• Acetylcholine is the chemical transmitter at the skeletal neuromuscular junction; the somatic division supplies excitatory innervation of skeletal muscle through the ventral roots.
2. Clinical basis:
• Low levels of ACh and loss of ACh neurons are found in Alzheimer's disease, with deterioration of memory, reasoning and language.
3. Distinction:
• The neuromuscular junction lies between a motor neurone terminal and a skeletal muscle fibre and uses acetylcholine; a synapse between neurons lies between an axon terminal and a dendrite, soma or axon and uses many transmitters (acetylcholine, serotonin, GABA, dopamine, norepinephrine, endorphins, glutamate).
questions.question:
Answer the following on neuromuscular transmission:
1. Describe transmission at the neuromuscular junction under these headings: anatomy of the junction, sequence of events, the transmitter and the receptors.
2. Explain the clinical basis of disturbances of cholinergic transmission.
3. Distinguish the neuromuscular junction from a synapse between two neurons.

questions.answerText:
1. Gas exchange:
• Air compositions: alveolar air is partially replaced by atmospheric air at each breath, oxygen constantly diffuses into the capillaries, carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into alveolar air, and dry inspired air is humidified in the passages.
• Respiratory membrane: a fluid layer with surfactant, alveolar epithelium, epithelial basement membrane, thin interstitial space, capillary basement membrane and capillary endothelium; thickness averages about 0.6 micrometre and is as little as 0.2 micrometre in places.
• Fick's law: diffusing capacity is proportional to pressure gradient x surface area / thickness; solubility and molecular weight give the diffusion coefficient (proportional to S/square root of MW); diffusing capacity is the volume of gas that diffuses each minute for a 1 mmHg pressure difference.
• Values: for oxygen 21 ml/min/mmHg at rest, rising to about 65 (three times); for CO2 about 400 to 450 at rest, rising to about 1200 to 1300 in exercise.
• Alveoli: about 300 million alveoli of 0.3 to 0.5 mm diameter with total area about 70 square metres, each in a basket of pulmonary capillaries; type I cells allow rapid diffusion and type II cells secrete surfactant.
2. Impaired exchange and exercise:
• Removing a lung halves the surface area; in emphysema alveolar walls dissolve and area falls up to fivefold, and with a fall to one third or one quarter of normal exchange is impeded even at rest.
• Oedema and fibrosis increase membrane thickness; a thickness of two to three times normal interferes significantly with exchange.
• Exercise raises diffusing capacity by opening previously dormant capillaries or dilating open ones, increasing surface area, and by a better ventilation-perfusion ratio.
3. Distinctions:
• Alveolar versus inspired air: partial replacement per breath, continual O2 uptake, CO2 addition and humidification.
• Alveolar versus expired air: dead space air mixes with alveolar air, so expired air has higher oxygen tension and lower carbon dioxide tension than alveolar air.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide (mechanism of gaseous exchange):
1. Describe gas exchange between the alveoli and the pulmonary capillaries under these headings: composition of inspired, alveolar and expired air, the respiratory membrane, Fick's law and the factors governing diffusing capacity, and normal diffusing capacities.
2. Explain why gas exchange is impaired in certain states (emphysema, oedema, fibrosis, removal of a lung) and how diffusing capacity increases in exercise.
3. Distinguish between alveolar air and inspired air, and between alveolar air and expired air.

questions.answerText:
1. Motility:
• The four major activities of the tract are motility, secretion, digestion and absorption.
• Mastication breaks food into small pieces, exposes it to salivary amylase and helps digestion of cellulose-containing food.
• Swallowing (mouth to stomach): buccal phase pushes food into the pharynx; pharyngeal phase passes food through the pharynx to the oesophagus; oesophageal phase carries food to the stomach by peristalsis.
• Oesophagus: a 25 cm tube guarded by an upper sphincter (prevents air entering the tract) and a lower sphincter (prevents reflux of gastric contents); peristalsis sweeps down it.
• Stomach: proximal area relaxes to store food; distal area mixes and empties chyme into the duodenum.
• Small intestine: segmentation and peristalsis mix, expose and propel contents.
• Colon: segmentation, mass movement and defecation.
2. Constipation:
• Constipation is abnormal, infrequent passage of faeces through the lower tract; it is not a disease but a symptom.
• Commoner in: inadequate fluid intake and immobility; drugs (anticholinergics, antacids such as aluminium hydroxide and calcium carbonate, opiates, antihistamines, iron); endocrine and metabolic disorders (hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia); pregnancy; depression and eating disorders.
• Treatment: more fibre, more fluid, regular exercise and treating the cause; laxatives for faecal impaction, pregnancy, surgery, poor diet and drug-induced constipation.
3. Distinctions:
• Segmentation mixes contents (in the small intestine and colon); peristalsis propels contents from oral to caudal.
• Mass movement propels contents of one colonic segment into the next; defecation involves involuntary and voluntary reflexes that evacuate the colonic content through the anal canal.
questions.question:
Answer the following on motility of the alimentary tract:
1. Describe motility of the alimentary tract under these headings: mastication, the three phases of swallowing, the oesophagus and its sphincters, gastric motility, small intestinal motility and colonic motility.
2. Explain the physiological basis of constipation: why it is commoner in certain states and how it is managed.
3. Distinguish between segmentation and peristalsis, and between mass movement and defecation.

Answer the following on the chemical control of respiration:
1. Describe the chemical control pathway of breathing: chemical stimuli, central and peripheral chemoreceptors, afferent input, integrating centres, efferent response and feedback.
2. State the threshold values and the factors that raise or lower ventilation, with the compensatory response to acid loads.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the changes in breathing when carbon dioxide or hydrogen ion levels are abnormal.
questions.answerText:
1. Chemical control:
• Stimuli: the concentration of CO2 and H+ in the blood; the major stimulus for respiration is carbon dioxide rather than oxygen.
• Central chemoreceptors lie in the brain and brainstem next to the respiratory rhythm centre; CO2 diffuses across the blood-brain barrier, raises hydrogen ions and lowers pH in the extracellular fluid, and the central chemoreceptors then stimulate the respiratory centres to contract the diaphragm and intercostals.
• Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid arteries and aortic arch) sense arterial H+ and large changes in dissolved oxygen; they cannot sense oxygen bound to haemoglobin.
• Integrating and efferent: signals go to the medulla, which drives the diaphragm and intercostal muscles; the response is dose-related, so a greater stimulus gives a greater response.
• Feedback: increased ventilation removes CO2, which lowers H+ and raises pH.
2. Values and modifiers:
• Peripheral chemoreceptors increase respiratory activity when blood oxygen falls to about 60 mmHg or less.
• Raise ventilation: rising CO2, falling pH (more acidic), lactic acid after strenuous exercise, low oxygen; lower ventilation: low CO2 and low H+ in the brain.
• Compensation: a large acid load stimulates breathing (respiratory compensation), removing CO2 and lowering H2CO3 to reduce the acidic shift in pH; chemical buffering is the first line of defence, the respiratory system the second and the kidneys the third.
3. Disturbances:
• Low blood CO2 leads to low H+ in the brain and a decrease in the rate and depth of ventilation, giving shallow, slow breathing.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the proprioceptors and the stretch receptor system:
1. Describe the proprioceptive system as a control pathway: static and dynamic position senses, receptors (muscle spindle, Golgi tendon organ, joint receptors), their structure and the sensory endings.
2. State the values and factors that raise or lower receptor firing and the compensatory role of the receptors.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the deficits when the position-sense pathway is damaged.
questions.answerText:
1. Proprioceptive system:
• Position senses are static (conscious perception of the orientation of body parts) and dynamic (kinesthesia, rate of movement).
• Muscle spindles: detect stretch and the rate of change of length and maintain muscle length; each has a capsule with two nuclear bag fibres and four or more nuclear chain fibres; the central region of the intrafusal fibres does not contract and acts as the sensory receptor; the primary ending responds to static length and to the rate of change (dynamic response) whereas the secondary ending responds mainly to static length.
• Tendon receptors (Golgi tendon organs): at the muscle-tendon junction, respond to maintained tension and to the rate of tension development and monitor total force exerted by the muscle.
• Joint receptors (Ruffini type): sense the degree of flexion, slowly adapting.
2. Values and modifiers:
• The primary sensory ending is about 17 micrometre and the secondary about 8 micrometre; the spindle is excited by lengthening the whole muscle or by contraction of the end portions of the intrafusal fibres; the receptors continue firing for at least several minutes if the spindle stays stretched.
• Tendon receptor firing rises with increasing muscle force.
• Compensation: the spindle maintains muscle length and the tendon organ signals force.
3. Damage:
• Position sense and kinesthesia travel in the dorsal column pathway, and are lost on the same side after hemisection of the cord (Brown-Sequard syndrome).
• Ataxia (inability to control body movements precisely) occurs in the thalamic syndrome.

1. Functions of leucocytes:
• Production (leukopoiesis) is stimulated by glycoprotein messengers, the interleukins and colony-stimulating factors (CSFs); WBCs average 5,000 to 10,000 per mm3.
• Neutrophils (40 to 70% of WBCs, 2 to 6 lobes): phagocytosis, degranulation and neutrophil extracellular traps; they release lysozyme, oxidants and defensins, congregate at infection sites and amplify inflammation through cytokines.
• Eosinophils (2 to 3%): release histaminase, phagocytose antigen-antibody complexes, act against parasitic worms and help break apart clots.
• Basophils (0.5 to 1%): become mast cells that liberate heparin, histamine and serotonin; they intensify inflammation and mediate hypersensitivity.
• Lymphocytes: smallest WBCs (8 to 10 micrometre); T cells, B cells and NK cells; B cells release antibodies, cytotoxic T cells release cytotoxic granules, helper T cells signal other cells, and memory cells respond to the same antigen later.
• Monocytes (3 to 8%, largest WBC): reach infection later than neutrophils but in larger numbers and differentiate into macrophages.
• Innate immunity is non-specific (barriers, chemicals, phagocytes); acquired immunity is specific, adaptive and has memory.
2. Excess and deficiency:
• Leukocytosis is an increase in WBC number; leukopenia is a count below 5,000/mm3.
• High neutrophils: bacterial infection, burns, stress, inflammation; low: radiation, chemotherapy drugs, vitamin B12 deficiency, systemic lupus erythematosus.
• High eosinophils: allergic reactions, parasitic infection, autoimmune disease, adrenal insufficiency; low: certain drugs, stress, Cushing's syndrome.
• Basophils rise with stress and allergies; high monocytes: viral or fungal infection, tuberculosis, some leukaemias, chronic disease; a low monocyte count rarely occurs.
3. Distant effects:
• Eosinophil changes point to the adrenal glands (adrenal insufficiency or Cushing's syndrome).
• Neutrophil changes may reflect vitamin B12 deficiency, radiation, drugs or systemic disease.
• Basophil-mediated hypersensitivity may appear as anaphylaxis, asthma, atopic dermatitis and hay fever.
• WBCs live in blood, skin and mucosa of the respiratory tract and circulate to lymphoid organs, so their changes signal disease at these distant sites.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the white blood cells:
1. Describe the functions of the leucocytes under these headings: production and its regulation, granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils), agranulocytes (lymphocytes, monocytes), and innate and acquired immunity.
2. State how the counts of each cell type relate to pathologies of excess and deficiency (leukocytosis, leukopenia and the raised or lowered counts of each type).
3. Explain why a disturbance of white cell counts may reflect disease in a distant organ or system.

Answer the following on the functions of the thalamus:
1. Describe the functions of the thalamus under these headings: relay of sensation, nuclei and their inputs, projection to the cortex, role in pain and temperature, and corticofugal regulation.
2. State how its components relate to common pathologies (the thalamic syndrome and related excess and deficiency).
3. Explain why a thalamic disturbance may affect a distant part of the body and cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• The thalamus is a sensory way-station for the rest of the brain and is important through its connections with other limbic structures.
• All general and special senses have an obligate relay in the thalamus; the only exception is olfaction.
• The ventrobasal complex has the ventral posterolateral nucleus (medial lemniscal fibres), ventral posteromedial nucleus (trigeminal fibres) and posterior thalamic nuclei (anterolateral system); third-order fibres go to the somatosensory cortex; intralaminar nuclei receive relays from the reticular nuclei.
• Role in somatic sensation: relays tactile information to the cortex, works with the brainstem in the discrimination of pain and temperature, and receives regulatory corticofugal fibres (mainly inhibitory) from the cortex.
2. Pathologies:
• Thalamic syndrome: blockage by thrombosis of the posterior cerebral artery supplying the posteroventral thalamus, and the nucleus degenerates.
• Effects: loss of pain sensation from the opposite side of the body, ataxia, a higher threshold for sensory perception after some weeks, extreme unpleasantness or pleasantness of many affective sensations, and enhanced sensitivity to pain.
• Secondary hyperalgesia arises from facilitation of sensory transmission due to a lesion in the spinal cord or thalamus.
3. Distant effects:
• Because sensory pathways cross, thalamic damage causes loss of pain on the opposite side of the body.
• The deficit also includes ataxia, which is an inability to control body movements precisely.

1. Micturition:
• Micturition (voiding) is the expulsion of urine from the bladder; it is regulated by the nervous system and by the muscles of the bladder and urethra.
• Filling phase: urine passes from the kidneys along the ureters, which enter the bladder obliquely; the detrusor muscle relaxes so the bladder distends; the internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle) and the external sphincter (skeletal muscle) are both contracted.
• Voiding phase: once storage capacity is reached the detrusor, which had been relaxing, contracts, and the bladder and urethra work together.
• Afferent input: distension of the bladder wall is an interoceptive sensation; the parasympathetic division controls defecation and diuresis.
2. Values and compensation:
• The bladder stores about 350 to 400 ml of urine before it is expelled.
• The ureteral openings are not guarded by any sphincter; their oblique passage through the bladder wall prevents urine re-entering the ureters.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the control of micturition:
1. Describe the micturition pathway: the bladder and sphincters as effectors, the sensory input from the bladder, the nervous control and the storage and voiding phases.
2. State the normal values (bladder capacity), the factors that alter the process and the compensatory mechanism that prevents reflux.

questions.answerText:
1. Synaptic transmission:
• A synapse is the junction where an axon terminal contacts another neuron or cell; the sending neuron is presynaptic and the receiving neuron postsynaptic; types are electrical, chemical and conjoint; by connectivity they are axodendritic, axosomatic or axoaxonic.
• Chemical synapse: cleft 20 to 50 nm wide; presynaptic button with synaptic vesicles (about 50 nm) and dense core vesicles (about 100 nm); active zones release transmitter and the postsynaptic density holds receptors.
• Requirements: synthesis and packing of neurotransmitter into vesicles, vesicle release in response to an action potential, an electrical or biochemical response in the postsynaptic neuron, removal of transmitter from the cleft, and all done very rapidly.
• Events: action potential enters the terminal, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open, Ca2+ activates proteins so vesicles fuse and release transmitter by exocytosis, the transmitter binds the postsynaptic receptor, whose inner ionophore has an ion channel component (cation channels excite, anion channels inhibit) and a G-protein second messenger component (opens ion channels or activates enzymes that make second messengers).
• Fate: cleared by diffusion, enzymatic degradation, presynaptic reuptake then degradation or recycling, uptake by glia, or uptake by the postsynaptic neuron with desensitisation.
• Transmitters include acetylcholine, serotonin, GABA, dopamine, norepinephrine, endorphins and glutamate.
2. Clinical basis:
• Understanding synaptic transmission is necessary for the actions of psychoactive drugs, the causes of mental disorders and the neural basis of learning and memory; transmitters must be cleared to permit another round of transmission.
• Alzheimer's disease shows deterioration of memory, reasoning and language with low acetylcholine and loss of ACh neurons.
• Too much dopamine is involved in schizophrenia, cocaine and nicotine mimic dopamine, and loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra causes Parkinson's disease.
3. Electrical versus chemical synapses:
• Electrical: direct transfer of ionic current through gap junctions, bidirectional, cells electronically coupled, very fast, common in non-neuronal cells and important in development.
• Chemical: transmitter released across a cleft, with receptors that convert the signal into a chemical or membrane potential change.
questions.question:
Answer the following on synaptic transmission:
1. Describe synaptic transmission under these headings: types of synapse, parts of a chemical synapse, requirements, sequence of events, the receptor components and the fate of neurotransmitters.
2. Explain the clinical basis of disturbances of synaptic transmission: why neurotransmitter imbalance is important in certain diseases and drugs.
3. Distinguish between electrical and chemical synapses.

Answer the following on the functions of the respiratory tract and lungs:
1. Describe the functions of the air passages, lungs and pulmonary circulation under these headings: pathway of air, mucus and cilia (mucociliary escalator), alveoli and surfactant, and the respiratory muscles.
2. State how the components relate to common respiratory disorders (airway, lung tissue and lung circulation disease) and the factors that cause them.
3. Explain why a respiratory disturbance may affect a distant organ or system.
questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• Air passages: nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, primary bronchi, secondary (lobar), tertiary (segmental) bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles (each bronchiole gives rise to 50 to 80), respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs; they filter, moisten, warm and conduct air; the conducting portion ends at the terminal bronchioles.
• Mucus from goblet cells and submucosal glands humidifies and filters air; ciliated epithelium (about 200 cilia per cell beating 10 to 20 times per second, upward in the lower tract and downward in the nose) moves trapped particles, forming the mucociliary escalator.
• Alveoli: about 300 million, area about 70 m2, each in a basket of capillaries; type I cells permit rapid diffusion and type II cells (5%) secrete surfactant that prevents collapse; the pulmonary circulation and alveoli together form the respiratory membrane.
• Muscles: diaphragm and external intercostals (inspiration); internal intercostals and abdominal muscles in forced expiration.
2. Disorders:
• Respiratory disorders are irregular or abnormal functioning, physiological or anatomical, resulting from genetics, allergies, lifestyle (smoking), air pollution and infections.
• Categories: airway disease, lung tissue disease and lung circulation disease; examples are asthma, COPD, emphysema, occupational disorders, sinusitis and lung cancer.
• Restrictive diseases (fibrosis, sarcoidosis) reduce volumes; obstructive diseases (emphysema, chronic bronchitis, asthma) increase residual volume; emphysema destroys alveolar walls.
• Drug groups: bronchodilators, antihistamines, antitussives, decongestants, expectorants, leukotriene modifiers, lung surfactants and mucolytics.
3. Distant effects:
• Impaired gas exchange reduces oxygen delivery to all tissues and reduces CO2 removal, changing blood pH.
• Pulmonary embolism dangerously impairs the ability to obtain oxygen; left heart failure backs blood into the lungs as pulmonary oedema.
• Smoking raises carbon monoxide occupancy of haemoglobin to as much as 10%.

1. Conducting system:
• The system consists of special conducting cells and fibres (not nervous tissue) that self-excite, conduct rapidly and coordinate the chambers; both atria contract together and first, then both ventricles.
• SA node: primary impulse initiator and physiological pacemaker; generates about 75 impulses per minute.
• AV node: secondary pacemaker and conduit; the atria are separated from the ventricles by a cartilaginous septum that cannot conduct, so the AV node is the only pathway; it delays the impulse about 0.1 second.
• Bundle of His: the initial segment penetrating the fibrous trigone into the interventricular septum; it allows only forward movement of action potentials and bifurcates into right and left bundle branches.
• Purkinje fibres: subendocardial branches extending to the apex and then up the ventricular walls; they have many more gap junctions than AV nodal cells, giving almost instantaneous transmission to the ventricle.
• ECG: electrodes on the skin record current spreading from the heart; there are bipolar leads (I, II, III), unipolar limb leads (aVR, aVL, aVF) and chest leads V1 to V6, twelve in all.
2. Normal values and modifiers:
• P wave (atrial depolarisation) 0.1 s, 0.1 to 0.12 mV; QRS (ventricular depolarisation) 0.08 to 0.10 s; T wave (ventricular repolarisation) 0.2 s, 0.3 mV; PR interval 0.12 to 0.2 s; ST segment 0.08 s; RR interval 0.8 s (one cardiac cycle, used for heart rate).
• Compensation: the rapid Purkinje conduction compensates for the delay at the AV node and lets the ventricles contract shortly after the atria.
• Ion levels and other factors that change the trace include potassium (hyperkalemia, hypokalemia), calcium and thyrotoxicosis.
3. Basis of ECG changes in failure:
• P wave: taller and wider in atrial enlargement; absent in hyperkalemia, atrial fibrillation or sinoatrial block.
• PR interval: prolonged in bradycardia and first degree heart block; shortened in tachycardia.
• QRS: prolonged in bundle branch block and hyperkalemia.
• ST segment: elevated in myocardial infarction, left bundle branch block, acute pericarditis; depressed in acute myocardial ischaemia, posterior infarction, ventricular hypertrophy, hypokalemia.
• T wave: tall and broad-based in acute ischaemia; flat or inverted in myocardial infarction, ventricular hypertrophy, pericarditis; U wave prominent in hypokalemia.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the conducting system of the heart and the electrocardiogram:
1. Describe the conducting system as a control pathway: initiator (pacemaker), conduction route through the SA node, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches and Purkinje fibres, and how ECG leads record it.
2. State the normal ECG values (durations and amplitudes of waves, intervals and segments), the factors that alter them and the compensatory role of the Purkinje fibres.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the ECG changes when the pathway fails or is damaged.

questions.answerText:
1. Erythrocyte functions:
• Structure: biconcave disc (6 to 9 micrometre diameter, 1 to 2 micrometre thick), deformable to pass the smallest vessels, no nucleus or mitochondria, about 33% haemoglobin; over 97% of the dry cell is haemoglobin.
• Haemoglobin: globin (two alpha and two beta chains) bound to haem, each haem bearing an iron atom that binds one O2 reversibly, so one Hb carries four O2; one cell holds about 250 million Hb molecules; normal Hb is 13 to 18 g/100 ml in adult males, 12 to 16 in females and 14 to 20 in infants.
• Functions: transport oxygen and assist CO2 transport, regulate acid-base balance to prevent large pH changes, assist clot formation; erythrocytes are the major factor in blood viscosity.
• Production: stimulated by erythropoietin (made mainly by the kidneys) in response to tissue oxygenation; a 70 kg man produces about 2.3 x 10^6 red cells per second.
• Destruction: life span 100 to 120 days; anucleate cells cannot synthesise protein, become rigid and fragile and are trapped in the spleen (the red blood cell graveyard) and engulfed by macrophages; haem is split from globin, globin to amino acids, iron stored as ferritin or haemosiderin and haem to bilirubin, carried on albumin, taken up by liver, secreted in bile and metabolised to urobilinogen and stercobilin in faeces; spilled Hb is captured by haptoglobin.
2. Deficiency and excess:
• Anaemia: blood with abnormally low oxygen-carrying capacity, from insufficient red cells (haemorrhagic, haemolytic, aplastic), from low Hb content (iron-deficiency, pernicious) or from abnormal Hb.
• Abnormal Hb: in thalassaemia one globin chain is absent or faulty and cells are thin and deficient in Hb; in sickle-cell anaemia one of 146 amino acids in a beta chain is changed, so HbS links into stiff rods under low oxygen and cells become spiky.
• Polycythaemia: an abnormal excess of erythrocytes that increases viscosity so blood sludges; polycythaemia vera, a bone marrow cancer, has 8 to 11 million cells/microlitre and haematocrit up to 80%, with dizziness.
3. Distant effects:
• Because the erythrocyte delivers oxygen to every tissue, anaemia leaves oxygen inadequate for normal metabolism and gives fatigue, pallor, breathlessness and chilliness.
• Sickle cells interfere with oxygen delivery, leaving victims gasping for air and in extreme pain.
• Aplastic anaemia from marrow destruction (drugs, radiation, viruses) impairs formation of all formed elements, so anaemia is one sign among several.
• Sluggish flow in polycythaemia impairs circulation generally.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the erythrocyte and haemoglobin:
1. Describe the functions of the erythrocyte and haemoglobin under these headings: structure, production and its regulation, oxygen and carbon dioxide transport, acid-base role, life span and destruction.
2. State how erythrocyte and haemoglobin disorders relate to pathologies of deficiency (the anaemias) and of excess (polycythaemia), including the abnormal haemoglobins.
3. Explain why these disturbances produce effects in distant organs and a functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• Meninges: three layers from outside inward, the dura mater (thick, lines the skull), the arachnoid mater (thin, web-like; the subdural space lies between them) and the pia mater (follows the folds; the subarachnoid space lies between arachnoid and pia).
• CSF: clear colourless fluid produced by ependymal cells in the choroid plexuses and absorbed in the arachnoid granulations; volume about 150 ml, production about 550 ml/day, turnover about 3.7 times per day.
• Formation: plasma is passively filtered across the choroidal capillary endothelium, then water and ions are secreted across the choroidal epithelium (HCO3-, Cl- and K+ through apical channels, with aquaporins for water); CSF is nearly protein-free.
• Circulation: lateral ventricles, interventricular foramina, third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, fourth ventricle, then the subarachnoid space through the median and lateral apertures and the central canal of the cord.
• Functions: buoyancy (brain of about 1500 g behaves as 25 to 50 g), protection as a shock absorber, prevention of ischaemia (reducing CSF lowers intracranial pressure and aids perfusion), homeostasis and removal of waste.
• Blood-brain barrier: a selective semipermeable border formed by tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells and choroid epithelial cells, with astrocyte end-feet and pericytes; it keeps out pathogens, limits large or hydrophilic molecules, allows hydrophobic molecules (O2, CO2, hormones) and small polar molecules, and actively transports glucose.
2. Pathologies:
• Clinical significance: hydrocephalus, lumbar puncture, anaesthesia and chemotherapy, kernicterus and drug administration.
• Causes of CNS disorders: trauma, infections (cryptococcal meningitis, malaria, leprosy, viruses), degeneration (Parkinson's disease), structural defects (anencephaly), tumours, autoimmune disorders (acute disseminated encephalomyelitis attacks myelin) and stroke.
• Cerebral oedema (swelling from the inflammatory response) may compress and kill brain tissue.
3. Distant effects:
• Metabolic waste diffuses into CSF and is removed into the blood as CSF is absorbed, so failure of drainage affects the whole brain.
• Stroke from interrupted blood supply kills tissue in the affected area, giving loss of function.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the cerebrospinal fluid, meninges and blood-brain barrier:
1. Describe the functions of the meninges, cerebrospinal fluid (formation, circulation, functions) and blood-brain barrier (structure, functions).
2. State how the components relate to common pathologies of excess and deficiency and the causes of CNS disorders.
3. Explain why a disturbance of these protective systems may affect distant parts of the nervous system and cause a functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• Location: deep in the temporal lobe on its medial aspect, forming the medial wall of the lateral ventricle; an ancient cortex of three layers, shaped like a seahorse.
• Memory: essential for the formation of new memories about past experiences and for retrieval; it underlies declarative (explicit) memory of facts and events, which depends on the medial temporal lobe and the hippocampal-entorhinal relationship; implicit memory is the learning of skills and conditioned and emotional responses; it plays a critical role in short-term memory, which is necessary to establish long-term patterns.
• Spatial function: understanding spatial relations, with the dentate gyrus and dorsal hippocampus generating new adult-born granule cells that support pattern separation, and the left hippocampus involved in recall of spatial memories.
• It helps control corticosteroid production.
2. Pathologies:
• Damage usually causes profound difficulty forming new memories (anterograde amnesia) and may affect access to earlier memories (retrograde amnesia), usually extending some years before the damage.
• Alzheimer's disease is a progressive degenerative disease, mostly in the elderly, with memory loss, irritability, confusion and ultimately hallucinations and death.
3. Distant effects:
• Lesions do not affect old established memories, which involve association areas in the frontal lobe and the parieto-temporo-occipital cortex; the hippocampus becomes less important in storage over time.
• The hippocampus sends output to the hypothalamus through the fornix.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the functions of the hippocampus:
1. Describe the functions of the hippocampus under these headings: location and structure, memory (declarative and non-declarative), spatial function, and other regulatory roles.
2. State how damage to or dysfunction of the hippocampus relates to common pathologies.
3. Explain why a hippocampal disturbance may affect distant memory stores and cause a functional deficit.

Answer the following on the nervous control of respiration:
1. Describe the control pathway for breathing: receptors, afferent pathways, integrating centres in the brain, efferent nerves, effector muscles and feedback reflexes.
2. State the normal values for breathing, the factors that raise or lower ventilation and the compensatory response during exercise.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the signs and symptoms when the pathway is disturbed.
questions.answerText:
1. Nervous control of respiration:
• Voluntary control is through the motor cortex of the cerebrum, with inputs from the limbic system and hypothalamus; involuntary control is by neurons in the pons and medulla.
• Medullary respiratory centre: sets the basic rhythm; the dorsal respiratory group (DRG) integrates input from stretch receptors and peripheral chemoreceptors and maintains the rhythm by stimulating the diaphragm and intercostals (inspiration); when DRG activity ceases the muscles relax (expiration); the ventral respiratory group (VRG) generates the rhythm, is involved in forced breathing and stimulates accessory muscles of forced inspiration and expiration.
• Pontine respiratory group: the apneustic centre stimulates the DRG, controlling the depth of inspiration; the pneumotaxic centre inhibits the DRG, allowing relaxation after inspiration and controlling the overall rate.
• Efferent and effectors: phrenic and intercostal nerves stimulate the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles to contract, producing inspiration; when stimulation stops the muscles relax and expiration occurs.
• Feedback and receptors: aortic and carotid bodies monitor PCO2, PO2 and pH; the hypothalamus monitors emotional state and body temperature; proprioceptors report joint and muscle movement; the inflation reflex protects the lungs from over-inflating and pulmonary irritant reflexes protect the respiratory zones from foreign material.
2. Values, modifiers and compensation:
• Values: adult respiratory rate about 12 to 18 breaths per minute (about 18 to 30 in a 10-year-old); tidal volume 500 ml and pulmonary ventilation 12 x 500 = 6000 ml/min.
• Factors affecting respiration: exercise, temperature, smoking, quantity and quality of air, internal ratio of CO2 and O2, blood pH, respiratory disorders, and drugs including alcohol.
• Compensation in exercise: oxygen demand rises, so tidal volume and breathing rate increase; chemoreceptors (aortic arch and carotid arteries, detecting blood acidity) and proprioceptors (joint and muscle movement) send messages to the medulla oblongata.
3. Disturbance:
• The mechanisms available to protect the lungs are the cough reflex, the sneeze reflex, the inflation reflex and the pulmonary irritant reflexes.

1. Functions of the pancreas:
• Endocrine: secretes insulin and glucagon from the islets of Langerhans.
• Exocrine: secretes pancreatic juice with an aqueous component (contains HCO3-, neutralises stomach acid in the duodenum so enzymes can function) and an enzymatic component (trypsin, chymotrypsin, lipase and amylase) essential for digesting and absorbing carbohydrates, fats and proteins.
• Enzyme actions: pancreatic amylase converts starch to maltose and maltotriose (pH 7.0); lipase with colipase converts triglyceride to monoglyceride and fatty acids (pH 8.0); enterokinase converts trypsinogen to trypsin and chymotrypsinogen to chymotrypsin, which reduce protein to polypeptides, and carboxypeptidase yields amino acids.
2. Pathologies:
• Diabetes mellitus (Type 1 IDDM and Type 2 NIDDM) is shown by raised plasma glucose.
• Pancreatic insufficiency is listed as a cause of diarrhoea.
3. Distant effects:
• Incomplete fatty acid oxidation in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus produces ketone body acids, adding a non-volatile acid load for the kidneys and buffers to handle.
• Lipids, proteins and lipoproteins are markers in diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease.
• Insulin and glucagon are degraded by the kidneys.
• Loss of pancreatic enzymes and bicarbonate impairs digestion and absorption in the intestine, producing diarrhoea.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the functions of the pancreas:
1. Describe the functions of the pancreas under these headings: endocrine secretion, exocrine secretion (aqueous and enzymatic components), actions in the duodenum and regulation.
2. State how the pancreatic components relate to common pathologies of excess and deficiency.
3. Explain why a disturbance of the pancreas may affect a distant organ or system.

questions.answerText:
1. Erythropoiesis:
• Sites: haemopoiesis occurs in embryonic sites (yolk sac, liver, spleen, thymus, lymph nodes, bone marrow) and after birth in the red bone marrow.
• Stem cells: blood cells arise from a common pluripotent haemopoietic stem cell that can self-renew or differentiate into committed progenitors (the colony-forming unit-erythrocyte, CFU-E, for red cells); interleukin-3 promotes proliferation of pluripotent stem cells and CFU-E; differentiation is stimulated by differentiation inducers.
• Erythropoietin (EPO): made mainly by the kidneys and in small amounts by the liver; it stimulates production of proerythroblasts from CFU-E.
• Stages: pluripotent stem cell, pronormoblast (earliest recognised cell; large, basophilic, about 1% Hb), basophilic normoblast, polychromatophilic normoblast (Hb production), orthochromatic normoblast (final nucleated stage), reticulocyte (no nucleus, about 95% Hb, circulates 1 to 2 days) and then mature RBC.
• Regulation: the basic regulator is tissue oxygenation; RBC production is proportional to 1/tissue oxygenation, so anaemia from haemorrhage, low atmospheric oxygen, lung disease, blood doping or altitude increases production.
• Requirements: amino acids, iron (for haem), vitamin B12 and folic acid (final maturation and DNA synthesis), vitamin B6 (DNA and haem synthesis), vitamin C (folate metabolism and iron absorption); copper and cobalt are essential in other animals but not shown in humans.
2. Basis of anaemia from disturbed production:
• Lack of vitamin B12 or folic acid slows proliferation of erythroblasts, so cells develop into large, irregular or oval erythrocytes with higher fragility and shorter life, leading to megaloblastic anaemia; these vitamins are needed for purine and pyrimidine synthesis and DNA, and a great demand is made in adult erythropoiesis (10 to 20 g of cells formed per day).
• Vitamin B12 absorption needs intrinsic factor from the stomach mucosa; in most pernicious anaemia intrinsic factor is deficient, in an autoimmune disease with atrophy of the stomach mucosa that most often affects the elderly; diet is rarely the problem except for strict vegetarians.
• Iron-deficiency anaemia is generally a secondary result of haemorrhagic anaemias but also results from inadequate intake of iron-containing foods and impaired iron absorption.
• Anaemia is a sign of some disorder, with blood oxygen levels inadequate to support metabolism; anaemic individuals are fatigued, pale, short of breath and chilly.
3. Megaloblastic versus iron-deficiency anaemia:
• Megaloblastic (pernicious): due to lack of vitamin B12 or folic acid, developing erythrocytes grow but do not divide, giving large pale macrocytes.
• Iron-deficiency: haemoglobin content is low, and the erythrocytes produced are small and pale microcytes.
questions.question:
Answer the following on erythropoiesis:
1. Describe erythropoiesis under these headings: sites, stem cells and growth factors, stages of red cell development, regulation by tissue oxygenation and erythropoietin, and the dietary requirements for red cell maturation.
2. Explain the basis of the anaemias that arise from disturbed red cell production: why deficiency of vitamin B12, folic acid or iron produces anaemia and why it is commoner in some people.
3. Distinguish between megaloblastic (pernicious) anaemia and iron-deficiency anaemia.

questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• The limbic system combines higher mental functions and primitive emotion into a single system, the emotional nervous system; its components are the amygdala, hippocampus, thalamus, hypothalamus, basal ganglia and cingulate gyrus.
• Thalamus: a sensory way-station connected with other limbic structures; hypothalamus: primary output node with endocrine, behavioural, autonomic and sexual centres; hippocampus: formation of new memories; amygdala: coordinates behavioural, autonomic and endocrine responses, mostly to fear and anxiety.
• Cingulate gyrus: focuses attention on emotionally significant events and associates memories with smells and pain, providing a pathway from the thalamus to the hippocampus.
• Ventral tegmental area: dopamine pathways responsible for pleasure.
• Basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, substantia nigra): repetitive behaviours, reward and focusing attention.
• Prefrontal cortex: thinking about the future, planning, action, and the same dopamine pathways of pleasure and addiction; the olfactory cortex connects to the amygdala and hypothalamus, influencing emotional and endocrine reactions.
2. Pathologies:
• Damage to the ventral tegmental area leaves difficulty getting pleasure, and people often turn to alcohol, drugs, sweets and gambling.
• Prefrontal damage causes poor abstract reasoning, judgment and mood; depression is linked to increased medial frontal activity and decreased posterior cingulate activity.
• Amygdala lesions reduce stress responses and stimulation produces rage; hippocampal damage causes amnesia; Parkinson's disease involves degeneration of dopamine cells in the basal ganglia (substantia nigra).
3. Distant effects:
• The hypothalamus controls autonomic responses through the brain stem and endocrine functions through projections to the median eminence, so limbic changes alter organ function.
• The autonomic nervous system, with its opposing sympathetic and parasympathetic parts, plays a powerful part in emotional life.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the limbic system and emotions:
1. Describe the functions of the limbic system under these headings: components, the roles of the thalamus, hypothalamus, hippocampus and amygdala, and the related areas (cingulate gyrus, ventral tegmental area, basal ganglia, prefrontal cortex, olfactory cortex).
2. State how its components relate to common pathologies of excess and deficiency.
3. Explain why a limbic disturbance may affect a distant organ or system and cause a functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
1. Olfactory pathway:
• The olfactory epithelium (about 5 cm2 in the roof of the nasal cavity) has 10 to 20 million bipolar olfactory sensory neurons among supporting (sustentacular) cells and basal stem cells; each neuron has a dendrite ending in a knob with 10 to 20 cilia bearing odorant receptors, covered by mucus from Bowman's glands.
• Transduction: odorants dissolve in mucus and bind G-protein-coupled receptors, which activate adenylyl cyclase and cAMP, opening cation channels; Na+ and Ca2+ enter and depolarise the cell.
• Axons pass through the cribriform plate into the olfactory bulb, where they contact mitral and tufted cell dendrites in glomeruli; mitral and tufted axons run through the intermediate and lateral olfactory striae to the olfactory cortex (anterior olfactory nucleus, olfactory tubercle, piriform cortex, amygdala, entorhinal cortex).
• There is no thalamic relay in the primary smell pathway; conscious discrimination depends on the pathway to the orbitofrontal cortex (greater on the right); the amygdala pathway gives emotional responses and the entorhinal cortex olfactory memories; olfactory cortex also projects via the hypothalamus.
2. Modifiers and adaptation:
• Rapid adaptation is mediated by Ca2+ acting through calmodulin on cyclic nucleotide-gated channels.
• The olfactory threshold increases with age: more than 75% of humans over 80 have impaired ability to identify smells; pregnancy commonly gives oversensitivity (hyperosmia).
3. Abnormalities:
• Anosmia (absence), hyposmia (diminished) and dysosmia (distorted); anosmia is associated with hypogonadism (Kallmann's syndrome).
• Causes: nasal congestion, fracture of the cribriform plate, tumours (neuroblastoma, meningioma), infections and abscesses, and Alzheimer's disease; dysosmia arises from sinus infections, partial nerve damage and poor dental hygiene.
questions.question:
Answer the following on olfaction (smell):
1. Describe the olfactory pathway as a control system: receptor cells and epithelium, transduction, olfactory bulb, olfactory tract, olfactory cortex and central connections.
2. State the normal features (numbers, adaptation), the factors that raise or lower olfactory sensitivity and the adaptation response.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the abnormalities of smell.

Answer the following on the physiology of hearing:
1. Describe hearing under these headings: functions of the external, middle and inner ear, the structure of the cochlea and organ of Corti, transduction in the hair cells, and coding of loudness and pitch.
2. Explain why hearing loss arises in certain states (conduction and nerve deafness) and how the middle ear protects the ear.
3. Distinguish between conduction deafness and nerve (sensorineural) deafness, and between the inner and outer hair cells.
questions.answerText:
1. Physiology of hearing:
• The ear houses receptors for hearing and equilibrium; the external ear, middle ear and cochlea serve hearing, while the semicircular canals, utricle and saccule serve equilibrium.
• Outer ear gathers sound to the tympanic membrane; the middle ear is an air-filled cavity in the temporal bone with the auditory tube, ossicles, oval and round windows; the stapes footplate closes the oval window and the round window is closed by the secondary tympanic membrane.
• Inner ear: bony labyrinth filled with perilymph containing the membranous labyrinth filled with K+-rich endolymph (no communication between them); the cochlea has three scalae; the organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane, and the hair cell processes are bathed in endolymph while their bases are bathed in perilymph.
• Transduction: basilar membrane vibration bends the cilia; K+ and Ca2+ enter through mechanically gated channels, depolarising the cell; voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open and transmitter is released, stimulating the cochlear nerve.
• Coding: loudness by amplitude, frequency of firing and recruitment of hair cells; pitch by frequency.
2. Basis of loss and protection:
• Tensor tympani and stapedius protect against loud noise and mask low-frequency sound.
• Conduction deafness follows wax plugs, foreign bodies, ossicle destruction or a thickened eardrum; nerve deafness follows aminoglycoside antibiotics, loud noise, a tumour of cranial nerve VIII or vascular damage in the medulla.
3. Distinctions:
• Conduction deafness: impaired transmission in the external or middle ear; nerve deafness: damage to hair cells or neural pathways.
• Inner hair cells form a single row and outer hair cells form 3 to 4 rows.

questions.question:
Answer the following on venous return and the control of blood pressure:
1. Describe the system that returns blood to the heart and regulates blood pressure: determinants of venous return, the structures and forces that aid it, and the vascular and neural effectors of blood pressure.
2. State the normal values (venous pressures, blood storage, cardiac output) and the factors that raise or lower venous return and blood pressure.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the signs and symptoms when the pathway fails.
questions.answerText:
1. Venous return and pressure control:
• Venous return is determined by total blood volume and venous pressure; veins are more compliant than arteries and act as capacitance vessels.
• Aids: sympathetic activity contracts venous smooth muscle and reduces compliance; the skeletal muscle pump squeezes veins; the thoracic-abdominal pressure difference promotes flow; one-way valves prevent backflow, and blood also relies on gravity and inertia.
• Blood pressure controls: hormones and autonomic signals alter heart rate and contraction strength; sympathetic vasoconstriction narrows arteries and raises pressure while vasodilation widens them; blood volume and viscosity also affect pressure.
• Flow relation: flow = pressure difference/resistance; precapillary sphincters and metarterioles regulate capillary flow.
2. Values and modifiers:
• Veins store about 70% of blood volume; pressure is about 10 mmHg at the venules and about 0 mmHg at the vena cava-right atrium junction; mean venous pressure is about 2 mmHg; cardiac output at rest is about 5 L/min (4 to 6).
• Raise return: sympathetic venoconstriction, muscle pump, higher blood volume, exercise; lower: blood loss.
• Raise pressure: greater contractile force and heart rate, vasoconstriction, higher blood volume, thicker viscous blood.
• Lower pressure: vasodilation after the fight-or-flight response or under hormones and chemicals.
3. Failure:
• Blood loss and extremely rapid heartbeat decrease stroke volume.
• Right-sided heart failure causes peripheral oedema and left-sided failure pulmonary oedema.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the functions of the kidney:
1. Describe the functions of the kidney under these headings: excretion, regulation of fluid, ions and acid-base balance, hormones synthesised or degraded, and the roles of the parts of the nephron.
2. State how the regulatory components of the nephron and the kidney's hormonal roles relate to common pathologies of excess and deficiency.
3. Explain why kidney disturbance may affect a distant organ or system and cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Functions of the kidney:
• The renal system produces, transports and stores urine (kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra and their muscles).
• Regulates osmolality of body fluids by excreting dilute or concentrated urine; regulates plasma Na+, K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, Cl-, bicarbonate, phosphate and sulphate; regulates extracellular fluid volume by controlling Na+ and water excretion; helps regulate arterial pressure by adjusting Na+ excretion and producing renin.
• Acid-base balance: excretes H+ when there is excess acid or HCO3- when there is excess base; synthesises ammonia.
• Eliminates urea, uric acid (purine metabolism) and creatinine (muscle metabolism), and excretes drugs and toxic compounds.
• Hormones: major production sites of erythropoietin and 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D3; degrades insulin, glucagon and parathyroid hormone; synthesises prostaglandins, thromboxane A2 and kallikrein (which leads to kinins).
• Nephron: glomerulus filters protein-free plasma into Bowman's capsule; proximal tubule does uncontrolled reabsorption and secretion; loop of Henle sets the medullary osmotic gradient; distal tubule and collecting duct do variable, controlled reabsorption of Na+ and water and secretion of K+ and H+; the juxtaglomerular apparatus produces substances that control kidney function.
2. Pathologies:
• Plasma urea nitrogen and creatinine are measures of kidney function, and GFR is an index of the kidneys' functionality (normal 125 ml/min).
• Hypercalcaemia occurs, for example, in renal failure; alkaline phosphatase is raised in kidney disorders.
3. Distant effects:
• Erythropoietin is made mainly by the kidneys and stimulates red cell production, so kidney function links to blood.
• The kidneys convert vitamin D into its active form, allowing calcium absorption in the small intestine.
• Kidney control of Na+, water and renin affects arterial blood pressure and extracellular fluid volume; acid-base regulation depends on kidney excretion of H+ and addition of HCO3- to the ECF.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the cough and sneeze reflexes:
1. Describe the cough reflex as a control pathway: stimulus, receptors, afferent nerves, medullary centre, efferent nerves, effectors and the sequence of the act.
2. State the normal values in the act of coughing, the factors that trigger it and how it compensates for irritants, and compare with the sneeze reflex.
questions.answerText:
1. Cough reflex:
• Stimulus: irritant agents; receptors are situated in several locations.
• Afferent fibres pass via the vagus, trigeminal, glossopharyngeal and phrenic nerves to the centre in the medulla oblongata.
• Efferent fibres arise from the medullary centre and pass through the vagus, phrenic and spinal motor nerves to activate the primary and accessory respiratory muscles; the effectors are the muscles of inspiration.
• Sequence: about 2 to 5 litres of air is inspired, the epiglottis and vocal cords close tightly, abdominal and intercostal muscles contract forcefully against the diaphragm, then sudden wide opening of the cords and epiglottis makes air explode outward carrying the foreign body from the bronchi and trachea.
2. Values and comparison:
• Values: pressure in the lungs rises to about 100 mmHg.
• Compensation: the reflex clears foreign material from the trachea and bronchi; the mucociliary escalator (cilia beating 10 to 20 times per second with mucus) also removes trapped particles.
• Sneeze: stimulated by irritants in the nasal mucosa; receptors are olfactory receptors and trigeminal endings; afferents run in the trigeminal and olfactory nerves to the medullary centre; efferents run through the trigeminal, facial, glossopharyngeal, vagus and intercostal nerves to pharyngeal, tracheal and respiratory muscles; it resembles the cough but the uvula is depressed so air passes rapidly through the nose to clear the nasal passages.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the transport of carbon dioxide in the blood:
1. Describe carbon dioxide transport under these headings: the three chemical forms, the reactions in the red cell, the chloride shift, and the reverse reactions in the lungs.
2. Explain why active tissues unload more oxygen (the link between CO2 loading, hydrogen ions and oxygen dissociation).
3. Distinguish between the chloride shift and the reverse chloride shift, and between carbaminohaemoglobin and bicarbonate transport.
questions.answerText:
1. CO2 transport:
• About 4 ml of CO2 is transported from tissues to lungs in each 100 ml of blood: 10% dissolved, 30% combined with haemoglobin and plasma proteins as carbamino-Hb (CO2 reacts with the amino group), and 60% as HCO3-.
• In the red cell dissolved CO2 reacts with water to form carbonic acid, catalysed by carbonic anhydrase (about 5000-fold faster); carbonic acid dissociates into H+ and HCO3-; most H+ combine with haemoglobin.
• Chloride shift: bicarbonate diffuses out of the red cell into plasma while chloride diffuses in, so venous red cells contain more chloride than arterial cells.
• In the lungs the reactions reverse: as haemoglobin loads oxygen its affinity for H+ declines, H+ dissociates and combines with HCO3- entering the red cell, chloride moves out (reverse chloride shift), free CO2 is regenerated and diffuses into the alveolus, together with CO2 released from carbaminohaemoglobin and dissolved CO2.
2. Link to oxygen unloading:
• Active tissues generate extra CO2, which raises H+ and lowers pH; this shifts the oxygen-haemoglobin curve to the right (Bohr effect) and promotes oxygen availability.
• CO2 loading releases hydrogen ions in the erythrocyte, and hydrogen ions promote O2 dissociation.
3. Distinctions:
• Chloride shift occurs in the tissues (HCO3- out, Cl- in); the reverse chloride shift occurs in the lungs (Cl- out, HCO3- in).
• Carbaminohaemoglobin carries about 30% of CO2 bound to the amino group of Hb; bicarbonate carries about 60%, formed through carbonic anhydrase.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the digestion and absorption of fats:
1. Describe fat digestion and absorption under these headings: role of bile and the gallbladder, pancreatic lipase and colipase, formation of micelles, uptake by the intestinal epithelium, formation of chylomicrons and VLDL, and routes into the circulation.
2. Explain why impaired fat absorption is more serious in some states (for example liver disease) and how it leads to a bleeding disorder.
3. Distinguish between micelles and chylomicrons, and between the lymphatic and venous routes of absorbed nutrients.
questions.answerText:
1. Fat digestion and absorption:
• Bile is required for fat digestion and absorption; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it, and it reaches the duodenum when digestion takes place.
• Pancreatic lipase with colipase converts triglyceride to monoglyceride and fatty acids (optimum pH 8.0); cholesterol esterase and phospholipase A2 also act.
• Fatty acids, monoglycerides, cholesterol and phospholipids with bile salts form micelles that carry lipids to the epithelium; in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum triglycerides and cholesterol esters are re-formed, and in the Golgi they are packaged with apoprotein B into chylomicrons or very low density lipoprotein (VLDL) particles.
• These leave the cell by exocytosis and enter lymph vessels (lacteals) or the venous system; lymph absorbs fatty acids and fats as chyle and transports lipids to the bloodstream.
• The absorptive surface is enlarged by folds, villi and microvilli.
2. Basis of vulnerability:
• Vitamin K is fat-soluble and is absorbed into the blood along with fats, so vitamin K deficiency occurs if fat absorption is impaired.
• Liver cells need vitamin K to make clotting factors; in liver disease the nonfunctional liver cells fail to produce procoagulants and also bile, which is required for fat and vitamin K absorption.
• Vitamin K deficiency is common in newborns and after systemic antibiotics; dietary lack is rarely a problem because bacteria in the large intestine produce vitamin K; the result is abnormal and often severe bleeding.
3. Distinctions:
• Micelles are bile salt aggregates in the lumen carrying fatty acids, monoglycerides, cholesterol and phospholipids to the epithelium; chylomicrons are lipoprotein particles assembled inside the cell (with apoprotein B) for export.
• Lymphatic route: lacteals carry lipids to the bloodstream as chyle; venous route: absorbed material enters the venous system directly.

1. Oxygen transport:
• Forms: dissolved in plasma 0.3 ml/100 ml (1.5%) and combined with haemoglobin 19.4 ml/100 ml (98.5%); 100 ml of blood at full saturation carries 19.7 ml of oxygen.
• Haemoglobin: four globin chains each with one haem; each haem binds one O2 at its ferrous ion, so one Hb carries up to four O2, loosely and reversibly.
• Release: arterial blood (PO2 95 mmHg, 97% saturated) holds about 19.4 ml/100 ml and falls to 14.4 ml (PO2 40 mmHg, 75% saturated) in the tissues, so about 5 ml is delivered per 100 ml; this 22% is the utilization coefficient; the remainder is a venous reserve that can sustain life for 4 to 5 minutes; in strenuous exercise the coefficient rises to 75 to 80%.
• Dissociation curve: at low PO2 it rises slowly, then rapidly, then levels off near 100% saturation; binding of the first O2 changes Hb shape and raises affinity for the next; high PO2 in pulmonary capillaries loads O2 and low PO2 in tissue capillaries unloads it.
• Shifts to the right (promoting unloading): low ambient PO2 in active tissues, raised temperature, 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPG, raised by fever or exercise) and raised PCO2 with lowered pH (Bohr effect).
2. Basis of vulnerability:
• Carbon monoxide binds the ferrous ion of haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, competes with oxygen for the same site and binds 210 times as tightly, tying up haemoglobin for a long time.
• Less than 1.5% of Hb is occupied by CO in most nonsmokers, up to 3% in residents of polluted cities and up to 10% in heavy smokers; 0.1% CO in air binds 50% of Hb and 0.2% is quickly lethal.
• Active tissues consume O2 rapidly, keeping tissue PO2 low, warmer and more acidic, so the curve shifts right and utilization may reach 80% in exercising muscle.
3. Distinctions:
• Oxyhaemoglobin (HbO2) is Hb bound to O2; deoxyhaemoglobin (HHb) has no oxygen bound.
• Oxyhaemoglobin binds oxygen reversibly and loosely; carboxyhaemoglobin (HbCO) is formed by CO, which competes for the same site with 210 times the affinity.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the transport of oxygen in the blood:
1. Describe oxygen transport under these headings: forms of transport, haemoglobin binding, amount released at the tissues (utilization coefficient), the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve and the factors that shift it.
2. Explain why carbon monoxide poisoning is so dangerous and how tissues with higher metabolic needs obtain more oxygen.
3. Distinguish between oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin, and between oxyhaemoglobin and carboxyhaemoglobin.

questions.answerText:
1. Cardiac cycle:
• Definition: the repeating pattern of contraction (systole) and relaxation (diastole); both atria contract almost simultaneously and both ventricles about 0.1 to 0.2 second later; diastolic systemic arterial pressure is about 80 mmHg.
• Isovolumetric contraction: ventricular pressure rises, the AV valves snap shut, and the ventricles neither fill nor eject.
• Ejection: when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic (about 120 mmHg) and pulmonary artery (about 25 mmHg) pressure the semilunar valves open; afterwards the semilunar valves close and arterial pressures fall to about 80 and 8 mmHg while ventricular pressure falls to about 0 mmHg; the dicrotic notch is a brief rise in aortic pressure from backflow.
• Isovolumetric relaxation: all valves are closed while ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.
• Rapid filling: the AV valves open when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.
• Atrial contraction: empties the final blood into the ventricles.
• Volumes: about 80 ml at end of systole, about 130 ml after passive filling, active atrial filling adds about 25% (to 150 ml), and about 70 ml is ejected.
• Heart sounds: closing of valves gives "lub-dub".
2. Basis of disturbance:
• Passive filling dominates, which explains why filling is still possible in atrial fibrillation.
• Valve disease: regurgitation is leakage because the valve does not close completely (blood flows back into the atria or ventricles); stenosis is narrowing or stiffening that suppresses flow, so the heart pumps with increased force; mitral valve prolapse is also listed.
3. Distinctions:
• First sound ("lub"): closure of the AV valves during isovolumetric contraction at the start of systole; second sound ("dub"): closure of the semilunar valves when ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure at the start of diastole.
• Isovolumetric contraction: pressure rises, AV valves shut, semilunar valves not yet open; isovolumetric relaxation: pressure falls, both valve sets closed.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the cardiac cycle:
1. Describe the cardiac cycle under these headings: definition of systole and diastole, phases, pressure and volume changes, and heart sounds.
2. Explain why ventricular filling remains possible when atrial contraction is lost (for example in atrial fibrillation) and how valve disease alters the pumping of the heart.
3. Distinguish between the first and second heart sounds, and between isovolumetric contraction and isovolumetric relaxation.

questions.answerText:
1. Functions of the stomach:
• Anatomy and motility: the stomach has a fundus, body and pylorus; the proximal area (fundus and body) is thin-walled, contracts weakly and infrequently and holds large volumes of food through receptive relaxation; the distal area (pylorus) is thick-walled with strong, frequent peristaltic contractions that mix food and propel it into the duodenum (gastric emptying).
• Hydrochloric acid: activates pepsinogen to pepsin, provides the optimum pH for pepsin and protein digestion, kills bacteria in food, helps absorption of Fe2+ and Ca2+, and promotes pancreatic, small intestinal and bile secretion.
• Mucus: soluble mucus mixes with the contents and lubricates chyme; insoluble mucus forms a protective barrier against the high acidity.
• Intrinsic factor: helps in the absorption of vitamin B12.
• GI secretions overall lubricate, protect, sterilise (HCl), neutralise (HCO3-) and digest (enzymes), about 6 to 8 L per day.
2. Pathologies:
• Peptic ulcer disease is a lesion in the lining of the stomach or duodenum caused by the digestive action of pepsin and gastric acid.
• Causes: NSAIDs, H. pylori infection, inadequate mucosal defence against HCl, increased HCl secretion (for example Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), steroid therapy, smoking, excess alcohol, chemotherapy, stress and genetic factors.
• Symptoms: epigastric pain, nausea, oral flatulence, bloating, distension and intolerance of fatty food, heartburn, and pain radiating to the back.
• Treatment approaches: eradicate H. pylori (amoxycillin, clarithromycin, metronidazole, tetracycline); reduce acid with H2-receptor antagonists (cimetidine, ranitidine, famotidine, nizatidine) or PPIs (omeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole); protect the mucosa (misoprostol); neutralise acid (antacids, sucralfate); anticholinergics.
• Deficiency of intrinsic factor causes pernicious anaemia (vitamin B12 deficiency).
3. Distant effects:
• Without intrinsic factor vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed, so erythrocytes grow but do not divide and large pale macrocytes result; pernicious anaemia is an autoimmune disease with atrophy of the stomach mucosa, most often in the elderly.
• Atrophy of the gastric mucosa is listed among the diseases that cause blood disorders.
• Peptic ulcer pain can radiate to the back.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the functions of the stomach:
1. Describe the functions of the stomach under these headings: motility (fundus, body, pylorus), gastric secretions (hydrochloric acid, mucus, intrinsic factor, pepsin) and the functions of each.
2. State how the components of gastric function relate to common pathologies of excess and deficiency (peptic ulcer disease, lack of intrinsic factor).
3. Explain why a disturbance of the stomach may affect a distant organ and cause a functional deficit.
