(c) Explain why choosing the wrong type of medium for a given specimen (e.g. a non-enriched medium for a fastidious organism) can lead to an inaccurate or invalid (false-negative) result.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Visible clumping within about 10 seconds of mixing the organism with rabbit plasma on a slide is a positive slide coagulase test, indicating the presence of bound coagulase (clumping factor), an adhesin that binds fibrinogen in the plasma to the bacterial cell wall.
(ii)
The result is recorded as "Slide coagulase test: positive".
(iii)
A positive result indicates Staphylococcus aureus, the most commonly isolated coagulase-positive Staphylococcus species (a small number of other species such as S. schleiferi and S. lugdunensis may also give positive slide results); a negative result suggests a coagulase-negative Staphylococcus such as S. epidermidis or S. saprophyticus.
(iv)
Follow-up: because the slide test can give false negatives, the tube coagulase test (the definitive test) should be performed - the organism is mixed into a larger volume of plasma in a test tube and observed for clot formation over up to 24 hours; formation of a clot of any size within 24 hours confirms a positive (coagulase-producing) result.
questions.question:
(i) A slide coagulase test on a Gram-positive coccal isolate from a wound shows visible clumping of bacterial cells within 10 seconds of mixing with rabbit plasma. Interpret this result.
(ii) State how the result is recorded.
(iii) State what this result indicates about the isolate's identity.
(iv) State the follow-up action if the slide test is negative but Staphylococcus aureus is still suspected.

(a) Describe urogenital specimen examination under the following headings: (i) specimens collected in males and females, (ii) transport requirements for the different suspected pathogens, (iii) culture media used for each organism.
(b) Explain why only organisms known to be pathogenic at genital sites are reported, given that the genital tract is normally colonised with bacteria.
(c) Distinguish the specimen/transport requirements for Neisseria gonorrhoeae from those for Chlamydia trachomatis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Specimens: in males, a urethral swab is taken; in females, high vaginal/vaginal, cervical or urethral swabs are taken, depending on the suspected infection (cervicitis, urethritis, vulvo-vaginitis, bacterial vaginosis or pelvic inflammatory disease).
• Transport requirements: female cervical and male urethral swabs for isolation of N. gonorrhoeae should be placed in charcoal-containing transport media/Stuart's medium, which preserves the organism, and delivered to the laboratory as soon as possible. Swabs for detection of Chlamydia trachomatis should not be put into transport medium but delivered to the laboratory immediately. A vaginal swab for detection of Group B beta-haemolytic streptococcus in pregnant women (34-37 weeks of gestation) is placed in transport media.
• Culture media: non-selective chocolate agar and selective Modified Thayer-Martin (MTM) agar are used for N. gonorrhoeae; Sabouraud dextrose agar is used for Candida albicans; bi-layer Tween 80 blood agar is used for Gardnerella vaginalis; Trichomonas medium is used for T. vaginalis.
(b)
Because the genital tract is normally colonised with commensal bacteria, confirmation of infection at these sites must be made by detecting and reporting only organisms known to be pathogenic at those sites (e.g. N. gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Candida, Trichomonas vaginalis, Haemophilus ducreyi, Gardnerella vaginalis in association with anaerobes), rather than every organism cultured, to avoid mistaking normal flora for the cause of disease.
(c)
For N. gonorrhoeae, the swab is placed in charcoal-containing transport medium/Stuart's medium (which preserves the organism) and delivered promptly, whereas for Chlamydia trachomatis, the swab must not be placed in transport medium at all but delivered immediately to the laboratory, reflecting the differing survival requirements of the two organisms outside the body.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of the intestinal protozoa of man into amoebae, flagellates, ciliates and coccidia.
(b) State how the diagnostic stage (trophozoite versus cyst) is selected/expected for each class when examining a stool specimen.
(c) Explain why examining only a single stool specimen can lead to a false-negative result for organisms such as Giardia lamblia.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Common intestinal protozoa of man are classified into amoebae (e.g. Entamoeba histolytica, E. coli, Endolimax nana, Iodamoeba butschlii, Dientamoeba fragilis), flagellates (e.g. Giardia lamblia, Chilomastix mesnili, Trichomonas hominis), ciliates (Balantidium coli, the only ciliate parasitising man) and coccidia (e.g. Isospora hominis).
(b)
Application: in general, only two stages occur - the motile trophozoite and the resistant cyst - and either may serve as the diagnostic stage, but only the cyst is generally infective (Trichomonas species and Dientamoeba fragilis lack a cyst stage, so their trophozoite serves as both diagnostic and infective stage); Balantidium coli is unusual in that both stages may serve as the diagnostic form, though only the cyst is infective; coccidia (Isospora) have a more complex life history involving both asexual and sexual generations.
(c)
Because Giardia lives in the small intestine and is shed from the body intermittently ("in showers"), its cysts may be found only intermittently in stool; a single negative stool examination therefore does not rule out infection, and repeated stool examinations on different days are required to reliably detect the organism, since a false-negative result can otherwise be wrongly interpreted as absence of infection.

questions.question:
(i) A stool culture on MacConkey agar shows bright pink, mucoid colonies. Identify the likely organism group and the basis for the colour observed.
(ii) State the basic technique/medium principle used to detect this finding.
(iii) State how the finding is recorded/reported.
(iv) State the follow-up practical step needed to identify the organism to species level.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Bright pink colonies on MacConkey agar indicate a lactose-fermenting organism; large, dome-shaped, mucoid pink colonies are typical of Klebsiella pneumoniae (capsulated), while smaller pink colonies are typical of Escherichia coli.
(ii)
Technique: MacConkey agar is a selective and indicator (differential) medium - bile salts inhibit Gram-positive organisms while allowing Gram-negative bacilli to grow, and lactose fermentation lowers the pH, turning the neutral red indicator pink; this classifies the isolate as a "lactose fermenter".
(iii)
The finding is recorded/reported as "lactose-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli isolated, colony morphology consistent with Klebsiella/E. coli", pending confirmatory biochemical testing.
(iv)
Follow-up: perform IMViC biochemical tests. E. coli is typically Indole positive, Methyl Red positive, Voges-Proskauer negative and Citrate negative, whereas Klebsiella pneumoniae is typically Indole negative, Methyl Red negative, Voges-Proskauer positive and Citrate positive, and is urease positive, allowing the two organisms to be distinguished.

(a)
• Direct examination methods include direct wet mount, India ink, KOH/calcofluor mounts, lactophenol cotton blue (LPCB) mounts, frozen section of tissue biopsies, and a modified Kinyoun acid-fast stain for Nocardia; these give a presumptive diagnosis and guide the choice of appropriate culture media.
• Culture: two general types of media are used - non-selective media (e.g. brain-heart infusion, permitting growth of virtually all clinically relevant fungi) and more selective/enriched media; using Sabouraud dextrose agar alone as the sole primary recovery medium is discouraged because it is insufficiently rich for fastidious pathogens such as the dimorphic fungi, so Potato Flake Agar, Inhibitory Mold Agar, or Sabouraud dextrose combined with heart infusion (SABHI) agar is recommended, with 5-10% sheep blood added for Histoplasma capsulatum media. Samples are typically cultured on two sets of media at two temperatures (30°C room temperature and 35°C) and incubated for a minimum of 30 days before being discarded as negative.
• Confirmatory tests: the germ tube test is performed by inoculating a yeast colony into human/horse serum and incubating at 35-37°C for 2-3 hours before examining for tube-like outgrowths (germ tubes); sprouting confirms Candida albicans, while its absence indicates a yeast other than C. albicans. Chlamydospore production on corn-meal or rice-tween 80 agar is another confirmatory feature of C. albicans.
(b)
Early and accurate diagnosis is clinically important because fungi are a common cause of infection, particularly in immunocompromised patients (e.g. Candida and Aspergillus species), and prompt diagnosis allows timely commencement of antifungal therapy while decreasing the unnecessary use of toxic antifungal agents.
(c)
India ink is added to specimens such as spinal fluid or exudates to provide a dark background that highlights hyaline yeast cells and capsular material as a "halo" effect, and is used specifically to look for Cryptococcus neoformans (white blood cells can be distinguished from C. neoformans by the irregular edge of the halo and pale cell wash). KOH mounts are instead used mainly for skin and nail specimens (40% and 10% KOH respectively), dissolving the epithelial cells/keratin to aid visualisation of fungal elements within the specimen, rather than providing a contrasting background stain for capsulated yeasts.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the laboratory diagnosis of fungal infection under the following headings: (i) direct examination methods (India ink, KOH, LPCB mounts), (ii) culture media and incubation conditions, (iii) confirmatory tests such as the germ tube test.
(b) Explain the clinical significance of early and accurate diagnosis of fungal infection.
(c) Distinguish the India ink method from the KOH mount method of direct examination.

(i) A patient with a chronic cough of more than two weeks, weight loss and evening fever submits a sputum sample for suspected tuberculosis. Identify the specimen and the staining reagents required for the standard smear technique used on it.
(ii) State the principle of the staining technique.
(iii) Outline the step-by-step staining procedure.
(iv) State the expected observed result and how a positive smear is interpreted.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Specimen: sputum (the usual specimen for diagnosis of tuberculosis); other samples that can be used include bronchial washings, biopsies, gastric aspirates, CSF and pleural fluid. Reagents for the Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) technique: strong (1%) carbol fuchsin as primary stain, acid-alcohol (3% hydrochloric acid in alcohol, or 20-25% sulphuric acid in water) as decolouriser, and 0.1% methylene blue as counterstain.
(ii)
Principle: the primary stain (carbol fuchsin) penetrates the lipid-rich, mycolic-acid cell wall of the bacillus; intense decolorisation with acid-alcohol does not release the primary stain from the cell wall of acid-fast bacilli (AFB), so the organism retains the red colour of the primary stain while the counterstain provides a contrasting background.
(iii)
Procedure: apply 1% carbol fuchsin to the heat-fixed smear and heat until steam rises, leaving it for 5 minutes; decolourise with acid-alcohol until faintly pink; counterstain with 0.1% methylene blue for 30 seconds; wash, air-dry and examine under oil immersion (1000x).
(iv)
A well-stained smear shows strong red acid-fast bacilli against a weak blue background, with no red artefacts. Grading follows the IUATLD/WHO scale: negative (0 AFB/length), scanty (1-9 AFB/length), 1+ (10-99 AFB/length), 2+ (1-10 AFB/field on average) and 3+ (>10 AFB/field on average); any AFB seen indicates a positive result requiring further TB work-up.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the general characteristics of Proteus species, including their morphology and the phenomenon of swarming.
(b) State the standard method used to inhibit swarming when a pure culture is required on solid media.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the Weil-Felix agglutination reaction observed with certain nonmotile Proteus strains.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Proteus is a genus of non-capsulated, pleomorphic, motile rods, lactose non-fermenters, named after the Greek god Proteus who could assume any shape, reflecting the organism's pleomorphism; flagellated strains growing on agar form a thin surface film resembling breath-mist on glass, called the Hauch (film) form, giving rise to the O (somatic, "ohne Hauch"/without film in nonflagellated strains) and H (flagellar, "Hauch") antigen naming convention. On culture, Proteus produces a putrefactive (fishy/seminal) odour and shows swarming (a wavy growth pattern in concentric circles on nutrient or blood agar); it is urease positive and phenylalanine deaminase (PPA) positive.
(b)
Standard method to inhibit swarming: incorporating agents such as 6% agar, sodium azide (1:500), alcohol (5-6%), sulphonamide, chloral hydrate (1:500), surface-active agents or boric acid (1:1000) into the medium prevents swarming and allows isolated colonies to be obtained for identification, e.g. on MacConkey and DCA agar, where Proteus instead grows as pale, non-swarming colonies.
(c)
Basic reasoning: certain nonmotile Proteus strains (OX2, OX19 and OXK) share a carbohydrate hapten (antigen) with certain Rickettsia species; because rickettsial infection stimulates production of antibodies that cross-react with this shared hapten, patient serum from a rickettsial infection agglutinates these Proteus strains, forming the basis of the Weil-Felix reaction used to diagnose rickettsial disease.

(a)
Symbiotic relationships between microorganisms and their host can take the form of mutualism (an association in which both partners benefit, e.g. gut bacteria and the host's synthesis of vitamins K and B), commensalism (an association in which one partner benefits and the other is unharmed, e.g. the normal microbiota/flora living on the skin) or parasitism (a relationship in which one partner, the parasite, benefits at the expense of the other, the host).
(b)
Application: when a microorganism is isolated from a patient specimen, its normal habitat and typical behaviour must be considered - an organism recovered from a site where it is a recognised commensal (e.g. Staphylococcus epidermidis on skin, or normal flora in the genital tract) is not automatically the cause of disease, whereas an organism recovered from a normally sterile site, or a known pathogen recovered even in small numbers from its typical infection site, is more likely to represent true infection.
(c)
Misclassifying a commensal as an infecting parasite (e.g. reporting normal skin or genital flora as the causative organism of an infection) can lead to unnecessary antibiotic treatment, masking of the true causative pathogen, and a false laboratory conclusion about the source of a patient's illness; this is why, in genital tract specimens, only organisms known to be pathogenic at that site are detected and reported, even though the tract is normally colonised with bacteria.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of host-parasite relationships into mutualism, commensalism and parasitism.
(b) State how each type of relationship is recognised/applied when assessing a microorganism found in or on a patient.
(c) Explain why misclassifying a commensal organism as an infecting parasite can lead to an inappropriate clinical or laboratory conclusion.

(a) Describe the general characteristics of Salmonella species, including their morphology and antigenic (O, H, Vi) classification.
(b) State the standard selective culture media used to isolate Salmonella from clinical specimens.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind why serological identification of Salmonella must always be confirmed biochemically rather than relying on serology alone.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Salmonella is a genus of rod-shaped, Gram-negative, non-spore-forming, predominantly motile bacteria of the family Enterobacteriaceae, moving by peritrichous flagella; they are facultative anaerobes and intracellular pathogens. The genus comprises two species, S. enterica (with six subspecies) and S. bongori; serotypes are classified according to the Kauffmann-White scheme, based on the somatic O (lipopolysaccharide) and flagellar H antigens, giving rise to more than 2,500 recognised serotypes.
(b)
Standard media: selective media containing agents such as bile salts, sodium desoxycholate (as in xylose lysine desoxycholate, XLD, agar) or desoxycholate citrate agar (DCA) are used to inhibit normal faecal flora while allowing Salmonella to grow; Salmonella typically produces hydrogen sulphide, readily detected on media containing ferrous sulphate such as the triple sugar iron (TSI) test.
(c)
Basic reasoning: serological identification of Salmonella without biochemical confirmation is unreliable because of the many cross-reactions with commensal gut flora that share similar surface antigens, so biochemical screening (fermentation reactions on combination media such as Kligler iron agar or TSI, decarboxylation/dehydrogenation reactions, and H2S production) must first narrow the identification before full serological (O/H) typing is performed to confirm the genus and serotype.

(i)
Specimen: CSF (other specimens for suspected Neisseria meningitidis infection include blood, nasopharyngeal swab, pus from an infected joint, and skin lesion aspirate); N. meningitidis is very fragile and dies easily outside body temperature, so the sample should be processed without delay. Medium: chocolate agar, incubated in a moist, enriched CO2 atmosphere (a candle jar can be used to provide this atmosphere); the selective medium is Modified Thayer-Martin medium.
(ii)
Principle: N. meningitidis is fastidious and requires the growth factors released by heating blood (chocolate agar) and an elevated CO2 tension (it is capnophilic) for optimal growth; a candle jar, in which a lit candle burns until extinguished by oxygen deprivation, generates a CO2-rich, oxygen-poor atmosphere suitable for such organisms.
(iii)
Procedure: a Gram-stained smear is made from the sediment of centrifuged CSF; the specimen is also inoculated onto chocolate agar and incubated at 37°C in a CO2-enriched (candle jar) atmosphere for 24 hours.
(iv)
A Gram-stained smear showing Gram-negative diplococci is a strong presumptive finding. After 24 hours' incubation, colonies on chocolate agar are small (about 1 mm), round, smooth, grey and glistening with a clearly defined edge (growth is less luxuriant on blood agar); an oxidase test is strongly positive, and carbohydrate utilisation shows fermentation of glucose and maltose, confirming N. meningitidis and indicating bacterial meningitis due to this organism.
questions.question:
(i) A cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample is received from a patient with suspected bacterial meningitis. Identify the specimen handling requirement and the culture medium of choice.
(ii) State the principle behind using an enriched, moist CO2-enriched medium for this organism.
(iii) Outline the procedure for direct examination and culture.
(iv) State the expected microscopic and colonial findings and how they are interpreted.

(a) Describe the structure, natural habitat and dimorphism of Histoplasma capsulatum.
(b) State the standard specimen types and antigen testing method used to diagnose histoplasmosis.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution that culturing H. capsulatum poses a severe biohazard to laboratory personnel.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic, ascomycetous fungus, growing as a mould in nature or in culture at room temperature but converting to a small (1-5 micrometre) budding yeast at 37°C and during invasion of host cells. It produces two types of conidia in its mould form - large, tuberculate macroconidia (8-15 µm) and smaller, smooth or finely roughened microconidia (2-4 µm). The fungus is strongly associated with soil enriched by bird droppings and with bat droppings; bats can become infected and transmit the fungus through their droppings, whereas birds cannot be infected but their excretions enrich the soil for mycelial growth.
(b)
Standard testing: combined urine and serum antigen testing gives a sensitivity of about 90% for disseminated disease, with bronchoalveolar lavage antigen testing being even more sensitive than urine antigen testing; specimens for histopathology and culture include sputum, blood, bone marrow and tissue biopsy.
(c)
Basic reasoning: because culturing H. capsulatum in its infectious mould/conidial form can generate airborne spores that are highly infectious by inhalation, the laboratory must be notified of the suspected diagnosis in advance so that appropriate biosafety precautions (handling in a biosafety cabinet) are taken, preventing laboratory-acquired infection.

(a)
• Smear microscopy: brightfield microscopy uses carbol fuchsin as the primary stain and methylene blue as the counterstain (Ziehl-Neelsen technique); fluorescence microscopy uses Auramine O as the primary stain and potassium permanganate as the counterstain. In ZN staining, the primary stain penetrates the cell wall and intense decolorisation does not release it from the acid-fast cell wall, so colour is based on the primary stain with the counterstain providing contrast; in fluorescence (Auramine) staining, the fluorochrome dye forms a complex with mycolic acids in the acid-fast cell wall that resists decolorisation by acid-alcohol, and the potassium permanganate counterstain renders tissue debris non-fluorescent, reducing artefacts.
• Culture methods: cultural techniques may be solid (egg-based Lowenstein-Jensen or Ogawa medium, or agar-based 7H10/7H11) or liquid (Middlebrook 7H9, as used in the BACTEC MGIT 960 system). Egg-based media are cheap, easy to prepare and have a long shelf-life (up to 12 weeks at 4°C), but take up to 8 weeks for evident growth; liquid media give a much shorter recovery time (about 8 days for smear-positive, 16 days for smear-negative specimens) with increased sensitivity, especially for CSF, pleural fluid and biopsies, but are more prone to contamination and carry a greater biosafety risk.
• Molecular techniques: GeneXpert MTB/RIF is an automated system using PCR (hemi-nested real-time PCR) to detect TB and rifampicin resistance within about 2 hours; the Line Probe Assay (LPA) uses DNA probes immobilised on a strip, based on reverse hybridisation of amplified, labelled PCR products, to identify the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex and resistance to rifampicin, isoniazid, fluoroquinolones and/or aminoglycosides within 8-24 hours.
(b)
Smear microscopy remains the first-line method because it is the best choice among diagnostic methods for immediate assessment, is required for treatment follow-up (molecular tests such as Xpert are not recommended for this purpose), and is far cheaper and simpler to perform than culture or molecular methods, even though molecular techniques (Xpert, 2 hours; LPA, 8-24 hours) are faster than culture (liquid, 4-21 days; solid, 8-10 weeks) for initial diagnosis.
(c)
The Ziehl-Neelsen method is a brightfield technique in which a well-stained smear shows strong red AFB against a weak blue background, examined under an ordinary light microscope; the Auramine (fluorescence) technique shows AFB as yellow or green fluorescence against a dark background, viewed with a fluorescence microscope, and is generally read at a lower magnification (20x or 40x objective), allowing a larger area to be scanned more quickly than ZN microscopy.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the laboratory diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis under the following headings: (i) smear microscopy methods and their staining principles, (ii) culture methods and media used, (iii) molecular diagnostic techniques.
(b) Explain why smear microscopy remains the mainstay first-line diagnostic method despite the availability of molecular techniques.
(c) Distinguish between the Ziehl-Neelsen (brightfield) and fluorescence (Auramine O) staining techniques for acid-fast bacilli.

(i) A stool sample is submitted from a patient with suspected intestinal protozoan infection. Identify the specimen and the reagent used for the routine direct examination.
(ii) State the principle behind the use of this reagent in the preparation.
(iii) Outline the procedure for preparing and examining the specimen.
(iv) State the expected findings and how the diagnostic and infective stages are interpreted.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Specimen: faeces. Reagent: normal saline (for a saline wet mount) and iodine (for an iodine wet mount), used to examine for trophozoites and cysts of intestinal protozoa such as the amoebae, flagellates, ciliates and coccidia.
(ii)
Principle: in general, only two stages occur in these protozoa - the motile trophozoite and the resistant cyst - and either stage may serve as the diagnostic form, but only the cyst is generally infective (trophozoites are fragile and disintegrate outside the body). Iodine stains the nuclear structure and glycogen of cysts, making internal morphology easier to see for identification, while saline preparations preserve motility for observing trophozoites.
(iii)
Procedure: emulsify a small portion of stool in a drop of saline (and, on a separate slide, in a drop of iodine) on a glass slide, cover with a coverslip, and examine systematically under the low and high power objectives of the microscope for trophozoites and cysts.
(iv)
Findings: motile trophozoites (e.g. of Entamoeba histolytica or Giardia lamblia) may be seen in the saline mount, while cysts with their nuclear detail are more clearly seen in the iodine mount. Because organisms such as Giardia are shed intermittently ("in showers"), a single negative stool does not exclude infection; repeat or multiple stool examinations may be needed before a negative result is accepted.

questions.question:
(i) An oxidase test performed by rubbing a colony onto filter paper soaked in Kovacs' oxidase reagent produces a dark purple colour within 5-10 seconds. Interpret this result.
(ii) State how the result is recorded.
(iii) State what this result indicates about the organism's identity.
(iv) State the follow-up action needed to complete identification.
questions.answerText:
(i)
A colour change to dark purple within 5-10 seconds indicates a positive oxidase test, showing the presence of cytochrome oxidase, which oxidises the reduced colourless reagent to an oxidised, coloured product; a colour change taking 60-90 seconds is delayed-positive, and no change (or a change taking over 2 minutes) is oxidase negative.
(ii)
The result is recorded as "Oxidase test: positive".
(iii)
A positive oxidase result is consistent with organisms such as Pseudomonas, Vibrio cholerae and Neisseria species, which are oxidase positive, and excludes members of the Enterobacteriaceae (e.g. E. coli, Klebsiella, Salmonella), which are oxidase negative; oxidase-negative results, together with reduction of nitrate and fermentation of glucose with acid production, are three key screening properties for Enterobacteriaceae.
(iv)
Follow-up: further biochemical and cultural tests (e.g. TSI reaction, growth on selective media such as MacConkey or TCBS, pigment production) should be performed to identify the oxidase-positive isolate to genus/species level, since oxidase positivity alone only narrows the possibilities.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the general characteristics and classification of Streptococcus species, including their morphology, arrangement, and classification by haemolysis and by Lancefield grouping.
(b) State the standard culture medium and conditions used for isolating Streptococcus species.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind requiring an enriched medium for the successful cultivation of Streptococcus pyogenes.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Streptococcus is a genus of Gram-positive bacteria with a spherical (coccal) shape, arranged in chains or pairs, non-spore-forming, and facultatively anaerobic and fastidious; medically relevant species include S. pyogenes, S. pneumoniae and S. agalactiae. Classification is based on haemolytic properties (alpha-, beta- or gamma-/non-haemolytic) and on serologic (Lancefield) grouping, in which beta-haemolytic species are classified into Groups A to U, with Groups A (S. pyogenes) and B (S. agalactiae) being the clinically significant groups; viridans streptococci (e.g. S. mutans) are alpha- or gamma-haemolytic.
(b)
Standard medium/conditions: enriched culture media are required for isolation, such as blood or chocolate agar; colonies on blood agar are 0.5-2 mm in diameter, raised, round or oval, smooth (mucoid in S. pneumoniae) and greyish to slightly translucent. Optimal incubation conditions for most streptococcal strains are 35-37°C in the presence of 5% CO2 or under anaerobic conditions, though growth also occurs (more slowly) in ambient air.
(c)
Basic reasoning: S. pyogenes is a fastidious organism requiring a minimum concentration of nutrients such as sugars and peptides for best growth, so an enriched medium such as blood agar (supplemented sheep blood) is needed to provide these nutrients and support visible, characteristic (beta-haemolytic) colony growth that would not occur on simple, unenriched media.

questions.question:
(i) A germ tube test performed on a yeast isolate incubated in serum for 2-3 hours shows no tube-like outgrowths under the microscope. Interpret this result.
(ii) State how the result is recorded.
(iii) State what this result indicates about the organism's identity.
(iv) State the follow-up test needed to identify the yeast further.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Absence of sprouting (tube-like outgrowths, germ tubes) from the yeast cells after incubation in serum at 35-37°C for 2-3 hours is a negative germ tube test.
(ii)
The result is recorded as "Germ tube test: negative - yeast other than Candida albicans isolated".
(iii)
This indicates that the yeast is not Candida albicans (which characteristically produces germ tubes under these conditions), and another yeast species (e.g. C. tropicalis, C. krusei, C. glabrata) should be considered.
(iv)
Follow-up: inoculate the yeast onto corn-meal (or rice-tween 80) agar to look for chlamydospore production (a feature of C. albicans not always mirrored by other species when germ-tube negative) and perform sugar assimilation/fermentation tests (glucose, maltose, lactose, dulcitol, galactose) to identify the yeast species definitively.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of infection transmission into direct contact, indirect (fomite/vehicle-borne), and vector-borne routes, using examples from the documents.
(b) State how infection-control precautions are selected according to the mode of transmission of a given organism.
(c) Explain why applying the wrong type of infection-control precaution (based on a misclassified transmission route) can fail to prevent spread of the organism.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diseases can be transmitted directly (e.g. syphilis by sexual contact, streptococcal pharyngitis by person-to-person contact via nasal secretions or saliva droplets), indirectly via fomites/vehicles (e.g. Salmonella spread when stool from an infected person contaminates hands, food, water or objects such as toys, or Staphylococcus transmitted efficiently from person to person and via contaminated hospital surfaces/equipment), or by an arthropod vector (e.g. Rickettsia by lice, fleas, ticks or mites; malaria by mosquitoes; relapsing fever by lice or ticks).
(b)
Application: infection-control precautions are matched to the transmission route - enteric precautions (hand hygiene, careful handling of faeces/contaminated linen) are applied for faecal-oral pathogens such as Salmonella and Shigella; contact/droplet precautions are applied for directly transmitted respiratory or skin pathogens such as Streptococcus pyogenes; vector control (insecticides, repellents, avoidance of vector habitats) is applied for arthropod-borne diseases such as rickettsioses and malaria.
(c)
Applying the wrong type of precaution can fail to prevent spread because each transmission route requires a specific interruption strategy - for example, focusing only on hand hygiene (appropriate for a faecal-oral pathogen) would not interrupt transmission of a vector-borne disease that depends on control of the arthropod vector, so the organism would continue to spread via its actual transmission route despite the (misdirected) infection-control effort.

(a)
The protective immune response to parasitic infection has four arms: cytotoxic T cells, natural killer cells and activated macrophages, which together constitute cell-mediated immunity, and antibody (produced by B cells), which constitutes humoral immunity.
(b)
Application: because microparasites (protozoa) are small and multiply within the vertebrate host, often intracellularly, they pose an immediate threat that must be contained by a prompt immune response, engaging both cell-mediated mechanisms (important against intracellular protozoa such as Leishmania) and humoral antibody responses; macroparasites (helminths) are large and do not multiply within the host, so they do not pose an immediate threat after initial infection, but the host must still mount a response against large infections and against infective stages, tending to elicit a more limited overall immune response than microparasites.
(c)
Immunological protection against parasitic infection is generally less efficient than against bacterial or viral infection because parasites are large and structurally/antigenically complex, so the immune system may fail to mount an effective response against their genuinely protective antigens; many protozoan parasites (e.g. Leishmania spp.) are intracellular, shielding them from immunological attack; many parasites live within the intestinal lumen, a location that limits the efficiency of immune attack and facilitates dispersal of infective stages; and some parasites undergo antigenic variation (e.g. Trypanosoma brucei) or use other immune-evasion strategies. This inefficiency, together with the fact that immunity in most parasitic infections lasts only while the original infection remains active (concomitant immunity), has made the production of effective vaccines against eukaryotic parasites extremely difficult.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of immune mechanisms against parasitic infection into cell-mediated (cytotoxic T cells, natural killer cells, activated macrophages) and humoral (antibody, B cells) arms.
(b) State how these mechanisms are applied differently against microparasites (e.g. protozoa) compared with macroparasites (e.g. helminths).
(c) Explain why immunological protection against parasitic infection is generally less efficient than that against bacterial or viral infection, and why this affects vaccine development.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Specimen: skin scrapings taken from the periphery of the lesion (not the centre), collected after cleaning the area with 70% alcohol to remove fatty material and make the scaling more obvious; scrapings are collected into a dry sterile container, envelope or folded paper. Reagent: 10-20% potassium hydroxide (KOH).
(ii)
Principle: KOH dissolves the keratin and epithelial cells of the specimen without destroying fungal elements, thereby clearing the background and making any septate hyphae or arthrospores easier to visualise.
(iii)
Procedure: place the sample of skin scrapings on a clean glass slide with a drop of 10-20% KOH, add a coverslip and heat the slide gently over a Bunsen flame (without boiling), or allow it to stand for 15-20 minutes at room temperature to clear; examine the cleared preparation under the microscope for septate hyphae and/or arthrospores.
(iv)
A positive finding is the presence of septate hyphae and/or arthrospores in the cleared preparation, consistent with dermatophyte (ringworm/Tinea) infection; this direct microscopy result is reported as "fungal elements seen" and should be followed by culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar with chloramphenicol and cycloheximide for species identification.
questions.question:
(i) A skin scraping is submitted from a patient with a scaly, ring-shaped lesion suspected to be ringworm. Identify the specimen collection requirement and the reagent used for direct microscopy.
(ii) State the principle of the reagent's action on the specimen.
(iii) Outline the procedure for preparation and microscopic examination.
(iv) State the expected microscopic finding and how it is interpreted.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Anaerobic bacteria are classified by spore formation and Gram reaction: anaerobic non-spore-formers include Gram-negative rods (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium), Gram-positive rods (Actinomyces, Eubacterium, Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, Propionibacterium), Gram-positive cocci (Peptostreptococcus, Peptococcus) and Gram-negative cocci (Veillonella, Acidaminococcus); anaerobic spore-formers are Gram-positive rods of the genus Clostridium (e.g. C. tetani, C. perfringens, C. botulinum).
(b)
Application: the McIntosh-Fildes jar or GasPak system is selected for strict/obligate anaerobes (e.g. Clostridium, Bacteroides) that require a fully oxygen-free environment; a candle jar is instead selected for capnophilic/microaerophilic organisms that need a CO2-enriched but not fully anaerobic atmosphere (e.g. Neisseria meningitidis, Brucella, Streptococcus pneumoniae).
(c)
Exposure of the specimen or culture to atmospheric oxygen during processing can invalidate the result because strict anaerobes lack the enzymes (catalase, superoxide dismutase, peroxidase) needed to detoxify the reactive oxygen products generated on exposure to air, so oxygen exposure can kill the organisms or prevent their growth even though they were originally present, producing a false-negative culture; this is why specimens for anaerobic culture must be transported and processed with minimal air exposure and examined by Gram stain to correlate a positive smear with a negative culture, which can indicate such technical failure.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of anaerobic bacteria into spore-forming (e.g. Clostridium) and non-spore-forming (e.g. Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus) groups, by Gram reaction.
(b) State how the choice of anaerobic culture apparatus (McIntosh-Fildes jar, GasPak, candle jar) is selected according to the type of organism suspected.
(c) Explain why exposure of the specimen or culture to atmospheric oxygen during processing can invalidate an anaerobic culture result.

(i) A Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion antibiotic sensitivity plate shows a clear zone of inhibition of 22 mm around one antibiotic disc and no zone around another. Interpret these two readings.
(ii) State how the result should be recorded/reported in standard practical format.
(iii) State what the result indicates about the isolate's antibiotic susceptibility.
(iv) State the follow-up action required based on the reading.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The zone of inhibition is the area around the disc where no bacterial growth is visible to the unaided eye; a large, clear 22 mm zone indicates that the organism is inhibited by that antibiotic, while no zone around the second disc indicates growth right up to the disc, meaning that antibiotic has no inhibitory effect on the isolate at the concentration tested.
(ii)
The diameter of each zone is measured (preferably with a Vernier scale or a ruler graduated to 0.5 mm), rounded to the nearest millimetre, and compared with the interpretive criteria for that specific antimicrobial agent published by CLSI.
(iii)
Based on the comparison with the CLSI interpretive chart, the isolate is reported as Sensitive (S), Intermediate (I) or Resistant (R) to each antibiotic tested; the organism with the 22 mm zone would typically be reported as sensitive, and the one with no zone as resistant, subject to the specific breakpoints for that drug and organism.
(iv)
Follow-up: plates with overlapping zones, non-circular/distorted zones, isolated colonies, or a batch whose control strain zones fall outside the expected limits must be rejected and the test repeated; the reported sensitivity/resistance pattern is used to guide the choice of antimicrobial therapy.

questions.question:
(i) A throat swab is submitted from a child with a grey pseudomembrane over the tonsils, suspected diphtheria. Identify the specimen and the selective culture medium used.
(ii) State the principle behind the selective medium's action.
(iii) Outline the procedure for staining and culture.
(iv) State the expected colonial appearance and how the result is interpreted.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Specimen: throat swab, taken from beneath the edge of the pseudomembrane where possible. Medium: tellurite blood agar (potassium tellurite medium), used as a selective medium for isolation of Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
(ii)
Principle: tellurite inhibits the growth of most secondary (commensal) throat bacteria without an inhibitory effect on diphtheria bacilli; C. diphtheriae reduces the tellurite to metallic tellurium, which has a black colour, so the medium is also an indicator medium as the diphtheria bacilli produce black colonies.
(iii)
Procedure: a Gram stain is performed to show Gram-positive rods in a typical arrangement; the swab is also inoculated onto blood tellurite agar and Loeffler's serum slope and incubated aerobically at 37°C.
(iv)
On blood tellurite medium, C. diphtheriae reduces the tellurite and yields grey to black colonies, with three biological types (gravis, mitis, intermedius) giving distinctive colonial appearances; a positive culture, together with a compatible Gram stain, is reported as "Corynebacterium diphtheriae isolated" and should prompt urgent clinical management given the risk of exotoxin-mediated disease.

questions.question:
(i) A triple sugar iron (TSI) agar slant inoculated with a stool isolate shows an alkaline (red) slant, an acid (yellow), blackened butt, and gas bubbles in the medium. Interpret this reaction.
(ii) State how the reaction is recorded in standard practical format.
(iii) State what this reaction indicates about the organism's likely identity.
(iv) State the follow-up test needed to confirm the identification.
questions.answerText:
(i)
An alkaline (red) slant with an acid (black) butt and gas indicates that the organism has fermented glucose (acid butt) but not lactose or sucrose (alkaline slant), has produced hydrogen sulphide (blackening of the medium) and gas.
(ii)
The result is recorded in the standard format "Slant: K (alkaline)/Butt: A (acid), Gas: +, H2S: +".
(iii)
This reaction pattern (alkaline slant/acid butt/H2S positive) is characteristic of non-lactose-fermenting, H2S-producing organisms such as Salmonella spp., Proteus spp. and Citrobacter spp.
(iv)
Follow-up: further biochemical tests (e.g. indole, citrate, urease, lysine decarboxylase) and serological (slide agglutination) testing with specific Salmonella or Proteus antisera are required to confirm the genus and, where relevant, the serotype, since TSI results alone cannot distinguish between these genera.

(a)
Neisseria species are Gram-negative cocci occurring in pairs with flattened or concave opposing sides (diplococci); they are non-motile and generally fastidious in their growth requirements, catalase positive, oxidase positive, and attack carbohydrates oxidatively. Of the 11 species, only two are pathogenic for man - N. meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae.
(b)
Standard medium/conditions: N. meningitidis grows best on an enriched medium (chocolate agar) in a moist, enriched CO2 atmosphere, with Modified Thayer-Martin medium as the selective medium; N. gonorrhoeae is similarly isolated on chocolate agar and Modified Thayer-Martin (MTM) agar. Both are incubated at 37°C, with N. meningitidis colonies appearing after 24 hours as small (about 1 mm), round, smooth, grey, glistening colonies with a clearly defined edge, growing less readily on blood agar.
(c)
Basic reasoning: N. meningitidis is very fragile and dies easily outside body temperature, so the specimen (e.g. CSF) should be processed without delay to avoid loss of viable organisms before culture, which would otherwise give a false-negative result despite true infection.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general characteristics and morphology of Neisseria species, including their microscopic appearance and growth requirements.
(b) State the standard culture medium and atmospheric conditions used for isolating Neisseria meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution of processing specimens for N. meningitidis without delay.

(a) Describe culture media under the following headings: (i) basic nutritional and gaseous requirements supported by media, (ii) classification of media based on consistency, (iii) classification of media based on chemical composition, giving one named example of each special type.
(b) Explain why selective and enrichment media are important in clinical bacteriology.
(c) Distinguish between selective media and differential (indicator) media, giving one example of each.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Culture media give an artificial environment simulating the natural conditions necessary for bacterial growth, providing similar environmental and nutritional conditions to those in the organism's natural habitat, and contain natural and/or synthetic constituents intended to support multiplication or preserve viability. Basic nutritional requirements include water, a carbon source, a nitrogen source, inorganic salts (phosphates, sulfates, sodium, potassium, magnesium, iron, manganese, calcium) and vitamins (thiamine, riboflavin, nicotinic acid, pyridoxine, folic acid, vitamin B12). Gaseous requirements relate to oxygen (obligate aerobes, facultative anaerobes, microaerophilic, obligate anaerobes) and carbon dioxide (capnophilic organisms).
• Based on consistency: solid media (used for isolation of bacteria as pure culture and for studying colony characters; agar is the usual solidifying agent, e.g. nutrient agar), and liquid media (used for profuse growth, e.g. blood culture broth, though mixed organisms cannot be separated in liquid media).
• Based on chemical composition, routine laboratory media are classified into basal media (e.g. nutrient broth/agar, peptone water - support growth without enrichment), enriched media (e.g. blood agar, chocolate agar, Lowenstein-Jensen medium, enriched with blood, serum or egg), selective media (e.g. MacConkey agar, which favours Gram-negative growth by inhibiting Gram-positives), indicator/differential media (e.g. MacConkey agar with neutral red, which distinguishes lactose fermenters from non-fermenters), transport media (e.g. Cary-Blair, Stuart's or Amies medium) and storage media (e.g. egg saline medium, chalk cooked meat broth); synthetic/defined media, prepared from pure chemicals of known composition, are used mainly in research.
(b)
Selective and enrichment media are important because clinical specimens (e.g. faeces) are heavily contaminated with commensal or non-pathogenic organisms; an inhibitory substance is incorporated to suppress the unwanted flora and allow the target pathogen to be recovered, increasing the diagnostic yield for organisms such as Salmonella, Shigella and Vibrio cholerae.
(c)
A selective medium contains an inhibitory substance added to suppress unwanted organisms while allowing the target organism to grow on solid media, e.g. MacConkey's agar, which inhibits Gram-positive organisms via bile salts. A differential (indicator) medium instead includes an indicator that changes visibly (e.g. colour) in the presence of a particular metabolic activity, allowing organisms to be distinguished from one another on the same plate, e.g. MacConkey agar, which is also indicator/differential because lactose fermenters turn pink while non-fermenters remain colourless; enrichment media (e.g. Selenite F broth for Salmonella/Shigella, alkaline peptone water for Vibrio cholerae) are liquid media that give the pathogen of interest a competitive advantage before subculture onto selective solid media.

(a)
• Clinical indications: blood cultures are performed most often when sepsis, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, meningitis or pneumonia is suspected.
• Medium/system: blood is inoculated into a broth-blood culture system or common nutrient broths such as thioglycollate, dextrose or brain-heart infusion broth, which support profuse growth of any organisms present.
• Organisms most frequently isolated: two Gram-positive cocci, Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae, and three Gram-negative rods, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
(b)
A liquid enrichment broth is used because blood from a septic patient typically contains only very small numbers of circulating organisms; a nutrient-rich liquid medium allows these organisms to multiply to detectable levels (visible turbidity/heavy deposit) before identification, which would not be reliably achieved by direct plating of a small blood volume onto solid media.
(c)
In routine specimen (e.g. swab) culture, the specimen is usually plated directly onto solid selective/differential media because it already contains relatively larger numbers of organisms (e.g. from a wound or the genital tract); blood culture, by contrast, requires an initial liquid enrichment step because of the low bacterial load in blood, and once growth (turbidity) is detected, the broth must then be subcultured onto solid media (blood agar, MacConkey agar, chocolate agar) for identification and susceptibility testing, an additional handling step not usually required for a heavily colonised swab specimen.
questions.question:
(a) Describe blood culture under the following headings: (i) clinical indications, (ii) the culture medium/system used, (iii) the organisms most frequently isolated.
(b) Explain why a liquid enrichment broth, rather than direct plating, is used as the primary blood culture medium.
(c) Distinguish blood culture technique from routine swab/specimen culture in terms of the volume of organisms typically present and the handling required.

(i) A stool culture on MacConkey agar shows pale, colourless, non-lactose-fermenting colonies from a patient with dysentery. Identify the likely organism group.
(ii) State the basic technique used to differentiate these colonies further.
(iii) State how the finding is recorded and reported at this stage.
(iv) State the follow-up practical step required for definitive identification.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Pale, colourless (non-lactose-fermenting) colonies on MacConkey agar in a patient with dysentery-type symptoms suggest Salmonella or Shigella species.
(ii)
Technique: inoculation of the pale colony onto combination biochemical media such as Kligler iron agar or triple sugar iron (TSI) agar, which incorporates multiple sugars and pH indicators in one tube to differentiate the organisms by their fermentation and hydrogen-sulphide-producing pattern.
(iii)
The finding at this stage is recorded/reported as "non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli isolated - Salmonella/Shigella suspected, biochemical confirmation pending".
(iv)
Follow-up: read the TSI reaction - Salmonella typically gives an alkaline slant/acid butt with gas and H2S production (blackening of the medium), while Shigella gives an alkaline slant/acid butt with no gas and no H2S; this, together with serological (slide agglutination) testing with specific antisera, confirms the genus and serotype.

questions.question:
(i) A semen sample is received in the laboratory for fertility assessment. Identify the specimen requirement and the correct collection method.
(ii) State the principle behind allowing the sample to liquefy before analysis.
(iii) Outline the procedure for the macroscopic examination of the sample.
(iv) State the normal reference values obtained and how an abnormal finding is interpreted.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Specimen: the entire ejaculate, collected preferably by masturbation into a clean, wide-mouthed sterile container after 2-6 days of abstinence, since the first (30%) portion of the ejaculate contains the majority of the sperm-rich fractions and must not be lost. The sample should be kept at body temperature, away from sunlight, and delivered to the laboratory within one hour of collection.
(ii)
Principle: normal semen liquefies within 15-30 minutes of ejaculation; the sample must be mixed well and allowed to liquefy so that sperm trapped in unliquefied jelly are freed and an accurate concentration/motility assessment can be made - a lumpy sample after 60 minutes may indicate prostatic infection or lack of prostatic protease.
(iii)
Procedure: examine appearance (normal is whitish to grey opalescent), record the time to liquefaction, assess viscosity (normal is smooth and watery), and measure volume with a pipette after thorough mixing.
(iv)
Normal reference values (WHO 2010 lower reference limits) include: semen volume 1.5 ml, sperm concentration 15x10^6/ml, total sperm number 39x10^6/ejaculate, progressive motility 32%, total motility 40%, vitality 58%, normal morphology 4%, and pH ≥7.2. A volume below 1.5 ml (hypospermia) suggests a problem with the seminal vesicles/prostate such as blockage, retrograde ejaculation, infection or androgen deficiency, and cannot adequately neutralise vaginal acidity.

(a)
Intestinal cestodes belong to two orders: Pseudophyllidea (e.g. Diphyllobothrium, Spirometra), whose scolex has a pair of longitudinal grooves (bothria) rather than suckers, and Cyclophyllidea (e.g. Taenia, Echinococcus, Hymenolepis), whose scolex possesses four suckers (acetabula), sometimes with an apical rostellum that may or may not bear hooks (as in Taenia solium).
(b)
Application: Cyclophyllidean eggs are covered by two layers (egg shell and embryophore), are spherical, embryonated from the start, non-operculated, with a non-ciliated embryo; Pseudophyllidean eggs are covered by one layer (egg shell), are ovoid, unembryonated when freshly passed, operculated, with a ciliated embryo. Observing whether an egg is operculated or non-operculated, together with its shape, therefore allows the examiner to assign it to the correct order and narrow the genus.
(c)
Misreading the operculum status can lead to an incorrect genus assignment because operculation is one of the key distinguishing features between the two orders; for example, mistaking a Pseudophyllidean (operculated, e.g. Diphyllobothrium) egg for a Cyclophyllidean (non-operculated, e.g. Taenia) egg, or vice versa, would place the parasite in the wrong life-cycle group, with consequent errors in reporting the intermediate hosts and the disease risk associated with the parasite.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of intestinal cestodes into the orders Pseudophyllidea and Cyclophyllidea, based on scolex structure and egg morphology.
(b) State how the egg characteristics (operculated versus non-operculated) are used to select the correct genus during microscopic examination.
(c) Explain why misreading an operculated egg as non-operculated (or vice versa) can lead to an incorrect identification of the tapeworm genus.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Immediate bubble formation (oxygen and water) when 3% hydrogen peroxide is added to a colony indicates the presence of the enzyme catalase, which breaks down the toxic hydrogen peroxide; observing against a dark background enhances readability.
(ii)
The result is recorded as "Catalase test: positive".
(iii)
A positive catalase result is characteristic of Staphylococcus spp. (as opposed to catalase-negative Streptococcus spp.), and this test is essential for differentiating catalase-positive Micrococcaceae from catalase-negative Streptococcaceae; it can also help distinguish, among Gram-positive bacilli, Bacillus (catalase positive) from Clostridium (catalase negative).
(iv)
Follow-up: since Staphylococcus is confirmed, a coagulase test (slide and/or tube method) should be performed next to distinguish coagulase-positive S. aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci such as S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus.
questions.question:
(i) A catalase test performed by adding 3% hydrogen peroxide to a colony on a slide produces immediate bubbling. Interpret this result.
(ii) State how the result is recorded.
(iii) State what this result indicates about the organism's identity.
(iv) State the follow-up test needed to further identify the organism.

(i) A Gram-stained smear of a centrifuged CSF sediment from a suspected meningitis patient shows Gram-negative diplococci within pus cells. Identify the likely organism and finding.
(ii) State the basic technique used to detect this organism from the specimen.
(iii) State how the result is recorded/reported.
(iv) State the follow-up practical step required for confirmation.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Gram-negative diplococci with flattened or concave opposing sides seen in CSF are characteristic of Neisseria meningitidis, the cause of cerebrospinal meningitis and meningococcal septicaemia.
(ii)
Technique: Gram staining of the sediment of centrifuged CSF (or other specimen), examined under oil immersion for the characteristic diplococcal morphology.
(iii)
The finding is recorded/reported as "Gram-negative diplococci seen", a strong presumptive indication of meningococcal meningitis, which should be communicated urgently to the clinician given the acute nature of the disease.
(iv)
Follow-up: culture of the CSF/specimen on chocolate agar incubated in a CO2-enriched atmosphere, followed by an oxidase test (strongly positive) and carbohydrate utilisation testing (glucose and maltose fermented) to confirm N. meningitidis, since Modified Thayer-Martin selective medium can be used if a mixed specimen is expected.

questions.question:
(i) A Weil-Felix slide agglutination test on a febrile patient's serum shows strong agglutination with Proteus OX19 antigen but no agglutination with OX2 or OXK. Interpret this result.
(ii) State how the result is recorded.
(iii) State what this result indicates about the likely rickettsial disease.
(iv) State the follow-up action needed given the limitations of this test.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Strong agglutination with OX19 antigen alone, with no reaction to OX2 or OXK, is the pattern of a positive Weil-Felix reaction attributable to cross-reacting antibodies against epidemic or endemic typhus.
(ii)
The result is recorded as "Weil-Felix test: OX19 positive, OX2 and OXK negative".
(iii)
This pattern indicates likely epidemic typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii) or endemic (murine) typhus (R. typhi), since strong agglutination with OX19 alone is associated with typhus, whereas agglutination with both OX19 and OX2 suggests spotted fever, and agglutination with OXK alone suggests scrub typhus.
(iv)
Follow-up: because the Weil-Felix test relies on a heterophile cross-reaction between rickettsial antibodies and Proteus OX antigens rather than the rickettsial antigen itself, a more specific confirmatory test such as immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) detection of rickettsial antigen, or other serological tests such as complement fixation or enzyme immunoassay, should be performed.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the identification of Staphylococcus species by the coagulase test under the following headings: (i) principle, (ii) the slide method, (iii) the tube method.
(b) Explain why the coagulase test is clinically important in distinguishing S. aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci.
(c) Distinguish the slide coagulase test from the tube coagulase test in terms of speed, reliability and the mechanism detected.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principle: coagulase is an enzyme-like protein that causes plasma to clot by converting fibrinogen to fibrin; Staphylococcus aureus produces two forms, bound coagulase (clumping factor), which is bound to the bacterial cell wall and reacts directly with fibrinogen, and free coagulase, which activates a plasma coagulase-reacting factor (a modified thrombin) to form a complex that in turn converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.
• Slide method: a suspension of bacterial cells is mixed into a drop of rabbit plasma on a microscope slide; if bound coagulase is present, the plasma causes visible clumping of the cells because the clumping factor (an adhesin) binds fibrinogen in the plasma, giving a result within about 10 seconds.
• Tube method: bacterial cells are mixed into a larger volume of plasma in a small test tube; as the bacteria multiply, they secrete staphylocoagulase, which activates prothrombin and, via a coagulase-CRP complex, cleaves fibrinogen to fibrin, forming a visible clot within 24 hours; EDTA plasma should be used and the free coagulase (tube) test should be read within 4 hours in some protocols.
(b)
The coagulase test is clinically important because Staphylococcus aureus (coagulase positive) is generally the most virulent and pathogenic staphylococcal species, associated with abscesses, pyogenic infections, toxic shock syndrome and food poisoning, whereas coagulase-negative species such as S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus are typically less virulent commensals that cause infection mainly in specific settings (e.g. indwelling devices, urinary tract in young women); differentiating them therefore directly guides clinical management.
(c)
The slide test is simple and rapid, giving results within about 10 seconds, but can give false negatives (some strains that are bound-coagulase negative may still be free-coagulase positive); the tube test is the definitive test but is slower, taking up to 24 hours, and detects free coagulase activity via the fibrinogen-to-fibrin clotting cascade rather than the direct clumping-factor mechanism detected by the slide test.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the antigenic structure of Escherichia coli, including its O, H and K antigens and how the antigenic pattern of a strain is written.
(b) State the standard laboratory culture medium used to identify E. coli, and the biochemical pattern (IMViC) it typically shows.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind why the K antigen can render a strain inagglutinable by O antiserum.
questions.answerText:
(a)
E. coli possesses three types of surface antigen: O = somatic antigen, K = capsular antigen, and H = flagellar antigen; more than 170 O types, 100 H types and 75 K types have been identified, and the antigenic pattern of a strain is written using these designations, e.g. O111:K58:H2.
(b)
Standard medium: MacConkey agar, on which E. coli produces bright pink colonies due to lactose fermentation; biochemically, E. coli shows the IMViC pattern ++-- (Indole positive, Methyl Red positive, Voges-Proskauer negative, Citrate negative), is gelatin negative, H2S negative and urease negative, and ferments glucose, lactose, mannitol, maltose and many other sugars with acid and gas production (sucrose is generally not fermented).
(c)
Basic reasoning: the K antigen is an acidic polysaccharide antigen located in the envelope or microcapsule (K for "kapsel", German for capsule) that encloses the O antigen; because it physically surrounds and masks the O antigen, it prevents O-specific antiserum from binding and agglutinating the strain, rendering the strain inagglutinable by O antiserum unless the K antigen is first removed (e.g. by heating).

(a)
Confirmatory tests for yeasts include the germ tube test (Candida albicans forms tube-like outgrowths after 2-3 hours in serum at 35-37°C), chlamydospore production (on corn-meal or rice-tween 80 agar, C. albicans produces spherical macroconidia/chlamydospores), and carbon/nitrogen assimilation and sugar utilisation tests (using glucose, maltose, lactose, dulcitol and galactose, with characteristic positive/negative patterns for each species).
(b)
Application: the germ tube test is typically applied first as a rapid screening test; if positive, C. albicans is presumptively identified; if negative, chlamydospore production and sugar assimilation/fermentation tests are applied in sequence to identify the yeast to species level among the many other Candida species (e.g. C. tropicalis, C. krusei, C. glabrata) and other yeasts of medical importance.
(c)
Relying on the germ tube test alone can be misleading because it only screens for C. albicans specifically; a negative result does not identify which other yeast species is present, and without following up with chlamydospore production and sugar assimilation/fermentation testing, the laboratory cannot reliably distinguish between the many non-albicans yeast species, some of which have different antifungal susceptibility and clinical significance.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of biochemical/confirmatory tests used to identify medically important yeasts, including the germ tube test, chlamydospore production, and sugar assimilation/fermentation tests.
(b) State how these tests are selected in sequence when a yeast isolate needs to be identified to species level.
(c) Explain why relying on a single test (e.g. germ tube alone) without further confirmatory testing can lead to an incorrect species identification.

(i) A serum sample from a patient with prolonged fever is sent for a Widal test to investigate suspected enteric (typhoid) fever. Identify the specimen and the reagents used.
(ii) State the principle of the test.
(iii) Outline the general procedure for performing the test.
(iv) State how the result (titre) is interpreted.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Specimen: serum. Reagents: killed Salmonella O and H antigen suspensions (used in a serial dilution against the patient's serum). The Widal test is used specifically for diagnosis of enteric fever.
(ii)
Principle: serological agglutination tests are a direct measurement of antibody binding to antigen - the particulate Salmonella antigens clump (agglutinate) in the presence of specific antibody (agglutinin) in the patient's serum; this is a quantitative serologic assay in which a rising or changing titre on serial testing is more important for confirming disease than a single reading.
(iii)
Procedure: doubling (serial) dilutions of the patient's serum are prepared and a fixed amount of antigen is added to each dilution; the tubes/wells are examined for visible agglutination (clumping), and the highest dilution (last tube) still showing agglutination is recorded as the titre.
(iv)
A single raised titre has limited value, particularly in the first 7-10 days of illness (serological tests generally become positive only after this period); a significantly rising titre on paired (acute and convalescent) samples taken 5-7 days apart is required to confirm the diagnosis of enteric fever, since a low titre with no rise on repeat testing has no diagnostic value.

(a)
Fungi are eukaryotic organisms, heterotrophic, and dependent on enzyme systems to derive energy from organic substrates; they may exist as yeasts (single-celled, budding organisms producing soft, moist colonies resembling bacterial cultures) or as moulds/hyphae (filamentous, multicellular structures). Some fungi occur in both forms and are called dimorphic fungi, existing as a yeast (parasitic/pathogenic) form in tissue/exudates or at 37°C in culture, and as a mycelium (saprophytic) form in nature or at 26°C in culture.
(b)
Standard method: culturing the specimen at two temperatures (room temperature, about 25-30°C, and 35-37°C) demonstrates the mould-to-yeast conversion characteristic of dimorphic fungi such as Histoplasma capsulatum, which grows as a mould at room temperature but converts to a small budding yeast at 37°C and during invasion of host cells.
(c)
Basic reasoning: conversion to the yeast form appears essential for pathogenicity because most pathogenic dimorphic fungi are thermotolerant in this form and can resist the effects of active oxygen radicals released during the phagocyte respiratory burst, allowing them to withstand host defences; establishment of mycotic infection also depends on the size of the inoculum and the resistance of the host, but the yeast-phase conversion specifically equips the organism to survive within the human host environment.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general morphology, classification (yeast vs mould) and dimorphism of medically important fungi.
(b) State the standard laboratory method (dual-temperature culture) used to demonstrate dimorphism.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind why conversion to the yeast form is considered essential for pathogenicity in dimorphic fungi.

(i) A throat swab culture on blood agar shows large zones of beta-haemolysis around small colonies from a child with pharyngitis. Identify the likely organism.
(ii) State the technique used to distinguish this organism from other beta-haemolytic streptococci.
(iii) State how the result of this technique is recorded/reported.
(iv) State the follow-up practical step for further confirmation.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Beta-haemolytic colonies on blood agar from a throat swab of a child with pharyngitis are consistent with Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus, GAS), a fastidious organism requiring a minimum concentration of nutrients such as sugars and peptides, cultured on Trypticase Soy Agar (TSA) with 5% sheep blood, the gold-standard culturing method.
(ii)
Technique: the bacitracin susceptibility test - the strain is streaked on a sheep blood agar plate and a disc containing 0.04 units of bacitracin is placed on the plate; after overnight incubation at 35°C in 5% CO2, the plate is examined for a zone of inhibition around the disc.
(iii)
A zone of inhibition around the bacitracin disc indicates susceptibility, consistent with S. pyogenes (Group A), and is recorded/reported as "bacitracin-sensitive beta-haemolytic streptococcus - Group A (S. pyogenes)". Resistance suggests a different beta-haemolytic streptococcus, such as Group B (S. agalactiae).
(iv)
Follow-up: a catalase test (negative, confirming a streptococcus rather than staphylococcus) and Lancefield antigen grouping (agglutination with group-specific antisera) are performed for definitive confirmation of the Lancefield group.

questions.question:
(a) Describe anaerobic culture technique under the following headings: (i) principle of oxygen removal, (ii) apparatus used (McIntosh and Fildes' jar, GasPak system, candle jar), (iii) indicators used to confirm anaerobiosis.
(b) Explain why Gram staining of the specimen is performed before anaerobic culture is set up.
(c) Distinguish a candle jar from the GasPak/McIntosh-Fildes anaerobic jar in terms of the atmosphere produced and the organisms each is suited to.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principle: the main principle is to reduce the oxygen content of the culture medium and remove any oxygen already present in the system or medium, since anaerobes lack the enzymes (superoxide dismutase, catalase, peroxidase) that aerobic and facultative organisms use to detoxify the superoxide and hydrogen peroxide generated during aerobic respiration.
• Apparatus: the McIntosh and Fildes' jar works by evacuation and replacement - air is evacuated and replaced with a gas mixture (5% CO2, 10% H2, 85% N2), and residual oxygen is converted to water using a heated palladium/platinum catalyst. The GasPak system is a more convenient modern replacement, in which a gas-generating sachet (containing sodium bicarbonate and sodium borohydride) produces hydrogen and carbon dioxide on addition of water; the hydrogen reacts with residual oxygen (catalysed by palladium) to form water, and carbon dioxide replaces the removed oxygen. A candle jar, by contrast, is used for microaerophilic/capnophilic organisms (which need lower oxygen and higher CO2 than atmospheric levels): a lit candle burns until extinguished by oxygen deprivation, creating a CO2-rich, oxygen-poor (but not fully anaerobic) atmosphere.
• Indicators: anaerobic indicator strips impregnated with methylene blue remain colourless anaerobically but turn blue on exposure to oxygen; strips impregnated with resazurin are colourless (white) anaerobically but turn pink in the presence of oxygen. A biological indicator can also be used - a plate inoculated with Pseudomonas (an obligate aerobe) is incubated alongside the anaerobic cultures, and absence of its growth confirms that anaerobiosis was achieved.
(b)
Gram staining is performed before anaerobic culture because all specimens submitted for anaerobic culture should be examined by Gram stain first; it reveals the types and relative numbers of microorganisms and host cells present, serves as a quality control measure for the adequacy of the anaerobic technique, and allows the clinical relevance of any isolate later recovered to be correlated with the initial Gram stain findings (e.g. a positive Gram stain but negative culture may indicate poor transport, excessive air exposure, inadequate media, failure to achieve anaerobiosis, or prior antimicrobial therapy).
(c)
The candle jar produces a CO2-enriched, still partly oxygenated atmosphere suited to capnophilic/microaerophilic organisms such as Neisseria meningitidis, Brucella spp. and Streptococcus pneumoniae, whereas the McIntosh-Fildes and GasPak jars actively remove virtually all oxygen to create a true anaerobic atmosphere required for obligate anaerobes such as Clostridium spp.

questions.question:
(i) A Gram- and Albert-stained throat smear shows Gram-positive, club-shaped rods arranged in a "Chinese letter" or palisade pattern. Identify the likely organism.
(ii) State the basic technique used to detect this organism's characteristic granules.
(iii) State how the finding is recorded/reported.
(iv) State the follow-up practical step needed for confirmation.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Gram-positive, non-sporing, non-motile, non-capsulated rods arranged in pairs, palisades or "Chinese letters", often club-shaped and swollen at the poles, are characteristic of Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
(ii)
Technique: Albert staining (or Neisser staining) is performed specifically when Corynebacterium infection is suspected, to demonstrate the characteristic metachromatic (volutin) granules within the rod-shaped cells.
(iii)
The finding is recorded/reported as "Gram-positive club-shaped rods in Chinese-letter/palisade arrangement seen, with metachromatic granules on Albert stain - morphology consistent with Corynebacterium diphtheriae".
(iv)
Follow-up: culture on blood tellurite agar and Loeffler's serum slope, incubated aerobically at 37°C; C. diphtheriae reduces tellurite to give grey-black colonies, and toxigenicity testing (e.g. Elek's test) may be required to confirm that the isolate produces the diphtheria exotoxin.

(i)
Strong red bacilli retaining the primary stain against a weak blue counterstained background on a Ziehl-Neelsen smear indicate acid-fast bacilli (AFB), consistent with Mycobacterium (e.g. M. tuberculosis).
(ii)
Technique: grading follows the IUATLD/WHO scale for ZN smears at 1000x magnification (1 length = 100 high-power fields): negative (0 AFB/length), scanty (1-9 AFB/length), 1+ (10-99 AFB/length), 2+ (1-10 AFB/field on average), 3+ (>10 AFB/field on average).
(iii)
The result is recorded/reported according to the grading obtained, e.g. "AFB smear positive, grade 2+", or "AFB smear negative" if no AFB are seen in one length.
(iv)
Follow-up: culture on solid (Lowenstein-Jensen/Ogawa) or liquid (Middlebrook 7H9, e.g. BACTEC MGIT 960) media for confirmation, and/or a molecular technique such as GeneXpert MTB/RIF (based on PCR, giving results in about 2 hours and simultaneously testing for rifampicin resistance) or a Line Probe Assay for resistance to rifampicin, isoniazid, fluoroquinolones and/or aminoglycosides.
questions.question:
(i) A Ziehl-Neelsen-stained sputum smear shows strong red bacilli against a blue background. Identify the likely organism and finding.
(ii) State the basic technique used to grade this finding.
(iii) State how the result is recorded/reported.
(iv) State the follow-up practical step for confirmation and drug-resistance testing.

(a) Describe serological (antigen-antibody) tests under the following headings: (i) the main types of test (agglutination, precipitation, fluorescent antibody, ELISA), (ii) their principle, (iii) their common diagnostic uses.
(b) Explain why serological tests have limited diagnostic value in the early phase (7-10 days) of an infection.
(c) Distinguish agglutination tests from precipitation tests in terms of the physical form of the antigen used.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Types of serological test: agglutination, precipitation (with flocculation as a modification of precipitation), fluorescent antibody tests, ELISA (enzyme-linked immuno-absorbed assay), radioimmunoassay, electrophoresis and immunoelectrophoresis.
• Principle: in agglutination, the antigen is in particulate form, and antigen and antibody form visible clumps - a direct measurement of antibody binding used in quantitative serologic assays (antibodies here are called agglutinins); the antigen may be part of a bacterium, forming an agglutinate, or may be bound to red blood cells, giving haemagglutination or, when the antigen is attached to RBCs artificially, passive haemagglutination. In precipitation, the antigen is in soluble (insoluble-forming) form, and the antibodies producing the reaction are called precipitins; precipitation can occur in liquid media (with serial dilution determining a titre) or in semisolid (gel) media, as in the Ouchterlony gel diffusion technique, which may be single or double radial immunodiffusion.
• Diagnostic uses: serological tests are used for identification of microorganisms, detection of antibody, autoantibody or offending drugs, immunoassay of hormones, and detection of immunologic abnormalities; specific examples include the Widal test for enteric fever and agglutination tests for ABO blood grouping, while non-specific tests give evidence for diseases such as syphilis and SLE.
(b)
Serological tests have little value in the first 7-10 days of illness because it takes this long for the immune system to mount a detectable antibody response; a rising (changing) titre is more important than a single reading for confirming disease, and if the titre remains low with no rise on repeat testing 5-7 days later, the test has no diagnostic value.
(c)
Agglutination tests use antigen in a particulate form (e.g. whole bacterial cells or antigen-coated red cells), so that antigen-antibody binding produces visible clumping; precipitation tests use antigen in a soluble form, so that the antigen-antibody complex instead forms a visible precipitate whose amount depends on the relative concentrations of antigen and antibody, rather than simple particulate clumping.

questions.question:
(a) Describe biochemical enzyme-based bacterial identification tests under the following headings: (i) classification of bacterial enzymes by site of reaction (endoenzymes vs exoenzymes), (ii) classification by production (inducible vs constitutive), (iii) examples of enzymatic reactions used in identification.
(b) Explain why understanding enzyme principles is important for interpreting biochemical identification tests.
(c) Distinguish endoenzymes from exoenzymes, giving one example of each.
questions.answerText:
(a)
