• In the microbiology laboratory, biochemical tests rely on enzymes (glycoproteins or proteins that act as catalysts by lowering the activation energy of a biological reaction); bacterial enzymes can be used to identify and distinguish between bacterial species.
• Classification by site of reaction: endoenzymes react with their substrate inside the cell (e.g. oxidase, catalase, urease); exoenzymes react with their substrate outside the cell (e.g. free coagulase, gelatinase, amylase).
• Classification by production: inducible enzymes are produced only when needed or induced by the presence of substrate; constitutive enzymes are produced continuously regardless of substrate presence.
• Examples of enzymatic reactions used in identification include the breakdown of toxic wastes such as hydrogen peroxide or urea (e.g. catalase, urease), the reduction of nitrate or oxygen (e.g. nitrate reductase, cytochrome oxidase), the degradation of specific amino acids (e.g. tryptophanase for the indole test), and the utilisation of non-carbohydrate carbon sources for growth (e.g. citrate utilisation via citrate lyase).
(b)
Understanding enzyme principles is important because each biochemical test is essentially a controlled demonstration of a specific bacterial enzyme's activity (e.g. catalase splitting hydrogen peroxide into oxygen and water, producing visible bubbles); knowing the reaction and its expected end-product colour change or effect allows the laboratory scientist to correctly perform, read and interpret the test, and to understand why particular organisms give positive or negative results.
(c)
Endoenzymes act on substrate that has entered the cell (e.g. oxidase acting on the reagent taken up by the organism, catalase acting on intracellular hydrogen peroxide generated by aerobic respiration), whereas exoenzymes are secreted by the organism to act on substrate in the surrounding environment before or without entering the cell (e.g. free coagulase secreted by Staphylococcus aureus acting on plasma fibrinogen outside the bacterial cell, and gelatinase/amylase acting on extracellular gelatin/starch).

(i)
The Gram-positive cocci occurring in clusters, pairs or singly are characteristic of Staphylococcus spp. Gram stains should be performed on young (18-24 hour) cultures, since very old cells may lose their ability to retain crystal violet and appear Gram-variable or Gram-negative.
(ii)
The coagulase test (slide or tube method) is used: bacterial cells are mixed with rabbit plasma; if bound coagulase (clumping factor) is present, the plasma causes the cells to clump on a slide within about 10 seconds (slide test), while the tube test, in which staphylocoagulase converts fibrinogen to fibrin, forms a definitive clot and may take up to 24 hours to complete.
(iii)
Clumping or a clot of any size is recorded as coagulase-positive; the organism is reported as "Staphylococcus aureus isolated - coagulase positive". Absence of clumping/clot is reported as coagulase-negative staphylococcus (CoNS), e.g. S. epidermidis or S. saprophyticus.
(iv)
Follow-up: culture on mannitol salt agar, on which S. aureus ferments mannitol and produces a yellow halo around golden-yellow, beta-haemolytic colonies on blood agar, distinguishing it from coagulase-negative staphylococci, which are typically white/non-pigmented and do not (or only weakly) ferment mannitol.
questions.question:
(i) A Gram stain of pus from a boil shows Gram-positive cocci arranged in clusters. Identify the likely organism and structure observed.
(ii) State the technique used to further identify the organism from culture.
(iii) State how a positive result of this technique is recorded/reported.
(iv) State the follow-up practical step needed to distinguish this organism from related species.

(i) A stool sample plated onto Thiosulphate Citrate Bile Salt Sucrose (TCBS) agar produces yellow colonies from a patient with profuse watery ("rice-water") diarrhoea. Identify the likely organism.
(ii) State the basic technique/principle behind the colour change observed.
(iii) State how the finding is recorded/reported.
(iv) State the follow-up practical step used to confirm the identification.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Yellow colonies on TCBS agar from a patient with profuse, rice-water diarrhoea are characteristic of Vibrio cholerae.
(ii)
Principle: TCBS agar is a selective, alkaline medium (widely used for Vibrio); V. cholerae ferments the sucrose in the medium, producing acid that turns the colonies yellow; on further incubation the colonies may turn green.
(iii)
The finding is recorded/reported as "yellow, sucrose-fermenting colonies on TCBS, morphology consistent with Vibrio cholerae".
(iv)
Follow-up: perform a Gram stain (comma-shaped, Gram-negative rods), dark-field microscopy (shows highly motile organisms described as "shooting stars"), and biochemical confirmation - V. cholerae is oxidase positive and catalase positive, ferments glucose, mannitol, maltose and sucrose with acid, and gives a positive "cholera red" reaction (development of a pink colour on adding concentrated sulphuric acid to a peptone-water culture, due to nitroso-indole).

questions.question:
(a) Describe the general morphology of the Arthropoda phylum relevant to medical parasitology, including the exoskeleton and body segmentation.
(b) State the standard method used by entomologists/parasitologists to classify arthropods for medical purposes (the four-subphylum/class system).
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution of controlling arthropod vectors as part of disease prevention, using Cyclops as an example.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Arthropods are invertebrate animals possessing an exoskeleton, a segmented body and jointed appendages; the exoskeleton is hard, composed of chitin, protects the arthropod, and cannot grow, so it must be shed periodically (moulted) to allow growth. All arthropods have segmented bodies divided into head, thorax and abdomen (with fusion of head and thorax, forming a cephalothorax, in some groups such as crabs and lobsters) and jointed appendages that allow varied locomotion (walking, crawling, climbing, hopping, flying, gliding, swimming).
(b)
Standard classification: the general classes of medical importance are Crustacea (cephalothorax and abdomen, legs on thoracic and abdominal segments), Arachnida (adults with 4 pairs of legs, 2 pairs of mouthparts, no antennae or wings), Pentastomida, Insecta (largest group, adults with 3 pairs of legs, body in 3 parts) and the Myriapoda (Diplopoda, Chilopoda).
(c)
Basic reasoning: Cyclops (order Copepoda, subphylum Crustacea) serve as an intermediate host for the larval stages of the broad fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum) and the dragon worm (Dracunculus medinensis); because these parasites cannot complete their life cycle without passing through the intermediate arthropod host, controlling or eliminating exposure to the vector (e.g. avoiding untreated water containing infected Cyclops) is an effective preventive measure against the diseases they transmit.

(i)
Specimen: faeces/rectal swab. Selective media: MacConkey agar, and more strongly selective media such as Xylose Lysine Deoxycholate (XLD) agar, Salmonella-Shigella (SS) agar, or Deoxycholate Citrate Agar (DCA).
(ii)
Principle: these media contain bile salts (and, in DCA/XLD, sodium desoxycholate) that inhibit the normal bowel commensal flora while still allowing enteric pathogens such as Shigella to grow; lactose (with a pH indicator such as neutral red) is incorporated so lactose-fermenting commensals (pink/red colonies) can be distinguished from non-lactose-fermenting pathogens (pale/colourless colonies).
(iii)
Procedure: inoculate the specimen onto MacConkey agar and the more selective medium, incubate aerobically at 37°C for 18-24 hours, and examine for lactose-fermenting versus non-lactose-fermenting colonies; suspect non-lactose-fermenting colonies are then picked for biochemical screening on combination media such as Kligler iron agar or triple sugar iron (TSI) agar.
(iv)
Shigella produces pale, non-lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar. On TSI, Shigella characteristically gives an alkaline (red) slant over an acid (yellow) butt with no gas and no H2S production, distinguishing it from Salmonella (alkaline slant/acid butt with gas and H2S) and from lactose-fermenting coliforms (acid slant/acid butt).
questions.question:
(i) A stool sample from a child with dysentery-like symptoms is submitted for suspected Shigella infection. Identify the specimen and the selective culture media used.
(ii) State the principle behind the choice of selective/differential media for this specimen.
(iii) Outline the procedure for inoculation and reading.
(iv) State the expected colonial appearance and biochemical confirmation.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Yeast cells surrounded by a large, unstained halo on India ink preparation of CSF are characteristic of the polysaccharide capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans, an opportunistic yeast affecting the lungs, brain and meninges, associated with HIV disease.
(ii)
Technique: India ink is added to CSF or exudate to provide a dark background that highlights the hyaline yeast cells and their capsular material as a clear "halo"; white blood cells can be distinguished from C. neoformans by the irregular edge of the halo and pale cell wash, whereas the fungal capsule gives a smooth, well-defined halo.
(iii)
The finding is recorded/reported as "encapsulated yeast cells seen on India ink preparation, morphology consistent with Cryptococcus neoformans".
(iv)
Follow-up: culture on Sabouraud agar at 35-37°C, on which C. neoformans appears as cream-coloured mucoid colonies that turn brown with age due to melanin production (it is urease positive); a latex agglutination test for cryptococcal capsular antigen in CSF (positive in up to 70% of cryptococcal meningitis cases) provides serological confirmation, being more sensitive than direct microscopy.
questions.question:
(i) An India ink preparation of CSF from an HIV-positive patient with headache and vision problems shows yeast cells surrounded by a wide, unstained halo. Identify the likely organism and finding.
(ii) State the basic technique used and its principle.
(iii) State how the result is recorded/reported.
(iv) State the follow-up practical step for confirmation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition/principle: the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) is the lowest concentration of a chemical/antimicrobial agent that will inhibit the visible growth of a microorganism after overnight incubation; it reflects the effect of the antimicrobial agent against the organism and is expressed in micrograms/ml or mg/L, often measured as the concentration associated with a 50% effect (IC50).
• Procedure: a known quantity of the test organism is placed into multiple tubes/wells, and increasing concentrations of the antibiotic (typically in log2/doubling dilutions) are added to consecutive tubes; after overnight incubation the lowest concentration showing no visible turbidity (growth) is recorded as the MIC. The full procedure involves serial dilution of the chosen antimicrobial, preparation of the culture media, preparation of pure isolates, and in-vitro determination of the MIC value, graded against standardised breakpoint values from CLSI, BSAC or EUCAST.
• Related terms: the Minimum Bactericidal Concentration (MBC) is the lowest concentration that results in a 99.9% reduction in bacterial growth (i.e. kills the bacteria), determined by subculturing an aliquot from MIC tubes onto antibiotic-free agar; the minimum effective concentration is the lowest drug concentration in blood required to show a therapeutic response; the maximum safe concentration is the highest blood concentration above which undesired responses generally occur.
(b)
Standardisation is important because MICs are used in diagnostic laboratories to confirm antibiotic sensitivity/resistance patterns, in drug-discovery laboratories to determine the effectiveness of new antimicrobial agents, and in clinical settings to choose the most effective antibiotic and dose for a patient's infection; the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI), building on earlier work standardising broth dilution turbidity assessment (originally developed by Alexander Fleming), consolidated and standardised MIC determination and clinical usage from 1980 onward, working with regulatory bodies such as the FDA as new pathogens and drugs emerge.
(c)
MIC is the lowest concentration that merely inhibits visible growth (the organism may still be viable but not multiplying), whereas MBC is the lowest concentration that actually kills the organism (99.9% reduction in viable count); MBC is therefore always equal to or higher than the MIC for the same organism-drug combination, and is determined by a subculture step after the MIC has been established.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the determination of Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) under the following headings: (i) definition and principle, (ii) procedure, (iii) related terminologies such as Minimum Bactericidal Concentration (MBC), minimum effective concentration and maximum safe concentration.
(b) Explain why standardisation of MIC breakpoints (by bodies such as CLSI) is important in clinical and drug-discovery laboratories.
(c) Distinguish MIC from MBC.

(i) An indole test performed on a Gram-negative bacillus isolated from urine develops a pink-to-red "cherry-red ring" after Kovac's reagent is added. Interpret this result.
(ii) State how the result is recorded.
(iii) State what this result indicates about the likely identity of the organism.
(iv) State the follow-up biochemical test needed for further identification.
questions.answerText:
(i)
A pink-to-red "cherry-red ring" forming in the reagent layer within seconds of adding Kovac's reagent is a positive indole test, indicating that the organism has degraded the amino acid tryptophan to produce indole; a negative test leaves the reagent layer yellow or slightly cloudy.
(ii)
The result is recorded as "Indole test: positive".
(iii)
A positive indole result is consistent with Escherichia coli or Vibrio cholerae (both indole positive), and rules against Klebsiella, Salmonella and Shigella spp., which are indole negative, helping to distinguish E. coli from Klebsiella within the Enterobacteriaceae.
(iv)
Follow-up: the citrate utilisation test should be performed next as part of the IMViC battery - E. coli is citrate negative (cannot use citrate as its sole carbon source, shown by no colour change and no growth on Simmons citrate medium) whereas Klebsiella is citrate positive (growth with a colour change from green to Prussian blue), completing the differentiation.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the morphology and virulence characteristics of Candida albicans, including its polymorphic nature and putative virulence factors.
(b) State the standard culture medium and incubation conditions used to grow C. albicans.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind why C. albicans, though a normal commensal, becomes pathogenic mainly in debilitated or immunosuppressed patients.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Candida albicans is a polymorphic yeast producing yeast cells, hyphae and pseudohyphae; on direct microscopy the yeasts are small, oval cells measuring 2-4 µm in diameter, Gram positive, often seen attached to pseudohyphae with single budding. Putative virulence factors include adherence, dimorphism, germ tube formation, rapid switching of expressed phenotype, surface hydrophobicity, interference with phagocytosis/immune defences/complement, extracellular hydrolases (proteinases, lipases), synergism with certain bacteria, killer toxins, acidic metabolites, and an undemanding nutrient requirement with a rapid growth rate.
(b)
Standard medium: Sabouraud agar, incubated at 35-37°C for 24-48 hours, producing cream-coloured, pasty colonies with a distinctive yeast smell; corn-meal agar demonstrates pseudohyphae and chlamydospore formation.
(c)
Basic reasoning: C. albicans is an endogenous commensal found in 40-80% of normal humans, mainly in the gastrointestinal tract; most Candida infections are opportunistic, occurring in debilitated persons, and are associated with prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy or invasive procedures (cardiac surgery, indwelling catheters) that alter host physiology, or with conditions of impaired immunity (e.g. HIV disease), which remove the normal checks that keep this commensal organism in balance and allow it to overgrow and invade tissue.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the structural features of spirochetes, including their shape, motility apparatus (axial filaments) and the exception seen in Treponema.
(b) State the standard microscopic method used to visualise spirochetes given their thinness.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind why dark-field microscopy, rather than ordinary light microscopy, is required to see live spirochetes.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Spirochetes are long, slender, tightly coiled bacteria, usually a fraction of a micron in diameter but 5-250 microns long, resembling miniature springs; they possess axial filaments, similar to bacterial flagella, that run along the outside of the protoplasm but inside an outer sheath, enabling movement by rotation. Treponema is the only genus lacking this outer sheath.
(b)
Standard method: dark-field microscopy (or staining with silver salts) is used, since many spirochetes are too slender to be seen by ordinary light microscopy.
(c)
Basic reasoning: because spirochetes are extremely thin (a fraction of a micron in diameter), they do not sufficiently refract or absorb light under ordinary brightfield illumination to be visible; dark-field microscopy illuminates the specimen obliquely so that only light scattered by the organism reaches the observer's eye, making the thin spirochete appear bright against a dark background and revealing its characteristic rotational, corkscrew motility, which is diagnostic (e.g. for Treponema pallidum in primary/secondary syphilis).

questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification of arthropods of medical importance into Crustacea, Arachnida, Insecta and Myriapoda.
(b) State how identification of the vector species is applied to guide vector-control measures for a given disease.
(c) Explain why misidentifying the arthropod vector responsible for transmission can lead to an ineffective disease control programme.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Arthropods of medical importance are classified into Crustacea (main body divisions are cephalothorax and abdomen; e.g. Cyclops), Arachnida (adults with four pairs of legs, two pairs of mouthparts, no antennae or wings; e.g. ticks, mites), Insecta (largest group; three pairs of legs, body divided into head, thorax and abdomen; e.g. mosquitoes, lice, fleas) and Myriapoda (Diplopoda and Chilopoda).
(b)
Application: correctly identifying the vector species allows control measures to be targeted appropriately - for example, since Cyclops (Crustacea) is the intermediate host for Dracunculus medinensis and Diphyllobothrium latum, control focuses on water filtration/treatment, whereas control of arachnid vectors (ticks, mites) for rickettsial diseases focuses on tick/mite avoidance and acaricide use, and control of insect vectors (mosquitoes, lice, fleas) focuses on insecticide use, bed nets, or delousing measures as appropriate to that vector's biology and behaviour.
(c)
Misidentifying the vector can render a control programme ineffective because control measures are highly vector-specific (e.g. measures effective against a mosquito vector, such as bed nets or larviciding of standing water, would have no effect on a tick- or louse-borne disease); resources spent on the wrong vector's control measures fail to interrupt the actual transmission cycle, allowing the disease to persist despite intervention.

(a)
• Principle: the Weil-Felix test, also known as the heterophile agglutination test, is an agglutination test based on cross-reactions that occur between antibodies produced in acute rickettsial infections and antigens of non-motile strains of Proteus species (OX19, OX2 and OXK).
• Antigens used: OX19, OX2 and OXK antigens, derived from non-motile Proteus strains, which share a carbohydrate hapten with certain Rickettsia species.
• Procedure: in the slide method, a small amount of the patient's serum is placed on a slide with a drop of the desired antigen, mixed and observed for visible agglutination, with positive results further titrated by the tube method; in the tube method, serum is diluted in three separate series of tubes, an equal amount of OX19, OX2 or OXK antigen is added to each series, and the tubes are incubated at 50-55°C for 4-6 hours before observing for agglutination.
(b)
This test can diagnose rickettsial infection despite not using rickettsial antigen directly because certain strains of Proteus share a carbohydrate hapten (antigen) with Rickettsia species, so antibodies raised against Rickettsia during infection cross-react with and agglutinate the Proteus OX strains, making this heterophile agglutination a practical surrogate for detecting rickettsial antibodies.
(c)
Strong agglutination with OX19 alone indicates epidemic or endemic typhus; strong agglutination with both OX19 and OX2 indicates spotted fever; strong agglutination with OXK alone indicates scrub typhus - the differing antigen reactivity pattern therefore helps distinguish among the rickettsial disease groups.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the Weil-Felix test under the following headings: (i) principle, (ii) antigens used, (iii) procedure (slide and tube methods).
(b) Explain why this heterophile agglutination test can be used to diagnose rickettsial infections even though it does not use rickettsial antigen directly.
(c) Distinguish the interpretation of a Weil-Felix result showing agglutination with OX19 alone from one showing agglutination with both OX19 and OX2, and from one showing agglutination with OXK alone.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Collection methods: masturbation (directing semen into a clean sample cup, without lubricant, which can kill sperm), coitus interruptus (withdrawal before ejaculation into a clean sample cup), coitus using a special silicone condom without spermicide, and assisted ejaculation (e.g. electro-ejaculation in paraplegic patients).
• Fractions of the ejaculate: the pre-ejaculatory secretion from the urethral and bulbourethral glands (no sperm); dilute fluid from the prostate gland (no sperm); the major portion of sperm from the vas deferens and distal epididymis (about 5% of volume); and seminal vesicle secretion (few sperm). The first three fractions make up about 30% of the total volume and contain most of the sperm, so it is important to ensure this first portion is collected; the whole sample must also be mixed well before analysis.
• Macroscopic parameters: appearance (normal is whitish to grey opalescent), liquefaction time (normal 15-30 minutes), viscosity (normal is smooth and watery), and volume (normal 1.5 ml or more).
(b)
Semen analysis to test the effectiveness of a vasectomy is done 6 weeks after the procedure, and because samples vary from day to day, 2-3 samples should be evaluated within a 3-6 month period for accurate assessment. The WHO 2010 reference range is derived from the semen quality of 4,500 fertile men whose partners achieved pregnancy within 12 months; the 5th percentile is given as the lower reference limit, and no high-value reference range is given because a value above the median is not considered detrimental to fertility.
(c)
Masturbation directs semen straight into a clean cup and avoids lubricants that may kill sperm; coitus interruptus depends on timely withdrawal before ejaculation; coitus using a special silicone condom (without spermicide) allows collection during intercourse itself, since ordinary condoms usually contain spermicide that would harm the specimen; assisted (electro-)ejaculation is reserved for patients (e.g. paraplegics) unable to ejaculate by the other methods.
questions.question:
(a) Describe semen analysis under the following headings: (i) sample collection methods, (ii) the fractions of the ejaculate and their sperm content, (iii) the macroscopic parameters examined.
(b) Explain why the WHO 2010 reference criteria give only a lower reference limit and no upper limit for most parameters.
(c) Distinguish the different methods of sperm collection (masturbation, coitus interruptus, coitus with a special condom, and assisted ejaculation).

(a) Describe the classification of food-borne diseases into food-borne infections and food-borne intoxications, with organism examples for each.
(b) State how the choice of specimen and laboratory approach is selected depending on whether an infection or an intoxication is suspected.
(c) Explain why treating a food-borne intoxication (e.g. from a preformed toxin) in the same way as a food-borne infection could lead to an inappropriate or delayed clinical response.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Food-borne diseases are classified into food-borne infections, caused by the entrance of pathogenic microorganisms contaminating food into the body and the tissue reaction to their presence (which may be bacterial, fungal, viral or parasitic, and tend to have long incubation periods with fever - e.g. cholera, salmonellosis, typhoid fever, shigellosis, and viral infections such as hepatitis A), and food-borne intoxications, caused by ingestion of a preformed toxin already present in the food, without the organism itself needing to establish infection.
(b)
Application: for a suspected food-borne infection, specimens such as stool, blood or vomitus are cultured to isolate and identify the causative organism (as the pathogen itself must be present and multiplying); for a suspected intoxication, the food remnant, vomitus or a clinical specimen may instead be tested for the toxin itself, since the causative organism may no longer be viable or may not even be recoverable from the patient despite the illness being present.
(c)
Treating an intoxication as though it were an infection could lead to an inappropriate response because intoxications typically have a short incubation period related to the amount of preformed toxin ingested rather than bacterial multiplication in the host, so antimicrobial therapy aimed at killing a live organism would not address a toxin already causing illness, and the clinical/laboratory approach (seeking to identify a live pathogen through prolonged culture) would be mismatched to the true, and often more rapidly resolving, cause of the illness.

(i)
Specimen: blood (finger-prick or venous, collected during a febrile episode). Two films are prepared: a thick film and a thin film.
(ii)
Principle: the thick film concentrates a larger volume of blood in a small area (red cells are lysed on staining), increasing the chance of detecting a low parasitaemia, while the thin film preserves the morphology of the red cells and the parasite, allowing species identification.
(iii)
Procedure: the films are air-dried; the thin film is fixed with methanol; both films are then stained with a Romanowsky-type stain such as Giemsa (or Leishman) stain, which is the stain also used generally for demonstrating blood parasites such as microfilariae and rickettsiae.
(iv)
The thick film is examined first (under oil immersion) to detect the presence of parasites; the thin film is then examined to identify the species and stage present (e.g. ring forms, trophozoites, schizonts, gametocytes for Plasmodium, or microfilariae for filarial infections) and to estimate parasitaemia; a positive result is reported with the organism/stage seen, and treatment/further testing follows from the identification.
questions.question:
(i) A blood sample is collected from a febrile patient returning from a malaria-endemic area. Identify the specimen and the two types of blood film prepared.
(ii) State the principle behind preparing both a thick and a thin film.
(iii) Outline the procedure for staining the films.
(iv) State how the films are examined and interpreted.

(a) Describe the classification of the genera within the spirochetes pathogenic for man - Treponema, Borrelia and Leptospira - and the diseases each causes.
(b) State how the diagnostic method is selected according to which genus and stage of disease is suspected.
(c) Explain why relying on serology alone in early primary syphilis can produce a false-negative (invalid) result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Three genera of spirochetes are pathogenic for man: Treponema (T. pallidum causes syphilis, transmitted by sexual contact; related species cause the non-venereal treponematoses yaws, T. pertenue, and pinta, T. carateum), Borrelia (causes relapsing fever - epidemic, via B. recurrentis and lice, or endemic, via other Borrelia species and ticks; B. burgdorferi causes Lyme disease via Ixodes ticks) and Leptospira (causes leptospirosis, a zoonosis with rodents/domestic animals as reservoirs; L. interrogans icterohaemorrhagiae causes Weil's disease).
(b)
Application: in primary and secondary syphilis, dark-field microscopy of fresh exudate from the lesion is selected because organisms are present in the lesion and serological tests may not yet be reactive; flocculation tests for Wasserman antibody (e.g. VDRL, RPR) and treponemal antibody tests (TPI, FTA, TPHA) are selected once sufficient time has passed for antibody development. For Borrelia relapsing fever, microscopic examination of blood during a febrile attack (dark-field or stained smear) is selected, since serological tests are of little value due to numerous antigenic variants. For leptospirosis, blood or urine culture and animal inoculation, together with direct microscopy by experienced observers, are used.
(c)
Relying on serology alone in early primary syphilis can give a false-negative result because the Wasserman antibody is usually detected only 1-3 weeks after the primary lesion appears, so dark-field microscopy of the chancre exudate is essential before serological tests become reactive; a negative serological test at this early stage does not exclude syphilis.

questions.question:
(i) A patient with suspected sepsis has blood drawn for culture. Identify the specimen and the type of medium into which it is inoculated.
(ii) State the principle of using a liquid enrichment medium for this specimen.
(iii) Outline the procedure, including handling of the sample once growth is detected.
(iv) State the organisms most frequently isolated and how a positive culture is interpreted.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Specimen: blood, collected when sepsis, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, meningitis or pneumonia is suspected. It is inoculated into a broth-blood culture system/enrichment broth (such as thioglycollate, dextrose broth or brain-heart infusion broth).
(ii)
Principle: blood normally contains few organisms, so a nutrient-rich liquid medium is used to allow any bacteria present to multiply to detectable numbers (general turbidity/heavy deposit) before they are subcultured onto solid media for identification.
(iii)
Procedure: inoculate the blood aseptically into the culture bottle/broth and incubate; examine daily for turbidity or other signs of growth; once growth is detected, subculture onto solid media (e.g. blood agar, MacConkey agar, chocolate agar) and perform a Gram stain on the broth for a rapid presumptive identification while awaiting subculture results.
(iv)
The organisms most frequently isolated from blood cultures are two Gram-positive cocci, Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae, and three Gram-negative rods, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. A positive blood culture, correlated with clinical findings, is interpreted as evidence of bacteraemia/septicaemia caused by the isolated organism.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of nematodes into intestinal nematodes and blood/tissue nematodes, giving examples of each.
(b) State how the specimen selected for laboratory diagnosis differs according to which category the suspected nematode belongs to.
(c) Explain why using a stool specimen alone would give a false-negative result for a blood/tissue nematode such as Wuchereria bancrofti.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Nematodes are classified into intestinal nematodes (e.g. Enterobius vermicularis, Trichuris trichiura, Ascaris lumbricoides, Ancylostoma duodenale/Necator americanus, Strongyloides stercoralis, Trichinella spiralis) and blood and tissue nematodes (e.g. Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia malayi causing lymphatic filariasis, Onchocerca volvulus causing river blindness, Dracunculus medinensis causing Guinea worm disease).
(b)
Application: for intestinal nematodes, stool examination (direct wet mount, concentration techniques) is used to detect eggs or larvae passed in the faeces; for blood and tissue nematodes such as Wuchereria bancrofti, a blood specimen (thick and thin films, ideally collected at the time of peak microfilarial periodicity) is required, since the infective/diagnostic microfilarial stage circulates in the peripheral blood rather than being passed in stool.
(c)
Using a stool specimen alone would give a false-negative result for W. bancrofti because this organism does not pass through the intestinal lumen at any diagnostic stage - its microfilariae circulate in the blood and lymphatics - so no eggs or larvae would ever be found in faeces regardless of how thoroughly the stool is examined; the correct specimen (blood, collected at the appropriate time) is essential for accurate diagnosis.

questions.question:
(i) A urease test on Christensen's urea agar shows the slant turning bright pink (fuchsia) within 2 hours of incubation. Interpret this result.
(ii) State how the result is recorded.
(iii) State what this result indicates about the organism's identity.
(iv) State the follow-up consideration if the colour change appears only after prolonged incubation.
questions.answerText:
(i)
A rapid colour change of the slant to bright pink (fuchsia) within 1-6 hours is a rapidly positive urease reaction, indicating that the organism has hydrolysed urea to ammonia, which alkalinises the medium and turns the phenol red indicator pink.
(ii)
The result is recorded as "Urease test: positive (rapid)".
(iii)
A rapid, strongly positive reaction is characteristic of Proteus spp. and Morganella morganii (rapidly urease-positive Proteeae); a delayed, weaker positive reaction after 6 hours (intensifying over up to 6 days) is instead typical of Klebsiella or Enterobacter; a negative (yellow, unchanged) reaction is typical of E. coli.
(iv)
Follow-up: because prolonged incubation can cause a false-positive reaction due to hydrolysis of proteins in the medium, a control medium lacking urea should be used to confirm that the colour change is genuinely due to urease activity and not a false positive from protein breakdown.

questions.question:
(a) Describe antibiotic susceptibility testing under the following headings: (i) the dilution technique, (ii) the diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) technique, (iii) how results are read and reported.
(b) Explain why the disk diffusion method is preferred for routine qualitative susceptibility testing in many laboratories.
(c) Distinguish the disk diffusion technique from the Stokes method of susceptibility testing.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Dilution technique: this can be agar- or broth-based and measures the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) and can be used to measure the Minimum Bactericidal Concentration (MBC) of a drug; it is performed by adding dilutions of the antimicrobial agent to broth or agar medium, inoculating with a standardised bacterial suspension, incubating overnight at 35°C, and examining for visible growth (turbidity) - the lowest concentration preventing visible growth is the MIC.
• Diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) technique: an inoculum is prepared by emulsifying colonies in broth and comparing its turbidity to a 0.5 McFarland standard; the surface of Mueller-Hinton agar is swabbed with the suspension, and antimicrobial discs are placed on the surface (20 mm apart, 25 mm from the plate edge; 6 discs for a 90 mm plate, 9 discs for a 120 mm plate); the plate is incubated aerobically at 35°C for 18-24 hours, and the zone of inhibition around each disc is measured and compared with an interpretive chart.
• Reading and reporting: the diameter of the zone of inhibition is measured (preferably with a Vernier scale or ruler graduated to 0.5 mm) and rounded to the nearest millimetre; the result is compared with CLSI interpretive criteria and reported as Sensitive (S), Resistant (R) or Intermediate (I).
(b)
The disk diffusion method is preferred for routine qualitative testing because it is a relatively inexpensive, easy-to-use and flexible agar-based method that provides qualitative results, and Mueller-Hinton agar (the medium of choice) shows good batch-to-batch reproducibility and allows true zones of inhibition to form due to its loose consistency, which permits good diffusion of the antibiotic.
(c)
In the standard Kirby-Bauer method, only the test organism is inoculated on the plate and the zone is compared against a fixed interpretive chart; in the Stokes method, both the test organism and a control organism of known sensitivity are inoculated on the same plate, and the zone of inhibition of the test organism is compared directly with that of the control, which corrects for plate-to-plate and reagent variability rather than relying solely on a standard chart.

(a)
Dermatophytes are a group of closely related fungi classified into three genera - Trichophyton, Epidermophyton and Microsporum - distinguished by the morphology of their large asexual spores; because of their ability to use keratin, they invade and live in keratinised tissue (skin, hair, nails), growing best at 25-28°C. In culture they develop three types of asexual spores: macroconidia (large, multicellular, thick-walled, typical of Microsporum and Trichophyton), microconidia (small, unicellular, thin-walled, typical of Epidermophyton and Trichophyton) and aleurioconidia (small, unicellular, thin-walled, typical of Trichophyton and Microsporum); in tissue, however, they form only hyphae and arthrospores.
(b)
Standard medium: Sabouraud Dextrose Agar, to which cycloheximide is added to inhibit growth of common contaminants without affecting the dermatophytes; scales, hair, nail scrapings or clippings are inoculated onto slopes of Sabouraud's dextrose agar containing chloramphenicol and cycloheximide and incubated for 6-8 weeks at room temperature (and, where available, in parallel at 32°C for more rapid growth of pathogens common in Nigeria) before being discarded as negative.
(c)
Basic reasoning: the skin or scalp is cleaned with 70% alcohol before collection to remove natural fatty (sebaceous) substances, which makes the area of scaling more obvious and improves the chance of collecting material that actually contains fungal elements, rather than obscuring or diluting the specimen with skin oils.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the structure and classification of the dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Epidermophyton, Microsporum), including their asexual spore types.
(b) State the standard medium used for isolation of dermatophytes, and the additive used to inhibit contaminants.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution of cleaning the collection site with alcohol before taking a specimen for dermatophyte diagnosis.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Fungi are clinically categorised into superficial/cutaneous mycoses (involving hair, skin or nails without invasion of deeper tissue, e.g. the dermatophytes causing ringworm/athlete's foot), subcutaneous mycoses (confined to subcutaneous tissue without dissemination, e.g. chromoblastomycosis, mycetoma), systemic mycoses (caused by genera including Blastomyces, Coccidioides, Histoplasma and Paracoccidioides, primarily involving the lungs but able to disseminate widely) and opportunistic mycoses (e.g. candidiasis, cryptococcosis, occurring mainly in immunocompromised patients).
(b)
Application: specimens are selected according to the suspected category and site - skin/nail/hair scrapings and KOH mounts for cutaneous mycoses; tissue biopsy for subcutaneous mycoses; sputum, blood, bone marrow or CSF for systemic/opportunistic mycoses; cultures for dimorphic systemic fungi (e.g. Histoplasma) are set up at two temperatures, room temperature (25-30°C) to obtain the mould/mycelial form, and 35-37°C to obtain the yeast form, since the correct diagnostic morphology depends on the temperature of incubation.
(c)
Using the wrong incubation temperature for a dimorphic fungus can give a misleading result because the organism shows a completely different morphology at each temperature (mould at room temperature versus yeast at 37°C); if only one temperature is used, or the wrong one for the type of confirmation needed, the characteristic dimorphic conversion cannot be demonstrated, potentially leading to a missed or incorrect identification.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of fungal infections (mycoses) into superficial/cutaneous, subcutaneous, systemic and opportunistic categories.
(b) State how the specimen type and incubation temperature are selected according to the suspected category of mycosis.
(c) Explain why using the wrong incubation temperature for a dimorphic fungus can produce a misleading or invalid culture result.

(i) A Simmons citrate slant inoculated with a Gram-negative bacillus turns from green to Prussian blue after incubation. Interpret this result.
(ii) State how the result is recorded.
(iii) State what this result indicates about the organism's identity.
(iv) State the follow-up action if the slant instead remains green with no growth.
questions.answerText:
(i)
A colour change from green to Prussian (intense) blue on Simmons citrate agar, with visible growth on the slant, indicates a positive citrate test - the organism has used citrate as its sole carbon source, producing alkaline by-products (carbonates and bicarbonates) that raise the pH of the medium and change the bromothymol blue indicator from green to blue.
(ii)
The result is recorded as "Citrate utilisation test: positive".
(iii)
This is consistent with organisms such as Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Citrobacter, Salmonella, Proteus, Providencia and Serratia, which are citrate positive, and rules out E. coli, which is citrate negative.
(iv)
Follow-up: if the slant remains the deep forest-green colour of the uninoculated medium with trace or no growth, the test is negative (e.g. as with E. coli); the citrate result should then be combined with the other IMViC results (indole, methyl red, Voges-Proskauer) to complete identification of the isolate to genus/species level.

(a)
Trematodes are classified by habitat: blood flukes (Schistosoma haematobium in the vesical and pelvic venous plexus, S. mansoni in the inferior mesenteric vein, S. japonicum in the superior mesenteric vein), biliary tract/liver flukes (Clonorchis sinensis, Fasciola hepatica, Opisthorchis spp.), intestinal flukes (Fasciolopsis buski) and lung flukes (Paragonimus westermani).
(b)
Application: the diagnostic specimen depends on the fluke's habitat and route of egg excretion - urine is examined for S. haematobium eggs (habitat: vesical/pelvic venous plexus, draining to the bladder), faeces are examined for S. mansoni and S. japonicum eggs (habitat: mesenteric veins, draining to the intestinal lumen) and for Fasciola/Fasciolopsis eggs (intestinal/biliary flukes), while sputum is examined for Paragonimus westermani eggs (lung fluke).
(c)
Examining urine alone would miss S. mansoni infection because this species resides in the inferior mesenteric vein and its eggs are released into the intestinal lumen and passed in faeces, not into the urinary tract; only S. haematobium, which inhabits the vesical/pelvic venous plexus, characteristically produces eggs detectable in urine, so selecting the wrong specimen for the wrong species would give a false-negative result even in a genuinely infected patient.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of trematodes by habitat into blood flukes, liver (biliary) flukes, intestinal flukes and lung flukes, with genus examples for each.
(b) State how the diagnostic specimen is selected according to the habitat/classification of the suspected fluke.
(c) Explain why examining urine alone (rather than stool) would miss infection with Schistosoma mansoni.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Phage typing is a method for detecting single strains of bacteria, exploiting the fact that bacteriophages (viruses that infect bacteria) can sometimes infect only a single strain of a bacterial species. Serotyping (serology in bacterial identification) usually involves detection of antigens by enzyme or fluorescence immunoassays, and can confirm identification obtained by other methods, e.g. Salmonella species identified biochemically are further processed for serotyping by slide agglutination, as is Vibrio cholerae.
• Procedure for phage typing: a culture of the strain is grown on agar and dried, a grid is drawn on the base of the Petri dish to mark different regions, and each square of the grid is inoculated with a different phage; after the phage drops dry, the plate is incubated, and susceptible phage regions show a circular clearing where the bacteria have been lysed, which is used for differentiation. Procedure for serotyping: antibodies against specific surface antigens (e.g. O, H or K antigens) are reacted with the isolate in a slide agglutination test, and the pattern of agglutination defines the serotype.
• Uses: phage typing is used to trace the source of outbreaks of infection by identifying different strains within a single bacterial species; serotyping is used for definitive/formal identification and epidemiological investigation, e.g. Salmonella serotypes are defined by somatic (O) and flagellar (H) antigens using the Kauffmann-White classification.
(b)
Phage typing is particularly useful for outbreak tracing because it can distinguish between different strains of the same species that would otherwise appear identical by routine biochemical and serological testing, allowing investigators to link cases to a common source strain.
(c)
Phage typing exploits the specific susceptibility of a bacterial strain to lysis by particular bacteriophages, whereas serotyping exploits the antigenic (surface antigen) composition of the organism as detected by specific antisera; the two methods therefore probe different biological properties (susceptibility to viral infection versus antigenic structure) to achieve strain- or serotype-level discrimination.
questions.question:
(a) Describe phage typing and serotyping as bacterial identification techniques under the following headings: (i) principle of each, (ii) procedure of each, (iii) their respective uses.
(b) Explain why phage typing is particularly useful for tracing the source of an outbreak.
(c) Distinguish phage typing from serotyping in terms of what property of the bacterium each method exploits.

(i) A broth dilution test shows no visible turbidity in tubes containing 2 µg/ml and higher concentrations of an antibiotic, but turbidity in tubes below 2 µg/ml. Interpret this finding.
(ii) State how the result is recorded/reported.
(iii) State what the result indicates about the isolate.
(iv) State the follow-up test that can determine whether the drug is bactericidal at this concentration.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The lowest concentration of antibiotic that shows no visible growth (turbidity) after overnight incubation at 35°C is the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC); here, the MIC is 2 µg/ml, since this is the lowest concentration preventing visible growth.
(ii)
The result is recorded/reported as "MIC = 2 µg/ml" for the antibiotic tested against the isolate, expressed quantitatively in µg/ml or mg/L.
(iii)
This value indicates the effect of the antimicrobial agent against the organism and can be compared against standardised breakpoint values (from CLSI, BSAC or EUCAST) to classify the isolate as susceptible, intermediate or resistant, and can guide selection of the most effective antibiotic and dose for the patient's infection.
(iv)
Follow-up: an aliquot (0.1 ml) from the tubes showing no visible growth (i.e. at or above the MIC) is subcultured onto an antibiotic-free agar plate; the lowest concentration that inhibits at least 99.9% of the original bacterial inoculum (i.e. yields no or minimal colony growth) is the Minimum Bactericidal Concentration (MBC), distinguishing a bactericidal from a merely bacteriostatic (growth-inhibiting) effect.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the Gram stain technique under the following headings: (i) reagents used, (ii) procedure, (iii) principle behind the differential staining.
(b) Explain why Gram stains should be performed on young cultures.
(c) Distinguish the Gram stain from the Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) stain in terms of the organisms detected and the mechanism of colour retention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Reagents: crystal violet (primary stain), Gram's iodine (mordant), acetone/alcohol (decoloriser) and a counterstain such as safranin or dilute carbol fuchsin.
• Procedure: a heat-fixed smear is stained with crystal violet, treated with Gram's iodine to fix the dye-iodine complex, decolorised briefly with acetone/alcohol, and then counterstained; Gram-positive organisms retain the primary violet stain, while Gram-negative organisms lose it and take up the pink/red counterstain.
• Principle: staining of the isolated bacteria is the foremost and most important step in identification; the Gram stain differentiates bacteria into Gram-positive and Gram-negative types, which can be either cocci or bacilli (or vibrios for Gram-positive), based on differences in cell wall structure that determine whether the crystal violet-iodine complex is retained (thick peptidoglycan, Gram-positive) or washed out (thin peptidoglycan with an outer membrane, Gram-negative).
(b)
Gram stains should be performed on young (18-24 hour) cultures because very old cells may lose their ability to retain crystal violet and appear Gram-variable or Gram-negative even though the organism is truly Gram-positive, which could lead to a false identification.
(c)
The Gram stain distinguishes Gram-positive pathogens (e.g. staphylococci, streptococci, pneumococci) from Gram-negative pathogens (e.g. E. coli, Klebsiella, Salmonella, Shigella) based on differential retention of crystal violet. The Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) stain, by contrast, is performed specifically when Mycobacterial infection (e.g. tuberculosis, leprosy) is suspected; it relies on the lipid-rich, mycolic-acid-containing cell wall of acid-fast bacilli resisting decolorisation with acid-alcohol after staining with carbol fuchsin, so that the organism retains the red primary stain regardless of Gram reaction, rather than depending on peptidoglycan thickness as in the Gram stain.

questions.question:
(i) A saline wet mount of a fresh stool sample shows a motile trophozoite with ingested red blood cells. Identify the likely organism and stage.
(ii) State the basic technique used to examine this specimen.
(iii) State how the finding is recorded/reported.
(iv) State the follow-up practical step needed given the intermittent shedding of this organism.
questions.answerText:
(i)
A motile trophozoite containing ingested red blood cells in a fresh stool wet mount is characteristic of Entamoeba histolytica, the most important pathogenic intestinal amoeba.
(ii)
Technique: direct saline wet mount microscopy of fresh (warm) stool, since trophozoites are motile and fragile and disintegrate outside the body; an iodine wet mount of the same or a further sample can be used to examine cyst nuclear detail if trophozoites are not seen.
(iii)
The finding is recorded/reported as "motile trophozoites with ingested red blood cells seen, morphology consistent with Entamoeba histolytica (haematophagous trophozoite)".
(iv)
Follow-up: because the cyst (not the trophozoite) is the infective stage and shedding can be intermittent, repeat stool examination on separate days (and examination for cysts using an iodine mount) is recommended if the first specimen is negative but clinical suspicion remains.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the cell wall structure of Mycobacterium species and how it relates to acid-fastness.
(b) State the standard staining and culture methods used to identify Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the biosafety precaution of processing sputum in a biosafety cabinet and decontaminating specimens before TB culture.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Mycobacteria are aerobic, non-motile, acid-fast bacilli, straight or slightly curved rods 0.2-0.6 µm wide by 1.0-10 µm long, with a cell wall thicker than in many other bacteria, hydrophobic, waxy and rich in mycolic acids; this lipid-rich cell wall confers resistance to decolorisation with acid-alcohol, which is why the organisms are termed "acid-fast bacilli" and appear mould-like when grown in liquid media (giving rise to the genus name, from the Greek "myco-" meaning fungus).
(b)
Standard methods: staining is by the Ziehl-Neelsen or fluorescence (Auramine O) technique; culture uses egg-based Lowenstein-Jensen or Ogawa medium, agar-based Middlebrook 7H10/7H11, or liquid Middlebrook 7H9 (as in the BACTEC MGIT 960 system).
(c)
Basic reasoning: most clinical specimens, especially sputum, are contaminated with normal flora that would rapidly outgrow the slow-growing tubercle bacilli in culture; processing (digestion and decontamination with agents such as NALC-NaOH, followed by concentration by centrifugation) frees the bacilli from mucus and cells and eliminates faster-growing contaminants, while work in a biosafety cabinet protects laboratory personnel from the highly infectious, aerosol-transmissible nature of M. tuberculosis.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the general characteristics of Bacillus anthracis, including its morphology, capsule and spore formation.
(b) State the standard culture medium and appearance used to identify B. anthracis.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the biosafety precaution of handling anthrax specimens with protective gloves, a face mask and formalin decontamination.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Bacillus anthracis is a large, 5-8 by 1-5 µm, Gram-positive (or Gram-variable) non-motile bacillus, often appearing joined end to end in chains; in smears from specimens the bacilli are capsulated, with capsular material often appearing irregular and fragmented, while in smears from aerobic cultures the bacilli are non-capsulated but contain oval spores of the same diameter as the bacillus, giving the organism a "beaded" appearance. It produces a polypeptide capsule that is anti-phagocytic, together with a toxin affecting the central nervous system leading to respiratory distress, shock, cardiac collapse and death.
(b)
Standard medium: B. anthracis grows aerobically and anaerobically (it is a facultative anaerobe), with an optimum temperature of 35-37°C; on blood agar it produces large (2-5 mm), grey-white, irregular colonies with wavy edges that are non-haemolytic or only slightly haemolytic, in contrast to the markedly haemolytic saprophytic Bacillus species.
(c)
Basic reasoning: B. anthracis is a high-risk infectious pathogen, so specimens and infected material must be handled with care using protective gloves and a face mask, and decontaminated with 4% w/v formalin solution, because the organism's resistant endospores and the severity of the resulting disease mean that even small accidental exposures can cause serious, potentially fatal infection in laboratory personnel.

questions.question:
(i) A high vaginal swab (HVS) is received from a woman with vaginal discharge for detection of Trichomonas vaginalis and Candida. Identify the specimen and the appropriate wet-preparation method.
(ii) State the principle of the wet mount examination.
(iii) Outline the procedure for both the wet preparation and the culture set-up.
(iv) State the expected microscopic findings for each organism and how they are reported.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Specimen: high vaginal swab (HVS)/vaginal swab. Method: wet preparation in saline. Culture media: Trichomonas medium for T. vaginalis, and Sabouraud dextrose agar for Candida albicans.
(ii)
Principle: T. vaginalis has no cyst stage, so the motile trophozoite is both the diagnostic and infective stage and must be examined promptly while still motile in a fresh wet mount; Candida is a budding yeast that can be seen directly on microscopy or grown in culture on Sabouraud agar.
(iii)
Procedure: immerse the vaginal swab in a sterile tube containing 0.5 ml saline; place a drop of the fluid on a glass slide, cover with a coverslip and examine under the x10 and x40 objectives for motile organisms and clue cells. For culture, immerse a swab in Trichomonas medium and incubate for 7 days, examining a drop of the medium daily under a coverslip for motile T. vaginalis; inoculate a second swab onto Sabouraud dextrose agar for Candida.
(iv)
Findings: T. vaginalis appears as a motile, pear-shaped flagellate with an undulating membrane, seen directly in the wet mount or in the daily examinations of the Trichomonas medium culture; Candida appears as Gram-positive, oval budding yeast cells, sometimes with pseudohyphae, and Candida albicans is confirmed by cream-coloured colonies on Sabouraud agar with a distinctive yeast smell. Results are reported as "Trichomonas vaginalis seen/isolated" or "Candida sp. isolated" as appropriate.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of water-borne diseases into bacterial, viral and protozoal categories, with organism examples for each.
(b) State how indicator organisms (E. coli, Streptococcus faecalis, Clostridium perfringens) are selected and applied to assess faecal contamination of a water supply.
(c) Explain why the absence of coliform bacteria alongside the presence of Clostridium perfringens spores can still indicate a water-safety problem, rather than being interpreted as clean water.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Water-borne diseases are classified as bacterial (e.g. cholera, typhoid, paratyphoid, diarrhoea, bacillary dysentery, Yersinia enterocolitica and Campylobacter infections), viral (e.g. Hepatitis A, Hepatitis E, poliomyelitis, rotavirus diarrhoea) and protozoal (e.g. amoebiasis, giardiasis, Balantidium coli diarrhoea).
(b)
Application: E. coli (and coliform bacteria as a whole) is used as the primary indicator because it is discharged only from the human or animal intestine and survives in water for only a few days, so its presence signals recent faecal pollution; Streptococcus faecalis found together with E. coli provides confirmatory evidence of recent faecal contamination; Clostridium perfringens, which also occurs in stool but forms resistant spores, is used as an indicator of faecal contamination that may have occurred some time ago.
(c)
Absence of coliforms with the presence of C. perfringens spores does not mean the water is safe, because coliforms die off relatively quickly in the environment while the resistant spores of C. perfringens can persist long after the coliforms have disappeared; this pattern therefore indicates that faecal pollution occurred at some point in the past even though it may no longer be recent or ongoing, and the water source should still be regarded as having a contamination history requiring further investigation.

(i)
Water is said to be contaminated when it contains bacterial, parasitic or viral agents, or other wastes/sewage; a safe water supply must not harm the consumer even over prolonged ingestion. The main indicator organism tested for is Escherichia coli, together with coliform bacteria as a whole.
(ii)
Principle: E. coli is discharged only from the human or animal intestine (about 200-400 billion organisms are shed by a person per day) and survives in water for only a few days, so its presence indicates recent faecal/excretal pollution of the water rather than requiring the laborious direct search for specific enteric pathogens.
(iii)
Procedure: water samples are examined for total and faecal coliforms as fecal indicator bacteria; correlations between indicator organism concentrations (total and faecal coliforms) have been documented in pooled water-quality data sets, supporting their use as a screening tool.
(iv)
Streptococcus faecalis found together with E. coli is a confirmatory sign of recent faecal contamination, since S. faecalis is present in excreta in smaller numbers than E. coli. Clostridium perfringens, also present in stool in small numbers, forms resistant spores; its presence in the absence of coliform bacteria indicates that faecal pollution occurred some time ago rather than recently, since coliforms die off faster than the spores.
questions.question:
(i) A water sample is submitted to assess safety for drinking. Identify the type of organism tested for as an indicator of contamination.
(ii) State the principle behind using this organism as an indicator rather than testing directly for pathogens.
(iii) Outline the general approach used to detect this indicator in the sample.
(iv) State how the presence of the indicator, together with other indicator organisms, is interpreted.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Macroscopic/microscopic identification: a needle mount is prepared by removing a small portion of sporing surface midway between the centre and periphery of a colony, teasing it apart in lactophenol cotton blue stain, covering with a coverslip and examining; alternatively, adhesive tape can be pressed onto the colony surface and examined similarly. A slide culture is set up by cutting a small agar block from Sabouraud dextrose agar, inoculating its four edges with the fungus, covering with a coverslip, and incubating in a moist chamber before examining the adherent culture for sporing structures.
• Urease test: colonies are inoculated onto Christensen's urea medium and incubated at room temperature; a colour change (typically to pink) indicates urease production.
• Hair penetration test: sterilised hair strands are placed in water containing yeast extract, inoculated with fragments of the fungus, incubated at room temperature for 4 weeks, and examined under the microscope in 30% KOH for transverse wedge-shaped perforations (a positive result). The rice-grain test involves inoculating rice-grain medium with a small portion of the fungus and incubating at room temperature for 3 weeks, observing whether growth occurs.
(b)
A slide culture is performed when the microscopic appearance of a routine (needle mount) culture is atypical and characteristic sporing features are not seen, because the intact, undisturbed sporing structures produced directly on the slide culture agar block give a clearer, more characteristic view of the conidial arrangement needed for accurate species identification.
(c)
In the urease test, Trichophyton mentagrophytes is positive within 7 days, whereas Trichophyton rubrum is negative or only weakly positive, helping to distinguish the two closely related species. In the rice-grain test, Microsporum audouinii fails to grow on rice-grain medium, whereas Microsporum canis and Microsporum gypsum do grow, providing a simple way to identify M. audouinii among the Microsporum species.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of dermatophyte identification tests under the following headings: (i) macroscopic/microscopic culture identification (needle mount, slide culture), (ii) the urease test, (iii) the hair penetration test and rice-grain test.
(b) Explain why a slide culture is performed when the microscopic appearance of a routine culture is atypical.
(c) Distinguish the urease test result of Trichophyton mentagrophytes from that of Trichophyton rubrum, and the rice-grain test result of Microsporum audouinii from other Microsporum species.

(a) Describe the general characteristics and structure of Staphylococcus species, including their morphology, arrangement, and pigmentation.
(b) State the standard laboratory method used to identify and distinguish Staphylococcus species in practice.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution of using young (18-24 hour) cultures for Gram staining and morphological examination.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Staphylococcus spp. are Gram-positive cocci, nonmotile and non-spore-forming, occurring singly, in pairs or characteristically in grape-like clusters, about 1 µm in diameter; they are a heterogenous group and are normal colonisers of skin and mucosal surfaces. S. aureus (named from the Latin for "golden") forms part of the normal flora of the skin, upper respiratory tract and intestinal tract, is carried in the nose of 20-40% of healthy individuals, grows on many media fermenting carbohydrates without gas, is halophilic (salt-loving), and its colonies may be white, grey or golden yellow due to production of the pigment staphyloxanthin.
(b)
Standard method: Gram staining of the specimen, followed by culture on 5% sheep blood agar and chocolate agar (with selective media such as mannitol salt agar, phenylethyl alcohol or CNA agar for heavily contaminated specimens), and biochemical tests including catalase and coagulase; S. aureus colonies on blood agar are medium-to-large, smooth, slightly raised, creamy-yellow and usually beta-haemolytic, and produce a yellow halo on mannitol salt agar due to mannitol fermentation.
(c)
Basic reasoning: Gram stains should be performed on young cultures because very old cells may lose their ability to retain crystal violet and appear Gram-variable or Gram-negative, which could lead to a false Gram reaction and misidentification of an organism that is actually Gram-positive.

questions.question:
(i) A Gram stain of a wound swab from a case of suspected tetanus shows Gram-positive rods with terminal, round spores giving a "drumstick" appearance. Identify the likely organism.
(ii) State the basic technique used to detect this organism, given its growth requirements.
(iii) State how the finding is recorded/reported.
(iv) State the follow-up practical step needed given the risk this organism poses.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Gram-positive rods with a terminal spore within a swollen sporangium, giving a distinctive "drumstick" appearance, are characteristic of Clostridium tetani.
(ii)
Technique: because C. tetani is an obligate (strict) anaerobe, the specimen must be cultured under anaerobic conditions (e.g. using a McIntosh-Fildes jar, GasPak system, or Robertson's cooked meat medium) rather than by routine aerobic culture; spores are rarely seen in smears from infected tissue itself, so terminal-spore morphology is most often demonstrated once the organism is subcultured.
(iii)
The finding is recorded/reported as "Gram-positive rods with terminal drumstick spores seen, morphology consistent with Clostridium tetani", and the clinician should be alerted immediately given the severity of tetanus.
(iv)
Follow-up: because endospores allow the organism to survive UV light, desiccation, high temperature and chemical disinfectants, strict decontamination of the culture area and equipment is required; the position of the spore (terminal for C. tetani versus oval sub-terminal for C. botulinum) should be documented as it is useful for species identification.

(i)
Small, oval, budding yeast cells (2-4 micrometres) attached to pseudohyphae, Gram-positive on staining, are characteristic of Candida albicans.
(ii)
Technique: the germ tube test - a yeast colony is inoculated into human serum and incubated at 35-37°C for 2-3 hours, then examined microscopically for tube-like outgrowths (germ tubes) from the yeast cells.
(iii)
If sprouting yeast cells (germ tubes) are seen, the result is reported as "Candida albicans isolated"; if no sprouting is seen, it is reported as "yeast other than C. albicans isolated".
(iv)
Follow-up: culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar, on which C. albicans grows as cream-coloured, pasty colonies with a distinctive yeast smell after 24-48 hours at 35-37°C; inoculation onto corn-meal agar demonstrates formation of pseudohyphae and chlamydospores, providing further confirmation.
questions.question:
(i) A wet preparation of a vaginal/oral swab shows small, oval, budding yeast cells attached to pseudohyphae. Identify the likely organism.
(ii) State the basic technique used to confirm the identification.
(iii) State how a positive result of this technique is recorded/reported.
(iv) State the follow-up practical step for culture confirmation.

(i) A Widal test on a febrile patient's serum shows agglutination up to a dilution of 1:160 for Salmonella typhi O antigen, with no agglutination for the H antigen. Interpret this titre reading.
(ii) State how the result should be recorded.
(iii) State what this titre indicates about the patient's likely infection status.
(iv) State the follow-up action needed to confirm the diagnosis.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The titre is the highest dilution of serum at which visible agglutination with the antigen still occurs; here, agglutination with the O antigen persisting to a 1:160 dilution, with no agglutination of the H antigen, is the reading obtained.
(ii)
The result is recorded as "Widal test: O antigen titre 1:160, H antigen titre negative/<1:20" (or as tested), noting the specific antigen and dilution.
(iii)
A single raised O titre is suggestive of but not confirmatory of current or recent Salmonella infection, since serological tests have little diagnostic value in the first 7-10 days of illness and a changing (rising) titre is far more significant than a single reading; false positives can occur due to past infection or vaccination.
(iv)
Follow-up: a repeat (convalescent) serum sample should be taken 5-7 days later to check for a rising titre, which is required for confirmation; blood, stool or urine culture for isolation of Salmonella typhi remains the definitive diagnostic method and should be pursued alongside serology.

(a)
• Role: animal inoculation was the first method of virus cultivation and for many years the only means of propagation; besides propagating the virus, inoculation of various animal hosts is important in identifying an unknown virus, and can reproduce the clinical illness in another member of the same species to confirm the infectious nature of a disease.
• Species and routes: monkeys are frequently used in medical virology because many human diseases with similar clinical symptoms can be reproduced in them; a wide variety of other laboratory animals (dogs, cats, mice, rats, guinea pigs, rabbits, hamsters) are also used. Viruses producing encephalitis are usually inoculated intracerebrally, poxviruses intradermally, and respiratory-group viruses intranasally; other routes include the scarified cornea of a rabbit, the scarified epithelium of the mouth/tongue of calves, or the footpad of a guinea pig. Rabies diagnosis in some cases must be made by animal inoculation because Negri bodies cannot always be demonstrated directly in brain tissue.
• Precautions: experimental animals must be healthy before use and properly cared for during the experiment; the material inoculated must be filtered or treated with antibiotics to ensure it is bacteriologically sterile and does not carry a concurrent bacterial infection that would complicate the clinical picture; animals should be examined once or twice daily for signs of disease, and rectal temperatures recorded where possible.
(b)
In distinguishing viruses producing similar lesions such as foot-and-mouth disease and vesicular stomatitis of cattle, calves and horses are inoculated: calves are susceptible to both viruses, whereas horses are insusceptible to foot-and-mouth disease virus but readily contract vesicular stomatitis, so the differential susceptibility of the two animal species allows the two viruses to be distinguished.
(c)
Animal inoculation reproduces the whole-organism host response (immunology, pathogenicity, vaccine efficacy) and is used for virus isolation, study of pathogenicity and host immune reactions, testing and developing vaccines, and raising monoclonal or polyclonal antibodies; it is more expensive and less convenient than the embryo (or cell culture) method of virus propagation, which instead grows the virus in isolated cells/tissue or the developing chick embryo without the need for a whole susceptible animal.
questions.question:
(a) Describe animal inoculation as a technique in medical microbiology under the following headings: (i) its role in virus cultivation and identification, (ii) the animal species and routes of inoculation used for different pathogens, (iii) precautions taken with experimental animals.
(b) Explain why animal inoculation is used to distinguish between viruses producing similar lesions, using the example of foot-and-mouth disease and vesicular stomatitis viruses.
(c) Distinguish animal inoculation from cell/embryo culture as a method of virus propagation.

(i) A thin blood film examined at night from a patient with recurrent fever shows sheathed, motile larval worms. Identify the likely organism and finding.
(ii) State the basic technique used to detect this organism, including the reason for timing of collection.
(iii) State how the finding is recorded/reported.
(iv) State the follow-up practical step for species confirmation.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Sheathed, motile larval worms seen in a blood film are microfilariae, consistent with lymphatic filariasis caused by Wuchereria bancrofti.
(ii)
Technique: a thick and thin blood film stained with Giemsa is examined; blood should be collected at the time of day when microfilariae show peak periodicity in the peripheral blood (classically at night for W. bancrofti), since numbers circulating in the blood vary with a periodic pattern.
(iii)
The finding is recorded/reported as "microfilariae seen on blood film, consistent with lymphatic filariasis" and the time of collection should be documented, since timing affects the sensitivity of the test.
(iv)
Follow-up: the morphology of the microfilaria (presence/absence of a sheath, and the arrangement of nuclei at the tail tip) is examined on the thin film to distinguish the species (e.g. Wuchereria bancrofti from Brugia malayi), and repeat sampling at the appropriate time may be needed if the initial specimen was collected outside the peak period.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the general characteristics of Rickettsia, including its obligate intracellular nature, cell membrane structure, and staining behaviour.
(b) State the standard specimen handling and culture requirements for Rickettsia given its growth characteristics.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution of handling Rickettsia specimens with extra care in the laboratory.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Rickettsia are obligate intracellular parasites, small coccobacilli (0.3-0.5 µm) with a cell membrane similar to Gram-negative bacteria, containing lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and peptidoglycan; they will not show up on Gram stain but can be seen with Giemsa stain, require growth co-factors, and (except Coxiella) are all transmitted by arthropod vectors such as fleas, ticks, mites and lice.
(b)
Standard requirements: Rickettsia will not grow on artificial media and must be grown in embryonated eggs or tissue culture; specimens are blood, collected during febrile illness.
(c)
Basic reasoning: cultivation of Rickettsia is technically difficult and dangerous because aerosol transmission can easily occur, and the organisms are highly infectious; specimens should therefore be handled very carefully, and where isolation is attempted, animal inoculation (into guinea pigs/mice, observed over 3-4 weeks for temperature rise and, for some species, scrotal inflammation/necrosis) is used instead of routine culture, minimising the risk of laboratory-acquired infection from direct culture manipulation.

(i)
Specimen: urethral swab (in the female, high vaginal/cervical/urethral swab is used instead). Transport medium: charcoal-containing transport medium/Stuart's medium, which preserves Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and the specimen should be delivered to the laboratory as soon as possible. Culture media: non-selective chocolate agar and the selective Modified Thayer-Martin (MTM) medium.
(ii)
Principle: because the genital tract is normally colonised with commensal bacteria, a selective medium such as MTM is required to suppress the accompanying flora while allowing the fastidious N. gonorrhoeae to grow; chocolate agar (heated blood agar) supplies the growth factors released by heating that N. gonorrhoeae requires.
(iii)
Procedure: inoculate the swab onto the MTM and chocolate agar plates using a roll-on (impression smear) method, then incubate the plates at 37°C in a candle jar (CO2-enriched atmosphere) and examine after 24 hours, re-incubating negative or pinpoint-growth plates for a further 24 hours.
(iv)
Result: N. gonorrhoeae produces smooth, colourless, raised colonies about 1-2 mm in diameter. An oxidase test performed on the suspect colony is strongly positive, and a Gram stain of the oxidase-positive colony shows Gram-negative diplococci, confirming the identification.
questions.question:
(i) A male patient presents with urethral discharge and a swab is taken for suspected gonococcal infection. Identify the specimen, the transport medium and the culture media required.
(ii) State the principle underlying the choice of the selective culture medium.
(iii) Outline the procedure for inoculation and incubation.
(iv) State the expected colonial appearance and the confirmatory biochemical/staining result.

(a) Describe the classification of antimicrobial susceptibility testing methods into dilution techniques and diffusion techniques.
(b) State how the choice between a qualitative (disc diffusion) and quantitative (MIC) method is selected depending on the clinical or laboratory need.
(c) Explain why using the disc diffusion method without following CLSI-standardised inoculum density and interpretive breakpoints can give an invalid result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing methods are classified into dilution techniques (agar or broth based, measuring MIC and, with a follow-up subculture step, MBC) and diffusion techniques (the Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion method, and the Stokes method, which compares the test organism directly with a control organism on the same plate).
(b)
Application: the qualitative disc diffusion method is selected for routine clinical reporting of Sensitive/Intermediate/Resistant status, being inexpensive, flexible and easy to perform; the quantitative MIC/dilution method is selected when a precise numerical drug concentration is needed, such as in drug-discovery laboratories assessing a new antimicrobial agent, or in clinical settings requiring dose optimisation for a specific patient's infection.
(c)
