Using the disc diffusion method without a correctly standardised inoculum (compared to a 0.5 McFarland turbidity standard) and without following CLSI interpretive breakpoints can give an invalid result because the zone size is directly affected by the density of the bacterial inoculum and by plate/medium factors (e.g. Mueller-Hinton agar depth and preparation); an inoculum that is too light or too heavy will produce an artificially large or small zone of inhibition that does not reflect the organism's true susceptibility, and without the harmonised CLSI breakpoints, results cannot reliably be compared between laboratories or interpreted clinically.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the general characteristics of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, including its morphology, growth conditions and pigment production.
(b) State the standard biochemical tests used in the laboratory to identify Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the infection-control precaution of considering moist hospital equipment (e.g. catheters) as a potential reservoir for this organism.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an encapsulated, Gram-negative, aerobic-facultatively anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium; it thrives not only in normal atmospheres but also in low-oxygen atmospheres and is found in soil, water, skin flora and most human-made environments. It produces phenazine pigments (including pyocyanin), which are involved in quorum sensing, virulence and iron acquisition.
(b)
Standard tests: P. aeruginosa is citrate positive, catalase positive and oxidase positive, distinguishing it from the oxidase-negative Enterobacteriaceae.
(c)
Basic reasoning: because P. aeruginosa thrives on moist surfaces, it is commonly found on and in medical equipment, including catheters, causing cross-infections in hospitals and clinics; recognising moist equipment as a reservoir underlies infection-control precautions such as proper cleaning/disinfection of equipment and hand hygiene among healthcare workers to prevent the organism from being spread by contaminated devices or hands.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of the Gram-positive cocci of medical importance (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Enterococcus) based on Gram reaction, arrangement and haemolysis.
(b) State how the catalase and coagulase tests are selected and applied to differentiate between these groups.
(c) Explain why an incorrectly read catalase or coagulase test can lead to an invalid identification result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Gram-positive cocci are classified based on the Gram stain reaction of the bacterial cell and its microscopic morphology/arrangement; members include Staphylococcus spp. (clusters), Streptococcus spp. (chains/pairs) and Enterococcus spp. Streptococcus is further classified by haemolytic pattern (alpha-, beta- or gamma-haemolytic) and by Lancefield serogroup (A to U for beta-haemolytic species).
(b)
Application: the catalase test is applied first to distinguish catalase-positive Staphylococcus/Micrococcaceae from catalase-negative Streptococcus/Streptococcaceae; once an isolate is identified as Staphylococcus by a positive catalase test, the coagulase test (slide and/or tube) is applied to differentiate coagulase-positive S. aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci such as S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus.
(c)
An incorrectly read catalase test can occur if red blood cells are inadvertently carried over from a blood-agar colony into the test, producing a false-positive bubbling reaction; an incorrectly read coagulase test (e.g. reading the rapid slide test alone without confirming an equivocal or negative result with the definitive tube test) can miss a true coagulase-positive organism or wrongly call a coagulase-negative isolate positive. Either error would misclassify the organism (e.g. reporting a less virulent coagulase-negative staphylococcus as S. aureus, or vice versa), leading to inappropriate clinical interpretation and management.

(a)
• Direct microscopy: Gram stain of a urogenital specimen may show Gram-negative intracellular diplococci (Neisseria gonorrhoeae), Gram-variable bacilli attached to epithelial cells known as "clue cells" (Gardnerella vaginalis), or Gram-positive yeast-like cells (Candida). Giemsa staining (1:40 for 1 hour) may reveal blue-mauve inclusion bodies characteristic of Chlamydia trachomatis.
• Culture: chocolate agar and Modified Thayer-Martin agar are used for N. gonorrhoeae, which on culture produces smooth, colourless, raised colonies about 1-2 mm in diameter; Sabouraud dextrose agar is used for Candida; bi-layer Tween 80 blood agar is used for Gardnerella vaginalis.
• Confirmatory testing: an oxidase test is performed on suspected N. gonorrhoeae colonies on chocolate agar (positive), and a Gram stain of the oxidase-positive colony confirms Gram-negative diplococci.
(b)
Culture and microscopy are both required because microscopy alone gives only a rapid presumptive impression (which may be equivocal, particularly in women where normal vaginal flora can resemble pathogenic diplococcal morphology), while culture provides a viable isolate for definitive biochemical/serological confirmation, antibiotic susceptibility testing, and detection of organisms present in numbers too low to see directly on the smear.
(c)
N. gonorrhoeae appears as Gram-negative diplococci, often located intracellularly within pus cells; Gardnerella vaginalis appears as Gram-variable bacilli adherent to the surface of vaginal epithelial cells, producing the characteristic "clue cell" appearance; Candida appears as Gram-positive, oval, budding yeast-like cells, sometimes with attached pseudohyphae - each giving a distinct and recognisable Gram-stain picture.

(b) Explain why culture and microscopy are both required rather than relying on microscopy alone in urogenital specimen examination.
(c) Distinguish the Gram-stain appearance of Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Gardnerella vaginalis and Candida in a urogenital specimen.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Enterobacteriaceae species are grouped into tribes, including Tribe I Escherichieae (Escherichia, Edwardsiella, Citrobacter, Salmonella, Shigella), Tribe II Klebsielleae (Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Hafnia, Serratia), Tribe III Proteeae (Proteus, Morganella, Providencia) and Tribe IV Erwinieae (Erwinia). All are Gram-negative rods that ferment glucose, reduce nitrate, are catalase positive and oxidase negative; lactose is fermented by Escherichia, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Citrobacter and Serratia, but not by Proteus, Salmonella, Shigella and Yersinia.
(b)
Application: MacConkey agar is used as a general screening medium for all Enterobacteriaceae, distinguishing lactose fermenters (pink colonies) from non-fermenters (colourless colonies); XLD (xylose lysine deoxycholate) and DCA (deoxycholate citrate agar) are more strongly selective media chosen specifically to isolate Salmonella and Shigella from faecal specimens, since their higher bile-salt/desoxycholate content further suppresses normal bowel commensals while still permitting these pathogens to grow.
(c)
Relying on colonial morphology alone can cause misidentification because several genera share the same lactose-fermentation status (e.g. both E. coli and Klebsiella are lactose fermenters, and both Salmonella and Shigella are non-fermenters), so a full biochemical battery (IMViC, TSI, urease, motility) plus serological confirmation is required to reliably distinguish the genus and species; using colony colour alone risks confusing organisms with very different clinical significance, such as a non-pathogenic non-fermenter with a true enteric pathogen.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of the family Enterobacteriaceae into tribes and major genera, and the biochemical properties (lactose fermentation, oxidase, motility) that distinguish them.
(b) State how selective/differential media such as MacConkey, XLD and DCA agar are selected according to the genus suspected.
(c) Explain why relying on colonial morphology alone (e.g. lactose fermentation on MacConkey agar) without a full battery of biochemical tests can lead to misidentification of an Enterobacteriaceae isolate.

(a) Describe the IMViC biochemical test battery under the following headings: (i) the four component tests, (ii) their individual principles, (iii) their combined use in identifying Enterobacteriaceae.
(b) Explain why IMViC was originally developed as a tool to detect faecal contamination of food and water.
(c) Distinguish the IMViC pattern of Escherichia coli from that of Enterobacter, and state how this differentiates a faecal from a non-faecal (environmental) coliform.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The four component tests are Indole, Methyl Red, Voges-Proskauer (VP) and Citrate.
• Principles: the indole test detects the ability of an organism to degrade tryptophan to indole, shown by a pink-to-red "cherry-red ring" with Kovac's reagent. The methyl red test identifies bacteria that produce strong, stable acids from glucose fermentation, shown by a red colour with methyl red indicator at low pH. The Voges-Proskauer test detects production of acetoin (acetyl methyl carbinol) from pyruvate, a fermentation product of the Klebsiella-Enterobacter-Serratia-Hafnia group, converted to a red complex by alpha-naphthol and potassium hydroxide. The citrate test screens for the ability to use citrate as the sole carbon and energy source, shown by growth and a colour change (green to Prussian blue) on Simmons citrate medium due to alkaline by-products raising the pH.
• Combined use: applying all four tests together to a Gram-negative bacillus produces a characteristic pattern that helps identify the genus within the Enterobacteriaceae; most species that are Voges-Proskauer positive are methyl red negative, and vice versa, giving reciprocal patterns that aid differentiation.
(b)
IMViC was originally developed to detect faecal contamination of food and water because it differentiates faecal coliforms (such as E. coli, indicating recent faecal pollution) from environmental/non-faecal coliforms (such as Enterobacter, which occurs naturally in soil and aquatic environments) based on their differing metabolic by-products.
(c)
E. coli shows the pattern Indole positive, Methyl Red positive, Voges-Proskauer negative, Citrate negative (I+M+VP-C-), whereas Enterobacter shows the opposite pattern, Indole negative, Methyl Red negative, Voges-Proskauer positive, Citrate positive (I-M-VP+C+); the E. coli pattern (a true faecal coliform) indicates recent faecal contamination when found in water or food, while the Enterobacter pattern indicates an environmental, non-faecal source.

questions.question:
Q4
1. Describe the basic composition and forms of EDTA as used in haematology, including its identifying features.
2. State the standard method/setting in which it is used in practice.
3. Explain the basic reasoning behind a common precaution associated with it.
questions.answerText:
1.
• EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) is the most frequently used anticoagulant, also known as sequestrene EDTA or Versenmate; it is an amino carboxylic acid and a colourless, water-soluble solid.
• It exists in different forms: di-potassium salt (K2EDTA, known as Sequestrene), di-sodium EDTA (Na2EDTA, known as Versene) and di-lithium EDTA.
• It is identified by its stopper colour code: a lavender (purple) stopper tube, with no other additive, is used for collection of whole blood for most haematology tests.
2.
• In standard practice, EDTA is used at a concentration of 0.5-2.0 mg per ml of blood, which preserves blood excellently for at least 6 hours, and is prepared in the laboratory as a dried vial (bulb) containing about 0.8 mg of dry chemical per 20 microlitres of solution.
• It is the standard anticoagulant for making blood smears for cell morphology studies and for a complete blood count (CBC), since it preserves the staining and morphology of leucocytes.
• It acts by chelating/removing ionised calcium, which is required for blood to clot; because it prevents clumping of platelets, it is the anticoagulant of choice where a total platelet count is required.
3.
• A common precaution is to avoid using an excessive concentration of EDTA relative to the blood volume collected.
• This is because excessive EDTA causes shrinkage of RBCs, giving erroneous PCV, MCV and MCHC results.
• Excess EDTA also interferes with blood chemistry, falsely decreasing alkaline phosphatase by binding Mg++.
• It further decreases the CO2 combining power of blood and interferes with Jaffe's reaction for creatinine testing.
• It also decreases or alters Na+, K+ and Ca2+ concentrations in plasma.
• The precaution of using the correct blood-to-EDTA ratio therefore protects both cell morphology/indices and chemistry results from these errors.

questions.question:
Q7
1. Describe the basic composition and forms of sodium citrate as used in haematology, including its identifying features.
2. State the standard method/setting in which it is used in practice.
3. Explain the basic reasoning behind a common precaution associated with it.
questions.answerText:
1.
• Sodium citrate is identified by its light blue stopper tube; the formal citrate solution (Dacie's solution), used as a diluent for counting RBCs and platelets, is prepared by dissolving 3.13 g of trisodium citrate in 100 ml of water with 1 ml of formaldehyde added per 99 ml of solution.
• Trisodium citrate used for coagulation testing is used in a liquid form at a concentration of 3.8%.
• It acts by combining with calcium to form an insoluble salt of calcium citrate, binding calcium in the same general manner as other calcium chelators.
2.
• In standard practice, for Prothrombin Time (PT), 3.8% tri-sodium citrate is used at a ratio of 1:9 (1 part anticoagulant to 9 parts blood), for example 200 microlitres of citrate with 1.8 ml of blood.
• For ESR by the Westergren method, 1 part of 3.8% tri-sodium citrate is mixed with 4 parts of blood, a ratio of 1:4, for example 400 microlitres of citrate with 1.6 ml of blood.
• Sodium citrate is the anticoagulant of choice for platelet function and morphology and is the preferred anticoagulant for coagulation studies, binding calcium in the blood specimen.
3.
• A common precaution is to use the correct anticoagulant-to-blood ratio (1:9 for PT, 1:4 for ESR), since an incorrect ratio changes the proportion of calcium available relative to the coagulation factors or sedimenting cells being tested.
• This precaution matters because sodium citrate does not preserve cell morphology and, used alone, preserves blood for only a few minutes, so timing of testing after collection is also important.
• Sodium citrate has a tendency to shrink cells, and because of the 10% dilution of blood it causes, it is generally not used for a complete blood count.
• It also interferes with many chemical tests, so it is reserved specifically for the coagulation and ESR purposes for which it is validated.
• An incorrect citrate-to-blood ratio would therefore either leave excess free calcium (understating clotting times) or over-dilute the sample, both of which invalidate PT, APTT or ESR results.
• This is why the sample must be collected from a clean venepuncture and the correct ratio strictly observed for these tests.

questions.question:
Q56
1. Describe the basic sources and preparation of antisera used in blood grouping, including identifying features.
2. State the standard method/setting in which good antisera are assessed in practice.
3. Explain the basic reasoning behind a precaution/quality requirement associated with antisera.
questions.answerText:
1.
• Antisera can be prepared from both plant and animal sources; in plants they are Lectins, which are monoclonal in nature, while in animal sources they are usually polyclonal and later purified by absorption/adsorption to become monoclonal for specific groups.
• Lectin antisera include Dolichos biflorus (anti-A1), Vicia cracea (anti-A) and roots of Ononis spinosa (anti-H).
• In animals, antisera are produced by hybridoma technology, whereby harvested spleen cells of A-, B- or AHG antigen-immunised sheep are fused with mouse myeloma cells, eventually producing monoclonal antibodies.
2.
• In standard practice, monoclonal antibodies are used because the reagent is free from infections such as HIV and there is a guarantee of a continuous supply of high-quality antisera, although they will not detect other variants of the blood group.
• Polyclonal antibodies are used where recognition of multiple epitopes is needed, though they are only of animal origin.
3.
• A good antisera must have a crystal-clear physical appearance and show clear reactivity, void of rouleaux, gel formation or haemolysis.
• It must show good avidity, that is, speed and strength of agglutination within 13 seconds.
• It must show specificity, reacting only with the specific red cell antigen, and potency, meaning it is effective and functional in its ability.
• It must also be stable, with a shelf life of about 2 years.
• The reasoning behind these quality requirements is that a weak, slow, or non-specific antisera would fail to correctly agglutinate or would give a false or ambiguous reaction.
• Requiring clarity and freedom from rouleaux or gel formation similarly ensures that any observed agglutination is a true antigen-antibody reaction rather than an artefact of the reagent itself.
• These qualities together (appearance, reactivity, avidity, specificity, potency, stability) are therefore the basis on which an antisera's suitability for blood grouping is judged before use.

questions.question:
Q19
1. Describe the general classification/types of special stains used in haematology.
2. State how each type is applied or selected in the laboratory.
3. Explain why using the wrong special stain leads to an incorrect differentiation of cells.
questions.answerText:
1.
Special stains include Periodic Acid Schiff (PAS), Perls' Prussian Blue reaction, Kleihauer-Betke stain, Leucocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP), Myeloperoxidase, Sudan Black B, Toluidine Blue, specific esterases, non-specific esterases, and Tartrate Resistant Acid Phosphatase.
2.
• PAS is applied where periodic acid oxidises 1-2 glycol groups to give a red reaction with Schiff's reagent; it gives granular positivity in proerythroblasts, homogenous positivity in normoblasts, and block/coarse granular positivity in lymphoblasts.
• Perls' Prussian Blue reaction is applied to identify iron in nucleated red blood cells (sideroblastic iron) or to identify Pappenheimer bodies in erythrocytes, unmasking ferric iron which reacts with potassium ferrocyanide to form Prussian Blue.
• Kleihauer-Betke stain is applied to demonstrate fetal haemoglobin in red cells; adult haemoglobin is dissolved out of red cells by a citric acid phosphate buffer, leaving HbA-containing cells unstained while HbF-containing cells stain bright red.
• LAP is applied as a screening test to differentiate chronic myelogenous leukaemia from leukaemoid reactions and other myeloproliferative disorders, giving a blue, granular reaction product interpreted based on a score.
• Myeloperoxidase is applied to differentiate a myelogenous or monocytic leukaemia from acute lymphocytic leukaemia, with promyelocytes and myelocytes staining strongly.
• Sudan Black B is applied where it gives a positive stain with a black-stained cytoplasm in myeloblasts, as in acute myeloid leukaemia (AML).
• Specific esterases are applied to confine red colouration to cells of the neutrophil series and mast cells, while non-specific esterases identify monocytic cells with a red/brown coloration that does not stain granulocytes or eosinophils.
3.
• Using PAS where Perls' stain is needed, for example, would fail to demonstrate iron in sideroblasts or Pappenheimer bodies, since PAS positivity instead reflects carbohydrate/glycogen content.
• Using Myeloperoxidase or Sudan Black B where a monocytic lineage is suspected, instead of non-specific esterase, could fail to reveal the red/brown monocytic reaction that distinguishes it from granulocytic cells.
• Since specific esterases stain only neutrophil-series and mast cells while non-specific esterases stain monocytic cells, applying the wrong esterase would misclassify the lineage of the leukaemic cells being examined.
• Because each special stain is confined to specific cell features (carbohydrate content, iron, fetal haemoglobin, enzyme activity), using a stain not suited to the diagnostic question therefore gives a falsely negative or misleading differentiation of the cell type or disease under investigation.

questions.question:
Q36
A manual WBC differential count on a blood film reveals 15 nucleated red blood cells (NRBCs) per 100 WBCs counted, and the instrument-reported WBC count is 5000/microlitre.
1. Interpret why this WBC count needs correction.
2. State how the corrected WBC count is calculated and recorded.
3. State what the corrected value indicates about the true white cell count.
4. State the action that follows from this reading.
questions.answerText:
1.
The count needs correction because 10 or more NRBCs were seen on the differential count, and NRBCs are counted by automated instruments alongside true white cells, inflating the reported WBC count.
2.
The corrected WBC count is calculated using the formula: corrected WBC count = WBC x 100 / (NRBC + 100); here this is 5000 x 100 / (15 + 100) = 4347.8.
3.
The corrected value indicates that the true white cell count is lower than the instrument-reported value, since the NRBCs were being counted as if they were leucocytes.
4.
The corrected WBC count of approximately 4347.8/microlitre should be reported instead of the uncorrected 5000/microlitre, following the same approach demonstrated for a value of 5,000 with 10 NRBCs, which corrects to 4545.50.

questions.question:
Q14
1. Describe the basic composition/preparation of Wright's stain, including its identifying features.
2. State the standard method/setting in which it is used in practice.
3. Explain the basic reasoning behind a common precaution associated with it.
questions.answerText:
1.
• Wright's stain used heated methylene blue, which produces a polychrome methylene blue, combined with Eosin Y.
• The heated methylene blue with Eosin Y is allowed to precipitate to form an eosinate, which is then dissolved with methanol to give the working stain.
• Wright's stain is used to differentiate the nuclear and/or cytoplasmic morphology of platelets, RBCs, WBCs and parasites.
2.
• In standard practice for thin blood films (dip method), an air-dried film is dipped in the undiluted stain for 15 to 30 seconds (double the time for bone marrow smears), then decolourised by immersion in distilled or deionised water and air-dried in a vertical position.
• In the rack method, air-dried slides are flooded with stain for 10 to 15 seconds, an equal volume of water is added and left for 10 seconds, and the slide is rinsed by dipping in distilled/deionised water for 30 seconds.
• It is also used to stain urine samples to diagnose urinary tract infection and interstitial nephritis by detecting eosinophils, and in cytogenetics to detect chromosomal defects.
3.
• A common precaution is to ensure all slides are completely clean before making the blood or bone marrow smear.
• This is because, if slides are not completely clean, the stain will not absorb into the smear.
• Another precaution for thick films is that they must be air-dried thoroughly for several hours or overnight and must not be dried in an incubator or by heat.
• This is because heat-drying will fix the blood and interfere with the lysing of the RBCs that is needed for a thick film.
• Thick films must also be laked by immersion in distilled or deionised water for 10 minutes before methanol fixation, since they are not fixed before staining in the way thin films are.
• These precautions ensure that the stain properly penetrates and differentiates the cells, rather than failing to bind or distorting cell lysis and morphology.

1.
Blood is diluted in a solution of potassium ferricyanide and potassium cyanide; the ferricyanide oxidises haemoglobin to methaemoglobin, and potassium cyanide provides cyanide ions to form cyanmethaemoglobin, whose absorbance is measured at 540 nm.
2.
The reagent is a detergent-modified Drabkin's solution containing potassium ferricyanide (200 mg), potassium cyanide (50 mg), potassium dihydrogen phosphate (140 mg) and a non-ionic detergent (1 ml) made up to 1000 ml with distilled water.
3.
• Take about 5 ml (4.98 ml) of Drabkin's solution in a test tube, add 20 microlitres of well-mixed anticoagulated venous blood, rinse the pipette and mix well.
• Allow the mixture to stand at room temperature for 3-10 minutes, then measure the absorbance against a reagent blank at 540 nm in a spectrophotometer or colorimeter.
4.
The reagent should be clear, pale yellow, with pH 7-7.4, and should read zero absorbance against a water blank at 540 nm; it must be stored at room temperature in a brown borosilicate bottle away from sunlight and checked periodically for turbidity or pH change.
5.
Increased absorbance not due to haemoglobin may be caused by turbidity from abnormal plasma proteins, hyperlipaemia, a high WBC count or fat droplets, so these must be considered when reading results.
6.
It is preferred as the reference method because it converts all forms of Hb except sulphaemoglobin readily to HiCN, allows direct comparison with a stable HiCN standard, and the diluted sample and standard are stable, with reagents readily available.
7.
• In the oxyhaemoglobin method, blood is instead diluted in weak alkali (0.04% ammonium hydroxide, specific gravity 0.88), which lyses the red cells so oxyhaemoglobin is released into solution, and the resulting colour is read at 540 nm.
• The oxyhaemoglobin procedure adds 0.02 ml of blood to 4 ml of the ammonia solution, mixes by inverting, and reads with a yellow-green filter; if absorbance exceeds 0.7, the sample is further diluted with an equal volume of water.
• An advantage of the oxyhaemoglobin method is that no time is required for colour development and it is a simple, fast and economical method with an error of only 2-3%.
• A disadvantage of the oxyhaemoglobin method, unlike the HiCN method, is that its standard solution is not easily available and is unstable, and methaemoglobin and carboxyhaemoglobin are not accurately detected.
• Because of these limitations, the cyanmethaemoglobin method is the preferred and most accurate method for determining haemoglobin concentration in the laboratory.
questions.question:
Q42
1. State the principle of the cyanmethaemoglobin (HiCN) method for haemoglobin estimation.
2. List the reagent and its composition.
3. Outline the procedure.
4. State the precautions to be observed.
5. State how the result is reported/calculated.
6. Explain why this technique is preferred as the reference method in practical haematology.
7. Distinguish it from the oxyhaemoglobin method.

questions.answerText:
1.
The specimen is anticoagulated venous blood diluted in Drabkin's solution (potassium ferricyanide, potassium cyanide, potassium dihydrogen phosphate and a non-ionic detergent), used in the cyanmethaemoglobin (HiCN) method.
2.
The principle is that the ferricyanide in the reagent oxidises haemoglobin to methaemoglobin, and potassium cyanide provides cyanide ions to form cyanmethaemoglobin, whose absorbance can be measured spectrophotometrically.
3.
The pipette used to add the blood is rinsed and mixed well with the solution, which is then allowed to stand at room temperature for 3-10 minutes before the absorbance is measured against a reagent blank at 540 nm in a spectrophotometer or colorimeter.
4.
The absorbance reading at 540 nm is compared with the HiCN standard to obtain the haemoglobin concentration, bearing in mind that increased absorbance not due to haemoglobin may result from turbidity caused by abnormal plasma proteins, hyperlipaemia, a high WBC count or fat droplets.
questions.question:
Q39
20 microlitres of well-mixed anticoagulated venous blood is added to about 5 ml of Drabkin's solution in a test tube for haemoglobin estimation.
1. Identify the specimen/reagent and the method being used.
2. State the underlying principle of this method.
3. Outline the procedure that follows.
4. State how the result is obtained/interpreted.

Q52
A patient's PT and APTT are both prolonged compared with control; a mixing study using equal parts of the patient's plasma and normal control plasma is performed and the prolonged times are corrected.
1. Interpret what the correction on mixing indicates.
2. State how this should be recorded.
3. State what this indicates about the mechanism of the prolongation.
4. State the action/further step that would follow if correction had NOT occurred.
questions.answerText:
1.
When PT/APTT/TT are prolonged, a correction study is performed by mixing equal parts of test plasma and control plasma and repeating the test; if the prolonged time is corrected, the study indicates a factor deficiency.
2.
This should be recorded as PT and APTT prolonged at baseline, with correction of both to within the normal difference from control (PT within 3 seconds, APTT within 5 seconds) on 1:1 mixing with normal plasma.
3.
The correction indicates that the patient's own plasma is missing one or more coagulation factors, which are supplied by the normal plasma in the mixture, rather than the patient's plasma containing an inhibitor.
4.
If lack of correction had instead been observed, this would indicate the presence of an inhibitor in the patient's plasma, with common inhibitors being heparin, lupus anticoagulant, or an antibody to one of the coagulation factors.

questions.question:
Q15
1. Describe the basic composition of the reagents used to prepare J.S.B. stain, including its identifying features.
2. State the standard method/setting in which the stain is used in practice.
3. Explain the basic reasoning behind a precaution taken when handling specimens for this stain.
questions.answerText:
1.
• J.S.B. stain (Jaswant-Singh-Bhattacharji stain) uses eosin yellow (water-soluble) and methylene blue as its two principal dyes.
• Other materials and reagents used in its preparation include potassium dichromate, di-sodium hydrogen phosphate (dihydrate), and 1% sulphuric acid.
• Its preparation also requires apparatus such as a round-bottom flask (2 litres), a heating mantle, distilled water and staining jars.
2.
• In standard practice, the stain is prepared and used in two separate staining solutions, J.S.B. I and J.S.B. II, applied in sequence to fixed thin smears.
• It is used specifically for the preparation and staining of blood smears made for malarial parasite screening.
• The stained smear is examined under oil immersion after the two-stage dip-and-wash sequence.
3.
• A precaution taken when handling specimens for this stain is to observe universal precautions while preparing the smears for malarial parasites.
• This includes using gloves, using only disposable needles/lancets, and washing hands.
• It also includes handling and disposing of the sharp instruments and other materials contaminated with blood carefully, to avoid injury.
• The reasoning is that the specimen used for this stain is fresh capillary blood obtained by finger prick, which carries a risk of bloodborne exposure to the person collecting or handling it.
• Careful handling and disposal of sharps also protects against cross-contamination between smears prepared from different patients.
• These precautions therefore protect both the person preparing the smear and the integrity of the specimen being screened for malarial parasites.

1.
Blood group typing techniques include classical methods such as the slide/tile test and the tube test, and relatively modern methods such as microplate testing, column agglutination, solid-phase techniques, and automated testing platforms.
2.
• The slide/tile method is selected for emergency cases because of its prompt results, though it is the least sensitive method among these techniques.
• The tube method is selected for routine transfusion work because it is more sensitive and reliable, allowing both forward and reverse grouping.
• The microplate method is selected where many samples must be tested economically, since one microplate can do the work of 96 test-tubes, using far less antisera and being reusable and cost-effective.
• Column agglutination, using gel or glass beads in a card or strip of microtubes, is selected for direct red cell typing and for the direct or indirect antiglobulin test (DAT/IAT), since serum remains on top of the column after centrifugation, avoiding the need for saline washing.
• Solid-phase techniques, similar to ELISA, are selected where red cell antigens or antibodies are immobilised in microplate wells to detect antigen-antibody interactions using anti-IgG-coated indicator cells.
• Automated testing platforms are selected for high-throughput work, performing multiple tests using solid phase, column agglutination or microtiter plate technology under computerised control with barcode identification.
3.
• False-positive reactions in ABO/D grouping can be caused by rouleaux, cold autoagglutination and cold-reacting alloantibodies, T-activation/polyagglutination, acquired B phenomenon, potentiators, or in vitro bacterial contamination.
• False-negative reactions can be caused by failure to add reagents, loss of reagent potency, failure to identify lysis, or a mixed-field appearance.
• Drying up of the reaction mixture in the slide method can specifically cause aggregation of cells, giving a false positive result.
• The tube method's reliance on centrifugation and correct reagent volumes means that errors here (for example failure to add antisera) directly lead to false-negative or invalid readings.
• An uncorrected technical error at any stage of these methods therefore produces a discrepancy between the true ABO/Rh type of the specimen and the reported result, which is why positive and negative controls are included with every test batch.
questions.question:
Q53
1. Describe the general classification of blood group (BG) typing techniques.
2. State how each type is applied or selected in the laboratory.
3. Explain why a basic error in technique causes a discrepancy in ABO/D grouping results.

questions.answerText:
1.
J.S.B. stain uses two staining solutions (J.S.B. I and J.S.B. II) applied in sequence to fixed thin smears, chiefly for screening malarial parasites.
2.
Materials/reagents: eosin yellow (water-soluble), methylene blue, potassium dichromate, di-sodium hydrogen phosphate (dihydrate), 1% sulphuric acid, a round-bottom flask, a heating mantle, distilled water and staining jars.
3.
• Prepare thin and thick smears from the case on micro slides, de-haemoglobinise the thick smear, and fix the thin smear in methanol for a few minutes.
• Using three staining jars (J.S.B. I, J.S.B. II and tap water), dip the smears in J.S.B. II for a few seconds and immediately wash in water, then drain the slides free of excess water.
• Dip the smears in J.S.B. I for 30-40 seconds, wash well in water, dry, and examine under oil immersion.
4.
Universal precautions must be observed while preparing the smears for malarial parasites: use gloves, use only disposable needles/lancets, wash hands, and handle and dispose of sharp instruments carefully to avoid injury.
5.
The smear is examined under oil immersion, with slide numbers marked on the thin smear using a lead pencil.
6.
It is used/preferred for screening malarial parasites because it uses a defined two-solution sequence (J.S.B. II briefly, then J.S.B. I for a longer, fixed time) suited to routine thin/thick smear staining.
7.
• The Jenner stain, by contrast, is a mixture of several thiazine dyes in a methanol solvent, involving ionic and non-ionic forces, with negatively charged phosphoric acid groups of DNA attracting the purple polychromatic cationic dyes to the nuclei.
• In the Jenner immersion staining protocol, thoroughly dried smears are fixed in absolute methanol for 15 seconds to 5 minutes, stained in Jenner's Stain Solution for 2 minutes, then stained in a mixture of Jenner's Stain Solution with pH 6.6 phosphate buffer and deionised water for 5 minutes.
• The Jenner staining protocol alternative floods the smear with methanol for 15-30 seconds, then with 1 ml Jenner's Stain Solution for 3 minutes, then adds phosphate buffer and deionised water for 45 seconds, followed by a brief rinse.
• J.S.B. staining therefore uses two dedicated J.S.B. solutions in a short-then-longer immersion sequence specifically for malaria screening, while Jenner staining uses a single thiazine-dye stain solution combined separately with a buffer step, in timings measured in minutes rather than seconds.
questions.question:
Q16
1. State the principle of the J.S.B. (Jaswant-Singh-Bhattacharji) stain technique.
2. List the materials/reagents required.
3. Outline the procedure.
4. State the precautions to be observed.
5. State how the stained smear is examined.
6. Explain why this technique is used/preferred in practical haematology.
7. Distinguish it from the Jenner stain technique.

Q58
1. State the principle behind producing monoclonal antisera by hybridoma technology.
2. List the materials/cells involved.
3. Outline the procedure.
4. State the precautions/quality checks to be observed.
5. State how the resulting antisera is assessed/reported.
6. Explain why monoclonal antisera is used/preferred in practical blood grouping.
7. Distinguish it from polyclonal and plant-derived (lectin) antisera preparation.
questions.answerText:
1.
Antibodies of a single specificity are produced by fusing antibody-producing spleen cells with myeloma cells, so that the resulting hybridoma continuously produces monoclonal antibodies against a specific blood group antigen.
2.
Materials/cells: spleen cells harvested from a sheep immunised with A, B or AHG antigen, and mouse myeloma cells.
3.
• The harvested spleen cells of the immunised sheep are fused with mouse myeloma cells.
• This fusion eventually produces the monoclonal antibodies used as antisera.
4.
The resulting antisera must still meet the general quality requirements of a good antisera: crystal-clear appearance, clear reactivity void of rouleaux/gel formation/haemolysis, good avidity (agglutination within 13 seconds), specificity, potency and stability (shelf life about 2 years).
5.
The antisera is assessed by its ability to react specifically and strongly with the intended red cell antigen, without cross-reacting inappropriately.
6.
It is used/preferred because the reagent is free from infections such as HIV, and there is a guarantee of a continuous supply of high-quality antisera.
7.
• A disadvantage of monoclonal antisera, distinguishing it from polyclonal antisera, is that it will not detect other variants of the blood group.
• Polyclonal antisera, produced in animal sources, is instead usually polyclonal in nature and is later purified by absorption/adsorption processes to become monoclonal for specific groups when needed.
• An advantage of polyclonal antibodies, unlike monoclonal ones, is that they recognise multiple epitopes, though a disadvantage is that they are only of animal origin.
• Lectin antisera, by contrast, are derived from plants and are monoclonal in nature; examples include Dolichos biflorus (anti-A1), Vicia cracea (anti-A) and roots of Ononis spinosa (anti-H).
• The three preparation routes (hybridoma-derived monoclonal, purified animal polyclonal, and plant lectin) therefore differ in source and in epitope specificity, though all must meet the same final quality criteria before use in blood grouping.

questions.question:
Q8
1. State the principle behind preparing an EDTA vial (bulb) in the laboratory.
2. List the materials required.
3. Outline the procedure.
4. State the precautions to be observed.
5. State the reporting/calculation associated with the preparation.
6. Explain why EDTA is prepared and used this way in practical haematology.
7. Distinguish it from the preparation of double oxalate solution.
questions.answerText:
1.
The principle is that a measured amount of EDTA powder is dissolved in distilled water to a set percentage, then a small dried volume is deposited per vial so that each vial chelates the calcium in a fixed volume of blood, preventing clotting.
2.
Materials required: physical balance, EDTA powder, distilled water, conical flask, measuring cylinder, micropipette (20 microlitre capacity), spatula, hot air oven, vials and storing bottles.
3.
• Weigh 4 g of EDTA powder on a balanced physical balance, dissolve it in 100 ml of distilled water measured with a measuring cylinder in a conical flask, applying heat if needed for proper mixing.
• Pipette 20 microlitres of the anticoagulant solution into each clear, dry vial, then place the vials in a hot air oven at 60 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes to dry.
• After drying, the EDTA powder remains attached at the bottom of the vials; store the vials with a lid in a safe place, each ready for 1-2 ml of blood.
4.
The oven temperature must not exceed 60 degrees Celsius, to avoid denaturing the EDTA or reducing its power of action.
5.
Calculation: 4 g of EDTA in 100 ml of water gives 4000 mg in 100,000 microlitres, so 20 microlitres of this solution contains 0.8 mg of EDTA, sufficient for 1-2 ml of blood.
6.
It is prepared this way so each vial delivers a controlled, reproducible dose of EDTA that chelates calcium without altering cell size or causing haemolysis, since EDTA preserves the staining and morphology of leucocytes and is used for most haematology tests.
7.
• Double oxalate solution, by contrast, is prepared by dissolving ammonium oxalate and potassium oxalate together (for example 2.4 g ammonium oxalate and 1.6 g potassium oxalate in 100 ml distilled water) rather than a single salt.
• For double oxalate, 0.2 ml of the stock solution (containing 8 mg of oxalates) is used per vial to prevent clotting of 3-4 ml of blood, compared with 20 microlitres of EDTA solution (0.8 mg) per 1-2 ml of blood.
• Double oxalate vials are also dried at 60 degrees Celsius, but the resulting anticoagulant is not suitable for peripheral blood film examination or blood banking, unlike EDTA which is preferred for blood smears and CBC.
• The two anticoagulants therefore differ in their chemical basis (a single chelator versus a balanced mixture of two oxalate salts) and in the laboratory purposes for which their prepared vials may be used.

questions.question:
Q32
On low power (10x) examination of a blood film, red cells are seen aligned one upon another resembling stacks of coins in one area, while in another area red cells show more irregular, round clumping.
1. Identify the two findings being described.
2. State the technique used to detect and distinguish them.
3. State the conditions in which each finding is seen.
4. State the follow-up point to note when either finding is observed.
questions.answerText:
1.
The first finding (cells aligned one upon another like stacks of coins) is rouleaux formation, while the second (irregular, round clumping) is agglutination.
2.
Both are assessed on low power (10x) at the start of microscopic analysis of the film, when checking whether red cell agglutination or excessive rouleaux formation is present.
3.
Rouleaux formation occurs in paraproteinaemia (monoclonal gammopathy) and with elevated plasma fibrinogen or globulin levels, whereas agglutination is seen with cold agglutinin, anti-RBC antibody, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and macroglobulinaemia.
4.
Since agglutination is more irregular and round compared with the linear stacking of rouleaux, correctly distinguishing the two on low power is the follow-up point to note before proceeding to assess leucocyte number, distribution and staining, and to find an area where red cells are evenly distributed for detailed analysis.

1.
• RBC colour on a blood film is classified as normochromic (normal intensity of staining), hypochromic, hyperchromic, or anisochromic.
• Colour is determined by the haemoglobin content of the RBC, and normal haemoglobin concentration is about 150±20 g/l in males and 135±15 g/l in females.
2.
• Hypochromic cells show a decrease in haemoglobin content with an increase in central pallor to more than a third of the cell, and decreased MCH and MCHC; they are seen in iron deficiency anaemia and thalassaemia.
• Hyperchromic cells stain deeply with less central pallor and an increase in MCH; they are seen in megaloblastic anaemia and in hereditary spherocytosis (where MCH is normal but MCHC is increased).
• Anisochromia is the presence of hypochromic and normochromic cells in the same film, also called a dimorphic blood picture, seen in sideroblastic anaemia, some weeks after iron therapy, and after transfusion of normal cells into a hypochromic anaemia.
• Polychromatophilia, a blue-grey tint due to residual Hb and RNA in young cells, implies reticulocytosis and is seen in haemolysis and acute blood loss.
3.
• A normal RBC is a circular, homogenous disc of fairly uniform size (6-8 micrometres) with deep pink cytoplasm and central pallor less than one third of the cell diameter.
• If the smear is too thick, cells overlap and central pallor cannot be assessed properly, so hypochromia or hyperchromia may be wrongly read or missed.
• If staining is faulty (for example, an excessively pink stain from insufficient staining time), erythrocytes appear bright red or orange, which can be mistaken for true hypochromia.
• Conversely, an excessively blue stain from prolonged staining or too high alkalinity makes erythrocytes appear blue-green, which can obscure the correct colour assessment.
• Since colour classification depends on the intensity of haemoglobin staining, any preparation or staining artefact directly distorts the reading of normochromia, hypochromia or hyperchromia.
• Correct classification therefore requires a well-made, evenly stained film examined in the zone of morphology where red cells are evenly distributed and not distorted.
questions.question:
Q23
1. Describe the general classification of red blood cell colour variations seen on a blood film.
2. State how each type is applied/recognised in the laboratory as a diagnostic clue.
3. Explain why a basic error in film preparation or reading leads to an inaccurate classification of RBC colour.

questions.answerText:
1.
• Haemoglobin estimation methods are classified as colour-based methods (based on the colour of haemoglobin or its derivative), physical methods (based on specific gravity), chemical methods (based on iron content), gasometric methods (based on oxygen-combining capacity), and spectrophotometric methods.
• Colour-based (visual comparison) methods include the Talliquist scale method, Dare's method, WHO haemoglobin colour scale, Spencer method, Sahli's (acid haematin) method, alkaline haematin method, and Haldane's carboxyhaemoglobin method.
• Spectrophotometric methods include the cyanmethaemoglobin (HiCN) method and the oxyhaemoglobin method, both based on Beer's and Lambert's law relating optical density to concentration.
2.
• The Talliquist and Dare's methods, based on direct visual matching, are noted to be totally unsatisfactory with a high degree of error (plus or minus 20-50%), so they are selected only where nothing more accurate is available.
• The WHO haemoglobin colour scale is selected for simple, inexpensive, reliable estimation in communities where photometric measurement is not possible, and is used in blood donor selection.
• The specific gravity (copper sulphate) method is selected as a blood donor screening procedure to ensure a donor is not anaemic, since there is no need to know the donor's exact Hb value, only whether it meets a cut-off.
• The chemical (iron content) and gasometric (oxygen-combining capacity) methods are selected as reference methods for accuracy, such as in preparing the cyanmethaemoglobin standard, but are too complex and time-consuming for routine clinical laboratory use.
• The cyanmethaemoglobin method is selected as the preferred routine and reference method, being simple, accurate, and giving a stable diluted sample comparable with a stable standard.
3.
• Sources of error in haemoglobinometry include errors in sampling, such as inadequate flow of blood from a finger prick, excessive squeezing of the finger, or prolonged use of a tourniquet, which concentrates blood cells.
• Further sources of error include insufficient mixing of venous blood, small clots from inadequate mixing with EDTA, adding too little blood to the diluting fluid, and air bubbles trapped in pipettes.
• Reagents left exposed to prolonged light or allowed to freeze, or a reference preparation that is out of date or deteriorated, are also recognised sources of error, along with faulty or dirty equipment such as broken or chipped pipettes.
• Selecting a method inappropriate to the setting (for example a screening method where an exact reference value is required) or committing any of these sampling/reagent/equipment errors will therefore give a haemoglobin value that does not reflect the true concentration in the specimen.
questions.question:
Q44
1. Describe the general classification of methods for estimating haemoglobin.
2. State how each type is applied or selected in the laboratory.
3. Explain why a basic error in method selection or technique leads to an inaccurate haemoglobin result.

questions.answerText:
1.
The reading was obtained by allowing the acid haematin brown colour to develop for at least 10 minutes, diluting with distilled water drop by drop with continuous mixing, and matching the colour with the glass plates in the comparator at eye level against natural light.
2.
The result should be recorded as the level of the fluid at its lower meniscus, read on the graduated scale in grams per decilitre, giving 11.5 g/dl.
3.
This result indicates the haemoglobin concentration of the specimen as estimated by this method, to be interpreted against the normal ranges (13-18 g/dl for men, 11-16 g/dl for women).
4.
A relevant precaution/limitation is that the reading must be taken without undue delay, since the brown colour of acid haematin is not stable, and forms of haemoglobin such as carboxyhaemoglobin, methaemoglobin and sulphaemoglobin are not converted to acid haematin and so would not be reflected in this reading.
questions.question:
Q41
A blood specimen is tested by Sahli's method: blood is drawn to the 20 mm mark and added to N/10 HCl in the graduated tube, left to stand for 10 minutes, then diluted with distilled water until the colour matches the comparator, giving a reading at the lower meniscus of 11.5 g/dl.
1. Interpret how this reading was obtained.
2. State how the result should be recorded.
3. State what this result indicates about the specimen.
4. State a precaution/limitation relevant to accepting this reading.

questions.answerText:
1.
The specimen is a drop of the patient's blood tested against anti-A, anti-B and anti-D reagents on a glass slide or white porcelain support, using the slide/tile method of blood grouping.
2.
The principle is a distinct chemical reaction between specific antibodies and blood group antigens, monitored as agglutination or blood clumping, to determine the ABO and rhesus D (RhD) type of the blood.
3.
The slide is divided into three parts, and a drop of the blood is mixed with anti-A, anti-B and anti-D separately in each part; the agglutination pattern is then visually observed.
4.
From the agglutination pattern, the ABO and RhD type can be determined; the test completes in 5-10 minutes and is valuable for prompt results in emergencies, but it is an insensitive method that cannot detect weakly or rarely reactive antigens and drying of the reaction mixture can cause false-positive aggregation, so it is used only for preliminary matching.
questions.question:
Q57
A glass slide divided into three parts has a drop of a patient's blood mixed separately with anti-A, anti-B and anti-D reagents, for an urgent emergency blood grouping request.
1. Identify the specimen/reagents and the method being used.
2. State the underlying principle of this method.
3. Outline the procedure.
4. State the expected result/interpretation and a limitation to note.

questions.answerText:
1.
• Platelets are formed from megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, and the normal platelet count is 150-450 x10^9/l, with a lifespan of 8-9 days.
• On a stained blood smear, platelets are anucleate, round or discoid bodies, 1-2 micrometres in size, with fine purple-pink granules.
• The platelet has a phospholipid cell membrane into which are inserted glycoproteins (GP) that act as major cell receptors and antigens of the platelet, such as GPIb-IX (receptor for von Willebrand factor) and GPIIb-IIIa (receptor for fibrinogen).
2.
• In standard practice, platelets are assessed on the same blood film area used for WBC and platelet estimates, with the red cells barely touching, and it is expected to see approximately 7-15 platelets per oil-immersion (x100) field.
• A platelet count per high-power field is used to estimate circulating platelets, where one platelet per field is equivalent to approximately 15,000-20,000 platelets in circulation; an increase is termed thrombocytosis and a decrease thrombocytopenia.
• All platelet counts must be verified by a blood smear as part of standard screening for haemostasis.
3.
• A common precaution is to collect the specimen into an anticoagulant that does not cause platelet clumping, since normal platelet number and clumping status directly affect count accuracy.
• EDTA is preferred for this purpose because sequestrene (EDTA) prevents the clumping of platelets and is therefore the anticoagulant of choice where a total platelet count is required.
• A platelet count done from a finger prick specimen is not considered reliable, so venous blood collected into the correct anticoagulant is used instead for screening tests.
• This reasoning matters because platelet adhesion and aggregation depend on normal platelet number and functioning membrane glycoprotein receptors, so an artefactually low or clumped count could be misread as true thrombocytopenia.
• Careful specimen handling therefore protects the accuracy of both the platelet count and the assessment of platelet morphology on the film.
• This is consistent with the broader principle that an anticoagulant for haematological examination must minimise platelet aggregation as one of its key required characteristics.
questions.question:
Q33
1. Describe the basic structure of the platelet as seen on a stained blood film, including its identifying features.
2. State the standard method/setting in which platelets are assessed in practice.
3. Explain the basic reasoning behind a common precaution needed when handling a specimen for platelet assessment.

Q11
1. Describe the basic composition of Giemsa stain, including its identifying features.
2. State the standard method in which it is used in practice.
3. Explain the basic reasoning behind a common precaution associated with it.
questions.answerText:
1.
• Giemsa stain is mainly composed of Eosin Y, an acidic component that stains basic components of cells such as haemoglobin.
• It also contains Azure B (methylene blue), a basic component that stains acidic components of cells such as the DNA/RNA of the WBC nucleus.
• Materials associated with it include a slide holder/rack, the stain reagent itself, and methanol, which is used to fix the cells on the slide.
• A buffer (0.05M Na2PO4, pH 6.4) and distilled water kept in a glass bottle for at least 24 hours at pH 6.4-6.8 are also required.
2.
• In standard practice, the smear is put into methanol and fixed for 1-2 minutes, then excess methanol is removed from the smear.
• The smear is then inserted into the stain jar and left in the stain for 2 minutes.
• It is next inserted into a buffer jar and allowed to stand for 4-8 minutes, then rinsed thoroughly with a stream of distilled water.
• It is allowed to air dry, ready for differentiation of blood cells on a peripheral smear.
3.
• The staining time varies from manufacturer to manufacturer, so the exact time given in the kit manual of each procedure must be followed.
• This precaution exists because the concentration of the stain and the time of exposure to the stain and buffer determine the quality of staining.
• A low concentration or too short an exposure time produces pale, under-stained cells, while a high concentration or too long an exposure produces an over-stained, dark smear.
• Following the manufacturer's stated timing therefore prevents faulty staining that would distort interpretation of cell morphology.

questions.question:
Q31
1. Describe the general classification of red blood cell size variation (anisocytosis) seen on a blood film.
2. State how each type is applied or recognised in the laboratory as a diagnostic clue.
3. Explain why the MCV becomes unreliable as a measure of size in certain circumstances.
questions.answerText:
1.
• Anisocytosis is variation in the size of red blood cells; the normal MCV is 80-100 fl, with microcytes defined as MCV less than 80 fl and macrocytes as MCV greater than 100 fl.
• Microcytes are seen when hemoglobin synthesis is defective, as in iron deficiency anaemia, thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease, and sideroblastic anaemia.
• Macrocytes are seen when the MCV is increased; macro-ovalocytes are seen in megaloblastic anaemia and myelodysplastic syndrome, while round macrocytes are seen in alcoholism and liver disease.
2.
• Anisocytosis is a feature of most anaemias, so its presence on a blood film is applied as a general, non-specific clue that red cell size is not uniform.
• Distinguishing macro-ovalocytes from round macrocytes is applied diagnostically to separate megaloblastic/myelodysplastic causes from alcoholism/liver disease as the underlying cause of macrocytosis.
• The RBC Distribution Width (RDW), an index of RBC size variation with a normal range of 11.5% to 14.5%, is applied to quantitate the amount of anisocytosis seen on the peripheral blood smear.
3.
• MCV is the average size of the RBC, calculated as haematocrit x 10 divided by the RBC count (in millions), and RBCs are considered normocytic if this falls in the 80-100 fl range.
• MCV is stated not to be reliable when there is marked anisocytosis, since it represents an average of red cell sizes.
• Where there is marked anisocytosis, for example a mixed population of microcytes and macrocytes (as in a dimorphic blood picture), the calculated average MCV can fall within the normal range even though individual cells are abnormally small or large.
• This is why microscopic examination of the peripheral blood smear is required for evaluation of anaemia, in addition to the automatically calculated RBC indices.
• The RDW is therefore used alongside MCV specifically because it can flag significant size variation that a normal average MCV might otherwise conceal.
• Relying on MCV alone, without smear examination or RDW, can therefore give a false impression of a uniform red cell population when marked anisocytosis is actually present.

1.
In the tube method, both forward (cell) grouping and reverse (serum) grouping are carried out, using antibody-antigen agglutination to determine ABO and Rh type.
2.
Materials/reagents: test tubes, saline as a diluent, anti-A and anti-B reagents (and anti-D for Rh typing), and RBC reagent groups of A1 and B for reverse grouping.
3.
• For forward grouping, blood cells are placed in two test tubes with saline, and one drop of anti-A and anti-B is added separately to each; the tubes are centrifuged for a few minutes and the resultant matrix is gently shaken to observe agglutination.
• For reverse grouping, the patient's serum is treated against RBC reagent groups of A1 and B, and the resulting agglutination pattern is monitored.
4.
Positive and negative controls should be included with every test or batch of manual tests.
5.
Results are read and graded by observing the agglutination pattern; the method allows fairly long incubation without the tube drying up.
6.
• It is preferred because it is more sensitive and reliable than the slide test, uses a low volume of reagents, allows some unexpected antigens to be detected, and centrifugation enhances the reaction, allowing weaker antigens and antibodies to be detected.
• A disadvantage is that in infants, reverse grouping is somewhat difficult to perform since they produce insufficient antibody for the test.
7.
• The slide/tile method, by contrast, divides a glass slide or white porcelain support into three parts, mixing a drop of blood separately with anti-A, anti-B and anti-D, and observing the agglutination pattern visually.
• The slide method completes in 5-10 minutes, is inexpensive and requires only a small volume of reagents, making it valuable for prompt results in emergency cases.
• However, the slide method is an insensitive method that cannot be conducted for weakly or rarely reactive antigens, is only useful for preliminary matching, and drying of the reaction mixture can cause aggregation of cells giving false positive results.
• The tube method is therefore generally used for reliable, transfusion-grade grouping, while the slide method is reserved for rapid preliminary matching in emergencies.
questions.question:
Q54
1. State the principle of the tube method for ABO/Rh blood grouping.
2. List the materials/reagents required.
3. Outline the procedure.
4. State the precautions/controls to be observed.
5. State how the result is reported.
6. Explain why the tube method is used/preferred in practical haematology.
7. Distinguish it from the slide/tile method.

Q9
1. State the principle of the wedge (slide) blood smear technique.
2. List the apparatus/materials required.
3. Outline the procedure for making the smear.
4. State the precautions to be observed.
5. State how a well-made smear is reported/recognised.
6. Explain why this technique is used/preferred in practical haematology.
7. Distinguish it from the coverslip technique and the spin technique.
questions.answerText:
1.
A drop of blood is spread thinly across a slide using a spreader slide held at an angle, producing a tongue-shaped film for single-layer microscopic examination.
2.
Apparatus: spreaders, clean slides, and a blood capillary tube or micropipette (10 microlitres); the blood used is EDTA-anticoagulated or fresh finger-prick blood.
3.
• A 2-3 mm drop of blood is placed about 1 cm from one end of the slide, with the slide held flat on a surface.
• A spreader slide is held at a 30-45 degree angle against the drop, drawn back, then pushed forward with one light, smooth, moderate-speed stroke.
• One edge is labelled with the patient name, lab ID and date, and the film is rapidly air-dried by waving the slide or using an electric fan.
4.
• A correctly sized drop must be used and the spreader pushed smoothly and completely across the slide with its clean edge kept flush against the slide at the correct angle.
• The film must be fixed promptly, since a delay in fixing or methanol contaminated with water causes cellular degenerative changes.
5.
A good smear is tongue-shaped with a smooth tail, does not cover the entire slide, has both thick and thin areas with a gradual transition, and is free of lines or holes.
6.
• It is preferred because it allows evaluation of anaemia and thrombocytopenia/thrombocytosis, and identification of abnormal cells such as blasts, abnormal promyelocytes and atypical lymphoid cells.
• It also allows detection of infections such as malaria and microfilaria, and of inclusions such as basophilic stippling, Howell-Jolly bodies and Cabot rings.
7.
• In the coverslip technique, a drop is touched onto a coverslip which is placed crosswise on a second coverslip film-side down, pulled apart quickly, then dried, stained and mounted film-side down on a slide.
• In the spin technique, which is automated, a drop placed at the centre of a slide is spun at high speed in a special cytospin centrifuge so the blood spreads uniformly, then it is dried and stained.

questions.question:
Q21
A Romanowsky-stained peripheral blood film from a patient is examined under oil immersion and shows numerous red cells that are boat-shaped or crescent-shaped rather than the usual biconcave disc shape.
1. Identify the abnormal red cell finding.
2. State the technique/stain used to detect this finding.
3. State the condition/haemoglobin type in which this finding is characteristically present.
4. State how the finding should be recorded/reported and any follow-up point to note.
questions.answerText:
1.
The cells described are sickle cells, which are sickle (boat-shaped) or crescent-shaped red cells.
2.
They are detected by examination of a peripheral blood film stained with a Romanowsky stain (e.g. Wright's or Leishman's stain) under oil immersion.
3.
Sickle cells are present in the film of patients with homozygosity for Hb S.
4.
• The finding should be recorded on the blood film report as the presence of sickle cells.
• It should be noted that sickle cells are usually absent in neonates and are rare in patients with a high percentage of Hb F, which is a relevant follow-up consideration in interpreting the film, for example in a very young patient.

questions.question:
Q20
1. Describe the basic structure of a normal red blood cell as seen on a stained blood film, including its identifying features.
2. State the standard method/setting in which this description is applied in practice.
3. Explain the basic reasoning behind a common precaution needed when assessing it.
questions.answerText:
1.
• The normal red blood cell is a biconcave disc shape, with central pallor of approximately one third of the red cell diameter, and lacks intracytoplasmic inclusions.
• In the blood of a healthy person, RBCs are circular, homogenous discs of nearly uniform size (6-8 micrometres), with deep pink cytoplasm and central pallor less than a third of the diameter.
• Red cells are pink in colour when stained with Romanowsky dye, since eosin in the stain yields red erythrocytes.
2.
• This structural description is used in practice as the reference point for peripheral blood film examination, against which abnormal variations in cell size, shape and colour, or the presence of intracellular inclusions, are compared to suggest a range of abnormalities.
• It is applied specifically when the microscopic analysis begins on low power (10x) to find an area where red cells are evenly distributed and not distorted, before detailed analysis is carried out on high power or oil immersion (100x).
3.
• A common precaution is to examine red cells only in the correctly prepared zone of the film, since the normal red cell's biconcave shape and central pallor can only be reliably assessed where the film is neither too thick nor too thin.
• In too thin an area or too thick an area of a film, cells may appear artificially distorted or overlapping, so the true central pallor and size cannot be accurately judged.
• The reasoning behind this precaution is that identification of abnormal variations such as hypochromia, anisocytosis or poikilocytosis depends entirely on comparison with the normal biconcave, centrally pale disc.
• If the reference appearance of the normal red cell is not correctly recognised due to a poorly made film, apparent abnormalities may be wrongly reported.
• The precaution therefore also requires that staining be satisfactory and cell distribution uniform before evaluation is attempted.
• Only once these conditions are met can size, shape, colour, arrangement and inclusions of the red blood cells be reliably evaluated.
• This underlies why peripheral blood smear examination begins with a macroscopic check of the quality of the smear and a low-power scan before proceeding to detailed morphological assessment.

1.
Screening tests for haemostasis include the full blood count (platelet count), bleeding time (BT), prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), and thrombin time (TT).
2.
• The platelet count from the FBC is applied first, and all platelet counts must be verified by a blood smear as part of screening.
• Bleeding time, measuring the platelet-vessel wall interaction, is applied using the Template method (normal 2-9 minutes) or the Ivy method (normal 2-6 minutes), though it is now accepted not to be a routine screening test.
• PT is applied to detect abnormalities of the extrinsic and common pathways (factors I, II, V, VII and X), measured as the time for citrated plasma to clot on addition of tissue thromboplastin and calcium chloride, with a normal manual value of 12-14 seconds.
• APTT is applied to measure all coagulation factors except FVII and FXIII, testing the intrinsic and common pathways, with a normal manual value of 30-35 seconds, and is used to monitor heparin therapy.
• TT is applied to measure clottable fibrinogen, with a normal value of 12-14 seconds, and is increased in deficiency of factor I, dysfibrinogenaemia, presence of heparin, and elevated FDP levels.
3.
• The blood samples for screening must be correctly collected: 1-2 ml in EDTA for the complete blood count, and 4.5 ml venous blood mixed with 0.5 ml of 3.2% sodium citrate for plasma clotting tests, from a clean venepuncture.
• If sampling is done from a central line, it must be flushed with normal saline and the first 4-5 ml of blood discarded before the test sample is drawn, and the sample must be processed within 1-2 hours.
• PT is considered prolonged if the test and control values show a difference greater than 3 seconds, and a control plasma is always run with the test; an incorrect or missing control invalidates interpretation of the result.
• When PT, APTT or TT are prolonged, a correction study is performed by mixing equal parts of test and control plasma and repeating the test; correction indicates a factor deficiency, while lack of correction indicates an inhibitor such as heparin or lupus anticoagulant.
• Since bleeding time is very operator dependent, an inconsistent standard wound or technique directly affects the reliability of the result, which is one reason it is a poor predictor of abnormal surgical bleeding.
• An incorrectly collected, delayed, or under-diluted/over-diluted citrate specimen will therefore give a falsely shortened or prolonged clotting time that does not reflect the patient's true coagulation status.

questions.answerText:
1.
The stated procedure specifies that if the cut bleeds for more than 10 minutes, the test should be discontinued, so this observation has reached that limit.
2.
The action to be taken is to discontinue the test at this point rather than continue timing further.
3.
This should be recorded as a bleeding time greater than 10 minutes (test discontinued), rather than as a specific numeric result, since the normal bleeding time is 3-5 minutes and the test is not continued beyond 10 minutes.
4.
A relevant limitation is that this method is the least standardised of the bleeding time methods, has less precision and accuracy, and it is difficult to obtain a standardised wound, which should be considered before drawing firm conclusions from a prolonged result.

1.
The inclusions described are Howell-Jolly bodies, smooth single large round inclusions that are remnants of nuclear chromatin.
2.
They are detected by microscopic examination of a Romanowsky-stained peripheral blood film under oil immersion.
3.

questions.answerText:
1.
The specimen is whole blood mixed with 3.8% tri-sodium citrate in a 1:4 ratio (blood to citrate), loaded into a 200 mm tube, which is the Westergren method for ESR.
2.
The principle is that erythrocytes are allowed to sediment at room temperature in a standard narrow-bore glass tube, and the rate of sedimentation, determined by plasma proteins, measures the distance in millimetres that the cells fall in 1 hour.
3.
The mixed blood/citrate specimen is placed upright in the 200 mm Westergren tube and allowed to stand undisturbed at room temperature for 1 hour, with plasma remaining above the sedimenting red cells.
