Q10
1. Describe the general classification/types of Romanowsky stains used in haematology.
2. State how each type is applied or selected in the laboratory.
3. Explain why a basic error in handling or technique with these stains leads to an inaccurate or invalid result.
questions.answerText:
1.
• Romanowsky stains include Leishman stain, Giemsa stain, Wright and Wright-Giemsa stain, May-Grunwald stain, Field stain, Jenner stain and J.S.B (Jaswant-Singh-Bhattacharji) stain.
• All these combinations have two essential ingredients: methylene blue (or azure, a basic dye) and eosin (an acidic dye).
2.
• Leishman and Wright stains are applied to differentiate and identify leucocytes, malaria parasites and trypanosomes on thin blood films.
• Giemsa stain is applied mainly for examination of blood films for parasitic infections, particularly malaria, and as a differential stain for erythrocytes, platelets and leucocytes.
• Field stain is selected for rapid diagnosis, using separate short-duration dips in Field's stain A (methylene blue) and stain B (eosin) for thin films, and a modified sequence for thick films that are not methanol-fixed.
• J.S.B stain is selected for staining smears prepared for malarial parasite screening, using J.S.B. II followed by J.S.B. I in separate staining jars.
3.
• Faulty staining can produce an excessively blue stain, caused by too-thick films, prolonged staining, inadequate washing, or too high alkalinity of the stain or diluent.
• On an excessively blue-stained film, erythrocytes appear blue-green and nuclear chromatin appears deep blue to black, which can be corrected by using ideal film thickness, reducing staining time, using less stain with more diluent, and prolonging washing.
• Faulty staining can also produce an excessively pink stain, caused by insufficient staining time, prolonged washing, or too high acidity of the stain or buffer.
• On an excessively pink-stained film, erythrocytes appear bright red or orange and nuclear chromatin appears pale blue, corrected by prolonging staining time, reducing washing, or adjusting the buffer pH.
• A precipitate on the film can also occur from unclean slides, drying during staining, inadequate washing, or use of unfiltered stain, and is corrected by using clean slides, avoiding drying, washing until thinner parts look pinkish, and filtering the stain.
• Since the pH of the buffered water is mainly responsible for the staining reactions, an uncorrected pH or timing error therefore distorts the colour of cell nuclei and granules and invalidates cell identification.

questions.question:
Q12
1. State the principle of the Giemsa stain technique.
2. List the materials/reagents required.
3. Outline the procedure.
4. State the precautions to be observed.
5. State how the stained film is examined/reported.
6. Explain why this technique is used/preferred in practical haematology.
7. Distinguish it from the May-Grünwald-Giemsa (MGG) combined procedure.
questions.answerText:
1.
Giemsa stain differentiates blood cells using a stock solution prepared by mixing Giemsa powder with glycerine and methyl alcohol, diluted in buffered water before use.
2.
Materials/reagents: 0.15 g Giemsa powder, 12.5 ml glycerine, 12.5 ml methyl alcohol (for the stock solution), and buffered water for dilution (1 volume of stock to 9 volumes of buffered water).
3.
• Prepare the stock solution by mixing 0.15 g Giemsa powder in 12.5 ml glycerine and 12.5 ml methyl alcohol, then before use dissolve one volume of stock solution in nine volumes of buffered water (dilution 1:9).
• Fill a staining dish with the diluted staining solution, place thin and thick films into the dish, and stain the blood slides for 45 minutes.
• Wash the slides in water, dry them, and examine under the oil immersion lens of the microscope.
4.
It is used as a special stain for examination of blood films for parasitic infections, particularly malaria; it is important to note that films may be under- or over-stained if the concentration, dilution ratio or staining time is not followed exactly.
5.
On this stain, it produces a blue-purple coloured staining of the nucleus and red-pink coloration of the cytoplasm and cytoplasmic granules.
6.
It is used/preferred because, as well as differentiating erythrocytes, platelets and leucocytes and their nuclear/cytoplasmic components, it is used in cytogenetics and histopathology for diagnosis of malaria, spirochetes, other blood parasites, and organisms such as Chlamydia trachomatis inclusion bodies, Borrelia spp, Yersinia pestis, Histoplasma spp and Pneumocystis jiroveci cysts.
7.
• The May-Grünwald-Giemsa procedure, by contrast, is a two-step staining procedure combining a May-Grünwald stain step with a Giemsa stain step to produce the Romanowsky effect (a wide range of hue/colour).
• In one MGG protocol, Giemsa stain is diluted 1:20 with deionised water (or pH 7.2 buffered water for a bluer colouration), slides are placed in May-Grünwald stain for 5 minutes, then in working phosphate/Trizma buffer (pH 7.2) for 1.5 minutes.
• Slides are then placed in the dilute Giemsa solution for 15-20 minutes, rinsed briefly in deionised water, and air-dried; a caution given is that thick films need careful rinsing since they are not fixed before staining, and improper rinsing causes loss of blood from the film.
• The straightforward Giemsa procedure therefore uses a single stain diluted 1:9 for a fixed 45-minute stain, while the MGG procedure sequentially combines two different stains (May-Grünwald then Giemsa) with separate buffer steps, taking longer overall and producing a more intense colour, as May-Grünwald-Giemsa staining takes longer to perform than Wright-Giemsa staining and produces intense colour after staining.

1.
Antigen-antibody agglutination is detected in the small wells of a microwell plate, which are rapidly replacing test tubes in many laboratories for blood group typing.
2.
A microplate consists of a small tray with 96 small wells, each able to hold between 200 and 300 microlitres of reagent, along with antisera and a saline suspension of the patient's red cells.
3.
• Place 1 drop (25 microlitres) of antisera into each appropriate well of the plate, then add 1 drop of a 2-3% saline suspension of the patient's red cells to each antisera.
• Test anti-A, anti-B and anti-AB (if used) with A, B and O cells to control the reagents, then incubate at room temperature (20-23 degrees Celsius) for 60 minutes.
• Mix the plate gently to resuspend unagglutinated cells and examine the plate over a white surface, then record the reactions.
4.
Positive and negative controls (A, B and O cells against the antisera) should be included, and the plate must be handled carefully to avoid contamination if not thoroughly cleaned between uses.
5.
Reactions are recorded after examining the plate over a white surface following gentle mixing to resuspend unagglutinated cells.
6.
It is preferred because one microplate can do the work of 96 test tubes, it uses far less antisera, is very cost-effective, and the microwell plates can be reused.
7.
• The column agglutination technique, by contrast, uses gel or glass beads to trap agglutinated red cells in a card or strip of several microtubes that allow performance of several tests simultaneously.
• In column agglutination, red cells interact with antibodies in chambers at the top of each column, and the columns are then centrifuged to force the red cells into the column.
• The column medium separates agglutinated red cells, which are too large to enter the gel matrix and remain at the top, from non-agglutinated cells that pass through the gel pores to the bottom.
• A key advantage of column agglutination not shared by the microplate method is that, as red cells enter the column, serum remains on top, obviating the need for saline washing in antiglobulin tests.
questions.question:

1. State the principle of the microplate method for blood grouping.
2. List the materials/apparatus required.

Q29
1. Describe the general classification/types of red blood cell inclusions seen on a blood film.
2. State how each type is applied or selected as a diagnostic clue in the laboratory.
3. Explain why a basic error in staining choice leads to an inaccurate identification of an inclusion.
questions.answerText:
1.
RBC inclusions include basophilic stippling (punctate basophilia), Howell-Jolly bodies, Pappenheimer bodies, Heinz bodies, Cabot rings, and malarial stippling.
2.
• Basophilic stippling consists of irregular basophilic granules of variable size that stain deep blue with Wright's stain; fine stippling is seen with increased polychromatophilia, while coarse stippling is seen with lead/heavy metal poisoning and disturbed erythropoiesis.
• Howell-Jolly bodies are smooth, single, large, round inclusions that are remnants of nuclear chromatin, seen singly in megaloblastic anaemia, haemolytic anaemia and post-splenectomy, or multiply in megaloblastic anaemia and abnormal erythropoiesis.
• Pappenheimer bodies are small, single or multiple, peripherally sited, angular basophilic inclusions, smaller than Howell-Jolly bodies and composed of haemosiderin; they are seen in sideroblastic erythropoiesis, hyposplenism, myelodysplastic syndrome and haemolytic anaemia.
• Heinz bodies are purple/blue, large, single or multiple inclusions attached to the inner surface of the red cell, representing precipitated haemoglobin; they are seen post-splenectomy, in oxidative stress and G6PD deficiency, but are not seen on Romanowsky stain (only on supravital stains).
• Cabot rings are ring-shaped or figure-of-eight or loop-shaped, red or reddish-purple with Wright's stain, and are observed rarely in pernicious anaemia and lead poisoning.
• Malarial stippling consists of fine, purplish-red granules of plasmodium vivax on Wright stain, with the infected red cells appearing larger than normal.
3.
• Pappenheimer bodies can be confirmed in nature by Perls' stain, since they are composed of haemosiderin (iron), while Heinz bodies specifically require a supravital stain and are not seen with the routine Romanowsky stain.
• If only a Romanowsky-stained film is examined, Heinz bodies will be missed entirely because they are not seen on this type of stain, leading to a false-negative identification of oxidative haemoglobin damage.
• Conversely, using Perls' stain when Pappenheimer bodies are suspected but not confirming the iron nature of the inclusion could lead to it being mistaken for basophilic stippling or another basophilic inclusion.
• An error in staining choice therefore means an inclusion that requires a specific stain (supravital for Heinz bodies, Perls' for confirming Pappenheimer bodies) may either be missed or misidentified as a different inclusion.
• Correct identification of the inclusion type consequently depends on selecting and correctly applying the staining method appropriate to that inclusion, not on the Romanowsky stain alone.

questions.question:
Q3
A laboratory scientist receives a venous blood sample collected into a lavender (purple)-stopper tube for a complete blood count and blood film request.
1. Identify the specimen/anticoagulant presented.
2. State the underlying principle of using this anticoagulant for this purpose.
3. Outline the procedure that follows once the specimen is confirmed suitable.
4. State the expected result/interpretation of a well-processed sample.
questions.answerText:
1.
The specimen is whole blood anticoagulated with EDTA (lavender/purple stopper), the standard collection tube for most haematology tests.
2.
EDTA acts by chelating/removing ionised calcium, which is required for blood to clot, so the anticoagulant combines with and removes calcium ions, keeping the blood in a fluid state without altering leucocyte staining or causing platelet clumping.
3.
A blood smear is made from the EDTA-anticoagulated blood within 1 hour of collection to avoid distortion of cell morphology, using the wedge technique with a spreader slide, and the smear is stained with a Romanowsky stain before examination.
4.
A correctly processed EDTA sample gives preserved red cell, white cell and platelet morphology on the film and a full blood count reflecting the patient's true cellular picture, since EDTA is the anticoagulant of choice for CBC and total platelet count.

questions.question:
Q25
A reticulocyte count performed on a patient using new methylene blue supravital stain gives a value of 6% of erythrocytes, in a patient being treated for anaemia.
1. Interpret what this reticulocyte value indicates relative to the normal range.
2. State how the corrected reticulocyte value should be calculated and recorded.
3. State what this result indicates about bone marrow activity.
4. State the action/significance that follows from this reading.
questions.answerText:
1.
The normal range for the reticulocyte count is 0.5-2.0% of all erythrocytes, so 6% is elevated above normal.
2.
The reticulocyte count is recorded after correction using the standard reticulocyte correction formula: the retic count multiplied by the patient's HCT, divided by the expected/standard HCT (45%), multiplied by 100.
3.
Reticulocytes are non-nucleated RBCs that still contain RNA, visualised by staining with supravital dyes such as new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue, and the reticulocyte count is useful in determining the response and potential of the bone marrow.
4.
An increase in the reticulocyte count indicates that the bone marrow is responding to the anaemia by increasing red cell production, which is the significant action point in this patient's monitoring.

1.
The cells described are tear drop cells (dacrocytes), in which one side of the cell is tapered and the other is blunt.
2.
They are detected by microscopic examination of a Romanowsky-stained peripheral blood film under oil immersion.
3.
Tear drop cells are seen in myelofibrosis, thalassaemia, haemoglobin E heterozygous and homozygous states, HbH disease, HbC trait, one HbO Arab disease, Hb Lepore heterozygous and homozygous states, HbD disease, iron deficiency, and Hb Lepore trait.
4.
The finding should be recorded as the presence of tear drop cells (dacrocytes), with a follow-up note that, since myelofibrosis is among the conditions associated with this finding, correlation with other film features and clinical information is advisable.
questions.question:
Q27
A blood film shows red cells that are tapered to a point on one side and blunt on the other, giving a tear-drop appearance.
1. Identify the abnormal red cell finding.
2. State the technique/stain used to detect this finding.
3. State the conditions in which this finding is seen.
4. State how the finding should be recorded/reported and any follow-up point to note.

questions.answerText:
1.
• Leucocytes are classified as granulocytes, which include neutrophils (polymorphonuclear leucocytes), eosinophils and basophils, and agranulocytes, which include lymphocytes and monocytes.
• Mature neutrophils have a segmented nucleus with 2 to 5 lobes joined by a thin filament, and less mature forms include band (stab, juvenile) forms, metamyelocyte, myelocyte, promyelocyte and myeloblast in that order.
2.
• Before evaluating leucocytes, it must be confirmed that the film is well made, that cell distribution is uniform, and that staining is satisfactory; while scanning, the total leucocyte count is estimated, and the differential count is done at oil immersion.
• The scanning technique examines ten microscopic fields vertically from bottom to top (or top to bottom), then moves the slide horizontally to the next field, repeating in a zig-zag motion until 100 WBCs have been counted.
• The manual WBC differential count is done in the same area as the WBC and platelet estimates, with red cells barely touching, using the zig-zag method under x100 (oil), counting 100 WBCs including all cell lines from immature to mature.
• Results are reported as absolute number of cells per microlitre, calculated as the percentage of a cell type in the differential multiplied by the white cell count.
• If 10 or more nucleated RBCs (NRBCs) are seen, the WBC count is corrected using the formula: corrected WBC count = WBC x 100 / (NRBC + 100).
3.
• Normally, about 2 to 5 leucocytes are seen per high-power field, and a leucocyte per high-power field approximates about 200 and 2000 cells in peripheral blood at x10 and x100 objectives respectively.
• Leucocytosis is suspected when WBC counts exceed 5 leucocytes per high-power field and leucopenia when less than 2 cells per high-power field, so a poorly distributed or poorly stained film can lead to a wrongly estimated total count.
• If the film is not well made, with uneven cell distribution or unsatisfactory staining, the identification and proportion of the 100 counted cells will not reflect the true differential picture.
• Similarly, if the presence of 10 or more NRBCs is not recognised and corrected for using the stated formula, the reported WBC count will be falsely elevated.
• An invalid film or an uncorrected NRBC-contaminated count therefore produces a differential and total WBC result that misrepresents the patient's true leucocyte picture.

2. State how the differential count of each type is applied/performed in the laboratory.

questions.answerText:
1.
The principle is that when a standard cut is made on the surface of the earlobe, all clotting mechanisms are activated to stop the bleeding, and the time from the cut until bleeding stops without assistance is the bleeding time.
2.
Materials needed: alcohol swab, sterile lancet, stopwatch and filter paper.
3.
• Clean the earlobe with a spirit swab, hold a glass slide behind it, puncture the lower edge to a depth of about 3 mm with a disposable sterile lancet, and start the stopwatch immediately.
• Discard the glass slide, then allow drops of blood to fall onto filter paper without touching the earlobe, gently touching each new drop onto a fresh area of the paper.
• Stop the watch when no more blood comes onto the filter paper and note the time; count the number of drops on the paper and multiply by 30 seconds, reporting to the closest minute.
4.
If the cut bleeds for more than 10 minutes, the test is discontinued.
5.
The normal bleeding time by this method is 3-5 minutes.
6.
• It is used because it is easy to perform, requires minimal equipment, gives quite good blood flow, and the earlobe contains abundant subcutaneous tissue and is vascular.
• However, it is the least standardised of the bleeding time methods, has less precision and accuracy, and it is difficult to get a standardised wound.
7.
• The Template method gives a normal bleeding time of 2-9 minutes, while the Ivy method gives a normal bleeding time of 2-6 minutes; both measure the platelet-vessel wall interaction.
• These bleeding time methods are very operator dependent, and it is accepted that bleeding time is not indicated as a routine screening test since a well-taken history is just as reliable and it is a poor predictor of abnormal surgical bleeding.
• Where indicated, bleeding time is used to assess platelet function 4-5 days after stopping aspirin, to assess platelet function in mild thrombocytopenia (platelet count greater than 50x10^9/l), to diagnose VWD and platelet dysfunction, and to evaluate response to FFP, cryoprecipitate or desmopressin in VWD prior to surgery.

questions.answerText:
1.
The cells described are target cells, showing a central round stained area and a peripheral rim of cytoplasm.
2.
They are detected by microscopic examination of a Romanowsky-stained peripheral blood film, assessed under oil immersion once the film quality and staining have been confirmed satisfactory.
3.
Target cells are seen in thalassaemia, chronic liver disease, hereditary hypobetalipoproteinaemia, iron deficiency anaemia, haemoglobinopathies (Hb C, Hb H, sickle cell anaemia), and post-splenectomy.
4.
The finding should be recorded on the film report as the presence of target cells, with a follow-up note that, because they occur in several different conditions, they should be interpreted together with the patient's other red cell indices and clinical picture.
questions.question:

A blood film shows red cells with a central round stained area surrounded by an area of pallor and then a peripheral rim of stained cytoplasm, resembling a target or bullseye.
1. Identify the abnormal red cell finding.
2. State the technique/stain used to detect this finding.
3. State the conditions in which this finding is seen.

questions.answerText:
1.
The specimen is capillary blood from the earlobe, obtained using a disposable sterile lancet, with a glass slide held behind the earlobe, a stopwatch, and filter paper as the apparatus involved.
2.
The principle is that a standard cut made on the earlobe surface activates all clotting mechanisms to stop the bleeding, and the bleeding time is the time spent from the cut until bleeding stops without any assistance.
3.
The earlobe is punctured to a depth of about 3 mm, the stopwatch is started immediately, the glass slide is discarded, and drops of blood are allowed to fall onto filter paper without touching the earlobe, gently touching each new drop on a fresh area of the paper.
4.
The watch is stopped when no more blood comes onto the filter paper; the number of drops is counted and multiplied by 30 seconds, reported to the nearest minute, with a normal bleeding time of 3-5 minutes, and the test is discontinued if the cut bleeds for more than 10 minutes.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
1.
• The ABO genes do not directly code for the ABO antigens; instead they code for specific glycosyltransferases that add sugars to a basic precursor structure (Type 2), formed from Type 1 (paragloboside).
• The H gene codes for an enzyme, L-fucosyltransferase, which transfers L-fucose from a donor nucleotide (GDP-Fuc) to the terminal galactose of the precursor chain, forming the H substance.
• The A allele encodes a glycosyltransferase that produces the A antigen (immunodominant sugar N-acetylgalactosamine), and the B allele encodes a glycosyltransferase that produces the B antigen (immunodominant sugar D-galactose); the O allele's enzyme has no function, leaving the H antigen unchanged.
• These antigens are incorporated into oligosaccharide chains, with type 2 being the most common in the antigen-carrying molecules of RBC membranes; each human RBC expresses about 2 million ABO blood group antigens.
2.
• In standard practice, this structural knowledge underlies why blood is typed as A, B, AB or O based on which glycosyltransferase(s) are present and functional, since the ABO antigens remain the most immunogenic of all blood group antigens in transfusion medicine.
• It is also applied in understanding secretor status: 'secretors' have at least one functional Se allele that produces H antigen in bodily secretions, which is then processed into A and/or B antigens depending on ABO genotype.
3.
• The H gene is very common, with 99.99% of people inheriting it, but the genotype hh is extremely rare and is called the Bombay phenotype.
• In the Bombay phenotype, the absence of a functional H gene means the precursor structure cannot be converted to H substance.
• Since the A and B glycosyltransferases act on the H substance as their substrate, an individual lacking H substance cannot express A or B antigens even if they carry functional A or B alleles.
• The precaution/reasoning is that Bombay phenotype red cells will type as apparent group O on routine forward grouping, but their serum contains antibodies against A, B and H antigens.
• Transfusing ordinary group O blood to a Bombay phenotype individual would therefore be incompatible, since their anti-H antibody would react against the H antigen present even on group O cells.
• Recognising this rare genotype is therefore important so that such patients are correctly identified and given compatible blood, rather than being assumed to be routine group O donors or recipients.
questions.question:
Q60
1. Describe the basic biochemical structure of the ABO blood group antigens, including their identifying features.
2. State the standard method/setting in which knowledge of this structure is applied in practice.
3. Explain the basic reasoning behind a precaution taken regarding rare Bombay-phenotype individuals.

questions.answerText:
1.
The ESR is the rate of sedimentation of erythrocytes in a whole blood specimen enclosed in a standard narrow-bore glass tube, measuring the distance, in millimetres, that erythrocytes fall in 1 hour.
2.
Materials/reagent: anticoagulated whole blood, mixed in a ratio of 4 parts whole blood to 1 part sodium citrate, and a narrow-bore glass tube.
3.
• The anticoagulated whole blood and sodium citrate mixture is placed in the narrow-bore glass tube.
• The erythrocytes are allowed to sediment at room temperature, with plasma above the sedimenting red cells in the blood column.
• The distance the red cells have fallen is read after a fixed period.
4.
The rate of sedimentation is determined by plasma proteins, and ESR increases with the acute phase response, so it is used as an indirect determination of inflammation.
5.
The result is reported as the distance, in millimetres, that erythrocytes fall in 1 hour.
6.
It is used/preferred because it is a simple indirect test of inflammation, used to follow conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, vasculitis and many other inflammatory conditions.
7.
• The Westergren method uses a 200 mm tube, while the Wintrobe method uses a shorter, 100 mm tube.
• Modern semi-automated methods measure sedimentation using infra-red light over a shorter period than 1 hour and extrapolate the result to give an equivalent Westergren ESR, and can interface with a laboratory information system.
• For the Westergren method specifically, 1 part of 3.8% tri-sodium citrate is mixed with 4 parts of blood (ratio 1:4).
• The Wintrobe method, by contrast, can also be performed using double oxalate anticoagulated blood, which is one of the recognised uses for that anticoagulant.
questions.question:
Q46
1. State the principle of the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) test.
2. List the materials/reagent required.
3. Outline the procedure.
4. State the precautions to be observed.
5. State how the result is reported.
6. Explain why this technique is used/preferred in practical haematology.
7. Distinguish the Westergren method from the Wintrobe method.

Q51
1. State the principle of the Prothrombin Time (PT) test.
2. List the reagents/specimen required.
3. Outline the procedure.
4. State the precautions to be observed.
5. State how the result is reported.
6. Explain why this technique is used/preferred in practical haematology.
7. Distinguish it from the APTT test.
questions.answerText:
1.
PT is the time taken for citrated plasma to clot on the addition of tissue thromboplastin and calcium chloride, measuring the extrinsic and common pathways.
2.
Reagents/specimen: 4.5 ml venous blood mixed with 0.5 ml of 3.2% sodium citrate (or 3.8% tri-sodium citrate at a 1:9 ratio), tissue thromboplastin reagent, and calcium chloride.
3.
• Blood is collected by clean venepuncture into the sodium citrate anticoagulant and processed within 1-2 hours; tissue thromboplastin and calcium chloride are added to the citrated plasma and the clotting time is measured.
• A control plasma is always run alongside the test plasma.
4.
PT is considered prolonged if the test and control values show a difference greater than 3 seconds; if PT is prolonged, a correction study is performed by mixing equal parts of test and control plasma and repeating the test.
5.
The normal PT by the manual technique is 12-14 seconds; for patients on oral anticoagulants, PT is reported as the International Normalised Ratio (INR), calculated as (Patient's PT divided by Mean normal PT) to the power of the ISI, with a normal INR of 0.9-1.2.
6.
It is used/preferred because it detects abnormalities of factors I, II, V, VII and X, and a mild elevation of the PT is an early indication of deranged hepatocellular dysfunction; the ISI value assigned to commercial thromboplastins, after comparison with a WHO standard, allows the INR to correct for varying thromboplastin sensitivities.
7.
• APTT, by contrast, measures all the coagulation factors except FVII and FXIII, testing the intrinsic and common pathways, and has replaced the old, insensitive Clotting Time (CT) test.
• The normal manual APTT is 30-35 seconds, and a difference greater than 5 seconds from the control is significant, whereas for PT a difference greater than 3 seconds is significant.
• A persistently short APTT (less than 25 seconds) indicates a hypercoagulable state, and APTT is specifically used to monitor heparin therapy, which is not the primary monitoring use of PT.
• Where PT and APTT are both prolonged, correction studies distinguishing factor deficiency from an inhibitor (heparin, lupus anticoagulant, or an antibody to a coagulation factor) apply to both tests in the same way.
• The two tests therefore test different pathways of the coagulation cascade (extrinsic/common for PT versus intrinsic/common for APTT) and are used together with thrombin time to localise where a coagulation abnormality lies.

1.
• Mature neutrophils (polymorphonuclear leucocytes) make up 40 to 80 percent of the total WBC count (2.0-7.0 x10^9/l) and have a diameter of about 13 micrometres.
• They have a segmented nucleus, usually with 2 to 5 lobes (trilobed being usual, with a small percentage having four or occasionally five lobes), joined by a thin filament, with pink/orange cytoplasm and fine granulation (0.2-0.3 micrometres) staining tan to pink with Wright's stain.
• Less mature forms, in order, include band (stab, juvenile) forms, metamyelocyte, myelocyte, promyelocyte and myeloblast; up to 8% of circulating neutrophils are unsegmented or partly segmented band forms.
2.
• In standard practice, this structural knowledge is used to recognise a 'left shift', where non-segmented neutrophils exceed 5%, which means increased bands and usually indicates acute infection, typically bacterial.
• It is also applied when assessing neutrophil granules, since toxic granulation (an increase in staining density and number of granules) is seen with bacterial infections and other inflammation.
• This structural assessment is carried out as part of the WBC differential count, performed under oil immersion (x100) using the zig-zag scanning method until 100 WBCs have been counted.
3.
• A common precaution is to ensure the film is well made and staining is satisfactory before assessing nuclear lobulation or granulation, since these are the features used to judge maturity and toxic change.
• This is because faulty staining directly distorts the appearance of granules; for example, an excessively blue stain makes neutrophil granules appear deeply stained, large and prominent.
• Conversely, an excessively pink stain, from insufficient staining time or too high acidity, can make granules barely visible.
• Since band forms and segmented forms are distinguished by the appearance of the nuclear filament/lobes, a poorly stained or poorly fixed film could cause a band form to be mistaken for a segmented form or vice versa.
• This would in turn distort the assessment of a left shift, since an inaccurate proportion of band forms would misrepresent whether an acute infective process is present.
• Correct identification of neutrophil maturity and granulation therefore depends on the same standards of film and staining quality required for the differential count generally.

questions.answerText:
1.
Tubes are classified by stopper colour: red (no additive), lavender/purple (EDTA), green (sodium or lithium heparin), light blue (sodium citrate), and gray (sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate, or sodium iodoacetate).
2.
• The red-stopper tube (no additives) is used for blood bank work and some biochemistry, for collection of serum, and requires 10-15 minutes to allow blood to clot before centrifugation.
• The lavender/purple-stopper tube (EDTA) is used for collection of whole blood, since it binds calcium, and is used for most haematology tests.
• The green-stopper tube (sodium or lithium heparin) inhibits thrombin activation and is used for chemistry studies.
• The light blue-stopper tube (sodium citrate) binds calcium and is used for coagulation studies (PT, APTT) and for ESR.
• The gray-stopper tube (sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate, which inhibits enolase, or sodium iodoacetate, which inhibits glucose-3-phosphate dehydrogenase) is used for glucose determination in chemical pathology, since it stabilises glucose in plasma.
3.
• An anticoagulant for haematological examination must not alter the size of cells, must not cause haemolysis, must minimise platelet aggregation, and must not disrupt leucocyte staining/morphology.
• If a red (serum) tube is used instead of an EDTA tube for a CBC, the sample would clot rather than remain as anticoagulated whole blood, making cell counting and film preparation impossible.
• If a green (heparin) tube is used for coagulation studies instead of a light-blue (citrate) tube, the result is invalid because heparin only delays clotting rather than binding calcium in the standardised way citrate does, and heparin also interferes with agglutination and coagulation tests.
• If a gray (fluoride/oxalate) tube is used for a test other than glucose, the fluoride's inhibition of enzymes could interfere with tests such as urea and other enzyme-based determinations.
• Using sodium citrate (light blue) for a CBC is also inappropriate, since it causes a 10% dilution of the blood and has a tendency to shrink cells, distorting cell counts and indices.
• Selecting the correct stopper colour/anticoagulant for each specific test therefore prevents the anticoagulant itself from introducing an artefact into the measured parameter.

1.
• The composition of the Rh system complex is thought to be a tetramer, consisting of two molecules of Rh-associated glycoprotein (RhAG) and two molecules of Rh proteins.
• The Rh proteins may be RhD, carrying the D antigen, or RhCE, carrying the C or c antigen and the E or e antigen.
• The Rh antigen is a transmembrane polypeptide and an integral part of the red cell membrane, and this complex is only expressed in cells of the erythroid line, so Rh antigens are only expressed on RBCs.
• The D antigen contains over 30 epitopes, and variations of the D phenotype arise when these epitopes are weakly expressed, giving rise to the 'weak D' (or Du) phenotype.
2.
• In standard practice, routine blood typing for Rh D status in both blood donors and transfusion recipients is carried out to reduce the incidence of transfusion reactions caused by anti-D.
• Rh antibodies, mostly of the IgG type, are considered a potential cause of haemolytic transfusion reactions (HTR) and haemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN), so this structural knowledge underlies routine antenatal and transfusion screening.
3.
• Weak D (Du) phenotype means all D antigen epitopes are present but are under-expressed; it is found in less than 1% of Caucasians and is only slightly more common in African Americans.
• It can arise as genetic weak D, C-in-trans, or D mosaic.
• The precaution taken is that individuals with these uncommon Rh phenotypes should be transfused with Rh-negative blood.
• The reasoning is that, although the D antigen epitopes are present, weak expression could otherwise lead to inconsistent typing results and potential exposure of the recipient to functional D antigen.
• Since Rh antibodies rarely bind complement, RBC destruction from Rh incompatibility is mediated almost exclusively via macrophages in the spleen (extravascular haemolysis), which remains clinically significant even when the causative antigen is weakly expressed.
• Transfusing Rh-negative blood to a patient with a weak D phenotype therefore avoids the risk of sensitisation or a delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction that could result from exposure to full-strength D antigen.

1.
• The main parts of Sahli's haemoglobinometer are a graduated glass tube, colour comparators, a glass stirrer, and Sahli's pipette, which measures 20 microlitres of blood.
• The tubes commonly used are square, with graduations in percent on one side and grams per 100 ml on the other.
• The colour comparators are made of brown-coloured glass, and some better instruments have glass prisms as an identifying feature.
2.
• In standard practice, N/10 hydrochloric acid is placed in the tube up to the lowest mark, and blood drawn up to the 20 mm mark in the pipette is transferred into the acid and mixed by shaking.
• The mixture is allowed to stand for at least 10 minutes to allow the brown colour of acid haematin to develop, then diluted with distilled water drop by drop, using the glass rod, until the colour matches the comparator.
• The reading is taken at the level of the lower meniscus of the fluid, read as grams per decilitre, when the colour of the solution exactly matches the comparator at eye level against natural light.
3.
• A common precaution is to allow a minimum of 10 minutes for the reaction before matching, since a minimum of 10 minutes is required for the conversion of Hb to acid haematin to be almost complete.
• This is because 95% of Hb is converted at the end of 10 minutes, 98% of the colour develops at the end of 20 minutes, and maximum colour is reached after about 1 hour, so premature reading gives a biological false negative result.
• Another precaution is to avoid delay in reading once colour development is complete, since the brown colour of acid haematin is not stable and undue delay affects the reading.
• Care must also be taken with the quality of the colour comparators, since old or faded glass blocks cause wrong results.
• Matching should be done carefully at eye level against natural light, and the glass rod should not be left inside the tube while comparing, since the reading is inherently subjective and can vary from person to person.
• These precautions collectively address the recognised sources of error in the method: technical errors in pipetting/mixing, visual errors in colour matching, and interference from substances such as carboxyhaemoglobin, methaemoglobin and sulphaemoglobin, which are not converted to acid haematin.

questions.answerText:
1.
The finding described is toxic granulation of the neutrophils, an increase in staining density and number of granules.
2.
It is detected by microscopic examination of a Romanowsky-stained peripheral blood film during the WBC differential count, assessed once the film is confirmed well made and satisfactorily stained.
3.
Toxic granulation is seen with bacterial infections and other inflammation.
4.
The finding should be recorded on the differential count report as toxic granulation present in neutrophils, with a follow-up note to also check for a left shift (non-segmented neutrophils greater than 5%), since increased bands together with toxic granulation usually mean acute infection, typically bacterial.

1.
The specimen is citrated plasma, collected from a clean venepuncture; if from a central line, the line must be flushed with normal saline and the first 4-5 ml of blood discarded before the sample is drawn, and it must be processed within 1-2 hours.
2.
PT measures the time for citrated plasma to clot on addition of tissue thromboplastin and calcium chloride, testing the extrinsic and common pathways, while APTT measures all coagulation factors except FVII and FXIII, testing the intrinsic and common pathways.
3.
A control plasma is always run with the test plasma; PT is considered prolonged if the difference from control exceeds 3 seconds, and APTT if the difference exceeds 5 seconds; if either is prolonged, a correction study mixing equal parts of test and control plasma is performed.
4.
The normal manual PT is 12-14 seconds and the normal manual APTT is 30-35 seconds; correction of a prolonged result on mixing indicates a factor deficiency, while lack of correction indicates the presence of an inhibitor such as heparin or lupus anticoagulant.

1.
Field stain uses separate short immersions in Field's stain B (eosin) and Field's stain A (methylene blue) to rapidly differentiate blood cells and parasites on a fixed thin film.
2.
Materials: methanol (absolute), Field stains A and B, a tube with water, staining dishes, and filter paper.
3.
• Fix the thin film with methanol for 1 minute, then dry the microscope slide on filter paper.
• Immerse the slide in Field's stain B (eosin) for 5 seconds, then immediately wash with water.
• Immerse the slide in Field's stain A (methylene blue) for 10 seconds, then immediately wash with water and dry the thin film.
4.
The timings for each stain (5 seconds for eosin, 10 seconds for methylene blue) must be followed precisely, and washing must occur immediately after each immersion.
5.
The dried, stained thin film is examined microscopically for blood cell and parasite morphology.
6.
It is used/preferred because it is a rapid staining method suited to quick examination of thin films.
7.
• For the thick film, by contrast, methanol fixation is not used ('Methanol No!'), since thick films need to be haemolysed and are therefore not fixed with methanol.
• The thick film procedure instead immerses the film in Field's stain A (methylene blue) for 3 seconds, rinses immediately in tap water, then immerses it in Field's stain B (eosin) for 3 seconds before rinsing again and allowing it to dry carefully.
• The thin film procedure stains with eosin (stain B) first for 5 seconds then methylene blue (stain A) for 10 seconds, while the thick film procedure stains with methylene blue (stain A) first for 3 seconds then eosin (stain B) for 3 seconds, a reversed order with shorter, equal timings.
• The thin film procedure therefore combines methanol fixation with longer, unequal staining times, while the thick film procedure omits fixation entirely and uses shorter, equal immersion times in the reverse staining order.

1.
• Anticoagulants may be classified as calcium chelators, which include oxalates (ammonium, potassium, double oxalate), EDTA and citrates (sodium citrate, ACD).
• They may also be classified as non-calcium chelators, which include sodium heparin and warfarin.
• By type of use, they are also grouped as physiological/circulatory (e.g. heparin), therapeutic (heparin, warfarin), transfusion anticoagulants (CPD-A, ACD) and laboratory anticoagulants (EDTA, heparin, oxalates and citrates).
2.
• EDTA (lavender stopper) is used for whole blood collection for most haematology tests, since it binds calcium and preserves the staining and morphology of leucocytes, making it the anticoagulant of choice for total platelet counts.
• Double oxalate can be used for Hb, TLC, RBC count and ESR by the Wintrobe method, but is not suitable for peripheral blood film examination or blood banking because leucocyte morphology is not well preserved and the calcium oxalate formed is toxic.
• Sodium citrate (light blue stopper) is the anticoagulant of choice for platelet function/morphology and for coagulation studies such as PT (1:9 ratio) and ESR by the Westergren method (1:4 ratio).
• Heparin (green stopper) is used for blood pH, gas analysis and acid-base balance, but is not suitable for agglutination tests or coagulation studies since clotting is only delayed, not prevented.
• Sodium fluoride with potassium oxalate (gray stopper) is used for glucose determination, since sodium fluoride inhibits the glycolytic enzymes responsible for glucose breakdown.
3.
• An anticoagulant for haematological examination must not alter the size of cells, must not cause haemolysis, must minimise platelet aggregation and must not disrupt the staining and morphology of leucocytes.
• Using ammonium oxalate causes swelling of the RBC while potassium oxalate causes shrinkage, so either alone is unsuitable for PCV, ESR and cell morphology studies, giving erroneous results.
• Excessive concentration of EDTA causes shrinkage of RBCs, giving erroneous PCV, MCV and MCHC results, and it also interferes with several blood chemistry tests.
• Using the wrong anticoagulant for a given test therefore invalidates the result because each anticoagulant acts differently on cell size, morphology, or specific analytes measured in that test.

questions.answerText:
1.
• Double oxalate (also called Paul and Heller mixture, Balanced Oxalate, or Wintrobe anticoagulant) is a mixture of ammonium oxalate and potassium oxalate.
• One preparation combines 2.4 grams of ammonium oxalate and 1.6 grams of potassium oxalate dissolved in 100 ml of distilled water, giving 0.2 ml of solution containing 8 mg of oxalates, which prevents clotting of about 3-4 ml of blood.
• Another preparation uses 6 grams of ammonium oxalate and 4 grams of potassium oxalate dissolved in 100 ml distilled water as a 10% stock solution, of which 0.5 ml is distributed into universal bottles and dried at 60 degrees Celsius.
2.
• In standard practice, double oxalate can be used for Hb estimation, total leucocyte count, RBC count, and ESR by the Wintrobe method.
• It acts by chelating calcium, forming an insoluble precipitate of calcium oxalate, thereby removing free calcium ion from the blood.
• The two salts are combined in the required proportions specifically to counter the swelling effect of ammonium oxalate and the shrinking effect of potassium oxalate on the red cells.
3.
• A common precaution is that double oxalate should not be used for peripheral blood film examination or for blood banking applications.
• This is because leucocyte morphology is not well preserved by this anticoagulant, so cellular detail needed for blood film examination is distorted.
• It is also because the calcium chelated is precipitated as calcium oxalate, a toxic substance, making it unsuitable wherever blood is destined for transfusion use.
• Ammonium oxalate alone causes cells to swell while potassium oxalate alone causes cells to shrink, so the two salts must be kept in the correct proportion to avoid either artefact.
• Potassium oxalate alone causes about 8% shrinkage in the PCV and is therefore not recommended for ESR when used on its own.
• Careful attention to the mixing ratio and choice of application therefore prevents the anticoagulant itself from introducing artefactual changes into the result.

Q18
1. Describe the general classification of staining faults seen on Romanowsky-stained blood films.
2. State how each fault is recognised and corrected in the laboratory.
3. Explain why an uncorrected staining fault leads to an inaccurate or invalid morphological result.
questions.answerText:
1.
Staining faults are classified as an excessively blue stain, an excessively pink stain, and a precipitate on the film.
2.
• An excessively blue stain is caused by too-thick films, prolonged staining, inadequate washing, or too high alkalinity of the stain or diluent, and is corrected by preparing films of ideal thickness, reducing staining time, using less stain with more diluent, prolonging washing, or adjusting the buffer pH.
• An excessively pink stain is caused by insufficient staining time, prolonged washing, or too high acidity of the stain or buffer, and is corrected by prolonging staining time, reducing washing, or adjusting the buffer pH.
• A precipitate on the film is caused by unclean slides, drying during staining, inadequate washing at the end of staining, or use of unfiltered/inadequately filtered stain, and is corrected by using clean slides, avoiding drying, washing until thinner parts of the film look pinkish, and filtering the stain.
• Quality control of staining is applied by testing a new batch of stain at several staining times (e.g. 5, 7, 10, 12, 15 minutes) on films from the same blood and comparing results with a stained control blood film.
• The pH of newly prepared buffer water is checked and rechecked at weekly intervals, since it must be correct (6.8), as pH is mainly responsible for the staining reactions.
3.
• On an excessively blue-stained film, erythrocytes appear blue-green, nuclear chromatin appears deep blue to black, and neutrophil granules appear deeply stained, large and prominent, distorting normal colour-based interpretation.
• On an excessively pink-stained film, erythrocytes appear bright red or orange, nuclear chromatin appears pale blue, and eosinophil granules appear sparkling brilliant red, which can mimic true hypochromia or mask basophilic structures.
• A precipitate on the film can obscure cellular detail and mimic inclusions, particularly if the stain was unfiltered or the slide dried during staining.
• If white cells look too blue and red cells look too grey, the stain/buffer is too alkaline, while if white cell granules are barely visible and red cells look too pale, the stain/buffer is too acidic; recognising this pattern guides correction.
• Re-staining after washing with methanol is possible but should only be done when it is not possible to make a new smear, since repeated processing risks further artefact.
• An uncorrected staining fault therefore changes the true colour relationships between cell components that morphological classification (e.g. of hypochromia, granulation, or inclusions) depends upon, invalidating the reading.

1.
Leishman stain differentiates blood cells using a methanolic mixture of polychromed methylene blue and eosin, which combines fixation and staining of the smear.
2.
Apparatus/materials: Leishman powder, acetone-free methyl alcohol, Whatman filter paper, a dark brown stock bottle, buffered water and a microscope with an oil immersion lens.
3.
• Dissolve 0.2 g of powdered Leishman's dye in 100 ml of acetone-free methyl alcohol, warm to 50 degrees Celsius for half an hour with occasional shaking, then cool and filter.
• Pour the stain dropwise onto the slide and wait 2 minutes to allow fixation, then add double the quantity of buffered water dropwise and mix by rocking for 8 minutes.
• Wash in water for 1 to 2 minutes, dry in air, and examine under the oil immersion lens of the microscope.
4.
As a quality-control check, the prepared stain should be a clear blue-coloured solution without any particles, confirmed by staining and microscopic examination.
5.
On the stained film, red cells appear pink with a central pale area, leucocyte nuclei stain blue to purple, eosinophilic granules appear red-orange and platelets show violet granules.
6.
It is used/preferred because it differentiates and identifies leucocytes, malaria parasites and trypanosomes, with the methanol in the stain acting as a fixative that prevents perforation of the cells.
7.
• Wright's stain, by contrast, differentiates the nuclear/cytoplasmic morphology of platelets, RBCs, WBCs and parasites using a dip method: an air-dried thin film is dipped in undiluted stain for 15 to 30 seconds, then decolorised in distilled water and air-dried vertically.
• In the rack method for Wright's stain, air-dried slides are flooded with stain for 10 to 15 seconds, an equal volume of water is added and left for 10 seconds, then the slide is rinsed by dipping for 30 seconds.
• Thick films for Wright's stain are air-dried for hours or overnight (never by heat, which would interfere with lysing of the RBCs), then laked in water for 10 minutes and fixed in absolute methanol for 30 seconds before staining.
• Wright's stain fixation also requires that slides be completely clean before the smear is made, since if the slide is not clean the stain will not absorb into the smear.

questions.answerText:
1.
Variation in shape is called poikilocytosis and includes elliptocytes, spherocytes, target cells, schistocytes, acanthocytes, echinocytes, keratocytes, leptocytes, stomatocytes, sickle cells and tear drop cells.
2.
• Elliptocytes are elliptical in shape and most abundant in hereditary elliptocytosis, but are also seen in iron deficiency anaemia, myelofibrosis with myeloid metaplasia, megaloblastic anaemia and sickle cell anaemia.
• Spherocytes are nearly spherical, smaller in diameter than normal and lack a central pale area; they are seen in hereditary spherocytosis, some cases of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, and direct physical or chemical injury.
• Target cells show a central round stained area with a peripheral rim of cytoplasm and are seen in thalassaemia, chronic liver disease, iron deficiency anaemia and haemoglobinopathies such as Hb C, Hb H and sickle cell anaemia, and post-splenectomy.
• Schistocytes are fragmented erythrocytes, smaller than normal and of varying shape, seen in genetic disorders like thalassaemia, acquired disorders of RBC formation, mechanical stress (MAHA) and direct thermal injury.
• Echinocytes (crenated cells) have numerous short regular projections and commonly occur as an artefact of film preparation, such as with overnight-stored blood or water contaminating the stain/methanol.
• Tear drop cells are tapered on one side and blunt on the other, and are seen in myelofibrosis, thalassaemia, and various haemoglobin variant conditions.
3.
• Producing a good quality smear requires practice and is influenced by the speed, angle and drop size used, since shape artefacts can be introduced by the technique itself.
• A drop of blood that is too large or too small, or a spreader slide pushed in a jerky manner, is a common cause of a poor blood smear that can distort cell shape assessment.
• Echinocytes specifically are noted to commonly occur as an artefact during film preparation, for example from overnight-stored blood before films are made, or water contaminating the stain.
• Cellular degenerative changes also occur from a delay in fixing, inadequate fixing time, or methanol contaminated with water, which can mimic or mask true poikilocytosis.
• Correct identification of true pathological poikilocytes therefore requires ruling out these preparation artefacts, since misreading an artefact as a pathological shape change invalidates the diagnostic interpretation.

Q30
A blood film from a patient with suspected Vitamin B12 deficiency shows oval macrocytes and neutrophils with more than 5 lobes in more than 5% of cells, together with increased anisocytosis, poikilocytosis and occasional Howell-Jolly bodies.
1. Identify the overall blood picture being described.
2. State the technique/stain used to detect this finding.
3. State the other laboratory findings that would support this picture.
4. State the follow-up investigation indicated by this blood picture.
questions.answerText:
1.
This blood picture (oval macrocytes, hyper-segmented neutrophils, anisocytosis, poikilocytosis and Howell-Jolly bodies) is the blood film picture of megaloblastic (Vitamin B12 deficiency) anaemia.
2.
It is detected by microscopic examination of a Romanowsky-stained peripheral blood film, with hyper-segmented neutrophils defined as more than 5% having more than 5 lobes.
3.
Supporting full blood count findings would be decreased PCV and Hb, a high MCV (greater than 95 fl, often 120-140 fl in severe cases), increased MCH, and decreased total WBC, platelet and reticulocyte counts.
4.
The follow-up investigation indicated is a serum B12 assay (reference value 180-914 ng/L, with less than 180 ng/L suggestive and less than 150 ng/L highly suggestive of cobalamin deficiency), and bone marrow biopsy analysis if needed to show megaloblastic red cell precursors.

1.
Haemoglobin is converted to acid haematin by N/10 HCl, and the resulting brown colour, whose intensity depends on the amount of acid haematin (and hence haemoglobin) produced, is compared with standard brown glass reference blocks.
2.
Reagents/instruments: N/10 hydrochloric acid, distilled water for dilution, blood anticoagulated with EDTA, and Sahli's haemoglobinometer (graduated tube, colour comparators, glass stirrer, Sahli's pipette).
3.
• Place N/10 HCl in the tube up to the lowest mark, draw blood up to the 20 mm mark in the pipette, transfer it to the acid, rinse the pipette by drawing and re-expressing the acid, and mix well.
• Allow the mixture to stand for at least 10 minutes to allow the brown colour to develop, then dilute with distilled water drop by drop with continuous mixing using the glass rod provided.
• Match the colour with the glass plates in the comparator at eye level against natural light, taking care not to leave the glass rod inside the tube, and read the level of the lower meniscus in grams per decilitre.
4.
Sources of error include improper mixing of blood, pipetting errors, tissue fluid contaminating capillary blood, and the subjective, person-to-person variability of visual colour matching.
5.
Carboxyhaemoglobin, methaemoglobin and sulphaemoglobin are not converted to acid haematin, so their presence causes false results, and non-haemoglobin substances such as protein interfere with the colour.
6.
It is used because it is a simple visual comparison method requiring only Sahli's haemoglobinometer and basic reagents, giving a reading in grams per decilitre without complex equipment.
7.
• In the alkaline haematin method, haemoglobin is instead converted to alkali haematin by the addition of N/10 NaOH, producing a brown colour read against comparator standards or in a colorimeter using a green filter.
• The alkaline haematin technique requires adding 0.05 ml of blood to 4.95 ml of N/10 NaOH, mixing and boiling for 4 minutes alongside 5 ml of Gibson and Harrison's standard solution, then cooling quickly and matching in a colorimeter.
• Unlike Sahli's method, carboxyhaemoglobin and sulphaemoglobin are converted to alkali haematin in the alkaline method, and this method is also used to determine foetal haemoglobin, which is resistant to denaturation by alkali.
• A disadvantage of the alkaline method is that the Hb solution has to be heated to ensure complete denaturation, and matching must be done within 30 minutes after boiling, whereas Sahli's method needs no heating step.

questions.answerText:
1.
An ESR of 62 mm in 1 hour is an increased ESR, since the ESR measures the distance in millimetres that erythrocytes fall in 1 hour.
2.
The result should be recorded as the distance fallen in millimetres in 1 hour, by the Westergren method, using the standard 200 mm tube.
3.
Since the rate of sedimentation is determined by plasma proteins and the ESR increases with the acute phase response, this result indicates an indirect finding of inflammation in the patient.
4.
This finding is used to follow conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, vasculitis and other inflammatory conditions, so it should be interpreted alongside the patient's clinical picture and other inflammatory markers.

An ESR is set up by the Westergren method (4 parts anticoagulated whole blood to 1 part sodium citrate in a 200 mm narrow-bore tube) and, after standing at room temperature, the red cells are found to have fallen 62 mm in 1 hour.

Q22
A full blood count on an adult patient shows a decreased haemoglobin and packed cell volume, with an MCV of 118 fl (often as high as 120-140 fl in severe cases) and an increased MCH; the total WBC and platelet counts are decreased, and the reticulocyte count is decreased.
1. Interpret what this set of results indicates about the red cell picture.
2. State how this MCV/MCH pattern should be classified and recorded.
3. State what this result indicates about the underlying process.
4. State the action/further investigation that follows from this reading.
questions.answerText:
1.
An MCV greater than 100 fl indicates macrocytes, so this is a macrocytic anaemia with an increased MCH.
2.
The result should be recorded as a decreased Hb and PCV with a raised MCV (macrocytic indices) and increased MCH, alongside decreased WBC, platelet and reticulocyte counts.
3.
This pattern of full blood count changes is described as the laboratory diagnosis picture of Vitamin B12 deficiency (megaloblastic) anaemia.
4.
The decreased reticulocyte count together with decreased WBC and platelet counts should prompt examination of the blood film for oval macrocytes and hyper-segmented neutrophils, and further tests such as serum B12 assay.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of methods used for embalming a dead body.
(b) State how each method of embalming is applied or selected.
(c) Explain why an error in the embalming procedure leads to inadequate preservation of the body.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Methods of embalming a dead body are classified into natural methods and non-natural methods.
• Natural methods include mummification and preservation in cold or icy conditions.
• Non-natural methods include the conventional method of embalming and refrigeration.
(b)
• Mummification occurs naturally in a dry and hot atmosphere, such as the Sahara desert, causing the body to become dehydrated, withered and dark.
• Preservation in cold or icy conditions occurs naturally where the body is kept in a dry, cold atmosphere, as in the highlands of Peru.
• The conventional method has four parts: arterial embalming (injection of chemicals into the blood vessels), cavity embalming (suction and injection into body cavities using an aspirator and trocar), hypodermic embalming (injection under the skin) and surface embalming (used to supplement the other methods on visibly injured parts).
• Refrigeration involves preserving the cadaver in a specially made refrigerator.
(c)
• In arterial embalming, embalming solution is injected via the right common carotid artery while blood is displaced from the right jugular vein, and the embalmer massages the corpse to ensure proper distribution of the fluid in case of poor circulation, using other injection points if needed.
• If poor circulation is not corrected by massage or alternative injection points, the embalming fluid will not be evenly distributed through the tissues, leaving areas unpreserved.
• Cavity embalming requires proper suction of internal fluids before injecting chemicals; incomplete suction leaves fluids that can support decomposition despite arterial treatment.
• Care after embalming, such as keeping the body dry, cleaning off mould with dry tissue and coating with pomade in dry seasons, is required, and failure to do this allows deterioration even after correct embalming.
• Because embalming exists to forestall decomposition and make a body suitable for viewing, any step performed incorrectly (wrong injection route, poor fluid distribution or poor after-care) reverses this purpose and allows decomposition to proceed.

(a)
• The ingredients recommended for making up embalming fluid are formalin, phenol, methylated spirit, glycerin and alcohol.
• Formaldehyde, discovered by the German chemist August Wilhelm Von Hofmann in 1867, was found to have preservative properties that became the foundation of modern embalming methods.
• Modified embalming fluid formulae have also been reported, such as one containing 95% ethyl alcohol as the base, 35% formalin as a fixative, diethylene glycol as a preservative and liquefied phenol as a mould preventative, plus water.
• A formaldehyde-free system has also been described, comprising ethanol, glycerine and thymol, injected arterially, with the body afterwards immersed in ethanol.
(b)
• In arterial embalming, the embalming fluid is injected into the blood vessels, usually via the right common carotid artery, with blood displaced from the right jugular vein.
• The embalming solution is injected through a mechanical pump, and the embalmer massages the corpse to ensure proper distribution of the fluid, using other injection points if circulation is poor.
• Cavity embalming supplements arterial embalming by suctioning internal fluids and injecting chemicals into body cavities using an aspirator and trocar, and hypodermic embalming injects the chemicals under the skin as needed.
(c)
• The precautions include always wearing laboratory clothing such as surgical gloves, a laboratory coat and rain boots, and always masking the face when embalming.
• The corpse should be tidied with disinfectants before embalming commences, and the embalming fluid must not be allowed to come into contact with the embalmer's body.
• For health reasons, embalming should be carried out in a well-ventilated area, since the fluid contains formalin and phenol, which are strong chemical preservatives.
• Hands must be washed properly after embalming to remove any residual chemical contact.
• These precautions are necessary because the reagents used (formalin, phenol, methylated spirit) are the same coagulant/preservative chemicals known to irritate skin and mucous membranes if handled without protection.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Fixation of the smear is done immediately with a fixative such as 95% alcohol or a cytofix spray, to avoid air drying of the cells.
• The smear should be a monolayer to allow proper penetration of the cell surface by the fixative.
• The slide should be labelled properly with the patient's name, identification number and other details, and detailed history and clinical examination findings should be recorded and maintained in a register.
(b)
• 95% alcohol is a standard fixative for smears intended for Papanicolaou staining, and smears to be Papanicolaou stained should be fixed while still wet.
• Cytofix spray is an alternative fixative used for the same purpose of preventing air drying.
• Dry smears do not stain well with the Papanicolaou technique and appear yellowish red, which is why immediate wet fixation is standard practice.
(c)
• The spray fixative should be kept at about 10 inches from the slide to avoid destruction of cells by the propellant in the spray.
• If the spray is held too close, the force and chemicals of the propellant can damage the cells before the fixative itself has a chance to preserve them.
• A monolayer smear is required for proper penetration of the cell surface by the fixative; a thick, multilayered smear would prevent the fixative from reaching and preserving the deeper cells adequately.
• Because more diagnostic problems arise from improper sampling and fixation than from screening itself, these precautions directly affect whether the final stained smear will be interpretable.
• Air drying before fixation causes cells to distort and stain poorly, appearing yellowish red rather than showing the true nuclear and cytoplasmic detail expected of a properly fixed Papanicolaou smear.
• Following the correct spray distance and achieving a monolayer smear are therefore basic precautions that protect the diagnostic value of the specimen before it even reaches the staining stage.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Based on centromere position, chromosomes are classified as metacentric (two arms of equal length), submetacentric/heterobrachal (chromatids of one side slightly longer), acrocentric (centromere closer to one end, with a satellite structure) and telocentric (centromere at the end; not seen in human cells).
(b)
• Based on the number of centromeres, chromosomes are classified as acentric (no centromere), monocentric (one centromere), dicentric (two centromeres) or polycentric (more than two centromeres).
• Chromosomes may also show a secondary constriction in addition to the primary centromeric constriction; the region between this and the nearest telomere is the satellite, and chromosomes with this feature are called satellite (Sat) chromosomes.
(c)
• A karyotype describes the number and appearance of chromosomes, paying attention to length, centromere position, banding pattern and differences between sex chromosomes, so centromere-position classification (metacentric, submetacentric, acrocentric) is used to identify and pair individual chromosomes.
• Human somatic cells have 10 satellite chromosomes, and the secondary constriction of satellite chromosomes is also known as the Nucleolus Organizer Region (NOR), containing genes coding for ribosomal RNA.
• Centromere-number classification (monocentric versus dicentric/polycentric/acentric) is applied to detect structural chromosomal abnormalities during karyotype analysis.
(d)
• Chromosome size shows remarkable variation depending on the stage of cell division: chromosomes are longest and thinnest in interphase, progressively shorter and thicker in prophase, and smallest in anaphase.
• Chromosomes are most easily observed during metaphase, when they are thick, quite short and well spread in the cell, which is why chromosome measurements are generally taken during mitotic metaphase.
• If chromosomes from one preparation are measured at metaphase and another at interphase or anaphase, their apparent lengths and shapes would not be genuinely comparable.
• This would compromise centromere-position classification (metacentric versus acrocentric, for example), since the relative arm lengths used for this classification only give a consistent picture at a defined stage of condensation.
• An error of this kind would therefore give an inaccurate or invalid karyotype interpretation, since the chromosomal aberrations, taxonomic relationships or evolutionary information sought from a karyotype depend on comparing like with like.
• Standardising analysis to metaphase spreads is therefore the precaution that keeps chromosome classification and comparison valid.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Staining is the application of dyes onto tissue sections or smears to bring about optical differentiation of cell and tissue components, and the dye used depends on the substance to be stained.
• The Papanicolaou stain is a multichromatic cytological staining technique developed by George Papanicolaou.
(b)
The reagents used include Harris Haematoxylin, 1% acid alcohol, OG6 and EA50, together with graded alcohols, xylene and a neutral synthetic mounting medium.
(c)
• Smears are removed from the fixative and rinsed through descending grades of alcohol (80%, 70%, 50%) and water for 10 seconds each.
• The smear is stained in Harris Haematoxylin for 2 minutes, rinsed, differentiated in 1% acid alcohol, washed and blued in tap water, then passed through 70% and 95% alcohol, stained in OG6 and EA50, rinsed in 95% alcohol, dehydrated in absolute alcohol, cleared in xylene and mounted.
(d)
Nuclei stain blue, acidophilic (superficial) cells stain reddish-pink, basophilic (intermediate and parabasal) cells stain blue/green, Candida albicans stains red to pale pink and Trichomonas vaginalis stains grey-green.
(e)
• The Papanicolaou stain gives good nuclear detail and stains the nucleus, chromatin and nucleolus well, enhancing differentiation between malignant and non-malignant cells.
• It stains the cytoplasm and its contents such as keratin, vacuoles and granules, differentiates acidophilic from basophilic materials, stains non-cellular substances such as fibrin, crystals and pigments, and identifies keratin in normal squamous cells.
• It also stains fungi and bacteria, although it does not give the differential staining characteristics seen with Gram staining.
(f)
• Smears to be stained by the Papanicolaou technique should be fixed while still wet, since dry smears do not stain well and appear yellowish red.
• Romanowsky stains may also be used for wet-fixed slides but are primarily applied to air-dried smears, unlike the Papanicolaou technique, which requires wet fixation.
• Consistency and reliability are most important in cytological interpretation, since cytologists rely heavily on the quality and appearance of the stain used.

(b) State the reagents/solutions used in manual Papanicolaou staining.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Fungal cell walls are rich in polysaccharides, which can be converted by oxidation to dialdehydes, and these dialdehydes are then detected by a silver solution.
(b)
The reagents used in the GMS technique are 4% chromic acid, 1% sodium bisulfite, 5% sodium thiosulfate, 0.21% silver nitrate (stock), 0.1% aqueous gold chloride solution and a light green counterstain solution.
(c)
Results show fungi, Pneumocystis and melanin staining black, mucin and glycogen staining dark grey, and the background staining pale green, with hyphae and yeast forms sharply delineated in black against the green background.
(d)
• The dialdehyde groups produced by oxidation of the polysaccharide-rich fungal cell wall reduce the methenamine silver solution to elemental silver at the site of the dialdehydes, giving a sharp, specific black outline of the organism.
• Because fungal walls consistently contain these reactive polysaccharides, the technique reliably outlines fungi such as Histoplasma, Candida and Cryptococcus, and a control tissue containing cryptococcal yeast can serve as a control for PAS, mucicarmine and GMS stains together.
(e)
• The Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) technique oxidises the polysaccharides of fungal cell walls to dialdehydes, which reduce methenamine silver to give fungi, Pneumocystis and melanin a black colour against a pale green background.
• The periodic acid-methenamine silver (Jones/PAM) technique instead oxidises the carbohydrate moieties of the basement membrane to aldehydes using periodic acid, which then reduce the methenamine silver to elemental silver at the basement membrane.
• The Jones/PAM technique is used to investigate glomerular lesions in the kidney, where deposits of immunoglobulin such as IgA may cause puncture holes or splitting of the basement membrane visible with this stain.
• Both techniques rely on the same underlying methenamine-silver chemistry (aldehyde groups reducing silver), but GMS targets fungal cell wall polysaccharides while the Jones/PAM stain targets basement membrane carbohydrate moieties.
• In both techniques the excess unreacted silver is removed by a reaction with sodium thiosulfate once the reduction reaction is complete.
• GMS is applied broadly to skin, lung and other tissues where a fungal or Pneumocystis infection is suspected, whereas the Jones/PAM technique is most commonly applied to renal biopsies.
• Selecting between the two techniques therefore depends on whether the diagnostic question concerns a suspected fungal organism (GMS) or the structural integrity of a basement membrane (Jones/PAM).

The faded reaction is the Perls' Prussian blue reaction, used to demonstrate iron on gross museum specimens.
(b)
Gross specimens are demonstrated by placing thoroughly fixed and washed tissue in acidified potassium ferrocyanide for one to two hours, then transferring to distilled water until the blue colour develops and mounting in Kaiserling III solution; the blue ferric ferrocyanide compound formed can fade over time.

This pattern, with abundant parabasal cells and occasional basal cells, indicates low oestrogen (atrophic) activity, which is typical of women who have reached menopause.
(b)
• The Maturation Index is calculated from a differential count of at least 200 squamous cells classified as parabasal, intermediate and superficial cells, each expressed as a percentage; low oestrogen activity is indicated by a preponderance of parabasal cells, since basal cells are rarely seen in smears generally.
• The degree of cell maturation is determined by cell morphology and staining reaction, reflecting the influence of estrogen on proliferation and maturation of the vaginal epithelium.
(c)

• Because interpretation is ultimately subjective, correlation with clinical findings and, where relevant, comparison with the patient's previous smears is required before a definitive hormonal status is reported.
