A tissue block from a suspected case of systemic amyloidosis is submitted to the laboratory.
(a) State the technique appropriate for confirming amyloid in this specimen.
(b) State the principle of this technique.
(c) State the materials/reagents required.
(d) State a common source of error affecting this technique.
(e) State the precaution taken to avoid this error.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The technique appropriate for confirming amyloid is the Congo red technique, examined under polarized light.
(b)
Congo red is a linear dye that stains amyloid by hydrogen bonding to the antiparallel beta-pleated sheet configuration of the amyloid protein; under polarized light, Congo red-stained amyloid shows apple-green birefringence, and this depends on both the linearity of the dye molecule and the beta-pleated configuration of the amyloid.
(c)
The materials required are 0.5% Congo red in 50% alcohol and 0.2% potassium hydroxide in 80% alcohol for differentiation; fixation is not critical for this technique.
(d)
Section thickness is a common source of error: a section that is too thin shows only a faint red colour, while a section that is too thick shows yellow rather than the diagnostic apple-green birefringence.
(e)
The precaution is to cut sections at the ideal thickness of 8-10 µm, and, where AA and AL amyloid need to be differentiated, to pretreat sections with trypsin or potassium permanganate, since AA amyloid loses affinity for Congo red while AL amyloid remains resistant.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the basic structure and chemical composition of a chromosome.
(b) State the standard stage of cell division at which chromosomes are studied and measured in practice.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind studying chromosome size and shape specifically at this stage.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A chromosome is an organized structure of DNA and protein found in the cell nucleus, consisting of a single piece of coiled DNA containing many genes and regulatory sequences, along with DNA-bound proteins that package the DNA and control its function.
• In the nucleus, DNA is tightly coiled many times around proteins called histones to form thin threads called chromatin fibres.
• Interphase chromatin consists of about 30-40% DNA, 50-65% protein and 1-10% RNA, while metaphase chromosomes contain 15-20% DNA, 10-15% RNA and 65-75% protein.
• Histones are highly basic proteins abundant in lysine and arginine residues; they act as a pole around which DNA winds to create nucleosomes, the basic structural unit of DNA packaging.
• A chromosome has a kinetochore, the protein structure where spindle fibres attach to pull chromosomes apart during cell division, and telomeres, the stable ends of the chromosome required for replication and stability.
(b)
• Chromosomes are longest and thinnest in interphase, progressively decrease in length with increasing thickness in prophase, and are most easily observed during metaphase, when they are thick, quite short and well spread in the cell.
• Chromosomes are smallest in anaphase, so chromosome measurements are generally taken during mitotic metaphase.
• A karyotype describes the number and appearance of chromosomes in the nucleus, paying attention to their length, the position of the centromere, banding pattern and any differences between the sex chromosomes.
(c)
• Because chromosome size shows remarkable variation depending on the stage of cell division, measuring at inconsistent stages would give inconsistent results for the same chromosome set.
• At metaphase, chromosomes are thick, quite short and well spread in the cell, which makes their length, centromere position and banding pattern easiest to observe and compare accurately.
• Karyotypes prepared at metaphase are used to study chromosomal aberrations, cellular functions, taxonomic relationships and past evolutionary events, all of which require consistent, comparable chromosome morphology.
• If chromosomes were instead measured at interphase (longest and thinnest) or anaphase (smallest), size and shape comparisons between individuals or species would not be valid.

(a)
The blue granules within macrophages are consistent with hemosiderin, a breakdown product of haemoglobin composed of ferric iron and protein.
(b)
The principle of Perls' stain is unmasking of ferric iron in hydroxide form by dilute hydrochloric acid; ferric hydroxide then reacts with potassium ferrocyanide to form ferric ferrocyanide, an insoluble blue compound, giving iron a blue colour and nuclei a red colour with the neutral red or safranin counterstain.
(c)
• The finding should be recorded as a positive Perls' (Prussian blue) reaction for ferric iron; the best positive control for this reaction is postmortem lung tissue containing iron-positive macrophages (heart failure cells).
• If iron is suspected but the reaction is negative in a haemoglobin- or myoglobin-rich area, the section should be treated with hydrogen peroxide first, since iron tightly bound within these proteins is not demonstrated by the traditional technique until it is released by this pretreatment.
questions.question:
A tissue section stained with Perls' technique shows blue granules within macrophages, with nuclei counterstained red.
(a) Identify the pigment demonstrated.

(a) Describe the composition of the reagents used in the Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) technique.
(b) State the standard control material recommended for the GMS technique.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind using a control tissue when performing the GMS technique.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The GMS technique uses 4% chromic acid as the oxidising agent, 1% sodium bisulfite, 5% sodium thiosulfate, 0.21% silver nitrate (stock), 0.1% aqueous gold chloride solution and a light green counterstain solution.
• Chromic acid oxidises the polysaccharides of the fungal cell wall to dialdehydes, which then reduce the methenamine silver solution to metallic silver, giving the black staining reaction.
• Gold chloride is used in the toning step, and sodium thiosulfate removes unreacted excess silver from the section.
(b)
• A control tissue containing cryptococcal yeast forms can be used as a control for the PAS, mucicarmine and GMS stains together.
• Control tissues for the demonstration of organisms should be matched to the organism expected in the diagnostic section.
• Control tissues can best be stored as paraffin blocks or slides, and it may be advantageous to have multiple tissues represented on some control slides for silver-based stains.
(c)
• The purpose of a positive control is to demonstrate that the stain is working with a proper signal-to-noise ratio, that is, a proper stain-to-background ratio.
• Silver solutions are very susceptible to degradation, and proteins, ions or metal contact with glassware can cause nonspecific silver deposition, so a control confirms the reagents themselves are functioning correctly on that staining run.
• Many tumours or altered tissues stain poorly compared with normal tissue, so this must be considered when choosing and evaluating a control for GMS.
• Without a matched positive control, a weak or absent black reaction in the test section could be wrongly read as a true negative for fungal organisms when it may instead reflect a technical staining failure.
• The use of a control tissue therefore separates a genuine absence of fungal organisms from a failure of the silver-reduction chemistry itself.
• This precaution is applied generally across silver stains, since instability of reagents and variability of staining with fixation and tissue type are recognised technical problems associated with silver-based methods.

(a)
• The Warthin-Starry method is based on the principle that bacteria in general, and spirochetes in particular, have the ability to bind silver ions.
• The method involves impregnation of the spirochetes in the tissue with silver ions, with subsequent reduction of these ions to metallic silver using a developer containing hydroquinone.
(b)
The reagents used are an acetate buffer at pH 3.6 and 1% silver nitrate.
(c)
The stain demonstrates black spirochetes against a yellow to pale brown background.
(d)
• The spiral morphology of spirochetes can be fully appreciated by the use of this method, since the black silver deposit outlines the bacterium clearly against the pale background.
• Spirochetes belong to the group of organisms, including Treponema pallidum and Leptospira, that can be diagnosed using silver staining as a general diagnostic tool for bacterial infections.
• Silver staining is simple to perform, reliable and very sensitive, and its permanence and simplicity make it better than a fluorescent probe for this purpose.
• Fixation must be considered when using this method, since argentaffin/silver-based staining is reduced in tissues fixed with alcohol-containing fixatives.
(e)
• The Warthin-Starry method uses an acetate buffer and silver nitrate with a hydroquinone developer, and is used specifically to demonstrate spirochetes, staining them black against a yellow-brown background.
• The Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) method uses chromic acid, sodium bisulfite, sodium thiosulfate, silver nitrate and gold chloride, and is used to demonstrate fungi and Pneumocystis organisms.
• In GMS, fungi, Pneumocystis and melanin stain black, mucin and glycogen stain dark grey, and the background stains pale green, which is a different colour scheme from the Warthin-Starry result.
• The two methods are therefore selected according to the organism suspected: Warthin-Starry for spirochetes and GMS for fungal or Pneumocystis infections.

(b) State the reagents used in the Warthin-Starry method.
(c) State the result obtained with the Warthin-Starry method.
(d) Explain why the Warthin-Starry method is preferred for demonstrating spirochetes.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Fixatives are broadly classified as coagulant (denaturant) fixatives, such as ethanol, picric acid and mercury chloride, and noncoagulant fixatives, such as formaldehyde, osmium tetroxide and acetic acid, or as fixative mixtures such as alcohol-formalin, Bouin's fluid and Carnoy's fluid.
• The general protocol for histological and histochemical study includes sampling, fixation, dehydration and clarification, impregnation and embedding, sectioning, adhesion of the section to a slide, staining, dehydration and mounting.
(b)
• Because a lot of lipids are soluble in organic solvents, the fixatives used must not be of an organic nature, and lipids must be treated to become insoluble before paraffin embedding, or frozen sections must be used instead.
• One protocol fixes tissue in a mixture of 5% potassium bichromate, formalin and acetic acid for 12 hours, then washes with 3% potassium bichromate before frozen sectioning or paraffin embedding.
• A second protocol fixes tissue in formalin-calcium for 6 to 12 hours, then treats it with 3% potassium bichromate at 60°C for 2 days before frozen sectioning or paraffin embedding.
• The best fixative for simple lipids is formal calcium (2% calcium acetate plus 10% formalin), and simple lipid is best demonstrated using fresh frozen sections.
(c)
• If lipids are carried through the organic solvents used in routine paraffin processing without prior insolubilization, the lipid will be dissolved out of the tissue before it can be stained.
• Lipids with a melting point below the staining temperature can be stained with fat stains, so only lipids that are liquid at staining temperature are stained; those in a solid or crystalline state remain unaffected.
• Melting point of a lipid is inversely related to its fatty acid chain length, so a wrong assumption about a lipid's physical state at staining temperature can cause it to be missed.
• Sudan black B fails to stain crystalline cholesterol, lecithin and free fatty acids unless bromine pretreatment is used to convert crystalline cholesterol to oily derivatives that are permeable to the dye.
• Choosing an inappropriate fixation or insolubilization protocol for lipids will therefore give a false-negative or patchy staining result that does not reflect the true lipid content of the tissue.
• Effects of fixation generally include immobilization of cell components, inhibition of autolysis and putrefaction, and modification of tissue refractive index, so a poorly chosen fixative undermines every later step of the technique.

questions.answerText:
(a)
As soon as blood or material appears in the hub, aspiration should be stopped immediately, but the needle should not be removed from the mass until pressure on the plunger is released.
(b)
• Releasing the plunger before withdrawal allows the cells to remain contained within the needle hollow rather than being drawn into the syringe barrel; if suction is not released, the aspirated material enters the barrel of the syringe and cellular material becomes difficult to recover.
• The needle used is a disposable 23 or 25-gauge needle with a syringe of 10-20 mL capacity, and the back-and-forth movement of the needle within the mass, in different directions, produces the cutting action that retains cells in the needle hollow.
(c)
• The sample should be placed directly into a labelled container or onto a labelled, clean, grease-free slide, a smear made, and it should be submitted with a separate requisition; if more than one site is sampled, each slide must be labelled as to which site it represents.
• If the lesion is found to be cystic, as much fluid as possible should be aspirated and placed in a container, and any residual mass should be resampled following the same aspiration procedure.
