(c) Explain why a basic error in specimen collection or submission leads to an inaccurate or invalid cytological result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Methods of cytology specimen collection are classified as exfoliative cytology, fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) and body fluid sampling.
• Exfoliative cytology is the study of cells that have been shed or removed from the epithelial surface of various organs, obtained from natural secretions or by artificial means such as paracentesis, lavage, scraping, swabbing or surface washing.
(b)
• FNAC is used for organs that do not shed cells spontaneously, such as breast, thyroid, lymph nodes, liver, lungs, skin, soft tissues and bones.
• Body fluid sampling is applied to specimens such as urine, pleural fluid, pericardial fluid, cerebrospinal fluid, synovial fluid and ascitic fluid.
• Cervical and vaginal smears are collected as exfoliative specimens for evaluating conditions such as cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, which can progress to squamous cell carcinoma over 10-20 years, hence early detection through the Pap smear.
(c)
• Proper specimen collection and submission is essential because at least one half to two thirds of false negatives result from patient conditions present at the time of collection, submission, or the skill of the person obtaining the specimen.
• The requisition form must include the patient's name, age or date of birth, menstrual status and any previous abnormal cytology result, treatment, biopsy or surgical procedure, since the laboratory relies on this information for risk assessment.
• Slides must be labelled with a unique identifier, such as the patient's name plus a second identifier like date of birth or collection date, in solvent-resistant pen on the frosted end for glass slides.
• Variability in specimen collection and submission gives inaccurate, imprecise, unreliable and inconsistent results, so the laboratory must have a written procedure specifying requirements for proper collection, submission, identification and processing.
• Each specimen type has its own guideline for transport, with some specimens requiring consideration of temperature, agitation and dryness, and no delay should occur before the specimen reaches the laboratory.
• Using ink instead of pencil to label slides can cause the label to come off in the stainer, and placing adhesive labels on slides can affect proper staining, both of which are basic collection/labelling errors that invalidate the result.
• The skill and knowledge of the individual who obtains the specimen is therefore of utmost importance, since an error at this stage cannot be corrected later in processing or staining.

questions.question:
A tissue section stained by the Van Gieson technique shows collagen bright red, while nuclei stain blue-black and muscle, cytoplasm, elastin and reticulin stain yellow.
(a) Identify the technique that has produced this colour pattern.
(b) State the basic principle behind this colour differentiation.
(c) State the correct next step in reporting this finding.
questions.answerText:
(a)
This colour pattern is produced by the Van Gieson technique, which uses Weigert's iron haematoxylin, saturated picric acid solution and acid fuchsin.
(b)
The reagents differentially colour connective tissue components: collagen takes up the acid fuchsin to appear bright red, while muscle, cytoplasm, elastin and reticulin take up the picric acid component to appear yellow, and nuclei are stained blue-black by the iron haematoxylin.
(c)
• This pattern should be reported as demonstrating collagen (bright red) as distinct from muscle and other non-collagenous elements (yellow), which is useful for identifying an increase in collagenous tissue or confirming fibrotic change.
• The fixative record should be checked, since the effect of fixation on trichrome-type stains means that formaldehyde-fixed tissue further treated with picric acid or mercuric chloride solution gives enhanced intensity and radiance of the reaction; recommended fixatives include Bouin's, Zenker's, formal-mercury and zinc formalin.

questions.question:
A gross bone specimen with a suspected osteogenic lesion needs the fine bony architecture preserved and displayed free of soft tissue.
(a) Identify the technique that should be used to prepare this specimen.
(b) State the principle/procedure of this technique.
(c) State how the prepared specimen should be finished and recorded for the museum.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Maceration is the technique that should be used, since it is used to demonstrate bony lesions such as osteogenic sarcomas, chronic osteomyelitis, osteomas and tuberculosis.
(b)
• For preservation of the finest bony spicules, a putrefaction method is used: the specimen is boiled in tap water or very dilute sodium hydroxide, and softened tissue is removed from the specimen at intervals during boiling.
• A gross method for hard compact bone instead involves autoclaving the bone in sodium hydroxide for 5 minutes, although this method also removes fine bony spicules along with the soft tissue, so the delicate putrefaction method is preferred where fine spicules must be kept.
(c)
• After soft tissue removal, the bone is immersed in chloroform for 3-4 hours to remove fat (degreasing), dried in an incubator, and bleached in hydrogen peroxide.
• The macerated bone is finally mounted dry, either on a central plate or on a Perspex support designed for the individual specimen, and fixed in place with nylon wires for museum display.

(a)
The first and most critical processing step is fixation, since mistakes made at this stage render the whole electron microscopy study useless.
(b)
Glutaraldehyde, a di-aldehyde, is often used because it cross-links cellular structures into a matrix, preserving structure with minimum loss of cellular constituents, morphology, volume or spatial relationships, though it penetrates more slowly than the monoaldehyde paraformaldehyde; a mixture of both may be used for larger tissues.
(c)
• After aldehyde fixation, the sample must be rinsed/washed with a buffer, such as sodium cacodylate buffer (effective range pH 5.1-7.4), to remove traces of aldehyde before osmium tetroxide post-fixation, since residual aldehyde can form a precipitate with the osmium.
• The follow-up steps are dehydration through graded acetone concentrations, infiltration and embedding in an epoxy, polyester or methacrylate resin, and trimming of the block to a pyramid with about 45-degree facets before ultrathin sectioning on an ultra-microtome.
questions.question:
A tissue sample intended for electron microscopy is received in the laboratory and must retain its fine ultrastructure with minimal loss of cellular constituents.
(a) Identify the processing step that must be performed first and correctly for the study to be valid.
(b) State the technique/principle applied at this step.
(c) State how the sample should be handled next, and the follow-up step required before sectioning.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The Van Gieson technique uses Weigert's iron haematoxylin as the nuclear stain, a saturated picric acid solution, and acid fuchsin.
• Weigert's iron haematoxylin is also the nuclear stain used in Masson's trichrome technique, since it is more resistant to the acidity of the dye solutions than alum haematoxylin, which becomes decolorized.
• Acid fuchsin, phosphomolybdic acid and picric acid are components shared, in different combinations, between the Van Gieson and Masson's trichrome reagent systems used for connective tissue staining.
(b)
• The Van Gieson technique is used to demonstrate collagen, giving a bright red colour, while nuclei stain blue/black and cytoplasm, muscle, red blood cells, elastin and reticulin stain yellow.
• It is used to identify an increase in collagenous tissue, distinguish collagen from other connective tissue elements, and to confirm fibrotic change seen on routine sections.
• Collagen fibre stains generally used for this purpose include Masson's trichrome, Van Gieson's stain, Mallory's phosphotungstic acid haematoxylin, the MSB technique, PAS, Heidenhain's Azan stain, Lillie's allochrome method and Luxol fast blue G.
(c)
• 10% neutral buffered formalin (NBF) will not yield optimal results for trichrome-type collagen stains.
• Treatment of formaldehyde-fixed tissue with a picric acid or mercuric chloride solution enhances the intensity and radiance of the trichrome-type reaction.
• Recommended fixatives for optimal collagen staining are Bouin's, Zenker's, formal-mercury and zinc formalin.
• Because tissue permeability and dye molecular size determine the staining reaction, and heat increases the rate of staining and penetration, an unsuitable fixative can leave the dense collagen network too impermeable for the dye to penetrate properly.
• A low pH of 1.5 to 3 is required for these staining solutions, so using an inappropriately buffered or fixed tissue can prevent the correct colour differentiation between collagen and muscle/cytoplasm.
• Choosing the correct fixative before staining is therefore a precaution that ensures the collagen network is left in a state that will take up the dye correctly and give an interpretable, reliable colour contrast.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition of the reagents used in the Van Gieson technique.
(b) State the standard use of the Van Gieson technique in practice.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind the precaution of using an appropriate fixative before applying the Van Gieson/trichrome-type stains.

(a) Describe the composition of the solutions used in the Congo red technique for amyloid.
(b) State the standard section thickness recommended when using the Congo red technique.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind this recommended section thickness.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The Congo red technique uses a solution of 0.5% Congo red in 50% alcohol.
• A differentiating solution of 0.2% potassium hydroxide in 80% alcohol is also used.
• Congo red is an acidic dye made of two identical halves, each with a phenyl ring bound to a naphthalene moiety by a diazo group, joined by a diphenyl bond to give a linear dye molecule.
• The alkaline Congo-red variant uses a high concentration of sodium chloride to reduce background electrochemical staining and enhance the hydrogen bonding of the dye specifically to amyloid.
(b)
• The standard, ideal section thickness for the Congo red technique is 8-10 µm.
• Fixation is not critical for this technique, but section thickness is treated as a critical variable.
• Results are read as amyloid staining red and nuclei staining blue under ordinary light, and as apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
(c)
• A section that is too thin will show only a faint red colour, which can be mistaken for a negative or weak result even when amyloid is present.
• A section that is too thick will show yellow birefringence rather than the diagnostic apple-green birefringence, which can also be misread.
• The Congo red-amyloid reaction depends on the linearity of the dye molecule and the beta-pleated sheet configuration of amyloid; if the section thickness distorts how this configuration is viewed under polarized light, the colour observed will not reflect the true amyloid content.
• Because apple-green birefringence under polarized light is currently the most reliable diagnostic test for amyloid, an incorrect section thickness directly undermines the reliability of this diagnostic step.
• Correct thickness therefore ensures that the true colour and birefringence pattern of amyloid, rather than an artefact of section thickness, is what is being interpreted.

(a)
• Superficial cells are the most mature cells of the ectocervix, polygonal with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, a small pyknotic nucleus (5-6 µm) and cytoplasmic keratohyaline granules.
• Intermediate cells are polygonal with abundant bluish cytoplasm and a larger nucleus with granular chromatin, and are most abundant during the secretory phase under progesterone influence.
• Parabasal cells are immature squamous cells, round to oval in shape, with a relatively larger vesicular nucleus (nucleus:cytoplasm ratio 1:2), fine reticular chromatin and a smaller, granular, dense cytoplasm.
• Basal cells are small (8-10 µm), round to oval, with dense cyanophilic cytoplasm and a large nucleus with fine reticular chromatin and small nucleoli.
(b)
• Hormones affect the vaginal epithelium in three ways: proliferation, maturation and exfoliation of cells, and these changes are noted for cell type in the smear, whether cells lie flat or folded, and whether they appear singly or in clumps.
• High oestrogen activity is indicated by a preponderance of superficial cells, while low oestrogen activity is indicated by a preponderance of parabasal cells; basal cells are rarely seen in smears.
• Numerical indices such as the Maturation Index, Eosinophilic Index and Cornification/Karyopyknotic Index are calculated from a differential count of 200 squamous cells to express the degree of oestrogenic effect.
• Women who have reached menopause show abundant parabasal cells with occasional basal cells in their vaginal smears.
(c)
• Specimens for hormone assessment should be collected from the posterior third of the vaginal wall, either by aspiration of vagino-cervical secretion from the posterior fornix or gentle scraping from the lateral mid-third of a healthy vaginal wall, to eliminate inflammatory cells.
• The smear should be made thickly to avoid air drying, and the staining method used should provide good nuclear morphology and clear cytoplasmic differentiation.
• For useful interpretation, information such as the patient's age, menstrual history and previous hormonal therapy, surgery or irradiation must be taken into account.
• Because interpretation is still ultimately subjective, smears are taken at about 3 or 4 day intervals throughout the menstrual cycle and correlated with clinical symptoms and previous smears.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the structural features of the squamous epithelial cell types seen in a normal vaginal smear.
(b) State the standard use of these cell types in the assessment of hormonal status.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind the recommended site and preparation for collecting the specimen used for hormonal cytological evaluation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Carbohydrate staining techniques include the Periodic Acid Schiff (PAS) technique, the Alcian blue method, the combined Alcian blue-PAS technique, the Mucicarmine technique, the colloidal iron technique, metachromatic staining, iodine staining for glycogen and enzymatic digestion techniques such as diastase, sialidase and hyaluronidase digestion.
• Carbohydrates are classified as simple carbohydrates (monosaccharides, oligosaccharides, polysaccharides) or glycoconjugates (proteoglycans, mucins and other glycoproteins).
• Mucins are further classified as neutral mucins (found in gastric mucosa, Brunner's glands, prostatic epithelia), sialomucins (bronchial submucous glands, goblet cells, salivary glands) and sulfomucins (bronchial mucous glands); sialomucins and sulfomucins are acidic mucins.
(b)
• The PAS technique is selected to demonstrate glycogen, mucin, basement membrane, alpha-antitrypsin, reticulin and fungal capsules, giving a magenta result.
• Alcian blue at pH 2.5 is selected to demonstrate acidic mucins (sialomucin, sulfomucin), proteoglycans and hyaluronic acid, which stain blue, while neutral mucins are not reactive with Alcian blue.
• The combined Alcian blue-PAS technique is selected to differentiate acid mucin (stained blue by Alcian blue first) from neutral mucin (stained magenta by the subsequent PAS reaction).
• The Alcian blue technique with varying electrolyte concentrations is selected to differentiate acidic carbohydrates and proteoglycans based on their different critical electrolyte concentration values.
(c)
• The PAS technique depends on oxidation of hydroxyl groups on adjacent carbon atoms of the carbohydrate to form two free aldehyde groups, which then react with Schiff reagent to give the coloured end product.
• Other oxidants such as potassium permanganate or chromic acid are not used in place of periodic acid because they further oxidize the aldehyde groups to carboxylic groups, which are no longer reactive with Schiff reagent.
• Using such an oxidant in place of periodic acid would therefore give a false-negative or weak PAS result even though carbohydrate is genuinely present in the tissue.
• Similarly, fixatives containing glutaraldehyde interfere with the PAS technique, so using this fixative introduces another basic source of error in carbohydrate demonstration.
• Because neutral mucins are not reactive with Alcian blue at pH 2.5, applying Alcian blue alone to a specimen and expecting it to reveal neutral mucin content would also give an invalid, incomplete result.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of stains used for the demonstration of carbohydrates.
(b) State how each carbohydrate stain is applied or selected in the laboratory.
(c) Explain why using the wrong oxidizing agent leads to an inaccurate carbohydrate staining result.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The Warthin-Starry method is the technique appropriate for demonstrating spirochetes.
(b)
The principle is that bacteria in general, and spirochetes in particular, have the ability to bind silver ions; the method involves impregnation of the spirochetes with silver ions, with subsequent reduction to metallic silver using a developer containing hydroquinone, producing black spirochetes against a yellow to pale brown background.
(c)
The materials required are an acetate buffer at pH 3.6 and 1% silver nitrate, together with the hydroquinone-containing developer.
(d)
Fixation is a factor that can interfere with the reliability of this and other silver-based techniques, since staining is reduced in tissues fixed with alcohol-containing fixatives, and glutaraldehyde fixation or short exposure to formalin may cause non-specific staining.
(e)
The precaution is to avoid alcohol-containing fixatives where possible, to use control tissues matched to the organism expected, and to keep glassware chemically clean and free of metal contact, since silver solutions are very susceptible to degradation and contamination.
questions.question:
A tissue block requires demonstration of spirochetes as part of the diagnostic work-up.
(a) State the technique appropriate for this purpose.
(b) State the principle of the technique.
(c) State the materials/reagents required.
(d) State a factor that can interfere with the reliability of this technique.
(e) State the precaution taken to avoid this interference.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The equipment for FNAC includes a disposable 10-20 mL plastic syringe and a disposable 23 or 25-gauge needle, preferably with a clear plastic hub.
(b)
• The skin over the lesion is cleansed with an alcohol swab, and the mass is fixed between the fingers to immobilize it during the needle passes.
• The needle is carefully poised at right angles to the skin surface, quickly introduced through the skin into the mass, and strong suction is applied once the needle is within the mass.
• Negative pressure is applied to the syringe and the needle is moved back and forth within the mass and in different directions to effect a cutting action and retain cells in the needle hollow.
• The moment blood or material appears in the hub, aspiration is stopped, but the needle is not removed from the mass until pressure on the plunger is released, so that cells remain in the needle rather than the syringe barrel.
• The sample is placed directly into a labelled container or onto a labelled, clean, grease-free slide, a smear is made, and it is submitted with a separate requisition; for a cystic lesion, fluid is aspirated first and any residual mass is resampled.
(c)
• If material from more than one site is submitted, each slide must be labelled as to which site it represents, so results are not misattributed if the cytology differs between sites.
• For any fluid other than peripheral blood, the tube must indicate what fluid it is, such as bile or peritoneal fluid.
(d)
• FNAC is used specifically because organs such as breast, thyroid, lymph nodes, liver, lungs, skin, soft tissues and bones do not shed cells spontaneously and therefore cannot be sampled by exfoliative methods.
• The suction and cutting action of the needle actively removes cells from within the mass, providing cellular material that would not otherwise be obtainable.
(e)
• FNAC obtains its specimen by actively inserting a needle into a mass and applying suction to withdraw cells from within the tissue.
• Exfoliative cytology instead relies on cells that have already been shed or removed from an epithelial surface, obtained by natural secretion or by scraping, swabbing, aspirating or surface washing of an accessible surface.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the equipment used for fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC).
(b) Outline the procedure for FNAC of a superficial mass.
(c) State the precautions observed during FNAC.
(d) Explain why FNAC is preferred for sampling organs that do not shed cells spontaneously.
(e) Distinguish FNAC from exfoliative cytology in terms of how the specimen is obtained.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The Feulgen technique uses 1M hydrochloric acid for acid hydrolysis, Schiff reagent to demonstrate the resulting aldehydes, and a bisulfite solution.
(b)
• The 1M hydrochloric acid is preheated to 60°C and used to break the purine-deoxyribose bond and yield an aldehyde group; the time in minutes depends on the fixative used, for example 8 minutes for Carnoy's or formalin-fixed tissue.
• Tissue is first fixed, most often in Carnoy's or Flemming's fluid, though numerous other fixatives are possible, followed by tissue block preparation in wax and tissue cutting before acid hydrolysis and Schiff reagent are applied.
(c)
Results show DNA staining red-purple and the cytoplasm staining green.
(d)
• The Feulgen technique demonstrates DNA by targeting the sugar (deoxyribose) component, since acid hydrolysis specifically breaks the purine-deoxyribose bond to produce the aldehyde that reacts with Schiff reagent.
• A control method for the standard Feulgen technique, the Naphthoic acid hydrazide (NAH) method, gives results identical to the true Feulgen reaction, supporting its reliability.
• A blue thionin-Feulgen reaction variant is used for studying cancer cell nuclear morphology and ploidy, where DNA is stained blue and the cytoplasm remains unstained.
(e)
• The Feulgen technique demonstrates DNA by detecting the sugar (deoxyribose) after acid hydrolysis, giving DNA a red-purple colour and cytoplasm green.
• The methyl green-pyronin method instead demonstrates the phosphate group of DNA using methyl green, whose amino group reacts with DNA phosphate, giving DNA a green-blue colour.
• In the methyl green-pyronin method, pyronin binds RNA (and also acid mucins and cartilage) and stains RNA red, allowing DNA and RNA to be seen together in the same section.
• Because RNA's ribose-purine bond is unaffected by 1M hydrochloric acid hydrolysis, the Feulgen technique cannot demonstrate RNA at all, whereas methyl green-pyronin can demonstrate both DNA and RNA simultaneously.
• The two techniques therefore differ in which chemical group of the nucleic acid they exploit (sugar versus phosphate) and in whether they can visualize RNA alongside DNA.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the solutions used in the Feulgen technique for demonstrating DNA.
(b) Outline the procedure of the Feulgen technique.
(c) State the results obtained with the Feulgen technique.
(d) Explain why the Feulgen technique is preferred as a method for demonstrating DNA specifically.
(e) Distinguish the Feulgen technique from the methyl green-pyronin technique for demonstrating nucleic acids.

(a) Describe the classification of silver stains used in histopathology.
(b) Describe the theoretical basis of each class of silver stain.
(c) State how each type of silver stain is applied or selected in the laboratory.
(d) Explain why an error in tissue fixation can lead to an inaccurate silver staining result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Silver stains are classified into argentaffin stains (silver reduction stains) and argyrophil stains (silver absorption stains).
(b)
• In argentaffin stains, melanin and certain other compounds have sufficient reducing strength to reduce ionic silver to metallic silver in a basic (ammoniacal) solution, and the excess ionic silver is solubilized by sodium thiosulfate.
• In argyrophil stains, specific cells with peptide-containing granules absorb silver, as in the Grimelius and related methods, and most of these cells arise embryologically from the neural crest area.
• Argyrophil cells take up amino acid precursors such as tyrosine and remove carboxyl groups from them to form amines, so the method identifies subpopulations of the Dispersed Neuroendocrine System.
(c)
• Argentaffin methods such as the Fontana-Masson technique are selected to stain melanomas, argentaffin secretory granules in midgut carcinoid tumours, and cells of the adrenal medulla and some paragangliomas.
• Amelanotic melanomas that cannot be stained by the Fontana-Masson technique are stained instead using acid silver solutions.
• The Warthin-Starry method, based on the ability of bacteria and spirochetes to bind silver ions, is selected for the demonstration of spirochetes.
• Reticulin stains are selected to demonstrate the supporting framework of the liver, spleen and lymph nodes, while the periodic acid-methenamine silver (Jones/PAM) stain is selected to investigate basement membranes and glomerular lesions.
(d)
• Argentaffin staining intensity is reduced in tissues fixed with fixatives containing alcohol, since alcohol solubilizes the argentaffin substance.
• Dissolution of argentaffin molecules by organic solvents such as alcohol before additive crosslinking fixation may therefore give a false-negative result.
• Fixation in glutaraldehyde, or even a short exposure to formalin, may cause non-specific staining with the silver solution, giving a misleading result.
• Because silver solutions are very susceptible to degradation and can react with proteins, ions or metal on glassware and instruments, control tissue slides must be used to judge staining quality and aid correct interpretation.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the patient preparation required before a Pap smear is taken.
(b) Outline the procedure for taking a Pap smear.
(c) State how the Pap smear specimen is fixed and labelled after collection.
(d) Explain why proper technique in taking a Pap smear is emphasised over the screening step itself.
(e) Distinguish sampling of the ectocervix using the Ayre's spatula from sampling of the endocervix using the cytobrush.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The vagina should not be douched for at least 24 hours before examination, and intravaginal drugs or preparations should not be used for at least one week before the smear is taken.
• The patient should abstain from coitus for at least 24 hours before the smear, and the smear should not be collected during menses; a postpartum smear should only be taken after 6-8 weeks of delivery.
(b)
• The patient is placed in the dorsal position with good illumination, and a Cusco's speculum is inserted to visualise and fix the cervix, with any findings on inspection noted.
• The Ayre's spatula is inserted first, placed at the cervical os so that the longer end goes into the cervical canal and the smaller end rests on the ectocervix, then rotated through 360 degrees while maintaining contact with the ectocervix.
• Too much force should not be used, to avoid bleeding or pain, and too little force should not be used, to avoid an inadequate sample; both sides of the spatula are smeared onto the slide.
• The endocervical sample is collected using an endocervical brush inserted into the canal so that the last bristles are visible, then rotated through 180 degrees, since more rotations increase the chance of bleeding.
(c)
• The sample is smeared evenly on the slide and fixed immediately, and the endocervical sample is rolled onto the slide and also fixed immediately.
• The slide should be labelled properly with the patient's name, identification number and details, with detailed history and clinical findings recorded and maintained in a register, and advice given regarding follow-up and treatment.
(d)
• More problems in Pap smear screening arise from improper sampling than from the screening process itself.
• Conventional cytology has a specificity of 98% but a sensitivity of only 51%, and false negative rates are due to faulty sampling, improper fixation or interpretation problems, so correct technique at collection directly determines test reliability.
(e)
• The Ayre's spatula samples the ectocervix by rotation through 360 degrees while maintaining contact, sampling the exocervical/ectocervical transformation zone with both sides of the spatula smeared onto the slide.
• The endocervical (cytobrush) sample instead targets the endocervical canal, inserted until the last bristles are visible and rotated only 180 degrees (fewer rotations than the spatula) because more rotation of the brush increases the risk of bleeding.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of methods used to demonstrate melanin.
(b) State how each melanin demonstration method is applied or selected.
(c) Explain why a positive silver-reduction reaction is a basic source of error when identifying melanin.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Melanin can be demonstrated by reducing methods, enzyme methods, solubility and bleaching characteristics, fluorescent methods, or immunohistochemistry.
• Reducing methods include the Masson-Fontana silver technique and Schmorl's ferric-ferricyanide reduction test.
• The enzyme method for melanin is the DOPA reaction.
(b)
• The Masson-Fontana stain relies on melanin's argentaffin property, using Fontana's silver solution; melanin is blackened by the acid silver nitrate solution, giving melanin black and nuclei red.
• Schmorl's ferric-ferricyanide reduction test is applied where melanin reduces ferricyanide to ferrocyanide, producing Prussian blue in the presence of ferric salts, giving melanin a dark blue colour and nuclei red.
• The enzyme (DOPA) method, solubility/bleaching characteristics, fluorescent methods and immunohistochemistry are selected as alternative or confirmatory approaches when a silver-reduction result needs further verification.
(c)
• The argentaffin reaction, which underlies the Masson-Fontana technique, is a reduction of an ammoniacal silver solution to form metallic silver without the use of an extraneous reducer.
• A positive reaction with this method is not specific for melanin, since other reducing substances can also convert the silver ions to metallic silver.
• Endogenous pigments, especially brown-black pigments other than melanin, could therefore give an incorrect interpretation if the Masson-Fontana or Schmorl reaction alone is relied upon.
• Because dissolution of argentaffin molecules by organic solvents such as alcohol before fixation may also give false-negative results, both false-positive and false-negative errors are possible with these reducing methods.
• This is why melanin demonstration is classified into several different method types (reducing, enzyme, solubility/bleaching, fluorescent, immunohistochemical), so that a doubtful reducing-method result can be checked against a different principle.
• Relying on a single reducing silver method without considering these confirmatory alternatives is therefore a basic error that can lead to an inaccurate identification of melanin in a tissue section.

questions.question:
An autoradiography slide processed and developed shows black silver deposits concentrated over a specific region of the tissue section, after counterstaining with toluidine blue.
(a) Identify what the black deposits represent.
(b) State the basic principle behind why the black deposits form at that location.
(c) State the correct next step in confirming and reporting this finding.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The black silver deposits represent the site and amount of radioactivity localized in the tissue, since autoradiography demonstrates the sites of radioactive isotopes in a section.
(b)
The basic principle is that radioactive isotopes in the tissue section reduce silver salts in the photographic film, plate or emulsion to black metallic silver deposits; this reduction occurs specifically where the radioactive compound has localized in the tissue.
(c)
• The result should be compared with control sections obtained from laboratory animals previously injected with radioactive compounds, since these controls confirm that the black deposits are a genuine radioactive signal rather than a fogging artefact.
• A densitometer may be used for quantitative estimation of the radioactivity, and the record should note the counterstain used (commonly Haematoxylin and Eosin, Methylene Blue, Basic Fuchsin or toluidine blue) and confirm that the whole process up to development of the photographic material was carried out in the dark to prevent false blackening by light.

(a)
The appropriate technique is the conventional Pap smear, using an Ayre's spatula for the ectocervix and an endocervical brush for the endocervical canal.
(b)
The transformation zone must be adequately represented, since cervical cancer develops through a sequence of intraepithelial changes over 10-20 years, and early detection depends on obtaining representative squamous and endocervical cells that are fixed before they can air dry.
(c)
The equipment required includes a Cusco's speculum, an Ayre's spatula, an endocervical brush (cytobrush), a glass slide, and a fixative such as 95% alcohol or cytofix spray.
(d)
A common source of error is improper sampling technique, such as using too much force (causing bleeding/pain) or too little force (giving an inadequate sample), or delayed fixation leading to air drying.
(e)
The precaution is to rotate the spatula through 360 degrees and the endocervical brush through only 180 degrees while maintaining gentle, even contact, to smear both sides of the spatula evenly onto the slide, and to fix the smear immediately, since more problems in screening result from improper sampling than from the screening process itself.
questions.question:
A cervical smear specimen is to be collected from a patient attending for routine cervical cytology screening.
(a) State the appropriate technique for collecting this specimen.
(b) State the principle underlying correct sampling of this specimen.
(c) State the equipment required.
(d) State a common source of error in this procedure.
(e) State the precaution(s) taken to avoid this error.

(a) Describe the principle of Masson's trichrome technique.
(b) State the reagents used in Masson's trichrome technique.
(c) State the results obtained with Masson's trichrome technique.
(d) State the factors that affect trichrome staining.
(e) Explain why Masson's trichrome technique is used in histopathology practice.
(f) Distinguish Masson's trichrome technique from the Van Gieson technique in terms of reagents and colour results.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Masson's trichrome technique demonstrates collagen and muscle by exploiting differences in tissue permeability and dye molecular size; erythrocyte protein forms a dense network with small pores, muscle cells have larger pores, and collagen has the least dense, most porous network.
(b)
The reagents used are Weigert's iron haematoxylin, acid fuchsin, glacial acetic acid, phosphomolybdic acid and methyl blue.
(c)
Results show nuclei staining blue/black, cytoplasm, muscle and red blood cells staining red, and collagen staining blue.
(d)
• Heat increases the rate of staining and penetration, and a low pH of 1.5 to 3 is used for the staining solutions.
• Iron haematoxylin is preferred as the nuclear stain for trichrome because it is more resistant to the acidity of the dye solutions than alum haematoxylin, which becomes decolorized.
• 10% neutral buffered formalin (NBF) will not yield optimal trichrome results; treatment of formaldehyde-fixed tissue with picric acid or mercuric chloride solution enhances the intensity and radiance of the stain, and recommended fixatives are Bouin's, Zenker's, formal-mercury and zinc formalin.
(e)
• Masson's trichrome is used to demonstrate collagen and muscle in normal tissue, differentiate collagen from muscle in tumours, identify an increase in collagenous tissue, and indicate fibrotic change in conditions such as cirrhosis of the liver and pyelonephritis.
• It is also used to distinguish tumours arising from muscle cells from those arising from fibroblasts.
(f)
• Masson's trichrome uses Weigert's iron haematoxylin, acid fuchsin, phosphomolybdic acid and methyl blue, giving nuclei blue/black, cytoplasm/muscle/red blood cells red, and collagen blue.
• The Van Gieson technique uses Weigert's iron haematoxylin, saturated picric acid solution and acid fuchsin.
• In the Van Gieson technique, collagen stains bright red while nuclei stain blue/black and cytoplasm, muscle, red blood cells, elastin and reticulin stain yellow, which is the reverse colour assignment for collagen compared with Masson's trichrome.
• The two techniques therefore use different chromogens for collagen (blue in trichrome versus red in Van Gieson) even though both share the same iron haematoxylin nuclear stain and acid fuchsin component.

questions.question:
A sputum smear stained by the Ziehl-Neelsen method shows bright red, beaded bacilli against a pale blue background, with very pale greyish-blue caseous material.
(a) Identify the organism/finding suggested by this appearance.
(b) State the technique/principle used to detect it.
(c) State how the result should be recorded and any follow-up step.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The bright red bacilli against a pale blue background are consistent with acid-fast bacilli, suggesting Mycobacterium infection.
(b)
• Mycobacteria possess a capsule containing mycolic acid, which is hydrophobic and resists decolorization by acid-alcohol once stained with a strong stain such as carbol fuchsin, hence the term acid- and alcohol-fastness demonstrated by the Ziehl-Neelsen technique.
• Reagents used are carbol fuchsin solution, 1% acid alcohol and 0.1% methylene blue solution, giving acid-fast bacilli a bright red colour, other tissue pale blue, and caseous material very pale greyish blue.
(c)
• The finding should be recorded as acid-fast bacilli (AFB) positive, noting that the blue counterstain may appear patchy if extensive caseation is present and that over-counterstaining should be avoided since scant organisms can easily be obscured.
• If the specimen required decalcification, the record should confirm that formic acid, not a strong mineral acid, was used, since strong acids may destroy acid-fastness and produce a false-negative result.

(a)
• The principle of the Perls' stain is unmasking of ferric iron in hydroxide form by dilute hydrochloric acid.
• In the Prussian blue reaction, ferric hydroxide reacts with potassium ferrocyanide to form ferric ferrocyanide, an insoluble blue compound.
(b)
The reagents used are 2% aqueous potassium ferrocyanide and 2% hydrochloric acid, with a counterstain of 1% neutral red or safranin.
(c)
Results show ferric iron staining blue and nuclei staining red.
(d)
• The best positive control is postmortem lung tissue, which contains a reasonable amount of iron-positive macrophages (heart failure cells).
• In haemoglobin and myoglobin, iron is bound tightly within the protein complex and cannot be demonstrated by the traditional technique; treatment with hydrogen peroxide releases the iron so that it can then be stained with Perls' stain.
(e)
• Hemosiderin is a breakdown product of haemoglobin composed of ferric iron and protein, seen as yellow-brown granules, and the Perls' reaction specifically targets ferric iron by forming a distinctly coloured insoluble blue compound.
• Because the reaction unmasks ferric hydroxide with dilute acid before forming the blue ferric ferrocyanide complex, it gives a clear, specific blue colour that is easy to distinguish from the red counterstained background.
• Three methods exist for demonstrating hemosiderin: Perls' Prussian blue reaction for ferric iron, Lillie's method for ferrous iron, and the Hukill and Putt method for both ferric and ferrous iron.
(f)
• The Perls' Prussian blue reaction demonstrates ferric iron specifically, using potassium ferrocyanide and hydrochloric acid to form a blue ferric ferrocyanide compound.
• Lillie's method instead demonstrates ferrous iron, the other oxidation state of iron found in tissue.
• The Hukill and Putt method is used when both ferric and ferrous iron need to be demonstrated together, unlike Perls' or Lillie's methods, which each detect only one iron oxidation state.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle of the Perls' Prussian blue reaction.
(b) State the reagents used in the Perls' stain.
(c) State the results obtained with the Perls' stain.
(d) State the precautions/notes associated with the Perls' stain.
(e) Explain why the Perls' stain is preferred for demonstrating hemosiderin in tissue.
(f) Distinguish the Perls' Prussian blue reaction from Lillie's method for iron.

(a) Describe the composition of Sudan black B and the solvents used to apply it.
(b) State the standard use of Sudan black B in demonstrating lipids.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind the precaution of pretreating crystalline cholesterol with bromine before staining with Sudan black B.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Sudan black B is the most sensitive of all the fat dyes; the first Sudan dye developed was Sudan 3.
• Sudan dyes must be dissolved in organic solvents to penetrate fats, and solvents used include 70% ethanol, isopropanol, propylene glycol and triethyl phosphate.
• Sudan black B has two staining fractions: the first stains neutral fats blue-black, and the second stains phospholipids grey.
(b)
• Sudan black B is used to demonstrate lipids that are liquid at the staining temperature, since lipids with a melting point below the staining temperature can be stained while those in a solid or crystalline state remain unaffected.
• Simple lipid is best demonstrated using fresh frozen sections, with formal calcium (2% calcium acetate plus 10% formalin) as the best fixative.
• The grey phospholipid reaction of Sudan black B can be enhanced and seen as a bronze dichroism if the section is viewed in polarised light.
(c)
• Sudan black B fails to stain crystalline cholesterol, lecithin and free fatty acids in their normal state.
• Bromine pretreatment converts crystalline cholesterol to oily derivatives, which are then permeable to the Sudan dye.
• Without this pretreatment, crystalline cholesterol present in a tissue would remain unstained and could be wrongly interpreted as an absence of lipid.
• Because melting point is inversely related to fatty acid chain length, lipids that are solid at room/staining temperature will similarly be missed unless a comparable pretreatment or a different technique is used.
• The precaution therefore ensures that lipids present in a non-liquid, non-permeable state are converted into a form the Sudan dye can actually penetrate, avoiding a false-negative fat stain.
• This is particularly important because Sudan black B is otherwise the most sensitive of the fat dyes, so a preventable false negative would undermine its main advantage.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the basic structure and features of the ultra-microtome.
(b) State the standard setting in which the ultra-microtome is used.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind the precaution of trimming the tissue block to a pyramid with facets of about 45 degrees before cutting.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The ultra-microtome is a highly specialized precision instrument designed to cut sections from hard synthetic resins.
• It cuts sections in the order of 0.005 to 0.1 µm (50-1000 Angstroms), suitable for electron microscopy work, and can also cut 1-2 µm sections for light microscopy.
• The knife is stationary with its cutting edge uppermost, while the tissue block moves up and down vertically as sections are cut.
• A low-power binocular microscope is attached to the front of the microtome above the tissue block, used for easy manipulation of the block and sections, and the feed mechanism is actuated by turning a wheel at the side of the microtome.
• The knife is prepared from diamond or plate glass, suitable for cutting tissue embedded in hard synthetic resin media, and cut sections fall into a trough beneath the knife where they are picked up for electron microscopy.
(b)
• The ultra-microtome is used in the trimming and sectioning stage of electron microscopy tissue processing, after infiltration and embedding of the specimen in resin.
• Before sectioning, excess plastic surrounding the tissue is trimmed away, while viewing under a dissecting microscope, using old glass knives or knives unsuitable for actual sectioning.
• The capsule mould is trimmed to a pyramid shape, in which the pyramid tip and sides are the exposed tissue to be sectioned.
(c)
• The angle of the pyramid sides (called facets) should be about 45 degrees so that the exposed tissue face presented to the diamond or glass knife is a manageable square or rectangular shape.
• If the block is not trimmed correctly, the section produced will not be a clean square or rectangle, making it difficult to obtain the very thin, evenly cut sections required for electron microscopy.
• Because very thin sections are required for electron microscopy, owing to the poor penetrating power of electrons, a poorly trimmed block increases the chance of thick, uneven or torn sections that will not image correctly.
• Correct trimming therefore protects both the knife edge and the quality of the resulting ultrathin sections, since the tissue moves vertically against a stationary knife and any excess resin at odd angles can damage the cutting edge or distort the section.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of fixatives based on their mode of action.
(b) State the composition of common fixative mixtures used in tissue preparation.
(c) State the standard duration for which each of these fixatives is used in practice.
(d) Explain the reasoning behind avoiding alcohol-containing fixatives for certain staining techniques.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Fixatives are classified as denaturant (coagulant) fixatives or noncoagulant fixatives.
• Coagulant fixatives include ethanol (70% to 100%), picric acid and mercury chloride.
• Noncoagulant fixatives include formaldehyde, osmium tetroxide and acetic acid.
(b)
• Fixative mixtures include alcohol-formalin, Bouin's fluid and Carnoy's fluid.
• Ethanol is mainly used to preserve mineral elements, osmium tetroxide reacts with lipids such as the phospholipids of the cell membrane, and acetic acid is a good fixative for the nucleus.
(c)
• Bouin's fluid is used for a fixation duration of 24 to 48 hours.
• Carnoy's fluid is used for a fixation duration of about 4 hours.
• Formalin can be used to fix tissue indefinitely.
• Fixation can be carried out by immersion, by perfusion for fragile tissues such as brain tissue, or by osmium tetroxide vapour, which is used essentially to fix a blood smear.
(d)
• Tissues to be stained with argentaffin stains should not be fixed in alcohol-containing fixatives, as alcohol solubilizes the argentaffin substance and decreases staining intensity.
• Bouin's fixative is not suitable for nucleic acid staining, as it causes over-hydrolysis of the nucleic acid during fixation.
• Effects of fixation generally include immobilization of cell components, inhibition of autolysis and putrefaction, tissue hardening, modification of the tissue refractive index and effects on dye affinity, all of which influence how a stain later reacts with the tissue.

questions.question:
A tissue section stained by the Periodic Acid Schiff method shows bright magenta staining within hepatocytes, with blue-stained nuclei.
(a) Identify the tissue component responsible for the magenta staining.
(b) State the basic technique/principle used to demonstrate this component.
(c) State how this finding should be recorded and what follow-up step confirms it.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The magenta-staining material within the hepatocytes is most likely glycogen, one of the components demonstrated by the PAS reaction.
(b)
• The PAS technique is based on oxidation of hydroxyl groups on adjacent carbon atoms of the carbohydrate by periodic acid, producing two free aldehyde groups, which then react with Schiff reagent to give a bright red/magenta end product.
• PAS-reactive components in tissue include glycogen, mucin, basement membrane, fungal capsules and several others, so the specific identity of the magenta material must be confirmed rather than assumed.
(c)
• The magenta reaction should be recorded as PAS-positive, with the pattern (diffuse cytoplasmic, in this case) noted, and the fixative used checked, since glutaraldehyde-containing fixatives should be avoided for PAS staining.
• The follow-up step is to repeat the stain on a diastase-digested control section; glycogen is removed by diastase digestion, so loss of the magenta reaction after digestion confirms glycogen, while persistence of staining suggests a different PAS-positive substance such as mucin.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of numerical indices used to assess oestrogenic (hormonal) effect on a vaginal smear.
(b) State how each numerical index is applied/calculated in the laboratory.
(c) Explain why relying on a single smear and a single method of assessment is a basic error that leads to an unreliable hormonal cytology result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The degree of oestrogenic effect in a vaginal smear can be established either by numerical indices or by subjective assessment.
• Numerical indices include the Maturation Index (MI), the Eosinophilic Index (EI) and the Cornification Index (CI), also called the Karyopyknotic Index (KPI).
(b)
• The Maturation Index involves a differential count of at least 200 squamous cells classified into parabasal, intermediate and superficial cells, each expressed as a percentage; high oestrogen activity shows a preponderance of superficial cells, and low oestrogen activity shows a preponderance of parabasal cells.
• The Eosinophilic Index is based on cytoplasmic staining, in which 200 squamous cells are counted and those showing red or pink eosinophilic staining are expressed as a percentage.
• The Cornification/Karyopyknotic Index counts 200 squamous cells for superficial cells with condensed, deeply stained nuclei and pink or red cytoplasm; this index is considered more reliable because it relies on the more stable nuclear morphology rather than cytoplasmic staining.
• Subjective assessment instead depends on the observer's impression of the proportion of basal, intermediate and superficial cells and their distribution pattern, whether lying flat and singly or folded and clumped.
(c)
• Basal cells are rarely seen in normal smears, and menopausal women show abundant parabasal cells with occasional basal cells, so a single smear read in isolation may not reflect the true hormonal status across the cycle.
• In order to obtain a meaningful assessment of oestrogenic influence, smears should be taken at about 3 or 4 day intervals throughout the menstrual cycle, not from a single sample.
• Whether numerical indices or subjective assessment are used, the ultimate interpretation of a vaginal smear depends on correlating clinical symptoms and signs with the smear findings and comparing them with known normal physiological patterns and with the patient's previous smears.
• Because the assessment is, in the final analysis, still subjective, using only one index or only one smear increases the risk of misclassifying the hormonal status, especially near phase transitions such as the periovulatory period.
• Cell types, whether cells lie flat or are folded at the edges, and whether cells appear singly or in clumps, must all be considered together; relying on a single criterion in isolation is itself a source of misinterpretation.
• A basic error of relying on a single smear/single-index approach therefore gives a result that does not account for the natural cyclical variation in cell maturation, making the hormonal assessment unreliable.

questions.question:
A liver biopsy is submitted with a clinical suspicion of a glycogen storage disorder.
(a) State the technique appropriate for demonstrating the suspected substance.
(b) State the principle of this technique.
(c) State the materials/reagents required.
(d) State a common source of error/interference in this technique.
(e) State the precaution(s) taken to avoid this error.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The Periodic Acid Schiff (PAS) technique is appropriate for demonstrating glycogen in this biopsy.
(b)
The technique depends on oxidation of the hydroxyl groups on adjacent carbon atoms (1,2-glycols) of the carbohydrate by periodic acid, forming two free aldehyde groups that then react with Schiff reagent to give a bright red/magenta end product; the intensity of colour reflects the tissue concentration of reactive glycol structures.
(c)
The materials required are periodic acid (a 0.5-1% solution used for 5-10 minutes) and Schiff reagent.
(d)
Fixatives containing glutaraldehyde interfere with PAS staining, and using an alternative oxidant such as potassium permanganate or chromic acid in place of periodic acid over-oxidises the aldehyde groups to carboxylic groups, which no longer react with Schiff reagent.
(e)
The precaution is to avoid glutaraldehyde-containing fixatives for tissue that will be PAS stained, to use periodic acid as specified rather than substitute oxidants, and to confirm true glycogen with a diastase-digestion control, since glycogen storage disorders such as Von Gierke, Pompe's, Forbes-Cori, Andersen's and McArdle disease are all associated with abnormal PAS-positive glycogen accumulation.

(a)
This pattern, consisting almost entirely of superficial cells with pyknotic nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm and a clean background, is characteristic of the ovulatory phase (15th-16th day) of the menstrual cycle.
(b)
• Estrogen promotes proliferation and maturation of the vaginal squamous epithelial cells, including the superficial cells, and deposition of glycogen within the vaginal epithelium, so high oestrogen activity is indicated by a preponderance of superficial cells.
• High oestrogen activity is particularly obvious and reaches a maximum level during the ovulatory period, when the cornification/karyopyknotic index is highest.
(c)
• The finding should be confirmed by calculating a numerical index, such as the Maturation Index or the Cornification (Karyopyknotic) Index, from a differential count of at least 200 squamous cells.
• Because interpretation is ultimately subjective, the result should be correlated with the patient's age, menstrual history and any previous hormonal therapy, and, where possible, smears should be repeated at 3-4 day intervals across the cycle before a final hormonal assessment is reported.
questions.question:
A vaginal smear is found to consist predominantly of superficial squamous cells with small pyknotic nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, lying flat and singly, with a very clean background.
(a) Identify the hormonal phase that this cellular pattern indicates.
(b) State the basic principle behind why this cell pattern appears at this phase.
(c) State the correct next laboratory step for confirming and reporting this pattern.

(a) Describe the principle of the Fontana-Masson technique for demonstrating melanin.
(b) State the application of the Fontana-Masson technique.
(c) State the precautions and problems associated with the Fontana-Masson and other argentaffin stains.
(d) Explain why the Fontana-Masson technique is preferred for demonstrating melanin in tissue.
(e) Distinguish the Fontana-Masson (argentaffin) technique from the Grimelius (argyrophil) technique.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The Fontana-Masson technique relies on melanin's argentaffin property, in which melanin reduces ionic silver in an ammoniacal (basic) silver solution to metallic silver, producing a black deposit.
(b)
• The technique stains melanomas and, using acid silver solutions, can also stain amelanotic melanomas that cannot be stained by the standard Fontana-Masson method.
• It also stains argentaffin secretory granules in midgut carcinoid tumours and cells of the adrenal medulla and some paragangliomas.
(c)
• A positive reaction is not specific for melanin, and endogenous pigments, especially brown-black pigments, could give an incorrect interpretation.
• Some procedures require exposure of sections to the alkaline silver solution for up to 24 hours, during which sections may separate from the glass slides.
• Glassware used in the staining procedure must be free of contamination, particularly protein residue and chloride ions, which may precipitate the silver.
• Dissolution of argentaffin molecules by organic solvents, especially alcohol, before additive crosslinking fixation may give false-negative results.
(d)
• Melanin has sufficient reducing strength to reduce ionic silver to metallic silver without the use of an extraneous reducer, giving melanin pigment (black) with nuclei counterstained red.
• The result is a clear black deposit that identifies melanin-containing lesions such as malignant melanoma and can also demonstrate Cryptococcus organisms.
(e)
• The Fontana-Masson technique is an argentaffin (silver reduction) stain, relying on melanin's own reducing strength to convert silver ions to metallic silver.
• The Grimelius technique is an argyrophil (silver absorption) stain, in which peptide-containing granules of neural-crest-derived cells absorb silver without themselves reducing it.
• Argyrophil methods therefore require a separate reducing/developing step, whereas argentaffin methods such as Fontana-Masson do not.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of pigments encountered in histopathology.
(b) State how the demonstration method is applied or selected for each class of pigment.
(c) Explain why haemoglobin- or myoglobin-bound iron cannot be demonstrated by the traditional Perls' technique without an additional step, and why omitting this step is a basic error.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pigments in tissue are classified as endogenous pigments (hematogenous and non-hematogenous), exogenous pigments and artifact pigments.
• Exogenous pigments include asbestos, silica and lead, while artifact pigments include formalin pigment, malaria pigment, mercury pigment and schistosome pigment.
(b)
• Hemosiderin, a hematogenous pigment that is a breakdown product of haemoglobin composed of ferric iron and protein, is demonstrated by Perls' Prussian blue reaction (ferric iron), Lillie's method (ferrous iron) or the Hukill and Putt method (both ferric and ferrous iron).
• Bile pigment is demonstrated by the Modified Fouchet's technique, using Fouchet's reagent (aqueous trichloroacetic acid and ferric chloride) combined with Van Gieson stain, giving bile pigment an emerald to blue-green colour.
• Melanin is demonstrated by reducing methods such as the Masson-Fontana silver technique or Schmorl's ferric-ferricyanide reduction test, by enzyme methods such as the DOPA reaction, by solubility and bleaching characteristics, by fluorescent methods, or by immunohistochemistry.
• Calcium is demonstrated by the Von Kossa technique, and copper by the Orcein stain or Rhodanine blue.
(c)
• In haemoglobin and myoglobin, iron is bound tightly within the protein complex and cannot be demonstrated by the traditional Perls' technique in this bound state.
• Treatment with hydrogen peroxide releases the iron from this tightly bound protein complex, after which it can be stained with Perls' stain.
• If this hydrogen peroxide pretreatment step is omitted, the Perls' reaction will fail to demonstrate iron that is genuinely present but still protein-bound, giving a false-negative result.
• This is a basic error because it assumes all tissue iron is in a freely reactive ferric hydroxide form, when in fact some iron is masked within haemoglobin or myoglobin and needs to be unmasked first.
• The best positive control for the Perls' reaction is postmortem lung tissue containing iron-positive macrophages (heart failure cells), which should demonstrate a positive reaction without needing hydrogen peroxide pretreatment, helping to confirm the reagents are working.
• Omitting the correct pretreatment for protein-bound iron therefore leads directly to an inaccurate, falsely negative interpretation of the tissue's true iron content.

questions.question:
A skin biopsy from a patient with a chronic non-healing lesion is submitted with a request to rule out a fungal infection.
(a) State the technique appropriate for this specimen.
(b) State the principle of the technique.
(c) State the materials/reagents required.
(d) State a common source of error in this technique.
(e) State the precaution taken to avoid this error.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The Gomori/Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) technique is appropriate for demonstrating a fungal infection in this specimen.
(b)
Fungal cell walls are rich in polysaccharides, which are oxidised to dialdehydes; these dialdehydes then reduce the methenamine silver solution to metallic silver, giving a black reaction.
(c)
The materials required are 4% chromic acid, 1% sodium bisulfite, 5% sodium thiosulfate, 0.21% silver nitrate (stock), 0.1% aqueous gold chloride solution and a light green counterstain.
(d)
A common source of error is degradation or contamination of the silver solution, since proteins, ions such as chloride, or metal from forceps or slide holders on glassware may react with or precipitate the silver, causing a high or erratic background.
(e)
The precaution is to chemically clean all glassware with commercial cleaning agents, concentrated nitric acid or bleach, rinse in distilled water, prepare solutions with distilled water, avoid any metal contact with the silver solution, and run a matched positive control tissue, such as one containing cryptococcal yeast forms, to confirm the stain is working correctly.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition of the reagents used in the Periodic Acid Schiff (PAS) technique.
(b) Describe how the reactive end-product of the PAS technique is formed.
(c) State the standard setting in which the PAS technique is used in practice.
(d) Explain the reasoning behind avoiding certain fixatives and oxidants when using the PAS technique.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The PAS technique uses periodic acid as an oxidant and Schiff reagent, which reacts with free aldehyde groups to form a bright red/magenta end product.
• A 0.5-1% solution of periodic acid is used for 5-10 minutes as the oxidising agent.
(b)
• The initial step is oxidation of hydroxyl groups attached to adjacent carbon atoms (1,2-glycols) within the carbohydrate.
• This oxidation cleaves the adjoining carbon-to-carbon bond and forms two free aldehyde groups.
• The intensity of the colour that develops after reaction with Schiff reagent depends on the tissue concentration of the reactive glycol structures.
(c)
• The PAS technique is used to demonstrate glycogen, starch, mucin, basement membrane, alpha-antitrypsin, reticulin, fungal capsules, pancreatic zymogen granules, thyroid colloid, corpora amylacea and Russell bodies.
• Results show glycogen and mucins staining magenta and nuclei staining blue.
• It is used diagnostically for conditions such as glycogen storage disorders, staining macrophages in Whipple's disease, demonstrating mucins in adenocarcinoma of the large intestine, and demonstrating fungi.
(d)
• Fixatives containing glutaraldehyde should be avoided if tissues are to be stained with the PAS technique.
• Other oxidants such as potassium permanganate or chromic acid are not used because they further oxidise the aldehyde groups to carboxylic groups, which are no longer reactive to Schiff reagent.
• Staining of glycolipids may only be detected when frozen sections are used, so section type must be considered when interpreting a PAS result.
• The first histochemical use of the periodic acid-Schiff method was by McManus for the demonstration of mucin.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification/types of electron microscopes.
(b) State how each type of electron microscope is applied or selected for use.
(c) Explain why an error in specimen preparation leads to an inaccurate or invalid result in electron microscopy.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Electron microscopes are of three main types: the transmission electron microscope (TEM), the scanning electron microscope (SEM) and the scanning tunnelling electron microscope (STEM).
• All electron microscopes use electromagnetic and/or electrostatic lenses to control the path of the electron beam, which illuminates the specimen instead of light as in light microscopy.
(b)
• The TEM works by shooting a beam of electrons at a thin, plastic-embedded slice of a sample and detecting the electrons that pass through, making it particularly good for studying cell organelles and identifying viruses, bacteria, protozoa and fungi.
• The SEM scans the surface of coated specimens with an electron beam and forms an image from secondary electrons scattered from the surface, giving a three-dimensional-looking image of bulk samples.
• The STEM studies the structure of a surface using a stylus that scans at a distance of only an atom's diameter, producing a computer-generated contour map, and has been used to study DNA molecules.
• The TEM offers magnification potentially over one million times with high-quality, detailed images and information on element and compound structure.
(c)
• In SEM, all water must be removed from the sample because it would vaporise in the vacuum, and non-conductive specimens require a thin surface coating of gold to increase secondary electron detection; without this the image will be dark or absent.
• In TEM, fixation is the first and most important step, since mistakes at this point render the whole project useless, and glutaraldehyde is often used because it cross-links cellular structures to preserve morphology with minimum loss of cellular constituents.
• If rinsing after aldehyde fixation and before osmium tetroxide post-fixation is skipped, traces of aldehyde can contaminate the tissue by forming a precipitate with the osmium.
• Very thin sections are required because electrons have poor penetrating power; an ultra-microtome is needed, and if ordinary paraffin wax is used for embedding it is not firm enough and will melt under the electron beam.
• A very small area of the specimen is examined in electron microscopy, so this may not give a true representation of the whole specimen if sampling and trimming are done poorly.
• Living cells and tissues cannot be examined by electron microscopy, and the structure of the sample may be changed during the preparation process, so any deviation from the correct fixation, dehydration, infiltration and embedding steps invalidates the final image.

(a)
• Amyloid is extracellular, amorphous, eosinophilic material composed of protein in an antiparallel beta-pleated sheet configuration.
• Congo red is an acidic dye composed of two identical halves, each with a phenyl ring bound to a naphthalene moiety by a diazo group, giving a linear dye molecule; it stains amyloid by hydrogen bonding.
(b)
The solution used is 0.5% Congo red in 50% alcohol, with 0.2% potassium hydroxide in 80% alcohol used for differentiation.
(c)
• Fixation is not critical for the Congo red technique.
• Results show amyloid staining red and nuclei staining blue.
(d)
• Section thickness is critical, with 8-10 µm considered ideal; too thin a section shows a faint red colour, while too thick a section shows yellow birefringence.
• To differentiate AA and AL amyloid, sections are pretreated with trypsin or potassium permanganate; AA amyloid loses its affinity for Congo red, while AL amyloid is resistant.
(e)
• Under polarized light, Congo red-stained amyloid exhibits apple-green birefringence, which is currently the most reliable diagnostic test for amyloid.
• The reaction depends on the linearity of the dye molecule and the beta-pleated sheet configuration of amyloid, so if the spatial configuration of either is altered the reaction fails.
• Other structures can give apple-green birefringence, such as the neurofibrillary tangles of Alzheimer's disease, intracellular inclusions in adrenal cortical cells, cellulose, chitin and dense collagen, so the polarizing step is essential for correct interpretation.
(f)
• The standard Congo red technique uses 0.5% Congo red in 50% alcohol with potassium hydroxide-alcohol differentiation and relies on hydrogen bonding to amyloid.
• The alkaline Congo-red technique uses a high concentration of sodium chloride, which reduces background electrochemical staining of other tissue components and enhances the hydrogen bonding of Congo red specifically to amyloid.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle of the Congo red technique for amyloid.
(b) State the reagents/solutions used in the Congo red technique.
(c) State the results obtained with the Congo red technique.
(d) State the precautions observed when using the Congo red technique.
(e) Explain why the Congo red technique, viewed under polarized light, is the preferred method for confirming amyloid.
(f) Distinguish the standard Congo red technique from the alkaline Congo-red technique.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The blue-staining fibrous material is collagen, differentiated from the red-staining muscle and cytoplasm by Masson's trichrome technique.
(b)
• The staining reaction depends on tissue permeability and dye molecular size: erythrocyte protein forms a dense network with small pores, muscle cells have larger pores, and collagen has the least dense and most porous network, allowing the larger dye molecules to be retained differently in each tissue type.
• Iron haematoxylin is used as the nuclear stain because it is more resistant to the acidity of the trichrome dye solutions than alum haematoxylin, which would be decolorized.
(c)
• The finding should be reported as an increase in collagenous (fibrous) tissue if this exceeds what is normal for the organ, since Masson's trichrome is used to identify increased collagen and to indicate fibrotic change, for example in cirrhosis of the liver or pyelonephritis.
• The fixative record should be checked, since 10% neutral buffered formalin alone does not give optimal results; treatment of formaldehyde-fixed tissue with picric acid or mercuric chloride solution, or use of a fixative such as Bouin's, Zenker's, formal-mercury or zinc formalin, enhances the intensity of the trichrome reaction.
questions.question:
A tissue section stained by Masson's trichrome shows fibrous areas staining blue, with muscle and cytoplasm staining red and nuclei staining blue-black.
(a) Identify the tissue component stained blue.
(b) State the basic principle behind why collagen and muscle take up different colours in this technique.
(c) State the correct next step in reporting this finding.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The conventional method of embalming, primarily arterial embalming, is the technique appropriate for preserving the body for viewing.
(b)
Arterial embalming involves injection of embalming chemicals into the blood vessels, usually via the right common carotid artery, with blood displaced from the right jugular vein, so that the chemicals are distributed throughout the vascular network.
(c)
The materials/equipment required include the anatomical (aspirator) bottle, a scalpel (surgical) blade, and embalming fluid made up of formalin, phenol, methylated spirit, glycerin and alcohol; hand gloves, laboratory coat and rubber boots are also required.
(d)
Poor circulation in the corpse can interfere with even distribution of the embalming fluid through the vascular system.
(e)
• The interfering effect of poor circulation is managed by the embalmer massaging the corpse to aid distribution and by using other injection points where necessary.
• Personnel should always wear laboratory clothing (surgical gloves, laboratory coat, rain boots), mask the face, tidy the corpse with disinfectants beforehand, avoid the embalming fluid contacting the body, work in a well-ventilated area, and wash hands thoroughly after the procedure.
questions.question:
A human cadaver is to be preserved for viewing at a funeral following a traumatic death.
(a) State the technique appropriate for this purpose.
(b) State the principle of this technique.
(c) State the materials/equipment required.
(d) State a factor that can interfere with even distribution of the preservative.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Demonstration of nucleic acids depends either on the reaction of dyes with phosphate groups, or on production of aldehydes from the sugar (deoxyribose); no histochemical method demonstrates the nitrogenous base directly.
• DNA can be demonstrated by the Feulgen technique (demonstrating the sugar), the methyl green-pyronin technique (demonstrating the phosphate group), acridine orange (a fluorescent method) or the Gallocyanin-chrome alum method.
• The Gallocyanin-chrome alum method demonstrates both DNA and RNA, staining both blue, and a suitable extraction technique must be used to separate the two nucleic acids.
(b)
• In the Feulgen technique, 1M hydrochloric acid is used for acid hydrolysis to break the purine-deoxyribose bond and yield an aldehyde, which is then demonstrated by Schiff reagent, giving DNA a red-purple colour and cytoplasm green.
• In the methyl green-pyronin method, methyl green is specific for DNA because its amino group reacts with the phosphate of DNA, while pyronin binds RNA (and also acid mucins and cartilage), giving DNA green-blue and RNA red.
• Extraction techniques used to separate DNA and RNA include digestion methods (deoxyribonuclease digests DNA, ribonuclease digests RNA) and chemical methods such as perchloric acid, trichloroacetic acid or hydrochloric acid treatment.
• The most suitable technique for identifying DNA is in-situ hybridization, and a control method for the standard Feulgen technique is the Naphthoic acid hydrazide (NAH) method.
(c)
• Bouin's fixative is not suitable for nucleic acid demonstration, as it causes over-hydrolysis of the nucleic acid during fixation.
• RNA cannot be demonstrated by the Feulgen stain because the ribose-purine bond is unaffected by hydrolysis with 1M hydrochloric acid, so applying Feulgen to detect RNA would give a false-negative result.
• If an unsuitable fixative such as Bouin's is used, the nucleic acid content may already be degraded before the Feulgen hydrolysis step even begins, invalidating the result regardless of technique.
• The time of hydrolysis in 1M hydrochloric acid depends on the fixative used (for example, 8 minutes for Carnoy's or formalin fixed tissue), so using the wrong hydrolysis time for a given fixative would under- or over-hydrolyse the tissue.
• The blue thionin-Feulgen reaction, used to study cancer cell nuclear morphology and ploidy, similarly depends on correct hydrolysis; an error here would misrepresent the DNA content being assessed.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of stains/methods used to demonstrate nucleic acids.
(b) State how each nucleic acid demonstration method is applied or selected.
(c) Explain why a basic error in fixative choice leads to an inaccurate nucleic acid staining result.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Mycobacteria possess a capsule containing a long-chain fatty acid (mycolic acid) that makes them hydrophobic, so they can be stained by a strong stain such as carbol fuchsin.
• The fatty capsule resists removal of the stain by an acid-alcohol solution, a property known as acid- and alcohol-fastness.
(b)
The reagents used are carbol fuchsin solution, 1% acid alcohol, and 0.1% methylene blue solution.
(c)
Results show acid-fast bacilli as bright red, other tissue as pale blue and caseous material as very pale greyish blue.
(d)
• The blue counterstain may appear patchy if extensive caseation is present, and over-counterstaining should be avoided as scant organisms can easily be obscured.
• Decalcification using strong acids may destroy acid-fastness, so formic acid is recommended instead.
(e)
• Mycobacteria cannot be demonstrated by Gram's stain because their hydrophobic, mycolic-acid-containing capsule is not stained by the crystal violet/iodine complex in the same way as ordinary bacterial cell walls.
• Mycobacteria are PAS positive because of the carbohydrate content of their cell wall, but the ZN stain is preferred because it specifically exploits their acid-alcohol fastness for clear identification.
(f)
• The standard Ziehl-Neelsen technique uses incubation in preheated carbol fuchsin at 56°C for 60 minutes and decolorizes with 1% acid alcohol (20% sulphuric acid), and it demonstrates Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
• The Modified Fite technique uses a mixture of xylol and liquid paraffin prior to staining, incubates in carbol fuchsin at 37°C for 45 minutes, and decolorizes with 5% sulphuric acid in 25% alcohol.
• The Modified Fite technique demonstrates Mycobacterium leprae, staining it bright red against pale blue nuclei and other tissue elements.
• The two techniques therefore differ in pre-treatment, incubation temperature and time, and decolorizing agent, and are selected according to which organism (M. tuberculosis or M. leprae) is suspected.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle of the Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stain for acid-fast bacilli.
(b) State the reagents used in the Ziehl-Neelsen stain.
(c) State the results obtained with the Ziehl-Neelsen stain.
(d) State the precautions observed when performing the Ziehl-Neelsen stain.
