questions.answerText:
(a)
Chromosomes should be selected from cells at metaphase for accurate karyotype analysis.
(b)
• Chromosome size varies remarkably with the stage of cell division: chromosomes are longest and thinnest in interphase, progressively decrease in length with increasing thickness in prophase, and are smallest in anaphase, but at metaphase they are thick, quite short and well spread in the cell, making them easiest to observe and measure.
• Because chromosome measurements are generally taken during mitotic metaphase, selecting chromosomes from any other stage would give inconsistent, non-comparable measurements of length and centromere position.
(c)
• The selected metaphase chromosomes should be classified by their length, the position of the centromere (metacentric, submetacentric, acrocentric or telocentric), their banding pattern, and any differences between the sex chromosomes, in keeping with the definition of a karyotype.
• The record should also note the total chromosome number (46, or 23 pairs, in a normal human somatic cell) and identify the autosomes (the first 22 pairs) and the sex chromosomes/gonosomes (the 23rd pair, XX or XY).
questions.question:
A chromosome spread prepared from a cell culture is examined, and the cells are found to be at varying stages of the cell cycle, with some chromosomes appearing long and thin and others short and thick.
(a) Identify the stage of the cell cycle at which chromosomes should be selected for accurate karyotype analysis.
(b) State the principle/reasoning behind selecting this stage.
(c) State how the selected chromosomes should be recorded/classified for the karyotype.

(a) Describe the principle of arterial embalming as part of the conventional method of embalming.
(b) State the apparatus/materials used in embalming.
(c) State the precautions observed while carrying out arterial embalming.
(d) Explain why arterial embalming is the primary method used in the conventional embalming process.
(e) Distinguish arterial embalming from cavity embalming.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Arterial embalming involves the injection of embalming chemicals into the blood vessels, usually via the right common carotid artery, with blood displaced from the right jugular vein.
• The embalming solution is injected through a mechanical pump, and the embalmer massages the corpse to ensure proper distribution of the fluid; in case of poor circulation, other injection points are used.
(b)
• The basic apparatus normally used for embalming includes the anatomical (aspirator) bottle and a scalpel blade (surgical blade), with hand gloves, a laboratory coat and rubber boots also used.
• Embalming fluid ingredients include formalin, phenol, methylated spirit, glycerin and alcohol.
(c)
• The embalmer must always wear laboratory clothing such as surgical gloves, laboratory coat and rain boots, and must always mask the face when embalming.
• The corpse should be tidied up with disinfectants before embalming commences, and the embalming fluid must not be allowed to come into contact with the embalmer's body.
• For health reasons, embalming should be carried out in a well-ventilated area, and hands must be washed properly afterwards.
(d)
• Arterial embalming distributes the preservative chemicals throughout the whole vascular network of the body, giving the most complete and even preservation of the tissues.
• It is normally the first of the four parts of the conventional method, with cavity, hypodermic and surface embalming used to supplement it where arterial distribution alone is insufficient.
(e)
• Arterial embalming injects chemicals into the blood vessels (via the carotid artery) to preserve tissue throughout the vascular system, using a mechanical pump and massage for distribution.
• Cavity embalming instead involves suctioning the internal fluids of the corpse and injecting embalming chemicals directly into the body cavities, using an aspirator and a trocar.
• Cavity embalming therefore targets the body cavities directly, whereas arterial embalming relies on the vascular system to carry the preservative to the tissues.

questions.question:
A tissue section treated with an ammoniacal silver solution shows black-brown granular deposits within tumour cells, with nuclei counterstained red.
(a) Identify the pigment and the technique that has produced this reaction.
(b) State the basic principle behind why the black deposit appears.
(c) State the correct next step in handling this result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The black-brown deposit is consistent with melanin demonstrated by the Fontana-Masson (argentaffin) technique.
(b)
Melanin has sufficient reducing strength to reduce ionic silver to metallic silver in the basic (ammoniacal) silver solution, without an extraneous reducer, giving a black deposit, while excess ionic silver is removed by sodium thiosulfate.
(c)
• Because a positive reaction is not specific for melanin, and endogenous brown-black pigments could give an incorrect interpretation, the result should not be reported as melanin without further consideration.
• The correct next step is to check that the tissue was not fixed in an alcohol-containing fixative (which would reduce staining intensity), to ensure glassware used was free of protein residue and chloride ions, and, if needed, to confirm the finding with a different melanin method such as the DOPA reaction or immunohistochemistry.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the mechanism of the Periodic Acid Schiff (PAS) technique.
(b) State the reagents used in the PAS technique.
(c) State the results and the range of tissue components demonstrated by the PAS technique.
(d) State the notes/precautions associated with the PAS technique.
(e) Explain why the PAS technique is used or preferred in histopathology and cytology practice.
(f) Distinguish the PAS technique from the Alcian blue technique in terms of what each demonstrates.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The PAS technique is based on the reactivity of free aldehyde groups within carbohydrates with Schiff reagent to form a bright red/magenta end product.
• The initial step is oxidation of hydroxyl groups attached to adjacent carbon atoms (1,2-glycols) within the carbohydrate, forming two free aldehyde groups and cleaving the adjoining carbon-to-carbon bond.
(b)
The reagents used are periodic acid (the oxidant) and Schiff reagent, with a 0.5-1% solution of periodic acid used for 5-10 minutes.
(c)
• The first histochemical use of the PAS method was by McManus for the demonstration of mucin.
• PAS-reactive cells and tissue components include glycogen, starch, mucin, basement membrane, alpha-antitrypsin, reticulin, fungal capsules, pancreatic zymogen granules, thyroid colloid, corpora amylacea and Russell bodies.
• Results show glycogen and mucins staining magenta and nuclei staining blue.
(d)
• Fixatives containing glutaraldehyde should be avoided if tissue is to be stained with the PAS technique.
• Staining of glycolipids may be detected only when frozen sections are used, and other oxidants such as potassium permanganate or chromic acid are not used because they further oxidise the aldehyde groups to unreactive carboxylic groups.
(e)
• The intensity of the colour that develops after reaction with Schiff reagent depends on the tissue concentration of reactive glycol structures, allowing both identification and a rough estimate of carbohydrate content.
• The PAS technique is used diagnostically for conditions such as glycogen storage disorders, staining macrophages in Whipple's disease, demonstrating mucins in adenocarcinoma of the large intestine, and demonstrating fungi, making it a versatile general-purpose carbohydrate stain.
(f)
• The PAS technique demonstrates a broad range of PAS-positive substances (glycogen, mucin, basement membrane, fungal capsules, and others), staining them magenta through an aldehyde-Schiff reaction.
• The Alcian blue technique instead specifically demonstrates acidic mucins (sialomucins and sulfomucins) and proteoglycans/hyaluronic acid at pH 2.5, staining them blue, while neutral mucins are not reactive with Alcian blue; combining both (Alcian blue-PAS) is needed to differentiate acid mucin from neutral mucin in the same section.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle of autoradiography.
(b) State the materials/apparatus used in autoradiography.
(c) Outline the procedure of the autoradiography method.
(d) State the precautions observed during autoradiography.
(e) Explain why autoradiography is used in histopathology/cytology practice.
(f) Distinguish the stripping method of applying photographic emulsion from the coating method.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Autoradiography is the study and process of identifying radioactive isotopes in tissue sections, demonstrating the sites and amounts of radioactivity in tissues.
• Its basic principle depends on the ability of radioactive isotopes in a tissue section to reduce silver salts in a photographic film, plate or emulsion to black deposits of silver.
(b)
Materials include the photographic emulsion or film, a light-proof box, a refrigerator for storage, and counterstains such as Haematoxylin and Eosin, Methylene Blue, Basic Fuchsin or toluidine blue.
(c)
• Living cells are briefly exposed to a pulse of a specific radioactive compound, left for a variable time, then samples are taken, fixed and processed for light or electron microscopy.
• Sections are cut and overlaid with a thin film of photographic emulsion, then left in the dark for days or weeks depending on isotope activity, temperature and background radiation.
• The photographic emulsion is then developed as in conventional photography, and counterstaining with toluidine blue shows the histological details of the tissue.
(d)
• The whole process, up to the stage of development of the photographic material, must be done in the dark to prevent reduction of silver salts by light.
• Control sections are obtained from laboratory animals previously injected with radioactive compounds, and the counterstain used must penetrate the tissue without adversely affecting the emulsion.
(e)
• Autoradiography allows quantitative estimation of radioactive isotopes using a densitometer and demonstrates precisely where radioactivity is localized in a tissue.
• It is used to determine receptor distribution in neuro-degenerative disorders, to study cytogenesis of the fore-brain, and in radio-pharmaceutical and genetic studies.
(f)
• In the stripping method, a photographic plate with a thick gelatin base is cut and applied over the section, giving accurate location and resolution of radioactive isotopes in tissue sections.
• In the coating method, the section is dipped into liquefied photographic emulsion melted in a water bath, then the back of the slide is wiped clean and dried vertically before development, which is a faster but less precise application than stripping.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of stains used to demonstrate collagen fibres in connective tissue.
(b) State how each collagen stain is applied or selected in practice.
(c) Explain why using an unsuitable fixative is a basic error that leads to an inaccurate connective tissue staining result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Collagen fibre stains include Masson's trichrome technique, Van Gieson's stain, Mallory's Phosphotungstic Acid Haematoxylin, the MSB technique, PAS, Heidenhain's Azan stain, Lillie's allochrome method and Luxol fast blue G.
• Factors affecting trichrome-type staining include tissue permeability and dye molecular size, heat, pH of the staining solution, and the choice of nuclear counterstain.
(b)
• Masson's trichrome is selected to demonstrate collagen and muscle together, giving collagen a blue colour and muscle/cytoplasm a red colour, and is used to indicate fibrotic change such as in cirrhosis.
• Van Gieson's stain is selected when collagen needs to be shown in bright red against a yellow background of muscle, cytoplasm, elastin and reticulin.
• Iron haematoxylin is the preferred nuclear counterstain for these techniques, as it is more resistant to the acidity of the dye solutions than alum haematoxylin, which is decolorized; a Celestin blue-alum haematoxylin sequence can also be used.
(c)
• The protein component of tissue exposed to a fixative forms an insoluble protein network whose structure (pore size) is directly related to the staining reaction; erythrocyte protein forms a dense, small-pored network, muscle a larger-pored network, and collagen the least dense, most porous network.
• 10% neutral buffered formalin (NBF) will not yield optimal trichrome results, so relying on routine formalin fixation alone is a basic error for this stain.
• Treating formaldehyde-fixed tissue further with picric acid or mercuric chloride solution enhances the intensity and radiance of the trichrome reaction, which routine processing does not automatically provide.
• Recommended fixatives for optimal collagen staining are Bouin's, Zenker's, formal-mercury and zinc formalin; using a fixative outside this list without secondary treatment risks poor differentiation between collagen and muscle.
• Because heat increases the rate of staining and penetration and a low pH (1.5-3) is required, incorrect staining temperature or pH is also a basic technical error that can prevent proper colour differentiation.
• An unsuitable fixative therefore leaves the tissue's protein network in a state that does not take up the trichrome dyes correctly, so the resulting colours no longer reliably distinguish collagen from muscle or cytoplasm.
• This is why fixation is treated as inseparable from the staining step itself: an error introduced at fixation cannot be corrected by the staining protocol that follows.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition of the reagents used in argentaffin silver staining.
(b) State the standard practice for handling glassware and solutions used in silver staining.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind this precaution regarding glassware and reagent handling in silver staining.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Argentaffin staining uses an ammoniacal (basic) silver solution, in which melanin and certain other reducing compounds convert ionic silver to metallic silver.
• Excess ionic silver in the process is solubilized by reaction with sodium thiosulfate.
• The Warthin-Starry method for spirochetes uses an acetate buffer at pH 3.6 and 1% silver nitrate, with a developer containing hydroquinone to reduce silver ions to metallic silver.
• The Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) technique uses reagents including 4% chromic acid, 1% sodium bisulfite, 5% sodium thiosulfate, 0.21% silver nitrate (stock), 0.1% gold chloride and a light green counterstain.
(b)
• All glassware used in silver staining procedures must be chemically cleaned with commercial cleaning agents, concentrated nitric acid, or bleach, and rinsed in distilled water.
• Solutions should be made with distilled water, and no metal should be allowed to contact the silver solutions.
• Control tissues, matched to the organism or substance expected, should be used to judge the quality of staining and aid interpretation.
(c)
• Proteins and ions attached to the walls of glassware may react with silver solutions, and ions such as chloride in non-distilled water may precipitate the silver.
• Silver solutions may also react with any metal used in the staining procedure, such as forceps or slide holders, causing nonspecific silver deposition.
• Because silver solutions are very susceptible to degradation, high temperatures could cause nonspecific silver deposition, and oxidizing solutions may lose their oxidizing power on aging.
• Fixation in glutaraldehyde, or even a short exposure to formalin, may also cause non-specific staining with the silver solution, adding another route to a false result.
• Following these handling precautions therefore prevents the high, erratic background and unreliable staining that silver stains are otherwise prone to, ensuring that a positive result genuinely reflects the tissue component being sought rather than glassware or reagent contamination.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of stains used to demonstrate acid-fast bacilli.
(b) State how each acid-fast staining method is applied or selected according to the organism suspected.
(c) Explain why decalcifying bony/calcified tissue with a strong acid before staining is a basic error that invalidates an acid-fast staining result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Acid-fast bacilli can be demonstrated by the standard Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stain or by the Modified Fite technique.
• Both techniques rely on the ability of a strong stain, carbol fuchsin, to penetrate the hydrophobic, mycolic-acid-containing capsule of mycobacteria, which then resists decolorization by acid-alcohol.
(b)
• The standard Ziehl-Neelsen technique uses carbol fuchsin, incubated in preheated solution at 56°C for 60 minutes, decolorized with 1% acid alcohol (20% sulphuric acid), and is selected to demonstrate Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
• The Modified Fite technique uses a mixture of xylol and liquid paraffin prior to staining, incubates in carbol fuchsin at 37°C for 45 minutes, decolorizes with 5% sulphuric acid in 25% alcohol, and is selected to demonstrate Mycobacterium leprae.
• In both techniques, acid-fast bacilli stain bright red while other tissue elements and nuclei stain pale blue, and caseous material stains very pale greyish blue in the ZN technique.
• The choice between ZN and Fite technique is therefore selected according to whether tuberculosis (ZN) or leprosy (Fite) is clinically suspected.
(c)
• Decalcification using strong acids may destroy acid-fastness in the tissue.
• Formic acid is recommended instead of strong mineral acids for decalcifying tissue that will subsequently be stained for acid-fast organisms.
• If a strong acid is used for decalcification, the mycolic-acid capsule that confers acid-alcohol fastness on the bacilli may itself be damaged before the ZN or Fite stain is even applied.
• This would cause the bacilli to lose their acid-fastness and fail to retain the red carbol fuchsin during the acid-alcohol decolorization step of the stain, giving a false-negative result even if organisms were originally present.
• Over-counterstaining with methylene blue is a related basic error, since it can obscure scant organisms and again lead to a false-negative interpretation.
• Choosing the correct decalcifying agent and counterstaining carefully are therefore both essential precautions for a valid acid-fast result, whichever of the two techniques is used.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the basic structure of a transmission electron microscope.
(b) State the standard use of each major part of the transmission electron microscope.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind the precaution of using an ultra-microtome to cut sections for electron microscopy.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A transmission electron microscope has four major parts: the electron source, the electromagnetic lens system, the sample holder and the imaging system.
• The electron source is an electron gun consisting of a tungsten filament that emits electrons when heated.
• The electromagnetic lens system consists of a solenoid, a coil of wire through which a current is passed to induce an electromagnetic field that focuses the electron beam.
• The sample holder consists of a mechanical arm that holds the specimen, and the imaging system consists of a further electromagnetic lens system and a phosphorescent screen that glows when struck by electrons.
(b)
• The electron source generates and emits the electron beam, which is focused onto the specimen by the condenser lenses (magnetic lenses).
• The sample holder positions the specimen in the path of the beam, and the imaging system's phosphorescent plate displays the image formed after electrons pass through the specimen.
• The electron beam passes through the centre of the solenoids on its way down the column of the microscope towards the sample.
(c)
• The ultra-microtome is a highly specialized precision instrument designed to cut sections from hard synthetic resins, cutting in the order of 0.005 to 0.1 µm, which is suitable for electron microscopy.
• The knife of the ultra-microtome is stationary with the cutting edge uppermost, while the tissue block moves up and down vertically as sections are cut, and the knife is prepared from diamond or plate glass suitable for the hard resin.
• Very thin sections are required for electron microscopy because electrons have poor penetrating power, so an ordinary microtome cannot produce sections thin enough for the electron beam to pass through.
• Excess plastic surrounding the tissue must first be trimmed to a pyramid with facet angles of about 45 degrees, viewed under a dissecting microscope, so that the block can be cut into square or rectangular ultrathin sections.
• Paraffin wax is not firm enough for ultrathin sections and would melt under the electron beam, which is why hard epoxy, polyester or methacrylate resins are used for embedding instead.

questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient in diabetic ketoacidosis prioritises which intervention first, according to standard emergency management principles?
options: Withholding all fluids until glucose normalises
Immediate administration of a large glucose bolus
Delaying treatment until formal endocrinology consultation
questions.explanation: In diabetic ketoacidosis, patients are typically significantly dehydrated due to osmotic diuresis from hyperglycaemia, so initial management prioritises fluid resuscitation to restore circulating volume and improve tissue perfusion, followed by careful insulin therapy to correct the underlying hyperglycaemia and ketosis. Administering a glucose bolus would worsen hyperglycaemia rather than help, and oral hypoglycaemics are not appropriate in this acute insulin-deficient state. This structured approach reflects evidence-based emergency management priorities.

questions.question: The alar plates of the myelencephalon contain how many groups of sensory nuclei?
questions.explanation: The alar plates of the myelencephalon contain three groups of sensory nuclei. Similarly, the basal plates contain three groups of motor neurons which form cranial nerve nuclei in the medulla. These nuclei are arranged in distinct columns.

questions.question: The seminal vesicles prostate gland and bulbourethral glands are male accessory sex glands. Their primary contribution to semen is which of the following?
options: Producing spermatozoa as an additional sperm source
Filtering sperm removing abnormal cells before ejaculation
Providing oxygen for sperm metabolism during ejaculation
questions.explanation: Male accessory sex glands contribute secretions forming semen: seminal vesicles provide approximately 60% of semen volume containing fructose as sperm energy source, prostaglandins that stimulate female reproductive tract contractions, and coagulation proteins; the prostate contributes approximately 30% with zinc for sperm motility, PSA protease that liquefies semen, and acid phosphatase; bulbourethral glands secrete mucus neutralizing urethral acidity and providing pre-ejaculatory lubrication.

questions.question: What condition results from median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel?
questions.explanation: results from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel. This causes sensory disturbances in the lateral three and one-half fingers (palmer aspect) and weakness of thenar muscles. The condition commonly occurs from inflammatory reactions in flexor tendon synovial sheaths or space-occupying lesions.

questions.question: A nurse notes an older client has orthostatic hypotension identified during vital sign assessment. This finding is clinically significant primarily because it increases risk for:
options: No meaningful impact on mobility or safety
Reduced risk of any position-related symptoms
Enhanced blood flow to the lower extremities
Falls related to dizziness upon standing
Improved balance when changing position quickly
questions.explanation: Orthostatic hypotension causes dizziness or lightheadedness upon standing due to a drop in blood pressure, significantly increasing fall risk in older adults, particularly during transfers or ambulation. This is the opposite of improved balance or reduced symptom risk. Nursing interventions such as slow position changes and monitoring help reduce this risk.

options: Renal function is unrelated to haemolysis
Haemolysis always causes permanent kidney failure
The spleen filters blood through the kidneys
Free haemoglobin can damage the renal tubules
The kidneys produce red blood cells directly
questions.explanation: Massive intravascular haemolysis releases free haemoglobin into the plasma, which can precipitate in renal tubules and cause acute kidney injury. Monitoring urine output, colour, and renal function tests allows early detection of this complication. Adequate hydration helps protect renal perfusion during recovery.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient recovering from a haemolytic crisis should monitor renal function closely because:
Which part of the humerus is most commonly associated with radial nerve injury?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve winds around the spiral groove of the humerus accompanied by profunda brachii vessels. Midshaft humeral fractures frequently damage the radial nerve at this location. This results in wrist drop due to paralysis of extensor muscles and sensory loss over the dorsal hand.

questions.question: Androgen insensitivity syndrome results from:
questions.explanation: Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) results from X-linked mutations causing non-functional androgen receptors. Complete AIS produces 46,XY individuals with female external genitalia, absent internal female structures (MIS effect), and undescended testes. They're raised female and present with primary amenorrhea. Partial AIS causes ambiguous genitalia. Gonadectomy after puberty prevents malignancy.

questions.question: A midwife caring for a woman with severe, persistent vomiting in early pregnancy, weight loss, and ketonuria diagnoses:
questions.explanation: Hyperemesis gravidarum is characterised by severe, persistent vomiting in pregnancy leading to weight loss, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and ketonuria, distinguishing it from the more common, milder nausea and vomiting of normal early pregnancy. This condition may require hospital admission for intravenous fluid replacement, antiemetics, and correction of electrolyte disturbances. Other causes of vomiting, such as gastroenteritis or appendicitis, should be considered and excluded as part of a thorough assessment.

questions.question: During inhalational induction with sevoflurane, a child suddenly develops stridor and suprasternal retraction. The nurse should suspect
options: an allergic drug reaction to sevoflurane
questions.explanation: Stridor with suprasternal retraction during induction indicates laryngospasm, a partial or complete closure of the vocal cords triggered by airway irritation during the light planes of anaesthesia. This requires immediate management such as jaw thrust, positive pressure oxygen, and deepening of anaesthesia if needed. It is not a normal or expected finding during smooth induction.

options: Further impacts the anterior shoulder against the symphysis pubis and risks uterine rupture
Reduces the risk of brachial plexus injury
Is the standard first-line manoeuvre recommended
Has no effect on the outcome
questions.question: During management of shoulder dystocia, a midwife is taught that fundal pressure should be avoided because it:
questions.explanation: Fundal pressure in shoulder dystocia pushes the anterior shoulder more firmly against the symphysis pubis, worsening impaction and increasing the risk of uterine rupture and further birth trauma. It is not a recommended manoeuvre and should be actively avoided. Effective management relies on manoeuvres that increase pelvic space or rotate the fetal shoulders instead.

options: Antidepressants (amitriptyline or duloxetine) or anticonvulsants (gabapentin, pregabalin)
Morphine and diclofenac with a proton pump inhibitor
Corticosteroids combined with muscle relaxants for nerve inflammation
Strong opioids alone titrated to the patient's response
Codeine combined with paracetamol at maximum daily doses
questions.question: When treating neuropathic pain in a diabetic patient, the most appropriate first-line pharmacological combination is:
questions.explanation: Diabetic neuropathy is a neuropathic pain condition that requires pharmacological agents targeting the aberrant nerve signaling rather than conventional analgesics. First-line agents include tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline), SNRIs (duloxetine), and anticonvulsants (gabapentin, pregabalin). Topical agents (lidocaine patches, capsaicin cream) may also be used for localized symptoms. Opioids are typically reserved for cases refractory to these agents due to their higher risk profile.

questions.question: The gallbladder has a storage capacity of approximately:
questions.explanation: The gallbladder can store 30-50 ml of concentrated bile between meals, representing about 12 hours of hepatic bile production. The pear-shaped organ concentrates bile 5-fold through water absorption, storing it until CCK-stimulated contraction releases it during meals. Despite this small capacity, the gallbladder plays an important role in coordinating bile availability with fat digestion.

questions.question: A midwife caring for a woman six weeks postpartum at her final postnatal check confirms the uterus is no longer palpable abdominally. This finding indicates:
questions.explanation: By six weeks postpartum, the uterus should have returned to its approximate pre-pregnancy size and is no longer palpable abdominally, confirming completion of normal involution. This is a reassuring finding consistent with expected postpartum recovery, not a cause for concern. Continued abdominal palpability of the uterus at this stage would instead suggest subinvolution, which requires further evaluation.
options: Evidence of retained products of conception

questions.explanation: Axillary and pubic hair development is significantly influenced by adrenal androgens, so their absence, particularly when otherwise unexpected given the patient's overall development, can indicate adrenal androgen insufficiency and warrants further endocrine evaluation. This is distinct from normal variation, which should be considered but not assumed without further assessment given the specific hormonal link. Recognising this connection supports a more targeted evaluation of adrenal function.
options: Normal variation requiring no further evaluation in every case
Isolated vitamin deficiency unrelated to hormones
questions.question: A nurse notes that a patient reports absent axillary and pubic hair despite otherwise normal secondary sexual development. What underlying disturbance should this finding prompt the nurse to consider?
When assessing a new patient in the ophthalmic clinic, the ophthalmic nurse's FIRST action should be to:
options: Refer the patient directly to the ophthalmologist
Perform tonometry to measure intraocular pressure
Obtain history of the present condition
questions.explanation: Obtaining a thorough history of the present condition is the initial step in the nursing process and guides all subsequent assessments and interventions. This baseline information enables the nurse to prioritize care, identify urgency, and direct the patient appropriately. Performing diagnostic tests without first gathering a history would compromise the quality and safety of patient-centered care in the ophthalmic setting.

questions.question: Family planning programs empower communities by:
options: Involving them in decision-making and implementing culturally suitable interventions
Distributing contraceptives to all community members without prior consultation
Replacing community health workers with formally trained medical professionals
Mandating compliance with national contraceptive targets at community level
Establishing community-level penalties for non-compliance with family planning
questions.explanation: Family planning programs empower communities by involving them in decision-making processes and implementing suitable interventions through collaboration between community members and healthcare providers. This participatory approach fosters awareness, dispels myths and misconceptions, and ensures that services and information are tailored to local needs. Community empowerment in family planning leads to greater program ownership, utilization, and sustainability.

options: Improved swallowing reflex efficiency with age
Oesophageal motility and swallowing muscle coordination
Enhanced oesophageal motility compared to youth
Increased saliva production aiding swallowing overall
No expected age-related change in swallowing
questions.explanation: Age-related changes in oesophageal motility and coordination of swallowing muscles, sometimes called presbyphagia, can contribute to difficulty swallowing and increased aspiration risk in older adults. This is the opposite of improved or enhanced swallowing function. Recognising these changes supports careful assessment and appropriate dietary modifications to reduce aspiration risk.
questions.question: An older client reports difficulty swallowing certain foods, occasionally coughing during meals. The nurse recognises this may relate to age-related changes affecting:
A nurse caring for a patient who has just started tube feeding reports new abdominal distension and high gastric residual volumes. The nurse's priority action is to:
questions.explanation: High residual volumes and distension suggest delayed gastric emptying or intolerance, and continuing to feed at the same rate increases the risk of vomiting and aspiration. Pausing the feed to reassess, and notifying the physician if the problem persists, is the safer initial response. Gradual reintroduction follows once tolerance improves.
options: Pause the feed and reassess before resuming
Reposition the patient flat and continue feeding
Increase the feeding rate to clear the stomach
Administer a full bolus feed immediately
Ignore the finding and continue as prescribed

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C7, C8, T1). The medial cord also gives rise to the medial pectoral nerve, medial cutaneous nerve of arm and forearm, and the medial root of the median nerve. Injury to the medial cord affects all these structures.
questions.question: Which cord of the brachial plexus gives rise to the ulnar nerve?

questions.explanation: The tympanic membrane (eardrum) is the first structure to vibrate in response to sound waves funneled through the external auditory canal. These vibrations are mechanically amplified through the ossicular chain (malleus, incus, stapes) before reaching the oval window. The tympanic membrane's large surface area relative to the oval window provides mechanical advantage in impedance matching.
questions.question: Sound waves entering the external ear ultimately cause vibration of which middle ear structure first?

options: Introduce formula at 3 months to prepare for return to work
Breastfeed before leaving for work and maintain pumping schedule
Gradually wean the infant 2 weeks before returning to work
Offer mixed feeding from birth to maintain supply flexibility
Continue breastfeeding only during weekday evening hours
questions.question: For employed breastfeeding mothers, the nurse should advise that they:
questions.explanation: Employed breastfeeding mothers should be counselled to breastfeed the infant before leaving for work and then adhere to a set schedule of pumping and feeding each day while at work. Breastfeeding should be resumed during the evening and throughout weekends to maintain milk supply. Proper expression and storage of breast milk should be taught, including sterilisation of equipment and safe storage practices.

options: Sciatic nerve block at the popliteal fossa
Femoral nerve block at the inguinal ligament
Peripheral nerve block at the thoracic level
Epidural anaesthesia in the epidural space
questions.question: An anaesthetic nurse is preparing for a patient undergoing labour. Which invasive anaesthesia technique is MOST commonly used for labour analgesia?
questions.explanation: Epidural anaesthesia involves injection of local anaesthetic into the epidural space surrounding the spinal cord and is widely used for labour analgesia. It provides effective pain relief while allowing the mother to remain conscious and actively participate in the birthing process. Spinal anaesthesia, though related, is typically used for caesarean sections rather than continuous labour analgesia.

The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament), a lateral extension of the broad ligament, suspends the ovary from the lateral pelvic wall and contains the ovarian artery (from aorta) and ovarian vein (to IVC on right, left renal vein on left), along with ovarian nerves and lymphatics. This ligament must be clamped and divided during oophorectomy. The ovarian ligament connects the ovary to the uterus medially, while the broad ligament provides only indirect support via the mesovarium. The round ligament extends from uterus to labium majus via the inguinal canal.
questions.question: The ovary is suspended by which ligament from the pelvic wall?
In the menstrual cycle, high estrogen levels stimulate the sudden LH surge. This surge occurs around which day of a 28-day cycle?
questions.explanation: High estrogen levels cause the LH surge around day 12-13 of a 28-day cycle. This positive feedback effect - where high estrogen triggers rather than suppresses LH - is unusual but critical for reproductive function. The surge lasts approximately 48 hours and leads to ovulation on day 14. This mechanism forms the basis of LH detection kits used for home ovulation prediction in couples trying to conceive.

Neutrophil nuclei typically contain 2-6 lobes connected by thin chromatin strands, giving them the alternate name "polymorphonuclear leukocytes" (PMNs). Nuclear lobulation increases with cell age, with younger neutrophils (bands) showing less segmentation than mature forms.
questions.question: What characterizes the nucleus of a neutrophil?
Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the oral cavity proper?
questions.explanation: The palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar of fauces) forms the posterior boundary of the oral cavity proper, separating it from the oropharynx. The arch extends from the soft palate to the side of the tongue and contains the palatoglossus muscle. The isthmus of fauces is the opening between the two palatoglossal arches connecting the oral cavity with the oropharynx.

options: Neutral position without any neck extension
Neck extended in supine position for access
Neck flexed forward with chin tucked to chest
Lateral position with head tilted to one side
questions.explanation: During cricothyrotomy, the patient lies supine with the neck extended to maximise exposure of the anterior neck and the cricothyroid membrane. Extension of the neck stretches the skin and subcutaneous tissues, making the cricothyroid membrane more prominent and easier to palpate and incise. This position also optimises subsequent tube passage into the trachea through the incision.
questions.question: During cricothyrotomy, the patient is positioned with the neck in which position to facilitate the procedure?

questions.explanation: Erb's palsy, the most common form of brachial plexus injury, results from traction damage to the upper brachial plexus roots at the fifth and sixth cervical levels, typically following shoulder dystocia or difficult delivery of the shoulders. This produces the characteristic 'waiter's tip' posture with the arm adducted, internally rotated, and the wrist flexed. Klumpke's palsy, in contrast, involves the lower nerve roots and presents with hand weakness rather than shoulder involvement.
options: The entire brachial plexus without exception
The third and fourth cervical nerve roots
The first and second thoracic nerve roots
The fifth and sixth cervical nerve roots
The seventh and eighth cervical nerve roots
questions.question: Erb's palsy results from injury to which cervical nerve roots during a difficult delivery?
What is the marginal artery of the heart?
questions.explanation: The right marginal artery is a branch of the right coronary artery that descends along the acute margin (right border) of the heart to supply the right ventricle. The left marginal artery (branch of the circumflex or left coronary artery) supplies the left border of the heart. These marginal branches are important anatomical landmarks in cardiac catheterization and surgery.

questions.question: Anxiety related to floaters in a patient with PDR MOST appropriately requires which nursing intervention?
questions.explanation: For anxiety related to floaters in PDR, the nurse provides factual explanation about the cause of floaters (vitreous hemorrhage from fragile neovascular vessels), what they indicate, and when they require urgent medical attention (sudden large increase in floaters or loss of vision). Coping strategies are taught, and the patient is encouraged to express their concerns. While acknowledging the understandable anxiety, the nurse guides the patient toward adaptive responses and reinforces the importance of regular ophthalmological monitoring.
options: Advising the patient to ignore floaters as they are always benign
Providing factual explanation and coping strategies while addressing concerns
Performing an immediate bedside dilated fundus examination
Administering sedatives and anti-anxiety medication immediately
Applying cool compresses to reduce vitreous inflammation causing floaters
Magnesium sulphate 4 g IV over 5–10 minutes
Labetalol 20 mg IV bolus to lower the blood pressure
Diazepam 10 mg IV to terminate the acute seizure
Lorazepam 4 mg IV as a first-line benzodiazepine
Phenytoin 15 mg/kg IV for status epilepticus management
questions.question: In the management of an eclamptic seizure, after securing the airway, which drug is administered first?
questions.explanation: In an eclamptic seizure, after ensuring the airway is clear (left lateral position, call for help, oxygen via face mask), the first drug administered is magnesium sulphate 4 g IV over 5-10 minutes as a loading dose, to terminate the seizure and prevent recurrence. MgSO4 is superior to diazepam and phenytoin in preventing recurrent eclamptic seizures (Magpie Trial). Antihypertensives are given concurrently once the seizure is controlled, but MgSO4 takes priority as the anticonvulsant.

options: Administer the patient's scheduled insulin dose immediately
Position the patient in Trendelenburg position for shock
Administer IV dextrose 10% over the next 4 hours slowly
Contact the physician before taking any nursing action
Obtain blood glucose and provide treatment for hypoglycemia
questions.question: A patient with diabetes presents with cool, clammy skin and a diminished level of consciousness. The priority nursing action is:
questions.explanation: Cool, clammy (moist) skin and a diminished level of consciousness are classic clinical manifestations of hypoglycemia in a diabetic patient. The priority nursing action is to recognize hypoglycemia, obtain blood glucose confirmation, and immediately treat with orange juice (for a conscious patient) or IV 50% dextrose or a glucagon injection (for an unconscious patient), followed by retesting blood glucose in 10-15 minutes. Delayed treatment of hypoglycemia can result in irreversible brain damage.

Prophylactic antimicrobials are given to close contacts to eradicate potential nasopharyngeal carriage of Neisseria meningitidis and prevent secondary cases from developing. It is not intended to treat an infection the contacts do not yet have, nor to reduce fever, since they may be asymptomatic. It does not provide long-term immunity or protect against unrelated respiratory illnesses.
questions.question: Close contacts of a patient recently diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis are advised to take prophylactic antibiotics. What is the primary purpose of this measure?

questions.explanation: The neural tube forms three brain flexures: the cephalic (midbrain) flexure which is ventral, the cervical flexure at the junction of hindbrain and spinal cord which is ventral, and the pontine flexure which is dorsal. There is no lumbar flexure in brain development.
questions.question: Brain flexures include all of the following EXCEPT:
Which of the following symptoms is shared by BOTH menopause and andropause?
questions.explanation: Both menopause and andropause share common symptoms including depression, anxiety, mood swings, hot flushes, night sweats, weight gain, hair loss, low libido, brain fog, and lack of energy. These shared symptoms reflect the common physiological effects of declining sex hormones on multiple organ systems. Recognising these shared symptoms helps healthcare providers offer appropriate support to both men and women experiencing hormonal changes during midlife.
options: Irregular menstrual periods and absence of ovulation
Cessation of sperm production and vaginal atrophy
Depression, anxiety, mood swings, and hot flushes

questions.question: A patient presents with a small asymptomatic conjunctival cyst. The MOST appropriate initial management is:
questions.explanation: Small, asymptomatic conjunctival cysts are best managed conservatively through watchful observation, as they often remain stable or may spontaneously regress over time. Surgical intervention is reserved for larger or symptomatic cysts that cause discomfort, visual disturbances, or difficulty closing the eyelid. This approach minimizes unnecessary procedural risk while ensuring that patients who develop complications are identified and treated appropriately.
options: Sclerotherapy injection to collapse the cyst immediately
Drainage under local anesthesia in the outpatient clinic
Watchful observation, as many cysts remain stable or regress
Administration of topical corticosteroids for three months
Immediate surgical excision to prevent rupture and infection

questions.question: Syndactyly occurring as part of Apert's syndrome is most characteristically associated with which additional feature?
options: Complete absence of the corpus callosum
Isolated congenital deafness without other features
Premature fusion of the skull sutures (craniosynostosis)
Isolated cleft palate without craniofacial involvement
Bilateral congenital cataracts without limb involvement
questions.explanation: Apert's syndrome combines syndactyly, typically of the hands and feet, with craniosynostosis, in which premature fusion of the cranial sutures leads to a characteristic skull shape and midface hypoplasia, reflecting the syndrome's basis in a fibroblast growth factor receptor mutation. This combination of limb and craniofacial features distinguishes Apert's syndrome from isolated syndactyly occurring without other anomalies. Multidisciplinary care involving craniofacial and hand surgery is typically required.

questions.question: The thyroid gland produces which hormones?
questions.explanation: The thyroid produces triiodothyronine (T3), thyroxine (T4), and calcitonin. T3 and T4 regulate metabolism, while calcitonin lowers blood calcium. T4 is the major secretory product but T3 is more biologically active. Most T3 is produced by peripheral conversion from T4.

ACE inhibitors used in the second and third trimesters cause fetal renal tubular dysplasia leading to oligohydramnios (reduced amniotic fluid) due to impaired fetal urine production, and can result in neonatal renal failure, pulmonary hypoplasia (from oligohydramnios), limb contractures, and neonatal death. The fetal renin-angiotensin system, which ACE inhibitors block, is critical for renal development. Women on ACE inhibitors for hypertension or heart disease must switch to safer alternatives before conception.
options: Neural tube defects in the first trimester
Fetal renal tubular dysplasia, oligohydramnios, and neonatal renal failure
Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus
questions.question: ACE inhibitors (e.g., enalapril, lisinopril) are contraindicated in the second and third trimesters of pregnancy because they cause:

questions.explanation: Sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, and tachycardia following a period of immobility are classic features suggesting pulmonary embolism secondary to venous thromboembolism. This presentation requires urgent evaluation rather than being dismissed as anxiety or a musculoskeletal issue. Prompt recognition allows timely anticoagulation or thrombolytic therapy consideration.
questions.question: A patient develops sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, and tachycardia after prolonged immobility. The nurse should have a high index of suspicion for:
options: Musculoskeletal chest pain from inactivity alone
Simple anxiety attack unrelated to physical illness
Chronic bronchitis exacerbation from prolonged rest

questions.explanation: The pronormoblast (proerythroblast) is the earliest recognizable cell committed to erythrocyte lineage. This large cell with basophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleus undergoes progressive maturation through normoblast stages, eventually losing its nucleus to become a reticulocyte.
questions.question: What cell is the erythrocyte precursor?

options: An optional addition only for paediatric patients
A component unrelated to the teaching process itself
A task reserved exclusively for the hospital chaplain
A replacement for factual information about the procedure
Addressing patient fears and providing reassurance throughout teaching
questions.question: Emotional support as a component of preoperative teaching is MOST accurately described as:
questions.explanation: Emotional support involves acknowledging and addressing patient fears and providing reassurance as an integrated part of the teaching process, not a separate or optional task. It complements, rather than replaces, factual information delivery. Attending to emotional needs alongside content improves the patient's overall receptiveness to teaching.

These are classic symptoms of acute myocardial infarction, and rapid ECG acquisition is essential to identify ST-segment changes guiding urgent reperfusion therapy. Time to treatment directly affects the amount of myocardium salvaged. Physical exertion and delay could worsen ischaemic injury.
options: Document the complaint for the next assessment round
Obtain a 12-lead ECG and notify the physician immediately
Apply a warm compress to the chest
Offer a light snack to settle the stomach
Encourage the patient to walk to relieve discomfort
questions.question: A patient reports crushing substernal chest pain radiating to the left arm, associated with sweating and nausea. The nurse's priority action is to:

options: Normal response to rupture of membranes
questions.question: A midwife caring for a labouring woman notices sudden maternal collapse, severe dyspnoea, and hypotension shortly after spontaneous rupture of membranes with strong contractions. This presentation raises suspicion of:
questions.explanation: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare but catastrophic event presenting with sudden maternal collapse, respiratory distress, hypotension, and often coagulopathy, typically occurring around the time of membrane rupture or delivery. It requires immediate resuscitation and multidisciplinary emergency management. This presentation is far more severe than normal physiological responses to labour and must be recognised rapidly.

questions.question: A 47-year-old woman who smokes heavily asks whether her habit could explain why she began menopause earlier than her mother did. What is the most accurate response?
questions.explanation: Smoking is a recognised lifestyle factor associated with earlier onset of menopause due to its toxic effects on ovarian follicles. Other factors such as certain autoimmune conditions and chemotherapy can similarly hasten menopause. Counselling women on modifiable risk factors is a relevant preventive nursing role.
options: Smoking has no relationship with menopausal timing
Smoking always delays menopause by several years
Smoking only affects fertility, not menopausal timing
Smoking guarantees a later, more severe menopause
Smoking is linked to earlier menopause onset

questions.explanation: In the early stages of hypovolaemic shock, the body compensates through tachycardia while blood pressure may remain normal or only slightly reduced, making heart rate an important early warning sign that can precede a dramatic drop in blood pressure. Profound hypotension, absent pulses, and loss of consciousness represent later, more severe stages of shock. Early recognition of tachycardia allows for prompt intervention before decompensation occurs.
options: Tachycardia with normal or slightly low blood pressure
questions.question: A midwife recognises early signs of hypovolaemic shock in a woman with ongoing postpartum haemorrhage. Which finding would appear EARLIEST in the progression of shock?
A patient with heart failure secondary to cardiomyopathy is prescribed furosemide. The nurse's priority assessment before and after administration is:
questions.explanation: Furosemide (a loop diuretic) promotes renal potassium excretion, predisposing to hypokalaemia (which increases arrhythmia risk, especially in patients on digoxin). The nurse must monitor serum potassium levels regularly and observe for hypokalaemia symptoms (muscle weakness, ECG changes). Urine output monitoring quantifies diuretic efficacy, and blood pressure monitoring detects hypotension from over-diuresis. Potassium supplementation is frequently prescribed alongside furosemide, and nurses must ensure compliance.
options: Blood glucose level and dietary history
Serum potassium, urine output, and blood pressure

questions.explanation: Before surgical closure, the open spina bifida lesion must be handled with utmost care to preserve the integrity of the sac and limit the risk of meningitis. The lesion should be covered with a non-adherent, sterile, moist dressing. The baby should not be positioned in a way that puts pressure on the sac, and unnecessary handling should be minimised. Urgent referral to a paediatric surgeon for possible surgical closure within 24 to 48 hours is essential.
questions.question: In the management of a neonate with an open spina bifida lesion before surgical closure, the midwife's priority nursing care should include:
options: Irrigating the sac with normal saline every four hours until surgery
Covering the open lesion with a non-adherent dressing and handling with care
Wrapping the sac tightly with a pressure bandage to reduce swelling
Applying antiseptic cream directly to the exposed neural tissue
Positioning the neonate prone to expose the sac to drying air

questions.explanation: Nifedipine, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, inhibits uterine contractions by blocking the influx of calcium ions through L-type calcium channels in myometrial smooth muscle cells. Calcium is essential for smooth muscle contraction, and its blockade leads to myometrial relaxation. Nifedipine is preferred over betamimetics (e.g., salbutamol, ritodrine) as a tocolytic agent due to its better side effect profile, oral administration, and comparable efficacy. It also lowers blood pressure, which can be beneficial or detrimental depending on the clinical context.
questions.question: Nifedipine is used as a tocolytic agent in preterm labour. Its mechanism of action to inhibit uterine contractions is:
options: Blocking calcium influx into myometrial smooth muscle cells

questions.explanation: Antenatal corticosteroids promote maturation of fetal organ systems, including the lungs and the fragile cerebral vasculature, and by reducing the severity of respiratory distress and the associated haemodynamic instability after birth, they lower the incidence and severity of periventricular-intraventricular haemorrhage in preterm infants. They do not repair haemorrhage that has already occurred, nor do they reliably delay labour indefinitely. Their main benefit lies in reducing complications once preterm birth occurs.
questions.question: Antenatal corticosteroid administration to a mother in threatened preterm labour reduces the risk of periventricular haemorrhage primarily by:
options: Reversing haemorrhage that has already occurred
Preventing preterm labour from occurring entirely
Directly repairing existing germinal matrix damage
Accelerating fetal lung and vascular maturity before birth
Eliminating the need for any postnatal ventilation
Reproductive health applies only during the childbearing years
Menopause falls outside reproductive health scope
Menopause management is included across the lifespan
Reproductive health is limited to fertility services
questions.question: A postmenopausal woman is refused counselling on hormone therapy because staff consider her 'past reproductive age.' Which principle is violated?
questions.explanation: Reproductive health explicitly includes management of menopause and andropause, recognising that hormonal transitions affect wellbeing beyond fertile years. Refusing care based on age contradicts the life-course approach to reproductive health. Nurses should provide counselling and support regardless of reproductive stage.

options: Cycles occurring at intervals longer than thirty-five days
Cycles occurring at intervals shorter than twenty-one days
Cycles occurring at regular twenty-eight day intervals
Cycles occurring twice within a single calendar month
Cycles occurring at intervals of exactly thirty days
questions.explanation: Oligomenorrhoea describes menstrual cycles occurring at intervals longer than thirty-five days, reflecting infrequent menstruation often associated with anovulation, as seen in conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome. This differs from polymenorrhoea, where cycles occur more frequently than every twenty-one days. Establishing the correct cycle pattern helps direct further hormonal and structural investigation.
questions.question: A woman is diagnosed with oligomenorrhoea after describing her menstrual pattern to the nurse. How frequently do her cycles occur to meet this definition?

questions.explanation: Haemoglobin electrophoresis identifies the specific haemoglobin genotype, distinguishing normal, carrier (trait), and disease states, which is essential information for genetic counselling and reproductive decision-making, particularly if her partner's genotype is also relevant to the risk of an affected child. The other listed tests do not provide information about haemoglobinopathy status. This investigation is a standard component of comprehensive preconception and family planning counselling in populations where sickle cell disease is prevalent.
questions.question: A woman with a family history of sickle cell disease requests family planning counselling. The most appropriate investigation to guide this counselling is:

questions.explanation: Polycystic ovary syndrome is characterised by the combination of oligomenorrhoea or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism such as hirsutism and acne, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound, often associated with insulin resistance and obesity. It is one of the most common causes of anovulatory infertility in women of reproductive age. Management includes lifestyle modification, ovulation induction, and metabolic risk reduction.
options: Polycystic ovary syndrome, a common endocrine disorder
Premature ovarian insufficiency, causing early menopause
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia, presenting in adulthood
questions.question: A woman presents with oligomenorrhoea, hirsutism, acne, and obesity, and ultrasound reveals polycystic ovarian morphology. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
A woman presents with HELLP-like laboratory findings but no hypertension or proteinuria. Before confirming atypical HELLP syndrome, which other conditions must first be excluded?
questions.explanation: Because thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and haemolytic uraemic syndrome can mimic HELLP with haemolysis and thrombocytopenia, these thrombotic microangiopathies must be excluded before confirming atypical HELLP without hypertension or proteinuria. Distinguishing features include ADAMTS13 activity and the degree of renal involvement. Correct diagnosis is essential since management strategies differ markedly between these conditions.
options: thrombotic microangiopathies such as TTP and HUS

questions.explanation: Amsel's criteria for bacterial vaginosis require at least three of four features: characteristic discharge, vaginal pH above 4.5, a positive amine (whiff) test, and clue cells on microscopy. Motile flagellated protozoa are instead the diagnostic hallmark of trichomoniasis, not bacterial vaginosis. Distinguishing these two conditions is important because their first-line treatments and implications differ.
options: Positive whiff test with added potassium hydroxide
Presence of clue cells on microscopy
Presence of motile flagellated protozoa on wet mount
Vaginal pH greater than four point five
questions.question: The Amsel criteria used to diagnose bacterial vaginosis include all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Ice should be applied for fifteen to twenty minutes using an ice pack or slush bath, repeated every two to three hours while the client is awake. Applying ice continuously for an hour or two days risks tissue and skin damage from excessive cold. Five seconds is too brief to achieve any therapeutic vasoconstrictive effect.
questions.question: A client with a Grade II ankle sprain is taught the RICE method. When applying ice, the nurse should instruct the client to use it for how long, and how often?

questions.explanation: Uterine inversion is a surgical emergency causing severe haemorrhage and neurogenic shock. The immediate management priority is manual replacement (repositioning) of the uterus as soon as possible before the cervical ring contracts and traps the fundus. Oxytocin and ergometrine must be stopped (as they will tighten the cervical ring and make replacement harder). If the placenta is still attached, it should NOT be removed before repositioning. Uterotonic agents are given AFTER successful replacement to contract the uterus.
options: Manual replacement of the uterus (repositioning) as soon as possible before the cervix contracts
Administration of IV oxytocin before repositioning
Waiting for anaesthesia before attempting any manipulation
Removing the placenta before attempting uterine replacement
questions.question: Uterine inversion is a rare but life-threatening complication of the third stage of labour. The immediate management priority is:

questions.explanation: Oxygen flow rates above 4 liters per minute typically require humidification because unhumidified gas dries the nasal mucosa, causing irritation and discomfort. Adding a humidifier addresses the symptom without discontinuing necessary oxygen therapy. This intervention improves patient tolerance and adherence to treatment.
options: Add humidification to the oxygen delivery system
Switch to a simple face mask without humidification
Increase the flow rate to improve comfort
Instruct the patient to breathe through the mouth
questions.question: A patient receiving oxygen via nasal cannula at 6 liters per minute reports nasal dryness and irritation. The nurse's priority action is to:

options: Increase supervision without addressing the regimen itself
Collaborate with the prescriber to simplify the regimen where possible
Discontinue all medications to eliminate the complexity
Instruct the client to memorise the complex schedule exactly every time
Assume the client will manage without any further support whatsoever
questions.question: A nurse assessing an older client's medication regimen notes several medications are taken at different times throughout the day with complex instructions. The most appropriate nursing intervention to support adherence is to:
questions.explanation: Simplifying complex medication regimens, where clinically appropriate, through strategies such as combination products or aligned dosing times, is an effective, evidence-based way to improve adherence in older adults. Simply expecting memorisation or increasing supervision without addressing complexity does not solve the underlying problem. Collaborative regimen review supports both safety and independence.

Kussmaul breathing — deep, rapid, labored breathing — is a compensatory respiratory response to the metabolic acidosis of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). In DKA, the absence of insulin leads to uncontrolled ketogenesis, producing ketone acids (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate) that lower blood pH. The respiratory center responds to the acidosis by increasing the depth and rate of breathing to blow off CO2 (carbonic acid), thereby raising blood pH toward normal. Kussmaul breathing is a hallmark clinical sign indicating severe metabolic acidosis requiring emergency intervention.
options: Hypoglycemia causes central nervous system depression
High blood glucose stimulates the respiratory centers directly
Osmotic diuresis from glucose causes respiratory fluid loss
Diabetic ketoacidosis causes metabolic acidosis requiring increased ventilation
Insulin deficiency directly impairs the diaphragm muscle function
questions.question: A patient with uncontrolled diabetes presents with Kussmaul breathing. The nurse understands this respiratory pattern occurs because:

options: A patient requesting a repeat prescription for lubricating drops
A patient presenting with acute angle-closure glaucoma
A patient with stable well-controlled diabetic retinopathy
A patient needing routine follow-up after cataract surgery
A patient with mild seasonal allergic conjunctivitis
questions.question: In which of the following situations would an ophthalmic nurse refer a patient directly to the emergency room?
questions.explanation: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is a true ocular emergency characterized by sudden severe eye pain, blurred vision, nausea, and vomiting, and requires immediate referral to the emergency room to prevent blindness. The rapid rise in intraocular pressure can cause irreversible optic nerve damage within hours if untreated. Non-emergency conditions like allergic conjunctivitis or routine follow-up do not warrant emergency referral.

Respiratory acidosis occurs when hypoventilation or impaired gas exchange causes CO₂ retention, increasing blood PCO₂ above 45 mmHg and lowering pH below 7.35. Causes include COPD, respiratory depression from drugs/CNS disorders, airway obstruction, or neuromuscular disease. The retained CO₂ combines with water to form carbonic acid (H⁺ O₂, which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻, acidifying blood. Renal compensation takes days, retaining bicarbonate to buffer the acid. Treatment addresses the underlying cause (bronchodilators, mechanical ventilation) rather than just giving bicarbonate.
questions.question: Respiratory acidosis results from:

options: Administering oral glucose immediately to treat hypoglycemia
Restricting IV fluids until blood glucose results are confirmed
Administering subcutaneous insulin without waiting for lab results
Checking blood glucose, obtaining IV access, and notifying the physician
Placing the patient on NPO and scheduling an urgent abdominal CT
questions.question: Which nursing intervention takes priority when a nurse suspects a patient is developing diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.explanation: When DKA is suspected, the priority nursing actions are: (1) check blood glucose immediately to confirm hyperglycemia, (2) check blood or urine ketones, (3) obtain IV access for fluid and insulin therapy, and (4) notify the physician urgently for orders. DKA treatment requires IV normal saline (1-2 liters initially to correct dehydration), IV regular insulin infusion (NOT subcutaneous), potassium replacement, and close monitoring. Early recognition and rapid intervention are critical to prevent DKA-related complications including cerebral edema and cardiovascular collapse.

options: Easier to perform without specialised training or equipment
Faster procedure completion in less than 30 seconds
Higher rescue success with fewer complications
Lower risk of subcutaneous emphysema development
Less bleeding from the highly vascular thyroid region
questions.question: Emergency front of neck access (eFONA), also called open scalpel cricothyrotomy, is now PREFERRED over needle cricothyroidotomy because it achieves which outcome?
questions.explanation: Open cricothyrotomy (emergency front of neck access, eFONA) is now preferred as it achieved higher rescue success with fewer complications than needle cricothyroidotomy when an emergency surgical airway was required. The open approach provides a more secure airway and allows insertion of a cuffed tube that can be connected to a ventilator, whereas needle approaches are more prone to failure and complications.

questions.question: A nurse assesses feeding practices in a child classified with a moderate illness under IMCI. This feeding assessment specifically includes checking for:
questions.explanation: IMCI feeding assessment for any child with moderate or severe illness includes checking breastfeeding practices, frequency, other foods and fluids given, and any difficulties experienced during feeding, since illness can significantly affect nutritional intake and recovery. This assessment allows targeted feeding counselling tailored to the child's specific situation. Addressing feeding problems identified during illness supports both recovery and longer-term nutritional status.

questions.question: A nurse evaluates that a client's chronic pain care plan, focused solely on medication, has not improved the client's overall function or quality of life. What is the MOST appropriate revision to this plan?
questions.explanation: When a chronic pain plan focused only on medication fails to improve function and quality of life, revising the plan to incorporate additional non-pharmacological strategies and specific functional goals, such as improved mobility or participation in daily activities, reflects a more holistic and effective approach to chronic pain management. Simply escalating medication without addressing broader functional goals often fails to address the full impact of chronic pain on a client's life. This revision aligns with current best practice emphasizing function and quality of life as key outcomes in chronic pain care.
options: Incorporate additional non-pharmacological and functional goals into the plan
Simply increase the medication dose indefinitely without further changes
Discontinue all follow-up care for this client immediately
Conclude that no further improvement is possible for this client
Remove all documentation of the client's pain from the record

questions.question: A global partnership brings together governments, UN agencies, and civil society to advance both maternal and child survival goals under a unified advocacy platform. Which initiative is this?
questions.explanation: Every Woman Every Child is a global partnership uniting governments, UN agencies, and civil society around a shared platform advancing both maternal and child survival goals together. This broad coalition-building approach differs from the more narrowly facility-focused Saving Mothers, Giving Life initiative. Coordinated multi-stakeholder advocacy strengthens global commitment to maternal and child health.

questions.question: A critique of a hospital's postoperative handover process identified a key gap as the absence of:
questions.explanation: A commonly identified deficiency in handover processes is the lack of a standardised, structured format, which increases the risk of information being omitted or miscommunicated. Staffing presence, lighting, and instrument supply are separate operational issues unrelated to handover structure itself. Implementing standardised tools such as SBAR addresses this specific gap.

Vitreous hemorrhage in the posterior segment from proliferative retinopathy
Intraocular lens centration and position to ensure optimal optical alignment
questions.explanation: After cataract surgery in a diabetic patient, blood glucose levels must be carefully monitored because hyperglycemia impairs wound healing, increases infection risk, and can exacerbate diabetic macular edema post-operatively. The stress of surgery can also cause significant glucose fluctuations in diabetic patients. The nursing role includes pre-operative glycemic optimization, intraoperative glucose monitoring, and post-operative blood sugar management in collaboration with the endocrinology team to minimize surgical complications.

The amplification cascade allows single photon detection in dark-adapted rods.

questions.explanation: The nursing diagnosis of deficient fluid volume related to excessive blood loss evidenced by hypotension applies to patients with APH or PPH presenting with signs of hypovolaemia, including hypotension, tachycardia, and reduced urine output. Appropriate nursing interventions include establishing large-bore IV access, administering prescribed IV fluids (e.g., Ringer's lactate or normal saline), monitoring vital signs, and preparing for potential blood transfusion.

questions.explanation: When evaluation reveals that goals have not been met, such as persistent severe pain despite planned interventions, the nurse should reassess the situation and revise the plan of care accordingly, which may involve adjusting medication, trying additional non-pharmacological strategies, or investigating for a change in underlying condition. Continuing an ineffective plan unchanged would fail to address the client's ongoing suffering. This reflects the cyclical, dynamic nature of the nursing process, particularly for a dynamic symptom like pain.
options: Continue the exact same plan without any changes
Discontinue all documentation of the client's pain
Assume the client is not being truthful about their pain
Wait several days before any further evaluation
Reassess and revise the plan of care based on current findings

questions.explanation: Aldosterone deficiency in Addison's disease reduces sodium and water retention, leading to decreased circulating blood volume, which predisposes the patient to orthostatic hypotension when changing position quickly due to inadequate compensatory vascular response. This explains why patients are often taught to change positions slowly and are monitored for postural blood pressure changes. It is a direct physiological consequence of the underlying aldosterone deficiency rather than an unrelated symptom.
options: This symptom is unrelated to their adrenal condition
Excess cortisol is causing this specific symptom
This is caused by excess aldosterone activity
Aldosterone deficiency reduces blood volume, leading to orthostatic hypotension
This symptom only occurs in patients with diabetes
questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient recently diagnosed with Addison's disease who asks why their blood pressure drops significantly when standing up quickly. What should the nurse explain?

options: Monitoring blood pressure every 4 hours and adjusting IV fluid rate
Restricting sodium intake and encouraging the DASH diet for blood pressure control
Applying a transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation unit for 30 minutes
Administering prescribed antihypertensive medication at scheduled times
Using non-pharmacological methods such as distraction, imagery, and relaxation
questions.explanation: Non-pharmacological pain management methods - including distraction, guided imagery, relaxation techniques, and massage - specifically address the psychological dimension of the pain experience. These techniques can prompt release of endogenous opioids, interrupt the pain-distress cycle, reduce anxiety, and improve the patient's perception of control over their pain. They complement pharmacological interventions and are particularly valuable for patients with chronic pain where the psychological component substantially influences pain intensity and functional outcomes.

Serve in national armed forces and security services
Form the primary tax-paying workforce of the nation

This argument connects adolescent reproductive health to broader development outcomes including democratic governance and national prosperity.

questions.explanation: Osteoarthritis is characterized by morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes, while rheumatoid arthritis typically causes morning stiffness lasting more than an hour, along with persistent joint pain, swelling, fatigue, fever, and weight loss. The reverse pattern does not align with the clinical features of these conditions. Neither stiffness lasting only seconds nor the complete absence of stiffness is consistent with the described presentations, and rheumatoid arthritis stiffness does not resolve within 5 minutes.
options: Neither condition causes any morning stiffness
Both conditions cause stiffness lasting only seconds
Rheumatoid arthritis morning stiffness typically resolves within about 5 minutes
Osteoarthritis morning stiffness typically lasts noticeably longer than rheumatoid arthritis stiffness in the majority of affected patients
Osteoarthritis morning stiffness lasts less than 30 minutes; rheumatoid arthritis stiffness lasts more than an hour

questions.explanation: The two major complications of ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunts in hydrocephalus management are shunt blockage and shunt infection. Blockage prevents adequate CSF drainage, causing a rapid rise in intracranial pressure with vomiting, severe headache, irritability, and lethargy. Infection (usually Staphylococcus epidermidis or aureus) manifests with fever, redness along the shunt tract, and fluid around the shunt valve. Regular monitoring for both complications is essential.
options: Peritoneal adhesions and hepatic failure from CSF absorption
Meningitis and subdural haematoma from overshunting
