It is absorbed transdermally or enterically, binds plasma proteins and distributes widely with affinity for fatty tissue; it is metabolized in the liver by cytochrome P450 oxidation, ester hydrolysis (carboxylesterases) and conjugation to glucuronide or sulfate, and metabolites are excreted mainly in bile and feces with little in urine.
(d)
It controls ticks, mites, flies, fleas and lice on cattle, sheep, goats, horses, dogs and cats, and varroatosis in bee hives, as topical solution or spray, collar, dip or bath and ear tag.
(e)
Adverse effects are local irritation, systemic toxicity (lethargy, vomiting, diarrhoea, seizures, tremors, more likely in smaller animals), hypersensitivity, behavioural changes (especially cats) and possible reproductive effects, so caution applies in pregnant or lactating animals.
(f)
Dogs and livestock generally tolerate it well, cats are more susceptible because of glucuronidase deficiency, and it should not be applied topically on extended skin lesions.
(g)
In humans it causes skin and eye irritation, respiratory irritation, neurological symptoms (dizziness, headaches, seizures) and allergic reactions, so gloves and masks are advised.
(h)
It partitions into organic matter and sediment, runs off into water from excreta and washed wool, and is highly toxic to fish, crustaceans and insects at very low concentrations.
(i)
Careful management practices are needed to delay resistance.
(j)
Treated animals should be monitored for adverse reactions with prompt veterinary care, and reactions should be reported to the appropriate authorities to improve safety guidelines.

(a)
Ivermectin is an antiparasitic of the avermectin (macrocyclic lactone) family, a semi-synthetic derivative of avermectins cultivated from Streptomyces avemitilis and S. cyanogriseus; it was discovered in 1975 and such products are labelled 3-AV.
(b)
It binds selectively with high affinity to glutamate-gated chloride channels in invertebrate nerve and muscle cells, holding them open so chloride influx causes hyperpolarization, paralysis and death of the cell.
(c)
It was first used in veterinary medicine for heartworm and acariasis, is active against most nematode types and all development stages, and is used in salmonid fish against sea lice (Lepeophtheirus salmonis, Caligus elongatus, Caligus rogercresseyi) at all developmental stages.
(d)
Livestock doses are 0.2 mg/kg by injection and 0.5 mg/kg pour-on; in salmon 0.05 mg/kg in feed twice a week removed about 90% of parasites; forms include a 1% injectable solution, 1% oral drench and 0.6% oral premix for pigs.
(e)
It is metabolized mainly by CYP450 3A4, with CYP450 3A5 and 2C9 also contributing, giving 3''-O-demethylated, C4-methyl hydroxylated and C25 isobutyl-/isopropyl-hydroxylated metabolites.
(f)
At low concentrations P-glycoprotein (MDR1) effluxes it slowly; at higher concentrations MRP1, MRP2 and MRP3 take part, ivermectin significantly inhibits BCRP1 (ABCG2) and moderately inhibits OATP1B1 and OATP1B3.
(g)
In salmon a single oral 0.2 mg/kg gave 2-5% mortality and double the dose gave 24% mortality (narrow safety margin); pregnancy and neurotoxicity in some breeds of dogs are contraindications.
(h)
Co-administration with potent inhibitors or inducers of CYP3A4 or MDR1 (P-gp) may cause interactions, polymorphisms in transporters and CYP3A4 may alter response, and ivermectin weakly inhibits CYP2C9, 2C19 and 2D6 and also inhibits CYP3A4.
(i)
It is excreted in animal feces, is persistent in soil (half-lives of weeks to months), binds strongly to organic matter, has low water solubility, bioaccumulates in aquatic organisms, and residues in dung reduce dung decomposition by dung beetles.
(j)
Overuse and improper disposal contribute to resistance in parasite populations.
(k)
Ivermectin has never been officially licensed for fish and was used off-label in Ireland, Canada and Chile until 2000; environmental risk assessment (ERA) schemes evaluate veterinary medicinal products in aquaculture, and existing ERA guidelines have limitations.

(a)
One Health is an integrated, unifying approach that aims to sustainably balance and optimize the health of people, animals and ecosystems.
(b)
The health of humans, animals and ecosystems is closely interlinked; about 60% of emerging infectious diseases reported globally come from animals, and over 30 new human pathogens were detected in three decades, 75% of them from animals.
(c)
Stressors are animal trade, agriculture, livestock farming, urbanization, extractive industries, climate change, habitat fragmentation and encroachment into wild areas.
(d)
It applies to antimicrobial resistance, zoonotic diseases, vector-borne diseases, food safety and foodborne diseases, and environmental health.
(e)
Zoonoses are infectious diseases spread between animals and people, such as Ebola, avian influenza and rabies.
(f)
Vector-borne diseases affect people bitten by vectors (mosquitoes, ticks, lice, fleas) and include dengue fever, West Nile virus, Lyme disease and malaria.
(g)
Foodborne diseases arise from contamination at any stage of production, delivery and consumption, such as norovirus, salmonella and listeria.
(h)
Environmental health covers water pollution, air pollution and climate change, and antimicrobial resistance is the first listed issue.
(i)
Domestic animals can act as monitors of environmental hazards and give early warning of disease in man.
(j)
Zoonoses such as anthrax and bovine tuberculosis, and resistance selected by growth promoters, can reach humans from animals.
(k)
Related trade-offs include the benefits of growth promoters against the risk of resistance.

(a)
Tylosin is a macrolide with a 16-membered lactone ring, produced by fermentation of Streptomyces fradiae (C46H77NO17), discovered in the 1950s, with factors A, B, C and D of which A is the most pharmacologically active.
(b)
It binds the 50S ribosomal subunit, blocking peptide translocation and protein synthesis; it acts against Gram-positive bacteria, some Gram-negative bacteria (Pasteurella, Haemophilus) and mycoplasmas, with limited effect on Gram-negative organisms.
(c)
It is given orally, intramuscularly or intravenously; it is well absorbed orally (lower in ruminants), concentrates in lungs, liver, kidneys and bile, crosses the placenta, enters milk, is partly metabolized in the liver (demethylation, dehydroxylation) and is excreted mainly in bile and faeces with enterohepatic recirculation prolonging half-life.
(d)
Broilers get 5-55 ppm in feed for weight gain and 880-1100 ppm for chronic respiratory disease, layers 22-55 ppm, pigs 10-100 ppm (production) or 40-100 ppm (swine dysentery), cattle 50-100 mg/animal/day, with intramuscular 5-10 mg/kg/day in cattle and pigs and 10 mg/kg/day in sheep and goats for contagious agalactia and caprine pleuropneumonia.
(e)
Adverse effects are hypersensitivity, diarrhoea and GIT disturbances after oral use (especially in horses), injection-site inflammation, itchiness and pain, and raised ALT and AST.
(f)
Acute oral LD50 is above 5000 mg/kg in rat and mouse and above 800 mg/kg in dog (salivation, emesis, defecation); intravenous LD50 in female rats is 321 mg/kg with tremors, clonic convulsions and leg weakness.
(g)
It is for veterinary use only and protective clothing is required to avoid rash.
(h)
Tylosin A, B, C and D residues are microbiologically active, so MRLs and daily intake estimates are set, and residues have been found in milk and sheep meat.
(i)
Resistance in Gram-positive bacteria involves tlrB and tlrD methyltransferases adding methyl groups at 23S rRNA nucleotides G748 and A2058 in synergy, specific to tylosin and mycinamycin.
(j)
Mitigation includes stewardship, combination therapy, resistance monitoring, new antibiotics, bacteriophage and vaccines; tylosin was banned as an EU growth promoter in 1999 because its class is used in human medicine.

(a)
Botanical insecticides include pyrethrum (Chrysanthemum cinerariifolium flower heads), Derris and Lonchocarpus (dried roots and rhizomes), tobacco (Nicotiana species leaves) and neem (Azadirachta indica); contact poisons are grouped as pyrethrins-pyrethroids, nicotine-nicotinoids and rotenone-rotenoids.
(b)
Pyrethroids block Na+ and K+ transport, causing paralysis.
(c)
Neem leaf extracts are applied topically to ectoparasites such as lice and mites on cattle, sheep, goats and poultry, and fresh neem leaves are spread in the henhouse; Margosan-O is marketed for limited use on non-food crops.
(d)
Dried neem leaves are macerated and applied topically, neem oil comes from the seed (fixed oil with nimbin, nimbinin, nimbidol) and azadirachtin, a tetranortriterpenoid, is the insecticidal constituent.
(e)
Pyrethrin II gives rapid knock-down and pyrethrin I high lethality with low mammalian toxicity.
(f)
Derris and Lonchocarpus, containing rotenone, deguelin and a chloroform extractive, act more slowly but are lethal.
(g)
Tobacco contains nicotine, nornicotine and anabasine, and natural nicotinoids are active but not safe.
(h)
Azadirachtin is biodegradable, non-mutagenic and non-toxic to birds, fish and warm-blooded animals.
(i)
Pyrethrins are natural templates, whereas pyrethroids are synthetic derivatives that are more potent.
(j)
Rotenone comes from Derris and Lonchocarpus roots (rotenoids), whereas nicotine comes from tobacco leaves (nicotinoids).
(k)
Neem acts through azadirachtin, whereas derris acts through rotenone and deguelin.
(l)
Organophosphates such as diazinon inhibit acetylcholinesterase and carry human safety concerns, whereas azadirachtin is described as non-toxic to warm-blooded animals.

(a)
Sulfonamides are synthetic antimicrobial agents (sulfa drugs) containing the -SO2NH2 or -SO2NH- group, often with a 5- or 6-membered heterocyclic ring; the first was synthesized in 1908 by Paul Gelmo, antibacterial activity was found in 1931, and Domagk's work on prontosil earned the 1939 Nobel Prize.
(b)
Short-acting (sulfamethoxazole), intermediate-acting (sulfadiazine), long-acting (sulfamethoxypyridazine) and topical (silver sulfadiazine).
(c)
They are competitive inhibitors of dihydropteroate synthase, blocking conversion of PABA to dihydropteroic acid and so tetrahydrofolate synthesis, which deprives bacteria of purines and pyrimidines for DNA and RNA and gives a bacteriostatic effect.
(d)
They act on Gram-positive and some Gram-negative bacteria and on some protozoa (coccidia), and treat respiratory infections (cattle, pigs, horses, poultry), urinary tract infections (dogs, cats), skin and soft tissue infections (sulfadimethoxine, not effective with purulent debris), coccidiosis, mastitis, foot rot and enteritis.
(e)
Bacteria synthesize folate de novo while humans acquire folate from the diet, so sulfonamides block bacterial folate production without affecting human folate metabolism.
(f)
The effect is bacteriostatic, and sulfonamides are ineffective against most obligate anaerobes and should not be used for serious anaerobic infections.
(g)
They are metabolized by acetylation, glucuronide conjugation and aromatic hydroxylation, with metabolites varying with species, age, diet, environment, disease and (except in pigs and ruminants) sex; dogs cannot acetylate them to any significant degree, N4-acetyl metabolites are inactive and hydroxymetabolites keep 2.5-39.5% of activity.
(h)
Resistance arises through altered DHPS or decreased cellular permeability; adverse effects include diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, folate deficiency and candidiasis, with serious allergic reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis) in about 3-8%.
(i)
Sulfamethazine is widely used for livestock diseases, whereas sulfadiazine is combined with pyrimethamine to treat toxoplasmosis in warm-blooded animals.
(j)
Antibiotic sulfonamides include sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim, sulfasalazine and sulfisoxazole; non-antibiotic ones include acetazolamide, bumetanide, celecoxib, glyburide, tolbutamide, hydrochlorothiazide, furosemide and probenecid.
(k)
Trimethoprim inhibits another enzyme in the folate pathway, so combination enhances efficacy and reduces resistance.
(l)
In pigs sulfamethazine gives N4-acetylsulfamethazine, desaminosulfamethazine and an N4-glucose conjugate; desaminosulfamethazine has an elimination half-life of 1 to 9 days while sulfamethazine and other metabolites have 10 to 20 hours.

(a)
Pseudopregnancy in a dog; EE2 is a synthetic steroidal estrogen that helps regulate the hormonal imbalance causing pseudopregnancy symptoms by modifying feedback mechanisms.
(b)
It diffuses into target cells and binds estrogen receptors alpha and beta (nuclear and membrane receptors); the complex activates response elements in gene promoters and begins transcription.
(c)
EE2 is a common oral estrogen (the oral contraceptive pill component and high-dose oral estrogen for in vitro fertilization cycles).
(d)
It is extensively metabolized when given orally in solution to dogs, with metabolism in both the gut wall and the liver; sulfates are major circulating metabolites, and oral bioavailability is about 60%, confirming a substantial first-pass effect.
(e)
EE2 must be used cautiously because of potential side effects, and oral estrogen causes modest changes in serum lipid concentration.
(f)
Other uses: mammary tumours (with other therapies), suppression of unwanted male behaviours, induction of parturition in livestock, osteoporosis after ovariohysterectomy, benign prostatic hyperplasia in male dogs, growth promotion in livestock and estrus synchronization with progestogens.
questions.question:
A bitch shows signs of pseudopregnancy, and the veterinarian considers ethinyl estradiol (EE2).
(a) Identify the condition and the drug and its class.
(b) State the mechanism of action.
(c) State the dosage form, route and dose.
(d) State the pharmacokinetic features that guide dosing.
(e) State the key adverse effect or precaution.
(f) State the other veterinary uses of the drug.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Flumethrin, a second-generation synthetic pyrethroid used mainly as an acaricide, one of the key actives in sheep dips.
(b)
It prolongs the transient rise in sodium permeability of the nerve membrane by blocking closure of sodium channel gates during repolarization, causing repetitive firing; low concentrations cause hyperactivity and high concentrations paralysis (knock-down) and death in arthropods.
(c)
It is used in dips and baths for livestock, giving broad coverage against parasites.
(d)
Follow the manufacturer's guidelines, wear protective gloves and masks, and store products away from children and pets; sustained skin exposure or open wounds can raise mammalian toxicity.
(e)
Prevent contamination of water bodies through proper disposal of containers and residual product; wool and hides processed by fellmongers and wool scourers release dip into ground and surface water, and flumethrin is highly toxic to fish, crustaceans and insects.
(f)
Careful management practices are essential to mitigate environmental risks and delay development of resistance.
questions.question:
A sheep flock has infestations of ticks, itch mites (Psoroptes ovis) and lice, and flumethrin dipping is proposed.
(a) Identify the agent and its class.
(b) Explain its mode of action.
(c) State the route and schedule.
(d) State the precautions for handling and storage.
(e) State the environmental precautions and the fate of the dip.
(f) State the limitations and the resistance risk.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Chlorfenvinphos is an organophosphorus insecticide and acaricide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase.
(b)
Alone it controls buffalo fly; for superficial wounds it is applied undiluted at 0.5-1 mL (max) per 5 kg live weight, and with cypermethrin it controls resistant tick strains in beef and dairy cattle, horses, deer, sheep and goats.
(c)
General population exposure is primarily through residues in food, infrequent monitoring suggests limited exposure, and humans can also be exposed through contaminated water, inhalation and skin contact.
(d)
Exposure can cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, muscle weakness and respiratory distress, and in severe cases coma and death; animal studies suggest reproductive and developmental effects.
(e)
It has been banned or phased out in many countries including the United States, with use restrictions, stricter monitoring and enforcement and education advised.
(f)
Use integrated pest management (prevention, monitoring, biological control, resistant breeds, hygiene), less toxic insecticides such as pyrethroids and avermectins, and non-chemical methods such as physical removal of parasites and good sanitation.
questions.question:
A beef and dairy cattle herd with buffalo fly infestation and superficial wounds is treated with chlorfenvinphos, and the animals are products of the food chain.
(a) Identify the drug and its class.
(b) State the use and dose for wounds and the combination used for ticks.
(c) State the residue concern and human exposure routes.
(d) State the public health implications.
(e) Name the regulatory requirements and the record-keeping requirement.
(f) State the preventive measures and alternatives.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Ivermectin is a semi-synthetic avermectin (macrocyclic lactone); the risk is mortality because of a narrow safety margin: a single oral dose of 0.2 mg/kg killed 2-5% of fish and doubling it killed 24%.
(b)
The only basis given is the narrow safety margin.
(c)
0.05 mg/kg twice a week in feed removed about 90% of parasites without fatalities and is toxic to the parasites but tolerated by the fish; emamectin benzoate is the most prevalent avermectin used in fish.
(d)
Sea lice (Lepeophtheirus salmonis, Caligus elongatus, Caligus rogercresseyi) are ectoparasitic copepods that feed on the blood, epidermis and mucus of the fish and passively carry other pathogens.
(e)
Ivermectin has never been licensed for fish (off-label use in Ireland, Canada and Chile until 2000), it is highly toxic to Daphnia and other aquatic invertebrates, persists in water and sediment and bioaccumulates, so unused medication must be disposed of properly and the environment monitored.
(f)
Environmental risk assessment (ERA) schemes weigh fate, exposure and ecotoxicological effects in surface water, sediment and dung, and existing guidelines have limitations such as an inadequate initial action limit and unclear higher-tier instructions.
questions.question:
Farmed salmon are given ivermectin orally against sea lice, and some fish die.
(a) Identify the drug, its class and the risk.
(b) Explain the basis of the vulnerability.
(c) State the safer dosing regimen and an alternative drug.
(d) Name the parasites targeted and their effects on the host.
(e) State the precautions on licensing and the environment.
(f) State the regulatory tools used to assess environmental risk.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Trypanosomiasis (nagana in animals), caused by protozoa of the genus Trypanosoma and transmitted by tsetse flies into the bloodstream; untreated animals often die, and the tsetse fly is restricted to the humid parts of sub-Saharan Africa.
(b)
Trypanocidal drugs: diminazene aceturate (a diamidine), isometamidium chloride (a phenanthridine) and suramin (a sulfonated naphthylamine); they are grouped as effective in the acute phase or in the chronic phase.
(c)
Diminazene binds the parasite's DNA, inhibiting replication and transcription.
(d)
Diminazene is rapidly absorbed and widely distributed with a relatively short half-life, so repeated dosing is needed to maintain therapeutic levels.
(e)
It is toxic at high doses, and resistance arises through mutations in the parasite's transport proteins that reduce drug uptake, together with selective pressure.
(f)
Isometamidium is used mainly as a prophylactic because of its long half-life and persistence in tissues; it intercalates into parasite DNA, and its persistence raises concern about non-target toxicity and residues in animal products.
(g)
Suramin is especially effective in early stages, is not extensively metabolized (long action, long half-life, extensive protein binding), and causes nephrotoxicity and hypersensitivity, so careful dose management and monitoring are needed.
(h)
Drug resistance is a significant challenge, so new drugs or combinations are continually needed.
questions.question:
Cattle in a humid part of sub-Saharan Africa show fever, anaemia and lethargy after tsetse fly exposure.
(a) Identify the condition, its cause and its vector.
(b) Name the drugs indicated and their classes.
(c) State the mechanism of action of diminazene aceturate.
(d) State the pharmacokinetic features that guide dosing, and the dosage form, route and dose.
(e) State the adverse effects and limitations of diminazene.
(f) State the role and mechanism of isometamidium chloride.
(g) State the features and precautions of suramin.
(h) State the key problem that limits treatment.

A sheep flock is infested with ticks, lice and scab or itch mites and is at risk of blowfly strike (Lucilia cuprina), and diazinon dipping is chosen.
(a) Identify the conditions and the drug class.
(b) State the mechanism of action.
(c) State the dosage form and how the dip is prepared and used, and the concentration.
(d) Name other diazinon dosage forms for livestock and pets.
(e) State the metabolism and elimination features relevant to dosing.
(f) State the key adverse effects and toxicity.
(g) State the precautions, resistance and regulatory limits.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Ectoparasite infestation (ticks, lice, scab and itch mites) and prevention of blowfly strike; diazinon is an organophosphate insecticide, acaricide and nematicide.
(b)
It inhibits acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors, altering neurotransmission at cholinergic synapses and neuromuscular junctions; it is a non-systemic contact, stomach and respiratory poison.
(c)
A sheep dip: a measured amount of insecticide solution is put into a large bath of water and the sheep are immersed completely to cover the fleece and entire body (it can also be applied on the wool).
(d)
Ear tags for cattle and sheep, shampoos, collars for dogs and cats, and sprays for horse stables and livestock premises.
(e)
It is oxidized to diazoxon, a more potent acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, and rapidly metabolized with most metabolites excreted in urine within 48 hours; first-pass metabolism cuts bioavailability by up to 65%.
(f)
Livestock and domestic animals suffer neurological disturbances and death, birds such as ducks and quail are sensitive, and human contact causes runny eyes and nose, emesis and muscular paralysis.
(g)
It has no effect in organophosphate-resistant organisms (other insecticides are used), its use is heavily regulated and banned in residential areas, and it is no longer used as a sheep dip because of environmental hazards and aquatic and terrestrial toxicity.

(a)
The risk is teratogenicity: a teratogen disturbs development of the embryo or fetus, and can halt pregnancy or produce a congenital malformation; thalidomide is contraindicated in pregnancy and in women of childbearing age.
(b)
Pregnant cats tolerated 500 mg/kg/day with no fetal toxicity and many rat strains showed no teratogenic effects at 4000 mg/kg/day, although its teratogenic effects are well described in several animal models.
(c)
Susceptibility depends on the nature of the teratogen, the timing of exposure (the embryo is most susceptible during rapid differentiation and cell division), the genotype of mother and fetus, the dose (effects increase with dose) and the ability to cross the placenta.
(d)
Mechanisms include toxicity and necrosis, triggering apoptosis, altering gene expression, inhibiting cell interactions and blocking morphogenetic cell movements; abnormalities may affect structure, function, growth or survival.
(e)
Thalidomide is contraindicated in pregnancy; heparin does not cross the placenta because of its high molecular weight and is therefore not teratogenic.
(f)
Avoid exposure during early gestation, since teratogens act for a short period early in gestation; thalidomide's adverse reactions include peripheral neuropathy, nausea, vomiting, constipation, dry mouth, headache, rashes and CNS depression.
questions.question:
Thalidomide is considered for use during pregnancy in cats and rats, since it has shown different effects across species.
(a) Identify the risk.
(b) State the species difference observed and the basis for it.
(c) State the determinants of teratogenic susceptibility.
(d) State the mechanisms of teratogenic action.
(e) State the management or safer alternative.
(f) State the precautions to be taken.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Chlorfenvinphos is a synthetic organophosphorus insecticide and acaricide that does not occur naturally in the environment.
(b)
Water solubility is 130 mg/l with moderate adsorption to particles, Koc is 295 (moderate soil mobility), it hydrolyzes slowly (half-lives above 700 hours at pH 1.1 and above 400 hours at pH 9.1) and its estimated bioconcentration factor is 28.
(c)
It is detoxified in mammals mainly by O-dealkylation; rats excrete mostly the glucuronide (41%) and monoethyl phosphate (32.3%), dogs mostly the monoethyl phosphate (69.6%) and after intravenous dosing 83% as the O-desethyl analogue, about 90% is excreted in urine in rats and dogs, and in sheep esterases and cytochrome P450 produce polar water-soluble metabolites excreted mainly in urine.
(d)
It controls buffalo fly, ticks and sheep blowfly strike on cattle, horses, goats, deer, sheep and working dogs (with cypermethrin it controls resistant tick strains except Pankhurst and Ultimo), applied by stencil brush or pressure sprayer and repeated as necessary, and cattle wounds are treated undiluted at 0.5-1 mL (max) per 5 kg live weight.
(e)
It inhibits acetylcholinesterase, disrupting nerve impulses; in rats oral doses up to 1 mg/kg did not affect cholinesterase but doses over 2 mg/kg significantly reduced it and altered EEG, and in humans it causes nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, muscle weakness, respiratory distress and, in severe cases, coma and death.
(f)
It is very toxic to fish (acute toxicity between 25 micrograms/l and 1 mg/l) and some zooplankton do not survive short exposure above 0.4 micrograms/l.
(g)
Animal studies suggest reproductive and developmental effects.
(h)
General population exposure is mainly through residues in food, humans can also be exposed through contaminated water, skin contact, inhalation and lanolin-containing products.
(i)
The combination with cypermethrin controls resistant tick strains.
(j)
It has been banned or phased out in many countries including the United States, use restrictions, monitoring and enforcement and education are advised, and alternatives are integrated pest management, pyrethroids, avermectins and non-chemical methods.

questions.question:
Milk from a lactating cow herd and meat from sheep and pigs treated with tylosin are to be marketed for human consumption.
(a) Identify the drug and its class.
(b) State the withdrawal period and the general meaning of the term.
(c) State the residue concern, including the active forms found and the limits set.
(d) State the public health implications.
(e) State the effect of cooking on residues.
(f) Name the regulatory requirements.
(g) State the preventive measures.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Tylosin is a macrolide antibiotic (16-membered lactone ring) produced by Streptomyces fradiae.
(b)
Withdrawal period is generally the time between the last dose and when residue levels in animal tissues or products fall below the maximum residue limit (MRL).
(c)
Tylosin A, B, C and D residues are found in tissues and are microbiologically active; WHO and FAO concluded use should not give rise to detectable residues in edible products, MRLs and daily intake estimates are set, and residues have been detected in milk (a Nigerian study found residues in fresh milk below the MRL) and in sheep meat (71.80 microgram/kg).
(d)
Residues can disrupt the colonization barrier of the human gastrointestinal tract (most susceptible: Bifidobacterium and Clostridium), cause allergic reactions or dermatitis, and have been linked to metabolic issues (obesity, hepatic steatosis, insulin resistance); no genotoxic or carcinogenic ability was found, and resistance is a concern.
(e)
Raw meat has more residues than microwaved or cooked meat, so cooking reduces the amount.
(f)
Tylosin is prescription-only in many countries, a veterinary prescription is required, label claims and dosing instructions are regulated, residues in animal tissues are monitored, Codex Alimentarius sets MRLs, and it is approved by the FDA (swine, poultry, cattle) and the EMA.
(g)
Prevention: antimicrobial stewardship (use only when necessary), combination therapy, monitoring resistance patterns, alternatives such as probiotics, prebiotics and vaccines, and regulatory obedience.

(a)
Ivermectin enters through agricultural runoff, wastewater effluent, industrial effluent and animal feces; tylosin through excretion, manure application, runoff and leaching; and EE2 through human urine, livestock wastewater and manure runoff and sewage sludge.
(b)
Ivermectin has been found in water at 0.05 to 100 micrograms/L, in sediment up to 10 mg/kg and in soil up to 100 micrograms/kg, and sulfonamides occur in rivers, lakes and oceans at nanograms to micrograms per litre.
(c)
ERA evaluates the ecotoxicological risk of veterinary medicinal products by assessing fate, exposure, effects and risks, with risk indicators in surface water, sediment and dung compartments.
(d)
The initial action limit may not protect against substances such as ivermectin, the tiered exposure approach may not suit substances that accumulate in soil, higher-tier guidance (field studies, dung) is unclear, and future work aims to improve exposure and effect assessments and guidelines for aquaculture.
(e)
Ivermectin persists in soil with half-lives of weeks to months, binds strongly to organic matter, has low water solubility, photodegrades in water, is not volatile and can bioaccumulate in aquatic organisms.
(f)
Tylosin degrades with a half-life of about 8 days (4-8 days in a soil-feces matrix), about 90% is excreted as the active compound, sorption to soil is strong, and algae are highly sensitive (EC50 0.22 mg/L) while birds and earthworms are practically unaffected.
(g)
Algae are the most sensitive aquatic organisms to sulfonamides, followed by crustaceans and fish; residues were detected up to 18 years in soil, and plants take them up.
(h)
Olaquindox has a bioconcentration factor of 3, flumethrin has a water half-life of 24-48 hours and is highly toxic to aquatic organisms, and chlorfenvinphos has a bioconcentration factor of 28 and is very toxic to fish.
(i)
Drug residues harm non-target organisms such as Daphnia, dung beetles, earthworms and algae, disturbing food webs and reducing biodiversity.
(j)
Contaminated groundwater and surface water can reach drinking water, and antibiotic residues promote resistance in bacteria that threatens human and animal health.
(k)
Current guidelines lack tailored guidance for soil-accumulating substances and clear instructions for higher-tier assessments.
(l)
Ivermectin remains a valuable tool for disease control, but responsible use, proper disposal of unused medication, careful management of treated livestock and ongoing monitoring are essential.

(a)
Members named are benzylpenicillin (Pen G), phenoxymethylpenicillin (Pen V), procaine benzylpenicillin, flucloxacillin and amoxicillin, together with the penicillinase-stable lactams methicillin and cloxacillin.
(b)
Pen G and Pen V are used across animal species, procaine benzylpenicillin treats mastitis in dry cows, flucloxacillin treats penicillin-resistant staphylococcal infections in cats and dogs, and penicillin is a main drug for anthrax in livestock.
(c)
Amoxicillin is given intramuscularly (cattle, sheep, pigs), orally in drinking water and subcutaneously (calves, piglets, poultry) and by all routes in cats and dogs; absorption is rapid from aqueous solution and delayed in oil vehicles.
(d)
Penicillins are sensitive to heat, light, extreme pH, heavy metals, nucleophiles, electrophiles and oxidising and reducing agents, so they must be freshly prepared.
(e)
Penicillins are not for small mammals, whereas cephalosporins are useful in rabbits and rodents.
(f)
Most Staphylococcus aureus strains produce penicillinases that break down penicillins; methicillin, cloxacillin and flucloxacillin resist this because the shape of their side chain precludes lactamase binding.
(g)
Widespread use led to MRSA, which resists lactamase through an alternative mechanism and is often resistant to erythromycin, clindamycin, tetracycline and many aminoglycosides; Streptococcus pyogenes remaining penicillin-sensitive after sixty years is described as very rare.
(h)
Pen G is benzylpenicillin and Pen V is phenoxymethylpenicillin.
(i)
Procaine benzylpenicillin is used for mastitis in dry cows, whereas flucloxacillin is used for penicillin-resistant staphylococcal infections in cats and dogs.
(j)
Amoxicillin is active against Gram-negative organisms and can be given by many routes, as listed above.
(k)
Cephalosporins are stable at pH 6-7 and useful in rabbits and rodents, whereas penicillins are not recommended for small mammals.

(a)
EE2 is a synthetic (semi-synthetic) steroidal estrogen; natural estrogens include estrone (E1), estradiol (E2), estriol (E3) and estetrol (E4), and it is a component of the FDA-approved oral contraceptive pill.
(b)
It diffuses into target cells and binds estrogen receptors alpha and beta (nuclear and membrane receptors), and the complex activates response elements in gene promoters to start transcription.
(c)
It is extensively metabolized when given orally to dogs; in rats 40% is metabolized by the gut wall and 60% of the portal drug by the liver, sulfates are the main circulating metabolites, and oral bioavailability is about 60%, confirming a substantial first-pass effect.
(d)
It is used for hormone-responsive mammary tumours with other therapies, pseudopregnancy in dogs, unwanted male behaviour, induction of parturition in livestock (with other hormones), osteoporosis, benign prostatic hyperplasia in male dogs, growth promotion and estrus synchronization with progestogens.
(e)
It is used cautiously in prostate disease because of potential side effects, and oral estrogen causes modest changes in serum lipid concentration.
(f)
It is highly effective at disrupting endocrine systems, causing feminization of male fish, intersex conditions and reduced fertility, and it accumulates in the tissues of aquatic organisms.
(g)
Growth promotion is less common because of regulations and consumer preferences.
(h)
Some metabolites keep estrogenic activity, the half-life in fresh water ranges from under a day to about 50 days under aerobic conditions, and manure, livestock wastewater and sewage sludge carry it into soil and water.
(i)
Pollutant levels have been linked with breast cancer in women and prostate cancer in men, and mitigation includes better wastewater treatment, sustainable manure management, eco-friendly alternatives, responsible prescribing and public awareness.

(a)
Quinolones (mequinate, clopidol), sulphonamides, nitrofurans and ionophoric antibiotics such as narasin are listed; sulfonamides treat and prevent coccidiosis in cattle, poultry and other animals.
(b)
Sulfonamides competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthase, blocking the conversion of PABA to dihydropteroic acid, so folate and then purine and pyrimidine synthesis fails and growth is inhibited (bacteriostatic action).
(c)
Tylosin is not a direct antibiotic against coccidia but helps control the secondary bacterial infections that often accompany coccidiosis in poultry.
(d)
Sulfonamide adverse effects include diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, candidiasis, folate deficiency and hypersensitivity (allergic reactions in about 3-8%), and they are not readily biodegradable.
(e)
Resistance arises from altered DHPS or decreased cellular permeability, and combination with trimethoprim enhances efficacy and reduces resistance.
questions.question:
A poultry flock and a cattle herd have coccidiosis, an intestinal parasitic infection.
(a) Identify the agents used for treatment and prevention.
(b) Explain the principle of the sulfonamide group.
(c) State the role of tylosin in the flock.
(d) State the precautions.
(e) State the limitations and the risk of resistance.

questions.answerText:
(a)
An ointment or cream (for example skinoment) applied topically.
(b)
It is often extremely effective because the drug is in immediate contact with the affected part; the vehicle matters because it affects the degree of hydration, may have a mild anti-inflammatory effect and may facilitate absorption through the skin.
(c)
Clip the area and remove hair, fur or debris using appropriate antiseptics.
(d)
Apply before feeding or exercise so the animal does not lick it.
(e)
Fit a restraint such as an Elizabethan collar (made of cardboard in the shape of a lamp shade), because licking amplifies the wound or lesion.
(f)
Shampoos (for example chlorhexidine and miconazole) clean the skin without causing allergic reactions and suit seborrheic conditions and skin disinfection, but they are rinsed off after a short time so repeated administration is needed.
questions.question:
A dog has a localized skin lesion, and the veterinarian chooses an ointment or cream.
(a) Identify the suitable dosage form.
(b) Justify the choice and the importance of the vehicle.
(c) Outline how the site is prepared.
(d) State when the product should be applied.
(e) State how licking is prevented.
(f) Name the alternative form for seborrheic conditions and its drawback.

Piglets on a pig farm receive olaquindox in starter and grower feed as a growth promoter, and the pork will enter the human food chain.
(a) Identify the drug and its class and uses.
(b) State the dose in feed and the restrictions on its use.
(c) State the residue concern, including excretion and the forms excreted.
(d) State the public health implications.
(e) Name the regulatory requirement and the record-keeping requirement.
(f) State the preventive measures.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Olaquindox is a synthetic, orally active quinoxaline antimicrobial that inhibits DNA, RNA and protein synthesis in bacteria; it is used as a growth promoter in pigs and to control pig dysentery and bacterial gastro-enteritis.
(b)
It is given at 25-100 mg/kg feed in starter or grower rations but not finisher rations, and may be used in pigs up to four months of age.
(c)
It is rapidly absorbed, with more than 90% excreted in urine within 48 hours and about 5% in faeces; olaquindox itself is the major excreted product (over 60% of the dose) with four other metabolites, and tissues were examined 48 hours after a 2 mg/kg dose.
(d)
It raises concern about antibiotic resistance and its bioaccumulation in fish may make them unsafe for human consumption; it also decreases intestinal mucosal immunity in piglets.
(e)
Use is subject to specific regulations and restrictions in countries where it is approved.
(f)
Restrict use to the labelled rations and age, observe the withdrawal period, manage swine manure to limit environmental release, and consider alternatives such as improved hygiene.

(a)
Natural pyrethrins come from dried flower heads of pyrethrum (Chrysanthemum cinerariifolium, Compositae) and are esters of chrysanthemic and pyrethric acids; first-generation synthetics (1950s) include allethrin, bioallethrin, tetramethrin, phenothrin, resmethrin, bioresmethrin and kadethrin; second-generation photostable ones (1970s) include permethrin, cypermethrin, fenvalerate, deltamethrin and flumethrin.
(b)
They cause paralysis following blockade of Na+ and K+ transport; flumethrin prolongs the normally transient rise in sodium permeability of the nerve membrane by blocking closure of sodium channel gates during repolarization, causing repetitive firing, hyperactivity at low concentrations and paralysis (knock-down) and death at high concentrations.
(c)
Flumethrin controls ticks, mites, flies, fleas and lice on cattle, sheep, goats, horses, dogs and cats, and is marketed for varroatosis in bee hives; permethrin and deltamethrin are insecticides and acaricides.
(d)
Flumethrin is given as a topical solution or spray (back or neck), collar, dip or bath, and ear tag.
(e)
Pyrethrins and pyrethroids have rapid onset but short duration of action; synergists piperonylbutoxide and n-octylbicycloheptene are used to prolong activity.
(f)
Natural pyrethrins are extremely safe on cats and dogs, whereas cats are more susceptible than dogs to synthetic pyrethroids because of glucuronidase deficiency.
(g)
First-generation pyrethroids have low photostability, limiting them mainly to household insecticidal sprays; second-generation compounds are photostable with residual activity of several weeks on the skin and in the environment.
(h)
Flumethrin toxicity is about 1000 times higher in insects and other arthropods than in mammals, although sustained skin exposure, inhalation or contact with open wounds can raise toxicity in mammals.
(i)
Pyrethrin II gives rapid knock-down action, whereas pyrethrin I gives high lethality.
(j)
Natural pyrethrins have low mammalian toxicity; synthetic pyrethroids are analogues made using pyrethrins as templates and are more potent.
(k)
First-generation pyrethroids are poorly photostable and used mainly in homes; second-generation pyrethroids are photostable and persist for weeks.
(l)
Permethrin and deltamethrin are both insecticides and acaricides, whereas flumethrin is mainly an acaricide (a fat-soluble type II pyrethroid whose cyano group on the phenoxy-fluorobenzyl alcohol moiety is responsible for long-lasting prolongation of sodium permeability).

questions.question:
A herd of cattle is diagnosed with pneumonia (bovine respiratory complex, shipping fever), foot rot caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum, and acute mastitis, and the veterinarian selects tylosin.
(a) Identify the class, source and chemical nature of the drug indicated for these conditions.
(b) State its mechanism of action and spectrum of activity.
(c) List the dosage forms available.
(d) State the route and dose for these cattle conditions, and the soluble powder dose for calves to prevent pneumonia.
(e) Explain how absorption differs in ruminants and name the tissues and fluids where the drug is concentrated.
(f) State the common adverse effects.
(g) State the key toxicity, residue and handling precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Tylosin is a macrolide antibiotic with a 16-membered lactone ring, produced by fermentation of Streptomyces fradiae (formula C46H77NO17); it is used against respiratory infections, foot rot and mastitis in cattle.
(b)
It binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and blocks peptide translocation during translation, inhibiting protein synthesis (growth inhibition or cell death depending on concentration and susceptibility); it is active against Gram-positive bacteria (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Corynebacterium), some Gram-negative bacteria (Pasteurella, Haemophilus) and mycoplasmas.
(c)
Dosage forms: feed premixes, soluble powders and formulations for intramuscular injection.
(d)
Intramuscular injection of 5-10 mg/kg body weight/day treats pneumonia, foot rot, diphtheria, metritis and acute mastitis in cattle; calves receive 1.0 g/animal twice daily (soluble powder) to prevent pneumonia associated with bovine respiratory mycoplasma and Pasteurella multocida.
(e)
Oral bioavailability is generally lower in ruminants because of degradation by rumen microflora; the drug reaches high concentrations in lungs, liver, kidneys and bile, crosses the placenta and is found in milk.
(f)
Adverse effects: hypersensitivity reactions, diarrhoea and GIT disturbances after oral use, inflammation, itchiness and pain at the injection site, and raised serum ALT and AST.
(g)
Residues (tylosin A, B, C and D) are microbiologically active, so maximum residue limits and daily intake estimates are set; the drug is for veterinary use only and protective clothing is required when handling to avoid rash.

questions.question:
A dog presents with a urinary tract infection and a skin and soft tissue infection, and a sulfonamide such as sulfadimethoxine is considered.
(a) Identify the conditions and the drug class indicated.
(b) State the mechanism of action.
(c) Explain why the class suits urinary infections.
(d) State the species-specific metabolism that affects dosing in the dog.
(e) State the adverse effects.
(f) State the limitations and precautions, including combination therapy.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Urinary tract infection and skin and soft tissue infection in dogs, treated with a sulfonamide (a synthetic antimicrobial; sulfadimethoxine is indicated for skin and soft tissue infections in dogs and cats).
(b)
Sulfonamides competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthase, blocking conversion of PABA to dihydropteroic acid and so tetrahydrofolate synthesis, which stops bacterial purine and pyrimidine production and gives a bacteriostatic effect.
(c)
They are readily excreted in urine and so reach high concentrations in the urinary tract.
(d)
Dogs are unable to acetylate sulfonamides to any significant degree; N4-acetyl metabolites have no antimicrobial activity and hydroxymetabolites keep 2.5-39.5% of the parent's activity.
(e)
Non-allergic effects include diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, candidiasis, folate deficiency and headaches; serious allergic reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis) occur, with allergy in about 3-8%.
(f)
Sulfadimethoxine is not effective in infections with purulent debris such as abscesses, sulfonamides are ineffective against most obligate anaerobes, resistance arises from altered DHPS or decreased permeability, and combination with trimethoprim enhances efficacy and reduces resistance.

questions.question:
A cattle, sheep and goat farm in an anthrax-endemic area reports sudden deaths among its livestock.
(a) Identify the causative agent, its nature and the form of disease commonly seen in livestock.
(b) Name the antimicrobials used for infected animals.
(c) Name the vaccine used and its type.
(d) Explain the principle of the vaccine and of the drugs.
(e) State the precautions needed to stop spread.
(f) State the role of the veterinary pharmacist.
(g) State the limitations of treatment.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Bacillus anthracis, a spore-forming zoonotic bacterium; in livestock the common form is septicaemic or peracute, often causing sudden death (cutaneous, inhalational and gastrointestinal forms depend on the route of exposure).
(b)
Penicillin and oxytetracycline are the most commonly used drugs for infected animals.
(c)
The Sterne strain vaccine, a live attenuated vaccine, is commonly used to immunize livestock.
(d)
Regular vaccination builds herd immunity and prevents outbreaks.
(e)
Environmental decontamination and proper disposal of carcasses prevent spread of spores, which can persist in the environment for decades and transmit to humans.
(f)
Veterinary pharmacists play a pivotal role in implementing the prevention strategies.
(g)
Antibiotic efficacy diminishes once disease progresses and severe cases die rapidly, leaving little time for treatment, so early intervention and prophylaxis are vital.

(a)
The choice depends on a broad and appropriate spectrum (reaching the MIC at the infection site), species or breed, age (which affects dose and route), intrinsic toxicity in a species or disease condition (for example liver and renal impairment), and avoidance of resistance by following approved protocols and drug combinations.
(b)
Cats are poor metabolizers of chloramphenicol, penicillins are not for small mammals, cephalosporins are useful in rabbits and rodents, and aminoglycosides (gentamicin, kanamycin, neomycin) cause ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity and neuromuscular blockade.
(c)
Oxytetracycline resistance arises through efflux pumps (tetA in E. coli), ribosomal protection proteins (tetM), enzymatic inactivation and target-site mutations, and spreads by horizontal gene transfer (conjugation, transformation, transduction).
(d)
Mitigation: use antibiotics only when necessary, use combination therapy, monitor resistance patterns, develop new antibiotics, use bacteriophage, and develop vaccines.
(e)
An antibiotic growth promoter is a medicine that destroys or inhibits bacteria given at a low sub-therapeutic dose; it improves daily growth by 1-10%, with less fat and more protein, and works best in sick animals or those kept in cramped, unhygienic conditions.
(f)
A link between chloramphenicol residues in meat and human aplastic anaemia cannot be ruled out, and its overuse in animals is believed to have raised Salmonella resistance (including S. typhi), although over-the-counter availability is an alternative explanation.
(g)
Avoparcin, a glycopeptide, was linked to vancomycin-resistant enterococci because van genes confer cross-resistance to vancomycin and teicoplanin; after the European ban, VRE contamination of poultry meat fell from 18.8% to 9.6%, but the fall in pork (9.7% to 6.9%) was not significant.
(h)
Monensin is not a medically important class, showed no real adaptation of rumen microbes after 96-146 days, and its effects disappear within hours of withdrawal, whereas virginiamycin use selected resistant bacteria.
(i)
Matching the drug to species, age and disease avoids toxicity and treatment failure, and growth promoters improved production in intensive systems.
(j)
Residue effects in meat are insignificant compared with selection of resistant bacteria (Salmonella, Campylobacter, E. coli, enterococci), which can mean prolonged illness, more toxic alternative drugs, treatment failure and death.
(k)
After Sweden's 1985 ban, weaned pigs showed more scouring, a 1.5% rise in mortality (about fifty thousand pigs) and 5-6 extra days to reach 25 kg, so housing and hygiene had to be improved.
(l)
Antibiotic use fell by 50% by 1993, but thousands of pigs and chickens probably died, Swedish produce became more expensive and less competitive, and the costs were high.

(a)
Dips totally immerse the animal so all areas are covered against external parasites; actives include organophosphates, diazinon, rotenone, amitraz and propetamphos, and dips should be kept in their original containers, away from children and animals, and not mixed with other products.
(b)
Teat dips are antiseptic washes or dips used before and immediately after milking to keep surface bacteria from the mammary gland, especially in mastitis, which can occur in sheep, goats, cattle and swine and reduces milk production.
(c)
Pour-on liquids act systemically when poured on the backline or applied as one spot; spot-on forms (for example levamisole) are mainly for grubs and lice, 1% ivermectin drops on the neck of birds treat tracheal mites or gapeworm, and the solvents are DMSO or aromatic hydrocarbons.
(d)
In dust bags, cattle brush against a bag of insecticide, pesticide or antibiotic powder to control flies and lice; aerosol dispensers deliver spray, stream or foam directly to the affected area without mechanical irritation and without contaminating the remaining material.
(e)
Vaporous collars release a high vapour pressure liquid pesticide, and powder-producing collars form a coating of particles (a bloom) that kills ticks and fleas on contact; both contain the insecticide and a plasticized solid thermoplastic resin.
(f)
Ointments and creams give immediate contact, the vehicle affects hydration and absorption, and they should be applied before feeding or exercise with an Elizabethan collar to stop licking.
(g)
Shampoos such as chlorhexidine and miconazole clean the skin and treat seborrheic conditions, but they are rinsed off quickly so repeated use is needed.
(h)
Oxytetracycline in aquaculture is given by feed, bath or injection, with oral use most popular because of little chance of ecological contamination; tylosin is given orally, intramuscularly or intravenously, and ivermectin is given at 0.2 mg/kg by injection or 0.5 mg/kg pour-on.
(i)
Pour-on forms remove injection trauma, need no special skills and dose troublesome animals quickly, while dips cover all areas of the body.
(j)
Dip actives raise human safety concerns from contact, so protective gloves and masks are advised for products such as flumethrin, and washing of dipped wool releases dip into ground and surface water.
(k)
Shampoos are rinsed off quickly, animals may lick topical products, and oral bioavailability is lower in ruminants because of rumen degradation.
(l)
Organophosphate dips brought safety concerns and diazinon dipping was banned, and the oral route in aquaculture limits ecological contamination yet oxytetracycline use is linked to antibiotic-resistance genes in the aquatic environment.

questions.question:
Farmed fish with furunculosis or vibriosis are treated with oxytetracycline in feed, and the fish are to be sold for human consumption.
(a) Identify the drug, its class, mechanism, dose and the diseases treated.
(b) State the withdrawal period.
(c) State the residue concern.
(d) State the public health implications.
(e) Name the regulatory requirements.
(f) State the preventive measures.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Oxytetracycline is a broad-spectrum tetracycline antibiotic (from Streptomyces rimosus) that binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and blocks aminoacyl-tRNA attachment; the dose is 60-100 mg/kg every 24 hours for 5-10 days, most commonly 75 mg/kg orally in feed, for furunculosis, aeromonosis, pseudomonosis, lactococcosis and vibriosis.
(b)
In the EU use is subject to strict withdrawal periods so residues do not remain in meat, milk or eggs.
(c)
Antibiotic residues remain in the edible tissues of treated fish and in plants irrigated with contaminated water, and the drug is excreted largely unchanged in urine and feces.
(d)
Residue consumption can cause allergic reactions, disrupt gut microbiota and spread antibiotic-resistant bacteria, and resistance genes can transfer from aquatic to terrestrial ecosystems and to humans.
(e)
In the US the FDA (Center for Veterinary Medicine) makes prescription use mandatory under a licensed veterinarian, the EMA authorizes use in the EU, and residue monitoring and regulation enforcement are required.
(f)
Use probiotics and phytochemicals as alternatives, apply biosecurity and vaccination, treat effluent and manage sediment, and monitor residues; the oral route is preferred because of little chance of ecological contamination.

(a)
Olaquindox is a synthetic, orally active quinoxaline-based antimicrobial.
(b)
It inhibits DNA, RNA and protein synthesis in bacteria and is active against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria and some protozoa (coccidia and trichomonads); it absorbs UV light at 375 nm and hydrolyzes under environmental conditions (pH 5 to 9).
(c)
In rats about 90% is absorbed and about 85% excreted in urine (about 80% unchanged), in dogs 65% is recovered in urine within 3 days, in pigs over 90% is excreted in urine within 24-48 hours, in chickens 15 metabolites appear in plasma 2 hours after dosing, and liver microsomes gave 13 metabolites in rats against 7 in pigs and chickens.
(d)
It is a growth promoter in pigs and controls pig dysentery and bacterial gastro-enteritis, at 25-100 mg/kg feed in starter or grower rations (not finisher) for pigs up to four months of age.
(e)
It stimulates growth and decreases intestinal mucosal immunity in piglets.
(f)
In fish it alters blood cell counts, enzyme activity and organ function, weakening fish and affecting growth, and it shows some potential for bioaccumulation in fish tissues.
(g)
It is not for finisher rations and not beyond four months of age.
(h)
Olaquindox itself is the major excreted product in pigs (over 60% of the dose), at least 80% of urinary activity is parent drug, and its bioconcentration factor is estimated at 3, indicating low bioconcentration in aquatic organisms.
(i)
Its antimicrobial properties raise concern about promoting antibiotic resistance in terrestrial bacteria.
(j)
It is approved in many countries (EU, US, Australia) subject to specific regulations; it has very high to high soil mobility (Koc 46-116), biodegradation half-lives of 5.8-8.8 days in soil slurries, and reaches soil through swine manure used as fertilizer.

options: Administer 10 IU oxytocin IM to stop the bleeding
Perform a vaginal examination to identify the bleeding source
Transfer immediately to theatre for emergency caesarean section
Apply a maternity pad and quantify the bleeding accurately
Establish large-bore IV access and initiate rapid fluid resuscitation
questions.question: A woman with APH is in hypovolaemic shock. Which immediate nursing intervention has the highest priority?
questions.explanation: In hypovolaemic shock from APH, the immediate priority is securing two large-bore IV cannulae and initiating rapid IV fluid resuscitation (crystalloid while blood is prepared). Simultaneously, blood is taken for FBC, cross-match, clotting studies, and group and save. Vaginal examination is absolutely contraindicated until placenta praevia is excluded by ultrasound. Theatre transfer follows resuscitation, not vice versa. Oxygen is administered via a face mask.

options: Occiput — vertex used for vertex presentation
Sacrum — used as the breech presentation denominator
Mentum — chin used for face presentation
Sinciput — brow used for brow presentation
questions.question: In breech presentation, what is the denominator used to describe fetal position?
questions.explanation: In breech presentation, the fetus lies longitudinally with the buttocks in the lower pole. The denominator is the sacrum. Types of breech include frank breech (hips flexed, knees extended), complete breech (both hips and knees flexed), and footling breech (one or both feet presenting). ECV is offered at 36-37 weeks to convert breech to cephalic presentation.

options: Luteal cells from the granulosa layer after ovulation
Stromal cells producing inhibin B to suppress FSH
Theca externa cells providing structural support
Theca interna cells secreting androgens from cholesterol
Granulosa cells expressing aromatase to convert androgens to oestrogen
questions.explanation: Granulosa cells express the enzyme aromatase (CYP19A1), which converts androgens (produced by theca interna cells) to oestrogens (oestradiol). This is the "two-cell, two-gonadotrophin" theory: LH stimulates theca cells to produce androgens, while FSH acts on granulosa cells to upregulate aromatase. The resulting oestradiol drives endometrial proliferation and the positive feedback LH surge.
questions.question: Which cells surrounding the primary follicle express aromatase activity to produce oestrogen?

options: Cervical cancer at an advanced stage
Normal findings in a postmenstrual examination
questions.explanation: Cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, and adnexal tenderness constitute the classic clinical triad of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). These minimum diagnostic criteria, as defined by the CDC, justify empirical treatment to prevent long-term sequelae such as infertility, chronic pelvic pain, and ectopic pregnancy. IUD insertion is absolutely contraindicated in the presence of active PID.
questions.question: A nurse in a family planning clinic identifies a client with cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, and adnexal tenderness. These clinical findings most strongly suggest:

questions.explanation: Microcephaly is defined as an occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) more than two standard deviations below the normal mean for gestational age. The disproportionately small head reflects impaired brain growth and is associated with causes including intrauterine infection (e.g., rubella, CMV, Zika virus), fetal alcohol syndrome, and trisomic chromosomal disorders. Mental impairment is almost invariably present in affected infants.
questions.question: Microcephaly in a neonate is most accurately defined as:
options: Head circumference below the 50th percentile for gestational age
Any head circumference below 33 cm at term gestation
Premature fusion of all cranial sutures causing head deformity
Head circumference more than two standard deviations below normal for gestational age
Head circumference at the 3rd percentile with normal brain development
Single gene disorder inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern
Chromosome and gene abnormalities with an extra chromosome
Multifactorial causes combining genetic and environmental factors
Teratogenic causes from maternal drug exposure
Unknown causes that cannot be linked to any identifiable factor
questions.explanation: Down's syndrome results from trisomy 21, where there are three copies of chromosome 21 instead of the normal two. This is a chromosomal abnormality arising from non-disjunction during meiosis, resulting in an excess of chromosomal material. Chromosomal abnormalities may involve addition, loss, or structural alteration of chromosomes. Down's syndrome is not caused by a single teratogen or multifactorial interaction.
questions.question: Down's syndrome (Trisomy 21) belongs to which category of congenital malformations?

questions.explanation: Grade 3 intraventricular haemorrhage occurs when blood extends into the lateral ventricles and causes blockage of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) outflow. As the choroid plexus normally produces CSF, obstruction to its outflow leads to progressive ventricular dilation — post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus. This distinguishes Grade 3 (with ventricular dilation) from Grade 2 (blood in ventricles without dilation) and Grade 4 (parenchymal extension).
options: Blockage of CSF outflow causing ventricular dilation (post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus)
Bilateral symmetrical haemorrhage into the choroid plexus exclusively
Haemorrhage limited to the germinal matrix only without extension
Extension of blood into adjacent cerebral white matter parenchyma
Haemorrhage into the subarachnoid cisterns around the brainstem
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the pathogenesis of periventricular haemorrhage (Grade 3) in preterm neonates?

questions.explanation: Fertility returns rapidly after stopping combined oral contraceptives because the hormones do not accumulate or cause lasting suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis. Many women can conceive within the very first cycle off the pill. This rapid return distinguishes COCs from injectable progestins, where return of fertility can be delayed by several months.
questions.question: A client asks how quickly fertility returns after discontinuing combined oral contraceptive pills. The correct response is that fertility:
options: Returns only after a mandatory six-month wait
Is permanently reduced after five years of use
Requires ovulation induction drugs to restore
Remains suppressed for approximately two years
Returns promptly, often within the same cycle
MRI of the pelvis with contrast to visualise endometriotic deposits
Pelvic ultrasound as the definitive diagnostic investigation
Endometrial biopsy to confirm retrograde menstruation histologically
Serum CA-125 level as the sole diagnostic blood test needed
Referral for diagnostic laparoscopy as the gold standard
questions.question: The most appropriate investigation for a woman presenting with chronic pelvic pain and suspected endometriosis in a family planning setting is:
questions.explanation: Laparoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosing endometriosis, providing direct visualisation of endometriotic lesions, ovarian endometriomas, and pelvic adhesions, with the ability to biopsy lesions for histological confirmation. While pelvic ultrasound can detect ovarian endometriomas (chocolate cysts) and MRI can assess deep infiltrating endometriosis, neither can diagnose peritoneal endometriosis — the most common form — without laparoscopy. Clients with suspected endometriosis should be referred for specialist evaluation.

options: Sudden chest pain with no leg symptoms at all
Bilateral ankle swelling without any associated pain
Generalised muscle weakness without any localised finding
Widespread pruritic rash affecting both lower limbs
Unilateral calf pain, swelling, warmth, and redness
questions.question: Deep vein thrombosis in the puerperium classically presents with which combination of clinical findings?
questions.explanation: Puerperal deep vein thrombosis typically presents with unilateral leg symptoms including calf pain, swelling, warmth, and redness, reflecting localised venous obstruction and inflammation, and pregnancy and the puerperium constitute a hypercoagulable state that increases this risk. Bilateral symptoms or symptoms without a clear localised limb finding would suggest an alternative diagnosis. Doppler ultrasound is the investigation of choice to confirm the clinical suspicion.

options: It can cause significant hypovolaemia from large blood loss
It is always confined by suture lines tightly
It never requires any laboratory monitoring afterward
It resolves completely within twenty-four hours
It is associated exclusively with forceps delivery
questions.question: Which feature makes subgaleal (subaponeurotic) haemorrhage potentially more dangerous than cephalhaematoma?
questions.explanation: Subgaleal haemorrhage occurs in the potential space between the galea aponeurotica and the periosteum, an area that can accommodate a large volume of blood and is not limited by suture lines, so bleeding can be extensive enough to cause hypovolaemic shock and coagulopathy. Cephalhaematoma, being confined beneath the periosteum, generally involves a smaller and self-limiting blood volume. Close monitoring of haemoglobin and vital signs is essential when subgaleal haemorrhage is suspected.

The uterosacral ligaments extend from the posterior aspect of the cervix and upper vagina to the front of the sacrum at the S2-S4 level, passing on either side of the rectum. They form the lateral boundaries of the pouch of Douglas and help maintain the anteverted position. Endometriosis nodules commonly implant on these ligaments.
questions.question: The uterosacral ligaments run from the cervix to which posterior structure?
options: Lateral pelvic sidewall at the obturator fascia
Pubic symphysis anteriorly via the pubocervical fascia
Ischial spine, used as the station landmark in labour
Sacral promontory anteriorly at the pelvic brim level
Posterior sacrum at the S2 to S4 vertebral level

questions.explanation: Persistent insomnia without apparent reason in the postnatal woman is an important early warning sign of puerperal psychosis. Other early warning signs include refusing meals, loss of interest in the baby, and restlessness. Early recognition and prompt referral to psychiatric services are critical to prevent progression to more severe manifestations including hallucinations, suicidal ideation, and risk of harm to the infant.
questions.question: Persistent insomnia without apparent reason in a newly delivered woman is most importantly significant because it:
options: Suggests the woman is experiencing anaemia from delivery
Indicates inadequate pain relief following perineal repair
Is expected and normal in the immediate postnatal period
Serves as an early warning sign of puerperal psychosis
Confirms postnatal depression has developed fully
Simple progression of her chronic hypertension alone
Gestational hypertension unrelated to her chronic disease
A normal physiological rise in blood pressure
Superimposed pre-eclampsia on her chronic hypertension
Resolution of her pre-existing hypertensive disease
questions.question: A woman with chronic hypertension becomes pregnant and later develops new-onset proteinuria and worsening blood pressure control. What does this combination indicate?
questions.explanation: Superimposed pre-eclampsia is diagnosed when a woman with pre-existing chronic hypertension develops new proteinuria, worsening hypertension, or other organ dysfunction after twenty weeks gestation, distinguishing it from a simple continuation of her baseline chronic disease. This combination carries a higher risk of adverse maternal and fetal outcomes than either condition alone. Careful antenatal surveillance helps detect this transition early.

questions.question: Thick meconium-stained amniotic fluid primarily requires which action at delivery?
options: Paediatric presence at delivery for active airway management
Thin meconium only requires oxytocin augmentation to speed delivery
It requires immediate caesarean section to prevent aspiration
It confirms fetal death and necessitates immediate delivery
It confirms that labour has been prolonged beyond 42 weeks
questions.explanation: Thick meconium (pea-soup consistency) is associated with meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS). Current guidelines recommend the paediatric/neonatal team attend delivery for thick MSAF, with preparation for airway suctioning if the baby is non-vigorous at birth. Vigorous babies with MSAF do not require routine tracheal suctioning. Thin meconium with normal CTG can be managed expectantly with close monitoring.

questions.question: In managing a newborn with Klumpke's palsy, what additional clinical condition must be specifically assessed for?
options: Horner's syndrome from associated cervical sympathetic nerve trauma
Erb's palsy on the contralateral side from compensatory injury
Phrenic nerve palsy from C4 root involvement and diaphragmatic paralysis
Fracture of the femur from the breech delivery mechanism
Facial nerve palsy from concurrent VII cranial nerve compression
questions.explanation: Klumpke's palsy results from trauma to C8 and T1 nerve roots. When the cervical sympathetic nerve chain (which runs adjacent to these nerve roots) is also traumatised, Horner's syndrome develops on the affected side. This presents with miosis (pupillary constriction), ptosis (eyelid drooping), anhidrosis (absence of sweating), and loss of sensation on the affected side. The presence of Horner's syndrome with Klumpke's palsy indicates a more extensive injury and may carry a worse prognosis for recovery.

questions.question: A midwife explains to a new mother that her fundus should be at approximately the level of the umbilicus immediately after birth and will progressively descend. Over what period does the uterus typically involute back to its pre-pregnancy size?
options: Approximately six weeks, the duration of the puerperium
questions.explanation: The puerperium, the period during which the reproductive organs return to their pre-pregnancy state, lasts approximately six weeks, during which the uterus undergoes progressive involution from its immediate postpartum size back to its normal weight and dimensions. Delayed involution beyond this expected timeframe may suggest retained products or infection requiring further assessment. Regular fundal height assessment in the early postnatal period tracks this normal process.

options: Repeat testing is required only after menopause
Repeat co-testing may be deferred for approximately five years
Repeat testing must be performed every six months
Repeat testing must be performed within one month
No further screening is required for life
questions.explanation: When cytology and HPV co-testing are both negative, current guidelines allow extension of the screening interval to approximately every five years because the combined negative predictive value is very high, reducing unnecessary procedures while maintaining safety. Screening every six months or requiring lifelong cessation would either be excessive or unsafe. Screening continues at appropriate intervals until the recommended upper age limit is reached.
questions.question: Which statement correctly reflects current guidance on the interval for repeat Pap smear testing in a woman with a normal result and negative HPV co-test at age 35?

The head is deflexed, giving a larger presenting diameter
The head is extended, presenting the mentovertical diameter
The neck is hyperextended, presenting the face
The head is asynclitic, tilted to one side
questions.explanation: The suboccipitobregmatic diameter, measuring about 9.5 cm, is the smallest anteroposterior diameter of the fetal skull and presents only when the head is well flexed in vertex presentation. Good flexion allows the smallest diameter to negotiate the pelvis, facilitating normal descent. Poor flexion increases the presenting diameter and can slow labour progress.
questions.question: A midwife measuring an engaged fetal head in vertex presentation notes the suboccipitobregmatic diameter is presenting. What does this indicate about neck flexion?

Directly posterior in the midline (median episiotomy)
questions.question: A true mediolateral episiotomy should be angled at what direction from the midline?
questions.explanation: A true mediolateral episiotomy should be directed at approximately 40-60 degrees from the midline (usually toward the right ischial tuberosity). This angle avoids the midline structures (external anal sphincter and Bartholin's gland duct) and reduces the risk of extension into a third- or fourth-degree tear. Episiotomies cut too close to the midline increase the risk of OASI.
