Retroplacental clot forming behind an intact placenta

questions.explanation: PID causes inflammatory damage and scarring of the fallopian tube epithelium and muscularis, impairing the cilia-mediated and peristaltic transport of the fertilised oocyte towards the uterus. This transport failure leads to implantation within the fallopian tube — ectopic pregnancy — which can cause tubal rupture, life-threatening intraperitoneal haemorrhage, and death if not promptly diagnosed and treated. The risk of ectopic pregnancy increases with each episode of PID.
questions.question: In a family planning context, which statement correctly describes the relationship between PID and ectopic pregnancy?
options: PID protects against ectopic pregnancy by creating fallopian tube spasms
Ectopic pregnancy caused by PID is always located in the ovary
Ectopic pregnancy only occurs in women who have never had PID
PID causes fallopian tube scarring, increasing the risk of ectopic pregnancy
PID always results in ectopic pregnancy in the subsequent conception

questions.question: Progestin-only injectable contraceptives (DMPA) are relatively contraindicated in women at risk of osteoporosis primarily because:
options: Injectable progestins cause direct osteoclast activation in bone
DMPA increases parathyroid hormone levels reducing bone formation
DMPA suppresses oestrogen, reducing bone mineral density over time
Progestin increases calcium excretion through the renal pathway
Progestin-only methods interfere with vitamin D metabolism in bone
questions.explanation: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injectable contraceptives suppress ovarian oestrogen production, which is essential for maintaining bone mineral density. Long-term use leads to a reduction in bone density that may predispose susceptible women to osteoporosis and fractures, particularly those who are already at risk — including adolescents, perimenopausal women, and those with low calcium intake. Bone density generally recovers after discontinuation.

options: Presence of bright red vaginal bleeding
Presence of significant pain and uterine tenderness
Occurrence of bleeding in the third trimester
questions.explanation: Placental abruption is characteristically associated with significant abdominal pain and a tender, sometimes woody-hard uterus due to concealed or revealed retroplacental bleeding, unlike the painless bleeding typical of placenta praevia. This clinical distinction, alongside ultrasound findings, guides the initial differential diagnosis before further investigation. Recognising pain as a key differentiator supports rapid, appropriate triage.
questions.question: A midwife is asked to identify the main clinical feature that distinguishes placental abruption from placenta praevia. Which feature is this?

options: Allow immediate pushing since transition indicates full dilatation
Assess the cervical dilatation before allowing her to push
Administer pethidine 100 mg IM to reduce expulsive distress
Transfer urgently to the theatre for assisted delivery
Encourage an epidural top-up to relieve expulsive sensation
questions.explanation: Pushing before full cervical dilatation can cause cervical oedema, tearing, and obstruction. The urge to push may begin before 10 cm, especially in rapid labours. The midwife must confirm full dilatation (10 cm) by vaginal examination before directing pushing. If not fully dilated, the woman should pant or breathe through contractions to resist the urge.
questions.question: A primigravida in the transition phase (8–10 cm) feels an urge to push. What is the MOST important nursing action?

options: Absence of one or more limbs entirely at birth
Two or more fingers fused together at birth
Short, deformed limbs from epiphyseal plate defect
More than the normal number of fingers or toes
An abnormally large head circumference from birth
questions.explanation: Polydactyly is defined as having more than the normal number of fingers, toes, or both. It is usually inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. The extra digit may be fully formed or attached by a pedicle. If there is no bone in the rudimentary digit, it may be ligated at the base and allowed to necrose. More complex attachments require surgical removal. The condition is distinct from syndactyly, where digits are fused together.
questions.question: Polydactyly is defined as a condition in which the infant has:

questions.explanation: Progesterone secreted by the corpus luteum after ovulation is thermogenic, raising basal body temperature by approximately 0.3-0.5°C. This rise persists throughout the 14-day luteal phase and falls just before menstruation if fertilization does not occur. The BBT chart is used in the symptothermal method of family planning to identify the post-ovulatory infertile period.
questions.question: Which hormone causes the rise in basal body temperature of approximately 0.5°C after ovulation?
options: Human chorionic gonadotrophin, rescuing the corpus luteum
Progesterone, secreted by the newly formed corpus luteum
Luteinising hormone, causing the preovulatory surge
Oestrogen, peaking just before the time of ovulation

questions.question: Congenital syphilis in a neonate born to an untreated infected mother most characteristically presents with which clinical feature?
questions.explanation: Congenital syphilis classically presents with persistent nasal discharge known as snuffles, along with skin rash, hepatosplenomegaly, and skeletal abnormalities such as periostitis, resulting from transplacental spirochaete transmission. The sunset sign is instead associated with hydrocephalus, while cataracts and cardiac murmurs are more typical of congenital rubella syndrome. Early recognition allows prompt penicillin treatment of both mother and infant.
options: Absent red reflex in both eyes
Sunset sign of both eyes bilaterally
Cataracts present at the time of birth

questions.explanation: Prenatal administration of corticosteroids (e.g., betamethasone or dexamethasone) to mothers at risk of premature birth stimulates fetal lung surfactant production, reducing the severity of respiratory distress syndrome. Corticosteroids also have a neuroprotective effect on the developing brain, and when followed by postnatal artificial surfactant administration, they significantly reduce the incidence of periventricular and intraventricular haemorrhage in preterm infants.
options: Stimulates maturation of surfactant and has a neuroprotective effect
Reduces maternal blood pressure lowering fetal haemodynamic stress
Suppresses maternal infection reducing fetal inflammatory cascade
Prevents fetal movement that could cause mechanical haemorrhage
Directly strengthens the germinal matrix capillary walls prenatally
questions.question: The prenatal administration of corticosteroids to mothers threatening premature labour is relevant to periventricular haemorrhage prevention because it:
Which oral antihypertensive is used as a fast-acting agent for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy?
options: Hydralazine 25 mg orally for mild hypertension
Methyldopa 250 mg orally for chronic hypertension
Labetalol IV infusion for acute severe hypertension
Amlodipine 5 mg orally as a slow-onset calcium blocker
questions.explanation: Nifedipine (immediate-release/short-acting) 10 mg orally (or sublingually) is a fast-acting calcium channel blocker used for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy where IV access is not available. It reduces systolic and diastolic BP within 15-30 minutes. IV labetalol and IV hydralazine are the IV first-line choices in hospital settings. Immediate-release nifedipine has largely replaced the sublingual capsule (which caused unpredictable hypotension).

Eclampsia is defined as the occurrence of one or more generalised seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia, in the absence of other causes such as epilepsy. It represents a severe complication requiring emergency management including magnesium sulphate and expedited delivery. Prompt recognition distinguishes it from other causes of seizure in pregnancy.
options: Severe pre-eclampsia, without a change in diagnosis
HELLP syndrome, defined primarily by seizure activity
Eclampsia, defined by seizures in a pre-eclamptic woman
questions.question: A woman develops seizures in the presence of pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks gestation. According to standard obstetric definitions, what has she now developed?
A midwife palpates a boggy fundus above the umbilicus two hours after delivery with heavy bleeding. Which uterine layer's failure to contract is responsible?
options: Myometrium, failing to compress the spiral arterioles
Perimetrium, failing to seal the peritoneal surface
Decidua basalis, failing to separate cleanly
Endometrium, failing to regenerate its glands
Parametrium, failing to support the cervix
questions.explanation: The myometrium's interlacing muscle fibres normally compress the spiral arterioles as living ligatures after placental separation. When it fails to contract adequately, atony results and vessels remain open, causing heavy postpartum bleeding. Uterine massage and uterotonics restore this contractile compression.

options: Prolactin secretion from the anterior pituitary gland
Milk ejection (let-down) via myoepithelial cell contraction
Alveolar cell synthesis and secretion of new milk proteins
Ductal proliferation and new lobular glandular development
Increased mammary blood flow improving nutrient delivery
questions.question: Oxytocin released from the posterior pituitary during breastfeeding stimulates which response?
questions.explanation: Oxytocin is released from the posterior pituitary in response to suckling via a neuroendocrine reflex. It acts on myoepithelial cells surrounding the alveoli, causing them to contract and eject milk into lactiferous ducts - the "let-down reflex." Prolactin, not oxytocin, synthesises milk. Oxytocin also causes uterine afterpains during breastfeeding postpartum.

questions.question: Fetal movements are typically first perceived by a primigravida at approximately what gestational age?
options: 22–24 weeks — when fetal muscle strength increases
24–26 weeks — when the fetal nervous system matures
14–16 weeks — quickening early in the second trimester
questions.explanation: Quickening (first maternal perception of fetal movements) typically occurs at approximately 18-20 weeks in primigravidae and earlier (16-18 weeks) in multigravidae, who recognise the sensation from previous pregnancies. Fetal movements actually begin much earlier (8-10 weeks) but are not perceived until sufficient strength develops. Absent movements after 28 weeks should prompt fetal wellbeing assessment.

questions.question: The Brandt-Andrews method for placental delivery involves which technique?
options: Gentle sustained traction on the cord with the uterus unsupported
Manual compression of the uterine body through the abdomen
Controlled cord traction while stabilising the uterus suprapubically
Fundal pressure applied with the mother bearing down
Maternal pushing combined with oxytocin injection
questions.explanation: The Brandt-Andrews method involves placing one hand suprapubically to stabilise and guard the uterus (preventing inversion), while applying steady, controlled downward traction to the clamped umbilical cord with the other hand during a contraction. Traction must never be applied without counter-pressure - unguarded cord traction causes uterine inversion, a life-threatening complication.

Primary infertility is defined as failure to achieve a clinical pregnancy after 12 months or more of regular unprotected sexual intercourse in a couple who have never previously conceived. Secondary infertility is failure to conceive after a previous pregnancy (regardless of outcome). The investigation threshold is reduced to 6 months for women over 35, known ovulatory disorders, known tubal damage, or male factor infertility (severe oligospermia).
options: Failure to carry a pregnancy to viability (recurrent miscarriage)
Failure to conceive after 12 months of unprotected regular intercourse with no prior pregnancy
Inability to conceive after 6 months of unprotected intercourse
Failure to conceive after 24 months regardless of prior pregnancies
Inability to conceive due to anovulation only
questions.question: Primary infertility is correctly defined as:

questions.explanation: A notable advantage of the female condom is that it can be inserted into the vagina some time before intercourse, giving the woman greater control over its use compared with the male condom, which is applied by the male partner immediately before penetration. Both condom types, when used correctly, provide protection against pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections. This flexibility can improve consistent use among women who want more control over barrier protection.
questions.question: Which statement correctly describes a key difference between the male and female condom?
options: The female condom needs a partner's active participation
The female condom can be inserted before intercourse begins
The female condom cannot be used without spermicide
The male condom must be fitted by a clinician
The male condom offers no infection protection

questions.explanation: Blood grouping and Rh factor determination in preconception counselling primarily address the risk of Rh incompatibility. An Rh-negative woman carrying an Rh-positive fetus risks developing anti-D antibodies after sensitisation, which can cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn in subsequent pregnancies. Anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis during pregnancy and after delivery prevents sensitisation. Early identification of Rh-negative status allows appropriate antenatal and peripartum management.
questions.question: The purpose of blood grouping and Rh factor determination as part of preconception investigation is primarily to:
options: Identify maternal blood group for organ donation registration
Screen for rare blood group antibodies causing autoimmune disease
Determine fetal blood group using maternal blood sample
Ensure compatibility for planned blood transfusions during delivery
Address Rh incompatibility risk between mother and fetus
Ergometrine + controlled cord traction + fundal pressure
Misoprostol + delayed cord clamping + uterine massage
Oxytocin + controlled cord traction + uterine massage
questions.question: The standard regimen for active management of the third stage of labour as recommended by WHO includes which three components?
questions.explanation: WHO's Active Management of the Third Stage of Labour (AMTSL) consists of three components: (1) uterotonic drug administration - oxytocin 10 IU IM (preferred) immediately after delivery of the baby (or anterior shoulder); (2) controlled cord traction (CCT) with counter-pressure (Brandt-Andrews technique) after signs of placental separation; and (3) uterine massage after delivery of the placenta to encourage continued uterine contraction. Early (within 1-3 minutes) cord clamping is also recommended unless delayed cord clamping is indicated.

questions.question: A woman using combined oral contraceptives reports missing two consecutive pills in the second week of her pack. The most appropriate advice is to:
questions.explanation: Missing two pills reduces contraceptive efficacy and requires the woman to take the most recently missed pill immediately, continue the remaining pack as scheduled, and use a backup method such as condoms for seven days. Discarding the pack unnecessarily increases the risk of an unintended pregnancy. Emergency contraception should also be considered if unprotected intercourse occurred in the preceding days.
options: Discard the pack and restart after her next period
Stop the pack immediately and await withdrawal bleeding
Take the missed pills now and use backup contraception
Continue as scheduled without any additional precaution
Double the next scheduled dose only once

questions.question: During delivery of the head in vertex presentation, the midwife applies gentle pressure to control its exit. What complication is this manoeuvre primarily intended to prevent?
questions.explanation: Guarding the perineum during crowning controls the speed of the head's delivery, preventing sudden expulsion that could cause extensive perineal tears including third- or fourth-degree injury. This gentle, controlled approach also reduces the force transmitted to the fetal head. It is a core component of safe vaginal delivery technique.
options: Retained placenta in the third stage
Rapid, uncontrolled delivery causing perineal trauma
To manually remove retained placental fragments
To assess for a possible cervical laceration
To reposition an inverted uterus back into place
To compress the uterus manually and control bleeding
To measure the extent of blood loss precisely
questions.question: A midwife caring for a woman with uterine atony and ongoing haemorrhage performs bimanual uterine compression as an initial procedure. What is the primary purpose of this technique?
questions.explanation: Bimanual uterine compression involves one hand in the vagina pressing against the anterior uterine wall and the other on the abdomen compressing the fundus posteriorly, mechanically controlling bleeding from an atonic uterus while pharmacological measures take effect. It is a bridging measure used when uterotonics alone are insufficient. This technique buys time while preparing for further intervention such as surgery if needed.

questions.question: Which skull suture separates the two parietal bones in the fetal skull?
options: Coronal suture between the frontal and parietal bones
Lambdoid suture between the parietal and occipital bones
Squamosal suture between the parietal and temporal bones
Sagittal suture between the two parietal bones
Metopic suture between the two frontal bones
questions.explanation: The sagittal suture runs longitudinally from the anterior fontanelle (bregma) to the posterior fontanelle (lambda), separating the two parietal bones. It is palpated on vaginal examination during labour to determine fetal head position. The position of the anterior fontanelle relative to the sagittal suture helps determine synclitism or asynclitism.

questions.question: A woman is diagnosed with secondary infertility after successfully conceiving and delivering a child previously. How is this specific term correctly defined?
questions.explanation: Secondary infertility is defined as difficulty conceiving or carrying a pregnancy to term in a woman who has previously achieved at least one successful pregnancy, regardless of the outcome of that pregnancy. This distinguishes it from primary infertility, where no previous pregnancy has ever occurred. Identifying which category applies helps direct the focus of subsequent investigations, as causes can differ between the two.
options: Failure to conceive with no previous pregnancy ever
Failure to sustain a pregnancy beyond twenty weeks
Failure to ovulate despite a regular menstrual cycle
Failure of a previous pregnancy to reach term
Failure to conceive after a previous successful pregnancy

questions.question: The primary reason progestin-only pills must be taken at the same time each day, with minimal flexibility, is that:
questions.explanation: Traditional progestin-only pills have a short duration of action on cervical mucus thickening, meaning a delay of more than three hours can allow mucus to thin and permit sperm penetration. This narrow window contrasts with combined pills, which allow a twelve-hour margin. Strict timing is therefore emphasised during counselling for this method.
options: Their contraceptive effect on mucus wanes quickly
They interact significantly with most antibiotics
They contain a much higher hormone dose
They cause irreversible changes if delayed
They require food for adequate gut absorption

questions.question: A client presents with unexplained vaginal bleeding. Which investigation is most urgently indicated to exclude endometrial pathology?
questions.explanation: Unexplained or abnormal uterine bleeding may indicate endometrial polyps, fibroids, hyperplasia, or carcinoma. Pelvic ultrasound provides initial imaging to assess the uterine cavity and endometrial thickness, while endometrial biopsy provides histological diagnosis. Together, they are the most appropriate initial investigations to exclude serious endometrial pathology before proceeding with family planning.
options: High vaginal swab and cervical culture
Hormonal assay for FSH and oestradiol
Complete blood count and coagulation profile
Thyroid function tests and prolactin level

questions.question: Couvade syndrome refers to which condition associated with obstetric pathology?
options: A large subchorionic haematoma causing a marginal APH
Bleeding from the placental margin in a low-lying placenta
Bleeding from a retroplacental haematoma without pain
Concealed abruption with no visible vaginal bleeding
Sympathy symptoms in the male partner of a pregnant woman
questions.explanation: Concealed placental abruption describes a situation where the placenta has separated partially or completely from the uterine wall but the blood is trapped behind the placenta (retroplacental haematoma) and does not escape through the cervix. There is no visible vaginal bleeding. The woman presents with severe abdominal pain, a tense, tender, board-like uterus, and signs of maternal and fetal compromise disproportionate to any external blood loss. This is the most dangerous form of abruption.

questions.question: Which statement about the integration of laboratory investigations with family planning services is most accurate?
options: Laboratory investigations are not relevant in family planning
Tests are selected based on the client's medical history
Routine laboratory testing is compulsory for all clients
Testing is reserved only for clients with chronic disease
All clients must complete a full hormonal profile first
questions.explanation: Laboratory investigations in family planning should be personalised based on the individual's medical history, age, presenting symptoms, and chosen contraceptive method. Routine blanket testing is not universally required; rather, investigations are guided by clinical judgment and specific indications identified during history taking and physical examination.

questions.question: A couple has been trying to conceive for 14 months without success. Which initial investigation for the male partner is most important?
questions.explanation: Semen analysis (spermogram) is the essential first-line investigation for male partner infertility assessment. It evaluates semen volume, sperm concentration, total sperm count, motility (progressive and total), and morphology (using Kruger strict criteria). WHO 2021 reference values: volume =1.4 mL, concentration =16 million/mL, total motility =42%, progressive motility =30%, normal morphology =4%. Azoospermia (no sperm), oligospermia (<16 million/mL), or asthenospermia (reduced motility) guides further investigations.
options: Semen analysis (spermogram) assessing volume, count, motility, and morphology
Serum testosterone level to assess androgen production
Testicular biopsy to assess spermatogenesis histologically
Serum FSH to assess pituitary function
Scrotal ultrasound to detect varicocele or hydrocele

questions.question: A woman is screened for gestational diabetes mellitus using a standard screening tool recommended in antenatal care. Which test is most commonly used for this purpose?
questions.explanation: The oral glucose tolerance test, typically performed between twenty-four and twenty-eight weeks gestation, is the standard screening and diagnostic tool for gestational diabetes mellitus, involving a fasting sample followed by measurement after a glucose load. Random glucose testing and urine dipstick are insufficiently sensitive for reliable diagnosis. Early identification through this test allows timely dietary or pharmacological management to reduce maternal and fetal complications.
options: Oral glucose tolerance test, performed at twenty-four to twenty-eight weeks
Random blood glucose test, performed at every antenatal visit
Haemoglobin A1c testing, performed once at booking only
Urine dipstick testing for glucose, performed weekly
Fasting blood glucose alone, performed once at booking

questions.question: Uterine fibroids (leiomyomata) are classified by their location. Which type is most associated with heavy menstrual bleeding?
questions.explanation: Submucosal fibroids (type 0, 1, 2 by the FIGO classification) protrude into the uterine cavity and distort the endometrial surface. They are the most strongly associated with heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB), because they increase the endometrial surface area, interfere with normal uterine contractility, and impair haemostasis. They are also the most strongly associated with infertility and recurrent miscarriage. Hysteroscopic myomectomy is the treatment of choice for type 0 and 1 submucosal fibroids.
options: Intramural fibroids — within the uterine wall muscle
Pedunculated fibroids — attached by a stalk to the uterus
Broad ligament fibroids — extending into the broad ligament
Submucosal fibroids — protruding into the uterine cavity
Subserosal fibroids — projecting outward from the uterine surface

questions.explanation: The symptothermal method combines two indicators: cervical mucus observation (for the pre-ovulatory fertile phase - Billings/Creighton approach) and basal body temperature charting (for confirming the post-ovulatory infertile phase - a BBT rise of 0.2-0.5°C confirmed on three consecutive mornings). Combining two methods improves accuracy. With correct use, the symptothermal method has a failure rate of 0.4-2.3%, making it the most effective natural method.
questions.question: Which fertility awareness method combines basal body temperature monitoring and cervical mucus observation?
options: Creighton model based on cervical mucus alone
Symptothermal method combining BBT and cervical mucus
Calendar (rhythm) method based on cycle length only
Standard Days Method using beads and cycle length
Lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM) for postpartum women

questions.question: A woman with endometriosis and pelvic pain is prescribed gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists. What is the expected effect on menstruation?
options: Shorter cycles from reduced luteal phase activity
Heavier periods due to endometrial proliferation
Normal cycles with reduced prostaglandin production
Amenorrhoea due to oestrogen suppression (medical menopause)
questions.explanation: GnRH agonists (leuprorelin, goserelin, buserelin) initially cause a "flare" of LH and FSH (days 1-2), followed by pituitary downregulation (receptor desensitisation), leading to markedly reduced LH and FSH, hypo-oestrogenism, and amenorrhoea. This "medical menopause" (pseudomenopause) causes regression of endometriotic implants. It is used for 6 months maximum to avoid bone loss. Add-back therapy (low-dose HRT) is given to reduce hypo-oestrogenic side effects (hot flushes, bone loss).

questions.question: Atrial septal defect (ASD) is characterised on auscultation by:
options: Harsh pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border
Opening snap followed by mid-diastolic murmur at the apex
Continuous machinery murmur heard below the left clavicle
Ejection systolic murmur with single second heart sound loudly
Fixed widely split second heart sound throughout respiration
questions.explanation: Atrial septal defect (ASD) produces a characteristic fixed, widely split second heart sound on auscultation, caused by prolonged right ventricular ejection time from the increased right-sided volume load. Normally the second heart sound splits with inspiration but closes with expiration; in ASD, the split is fixed and does not vary with respiration. A pulmonary systolic flow murmur may also be heard from increased pulmonary blood flow.

questions.question: Pap smear screening for cervical cancer should begin at age 21 and, for women aged 30 to 65, is recommended every how many years when combined with HPV co-testing?
options: Every three years with Pap smear alone from age 30
Every two years with Pap smear alone only
Every year for maximum early detection sensitivity
Every five years with Pap smear and HPV co-testing
Every ten years if the previous two tests were normal
questions.explanation: Current guidelines recommend that women begin cervical cancer screening at age 21, with Pap smear alone every three years until age 29. From ages 30 to 65, the preferred strategy is Pap smear combined with HPV co-testing every five years. This co-testing strategy has greater sensitivity for detecting high-grade cervical lesions (over 90%) compared to Pap smear alone (approximately 70%), allowing for safe extension of the screening interval.

questions.question: A lipid profile is most indicated in family planning for a client who intends to use which contraceptive method?
questions.explanation: Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) contain oestrogen, which can alter lipid metabolism by increasing triglycerides and LDL cholesterol while reducing HDL cholesterol, thereby increasing cardiovascular risk. A baseline lipid profile is therefore indicated before initiating COCs in clients with risk factors for cardiovascular disease. Dyslipidaemia is a relative contraindication for oestrogen-containing contraceptives.

Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common cause of tubal factor infertility, as ascending infection can cause silent salpingitis leading to tubal scarring, adhesions, and blockage even without an obvious acute illness. Screening and prompt treatment of chlamydial infection are important preventive strategies against this complication. Tubal patency testing is often required in women with a history of pelvic infection presenting with infertility.
questions.question: A woman with a history of pelvic inflammatory infection is investigated for tubal factor infertility. Which sexually transmitted infection is the most common cause of this specific type of infertility?
options: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, causing isolated cervical infection only
Treponema pallidum, causing systemic disease without tubal damage
Human papillomavirus, causing cervical dysplasia only
Chlamydia trachomatis, causing tubal scarring and blockage
Herpes simplex virus, causing genital ulceration only

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why progestin-only contraceptives are generally preferred over combined oral contraceptives (COCs) for lactating women?
questions.explanation: Progestin-only methods (mini-pill, DMPA injectable, implants) are preferred for lactating women because progestin alone does not adversely affect milk volume or composition. Combined oral contraceptives contain oestrogen, which can reduce milk production by inhibiting prolactin-mediated lactogenesis. Maintaining adequate breast milk supply is essential for infant nutrition and the success of breastfeeding, making progestin-only methods the appropriate choice in the postpartum lactating period.
options: COCs are completely absorbed by breast tissue before reaching milk
Progestin-only methods do not adversely affect milk production volume
Progestin increases milk fat content improving neonatal nutrition
Progestin-only methods have superior contraceptive efficacy in lactating women
COCs cause galactorrhoea by stimulating prolactin release excessively

questions.question: Which is the first cardinal movement of labour in vertex presentation?
options: Internal rotation to the anteroposterior diameter
Engagement of the biparietal diameter at the inlet
Flexion to present the smaller suboccipitobregmatic diameter
Restitution restoring the head to its original alignment
questions.explanation: The first cardinal movement is engagement, defined as the passage of the widest transverse diameter of the fetal head (biparietal diameter, 9.5 cm) through the pelvic inlet. In primigravidae, engagement typically occurs 2-4 weeks before labour; in multigravidae, it may not occur until labour begins. It is confirmed when only 2/5 of the head is palpable abdominally.

options: Syncytiotrophoblast — the invasive outer cellular layer
Cytotrophoblast — the inner cellular trophoblast layer
Epiblast (inner cell mass/embryoblast) — the embryonic layer
questions.explanation: The blastocyst has an inner cell mass (embryoblast), which differentiates into the epiblast and hypoblast, and the outer trophoblast. The inner cell mass gives rise to all embryonic tissues (and eventually the fetus). The epiblast will form the three primary germ layers - ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm - via gastrulation in the third week. The trophoblast forms the placenta.
questions.question: The blastocyst has two distinct cell populations. Which layer will form the fetus itself?
A woman presents with a vulval lump and swelling is traced through lymphatics to enlarged inguinal nodes. Which lymphatic pathway explains this spread?
options: Para-aortic nodes draining the ovary directly
Internal iliac nodes draining the cervix primarily
Obturator nodes draining the bladder base
Superficial inguinal nodes draining the vulva directly
External iliac nodes draining the uterine body
questions.explanation: The vulva drains primarily to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes, unlike the cervix and uterine body which drain to pelvic node groups. This explains why vulval cancers characteristically metastasise to groin nodes early. Clinical examination of the groin is therefore essential in suspected vulval malignancy.

questions.question: A woman develops sudden shoulder dystocia after delivery of the fetal head, with the anterior shoulder trapped behind the symphysis pubis. What is the recommended first-line manoeuvre?
questions.explanation: The McRoberts manoeuvre, hyperflexing the maternal hips onto the abdomen, combined with suprapubic pressure to dislodge the anterior shoulder, is the recommended first-line approach to shoulder dystocia and resolves the majority of cases. Fundal pressure is avoided as it can worsen impaction and risks uterine rupture. If first-line measures fail, further internal manoeuvres are attempted by a skilled obstetric team.
options: Immediate fundal pressure to expel the shoulder
Zavanelli manoeuvre to replace the fetal head
Aggressive downward traction on the fetal head

questions.question: A neonate presents with facial asymmetry noted only when crying, with the affected side failing to move while the unaffected side wrinkles normally. This is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Facial nerve palsy in the newborn commonly results from pressure on the facial nerve during delivery, often related to forceps application, and is recognised by asymmetric facial movement that becomes most apparent during crying, with the affected side failing to wrinkle or move while the unaffected side functions normally. Brachial plexus injuries instead affect limb movement rather than facial expression. Most cases resolve spontaneously within weeks as nerve compression subsides.
options: Klumpke's palsy affecting the lower limb
Erb's palsy affecting the upper limb
Facial nerve palsy from birth trauma

questions.question: A woman with sharp groin pain in the third trimester is reassured this is common in pregnancy. Stretching of which structure explains this pain?
questions.explanation: The round ligament runs from the uterine cornua through the inguinal canal to the labium majus, and hypertrophies during pregnancy to help support the anteverted uterus. Rapid stretching, especially with sudden movement, causes sharp groin or lower abdominal pain. This round ligament pain is benign and self-limiting.
options: Broad ligament, compressed by the enlarging fetus
Round ligament, hypertrophied and stretched by the growing uterus
Uterosacral ligament, pulled posteriorly toward the sacrum
Ovarian ligament, tethered near the pelvic sidewall
Cardinal ligament, stretched at the cervix
Inability to suck effectively due to unilateral facial muscle weakness
Vomiting from impaired lower oesophageal sphincter function
Diarrhoea from impaired innervation of the intestinal wall
Choking from paralysis of the pharyngeal swallowing muscles
Excessive hunger from insufficient caloric intake and metabolic demand
questions.explanation: Facial nerve palsy (VII cranial nerve) causes unilateral facial muscle weakness including the orbicularis oris, which is essential for creating the seal around the nipple or teat needed for effective sucking. The affected baby drools excessively, cannot create adequate negative pressure for sucking, and may be unable to feed effectively from the breast or bottle. Alternative feeding positions and feeding aids may help. This problem usually resolves as the nerve trauma heals.
questions.question: The feeding difficulty most commonly associated with facial nerve palsy in a neonate is:

questions.explanation: Infertility is associated with significant psychological distress, anxiety, depression, and relationship strain. Supportive measures during the referral process include providing emotional support and counselling to both partners to manage the stress of investigations and uncertainty. Couples should also be educated about lifestyle modifications, encouraged to continue tracking menstrual cycles, and counselled to continue attempting conception (unless there is an absolute contraindication) while awaiting specialist review.
options: Separating the couple for individual counselling without joint sessions
Prescribing anxiolytic medications to both partners before referral
Advising the couple to avoid intercourse until investigations are complete
Recommending adoption as the only realistic option for infertile couples
Providing emotional support and counselling to manage anxiety and stress
questions.question: Supportive measures during infertility referral should include which psychosocial intervention?

questions.explanation: Typical-use effectiveness accounts for user error, and barrier methods such as condoms show markedly higher real-world failure rates than long-acting reversible or permanent methods because correct use depends on the couple every act of intercourse. Implants, IUDs, and sterilisation are largely independent of user behaviour once in place. This distinction guides counselling on method choice for clients prioritising high efficacy.
options: Male condom used inconsistently by young couples
Copper intrauterine device left in situ correctly
questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs a contraceptive method with its typical-use failure rate being comparatively HIGH?

questions.explanation: Anteversion means the uterus is tilted forward over the bladder relative to the vaginal axis. Anteflexion means the body of the uterus bends forward on the cervix. This combined anteverted-anteflexed position is the normal position of the uterus in most women. Retroversion with retroflexion is the reverse and can be associated with dysmenorrhoea.
questions.question: During a bimanual examination, the uterus is anteverted and anteflexed. What does this describe?
options: Uterus tilted forward over the bladder with forward body angle
Uterus in a neutral midline position with no angulation
Uterus retroverted with retroflexion of the uterine body
Uterus tilted laterally toward the right adnexal structures
Uterus tilted backward with the cervix pointing anteriorly

questions.explanation: Isoniazid (INH), used to treat active tuberculosis in pregnancy (which must be treated to protect both mother and fetus), acts as a vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) antagonist by inhibiting pyridoxal phosphokinase. This can cause peripheral neuropathy. Pyridoxine 25-50 mg daily is co-prescribed with isoniazid to prevent this complication. Active TB in pregnancy is treated with rifampicin + isoniazid + ethambutol (avoid pyrazinamide in first trimester if possible).
questions.question: Which drug used in pregnancy acts as a vitamin B6 antagonist, requiring supplementation to prevent peripheral neuropathy?
options: Metronidazole used for treating bacterial vaginosis
Metformin used for gestational diabetes management
Amoxicillin used for urinary tract infection in pregnancy
Isoniazid used to treat active tuberculosis in pregnancy
Azithromycin used for chlamydial infection treatment

questions.explanation: The copper IUD is the most effective form of emergency contraception, with greater than 99% efficacy, and can be inserted up to 5 days (120 hours) after unprotected intercourse. It provides ongoing highly effective contraception after insertion. At 60 hours post-intercourse, levonorgestrel EC (effective within 72 hours) is still an option, but the copper IUD is superior in efficacy. Ulipristal acetate is effective up to 120 hours, but the copper IUD remains the gold standard for maximum effectiveness.
questions.question: A 24-year-old woman presents to the family planning clinic requesting emergency contraception 60 hours after unprotected sexual intercourse. The most effective option available is:
options: Ulipristal acetate 30 mg oral single dose exclusively within 48 hours
Progestin-only mini-pill taken twice daily for 3 days
Copper IUD insertion within 5 days of unprotected intercourse
Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg oral EC pill as a single dose
Combined oral contraceptive pills (Yuzpe method) for 2 days

questions.explanation: Petechiae confined to the face and upper chest following a rapid or precipitate delivery typically result from transient increased venous pressure during birth rather than an underlying bleeding disorder, and they usually fade spontaneously within a few days without specific treatment. Widespread petechiae involving other body areas, or petechiae accompanied by other signs of illness, would instead warrant further investigation for thrombocytopenia or infection. Reassuring the parents while observing for resolution is appropriate in this isolated presentation.
questions.question: Petechiae noted over the face and upper chest of a newborn following a precipitate delivery are most appropriately managed by:
options: Reassurance, since they typically resolve without treatment
Urgent screening for a bleeding disorder before discharge
Systemic corticosteroids to reduce capillary fragility
Immediate platelet transfusion to correct thrombocytopenia

questions.question: Normal amniotic fluid volume at term is approximately how much?
questions.explanation: Normal amniotic fluid volume at term is approximately 700-1000 mL (average ~800 mL), peaking at approximately 34 weeks (~1000 mL). Polyhydramnios is diagnosed when AFI exceeds 24 cm or a single deepest pocket exceeds 8 cm. Oligohydramnios is AFI less than 5 cm. Amniotic fluid is produced by fetal urine production and lung secretions, absorbed via fetal swallowing.
options: 200–400 mL — less than the normal average volume
400–600 mL — slightly below the normal average volume
700–1000 mL — within the normal range at term

questions.explanation: Uterine rupture through a previous LSCS scar classically presents as sudden cessation of uterine contractions, acute severe abdominal pain, loss of fetal station (presenting part recedes), profound fetal bradycardia, and signs of maternal haemorrhagic shock. Immediate emergency laparotomy is required. The risk in VBAC is approximately 0.5%, and continuous CTG monitoring throughout VBAC labour is mandatory.
options: Prolonged latent phase requiring oxytocin augmentation
Variable decelerations on CTG with intact membranes
Sudden cessation of contractions with fetal bradycardia and pain
Maternal tachycardia with mild uterine tenderness
questions.question: During VBAC labour, which sign most immediately suggests uterine scar rupture?

options: Ovulation occurs and the oocyte enters the tube
A spermatozoon penetrates the zona pellucida and oocyte membrane
Progesterone from the corpus luteum stimulates meiosis II
The LH surge triggers the final meiotic division
Capacitation is complete and sperm are hyperactivated
questions.explanation: The secondary oocyte released at ovulation is arrested at metaphase II. It only completes meiosis II (producing a mature ovum and a second polar body) after penetration by a spermatozoon triggers an increase in intracellular calcium. If fertilization does not occur, the oocyte degenerates without completing meiosis. The second polar body is a byproduct preserving cytoplasm in the ovum.
questions.question: The secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II completes meiosis II only when which event occurs?

options: Patency of the fallopian tubes and uterine cavity shape
Endometrial thickness during the luteal phase
Cervical mucus quality around ovulation time
Ovarian reserve through hormone level measurement
questions.explanation: A hysterosalpingogram involves injecting contrast medium through the cervix under fluoroscopy to outline the uterine cavity and demonstrate whether the fallopian tubes are patent, an important step in evaluating tubal factor infertility. It does not assess ovarian reserve, sperm parameters, or cervical mucus, which require separate specific tests. Findings guide decisions about surgical correction or referral for assisted reproduction.
questions.question: A couple undergoing infertility investigation is scheduled for a hysterosalpingogram. The primary purpose of this test is to assess:

questions.explanation: The window period is the interval following HIV exposure during which the virus is present but the body has not yet produced detectable antibody levels, potentially causing a false-negative antibody test result. Repeat testing after this period, or use of a fourth-generation combination antigen-antibody assay, improves detection reliability. Understanding this concept is essential for accurate counselling after a recent possible exposure.
options: The period during which viral load is undetectable
The time before detectable antibodies appear after exposure
The interval between two doses of antiretroviral therapy
The time needed for CD4 count to normalise
The duration antiretroviral prophylaxis remains effective
questions.question: A client recently diagnosed with HIV asks about the window period for antibody-based testing. The nurse should explain that this refers to:

options: Retinal haemorrhage from traumatic birth injury
Neonatal jaundice causing retinal bilirubin deposition
Congenital glaucoma from impaired aqueous drainage
Congenital cataract from intrauterine rubella infection
questions.question: Sun-setting sign of the eyes in a neonate with increasing head circumference is most indicative of:
questions.explanation: The sun-setting sign (setting sun sign) in a neonate refers to downward deviation of the eyes with sclera visible above the iris, caused by raised intracranial pressure compressing the mesencephalic tegmentum and producing paralysis of upward gaze. Combined with an inappropriately large or rapidly increasing occipitofrontal circumference, bulging fontanelle, splayed skull sutures, and irritability, it indicates hydrocephalus requiring urgent assessment and treatment.

options: The client's employer and immediate family members
Healthcare providers who previously examined the client
Recent sexual partners within the exposure window period
The client's entire community for public health awareness
All previous sexual contacts from the past five years
questions.question: A nurse conducting contact tracing for a client diagnosed with gonorrhoea should prioritise notifying:
questions.explanation: Contact tracing for gonorrhoea and other STIs focuses on notifying recent sexual partners within the relevant exposure window period, typically the past 60 days or the most recent partner if longer. This allows partners to be tested and treated to break the chain of transmission and prevent reinfection. The process should be conducted confidentially and sensitively.

Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome results from spread of infection, typically gonococcal or chlamydial, from the pelvis to the liver capsule, producing perihepatic adhesions and right upper quadrant pain that can mimic cholecystitis. It is a recognised extragenital complication of ascending pelvic inflammatory disease. Awareness of this presentation prevents misdiagnosis and ensures appropriate antibiotic management targeting the underlying pelvic infection.
questions.question: The Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, a recognised complication of PID, is characterised by:
options: Ovarian cyst formation with torsion risk
Perihepatic inflammation causing right upper quadrant pain
Bilateral tubal blockage without any pain symptoms

questions.explanation: Haemoglobin electrophoresis is the gold standard investigation to determine whether a client carries the sickle cell trait (HbAS), has sickle cell disease (HbSS), or other haemoglobin variants. This information is essential in family planning counselling to assess the risk of passing sickle cell disease to offspring, guide preconception advice, and identify contraceptive methods that are safe given the coagulation implications of sickle cell disease.
options: Peripheral blood film for abnormal red cell morphology
Haemoglobin electrophoresis to determine sickle cell trait or disease
Bone marrow biopsy to assess red cell precursor abnormalities
Serum iron and ferritin levels to assess iron storage
Full blood count with differential white cell count
questions.question: During a routine family planning consultation, a woman discloses a family history of sickle cell anaemia. The most appropriate investigation to guide her contraceptive counselling is:

questions.explanation: A boggy (soft, relaxed) uterus after delivery with heavy vaginal bleeding is the classic presentation of uterine atony - the most common cause of primary PPH, accounting for approximately 70-80% of PPH cases. Management includes bimanual uterine compression, uterotonics (oxytocin, ergometrine, misoprostol), balloon tamponade, B-Lynch suture, and hysterectomy if refractory.
options: Placenta accreta with abnormal trophoblast invasion
Cervical laceration presenting as ongoing slow haemorrhage
Uterine atony causing primary postpartum haemorrhage
Uterine inversion with the fundus descending into vagina
Retained placenta with clot formation in the uterus
questions.question: After delivery, a midwife finds the uterus is relaxed and boggy. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: The correct sequence in the referral process begins with stabilising the patient — administering medications, fluids, or oxygen as needed, controlling haemorrhage, managing seizures, and providing pain relief. Only after stabilisation should transport be arranged and communication established with the receiving facility. Notifying the referral centre in advance allows them to prepare for the patient's arrival and confirm capacity to manage the specific condition.
options: Arranging transport before stabilising the patient
Obtaining written consent before any emergency stabilisation
Stabilising the patient then communicating with the receiving facility
Notifying the family before contacting the referral centre
Documenting findings before administering any treatment
questions.question: The referral process for a high-risk pregnant woman should begin with which priority action?

questions.explanation: CA-125 is commonly used as a tumour marker in the assessment and monitoring of epithelial ovarian masses, though it lacks specificity as it can also be elevated in benign conditions such as endometriosis and fibroids. It is most useful when interpreted alongside imaging findings and clinical risk assessment tools. Other markers such as alpha-fetoprotein are more relevant to germ cell tumours rather than epithelial ovarian disease.
questions.question: A woman with a suspected ovarian mass is being investigated, and the nurse explains the role of a specific tumour marker used in monitoring epithelial ovarian conditions. Which marker is this?
options: CA-125, a non-specific marker used in ovarian monitoring
Alpha-fetoprotein, specific to germ cell tumours
Human chorionic gonadotrophin, specific to trophoblastic disease
Prostate-specific antigen, specific to male reproductive tissue
Carcinoembryonic antigen, specific to gastrointestinal malignancy
The entire brachial plexus without exception
The third and fourth cervical nerve roots
The first and second thoracic nerve roots
The fifth and sixth cervical nerve roots
The seventh and eighth cervical nerve roots
questions.explanation: Erb's palsy, the most common form of brachial plexus injury, results from traction damage to the upper brachial plexus roots at the fifth and sixth cervical levels, typically following shoulder dystocia or difficult delivery of the shoulders. This produces the characteristic 'waiter's tip' posture with the arm adducted, internally rotated, and the wrist flexed. Klumpke's palsy, in contrast, involves the lower nerve roots and presents with hand weakness rather than shoulder involvement.
questions.question: Erb's palsy results from injury to which cervical nerve roots during a difficult delivery?

options: From 16 weeks of gestation until delivery
From 12 weeks of gestation until 36–37 weeks
From 6 weeks of gestation, as early as possible
From 20 weeks of gestation until term
From 28 weeks of gestation in the third trimester
questions.explanation: Low-dose aspirin (75-150 mg nocte) is recommended from 12 weeks (ideally 11-14 weeks) of gestation until 36-37 weeks in women at high risk of pre-eclampsia. The mechanism involves inhibiting thromboxane A2 (platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction) while relatively sparing prostacyclin (vasodilation). Meta-analyses show it reduces the risk of pre-eclampsia by approximately 20% and preterm pre-eclampsia by up to 62% when started before 16 weeks.
questions.question: Low-dose aspirin (75–150 mg) is recommended from which gestational week to prevent pre-eclampsia in high-risk women?

options: It directly stimulates uterine smooth muscle contraction
It replaces clotting factors lost through bleeding
It constricts uterine blood vessels directly
It inhibits fibrinolysis, stabilising formed blood clots
It reduces uterine blood flow by vasoconstriction
questions.explanation: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic agent that inhibits the breakdown of fibrin clots, helping to stabilise clot formation at the bleeding site rather than acting on uterine muscle tone. It is used as an adjunct to uterotonics in the management of postpartum haemorrhage, and evidence supports its use when given early after bleeding begins. It does not replace the need for uterotonic therapy.
questions.question: A woman with ongoing postpartum haemorrhage is given tranexamic acid alongside uterotonics. What is the primary mechanism of action of this adjunct drug?

questions.explanation: Bimanual palpation allows the clinician to assess the size, shape, and position of the uterus as well as identify ovarian or adnexal masses that may affect contraceptive choice or indicate pathology. This examination is essential before inserting an IUD or selecting any intrauterine contraceptive device. The other assessments listed require different diagnostic techniques.
options: Depth and integrity of the vaginal fornices
Uterine size, position, and adnexal masses
questions.question: A bimanual pelvic examination in family planning is primarily used to evaluate which of the following?

questions.explanation: In a woman with antepartum haemorrhage and signs of hypovolaemic shock, the immediate nursing priority is to secure large-bore intravenous access and commence fluid resuscitation while summoning urgent obstetric and anaesthetic support. Vaginal examination is deferred until placenta praevia has been excluded by ultrasound, as it can provoke severe bleeding. Rapid restoration of circulating volume is essential to prevent maternal deterioration.
options: Perform a detailed vaginal examination immediately
Establish intravenous access and begin fluid resuscitation
Arrange non-urgent ultrasound before any treatment
Administer oral fluids to correct her hypovolaemia
Delay treatment until the bleeding source is confirmed
questions.question: A woman presents with antepartum haemorrhage and is found to be in hypovolaemic shock with tachycardia and hypotension. What is the immediate nursing priority?
A client asks about the difference between pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for HIV. The correct distinction is that PEP:
options: Consists of a single antiretroviral tablet only
Is started within seventy-two hours after a possible exposure
Is taken continuously before any anticipated exposure occurs
Provides lifelong immunity after one completed course
Is only appropriate for pregnant women specifically
questions.explanation: Post-exposure prophylaxis must be initiated as soon as possible and within seventy-two hours of a suspected HIV exposure, then continued as a twenty-eight-day antiretroviral course to reduce the likelihood of infection becoming established. PrEP, in contrast, is taken continuously by HIV-negative individuals at ongoing risk before exposure occurs. Neither approach confers lasting immunity beyond the treatment period.

questions.question: Which physical finding during a family planning consultation is an absolute contraindication to combined oral contraceptives?
options: Mild anaemia with haemoglobin of 10 g/dL
BMI of 27 kg/m2 with no complications
A uterus that is slightly anteverted on examination
A regular menstrual cycle of 28 days duration
questions.explanation: Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) containing oestrogen are contraindicated in hypertension because they further elevate blood pressure and increase the risk of cardiovascular events such as stroke and myocardial infarction. A blood pressure averaging 145/95 mmHg exceeds acceptable thresholds for COC use. The other findings listed do not constitute absolute contraindications to COC therapy.

Clients with a personal or family history of chromosomal or genetic disorders such as sickle cell anaemia, cystic fibrosis, or Klinefelter syndrome require referral to a genetic counsellor. Genetic counselling, karyotyping, and DNA analysis provide information on the risk of passing genetic conditions to offspring, enabling informed reproductive decisions and family planning.
options: A reproductive endocrinologist for IVF planning
A urologist for male infertility evaluation
An oncologist for cancer screening and staging
A genetic counsellor for karyotyping and DNA analysis
questions.question: For a client with a suspected chromosomal or genetic disorder seeking family planning advice, the most appropriate referral is to:

options: A general statement that she needs review
The names of all staff currently on duty
The referring facility's opening hours only
Gestational age, clinical findings, and reason for referral
Only the woman's name and home address
questions.question: A referral letter for a pregnant woman being transferred to a higher-level facility for suspected intrauterine growth restriction must, at minimum, include:
questions.explanation: A complete referral letter must include essential clinical information such as gestational age, relevant findings including fundal height and any Doppler or ultrasound results, and the specific reason prompting referral, to enable the receiving team to provide appropriate and timely care without delay. Omitting these details, or providing only administrative information, could compromise patient safety by delaying accurate assessment on arrival. Comprehensive documentation is a fundamental component of safe obstetric referral practice.

options: Painless bleeding at membrane rupture, fetal bradycardia, and fetal exsanguination
Painless bleeding, soft uterus, and maternal haemorrhagic shock
Postpartum bleeding with retained placental fragments
Antepartum haemorrhage with placenta covering the os
Painful bleeding, tender uterus, and fetal bradycardia
questions.question: Vasa praevia is a rare but catastrophic condition. Which combination of features is pathognomonic?
questions.explanation: Vasa praevia occurs when fetal blood vessels (from a velamentous cord insertion or succenturiate lobe) traverse the membranes over the internal os. When membranes rupture (SROM or AROM), these fetal vessels are torn, causing fetal haemorrhage (not maternal). The combination of painless bleeding at membrane rupture + sudden severe fetal bradycardia + sinusoidal FHR pattern indicates fetal exsanguination. Maternal haemoglobin is unaffected. Emergency caesarean section is required immediately.

options: Neonatal sepsis from Group B Streptococcus colonisation
Neonatal jaundice from tetanus-related red cell haemolysis
Congenital tetanus from transplacental toxin transmission
Respiratory distress syndrome from Clostridium perfringens toxins
Neonatal tetanus from contaminated cord care practices
questions.question: During antenatal care, routine tetanus toxoid immunisation is primarily aimed at preventing which condition in the newborn?
questions.explanation: Tetanus toxoid immunisation during pregnancy generates maternal antibodies that cross the placenta to protect the neonate against neonatal tetanus (tetanus neonatorum). Neonatal tetanus is caused by Clostridium tetani infecting the umbilical stump through unclean cord care practices during delivery. It remains a significant cause of neonatal mortality in low-resource settings. Adequate maternal immunisation combined with clean delivery and cord care is the most effective prevention strategy.

At the primary care level, high-risk pregnancies should be closely monitored while managing pre-existing conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, or anaemia with appropriate medications. Antenatal care visits should be more frequent, and the threshold for referral should be low when conditions deteriorate or exceed primary care management capacity. Stabilisation before referral is essential, and timely communication with the receiving facility ensures safe transfer and continuity of care.
questions.question: Which statement most accurately reflects the management of high-risk pregnancy at the primary care level before referral?
options: High-risk conditions should be monitored closely while managing pre-existing conditions
High-risk pregnancy should be immediately transferred to a tertiary hospital without stabilisation
Only obstetric emergencies require referral while stable conditions are managed locally
All high-risk conditions should be managed at primary care with extra monitoring
Primary care should initiate delivery before referring to higher-level facilities

questions.question: A woman with recurrent uterine prolapse asks which supporting ligament is most important in preventing descent of the uterus. Which structure is this?
options: Round ligament running through the inguinal canal
Ovarian ligament connecting the ovary to the uterus
Broad ligament draping over the pelvic organs
Transverse cervical (cardinal) ligament at the pelvic sidewall
Uterosacral ligament running toward the sacrum posteriorly
questions.explanation: The transverse cervical, or cardinal, ligaments extend from the cervix and lateral vaginal fornices to the pelvic sidewall and provide the main mechanical support preventing uterine descent. Weakness of these ligaments, often from childbirth trauma, is a major contributor to uterine prolapse. Uterosacral ligaments provide secondary posterior support.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the Pap smear in family planning consultations?
options: It screens for cervical dysplasia and cancer
It detects chromosomal abnormalities in cells
It confirms ovulation by detecting LH surge
questions.explanation: The Pap smear (cervical cytology) is a screening tool for cervical dysplasia and carcinoma, collecting cells from the transformation zone of the cervix for microscopic examination. In family planning, it is used to identify precancerous changes or cancers that may influence the choice of contraceptive method and necessitate referral for colposcopy or further investigation.

When a contraceptive patch has been detached for more than twenty-four hours, contraceptive protection cannot be assured, so a new patch should be applied promptly and additional barrier contraception used for seven days while hormone levels re-establish. Reapplying the same detached patch is unhygienic and unreliable since adhesion and hormone delivery may be compromised. Discarding the pack unnecessarily would not address the immediate risk of reduced protection.
options: Apply a new patch and use backup contraception for a week
Wait until the next scheduled change day only
Discard the entire pack and await her next period
Reapply the same detached patch immediately without concern
Continue the current cycle without any additional precaution
questions.question: A woman using the combined contraceptive patch reports it detached for more than 48 hours mid-cycle. The most appropriate advice is to:

options: Umbilical vein carrying oxygenated blood from the placenta
Descending aorta distributing blood to the lower body
Superior vena cava returning deoxygenated blood from the head
Umbilical arteries carrying blood from the fetal aorta
Pulmonary artery carrying blood from the right ventricle
questions.explanation: The umbilical vein carries oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus and has the highest oxygen saturation in the fetal circulation (approximately 80%). The two umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the fetal aorta to the placenta. After birth, the umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments, and the umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres.
questions.question: Which fetal vessel carries the highest oxygen saturation?
The complete blood count (CBC) is most relevant in family planning for clients considering which procedure?
options: Adoption of natural family planning methods
Use of barrier methods such as diaphragm
questions.explanation: Before sterilisation by tubal ligation, a complete blood count is required to assess overall health status, detect anaemia that could complicate surgical haemostasis, and ensure the client is fit for surgery. Blood grouping and cross-matching are also required in case of unexpected haemorrhage. Coagulation studies complement the CBC to ensure surgical safety.

options: Immediate surgical nerve grafting within the first week
High-dose systemic corticosteroids started at birth
Gentle passive range-of-motion exercises started after initial rest
Complete immobilisation of the limb for many months
Amputation of the affected limb if severe
questions.explanation: Most cases of neonatal brachial plexus palsy are managed conservatively, beginning with a brief period of rest to allow initial swelling to settle, followed by gentle passive range-of-motion exercises to prevent joint contractures while awaiting spontaneous nerve recovery. Surgery is reserved for cases showing no recovery after a period of observation, typically several months. Corticosteroids and amputation have no established role in this condition.
questions.question: The recommended initial management approach for a neonate diagnosed with brachial plexus palsy is:

options: Controlling the spread of infection and compiling epidemiological statistics
Immediate transfer of all pyrexial postnatal women to teaching hospitals
Routine prophylactic antibiotic administration to all postnatal women
Legal prosecution of birth attendants associated with infected deliveries
Mandatory quarantine of all postnatal women with fever above 37.5°C
questions.explanation: Puerperal pyrexia is a notifiable condition in both developed and developing countries, including Nigeria. Notification serves two essential public health purposes: to facilitate control of the spread of infection (particularly in cases of infectious puerperal sepsis that may affect others) and to compile epidemiological statistics that inform national maternal morbidity reporting, policy development, and resource allocation for maternal health services.
questions.question: The national policy in Nigeria regarding puerperal pyrexia describes it as a notifiable condition primarily to enable:
Which laboratory investigation specifically evaluates ovarian reserve in a woman being investigated for infertility?
questions.explanation: Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) is produced by granulosa cells of preantral and antral follicles and is the most accurate biochemical marker of ovarian reserve. A low AMH level indicates diminished ovarian reserve and reduced fertility potential, guiding decisions about urgency of fertility treatment and stimulation protocols. AMH is relatively stable throughout the menstrual cycle, making it convenient to measure at any time. It is increasingly used in infertility evaluation before referral.
options: Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) reflecting the remaining primordial follicle pool
Mid-luteal serum progesterone confirming ovulation in the current cycle
Basal serum LH to assess hypothalamic-pituitary function on day 2
Cervical mucus assessment at mid-cycle for sperm penetration capacity
Serum oestradiol level throughout the follicular phase of the cycle

questions.question: The most common cause of secondary postpartum haemorrhage is:
options: Uterine inversion following mismanagement of the third stage
Trauma to the cervix during precipitate labour and delivery
Coagulation disorder developing after the third stage of labour
Subinvolution of the uterus due to infection or retained products
Atonic uterus from prolonged oxytocin infusion during labour
questions.explanation: Subinvolution is the most common cause of secondary postpartum haemorrhage, which occurs after 24 hours up to 12 weeks following delivery. Subinvolution is most often caused by infection related to retained placental fragments or membranes, which prevent the normal physiological shrinkage of the uterus. Multiparity, prolonged labour, and premature delivery are additional contributing factors.

options: Failure of the uterus to descend into the pelvis after delivery
Prolapse of the uterus into the vaginal canal postpartum
Displacement of the uterus due to a full bladder after delivery
Inability of the uterus to return to its normal size after birth
Abnormal contraction of the uterus causing retained placenta
questions.explanation: Subinvolution is defined as the inability of the uterus to return to its normal non-pregnant size and state following delivery of the baby. In subinvolution, the uterine height is greater than expected for the particular postnatal day. It is the most common cause of secondary postpartum haemorrhage and is more common in multiparous women, tending to recur in subsequent pregnancies.
questions.question: Subinvolution of the uterus is best defined as:

questions.explanation: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic drug that competitively inhibits the activation of plasminogen to plasmin, thereby preventing the breakdown of fibrin clots. In PPH, it reduces blood loss and mortality when given within 3 hours of delivery. The WHO recommends tranexamic acid 1 g IV as an adjunct to uterotonics in PPH management. It does not cause uterine contraction - that is the role of oxytocin and ergometrine.
options: It replaces clotting factors lost in haemorrhage
It constricts uterine arteries reducing arterial blood flow
It inhibits fibrinolysis by blocking plasminogen activation
It stimulates uterine smooth muscle contraction
It promotes platelet aggregation at the uterine sinusoids
questions.question: Tranexamic acid is used in the management of PPH. What is its mechanism of action?
A woman with hyperemesis gravidarum is distinguished from a woman with simple morning sickness during assessment. Which combination of criteria supports this specific diagnosis?
options: Occasional nausea without vomiting throughout the day
Mild nausea resolving spontaneously by early afternoon
Vomiting only after eating specific trigger foods
Nausea limited strictly to the first six weeks
Persistent vomiting causing weight loss, dehydration, and ketonuria
questions.explanation: Hyperemesis gravidarum is distinguished from simple morning sickness by persistent, severe vomiting leading to significant weight loss, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and ketonuria, often requiring hospital admission for intravenous fluid and antiemetic therapy. Simple morning sickness, while uncomfortable, does not typically cause these severe metabolic consequences. Recognising these distinguishing features ensures timely, appropriate treatment for the more severe condition.

questions.question: HELLP syndrome stands for which combination of laboratory findings?
questions.explanation: HELLP syndrome stands for Haemolysis (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia - elevated LDH, abnormal blood film), Elevated Liver enzymes (raised ALT/AST due to hepatic ischaemia and periportal necrosis), and Low Platelets (thrombocytopaenia <100 × 10?/L). It is a severe variant of pre-eclampsia, complicating 0.5-0.9% of all pregnancies. Management includes delivery, magnesium sulphate, and blood product replacement.
options: Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets
Hypertension, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets

questions.question: Which investigation is routinely performed at the first antenatal (booking) visit for all pregnant women in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: At the booking visit, routine investigations include: ABO blood group and Rhesus factor; haemoglobin (Hb) for anaemia; VDRL or RPR for syphilis (a cause of congenital infection); HIV screening (with pre-test counselling); hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg); urinalysis for protein and glucose; and malaria parasite testing in endemic areas. These investigations follow the NMCN and Nigerian National Guidelines for Antenatal Care and are essential for identifying risks that can be addressed to improve maternal and neonatal outcomes.
options: Glucose tolerance test, full blood count, and biophysical profile
Urine culture, vaginal swab for GBS, and thyroid function tests
Cervical smear, serum folate, and hepatitis B surface antigen
Blood group, Rhesus factor, haemoglobin, VDRL/RPR, and HIV screening
Urea and electrolytes, LFTs, and thrombophilia screen
Diagnostic laparoscopy with histological biopsy confirmation
Hysteroscopy identifying endometrial lesions in the cavity
CA-125 serum level elevated in endometriosis
MRI pelvis showing deep infiltrating endometriosis
questions.question: Which investigation is considered the gold standard for diagnosing endometriosis?
questions.explanation: Diagnostic laparoscopy with direct visualisation of lesions (bluish-black "powder burn" or "gunshot" lesions, white fibrotic nodules, red implants) and histological biopsy confirming endometrial-like glands and stroma is the gold standard for diagnosing endometriosis. Transvaginal ultrasound can identify endometriomas and deep infiltrating endometriosis but cannot diagnose peritoneal disease. MRI is used for mapping deep infiltrating endometriosis. A clinical diagnosis may be made in typical presentations.

The true conjugate (conjugate vera) is measured from the sacral promontory to the upper inner border of the pubic symphysis, measuring approximately 11 cm. The obstetric conjugate (approximately 10.5 cm) is from the promontory to the nearest symphysis point. The diagonal conjugate (approximately 12.5 cm) is the clinically measurable one from which 1.5 cm is subtracted to estimate the true conjugate.
options: 10 cm from sacral promontory to upper symphysis surface
9 cm — the obstetric conjugate used clinically
12 cm from sacral promontory to outer symphysis surface
13 cm — the widest transverse pelvic brim diameter
11 cm from sacral promontory to inner symphysis border
questions.question: The anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic inlet known as the conjugate vera measures approximately how much?

questions.explanation: The standard recommendation for low-risk women is folic acid 0.4 mg (400 mcg) daily, started at least 4 weeks (ideally 3 months) before conception and continued through the first 12 weeks of pregnancy (the period of neural tube closure). High-risk women (previous NTD pregnancy, epilepsy on anticonvulsants, BMI >30, diabetes, malabsorption) require 5 mg daily. Folic acid is a B vitamin essential for DNA synthesis and cell division during rapid embryogenesis.
options: 0.1 mg (100 mcg) daily from conception onwards
1 mg daily from the time of positive pregnancy test
0.4 mg (400 mcg) daily from at least 4 weeks before conception
5 mg daily for all women regardless of risk status
2.5 mg daily throughout the entire pregnancy
questions.question: Folic acid supplementation is recommended periconceptionally to prevent neural tube defects. What is the standard dose for low-risk women?
A woman at high risk of pre-eclampsia is counselled on prophylactic low-dose aspirin. From which gestational week is this typically recommended to begin?
questions.explanation: Low-dose aspirin, typically 75 to 150 mg daily, is recommended from around twelve weeks gestation in women at high risk of pre-eclampsia, as it helps reduce placental vascular resistance and lowers the incidence of the condition. Starting later in pregnancy significantly reduces its preventive benefit. This is now a standard component of antenatal risk reduction in high-risk women.
options: Only after a diagnosis of pre-eclampsia is made
From the first day of the last menstrual period

questions.question: Which of the following best defines the role of family planning clinics in the referral process for PID patients?
questions.explanation: Family planning clinics play an important role in the PID referral process through three key functions: early identification of severe or complicated cases during initial assessment, establishing clear referral pathways with partnerships with higher-level healthcare facilities for seamless transfer, and monitoring referred clients after treatment to ensure recovery and address ongoing family planning needs. Definitive surgical management is beyond their scope and requires specialist referral.
options: Performing laparoscopy to assess the extent of tubal damage
Providing definitive inpatient antibiotic therapy independently
Providing long-term psychological counselling for infertile couples
Early identification, clear referral pathways, and post-treatment follow-up
Independently managing all complications including abscess drainage

questions.question: Which type of cells lines the endometrium and forms its glandular structure?
questions.explanation: The endometrium is lined by simple columnar epithelium with underlying uterine glands opening into the uterine cavity, supported by a vascular stroma. The functional layer (stratum functionalis) with its glands and spiral arteries is shed at menstruation. The basal layer (stratum basalis) remains to regenerate the functional layer in the next cycle.
options: Simple columnar epithelium with underlying uterine glands
Stratified cuboidal epithelium located in the basal zone
Pseudostratified ciliated epithelium with interspersed goblet cells
Transitional epithelium capable of significant stretching
Squamous epithelial cells forming stratified protective layers

questions.explanation: In a gynecoid pelvis, the subpubic arch is 90 degrees or more (typically 90-100°). A wide subpubic arch allows the fetal head to use the full width of the pelvic outlet and emerge under the symphysis pubis.
