In the android pelvis, the narrow arch (less than 70-80°) forces the head away from the arch, reducing the effective outlet diameter and increasing perineal trauma risk.
questions.question: The subpubic angle in a gynecoid pelvis is typically how wide?
options: 90 degrees or more — the wide gynecoid arch
Less than 70 degrees — a narrow acute angle
More than 120 degrees — typical of platypelloid pelvis
70–80 degrees — characteristic of the android pelvis
Permanently eliminate the latent virus from the body
Replace the need for safer sexual practices entirely
Prevent all future pregnancies from being affected
Cure any active outbreak within twenty-four hours
Reduce the frequency of symptomatic recurrent outbreaks
questions.explanation: Suppressive antiviral therapy, typically with daily acyclovir or valacyclovir, reduces the frequency and severity of recurrent herpes outbreaks and lowers the risk of viral shedding and transmission to partners, but it does not eradicate the latent virus residing in nerve ganglia. Safer sexual practices remain important even with suppressive treatment. This distinction should be clearly communicated during client counselling.
questions.question: A client with recurrent genital herpes outbreaks asks about suppressive therapy. The nurse should explain that long-term suppressive antiviral therapy is used primarily to:
Iatrogenic skin injury in newborns most commonly results from:
questions.explanation: Iatrogenic skin injuries in newborns result from obstetric instruments used during delivery. Forceps blades can cause bruising or superficial fat necrosis, vacuum extractor cups can cause scalp abrasions, scalp electrodes cause puncture wounds, and scalpels during caesarean section can occasionally lacerate the baby's skin. These injuries are primarily detected on physical examination immediately after birth.
options: Maternal systemic infection transmitting through the placenta
Forceps blades, vacuum extractor cups, scalp electrodes, and scalpels
Immune-mediated destruction of skin cells after neonatal transfusion
Neonatal dermatitis from contact with vernix caseosa after delivery

questions.explanation: Pre-eclampsia is defined as new-onset hypertension developing after twenty weeks gestation in a previously normotensive woman, accompanied by proteinuria or evidence of other maternal organ dysfunction such as renal or liver impairment. This distinguishes it from chronic hypertension, which predates pregnancy or the twenty-week threshold. Accurate definition guides correct diagnosis and subsequent management planning.
questions.question: A woman diagnosed with pre-eclampsia asks how this condition is defined in relation to her blood pressure and gestational age. What is the standard definition?
options: Hypertension present before conception in any woman
Elevated blood pressure only during the first trimester
New hypertension after twenty weeks with proteinuria or organ dysfunction
Hypertension diagnosed exclusively in the postpartum period
Any blood pressure reading above the non-pregnant baseline

questions.question: Which of the following is the most accurate indication for prolactin level measurement in a family planning setting?
questions.explanation: Elevated prolactin levels (hyperprolactinaemia) can cause irregular or absent menstrual cycles, galactorrhoea, and infertility. Measuring serum prolactin is indicated when these symptoms are present, as hyperprolactinaemia may indicate a pituitary adenoma or hypothyroidism. Identifying this condition affects contraceptive choice and may require treatment before effective family planning can be achieved.
options: Client requests emergency contraception after unprotected sex
Client uses barrier methods and wants STI screening
Client is a primigravida requesting postpartum contraception
Client has irregular cycles and galactorrhoea

questions.question: The platypelloid (flat) pelvis is characterised by which combination of diameters?
questions.explanation: The platypelloid (flat) pelvis has a wide transverse diameter but a significantly reduced anteroposterior diameter, giving a kidney-shaped or oval inlet. This shape forces the fetal head to engage in the transverse position and does not permit spontaneous rotation. It is the rarest pelvic type and may result from rickets (nutritional deficiency) causing the sacrum to fall forward.
options: Heart-shaped inlet with convergent sidewalls and deep sacrum
Equal transverse and AP diameters producing a round inlet
Long AP diameter with a narrow transverse diameter
Wide transverse diameter with a significantly reduced AP diameter
Narrow transverse with a very prominent sacral promontory

questions.question: During antenatal care, which investigation is performed routinely at the 28-week visit for all Rh-negative women?
questions.explanation: At 28 weeks, all Rh-negative unsensitised women should receive: (1) routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis (500 IU IM or 1500 IU depending on local guidelines); and (2) an indirect Coombs test (antibody screen/MSAFP/red cell alloantibody screen) to ensure the woman has not already become sensitised. If alloantibodies are detected, anti-D will not help and specialist monitoring for haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN) is initiated. Both are essential components of the 28-week antenatal visit.
options: Indirect Coombs test (antibody screen) for alloimmunisation
Both anti-D administration and indirect Coombs test
Complete blood count and serum ferritin assessment

questions.question: The transverse diameter of the pelvic outlet is measured between which bony points?
options: Between the sacral promontory and the pubic crest
Between the inner surfaces of the ischial tuberosities
Between the two anterior superior iliac spines
Between the ischial spines (the interspinous diameter)
Between the two iliopectineal eminences of the brim
questions.explanation: The transverse diameter of the pelvic outlet is the intertuberous diameter, measured between the inner surfaces of the ischial tuberosities, approximately 11 cm. It is clinically estimated by placing a closed fist between the tuberosities; if a standard fist (approximately 8 cm) fits, the outlet is adequate. A value less than 8 cm is considered contracted.

At term, placental intervillous blood flow is approximately 500-800 mL per minute. This massive flow through the placenta is why uterine atony (failure of the uterus to contract after delivery) leads to catastrophic haemorrhage so rapidly - the open uterine sinusoids bleed at the full intervillous flow rate until the uterus contracts (the "living ligature" mechanism). This explains why uterotonics and uterine massage must be prompt.
questions.question: Blood flow through the placental intervillous space at term is approximately how much per minute?
options: 250–350 mL per minute through the intervillous space
1000–1200 mL per minute at maximum flow
100–200 mL per minute at normal uteroplacental flow
50–100 mL per minute in a resting non-labouring state
500–800 mL per minute through the intervillous space

questions.question: Syndactyly that is part of Apert's syndrome is associated with which additional features?
questions.explanation: Apert's syndrome is a congenital condition in which syndactyly (fusion of fingers and toes) occurs as part of a broader syndrome that includes premature fusion of the cranial sutures (craniosynostosis), cleft palate, and complete syndactyly of both hands and feet. The premature suture fusion can restrict brain growth and must be addressed surgically. Apert's syndrome demonstrates how syndactyly can be part of a larger malformation syndrome.
options: Clubfoot deformity requiring immediate orthopaedic correction
Extra digits on the hands and feet in an autosomal dominant pattern
Premature skull suture fusion, cleft palate, and complete hand and foot syndactyly
Short limbs with large head and marked lumbar lordosis
Hip dysplasia with absent femoral head and acetabular deformity

questions.explanation: Well-established risk factors for pre-eclampsia include: nulliparity (3× risk); previous pre-eclampsia; multiple pregnancy; obesity (BMI >35); advanced maternal age (>40); pre-existing hypertension; diabetes (pre-gestational); renal disease; antiphospholipid syndrome; and family history of pre-eclampsia. Low-dose aspirin (150 mg nocte) from 12 weeks reduces the risk by approximately 20% in high-risk women.
options: Nulliparity, low folate intake, anaemia, and urinary tract infection
Multiparity, BMI <18.5, thrombophilia, and male fetus
Nulliparity, BMI >35, age >40, multiple pregnancy, and previous pre-eclampsia
Multiparity, diabetes without hypertension, and iron deficiency
Multiparity, young maternal age, low BMI, and smoking
questions.question: Risk factors specifically associated with the development of pre-eclampsia include which combination?
The corpus luteum of pregnancy is maintained beyond its usual 14-day lifespan by which hormone?
questions.explanation: Human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG), secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast from about day 8 post-fertilization, rescues the corpus luteum from degeneration by its LH-like action on luteal cells. The corpus luteum then continues secreting progesterone to maintain the decidua until the placenta takes over at 8-10 weeks - the luteoplacental shift.
options: Progesterone secreted by the corpus luteum itself
Human chorionic gonadotrophin secreted by the trophoblast
Follicle-stimulating hormone secreted by the anterior pituitary
Oestradiol produced by the dominant developing follicle
Luteinising hormone released during the preovulatory LH surge

questions.question: The cortical reaction occurs immediately after one sperm penetrates the oocyte. What is its primary purpose?
questions.explanation: The cortical reaction involves exocytosis of cortical granules from the oocyte, releasing enzymes that modify the zona pellucida (zona reaction), making it impenetrable to additional sperm. This is the primary block to polyspermy. A secondary fast block involves membrane depolarisation. Together these ensure only one sperm contributes genetic material, maintaining the correct diploid chromosome number.
options: Hardening the zona pellucida to prevent additional sperm entry
Promoting implantation of the blastocyst in the endometrium
Stimulating the secondary oocyte to complete meiosis I
Initiating capacitation of the remaining spermatozoa in the tube
Triggering the release of hCG from the newly formed blastocyst

questions.question: In vertex presentation, the position described as LOA means the occiput is directed where?
questions.explanation: LOA stands for Left Occipito-Anterior, meaning the occiput (denominator in vertex presentation) is directed toward the left anterior quadrant of the maternal pelvis. LOA is the most common and favourable position for delivery, allowing the head to rotate anteriorly to direct OA for delivery. Other presentation denominators: face (mentum), brow (sinciput), breech (sacrum).
options: Left Oblique Axis — direction of the sagittal suture
Left Occipital-Angle — position of the head at the pelvic brim
Lower Occipito-Anterior — position in the mid-pelvic cavity
Left Occipito-Anterior — occiput directed to the left-anterior quadrant
Left Occiput-Apex — relationship of vertex to the pelvis

questions.explanation: Relaxin, produced by the corpus luteum and later the placenta, softens and relaxes pelvic ligaments and the pubic symphysis, increasing pelvic joint mobility. This allows slight widening of pelvic dimensions during labour. The pubic symphysis normally widens by 2-3 mm in pregnancy (normal non-pregnant gap 4-5 mm). Excessive relaxation causes symphysis pubis dysfunction (SPD).
options: Causes hypertrophy of the obturator internus muscle
Softens and relaxes pelvic ligaments and symphyseal cartilage
Constricts the sacroiliac joints to stabilise the pelvis
Increases bone density to support the growing gravid uterus
Stimulates calcium deposition into the pubic symphysis
questions.question: Relaxin is a hormone that prepares the pelvis for childbirth. What is its primary action on pelvic structures?

questions.explanation: A personal history of venous thromboembolism is an absolute contraindication to combined hormonal contraceptives, as the oestrogen component further increases clotting risk in women already predisposed to thrombosis. Progestogen-only methods are generally considered safer alternatives in this context. Thorough risk assessment before prescribing hormonal contraception helps prevent recurrent thrombotic events.
questions.question: A woman using combined oral contraceptives has a strong personal history of deep vein thrombosis. Which pregnancy-related condition would also make oestrogen-containing contraception absolutely contraindicated?
options: A previous uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery
A personal history of any venous thromboembolism
A previous pregnancy affected by mild anaemia
A previous pregnancy with mild nausea and vomiting
A family history of migraine without aura

questions.explanation: As the blood in a cephalhaematoma is absorbed, haemolysis of the extravasated red blood cells releases haem, which is converted to bilirubin. This can cause hyperbilirubinaemia (jaundice) in the affected neonate, potentially requiring phototherapy. The primary nursing intervention is to monitor serum bilirubin levels closely during the period of cephalhaematoma resolution and initiate phototherapy if bilirubin rises to treatment threshold levels. Surgical drainage is not indicated for cephalhaematoma management.
options: Restricting fluids to prevent bilirubin excretion into the kidneys
Administering intravenous immunoglobulin to suppress haemolysis
Phototherapy prophylactically immediately after birth for all affected neonates
Monitoring serum bilirubin levels as the cephalhaematoma reabsorbs
Surgically draining the cephalhaematoma to prevent haemolysis
questions.question: The primary nursing intervention for preventing neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia related to a cephalhaematoma is:
The treatment of cracked nipples in a breastfeeding mother includes resting the affected breast for:
questions.explanation: A cracked nipple is a serious condition predisposing to breast infection. The baby should be taken off the affected breast for 48 to 72 hours to rest the nipple and promote healing of the fissure. During this period, the breast is manually expressed — not with a breast pump — to maintain milk supply and relieve engorgement. The condition predisposes to mastitis and must be managed promptly.
options: 7 days with complete cessation of breastfeeding
Until the infant is weaned from breastfeeding entirely
12 to 24 hours while expressing milk manually
6 to 12 hours and then resuming breastfeeding normally
48 to 72 hours to promote healing of the fissure

questions.question: Fetal station during labour is measured in relation to which landmark?
options: The pelvic outlet, where delivery will finally occur
The pelvic inlet (brim), where engagement begins
The ischial spines, which define zero station
The sacral promontory at the posterior inlet
The interspinous diameter as the narrowest pelvic level
questions.explanation: Fetal station is measured in centimetres above or below the ischial spines (station 0). Negative stations (-1 to -5) indicate the presenting part above the spines; positive stations (+1 to +5) indicate descent below. The presenting part is considered engaged at station 0 or when the widest diameter has passed through the inlet. This guides labour management decisions and assessment of progress.

options: Mastitis, an infection localised to the breast tissue
Urinary tract infection, unrelated to the uterus itself
Deep vein thrombosis, presenting with leg swelling
Puerperal sepsis, an infection of the reproductive tract
Postpartum psychosis, presenting with behavioural changes
questions.question: A midwife caring for a postpartum woman identifies fever, offensive lochia, and uterine tenderness as key features of a specific postpartum complication. Which condition does this triad describe?
questions.explanation: Puerperal sepsis is characterised by fever of at least 38 degrees Celsius, offensive or purulent lochia, and uterine tenderness, reflecting infection of the reproductive tract following childbirth, most commonly caused by ascending bacterial infection. Prompt recognition and treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics are essential to prevent progression to severe sepsis or septic shock. This condition remains an important cause of maternal morbidity and mortality globally.

options: Direct destruction of ovarian follicular reserve alone
Pelvic adhesions and distorted tubo-ovarian anatomy
Complete obstruction of the cervical canal alone
Autoimmune destruction of sperm within the uterus
questions.question: A woman with endometriosis is being counselled on how this condition can contribute to infertility. Through which mechanisms does endometriosis primarily impair fertility?
questions.explanation: Endometriosis causes infertility primarily through pelvic inflammation, adhesion formation, and distortion of normal tubo-ovarian anatomy, which impair oocyte release, tubal transport, and fertilisation. Endometriomas can also directly reduce ovarian reserve. Management of infertility in endometriosis may involve surgical treatment of adhesions or assisted reproduction depending on severity.

questions.question: Antepartum haemorrhage (APH) is defined as bleeding from the genital tract after which gestational age?
options: 22 weeks, the threshold of fetal viability
24 weeks, when the fetus is considered potentially viable
28 weeks, in the third trimester of pregnancy
20 weeks, before which all bleeding is considered miscarriage
32 weeks, when major complications are more common
questions.explanation: APH is defined as bleeding from the genital tract after 24 weeks of gestation and before the onset of labour. It complicates approximately 3-5% of pregnancies. Bleeding before 24 weeks is classified as a threatened, inevitable, or incomplete miscarriage depending on the clinical context. Accurate classification guides triage, investigation, and management.

questions.question: The normal umbilical cord contains how many blood vessels?
options: One vein and two arteries (three vessels total)
One vein and one artery (two vessels total)
Two veins and one artery (three vessels total)
Two veins and two arteries (four vessels total)
One vein only (the single umbilical vessel)
questions.explanation: The normal umbilical cord contains three blood vessels: one umbilical vein (carrying oxygenated blood from placenta to fetus) and two umbilical arteries (carrying deoxygenated blood from fetus to placenta). They are embedded in Wharton's jelly covered by amniotic membrane. A two-vessel cord (single umbilical artery) is associated with congenital anomalies and growth restriction.

questions.question: Chronic hypertension in pregnancy is defined as hypertension that:
options: Only develops in the third trimester with no prior history
Occurs exclusively in nulliparous women over 40 years
Develops after 20 weeks and resolves postpartum
Is present before pregnancy or diagnosed before 20 weeks
Is caused solely by pre-existing renal disease
questions.explanation: Chronic (pre-existing) hypertension is defined as hypertension present before pregnancy or diagnosed before 20 weeks of gestation, and typically persists beyond 6 weeks postpartum. It must be distinguished from pre-eclampsia (which develops after 20 weeks in previously normotensive women). Women with chronic hypertension are at increased risk of developing superimposed pre-eclampsia, which carries a significantly worse prognosis than either condition alone.

questions.question: Eclampsia is defined as the occurrence of which event in a woman with pre-eclampsia?
options: Renal failure with oliguria less than 30 mL per hour
Proteinuria greater than 5 grams in a 24-hour collection
Convulsions (tonic-clonic seizures) not attributed to other causes
HELLP syndrome with haemolysis and elevated enzymes
Severe hypertension with diastolic BP above 110 mmHg
questions.explanation: Eclampsia is defined as the occurrence of one or more convulsions (tonic-clonic seizures) in a woman with pre-eclampsia, not attributable to other neurological causes. Convulsions may occur antepartum (50%), intrapartum (25%), or postpartum (25%, most within 48 hours). It is a life-threatening emergency. Magnesium sulphate is the drug of choice for both treating eclamptic seizures and preventing recurrence. It is also the drug for prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia.

options: Eliminating the need for postnatal newborn checks
Guaranteeing a completely uncomplicated labour outcome
Replacing the need for any skilled birth attendance
Substituting for proper nutrition throughout pregnancy
Protecting both mother and baby from specific preventable infections
questions.question: The purpose of routine immunisation given during antenatal care, according to standard maternal health education, is best summarised as:
questions.explanation: Antenatal immunisation, most notably tetanus toxoid, is intended to protect both the mother and her newborn from specific vaccine-preventable infections that could otherwise cause serious morbidity or mortality around the time of birth. It does not replace the need for skilled birth attendance, postnatal assessment, or adequate maternal nutrition, all of which remain essential components of comprehensive antenatal and perinatal care. Health education should present immunisation as one part of a broader package of care.

options: S2, S3, S4 — sacral plexus nerve roots
T10, T11, T12 — lower thoracic intercostal nerves
L1, L2, L3 — contributions from the lumbar plexus
S1, S2, S3 — only the upper sacral roots
L4, L5, S1 — fibres from the lumbosacral trunk
questions.question: The pudendal nerve, which supplies the perineum, arises from which nerve roots?
questions.explanation: The pudendal nerve arises from the sacral plexus, derived from ventral rami of S2, S3, and S4. It exits through the greater sciatic foramen, winds around the ischial spine, and re-enters via the lesser sciatic foramen into Alcock's canal. It innervates the external genitalia, external urethral sphincter, and external anal sphincter. The ischial spine is the landmark for pudendal nerve block.

questions.question: A pregnant woman is diagnosed with genital chlamydia at 32 weeks gestation. Doxycycline is avoided in her treatment primarily because it:
questions.explanation: Doxycycline, a tetracycline-class antibiotic, is contraindicated in pregnancy because it binds to calcium in developing bone and teeth, causing permanent discolouration and potential effects on skeletal growth in the fetus. Azithromycin is therefore preferred for treating chlamydia during pregnancy. This teratogenic risk is specific to tetracyclines and does not apply to macrolide antibiotics.
options: Requires refrigeration unavailable in most clinics
Cannot be absorbed adequately in pregnancy
Increases the risk of neonatal conjunctivitis
Is completely ineffective against Chlamydia trachomatis
Can cause discolouration of the fetal teeth and bones

questions.question: The most common pathogens responsible for causing late-onset neonatal sepsis in the NICU environment are:
options: Chlamydia trachomatis from maternal genital tract colonisation at delivery
Rubella virus and cytomegalovirus from peripartum maternal viraemia
Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Treponema pallidum from maternal STIs
Coagulase-negative Staphylococci and Gram-negative hospital organisms
Group B Streptococcus acquired during passage through the birth canal
questions.explanation: Late-onset neonatal sepsis in the NICU is predominantly caused by hospital-acquired (nosocomial) organisms. Coagulase-negative Staphylococci (particularly Staphylococcus epidermidis) are the most common pathogens associated with central venous catheters and parenteral nutrition. Gram-negative organisms including Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Escherichia coli are also common nosocomial pathogens in the NICU, particularly in ventilated infants.

HPV co-testing (combining Pap smear with HPV test) achieves a sensitivity of over 90% for detecting high-grade cervical lesions, compared to approximately 70% for Pap smear alone. This significantly improved sensitivity is the rationale for extending the screening interval to every five years in women aged 30 to 65 who receive co-testing with normal results. A negative HPV test with a normal Pap smear provides high reassurance against cervical pathology.
questions.question: The sensitivity of HPV co-testing (Pap smear combined with HPV test) for detecting high-grade cervical lesions is approximately:
options: 60%, slightly better than visual inspection with acetic acid
70%, which is the same as Pap smear sensitivity alone
50%, similar to Pap smear alone in clinical practice
Over 90%, significantly higher than Pap smear alone
100%, eliminating the need for any further diagnostic workup

questions.question: The prognosis of puerperal psychosis in tropical countries compared to temperate climates is:
questions.explanation: The prognosis of puerperal psychosis is generally very good, with high rates of complete recovery. The prognosis is reported to be even better in tropical countries, where recovery rates exceed the 75 to 80 percent reported in temperate countries. Early diagnosis, prompt psychiatric intervention, antibiotic treatment where infection is the aetiology, and adequate nursing care contribute to favourable outcomes.
options: Variable based entirely on the severity of the initial presentation
Better in the tropics, with higher complete recovery rates reported
The same, with 75 to 80 percent recovering completely in both
Consistently poor regardless of geographical location globally
Significantly worse due to limited psychiatric services available

questions.explanation: The posterior fornix of the vagina is closely related to the pouch of Douglas (rectouterine pouch). This anatomical relationship is clinically significant because blood, pus, or fluid in the pouch of Douglas can be drained via posterior colpotomy through the posterior vaginal wall. The rectum lies behind, separated by the pouch of peritoneum.
questions.question: Which structure marks the posterior relation of the vagina at its upper third?
options: Pouch of Douglas (rectouterine pouch of peritoneum)
Urinary bladder resting directly on the anterior vaginal wall
Urethra lying immediately in front below the bladder
Perineal body forming the posterior inferior vaginal support
Anal canal inferior and posterior to the vaginal fornix

questions.question: The action line on the WHO partograph triggers intervention when labour progress:
options: Shows decelerations on continuous CTG monitoring
Falls behind the alert line by 2 cm in 1 hour
Lags 4 hours behind the alert line of the partograph
Drops to below 2 cm dilatation per hour for primigravidae
Reaches 4 cm dilatation in active labour
questions.explanation: The WHO partograph has an alert line (expected progress of 1 cm/hour from 4 cm onwards) and an action line positioned 4 hours to the right. If labour progress crosses the action line (cervical dilatation is 4 hours behind the expected rate), it triggers the need for medical review and consideration of obstetric intervention - augmentation, operative delivery, or caesarean section.

2% for cleft lip with or without cleft palate

9% for cleft lip with or without cleft palate
questions.question: In genetic counselling for cleft palate, the recurrence risk when one parent and one sibling are already affected is approximately:
questions.explanation: Non-syndromic cleft lip and palate has multifactorial inheritance. For isolated cleft palate, when one parent and one sibling are already affected, the recurrence risk rises to approximately 17%. For cleft lip with or without cleft palate: one parent gives 2%, one sibling gives 4%, two siblings gives 9%, and one parent plus one sibling gives 15%. These figures demonstrate the additive nature of risk with multiple affected family members.

Pelvic ultrasound before IUD insertion assesses uterine anatomy to identify conditions that may prevent safe or effective IUD placement. These include uterine fibroids that distort the uterine cavity, congenital uterine anomalies (e.g., bicornuate uterus, septate uterus), uterine polyps, or significant variations in uterine size. Identifying these abnormalities allows the clinician to modify the insertion technique, select an appropriate IUD size, or refer for specialist insertion under ultrasound guidance.

Measure endometrial thickness to guide selection of IUD type

questions.question: The purpose of performing a pelvic ultrasound before IUD insertion in a family planning setting is to:

options: Interventions and treatments already provided before referral
The waiting time experienced at the referring health facility
The financial arrangements made for the patient's inpatient care
The names of all family members accompanying the patient
The patient's religious preference and dietary requirements
questions.question: The referral letter for a pregnant woman being transferred to a higher level facility for complications must NOT omit which critical piece of information?
questions.explanation: The referral letter must include all interventions and treatments already provided, such as medications administered (oxytocics, antihypertensives, antibiotics, IV fluids), blood transfusions given, and procedures performed. This information is critical because it prevents duplication of treatments, informs the receiving team about the clinical course, and identifies what has been attempted and what remains to be done. Omission of this information risks patient safety through dangerous gaps in care.

Rubin II — internal rotation of the posterior shoulder
Wood's screw manoeuvre to rotate the anterior shoulder
Fundal pressure to push the baby downward
Zavanelli manoeuvre — replacing the head into the uterus
questions.explanation: The McRoberts manoeuvre is first-line for shoulder dystocia. It involves hyperflexing the maternal thighs onto the abdomen, which straightens the lumbar lordosis, rotates the pubic symphysis superiorly, and widens the pelvic inlet, freeing the impacted anterior shoulder. It is simple, rapid, and effective alone in up to 90% of cases. Simultaneous suprapubic pressure (not fundal) is also applied.

options: A single method is always insufficient to prevent pregnancy
To reduce the cost of contraception per unit of protection
To improve convenience and ease of contraceptive compliance

To simultaneously prevent STIs and unintended pregnancy
questions.question: The most important reason why family planning services promote dual protection (condom plus another contraceptive method) is:
questions.explanation: Dual protection promotes the simultaneous use of condoms alongside another contraceptive method to achieve two distinct goals: prevention of sexually transmitted infections and prevention of unintended pregnancy. This is particularly important in family planning settings where clients may be at risk for both STIs and unintended pregnancy. No hormonal or intrauterine contraceptive method provides protection against STIs, making condom use essential for comprehensive sexual health protection.

options: Progesterone-only injectable administered every three months
A copper IUD as first-line despite the history of ectopic pregnancy
Natural family planning methods based on basal body temperature
Combined oral contraceptive pill for high contraceptive efficacy
A long-acting progestin implant or hormonal IUS to prevent ovulation
questions.question: In managing a client with a history of ectopic pregnancy who now desires contraception, which method is most strongly recommended?
questions.explanation: For women with a history of ectopic pregnancy, long-acting progestin-containing methods such as the subdermal implant or levonorgestrel-releasing IUS are strongly preferred because they suppress ovulation and prevent any fertilised oocyte from implanting in the fallopian tube. The copper IUD, while highly effective for contraception, does not suppress ovulation and carries a slightly higher proportional risk of ectopic implantation if contraceptive failure occurs.

The cervix of the non-pregnant uterus measures approximately 2.5 cm in length and 2 cm in width. It projects into the vagina as the portio vaginalis. The external os is round in nulliparous women and a transverse slit after delivery. The internal os connects the cervical canal to the uterine cavity and is the site assessed for incompetent cervix.
questions.question: How long does the cervix measure in a non-pregnant woman on average?

5.0 cm long, between internal and external os
2.5 cm long and 2 cm wide on average
3.5 cm long and 2.5 cm in the parous uterus
4.0 cm long, equal to the length of the uterine body

questions.explanation: Rubella IgG antibody measurement is used in preconception counselling to confirm whether the woman has protective immunity from previous infection or vaccination. Women found to be non-immune (IgG negative) should be vaccinated with the MMR vaccine before conception to prevent congenital rubella syndrome, which can cause severe fetal abnormalities including cataracts, deafness, and congenital heart defects if infection occurs in the first trimester.

Throat swab culture for rubella virus isolation and identification
Rubella IgG antibody titre to confirm past immunity or vaccination

questions.explanation: Linear skull fractures in newborns usually require no specific treatment because they are not displaced and heal spontaneously with good outcomes in the absence of associated complications. Depressed skull fractures, on the other hand, may require surgical intervention. Antibiotic therapy is indicated only if there is cerebrospinal fluid leakage through the ear or nose, suggesting meningeal breach and risk of meningitis.

Prophylactic antibiotics and lumbar puncture for CSF analysis
No specific treatment as linear fractures usually heal spontaneously
Emergency neurosurgical craniectomy to release intracranial pressure
Skull traction device to realign the fractured bone segments
questions.question: Linear skull fracture in a newborn detected after a prolonged or difficult instrumental birth most commonly requires:
Which of the following is the correct duration of protection provided by a single dose of depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA)?
questions.explanation: DMPA is administered by intramuscular or subcutaneous injection every twelve weeks, giving roughly three months of contraceptive cover per dose. Clients returning more than two weeks late for a repeat injection should be assessed for pregnancy before revaccination. This scheduling distinguishes DMPA from daily or long-acting reversible methods.

options: Thyroid-stimulating hormone testing routinely for all women
Serum calcium level testing routinely for all women
Chest radiograph screening routinely for all women
questions.question: A woman at her first antenatal booking visit undergoes a panel of routine investigations recommended for all pregnant women. Which test specifically screens for a common chronic viral infection with vertical transmission risk?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B surface antigen testing is a standard component of the first antenatal booking panel, as maternal infection carries a significant risk of vertical transmission to the neonate, which can be substantially reduced with appropriate neonatal immunoprophylaxis. Other routine booking investigations include full blood count, blood group and antibody screen, HIV, and syphilis serology. Early identification allows timely planning to protect the newborn.

options: Weeks 10 to 14; closes only after birth in response to suckling
Weeks 4 to 7; fuses simultaneously in both sexes at the same time
Weeks 6 to 9; closes one week later in females than in males
Weeks 9 to 12; closes two weeks earlier in females than males
Weeks 3 to 6; fuses earlier in females due to oestrogen effects
questions.question: The secondary palate forms between which weeks of gestation, and when does it fuse in female fetuses compared to males?
questions.explanation: The secondary palate forms between the 6th and 9th weeks of gestation when the palatal shelves change from a vertical to a horizontal position and fuse in the midline. Importantly, the secondary palate closes one week later in female fetuses than in male fetuses. This difference in timing explains why females have a higher incidence of isolated cleft palate — if the fusion process is disturbed, the later closing timeline in females provides a longer window for disruption to occur.

options: Short-acting beta-agonists, used for acute relief
Inhaled corticosteroids, used for maintenance therapy
Non-selective beta-blockers, which can worsen bronchospasm
Oral corticosteroids, used for severe exacerbations
Oxygen therapy, used to correct hypoxaemia
questions.question: A woman at 28 weeks with known asthma develops acute breathlessness and audible wheeze. Which category of drug should be avoided in her acute management if possible?
questions.explanation: Non-selective beta-blockers can precipitate or worsen bronchospasm in patients with asthma by blocking bronchodilating beta-2 receptors, and should generally be avoided when safer alternatives exist. Short-acting beta-agonists, inhaled and oral corticosteroids, and oxygen remain standard components of acute asthma management in pregnancy. Careful drug selection ensures effective asthma control without compromising respiratory function.

The Bardach two-flap technique for cleft palate repair involves making medial incisions to separate the oral and nasal mucosa, followed by lateral incisions at the junction of the palate and alveolar ridge. Flaps are then elevated while preserving the greater palatine artery, the velar muscles are detached from the posterior palate, and the repair is closed in three layers (nasal mucosa, muscle, and oral mucosa). The trend in modern surgery is towards techniques with less scarring and tension.
questions.question: The Bardach two-flap technique for cleft palate repair involves which sequence of surgical steps?
options: Primary bone grafting followed by soft tissue closure in a single stage
Pharyngeal flap attachment prior to hard palate repair in two stages
Uvular repair first, then soft palate closure and hard palate grafting
Vomer flap repair of the nasal floor followed by buccal mucosa grafting
Medial oral-nasal incisions, lateral incisions, flap elevation preserving palatine artery, three-layer closure

questions.question: The O'Sullivan technique for managing uterine inversion involves which intervention?
questions.explanation: Uterine inversion is a third-stage emergency causing profound haemorrhage and neurogenic shock. The O'Sullivan hydrostatic method infuses warm saline (2-3 litres) into the vagina to create hydraulic pressure that repositions the uterus. Johnson's manual replacement is an alternative. Oxytocics are withheld until after replacement, as they can make reduction impossible by contracting the cervical ring.
options: Immediate manual removal of the placenta then uterine replacement
Aggressive fundal pressure to assist placental delivery
IV ergometrine to contract the uterus around the inversion
Caesarean hysterectomy as the definitive first-line treatment
Hydrostatic replacement using warm saline infusion into the vagina

questions.question: A midwife performing internal pelvimetry cannot reach the sacral promontory. What does this finding suggest?
questions.explanation: When the sacral promontory cannot be reached during vaginal examination, it suggests the diagonal conjugate is likely greater than 12.5 cm, giving an estimated obstetric conjugate of at least 11 cm - an encouraging sign of adequate pelvic inlet dimensions. Conversely, if the promontory is easily felt, it may indicate a reduced AP diameter.

During the proliferative phase, rising oestrogen from the maturing follicle stimulates regrowth of the functional endometrial layer. Glands become straight and narrow, and the stroma proliferates. Endometrial thickness increases from approximately 2 mm after menstruation to 8-10 mm at ovulation. This phase corresponds to follicular development and ends at ovulation.
questions.question: What structural endometrial change occurs during the proliferative (follicular) phase?
options: Straight glands and stroma proliferate under oestrogen stimulation
Endometrial lining sheds with prostaglandin-mediated vasoconstriction
Decidualisation of the stroma occurs under combined hormones
Secretory glands accumulate glycogen under progesterone influence
Spiral arteries become coiled and glands become tortuous

questions.explanation: The Billings ovulation method (BOM) relies on the woman observing and recording the characteristics of cervical mucus (vaginal discharge) throughout her menstrual cycle. In the periovulatory period, oestrogen causes the cervical mucus to become clear, slippery, stretchy (Spinnbarkeit), and abundant - like raw egg white - indicating the fertile window. After ovulation, progesterone transforms mucus to thick, cloudy, and scant (infertile). Correct use requires daily observation and charting, with trained counselling.
questions.question: The Billings ovulation method (cervical mucus method) of fertility awareness is based on which physiological observation?
options: Counting cycle days from the first day of menstruation
Observing the characteristics of cervical mucus throughout the cycle
Monitoring basal body temperature rise after ovulation
Measuring urinary LH levels to detect the preovulatory surge
Uterotonic administration, manual placental removal, and antibiotics
Uterotonic administration, controlled cord traction, and uterine massage
Delayed cord clamping, uterine massage, and immediate breastfeeding
Controlled cord traction, episiotomy, and uterine massage
Uterotonic administration, cervical examination, and fundal massage
questions.explanation: Active management of the third stage of labour, as recommended by WHO, comprises three key components: administration of a uterotonic drug, usually oxytocin, shortly after birth, controlled cord traction to assist placental delivery once separation is confirmed, and uterine massage after placental delivery to maintain good uterine tone. This package has been shown to significantly reduce the incidence and severity of postpartum haemorrhage compared with expectant management. Consistent application of all three components maximises the protective benefit.
questions.question: A midwife is asked to explain the standard WHO regimen for active management of the third stage of labour as a complete package. Which three components make up this regimen?
A newborn is given vitamin K shortly after birth as a routine preventive measure. What is the primary purpose of this administration?
options: Preventing neonatal jaundice from excess bilirubin
Preventing neonatal hypoglycaemia in the first days
Preventing vitamin K deficiency bleeding in the neonate
Preventing neonatal sepsis from maternal transmission
Preventing congenital heart defects from developing
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is administered to all newborns shortly after birth to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding, since neonates have low vitamin K stores and immature liver synthesis of clotting factors at birth. This can present as early, classical, or late bleeding depending on timing, with the late form carrying particular risk of intracranial haemorrhage. A single intramuscular dose provides effective long-term prevention.

options: Within the first twenty-four hours after birth
Between twenty-four hours and six weeks postpartum
Only after six weeks following delivery
Exclusively within the first week after birth
Only during the antenatal period before delivery
questions.question: A woman develops secondary postpartum haemorrhage with offensive lochia and uterine tenderness ten days after delivery. Within which typical timeframe does secondary PPH usually occur?
questions.explanation: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage is defined as excessive bleeding occurring between twenty-four hours and six weeks after delivery, most commonly caused by retained products of conception or endometritis. The combination of offensive lochia and uterine tenderness in this case suggests an infective component requiring antibiotics alongside evaluation for retained tissue. This differs from primary PPH, which occurs within the first twenty-four hours.

questions.question: A woman with placental abruption develops widespread bleeding from venepuncture sites and abnormal clotting studies. Which mechanism explains this complication?
options: Direct mechanical damage to platelets from uterine bleeding
Release of thromboplastin triggering disseminated intravascular coagulation
Excessive uterotonic use causing consumptive coagulopathy
Amniotic fluid embolism causing widespread clot formation
questions.explanation: Placental abruption releases large amounts of tissue thromboplastin into the maternal circulation, activating the clotting cascade excessively and consuming clotting factors and platelets, which precipitates disseminated intravascular coagulation. This presents as widespread bleeding, low fibrinogen, and deranged clotting studies. Prompt delivery and correction of coagulopathy with blood products are essential to manage this life-threatening complication.

options: Relaxin, softening the cervix in early pregnancy
Oestrogen, to proliferate the endometrial lining

Progesterone, to maintain the decidualised endometrium
questions.question: The corpus luteum rescued by hCG primarily secretes which hormone to sustain early pregnancy?
questions.explanation: The corpus luteum, rescued by hCG, continues secreting progesterone (and some oestrogen). Progesterone is essential to maintain the decidua, inhibit uterine contractions, and support implantation. The luteoplacental shift occurs at 8-10 weeks when the placenta takes over progesterone production. Removal of the corpus luteum before this shift may cause miscarriage.

Intramuscular ceftriaxone, given once at booking
Oral erythromycin, given throughout the third trimester
Intravenous vancomycin, given routinely regardless of allergy
questions.question: A woman is screened for Group B Streptococcus colonisation, and results are positive. Which antibiotic is considered the drug of choice for intrapartum prophylaxis in this situation?
questions.explanation: Intravenous penicillin administered during labour is the first-line intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for women colonised with Group B Streptococcus, significantly reducing the risk of early-onset neonatal GBS infection. Alternative antibiotics such as clindamycin or vancomycin are reserved for women with penicillin allergy, depending on the type of reaction and local resistance patterns. Timely administration once labour begins, rather than earlier in pregnancy, is essential for effectiveness.

options: Amenorrhoea, describing complete absence of menstruation
questions.explanation: Polymenorrhoea describes menstrual cycles occurring more frequently than every twenty-one days, often reflecting a shortened follicular or luteal phase, and can be associated with anovulatory cycles or hormonal imbalance. This is distinct from menorrhagia, which describes the volume of bleeding rather than its frequency. Correctly distinguishing these terms guides appropriate hormonal investigation and management.
questions.question: A woman describes her menstrual cycles as occurring more frequently than every twenty-one days. Which term correctly describes this menstrual pattern?
A pregnant woman at 30 weeks develops a severe frontal headache, blurred vision, and epigastric pain. Her BP is 165/110 mmHg and urine protein is 3+. Which immediate nursing action is the priority?
questions.explanation: This presentation is severe pre-eclampsia with imminent eclampsia (BP =160/110, proteinuria, headache, visual disturbances, epigastric pain - Korotkoff signs of impending eclampsia). The immediate nursing priority is to alert the obstetric and anaesthetic team urgently and initiate the eclampsia/severe pre-eclampsia protocol: IV magnesium sulphate (anti-convulsant), IV antihypertensive (labetalol or hydralazine), IV access, urinary catheter, and preparation for possible delivery.

Insert a urinary catheter and measure hourly urine output
Perform a vaginal examination for cervical dilatation
Alert the obstetric team and prepare for eclampsia protocol
Administer IV dextrose 10% for the headache symptom

questions.question: Which drug used to treat hyperemesis gravidarum has been associated with neonatal extrapyramidal effects if used near term?
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide (a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist) is used for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. If used near term, it can cross the placenta and cause neonatal extrapyramidal side effects (dystonic reactions, oculogyric crises) due to its dopamine-blocking action on the neonatal striatum. Maternal side effects include tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use. It is still used in pregnancy where benefits outweigh risks, but with caution in the third trimester and near term.

questions.question: The antidote for magnesium sulphate toxicity is which drug?
questions.explanation: Magnesium sulphate toxicity causes loss of deep tendon reflexes (first sign, MgSO4 level >5 mmol/L), respiratory depression (>7 mmol/L), and cardiac arrest (>15 mmol/L). The antidote is calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% solution (1 g) given slowly IV over 10 minutes. Calcium directly antagonises the neuromuscular effects of magnesium. During MgSO4 infusion, deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate (>12/min), and urine output (>25 mL/hr) must be monitored every 30 minutes.

questions.question: A woman with a large endometrioma measuring four centimetres wishes to preserve her fertility while undergoing surgical treatment. What is the primary surgical consideration in her case?
questions.explanation: In a woman wishing to preserve fertility, surgical management of an endometrioma should use careful cystectomy technique that removes the cyst wall while preserving as much healthy ovarian cortex and follicular reserve as possible. Aggressive excision can further reduce ovarian reserve, while incomplete removal risks recurrence. Balancing complete lesion removal against ovarian preservation is a key surgical consideration in this population.
options: Complete oophorectomy to prevent any disease recurrence
Bilateral salpingectomy to eliminate future tubal disease
Total hysterectomy to remove all endometriotic tissue
Careful cystectomy technique to preserve healthy ovarian tissue
Radical pelvic clearance regardless of fertility wishes

questions.question: Azoospermia is defined as the complete absence of sperm in the ejaculate. What are the two main categories?
questions.explanation: Azoospermia is classified as: obstructive azoospermia (OA) - sperm is produced but cannot reach the ejaculate due to obstruction (vas deferens obstruction, congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens/CBAVD, epididymal obstruction); and non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA) - impaired or absent spermatogenesis (Sertoli cell-only syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome XXY, cryptorchidism, post-chemotherapy). FSH is elevated in NOA (indicating primary testicular failure) and normal in OA. Surgical sperm retrieval (TESA/PESA) is used with IVF-ICSI.

Doderlein's bacilli (Lactobacillus acidophilus) are normal commensals of the vagina that ferment glycogen from desquamated epithelial cells into lactic acid. This lactic acid maintains the vaginal pH between 4.0 and 4.5. This acidic environment provides a natural defence against ascending infection and pathogen colonisation.

Squamous epithelial cells directly secreting hydrogen ions

Uterine secretions draining downward to acidify the canal

Mild acne unrelated to hormonal fluctuation

Family history of migraine without aura
questions.question: A woman with a history of migraine with aura asks whether she can use combined oral contraceptives. Which of her conditions represents an absolute contraindication?
questions.explanation: Migraine with aura is an absolute contraindication to combined hormonal contraceptives because the oestrogen component further increases an already elevated risk of ischaemic stroke in these women. Progestogen-only methods are generally considered safer alternatives for women with this history. Careful history-taking before prescribing hormonal contraception helps identify such contraindications.

questions.question: Metformin is used in gestational diabetes when dietary management alone is insufficient. What is its primary mechanism of action?
options: Stimulating GLP-1 release from intestinal L-cells
Increasing renal glucose excretion by blocking SGLT-2
Blocking intestinal glucose absorption from dietary carbohydrates
Reducing hepatic glucose production (gluconeogenesis) and increasing insulin sensitivity
Stimulating insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells
questions.explanation: Metformin is a biguanide that acts primarily by reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis (inhibiting complex I of the mitochondrial electron transport chain), thereby reducing fasting blood glucose. It also increases peripheral insulin sensitivity (muscle glucose uptake) and reduces intestinal glucose absorption. It does not cause hypoglycaemia (as it does not stimulate insulin secretion). Metformin crosses the placenta but has not been shown to cause fetal harm; it is used as an adjunct or alternative to insulin in GDM.

options: Anthropoid pelvis with its long AP diameter
Gynecoid pelvis with adequate round inlet shape
Android or platypelloid pelvis with a contracted inlet
Rachitic pelvis caused by childhood vitamin D deficiency
questions.question: Which pelvic type most commonly causes cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD)?
questions.explanation: CPD most commonly results from a contracted pelvis - most often the android type (narrow forepelvis) or platypelloid type (flat inlet with reduced AP diameter). An obstetric conjugate of less than 10 cm or intertuberous diameter less than 8 cm is considered contracted. CPD leads to failure of engagement, prolonged labour, and ultimately caesarean section.

Polymenorrhoea (epimenorrhoea) describes cycles with a frequency of less than 21 days. It may result from a shortened follicular phase, luteal phase defect, or anovulatory cycles. Oligomenorrhoea describes infrequent cycles (greater than 35 days). Dysmenorrhoea is painful menstruation, amenorrhoea is absence of periods, and menorrhagia is excessive loss - all distinct NMCN-tested definitions.

questions.explanation: A normal umbilical cord contains three vessels: two umbilical arteries carrying deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta, and one umbilical vein carrying oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus. The presence of only two vessels, a single umbilical artery, is associated with an increased risk of congenital anomalies and warrants further neonatal assessment. Documenting vessel number at birth is a routine part of newborn examination.

Three vessels, comprising two arteries and one vein
Four vessels, comprising two arteries and two veins
One vessel only, functioning as a combined conduit
Five vessels, comprising three arteries and two veins

2000 grams — at the height of post-delivery size
questions.question: Immediately postpartum, the uterus weighs approximately how much?
questions.explanation: Immediately after delivery, the uterus weighs approximately 900-1000 grams, with the fundus palpable at the umbilicus. Involution occurs progressively: by 7 days approximately 500 g, by 14 days approximately 300 g, and by 6 weeks it returns to the non-pregnant weight of approximately 60-80 g. Involution is aided by breastfeeding via oxytocin release causing uterine contractions.

questions.question: The "four T's" mnemonic for causes of postpartum haemorrhage lists which four categories?
questions.explanation: The 4 T's of PPH are: Tone (uterine atony - most common, ~70%); Trauma (lacerations of cervix, vagina, perineum, uterine rupture); Tissue (retained placenta or placental fragments); and Thrombin (coagulopathy - DIC, pre-existing clotting disorders). This mnemonic guides systematic assessment and management. Uterine atony must always be excluded and treated first.

questions.question: A woman is found to have a blood pressure reading of 165/115 mmHg at 32 weeks gestation with significant proteinuria. How should this finding be classified?
questions.explanation: Severe pre-eclampsia is indicated by a blood pressure of at least 160/110 mmHg accompanied by significant proteinuria, distinguishing it from milder gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia. This classification triggers closer monitoring, antihypertensive therapy, and consideration of timing of delivery based on gestational age and maternal-fetal status. Recognising severity accurately guides the urgency of management.
options: Severe pre-eclampsia, given the markedly elevated readings
Mild pre-eclampsia, within an acceptable range
White coat hypertension requiring repeat measurement only

questions.explanation: Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant condition caused by a defect in the ossification of the epiphyseal plate. It presents with a disproportionately large head, very short limbs, and pronounced lumbar lordosis. Cognitive development is typically not impaired. No specific treatment is required for the condition itself, though supportive care and psychological support for parents are important components of management.

Autosomal dominant condition with large head, short limbs, and lordosis
Autosomal recessive mutation causing severe cognitive impairment
X-linked recessive inheritance affecting male infants exclusively
Chromosomal trisomy causing intellectual disability and cardiac defects

Which uterine ligament is the most important in preventing uterine prolapse?
questions.explanation: The transverse cervical (cardinal or Mackenrodt's) ligament runs from the cervix and upper vagina to the lateral pelvic wall, providing the primary mechanical support against uterine descent. Damage to this ligament during childbirth can lead to uterine prolapse. The uterosacral ligaments provide additional posterior support.

Ovarian ligament connecting the ovary to the uterine cornua
Round ligament passing through the inguinal canal
