Clara cells divide rapidly to replace damaged epithelium

questions.explanation: Juxtamedullary nephrons possess long loops of Henle that extend deep into the medulla, enabling production of concentrated urine. Their efferent arterioles give rise to vasa recta rather than peritubular capillaries, supporting the countercurrent exchange system. Cortical nephrons with short loops are primarily involved in excretion rather than concentration.
options: Cortical nephrons lack a loop of Henle structure
Juxtamedullary nephrons have longer loops of Henle
Cortical nephrons possess more extensive glomeruli
Juxtamedullary nephrons filter blood more efficiently
Cortical nephrons produce more concentrated urine
questions.question: What is the primary difference between cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons?

questions.explanation: Serous cells in bronchial submucosal glands produce watery secretions containing lysozyme and other antimicrobial proteins. These secretions hydrate and dilute the mucus layer, maintaining optimal consistency for mucociliary clearance. Pure mucous secretions would be too viscous for effective ciliary transport.
options: Serous cells produce mucus for airway lubrication
Serous cells secrete watery fluid diluting mucus
Serous cells generate antibodies for immune protection
Serous cells produce surfactant for alveolar function
Serous cells create acidic secretions killing bacteria
questions.question: What is the function of serous cells in submucosal glands?

questions.explanation: Mumps is a viral infection (paramyxovirus) primarily affecting the parotid glands, causing painful bilateral swelling. The virus spreads by respiratory droplets and can affect other organs (testes, pancreas, CNS). Vaccination has markedly reduced incidence. Complications include orchitis, meningitis, and rarely, permanent hearing loss.
options: Bacterial infection of salivary glands causes mumps
Autoimmune destruction of salivary tissue causes mumps
Paramyxovirus infection of parotid glands causes mumps
Salivary duct obstruction by stones causes mumps
Tumor formation in parotid gland causes mumps
questions.question: What causes mumps infection?

questions.explanation: Acetylcholine released from motor neuron terminals binds to nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate, triggering muscle fiber depolarization. The neurotransmitter is then rapidly degraded by acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft. This ensures precise temporal control of muscle activation.
questions.question: Which neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction to initiate skeletal muscle contraction?

options: Excessive mucus production obstructs airways completely
Fibrosis of interalveolar septa impairs diffusion
Inflammation of bronchioles causes airway narrowing
Destruction of alveolar walls reduces gas exchange surface
Pulmonary edema floods alveoli with fluid
questions.explanation: Emphysema involves progressive destruction of alveolar walls and loss of elastic fibers, reducing gas exchange surface area and impairing elastic recoil. This causes air trapping and hyperinflation. Smoking is the primary cause through protease-antiprotease imbalance. The condition is irreversible and part of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
questions.question: What characterizes emphysema pathologically?

options: Achalasia develops from prolonged acid exposure
Barrett esophagus shows metaplastic epithelial changes
Esophageal varices form due to reflux damage
Zenker diverticulum results from chronic reflux
Esophageal atresia follows severe acid injury
questions.explanation: Barrett esophagus is a metaplastic condition where stratified squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium due to chronic acid exposure. This intestinal-type metaplasia is a premalignant condition increasing esophageal adenocarcinoma risk. Regular endoscopic surveillance is recommended for affected patients.
questions.question: What condition results from chronic gastroesophageal reflux?
What membrane immediately surrounds the developing embryo/fetus?
questions.explanation: The amnion is the innermost fetal membrane forming a fluid-filled sac around the embryo/fetus. Amniotic fluid cushions the fetus, permits movement, and maintains temperature. The amnion is avascular, receiving nutrients by diffusion from maternal blood.

The blood-air barrier consists of type I alveolar cells, fused basement membranes, and capillary endothelium, totaling less than 0.5 micrometers thickness. This minimal barrier facilitates rapid gas diffusion while maintaining separation between air and blood. The total surface area available for gas exchange approximates 70 square meters.
options: Thick connective tissue separating air from blood compartments
Multiple layers of epithelial cells preventing gas passage
Surfactant layer forming an impermeable barrier structure
Alveolar epithelium and capillary endothelium with fused basement membranes
Alveolar macrophages creating a defensive cellular barrier
questions.question: What composes the blood-air barrier?

questions.explanation: Fibrocartilage contains thick bundles of type I collagen fibers providing tensile strength in structures subject to compression and shear forces. It lacks a perichondrium and shows gradual transitions to dense connective tissue. This cartilage type resists both tension and compression.
questions.question: What type of cartilage contains type I collagen and is found in intervertebral discs?
What characterizes granulation tissue?
questions.explanation: Granulation tissue is new connective tissue rich in capillaries (angiogenesis), fibroblasts secreting collagen (initially type III), and macrophages. It fills wound defects during proliferative phase. The pinkish granular appearance reflects new vessel formation.

questions.question: What protects the gastric mucosa from acid and pepsin?
questions.explanation: The gastric mucosal barrier consists of surface mucus (forming a continuous gel layer) and bicarbonate secretion (creating a pH gradient within the mucus). Prostaglandins stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion and maintain mucosal blood flow. NSAIDs damage this barrier by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis.
options: Thick keratin layer on epithelial surface
Tight epithelial junctions preventing acid penetration
Continuous epithelial cell renewal without mucus
Absence of blood flow to mucosa

questions.question: Which direction do smooth muscle fibers run in the bronchiolar wall?
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle in bronchiolar walls is arranged primarily in a circular or spiral pattern around the airway lumen. Contraction narrows the lumen (bronchoconstriction), while relaxation causes dilation (bronchodilation). This muscle layer becomes proportionally thicker as bronchi branch into smaller airways lacking cartilage.
options: Smooth muscle spirals longitudinally along bronchiolar length
Smooth muscle extends radially outward from lumen
Smooth muscle runs randomly without organized pattern
Smooth muscle alternates between all three orientations
Smooth muscle courses circumferentially around bronchioles

questions.explanation: Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation affecting any part of the GI tract (mouth to anus) with skip lesions (diseased segments separated by normal bowel). Histology shows noncaseating granulomas, fissures, and fistulas. This contrasts with ulcerative colitis which shows continuous mucosal inflammation limited to the colon.
options: Continuous superficial inflammation of the colon
Inflammatory changes limited to the mucosa only
Uniform inflammation throughout the entire colon
Inflammation confined to the terminal ileum exclusively
Transmural inflammation with skip lesions anywhere in GI tract
questions.question: What characterizes Crohn disease histologically?
What characterizes the renal medullary pyramids?
questions.explanation: Medullary pyramids contain the loops of Henle from juxtamedullary nephrons and the collecting ducts converging toward the papillae. The parallel arrangement of these tubules creates the striated appearance characteristic of the medulla. This organization is essential for establishing and maintaining the osmotic gradient required for urine concentration.
options: They house the loops of Henle and collecting ducts
They contain primarily cortical nephron components exclusively
They are separated by columns of adipose tissue
They filter blood through extensive capillary networks
They produce erythropoietin in response to oxygen levels

questions.explanation: Osteons (Haversian systems) are cylindrical structures forming the basic organizational unit of compact bone. Each contains a central canal with blood vessels and nerves surrounded by concentric bone lamellae. Osteocytes reside in lacunae between lamellae, connected by canaliculi.
questions.question: What structural unit consists of concentric lamellae surrounding a central Haversian canal?

options: The prostatic urethra measures approximately 15 centimeters
The spongy urethra spans roughly 15 centimeters
The membranous urethra extends about 15 centimeters
The penile urethra reaches approximately 3 centimeters
The bulbar urethra extends for about 15 centimeters
questions.question: Which portion of the male urethra is longest?
questions.explanation: The spongy (penile) urethra is the longest segment of the male urethra at approximately 15 cm, extending through the corpus spongiosum. This portion is lined initially by pseudostratified columnar epithelium, transitioning to stratified squamous epithelium distally. The prostatic and membranous segments are much shorter at 3-4 cm and 1-2 cm respectively.

options: Excessive mucus production causes voice changes
Edema of vocal folds impairs vibration causing hoarseness
Vocal fold paralysis causes hoarseness exclusively
Tumor formation on folds causes voice changes
Atrophy of vocal muscles produces hoarseness
questions.question: What causes hoarseness in laryngitis?
questions.explanation: Laryngitis involves inflammation and edema of the vocal folds and other laryngeal structures, altering their mass and vibratory characteristics. This produces hoarseness or complete voice loss (aphonia). Viral infection is the most common cause. Chronic laryngitis from irritants, voice overuse, or reflux can cause permanent voice changes.

Thyroid follicular cells form simple cuboidal to low columnar epithelium surrounding colloid-filled follicles. Cell height varies with activity level: taller when active (TSH stimulation), flatter when inactive. These cells synthesize thyroglobulin and concentrate iodide for thyroid hormone production.
questions.question: What type of epithelial cells line thyroid follicles and synthesize thyroglobulin?

questions.explanation: The extrinsic pathway is initiated by death ligands (FasL, TNF, TRAIL) binding death receptors, recruiting adaptor proteins and caspase-8. This directly activates executioner caspases. The pathway is important in immune regulation and tissue homeostasis.
questions.question: Which pathway of apoptosis involves death receptors like Fas?
Where do spermatozoa undergo final maturation and acquire motility?
questions.explanation: The epididymis is a highly coiled duct where spermatozoa spend 2-3 weeks maturing, acquiring motility and fertilizing capacity. Epididymal epithelium reabsorbs fluid and secretes glycoproteins modifying sperm surface. Stereocilia increase surface area for absorption.

questions.question: Which cells produce pulmonary surfactant?
options: Type I alveolar cells synthesize and secrete surfactant
Alveolar macrophages generate surfactant components continuously
Capillary endothelial cells produce surfactant molecules
Interstitial fibroblasts secrete surfactant into alveolar spaces
Type II alveolar cells manufacture and release surfactant
questions.explanation: Type II alveolar cells (great alveolar cells) synthesize, store, and secrete pulmonary surfactant from distinctive lamellar bodies. These cuboidal cells contain abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum and well-developed Golgi apparatus for surfactant production. Surfactant secretion increases with deep breathing and is regulated by various stimuli.

questions.question: Which organelle is responsible for the post-translational modification and sorting of proteins destined for secretion?
questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus modifies proteins through glycosylation, sulfation, and phosphorylation, then sorts them to appropriate destinations. Proteins move through cis, medial, and trans cisternae undergoing sequential modifications. The trans-Golgi network packages modified proteins into vesicles for delivery.

Positive selection in the thymic cortex ensures T cells can recognize self-MHC molecules. Thymocytes whose receptors bind cortical epithelial cell MHC with appropriate affinity survive; others die by neglect. This selects for MHC restriction.
questions.question: What process occurs in the thymic cortex during T cell development?

questions.explanation: Microvilli are finger-like projections containing bundled actin filaments that form the brush border of intestinal epithelial cells. Each cell possesses thousands of microvilli creating a striated appearance under light microscopy. This massive surface area enhancement is critical for efficient nutrient absorption.
questions.question: What specialized structure increases the apical surface area of intestinal absorptive cells by approximately 20-fold?

options: Excessive mucus production overwhelms drainage capacity completely
Bacterial infection destroys the epithelial lining tissue
Defective ciliary motility impairs mucus clearance mechanisms
Anatomical obstruction blocks all sinus drainage pathways
Autoimmune destruction of ciliated cells occurs progressively
questions.question: What causes chronic sinusitis in primary ciliary dyskinesia?
questions.explanation: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) results from defective dynein or other ciliary proteins causing immotile cilia. Impaired mucociliary clearance in sinuses and airways leads to chronic sinusitis and bronchitis. The condition also causes male infertility due to immotile sperm flagella.

After ovulation, the ruptured follicle fills with blood (corpus hemorrhagicum) then transforms into the corpus luteum as granulosa and theca cells luteinize. Without pregnancy, the corpus luteum degenerates after ~14 days into the corpus albicans (white scar tissue).
questions.question: What structure forms after ovulation if fertilization does not occur?

questions.explanation: The exocrine pancreas secretes approximately 1.5 L daily of pancreatic juice containing digestive enzyme precursors and bicarbonate-rich fluid. Acinar cells produce enzymes while centroacinar and ductal cells secrete bicarbonate. This secretion neutralizes gastric acid and provides optimal pH for enzyme activity in the duodenum.
questions.question: What is the exocrine secretion of the pancreas?
options: Pancreatic juice containing only enzymes is secreted
Pancreatic juice with enzymes and bicarbonate is produced
Only bicarbonate without enzymes is secreted
Insulin and glucagon comprise the exocrine secretion
Mucus is the primary pancreatic exocrine product
Easier to isolate than embryonic stem cells
Higher potency than embryonic stem cells
questions.explanation: iPSCs are generated from adult somatic cells by introducing transcription factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc), avoiding embryo destruction. They can form patient-specific cells for therapy, reducing rejection risk. However, reprogramming efficiency and safety concerns remain.
questions.question: What is the primary advantage of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs)?
Which cell type produces surfactant apoprotein?
options: Type I alveolar cells synthesize surfactant proteins
Type II alveolar cells produce surfactant apolipoproteins
Clara cells manufacture all surfactant proteins
Capillary endothelial cells create surfactant proteins
questions.explanation: Type II alveolar cells synthesize surfactant proteins (SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, SP-D) along with phospholipids. SP-B and SP-C are hydrophobic proteins essential for surfactant function, while SP-A and SP-D are hydrophilic proteins involved in innate immunity and surfactant homeostasis. Genetic deficiencies in these proteins cause respiratory disease.

questions.question: What type of electron microscopy is used to study three-dimensional surface structures?
questions.explanation: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) scans specimen surfaces with focused electron beams, detecting secondary electrons to create 3D images. Specimens are typically coated with gold or platinum for conductivity. SEM provides detailed surface topography information.

questions.question: What determines whether tissue repair proceeds by regeneration or fibrosis?
questions.explanation: Regeneration requires stem/progenitor cells, intact tissue framework, appropriate growth factors, and limited injury. Extensive damage, loss of architecture, chronic inflammation, or tissues with poor regenerative capacity (heart, CNS) favor fibrotic scarring over regeneration. AGING

Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells create the blood-testis barrier, dividing the seminiferous epithelium into basal and adluminal compartments. This immunologically privileged environment protects developing germ cells expressing novel antigens from autoimmune attack. Meiotic and post-meiotic cells reside in the adluminal compartment.
options: Isolate developing germ cells from immune system
questions.question: What is the function of the blood-testis barrier formed by Sertoli cell tight junctions?
What initiates the swallowing reflex?
questions.explanation: Swallowing is initiated voluntarily but becomes an involuntary reflex once food contacts pharyngeal mechanoreceptors. The swallowing center in the medulla coordinates the complex sequence involving oral, pharyngeal, and esophageal phases. This includes soft palate elevation, laryngeal closure, pharyngeal contraction, and esophageal peristalsis. Neurological damage can impair the reflex causing dysphagia.
options: Voluntary muscle contraction alone initiates swallowing
Gastric distension stimulates the swallowing reflex
Food contact with pharyngeal receptors triggers the reflex
Low blood glucose activates swallowing mechanisms
Conscious thought alone initiates all swallowing

questions.explanation: Sertoli cells form tight junctions creating the blood-testis barrier and provide structural and metabolic support for developing spermatogenic cells. They respond to FSH and testosterone, regulating spermatogenesis. These cells also phagocytose residual bodies and secrete androgen-binding protein.
questions.question: Which cells in seminiferous tubules respond to FSH and support developing germ cells?
Which substance causes vasodilation of the afferent arteriole?
questions.explanation: Prostaglandins, especially PGE2 and PGI2, cause afferent arteriole vasodilation, helping maintain GFR when renal perfusion is threatened. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, potentially causing acute kidney injury in volume-depleted states by eliminating this protective vasodilation. Prostaglandins counterbalance angiotensin II and sympathetic vasoconstriction.
options: Angiotensin II dilates the afferent arteriole markedly
Endothelin dilates afferent arterioles increasing GFR
Norepinephrine dilates afferent arterioles under stress
Vasopressin dilates afferent arterioles during dehydration

questions.explanation: The cardia and pylorus contain primarily mucus-secreting glands lacking parietal and chief cells. These regions produce protective mucus rather than digestive secretions. The fundus and body contain typical gastric glands with all cell types including parietal and chief cells.
options: The cardia and pylorus lack parietal and chief cells
The fundus contains no parietal or chief cells
The body lacks both these cell types
The greater curvature has no parietal or chief cells
All stomach regions contain parietal and chief cells
questions.question: Which region of the stomach lacks parietal and chief cells?

options: Mitochondria are the primary target of alcohol damage
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum proliferates with chronic alcohol
Lysosomes are destroyed by alcohol exposure
Golgi apparatus undergoes fragmentation from alcohol
Nuclei shrink and condense from alcohol damage
questions.explanation: Chronic alcohol consumption induces proliferation of smooth endoplasmic reticulum in hepatocytes, increasing cytochrome P450 enzymes for alcohol metabolism. This adaptation increases alcohol tolerance but also enhances metabolism of other drugs and production of toxic metabolites. Mitochondria are also damaged, impairing energy production and fatty acid oxidation.
questions.question: Which hepatocyte organelle is most affected by alcohol?

options: Filiform papillae form this distinctive pattern
Fungiform papillae create this arrangement specifically
Foliate papillae establish this characteristic configuration
Conical papillae organize into this formation
Circumvallate papillae compose this V-shaped row
questions.explanation: Circumvallate (vallate) papillae are arranged in an inverted V-shape along the sulcus terminalis, numbering 7-12 in humans. Each is surrounded by a deep trough into which serous glands (von Ebner's glands) secrete, washing the taste buds. These are the largest but least numerous lingual papillae.
questions.question: Which papillae are arranged in a V-shape on the tongue?

questions.explanation: The contractile ring composed of actin and myosin filaments forms at the cell equator and constricts to divide the cytoplasm. This creates a cleavage furrow that deepens until the cell completely divides. The process is coordinated with nuclear division.
questions.question: What structure divides the cytoplasm during animal cell cytokinesis?
What type of muscle composes the tongue?
questions.explanation: The tongue consists of interlacing bundles of skeletal muscle fibers arranged in three planes, providing complex mobility. Intrinsic muscles alter tongue shape while extrinsic muscles move the entire tongue. This muscular complexity enables precise movements necessary for speech, mastication, and swallowing.
options: Smooth muscle arranged in multiple directions throughout
Cardiac muscle forms the core tongue structure
Mixed smooth and skeletal muscle fibers together
Oblique cardiac muscle layers compose tongue substance
Skeletal muscle in intrinsic and extrinsic groups

questions.question: What specialized structure allows distal tubule cells to monitor sodium concentration in filtrate?
questions.explanation: The macula densa is a specialized region of the distal tubule epithelium that senses tubular fluid sodium concentration. These cells are part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus and regulate renin release from juxtaglomerular cells. This provides feedback control of glomerular filtration.

questions.question: What histological feature distinguishes Crohn's disease from ulcerative colitis?
questions.explanation: Crohn's disease shows transmural inflammation (all layers) with noncaseating granulomas, skip lesions, and fissures. Ulcerative colitis exhibits superficial mucosal inflammation limited to colon with continuous involvement from rectum. These distinct patterns guide diagnosis and treatment.

options: Brunner's glands secrete acidic fluid with pH 2.0
Brunner's glands produce neutral secretions at pH 7.0
Brunner's glands generate alkaline fluid with pH 8.1-9.3
Brunner's glands create basic secretions at pH 10.0
Brunner's gland secretions vary widely in pH
questions.question: What is the pH of secretions from Brunner's glands?
questions.explanation: Brunner's glands secrete alkaline mucus with pH 8.1-9.3, which neutralizes acidic chyme entering from the stomach and protects the duodenal mucosa. This alkaline environment also provides optimal pH for pancreatic enzyme activity. The bicarbonate-rich secretion complements pancreatic bicarbonate in acid neutralization.

Spironolactone and eplerenone are potassium-sparing diuretics that competitively block aldosterone receptors in principal cells of collecting ducts. This prevents sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. These diuretics are used for heart failure, hypertension, and hyperaldosteronism. Side effects include hyperkalemia and, with spironolactone, gynecomastia.
questions.question: Which diuretic blocks aldosterone receptors?
Which microscopy technique produces high-contrast images of living specimens without staining by using refraction and interference?
questions.explanation: Phase contrast microscopy converts phase shifts in light passing through specimens into amplitude changes visible as contrast differences. This allows visualization of transparent living cells without staining or fixation. The technique is particularly useful for observing intracellular structures and dynamic cellular processes.

BALT consists of lymphoid aggregates in bronchial walls that monitor inhaled antigens and initiate immune responses. Similar to gut-associated lymphoid tissue, it contains B and T cells. BALT is more prominent in children and in response to chronic stimulation.
questions.question: What is the main function of bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue (BALT)?
Which hormone is produced by the syncytiotrophoblast and is the basis for pregnancy tests?
questions.explanation: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is synthesized by syncytiotrophoblast starting soon after implantation. Its detection in maternal blood/urine forms the basis of pregnancy tests. hCG maintains the corpus luteum, ensuring continued progesterone production in early pregnancy.

questions.question: What composes a portal triad?
options: Portal vein, hepatic artery, and central vein together
Hepatic artery, central vein, and bile duct together
Bile duct, portal vein, and central vein together
Portal vein, bile duct, and hepatic artery together
Lymphatic, portal vein, and hepatic artery together
questions.explanation: Portal triads (portal areas) contain branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct surrounded by connective tissue at lobule periphery. Lymphatics and nerves are also present. These structures bring blood and drain bile from hepatic parenchyma. Multiple portal triads surround each hepatic lobule.

questions.question: What is the functional significance of hepatocyte binucleation?
options: Binucleate cells are always pathological in liver
Binucleate hepatocytes indicate imminent cell division
Binucleation occurs only in cirrhotic liver tissue
Binucleate cells have reduced metabolic function
questions.explanation: Approximately 25-30% of normal hepatocytes are binucleate, representing a form of polyploidy that increases cellular metabolic capacity without cell division. This polyploidy increases with age and liver regeneration. Binucleate hepatocytes can perform all normal hepatocyte functions and may actually have enhanced metabolic capabilities.

options: The gallbladder produces bile for lipid digestion
The gallbladder absorbs fats from bile secretions
The gallbladder concentrates bile by absorbing water
The gallbladder reabsorbs bile acids exclusively
The gallbladder has no absorptive function
questions.explanation: The gallbladder concentrates bile 5-20 fold by absorbing water and electrolytes through its columnar epithelium while retaining bile salts and other organic components. This concentrating function is crucial for efficient fat digestion. During fasting, bile is stored in the gallbladder; CCK stimulates its release during meals.
questions.question: What characterizes the gallbladder's absorptive function?

questions.explanation: Filiform papillae are numerous conical structures covering the anterior tongue dorsum that lack taste buds. They increase friction for food manipulation and are heavily keratinized. Their mechanical function contrasts with taste-bearing papillae.
questions.question: Which lingual papillae lack taste buds and function primarily in mechanical processing?

options: Glucose is the primary fuel for cardiac myocytes
Amino acids are the main cardiac energy substrate
Ketone bodies primarily fuel cardiac contraction
Lactate is the principal cardiac energy source
Fatty acids provide most cardiac energy under normal conditions
questions.question: What is the primary energy source for cardiac muscle?
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle derives 60-70% of its energy from fatty acid oxidation under normal conditions, with glucose, lactate, and ketones providing the remainder. The heart is metabolically flexible, switching fuels based on availability. During ischemia, the heart relies more on anaerobic glycolysis, producing less ATP and lactate accumulation.

options: The duodenum is the main B12 absorption site
The jejunum absorbs most vitamin B12
The colon absorbs the majority of B12
The terminal ileum is the primary B12 absorption site
Vitamin B12 is absorbed throughout the intestine
questions.question: What is the primary site of vitamin B12 absorption?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor is absorbed specifically in the terminal ileum through cubilin receptors. Ileal resection or disease (Crohn's disease) causes B12 malabsorption despite adequate intrinsic factor. The ileum is the only site with the specific receptor for the B12-IF complex, making it crucial for B12 absorption.

Type I pneumocytes are extremely thin, squamous cells covering ~95% of alveolar surface area despite being fewer in number than type II cells. Their minimal thickness (~25 nm in places) facilitates rapid gas diffusion across the air-blood barrier.
questions.question: Which cells form the majority of alveolar surface area for gas exchange?
Which cells in the olfactory epithelium are bipolar neurons detecting odors?
questions.explanation: Olfactory receptor neurons are bipolar neurons with dendrites extending to the epithelial surface bearing cilia containing odorant receptors. Their axons form the olfactory nerve projecting to the olfactory bulb. These neurons are continuously replaced throughout life from basal stem cells.

options: Surface cells produce acidic mucus while neck cells produce alkaline mucus
Surface cells secrete alkaline mucus while neck cells secrete acidic mucus
Surface cells lack secretory granules unlike neck cells
Surface cells are located in gastric pits while neck cells are in gland necks
Surface cells produce pepsinogen while neck cells secrete acid
questions.explanation: Surface mucous cells lining gastric pits and surface produce alkaline mucus (pH 7-8) that protects the epithelium from acid. Mucous neck cells in gland necks produce acidic mucus. Both are columnar with apical secretory granules, but differ in mucus composition and location.
questions.question: What distinguishes surface mucous cells from mucous neck cells?

questions.explanation: The true vocal folds are covered by stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium without glands or taste buds, minimizing mass for optimal vibration. The laryngeal surface of the epiglottis and other structures have respiratory epithelium with occasional taste buds. The lingual epiglottic surface may have scattered taste buds.
questions.question: Which laryngeal structures lack taste buds?
options: The epiglottic lingual surface has abundant taste buds
The false vocal folds contain taste bud structures
All laryngeal structures contain some taste buds
The aryepiglottic folds have numerous taste buds
The true vocal folds lack taste buds entirely

questions.question: What is demonstrated by enzyme histochemistry?
questions.explanation: Enzyme histochemistry uses substrates that produce visible colored or fluorescent products at sites of enzyme activity. This localizes and quantifies enzyme distribution in tissues. Fresh or frozen sections are required since most enzymes are inactivated by fixation.

Intramembranous ossification occurs when mesenchymal cells differentiate directly into osteoblasts and produce bone matrix. This process forms flat bones of the skull and facial bones. Ossification centers develop and expand radially, eventually fusing at suture lines.
questions.question: What type of ossification involves bone formation directly from mesenchymal tissue without a cartilage model?
Which cells are found in the space of Disse?
options: Kupffer cells reside in the space of Disse
Hepatocytes directly contact the space of Disse
Bile duct cells are present in Disse's space
Red blood cells accumulate in Disse's space
Hepatic stellate cells occupy the space of Disse
questions.explanation: Hepatic stellate (Ito) cells reside in the space of Disse between hepatocytes and sinusoidal endothelium, storing vitamin A in lipid droplets. In liver injury, they activate into myofibroblasts producing collagen and causing fibrosis. The space also contains hepatocyte microvilli and sparse extracellular matrix.

T3 is 3-4 times more potent than T4 and represents the active form. Most T4 (80%) is converted to T3 peripherally by deiodinases. T3 binds nuclear receptors regulating gene transcription, affecting metabolism, growth, and development.
questions.question: Which thyroid hormone is more potent and biologically active?
Which pancreatic hormone regulates blood glucose levels?
questions.explanation: Insulin (from beta cells) lowers blood glucose by promoting cellular uptake and storage, while glucagon (from alpha cells) raises it by stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. These hormones work antagonistically to maintain blood glucose within narrow limits. Dysregulation causes diabetes mellitus (insulin deficiency) or hypoglycemia (excess insulin).
options: Somatostatin is the primary glucose-regulating hormone
Insulin and glucagon together regulate blood glucose

questions.question: What structures mark the transition from conducting to respiratory portions of the airways?
questions.explanation: Respiratory bronchioles have occasional alveoli in their walls, marking the beginning of the respiratory zone. They branch from terminal bronchioles and lead to alveolar ducts. This is where both air conduction and gas exchange occur.

options: Vitamin A is produced by colonic bacteria
Vitamin C is synthesized by intestinal bacteria
Vitamin D is generated by colonic microbiota
Vitamin E is synthesized by intestinal flora
Vitamin K is produced by colonic bacteria
questions.question: Which vitamin is synthesized by colonic bacteria?
questions.explanation: Colonic bacteria synthesize vitamin K (especially menaquinone, vitamin K2), which is absorbed and contributes to the body's vitamin K status. This is clinically significant because prolonged antibiotic use can reduce bacterial populations causing vitamin K deficiency with bleeding tendency. Newborns have sterile intestines and receive vitamin K prophylaxis.

questions.question: What is xerostomia?
options: Xerostomia is dry mouth from inadequate saliva
Xerostomia is inflammation of salivary glands
Xerostomia is a salivary gland tumor
questions.explanation: Xerostomia (dry mouth) results from inadequate saliva production due to medications (anticholinergics, antihistamines), radiation therapy, Sjögren's syndrome, or other conditions affecting salivary glands. It causes difficulty chewing, swallowing, and speaking, increases dental caries risk, and reduces quality of life. Treatment focuses on stimulating remaining function or artificial saliva.

The LH surge from anterior pituitary, triggered by high estrogen levels, induces final oocyte maturation and follicle rupture. This occurs ~36 hours before ovulation. The surge also initiates luteinization of granulosa and theca cells forming corpus luteum.
questions.question: What hormone surge triggers ovulation?

options: They filter blood plasma through fenestrated membranes
They produce basement membrane components exclusively
They generate erythropoietin in response to hypoxia
They provide structural support and regulate filtration
They secrete renin when blood pressure falls
questions.question: What is the primary function of mesangial cells?
questions.explanation: Mesangial cells provide structural support to glomerular capillaries and can contract to regulate glomerular filtration rate. They also phagocytose trapped material from the basement membrane and produce extracellular matrix components. These cells play crucial roles in maintaining glomerular capillary architecture and function.

questions.question: Which process transforms round spermatids into mature spermatozoa?
questions.explanation: Spermiogenesis involves dramatic morphological changes: acrosome formation, nuclear condensation, flagellum development, and cytoplasm removal. This transformation occurs without cell division. Residual bodies containing excess cytoplasm are phagocytosed by Sertoli cells.

SRP recognizes signal sequences on nascent polypeptides emerging from ribosomes and directs ribosome-mRNA complex to ER membrane. SRP receptor on ER facilitates ribosome docking. This targets secretory and membrane proteins to the endomembrane system.
questions.question: What is the function of the signal recognition particle (SRP) in protein synthesis?

questions.explanation: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum in hepatocytes contains cytochrome P450 enzymes that detoxify drugs, alcohol, and other xenobiotics through oxidation. It also participates in cholesterol synthesis, lipoprotein production, and glycogen metabolism. SER proliferates in response to certain drugs like phenobarbital.
options: Protein synthesis for secretion into blood
questions.question: What is the primary metabolic role of smooth endoplasmic reticulum in hepatocytes?
Which structure contains the greatest amount of cartilage in the bronchial tree?
questions.explanation: The main (primary) bronchi contain the most extensive cartilage, with nearly complete rings similar to but more irregular than tracheal cartilage. As bronchi branch and decrease in diameter, cartilage becomes progressively more sparse, appearing as irregular plates. Bronchioles lack cartilage completely, relying on smooth muscle and elastic tissue.
options: The main bronchi possess the most extensive cartilage
The terminal bronchioles have the most cartilage support
The respiratory bronchioles contain abundant cartilage plates
The lobar bronchi have maximal cartilaginous reinforcement
The segmental bronchi contain the greatest cartilage amount

questions.explanation: The ileum contains the most abundant lymphoid tissue, including numerous large Peyer's patches in the submucosa. This reflects the increasing bacterial load toward the large intestine and the ileum's role in immune surveillance. Individual lymphoid nodules are also present throughout the intestinal lamina propria.
questions.question: Which segment of small intestine has most lymphoid tissue?
options: The duodenum contains the most lymphoid aggregates
The jejunum has the greatest lymphoid tissue amount
The ileum possesses the most abundant lymphoid tissue
All small intestinal segments have equal lymphoid tissue
No lymphoid tissue exists in the small intestine

questions.explanation: Type I (slow-twitch) fibers are rich in myoglobin and mitochondria, relying on oxidative metabolism for sustained ATP production. These fibers contract slowly but resist fatigue, making them ideal for postural maintenance and endurance activities. They appear red due to high myoglobin content.
questions.question: Which muscle fiber type is characterized by high myoglobin content, numerous mitochondria, and resistance to fatigue?

questions.explanation: The initial segment (trigger zone) at the axon hillock contains high concentrations of voltage-gated sodium channels. This region has the lowest threshold for action potential generation due to its high density of ion channels. Summation of excitatory and inhibitory inputs determines whether threshold is reached.
questions.question: What structure at the axon hillock integrates incoming signals to determine if an action potential will be generated?

options: Smooth muscle cells secrete the primary prostatic fluid
Transitional epithelial cells produce the secretory products
Simple columnar epithelial cells generate the secretions
Stratified squamous cells manufacture prostatic components
Mesenchymal stromal cells synthesize the secretory material
questions.explanation: The secretory alveoli of the prostate are lined by simple columnar or cuboidal epithelium that produces the prostatic secretion. This slightly acidic fluid contains citric acid, acid phosphatase, fibrinolysin, and other enzymes that liquefy semen. The epithelial cells show secretory granules in their apical cytoplasm.
questions.question: Which cells in the prostate produce prostatic secretions?
Which layer of blood vessel walls contains smooth muscle cells?
questions.explanation: The tunica media contains circumferentially arranged smooth muscle cells and elastic fibers. Vessel diameter and blood flow are regulated by smooth muscle contraction/relaxation. The media is thickest in arteries, particularly muscular arteries.

Minor salivary glands scattered throughout the oral mucosa contribute approximately 10% of total saliva volume but account for 70% of mucus secreted. These small glands provide continuous baseline secretion maintaining oral moisture. The major salivary glands contribute the remaining 90% of volume.
questions.question: What percentage of total saliva volume comes from minor salivary glands?
options: Minor salivary glands contribute approximately 5 percent
Minor salivary glands generate roughly 25 percent volume
Minor salivary glands secrete around 50 percent total
Minor salivary glands account for about 70 percent
Minor salivary glands produce about 10 percent total

questions.explanation: The proximal tubule reabsorbs ~65% of filtered sodium, water, and virtually all filtered glucose and amino acids. Cells have extensive apical brush border and basolateral membrane infoldings with numerous mitochondria. This high metabolic activity supports active transport.
questions.question: Which segment of the nephron is responsible for most sodium and water reabsorption?

questions.explanation: Flow cytometry analyzes individual cells passing through laser beams, detecting fluorescence from labeled antibodies. FACS (Fluorescence-Activated Cell Sorting) physically separates cell populations based on markers. This enables phenotyping, cell cycle analysis, and purification of specific populations.
questions.question: Which technique allows cell sorting based on fluorescently labeled surface markers?

options: Genetic programs alone control lung development
Amniotic fluid composition regulates lung formation
Fetal breathing movements stimulate lung growth
Placental factors exclusively control lung development
questions.question: What triggers lung development in the fetus?
questions.explanation: Fetal breathing movements, though not ventilating the lungs, provide mechanical stimulation essential for lung development. These movements begin around 10 weeks gestation and help expand airways and promote alveolar development. Oligohydramnios limiting fetal movements can cause pulmonary hypoplasia. Hormones, growth factors, and genetic programs also regulate development.

Colonocytes preferentially use short-chain fatty acids (butyrate, propionate, acetate) produced by bacterial fermentation of dietary fiber as their main energy source. Butyrate is the preferred fuel, supplying about 70% of colonocyte energy needs. This unique metabolism explains why fiber deprivation can lead to colonic atrophy.
options: Glucose from the bloodstream fuels colonocytes primarily
Short-chain fatty acids (especially butyrate) fuel colonocytes
Amino acids provide the main colonocyte energy
Ketone bodies are the primary colonocyte fuel
Lactate serves as the main colonocyte energy source
questions.question: What is the primary energy source for colonocytes?

options: The acinus is centered on a central vein
The acinus is identical to the classical lobule
The acinus has no relevance to liver pathology
The acinus is a diamond-shaped unit between portal triads and central veins
The acinus is purely a theoretical construct
questions.explanation: The hepatic acinus is a diamond-shaped functional unit with portal triads at the narrow ends and central veins at the wide ends. It is divided into three zones based on oxygen and nutrient gradients from portal blood. This model best explains patterns of hepatic injury and metabolic zonation.
questions.question: What characterizes the hepatic acinus of Rappaport?
Which paranasal sinuses are lined with the thinnest respiratory epithelium?
options: All paranasal sinuses have equally thin epithelium
The frontal sinuses have the thinnest epithelial lining
The maxillary sinuses possess minimal epithelial thickness
The ethmoid sinuses contain the least epithelium
The sphenoid sinuses show the thinnest respiratory lining
questions.explanation: All paranasal sinuses are lined with thinner respiratory epithelium than the main nasal cavity, containing fewer goblet cells. The lamina propria is thin with few glands and is continuous with periosteum. This simpler structure reflects the sinuses' function in reducing skull weight and resonating sound.

Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) are resident phagocytes in alveolar spaces that remove inhaled particles and microorganisms. They arise from blood monocytes and can migrate to airways for mucociliary clearance. These cells are vital for maintaining sterile alveolar environment.
questions.question: Which immune cells patrol alveoli, phagocytosing inhaled particulates and pathogens?

options: Ammonia is directly excreted by the kidneys
Ammonia is converted to urea via the urea cycle
Ammonia is exhaled by the lungs unchanged
Ammonia is stored in hepatocytes indefinitely
Ammonia is secreted into bile for elimination
questions.explanation: Hepatocytes convert toxic ammonia (from amino acid deamination and bacterial colonic production) to urea via the urea cycle. Urea is then filtered by glomeruli and excreted in urine. Liver failure impairs urea synthesis causing hyperammonemia, which crosses the blood-brain barrier causing hepatic encephalopathy with altered mental status.
questions.question: What is the fate of ammonia produced in the liver?
What color does eosin impart to cytoplasm in H&E staining?
questions.explanation: Eosin is an acidic dye that binds basic cytoplasmic components (proteins), coloring them pink-red. Acidophilic structures (cytoplasm, collagen) appear pink. The combination of hematoxylin (blue nuclei) and eosin (pink cytoplasm) provides excellent tissue contrast.

Residual paraffin or wax prevents stain penetration, as does insufficient staining time. Proper deparaffinization using xylene or substitutes and adequate staining duration ensure uniform coloration. Nuclear pallor may indicate poor fixation or improper hematoxylin ripening.
questions.question: What causes tissue to appear pale or unstained in certain areas?
Which special stain demonstrates reticular fibers by silver impregnation?
questions.explanation: Reticulin stains (silver impregnation) blacken reticular fibers (type III collagen) due to their high carbohydrate content. This technique visualizes delicate connective tissue frameworks in lymphoid organs, liver, and bone marrow. The fibers appear black against pale backgrounds.

questions.question: What is the role of atrial natriuretic peptide?
options: ANP increases sodium reabsorption in kidneys
ANP promotes sodium excretion and vasodilation
ANP stimulates aldosterone and renin release
ANP increases blood pressure through vasoconstriction
questions.explanation: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), released from atrial myocytes in response to atrial stretch from volume expansion, promotes natriuresis (sodium excretion) by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in collecting ducts. ANP also causes vasodilation, inhibits renin and aldosterone secretion, and increases GFR. These effects reduce blood volume and pressure.

Striated ducts modify saliva by reabsorbing sodium and chloride while secreting potassium and bicarbonate, making saliva hypotonic relative to plasma. The extensive basal membrane infoldings with associated mitochondria provide energy for these active transport processes. This modification occurs in both parotid and submandibular glands.
questions.question: Which duct type is responsible for modifying saliva composition?
options: Intercalated ducts actively transport ions to modify saliva
Interlobular ducts concentrate saliva by water absorption
Excretory ducts remove sodium and add mucus proteins
Main ducts acidify saliva through proton secretion
Striated ducts reabsorb sodium and secrete potassium

questions.explanation: The anal canal transitions from simple columnar rectal epithelium to stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium in the mid-portion, then to keratinized stratified squamous epithelium at the external anal orifice. This reflects the transition from internal mucosa to external skin. The keratinized epithelium provides protection against abrasion.
options: Simple columnar epithelium lines the anal canal
Pseudostratified ciliated epithelium covers the anal canal
Transitional epithelium allows anal canal distension
Stratified squamous keratinized epithelium lines it distally
Simple cuboidal epithelium forms the anal lining
questions.question: Which epithelium lines the anal canal?

questions.explanation: Elastic cartilage contains numerous elastic fibers in addition to type II collagen, providing flexibility while maintaining shape. This is evident in the auricle, external auditory canal, and epiglottis. The elastic fibers can be visualized using special stains like Verhoeff's.
questions.question: What distinguishes elastic cartilage from hyaline cartilage histologically?

options: Insufficient gastric acid production causes malabsorption
Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells occurs
Gastric outlet obstruction causes acid retention
Gastrin-secreting tumor causes excessive acid production
questions.explanation: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome results from a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma), usually in the pancreas or duodenum. Excessive gastrin stimulates massive acid secretion, causing severe peptic ulcers often in unusual locations (jejunum). Patients develop diarrhea from acid inactivating pancreatic enzymes. Treatment includes proton pump inhibitors and tumor resection.
questions.question: What characterizes Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?

options: Elastic fibers prevent alveolar overdistension during inspiration
Elastic fibers maintain constant alveolar diameter throughout breathing
Elastic fibers produce surfactant to reduce surface tension
Elastic fibers anchor alveoli to bronchiolar structures
Elastic fibers facilitate alveolar collapse during expiration
questions.question: What is the primary function of elastic fibers in alveolar walls?
questions.explanation: Elastic fibers in alveolar walls store energy during inspiration and facilitate passive recoil during expiration. This elastic recoil helps expel air from alveoli without muscular effort and maintains alveolar architecture. Loss of elastic fibers in emphysema impairs expiration and causes air trapping.

questions.question: Which second messenger is produced by activation of phospholipase C?
questions.explanation: Phospholipase C cleaves PIP2 into IP3 (inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate) and DAG (diacylglycerol). IP3 releases calcium from ER stores while DAG activates protein kinase C. This signaling pathway mediates many hormone and neurotransmitter responses.

Verhoeff's elastic stain uses hematoxylin-ferric chloride solution to color elastic fibers black. This demonstrates elastic tissue distribution in arteries, lungs, and skin. Van Gieson stain can be used as counterstain, coloring collagen red.
questions.question: Which stain is used to visualize elastic fibers?
What stimulates saliva production by salivary glands?
options: Sympathetic stimulation produces copious watery saliva primarily
Somatic motor nerves directly trigger salivary secretion
Parasympathetic stimulation causes vasodilation and abundant secretion
Hormonal signals from the pituitary control saliva production
Local tissue stretch activates salivary cell secretion
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic stimulation via facial and glossopharyngeal nerves produces vasodilation and copious watery saliva secretion in response to taste or smell of food. Sympathetic stimulation produces smaller volumes of more viscous, protein-rich saliva. Both divisions are active to varying degrees during secretion.

Pancreatic acinar cells synthesize and secrete digestive enzymes (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, amylase, lipase) in zymogen granules. These serous cells have basophilic cytoplasm and apical eosinophilic granules. Enzymes are released into the ductal system in inactive forms.
questions.question: What is the exocrine product of pancreatic acinar cells?

questions.explanation: Parietal (oxyntic) cells in gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid through an active transport mechanism involving H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump). These large eosinophilic cells also produce intrinsic factor necessary for vitamin B12 absorption. The acid activates pepsinogen and provides optimal pH for pepsin activity.
questions.question: Which cells produce hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
options: Chief cells secrete hydrochloric acid into gastric lumen
Mucous neck cells generate acid for digestion
G cells synthesize and release hydrochloric acid
Parietal cells produce and secrete hydrochloric acid
Surface mucous cells create the acidic environment

questions.question: Which hormone raises blood calcium levels by stimulating osteoclastic bone resorption?
questions.explanation: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) increases serum calcium by stimulating osteoclast activity, enhancing renal calcium reabsorption, and promoting vitamin D activation. PTH acts indirectly on osteoclasts through osteoblast-mediated signaling involving RANKL. This hormone is essential for maintaining calcium homeostasis.

Basal keratinocytes include stem cells that continuously divide to renew the epidermis. Some daughter cells remain in the basal layer (self-renewal) while others differentiate and migrate upward. This maintains homeostatic balance in epidermal turnover.
questions.question: Which cells in the epidermis serve as stem cells for epidermal renewal?
What causes acute tubular necrosis?
options: Ischemia or toxins cause acute tubular cell death
Chronic hypertension damages tubular epithelium slowly
Autoimmune attack destroys tubular cells acutely
Genetic defects cause tubular cell necrosis
Dietary deficiencies lead to tubular necrosis
questions.explanation: Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) results from severe ischemia (shock, surgery) or nephrotoxins (aminoglycosides, contrast agents) causing tubular epithelial cell death and acute kidney injury. The proximal tubule and thick ascending limb are most vulnerable. ATN is potentially reversible if the underlying cause is corrected promptly.

questions.question: Which region of the GI tract has mucosa-associated glands (Brunner's glands) that secrete alkaline mucus?
questions.explanation: Brunner's glands in the duodenal submucosa secrete alkaline mucus-rich fluid that neutralizes acidic chyme from the stomach. This protects the duodenal mucosa and creates optimal pH for pancreatic enzyme activity. These compound tubular glands extend into the mucosa.

options: The proximal convoluted tubule exhibits this feature
The distal convoluted tubule has extensive microvilli
The thin segment of Henle's loop displays it
The collecting duct possesses the tallest microvilli
The macula densa region shows prominent borders
questions.explanation: The proximal convoluted tubule possesses abundant apical microvilli forming a prominent brush border that greatly increases surface area. This structural adaptation facilitates the massive reabsorption of glucose, amino acids, proteins, and other nutrients from the filtrate. The eosinophilic cytoplasm reflects numerous mitochondria required for active transport processes.
questions.question: Which segment of the nephron has the most prominent brush border?

questions.explanation: Estrogen from developing ovarian follicles stimulates endometrial proliferation, increasing gland and stromal cellularity. Blood vessels elongate and spiral arteries develop. This prepares the endometrium for potential implantation. The proliferative phase lasts from menstruation until ovulation.
questions.question: What hormone stimulates endometrial proliferation during the follicular phase?

questions.explanation: Gap junctions within intercalated discs provide electrical coupling between cardiac myocytes, allowing rapid action potential propagation. This creates functional syncytium enabling coordinated contraction. Desmosomes and fascia adherens in intercalated discs provide mechanical coupling.
questions.question: Which cardiac muscle feature allows synchronized contraction of the myocardium?

questions.explanation: Corpora arenacea (brain sand) are calcified deposits increasing with age. They're visible on skull X-rays and CT scans, serving as anatomical landmarks. Their composition includes calcium phosphate and carbonate. Functional significance is uncertain.
questions.question: What are corpora arenacea in the pineal gland?

options: Celiac disease from gluten sensitivity develops
Whipple's disease from bacterial infection occurs
questions.explanation: Lactase deficiency (hypolactasia) prevents lactose digestion, causing it to be fermented by colonic bacteria producing gas, bloating, and diarrhea after dairy consumption. Primary lactase deficiency is common in adults worldwide, varying by ethnicity. Secondary lactase deficiency can result from intestinal diseases.
questions.question: What disease results from lactase deficiency in adults?

questions.explanation: Kupffer cells are specialized macrophages attached to sinusoidal endothelium or free in the lumen, comprising about 15% of liver cells. They phagocytose aged erythrocytes, bacteria from the portal blood, and other debris. Kupffer cells are most numerous in periportal regions where they first encounter portal blood.
questions.question: Which cells in liver sinusoids are phagocytic?
options: Hepatocytes perform phagocytosis in the sinusoids
Kupffer cells are macrophages in sinusoid lumens
Stellate cells remove debris from sinusoidal blood
Endothelial cells phagocytose particles passing through
Bile duct cells ingest foreign material actively
Skeletal muscle of the pelvic floor forms it
Smooth muscle of the detrusor creates this sphincter
Cardiac muscle fibers encircle the urethral lumen
Oblique smooth muscle layers compose this structure
Circular cardiac muscle surrounds the urethra
questions.explanation: The external urethral sphincter consists of skeletal muscle fibers from the pelvic floor musculature surrounding the urethra. This voluntary sphincter provides conscious control over micturition, contrasting with the involuntary smooth muscle internal sphincter. Damage to this sphincter can result in urinary incontinence.
questions.question: What muscle forms the external urethral sphincter?
What is the primary component of the interalveolar septum?
questions.explanation: The interalveolar septum consists primarily of a capillary network with minimal supporting connective tissue containing elastic and reticular fibers. The thin septum minimizes diffusion distance while maintaining structural integrity. Excessive connective tissue deposition in pulmonary fibrosis impairs gas exchange.
options: Dense collagenous connective tissue forms the septum
Smooth muscle bundles constitute septal structure
Cartilage plates provide septal rigidity throughout
Adipose tissue fills the interalveolar spaces
Capillaries and minimal connective tissue compose it

questions.question: What structure occupies the core of intestinal villi?
options: Loose connective tissue with vessels forms the core
Dense connective tissue forms the villus core
Smooth muscle bundles fill the villus center
Adipose tissue occupies the central villus region
Cartilage supports the villus structure centrally
questions.explanation: Each villus has a core of loose connective tissue (lamina propria) containing a capillary network, a central lacteal lymphatic vessel, smooth muscle cells, and scattered immune cells. This highly vascularized core allows efficient absorption of nutrients into blood and lymph. Smooth muscle contractions aid in pumping lymph from lacteals.

Parafollicular C cells (clear cells) reside between follicles and produce calcitonin in response to hypercalcemia. Calcitonin inhibits osteoclast activity, lowering blood calcium. These cells originate from neural crest, unlike follicular cells from endoderm.
questions.question: What cells surround thyroid follicles and produce calcitonin?

questions.explanation: The total alveolar surface area in adult lungs approximates 160 square meters, roughly equal to a tennis court and 80 times the body's skin area. This enormous surface maximizes gas exchange efficiency despite lungs occupying relatively small thoracic volume. The surface area decreases with age and in emphysema.
options: Alveolar surface approaches 160 square meters overall
Alveolar surface approximates 10 square meters total
Alveolar surface reaches about 50 square meters
Alveolar surface extends to 300 square meters
Alveolar surface measures roughly 500 square meters
questions.question: What is the total surface area of alveoli in adult human lungs?

questions.explanation: Metaphase is characterized by chromosome alignment at the metaphase plate (cell equator) with kinetochores attached to spindle fibers. The metaphase checkpoint ensures proper chromosome attachment before anaphase progression. This alignment is critical for equal chromosome segregation.
questions.question: During which mitotic phase do chromosomes align at the cell's equator?

questions.explanation: Different fluorophores (FITC, rhodamine, Cy3, Cy5) with distinct emission spectra allow simultaneous detection of multiple antigens. This permits colocalization studies and analysis of protein interactions. Fluorescence intensity can also indicate relative expression levels.
questions.question: What is the advantage of using fluorescent secondary antibodies in immunofluorescence?
What prevents backflow of urine from bladder to ureters?
questions.explanation: The ureters enter the bladder obliquely through its posterior wall, creating a valve mechanism that prevents vesicoureteral reflux. As the bladder fills and wall tension increases, the intramural portion of the ureter is compressed closed. This anatomical arrangement functions without specialized sphincter muscles.
options: Specialized circular sphincters surround each ureteric orifice
Transitional epithelium forms one-way valve structures
Oblique passage of ureters through bladder wall
Smooth muscle peristalsis maintains forward flow only
External compression by detrusor muscle prevents reflux

questions.explanation: Caspases are cysteine proteases that cleave target proteins at aspartate residues. Initiator caspases (8, 9) activate executioner caspases (3, 6, 7), which dismantle cellular structures. Caspase activation is a point of no return in apoptosis.
questions.question: What are the executioner enzymes of apoptosis?
Which enzyme is secreted by serous demilunes in submandibular glands?
options: Amylase breaks down complex carbohydrates into sugars
Lipase digests dietary fats into fatty acids
Pepsinogen initiates protein digestion in saliva
Nuclease degrades nucleic acids in oral cavity
Lysozyme hydrolyzes bacterial cell wall components
questions.explanation: Serous demilunes in submandibular and sublingual glands secrete lysozyme, an antimicrobial enzyme that hydrolyzes peptidoglycan in bacterial cell walls. This provides innate immune protection in the oral cavity. The demilunes also secrete IgA and other protective proteins.

Four parathyroid glands (two superior, two inferior) are typically embedded in the posterior thyroid capsule. Number varies (2-6 glands). They develop from pharyngeal pouches and can have ectopic locations, complicating surgical identification.
questions.question: How many parathyroid glands are typically present?
What glands secrete serous fluid that rinses the trenches around circumvallate papillae?
questions.explanation: Von Ebner's glands are serous glands opening into the trenches of circumvallate and foliate papillae. Their watery secretion contains lipase and washes away taste stimuli, allowing rapid stimulus changes. This enables detection of new taste sensations.

Juxtaglomerular cells (modified smooth muscle in afferent arterioles) are the sole source of renin in the kidney. Renin release is stimulated by decreased renal perfusion pressure, sympathetic activation, and signals from macula densa. This initiates the RAAS cascade.
questions.question: What structure in the kidney produces renin?

options: Simple columnar epithelium with microvilli lines it
Simple squamous epithelium lines the gallbladder
Stratified columnar epithelium forms the lining
Pseudostratified epithelium with goblet cells lines it
questions.explanation: The gallbladder is lined by simple tall columnar epithelium with short microvilli that actively absorb water and electrolytes from bile. The cells are joined by tight junctions preventing bile leakage. No goblet cells are present. The epithelium rests on a lamina propria and muscular layer without a muscularis mucosae.
questions.question: Which cell type lines the gallbladder?
Which region of the GI tract has both submucosal and mucosal glands?
questions.explanation: The duodenum uniquely possesses Brunner's glands in the submucosa (secreting alkaline mucus) and Crypts of Lieberkühn in the mucosa (containing stem cells, Paneth cells, goblet cells). This dual gland distribution protects against gastric acid and supports rapid cell turnover.

questions.question: Which structure prevents gastroesophageal reflux?
questions.explanation: The lower esophageal sphincter, formed by thickened circular smooth muscle at the gastroesophageal junction, prevents reflux of acidic gastric contents. The acute angle of entry (angle of His) and diaphragmatic crura also contribute to the antireflux mechanism. Sphincter incompetence causes gastroesophageal reflux disease.
options: The upper esophageal sphincter prevents acid reflux completely
Specialized valves in the esophagus block retrograde flow
The angle of His has no role in preventing reflux
The lower esophageal sphincter inhibits reflux normally
Esophageal peristalsis alone prevents all gastric reflux

questions.question: What prostatic secretion contributes to semen liquefaction?
questions.explanation: PSA (kallikrein-related peptidase 3) is a serine protease that liquefies coagulated semen by cleaving seminogelin and fibronectin. This allows sperm motility in the female reproductive tract. Elevated serum PSA may indicate prostate pathology.

questions.question: What type of glands are found throughout the esophageal submucosa?
questions.explanation: Esophageal glands proper in the submucosa are compound tubuloalveolar mucous glands producing lubricating secretions. Their ducts penetrate the muscularis mucosae to open onto the esophageal lumen. These glands are scattered throughout the esophageal length and increase secretion during swallowing.
options: Serous glands producing enzyme-rich secretions predominate
Mixed seromucous glands with both components
Mucous glands secreting protective lubricating fluid

questions.explanation: Thick ascending limb cells actively transport NaCl into the medullary interstitium while remaining impermeable to water, creating and maintaining the osmotic gradient. This countercurrent multiplier system allows urine concentration. The gradient is preserved by vasa recta countercurrent exchange and urea recycling.
options: Proximal tubule cells establish the osmotic gradient
Thin limb epithelium maintains the gradient passively
Collecting duct cells generate the osmotic gradient
Thick ascending limb cells actively create the gradient
Glomerular cells produce the medullary gradient
questions.question: Which cell maintains the medullary osmotic gradient?

questions.explanation: The submandibular gland produces mixed seromucous secretions with approximately 90% serous acini and 10% mucous tubules capped by serous demilunes. This combination provides both enzymatic activity and lubrication. The mixed secretion contributes significantly to total saliva composition.
questions.question: What composition characterizes submandibular gland secretions?
options: The submandibular produces purely mucous secretions exclusively
The submandibular creates mixed seromucous secretions
The submandibular generates only serous watery saliva
The submandibular manufactures predominantly lipid-rich saliva
The submandibular secretes primarily glycogen-containing fluid

questions.question: What stimulates aldosterone secretion from zona glomerulosa?
questions.explanation: Aldosterone secretion is primarily stimulated by angiotensin II (via RAAS) and elevated plasma potassium. ACTH has minor effects. Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in the distal nephron, regulating blood pressure and electrolytes.

Cartilage progresses from nearly complete rings in main bronchi to irregular crescentic plates in smaller bronchi, eventually disappearing entirely in bronchioles. This structural change parallels the decreasing diameter and the transition from cartilaginous to smooth muscle support. The loss of cartilage makes bronchioles susceptible to collapse during forced expiration.
options: Cartilage becomes more abundant in distal branches
Cartilage changes from hyaline to elastic type
Cartilage increases in thickness toward periphery
Cartilage persists throughout all bronchiolar branches
Cartilage transforms from rings to irregular plates
questions.question: What happens to cartilage distribution along the bronchial tree?
What artifact appears as brown-black granular deposits in formalin-fixed tissues?
questions.explanation: Formalin pigment (acid hematin) forms when acidic formalin reacts with blood, creating brown-black granules. It's removable by treating sections with saturated alcoholic picric acid or treating tissues with buffered formalin. Proper pH-buffered fixatives prevent formation.

questions.question: What enzyme is commonly conjugated to secondary antibodies for chromogenic detection?
questions.explanation: Horseradish peroxidase (HRP) and alkaline phosphatase (AP) are commonly used enzyme labels. HRP produces brown precipitates with DAB substrate while AP yields blue/red products with various substrates. These create permanent, light-stable staining visible by light microscopy.

Barrett's esophagus shows replacement of normal stratified squamous epithelium with intestinal-type columnar epithelium containing goblet cells. This metaplasia results from chronic acid reflux. It predisposes to adenocarcinoma, requiring surveillance.
questions.question: What epithelial change in Barrett's esophagus represents intestinal metaplasia?

options: Supporting cells divide to replace all epithelial types
Basal cells generate new olfactory neurons throughout life
Olfactory neurons themselves undergo continuous division
Brush cells proliferate to maintain the epithelium
Bowman's gland cells migrate to replenish surface cells
questions.question: Which cells in olfactory epithelium serve as stem cells?
questions.explanation: Basal cells are stem cells that continuously divide to produce new olfactory receptor neurons, making them unique among neurons in their regenerative capacity. This turnover is necessary because olfactory neurons are directly exposed to environmental insults. The entire olfactory epithelium can regenerate after injury.

options: Serous glands produce watery enzyme-rich secretions
Mucous glands secrete protective glycoproteins abundantly
Mixed glands contribute both mucous and serous
Sebaceous glands provide lipid-based secretions regularly
Endocrine glands release hormones into the circulation
questions.question: What type of glands are associated with circumvallate papillae?
questions.explanation: Circumvallate papillae are surrounded by serous glands (von Ebner's glands) that secrete a watery, enzyme-containing fluid. This secretion washes the taste pores clean of food particles and taste stimulants, preparing the receptors for new stimuli. The continuous flow also helps maintain the microenvironment necessary for optimal taste receptor function.

ADH (vasopressin) release is primarily regulated by osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detecting plasma osmolarity changes. Increased osmolarity triggers ADH secretion, promoting water reabsorption in collecting ducts. Volume receptors and blood pressure also influence ADH release.
questions.question: What regulates ADH release from the neurohypophysis?

options: Excessive red blood cell destruction overwhelms liver
Bile duct obstruction prevents bilirubin excretion
Hemolytic disease destroys fetal red blood cells
Immature hepatocyte smooth ER has inadequate conjugating enzymes
questions.question: What causes neonatal jaundice in premature infants?
questions.explanation: Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia occurs because premature infant hepatocytes have underdeveloped smooth endoplasmic reticulum with insufficient glucuronyltransferase for bilirubin conjugation. Unconjugated bilirubin accumulates, causing jaundice and potential neurotoxicity (kernicterus). Phototherapy converts bilirubin to water-soluble photoisomers excretable by kidneys.

questions.question: Which cyclin-CDK complex regulates the G1/S checkpoint?
questions.explanation: Cyclin E-CDK2 complex promotes entry into S phase by phosphorylating proteins required for DNA replication initiation. This checkpoint ensures favorable growth conditions and absence of DNA damage before committing to replication. p53 and Rb proteins regulate this transition.

questions.question: What is the most common renal tumor in adults?
options: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) is most common in adults
Transitional cell carcinoma predominates in adult kidneys
Renal cell carcinoma is the most frequent renal tumor
Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type
Adenoma is the most frequent adult renal tumor
questions.explanation: Renal cell carcinoma arising from proximal tubule epithelium is the most common kidney malignancy in adults (85% of renal tumors). It often presents late with hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass. The tumor is highly vascular and may produce paraneoplastic syndromes including erythrocytosis from erythropoietin production.

questions.question: Which accessory gland contributes fructose-rich alkaline fluid comprising ~70% of semen volume?
questions.explanation: Seminal vesicles produce fructose (energy source for sperm), prostaglandins, and coagulating proteins. Their secretion is alkaline, neutralizing vaginal acidity. The highly folded mucosa increases secretory surface area.

Cirrhosis shows nodules of regenerating hepatocytes surrounded by dense fibrous septa bridging portal tracts and central veins. This disrupts normal architecture and blood flow. Progressive fibrosis from chronic injury (alcohol, hepatitis) leads to liver failure and portal hypertension.
questions.question: What histological change characterizes cirrhosis of the liver?

options: Asthma results from ciliary immotility exclusively
Cystic fibrosis primarily affects ciliary motility
Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) causes immotile cilia
Chronic bronchitis results from ciliary paralysis
questions.explanation: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) is caused by defective dynein or other ciliary proteins, resulting in immotile cilia and flagella. This causes chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and male infertility (immotile sperm). The condition may be associated with situs inversus due to defective embryonic ciliary function.
questions.question: Which respiratory disease involves immotile cilia?

questions.explanation: Transitional epithelium appears multilayered when relaxed but stretches to appear thinner when distended. The surface cells are characteristically large and dome-shaped in the relaxed state. This specialized epithelium is uniquely adapted to withstand mechanical stress and volume fluctuations.
questions.question: Which type of epithelium lines the urinary bladder and can accommodate significant volume changes?

questions.explanation: Taste buds contain 50-100 taste receptor cells, supporting cells, and basal cells within taste pores. They occur mainly on tongue papillae (fungiform, foliate, circumvallate) but also on soft palate and pharynx. Taste cells are chemoreceptors detecting sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami.
questions.question: Where are taste receptor cells located?

questions.explanation: Fixation causes protein cross-linking and ~10% shrinkage; dehydration removes water causing further shrinkage; clearing and embedding introduce additional dimensional changes. The cumulative effect can reduce tissue volume by 20-30%. Proper technique minimizes but cannot eliminate artifacts.
questions.question: What causes tissue shrinkage during processing?
What cells line the collecting ducts in the kidney?
options: Simple squamous epithelium lines collecting ducts
Stratified columnar epithelium forms duct lining
Pseudostratified epithelium with cilia lines ducts
Cuboidal epithelium with principal and intercalated cells
questions.explanation: Collecting ducts are lined by simple cuboidal epithelium consisting of pale-staining principal cells (involved in Na+/K+ exchange and water reabsorption) and darker intercalated cells (involved in acid-base balance). Cell boundaries are distinct unlike in proximal tubule. The epithelium becomes taller (columnar) in larger collecting ducts.

Approximately 20% of renal plasma flow is filtered at the glomerulus (filtration fraction = GFR/RPF). This balance maintains adequate filtration while preventing excessive protein concentration in post-glomerular blood. Changes in filtration fraction affect tubular reabsorption.
questions.question: What is the filtration fraction in normal kidneys?

questions.explanation: Type II alveolar cells serve as progenitor cells that proliferate after injury and can differentiate into type I cells to restore the alveolar epithelium. Type I cells are terminally differentiated and cannot divide. This regenerative capacity is crucial for lung repair after conditions like acute respiratory distress syndrome.
options: Type I alveolar cells divide to replace damage
Alveolar macrophages transform into epithelial cells
Capillary endothelial cells become alveolar epithelium
Type II alveolar cells differentiate to replace type I cells
questions.question: Which cells replace damaged alveolar epithelium?
Which anterior pituitary cells secrete growth hormone?
questions.explanation: Somatotrophs (most abundant acidophil) secrete growth hormone (GH), which promotes growth and regulates metabolism. GH secretion follows pulsatile patterns with nocturnal surges. GH acts directly and via IGF-1 produced in the liver.

The stomach's muscularis externa includes an inner oblique layer not found in other GI regions, in addition to the usual middle circular and outer longitudinal layers.
