Other autoantibodies listed are associated with different autoimmune conditions such as liver or vasculitic disease. Serological monitoring complements clinical assessment of growth and symptom control.

Asterixis (hepatic flap or flapping tremor), elicited by outstretched hands, is a sign of hepatic encephalopathy caused by impaired neuromuscular coordination from ammonia and other toxin accumulation. It is not specific to liver disease but is prominent and early in hepatic encephalopathy.
questions.question: Asterixis (flapping tremor) is a sign of which complication in portal hypertension?

questions.explanation: The starry-sky appearance on histology, caused by macrophages ingesting apoptotic tumour cells scattered among a background of rapidly proliferating malignant lymphocytes, is characteristic of Burkitt lymphoma or its leukaemic counterpart. This is one of the fastest-growing human tumours, requiring urgent diagnosis and treatment.
questions.question: A 3-year-old presents with fever, pallor, and generalised lymphadenopathy. Peripheral blood film shows numerous blasts with a starry-sky appearance suspected on marrow biopsy. Which malignancy is most likely?

questions.explanation: Genu valgum in rickets results from retarded growth on the lateral aspect of the growth plate, causing the limb to angle inward, in contrast to genu varum where medial retardation causes outward bowing. Understanding this asymmetry helps predict deformity patterns during treatment. Correction of the underlying rickets allows the growth plate abnormality to gradually resolve.
options: Retarded growth on the lateral side of plate
Retarded growth on the medial side of plate
Symmetrical growth retardation on both sides
Accelerated growth on the lateral side of plate
Retarded growth confined to the diaphysis only
questions.question: A child with knock knees is being evaluated for underlying rickets. Which growth plate change BEST explains the direction of this specific deformity?

questions.explanation: Bacterial causes of neonatal cholestasis include syphilis, E. coli (beta-haemolytic), Listeria monocytogenes, Tuberculosis, and Staphylococcus aureus. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is not specifically listed among the bacterial causes of neonatal cholestasis in the documents provided.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a bacterial cause of neonatal cholestasis?

questions.explanation: Norovirus belongs to the family Caliciviridae and is the most common cause of epidemic non-bacterial gastroenteritis across all age groups worldwide. It spreads via the faecal-oral route and contaminated food, and typically causes a self-limiting illness of 1–3 days.
questions.question: Norovirus belongs to which family of viruses and is the commonest cause of epidemic gastroenteritis across which age group?
The BEST treatment for endemic cretinism to prevent neurological damage is:
options: Neonatal thyroxine replacement within 2 weeks of birth
Iodised salt before and during pregnancy
questions.explanation: The best treatment for endemic cretinism is prevention through correction of iodine deficiency using iodised salt or dietary supplements before and during pregnancy. Neurological damage once established during the critical fetal brain development period is untreatable. Levothyroxine given postnatally treats hypothyroidism but cannot reverse established fetal neurological injury.

A soft tissue mass with relative gaslessness (airless area) in the right lower quadrant on plain abdominal X-ray is the most specific finding for intussusception, representing the intussusceptum displaced into the ascending or transverse colon. Other findings (dilated bowel, air-fluid levels) are non-specific. However, plain X-ray may be completely normal in up to 25% of intussusception cases.
questions.question: Which imaging finding is MOST specific for intussusception on plain X-ray?
options: Multiple air-fluid levels throughout the bowel
Ground glass appearance in the pelvis
The child only, if aged over 10 years
The haematology department on the child's behalf
The ward sister as part of standard nursing documentation
Parents or legal guardians before transfusion
Consent is implicit in the emergency setting and not required
questions.explanation: Informed consent for blood transfusion must be obtained from parents or legal guardians (and from the child themselves where they have sufficient understanding), as transfusion carries real risks including infection, alloimmunisation, and transfusion reactions. The process involves explaining the indication, risks, alternatives, and the right to refuse. Documentation of consent is a medicolegal requirement. In genuine emergencies where consent cannot be obtained and the child's life is at risk, transfusion may proceed under emergency provisions.
questions.question: In paediatric blood transfusion practice, informed consent must be obtained from whom?

questions.explanation: Human tetanus immunoglobulin (HTIG) for neonatal tetanus is 500 IU IM. For children (post-neonatal tetanus), HTIG is 2,000 IU IM. Equine antitetanus serum (ATS) is given at 10,000–20,000 IU IM for all ages. Confusing neonatal (500 IU) and child (2,000 IU) HTIG doses—or confusing HTIG with equine ATS (10,000–20,000 IU)—is a common examination error.
questions.question: A 4-month-old presents with trismus, poor feeding, and generalised stiffness after delivery at home. In neonatal tetanus, what is the dose of human tetanus immunoglobulin (HTIG) for neonates specifically?

options: PNH occurs only in children under 5 years
PNH is always associated with hypersplenism
PNH produces basophilic stippling on peripheral smear
PNH is caused by antibody-mediated destruction of RBCs
questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) from other extrinsic causes of haemolysis?
questions.explanation: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria results from a somatic mutation in the PIG-A gene, leading to deficiency of GPI-anchored complement regulatory proteins (CD55 and CD59) on the red cell surface. This renders RBCs susceptible to complement-mediated lysis, particularly during sleep when slight respiratory acidosis activates the complement pathway. It is classified among extrinsic haemolytic anaemias due to the acquired susceptibility to complement.

Acute stroke in sickle cell disease is a medical emergency treated with urgent exchange blood transfusion to rapidly lower the percentage of sickle haemoglobin and improve cerebral perfusion, reducing the risk of extension or recurrence. Corticosteroids, hydroxyurea loading, watchful waiting, and antibiotics alone do not address the acute vaso-occlusive event causing the stroke. Rapid recognition and transfusion significantly improve neurological outcome.
questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease presents with sudden hemiparesis and slurred speech. Neuroimaging confirms an acute ischaemic stroke. The IMMEDIATE treatment of choice is:
options: Exchange blood transfusion to rapidly reduce HbS percentage
Oral hydroxyurea started at a high loading dose
Watchful waiting with serial neurological examinations only
Accurate molecular diagnosis of the proband
Discussing termination of pregnancy options immediately
Requesting all available genetic tests simultaneously
questions.explanation: Accurate diagnosis of the proband is the first and most essential step in genetic counselling. Without a precise diagnosis, recurrence risks, mode of inheritance, natural history, and management options cannot be meaningfully discussed. Ancillary genetic testing, molecular confirmation, and specialist review may be needed to establish an accurate diagnosis before counselling can proceed.
questions.question: The MOST important first step in genetic counselling before calculating recurrence risks is:
Abdominal ultrasound scan in hepatitis is primarily used to assess:
questions.explanation: Abdominal ultrasound in chronic liver disease and hepatitis assesses liver size, echogenicity (cirrhosis appears heterogeneous), portal vein patency and diameter, splenomegaly, ascites, and focal lesions. Doppler ultrasound can evaluate portal haemodynamics for portal hypertension.
options: Hepatic architecture, portal vein patency, and presence of focal lesions or ascites

questions.question: The subunit of TSH that provides TSH-specific biological activity and receptor binding (distinct from the alpha subunit shared with gonadotrophins) is the:
questions.explanation: TSH has alpha and beta subunits. The alpha subunit is common to LH, FSH, hCG, and TSH. The beta subunit is TSH-specific and is required for binding to the TSH receptor and conferring full biological activity. This shared alpha subunit structure explains cross-reactivity of very high hCG with TSH receptors in trophoblastic disease.

questions.question: Rapid-acting insulin analogue (Insulin Aspart) differs from regular short-acting insulin primarily in that it has:
questions.explanation: Insulin Aspart has a faster onset and shorter duration than regular crystalline insulin, making it ideally suited for administration at meal times. It more closely mimics the physiological postprandial insulin spike, reduces post-meal hyperglycaemia, and minimises the risk of late hypoglycaemia compared to standard short-acting insulin.

questions.question: A child with coarse facial features, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly, and joint stiffness is diagnosed with a mucopolysaccharidosis. Which enzyme deficiency underlies this presentation?
questions.explanation: Hurler syndrome, mucopolysaccharidosis type I, results from alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency causing glycosaminoglycan accumulation that produces coarse facial features, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly, and progressive joint stiffness. Early enzyme replacement or stem cell transplantation can modify disease progression if started early. Multisystem involvement requires a coordinated specialist team approach.

questions.question: Which investigations are used to screen for haemochromatosis in portal hypertension evaluation?
options: Alpha-1 antitrypsin phenotype and serum iron studies
Serum bile acids and liver biopsy
questions.explanation: Haemochromatosis screening involves serum ferritin (elevated) and transferrin saturation (>45–50%). HFE gene mutation testing confirms hereditary haemochromatosis. Ceruloplasmin and copper are for Wilson's disease; alpha-1 antitrypsin phenotype screens for A1AT deficiency.

A firm, non-transilluminating scrotal mass with markedly elevated alpha-fetoprotein in a young child is highly suggestive of a testicular yolk sac tumour, the commonest prepubertal testicular malignancy. Alpha-fetoprotein serves as a valuable tumour marker for diagnosis and monitoring treatment response.
questions.question: A 4-year-old boy presents with painless gross haematuria and a firm scrotal mass that does not transilluminate. Alpha-fetoprotein is markedly elevated. Which diagnosis is most likely?
Which of the following is NOT a cause of DIC?
questions.explanation: Beta-thalassaemia trait (minor) is a benign carrier state with mild microcytic anaemia but without any coagulopathy or haemostatic disorder. It does not cause DIC. Recognised causes of DIC include homozygous protein C and S deficiency (causing neonatal purpura fulminans), malignancies (releasing tissue factor), haemolytic transfusion reactions (releasing RBC stroma activating coagulation), massive trauma (releasing tissue thromboplastins), infections, and giant haemangioma.

In Social Paediatrics, behaviour is understood as a function of knowledge, beliefs, attitudes, actual experiences, societal norms, and enabling factors such as poverty. These behavioural determinants affect the presentation, course, and final outcome of disease. Genetics, parental influence, and outcome effects are all encompassed within, not separate from, behavioural determinants.
options: Behaviour reflects knowledge, beliefs, and societal norms
Behaviour is genetically fixed and cannot be modified
Behaviour affects only the presentation but not the final outcome of disease
Parental behaviour has no influence on child health outcomes
Behavioural determinants apply only to infectious diseases
questions.question: Which statement MOST accurately describes the role of behaviour in Social Paediatrics, as it relates to disease outcomes in children?

questions.explanation: Abdominal pain during a vaso-occlusive crisis often resembles the child's previous crisis pattern and lacks true peritoneal signs such as rebound tenderness, guarding, or a rigid abdomen, which would instead suggest a surgical cause requiring urgent evaluation. Careful clinical assessment helps differentiate these overlapping presentations.
options: Fever with a tender, palpable mass
Pain pattern consistent with the child's previous typical crises and absence of peritonism
questions.question: A 5-year-old with sickle cell disease develops acute severe abdominal pain mimicking an acute abdomen during a painful crisis. Which feature would most favour vaso-occlusive crisis over a surgical cause?
Niemann-Pick disease Type A results from sphingomyelinase deficiency, causing progressive neurodegeneration. The hallmark funduscopic finding shared with Tay-Sachs disease is:
questions.explanation: A cherry-red macular spot on funduscopy is the hallmark of several lysosomal storage diseases including Tay-Sachs (GM2 gangliosidosis), Niemann-Pick Type A, Sandhoff disease, and generalised gangliosidosis. It results from normal macular ganglion cells appearing red against a white perimacula where lipid has accumulated in the retinal ganglion cells surrounding the fovea.

questions.question: Adolescents are increasingly used to incite violence during elections, and internet addiction with exposure to pornography is rising. These risks are classified under which broad challenge category in the adolescence framework?
questions.explanation: Accidents and violence (including being used to incite electoral violence) and internet addiction (pornography, sexting) are categorised as separate challenges from physical health, mental health, nutrition, and sexual risks. The lecture lists them under 'Challenges—continued' as distinct items. Conflating violence and internet risks with mental health or sexual activity challenges is a common error.

questions.question: SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate ADH) in paediatric oncology is caused by which specific drug?
options: Vincristine, causing SIADH as a known neurological side effect
Methotrexate, through folate depletion affecting ADH regulation
Cyclophosphamide, through bladder toxicity triggering ADH release
Doxorubicin, through cardiac toxicity stimulating ADH release
questions.explanation: Vincristine causes SIADH as a specific neurological side effect through its toxic effects on hypothalamic-pituitary ADH regulation via peripheral and autonomic nervous system damage. Other causes of SIADH in oncology include CNS and pulmonary tumours, lymphoma, leukaemia, stress, pain, surgery, mechanical ventilation, and tumours producing ADH-like substances. SIADH presents with hyponatraemia, concentrated urine despite plasma hypo-osmolality, and neurological symptoms that can progress to seizures and coma.

Vibrio cholerae produces cholera toxin (CT), which activates adenylyl cyclase causing massive chloride secretion and water efflux into the intestinal lumen—a pure secretory mechanism. There is little or no structural mucosal damage in cholera.
questions.question: Which mechanism underlies the diarrhoea caused by Vibrio cholerae O1?

questions.explanation: Immediate management of ruptured exomphalos requires placing the exposed bowel in a sterile warm saline intestinal bag to prevent hypothermia, desiccation, and infection. Simultaneously, IV access, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, and vitamin K are commenced. These resuscitative measures must be performed in the delivery room before transfer to the NICU. Resuscitation precedes surgery.
questions.question: In the immediate resuscitation of a neonate with ruptured exomphalos, which of the following is the FIRST priority?

questions.explanation: Eye prophylaxis at birth is specifically directed at preventing ophthalmia neonatorum, conjunctivitis acquired from passage through an infected birth canal, most classically due to gonococcal or chlamydial infection, which can cause rapid corneal damage if untreated. It has no role in preventing congenital cataract, congenital glaucoma, retinopathy of prematurity, or strabismus, which have entirely different causes and prevention strategies. This simple, low-cost intervention remains an important component of routine newborn care.
questions.question: Eye prophylaxis with antimicrobial drops is administered to all neonates shortly after birth. This intervention is specifically aimed at preventing:
options: Ophthalmia neonatorum from maternal genital infection

questions.explanation: Dysentery is specifically defined as diarrhoea with visible blood in the stool and indicates mucosal invasion, most commonly by Shigella, Entamoeba histolytica, or enteroinvasive E. coli. It must be distinguished from acute watery or persistent diarrhoea.
questions.question: Diarrhoea with visible blood in the stool defines which clinical entity?

questions.explanation: Henoch-Schonlein purpura is an IgA-mediated small vessel vasculitis presenting with palpable purpura typically over the buttocks and lower limbs, abdominal pain, arthritis or arthralgia, and renal involvement with haematuria or proteinuria. Abdominal pain in this condition can also predispose to intussusception, requiring careful monitoring.
questions.question: A 4-year-old boy presents with sudden onset severe abdominal pain, palpable purpura on the buttocks and lower limbs, joint pain, and haematuria. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Intussusception alone without an underlying cause
Ureterocele from the lower pole moiety
Ectopic ureter from the upper pole of a duplex system
questions.explanation: In a duplex kidney system, the upper pole moiety ureter often inserts ectopically, sometimes below the external urethral sphincter, bypassing normal bladder neck control and causing continuous dribbling incontinence in addition to recurrent infections, following the Weigert-Meyer rule which describes the crossed relationship of the ureters in duplex systems.
questions.question: A 5-year-old presents with recurrent urinary tract infections and is found to have a duplex kidney with the upper pole moiety draining ectopically below the bladder neck, causing continuous dribbling incontinence. Which anomaly best explains this presentation?

A health facility record shows Vitamin A supplementation was given at 6 months and again at 12 months rather than at the recommended intervals. To correct future practice, the team should ensure doses are spaced:
questions.explanation: The Nigerian schedule recommends Vitamin A supplementation from 6 months of age, repeated at approximately six-month intervals to maintain adequate serum levels and reduce child mortality and morbidity from deficiency. Restricting doses to once in five years or to campaign periods alone would leave prolonged gaps in coverage. Correcting the interval to six months, not twelve, aligns practice with the recommended schedule.
options: Only during Supplemental Immunisation Activity campaigns
At approximately six-month intervals from 6 months of age
At every routine vaccination visit regardless of age
Only once in a child's entire first five years
At exactly twelve-month intervals starting from birth

questions.explanation: The first-line treatment for cerebral malaria in children is IV Quinine 10mg/kg in 10ml/kg of 10% dextrose water over 2 hours, repeated every 8 hours until the child can tolerate oral therapy, then switched to oral quinine or Coartem to complete 7 days. IV Artesunate and IM Artemether are second-line agents. Oral Coartem is used as step-down after IV quinine. Chloroquine resistance makes it ineffective for P. falciparum.
questions.question: The first-line treatment for cerebral malaria in children, as per the lecture, is:
options: Oral Coartem (artemether-lumefantrine) as soon as oral feeding resumes
IV Artesunate 2.4mg/kg stat, then 1.2mg/kg at 12 hours
Brief febrile convulsion in child 6 months–5 years, no CNS infection

questions.explanation: Rasburicase, a recombinant urate oxidase enzyme, rapidly converts uric acid to allantoin, which is more soluble and easily excreted, providing faster and more effective uric acid reduction than allopurinol in children at high risk of tumour lysis syndrome before chemotherapy begins.
questions.question: A 5-year-old with newly diagnosed leukaemia has a serum uric acid of 15 mg/dL before chemotherapy. Which agent most rapidly lowers uric acid in this pre-treatment setting?

questions.explanation: The four Rs of fractionated radiotherapy are: Repair (of sub-lethal DNA damage between fractions, favouring normal tissues with better repair capacity); Repopulation (tumour cells repopulate between fractions, which accelerated fractionation aims to counter); Reoxygenation (hypoxic tumour cells, which are radioresistant, reoxygenate between fractions as oxygen becomes available following death of better-oxygenated outer cells, increasing radiosensitivity); and Redistribution (cells progress through the cell cycle between fractions, redistributing into more radiosensitive phases like G2/M).
questions.question: The four Rs of fractionated radiotherapy explain its biological basis. Which option correctly lists all four Rs?

options: Stimulating insulin secretion from residual beta cells
questions.question: Alcohol consumption in diabetic adolescents causes hypoglycaemia primarily by:
questions.explanation: Alcohol impairs hepatic gluconeogenesis, eliminating a critical counter-regulatory response to falling blood glucose. This leads to severe and prolonged hypoglycaemia, especially without adequate carbohydrate intake. Diabetic adolescents must eat complex carbohydrates while drinking, measure blood glucose before bed, and ensure companions are aware of their condition.

A varicocele results from dilatation of the pampiniform venous plexus within the scrotum, classically described as feeling like a 'bag of worms', which becomes more prominent on standing due to increased venous pressure and decreases or disappears when lying flat as venous drainage improves.
questions.question: A 6-year-old boy presents with a scrotal swelling described as a 'bag of worms' that increases in size on standing and decreases when lying flat. Which diagnosis is most likely?
Prenatal diagnosis of gastroschisis by maternal serum alphafetoprotein would show:
questions.explanation: Maternal serum alphafetoprotein (MSAFP) is markedly elevated in gastroschisis because the exposed, sac-less bowel allows AFP to leak directly into the amniotic fluid and transplacentally into the maternal circulation. In exomphalos with intact membrane, the elevation is less dramatic but still elevated. Both conditions are reliably diagnosable on fetal ultrasound from 11-14 weeks.

Vesicoureteric reflux refers to the retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into the ureter and renal pelvis during voiding, predisposing affected children to recurrent febrile urinary tract infections and, if severe or longstanding, progressive renal scarring known as reflux nephropathy.
questions.question: A 4-year-old girl presents with recurrent febrile urinary tract infections. Micturating cystourethrogram shows retrograde flow of contrast into the ureter and renal pelvis during voiding. Which diagnosis is most likely?

questions.explanation: Serial monitoring of haemoglobin alongside the reticulocyte count best tracks the trajectory of ongoing haemolysis in a hyperhaemolytic crisis, guiding decisions about transfusion support and identifying deterioration promptly. A single electrolyte, glucose, or urinalysis measurement does not capture the dynamic, ongoing process of red cell destruction. A chest radiograph is relevant for suspected acute chest syndrome but does not monitor haemolysis itself.
options: Serum electrolytes measured once at presentation only
Serial haemoglobin and reticulocyte count monitoring
A single random blood glucose measurement
A one-off chest radiograph at admission
Urinalysis for glucose and ketones exclusively
questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease develops rapidly worsening anaemia, jaundice, and a rising reticulocyte count during an acute illness. The BEST bedside test to monitor ongoing red cell destruction in this hyperhaemolytic crisis is:
A neonate develops encephalopathy, poor feeding, and a distinctive sweet caramel odour to the urine within the first week of life. Which enzyme deficiency is responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease results from deficiency of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, and valine derivatives that produce the characteristic sweet, caramel-like urine odour alongside severe neonatal encephalopathy. Urgent dietary restriction of branched-chain amino acids and metabolic stabilisation are required to prevent death or severe brain injury. Newborn screening allows earlier detection before symptomatic crisis.

options: Hepatic synthesis of fibrin fragments during coagulation
Endothelial cell synthesis of fibrin monomers
Plasmin-mediated lysis of fibrinogen and fibrin clots formed in DIC
Factor XIII cross-linking of fibrin monomers
questions.question: Fibrin degradation products (FDP) in DIC arise from:
questions.explanation: Fibrin degradation products (FDP) and D-dimers result from plasmin-mediated fibrinolysis of fibrinogen and cross-linked fibrin clots generated in DIC. Secondary fibrinolysis is activated as a physiological response to the widespread microvascular fibrin deposition. Plasmin cleaves fibrin at specific sites producing FDP fragments (X, Y, D, E fragments) and D-dimers (from cross-linked fibrin only). Elevated FDP/D-dimers confirm fibrin turnover and are an important diagnostic marker for DIC.

Magnetic resonance imaging detects early marrow oedema and ischaemic changes in avascular necrosis well before structural changes become apparent on plain radiographs, allowing for earlier intervention. This makes MRI the investigation of choice when avascular necrosis is clinically suspected in sickle cell disease.
questions.question: Which imaging modality is most sensitive for early detection of avascular necrosis of the femoral head in a child with sickle cell disease before changes are visible on plain X-ray?

questions.explanation: Liver biopsy provides histological diagnosis including degree of fibrosis (staging), inflammatory activity (grading), and specific aetiological features (PAS-positive A1AT globules, copper deposits for Wilson's, iron overload for haemochromatosis). This information is not obtainable by non-invasive means.
options: Histological diagnosis—degree of fibrosis, activity, and specific aetiology
questions.question: Liver biopsy in the evaluation of portal hypertension provides which information NOT available from laboratory and imaging studies?

questions.explanation: The Social Paediatrics home visit experience is designed to shift students toward a holistic, biopsychosocial approach, understanding that health extends beyond clinical findings to context, environment, and social circumstances. Pharmacotherapy, laboratory interpretation, physical examination, and pathophysiology are competencies developed through other components of medical training.
questions.question: A medical student reports that after conducting a home visit, they understood that 'patients are not just clinical but also their context, with biopsychosocial circumstances.' This learning outcome PRIMARILY reflects which goal of Social Paediatrics education?
options: Enhanced ability to interpret laboratory results
A holistic, biopsychosocial approach to child health care
Competency in performing paediatric physical examination
CT scan with IV contrast as the first-line investigation
MRI of the abdomen without contrast
Renal biopsy under general anaesthesia immediately
questions.explanation: For kidney masses and Burkitt's lymphoma staging, the lecture specifically mentions IVU (intravenous urography) for kidney masses and abdominal ultrasound as key investigations. In a resource-limited Nigerian setting, IVU and USS are the accessible first-line tools for renal mass evaluation. CT with IV contrast is more definitive but may not be the initial investigation in this context. Renal biopsy and urine cytology are not first-line staging investigations.
questions.question: Wilms' tumour (nephroblastoma) accounts for 8.5% of childhood tumours in Ibadan. Which investigation is MOST appropriate for initial assessment of a child with a suspected renal mass in Burkitt's lymphoma staging?
Nappy rash (irritant contact dermatitis) in infants is a common paediatric dermatological condition. Which statement about nappy rash is MOST accurate clinically?
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasises that 'any disorder could also affect the nappy area'—meaning psoriasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, and other conditions can present in the nappy region, not just irritant or Candida nappy rash. Assuming all nappy rash is Candida-related or irritant-only can lead to diagnostic error. It is not exclusively a premature infant problem, does not automatically indicate neglect, and may require specific treatment depending on aetiology.
options: It is exclusively caused by Candida albicans infection
It exclusively affects premature infants due to thin skin
It is a sign of child neglect and must be reported immediately
Any skin disorder may affect the nappy area
It is always self-limiting and requires no treatment or parent education

questions.explanation: Iron deficiency anaemia produces small, pale red cells with variable size and shape, described as microcytic hypochromic anisopoikilocytosis, reflecting impaired haemoglobin synthesis during erythropoiesis. Target cells and basophilic stippling suggest thalassaemia or lead poisoning, while macrocytosis suggests megaloblastic causes.
questions.question: Which finding on peripheral blood film is most characteristic of iron deficiency anaemia in a toddler?
A non-compressible, blind-ending tubular structure >6 mm in diameter with periappendiceal fat stranding on USS is consistent with:
questions.explanation: A non-compressible, blind-ending tubular structure exceeding 6 mm in outer diameter on ultrasound, with periappendiceal fat stranding and tenderness, is the ultrasound criterion for acute appendicitis. A normal-appearing appendix <6 mm reliably excludes appendicitis when well-visualised.
options: Crohn's disease of the terminal ileum

questions.question: Early signs of shock include sinus tachycardia, delayed capillary refill, and irritability. Bradycardia in a shocked child is a LATE sign. What does the development of bradycardia in a previously tachycardic shocked child indicate?
questions.explanation: Bradycardia is a late sign of shock, appearing after tachycardia fails to maintain perfusion. The progression from compensated tachycardia to bradycardia indicates failure of compensatory mechanisms and imminent cardiopulmonary arrest—not stabilisation or recovery. This transition point demands immediate, aggressive intervention. Electrolyte correction causing benign arrhythmia and SVR-related resolution are reassuring scenarios inconsistent with the declining trajectory described.
options: Adequate fluid resuscitation restoring normal heart rate
Development of a benign sinus arrhythmia from electrolyte correction
The onset of the resolution phase as SVR decreases
Less than 2% only after age 2 years
questions.question: Haemoglobin A2 (HbA2) constitutes what percentage of normal adult haemoglobin?
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin A2 (alpha2-delta2) constitutes 2.5-3.5% of total haemoglobin in normal adults. An elevated HbA2 above 3.5% is the diagnostic hallmark of beta-thalassaemia trait (minor), resulting from compensatory upregulation of delta-globin chain production to substitute for reduced beta-chain output. Conversely, HbA2 is normal or low in iron deficiency anaemia (where all chain productions are reduced proportionally), making HbA2 measurement essential for distinguishing beta-thalassaemia trait from iron deficiency when both conditions co-exist.

High fever with high blood glucose and ketonuria in diabetic children is most commonly caused by bacterial infections. Management requires identifying and treating the infection focus, giving frequent subcutaneous short-acting insulin, and maintaining hydration. Viral infections more commonly cause low blood glucose with ketonuria from anorexia and reduced oral intake.
questions.question: In children with Type 1 diabetes, high fever with high blood glucose and ketonuria is MOST commonly caused by:

questions.explanation: Pellagra results from niacin (vitamin B3) or tryptophan deficiency and classically presents with the '4 Ds': dermatitis (photosensitive, symmetric 'Casal's necklace'), diarrhoea, dementia, and death if untreated. It is common in populations subsisting on maize-based diets without lime processing.
questions.question: Pellagra is caused by deficiency of which vitamin and presents with the classic 'four Ds'?
options: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine); dysarthria, depression, dermatitis, diarrhoea
Riboflavin (B2); dermatitis, dim vision, dysphagia, dysuria
Niacin (vitamin B3); dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia, death

questions.question: A child has MUAC of 10.5 cm and weight-for-height Z-score of –3.5. This child has:
questions.explanation: Severe acute malnutrition is defined as MUAC <11.5 cm OR weight-for-height Z-score <–3 SD (or by oedema). This child has both a MUAC of 10.5 cm and a WHZ of –3.5, clearly meeting SAM criteria and requiring therapeutic feeding with F-75/F-100 or RUTF.

questions.question: The definitive surgical treatment for anorectal malformation with low fistula in a neonate is:
questions.explanation: Low anorectal malformations, where the rectum ends below the levator ani, are managed by primary anoplasty which involves moving the misplaced opening to the correct anatomical position within the external sphincter. There is no need for a prior colostomy in low lesions. This single-stage approach has excellent functional outcomes.

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed by an ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear (PMN) neutrophil count exceeding 250 cells/mm³, regardless of Gram stain or culture results. Empirical third-generation cephalosporin treatment is initiated immediately. SBP is a leading cause of mortality in cirrhosis.
questions.question: The defining investigation for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is:
options: Blood culture positive for Gram-negative organisms

questions.question: Eye prophylaxis with silver nitrate drops is administered to neonates at birth. What specific neonatal infection is being prevented?
options: Chlamydial conjunctivitis from birth canal exposure
questions.explanation: Silver nitrate drops (or antibiotic eye ointment in modern practice) are administered to neonates to prevent gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum—neonatal conjunctivitis acquired during passage through a gonorrhoea-infected birth canal. Without prophylaxis, this can rapidly progress to corneal ulceration and blindness. Rubella and toxoplasmosis are transplacental; neonatal herpes keratitis and chlamydial conjunctivitis require different prophylaxis protocols.

questions.question: Adolescence is described as a critical period for developing habits and skills that create a strong foundation for healthy lifestyles. Which of the following BEST justifies why investing in adolescent health benefits future adult populations?
questions.explanation: Adolescence is a time of major transitions when young people develop habits, patterns of behaviour, and relationships they carry into adult life. Investing in adolescent health reduces future adult disease burden, protects human capital, and is a human rights imperative. Adolescent disease can have lasting sequelae (e.g., STI complications), and healthcare costs are not uniquely lower in this age group.
options: Adolescents have higher healthcare costs than younger children
Adolescents are legally protected from receiving medical care without consent
Habits formed in adolescence are carried into adult life
Adolescent diseases are exclusively acute and resolve without sequelae
Adolescent healthcare is cheaper to provide than paediatric healthcare

questions.question: A critically ill child is assessed using the ABCDE approach. Under 'D—Disability,' which parameter is MOST critically assessed?
options: Degree of anaemia on conjunctival examination
questions.explanation: In the ABCDE primary assessment, 'D—Disability' specifically refers to assessment of conscious level and neurological status, including responsiveness, pupillary response, and signs of raised intracranial pressure. Capillary refill is part of 'C—Circulation.' Oedema, anaemia assessment, and medication history are not the primary targets of the Disability component of ABCDE.

Burkitt's lymphoma staging is based on the number and combination of anatomical sites involved, with multiple sites such as combined abdominal and jaw involvement indicating a higher disease burden and more advanced stage than a single, resectable site. Jaw involvement alone, when it is the sole site, generally corresponds to an earlier stage rather than the most advanced. Staging systems specifically incorporate site distribution and resectability, not solely the patient's age.
questions.question: Staging of Burkitt's lymphoma is based on anatomical extent of disease. A child with an intra-abdominal tumour AND a jaw tumour, both incompletely resected, would be classified at a MORE advanced stage primarily because:
options: Jaw involvement alone always defines the lowest stage
Staging depends only on the child's age, not tumour sites
Multiple extra-abdominal sites indicate higher disease burden
A single site of disease always defines advanced stage
Abdominal involvement is disregarded in staging systems

questions.question: Homocystinuria from cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency causes a clinical picture resembling Marfan syndrome. The MOST life-threatening complication is:
questions.explanation: The most life-threatening complication of homocystinuria is arterial and venous thromboembolic disease (strokes, pulmonary embolism, coronary artery disease), which can occur at any age including childhood. Homocysteine damages vascular endothelium and promotes platelet aggregation. Other features include ectopia lentis, Marfanoid habitus, intellectual disability, and osteoporosis.

options: Lead pipe sign, suggesting ulcerative colitis
Double bubble sign, suggesting duodenal atresia
Apple core sign, suggesting colonic malignancy
String sign of Kantor, suggesting Crohn's disease
questions.explanation: The string sign of Kantor on barium follow-through reflects severe luminal narrowing from mural thickening and spasm in a segment of diseased bowel, classically associated with Crohn's disease affecting the terminal ileum. This differs from the lead pipe appearance of chronic ulcerative colitis, which reflects loss of normal colonic haustration. Recognising these distinct radiological patterns supports differentiation between the two major forms of inflammatory bowel disease.
questions.question: A child with chronic abdominal pain and suspected inflammatory bowel disease undergoes barium follow-through, which shows separation and thickening of bowel loops with a string-like narrowed segment. Which sign and underlying diagnosis does this represent?

questions.explanation: Sickle cell trait (HbAS) typically does not cause anaemia, significant splenomegaly, or clinical sickling under normal physiological conditions. Sickling occurs only under extreme hypoxia (e.g., high altitude, pressurised aircraft). The clinical presentation of symptomatic anaemia and splenomegaly at 2 years points to a compound heterozygous or homozygous state. HbAS individuals are carriers with near-normal haematological indices and minimal clinical manifestations.
questions.question: A 2-year-old presents with pallor, Hb 6 g/dL, splenomegaly, and a positive sickling test. Which form of the sickling disorder is LEAST consistent with this presentation?

questions.explanation: Antithyroid drugs such as carbimazole and propylthiouracil primarily inhibit organification of iodine within the thyroid gland, reducing synthesis of new thyroid hormone. This differs from mechanisms such as radioactive iodine ablation, which destroys thyroid tissue directly. Regular monitoring of thyroid function guides dose titration during treatment.
options: Blocks TSH receptor binding on thyroid cells
Inhibits iodine organification within the thyroid
Blocks peripheral T4 to T3 conversion only
Increases renal excretion of circulating thyroxine
questions.question: A child with Graves disease is started on antithyroid drug therapy. Her mother asks how this medication works. Which mechanism is CORRECT?

options: Iron deficiency from inadequate maternal iron stores
Vitamin K deficiency causing spontaneous haemorrhage
Feto-maternal haemorrhage, twin-twin transfusion, or birth trauma causing internal haemorrhage
High haematocrit from delayed cord clamping
questions.question: Anaemia in the newborn from blood loss can result from which of the following causes?
questions.explanation: Blood loss causing neonatal anaemia can occur through feto-maternal haemorrhage (fetal blood entering the maternal circulation through placental disruption, diagnosed by Kleihauer-Betke test), twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (chronic placental vascular anastomoses causing unequal blood distribution between twins), and birth trauma causing internal haemorrhage (adrenal, subaponeurotic, hepatic, or splenic haemorrhage). These must be distinguished from haemolytic and hypoproductive causes to guide appropriate management.

questions.question: In acute adrenal crisis, the MOST critical initial pharmacological treatment is:
questions.explanation: IV hydrocortisone is the critical initial treatment in acute adrenal crisis, providing both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity. IV normal saline is given for fluid resuscitation and glucose for hypoglycaemia. Fludrocortisone (oral mineralocorticoid) is used for long-term maintenance but is not suitable for acute crisis management.

questions.question: Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD) includes diabetes mellitus alongside diabetes insipidus, optic atrophy, and:
questions.explanation: Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD) is the combination of Diabetes Insipidus, Diabetes Mellitus, Optic Atrophy, and Deafness. It is a rare autosomal recessive disorder from mutations in the WFS1 gene. It is classified under genetic defects of beta-cell function as a cause of secondary diabetes.

questions.question: In paediatric portal hypertension, which blood count abnormality from hypersplenism increases bleeding risk?
questions.explanation: Hypersplenism in portal hypertension causes splenomegaly with sequestration of platelets, leading to thrombocytopaenia. This impairs primary haemostasis and increases the risk of bleeding complications, particularly from varices. Combined with coagulopathy from liver failure, bleeding risk is compounded.

Relative adrenal insufficiency describes critically ill patients whose absolute cortisol may be within the normal range but is insufficient given the degree of physiological stress—they fail to mount the expected cortisol stress response. This concept guides empirical stress-dose hydrocortisone administration in critically ill patients with refractory shock. Subtopic 5: Inborn Errors of Metabolism
options: Have complete absence of adrenal function
Have secondary ACTH deficiency from pituitary disease
Fail adequate cortisol response to illness
questions.question: Relative adrenal insufficiency in critically ill patients describes patients who:

questions.explanation: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease typically presents later in childhood or adulthood with bilateral enlarged kidneys containing numerous cysts of varying size, and a positive family history reflects its autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, distinguishing it from the earlier-presenting, more severe autosomal recessive form typically diagnosed in infancy.
questions.question: A 5-year-old presents with progressive abdominal distension, and imaging reveals bilateral enlarged kidneys with numerous cysts of varying sizes and a family history of a similar condition in a parent. Which diagnosis is most likely?

questions.explanation: Classic infantile Tay-Sachs disease presents at 3–6 months after apparently normal early development, with progressive developmental regression, hyperacusis (exaggerated startle response to sound), progressive visual loss, and a cherry-red macular spot. Seizures, hypotonia, and vegetative state follow, with death by 2–4 years. Ashkenazi Jewish populations have a carrier frequency of approximately 1 in 30.
questions.question: Tay-Sachs disease (GM2 gangliosidosis) from hexosaminidase A deficiency presents in the classic infantile form with developmental regression beginning at:

questions.explanation: An appendiceal mass/phlegmon that has formed after 5 days of symptoms is best managed conservatively with IV antibiotics, bowel rest, and close clinical monitoring. Attempting appendicectomy through an established mass risks bowel injury, vascular injury, and faecal fistula. Interval appendicectomy is planned 6-8 weeks later after the inflammation fully resolves.
questions.question: An appendiceal mass (phlegmon) in a child with 5 days of symptoms is best managed initially by:

questions.explanation: Serum potassium must be checked before starting insulin in DKA because insulin therapy drives potassium into cells, potentially causing life-threatening hypokalaemia. If renal failure is suspected, potassium is withheld until electrolytes are available and urine output is confirmed. Hypokalaemia on ECG (U waves, flat T waves) requires correction before commencing insulin.
questions.question: Before starting insulin in DKA, which investigation is MOST critical to check first to prevent fatal arrhythmia?

questions.explanation: Oral rehydration therapy is inappropriate as sole initial treatment when a child shows signs of shock or cannot drink at all, since these situations require immediate intravenous or nasogastric intervention to prevent rapid deterioration. Mild stools, a single vomiting episode, low-grade fever, and normal activity with good appetite do not preclude oral therapy. Recognising true contraindications prevents dangerous delay in escalating care.
options: Signs of shock or an inability to drink
Normal activity level and good appetite
Low-grade fever below thirty-eight degrees Celsius
Mild loose stools without any other symptoms
A single episode of non-bloody vomiting
questions.question: Oral rehydration therapy is considered INAPPROPRIATE as the sole initial treatment when a child with diarrhoea also has:
A child with untreated CAH develops early epiphyseal fusion due to prolonged androgen excess. What is the LONG-TERM consequence of this on final adult height?
questions.explanation: Chronic androgen excess in undertreated or untreated CAH causes early childhood growth acceleration but also premature epiphyseal fusion, ultimately resulting in reduced final adult height despite the child appearing tall for age earlier in childhood. This underscores the importance of adequate glucocorticoid suppression of excess androgens from an early age. Growth and bone age monitoring help guide treatment adjustments to optimise final height outcomes.
options: Reduced final adult height despite early tall stature
No effect on final adult height at all
Final height improves without any treatment needed
Increased final adult height compared with peers
Final height determined solely by genetic potential

questions.explanation: Cholestasis impairs absorption of fat-soluble vitamin K, leading to deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors and a coagulopathy that can be corrected with parenteral vitamin K administration, particularly important before any invasive procedure. This differs from a primary synthetic coagulopathy from severe hepatocellular dysfunction, which may not fully correct with vitamin K alone. Distinguishing between these two mechanisms of coagulopathy helps guide appropriate correction strategies before procedures.
options: Isolated fibrinogen deficiency unrelated to vitamin K
Isolated haemoglobin deficiency unrelated to vitamin K
Isolated albumin deficiency unrelated to vitamin K
questions.question: A neonate with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia requires IV vitamin K administration prior to an invasive procedure. Which specific deficiency is this treatment addressing in the context of cholestasis?

questions.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome results from a 22q11.2 microdeletion causing failure of development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, leading to thymic aplasia or hypoplasia (impairing T-cell development), hypoparathyroidism (causing hypocalcaemia), conotruncal cardiac defects, and dysmorphic facial features. T-cell immunodeficiency ranges from mild to severe depending on the degree of thymic hypoplasia.
options: BTK gene mutation blocking B-cell maturation
Adenosine deaminase deficiency blocking all lymphocyte development
Thymic aplasia or hypoplasia impairing T-cell development
questions.question: DiGeorge syndrome from 22q11.2 microdeletion causes T-cell immunodeficiency because of:

questions.explanation: The four basic clinical signs of paediatric heart failure are tachycardia, tachypnoea, hepatomegaly, and cardiomegaly, reflecting compensatory and congestive changes across the cardiovascular and hepatic systems. Bradycardia, hypothermia, jaundice, and splenomegaly are not part of this core recognised tetrad. Identifying these four signs together supports a prompt clinical diagnosis before echocardiographic confirmation.
questions.question: The four basic clinical signs used to recognise heart failure in a child include tachycardia, tachypnoea, hepatomegaly, and:

questions.explanation: Familial hypophosphataemic rickets is treated with high-dose vitamin D (or calcitriol) combined with oral phosphate supplementation (1.5–2 g in 4–6 divided doses daily). Phosphate alone worsens secondary hyperparathyroidism; vitamin D alone does not correct the primary renal phosphate wasting. Both are required for effective treatment of this X-linked dominant condition.
questions.question: Familial hypophosphataemic rickets (vitamin D-resistant rickets) is treated with the combination of:

options: New parasitic infestation unrelated to radiotherapy
New lymphatic obstruction unrelated to radiotherapy
New pancreatic exocrine insufficiency unrelated to radiotherapy
New autoimmune villous atrophy unrelated to radiotherapy
questions.question: A child recently completed abdominal radiotherapy for a malignancy and subsequently develops chronic diarrhoea and malabsorption. Which mechanism BEST explains this complication?
questions.explanation: Radiotherapy directed at the abdomen can cause direct damage to the small intestinal mucosa, resulting in malabsorption that may be acute or, in some cases, chronic and progressive due to fibrosis and vascular changes. This iatrogenic cause of malabsorption should be considered in any child with a relevant treatment history. Management is largely supportive, addressing specific nutrient deficiencies as they arise.

Direct portal pressure measurement is avoided because of its invasive nature, significant complication risk (haemorrhage, infection), and the fact that anaesthetic agents alter portal haemodynamics, making results unreliable. Indirect measurement via hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) is preferred.
questions.question: Direct portal pressure measurement is generally avoided primarily because:
options: Results are identical to non-invasive Doppler measurements
Invasive nature, risk of complications, and interference of anaesthetics on portal haemodynamics

questions.explanation: Potassium replacement must be commenced as soon as resuscitation is completed and BEFORE starting the insulin infusion. Insulin drives potassium into cells, risking life-threatening hypokalaemia if potassium is not replaced first. DKA is always accompanied by severe total body potassium depletion even when serum potassium appears normal or elevated.
questions.question: Potassium replacement in DKA must be commenced immediately after resuscitation and specifically BEFORE:

questions.explanation: The management states: IV 50% D/W 1ml/kg (1:4 dilution). A 1:4 dilution means 1 part 50% dextrose in 4 parts water, resulting in 12.5% dextrose. The 1ml/kg of 50% D/W diluted 1:4 gives 2.5ml/kg of 12.5% solution (0.125g/ml × 2.5ml/kg ≈ 0.3g/kg glucose), followed by a 10% dextrose water infusion. Alternatively, 2–4ml/kg of 10% dextrose water directly provides the same glucose load without dilution calculations.
options: 1ml/kg of undiluted 50% dextrose, giving 0.5g/kg of glucose
2ml/kg of undiluted 25% dextrose providing 0.5g/kg of glucose
1ml/kg of 50% dextrose diluted in 9ml of normal saline giving 5% glucose
questions.question: In the management of hypoglycaemia in a convulsing child, IV 50% dextrose is used at 1ml/kg but MUST be diluted 1:4. What is the resulting dilution administered and how is it calculated?
Clinically significant hyperleukocytosis in CML occurs at WBC counts greater than:
questions.explanation: Clinically significant hyperleukocytosis occurs at different WBC thresholds for different leukaemia types, reflecting differences in blast cell size and stickiness: AML (myeloblasts, large and sticky) at >200,000/mm³; ALL (lymphoblasts, smaller) at >300,000/mm³; CML (mature myeloid cells, smaller and less sticky) at >600,000/mm³. CML blasts are more mature and less adhesive than AML myeloblasts, explaining why a higher count is needed before clinically significant leucostasis occurs in CML.

questions.question: The rectal biopsy in Hirschsprung's disease confirms the diagnosis by demonstrating absence of:
questions.explanation: Full thickness or suction rectal biopsy confirms Hirschsprung's disease by showing absence of ganglion cells in both the submucosal (Meissner's) and myenteric (Auerbach's) plexuses, along with hypertrophied nerve fibres and increased acetylcholinesterase staining. This histological finding is the gold standard for diagnosis, with 95% accuracy on suction biopsy.

Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC), like Shigella, directly invades and destroys colonic mucosal cells, causing dysentery with blood and mucus. ETEC and V. cholerae produce secretory diarrhoea without mucosal invasion. Rotavirus and Norovirus cause watery, non-bloody diarrhoea.
questions.question: Which of the following organisms invades the colonic mucosa and causes inflammatory diarrhoea with blood and mucus in the stool?

options: Transudative ascites from portal hypertension or hypoalbuminaemia
questions.question: Ascitic fluid showing low protein (<25 g/L) and high SAAG (>1.1 g/dL) indicates which aetiology?
questions.explanation: A serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) >1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension as the cause of ascites (transudative). Low ascitic protein (<25 g/L) supports a transudative mechanism from increased hydrostatic pressure (portal hypertension) rather than malignancy or infection.

options: Only bacterial infections as viral infections are self-limiting
Parasitic infections exclusively because malaria predisposes to lymphoma
Antibiotic prophylaxis only without treatment of active infections
Bacterial, viruses, and fungi with empirical antibiotics and cultures
Infections are ignored during active chemotherapy as they resolve spontaneously
questions.question: Supportive care in paediatric oncology includes management of which specific infections?
questions.explanation: Supportive care in paediatric oncology includes aggressive management of infections in immunocompromised patients. Bacterial infections (Staphylococcus aureus, Gram-negative rods) are treated by taking appropriate cultures and starting empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately without awaiting culture results. Viral infections (herpes, CMV, influenza) and fungal infections (Candida, Aspergillus) are also significant in immunocompromised oncology patients. This approach follows the axiom: fever plus neutropaenia equals emergency—start antibiotics.

questions.question: HbA1c reflects average blood glucose control over the preceding:
questions.explanation: HbA1c reflects average blood glucose control over the preceding 4–6 weeks in most paediatric references. The red blood cell lifespan is approximately 120 days, but glycation reflects the most recent period most heavily. In clinical paediatric diabetes, HbA1c is checked every 3 months and most clinicians aim for values of 7–9%.

questions.question: IV vitamin K administration in the portal hypertension case was directed at correcting which deficiency?
options: Absolute hepatic synthetic failure of coagulation factors
Fat-soluble vitamin K malabsorption from cholestasis
questions.explanation: IV vitamin K supplementation in cholestatic jaundice corrects vitamin K deficiency caused by impaired fat-soluble vitamin absorption from cholestasis. If the coagulopathy responds to vitamin K, it indicates hepatocellular synthetic function is partially preserved; non-response suggests intrinsic synthetic failure.

Malignancies cause DIC primarily through aberrant expression and release of tissue factor and other procoagulant substances (cancer procoagulant, phosphatidylserine-rich microparticles) by tumour cells. This directly activates the extrinsic coagulation pathway and triggers systemic thrombin generation. Leukaemias (particularly APL) are classically associated with severe DIC. The recognised malignancies listed as DIC causes include various paediatric cancers as part of the systemic procoagulant response to cancer.
questions.question: Malignancy causes DIC most commonly through which mechanism?
options: Thrombocytopaenia from marrow infiltration causing platelet-induced coagulopathy
Anti-platelet antibodies produced by the immune response to tumour antigens
Hepatic metastases reducing coagulation factor synthesis to critical levels
Release of tissue factor and procoagulant phospholipids by tumour cells activating coagulation
Tumour necrosis factor causing endothelial injury and complement activation

questions.question: Which investigation is the gold standard for assessing portal venous pressure non-invasively?
options: Hepatic venous pressure gradient via transjugular hepatic vein catheterisation
questions.explanation: Hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) measured via transjugular catheterisation is the gold standard for assessing portal pressure indirectly. HVPG = wedged hepatic venous pressure – free hepatic venous pressure. Values >5 mmHg = portal hypertension; >12 mmHg predicts variceal bleeding risk.

questions.question: A child with severe acute malnutrition is found to have blood glucose below the defined threshold on admission. Which immediate management step is MOST appropriate?
options: Delay treatment until formal laboratory confirmation returns
Immediate correction with intravenous insulin therapy
Immediate initiation of high-volume rehabilitation feeds
Prompt treatment of hypoglycaemia with feeds or glucose
questions.explanation: Hypoglycaemia in severe acute malnutrition, defined below a specific threshold, requires prompt treatment with feeds or glucose to prevent seizures, coma, or death, since malnourished children have depleted glycogen reserves and limited capacity to maintain normoglycaemia during fasting. High-volume feeding is inappropriate at this stage and belongs to a later rehabilitation phase. Frequent feeding, including through the night, helps prevent recurrent hypoglycaemic episodes during stabilisation.

In the cited study from OTCHEW in 2004, anaemia due to malaria was the leading indication for blood transfusion. Malaria-induced severe anaemia from haemolysis, splenic sequestration, and dyserythropoiesis represents the most common transfusion indication in sub-Saharan African paediatric practice. This reflects the high burden of Plasmodium falciparum malaria in Nigeria and other tropical African countries, where malaria is the primary driver of both admissions and blood transfusion needs.
questions.question: Which malaria-related factor most commonly indicated blood transfusion in the OTCHEW study population?

questions.explanation: Idiopathic intussusception most commonly presents between 5 and 10 months of age, coinciding with the period of weaning and dietary change, lymphoid hyperplasia from viral upper respiratory tract infections, and introduction of rotavirus vaccine. It predominantly affects previously healthy infants. After 3 years of age, a pathological lead point must be actively sought.
questions.question: The peak age of presentation of idiopathic intussusception is:

questions.explanation: C3 deficiency impairs opsonisation (coating bacteria for phagocytosis) and activation of the membrane attack complex, predisposing to recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria—the same organisms as in antibody deficiencies. Terminal complement deficiencies (C5–C9) specifically predispose to Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections, due to the importance of the MAC in killing Neisseria species.
questions.question: Complement C3 deficiency predisposes children to recurrent infections with which organisms?

questions.explanation: The caput medusae sign, dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus, reflects portosystemic collateral formation through recanalised umbilical or periumbilical veins in portal hypertension. This finding, alongside splenomegaly and ascites, supports the clinical diagnosis of significant portal hypertension. Further imaging is used to characterise the specific site and cause of the underlying portal venous obstruction.
questions.question: A child with portal hypertension is examined and found to have dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus. What does this specific physical sign indicate?
options: Portosystemic collateral formation around the umbilicus
Isolated inferior vena cava obstruction only
Priapism from vaso-occlusion in penile vessels
Nephrotic syndrome from sickle cell nephropathy
questions.explanation: Bladder hypertrophy from detrusor muscle sickling is not a recognised complication of SCD. Genuine genitourinary complications include: priapism (sustained painful erection from vaso-occlusion in the corpora cavernosa), hyposthenuria (inability to concentrate urine from renal medullary infarction), haematuria (medullary ischaemia), pyelonephritis (dilute urine favouring bacterial growth), progressive azotaemia/renal failure, nephrotic syndrome, and renal medullary carcinoma (a rare but specific SCD-associated malignancy).
questions.question: Genito-urinary complications of SCD include all of the following EXCEPT:
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is the definitive curative treatment for all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Selective IgA deficiency does NOT require haematopoietic stem cell transplantation; it is managed with infection surveillance and treatment, with IVIG contraindicated due to anaphylaxis risk from anti-IgA antibodies. HSCT is curative for SCID, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, CGD, leukocyte adhesion deficiency, and other severe primary immunodeficiencies where the life-threatening risk justifies the transplant-related morbidity.

questions.question: A child with chronic liver disease develops lethargy, increased irritability, and disturbed sleep patterns without overt confusion. Which complication of portal hypertension does this EARLY presentation MOST likely represent?
questions.explanation: Subtle behavioural changes such as lethargy, irritability, and altered sleep patterns represent early, grade one hepatic encephalopathy, resulting from accumulation of neurotoxic substances such as ammonia due to impaired hepatic clearance and portosystemic shunting. Early recognition allows prompt treatment before progression to more severe confusion or coma. Identifying and correcting precipitating factors, such as infection or gastrointestinal bleeding, is an important part of management.

options: Haemorrhoids from constipation secondary to diuretics
questions.explanation: Rectal haemorrhoids in portal hypertension represent portal-systemic collaterals formed through anastomoses between the superior rectal (portal territory) and middle/inferior rectal veins (systemic territory). They differ from primary haemorrhoids and may cause significant bleeding.
questions.question: Rectal haemorrhoids in portal hypertension represent:

questions.explanation: Satellite lesions extending into the skin creases are a classic feature of candidal superinfection complicating napkin dermatitis, distinguishing it from simple irritant dermatitis, which spares the deep folds. Staphylococcal infection can complicate nappy rash but does not typically produce this satellite-lesion pattern, and herpes simplex, molluscum, and HPV present with distinctly different lesion morphologies. Recognising candidal superinfection prompts the addition of a topical antifungal agent to standard barrier care.
questions.question: A 6-month-old with a persistent nappy rash unresponsive to standard barrier cream is examined and found to have satellite erythematous papules extending into the skin creases. This finding suggests superimposed infection with:

questions.explanation: The VACTERL association describes the non-random co-occurrence of vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, and limb anomalies, and neonates diagnosed with oesophageal atresia should be systematically screened for these associated defects, as their presence significantly influences overall management and prognosis.
options: Vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, and limb anomalies (VACTERL)
questions.question: Which combination of anomalies should be actively screened for in a neonate diagnosed with oesophageal atresia, given the recognised association?

A paediatric team reviews a case where a child's recurrent hospital admissions are linked to a parent's alcohol dependency, domestic violence, and homelessness. Which component of the social determinants framework MOST directly explains this pattern?
questions.explanation: Social structure, family units, resources, and socio-economic status are named social determinants of health. Parental alcohol dependency, domestic violence, and homelessness are socio-economic and family structural determinants that directly drive child health outcomes. Genetics, microbial virulence, hospital capacity, and pharmacotherapy are factors in the biomedical, not social, domain.

questions.question: Antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) positivity is specifically associated with:
questions.explanation: Antimitochondrial antibody (AMA), particularly M2, is highly specific for primary biliary cirrhosis (cholangitis). Antinuclear antibody (ANA) is associated with autoimmune hepatitis. Differentiating these conditions is important as their management differs significantly (ursodeoxycholic acid vs immunosuppression).

questions.question: Which pathophysiologic mechanism primarily explains diarrhoea due to enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC)?
questions.explanation: ETEC produces heat-labile (LT) and heat-stable (ST) enterotoxins that stimulate adenylyl cyclase and guanylyl cyclase respectively, leading to increased cAMP and cGMP and consequent active chloride secretion—a classic secretory mechanism with little structural damage.

questions.question: Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) in portal hypertension provides which specific information NOT obtainable by standard ultrasound?
options: Quantitative portal venous and azygos blood flow data
questions.explanation: MRI angiography detects portosystemic collaterals and obstruction of portal vasculature AND provides quantitative data on portal venous and azygos blood flow—information not obtainable by standard ultrasound. MRI also provides qualitative information similar to CT without radiation.

options: Conservative management with nasogastric decompression only
questions.explanation: In duodenal atresia with gas in the distal bowel (suggesting incomplete obstruction or a wind-related artifact), duodenoduodenostomy remains the definitive treatment once the patient is stabilized. The patient is not a surgical emergency per se but requires resuscitation followed by surgery. Barium enema is not indicated in confirmed duodenal atresia.
questions.question: A 2-day-old male neonate with Down's syndrome fails to pass meconium, has bilious vomiting, and a plain X-ray shows a double bubble sign with gas in the distal bowel. The next most appropriate step is:

options: Stimulating PTH release from the parathyroids
Increasing calcium absorption from the gut
questions.question: The MOST important bioeffect of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (calcitriol) on calcium homeostasis is:
questions.explanation: The most important biological effect of calcitriol is increasing calcium (and phosphate) absorption from the intestinal mucosa. Along with PTH, it also releases calcium from bones. The anti-rachitogenic effects of vitamin D include mobilisation of calcium and phosphate and support for normal bone mineralisation.

Prolonged jaundice, excessive sleepiness, hoarse cry, poor feeding, hypotonia, macroglossia, large fontanelles, umbilical hernia, and constipation in a neonate are classical features of congenital hypothyroidism. Urgent TSH and T4 measurement and levothyroxine therapy must be commenced promptly to prevent irreversible neurological damage.
questions.question: A neonate who is excessively sleepy ('good baby'), has prolonged jaundice, hoarse cry, and umbilical hernia should prompt urgent screening for:

questions.explanation: Sweat chloride testing (pilocarpine iontophoresis) is performed to screen for cystic fibrosis in cholestatic neonates. A sweat chloride >60 mmol/L is diagnostic of CF. This is included in the standard workup of neonatal cholestasis alongside metabolic screens and cultures.
questions.question: Sweat chloride testing in neonatal cholestasis evaluation screens for:

options: It represents the time between first sickling and irreversible cell damage
It determines the interval between vaso-occlusive crises
It represents the time required for hydroxyurea to induce HbF production
It is inversely proportional to the 15th-35th power of HbS concentration, meaning small changes in HbS concentration markedly affect sickling
It is the time delay before cells become irreversibly sickled after repeated cycles
questions.explanation: The delay time (latency phase before HbS polymer formation) is inversely proportional to the 15th-35th power of HbS concentration. This extreme non-linear relationship means even small reductions in intracellular HbS concentration produce dramatic prolongation of the delay time, effectively preventing sickling during capillary transit. This principle underlies hydroxyurea therapy (which induces HbF to dilute HbS) and chronic transfusion programmes to reduce HbS below 30%.
questions.question: The delay time before HbS polymerisation and irreversible sickling occurs is best described by which of the following?
Which structure must be excised along with a sacrococcygeal teratoma during surgical resection to minimise the risk of local recurrence?
questions.explanation: Complete excision of a sacrococcygeal teratoma must include the coccyx, as residual coccygeal tissue is strongly associated with local tumour recurrence, even when the visible mass itself has been fully removed. This principle is fundamental to achieving surgical cure in this condition.

questions.question: A toddler with rachitic bow legs is assessed clinically. Which measurement finding would classify the deformity as requiring surgical referral rather than continued medical treatment alone?
questions.explanation: An intercondylar distance beyond the defined threshold in genu varum indicates a severe deformity that is unlikely to correct with medical therapy alone and warrants orthopaedic surgical assessment. Milder deformities usually improve spontaneously once the underlying rickets is treated. Persistent severe bowing risks long-term gait and functional problems.
options: Serum phosphate remaining within normal range
Alkaline phosphatase falling after vitamin D therapy
Radiographic cupping resolving after treatment begins
Intercondylar distance exceeding the defined threshold
Intercondylar distance below the defined threshold

questions.question: Vaso-occlusive crisis in sickle cell disease can cause acute abdomen through:
questions.explanation: Vaso-occlusive (sickle cell) crisis causes acute abdomen through ischaemia and infarction of abdominal organs (spleen, mesentery, bowel) secondary to vascular sludging and occlusion by sickled erythrocytes. This must be distinguished from surgical causes of acute abdomen as management (hydration, opioids, and supportive care) differs fundamentally from surgical intervention.

options: Requires general anaesthesia for every insertion
Cannot be inserted without direct laryngoscopy at all
Is contraindicated in every paediatric age group
Does not protect against aspiration of gastric contents
questions.explanation: A laryngeal mask airway sits above the glottis and does not provide a secure seal against the trachea, so it does not reliably protect against aspiration of gastric contents, unlike a cuffed endotracheal tube. It can be inserted blindly without direct laryngoscopy, which is actually an advantage in emergencies, and is used across paediatric age groups as a bridging airway. It is not a definitive long-term airway solution.
questions.question: A child requires emergency airway management, and a laryngeal mask airway is considered. A significant disadvantage of this device in paediatric emergency care is that it:

questions.explanation: For an X-linked recessive condition, a carrier mother transmits the affected X chromosome to fifty percent of her sons on average, who will then be affected, while fifty percent of her daughters will be carriers. This differs fundamentally from autosomal recessive inheritance risk calculations. Accurate explanation of sex-specific risk is central to genetic counselling in X-linked conditions.
questions.question: A couple with a family history of an X-linked recessive condition seek genetic counselling. Their unaffected daughter is confirmed as a carrier. What is the CORRECT risk that each of her future sons will be affected?
options: A seventy-five percent chance of being affected
No risk since the mother is unaffected herself
A fifty percent chance of being affected
A one hundred percent chance of being affected
A twenty-five percent chance of being affected

questions.question: Denys-Drash syndrome must be distinguished from which other WT1-associated syndrome by the presence of nephropathy rather than aniridia?
questions.explanation: Denys-Drash syndrome (DDS: Wilm's tumour + nephropathy + genital abnormalities) is distinguished from WAGR syndrome (Wilm's tumour + Aniridia + Genitourinary malformation + mental Retardation) by the presence of nephropathy (mesangial sclerosis causing nephrotic syndrome) in DDS, versus aniridia and intellectual disability in WAGR. Both involve WT1 gene abnormalities on chromosome 11p13: DDS from point mutations and WAGR from larger contiguous deletions. Neither condition presents with DDS' specific diffuse mesangial sclerosis in WAGR, and vice versa.

Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome describes bilateral adrenal haemorrhage complicating overwhelming sepsis, classically meningococcaemia, causing acute adrenal insufficiency and refractory shock. Prompt recognition and immediate hydrocortisone administration alongside sepsis management are critical for survival. Imaging showing bilateral adrenal enlargement or haemorrhage supports the diagnosis in this clinical context.
questions.question: A child recovering from severe meningococcal septicaemia develops sudden hypotension and shock unresponsive to fluids, with imaging showing bilateral adrenal enlargement. Which syndrome does this presentation suggest?
options: Cushing syndrome from ectopic ACTH secretion

questions.explanation: When peripheral intravenous access fails after limited attempts in a critically ill child, intraosseous access provides rapid, reliable vascular access for fluids and drugs and should be pursued promptly rather than persisting with further failed peripheral attempts. Elective radiology-guided central access is too slow for an emergency. Oral or subcutaneous routes cannot deliver adequate volumes in shock.
options: Oral rehydration therapy as an alternative
Repeated peripheral attempts for ten more minutes
Elective central line placement in radiology
questions.question: A 4-year-old in shock requires vascular access urgently but two peripheral attempts have failed. The MOST appropriate NEXT step is:

options: Chronic anaemia and increased metabolic demand from haemolysis
questions.explanation: Chronic anaemia increases metabolic demand and reduces oxygen delivery to tissues, while ongoing haemolysis diverts nutritional resources, both contributing to growth delay and pubertal delay commonly observed in children with sickle cell disease. Adequate nutrition and disease control can help mitigate these effects.
questions.question: A 6-year-old with sickle cell disease is noted to have delayed growth and pubertal development compared to peers. Which factor most commonly contributes to this in sickle cell disease?

questions.explanation: A regular chronic blood transfusion programme reduces the proportion of sickle haemoglobin and has been shown in clinical trials to significantly lower the risk of first stroke in children with sickle cell disease identified as high risk by elevated transcranial Doppler velocities. This requires ongoing monitoring for iron overload with chelation therapy.
questions.question: A 4-year-old with sickle cell disease has persistently elevated transcranial Doppler velocities. Which management strategy is most appropriate to reduce stroke risk?

options: Routine immunisation intensification at fixed facilities only
Withholding vaccination until laboratory confirmation in all suspected cases
Mop-up campaigns targeting the school population and close contacts
Administering prophylactic antibiotics to all unvaccinated contacts only
Closing all schools in the state pending national vaccination roll-out
questions.explanation: Vaccines are specifically used to control outbreaks through supplemental immunisation, including mop-up campaigns targeting affected populations and close contacts. Meningococcal vaccine is recommended for outbreak control. Fixed-facility routine immunisation alone is insufficient for outbreak containment. Laboratory confirmation should not delay immunisation of contacts; antibiotic prophylaxis complements but does not replace vaccination in outbreak response.
