Use a standardised (0.5 McFarland) inoculum spread evenly to give confluent growth, apply discs of the correct potency within 15 minutes of inoculation, and incubate at the correct temperature for the standard duration, since deviations from the standardised protocol distort zone sizes and give misleading susceptibility results.
questions.question: A 42-year-old woman presents with her fourth urinary tract infection in eight months, with previous partial responses to standard first-line antibiotics, and the attending doctor, suspecting recurrent UTI needing individualised therapy, refers the patient for a disc diffusion antibiotic susceptibility test on a pure isolate from urine culture specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

A 19-year-old student presents with a stepwise rising fever, headache and relative bradycardia for eight days, and the attending doctor, suspecting enteric (typhoid) fever, refers the patient for a blood culture on a blood specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the blood culture because blood culture is most sensitive in the first week of typhoid fever, before the organism becomes established in the stool, and it also permits antibiotic sensitivity testing given rising fluoroquinolone resistance. Principle: The specimen is inoculated onto appropriate general and selective/differential media and incubated under suitable atmospheric conditions to allow the causative organism to grow into discrete colonies; the isolate is then identified by colonial and biochemical characteristics and tested against a panel of antibiotics by disc diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) to determine susceptibility. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no significant growth of a pathogen is obtained (sterile culture, or growth confined to insignificant colony counts of commensals); Growth of Salmonella Typhi confirms typhoid fever and directs targeted therapy; no growth after 5-7 days of incubation with subculture is reported as sterile, though this does not fully exclude typhoid if antibiotics were taken before sampling. Precautions: Draw blood using strict aseptic skin antisepsis (70% alcohol followed by chlorhexidine or iodine, allowed to dry) before venepuncture to prevent skin-commensal contamination; collect an adequate volume into the correct blood-to-broth ratio bottles, and inoculate aerobic and anaerobic bottles before the specimen clots or dries. Use fresh, adequately labelled media within their expiry date, incubate at the correct temperature/atmosphere (e.g. 5-10% CO2 for fastidious organisms) for the recommended duration, and avoid specimen collection after the patient has already started antibiotics, which can suppress growth and give a false-negative culture.

questions.question: A 3-year-old child presents with fever, lethargy, and bulging fontanelle, and CSF culture is requested to investigate pneumococcal meningitis. State the rationale, the principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions needed to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading cause of bacterial meningitis in young children, so CSF culture is requested to confirm the organism and guide appropriate antibiotic therapy. The principle involves culturing CSF on blood agar and chocolate agar, where Streptococcus pneumoniae produces small, alpha-haemolytic colonies that are optochin-sensitive and undergo autolysis (bile solubility) confirming its identity. A normal CSF culture shows no bacterial growth; growth of optochin-sensitive colonies confirms pneumococcal meningitis. Precautions include transporting the CSF specimen promptly and without cooling, since delays can reduce the fragile organism's viability, and using fresh optochin discs and bile solubility reagents to avoid false identification results.

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy presents with a discharging leg wound from which catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci in chains were isolated, and the attending doctor, suspecting wound isolate requiring pathogen versus commensal distinction, refers the patient for a catalase test on a pure isolate from wound culture specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the catalase test as an initial step to confirm the isolate belongs to the streptococci (catalase-negative) rather than the staphylococci (catalase-positive), directing further group-specific testing. Principle: A colony is emulsified in hydrogen peroxide; catalase-positive organisms possess the enzyme catalase, which breaks down H2O2 into water and oxygen, producing visible effervescence (gas bubbles), while catalase-negative organisms show no bubbling. Normal result and deviation: In this context, a negative reaction (no bubbling) is expected when a catalase-negative organism such as a streptococcus is tested; A negative catalase reaction is consistent with Streptococcus, prompting further testing (such as bacitracin sensitivity) to confirm Group A Streptococcus specifically; a positive reaction would instead redirect identification towards Staphylococcus. Precautions: Cleanse the wound surface of surface debris/exudate first, then swab the base or deep margin of the lesion using a sterile swab and place immediately into transport medium to preserve fastidious organisms and prevent overgrowth by skin commensals. Avoid picking up traces of blood agar (which contains catalase-positive red cells) along with the colony, as this gives a false-positive reaction; use an 18-24 hour pure culture and a fresh bottle of hydrogen peroxide.

Reason for the test: The doctor requested the blood culture because clinical signs of neonatal sepsis are non-specific, and blood culture is the gold standard to confirm bacteraemia and guide antibiotic therapy in this vulnerable age group. Principle: The specimen is inoculated onto appropriate general and selective/differential media and incubated under suitable atmospheric conditions to allow the causative organism to grow into discrete colonies; the isolate is then identified by colonial and biochemical characteristics and tested against a panel of antibiotics by disc diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) to determine susceptibility. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no significant growth of a pathogen is obtained (sterile culture, or growth confined to insignificant colony counts of commensals); Growth of a recognised pathogen at a significant colony count confirms sepsis; growth of coagulase-negative staphylococci in only one of two bottles more often reflects skin contamination than true infection and should be interpreted with the clinical picture. Precautions: Draw blood using strict aseptic skin antisepsis (70% alcohol followed by chlorhexidine or iodine, allowed to dry) before venepuncture to prevent skin-commensal contamination; collect an adequate volume into the correct blood-to-broth ratio bottles, and inoculate aerobic and anaerobic bottles before the specimen clots or dries. Use fresh, adequately labelled media within their expiry date, incubate at the correct temperature/atmosphere (e.g. 5-10% CO2 for fastidious organisms) for the recommended duration, and avoid specimen collection after the patient has already started antibiotics, which can suppress growth and give a false-negative culture.
questions.question: A 3-day-old neonate presents with lethargy, poor feeding, temperature instability and grunting respiration, and the attending doctor, suspecting neonatal sepsis, refers the patient for a blood culture on a blood specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: Neonates present with non-specific signs of infection, so blood culture is requested to confirm or exclude sepsis, a potentially rapidly fatal condition in this age group if untreated. The principle relies on enrichment of any bacteria present in the small blood sample within a nutrient broth, followed by subculture for identification once growth is detected. A normal result shows no bacterial growth; growth of a pathogenic organism confirms neonatal sepsis and guides urgent antibiotic therapy. Precautions include collecting an adequate blood volume relative to body size to maximise sensitivity despite typically low bacterial counts in neonatal sepsis, and using strict aseptic technique to avoid contamination that could be mistaken for a true pathogen.
questions.question: A neonate with poor feeding, temperature instability, and lethargy is investigated with blood culture to rule out neonatal sepsis. State why this test was requested, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must observe.

questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the TPHA/FTA-ABS confirmatory test to distinguish a true treponemal infection from a biological false positive, which is well recognised in autoimmune conditions such as lupus. Principle: Patient serum is reacted with Treponema pallidum-specific antigen (fixed on sheep red cells for TPHA, or whole treponemes for FTA-ABS); specific antibody present in the serum causes agglutination or fluorescent labelling, confirming true treponemal infection rather than a biological false positive. Normal result and deviation: In this context, a non-reactive result is normal and, once positive, this test generally stays positive for life regardless of treatment, so it is used only to confirm past or present treponemal infection, not to monitor treatment response; A non-reactive TPHA/FTA-ABS in the presence of a reactive VDRL confirms a biological false positive rather than true syphilis; a reactive confirmatory test instead indicates genuine past or current treponemal infection requiring treatment. Precautions: Collect blood without anticoagulant, allow it to clot fully, separate serum by centrifugation and avoid haemolysis, which can interfere with agglutination and immunoassay readings. Ensure adequate absorption of cross-reacting antibodies where required (FTA-ABS) to prevent false positives from non-pathogenic treponemes/spirochaetes, and use appropriately diluted, non-haemolysed serum.
questions.question: A 35-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with a reactive VDRL result found incidentally with no history or signs suggestive of syphilis, and the attending doctor, suspecting biological false positive syphilis test, refers the patient for a TPHA/FTA-ABS confirmatory test on a serum specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: Blood culture is requested early in the illness because bacteraemia is highest in the first week of typhoid fever, making this the most sensitive window for isolating the causative organism. The principle involves inoculating blood into a nutrient-rich broth that supports bacterial multiplication, followed by subculture onto selective and differential media to identify Salmonella Typhi by its biochemical and serological characteristics. A normal (negative) culture shows no bacterial growth after the incubation period; growth of Salmonella Typhi confirms the diagnosis and allows antimicrobial susceptibility testing. The scientist must collect an adequate blood volume before starting antibiotics, use strict aseptic technique to prevent skin-flora contamination, and maintain the correct blood-to-broth ratio to avoid inhibiting bacterial growth.
questions.question: A 19-year-old man in the first week of fever, headache, and malaise is referred for blood culture to confirm suspected typhoid fever. Explain the rationale for the test, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions to avoid a false result.

A febrile 8-year-old child with abdominal distension and rose-coloured spots on the trunk is referred for a Widal agglutination test. State why the test was requested, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must take.
questions.answerText: The presence of rose spots with fever and abdominal distension is a classic, though not exclusive, sign of typhoid fever in children, so Widal serology is requested to support the clinical diagnosis. The principle is antigen-antibody agglutination, where the child's serum is serially diluted and mixed with O and H antigen suspensions to detect specific agglutinating antibodies. A normal result shows no clumping at diagnostic dilutions; a titre meeting or exceeding the locally validated threshold, especially with a rising trend, supports active infection. The scientist must ensure the antigen suspensions are not over- or under-concentrated, must incubate tubes or slides for the correct time and temperature, and must be cautious of false positives from malaria or other febrile illnesses that can cause non-specific cross-reactions.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man presents with completion of a two-week H. pylori eradication regimen for a previously confirmed infection, and the attending doctor, suspecting confirmation of H. pylori eradication, refers the patient for a H. pylori stool antigen test on a stool specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the H. pylori stool antigen test to confirm successful eradication of the organism after treatment, since persistent infection risks ulcer recurrence and, rarely, gastric malignancy. Principle: An immunoassay detects Helicobacter pylori-specific antigens shed in the stool, using antibody-coated particles that bind the antigen and produce a visible line, reflecting active gastric infection. Normal result and deviation: In this context, a negative result is normal; A negative repeat stool antigen test (taken at least four weeks after completing therapy and off proton pump inhibitors) confirms successful eradication; a persistently positive result indicates treatment failure and the need for a second-line regimen. Precautions: Collect a fresh stool sample (not one contaminated with urine or water), use a clean wide-mouthed container, and examine or place in transport/enrichment medium within the recommended time, since delay allows overgrowth of commensal flora and loss of fragile pathogens or motile trophozoites. Advise the patient to stop proton pump inhibitors, antibiotics, and bismuth compounds for the recommended period before testing, as these suppress the organism and cause false-negative results, and test a fresh, unrefrigerated-beyond-recommendation stool specimen.

Reason for the test: The doctor requested the saline wet mount as a quick bedside test to look for the motile flagellated parasite responsible, allowing same-visit diagnosis and treatment along with partner notification. Principle: A drop of vaginal/urethral discharge is mixed with a drop of warm normal saline on a slide and examined immediately under the microscope for the characteristic jerky, twitching motility of flagellated Trichomonas vaginalis trophozoites. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no motile flagellated organisms are seen in a normal wet preparation; Motile, pear-shaped flagellates with characteristic jerky movement confirm trichomoniasis; a negative wet mount does not fully exclude the diagnosis given its lower sensitivity compared with culture or NAAT, so a negative result in a strongly suggestive case should prompt further testing. Precautions: Collect the high vaginal swab using a bivalve speculum without lubricant (which can be bacteriostatic), sample the posterior fornix, and transport in Amies/Stuart medium promptly to preserve fastidious and anaerobic organisms. Examine the slide within 10-20 minutes of collection at body-temperature range, since Trichomonas motility rapidly declines and organisms become difficult to distinguish from leucocytes once movement stops.
questions.question: A 27-year-old woman presents with a frothy, yellow-green, malodorous vaginal discharge with vulval irritation, and the attending doctor, suspecting trichomonal vaginitis, refers the patient for a saline wet mount on a vaginal discharge specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the culture and sensitivity to identify the organism responsible for the post-operative infection and guide targeted antibiotic therapy, reducing the risk of wound dehiscence or deeper infection. Principle: The specimen is inoculated onto appropriate general and selective/differential media and incubated under suitable atmospheric conditions to allow the causative organism to grow into discrete colonies; the isolate is then identified by colonial and biochemical characteristics and tested against a panel of antibiotics by disc diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) to determine susceptibility. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no significant growth of a pathogen is obtained (sterile culture, or growth confined to insignificant colony counts of commensals); Significant growth of E. coli with sensitivity results allows targeted therapy; scanty growth of skin commensals alone in a wound with minimal inflammation may not represent true infection and can be managed with dressing care alone. Precautions: Cleanse the wound surface of surface debris/exudate first, then swab the base or deep margin of the lesion using a sterile swab and place immediately into transport medium to preserve fastidious organisms and prevent overgrowth by skin commensals. Use fresh, adequately labelled media within their expiry date, incubate at the correct temperature/atmosphere (e.g. 5-10% CO2 for fastidious organisms) for the recommended duration, and avoid specimen collection after the patient has already started antibiotics, which can suppress growth and give a false-negative culture.
questions.question: A 44-year-old woman presents with wound discharge and redness five days after abdominal hysterectomy, and the attending doctor, suspecting surgical site infection, refers the patient for a culture and sensitivity on a wound swab/pus specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

A 55-year-old man presents with thickened, discoloured, crumbling toenails, and the attending doctor, suspecting onychomycosis (fungal nail infection), refers the patient for a Potassium hydroxide (KOH) mount on a nail clippings/scrapings specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the Potassium hydroxide (KOH) mount to confirm a fungal cause before committing the patient to a prolonged course of oral antifungal therapy, which carries potential liver toxicity. Principle: The specimen (skin scraping, hair, nail, or vaginal discharge) is mixed with 10-20% potassium hydroxide, which digests keratin and host cellular debris, clearing the background so that fungal hyphae, spores, or budding yeasts become visible under the microscope. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no fungal hyphae, spores, or pseudohyphae are seen in a normal preparation; Visible hyphae within the nail material support onychomycosis, justifying antifungal treatment; a negative KOH mount should prompt fungal culture, since nail material can be difficult to clear fully and false negatives are relatively common. Precautions: Scrape the active advancing edge of the lesion with a blunt scalpel onto a clean slide or into a folder, since scraping the centre of an old lesion under-samples viable fungal elements. Allow adequate time (10-20 minutes, or gentle warming) for the KOH to fully digest keratin before examination, since inadequate clearing can mask hyphae, and avoid mistaking cotton or textile fibres and mosaic artefacts for true fungal elements.

questions.question: A 35-year-old butcher presents with a painless black-eschar skin lesion with surrounding oedema after handling a sick animal carcass, and the attending doctor, suspecting cutaneous anthrax, refers the patient for a culture and sensitivity on a lesion exudate/eschar edge specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the culture and sensitivity to confirm this occupationally-acquired diagnosis definitively, given the serious public health and biosecurity implications of a confirmed anthrax case, while treatment is started immediately on clinical suspicion. Principle: The specimen is inoculated onto appropriate general and selective/differential media and incubated under suitable atmospheric conditions to allow the causative organism to grow into discrete colonies; the isolate is then identified by colonial and biochemical characteristics and tested against a panel of antibiotics by disc diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) to determine susceptibility. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no significant growth of a pathogen is obtained (sterile culture, or growth confined to insignificant colony counts of commensals); Growth of large, Gram-positive, spore-forming rods with a characteristic 'medusa head' colonial appearance confirms Bacillus anthracis; strict laboratory biosafety precautions are required throughout, since the organism's spores are highly resistant and potentially hazardous to handle. Precautions: Sample the vesicle fluid or the edge of the eschar/lesion with a sterile swab or scraping before any topical antiseptic is applied, and handle with the biosafety precautions appropriate to the suspected organism. Use fresh, adequately labelled media within their expiry date, incubate at the correct temperature/atmosphere (e.g. 5-10% CO2 for fastidious organisms) for the recommended duration, and avoid specimen collection after the patient has already started antibiotics, which can suppress growth and give a false-negative culture.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man with a family history of gastric cancer undergoes Helicobacter pylori stool antigen testing as part of a screening and eradication strategy. Explain why this test was requested, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must observe.
questions.answerText: Chronic Helicobacter pylori infection is a recognised risk factor for gastric cancer, so screening with stool antigen testing is requested in someone with a relevant family history to identify and treat infection before significant mucosal damage occurs. The principle involves an immunoassay detecting Helicobacter pylori surface antigens present in the stool sample, using specific antibodies to generate a measurable signal. A normal (negative) result shows no antigen detected, suggesting no active infection; a positive result confirms infection warranting eradication therapy given the associated cancer risk. Precautions include confirming the patient has not recently used antibiotics, bismuth, or acid-suppressing medication that could cause a false-negative result, and using a properly validated assay kit with appropriate controls run alongside patient samples.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman presents with a thin, greyish, fishy-smelling vaginal discharge, and the attending doctor, suspecting bacterial vaginosis, refers the patient for a Gram stain on a high vaginal swab smear specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the Gram stain to demonstrate the shift in vaginal flora that characterises bacterial vaginosis, which cannot be diagnosed by culture alone since the causative organisms are also found in healthy women. Principle: The specimen is smeared, heat-fixed and sequentially stained with crystal violet, Lugol's iodine (mordant), acetone-alcohol (decolouriser) and safranin (counterstain); Gram-positive organisms retain the crystal violet-iodine complex within their thick peptidoglycan wall and appear purple/blue, while Gram-negative organisms lose it on decolourisation and take up the safranin, appearing pink/red. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no organisms or only mixed scanty commensal flora are seen; Epithelial cells studded with adherent coccobacilli obscuring the cell border ('clue cells'), with a marked reduction in normal Gram-positive lactobacilli, support the diagnosis; a smear dominated by normal lactobacilli argues against bacterial vaginosis. Precautions: Collect the high vaginal swab using a bivalve speculum without lubricant (which can be bacteriostatic), sample the posterior fornix, and transport in Amies/Stuart medium promptly to preserve fastidious and anaerobic organisms. Prepare a smear of optimal thinness and heat-fix gently (excessive heat distorts morphology); do not over-decolourise with acetone-alcohol, as this can make Gram-positive organisms falsely appear Gram-negative, while under-decolourising can make Gram-negatives falsely appear Gram-positive; always include a known control organism.

Reason for the test: The doctor requested the dark-field microscopy to attempt direct visualisation of the organism very early in the illness, before serology becomes reliably positive. Principle: A wet preparation of exudate/serum is examined under dark-field illumination, where light is scattered obliquely so that thin, motile spirochaetes stand out brightly against a dark background, since they are too thin to be seen by ordinary bright-field microscopy or Gram stain. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no spirochaetes are seen in a normal specimen; Thin, tightly coiled, actively motile spirochaetes with hooked ends support leptospirosis; however, this method has low sensitivity and a negative result does not exclude the diagnosis, so serology (MAT) on a later sample remains the mainstay of confirmation. Precautions: Collect capillary or EDTA venous blood and prepare thick and thin films promptly (ideally at the bedside or within the hour) before parasitaemia patterns are lost or morphology distorted by prolonged anticoagulant contact. Examine the wet preparation immediately while organisms remain motile, since spirochaetes lyse and lose motility quickly if the preparation dries out or is delayed, and avoid specimens from an area recently cleaned with antiseptic, which kills the organisms and gives a false negative.
questions.question: A 32-year-old sewage worker presents with fever and severe muscle pain in the first few days of illness, before antibodies have developed, and the attending doctor, suspecting leptospirosis (direct dark-field of blood), refers the patient for a dark-field microscopy on a fresh blood/urine specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: Extrapulmonary specimens usually contain very few bacilli, so culture is chosen over smear microscopy because it can detect even a small number of viable organisms that a direct smear would miss. The principle involves inoculating decontaminated pleural fluid onto specialised mycobacterial media, allowing slow-growing colonies to develop over several weeks under controlled incubation. A normal result is no growth after the full incubation period; growth of acid-fast colonies confirms tuberculous involvement of the pleura. Precautions include processing the fluid promptly to prevent bacterial overgrowth by contaminants, centrifuging to concentrate any organisms present, and maintaining strict sterile technique throughout inoculation to avoid false-positive contamination.
questions.question: A 33-year-old man with extrapulmonary symptoms and a suspected tuberculous pleural effusion has pleural fluid sent for mycobacterial culture. Explain why culture rather than smear was chosen, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must observe.

A 58-year-old man with a urinary catheter develops fever and rigors, and blood cultures are requested alongside urine culture to determine whether urosepsis has occurred. Explain the reasoning, the principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must take.
questions.answerText: Fever and rigors in a catheterised patient raise concern that a urinary tract infection has progressed to bloodstream invasion, so blood cultures are requested together with urine culture to establish whether the same organism is present in both sites. The principle involves enrichment of the blood sample in broth to detect circulating organisms, paralleling the quantitative approach used for urine culture, with organism identification and susceptibility testing performed on any isolate recovered. A normal blood culture shows no growth; growth of the same organism recovered from the urine, such as a Gram-negative rod, confirms urosepsis. Precautions include collecting blood cultures from a site distant from the catheter to avoid contamination, and ensuring prompt processing of both specimens to allow timely, concordant identification of the causative organism.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with an infected central venous catheter develops fever, and paired blood cultures from the catheter and a peripheral vein are requested to investigate catheter-related bloodstream infection. Explain the rationale, the principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions needed.
questions.answerText: Comparing cultures drawn simultaneously from the catheter and a peripheral vein helps determine whether the catheter itself is the infection source, so paired cultures are requested rather than a single sample. The principle involves enrichment culture of each sample in broth, with time-to-positivity compared between the two sites; significantly earlier growth from the catheter sample supports a catheter-related infection. A normal result shows no growth from either site; growth from both sites with earlier positivity from the catheter sample strongly supports catheter-related bloodstream infection. Precautions include clearly labelling each sample by its collection site, collecting both samples as close together in time as possible, and using strict aseptic technique at both sites to avoid contamination that could obscure the comparison.

Reason for the test: The doctor requested the Microscopic agglutination test (MAT) to confirm the diagnosis in an occupationally exposed patient presenting with the severe icteric form of the disease, guiding urgent antibiotic and supportive renal care. Principle: Patient serum is reacted with live or formalised suspensions of different Leptospira serovars; specific antibody agglutinates the corresponding leptospires, observed under dark-field microscopy, identifying the infecting serogroup and titre. Normal result and deviation: In this context, a titre below the diagnostic cut-off, or absence of a four-fold rise between acute and convalescent samples, is regarded as negative; A significant titre supports severe leptospirosis (Weil's disease), reinforcing the need for aggressive supportive management alongside antibiotics; a negative early titre should be repeated in a convalescent sample before leptospirosis is excluded, given the delayed antibody response. Precautions: Collect blood without anticoagulant, allow it to clot fully, separate serum by centrifugation and avoid haemolysis, which can interfere with agglutination and immunoassay readings. Test paired acute and convalescent sera to demonstrate a rising titre since a single titre can reflect past exposure, maintain live leptospiral cultures correctly for the antigen panel, and read promptly under dark-field microscopy before agglutinates settle or degrade.
questions.question: A 44-year-old sewage worker presents with fever, jaundice and reduced urine output, and the attending doctor, suspecting occupational leptospirosis (sewage worker), refers the patient for a Microscopic agglutination test (MAT) on a serum specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

A 45-year-old miner reports a persistent cough with occasional streaks of blood in his sputum over two months. The physician requests three early-morning sputum smears for AFB. What is the justification for the test, its underlying principle, the expected normal finding, and the precautions needed to avoid an inaccurate result?
questions.answerText: Haemoptysis with a prolonged cough in a person with occupational dust exposure raises strong suspicion of pulmonary tuberculosis, so sputum AFB smears are ordered to confirm infectious bacilli quickly and cheaply. The test works because mycobacterial mycolic acids bind carbol fuchsin so tightly that the dye resists decolourisation by acid-alcohol, leaving bright red bacilli visible on Ziehl-Neelsen staining. Normally no acid-fast bacilli are seen in 100 high-power fields; any bacilli seen are graded and reported, with higher grades correlating with greater infectiousness. To avoid false results the scientist must ensure the specimen is genuine sputum and not saliva, use adequate smear thickness, heat-fix properly without charring, stain with quality-controlled reagents, and examine systematically to avoid missing scanty bacilli.

With malaria excluded and fever persisting beyond a week, blood culture is requested because prolonged undifferentiated fever in endemic settings is frequently due to enteric fever, and culture remains the most specific confirmatory test. The principle relies on enrichment of any bacteria present in the blood sample within a nutrient broth, followed by isolation on selective media and biochemical or serological confirmation of the organism. Normally, no growth occurs, indicating a sterile blood sample; growth of Salmonella Typhi confirms bacteraemic typhoid fever. Precautions include disinfecting the venepuncture site thoroughly to prevent contamination with skin flora, drawing blood before antibiotic administration, and incubating cultures for the full recommended period since some isolates grow slowly.
questions.question: A 24-year-old woman with fever for ten days and no localising signs is referred for blood culture after a negative malaria test. State why this test is appropriate, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must take.

A 19-year-old university student with cough, fever, and a positive tuberculin skin test is referred for a liquid culture system (such as MGIT) to confirm active disease. Give the reason for the test, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions to avoid false outcomes.
questions.answerText: A positive tuberculin test only indicates exposure, not active disease, so a liquid culture system is requested to confirm whether viable, actively multiplying bacilli are present. The principle of the mycobacterial growth indicator tube relies on a fluorescence-quenching oxygen sensor at the tube base that fluoresces as growing organisms consume oxygen, allowing automated detection of growth days to weeks earlier than solid media. A normal result is no fluorescence signal, indicating no growth; a positive signal confirms viable mycobacteria requiring identification and susceptibility testing. The scientist must supplement the broth correctly, inoculate under aseptic conditions to prevent contamination, and monitor incubation continuously since delayed reading of a positive tube can allow overgrowth that complicates further testing.

Reason for the test: The doctor requested the Malaria rapid diagnostic test (RDT) to rapidly screen for malaria as a cause of fever in a returning traveller, given the risk of rapid progression to severe disease if the infecting species is Plasmodium falciparum. Principle: An immunochromatographic strip captures Plasmodium-specific antigens (e.g. HRP-2 or pLDH) from a finger-prick blood sample using monoclonal antibodies bound to the strip, producing a visible test line within minutes if antigen is present. Normal result and deviation: In this context, a negative result is normal; A positive result confirms malaria and mandates urgent treatment and assessment for features of severity; a negative result in a returning traveller with ongoing fever should not be fully reassuring and warrants a blood film (which is more sensitive) and consideration of other travel-related causes of fever. Precautions: Collect capillary or EDTA venous blood and prepare thick and thin films promptly (ideally at the bedside or within the hour) before parasitaemia patterns are lost or morphology distorted by prolonged anticoagulant contact. Follow the manufacturer's timing strictly when reading the result, since reading too early or too late can give a false result, and confirm a negative result with microscopy in a strongly suspicious case since RDTs can miss low-density parasitaemia; note some tests remain positive for weeks after successful treatment (persistent antigenaemia) so cannot be used to monitor cure.
questions.question: A 33-year-old woman presents with fever ten days after returning from a malaria-endemic country, and the attending doctor, suspecting returning traveller with fever (RDT), refers the patient for a Malaria rapid diagnostic test (RDT) on a finger-prick blood specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

A newborn develops multiple pustular skin lesions in a hospital nursery, prompting a wound swab culture to investigate a possible staphylococcal outbreak. Explain why this test was requested, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must observe.
questions.answerText: Pustular lesions in a nursery setting raise concern for a Staphylococcus aureus outbreak, so culture is requested both to confirm the organism and, if needed, to support strain typing for infection control. The principle relies on culturing the pustule exudate on blood agar, where Staphylococcus aureus produces golden colonies with clear beta-haemolysis, and confirming pathogenicity with a positive coagulase test. A normal culture from healthy skin shows no growth of a dominant pathogen; confirmed growth of coagulase-positive Staphylococcus aureus supports the outbreak diagnosis and prompts infection control measures. Precautions include collecting the specimen before topical antiseptics are applied, since these can suppress bacterial growth and cause a false-negative culture, and maintaining strict aseptic swabbing technique to avoid contaminating the sample with normal skin flora.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents with routine blood donation screening panel, and the attending doctor, as part of blood donor hepatitis B screening, refers the patient for a HBsAg test on a serum specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the HBsAg test as a mandatory screening step to prevent transfusion-transmitted hepatitis B, since chronically infected donors may have no symptoms at all. Principle: An immunoassay (ELISA or rapid immunochromatographic strip) detects the surface antigen of the hepatitis B virus in the patient's serum using antibody-coated particles that bind HBsAg and generate a visible line or colour change. Normal result and deviation: In this context, a negative result is normal; A positive HBsAg result excludes the donor and prompts referral for further hepatitis B work-up (viral load, liver function) and counselling; a negative result allows the unit to proceed, understanding that a very recent infection within the window period could rarely still be missed. Precautions: Collect blood without anticoagulant, allow it to clot fully, separate serum by centrifugation and avoid haemolysis, which can interfere with agglutination and immunoassay readings. Confirm any positive/borderline screening result with a more specific supplemental test, avoid gross haemolysis or lipaemia in the sample which can interfere with the assay, and be aware of the diagnostic window period shortly after infection when the antigen may not yet be detectable.

Reason for the test: The doctor requested the Microscopic agglutination test (MAT) to confirm the specific infecting serogroup, since the flooding exposure history strongly raises suspicion of leptospirosis, which can progress to severe multi-organ disease (Weil's disease) if untreated. Principle: Patient serum is reacted with live or formalised suspensions of different Leptospira serovars; specific antibody agglutinates the corresponding leptospires, observed under dark-field microscopy, identifying the infecting serogroup and titre. Normal result and deviation: In this context, a titre below the diagnostic cut-off, or absence of a four-fold rise between acute and convalescent samples, is regarded as negative; A significant titre, or ideally a rising titre on paired acute and convalescent samples, confirms leptospirosis and identifies the likely serogroup for epidemiological purposes; a single low titre taken very early in the illness may be falsely reassuring, since antibodies typically take about a week to become detectable. Precautions: Collect blood without anticoagulant, allow it to clot fully, separate serum by centrifugation and avoid haemolysis, which can interfere with agglutination and immunoassay readings. Test paired acute and convalescent sera to demonstrate a rising titre since a single titre can reflect past exposure, maintain live leptospiral cultures correctly for the antigen panel, and read promptly under dark-field microscopy before agglutinates settle or degrade.
questions.question: A 36-year-old man presents with fever, severe calf muscle pain and conjunctival redness after wading through floodwater, and the attending doctor, suspecting leptospirosis after flooding, refers the patient for a Microscopic agglutination test (MAT) on a serum specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the oxidase test to rapidly triage the Gram-negative rod isolated from blood culture into the Enterobacteriaceae (oxidase-negative) or the non-fermenters such as Pseudomonas (oxidase-positive), guiding urgent empirical antibiotic escalation while full identification is completed. Principle: A colony is smeared onto filter paper impregnated with the oxidase reagent (tetramethyl-p-phenylenediamine); organisms possessing cytochrome c oxidase rapidly oxidise the reagent, producing a deep purple colour within 10-15 seconds, while oxidase-negative organisms cause no colour change. Normal result and deviation: In this context, a negative reaction (no colour change) is expected with members of the Enterobacteriaceae; A negative oxidase reaction supports a member of the Enterobacteriaceae such as E. coli, generally more predictable in susceptibility; a positive reaction instead suggests Pseudomonas or a related non-fermenter, prompting broader anti-pseudomonal cover pending full sensitivity results. Precautions: Draw blood using strict aseptic skin antisepsis (70% alcohol followed by chlorhexidine or iodine, allowed to dry) before venepuncture to prevent skin-commensal contamination; collect an adequate volume into the correct blood-to-broth ratio bottles, and inoculate aerobic and anaerobic bottles before the specimen clots or dries. Use a platinum or plastic (never nichrome/iron) loop to transfer the colony, as metal loops can produce a false-positive reaction, and read strictly within 10-15 seconds since delayed colour change is not considered a true positive.
questions.question: A 57-year-old man presents with fever and hypotension with a Gram-negative rod isolated from blood culture, and the attending doctor, suspecting septicaemia (rapid coliform vs Pseudomonas triage), refers the patient for a oxidase test on a pure isolate from blood culture specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

A 55-year-old man develops abdominal distension, fever, and profuse diarrhoea while on antibiotics for a respiratory infection, and stool testing is requested to investigate pseudomembranous colitis caused by Clostridium difficile. State why this test was requested, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must observe.
questions.answerText: The combination of antibiotic exposure with systemic signs and severe diarrhoea raises concern for pseudomembranous colitis, so stool toxin testing is requested urgently to confirm Clostridium difficile as the cause and guide immediate targeted treatment. The principle involves detecting toxin A and/or B, the virulence factors directly responsible for colonic mucosal damage, using immunoassay or molecular amplification techniques applied to the liquid stool sample. A normal result shows no detectable toxin; a positive result confirms the diagnosis, supporting the clinical suspicion of pseudomembranous colitis. Precautions include ensuring the stool sample is appropriately liquid and fresh, since toxin can degrade over time at room temperature, and communicating a positive result promptly given the infection control implications for isolating the patient to prevent spread.

HBeAg status helps determine the level of active viral replication and infectivity in chronic hepatitis B, guiding treatment decisions, so this test is requested alongside routine monitoring. The principle involves immunoassay detection of the hepatitis B e antigen or its corresponding antibody in the patient's serum, using specific antibody binding and a labelled detection system. A normal pattern in a resolving or low-replicative phase would show HBeAg negative with anti-HBe positive; ongoing HBeAg positivity indicates high viral replication and infectivity. Precautions include interpreting results alongside viral load and liver function tests for a complete clinical picture, and using properly validated assays since certain viral mutations can affect antigen detection and produce misleading results if not accounted for.
questions.question: A 40-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B undergoes HBeAg and anti-HBe testing to assess viral replication activity and infectivity. State why this test was requested, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must observe.

A 30-year-old man with recent unprotected sexual exposure requests HIV testing, and the physician orders an ELISA screening test. Why was this test requested, what is its principle, what is the expected normal result, and what precautions must be taken to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: ELISA is requested as the initial screening test because it is highly sensitive, minimising the chance of missing a true infection, following a recognised exposure risk. The principle involves the patient's serum being incubated with HIV antigens fixed to a solid surface; if specific antibodies are present, they bind the antigen and are then detected using an enzyme-linked secondary antibody that produces a measurable colour change proportional to antibody concentration. A normal (non-reactive) result shows no significant colour change; a reactive result requires confirmation with a more specific test such as a Western blot or a combination antigen-antibody assay before a diagnosis is given. Precautions include testing at an appropriate interval after exposure to allow the window period for antibody development to pass, running proper positive and negative controls, and never disclosing a preliminary reactive screening result as a confirmed diagnosis without supplementary testing.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman presents with typical symptoms of an uncomplicated urinary tract infection with a positive urine culture, and the attending doctor, suspecting uncomplicated cystitis requiring confirmation of first-line therapy, refers the patient for a disc diffusion antibiotic susceptibility test on a pure isolate from urine culture specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the disc diffusion antibiotic susceptibility test to confirm susceptibility to the standard first-line oral agent before or shortly after starting empirical treatment, ensuring the chosen therapy will actually be effective. Principle: A standardised inoculum of the isolate is spread evenly on Mueller-Hinton agar and antibiotic-impregnated discs are applied; the antibiotic diffuses outward from the disc creating a concentration gradient, and the diameter of the resulting zone of inhibited growth is measured and compared with standard breakpoints to classify the isolate as sensitive, intermediate, or resistant. Normal result and deviation: In this context, a wide zone of inhibition around each disc, classifying the isolate as sensitive to first-line agents, is the expected/favourable pattern; A wide zone of inhibition around the first-line agent confirms it was an appropriate choice; an unexpectedly small zone (resistance) would prompt the clinician to switch to an alternative agent guided by the rest of the panel. Precautions: Collect a clean-catch, midstream early-morning specimen after proper genital cleaning to avoid contamination with periurethral flora, and deliver to the laboratory or refrigerate at 4°C within two hours to prevent bacterial overgrowth that falsifies the colony count. Use a standardised (0.5 McFarland) inoculum spread evenly to give confluent growth, apply discs of the correct potency within 15 minutes of inoculation, and incubate at the correct temperature for the standard duration, since deviations from the standardised protocol distort zone sizes and give misleading susceptibility results.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with diabetes presents with fever, rigors, and costovertebral angle tenderness. Blood and urine cultures are requested to investigate urosepsis. State why these tests were requested, the principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must observe.
questions.answerText: The combination of systemic sepsis features with flank tenderness suggests urosepsis, so both urine and blood cultures are requested to confirm the source organism, commonly Escherichia coli, and its extent of spread into the bloodstream. The principle for urine culture is quantitative plating to detect significant colony counts, while blood culture relies on enrichment broth to detect bacteraemia; both use selective and differential media to identify the causative organism. A normal result for both would show no significant growth; concordant growth of the same organism, such as Escherichia coli, in both specimens confirms urosepsis. Precautions include collecting both specimens before antibiotic administration wherever possible, using strict aseptic technique for venepuncture to avoid contamination, and processing both samples urgently given the potential severity of sepsis.

Reason for the test: The doctor requested the cefoxitin disc test (MRSA screen) urgently, since Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia carries high mortality, and methicillin resistance status critically determines whether empirical therapy needs immediate escalation. Principle: The isolate is tested against a cefoxitin disc (a surrogate marker for the mecA-mediated altered penicillin-binding protein PBP2a); a reduced zone of inhibition indicates methicillin/oxacillin resistance (MRSA) rather than testing oxacillin directly, which can give unreliable results at standard incubation temperature. Normal result and deviation: In this context, a full, unimpeded zone of inhibition around the cefoxitin disc (methicillin-susceptible) is the normal/favourable result; A reduced cefoxitin zone confirms MRSA bacteraemia, mandating a switch to a glycopeptide or other appropriate anti-MRSA agent without delay; a full zone confirms MSSA, for which a narrower-spectrum beta-lactam is actually more effective than a glycopeptide. Precautions: Draw blood using strict aseptic skin antisepsis (70% alcohol followed by chlorhexidine or iodine, allowed to dry) before venepuncture to prevent skin-commensal contamination; collect an adequate volume into the correct blood-to-broth ratio bottles, and inoculate aerobic and anaerobic bottles before the specimen clots or dries. Incubate at 30-35°C for the full 24 hours (some mecA-mediated resistance is poorly expressed at 37°C), and confirm borderline results with a molecular mecA/mecC or PBP2a test where available.
questions.question: A 66-year-old man presents with persistent fever and a positive blood culture for Staphylococcus aureus during a prolonged hospital stay, and the attending doctor, suspecting bloodstream MRSA infection, refers the patient for a cefoxitin disc test (MRSA screen) on a pure isolate from blood culture specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The recent timing of exposure with acute symptoms raises concern for early HIV infection, so a combination test capable of detecting both viral antigen and host antibody is requested to shorten the diagnostic window period compared with antibody-only assays. The principle involves simultaneously detecting the HIV p24 antigen, present early in infection before antibodies develop, and HIV-specific antibodies, which appear somewhat later, using a combined immunoassay format. A normal (non-reactive) result shows no significant signal for either component; a reactive result requires confirmatory testing to distinguish true early infection from a false-positive screening result. Precautions include being aware that even this combination test has a residual window period before either marker becomes detectable, and advising a repeat test after this period if the initial result is negative but exposure risk remains high.
questions.question: A 4th-generation combination antigen-antibody test is requested for a 28-year-old man presenting with a flu-like illness two weeks after a high-risk exposure, given the earlier detection window compared with antibody-only testing. Explain why this test was requested, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must observe.

questions.answerText: Pregnancy increases susceptibility to severe malaria and adverse outcomes for both mother and baby, so routine blood film screening is requested even in the absence of overt symptoms in high-risk settings. The principle involves examining Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood films under the microscope to detect and identify any malaria parasites present within red blood cells. A normal (negative) film shows no parasites after adequate examination; a positive film identifies infection requiring prompt, pregnancy-appropriate antimalarial treatment. Precautions include examining an adequate number of fields given that placental sequestration of parasites can sometimes make peripheral blood parasitaemia deceptively low, and correlating any negative result with the clinical picture, repeating testing if symptoms persist despite an initial negative film.
questions.question: A pregnant woman in an endemic area undergoes a blood film for malaria as part of routine antenatal screening given the increased risk of severe disease in pregnancy. State why this test was requested, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must observe.

A 39-year-old woman presents with recurrent flank pain and a lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod on urine culture, and the attending doctor, suspecting chronic pyelonephritis (citrate-negative coliform), refers the patient for a citrate utilisation test on a pure isolate from urine culture specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the citrate utilisation test to confirm the coliform's identity as E. coli by demonstrating that it cannot use citrate as a sole carbon source, distinguishing it from other Enterobacteriaceae with a similar colonial appearance. Principle: The organism is inoculated onto Simmons citrate agar; organisms able to use citrate as their sole carbon source alkalinise the medium, turning the bromothymol-blue indicator from green to Prussian blue (positive), while non-utilisers leave the medium unchanged (green). Normal result and deviation: In this context, a negative reaction (medium remains green) is expected with citrate-non-utilising organisms; A negative citrate test (medium remains green) is consistent with E. coli; a positive result would instead point towards Klebsiella, Enterobacter, or Citrobacter, altering the expected resistance profile and prognosis for recurrence. Precautions: Collect a clean-catch, midstream early-morning specimen after proper genital cleaning to avoid contamination with periurethral flora, and deliver to the laboratory or refrigerate at 4°C within two hours to prevent bacterial overgrowth that falsifies the colony count. Use only a light inoculum streaked on the slant surface (a heavy inoculum can cause false colour change from carry-over nutrients), and incubate for the full 24-48 hours before declaring a negative result.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man presents with routine pre-operative screening before elective hip replacement surgery, with no active infection, and the attending doctor, as part of MRSA nasal carriage screening, refers the patient for a culture on selective MRSA chromogenic agar on a nasal swab specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the culture on selective MRSA chromogenic agar to detect asymptomatic nasal carriage of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus before surgery, since carriers have a higher risk of post-operative surgical site infection and may need decolonisation therapy first. Principle: The specimen is inoculated onto appropriate general and selective/differential media and incubated under suitable atmospheric conditions to allow the causative organism to grow into discrete colonies; the isolate is then identified by colonial and biochemical characteristics and tested against a panel of antibiotics by disc diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) to determine susceptibility. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no significant growth of a pathogen is obtained (sterile culture, or growth confined to insignificant colony counts of commensals); Growth of characteristic coloured colonies on chromogenic MRSA agar, confirmed by cefoxitin disc testing, indicates carriage requiring decolonisation before surgery; no growth allows the patient to proceed to surgery as scheduled. Precautions: Rotate a moistened sterile swab against the anterior nasal mucosa of both nostrils to sample the carriage site adequately, and transport promptly in appropriate medium, since an inadequate or dry swab under-samples true carriers and gives a false-negative screen. Use fresh, adequately labelled media within their expiry date, incubate at the correct temperature/atmosphere (e.g. 5-10% CO2 for fastidious organisms) for the recommended duration, and avoid specimen collection after the patient has already started antibiotics, which can suppress growth and give a false-negative culture.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man presents with bloody, mucus-streaked diarrhoea and abdominal cramps. The physician requests stool microscopy for ova and parasites. Why was this test requested, what is its principle, what is the expected normal result, and what precautions must be taken to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: Bloody, mucus-streaked stool suggests amoebic dysentery, so stool microscopy is requested to directly visualise Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites or cysts and confirm the diagnosis. The principle involves examining a fresh stool sample, or a fixed and stained preparation, under the microscope to identify the organism's characteristic morphology, including trophozoites with ingested red blood cells in active dysentery or cysts with distinctive nuclear features in less acute presentations. A normal stool sample shows no such organisms; identification of trophozoites containing ingested erythrocytes strongly supports invasive amoebic disease. Precautions include examining the stool while still warm and fresh, since trophozoites lose their diagnostic motility and degenerate quickly once cooled, and examining multiple samples on different days to increase the chance of detecting intermittently shed organisms.

Erythema nodosum can follow streptococcal throat infection, so ASO titre is requested to establish evidence of recent infection supporting this underlying cause among the differential diagnoses. The principle relies on the patient's serum antibodies neutralising streptolysin O's ability to lyse red blood cells, with the titre representing the highest dilution still showing inhibition. A normal titre lies within the established reference range; an elevated titre supports a recent streptococcal trigger for the skin findings. Precautions include avoiding lipaemic or contaminated serum samples that can interfere with the haemolysis endpoint, and considering that some individuals, particularly with skin rather than throat streptococcal infections, may not mount a strong ASO response, requiring additional tests such as anti-DNase B.
questions.question: A 40-year-old woman with fever and painful, red nodules on her shins is investigated for erythema nodosum secondary to streptococcal infection using ASO titre. Give the rationale, the principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions needed to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the VDRL/RPR test because titres are typically very high during the secondary (disseminated) stage, making this an effective screening test at this point in the disease. Principle: Patient serum is mixed with a cardiolipin-lecithin-cholesterol antigen suspension on a card or slide; if reagin antibodies (produced in response to tissue damage by Treponema pallidum) are present, visible flocculation (clumping) occurs within minutes. Normal result and deviation: In this context, a non-reactive (negative) result, i.e. no flocculation, is normal; A strongly reactive result at high titre is typical of secondary syphilis and correlates with disease activity, useful also for monitoring treatment response by watching the titre fall; a weakly reactive or discordant result should be confirmed with a treponemal-specific test. Precautions: Collect blood without anticoagulant, allow it to clot fully, separate serum by centrifugation and avoid haemolysis, which can interfere with agglutination and immunoassay readings. Ensure the antigen suspension is freshly prepared and correctly standardised, avoid haemolysed or lipaemic serum which can obscure flocculation, and remember that biological false positives can occur in pregnancy, autoimmune disease, and some acute infections, so all reactive results must be confirmed with a specific treponemal test.
questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents with a widespread rash involving the palms and soles, with generalised lymphadenopathy, and the attending doctor, suspecting secondary syphilis, refers the patient for a VDRL/RPR test on a serum specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

A 25-year-old man completing treatment for malaria undergoes a follow-up blood film to confirm parasite clearance. Explain why this test was requested, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must observe.
questions.answerText: Follow-up blood film testing is requested to confirm that antimalarial treatment has successfully cleared the parasites and to detect any treatment failure or recrudescence early. The principle remains microscopic examination of Giemsa-stained blood films, looking for any remaining malaria parasites within red blood cells and assessing parasite density if present. A normal (negative) follow-up film supports successful treatment; continued or recurrent parasitaemia indicates treatment failure or reinfection requiring further management. Precautions include timing the follow-up film appropriately according to the treatment protocol, and maintaining consistent, high-quality staining and examination technique to allow reliable comparison between the pretreatment and follow-up results.

The characteristic honey-coloured crusting is typical of impetigo, and culture is requested to confirm whether Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, or both organisms are responsible, since management can differ. The principle involves plating the lesion exudate on blood agar, where Staphylococcus aureus produces golden, beta-haemolytic colonies confirmed by a positive coagulase test, while Streptococcus pyogenes produces smaller colonies with a wider zone of beta-haemolysis and is catalase-negative. A normal (healthy) skin swab would show no significant growth of either pathogen; growth of one or both organisms confirms the causative agent. Precautions include gently lifting or moistening the crust before swabbing to access the underlying exudate, and avoiding excessive delay in transport, which can allow overgrowth of contaminating skin flora.
questions.question: A 5-year-old child develops honey-coloured crusted skin lesions around the mouth, and a swab is sent for culture to confirm impetigo caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Explain the reasoning, the principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must take.

questions.answerText: Distinguishing between Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species is a key early step in identifying Gram-positive cocci, so the catalase test is performed as a rapid, simple way to separate these two genera before further testing. The principle relies on the presence or absence of the enzyme catalase, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen gas; adding a colony to hydrogen peroxide produces visible bubbling if the organism is catalase-positive. A normal (negative) result shows no bubbling, characteristic of Streptococcus species; a positive result with visible bubbling indicates a catalase-positive organism such as Staphylococcus. Precautions include using a fresh hydrogen peroxide solution, since degraded reagent can give a false-negative result, and picking the colony with a plastic or wooden stick rather than a metal loop, which can carry trace catalase-like activity and cause a false-positive reaction.
questions.question: A wound swab grows Gram-positive cocci in clusters, and the laboratory scientist performs a catalase test to help differentiate Staphylococcus from Streptococcus species. Why was this test requested, what is its principle, what is the expected normal result, and what precautions must be taken to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: Since Enterobacteriaceae are oxidase-negative while organisms such as Pseudomonas are oxidase-positive, this test is a key early step in narrowing the identification of Gram-negative rods. The principle relies on the bacterial enzyme cytochrome c oxidase oxidising a colourless reagent to a coloured end product, typically dark purple or blue, within seconds if the organism possesses the enzyme. A normal (negative) result shows no colour change, consistent with Enterobacteriaceae; a positive result with rapid colour change supports an oxidase-positive organism such as Pseudomonas. Precautions include using a non-metallic loop or applicator, since metal can cause a false-positive reaction, and reading the result within the specified short time frame, since delayed colour changes can occur non-specifically and lead to misinterpretation.
questions.question: A Gram-negative rod isolated from a wound culture is tested with the oxidase test to help distinguish Pseudomonas from Enterobacteriaceae. State why this test was requested, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must observe.

questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the C-reactive protein (CRP) as a rapidly responsive marker to help monitor the trend of inflammation over the course of treatment, complementing (not replacing) clinical assessment and repeat cultures. Principle: An immunoturbidimetric or latex agglutination assay measures C-reactive protein, an acute-phase protein synthesised by the liver in response to interleukin-6 during active inflammation or infection, with the concentration in serum rising rapidly and proportionally to the severity of the inflammatory process. Normal result and deviation: In this context, a low serum concentration (typically under about 6-10 mg/L, laboratory-dependent) is normal; A falling CRP over serial measurements supports a good response to treatment; a persistently high or rising CRP despite antibiotics should prompt reassessment for inadequate source control, an undrained collection, or antibiotic resistance. Precautions: Collect blood without anticoagulant, allow it to clot fully, separate serum by centrifugation and avoid haemolysis, which can interfere with agglutination and immunoassay readings. Avoid grossly lipaemic or haemolysed samples which can interfere with the turbidimetric reaction, and interpret the result alongside the clinical picture, since CRP is a non-specific marker that rises in any acute inflammatory process, not infection alone.
questions.question: A 5-day-old neonate presents with confirmed blood-culture-positive sepsis, now on treatment, with the clinical team assessing response, and the attending doctor, as part of neonatal sepsis severity monitoring, refers the patient for a C-reactive protein (CRP) on a serum specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

A 6-year-old child living with a grandparent who has active tuberculosis develops a persistent cough and poor weight gain. The paediatrician requests a gastric aspirate for AFB smear since the child cannot expectorate sputum. Explain why the test was ordered, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions required.
questions.answerText: Because young children often swallow rather than expectorate sputum, a gastric aspirate is collected to recover bacilli cleared from the airway overnight, and the test is ordered due to close contact with an infectious source case. The Ziehl-Neelsen technique detects the acid-fastness conferred by mycolic acids in the mycobacterial cell wall, which resist decolourisation and remain stained red. Normally the aspirate shows no acid-fast bacilli; a positive result confirms transmission has occurred and mandates treatment. Precautions include collecting the aspirate fasting and before the child rises in the morning, neutralising the acidic gastric contents promptly to preserve any bacilli, and processing the specimen quickly since gastric acid can otherwise destroy organisms and cause a false-negative result.

questions.question: An infant presents with irritability, poor feeding, and a bulging fontanelle. A lumbar puncture is performed and CSF is sent for Gram stain and culture. Explain why this test was requested, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions to prevent a false result.
questions.answerText: Non-specific signs such as irritability and a bulging fontanelle in an infant raise strong suspicion of meningitis, so CSF Gram stain and culture are requested to confirm bacterial infection despite the absence of classic adult symptoms. The Gram stain principle is based on the outer membrane structure of Gram-negative organisms like Neisseria meningitidis retaining the pink counterstain, allowing visualisation as diplococci within the specimen. A normal CSF sample is clear, with no organisms and minimal white cells; bacterial meningitis shows turbidity, neutrophilic pleocytosis, and visible bacteria on stain. Precautions include collecting an adequate CSF volume divided appropriately for cell count, chemistry, and microbiology, avoiding contamination from skin flora during the lumbar puncture, and inoculating culture media promptly since fastidious organisms may not survive prolonged transport.

questions.question: A newborn with congenital cataracts, heart defects, and hearing loss is investigated with rubella IgM testing to confirm congenital rubella syndrome. Explain the rationale, the principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions needed.
questions.answerText: The combination of congenital anomalies is classic for congenital rubella syndrome, so IgM testing in the newborn is requested to confirm active fetal infection, since IgM does not cross the placenta and therefore reflects the infant's own immune response. The principle involves an immunoassay detecting IgM antibodies specific to rubella virus in the infant's serum, using antibody-antigen binding and a labelled detection system. A normal (negative) result would be unexpected given the clinical picture; a positive IgM result confirms congenital rubella infection. Precautions include ensuring the blood sample is taken directly from the infant rather than contaminated with maternal blood, which could produce a misleading result, and correlating serology with the compatible clinical findings for a complete diagnosis.

questions.question: A 47-year-old man with a known valvular heart defect presents with persistent low-grade fever, malaise, and new heart murmur over three weeks, and the attending doctor, suspecting infective endocarditis, refers the patient for a blood culture on a blood (three separate sets) specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the blood culture because sustained or intermittent bacteraemia is the hallmark of infective endocarditis, and three sets taken from different sites over time increase the chance of isolating the causative organism and excluding contaminants. Principle: The specimen is inoculated onto appropriate general and selective/differential media and incubated under suitable atmospheric conditions to allow the causative organism to grow into discrete colonies; the isolate is then identified by colonial and biochemical characteristics and tested against a panel of antibiotics by disc diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) to determine susceptibility. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no significant growth of a pathogen is obtained (sterile culture, or growth confined to insignificant colony counts of commensals); Persistent growth of the same organism in multiple, separately drawn sets strongly supports endocarditis; a single positive bottle growing a skin commensal like coagulase-negative staphylococcus more likely represents contamination. Precautions: Draw blood using strict aseptic skin antisepsis (70% alcohol followed by chlorhexidine or iodine, allowed to dry) before venepuncture to prevent skin-commensal contamination; collect an adequate volume into the correct blood-to-broth ratio bottles, and inoculate aerobic and anaerobic bottles before the specimen clots or dries.
