The principle involves an immunoassay detecting antibodies against the hepatitis B surface antigen in the patient's serum, generated in response to either vaccination or past natural infection, using specific antibody binding and signal detection. A normal, protective result typically shows an antibody level above the accepted protective threshold; a level below this threshold suggests inadequate response, warranting revaccination or booster doses. Precautions include testing at the recommended interval after completing the vaccination series to allow adequate time for antibody development, and using a quantitative rather than purely qualitative assay to accurately assess whether the protective threshold has been reached.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man presents with high fever, rusty-coloured sputum, and pleuritic chest pain. Sputum culture is requested to investigate suspected pneumococcal pneumonia. Why was this test requested, what is its principle, what is the expected normal result, and what precautions must be taken to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: Rusty sputum with acute fever and pleuritic pain is classic for pneumococcal pneumonia, so sputum culture is requested to confirm Streptococcus pneumoniae as the cause and determine antibiotic susceptibility. The principle involves plating the sputum on blood agar, where Streptococcus pneumoniae produces small, alpha-haemolytic (greenish) colonies that are characteristically sensitive to optochin and soluble in bile, distinguishing it from other alpha-haemolytic streptococci. A normal sputum culture from a healthy person may show mixed normal oral flora without a dominant pathogen; a predominant growth of optochin-sensitive, bile-soluble colonies confirms pneumococcal infection. Precautions include obtaining a good-quality, purulent sputum sample rather than saliva, transporting it promptly to prevent overgrowth of contaminating oral flora, and performing the optochin and bile solubility tests correctly to avoid misidentifying other streptococci as pneumococcus.

Reason for the test: The doctor requested the Potassium hydroxide (KOH) mount to confirm a fungal cause of the oral plaques before starting topical antifungal treatment, distinguishing thrush from simple milk residue. Principle: The specimen (skin scraping, hair, nail, or vaginal discharge) is mixed with 10-20% potassium hydroxide, which digests keratin and host cellular debris, clearing the background so that fungal hyphae, spores, or budding yeasts become visible under the microscope. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no fungal hyphae, spores, or pseudohyphae are seen in a normal preparation; Budding yeasts and pseudohyphae confirm oral candidiasis; the absence of fungal elements despite a suggestive appearance should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis, since milk curds can sometimes mimic thrush clinically. Precautions: Scrape the active advancing edge of the lesion with a blunt scalpel onto a clean slide or into a folder, since scraping the centre of an old lesion under-samples viable fungal elements. Allow adequate time (10-20 minutes, or gentle warming) for the KOH to fully digest keratin before examination, since inadequate clearing can mask hyphae, and avoid mistaking cotton or textile fibres and mosaic artefacts for true fungal elements.
questions.question: A 3-month-old infant presents with white plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa that do not wipe away easily, and the attending doctor, suspecting oral thrush in an infant, refers the patient for a Potassium hydroxide (KOH) mount on a oral swab/scraping specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the Ziehl-Neelsen (AFB) smear as the fastest, cheapest first-line test to look for acid-fast bacilli and identify infectious cases who need to start treatment and be isolated from others. Principle: The smear is flooded with strong carbol fuchsin and heated to drive the stain into the waxy mycolic-acid-rich cell wall, then decolourised with acid-alcohol (which only acid-fast organisms resist) and counterstained with methylene blue; acid-fast bacilli retain the red stain against a blue background. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no acid-fast bacilli are seen on a normal smear; Red, beaded acid-fast bacilli against a blue background confirm a smear-positive case, indicating high infectiousness; a negative smear does not exclude tuberculosis (paucibacillary disease is common), and a repeat sample or a more sensitive test such as GeneXpert should be requested if suspicion remains high. Precautions: Instruct the patient to rinse the mouth with water and produce a deep cough specimen (not saliva) under supervision, preferably an early-morning sample, and transport promptly to avoid overgrowth of oral commensals that could mask the true pathogen. Avoid over- or under-decolourisation with acid-alcohol, which respectively causes false-negative or false-positive results, examine a minimum number of oil-immersion fields before reporting a smear negative, and use a positive control smear to confirm reagent performance.
questions.question: A 41-year-old man presents with a chronic cough for over three weeks, night sweats and weight loss, and the attending doctor, suspecting pulmonary tuberculosis (initial smear), refers the patient for a Ziehl-Neelsen (AFB) smear on a sputum specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

A 32-year-old woman with recurrent urinary tract infections undergoes urine culture with antibiotic sensitivity testing to guide long-term management. Explain the reasoning, the principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions needed to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Recurrent infections raise concern for resistant organisms or an unresolved anatomical or functional predisposing factor, so culture with sensitivity testing is requested to identify the current causative strain, often Escherichia coli, and select an effective antibiotic. The principle involves quantitative urine culture followed by disc diffusion or another susceptibility method applied to a pure isolate to determine which antibiotics inhibit growth. A normal result shows no significant growth; significant growth of Escherichia coli with a documented resistance pattern guides more effective, targeted therapy. Precautions include collecting the sample before starting or restarting antibiotics wherever possible, and ensuring the isolate tested for sensitivity is pure and correctly identified, since a mixed culture can produce an inaccurate or uninterpretable antibiogram.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man with advanced HIV infection presents with progressive headache and confusion over two weeks, and the attending doctor, suspecting cryptococcal meningitis (culture), refers the patient for a fungal culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar on a CSF specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the fungal culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar to confirm a positive India ink finding with a definitive culture and to obtain an isolate for antifungal susceptibility, given the high mortality of untreated cryptococcal meningitis. Principle: The specimen is inoculated onto appropriate general and selective/differential media and incubated under suitable atmospheric conditions to allow the causative organism to grow into discrete colonies; the isolate is then identified by colonial and biochemical characteristics and tested against a panel of antibiotics by disc diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) to determine susceptibility. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no significant growth of a pathogen is obtained (sterile culture, or growth confined to insignificant colony counts of commensals); Growth of mucoid, cream-coloured yeast colonies confirms Cryptococcus neoformans; a negative culture despite a positive India ink test is unusual and should prompt repeat testing or cryptococcal antigen testing, which is more sensitive. Precautions: Collect CSF by lumbar puncture under strict aseptic technique into sterile sequential containers, avoid a traumatic tap that introduces peripheral blood, transport immediately at room temperature (never refrigerate) and process without delay because fastidious organisms such as N. meningitidis die rapidly outside the body. Use fresh, adequately labelled media within their expiry date, incubate at the correct temperature/atmosphere (e.g. 5-10% CO2 for fastidious organisms) for the recommended duration, and avoid specimen collection after the patient has already started antibiotics, which can suppress growth and give a false-negative culture.

The progression from a respiratory infection to meningeal symptoms suggests haematogenous spread of Neisseria meningitidis to the central nervous system, so a combination of Gram stain, culture, and rapid antigen testing is requested to confirm the diagnosis quickly. The Gram stain principle relies on the organism's Gram-negative cell wall retaining the pink counterstain to reveal diplococci, while latex agglutination detects capsular polysaccharide antigen through visible clumping of antibody-coated latex particles. A normal CSF sample shows no organisms, no antigen reaction, and normal cell counts; a positive Gram stain, culture, or antigen test confirms bacterial meningitis. Precautions include running the antigen test with proper positive and negative controls to avoid false agglutination, and ensuring the CSF specimen is not haemolysed, as blood contamination can cause non-specific reactions.
questions.question: A 26-year-old woman presents with fever, severe headache, and confusion following a recent upper respiratory infection. CSF is collected for Gram stain, culture, and latex agglutination antigen testing. Explain the rationale, the underlying principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must observe.

A 33-year-old woman recently returned from travel presents with fever, rigors, and jaundice, and blood cultures are requested alongside other tests to investigate possible bacteraemia. State why this test was requested, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must observe.
questions.answerText: Fever with jaundice after travel raises a broad differential including bacteraemic causes, so blood culture is requested to identify or exclude a bacterial pathogen alongside other travel-related investigations. The principle relies on enrichment of the blood sample in broth to allow any bacteria present to multiply to detectable levels before subculture and identification. A normal result shows no bacterial growth; growth of an organism identifies the cause and directs antibiotic therapy, while a negative result supports consideration of non-bacterial travel-related causes. Precautions include collecting the sample before starting empirical antibiotics wherever clinically safe, using aseptic technique to avoid contamination, and communicating relevant travel history to the laboratory so appropriate extended or specialised culture conditions can be considered if standard culture remains negative.

Trichomonas vaginalis infection in pregnancy is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight, so wet mount testing is requested to confirm or exclude this treatable infection as a contributing factor. The principle involves examining a fresh sample of vaginal discharge under the microscope, identifying the organism by its motile, flagellated appearance when live and active. A normal wet mount shows no such organisms; identification of motile trichomonads confirms infection, prompting appropriate treatment during pregnancy. Precautions include examining the specimen without delay, since motility diminishes rapidly, and considering culture or molecular testing as a more sensitive back-up if the wet mount is negative but clinical suspicion remains high, given the wet mount's relatively modest sensitivity.
questions.question: A pregnant woman with vaginal discharge and preterm labour risk factors undergoes wet mount testing to investigate Trichomonas vaginalis given its association with adverse pregnancy outcomes. Give the rationale, the principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must take.

A 33-year-old man with HIV infection presents with a persistent cough and two negative sputum smears despite ongoing symptoms, and the attending doctor, suspecting tuberculosis in a smear-negative HIV patient, refers the patient for a GeneXpert MTB/RIF (automated PCR) on a sputum specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the GeneXpert MTB/RIF (automated PCR) because this molecular test is considerably more sensitive than smear microscopy, particularly important in HIV-positive patients who often have paucibacillary, smear-negative disease. Principle: Nucleic acid amplification technology (PCR/GeneXpert) uses specific primers to exponentially amplify a target gene sequence unique to the pathogen, then detects the amplified product (often in real time using fluorescent probes), allowing detection of even very small numbers of organisms with high sensitivity and specificity. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no amplifiable target DNA/RNA is detected (negative/not detected) in a normal or successfully treated specimen; A positive result confirms tuberculosis even when smears were negative, allowing prompt treatment initiation; a negative result substantially lowers the likelihood of tuberculosis but, in a strongly suspicious case, should still be followed by culture, which remains slightly more sensitive for very low bacillary loads. Precautions: Instruct the patient to rinse the mouth with water and produce a deep cough specimen (not saliva) under supervision, preferably an early-morning sample, and transport promptly to avoid overgrowth of oral commensals that could mask the true pathogen. Strictly avoid cross-contamination between specimens or with previously amplified product, which causes false positives, and use dedicated pre- and post-amplification work areas; also collect the specimen before, not after, antimicrobial therapy has begun to avoid a false negative from suppressed organism load.

The delayed onset of joint pain and cardiac involvement after a preceding sore throat suggests rheumatic fever, an immune-mediated complication of Streptococcus pyogenes infection, so an ASO titre is requested to provide serological evidence of recent streptococcal infection. The principle relies on detecting antibodies against streptolysin O, a toxin produced by the organism, by observing inhibition of red cell lysis when patient serum containing anti-streptolysin O antibodies is mixed with streptolysin reagent and red blood cells. A normal titre is below the age-adjusted upper limit; an elevated or rising titre supports recent streptococcal infection, supporting the diagnosis of rheumatic fever in the correct clinical context. Precautions include using fresh, non-haemolysed serum, since haemolysis can interfere with the red cell lysis endpoint, and comparing results against locally established normal ranges since baseline titres vary by population and age.
questions.question: A 9-year-old child develops joint pain, fever, and a new heart murmur three weeks after a sore throat. The physician requests an ASO titre to investigate possible rheumatic fever. Why was this test requested, what is its principle, what is the expected normal result, and what precautions must be taken to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the TPHA/FTA-ABS confirmatory test to confirm that the reactive screening result truly reflects treponemal infection before committing the patient to a diagnosis of syphilis and contact tracing. Principle: Patient serum is reacted with Treponema pallidum-specific antigen (fixed on sheep red cells for TPHA, or whole treponemes for FTA-ABS); specific antibody present in the serum causes agglutination or fluorescent labelling, confirming true treponemal infection rather than a biological false positive. Normal result and deviation: In this context, a non-reactive result is normal and, once positive, this test generally stays positive for life regardless of treatment, so it is used only to confirm past or present treponemal infection, not to monitor treatment response; A reactive confirmatory test supports true syphilis and should prompt staging and treatment along with partner notification; because this test remains positive for life even after successful treatment, it cannot be used to monitor treatment response, unlike the VDRL/RPR. Precautions: Collect blood without anticoagulant, allow it to clot fully, separate serum by centrifugation and avoid haemolysis, which can interfere with agglutination and immunoassay readings. Ensure adequate absorption of cross-reacting antibodies where required (FTA-ABS) to prevent false positives from non-pathogenic treponemes/spirochaetes, and use appropriately diluted, non-haemolysed serum.
questions.question: A 29-year-old man presents with a genital ulcer with a reactive screening VDRL test, and the attending doctor, suspecting confirmed primary syphilis needing definitive diagnosis, refers the patient for a TPHA/FTA-ABS confirmatory test on a serum specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

A 70-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease develops worsening cough and purulent sputum. Sputum culture is requested to investigate a possible pneumococcal exacerbation. Explain why this test was requested, its principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions the laboratory scientist must observe.
questions.answerText: Underlying chronic lung disease predisposes to bacterial exacerbations, commonly involving Streptococcus pneumoniae, so sputum culture is requested to identify the pathogen and select effective antibiotic therapy. The principle relies on culturing the sputum on blood agar, where pneumococcal colonies appear small and alpha-haemolytic, confirmed as Streptococcus pneumoniae through sensitivity to optochin and solubility in bile salts, unlike other alpha-haemolytic streptococci. A normal sputum sample would show scanty mixed flora without a predominant pathogen; heavy, pure growth of optochin-sensitive organisms supports the diagnosis. Precautions include using a Gram stain to assess sputum quality before culture, rejecting samples with excessive squamous cells suggesting salivary contamination, and processing the specimen quickly since pneumococci can autolyse and die if left standing.

questions.question: A 26-year-old man presents with fever, rash and sore throat three weeks after a high-risk sexual exposure, and the attending doctor, suspecting acute retroviral syndrome, refers the patient for a HIV ELISA (screening), ideally with a combination antigen/antibody assay on a serum specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the HIV ELISA (screening), ideally with a combination antigen/antibody assay to investigate a possible acute HIV infection, although early testing may still fall within the window period before antibodies (or even antigen) become detectable. Principle: Patient serum/plasma is added to wells coated with HIV antigens; specific antibody, if present, binds the antigen and is detected by an enzyme-linked anti-human-antibody conjugate that produces a measurable colour change on addition of substrate, proportional to the amount of antibody present. Normal result and deviation: In this context, a non-reactive result is normal; A reactive result at this stage supports acute HIV infection and warrants urgent confirmatory testing and viral load measurement; a non-reactive result during the window period does not exclude infection, and repeat testing after the window period, or HIV RNA testing, is required. Precautions: Collect blood without anticoagulant, allow it to clot fully, separate serum by centrifugation and avoid haemolysis, which can interfere with agglutination and immunoassay readings. Follow the recommended testing algorithm (screening test confirmed by a second, different assay) since a single reactive screening test can be a false positive, observe the correct window period before testing after a possible exposure, and avoid contamination between wells that can cause false positives.

Reason for the test: The doctor requested the culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar to confirm a fungal cause and identify the exact Candida species, since some non-albicans species show reduced susceptibility to first-line antifungal agents. Principle: The specimen is inoculated onto appropriate general and selective/differential media and incubated under suitable atmospheric conditions to allow the causative organism to grow into discrete colonies; the isolate is then identified by colonial and biochemical characteristics and tested against a panel of antibiotics by disc diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) to determine susceptibility. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no significant growth of a pathogen is obtained (sterile culture, or growth confined to insignificant colony counts of commensals); Growth of creamy, dome-shaped colonies identified as Candida albicans supports the diagnosis and guides antifungal choice; growth of a non-albicans species may explain treatment failure and require a different antifungal agent. Precautions: Collect the high vaginal swab using a bivalve speculum without lubricant (which can be bacteriostatic), sample the posterior fornix, and transport in Amies/Stuart medium promptly to preserve fastidious and anaerobic organisms. Use fresh, adequately labelled media within their expiry date, incubate at the correct temperature/atmosphere (e.g. 5-10% CO2 for fastidious organisms) for the recommended duration, and avoid specimen collection after the patient has already started antibiotics, which can suppress growth and give a false-negative culture.
questions.question: A 30-year-old woman presents with recurrent thick, curd-like vaginal discharge and itching not responding to standard antifungal cream, and the attending doctor, suspecting candidal vaginitis (culture), refers the patient for a culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar on a high vaginal swab specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

A 4-month-old infant presents with a persistently discharging swelling at the BCG vaccination site, and the attending doctor, as part of post-BCG lymphadenitis query, refers the patient for a Ziehl-Neelsen (AFB) smear on a pus from discharging node specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the Ziehl-Neelsen (AFB) smear to look for acid-fast organisms in the discharge, supporting a diagnosis of BCG-related lymphadenitis, a recognised complication of the vaccine. Principle: The smear is flooded with strong carbol fuchsin and heated to drive the stain into the waxy mycolic-acid-rich cell wall, then decolourised with acid-alcohol (which only acid-fast organisms resist) and counterstained with methylene blue; acid-fast bacilli retain the red stain against a blue background. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no acid-fast bacilli are seen on a normal smear; Acid-fast bacilli seen on smear are consistent with mycobacterial lymphadenitis, most likely related to the recent BCG vaccination in this age group and site; culture with species identification is needed to formally distinguish vaccine-strain BCG from other mycobacteria. Precautions: Aspirate frank pus with a sterile syringe/needle rather than swabbing where possible, to obtain a larger, less contaminated and better-preserved sample, and transport in anaerobic transport medium promptly. Avoid over- or under-decolourisation with acid-alcohol, which respectively causes false-negative or false-positive results, examine a minimum number of oil-immersion fields before reporting a smear negative, and use a positive control smear to confirm reagent performance.

Reason for the test: The doctor requested the nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT/PCR) because Chlamydia is an intracellular organism that does not grow on routine bacterial culture media, so molecular testing is required to reliably detect it and prevent progression to pelvic inflammatory disease. Principle: Nucleic acid amplification technology (PCR/GeneXpert) uses specific primers to exponentially amplify a target gene sequence unique to the pathogen, then detects the amplified product (often in real time using fluorescent probes), allowing detection of even very small numbers of organisms with high sensitivity and specificity. Normal result and deviation: In this context, no amplifiable target DNA/RNA is detected (negative/not detected) in a normal or successfully treated specimen; A positive result confirms chlamydial infection, prompting treatment of the patient and her partner(s); a negative result makes chlamydia unlikely, though the specimen must have been correctly taken from the endocervical canal (not just vaginal discharge) for the result to be reliable. Precautions: Remove cervical mucus first, then firmly rotate the swab in the endocervical canal for adequate cellular yield, and transport in appropriate medium (e.g. charcoal transport medium) without delay, since the causative organisms are fragile outside the host. Strictly avoid cross-contamination between specimens or with previously amplified product, which causes false positives, and use dedicated pre- and post-amplification work areas; also collect the specimen before, not after, antimicrobial therapy has begun to avoid a false negative from suppressed organism load.
questions.question: A 23-year-old woman presents with a mild mucopurulent cervical discharge and intermenstrual bleeding, with a negative gonorrhoea culture, and the attending doctor, suspecting chlamydial cervicitis, refers the patient for a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT/PCR) on a endocervical swab specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: Reason for the test: The doctor requested the HBsAg test as part of the standard work-up for chronic liver disease, since chronic hepatitis B is a common, often previously undiagnosed, cause of ongoing liver damage. Principle: An immunoassay (ELISA or rapid immunochromatographic strip) detects the surface antigen of the hepatitis B virus in the patient's serum using antibody-coated particles that bind HBsAg and generate a visible line or colour change. Normal result and deviation: In this context, a negative result is normal; A positive result identifies chronic hepatitis B as a likely contributor to his liver disease and prompts further staging (viral load, e-antigen status) and consideration of antiviral therapy; a negative result directs the work-up towards other causes such as alcohol, hepatitis C, or fatty liver disease. Precautions: Collect blood without anticoagulant, allow it to clot fully, separate serum by centrifugation and avoid haemolysis, which can interfere with agglutination and immunoassay readings. Confirm any positive/borderline screening result with a more specific supplemental test, avoid gross haemolysis or lipaemia in the sample which can interfere with the assay, and be aware of the diagnostic window period shortly after infection when the antigen may not yet be detectable.
questions.question: A 50-year-old man presents with longstanding fatigue and mildly deranged liver function tests found incidentally, and the attending doctor, suspecting chronic liver disease work-up, refers the patient for a HBsAg test on a serum specimen. As the laboratory scientist handling this request, explain why this test was requested, the principle behind it, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions you must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The combination of prior urethritis and an acutely inflamed joint suggests haematogenous spread of gonococci, so joint fluid Gram stain and culture are requested to confirm septic arthritis of gonococcal origin. The Gram stain principle relies on the Gram-negative envelope of the organism retaining the pink counterstain, appearing as intracellular diplococci within neutrophils recruited into the inflamed joint space. A normal joint fluid Gram stain shows no organisms and few cells; a positive smear supports the diagnosis, although the organism is notoriously difficult to see or culture from joint fluid in disseminated disease. Precautions include inoculating culture media immediately at the bedside since Neisseria gonorrhoeae is fastidious and sensitive to cooling and drying, and avoiding delays in transport that reduce organism viability.
questions.question: A 33-year-old man presents with a swollen, painful knee and a history of urethral discharge two weeks earlier. Give the rationale, the principle, the expected normal result, and the precautions required.

questions.question:
(a) State the indications for Tibiofemoral Distraction.
(b) Describe the patient position for Tibiofemoral techniques, including progression and rotation of the tibia.
(c) Describe the hand placement and mobilizing force for Tibiofemoral Distraction.
(d) State the indication for Tibiofemoral Posterior Glide.
(e) Describe the patient position, hand placement and mobilizing force for Tibiofemoral Posterior Glide.
(f) State the indication, patient positions and mobilizing force for Anterior Gliding of the tibia.
(g) Explain the rationale for adding internal or external rotation of the tibia to the traction force.
(h) Explain the rationale for the alternative sitting position used for the posterior glide.
(i) Distinguish the indication of Posterior Glide from that of Anterior Glide.
(j) Distinguish the patient positions used for the posterior and anterior glides.
(k) Distinguish the direction and source of the mobilizing force between the two glides.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Tibiofemoral Distraction is indicated for testing, initial treatment, pain control and general mobility.

(b)
Patient position: sitting, supine, or prone, beginning with the knee in the resting position, progressing to positioning the knee at the limit of the range of flexion or extension; rotation of the tibia may be added prior to applying the traction force, using internal rotation at end-range flexion and external rotation at end-range extension.

(c)
Hand placement for Distraction: grasp around the distal leg, proximal to the malleoli, with both hands; mobilizing force: pull on the long axis of the tibia to separate the joint surfaces.

(d)
Tibiofemoral Posterior Glide is indicated for testing and to increase flexion.

(e)
Patient position for Posterior Glide: supine, with the foot resting on the table (the drawer-test position can be used to mobilize the tibia either anteriorly or posteriorly, though no Grade I distraction can be applied with the glides); the therapist sits on the table with the thigh fixating the patient's foot, grasping around the tibia with both hands, fingers pointing posteriorly and thumbs anteriorly; mobilizing force: extending the elbows and leaning the body weight forward, pushing the tibia posteriorly with the thumbs (an alternative sitting method progresses to near 90° of flexion with the tibia in internal rotation, applying force by leaning body weight onto the tibia to glide it posteriorly).

(f)
• Anterior Gliding is indicated to increase extension; patient positions: prone, beginning with the knee in resting position and progressing to the end of available range, with a small pad under the distal femur to prevent patellar compression (or the drawer-test position, with the mobilizing force from the fingers on the posterior tibia as the therapist leans backward); mobilizing force: applied with the hand on the proximal tibia in an anterior direction, which may be directed to the lateral or medial tibial plateau to isolate one side of the joint.
• Hand placement for Anterior Gliding: grasp the distal tibia with the hand closer to it, and place the palm of the proximal hand on the posterior aspect of the proximal tibia.

(g)
Rotation of the tibia is added to the traction force because internal rotation at end-range flexion or external rotation at end-range extension helps direct the distraction toward the specific restricted motion being treated.

(h)
The alternative sitting position for the posterior glide (near 90° flexion, tibia internally rotated) allows the therapist to progress the glide toward the end of the available flexion range by leaning body weight onto the tibia, rather than only through the supine drawer-test position.

(i)
Posterior Glide is used to increase flexion, whereas Anterior Glide is used to increase extension.

(j)
Posterior Glide is performed supine with the foot resting on the table (therapist sitting with thigh fixating the foot), whereas Anterior Glide is performed prone (or using the drawer-test position).

(k)
For Posterior Glide, force is applied by the thumbs pushing the tibia posteriorly as the therapist leans forward; for Anterior Glide, force is applied by the hand on the proximal tibia pushing anteriorly, or by the fingers on the posterior tibia as the therapist leans backward in the drawer-test position.

(a)
Fibromyalgia (FM) – a chronic condition characterised by widespread pain covering half of the body (right/left or upper/lower half) lasting more than three months, with 11 of 18 tender points at specific sites, non-restorative sleep, morning stiffness, and fatigue with subsequent reduced exercise tolerance.

(b)
Contributing factors/pathophysiology: symptoms can start at any age but usually occur during early to middle adulthood, and in over 30% of cases symptoms develop after physical trauma such as a motor vehicle accident or a viral infection; pain is usually muscular in origin and predominantly reported in the scapular, head, neck, chest and low back regions, and symptoms fluctuate, with pain-free days interspersed with days of serious pain; FM is a non-inflammatory, non-degenerative, non-progressive disorder, but environmental stresses (weather changes, especially barometric pressure change, cold, dampness, fog, rain, fluorescent light), physical stresses (repetitive activities, prolonged sitting/standing, rotating shifts) and emotional stresses affect the severity of a flare; individuals with FM may have a higher incidence of tendinitis, headache, irritable bowel, TMJ dysfunction, restless leg syndrome, mitral valve prolapse, anxiety, depression and memory problems.

(c)
Management: aerobic exercise and resistance exercise; instruction in pacing of activities to avoid fluctuations in symptoms; avoidance of stress factors; decreasing alcohol and caffeine consumption; diet modification; prescription and over-the-counter medication (as adjuncts).
questions.question:
A patient reports chronic widespread pain covering half of the body (right/left or upper/lower half) for more than three months, with morning stiffness, non-restorative sleep and fatigue with reduced exercise tolerance. Examination reveals multiple tender points at specific sites.
(a) State the diagnosis.
(b) Describe the contributing factors and pathophysiology.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Assessment findings: restricted anterior (ventral) glide of the fibular head at the proximal tibiofibular articulation, sometimes with a posteriorly subluxed head noted on assessment; restricted anterior or posterior glide at the distal tibiofibular articulation.

(b)
Techniques: Proximal Tibiofibular Articulation – Anterior (Ventral) Glide, indicated to increase movement of the fibular head and to reposition a posteriorly subluxed head; Distal Tibiofibular Articulation – Anterior (Ventral) or Posterior (Dorsal) Glide.

(c)
Starting position/hand placement: for the proximal joint, the patient is side-lying, trunk and hips rotated partially toward prone, with the top leg flexed forward so the knee and lower leg rest on the table or a pillow; the therapist stands behind the patient, placing one hand under the tibia to stabilize it and the base of the other hand posterior to the head of the fibula, wrapping the fingers anteriorly. For the distal joint, the patient is supine or prone; working from the end of the table, the fingers of the more medial hand are placed under the tibia and the thumb over the tibia to stabilize it, while the base of the other hand is placed over the lateral malleolus with the fingers underneath.

(d)
Dosage/progression: for the proximal joint, force is applied through the heel of the hand against the posterior aspect of the fibular head in an anterior-lateral direction; for the distal joint, force is applied against the fibula in an anterior direction when the patient is prone, and in a posterior direction when the patient is supine.

(e)
Complications/precautions: absolute contraindications – malignancy in the area, infectious arthritis, metabolic bone disease, neoplastic disease, fusion or ankylosis, osteomyelitis, fracture or ligament rupture; relative contraindications – excessive pain or swelling, arthroplasty, pregnancy, hypermobility, spondylolisthesis, rheumatoid arthritis, vertebrobasilar insufficiency; the tibia must be adequately stabilized throughout to isolate the mobilizing force to the tibiofibular joint.
questions.question:
A patient has restricted mobility of the proximal fibular head following a lateral ankle/knee-region injury, with reduced accessory movement noted on assessment.
(a) State the assessment findings expected (restricted joint play at the proximal and/or distal tibiofibular joints).
(b) State the techniques named.
(c) Describe the starting position, hand placement and stabilization.
(d) State the dosage and progression.
(e) State the complications and precautions.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Glenohumeral Distraction is indicated for testing; initial treatment (sustained Grade II); pain control (Grade I or II oscillations); and general mobility (sustained Grade III).

(b)
Patient position for Distraction: supine, arm in resting position, forearm supported between the therapist's trunk and elbow; hand placement: the hand nearer the part treated is placed in the patient's axilla, thumb just distal to the joint margin anteriorly and fingers posteriorly, while the other hand supports the humerus from the lateral surface.

(c)
Mobilizing force for Distraction: with the hand in the axilla, the humerus is moved laterally.

(d)
Glenohumeral Posterior Glide (resting position) is indicated to increase flexion and to increase internal rotation.

(e)
Patient position for Posterior Glide: supine, arm in resting position; the therapist stands with back to the patient between the trunk and arm, supporting the arm against the trunk and grasping the distal humerus with the lateral hand (providing Grade I distraction), with the lateral border of the top hand placed just distal to the anterior joint margin, fingers pointing superiorly.

(f)
Mobilizing force for Posterior Glide: the humeral head is glided posteriorly by moving the entire arm as the therapist bends the knees.

(g)
The rationale rests on the concave glenoid fossa receiving the convex humeral head, with the treatment plane lying in the glenoid fossa and moving with the scapula as it rotates; the scapula is fixated with a belt or an assistant so the mobilizing force is applied accurately relative to this plane.

(h)
A Grade I distraction is built into the hand placement of most glides (e.g. the axilla hand, or the hand supporting the distal humerus) to unload the joint surfaces before the gliding force is applied, consistent with the general principle that distraction and gliding movements cause synovial fluid motion and reduce compressive stress during the technique.

(i)
Anterior Glide is indicated to increase extension and to increase external rotation, whereas Posterior Glide is indicated to increase flexion and internal rotation.

(j)
Anterior Glide is performed prone (or supine), with the arm in resting position supported over the edge of the table on the therapist's thigh, whereas Posterior Glide is performed supine with the arm supported against the therapist's trunk.

(k)
For Anterior Glide, the mobilizing force is directed anteriorly and slightly medially using the ulnar border of the hand placed just distal to the posterior angle of the acromion, moved by bending both knees; for Posterior Glide, the force is directed posteriorly using the lateral border of the top hand placed distal to the anterior joint margin.

(l)
Because of the danger of subluxation when an anterior glide is combined with the humerus externally rotated, external rotation range is instead gained using a distraction progression or an elevation progression rather than a direct anterior glide.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Indications: arthritis is an indication; the primary effects sought are pain reduction, improved range of motion and improved quality of joint movement; Hip Distraction is indicated for testing, initial treatment, pain control and general mobility, and Hip Posterior Glide is specifically indicated to increase flexion and internal rotation.

(b)
Contraindications: absolute – malignancy in the area, infectious arthritis, metabolic bone disease, neoplastic disease, fusion or ankylosis, osteomyelitis, fracture or ligament rupture; relative – excessive pain or swelling, arthroplasty, pregnancy, hypermobility, spondylolisthesis, rheumatoid arthritis, vertebrobasilar insufficiency.

(c)
Technique: the concave acetabulum receives the convex femoral head. Hip Posterior Glide is selected: patient supine with hips at the end of the table, opposite hip held flexed to stabilize the pelvis and lumbar spine; the therapist stands medial to the thigh, uses a belt around the shoulder and under the thigh, places the distal hand under the belt/distal thigh and the proximal hand anteriorly on the proximal thigh, then applies force posteriorly through the proximal hand by flexing the knees with elbows extended; this may be preceded by Hip Distraction (Caudal Glide), applying long-axis traction with a belt around the trunk and the ankle, for testing/initial treatment/pain control/general mobility, avoiding this specific supine-knee-extended position if knee dysfunction is present.

(d)
Effects/outcome: mitigation of capsular restriction, breaking of adhesions, distraction of impacted tissue and improved cartilage lubrication; pain reduction and decreased muscle tension via mechanoreceptor stimulation; expected outcome is increased hip flexion and internal rotation with improved joint quality.

(e)
Precautions: avoid mobilization in the presence of any absolute contraindication and proceed cautiously with relative contraindications; avoid the standard supine, knee-extended distraction position if knee dysfunction is present, using the alternate position instead; keep Grade I/II oscillations pain-free; assess pain and stiffness after each set of oscillations and stop or modify if the technique causes more than slight discomfort or is not tolerated.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Myofascial trigger points with a specific referred pattern of pain located in the muscle, producing decreased range of motion, reduced muscle strength and increased pain with stretching.

(b)
Impairments: trigger points as hyper-irritable areas in a tight band of muscle; pain from the trigger points described as dull, aching and deep; decreased range of motion when the muscle is stretched; reduced muscle strength; increased pain with muscle stretching.

(c)
Goals of treatment: eliminate the trigger points; correct the contributing factors (such as chronic or acute muscle overload, poor conditioning, postural stresses, or poor body mechanics); restore range of motion; and subsequently strengthen the muscle.

(d)
Strengthening programme: the three main components of MPS treatment are eliminating the trigger points, correcting the contributing factors, and strengthening the muscle; techniques for eliminating the trigger point include contract-relax, trigger point release, spray and stretch, and dry needling or injection; precaution – if chronic overload is the cause of the trigger point, the contributing factor is eliminated before addressing the trigger point, and muscle strengthening is initiated only once range of motion has been restored and the trigger point has been addressed.
questions.question:
A patient with myofascial pain syndrome has trigger points causing decreased range of motion when the affected muscle is stretched, reduced muscle strength, and increased pain with stretching.
(a) State the physiotherapy problem list.
(b) Outline the impairments present, including weakness, tight band/stiffness, pain and restricted ROM.
(c) State the goals of treatment.
(d) Outline the strengthening programme, including precautions.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Joint stability is a joint's ability to resist dislocation, specifically its ability to resist displacement of one bone end with respect to another while preventing injury to the ligaments, muscles and tendons surrounding the joint.

(b)
Factors influencing joint stability: the contact area between the articulating bone surfaces (the larger the contact area, the more stable the joint); joint structure (reciprocally shaped articulating surfaces fit together, increasing stability); connective tissues (ligaments, muscles and tendons); and fatigue.

(c)
• Joint flexibility is the range of motion allowed at each of the planes of motion at a joint; static flexibility is the range of motion when a body segment is passively moved, as by a physiotherapist, while dynamic flexibility is the range of motion achieved by actively moving a body segment through muscle contraction; static and dynamic flexibility are independent of each other, and static flexibility is a better indicator of relative tightness or laxity for injury-potential purposes.
• Dynamic flexibility must be sufficient not to restrict the range of motion needed for activities of daily living.

(d)
• Factors influencing joint flexibility: the shapes of the articulating bone surfaces; intervening muscle/fatty tissue, which may terminate movement at the extreme of range; and the laxity and/or extensibility of the collagenous tissues and muscles crossing the joint.
• Flexibility is joint-specific, so extreme flexibility at one joint does not guarantee the same degree of flexibility at all other joints.
• Reduction in joint flexibility with aging is due to reduced levels of physical activity, not to changes caused by the aging process itself.

(e)
Because contact area and reciprocal joint structure increase stability, a joint judged to have low contact area or poorly matched surfaces (naturally less stable, such as the knee or shoulder) is approached with greater reliance on the surrounding soft tissues for stability, whereas a joint with large, well-matched surfaces already has inherent bony stability guiding a more mobility-focused approach.

(f)
Because weak and lax connective tissues cause low stability while strengthening them increases stability, and fatigued muscles are less able to contribute to joint stability, strengthening of the muscles, ligaments and tendons crossing an unstable joint (particularly joints such as the knee and shoulder, where bone configuration is not particularly stable) is prioritised over aggressive mobilization when instability rather than hypomobility is the primary problem.

(g)
Risk of injury is increased when joint flexibility is extremely low, extremely high, or unbalanced between the dominant and non-dominant sides of the body; high strength and flexibility together are desirable for injury prevention.

(h)
Weak and lax connective tissues cause low joint stability, whereas strengthening of ligaments, muscles and tendons results in increased stability, since tension in these tissues helps hold the articulating bone ends together, particularly at joints such as the knee and shoulder where the bone configuration itself is not particularly stable.

(i)
Fatigued muscles are less able to contribute to joint stability, which is why injuries are more common in sporting activities once fatigue has set in.

(b) List the factors influencing joint stability.
(c) Define joint flexibility and distinguish static from dynamic flexibility.

(a) State the indications for Humeroulnar Distraction and Progression.
(b) Describe the patient position for Humeroulnar Distraction.
(c) Describe the hand placement for Humeroulnar Distraction.
(d) Describe the mobilizing force for Humeroulnar Distraction.
(e) Describe the patient position and hand placement for Humeroradial Distraction.
(f) Describe the mobilizing force for Humeroradial Distraction.
(g) Explain the rationale for applying force at a 45° angle to the ulna in the humeroulnar techniques.
(h) Explain the indication (rationale) for using Humeroradial Distraction specifically.
(i) Distinguish the indications of Humeroulnar Distal Glide from Humeroulnar Distraction.
(j) Distinguish the indications of Humeroradial Dorsal Glide from Humeroradial Volar Glide.
(k) Distinguish the therapist's hand grip between Humeroulnar and Humeroradial techniques.
(l) State the precaution regarding which forearm bone must not be grasped during Humeroradial Distraction.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Humeroulnar Distraction and Progression is indicated for testing; initial treatment (sustained Grade II); pain control (Grade I or II oscillation); and to increase flexion or extension (Grade III or IV).

(b)
Patient position: supine, with the elbow over the edge of the treatment table or supported with padding just proximal to the olecranon process; the patient's wrist rests against the therapist's shoulder, with the elbow in resting position for initial treatment, or positioned at the end of its available range to stretch into flexion or extension.

(c)
Hand placement: in resting position or at end-range flexion, the fingers of the medial hand are placed over the proximal ulna on the volar surface, reinforced by the other hand; at end-range extension, the base of the proximal hand is placed over the proximal ulna, with the other hand supporting the distal forearm.

(d)
Mobilizing force: applied against the proximal ulna at a 45° angle to the shaft of the bone.

(e)
Humeroradial Distraction: patient position is supine or sitting with the arm resting on the treatment table; the therapist positions on the ulnar side of the patient's forearm, stabilizes the humerus with the superior hand, and grasps around the distal radius with the fingers and thenar eminence of the inferior hand.

(f)
Mobilizing force for Humeroradial Distraction: the radius is pulled distally, since long-axis traction causes joint traction.

(g)
The 45° angle to the ulna is used because it directs the distraction force appropriately to separate the humeroulnar joint surfaces while the joint is supported near the olecranon.

(h)
Humeroradial Distraction is indicated to increase mobility of the humeroradial joint and to manipulate a "pushed" elbow (proximal displacement of the radius).

(i)
Humeroulnar Distal Glide is used with the elbow positioned at the end-range of flexion, applying distraction at 45° to the ulna and then, while maintaining distraction, directing the force distally along the long axis of the ulna in a scooping motion, whereas Humeroulnar Distraction is used more broadly, including in resting position, for testing, initial treatment, pain control and general progression into flexion or extension.

(j)
Humeroradial Dorsal Glide (of the head of the radius) is used to increase elbow extension, whereas Humeroradial Volar Glide is used to increase flexion.

(k)
In the humeroulnar techniques, the therapist's hand grasps the proximal ulna on its volar (or, at end-range extension, its proximal) surface, whereas in Humeroradial Distraction the therapist's hand grasps around the distal radius with the fingers and thenar eminence.

(l)
During Humeroradial Distraction, the therapist must be sure not to grasp around the distal ulna, since the technique is directed specifically at traction of the radius.

(a)
Anatomically, all articular surfaces are either convex or concave, although some joint surfaces are not overtly either shape, in which case fibrocartilage enhances and modifies the contour; on a convex surface, more cartilage is found at the centre, while on a concave surface, more cartilage is found at the periphery.

(b)
When the concave surface is stationary and the convex surface is moving, the gliding movement of the joint occurs in a direction opposite to the bone movement.

(c)
Conversely, when the convex surface is fixed and the concave surface is mobile, the gliding motion occurs in the same direction as the bone movement.

(d)
This occurs because the convex bone surface always maintains an axis of rotation during joint motion.

(e)
At the glenohumeral joint, the concave glenoid fossa receives the convex humeral head; the glenoid (concave, fixed by the scapula) is stationary while the humeral head (convex) moves, so glides such as the posterior glide are applied to increase flexion/internal rotation and the anterior glide to increase extension/external rotation, in line with the rule.

(f)
At the hip joint, the concave acetabulum receives the convex femoral head; because of the deep configuration of this joint, traction applied perpendicular to the treatment plane causes lateral glide of the superior, weight-bearing surface.

(g)
In general, the direction of mobilization is chosen according to the convex-concave rule so that the glide restores the specific restricted motion (for example, a posterior glide to increase flexion and internal rotation, or an anterior glide to increase extension and external rotation).

(h)
When ROM is decreased due to stiffness, joint hypomobility (capsular restriction) limits movement of the joint, presenting as difficulty moving the joint or apparent loss of range of motion.

(i)
Applying a mobilizing force in the direction opposite to that indicated by the convex-concave rule would not correctly elongate the restricted capsular or ligamentous tissue and so would fail to restore the intended motion.

(j)
The treatment plane lies in the glenoid fossa and moves with the scapula as it rotates, so the direction of the mobilizing force must be aligned with this plane for the glide to be effective.

(k)
Correctly directed mobilization, applied according to the rule, mitigates capsular restrictions, breaks adhesions, and distracts impacted tissue while providing movement and lubrication for the articular cartilage.

(l)
Stabilizing the non-moving bone (for example, fixating the scapula with a belt or an assistant at the shoulder, or stabilizing the pelvis at the hip) ensures the mobilizing force is applied correctly relative to the fixed surface, as required by the convex-concave rule.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Indications: arthritis is an indication; the primary effects sought are pain reduction, improved range of motion and improved quality of joint movement; Tibiofemoral Distraction is indicated for testing, initial treatment, pain control and general mobility, and Tibiofemoral Posterior Glide is specifically indicated for testing and to increase flexion.

(b)
Contraindications: absolute – malignancy in the area, infectious arthritis, metabolic bone disease, neoplastic disease, fusion or ankylosis, osteomyelitis, fracture or ligament rupture; relative – excessive pain or swelling, arthroplasty, pregnancy, hypermobility, spondylolisthesis, rheumatoid arthritis, vertebrobasilar insufficiency.

(c)
Technique: Tibiofemoral Posterior Glide is selected – patient supine with the foot resting on the table, the therapist sitting on the table with the thigh fixating the patient's foot, grasping around the tibia with both hands (fingers pointing posteriorly, thumbs anteriorly), and applying force by extending the elbows and leaning the body weight forward to push the tibia posteriorly with the thumbs; this may be preceded by Tibiofemoral Distraction, beginning with the knee in resting position and progressing toward end-range flexion, with internal rotation of the tibia added at end-range flexion, grasping around the distal leg proximal to the malleoli with both hands and pulling along the long axis of the tibia.

(d)
Effects/outcome: mitigation of capsular restriction, breaking of adhesions, distraction of impacted tissue and improved cartilage lubrication (with synovial fluid motion bringing nutrition to the avascular portion of the joint); pain reduction and decreased muscle tension via mechanoreceptor stimulation; expected outcome is increased knee flexion with improved joint quality.

(e)
Precautions: avoid mobilization in the presence of any absolute contraindication and proceed cautiously with relative contraindications; keep Grade I/II oscillations pain-free; assess pain and stiffness after each set of oscillations and stop or modify if the technique produces more than slight discomfort or is not tolerated; note that no Grade I distraction can be applied together with the glide techniques.
questions.question:
A patient has restricted knee range of motion, with limited flexion, thought to be due to capsular restriction of the tibiofemoral joint.
(a) State the indications for joint mobilization in this patient.
(b) State the contraindications to be excluded before mobilizing.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Hip Distraction of the Weight-Bearing Surface (Caudal Glide) is indicated for testing, initial treatment, pain control and general mobility.

(b)
Patient position: supine, with the hip in resting position and the knee extended; the therapist stands at the end of the treatment table, places a belt around the trunk, crosses the belt over the patient's foot and around the ankle, and places the hands proximal to the malleoli under the belt.

(c)
Mobilizing force: a long-axis traction is applied by pulling on the leg as the therapist leans backward, the belt allowing use of body weight.

(d)
Hip Posterior Glide is indicated to increase flexion and to increase internal rotation.

(e)
Patient position for Posterior Glide: supine, with the hips at the end of the table, the patient helping to stabilize the pelvis and lumbar spine by flexing the opposite hip and holding the thigh to the chest; the therapist stands on the medial side of the patient's thigh, with a belt around the shoulder and under the patient's thigh, the distal hand under the belt and distal thigh, and the proximal hand on the anterior surface of the proximal thigh.

(f)
Mobilizing force for Posterior Glide: with elbows extended, the therapist flexes the knees and applies force through the proximal hand in a posterior direction.

(g)
Because of the deep configuration of the hip joint, traction applied perpendicular to the treatment plane causes a lateral glide of the superior, weight-bearing surface of the acetabulum (the concave acetabulum receiving the convex femoral head).

(h)
A belt is used so the therapist can use body weight, rather than arm strength alone, to apply the mobilizing or traction force, and to help support the weight of the patient's leg during the technique.

(i)
Hip Anterior Glide is indicated to increase extension and to increase external rotation, whereas Hip Posterior Glide is indicated to increase flexion and internal rotation.

(j)
Anterior Glide is performed prone, with the trunk resting on the table and the hips over the edge (or alternatively side-lying with the thigh supported by pillows), whereas Posterior Glide is performed supine with the hips at the end of the table.

(k)
For Anterior Glide, the force is applied through the proximal hand, placed posteriorly on the proximal thigh, in an anterior direction with the therapist's knees flexed and elbow extended; for Posterior Glide, the force is applied through the proximal hand, placed anteriorly on the proximal thigh, in a posterior direction.

(l)
The standard supine Hip Distraction position (knee extended) should not be used in the presence of knee dysfunction, for which an alternate position is used.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Muscle performance is the ability/capacity of a muscle to do work, and is a complex component of functional movement; linear work is defined as force multiplied by distance, while rotational work is defined as torque (force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation) multiplied by the arc of movement.

(b)
Muscle strength is the force exerted by a muscle or group of muscles to overcome a resistance in one maximal effort, expressed as the one repetition maximum (1RM) of a resistance exercise; muscle power is work produced per unit of time, or the product of strength and speed; muscle endurance is the ability of the muscle to contract repeatedly over time.

(c)
Strength training uses heavy loads to recruit as many fibres as possible within a muscle to generate near-maximal forces and stimulate the nervous and muscular systems to adapt; it typically involves a load/intensity of 80-100% of 1RM, using approximately 1 to 6 repetitions.

(d)
Power training requires a primary component of velocity of movement; since velocity is inversely proportional to the load lifted, the load is relatively lighter than in strength training to accomplish the necessary velocity, though power training does require a foundation of strength.

(e)
Endurance training involves many methods (such as circuit training) but is characterised by high repetitions with lighter loads; the relative work-to-rest ratio is the lowest among the three primary parameters of muscle performance.

(f)
Named resistance/training-load regimens: the DeLorme regimen, the Oxford regimen, the Daily Adjusted Progressive Resistance Exercise (DAPRE) technique, and the OMNI-RES (Oddvar Holten) method.

(g)
Endurance training can be a method to achieve hypertrophy training, since moderate loads and a repetition range of 8-12 repetitions are used for hypertrophy training.

(h)
Training-session terminology: tempo is the speed of movement; number of repetitions is a single cycle of lifting and lowering a weight in a controlled manner; sets are several repetitions performed one after another with no break between them; repetitive maximum is the number of repetitions performed at a certain weight.

(i)
Strength and power training can require similar components of training, whereas endurance training is fairly unique, being high repetitions with lighter loads and having the lowest relative work-to-rest ratio among the three parameters.

(a) State the classification system used to guide treatment decisions in Legg-Calvé-Perthes syndrome and its two groups.
(b) State the factors on which treatment decisions are based.
(c) State the goal of conservative (containment) treatment.
(d) List the components of conservative treatment.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Hips are categorised using the Salter-Thompson classification system into group A (less than 50% of the femoral head involved; relatively good prognosis) and group B (more than 50% of the femoral head involved; relatively poor prognosis).

(b)
Treatment decisions are based on the child's age and the extent of femoral head involvement.

(c)
The goal of conservative treatment is to optimise containment of the femoral head within the acetabulum by maintaining hip abduction, which places the femoral head deepest into the acetabulum, and to prevent further flattening of the femoral head while encouraging remodelling back into a spherical shape.

(d)
Conservative treatment for group A may include observation (no treatment, as many cases resolve), mobilization exercises, traction, use of a wheelchair to limit weight-bearing, and bilateral long-leg casts with a fixed abduction bar (Petrie casts) or braces.

(e)
Group A (less than 50% involvement) has a relatively good prognosis, while group B (more than 50% involvement) has a relatively poor prognosis.

(f)
There is no consensus on the best treatment for Legg-Calvé-Perthes syndrome, or even on whether surgery is needed.

(g)
Surgical options: tenotomy to lengthen shortened muscles, proximal varus osteotomy of the femur to reposition the femoral head securely in the acetabulum, and shelf osteoplasty to deepen the acetabulum and provide better coverage of the femoral head.

(h)
• Pain relief modifications used before/alongside active exercise include ultrasound, HCP or another electro-analgesic current such as TENS, and instruction in crutch walking to reduce weight-bearing in severe pain while keeping the child active.
• Active and muscle-strengthening exercises are then used, with aquatic exercise noted as a great resource, since frequent muscle spasms, pain or an altered gait pattern lead to decreases in hip abduction range of motion.
• Home exercise programmes are used to increase hip abduction and external rotation, and strength, because these positions place the femoral head deepest into the acetabulum.

(i)
Activity choices likely to increase pain, such as distance running and football, should be avoided, and patient/caregiver education on this should be provided.

questions.question:
(a) List the quantitative methods of determining muscle strength.
(b) State the qualitative method of determining muscle strength.
(c) Describe the method of resisted isometric testing.
(d) State the principle used to interpret the findings of resisted isometric testing (contractile versus inert tissue).
(e) State how manual muscle testing (MMT) is performed and by whom it was developed.
(f) Distinguish the break test from the make test in manual resistance testing.
(g) Describe how a handheld dynamometer (HHD) is used and what factors affect its readings.
(h) Describe how an isokinetic dynamometer is used.
(i) State the interpretation for a finding of "strong and painless" and "strong and painful".
(j) State the interpretation for a finding of "weak and painless" and "weak and painful".
(k) State when a resisted isometric test would prompt further testing with MMT or a dynamometer.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Quantitative methods of determining muscle strength: manual muscle testing (MMT), Oxford muscle grading, handheld dynamometry, isokinetic dynamometry, and electromyography (EMG) to analyse the muscles.
• Electromyography (EMG) is a diagnostic procedure that evaluates the health condition of muscles and the nerve cells that control them.

(b)
The qualitative method is resisted isometric testing.

(c)
In resisted isometric testing, the therapist places the patient's joint midway through the range of motion, so that minimal tension is put on inert structures; the body part proximal to the joint is well stabilized to minimise extraneous muscle substitutions; the patient holds the position while the therapist gradually applies resistance, and joint movement is strictly avoided.

(d)
Increased pain during a resisted isometric contraction, caused by shortening of the muscle and pulling on the tendon, helps confirm involvement of contractile tissues (sometimes more pain is felt when the contraction is released and lengthening occurs, which is still a positive finding); a lack of pain during resisted isometric testing, together with pain on limited accessory joint motions, a capsular pattern of restriction, or particular end-feels during passive ROM and accessory motions, helps confirm involvement of inert tissues instead.

(e)
Manual muscle testing was developed by Wright and Lovett, beginning in 1912, as a means of testing and grading muscle strength based on gravity and manually applied resistance; both commonly used methods use arc of motion, gravity, and manually applied resistance to test and determine muscle grades. The patient is positioned so the muscle/muscle group must move or hold against gravity; if tolerated, manual resistance is applied gradually to the distal end of the body part, in a direction opposite the torque produced by the muscle; weaker muscles are repositioned to move through a gravity-minimised (horizontal) plane of motion.

(f)
In a break test, the patient holds a joint position until the therapist gradually overpowers the patient and an eccentric contraction begins, occurring at the end of range for one-joint muscles and at mid-range for two-joint muscles; in a make test (active resistance test), manual resistance is applied while the patient moves through the range, so the muscle's ability to contract concentrically against maximal resistance can also be determined.

(g)
A handheld dynamometer is a portable device placed between the therapist's hand and the patient's body that measures mechanical force at the point of application, applied perpendicular to the body segment at an established location; the force measured varies with the method of applying resistance (make or break test), the patient's body position relative to gravity, joint angle, dynamometer placement (lever arm), stabilization to prevent muscle substitution, and the therapist's strength; results are recorded in newton-metres or kilogram-force (kgf) metres.

(h)
Isokinetic dynamometers are stationary, electromechanical devices that control the velocity of a moving body segment by resisting and measuring the patient's effort so the segment cannot accelerate beyond a preset angular velocity, measuring torque and range of motion as a function of time; they can measure torque during isometric (velocity set to 0°/second), concentric and eccentric contractions, and are especially helpful in examining large, strong muscle groups such as those at the knee, shoulder and back.

(i)
Strong and painless: there is no lesion or neurological deficit involving the tested muscle and tendon; strong and painful: there is a minor lesion of the tested muscle or tendon.

(j)
Weak and painless: there is a disorder of the nervous system or neuromuscular junction, a complete rupture of the tested muscle or tendon, or disuse atrophy; weak and painful: there is a serious, painful pathology such as a fracture or neoplasm, an acute inflammatory process inhibiting contraction, or a partial rupture of the tested muscle or tendon.

(k)
In addition to noting the presence or absence of pain, the therapist notes the strength of the muscle contraction during resisted isometric testing; if weakness is found, more extensive testing of muscle strength should be performed using MMT or dynamometers.

(a)
Radiocarpal Distraction is indicated for testing, initial treatment, pain control and general mobility of the wrist.

(b)
Patient position: sitting, with the forearm supported on the treatment table, wrist over the edge of the table.

(c)
Hand placement: with the hand closer to the patient, the therapist grasps around the styloid processes and fixates the radius and ulna against the table; the other hand grasps around the distal row of carpals.

(d)
Mobilizing force: a pull in a distal direction with respect to the arm.

(e)
For the Radiocarpal Joint General Glides and Progression, the patient sits with the forearm resting on the table, in pronation for the dorsal and volar glide techniques and in midrange position for the radial and ulnar glide techniques, progressing by moving the wrist to the end of the available range before gliding.

(f)
The four directions and their effects: dorsal glide increases flexion; volar glide increases extension; ulnar glide increases radial deviation; radial glide increases ulnar deviation.

(g)
The radius and ulna are fixated against the table during Radiocarpal Distraction so that the distal row of carpals can be pulled distally relative to a stabilized forearm, ensuring the distraction force is isolated to the radiocarpal joint rather than moving the whole forearm.

(h)
Pronation is used to position the forearm appropriately for accessing the dorsal and volar surfaces for those glides, while a midrange forearm position is used for the radial and ulnar glides, allowing the wrist to be moved toward end-range in the radial/ulnar deviation plane before the glide is applied.

(i)
Dorsal Glide is used to increase flexion, whereas Volar Glide is used to increase extension.

(j)
Ulnar Glide is used to increase radial deviation, whereas Radial Glide is used to increase ulnar deviation.

(k)
• Specific techniques to mobilize individual carpal bones may be necessary to gain full range of motion of the wrist; to glide one carpal on another, or on the radius, the patient sits with the elbow hanging unsupported as the therapist grasps the hand, the weight of the arm providing slight distraction so only the glide itself needs to be applied.
• For individual carpal mobilization, the index fingers are placed on the volar surface of the bone to be stabilized, and the overlapping thumbs are placed on the dorsal surface of the bone to be mobilized, with the rest of the fingers holding the patient's hand relaxed.
