questions.answerText:
(a)
Legg-Calvé-Perthes (LCP) syndrome.

(b)
Pathophysiology: the proximal femur receives its blood supply from the extracapsular arterial ring (medial and lateral femoral circumflex vessels), the ascending cervical vessels, and the vessel of the ligamentum teres; interruption of blood flow from the medial femoral circumflex artery is suspected to lead to aseptic avascular necrosis of the femoral head and bone reabsorption. Hips are categorised by the Salter-Thompson classification into group A (less than 50% of the femoral head involved, relatively good prognosis) and group B (more than 50% involved, relatively poor prognosis); the necrotic tissue is gradually replaced with new bone, and compression encourages congruent, spherical reshaping of the femoral head.

(c)
Management: pain relief using ultrasound, HCP or another electro-analgesic current such as TENS, and instruction in crutch walking to reduce weight-bearing in severe pain while keeping the child active; active and muscle-strengthening exercises (aquatic exercise is a useful resource), since frequent muscle spasms, pain or an altered gait pattern reduce hip abduction range of motion; hip abduction and external rotation are the best positions for placing the femoral head into the acetabulum, so home exercise programmes to increase abduction, external rotation and strength are used; patient/caregiver education on activity choices, avoiding activities such as distance running and football that are likely to increase pain. For Salter-Thompson group A, conservative treatment is often used, including observation (many cases resolve without treatment), mobilization exercises, traction, use of a wheelchair to limit weight-bearing, and bilateral long-leg casts with a fixed abduction bar (Petrie casts) or braces, with the goal of optimising containment of the femoral head within the acetabulum by maintaining hip abduction, preventing further flattening, and encouraging remodelling. Surgical treatment (tenotomy to lengthen shortened muscles, proximal varus femoral osteotomy, and shelf osteoplasty to deepen the acetabulum) may be considered, though there is no consensus on the best treatment or on whether surgery is needed.
questions.question:
A child presents with an insidious-onset limp, characterised by a drop in the pelvis of the swinging leg and the trunk leaning toward the stance side. The child does not complain much of pain unless prompted, and reports that pain is aggravated by activity and relieved by rest, sometimes referred to the antero-medial thigh or knee.
(a) State the diagnosis.
(b) Describe the contributing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) Outline the physiotherapy management.

(a) State the two important functions of articular cartilage.
(b) Describe the structural properties of articular cartilage (composition, porosity, response to loading, ability to heal).
(c) State the forms in which articular fibrocartilage exists and give examples.
(d) List the possible roles of articular fibrocartilage.
(e) Explain how these structural properties guide the choice of joint mobilization as a technique (mechanical effect on synovial fluid and cartilage nutrition).
(f) Explain how the limited healing capacity of cartilage guides caution in technique selection/grading.
(g) Explain how the roles of fibrocartilage (load distribution, fit improvement, shock absorption) guide technique selection at joints containing menisci or discs.
(h) Explain the effect on function when articular cartilage is damaged (progression toward arthritis).
(i) Explain the effect of cartilage's stress-distribution role being impaired (increased contact stress).
(j) Explain the effect on function when the fibrocartilage's shock-absorption/limitation-of-translation role is impaired.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Articular cartilage distributes loads at the joint over a wide area to ensure that the amount of stress at any contact point is reduced, and it allows movement of the articulating bones at the joint with minimal friction and wear.

(b)
• Articular cartilage is a dense, white connective tissue that is soft, porous and permeable, and it is hydrated; it deforms under loading, thereby exuding synovial fluid, and it has little or no ability to heal or regenerate on its own once damaged.
• Regular exercise and loading, unlike for cartilage, allow tendons and ligaments (composed primarily of collagen and elastic tissue) to hypertrophy and increase in strength of their bony attachments, but when stretched beyond their elastic limits they remain stretched and can only be returned to original length through surgery.
• Articular cartilage increases as a child's height increases during normal growth, though weight change was not found to correlate with cartilage accrual at the knee, indicating its accrual is linked to growth rather than loading alone.

(c)
Articular fibrocartilage exists as a fibrocartilaginous disc or as partial discs known as menisci, present between articulating bones; examples given are the intervertebral discs and the menisci of the knee.

(d)
Possible roles of articular fibrocartilage: distribution of loads over joint surfaces, improvement of the fit of the articulating surfaces, limitation of translation or slip of one bone relative to another, protection of the periphery of the articulation, lubrication, and shock absorption.

(e)
Small-amplitude distraction or gliding movement of a joint, as used in mobilization, causes synovial fluid motion, which brings nutrition to the avascular portion of the articular cartilage, so mobilization is chosen partly for this mechanical/nutritive effect.

(f)
Because cartilage can reduce contact stress at a joint by 50% but has little or no ability to heal once damaged, and injuries to it tend to progress toward more of the protective coating being worn away, mobilization technique and grade should be chosen and progressed cautiously to avoid excessive compressive stress on already compromised articular surfaces.

(g)
Because fibrocartilage such as the meniscus distributes load, improves joint fit and provides shock absorption, mobilization or manual techniques at joints containing these structures (for example, the knee) are selected with attention to protecting these functions during joint play or gliding.

(h)
When articular cartilage is damaged, injuries tend to progress, with more and more of the protective coating of the articulating bone ends being worn away, thereby leading to arthritis.

(i)
Articular cartilage normally reduces contact stress at a joint by up to 50%; if its load-distributing function is impaired, contact stress at the joint increases.

(j)
If the shock-absorption or translation-limiting role of the fibrocartilage (for example, the meniscus) is impaired, greater load and slip are transmitted directly between the articulating bones, reducing the protection normally afforded to the periphery of the articulation.

questions.question:
A patient with fibromyalgia reports fatigue with reduced exercise tolerance and widespread muscular pain that fluctuates with environmental, physical and emotional stresses.
(a) State the physiotherapy problem list.
(b) Outline the impairments present, including weakness/fatigue, stiffness, pain and restricted tolerance.
(c) State the goals of treatment.
(d) Outline the strengthening programme, including precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Widespread muscular pain and fatigue with reduced exercise tolerance, morning stiffness and non-restorative sleep, consistent with fibromyalgia.

(b)
Impairments: widespread pain covering half of the body, usually muscular in origin and predominant in the scapular, head, neck, chest and low back regions; morning stiffness; fatigue with reduced exercise tolerance; symptoms fluctuate, with pain-free days interspersed with days of serious pain.

(c)
Goals of treatment: reduce symptom severity and flares; improve exercise tolerance through graded aerobic and resistance exercise; avoid triggering environmental, physical or emotional stress factors; support pacing of activities.

(d)
Strengthening programme: resistance exercise together with aerobic exercise; instruction in pacing of activities to avoid symptom fluctuations; precautions – avoid or manage environmental stresses (weather changes, especially barometric pressure change, cold, dampness, fog, rain, fluorescent light) and physical stresses (repetitive activities such as typing, playing piano, vacuuming, prolonged sitting/standing, working rotating shifts), which can trigger a flare; decrease alcohol and caffeine consumption and modify diet; avoid emotional stress factors as part of the overall programme alongside prescription and over-the-counter medication.

questions.question:
A child with Legg-Calvé-Perthes syndrome has frequent muscle spasms and an altered gait pattern.
(a) State the physiotherapy problem list.
(b) Outline the impairments present, including weakness, stiffness/spasm, pain and restricted range of motion.
(c) State the goals of treatment.
(d) Outline the strengthening programme, including precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Reduced hip abduction range of motion and reduced hip abductor/lower-limb strength secondary to Legg-Calvé-Perthes syndrome, with an altered gait pattern.

(b)
Impairments: frequent muscle spasms and pain; an altered gait pattern (insidious-onset limp with pelvic drop of the swinging leg and trunk lean toward the stance side); decreased hip abduction range of motion resulting from the spasms, pain and altered gait.

(c)
Goals of treatment: pain relief; optimisation of containment of the femoral head within the acetabulum by maintaining hip abduction; prevention of further flattening of the femoral head and encouragement of remodelling back into a spherical shape; improvement of hip abduction and external rotation range and strength; education of the patient/caregiver on activity choices.

(d)
Strengthening programme: active and muscle-strengthening exercises, with aquatic exercise noted as a great resource; hip abduction and external rotation are the best positions for placing the femoral head into the acetabulum, so a home exercise programme is used to increase abduction, external rotation and strength; for Salter-Thompson group A, conservative measures such as mobilization exercises, and use of a wheelchair or Petrie casts/braces to limit weight-bearing, may accompany the strengthening programme; precautions: pain relief (ultrasound, HCP or an electro-analgesic current such as TENS) and crutch walking to reduce weight-bearing are used first if pain is severe, while keeping the child active; activities such as distance running and football should be avoided as they are likely to increase pain.

(a)
Myofascial Pain Syndrome (MPS) – a chronic regional pain syndrome with myofascial trigger points showing a specific referred pattern of pain located in the muscle; trigger points are hyper-irritable areas in a tight band of muscle, producing pain that is dull, aching and deep, with other impairments including decreased range of motion when the muscle is stretched, reduced muscle strength, and increased pain with muscle stretching.

(b)
Contributing factors/pathophysiology: the aetiology is not completely known, but possible causes include chronic overload of muscle from repetitive activities or activities that maintain the muscle in a shortened position, acute overload of muscle (such as slipping and catching oneself, lifting an unexpectedly heavy object, or trauma such as a motor vehicle accident), poorly conditioned muscles as opposed to regularly exercised muscles, postural stresses (such as prolonged sitting in an ergonomically incorrect workstation, and leg length differences), and poor body mechanics during lifting and other activities.

(c)
Management: three main components – eliminating the trigger points, correcting the contributing factors, and strengthening the muscle; if chronic overload is the cause of the trigger point, the contributing factor is eliminated before addressing the trigger point, and once range of motion has been restored and the trigger point addressed, muscle strengthening is initiated. Techniques for eliminating the trigger point include contract-relax, trigger point release, spray and stretch, and dry needling or injection.

(a) State the diagnosis.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Indications: arthritis and ankle sprains are indications for mobilization; the primary effects sought are pain reduction, improved range of motion and improved quality of joint movement; Talocrural Distraction is indicated for testing, initial treatment, pain control and general mobility, and Talocrural Dorsal (Posterior) Glide is specifically indicated to increase dorsiflexion.

(b)
Contraindications: absolute – malignancy in the area, infectious arthritis, metabolic bone disease, neoplastic disease, fusion or ankylosis, osteomyelitis, fracture or ligament rupture; relative – excessive pain or swelling, arthroplasty, pregnancy, hypermobility, spondylolisthesis, rheumatoid arthritis, vertebrobasilar insufficiency.

(c)
Technique: Talocrural Dorsal (Posterior) Glide is selected – patient supine, leg supported on the table with the heel over the edge; the therapist stands to the side, stabilizes the leg with the cranial hand or a belt, places the palmar web space of the other hand over the talus just distal to the mortise, wraps the fingers and thumb around the foot to maintain resting position, applies a Grade I distraction force in a caudal direction, and glides the talus posteriorly with respect to the tibia; this may be preceded by Talocrural Distraction (supine, lower extremity extended, ankle in resting position progressing to end-range of dorsiflexion or plantarflexion, fingers of both hands wrapped over the dorsum of the foot distal to the mortise, thumbs on the plantar surface, pulling the foot along the long axis of the leg in a distal direction by leaning backward).

(d)
Effects/outcome: mitigation of capsular restriction, breaking of adhesions, distraction of impacted tissue and improved cartilage lubrication; pain reduction and decreased muscle tension via mechanoreceptor stimulation; expected outcome is increased dorsiflexion with improved joint quality.

(e)
Precautions: avoid mobilization in the presence of any absolute contraindication and proceed cautiously with relative contraindications, including with a history of ankle sprain where excessive pain or swelling is present; keep Grade I/II oscillations pain-free; assess pain and stiffness after each set of oscillations and stop or modify if the technique produces more than slight discomfort or is not tolerated.
questions.question:
A patient has restricted ankle range of motion, with limited dorsiflexion, thought to be due to capsular restriction of the talocrural joint.
(a) State the indications for joint mobilization in this patient.
(b) State the contraindications to be excluded before mobilizing.
(c) State the mobilization technique selected, including grade, direction and position.
(d) State the effects and expected outcome.
(e) State the precautions and when to stop treatment.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Joint mobilization is a type of manual therapy involving passive movement of a specific joint; physiologic mobilizations follow the same pattern of movement produced by voluntary muscle contraction, while accessory mobilizations are performed passively, in a pattern that cannot be produced voluntarily, usually in the midrange (open-pack) position.

(b)
Maitland grades: Grade I – small amplitude, short of resistance; Grade II – large amplitude, short of resistance; Grade III – large amplitude to 50% of R1-R2; Grade IV – small amplitude to 50% of R1-R2; Grade V – small amplitude, high-velocity thrust at the end of available range (R1 = first perceptible onset of resistance, R2 = limit of resistance).

(c)
If physiologic mobilization Grades I and II cause pain when treating pain, accessory Grades I and II should be performed instead; if 50% of physiologic active ROM is unavailable due to pain, accessory Grades I and II are used (the 50/50 rule).

(d)
Small-amplitude distraction or gliding causes synovial fluid motion bringing nutrition to avascular portions of the joint; vigorous joint play elongates hypomobile ligaments and capsular tissue; gliding techniques restore functional immobility; chronic hypomobility is treated with joint play at a higher grade plus advanced techniques.

(e)
Pain reduction and decreased muscle tension occur through stimulation of fast-conducting fibres (type A-β and A-α) blocking small pain fibres (type C afferents), and through activation of dynamic mechanoreceptors producing reflexive relaxation; small-amplitude oscillatory and distraction movements inhibit nociceptive transmission at the spinal cord and brain stem level.

(f)
When ROM is decreased due to pain, Grade I and II mobilizations should be performed in the pain-free range for 30 seconds or longer, and function reassessed afterward.

(g)
• For stiffness, 60 seconds of accessory mobilization is followed by 60 seconds of physiologic mobilization, with the effect assessed; this sequence is performed three times.
• Assessment for pain or stiffness should be made after each set of oscillations during any mobilization treatment to determine the effect achieved.

(h)
If both pain and stiffness are present, the therapist decides which is primary: if pain occurs before resistance, control pain first before progressing; if pain occurs with resistance, mobilize with caution; if pain occurs after resistance, vigorous mobilization for stiffness may be used followed by techniques for pain.

(i)
Primary effects: pain reduction, improved range of motion, and improved quality of joint movement; indicated conditions include arthritis, rotator cuff tears and sprain, adhesive capsulitis, medial or lateral epicondylitis, facet joint locking and spinal misalignments, whiplash, ankle sprains, and sciatica or other nerve impingement syndromes.

(j)
Absolute contraindications: malignancy in the area of treatment, infectious arthritis, metabolic bone disease, neoplastic disease, fusion or ankylosis, osteomyelitis, and fracture or ligament rupture.

(k)
Relative contraindications: excessive pain or swelling, arthroplasty, pregnancy, hypermobility, spondylolisthesis, rheumatoid arthritis, and vertebrobasilar insufficiency.

(f) State the length-tension relationship and the role of the Series Elastic Component.
(g) State the difference in the length at which peak tension is produced between parallel-fibered and pennate-fibered muscles.
(h) Define the stretch-shortening cycle and its effect on force production.
(i) State the contributors to the stretch-shortening cycle.
(j) Define electromechanical delay and state its physiological basis.
(k) State how electromechanical delay differs by fibre-type dominance and by age.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Concentric contraction occurs when muscular tension produces a torque greater than the resistive torque at the joint, so the muscle shortens and the joint angle changes; the external force (load) is less than the muscle's internal force, and the resulting joint movement is in the direction of the net torque generated by the muscle; a single muscle fibre can shorten to approximately half its normal resting length.

(b)
Isometric contraction occurs when the opposing torque at the joint equals the torque produced by the muscle (net torque = 0), i.e. the external force equals the muscle's internal force; muscle length remains unchanged and no joint movement occurs, though the cross-sectional area of the tense muscles increases when opposing muscles contract isometrically together.

(c)
Eccentric contraction occurs when the opposing joint torque is greater than the tension produced by the muscle, so the muscle lengthens as it contracts, with movement in the direction opposite to the net torque; it acts as a braking mechanism to control movement speed; an example is tension in the elbow flexors during elbow extension (and vice versa).

(d)
The maximal force a muscle can develop is determined by the velocity of the muscle's shortening or lengthening; this relationship holds for maximally activated muscle but not for muscle action during most daily activities.

(e)
Most activities of daily living require slow, controlled movements of submaximal loads, so with such loads the velocity of muscle shortening depends on volitional control, with only the number of motor units needed being activated.

(f)
The amount of maximum isometric tension a muscle can produce largely depends on its length; force generation is at its peak when the muscle is slightly stretched and is lesser following muscle shortening; this length-tension relationship is due to the contribution of the elastic components of muscle, primarily the Series Elastic Component (SEC).

(g)
Parallel-fibered muscles produce maximum tension at just over resting length, while pennate-fibered muscles generate maximum tension at between 120% and 130% of resting length.

(h)
The stretch-shortening cycle is the pattern of eccentric contraction followed immediately by concentric contraction; when an actively tensed muscle is stretched before contracting, the resulting contraction is more forceful, and a muscle can perform substantially more work with less metabolic cost than when it simply contracts without pre-stretch.

(i)
The Series Elastic Component contributes through its elastic recoil effect enhancing force production, and activation of the stretch reflex provoked by forced lengthening of the muscle is another potential contributor.

(j)
Electromechanical delay (EMD) is the brief period that elapses between the time a muscle is stimulated and the time it begins to develop tension; the delay is required for the contractile component of the muscle to stretch the Series Elastic Component, eliminating muscle laxity before tension development proceeds.

(k)
Muscles with a higher percentage of fast-twitch fibres have a shorter EMD than those with a higher percentage of slow-twitch fibres, and higher contraction force is associated with a shorter EMD; EMD is significantly longer in children than in adults, and is longer immediately after passive stretching, several days after eccentric exercise causing muscle damage, after endurance training, and when contraction is initiated from a resting rather than an activated state.

(a)
McMurray's test, a test for meniscus lesions of the knee.

(b)
The meniscus is a fibrocartilage structure that improves the fit of the articulating surfaces and provides shock absorption between the femur and tibia; during full extension and flexion with the foot internally and then externally rotated, a torn portion of the meniscus catches between the articulating surfaces, producing a reproducible "pop or click" that is felt or heard, which is the positive sign of a meniscus lesion.

(c)
Differential: the Apley Grind/Distraction test differentiates a meniscus lesion from a ligamentous injury – the patient lies prone with the knee flexed to 90°, and the examiner applies a compressive force on the heel while rotating the tibia and palpating the joint line for crepitation (positive for meniscus if pain or crepitation occurs); the test is then repeated with a distractive force applied to the leg, and if pain is elicited during distraction, this indicates a ligamentous injury rather than a meniscus injury.

(d)
Clinical reasoning: because the meniscus is fibrocartilage with roles in load distribution, improving joint fit and shock absorption, and has limited capacity to heal (similar to articular cartilage), treatment reasoning favours protecting the joint from excessive compressive/rotational stress (for example, avoiding vigorous compressive mobilization grades at the tibiofemoral joint) while addressing any accompanying restriction with lower-grade, pain-free mobilization and strengthening of the surrounding musculature to support the joint, rather than aggressive end-range techniques that would reproduce the mechanical catching.
questions.question:
A patient lies supine while the examiner fully extends and flexes the knee, placing one hand over the joint line to feel for clicks or pops; the test is then repeated with the foot internally rotated and again externally rotated, with a reproducible click noted.
(a) Identify the test and the structure being examined.
(b) State the affected structures and the mechanism producing the positive sign.
(c) State a differential test and finding that would instead suggest a ligamentous injury.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for the treatment choice, justifying one approach.

(a) State how the tension in a two-joint or multi-joint muscle affects the joints it crosses.
(b) List the factors determining the effectiveness of a two-joint or multi-joint muscle in causing movement at a joint it crosses.
(c) Define active insufficiency and give an example.
(d) Define passive insufficiency and give examples.
(e) Explain how active insufficiency guides the choice of exercise/stretching position for a two-joint muscle.
(f) Explain how passive insufficiency guides the choice of positioning during a strengthening or stretching technique.
(g) Explain the effect on function of active insufficiency (impact on producing full ROM at all crossed joints simultaneously).
(h) Explain the effect on function of passive insufficiency (impact on ROM in the opposite direction at all crossed joints).
(i) Explain, using the ankle/knee example, how relaxing a two-joint muscle at one joint increases available range at another.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Tension in a muscle is constant throughout its length and at the sites of its tendinous attachments to bone, so a two-joint or multi-joint muscle affects motion at both, or all, of the joints it crosses simultaneously.
• A one-joint muscle produces force directed primarily in line with a body segment, but a two-joint muscle can produce force with a significant transverse component, and the disadvantages of two-joint or multi-joint muscles are active and passive insufficiency.

(b)
The effectiveness of a two-joint or multi-joint muscle in causing movement at any joint it crosses depends on the location and orientation of the muscle's attachments relative to the joint, the tightness or laxity present in the musculotendinous unit, and the action of other muscles crossing the joint.

(c)
Active insufficiency refers to the inability of a two-joint muscle to shorten (stretch) to the extent required to produce a full range of motion at all the joints it crosses simultaneously; an example is that the finger flexors cannot produce as tight a fist as possible when the wrist is flexed as when the wrist is in a neutral position.

(d)
• Passive insufficiency occurs when a two-joint or multi-joint muscle is unable to stretch to the extent required for full range of motion in the opposite direction at all the joints it crosses; examples given are that a larger range of wrist extension is possible when the fingers are not fully extended than when fully extended (as extensor digitorum longus is relaxed over the fingers), and a larger range of ankle dorsiflexion is possible when the knee is slightly flexed, relaxing the gastrocnemius at the knee.
• These properties (active and passive insufficiency) are disadvantages of two-joint or multi-joint muscles compared with one-joint muscles.

(e)
Because active insufficiency limits full shortening across all crossed joints simultaneously, exercises aiming for maximal contraction/shortening of a two-joint muscle (such as gripping) are reasoned to be performed with the proximal joint in a position (e.g. wrist neutral rather than flexed) that avoids placing the muscle in an already-shortened position at the other joint.

(f)
Because passive insufficiency limits full lengthening across all crossed joints simultaneously, stretching or mobilizing techniques for a two-joint muscle are reasoned to position one of the crossed joints so as to relax the muscle there, allowing a fuller stretch or range to be achieved at the joint being targeted.

(g)
Active insufficiency means the muscle cannot produce as complete a shortening-based movement (such as a tight fist) when the other joint it crosses is already positioned to shorten the muscle.

(h)
Passive insufficiency means the muscle cannot allow as complete a lengthening-based movement (such as full wrist extension with fingers extended) when the other joint it crosses is already positioned to lengthen the muscle.

(i)
• In the ankle/knee example, dorsiflexion range at the ankle is greater when the knee is slightly flexed, because this relaxes the gastrocnemius (which crosses both the knee and ankle), demonstrating how relieving tension at one joint crossed by a two-joint muscle increases available range at the other joint it crosses.
• Similarly, a larger range of wrist extension is possible when the fingers are not fully extended, because the extensor digitorum longus (crossing both the wrist and fingers) is relaxed over the fingers.

(a)
Joint stiffness with disuse muscle weakness and loss of range of motion following a period of immobilization; immobilization, surgery, soft-tissue injury and overuse are among the causes of joint stiffness.

(b)
Impairments: joint stiffness (sensation of difficulty moving the joint / apparent loss of range of motion), often accompanied by pain and swelling; disuse-related loss of muscle performance; restricted range of motion within the permitted post-injury limits.

(c)
Goals of treatment (Phase I – Immediate rehabilitation): protection of the integrity of the involved tissue; restoration of range of motion within restrictions; diminishment of pain and inflammation; prevention of muscular inhibition.

(d)
Strengthening programme: begin with Phase I exercises within restrictions; progress to Phase II when there is minimal pain with all Phase I exercises, range of motion is about 75% of the non-involved side, and proper muscle firing patterns are present for initial exercises; Phase II continues protection of the tissue while restoring function of the region; progress to Phase III once range of motion/muscle length/joint play are close to full and strength is about 60% of the uninjured side, adding restoration of muscular endurance and strength, cardiovascular endurance, and neuromuscular control/balance/proprioception; progress to Phase IV, focused on return to full function, once strength is greater than 70-80% of the non-involved side and initial agility drills can be performed with proper form; precaution: do not advance a phase until its criteria are met, and during advanced drills avoid uncoordinated or asymmetrical movement such as medial collapse of the lower extremities.
questions.question:
A patient presents with a stiff joint and disuse weakness following a period of immobilization after an injury, with reduced ability to move the joint through its full range.
(a) State the physiotherapy problem list for this presentation.
(b) Outline the impairments present, including weakness, stiffness, pain and restricted range of motion.
(c) State the goals of treatment.
(d) Outline the strengthening programme, including grading, progression and precautions.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Assessment findings: restricted accessory glide/joint play at the acromioclavicular (AC) joint limiting overall shoulder girdle mobility; restricted anterior glide/caudal glide or posterior/superior glide at the sternoclavicular (SC) joint limiting protraction/elevation or retraction/depression of the clavicle; restricted scapulothoracic soft-tissue mobility limiting elevation, depression, protraction, retraction, upward/downward rotation and winging of the scapula.

(b)
Techniques: Anterior Glide of the Clavicle on the Acromion (AC joint); Sternoclavicular Anterior Glide and Caudal (Inferior) Glide; Sternoclavicular Posterior Glide and Superior Glide; Scapulothoracic Soft-Tissue Mobilization.

(c)
Starting position/hand placement/stabilization: AC joint – stabilize the scapula with the more lateral hand around the acromion process; with the patient sitting, stand behind and stabilize the acromion with the fingers of the lateral hand while the thumb of the other hand pushes down through the upper trapezius, placed posteriorly on the clavicle just medial to the joint space (with the patient prone, stabilize the acromion with a towel roll under the shoulder). SC joint – fingers placed superiorly and thumb inferiorly around the clavicle for the anterior/caudal glides; thumb on the anterior surface of the proximal clavicle with the flexed index finger's middle phalanx supporting along the caudal surface for the posterior/superior glides. Scapulothoracic – begin prone (progressing to side-lying facing the therapist) with the patient's arm draped over the therapist's inferior arm to relax the scapular muscles; the superior hand is placed across the acromion to control direction while the fingers of the inferior hand scoop under the medial border and inferior angle of the scapula.

(d)
Dosage/progression: apply the general Maitland grading principles for peripheral joint mobilization – small-amplitude Grade I/II oscillations at 3-4 per second, progressing to larger-amplitude Grade III/IV mobilizations toward the end of range as tolerated, with the effect assessed after each set of oscillations.

(e)
Complications/precautions: absolute contraindications – malignancy in the area, infectious arthritis, metabolic bone disease, neoplastic disease, fusion or ankylosis, osteomyelitis, fracture or ligament rupture; relative contraindications – excessive pain or swelling, arthroplasty, pregnancy, hypermobility, spondylolisthesis, rheumatoid arthritis, vertebrobasilar insufficiency; adequate stabilization of the acromion/scapula is required to prevent substitution movement during the mobilizing force.
questions.question:
A patient has restricted mobility of the shoulder girdle, with reduced accessory joint play at the acromioclavicular and sternoclavicular joints and restriction of scapular movement.
(a) State the assessment findings expected (restricted joint play/movement at the AC, SC and scapulothoracic regions).
(b) State the techniques used for these joints.
(c) Describe the starting position, hand placement and stabilization for each technique.
(d) State the dosage and progression.
(e) State the complications and precautions.

(a) State the three main components of Myofascial Pain Syndrome treatment (the principle of sequencing).
(b) State the techniques used for eliminating the trigger point.
(c) State the principle governing when strengthening is introduced relative to the other components.
(d) State the precaution regarding chronic overload as a contributing factor.
(e) State the other contributing factors that may need to be corrected as a precautionary/complication-avoidance measure.
(f) State the basis for modifying management when acute overload rather than chronic overload is the cause.
(g) State the basis for modifying management according to the presence of postural stresses.
questions.answerText:
(a)
There are three main components to MPS treatment: eliminating the trigger points, correcting the contributing factors, and strengthening the muscle.

(b)
Techniques for eliminating the trigger point include contract-relax, trigger point release, spray and stretch, and dry needling or injection.

(c)
Muscle strengthening should be initiated only once range of motion has been restored and the trigger point has been addressed.

(d)
If chronic overload of the muscle from repetitive activities, or from activities that maintain the muscle in a shortened position, is the cause of the trigger point, the contributing factor is eliminated before addressing the trigger point itself.

(e)
Other possible contributing factors that may need correcting include acute overload of the muscle, poorly conditioned muscles (as opposed to those exercised regularly), postural stresses such as prolonged sitting at an ergonomically incorrect workstation and leg length differences, and poor body mechanics during lifting and other activities.

(f)
Acute overload may arise from events such as slipping and catching oneself, picking up an object of unexpected weight, or trauma such as a motor vehicle accident, and correcting the precipitating activity or exposure is part of correcting the contributing factor in this situation, just as it is for chronic overload.

(g)
Where postural stresses such as an ergonomically incorrect workstation, prolonged sitting or standing, or a leg length difference are identified as contributing factors, correction of these postural/ergonomic factors forms part of the "correcting the contributing factors" component before or alongside trigger point elimination and strengthening.

(a)
Three factors are significant determinants of the magnitude of the force generated by a muscle: the velocity of muscle shortening, the length of the muscle when it is activated, and the period of time since the muscle received a stimulus.

(b)
A muscle's moment arm is affected by two equally important factors: the distance between the muscle's anatomical attachment to the bone and the axis of rotation at the joint centre, and the angle of the muscle's attachment to the bone, which is a function of the relative joint angle.

(c)
Maximum torque is produced by maximum tension in a muscle that is oriented at a 90° angle to the bone and anatomically attached as far from the joint centre as possible.

(d)
The force (tension) generating capability of a muscle per cross-sectional area is 90 N/cm².

(e)
Because peak isometric tension is produced when a muscle is slightly stretched, and maximum torque requires both this tension and a long moment arm (attachment far from the joint centre, at 90° to the bone), resistance in a strengthening exercise is positioned to work the muscle near this favourable length and joint angle to maximise the torque generated for a given effort.

(f)
Because the maximal force a muscle can develop is determined by the velocity of shortening or lengthening, and most activities of daily living use slow, controlled movements of submaximal loads with volitional control of motor unit recruitment, the speed and load of a strengthening exercise are selected according to whether the goal is maximal force (slower, heavier loads, as in strength training) or velocity-dependent power (lighter loads permitting faster movement, as in power training).

(g)
If a muscle's moment arm is reduced (attachment closer to the joint centre, or attachment angle away from 90° to the bone), less torque is produced for the same muscle tension, reducing the muscle's effective strength at that joint.

(h)
If a muscle is worked at a length shorter than its optimal length (following shortening), tension development is lesser than at the peak, so force generation and the resulting torque are reduced; parallel-fibered muscles peak at just over resting length and pennate-fibered muscles peak between 120% and 130% of resting length, so working outside these ranges reduces force output.

(i)
• Muscular power is the product of muscular force and the velocity of muscle shortening, more generally the rate of torque production at a joint, or the product of net torque and angular velocity; maximum muscular power occurs at approximately one-third of maximum velocity and approximately one-third of maximum concentric force.
• Individuals with a larger percentage of fast-twitch fibres generate more power at a given load and reach maximum power at faster velocities of shortening than those with predominantly slow-twitch fibres, since fast-twitch fibres develop tension more rapidly; the ratio for maximum peak power production by fibre type is 10:5:1 for type IIb, IIa and type I fibres respectively.
• Muscular endurance refers to a muscle's ability to exert tension over time, and training for it typically involves large numbers of repetitions against relatively light resistance, which is a different force-generation demand from the maximal-torque and maximal-power conditions described above.
• Body temperature increase shifts the force-velocity curve, producing higher maximum isometric tension and higher maximum velocity of shortening at any given load, with fewer motor units needed to sustain a given load, providing the rationale for warming up before exercise; muscle function is most efficient at 38.5 °C, with temperatures above this being dangerous for body function.
questions.question:
(a) State the three factors that are significant determinants of the magnitude of force generated by a muscle.
(b) State the two factors affecting a muscle's moment arm.
(c) State the muscle orientation and attachment condition that produces maximum torque.
(d) State the value for a muscle's tension-generating capability per cross-sectional area.
(e) Explain how the length-tension relationship and moment-arm factors together guide the positioning used when applying resistance during a strengthening exercise.
(f) Explain how knowledge of the force-velocity relationship guides the speed/load selected for a strengthening exercise.
(g) Explain the effect on function (torque production) when a muscle's moment arm is reduced.
(h) Explain the effect on function when a muscle is worked outside the length range at which it generates peak tension.
(i) Explain the effect on power output when velocity or load moves away from the values associated with maximum muscular power.

A patient stands on the test-side extremity in a unilateral stance while the therapist observes from behind. The pelvis is seen to drop toward the unsupported (swinging) limb.
(a) State the diagnosis suggested by this classic sign.
(b) Describe the contributing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) Outline the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A positive Trendelenburg Test, indicating weakness of the gluteus medius muscle during unilateral weight bearing.

(b)
Pathophysiology: the Trendelenburg Test is performed with the therapist positioned behind the patient to observe the pelvis, as the patient assumes a unilateral stance on the test-side extremity; a positive sign is indicated by the pelvis dropping toward the unsupported limb, reflecting the inability of a weak gluteus medius to stabilize the pelvis on the weight-bearing side during single-leg stance; this pattern of pelvic drop and trunk lean toward the stance side is also described as part of the gait presentation in conditions such as Legg-Calvé-Perthes syndrome, where hip abductor function is compromised.

(c)
Management: because impairments involving muscle weakness are addressed through a graded strengthening programme, management follows the general strengthening approach – progressing exercise through the phases of rehabilitation (protecting the tissue and restoring range of motion within restriction, then restoring function of the region, then restoring muscular endurance and strength together with neuromuscular control/balance, and finally returning to full activity), with progression criteria at each phase based on pain level, range of motion compared with the non-involved side, and strength compared with the uninjured side; hip abduction strengthening in particular is supported by positioning the hip in abduction, as this is the position that helps stabilize and optimally place the hip joint.

questions.question:
(a) List the training-program design principles for a muscle strengthening programme.
(b) Describe the exercise-selection principle, including multi-joint versus isolation exercises and the order in which they are performed.
(c) Describe the role of training-equipment availability, exercise volume and periodization.
(d) State the training-frequency categories.
(e) Describe the exercise-order principle.
(f) State the recognised resistance/training-load regimens.
(g) State the criterion (precaution against premature progression) for advancing from Phase I to Phase II of rehabilitation.
(h) State the criterion for advancing from Phase II to Phase III.
(i) State the criterion for advancing from Phase III to Phase IV.
(j) Describe the goals of Phase I, as the basis for how the programme is modified in the acute/immediate situation.
(k) Describe the goals of Phases II to IV, as the basis for how the programme is modified as the patient advances.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The programme principles are exercise selection, availability of training equipment, training frequency, exercise order, rest interval, and resistance/training load.

(b)
Multi-joint exercises involve many muscle groups in one exercise (e.g. squats, deadlifts, bench presses, push jerks) and are typically done first because they are most fatiguing and are recommended most for increasing muscle and bone strength; isolation (supplementary) exercises are primarily single-joint, single-plane exercises (e.g. knee extensions), and progression to multi-joint exercise requires more instruction and time to establish safe, effective coordination; performing large-muscle-mass, multi-joint exercises early in a workout produces significant elevations in anabolic hormones.

(c)
A lack of certain equipment necessitates changes to, or prevents, some exercises; volume is the number of muscles worked, exercises, sets and repetitions performed during a session; periodization is the modulation of volume, intensity and frequency over time to stimulate gains while allowing recovery.

(d)
Training frequency is categorised as low (1 day per week), medium (2 days per week), or high (3 or more days per week).

(e)
Large muscle groups are exercised before small muscles and multiple-joint exercises before single-joint exercises; an adequate warm-up is used, and high-intensity exercises are performed before lower-intensity exercises.

(f)
Named resistance/training-load regimens: the DeLorme regimen, the Oxford regimen, the Daily Adjusted Progressive Resistance Exercise (DAPRE) technique, and the OMNI-RES (Oddvar Holten) method.

(g)
Major criteria for progression from Phase I to Phase II include minimal pain with all Phase I exercises, range of motion equal to about 75% of the non-involved side, and proper muscle firing patterns for the initial exercises.

(h)
Criteria for progression from Phase II to Phase III include range of motion/muscle length/joint play close to full, and strength of the primarily involved musculature about 60% of that on the uninjured side.

(i)
Criteria for progression from Phase III to Phase IV include strength greater than 70-80% of the non-involved side and demonstration of initial agility drills with proper form, such as avoidance of medial collapse of the lower extremities and coordinated, symmetrical movement of all extremities.

(j)
Phase I (Immediate rehabilitation) is characterised by tissue/joint inflammation and pain, disuse, detraining, loss of muscle performance and potential immobilization, so its goals are protection of the involved tissue, restoration of range of motion within restrictions, diminishment of pain and inflammation, and prevention of muscular inhibition.

(k)
Phase II (Intermediate) continues tissue repair with decreased inflammation and improved muscle performance, aiming to continue protecting the involved tissue and restore function of the region; Phase III (Advanced) restores normal joint kinematics, range of motion and continued muscle performance, aiming to restore muscular endurance and strength, cardiovascular endurance, and neuromuscular control/balance/proprioception; Phase IV (Return to function) focuses on activities that return the patient to full function in their preferred activity and prevention of re-injury.

questions.question:
(a) State the basis used for classifying joints, and name the three broad categories.
(b) Describe immovable joints (synarthroses) and their two types, with examples.
(c) Describe slightly movable joints (amphiarthroses) and their two types, with examples.
(d) Describe freely movable joints (diarthroses) and list their six types with an example of each.
(e) State the principle/physiological effect of the classification into uniaxial, biaxial, triaxial and nonaxial joints.
(f) State the physiological function of articular cartilage that relates to this classification.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Physiotherapists classify joints on the basis of motion capabilities, broadly into immovable joints, slightly movable joints, and freely movable joints.

(b)
Immovable joints (synarthroses) can absorb shock but permit little or no motion of the articulating bones; they are of two types – sutures (regularly grooved articulating bone sheets tightly connected by fibres continuous with the periosteum, which ossify in early adulthood; the only human example is the sutures of the skull) and syndesmoses (bones banded together by dense fibrous tissue permitting only extremely limited movement, examples being the coracoacromial joint, the mid-radioulnar joint, the mid-tibiofemoral joint and the inferior tibiofibular ligament).

(c)
Slightly movable joints (amphiarthroses) absorb shock and permit more motion than synarthroidal joints; they are of two types – synchondroses (articulating bones held together by a thin layer of cartilage, examples being the sternocostal joints and epiphyseal plates before ossification) and symphyses (thin plates of hyaline cartilage separating a disc of fibrocartilage from the bone, examples being the vertebral joints and the pubic symphysis).

(d)
Freely movable joints (diarthroses or synovial joints) have articulating bone surfaces covered by articular cartilage, surrounded by an articular capsule with a synovial membrane secreting synovial fluid; the six types are: gliding (plane/arthroidal) joints, permitting only non-axial gliding (example: intercarpal joints); hinge (ginglymus) joints, restricted by strong collateral ligaments to planar hinge-like motion (example: interphalangeal joints); pivot (screw/trochoid) joints, permitting rotation around one axis (example: atlantoaxial joint); condyloid (ovoid/ellipsoidal) joints, permitting flexion, extension, adduction, abduction and circumduction (example: metacarpophalangeal joints); saddle (sellar) joints, permitting movements like condyloid joints but with greater range (example: carpometacarpal joint of the thumb); and ball-and-socket (spheroidal) joints, permitting rotation in three planes (example: hip and shoulder joints).

(e)
Synovial joints are also categorised by the number of axes of rotation as uniaxial, biaxial, triaxial (permitting motion around one, two or three axes respectively) or nonaxial (only limited motion permitted in any direction); joint motion capability can also be described in terms of degrees of freedom, with uniaxial, biaxial and triaxial joints having one, two and three degrees of freedom respectively.

(f)
Articular cartilage, a dense white connective tissue, distributes loads at the joint over a wide area to reduce stress at any contact point, and allows the articulating bones to move with minimal friction and wear, relevant across all freely movable joint types.

(a)
Management of fibromyalgia includes aerobic exercise and resistance exercise as the exercise-based components of the programme.

(b)
Instruction is given in pacing of activities to avoid fluctuations in symptoms.

(c)
Other components include prescription medication, over-the-counter medication, avoidance of stress factors, decreasing alcohol and caffeine consumption, and diet modification.

(d)
Environmental stresses that can provoke a flare include weather changes, especially significant changes in barometric pressure, cold, dampness, fog, rain and fluorescent light.

(e)
Physical stresses that can provoke a flare include repetitive activities such as typing, playing piano and vacuuming, prolonged sitting and/or standing, and working rotating shifts.

(f)
Emotional stresses are among the factors that affect the severity of symptoms, alongside environmental and physical stresses, so avoidance of stress factors generally is part of management.

(g)
• Because symptoms fluctuate, with pain-free days interspersed with days of serious pain, the exercise and activity programme is paced rather than fixed, and adjusted around the presence of a flare.
• Because fibromyalgia is a non-inflammatory, non-degenerative, non-progressive disorder, the modifications made are aimed at managing symptom severity and triggers rather than treating structural disease progression.

(h)
Individuals with fibromyalgia may have a higher incidence of tendinitis, headache, irritable bowel, TMJ dysfunction, restless leg syndrome, mitral valve prolapse, anxiety, depression and memory problems, so the presence of these associated conditions may be a basis for further modification of the overall management plan.

(a) State the principle underlying the dosage/type of exercise used in fibromyalgia management.
(b) State the principle of pacing used in the management programme.
(c) State the other non-exercise components of the management programme.
(d) State the precautions/complications relating to environmental stress factors that can provoke a flare.
(e) State the precautions relating to physical stress factors that can provoke a flare.
(f) State the precautions relating to emotional stress factors.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Lachman's test, designed to detect anterior instability of the knee, indicating a torn anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) when there is excessive forward translation.

(b)
The ACL normally restrains anterior translation of the tibia on the femur; the test is performed with the knee flexed to 15–30° (the functional position of the knee) while the thigh is stabilized, so that the drawer manoeuvre isolates translation at the tibiofemoral joint; excessive forward translation indicates the ACL is torn and no longer restraining this motion. This test is considered more sensitive than the Anterior Drawer Test because it is performed in the knee's functional position.

(c)
Differential: in the related Anterior/Posterior Draw (sign) test, performed with the knee flexed 90°, excessive anterior movement of the tibia under the examiner's thumbs indicates an ACL lesion, whereas excessive posterior movement of the tibia would instead indicate a PCL lesion.

(d)
Clinical reasoning: because the positive sign reflects ligamentous laxity (structural instability) rather than joint hypomobility, treatment reasoning favours strengthening of the surrounding musculature and joint-stability-focused management over aggressive joint mobilization, consistent with the general principle that connective tissues (ligaments, muscles, tendons) determine joint stability, and that weak or lax connective tissue reduces stability while strengthening the muscles crossing the joint increases it – particularly relevant at the knee, a joint noted as not being particularly stable from bone configuration alone.
questions.question:
A patient's knee is examined supine with the knee flexed to 15–30°; the examiner stabilizes the thigh on the table and performs a drawer manoeuvre, noting excessive forward translation of the tibia on the femur.
(a) Identify the test and the structure being examined.
(b) State the affected structures and the mechanism producing the positive sign.
(c) State the differential finding that would instead suggest a posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) lesion.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for the treatment choice, justifying one approach.

questions.answerText:
(a)
When range of motion is decreased due to pain, Grade I and II mobilizations should be performed, in the pain-free range, for 30 seconds or longer, and function should be assessed afterward to determine whether a change has been achieved.

(b)
When range of motion is decreased due to stiffness, Grade I and II mobilizations are likewise performed in the pain-free range for 30 seconds or longer, with function assessed after mobilization to determine whether any change has been achieved.

(c)
The 50/50 rule: if 50% of physiologic active range of motion is not available due to pain, accessory Grades I and II should be used to treat the pain.

(d)
When treating stiffness with Grades III and IV, the therapist performs 60 seconds of an accessory mobilization followed by 60 seconds of a physiologic mobilization and then assesses the effect; this sequence is performed three times.

(e)
During any mobilization treatment, an assessment should be made after each set of oscillations, for either pain or stiffness, to determine the effect of the mobilization.

(f)
Absolute contraindications: malignancy in the area of treatment, infectious arthritis, metabolic bone disease, neoplastic disease, fusion or ankylosis, osteomyelitis, and fracture or ligament rupture.

(g)
Relative contraindications: excessive pain or swelling, arthroplasty, pregnancy, hypermobility, spondylolisthesis, rheumatoid arthritis, and vertebrobasilar insufficiency.

(h)
If pain occurs before resistance is met in the range, techniques to control the pain are used before progressing to more aggressive treatment.

(i)
If pain occurs with resistance, mobilizations may be used with caution; it is customary to treat the pain first and then the stiffness.

(j)
If pain occurs after the resistance, vigorous mobilization may be used to treat the stiffness, followed by techniques for the pain.

(k)
• If pain is being treated and physiologic mobilization Grades I and II cause pain, accessory Grades I and II should be performed instead.
• Accessory mobilizations should be performed in the midrange of joint motion (open-pack position), since this allows for more joint play or motion.
questions.question:
(a) State the principle for choosing a mobilization grade when range of motion is decreased due to pain.
(b) State the principle for choosing a mobilization grade when range of motion is decreased due to stiffness.
(c) State the 50/50 rule.
(d) State the dosage/sequence used when treating stiffness with Grades III and IV.
(e) State the precaution to observe during any mobilization treatment.
(f) State the absolute contraindications (complications to avoid) to joint mobilization.
(g) State the relative contraindications to joint mobilization.
(h) State how the treatment plan is modified when pain occurs before resistance in the range.
(i) State how the treatment plan is modified when pain occurs with resistance in the range.
(j) State how the treatment plan is modified when pain occurs after resistance in the range.
(k) State how the type of mobilization is modified when physiologic Grade I/II causes pain.

A patient is positioned prone for examination. The examiner passively flexes the knee of the test extremity, and the ipsilateral buttock rises off the plinth.
(a) Identify the muscle/test being demonstrated.
(b) State the affected structures and the mechanism producing the positive sign.
(c) State the differential problem and how it is distinguished.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for the treatment choice, justifying one approach.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Ely's Test, a test to determine if a patient has shortening of the rectus femoris muscle.

(b)
The rectus femoris is a two-joint muscle (crossing the hip and knee); because tension in a muscle is constant throughout its length and at its tendinous attachments, a two-joint muscle affects motion at both joints it crosses simultaneously. Passive knee flexion in prone lengthens the rectus femoris over the knee; if the muscle is shortened, it cannot stretch to the extent required for full range of motion at both joints simultaneously (passive insufficiency), so the pelvis/hip is pulled into flexion, producing the ipsilateral buttock rise.

(c)
Differential: the Thomas Test differentiates rectus femoris tightness from iliopsoas tightness – the patient is supine, brings both knees to the chest, and the examiner passively lowers the test limb; if the limb remains up, a hip flexor contracture is suspected, and the examiner then passively extends the knee to place rectus femoris on slack – if the limb then lowers to the table, rectus femoris is shortened, but if the limb remains off the table with the knee flexed, iliopsoas is shortened.

(d)
Clinical reasoning: because rectus femoris is a two-joint muscle subject to passive insufficiency, treatment is reasoned to address its length across both the hip and knee simultaneously (a combined hip-extension/knee-flexion stretch position) rather than addressing either joint in isolation, since stretching across only one joint would not fully lengthen a two-joint muscle that is tight across both.

questions.question:
A patient has restricted shoulder movement, with limited elevation and limited external rotation, thought to be due to capsular restriction of the glenohumeral joint.
(a) State the indications for joint mobilization in this patient.
(b) State the contraindications to be excluded before mobilizing.
(c) State the mobilization technique selected, including grade, direction and position.
(d) State the effects and expected outcome.
(e) State the precautions and when to stop treatment.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Indications: arthritis, rotator cuff tears/sprain and adhesive capsulitis are conditions indicated for mobilization; the primary effects sought are pain reduction, improved range of motion and improved quality of joint movement; distraction is indicated for testing, initial treatment (sustained Grade II), pain control (Grade I or II oscillations) and general mobility (sustained Grade III).

(b)
Contraindications: absolute – malignancy in the area, infectious arthritis, metabolic bone disease, neoplastic disease, fusion or ankylosis, osteomyelitis, fracture or ligament rupture; relative – excessive pain or swelling, arthroplasty, pregnancy, hypermobility, spondylolisthesis, rheumatoid arthritis, vertebrobasilar insufficiency.

(c)
Technique: the concave glenoid fossa receives the convex humeral head; resting position is 55° abduction, 30° horizontal adduction, forearm in the plane of the scapula; the scapula is stabilized with a belt or an assistant. For limited elevation/external rotation, a Glenohumeral Posterior Glide in resting position is used (Grade I distraction with the lateral hand supporting the distal humerus, mobilizing force applied posteriorly with the top hand just distal to the anterior joint margin) to increase flexion and internal rotation, progressing to a Caudal Glide (sustained Grade III) with a hand in the axilla providing Grade I distraction while the other hand glides the humerus inferiorly to increase abduction; where external rotation is restricted, a distraction or elevation progression is used rather than an anterior glide, because of the danger of subluxation when combining anterior glide with external rotation.

(d)
Effects/outcome: mitigation of capsular restriction, breaking of adhesions, distraction of impacted tissue and improved lubrication of articular cartilage; pain reduction and decreased muscle tension through mechanoreceptor stimulation; expected outcome is increased elevation and external rotation with improved joint quality.

(e)
Precautions: do not mobilize in the presence of any absolute contraindication, and proceed cautiously with relative contraindications; Grade I and II oscillations should remain pain-free – stop or reduce the grade if pain occurs; assess pain and stiffness after each set of oscillations to judge whether to continue, and stop if the technique produces more than slight discomfort or is not tolerated.

questions.question:
A patient has restricted elbow range of motion, with limited flexion, following a period of stiffness affecting the elbow and forearm complex.
(a) State the assessment findings expected (restricted joint play/end-feel at the humeroulnar and humeroradial joints).
(b) State the technique used.
(c) Describe the starting position, hand placement and stabilization.
(d) State the dosage and progression.
(e) State the complications and precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Assessment findings: restricted accessory motion (joint play) at the humeroulnar joint, since accessory motions of varus and valgus (radial and ulnar glides) are necessary for full elbow flexion and extension; the elbow and forearm complex consists of four joints – humeroulnar, humeroradial, proximal radioulnar and distal radioulnar.

(b)
Technique: Humeroulnar Distraction and Progression, to increase flexion or extension (Grade III or IV), in addition to testing, initial treatment (sustained Grade II) and pain control (Grade I or II oscillation).

(c)
Starting position/hand placement: supine, with the elbow over the edge of the treatment table or supported with padding just proximal to the olecranon process; the patient's wrist rests against the therapist's shoulder, with the elbow in resting position for initial treatment, or positioned at the end of its available range to stretch into flexion or extension; the fingers of the medial hand are placed over the proximal ulna on the volar surface, reinforced by the other hand (or, at end-range extension, the base of the proximal hand is placed over the proximal ulna with the other hand supporting the distal forearm).

(d)
Dosage/progression: the mobilizing force is applied against the proximal ulna at a 45° angle to the shaft of the bone; progression follows the general Maitland grading principle of moving from Grade I/II (short of resistance, pain-free, 3-4 oscillations per second) toward Grade III/IV (toward end of range, may cause slight discomfort) as tolerated; for the Humeroulnar Distal Glide, distraction is first applied at 45° to the ulna, then, while maintaining distraction, the force is directed distally along the long axis of the ulna in a scooping motion.

(e)
Complications/precautions: absolute contraindications – malignancy in the area, infectious arthritis, metabolic bone disease, neoplastic disease, fusion or ankylosis, osteomyelitis, fracture or ligament rupture; relative contraindications – excessive pain or swelling, arthroplasty, pregnancy, hypermobility, spondylolisthesis, rheumatoid arthritis, vertebrobasilar insufficiency; assess for pain and stiffness after each set of oscillations to determine the effect.

questions.question:
A patient has restricted wrist range of motion, with limited flexion, following a period of stiffness affecting the wrist and hand complex.
(a) State the assessment findings expected (restricted joint play at the radiocarpal joint and carpal rows).
(b) State the technique used.
(c) Describe the starting position, hand placement and stabilization.
(d) State the dosage and progression.
(e) State the complications and precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Assessment findings: restricted accessory joint play at the radiocarpal joint, and at the proximal and distal rows of carpals when mobilized as a group; for full range of motion, individual carpal mobilizations/manipulations may also be necessary.

(b)
Technique: Radiocarpal Distraction, followed as needed by Radiocarpal Joint General Glides and Progression, with the dorsal glide used to increase flexion.

(c)
Starting position/hand placement: sitting, with the forearm supported on the treatment table, wrist over the edge; with the hand closer to the patient, the therapist grasps around the styloid processes and fixates the radius and ulna against the table, while the other hand grasps around the distal row of carpals. For the general glides, the patient sits with the forearm resting on the table, in pronation for the dorsal and volar techniques and in midrange position for the radial and ulnar techniques.

(d)
Dosage/progression: for Radiocarpal Distraction, the mobilizing force is a pull in a distal direction with respect to the arm; for the general glides, progression is made by moving the wrist toward the end of the available range and gliding in the defined direction (dorsal glide to increase flexion, volar glide to increase extension, ulnar glide to increase radial deviation, radial glide to increase ulnar deviation).

(e)
Complications/precautions: absolute contraindications – malignancy in the area, infectious arthritis, metabolic bone disease, neoplastic disease, fusion or ankylosis, osteomyelitis, fracture or ligament rupture; relative contraindications – excessive pain or swelling, arthroplasty, pregnancy, hypermobility, spondylolisthesis, rheumatoid arthritis, vertebrobasilar insufficiency; the radius and ulna must be adequately fixated against the table to avoid unwanted forearm movement during the distraction.

questions.question:
A patient is positioned side-lying with the test limb on top; the hip and knee of the limb closer to the plinth are flexed to stabilize the patient. The uppermost limb is passively positioned into abduction and extension, then allowed to slowly adduct toward the table; the test limb remains off the table.
(a) Identify the test/structure being examined.
(b) State the affected structures and the mechanism producing the positive sign.
(c) State a differential problem drawn from another hip provocative test.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for the treatment choice, justifying one approach.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Ober Test, a test to determine if the patient has tightness of the tensor fasciae latae (TFL) or the iliotibial band (ITB).

(b)
The uppermost limb is passively abducted and extended so the ITB passes over the greater trochanter; the pelvis is stabilized by the examiner to prevent substitution, and the test limb is allowed to adduct toward the table. If the TFL/ITB is tight, it does not permit the limb to lower fully, so the test limb remains off the table (a positive test); a greater stretch is felt with the knee in extension than in flexion.

(c)
Differential: the Piriformis Test differentiates tightness producing buttock/referred pain along the sciatic nerve distribution – the patient is side-lying, and the test limb is taken into flexion, adduction and internal rotation; a positive test reproduces gluteal pain or radicular symptoms, distinguishing piriformis tightness from an isolated TFL/ITB tightness found on Ober's Test.

(d)
Clinical reasoning: because the positive sign is produced specifically by the ITB/TFL being unable to lengthen as the limb adducts (with the pelvis stabilized to prevent substitution), treatment is reasoned to target stretching/lengthening of the TFL-ITB complex in the same abducted, extended limb position used in the test, rather than general hip mobilization, since the limitation is soft-tissue (muscle/band) tightness rather than joint hypomobility.

courses.title: Pharmacotherapeutics

questions.explanation: SSRIs like fluoxetine require several weeks of consistent dosing before full therapeutic antidepressant effect is achieved, typically 4 to 6 weeks, because downstream neuroadaptive changes in receptor sensitivity, rather than the immediate increase in synaptic serotonin, are thought to underlie the clinical antidepressant response.
questions.question: A patient starting fluoxetine for major depressive disorder asks how soon she can expect symptom improvement. What is the most accurate counseling point?
options: Full benefit typically occurs within 24-48 hours
Full benefit typically occurs within 3-5 days
No improvement should be expected before 6 months
Symptoms should worsen for the first month
Full therapeutic benefit typically takes 4-6 weeks
Combined estrogen/progestin therapy to prevent endometrial cancer
Phytoestrogen-based therapy for natural hormone replacement
Progestogen-only therapy to manage vasomotor symptoms
Estrogen therapy alone (low dose) without progestogen
Testosterone replacement to counteract adrenal androgen decline
questions.explanation: A low dose of estrogen alone (estrogen therapy without progestogen) is often suggested for women who have had a hysterectomy because they no longer have a uterus and therefore do not need endometrial protection. Without a uterus, there is no risk of endometrial hyperplasia or cancer from unopposed estrogen. Combined estrogen-progestogen therapy is reserved for women with an intact uterus to protect the endometrium from the proliferative effects of unopposed estrogen.
questions.question: HRT is available in many forms. Which formulation is specifically indicated for women who have had a hysterectomy without needing combined hormone therapy?
A woman experiencing hot flashes declines hormone therapy due to a personal history of breast cancer. Which non-hormonal agent is most appropriate for her vasomotor symptoms?
options: Conjugated equine estrogen at low dose
questions.explanation: Venlafaxine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, is an effective non-hormonal option for managing vasomotor symptoms in women for whom estrogen therapy is contraindicated, such as those with a history of hormone-sensitive breast cancer. It works centrally to stabilize thermoregulatory control in the hypothalamus.

options: Major depressive disorder with seasonal pattern
questions.question: A 34-year-old married woman seeks help for symptoms that worsen one week before menses and completely resolve by day 4 of her cycle. She has experienced this pattern for 8 months. The most accurate diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: PMS is defined as a cyclic disorder composed of physical and emotional changes occurring during the luteal phase, improving significantly or disappearing within the first several days of menstrual flow, and absent during the first week following menses. This woman's pattern-worsening premenstrually and resolving by day 4-fits PMS criteria. Importantly, lack of a symptom-free interval would suggest a psychiatric disorder or perimenopause rather than PMS.

options: Panic disorder and social anxiety disorder
questions.question: Schizoaffective disorder presents with symptoms of both schizophrenia and a mood disorder. The two mood disorders most commonly seen in schizoaffective disorder are:
questions.explanation: Schizoaffective disorder presents with symptoms of both schizophrenia (psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions) and a mood disorder-specifically depression or bipolar disorder. This combination of psychotic and affective features distinguishes schizoaffective disorder from pure schizophrenia (predominantly psychotic) and pure mood disorders (primarily affective). Treatment typically combines antipsychotic agents (for psychotic features) with mood stabilizers or antidepressants (for affective features), guided by the predominant mood component.

questions.question: A preterm infant on prolonged parenteral nutrition develops metabolic bone disease with fractures. Which two minerals are most critical to supplement adequately to prevent this?
questions.explanation: Preterm infants have high in-utero calcium and phosphate accretion rates during the third trimester that parenteral nutrition often fails to replicate, and inadequate supplementation of these minerals leads to metabolic bone disease of prematurity, presenting with poor mineralization, rickets-like changes, and pathological fractures.

Lithium is eliminated almost entirely unchanged by the kidneys, and renal impairment significantly increases the risk of toxicity due to reduced clearance; baseline and periodic renal function monitoring is therefore essential before and throughout lithium therapy, alongside thyroid monitoring for its separate long-term effects.
questions.question: A patient with bipolar I disorder is started on lithium for mood stabilization. Which baseline laboratory test is essential before initiation due to lithium's primary route of elimination?

questions.explanation: The Quick Start method requires a confirmed negative urine pregnancy test before the patient takes the first OC pill on the day of her office visit. A backup method of contraception should be used for at least 7 days since contraceptive protection is not immediate. Despite requiring a backup method, the Quick Start approach encourages immediate contraception initiation and is associated with higher continuation rates through the third cycle, improving overall contraceptive effectiveness.
questions.question: The Quick Start method for initiating oral contraceptives requires negative confirmation of which test before the patient takes the first pill on the day of the office visit?
A patient with drug-resistant focal epilepsy has failed three appropriately chosen antiepileptic drugs at adequate doses. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: Epilepsy is considered drug-resistant after failure of two or three appropriately chosen and adequately dosed antiepileptic drugs, and at this point, evaluation for epilepsy surgery or other non-pharmacological options such as vagus nerve stimulation should be pursued, since continued drug trials have progressively lower chances of achieving seizure freedom.
options: Continue trialing additional antiepileptic monotherapies indefinitely
Referral for evaluation of epilepsy surgery candidacy
Increase all current medications to toxic doses

questions.explanation: Quetiapine has low D2 receptor affinity and is less likely to worsen parkinsonian motor symptoms compared to typical antipsychotics or higher-potency atypical agents like risperidone, making it a preferred choice, alongside clozapine, when antipsychotic treatment is required in Parkinson's disease-related psychosis.
questions.question: If antipsychotic therapy becomes necessary for psychosis in a patient with Parkinson's disease, which agent is preferred due to minimal dopamine receptor blockade?

options: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine metabolism, requiring a slower titration
Valproate has no effect on lamotrigine dosing
Lamotrigine requires a faster titration schedule
questions.explanation: Valproate inhibits hepatic glucuronidation of lamotrigine, significantly increasing lamotrigine serum levels and the risk of severe skin reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome; when combined, lamotrigine must be titrated much more slowly and at a lower target dose than when used alone or with enzyme-inducing antiepileptics.
questions.question: A patient with epilepsy well-controlled on sodium valproate is started on lamotrigine as an adjunct for better seizure control. What pharmacokinetic interaction must be anticipated?
A patient with chronic kidney disease develops hyperphosphatemia despite dietary phosphate restriction. Which class of medication is used to further reduce phosphate absorption from the diet?
questions.explanation: Phosphate binders such as calcium carbonate, sevelamer, or lanthanum carbonate are taken with meals to bind dietary phosphate in the gut lumen, preventing its absorption and helping control hyperphosphatemia in chronic kidney disease patients who cannot achieve adequate control through dietary restriction alone.
options: Calcium channel blockers taken with meals
Vitamin D analogues taken between meals
Nutrition-focused medication management and drug-nutrient interaction identification
Ordering complete nutritional support without physician involvement
Performing anthropometric measurements and body composition analysis
Providing intravenous total parenteral nutrition independently
Conducting dietary recalls and meal planning exclusively
