questions.explanation: Proton pump inhibitors provide the most effective and reliable acid suppression for both healing established NSAID-induced peptic ulcers and preventing future ulceration with continued NSAID use, outperforming H2 receptor antagonists and other agents in comparative studies, making them the preferred co-therapy for patients requiring ongoing NSAID treatment.

questions.question: A patient with treatment-resistant depression is being considered for electroconvulsive therapy. What is the most appropriate indication prioritizing this treatment over further medication trials?
questions.explanation: Electroconvulsive therapy is particularly indicated for severe depression with psychotic features, catatonia, or acute suicidal risk requiring rapid response, situations where the slower onset of pharmacotherapy poses too great a risk, making ECT a first-line rather than last-resort option in these specific high-acuity presentations.
options: Severe depression with psychotic features or acute suicidality
Mild depression with good medication response so far
Preference for avoiding all medication side effects
Recently diagnosed depression with no prior treatment
Chronic mild dysthymia without acute risk features

questions.explanation: Women who recently have undergone menopause have a higher risk of excessive, unpredictable bleeding while receiving continuous-combined HRT; thus, this regimen is best reserved for women who are at least 2 years postmenopause. Initially, continuous-combined therapy causes unpredictable spotting or bleeding, which usually resolves within 6 to 12 months. Decreasing the estrogen dose or increasing the progestogen dose may also decrease or stop the spotting. Despite the initial bleeding issue, continuous-combined HRT is ultimately more acceptable than traditional cyclic therapy because it avoids monthly withdrawal bleeding.
questions.question: Continuous-combined estrogen-progestogen HRT is best reserved for women who are at least how many years postmenopause to reduce risk of excessive, unpredictable bleeding?

questions.explanation: PMDD has an estimated incidence of 3 to 8% among menstruating women, while clinically relevant PMS occurs in about 15 to 20% of the approximately 95% of women who experience some premenstrual changes. PMDD therefore represents a smaller but more clinically significant subset requiring more aggressive therapeutic intervention. The high prevalence of mild premenstrual symptoms versus the much smaller proportion with true PMDD is an important clinical distinction.
questions.question: The estimated incidence of PMDD among menstruating women is:
During Phase 3 (follow-up and recurrence prevention) of PEM management, follow-up visits typically begin within the first week after discharge and continue monthly for at least:
questions.explanation: In Phase 3, follow-up visits typically begin within the first week after discharge and continue monthly for at least six months. During these visits, the child's weight, height, appetite, developmental milestones, and general health status are assessed. Growth monitoring allows early detection of nutritional faltering and timely intervention. This extended follow-up period is critical for preventing relapse, as the social determinants of malnutrition (poverty, food insecurity, poor feeding practices) persist after discharge.

options: Spironolactone directly reduces portal hypertension pressure
Spironolactone improves hepatic synthetic protein function
Spironolactone counteracts secondary hyperaldosteronism in cirrhosis
Spironolactone reduces ammonia production in the gut
Spironolactone increases serum albumin production directly
questions.question: A patient with chronic liver disease and ascites is placed on a sodium-restricted diet. What is the primary pharmacological rationale for combining this with spironolactone?
questions.explanation: Cirrhosis with ascites is characterized by secondary hyperaldosteronism due to reduced effective circulating volume sensed by the kidneys; spironolactone, an aldosterone antagonist, counteracts this sodium and water retention, making it the preferred first-line diuretic in cirrhotic ascites, often combined with dietary sodium restriction.

questions.question: Vaginal spermicides prevent sperm from entering the cervical os by attacking sperm flagella and body, reducing mobility. The actual spermicidal agent in most products is a surfactant. Commonly used spermicidal agents include:
questions.explanation: Vaginal spermicides consist of a base combined with either nonoxynol-9 or octoxynol as the spermicidal agents. These surfactants destroy the sperm cell membrane, attacking sperm flagella and body to reduce mobility and disrupt fructolytic activity (inhibiting nourishment of sperm). Spermicides are inserted into the vagina before each coital act. They are generally used in combination with barrier methods (diaphragm, condom) rather than as sole contraceptive agents, as their standalone efficacy is relatively lower.

Normal menstrual blood loss ranges from 20 to 60 mL per cycle, with an average of 30 to 50 mL. A loss exceeding 80 mL per cycle is considered abnormal (menorrhagia) and is clinically associated with iron-deficiency anemia. This threshold is important in distinguishing normal from pathological menstrual bleeding and guiding therapeutic decisions.
questions.question: The average normal menstrual cycle lasts 28 days, and blood loss is considered abnormal when it exceeds which threshold per cycle?

questions.explanation: Estrogen therapy reduces bone turnover and increases bone density in postmenopausal women of all ages. However, the protective effect on bone persists only as long as treatment is maintained-with cessation of therapy, postmenopausal bone loss resumes at the same rate as in untreated women. This highlights the long-term nature of bone protection from HRT and the need to consider alternative therapies (bisphosphonates, SERMs) that have more durable effects on bone after discontinuation.
questions.question: HRT with estrogen has been shown to increase bone density in postmenopausal women of all ages. However, the protective effect on bone is only maintained under which condition?
options: In women who receive concurrent calcium supplementation
In women who also perform weight-bearing exercise regularly
When using transdermal rather than oral estrogen
Only for the first 5 years of menopause
As long as the HRT treatment is maintained

questions.question: In young infants, the most common cause of seizures is:
questions.explanation: In young infants, the most common causes of seizures are hypoxia or birth asphyxia (hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy), intracranial trauma during birth, metabolic disturbances (hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, hyponatremia), congenital malformations of the brain, and infections. These neonatal and early infantile seizures differ significantly from epilepsy in older children and adults in etiology, clinical presentation, and management. Identifying and treating the underlying cause is paramount in infant seizure management.
options: Febrile convulsion from any infectious cause
Idiopathic generalized epilepsy with genetic basis
Drug withdrawal from maternal opioid use
Brain tumors in the posterior fossa
Hypoxia or birth asphyxia, intracranial trauma, metabolic disturbances, and congenital malformations

questions.question: Levodopa is the gold standard treatment for Parkinson's disease despite its limitation of extracerebral (peripheral) metabolism. Why is levodopa combined with a dopa decarboxylase inhibitor?
questions.explanation: Levodopa is combined with a dopa decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa in Sinemet, benserazide in Madopar) that does NOT cross the blood-brain barrier. The inhibitor prevents peripheral (extracerebral) conversion of levodopa to dopamine by dopa decarboxylase in the gut, liver, and other tissues. This results in much higher plasma concentrations of levodopa available to cross the BBB, a prolonged plasma half-life, and significantly reduced peripheral dopaminergic side effects (nausea, vomiting, cardiovascular effects). Consequently, the required levodopa dose is dramatically reduced.
options: To enhance levodopa's ability to cross the blood-brain barrier
To prevent peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine, increasing CNS availability and reducing required dose
To slow the renal elimination of levodopa and extend its plasma half-life
To block dopamine receptors in the gut preventing nausea
To activate levodopa from an inactive prodrug form
Adult men over 50 years of age
Women of reproductive age and infants
Elderly men with chronic kidney disease
questions.question: Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide. The risk group at highest risk for iron-deficiency anemia includes:
questions.explanation: Women of reproductive age (due to menstrual blood loss) and infants (due to rapid growth outpacing iron stores and, in older infants, consumption of low-iron formula or complementary foods) are at highest risk for iron-deficiency anemia. Iron is essential for hemoglobin synthesis; deficiency causes microcytic hypochromic anemia with fatigue, pallor, reduced exercise tolerance, and impaired cognitive function. Prevention strategies include iron supplementation in pregnant women, fortification of infant foods, and screening of high-risk populations.

In one study, 59% to 81% of women who stopped oral contraceptives did so because of side effects. This high rate of discontinuation due to adverse effects underscores the critical importance of patient education and early reassessment (within 3 to 6 months) to identify and manage adverse effects, improve compliance, and prevent unintentional pregnancies. Many early side effects (nausea, bloating, breakthrough bleeding) improve spontaneously by the third cycle as the body adjusts to hormonal changes.
questions.question: Most women who stopped oral contraceptives in one study did so because of side effects, with what percentage citing adverse effects as the reason for discontinuation?

A patient with Crohn's disease is at risk for multiple vitamin and mineral deficiencies due to malabsorption. Which fat-soluble vitamin is specifically absorbed in the terminal ileum that is commonly affected in Crohn's disease?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) absorption occurs specifically in the terminal ileum through the intrinsic factor-cobalamin receptor (cubilin). Crohn's disease commonly affects the terminal ileum, causing inflammation and malabsorption that specifically impairs B12 absorption. This is distinct from the dietary B12 deficiency seen in vegans-it is a malabsorption-related deficiency. Patients with terminal ileal Crohn's disease or those who have had ileal resection require parenteral (intramuscular) B12 supplementation since oral B12 cannot be absorbed through the damaged or absent terminal ileum.

Vitamin E (tocopherol) deficiency in premature infants causes hemolytic anemia because Vitamin E serves as a critical antioxidant protecting red blood cell membranes from oxidative damage. Premature infants have low Vitamin E stores at birth and are particularly vulnerable to hemolytic anemia from Vitamin E deficiency. Adults with fat malabsorption syndromes are also at risk and may develop neurological symptoms (peripheral neuropathy, ataxia) from Vitamin E deficiency. The fat-soluble nature of Vitamin E means deficiency is particularly associated with fat malabsorption conditions.
questions.question: Hemolytic anemia in premature infants is a specific manifestation of deficiency of which fat-soluble vitamin?
During perimenopause, high concentrations of FSH should NOT be used alone to diagnose menopause because:
questions.explanation: During perimenopause, FSH concentrations may rise to the postmenopausal range during some cycles but return to premenopausal levels during subsequent cycles. This cycle-to-cycle variability means that a single high FSH measurement is not reliable for diagnosing menopause in perimenopausal women. The diagnosis of menopause requires 12 consecutive months of amenorrhea (determined retrospectively). Despite this diagnostic limitation, vasomotor symptoms in perimenopausal women may still require treatment even when FSH levels are not consistently in the menopausal range.
options: FSH may rise to postmenopausal range in some cycles but return to premenopausal levels in subsequent cycles
FSH assays are inaccurate in the perimenopausal range
FSH is produced by the ovary rather than the pituitary in perimenopause
LH is a more reliable marker than FSH for menopausal diagnosis
High FSH only occurs after 5 or more years of perimenopausal transition

questions.explanation: Simple partial seizures can progress to complex partial seizures when unconsciousness (altered consciousness) is involved. In simple partial seizures, the patient remains fully conscious and the clinical manifestation depends on the area of discharge (e.g., jerking of a limb, abnormal sensations). The addition of impaired consciousness converts the seizure classification to complex partial. Complex partial seizures can further progress to secondarily generalized seizures through spread of the ictal discharge to involve both hemispheres.
options: When jerking movements spread from one limb to both sides
When the EEG shows bilateral spike-wave discharges
When post-ictal confusion lasts more than 30 minutes
When autonomic features like sweating and palpitations appear
questions.question: Simple partial seizures can progress to complex partial seizures when which additional feature develops?

options: Glycogen -> muscle protein -> adipose tissue fat
Adipose tissue fat -> glycogen -> muscle protein
Glycogen -> adipose tissue fat -> muscle protein
Muscle protein -> adipose tissue fat -> glycogen
All stores are mobilized simultaneously from the onset
questions.question: In marasmus, the body draws on its own stores in response to insufficient energy intake. The correct sequence of fuel mobilization is:
questions.explanation: In starvation (marasmus), the body mobilizes fuels in a sequential, prioritized manner: first glycogen stores (hepatic and muscle, lasting about 24 hours), then adipose tissue fat (the primary fuel source during prolonged starvation, resulting in the emaciation seen in marasmus), and finally muscle protein when fat stores are depleted. The body preferentially preserves vital proteins (visceral and immune proteins) by breaking down muscle first. This is why advanced marasmus shows profound muscle wasting along with complete loss of subcutaneous and visceral fat.

Caloric restriction to 60-80% during Phase 1 is specifically to avoid refeeding syndrome-a potentially fatal clinical syndrome caused by sudden carbohydrate reintroduction after prolonged starvation. When glucose becomes suddenly available, it inhibits gluconeogenesis and triggers an insulin surge, causing rapid intracellular influx of potassium, magnesium, and phosphate, resulting in dangerously low serum levels. This leads to poor myocardial contractility, manifesting as excessive sweating, muscle weakness, tachycardia, and heart failure.
questions.question: During Phase 1 (resuscitation and stabilization) of PEM treatment, feeding is instituted carefully with caloric restriction to 60-80% of caloric requirements for age. The primary purpose of this restriction is to:
options: Prevent excessive weight gain during refeeding
Reduce the metabolic load on a damaged liver
Prevent overstimulation of malnourished digestive enzymes
Avoid refeeding syndrome from rapid carbohydrate introduction
Minimize costs of therapeutic nutrition formulas

questions.question: Iodine deficiency is particularly problematic in populations living in:
options: Iodine-deficient soils, commonly inland or mountainous regions
Coastal regions with access to seafood
Urban areas with poor sanitation and water treatment
Equatorial regions with high sunlight and vitamin D adequacy
Regions consuming excessive amounts of brassica vegetables
questions.explanation: Iodine deficiency is most prevalent in populations living in iodine-deficient soils, which are commonly found in inland, mountainous, and flood-prone regions where iodine has been leached from the soil. Coastal populations generally have adequate iodine intake through seafood and iodine-rich water. Universal salt iodization (adding potassium iodate to table salt) has been the primary public health intervention to address iodine deficiency globally, dramatically reducing the prevalence of goiter and cretinism in affected regions.

questions.question: Typical antipsychotics (FGAs) have high D2 antagonism. Their primary therapeutic effects are thought to be due to D2 antagonism at the:
questions.explanation: The primary therapeutic effects of first-generation antipsychotics (FGAs) are thought to be due to D2 antagonism at the limbic system (mesolimbic pathway), which controls behavior and emotion and is hypothesized to be overactive in schizophrenia (explaining positive symptoms). In contrast, extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS)-the major adverse effects of FGAs-are thought to be related to dopamine antagonism in the dorsal striatum (nigrostriatal pathway), which controls movement. This anatomical distinction explains why all effective antipsychotics carry some EPS risk.
options: Limbic system, which controls behavior and emotion

questions.explanation: First-line pharmacological treatments for OCD include paroxetine, fluoxetine, sertraline, fluvoxamine CR, and fluvoxamine. Second-line OCD treatments include clomipramine (a TCA with potent serotonin reuptake inhibition), venlafaxine, citalopram, and escitalopram. Venlafaxine XR is a first-line treatment for GAD but only a second-line option for OCD. The cornerstone of OCD pharmacotherapy is serotonergic agents, reflecting the serotonin hypothesis of OCD pathogenesis.
questions.question: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) first-line pharmacological treatments include all of the following EXCEPT:

options: During the hepatic first-pass metabolism of levodopa
During renal tubular secretion of levodopa
During intestinal absorption from the small intestine after gastric transit
During CNS uptake through the blood-brain barrier
During peripheral conversion to dopamine by dopa decarboxylase
questions.question: Levodopa's plasma concentration typically peaks between 1 and 2 hours after oral dose. Gastric emptying rate and gastric pH significantly affect this. When does absorption depend on these factors most critically?
questions.explanation: Levodopa is rapidly absorbed from the small intestine, but its absorption depends on the rate of gastric emptying (which determines how quickly levodopa reaches the absorptive site in the small intestine) and the pH of the gastric content (affecting solubility and stability). Delayed gastric emptying reduces peak plasma concentrations and delays clinical effect. This explains why levodopa should ideally be taken on an empty stomach, and why high-protein meals can reduce absorption (large neutral amino acids compete with levodopa for intestinal and BBB transport proteins).

options: Increased estrogen receptor sensitivity in the uterus
Increased aromatase activity converting androgens to estrogens
Endometrial proliferation leading to excess menstrual blood loss
Upregulation of LH receptors causing corpus luteum dysfunction
Vasoconstriction and uterine contractions independently of prostaglandins
questions.question: Leukotrienes contribute to dysmenorrhea primarily in women who do NOT respond to NSAID therapy because leukotrienes cause:
questions.explanation: Leukotrienes are inflammatory mediators that cause vasoconstriction and uterine contractions through pathways independent of prostaglandins. Women who do not respond to NSAIDs (which inhibit prostaglandin synthesis) may have elevated leukotriene levels as an alternative mediator of dysmenorrhea. Leukotrienes also increase the sensitivity of uterine pain fibers, further amplifying pain perception independently of the prostaglandin pathway.

Women with conditions including blood clots, cancer (such as breast, uterine, or endometrial), heart or liver disease, known or suspected pregnancy, and stroke should avoid HRT. These represent absolute contraindications because HRT (particularly the estrogen component) can exacerbate thrombotic disease, promote hormone-sensitive cancers, impair liver metabolism of hormones, and cause harm in established cardiovascular disease. Risk-benefit analysis must be individualized, considering personal and family medical history.
options: Known blood clots, breast cancer, or current stroke
questions.question: HRT is absolutely contraindicated in women with which of the following conditions?

questions.explanation: The triad of pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, and decreased consciousness is classic for opioid toxicity, and naloxone, a competitive opioid receptor antagonist, rapidly reverses these effects and is the specific antidote of choice, though its shorter half-life compared to many opioids means repeat dosing or infusion may be needed.
questions.question: A first responder needs to identify a medication overdose causing pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, and decreased consciousness. Which reversal agent should be administered?

questions.explanation: Rifampin is a potent inducer of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, including those responsible for warfarin metabolism, which accelerates warfarin clearance and reduces its anticoagulant effect; an increased warfarin dose is typically needed to maintain therapeutic INR while rifampin is co-administered, with careful monitoring during and after its discontinuation.
questions.question: A patient on a stable warfarin dose starts taking rifampin for tuberculosis treatment. What change in warfarin dosing should be anticipated?
options: A decreased warfarin dose will likely be needed
No dose adjustment will be needed at all
INR monitoring becomes unnecessary during rifampin use
An increased warfarin dose will likely be needed

questions.question: The formal thought disorder in schizophrenia in which a patient goes off on a tangent never to return to the original thought is called:
questions.explanation: Tangential thinking is the formal thought disorder in which the patient's thinking goes off on a tangent and never returns to the original thought. Circumstantial thinking involves talking in general terms around an idea but never directly addressing the topic. Derailment involves jumping from one idea to another without any connection. Loose associations (also called 'knight's move thinking') involve illogical connections between unrelated ideas. These thought disorders represent the clinical manifestations of disorganized thinking in schizophrenia, reflecting underlying dysfunction in prefrontal executive processing.

questions.question: Chronic excessive alcohol consumption causes deficiencies of multiple nutrients. Which mechanism specifically explains how alcohol causes vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency?
options: Alcohol directly destroys thiamine by oxidation in the stomach
Alcohol increases renal thiamine excretion through osmotic diuresis
Alcohol activates thiaminase enzymes that degrade thiamine in the blood
Alcohol displaces nutritious foods, impairs intestinal thiamine absorption, and reduces hepatic thiamine storage
Alcohol blocks thiamine incorporation into its active phosphate form
questions.explanation: Chronic excessive alcohol consumption causes thiamine deficiency through multiple mechanisms: alcohol displaces nutritious foods from the diet (calories from alcohol replace food-derived nutrients), impairs intestinal absorption of thiamine (alcohol damages intestinal mucosa and transport mechanisms), and reduces hepatic storage of thiamine (liver damage impairs thiamine phosphorylation and storage). This combination of inadequate intake, impaired absorption, and reduced storage makes alcoholics highly susceptible to thiamine deficiency and its neurological consequences (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome).

questions.question: Brain tumors are the cause of epilepsy in about one third of patients in which age range?
questions.explanation: Brain tumors are the cause of epilepsy in about one third of patients between the ages of 30 and 50 years. This is an important age-related etiology to consider when evaluating new-onset epilepsy in this age group, as newly presenting seizures in a middle-aged adult mandate neuroimaging to exclude an underlying neoplasm. Cerebrovascular disease is the most common cause of epilepsy in patients above 50 years of age, while idiopathic and cryptogenic epilepsy with trauma predominate in young adults.

questions.question: A patient on citalopram at a moderate dose is switched to tramadol for pain management and subsequently develops agitation, hyperthermia, and clonus. What condition does this presentation suggest?
questions.explanation: Combining an SSRI like citalopram with tramadol, which also has serotonergic activity, increases the risk of serotonin syndrome, characterized by the triad of altered mental status, autonomic instability with hyperthermia, and neuromuscular abnormalities including clonus and hyperreflexia, requiring prompt discontinuation of both agents and supportive care.

questions.question: Folic acid deficiency during early pregnancy is the primary preventable cause of which congenital abnormality?
options: Chromosomal abnormalities such as Down syndrome
Renal agenesis and urinary tract malformations
questions.explanation: Folic acid deficiency during early pregnancy (particularly in the first 4 weeks post-conception, often before pregnancy is confirmed) is the primary preventable cause of neural tube defects, including spina bifida (incomplete closure of the spinal column) and anencephaly (absence of major brain structures). Folate is essential for DNA/RNA synthesis and rapid cell division during neural tube formation. All women of childbearing age are recommended to take 400-800 mcg of folic acid daily, and higher doses for women with previous NTD-affected pregnancies.

Kwashiorkor occurs when there is adequate caloric intake but insufficient protein, commonly seen in regions where staple foods are high in carbohydrates but low in protein (e.g., cassava, yams, sweet potatoes, green bananas). Kwashiorkor is characterized by pitting edema (from hypoalbuminemia), moon face, sparse brittle hair, skin dermatosis ("flaky paint"), and hepatomegaly from fatty liver. This contrasts with marasmus, which features severe wasting, absent subcutaneous fat, and an "old-man" appearance without edema.
questions.question: A 2-year-old child in rural Africa presents with pitting edema of the legs, sparse and discolored hair, and skin dermatosis. His diet consists mainly of cassava and yams. The most likely diagnosis is:

options: After 6 months when symptoms typically resolve
After 1 year of continuous symptom control
Never, as symptoms recur immediately upon cessation
After 5 years as per WHI recommendations
questions.explanation: Hormone therapy for menopausal symptoms can generally be stopped about 2 to 3 years after starting, as the prevalence of hot flushes is highest in the first 2 postmenopausal years and tends to decrease over time. HRT should be used for the shortest time possible at the lowest effective dose. Evidence suggests that serious health risks such as blood clots, breast cancer, and stroke increase after five years of use, reinforcing the importance of reassessing the continued need for HRT at regular intervals.
questions.question: Hormone therapy for menopausal symptoms (hot flushes and vasomotor symptoms) can generally be stopped about how long after starting?

A schizophrenic patient in Stage III of the illness shows symptoms indistinguishable from florid psychosis, including features similar to organic psychosis. During which earlier stage were the defining characteristics of grandiosity and euphoria most prominent?
options: Stage II (acute mania with irritability and anger)
Residual phase after acute episode resolution
Prodromal phase before first acute episode
questions.explanation: This question refers to the three stages of the acute course of a manic episode in bipolar disorder (as described in the curriculum), not schizophrenia stages. Stage I corresponds to hypomania where euphoria and grandiosity predominate, with patients appearing happy, hyperactive, and impulsive but not psychotic. Stage II (acute mania) shows irritability, anger, flight of ideas, and fixed false beliefs (delusions). Stage III is indistinguishable from florid psychosis or organic psychosis. The rate of progression through these stages can be rapid but the sequence is usually consistent.

questions.question: A patient is started on a loading dose of a medication before beginning maintenance dosing. What is the primary pharmacokinetic rationale for using a loading dose?
options: To permanently reduce the drug's elimination half-life
To reduce the total maintenance dose required later
To eliminate the need for any further dosing
To achieve therapeutic plasma concentration rapidly
To reduce first-pass metabolism of the drug
questions.explanation: A loading dose is calculated to rapidly achieve a therapeutic plasma concentration without waiting for the drug to accumulate gradually through repeated maintenance dosing, which would otherwise take approximately four to five half-lives to reach steady state, making loading doses particularly important for drugs with long half-lives in urgent clinical situations.

options: Traumatic experience, stress, or drug/alcohol misuse
Brain tumor compressing the temporal lobe
Genetic mutations in dopamine receptor genes
questions.explanation: Psychosis can be caused by purely social factors without a biological component. Specifically, psychosis can be triggered by a traumatic experience, stress, drug misuse, alcohol misuse, side effects of prescribed medications, or a physical condition such as a brain tumor. The curriculum emphasizes that the cause of psychosis is generally unknown, with the interaction of biological and psychosocial factors contributing to development. This biopsychosocial model of psychosis etiology guides comprehensive treatment that addresses both biological (pharmacological) and psychosocial aspects.
questions.question: Psychosocial factors alone (without biological components) can cause psychosis. Which social trigger is specifically identified as a non-biological cause of psychosis?

options: Gradual tapering may be considered after a prolonged seizure-free period
Antiepileptic drugs should never be discontinued once started
Sudden discontinuation is preferred over gradual tapering
Withdrawal should be attempted within the first six months
Withdrawal decisions depend only on the patient's age
questions.explanation: After a substantial seizure-free period, typically two years or more, and with a low-risk epilepsy syndrome and normal EEG, gradual tapering of antiepileptic therapy may be considered under close medical supervision, since abrupt discontinuation carries a significant risk of rebound seizures, including status epilepticus.
questions.question: A patient with epilepsy well controlled for three years wants to know the general principle guiding when antiepileptic drug withdrawal might be considered. What is the most appropriate answer?

questions.explanation: SSRIs, particularly sertraline and paroxetine, are FDA-approved and considered first-line pharmacotherapy for PTSD, helping to reduce intrusive symptoms, hyperarousal, and avoidance behaviors, whereas benzodiazepines are generally avoided due to lack of efficacy for core PTSD symptoms and risk of dependence in this population.
questions.question: A patient with post-traumatic stress disorder is being started on pharmacotherapy. Which class of medication is considered first-line for this condition?

questions.explanation: When status epilepticus fails to respond to adequate benzodiazepine dosing, guidelines recommend proceeding to a second-line intravenous antiepileptic loading dose such as fosphenytoin, valproate, or levetiracetam, rather than repeating benzodiazepines further, which increases the risk of respiratory depression without added seizure control benefit.
options: Repeat a third dose of lorazepam immediately
Switch immediately to oral phenytoin therapy
Intravenous loading dose of a second-line agent such as fosphenytoin
Administer intramuscular diazepam as the next step
Wait and observe before further intervention
questions.question: A patient in status epilepticus does not respond adequately to two doses of intravenous lorazepam. What is the most appropriate next pharmacologic step?

options: Take it with milk to reduce gastric irritation
Take it with tea to improve palatability
Take it together with a calcium supplement
Take it with a high-fiber meal for tolerance
Take it with a source of vitamin C on an empty stomach
questions.question: A patient with iron-deficiency anemia is prescribed oral ferrous sulfate and asks how to maximize absorption. What is the most appropriate advice?
questions.explanation: Vitamin C enhances non-heme iron absorption by reducing ferric iron to the more absorbable ferrous form and forming a soluble complex, while calcium, tea (tannins), and high-fiber foods with phytates all inhibit iron absorption, so iron is best taken on an empty stomach with a vitamin C source when tolerated.

questions.question: A 2-year-old child from a food-insecure household presents with generalized edema, a distended abdomen, and reddish, thinning hair, but preserved subcutaneous fat. Which nutritional deficiency state does this describe?
questions.explanation: Kwashiorkor results from severe protein deficiency in the presence of adequate or near-adequate caloric intake, producing hypoalbuminemia that drives edema, along with characteristic hair depigmentation and a fatty liver causing abdominal distension. Marasmus, in contrast, results from total caloric deficiency and presents with severe wasting rather than edema.
options: Iron deficiency anemia in early childhood

questions.explanation: An abdominal heat patch provides analgesic effects that add to the relief provided by ibuprofen, demonstrating synergy between non-pharmacologic and pharmacologic approaches. The heat patch also has a faster onset of analgesic effect than drug therapy alone. Non-drug therapy, including heat, may be particularly beneficial for the estimated 15% of women who cannot tolerate or do not respond to non-prescription medications.
questions.question: The use of heat therapy for primary dysmenorrhea is considered most accurate in which statement below?
options: It is more effective than all NSAIDs when used alone
An abdominal heat patch can add to ibuprofen's analgesic effect
It works by suppressing prostaglandin synthesis directly
Its analgesic onset is slower than drug therapy in all patients
Evidence shows it is ineffective compared with placebo

questions.explanation: The LH surge occurring 28 to 32 hours before follicular rupture is the most clinically useful predictor of approaching ovulation. Ovulation typically occurs 24 to 36 hours after the estradiol peak and 10 to 16 hours after the LH peak. This timing is widely exploited in ovulation predictor kits and is critical for planning conception, as fertilization is most successful from two days before ovulation through the day of ovulation.
questions.question: The LH surge, which occurs 28 to 32 hours before follicular rupture, is clinically useful primarily as a predictor of:
A patient with Parkinson's disease develops visual hallucinations after a dose increase of his dopamine agonist. What is the most appropriate initial management step?
questions.explanation: Dopaminergic medications, particularly dopamine agonists, are a common cause of hallucinations in Parkinson's disease, and the first step in management is to reduce or discontinue the most recently added or highest-risk dopaminergic agent before considering antipsychotic therapy, since typical antipsychotics can worsen parkinsonian motor symptoms.
options: Add an anticholinergic agent for symptom control
Increase the levodopa dose to compensate
Reduce or discontinue the dopamine agonist first

questions.question: A patient with anorexia nervosa undergoing nutritional rehabilitation needs cardiac monitoring during the first week. Which electrolyte abnormality is the most immediately life-threatening if it develops during refeeding?
questions.explanation: Hypophosphatemia is the most immediately life-threatening electrolyte disturbance during refeeding because phosphate is essential for ATP synthesis and cardiac muscle function; severe depletion can precipitate cardiac arrhythmias, respiratory failure from diaphragmatic weakness, and sudden death if not anticipated and corrected proactively.

questions.question: A vegan patient presents with megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord with loss of proprioception. Which deficiency best explains both findings together?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia due to impaired DNA synthesis and additionally causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord from demyelination of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, producing proprioceptive loss. Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia but does not cause neurological demyelination.

Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is the most effective treatment for psychotic or delusional depression. When delusions are present, antidepressant drug therapy alone has much lower response rates. A combination of antidepressant and antipsychotic has a response rate of approximately 78%, while ECT remains the gold standard for this most severe form of depression. Fixed combination antidepressant-antipsychotic products are not recommended since antipsychotic use is needed for only a few weeks while the antidepressant is continued for at least 6 months.
questions.question: Delusional (psychotic) depression involves major depressive disorder with psychotic symptoms, especially delusions. What is the MOST effective treatment for delusional depression?

options: Negative symptoms (flat affect or poverty of speech)
Cognitive impairment in attention or memory
questions.explanation: To meet diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia, the patient must have experienced at least 2 of the following 5 symptoms: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized or catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms. Critically, at least 1 of the symptoms must be the presence of delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech. This requirement ensures that the diagnosis is anchored to the most characteristic psychotic features of schizophrenia, preventing its application to conditions with only negative symptoms or disorganized behavior.
questions.question: For diagnosis of schizophrenia, at least 2 of 5 specific symptoms must be experienced by the patient, and at least 1 of these must be which of the following?

options: Schwann cell protein in peripheral nerve sheaths
Myelin sheath (subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord)
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord through impaired methylmalonyl-CoA mutase activity, leading to abnormal fatty acid synthesis and defective myelin production. The posterior and lateral columns of the spinal cord are predominantly affected, causing peripheral neuropathy, loss of proprioception, and ataxia. Combined with megaloblastic anemia (from impaired DNA synthesis), B12 deficiency presents a unique dual hematological and neurological picture. Vegans and patients with pernicious anemia are particularly at risk.
questions.question: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia AND peripheral neuropathy. The neuropathy results from impaired synthesis of which component essential for neuronal integrity?
Contraction pressure in the uterus of a woman with severe primary dysmenorrhea can exceed which value, compared to the normal 50-80 mmHg?
questions.explanation: In dysmenorrhea, uterine contraction pressure can exceed 400 mmHg (compared to normal 50-80 mmHg), contractions may last longer than 90 seconds (vs. 15-30 seconds normally), and intervals between contractions may be less than 15 seconds. This markedly increased pressure and frequency contribute to profound intrauterine ischemia, tissue hypoxia, and the intense pelvic pain characteristic of dysmenorrhea.

questions.question:
Describe opium under the following headings, then explain its standards and quality control, and state its uses, its storage and how it differs from a related drug.
A(i) Biological source and family
A(ii) Method of collection or preparation
A(iii) Description and physical characters
A(iv) Chemical constituents
B(i) Chemical tests
B(ii) Solubility
B(iii) Standards
B(iv) Tests for purity or adulteration
B(v) Basis of commercial grades or classification
C(i) Uses
C(ii) Storage
C(iii) Distinction from poppy seeds and the other opium preparations
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Opium is the air-dried latex obtained by incision of the unripe capsules of Papaver somniferum L. or its variety P. album Decand. (Papaveraceae), the opium poppy; the caked latex is raw (crude or gum) opium; native to Turkey, with other sources including Yugoslavia, Iran, India, China and Tasmania.
A(ii)
A flowering annual herb with about eight capsules; the latex is collected 5-10 days after the petals fall, when lower leaves yellow and capsules turn from pale green to brownish green; incisions about 1 mm deep (the latex lies between epicarp and mesocarp) are made vertically or horizontally in dry weather, morning or evening; the latex solidifies in 8-14 hours and is scraped off with a knife or blade (often gathered in poppy leaves) as raw opium. Prepared opium: opiums from different sources are mixed, kneaded and moulded into cakes of definite size and shape with a fixed morphine content (standard powdered opium is adjusted with cocoa shell if morphine is too high).
A(iii)
Fresh latex is milky white and coagulates to brown. Turkish: sub-cylindrical cakes about 9 cm high and 15 cm across, coated with coarse powdered poppy leaves (greenish-grey mottled), pale chocolate-brown, uniformly slightly granular, moderately plastic when fresh and very hard when old. Yugoslavian: oblong cakes with rounded ends, 160-225 g, 18-20 × 6-7.5 × 1.5-2.4 cm, greyish-green with broken poppy leaves or dark brown without. Indian: dark brown to nearly black cubical blocks 8-9 cm across, about 1 kg, smooth and homogeneous inside, wrapped in thin white paper.
A(iv)
About 25 alkaloids: morphine (10-16%), codeine (0.8-2.5%), thebaine (0.5-2%), noscapine (4-8%), papaverine (0.5-2.5%) and narceine; classed as morphine, phthalide isoquinoline, benzyl isoquinoline and cryptopine types plus unclassified; meconic acid (about 5%, an analytical marker found only in opium); sugars, albuminous compounds, sulphates, mucilage, wax and Ca/Mg salts; tannin, oxalic acid and fats are absent.
B(i)
Aqueous extract with 10% FeCl₃ turns brown to deep reddish-purple, persisting on adding 2N HCl (meconic acid); a drop of a moistened sample added to 2N HCl and warmed gives a red colour (porphyroxine); Marquis reagent (conc. H2SO4 + formaldehyde): morphine and codeine dark violet, papaverine no colour, noscapine bright yellow; other colour tests include Mecke, Froehde, Mandelin and Liebermann.
B(ii)
For purification, 300 mg is dispersed in 2.5% acetic acid, made basic with ammonia to about pH 10 and extracted with chloroform-isopropanol (3:1), dried over anhydrous sodium sulphate, evaporated, redissolved in methanol and evaporated to leave morphine.
B(iii)
Standards: standardised opium has a more or less fixed morphine content (standard powder contains a definite percentage of morphine); opium tincture contains 10% powdered opium (about 1% morphine, denarcotised and deodorised); meconic acid must be present, so its detection is a quality check; value varies with season, weather and fertiliser.
B(iv)
Raw opium has plant fragments, meconic acid and porphyroxine; prepared opium has meconic acid but no recognisable plant fragments or porphyroxine; crude morphine has none of these nor the opium odour. Microscopy of the water-washed residue shows poppy capsule fragments with 5-6-sided thick-walled epidermis, infrequent anomocytic stomata and occasional pollen grains. Former adulterants (wheat flour, gums, powdered dates) are found by microscopy, moisture, morphine content, water-soluble extractive and ash value.
B(v)
Classified as natural/raw opium and prepared (standardised) opium, and by variety: Turkish, Indian, Yugoslavian, Chinese and Persian; Iranian opium occurs as bricks (15 × 8 × 6 cm, about 700 g) in bright-red paper, very hard, splintery and dark brown to nearly black; Indian as cakes and balls (about 1500 g) covered with poppy petals, rather soft, brown to nearly black; Turkish as cylindrical masses covered with poppy leaves.
C(i)
Standardised extracts and purified compounds are used in medicine: morphine as the main opioid analgesic; codeine as analgesic and mild sedative in cough mixtures; noscapine as emetic and central antitussive; papaverine as non-narcotic smooth-muscle relaxant for spasms; opium tincture as a bitter antidiarrhoeal; hypnotic and sedative; products include Benylin with codeine and opium tincture USP; preparations are strictly regulated and opioids are prescription-only.
C(ii)
Careful storage is needed to keep the morphine content: store under anaerobic conditions; opium dried at 60° C and stored with air loses morphine rapidly, while drying at 100° C and storing out of contact with air gives little loss (loss attributed to the enzyme opiase).
C(iii)
Poppy seeds contain opium alkaloids only through external contamination from the pod, not from inside the seed; raw, prepared and crude-morphine opium differ in plant fragments, meconic acid, porphyroxine and odour as above; meconic acid occurs only in opium.

questions.question:
Describe mineral matters used in pharmacy (chalk, talc, kieselguhr, kaolin, bentonite), relate their sources and preparation to representative examples, and explain why the approach is used and what limitation or hazard results.
A(i) State what mineral matters are and name them
A(ii) Describe chalk (source, composition, preparation)
A(iii) Describe talc and kieselguhr
A(iv) Describe kaolin and bentonite
B(i) Compare light and heavy kaolin
B(ii) Describe pharmaceutical uses
B(iii) Describe official preparations
B(iv) Describe industrial and other uses and bentonite types
C(i) Explain why mineral matters are used
C(ii) Explain why purification is required
C(iii) State the hazard of talc
C(iv) State the trade-off
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Crude drugs from natural sources made up mainly of inorganic materials, some from remains of microscopic plants (phytoplankton) or marine animals: chalk, talc, bentonite, kieselguhr, kaolin, asbestos.
A(ii)
Creta/English white: white, soft, earthy, amorphous, tasteless, odourless, insoluble in water, effervesces with acids; about 98% calcium carbonate, 0.5% magnesium carbonate, 0.5-1% silica; from coccolithophore shells (fine grains) and foraminifera etc. (coarse); North and South Downs and Dover (England), Champagne (France), Germany, Denmark; mined, ground, elutriated, moulded into cakes dried as whiting, further purified as small cones; prepared chalk has not more than 0.25 silica and iron/aluminium oxides.
A(iii)
Talc (French chalk): fine steatite/soapstone, greasy 'slip', insoluble in water, acids and alkalis, hydrated magnesium silicate Mg6(Si2O5)4(OH)4, 1-2% iron oxide gives grey-green tint; mined, purified by boiling with dilute HCl, washed, dried at 110° C; Piedmont (Italy), France, New York. Kieselguhr (diatomite): light brownish-grey, highly absorbent, 75-92% silica, from fossil diatoms (Bacillariaceae); mined, air-dried to 5-6% moisture, ground, graded by cyclone air separators, digested with dilute HCl, washed and dried; California, Virginia, Algeria, Denmark, Germany, Kenya, Scotland.
A(iv)
Kaolin (China clay): soft white clay, hydrated aluminium silicate Al2O3.2SiO2.2H2O, insoluble in water and unaffected by dilute acids and alkalis; from weathered granite feldspar (Cornwall, Devonshire); washed out with water jets, separated in drags, elutriated into light and heavy grades. Bentonite: pale greenish-grey powder, mainly montmorillonite (80%), absorbs 5-6 times its weight of water and swells 12-15 times, 2% dispersion pH 9-10; from decomposed volcanic ash (Italy, Canada, South Africa, Wyoming); mined as soapy lumps, steam-dried, powdered and sifted.
B(i)
Light kaolin (small, largely colloidal) forms a stiff sticky mass and suspends in water with little deposit, for internal use; heavy kaolin (coarse, no colloid) forms a plastic, less sticky mass that deposits leaving a clear supernatant, used for filtration, poultices and pill excipient.
B(ii)
Chalk: antacid, diarrhoea, face/tooth/dusting powders, tablet filler, phosphate binder in chronic renal failure; talc: dusting powders, pill coating, lubricant; kieselguhr: face/tooth powders, clarification and filtration, TLC stationary phase; light kaolin: diarrhoea absorbent; bentonite: sols and gels for emulsions, ointments and creams, bulk laxative, bentoquatam shield against urushiol, desiccant.
B(iii)
Prepared Chalk BP, Paediatric Chalk mixture BP, Aromatic Chalk with Opium mixture BP; Purified Talc BP, Talc Dusting Powder BP; Kaolin Mixture BP, Kaolin and Morphine Mixture BP, Paediatric Kaolin Mixture BP, Light and Heavy Kaolin BP, Kaolin Poultice BP.
B(iv)
Chalk: abrasive in toothpaste, food preservative/colour retainer, source of quicklime and slaked lime, raising soil pH; kieselguhr: nail polish, Berkefeld candle filters, mechanical insecticide; bentonite in cosmetic bases; types by predominant salt: sodium (best grade), calcium, potassium.
C(i)
Their inorganic composition and physical properties (absorbency, slip, swelling, inertness) suit powders, excipients, absorbents and suspending bases.
C(ii)
Native minerals contain impurities (silica and iron oxide in chalk, iron oxide in talc), so pharmaceutical grades are elutriated or acid-treated.
C(iii)
Talc contaminated with asbestos is classified by IARC as carcinogenic to humans (ovarian, lung, mesothelioma), while asbestos-free talc has not been confirmed carcinogenic; manufacturers must use asbestos-free talc and check samples by polarised light microscopy or transmission electron microscopy.
C(iv)
Cheap mined minerals give useful bulk properties but depend on purification and contamination control;.

questions.question:
Describe agar under the following headings, then explain its standards and quality control, and state its uses and how it differs from a related drug.
A(i) Biological source and family
A(ii) Method of collection or preparation
A(iii) Description and physical characters
A(iv) Chemical constituents
B(i) Chemical tests
B(ii) Solubility
B(iii) Standards
B(iv) Tests for purity or adulteration
B(v) Basis of commercial grades or classification
C(i) Uses
C(ii) Distinction from gelatin and tragacanth
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Dried colloidal concentrate from a decoction of various red algae, particularly species of Gelidium and Pterocladia (Gelidiaceae) and Gracilaria (Gracilariaceae); produced in Japan (about one third of world production), Korea, South Africa, the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the USA, Chile, Spain and Portugal; Gelidium supplies 35% of the source material.
A(ii)
Collected in Japan from May to October and manufactured from November to February; poles are planted in the sea to support the algae, which are stripped off, raked or collected by diving, dried, beaten and shaken to remove sand and shells, bleached by watering and sunlight and washed to remove salt; boiled with acidulated water (1:50-60) for several hours, filtered hot through linen, the jelly cut into bars and strips through wire netting, and moisture removed by freezing, thawing and drying at about 35° C.
A(iii)
Occurs as bundles of agglutinated, translucent yellowish-white strips about 60 × 0.4 cm, or as coarse powder or flakes; swells in cold water with only a small fraction dissolving; a 1% solution of Japanese agar in boiling water sets to a stiff jelly on cooling.
A(iv)
Hydrolysis gives D- and L-galactose; a heterogeneous polysaccharide of agarose (neutral galactose polymer free of sulphate, alternating 3,6-anhydro-L-galactose and D-galactose, giving gel strength) and agaropectin (sulphonated polysaccharide with galactose and uronic acid partly esterified with sulphuric acid, giving viscosity).
B(i)
Near boiling, 0.2% gives no precipitate with aqueous tannic acid; no ammonia is evolved on heating with soda lime; hydrolysis by boiling with dilute acid gives galactose (reduces Fehling's solution) and sulphate ions (precipitated by barium chloride); gives a deep crimson to brown colour with 0.05 M iodine; stains pink with ruthenium red.
B(ii)
Swells in cold water with only a small fraction dissolving; dissolves in boiling water and sets to a jelly on cooling.
B(iii)
Standards: gel strength is expressed by the concentration giving a similarly stiff jelly (1% Japanese, 0.7% New Zealand, 1% South African, 2% Austrian agar).
B(iv)
Residue of the ash treated with dilute HCl shows, under the microscope, silica skeletons of diatoms and sponge spicules; absence of ammonia with soda lime (no protein) and the tannic acid and iodine tests are also used.
B(v)
Classified by form (strips versus coarse powder/flakes) and by source, with different concentrations (0.7-2%) needed to give equal jelly stiffness.
C(i)
Preparation of culture media, emulsifying agent, treatment of chronic constipation; agar and agarose in affinity chromatography; pure agarose gels in protein electrophoresis.
C(ii)
Gelatin is a protein and evolves ammonia with soda lime whereas agar does not; agar gives a precipitate with lead acetate (acacia does not) and contains galactose and sulphate.

A(i)
Capsicum (chilies, cayenne pepper) is the dried ripe fruit of Capsicum annuum var. minimum (Miller) Heiser and small-fruited varieties of C. frutescens L. (Solanaceae); known as chili pepper, bell pepper, bird pepper; local names Ose (Igbo), Tatashe (Yoruba), Barkono (Hausa), Ata wewe, Ose mkpe.
A(ii)
Originated in Central and South America; cultivated in southern India, South America and Africa (producers include Brazil, Peru, Colombia, India, Thailand, Indonesia, Nigeria, Ghana).
A(iii)
Fertile, well-drained loamy soil of pH 6.0-6.8; seeds raised in nursery (8-10 weeks indoors) and transplanted after 4-6 weeks; harvest 60-90 days after transplanting (C. frutescens fruits mature 90-120 days after transplanting), picking blemish-free ripe fruit by hand; fruits are washed, sorted by size, colour and quality, dried (for storage or grinding) and stored in a cool dry place.
A(iv)
Pod narrowly ovoid or ovoid-conical, 12-20 mm long and 4-7 mm wide; cup-shaped calyx about 4 mm with 5 inconspicuous teeth; pericarp glabrous, shrunken, thin, translucent, leathery and orange-red; two loculi divided by a longitudinal dissepiment with axile placentation and 5-10 seeds each; seeds disc-shaped, 3-4 mm × 2.5-3 mm × 0.5-1.0 mm, testa pale buff, abundant oily endosperm with a narrow coiled embryo; odour characteristic but not powerful; taste extremely fiery and pungent.
A(v)
Pericarp of epidermis, mesocarp (with chromoplasts) and endocarp; stomata surrounded by a thick cuticle; unicellular hair-like trichomes; calcium oxalate as rosettes or prisms; vascular bundles in the mesocarp; seed coat a thick outer layer with oily/starchy endosperm.
A(vi)
Capsaicin (colourless crystals, the pungent principle; capsaicinoids include dihydrocapsaicin), a liquid alkaloid, fixed oil, carotenoids and red colouring matter (capsanthin, capsorubin), traces of starch, flavonoids, vitamins and minerals; pungency is destroyed by oxidation with potassium dichromate or permanganate and is not affected by 2% alcoholic potash.
B(i)
Extremely fiery pungent taste, translucent leathery orange-red pericarp, two loculi with axile placentation, disc-shaped seeds with coiled embryo, and pungency as an organoleptic marker.
B(ii)
Capsaicin pungency is destroyed by potassium dichromate or permanganate oxidation but not by 2% alcoholic potash.
B(iii)
Red chillies (C. frutescens) may be substituted by C. annuum (sub-standard variety by morphological resemblance); capsicum is itself used to adulterate ginger by adding pungency.
C(i)
Applied externally as stimulant and counter-irritant; internally a pungent carminative to dispel flatulence and rouse appetite; capsaicin creams for arthritis and nerve pain; spice, pepper sprays; stored in a cool, dry place (or refrigerated or sun-dried depending on use).
C(ii)
Varieties: Sierra Leone (most pungent, slender bright pod, stalk occasionally attached), Nyasaland (resembles Sierra Leone but brighter and freer of stalk), Zanzibar (dull, more stalky, shorter and broader pod, calyx and pedicel usually present in small amount); C. frutescens fruit is elongated, tapered and conical, 2-5 cm long and 0.5-1.5 cm wide.

Describe capsicum (chillies) under the following headings, then explain how it is identified and evaluated, and state its uses and how it differs from a related drug.
A(i) Synonym, biological source and family
A(ii) Geographical source
A(iii) Cultivation, collection and preparation
A(iv) Part used and macroscopic characters
A(v) Microscopic characters
A(vi) Chemical constituents
B(i) Key diagnostic features used for identification
B(ii) Chemical tests
B(iii) Adulterants or substitutes and how they are detected
C(i) Uses (with any storage or toxicity note)
C(ii) Distinction from its commercial varieties and related Capsicum species

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Crude drugs are vegetable or animal drugs of natural substances that have undergone only collection and drying; organised vegetable drugs are drugs with a definite cellular structure obtained from morphological parts of plants (leaves, roots, stems, bark), and almost all parts of a plant or the whole plant may be organised drugs.
A(ii)
Vegetable saps, extracts and secretions, e.g. dried latices, gums, oils, fats, waxes and resins.
A(iii)
Leaves: senna, digitalis, catharanthus; barks: cinnamon, cassia, cascara, cinchona; roots: rauwolfia, belladonna, ipecacuanha, aconite, liquorice; rhizomes: ginger, turmeric, podophyllum; seeds: strophanthus, cocoa, calabar bean, castor, kola; fruits: vanilla, cardamom, fennel, tamarind, capsicum.
A(iv)
Gums and mucilages (acacia, tragacanth, sterculia, agar), gelatin, aloes, opium (dried latex), balsams and resins (Peru, Tolu, storax, benzoin), waxes (beeswax, woolfat, spermaceti).
B(i)
Gums are pathological products formed by injury or drought through breakdown of cell walls (extracellular); mucilages are normal metabolic products formed within cells (intracellular), serving as storage material, water reservoir or protection of germinating seeds, found in senna leaf epidermis, linseed and psyllium seed coats, marshmallow root and slippery elm bark.
B(ii)
Organised drugs: macroscopic/organoleptic and microscopic (histological) features. Unorganised drugs: chemical tests and physical constants are the important parameters, e.g. aloes confirmed by the test for anthraquinone derivatives.
B(iii)
Powdered leaves: epidermis with stomata, cellulose parenchyma, small vascular elements, chlorophyll; often trichomes, palisade cells, calcium oxalate, collenchyma, pericyclic fibres. Powdered barks: always sieve tubes and cellulose parenchyma; chlorophyll and aleurone absent; cork, fibres, sclereids, starch, calcium oxalate and secretory tissue frequent; xylem absent or scanty.
B(iv)
Origin, common names, biological source and family, geographical source, cultivation, collection, preparation and storage, macroscopic, organoleptic and microscopic evaluation, constituents, uses, substitutes and adulterants.
C(i)
It directs the method of study and evaluation: cellular structure allows microscopy for organised drugs, while secretions without structure rely on chemical and physical tests; it is also the basis of morphological classification.
C(ii)
Morphological classification is particularly useful for identifying specific drugs and detecting adulterants; the form of the drug indicates the detection method (morphology for whole drugs, microscopy for powders, chemical and physical standards for liquids/secretions).
C(iii)
Similar morphological parts from different plants do not have similar constituents (cascara, cinnamon and cinchona barks differ), and morphological grouping is unsuitable for storage.
C(iv)
The structural distinction aids identification but tells little about chemistry or activity; other systems are needed for those.
questions.question:
Distinguish organised from unorganised vegetable drugs, relate the distinction to representative examples and plant parts, and explain why the distinction is used and what limitation results.
A(i) Define crude drugs and organised drugs
A(ii) Define unorganised drugs
A(iii) Give examples of organised drugs by part
A(iv) Give examples of unorganised drugs
B(i) Compare gums and mucilages
B(ii) Compare the identification tools used for each class
B(iii) Describe diagnostic features of powdered leaves and barks
B(iv) Describe the features studied in systematic study of organised drugs
C(i) Explain why the distinction is used
C(ii) Relate the distinction to adulteration detection
C(iii) State the limitation
C(iv) State the trade-off

Describe the histochemical techniques of clearing and disintegration used for crude drugs, relate each reagent to representative examples, and explain why they are used and what limits they have.
A(i) State why clearing agents and stains are needed
A(ii) Describe chloral hydrate and sodium hypochlorite
A(iii) Describe potash solutions and ether-ethanol
A(iv) Describe disintegration with oxidising agents
B(i) Describe chromic-nitric mixtures
B(ii) Describe dilute acids and alkalis
B(iii) Describe the stains for walls
B(iv) Describe microscopic technique steps
C(i) Explain why the approach is used
C(ii) Explain why reagent choice depends on the tissue
C(iii) State a limitation
C(iv) State the trade-off
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Plant structures are not properly seen because of abundant cell contents, colouring matter and shrinkage of cell walls; reagents remove contents, bleach and restore wall shape; cleared samples are washed and mounted in another medium (glycerine, alcohol, carbolic acid, lactophenol, clove oil have some clearing effect).
A(ii)
Chloral hydrate dissolves proteins, starch, chlorophyll, resins and volatile oils, expands shrunken cells, used for sections, whole leaf, flowers and seeds, does not dissolve calcium oxalate. Sodium hypochlorite bleaches dark sections (e.g. bark) and removes leaf chlorophyll; prolonged contact removes starch and lignin.
A(iii)
5% aqueous KOH clears, dissolves starch and protein quickly, swells walls, separates heavily cuticularised leaf epidermis, isolates secretory tissue and lignified elements (suberised and cutinised tissue resist); 0.3% dissolves aleurone grains; wash out soon. Ether-ethanol (equal parts, 96% ethanol) removes fixed oils, fats, resins, volatile oils, tannins and chlorophyll (defatting of oily seeds).
A(iv)
Woody tissue is disintegrated by oxidising away the lignin-rich middle lamella: wood placed in 50% nitric acid with small amounts of potassium chlorate added at intervals until it breaks up, then washed free of acid.
B(i)
Equal parts of 10% chromic acid and 10% nitric or sulphuric acid disintegrate sclerenchymatous tissue (testas of capsicum, seeds of bitter cucumber) and separate lignified hairs of nux vomica and strophanthus; dilute nitric acid has a marked effect on wood.
B(ii)
Pectic substances are soluble in dilute acids or alkalis; pure cellulose resists hydrolysing and oxidising agents (stability in boiling 5% potash separates cotton from wool); mannans, galactans, pectin, hemicelluloses, gums and lichen are readily attacked.
B(iii)
Phloroglucinol with hydrochloric acid shows lignified walls; chlor-zinc-iodine shows cellulose, lignified wall and starch.
B(iv)
Dried leaves are softened in a moist atmosphere, dried bark or root is boiled in water; sections for mucilage or water-soluble contents; disintegration to isolate tissues; bleaching for deeply coloured material; defatting for fatty seeds.
C(i)
It makes tissues and cell structure visible for identification of crude drugs and for study of adulterants in powders.
C(ii)
Reagents act on specific wall components, especially the middle lamella; strength and exposure time vary with the plant material.
C(iii)
Prolonged exposure removes useful structures (hypochlorite removes starch and lignin; potash dissolves starch and protein), and chloral hydrate does not dissolve calcium oxalate.
C(iv)
Stronger clearing improves visibility but may destroy diagnostic contents;.

questions.question:
Describe fennel under the following headings, then explain how it is identified and evaluated, and state its uses.
A(i) Synonym, biological source and family
A(ii) Geographical source
A(iii) Cultivation, collection and preparation
A(iv) Part used and macroscopic characters
A(v) Microscopic characters
A(vi) Chemical constituents
B(i) Key diagnostic features used for identification
B(ii) Adulterants or substitutes and how they are detected
C(i) Uses (with any storage or toxicity note)
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Fennel consists of the dried ripe fruits of cultivated Foeniculum vulgare Mill. var. vulgare (Umbelliferae); sweet fennel, wild fennel, fennel seeds, finocchio (Italy).
A(ii)
Indigenous to Europe (Mediterranean origin); cultivated in many parts of Europe; commercial supplies from India and China with small quantities from Egypt; also cultivated in Nigeria.
A(iii)
Thrives in temperate climate but adapts to tropical/subtropical; well-drained loamy or sandy soil, pH 6.0-7.0, full sun; propagated by seeds sown directly or in nurseries, in the cool season (autumn or early spring) at 1-2 cm depth with rows 30-45 cm apart; irrigation, weeding and nitrogen/phosphorus fertilizers; harvested 4-5 months after sowing when fruits turn greenish-brown, cutting flowering stems below the umbels in dry weather; umbels sun-dried, threshed and winnowed; seeds stored in airtight containers or sacks in a cool dry place.
A(iv)
Fruit (a cremocarp) small, oval to oblong and slightly curved, 4-10 mm long and 2-4 mm in diameter; greenish-brown to yellowish-brown; glabrous with prominent, straight, pale straw-coloured primary ridges on each mericarp; fracture short and granular; odour strong, sweet, aromatic; taste sweet, slightly pungent, anise/liquorice-like.
A(v)
Epicarp of polygonal cells with a thin cuticle, stomata and a few hairs; mesocarp of parenchyma with scattered vascular bundles and 6-8 oil ducts in each mericarp; endocarp of elongated, thick-walled, lignified sclerenchymatous cells; vascular bundles beneath the ridges run longitudinally.
A(vi)
Volatile oil 1-3% (50-60% anethole and about 20% fenchone; fenchone is a colourless liquid with pungent camphoraceous taste), proteins and fixed oil; phenolic acids (ferulic, gallic, o-coumaric) and limonene, α-thujone, β-fenchol, α-terpinene and β-myrcene in the essential oil.
B(i)
Strong sweet aromatic odour typical of umbelliferous fruits, prominent pale ridges on each mericarp, 6-8 oil ducts per mericarp and lignified endocarp.
B(ii)
Fennel is liable to adulteration by replacement with exhausted fruits (a costly drug re-used after extraction).
C(i)
Agreeable aromatic and carminative; flavouring agent; ethnomedicinal use for indigestion, bloating, respiratory issues and menstrual cramps, as eye wash and diuretic; commercial products are volatile oil, powdered fennel and dried seed; stored in airtight containers in a cool dry place.

questions.question:
Describe nutmeg under the following headings, then explain how it is identified and evaluated, and state its uses and how it differs from a related drug.
A(i) Synonym, biological source and family
A(ii) Geographical source
A(iii) Cultivation, collection and preparation
A(iv) Part used and macroscopic characters
A(v) Microscopic characters
A(vi) Chemical constituents
B(i) Key diagnostic features used for identification
B(ii) Chemical tests
B(iii) Adulterants or substitutes and how they are detected
C(i) Uses (with any storage or toxicity note)
C(ii) Distinction from Papua and Bombay nutmegs
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Nutmeg consists of the dried kernels of the seeds of Myristica fragrans Houtt. (Myristicaceae); mace is the red aril; synonyms include M. aromatica Lam., M. moschata Thunb., M. officinalis L.f., M. philippensis Lam and M. laurifolia Salisb; local names gujiya dan miya (Hausa), Ariwo (Yoruba), Ehuru/Ehiri (Igbo); common names nutmeg tree, Banda tree, Muscadier.
A(ii)
An evergreen tree 10-20 m high, indigenous to the Molucca Islands and now cultivated in Indonesia and Malaysia (Molucca Islands, Sumatra, Java, Penang), Ceylon and the West Indies (Grenada).
A(iii)
Grown from seeds that germinate in 5 weeks, seedlings transplanted after 6 months, male trees reduced to 10% by 5-8 years; in Grenada females are propagated by marcotting and grafting; fruiting starts at 8-9 years and lasts 20-30 years; the ripe fruit splits to show the seed and red aril, the pericarp is removed on the spot and mace is dried immediately; nutmegs are dried 3-6 weeks until the shell is brittle, cracked, graded by size and exported in barrels or cases (yield 250-500 kg nutmeg and 50-100 kg mace per acre).
A(iv)
Kernel broadly oval, 2-3 cm × 2 cm, brown/greyish-brown with a reticulated surface, a light patch at one end, radiating lines, a raised ring and a dark depression from raphe to chalaza; aromatic odour and pungent, bitter taste; longitudinal section marbled (dark brown perisperm in light brown endosperm) with fibrovascular bundles in the perisperm aligned with surface furrows.
A(v)
Outer perisperm cells radially flattened with brownish contents insoluble in KOH or chloral hydrate, a few with prismatic or disc-shaped crystals (thought to be potassium acid tartrate); inner perisperm with lamellae of thin-walled brown parenchyma and oval oil cells and lignified spiral vessels; endosperm of thin-walled brown parenchyma with simple or 2-10 compound starch grains (up to 22 µm), aleurone grains with crystalloids and feathery fat crystals; scattered tannin cells.
A(vi)
5-15% volatile oil (4-8% myristicin, elemicin and safrole); 30-40% fat (fixed oil mainly myristic acid about 60%, with oleic and lauric acids); phytosterin, starch, amylodextrin, colouring matter, saponin, tannins, flavonoids and alkaloids; about 3% total ash and about 0.2% acid-insoluble ash.
B(i)
Reticulated surface, marbled section, aromatic odour with pungent bitter taste, brown perisperm contents, oil cells, starch grains up to 22 µm and aleurone grains; total ash about 3% and acid-insoluble ash about 0.2%.
B(ii)
Perisperm contents are insoluble in KOH or chloral hydrate; ash values as above.
B(iii)
Papua (Macassar, long or wild) nutmegs from M. argentea have a uniform scurfy surface, little odour and a disagreeable taste; Bombay nutmegs from M. malabarica are very long and narrow and lack the characteristic aroma; they are recognised by these morphological and sensory features.
C(i)
Flavouring and carminative (nutmeg, mace and their oils); aqueous extract used for infantile diarrhoea in traditional Indian medicine; added to shampoos and conditioners; used in spices, processed foods and beverages and in ayurvedic and unani remedies; excessive consumption causes hallucinations, nausea and palpitations (myristicin and safrole); improved drying and storage maintain quality.
C(ii)
Papua nutmegs (M. argentea, New Guinea) and Bombay nutmegs (M. malabarica, India) differ from genuine nutmeg as described above: scurfy surface, little odour and disagreeable taste for Papua; very long, narrow shape and lack of aroma for Bombay.

questions.question:
Describe the chemical, microchemical and biological evaluation of crude drugs, relate the tests to representative examples, and explain why the approach is used and what limitation results.
A(i) Describe chemical evaluation
A(ii) Describe microchemical tests on the cell wall
A(iii) Give chemical tests for named organised drugs
A(iv) Give chemical tests for named unorganised drugs
B(i) Describe wax and balsam constants
B(ii) Describe biological evaluation
B(iii) Describe histochemical clearing and disintegration reagents
B(iv) Describe when biological methods are chosen
C(i) Explain why chemical tests are used
C(ii) Explain why microchemical tests are used
C(iii) State a limitation
C(iv) State the trade-off
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Determines active constituents; useful for powdered organised drugs and important for unorganised drugs; includes quantitative constants (acid, saponification, ester and iodine values), instrumental methods and phytochemical profiling.
A(ii)
Cellulose: blue with chlor-zinc-iodine or cuoxam; lignin: red with phloroglucinol and conc. HCl; suberin (cork, endodermis) and cutin (leaf cuticle): red with Sudan III on heating; mucilage: red/pink with ruthenium red.
A(iii)
Cinnamon: KOH gives potassium eugenate needles and Sudan III shows orange-red oil globules; cinchona: emerald-green with bromine water and ammonia, red fumes with acetic acid, blue fluorescence under UV; cascara: Borntrager's test (pink/red/violet in ammonia layer).
A(iv)
Opium: ferric chloride deep purplish-red (meconic acid) and red with HCl (porphyroxine), Marquis reagent colours; gelatin: biuret violet, ninhydrin deep blue, ammonia with soda lime; acacia: no lead acetate precipitate, no iodine colour; benzoins: KMnO₄ benzaldehyde odour and ferric chloride colours.
B(i)
Waxes: acid, saponification, ester (saponification minus acid) and iodine values; woolfat: cholesterol test (chloroform, acetic anhydride, drops of conc. H2SO4 give deep green); balsam of Peru: 45-75% esters by gravimetric analysis.
B(ii)
Bioassay of potency by effect on bacteria, fungi, tissues or animals: toxic, symptomatic and tissue methods; examples hepatoprotective, anti-inflammatory, hypoglycaemic and anti-ulcer.
B(iii)
Chloral hydrate dissolves proteins, starch, chlorophyll, resins and volatile oils but not calcium oxalate; sodium hypochlorite bleaches; KOH (5%) clears but dissolves starch and protein; ether-ethanol defats; nitric acid with potassium chlorate, chromic-nitric mixture disintegrate woody and sclerenchymatous tissue.
B(iv)
When standardisation is not adequate by chemical or physical means, and to confirm therapeutic activity of raw material or finished products.
C(i)
The usefulness of drugs is due to their chemicals, and tests identify them in powdered organised and unorganised drugs.
C(ii)
They give specific identification reactions on slides for wall materials and cell contents.
C(iii)
Colour tests indicate a class of compound only, e.g. Borntrager's test shows anthraquinones; the benzidine test is no longer used because benzidine is carcinogenic; bioassay needs living material.
C(iv)
Chemical and biological methods give information on constituents and potency but need reagents, instruments or animals;.

A(i)
Digitalis (purple foxglove leaves) consists of the dried leaves of Digitalis purpurea L. (Scrophulariaceae), a biennial or perennial herb about 1 m high.
A(ii)
The USA, Bulgaria, Hungary and South America; the USA once had domestic supplies of digitalis but now obtains it from Bulgaria, Hungary and South America.
A(iii)
Leaf sessile, linear to lanceolate, about 30 cm long and 4 cm broad, apex acute, margin entire, midrib at a very acute angle.
A(iv)
Upper epidermis single-layered with a thick cuticle and wavy thick-walled cells; multicellular uniseriate glandular trichomes; stomata occasionally on the upper epidermis; mesophyll differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma with no calcium oxalate crystals; lower epidermis similar but with more stomata and trichomes; midrib dorsal surface convex with strips of collenchyma and vascular bundles surrounded by a distinct endodermal layer.
A(v)
Cardiac glycosides and aglycones: digitoxin, digoxin, digitoxigenin, gitoxigenin and gitaloxigenin.
B(i)
Sessile lanceolate leaf with entire margin, wavy-walled epidermis with thick cuticle, uniseriate glandular trichomes, palisade and spongy mesophyll and absence of calcium oxalate crystals.
B(ii)
Adulterants: mullein leaves (Verbascum thapsus), comfrey (Symphytum officinale), primrose (Primula vulgaris), nettle (Urtica dioica) and Catharanthus roseus; digitalis very low in glycosides is also used as a diluent in preparing 'prepared digitalis'.
C(i)
Digitalis preparations act on cardiac muscle and are used as tablets or capsules for congestive heart failure, paroxysmal atrial tachycardia, atrial flutter and atrial fibrillation (derived products include Digoxin-Sandoz tablets and Digiglusin); the leaves are known to be poisonous.

A(i)
A balsam obtained from the trunk of Liquidambar orientalis (Hamamelidaceae), a small tree of south-western Turkey; the allied drug comes from L. styraciflua, a large tree found along the Atlantic coast from Central America to Connecticut.
A(ii)
The bark is wounded by bruising and incisions and, much later in autumn, pieces of bark are removed and pressed in horsehair bags in the cold and then in boiling water to give crude storax; crude storax is dissolved in alcohol and filtered (the insoluble matter is vegetable debris and resin) and the alcohol recovered at low temperature to give purified (Levant) storax without losing volatile constituents.
A(iii)
Crude storax: grey viscous fluid, pleasant odour, bitter taste, containing 20-30% water. Levant storax: brown viscous semi-solid, pleasant odour, bitter taste.
A(iv)
30-47% total balsamic acids, especially cinnamic acid; vanillin; phenylethylene; resin alcohols.
B(i)
An odour of benzaldehyde is produced on oxidation with KMnO₄ because of cinnamic acid.
B(ii)
Crude storax is 82-87% soluble in alcohol; Levant storax is completely soluble in alcohol and partially in ether.
B(iii)
Standards: Levant storax loses not more than 5% of its weight when dried for one hour on a water bath and is completely soluble in alcohol.
B(iv)
Alcohol solubility (82-87% for crude), loss on drying (not more than 5%) and the KMnO₄ benzaldehyde test.
B(v)
Two forms: crude storax and purified (Levant) storax; the allied drug is from L. styraciflua.
C(i)
Used in the preparation of Friars' balsam and of benzoin inhalation.
C(ii)
Storax is from Hamamelidaceae, whereas balsams of Peru and Tolu are from Myroxylon (Fabaceae) and benzoins from Styrax (Styracaceae); all give a benzaldehyde odour with KMnO₄ (cinnamic acid) except Siam benzoin; storax is a grey/brown viscous balsam rather than a hardening paste (Tolu) or reddish-brown fluid (Peru).
