questions.answerText:
A(i)
Calabar bean (ordeal bean; Esere in Yoruba, Esero in Igbo) consists of the dried ripe seeds of Physostigma venenosum Balfour (Fabaceae/Leguminosae).
A(ii)
Indigenous to the west coast of Africa, especially near the mouths of the old Calabar and Niger rivers; native to tropical West Africa (Nigeria, Cameroon, Gabon, Congo) in humid rainforests and riverine areas.
A(iii)
A large woody-based herbaceous climbing perennial (stem up to 5 cm thick, about 15 m high) grown in fertile, well-drained soil, propagated by seeds and transplanted, often shaded; it matures in 10-12 months and seeds are hand-harvested when pods turn brown and split; gloves are recommended because of the toxic physostigmine.
A(iv)
Seeds oblong-reniform, about 25-30 mm long, 15-18 mm wide and 10-15 mm thick (another account: 1-2 cm long); testa dark reddish-brown, hard, thick, shiny and slightly rough; hilum a deep black groove about 2 mm wide along the whole curved edge and round the blunt end; two concavo-convex starchy cotyledons with an air-filled hollow so the seeds float in water; no odour, bean-like taste; very poisonous (exalbuminous seed with starchy cotyledons).
A(v)
Seed coat of rectangular/polygonal epidermal cells, loosely arranged parenchyma with starch, and lignified cells; endosperm parenchyma with large polygonal starch granules and oil globules; cotyledons packed with starch and a small radicle near the hilum; needle-shaped colourless physostigmine crystals in parenchyma cells; starch grains polygonal or globular and birefringent in polarised light.
A(vi)
Physostigmine (eserine, C15H21N3O2, the major alkaloid), eseramine, physovenine, geneserine, calabatine and calabacine (pyridostigmine is also listed in one account), with starch, proteins and fixed oil.
B(i)
Black hilum groove, floating seeds, starchy cotyledons, oblong-reniform shape and physostigmine needle crystals in the parenchyma.
C(i)
Source of physostigmine used to contract the pupil (against mydriatics) and in glaucoma, as antidote in anticholinergic or strychnine poisoning, and in tetanus and locomotor ataxy (physostigmine salicylate used intravenously); ordeal poison among the Efik of Old Calabar, where survival of the accused meant innocence; physostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase causing salivation, twitching, convulsions, respiratory failure and death by asphyxia, and overdose raises blood pressure.

A(i)
Active constituent percentages are quoted on an air-dried basis; moisture is minimised to prevent decomposition or microbial contamination and is found by heating at 105° C to constant weight; toluene distillation is used for drugs that lose volatile constituents or change at 100° C.
A(ii)
Ash is the residue after incineration (about 2 g incinerated at 450° C) representing inorganic salts natural, adhering or added; total ash includes carbonates, phosphates, silicates and silica; acid-insoluble ash (boiled with 25 mL dilute HCl, filtered, ignited) indicates adhering dirt and sand; % = 100 × (Z-A)/B.
A(iii)
Measures the water-absorbing power due to mucilage, used for seeds: 1 g in a 25 mL stoppered cylinder with water to 20 mL, shaken occasionally, stood for 12 hours and the volume occupied by the swollen material measured.
A(iv)
Water-soluble (10 g in 100 mL chloroform water, 4 h; for tannins, sugars, acids, mucilage, glycosides) and alcohol-soluble (95% ethanol; tannins, resins) extractives; limits: aloes not more than 10.0% w/w, rhubarb not less than 30.0%, ginger not less than 4.5%; alcohol-insoluble extractive applies to resinous drugs such as myrrh and benzoin.
B(i)
Parts of the source organism other than those named, excess of named parts, or material from another source; 10 g spread on a tile and picked out by eye or lens and weighed.
B(ii)
For powdered drugs: lycopodium spores are uniform (25 µm, about 94,000 per mg) and are counted against defined particles (starch or pollen grains) to compute content; applicable to powdered clove, ginger and umbelliferous fruits.
B(iii)
Residue of resistant tissue after treatment of 2 g of powder with 50 mL 10% nitric acid (boiled 30 s), then 50 mL 2.5% sodium hydroxide (boiled 30 s), washed, dried and weighed.
B(iv)
Specific gravity, density, melting point, optical rotation by polarimeter (drugs with sugars), chromatography (TLC Rf, HPLC, GC) and IR/NMR spectroscopy.
C(i)
Moisture control prevents decomposition and microbial growth; ash is a criterion of identity and purity because it shows added or adhering inorganic matter.
C(ii)
Extractives give an approximate measure of constituents (tannins, resin, sugars) in diverse drugs; the solvent must dissolve substantial amounts of the desired substances.
C(iii)
Heating at 100° C may drive off volatile constituents, so moisture by oven can mislead; extractives are only approximate indicators.
C(iv)
Simple gravimetric tests are inexpensive but give only bulk measures; chromatography and spectroscopy give detail but need instruments;.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Biological sources relate to the plant (or organism) from which the drug is derived; natural sources are plant sources and marine sources.
A(ii)
Leaf: Digitalis purpurea (digoxin); bark: Cinchona officinalis (quinine); fruit: Papaver somniferum (morphine); stem: Chondrodendron tomentosum (tubocurarine); root: Rauwolfia serpentina (reserpine).
A(iii)
Most drugs come from spermatophytes: gymnosperms (pines and firs; Pinus palustris turpentine oil, Ephedra sinica ephedrine) and angiosperms (monocots such as grasses, lilies, palms; dicots give more useful drugs); algae give agar and alginic acid (Gelidium amansii); lichens and mosses contribute little; pteridophytes are known for taenicidal ferns.
A(iv)
Sponges give compounds with anti-inflammatory, antiviral and anticancer activity: Discodermia dissoluta (discodermolide, anticancer), Celtodoryx girardae (anti-herpes), Bugula neritina (bryostatin, anticancer), Spongia officinalis (anti-inflammatory).
B(i)
Folk medicine, herbaria, pharmacopoeias and publications.
B(ii)
Folk (traditional) medicine is knowledge and practice from indigenous cultures using plant, animal products and minerals, relied on by 80% of the world population. A herbarium is a store of dried, mounted plant specimens used for naming, identification and classification, confirming a plant's identity and teaching.
B(iii)
Pharmacopoeias set standards and quality specifications for pharmaceutical preparations as reference material for countries (USP, BP, African Pharmacopoeia, Indian Pharmacopoeia). Publications are research disseminated in journals or books stating the problem, methods, key findings and conclusions.
B(iv)
Each example above (digitalis, cinchona, poppy, rauwolfia) is traced to a named species and family through these sources.
C(i)
It identifies the genuine plant and its constituents (e.g. species named with the active compound), which is the first element in the systematic description of a drug.
C(ii)
Each records different things: tradition, preserved specimens, official standards and research findings.
C(iii)
Folk medicine includes knowledge explicable or inexplicable, and herbaria are only reference material; the limits of pharmacopoeias are that they serve as source material for adaptation by each country.
C(iv)
Drugs from higher plants are abundant but those from algae, lichens and mosses are limited; marine sources offer interesting activities;.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Grains of paradise are the seeds of Aframomum melegueta Roscoe (K. Schum.) (syn. Amomum melegueta), Zingiberaceae; also called Guinea grains, melegueta pepper, ossame, fom wisa and alligator pepper; Ataare/Ata ire (Yoruba), Ose oji (Igbo), Chitta (Hausa).
A(ii)
Native to the West African coast around the Gulf of Guinea: Ghana (a major producer), Nigeria, Cote d'Ivoire, Liberia, Togo, Cameroon and Sierra Leone, in warm humid forested or swampy habitats.
A(iii)
A perennial herb with a tufted leafy stem up to 1.5 m, grown at 20-30° C with 1,500-2,000 mm rainfall in well-drained loamy soil of pH 5.5-7, from rhizome cuttings (2-3 nodes, 5-8 cm deep) or seeds; flowering 10-12 months after planting and fruits mature 5-6 months later; pods are harvested when reddish-brown or dry, opened, seeds separated, washed, shade-dried to 10-12% moisture and stored in airtight containers in a cool dry place (vacuum sealing or refrigeration for long-term).
A(iv)
Fruit ovoid, pointed, about 10 cm long with many seeds; seeds hard, reddish-brown (to blackish-brown), about 2-5 mm, inverted sub-pyramidal and four-sided with rounded angles, testa minutely papillose, with a pale fibrous funicle forming a projecting point; fracture short and brittle; crushed seed faintly to strongly aromatic and peppery; taste intensely pungent; internally resembles cardamom seed.
A(v)
Testa of thick-walled polygonal cells with reddish-brown tannin pigment and a papillose surface; parenchyma with oval starch grains with a central hilum and aromatic oil cells; sclerenchymatous fibrous layer; oil globules; abundant white starchy perisperm around a small ovoid yellowish horny endosperm containing a pale embryo; sparse unicellular non-glandular trichomes and calcium oxalate prisms or rosettes.
A(vi)
About 0.5% volatile oil (principally β-caryophyllene, α-humulene and their epoxides); paradol (a yellowish, extremely pungent oil resembling gingerol whose pungency is not destroyed by caustic potash), shogaol and gingerol; also flavonoids, tannins, sterols, triterpenes, resins and phenolic acids (caffeic, ferulic).
B(i)
Papillose reddish-brown testa, sub-pyramidal seeds with a funicle point, intense pungency, starchy perisperm around horny endosperm, and resemblance to cardamom seed internally.
B(ii)
The pungency of paradol is not destroyed by caustic potash (unlike gingerol in ginger).
B(iii)
Allied or similar drugs named are cardamom, black cardamom (Amomum subulatum), black pepper (Piper nigrum), Capsicum spp. and other Aframomum species.
C(i)
Stimulant, condiment, domestic remedy for toothache, veterinary use and alcoholic liquors; ethnomedical use for stomach upset, diarrhoea, inflammation and pain; commercial oleoresin, essential oil and paradol; excessive consumption leads to ocular toxicity; stored in airtight containers in a cool dry place.
C(ii)
Cardamom (Elettaria cardamomum) is in the same family and shares a similar aromatic profile, and grains of paradise resemble cardamom seed internally; in ginger the pungent gingerol is destroyed by baryta water, whereas paradol, which resembles gingerol, is not destroyed by caustic potash.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Dried gummy exudate of Sterculia urens (Sterculiaceae), produced in India, Pakistan and Africa; synonyms Karaya gum, Indian tragacanth, Bassora tragacanth; formerly regarded as an adulterant or inferior substitute of tragacanth, now superior in many respects and official in the BP.
A(ii)
Collected twice a year (April-June and September), the first collection giving the best gum; blazes up to a square foot are cut in larger trees and smaller trees are tapped, the flow being greatest in the first 24 hours and continuing several days; dried irregular masses are picked off and taken to village purchase centres for Bombay merchants, who remove bark and sort into two grades; graded further in Europe and the USA by colour and foreign organic matter (especially bark) and sold as granulated crystal or fine powder; over-tapping is reducing the tree population and in vitro propagation (seedling and nodal explants, somatic embryogenesis) is being researched.
A(iii)
Good quality gum occurs as irregular, almost colourless, translucent, striated masses of up to 25 g or more; medium grades have a pinkish tinge; lower grades are very dark with much bark; low solubility in water but swells many times its volume; fine powder gives a homogeneous dispersion while coarser granules give a discontinuous grainy dispersion.
A(iv)
Partial hydrolysis yields D-galactose, L-rhamnose, D-galacturonic acid, aldobiouronic acid, an acid trisaccharide and acetic acid; uronic acid represents 37% of the gum; contains no starch.
B(i)
Marked odour of acetic acid on hydrolysis with 5% phosphoric acid (volatile acidity not less than 14%, versus 2% for tragacanth); boiled with potash it turns slightly brownish (tragacanth gives canary yellow); stains pink with ruthenium red; contains no starch.
B(ii)
Low solubility in water, swelling many times its original volume.
B(iii)
Standards: official in the BP; a volatile acidity of not less than 14% is stated.
B(iv)
Detected as an adulterant or substitute of tragacanth by gel formation in alcoholic solution or by the acidity test; absence of starch and the potash colour also distinguish it.
B(v)
Two grades by merchants (bark removed), then graded further by colour and the presence of foreign organic matter such as bark; also classed by form: granulated crystal or fine powder.
C(i)
Granular grades as bulk laxative; powdered gum in lozenges, pastes and denture fixative powders; adhesive for stoma appliances; combined with frangula in granular form as stimulant and bulk laxative.
C(ii)
Compared with tragacanth: sterculia has volatile acidity of not less than 14% (tragacanth 2%), turns slightly brownish with potash (tragacanth canary yellow), contains no starch and stains pink with ruthenium red, and swells strongly while being only slightly soluble.

A(i)
Determine size, shape and arrangement of cells and tissues, the form and chemical nature of cell contents and of cell walls (phloroglucinol + HCl for lignified walls; chlor-zinc-iodine for cellulose, lignified walls and starch).
A(ii)
Average number of palisade cells beneath each epidermal cell; clear leaf in chloral hydrate, trace four epidermal cells with a camera lucida and count palisade cells beneath (count if more than half lies within), divide by 4, repeat for five groups and average; sufficiently constant to separate species of one genus in some instances.
A(iii)
Vein-islet number is the number of small green areas surrounded by veinlets per sq. mm midway between midrib and margin; independent of leaf size and age (Azadirachta indica 10-18, Momordica charantia 7-12, Nicotiana tabacum 12-20); vein-termination number counts ultimate free veinlet endings per sq. mm; both counted in 1 mm squares and averaged over four adjacent squares.
A(iv)
Stomatal number is average stomata per sq. mm of epidermis (varies with age, size and conditions); stomatal index SI = S/(E+S) × 100 where S is stomata and E epidermal cells per unit area; constant for a species and used on entire or powdered leaf.
B(i)
Powder cleared in chloral hydrate, stained with phloroglucinol and HCl, measured with a calibrated eyepiece micrometer against a stage micrometer; length and width of about 25 fibres averaged; same technique for starch-grain diameter, trichome length and stone-cell size.
B(ii)
Stage micrometer: slide 7.6 × 2.5 cm with a 1 mm scale divided into 0.01 mm (10 µm) parts; eyepiece micrometer is a linear or squared scale calibrated for each optical combination.
B(iii)
Epidermal cell shape, size and wall; stomata form and distribution; trichome form and abundance; mesophyll palisade/spongy arrangement; collenchyma, sclerenchyma, oil or mucilage cells, ducts; calcium oxalate crystals; reticulate venation (dicots) versus parallel (monocots).
B(iv)
Senna: isobilateral leaflets, paracytic stomata, prismatic crystals, non-lignified trichomes; digitalis: wavy thick-walled epidermis, uniseriate glandular trichomes, no crystals.
C(i)
They help distinguish closely related leaves in powder and entire form, because stomatal index and palisade ratio stay constant for a species.
C(ii)
Stomatal number varies with leaf age, size and environment, whereas stomatal index is constant for a species.
C(iii)
Requires clearing, camera lucida tracing and repeated counts; the palisade ratio is only constant in some instances for species of one genus.
C(iv)
Quantitative counts give objective discrimination but need more time and equipment than qualitative inspection;.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Classification arranges substances into smaller groups on the basis of similarities and dissimilarities; crude drugs come from a large variety of natural sources (almost all parts of plants and animals, plus exudates, juices and extracts), and are classified for ease of study, description and storage.
A(ii)
Alphabetical, taxonomical, morphological, pharmacological/therapeutic and chemical/biogenetic systems.
A(iii)
Drugs are arranged by Latin or vernacular names, as used by pharmacopoeias and other official publications.
A(iv)
Drugs are arranged by the plants they come from (classes, orders, families, genera, species); e.g. plants of Solanaceae are grouped as Solanaceous drugs.
B(i)
Drugs are grouped by the morphology of the parts used: organised drugs (leaves, flowers, fruits, seeds, bark, rhizomes, roots) and unorganised drugs (dried latices, extracts, gums, oils, fats, waxes and resins).
B(ii)
Drugs with similar action are grouped irrespective of morphology, taxonomy or chemistry; e.g. anticancer activity of Podophyllum (rhizome), Catharanthus (leaves) and Ginseng (root).
B(iii)
Drugs are grouped by principal chemical constituents or biosynthetic pathways, e.g. drugs containing volatile oils or alkaloids are grouped together irrespective of activity.
B(iv)
Alphabetical: simplest, suitable for quick reference. Taxonomical: shows natural relationship/phylogeny and similar constituents (Solanaceous drugs contain tropane alkaloids). Morphological: useful for identifying drugs and detecting adulterants. Pharmacological: gives information on activity, ideal for pharmacists. Chemical: ideal for study and storage because action depends on constituents.
C(i)
Because crude drugs are so varied, grouping makes study, description and storage manageable and each system serves a different purpose (reference, phylogeny, identification, activity, or chemistry).
C(ii)
Alphabetical: gives no information on interrelationship, so unrelated drugs are grouped together. Morphological: unsuitable for storage, and similar parts of different plants differ chemically (cascara bark has anthraquinone glycosides, cinnamon bark volatile oil, cinchona bark alkaloids).
C(iii)
Pharmacological: possible contamination in storage and incompatibility in formulation if used carelessly. Chemical: drugs with several active principles of different phytochemical groups are hard to categorise, e.g. liquorice (flavonoids and polysaccharides) and ginseng (steroidal saponins and peptides).
C(iv)
No single system is complete: each gains one benefit (simplicity, phylogeny, ease of identification, activity information or chemical grouping) at the cost of the limitations above;.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Rauwolfia (Indian snakeroot) consists of the dried rhizome and roots of Rauwolfia serpentina L. Benth. ex Kurz (Apocynaceae); another account adds the dried root and rhizome of R. vomitoria Afz., the common African Rauwolfia.
A(ii)
R. serpentina is a small shrub found in India, Pakistan, Burma, Thailand and Java (also Myanmar, Malaysia, Indonesia); geographical source influences alkaloid content and India and Pakistan are preferred; R. vomitoria is a tree widely distributed in tropical Africa from the west coast to Mozambique; limitation of Indian exports shifted supply to Thailand.
A(iii)
Collected mainly from wild plants, leaving some roots in the ground for regeneration; the drug is cut transversely and dried; cultivation by nodal and cell culture is encouraged because wild plants are depleted, root collection is destructive, seed viability is low and the plant is endangered.
A(iv)
Roots rarely branched; bark of older pieces readily falls off leaving patches of exposed wood; longitudinal wrinkles on young and ridges on old pieces; rhizome differs from root by a small central pith and occasional aerial stems; cylindrical or slightly tapering tortuous (wavy) pieces 2-10 cm long and 5-22 mm in diameter; greyish-yellow or brown; fracture short; odour slight, decreasing with age; taste bitter.
A(v)
Cork in 2-8 zones where small suberised unlignified cells alternate with larger lignified cells; secondary cortex parenchymatous with starch; phloem parenchymatous with sieve tubes and calcium oxalate crystals or prisms, sclerenchyma absent; xylem totally lignified with 3-6 growth rings; medullary rays contain starch; secondary xylem of vessels, fibres and parenchyma, vessels under 57 µm in diameter.
A(vi)
0.7-2.4% indole alkaloids (at least 40 alkaloids): ajmaline group (ajmaline, ajmalinine, ajmalicine) and serpentine group (serpentine, serpentinine, yellow); most important are reserpine and rescinnamine; also phytosterols, fatty acids, unsaturated alcohols, dextrose, sucrose, fumaric acid and a fluorescent substance; African Rauwolfia has additional alkaloids (reserpoxidine, seredine, alstonine, yohimbine) and is used commercially to extract reserpine (about 2.0%).
B(i)
Wavy (tortuous) shape of the pieces, short fracture, bitter taste, cork zones with alternating suberised and lignified cells, absence of sclerenchyma in the phloem, vessels under 57 µm and 3-6 xylem growth rings.
B(ii)
The alkaloid content (0.7-2.4%) is the stated chemical measure.
B(iii)
Eighty-six Rauwolfia species are known, many used to adulterate R. serpentina; allied drugs include R. vomitoria and R. tetraphylla, and roots/rhizomes of R. tetraphylla and R. nitida have been substituted; detection is by the absence of phloem sclerenchyma and vessel diameter under 57 µm in R. serpentina.
C(i)
Reserpine for hypertension and mental disorders, rescinnamine for hypertension, ajmaline for cardiac arrhythmias, ajmalicine for blood circulatory diseases; Rauwolfia preparations lower blood pressure and depress the nervous system.
C(ii)
R. vomitoria (African species) closely resembles R. serpentina microscopically but has a large proportion of sclereids in the phloem, pericycle and phelloderm and vessels under 180 µm (versus under 57 µm); it contains extra alkaloids (reserpoxidine, seredine, alstonine, yohimbine).

questions.question:

A(i) Biological source
A(ii) Method of collection or preparation
A(iii) Description and physical characters
A(iv) Chemical constituents
B(i) Chemical tests
B(ii) Solubility
B(iii) Standards
B(iv) Tests for purity or adulteration
B(v) Basis of commercial grades or classification
C(i) Uses
C(ii) Distinction from Siam benzoin and Palembang benzoin
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A balsamic resin obtained from the incised stem of Styrax benzoin Dryand; produced from cultivated trees in Sumatra; a pathological product formed by incision and fungal attack.
A(ii)
Seeds are grown with rice, which protects the young trees to maturity at 7 years; triangular incisions are made on the trunk 40 cm apart and the bark between scraped off; the first secretion is amorphous and sticky and is rejected; incisions are increased every 3 months and a harder, crystalline secretion is obtained; the drug is scraped every 6 weeks (outer layer finest, next intermediate, innermost lowest quality, darker with bark fragments) and the process continues with fresh incisions higher up the tree.
A(iii)
Brittle masses with opaque whitish or reddish tears embedded in a reddish-brown or greyish-brown resinous matrix; odour agreeable and balsamic but not marked; taste slightly acrid; on heating, white fumes of cinnamic and benzoic acids condense as white crystals on a cool surface.
A(iv)
20-30% free cinnamic and benzoic acids (cinnamic acid about twice as much); esters of cinnamic and benzoic acids; triterpenoid acids such as 19-hydroxyoleanolic acid and 6-hydroxyoleanolic acid.
B(i)
An odour of benzaldehyde on oxidation with KMnO₄ (cinnamic acid); yellow colour with alcoholic ferric chloride; sublimation of white crystals on heating.
B(ii)
Alcohol-insoluble extractive values are applicable to resinous drugs such as benzoin and myrrh.
B(iii)
Standards: the alcohol-insoluble extractive applies to benzoin.
B(iv)
Adulterant: dammar gum, a copal resin from Hopea, Shorea and Vateria species (Dipterocarpaceae) used in varnishes.
B(v)
The three qualities (outer, intermediate, inner) are blended in different proportions to give commercial benzoin grades, the worst grade being abundant in resinous matrix; Palembang benzoin is an inferior variety.
C(i)
Expectorant, antiseptic, ingredient of Friars' balsam and odourant.
C(ii)
Siam benzoin (Styrax tonkinensis) lacks cinnamic acid, so gives no benzaldehyde odour with KMnO₄ and gives a green colour with alcoholic FeCl₃ (Sumatra gives yellow); Palembang benzoin is inferior, light in weight with an irregular porous fracture and few small tears in reddish-brown resin, used as a natural source of benzoic acid.

A(i)
Senna (Folia sennae, Alexandrian, Cassia senna) consists of the dried leaflets of Cassia senna L. (C. acutifolia Delile), family Fabaceae.
A(ii)
Indigenous to Somalia, Arabia, Sind and the Punjab and cultivated in South India (Tinnevelly); also native to Egypt, Sudan, Nigeria, Nubia, India, Pakistan and China; the Alexandrian and Tinnevelly varieties are of desert origin.
A(iii)
A low-branching shrub (about 3 feet) with a straight woody stem and yellow flowers; leaflets have stout petiolules, an entire margin, an asymmetric base and an acute apex; odour faint and taste bitterish and unpleasant.
A(iv)
Isobilateral leaflets with walled epidermal cells; non-lignified trichomes; paracytic stomata; prismatic calcium oxalate crystals.
A(v)
Anthraquinone glycosides: sennosides A, B, C and D, with sennidin A and sennidin B.
B(i)
Asymmetric leaflet base with acute apex and entire margin, isobilateral structure, paracytic stomata, non-lignified trichomes and prismatic crystals; stomatal index, palisade ratio and vein-islet number are the quantitative leaf constants available for closely related leaves.
B(ii)
The anthraquinone derivatives of senna respond to Borntrager's test (as for cascara and frangula).
B(iii)
Adulterants: Cassia obovata (Italian senna), Arabian senna, Mecca senna, Bombay senna; substitutes: Argel leaves (Solenostoma argel, Asclepiadaceae), Tephrosia apollinea (Fabaceae) and Globularia alypum (Globulariaceae); broken C. obovata leaf mixed with broken senna is recognised by the papillose cells of the lower epidermis; Alexandria senna substituted by Arabian senna is also cited.
C(i)
Treatment of constipation (stimulates the intestinal coat and produces purgation), bowel clearing before colonoscopy, and use in irritable bowel syndrome, haemorrhoids and weight loss; derived products include Dakin's herb tea, Black draught, Dr. Caldwell's Senna Laxative, Garfield's Tea and Swiss Kriss.
C(ii)
Cassia obovata (Italian senna), cultivated in Italy, has constituents similar to senna (total oxymethylanthraquinones 3.8%, about equal in activity) and is recognised by the papillose cells of its lower epidermis.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Air-dried gummy exudate, flowing naturally or from incisions in the trunk and branches of Astragalus gummifer Labillardiere (Fabaceae) and certain other Astragalus species from Western Asia; the principal species is A. microcephalus with smaller amounts of A. gummifer and A. kurdicus; Persian tragacanth is used in the UK, Anatolian in Europe, and 'Persian' denotes the better grades from Iran and Turkish Kurdistan.
A(ii)
Thorny shrubs at 1000-3000 m, usually tapped in their second year; earth is removed to 5 cm depth, the exposed part incised with a thin sharp knife, a wedge-shaped piece of wood forces the incision open and is left 12-24 hours, and gum is collected after 2 days; burning the top of the plant after incision gives more gum but low-quality, reddish, dirty gum and may kill the plant. The gum is preformed: pith and medullary ray cell walls change to gum (gummosis) and exude immediately after injury.
A(iii)
Flattened ribbons up to 25 mm long and 12 mm wide with ridges (temporary stoppage of flow) and fine edges parallel to the incision margin; white or very pale yellowish, translucent and horny; very short fracture; odourless with little taste; swells to a gelatinous mass in water with only a small portion dissolving.
A(iv)
Tragacanthin (water-soluble) and bassorin (water-insoluble), both insoluble in alcohol and separable by filtering a very dilute mucilage; the best grade has the least tragacanthin; hydrolysis gives galacturonic acid, D-galactopyranose, L-arabinofuranose and D-xylopyranose; methoxylation and bassorin content determine viscosity (heating and powdering demethoxylate the gum and reduce viscosity); peroxidase is usually considered absent but has been detected in genuine commercial samples; starch content is high.
B(i)
Blue points appear on a fragment soaked in water on adding dilute iodine solution (distinction from Smyrna tragacanth, which has more starch) and a green colour with strong iodine; it gives a precipitate with lead acetate (acacia does not); boiling with potash gives a canary yellow colour (sterculia gives slightly brownish); volatile acidity about 2%.
B(ii)
Swells to a gelatinous mass in water, only a small portion dissolving; tragacanthin dissolves in water and bassorin does not; both are insoluble in alcohol.
B(iii)
Standards: because it is used as a food additive, precise botanical specification of the species and strict analytical procedures are required; the best grades form the official drug.
B(iv)
Adulterants/allied gums: non-pharmaceutical grades (hog gum or hog tragacanth), chiral gum of Indian commerce, Sterculia gum (detected by gel formation in alcoholic solution or an acidity test) and insoluble Shiraz gum (distinguished by the oxidase reaction and absence of starch).
B(v)
Grades are set by exporters and middlemen; the best grades form the official drugs while lower grades go to food, textile and other industries; Persian (better, Iran and Turkish Kurdistan) versus Anatolian; the gum is expensive because of short supply and the extra treatment and tests needed to meet the official standard.
C(i)
Suspending agent for insoluble powders, binding agent in pills and tablets, and in the food industry.
C(ii)
Acacia is slowly produced after injury while tragacanth is preformed and exudes immediately; tragacanth gives a lead acetate precipitate and blue points with iodine, acacia gives neither; Sterculia gum gives volatile acidity of not less than 14% (2% for tragacanth), turns slightly brownish with potash (tragacanth canary yellow) and contains no starch.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The origin or locality of the plant drug, i.e. where it is commonly found or mostly cultivated; many plants grow well in several localities with similar climate.
A(ii)
Suitability of the plant to the environment, economic factors in production, government policies on export of raw materials, political considerations, and national or international restrictions.
A(iii)
Indian limitation of crude rauwolfia root export moved supply to Thailand; change in legal cultivation of medicinal cannabis in Nigeria moved sourcing to Malawi; Mexican diosgenin nationalised, prices rose, makers turned to hecogenin (sisal) and solasodine (Solanum).
A(iv)
Cinnamon from Sri Lanka now cultivated successfully in Seychelles (it has become a weed) and grows well in West Africa but is not commercially used; the USA moved from domestic Solanaceous drugs and digitalis to Bulgaria, Hungary and South America; scarcity of Sudan acacia led to Nigerian gum; Jamaican ginger decline led to African and Chinese ginger; Brazilian ipecacuanha shortage led to Cartagena, Nicaragua and Panama varieties.
B(i)
To avoid overexploitation, national and international restrictions are placed on collection from the wild, e.g. CITES lists all Aloe species except A. vera, causing shortage of aloes from the usual species.
B(ii)
Geographical source influences alkaloid content: rauwolfia from India and Pakistan is preferred by manufacturers; senna is cultivated in Tinnevelly; Kordofan acacia is the best gum and Senegal and Nigeria also give good gum.
B(iii)
Capsicum varieties (Sierra Leone, Nyasaland, Zanzibar), cardamom varieties (Aleppy, Mysore, Malabar, Mangalore), ginger varieties (Jamaican, Nigerian, Chinese, Cochin) and opium varieties (Turkish, Iranian, Indian).
B(iv)
Political instability can affect availability of crude drugs once peculiar to one location, as in the diosgenin example.
C(i)
It shapes supply, price and sometimes composition (alkaloid content), so buyers and pharmacists need to know it.
C(ii)
Economic, political and legal pressures and the suitability of other regions drive the change, as in the examples above.
C(iii)
Supply from one region can fail through policy, instability or protection laws, forcing substitution by varieties of different quality (e.g. Nigerian ginger is darker, more pungent, less aromatic and lower in oil than Jamaican).
C(iv)
Protection of wild species (CITES) preserves plants but creates shortage; cultivation elsewhere secures supply but may change quality;.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Cardamom consists of the dried, nearly ripe fruits (capsules) of Elettaria cardamomum Maton var. minuscula Burkill (Zingiberaceae); synonyms Capalaga, Malabar cardamums, Ilachi, Ailum; known as the 'Queen of Spices'; the seeds are the part used and are kept in the fruit until required.
A(ii)
Principal producers are Sri Lanka, southern India and Guatemala; it grows wild in the forests of southern India, is cultivated in Ceylon, and the Malabar coast is the source of the official drug.
A(iii)
Mainly from cultivated plants (propagation by seedlings or vegetatively, the latter risking mosaic or katte virus); the reed-like plant, 4 m or more high, has fruits on a raceme ripening at different times, so each fruit is cut with short-bladed scissors when nearly ripe and before splitting; most of the crop is collected October-December; fruits are dried slowly outdoors or in a curing house (rapid drying splits fruits; sun-bleaching or sulphur-bleaching improves appearance; green curing may use a 10-minute soak in 2% sodium carbonate); calyx and stalk are removed and fruits graded by sieves into longs, mediums, shorts and tiny.
A(iv)
Inferior, ovoid or oblong, three-sided capsule 1-2 cm long, greenish to pale buff/yellowish with a dry woody pericarp, shortly beaked apex and rounded base; three loculi with membranous septa, axile placentation and a double row of seeds in each loculus, the seeds adhering as one mass (about 70% of the weight); each seed about 3-4 mm long, angular, covered by a colourless membranous aril, testa dark reddish-brown (paler if unripe) with 6-8 transverse wrinkles, a raphe groove and hilum depression; odour strongly aromatic and taste pleasantly aromatic and somewhat pungent. Varieties: Aleppy, Mysore, Malabar and Mangalore.
A(v)
Thin yellow aril of collapsed oil-containing cells; testa of an outer epidermis of longitudinally elongated cells, 1-2 layers of parenchyma, a layer of large volatile-oil cells, flattened parenchyma, and an inner epidermis of radially elongated, strongly thickened reddish-brown sclerenchymatous cells with a bowl-shaped lumen holding a silica nodule (also forming the operculum); perisperm of parenchyma packed with minute starch grains about 4 µm wide with a small prismatic calcium oxalate crystal in each cell; endosperm and embryo thin-walled and rich in protein.
A(vi)
Powder: cardamom pericarps (husks) used to adulterate powdered drug are identified by pitted fibres, spiral vessels of the fibrovascular bundles and abundant empty parenchymatous cells.
A(vii)
Seed yields 2.8-6.2% volatile oil (BP not less than 4.0%), with up to 50% starch, 1-10% fixed oil and calcium oxalate; α-terpineol and 1,8-cineole are shown as constituents.
B(i)
Seeds kept in the fruit; three loculi with axile placentation; transversely wrinkled testa with aril; silica nodule in the inner epidermal cells; perisperm with 4 µm starch grains and prismatic crystals; strongly aromatic odour.
B(ii)
Iodine staining of cut seeds shows starch in the perisperm while the endosperm and embryo are free of starch; volatile oil content (BP not less than 4.0%).
B(iii)
Pericarps/husks are used to adulterate powdered cardamom and are recognised by pitted fibres, spiral vessels and empty parenchyma; allied or substitute drugs are the long wild native cardamom (var. major) and Amomum aromaticum / A. subulatum.
C(i)
Flavouring agent in curries, cakes and liqueurs, Gahwa (cardamom coffee) in the Middle East, and aromatic carminative; ethnomedicinal anti-microbial, anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antispasmodic and gastroprotective uses; seeds are kept inside the fruit until needed to prevent loss of volatile oil.
C(ii)
Long wild native cardamoms of Sri Lanka (E. cardamomum var. major Thwaites) are much longer, sometimes about 4 cm, with dark brown, coarsely striated pericarps and an oil used in liqueurs; Amomum aromaticum (Bengal cardamom, from Bengal and Assam) and A. subulatum (Nepal or Greater cardamom, from Nepal, Bengal, Sikkim, Assam) are the other allied drugs.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Cola nitida (Vent.) Schott & Endlicher is the kola nut (cotyledons of the seeds), of the mallow family Malvaceae, sub-family Sterculiaceae; synonyms Cola vera, Sterculia nitida (Ventenat), Cola acuminata (Engler); Obi (Yoruba), Oji (Igbo), Goro (Hausa), Oka (Ghana).
A(ii)
A large evergreen tree native to the tropical rainforests of West Africa (Nigeria, Cameroon, Ghana, Sierra Leone); cultivated in tropical South and Central America, the West Indies, Sri Lanka, Malaysia (also Brazil and Java); grows in hot lowland forest with rainfall over 8 months at 23-28° C, mainly between 6 and 7° north.
A(iii)
Propagated traditionally by seed and now commonly by cuttings (preferred for the market-favoured white-seeded strain); in southern Nigeria seeds germinate in boxes or polythene bags of top soil with sand or sawdust, or in nursery beds, within about 80 days, and seedlings are planted out at 6-8 months at 7-10 cm depth (avoid over-watering because of fungal infections); trees bear after 4-5 years and are fully productive in 7-10 years; ripe yellow/brown pods are picked and nuts extracted; dried nuts are stored for several months in airtight containers in a cool dry place.
A(iv)
Hard, reddish-brown to dark brown, shiny, smooth seeds, ovoid, oblong or plano-convex, 2.5-5 cm long and 2-4 cm wide (another account: flat on one side, curved on the other, wedge-shaped or irregularly six-sided), paler internally with a uniform section; fresh seeds taste bitter and astringent (not perceived in dry seed); odour faintly aromatic when fresh.
A(v)
Testa epidermis of polygonal cells with straight walls and reddish-brown pigment granules; thin-walled parenchyma of testa and cotyledons loaded with starch; irregular, thick-walled lignified sclereids beneath the epidermis; fibrovascular bundles with sclerenchymatous fibres in the cotyledons; scattered oil cells with fixed-oil droplets; calcium oxalate prisms or rosettes in parenchyma; caffeine and theobromine stored in parenchyma cells.
A(vi)
Seed contains 13.5% water, 9.5% crude protein, 1.4% fat, 45% sugar and starch, 7.0% cellulose, 3.8% tannin, 3% ash, caffeine 2.8% and theobromine 0.05%; kolatin and kolatein (an oxidase enzyme) are also listed.
B(i)
Reddish-brown shiny ovoid or plano-convex seeds with uniform section, starch-loaded parenchyma, sclereids beneath the epidermis, oil cells, calcium oxalate crystals and caffeine in parenchyma cells.
C(i)
Nerve stimulant (caffeine and theobromine); used in energy drinks, capsules, herbal teas, tinctures (digestion, mild diuretic) and for cough and wounds; historically in cola beverages; extracts used in creams, lotions and shampoos for antioxidant properties; stored in airtight containers in a cool dry place.
C(ii)
Varieties are distinguished mainly by nut colour: black kola (dark brown or black, among the most common), red kola (reddish-brown) and white kola (lighter, pinkish or yellowish); the colour differences are associated with slight differences in taste and chemical composition.

A(i)
Cinnamon (Ceylon cinnamon, Dalchini, Cortex Cinnamoni) is the dried bark of the shoots of Cinnamomum zeylanicum Blume (Lauraceae), grown on cut stock and freed from the outer cork and underlying cortex/parenchyma.
A(ii)
Cultivated mostly in Sri Lanka (formerly Ceylon), India, Seychelles, Madagascar, Jamaica and Brazil.
A(iii)
Seeds are planted and grown 2-3 years, then cut near the ground so that 5-6 shoots grow from the stump (kept vertical by pruning); after about 18 months, when shoots are about 3 m high and 2 cm thick, they are harvested and trimmed, and after a few hours of fermentation the bark is removed with a non-ferrous knife; the bark is stretched and the outer cork and cortex scraped off; pieces are placed one inside another to form compound quills, dried in the open air away from direct sunlight.
A(iv)
Part used is the bark, in quills (single, double, compound of 10-40 pieces) about 20 cm long and 1-4 mm thick; outer surface yellowish-brown with shining longitudinal wavy lines (pericyclic fibres) and scars/holes of leaves and twigs; inner surface dark brown with fine longitudinal striations; fracture short and splintery; odour fragrant and aromatic; taste sweet, agreeable and warm.
A(v)
Cork and cortex absent; the outermost layer is the pericycle of 3-4 layers of lignified sclereids with lignified pericyclic fibres 1000-2500 µm long; primary phloem not distinguishable; secondary phloem has phloem parenchyma (oil cells, mucilage cells, starch grains under 10 µm, acicular calcium oxalate crystals 5-8 µm, tannins), phloem fibres (lignified, more abundant in inner bark, under 30 µm wide, 200-600 µm long) and medullary rays 7-14 cells high with numerous acicular crystals.
A(vi)
Volatile oil over 1.2% (65-75% cinnamic aldehyde, 4-10% phenols mainly eugenol, hydrocarbons, ketones, alcohols, esters); another account gives 0.5-1% oil with about 90% cinnamaldehyde plus ethyl cinnamate, β-caryophyllene, linalool and methyl chavicol; also phlobatannins, mucilage (1.6-2.9%), calcium oxalate and starch.
B(i)
Quill form, yellowish-brown colour with shining wavy lines, short splintery fracture, aromatic odour and sweet warm taste; microscopically absence of cork and cortex, pericycle sclereids and fibres, starch grains under 10 µm and acicular calcium oxalate crystals (starch grains within sclereids are noted as diagnostic in cinnamon and cassia).
B(ii)
Powder + 50% KOH gives needle crystals of potassium eugenate; powder + Sudan III examined under the microscope shows orange-red oil globules, indicating volatile oil.
B(iii)
Adulterants/allied drugs: jungle cinnamon, cinnamon chips (pieces of untrimmed bark), Java cinnamon, Cayenne cinnamon (older branches of C. zeylanicum) and C. loureirii; starch-grain diameter (about 10 µm in C. cassia) is useful microscopically for detecting adulterants.
C(i)
Carminative in flatulence, distension and mild digestive upsets (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea); mild astringent; flavouring agent (also in astringent powders and tinctures); warming stimulant; antispasmodic in mild cramp-like GIT disorders; cinnamic aldehyde used as sedative and analgesic; hypolipidaemic and germicidal properties.
C(ii)
Cassia bark is the dried bark of the stem and branches of Cinnamomum cassia Blume with outer cork and cortex partly present, from south-eastern China; channelled pieces or single quills up to 10 cm long, 1-2 cm wide, 1-3 mm thick, darker with patches of grey cork, coarser odour, slightly sweet and more astringent taste, short granular fracture; cork and cortex with sclereids present; starch grains over 10 µm and phloem fibres 30-40 µm wide; oil about 1.2% with at least 85% cinnamic aldehyde and no eugenol; mucilage 10%; uses antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, spice and flavourant.

A(i)
Obtained by incision from the trunk of Myroxylon balsamum (L.) Harms var. balsamum H.B.K. (Fabaceae), a tree found in Colombia and Venezuela.
A(ii)
V-shaped incisions are made in the bark and the balsam is received in a calabash at the angle of the V; the yield is 8-10 kg per tree.
A(iii)
Freshly collected, it is a soft, yellow, semi-solid paste that solidifies and hardens to a hard, brown, brittle solid on keeping; taste and odour aromatic and fragrant; acidic to litmus.
A(iv)
About 30% resin derived from resin alcohols combined with cinnamic and benzoic acids; 12-15% free cinnamic acid; about 8% free benzoic acid; esters such as benzyl benzoate and benzyl cinnamate; vanillin; resinotannols.
B(i)
Gives a green colour with ferric chloride (resinotannol); an odour of benzaldehyde is produced on oxidation with KMnO₄ (cinnamic acid); microscopic examination shows crystals of cinnamic acid, amorphous resin and vegetable debris.
B(ii)
Almost entirely soluble in alcohol.
C(i)
Antiseptic, added to cough mixtures, flavourant and odourant.
C(ii)
Balsam of Peru is from M. balsamum var. pereirae, a pathological product from stripped bark, a reddish-brown fluid with 45-75% esters and used as antiseptic dressing, parasiticide and for catarrh and diarrhoea; Tolu is a semi-solid becoming hard and is rich in free cinnamic and benzoic acids.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Ginger is the scraped or unscraped rhizome of Zingiber officinale Roscoe (Zingiberaceae); deprived of its root it is known commercially as unbleached ginger.
A(ii)
Indigenous to south-eastern Asia and cultivated in many tropical countries including the West Indies, India, China and West African countries such as Nigeria.
A(iii)
Grown vegetatively from rhizome pieces each bearing a bud, planted in holes; planting March-April and harvest December-January; needs subtropical temperatures, annual rainfall over 1.98 m, clayey loamy soil and fertilizer; unscraped ginger may be converted to scraped ginger by boiling in water, peeling, washing and sun-drying for about 8 days, giving a whiter product.
A(iv)
Unscraped rhizome is brownish because of the outer cork; scraped rhizome is light yellow (no cork); 7-15 cm long and 1-1.5 cm broad with branches 1-3 cm long; longitudinal striations; fracture short with projecting fibrovascular bundles; odour aromatic and agreeable; taste pungent.
A(v)
Unscraped rhizome shows a cork zone (outer irregularly arranged cells, inner radially arranged cells); outer cortex of flattened parenchyma and inner cortex of normal parenchyma, both rich in starch, with numerous oil cells holding yellow-brown oleo-resin and non-lignified fibrous vascular bundles (no marked lignin reaction with phloroglucinol and conc. HCl); a starch-free single-layered endodermis encloses the stele, which has a ring of vascular bundles beside the endodermis, scattered bundles, starch-bearing parenchyma and numerous oil cells; cork is absent from scraped ginger.
A(vi)
The presence of non-lignified vessels in powders of ginger (and rhubarb) is cited as indicating adulteration, and the lycopodium spore method is used to evaluate powdered ginger.
A(vii)
Volatile oil 1-2% (over 50 constituents including zingiberene, zingiberol, zingerone; monoterpenes and sesquiterpene hydrocarbons) responsible for aroma but not pungency; pungency is due to gingerol, an oily liquid of homologous phenols ([6]-, [8]-, [10]-gingerol), which is decomposed to zingerone (pungent but sweet-aromatic) by baryta water, Ba(OH)₂.H₂O; also 5-8% resinous matter, about 56% starch and mucilage.
B(i)
Pungent taste with aromatic odour; scraped (light yellow) versus unscraped (brownish) appearance; short fracture with projecting fibrovascular bundles; oil cells with oleo-resin, abundant starch, non-lignified bundles and a starch-free endodermis; alcohol-soluble extractive of not less than 4.5%.
B(ii)
Gingerol is decomposed to zingerone by baryta water (Ba(OH)₂.H₂O); vascular bundles give no marked lignin reaction with phloroglucinol and conc. HCl.
B(iii)
Exhausted ginger is mixed with starch and coloured to the proper shade; powdered or exhausted ginger may be given extra pungency by adding Capsicum annuum or Aframomum melegueta; detection is by microscopy (non-lignified vessels in powder), the lycopodium spore method for powder and the alcohol-soluble extractive limit (not less than 4.5%).
C(i)
Carminative, stimulant, antiemetic, aromatic stimulant, spice and condiment.
C(ii)
Turmeric is the dried rhizome of Curcuma longa (Zingiberaceae); it resembles ginger but is yellow and bitter, colours saliva yellow when chewed, has about 5% volatile oil, resin, starch and curcumin, is adulterated with C. zedoaria and is used as condiment, colouring agent and dye. Among ginger varieties the pharmaceutical drug is Jamaican ginger; Nigerian ginger resembles it but is darker, more pungent, less aromatic and yields less volatile oil (0.7-1.0%); Chinese and Cochin (Indian) varieties are also named.

Describe aloes under the following headings, then explain its standards and quality control, and state how it differs from a related drug.

A(iv) Chemical constituents

B(ii) Solubility
B(iii) Standards
B(iv) Tests for purity or adulteration
B(v) Basis of commercial grades or classification
C(i) Distinction from the other commercial aloes
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Aloes is the residue obtained by evaporating to dryness the liquid oozing from the leaves of various aloes, family Liliaceae: Cape aloes from Aloe ferox (South Africa), Curacao aloes from Aloe vera (West Indies, highland of Barbados), and Socotrine and Zanzibar aloes from A. perryi.
A(ii)
Leaves are cut and the yellow juice from the secretory cells (surrounded by vascular bundles) is collected in a pot and evaporated by boiling in pans, impurities that precipitate being removed from time to time; the way boiling is carried out and the stage at which it is stopped affect the appearance of the drug: hepatic (livery) aloe, opaque because small barbaloin crystals form, is made by stopping heating midway and cooling at room temperature; vitreous (glassy) aloe is made by boiling until the concentrated juice solidifies at once on cooling, leaving no suitable condition for crystallisation (stated as free of barbaloin).
A(iii)
Hepatic aloe looks like liver and is opaque because of small crystals of barbaloin embedded throughout the mass; vitreous aloe is glassy.
A(iv)
Barbaloin (pale yellow, water-soluble crystalline anthraquinone glycoside present in both Cape and Curacao aloes); β-barbaloin (amorphous, water-soluble isomer formed on heating the juice, up to 8% in Cape aloe, little or none in other varieties); isobarbaloin (crystalline isomer in Curacao and a minute amount in Cape aloe, absent from Zanzibar and Socotrine); collectively aloin: about 30% in Curacao and 10% in Cape.
B(i)
Barbaloin gives a positive Borntrager's test like cascara, frangula and senna; aloe, as an unorganised drug, is confirmed by the chemical test for anthraquinone derivatives.
B(ii)
Barbaloin is water-soluble; for aloin preparation, aloe is dissolved in about 10 times its weight of boiling water, dilute sulphuric acid is added to precipitate the resin, the clear filtrate is neutralised and concentrated under reduced pressure, crystallised with a few aloe crystals, and the crystals are washed with a little alcohol, dissolved in minimum hot alcohol and recrystallised (yield 10-20% aloin).
B(iii)
Standards: alcohol-soluble extractive for aloes not more than 10.0% w/w; the official varieties are Cape and Curacao, both containing barbaloin.
B(iv)
Chemical test for anthraquinone derivatives (Borntrager's) confirms identity; barbaloin/aloin content differs between varieties.
B(v)
Classified by geographical/biological source (Cape, Curacao, Socotrine, Zanzibar), by aloin content and isobarbaloin/β-barbaloin pattern, and by method of preparation (hepatic versus vitreous); CITES protection of all Aloe species except A. vera has caused a shortage of the usual aloes.
C(i)
Cape aloe (A. ferox; South Africa) contains up to 8% β-barbaloin and about 10% aloin; Curacao aloe (A. vera; West Indies) contains isobarbaloin and about 30% aloin; Zanzibar and Socotrine aloes (A. perryi) lack isobarbaloin.

A(i)
A seed is the fertilised ripened ovule containing an embryo capable of germination; a fruit is the seed-bearing structure formed from the ovary after flowering, serving seed dissemination, and may be fleshy or dry.
A(ii)
Exalbuminous (large embryo within testa, no endosperm): oily cotyledons with straight or folded embryo, starchy cotyledons with straight embryo (calabar bean). Albuminous (embryo in endosperm): straight embryo (strophanthus, castor, cocoa), coiled, folded or minute embryo.
A(iii)
Simple dry: cremocarps (fennel, dill, coriander), legumes (senna, tamarind), capsules (cardamom, vanilla, poppy); succulent: drupes (prune, laurel), berries (capsicum, orange, lemon); aggregate: achenes (hips), follicles (star anise); compound: figs, mulberry, long pepper.
A(iv)
Seeds: shape, size, colour, hilum, micropyle, testa texture, hairs, perisperm, endosperm, embryo and cotyledons. Fruits: shape, dehiscence, pericarp colour/texture/sutures, odour, taste and food reserve.
B(i)
Seeds: epidermal cells (lignified?), sclereids, characteristic hairs, chemical tests for food reserve. Fruits: pericarp layers (epicarp, mesocarp, endocarp), placentation, seed number, stomata and hairs, fibres and sclereids in dry fruits, oil ducts and latex tissue.
B(ii)
Strophanthus (k-strophanthin, cymarin), cocoa (theobromine, caffeine, cocoa butter), calabar bean (physostigmine), castor (fixed oil), kola (caffeine), grains of paradise (paradol), cannabis tops (Δ9-THC).
B(iii)
Tamarind (tartaric, citric, malic acids), vanilla (vanillin; curing converts glucovanillin), fennel (anethole, fenchone), cardamom (volatile oil), capsicum (capsaicin).
B(iv)
Vanilla curing by fermentation, sweating and slow drying; ordeal use of calabar bean; cocoa fermentation then sun-drying; castor seeds sun-exposed so capsules burst.
C(i)
Classifying by embryo, endosperm and fruit type organises the many seed/fruit drugs and points to the features to examine for identification.
C(ii)
Some drugs need specific storage (cannabis thoroughly dried and well closed).
C(iii)
Structural classes do not predict constituents (cocoa and castor share a straight embryo but differ chemically).
C(iv)
Morphology allows quick recognition but needs microscopy and chemistry to confirm;.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Gelatin (Puragel, Gelatinum, Gelfoam) is a heterogeneous mixture of water-soluble proteins of high molecular weight (a scleroprotein/albumoid), derived from collagen by hydrolytic action and not found in nature; obtained from skin, tendons, bones and ligaments of domestic animals (horse, sheep, cow); plant family: not applicable (animal source).
A(ii)
Animal tissues are treated with hot water, converting insoluble collagen to soluble gelatin; the aqueous extract is evaporated, and the solution purified and concentrated to a solid form.
A(iii)
Sheets, shreds or coarse granular powder, colourless to pale yellow, translucent, odourless and tasteless, hard and brittle (bends then breaks with a short fracture); absorbs 5-10 times its weight of water and forms a gel below 35-40° C; a 2% solution forms a jelly on cooling; amphoteric; stable dry but attacked by bacteria when moist; prolonged boiling reduces gelatinising power.
A(iv)
The protein glutin, which gives on hydrolysis glycine, lysine, histidine, alanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, cystine, cysteine, methionine, tyrosine, aspartic acid, glutamic acid and arginine, but no tryptophan; the gelatinising compound is chondrin and the adhesive nature is due to glutin.
B(i)
Biuret test (alkaline copper sulfate): violet; xanthoproteic (conc. HNO₃): yellow precipitate; Millon's reagent: red on heating (tyrosine); ninhydrin: deep blue; 1 g heated with soda lime: ammonia released; 1% gelatin + 10% NaCl added to 1% tannin: white-buff precipitate; picric acid: mahogany-red solution (another account gives a yellow precipitate); no sulphur, so no blackening with lead acetate and KOH.
B(ii)
Insoluble in cold water and in alcohol and ether; soluble in hot water, glycerol and acetic acid; swells in cold water; boiled with dilute HCl it is converted to glutin hydrochloride.
B(iii)
Standards: quality is judged by jelly strength (important for suppositories and pessaries); a 2% aqueous solution must gelatinise on cooling (lost on prolonged boiling).
B(iv)
Purity: it should be free of chondrin (then fully soluble in acetic acid and giving no precipitate with lead acetate, alum or ferric chloride solutions); absence of sulphur distinguishes it from albumin; ammonia with soda lime shows nitrogen (unlike agar).
B(v)
Two types: Type A (isoelectric point pH 7-9), incompatible with anionic compounds such as tragacanth, agar and acacia; Type B (isoelectric point pH 4.7-5), compatible with anionic mixtures; it is usually coloured with a certified colour for capsules and tablet coating.
C(i)
Pastilles, pastes, suppositories, capsules, pill coatings and gelatin sponge; suspending agent, tablet binder and coating agent; stabiliser, thickener in food; culture medium and nutrient; styptic; absorbable gelatin sponge (absorbs about 50 times its weight of water and 45 times of blood, local haemostatic) and absorbable gelatin film (neurosurgery, thoracic and ocular surgery); also adhesives, photographic films and other industrial uses.
C(ii)
Storage: stable in air when dry but attacked by bacteria when moist.
C(iii)
Agar is a polysaccharide giving no ammonia with soda lime, whereas gelatin is a protein giving ammonia; albumin contains sulphur (blackens with lead acetate and KOH) while gelatin does not.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Cinchona (Peruvian bark, Jesuit's bark) is the dried stem or root bark of Cinchona succirubra Pavon (red cinchona) or its hybrids, or of C. ledgeriana, C. calisaya Weddell (calisaya/yellow cinchona) or hybrids; C. officinalis Linn. is also listed; family Rubiaceae; contains over 6.5% total alkaloids, of which 30-60% are quinoline alkaloids.
A(ii)
Large trees indigenous to South America (Colombia, Ecuador, Bolivia, Peru); other sources listed are Indonesia, India, Tanzania, Kenya and Guatemala.
A(iii)
Collection from wild trees involved felling and has been replaced by cultivation because of possible extermination; cultivation involves grafting high-yielding varieties onto C. succirubra, the hardiest species; seedlings need protection from the fungus Phytophthora cinnamomi, which lowers alkaloid content and may kill the tree.
A(iv)
Stem bark: single quills or small curved pieces up to about 30 cm long and 2-6 mm thick; cork may bear mosses or lichens, with or without longitudinal wrinkles and usually transverse cracks; inner surface striated, yellowish-brown to reddish-brown; fracture short in outer bark and fibrous in inner bark; odour slight; taste bitter and astringent. Root bark: channelled, twisted pieces 2-7 cm long, outer surface scaly, inner surface striated and of similar colour.
A(v)
Cork of radial rows of thin-walled polygonal cells; secondary cortex (phelloderm) of regular dark-walled cells; primary cortex of thin-walled cells with starch grains 6-10 µm and idioblasts (calcium oxalate and secretory cells); phloem of parenchyma, narrow sieve tubes with transverse sieve plates and spindle-shaped phloem fibres, whose distribution and size differentiate species; sclereids absent.
A(vi)
Quinoline alkaloids (quinine, quinidine, cinchonidine, cinchonine; quinetum also listed), tannins (cinchotannic acid, phlobatannin) and quinovin (hydrolyses to quinovic acid and the sugar quinovose).
B(i)
Quills with short outer and fibrous inner fracture, bitter astringent taste, mosses/lichens on the cork, spindle-shaped phloem fibres whose size and distribution differ between species, absence of sclereids, and total alkaloids above 6.5%.
B(ii)
Bark extract (0.5 g) + 2 mL dilute H2SO4 + 2 drops bromine water + 1 mL dilute ammonia gives an emerald green colour; powdered bark heated with glacial acetic acid gives red fumes condensing on the upper test tube; powdered bark + dilute H2SO4 under UV light gives blue fluorescence (each indicates cinchona is suspected).
B(iii)
Substitutes: Cuprea bark (Remijia pedunculata) and Remijia purdieana, and various species of Cascarilla, Exostemma and Stenostoma, which contain none of the cinchona alkaloids.
C(i)
Quinine for antimalarial use (including chloroquine-resistant malaria, though largely superseded by synthetic antimalarials); quinidine for prevention of cardiac arrhythmias and treatment of atrial fibrillation; cinchonine and cinchonidine as antirheumatics; decoction or acid infusion as astringent gargle (tannins); bitter tonic and stomachic.
C(ii)
Cuprea bark (Remijia spp., Rubiaceae) differs morphologically from cinchona but contains quinine, quinidine, cinchonine and cinchonamine; one account states that false cuprea (R. purdieana) lacks quinine and contains cinchonine and cinchonamine, while another lists it as containing quinine, cupreine and quinidine; the Cascarilla, Exostemma and Stenostoma barks contain none of the cinchona alkaloids.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
A yellowish-brown or yellowish-white solid obtained by melting and purifying the honeycomb of Apis mellifica (Apidae) and other bee species; waxes are esters of long-chain fatty acids and high-molecular-weight alcohols (animal source, so no plant family).
A(ii)
Worker bees secrete yellow beeswax in cells on the lower four abdominal segments to build the comb; after the honey is extracted the comb is cut up and melted in water (honey dissolves, impurities sink), and on cooling the yellow wax floats and is strained into moulds; white beeswax is made by sun-bleaching thin strips or by treatment with KMnO₄, chromic acid, chlorine or H₂O₂.
A(iii)
Yellowish or white solid; melting point range 41-68° C.
A(iv)
About 80% myricyl palmitate and about 15% cerotic acid, with aromatic substances (cerolein), a cholesteryl ester, myristolactone, myricyl alcohol and ceryl alcohol.
B(i)
Chemical standards for waxes: acid value (mg KOH to neutralise free acids in 1 g), saponification value (mg KOH to neutralise free acids and hydrolyse esters in 1 g), ester value (saponification value minus acid value) and iodine value (parts of iodine absorbed by 100 parts of substance); waxes are saponified by alcoholic but not aqueous alkali and contain no triglycerides.
B(ii)
Sparingly soluble in cold alcohol, soluble in ether, fixed and volatile oils, and insoluble in water.
B(iii)
Standards are expressed by acid, saponification, ester and iodine values and melting range.
B(iv)
Adulterants: carnauba wax (leaf of Copernicia), Japan wax (berries of Toxicodendron vernicifluum), solid paraffin, colophony, and other fats and oils; paraffin wax tinged yellow is a cited substitute.
B(v)
Available in two qualities: yellow beeswax (cera flava) and white beeswax (cera alba).
C(i)
Plasters, ointments and polishes; hardening ointments; dental moulds; cosmetics (lipsticks, face creams); candles; ingredient in chewing gums.
C(ii)
Woolfat (anhydrous lanolin, from sheep wool grease) contains at least 30% cholesterol and gives a deep green colour in the cholesterol test, is light yellow and tenacious, and is an emollient base; spermaceti (from the sperm whale head) is mainly cetyl palmitate, melts at about 50° C and congeals at 45° C, whereas beeswax is mainly myricyl palmitate.

A(i)
Epidermal trichomes of the seeds of Gossypium herbaceum and other Gossypium species (Malvaceae); raw cotton is ginned, about 90% cellulose with wax, fat and ash, a unicellular fibre up to 5 cm and 9-24 µm wide with a waxy cuticle (non-absorbent; stains red with ruthenium red); absorbent cotton is made by heating with dilute NaOH and Na2CO3 at 1-3 atm for 10-15 h, treated with dilute HCl and bleached with sodium hypochlorite; it is pure cellulose of glucose units joined by 1,4-β-glucosidic links.
A(ii)
Blue with N/50 iodine + 80% H2SO4 (unlike wool and silk); soluble in 80% H2SO4 but insoluble in 60% H2SO4; raw cotton balloons in ammoniacal copper oxide leaving cuticle, absorbent swells and dissolves; burns with white ash and little odour; no pink with Millon's reagent, no yellow with picric acid, no stain with phloroglucinol-HCl.
A(iii)
From spruce (Picea) wood pulp or cotton linters: NaOH removes hemicellulose, carbon disulphide gives sodium cellulose xanthate, spun through a spinneret into dilute H2SO4/Na2SO4; pure cellulose, fibres 15-20 µm, no loss of absorbency on storage but loses about 60% of tensile strength when wet; distinguished from cotton by solubility in 60% H2SO4; used in surgical dressings.
A(iv)
Jute: phloem fibres of Corchorus species (Tiliaceae), retted, lignified, deep pink/red with phloroglucinol-HCl, used for eco-friendly packaging. Flax: pericyclic fibres of Linum usitatissimum, mostly cellulose, strong but less elastic, capillary action, allergen-free, bandages. Hemp: pericyclic fibres of Cannabis sativa, cellulose with some lignin, pink/red with phloroglucinol, filter paper.
B(i)
From the cocoon of Bombyx mori and others; cocoons heated at 60-80° C, beaten in hot water, threads scoured with hot soap to remove sericin; no cellular structure, 10-20 µm, fibroin (glycine 44%, alanine 27%, serine 11%, tyrosine 5%); dissolves in ammoniacal copper oxide and rapidly in conc. HCl; no PbS (no sulphur); used as non-absorbable suture.
B(ii)
Fleece of Ovis aries; keratin (α, reversibly β when stretched), cuticle, cortex and medulla; elastic; coloured blue by ammoniacal copper oxide; black PbS precipitate (sulphur); insoluble in conc. HCl; stains yellow with picric acid and pink with Millon's reagent; used in medical devices, paddings, dressings and filters.
B(iii)
Absorbable gelatin sponge (about 50 times its weight of water, 45 of blood, haemostatic) and absorbable gelatin film for neurosurgery, thoracic and ocular surgery.
B(iv)
Cotton: cleaning skin and dressing wounds; viscose rayon: surgical dressings; silk: non-absorbable suture; flax: wound bandages (moisture channelled away, allergen-free); hemp: filter paper for pharmaceutical research; jute: eco-friendly packaging; wool: medical devices, paddings, dressings and filter media.
C(i)
Several fibres look alike, so solubility, colour and microscopic tests distinguish cellulose, lignocellulose, protein and keratin fibres.
C(ii)
Removing the waxy cuticle makes the fibre absorbent for dressings.
C(iii)
Viscose rayon behaves like cotton in most tests and differs only in solubility in 60% H2SO4, and loses strength when wet; old stems give harsh flax.
C(iv)
Natural fibres have uses suited to application (silk suture non-absorbable; wool elastic; flax strong but less elastic);.

C(ii) Storage
C(iii) Distinction from Sumatra benzoin
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A balsam from Styrax tonkinensis (Pierre) Craib ex Hartwich (Styracaceae), an East Asian tree cultivated in Thailand, Vietnam and Sumatra at 600-2500 m altitude, which is necessary for resin production.
A(ii)
Collected much as for Sumatra benzoin: incisions through the bark to the wood; the tissue formed when the bark heals contains secretory ducts that produce a yellowish-white balsam which later solidifies.
A(iii)
Flattened, sometimes curved tears up to 3 cm long; outer surface yellowish-white to reddish; tears cemented by a brownish resin which increases through oxidation during storage; fracture milky white with a vanilla-like odour.
A(iv)
60-70% coniferyl benzoate, 10-20% free benzoic acid, about 2% cinnamyl benzoate, about 1% vanillin, and triterpenoid acid and esters; cinnamic acid is absent.
B(i)
No benzaldehyde odour on warming with KMnO₄ (no cinnamic acid); a green colour with alcoholic FeCl₃ (Sumatra benzoin gives yellow).
B(ii)
The KMnO₄ and FeCl₃ tests are used to detect adulteration of Siam benzoin with the cheaper Sumatra benzoin.
C(i)
Uses similar to Sumatra benzoin (expectorant, antiseptic, ingredient of Friars' balsam, odourant).
C(ii)
Storage: the brownish cementing resin increases through oxidation during storage.
C(iii)
Sumatra benzoin (Styrax benzoin) contains 20-30% free cinnamic and benzoic acids, so gives a benzaldehyde odour with KMnO₄ and a yellow colour with alcoholic FeCl₃; its tears are opaque whitish or reddish in a reddish-brown matrix, whereas Siam tears are flattened and yellowish-white with a milky fracture and vanilla-like odour.

A(i)
Cascara (cascara sagrada, sacred bark, chittem bark, Cortex Rhamni purshianae) is the dried bark of Rhamnus purshianus DC (Frangula purshiana (DC) A. Gray ex J.C. Cooper), family Rhamnaceae; it is collected at least one year before use.
A(ii)
Indigenous to North America and Canada; obtained from wild and cultivated shrubs and small trees in North Carolina, Washington and Oregon regions of the USA, and also cultivated in western Canada and Kenya.
A(iii)
Bark is collected from wild trees 6-18 m high between April and August when it is easily removed; 'natural cascara' is bark dried in the shade with the cork facing upwards; 'processed', 'compact' or 'evenized' cascara is the commercial drug made from natural cascara by size reduction; it is prepared and stored dry, free from dampness, to prevent mould and partial extraction of constituents, and stored at least a year before use because fresh bark causes griping and nausea.
A(iv)
Part used is the bark: channelled or single quills (branches) or nearly flat pieces (trunk), about 20 cm long (5-20 cm), 1-4 mm thick, up to 2 cm wide; outer surface with patchy silvery-grey lichen or moss, dark purplish-brown cork and transverse lenticels; inner surface purplish-brown to black with longitudinal striations and faint transverse corrugations; fracture short and granular in outer bark and fibrous in inner bark/phloem; odour faint; taste persistently bitter and nauseous.
A(v)
Cork of 10-15 layers of flattened cells; cortex of collenchyma, parenchyma and groups of sclereids (collenchyma and parenchyma contain chloroplasts and starch; ovoid yellowish sclereids are encircled by cells containing calcium oxalate prisms); phloem with elongated groups of yellow lignified fibres 8-15 µm wide in tangential rows, parenchyma with calcium oxalate prisms, plastids, starch and a material staining violet with alkali, sieve tubes with sieve plates, and medullary rays 1-5 cells wide and 15-25 cells deep.
A(vi)
Anthracene derivatives (6-9%): cascarosides A, B, C and D (O- and C-glycosides of aloin and chrysophanol), barbaloin and chrysaloin, O-glycosides of emodin, oxanthrone, aloe-emodin and chrysophanol, free aloe-emodin, emodin and chrysophanol, dianthrones and heterodianthrones (palmidins A, B, C); fresh bark contains anthranol derivatives (griping and emetic), oxidised to anthraquinones during at least one year of storage.
B(i)
Channelled/quill form, silvery-grey lichen on dark purplish-brown cork with transverse lenticels, striated and corrugated inner surface, short granular fracture, persistently bitter taste; microscopically 10-15 cork layers, cortical sclereids with oxalate prisms, yellow lignified phloem fibres and a violet reaction with alkali.
B(ii)
Borntrager's test: bark extract boiled with dilute H2SO4 (10 mL) and filtered hot; filtrate shaken with 5 mL benzene; benzene layer shaken with half its volume of 10% ammonia; a pink, red or violet colour in the lower ammonia phase indicates anthraquinones.
B(iii)
Substitutes listed: Rhamnus californica Eschsolz, R. fallax Boiss., Prunus bark and frangula bark.
C(i)
Purgative (larger doses), emetic, tonic and stomachic (bitter stomachic in small doses); correction of habitual constipation; derived products include Cas-Evac, Caroid, Nature's Remedy, Kondremul and Stimulax; storage: dry and free from dampness, aged at least a year.
C(ii)
Differences between cascara and its substitute barks (R. californica, R. the substitutes are listed only by name.

Describe adulteration of crude drugs, its reasons and methods, relate each method to representative examples, and explain the remedies and their limitations.
A(i) Define adulteration and related terms
A(ii) State reasons for adulteration
A(iii) Describe replacement by exhausted drugs and by similar inferior drugs
A(iv) Describe artificial substitutes and sub-standard varieties
B(i) Describe organic matter from the same plant and synthetic additions
B(ii) State remedies
B(iii) Describe how identification confirms genuineness
B(iv) Relate to specific example drugs
C(i) Explain why these categories are used
C(ii) Explain why evaluation is needed
C(iii) State a limitation
C(iv) State the trade-off
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Adulteration is substitution of the original crude drug partly or fully with other substances free of or inferior in therapeutic and chemical properties; the adulterant resembles the genuine drug morphologically and may be deliberate or accidental. Deterioration is impaired quality; admixture is addition of one article to another (ignorance or accident); sophistication is deliberate adulteration; substitution is selling an entirely different article in place of the required one.
A(ii)
Overexploitation or high price, non-availability of the drug, ignorance and inadequate knowledge of collectors, and regional or linguistic nomenclature; it is common with illegally sold drugs and the extent depends on whether the drug is indigenous or imported.
A(iii)
Exhausted costly drugs (cloves, saffron, fennel, ginger) are re-used, exhausted saffron is coloured and ginger is mixed with coloured starch; superficially similar inferior drugs: cloves with mother cloves, saffron with safflower, low-glycoside digitalis as diluent.
A(iv)
Yellow-tinged paraffin wax for yellow beeswax, artificial invert sugar in honey; sub-standard varieties: Capsicum annuum for C. frutescens, Picrorhiza kurroa for Gentiana lutea, Arabian for Alexandria senna, Strychnos nux-blanda or S. potatorum for nux-vomica.
B(i)
Cloves mixed with clove stalks; caraway and anethum fruits mixed with other inflorescence parts; synthetic constituents added: benzyl benzoate to balsam of Peru, citral to lemon grass oil, camphor and eucalyptus oil in rosemary oil.
B(ii)
Cultivation of medicinal plants, collection at the right time, building a herbarium and museum, and drug evaluation (identification and authentication).
B(iii)
Identification confirms genuineness of raw materials through evaluation of the crude drug; the form of the drug indicates the method (morphology for whole drugs, microscopy for powder, chemical/physical tests for liquids).
B(iv)
Senna: Cassia obovata (papillose lower epidermal cells); ginger/capsicum and Aframomum for pungency; cardamom husks (pitted fibres, spiral vessels); benzoin with dammar; beeswax with carnauba, Japan wax, paraffin, colophony.
C(i)
They describe how adulteration happens so each can be targeted by an appropriate test.
C(ii)
Because of biochemical variation, deterioration from treatment and storage, and substitution/adulteration.
C(iii)
An adulterant resembles the genuine drug morphologically, so macroscopic checks can fail.
C(iv)
Costly drugs are most exposed to adulteration; remedies such as cultivation and herbaria take time and resources.

A(i)
Evaluation confirms identity and determines quality and purity and detects the nature of adulteration; needed because of biochemical variation, deterioration from treatment and storage, and substitution and adulteration.
A(ii)
Organoleptic (morphological), microscopic, physical, chemical and biological evaluation.
A(iii)
Uses macroscopic and sensory characters (colour, odour, taste, size, shape, touch, texture, sound, trichomes, ridges and markings). Diagnostic examples: aromatic odour of umbelliferous fruits, quill of cinnamon, ribbon shape of tragacanth, wavy shape of rauwolfia, pungent taste of ginger and capsicum, odour and taste of nutmeg and black pepper.
A(iv)
Detailed examination of cells, tissues, cell walls and contents, starch grains, calcium oxalate, trichomes, fibres and vessels in thin sections; qualitative (stomata, trichomes, starch, vessels, crystals) and quantitative (stomata number and index, vein-islet and vein-termination number, palisade ratio); e.g. non-lignified vessels in powdered rhubarb and ginger indicate adulteration and starch grain diameter in Cinnamomum cassia is about 10 µm.
B(i)
Specific gravity, density, optical rotation, refractive index, melting point, viscosity, solubility and extractives; moisture, ash, swelling factor, foreign organic matter, crude fibre; chromatography (TLC with Rf, paper, HPLC, GC, column) and IR/NMR; optical rotation (polarimeter) for drugs with sugars.
B(ii)
Determines active constituents; chemical tests help identify powdered organised drugs and are important for unorganised drugs (aloes by test for anthraquinones); quantitative tests (acid and saponification values), instrumental methods (colorimetry for alkaloids, spectroscopy for strychnine) and phytochemical investigation for the chemical profile.
B(iii)
Bioassay estimates potency by effect on living organisms (bacteria, fungi, tissues or animals); used when chemical or physical standardisation is inadequate and to confirm therapeutic activity; types: toxic, symptomatic (animals) and tissue methods (isolated organs); examples: hepatoprotective, anti-inflammatory, hypoglycaemic, anti-ulcer.
B(iv)
Morphological characters may suffice for whole drugs, microscopy is needed for powders, and chemical tests plus physical standards such as specific gravity, optical rotation and solubility help for liquid drugs.
C(i)
Crude drugs vary in source and chemistry, so they are standardised by different techniques (morphological, histological and chemical studies).
C(ii)
Adulterants resemble the genuine drug in appearance, so morphology alone may not detect them; powders need microscopy.
C(iii)
Some substances lose volatile constituents at 100° C, so moisture by oven can mislead (toluene distillation is used); bioassay is used only where chemical or physical standardisation is inadequate.
C(iv)
Simple methods are quick but less specific, whereas microscopic, chemical and biological methods give detail but need more procedure;.
