Describe acacia gum (gum arabic) under the following headings, then explain its standards and quality control, and state its uses, its storage and how it differs from a related drug.
A(i) Biological source and family
A(ii) Method of collection or preparation
A(iii) Description and physical characters
A(iv) Chemical constituents
B(i) Chemical tests
B(ii) Solubility
B(iii) Standards
B(iv) Tests for purity or adulteration
B(v) Basis of commercial grades or classification
C(i) Uses
C(ii) Storage
C(iii) Distinction from tragacanth and other gums
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Dried gum from the stem and branches of Acacia senegal Willd and other Acacia species, family Leguminosae; obtained in Kordofan (Sudan) and Senegambia and Nigeria (known as Hashab and Verek); Kordofan gives the best gum. Gums are amorphous translucent solids and are pathological products formed on injury or in drought by breakdown of cell walls (extracellular formation).
A(ii)
Trees about 6 years old are tapped in February-March, or earlier in September after the rains when leaves have fallen; a transverse incision is made in a branch with a small axe up to the cambium and twisted so the bark loosens, and strips about 0.5-1.0 × 5.0-7.5 cm are pulled off above and below the cut.
A(iii)
Bleached Kordofan: rounded or ovoid tears up to 3 cm, outer surface with fine cracks (formed on ripening) that make the gum opaque, glassy fracture in small pieces, colourless, bland mucilaginous taste. Cleaned Kordofan: more yellowish or pinkish, fewer cracks, more transparent, less uniform tears. Solution is viscid but not glary and does not deposit on dilution; it is laevorotatory.
A(iv)
Arabin (calcium, with traces of magnesium and potassium salts of arabic acid); hydrolysis with sulphuric acid gives L-rhamnopyranose, D-galactopyranose, L-arabinofuranose and the aldobionic acid 6-β-D-glucuronosido-D-galactose; contains oxidase enzyme, 14% water and 2.7-4% ash.
B(i)
A 10% solution gives no precipitate with dilute lead acetate (tragacanth and agar do); no colour with iodine (no starch or dextrin); no tannin reaction with ferric chloride; mucilage gives a blue colour with benzidine and a few drops of hydrogen peroxide (peroxidase enzyme), a possible distinction from tragacanth, but the benzidine test is no longer used because benzidine is carcinogenic; the solution is slightly acid and becomes more acid on keeping, especially with hot water.
B(ii)
Completely soluble in water but dissolves slowly, giving a slightly acid, viscid solution.
B(iii)
The constituent figures given are about 14% water and 2.7-4% ash, and spray-dried acacia is valued for its low viable bacterial count.
B(iv)
Purity is judged by the tests above (no lead acetate precipitate, no iodine colour, no tannin reaction, peroxidase test); allied gums to be distinguished include talka gum and ghatti (Indian) gum from Anogeissus latifolia (Combretaceae).
B(v)
Three varieties: Kordofan gum (3 grades quoted in London: hand-picked selected (hps) Kordofan, cleaned Kordofan, talka gum); Senegal gum, used largely for pharmaceutical purposes, in 3 grades (gomme du bas du fleuve, gomme du haut du fleuve, gomme friable); and imported spray-dried acacia, increasingly important for its low viable bacterial count.
C(i)
General stabiliser in emulsions; pharmaceutical necessity in lozenges; demulcent in cough, diarrhoeal and throat preparations; used in food, drinks and other industries.
C(ii)
The gum is incompatible with readily oxidised materials such as phenols and vitamin A of cod liver oil.
C(iii)
Tragacanth exudes immediately after injury (preformed) whereas acacia gum is produced slowly; tragacanth gives a lead acetate precipitate and swells to a gelatinous mass, acacia does not; Sterculia and tragacanth are also distinguished from acacia by their swelling and starch/acidity behaviour (see their own tests).

A(i)
Obtained from Myroxylon balsamum (L.) Harms var. pereirae (Royle) Harms (Fabaceae), a tall tree of Central America; balsams are sweet-smelling resinous mixtures from plants rich in aromatic compounds such as acids and esters.
A(ii)
A pathological product formed when the tree is injured: in November or December the bark is loosened on four parts of the trunk circumference by beating and burned a week later; the next week strips of bark (about 30 × 15 cm) are pulled off, leaving bark intact between segments so the tree survives; the oozing balsam is absorbed in cloths wrapped round the trunk and by boiling the bark strips in water; the balsam is recovered by boiling the cloths, separating on cooling and sinking to the bottom, the water being decanted.
A(iii)
A reddish-brown fluid with an acrid, slightly bitter taste.
A(iv)
Esters of cinnamic and benzoic acids, especially benzyl cinnamate, cinnamyl cinnamate and benzyl benzoate; a resin of peruresinotannols combined with cinnamic and benzoic acids and alcohols; vanillin and free cinnamic acid.
B(i)
The ester content is determined by gravimetric analysis.
B(ii)
The official drug must contain 45-75% w/w esters, assayed gravimetrically.
B(iii)
Physicochemical properties are used to detect adulteration with fixed oils, alcohol, kerosene and similar materials; benzyl benzoate may also be added as a synthetic adulterant.
C(i)
Antiseptic dressing for wounds, parasiticide, and treatment of catarrh and diarrhoea.
C(ii)
Balsam of Tolu comes from M. balsamum var. balsamum (Colombia, Venezuela) by V-shaped incisions (8-10 kg per tree), is a soft yellow semi-solid paste that hardens to a brittle brown solid, is almost entirely soluble in alcohol and gives a green colour with ferric chloride; Peru balsam is a pathological fluid obtained from stripped bark and is reddish-brown.

questions.explanation: The cell-division cycle is both the mechanism for embryonic development from a single fertilized egg and the continuous renewal of cells in self-renewing tissues like skin and blood. Disruption of this cycle underlies both developmental defects and malignancies. Terminal differentiation, by contrast, is the process by which cells stop dividing and specialize.
questions.question: The cell division process by which a single-celled fertilized egg ultimately develops into a mature organism and by which certain tissues (skin, blood) are continuously renewed is best described as which of the following?

questions.explanation: Nephron formation (nephrogenesis) is complete at birth, with over 1 million nephrons in each kidney. No new nephrons form after birth, though existing ones continue to mature and grow. This finite nephron number explains why kidney disease in childhood can have lifelong consequences. Low birth weight and prematurity are associated with reduced nephron number.
questions.question: Which statement about nephron formation is correct?
The hepatic acinus (acinus of Rappaport) is divided into three zones. Zone 3 of the acinus, being furthest from the blood supply, is most vulnerable to:
questions.explanation: Zone 3 of the hepatic acinus receives the most deoxygenated, nutrient-depleted blood as it is furthest from the portal tract (short axis) and adjacent to the central vein. This makes Zone 3 hepatocytes most susceptible to ischemic (centrilobular) necrosis in conditions of right heart failure or shock. Zone 1 (periportal) is most susceptible to toxic damage from substances entering via the portal blood.

The outer layer of mesenchymal tissue overlying the anterior aspect of the eye forms the substantia propria of the cornea. Vacuolization of this mesenchymal tissue creates the anterior chamber. The inner mesenchymal layer forms the iridopupillary membrane, which later disappears to establish communication between anterior and posterior chambers.
questions.question: The substantia propria of the cornea develops from which embryonic layer?

options: Beta cells (~70%) centrally; alpha cells (~20%) peripherally; delta cells also present
Alpha cells are central and beta cells are peripheral in all islets
Only two cell types exist in equal proportions
All islet cells produce identical hormone mixtures without specialization
Alpha cells produce insulin and beta cells produce glucagon opposite to the traditional teaching
questions.question: The islets of Langerhans in the pancreas contain alpha cells producing glucagon and beta cells producing insulin. Which of the following correctly describes their arrangement?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic islets contain beta cells at approximately 70% concentrated in the islet center producing insulin that lowers blood glucose; alpha cells at approximately 20% in the islet periphery producing glucagon that raises blood glucose; and delta cells at approximately 10% producing somatostatin that paracrine inhibits both alpha and beta cells. This architectural arrangement facilitates paracrine signaling between cell types. Type 1 diabetes involves autoimmune destruction of beta cells.

options: Its mesentery fuses with posterior wall
questions.explanation: The duodenum becomes secondarily retroperitoneal as it rotates to the right and loses its dorsal mesentery through fusion with the posterior abdominal wall. The pancreas, developing in the duodenal mesentery, also becomes retroperitoneal. Only the first inch of duodenum retains its mesentery as the hepatoduodenal ligament.
questions.question: The duodenum becomes secondarily retroperitoneal because:

questions.explanation: The stratum basale contains the stems cells and gland bases that regenerate the entire stratum functionale after it is shed during menstruation. It is not shed because it receives blood from the straight (basal) arteries, which do not undergo the vasoconstriction that precipitates menstruation. The stratum functionale, supplied by spiral arteries (responsive to progesterone withdrawal), is the layer that proliferates, secretes, and is shed cyclically.
questions.question: The endometrium undergoes cyclical changes under hormonal control. The stratum functionale is shed during menstruation, while the stratum basale remains. The stratum basale is responsible for:
options: Regeneration of the stratum functionale after menstruation
Production of progesterone during the luteal phase
Formation of the decidua basalis only in pregnancy

questions.question: The alveolar septa (interalveolar walls) are the thin tissue partitions between adjacent alveoli. Their structural components include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The alveolar septa contain: Type I pneumocytes (lining most of the surface), Type II pneumocytes (surfactant production), capillary endothelial cells, a shared basal lamina, elastic fibers (allowing alveolar recoil during expiration), collagen fibers (structural support), and occasional alveolar macrophages. Smooth muscle cells are NOT present in alveolar septa — they are found in bronchioles and pulmonary vessels. Loss of elastic fibers causes alveolar collapse (emphysema).

Each horn of the sinus venosus receives three veins: one vitelline vein (from the yolk sac), one umbilical vein (from the placenta), and one common cardinal vein (from the body wall). The sinus venosus is the first area of the heart to receive venous blood.
questions.question: How many veins join each horn of the sinus venosus?

questions.explanation: Turner syndrome results from monosomy X (45,X karyotype), where there is only one X chromosome and no second sex chromosome. Affected individuals are phenotypically female with characteristic features including short stature, ovarian dysgenesis, webbed neck, and cardiovascular abnormalities.
questions.question: Turner syndrome results from which sex chromosome constitution?
Lanugo hair is characterized by being:
questions.explanation: Lanugo is fine, soft, lightly pigmented downy hair that appears around the 12th week and is the first hair to develop. It is replaced by coarser hairs during the perinatal period. Lanugo persists over most of the body but is eventually replaced by vellus or terminal hairs.

options: Excess aldosterone and cortisol causing hypertension
Cortisol deficiency, aldosterone deficiency, and ACTH-driven hyperpigmentation
Deficiency of epinephrine causing bradycardia only
Isolated aldosterone deficiency without cortisol effects
questions.explanation: Addison's disease destroys all cortical zones causing: cortisol deficiency from zona fasciculata destruction producing weakness fatigue hypoglycemia and impaired stress response; aldosterone deficiency from zona glomerulosa destruction causing salt wasting hyponatremia hyperkalemia hypotension and salt craving; and adrenal androgen deficiency from zona reticularis destruction. Loss of negative feedback causes excess ACTH and MSH from the anterior pituitary producing the characteristic bronzed hyperpigmentation especially in sun-exposed areas and pressure points.
questions.question: A patient with Addison's disease has primary adrenal insufficiency destroying the entire adrenal cortex. Which combination of hormonal deficiencies and clinical features would result?
Canaliculi in bone serve which of the following critical physiological functions?
questions.explanation: Canaliculi are minute tunnels radiating from each osteocyte lacuna, containing cytoplasmic processes of osteocytes that form gap junctions with adjacent osteocytes. Since metabolites cannot diffuse through calcified matrix, this canalicular network creates a 'bucket brigade' relay system for nutrients, oxygen, hormones, and waste products between blood vessels in Haversian canals and the most distant osteocytes. Osteocytes also sense mechanical strain through canalicular fluid flow.
options: Allow osteoclasts to migrate between different bone surfaces
Store calcium phosphate reserves for blood calcium regulation
Serve as channels for osteoblast migration during bone remodeling
Provide direct routes for nerve fibers to reach osteocytes
Allow osteocytes to exchange nutrients with blood vessels via gap junctions

questions.explanation: The lienorenal (splenorenal) ligament connects the spleen to the left kidney and is derived from the dorsal mesogastrium. It contains the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas. Together with the gastrosplenic ligament, it forms the lateral boundary of the lesser sac. These ligaments must be divided during splenectomy.
questions.question: The lienorenal ligament connects:
Which structure serves as the primary inducer during primary embryonic induction?
questions.explanation: During primary embryonic induction, the mesoderm (particularly the notochord and prechordal mesoderm) serves as the primary inducer of neural tissue. These structures secrete factors like noggin, chordin, and follistatin that induce the overlying ectoderm to form neural tissue.

questions.question: A cell type in connective tissue that is the most abundant fixed cell and is responsible for synthesizing extracellular matrix components including collagen and ground substance is which of the following?
questions.explanation: Fibroblasts are the most numerous and principal cells of connective tissue proper, responsible for synthesizing and secreting all components of the extracellular matrix — collagen, elastic fibers, reticular fibers, proteoglycans, and glycoproteins. They are spindle-shaped cells with elongated nuclei that align with collagen fibers. Fibroblast dysfunction underlies excessive scarring (keloid, fibrosis) and wound healing defects.

The prostate gland develops from endodermal epithelial outgrowths (buds) of the pelvic part of the urogenital sinus, which penetrate surrounding mesenchyme. Development is stimulated by dihydrotestosterone from the fetal testes. The mesenchyme forms the fibromuscular stroma, while the endoderm forms the glandular epithelium. Prostatic development continues through puberty.
questions.question: The prostate gland develops from:
The functional unit of the kidney responsible for filtration, reabsorption, secretion, and excretion is the:
questions.explanation: The nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney. It consists of the renal corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman's capsule), proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle (thin and thick limbs), and distal convoluted tubule. The collecting duct, while functionally important, is technically not part of the nephron. Each kidney contains approximately 1–1.5 million nephrons.

questions.question: Ovarian descent is limited compared to testicular descent because:
questions.explanation: Ovarian descent is limited because the female gubernaculum attaches to the developing uterus, dividing into two structures: ovarian ligament (from ovary to uterus) and round ligament (from uterus through inguinal canal to labium majus). This attachment prevents descent beyond the pelvis. Ovaries descend from their origin near the kidneys to the pelvic brim but normally remain in the pelvis.

Peyer's patches are large aggregates of lymphoid follicles located predominantly in the distal ileum, where they can extend from the lamina propria into the submucosa. They are part of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) and play a crucial role in immune surveillance of intestinal contents. Isolated lymphoid nodules are distributed throughout the small intestine but aggregated patches characterize the ileum.
questions.question: Peyer's patches are aggregated lymphoid nodules found predominantly in which segment of the small intestine?
The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into:
questions.explanation: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into the ventral urogenital sinus and the dorsal rectum/cranial anal canal. This septum grows from mesoderm at the junction between the connecting stalk and yolk sac. By the 7th week, it fuses with the cloacal membrane, dividing it into anal and urogenital membranes.

The ascending reticular activating system connects to areas in the thalamus, hypothalamus, and cortex, and is responsible for the sleep-wake cycle, mediating various levels of alertness and consciousness. It is critical for maintaining the conscious state.
questions.question: The ascending reticular activating system is responsible for which function?

questions.explanation: ADH and oxytocin are produced by hypothalamic neurons in supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei respectively and released from the posterior pituitary or neurohypophysis not the anterior pituitary. The anterior pituitary or adenohypophysis secretes GH, Prolactin, ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH, and MSH. This distinction is essential for understanding pituitary disorders where anterior and posterior functions are independently affected.
questions.question: The anterior pituitary secretes multiple tropic hormones. Which of the following is correctly identified as a posterior pituitary hormone not an anterior pituitary hormone?

questions.explanation: The ENS contains approximately 100 million (10^8) neurons — more than the spinal cord — organized into the myenteric and submucosal plexuses. This vast neuronal network enables autonomous regulation of GIT motility, secretion, and blood flow, earning the ENS its designation as the 'second brain.' The ENS communicates bidirectionally with the CNS via the vagus nerve and sympathetic pathways.
questions.question: The enteric nervous system (ENS) is called the 'second brain'. What is the total approximate number of neurons in the ENS?
The classic signs of inflammation described by Celsus include all of the following EXCEPT which of the following?
questions.explanation: The cardinal signs of inflammation described by Celsus (1st century CE) are: redness (rubor), heat (calor), swelling (tumor), and pain (dolor), to which Galen later added disturbed function (functio laesa). Pallor (pallidus — whiteness) is notably absent; in fact inflammation typically causes redness, the opposite of pallor. The five cardinal signs remain the clinical hallmark of acute inflammation.

Ectopic gastric mucosa in Meckel's diverticulum can produce acid, leading to peptic ulceration of adjacent ileal mucosa and bleeding. Pancreatic acini may also be present. These heterotopic tissues make Meckel's diverticulum clinically significant despite being a common anatomical variant. The classic presentation is painless rectal bleeding.
questions.question: Ectopic gastric mucosa in Meckel's diverticulum can cause:
Which cell type in the intestinal epithelium produces mucus to lubricate and protect the intestinal lining?
questions.explanation: Goblet cells are unicellular mucous glands scattered throughout the intestinal epithelium. They produce and secrete mucins that form the protective mucus layer overlying the epithelium. Their numbers increase from duodenum to rectum. Deficiency of mucus production, as seen in inflammatory bowel disease, exposes the epithelium to luminal damage.

questions.question: The CNS is protected by three connective tissue meningeal layers named from outermost to innermost as which of the following?
questions.explanation: The three meninges from outside to inside are: dura mater or pachymeninx which is the thickest toughest layer containing dural venous sinuses; arachnoid which is the middle spider web-like layer with CSF-containing subarachnoid space below it; and pia mater which is the thinnest highly vascular layer that intimately follows the brain and spinal cord surface. The subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia contains cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.question: The respiratory system is divided into a conducting zone and a respiratory zone. Which of the following is the FIRST structure in the respiratory zone where gas exchange begins?
questions.explanation: The respiratory zone begins at the respiratory bronchioles, which are the first airways to bear alveoli in their walls and thus the first sites of gas exchange. Terminal bronchioles are the last purely conducting airways. Beyond respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs are entirely surrounded by alveoli. The conducting zone (nasal cavity to terminal bronchioles) conditions air but does not participate in gas exchange.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly defines histology in terms of its Greek etymological roots?
questions.explanation: Histology derives from the Greek 'histos' meaning web or tissue, and 'logia' meaning the study of a science. It specifically focuses on the microscopic anatomy of cells and tissues. Understanding this etymology distinguishes histology from gross anatomy, cytology, and biochemistry.
options: Study of living organisms using electron beams
Study of tissues derived from 'histos' and 'logia'
Study of cells using biochemical markers only
Anatomical study limited to the gross level
Study of body fluids and their components

questions.question: The septum primum grows from the roof of the common atrium toward which structure?
questions.explanation: At the end of the fourth week, a sickle-shaped crest (septum primum) grows from the roof of the common atrium into the lumen. The two limbs of this septum extend toward the endocardial cushions in the atrioventricular canal. The opening between the septum primum and endocardial cushions is called the ostium primum.

The cephalic flexure is a ventral flexure that forms in the midbrain region. The cervical flexure (also ventral) forms at the junction of the hindbrain and spinal cord. The pontine flexure (dorsal) forms later and is responsible for the diamond shape of the fourth ventricle.
questions.question: The cephalic flexure forms in which brain region?

questions.explanation: The stomach uniquely possesses three smooth muscle sublayers: inner oblique, middle circular, and outer longitudinal. This arrangement allows the mechanical churning and mixing of food necessary for gastric digestion. All other GIT regions have only two layers (inner circular and outer longitudinal) in the muscularis externa.
questions.question: On a histological slide, three distinct smooth muscle sublayers are seen in the muscularis of one GIT region. This finding is characteristic of which region?
The white line (anocutaneous line) marks where epithelium changes from:
questions.explanation: The white line (anocutaneous line), located approximately 2 cm superior to the anus, marks where the anal epithelium changes from columnar to stratified squamous epithelium. This is distinct from the pectinate line, which marks the junction between endodermal and ectodermal portions. These landmarks have clinical significance for innervation and venous drainage.

Both male and female germ cells have a common origin from primordial germ cells in the posterior wall of the yolk sac. These cells start migrating by the 4th week and reach the gonad by the 5th week, where they differentiate into either spermatogonia or oogonia.
questions.question: Primordial germ cells first appear in which location?

options: Multipolar motor neurons with ventral horn characteristics
Large pseudounipolar neurons with satellite glia in a connective tissue capsule
Bipolar neurons identical to retinal bipolar cells
Interneurons connecting ascending sensory and descending motor pathways
Oligodendrocytes that exclusively produce myelin in the CNS
questions.explanation: Dorsal root ganglia contain large pseudounipolar sensory neurons whose single T-shaped process divides into a peripheral branch to sensory receptors and a central branch entering the spinal cord. Each neuron is surrounded by satellite cells which are glial cells that regulate the local ionic environment around the neuron cell body. The entire ganglion is enclosed in dense connective tissue continuous with the epineurium of the nerve.
questions.question: A section through the dorsal root ganglion would show which cell types?

options: DCT has a brush border while PCT does not
DCT cells have more mitochondria than PCT cells
DCT is lined by cuboidal cells with no brush border, while PCT
DCT cells are taller and more eosinophilic than PCT cells
DCT has a larger lumen than PCT
questions.explanation: The DCT is lined by simple cuboidal cells with NO brush border (or only minimal microvilli), making the lumen appear relatively clear and larger compared to the PCT. PCT cells, in contrast, have a prominent brush border that significantly reduces the apparent lumen diameter. Both have abundant mitochondria and basolateral infoldings, but the absence of a brush border is the key histological criterion distinguishing DCT from PCT.
questions.question: The distal convoluted tubule (DCT) differs from the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) in which histological characteristic?

questions.explanation: The dorsal part of the maxillary process forms the premaxilla, maxilla, zygomatic bone, and part of the temporal bone. The mandible is formed from mesenchyme surrounding Meckel's cartilage in the mandibular process (dorsal part) of the first arch, not from the maxillary process.
questions.question: The maxillary process of the first arch forms all EXCEPT:
The facial colliculus in the floor of the fourth ventricle is formed by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus is formed by the facial nerve (CN VII) wrapping around the abducens nucleus (CN VI) before exiting the brainstem. This occurs at the level of the lower pons. The facial nucleus is located in the ventrolateral pontine tegmentum.

questions.question: The term 'basophilic' in histology refers to structures that stain with basic dyes due to their net negative charge and includes which of the following?
questions.explanation: Basophilic structures contain abundant nucleic acids (DNA in nuclei, RNA in ribosomes and rough ER), which carry negatively charged phosphate groups that attract positively charged (basic) dyes like hematoxylin. This gives nuclei and ribosomes the characteristic blue-purple staining in H&E sections. Cytoplasm rich in rough ER (ribosomes) is also basophilic.

questions.question: Polyhydramnios associated with esophageal atresia results from:
questions.explanation: Polyhydramnios (excess amniotic fluid) associated with esophageal atresia results from impaired fetal swallowing of amniotic fluid. Normally, the fetus swallows amniotic fluid, which is absorbed in the intestines. When esophageal atresia prevents this, amniotic fluid accumulates. Polyhydramnios should prompt evaluation for GI tract anomalies.

Renal ectopia refers to an abnormally positioned kidney, most commonly pelvic kidney (failure to ascend) or crossed renal ectopia (kidney on wrong side). Simple ectopic kidneys are usually unilateral and asymptomatic. The ectopic kidney may receive blood supply from nearby vessels and is prone to trauma, infection, and obstruction due to its abnormal position.
questions.question: Renal ectopia refers to:
A researcher studying the stomach notices that the lamina propria is highly vascularized to support gastric pits and glands. This rich vascularity is essential for which function?
options: Direct absorption of digested nutrients in the stomach
Supply of substrates for HCl synthesis
questions.explanation: The rich vascularity of the gastric lamina propria serves multiple critical functions: it delivers CO2, water, and substrates needed for acid production; it transports oxygen to support the high metabolic activity of parietal and chief cells; it carries regulatory hormones and neural signals to epithelial cells; and it rapidly clears absorbed substances and waste products. Any disruption of this blood supply (as in mucosal ischemia) quickly compromises the gastric mucosal barrier.

Parafollicular C cells scattered between thyroid follicles produce calcitonin which lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclast activity reducing bone resorption and promoting calcium deposition in bone. It opposes parathyroid hormone action. While important pharmacologically for treating Paget's disease and hypercalcemia, calcitonin's physiological role in human calcium homeostasis is less critical than that of PTH.
options: Stimulating thyroid hormone production by follicular cells
Raising blood calcium by stimulating osteoclasts
Regulating sodium reabsorption in the kidney
Mediating the stress response through cortisol release
Suppresses bone resorption and increases calcification, lowering blood calcium
questions.question: Parafollicular C cells of the thyroid gland produce calcitonin which has which physiological action?

questions.explanation: Type II pneumocytes (pneumonocytes) are cuboidal cells with characteristic lamellar bodies — the organelles that synthesize and store pulmonary surfactant. Surfactant (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine + proteins) reduces alveolar surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse. Deficiency in premature infants causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Type II cells also serve as progenitors for Type I pneumocytes after lung injury.
questions.question: Type II pneumocytes represent only 5% of alveolar surface but have a critical metabolic function. This function is:

options: Two layers — inner circular, outer longitudinal throughout
Skeletal muscle in the upper third
No peristalsis — urine flows by gravity alone
questions.explanation: The ureter has two smooth muscle layers in its upper two-thirds (inner longitudinal and outer circular) and three layers in its lower third near the bladder (inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal). Peristaltic waves generated by pacemaker cells in the renal pelvis propel urine downward toward the bladder. The oblique entry of the ureter into the bladder wall creates a valve mechanism preventing vesicoureteral reflux during bladder filling and micturition.
questions.question: The renal pelvis collects urine from the major calyces and connects to the ureter. What type of smooth muscle arrangement in the ureter drives urine downward by peristalsis?
The pharynx is histologically characterized by which type of epithelium in its respiratory portion?
questions.explanation: The nasopharynx is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium (respiratory epithelium) with goblet cells. The oropharynx and laryngopharynx, being food-conducting portions, transition to non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. This distinction reflects the dual role of the pharynx in both respiratory and digestive pathways.

The lens placode becomes visible at Carnegie stage 13 (approximately 28 days). At this stage, other features include the 4th pair of pharyngeal arches, appearance of upper and lower limb buds, an attenuated tail, and closure of the caudal neuropore. The lens placode is the primordium of the lens of the eye.
questions.question: The lens placode first becomes visible at which Carnegie stage?

questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus receives proteins from the rough ER, modifies them (glycosylation, phosphorylation, proteolytic cleavage), sorts them, and packages them into vesicles directed to the cell surface (secretion), lysosomes, or other organelles. It functions as the cell's postal sorting and processing center. The 'cis' face receives from the ER while the 'trans' face dispatches vesicles.
options: Sorting, modifying, and packaging proteins for secretion
Generating cellular energy through oxidative phosphorylation
Detoxification of drugs and metabolic byproducts
questions.question: The Golgi apparatus is primarily responsible for which of the following cellular functions?

questions.explanation: By the 7th week of development, the pleuropericardial membranes fuse with mesenchyme ventral to the esophagus, forming the primordial mediastinum. This fusion closes the pleuropericardial openings and separates the pleural cavities from the pericardial cavity. The right opening typically closes slightly earlier than the left.
questions.question: By which week do the pleuropericardial membranes fuse to close the pleuropericardial openings?

questions.explanation: Osteitis fibrosa cystica results from primary or secondary hyperparathyroidism, where excess PTH chronically stimulates osteoclasts to resorb bone matrix. The removed bone is replaced by fibrous tissue and hemorrhagic cysts called brown tumors. Histologically, increased osteoclast activity with tunneling resorption, fibrous stroma, and cyst formation are the characteristic findings.
options: Vitamin D deficiency causing impaired mineralization of osteoid
Increased osteoblast activity without corresponding osteoclast activity
Excess osteoclast-mediated bone resorption with fibrous tissue replacement
Deficiency of type I collagen synthesis by osteoblasts
Failure of endochondral ossification at the growth plate
questions.question: Osteitis fibrosa cystica is the bone disease associated primarily with which of the following?

options: Lipids in cell membranes with negative surface charges
Myofilaments of actin and myosin in the sarcomere
Collagen fibers with hydroxylysine and hydroxyproline residues
Phosphate groups on nucleic acids attract the cationic hematoxylin dye
questions.explanation: Hematoxylin is a basic (positively charged at acidic pH after mordanting) dye that is attracted to the negatively charged phosphate groups of nucleic acids — DNA in nuclei and RNA in nucleoli, ribosomes, and rough ER. This explains why cell nuclei stain blue-purple (basophilic) while collagen-rich cytoplasm and extracellular matrix stain pink (eosinophilic) with eosin in H&E. The degree of basophilia reflects RNA/ribosome content.
questions.question: Hematoxylin stains nuclei blue-purple in H&E sections. This basophilic staining occurs because nuclei predominantly contain which of the following?

questions.explanation: Simple renal cysts in children (unlike adults, where they're common and benign) usually indicate underlying disease such as tuberous sclerosis, von Hippel-Lindau disease, or other syndromes. Isolated simple cysts are rare in children. Any cystic renal lesion in a child warrants investigation for syndromic or genetic conditions. Simple cortical cysts become increasingly common with age in adults.
questions.question: Simple renal cysts in children usually indicate:
Epispadias is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Epispadias is characterized by the urethral opening on the dorsal (upper) surface of the penis due to faulty positioning of the genital tubercle and inadequate ectodermal ingrowth. It is much less common than hypospadias and is often associated with bladder exstrophy. The penis is typically short, broad, and curves dorsally. Surgical reconstruction is required.

questions.question: In the late secretory phase of the endometrial cycle (days 25–28), just before menstruation, the endometrium shows which specific vascular change?
questions.explanation: In the late secretory phase, falling progesterone (and estrogen) levels trigger intense vasospasm of the spiral arteries of the stratum functionalis. This ischemia causes breakdown of the functionalis. The subsequent reperfusion causes lysis of the ischemic tissue, which sloughs as menstrual flow. Prostaglandins (particularly PGF2α) mediate this spiral artery vasospasm. Excessive prostaglandin production causes dysmenorrhea; NSAIDs treat dysmenorrhea by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis.

Monosomy X (Turner syndrome, 45,X) is the only viable human monosomy. All autosomal monosomies are lethal and result in early miscarriage. Even monosomy X has a high rate of spontaneous abortion; about 99% of 45,X conceptuses are lost during pregnancy.
questions.question: The only viable human monosomy is which condition?

questions.explanation: Sebaceous glands develop from buds of the epidermal root sheaths of hair follicles. The glandular buds grow into surrounding connective tissue and branch to form alveoli and ducts. Central cells of the alveoli break down to form the oily secretion called sebum.
questions.question: Sebaceous glands develop from:
The inferior parathyroid gland develops from which pharyngeal pouch?
questions.explanation: The inferior parathyroid gland develops from the dorsal part of the third pharyngeal pouch in the 5th week. It develops along with the thymus and descends with it into the thorax. There are four parathyroid glands total, with the superior pair developing from the fourth pouch.

The osteon or Haversian system is the basic structural unit of compact bone consisting of a central Haversian canal containing blood vessels and nerves surrounded by 5 to 20 concentric lamellae of mineralized matrix. Osteocytes reside in lacunae between lamellae connected by canaliculi extending to the central canal and adjacent osteocytes. Osteons run parallel to the bone long axis and are the result of bone remodeling where osteoclasts create tunnels subsequently filled by osteoblasts depositing concentric lamellar bone.
questions.question: A section of compact bone stained with hematoxylin and eosin shows concentric lamellae, lacunae, canaliculi, and a central canal. The entire cylindrical structure is called which of the following?
Ankyloglossia results from:
questions.explanation: Ankyloglossia (tongue-tie) is characterized by an unusually short, thick lingual frenulum that may decrease tongue mobility. It is a congenital oral anomaly that can affect speech and feeding. Severe cases may require surgical intervention (frenulotomy) to improve tongue movement.

questions.question: The tunica intima of blood vessels consists of which three components in the correct sequence from the lumen outward?
options: Basement membrane → smooth muscle → elastic lamina
Endothelium → external elastic lamina → smooth muscle
questions.explanation: The tunica intima is the innermost layer of blood vessels and consists of: (1) endothelium — a single layer of squamous cells lining the lumen, (2) a basement membrane, and (3) a subendothelial layer of loose connective tissue. In larger arteries, the intima is separated from the tunica media by the internal elastic lamina (IEL). The endothelium is metabolically active, producing NO, prostacyclin, and von Willebrand factor.

Primary oocytes begin meiosis I during fetal life but are arrested in prophase I (specifically diplotene stage) until puberty. At puberty, with each ovarian cycle, one or more primary oocytes complete meiosis I to form secondary oocytes, which are then arrested in metaphase II.
questions.question: Primary oocytes are arrested in which stage of meiosis until puberty?
The crypts of Lieberkühn in the small intestine are structurally defined as:
options: Finger-like mucosal projections into the lumen
Lymphoid follicles scattered in the lamina propria
Goblet cell clusters in the epithelium
questions.explanation: Intestinal glands — the crypts of Lieberkühn — are simple tubular glands that extend through the full thickness of the mucosal lamina propria. They open at the base of the villi and contain stem cells, goblet cells, Paneth cells, and enteroendocrine cells. They are the proliferative compartment of the intestinal epithelium, constantly renewing the villous epithelium.

The foregut extends from the oral cavity to the ampulla of Vater (opening of the bile duct into the duodenum). This division is based on arterial supply, with the celiac trunk supplying foregut derivatives. The midgut extends from the ampulla of Vater to the proximal 2/3 of the transverse colon.
questions.question: The foregut extends from the oral cavity to:
In females, the mesonephric duct remnant may persist as:
questions.explanation: In females, the mesonephric duct may persist as Gartner's duct, a vestigial structure in the lateral vaginal wall. The epoophoron and paroophoron in the broad ligament also represent mesonephric remnants. These structures are usually clinically insignificant but may occasionally form cysts. In males, the mesonephric duct becomes the ductus deferens and related structures.

questions.question: The nasal pits are surrounded by which prominences?
questions.explanation: The nasal placodes form nasal pits, which are primordia of the anterior nares (nostrils) and nasal cavities. Ridges of tissue surrounding the nasal pits form the medial and lateral nasal prominences. These prominences are important for subsequent facial development.

questions.question: The inferior colliculus is associated with which sensory system?
questions.explanation: The inferior colliculus, located in the tectum of the lower midbrain, is part of the auditory pathway. It receives input from the lateral lemniscus and projects to the medial geniculate body of the thalamus, which then projects to the auditory cortex.

Loose (areolar) connective tissue is characterized by abundant ground substance, relatively few loosely arranged fibers, and a diversity of cell types including fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells, plasma cells, and leukocytes. The abundant intercellular spaces allow for the exchange of nutrients, gases, and waste products between blood vessels and neighboring cells. It forms the lamina propria and fills spaces between organs.
questions.question: Loose (areolar) connective tissue is distinguished from dense connective tissue primarily by which of the following characteristics?
options: Abundant ground substance, numerous cells of multiple types
Absence of any fibroblasts or macrophages
Exclusive presence under epithelial surfaces only
Composed mainly of elastic fibers in a watery matrix

questions.question: The adrenal glands develop from:
questions.explanation: The adrenal glands have dual embryological origin: the cortex develops from intermediate mesoderm (coelomic epithelium) and the medulla from neural crest cells (sympathetic ganglion cells). During kidney ascent, the adrenals remain in their original position at the superior poles. Initially, the adrenal glands are much larger relative to the kidneys than in adults, and the fetal cortex (which produces fetal zone steroids) involutes after birth.

options: Forming the thick filaments that generate force during contraction
Providing the elasticity that returns the sarcomere to its resting length
Connecting Z discs to the sarcolemma, maintaining sarcomere alignment during contraction
Anchoring the motor end plate to the sarcolemma
Transporting calcium from the SR to the troponin complex
questions.question: Desmin intermediate filaments in muscle primarily serve which function?
questions.explanation: Desmin intermediate filaments form a three-dimensional cytoskeletal lattice that encircles Z discs and connects adjacent sarcomeres to each other and to the sarcolemma and nuclear envelope. This maintains the lateral register of sarcomeres ensuring all contract synchronously and transmits contractile force to the ECM. Desmin mutations cause desminopathies including cardiomyopathies and skeletal muscle diseases with Z disc disruption.

questions.question: Atherosclerosis begins with endothelial dysfunction and subendothelial lipid deposition. The 'fatty streak' — the earliest macroscopic lesion — is composed histologically of:
questions.explanation: The fatty streak is the earliest atherosclerotic lesion, appearing in the aorta in children and adolescents. Histologically, it consists of accumulations of foam cells — macrophages that have ingested oxidized LDL via scavenger receptors — in the subintimal space. Foam cells appear as large pale cells with foamy cytoplasm (lipid-filled vacuoles). Fatty streaks are reversible and their progression to advanced plaques depends on continued oxidative stress, inflammation, and endothelial injury.

questions.question: Hypertrichosis is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Hypertrichosis is characterized by excessive hairiness resulting from an abundance of hair follicles. This can be localized or generalized and may be congenital or acquired. The condition differs from hirsutism, which is hormone-dependent excessive hair growth in specific distribution patterns.

questions.question: The right and left main bronchi appear during which week?
questions.explanation: The right and left main bronchi appear during the early 5th week as lateral outpocketings of the lung bud. The right bronchus subsequently divides to form three secondary bronchi, while the left forms two. This asymmetric branching establishes the foundation for the three-lobed right lung and two-lobed left lung.

Kupffer cells are fixed macrophages lining the hepatic sinusoids. Their strategic position allows them to phagocytose particulate matter, old red blood cells, bacteria, and endotoxins arriving via the portal circulation from the intestine. They are the largest pool of fixed macrophages in the body, playing a critical role in immune surveillance and iron recycling from hemoglobin breakdown.
questions.question: Kupffer cells are resident macrophages of the liver. Their location within hepatic sinusoids allows them to perform which primary function?
Which structure do neural crest cells NOT contribute to forming?
questions.explanation: Neural crest cells give rise to many structures including dorsal root ganglia, autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, and leptomeninges. Motor neurons of the spinal cord are derived from the basal plate of the neural tube, not from neural crest cells.

questions.question: Intramembranous ossification, which forms flat bones of the skull, begins with which of the following initial events?
questions.explanation: Intramembranous ossification begins with the condensation (aggregation) of mesenchyme cells in a highly vascularized region, followed by their direct differentiation into osteoblasts without any cartilage intermediate. These osteoblasts secrete osteoid (collagen + ground substance) that subsequently mineralizes, forming primary ossification centers. The skull bones, mandible, clavicle, and some facial bones form by this direct membrane bone formation pathway.
options: Formation of a cartilage template that is subsequently replaced by bone
Endochondral replacement of previously formed cartilage
Mesenchyme cells differentiating directly into osteoblasts without a cartilage intermediate
Migration of osteoblasts from the marrow cavity to the periosteum
Dedifferentiation of mature osteocytes into osteoprogenitor cells

questions.question: Gastric pits are invaginations of the surface epithelium into the lamina propria. The ratio of gastric pit depth to total gland length is GREATEST in which gastric region?
questions.explanation: In the pyloric region, gastric pits are notably deep — occupying approximately half the mucosal thickness — while the associated glands are shorter and more coiled. In the fundus and body, the glands are longer and pits shallower by proportion. This morphological difference is a key histological criterion for distinguishing pyloric from fundic/body mucosa.

RET gene mutations are associated with Hirschsprung disease. RET is a tyrosine kinase receptor involved in neural crest cell migration. Mutations impair the migration of neural crest cells into the distal colon, resulting in absence of ganglia. Genetic testing can help diagnose and counsel families about recurrence risks.
questions.question: The RET gene mutation is associated with:
Primordial germ cells reach the gonad by which week?
questions.explanation: Primordial germ cells start migrating by the 4th week and reach the gonad (genital ridge) by the 5th week of development. They migrate along the wall of the hindgut and through the dorsal mesentery to reach the developing gonads.

questions.question: The phallic part of the urogenital sinus gives rise to:
questions.explanation: The phallic part of the urogenital sinus gives rise to the penile (spongy) urethra in males and the vestibule in females. This portion grows toward and into the genital tubercle. In males, the terminal glandular urethra is formed by an ectodermal cord that grows inward from the glans and later canalizes.

Neurulation is the process involved in formation of the neural plate, neural groove, neural folds, and fusion of the folds to form the neural tube. The process is completed by the end of the 4th week with closure of the neural tube. The neural tube is the primordium of the central nervous system.
questions.question: Neurulation is completed by the end of which week with closure of the neural tube?

questions.explanation: On day 9, some hypoblast cells migrate and form a thin membrane termed the exocoelomic membrane of Heuser. Heuser's membrane together with hypoblast cells lines the blastocystic cavity, forming the primitive (primary) yolk sac.
questions.question: Heuser's membrane is formed by migration of cells from which layer?
The canalicular period is characterized by formation of:
questions.explanation: The canalicular period (16-26 weeks) is characterized by division of terminal bronchioles into respiratory bronchioles, which then divide into alveolar ducts. Primitive alveoli begin forming, and capillaries establish close contact with developing air spaces. Fetuses born at the end of this period may survive with intensive care.

questions.question: Vernix caseosa is composed of:
questions.explanation: Vernix caseosa is a white, greasy substance composed of sebum (from sebaceous glands) and desquamated peridermal cells. It covers fetal skin and protects against constant exposure to amniotic fluid with its high urine content. Vernix also facilitates birth by providing lubrication.

questions.question: The accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini) opens at:
questions.explanation: The accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini), when present, opens at the minor duodenal papilla, located approximately 2 cm proximal to the major papilla. It represents the proximal part of the dorsal pancreatic bud duct. The main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung) opens at the major duodenal papilla along with the common bile duct.

Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic phenomenon where certain genes are expressed in a parent-of-origin-specific manner. Some genes are only expressed from the maternal allele, others only from the paternal allele. Abnormalities in imprinting can cause disorders like Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes.
questions.question: Genomic imprinting refers to which phenomenon?

questions.explanation: Volvulus (twisting) of the midgut can result from malrotation, which creates a narrow mesenteric base predisposing to twisting around the superior mesenteric artery. This can cause intestinal obstruction and ischemia. Midgut volvulus is a surgical emergency requiring prompt intervention to prevent bowel necrosis. It typically presents with bilious vomiting in infants.
questions.question: Volvulus of the midgut can result from:

questions.explanation: The autosomal recessive form of polycystic kidney disease typically presents in infancy or early childhood with enlarged kidneys and progressive renal failure. This contrasts with the autosomal dominant form (adult polycystic kidney disease), which usually presents in the third or fourth decade. Both forms involve multiple renal cysts but differ in age of onset and inheritance pattern.
questions.question: Polycystic kidney disease (autosomal recessive form) typically presents:
The epidermis is derived from which embryonic germ layer?
questions.explanation: The epidermis is derived entirely from surface ectoderm, which provides the epithelial component of skin. The dermis, in contrast, develops from mesoderm. This dual origin explains the distinct tissue types and functions of these two skin layers.

Blood consists of approximately 55% plasma which is 90% water with proteins including albumin immunoglobulins and clotting factors plus electrolytes and solutes, and 45% formed elements by volume known as the hematocrit. The formed elements comprise erythrocytes accounting for approximately 99% of cells, leukocytes of five types, and platelets which are cell fragments. This ratio is maintained by continuous hematopoiesis in bone marrow.
options: Equal parts plasma, leukocytes, and erythrocytes
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the components of whole blood and their approximate proportions?

Capillaries are classified into three types based on their endothelium. Which type is found in the kidney glomeruli, pancreatic islets, and intestinal villi, and is characterized by cytoplasmic pores called fenestrations?
questions.explanation: Fenestrated capillaries have numerous transcytoplasmic pores (fenestrae, ~80nm diameter) covered by thin diaphragms. They are found in organs with high filtration/secretion/absorption requirements: kidney glomeruli, intestinal villi, endocrine glands, and choroid plexus. The fenestrae increase permeability to water and small molecules compared to continuous capillaries. In the glomerulus, fenestrae lack diaphragms to maximize filtration.

A rectovesical fistula is an abnormal communication between the rectum and urinary bladder. This results from incomplete separation of the cloaca by the urorectal septum. Boys with high anorectal malformations may have rectovesical or rectourethral fistulas. These require surgical correction to separate the systems.
questions.question: A rectovesical fistula connects the rectum to:

questions.explanation: The sinoatrial nodal artery supplies the SA node and arises from the right coronary artery (RCA) in approximately 55–60% of individuals and from the left circumflex artery in the remaining 40–45%. This is clinically important because RCA territory myocardial infarctions (inferior MI) can cause sinus node dysfunction (bradycardia, sick sinus syndrome). Understanding coronary artery anatomy and conduction system blood supply is essential for interpreting ECG changes in MI.
questions.question: The sinoatrial (SA) node is located in the wall of the right atrium. The artery supplying the SA node arises from which coronary artery in most individuals?
The kidneys initially receive blood supply from:
questions.explanation: The kidneys initially receive blood supply from the common iliac arteries when they are pelvic organs. As the kidneys ascend, they receive new arterial branches successively from higher levels of the aorta. Eventually, they receive their definitive blood supply from the renal arteries arising from the abdominal aorta. Accessory renal arteries represent persistence of embryonic vessels.

questions.question: Karyotyping is performed during which phase of the cell cycle?
questions.explanation: Karyotyping is performed on metaphase chromosomes because they are maximally condensed and individually distinguishable at this stage. Cells are arrested in metaphase, chromosomes are stained, photographed, and arranged by size and banding pattern to identify abnormalities.

Sinusoidal capillaries (sinusoids) have large, tortuous lumens, fenestrated endothelium without diaphragms, large gaps between cells, and a discontinuous or absent basement membrane. This structure permits passage of blood cells, large proteins, and even entire cells between blood and tissue. They are found in the liver (hepatic sinusoids), spleen (splenic sinusoids), and bone marrow, all sites of cell production or destruction.
questions.question: Sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillaries are found in which organs where maximum exchange of cells and large molecules with blood is required?

questions.explanation: The colonic crypts of Lieberkühn are lined predominantly by goblet cells that produce mucus to lubricate the passage of increasingly solid fecal material. The crypts also contain stem cells (at the base) that continuously renew the surface epithelium every 4–6 days. Unlike the small intestinal crypts, colonic crypts contain very few Paneth cells (absent in adult human colon) and no absorptive enterocytes comparable to those in the small intestine.
questions.question: The large intestine absorbs water and forms feces. The colonic mucosa has no villi but has abundant crypts. The primary function of the crypts of Lieberkühn in the colon is:

questions.explanation: T follicular helper cells in germinal centers provide critical help to B cells through: CD40L-CD40 interaction which is the contact-dependent signal preventing B cell apoptosis and driving proliferation; IL-21 which drives somatic hypermutation and promotes plasma cell differentiation; and IL-4 which promotes class switching to IgG1 and IgE. Without Tfh help, B cells in germinal centers undergo apoptosis rather than completing affinity maturation. This Tfh-B cell interaction is disrupted in common variable immunodeficiency.
options: CD8 cytotoxic signals killing infected B cells
Mast cell degranulation and histamine release signals
Neutrophil oxidative burst and degranulation signals
CD40L–CD40 and IL-21/IL-4 driving B-cell proliferation and class switching
questions.question: The germinal center reaction in secondary follicles requires T follicular helper cells providing which signals to activate B cells?

In the context of membrane transport, the movement of glucose into a cell via a glucose transporter (GLUT) without requiring direct ATP expenditure but utilizing a concentration gradient is classified as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion moves substances down their concentration gradient through specific membrane protein channels or carriers, requiring no energy expenditure (ATP). GLUT transporters move glucose down its gradient from high extracellular to lower intracellular concentrations. By contrast, primary active transport (e.g., Na+/K+ ATPase) uses ATP to move substances against concentration gradients.

options: Action potentials jumping node to node, dramatically increasing conduction speed
They are sites of synaptic transmission between neurons
They represent areas where myelin synthesis is slowest
They contain the highest density of potassium channels for repolarization
They allow Schwann cells to phagocytose damaged axon segments
questions.question: The nodes of Ranvier enable saltatory conduction of action potentials. This increases conduction velocity by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Nodes of Ranvier are unmyelinated gaps approximately 1 micrometer wide where voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated. Action potentials are regenerated only at nodes jumping from node to node in saltatory conduction which is approximately 50 times faster than continuous conduction and requires less energy since fewer membrane areas need repolarization. Multiple sclerosis disrupts myelin converting saltatory to continuous slower conduction causing the characteristic delayed nerve conduction.

The lingual (upper/oral) surface of the epiglottis and the anterior portion of its laryngeal surface are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, continuous with the oropharyngeal epithelium. The posterior laryngeal surface and the epiglottis below the transition zone are covered by respiratory epithelium. This distinction reflects the dual role of the epiglottis in both digestive and respiratory passages.
questions.question: The epiglottis is a cartilaginous flap that closes the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. On its lingual (superior) surface, it is covered by which epithelium?

questions.explanation: Macrophages originate from monocyte precursor cells produced in the bone marrow, which circulate in the blood and then migrate into connective tissues where they differentiate into tissue macrophages. This monocyte-macrophage lineage is part of the Mononuclear Phagocyte System (MPS). The process of differentiation involves changes in size, surface markers, and the acquisition of pronounced phagocytic capacity.
questions.question: Macrophages originate from which precursor cells in the bone marrow and subsequently differentiate in connective tissues?
Which connective tissue cell type acts as an antigen-presenting cell (APC) in the skin epidermis and is specifically named after the scientist who described it?
questions.explanation: Langerhans cells are specialized antigen-presenting macrophages resident in the skin epidermis, named after Paul Langerhans who also described the pancreatic islets. They capture antigens entering through the skin and migrate to draining lymph nodes to present antigens to T lymphocytes, initiating adaptive immune responses. They are part of the MPS and contain characteristic tennis racket-shaped cytoplasmic Birbeck granules.

questions.question: The lens of the eye achieves accommodation for near vision by which mechanism?
options: Changing the curvature of the cornea through ciliary muscle contraction
Rotating the eyeball to shift the angle of refraction
Adjusting aqueous humor volume in the anterior chamber
Ciliary muscle contraction reduces zonular tension, allowing the lens to round up
Pupil constriction reducing spherical aberration for near objects
questions.explanation: Accommodation for near vision involves ciliary muscle contraction which relaxes the circular zonular fibers attached to the lens, allowing the elastic lens to recoil into a more spherical shape with greater refractive power to focus near objects on the retina. For far vision, ciliary muscle relaxes causing zonular fibers to tighten and flatten the lens. The lens loses elasticity with age causing presbyopia with reduced near vision accommodation.

questions.question: The rectal mucosa differs from the rest of the colon in that the anal canal shows a transition from simple columnar to which other epithelium?
questions.explanation: At the pectinate (dentate) line in the anal canal, the simple columnar epithelium of the rectum transitions first to non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and then to keratinized stratified squamous epithelium continuous with the perianal skin. This zone is clinically important as it is the site of hemorrhoids and a transition zone for certain types of anal carcinoma.

The pharyngeal tonsils (adenoids) are part of Waldeyer's ring — a ring of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) at the pharyngeal entrance. Unlike lymph nodes and spleen (encapsulated secondary lymphoid organs), tonsils are unencapsulated lymphoid tissues within mucous membranes. The adenoids are covered by respiratory epithelium and lack crypts. Enlarged adenoids in children can obstruct the nasopharynx, impairing breathing and Eustachian tube drainage.
options: Secondary lymphoid organ with a capsule
questions.question: The pharyngeal tonsils (adenoids) are located in the nasopharynx. They represent which type of lymphoid tissue?

questions.explanation: Reticular connective tissue consists of type III collagen fibers (reticular fibers) forming a delicate network supporting free cells. It forms the stroma of hematopoietic organs (bone marrow, spleen) and lymphoid organs (lymph nodes, thymus), providing the scaffold that supports blood cell development and immune cell interactions. The reticular fibers are produced by specialized fibroblasts called reticular cells.
options: Bone marrow, lymph nodes, spleen, liver, and pancreas
Cartilage matrix and calcified bone matrix
Brain white matter and peripheral nerves
questions.question: Reticular connective tissue is unique in forming the structural framework (stroma) of which of the following organs?
The bony core of the cochlea called the modiolus contains which structure of critical auditory importance?
questions.explanation: The modiolus is the conical bony core around which the cochlea spirals and it contains the spiral ganglion housing the cell bodies of bipolar primary auditory neurons. The central processes of these neurons form the cochlear nerve which is a branch of cranial nerve VIII traveling to the cochlear nuclei in the brainstem. The modiolus also transmits blood vessels to the cochlea and is targeted during cochlear implant electrode array insertion.
options: The organ of Corti with hair cells
Spiral ganglion housing CN VIII auditory neuron cell bodies
The stapes footplate in the oval window
The endolymphatic sac in the temporal bone

questions.explanation: Enteroendocrine cells (also called APUD cells or diffuse neuroendocrine cells) are scattered throughout the GIT epithelium and release hormones and peptides — such as gastrin, somatostatin, and secretin — into the lamina propria vasculature. They are characterized by basal granules visible on electron microscopy. They constitute the largest endocrine system in the body.
questions.question: Enteroendocrine cells in the stomach are best characterized by which feature?
options: They are the most numerous cells lining gastric pits
They release hormones into the bloodstream
They produce HCl and intrinsic factor
They are exclusively found in the pyloric glands
They stain intensely with PAS reagent for mucus

questions.question: Ground substance of bone matrix contains which important non-collagenous proteins that participate in mineralization regulation?
questions.explanation: Bone matrix non-collagenous proteins include osteocalcin which binds calcium and regulates mineral crystal growth, osteopontin which mediates osteoclast attachment and cell signaling, and bone sialoprotein which nucleates hydroxyapatite crystallization. These proteins are synthesized by osteoblasts and regulate mineralization. Osteocalcin is also used as a serum marker of bone formation activity in metabolic bone disease assessment.
options: Hyaluronic acid and heparan sulfate predominantly
Type II collagen and aggrecan proteoglycan

questions.question: The musculature of the tongue develops from which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation: Tongue musculature develops from occipital myotomes (somites). These myoblasts migrate into the developing tongue, bringing their nerve supply (hypoglossal nerve, CN XII) with them. This is why the hypoglossal nerve innervates all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles.

options: Fundus/body secrete mucus; cardia/pylorus secrete acid
All regions secrete equal amounts of mucus and acid
Cardia/pylorus secrete mucus; fundus/body secrete acid
Pylorus is the sole site of pepsinogen production
Cardia is the only region with parietal cells
questions.explanation: The cardia and pylorus contain glands that predominantly produce mucus to protect the mucosa at junctional zones. The fundus and body contain the main gastric glands with parietal cells (HCl and intrinsic factor) and chief cells (pepsinogen). This regional specialization ensures protection at the gastroesophageal and gastroduodenal junctions.
questions.question: Histologically, the fundus and body of the stomach are identical, while the cardia and pylorus are similar. The primary secretory difference between these regions is:

questions.explanation: Arterioles are small muscular vessels (diameter < 0.3 mm) whose tunica media contains 1–3 layers of smooth muscle cells. Contraction or relaxation of this smooth muscle changes the arteriolar diameter, directly controlling peripheral vascular resistance and blood flow distribution. This is the primary mechanism regulating blood pressure at the tissue level and is the target of antihypertensive drugs like calcium channel blockers.
questions.question: Arterioles are the principal site of peripheral vascular resistance. This resistance is regulated by contraction of smooth muscle in which layer?
The liver produces the majority of serum proteins. Which protein, synthesized exclusively by hepatocytes, is the most abundant in plasma and maintains oncotic pressure?
questions.explanation: Albumin is synthesized exclusively by hepatocytes (approximately 12g/day) and is the most abundant plasma protein (35–50 g/L). It maintains plasma oncotic pressure (preventing edema), transports fatty acids, bilirubin, hormones, and drugs, and acts as a buffer. In chronic liver failure, reduced albumin synthesis causes hypoalbuminemia, leading to peripheral edema and ascites. Serum albumin level is a sensitive marker of synthetic function in chronic liver disease.

questions.question: S-shaped tubules in kidney development give rise to:
questions.explanation: S-shaped tubules formed from metanephric vesicles give rise to the nephrons (excretory units). One end develops into Bowman's capsule around a developing glomerulus, while the other end connects to a collecting tubule. The middle portion elongates to form the proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, and distal convoluted tubule. Each kidney contains over 1 million nephrons.

As a result of brain growth and cephalic folding of the embryo, the buccopharyngeal membrane is pulled forward while the heart and pericardial cavity move first to the cervical region and finally to the thorax. This repositioning is essential for establishing the normal anatomical relationships of the heart.
questions.question: As a result of cephalic folding, the heart moves from the cervical region to which final location?

questions.explanation: Structures at 0.5 nm are well below the resolving limit of light microscopy (0.2 μm = 200 nm), requiring an electron microscope. The transmission electron microscope achieves resolution of ~0.1 nm, making it suitable for visualizing macromolecules and subcellular structures. Phase contrast and fluorescence microscopes are variants of light microscopy with the same inherent resolution limit.
questions.question: A histologist wishes to visualize structures that are 0.5 nm in size. Which microscope should be used?

questions.explanation: At the neuromuscular junction, motor neurons release acetylcholine from synaptic vesicles into the synaptic cleft. Acetylcholine binds nicotinic ACh receptors which are ligand-gated ion channels on the muscle fiber's motor end plate, causing sodium influx and depolarization that triggers the action potential propagating along T-tubules to initiate excitation-contraction coupling. Acetylcholinesterase rapidly hydrolyzes ACh to terminate the signal.
questions.question: The neuromuscular junction uses which neurotransmitter binding to which receptor type on the skeletal muscle fiber?
options: Norepinephrine binding to beta-adrenergic smooth muscle receptors
Acetylcholine on nicotinic motor end plate receptors causing Na⁺ influx
Glutamate binding to ionotropic postsynaptic NMDA receptors
Substance P binding to NK1 pain receptors
Dopamine binding to postsynaptic D2 dopamine receptors

questions.question: High anorectal malformations are characterized by:
questions.explanation: High anorectal malformations are characterized by the rectum ending above the levator ani muscle, often with a fistula to the urinary tract (males) or vagina (females). Low malformations involve the rectum ending below the levator ani. This classification is important for surgical planning, as high malformations require more extensive reconstruction.

Both the visceral (lung) and parietal (chest wall, diaphragm, mediastinum) pleura are lined by a continuous layer of mesothelial cells — simple squamous epithelial cells of mesodermal origin. Mesothelial cells produce lubricating serous fluid that allows friction-free lung movement during breathing. In pleural mesothelioma (associated with asbestos exposure), these cells undergo malignant transformation. Mesothelial cells are identified immunohistochemically by calretinin, WT1, and CK5/6.
questions.question: The lung pleura is composed of two layers — visceral and parietal. Both are lined by which cell type?

questions.explanation: The mesenchyme for formation of the head and neck region is derived from paraxial mesoderm, lateral plate mesoderm, neural crest cells, and ectodermal placodes. Endoderm contributes to epithelial linings of pharyngeal pouches but not to mesenchymal structures. Each of these sources contributes specific tissues.
questions.question: The mesenchyme for head and neck formation is derived from all EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: The visceral pleura is derived from splanchnic mesoderm covering the outside of the developing lungs. The parietal pleura develops from somatic mesoderm lining the body wall. The pleural cavity forms between these two layers as the lungs expand into the body cavity.
questions.question: The visceral pleura is derived from:

questions.explanation: In crossed fused renal ectopia, both kidneys are most commonly on the left side (though right-sided can occur). One kidney crosses the midline during development and fuses with the other. The ureters still insert normally in the bladder on their respective sides. The fused kidneys typically function normally. Various fusion patterns exist (inferior, sigmoid, lump, disc). The condition is usually discovered incidentally.
questions.question: Crossed fused renal ectopia most commonly involves:
The canalicular network in bone allows which of the following physiological exchanges?
questions.explanation: Canaliculi are minute tunnels containing cytoplasmic processes of osteocytes that extend from each lacuna connecting to adjacent osteocytes via gap junctions. Since metabolites cannot diffuse through calcified matrix this canalicular network creates a bucket brigade relay for nutrients oxygen hormones and waste products between blood vessels in Haversian canals and the most distant osteocytes. Osteocytes also sense mechanical strain through canalicular fluid flow and signal bone remodeling accordingly.
options: Osteoclasts to migrate between different bone surfaces
Calcium phosphate to be stored between osteocytes
Osteoblasts to migrate through mineralized matrix
Nerve fibers to reach individual osteocytes
Osteocytes exchange nutrients with blood vessels via cytoplasmic processes

questions.question: Malrotation of the midgut can lead to:
questions.explanation: Malrotation of the midgut can lead to volvulus, which is rotation of an intestinal loop around a branch of the superior mesenteric artery. This can cause intestinal obstruction or even gangrene. Volvulus requires emergency surgical intervention to prevent bowel ischemia and necrosis.

The vesical (upper) part of the urogenital sinus is continuous with the allantois, which constricts to form the urachus connecting the bladder apex to the umbilicus. The vesical portion forms most of the urinary bladder. The allantois eventually obliterates to become the median umbilical ligament in the adult.
questions.question: The vesical part of the urogenital sinus is continuous with:

options: Absence of fibroblasts in the cartilage matrix
Immune suppression preventing any cellular activity
Type II collagen being unable to be synthesized by mature chondrocytes
Avascular with few cells and no perichondrium, severely limiting regenerative capacity
Synovial fluid preventing cell migration to damage sites
questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has destruction of articular cartilage. The inability of this cartilage to repair itself is primarily explained by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Articular hyaline cartilage lacks blood vessels nerves and lymphatics and has no perichondrium. Its sparse chondrocytes cannot migrate being trapped in lacunae and have minimal proliferative capacity. Damage cannot be repaired through the usual healing cascade requiring vascular invasion. Fibrocartilage rather than hyaline cartilage forms any repair tissue which has inferior mechanical properties explaining the progressive joint destruction in rheumatoid and osteoarthritis.

questions.question: The midgut loop rotates a total of how many degrees?
questions.explanation: The midgut loop undergoes a total rotation of 270 degrees counterclockwise around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery. An initial 90-degree rotation occurs while in the umbilical cord, followed by an additional 180-degree rotation during return to the abdomen. This rotation is essential for proper intestinal positioning.

The pharyngeal constrictor muscles (superior, middle, inferior) are derived from the fourth pharyngeal arch and are innervated by the vagus nerve (CN X) via the pharyngeal plexus. These muscles are essential for swallowing. The stylopharyngeus (from third arch) is innervated by CN IX.
questions.question: The pharyngeal constrictors are innervated by which cranial nerve?

The renal papilla is the apex of a medullary pyramid where urine drains into the minor calyx. It contains the openings of papillary ducts (ducts of Bellini). The epithelium lining the minor calyx that receives this urine is:
questions.explanation: From the renal papilla outward — through the minor calyces, major calyces, renal pelvis, ureter, and bladder — the entire collecting system is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium). This barrier epithelium is impermeable to urea and urine, preventing urine reabsorption. Transitional epithelium can stretch considerably (2–6 layers when relaxed versus 2–3 when distended).

questions.question: The embryonic organizer refers to which group of cells?
questions.explanation: The migratory cells which invaginate from the surface during gastrulation and induce development of the neural tube are termed the embryonic organizer. These mesodermal cells (including the notochord) secrete factors that induce the overlying ectoderm to form neural tissue.

Duplication of the ureter results from development of two ureteric buds from the mesonephric duct instead of one. Complete duplication produces two separate ureters, while incomplete duplication (bifid ureter) produces a Y-shaped ureter. The duplicated ureter may have ectopic opening into the urethra or vagina.
questions.question: Duplication of the ureter results from:

questions.explanation: Six mesenchymal proliferations called auricular hillocks develop from the dorsal ends of the 1st and 2nd pharyngeal arches (three on each side of the meatus). These hillocks fuse to form the definitive auricle. The complex adult shape of the auricle reflects contributions from multiple hillocks.
questions.question: How many auricular hillocks contribute to the formation of the definitive auricle?
