questions.explanation: Reciprocal induction involves interactions between different tissues in which cells in one tissue express a set of inductive signals to which cells in the other tissue respond. The responding cells then express signals that affect the inducing tissue. Many organs develop through reciprocal induction.
questions.question: Reciprocal induction involves which type of interaction?

options: Rapid insertion of aquaporin-2 channels via exocytosis
Activation of V2 receptors on the cell membrane
questions.explanation: Aldosterone is a steroid hormone that diffuses into principal cells and binds cytosolic mineralocorticoid receptors (MR). The aldosterone-MR complex translocates to the nucleus and acts as a transcription factor, increasing expression of: ENaC (apical sodium channels), Na+/K+-ATPase (basolateral sodium pump), and ROMK (potassium channels). This genomic action takes 30–60 minutes to manifest. Spironolactone and eplerenone are MR antagonists used clinically to block aldosterone's effects.
questions.question: Aldosterone acts on principal cells of the collecting duct to increase sodium reabsorption. Its mechanism involves which action on gene expression?

options: Intrinsic GI nervous system with independent control of motility and secretion
The sympathetic chain ganglia innervating the intestine
The somatic motor system controlling intestinal smooth muscle
The central nervous system extension into the gut wall
The lymphatic plexus draining intestinal villi
questions.explanation: The enteric nervous system is a complex intrinsic neural network within the GI wall containing approximately 500 million neurons organized into Meissner's submucosal plexus which regulates secretion and blood flow and Auerbach's myenteric plexus between circular and longitudinal muscle layers which controls motility. The ENS can function autonomously without input from the CNS and is often called the second brain. It is derived from neural crest cells and contains as many neurons as the spinal cord.
questions.question: The submucosal Meissner's plexus and myenteric Auerbach's plexus together constitute which nervous system component?

questions.explanation: Meckel's diverticulum can result from persistence of the vitelline duct (yolk stalk). This is the most common congenital malformation of the gastrointestinal tract, occurring in about 2% of the population. It is typically located about 2 feet from the ileocecal valve on the ileum.
questions.question: Meckel's diverticulum represents persistence of which embryonic structure?
Myelin is produced in the peripheral nervous system by which specific cell type?
questions.explanation: In the peripheral nervous system, Schwann cells produce myelin by spirally wrapping their cytoplasm around a single axon segment compacting the membrane into the myelin sheath. In the CNS, oligodendrocytes produce myelin and can myelinate segments of multiple axons simultaneously unlike Schwann cells which myelinate only one axon segment each. This difference has important implications for regeneration after nerve injury.

questions.question: Imperforate hymen results from failure of:
questions.explanation: Imperforate hymen results from failure of complete canalization of the vaginal plate, leaving a membrane blocking the vaginal opening. This is often asymptomatic until menarche, when menstrual blood accumulates (hematocolpos). The condition may present with cyclic pelvic pain, primary amenorrhea, or abdominal mass. Treatment is simple surgical opening (hymenotomy).

The transverse mesocolon fuses with the greater omentum but maintains its mobility. This creates a four-layered structure posterior to the stomach. The fusion occurs as the greater omentum grows inferiorly from the greater curvature. Despite fusion, the transverse colon retains significant mobility unlike the ascending and descending colons.
questions.question: The transverse mesocolon fuses with:

questions.explanation: At the end of the 4th week, five mesenchymal prominences can be recognized surrounding the stomodeum: one frontonasal prominence, two mandibular prominences, and two maxillary prominences. These prominences are derived from neural crest cells and play crucial roles in facial development.
questions.question: At the end of the 4th week, how many mesenchymal prominences surround the stomodeum?

questions.explanation: The chorion is histologically composed of four layers: cellular layer, dense reticulum, pseudo-basement membrane, and outer trophoblast. The chorion is the outer membrane of the fetal membranes, is in contact with the uterine wall, and is attached to the margins of the placenta.
questions.question: The chorion is histologically composed of how many layers?

questions.explanation: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus is the parasympathetic component of the oculomotor nuclear complex in the upper midbrain. It provides parasympathetic innervation to the sphincter pupillae (pupil constriction) and ciliary muscle (accommodation). It is essential for the pupillary light reflex.
questions.question: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus is associated with which cranial nerve?

questions.explanation: The kidneys attain their adult position in the abdomen by the 9th week of development. This "ascent" occurs through disproportionate growth of the lumbar and sacral regions. During ascent, the kidneys rotate medially approximately 90 degrees, bringing their hila to face anteromedially. Blood supply changes from iliac to aortic branches.
questions.question: Kidneys attain their adult position by which week?

questions.explanation: On days 11-12, new cells appear between the cytotrophoblast and Heuser's membrane to form extraembryonic mesoderm. Spaces appear in this mesoderm to form the chorionic cavity (extraembryonic coelom), which will eventually surround the amnion and yolk sac.
questions.question: Extraembryonic mesoderm appears between which two structures?

questions.explanation: Birth normally occurs 266 days or 38 weeks after fertilization (280 days or 40 weeks after the last normal menstrual period). The fetus is considered full term at this point. Gestational age is usually calculated from the last menstrual period rather than fertilization.
questions.question: Birth normally occurs how many days after fertilization?
Which cells in the gastric mucosa secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor?
questions.explanation: Parietal (oxyntic) cells are large, rounded or pyramidal cells with intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm due to abundant mitochondria. They secrete both hydrochloric acid, which creates the acidic environment for protein digestion, and intrinsic factor, which is essential for vitamin B12 absorption. Deficiency of intrinsic factor causes pernicious anemia.

options: Isolated renal failure without other effects
questions.explanation: Bilateral renal agenesis (Potter syndrome) prevents fetal urine production, causing oligohydramnios (markedly reduced amniotic fluid). This leads to the Potter sequence: pulmonary hypoplasia (lack of fluid for lung expansion), limb contractures (restricted movement), and characteristic Potter facies (flattened nose, low-set ears, epicanthal folds, recessed chin from oligohydramnios compression). It is invariably lethal due to pulmonary insufficiency. Amniotic fluid is essential for normal fetal lung development.
questions.question: The fetal kidney produces urine, which becomes the primary source of amniotic fluid from the second trimester. Bilateral renal agenesis causes which condition?

questions.explanation: Digital rays in the hand plate first appear during the 6th week of development. At this time, there is rapid growth of the upper limbs, a groove develops between the 1st and 2nd pharyngeal arches (forming the external acoustic meatus), and swelling around this groove forms the auricular hillocks.
questions.question: Digital rays in the hand plate first appear during which week?

questions.explanation: Kupffer cells (hepatic macrophages) are derived from mesenchyme of the septum transversum, along with fibrous tissue and hematopoietic tissue. The hepatic epithelial cells (hepatocytes and bile duct epithelium) are derived from endoderm of the hepatic diverticulum. This dual origin creates the complex cellular composition of the liver.
questions.question: Kupffer cells in the liver are derived from:

questions.explanation: The hinge points are areas where the neural plate attaches to adjacent tissues during neurulation. The median hinge point is attached to the notochord, while paired dorsolateral hinge points are attached to adjacent epidermal ectoderm. At these points, neuroepithelial cells become wedge-shaped and the neural plate undergoes furrowing. SECTION C: EMBRYONIC FOLDING AND BODY FORM
questions.question: The hinge points during neurulation are areas of neural plate attachment to which structures?
The mucous blanket of the conducting airways consists of two layers. The more superficial, viscous gel layer traps particles, while the deeper, watery sol layer contains:
questions.explanation: The periciliary layer (sol layer) is a low-viscosity watery fluid surrounding the cilia of ciliated epithelial cells in the conducting airways. Cilia beat within this sol layer, propelling the more viscous, particle-laden gel (mucus) layer above them toward the pharynx for clearance. In cystic fibrosis, dehydration of the periciliary layer collapses the cilia and renders the mucus immovable. In primary ciliary dyskinesia, structurally abnormal cilia cannot beat effectively.

questions.question: The preparation of tissue sections for electron microscopy differs from light microscopy preparation in requiring which of the following?
questions.explanation: Electron microscopy requires ultra-thin sections (50–100 nm) because electrons cannot penetrate thicker tissue. Specimens are fixed with glutaraldehyde and osmium tetroxide, embedded in epoxy resin (not paraffin), cut on an ultramicrotome, and contrast-stained with heavy metals (uranium, lead) that scatter electrons differentially. These differences from light microscopy preparation are fundamental.
options: Ultra-thin sections stained with heavy metal salts
Routine H&E staining and glass slides

questions.explanation: The proliferative phase beginning approximately days 3 to 5 post-injury involves fibroblasts invading the wound and initially depositing type III collagen forming provisional granulation tissue. Over weeks to months during the remodeling phase type III collagen is progressively replaced by stronger type I collagen and cross-linking increases gradually restoring tensile strength reaching maximum approximately 80% of original. This temporal collagen transition is fundamental to wound healing biology.
options: Type IV collagen is deposited first then replaced by type I
Type I collagen is deposited first without any subsequent change
Type III collagen deposited first, then replaced by type I during remodeling
Type II collagen is deposited only then replaced by type III
Elastic fibers are deposited first before any collagen
questions.question: During wound healing, which type of collagen is initially deposited by fibroblasts in the proliferative phase and what subsequently replaces it?

questions.explanation: Amniotic fluid is derived from active secretion by amniotic epithelium, transudation from fetal circulation, fetal urine (important source in later pregnancy), and transudation from maternal circulation. The fetal liver does not directly contribute to amniotic fluid production.
questions.question: Amniotic fluid is derived from all sources EXCEPT:
Embryonic induction is involved in development of all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Embryonic induction is involved in development of many organs including eyes (lens, optic cup), ears, limbs, kidney, teeth, hair, salivary glands, and pancreas. Blood cell development (hematopoiesis) occurs through intrinsic differentiation programs rather than classical tissue-to-tissue induction.

questions.question: Lymph nodes filter lymph and contain B cell follicles and T cell zones. The germinal center of a lymphoid follicle represents:
questions.explanation: Germinal centers are specialized microenvironments within secondary lymphoid follicles where antigen-activated B cells undergo rapid clonal expansion (centroblasts → centrocytes), somatic hypermutation of immunoglobulin genes (affinity maturation), and class-switch recombination. The resulting high-affinity antibody-secreting plasma cells and long-lived memory B cells are the products of the germinal center reaction. Abnormal germinal centers are the origin of most B-cell lymphomas.
options: The primary B cell zone in a non-stimulated lymph node
The T cell-rich area around the follicle
A site of active B cell proliferation, somatic hypermutation,
The site of T cell receptor gene rearrangement

questions.question: Horseshoe kidney ascent is prevented by:
questions.explanation: Normal ascent of horseshoe kidney is prevented by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery, which acts as a mechanical barrier to the fused kidneys. The kidneys typically lie in the lower lumbar region with the isthmus (fusion point) at or near the level of the IMA origin. Despite their low position, horseshoe kidneys usually function normally.

The cervical sinus is formed during the 5th week when the hyoid (2nd) pharyngeal arch overgrows the 3rd and 4th arches. This creates a depression called the cervical sinus, which normally disappears during development. Persistence of this structure can lead to cervical cysts or fistulas. SECTION D: CARDIOVASCULAR DEVELOPMENT
questions.question: The cervical sinus is formed by overgrowth of which pharyngeal arch?

questions.explanation: The early ectoderm produces bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), especially BMP-4. Neural inducers (noggin, chordin, and follistatin) from the notochord and primitive node bind to BMPs, neutralizing them. This prevents the ectoderm from forming epidermis and allows it to form neural ectoderm instead.
questions.question: Neural induction occurs by preventing ectoderm from forming which tissue?

options: Bile pigment processing and bilirubin conjugation only
Lipid synthesis and detoxification of drugs
Urea cycle and albumin synthesis equally in all zones
questions.explanation: Zone 1 (periportal) hepatocytes receive well-oxygenated blood rich in nutrients and are therefore specialized for oxygen-dependent processes: oxidative phosphorylation, fatty acid oxidation, gluconeogenesis, and amino acid metabolism (including urea synthesis). Zone 3 (centrilobular) hepatocytes, receiving less oxygen, are specialized for glycolysis, lipogenesis, and drug biotransformation (high CYP450). This metabolic zonation explains why different liver diseases affect different zones.
questions.question: Hepatocytes in Zone 1 (periportal) of the hepatic acinus are specialized for which metabolic function?

options: They produce PTH as the sole parathyroid hormone source
They produce calcitonin supplementing thyroid C cells
They produce aldosterone in hypoparathyroid states
They are the sole producers of vitamin D binding protein
Post-pubertal cells with abundant mitochondria; may be exhausted chief cells
questions.explanation: Oxyphil cells appear after puberty in increasing numbers and have abundant mitochondria giving them their eosinophilic granular cytoplasm. Their function remains incompletely understood. They are thought to represent a transitional or exhausted form of chief cells that may retain some limited PTH secretory capacity. In parathyroid adenoma and hyperplasia, oxyphil cells may proliferate. They do not have the prominent Golgi or secretory granules of active chief cells.
questions.question: The parathyroid glands contain chief cells and oxyphil cells. The function of oxyphil cells is which of the following?

questions.explanation: The perpendicular alternation of collagen fiber orientation between adjacent lamellae (visible as alternating bright and dark bands under polarized light) is structurally analogous to plywood — it provides resistance to mechanical stress from multiple directions. This arrangement prevents crack propagation through bone and provides optimal mechanical resistance to the combined torsional, bending, and compressive forces that bones encounter during locomotion.
options: Provides resistance to stress from multiple directions against twisting, bending, and compression
Facilitates faster mineralization of new lamellae
Allows the osteon to expand during bone remodeling
Prevents canalicular fluid flow between lamellae
Creates the alternating light and dark pattern seen under polarized light but has no mechanical significance
questions.question: The collagen fibers within adjacent lamellae of an osteon are oriented at different angles to each other. What is the primary biomechanical significance of this arrangement?

questions.explanation: Mitochondria are the powerhouses of the cell, generating the majority of ATP through oxidative phosphorylation in their inner membrane (electron transport chain) using oxygen and metabolic substrates. They also regulate calcium homeostasis, apoptosis, and contain their own DNA (mtDNA) and ribosomes reflecting bacterial ancestry. Cells with high energy demands (cardiac muscle, neurons) are particularly rich in mitochondria.
options: Protein synthesis exclusively for cytoskeletal components
Production of secretory vesicles for exocytosis
Forming the contractile apparatus in all cell types
questions.question: Mitochondria are specifically essential for cell survival primarily due to which of the following functions?
Lymphatic capillaries differ from blood capillaries in which important structural feature?
questions.explanation: Lymphatic capillaries begin as closed-ended tubes in the tissue spaces. Their endothelial cells have overlapping (valve-like) edges and are anchored to surrounding connective tissue by anchoring filaments. These features allow tissue fluid to enter one-way but not re-enter the interstitium. Lymphatic capillaries have a thin or absent basement membrane and no pericytes, distinguishing them from blood capillaries.
options: Lymphatic capillaries have a thicker basement membrane
Lymphatic capillaries are lined by fenestrated endothelium
Lymphatic capillaries contain red blood cells
Lymphatic capillaries closed at one end
Lymphatic capillaries are surrounded by smooth muscle

questions.question: A neuron with an axon 1 meter long (e.g., motor neuron to the foot) demonstrates which cellular challenge most dramatically?
questions.explanation: Motor neurons with meter-long axons cannot rely on diffusion to supply synaptic terminals with neurotransmitters, organelles, and trophic factors synthesized in the cell body. Fast anterograde axonal transport (via kinesin on microtubule tracks at ~400 mm/day) and retrograde transport (via dynein at ~200 mm/day) are essential for neuronal survival and function. Disruption of axonal transport underlies several neurodegenerative diseases.
options: The need for axonal transport to deliver organelles from cell body to distant terminals
The necessity for multiple nuclei to support such a long cell
The requirement for lysosomes at each node of Ranvier
The generation of a large number of synaptic vesicles in the cell body only
The need for peroxisomes to oxidize myelin along the axon length

questions.question: The aorticopulmonary (A(ΔP) septum forms by fusion of ridges that grow in what pattern?
questions.explanation: The aorticopulmonary septum divides the truncus arteriosus into the aorta and pulmonary trunk. It forms by fusion of pairs of opposing ridges (truncal and bulbar ridges) that grow in a spiral fashion, not straight. This spiral arrangement is crucial for proper alignment of the great vessels.

Three disc-like flattened outpocketings develop from the utricular portion of the otic vesicle to form the semicircular canals. The central portions of these outpocketings oppose and fuse, then disappear, leaving the peripheral unfused parts. These peripheral portions become the semicircular ducts housed within the semicircular canals.
questions.question: The semicircular canals develop from which portion of the otic vesicle?
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies which pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is the nerve of the third pharyngeal arch. It provides both motor and sensory innervation to structures derived from this arch, including the stylopharyngeus muscle and portions of the tongue (posterior one-third).

options: Neurons do not require energy from mitochondria
Neurons are amitotic and cannot divide
questions.question: Centrioles are organelles present in most cells but conspicuously absent in neurons. Their absence in neurons is most consistent with which of the following characteristic of neurons?
questions.explanation: Centrioles organize the mitotic spindle during cell division, a function unnecessary in neurons since they are amitotic (permanently post-mitotic after final differentiation). The absence of centrioles is directly consistent with the inability of neurons to undergo mitosis and therefore regenerate after destruction. This is why CNS neuron loss (e.g., in stroke, trauma) is permanent.

The circumferences of the head and abdomen become approximately equal at 36 weeks. The crown-rump length is about 360 mm and weight about 3400 grams at this time. The fetus is growing more slowly before birth compared to earlier weeks.
questions.question: The circumferences of the head and abdomen become equal at approximately which week?

questions.explanation: The three concentric tunics of the eye are: the outer fibrous tunic consisting of the sclera which is white and protective and the cornea which is transparent and refractive; the middle vascular tunic or uvea consisting of the choroid for nutrition, the ciliary body for accommodation and aqueous humor production, and the iris for pupil control; and the inner nervous tunic which is the retina containing photoreceptors and neurons for vision.
options: Uveal tract → Fibrous tunic → Nervous tunic
Fibrous (sclera/cornea), vascular uvea, and nervous tunic (retina)
questions.question: The eye is composed of three concentric layers. From outside to inside these are correctly named as which of the following?

questions.explanation: Exstrophy of the cloaca is a rare, severe ventral body wall defect occurring in approximately 1 in 30,000 births. It results from inhibition of mesoderm migration to the midline and failure of the tail fold to progress. The defect includes bladder exstrophy, spinal defects with or without meningomyelocele, and imperforate anus.
questions.question: Exstrophy of the cloaca is a more severe defect than bladder exstrophy and occurs in:
The umbilical cord typically contains how many blood vessels?
questions.explanation: The umbilical cord typically contains two arteries and one vein surrounded by Wharton's jelly. The umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta, while the umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus. Single umbilical artery is associated with congenital anomalies.

questions.question: Brain flexures include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The neural tube forms three brain flexures: the cephalic (midbrain) flexure which is ventral, the cervical flexure at the junction of hindbrain and spinal cord which is ventral, and the pontine flexure which is dorsal. There is no lumbar flexure in brain development.

The nervous system has two fundamental cell categories: neurons are the electrically excitable conducting cells that transmit electrochemical impulses, and neuroglia or glial cells are the non-conducting support cells far more numerous than neurons that retain the ability to undergo mitosis. The term neuroglia means nerve glue reflecting the originally conceptualized function of physically supporting neurons.
options: Neurons as supporting cells and oligodendrocytes as conducting cells
Neurons that conduct impulses and mitotically capable neuroglia that provide support
Astrocytes that conduct and Schwann cells that only support in CNS
Microglia that conduct and astrocytes that provide energy
Both neuroglia and neurons conduct impulses equally
questions.question: The two main cell types in nervous tissue and their primary distinction are which of the following?
The metanephric blastema is induced by:
questions.explanation: The metanephric blastema (metanephric mesenchyme) is induced by the ureteric bud. Reciprocal induction between these two tissues is essential for kidney development. The ureteric bud induces the blastema to form nephrons (excretory units), while the blastema induces the ureteric bud to branch and form the collecting system.

questions.question: The bladder in newborns is located:
questions.explanation: The bladder in newborns is located partly in the abdomen, projecting above the pelvic brim. As the pelvis enlarges with growth, the bladder descends to become entirely a pelvic organ by adulthood. This explains why the bladder is more easily palpable abdominally in infants. The peritoneal reflection is also higher in infants.

The uncinate process does NOT develop from the dorsal pancreatic bud; it develops from the ventral bud along with part of the head. The dorsal bud forms the body, tail, and remainder of the head of the pancreas. The accessory pancreatic duct (when present) is formed from the proximal part of the dorsal bud duct.
questions.question: Which structure does NOT develop from the dorsal pancreatic bud?
Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) cells have numerous apical microvilli (brush border) and extensive basolateral infoldings. These adaptations are designed for:
questions.explanation: The PCT reabsorbs approximately 65% of the glomerular filtrate — including virtually all glucose and amino acids, most sodium, water, potassium, and bicarbonate. The brush border greatly increases the apical surface area, while basolateral infoldings and abundant mitochondria support the energy-intensive Na+/K+-ATPase-driven active transport. PCT cells are the most metabolically active cells in the kidney.

questions.question: The zona pellucida is a glycoprotein coat surrounding the oocyte. It first becomes visible at which stage of follicular development?
questions.explanation: The zona pellucida first becomes visible as follicular cells proliferate from a single to multiple layers (multilaminar primary/early secondary follicle stage). It is a thick, acidophilic, PAS-positive glycoprotein layer secreted jointly by the oocyte and granulosa cells. The zona pellucida contains ZP3 (sperm receptor) and plays critical roles in sperm binding and the block to polyspermy.

questions.question: Which cells in the respiratory epithelium serve as stem cells capable of regenerating other epithelial cell types after injury?
questions.explanation: Basal cells are the stem cells of the pseudostratified respiratory epithelium. They are small, triangular cells attached to the basement membrane but not reaching the luminal surface. After injury, basal cells proliferate and differentiate into ciliated cells, goblet cells, and other cell types to restore the epithelium. This regenerative capacity is critical for airway repair after viral infections and toxic exposures.

questions.question: When macrophages encounter a foreign body too large to phagocytose (e.g., a splinter), they may fuse together to form which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: When a foreign body is too large for a single macrophage to engulf, multiple macrophages can fuse to form multinucleated foreign body giant cells. These cells accumulate at invasion sites and sites of chronic inflammation, attempting to isolate and destroy the foreign material. This fusion response is a hallmark histological feature of granulomatous inflammation.

The intermediate mesoderm in the sacral region gives rise to the metanephric blastema (metanephric mesenchyme), which forms the nephrons of the permanent kidney. More cranially, intermediate mesoderm gives rise to the pronephros (cervical) and mesonephros (thoracolumbar). The gonads develop from intermediate mesoderm but in a different region (urogenital ridge).
questions.question: The intermediate mesoderm in the sacral region gives rise to:

questions.explanation: Appositional growth of cartilage occurs from the periphery — the inner chondrogenic layer of the perichondrium contains chondroprogenitor cells that differentiate into chondroblasts, depositing new cartilage matrix on the outer surface. This increases cartilage width. Interstitial growth (from within) occurs by mitosis of chondrocytes within lacunae, increasing cartilage length especially in young growing cartilage.
options: Mitosis of existing chondrocytes already in lacunae
Vascular invasion delivering osteoblasts from the periosteum
Hypertrophy of central chondrocytes without matrix deposition
Endochondral ossification converting cartilage to bone
Perichondrial cells become chondroblasts depositing matrix on the outer surface
questions.question: The appositional growth of cartilage that increases its width occurs by which mechanism?
Osteomalacia (adult) and osteitis fibrosa cystica represent opposite extremes of bone pathology because of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Osteomalacia involves vitamin D deficiency leading to failure of osteoid mineralization, with accumulation of unmineralized osteoid seams and soft, painful bones. Osteitis fibrosa cystica (von Recklinghausen disease of bone) results from hyperparathyroidism causing excessive osteoclast activity, which removes both mineral and organic matrix and replaces it with fibrous tissue and cysts. Tetracycline labeling diagnostically distinguishes these opposite metabolic bone disorders.
options: Osteomalacia involves osteoclast hyperactivity; osteitis fibrosa involves mineralization failure
They both result from identical biochemical defects in collagen synthesis
Osteomalacia involves excessive mineralization; osteitis fibrosa involves matrix dissolution
Osteomalacia involves impaired mineralization; osteitis fibrosa involves excess osteoclast activity
They are the same disease at different ages

questions.explanation: The myelencephalon (medulla oblongata) differs from the spinal cord in that its lateral walls are everted (spread apart). Alar and basal plates separated by the sulcus limitans can still be clearly distinguished, but their arrangement differs from the spinal cord.
questions.question: The myelencephalon differs from the spinal cord in which way?
Ectopic lung lobes may arise from:
questions.explanation: Ectopic lung lobes may arise from the trachea or esophagus rather than from the normal bronchial tree. These accessory lung buds develop independently. Ectopic lobes are usually non-functional and may become infected. They result from abnormal budding of the respiratory diverticulum or foregut.

questions.question: A spleen histology section shows a periarteriolar lymphoid sheath surrounding a central artery and an adjacent lymphoid follicle with a germinal center. These structures collectively constitute which of the following?
questions.explanation: The white pulp of the spleen consists of the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath containing predominantly T lymphocytes encircling the central arteriole, and adjacent lymphoid follicles containing B lymphocytes that form germinal centers during immune responses. Together they constitute the immunologically active white pulp compartment strategically positioned for contact with blood-borne antigens. The marginal zone between white and red pulp contains marginal zone B cells and macrophages bridging innate and adaptive immunity.
options: Red pulp with venous sinuses and splenic cords
Trabecular framework and capsule of the spleen
White pulp T-cell PALS and B-cell follicles as immunologically active zones
Marginal zone alone without organized lymphocyte aggregates
Perivascular sheath containing only vascular smooth muscle cells

questions.question: Alveoli at birth are approximately what fraction of the adult number?
questions.explanation: At birth, alveoli number approximately 1/6th of the adult number. The remaining 5/6ths develop postnatally, primarily during the first 10 years of life. This continued alveolar development explains why lung function continues to improve during childhood. Factors affecting early lung development can have lifelong consequences.

The submucosal venous plexus of the lower esophagus forms portosystemic anastomoses between the portal venous system and systemic venous circulation. In portal hypertension, blood is diverted through these vessels causing esophageal varices — dilated submucosal veins. Rupture of esophageal varices can cause life-threatening hemorrhage.
questions.question: Which layer of the esophageal wall contains a rich venous plexus clinically significant in portal hypertension?

questions.explanation: The epithelium of the entire female urethra is derived from endoderm of the urogenital sinus. This contrasts with the male urethra, where the terminal glandular portion is derived from surface ectoderm. The connective tissue and smooth muscle of both male and female urethras are derived from surrounding splanchnic mesenchyme.
questions.question: The epithelium of the female urethra is entirely derived from:

questions.explanation: The caudal neuropore closes at Carnegie stage 13, which corresponds to approximately 28 days of development. At this stage, the 4th pair of pharyngeal arches appear, upper and lower limb buds are visible, lens placodes are present, and the tail is attenuated. This closure is critical for normal neural tube development.
questions.question: At which Carnegie stage does the caudal neuropore close?

questions.explanation: The fluid mosaic model describes the plasma membrane as a fluid phospholipid bilayer (the 'fluid' component) in which membrane proteins are embedded and can diffuse laterally (the 'mosaic' pattern). Cholesterol modulates the fluidity. The model replaced earlier static membrane models and explains the dynamic lateral movement of membrane components observed in experiments like FRAP (fluorescence recovery after photobleaching).
options: Membrane proteins are fixed in place within a rigid lipid framework
Lipids exist in a solid gel phase stabilized by cholesterol exclusively
Membrane proteins float freely within a fluid phospholipid bilayer like a mosaic
The membrane is composed only of proteins with lipids as minor components
All membrane components move in a synchronized coordinated pattern
questions.question: The 'fluid mosaic model' of cell membrane structure, proposed by Singer and Nicolson, best describes which of the following?

questions.explanation: The submucosa, composed of dense irregular connective tissue rich in collagen type I and elastic fibers, provides the primary tensile strength to the GIT wall. This is why surgeons place sutures through the submucosa during intestinal anastomoses — it is the holding layer. In conditions like diverticular disease, weakness of the submucosa and muscularis allows mucosal herniation through the wall.
questions.question: The GIT wall is described as a hollow tube with four layers. Which layer represents the structural foundation providing tensile strength to resist luminal pressure?

questions.explanation: ADH (vasopressin), released from the posterior pituitary in response to increased plasma osmolality or decreased blood volume, acts on V2 receptors on principal cells of the collecting duct. This triggers insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane, making the collecting duct permeable to water. Water then moves osmotically into the hypertonic medullary interstitium, concentrating the urine. Absence of ADH causes diabetes insipidus.
questions.question: The collecting duct plays a central role in final urine concentration. Which hormone directly acts on principal cells of the collecting duct to insert aquaporin-2 channels?

options: Multiple peripheral nuclei, identical to typical skeletal muscle fibers
Uniform smooth histological appearance without visible cross-striations
Intercalated discs with gap junctions for coupling and desmosomes for cohesion
Satellite cells providing regeneration after myocardial infarction
Voluntary motor control through upper alpha motor neurons
questions.explanation: Intercalated discs are the unique structural feature of cardiac muscle at the junctions between cardiomyocytes. They contain gap junctions that electrically couple adjacent cells allowing rapid action potential propagation throughout the myocardium creating a functional syncytium; desmosomes providing mechanical cohesion during vigorous contraction; and fascia adherens for myofibril anchoring. This organization enables the coordinated, rhythmic heart contractions.
questions.question: Cardiac muscle is unique among the three muscle types in possessing which structural feature?

options: Only thick myosin filaments with no actin
Both thick and thin filaments in maximum overlap
The M line with myomesin cross-linking thick filaments
Only titin spanning from M line to Z disc
Thin actin filaments only, bisected by the Z disc; no myosin overlap
questions.explanation: The I band consists only of thin actin filaments without any overlapping thick myosin filaments. Each I band is bisected by a Z disc to which the thin filaments are anchored. During contraction, actin filaments slide deeper into the A band, narrowing the I band and H zone but not the A band. The degree of I band narrowing reflects the degree of muscle shortening.
questions.question: The I band of a sarcomere which appears light under polarized microscopy contains which of the following?

questions.explanation: Glucagon-producing alpha cells of the pancreatic islets begin functioning around the 15th week, approximately 5 weeks after insulin-producing beta cells (10th week). Both cell types develop from pancreatic epithelium and aggregate to form islets of Langerhans. The islets are surrounded by exocrine pancreatic tissue.
questions.question: Glucagon-producing cells begin functioning around:
The epiploic foramen (of Winslow) provides communication between:
questions.explanation: The epiploic foramen (of Winslow) provides communication between the greater peritoneal sac and the lesser sac (omental bursa). Its boundaries are: anteriorly - hepatoduodenal ligament (free edge of lesser omentum); posteriorly - inferior vena cava; superiorly - caudate lobe of liver; inferiorly - first part of duodenum. Understanding this anatomy is important for surgical access to the lesser sac.

questions.question: Which type of pancreatic duct cell is stimulated by secretin to produce the bicarbonate-rich component of pancreatic juice?
questions.explanation: Secretin, released from S-cells in the duodenum in response to acid, stimulates centroacinar cells and small pancreatic duct cells to secrete large volumes of water and bicarbonate. This alkaline fluid (pH ~8) neutralizes gastric acid in the duodenum and creates the optimal pH for pancreatic enzyme activity. In cystic fibrosis, CFTR mutations impair this bicarbonate secretion.

Renal pyramids are formed by collecting tubules of the 5th and successive generations that elongate considerably and converge on each minor calyx. The tubules run parallel to each other, creating the striated appearance of the pyramids. Each pyramid with its overlying cortex represents a renal lobe. The apex of each pyramid (papilla) projects into a minor calyx.
options: Collecting tubules converging on minor calyx
questions.question: Renal pyramids are formed by:
The conotruncal septum of the heart is formed by cells from which source?
questions.explanation: Neural crest cells migrate into the developing heart and contribute to formation of the conotruncal (aorticopulmonary) septum, which divides the truncus arteriosus into the aorta and pulmonary trunk. Abnormalities in neural crest migration can result in conotruncal defects like persistent truncus arteriosus or transposition of great vessels.

questions.question: The zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex produces cortisol. The cells in this zone appear vacuolated or spongy in histological sections because of which characteristic?
questions.explanation: The cells of zona fasciculata are called spongiocytes because their abundant cytoplasmic lipid droplets containing stored cholesterol esters which are the substrate for steroid hormone synthesis are dissolved by organic solvents during standard histological dehydration and clearing, leaving a characteristic spongy or vacuolated cytoplasm. In electron microscopy they are rich in smooth ER for steroidogenesis and mitochondria with tubular cristae.
options: Lipid droplets dissolved during histological processing create a spongy appearance
They have a meshwork of interconnected cell processes
They contain large amounts of glycogen creating empty-appearing spaces
They are post-apoptotic cells with fragmented nuclei

questions.explanation: In the classic hepatic lobule, blood flows from the portal triads at the periphery which contain branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct, through the sinusoids between hepatocyte cords toward the central vein at the lobule center, which then drains into hepatic veins and the inferior vena cava. This centripetal blood flow exposes hepatocytes to portal blood first at the periportal zone accounting for zone 1 being most vulnerable to toxins in portal blood.
questions.question: The histological appearance of the liver lobule shows hepatocytes arranged in radiating cords from the central vein to the portal tracts. Blood flows from which direction through the hepatic sinusoids?
options: From the central vein outward toward portal tracts
From portal tracts (hepatic artery and portal vein) toward the central vein
Bidirectionally through hepatic sinusoids without directional preference
From hepatic veins retrograde toward portal tracts
Only from hepatic artery branches without any portal venous component

questions.question: During cell cycle arrest, a cell accumulates in which phase if it fails to complete DNA replication?
questions.explanation: DNA replication occurs during the S (synthesis) phase of interphase; if replication is incomplete or damaged, checkpoint mechanisms arrest the cell in S phase or at the S/G2 boundary. Checkpoints prevent progression to mitosis until DNA integrity is confirmed. Arrest in S phase occurs when replication forks stall or when DNA damage is detected during replication.

Wait — the standard description: The inner sublayer of the muscularis externa is arranged circularly, and the outer sublayer is longitudinal. The circular layer's contraction decreases lumen diameter and propels contents forward. The stomach uniquely has three layers including an additional oblique layer. Answer: C (Circular).
questions.question: The innermost sublayer of the muscularis externa throughout most of the GIT is arranged in which orientation?
The glomerular basement membrane (GBM) has a trilaminar structure on electron microscopy. The three layers from Bowman's space inward are:
questions.explanation: The GBM has a trilaminar ultrastructure on electron microscopy: (1) Lamina rara interna — adjacent to the endothelium, contains heparan sulfate (charge barrier); (2) Lamina densa — central electron-dense layer of type IV collagen and laminin (size barrier); (3) Lamina rara externa — adjacent to podocyte foot processes, also contains heparan sulfate. Goodpasture syndrome involves autoantibodies targeting type IV collagen (alpha-3 chain) in the lamina densa.
options: Lamina rara externa → Lamina densa → Lamina rara interna
Lamina densa → Lamina rara externa → Lamina rara interna
Lamina rara interna → Lamina densa → Lamina rara externa
Only two layers — lamina rara and lamina densa
The GBM is a single homogeneous layer

questions.question: Which cranial nerves emerge from the medulla?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), accessory (XI), and hypoglossal (XII) cranial nerves emerge from the medulla oblongata. The hypoglossal nerve emerges between the pyramid and olive, while IX, X, and XI emerge posterior to the olive.

options: One or two centrally placed nuclei
Multiple peripherally placed nuclei like skeletal muscle
A single very large lobulated nucleus
Multiple nuclei arranged only at the intercalated disc
questions.explanation: Cardiomyocytes are mononucleated and occasionally binucleated cells with centrally placed nuclei, in contrast to skeletal muscle fibers with multiple peripheral nuclei reflecting their syncytial origin from myoblast fusion. The central nuclear position in cardiac muscle reflects that cardiomyocytes are individual cells joined at intercalated discs rather than true syncytia. This distinction is diagnostically useful in differentiating cardiac from skeletal muscle in tissue sections.
questions.question: Cardiac muscle cells have which of the following nuclear arrangement that distinguishes them from skeletal muscle fibers?

questions.explanation: The first indication of respiratory system development is the respiratory diverticulum (lung bud), which appears during the 4th week as an outgrowth from the ventral wall of the foregut. This location is determined by transcription factor TBX4. The diverticulum subsequently elongates and divides to form the respiratory tree.
questions.question: The first indication of respiratory system development is:

questions.explanation: Recanalization of the esophageal lumen normally occurs by the end of the embryonic period (8th week). During the 4th-7th weeks, epithelial proliferation partly or completely obliterates the lumen temporarily. Failure of proper recanalization leads to esophageal stenosis or atresia. This process of obliteration and recanalization occurs throughout the GI tract.
questions.question: Recanalization of the esophageal lumen normally occurs by:

options: Permanent destruction of lymph node structure
Lymphocyte proliferation and germinal center formation
Viral infection of macrophages causing their enlargement
questions.explanation: Lymph node enlargement reflects massive lymphocyte proliferation in response to antigens drained from the infected tissue and trapped in the node. B cells proliferate in germinal centers producing antibodies while T cells proliferate in the paracortex. Germinal center reaction produces plasma cells and memory B cells. Persistent lymphadenopathy requires investigation to exclude malignancy or systemic infection.
questions.question: Lymph nodes function as filters for lymph and sites of adaptive immune responses. Swollen lymph nodes at a site of infection indicate which of the following?

options: Blood supply, innervation, and lymphatic drainage
questions.explanation: The pectinate line marks differences in blood supply (superior rectal artery above, inferior rectal artery below), innervation (visceral above, somatic below), lymphatic drainage (internal iliac nodes above, superficial inguinal nodes below), and epithelium (columnar above, stratified squamous below). These differences reflect the dual embryological origin of the anal canal.
questions.question: The pectinate line is clinically significant because it marks differences in:
The primitive streak first appears at which location on the embryonic disc?
questions.explanation: At the beginning of the 3rd week, epiblast cells proliferate and migrate to the median plane of the germ disc, forming the primitive streak. As the primitive streak elongates, its cranial part forms the primitive node. The primitive groove appears in the streak and is continuous with the primitive pit.

Tetracycline chelates calcium with high affinity and is incorporated into newly mineralizing bone matrix at the calcification front, creating a fluorescent label visible with fluorescence microscopy. Administering two tetracycline doses separated by a known interval (e.g., 5 days) creates two parallel fluorescent lines; the distance between them divided by the interval gives the bone apposition rate. This method is diagnostic for osteomalacia and metabolic bone diseases.
options: Newly mineralized bone matrix at the calcification front
Hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow
questions.question: The tetracycline antibiotic fluorescence method for measuring bone apposition rate works because tetracycline interacts specifically with which of the following?
Respiratory epithelium (pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium) lines most of the conducting airways. Which cell type in this epithelium is most numerous?
questions.explanation: Ciliated columnar cells are the most numerous cells in the respiratory epithelium of the conducting airways. Each cell bears approximately 300 cilia on its apical surface. Coordinated ciliary beating propels the mucus blanket (produced by goblet cells) with trapped particles toward the pharynx — the mucociliary escalator. Dysfunction of cilia (as in primary ciliary dyskinesia) leads to chronic respiratory infections.

options: Red marrow of flat bones, vertebrae, and long bone epiphyses
Liver as the primary adult hematopoietic organ
Spleen as the sole adult hematopoietic organ
Thymus for all blood cell lineages equally
Lymph nodes for erythrocyte production mainly
questions.question: Hematopoiesis in postnatal life primarily occurs in which location?
questions.explanation: In postnatal life, hematopoiesis occurs in red bone marrow of flat bones including sternum, ribs, vertebrae, and ilium, and in proximal epiphyses of long bones. The liver and spleen are primary fetal hematopoietic organs that normally cease this function after birth but can resume extramedullary hematopoiesis in disease states such as myelofibrosis or severe anemia. The thymus is only for T cell maturation not all lineages.

Dense irregular connective tissue has collagen fiber bundles oriented randomly in multiple planes, conferring tensile strength resistant to forces from all directions rather than a single direction. This is optimal for skin dermis, organ capsules, joint capsules, and the tunica albuginea, which must withstand multidirectional mechanical stresses. The irregular arrangement distinguishes it functionally and structurally from the unidirectional dense regular type.
questions.question: Dense irregular connective tissue, found in the dermis of skin and organ capsules, differs from dense regular connective tissue in which of the following ways?
options: Collagen bundles arranged randomly to resist tearing from all directions
It contains only elastic fibers arranged haphazardly
It is composed entirely of reticular fibers
It has a much lower collagen content than loose connective tissue
Its fiber bundles run parallel like those of tendons

questions.question: The epithelium of most of the male urethra is derived from:
questions.explanation: The epithelium of most of the male urethra is derived from endoderm of the urogenital sinus. Only the terminal part in the glans penis is derived from a solid cord of ectodermal cells that grows inward. The connective tissue and smooth muscle are derived from splanchnic mesenchyme.

The otic placode appears around the 22nd day as a thickening of surface ectoderm beside the myelencephalon (future medulla oblongata). This placode invaginates to form the otic vesicle. The otic vesicle subsequently divides into dorsal and ventral parts, giving rise to various inner ear structures.
questions.question: The otic placode first appears as a thickening of surface ectoderm beside which brain structure?
Surfactant secretion by type II pneumocytes begins during which weeks?
questions.explanation: Secretion of surfactant (a surface-active lipid) begins during 21-25 weeks. Surfactant maintains the patency of developing alveoli of the lungs and prevents collapse. Adequate surfactant production is essential for survival of premature infants; deficiency causes respiratory distress syndrome.

A fresh cut section of the spleen shows easily distinguishable red pulp which appears dark red due to its massive blood content in sinuses and cords, and white pulp which appears as white or gray nodular areas along the branches of the splenic artery. The white pulp lymphoid nodules were originally described as Malpighian bodies or corpuscles in the unfixed spleen where this macroscopic distinction is most visible. Processing changes these appearances.
options: Entirely white throughout with no distinction between areas
Entirely red pulp throughout without white pulp areas
Yellow-gray coloration throughout due to extensive adipose tissue infiltration
Uniformly brown from bile pigment and hemosiderin accumulation
Dark red pulp from blood cells and white-gray nodules of white pulp
questions.question: Which of the following describes the histological appearance of the spleen when the organ is freshly sectioned, without tissue processing?

questions.explanation: After removal from the body, tissues lose their blood supply, causing cellular enzymes (lysosomes) to begin digesting cellular components (autolysis) and the tissue to dry out. Immediate fixation halts these processes by cross-linking proteins and denaturating enzymes. Delay in fixation results in artefacts that compromise histological and diagnostic interpretation.
options: Fixed tissues take up stain more selectively
Cells rapidly deteriorate through drying out and autolysis after removal
Fixation prevents tissue shrinkage during microtomy
Unfixed tissues react with embedding media
Blood supply continues to alter tissue composition after removal
questions.question: Which of the following correctly explains why tissue fixation must be performed immediately after tissue removal from the body?

questions.explanation: The portal lobule is defined by bile flow rather than blood flow. It is organized as a triangle with the portal tract at its center, and central veins at the three corners. Bile produced by hepatocytes flows from the periphery (near central veins) toward the central portal tract, the opposite direction of blood flow. This model emphasizes the exocrine secretory function of hepatocytes.
questions.question: In the portal lobule model of liver organization, what structure is at the center of the lobule?
The inferior olivary complex is a characteristic feature of which medullary level?
questions.explanation: The inferior olivary complex (principal, medial accessory, and dorsal accessory olivary nuclei) is a characteristic feature of the mid-medulla level. The olive appears as a prominent landmark on the ventral surface of the medulla. It projects to the cerebellum via climbing fibers.

options: Random arrangement of collagen fibers with abundant ground substance
Predominantly elastic fibers with few collagen fibers
Large amounts of adipose cells with sparse collagen
Parallel bundles of collagen fibers with sparse fibroblasts aligned along fibers
Predominantly reticular fibers forming a supporting meshwork
questions.explanation: Dense regular connective tissue is characterized by closely packed, parallel bundles of type I collagen fibers, with few but elongated fibroblasts (tenocytes) aligned between the fiber bundles. This parallel arrangement provides maximal tensile strength in a single direction — ideal for tendons and ligaments that must withstand strong unidirectional forces. The sparse ground substance and cells reflect prioritization of mechanical performance over cellular activity.
questions.question: Dense regular connective tissue, as found in tendons and ligaments, is characterized by which of the following structural features?
Collagen type I is found predominantly in which of the following tissues?
questions.explanation: Type I collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body, forming thick fibrillar bundles in dermis, bone, tendons, ligaments, fascia, and the corneal stroma. It provides high tensile strength. Type II collagen is specific to cartilage and vitreous, type III (reticular) predominates in loose connective tissues and vessels, and type IV forms non-fibrillar sheets in basement membranes.

questions.question: The main macromolecules broken down during GIT digestion include proteins, complex carbohydrates, nucleic acids, and fats. The products of digestion are absorbed primarily through the lining of which structure?
questions.explanation: The small intestine is the primary site of nutrient absorption. Its mucosa is extensively modified with plicae circulares, villi, and microvilli to maximize surface area. Digested macromolecules — amino acids, monosaccharides, fatty acids — cross the epithelium here into blood and lymphatic vessels for systemic distribution.

The greater omentum extends from the greater curvature of the stomach and hangs inferiorly like an apron over the intestines. It is derived from the dorsal mesogastrium and fuses with the transverse mesocolon. The greater omentum contains fat and lymphoid tissue and can wall off infections or inflammation in the abdominal cavity.
questions.question: The greater omentum extends from the:

questions.explanation: The combination of absent villi, abundant goblet cells, and teniae coli (three bands of longitudinal muscle) is pathognomonic for the colon. The colon lacks villi entirely, unlike all three segments of the small intestine. Goblet cells are more numerous in the colon than anywhere else in the GIT. The teniae coli are the most distinctive gross and microscopic feature of the colon.
questions.question: A histological section shows a segment of gut with no villi, extremely numerous goblet cells, and three distinct longitudinal muscle bands. This is most consistent with:

questions.explanation: The paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) is most essential for maintenance of equilibrium and coordination of eye movements. The paramedian neurons are connected to the vestibular nuclei. The reticular formation overall is concerned with somatic motor functions via the reticulospinal tract.
questions.question: The paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) is essential for which function?

options: Protein fibers (collagen, elastic, reticular) and ground substance
Cellular debris and metabolic waste products
Blood plasma proteins and immunoglobulins only
Basement membrane only with no other components
questions.question: The extracellular matrix (ECM) of connective tissue is composed of which of the following?
questions.explanation: The ECM is the non-cellular material of connective tissue consisting of protein fiber networks (collagen for tensile strength, elastic for extensibility, reticular for support scaffolding) and ground substance (proteoglycans providing hydration and compressive resistance, adhesive glycoproteins like fibronectin and laminin). The composition varies among connective tissue types to fulfill specific mechanical and functional requirements.

The A band corresponds to the full length of thick myosin filaments including the regions where thin actin filaments overlap with myosin at both ends. The central H zone within the A band contains only thick myosin filaments with no actin overlap at rest. During contraction, actin slides inward narrowing the H zone and I band while the A band width remains constant — a key observation confirming the sliding filament model.
questions.question: The A band of a sarcomere corresponds to which ultrastructural components?
options: Full thick myosin filament length including regions overlapping actin at both ends
The region containing only thin actin filaments with no myosin
The H zone where thin filaments overlap maximally
The region between Z lines exclusive of all thick filaments

questions.explanation: Triploidy (69 chromosomes, three complete sets) is a lethal condition usually resulting from fertilization of an egg by two sperm (dispermy) or failure of meiotic division. Most triploid conceptuses are spontaneously aborted. Tetraploidy (92 chromosomes) is even rarer and also lethal.
questions.question: A person with 69 chromosomes has which condition?

questions.explanation: Bile canaliculi are sealed from the perisinusoidal space by tight junctions (zonulae occludentes) between adjacent hepatocytes. This prevents bile — which contains potentially toxic bile salts — from leaking into the space of Disse and entering the bloodstream. Disruption of these tight junctions in cholestasis leads to regurgitation of bile into the hepatic sinusoids, causing jaundice.
questions.question: The bile canaliculi between hepatocytes are sealed by which intercellular junctions to prevent bile from leaking into the space of Disse?

questions.explanation: Keloids are benign fibroproliferative lesions caused by abnormal collagen accumulation beyond the original wound margins. They are significantly more prevalent in individuals of Black African descent due to genetic factors influencing fibroblast activity. Clinical management is challenging because surgical excision is almost always followed by recurrence; combined modalities (excision + steroid injection or radiation) are used.
options: Occurring exclusively in patients with oculocutaneous albinism
Self-limiting regression without any treatment over time
Occurring only on the face and neck regions
Commoner in Black Africans; prone to recurrence post-excision
Representing malignant transformation of resident dermal fibroblasts
questions.question: Keloid formation represents an abnormal accumulation of collagen in skin scars and is clinically notable for which of the following characteristics?

questions.explanation: The corticomedullary junction represents the meeting point between the adrenal cortex derived from mesodermal coelomic epithelium and the adrenal medulla derived from neural crest cells that migrated and became encapsulated by the cortex. Histologically the boundary shows the transition from cortical zona reticularis cells to larger medullary chromaffin cells with their prominent eosinophilic granules. This dual developmental origin explains why cortical and medullary function is regulated by entirely different signaling systems.
options: The site of aldosterone synthesis switching to cortisol production
A watershed zone with the lowest blood supply
The location of the adrenal capsule blood vessels
A region containing only adipocytes with no endocrine cells
Boundary between mesodermal cortex and neural crest-derived chromaffin medulla
questions.question: The corticomedullary junction of the adrenal gland is significant histologically because it represents which of the following?
The folds of the stomach mucosa and submucosa visible to the naked eye when the stomach is empty are called:
questions.explanation: The rugae are longitudinal folds of the gastric mucosa and submucosa visible when the stomach is empty. They allow the stomach to expand greatly when filled with food. These folds flatten as the stomach distends. Plicae circulares are found in the small intestine and cannot be flattened, distinguishing them from gastric rugae.

questions.question: Enterocytes in the small intestinal villi contain which enzyme system on their brush border that is critical for final carbohydrate digestion?
questions.explanation: The brush border of enterocytes is embedded with numerous disaccharidases (sucrase, maltase, lactase) and peptidases responsible for terminal digestion of carbohydrates and proteins. Lactase deficiency causes lactose intolerance — the most common brush border enzyme deficiency. These enzymes are part of the glycocalyx covering the microvilli and are directly linked to absorption.

questions.question: Vitamin D deficiency in children causes rickets while in adults it causes osteomalacia. The underlying histological defect common to both is which of the following?
questions.explanation: Vitamin D deficiency impairs intestinal calcium absorption and bone mineralization. Without adequate calcium and phosphate, osteoblasts continue to produce osteoid but it cannot be mineralized, accumulating as wide seams of unmineralized matrix. In children, the epiphyseal plate also fails to mineralize properly causing characteristic bowing of weight-bearing bones and epiphyseal widening in rickets. In adults the same osteoid accumulation causes bone pain and stress fractures of osteomalacia. The tetracycline labeling distance is reduced in osteomalacia.
options: Decreased osteoclast activity causing excessive bone density
Increased osteoblast apoptosis reducing bone formation
Inflammatory destruction of bone collagen matrix
Unmineralized osteoid accumulation from impaired bone mineralization
Complete absence of osteoid synthesis by osteoblasts

questions.explanation: Implantation begins on day 7 and ends on day 13. The blastocyst is enclosed within the zona pellucida and lies free in the uterus cavity before implantation. The zona pellucida must disappear before implantation can occur.
questions.question: Implantation of the blastocyst begins on which day?
The female reproductive cycle is approximately 28 days. The interval between ovulation and menstruation (luteal phase) is consistently which duration?
questions.explanation: The luteal phase (from ovulation to the onset of menstruation) is consistently approximately 14 days in all women with normal cycles, regardless of total cycle length. This is because it corresponds to the fixed lifespan of the corpus luteum (14 ± 2 days) in the absence of pregnancy. Cycle length variation arises from differences in the follicular phase (proliferative phase duration). This constancy is the basis of counting back 14 days from the next expected period to estimate ovulation date.

options: Type III collagen (encoded by COL3A1 gene)
Type I collagen (most abundant fibrillar collagen)
questions.explanation: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome vascular type (EDS-IV) results from autosomal dominant mutations in COL3A1, which encodes type III procollagen — the main collagen of reticular fibers in arterial walls and intestines. Abnormal type III collagen makes these structures fragile and prone to spontaneous rupture, a life-threatening complication. Clinically: thin translucent skin with visible veins, easy bruising, hypermobile fingers, and high risk for arterial dissection.
questions.question: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type IV is specifically caused by a deficiency of which collagen type, leading to rupture of arteries and intestines?
Alpha-fetoprotein (AF(ΔP) levels are increased in which conditions?
questions.explanation: Alpha-fetoprotein (AF(ΔP) is produced by the fetal liver, yolk sac, and intestine. AFP levels are increased in maternal serum and amniotic fluid in cases of neural tube defects (NTDs) and ventral wall defects (VWDs). AFP is decreased in Down syndrome and trisomy 18.

The ureteric bud (metanephric diverticulum) sprouts from the distal end of the mesonephric duct at about 5 weeks. This outgrowth induces the surrounding intermediate mesoderm to form metanephric blastema. Reciprocal induction between the ureteric bud and metanephric blastema is essential for proper kidney development.
questions.question: The ureteric bud arises from which structure?

options: Exclusively inner circular and outer longitudinal layers
Three layers — oblique, circular, and longitudinal
Circular constrictors and longitudinal elevator muscles
questions.explanation: The pharyngeal wall contains circular constrictor muscles (superior, middle, and inferior pharyngeal constrictors) and longitudinal elevator muscles (stylopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus). This arrangement allows coordinated constriction and elevation during swallowing. The pharynx is also notable for having skeletal muscle throughout — unlike the esophagus which transitions to smooth muscle.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the arrangement of smooth muscle in the pharyngeal wall?
The metencephalon gives rise to which two structures?
questions.explanation: The metencephalon, derived from the rhombencephalon, gives rise to the pons and cerebellum. The dorsolateral parts of the alar plates bend medially to form rhombic lips, which develop into the cerebellum. The remaining portion forms the pons.

questions.question: Erythropoiesis shifts from the liver to which organ by the end of the 28th week?
questions.explanation: By the 28th week, the spleen has been an important site of hematopoiesis, but hematopoiesis shifts to the bone marrow by the end of this week. Earlier, erythropoiesis occurs primarily in the liver (starting around 6 weeks) and later in the spleen (starting around 12 weeks).

questions.question: The periderm (epitrichium) is typically replaced completely by which gestational week?
questions.explanation: The periderm, which is the outermost layer of early fetal skin, is completely replaced by the 21st week of gestation. Peridermal cells continually undergo keratinization and desquamation, being replaced by cells from the basal layer. Exfoliated peridermal cells contribute to the formation of vernix caseosa.

questions.question: The liver in the 5th-10th weeks comprises what percentage of total body weight?
questions.explanation: During weeks 5-10, the rapidly growing liver comprises about 10% of total body weight, filling a large part of the abdominal cavity. This disproportionate size contributes to physiological herniation of the midgut. As other organs grow, the liver's relative size decreases. The large fetal liver reflects its hematopoietic function.

questions.question: The stomach secretes approximately 2–3 liters of gastric juice daily. The acidic gastric juice is produced by parietal cells via which molecular mechanism?
questions.explanation: Parietal cells secrete HCl via H+/K+-ATPase (the proton pump) on the intracellular canalicular membranes. This enzyme pumps H+ into the canalicular lumen in exchange for K+, driven by ATP hydrolysis. CO2 + H2O (via carbonic anhydrase) generates H+ and HCO3-. Cl- enters the lumen via Cl- channels. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs like omeprazole) irreversibly block H+/K+-ATPase, the most effective pharmacological reduction of gastric acid.
options: Na+/K+-ATPase pumping H+ into the lumen
Passive diffusion of H+ through tight junctions
Na+/H+ exchanger on the apical membrane

questions.question: Kupffer cells in the liver sinusoids are the most numerous tissue macrophages in the body. They perform which primary functions?
options: Synthesizing albumin for plasma oncotic pressure
Storing vitamin A in lipid droplets which is the function of hepatic stellate cells
Phagocytosing aged erythrocytes and bacteria from portal blood; antigen presentation
questions.explanation: Kupffer cells are liver-resident macrophages lining the hepatic sinusoids representing approximately 80 to 90% of all fixed tissue macrophages in the body. They phagocytose aged RBCs contributing to heme and bilirubin metabolism, bacteria from portal blood as first defense against gut-derived pathogens, endotoxin or LPS, immune complexes, and cellular debris. They are part of the MPS and contribute to liver inflammation in alcoholic hepatitis and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

questions.question: Which GIT wall layer contains the largest concentration of lymphoid tissue including Peyer's patches?
questions.explanation: Lymphoid tissue in the GIT is distributed throughout the mucosa (lamina propria contains diffuse lymphoid tissue and isolated nodules) and the submucosa (where larger aggregates like Peyer's patches can extend). The gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) constitutes the largest immunological organ in the body. This strategic positioning allows surveillance of luminal antigens at the interface between the external environment and internal tissues.

Vernix caseosa is formed from fatty secretions from fetal sebaceous glands and dead epithelial cells. It covers the fetal skin during 17-20 weeks and protects the skin from abrasions, chapping, and hardening that could result from exposure to amniotic fluid. It is a white, cheese-like substance.
questions.question: Vernix caseosa is formed from which substances?
options: Fatty secretions and dead epithelial cells
Rough endoplasmic reticulum specialized for protein synthesis
Sarcoplasmic reticulum specialized for calcium storage and release
Golgi apparatus specialized for vesicle production
questions.question: The sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle cells is a modified form of which cellular organelle?
questions.explanation: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a highly specialized form of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in muscle cells. It functions primarily as a regulated calcium store, sequestering calcium during relaxation via SERCA pumps and releasing it rapidly upon electrical stimulation to trigger contraction. The SR is most highly developed in skeletal muscle where its rapid calcium release enables the fast forceful contractions needed for locomotion.

Smooth muscle cells are fusiform spindle-shaped, mononucleated with a central nucleus, and lack the organized sarcomere structure responsible for striation in skeletal and cardiac muscle. They contain actin and myosin filaments but arranged in a non-parallel diagonal network rather than aligned sarcomeres. Contraction is slow and sustained, regulated by autonomic nerves and hormones, and they form the walls of blood vessels, GI tract, airways, and glands.
options: Smooth muscle has the most organized sarcomere structure of all three types
Lacks sarcomeres and striations; has a single central nucleus and fusiform cell shape
Smooth muscle has more mitochondria than cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle contracts faster than skeletal muscle
Smooth muscle is derived from the neuroectoderm rather than mesoderm
questions.question: Smooth muscle cells differ from skeletal and cardiac muscle cells structurally in which of the following ways?
Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) arises from:
questions.explanation: Wilms tumor arises from persistent metanephric blastema (embryonal renal tissue) that fails to differentiate into mature nephrons. It is the most common primary renal malignancy in children, typically presenting before age 5 with abdominal mass, hematuria, or hypertension. Histologically, it contains blastemal, stromal, and epithelial elements. Associated syndromes include WAGR (Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary abnormalities, mental Retardation) and Denys-Drash syndrome.

The muscularis mucosae is a thin layer of smooth muscle that separates the mucosa from the submucosa. Its contractions produce local movements of the mucosa, improving contact with luminal contents. It should not be confused with the muscularis externa, which drives peristalsis. The myenteric plexus lies between the layers of the muscularis externa, not mucosae.
questions.question: Which statement about the muscularis mucosae is MOST accurate?
options: It is composed of skeletal muscle in the upper GIT
It is the thickest layer of the GIT wall
It contains the myenteric plexus between its two sublayers
It generates peristaltic waves throughout the GIT

questions.explanation: The proliferative zone is characterized by rapid mitotic division of chondrocytes that organize into longitudinal columns stacked like coins and oriented parallel to the bone's long axis. This zone is responsible for actual bone lengthening through interstitial growth. The columns of cells reflect the directional pressure of growth and guide subsequent events of hypertrophy calcification and replacement by bone in the zones closer to the diaphysis.
questions.question: In which zone of the epiphyseal growth plate do chondrocytes actively divide and arrange themselves in longitudinal columns parallel to the long axis of the bone?

options: Lateral nasal and medial nasal prominences
questions.explanation: By the 3rd month, mesenchyme between the sensory epithelium and olfactory bulb forms the cartilaginous lamina cribrosa of the ethmoid. This structure later ossifies to form the cribriform plate through which olfactory nerves pass. The cribriform plate has numerous perforations for olfactory nerve fascicles.
questions.question: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone forms from mesenchyme located between:

options: The wall of the heart ventricular myocardium
The iris and ciliary body of the eye
questions.explanation: The ventricular myocardium of the heart is composed of cardiac muscle not smooth muscle. Cardiac muscle is a striated involuntary muscle type restricted to the heart and great vessel roots. Smooth muscle forms the walls of hollow viscera including GI tract, bladder, and uterus, the tunica media of blood vessel walls, airways, and the iris and ciliary body of the eye.
questions.question: The prominent locations of smooth muscle in the body include all of the following EXCEPT which of the following?
Ventricular septal defects most commonly involve which septum?
questions.explanation: Ventricular septal defects (VSDs) most commonly involve the membranous portion of the interventricular septum. VSD is the most common congenital cardiac malformation, occurring in 12/10,000 births. These defects allow abnormal left-to-right shunting, potentially causing pulmonary overcirculation and heart failure.

The brainstem consists of three parts: the midbrain (mesencephalon), pons (part of metencephalon), and medulla oblongata (myelencephalon). The brainstem is the lowest part of the brain, acting as a pathway between the upper brain and spinal cord, and containing centers for vital functions.
questions.question: The brainstem consists of which three parts?

questions.explanation: Chorionic villi consist of a core of mesoderm (connective tissue containing fetal capillaries) covered by two layers of trophoblast: an inner cytotrophoblast layer and an outer syncytiotrophoblast layer. The villi become tertiary when umbilical blood vessels invade the mesenchymal core in the 3rd week.
questions.question: Chorionic villi consist of a core of which tissue type?

questions.explanation: Meckel's diverticulum occurs in approximately 2% of normal individuals and represents persistence of the proximal part of the vitelline duct. It follows the "rule of 2s": 2% prevalence, 2 feet from ileocecal valve, 2 inches long, and may contain 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric and pancreatic).
questions.question: Meckel's diverticulum occurs in what percentage of normal individuals?
The inner cell mass of the blastocyst is also termed which structure?
questions.explanation: The blastocyst consists of an outer cell layer (trophoblast) and a group of centrally located cells called the inner cell mass or embryoblast. The embryoblast gives rise to the embryo proper, while the trophoblast gives rise to the chorion and ultimately the fetal part of the placenta.

questions.question: Which component of the GIT wall forms an important physical barrier between luminal contents and the body's deeper tissues?
questions.explanation: The inner epithelial lining of the mucosa acts as the primary barrier separating the potentially harmful luminal environment from underlying tissues. This epithelium is also the interface for absorption and secretion. The lamina propria, submucosa, and other layers provide structural support but are not the primary barrier.

The cloacal membrane is located on the caudal end of the primitive streak and develops into the future anus.
