This covering differentiates omphalocele from gastroschisis, where bowel is exposed directly to amniotic fluid without membrane coverage. The membrane may rupture during or after delivery.

questions.question: Mesenchyme, the embryonic connective tissue from which all adult connective tissues are derived, is best characterized by which of the following?
options: Dense collagen bundles with polarized epithelial cells
Abundant mature elastic fibers and fibroblasts throughout
Sparse stellate cells in watery matrix with few collagen fibers
Completed differentiated adipocytes in an embryonic setting
Organized lymphoid follicles with germinal centers
questions.explanation: Mesenchyme is the embryonic loose connective tissue consisting of sparse, undifferentiated stellate (star-shaped) cells that can give rise to all adult connective tissue types (fibroblasts, chondrocytes, osteoblasts, adipocytes, smooth muscle cells). The cells are embedded in a watery matrix with minimal collagen. It is found in the mesodermal layer of early embryos and persists in Wharton's jelly of the umbilical cord.

questions.question: The laryngeal cartilages are derived from which pharyngeal arches?
questions.explanation: The laryngeal cartilages (thyroid, cricoid, arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform) are derived from the 4th and 6th pharyngeal arches. The muscles of the larynx are also derived from these arches. This explains their innervation by branches of the vagus nerve (superior and recurrent laryngeal nerves).

questions.question: Intrinsic muscles of the larynx are derived from which pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation: The intrinsic muscles of the larynx are derived from the sixth pharyngeal arch. The fourth arch gives rise to the cricothyroid, levator palatini, and constrictor muscles of the pharynx. Both fourth and sixth arches contribute to formation of laryngeal cartilages.

From lumen outward, the GIT wall layers are: mucosa (epithelium + lamina propria + muscularis mucosae), submucosa, muscularis externa, and serosa/adventitia. The submucosa therefore lies between the muscularis mucosae (innermost smooth muscle layer) and the muscularis externa (outer thick smooth muscle). This sequence is consistent throughout the GIT.
questions.question: Which statement regarding the relationship between the four layers of the GIT wall is CORRECT?
options: The submucosa lies between mucosae and externa
The serosa is directly adjacent to the muscularis mucosae
The mucosa is the deepest layer of the GIT wall
The muscularis externa is directly beneath the epithelium
The lamina propria is located outside the muscularis mucosae

questions.question: The posterior one-third of the tongue develops from which structure?
questions.explanation: The posterior one-third of the tongue is formed by the cranial part of the hypobranchial eminence (cupola or second median swelling). The hypobranchial eminence is derived from the second, third, and fourth pharyngeal arches. The boundary between anterior and posterior parts is marked by the terminal sulcus.

Proteins such as fibroblast growth factor (FGF) and activin, belonging to peptide growth factors, play key roles in programming mesodermal cells to induce overlying ectoderm to differentiate into neural structures. These factors are part of the complex signaling that establishes the nervous system.
questions.question: Which growth factor plays a key role in programming mesodermal cells to induce neural structures?

questions.explanation: Anorectal malformations most commonly result from abnormal development of the urorectal septum, causing incomplete separation of the cloaca into urogenital and anorectal portions. This can lead to various types of fistulas between the rectum and urogenital structures, as well as imperforate anus and rectal atresia.
questions.question: Anorectal malformations most commonly result from abnormal development of:
The endothelium lining blood vessels is metabolically active and produces multiple vasoactive substances. Which endothelial product causes vasodilation and inhibits platelet aggregation?
questions.explanation: Endothelial cells produce nitric oxide (NO, via eNOS stimulated by shear stress) and prostacyclin (PGI2), both of which cause vasodilation and inhibit platelet aggregation, maintaining vascular homeostasis. In contrast, damaged endothelium produces less NO/PGI2 and releases endothelin-1 (vasoconstrictor), PAI-1 (pro-thrombotic), and von Willebrand factor (platelet adhesion). This balance between vasodilatory and vasoconstrictive endothelial products underlies the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis and hypertension.

Prune belly syndrome (Eagle-Barrett syndrome) is characterized by deficiency of abdominal wall muscles, giving the abdomen a wrinkled, prune-like appearance. It is associated with urinary tract abnormalities including megacystis, hydroureter, and cryptorchidism. The condition occurs almost exclusively in males and has a complex, poorly understood etiology.
questions.question: Prune belly syndrome is associated with:

questions.explanation: Embryonic induction is a process by which the presence of one tissue influences the development of others. The inducing tissue directs the differentiation of adjacent responding tissue. Absence of the inducing tissue results in lack of or improper development of the induced tissue.
questions.question: Embryonic induction refers to which developmental process?
The germinal center within a lymph node secondary follicle is the site of which critical immunological process?
options: T cell positive selection on MHC molecules
Plasmacytoid dendritic cell production of type I interferons
B cell clonal expansion, hypermutation, affinity maturation, and class switching
Mast cell IgE production following allergen exposure
questions.explanation: Germinal centers form in secondary lymphoid follicles when antigen-activated B cells with T cell help undergo rapid clonal expansion. Within germinal centers, activation-induced cytidine deaminase causes somatic hypermutation of immunoglobulin variable regions; selection retains high-affinity mutants in affinity maturation; class switch recombination changes immunoglobulin isotype from IgM to IgG, IgA, or IgE; selected cells differentiate into long-lived plasma cells or memory B cells.

Ureteral ectopia in females, where the ureter opens into the urethra or vagina (distal to the urinary sphincter), results in continuous urinary incontinence despite normal voiding. The ectopic ureter bypasses the sphincter mechanism. In males, ectopic ureters usually open into structures proximal to the external sphincter and don't cause incontinence. Surgical reimplantation is required.
questions.question: Ureteral ectopia in females may result in:
Podocytes are specialized cells of the visceral epithelium of Bowman's capsule. The spaces between their foot processes are called filtration slits, which are bridged by:
questions.explanation: Filtration slits between podocyte foot processes are bridged by thin protein structures called slit diaphragms, composed primarily of nephrin and podocin. The slit diaphragm acts as the final filtration barrier, preventing proteins above 8nm from passing into Bowman's space. Mutations in nephrin (NPHS1 gene) cause congenital nephrotic syndrome with complete loss of slit diaphragms.

questions.question: The esophageal wall contains a rich submucosal venous plexus. In which pathological condition does this plexus become clinically life-threatening?
questions.explanation: In portal hypertension (e.g., from liver cirrhosis), increased pressure in the portal venous system is transmitted to the submucosal venous plexus of the lower esophagus via portosystemic anastomoses. This causes dilation of these submucosal veins into esophageal varices. Variceal rupture during vomiting or Valsalva can cause massive, life-threatening upper GI hemorrhage. Endoscopic band ligation or sclerotherapy is used to obliterate these vessels.

Each osteon (Haversian system) is the basic structural unit of compact bone, consisting of 5–20 concentric lamellae of mineralized matrix (with alternating collagen fiber orientations) surrounding a central Haversian canal containing small arterioles, venules, nerves, and loose connective tissue. Osteocytes reside in lacunae between lamellae and communicate via canaliculi that penetrate all lamellae to reach the central canal.
questions.question: Compact (cortical) bone is organized into cylindrical structures called osteons (Haversian systems), each of which consists of which of the following?
options: A central nutrient foramen surrounded by randomly arranged trabecular bone
Concentric lamellae surrounding a central Haversian canal with blood vessels and nerves
A solid block of mineralized matrix with no canal system
Interconnecting trabeculae with red marrow in all spaces
A single osteocyte surrounded by ground substance only

questions.question: The lesser omentum extends between:
questions.explanation: The lesser omentum extends between the liver and stomach (lesser curvature), connecting the lesser curvature of the stomach to the inferior surface of the liver. It develops from the ventral mesogastrium. The lesser omentum contains the hepatic artery, portal vein, and bile duct in its free edge.

questions.question: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) is activated when juxtaglomerular cells secrete renin. Renin acts on which substrate to begin the cascade?
questions.explanation: Renin is a protease enzyme secreted by juxtaglomerular cells that cleaves angiotensinogen — a glycoprotein produced by the liver — to form angiotensin I (a decapeptide). ACE (in pulmonary endothelium) then converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex, increasing sodium reabsorption and blood pressure. ACE inhibitors block this step therapeutically.
options: Aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct

questions.question: The appendix is a blind-ended tubular appendage of the cecum. Its histological hallmark that distinguishes it from the rest of the large intestine is:
questions.explanation: The appendix is characterized histologically by the presence of numerous lymphoid follicles that may extend from the mucosa into the submucosa. This prominent lymphoid tissue has led to the appendix being called a gut tonsil or abdominal tonsil. It is thought to function in immune surveillance. In chronic inflammation, this lymphoid tissue may atrophy in elderly individuals.

Excitable cells (neurons, muscle cells, some gland cells) are capable of responding to stimuli by rapidly reversing their membrane potential (action potential/depolarization). All cells maintain an electrical potential across their membrane, but only excitable cells can rapidly and significantly change this potential to propagate a signal. This property is the basis of nerve impulse transmission and muscle contraction.
questions.question: When a cell is described as 'excitable' or 'irritable' in the context of membrane physiology, this specifically means which of the following?
options: It can rapidly change its membrane electrical potential in response to stimuli
It is easily damaged by mechanical force
It secretes large quantities of hormones in response to signals
It undergoes rapid division when stimulated
It migrates toward the source of a chemical signal

questions.question: Bladder extrophy is associated with which other anomaly?
questions.explanation: Bladder exstrophy is almost always associated with epispadias (urethral opening on dorsal surface of penis). Both result from defective development of the anterior abdominal wall. The bladder mucosa is exposed, the pubic bones are separated, and the external genitalia are abnormal. The condition requires staged surgical reconstruction.

questions.question: The mesonephric tubules in males contribute to formation of:
questions.explanation: In males, some caudal mesonephric tubules persist to form the efferent ductules connecting the testis to the epididymis. The mesonephric duct itself becomes the ductus deferens, epididymis, and ejaculatory duct. In females, mesonephric structures largely degenerate, with only vestigial remnants (epoophoron, paroophoron) persisting.

questions.question: Muscles of mastication are derived from which pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation: Muscles of the first pharyngeal arch include the muscles of mastication (temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids), anterior belly of digastric, mylohyoid, tensor tympani, and tensor palatini muscles. These muscles are innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V).

questions.question: The large intestine contains bacteria (microbiome) that produce vitamin K and certain B vitamins. These vitamins are primarily absorbed in which colonic segment?
questions.explanation: The ascending colon and proximal colon (cecum and ascending colon) are the primary sites of bacterial fermentation and vitamin K / B-vitamin production and absorption. These regions also absorb the majority of the remaining water and electrolytes. Fermentation in the proximal colon produces short-chain fatty acids (butyrate, acetate, propionate) that are absorbed and serve as major energy sources for colonocytes.

questions.question: General sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is provided by which nerve?
questions.explanation: General sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is provided by the lingual branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3). Special taste sensation to this region is from the chorda tympani (CN VII). The posterior one-third receives both general and taste sensation from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

questions.question: The secondary oocyte completes meiosis II at which time?
questions.explanation: The secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II and is ovulated in this state. It only completes meiosis II if fertilization occurs. The penetration of the sperm triggers completion of meiosis II, with extrusion of the second polar body. Without fertilization, the oocyte degenerates.

questions.question: G-cells of the stomach primarily secrete which hormone that stimulates gastric acid production?
questions.explanation: Wait — G-cells are enteroendocrine cells that secrete gastrin. Secretin is produced by S-cells in the duodenum. Gastrin stimulates parietal cells to secrete HCl and promotes gastric motility. This is a key distinction in GIT endocrinology. Answer: D (Gastrin).

questions.question: After birth, the ligamentum teres of the liver is formed from:
questions.explanation: The left umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres (round ligament) of the liver after birth and closure. The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum. The umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments. These fibrous remnants mark the locations of important fetal vessels.

options: Type IV collagen of basement membranes
questions.explanation: Elastic fibers require special staining techniques because they are not well visualized by H&E. Weigert's resorcin-fuchsin and orcein stains specifically stain elastic fibers dark blue-black or brown, allowing their visualization in vessels, lung, and ligamentum flavum. Silver stains, by contrast, stain reticular (type III collagen) fibers. This differential staining is important for diagnosing conditions affecting elastic tissue (e.g., emphysema, aortic aneurysm).
questions.question: Which connective tissue fiber type is best demonstrated by the Weigert's or orcein staining techniques?

questions.explanation: Reticular fibers, composed mainly of type III collagen, are not visible in routine H&E preparations but are stained black by silver impregnation due to their argyrophilic nature. This property reflects their high carbohydrate content associated with the sugar chains on these fibers. PAS also stains them positively due to the same sugar chain content.
questions.question: Reticular fibers are best visualized in histological sections by impregnation with which of the following staining methods?

options: Sound vibrations converted to nerve impulses
Macular otolith organs (linear) and semicircular cristae (angular acceleration)
Only static head position without any dynamic movement detection
questions.explanation: The vestibular apparatus detects two types of motion through distinct receptor organs: the maculae of the utricle and saccule contain hair cells with overlying otolithic membranes carrying calcium carbonate crystals called otoliths that respond to linear acceleration and gravity; and the cristae ampullares in the three semicircular ducts oriented in the three planes of space detect angular acceleration and rotation. Together these five receptor organs provide complete three-dimensional vestibular sensing.
questions.question: The vestibular apparatus of the inner ear detects which types of motion through its specialized sensory receptor structures?

questions.explanation: Spermiogenesis is the structural modification of spermatids (which have already completed meiosis) into spermatozoa. It involves cytoplasm shedding, nucleus condensation, formation of neck, middle piece and tail, and acrosome formation. Meiotic division occurs earlier during conversion of spermatocytes to spermatids.
questions.question: Spermiogenesis involves all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Hassall's corpuscles are spherical structures in the thymic medulla composed of concentrically arranged keratinized medullary epithelial cells forming onion-skin-like whorls. They appear in increasing numbers with age and thymic involution. Recent evidence shows they produce thymic stromal lymphopoietin that activates medullary dendritic cells to induce regulatory T cells contributing to self-tolerance. They are pathognomonic for thymic tissue identification in histological sections.
options: Clusters of mature T lymphocytes expressing CD8
Keratinized epithelial whorls involved in regulatory T cell induction
Macrophages that have phagocytosed dying thymocytes
Type IV collagen deposits forming the blood-thymus barrier
questions.question: The Hassall's corpuscles found exclusively in the thymic medulla are composed of which of the following?
The embedding medium used in standard paraffin histology processing primarily provides tissues with which of the following properties?
options: Firmness to support sectioning on the microtome
questions.explanation: Paraffin wax infiltrates dehydrated tissue and, upon solidifying, provides the mechanical support necessary for cutting thin, consistent sections (3–10 μm) on a microtome. The wax must be removed (deparaffinization) before staining since it interferes with water-based stains. Embedding is a critical intermediate step between fixation and staining.

questions.question: Hirschsprung disease is more common in:
questions.explanation: Hirschsprung disease is more common in males than females, with a male:female ratio of approximately 4:1. It is a dominantly inherited multigenic disorder. The disease is the most common cause of neonatal colonic obstruction, occurring in approximately 1 in 5000 live births.

questions.question: The bronchopulmonary segments are the smallest independently functional lung units with their own bronchus, artery, and vein. Which surgical implication arises from this segmental anatomy?
options: Only entire lobes can be surgically removed
Individual bronchopulmonary segments can be surgically resected
Each segment has its own pleural covering preventing pneumothorax
Segments are too small to be identified radiologically
Segments share venous drainage making individual resection impossible
questions.explanation: Because each bronchopulmonary segment has its own segmental bronchus and artery (note: veins run in intersegmental septa between segments), individual segments can be surgically resected (segmentectomy) while preserving adjacent healthy lung tissue. This is advantageous in patients with limited pulmonary reserve who cannot tolerate lobectomy. Understanding segmental anatomy is also critical for interpreting chest CT, bronchoscopy findings, and postural drainage positions.

The combination of eccentric nucleus with clock-face chromatin arrangement and strongly basophilic cytoplasm (due to abundant rough ER for antibody synthesis) is pathognomonic for plasma cells. These cells are terminally differentiated B lymphocytes specialized for immunoglobulin production. The well-developed Golgi body adjacent to the nucleus creates the paranuclear pale zone called the 'Hof.'
questions.question: A histology student observes a tissue section where cells show large basophilic cytoplasm with eccentric nuclei having a clock-face chromatin pattern. These cells are most likely which of the following?

options: Sensorineural hearing loss from hair cell damage
Central hearing loss from brainstem damage
Mixed hearing loss with retrocochlear component
Fixed stapes preventing vibration transmission: conductive hearing loss
questions.explanation: Otosclerosis involves abnormal bony remodeling that fixes the stapes footplate in the oval window preventing its normal piston-like movement. Since the stapes footplate normally transmits vibrations from the ossicular chain into the cochlear perilymph, its fixation blocks sound transmission to the inner ear causing conductive hearing loss. The inner ear hair cells are unaffected so sensorineural function is intact. Stapedectomy with prosthesis replacement restores hearing in most cases.
questions.question: The middle ear ossicle pathology in otosclerosis where abnormal bone formation fixates the stapes footplate causes which hearing deficit?
The liver parenchyma is predominantly composed of hepatocytes, but which additional cell type lines the hepatic sinusoids and has fenestrated cytoplasm?
questions.explanation: Hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) are specialized endothelial cells with numerous transcytoplasmic pores (fenestrae) arranged in groups called sieve plates. This fenestrated structure allows free passage of plasma and macromolecules (but not blood cells) between the sinusoidal blood and the space of Disse, facilitating hepatocyte exchange. Loss of fenestration in hepatic disease impairs liver function.

Tooth development requires reciprocal inductive interactions between mesenchyme (neural crest-derived) and epithelium (ectodermal). The epithelium induces the mesenchyme to form dental papilla and dental follicle, while the mesenchyme induces the epithelium to form enamel organ. Both tissues are required.
questions.question: Tooth development requires inductive stimuli from which tissue?
The placenta produces all of the following hormones EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The placenta produces hormones including progesterone, estrogens (especially estriol), human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), and human placental lactogen (somatomammotropin). It does not produce follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland.

questions.question: Cholangiocytes are the epithelial cells lining the bile ducts. What type of epithelium lines the large intrahepatic bile ducts?
questions.explanation: Intrahepatic bile ducts are lined by cholangiocytes — simple cuboidal epithelium in smaller ducts transitioning to simple columnar epithelium in larger ducts. These cells regulate bile composition through secretion and reabsorption. Cholangiocytes are targets of autoimmune destruction in primary biliary cholangitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis, causing progressive biliary cirrhosis.

The cornea provides approximately two-thirds of the total refractive power of the eye at about 43 diopters of the approximately 58 total, making it the primary refractive surface. The lens provides the remaining one-third and fine-tunes focus through accommodation. The cornea's refractive power is fixed while the lens changes shape. Corneal transparency depends on its regular collagen fiber arrangement, avascularity, and the endothelial fluid pump.
questions.question: The cornea as part of the eye's optical apparatus provides approximately what proportion of the eye's total refractive power?
options: Two-thirds of total refractive power; primary refraction site
All refractive power without the lens
Only 10 percent of total refractive power
Equal contribution to the lens of 50 percent each

questions.question: The volume of amniotic fluid at mid-pregnancy is approximately:
questions.explanation: The volume of amniotic fluid is about 400 ml at mid-pregnancy. It reaches about 1000 ml at 36-38 weeks, then decreases later to be scanty in post-term pregnancy. The fluid is continuously turned over, with approximately 500 ml replaced every hour.

options: Digest ingested material, worn-out organelles, and debris
questions.question: Lysosomes are organelles that contain hydrolytic enzymes and primarily function to perform which of the following?
questions.explanation: Lysosomes are membrane-bound vesicles containing over 50 acid hydrolases active at pH ~4.5, enabling intracellular digestion of phagocytosed material (heterophagy), worn-out organelles (autophagy), and cellular debris. Their role in fusing with phagosomes (forming phagolysosomes) is central to macrophage-mediated immunity. Lysosomal storage diseases result from deficiency of specific hydrolases.

questions.question: The pancreas has both exocrine and endocrine functions. The ratio of exocrine to endocrine tissue in the normal adult pancreas is approximately:
questions.explanation: In the adult pancreas, approximately 80–85% of the parenchyma is exocrine acinar tissue producing digestive enzymes. The ductal system comprises another 10–15%. The islets of Langerhans constitute only about 1–2% of the total pancreatic mass, yet they have profound systemic significance. The pancreatic stroma (connective tissue, blood vessels, nerves) accounts for the remainder. This ratio is important in understanding pancreatitis and its preferential exocrine destruction.

questions.question: Respiratory distress syndrome in premature infants primarily results from:
questions.explanation: Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in premature infants primarily results from insufficient surfactant production by immature type II pneumocytes. Without adequate surfactant, alveoli collapse during expiration, requiring greater effort for breathing. Treatment includes surfactant replacement therapy and respiratory support.

options: Synthesizing ATP directly through oxidative phosphorylation
Regulating calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Storing and diffusing oxygen within muscle cells to support aerobic metabolism
Acting as a structural protein anchoring actin to the Z disc
Catalyzing the breakdown of glycogen for anaerobic glycolysis
questions.question: Myoglobin in skeletal muscle primarily serves which of the following functions?
questions.explanation: Myoglobin is a single-chain oxygen-binding heme protein in muscle cells that stores oxygen and facilitates its diffusion from the sarcolemma to mitochondria. This oxygen reserve allows continued aerobic metabolism during brief periods of reduced blood flow during contraction. Type I slow oxidative muscle fibers are rich in myoglobin appearing red while type II fast glycolytic fibers have less myoglobin appearing white.

The azygos lobe is an anatomical variant (found in approximately 1% of people) where the azygos vein migrates through the lung during development, carrying a double layer of pleura (visceral and parietal) with it to form an accessory fissure. The tissue within the azygos lobe is otherwise completely normal pulmonary parenchyma. It is clinically significant because it can be mistaken for a pathological lesion on chest radiography and may complicate surgical procedures.
questions.question: The azygos lobe is an accessory lobe of the right lung created by an anomalous azygos vein cutting through the lung tissue. Histologically, the tissue within the azygos lobe is:
What percentage of conceptions are estimated to be chromosomally abnormal?
questions.explanation: It is estimated that 10-15% of all conceptions are chromosomally abnormal. Most of these (about 95%) result in spontaneous abortion, usually in the first trimester. Chromosomal abnormalities are the leading cause of pregnancy loss and account for about 50% of first-trimester miscarriages.

questions.question: The nipple typically rises from the mammary pit:
questions.explanation: After birth, nipples rise from mammary pits through proliferation of surrounding connective tissue of the areola. In newborn infants, nipples are poorly formed and depressed. Late in fetal life, the epidermis at the site of mammary gland origin becomes depressed, forming a shallow mammary pit.

questions.question: Aqueous humor fills the anterior and posterior chambers of the eye and is produced by which structure?
questions.explanation: Aqueous humor is produced by the ciliary body's non-pigmented epithelium through active secretion from blood plasma. It flows from the posterior chamber through the pupil into the anterior chamber and drains at the iridocorneal angle through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal. Impaired drainage in glaucoma increases intraocular pressure damaging the optic nerve. Aqueous humor provides nutrients to the avascular lens and cornea.
options: The corneal endothelium through active secretion
The ciliary body epithelium by active secretion from capillaries
The vitreous humor flowing into the anterior chamber
The iris stroma through filtration of plasma

questions.explanation: The hallmark of nephrotic syndrome at the ultrastructural level is effacement (fusion/retraction) of podocyte foot processes, which eliminates the slit diaphragms that are the final size-selective filter. Without slit diaphragms, proteins — primarily albumin — leak freely into the filtrate, causing proteinuria. In minimal change disease, foot process effacement is the only ultrastructural abnormality (no deposits, normal light microscopy). This effacement is reversible with corticosteroid treatment in minimal change disease.
questions.question: The nephrotic syndrome is characterized by massive proteinuria (>3.5g/day), hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia. The podocyte lesion that results in loss of selective filtration is:

questions.explanation: Anal stenosis is characterized by narrowing of the anus and anal canal, which are in the normal position but constricted. This may result from incomplete recanalization after the solid epithelial stage. Mild stenosis may only become apparent when the infant begins passing formed stools. Surgical dilation or anoplasty may be required.
questions.question: Anal stenosis results from:
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is caused by a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma). Histologically, the gastric mucosa in this condition would show:
options: Replacement of gastric epithelium by intestinal metaplasia
Infiltration of the mucosa by goblet cells
questions.explanation: In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, excessive gastrin from a gastrinoma (often in the duodenal wall or pancreas) continuously stimulates parietal cell HCl secretion and promotes mucosal growth. This causes hypertrophy and hyperplasia of fundic glands, particularly parietal and chief cells, with markedly thickened, prominent rugae. Patients develop severe, refractory peptic ulcers. This is the opposite of gastric atrophy seen in pernicious anemia.

options: Zona reticularis producing aldosterone, zona fasciculata producing androgens, and zona glomerulosa producing cortisol
Zona medullaris producing epinephrine, zona fasciculata producing cortisol, and zona reticularis producing aldosterone
Zona glomerulosa (aldosterone), zona fasciculata (cortisol), zona reticularis (androgens) — GFR
Zona granulosa producing estrogen, zona lutea producing progesterone, and zona basalis producing testosterone
Cortex producing all three hormones uniformly without zonal distinction
questions.explanation: The adrenal cortex from outer to inner consists of: zona glomerulosa at approximately 15% with rounded cell clusters producing aldosterone regulated by angiotensin II and potassium; zona fasciculata at approximately 75% with parallel cords of spongiocytes producing cortisol regulated by ACTH; and zona reticularis at approximately 10% with irregular cords producing androgens such as DHEA regulated by ACTH. The mnemonic GFR from surface inward aids recall.
questions.question: The adrenal cortex is organized into three zones from outside to inside. Which of the following correctly names these zones and their hormone products?

questions.explanation: After the 13th week, bile entering the duodenum gives meconium its characteristic dark green color. Bile formation by hepatic cells begins around the 12th week. Meconium accumulates in the fetal intestines throughout gestation and is normally passed within the first 24-48 hours after birth. Delayed passage may indicate intestinal obstruction.
questions.question: Bile entering the duodenum gives meconium its characteristic color around:
Microtubules within the cytoskeleton serve which of the following primary functions?
questions.explanation: Microtubules (25 nm diameter, hollow cylinders of tubulin dimers) provide structural rigidity to maintain cell shape and serve as tracks for motor proteins (kinesins and dyneins) carrying organelles and vesicles throughout the cell. They also form the mitotic spindle during cell division. Their dynamic instability allows rapid reorganization in response to cellular needs.
options: Provide the contractile force for muscle contraction
Generate cell surface projections like microvilli
Provide rigidity and tracks for organelle movement

questions.question: Type A spermatogonia undergo mitosis to produce which cells?
questions.explanation: Type A spermatogonia undergo mitosis to produce more type A spermatogonia (maintaining the stem cell pool) and type B spermatogonia. Type B spermatogonia then differentiate into primary spermatocytes, which undergo meiosis to eventually produce spermatozoa.

Omphalocele is characterized by herniation of abdominal viscera through a large umbilical ring defect. The herniated viscera are covered by peritoneal and amniotic membranes. About 50% of cases have other serious congenital or chromosomal abnormalities. The defect results from failure of intestinal return or body wall closure.
questions.question: Omphalocele is characterized by:

questions.explanation: The mesencephalon (midbrain vesicle) gives rise to the midbrain in the adult brain. The three primary brain vesicles are prosencephalon (forebrain), mesencephalon (midbrain), and rhombencephalon (hindbrain). These later subdivide into five secondary brain vesicles.
questions.question: The mesencephalon gives rise to which adult brain structure?

questions.explanation: Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses are herniations of the gallbladder mucosal epithelium into and through the muscularis layer. While small sinuses may be considered a normal variant, prominent ones are a pathological feature of chronic cholecystitis (chronic gallbladder inflammation). They are significant because they can harbor bacteria within the muscular wall, contributing to recurrent infections, and can be mistaken for adenomyomatosis on imaging.
questions.question: The gallbladder mucosa shows Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses on histological examination. These sinuses represent:
options: Normal mucosal invaginations without pathological significance
Lymphoid aggregates in the lamina propria

questions.question: The glycocalyx, which surrounds the cell membrane, is composed primarily of which of the following?
questions.explanation: The glycocalyx is a fuzzy extracellular coat composed of carbohydrate chains covalently attached to membrane proteins (glycoproteins) and lipids (glycolipids). It plays roles in cell recognition, adhesion, and protection from mechanical damage. Its presence is detectable in electron micrographs as an electron-dense coating on the outer surface of the plasma membrane.

options: A primary oocyte arrested in meiosis I surrounded by a single layer of flattened follicular
A primary oocyte surrounded by several layers of granulosa cells with a zona pellucida
A secondary oocyte with a fully formed antrum
A secondary oocyte surrounded by cumulus oophorus
A mature egg with zona pellucida and corona radiata only
questions.explanation: Primordial follicles consist of a primary oocyte arrested in prophase I of meiosis, surrounded by a single layer of flattened (squamous) follicular cells. These are the smallest and most numerous follicles in the ovary and represent the ovarian reserve. Activation of primordial follicles triggers their transition to primary follicles, where follicular cells become cuboidal and begin proliferating.
questions.question: The female ovary contains follicles at various stages of development. Primordial follicles consist of:

questions.explanation: Satellite cells are the adult stem cells of skeletal muscle, residing between the sarcolemma and the overlying basal lamina. They are normally quiescent but are activated by muscle injury, proliferate, and either fuse with damaged fibers or form new fibers, providing the limited but genuine regenerative capacity of skeletal muscle. Progressive depletion of satellite cells contributes to the sarcopenia seen with aging.
options: Between sarcomeres inside muscle fibers where they synthesize myosin
Within the endomysium where they produce collagen for muscle connective tissue
At the neuromuscular junction where they remyelinate motor nerves
In the perimysium where they differentiate into fibroblasts after injury
Between the sarcolemma and overlying basal lamina, serving as adult muscle stem cells
questions.question: Satellite cells in skeletal muscle are located in which specific position and serve which primary function?
The Nissl substance visible in neuronal cell bodies corresponds to which ultrastructural organelle and what does its dissolution (chromatolysis) indicate?
options: Mitochondria with chromatolysis indicating increased ATP demand
Golgi apparatus with chromatolysis indicating secretory cell activation
Lipofuscin granules with chromatolysis indicating cellular aging
Rough ER with ribosomes; chromatolysis indicates neuronal injury after axonal damage
Melanin granules with chromatolysis indicating decreased dopamine production
questions.explanation: Nissl bodies are stacks of rough ER visible with basic dyes in neuronal cell bodies reflecting the neuron's high capacity for protein synthesis. Chromatolysis is the dissolution of Nissl substance occurring as the histological hallmark of the axonal reaction after peripheral axon injury, characterized by cell body swelling, nuclear eccentricity, and dispersal of Nissl substance as the neuron redirects synthetic activity toward axon regeneration proteins.

questions.question: M cells (microfold cells) in the small intestinal epithelium overlie Peyer's patches. Their primary function is:
questions.explanation: M cells are specialized epithelial cells overlying Peyer's patches that lack a conventional brush border and instead have an irregular apical surface. They transcytose antigens, bacteria, and macromolecules from the intestinal lumen to the underlying lymphoid tissue for immune processing. This makes them critical portals for mucosal immunity but also pathogen entry points.

questions.question: The septum secundum forms as a crescent-shaped fold in which direction from the septum primum?
questions.explanation: Shortly after the ostium secundum forms, a second crescent-shaped fold (septum secundum) appears to the right of the septum primum. The septum secundum never forms a complete partition. The opening left by the septum secundum is called the foramen ovale.

The oviduct is lined by simple columnar epithelium containing two cell types: ciliated cells (whose cilia beat toward the uterus, propelling the oocyte) and secretory (peg) cells (which produce nutrient secretions to support the oocyte and early embryo). The mucosa of the ampulla (site of fertilization) is especially complex with elaborate mucosal folds. Loss of ciliary function impairs oocyte transport and increases ectopic pregnancy risk.
questions.question: The oviduct (fallopian tube) is lined by which type of epithelium that facilitates the transport of the oocyte?
The plasma membrane's glycocalyx performs which of the following functions that most directly relates to cell-to-cell recognition?
questions.explanation: The glycocalyx's carbohydrate chains serve as recognition molecules for cell-cell adhesion, immune recognition (self vs. non-self), and receptor-ligand interactions including microbial adhesion to host cells. Blood group antigens (ABO system) are glycocalyx components. The unique carbohydrate sequences on different cell types allow specific cellular recognition and communication.
options: Cell recognition, adhesion, and immune self/non-self identification
Generating the membrane potential across the bilayer
Regulating gene expression in the nucleus

questions.question: Which germ layer gives rise to the epithelial lining of the respiratory tract?
questions.explanation: The endoderm gives rise to the epithelial lining of the respiratory tract (pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs). The connective tissue, cartilage, and smooth muscle of the respiratory system are derived from splanchnic mesoderm. The yolk sac endoderm contributes to this epithelium.

options: Give the cell rigid structural support
Act as tracks for organelle movement
questions.question: Microfilaments of actin within the cytoskeleton primarily enable cells to perform which of the following functions?
questions.explanation: Actin microfilaments (7 nm diameter) are the thinnest cytoskeletal filaments and generate the forces necessary for cell shape changes, movement, and cell division through dynamic polymerization and depolymerization. They are concentrated beneath the plasma membrane forming the cell cortex. They work with myosin motors in muscle contraction and in non-muscle cell motility.

options: Only a single layer of simple squamous epithelium
Two layers of keratinized squamous epithelium enclosing air
Three layers: outer keratinized skin, middle fibrous layer, inner simple squamous epithelium
Stratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells identical to respiratory mucosa
Fibrocartilage identical to the ear pinna
questions.explanation: The tympanic membrane has three layers: an outer lateral layer continuous with the skin of the external auditory canal with thin keratinized stratified squamous epithelium; a middle fibrous layer of radially and circularly arranged collagen and elastic fibers providing structural integrity; and an inner medial layer of simple squamous to low cuboidal epithelium continuous with the middle ear mucosa. The tympanic membrane vibrates in response to sound waves transmitting them to the malleus handle attached to its inner surface.
questions.question: The tympanic membrane or eardrum consists of which layers and performs which function?

questions.explanation: Hepatocytes are large polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm reflecting their high metabolic activity (rich in mitochondria, ER, and glycogen). They have round, vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli, and about 25% are binucleate — a feature of polyploidy indicating high metabolic demand. These features readily distinguish hepatocytes from other liver cell types.
questions.question: Hepatocytes are the main functional cells of the liver. Which description best characterizes their light microscopic appearance?
options: Small dark nuclei with scanty cytoplasm
Elongated fusiform cells with dark basophilic cytoplasm
Cuboidal cells with apical microvilli and basal nuclei
Large polygonal eosinophilic cells with round nuclei

questions.explanation: Erythropoiesis progresses: proerythroblast (large cell with prominent nucleolus basophilic cytoplasm) to basophilic erythroblast (active ribosome synthesis) to polychromatic erythroblast (hemoglobin accumulation mixed colors) to orthochromatic erythroblast (pyknotic nucleus pink cytoplasm) where the nucleus is extruded to form a reticulocyte (still contains ribosomes staining with supravital dyes) which matures into an erythrocyte. This 5 to 7 day process is driven by erythropoietin from the kidney.
options: Proerythroblast → basophilic → polychromatic → orthochromatic erythroblast → reticulocyte → erythrocyte
Myeloblast then promyelocyte then myelocyte then metamyelocyte then erythrocyte
Lymphoblast then prolymphocyte then lymphocyte then erythrocyte
Stem cell directly producing mature erythrocytes without intermediate stages
questions.question: The process of erythropoiesis involves a series of precursor stages. Which of the following correctly sequences erythroid development from earliest to most mature in bone marrow?

questions.explanation: Hematopoiesis begins in the liver during the 6th week, giving the organ a dark red color. The liver serves as the major hematopoietic organ during fetal life. By the 9th week, the rapidly growing liver comprises about 10% of total body weight.
questions.question: Hematopoiesis in the liver begins during which week?

questions.explanation: During cephalocaudal folding and brain growth, the buccopharyngeal membrane is pulled forward, while the heart and pericardial cavity move from dorsal to cervical and finally to thoracic position. This folding transforms the flat embryonic disc into a three-dimensional embryo with distinct body cavities.
questions.question: During embryonic folding, the buccopharyngeal membrane moves:

questions.explanation: Cryptorchidism most commonly involves retention in the inguinal canal (70% of cases). Abdominal retention accounts for about 20%, and other locations 10%. The condition may be bilateral or unilateral (right side more common). Orchiopexy (surgical placement into scrotum) is recommended by 12-18 months to preserve fertility and reduce malignancy risk.
questions.question: Undescended testis (cryptorchidism) most commonly involves:
Which condition would most directly result from premature closure of the epiphyseal growth plate?
options: Rickets due to vitamin D deficiency
Osteoporosis from reduced bone mineral density
Osteosarcoma arising from osteoblast precursor cells
Arrested longitudinal growth causing short stature before full height
Osteomalacia from impaired bone matrix mineralization
questions.explanation: The epiphyseal growth plate is responsible for longitudinal bone growth through endochondral ossification. Premature closure, whether from trauma, infection, or corticosteroids, arrests longitudinal growth of that bone. If bilateral, this leads to short stature proportional to the extent and timing of premature closure. Conversely, delayed closure as in growth hormone excess before puberty leads to gigantism.

The peritoneal cavity loses its connection with the extraembryonic coelom during the 10th week of development. Initially, the greater part of each limb of the intraembryonic coelom opens laterally into the extraembryonic coelom. Horizontal folding brings the limbs together ventrally and eventually closes this connection.
questions.question: The peritoneal cavity loses its connection with the extraembryonic coelom during which week?
A histology student is instructed to make drawings of tissue sections observed under the light microscope. This practice is specifically aimed at achieving which primary objective?
questions.explanation: Making drawings of observed tissue sections trains students to carefully observe and accurately record the spatial arrangement of cells and tissue components. This active observation develops the ability to identify tissue types and pathological changes from microscopic examination. It is a core component of histology practical training.
options: Memorizing staining patterns by color alone
Learning to operate the microscope mechanically
Accurate recognition of cellular and tissue architecture

questions.question: The notochordal process extends cranially to which structure?
questions.explanation: In the third week of development, mesenchymal cells from the primitive node form the notochordal process. This process extends cranially between the ectoderm and endoderm to reach the prechordal plate. The primitive pit extends into the notochordal process to form the notochordal canal.

Metachromasia refers to the property of certain dyes, including toluidine blue, to color tissue components differently from their own intrinsic color. Mast cell granules contain heparin (a sulfated glycosaminoglycan) which shifts the color from the dye's native blue to purple or violet. This color shift is diagnostic for identifying mast cells in tissue sections.
questions.question: Mast cell granules stained metachromatically with toluidine blue produce which of the following colors?
The bulbus cordis eventually forms which adult heart structure?
questions.explanation: The bulbus cordis gives rise to the smooth part of the right ventricle, while the primitive ventricle forms the trabeculated parts of both ventricles. The proximal part of the bulbus is called the conus cordis, and the distal part is the truncus arteriosus, which is continuous with the aortic sac.

questions.question: The stomach is divided into four regions. Which pair of regions is histologically IDENTICAL?
questions.explanation: The fundus and body of the stomach are histologically identical, both containing branched tubular gastric glands with parietal cells, chief cells, mucous neck cells, and enteroendocrine cells. The cardia and pylorus are histologically similar to each other, containing predominantly mucus-secreting glands. This regional identity is consistently tested in histology examinations.

questions.question: A student views a specimen and finds it cannot be examined directly because of its thickness. Which instrument is most appropriate to produce thin translucent sections?
questions.explanation: A microtome is the specialized instrument used to cut tissue blocks into thin sections (typically 3–10 μm) that allow light transmission for microscopy. The cryostat is a variant used for frozen sections. A centrifuge separates components and an autoclave sterilizes, neither producing histological sections.

The endocardium, forming the internal endothelial lining of the heart, develops from splanchnic mesoderm. The myocardium (muscular wall) and epicardium (visceral pericardium) also develop from splanchnic mesoderm. Initially, right and left endothelial heart tubes form and subsequently fuse.
questions.question: The endocardium develops from which embryonic layer?
The neck is formed by elongation of the region between which two structures?
questions.explanation: The neck is formed by elongation of the region between the stomodeum and pericardium. This elongation is caused by descent of the developing heart and appearance of the pharyngeal (branchial) arches in the 4th and 5th weeks of development. The developing brain is separated from the future thorax by the stomodeum.

Mallory-Denk bodies (Mallory bodies) are eosinophilic, irregular cytoplasmic inclusions within hepatocytes composed of aggregated cytokeratin intermediate filaments. They are characteristically seen in alcoholic hepatitis and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). Their presence indicates hepatocyte injury with cytoskeletal disruption. They can also be seen less commonly in Wilson's disease and primary biliary cholangitis.
questions.question: Rosenthal fibers and Mallory bodies are cytoplasmic inclusions of hepatocytes. The Mallory body (Mallory-Denk body) is characteristically associated with:

questions.explanation: Nondisjunction (failure of separation of homologous chromosomes in anaphase I or sister chromatids in anaphase II) can result in abnormal gametes. Normal gametes have 23 chromosomes (22 + X or 22 + Y). Nondisjunction produces gametes with 24 chromosomes (23 + X or 23 + Y) or 22 chromosomes (21 + X or 21 + Y).
questions.question: Nondisjunction during oogenesis can result in gametes with which chromosome number?

questions.explanation: At about day 20, the paraxial mesoderm differentiates to form the first pair of somites on each side of the neural tube. Four somites are formed per day during the somite period (days 20-30). By the end of this period, approximately 42-44 somites have been formed.
questions.question: By which day are approximately 42-44 somites formed?
Intermediate filaments, the cytoskeletal elements between actin and microtubules in diameter, primarily serve which of the following roles?
questions.explanation: Intermediate filaments (8–12 nm) provide the primary mechanical support for cells, reinforcing their shape against deformation and anchoring the nucleus and other organelles. Different cell types express different intermediate filament proteins (vimentin in mesenchymal cells, cytokeratins in epithelial cells, desmin in muscle, neurofilaments in neurons). Their stability makes them useful as cell-type identification markers in pathology.
options: Generate contractile forces in non-muscle cells
Form mitotic spindle during cell division
Reinforce the cell mechanically and maintain organelle position
Transport vesicles from ER to Golgi

questions.explanation: Primordial germ cells appear in the endodermal lining of the yolk sac wall. These cells later migrate to the developing gonads to form oogonia and spermatogonia. The yolk sac also functions in early blood development and contributes endoderm to various organs.
questions.question: Primordial germ cells appear in the endodermal lining of which structure?
The ductus arteriosus connects which two vessels?
questions.explanation: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta, allowing most blood from the right ventricle to bypass the non-functional fetal lungs. After birth, the ductus arteriosus closes and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. Failure of closure results in patent ductus arteriosus.

questions.question: Merkel cells are primarily associated with:
questions.explanation: Merkel cells are sensitive mechanoreceptors essential for light touch sensation and discrimination of shapes and textures. They appear in human fetal skin at 18 weeks of gestation. These cells are joined by desmosomes to keratinocytes and contact sensory nerve fibers at their basolateral surfaces.

questions.question: Attachment of the blastocyst to endometrial epithelium is mediated by which molecule on the trophoblast?
questions.explanation: Attachment of the blastocyst to the endometrial epithelium is mediated by L-selectin on the trophoblast and its receptor on the endometrial epithelium. This is the first stage of implantation and occurs after the zona pellucida has disappeared.

questions.question: Interstitial nephritis is inflammation of the renal interstitium. The characteristic histological finding of acute interstitial nephritis (typically drug-induced) is:
options: Subepithelial immune deposits on electron microscopy
questions.explanation: Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is characterized histologically by edema and dense inflammatory infiltrate in the renal interstitium — predominantly lymphocytes, plasma cells, monocytes, and characteristically eosinophils (suggesting drug-induced type). Tubular injury (tubulitis — inflammatory cells invading the tubular epithelium) is a key feature. Glomeruli are typically normal or show minor changes. NSAIDs, beta-lactam antibiotics, and PPIs are common causes. AIN is an important reversible cause of acute kidney injury.

questions.question: The amniotic cavity appears as spaces within which layer on day 8?
questions.explanation: On day 8, spaces occur within the epiblast layer to form the amniotic cavity. This cavity will expand greatly and eventually surrounds the entire embryo. The cells lining the amniotic cavity are derived from epiblast and are called amnioblasts.

questions.question: The kidney is enclosed by three layers of supporting tissue. Which layer, immediately adjacent to the renal capsule externally, consists of perinephric fat?
questions.explanation: The three layers from innermost outward are: (1) fibrous (true) capsule — tightly adherent to renal parenchyma; (2) adipose (perinephric fat) capsule — layer of perinephric fat providing cushioning; (3) renal (Gerota's) fascia — outer fibrous layer anchoring the kidney to surrounding structures. This fat layer acts as a protective shock absorber. In thin patients, loss of perinephric fat contributes to renal ptosis (nephroptosis).

Heparin within mast cell granules is a sulfated glycosaminoglycan that acts locally as an anticoagulant by activating antithrombin III, which inhibits clotting factors. The local anticoagulant effect may facilitate cell migration through connective tissue during inflammatory responses. Clinically, heparin extracted from mast cell-rich tissues (lung, intestinal mucosa) is used as a therapeutic anticoagulant.
questions.question: Mast cell granules contain heparin, which acts locally in connective tissue as which of the following?
options: A vasoconstrictor reducing blood flow to inflamed areas
An antibacterial peptide directly killing bacteria
An anticoagulant preventing blood clot formation in the tissue
A growth factor stimulating fibroblast proliferation

questions.explanation: Reichert's cartilage is the cartilage of the second pharyngeal arch. Its dorsal part forms the stapes, styloid process of temporal bone, and stylohyoid ligament. The ventral part forms the lesser horn of the hyoid bone and the upper part of the body of the hyoid bone.
questions.question: Reichert's cartilage is associated with which pharyngeal arch?
The heart and blood vessels are derived from which germ layer?
questions.explanation: The heart and all blood vessels are mesodermal in origin. The mesoderm constitutes the cardiogenic field or area, which is closely related to the pericardial cavity and heart tube. This cardiogenic mesoderm differentiates to form the endocardium, myocardium, and epicardium.

questions.question: The tympanic membrane receives contributions from which embryonic layers?
questions.explanation: The tympanic membrane is formed by contributions from all three germ layers. The external epithelial lining comes from ectoderm of the first pharyngeal cleft, the middle fibrous layer from mesoderm, and the internal lining from endoderm of the first pharyngeal pouch (tubotympanic recess).

questions.question: The parietal layer of Bowman's capsule is lined by which type of epithelium?
questions.explanation: The parietal layer of Bowman's capsule is lined by simple squamous epithelium. This thin, flat epithelium forms the outer boundary of the urinary space (Bowman's space) between the parietal and visceral (podocyte) layers. In rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, parietal epithelial cells proliferate to form crescents, a pathological hallmark of severe glomerular injury.

The duodenum uniquely has Brunner's glands located in its submucosa. These glands secrete alkaline mucus to neutralize the acidic chyme entering from the stomach. The esophagus also has glands in its submucosa (esophageal glands proper), but Brunner's glands are the most clinically significant submucosal glands in the GIT.
questions.question: A histological preparation shows a GIT wall segment where the submucosa contains glands. This is a unique feature of which region?
Which of the following correctly describes spongy (cancellous) bone compared to compact (cortical) bone?
questions.explanation: Spongy (cancellous/trabecular) bone consists of a three-dimensional lattice of bone trabeculae (thin struts and plates) with interconnected marrow-filled spaces, providing a lightweight yet strong architecture for weight-bearing and hematopoiesis. Compact bone forms the dense cortex with cylindrical osteons. Both types contain osteocytes in lacunae, but spongy bone's trabeculae are too thin to require Haversian canal systems.
options: Spongy bone is denser and forms the cortex of long bones
Spongy bone contains Haversian systems like compact bone
Spongy bone has no cells and is composed entirely of mineral
Spongy bone is found only in flat bones and absent in long bones
Spongy bone has a lattice-like trabecular structure with marrow-filled spaces

questions.question: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS) occurs in premature infants due to surfactant deficiency. Antenatal corticosteroids are given to accelerate fetal lung maturity by stimulating:
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids (betamethasone, dexamethasone) given antenatally accelerate fetal lung maturity by binding glucocorticoid receptors in Type II pneumocytes, stimulating maturation and increasing synthesis of dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) — the main surfactant phospholipid. This reduces surface tension in alveoli, decreasing the risk of NRDS. Lecithin:sphingomyelin (L:S) ratio >2 in amniotic fluid indicates adequate surfactant maturity.

The dorsal column nuclei (nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus) are characteristic features of the lower medulla (caudal to the pyramidal decussation level). These nuclei receive and relay sensory information from the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus).
questions.question: The dorsal column nuclei (gracile and cuneate) are found at which level?

options: Systemic elastic tissue disease with aortic dissection as a major complication
Cartilage throughout the body affected causing severe degenerative arthritis
Compact cortical bone affected causing repeated pathological fractures
Lymphoid tissue affected causing severe progressive immunodeficiency
Skeletal muscle affected causing dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
questions.explanation: Marfan syndrome from FBN1 fibrillin-1 mutations primarily affects tissues rich in elastic fibers since fibrillin-1 scaffolds elastin deposition. The aorta with its high elastic fiber content and constant high-pressure pulsatile stress is most critically affected, with progressive dilatation leading to aneurysm formation and potentially fatal acute aortic dissection or rupture. Additional manifestations include lens dislocation from zonular fiber weakness, and skeletal features from abnormal bone and connective tissue.
questions.question: A patient with Marfan syndrome has mutations in the FBN1 gene. Which tissue type is most critically affected and what is the life-threatening complication?

questions.explanation: The tunica adventitia is rich in type I collagen fibers (providing tensile strength and preventing overdistension at high pressures) and type III collagen (providing flexibility). Elastin fibers in the adventitia provide elasticity, while type I collagen acts as a 'safety net' limiting vessel diameter when maximally distended. Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome involves type III collagen deficiency, causing fragile vessel walls prone to spontaneous arterial rupture.
questions.question: In the tunica adventitia of large arteries, which structural proteins provide tensile strength and prevent overdistension?

options: Axon hillock and entire axonal arborization
questions.question: Nissl substance is absent from which two regions of the neuron?
questions.explanation: Nissl substance or rough ER is present throughout the cell body and extends into the main dendritic trunks but is notably absent from the axon hillock and throughout the entire axon. This distribution reflects the specialized function of the axon as an electrical conductor rather than a protein synthesis compartment. Proteins synthesized in the cell body are transported to axon terminals via axonal transport mechanisms.

Wait — Chief cells secrete pepsinogen (converted to pepsin by HCl) and gastric lipase. Gastrin is secreted by G-cells (enteroendocrine cells). The correct answer is C: Chief (zymogen) cells are basophilic cells in the base of gastric glands that produce pepsinogen and gastric lipase. Answer: C.
questions.question: Chief (zymogen) cells of the gastric glands are characterized by which secretory product?
The muscular interventricular septum develops in:
questions.explanation: The muscular interventricular septum develops in the floor of the common ventricle and grows toward the AV endocardial cushions. However, it stops short, leaving the interventricular foramen. Complete closure requires fusion of the membranous IV septum formed by right bulbar ridge, left bulbar ridge, and AV cushions.

The periurethral (Skene's) glands in the female urethra are the embryological homologs of the prostate gland. Both develop from the urogenital sinus under hormonal influence. Like prostatic tissue, Skene's glands express PSA and PSAP (prostate-specific acid phosphatase). Bartholin's glands are the female homologs of Cowper's (bulbourethral) glands in males. Understanding these homologies is important for embryology, pathology, and forensic medicine.
questions.question: The periurethral glands in the female urethra are histologically homologous to which structure?
Neutrophils are the first responders to bacterial infection primarily because of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are the dominant acute inflammatory cells and first responders to bacterial infection. They migrate rapidly via chemotaxis to infection sites within hours, phagocytose bacteria, and kill them through: oxidative burst where NADPH oxidase generates reactive oxygen species; azurophilic granule enzymes including myeloperoxidase and elastase; and defensins and lactoferrin. Their short lifespan of 1 to 2 days in tissues and abundant bone marrow production support rapid response.
options: They produce antibodies against bacterial antigens
They present antigens to T lymphocytes at infection sites
Rapidly recruited phagocytes killing bacteria via oxidative burst
They release histamine causing vascular dilation
They transform into macrophages at infection sites

questions.question: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is absorbed in which specific region of the intestine after binding to intrinsic factor?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor (IF, produced by gastric parietal cells) is specifically absorbed in the terminal ileum via cubilin receptors on enterocyte surfaces. This is a critical location because surgical resection or Crohn's disease affecting the terminal ileum will cause B12 malabsorption and megaloblastic anemia. The terminal ileum also specifically absorbs bile salts (enterohepatic circulation) — their malabsorption leads to bile salt-induced diarrhea.

questions.question: The trigone of the bladder has which embryological origin?
questions.explanation: The trigone of the bladder has mesodermal origin, derived from the caudal ends of the mesonephric ducts. The remainder of the bladder epithelium is endodermal, derived from the urogenital sinus. This dual origin explains the different epithelial characteristics: the trigone has unique smooth muscle and different innervation patterns.

The renal papillae (apices of renal pyramids) are formed by convergence of collecting ducts from each pyramid. The papillae project into minor calyces, and collecting duct openings (papillary ducts of Bellini) at the papillae drain urine into the calyces. Each kidney has 8-12 papillae corresponding to pyramids. Papillary necrosis can occur in certain disease states.
questions.question: The renal papillae are formed by:

questions.explanation: In the resting state, tropomyosin physically blocks myosin-binding sites on actin. When calcium is released from the SR, it binds troponin C as part of the troponin-tropomyosin complex on thin filaments, causing a conformational change that moves tropomyosin away from the myosin binding sites on actin. This exposes the binding sites allowing myosin cross-bridges to attach and the power stroke to occur.
options: Tropomyosin to displace it from actin binding sites
Titin to reduce the sarcomere resting length
Troponin C moves tropomyosin to expose actin's myosin-binding sites
Actin directly to activate its ATPase activity
questions.question: During skeletal muscle contraction, calcium ions bind to which protein to initiate the actin-myosin interaction?

questions.explanation: Most cases of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) are autoimmune, caused by antibodies against granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF). GM-CSF is required for terminal differentiation and surfactant-catabolizing function of alveolar macrophages. Without functional GM-CSF signaling, macrophages cannot clear surfactant, which accumulates in alveoli. Histologically, alveoli are filled with PAS-positive, acellular, granular material. Treatment is whole-lung lavage.
questions.question: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is characterized by accumulation of surfactant lipids and proteins in alveoli. The deficiency that causes most cases is:
options: Deficiency of surfactant proteins A and D
Excess production of type I collagen
Loss of ciliary function in bronchioles

questions.explanation: Autolysis is self-digestion resulting from release of lysosomal enzymes within dying cells, which hydrolyze cellular components. It is a key reason why tissues must be fixed immediately after removal. Necrosis is a broader term for cell death, while apoptosis is programmed cell death distinct from autolysis.
questions.question: Which cellular deterioration process occurring after tissue removal involves self-digestion by the cell's own enzymes?

questions.explanation: Polar bodies are small cells with minimal cytoplasm that result from asymmetric division during oogenesis. They contain genetic material but lack the cytoplasm and organelles needed for development. Polar bodies are nonfunctional cells that degenerate and serve to discard excess chromosomes.
questions.question: Polar bodies are characterized by which feature?

questions.explanation: The myocardium is the middle layer of the heart wall, composed of cardiac muscle cells (cardiomyocytes) organized into complex networks. It is the thickest layer, especially in the left ventricle, and is responsible for the contractile force that pumps blood. The endocardium lines the cardiac chambers internally, and the epicardium (visceral pericardium) covers the external surface.
questions.question: The heart wall has three layers. Which is the middle and thickest layer, composed of cardiac muscle, and is responsible for pumping function?

options: Ventral duct and distal dorsal duct
questions.question: The main pancreatic duct is formed from:
questions.explanation: The main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung) is formed from the duct of the ventral bud and the distal part of the dorsal bud duct. The proximal part of the dorsal bud duct often persists as the accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini). The main duct opens into the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla.

questions.question: The glomerulus is a tuft of capillaries enclosed within Bowman's capsule. The filtration barrier between blood and Bowman's space consists of which three layers?
options: Fenestrated endothelium → glomerular basement membrane → podocyte foot
Podocyte cell body → basement membrane → mesangial cell
Continuous endothelium → thick basement membrane → parietal epithelium
questions.explanation: The glomerular filtration barrier has three layers: (1) fenestrated glomerular capillary endothelium (without diaphragms) — provides size selectivity; (2) glomerular basement membrane (GBM) — provides charge and size selectivity; (3) podocyte foot processes with filtration slit diaphragms — provides the final size selectivity. Disruption of any layer (e.g., podocyte effacement in nephrotic syndrome) leads to proteinuria.

questions.question: A normal human somatic cell contains how many chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Normal human somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX in females, XY in males). Gametes (sperm and ova) contain 23 chromosomes (haploid number). The diploid number is restored at fertilization.

questions.question: The outer surface of the liver is covered by Glisson's capsule. What is the composition of this capsule?
questions.explanation: Glisson's capsule is a fibrous connective tissue capsule that encloses the liver parenchyma. Its outermost surface is covered by a thin layer of mesothelial cells derived from the visceral peritoneum. Fibrous septa extend from the capsule into the parenchyma, carrying branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile ducts (the portal triad). This capsule provides structural support to the liver.
options: Reticular fibers without an outer cellular lining
Fibrous connective tissue covered by a mesothelial cell
Nasopharynx equalizing pressure between middle ear and atmosphere
The inner ear labyrinth and cochlea directly
questions.explanation: The Eustachian or auditory tube connects the middle ear tympanic cavity to the nasopharynx, equalizing atmospheric pressure on both sides of the tympanic membrane. Swallowing and yawning open the tube momentarily allowing air exchange. Obstruction from upper respiratory infection or adenoid hypertrophy prevents pressure equalization causing negative middle ear pressure, tympanic membrane retraction, and fluid accumulation known as otitis media with effusion.
questions.question: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear cavity to which structure allowing pressure equalization?

options: Loops of Henle and collecting ducts
questions.explanation: The cortical labyrinth is the region of the renal cortex between the medullary rays. It contains: renal corpuscles (glomeruli with Bowman's capsule), proximal convoluted tubules (PCT), and distal convoluted tubules (DCT). Medullary rays, in contrast, contain the straight segments of tubules (pars recta of PCT and DCT) and the cortical collecting ducts running in parallel toward the medulla. This architectural division is essential for interpreting renal biopsy findings.
questions.question: The renal cortex can be divided into the cortical labyrinth and medullary rays. The cortical labyrinth specifically contains:
Bone tissue is described as highly vascularized and metabolically active. Which of the following best reflects this metabolic activity?
options: Bone does not participate in calcium homeostasis
Bone matrix is completely stable and undergoes no remodeling after skeletal maturity
Osteocytes are permanently quiescent after being trapped in lacunae
Bone is a calcium and phosphate reservoir continuously remodeled for blood mineral homeostasis
Bone marrow is metabolically inactive in adult life
questions.explanation: Bone serves as the body's major reservoir of calcium accounting for 99% of body calcium, which is released into or deposited from blood under hormonal control by PTH, calcitonin, and vitamin D. Adult bone undergoes continuous remodeling at approximately 10% of the skeleton per year through coordinated osteoclast resorption followed by osteoblast formation. This metabolic activity is reflected in the rich vascular supply essential for delivering hormones and nutrients to bone cells.

questions.question: Melanocytes originate from which embryonic source?
questions.explanation: Melanocytes are neural crest derivatives that migrate into the embryonic epidermis during the first three months of development. They migrate to the dermo-epidermal junction where they differentiate from melanoblasts. One melanocyte typically associates with 30-40 keratinocytes, forming an epidermal-melanin unit.

The corpus albicans (white body) is the hyalinized scar that remains after the corpus luteum degenerates. It appears as an irregular, eosinophilic mass of collagenous connective tissue on histological sections. It gradually diminishes in size over months. Older ovaries contain multiple corpora albicantia, reflecting the number of previous ovulations and luteal cycles throughout reproductive life.
options: A fluid-filled structure with granulosa cells lining its wall
A cluster of primordial follicles with flattened cells
A dark, hemorrhagic structure following ovulation
A mass of white, hyalinized fibrous tissue
A collection of interstitial cells secreting androgens
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the histological appearance of the corpus albicans?
Which muscle of the tongue is NOT supplied by the hypoglossal nerve?
questions.explanation: The palatoglossus muscle is supplied by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve (CN X), not the hypoglossal nerve. All other tongue muscles (intrinsic muscles, genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus) are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

questions.question: The ureteric bud arises from the mesonephric duct at approximately:
questions.explanation: The ureteric bud (metanephric diverticulum) arises from the mesonephric duct at approximately 5 weeks gestation, near its entrance into the cloaca. The exact position of ureteric bud origin is critical - abnormal positioning can lead to ectopic ureter or duplex systems. After forming, the bud grows dorsally to contact the metanephric mesenchyme, initiating reciprocal induction.

options: Only chronic inflammation involves vascular changes
Acute inflammation always leads to tissue fibrosis
Chronic inflammation lacks any cellular component
Acute: neutrophil-dominated; chronic: lymphocytes, macrophages, fibrosis
questions.question: Acute inflammation differs from chronic inflammation histologically primarily in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Acute inflammation is characterized by vascular changes and neutrophil (PMN) infiltration as the dominant cellular response, typically resolving within days. Chronic inflammation (lasting weeks to months) features a mononuclear cell infiltrate (lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells), tissue destruction, and attempts at healing/fibrosis. The temporal and cellular differences reflect distinct immunological mechanisms and different tissue repair outcomes.

questions.question: In fetal circulation, oxygenated blood from the placenta reaches the fetus via:
questions.explanation: Oxygenated blood from the placenta reaches the fetus through the umbilical vein, which joins the left branch of the portal vein. Most of this blood passes directly to the inferior vena cava through the ductus venosus, bypassing the liver. This ensures well-oxygenated blood reaches vital organs.

questions.question: Brown fat, which is important for heat production, forms during which period?
questions.explanation: Brown fat (brown adipose tissue) forms during 17-20 weeks and is an important site of heat production in the newborn. It is located primarily in the neck, between the scapulae, around the kidneys, and around the adrenal glands. Brown fat helps maintain body temperature after birth.

questions.question: Collecting tubules are derived from:
questions.explanation: Collecting tubules are derived from the ureteric bud through repeated branching (approximately 15 generations). The ureteric bud gives rise to the entire collecting system: ureter, renal pelvis, major and minor calyces, and collecting tubules. The metanephric blastema forms the nephrons (glomeruli and tubules from Bowman's capsule to distal convoluted tubule).

questions.question: The lateral plate mesoderm forms which laryngeal cartilages?
