questions.explanation: The lateral plate mesoderm forms the laryngeal cartilages, specifically the arytenoid and cricoid cartilages and their connective tissues. Other laryngeal cartilages (thyroid, corniculate, cuneiform) are derived from pharyngeal arch mesenchyme, which is of neural crest origin.

The aorticopulmonary (A(ΔP) septum divides the truncus arteriosus into the aorta and pulmonary trunk. Opposing truncal and bulbar ridges grow in a spiral fashion and fuse to form this septum. The spiral course explains the normal spiral relationship between the great vessels.
questions.question: The aorticopulmonary septum divides the truncus arteriosus into:

questions.explanation: Dehydration removes water from fixed tissue using ascending concentrations of alcohol, making tissue compatible with the hydrophobic wax or resin embedding medium. Water and wax are immiscible, so complete dehydration is essential before infiltration. Without this step, sectioning quality is compromised due to incomplete infiltration.
questions.question: During histological tissue preparation, dehydration is performed primarily to achieve which of the following?
options: Add color contrast for microscopic viewing
Dehydrate tissue for wax or resin infiltration
Increase tissue softness for easier cutting

questions.explanation: Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) predisposes to renal scarring (reflux nephropathy) from recurrent urinary tract infections, as bacteria can ascend from bladder to kidneys. Primary VUR results from inadequate length of intramural ureter or lateral positioning of ureteric orifice. High-grade reflux may require surgical reimplantation to prevent progressive renal damage and chronic kidney disease.
questions.question: Vesicoureteral reflux predisposes to:

options: The signal for Wallerian degeneration of the proximal stump
Cellular tubes guiding regenerating axon sprouts toward their target organs
New myelin directly without any axon present
The blood-nerve barrier preventing macrophage entry
Inhibitory proteoglycans that prevent aberrant regeneration
questions.explanation: After PNS injury, Schwann cells and their basal lamina form continuous tubes called bands of Büngner within the neurilemma that guide regenerating axon sprouts from the proximal cut end toward the target organ at approximately 1–3 mm per day. The neurilemma's guidance role and growth factor secretion explain why peripheral nerves can regenerate while CNS axons generally cannot, since CNS oligodendrocytes lack this guiding tube and produce inhibitory molecules.
questions.question: The neurilemma formed by Schwann cells plays a critical role in peripheral nerve regeneration primarily by providing which of the following?

questions.explanation: The tracheoesophageal septum is formed by fusion of two longitudinal tracheoesophageal ridges. This septum separates the respiratory diverticulum (ventrally) from the foregut/esophagus (dorsally). Abnormal formation of this septum, often due to abnormal growth of the ridges, results in tracheoesophageal fistulas with or without esophageal atresia.
questions.question: The tracheoesophageal septum is formed by fusion of:
Which of the following correctly classifies connective tissue into its two main fiber systems?
options: Collagen, reticular, and elastic fiber systems
Only collagen fibers and only elastic fibers
Reticular and smooth muscle fiber systems
Type I and Type II collagen systems only
questions.explanation: The two fiber systems in connective tissue are the collagen system (comprising collagen fibers and reticular fibers, both made of collagen protein) and the elastic system (comprising elastic, elaunin, and oxytalan fibers containing elastin and fibrillin). Collagen provides tensile strength while elastic fibers allow extensibility and recoil. The classification into these two systems reflects both compositional and functional differences.

questions.question: The axon hillock of a neuron is specifically important because it is the site of which of the following?
options: Myelin sheath formation by Schwann cells
Calcium influx triggering exocytosis of vesicles
Axon hillock integrating graded potentials into action potentials
Retrograde axonal transport of trophic factors
questions.explanation: The axon hillock is the specialized region at the junction of the cell body and axon containing the highest density of voltage-gated sodium channels and the lowest threshold for action potential generation. It functions as the integration point that sums excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials and fires an action potential only when depolarization reaches threshold, making it the decision-making point of the neuron.

questions.question: Ankyloglossia is also known as which condition?
questions.explanation: Ankyloglossia is commonly known as tongue tie. It results from an abnormally short lingual frenulum that restricts tongue movement. This can interfere with breastfeeding in infants and speech development in children. Treatment may involve surgical release of the frenulum.

questions.question: Which of the following statements most accurately distinguishes an electron microscope from a light microscope in terms of resolving power?
options: They have identical resolving power but different magnifications
Light microscopes have greater resolving power than electron microscopes
Electron microscopes use visible light of shorter wavelength
Electron microscopes achieve far greater resolving power by using electron beams
Both instruments have a resolving limit of 0.2 micrometers
questions.explanation: Electron microscopes use electron beams with wavelengths far shorter than visible light, enabling resolution at the nanometer scale (0.1–0.2 nm), thousands of times better than light microscopy (0.2 μm). This allows visualization of subcellular organelles and macromolecular complexes. The superior resolution comes at the cost of requiring special specimen preparation and vacuum conditions.

The common bile duct descends through the head of the pancreas and joins the main pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung) to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater). This empties into the second part of the duodenum, controlled by the sphincter of Oddi. Gallstones impacting this common channel can cause both obstructive jaundice and pancreatitis.
questions.question: The common bile duct joins which structure before emptying into the duodenum at the ampulla of Vater?

questions.explanation: The core of each intestinal villus is composed of loose connective tissue derived from the lamina propria. It contains fibroblasts, lymphocytes, plasma cells (secreting IgA), smooth muscle fibers (from the muscularis mucosae), fenestrated capillaries for nutrient uptake, and a central lacteal for lipid absorption. This rich cellular composition underlies the villus's absorptive and immune functions.
questions.question: The innermost layer of the small intestine villi consists of which connective tissue component with immune cells?
The white line (anocutaneous line) is located approximately how many centimeters above the anus?
questions.explanation: The white line (anocutaneous line) is located approximately 2 cm superior to the anus and marks where the anal epithelium changes from columnar to stratified squamous keratinized epithelium. This is distinct from the pectinate (dentate) line, which is more superior and marks the embryological junction between endoderm and ectoderm. Both lines have clinical significance.

Chemotaxis is the directed migration of cells along a concentration gradient of chemoattractant molecules (chemokines, complement fragments C3a and C5a, bacterial peptides). In inflammation, these signals attract neutrophils, monocytes, and other leukocytes specifically to sites of tissue injury or infection. This directional guidance ensures efficient recruitment of the appropriate immune cells to sites where they are needed.
options: Directed cell migration toward inflammation guided by chemical gradients
Non-directed random migration of leukocytes through tissues
Secretion of chemical mediators from mast cells
Phagocytosis of bacteria by neutrophils and macrophages
Vascular dilation in response to increased blood flow
questions.question: Chemotaxis in inflammation specifically refers to which of the following phenomena?

questions.explanation: Histology, also called microanatomy, is the study of the microscopic structure of cells, tissues, and organs. It is dependent on microscopes and molecular methods because cells and tissue components are too small to visualize with the naked eye. Gross anatomy by contrast examines structures visible to the unaided eye.
questions.question: The science of microanatomy, which studies the microscopic organization of cells, tissues, and organs, is most accurately referred to as which of the following?
Zymogenic (chief) cells contain abundant basophilic rough endoplasmic reticulum and produce pepsinogen. The basophilia of these cells reflects which feature?
questions.explanation: Chief (zymogenic) cells are basophilic because they contain an extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER) for the high-volume synthesis and processing of the zymogen pepsinogen. The rER contains RNA, which stains basophilically with hematoxylin. Apical acidophilic zymogen granules are also present. This combination of basal basophilia with apical granules is the hallmark of zymogenic/serous cells throughout the body.
options: Dense mucin granules in the cytoplasm
High content of rough ER for protein

questions.question: Duodenal atresia most commonly results from:
questions.explanation: Duodenal atresia most commonly results from incomplete recanalization of the duodenal lumen after the temporary solid stage (5-8 weeks). During the 2nd month, rapid epithelial proliferation obliterates the lumen, which should be recanalized by apoptosis. Failure of complete recanalization results in atresia or stenosis.

On day 9, the blastocyst is deeply embedded in the endometrium and the defect is plugged with a fibrin clot. Spaces called lacunae appear within the syncytiotrophoblast. These lacunae will later fill with maternal blood to establish uteroplacental circulation.
questions.question: Lacunae appear in the syncytiotrophoblast on which day?

questions.explanation: A reciprocal translocation involves exchange of segments between two non-homologous chromosomes. This is a balanced rearrangement if no genetic material is lost or gained. However, carriers may produce unbalanced gametes, leading to miscarriages or offspring with developmental abnormalities.
questions.question: A reciprocal translocation involves which process?
Processes of digestion include ingestion, mastication, peristalsis, secretion, hormone release, and absorption. Which additional process completes this list?
questions.explanation: The complete processes of GIT digestion include: ingestion, mastication, peristalsis/motility, secretions, hormone release, chemical digestion, absorption, and elimination. Elimination is the final step involving the expulsion of undigested materials as feces. Gluconeogenesis is a hepatic metabolic process, not a digestive process.

questions.question: Patau syndrome results from trisomy of which chromosome?
questions.explanation: Patau syndrome results from trisomy 13 (47,XX,+13 or 47,XY,+13). Features include holoprosencephaly, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, cardiac defects, and severe intellectual disability. Like trisomy 18, most affected infants die within the first year of life.

Temporary occlusion of the laryngeal lumen results from rapid proliferation of the laryngeal epithelium. This is followed by vacuolization and recanalization, creating the laryngeal ventricles bounded by vocal cord folds. Failure of proper recanalization can result in laryngeal atresia or webs, which are rare but serious anomalies.
questions.question: Temporary occlusion of the laryngeal lumen results from:

questions.explanation: Wait — the correct answer: The esophagus is lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, appropriate for a food-conducting passage exposed to mechanical trauma. Keratinization occurs in truly exposed skin surfaces like the skin. Option C is correct. Answer: C (non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium).
questions.question: The esophagus is lined by which type of epithelium that provides protection against mechanical abrasion?
The vasa vasorum are small blood vessels supplying the walls of larger vessels. They are most prominent in which layer of the vessel wall?
questions.explanation: The vasa vasorum (vessels of vessels) are small nutrient arteries and veins found primarily in the tunica adventitia of larger blood vessels. They also penetrate the outer portion of the tunica media. The inner layers of the media and intima receive oxygen and nutrients by diffusion from the blood in the lumen. In aortic disease (syphilis, giant cell arteritis), inflammation of the vasa vasorum leads to medial ischemia and aneurysm.

Microglia are the resident immune and phagocytic cells of the CNS derived from bone marrow monocyte precursors not neuroectoderm. They continuously survey the CNS parenchyma and respond to injury or infection by proliferating, migrating to the site, phagocytosing debris and pathogens, and presenting antigens. They are the CNS equivalent of the peripheral tissue macrophage within the Mononuclear Phagocyte System.
questions.question: Which glial cell type acts as the macrophage of the CNS performing phagocytic functions?

questions.explanation: The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus is located between the circular and longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa. It controls the peristaltic movements of the gut wall essential for propulsion of luminal contents. The Meissner plexus, in contrast, primarily regulates secretion and mucosal blood flow.
questions.question: Which autonomic nerve plexus is solely responsible for coordinating local peristaltic contractions of the muscularis externa?

questions.explanation: The dorsal part of the first pharyngeal cleft forms the external auditory meatus. The epithelial lining of the meatus contributes to formation of the external layer of the tympanic membrane. The ventral part of the first cleft disappears during development.
questions.question: The external auditory meatus develops from which structure?

questions.explanation: Haustra (singular: haustrum) are created because the three teniae coli are shorter than the total length of the colon. Their tonic contraction gathers the colon wall into pouches between them. Haustra disappear in conditions like ulcerative colitis (lead-pipe colon on imaging) due to loss of normal colonic architecture. They facilitate segmental mixing and slow colonic transit.
questions.question: Haustra are saccular pouches visible on the outer surface of the colon. They are produced by which mechanism?
options: Distension of the colon wall by fecal material
Submucosal lymphoid tissue causing outward protrusion
Hypertrophy of the circular muscle layer
Anaerobic glycolysis for ATP production in erythrocytes
The pentose phosphate pathway producing NADPH to regenerate glutathione
The synthesis of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate for oxygen affinity regulation
questions.explanation: Erythrocytes depend entirely on the pentose phosphate pathway for NADPH production since they lack mitochondria. NADPH is essential for regenerating reduced glutathione via glutathione reductase, which protects erythrocyte membranes and hemoglobin from oxidative damage. G6PD deficiency impairs this protection making RBCs vulnerable to oxidative stress from drugs such as primaquine, fava beans, or infection-induced reactive oxygen species, causing hemolysis. G6PD deficiency is the most common enzymatic RBC disorder worldwide.
questions.question: Deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase in erythrocytes leads to hemolytic anemia triggered by oxidative stress from drugs or infections. This is because G6PD is essential for which metabolic pathway in erythrocytes?

questions.explanation: The first major induction phenomenon occurs during the final stages of gastrulation of most animal embryos. This primary embryonic induction involves the mesoderm inducing the overlying ectoderm to develop into the neural tube. This establishes the basic body plan.
questions.question: The first major induction phenomenon occurs during which developmental stage?

questions.explanation: The respiratory diverticulum (lung bud) appears during the 4th week as an outgrowth from the ventral wall of the foregut. This location is controlled by transcription factor TBX4, upregulated by retinoic acid from adjacent mesoderm. The bud induces formation and promotes growth and differentiation of the lungs.
questions.question: The respiratory diverticulum appears during which week?

questions.explanation: The atrioventricular (AV) septum is formed by fusion of the dorsal and ventral AV endocardial cushions. This septum divides the AV canal into right and left AV canals. Failure of proper fusion can result in atrioventricular septal defects or univentricular heart.
questions.question: The atrioventricular septum is formed by fusion of:

questions.explanation: The outer ridge of epithelial cells in the cochlear duct forms rows of hair cells, which are the sensory cells of the auditory system. These hair cells are covered by the tectorial membrane. The inner ridge forms other supporting structures of the organ of Corti.
questions.question: Hair cells of the organ of Corti develop from which embryonic ridge?

questions.explanation: The restriction of Nissl substance or rough ER to the cell body and proximal dendrites while being absent from axons means that all axonal proteins must be synthesized in the cell body and transported to axon terminals via anterograde axonal transport using kinesin motor proteins on microtubule tracks. Fast axonal transport carries organelles and vesicles at up to 400 mm per day while slow transport carries cytoskeletal components at 0.1 to 3 mm per day. Disruption of axonal transport contributes to neurodegenerative diseases.
options: Axons synthesize their own proteins independently of the cell body
Only the nucleus synthesizes proteins not the cytoplasm
Neurons do not require protein synthesis after development
Ribosomes absent from axons; proteins must be transported from the cell body
All neuronal proteins are synthesized in Schwann cells and transferred to neurons
questions.question: Nissl substance is found in neuronal cell bodies and is absent from axons. What does this distribution indicate about protein synthesis in neurons?
The juxtaglomerular apparatus of the kidney consists of juxtaglomerular cells macula densa cells and extraglomerular mesangial cells. The juxtaglomerular cells perform which function?
questions.explanation: Juxtaglomerular cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole at the vascular pole of the glomerulus. They contain renin stored in secretory granules and release it in response to: decreased stretch from low blood pressure sensed by baroreceptors in the afferent arteriole; decreased sodium delivery sensed by macula densa cells; and sympathetic beta-1 adrenergic stimulation. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I initiating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis.
options: Filtering blood directly in place of the glomerulus
Producing erythropoietin to stimulate red blood cell production
Secreting aldosterone in direct response to angiotensin II stimulation
Secretes renin in response to low perfusion, low sodium, and sympathetic activation
Phagocytosing damaged and apoptotic glomerular mesangial cells

questions.question: The cloacal membrane is composed of:
questions.explanation: The cloacal membrane is composed of endoderm (lining the cloaca) and ectoderm (surface covering) without intervening mesoderm. This bilaminar membrane closes the caudal end of the hindgut. When the urorectal septum divides the cloaca, it also divides the cloacal membrane into the urogenital membrane ventrally and anal membrane dorsally. Both membranes normally rupture during the 7th-9th weeks.

options: Prevent acid from entering the stomach
Regulate the emptying of gastric contents
Generate peristaltic waves in the stomach
Produce mucus to neutralize gastric acid
questions.question: The pyloric sphincter is a thickening of the circular smooth muscle layer at the gastroduodenal junction. Its primary function is to:
questions.explanation: The pyloric sphincter regulates the rate of gastric emptying into the duodenum, ensuring that chyme is released in small, manageable quantities for digestion and absorption. It prevents duodenal contents from refluxing back into the stomach. Pyloric stenosis (hypertrophy of this sphincter) in infants causes projectile vomiting and is corrected surgically. The sphincter responds to both neural (vagal) and hormonal (gastrin, secretin, CCK) signals.

questions.question: The superior colliculus is primarily involved in which function?
questions.explanation: The superior colliculus, located in the tectum of the upper midbrain, is primarily involved in visual reflexes and eye movements. It receives visual input and projects to motor centers controlling eye and head movements. It is important for orienting to visual stimuli.

Melanocytes are pigment-producing cells derived from neural crest. They migrate from the neural crest to the developing skin, hair follicles, and eyes. Absence of melanocytes or their pigment production results in albinism. Neural crest cells also give rise to other pigmented cells.
questions.question: Melanocytes in the skin are derived from which source?

questions.explanation: Prune belly syndrome is characterized by abdominal muscle deficiency (wrinkled skin), cryptorchidism, and urinary tract abnormalities (megacystis, hydroureter, hydronephrosis), but NOT renal agenesis. The kidneys are present but often dysplastic. The syndrome occurs almost exclusively in males. The exact cause is unknown but may relate to early urethral obstruction.
questions.question: Prune belly syndrome is characterized by all EXCEPT:
Exstrophy of the bladder is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Exstrophy of the bladder is a ventral body wall defect in which bladder mucosa is exposed externally. This rare anomaly (2/100,000 live births) results from failure of mesoderm migration to the ventral midline. The exposed bladder mucosa is continuous with abdominal skin, and the condition requires surgical correction.

Facilitated diffusion uses integral membrane carrier proteins or channels to move substances down their concentration gradient, requiring no ATP. Simple diffusion moves lipid-soluble molecules directly through the bilayer without carriers. Osmosis is specifically water movement, and active transport requires ATP to move substances against gradients. Facilitated diffusion is intermediate: it needs proteins (like simple diffusion does not) but not energy (unlike active transport).
questions.question: The movement of a molecule across a membrane requiring carrier proteins, driven by a concentration gradient, without ATP expenditure, is BEST classified as which of the following?
The telencephalon develops from which primary brain vesicle?
questions.explanation: The prosencephalon (forebrain) divides into telencephalon and diencephalon. The telencephalon gives rise to the cerebral hemispheres (cortex, white matter, and basal nuclei), while the diencephalon forms the thalamus and hypothalamus. This subdivision occurs during formation of secondary brain vesicles.

questions.question: Macula densa cells are specialized cells of the distal convoluted tubule. Their primary function in the juxtaglomerular apparatus is to:
options: Produce erythropoietin in response to hypoxia
Reabsorb glucose from the glomerular filtrate
questions.explanation: Macula densa cells are tall, densely nucleated cells of the DCT wall that abut the JG apparatus. They act as salt sensors: when NaCl delivery to the DCT decreases (indicating low blood pressure or volume), macula densa cells signal JG cells to increase renin secretion. This activates the RAAS, ultimately raising blood pressure. The macula densa thus functions as a key component of tubuloglomerular feedback.

The third stage of implantation involves reparation of the implantation defect in the endometrium. The defect in the epithelium is filled with a closing plug (operculum) consisting of a blood clot and cellular debris. This seals the implantation site.
questions.question: The implantation defect in the endometrium is filled with which structure?

questions.explanation: By the 5th week of development, the lens vesicle has completely separated from the surface ectoderm and lies free within the rim of the optic cup. This separation allows the lens vesicle to develop independently while maintaining its position. The lens vesicle then undergoes further differentiation to form the definitive lens structure.
questions.question: At what gestational week does the lens vesicle separate from the surface ectoderm?
In females, how many ova result from each primary oocyte?
questions.explanation: Each primary oocyte produces only one ovum. During meiosis I, the primary oocyte produces one secondary oocyte and one first polar body. During meiosis II, the secondary oocyte produces one mature ovum and one second polar body. The polar bodies are nonfunctional and degenerate.

The morula (16-32 cell stage) enters the uterine cavity on day 4. Cleavage takes place partly in the uterine tube (during the first three days) and partly in the uterus (from day 4 to 6). Shortly after entering the uterus, the morula transforms into a blastocyst.
questions.question: The morula enters the uterine cavity on approximately which day?
The arrector pili muscles are derived from:
questions.explanation: Arrector pili muscles differentiate from mesenchyme surrounding the hair follicle and attach to the dermal root sheath and papillary dermis. Their contraction causes depression of skin at their attachment and elevation around hair shafts (goosebumps). These muscles are poorly developed in axillary hairs and absent in eyebrow and eyelash hairs.

The lesser omentum is derived from the ventral mesogastrium, not the dorsal mesogastrium. The dorsal mesogastrium gives rise to the greater omentum, gastrosplenic ligament, and lienorenal ligament. The ventral mesogastrium also forms the visceral peritoneum of the liver and falciform ligament.
questions.question: The dorsal mesogastrium gives rise to all EXCEPT:
The epithelium lining the respiratory tract from nasal cavity to small bronchi is characterized as which type and what is the functional significance of its goblet cells?
options: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells; mucociliary escalator
Simple squamous epithelium optimized for gas exchange
Stratified squamous keratinized epithelium for mechanical protection
Transitional epithelium capable of changing shape
Simple cuboidal epithelium with secretory function only
questions.explanation: Respiratory epithelium from nasal cavity through trachea and bronchi to small bronchioles is pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells. Goblet cells secrete viscous mucus that forms a protective blanket trapping inhaled particles, pathogens, and allergens. Approximately 200 cilia per cell beat at 10 to 15 Hz in coordinated waves propelling the mucus blanket with its trapped particles toward the pharynx for clearance. This mucociliary escalator is the primary mechanical defense of the respiratory tract, impaired in smoking and primary ciliary dyskinesia.

The adrenal medulla is derived from neural crest cells (sympathoadrenal progenitors) that migrate from the neural crest to the developing adrenal gland. Chromaffin cells of the medulla are modified post-ganglionic sympathetic neurons that secrete catecholamines — primarily epinephrine (80%) and norepinephrine (20%) — in response to sympathetic (cholinergic) stimulation. The adrenal cortex is derived from mesodermal cells of the genital ridge. This dual embryological origin explains why cortical and medullary tumors have completely different characteristics.
questions.question: The adrenal gland sits on top of the kidneys. The adrenal medulla is derived from which embryological structure and secretes which main product?

questions.explanation: Carnegie stage 11 corresponds to approximately 24 days of development. At this stage, the embryo shows the mandibular (1st) and hyoid (2nd) pharyngeal arches, is slightly curved with head and tail folds, and has a prominent heart. The rostral neuropore is closing at this stage.
questions.question: Carnegie stage 11 corresponds to approximately how many days of development?

questions.explanation: Adrenal medullary chromaffin cells are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons that upon preganglionic sympathetic stimulation via acetylcholine release catecholamines predominantly epinephrine at 80% and norepinephrine at 20% directly into the bloodstream. This hormonal output mediates the systemic fight-or-flight response including increased heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose through glycogenolysis, and bronchodilation.
questions.question: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla secrete which hormones in response to sympathetic nerve stimulation?
Collagen type IV found in basement membranes has which of the following structural characteristics that distinguish it from fibrillar collagens?
questions.explanation: Type IV collagen forms a non-fibrillar sheet-like or meshwork structure rather than fibrillar bundles. Type IV collagen molecules assemble into polygonal networks through end-to-end and lateral associations, forming the structural scaffolding of all basement membranes. Basement membranes also contain laminin, perlecan, nidogen, and other non-collagenous components. Goodpasture syndrome involves autoantibodies against type IV collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes.
options: Forms thick parallel bundles like type I collagen
Organizes into reticular fibers staining with silver salts
Forms non-fibrillar sheet-like networks rather than fibrillar bundles
Is produced exclusively by chondrocytes in cartilage
Contains no triple helical domains unlike other collagens

questions.explanation: Congenital lung cysts are formed by dilation of terminal or larger bronchi. These cysts may be single or multiple and can cause respiratory compromise if large. They result from abnormal branching morphogenesis or obstruction during development. Large cysts may require surgical resection.
questions.question: Congenital lung cysts are formed by:
Fetal movements are first felt by the mother during which weeks?
questions.explanation: Fetal movements (quickening) are typically felt by the mother during 17-20 weeks. Coordinated limb movements actually begin earlier (13-16 weeks), but they are too weak to be felt. Quickening is an important milestone in prenatal development and pregnancy monitoring.

questions.question: The intrinsic muscles of the larynx are supplied by:
questions.explanation: The intrinsic muscles of the larynx, derived from the 6th pharyngeal arch, are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The cricothyroid muscle (4th arch derivative) is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. Both are branches of the vagus nerve (CN X).

Most of the esophagus is located in the neck and thorax, where it lacks peritoneal covering and is therefore surrounded by adventitia — loose connective tissue that blends with surrounding structures. Only the short intraabdominal segment of the esophagus is covered by serosa (peritoneum). This has surgical significance as it affects how esophageal leaks are managed.
questions.question: The adventitia, rather than serosa, covers the esophagus in which portion?
options: The portion at the gastroesophageal junction

questions.explanation: The laryngeal muscles are derived from the 4th and 6th pharyngeal arches. The cricothyroid muscle (4th arch) is innervated by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. The intrinsic laryngeal muscles (6th arch) are innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Both nerves are branches of the vagus.
questions.question: The laryngeal muscles are derived from which pharyngeal arches?

options: Oropharynx has pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium; nasopharynx has stratified squamous
Both have identical pseudostratified columnar epithelium
Oropharynx has non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Oropharynx has transitional epithelium; nasopharynx has simple columnar
Both have non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
questions.explanation: The nasopharynx is a respiratory passageway lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar (respiratory) epithelium with goblet cells, continuous with the nasal cavity epithelium. The oropharynx and laryngopharynx are food-conducting passages that transition to non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium to withstand mechanical abrasion during swallowing. This epithelial transition at the pharyngeal isthmus is clinically relevant in nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
questions.question: Which structural feature distinguishes the oropharynx histologically from the nasopharynx?

questions.explanation: The action potential begins when membrane depolarization reaches threshold activating voltage-gated sodium channels, causing rapid sodium influx down its electrochemical gradient from high extracellular to low intracellular concentration. This rapid sodium entry reverses the membrane potential from approximately -70 mV to +30 mV. Subsequent potassium efflux through delayed rectifier channels repolarizes the membrane. The all-or-nothing nature ensures signal fidelity over long axonal distances.
questions.question: An action potential in a neuron is characterized as a reversal of the ionic gradient propagated along the neuronal plasma membrane. What triggers the initial depolarization?
options: Permanent irreversible change in the neuron membrane composition
Passive diffusion of glucose across the neuronal membrane
Release of neurotransmitters directly into the bloodstream
Synthesis of new proteins at the axon terminal
Voltage-gated sodium channels open, causing sodium influx and rapid depolarization

questions.question: Weibel-Palade bodies are found exclusively in endothelial cells. These organelles are used as a definitive immunohistochemical marker of endothelial cell origin using antibodies against:
questions.explanation: Von Willebrand factor (vWF, also known as Factor VIII-related antigen) stored in Weibel-Palade bodies is the most specific immunohistochemical marker of endothelial cell origin. It is routinely used in surgical pathology to confirm vascular tumors (hemangiomas, angiosarcomas) and to identify endothelial cells in tissue sections. CD31 (PECAM-1) is another highly sensitive endothelial marker. CD68 marks macrophages; smooth muscle actin marks smooth muscle cells.

questions.question: Congenital hydrocele results from:
questions.explanation: Congenital hydrocele results from patent processus vaginalis allowing peritoneal fluid to accumulate around the testis. Unlike an indirect inguinal hernia (where bowel can enter), a hydrocele contains only fluid. Communicating hydroceles vary in size with position/activity. Most resolve spontaneously by age 1-2 years as the processus vaginalis obliterates. Persistence beyond this age may require surgical repair.

The nuclear envelope consists of inner and outer lipid membranes separated by the perinuclear space (continuous with ER lumen). Nuclear pore complexes (~120 nm diameter) perforate both membranes and mediate selective bidirectional traffic: mRNAs and ribosome subunits exit to cytoplasm while transcription factors, histones, and polymerases enter. The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with rough ER.
questions.question: Which of the following describes the structure and function of the nuclear envelope?
options: A single lipid membrane with no pores that completely isolates nuclear contents
A double membrane perforated by nuclear pores regulating nucleocytoplasmic exchange
A rigid structure composed entirely of intermediate filaments
A membrane identical in composition to the plasma membrane
A structure that only allows RNA to exit while blocking all proteins from entering

questions.explanation: The mesonephros begins functioning during the 5th week, with urine draining along the mesonephric duct into the cloaca. The mesonephric kidney continues functioning as an interim kidney until the 10th week. By this time, the permanent metanephric kidneys have developed sufficiently.
questions.question: The mesonephros begins functioning during which week?

options: The M line of the sarcomere
The sarcolemma and its overlying myelin sheath
The Z line and attached titin proteins
One T-tubule flanked by two SR terminal cisternae
questions.explanation: The triad is the functional calcium-release unit of skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling, consisting of one transverse tubule, which is an invagination of the sarcolemma that rapidly propagates the action potential, flanked by two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Voltage sensors called dihydropyridine receptors in the T-tubule mechanically open ryanodine receptors in the SR, releasing calcium into the cytoplasm to trigger contraction.
questions.question: In skeletal muscle, which structure represents the functional unit for calcium release that triggers contraction?

questions.explanation: Patent urachus is characterized by persistent communication between the bladder and umbilicus, resulting in urine drainage from the umbilicus. This represents complete failure of urachus obliteration. The condition is evident at birth and requires surgical repair to prevent infection and establish normal urinary drainage.
questions.question: Patent urachus is characterized by:

questions.explanation: Ureteropelvic (UPJ) obstruction in children most commonly results from intrinsic narrowing or a crossing vessel (accessory lower pole renal artery) compressing the ureter. UPJ obstruction is the most common cause of hydronephrosis detected on prenatal ultrasound. Treatment (pyeloplasty) is indicated for symptoms, progressive hydronephrosis, or declining renal function.
questions.question: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction most commonly results from:
The urachus in adults becomes which structure?
questions.explanation: The urachus, which connects the apex of the bladder to the umbilicus, becomes the median umbilical ligament in adults. Initially, the bladder is continuous with the allantois, which constricts to form the urachus. In some cases, the urachus may persist as a patent canal, leading to urachal abnormalities.

options: To store calcium ions for intracellular signaling
To provide attachment sites for ribosomes during protein synthesis
To protect mitochondrial DNA from damage
To allow entry of oxygen molecules into the mitochondria
To increase the surface area for ATP-generating oxidative phosphorylation
questions.explanation: Cristae are infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane that vastly increase the surface area available for the electron transport chain complexes and ATP synthase. Greater surface area means more ATP can be generated per unit time. Cells with extremely high energy demands (like cardiac myocytes) have mitochondria with particularly densely packed cristae.
questions.question: The inner mitochondrial membrane is extensively folded into structures called cristae. The primary purpose of these cristae is which of the following?

questions.explanation: Folding of the embryo occurs in both the median (longitudinal) and horizontal (transverse) planes. Median plane folding includes the head fold and tail fold, which result from differential growth of the embryonic structures. This folding converts the flat embryonic disc into a cylindrical embryo.
questions.question: Longitudinal folding of the embryo occurs in which plane?

questions.explanation: The muscularis mucosae of the small intestine consists of two thin layers of smooth muscle: an inner circular and an outer longitudinal layer. Isolated smooth muscle cells from the muscularis mucosae extend into the lamina propria and up into the villi, where their contraction pumps lymph through the lacteals, facilitating fat absorption. This is distinct from the much thicker muscularis externa.
questions.question: The muscularis mucosae of the small intestine consists of which arrangement of smooth muscle?
options: Three layers — oblique, circular, and longitudinal
Inner circular and outer longitudinal thin layers

questions.question: Sinusoids are established in the syncytiotrophoblast on which days?
questions.explanation: On days 11 and 12, syncytiotrophoblast lacunae establish connections with maternal stromal capillaries to form sinusoids. This marks the beginning of uteroplacental circulation, allowing maternal blood to flow through the lacunae and provide nutrients and oxygen to the developing embryo.

options: Microbial sentinels mediating hypersensitivity via granule mediator release
Presenting antigens to T lymphocytes directly
Storing neutral fats and releasing them during fasting
Producing antibodies of the IgG class
questions.explanation: Mast cells function as tissue sentinels, strategically positioned near blood vessels and mucosal surfaces to detect antigens and pathogens. When activated (especially through IgE-antigen crosslinking), they rapidly release preformed mediators (histamine, heparin, tryptase) from their granules and synthesize new mediators (prostaglandins, leukotrienes). This response mediates both protective immunity and allergic/hypersensitivity reactions.
questions.question: Which of the following most accurately describes the primary function of mast cells in connective tissue?

questions.explanation: Nissl substance (or Nissl bodies) are the basophilic granular patches in neuronal cytoplasm that represent stacked rough ER cisternae with densely attached ribosomes. They reflect the neuron's high demand for new protein synthesis to maintain its extensive axonal and dendritic processes. Chromatolysis (dissolution of Nissl substance) following axonal injury is a histological sign of neuronal stress.
questions.question: The Nissl substance visible in neuronal cell bodies under light microscopy corresponds to which ultrastructural organelle?

questions.explanation: Horseshoe kidney, present in 0.2% of the population, usually results from fusion of the inferior poles of the kidneys. The fused kidney typically lies in the hypogastric region because normal ascent is prevented by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery. Most cases are asymptomatic as the collecting system develops normally.
questions.question: A horseshoe kidney results from fusion of the kidneys at which pole?

questions.explanation: At ovulation, the secondary oocyte is arrested at metaphase II of meiosis. The first meiotic division is completed just before ovulation, expelling the first polar body. Meiosis II is only completed if fertilization occurs, when the sperm's penetration provides the activating signal. The second polar body is then expelled. If not fertilized, the secondary oocyte degenerates without completing meiosis. This arrest mechanism prevents parthenogenetic activation.
questions.question: The secondary oocyte is released at ovulation and arrested at which stage of meiosis?

questions.explanation: In Hirschsprung's disease, absence of ganglion cells (aganglionosis) in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses of the affected bowel segment means it cannot relax — it remains in a state of tonic contraction, creating a functional obstruction. The proximal bowel dilates massively (megacolon) due to retained feces and gas. Diagnosis requires rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells. Treatment is surgical resection of the aganglionic segment.
options: Functional obstruction with failure of relaxation
questions.question: Hirschsprung's disease results from absence of the myenteric and submucosal plexuses in a segment of colon. This leads to which functional consequence?

options: Spiral ganglion neurons secreting potassium into the scala media
Basilar membrane vibration generating piezoelectric potentials
Stria vascularis maintaining high-K+ endolymph and the positive endocochlear potential
Outer hair cells through their electromotile activity
The round window membrane oscillating against the tectorial membrane
questions.explanation: The stria vascularis is a specialized epithelium on the lateral wall of the cochlear duct containing marginal cells, intermediate cells, and basal cells with extensive ion transport machinery including Na-K-ATPases and KCNJ10 potassium channels. It maintains the endolymph composition of high potassium and low sodium and generates the endocochlear potential of approximately +80 mV. This large potential difference drives potassium through mechanosensitive channels in hair cell stereocilia amplifying the transduction current.
questions.question: The endocochlear potential of approximately +80 mV in the scala media endolymph is generated by which structure and serves which function?
The metanephric blastema is derived from:
questions.explanation: The metanephric blastema (metanephric mesenchyme) is derived from intermediate mesoderm in the sacral region. This mesenchyme condenses around the ureteric bud and, through reciprocal induction, differentiates to form the nephrons (excretory units) of the permanent kidney. Without proper interaction between ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme, the kidney fails to develop.

Islets of Langerhans are clusters of endocrine cells scattered throughout the pancreatic parenchyma. They contain alpha cells (glucagon), beta cells (insulin — most numerous, centrally located), delta cells (somatostatin), and PP cells (pancreatic polypeptide). These hormones are secreted directly into the rich capillary networks within islets. The islets constitute only about 2% of pancreatic mass but have profound metabolic importance.
questions.question: Islets of Langerhans constitute which functional component of the pancreas?
options: Exocrine pancreas secreting digestive enzymes into the duodenum
Connective tissue stroma of the pancreas

questions.question: Renal columns (of Bertin) are composed of:
questions.explanation: Renal columns (of Bertin) are composed of cortical tissue that extends between the pyramids down to the renal sinus. They contain cortical nephrons and interlobular vessels. Prominent columns are normal variants but can be mistaken for masses on imaging. The columns represent the cortical tissue separating adjacent renal pyramids.

Unlike spermatogenesis which is continuous, oogenesis is cyclic and limited only to the period of sexual maturity (from puberty to menopause). Only about 400 ova are ovulated during a woman's reproductive life. No new oogonia are formed after birth.
questions.question: In females, oogenesis is characterized as which type of process?
Amniocentesis for genetic testing is typically performed after which week?
questions.explanation: Amniocentesis is typically performed after 14 weeks when there is about 200 ml of amniotic fluid, and 20-30 ml can be safely withdrawn. The procedure is performed under ultrasound guidance. The risk of inducing an abortion is approximately 0.5%.

Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is the most compatible with survival to term and beyond among autosomal trisomies. Trisomies 13 and 18 are compatible with survival to term but usually result in death within the first year. Most other autosomal trisomies are lethal in utero.
questions.question: Which autosomal trisomy is most compatible with survival to term?
Renal agenesis on ultrasound may show which associated finding?
questions.explanation: Bilateral renal agenesis shows oligohydramnios (decreased amniotic fluid) on ultrasound because the fetus cannot produce urine. Unilateral renal agenesis typically shows normal amniotic fluid because the contralateral kidney produces adequate urine. Other ultrasound findings in bilateral renal agenesis include non-visualization of kidneys and bladder. Oligohydramnios impairs ultrasound visualization and causes Potter sequence.

The tensor tympani muscle is derived from the first pharyngeal arch and is innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3). It attaches to the malleus and dampens sound. The tensor veli palatini (also first arch) is also innervated by CN V3.
questions.question: The tensor tympani muscle is innervated by which division of the trigeminal nerve?

options: Phagocytosing protein that leaks through the glomerular basement membrane
Secreting components of the glomerular basement membrane
Podocyte filtration slits with slit diaphragms as the final filtration barrier
Actively pumping water across the glomerular filtration barrier
Producing renin for blood pressure regulation
questions.question: The podocytes or visceral epithelial cells of the Bowman's capsule in the kidney have specialized foot processes. What is the functional significance of these foot processes?
questions.explanation: Podocytes extend major processes that branch into smaller foot processes or pedicels that interdigitate with those of adjacent podocytes. Between adjacent foot processes are filtration slits of 25 to 60 nm bridged by the slit diaphragm composed primarily of nephrin protein. The slit diaphragm is the final and most selective barrier to protein filtration. Nephrin mutations cause congenital nephrotic syndrome. In minimal change disease and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, foot process effacement is the pathological hallmark causing nephrotic syndrome.

questions.question: The thyroid gland stores thyroid hormones extracellularly in which unique structure?
options: Thyroid follicles filled with colloid containing iodinated thyroglobulin
Dense-core secretory granules within follicular cells
Thymic Hassall's corpuscles in the medulla
Intracellular lipid droplets in follicular cells
questions.explanation: The thyroid gland is unique among endocrine glands in storing its hormones extracellularly within thyroid follicles, spherical structures lined by follicular cells and filled with colloid which is iodinated thyroglobulin. When stimulated by TSH, follicular cells endocytose the colloid, cleave thyroid hormones from thyroglobulin, and secrete T3 and T4 into the bloodstream. This extracellular storage allows a 2 to 3 month hormone reserve.

questions.question: The parietal cell cytoplasm appears intensely eosinophilic in H&E staining. The organelle responsible for this staining property is:
questions.explanation: Parietal cells are intensely eosinophilic because they contain an exceptionally high density of mitochondria required for the energy-intensive process of HCl secretion via proton pumps. This is a distinctive feature that aids histological identification. Chief cells, by contrast, are basophilic due to abundant rough ER for protein synthesis.

options: Elastic tissue providing compliance during cardiac filling
Serous tissue secreting lubricating pericardial fluid
Dense irregular fibrous connective tissue anchoring the heart
questions.explanation: The fibrous pericardium is a tough, inextensible sac of dense irregular fibrous (collagenous) connective tissue that encloses the heart. It is anchored to the central tendon of the diaphragm, the sternum, and the great vessels. Its primary functions are: anchoring the heart in the mediastinum, preventing cardiac overdistension (cardiac tamponade physiology), and providing a barrier against infection. The serous pericardium (inner layer) secretes pericardial fluid for lubrication.
questions.question: The fibrous pericardium is the outermost covering of the heart. It is composed of which tissue and serves which primary function?
A 45-year-old develops Barrett's esophagus. Histologically, this condition is characterized by replacement of normal esophageal epithelium with:
questions.explanation: Barrett's esophagus is a metaplastic condition where the normal non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium of the esophagus is replaced by intestinal-type simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells (specialized intestinal metaplasia). This occurs due to chronic gastroesophageal acid reflux and carries a risk of progression to esophageal adenocarcinoma.
options: Intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells

questions.explanation: Permissive induction occurs when the responding cell is already committed to a certain fate and requires the inducing signals to proceed in the developmental pathway. An example is pancreas development, which depends on associated mesoderm to permit the endoderm to develop into pancreatic tissue.
questions.question: Permissive induction occurs when the responding cell is already committed to which state?
Insulin production by the pancreas begins around:
questions.explanation: Insulin production begins around the 10th week of pancreatic development, while glucagon production begins around the 15th week. The endocrine cells develop from pancreatic epithelium and aggregate to form islets of Langerhans. These islets are surrounded by exocrine pancreatic tissue.

questions.question: The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle is formed by which structures?
questions.explanation: The roof plate of the myelencephalon consists of a single layer of ependymal cells covered by vascular mesenchyme (pia mater), known together as the tela choroidea. Proliferation of this vascular mesenchyme produces saclike invaginations (choroid plexus) that project into the ventricular cavity and produce cerebrospinal fluid.

The cloacal membrane disappears during the 7th week, after the urorectal septum has divided it into anal and urogenital membranes. This breakdown exposes a ventral urogenital opening and a dorsal anal opening. The tip of the urorectal septum forms the perineal body.
questions.question: The cloacal membrane disappears during which week?

questions.explanation: Oligohydramnios (decreased amniotic fluid) is commonly associated with bilateral renal agenesis or severe renal dysfunction because the fetus cannot produce urine. Oligohydramnios causes Potter sequence: pulmonary hypoplasia, limb deformities, and characteristic facial features. The condition is incompatible with life due to pulmonary hypoplasia and renal failure.
questions.question: Oligohydramnios is commonly associated with:
Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) causes progressive replacement of renal parenchyma by cysts. The autosomal dominant form (ADPKD) involves mutations in which genes?
questions.explanation: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is caused by mutations in PKD1 (encoding polycystin-1, chromosome 16 — 85% of cases) or PKD2 (encoding polycystin-2, chromosome 4 — 15% of cases). Polycystins are membrane proteins involved in mechanosensation, cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions, and fluid flow sensing. Their dysfunction causes collecting duct cells to proliferate and form cysts. ADPKD is the most common hereditary kidney disease, causing end-stage renal disease in 50% of patients by age 60.

questions.question: The cricothyroid membrane connects the cricoid and thyroid cartilages of the larynx. In emergency airway obstruction, which procedure uses this membrane?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid membrane is the preferred emergency access point for securing the airway when conventional intubation fails (can't intubate, can't oxygenate — CICO scenario). It is accessible, avascular in its midline, and located below the vocal cords. Needle cricothyroidotomy provides temporary oxygenation, while surgical cricothyrotomy creates a definitive emergency airway. Knowledge of the cricothyroid membrane and its histological composition (fibrous/elastic tissue) is essential for airway management.

During the 6th week, pleuroperitoneal membranes extend ventromedially and fuse with the dorsal mesentery of the esophagus and septum transversum. This results in closure of the pericardioperitoneal openings, with the right opening closing slightly earlier than the left. These membranes are invaded by myoblasts during their development.
questions.question: During which week do the pleuroperitoneal membranes extend ventromedially to fuse with other structures?
The Mononuclear Phagocyte System (MPS) includes all of the following EXCEPT which of the following?
questions.explanation: The MPS includes all tissue macrophages regardless of location: Kupffer cells (liver), alveolar macrophages (lung), osteoclasts (bone), microglia (CNS), Langerhans cells (skin), and dendritic cells (lymph nodes). Mast cells, however, are NOT part of the MPS — they originate from a separate progenitor cell distinct from monocytes and are not phagocytic macrophages. This distinction is frequently tested.

A thyroglossal cyst results from persistence of a portion of the thyroglossal duct. The duct normally becomes solid and disappears, but if portions persist, they can form cysts anywhere along the path of thyroid descent from the foramen cecum to the final position in the neck.
questions.question: A thyroglossal cyst results from persistence of which embryonic structure?
The tympanic cavity develops from which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation: The distal expanded part of the first pharyngeal pouch forms the tympanic cavity, which gradually envelopes the bony ossicles. The proximal part of this pouch forms the auditory (Eustachian) tube. The first pharyngeal pouch is also called the tubotympanic recess.

questions.question: Which connective tissue element specifically transmits the force of skeletal muscle contraction to the skeleton?
questions.explanation: Tendons are the functional link between muscle and bone that transmit contractile force to the skeleton, producing movement. They form by convergence of the three muscle connective tissue layers at the muscle's ends, consisting predominantly of parallel type I collagen bundles of dense regular connective tissue with sparse tenocytes aligned between the fiber bundles. Tendons are among the strongest biological tissues per unit cross-sectional area.
options: Convergence of epimysium, perimysium, and endomysium
Endomysium surrounding individual muscle fibers directly

questions.explanation: Colonic diverticula (false diverticula) form at natural weak points in the muscularis where the vasa recta (arterial branches supplying the mucosa) penetrate the circular muscle layer. The increased intraluminal pressure from a low-fiber diet forces the mucosa and submucosa to herniate through these weak points. Diverticulosis is most common in the sigmoid colon where intraluminal pressures are highest due to the narrow lumen.
options: Anywhere along the entire colon equally
At the points where vasa recta (blood vessels)
Only in the sigmoid colon, not other regions
questions.question: Colonic diverticula are herniations of mucosa and submucosa through the muscularis externa. They form preferentially at which anatomical site?

questions.explanation: A secondary follicle with a germinal center forms in lymph nodes when antigen-activated B cells undergo clonal expansion within the center, forming the germinal center with large proliferating centroblasts and smaller centrocytes. This is surrounded by a mantle zone of small naive B cells forming a dark rim. Secondary follicles indicate active humoral immune responses with ongoing somatic hypermutation and affinity maturation. Primary follicles are smaller and uniformly cellular without germinal centers.
questions.question: A histology student examines a lymph node section and identifies a region with large dividing B cells surrounded by a mantle zone of small B cells. This structure is specifically called which of the following?
options: Primary follicle without germinal center or immune activation
Thymic cortex undergoing T-cell positive selection
Secondary follicle with germinal center indicating active immune response

questions.question: The serosa of the GIT is derived from which embryological structure?
questions.explanation: The serosa is derived from splanchnic mesoderm and is equivalent to the visceral peritoneum. It consists of a mesothelial cell layer over a thin layer of connective tissue. In retroperitoneal organs, this covering is replaced by the adventitia — a connective tissue layer without mesothelium.

questions.question: The tonsils of Waldeyer's ring encircle the entrances to the respiratory and digestive tracts. The palatine tonsils are covered by which epithelium?
options: Stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium in the lateral oropharynx
Pseudostratified ciliated epithelium with goblet cells
Simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells
Transitional urothelial epithelium of the bladder
questions.explanation: Palatine tonsils are located in the lateral walls of the oropharynx and are covered by stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium continuous with the oral cavity lining. Their deep crypts lined by this epithelium increase surface area for antigen sampling. Pharyngeal tonsils or adenoids are covered by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium reflecting their nasopharyngeal location. This epithelial difference is histologically diagnostic between the two tonsil types.

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia commonly occurs through a posterolateral defect in the diaphragm, most frequently on the left side. This defect results from incomplete fusion of the pleuroperitoneal membranes with other diaphragmatic components. The herniation causes the left lung to show hypoplasia due to compression by abdominal viscera.
questions.question: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia most commonly occurs through which defect?
The small intestine has specialized mucus produced by goblet cells. Which mucin glycoprotein predominates in the small intestinal goblet cells?
questions.explanation: MUC2 is the predominant mucin glycoprotein secreted by goblet cells throughout the intestine (both small and large intestine). It forms the structural backbone of the intestinal mucus gel layer. MUC5AC is the primary gastric surface mucous cell mucin; MUC6 is produced by gastric mucous neck cells and Brunner's glands. Deficiency of MUC2 (in MUC2 knockout mice) leads to spontaneous colitis, demonstrating its essential protective role.

questions.question: The definitive adult kidney originates from:
questions.explanation: The definitive adult kidney originates from the metanephros, which begins developing in the 5th week and starts functioning around the 12th week. The pronephros and mesonephros are transient embryonic kidneys that regress. The metanephros arises from reciprocal induction between the ureteric bud and metanephric blastema.

options: Clock-face or cartwheel pattern of heterochromatin
Multiple prominent nucleoli in a clear nucleus
Lobulated multilobed nucleus with fine chromatin
Pyknotic condensed nucleus against cell membrane
questions.explanation: Plasma cell nuclei display a distinctive 'clock-face' or 'cartwheel' pattern in which heterochromatin is arranged in clumps around the periphery of the nucleus, alternating with pale euchromatin regions. This pattern results from the heavy ribosome production needed for antibody synthesis. Plasma cells also have eccentrically placed nuclei and basophilic cytoplasm due to abundant rough ER.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the characteristic appearance of plasma cell nuclei in histological sections, making them easily identifiable?
Renal dysplasia refers to:
questions.explanation: Renal dysplasia refers to abnormal differentiation of kidney tissue during development, resulting in disorganized tissue with cartilage, primitive ducts, and undifferentiated mesenchyme. It may be unilateral or bilateral, focal or diffuse. Bilateral severe dysplasia is incompatible with life. Dysplasia often coexists with other urinary tract anomalies like ureteral obstruction.

options: Erythroblasts in the red bone marrow
Polyploid megakaryocytes shedding cytoplasmic fragments as platelets
questions.explanation: Platelets are anucleate cell fragments 1.5 to 3 micrometers in diameter released from the cytoplasm of megakaryocytes, which are polyploid bone marrow cells up to 128N that form an extensive demarcation membrane system defining platelet territories. Each megakaryocyte generates 2,000 to 3,000 platelets. Platelets circulate for 8 to 12 days and play essential roles in primary hemostasis forming a platelet plug at injury sites.
questions.question: Platelets are not cells but cell fragments derived from which parent cell?
In the female reproductive system, the corpus hemorrhagicum is formed immediately after ovulation as:
options: The mature Graafian follicle before ovulation
A blood clot that fills the ruptured follicle cavity
The first stage of follicular atresia
The fully formed corpus luteum with maximum progesterone output
questions.explanation: When a Graafian follicle ruptures at ovulation, blood fills the ruptured cavity forming the corpus hemorrhagicum (blood clot). This structure is then invaded by luteinizing granulosa and theca cells to form the corpus luteum. The blood clot is gradually resorbed as the corpus luteum develops its characteristic yellow appearance due to accumulating lutein (lipid-rich) cells under the influence of LH.

questions.question: The pronephric duct gives rise to:
questions.explanation: The pronephric duct persists after pronephric degeneration and becomes the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct. This duct is initially used by the mesonephros for urine drainage and later gives rise to the ureteric bud (which forms the collecting system of the kidney). In males, the mesonephric duct persists as the ductus deferens and related structures.

questions.question: Cardiac muscle cells differ from skeletal muscle cells in several ways. Which feature is UNIQUE to cardiac muscle?
options: Presence of actin and myosin filaments
Striated pattern due to sarcomere arrangement
Dependence on oxygen for sustained function
questions.explanation: Intercalated discs are specialized junctional complexes unique to cardiac muscle. They contain fascia adherens (anchoring myofibrils), desmosomes (mechanical coupling), and gap junctions (electrical coupling via connexins). Gap junctions allow rapid propagation of action potentials, making the heart function as an electrical syncytium. Skeletal muscle lacks intercalated discs; its cells are multinucleate with peripheral nuclei, unlike the central single nucleus of cardiomyocytes.

The external auditory meatus develops from the dorsal portion of the first pharyngeal cleft, forming the meatal plug. Initially, the epithelium proliferates and fills the meatus temporarily. Later recanalization occurs to establish the patent external auditory canal.
questions.question: The external auditory meatus develops from which pharyngeal structure?

questions.explanation: Placenta previa occurs when the placenta is implanted in the lower uterine segment and covers or is near the internal cervical os. This can cause painless vaginal bleeding in the third trimester and may necessitate cesarean delivery. Complete previa totally covers the os; partial previa partially covers it.
questions.question: Placenta previa refers to which abnormal condition?
The stylopharyngeus muscle is derived from which pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation: The stylopharyngeus muscle is the only muscle derived from the third pharyngeal arch. The skeletal elements of this arch include the greater horn of the hyoid bone and the inferior part of the body of the hyoid bone. The nerve of the third arch is the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

Distinct basal and alar plates, representing motor and sensory areas respectively, are found on each side of the midline in the rhombencephalon and mesencephalon, separated by the sulcus limitans. The basal plate is ventral (motor), and the alar plate is dorsal (sensory).
questions.question: The sulcus limitans in the brainstem separates which two functional areas?
The space of Disse is the perisinusoidal space that lies between:
options: The central vein and portal tract
questions.explanation: The perisinusoidal space of Disse separates the surface of hepatocytes from the endothelium of hepatic sinusoids. Hepatocyte microvilli project into this space, maximizing exchange of substances between blood and hepatocytes. Stellate cells (Ito cells) also reside in the space of Disse and store vitamin A. In hepatic fibrosis, stellate cells activate and deposit collagen, obliterating the space of Disse.

Brush cells (tuft cells) are solitary chemosensory cells found in the respiratory epithelium, including the trachea and bronchi. They have a characteristic tuft of blunt microvilli on their apical surface and express taste receptor proteins (T2R bitter taste receptors). When activated by bitter compounds (bacterial metabolites, irritants), they trigger rapid cholinergic reflexes causing bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion as a defense mechanism.
questions.question: The tracheal epithelium contains Basal cells, goblet cells, and ciliated cells. Which additional specialized cell type is found in the tracheal epithelium that monitors airway chemicals?

questions.explanation: Hyaline cartilage appears translucent and glassy in H&E because type II collagen fibrils are extremely fine with diameters of 10 to 20 nanometers, below the resolution limit of light microscopy. Additionally the collagen has a similar refractive index to the surrounding proteoglycan-rich ground substance preventing optical contrast. This contrasts with fibrocartilage where thick type I collagen bundles are visible and elastic cartilage where elastic fibers are visualized with special stains.
questions.question: Hyaline cartilage appears glassy and homogeneous in routine H&E sections because of which property of its matrix?
options: Absence of all collagen fibers in the matrix
Presence of extensive elastic fiber networks throughout the matrix
Type II collagen fibres are too thin to resolve by light microscopy
Calcification of the entire matrix creating opacity
Lipid infiltration of the matrix creating a homogeneous appearance

questions.question: Hypospadias results from:
questions.explanation: Hypospadias results from incomplete fusion of the urethral folds on the ventral surface of the penis, leaving the urethral opening on the underside rather than at the tip. Severity varies from glandular (near tip) to penoscrotal. It is one of the most common congenital anomalies in males. Associated chordee (ventral curvature) often requires surgical correction.

The stratified placodal base of the invaginating olfactory pits forms the olfactory epithelium containing neurosensory cells. The lateral walls around the pits become the surface ectodermal covering of nasal cavities. Placodal cells differentiate into neurosensory cells that give rise to olfactory nerve fibers.
questions.question: The olfactory epithelium is derived from which embryonic structure?

questions.explanation: Esophageal atresia is most commonly associated with tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF). The most frequent combination is proximal esophageal atresia with distal TEF. These defects result from abnormal development of the tracheoesophageal septum that separates the respiratory diverticulum from the foregut. Polyhydramnios often accompanies these defects.
questions.question: Esophageal atresia is often associated with:
Ground substance in connective tissue, which contains proteoglycans and glycoproteins, is NOT preserved in routine histological preparations for which of the following reasons?
options: It is destroyed by formalin fixation
It is dissolved by H&E staining
It is extracted during paraffin embedding processing
It stains identically to collagen and cannot be distinguished
An aqueous gel lost during histological dehydration processing steps
questions.explanation: Ground substance is a highly hydrated gel composed of proteoglycans (hyaluronan, chondroitin sulfate), adhesive glycoproteins, and interstitial fluid. During histological processing, the dehydration steps (alcohols) and clearing agents remove the water, dissolving and extracting most of the ground substance. This is why conventional H&E sections appear to show more space than exists in living tissue — the space was occupied by ground substance.

The endocardium is lined on its luminal surface by endothelium — a single layer of simple squamous cells continuous with the endothelium of blood vessels. Beneath the endothelium are a subendothelial layer of connective tissue and a deeper layer of smooth muscle and connective tissue. In the atria, the endocardium also contains ANP-secreting granules in the myocardium below it.
questions.question: The endocardium of the heart is lined by which cell type on its luminal surface?

questions.explanation: Nasal placodes appear around day 30 as thickenings on the right and left of the anteroinferior portion of the frontal prominence. They are located above the stomodeum and below the forebrain. These placodes appear after optic and otic placodes and after the neural tube has completely closed.
questions.question: The nasal placodes appear on approximately which day of development?

questions.explanation: Connective tissue derives its name from its fundamental function of connecting or binding cells and tissues together throughout the body. It maintains the form of organs and serves as a structural framework for other tissue types. Unlike epithelium, muscle, and nerve (which consist mainly of cells), connective tissue's dominant component is the extracellular matrix.
options: It forms the outer covering of all organs
It generates electrical impulses through gap junctions
It absorbs and secretes fluids in body cavities
It provides contractile force for body movement
It connects and binds cells and tissues together
questions.question: Connective tissue derives its name from which of the following primary functional characteristics?

questions.explanation: The wall of the fused neural tube is composed of neuroepithelial cells arranged in a pseudostratified epithelium. These neuroepithelial cells give rise to neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependymal cells. Microglia are derived from mesoderm, and Schwann cells from neural crest.
questions.question: The wall of the neural tube is initially composed of which type of cells?

questions.explanation: Macrophages of the spleen (red pulp), liver (Kupffer cells), and bone marrow phagocytose aged or damaged erythrocytes, break down hemoglobin, and recycle iron (releasing it for new hemoglobin synthesis) and heme (converted to bilirubin). This erythrophagocytosis and iron recycling is a critical metabolic function. Macrophages also participate in extrahepatic bile production through this heme degradation pathway.
options: Destroying aged erythrocytes and recycling iron from hemoglobin
Synthesizing transferrin for iron transport in blood
Storing iron only in bone marrow without degrading erythrocytes
Producing erythropoietin to stimulate red blood cell production
Converting bilirubin to iron in the gallbladder
questions.question: In the body, macrophages participate in iron metabolism by performing which of the following specific functions?
The definitive kidney begins functioning at approximately:
questions.explanation: The definitive metanephric kidney begins functioning at approximately 12 weeks gestation when glomerular filtration commences. Before this, the mesonephros serves as the interim kidney. Although the metanephric kidney is functional by 12 weeks, it doesn't perform true excretory function during fetal life - the placenta handles waste removal. The fetal kidneys primarily regulate amniotic fluid volume.

questions.question: The connective tissue layers of skeletal muscle from outside to inside are correctly named in which sequence?
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle has three nested connective tissue sheaths: epimysium is the outer dense irregular connective tissue covering the entire muscle belly; perimysium surrounds fascicles or bundles of muscle fibers; and endomysium is the thin connective tissue layer between individual muscle fibers. These layers merge at the ends to form tendons and carry nerves and blood vessels into the muscle substance.

questions.question: In the development of ovarian follicles, thecal cells differentiate from which surrounding ovarian structure?
questions.explanation: As a follicle grows beyond the primary stage, stromal cells surrounding the granulosa cell layer differentiate into theca cells. The theca organizes into two layers: theca interna (secretes androgens under LH stimulation, which granulosa cells aromatize to estrogens) and theca externa (fibrous structural support). This two-cell, two-gonadotropin model of sex steroid synthesis is fundamental to understanding ovarian function and PCOS pathophysiology.

questions.question: A student observes glands within the lamina propria on a GIT slide. These glands most likely represent:
questions.explanation: The lamina propria frequently contains small glands which open into the lumen, forming part of the secretory apparatus of the GIT. These are region-specific — gastric glands in the stomach, intestinal crypts in the intestines. Brunner's glands are specific to the duodenal submucosa, not the lamina propria.

The right and left endothelial heart tubes fuse to form a single tube that shows a series of four dilations: bulbus cordis, ventricle (primitive ventricle), atrium (primitive atrium), and sinus venosus. These dilations represent the primordial chambers of the developing heart.
questions.question: The endocardial heart tubes fuse to form a single tube showing how many dilations?

questions.explanation: The right 4th aortic arch gives rise to part of the right subclavian artery, while the left 4th arch forms the arch of the aorta. The 3rd arches form the carotid arteries, and the 6th arches form the pulmonary arteries. The 1st, 2nd, and 5th arches largely disappear.
questions.question: The 4th aortic arch gives rise to which vessels?

questions.explanation: Macrophages are normally long-lived cells that can survive in tissues for several months, unlike neutrophils which survive only hours to days. This longevity allows macrophages to serve as persistent sentinels against infection and to perform sustained phagocytic, antigen-presenting, and immunomodulatory functions. Long-lived macrophages also secrete enzymes like collagenase and cytokines that participate in tissue remodeling.
questions.question: The typical macrophage can survive in tissues for how long, reflecting its role as a long-term sentinel of immunity?

questions.explanation: Imperforate anus occurs in approximately 1 in 5000 newborn infants and is more common in males. It results from abnormal development of the urorectal septum, leading to incomplete separation of the cloaca. The condition may be associated with fistulas to the bladder, urethra, or vagina.
questions.question: Imperforate anus occurs in approximately how many newborns?

questions.explanation: During return of herniated intestines (10th week), the small intestine loops (cranial limb) return first and are situated to the right of the dorsal mesentery.
