Atrial septal defect is not part of this tetralogy. The condition results from unequal division of the conus by the AP septum.
questions.question: Tetralogy of Fallot includes all EXCEPT:
On which day does the cranial neuropore typically close?
questions.explanation: The neural tube formed during neurulation has two openings: the cranial (anterior) neuropore and the caudal (posterior) neuropore. The cranial neuropore closes on day 25, while the caudal neuropore closes on day 27. Failure of these neuropores to close results in neural tube defects.

questions.question: The blood-thymus barrier in the thymic cortex prevents circulating antigens from reaching developing thymocytes. This serves which critical immunological function?
questions.explanation: The blood-thymus barrier consists of capillary endothelium with tight junctions, pericytes, perivascular connective tissue, and enveloping cortical epithelial cells. It prevents blood-borne antigens from reaching developing thymocytes in the cortex, ensuring that T cells are educated exclusively on self-MHC and self-peptide complexes presented by thymic epithelial cells. This controlled environment is essential for generating a self-tolerant T cell repertoire avoiding autoimmunity.
options: Preventing T cells from leaving the thymus prematurely
Blocking antibody production within the thymus
Filtering out aged erythrocytes before they enter lymphoid tissue
Educating T cells on self-MHC to generate a self-tolerant repertoire

questions.question: Which of the following most accurately describes the molecular organization of the four components of the cell membrane?
questions.explanation: The molecular organization of the plasma membrane comprises: (1) the phospholipid bilayer forming the structural backbone; (2) transmembrane (integral) proteins spanning the bilayer; (3) an interior protein network including cytoskeletal connections; and (4) cell surface markers (glycocalyx). Each component contributes distinct structural or functional properties to membrane biology.
options: Phospholipid bilayer, transmembrane proteins, interior protein network
Single phospholipid layer, DNA, RNA, and cytoskeletal proteins
Collagen fibers, glycoproteins, nucleic acids, and lipid droplets
Actin filaments, myosin, troponin, and tropomyosin
Glycolipids only, with no protein components

questions.explanation: Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) has a risk of fetal loss of approximately 1%. Trophoblast cells are obtained by needle through the mother's abdominal and uterine wall under ultrasound guidance. There is also a risk of limb defects if the procedure is performed too early (before 10 weeks).
questions.question: Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) has what risk of fetal loss?

questions.explanation: The submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses together constitute the enteric nervous system of the GIT. This system can regulate motility, secretion, and blood flow independently of the CNS, hence it is sometimes called the 'gut brain'. This autonomy allows GIT function to continue even with disruption of extrinsic innervation.
questions.question: The local enteric nervous system of the GIT, which can function independently of the CNS, is constituted by which two plexuses?
The primitive pharynx gives rise to all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The liver develops from the hepatic diverticulum of the foregut, not from the primitive pharynx. The primitive pharynx gives rise to the thyroid gland, parathyroid glands, thymus gland, tympanic cavity, and contributes to trachea and lung development. These structures develop from pharyngeal pouches and floor of the pharynx.

Lysosomes fuse with phagosomes containing engulfed microorganisms to form phagolysosomes, where lysosomal hydrolases (active at pH ~4.5) digest the bacterial components. This is the primary intracellular killing mechanism of macrophages. The acidic pH of lysosomes both activates the hydrolases and denatures many bacterial proteins, contributing to efficient destruction.
questions.question: Phagocytosis of bacteria by a macrophage involves fusion of the phagosome with lysosomes to form a phagolysosome. This process specifically demonstrates which organelle's function?
The zona glomerulosa, fasciculata, and reticularis are the three zones of the adrenal cortex. Which zone primarily produces mineralocorticoids (aldosterone)?
questions.explanation: The zona glomerulosa is the outermost zone of the adrenal cortex and is the exclusive site of aldosterone synthesis (it uniquely expresses aldosterone synthase/CYP11B2). Aldosterone regulates sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the renal collecting duct. The zona fasciculata (middle, largest zone) produces cortisol (glucocorticoids), and the zona reticularis (innermost) produces weak androgens (DHEA). The adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine).

questions.question: Microglia cells in the nervous system are derived from which source?
questions.explanation: Cells of the nervous system are derived from three different origins. Neuroepithelium gives rise to neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependymal cells. Neural crest cells give rise to Schwann cells. Mesoderm gives rise to microglia, the immune cells of the central nervous system.

As a result of further deepening of the pontine flexure, the rhombic lips compress cephalocaudally and form the cerebellar plate. This plate differentiates into the cerebellum, with an external granular layer, cortex (with Purkinje cells), and deep nuclei.
questions.question: The cerebellar plate forms due to compression of which structures?

questions.explanation: Hepatic sinusoids are derived from the vitelline veins, which form a plexus around the developing hepatic cords. The hepatic cords (derived from endoderm) anastomose around these endothelium-lined spaces to create the characteristic sinusoidal architecture. The sinusoids eventually receive blood from both hepatic artery and portal vein.
questions.question: Hepatic sinusoids are derived from:

questions.explanation: Carnegie stage 22 corresponds to the 8th week when webbed digits of the hand are present. This is the final week of the embryonic period. At this stage, notches are also present between digits of the foot, the tail is still present, and the scalp vascular plexus is visible.
questions.question: Which Carnegie stage corresponds to the appearance of webbed digits of the hand?

questions.explanation: Histamine is the primary early vasoactive mediator of increased vascular permeability in acute inflammation. Released rapidly from mast cell and basophil granules upon activation, histamine causes postcapillary venule endothelial cell contraction, widening intercellular gaps and allowing fluid, proteins, and leukocytes to escape into the tissue. This increase in permeability produces the edema (tumor) and contributes to redness and heat.
questions.question: Increased vascular permeability during inflammation is primarily caused by the action of which vasoactive substance?
options: Histamine from mast cells and basophils
PTH raises blood calcium by stimulating bone resorption; calcitonin suppresses resorption
Calcitonin raises blood calcium; parathyroid hormone lowers it
Both hormones raise blood calcium through osteoclast activation
Parathyroid hormone only acts on kidneys with no effect on bone
Calcitonin stimulates osteoclast activity while parathyroid hormone activates osteoblasts
questions.question: Blood calcium levels are regulated by two hormones with opposing effects on bone resorption. Which of the following correctly describes this hormonal regulation?
questions.explanation: Parathormone (PTH) from parathyroid glands raises blood calcium by stimulating osteoclast-mediated bone resorption (releasing stored calcium), increasing renal calcium reabsorption, and promoting intestinal calcium absorption via vitamin D activation. Calcitonin (from thyroid C cells) opposes PTH by suppressing bone resorption (inhibiting osteoclasts) and increasing osteoid calcification. This PTH-calcitonin axis is the primary calcium homeostasis mechanism.

options: Regulating light entry through pupil diameter changes
Producing vitreous humor for the posterior chamber
Focusing light on the retina through refractive power
Providing oxygen and nutrients to the outer retinal layers including photoreceptors
Converting light energy to neural impulses in the photoreceptor layer
questions.question: The choroid layer of the uveal tract primarily serves which function for the retina?
questions.explanation: The choroid is a highly vascularized layer between the sclera and retinal pigment epithelium that provides the sole blood supply to the outer one-third of the retina including photoreceptors and RPE. The inner two-thirds of the retina receive blood from the central retinal artery. Choroidal blood flow is the highest per gram of tissue in the body reflecting the extremely high metabolic demand of photoreceptors. Age-related macular degeneration involves abnormal choroidal neovascularization.

questions.question: The fundic glands of the stomach body contain a characteristic cell type not found in the pyloric or cardiac regions. This cell type is:
questions.explanation: Parietal (oxyntic) cells are the defining cell type of the fundic and body glands of the stomach. They are large, pyramidal, eosinophilic cells that produce HCl and intrinsic factor. The cardiac and pyloric glands are predominantly mucous glands lacking parietal cells (or with very few in transitional zones). The unique presence of parietal cells in fundic glands is therefore the key histological criterion for identifying this region.

questions.question: The right main bronchus gives rise to how many secondary bronchi?
questions.explanation: The right main bronchus gives rise to three secondary bronchi, corresponding to the three lobes of the right lung. The left main bronchus forms two secondary bronchi for the two lobes of the left lung. These appear as lateral outpocketings during the early 5th week.

options: Goblet cells in the lamina propria
Smooth muscle cells of the muscularis
Stem cells in the base of colonic crypts
questions.question: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) involves APC gene mutations leading to hundreds of colonic polyps. These polyps arise from the abnormal proliferation of which cells?
questions.explanation: Colorectal polyps in FAP arise from the uncontrolled proliferation of crypt stem cells (colonocytes) in the base of colonic crypts. Normally, the APC protein controls Wnt signaling to regulate stem cell proliferation. Bi-allelic APC loss leads to unrestrained crypt cell division and upward migration, forming adenomatous polyps. Without prophylactic colectomy, virtually all FAP patients develop colorectal cancer by age 40.

questions.question: The renal medulla is organized into pyramids separated by renal columns. Renal columns (columns of Bertin) are composed of:
options: Medullary tissue extending toward the cortex
Inward extensions of cortical tissue between
questions.explanation: Renal columns (columns of Bertin) are inward projections of cortical tissue that separate adjacent medullary pyramids. They contain interlobar arteries and veins, as well as cortical nephrons extending into the columns. Prominent renal columns can be mistaken for renal masses on imaging — an important radiological consideration. They represent the normal infolding of cortex between the lobes of the kidney.

options: Hyaline cartilage, elastic cartilage, and vitreous body
questions.explanation: Type II collagen is the principal collagen of cartilage (both hyaline and elastic types) and the vitreous body of the eye. Its fibrils are finer than type I collagen and are embedded in the proteoglycan-rich cartilage matrix. Chondrocytes are the cell type that synthesizes type II collagen. Autoimmune destruction of type II collagen characterizes relapsing polychondritis and contributes to joint cartilage loss in rheumatoid arthritis.
questions.question: Type II collagen is specifically found in which of the following tissue locations?
The centroacinar cells of the pancreas are unique cells found within the lumen of pancreatic acini. Their primary function is:
questions.explanation: Centroacinar cells are the initial cells of the ductal system that extend into the lumen of the acinus. They secrete water and bicarbonate (stimulated by secretin) into the duct lumen, forming the aqueous component of pancreatic juice. This alkaline fluid neutralizes gastric acid in the duodenum. Cystic fibrosis impairs centroacinar cell function, causing thickened pancreatic secretions and ductal obstruction.

questions.question: The kidney has cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons. Juxtamedullary nephrons have longer loops of Henle that extend deeper into the medulla. Their primary functional advantage is:
questions.explanation: Juxtamedullary nephrons (approximately 15% of nephrons) have long loops of Henle that penetrate deep into the medulla. Their long ascending limbs actively transport more NaCl, creating a deeper and steeper medullary osmotic gradient. This allows the formation of highly concentrated urine when ADH is present. The vasa recta, which run alongside these loops, maintain this gradient via countercurrent exchange.

Melanocyte cell bodies are located in the basal layer of the epidermis, not in dermal papillae. Dermal papillae project upward into the epidermis and contain capillaries, sensory nerve endings, and connective tissue. These papillae are especially prominent in thick skin areas like palms and soles.
questions.question: The dermal papillae contain all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Cholesterol molecules intercalated between phospholipid tails regulate membrane fluidity: at high temperatures, cholesterol restricts phospholipid movement reducing fluidity; at low temperatures it prevents tight packing, maintaining fluidity. This temperature-buffering role is essential for membrane function across physiological temperature ranges. Cholesterol constitutes approximately 30–40% of mammalian plasma membrane lipids.
questions.question: Which component of the cell membrane stabilizes the phospholipid bilayer, increases its rigidity, and regulates fluidity?
The gallbladder develops from which part of the hepatic diverticulum?
questions.explanation: The gallbladder develops from the smaller caudal part of the hepatic diverticulum. The larger cranial part forms the liver parenchyma. The stalk of the diverticulum connecting these parts becomes the cystic duct. The bile duct forms from the stalk connecting to the duodenum. These structures undergo temporary occlusion and recanalization.

questions.question: A branchial fistula results from persistence of which structure?
questions.explanation: A branchial fistula results from persistence of a pharyngeal cleft (external) communicating with a pharyngeal pouch (internal), creating an abnormal passage from the pharynx to the external skin surface. Most commonly, this involves the second pharyngeal cleft and second pouch.

questions.question: The sinoatrial (SA) node is the pacemaker of the heart. Histologically, SA node cells differ from working cardiomyocytes in that they are:
questions.explanation: SA node cells (pacemaker cells) are pale-staining, small, ovoid to spindle-shaped cells with few myofibrils, sparse sarcoplasmic reticulum, and no intercalated discs. They spontaneously depolarize due to the 'funny current' (If) — a mixed Na+/K+ current that is unique to pacemaker cells. Working cardiomyocytes are larger, darker, striated, and rely on electrical input rather than generating it. SA node cells are connected to the myocardium by transitional cells.

questions.question: Caudal regression syndrome affects which body systems?
questions.explanation: Caudal regression syndrome (sacral agenesis) affects the lower limbs and caudal structures including lumbosacral spine, lower limbs, urogenital system, and hindgut. Severity ranges from minor sacral hypoplasia to complete absence of sacral and lumbar vertebrae with fused lower limbs (sirenomelia). The syndrome is associated with maternal diabetes and has high mortality.

questions.question: The tunica adventitia of blood vessels is primarily composed of which tissue?
questions.explanation: The tunica adventitia is the outermost layer of blood vessels, composed predominantly of dense irregular connective tissue containing type I collagen fibers, fibroblasts, and elastic fibers. It anchors the vessel to surrounding tissues and prevents overdistension. The adventitia also contains vasa vasorum (supplying the vessel wall), nervi vasorum (autonomic nerves), and lymphatic vessels.

questions.question: The facial nerve (CN VII) is the nerve of which pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) is the nerve of the second pharyngeal arch. It innervates muscles including stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric, auricular muscles, muscles of facial expression, occipitofrontalis, and platysma. Each pharyngeal arch has a specific cranial nerve association.

The trachea is supported by 16–20 C-shaped (horseshoe-shaped) rings of hyaline cartilage. The open (posterior) gap is bridged by the trachealis smooth muscle and fibroelastic membrane. This arrangement maintains an open lumen while allowing esophageal expansion during swallowing. As airways branch into bronchi and bronchioles, cartilage becomes irregular plates, then disappears at the bronchiolar level.
questions.question: The trachea and main bronchi are held open by which structural element?

options: Is lined by stratified squamous epithelium
Has no teniae coli, as the longitudinal muscle is
Contains Brunner's glands in its submucosa
Has three distinct layers of muscularis externa
questions.explanation: The rectum differs from the rest of the large intestine in that the teniae coli spread out into a complete longitudinal muscle layer (no longer forming three bands), and haustra are absent — giving the rectum a smooth, non-sacculated outline. This smooth muscle coat contributes to the rectal reservoir function. The rectum is lined by simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells, transitioning to stratified squamous in the anal canal.
questions.question: The rectum differs from the sigmoid colon histologically in that the rectum:

questions.explanation: The Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) on the apical membrane of thick ascending limb (TAL) cells transports 1 Na+, 1 K+, and 2 Cl- into the cell using the electrochemical gradient created by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase. This is the primary mechanism for NaCl reabsorption in the TAL, generating the medullary osmotic gradient. Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide) inhibit NKCC2, reducing NaCl reabsorption and preventing medullary gradient formation, producing a potent diuretic effect.
questions.question: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is impermeable to water but actively transports NaCl. Which transporter on the apical membrane of thick ascending limb cells accomplishes this?

questions.explanation: The superior 2/3 of the anal canal (endodermal portion) is supplied by the superior rectal artery, a branch of the inferior mesenteric artery. The inferior 1/3 (ectodermal portion) is supplied by the inferior rectal artery from the internal pudendal artery. This reflects the dual embryological origin of the anal canal.
questions.question: The superior 2/3 of the anal canal is supplied by:
Umbilical herniation with intestines occurs during which week?
questions.explanation: Umbilical herniation with intestine occurs during the 7th week of development. This is a normal developmental event. During this week, notches also appear between the digital rays of the hand. The intestines herniate into the umbilical cord due to rapid growth and limited abdominal space.

questions.question: The dermis of the skin is derived from which embryonic source?
questions.explanation: The dermis of the face is derived from neural crest cells, while dermis in the dorsal region of the head comes from paraxial mesoderm, and dermis of the body wall comes from lateral plate mesoderm. The epidermis is derived from surface ectoderm throughout the body.

options: At the ureterovesical junction (UVJ) as it enters the bladder
At the pelvic brim crossing anterior to iliac vessels
questions.question: The ureter descends retroperitoneally and crosses anterior to the common iliac artery. At which anatomical location does the ureter have the narrowest caliber, making it a common site for ureteral stone impaction?
questions.explanation: There are three natural constrictions of the ureter where ureteric stones commonly lodge: (1) ureteropelvic junction (UPJ); (2) as the ureter crosses the common iliac vessels at the pelvic brim; (3) ureterovesical junction (UVJ) — the narrowest point. The UVJ is the most common site for stone impaction because the ureter passes obliquely through the bladder wall (antireflux mechanism), creating the narrowest luminal diameter. Stones >5mm at the UVJ are unlikely to pass spontaneously.

questions.question: The philtrum of the upper lip is formed from which component of the intermaxillary segment?
questions.explanation: The intermaxillary segment has three components: the upper jaw component (carries four incisor teeth), the labial component (forms the philtrum of the upper lip), and the palatal component (forms the triangular primary palate). The segment forms by fusion of the two medial nasal prominences.

questions.question: A liver biopsy shows centrilobular necrosis (necrosis around the central veins). This pattern of injury is most consistent with which condition?
options: Right heart failure causing hepatic congestion
questions.explanation: Centrilobular (Zone 3) necrosis corresponds to hepatocyte death around the central veins — precisely where Zone 3 hepatocytes are located. These cells are most vulnerable to ischemia because they are furthest from the portal blood supply. Right heart failure causes venous congestion (nutmeg liver) with centrilobular necrosis. Acetaminophen toxicity also causes centrilobular necrosis via CYP2E1-mediated toxicity (concentrated in Zone 3).

Medullary sponge kidney is characterized by cystic dilation of collecting ducts in the renal pyramids, giving a sponge-like appearance. It is usually bilateral and often asymptomatic but may cause nephrolithiasis (kidney stones), hematuria, or urinary tract infections. The condition is typically diagnosed in young adults. The cortex and glomeruli are normal. It represents a developmental abnormality of collecting duct formation.
questions.question: Medullary sponge kidney is characterized by:

questions.explanation: The remaining part of the septum primum (after the upper part gradually disappears) becomes the valve of the foramen ovale. This creates a valvular aperture that allows blood to flow from right to left but not from left to right during fetal life.
questions.question: The valve of the foramen ovale is formed by which structure?
The term 'microanatomy' is used interchangeably with histology because both disciplines share which primary characteristic?
questions.explanation: Microanatomy and histology are synonymous terms referring to the study of microscopic structural organization of cells and tissues. Both use light and electron microscopy to examine structures below the resolution of the unaided eye. The prefix 'micro' in microanatomy reflects the scale of observation, precisely matching the etymological meaning of histology ('tissue science').
options: Both study organisms visible to the naked eye
Both use only electron microscopes for observation
Both focus exclusively on pathological changes in tissues
Both examine the microscopic structure of cells and tissues
Both are limited to the study of epithelial tissues
Neurons cannot produce new proteins after development
Neurons cannot receive synaptic signals from more than one cell
Neurons cannot transmit action potentials to adjacent cells
Neurons cannot develop myelin sheaths in the CNS
Destroyed neurons cannot be replaced since they lack the ability to divide
questions.question: Neurons are described as amitotic. The most significant clinical consequence of this property is which of the following?
questions.explanation: The permanent post-mitotic state of neurons means that destroyed neurons are not replaced by new neurons through division. This is why CNS injuries from stroke or trauma and neurodegenerative diseases cause permanent functional deficits proportional to the neurons lost. Limited adult neurogenesis in specific brain regions represents a minor exception. This amitotic nature also explains why brain tumors arise from glial cells as gliomas rather than from neurons.

The pupillary light reflex develops during 30-34 weeks as the nervous system matures. At this stage, the upper and lower limbs have a chubby appearance, the skin is pink and smooth, and infants born at 32 weeks usually survive with proper medical care.
questions.question: The pupillary light reflex develops during which weeks?
Which of the following best explains why histology is described as being dependent on the use of microscopes?
options: Cells and matrix are too small to visualize with the unaided eye
Staining reagents can only be applied under microscopic guidance
Tissue preparation cannot be done without microscopic feedback
Biochemical analysis requires prior microscopic confirmation
The human retina cannot detect color differences in tissues
questions.explanation: Histology depends on microscopes because the fundamental units of tissue — cells and extracellular matrix components — are measured in micrometers, far below the resolution of the unaided human eye (~0.1 mm). Light microscopes extend visualization to ~0.2 μm while electron microscopes reach the nanometer scale. This microscopic dependency is definitional to histology as a discipline.

options: Septum primum fuses with endocardial cushions
questions.question: The ostium primum is closed when:
questions.explanation: The ostium primum is obliterated when the septum primum fuses with the AV endocardial cushions. Before complete closure, perforations appear in the upper portion of septum primum. These perforations coalesce to form the ostium secundum, ensuring continued blood flow from right to left atrium.

Neurulation involves four major stages: transformation of general ectoderm into a thickened neural plate, shaping the plate so it becomes narrower and longer, lateral folding of the neural plate, and fusion of the two most lateral apical surfaces of the neural folds.
questions.question: Neural tube formation involves how many major stages?

questions.explanation: On day 8, the embryoblast differentiates into a hypoblast layer (adjacent to the blastocystic cavity) and an epiblast layer (adjacent to the amniotic cavity). The epiblast will give rise to all three germ layers of the embryo, while the hypoblast contributes to extraembryonic structures.
questions.question: On day 8, the embryoblast differentiates into which two layers?

options: To prevent contamination of the specimen
To allow staining solutions to penetrate faster
They are too thick for transmitted light to pass through
To reduce the size of the specimen on the slide
To improve resolution of the electron microscope
questions.explanation: Light microscopy requires transmitted light to pass through specimens, but intact tissues or organs are too thick to allow adequate light transmission. Thin sections, typically 3–10 micrometers, are mounted on glass slides to achieve the translucency required for microscopic examination. This is the fundamental reason for the sectioning step in histological preparation.
questions.question: Most tissues require slicing into thin sections before microscopic examination primarily because of which of the following reasons?

options: Proliferation of glands (becoming slightly tortuous), mitoses in glands
Straight glands with narrow lumens and compact stroma; thin endometrium
Coiled (spiral) glands with secretory vacuoles, subnuclear glycogen
questions.explanation: During the proliferative phase (days 5–14), rising estrogen levels stimulate endometrial growth: glands multiply and become slightly tortuous, stromal cells proliferate actively (mitoses visible), and the endometrium thickens from ~0.5mm (just after menstruation) to ~5mm. In the early proliferative phase, glands are narrow and straight; they become more tortuous later. This phase is dominated by mitotic activity in preparation for the secretory (luteal) phase.
questions.question: The endometrium in the proliferative phase is stimulated by estrogen from developing follicles. Which histological changes characterize this phase?

options: Mineral storage exclusively without any cellular function
Hematopoiesis — production of erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets
Synthesis of cortical bone matrix as the primary source
Production of cartilage matrix for endochondral ossification
Secretion of parathyroid hormone to regulate blood calcium
questions.question: The bone marrow housed in cancellous bone serves which of the following essential functions?
questions.explanation: Red bone marrow fills the spaces of cancellous bone and is the site of hematopoiesis — the continuous production of all formed elements of blood: erythrocytes, leukocytes, and megakaryocytes which produce platelets. Yellow marrow (fat-filled) predominates in adult long bone shafts but can revert to active red marrow during increased demand such as severe anemia or hemorrhage.

questions.question: The thymus develops from which pharyngeal pouch?
questions.explanation: The thymus develops from the endoderm of the ventral part of the third pharyngeal pouch in the 5th week. It is large at birth, reaches full size at puberty, and shrinks in old age. It has both cranial (neck) and caudal (thorax) parts and is invaded by vascular mesoderm containing lymphoblasts.

questions.question: The lymphatic system begins with lymphatic capillaries in tissues. These ultimately drain into lymphatic ducts that empty into the venous circulation at which anatomical sites?
questions.explanation: All lymphatic drainage ultimately returns to the bloodstream via the thoracic duct (draining left body below the diaphragm, left head/neck/arm) emptying into the left subclavian-jugular angle, and the right lymphatic duct (draining right head/neck/arm, right thorax) emptying into the right subclavian-jugular angle. This return of lymph to the venous circulation maintains plasma volume, returns plasma proteins, and allows immune cells to recirculate.

Potter sequence is characterized by oligohydramnios (not polyhydramnios), which leads to pulmonary hypoplasia, limb deformities, and characteristic facial features (low-set ears, epicanthal folds, flattened nose). The sequence results from bilateral renal agenesis or severe bilateral renal dysplasia. The condition is lethal due to pulmonary hypoplasia preventing adequate breathing after birth.
questions.question: Potter sequence is characterized by all EXCEPT:
The lens develops in response to induction from which structure?
questions.explanation: The lens develops from surface ectoderm in response to induction from the optic vesicle (an outgrowth of the diencephalon). The optic vesicle induces the overlying ectoderm to form the lens placode, which then invaginates to form the lens vesicle.

questions.question: The urinary bladder develops primarily from:
questions.explanation: The urinary bladder develops primarily from the vesical (upper) part of the urogenital sinus, which is endodermal. The trigone has dual origin: endodermal from UGS and mesodermal from incorporated mesonephric ducts. The smooth muscle and connective tissue are derived from surrounding splanchnic mesenchyme. The urachus (from allantois) connects to the bladder apex.

questions.question: Eosinophils are most characteristically elevated in which clinical conditions?
questions.explanation: Eosinophils are classically elevated in IgE-mediated allergic diseases including asthma atopic dermatitis and food allergy, and in parasitic helminth infections. Their bilobed nucleus and prominent orange-red granules containing major basic protein and eosinophil peroxidase allow cytotoxic killing of parasites too large to phagocytose. Eosinophil recruitment is directed by IL-5 from T helper 2 cells and eotaxin from tissue cells.

Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is more common in males than females (approximately 4:1 ratio). It typically presents at 2-8 weeks of age with progressive non-bilious projectile vomiting. A palpable olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant represents the hypertrophied pyloric muscle. The condition likely has a genetic component but exact etiology remains unclear.
questions.question: Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is more common in:

questions.explanation: Most inductive processes during embryonic development involve epithelial-mesenchymal interactions, including development of kidneys, gastrointestinal derivatives, respiratory system, and skin appendages. Skeletal muscles develop primarily from somitic mesoderm through intrinsic differentiation programs rather than epithelial-mesenchymal induction.
questions.question: Which organ system does NOT primarily develop through epithelial-mesenchymal interactions?
Which of the following correctly distinguishes primary from secondary lymphoid organs?
questions.explanation: Primary lymphoid organs are the sites where lymphocytes develop and acquire antigen recognition capability: bone marrow for B cells and thymus for T cells. Secondary lymphoid organs including lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils, Peyer's patches, and MALT are where mature naive lymphocytes encounter antigens and mount adaptive immune responses. This distinction reflects the two-stage model of lymphocyte differentiation: antigen-independent in primary organs and antigen-dependent in secondary organs.
options: Primary organs filter lymph while secondary organs filter blood
Primary organs for lymphocyte development; secondary organs for immune responses
Primary organs are larger than secondary organs
Secondary organs develop before primary organs in embryogenesis
They are functionally identical with only anatomical location differing

questions.explanation: Volkmann's canals (perforating canals) run perpendicular or oblique to the long axis of bone, connecting adjacent Haversian canals to each other and to the periosteum and marrow cavity. They are the primary route by which blood vessels from the marrow cavity reach the Haversian canals of individual osteons. Unlike Haversian canals, Volkmann's canals are NOT surrounded by concentric lamellae.
questions.question: Volkmann's canals in compact bone differ from Haversian canals primarily in which of the following ways?
options: Volkmann's canals contain larger blood vessels and no nerves
Volkmann's canals run parallel to the long axis of the bone
Volkmann's canals run perpendicular to the long axis of bone
Volkmann's canals are absent in mature bone and present only during development
Volkmann's canals are only found in spongy bone trabeculae

questions.question: The liver acinus is described as a 'diamond' shape. Which structures are located at the corners of the SHORT axis of this diamond?
questions.explanation: In the hepatic acinus (Rappaport's acinus), the diamond shape has portal tracts at the corners of the short axis (closer to blood supply, Zone 1) and central veins at the corners of the long axis (farther from blood supply, Zone 3). This arrangement defines the three zones based on proximity to the blood supply from the portal tract, with Zone 1 nearest and Zone 3 farthest.

questions.question: The three cell types found in bone tissue and their respective primary functions are best described by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Bone has three distinct cell types with complementary roles: osteoblasts are active matrix-synthesizing cells that produce osteoid (unmineralized matrix); osteocytes are mature osteoblasts entrapped in lacunae that maintain the matrix and act as mechanosensors; and osteoclasts are large multinucleated cells (monocyte-derived) that resorb bone through acid and lysosomal enzyme secretion. The balance between osteoblast and osteoclast activity determines bone mass.
options: Osteoblasts (synthesize osteoid), osteocytes (maintain matrix), and osteoclasts (resorb bone)
Fibroblasts, macrophages, and adipocytes performing structural roles
Osteoblasts and osteocytes performing identical functions with no resorption cells

questions.explanation: Fingerprints and footprints result from the microscopic ridge structures formed by the papillary layer of the dermis. These ridges create unique patterns that remain constant throughout life unless disrupted. The patterns are genetically determined and established during intrauterine development.
questions.question: Fingerprints and footprints result from the arrangement of:

questions.explanation: The pleuroperitoneal membranes form a large portion of the fetal diaphragm but represent a relatively smaller portion in infants due to differential growth. The body wall contributes the peripheral muscular part, while the septum transversum forms the central tendon. The dorsal mesentery of the esophagus forms the crura.
questions.question: Which component forms the largest portion of the fetal diaphragm but represents a smaller portion in infants?

options: Medial nasal and two maxillary prominences
questions.explanation: The upper lip is formed in the 6th week by fusion of the medial nasal prominence and the two maxillary prominences. The lower lip and jaw are formed by fusion of the two mandibular prominences in the midline. The cheeks and maxilla are formed by fusion of the maxillary prominences.
questions.question: The upper lip is formed by fusion of which structures?
The parietal pleura develops from:
questions.explanation: The parietal pleura develops from somatic mesoderm covering the internal surface of the body wall. The visceral pleura develops from splanchnic mesoderm surrounding the developing lungs. The pleural cavity between these layers is initially part of the intraembryonic coelom, which is partitioned during development.

The choroid fissure, located on the ventral surface of the optic cup, closes during the 7th week of development. Closure of this fissure is essential for proper optic nerve formation and vascularization. Failure of complete closure results in coloboma, a congenital defect affecting various ocular structures.
questions.question: The choroid fissure normally closes during which week of development?

questions.explanation: Mesangial cells are specialized pericyte-like cells within the mesangium (matrix between glomerular capillary loops). Their functions include: structural support and anchoring of glomerular capillaries; phagocytosis and removal of immune complexes, macromolecules, and cellular debris; contraction/relaxation to regulate capillary surface area available for filtration; and secretion of cytokines. In IgA nephropathy, mesangial IgA immune complex deposition causes mesangial cell proliferation and matrix expansion.
questions.question: The mesangium is the supporting tissue of the glomerulus between and within the glomerular capillary loops. Mesangial cells perform which functions?
options: Filtration of blood plasma through slit diaphragms
Structural support of capillary loops, phagocytosis

questions.question: Pores of Kohn are small openings in alveolar septa connecting adjacent alveoli. Their functional significance is:
questions.explanation: Pores of Kohn are natural fenestrations (1–15 μm) in the walls between adjacent alveoli in adult lungs. They allow collateral ventilation — movement of air between alveoli via pathways that bypass conventional airways. This is protective in obstructive lung disease as alveoli distal to an obstructed airway can still receive air via the pores. However, they also allow bacterial spread between alveoli during pneumonia, contributing to consolidation patterns.
options: They allow collateral ventilation between alveoli when
They are pathological openings only seen in emphysema
They are sites of gas exchange
They allow fluid to drain into lymphatics
They are channels for surfactant distribution

questions.question: Renal hypoplasia is defined as:
questions.explanation: Renal hypoplasia is defined as a small kidney with reduced nephron number but otherwise normal architecture and function. It differs from a small kidney secondary to chronic disease (where architecture is abnormal). True hypoplasia results from reduced branching of the ureteric bud or inadequate metanephric mesenchyme. Bilateral hypoplasia can cause chronic kidney disease. Unilateral hypoplasia with contralateral compensatory hypertrophy is usually asymptomatic.

questions.question: The allantois first appears around which day of development?
questions.explanation: The allantois first appears around day 16 as a small diverticulum projecting from the caudal end of the yolk sac into the connecting stalk. In humans, the allantois is vestigial and contributes to bladder development and formation of the urachus. In other species, it plays important roles in waste storage and gas exchange.

The first urine is produced around 12 weeks when the metanephric kidney becomes functional and glomerular filtration begins. Urine is excreted into the amniotic cavity and becomes a major component of amniotic fluid in the second half of pregnancy. Fetal urine is hypotonic compared to fetal plasma. The placenta handles waste excretion; the kidneys primarily regulate fluid balance.
questions.question: The first urine is produced around:

options: Production of mucus for airway lubrication
Production of IgA for mucosal immunity
Secretion of HCl to maintain airway pH
Production of lysozyme for antibacterial defense
questions.question: Clara cells (club cells) are non-ciliated secretory cells found primarily in terminal and respiratory bronchioles. Their secretion performs which function?
questions.explanation: Club cells (formerly Clara cells) in bronchioles secrete a surfactant-like lipoprotein that reduces surface tension in smaller airways. They also contain cytochrome P450 enzymes for detoxification of inhaled xenobiotics. Additionally, they serve as progenitor cells for bronchiolar epithelium. Their dome-shaped apical surface protrudes into the airway lumen — a useful histological feature for identification.

options: Thick, viscous, and cellular (late luteal phase mucus)
Thick and plug-like due to progesterone action
Thin, watery, acellular, and forms a ferning pattern on drying
questions.question: The cervical mucus changes in consistency throughout the menstrual cycle. At the time of ovulation, cervical mucus is maximally permeable to sperm because it becomes:
questions.explanation: At ovulation, high estrogen levels cause cervical mucus secreted by endocervical glands to become thin, watery, acellular, and highly elastic (spinnbarkeit — can be drawn into long strings). When dried on a glass slide, ovulatory mucus forms a characteristic ferning (arborization) pattern due to NaCl crystallization. This change facilitates sperm penetration. After ovulation, progesterone converts cervical mucus to thick, viscous, cellular mucus forming a 'plug' impenetrable to sperm.

Unilateral renal agenesis is often associated with ipsilateral genital anomalies (absent vas deferens in males, uterine anomalies in females) because both systems develop from adjacent mesoderm and share inductive interactions. The condition results from failure of ureteric bud formation or degeneration of the metanephric blastema. Most cases are compatible with normal life if the contralateral kidney is normal.
questions.question: Unilateral renal agenesis is often associated with:

questions.explanation: Integral (transmembrane) proteins span the entire thickness of the lipid bilayer and have exposed domains on both the cytoplasmic and extracellular faces. They include receptors, ion channels, transporters, and structural proteins (like integrins). Unlike peripheral proteins, they cannot be extracted without disrupting the membrane with detergents.
questions.question: A protein that spans the entire phospholipid bilayer, with domains both inside and outside the cell, is classified as which of the following?

questions.explanation: Meningomyelocele is a cystic form of spina bifida where both meninges and spinal cord tissue protrude through the vertebral defect. Other forms include spina bifida occulta (hidden, minimal defect) and meningocele (only meninges protrude). These result from failure of posterior neuropore closure.
questions.question: Meningomyelocele is a type of which congenital anomaly?
Nephrocalcinosis is calcification of the renal parenchyma. It is associated with which metabolic condition causing elevated urinary calcium and supersaturation of calcium salts?
questions.explanation: Nephrocalcinosis (renal parenchymal calcification) is most commonly caused by hypercalciuria from primary hyperparathyroidism (elevated PTH increases renal calcium loss) and distal renal tubular acidosis (RTA type 1 — inability to acidify urine causes calcium phosphate supersaturation). Other causes include medullary sponge kidney, hyperoxaluria, and sarcoidosis (elevated calcitriol). Dystrophic calcification can also occur in areas of papillary necrosis or chronic pyelonephritis.

questions.question: The prosencephalic organizing center (POC) is located in which position?
options: Rostral to notochord and ventral to prosencephalon
questions.explanation: Face development depends on inductive influences from two organizing centers. The prosencephalic organizing center (POC) is located rostral to the notochord and ventral to the prosencephalon. The rhombencephalic organizing center (ROC) is located ventral to the rhombencephalon.

The lower intercostal nerves supply sensory fibers to the peripheral region of the diaphragm, which is derived from the body wall. This peripheral portion brings its own nerve supply with it during development. The phrenic nerve supplies sensory fibers to all other parts of the diaphragm and motor supply to all diaphragmatic muscles. SECTION B: GASTRULATION AND TRILAMINAR GERM DISC
questions.question: Which nerve supplies sensory fibers to the peripheral region of the diaphragm?

questions.explanation: Intervillous spaces are filled with maternal blood from spiral arteries. Maternal blood bathes the chorionic villi, allowing exchange of nutrients, gases, and wastes between maternal and fetal circulations without direct contact. Blood flows from spiral arteries and drains into endometrial veins.
questions.question: Intervillous spaces contain which substance?
Respiratory movements begin before birth primarily to:
questions.explanation: Respiratory movements begin before birth primarily to practice breathing muscles (diaphragm and intercostals) and promote lung development. These movements do not accomplish gas exchange, which occurs at the placenta. Fetal breathing movements can be detected by ultrasound and are used to assess fetal well-being.

questions.question: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is an autoimmune disease targeting intrahepatic bile ducts. The characteristic histological finding in early PBC is:
options: Granulomatous destruction of interlobular bile ducts
Periportal fibrosis with plasma cell infiltrate
questions.explanation: The pathognomonic early histological lesion of primary biliary cholangitis is the 'florid duct lesion' — granulomatous inflammation with a dense lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltrate surrounding and destroying the interlobular bile ducts. This is mediated by autoreactive T cells targeting mitochondrial antigens (anti-mitochondrial antibodies/AMA are serological markers). Progressive bile duct destruction leads to cholestasis, fibrosis, and eventually cirrhosis.

Skeletal muscle fibers can be identified histologically by their multiple peripheral nuclei (pushed to the periphery by myofibrils), prominent cross-striations (due to regular sarcomere arrangement), and large diameter. Smooth muscle cells have a single central nucleus, no cross-striations, and are spindle-shaped. Cardiac muscle has central nuclei, cross-striations, and intercalated discs. These features allow confident identification of muscle type in the esophageal wall.
questions.question: The tunica muscularis of the esophagus in its middle third contains both skeletal and smooth muscle. These two muscle types can be distinguished histologically because skeletal muscle has:
options: A single central nucleus and faint cross-striations
A single peripheral nucleus without cross-striations

questions.explanation: Salivary glands develop as solid epithelial buds from the primordial oral cavity (ectoderm). These epithelial buds grow into surrounding mesenchyme through reciprocal inductive interactions. The mesenchyme induces branching and differentiation of the epithelial component.
questions.question: The salivary glands develop from which tissue interactions?

questions.explanation: The hepatic diverticulum appears as a ventral bud from the caudal part of the foregut during the 4th week. This diverticulum grows into the septum transversum and divides into a larger cranial part (liver primordium) and smaller caudal part (gallbladder and cystic duct).
questions.question: The hepatic diverticulum appears during which week?

options: Two layers from the start of the esophagus
No muscularis mucosae in the esophagus
A single longitudinal layer in the upper
questions.question: The esophageal muscularis mucosae is noteworthy because it consists of:
questions.explanation: The muscularis mucosae of the esophagus begins as a single longitudinal layer in the upper esophagus and develops into two layers (inner circular + outer longitudinal) in the lower esophagus. This is an important histological feature distinguishing the esophagus from the stomach, where the muscularis mucosae has two layers throughout. This developmental variation in the esophageal muscularis mucosae is a reliable landmark for esophageal identification.

options: To cool the lens and prevent heat damage
To increase the depth of focus significantly
To stain the specimen more uniformly
To increase the numerical aperture and resolving power
To reduce the total magnification produced
questions.question: In a compound microscope, the objective lens magnifying 100× is usually used together with immersion oil primarily for which of the following reasons?
questions.explanation: Immersion oil has a refractive index similar to glass, preventing light refraction at the interface between the coverslip and objective lens, thereby increasing numerical aperture. Higher numerical aperture directly improves the resolving power of the objective. This allows visualization of structures at very fine resolution approaching 0.2 micrometers.

questions.question: Somatostatin-producing D cells in the gastric antrum act as paracrine inhibitors of acid secretion. When stimulated, they primarily inhibit which cell type?
questions.explanation: D cells (delta cells) are enteroendocrine cells producing somatostatin, which acts as a potent paracrine inhibitor. Somatostatin inhibits gastrin secretion from G cells (reducing the stimulus for HCl production) and directly inhibits parietal cells and enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells. This provides a local negative feedback loop regulating gastric acid secretion. H. pylori infection suppresses D cell function, contributing to hypergastrinemia.

questions.question: Unilateral renal agenesis affects which kidney more commonly?
questions.explanation: Unilateral renal agenesis more commonly affects the left kidney and occurs in approximately 1 in 1000 neonates. Males are more frequently affected than females. The condition usually causes no symptoms because the contralateral kidney undergoes compensatory hypertrophy and performs the function of both kidneys.

Umbrella cells (superficial cells) of the urothelium have rigid, thickened apical plaques (asymmetric unit membranes composed of uroplakins — specific barrier proteins) and cytoplasmic fusiform vesicles. When the bladder is empty, excess membrane is stored as invaginated vesicles. During bladder filling, the vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane, adding membrane to accommodate distension. Uroplakins also create the highly effective barrier preventing urine from diffusing back into the tissue.
options: Large surface area with asymmetric unit membranes (plaques)
Tight junctions only, without special membrane features
questions.question: Transitional epithelium (urothelium) of the bladder has umbrella cells on its luminal surface. These cells are characterized by which unique structural feature adapting them to stretch?

questions.explanation: Maternal blood enters the intervillous spaces through spiral arteries, which become less convoluted and increase in diameter during pregnancy. This increases maternal blood flow to the placenta for gaseous exchange. Deoxygenated maternal blood flows back through endometrial veins.
questions.question: Maternal blood enters the intervillous spaces through which vessels?
Ring chromosomes result from which process?
questions.explanation: Ring chromosomes form when deletions occur at both ends of a chromosome, and the broken ends fuse together to form a ring structure. This results in loss of genetic material from both chromosome arms. The clinical effects depend on which genes are lost. SECTION L: BRAINSTEM DEVELOPMENT

Accessory (ectopic) pancreatic tissue is most commonly found in the stomach wall, duodenum, or jejunum. It represents aberrant pancreatic tissue that develops outside the normal pancreas, usually in the GI tract wall. Most accessory pancreatic tissue is asymptomatic and discovered incidentally, though it may rarely cause obstruction or bleeding.
questions.question: Accessory pancreatic tissue is most commonly found in:
The head fold causes the septum transversum to move to which region?
questions.explanation: As a result of growth of the brain and cephalic folding of the embryo, the buccopharyngeal membrane is pulled forward while the heart and pericardial cavity move first to the cervical region. Eventually, these structures move to their final position in the thorax. The septum transversum develops into the central tendon of the diaphragm.

questions.question: Interstitial cells of Leydig in the testis produce testosterone. They are found in which location within the testis?
questions.explanation: Leydig cells (interstitial cells) are located in the connective tissue stroma between the seminiferous tubules of the testis. They are large, polygonal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm (rich in smooth ER and mitochondria for steroidogenesis) and often contain Reinke crystals (elongated protein inclusions). LH from the pituitary stimulates Leydig cells to synthesize and secrete testosterone, which is essential for spermatogenesis, secondary sexual development, and male reproductive function.
options: Within the lumen of the rete testis

questions.explanation: Crown-rump length (CRL) or sitting height is used as the primary measurement method after the 4th week when the embryo begins to show significant curvature. This measurement is taken from the vertex of the skull to the midpoint between the apices of the buttocks, excluding the limbs.
questions.question: Crown-rump length (CRL) is primarily used for measuring embryos after which week?

options: Resolving power of the light microscope
The thickness of the glass slide
Using the wrong objective lens only
questions.explanation: Resolving power defines the minimum distance at which two distinct points can be perceived separately; at 0.2 micrometers this is the light microscope's limit. Structures closer than this threshold appear as a single fused image, regardless of magnification applied. This is a fundamental optical constraint, not a staining or preparation artifact.
questions.question: A histologist notes that two structures 0.15 micrometers apart appear as one object under a light microscope. This limitation is best attributed to which property?

questions.explanation: The gastric mucosal barrier consists of: mucus layer (traps bicarbonate), bicarbonate secretion (creates alkaline microenvironment at mucosa surface), tight junctions (prevent acid backflow), rapid cell renewal (replaces damaged cells), and rich blood supply. Pepsinogen granules in chief cells are precursors to the digestive enzyme pepsin — they are part of the digestive mechanism, not the protective barrier. NSAIDs disrupt the barrier by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis.
questions.question: The mucosa of the stomach is protected from self-digestion by a gastric mucosal barrier. Which component is NOT part of this barrier?
options: Mucus layer secreted by surface mucous cells
Bicarbonate secreted beneath the mucous layer
Tight junctions between surface epithelial cells

questions.question: A patient with pernicious anemia is found to have autoantibodies destroying parietal cells. Which essential substance becomes deficient as a direct consequence?
questions.explanation: Parietal cells produce both HCl and intrinsic factor. Intrinsic factor is essential for the absorption of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) in the terminal ileum. Destruction of parietal cells leads to intrinsic factor deficiency, preventing B12 absorption and causing megaloblastic anemia — termed pernicious anemia. This is one of the most important clinical correlates of gastric histology.

The trigone of the bladder is derived from the caudal ends of the mesonephric ducts, which become incorporated into the bladder wall. Although the trigone has mesodermal origin, the rest of the bladder epithelium is endodermal from the urogenital sinus. The trigone is the triangular area between the ureteric and urethral openings.
questions.question: The trigone of the bladder is derived from:

questions.explanation: The cecal swelling (diverticulum) in the caudal limb of the midgut loop marks the primordium of both the cecum and appendix. This swelling appears during the 6th week. The appendix initially arises from the distal end of the cecum but shifts to the medial side with unequal cecal wall growth.
questions.question: The cecal swelling marks the future:
After birth, the valve of the foramen ovale is pressed against which structure?
questions.explanation: After birth, when lung circulation begins and pressure in the left atrium increases, the valve of the foramen ovale is pressed against the septum secundum. This obliterates the foramen ovale and separates the right and left atria. Functional closure occurs immediately, but anatomical closure may take several months.

questions.question: The left vagus nerve innervates which surface of the adult stomach?
questions.explanation: The left vagus nerve innervates the anterior surface of the adult stomach due to the 90-degree rotation during development. The right vagus nerve innervates the posterior surface. Understanding this developmental rotation is clinically important for vagotomy procedures.

Wilms' tumor shows a classic triphasic histological pattern: (1) Blastemal cells — densely packed small cells with scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei, representing the undifferentiated metanephric mesenchyme; (2) Stromal cells — loose to dense mesenchymal tissue, sometimes with heterologous elements (muscle, fat, cartilage); (3) Epithelial cells — tubular or glomeruloid structures mimicking normal kidney development. WT1 and WT2 gene mutations are pathogenetically important.
options: Glomeruli, tubules, and medullary cells only
Uniform small blue cells without differentiation
Blastemal cells, stromal cells, and epithelial (tubular) cells
questions.question: Wilms' tumor (nephroblastoma) is the most common primary renal malignancy in children. Histologically, it recapitulates the developing kidney and shows a characteristic triphasic pattern of:

questions.explanation: The chorion frondosum (villous chorion) forms the fetal portion of the placenta. This is the part of the chorion where villi are well-developed and persist, in contrast to the chorion laeve (smooth chorion) where villi degenerate. The chorion frondosum is located at the embryonic pole.
questions.question: The chorion frondosum forms which part of the placenta?

questions.explanation: The granular appearance of the renal cortex results from the presence of numerous renal corpuscles (glomeruli enclosed in Bowman's capsule) and convoluted tubules (proximal and distal). These structures give the cortex its characteristic granular texture on gross and histological examination. The medullary pyramids, in contrast, contain straight tubules (loops of Henle, collecting ducts) giving them a striated appearance.
questions.question: The renal cortex contains granular-appearing regions because of which structures concentrated there?
The processus vaginalis normally:
questions.explanation: The processus vaginalis, an evagination of peritoneum that precedes testicular descent through the inguinal canal, normally obliterates after testicular descent (except for portion covering testis = tunica vaginalis). Patent processus vaginalis allows communication between peritoneal cavity and scrotum, predisposing to indirect inguinal hernia or hydrocele. Obliteration usually occurs shortly before or after birth.

The buccopharyngeal membrane, an ectodermal-endodermal membrane at the cranial end of the foregut, ruptures during the 4th week. This establishes an open connection between the oral cavity and the primitive gut. Before rupture, the membrane temporarily bounds the foregut anteriorly.
questions.question: The buccopharyngeal membrane ruptures during which week?

questions.explanation: Total magnification is calculated by multiplying the ocular lens magnification by the objective lens magnification (10 × 40 = 400×). Addition of the two values is a common misconception that gives an incorrect result. This principle applies consistently across all compound microscope configurations.
questions.question: The total magnification achieved when a 10× ocular lens is combined with a 40× objective lens is which of the following?
The vesical part of the urogenital sinus gives rise to:
questions.explanation: The vesical (upper) part of the urogenital sinus gives rise to most of the urinary bladder and is continuous with the allantois (which becomes the urachus). The pelvic part forms the prostatic and membranous urethra in males or the entire urethra in females. The phallic part grows toward the genital tubercle.

options: Glandular columnar epithelium with goblet cells
questions.question: Lingual tonsils located at the base of the tongue are covered by which epithelium?
questions.explanation: Lingual tonsils located in the lamina propria at the root of the tongue are covered by stratified squamous epithelium reflecting their location within the oral cavity where mechanical abrasion from food necessitates a protective stratified squamous surface. This is the same epithelial type as palatine tonsils. In contrast pharyngeal tonsils have respiratory pseudostratified ciliated epithelium reflecting their nasopharyngeal location.

questions.question: The ureter is lined by which type of epithelium that can accommodate changes in volume and distension?
questions.explanation: The entire urinary collecting system from the renal pelvis to the bladder is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium). In the relaxed state, it appears 5–6 cells thick with characteristic dome-shaped (umbrella) cells at the surface. When distended, it becomes 2–3 cells thick as cells flatten out. This remarkable ability to accommodate volume changes without losing barrier function is unique to urothelium.

questions.question: The extraembryonic mesoderm adjacent to the cytotrophoblast is termed which type?
questions.explanation: Extraembryonic mesoderm adjacent to the cytotrophoblast (and amnion) is called somatopleuric extraembryonic mesoderm. Extraembryonic mesoderm adjacent to the primitive yolk sac is called splanchnopleuric extraembryonic mesoderm. These terms are analogous to the intraembryonic mesoderm layers.

questions.question: Klinefelter syndrome is characterized by which karyotype?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome is characterized by a 47,XXY karyotype (or variants with additional X chromosomes). Affected individuals are phenotypically male with tall stature, small testes, gynecomastia, reduced fertility or infertility, and sometimes learning difficulties. This results from nondisjunction of sex chromosomes.

The thyroid gland reaches its final position in the 7th week in the neck, anterior to the trachea. The two lobes become connected by an isthmus attached to the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th tracheal rings. The thyroglossal duct becomes solid and normally disappears as the gland descends.
questions.question: The thyroid gland reaches its final position in the neck during which week?

questions.explanation: The Reid index measures bronchial mucous gland hypertrophy by calculating the ratio of mucous gland thickness to the total thickness of the bronchial wall between the epithelium and the perichondrium of the cartilage. Normal Reid index is < 0.4. In chronic bronchitis (defined clinically by productive cough for ≥3 months/year for ≥2 years), excessive smoking-induced gland hypertrophy raises the Reid index to > 0.5, reflecting the basis of increased mucus production.
options: The ratio of alveolar surface area to lung volume
The number of goblet cells per 100 epithelial cells
The ratio of mucous gland thickness to total bronchial wall
The thickness of the basement membrane beneath the epithelium
The ratio of cartilage to smooth muscle in the bronchial wall
questions.question: The bronchial submucosa contains mucous glands that contribute to the airway mucous blanket. In chronic bronchitis, these glands undergo hypertrophy. The Reid index measures this hypertrophy as:

questions.explanation: The isthmus is the transitional zone between the gastric pit and the gastric gland proper. It houses pluripotent stem cells that give rise to all epithelial cell types of the gastric mucosa. Stem cells can migrate upward to replace surface mucous cells or downward to replace secretory cells in the gland, ensuring mucosal renewal.
options: The deepest portion of the gland containing chief cells
The opening of the gland into the gastric pit
Gastric pit-gland junction with stem cells
The region producing the most mucus
The site of maximal parietal cell density
questions.question: Gastric pits in the stomach mucosa lead into gastric glands. The isthmus of the gastric gland is best defined as:

options: Deficiency of collagen leading to tissue atrophy
Selective loss of elastic fibers in skin
Excessive collagen accumulation in skin, digestive tract, and muscles
Mast cell infiltration causing widespread anaphylaxis
Replacement of connective tissue by adipose tissue
questions.explanation: Progressive systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) involves pathological overproduction of collagen by activated fibroblasts, resulting in fibrosis of multiple organs including skin, GI tract, lungs, kidneys, and muscles. The histological hallmark is replacement of normal tissue architecture by dense collagen bundles. The hardening (sclero-) and organ dysfunction reflect the replacement of functional tissue with excessive collagen.
questions.question: Progressive systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) is characterized histologically by which of the following?
The central lymphatic vessel within each intestinal villus is called:
questions.explanation: Each intestinal villus contains a central lymphatic channel called a lacteal. Lacteals absorb dietary long-chain fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamins packaged as chylomicrons. The absorbed lipids travel through the lymphatic system to the thoracic duct before entering the bloodstream — bypassing the portal circulation. This is why certain fat-soluble drugs avoid hepatic first-pass metabolism.

questions.question: The female urethra has para-urethral glands (Skene's glands) on its posterior wall. These glands are homologous to which male structure?
questions.explanation: Skene's glands (para-urethral glands) in females are the embryological homologs of the prostate gland in males, both derived from the urogenital sinus (endoderm). Like the prostate, Skene's glands express prostate-specific antigen (PSA). They open on either side of the urethral meatus and secrete a small amount of fluid. They are relevant clinically as a site of infection (causing paraurethral cysts or abscess) and as the glandular origin of female prostate cancer.

questions.question: The perineal body is formed from:
questions.explanation: The perineal body is formed from the tip of the urorectal septum at the point where it meets and divides the cloacal membrane. The perineal body is an important fibromuscular structure in the perineum where several muscles converge. It provides support for pelvic organs and is clinically important during childbirth and pelvic surgery.

questions.question: Placenta accreta involves abnormal adherence of placenta to which structure?
questions.explanation: Placenta accreta involves abnormal adherence of the placental villi directly to the myometrium due to defective decidua basalis. Placenta increta involves invasion into the myometrium, and placenta percreta involves penetration through the myometrium to the serosa. These conditions prevent normal placental separation at delivery.

questions.question: Cri-du-chat syndrome results from deletion of which chromosome?
questions.explanation: Cri-du-chat (cat cry) syndrome results from deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-). Affected infants have a characteristic high-pitched cry resembling a cat's cry, microcephaly, intellectual disability, and distinctive facial features. The severity depends on the size of the deletion.

questions.question: Which zone of the hepatic acinus receives the most oxygenated blood and the highest concentration of nutrients?
questions.explanation: Zone 1 (periportal zone) of the hepatic acinus is located adjacent to the portal tract (the short axis of the acinus) and therefore receives blood first as it enters the sinusoids. This zone has the highest oxygen tension and nutrient concentration, making it most metabolically active for oxidative metabolism and gluconeogenesis. Zone 1 is also most susceptible to toxic injury from substances absorbed via the portal circulation.

questions.question: The efferent arteriole of juxtamedullary nephrons is different from cortical nephrons in that it gives rise to:
questions.explanation: The efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons descend into the medulla as the vasa recta (straight vessels) rather than forming cortical peritubular capillaries. The descending and ascending vasa recta form a hairpin loop parallel to the loop of Henle. This countercurrent exchange in the vasa recta allows solutes to cycle (salt and urea recirculate) without being washed out of the medullary interstitium, maintaining the osmotic gradient essential for urine concentration.

The allantois plays a significant role in development of the urinary bladder through the urachus, which later becomes the median umbilical ligament. The urachus connects the apex of the bladder to the umbilicus. Persistence of the urachal lumen can result in urachal cysts or fistulas.
questions.question: The urachus later becomes which adult structure?
Supernumerary kidney results from:
options: Two ureteric buds on same side
questions.explanation: Supernumerary kidney results from development of two separate ureteric buds on the same side, each inducing separate metanephric tissue. This is extremely rare and differs from duplicated collecting system (bifid ureter), where a single ureteric bud branches early. Each supernumerary kidney has its own blood supply, ureter, and collecting system.

questions.question: Actin microfilaments enable cells to change shape, which is most critical in which of the following cellular processes?
options: Lipid synthesis in the smooth ER
Calcium sequestration in the sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation: Actin microfilament dynamics (polymerization at the leading edge and depolymerization at the trailing edge) drive cell migration, while actin-myosin rings power cytokinesis (cleavage furrow contraction). Phagocytosis also depends on actin polymerization to extend pseudopods around the target particle. These processes are all dependent on the ability of actin networks to rapidly reorganize their architecture.

questions.question: The omental bursa (lesser sac) forms as a result of:
questions.explanation: The omental bursa (lesser sac) forms as a result of 90-degree rotation of the stomach around its longitudinal axis. This rotation pulls the dorsal mesogastrium to the left, creating a space behind the stomach. The omental bursa communicates with the greater peritoneal cavity through the epiploic foramen.

Amniotic fluid volume in the third trimester is primarily regulated by fetal swallowing (removes ~500-1000 ml/day) and fetal urination (produces ~800-1200 ml/day). This dynamic balance maintains normal fluid volume. Disruption of either process leads to polyhydramnios (impaired swallowing from GI obstruction or neurological problems) or oligohydramnios (impaired urination from renal/urinary anomalies).
questions.question: Amniotic fluid volume in the third trimester is primarily regulated by:

questions.explanation: On day 8, the trophoblast differentiates into two layers: an inner cellular layer called cytotrophoblast and an outer multinucleated layer called syncytiotrophoblast. The syncytiotrophoblast is highly invasive and erodes maternal tissues to establish uteroplacental circulation.
questions.question: On day 8, the trophoblast differentiates into which two layers?

questions.explanation: Bipolar neurons are spindle-shaped with a single dendrite at one pole and a single axon at the opposite pole. They are specialized sensory neurons found in the retina as bipolar cells, in the cochlear spiral ganglion as first-order auditory neurons, in the vestibular ganglion, and in the olfactory epithelium. Their simple two-process form reflects their specialized role as first-order sensory transducer cells.
options: Motor neurons of the spinal cord ventral horn
Retinal, cochlear, and olfactory epithelium sensory neurons
questions.question: Bipolar neurons with a dendrite at one end and an axon at the other are found predominantly in which locations?
Which aortic arch gives rise to the left arch of the aorta?
questions.explanation: The fourth aortic arch on the left side gives rise to the arch of the aorta. The first and second arches form the carotid arteries, the third forms parts of the internal carotid, the fifth disappears, and the sixth forms the pulmonary arteries. The right fourth arch contributes to the right subclavian artery.

Neural crest cells form the dermis of the face, midfacial skeleton, pharyngeal arch skeleton, cartilage, bone, dentin, tendon, pia and arachnoid matter, sensory neurons, and glandular stroma. Voluntary craniofacial muscles are derived from paraxial mesoderm, not neural crest.
questions.question: Neural crest cells contribute to formation of all EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Mosaicism results from mitotic nondisjunction occurring post-zygotically, leading to two or more cell lines with different chromosome numbers in the same individual. The phenotype depends on the proportion and distribution of abnormal cells. Mosaicism generally results in milder phenotypes than complete aneuploidy.
questions.question: Mosaicism results from which event?

questions.explanation: The classic hepatic lobule is centered on the central vein (terminal hepatic venule). Portal tracts — containing branches of the hepatic artery, portal vein, and bile duct — are located at the periphery (corners of the hexagon). Blood flows from the portal tracts centripetally through sinusoids toward the central vein, while bile flows in the opposite direction toward the bile ducts in the portal tracts.
questions.question: The classic hepatic lobule is described as hexagonal. Which structure is located at the CENTER of this lobule?
The median umbilical ligament in adults represents:
questions.explanation: The median umbilical ligament in adults represents the obliterated urachus, which connected the apex of the bladder to the umbilicus during fetal life. The medial umbilical ligaments represent the obliterated umbilical arteries. The ligamentum teres represents the obliterated umbilical vein. These structures are useful anatomical landmarks during surgery.

questions.question: The large intestine lacks villi but retains crypts of Lieberkühn. What is the predominant cell type in these colonic crypts?
questions.explanation: The large intestine has no villi and is lined by simple columnar epithelium with numerous crypts (tubular glands). Goblet cells are the predominant secretory cell type in the colonic mucosa and are far more numerous than in the small intestine. The abundant mucus they produce lubricates the passage of increasingly solid fecal matter. Paneth cells are rare or absent in the adult colon.

questions.question: C-cells of the thyroid gland are derived from which pharyngeal structure?
questions.explanation: C-cells (parafollicular cells) of the thyroid gland are derived from the ultimobranchial body, which represents the fifth pharyngeal pouch. These cells are of neural crest origin and produce calcitonin, which regulates calcium metabolism. The follicular cells are derived from endoderm.

questions.question: The gastric mucosa undergoes rapid renewal. Surface mucous cells of the stomach are replaced approximately every:
questions.explanation: Surface mucous cells of the stomach are among the most rapidly renewed cells in the body, with a turnover rate of approximately 3–7 days. This rapid replacement is driven by the pluripotent stem cells in the isthmus of gastric glands, which continuously produce new cells that migrate upward to the surface. This rapid renewal is essential for maintaining mucosal integrity against the highly acidic and proteolytic gastric environment.

Folic acid supplementation (400-800 mcg daily) before conception and during early pregnancy significantly reduces the risk of neural tube defects (NTDs) such as spina bifida and anencephaly. Folic acid is essential for DNA synthesis and cell division during the critical period of neural tube closure.
questions.question: Folic acid supplementation during pregnancy is primarily recommended to prevent which abnormality?
Hair follicle development begins in which body regions first?
questions.explanation: Hair development first becomes recognizable in the eyebrows, upper lip, and chin regions, beginning around the 9th-12th week. Hair does not become easily visible until approximately the 20th week. This craniocaudal progression reflects the general pattern of embryonic development.

questions.question: Fibronectin and laminin are glycoproteins of the extracellular matrix that primarily serve which function?
