questions.explanation: Fibronectin in loose connective tissue ECM and laminin in basement membranes are adhesive multidomain glycoproteins that mediate cell attachment to the extracellular matrix. They have binding sites for both matrix components like collagen and heparan sulfate proteoglycans and for cell surface integrin receptors, acting as molecular bridges linking cells to their surrounding matrix. This adhesion is critical for cell migration, differentiation, and signaling. Fibronectin has RGD sequences recognized by multiple integrin heterodimers.
options: Providing tensile strength like type I collagen
Adhesive glycoproteins mediating cell-ECM attachment via integrin receptors
Catalyzing collagen cross-linking like lysyl oxidase
Inhibiting protease degradation of the ECM

questions.explanation: During diastole, when the aortic valve closes, the aortic sinuses (sinuses of Valsalva) fill with blood and create eddy currents that flow backward toward the valve. This prevents the valve cusps from apposing the aortic wall (which would obstruct the coronary ostia) and simultaneously fills the coronary ostia with blood, driving coronary perfusion during diastole. This is why the majority of coronary perfusion occurs during diastole, not systole.
options: Preventing regurgitation of blood into the ventricle
Acting as pressure reservoirs for the coronary circulation
Storing oxygenated blood for direct myocardial diffusion
Creating eddy currents that fill the coronary ostia with blood
questions.question: The coronary arteries supply the myocardium. They arise from the aortic sinuses (sinuses of Valsalva) just above the aortic valve. These sinuses serve which function during diastole?

questions.explanation: The female urethra (approximately 4cm long) transitions from transitional epithelium near the bladder to non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium near the external urethral orifice, with patches of pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium in between. This epithelial variability makes the female urethra susceptible to ascending infections, contributing to the higher incidence of UTIs in women compared to men.
questions.question: The urethra in females is shorter than in males. The female urethra is lined by which epithelium in its middle portion?

questions.explanation: Pancreas divisum results from failure of fusion between the ventral and dorsal pancreatic ducts. The dorsal duct drains most of the pancreas through the minor papilla, while the ventral duct drains only the uncinate process through the major papilla. This is the most common congenital pancreatic anomaly and is usually asymptomatic but may predispose to pancreatitis.
questions.question: Pancreas divisum results from:

questions.explanation: Mast cells express high-affinity surface receptors (FcεRI) for the Fc portion of IgE, allowing IgE molecules to bind to mast cells even in the absence of antigen. When antigen subsequently crosslinks the cell-bound IgE, this triggers degranulation. Most circulating IgE is therefore cell-bound on mast cells and basophils, with very little free in plasma — explaining why serum IgE levels are low even in atopic individuals.
options: IgE circulates freely in plasma at high concentrations
IgE activates complement directly without antigen
IgE is produced by mast cells themselves
Mast cells bear surface IgE receptors without prior antigen exposure
IgE can only activate neutrophils, not mast cells
questions.question: The IgE immunoglobulin type is uniquely important in mast cell activation because of which of the following specific features?

questions.explanation: The cytoplasm is the gel-like aqueous medium (cytosol) filling the space between the nucleus and cell membrane, containing suspended organelles, the cytoskeleton, inclusions, and dissolved metabolites, ions, and proteins. The cytosol (~70% water) forms the environment in which most metabolic reactions occur. It is not empty but rather a highly organized and crowded molecular space.
questions.question: Which of the following descriptions most accurately characterizes the structure of the cytoplasm?
options: A rigid crystalline compartment supporting all organelles
A gel-like aqueous medium containing organelles and cytoskeletal elements
An empty fluid space between the nucleus and cell membrane
A dense granular material composed exclusively of ribosomes
A lipid-rich compartment surrounding the nucleus only
Smooth muscle throughout its entire length
Cardiac muscle in the lower third
Skeletal muscle only in the upper third, mixed
Exclusively smooth muscle in its upper third
questions.question: On a histological section, the pharyngeal wall shows skeletal muscle throughout with no smooth muscle. This distinguishes the pharynx from the esophagus because the esophagus contains:
questions.explanation: The pharynx contains skeletal muscle throughout, reflecting its role in the voluntary phase of swallowing. The esophagus differs markedly: the upper third has skeletal muscle (voluntary deglutition), the middle third has mixed skeletal and smooth muscle (transition), and the lower third has smooth muscle only (involuntary peristalsis). This progressive change from skeletal to smooth muscle is a classic and regularly examined feature of esophageal histology.

After 90-degree clockwise rotation (viewed from above), the stomach's original dorsal border becomes the left surface and forms the greater curvature. The original ventral border becomes the right surface and forms the lesser curvature. The original left surface becomes anterior, and the original right surface becomes posterior. This rotation explains the vagal nerve distribution.
questions.question: The stomach's original dorsal border becomes which surface after rotation?
The midgut loop herniates into the umbilical cord during which week?
questions.explanation: Physiological umbilical herniation of the midgut loop occurs at the beginning of the 6th week due to rapid intestinal elongation and liver enlargement. The abdominal cavity becomes relatively too small to accommodate the growing intestines. The intestines return to the abdomen during the 10th week.

Piebaldism is an autosomal dominant trait characterized by localized lack of melanin in patches of skin and/or hair, often presenting with a white forelock. Unlike generalized albinism (autosomal recessive), piebaldism shows a predictable inheritance pattern. The condition results from mutations affecting melanocyte development or migration.
questions.question: Piebaldism is inherited as:

questions.explanation: Intestinal villi transition from broad, leaf-shaped forms in the duodenum to more slender, finger-like projections in the ileum. This progressive shape change reflects adaptation for absorption. The villi are tallest and most densely packed in the jejunum, which is the primary site of nutrient absorption, and become shorter in the ileum.
questions.question: The duodenal villi are typically described as leaf-shaped. How does their shape change as you progress to the ileum?
options: They disappear entirely in the ileum
They gradually assume a finger-like shape

questions.question: An osteoblast that becomes completely surrounded by the bone matrix it has secreted is henceforth called which of the following?
questions.explanation: When an active osteoblast secreting matrix becomes entrapped in the matrix it has produced, it transforms into an osteocyte. Osteocytes reside in lacunae and maintain the surrounding matrix through limited secretion and resorption. They extend cytoplasmic processes through canaliculi, connecting to neighboring osteocytes and to vascular channels, functioning as the primary mechanosensory cells of bone that regulate remodeling in response to mechanical loading.

questions.question: The urinary bladder wall contains the detrusor muscle, which is composed of which type of muscle and how is it arranged?
options: Smooth muscle in three interwoven layers
Cardiac muscle in a single layer
Two layers of smooth muscle (circular only)
Mixed skeletal and smooth muscle in two layers
questions.explanation: The detrusor muscle of the bladder is composed of three interwoven layers of smooth muscle: inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal. Unlike the GIT where layers are distinct, the bladder muscle layers are less clearly defined and fibers run in multiple directions, giving the bladder its unique distensibility. The internal urethral sphincter at the bladder neck is a thickening of the circular smooth muscle.

Vascular smooth muscle cells in the tunica media are connected by gap junctions (containing connexins), which allow direct electrical and chemical coupling between adjacent cells for coordinated vasoconstriction and vasodilation. They also have dense bodies (equivalent to Z-lines in striated muscle) on the inner surface of the plasma membrane and in the cytoplasm, which anchor actin and intermediate filaments of the contractile apparatus. This arrangement allows the smooth muscle to generate sustained tension.
questions.question: The tunica media of muscular arteries is composed predominantly of circular smooth muscle cells. These cells are connected to each other and to the extracellular matrix by which junction allowing coordinate contraction?

questions.explanation: Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis) results from abnormal neural crest cell development. It is characterized by deformities of the ears, eyes, cheekbones, and chin. The severity varies from mild to severe, and complications may include breathing problems, vision issues, cleft palate, and hearing loss.
questions.question: Treacher Collins syndrome results from abnormal development of which cells?

questions.explanation: Mammary glands are modified and highly specialized apocrine sweat glands. They develop from mammary buds that appear during the 6th week as solid downgrowths of epidermis. These buds give rise to secondary mammary buds that become lactiferous ducts and their branches.
questions.question: Mammary glands are modified forms of:
The ascending and descending colons become retroperitoneal through:
questions.explanation: The ascending and descending colons become secondarily retroperitoneal when their mesenteries press against and fuse with the posterior abdominal wall. This fusion obliterates the potential space behind these structures. The transverse and sigmoid colons retain their mesenteries and remain intraperitoneal. This anatomical arrangement has important surgical implications.

questions.question: The ventral pancreatic bud gives rise to:
questions.explanation: The ventral pancreatic bud gives rise to the uncinate process and part of the head of the pancreas. The dorsal bud forms most of the pancreas including the body, tail, and remainder of the head. The two buds fuse as the duodenum rotates, bringing the ventral bud dorsally.
options: Uncinate process and part of head

questions.question: Edwards syndrome is caused by trisomy of which chromosome?
questions.explanation: Edwards syndrome is caused by trisomy 18 (47,XX,+18 or 47,XY,+18). It is characterized by severe developmental abnormalities including clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, cardiac defects, and profound intellectual disability. Most affected infants die within the first year.

options: Resting → proliferative → hypertrophic → calcified cartilage → ossification
Ossification zone then calcified zone then hypertrophic zone then proliferative zone then resting zone
Only three zones exist: proliferative hypertrophic and ossification
Calcified zone is immediately adjacent to the resting zone
The proliferative zone is closest to the diaphysis
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the five zones of the epiphyseal growth plate from the epiphyseal to the diaphyseal side?
questions.explanation: The epiphyseal plate from epiphyseal to diaphyseal side has five zones: resting zone with quiescent hyaline cartilage chondrocytes; proliferative zone with rapidly dividing chondrocytes in longitudinal columns; hypertrophic zone with enlarged chondrocytes accumulating glycogen; calcified cartilage zone where matrix calcifies as chondrocytes die; and ossification zone where endochondral bone tissue appears as blood vessels and osteoblasts invade. This progression drives longitudinal bone growth.

The appendix initially arises from the distal (apical) end of the cecum during the 6th week. Due to unequal growth of the cecal wall, with the right side growing more rapidly, the appendix comes to lie on the medial side of the cecum. This explains the variable positions of the appendix in adults (retrocecal, pelvic, etc.).
questions.question: The appendix is initially located at which part of the cecum?
The function of the cell membrane is best described as which of the following?
options: Structural support and semipermeable barrier for molecular traffic
Synthesizing proteins for secretion outside the cell
Detoxifying foreign substances entering the cell
questions.explanation: The cell membrane provides structural integrity to the cell and, through its selectively permeable nature, controls which molecules enter and exit. Transport can be passive (down concentration gradient) or active (requiring energy, against gradient). The membrane also mediates cell signaling through surface receptors and cell-to-cell recognition through the glycocalyx.

Smooth muscle has the highest regenerative potential and can fully regenerate from surviving smooth muscle cells. Skeletal muscle has limited but real regeneration through satellite cell activation. Cardiac muscle has minimal regeneration; after myocardial infarction, lost cardiomyocytes are replaced by fibrous scar tissue rather than functional myocardium, causing permanent loss of contractile function proportional to the infarct size.
options: All three types have identical regenerative potential
Smooth > Skeletal > Cardiac in regenerative capacity
questions.question: The regeneration potential differs among the three muscle types. Which of the following correctly ranks their regenerative capacity?

questions.explanation: The juxtaglomerular apparatus develops from specialized cells in the distal convoluted tubule (macula densa) and the afferent arteriole (juxtaglomerular cells). This structure regulates renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate through the renin-angiotensin system. It forms during late fetal development and continues maturing postnatally. The JGA is important for blood pressure regulation and fluid homeostasis.
questions.question: The juxtaglomerular apparatus develops from:
The thyroglossal duct connects which two structures during development?
questions.explanation: The thyroglossal duct initially connects the developing tongue and thyroid gland. The foramen cecum becomes thickened below the surface to form this duct. The tip of the duct becomes bilobed, and cells proliferating at this bifid end form the two lobes of the thyroid gland.

The core disciplines essential for tissue biology include biochemistry, molecular biology, physiology, immunology, and pathology — but pharmacokinetics is not among them. Pharmacokinetics deals with drug absorption, distribution, and metabolism, which is outside the foundational scope of tissue biology. This distinction is important for understanding the integrative basis of histological science.
questions.question: Which of the following disciplines is NOT listed as essential for better knowledge of tissue biology in the context of histological study?
Peroxisomes differ from lysosomes primarily in which of the following aspects?
options: They are not enclosed by a membrane
They degrade proteins by proteolysis exclusively
They arise from the Golgi apparatus during biogenesis
They do not contain any enzymes
They use oxidative reactions rather than hydrolysis
questions.explanation: Peroxisomes perform oxidative reactions using molecular oxygen to generate hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as an intermediate, which is then detoxified by catalase within the same organelle. They oxidize very long chain fatty acids (beta-oxidation), metabolize glyoxylate, and detoxify alcohol. Lysosomes use acid hydrolases at low pH, whereas peroxisomes oxidize substrates at neutral pH — a fundamental mechanistic difference.

questions.question: The reticular formation consists of approximately how many nuclei?
questions.explanation: The reticular formation consists of more than 100,000 brainstem nuclei. These nuclei are divided into three subgroups: paramedian nuclear group, central/medial column group (magnocellular), and lateral group (parvocellular column). They acquire different names in different parts of the brainstem.

Mesonephric ridges appear during the 5th week of development and indicate the sites of the developing kidneys. During this week, the brain grows rapidly, the face contacts the heart prominence, the hyoid (2nd) arch overgrows the 3rd and 4th arches forming the cervical sinus, and upper limbs show elbows and hand plates.
questions.question: Mesonephric ridges, which indicate sites of future kidneys, appear during which week?

questions.explanation: The sliding filament model explains contraction through cross-bridge cycling: calcium binds troponin exposing myosin-binding sites on actin; myosin heads attach to actin; the power stroke pivots the head pulling actin toward the M line; ATP binding causes myosin head release; and ATP hydrolysis re-cocks the head. Repeated cycling slides actin over myosin, shortening the sarcomere without changing the length of individual filaments.
options: Shortening of individual myosin and actin filaments
Enzymatic degradation of titin elastic proteins
Disassembly of Z line proteins releasing actin filaments
Cross-bridge cycling: myosin heads bind actin, pivot, release, and re-cock
Calcium directly shortening thick filaments through conformational change
questions.question: In the sliding filament model of muscle contraction, shortening of the sarcomere is produced by which molecular events?
Hyaloid vessels primarily function to supply which developing structure during intrauterine life?
questions.explanation: The hyaloid vessels, which invade the optic cup through the choroid fissure, primarily supply the developing lens during intrauterine life. These vessels form a delicate network between the lens and retina. After birth, the hyaloid vessels normally regress, and their persistence can form cords or cysts.

questions.question: The pia and arachnoid mater (leptomeninges) are derived from which source?
questions.explanation: The pia and arachnoid mater (collectively called leptomeninges) are derived from neural crest cells. The dura mater is derived from mesoderm. Schwann cells, which myelinate peripheral nerves, are also derived from neural crest, while oligodendrocytes (CNS myelin) come from neural tube.

questions.question: The stomodeum is initially separated from the foregut by which membrane?
questions.explanation: Initially, the foregut is separated from the stomodeum by the buccopharyngeal membrane. This membrane breaks down so that the foregut opens to the exterior. At this stage, the head is represented by a bulge caused by the developing brain, and the pericardium occupies the region of the future thorax.

Maturation of villi occurs throughout fetal development. The chorionic villi become thinner, providing a minimal barrier to diffusion, while the number of fetal capillaries within them increases. The cytotrophoblast and its core become thinned out so fetal capillaries are separated from maternal blood only by thin layers.
questions.question: The placental barrier becomes progressively thinner due to which process?

questions.explanation: The GI tract wall contains an inner circular smooth muscle layer encircling the tube and an outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer running along its length. Coordinated contraction where the inner circular layer contracts while the outer longitudinal layer relaxes produces peristaltic waves that propel luminal contents aborally. The myenteric plexus of Auerbach between these layers coordinates their activity.
questions.question: Smooth muscle of the GI tract wall achieves peristalsis through which organization of its muscle layers?
options: Inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle in coordinated waves
Inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle layers
Inner striated and outer smooth muscle layers
Inner oblique and outer transverse layers only
A single layer with spiral orientation throughout

questions.question: Horizontal folding of the embryo results in incorporation of which structure into the midgut?
questions.explanation: Lateral (horizontal) folding rolls the sides of the embryonic disc and turns part of the yolk sac into the embryo as midgut. The rest is left outside as the yolk stalk and is incorporated into the umbilical cord. This folding brings the ventral body wall together and establishes the tubular gut.

The gallbladder notably lacks a muscularis mucosae layer — one of its key histological distinguishing features from other GIT structures. Its wall consists of mucosa (epithelium + lamina propria), a fibromuscular layer, perimuscular connective tissue, and serosa/adventitia. The absence of muscularis mucosae is paired with the absence of a submucosa, making the gallbladder structurally unique among tubular digestive organs.
questions.question: In a histology practical, a GIT segment is identified by its LACK of muscularis mucosae. This feature is characteristic of which structure?

options: 4× lens used for scanning wide fields
100× lens used with immersion oil for highest magnification
40× lens used for most detailed cellular work
60× lens standard in all compound microscopes
questions.explanation: The 100× objective lens is the oil immersion lens, requiring immersion oil between the lens and coverslip to prevent light refraction. It provides the highest magnification and best resolving power of the objective lenses in the standard set (4×, 10×, 40×, 100×). Without oil, light bends at the air-glass interface, drastically reducing resolution and brightness.
questions.question: Which objective lens is designated as the 'oil immersion' lens in a compound microscope and at what magnification?

questions.explanation: Annular pancreas results from bifurcation of the ventral pancreatic bud, with portions migrating in different directions around the duodenum. When these portions fuse with the dorsal bud, they form a ring of pancreatic tissue encircling the duodenum. This can cause duodenal obstruction requiring surgical intervention.
questions.question: Annular pancreas results from:
The arcuate arteries of the kidney run along the boundary between cortex and medulla. From these arteries, which vessels supply blood directly to the glomeruli?
questions.explanation: Blood flow to glomeruli follows: renal artery → segmental arteries → interlobar arteries → arcuate arteries → interlobular (cortical radiate) arteries → afferent arterioles → glomerular capillaries. After filtration, blood exits via efferent arterioles into peritubular capillaries (cortex) or vasa recta (medulla). This unique portal-like arrangement with two capillary beds allows independent regulation of filtration and tubular blood flow.

questions.question: The retina's rods and cones differ in which of the following ways?
options: Rods provide color vision and cones detect low light and movement
Both rods and cones function identically in all light conditions
Rods detect dim light and provide achromatic vision; cones detect color and high-acuity vision
Rods are concentrated at the fovea centralis and cones are in the peripheral retina
Only cones are present in humans as rods are vestigial structures
questions.explanation: Rods number approximately 120 million and contain rhodopsin, are extremely sensitive to low light, provide monochromatic peripheral vision, and are distributed throughout the retina except the fovea. Cones number approximately 6 to 7 million and come in three types for trichromatic color vision concentrated at the fovea centralis for maximum visual acuity. Cone-dominated foveal vision requires bright light.

Hematopoiesis (blood cell formation) first occurs in the yolk sac wall and allantois during the third week. It later shifts to the liver (6 weeks), then to the spleen (12 weeks), and finally to the bone marrow (which becomes the primary site by 28 weeks and throughout life).
questions.question: Hematopoiesis first occurs in which embryonic location?

options: Multiple dendrites and a single long axon like motor neurons
A single process always purely dendritic without any axon function
One process splits: peripheral branch to receptor, central branch to CNS
Two separate processes both classified as axons
No processes communicating only through gap junctions
questions.explanation: Pseudounipolar neurons appear structurally unipolar with a single process from the cell body but are functionally bipolar. Their single process divides T-shaped into a long peripheral branch conducting sensory information from receptor to cell body and a central branch entering the spinal cord or brainstem. Both branches conduct impulses toward the cell body making them both functionally dendritic. They are the primary sensory neurons for touch pain and proprioception.
questions.question: Pseudounipolar neurons serving as primary sensory neurons in dorsal root ganglia have which structural arrangement?
The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs sodium using which transport mechanism at its basolateral membrane?
options: Secondary active transport via SGLT2 on the basolateral side
Na+/K+-ATPase pumping sodium out into the peritubular space
questions.explanation: Na+/K+-ATPase on the basolateral membrane of PCT cells actively pumps 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per cycle, maintaining a low intracellular Na+ concentration. This creates the electrochemical gradient that drives Na+ entry from the tubular lumen across the apical membrane (via brush border cotransporters like SGLT2 for glucose-Na+ and NHE3 for H+-Na+ exchange). This is the fundamental mechanism for renal sodium reabsorption.

questions.question: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies which pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve, a branch of the vagus nerve (CN X), supplies the sixth pharyngeal arch. The superior laryngeal nerve supplies the fourth arch. These nerves innervate the muscles and provide sensation to structures derived from their respective arches.

In bone osteons, collagen fibers within adjacent lamellae are oriented at right angles to one another, creating anisotropy detectable with polarized light. Lamellae with fibers parallel to the polarizer appear dark (extinct) while those with perpendicular fibers appear bright, producing the characteristic alternating pattern. This structural arrangement gives bone its mechanical strength and resistance to multidirectional stress.
questions.question: A tissue section examined under polarized light shows alternating bright and dark layers corresponding to perpendicular collagen fiber orientation. This is most characteristic of which structure?
options: Reticular fiber networks in lymph nodes

questions.explanation: Bilateral renal agenesis is incompatible with life primarily due to pulmonary hypoplasia resulting from severe oligohydramnios, not due to renal failure (the placenta handles waste excretion in utero). Insufficient amniotic fluid prevents normal lung development. Affected neonates cannot breathe adequately after birth. The condition occurs in approximately 1 in 4,000 births and shows male predominance.
questions.question: Bilateral renal agenesis is incompatible with life primarily due to:

questions.explanation: The loop of Henle becomes functionally mature at approximately 1 year of age. At birth, infant kidneys cannot concentrate urine as effectively as adult kidneys because the loops of Henle are short and the medullary concentration gradient is not fully developed. This explains why infants produce dilute urine and are vulnerable to dehydration. Concentrating ability gradually improves during the first year.
questions.question: The loop of Henle becomes functionally mature:

questions.explanation: Eccrine sweat glands begin to function shortly after birth, although they are structurally mature by the 24th week of gestation. These glands develop as epidermal downgrowths into the underlying mesenchyme. They are distributed throughout most of the body and play crucial roles in thermoregulation.
questions.question: Eccrine sweat glands begin to function:
Megaureter refers to:
questions.explanation: Megaureter refers to a dilated ureter, which may result from obstruction (obstructive megaureter), reflux (refluxing megaureter), or aperistaltic segment (primary megaureter). Congenital causes include posterior urethral valves, ureteropelvic junction obstruction, or vesicoureteral reflux. Chronic dilation can lead to progressive loss of ureteral function and renal damage.

Bile flows from bile canaliculi (between hepatocytes) to Canals of Hering (transitional channels at the periphery of lobules), then to bile ductules, interlobular bile ducts, intrahepatic ducts, right and left hepatic ducts, common hepatic duct, and finally joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct which empties into the duodenum at the ampulla of Vater.
options: Bile ductules → Canals of Hering → common bile duct → duodenum
Interlobular ducts → Canals of Hering → bile ductules → common hepatic duct
Bile canaliculi → sinusoids → central vein → hepatic vein
Canals of Hering → bile ductules → interlobular bile ducts → intrahepatic ducts →
Bile canaliculi → space of Disse → portal vein → duodenum
questions.question: Bile canaliculi are spaces between adjacent hepatocyte plasma membranes. Bile flows from canaliculi in which sequential pathway toward the duodenum?
All mammalian cells contain a cytoplasm and a nucleus EXCEPT which of the following?
questions.explanation: Mature mammalian erythrocytes are unique in lacking a nucleus (anucleate) as well as most other organelles including mitochondria. This anucleate state is achieved during terminal differentiation and maximizes space for hemoglobin, optimizing oxygen-carrying capacity. All other cell types listed retain both nucleus and cytoplasm throughout their functional lifespan.

Wharton's jelly is a mucous connective tissue (gelatinous connective tissue) that surrounds and protects the umbilical blood vessels within the umbilical cord. It prevents compression and kinking of the vessels. The cord is typically 30-90 cm in length and 1-2 cm in diameter.
questions.question: Wharton's jelly is composed of which tissue type?

questions.explanation: TORCH is an acronym for congenital infections: Toxoplasmosis, Other (syphilis, VZV, HIV, parvovirus B19), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, and Herpes simplex. Influenza is not typically included in TORCH infections. These infections can cause serious fetal abnormalities when contracted during pregnancy.
questions.question: TORCH infections include all of the following EXCEPT:

The signal sequence on a newly synthesized protein directs it to the rough ER for translocation into the lumen. Proteins lacking this signal sequence are destined for which of the following locations?
questions.explanation: Proteins without the N-terminal signal sequence are synthesized on free cytoplasmic ribosomes and remain in the cytosol unless containing other targeting sequences directing them to mitochondria, peroxisomes, or the nucleus. Signal peptide-bearing proteins enter the rough ER for processing and eventual secretion or membrane insertion. This cotranslational targeting system, discovered by Blobel (Nobel Prize 1999), is fundamental to protein trafficking.
options: Remain cytosolic or are directed to cytoplasmic organelles
Are directed to the nucleus regardless of function
Are inserted into the outer mitochondrial membrane only

questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are identified histologically as submucosal lymphoid aggregates underlying the intestinal epithelium in the ileum. Their characteristic features include multiple secondary follicles with germinal centers, a dome-shaped villus-free follicle-associated epithelium overlying each aggregate, M cells interspersed in the FAE, and an interfollicular zone containing T lymphocytes. These features distinguish Peyer's patches from solitary intestinal lymphoid nodules and other GALT structures.
questions.question: A section through the ileum shows dome-shaped protrusions overlying lymphoid aggregates with follicle-associated epithelium containing M cells. This structure corresponds to which of the following?
options: Thymic lobule with cortex and medulla
Lymph node germinal center with B cells
Peyer's patches: ileal submucosal aggregates of lymphoid follicles

questions.question: "Apple peel" atresia involves:
questions.explanation: "Apple peel" atresia involves a large segment of the midgut loop derivatives (jejunum and ileum). A short segment of intestine distal to the atresia is coiled around the remnant of the superior mesenteric artery, resembling an apple peel. This results from vascular accidents rather than failure of recanalization.

questions.question: Cartilage is classified as which of the following tissue types and is characterized by which unique feature that distinguishes it from most other connective tissues?
options: Muscle tissue with highly specialized contractile cells
Avascular tissue with sparse cells in a firm matrix
Epithelial tissue lining the joint cavities
Specialized adipose tissue for joint cushioning
questions.explanation: Cartilage is a specialized connective tissue where chondrocytes are embedded within lacunae in a firm, gel-like matrix. Its most distinctive feature is avascularity — cartilage contains no blood vessels, nerves, or lymphatics; it receives nutrition by diffusion through the matrix from surrounding perichondrium or synovial fluid. This avascularity explains the slow healing of cartilage injuries compared to vascularized tissues.

questions.question: Foramen secundum atrial septal defects result from:
questions.explanation: Foramen secundum defects result from excessive resorption of septum primum, septum secundum, or both. This is the most common type of atrial septal defect (ASD). The defect allows abnormal left-to-right shunting after birth, potentially causing right heart volume overload.

At the 2- and 4-cell stages, blastomeres are loosely bound. With the third division producing 8 cells, compaction occurs, producing tightly bound cells. This compaction maximizes cell-to-cell contact and is essential for subsequent differentiation into inner cell mass and trophoblast.
questions.question: Compaction of blastomeres occurs at which cell stage?

questions.explanation: Persistent renal lobulation in infants is a normal variation representing incompletely fused renal lobes. The lobulated appearance typically disappears during infancy as nephrons grow. Each lobe consists of a pyramid and its overlying cortex. External lobulation should not be confused with renal scarring, which represents pathological loss of renal tissue usually from reflux nephropathy or infection.
questions.question: Renal lobulation that persists after birth is:
The anal canal below the pectinate line is supplied by which blood vessels, innervated by somatic nerves, and lined by what epithelium?
options: Inferior rectal artery, somatic (pudendal nerve) innervation, keratinized stratified
Superior rectal artery, autonomic innervation, simple columnar epithelium
Middle rectal artery, autonomic innervation, transitional epithelium
Superior rectal artery, somatic innervation, non-keratinized squamous epithelium
Internal iliac artery only, somatic innervation, simple cuboidal epithelium
questions.explanation: Below the pectinate (dentate) line, the anal canal is supplied by the inferior rectal artery (branch of the internal pudendal artery), is innervated by somatic fibers (pudendal nerve — pain, temperature, touch sensation), and is lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium continuous with perianal skin. Above the pectinate line, the mucosa is simple columnar, supplied by the superior rectal artery, and innervated by autonomic fibers (relatively insensitive to pain).

Taste buds are formed by inductive interaction between epithelial cells of the tongue and invading gustatory nerve cells from the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve (CN VII). This interaction is essential for taste bud development in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
questions.question: Taste buds form by inductive interaction between epithelial cells and which nerve?
Langerhans cells first appear in fetal skin at:
questions.explanation: Langerhans cells, which are antigen-presenting cells of the immune system, appear in fetal skin at 6 weeks of gestation. They demonstrate functional activity at around 12-14 weeks of gestation. These cells are part of the skin-associated lymphoid tissue (SALT) and play crucial roles in adaptive immunity.

questions.question: Which paranasal sinuses develop before birth?
questions.explanation: The maxillary and sphenoidal sinuses develop before birth as diverticula from the nasal cavity. The frontal and ethmoid sinuses develop after birth. Enlargement of all sinuses is associated with overall facial skeleton growth, providing space for jaw development and teeth eruption.

questions.question: Which structure forms from the pars iridica retinae of the optic cup?
questions.explanation: The anterior 1/5th of the inner layer of the optic cup, called pars iridica retinae, forms the inner layer of the iris. The pars ciliaris retinae forms the ciliary body epithelium. These anterior derivatives of the optic cup do not develop photoreceptors like the posterior portions.

questions.question: The mesonephros functions for approximately how many weeks?
questions.explanation: The mesonephros functions as an interim kidney for approximately 4 weeks (from weeks 6-10 of development). It appears late in the 4th week and degenerates toward the end of the first trimester. In males, some caudal tubules persist to form parts of the reproductive system, but in females, the mesonephros disappears almost completely.

The muscles of facial expression are derived from the second pharyngeal arch and are innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII). This includes muscles like orbicularis oculi, orbicularis oris, buccinator, platysma, and the occipitofrontalis. Paralysis of CN VII results in facial weakness (Bell's palsy).
questions.question: The muscles of facial expression are innervated by which cranial nerve?

questions.explanation: A vitelline fistula represents complete persistence of the vitelline duct, creating a communication between the ileum and umbilicus. Meconium (intestinal contents) oozes out of the umbilicus. This requires surgical repair to close the fistula and restore intestinal continuity. It differs from a urachal fistula, which would drain urine.
questions.question: A vitelline fistula is characterized by:

questions.explanation: The JGA has three components: (1) juxtaglomerular (granular) cells — modified smooth muscle of the afferent arteriole that secrete renin; (2) macula densa — specialized DCT cells that sense NaCl concentration and signal to JG cells; (3) extraglomerular mesangial cells (lacis cells) — mediators between macula densa and JG cells. Together they regulate renin release and hence blood pressure via the RAAS.
options: Podocytes, mesangial cells, and parietal cells
Collecting duct cells, juxtaglomerular cells, and podocytes
Macula densa, vasa recta, and PCT cells
Distal tubule cells, podocytes, and parietal epithelium
questions.question: The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) is a specialized structure that regulates blood pressure and filtration. Which three components make up the JGA?

questions.explanation: In membranous nephropathy, subepithelial immune complex deposits cause the GBM to appear diffusely thickened on light microscopy. With silver methenamine staining, the GBM shows characteristic 'spike and dome' or 'spike' formation — projections of GBM material growing up between and around the subepithelial deposits. Immunofluorescence shows granular IgG and C3 deposits in a peripheral (capillary wall) pattern. This is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults.
options: No visible changes on light microscopy
questions.question: In membranous nephropathy, immune complexes deposit on the subepithelial aspect of the GBM (between the GBM and podocyte foot processes). On light microscopy, the GBM shows:

questions.explanation: Crossing over (exchange of chromosome segments between homologous chromosomes) occurs during prophase I of meiosis, specifically during the pachytene stage. This occurs at points called chiasmata and results in new combinations of genes, increasing genetic diversity.
questions.question: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes occurs during which meiotic stage?
Two types of mast cells exist in connective tissue; the key difference between connective tissue mast cells and mucosal mast cells is which of the following?
options: Their surface receptors for IgE differ fundamentally
Connective tissue mast cells lack histamine while mucosal mast cells contain it
Connective tissue mast cells contain heparin; mucosal mast cells contain chondroitin sulfate
Connective tissue mast cells are found in the intestinal mucosa
questions.explanation: Connective tissue mast cells (found in skin, peritoneal cavity) contain heparin as their predominant proteoglycan in granules, while mucosal mast cells (in intestinal mucosa and lung) contain chondroitin sulfate instead of heparin. Mucosal mast cells are also smaller than connective tissue mast cells. This biochemical distinction has implications for anticoagulant activity at different body sites.

questions.question: The collecting system of the kidney (collecting tubules and ducts) is derived from which embryological structure, distinct from the nephrons?
questions.explanation: Kidney development involves two distinct embryological components: (1) the ureteric bud (metanephric diverticulum), which branches from the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct and gives rise to the collecting system — collecting tubules, papillary ducts, calyces, renal pelvis, and ureter; (2) the metanephric mesenchyme (blastema), which is induced by the ureteric bud to undergo mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition, forming the nephrons (glomeruli, proximal tubules, loop of Henle, distal tubules). Failure of ureteric bud induction causes renal agenesis.

questions.question: The liver is described as a modified exocrine gland. This classification reflects which feature of hepatocytes?
options: They secrete hormones into the bloodstream
They store glycogen like endocrine cells
They secrete bile into the bile canaliculi,
questions.explanation: Hepatocytes function as exocrine secretory cells by producing bile — approximately 600–1000 mL daily — which they secrete into bile canaliculi. Bile drains through the intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary tree into the duodenum where it aids fat digestion. This secretory product (bile) traveling through a duct system to a body surface (duodenum) is the defining characteristic of an exocrine gland. Hepatocytes also have endocrine functions (producing plasma proteins, clotting factors) making the liver a uniquely multifunctional organ.

The blood-air barrier consists of: (1) the thin cytoplasm of Type I pneumocytes, (2) a fused basement membrane shared between the pneumocyte and endothelial cells (the thinnest part of the barrier), and (3) the thin cytoplasm of the capillary endothelium. The total thickness is approximately 0.2–0.5 μm. This minimal diffusion distance allows rapid O2/CO2 exchange by passive diffusion.
questions.question: The blood-air barrier across which gas exchange occurs in the lung consists of which three layers in correct sequence from alveolar air to capillary blood?
options: Type I pneumocyte → capillary endothelium → basement membrane
Type I pneumocyte → fused basement membrane → capillary endothelium
Type II pneumocyte → basement membrane → capillary endothelium

questions.question: Type I pneumocytes cover approximately 95% of the alveolar surface. Their primary structural characteristic is:
options: Cuboidal shape with numerous lamellar bodies
Extremely thin, flattened cells allowing rapid gas
questions.explanation: Type I pneumocytes (type I alveolar cells) are extremely thin, squamous epithelial cells covering about 95% of the alveolar surface. Their thinness (0.2 μm) minimizes the diffusion distance for O2 and CO2 across the blood-air barrier. They cannot divide and are renewed from Type II pneumocytes. Damage to Type I cells (as in ARDS) severely impairs gas exchange.

questions.question: The renal corpuscle consists of the glomerular tuft and Bowman's capsule. The urinary space (Bowman's space) is located between which two structures?
options: Between the endothelium and the GBM
Between the GBM and podocyte foot processes
questions.explanation: Bowman's space (urinary space) is the crescent-shaped cavity between the visceral epithelium (podocytes) covering the glomerular capillaries and the parietal epithelium (simple squamous cells) lining the outer wall of Bowman's capsule. Ultrafiltrate crosses the filtration barrier into this space, then flows into the proximal convoluted tubule. In glomerulonephritis with crescents, proliferating parietal epithelial cells and infiltrating macrophages fill Bowman's space, compressing the glomerular tuft.

Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune demyelinating disease where T cells and antibodies target CNS myelin and oligodendrocytes. Loss of myelin disrupts saltatory conduction causing the variable neurological symptoms of optic neuritis weakness sensory loss and ataxia. CNS regeneration is limited because oligodendrocytes lack the neurilemma guidance provided by Schwann cells and inhibitory molecules prevent axon regrowth through plaques.
options: Schwann cells in peripheral nerve myelin
Oligodendrocytes as CNS myelin-producing cells targeted by autoimmune attack
Microglia phagocytosing myelin debris as a secondary response
Neurons in the gray matter predominantly
questions.question: A patient with multiple sclerosis has plaques of demyelination in the CNS white matter. The cell type most directly damaged in this condition is which of the following?

options: Increased LH receptor expression on theca cells
questions.question: Atresia is the process by which most ovarian follicles are destroyed. It can occur at any stage of follicular development. Which characteristic histological change marks follicular atresia?
questions.explanation: Follicular atresia is characterized histologically by: apoptosis and pyknosis of granulosa cells, shrinkage of the oocyte, thickening and eventual hyalinization of the zona pellucida, and invasion by macrophages. The theca interna cells may persist temporarily as interstitial cells. Atresia affects the vast majority of follicles — of the approximately 2 million primordial follicles at birth, only 400 will be ovulated during a woman's reproductive lifetime.

Failure of the cranial neuropore to close results in anencephaly, a severe neural tube defect. Failure of the caudal neuropore to close with bifid vertebral arch results in spina bifida. Neural tube defects occur in about 1 in 1,000 births and are collectively known as neural tube defects.
questions.question: Failure of the cranial neuropore to close results in which condition?

questions.explanation: The decidua basalis forms the maternal portion of the placenta. The fetal portion is formed by the chorion frondosum. The decidua basalis is the part of the endometrium located beneath the implanted embryo, where maternal blood vessels are modified to supply the placenta.
questions.question: The decidua basalis forms which part of the placenta?

questions.explanation: Transitional epithelium or urothelium is the specialized epithelium lining the renal pelvis, ureters, bladder, and proximal urethra. When the bladder is empty it appears stratified cuboidal to columnar with large rounded umbrella cells at the surface; when distended it stretches to appear much thinner and more squamous. The umbrella cells are joined by tight junctions forming an impermeable barrier and have specialized cytoplasmic plaques containing uroplakin proteins resistant to urine.
questions.question: In the classification of epithelium, the urinary bladder epithelium that can change from columnar to squamous depending on distension is specifically called which of the following?

options: Acinar cells are pale-staining with irregular nuclei
Acinar cells are large cells with central nuclei and clear cytoplasm
Acinar cells are pyramidal with basophilic cytoplasm and apical zymogen granules
Acinar cells are arranged in cords surrounded by fenestrated capillaries
questions.explanation: Pancreatic acinar cells are pyramidal or triangular cells with intensely basophilic basal cytoplasm (due to abundant rough ER for enzyme synthesis) and acidophilic apical zymogen granules (containing inactive digestive enzymes). They are arranged in rounded secretory units (acini). Islet cells (of Langerhans), in contrast, are paler-staining, spherical cells arranged in cords with rich capillary networks.
questions.question: The pancreatic acinar cells produce digestive enzymes. Which morphological feature distinguishes them from islet cells?

questions.explanation: Cortical migration follows an inside-out gradient pattern. The first wave of neuroblast migration forms the deepest layer (Layer VI), while subsequent waves migrate past earlier neurons to form progressively more superficial layers. The oldest cells are in the deepest layers, and the newest cells are in the most superficial layers.
questions.question: Cortical migration occurs in which pattern in the developing cerebral cortex?
The scala vestibuli and scala tympani are separated from the cochlear duct by which membranes?
questions.explanation: The scala vestibuli is separated from the cochlear duct by the vestibular (Reissner's) membrane, while the scala tympani is separated by the basilar membrane. These membranes are formed from mesenchyme surrounding the cochlear duct that differentiates into cartilage and subsequently vacuolizes. The basilar membrane supports the organ of Corti.

questions.question: Plasma cells are responsible for antibody production and are derived from which precursor cell type?
options: B lymphocytes following antigen activation and maturation
questions.explanation: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B lymphocytes that have undergone antigen activation, B cell receptor signaling, and somatic hypermutation, resulting in high-affinity antibody-secreting cells. They are the primary humoral immune effector cells, producing thousands of antibody molecules per second. Their unique morphology (eccentric clock-face nucleus, basophilic cytoplasm) reflects extreme adaptation for protein secretion.

The most serious consequence of oligohydramnios is pulmonary hypoplasia (underdeveloped lungs), which is often lethal. Normal amniotic fluid is essential for lung development through fetal breathing movements and adequate thoracic space. Severe oligohydramnios, especially in the second trimester, prevents normal lung development. Affected neonates cannot maintain adequate gas exchange after birth.
questions.question: The most serious consequence of oligohydramnios is:

questions.explanation: Emphysema is defined histologically by permanent, abnormal enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of alveolar walls without significant fibrosis. This destroys the elastic recoil of the lung and the blood-air barrier for gas exchange. Smoking activates alveolar macrophages and neutrophils that release elastases and proteases, overwhelming the lung's protective alpha-1-antitrypsin. The result is dynamic airway collapse and air trapping during expiration.
questions.question: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) encompasses emphysema and chronic bronchitis. Histologically, emphysema involves permanent abnormal enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles with:
options: Fibrosis and collagen deposition in alveolar walls
Destruction of alveolar walls without significant fibrosis
Excessive goblet cell metaplasia in alveoli
Abundant mucin granules for mucus secretion
questions.question: Paneth cells are found at the base of intestinal crypts and are best characterized by which morphological and functional feature?
questions.explanation: Paneth cells are distinctive for their large, apical, eosinophilic secretory granules that contain antimicrobial substances including alpha-defensins (cryptdins), lysozyme, and secretory phospholipase A2. These secretions play a critical role in innate immunity by regulating microbial colonization of the intestinal crypts. They are among the longest-lived cells in the intestinal epithelium.

questions.question: Glomerular filtration rate in newborns is approximately what fraction of adult values?
questions.explanation: Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in term newborns is approximately 1/3 of adult values when corrected for body surface area. GFR increases rapidly during the first two weeks, doubles by 2-3 months, and reaches adult values (per unit surface area) by 1-2 years. The low neonatal GFR reflects immature nephrons, low renal blood flow, and high renal vascular resistance. This affects drug dosing and fluid management in neonates.

The celiac trunk supplies the abdominal foregut derivatives, including the abdominal esophagus, stomach, proximal duodenum (to the ampulla of Vater), liver, gallbladder, and pancreas. The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, and the inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut.
questions.question: The celiac trunk supplies which embryonic gut division?

questions.explanation: PNS myelin is produced by Schwann cells where one Schwann cell myelinates one internode of one axon, and the Schwann cell cytoplasm and basal lamina form the neurilemma tube that guides axon regeneration. CNS myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes where one oligodendrocyte myelinates segments of multiple axons through cytoplasmic processes, without forming a cellular tube, and CNS environment contains inhibitory factors preventing regeneration. PNS myelin contains P0 protein as the major structural protein while CNS myelin contains MBP and PLP.
options: PNS myelin is thicker but has fewer lamellae than CNS myelin
CNS myelin contains more cholesterol than PNS myelin
PNS myelin has identical protein composition to CNS myelin
Both CNS and PNS myelin are produced by identical Schwann cells
PNS Schwann cell myelin enables regeneration; CNS oligodendrocyte myelin does not
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the structural and functional difference between myelin in the PNS versus CNS?
Esophageal glands proper are located in which layer of the esophageal wall?
questions.explanation: Esophageal glands proper are small mucous glands located in the submucosa throughout the esophagus. They produce mucus that lubricates the passage of food boluses. In contrast, esophageal cardiac glands are found in the mucosa near the gastroesophageal junction. This submucosal location is a useful histological landmark for identifying esophageal tissue.

The fetal period begins at 9 weeks after fertilization and ends at birth. It is characterized by rapid body growth and differentiation of tissues and organs that were established during the embryonic period. The major events are maturation and growth rather than organogenesis.
questions.question: The fetal period begins at which week after fertilization?
The myelencephalon develops into which adult brain structure?
questions.explanation: The myelencephalon is a brain vesicle that gives rise to the medulla oblongata. It differs from the spinal cord in that its lateral walls are everted. Alar and basal plates separated by the sulcus limitans can be clearly distinguished in the myelencephalon.

The primitive streak continues to produce mesoderm until the early 4th week, after which it regresses and becomes an insignificant structure in the sacrococcygeal region. It normally degenerates and disappears by the end of the 4th week. Persistence of the primitive streak results in a sacrococcygeal teratoma.
questions.question: By the end of which week does the primitive streak normally degenerate and disappear?

questions.explanation: Protein secretion requires synthesis at rough ER ribosomes, modification and packaging in the Golgi apparatus, and transport of secretory vesicles to the cell surface for exocytosis. Cells specialized for protein secretion (pancreatic acinar cells, antibody-secreting plasma cells) are therefore characterized by abundant rough ER (basophilic cytoplasm) and prominent Golgi complex. This constellation of organelles defines the secretory pathway.
questions.question: A cell that is actively secreting proteins would be expected to have especially abundant amounts of which of the following?
options: Peroxisomes and centrioles of the cytoskeleton
Rough ER, Golgi apparatus, and secretory vesicles

questions.explanation: The superior parathyroid gland develops from the fourth pharyngeal pouch in the 5th week, along with contributions to thyroid gland formation. It remains in the neck region along with the thyroid gland. The inferior parathyroid from the third pouch descends with the thymus.
questions.question: The superior parathyroid gland develops from which pharyngeal pouch?
The allantois appears as a diverticulum from which structure?
questions.explanation: The allantois appears as a sausage-like diverticulum from the caudal wall of the yolk sac that extends into the connecting stalk. It degenerates during the second month. Blood formation occurs in its wall, and its blood vessels persist as the umbilical vein and arteries.

options: Neutrophils and eosinophils of innate immunity
Megakaryocytes and platelets of the myeloid lineage
Macrophages and dendritic cells of the Mononuclear Phagocyte System
questions.question: Monocytes in the bloodstream are precursors that differentiate into which cell types upon emigrating into tissues?
questions.explanation: Monocytes circulate in blood for 1 to 3 days before emigrating into tissues where they differentiate into tissue-resident macrophages including Kupffer cells, alveolar macrophages, microglia, and osteoclasts, or into dendritic cells depending on tissue-specific signals. This monocyte-macrophage-dendritic cell lineage comprises the MPS. Monocytes are identified by their kidney-shaped nucleus and represent 2 to 8 percent of blood leukocytes.

Bronchopulmonary segments are established by the formation of tertiary (segmental) bronchi. There are ten on the right and eight on the left. Each segment represents a functional unit of lung tissue supplied by a segmental bronchus and its branches.
questions.question: Bronchopulmonary segments are established by formation of:
Lanugo helps to hold which substance on the fetal skin?
questions.explanation: Lanugo is fine, downy hair that appears during 17-20 weeks and helps hold the vernix caseosa on the skin. Lanugo is usually shed before birth or shortly after. Premature infants often have more lanugo than full-term infants.

options: A surge of LH causing corpus luteum regression
Rising FSH stimulating new follicular growth
An increase in GnRH causing endometrial shedding
Regression of the corpus luteum with falling progesterone
questions.explanation: In the absence of fertilization and implantation, there is no hCG to rescue the corpus luteum. The corpus luteum undergoes luteolysis (structural regression) after approximately 14 days, causing progesterone and estrogen levels to fall sharply. The withdrawal of progesterone (and estrogen) from the endometrium triggers spiral artery vasospasm, ischemic necrosis of the stratum functionalis, and menstrual shedding. Rising FSH from pituitary (released from negative feedback) simultaneously begins recruiting a new cohort of follicles.
questions.question: In the female, the ovarian cycle and endometrial cycle are closely coordinated. If fertilization does NOT occur, what event signals the end of the luteal phase and onset of menstruation?
The internal elastic lamina is a prominent layer separating the tunica intima from the tunica media. It is best developed in which type of artery?
questions.explanation: The internal elastic lamina is most prominent in muscular (distributing) arteries such as the femoral, radial, and coronary arteries. It appears as a wavy, bright eosinophilic band on H&E staining and stains black with Verhoeff elastic stain. Muscular arteries also have an external elastic lamina separating the media from the adventitia. These landmarks help distinguish muscular arteries from elastic arteries in histological sections.

Primary ossification centers appear in the skeleton (skull and long bones) during 9-12 weeks. During this period, there is also rapid growth in body length, decrease in relative head growth compared to earlier stages, and beginning of erythropoiesis by the liver and spleen.
questions.question: During which weeks do primary ossification centers appear in the skeleton?

questions.explanation: Shortly after the morula enters the uterus on day 4, fluid from the uterine cavity passes through the zona pellucida to form a single fluid-filled space called the blastocystic cavity, primitive chorionic cavity, or blastocoele. This transforms the morula into a blastocyst.
questions.question: The blastocystic cavity is also known as which structure?

questions.explanation: The pontine flexure, which is a dorsal flexure, is responsible for the diamond shape of the fourth ventricle. This flexure also serves as a template for development of the cerebellum. The other brain flexures (cephalic and cervical) are ventral flexures.
questions.question: The pontine flexure is responsible for the shape of which structure?
Bowman's capsule develops from:
questions.explanation: Bowman's capsule develops from metanephric vesicles, which form from the metanephric blastema. These vesicles elongate to form S-shaped tubules. One end of the tubule invaginates to form Bowman's capsule around a developing glomerulus. The other end connects to a collecting tubule, establishing continuity of the nephron.

questions.question: The small intestine renews its epithelium approximately every 3–5 days. This rapid renewal protects against environmental damage but also makes the intestinal epithelium particularly vulnerable to:
questions.explanation: The high proliferative rate of intestinal stem cells makes the intestinal epithelium one of the most sensitive targets of cytotoxic chemotherapy and radiation therapy, which preferentially damage rapidly dividing cells. This accounts for the GI toxicity (mucositis, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting) seen with these treatments. Intestinal stem cells in the crypts are the primary target, and their loss leads to villous atrophy and malabsorption.

questions.question: Capillary hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors. On histological examination, they consist of:
questions.explanation: Capillary hemangiomas are composed of closely packed, small caliber vascular channels lined by a single layer of benign endothelial cells. The channels are thin-walled (like capillaries) and are filled with red blood cells. The stroma contains minimal supporting connective tissue. Strawberry hemangiomas in infants are the most common type, involuting spontaneously. Cavernous hemangiomas have larger, dilated blood-filled spaces with thin walls.
options: Closely packed, small, thin-walled blood-filled channels

questions.explanation: Bone matrix is mineralized by calcium phosphate crystals organized in a structure similar to hydroxyapatite [Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2]. The minerals are deposited in and around type I collagen fibers (95% of bone matrix) and the ground substance. Bone's hardness comes from these mineral crystals while its resilience comes from the collagen organic framework — together providing optimal combination of strength and flexibility.
questions.question: Bone as a specialized connective tissue is mineralized by which of the following minerals that form crystals similar to hydroxyapatite?
options: Calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate as hydroxyapatite-like crystals
Calcium sulfate (gypsum) deposited in collagen fibers
Iron oxide embedded in type II collagen
The eyepiece magnifies the actual specimen while the objective produces a virtual image
The objective creates an enlarged real image; the eyepiece further magnifies it
Both lenses function identically with only placement differing
The eyepiece lens improves resolving power; the objective only magnifies
The objective is adjusted by the coarse focus; the eyepiece by the fine focus
questions.explanation: The objective lens creates an enlarged real, inverted intermediate image of the specimen based on its proximity to the object. The eyepiece then acts as a magnifying glass to further enlarge this intermediate image for the observer's eye. Only the objective lens determines resolving power; the eyepiece simply increases perceived magnification without improving resolution.
questions.question: Which of the following features best distinguishes the 10× eyepiece lens from a 10× objective lens in terms of function within a compound microscope?

questions.explanation: Paneth cells at the base of small intestinal crypts are the primary niche cells for intestinal Lgr5+ stem cells. Paneth cells provide essential stem cell maintenance signals including Wnt3a (activating the Wnt/β-catenin pathway), Delta-like ligands (Notch signaling), and EGF family members. This direct physical and signaling contact between Paneth cells and stem cells is essential for intestinal regeneration. In colonic crypts, Paneth-like cells or stromal cells fulfill this niche function.
questions.question: The intestinal stem cell niche is located at the base of intestinal crypts, where Lgr5+ stem cells reside. These stem cells are maintained by signals from which adjacent supporting cell type?

options: Thinning of all vessel wall layers with normal valve architecture
Replacement of venous wall by arterial tissue
Cartilaginous metaplasia of the vein wall
questions.explanation: Varicose veins show irregular remodeling of the vein wall: areas of smooth muscle hypertrophy alternating with atrophy and fibrosis in the media, intimal thickening, adventitial fibrosis, and calcification. Valve leaflets are thickened and fibrotic (incompetent). The irregular contraction of the remodeled smooth muscle makes varicose veins tortuous. These changes result from chronic venous hypertension due to gravitational stress and valve failure.
questions.question: Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous superficial veins caused by incompetent venous valves. Histologically, varicose veins show which changes compared to normal veins?

questions.explanation: Asthma causes reversible airway changes including goblet cell hyperplasia (mucus hypersecretion), subepithelial collagen deposition (thickened reticular basement membrane), smooth muscle hypertrophy/hyperplasia (increased bronchoconstriction potential), and eosinophilic/mast cell/T-lymphocyte infiltration. Destruction of alveolar walls (emphysematous change) is NOT part of asthma — it is a feature of emphysema (a separate COPD entity). This distinction is critical for understanding asthma pathophysiology.
questions.question: Asthma is characterized by reversible bronchoconstriction, airway hyperresponsiveness, and inflammation. The histological changes in the asthmatic airway include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Goblet cell hyperplasia and mucus hypersecretion

questions.explanation: The proximal straight tubule (pars recta, S3 segment) is a major site for secretion of organic anions and cations into the tubular lumen. Organic anion transporters (OAT1, OAT3) and organic cation transporters (OCT2) on basolateral membranes move drugs, metabolites, uric acid, and endogenous compounds from peritubular blood into tubular cells, which then export them apically into the lumen. This is the mechanism by which drugs like penicillin, probenecid, and methotrexate are excreted in urine.
questions.question: The proximal straight tubule (pars recta) of the nephron has an important detoxification role. Which group of substances does it secrete into the tubular lumen?
Polyhydramnios may be associated with which fetal condition?
questions.explanation: Polyhydramnios (excessive amniotic fluid, usually >2000 ml) may be associated with esophageal atresia or other conditions that prevent the fetus from swallowing amniotic fluid. It can also occur with anencephaly, where there is excessive CSF production. Oligohydramnios (too little fluid) is associated with renal agenesis.

questions.question: Which cellular organelle is correctly described as having its own DNA and ribosomes, and is thought to have originated from endosymbiosis with an ancient bacterium?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria contain their own circular DNA (mtDNA), 70S ribosomes, and double membrane — features consistent with endosymbiotic origin from an ancient alpha-proteobacterium engulfed by a proto-eukaryotic cell. Mitochondrial ribosomes are sensitive to the same antibiotics that inhibit bacterial ribosomes. mtDNA is inherited maternally in most species and is used for phylogenetic and forensic analysis.

questions.question: Megacystis (enlarged bladder) may result from:
questions.explanation: Megacystis (enlarged bladder) commonly results from posterior urethral valves in males, which cause bladder outlet obstruction. The increased pressure leads to bladder wall hypertrophy and trabeculation. Prolonged obstruction can cause bilateral hydronephrosis and renal damage. Diagnosis is often made prenatally by ultrasound. Endoscopic valve ablation is the treatment.

questions.question: The intrinsic muscles of the tongue are derived from:
questions.explanation: The muscles of the tongue are derived from occipital myotomes (somites) that migrate with the hypoglossal nerve. This explains why tongue muscles are innervated by cranial nerve XII despite developing from somitic mesoderm. The extrinsic and intrinsic tongue muscles share this developmental origin.

questions.question: Adipocytes (fat cells) in connective tissue are specialized for which of the following primary functions?
questions.explanation: Adipocytes are highly specialized connective tissue cells derived from mesenchyme that store neutral fat (triglycerides) as a single large droplet (unilocular white adipose tissue) or multiple small droplets (multilocular brown adipose tissue). Their metabolic functions include energy storage/release, thermal insulation, organ cushioning, and (importantly recognized now) endocrine signaling through adipokines like leptin and adiponectin.
options: Synthesis and secretion of immunoglobulins by plasma cells
Phagocytosis of debris from tissue injury
Secretion of histamine during allergic reactions
Cytoplasmic storage of neutral lipids for energy and insulation

questions.explanation: Dizygotic (fraternal) twins result from fertilization of two separate ova by two different spermatozoa. These twins have separate amnions, chorions, and placentas (though placentas may be fused). They are genetically no more similar than any siblings and may be of different sexes.
questions.question: Dizygotic twins result from fertilization of how many ova?

questions.explanation: Cholangiocytes are reliably identified by immunostaining for cytokeratin 7 (CK7) — a type II intermediate filament characteristic of biliary epithelial cells and some hepatic progenitor cells. CK7 positivity differentiates bile duct cells from hepatocytes (which are negative for CK7 but express albumin). CK7 immunostaining is used in liver biopsies to identify ductular reactions, bile duct proliferation, and metastatic carcinomas of biliary origin.
questions.question: The interlobular bile ducts in the portal tracts are lined by cuboidal to low columnar epithelial cells called cholangiocytes. Which immunohistochemical marker is most useful for identifying these cells?

questions.explanation: The superior olivary nucleus, found at the upper pons level, is part of the auditory pathway. It receives input from the cochlear nuclei bilaterally and projects to the lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus. It is involved in sound localization.
questions.question: The superior olivary nucleus is part of which pathway?

questions.explanation: The submucosa consists of dense irregular connective tissue that houses larger caliber blood vessels, lymphatics, and lymphoid tissue. This is in contrast to the lamina propria, which contains loose connective tissue with smaller vessels. The submucosa also contains the Meissner plexus of autonomic nerves.
questions.question: In a cross-section of the GIT wall, the layer identified as having the densest connective tissue with large blood and lymph vessels is the:
The definitive urinary bladder develops from which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation: The definitive urinary bladder develops from the urogenital sinus (part of the cloaca). The allantois contributes to formation of the urachus (median umbilical ligament). The trigone of the bladder is derived from incorporated portions of the mesonephric ducts.

questions.question: The red nucleus is located in which part of the midbrain?
questions.explanation: The red nucleus is located in the tegmentum of the upper midbrain. It receives input from the cerebellum and cerebral cortex and gives rise to the rubrospinal tract. It is involved in motor coordination. It appears reddish due to high vascularity and iron content.

questions.question: Fingernails reach the fingertips by approximately:
questions.explanation: Fingernails reach the fingertips by the 32nd week of gestation, while toenails reach toe tips by the 36th week. Development of fingernails precedes toenails by approximately 4 weeks. Nails begin developing at the tips of digits around the 10th week as thickened areas called nail fields.

questions.question: During the pseudoglandular period (5-16 weeks), which structures are absent?
questions.explanation: During the pseudoglandular period (5-16 weeks), branching continues to form terminal bronchioles, but respiratory bronchioles and alveoli are not yet present. The lung resembles a gland histologically during this period. Respiration is not possible if a fetus is born during this stage.

questions.question: The most common cause of bilateral hydronephrosis in male fetuses is:
questions.explanation: The most common cause of bilateral hydronephrosis in male fetuses is posterior urethral valves (PUV), which cause bladder outlet obstruction. PUV are membranous folds in the posterior urethra that obstruct urinary flow. Prenatal ultrasound shows bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, distended bladder, and oligohydramnios. Postnatal endoscopic valve ablation is required. Severe cases cause renal dysplasia and chronic kidney disease.

The epiphyseal plate (physis or growth plate) is the cartilaginous disc separating the primary ossification center (diaphysis) from secondary ossification centers (epiphyses) in growing long bones. It allows longitudinal bone growth through the process of endochondral ossification. Fusion of the epiphyseal plate (growth plate closure) at skeletal maturity halts further longitudinal growth; premature closure causes short stature while delayed closure extends growth.
questions.question: Secondary ossification centers in long bones develop after birth at the epiphyses. The region separating primary and secondary ossification centers during growth is called which of the following?

questions.explanation: General sensory innervation to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue is provided by the lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3). Special taste sensation from this area is provided by the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
questions.question: General sensation from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue is provided by:

questions.explanation: The definitive kidney formed from the metanephros becomes functional near the 12th week, when urine begins to be passed into the amniotic cavity. During fetal life, the placenta performs excretory functions. Urine mixed with amniotic fluid is swallowed by the fetus and recycled through the kidneys.
questions.question: The definitive kidney becomes functional near which week?

questions.explanation: The thyroid gland has a pathognomonic histological appearance of spherical follicles filled with eosinophilic homogeneous colloid which is iodinated thyroglobulin, lined by a single layer of follicular cells. The height of the follicular epithelium reflects activity: flat squamous cells in inactive thyroid and tall columnar cells in hyperstimulated thyroid. No other endocrine gland has this follicular colloid-filled architecture, making thyroid histology immediately recognizable.
options: Colloid-filled follicles lined by follicular epithelium
Parathyroid gland with chief cell cords
Pituitary gland with acidophils and basophils
questions.question: A tissue section shows a gland composed of spherical follicles filled with homogeneous pink material lined by a single layer of cuboidal cells. This histological picture is most consistent with which of the following organs?

options: Smooth muscle cells of the colon
questions.question: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) such as butyrate are produced by bacterial fermentation in the large intestine. Butyrate is the primary energy source for which cell type?
questions.explanation: Butyrate produced by colonic bacterial fermentation of dietary fiber is the primary metabolic fuel for colonocytes. Colonocytes preferentially oxidize butyrate (beta-oxidation) rather than glucose, deriving approximately 70% of their energy from this short-chain fatty acid. Butyrate also has anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative effects on the colonic epithelium. Deficiency (from low-fiber diets) may contribute to ulcerative colitis and colorectal cancer pathogenesis.

Extrahepatic biliary atresia typically presents with jaundice developing soon after birth due to obstruction of bile flow. This is the most common serious anomaly of the biliary system. If uncorrected surgically, it leads to progressive liver damage and death. Early diagnosis and surgical intervention (Kasai procedure) are critical.
questions.question: Extrahepatic biliary atresia typically presents with:

questions.explanation: The terminal sac period extends from 26 weeks to birth, during which terminal sacs (primitive alveoli) form and capillaries establish close contact with the epithelium. The epithelium thins from cuboidal to squamous, creating the blood-air barrier. Surfactant production by type II pneumocytes begins during this period.
questions.question: The terminal sac period of lung development extends from:
The functional unit of the kidney is the:
