questions.question: A physiotherapist applies manual pressure to a patient's pelvis to prevent unwanted movement while the hip is exercised. What is this technique called?

options: Tests only maximal isometric force production
Measures force-velocity relationship across multiple speeds
Quantifies proprioceptive joint position sense accuracy
Assesses endurance capacity rather than peak force
Is limited to testing only the quadriceps and hamstrings
questions.explanation: Isokinetic dynamometry maintains constant angular velocity through the entire range of motion, providing resistance equal to the force applied at every joint angle and velocity. This allows measurement of peak torque, total work, and power across multiple preset velocities (e.g., 60, 180, 300 degrees/second), revealing the force-velocity relationship for the joint being tested. Clinically, this enables bilateral comparison of limb symmetry, identification of velocity-specific deficits, and calculation of hamstring-to-quadriceps strength ratios, all of which guide return-to-sport decisions in knee rehabilitation.
questions.question: Isokinetic dynamometry in physiotherapy assessment provides information that differs from free weight or isometric strength testing primarily because it:

questions.explanation: Suitable strong muscles working against maximal resistance can be used to secure overflow of effort and ensure contraction of muscles working across an immobilised joint, for example activating Quadriceps and Hamstrings via strong contraction of hip and foot muscles of either leg. The patient is also taught to practise voluntary static contractions frequently, following the slogan 'five minutes in every hour'. This approach helps prevent rapid muscle wasting in coarse muscles such as Quadriceps, Deltoid, Gastrocnemius and Glutei.
questions.question: Which strategy is recommended to maintain Quadriceps and Hamstrings activity while the knee joint itself is immobilised after injury?
options: Complete rest of all muscles in the limb until the joint heals
Forced passive stretching of the immobilised muscles daily
Strong contraction of hip and foot muscles to produce overflow of effort into the immobilised muscles
Resisted exercise applied directly across the injured joint
Electrical stimulation used as the sole means of maintaining bulk

questions.question: Laura Mitchell's method of relaxation is based on which physiological principle?
options: Maximal contraction followed by sudden release
Reciprocal relaxation produced by actively changing joint position
Sustained traction applied along a joint's long axis
questions.explanation: Physiological relaxation, devised by Laura Mitchell, is based on reciprocal relaxation: the patient actively moves each joint out of a defined position of tension using precise voluntary orders, which relaxes the muscles that held the tense position. This differs fundamentally from the contrast method, which instead relies on a preceding strong contraction. Mitchell's method allows patients to self-administer relaxation at any time without needing a preliminary contraction.

questions.question: Rhythmic initiation is a relaxation technique specifically designed for which condition?
options: The spasticity of upper motor neurone lesions generally
The flaccidity following peripheral nerve injury
questions.explanation: Rhythmic initiation is described specifically as a relaxation technique for application to the rigidity of Parkinson's Disease, progressing from passive movement through active-assisted and resisted movement to free active movement while maintaining rhythm throughout. The technique helps Parkinson patients improve their ability to initiate movement. Maintaining the rhythm during each transition between stages is essential to the technique's success.

questions.question: During rhythmic stabilisation, why is the patient commanded simply to 'HOLD!' against resistance applied from varying directions rather than given a directional command?
options: Directional commands always cause complete relaxation
Directional commands eliminate the rotatory component
Directional commands are reserved for hold-relax only
Directional commands prevent any build-up of excitation
A directional command would produce isometric reversal of antagonists rather than the required co-contraction
questions.explanation: In rhythmic stabilisation the patient is commanded to 'HOLD' against resistance from any direction because a directional effort would instead produce an isometric reversal of antagonists rather than the simultaneous co-contraction the technique requires. The rotatory component receives special attention because it is important for 'locking in' the joint. This co-contraction builds excitation, increases strength, and improves circulation since the contraction energy is released as heat without movement.

options: Strengthening of the shortened muscles alone without addressing the antagonists
Complete immobilisation of the joint until muscle balance spontaneously returns
Passive stretching of the antagonist muscles exclusively
Static splintage of the joint in a neutral position only
Relaxation techniques for the shortened muscles combined with strengthening of their antagonists
questions.explanation: Persistent tension or hypertonicity of muscles on one aspect of a joint produces muscular imbalance leading to adaptive shortening of the tense muscles and progressive lengthening and weakening of the antagonists on the opposing aspect. Relaxation techniques for the shortened muscles combined with strengthening techniques for their antagonists, followed by integration of their reciprocal action, are used to restore the increased range of movement. Both agonist and antagonist muscles are inefficient once this imbalance develops, so both sides require attention rather than just one.
questions.question: Adaptive shortening of muscles on one side of a joint, with lengthening and weakening of the antagonists on the opposite side, is best addressed by which combined approach?

questions.explanation: When two equal forces act at a common point but in opposite directions, they cancel each other out and the body remains at rest. This is the basic definition of equilibrium produced by balanced opposing forces. Unequal opposing forces, by contrast, would cause movement toward the greater force.
questions.question: Two equal forces act at a common point in opposite directions on a body. What is the immediate mechanical result?

options: Facilitated or assisted movement to help initiate the response
Immediate resisted exercise against maximal load
Mass exercise performed in a large group
Unsupervised free exercise practised at home
questions.explanation: Patients who have suffered brain damage or are unable to initiate movement cannot cooperate in free exercises until performance has been facilitated and voluntary control established. Assisted exercise or facilitation techniques therefore precede the introduction of free exercise in such cases. This sequencing respects the patient's actual neuromuscular capacity rather than assuming free exercise is always the appropriate starting point.
questions.question: A patient with brain damage cannot initiate a movement through voluntary free exercise. What is the most appropriate initial active movement strategy?

options: Eccentric work always requires less concentration than concentric work
A recovering muscle may resist a load eccentrically before moving concentrically
Eccentric work eliminates the need for any external resistance
Eccentric work cannot occur in a muscle recovering from paralysis
Eccentric work always uses more energy than equivalent concentric work
questions.explanation: Because the physiological cost of eccentric work is lower, probably only about a quarter of that required for concentric work, a muscle recovering from paralysis may sometimes be persuaded to contract to resist a force before it is able to produce movement concentrically. This makes eccentric loading a useful early step in the progression of strengthening for a weak or recovering muscle. Considerable concentration is, however, still required to control the speed of these exercises, since eccentric work in natural movement tends to occur rapidly.
questions.question: Why does the physiological cost of eccentric muscle work being lower than concentric work make it a useful early strategy in muscle recovery after paralysis?

questions.explanation: As specific pathways are used for the production of specific movements, the patterns of movement used to obtain facilitation should match the patient's most urgent functional needs and remain the same each time the movement is repeated. Changing the pattern randomly would not reliably reinforce the same neuromuscular pathway. This principle underlies why PNF patterns closely mirror functional movements rather than abstract anatomical motions.
options: Variation always increases the risk of joint injury
Consistency eliminates the need for any resistance
Random variation produces faster strength gains
Pattern consistency is irrelevant to neuromuscular pathways
Specific pathways serve specific movements, so repetition must stay consistent
questions.question: Why must the pattern of movement used to obtain facilitation be kept the same on each repetition rather than varied randomly?

questions.explanation: The disadvantages of Group Treatment arise from the abuse or misunderstanding of the system, with faulty selection of patients, inadequate explanation, lack of or inefficient grading of groups, overcrowding, and poor technique of instruction identified as the most common causes of failure to benefit the patient. The keynote of success in Group Exercise, as in any exercise therapy, is to give the patient the right exercises at the right time and in the right way. Careful grading and re-grading of groups at frequent intervals is therefore essential to avoid these pitfalls.
options: It always results in complete cessation of all group activity
It has no relationship to the eventual benefit gained by patients
It is only relevant to Mass Exercise, never to Group Exercise
It leads to mismatched exercises that fail to suit individual patients' capacities within the group
It is corrected automatically through the presence of other patients
questions.question: Why is faulty selection of patients identified as one of the most common causes of failure in Group Treatment?

questions.explanation: To 'facilitate' means to make easy or easier, so Neuromuscular Facilitation is the process by which the response of the neuromuscular mechanism is made easier when the demands of voluntary effort are weakened. It works by supplying the demand necessary to elicit a satisfactory response and improving conductivity of the relevant nervous pathways. This is distinct from passive technique, since voluntary effort remains central to facilitation.
questions.question: What is the fundamental aim of Neuromuscular Facilitation as a treatment principle?
options: To eliminate all voluntary effort from movement
To replace active exercise with passive technique
To make the response of the neuromuscular mechanism easier
To increase joint range through forced stretching
To suppress reflex activity throughout treatment

questions.explanation: Exercise is safe and beneficial in chronic kidney disease, improving cardiorespiratory fitness, muscle strength, functional capacity, and quality of life without accelerating renal function decline. The high cardiovascular mortality in CKD is directly addressed by exercise-induced improvements in cardiac and metabolic risk factors. Pre-dialysis and dialysis patients both benefit from structured exercise programmes. Physiotherapists should provide exercise guidance adapted to renal function stage, dialysis schedule (intra-dialytic exercise is feasible and effective), and comorbidities.
questions.question: Exercise benefits for patients with chronic kidney disease managed by a physiotherapist include improved fitness because exercise:
options: Accelerates kidney deterioration by increasing protein catabolism
Worsens renal function by increasing creatinine production
Improves fitness, functional capacity, and quality of life
Provides no possible benefits for renal disease patients
Represents an absolute contraindication to all physical activity
Emotional state has no measurable influence on habitual posture
Unhappiness and conflict always produce postures dominated by extension
Only physical factors, never psychological ones, influence posture
Confidence is reflected exclusively by increased flexion of the trunk
Joy, happiness and confidence are reflected by an alert posture in which extension predominates
questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between emotional state and postural pattern, according to the described connection between mental attitude and posture?
questions.explanation: Emotion and mental attitude have a profound effect on the nervous system as a whole, reflected in posture: joy, happiness and confidence are stimulating and are reflected by an alert posture in which positions of extension predominate, while unhappiness, conflict and feelings of inferiority produce postures in which positions of flexion are most conspicuous. This connection between mental and physical attitude has long been recognised and used deliberately in dance and stage performance. It also raises the converse question of whether consciously adopting an extended, confident physical posture might in turn influence mental attitude.

options: It is the joint over which the weak muscles work and where movement is repeated
It is the area proximal to the weak muscles that maintains stability during the technique
It is the part distal to the pivot that 'locks in' during isometric work
It has no defined anatomical relationship to the pivot
It is always the strongest distal joint in the pattern
questions.question: In the technique of repeated contractions using timing for emphasis, what is the role of the 'stabilising part' of the body?
questions.explanation: In timing for emphasis, three elements are defined: the stabilising part, proximal to the joint where the weak muscles work, which maintains stability; the pivot, the joint where weak muscle activity is emphasised; and the handle, distal to the pivot, which 'locks in' so the limb moves as a single unit. Both the stabilising part and the handle work isometrically against maximal resistance while movement is initiated at the pivot. This structured arrangement allows irradiation to strengthen the weak muscles at the pivot from either proximal or distal strong components.

options: Concentration of attention, precision, and repetition
Assistance, resistance, and free exercise combined
questions.question: Which three essentials are described as central to the process of learning Frenkel's alternative method of movement control?
questions.explanation: The process of learning Frenkel's alternative method of movement control is similar to learning any new exercise, with the essentials being concentration of the attention, precision, and repetition. This mirrors the broader principle that establishing any new coordinated movement pattern, whether in re-education of ataxia or general skill learning, requires focused, accurate, and repeated practice. The ultimate aim is to establish control so the patient is confident in performing activities essential for independence in daily life.

questions.question: A patient with a weak grasp pattern is asked to perform a strong contralateral limb pattern, after which the weak hand pattern noticeably improves in strength during testing. Which PNF principle best explains this observed improvement?
questions.explanation: Re-inforcement always proceeds from strength to weakness, so the maximal contraction of a strong pattern can re-inforce the action of a weaker, related pattern through irradiation, the spread of excitation in the central nervous system caused by intense proprioceptive stimulation. This explains why strengthening one limb pattern can produce a measurable improvement in a related but weaker pattern elsewhere in the body. This principle underlies the deliberate use of strong patterns to support rehabilitation of weaker ones.
options: Irradiation from the strong pattern reinforces the weaker, related pattern
Successive induction of the antagonist alone explains the change
The improvement results purely from increased joint traction
Rhythmic initiation is responsible for the strength change
The change reflects accessory movement of the wrist only

questions.explanation: Stability depends largely on the size of the base of support, and standing on one leg drastically reduces this base compared with a wider stance. A smaller base makes it easier for the line of gravity to fall near or outside its margin with only slight displacement. This is why single-leg stance is used clinically to progressively challenge balance.
questions.question: Which factor chiefly explains why the human body is least stable when standing on one leg compared with standing with feet apart?
options: The centre of gravity is lowered
The base of support is markedly reduced
The line of gravity is eliminated
Gravity no longer acts on the body

questions.question: Why is dynamic posture generally considered more difficult to assess than static posture?
options: Dynamic posture never involves any alignment of body segments at all
Static posture always requires more muscular effort than dynamic posture
Dynamic posture is unrelated to the alignment used in static positions
It involves constant readjustment throughout the progress of movement rather than a single fixed alignment
Assessment difficulty has no relationship to whether posture is fixed or changing
questions.explanation: As dynamic postures involve constant readjustment to maintain the efficiency of the postural background throughout the progress of movement, they are much more difficult to assess than static postures, which represent a single, relatively fixed pattern. In many activities, however, the same alignment of body segments satisfactory in erect static postures forms the basis from which these ongoing adjustments are made, such as in walking or sitting and writing. In many dynamic postures the plane of this alignment becomes inclined or even horizontal, altering how gravity affects each segment and requiring correspondingly adjusted muscle work.

questions.question: A physiotherapist notices a patient with stiff shoulders compensating for lost elevation range by hyperextending the lumbar spine. What broader postural principle does this illustrate?
options: Joint stiffness never produces any compensatory postural change elsewhere
Lost range in one joint can be masked by adjacent joint mobility
Compensatory movement always occurs at exactly the same joint that is stiff
Hyperextension of the lumbar spine always indicates primary lumbar pathology
Compensation of this type has no bearing on postural assessment
questions.explanation: If joint stiffness has developed, specific mobility measures for the affected joint are needed to ensure that loss of range in that joint is not masked by a compensatory increase in mobility of adjacent joints, with stiff shoulders unable to permit full arm elevation readily compensated by hyperextension in the lumbar spine given as a specific example. Recognising this compensatory pattern is important during postural and mobility assessment, since treating only the visible compensation without addressing the true site of restriction would fail to resolve the underlying problem. This principle underlies why targeted, joint-specific mobility measures are preferred over generalised exercise alone in such cases.

options: Obese individuals have higher haemoglobin concentrations
The larger body mass requires more energy to move and support
Obese individuals use anaerobic metabolism preferentially
Fat tissue is more metabolically active than muscle during exercise
Higher cardiac output in obese individuals increases energy use
questions.explanation: Absolute energy expenditure during weight-bearing exercise (walking, stair climbing) increases proportionally with body mass because a greater force must be generated to move and support a larger mass against gravity and inertia. A 120 kg individual expends approximately twice the absolute calories walking at the same speed as a 60 kg individual. This means that even low-intensity exercise produces substantial energy expenditure in obese patients, and physiotherapists should account for this when prescribing and progressing exercise programmes for weight management.
questions.question: The primary physiological mechanism explaining why obese individuals have a higher absolute exercise energy expenditure than lean individuals at the same exercise intensity is:

questions.explanation: Instruction by passive movement is rarely necessary except for patients who are blind or deaf, or for those who have sustained long periods of inactivity during which the pattern of movement, as recorded by kinaesthetic sensation, has been forgotten. This makes passive movement a targeted, situation-specific teaching method rather than a general first-line approach, reserved for cases where verbal or visual instruction alone would be insufficient. It represents a distinct use of passive movement, separate from its roles in relaxation, joint maintenance, or mobilisation.
options: As the first-choice method for every new patient regardless of ability
Only for patients who are able to see a clear physical demonstration
Exclusively for teaching formal commands used in competitive activities
For patients who are blind, deaf, or have forgotten the pattern
As a substitute for verbal instruction in all group exercise sessions
questions.question: When is instruction by passive movement specifically indicated as a teaching method, according to the described circumstances of its use?

options: Completely curing all structural disc pathology
Core strengthening, flexibility, and gradual activity return
Eliminating all recurrence risk after one exercise course
Providing maximum benefits only in the acute phase
questions.question: Exercise benefits for low back pain management in physiotherapy are primarily related to which mechanism relevant to spine rehabilitation?
questions.explanation: Evidence-based physiotherapy for low back pain prioritises core stabilisation exercise (targeting transversus abdominis and multifidus), flexibility training (hip flexors, hamstrings, thoracic spine), and progressive return to functional activities. These components address the primary deficits in chronic LBP: reduced core muscle activation, movement avoidance behaviours, and physical deconditioning. Gradual progressive loading through graded activity principles reduces pain catastrophising and kinesiophobia while improving functional capacity.

questions.question: Which best explains why functional re-education places emphasis on activities the patient needs for everyday living rather than on isolated measurements of joint range or muscle power?
options: Isolated measurements are always more accurate than functional testing
Joint range and muscle power have no relationship to function at all
Functional activities cannot be recorded or reviewed over time
Functional re-education replaces the need for any assessment
Restoration of needed function, not isolated measurements, is the true criterion of progress
questions.explanation: Restoration of functions which are needed is described as the sole criterion of progress, since recorded measurements such as joint range or muscle bulk do not necessarily indicate functional efficiency or purposeful activity to the patient. Emphasising the specific purpose of each activity helps direct the patient's effort toward regaining abilities they actually need. This functional focus is central to motivating patients and demonstrating meaningful rehabilitation progress.

options: The therapeutic use of heat to relieve pain and stiffness
The therapeutic use of movement to restore, maintain, or improve function
The therapeutic use of electrical stimulation for muscle re-education
The therapeutic use of manual massage to improve circulation
The therapeutic use of medication to control inflammation
questions.explanation: Exercise therapy is fundamentally the use of movement, whether active, assisted, resisted, or passive, applied for a therapeutic purpose such as restoring or maintaining function. It is distinguished from other physical agents such as heat, electrotherapy, or massage, which may be used alongside it but are not movement-based in themselves. This distinction is foundational to classifying exercise therapy as a discrete treatment approach.
questions.question: Which of the following best defines exercise therapy as a treatment modality?

options: Resisted movement, then passive movement, then free active movement
Free active movement, then passive movement, then resisted movement
Passive movement, then active-assisted movement, then resisted movement, then free active movement
Active-assisted movement only, repeated without progression
Isometric holding, then passive movement, then resisted movement
questions.explanation: Rhythmic initiation begins by taking the limb passively and rhythmically through the pattern, progresses to active-assisted movement once relaxation has occurred, then to resisted movement, and finally to free active movement once the physiotherapist's hands are removed. Maintaining the rhythm throughout each transition is essential. This graded progression specifically aids initiation of movement in rigid Parkinsonian muscles.
questions.question: Which sequence correctly describes the progression of rhythmic initiation from start to finish?
Why is a general attitude of rest, such as reclining in a chair rather than sitting bolt upright, recommended before giving massage or passive movement to a supported limb?
questions.explanation: Massage and passive movement both presuppose relaxation of the area under treatment, and while local relaxation is obtained by applying the general principles already described to that specific area, a general attitude of rest assists the process, so an abducted, supported arm relaxes more readily when the patient reclines in a chair than when sitting bolt upright. This illustrates how whole-body positioning influences the success of even quite localised relaxation techniques. Preparing the whole patient for rest therefore complements the local measures applied to the specific area being treated.
options: It assists the process of local relaxation needed for effective massage and passive movement
It eliminates the need for any support of the limb itself
It converts the technique into an assisted active exercise
It has no bearing on the quality of local relaxation achieved
It is required only for patients experiencing pathological spasm

questions.question: A joint permits flexion and extension about one axis only, as seen at the interphalangeal joints. How is this joint classified?
questions.explanation: Uni-axial joints permit movement about one axis only, and a hinge joint such as the interphalangeal joints allows flexion and extension about that single axis. A pivot joint, the other uni-axial type, instead allows only rotation, as at the atlanto-axial joint. This classification is based purely on the number and type of axes of movement permitted, not on the size of the joint.

questions.question: The specific benefits of plyometric training for physiotherapy rehabilitation in lower limb explosive strength recovery include:
questions.explanation: Plyometric training exploits the stretch-shortening cycle (SSC): rapid eccentric pre-loading of elastic elements (titin, tendon) followed by immediate explosive concentric contraction. SSC training improves neuromuscular efficiency (rate of force development, motor unit synchronisation), elastic energy storage and return in tendon, and the stiffness regulation of the musculotendinous unit. These adaptations are specific to explosive activities (jumping, sprinting, change of direction) and are essential components of late-stage lower limb rehabilitation before return to sport.
options: Exclusively improving cardiovascular fitness without neuromuscular benefits
Strengthening only slow-twitch type I muscle fibres
Producing the same adaptations as static resistance training
Enhancing stretch-shortening cycle efficiency and explosive power

questions.question: Fast-twitch type IIa fibres differ from type IIb fibres in physiotherapy exercise prescription because type IIa fibres have:
questions.explanation: Type IIa (fast-twitch oxidative-glycolytic) fibres have substantially more mitochondria and higher oxidative enzyme capacity than Type IIb (fast-twitch glycolytic) fibres, giving them intermediate fatigue resistance. Type IIa fibres can sustain moderate-to-high intensity exercise for longer before fatiguing, making them important targets for interval training in physiotherapy. Type IIb fibres fatigue rapidly despite high force production, limiting their role to very short, maximal efforts.
options: Greater fatigue resistance from higher oxidative capacity
Higher maximal force output per unit cross-sectional area
Greater reliance on anaerobic glycolysis for energy
Larger motor neuron size for faster recruitment
Fewer mitochondria per unit volume of fibre

questions.explanation: The a-vO2 difference reflects peripheral oxygen extraction by tissues. During exercise, metabolically active muscles increase their oxygen extraction through several mechanisms: reduced local PO2 drives more oxygen off haemoglobin (rightward Bohr shift from CO2 and lactate), increased temperature, and muscle vasodilation increasing the oxygen diffusion surface area. At VO2 max, the a-vO2 difference reaches approximately 15-16 mL O2/dL blood, representing near-maximal peripheral extraction.
options: Pulmonary oxygen loading of haemoglobin increases
Cardiac output decreases, increasing extraction time
Blood oxygen carrying capacity increases with exercise
Venous blood becomes more oxygenated during exercise
Working muscles extract more oxygen from arterial blood
questions.question: During progressive exercise testing, the a-vO2 difference (arteriovenous oxygen difference) increases primarily because:

questions.explanation: Ligaments of white fibrous tissue are flexible and pliant, offering no resistance to the normal range of movement, but they are inelastic and unyielding so as to prevent excessive or abnormal movement at the joint. Hyaline cartilage, by contrast, provides a smooth, low-friction surface for movement rather than restraining it. Excessive stretching of ligamentous tissue stimulates pain receptors and causes protective muscular spasm.
options: The hyaline cartilage covering the bone ends
The synovial membrane lining the capsule
The ligaments of white fibrous tissue
The fibrocartilaginous discs within the joint
The fat pads enclosed by the synovium
questions.question: Which structural feature of synovial joints is described as inelastic and unyielding specifically to prevent excessive or abnormal movement?
Why do sticks generally allow a patient to take more weight through the affected leg compared with crutches?
questions.explanation: Sticks allow more weight to be taken through the affected leg than crutches do, since a single stick, particularly when used on the unaffected side so that the stick and affected leg are placed forward together, provides comparatively less overall external support than a pair of crutches. This makes sticks an appropriate progression once the patient's affected leg can tolerate greater load. Metal sticks are adjustable and therefore particularly useful during the assessment phase of determining the correct walking aid.
options: Sticks are always longer than crutches, increasing leverage
Sticks eliminate the need for any balance in standing
Sticks are used only once the patient no longer needs any support
Sticks require no assessment of arm strength beforehand
Sticks give less external support, so the leg bears more weight

questions.explanation: Relaxed passive movement maintains but does not increase mobility, and is used when active exercise in the same range is impossible or contra-indicated. This distinguishes it from passive manual mobilisation techniques, which are specifically intended to increase range. Freedom of accessory movement, included within relaxed passive movement, is necessary to maintain or regain full joint function.
options: A technique that always increases mobility beyond the existing range
A technique reserved exclusively for spastic paralysis
A technique that replaces the need for active exercise entirely
A technique used only after surgical manipulation
A technique that maintains but does not increase mobility
questions.question: Relaxed passive movement is described as which of the following with respect to joint range?
The hip joint allows flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction and rotation. Which classification of joint is this?
questions.explanation: Poly-axial joints permit movement about many axes, occurring in ball and socket joints such as the hip, which allow the four angular movements plus circumduction and rotation. This is distinct from bi-axial joints, such as the wrist, which permit the four angular movements and circumduction but not true rotation. The number of axes available directly determines the range of distinct movement types possible at a joint.

questions.question: A physiotherapist notices that a patient's inco-ordination is confined largely to fine, highly skilled hand movements while basic proximal movements remain relatively unaffected. According to principles of re-education, in what order should treatment generally progress?
options: From fine distal hand movements toward large proximal joint movements
Both proximal and distal movements must always be trained simultaneously from the outset
Only distal movements require any specific re-education approach
From large, basic movements of proximal joints toward finer, more accurate movements of distal joints
Progression order has no bearing on the success of re-education
questions.explanation: In re-education of inco-ordination, exercises which involve the more proximal joints and are large and basic in character are used first, with training in accuracy and finer, highly coordinated movements such as those of the hand deferred until basic movements and rhythm are established. This progression respects the natural developmental sequence in which proximal control typically develops before distal control. Applying this order helps ensure that the patient builds a stable foundation before attempting more demanding fine motor tasks.

When movement must be maintained despite pain in joints, assisted exercise is very useful, with Rheumatoid Arthritis cited as an example where this approach helps the patient continue moving the joint comfortably. The support given reduces load on painful structures while still allowing active muscular participation. This balances the need to preserve movement with the need to avoid aggravating an inflamed joint.
questions.question: A patient with Rheumatoid Arthritis experiences pain on active movement of an inflamed joint. Why might assisted exercise be particularly useful in this situation?
options: It eliminates all sensation of pain permanently
It always increases inflammation in the joint
It replaces the need for medical management of the disease
It converts active movement into mass exercise
It allows movement to continue despite joint pain, using support

questions.question: Why is it considered the physiotherapist's duty to prevent joint stiffness wherever possible, according to the principle that 'prevention is better than cure'?
questions.explanation: Whenever possible, it is the physiotherapist's duty to prevent a joint from stiffening, saving the patient pain and the possibility of permanent disability, while the period of rehabilitation can be considerably reduced in many cases, allowing a return to work where appropriate. This proactive principle underlies the use of early static muscle contraction, controlled active movement, and measures to control exudate formation. It reflects the broader emphasis in exercise therapy on prevention alongside treatment of existing limitation.
options: It eliminates the need for any future passive movement
It guarantees permanent immunity from future joint injury
It is required only in cases of bacterial joint infection
It reduces the patient's pain, shortens rehabilitation, and may allow an earlier return to work
It replaces the need for muscle strengthening entirely

questions.explanation: It is thought that an initiation centre exists in the brain stem which alerts the cerebral cortex, which is then responsible for planning the pattern of movement based on memories of patterns used on previous occasions. The cerebellum, by contrast, acts as a receiving station for kinaesthetic and other information used to make delicate adjustments that harmonise the interaction of different muscle groups during the movement. These adjustments are then conveyed to the anterior horn cells via extra-pyramidal or other descending pathways.
questions.question: Which structure is thought to act as an initiation centre that alerts the cerebral cortex to plan a pattern of voluntary movement?
options: A centre in the brain stem

questions.question: The energy cost of climbing stairs (ascending) versus walking on level ground that a physiotherapist should understand when designing exercise for cardiac rehabilitation is approximately:
questions.explanation: Stair climbing requires approximately 3-5 times the energy expenditure of level walking at comparable pace because the body must perform work against gravity to elevate the centre of mass with each step. This substantially higher energy cost means patients with limited cardiac reserve may experience significant cardiovascular stress ascending stairs that was absent during flat walking. Physiotherapists in cardiac rehabilitation should use stair assessment to determine functional capacity for home and workplace safety, and include stair training as a progressive functional goal in appropriate patients.
options: Stair climbing requires equivalent energy to level walking
Stair climbing requires 10-15 times the energy of level walking
Stair climbing requires 3-5 times the energy of level walking
Stair climbing requires only slightly more energy (1.1 times)
Stair climbing requires less energy because of gravity assistance

questions.question: Why is improving the circulation to an area affected by flaccid paralysis considered an important treatment goal?
questions.explanation: Paralysis leads to coldness and blueness of the affected area, indicating poor circulation, so maintaining circulation through active exercise of other normal muscles in the area, contrast baths, and similar means is important to ensure adequate nutrition for the paralysed muscles. Increased arterial blood flow during active work supplies oxygen and nutrients essential for repair, while local venous return is assisted by intermittent pressure from contracting muscles and joint movement. This circulatory support complements, rather than replaces, splintage and passive movement in managing flaccid paralysis.
options: It ensures adequate nutrition to the paralysed muscles to support recovery
It permanently restores voluntary control to the muscle immediately
It eliminates the need for any splintage or support
It has no influence on the condition of the paralysed muscle
It only matters in cases of spastic, not flaccid, paralysis

questions.question: Why is the knee joint typically rested in approximately 20 degrees of flexion rather than full extension following injury that risks adhesion formation?
options: It eliminates the need for any subsequent mobilisation
It gives equal tension on all capsule fibres, preventing folds
It permanently increases the joint's range of motion
It prevents synovial fluid production entirely
It reduces blood supply to the joint capsule
questions.explanation: The position of rest is chosen to ensure an equal degree of tension on all fibres of the joint capsule, since a slack portion of capsule prone to falling into folds is at greater risk of adhesions gluing those folds into tucks. For this reason the knee is rested in about 20 degrees of flexion, and the shoulder joint is rested partially abducted. This positioning principle aims to minimise later restriction of range caused by adhesion formation.

options: Improving immune function and cardiovascular health
Enhancing cardiovascular health through sympathetic activation
Raising disease risk via sustained cortisol elevation and inflammation
Improving glucose metabolism through stress hormone effects
Having no measurable physiological consequences whatsoever
questions.question: Chronic psychological stress increases disease risk through which sustained physiological mechanisms most relevant to physiotherapy assessment?
questions.explanation: Chronic psychological stress activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis sustaining cortisol elevation and maintains sympathetic nervous system activation. Chronically elevated cortisol impairs immune function (increased infection susceptibility, impaired wound healing), promotes visceral fat accumulation, increases blood pressure, and induces chronic low-grade systemic inflammation (elevated IL-6, TNF-alpha, CRP). These mechanisms accelerate atherosclerosis, impair insulin signalling, and increase cancer risk. Physiotherapists should recognise stress as a modifiable risk factor in their patients' health management.

Muscle extensibility is the passive property allowing a muscle to be lengthened beyond its normal resting length without tearing. It is distinct from flexibility (the range of motion at a joint) and elasticity (return to resting length after stretch). Reduced extensibility contributes to musculotendinous tightness and limited joint range of motion. Physiotherapists target extensibility through sustained static stretching and myofascial techniques that alter the viscoelastic properties of the muscle-tendon unit to increase passive muscle length.
questions.question: A physiotherapist assessing muscle extensibility should understand that this property allows muscles to:
options: Generate maximum force at optimal fibre length
Resist stretch through elastic recoil mechanisms
Maintain constant length during isometric loading
Lengthen passively beyond their normal resting length

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why displacement or tearing of an intracapsular fibrocartilage commonly produces a 'locked' joint?
questions.explanation: Displacement or tearing of an intracapsular fibrocartilage, or the presence of a foreign body within the joint, may limit both active and passive movement, and when accompanied by intense pain the joint frequently becomes locked by muscular spasm. This mechanical locking is a protective reflex response to pain rather than a structural block from adhesion or bone. Recognising this distinct cause helps differentiate it from the slower, progressive stiffness associated with adhesion formation.
options: The fibrocartilage prevents synovial fluid secretion entirely
The capsule becomes permanently glued by adhesions instantly
Intense pain from the displaced structure causes protective muscular spasm that blocks movement
Active range always exceeds passive range in this condition
Bony ankylosis develops immediately following the tear

questions.question: A patient stands in 'stride standing' rather than feet-together standing during early balance retraining. What mechanical advantage does this give?
questions.explanation: Stride standing widens the effective base of support bounded by the outer borders of the feet. A wider base allows the line of gravity to fall well within it even with greater body sway, increasing stability. This is why widening the base is a common early strategy in balance re-education.
options: A lower centre of gravity reduces effort
A neutral equilibrium prevents any sway
The line of gravity shifts outside the base

questions.question: A physiotherapist conducting return-to-sport testing for an ACL-reconstructed patient uses a limb symmetry index (LSI). The minimum LSI threshold considered safe for return to sport is generally accepted as:
options: Greater than 60% of the contralateral limb
Greater than 70% of the contralateral limb
Greater than 90% of the contralateral limb
Equal to 100% of the contralateral limb only
questions.explanation: A limb symmetry index (LSI) greater than 90% between the reconstructed and contralateral limb for strength (isokinetic quadriceps torque) and functional hop tests is the generally accepted minimum threshold for return to full sport after ACL reconstruction. This threshold reflects the need for near-symmetrical neuromuscular capacity to minimise re-injury risk. Research demonstrates that athletes returning with LSI below 90% have substantially higher ACL re-injury rates. Physiotherapists should measure multiple LSI parameters (strength, hop tests, reactive strength) before clearing patients for return to contact sport.

options: The muscle must be progressively extended over each joint until extended over all simultaneously
Only the most distal joint needs to be moved
The muscle should never be stretched over more than one joint at once
Resistance must be applied throughout to prevent shortening
The proximal joint must remain in mid-range at all times
questions.explanation: Muscles passing over two or more joints, such as Quadriceps, must be progressively extended over each joint involved until they are finally extended to their normal length across all the joints simultaneously. For Quadriceps this means the hip is extended while the knee is flexed to achieve full stretch. This careful sequencing maintains the extensibility of two-joint muscles during passive movement.
questions.question: When giving a relaxed passive movement to a muscle that crosses two joints, such as Quadriceps, what special consideration applies to achieve full muscle length?
During re-education of rolling from supine to side lying, the patient pulls strongly on a fixed bar with the leading hand. What is the primary functional purpose of this action?
questions.explanation: Rolling from supine to side lying requires total flexion-with-rotation of the body initiated and led by the head and neck, with trunk rotation facilitated by a strong pull on the hand grasping a fixture, since retraction of one shoulder facilitates protraction of the opposite shoulder. Strong limb activity is recruited to assist whenever available, including hooking and pushing actions of the legs. This functional pattern mirrors how rolling is achieved naturally rather than through isolated muscle action.
options: To facilitate trunk rotation through retraction of the leading shoulder
To eliminate the need for head and neck initiation of the roll
To fixate the pelvis and prevent any rotation
To substitute entirely for active lower limb involvement
To produce isolated distal hand strengthening only

questions.question: Understanding that the rate coding (firing frequency) of motor units increases force output in muscle is most practically applied by physiotherapists when:
questions.explanation: Force production in muscle is increased by two mechanisms: motor unit recruitment (adding more units) and rate coding (increasing firing frequency of already-recruited units). At high force levels above approximately 80-85% of maximum, rate coding becomes increasingly important as virtually all units are already recruited. Explosive speed-strength training increases the rate of motor unit discharge (rate of force development), which is the primary determinant of explosive athletic performance. Physiotherapists prescribing power development for athletes and fall prevention in elderly must incorporate rapid, explosive exercise to develop rate coding capacity.
options: Prescribing explosive speed-strength training for power
Teaching patients to perform exercises very slowly
Designing low-intensity maintenance programmes for elderly
Selecting stretching techniques for flexibility improvement
Assessing cardiovascular fitness with step testing
Extensor spasm in the leg is never associated with any functional benefit
The spasm may be functionally useful, allowing the patient to stand despite the underlying paralysis
Reducing spasm always improves circulation immediately in these patients
This type of spasm cannot be influenced by any relaxation technique
The spasm always indicates permanent, irreversible joint damage
questions.explanation: The relief of pathological spasm resulting from central nervous system lesions is only temporary unless voluntary control can be re-established, and care must be taken not to reduce spasm which is functionally useful through hyperactivity of the antagonistic reflex unless sufficient voluntary power is present, such as extensor spasm of the leg that allows a patient to stand. This highlights that not all spasm is purely pathological or undesirable in every clinical context. Reflex initiation techniques using the stretch reflex combined with voluntary effort can be used cautiously in these cases, balancing the goals of increased mobility against loss of functional support.
questions.question: Why is care taken to avoid reducing pathological extensor spasm of the leg in some spinal cord lesion patients, even though relaxation techniques could achieve this?

options: Timing for emphasis, proceeding from proximal to distal
Normal timing, proceeding from distal to proximal
questions.explanation: Normal timing in patterns of facilitation proceeds from distal to proximal, since distal parts such as the hands and feet normally receive most of the stimuli for activity, with movement completed first in distal, then intermediate, then proximal joints. This contrasts with timing for emphasis, which is deliberately altered to correct imbalances. Disruption of normal timing, for example by giving too much resistance to a distal component, reduces overall movement efficiency.
questions.question: A patient performs a PNF leg pattern in which the hand and foot complete their movement before the hip and shoulder reach the end of theirs. What principle of facilitation does this illustrate?

options: It eliminates the need for any subsequent practice of the whole sequence
It is required only for patients who are unable to hear verbal instruction
Complex activities can never be safely taught as a whole sequence
It has no bearing on the accuracy of the movements eventually performed
Otherwise attention becomes focused on remembering the sequence rather than performing the constituent movements accurately
questions.explanation: Many exercises and most activities consist of a series of simple movements, and for teaching purposes it is usually advisable to analyse the exercise and allow the patient to practise each simple movement before attempting to build them into the full sequence, since otherwise attention becomes focused on remembering the sequence rather than on accurate performance of the constituent movements. An example given is that transference of weight is perfected before the full sequence of movements constituting walking is attempted. This principle of breaking down complex tasks underlies effective teaching of virtually any multi-component functional activity.
questions.question: Why is it considered advisable to analyse a complex exercise or activity into its simple constituent movements before teaching the sequence as a whole?

options: Isometric co-contraction of antagonists is held while resistance alternates direction
A hypertonic muscle is held isometrically then voluntarily relaxed
A limb is passively guided through a pattern before active assistance is added
A strong agonistic pattern against maximal resistance reverses smoothly into the resisted antagonistic pattern without relaxation
Maximal resistance is applied only to the weaker of two unrelated patterns
questions.question: Which best describes the application of slow reversals as a PNF technique?
questions.explanation: Slow reversals involve movement in a strong agonistic pattern against maximal resistance followed immediately, without relaxation, by a smooth reversal into the antagonistic pattern, which is also resisted maximally. This is based on Sherrington's principle of successive induction, where excitability of the antagonist is increased immediately after the agonist's contraction. The technique always begins in the stronger pattern and ends in the weaker one to facilitate the weaker muscles.

options: The maximum ventilation achievable by the respiratory system
The exercise intensity where lactate begins accumulating and buffering increases ventilation
The onset of hyperventilation from respiratory muscle fatigue
The point where breathing becomes uncomfortable for patients
The maximal oxygen uptake at peak aerobic exercise intensity
questions.question: The ventilatory threshold during progressive exercise testing is clinically significant to physiotherapy because it represents:
questions.explanation: The ventilatory threshold (VT), also termed the anaerobic or lactate threshold, represents the exercise intensity above which lactate accumulation accelerates and is buffered by bicarbonate, releasing CO2 that disproportionately drives ventilation. VT is detectable as a non-linear increase in ventilation relative to oxygen uptake. In physiotherapy, VT is used to prescribe high-intensity interval training boundaries and to monitor training adaptations in cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation patients.

options: Increasing all training variables simultaneously as quickly as possible
Keeping training load completely constant throughout the programme
Applying the principle of progressive overload with adequate recovery
Reducing training intensity with every subsequent session
Avoiding any increase in training volume or intensity
questions.question: The most important principle of exercise progression in physiotherapy rehabilitation that prevents overuse injury while continuing to stimulate adaptation is:
questions.explanation: Progressive overload is the fundamental principle driving all training adaptations: the training stimulus must gradually increase beyond current capacity to continue stimulating improvement. However, progression must be balanced with adequate recovery to avoid the overtraining-injury continuum. The SAID principle (Specific Adaptations to Imposed Demands) requires that stimuli progressively exceed current capacity. Physiotherapists should increase load, volume, frequency, or complexity incrementally (10% rule per week is a commonly used guideline for runners) to optimise adaptation while managing injury risk.

questions.question: A physiotherapist selects ball games and scrubbing activities as part of a treatment plan for a stiff shoulder that has not responded well to localised mobilising exercises. What is the rationale for including such objective and diversional activities?
options: These activities are used only when a joint requires complete rest
The variety of natural movement involved may help 'shake loose' joints unresponsive to other methods
They eliminate the need for any measurement of joint range
They are unrelated to the joint mobility programme as a whole
They replace localised treatment entirely once introduced
questions.explanation: Objective, occupational and diversional activities such as ball exercises, scrubbing, and hiking interest the patient, increase circulation, and the variety of natural movement involved may help 'shake loose' joints which do not respond to other, more localised methods. These activities are described as always being a valuable adjunct to more localised treatment rather than a replacement for it. This illustrates how functional, motivating activities can complement formal mobilising technique.

questions.question: Progressive Resistance Exercise, as first described by de Lorme in 1945, is based on testing which measure before establishing a training poundage?
options: The patient's resting heart rate before exercise
The maximum passive range of the joint involved
The total surface area of the muscle being trained
The patient's subjective pain score during contraction
The repetition maximum (R.M.) for a given number of repetitions
questions.explanation: Progressive Resistance Exercise, used for restoring muscle power and volume after injury, is based on testing the repetition maximum, the greatest weight that can be lifted for a specified number of repetitions, most commonly a 10 R.M. test. Several published regimes, such as those of de Lorme and Watkins, Zinovieff, and MacQueen, are all based on this same 10 R.M. test but differ in how the lifts and sets are arranged. The poundage used throughout a programme is therefore individualised to the patient's tested capacity.

questions.question: Bony ankylosis differs from adhesion-related joint stiffness in which key respect?
options: Bony ankylosis is always reversible with passive stretching
Adhesions always produce a more severe restriction than bony ankylosis
Bony ankylosis only ever affects synovial joints, never cartilaginous joints
Bony ankylosis limits movement altogether, whereas adhesions cause a progressive but potentially reversible restriction
Adhesions and bony ankylosis are mechanically identical conditions
questions.explanation: Bony or fibrous ankylosis limits movement altogether, representing a more severe and generally fixed restriction, whereas adhesions, formed from organised exudate, cause a progressive limitation that may potentially be addressed through prompt management of exudate, mobilising techniques, or manipulation before they fully consolidate into scars. This distinction matters clinically because the treatment approach and prognosis differ significantly between the two. Recognising adhesion formation early offers a better opportunity to prevent progression toward more fixed restriction.

options: It eliminates the need for any fixation
It minimises tension in the antagonistic muscles that would otherwise resist the movement
It increases the resistance of gravity on the movement
It widens the base of support of the whole body
It converts the movement into a passive one
questions.explanation: During assisted exercise, every effort is made to reduce tension in muscles antagonistic to the intended movement, and the starting position is chosen to ensure this tension is minimal. Flexing the knee reduces tension in two-joint calf muscles that would otherwise resist ankle dorsiflexion. Selecting the right starting position is therefore one of the key technical principles of giving effective assisted exercise.
questions.question: A physiotherapist chooses a starting position in which the knee is flexed before assisting dorsiflexion of the foot. What is the main reason for this choice?

options: They always require greater muscular resistance
They focus the patient's attention on accuracy of the movement itself
They eliminate gravity from the exercise
They are easier to perform in any position
They replace the need for verbal instruction
questions.explanation: Subjective exercises are formal, anatomically precise movements in which the patient's attention is deliberately focused on the form and pattern of the exercise to ensure accuracy. Objective exercises, by contrast, direct attention toward achieving a goal, such as reaching a mark on the wall, which is more motivating but can sacrifice accuracy if introduced too soon. Establishing accuracy first provides a sound pattern before goal-directed practice is added.
questions.question: Why are subjective exercises typically introduced before objective exercises when teaching a new movement pattern?

options: The wrist flexors and finger extensors of the unaffected side
The hip abductors and extensors, the knee extensors, and the ankle plantar flexors
The neck flexors and shoulder rotators exclusively
The muscles of facial expression relevant to communication
The intrinsic muscles of the unaffected foot exclusively
questions.question: Before a patient begins non-weight-bearing crutch walking, which muscle groups of the unaffected leg require particular attention during assessment?
questions.explanation: For non-weight-bearing crutch walking, the mobility and strength of the unaffected leg should be assessed, paying particular attention to the hip abductors and extensors, the knee extensors, and the plantar flexors of the ankle, since these muscles must be sufficiently strong to take the patient's full weight during the swing phase. If required, the patient is also taught hip-hitching on the non-weight-bearing side. This assessment ensures the unaffected limb can safely bear the additional demand placed on it while the other leg is protected.

questions.question: Why must weight never be taken through the axillary pad of an axillary crutch during standing or walking?
questions.explanation: Weight must be transmitted down the arm to the hand piece with the elbow extended, and on no account should weight be taken through the axillary pad itself, since this could lead to a neuropraxia of the Radial Nerve or Brachial Plexus from sustained compression in the axilla. This is why correct crutch length and technique are checked carefully once the patient is standing, to ensure the axillary pad does not press into the axilla. Physiotherapist supervision during early crutch use is essential to prevent this potentially serious complication.
options: It causes immediate structural failure of the crutch itself
It has no clinical significance if used only briefly
It prevents any weight from reaching the hand piece at all
It only affects patients with pre-existing shoulder pathology
It risks causing a neuropraxia of the Radial Nerve or Brachial Plexus

questions.question: Vital capacity in lung function testing represents which respiratory measurement relevant to physiotherapy assessment?
questions.explanation: Vital capacity is the maximum volume of air that can be forcibly exhaled after a maximum inhalation (VC = IRV + TV + ERV). It represents the usable respiratory volume excluding residual volume. Physiotherapists measure vital capacity to assess respiratory muscle strength, chest wall compliance, and respiratory impairment in conditions including neuromuscular disease, COPD, and post-thoracic surgery. It is a key indicator of respiratory reserve available for exercise ventilation.
options: The volume of air remaining after maximum exhalation
The rate of air flow during a forced expiratory effort
The functional residual capacity at end-tidal breathing
The maximum air volume inhaled and exhaled in one breath
The total lung capacity minus the functional residual capacity
It always decreases the effect of the resistance regardless of speed change
Speed changes have no effect on concentric work intensity
It only affects resistance during eccentric, not concentric, work
It increases the effect of the resistance compared with working at natural speed
It eliminates the need for any other progression method
questions.explanation: Muscular contraction is most efficient at an optimum or natural speed, so increasing or decreasing this natural speed increases the effect of the resistance when the muscle works concentrically. For eccentric work the relationship is reversed: the slower the movement, the greater the effect of the resistance, since eccentric work in natural movement tends to be fairly rapid. This means speed alteration can be deliberately used as a fourth method of progressing resistance, alongside poundage, leverage, and duration.
questions.question: For concentric muscle work, increasing or decreasing the speed away from the muscle's natural rhythm has what general effect on perceived resistance?

questions.explanation: Active fixation of a joint is obtained by co-contraction of the muscles around it, as opposed to passive fixation achieved by external means such as manual pressure or straps. Asking the patient to hold the pelvis still using their own muscles is therefore active fixation. This improves the efficiency of the prime movers by securing their origin.
questions.question: During a trunk-strengthening exercise the physiotherapist asks the patient to keep their pelvis still through their own abdominal effort rather than manual support. Which mechanism is being used?

options: They function only to record deep pressure information from joints
They are unrelated to any alteration in body position relative to surroundings
They act solely to inhibit all muscular activity during standing
They help the head and body restore themselves to an erect position
They are activated exclusively by vestibular, not visual, information
questions.explanation: Visual sensation records any alteration in the position of the body with regard to its surroundings, and the eyes form one of the receptors for the 'righting' reflexes which enable the head and body to restore themselves to the erect position from other, less usual attitudes. This is one of several afferent sources, alongside the muscles and ears, that are integrated in the central nervous system to maintain and adjust posture. Loss or impairment of visual input can therefore significantly affect a patient's ability to maintain or correct their postural alignment.
questions.question: Why do the 'righting' reflexes involving the eyes matter for maintaining erect posture?

questions.explanation: Each PNF pattern has three components, two of which are angular and the third rotatory, with rotation considered of major importance because it gives direction to the movement as a whole. Rotation also starts the movement, even though its range is only partial. This is why special attention is paid to the rotatory component during techniques such as rhythmic stabilisation.
questions.question: In a PNF pattern, which component of movement is considered of major importance because it gives direction to the movement as a whole?

questions.explanation: On an inclined plane, the reaction of the plane is greatest when the incline is nearly horizontal, so resistance to the muscles is least at that point. As the incline approaches the vertical, the reaction of the plane decreases and the resistance offered by gravity increases correspondingly. This explains why steeper ramps demand greater muscular effort for upward movement.
options: It decreases as the incline nears vertical
It remains constant at every incline
It becomes gravity-free at any incline
It increases as the incline nears vertical
It is unaffected by the angle of incline
questions.question: A patient pushes a weighted sledge up a ramp that becomes progressively steeper. As the incline approaches vertical, what happens to the resistance offered to the working muscles?

questions.explanation: Regular aerobic exercise reduces cardiovascular disease risk through multiple pathways: lowering LDL cholesterol while raising HDL, reducing resting systolic and diastolic blood pressure through vascular adaptations, improving endothelial function (increasing nitric oxide production), reducing plasma fibrinogen and platelet aggregability, and improving insulin sensitivity. These cumulative effects substantially reduce atherogenic risk. Understanding these mechanisms allows physiotherapists to motivate patients by explaining the specific cardiovascular benefits of their exercise programme.
options: Increasing resting blood pressure and heart rate
Elevating LDL cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations
Improving lipid profile, blood pressure, and endothelial function
Reducing cerebral blood flow and cognitive circulation
Having no measurable cardiovascular benefits whatsoever
questions.question: Regular physical activity reduces cardiovascular disease risk through which combination of mechanisms most relevant to physiotherapy clinical practice?

questions.explanation: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction is triggered by airway drying and cooling during high ventilatory demand, particularly in cold and dry environments. The primary mechanism involves osmotic changes and mast cell activation in the airway epithelium. Wearing a face mask during cold weather exercise warms and humidifies inspired air before it reaches the airways, substantially reducing EIB triggers. Nasal breathing (rather than mouth breathing) also warms and humidifies air and should be encouraged during low-to-moderate intensity exercise.
options: Complete avoidance of all aerobic exercise permanently
Breathing exclusively through the mouth to increase air flow
Increasing exercise intensity to override bronchospasm
Using cold room exercise to desensitise airways
Wearing a face mask to warm and humidify inspired air
questions.question: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) is triggered by airway cooling and drying from cold air inhalation. A physiotherapist managing a patient with EIB should recommend which exercise modification?

questions.explanation: Commonly identified exercise barriers in clinical and community populations include lack of time (most frequently cited), limited access to facilities, insufficient motivation or enjoyment, lack of social support, fear of injury or exercise-related symptoms, pain, and low self-efficacy. Physiotherapists should systematically assess barriers during physical activity counselling using brief validated tools and address them specifically through problem-solving, community resource referral, home exercise programmes, and motivational strategies tailored to each patient.
options: Excessive amounts of free time available
Too many exercise facilities available nearby
Too much existing motivation for exercise
No obstacles to exercise exist for patients
Lack of time, facility access, motivation, and support
questions.question: Physical activity barriers commonly identified in physiotherapy patients that physiotherapists should routinely assess and address include:

questions.explanation: The primary physiological reason interval training is superior for VO2 max improvement is that brief high-intensity intervals (>90% VO2 max) drive cardiac output close to maximum, creating the stimulus for central cardiovascular adaptations (stroke volume increase, cardiac chamber enlargement) that continuous moderate training cannot consistently achieve. The accumulation of time spent near maximal cardiac output per session maximises the stimulus for eccentric cardiac hypertrophy and plasma volume expansion - the primary determinants of VO2 max improvement.
questions.question: The primary mechanism by which interval training is superior to continuous moderate-intensity training for improving VO2 max in physiotherapy is:
options: Longer total session duration increases total energy expenditure
Interval rest periods allow complete lactic acid clearance
Interval training exclusively develops the glycolytic energy system
Brief high-intensity intervals spend more time near maximal cardiac output
Continuous training cannot improve VO2 max at any intensity

questions.explanation: In lying positions, the posterior aspect of the whole body in contact with the supporting surface forms the base, which is generally larger and lower than the base available in sitting positions, making lying more stable overall. Crook lying, with the knees bent and feet flat, maintains this large area of ground contact while also reducing tension in structures such as the hamstrings. This combination of a low centre of gravity and a wide, stable base is why lying positions are consistently used for maximum stability during early rehabilitation.
questions.question: Which best explains why the human body is more stable in crook lying than in long sitting with the legs extended?
options: Crook lying eliminates the effect of gravity on the trunk
Long sitting always lowers the centre of gravity below that of crook lying
Long sitting increases the base of support compared with crook lying
Crook lying gives a larger area of body contact, creating a bigger base
Both positions provide an identical base of support
Measurement of the patient's overall muscle bulk
A complete record of the patient's occupational history
Measurement of the present range of joint movement
An estimate of the patient's pain tolerance threshold
A count of total adhesions present in the joint
questions.explanation: Measurement of the present range of joint movement is essential before treatment begins and at specified intervals afterward to permit assessment of progress. If progress proves unsatisfactory, the method of treatment must be modified or changed, and if still ineffective, further investigation of the underlying cause of limitation is required. This systematic measurement underpins evidence-based progression of joint mobility treatment.
questions.question: Before starting a course of joint mobilisation treatment, what must be established as a baseline to allow assessment of progress?

options: Mobilisations are always performed under general anaesthesia
Mobilisations are rhythmical and patient-controlled; manipulations are single and high-velocity
Manipulations are always slower than mobilisations
Mobilisations and manipulations are functionally identical techniques
Manipulations are always performed by the patient unaided
questions.explanation: Mobilisations are usually small, repetitive, rhythmical oscillatory movements performed in various amplitudes within available range under the patient's control, while manipulations are accurately localised, single, quick, decisive movements of small amplitude and high velocity, completed before the patient can stop them. Manipulations may be performed by physiotherapists or, under anaesthesia, by a surgeon or physician to gain further range that must then be maintained by the physiotherapist. This distinction in speed, control, and repetition is the defining difference between the two techniques.
questions.question: Which statement correctly differentiates a mobilisation from a manipulation as passive manual mobilisation techniques?
Cartilaginous or bony destruction within a joint typically produces limitation of movement through which mechanism?
options: Excessive accessory movement develops at the joint
Synovial fluid production increases beyond normal levels
Ligaments become more elastic and yielding
Active range exceeds passive range significantly
Pain limits movement and articular surfaces no longer slide easily upon one another
questions.explanation: Cartilaginous or bony destruction within a joint produces pain that may limit both active and passive movement, while the damaged articular surfaces no longer slide easily upon one another, further restricting range. Bony or fibrous ankylosis represents the most extreme outcome of this process, limiting movement altogether, while bony obstruction such as in myositis ossificans limits range specifically in the direction of the obstruction. This differs mechanically from adhesion-related stiffness, which arises from soft tissue gluing rather than joint surface damage.

Assisted exercise is used when muscle strength or coordination is inadequate to complete a movement unaided, so an external force such as support on a polished board compensates for the deficiency. The support reduces the load by counterbalancing gravity rather than replacing the patient's own effort entirely. As the muscle strengthens, the amount of support provided must be reduced proportionally.
questions.question: A physiotherapist supports a patient's weak forearm on a re-education board to allow elbow flexion to be practised. What type of exercise is this primarily?

questions.explanation: As muscles warm up to a task they become more efficient, so the effect of a given resistance decreases and the exercise feels easier initially, but if continued for a sufficient number of repetitions, fatigue reduces the muscles' efficiency again and the resistance appears to increase in difficulty. This illustrates how the fourth method of progression, increasing the duration of exercise, exerts its effect through the interplay of warm-up and subsequent fatigue. This pattern is used to explain why a task such as sawing wood can feel easier at first but becomes hard work by the end of an hour.
options: The actual resistance applied is automatically reduced partway through exercise
This pattern only occurs with isometric, never isotonic, muscle work
The muscle's blood supply is completely cut off during the exercise
This pattern indicates the resistance was set far too low from the start
Early warm-up increases efficiency, while later fatigue reduces it again as duration increases
questions.question: A muscle group that initially finds a resistance challenging seems to become easier to work against as the exercise continues, but later in the same session the resistance again feels harder. What explains this pattern?

questions.explanation: The physiotherapist's voice is used as a verbal stimulus to demand the patient's maximum voluntary effort, and brief, simple, accurate, and well-timed instructions suited to the patient's age, character, and ability to cooperate demand attention and effort at the right time and indicate the type of reaction required, even if the patient does not understand the spoken language. This shows that the timing and manner of commanding carries meaning independent of verbal comprehension. Well-executed commanding is therefore considered a skill in its own right within facilitation technique.
options: Commands have no functional purpose beyond general encouragement
Language comprehension is irrelevant to any aspect of PNF technique
Commands demand attention at the right time through tone and timing alone
Commands are only ever needed for isometric holding techniques
Commands must always be given in the patient's native language to work
questions.question: Why must a physiotherapist's commands during PNF technique be brief, simple, and well-timed even if the patient does not understand the spoken language?

questions.explanation: The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is a specialised smooth endoplasmic reticulum surrounding myofibrils that stores calcium at high concentrations when the muscle is at rest. Upon motor neuron activation, the action potential travels through T-tubules and triggers ryanodine receptor opening in the SR terminal cisternae, releasing calcium into the cytoplasm. Calcium binds troponin C, shifting tropomyosin to expose myosin-binding sites on actin, initiating contraction. The SR calcium pump (SERCA) then actively re-sequesters calcium during relaxation, requiring ATP. SERCA dysfunction contributes to muscle fatigue during sustained exercise.
questions.question: The primary role of the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) in excitation-contraction coupling is which function directly relevant to muscle physiology understanding in physiotherapy?
options: Producing ATP for myosin cross-bridge power strokes
Conducting action potentials along the muscle fibre length
Synthesising actin and myosin proteins for myofibril growth
Removing metabolic waste products from the muscle cytoplasm
Storing and releasing calcium to trigger muscle contraction
Ketoacidosis from insufficient basal insulin during exercise
