Exercise always increases blood glucose in type 1 diabetes
Hyperglycaemia from muscle glucose release during contraction
Insulin resistance improving permanently after single session
Complete muscle glycogen depletion after 10 minutes
questions.explanation: In type 1 diabetes, inadequate insulin availability during exercise (if basal insulin is insufficient) leads to unrestrained ketogenesis and hyperglycaemia, potentially precipitating diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Conversely, excessive insulin (taken before exercise) causes hypoglycaemia through the same GLUT4-mediated mechanisms as in type 2 diabetes. Physiotherapists must ensure type 1 diabetic patients have appropriate blood glucose levels (5-10 mmol/L) before exercise, have reduced pre-exercise insulin if needed, carry rapid-acting carbohydrate, and monitor blood glucose throughout sessions.
questions.question: A physiotherapist managing a patient with type 1 diabetes during an exercise session should specifically monitor for which unique metabolic risk not present in type 2 diabetes?
A physiotherapist notices a patient's tense, raised shoulders during relaxation training and asks them to actively lower and lengthen them, then feel the new position. Which method is being applied?
questions.explanation: Physiological relaxation involves defining the position of tension precisely, such as raised shoulders, and then guiding the patient through exact voluntary orders to change that position and register the new sensation. This registers the altered joint position and skin pressure at a cortical level, allowing the patient to learn to reverse tension deliberately. It is distinct from the contrast method, which instead relies on first generating, then releasing, a strong contraction.

questions.question: The physiological benefits of regular exercise for patients with osteoarthritis, as prescribed by physiotherapists, include:
options: Increased joint destruction and worsening inflammation
Complete disease cure from cartilage regeneration
Worsened symptoms from mechanical loading always
Reduced pain, improved function, no damage acceleration
No possible benefits for affected joint structures
questions.explanation: Appropriately dosed exercise for osteoarthritis consistently reduces joint pain and improves functional capacity, muscle strength around affected joints, and quality of life without accelerating radiographic progression. Exercise-induced benefits include reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines, improved cartilage nutrition through intermittent loading, strengthened periarticular muscles reducing compressive forces, and weight management. Both aerobic and resistance exercise are recommended by clinical guidelines for knee and hip OA as first-line conservative management.

Dr. H. S. Frenkel devised a method of systematic, graduated exercises to treat the ataxia that is a prominent symptom of tabes dorsalis, a condition he made a special study of at the Sanatorium 'Freihof' in Switzerland. Since then his methods have been extended to treat inco-ordination resulting from many other diseases, such as disseminated sclerosis. His technique relies on substituting intact senses, notably sight, sound, and touch, to compensate for the loss of kinaesthetic sensation characteristic of this condition.
questions.question: Frenkel's exercises were originally devised to treat the ataxia associated with which specific disease?
In flaccid paralysis, why must passive movement of an affected limb follow the natural pattern of group joint movement rather than isolated single-joint movement?
questions.explanation: Movement is associated in the brain with numerous sensory impulses from joints, muscles, skin and eyes, and in the absence of voluntary movement, stimulation of these impulses by passive movement may remind the brain of the natural pattern of movement in preparation for the eventual return of motor function. The passive movements given for this purpose must therefore follow the natural pattern of group joint movement rather than treating each joint in isolation. In this way, coordinated movement does not need to be entirely re-learned once muscle power returns.
options: Isolated single-joint movement always causes joint contracture
It helps stimulate the brain's memory of the coordinated movement pattern in preparation for recovery
Group movement is required only to increase local circulation
Natural patterns eliminate the need for full-range movement
Isolated movement is impossible to perform passively
Flexibility, intensity, time, and type of exercise
Frequency, intensity, time, and type of exercise
Force, interval, time, and training specificity
Fatigue, intensity, tempo, and training volume
Function, intensity, time, and therapeutic goals
questions.explanation: The FITT principle provides a structured framework for exercise prescription: Frequency (sessions per week), Intensity (work rate, percentage of maximum, or RPE), Time (session duration), and Type (exercise modality). All four components must be specified for a complete prescription that can be reliably followed and progressively modified. Physiotherapists should document all four FITT components in rehabilitation plans to ensure reproducibility, appropriate progression, and communication across the treatment team.
questions.question: The FITT principle for exercise prescription specifically requires physiotherapists to specify which four components for every exercise programme?

questions.explanation: Rhythmical swinging and pendular movements assist relaxation because the alternating reciprocal contraction and relaxation of opposing muscle groups required to sustain the movement helps restore the normal resting state. This reduces wasteful tension that would otherwise limit joint range and impair coordination. It is therefore used alongside other relaxation methods rather than for strengthening purposes.
questions.question: Rhythmical pendular swinging of a relaxed limb is most effective for which therapeutic purpose?
options: Localising fixation to a single joint
Promoting relaxation of hypertonic muscles around the joint

questions.explanation: Derived positions are modifications of the fundamental starting positions, adjusted in some specific way, for example by altering the base, the relationship to gravity, or the degree of support, to suit the particular aim of an exercise. They allow the physiotherapist to grade an exercise more precisely than the limited set of fundamental positions alone would permit. Half lying and stride sitting are common named examples of such derived positions.
questions.question: What is the principal purpose of using 'derived positions' such as half lying or stride sitting in exercise therapy practice?
options: To eliminate the need for any fixation
To increase resistance in every exercise
To modify a fundamental starting position to suit a specific exercise aim
To remove gravity from all movement

questions.question: Which statement correctly reflects the role of free exercise as a method of increasing joint mobility, in relation to its scheduling and supervision?
questions.explanation: Free exercise is described as a valuable method for increasing mobility because, once learnt, it can be carried out at frequent intervals by a cooperative patient, with pendular movement and pressing movements at the limit of range commonly used. Cooperation and accurate instruction to ensure correct movement are described as essential to achieving results. This makes free exercise particularly useful for sustaining gains made through other mobilising methods between treatment sessions.
options: It must always be performed under general anaesthesia
It requires constant manual resistance from the physiotherapist throughout
It is valuable because a cooperative, well-instructed patient can practise it independently at frequent intervals
It cannot be used to increase range, only to maintain it
It is unsuitable for any home-based practice
Speed of eccentric, pause, and concentric phases
Training frequency and session scheduling only
Rest intervals between sets and exercises
questions.explanation: Temporal velocity (repetition tempo) specifies the duration of each phase of a resistance exercise repetition: eccentric phase (lowering), isometric pause, and concentric phase (lifting), typically expressed as a four-digit code (e.g., 3-0-1-0 means 3 s eccentric, 0 s pause, 1 s concentric, 0 s between reps). Controlling tempo alters time under tension, motor unit recruitment patterns, and muscle damage. Slower eccentric velocities increase mechanical tension and muscle damage, promoting hypertrophy. Physiotherapists should specify tempo to standardise exercise dose and target specific neuromuscular adaptations.
questions.question: Temporal velocity in resistance training refers to which training variable that physiotherapists should specify in exercise prescriptions?

questions.explanation: Rotation occurs about a vertical axis, which lies parallel to the line of gravity, and the resulting movement takes place in the horizontal plane. This is distinct from flexion-extension and abduction-adduction, which use frontal and sagittal axes respectively. Trunk rotation exercises are therefore described using this third axis-plane pairing.
options: A sagittal axis, in a frontal plane
A vertical axis, in a horizontal plane
A frontal axis, in a sagittal plane
A horizontal axis, in a vertical plane
A transverse axis, in a frontal plane
questions.question: Rotation of the trunk in standing occurs about which axis and in which plane?

questions.explanation: As it is movements, and not individual muscles or even muscle groups, that are represented in the cerebral cortex, the importance of concentrating on the overall movement rather than the contraction of one specific muscle during re-education cannot be over-emphasised. Furthermore, since the movements represented are those to which the patient is accustomed, natural functional movements are given prime importance. This principle underlies why functional patterns, rather than isolated muscle drills, are favoured in re-education whenever possible.
options: Individual muscles are represented separately and exclusively in the cortex
Single-muscle focus always produces faster strength recovery
The cerebral cortex has no influence over voluntary movement patterns
Movements, not individual muscles, are represented in the cerebral cortex
Concentrating on individual muscles eliminates the need for synergists
questions.question: Why is concentrating on the overall pattern of movement, rather than on contraction of a single muscle, emphasised during muscle re-education?
An irregularly shaped splint is suspended successively from two different points to locate a reference point needed for fitting. Which mechanical principle is being applied?
questions.explanation: The centre of gravity of an irregular object can be found by suspending it from at least two points and marking the line taken by a plumb line at each suspension point. The intersection of these two lines locates the centre of gravity, which need not lie within the body itself. This classic method demonstrates how the centre of gravity is found practically rather than calculated.
options: Calculating the line of gravity through the base
Locating the centre of gravity using a plumb line
Establishing the axis of rotation of the splint
Measuring the base of support of the splint
Determining the equilibrium state of the splint

questions.question: A physiotherapist gives two full-range passive movements to a flaccid limb twice daily rather than many repetitions throughout the day. What is the rationale for this relatively limited frequency?
questions.explanation: For preventing adhesion formation and maintaining the present free range of movement, one passive movement well given at frequent intervals is sufficient, although usual practice is to put the joint through two movements twice daily. This reflects an efficient balance between adequate joint maintenance and avoiding unnecessary handling. The technique's effectiveness depends on quality and consistency rather than sheer repetition.
options: More frequent movement always causes joint damage
Flaccid muscles cannot tolerate any passive movement
One well-given movement at frequent intervals is sufficient to prevent adhesion formation and maintain range
Twice-daily movement is required only for spastic paralysis
Passive movement frequency has no relationship to adhesion prevention

questions.explanation: Increasing leverage means applying the same weight at a greater perpendicular distance from the fulcrum, the joint at which movement takes place, since the moment of force equals weight multiplied by perpendicular distance from the fulcrum. For example, a constant resistance applied to the Shoulder Abductors has a much greater effect when applied at the wrist than at the elbow. This is distinct from increasing poundage, which instead changes the magnitude of the weight itself rather than its point of application.
questions.question: Which of the four main methods of progressing resistance involves applying a constant weight further from the joint's axis of movement?
options: Alteration in the speed of movement
Increase in the duration of the exercise
Increase in the base of support
Permanent destruction of the motor unit
Immediate reflex inhibition of the muscle
Conversion of the cell into a dormant state
A reduction in the cell's threshold of excitability
questions.explanation: Sub-threshold stimuli fail to stimulate the Anterior Horn Cell but progressively lower its threshold of excitability, facilitating its response to subsequent stimuli. This is distinct from a strong threshold stimulus, which causes the cell to fire immediately. Repeated bombardment of even dormant cells by strong stimuli can eventually succeed in reducing their threshold sufficiently to allow a response.
questions.question: Repeated sub-threshold stimuli arriving at an Anterior Horn Cell fail to trigger firing but still produce a useful effect. What is this effect called?

questions.explanation: Synergists are muscles that work or relax to modify the action of prime movers, either altering the direction of pull or, where prime movers cross more than one joint, fixing or moving the joint where the main action is not required into the most advantageous position. The Wrist Extensors act as synergists here so that the power of the Finger Flexors is directed fully into finger flexion rather than being diverted into unwanted wrist flexion. This allows the extended wrist to act as a fulcrum, increasing the efficiency of the prime movers.
questions.question: In flexion of the fingers to make a fist, the Extensors of the Wrist contract to fix the wrist in extension. What role are these wrist extensors playing?
Why are painless, mobile and strong feet described as essential for good static and dynamic posture?
questions.explanation: Painless, mobile and strong feet form a stable base on which the weight of the body is balanced and supported, with the arches braced so that weight falls through the summit of the arch and is distributed evenly to the weight-bearing areas of the foot. In walking, weight is transferred progressively from one part of the weight-bearing area to the next, requiring healthy, functional feet throughout the gait cycle. Bracing exercises for the arches require the weight-bearing areas to remain in contact with the supporting surface to preserve the sensory stimulation needed for correct positioning.
options: They form a stable base on which body weight can be balanced and evenly distributed
They eliminate the need for any bracing of the arches during weight-bearing
They function independently of the overall alignment of the body above them
They are relevant only to dynamic posture, never to static standing
Their condition has no relationship to progressive weight transfer during walking

questions.explanation: When two training sessions occur within 8 hours, immediate post-exercise nutrition is critical because glycogen resynthesis and muscle protein synthesis must both occur within the short recovery window. Consuming combined carbohydrate (1.0-1.2 g/kg) and protein (20-40 g) within 30 minutes maximises both glycogen resynthesis rate (carbohydrate plus exercise-induced insulin sensitivity) and muscle protein synthesis (protein plus mTOR activation). The co-ingestion of protein with carbohydrate also modestly enhances glycogen resynthesis by synergistic insulin secretion.
questions.question: A physiotherapist advising on sports nutrition timing should recommend which post-exercise recovery strategy for an athlete with two training sessions within 8 hours?
options: Delay all nutrient intake for 2 hours post-exercise
Consume only water immediately following the session
Restrict protein until 24 hours after the first session
Consume combined carbohydrate and protein within 30 minutes
Consume high-fat foods only during the recovery window

questions.question: A physiotherapist applies resistance to a patient's arm during a strengthening exercise, describing the arrow used to represent this force. Which two properties does the arrow's direction and length represent?
questions.explanation: The application of a force to a body is specified by the direction of the force, which may be represented by the direction of an arrow, and the magnitude of the force, represented by the length of the arrow. The tail of the arrow represents the point of application of the force. This graphical convention is the basis for analysing composition of forces, such as when two forces are compounded or opposed.
options: The speed of the limb and its base of support
The direction of the force and its magnitude
The axis of movement and the plane of movement
The centre of gravity and the line of gravity
The type of equilibrium and the degree of stability

questions.explanation: Because relaxation must be maintained throughout a relaxed passive movement, the speed of performance must be uniform, fairly slow, and rhythmical. A sudden or uneven pace risks provoking protective muscle spasm or pain, which would defeat the purpose of the technique. This contrasts with manipulations, which deliberately use high velocity to bypass voluntary guarding.
questions.question: A physiotherapist gives passive movement to a recently injured ankle, performed slowly, smoothly, and within pain-free range. Why is uniform, slow speed emphasised during this technique?
options: Fast movement is needed to elicit the stretch reflex deliberately
Relaxation must be maintained throughout, which requires a steady rhythmical pace
Slow speed eliminates the need for fixation of the proximal bone
Uniform speed converts the technique into active assisted exercise
Slow movement is required only when treating spastic paralysis

questions.explanation: Among the values of Group Exercise, the patient learns to work with others and no longer considers themselves set apart from others because of their disability, with help at hand if needed while they take their place within the community of patients. Group treatment is also described as a progression from, and adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, individual treatment. This social and psychological benefit is distinct from, though related to, the physical benefits of endurance building and stimulated effort gained through group participation.
options: The patient avoids all contact with other patients during treatment
The patient relies entirely on the physiotherapist throughout every session
The patient learns to work with others and no longer feels set apart because of the disability
The patient is discouraged from any competitive activity whatsoever
The patient no longer requires any individual treatment at any stage
questions.question: Which of the following is listed as a specific value of Group Exercise for the patient's psychological adjustment to disability?

options: Acute inflammatory infiltration with neutrophil accumulation
Calcium hydroxyapatite crystal deposition in tendon substance
Bone erosion at the enthesis from inflammatory arthritis
questions.question: A physiotherapist treating a tennis player with lateral epicondylopathy (tennis elbow) should understand that the pathological changes in the common extensor tendon are characterised by:
questions.explanation: Lateral epicondylopathy is characterised by degenerative angiofibroblastic tendinosis rather than acute inflammatory changes. Histopathology reveals disordered collagen fibre organisation, increased tenocyte apoptosis, pathological neovascularity, and mucoid degeneration - all features of failed tendon healing rather than inflammation. This pathological understanding explains why NSAIDs (anti-inflammatory) are less effective than exercise-based tendon loading programmes. Physiotherapy targets include progressive eccentric and isometric loading to stimulate tenocyte activity and restore collagen organisation.

In crook lying the trunk is well supported on the floor while the hips and knees are flexed, leaving the pelvis free to tilt in an antero-posterior direction under voluntary control. This combination of trunk stability with pelvic freedom is precisely what is needed to learn pelvic tilting before progressing to less supported positions. Long sitting would demand far more postural control of the trunk, making isolated pelvic movement harder to learn.
questions.question: A physiotherapist selects 'crook lying' rather than 'long sitting' as the starting position for early pelvic tilting practice. What is the main mechanical reason for this choice?
options: It removes the line of gravity from the body
It eliminates the need for any muscular fixation
It supports the trunk while leaving the pelvis free to move
It widens the base to the maximum possible extent
It places the centre of gravity outside the base
The vertical plane reduces friction completely
The inclined plane removes all resistance
Movement in the horizontal plane is gravity-free
Gravity assists movement in this plane
The base of support is widened by the table
questions.question: A weak shoulder abductor manages to lift the arm only when the limb is supported flat on a polished table top. Why does this happen?
questions.explanation: Movement in the horizontal plane is not affected by gravity and is described as gravity-free, since the only resistance is the frictional resistance of the supporting surface. This allows weak muscles unable to lift a limb against gravity to succeed when the part is supported horizontally. It is therefore a useful starting position for very weak muscle grades.

options: Accelerated neuron loss and cognitive deterioration
Enhanced neuroplasticity, motor control, and reduced fall risk
Worsened movement disorders and balance problems
No possible benefits for neurological function
questions.question: Exercise benefits for Parkinson's disease patients in physiotherapy include which neurologically specific outcomes relevant to motor rehabilitation?
questions.explanation: Exercise in Parkinson's disease stimulates neuroplasticity through BDNF production, potentially enhancing remaining dopaminergic pathway function. Specific exercise benefits include improved motor control, gait velocity, stride length, and balance, all directly reducing fall risk. Aerobic exercise may have neuroprotective effects by reducing alpha-synuclein aggregation. Treadmill training, dance, cycling, and tai chi have all demonstrated significant functional improvements in clinical trials. Physiotherapists are central to delivering and progressing these neurological rehabilitation exercise programmes.

Careful active movements of the affected joint are begun as soon as possible and should progress rapidly, since they maintain the power of the working muscles, ensure freedom of tendons, and help the pattern of movement to be remembered. Passive movements can also be used, but they are more likely to cause minor trauma to the affected joint with further exudation, while their effect on the circulation is minimal. This is why active exercise, when tolerated, is generally favoured over passive movement once the acute phase allows it.
options: Active movement eliminates the need for any rest of the joint
Passive movement always improves circulation more than active movement
Active movement is contraindicated in almost all joint injuries
Passive movement carries no risk of further joint trauma
Active movement maintains muscle power and risks less further trauma
questions.question: Why are careful active movements of an affected joint begun as soon as possible after injury, in preference to relying mainly on passive movement?

options: Progressive bone mineral density loss affecting mobility
Declining maximal heart rate reducing cardiac output ceiling
Accumulation of oxidative damage in mitochondrial DNA
Increasing peripheral vascular resistance with ageing
Reduced respiratory drive from central chemoreceptor changes
questions.question: Ageing affects exercise capacity through multiple physiological mechanisms. The single greatest contributor to reduced VO2 max with advancing age is:
questions.explanation: VO2 max declines approximately 1% per year from age 25-30 in sedentary individuals, with the primary contributor being the progressive decline in maximal heart rate (approximately 1 beat/min/year). Since maximum cardiac output = maximum heart rate times stroke volume, declining maximum heart rate directly limits the oxygen delivery ceiling regardless of peripheral adaptations. While muscle mass loss, mitochondrial density reduction, and reduced arteriovenous oxygen difference also contribute, declining maximal heart rate accounts for the largest single portion of age-related VO2 max decline.

questions.question: Which best distinguishes an accessory joint movement from a relaxed passive movement?
questions.explanation: Accessory movements are gliding or rotational components present within normal joint movement, but they cannot be produced voluntarily by the patient in isolation and can only be isolated and performed by the physiotherapist. Relaxed passive movements, in contrast, follow the same range and direction as active movement. Both share the same underlying principles of fixation, support, and relaxation when being performed.
options: Accessory movements always require general anaesthesia
Accessory movements are performed only by the patient
Accessory movements are gliding or rotational components that cannot be performed voluntarily in isolation
Accessory movements involve high-velocity thrust techniques
Accessory movements replace active exercise entirely

questions.explanation: Manipulations performed by physiotherapists are accurately localised, single, quick decisive movements of small amplitude and high velocity, completed before the patient is able to stop them. Mobilisations differ in being repetitive, rhythmical, oscillatory movements performed under the patient's control. This distinction in speed and patient control is the key feature separating the two techniques.
questions.question: A physiotherapist performs a single, accurately localised, high-velocity movement of small amplitude at a joint, completed before the patient can resist it. What technique is this?

questions.explanation: Children have a higher surface area to body mass ratio than adults, which facilitates greater convective and radiative heat exchange from the environment into the body on hot days, actually increasing heat stress rather than dissipating it effectively. Additionally, children have fewer sweat glands per unit body surface area and lower absolute sweat rates than adults, reducing evaporative cooling capacity. Physiotherapists supervising paediatric exercise in hot conditions must increase monitoring frequency, enforce hydration, and reduce intensity more aggressively than for adults.
options: Superior heat dissipation and cooling capacity
Higher surface-to-mass ratio and lower sweat rate
questions.question: Children are at a thermoregulatory disadvantage during exercise in hot environments compared to adults primarily because of:
Why is traction commonly applied along the long axis of a joint during relaxed passive movement?
questions.explanation: Traction given in the long axis of a joint, with the proximal bone fixed to provide an opposing force, is thought to facilitate movement by reducing friction between the articular surfaces. This is a supportive technique used alongside, not instead of, proper fixation and patient relaxation. It allows the joint surfaces to be drawn slightly apart before or during the passive movement.
options: It permanently increases the joint's range beyond normal limits
It replaces the need for fixation of the proximal bone
It substitutes entirely for active exercise
It eliminates the need for patient relaxation
It is thought to reduce interarticular friction and facilitate the movement

questions.question: Why might a muscle classified as having 'functional' weakness still be capable of contracting under electrical stimulation or facilitation techniques despite the patient being unable to use it voluntarily?
options: There is no organic cause for the weakness, only a failure of normal voluntary function
The Anterior Horn Cells supplying the muscle have been permanently destroyed
The muscle tissue itself has undergone irreversible degeneration
The muscle is affected by an upper motor neurone lesion causing spasticity
The muscle is in a state of true flaccid paralysis from nerve injury
questions.explanation: In functional weakness there is no organic cause for the muscle not functioning, even though the muscle may be made to contract by electrical stimulation of the nerve or by methods of facilitation, distinguishing it clearly from true paralysis caused by destruction of motor neurones or muscle tissue. This distinction matters because the treatment approach for functional weakness differs significantly from that for organic paralysis. Recognising preserved excitability via external stimulation helps differentiate functional from structural causes of weakness.

When normal timing cannot be achieved, timing for emphasis is used as a means of correcting imbalances by deliberately adjusting the sequence of muscle contraction to reinforce weaker components. This contrasts with normal timing, which proceeds naturally from distal to proximal in unimpaired movement. Timing for emphasis is combined with reinforcement to direct the benefit of strong muscle contraction toward weaker muscle groups.
options: A deliberate adjustment of the normal sequence of contraction to reinforce a weaker component or pattern
The unaltered distal-to-proximal sequence seen in normal movement
A technique applied only to isometric holding without movement
A method of eliminating resistance from the stronger pattern
A technique used solely to test maximal resistance tolerance
questions.question: Which of the following best describes 'timing for emphasis' as used in PNF technique?
Adequate sleep supports physiotherapy patient recovery from exercise through which primary mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Sleep is the primary period for physical and psychological recovery from exercise: growth hormone (GH) is predominantly released during slow-wave sleep, supporting muscle protein synthesis and tissue repair; immune function including antibody production and lymphocyte activity peaks during sleep; and emotional regulation is restored through REM sleep processing. Sleep deprivation (below 7 hours) impairs muscle glycogen resynthesis, elevates cortisol, reduces motivation for exercise, increases perceived exertion, and impairs pain tolerance. Physiotherapists should assess and optimise sleep as a fundamental recovery variable.
options: Sleep increases stress hormones for tissue repair
Sleep deprivation improves performance through hormonal stimulation
Sleep does not meaningfully affect stress or recovery
Sleep supports recovery, immunity, and emotional regulation
Minimal sleep is optimal for exercise adaptation

questions.explanation: Maximal resistance to an isometric contraction is the greatest amount of resistance that can be applied without breaking the patient's hold, whereas maximal resistance to an isotonic contraction is the greatest resistance against which the patient can still perform a smooth, coordinated movement through full range. This distinction matters because exceeding either limit would cause either loss of the isometric hold or a jerky, uncoordinated isotonic movement. Both forms of maximal resistance are used to recruit the greatest possible number of motor units.
questions.question: Why is maximal resistance to an isometric contraction defined differently from maximal resistance to an isotonic contraction in PNF technique?
options: Both are defined identically regardless of the type of muscle work
Isometric maximal resistance refers only to passive movement
Isotonic maximal resistance ignores the muscle's available range
One resists without breaking a hold; the other allows smooth full-range movement
Neither definition relates to the patient's voluntary effort

questions.explanation: Cardiovascular drift occurs during prolonged exercise in the heat when progressive dehydration reduces plasma volume, decreasing venous return and stroke volume. Heart rate progressively rises to maintain cardiac output despite declining stroke volume. This drift means that a fixed heart rate target becomes an increasingly ineffective intensity guide over long exercise sessions, as the metabolic demand (VO2) remains relatively constant while heart rate increases without a corresponding increase in work rate.
questions.question: Cardiovascular drift during prolonged exercise involves progressive changes in cardiac function that a physiotherapist should anticipate. The primary mechanism is:
options: Increasing cardiac output from elevated stroke volume
Rising heart rate compensating for declining stroke volume
Falling heart rate from sympathetic nervous system fatigue
Stable cardiac output with constant stroke volume and rate

questions.question: Motor unit recruitment during progressive resistance exercise in physiotherapy follows which orderly pattern?
questions.explanation: Motor unit recruitment follows Henneman's size principle: small motor neurons (innervating type I slow-twitch fibres) have the lowest activation thresholds and are recruited first at low force levels. As force requirements increase, progressively larger motor neurons (innervating type IIa then type IIb fibres) are recruited in order. This orderly recruitment ensures metabolically efficient grading of muscle force. Understanding this principle helps physiotherapists design resistance training to target all motor unit types by prescribing loads that recruit fast-twitch units (greater than 70-80% of 1RM or training to volitional fatigue).
options: Large high-threshold units are recruited first for any load
All motor units are recruited simultaneously regardless of load
Fast-twitch units are always recruited before slow-twitch units
Small low-threshold units (type I) recruit first, with larger units added progressively
Motor unit recruitment is random and unpredictable

questions.explanation: Repeated sprint activities with 20-30 seconds between bouts (as in basketball's play-rest pattern) primarily use the ATP-PCr system for each brief maximal sprint, with PCr largely resynthesised between efforts via oxidative metabolism during the rest intervals. The ability to sustain repeated sprint quality is termed 'repeated sprint ability' and is determined by PCr resynthesis rate (aerobic capacity dependent) and glycolytic contribution during extended sprints. Physiotherapists designing basketball rehabilitation must include repeated sprint protocols that replicate this ATP-PCr/oxidative interaction.
options: Exclusively oxidative metabolism for all sprint bouts
Exclusively glycolytic without any PCr contribution
Fat oxidation via beta-oxidation providing primary substrate
Equal and constant contribution from all three energy systems
ATP-PCr resynthesised between sprints, glycolysis during sprints
questions.question: A physiotherapist evaluates a patient's sport-specific agility and considers which energy system primarily supports repeated change-of-direction sprints with 20-30 seconds between efforts in basketball rehabilitation:

options: The Hamstrings cannot contract at all unless both joints move simultaneously
Hip flexion eliminates the stretch reflex from the movement entirely
Two-joint muscles work most effectively when stretched over the joint not directly involved in the desired movement
The Hamstrings function only as hip extensors, never as knee flexors
Joint position has no influence on two-joint muscle efficiency
questions.explanation: Two-joint muscles are most effective in moving one joint when they are stretched over the other, since that other joint then acts as a fulcrum and the stretching of the muscle provides an additional stimulus to contraction. For the Hamstrings to work efficiently as knee flexors, the hip must therefore be flexed, or flexing, to keep the muscle appropriately stretched at its proximal attachment. The converse situation applies when the Hamstrings are required to work as hip extensors, requiring the knee to extend simultaneously.
questions.question: Why must the hip joint flex, or be flexed by synergic action, when the Hamstrings are required to work efficiently as knee flexors?

options: The base of support of the object
The line of gravity of the object
A point of unstable equilibrium only
The axis of rotation of the object
The centre of gravity of a uniform object
questions.question: A patient balances a rod on one finger and finds the point of exact balance halfway along its length. What does this point represent?
questions.explanation: A uniform rod will balance at a point exactly half-way along its length because this is its centre of gravity, the point through which the earth's attraction effectively acts regardless of the object's position. A rigid body will balance when supported only at its centre of gravity. This simple demonstration underlies the more complex methods used to locate the centre of gravity of irregular objects or the human body.

Warm-up facilitates gradual cardiovascular adjustment (progressive increase in heart rate, cardiac output, and muscle blood flow), increased muscle and tendon temperature (improving viscoelastic properties and enzymatic reaction rates), reduced blood viscosity, and neural activation. Elevated tissue temperature improves force-velocity relationships in muscle, increases nerve conduction velocity, and reduces stiffness of connective tissue, collectively reducing injury risk. Research supports that appropriate warm-up reduces acute musculotendinous injury during subsequent high-intensity exercise.
questions.question: The warm-up phase of a physiotherapy exercise session facilitates which primary physiological processes supporting exercise safety and performance?
options: Complete muscle fatigue before commencing activity
Immediate peak oxygen delivery to all muscle groups
Gradual cardiovascular adjustment, tissue warming, and injury prevention
No physiological benefits; warm-ups are unnecessary

questions.explanation: Flexibility training is most effective and safest when muscle and connective tissue temperature is elevated, which occurs post-exercise. Warm tissues have greater viscoelastic extensibility, lower resistance to stretch, and reduced injury risk. Performing intensive static stretching cold (before warm-up) can temporarily reduce strength and power. The post-exercise period also allows stretching to target the specific muscles and tendons loaded during the session, making it more functionally relevant.
questions.question: Flexibility training should optimally occur at which point in a physiotherapy session to maximise safety and effectiveness?
options: Only before exercise as a mandatory warm-up component
Only during the cool-down phase after aerobic exercise
Exclusively during morning sessions before any physical activity
After exercise when tissues are warm, or as a separate session
Never incorporated into supervised physiotherapy programmes
Demonstration is never useful under any circumstances in exercise teaching
Performing alongside patients always eliminates the need for verbal instruction
Prolonged demonstration wastes time the patient could spend actively practising
This approach is required only for patients unable to see the physiotherapist
Demonstration always improves patient understanding more than active practice
questions.explanation: Much valuable time may be wasted while the patient remains inactive watching a prolonged demonstration when they would be more profitably employed attempting to 'do' the exercise, so it is often preferable for the physiotherapist to perform the exercise alongside the patients in response to her own instructions, except when a rest period would be beneficial. A stop-watch can be used to usefully estimate the proportion of treatment time spent actually exercising versus time spent talking or demonstrating. This reflects the broader principle of maximising the patient's active participation within limited treatment time.
questions.question: Why might it be more valuable for a physiotherapist to perform an exercise alongside patients rather than give a prolonged demonstration before they begin?

questions.explanation: The 48-72 hour recovery period between resistance training sessions for the same muscle groups is the minimum time required for the post-exercise muscle protein synthesis window to complete and for satellite cell activation, myofibrillar remodelling, and restoration of muscle glycogen stores. Training the same muscles before this recovery is complete blunts the hypertrophic signal and increases overuse injury risk. Non-consecutive day scheduling ensures each session is performed in a recovered state, maximising the adaptive stimulus.
questions.question: The primary physiological reason for recommending resistance training frequency of 2-3 non-consecutive days per week in physiotherapy is to:
options: Limit the total training volume to prevent overexertion
Reduce the patient's commitment burden to the programme
Match the schedule of outpatient physiotherapy appointments
Prevent muscle fibre hypertrophy from becoming excessive
Allow adequate time for muscle protein synthesis between sessions

questions.question: A physiotherapist designs a 12-week aerobic training programme for a sedentary patient. Which physiological adaptation is most responsible for the observed reduction in submaximal heart rate at the same work intensity after 8 weeks?
options: Increased stroke volume allowing lower heart rate for same cardiac output
Increased maximum heart rate from cardiac conditioning
Reduced peripheral oxygen extraction by muscles
Reduced skeletal muscle oxygen demand at the same power
questions.explanation: Training-induced improvements in stroke volume (from increased end-diastolic volume, improved myocardial contractility, and enhanced ventricular compliance) allow the same or greater cardiac output to be achieved at a lower heart rate. This is quantified by the Fick equation: VO2 = HR x SV x (a-vO2 diff). With a larger SV, fewer beats per minute are required to achieve the same VO2 at submaximal exercise, explaining why trained individuals have lower submaximal heart rates (and lower resting heart rate - athlete's bradycardia). This is among the earliest and most measurable training adaptations in physiotherapy.

options: Spastic muscles are never subject to disuse of any kind
Spastic paralysis always involves complete destruction of the Anterior Horn Cells
Spastic muscles retain a motor nerve supply via the spinal reflex arc, maintaining some tone
Flaccid muscles receive a stronger reflex nerve supply than spastic muscles
Wasting severity is unrelated to the type of paralysis present
questions.explanation: In spastic paralysis, muscles receive a motor nerve supply only via a spinal reflex because they are cut off from higher centres by an upper motor neurone lesion, leaving them tense and hypertonic but not destroyed, so wasting is not marked. This contrasts with flaccid paralysis, where destruction or severe damage to the Anterior Horn Cells or peripheral nerve removes the motor supply entirely, leading to more rapid and severe wasting. This distinction guides differing treatment priorities for the two conditions.
questions.question: Why is wasting in spastic paralysis generally less marked than in flaccid paralysis?

options: Force is capable of changing either stillness or the pattern of ongoing motion
Force can only ever produce complete stillness in a moving body
Force is unrelated to any change in a body's state of motion
Force always increases the speed of a body's existing motion
Force acts only on bodies that are already in motion
questions.explanation: Force is defined as that which alters the state of rest of a body or its uniform motion in a straight line, meaning it can either set a stationary body into motion or change the speed or direction of a body already moving uniformly. This broad definition underlies why muscular contraction, gravity, and externally applied resistance are all classified as forces within exercise therapy. Recognising force in this general sense is foundational to analysing all subsequent mechanical principles.
questions.question: Why is force defined as something that can alter either the state of rest of a body or its uniform motion in a straight line?

options: Movement occurs toward the smaller force, equal to their sum
No movement occurs since the forces are opposite
Movement occurs equally in both directions simultaneously
Movement occurs toward the greater force, equal to the difference between the two forces
Movement occurs at a right angle to both forces
questions.question: Two forces of unequal magnitude act at the same point in opposite directions on a limb. What determines the direction and magnitude of the resulting movement?
questions.explanation: When two unequal forces act at a common point in opposite directions, movement results in the direction of the greater force. The magnitude of the movement-producing force equals the difference between the magnitudes of the two opposing forces. This principle underlies much of the physiotherapist's work in applying manual resistance that is deliberately less than, equal to, or greater than a patient's muscular effort.

Inner range work occurs when a muscle contracts concentrically from a position of partial contraction, roughly half-way between the limits of full range, to a position of full contraction. This range is used specifically to gain or maintain movement of a joint in the direction of the muscle's pull and to train extensor muscles responsible for joint stabilisation. It is distinguished from outer range work, which instead begins from a position of full stretch.
questions.question: A physiotherapist instructs a patient to flex the elbow from a position of half-flexion to full flexion, working concentrically. Which range of muscle work is being used?

options: Maintaining joint range and the extensibility of muscles
Inducing the myotatic stretch reflex permanently
Replacing the need for any active rehabilitation later
questions.explanation: In cases of flaccid paralysis, passive movement maintains joint range and the extensibility of muscles, with one or two full-range movements performed twice daily generally being sufficient. This prevents adaptive shortening and joint stiffness while voluntary control is absent or being re-established. It does not build muscle strength, since no active muscular work is occurring.
questions.question: A patient with flaccid paralysis of the leg receives daily passive movements of the hip, knee and ankle. What is the primary purpose of this intervention?
Why might rhythmical passive movement of the limbs be used as an adjunct to general relaxation training?
options: It eliminates the need for patient comfort and support
It substitutes for active fixation of proximal joints
It is the primary method of building muscle strength
It can have a soothing effect that helps induce further relaxation or sleep
questions.explanation: Continued rhythmical passive movement can have a soothing effect, and if successful the movement is made progressively slower and less perceptible as the patient relaxes further. It is generally given as a sequel to massage rather than as a standalone primary technique. This use of passive movement is supportive rather than corrective, distinguishing it from passive movement aimed at maintaining joint range.

options: Group work always progresses faster than individual treatment for every patient
Group work eliminates the need for any further individual attention
Group work is used only in the earliest stages before any control is present
Group work has no bearing on confidence or social independence
It teaches concentration on one's own effort, building social confidence
questions.question: Why is group work considered particularly valuable once a patient's control of movement has begun to improve during re-education of inco-ordination?
questions.explanation: As control improves, group work is of great value because it teaches the patient to concentrate on their own efforts without being distracted by those of other people, while also gaining confidence in walking and moving about with others, altering direction, and stopping to avoid bumping into them. This social dimension of re-education addresses functional independence beyond pure movement control. Skills such as climbing stairs and stepping on and off a kerb further extend this confidence toward genuine community independence.

questions.question: A formal command such as 'stride jump, with Arm lifting and lowering... On your marks... go!' is structured into which three recognised parts?
questions.explanation: Each formal command consists of three parts: a preparatory or descriptive word describing the exercise, a pause, and an executive word that specifies the precise moment the exercise is to begin, allowing many patients to perform it in unison or to a definite musical beat. Formal commands are now rarely used but remain a convenient method for starting a well-known exercise or achieving a fair start in competitive games and activities. This structured commanding differs from the informal explanation used for teaching new or individual movements.
options: Preparatory or descriptive word, pause, and executive word
Explanation, practice attempt, and final review

questions.question: Golgi tendon organs (GTOs) detect which mechanical stimulus and produce which protective motor response during physiotherapy resistance training?
questions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs are mechanoreceptors located at the musculotendinous junction that detect muscle tension (force) rather than length. When tension exceeds safe thresholds, GTOs activate Ib afferent fibres that synapse on inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord, causing autogenic inhibition (relaxation) of the same muscle. This protective mechanism prevents excessive force generation that could damage musculotendinous structures. PNF stretching techniques exploit GTO activation to achieve muscle relaxation and improved flexibility in physiotherapy.
options: Muscle length changes, causing facilitation of the stretched muscle
Joint angle, causing reciprocal inhibition of antagonist muscles
Velocity of stretch, causing facilitation of synergist muscles
Temperature changes, causing withdrawal reflex activation
Muscle tension, causing inhibition (autogenic inhibition) of the same muscle

questions.question: A physiotherapist prescribing aerobic training should understand that total peripheral resistance (TPR) during dynamic exercise primarily:
options: Decreases due to vasodilation in working muscles
Increases throughout exercise due to vasoconstriction
Remains unchanged from baseline resting values
Increases in proportion to exercise intensity
Is unaffected by exercise in hypertensive patients
questions.explanation: During dynamic exercise, metabolically active skeletal muscles undergo vasodilation driven by local metabolites (CO2, H+, adenosine, K+) and nitric oxide, dramatically reducing vascular resistance in the exercising limbs. This substantially decreases TPR despite sympathetically mediated vasoconstriction in inactive organs. The net result is reduced TPR alongside increased cardiac output, explaining why systolic blood pressure rises modestly while diastolic blood pressure typically remains stable or decreases during moderate aerobic exercise.

questions.question: Why does the physiotherapist encourage a patient to palpate their own contracting muscle during assisted exercise?
options: It is required to measure the exact joint angle achieved
It substitutes for the physiotherapist's manual assistance
It eliminates the need for verbal commands
Seeing and feeling the contraction helps maintain confidence and encourages maximal voluntary effort
It prevents adaptive shortening of the antagonist muscle
questions.explanation: The ability to see results and feel what is happening is a great help to the patient, so encouraging palpation of the contracting muscle reinforces the connection between effort and visible response. This supports confidence and concentrated effort, both of which are needed to encourage weak muscles to contribute maximally. It is a motivational and sensory feedback strategy rather than a substitute for proper manual technique.

options: General corrections are always more effective than individual corrections for every patient
General corrections eliminate the need for the physiotherapist to observe individual performance
Individual corrections are never appropriate in any group exercise setting
General corrections are given only when no patient in the group requires improvement
They allow the patient a chance to improve without drawing the group's attention specifically to their mistake
questions.question: Why are general, rather than individual, corrections sometimes preferred when addressing a mistake made by a nervous or inattentive patient during group exercise?
questions.explanation: For group work, corrections may be general or individual, with general corrections given when several group members would benefit or to give a nervous or inattentive patient a chance to improve their performance without drawing the group's attention to their specific mistake. Individual corrections, by contrast, involve addressing the patient by name, or the physiotherapist providing manual help and guidance by standing beside a shy or nervous patient. Selecting the appropriate type of correction reflects sensitivity to both the technical need for improvement and the patient's psychological comfort within the group setting.

options: Recommending complete rest immediately after high-intensity exercise
Passive stretching is the most effective post-exercise clearance strategy
Cold water immersion prevents all post-exercise lactate production
Lactate remains elevated for 24-48 hours regardless of recovery activity
Active recovery at low intensity accelerates lactate clearance
questions.question: Understanding the phenomenon of blood lactate clearance after exercise is clinically relevant to physiotherapy because it informs which practice?
questions.explanation: After high-intensity exercise, blood and muscle lactate is oxidised most rapidly when low-intensity active recovery (approximately 30-40% VO2 max) is performed rather than passive rest. Active recovery maintains elevated muscle blood flow, delivering lactate to cardiac muscle, slow-twitch fibres, liver, and kidneys where it is converted to glucose (Cori cycle) or oxidised as fuel. This active recovery strategy reduces blood lactate from post-exercise peaks to near-resting levels within 15-30 minutes, compared to 60-90 minutes for passive rest, supporting faster return to high-intensity work in training and rehabilitation.

Anti-gravity muscles are typically multi-pennate and fan-shaped, an arrangement that signifies powerful action as opposed to the ability to produce a wide range of movement at high speed. This structural feature, combined with a predominance of red muscle fibres capable of sustained low-fatigue contraction, equips these muscles well for their role in maintaining posture over long periods. Long fusiform muscles, by contrast, favour speed and range of movement but generate comparatively less power.
options: A long fusiform arrangement of parallel fibres
A multi-pennate, fan-shaped arrangement of fibres
An arrangement identical to fast phasic muscles
An absence of any red muscle fibres
A structure specialised only for rapid, brief bursts of activity
questions.question: Which structural characteristic of anti-gravity muscles particularly favours their function of powerful, sustained postural contraction?
In the non-weight-bearing crutch gait, why does the patient stand with a triangular base, positioning the crutches either in front of or behind the weight-bearing leg?
questions.explanation: In non-weight-bearing crutch walking, the patient should always stand with a triangular base, with the crutches placed either in front of or behind the weight-bearing leg, which provides a stable support arrangement from which the crutches can then be moved forward and weight taken through them as the unaffected foot is advanced. This triangular arrangement maximises stability throughout the gait cycle. Progression can then be made from placing the foot just behind the line of the crutches to placing it just in front, as balance and confidence improve.
options: It eliminates the need for any hand grip strength
It automatically increases the speed of walking achieved
It provides a stable base of support before weight is transferred forward
It removes the need for any balance assessment beforehand
It is required only for patients using gutter crutches

questions.question: A patient with a habitually stooped posture is found to have shortened pectoral muscles and weak scapular retractors. Which principle guides the muscular re-education approach for this postural defect?
questions.explanation: When joint stiffness or muscular imbalance is present, exercise for the muscles which have been stretched, such as the scapular retractors and upper back extensors, is essential to restore muscular balance, working alongside relaxation of their shortened antagonists such as the pectoral muscles. This dual approach directly addresses the imbalance responsible for the stooping pattern rather than treating either side of the imbalance in isolation. Correcting muscle power alone, without addressing associated tightness, would be unlikely to fully resolve the postural deviation.
options: Only the shortened muscles should ever be targeted for treatment
Strengthening the stretched muscles restores muscular balance while relaxation of their shortened antagonists is required
Only the weakened muscles should ever be targeted for treatment
Muscular re-education plays no part in correcting postural defects
The scapular retractors should be deliberately weakened further

questions.explanation: Stimulation of the muscle spindles under maximal resistance leads to a maximal increase in intramuscular tension and a spread of excitation to adjacent muscle groups, a phenomenon known as irradiation. The extent of this spread and which muscles are affected depends on the demands of the resistance applied. Irradiation is the physiological basis underlying both reinforcement and repeated contraction techniques.
questions.question: Maximal resistance applied during a strong PNF leg pattern causes a spread of muscular excitation into the trunk muscles. What is this spreading phenomenon called?

questions.explanation: Trapezius and Serratus Anterior pull on different points of the scapula in different directions, and unequal forces acting at different points in opposite directions produce rotation. This differs from forces acting at a single common point, which produce either equilibrium or linear motion. Scapular rotation during arm elevation is the textbook example of this mechanical principle.
questions.question: Trapezius and Serratus Anterior contract together to rotate the scapula. Which principle of force composition does this best demonstrate?
options: Equal forces at one point causing equilibrium
A single force causing linear movement
Unequal forces at different points causing rotation
Compounded forces along one line of pull
Forces neutralising at a common point

questions.question: Which statement best explains why disuse from splintage, rather than inability or unwillingness, can lead to muscle weakening even when a patient is physically capable of contracting the muscle?
questions.explanation: When a joint is fixed by splintage it becomes stable and unable to move, so there is no necessity for the patient to contract the surrounding muscles unless compelled by strong resistance offered to other muscles in the same series or by deliberate voluntary effort. Static muscle work is therefore essential during splintage to maintain circulation, muscle power, and tendon movement needed for recovery once the splint is removed. This represents one of three reasons given for muscle disuse, distinct from inability caused by pain or unwillingness caused by patient resistance to effort.
options: Splintage always physically destroys the Anterior Horn Cells of the muscle
Splintage prevents the muscle from contracting under any circumstances
Splintage automatically produces flaccid paralysis in the immobilised limb
Splintage stabilises the joint, removing any functional need to contract
Splintage has no relationship to the risk of muscle wasting
Fit young adults performing high-intensity interval training
Habitual sedentary persons performing unaccustomed vigorous exercise
Elderly aerobically trained individuals in low-intensity activity
Recreational athletes at moderate intensity during team sports
questions.explanation: The risk of cardiovascular events (sudden cardiac death, myocardial infarction) during exercise is disproportionately elevated in habitually sedentary individuals performing unaccustomed vigorous exercise. This population has the least cardiovascular adaptation, highest sympathetically driven heart rate and blood pressure response, and potentially undiagnosed cardiovascular disease. Regular exercisers have substantially lower exercise-related cardiovascular risk. This is why physiotherapists use pre-participation health screening tools (PAR-Q+) before initiating exercise programmes for sedentary patients.
questions.question: Cardiovascular disease risk during exercise is highest in which population, making physiotherapy pre-exercise screening most critical?
A physiotherapist prescribing resistance training for older adults should follow which frequency recommendation to optimise musculoskeletal adaptation?
questions.explanation: Current evidence recommends 2-3 days per week of resistance training per muscle group for older adults, with non-consecutive days to allow 48-72 hours of muscle protein synthesis and repair between sessions. Daily training of the same muscle groups in older adults exceeds their recovery capacity and may blunt adaptation or cause overuse injury. Non-consecutive training provides the necessary stimulus frequency for progressive strength gain while allowing adequate recovery for the age-related reductions in muscle repair efficiency.
options: 2-3 non-consecutive days per week, per muscle group
Daily training every day with no rest between sessions
No regular schedule needed for older adults

questions.question: Ballistic stretching differs from static stretching in physiotherapy practice primarily in that ballistic stretching:
questions.explanation: Ballistic stretching uses rapid, bouncing movements at the end range of motion to attempt to stretch the muscle through momentum. The rapid stretch stimulus may activate muscle spindle Ia afferents, triggering the stretch reflex (myotatic reflex) and causing muscle contraction rather than relaxation, potentially increasing injury risk. Static stretching held for 20-60 seconds at end range is preferred for most rehabilitation patients because it allows time for Golgi tendon organ autogenic inhibition and viscoelastic creep, producing safer muscle elongation. Ballistic stretching may be appropriate for advanced athletes once flexibility is established.
options: Produces greater lasting improvements in range of motion
Is safer than static stretching for all patient populations
Is the preferred method for patients with acute muscle tears
Involves isometric co-contraction of the stretched muscle
Uses rapid bouncing movements that may activate the stretch reflex

questions.question: A physiotherapist developing a strength training programme for a patient with osteoporosis should understand that bone mineral density adaptations from resistance training primarily occur through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Resistance training produces mechanical strain in cortical and trabecular bone that stimulates osteoblast activity through mechanosensory pathways involving osteocytes (lacunocanalicular network signalling). Above a minimum effective strain threshold (approximately 1500-3000 microstrain), bone remodelling shifts favourably toward net mineralisation. Ground reaction forces from weight-bearing exercise and joint reaction forces from muscular pull on bone insertions both contribute to the osteogenic stimulus. High-impact activities produce the greatest bone-forming stimulus, while low-impact activities like swimming provide insufficient mechanical strain for significant bone density improvements.
options: Mechanical loading stimulating osteoblast mineralisation activity
Increasing serum vitamin D through exercise metabolism
Reducing osteoclast activity through anti-inflammatory effects
Increasing intestinal calcium absorption through muscle contractions
Directly incorporating dietary calcium into bone crystal structure

questions.explanation: Phosphocreatine (PCr) stores in skeletal muscle are limited, approximately 75-80 mmol/kg dry muscle weight, and are nearly completely depleted during maximal exercise within 8-10 seconds. Resynthesis of PCr after maximal efforts requires approximately 3-5 minutes of aerobic recovery. The rate of PCr resynthesis determines the interval required between sprint bouts in athletic training and rehabilitation. Understanding PCr dynamics allows physiotherapists to optimise work-to-rest ratios in interval-based sprint rehabilitation programmes.
options: Accumulation of lactate in the cytoplasm of muscle cells
Reduction in muscle glycogen below the glycolytic threshold
Reduced activity of ATPase enzymes from acidosis
Depletion of intramuscular PCr stores during maximal effort
questions.question: The phosphagen (ATP-PCr) system's limited duration of maximum power output (approximately 8-10 seconds) is primarily determined by:
A physiotherapist should understand that during high-intensity anaerobic exercise, blood lactate accumulation causes which immediate physiological effect relevant to performance limitation?
options: Reducing pH impairing muscle contractile protein function
Directly causing the burning sensation in working muscles
Directly damaging mitochondrial DNA in muscle fibres
Increasing glycolytic enzyme activity to maintain energy
Increasing haemoglobin oxygen affinity to improve delivery
questions.explanation: The hydrogen ions (H+) produced alongside lactate during anaerobic glycolysis lower intracellular and blood pH (metabolic acidosis). This acidosis impairs contractile protein function (troponin-calcium interaction), reduces phosphofructokinase (rate-limiting glycolytic enzyme) activity, and impairs excitation-contraction coupling, contributing to fatigue and performance limitation. Note that lactate itself is not the cause of fatigue - it is a useful fuel and marker of metabolic stress. The H+ co-produced with lactate is the primary contributor to acidosis-related fatigue.

Flexion and extension movements take place about a frontal, or transverse, axis and occur within the sagittal plane. This axis lies parallel to the transverse suture of the skull and is horizontal and at right angles to the sagittal axis. The elbow, like most hinge joints, follows this standard relationship.
questions.question: Flexion and extension of the elbow occur about which axis?

questions.explanation: When a joint is injured or diseased, a sero-fibrinous exudate may soak the joint structures, and if not removed promptly, the fibrinous constituents 'glue' the collagenous fibres of ligaments and tendons together to form adhesions. These adhesions, initially soft, later consolidate and contract to form scars, which can progressively limit movement. The shoulder joint is given as an example where capsule folds can become glued if the joint is left immobile too long.
options: Formation of adhesions from a sero-fibrinous exudate
questions.question: Which factor is described as causing limitation of joint range through the 'gluing' of collagenous fibres of ligaments and tendons together?

options: Completely eliminates pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretion
Prevents progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes
Increases insulin resistance independent of body composition
Requires pharmacological adjuncts to achieve effectiveness
Only benefits patients with established type 2 diabetes
questions.question: Regular physical activity combined with modest weight loss is recommended by physiotherapists as the primary approach to preventing type 2 diabetes because it:
questions.explanation: The Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) demonstrated that lifestyle intervention combining regular physical activity (150 min/week moderate-intensity) with modest 5-7% weight loss reduced progression from impaired glucose tolerance to type 2 diabetes by 58%, outperforming metformin pharmacotherapy in all age groups except under 60 years. This evidence positions lifestyle physiotherapy intervention as a first-line prevention strategy. Physiotherapists are uniquely positioned to deliver structured exercise programmes as part of diabetes prevention in high-risk individuals.

questions.question: High-intensity interval training (HIIT) produces time-efficient fitness improvements. The specific physiological advantage most relevant to physiotherapy prescription is:
options: Time-efficient aerobic and anaerobic capacity improvements
No measurable fitness improvements occur with HIIT
HIIT produces only strength rather than aerobic development
HIIT decreases cardiovascular function over time
HIIT requires complete exercise avoidance between sessions
questions.explanation: HIIT simultaneously improves VO2 max (aerobic capacity) and anaerobic capacity more efficiently per unit time than continuous moderate-intensity training. HIIT protocols requiring 20-30 minutes (including rest intervals) produce adaptations equivalent to 60 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise. This time efficiency is particularly valuable in physiotherapy for patients with limited time, rapid reconditioning requirements (post-surgical), or high-performance sport rehabilitation where multiple fitness components must be developed within tight timelines.

The Tabata protocol involves 8 cycles of 20 seconds maximal-effort exercise alternating with 10 seconds of rest (total session: 4 minutes). This protocol was developed by Tabata et al. (1996) and demonstrated simultaneous improvements in both aerobic and anaerobic capacity. The extremely high intensity during work intervals (170% VO2 max) drives substantial metabolic adaptations. Physiotherapists use adapted Tabata or HIIT protocols (reduced intensity) in conditioning programmes for athletes and clinically stable patients requiring time-efficient cardiovascular training.
questions.question: Tabata protocol, a high-intensity interval training format used in physiotherapy conditioning, consists of:
options: Long slow distance training at low intensity
Maximal 20 s effort, 10 s rest, repeated 8 cycles
Minimal intensity exercise throughout the session
Hour-long exercise sessions at moderate intensity

questions.question: The physiological basis for prescribing cool-down after aerobic exercise in physiotherapy involves which primary cardiovascular safety mechanism?
questions.explanation: Abrupt cessation of aerobic exercise can cause venous pooling in the legs (as muscle pump action stops while vasodilation persists) and parasympathetic rebound, potentially causing post-exercise hypotension and syncope - a risk particularly in cardiac patients. A gradual cool-down maintains muscle pump action through continued low-intensity activity, allowing the cardiovascular system to progressively downregulate. Cool-down also facilitates lactate clearance and mental transition from exercise, reducing perceived muscle soreness in the immediate post-exercise period.
options: Maximising lactate removal in blood post-exercise
Reducing the total energy expenditure of the session
Eliminating the need for stretching after exercise
Preventing post-exercise BP and heart rate drop causing fainting
Increasing sympathetic nervous system activity progressively

questions.question: Strategies for long-term exercise adherence that physiotherapists should incorporate into discharge planning include:
questions.explanation: Long-term exercise adherence is maximised by combining multiple evidence-based strategies: setting realistic, specific, achievable goals with patient input (building self-efficacy), selecting intrinsically enjoyable activities that align with patient preferences, incorporating social support (exercise partners, group classes, family involvement), and building flexibility into scheduling to accommodate real-life variability. Physiotherapists should transition patients from supervised to independent exercise gradually while establishing these adherence supports to prevent the common post-discharge exercise dropout.
options: Maximum intensity immediately from the first session
Rigid inflexible programmes without patient input
Only unenjoyable and maximally challenging activities
Realistic goals, enjoyable activities, social support, flexible scheduling
Complete isolation from social support during exercise
Increasing cortisol production and sympathetic activation
Eliminating all life challenges and stressors permanently
Worsening existing anxiety through sympathetic stimulation
Lowering stress hormones and enhancing neurotransmitters
questions.explanation: Exercise reduces chronic stress through multiple neurobiological pathways: post-exercise reductions in cortisol, adrenaline, and sympathetic tone; increased serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine function improving mood regulation; endorphin release producing post-exercise euphoria; and BDNF-mediated neuroplasticity improving stress resilience. These mechanisms operate acutely (single session) and chronically (regular training programme) and are the physiological basis for incorporating exercise as an adjunct treatment for anxiety, depression, and stress-related disorders in physiotherapy.
questions.question: Exercise reduces stress hormones and enhances neurotransmitters, providing physiotherapy patients with psychological benefits primarily through which mechanism?

options: Rapidly increasing speed with constant elevation
Intermittent rest periods between increasing work stages
Cycling ergometer with increasing resistance every minute
Constant walking speed with progressively increasing grade
Arm ergometry protocol designed for non-ambulatory patients
questions.explanation: The Balke protocol is a treadmill test that maintains a constant walking speed (3.3 mph or 5.3 km/h) and increases the treadmill elevation by 1% per minute. This design is more tolerable for older or deconditioned patients because the constant speed avoids the abrupt speed increases in the Bruce protocol, which can be mechanically demanding. The gradual grade increase provides finer workload increments, making the Balke protocol preferred for clinical assessment in cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation.
questions.question: The Balke protocol for graded exercise testing features which specific design characteristic that differentiates it from the Bruce protocol?

options: Lying always eliminates the need for visual feedback entirely
Standing exercises are always introduced before any lying exercises
Support level has no relationship to the degree of achievable control
Progression follows the degree of disability, moving from more supported to less supported positions as control improves
All patients begin exercises identically regardless of disability severity
questions.explanation: According to the degree of disability, Frenkel's re-education exercises start in lying with the head propped up and the limbs fully supported, and progress is made to exercises in sitting and then standing as control develops. This graded reduction in support challenges the patient's control progressively as their ability to compensate through vision and precision improves. Progression is also made by altering the speed, range, and complexity of the exercises themselves as the patient advances.
questions.question: In Frenkel's exercise progression, why do exercises typically begin with the patient lying with limbs fully supported before progressing to sitting and then standing?

options: Functional responses and adaptations of the body to exercise
Biomechanical forces acting on the musculoskeletal system
questions.question: A physiotherapist defining exercise physiology for a new rehabilitation team member should describe it most accurately as the study of:
questions.explanation: Exercise physiology is defined as the study of acute functional responses and chronic adaptive changes in the body in response to physical exercise. This encompasses cardiovascular, respiratory, metabolic, neuromuscular, and endocrine responses to both single exercise bouts and training programmes. Understanding these mechanisms enables physiotherapists to design evidence-based exercise prescriptions for rehabilitation and health promotion.

options: Reduced assistance prevents the stretch reflex from occurring
Less assistance changes the movement into a passive one
Assistance has no relationship to muscle power at any stage
Greater assistance always shortens treatment time
Assistance must decrease in proportion as muscle power increases to avoid substituting for effort
questions.question: During an assisted exercise for weak hip flexors, why does the physiotherapist reduce manual assistance progressively as the patient's strength returns?
questions.explanation: The magnitude of assisting force must be sufficient only to augment muscular action, never to substitute for it, and as the power of the muscle increases the assistance given must decrease proportionally. If assistance is not reduced appropriately, the movement risks becoming effectively passive rather than actively assisted. This graded withdrawal of support is central to progressing assisted exercise toward independent active movement.

options: Maximum physical fitness and conditioning capacity
Confidence in ability to complete exercise tasks
Genetic predisposition to exercise performance outcomes
