Absence of any psychological factors in exercise
questions.explanation: Self-efficacy, as defined by Bandura, is an individual's belief in their own capacity to execute the behaviours required to achieve specific exercise goals. In physiotherapy, self-efficacy is one of the strongest predictors of exercise adherence and long-term health behaviour change. Physiotherapists can enhance patient self-efficacy through graduated mastery experiences (progressive exercise success), verbal encouragement, observational learning from peers with similar conditions, and reinterpreting physiological signals (breathlessness is normal, not dangerous).
questions.question: Self-efficacy for exercise, as defined in physiotherapy behavioural science, refers specifically to:
Which type of crutch is specifically designed for patients with Rheumatoid Disease who cannot take weight through the hands, wrists, and elbows because of deformity or pain?
questions.explanation: Gutter crutches, also called adjustable arthritic or forearm support crutches, are made with a padded forearm support and strap and are used for patients with Rheumatoid Disease who require support but cannot take weight through the hands, wrists, and elbows due to deformity or pain. They are adjustable in length, in the length of forearm support, and in the angle of the hand piece to accommodate these deformities. This differs from elbow crutches, which are suitable for patients with good balance and strong arms who transmit weight in the same way as with axillary crutches.

Outer range work involves the muscle contracting concentrically from a position of full stretch toward partial contraction, and this range is extensively used in re-education because a contraction is initiated more easily from stretch in most muscles. This relates to the stretch reflex mechanism, in which placing a muscle on stretch facilitates its subsequent contraction. This makes outer range work a useful starting point for very weak muscles that struggle to initiate contraction from a shortened position.
options: It eliminates the need for any external resistance
It guarantees the fastest possible strength gain in all cases
It avoids any involvement of the stretch reflex
It only applies to muscles working eccentrically
A contraction is initiated more easily from stretch in most muscles
questions.question: Why is outer range muscle work extensively used in early muscle re-education?

questions.explanation: Eight to twelve weeks of aerobic training produces substantial skeletal muscle adaptations: mitochondrial biogenesis (increased mitochondrial density and respiratory enzyme activity), enhanced fat oxidation capacity (increased fatty acid transport proteins and beta-oxidation enzyme activity), increased capillarisation (more capillaries per muscle fibre improving oxygen diffusion), and potentially type IIb to type IIa fibre conversion. These peripheral adaptations improve metabolic efficiency, allowing the same work rate to be sustained with less cardiovascular stress and lower perceived exertion - the foundation of improved submaximal exercise capacity in physiotherapy rehabilitation.
options: Decreased muscle glycogen storage from training depletion
Increased mitochondrial density, fat oxidation, and metabolic efficiency
Reduced skeletal muscle mitochondrial enzyme capacity
Decreased capillary density from arterial vasoconstriction adaptation
Reduced fibre type changes maintaining initial composition
questions.question: The specific physiological adaptations occurring in skeletal muscle after 8-12 weeks of aerobic training that most directly improve submaximal exercise economy in physiotherapy rehabilitation are:

options: Sensory ataxia from loss of kinaesthetic sensation
Inco-ordination from spasticity of the muscles
Functional inco-ordination with no organic cause
questions.question: Marked hypotonicity, easy fatigue, and a pronounced intention tremor with irregular swaying movement are most characteristic of which type of inco-ordination?
questions.explanation: Cerebellar ataxia is characterised by marked hypotonicity of the muscles, which tire easily, inadequate fixator action, and movement that is irregular and swaying with a marked intention tremor, reflecting loss of the cerebellum's coordinating function. This differs from sensory ataxia, in which the patient is unaware of body position because kinaesthetic sensation is lost, though muscles are similarly hypotonic and tire easily without the sensation of fatigue being recorded. Recognising these distinguishing features helps direct the appropriate re-education strategy for each type of inco-ordination.

options: Pulleys eliminate the effect of gravity on the working limb entirely
The angle of pull can be arranged to match the muscle's varying power
Pulleys always provide more total resistance than a directly applied weight
Pulleys remove the need for any relaxation stop in the circuit
Pulleys can only be used for isometric, not isotonic, muscle work
questions.question: Why does using a weight and pulley system, rather than a weight applied directly to a limb, offer an advantage for resisting a muscle group through its range?
questions.explanation: Because the angle of pull of the rope, and therefore the resistance applied, varies during the course of a movement, a pulley system can offer resistance that more accurately matches the variation of the muscle's power across different parts of its range than a weight applied directly to the limb or a spring. Resistance is typically arranged to act at right angles to the limb at the point of greatest muscular power, usually mid-range. A relaxation stop is incorporated into the circuit to ensure the joint is not strained between repetitions.

options: Both use an identical area regardless of position
Lying uses only the heels; standing uses the entire trunk
Lying uses the centre of gravity directly; standing does not
Lying has no defined base; standing always does
Lying uses the whole posterior body surface as base; standing uses the area between the feet
questions.question: Which best describes the difference between the base of a body in lying compared with stride standing?
questions.explanation: In lying, the posterior aspect of the whole body in contact with the supporting surface forms the base, which is large and contributes to high stability. In stride standing the effective base is the area bounded by the outer borders of the feet, which is considerably smaller. This difference in base size is the principal reason lying is the most stable posture and standing the least stable of common positions.

Grasping the distal phalanges while keeping the toes straight by traction and performing the movement at the metatarsophalangeal joints, usually with emphasis on flexion, is described as preferable because it more nearly approaches the correct functional movement of the toes in gripping the floor. This functional consideration guides the choice of technique even when an alternative grasp would achieve a similar passive range. Fixation and traction principles still apply regardless of which grasp is selected.
questions.question: During passive movement of the toe metatarsophalangeal joints, why is grasping the distal phalanges while keeping the toes straight by traction considered preferable to grasping the proximal phalanges?
options: It eliminates the need for any traction during the movement
It avoids the need to fix the metatarsal bones at all
It increases resistance applied to the interphalangeal joints
It more closely approaches the correct functional movement of the toes gripping the floor
It is the only method that allows abduction and adduction

questions.explanation: In concentric work the muscle's attachments are drawn toward its centre as it shortens and overcomes an opposing force, whereas in eccentric work the attachments are drawn apart as the muscle lengthens and pays out under control. Concentric work has a higher physiological energy cost than eccentric work for a comparable load. Both are forms of active isotonic movement, distinguished from isometric work in which no length change occurs.
questions.question: Which statement correctly differentiates concentric from eccentric active movement in terms of the muscle's behaviour?
options: Concentric work always uses more energy than eccentric work for equal load
Eccentric work shortens the muscle while concentric work lengthens it
Concentric work shortens the muscle; eccentric work lengthens it under control
Both types of work always result in equal joint movement
Eccentric work cannot occur during active free exercise
Immediate permanent abolition of the stretch reflex
Relaxation and lengthening of the spastic muscle
Conversion of isometric to isotonic work
Stimulation of the muscle spindle to increase tone
Formation of new adhesions within the joint
questions.explanation: Controlled sustained stretching can be used to overcome spasticity patterns of limbs, such as in a hemiplegic patient, because slow sustained stretch produces relaxation and lengthening of the affected muscle. This differs from a quick stretch, which would instead tend to elicit the stretch reflex and increase tone. Sustained stretch is therefore favoured specifically for managing spastic hypertonicity.
questions.question: A physiotherapist applies a steady, prolonged passive stretch to overcome a spasticity pattern in a hemiplegic patient's wrist flexors. What is the expected physiological effect?
A muscle's attachments are drawn closer together as it contracts to produce movement against an external force. What type of muscle work is this?
questions.explanation: When the attachments of a working muscle are drawn toward the centre of that muscle, it is said to work concentrically, becoming shorter and thicker as joint movement results from overcoming an opposing force. This is one of the two forms of isotonic work, distinguished from eccentric work in which the muscle lengthens under control as its attachments are drawn apart. Concentric work has a relatively high physiological cost since only about a quarter of the energy liberated is available as mechanical work.

options: Block the myosin-binding sites on actin filaments at rest
Bind calcium ions released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Generate the power stroke during cross-bridge cycling
Transmit force from sarcomeres to the tendon
Provide structural stability to the Z-disc of the sarcomere
questions.explanation: Tropomyosin is a regulatory protein that, in the resting state, physically covers the myosin-binding sites on actin filaments, preventing cross-bridge formation and muscle contraction. When calcium binds to troponin (part of the troponin-tropomyosin complex), a conformational change shifts tropomyosin away from the binding sites, allowing myosin heads to attach to actin and initiate the sliding filament mechanism. This regulation is fundamental to excitation-contraction coupling.
questions.question: Tropomyosin's primary function in skeletal muscle is to:

A physiotherapist increases the speed at which a free exercise is performed without changing the range of movement. According to mechanical principles, what is the most direct effect on the working muscles?
options: Greater tension is created in the muscle
The base of support is automatically widened
Equilibrium of the joint becomes unstable
The centre of gravity of the limb is lowered
questions.explanation: Tension created in working muscles is greater when an exercise is performed at a speed slower or faster than the natural rhythm of movement, and tension also increases with duration of effort. Increasing speed beyond the natural rate therefore raises the demand placed on the contracting muscle. This relationship between speed and tension underlies how free exercise intensity can be graded without adding external resistance.

questions.question: Why must the knee be flexed, rather than left straight, when passively mobilising the ankle into dorsiflexion?
questions.explanation: Tension on the calf muscles, which cross both the knee and ankle joints, must be slackened to avoid artificially limiting dorsiflexion, so a starting position with the knee bent, such as half lying with the knee over a firm pillow, is selected for this passive movement. If the knee remained straight, tightness in the two-joint Gastrocnemius would restrict the available ankle range. This illustrates the general principle of accounting for two-joint muscles when mobilising a joint they cross.
options: Knee flexion increases tension on the calf muscles deliberately
Knee flexion is required only to fix the talus
Knee position has no effect on ankle dorsiflexion range
Knee flexion prevents accessory movement at the subtaloid joint
Tension on the calf muscles must be slackened to avoid limiting dorsiflexion

questions.explanation: The oxygen deficit represents the delay between exercise onset and the achievement of steady-state oxygen uptake. During this period, ATP-PCr and glycolytic systems compensate for the initial oxidative shortfall. A gradual warm-up reduces the magnitude of the oxygen deficit by progressively activating the cardiovascular and oxidative systems before main exercise. This reduces early metabolic stress, lowering perceived exertion and decreasing risk of cardiovascular events at exercise onset.
questions.question: The oxygen deficit at exercise onset occurs because the oxidative energy system cannot immediately meet energy demands. The clinical implication for physiotherapy warm-up prescription is to:
options: Allow cardiovascular and oxidative system time to reach steady state
Begin exercise at maximum intensity to trigger oxygen delivery
Administer supplemental oxygen before exercise commencement
Perform passive stretching to reduce initial oxygen demand
Skip warm-up in patients with high aerobic fitness levels
Brief high-intensity exercise performed once per week only
Complete rest from all physical activity
Moderate intensity, 30 minutes, most days of the week
questions.question: Exercise at moderate intensity most days of the week for mental health is recommended at which specific dose for general psychological wellbeing?
questions.explanation: Current mental health exercise guidelines recommend moderate-intensity aerobic exercise for 30 minutes on most days of the week (equivalent to 150 minutes per week) for general psychological wellbeing, anxiety reduction, and mild-to-moderate depression management. This dose produces reliable acute and chronic reductions in anxiety and depressive symptoms through neurobiological mechanisms. Physiotherapists should routinely integrate mental health outcomes into exercise programme goals, as psychological and physical health are inseparable in comprehensive rehabilitation.

options: Myofibrillar protein accretion increasing fibre cross-sectional area
Increased number of muscle cells through mitosis
Addition of entirely new muscle fibres (hyperplasia) only
Enlargement of muscle nuclei without fibre changes
questions.question: Muscle hypertrophy from resistance training occurs through which cellular mechanisms that physiotherapy rehabilitation programmes should be designed to stimulate?
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle hypertrophy results primarily from net myofibrillar protein accretion: the balance between muscle protein synthesis (MPS) and muscle protein breakdown (MPB) shifts in favour of synthesis following resistance exercise and adequate protein intake. Actin and myosin filament content increases within existing fibres, enlarging their cross-sectional area and increasing force production capacity. Satellite cell activation also contributes myonuclei to support the expanded protein synthetic capacity in hypertrophied fibres. Hyperplasia (new fibre formation) is debated but not a primary mechanism in humans.

questions.question: Which method is specifically described for reducing joint exudate and so helping to prevent adhesion formation, aside from bacterial infection cases?
questions.explanation: Except in cases of bacterial infection, persistent efforts must be made to assist removal of exudate or swelling before adhesions become organised, achieved through elevation of the part, elastic bandaging, and rhythmical active exercise of muscles and joints in the vicinity to assist venous return. Other methods such as contrast baths, massage and heat may also be employed if required. This active approach to managing exudate is central to preventing the secondary stiffness that follows untreated joint swelling.
options: Elevation of the part, elastic bandaging, and rhythmical active exercise of muscles and joints nearby
Complete immobilisation of the limb in a dependent position
Avoidance of any movement until the joint is fully healed
Forceful passive stretching applied at maximal range
Application of strong resistance directly across the joint
They respond rapidly but fatigue very quickly under load
They contain no blood supply and rely on anaerobic metabolism
They are incapable of any sustained postural contraction
They are found exclusively in muscles producing fast movement
They contract slowly but can sustain contraction for a long time without fatigue
questions.question: Why are 'red' muscle fibres predominant in anti-gravity muscles such as Soleus rather than in muscles primarily responsible for fast movement?
questions.explanation: Red fibres, due to a rich blood supply and the presence of pigment, contract slowly in response to stimulation but can sustain contraction for a considerable time without fatigue, which is why they predominate in anti-gravity muscles such as Soleus that maintain posture. White fibres, by contrast, respond rapidly to stimulation but fatigue easily, predominating in muscles such as Gastrocnemius that are primarily responsible for movement. This fibre-type distribution reflects the differing functional demands placed on postural versus phasic muscles.

A small base and raised centre of gravity on a compliant surface mean small displacements progressively increase rather than being corrected, which defines unstable equilibrium. The line of gravity moves closer to the margin of the base until it falls outside it, forcing a corrective step. This is why single-leg stance on foam is used to challenge balance reactions.
questions.question: A patient balancing on one leg on a foam pad shows increasing sway until they step out to recover. Which equilibrium state is being demonstrated just before the step?

options: Approximately double the resting flow only
As much as ten times as great
Exactly equal to the resting blood flow
Reduced to half the resting blood flow
Unrelated to the intensity of the exercise performed
questions.explanation: Although blood flow is impeded during the actual muscular contraction, the amount of blood contained in the muscles immediately after contraction may be as much as ten times as great during strenuous exercise as the amount contained during rest. This dramatic post-exercise increase in blood flow continues for some time, supplying oxygen and nutrition while assisting the removal of metabolic waste products. This circulatory response underlies much of the systemic benefit attributed to resisted exercise beyond the local strengthening effect.
questions.question: Increased blood flow to working muscles immediately after strenuous resisted exercise can be how many times greater than the resting blood flow, according to the described physiological response?

questions.explanation: Resistance offered by water increases with both the speed of movement and the surface area of the part moved, and when the movement is vertical, buoyancy adds to resistance on the way down while cancelling much of the resistance on the way up. Springs, by contrast, offer resistance that increases progressively as they are stretched or compressed, and are considered a relatively crude method as their resistance cannot be precisely matched to a muscle's varying power and range. Each resistance medium therefore has its own distinctive resistance-versus-movement relationship that suits different clinical situations.
questions.question: Among the listed methods of providing resistance, which is described as offering resistance that increases with both the speed and the surface area of the part being moved?
The specific role of the thoracolumbar fascia in core stability during resistance exercise, which physiotherapists should understand for spinal rehabilitation, is that it functions as:
questions.explanation: The thoracolumbar fascia (TLF) is a multi-layered fibrous structure connecting the paraspinal muscles, latissimus dorsi, gluteus maximus, transversus abdominis, and oblique abdominals. When these muscles contract (particularly transversus abdominis creating hoop tension), the TLF transmits forces across the lumbopelvic region, enhancing spinal stiffness and load transfer between the spine, pelvis, and lower limbs. This force transmission mechanism is a key component of the integrated 'cylinder' model of core stability. Rehabilitation targeting TLF tension optimisation (through transversus abdominis activation) is central to lumbar stabilisation programmes.
options: A passive structure with no contribution to spinal loading
A force transmission mechanism linking spinal and limb muscles
The primary flexor of the lumbar spine during lifting
A source of direct compressive loading on lumbar discs
A proprioceptive organ providing joint position sense only

questions.question: Which factor most directly explains why static postural tone is greater in standing than in supported lying?
options: The muscle spindle circuit is inactive during standing
Reciprocal innervation is reversed in standing
Voluntary movement increases tone only in lying
The stretch reflex is absent in upright postures
Gravity stretches the postural muscles more strongly when unsupported in standing
questions.explanation: Postural tone is maintained by the myotatic, or stretch, reflex, which responds to the degree to which gravity stretches the anti-gravity muscles. In standing, gravity exerts a stronger stretching effect on these muscles than in recumbent positions where the body is fully supported. This is why fully supported lying positions are selected for training general relaxation.

questions.question: The physiological basis for prescribing blood flow restriction (BFR) training at low loads in physiotherapy rehabilitation is that partial arterial and venous occlusion causes:
options: Complete muscle hypoxia reducing all metabolic activity
Metabolite accumulation and fast-twitch recruitment at low loads
Increased oxygen delivery driving oxidative adaptation
Reduced motor unit recruitment from reduced force demands
Enhanced recovery through improved nutrient delivery
questions.explanation: Blood flow restriction training applies partial occlusion to restrict venous outflow while maintaining arterial inflow. This creates intramuscular hypoxia and accumulation of metabolites (H+, lactate, Pi), which causes early fatigue of type I fibres and consequent recruitment of type II (fast-twitch) fibres at loads as low as 20-40% of 1RM. Type II fibre recruitment at these low loads is the primary mechanism driving hypertrophic adaptation normally requiring 70-80% of 1RM. BFR enables tissue-protective strength training in post-surgical or pain-limited patients where heavy loading is contraindicated.

questions.question: The force-velocity relationship in skeletal muscle (Hill's curve) is most clinically relevant to physiotherapy when designing resistance training programmes because it demonstrates:
questions.explanation: The force-velocity relationship demonstrates an inverse relationship between shortening velocity and force production in concentric contractions: slower contractions allow more cross-bridges to form simultaneously, generating higher forces. Isometric (zero velocity) and near-isometric slow contractions produce maximum force; eccentric contractions produce even greater force (120-160% of isometric maximum) because external force can pull sarcomeres apart while cross-bridges resist. Physiotherapists use this principle to prescribe slow, controlled resistance movements for maximum force development and to include eccentric loading for tendon rehabilitation.
options: Maximum force is generated at maximum contraction speed
Force and velocity are directly proportional at all speeds
Force is unrelated to velocity during muscle contraction
Slow contractions (isometric and near-isometric) generate maximum force
Eccentric contractions generate less force than concentric
Progressive Resistance Exercise using a de Lorme boot
questions.explanation: Controlled sustained passive stretching is described as inhibiting spasm sufficiently to permit movement in spastic paralysis, used alongside reflex movement initiated through Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation techniques such as the stretch stimulus combined with a command for voluntary effort. Both approaches aim to develop any remaining voluntary control while reducing the masking effect of spasm. This differs from the strengthening-focused techniques such as Progressive Resistance Exercise, which are aimed at building muscle power rather than reducing hypertonicity.
questions.question: Which technique is described as helping to reduce hypertonic spasm sufficiently to permit movement, alongside reflex movement initiated through PNF stretch stimulus?

options: Greater maximum strength in one-repetition maximum testing
Superior explosive power output in jump testing
Faster motor unit discharge rates at all exercise intensities
Better fatigue resistance during prolonged submaximal tasks
Greater rate of force development during ballistic movements
questions.question: When a physiotherapist assesses the functional implications of different muscle fibre type distributions in patients, the clinical relevance is that individuals with a high proportion of type I (slow-twitch) fibres will demonstrate:
questions.explanation: Type I (slow-twitch, oxidative) fibres have higher mitochondrial density, greater capillarisation, slower ATPase activity (more economical ATP utilisation), and lower calcium cycling rates that collectively confer superior fatigue resistance during prolonged aerobic activities. Individuals with high type I proportions demonstrate greater endurance capacity, sustained force production during repetitive activities, and better recovery between efforts. This has clinical implications for physiotherapy when prescribing work assessment protocols, selecting appropriate rehabilitation exercise modes, and explaining individual patient responses to different exercise types.

options: Maximum cardiovascular stress and high-intensity effort
No stress reduction mechanisms unlike aerobic exercise
Physical activity, breath work, and mindfulness integration
questions.question: Mind-body exercises such as yoga and tai chi reduce stress and improve physiotherapy patient outcomes because they integrate:
questions.explanation: Mind-body exercises integrate physical movement with controlled breath work and mindfulness (present-moment awareness), simultaneously activating parasympathetic nervous system (vagal tone enhancement, reduced heart rate, lower cortisol), improving proprioception and balance, and cultivating cognitive stress regulation skills. Clinical trials demonstrate significant reductions in anxiety, blood pressure, and pain perception in yoga and tai chi practitioners. Physiotherapists should consider prescribing mind-body exercises for patients where stress, anxiety, or chronic pain are significant comorbidities.

Movement that takes place in the horizontal plane is gravity-free because only frictional resistance from the supporting surface opposes the muscle. Positioning the patient in side lying with the limb supported on a flat surface allows hip extension to occur in this gravity-eliminated plane. This is the rationale for grading exercise intensity through choice of starting position before progressing to movement against gravity.
questions.question: A physiotherapist wants a patient's weak hip extensors to lift the leg with the least possible muscular demand. Which starting position best achieves a gravity-eliminated plane for this movement?
options: Standing with the leg moving against gravity
Prone lying with the leg lifted vertically
Sitting with the leg moving in a vertical arc
Side lying with the leg supported on a horizontal surface
Crook lying with the leg held unsupported

questions.question: The centre of gravity of the human body in standing in the anatomical position lies approximately at the level of which structure?
questions.explanation: The centre of gravity of the human body in the anatomical standing position is reputed to lie in the vicinity of the body of the second sacral vertebra. Its exact position varies with build, being slightly higher in men and children due to greater upper body mass. This landmark is used as a general reference rather than an absolute fixed point.

questions.question: Graded exercise testing (GXT) in physiotherapy primarily assesses which functional outcome most relevant to cardiac rehabilitation?
questions.explanation: Graded exercise testing is the systematic incremental increase of exercise workload to assess cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2 max or peak), detect exercise-limiting symptoms (chest pain, dyspnoea, ECG changes, blood pressure abnormalities), and determine safe exercise intensity ranges for rehabilitation prescription. In cardiac rehabilitation, GXT identifies ischaemic threshold, arrhythmias, and haemodynamic responses to exercise that guide safe exercise prescription and risk stratification.
options: Maximum muscle strength during progressive loading
Cardiorespiratory fitness and detection of exercise-limiting symptoms
Proprioceptive accuracy across a range of joint angles
Pulmonary function during increasing ventilatory demands
Neuromuscular fatigue threshold during endurance efforts

questions.question: Exercise reduces stress and anxiety primarily through which neurobiological mechanisms most relevant to physiotherapy-based mental health management?
questions.explanation: Exercise reduces stress and anxiety through multiple neurobiological mechanisms: reducing cortisol and adrenaline levels after each session, increasing beta-endorphin (endogenous opioid) release producing post-exercise mood elevation, enhancing serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine neurotransmitter function, and promoting neuroplasticity through BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) production. Regular exercise produces lasting reductions in trait anxiety. These mechanisms support physiotherapy's expanding role in managing comorbid mental health conditions in rehabilitation patients.
options: Increasing cortisol production and sympathetic tone
Eliminating all life challenges and stressors permanently
Lowering stress hormones and enhancing neurotransmitters

questions.question: During supervised exercise testing of a pregnant patient, the physiotherapist should anticipate which primary cardiovascular response that differs from the non-pregnant state?
questions.explanation: Pregnancy causes significant cardiovascular changes: blood volume increases 40-50%, cardiac output rises 30-50%, and resting heart rate increases 10-20 beats/min above pre-pregnancy levels. Plasma volume expansion exceeds red cell mass increase, causing physiological anaemia that can reduce submaximal exercise tolerance. Physiotherapists must account for elevated baseline heart rate when using heart rate-based intensity targets during prenatal exercise, typically using perceived exertion scales as a more appropriate intensity guide in pregnancy.
options: Reduced heart rate at any given work intensity
Decreased blood volume requiring lower exercise intensity
Reduced ventilatory response to increasing exercise loads
Lower resting blood pressure from elevated systemic resistance
Elevated resting heart rate and cardiac output

questions.question: Long-term exercise maintenance is most strongly predicted by which psychological and behavioural factors in physiotherapy patients?
questions.explanation: Long-term exercise maintenance requires a constellation of psychosocial factors: intrinsic motivation (exercising for personal satisfaction, health, or enjoyment rather than external pressure), high self-efficacy (confidence in exercise ability), habitual automaticity (exercise becoming routine behaviour), and social support (from family, peers, or health professionals). Physiotherapists should identify which of these factors are limiting adherence for each patient and address them explicitly through motivational interviewing, goal-setting, and social support programming.
options: Initial high-intensity excessive training without adequate recovery
External rewards exclusively driving exercise behaviour
Perfect adherence without breaks from the outset
No psychological factors - only physical ability matters
Intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, habit strength, and social support

questions.question: What is the key functional difference between resisted exercise and assisted-resisted exercise in muscle re-education?
questions.explanation: Assisted-resisted exercise combines assistance and resistance within one movement, meeting the needs of partially weak muscles with greater accuracy than assistance alone, since muscle strength typically varies through range. Pure resisted exercise, by contrast, is used when a muscle is strong enough throughout range to work against an opposing force without needing assistance anywhere. The choice between the two depends on whether the muscle's deficit is uniform or confined to part of the range.
options: Assisted-resisted exercise adapts the external force to match the muscle's varying ability across the range
Resisted exercise can never be combined with assistance
Assisted-resisted exercise is always weaker than pure resistance
Resisted exercise is used only for fully paralysed muscles
Assisted-resisted exercise eliminates the need for muscle testing
It always causes immediate joint dislocation
It permanently abolishes the stretch reflex
It produces unstable equilibrium in the joint
questions.explanation: Forcing passive movement or applying strong resistance around the elbow soon after injury carries a recognised danger of provoking myositis ossificans, an abnormal deposition of bone in soft tissue. This is why gentle, controlled approaches are favoured in this region during the early stages of recovery from elbow trauma. The risk is specific to this joint region rather than a universal contraindication for all passive movement.
questions.question: Why is forceful passive movement or strong resistance contra-indicated soon after an elbow injury?

options: Decreased diastolic blood pressure from muscle vasodilation
Decreased systolic pressure from reduced cardiac output
Minimal blood pressure change throughout the contraction
Large increases in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure
Isolated systolic pressure increase with no diastolic change
questions.explanation: Sustained isometric contractions above approximately 15-30% of maximum voluntary contraction compress intramuscular vasculature, restricting muscle blood flow and stimulating metaboreceptors (group III and IV afferents). This triggers a pressor response mediated by the exercise pressor reflex, causing large increases in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure (and heart rate), with minimal increase in cardiac output. Unlike aerobic exercise where systolic rises while diastolic is stable, isometric exercise elevates both components. Physiotherapists must monitor blood pressure responses to isometric exercise, particularly in hypertensive patients.
questions.question: Blood pressure response to isometric exercise differs from dynamic aerobic exercise in physiotherapy assessment. Isometric exercise primarily causes:
A physiotherapist teaching patients about the energy continuum concept should explain that a 400-metre swim primarily relies on which combination of energy systems?
questions.explanation: A competitive 400-metre swim at racing pace takes approximately 4-5 minutes for trained swimmers, an exercise duration that spans the glycolytic-oxidative transition. At this duration, both the glycolytic system (contributing to the high-intensity anaerobic load of racing pace) and the oxidative system (sustaining ATP production over the 4-5 minute duration) contribute significantly, with the oxidative system becoming increasingly dominant as the effort extends. This contrasts with short sprints (ATP-PCr dominant) or prolonged distance swimming (oxidative dominant).
options: Glycolytic and oxidative systems in approximately equal proportion
Exclusively ATP-PCr for the entire duration
Predominantly oxidative metabolism with minimal glycolytic contribution

questions.explanation: Hold-relax involves isometric contraction of the hypertonic muscle held against maximal resistance to build excitation, followed by voluntary relaxation, after which successive induction facilitates the antagonist and reciprocal innervation increases the lengthening reaction of the hypertonic muscle. An attempt is then made to move further into the previously limited range. The technique is simple, effective, and pain-free, and is often followed by repeated contractions to consolidate any gain in range.
options: Isometric contraction is followed by relaxation, then successive induction facilitates the antagonist
Maximal resistance is applied continuously without any relaxation phase
The hypertonic muscle is stretched suddenly at high velocity
Reciprocal innervation is bypassed entirely during the technique
The antagonist muscle is fixed rather than facilitated
questions.question: A physiotherapist applies hold-relax to a hypertonic muscle group limiting range at a joint. What physiological sequence underlies the resulting increase in range?

questions.explanation: Normal timing may be defeated by the application of too much resistance to a particular component of the movement, such as the foot in leg movements, which decreases the efficiency of the overall pattern. This illustrates why resistance in PNF must be carefully graded across all three components of a movement rather than concentrated inappropriately. Correcting this requires re-establishing the natural distal-to-proximal sequence before progressing the exercise further.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices that a patient's distal foot movement is given disproportionately strong resistance during a leg pattern, reducing the overall efficiency of the exercise. What facilitation principle has been violated?
options: Maximal resistance has been correctly applied throughout
Re-inforcement has correctly proceeded from strength to weakness
Normal timing has been defeated by excessive resistance applied to a distal component
Rhythmic stabilisation has been appropriately performed
The stretch reflex has been correctly elicited

questions.explanation: At the onset of high-intensity exercise, TCA (Krebs) cycle flux must increase rapidly to meet elevated ATP demands. This is facilitated by anaplerotic reactions that expand the pool of TCA cycle intermediates (particularly succinate, fumarate, and oxaloacetate), most importantly through the purine nucleotide cycle converting amino acids (aspartate, glutamate) via fumarate to maintain adequate intermediate concentrations. This intermediate expansion is a critical early adaptation at exercise onset that sustains TCA flux until acetyl-CoA supply fully matches demand.
options: Carbon dioxide is recycled directly as a Krebs cycle substrate
Pyruvate completely replaces acetyl-CoA at high intensities
Anaplerotic reactions (especially from amino acids) maintain cycle intermediates
Fatty acid beta-oxidation inhibits the Krebs cycle at high intensities
The Krebs cycle capacity decreases above the anaerobic threshold
questions.question: The response of the Krebs cycle to increased exercise intensity that physiotherapists should understand is that TCA cycle intermediate expansion occurs because:
The innervation ratio in skeletal muscle directly determines which functional property most relevant to physiotherapy assessment?
options: Blood flow regulation within the muscle
Speed of action potential conduction along nerve fibres
questions.explanation: The innervation ratio is the number of muscle fibres innervated by a single motor neuron. Low innervation ratios (e.g., 3-6 fibres per motor neuron in extraocular or intrinsic hand muscles) enable fine motor control and precise force gradation. High innervation ratios (hundreds to thousands of fibres in postural muscles) enable powerful contractions but with less precision. Physiotherapists applying manual therapy or prescribing fine motor rehabilitation must understand how innervation ratio affects therapeutic exercise outcomes.

questions.question: Why is training of static postures in the erect position considered basic to postural re-education for most patients?
options: Static erect posture is never relevant to dynamic activities such as walking
Dynamic postures are always trained before any static postures are introduced
Erect posture training is required only for children, not adults
Most people spend most waking hours in static upright positions
Static posture has no influence on the alignment maintained during walking
questions.explanation: Training of static postures in the erect position is described as basic, largely because most people, apart from very small children, are compelled to spend most of their waking hours in relatively static upright positions such as standing and sitting. Even in walking, the alignment of the trunk remains more or less the same as in static standing, making the erect static posture a foundational reference point. Establishing the ability to remain still without undue effort is also considered a valuable habit to acquire in its own right.

questions.question: In a specific exercise scheme designed to treat a local condition, where are strengthening and mobilising exercises typically positioned relative to coordination and functional-use exercises?
questions.explanation: Within a specific scheme addressing a local condition, the arrangement can only be planned in broad outline, with exercises that are strengthening and mobilising in effect placed at the beginning, and those which train coordination and the functional use of the part predominating toward the end. An effort is also made to avoid using the same muscles strongly in consecutive exercises to prevent undue fatigue. This progression from foundational strength and mobility toward integrated functional use mirrors the overall philosophy of rehabilitation moving from impairment-focused to function-focused treatment.
options: Coordination exercises always precede any strengthening work
Functional exercises are placed exclusively at the very start of the scheme
Strengthening exercises begin the scheme; coordination exercises predominate later
Strengthening and coordination exercises are always given equal emphasis throughout
The arrangement of a specific scheme cannot be planned in any systematic way

questions.explanation: Forcing of passive movement or the application of strong resistance is specifically contra-indicated following recent injury to the elbow region because of the danger of myositis ossificans, the abnormal formation of bone within soft tissue. This contraindication is unique to the post-injury elbow rather than a universal rule for all joints. Gentler, more controlled approaches to mobility are therefore preferred in this region during early recovery.
questions.question: Why is forced passive movement specifically avoided in the elbow region following recent injury?
options: It always results in permanent joint dislocation
It eliminates all accessory movement in the joint
It is the only joint where adhesions never form
It carries a recognised risk of provoking myositis ossificans
It prevents the joint from being rested in any position
Crook lying eliminates any need to contract the abdominal muscles
Standing provides greater support to the trunk than crook lying
Crook lying prevents any hollowing of the lumbar spine from occurring
Pelvic tilt cannot be taught in any position other than crook lying
The trunk is supported in alignment while the pelvis remains free to move in an antero-posterior direction
questions.question: Voluntary control of the pelvic tilt is typically first taught in crook lying rather than in standing. What is the main reason for beginning in this position?
questions.explanation: In crook lying the trunk is supported in a position of alignment while the pelvis is free to move in an antero-posterior direction, making this an ideal starting position for teaching voluntary control of pelvic tilt, achieved through contraction of the hip extensors and straight abdominal muscles to tilt the pelvis backward, or hollowing of the lumbar spine for the reverse movement. Once this control is established it can be transferred to sitting and standing positions. This progression mirrors the broader principle of teaching new movement patterns in a supported position before challenging them in less supported postures.

questions.question: Muscle protein synthesis is maximised following resistance training by:
questions.explanation: Muscle protein synthesis (MPS) is maximally stimulated by combining resistance exercise with adequate leucine-containing protein intake of approximately 20-40 g per meal (0.25-0.40 g/kg body mass). This protein dose saturates the MPS response and provides essential amino acids (especially leucine as an mTOR activator) required for new protein synthesis. Physiotherapists should advise patients on post-exercise protein intake timing and quantity to optimise muscle building and repair during rehabilitation.
options: Avoiding all protein intake during the training phase
Resistance training with adequate protein intake (20-40 g per meal)
Consuming only carbohydrates within 30 minutes post-exercise
Training to complete muscular failure on every set
Extended fasting after training to promote hormonal response

questions.explanation: Mass movement patterns used in PNF are spiral and diagonal because they are closely allied to those of normal functional movement and lie in the line of action of the main muscle components responsible for the movement. This makes them more effective for facilitation than straight movements because the muscles work more efficiently along these pathways. Everyday examples include taking the hand to the mouth or chopping wood.
questions.question: Why are the patterns of movement used in Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation described as spiral and diagonal rather than straight-line movements?
options: They reduce the total resistance applied during treatment
They eliminate the rotatory component of movement
They are easier to perform than straight movements
They avoid the need for manual contact
They closely follow the natural line of pull of the muscles producing functional movement
Any free exercise automatically increases range regardless of technique
The mobilising effect depends largely on the manner in which the exercise is performed
Mobilising effect depends solely on the choice of starting position
Pendular movement can never influence joint range
Mobilising effect is unrelated to the speed of the movement
questions.question: A physiotherapist chooses pendular movement with a gradually increasing amplitude as a free exercise to mobilise a stiff shoulder. What is the key principle determining its mobilising effect?
questions.explanation: With free exercise it is emphasised that a mobilising effect results not so much from the choice of a particular exercise but depends largely on the manner in which it is performed, with full-range movement at natural speed and emphasis at the limit of range, repeated frequently, generally most effective. Sometimes more rapid movement or sustained contraction at the limit of range is used instead. This highlights technique and repetition as more important than the specific exercise selected.

questions.question: What is the key difference between the two described methods of partial weight-bearing crutch gait?
questions.explanation: The first method of partial weight-bearing is a progression from shadow walking, where the crutches and affected leg are taken forward and put down together before weight is taken through them while the unaffected leg is brought through, allowing a gradual increase in weight tolerance. The second method more closely simulates normal walking, with the right crutch and left leg moving together followed by the left crutch and right leg, taking more weight through the affected leg overall. The choice between methods depends on the patient's tolerance for weight-bearing and stage of rehabilitation.
options: One method requires no crutches at all, only sticks
Both methods are functionally identical in every respect
One method is used only for patients with Rheumatoid Disease
One progresses gradually from shadow walking; the other simulates normal walking
The second method takes less weight through the affected leg than the first

questions.explanation: Post-concussion management follows a graduated return-to-sport protocol: initial relative (not absolute) physical and cognitive rest, followed by sequential progression through light aerobic activity, sport-specific exercise, non-contact training drills, full-contact training, and finally return to competition. Each stage requires 24 hours of symptom-free participation before progression. Premature return increases risk of second impact syndrome (rare but catastrophic), and physiotherapists must supervise this protocol in collaboration with medical staff.
questions.question: A physiotherapist assessing a patient's exercise capacity after a concussion should apply which evidence-based return-to-activity protocol?
options: Immediate return to full contact competitive activity
Ignoring all post-concussion symptoms during rehabilitation
No medical evaluation necessary before resuming sport
Physical and cognitive rest then gradual return-to-play
Playing through head injury to avoid deconditioning

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes fixation from stabilisation as used in exercise therapy?
questions.explanation: Fixation describes a state of complete immobility of a joint, whereas stabilisation describes a state of relative immobility of an area providing a background for movement elsewhere. Both can be achieved by active muscular work or passive external means, so the distinction is not about method but about the degree of immobility produced. This distinction underlies how starting positions are selected for localised exercise.
options: Fixation is always passive; stabilisation is always active
Fixation uses gravity; stabilisation uses resistance
Fixation occurs distally; stabilisation occurs proximally
Fixation requires apparatus; stabilisation never does
Fixation is complete immobility; stabilisation is relative immobility

questions.question: Which sense is primarily substituted to compensate for loss of kinaesthetic sensation in Frenkel's approach to re-education?
questions.explanation: Frenkel aimed to establish voluntary control of movement using any part of the sensory mechanism that remained intact, notably sight, sound and touch, to compensate for the loss of kinaesthetic sensation, though sight is emphasised as the primary substitute given the technique's heavy reliance on the patient watching the limb throughout each exercise. The patient must be positioned and suitably clothed so the limbs can be seen during every exercise. This visual substitution allows conscious control to replace the missing automatic kinaesthetic feedback.

options: It eliminates the need for the patient to focus attention on the pattern at all
It works only when resistance is applied from a single known direction
It builds excitation and control across all muscle groups needed to maintain the posture against unpredictable disturbance
It has no relationship to any facilitation-based principle of muscle training
It is used exclusively for training dynamic, never static, postures
questions.explanation: Establishment of a new and satisfactory pattern of posture is accelerated by strong and prolonged holding against maximal resistance, applied first manually in directions known to the patient with a dynamic command to 'HOLD!' to focus attention, and later applied in quick succession from a variety of directions unknown to the patient. This progression from predictable to unpredictable resistance builds robust postural control able to withstand real-world disturbances rather than only a single, anticipated challenge. This use of resistance to consolidate posture closely parallels the rhythmic stabilisation technique used more broadly in facilitation-based treatment.
questions.question: Why is establishment of a satisfactory postural pattern accelerated by strong, prolonged holding against maximal resistance applied from a variety of directions?

options: The legs always initiate rolling before the head moves
Total flexion-with-rotation in rolling begins from the head and neck
Rolling cannot involve any rotation of the trunk
The head and neck are passive throughout the roll
Rolling is achieved through pure extension of the spine
questions.explanation: The roll from lying supine to side lying requires a total flexion-with-rotation of the body which is initiated from and led by the head and neck, with strong limb activity recruited to assist when available. This reflects the normal developmental and functional pattern of rolling seen in everyday movement. Re-education techniques for patients with movement disorders are based on reproducing this natural sequencing.
questions.question: Why is the head and neck described as initiating and leading the rolling movement from supine to side lying?

questions.explanation: When manipulation is performed under anaesthesia by a surgeon or physician to gain further range, the increase in movement gained must be maintained by the physiotherapist through subsequent treatment, so it is advantageous for the physiotherapist to be present during the procedure to see the range achieved. Without this prompt follow-up, the gained range risks being lost to new adhesion formation. This collaborative process underlines the close relationship between surgical and physiotherapeutic management of joint stiffness.
questions.question: Following a manipulation performed under anaesthesia by a surgeon, what is the physiotherapist's most important immediate responsibility?
options: Performing a second manipulation immediately afterward
Avoiding any treatment until the patient is fully ambulant
Maintaining the increase in range gained through subsequent treatment
Administering further anaesthesia for additional range
Allowing the joint to remain fully immobilised post-procedure

questions.question: Which factor is specifically identified as a chief predisposing condition for the healthy development of posture in a growing child?
options: Opportunity for plenty of natural free movement
Early specialisation in a single repetitive sporting activity
Prolonged static positioning to encourage postural stillness
Restriction of movement to prevent injury during growth
Avoidance of all extension-based movement during play
questions.explanation: The chief factors which predispose to the health and development of the muscles and postural reflex are a stable psychological background, good hygienic conditions, and opportunity for plenty of natural free movement, with activities such as running, jumping, and climbing, in which movements of active extension predominate, particularly valued in the growing child. This natural movement encourages harmonious development of the skeletal muscles supporting posture. Restricting a child's opportunity for such free movement is therefore seen as detrimental to healthy postural development rather than protective.

Tightness or spasticity limits passive as well as active movement because the antagonist muscles are unable, or able only with difficulty, to relax sufficiently to allow the movement to take place. This contrasts with simple muscular weakness, which limits active range because the muscle's power is insufficient against resistance, but does not necessarily restrict passive movement performed by an external force. Recognising whether a limitation is active-only or active-and-passive helps the physiotherapist identify spasticity as the underlying cause.
questions.question: Why does spasticity specifically limit passive, rather than only active, range of movement at a joint?
options: Spasticity destroys the articular cartilage directly
The antagonist muscles cannot relax sufficiently to allow the movement to take place
Spasticity always causes complete bony ankylosis
Spasticity is unrelated to passive movement at any joint
Spasticity increases the joint's synovial fluid volume

questions.explanation: Inactive postures are those adopted for resting or sleeping, chosen because they reduce essential muscular activity to a minimum and place least demand on respiration and circulation. Positions used for general relaxation training share these same characteristics. Active postures, by contrast, require the integrated and ongoing work of many muscles to maintain stability or movement.
options: An inactive posture used for rest or sleep
questions.question: A starting position in which the body segments are arranged to make minimal demands on postural muscles, supporting respiration and circulation, is best classified as which type of posture?

questions.explanation: In repeated contractions, when the patient's maximal isotonic contraction can progress no further, the stretch reflex is repeated to facilitate contraction of the weaker muscle groups and enable the patient to continue moving through range. Two or three repetitions of the stretch reflex may be used in this way, each given as a short, sharp stimulus. This technique builds strength and endurance specifically in weaker components of a pattern.
questions.question: In the repeated contractions technique, why is the stretch reflex applied again partway through a movement when the patient 'can go no further'?
options: To stop the movement permanently at that point
To switch the technique into rhythmic stabilisation
To facilitate further contraction of the weaker muscle groups so movement continues through range
To eliminate the need for maximal resistance
To convert isotonic work into purely isometric work
Static work always uses the least amount of energy of any muscle work
Static work eliminates the need for any blood flow to the muscle
The resistance demands the greatest possible increase in intra-muscular tension at that point
Static work is never fatiguing even when sustained for long periods
Static work always changes the length of the muscle being trained
questions.explanation: Static, or isometric, muscle work against maximal resistance provides the most rapid method for gaining hypertrophy of muscle at a particular point in the range, because the resistance demands the greatest possible increase in intramuscular tension at that specific joint angle. Although more economical than isotonic work overall, static work is fatiguing if sustained, largely because of the hindrance to circulation through the muscle caused by increased intramuscular tension. This makes static contraction a powerful but localised tool for building strength at a specific range.
questions.question: Why is static muscle work against maximal resistance described as the most rapid method for gaining hypertrophy at a specific point in range?

options: The muscular force exactly equals the opposing force of gravity
The muscular force is much greater than gravity
Gravity is eliminated by the seated position
The base of support prevents any movement
Unstable equilibrium is occurring at the knee
questions.question: A patient is asked to maintain an isometric quadriceps contraction while seated with the knee extended against gravity. Which mechanical principle explains why the limb remains still rather than moving?
questions.explanation: Movement of joints results when one force exceeds another, but when the force of muscular contraction exactly balances the force of gravity acting on the limb, the limb remains motionless. This balanced condition is the mechanical basis of an isometric or static muscular hold against gravity. If the contraction force fell below that of gravity, the limb would lower under gravity's effect.

options: Stroke volume continues to increase proportionally with heart rate to maximum
Heart rate alone determines maximum cardiac output during exercise
Stroke volume plateaus around 40-50% VO2 max while heart rate continues rising
Cardiac output remains constant while only oxygen extraction increases
Stroke volume decreases as heart rate increases to maximum
questions.question: Which statement most accurately describes the physiological relationship between stroke volume, heart rate, and cardiac output during maximal exercise that physiotherapists should understand?
questions.explanation: Stroke volume increases from rest to approximately 40-50% of VO2 max, then plateaus as higher heart rates shorten diastolic filling time proportionally, preventing further end-diastolic volume increase. Beyond this point, further increases in cardiac output are achieved entirely through heart rate increase. This stroke volume plateau is the reason that highly trained athletes achieve their high VO2 max primarily through larger stroke volumes (from eccentric cardiac hypertrophy) rather than higher maximum heart rates, which are similar to untrained individuals.

questions.question: In group action of muscles producing coordinated movement, which group's contraction directly results in movement of a joint?
questions.explanation: Coordinated movement is brought about by the integrated action of muscles grouped as prime movers, antagonists, synergists and fixators, with the prime movers responsible for the contraction that directly results in the movement of a joint. The antagonists relax reciprocally to control rather than impede the movement, while synergists and fixators serve supporting roles. This group action, superimposed on a basis of efficient postural activity, is what produces smooth, accurate and purposeful movement.

questions.question: A patient's foot drops into plantarflexion due to a lesion of the Anterior Tibial Nerve, with the unopposed Calf Muscles pulling the foot down. Why must a splint or toe-spring be worn?
questions.explanation: Normal muscles protect themselves from overstretching by a reflex contraction, but flaccidly paralysed muscles are incapable of this protective contraction and may become stretched beyond their physiological limit by gravity or the unopposed action of healthy antagonists. In anterior tibial nerve lesions, a splint or toe-spring prevents this overstretching of the paralysed dorsiflexors until their power of contraction is sufficient to restore muscle balance. This is a core principle in the early management of any flaccid paralysis affecting a specific muscle group.
options: To increase the workload placed on the paralysed muscles directly
To eliminate the need for any passive movement of the ankle
To prevent any circulation to the affected lower leg
To replace the need for resisted exercise of normal muscles nearby
To protect the paralysed muscles from being overstretched by gravity and the unopposed antagonist

questions.explanation: Heat produced by strenuous muscular activity stimulates the heat-regulating centre, causing vaso-dilatation in the skin following an initial vessel constriction that occurs to compensate for the increased blood flow directed to the muscles. With sufficient exercise the skin feels warm, possibly moist, and appears pink, indicating heat loss from the surface balancing the heat gained from muscle activity. This thermoregulatory response is a systemic effect of resisted exercise, distinct from its local strengthening action on the muscle itself.
options: Permanent vaso-constriction causing pallor of the skin
Complete cessation of sweating in the exercised limb
Vaso-dilatation causing the skin to feel warm and appear pink
Immediate cooling of the skin below resting temperature
No detectable change in skin temperature or colour
questions.question: Heat produced as a result of strenuous resisted exercise leads to which observable skin change once sufficient exercise has occurred?

options: It reduces interarticular friction along the joint's long axis
It eliminates the need for any manual contact
It mimics traction applied during flexion patterns
It simulates the normal circumstances of weight-bearing or pushing
It is unrelated to proprioceptive joint stimulation
questions.explanation: Approximation, or compression of joint surfaces, simulates the normal circumstances arising during weight-bearing or pushing and is therefore more effective for facilitating extension movements. Traction, by contrast, is most effective in flexion movements because lifted weight normally exerts traction in proportion to its own weight. Both techniques stimulate proprioceptive impulses arising from joint structures but are matched to opposite movement directions.
questions.question: Why is approximation, or joint compression, considered more effective for facilitating extension movements than flexion movements?

questions.explanation: DOMS results from mechanical disruption of muscle fibres (particularly from eccentric loading), which initiates an acute inflammatory response including prostaglandin and bradykinin release, sensory nerve sensitisation (C-fibre activation), and oedema from increased capillary permeability. The inflammatory cascade typically peaks 24-72 hours post-exercise, explaining the delayed onset of soreness. Lactic acid is cleared within 60-90 minutes post-exercise and does not cause DOMS. Physiotherapists should distinguish DOMS from muscle injury when designing progressive loading programmes.
questions.question: Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) peaks at 24-72 hours after unaccustomed exercise primarily because of:
options: Acute lactic acid accumulation causing direct tissue damage
Inflammatory response to mechanical muscle fibre disruption
Delayed onset of ATP depletion in type II fibres
Oxidative stress exceeding antioxidant defence capacity

questions.explanation: Recognised causes of limitation of range include tightness of skin restricting both active and passive range, muscular weakness or inefficiency limiting active range specifically, spasticity preventing relaxation and full passive movement, adhesion formation gluing collagenous structures together, and cartilaginous or bony destruction or obstruction. Occasionally no organic cause can be found despite the patient being unable to move a joint. Identifying which of these mechanisms predominates guides the selection of an appropriate mobilising method.
questions.question: Which combination of factors most commonly causes limitation of joint range according to the recognised causes of joint stiffness?
options: Tightness of skin, muscular weakness, spasticity, adhesion formation, and cartilaginous or bony destruction
Overactivity of the anti-gravity muscles alone

questions.question: The concept of neuromuscular fatigue during high-intensity exercise, relevant to physiotherapy sports rehabilitation, involves which peripheral mechanism as the primary contributor at the muscle level?
questions.explanation: Peripheral neuromuscular fatigue during high-intensity exercise is primarily attributed to inorganic phosphate (Pi) and hydrogen ion (H+) accumulation within muscle fibres. Pi reduces the sensitivity of contractile proteins to calcium and impairs SR calcium release, while H+ acidosis impairs troponin-calcium interaction, phosphofructokinase activity, and direct cross-bridge formation. These metabolic factors reduce force production capacity at the sarcomere level independently of neural drive. Understanding peripheral fatigue mechanisms guides physiotherapists in designing appropriate work-to-rest ratios for high-intensity rehabilitation protocols.
options: Reduced cerebral oxygen delivery impairing motor command
Glycogen depletion in liver preventing blood glucose maintenance
Accumulation of Pi and H+ impairing cross-bridge cycling
Impaired neuromuscular junction transmission from ACh depletion
Elevated serotonin impairing central motor drive

questions.explanation: Ataxic patients who are too unsteady to lift a standard lightweight frame forward may instead be able to use a rollator frame, which can be pushed rather than lifted, or a reciprocal frame, in which each side moves independently. These alternatives accommodate the specific balance and coordination challenges associated with ataxia, where the sudden unsupported phase of lifting a standard frame would pose a fall risk. Selecting the correct type of frame for the specific movement disorder present is therefore an important part of walking aid prescription.
options: A pushable rollator frame, or a reciprocal frame moving independently
A standard lightweight four-footed frame lifted with each step
A single wooden stick used on the unaffected side
A pair of axillary crutches used with a triangular base
Gutter crutches with a padded forearm support
questions.question: Which type of walking frame is specifically recommended for ataxic patients who are too unsteady to lift a standard frame forward?
A patient's centre of gravity rises and their base of support narrows as they move from lying to standing. What happens to their equilibrium?
options: It shifts to unstable equilibrium only in sitting
questions.explanation: Stability is greatest when the centre of gravity is low and the base of support is wide, as in lying. As the patient rises through sitting to standing, the centre of gravity is raised and the base is reduced, so equilibrium becomes progressively less stable. This is why standing balance training is more demanding than balance training in lying or sitting.

questions.question: A patient's elbow flexors can lift the forearm through part of the range against gravity but fail near the end of range. Which classification of active movement is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Assisted-resisted exercise combines assistance and resistance within a single movement so that the external force is adapted to the muscle's varying ability across the range. Since the muscle is adequate in part of range but deficient elsewhere, this matched approach is more accurate than either pure assistance or pure resistance. It is generally preferable to assisted exercise alone because it meets the muscle's true capacity more precisely.

options: A state of unstable equilibrium at the joint
Complete elimination of gravity acting on the limb
A distraction of the articular surfaces to facilitate movement with reduced friction
Conversion of the movement into a resisted exercise
A permanent increase in the joint's base of support
questions.question: A physiotherapist applies manual traction to a joint while simultaneously fixing the bone proximal to it. What overall mechanical effect is this combination intended to produce?
questions.explanation: Traction given along the long axis of a joint, combined with fixation of the proximal bone to provide an opposing force, draws the articular surfaces apart and is thought to facilitate the movement by reducing interarticular friction. This combination of two separate mechanical actions, fixation and traction, working together illustrates how basic mechanical principles are applied practically in technique. Neither traction nor fixation alone would achieve the same combined effect on joint movement.

options: 3-4 weeks of continuous hot weather exercise
A single prolonged heat exposure session
questions.question: Heat acclimatisation for a physiotherapy patient scheduled to exercise in a hot environment requires approximately how long to achieve meaningful physiological adaptations?
questions.explanation: Meaningful heat acclimatisation adaptations (expanded plasma volume, lower core temperature threshold for sweating onset, increased sweat rate, reduced heart rate at a given work intensity, decreased exercise perceived exertion in heat) develop over approximately 7-14 days of daily exercise in hot conditions. Initial adaptations (plasma volume expansion) occur within days, while complete acclimatisation including thermoregulatory efficiency improvements requires 10-14 days. Physiotherapists scheduling patients for exercise in hot environments should allow adequate pre-exposure acclimatisation time.

options: The ligament itself contracts to protect the joint
Synovial fluid production stops entirely after injury
Hyaline cartilage degenerates immediately after the injury
Excessive ligament stretching stimulates sensory receptors, causing pain and reflex spasm in antagonist muscles
Accessory joint movement increases permanently after the injury
questions.explanation: Excessive stretching of ligamentous tissue stimulates the sensory receptors with which it is freely supplied, causing pain and reflex spasm in the muscles antagonistic to the force responsible for the stretching. This protective spasm helps prevent further excessive movement at the injured joint. Recognising this mechanism explains why early management often focuses on relieving pain to reduce secondary muscular guarding.
questions.question: A patient reports pain and spasm after a ligament was stretched beyond its normal limit during a sporting injury. What is the physiological explanation for the resulting muscle spasm?

questions.explanation: Rapid glycogen resynthesis through high-carbohydrate intake (1.0-1.2 g/kg/hour) in the immediate post-exercise period is most critical for patients performing two training sessions within 24 hours (e.g., morning and afternoon sessions in sports rehabilitation), as this is the only scenario where full glycogen restoration is physiologically necessary. The post-exercise insulin sensitivity window (approximately 30-60 minutes) enhances GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake into muscle, making this the optimal timing for carbohydrate ingestion to maximise resynthesis rate.
options: Performing light recreational walking three times weekly
Training only once per week at low intensity
Completing prolonged or repeated exercise sessions the same day
questions.question: Post-exercise carbohydrate intake recommendation of 1.0-1.2 g/kg/hr to maximise glycogen resynthesis is most clinically relevant for physiotherapy patients who are:

questions.explanation: Economy of words is essential for clarity, and a single instruction which is carried out immediately leaves the patient in no doubt as to what is required, whereas numerous instructions and lengthy explanations are confusing, since the first instruction is often forgotten by the time the exercise is due to start. Constant repetition of unnecessary phrases is described as contributing little or nothing to the explanation and is better omitted. This principle of concise, direct instruction applies broadly across both individual and group teaching situations.
options: A single clear instruction leaves no doubt, unlike confusing lengthy explanations
Longer explanations always improve the accuracy of the movement performed
Economy of words is required only when working with large groups
Repeated phrases such as reassurance always aid understanding of an instruction
Verbal instruction is never used for teaching any active exercise
questions.question: Why is economy of words emphasised as essential when giving informal verbal instructions during active exercise?

questions.explanation: Exercise for rheumatoid arthritis is strongly evidence-supported for reducing pain, improving functional capacity, muscle strength, and aerobic fitness, and enhancing quality of life without accelerating cartilage damage or joint erosion. Contrary to historical concerns, appropriately dosed exercise does not worsen radiographic joint changes. Exercise also reduces cardiovascular risk, which is elevated in RA from chronic systemic inflammation. Physiotherapists should actively prescribe exercise during all phases of RA management, including during disease flares with appropriate modification.
questions.question: Exercise benefits for rheumatoid arthritis patients prescribed by a physiotherapist should emphasise which outcomes supported by current evidence?
options: Complete cessation of inflammatory disease activity
Replacement of all disease-modifying pharmacological treatment
Reduced pain and improved function without accelerating joint damage
Elimination of synovitis through mechanical joint compression
Immediate reversal of joint erosions seen on radiography

questions.explanation: The stretch stimulus places muscles on full stretch so tension is felt in all components, while the stretch reflex involves a sharp, controlled stretch at the limit of range synchronised with a dynamic command for maximum voluntary effort. Together these add the stimulus of stretching to the patient's own effort. This combination is a foundational technique used to initiate or accelerate the strengthening process in weak muscles.
options: The stretch stimulus combined with the stretch reflex
questions.question: A physiotherapist puts a weak muscle group on full stretch before applying a sharp, controlled stretch synchronised with a command for maximal effort. What technique is this combination known as?

questions.explanation: Exercise reduces hepatic steatosis in NAFLD primarily by reducing visceral adiposity (the main source of excess free fatty acids delivered to the liver via portal circulation), improving insulin sensitivity (reducing hepatic de novo lipogenesis), and directly increasing hepatic fat oxidation through AMPK activation. Both aerobic and resistance exercise produce meaningful reductions in liver fat content even without significant weight loss. Physiotherapists should prescribe a combination of aerobic and resistance training as part of NAFLD management.
options: Reducing visceral adiposity and hepatic lipid influx
Eliminating the need for all dietary interventions
questions.question: Regular aerobic and resistance exercise reduces liver fat in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) primarily by:

options: The prime movers of locomotion only
The intrinsic muscles of the hand
questions.question: Which muscles are chiefly responsible for maintaining the erect posture of the body against the effects of gravity?
questions.explanation: The groups of muscles most frequently employed to maintain active posture are those used to counteract the effects of gravity in the erect position, known as the anti-gravity muscles, whose action with regard to joints is usually one of extension. These muscles present structural characteristics, such as a multi-pennate, fan-shaped form, that favour powerful sustained action over speed or wide range of movement. Many of their constituent fibres are red, reflecting their capacity for sustained contraction without fatigue.

options: Active movement always exceeds the passive range available
Passive movement is limited entirely by ligament tension only
