Active and passive ranges are always identical at every joint
Active movement eliminates resistance from antagonist muscles
Reciprocal relaxation of opposing muscles is not always complete during active movement
questions.explanation: Active range is usually less than passive range owing to the reciprocal relationship of muscles; some residual tension in the antagonist muscle group during active movement limits the range achieved compared with movement produced entirely passively. Passive range therefore better reflects the true anatomical limit of the joint structures themselves. This distinction is clinically important when assessing whether a movement deficit is due to joint or muscular factors.
questions.question: Why is the active range of joint movement usually smaller than the passive range at the same joint?

options: Pressure applied opposite to the direction of movement
Pressure that avoids contact with skin entirely
questions.explanation: Manual contacts must be purposeful, directional, and comfortable to be effective: firm enough that the patient is aware of it, applied in the direction of the intended movement, and free from pain that would inhibit contraction. Pressure applied opposite to the movement or causing discomfort would inhibit rather than facilitate the response. Direct skin contact is preferred whenever possible to maximise stimulation of exteroceptors.
questions.question: Which quality is essential for a physiotherapist's manual contacts to be effective in facilitation techniques?

questions.explanation: Failure of systolic blood pressure to rise with increasing exercise intensity, or a drop in systolic blood pressure of more than 10 mmHg from peak, is an absolute indication for exercise test termination as it indicates a dangerous haemodynamic response suggesting cardiac output failure (cardiogenic shock, severe obstruction, or left ventricular dysfunction). Other absolute stop criteria include severe chest pain, ST changes indicating ischaemia, ventricular arrhythmias, and neurological symptoms. Moderate effort and expected physiological responses do not constitute termination criteria.
options: Patient reports moderate effort at 13 on the Borg RPE scale
Systolic blood pressure fails to rise or drops during exercise
Heart rate reaches 85% of age-predicted maximum
Respiratory rate exceeds 30 breaths per minute
Patient demonstrates mild perspiration and facial flushing
questions.question: A physiotherapist performing a graded exercise test terminates the test early. Which observation would be the most appropriate termination criterion?

questions.explanation: Movements at the intermetatarsal joints cannot be performed actively except in conjunction with other movements, but passive gliding movements between the distal ends of the bones help keep the foot resilient. A combination of upward pressure beneath the metatarsal heads and a stroking movement on the dorsum helps mould the anterior transverse arch into its normal non-weight-bearing position. This is a clear example of an accessory movement that the physiotherapist alone can isolate.
options: Gliding movements between bone ends that cannot be produced actively in isolation
Movements that can be fully reproduced by active toe flexion alone
Movements identical in range and type to active toe extension
Movements performed exclusively under general anaesthesia
Movements that replace the need for fixation entirely
questions.question: Accessory movements at the intermetatarsal joints of the foot are best described in which way?

options: It eliminates the need for the physiotherapist to give verbal instruction
It replaces the need for active practice of postural correction entirely
It helps the patient compare their own image with good alignment
It is used only for dynamic postures, never for static positions
It has no relationship to convincing the patient a new posture looks right
questions.explanation: A mirror, posture recorder, or photographs may be useful so the patient's image can be compared with pictures demonstrating a good general pattern of alignment, with video also mentioned as particularly impressive for training dynamic postures in activities such as tennis, diving, and lifting. This visual feedback helps convince the patient that a new posture 'looks' right and will prove efficient, addressing the discomfort many patients initially feel when adopting an unfamiliar position. The physiotherapist's role in 'selling' the new pattern of posture to the patient is described as essential to successful re-education.
questions.question: Why is a mirror, posture recorder, or video sometimes used when teaching a patient to assume a good pattern of posture?

Anaesthesia Techniques, Regional Blocks & Sedation: Q1–42
Physiological Monitoring & Anaesthetic Equipment: Q43–116
Airway Management & Difficult Intubation: Q117–161
Basic & Advanced Life Support (Resuscitation): Q162–205
Pain Physiology, Assessment & TENS: Q206–238
Anaesthetic & Analgesic Pharmacology: Q239–318
Perioperative Complications, Nursing Care & Professional/Legal Issues: Q319–384
courses.title: Anaesthetic Nursing

questions.explanation: Stridor with suprasternal retraction during induction indicates laryngospasm, a partial or complete closure of the vocal cords triggered by airway irritation during the light planes of anaesthesia. This requires immediate management such as jaw thrust, positive pressure oxygen, and deepening of anaesthesia if needed. It is not a normal or expected finding during smooth induction.
questions.question: During inhalational induction with sevoflurane, a child suddenly develops stridor and suprasternal retraction. The nurse should suspect
options: an allergic drug reaction to sevoflurane
Preferential glucose utilisation and glycogen storage
Enhanced immune function and increased antibody production
Anabolic metabolism with increased protein synthesis
Carbohydrate, protein, and fat catabolism and poor glucose utilisation
Improved wound healing from growth hormone release
questions.explanation: The endocrine system reacts to unrelieved pain by releasing an excessive amount of hormones, ultimately resulting in carbohydrate, protein, and fat catabolism, poor glucose utilisation, and other harmful effects. This catabolic state impairs wound healing and immune function, increases the risk of infection, and prolongs recovery. Adequate pain management is therefore essential not only for comfort but for physiological recovery.
questions.question: Unrelieved pain leads to excessive release of hormones from the endocrine system. What is the METABOLIC consequence of this hormonal response?

options: delays in starting the surgical procedure
the need for a second qualified checker
medication errors from similar drug names or packaging
excessive drug wastage in the department
the surgeon's dissatisfaction with preparation time
questions.explanation: Independent checking of drug labels against the prescription is a fundamental medication safety practice designed to prevent errors arising from similar-sounding drug names, look-alike packaging, or similar drug concentrations, which are recognised contributors to serious medication incidents in anaesthesia. This practice does not aim to reduce the need for double-checking; rather it forms part of a robust two-person verification process.
questions.question: An anaesthetic nurse preparing drugs for a case should independently check each drug label against the prescription PRIMARILY to prevent
Core temperature monitoring during prolonged surgery is important because unrecognised intraoperative hypothermia increases the risk of
questions.explanation: Unrecognised intraoperative hypothermia impairs platelet function and clotting enzyme activity, increasing bleeding and coagulopathy risk, and also impairs neutrophil function and wound oxygenation, increasing the risk of surgical site infection. It does not improve wound healing or immune function, and it typically delays rather than speeds emergence from anaesthesia due to prolonged drug metabolism.

options: To override the refusal in the patient's best interests
To contact the patient's family to obtain consent instead
To document the refusal and immediately notify hospital management
To seek a court order to compel the patient to accept treatment
To respect the patient's autonomous right to refuse treatment
questions.question: When a patient refuses treatment after being fully informed, what is the anaesthetic nurse's PRIMARY obligation?
questions.explanation: The anaesthetic nurse must respect the patient's autonomous right to refuse treatment when the patient has capacity and has been fully informed. Nurses will be acting unlawfully if they administer care without a patient's consent. The nurse's biggest responsibility is to ensure patients receive sufficient information and to enable them to feel less doubtful about accepting treatment, but ultimately the patient's decision must be respected.

Negligence in anaesthesia occurs when a healthcare professional deviates from the accepted standard of care AND that deviation causes harm to the patient. Both elements must be present: a breach of the standard of care and causation of harm. Medication errors, monitoring failures, equipment problems, communication breakdowns, and human judgement errors can all constitute negligence when they result in patient harm.
questions.question: Negligence in anaesthesia is defined as occurring when deviation from accepted standard of care has which ADDITIONAL requirement?
options: The deviation must be repeated more than once
The deviation must result in a patient complaint formally filed
The deviation must be witnessed by at least two healthcare workers
The deviation must cause harm to the patient
The deviation must be documented in the patient's record

questions.explanation: Once an advanced airway such as an endotracheal tube is secured during cardiac arrest, ventilation is delivered asynchronously at a rate of approximately one breath every 6 seconds (about 10 breaths per minute) without pausing chest compressions, since continuous uninterrupted compressions maximise coronary perfusion pressure. Synchronising breaths with compression pauses is only required before an advanced airway is placed.
questions.question: During an intraoperative cardiac arrest, once an advanced airway is in place, ventilation should be delivered at which rate WITHOUT pausing compressions?
Using the Aldrete scoring system, a patient is assessed as ready for discharge from the recovery room when the total score indicates
questions.explanation: The Aldrete score evaluates activity, respiration, circulation, consciousness, and oxygen saturation, and a sufficiently high total score indicates the patient has returned close enough to their pre-anaesthetic baseline status to be safely discharged from the recovery area. A fixed time interval alone, without clinical assessment, is not a valid discharge criterion, nor is surgeon sign-off a substitute for objective recovery scoring.
options: the patient remains deeply sedated but stable
the patient has a stable heart rate only
the surgeon has signed the discharge form
the patient has returned close to their baseline status
two hours have elapsed since surgery regardless of score

questions.explanation: Anaesthetic nurses have a legal and ethical responsibility to maintain competence by staying up to date on best practices and adhering to professional standards. This includes following protocols and procedures established by the facility and professional organisations, advocating for patient safety, questioning orders that do not seem right, and documenting accurately and thoroughly. Continuing education is essential for maintaining this competence.
questions.question: Anaesthetic nurses must maintain competence as a legal and ethical responsibility. This SPECIFICALLY requires which ongoing action?
options: Obtaining a new nursing qualification every 5 years
Staying up to date on best practices and adhering to professional standards
Completing at least 10 supervised anaesthetic cases annually
Publishing research in peer-reviewed anaesthesia journals
Attending one professional development course per decade

questions.explanation: Neck mobility less than 35 degrees of extension is a predictor of difficult intubation. Adequate neck extension is required for the sniffing position, which aligns the oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal axes to optimise laryngoscopic view. Conditions limiting neck extension include cervical spine disease, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and previous cervical spine surgery or fusion.
questions.question: Neck mobility less than what angle of extension is a predictor of difficult intubation?

options: On receptor sites in the CNS, particularly spinal and medullary dorsal horn
At the blood-brain barrier to reduce inflammatory mediators
On GABA receptors in the basal ganglia region
At the neuromuscular junction to reduce muscle spasm
At peripheral nociceptor terminals to reduce sensitivity
questions.question: Endorphins and enkephalins reduce pain transmission by acting at which sites in the nervous system?
questions.explanation: Endorphins and enkephalins are found in heavy concentrations in the central nervous system, particularly in the spinal and medullary dorsal horn, the periaqueductal gray matter, hypothalamus, and amygdala. They reduce pain transmission by stimulating inhibitory interneuronal fibres. Morphine and other opioid medications mimic these endogenous substances by acting at opioid receptor sites to suppress nociceptive excitation.

options: Ischaemia of peripheral nerve from vascular compression
Central sensitisation from repeated superficial skin stimulation
Persistent pain from functional changes in CNS after peripheral nerve injury
Psychosomatic amplification of normal nociceptive input
Activation of nociceptors by inflammatory chemical mediators
questions.question: Neuropathic pain is described as a sharp, shooting, devastating pain arising from which pathophysiological mechanism?
questions.explanation: Neuropathic pain is a persistent pain that arises from functional changes occurring in the CNS secondary to peripheral nerve injury. Once the nerve is damaged, the damaged nerve elicits sustained activation of nociceptors and nociceptive afferents. It is described as shooting, stabbing, or burning pain and may affect sensitivity to touch and temperature, making it challenging to manage with conventional analgesics.

questions.question: Rapid infusion of large volumes of 0.9% normal saline intraoperatively can predispose the patient to which acid-base disturbance?
questions.explanation: Large-volume administration of 0.9% saline, which has a chloride content higher than plasma, can cause a dilutional hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis due to the relatively high chloride load displacing bicarbonate. Balanced crystalloid solutions with a more physiological electrolyte composition are often preferred for large-volume resuscitation to reduce this risk. This is a metabolic, not respiratory, disturbance.

options: Increases coronary artery blood flow and perfusion pressure
Selectively decreases pulmonary vascular resistance only
Increases myocardial contractility and heart rate
Causes profound peripheral vasodilation and hypotension
Decreases myocardial contractility and heart rate by vagal stimulation
questions.explanation: Halothane decreases (reduces) myocardial contractility and decreases heart rate by vagal stimulation. This distinguishes it from isoflurane and desflurane, which primarily cause vasodilation. Adverse effects of halothane include decreased coronary perfusion, reduced gastrointestinal motility, and reduced uterine tone. It also increases the secretion of vasopressin, thyroxine, growth hormone, and corticosteroids.
questions.question: Halothane reduces metabolic rate and has which specific effect on the cardiovascular system that distinguishes it from other volatile agents?

questions.explanation: EEG monitoring involves electrodes attached to the patient's scalp, which capture electrical signals produced by the brain. These signals are then amplified, filtered, and displayed on a monitor for real-time observation. The standard EEG machine captures activity from multiple scalp regions simultaneously, providing comprehensive information about brain function during anaesthesia.
options: The forehead adjacent to the prefrontal cortex
The nasopharynx adjacent to the pituitary gland
The patient's scalp surface to capture brain signals
The mastoid process behind the external ear
The chest wall overlying the cardiac apex region
questions.question: EEG monitoring uses electrodes attached to which anatomical location to capture electrical brain signals?
Succinylcholine (suxamethonium) can increase intragastric pressure during fasciculations. This is clinically relevant because it may cause which complication?
options: Reflux of gastric contents with aspiration risk
Increased heart rate and cardiac output
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine mimics acetylcholine and produces initial muscle contractions (fasciculations), which increase intragastric pressure. This may be strong enough to overcome the tone of the lower oesophageal sphincter and allow reflux of gastric contents, creating aspiration risk. Patient factors including body habitus, NPO status, and comorbidities should be considered when assessing aspiration risk.

An axillary block numbs the arm and shoulder and is commonly used for surgeries involving the arm or shoulder. It is a type of brachial plexus block performed at the axillary level, providing effective anaesthesia for the distal upper extremity. Unlike the interscalene block which targets the shoulder primarily, the axillary approach anaesthetises the arm more comprehensively.
questions.question: An axillary block provides anaesthesia for which anatomical region?
options: The arm and shoulder for upper limb surgeries
The hand and wrist for carpal tunnel release
The foot and ankle for podiatric procedures
The thigh and knee for orthopaedic surgery
The shoulder and upper arm for rotator cuff repair

questions.explanation: The double tourniquet allows the distal cuff to be inflated over anaesthetised skin once the block has taken effect, and the proximal cuff deflated, reducing the tourniquet-site pain that develops with prolonged single-cuff inflation. It does not increase the anaesthetic dose or eliminate the need for monitoring. Systemic absorption can still occur if a cuff fails or is released early.
questions.question: A Bier's block (intravenous regional anaesthesia) requires a double tourniquet technique PRIMARILY to
options: increase the total dose of local anaesthetic given
prevent systemic absorption of the anaesthetic entirely
reduce tourniquet-site pain during the procedure
allow simultaneous surgery on both limbs
eliminate the need for patient monitoring

questions.explanation: Non-invasive anaesthesia may be more cost-effective than invasive methods due to reduced risks and faster recovery times. Patients who recover more quickly require shorter hospital stays, which reduces overall healthcare costs. Faster recovery also allows earlier return to normal activities, reducing indirect economic costs to patients and healthcare systems.
questions.question: Non-invasive anaesthesia is potentially more cost-effective than invasive methods primarily because of which factor?
options: Shorter duration of the surgical procedure itself
Reduced risks and faster recovery requiring less hospital stay
Less expensive drugs used in non-invasive techniques
Lower requirement for skilled anaesthetic personnel
Reduced need for specialised monitoring equipment

questions.explanation: Tracheal intubation is considered difficult if more than one attempt at optimised laryngoscopy and tracheal tube passage is made, a more experienced healthcare worker is required, or a change in technique or device is made. The American Society of Anaesthesiologists defines difficult intubation as requiring multiple attempts, emphasising anatomical difficulties in visualising the glottis or inserting the tube.
options: When the procedure takes longer than 5 minutes total
When two different laryngoscope blades are tried
When a more experienced clinician is required or technique changed
When the patient requires neuromuscular blocking drugs first
When the patient's Mallampati score is 2 or higher
questions.question: Difficult intubation is considered when more than one attempt at laryngoscopy is made OR when which other conditions apply?

options: Direct toxic effect on the glomerular basement membrane
Blockade of renin-angiotensin system activation by the kidney
Extra-renal effects including haemodynamic changes mitigated by hydration
Permanent reduction in renal blood flow through vasoconstriction
Direct inhibition of sodium-potassium ATPase in tubular cells
questions.explanation: Inhalational anaesthetics generally decrease glomerular filtration rate and urine output primarily through extra-renal effects that are mitigated by preoperative hydration. These haemodynamic effects, influenced by sympathetic activity and humoral regulation, are more prominent than any direct renal effects. The perioperative changes in renal function are typically transient and clinically negligible.
questions.question: Inhalational anaesthetics PRIMARILY reduce glomerular filtration rate (GFR) through which mechanism?

options: excessive anaesthetic depth or cerebral hypoperfusion
questions.explanation: A persistently low BIS value together with hypotension and bradycardia, despite reducing volatile agent delivery, suggests either excessive anaesthetic depth relative to the patient's needs or a physiological problem such as cerebral hypoperfusion affecting EEG activity, both of which require prompt clinical assessment. This pattern is not consistent with a normal, light, or appropriately titrated anaesthetic state.
questions.question: A patient under general anaesthesia develops a persistently low BIS value alongside hypotension and bradycardia despite reduced volatile agent delivery. This combination should raise concern for

options: satisfy hospital administrative record keeping only
reduce the total cost of anaesthetic gases
shorten the overall duration of surgery
detect faults before patient exposure to risk
replace the need for intraoperative monitoring
questions.explanation: A thorough pre-use check of the anaesthetic machine, including gas supplies, breathing circuit integrity, and vaporisers, is performed to detect faults or leaks before the patient is exposed to the equipment, preventing hypoxia or awareness from equipment failure. It is a patient safety measure, not primarily an administrative or cost-saving exercise, and does not replace ongoing monitoring during the case.
questions.question: Prior to induction of general anaesthesia, the anaesthetic nurse performs a full check of the anaesthetic machine PRIMARILY to
End-tidal CO2 (ETCO2) normal values for patients, regardless of demographic factors, range between which values?
options: 45-55 mmHg for patients on mechanical ventilation
20-30 mmHg for patients during controlled ventilation
questions.explanation: Normal ETCO2 values range between 35-45 mmHg, or about 5% CO2, regardless of patient age, sex, race, or size. Values above 45 mmHg indicate hypoventilation, while values below 35 mmHg indicate hyperventilation. These values are measured using capnography, providing continuous graphical display of CO2 concentration in exhaled gas.

options: Approximately 90% of all cardiac arrests occur out of hospital
Approximately 70% of all cardiac arrests occur out of hospital
Approximately 30% of all cardiac arrests occur out of hospital
Approximately 50% of all cardiac arrests occur out of hospital
Approximately 20% of all cardiac arrests occur out of hospital
questions.explanation: Approximately 70% of all cases of cardiac arrest occur out of hospital, often in the victim's home. Early intervention by a bystander-calling for the emergency services and initiating CPR-can materially improve eventual outcome. The sooner that BLS can be instituted the better the outcome, highlighting the critical importance of public training in CPR and defibrillation.
questions.question: Approximately what percentage of cardiac arrests occur outside the hospital, often in the victim's home?

options: Partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood
Minute ventilation and tidal volume continuously
Carbon dioxide concentration in exhaled breath
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry is a non-invasive and painless technique that measures the oxygen saturation (SpO2) of arterial haemoglobin using spectrophotometry and optical plethysmography. It detects hypoxia early, playing a crucial role in patient safety throughout the perioperative period. Capnography, not pulse oximetry, measures carbon dioxide in exhaled breath.
questions.question: Pulse oximetry is used as a non-invasive monitoring technique. It primarily measures which physiological parameter?
The monitoring standard requiring an anaesthetist to be present throughout the conduct of anaesthesia represents which ASA Standard?
questions.explanation: ASA Standard I requires that qualified anaesthesia personnel be present in the procedural room over the entirety of all general anaesthetics, regional anaesthetics, and Monitored Anaesthesia Care. This standard ensures continuous human oversight throughout the procedure. Standard II addresses the specific parameters that must be monitored.
options: ASA Standard IV for paediatric anaesthesia specifically
ASA Standard II for continual evaluation of vital parameters
ASA Standard III for advanced monitoring requirements
ASA Standard V for documentation and record keeping
ASA Standard I for personnel presence requirement

questions.question: During cricothyrotomy, the patient is positioned with the neck in which position to facilitate the procedure?
options: Neutral position without any neck extension
Neck extended in supine position for access
Neck flexed forward with chin tucked to chest
Lateral position with head tilted to one side
questions.explanation: During cricothyrotomy, the patient lies supine with the neck extended to maximise exposure of the anterior neck and the cricothyroid membrane. Extension of the neck stretches the skin and subcutaneous tissues, making the cricothyroid membrane more prominent and easier to palpate and incise. This position also optimises subsequent tube passage into the trachea through the incision.

questions.question: A thermistor is described as a semiconductor with which specific electrical property?
questions.explanation: A thermistor is a semiconductor whose electrical resistance falls as temperature increases; it responds rapidly to changes in temperature. This property makes thermistors ideal for intraoperative temperature monitoring where fast response times are essential. Thermistors are used in oesophageal temperature probes and within pulmonary artery catheters for thermodilution cardiac output measurement.
options: Its resistance changes only at extremes of temperature
It converts temperature changes into digital signal output
Its electrical resistance falls as temperature increases
It maintains constant resistance regardless of temperature
Its electrical resistance increases as temperature increases

questions.question: Train-of-four monitoring is used intraoperatively to assess
questions.explanation: Train-of-four (TOF) stimulation delivers four supramaximal electrical stimuli to a peripheral nerve and observes the resulting muscle twitches; the ratio and fade of these twitches indicate the degree of neuromuscular blockade present. This guides dosing of muscle relaxants and confirms adequate recovery before extubation. It does not assess anaesthetic depth, analgesia, or cardiac rhythm.
options: depth of anaesthesia and awareness risk
Increased survival to discharge for out-of-hospital arrests
Need for immediate termination of resuscitation efforts
Poor prognosis and decreased chance of survival
Indication of irreversible brain damage after arrest
questions.explanation: Gasping or agonal respirations are relatively common after cardiac arrest and are associated with increased survival to discharge for out-of-hospital cardiac arrests (OHCA). Gasping is a natural reflex that enhances oxygenation and circulation. Initiation of gasping after cardiac arrest has been linked to brainstem activity and adequate perfusion, indicating some preserved brain function.
questions.question: Signs of life in a collapsed patient include gasping, pupillary response, and any movements during CPR. Gasping after cardiac arrest is associated with which outcome?

options: Verbal confirmation from theatre porters only
Checking the surgeon's personal preference sheet
Confirming the availability of general anaesthesia
Site marking and a formal team time-out
questions.question: Prior to performing a peripheral nerve block, the anaesthetic nurse should confirm which safety step to prevent wrong-site block?
questions.explanation: Site marking combined with a formal surgical time-out, where the team verbally confirms patient identity, procedure, and laterality, is the recognised safety step to prevent wrong-site nerve blocks. This process directly addresses the risk of performing a block on the incorrect limb. Confirming general anaesthesia availability or dietary history does not address wrong-site risk.

options: Patients with a history of motion sickness
Patients with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus
Patients with a low body mass index
questions.question: Dexamethasone is commonly given intraoperatively as an antiemetic adjunct, but caution is advised in which patient group?
questions.explanation: Dexamethasone, a corticosteroid, can transiently raise blood glucose levels, so caution and closer glucose monitoring are advised in patients with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus when it is used as a postoperative nausea and vomiting prophylactic agent. It is not specifically contraindicated by motion sickness history, day-case status, regional anaesthesia use, or low body mass index.

questions.question: Nitrous oxide is 30 times more soluble than nitrogen in blood. This property PRIMARILY explains why nitrous oxide causes which gastrointestinal effect?
questions.explanation: Nitrous oxide is 30 times more soluble than nitrogen in blood and will diffuse into gas-containing cavities from the blood faster than nitrogen can diffuse out. This is especially important in the bowels, as gut distension correlates with the amount of gas already present, the duration of nitrous oxide administration, and the concentration administered. This limits its use in bowel surgery.
options: Reduced intestinal motility and postoperative ileus
Delayed gastric emptying after prolonged administration
Increased absorption of intestinal gases into blood
Bowel distension by diffusing into gas-containing cavities

questions.question: Early central nervous system signs of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity include which combination of symptoms?
questions.explanation: Early CNS signs of LAST typically include tinnitus, circumoral or perioral numbness, a metallic taste, and light-headedness, which can progress to seizures if unrecognised and untreated. Cardiovascular signs such as widened QRS complex and hypotension tend to occur later or with higher plasma concentrations. Recognising these early warning signs allows the nurse to stop injection promptly.

If it is absolutely necessary to continue anaesthesia without an essential monitor, the anaesthetic nurse should note the reasons in the anaesthetic record. This documentation requirement ensures accountability and reflects the clinical decision-making process. Continuation without documentation would be a breach of professional and legal standards of care in anaesthetic nursing practice.
questions.question: According to minimum monitoring standards, if an essential monitor becomes unavailable during anaesthesia, what MUST the anaesthetic nurse do?
options: Immediately stop the procedure and reschedule
Transfer the patient to a more equipped operating theatre
Replace it with any available alternative device
Note the reasons in the anaesthetic record and continue
Inform only the surgeon and proceed without documentation

questions.explanation: Vasopressin (commonly referred to as antidiuretic hormone) acts as a nonadrenergic peripheral vasoconstrictor at high doses during cardiac arrest. It is therefore an effective vasopressor during resuscitation. Unlike adrenaline, vasopressin does not act through adrenergic receptors but instead stimulates V1 receptors in vascular smooth muscle to cause vasoconstriction.
questions.question: The mechanism of action of vasopressin during cardiac arrest resuscitation is described as which type of vasoconstrictor?
options: Beta-adrenergic inotropic agent increasing cardiac output
Nonadrenergic peripheral vasoconstrictor at high doses
Dopaminergic renal vasodilator at low doses
Obese patients with increased neck circumference
Patients with cervical spine disease and fusion
Pregnant patients and those with severe anaphylaxis
Patients with previous tracheostomy and scarring
Elderly patients with atrophic laryngeal mucosa
questions.question: Oedema to the subglottic structures is listed as a CAUSE of failed intubation. This is MOST clinically relevant in which patient group?
questions.explanation: Oedema of the subglottic structures as a cause of failed intubation is most clinically relevant in pregnant patients (who have physiological airway oedema) and patients with severe anaphylaxis or airway burns. This subglottic oedema narrows the airway below the vocal cords, preventing passage of the endotracheal tube even when the cords are visualised. Management requires a smaller tube or surgical airway.

options: Degree of sensitivity to succinylcholine in atypical cases
Identification of phase II block from depolarising agents
Adequacy of reversal after administration of neostigmine
Recovery of neuromuscular function at various stages
Speed of onset of neuromuscular blockade at induction
questions.question: The 'double burst' and 'post-tetanic count' stimulation patterns are additional modalities used for assessing which aspect of neuromuscular function?
questions.explanation: Double burst stimulation and post-tetanic count are stimulation modalities for assessing neuromuscular blockade in addition to TOF stimulation. Post-tetanic count is particularly useful during deep block when TOF responses are absent. Anaesthetic departments are encouraged to use quantitative devices for accurate assessment of neuromuscular function throughout anaesthesia.

questions.question: A femoral nerve block is planned for a patient with a fractured neck of femur. Which landmark is used to correctly locate the femoral nerve?
questions.explanation: The femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral artery within the femoral triangle, so the artery pulse is palpated as a landmark before needle insertion lateral to it. Correct identification reduces the risk of accidental arterial puncture. The vein lies medial to the artery and is not the landmark used for nerve localisation.
options: Medial to the femoral vein position
Lateral to the femoral artery pulse
Two centimetres above the iliac crest
At the midpoint of the inguinal ligament
provides equivalent analgesia to strong opioids alone
eliminates the need for any other analgesics
carries a high risk of respiratory depression
reduces opioid requirements with a favourable safety profile
is contraindicated in almost all surgical patients
questions.question: Paracetamol is frequently included in a multimodal postoperative analgesia regimen PRIMARILY because it
questions.explanation: Paracetamol has a favourable safety profile with minimal respiratory or haemodynamic side effects and, when combined with other analgesics such as opioids and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, reduces overall opioid consumption and associated side effects such as sedation and nausea. It is generally weaker than strong opioids alone for severe pain, which is why it forms part of a multimodal, not standalone, approach.

options: Witnessed signature from an independent observer
Physician verification of patient understanding level
Documentation of the consent process formally
Legal review by hospital consent committee
Competency assessed by the treating physician only
questions.question: The four principles of informed consent include capacity, comprehension, voluntary consent, and which fourth principle?
questions.explanation: The four principles of informed consent are: capacity (patient ability to decide), comprehension (information must be understandable), voluntary consent (free from coercion), and documentation (the process is formally documented, usually with a signed form). Documentation provides a legal record of the consent process and the patient's agreement to treatment. Verbal assent may also be valid depending on the situation.

options: an allergic reaction to the surgical drape
the Bezold-Jarisch reflex from venous pooling
excessive fluid overload from intravenous therapy
malignant hyperthermia triggered by volatile agent
questions.explanation: In the seated beach-chair position, reduced venous return can trigger the Bezold-Jarisch reflex, a paradoxical bradycardia and hypotension mediated by cardiac mechanoreceptors responding to a relatively empty, vigorously contracting ventricle. Prompt recognition allows repositioning and treatment with fluids and vasopressors. Malignant hyperthermia presents with hyperthermia and hypercarbia rather than sudden bradycardia and hypotension.
questions.question: A patient undergoing shoulder arthroscopy under an interscalene block in the beach-chair position suddenly becomes hypotensive and bradycardic. The nurse should FIRST suspect

options: 5 compressions to 1 ventilation for adults only
15 compressions to 2 ventilations for all rescuers
questions.explanation: The recommended compression-to-ventilation ratio for adult CPR is 30 compressions to 2 ventilations. This ratio was adopted based on evidence that minimising interruptions to compressions maximises coronary perfusion pressure. When an advanced airway is in place during 2-person CPR, continuous compressions are delivered while breaths are given every 6-8 seconds without pausing.
questions.question: In adult CPR, the compression-to-ventilation ratio recommended for lay rescuers and healthcare providers is which ratio?

options: less motor block at equivalent analgesic doses
faster systemic absorption from the epidural space
stronger sedative effects on the fetus
questions.explanation: Ropivacaine produces relatively less motor blockade than bupivacaine at equianalgesic doses, allowing mothers in labour to retain more lower limb movement while still receiving effective analgesia, and it is also associated with a lower potential for cardiotoxicity. This sensory-motor separation is a key reason for its popularity in obstetric epidural infusions.
questions.question: Ropivacaine is often preferred over bupivacaine for epidural infusions in labour because it produces relatively

options: Avoiding neck movement during intubation attempts
Immediate pharmacological paralysis to prevent movement
Immediate tracheostomy to secure the definitive airway
Use of nasal rather than oral intubation exclusively
Awake fibreoptic intubation in all cervical spine cases
questions.explanation: In trauma patients with cervical spine injury, avoiding neck movement during intubation attempts is paramount to prevent secondary spinal cord injury. The rigid cervical collar used for immobilisation can result in higher Cormack-Lehane views of the larynx, increasing difficulty. Avoiding hypotension, hypoxia, and hypercarbia are also critically important in these patients.
questions.question: Trauma patients with cervical spine injury present an increased risk of difficult intubation. Which intervention is PARAMOUNT during intubation of these patients?

options: 3 plus 1 by an expert for a total of four attempts
2 maximum attempts by any clinician before stopping
As many as needed until oxygenation is achieved
1 attempt only before moving to surgical airway
questions.explanation: A maximum of 3 + 1 laryngoscopy attempts is emphasised in failed intubation management. The first three attempts can be made by the initial clinician, and the plus one attempt is reserved for situations when an expert arrives to help. It is unlikely that more than three attempts by the same clinician will be successful, and continued attempts can result in airway trauma and worsening conditions.
questions.question: In the ALS algorithm, how many maximum laryngoscopy attempts are recommended before declaring a failed airway situation?

questions.explanation: A sudden drop in end-tidal CO2 to near zero immediately after intubation is a hallmark sign of oesophageal intubation, since no CO2-containing gas from the lungs is being exhaled through the airway device. This finding requires immediate tube removal and reintubation. Correct tracheal placement would instead show a sustained, characteristic capnography waveform with each breath.
options: oesophageal rather than tracheal tube placement
questions.question: An abrupt fall of end-tidal CO2 to near zero immediately after intubation MOST strongly suggests

questions.explanation: In certain clinical situations, invasive arterial lines may be placed to provide continuous and more precise blood pressure monitoring beyond what non-invasive cuffs can offer. This is particularly important during major surgeries with significant haemodynamic changes or in critically ill patients where real-time continuous data is essential for management. Routine procedures use non-invasive blood pressure monitoring.
questions.question: Blood pressure monitoring is described as a non-invasive procedure. In which specific situation might invasive arterial lines replace non-invasive blood pressure monitoring?
options: When the patient is undergoing a procedure under sedation
When continuous and more precise BP monitoring is required
When the patient has difficult venous access peripherally
When non-invasive cuffs produce artefactual high readings
When the patient requires hourly blood pressure readings

questions.explanation: Inaccurate localisation of the target nerve is the most common reason for incomplete peripheral nerve block anaesthesia. The objective of peripheral nerve blocks is the precise administration of local anaesthetic agents near targeted nerves. Ultrasound guidance has significantly improved nerve localisation accuracy, reducing the incidence of block failure and complications.
questions.question: A patient undergoing a peripheral nerve block for surgery reports incomplete anaesthesia. Which factor MOST likely contributed to this outcome?
options: Selection of an agent with too prolonged duration
Administration of an unnecessarily concentrated solution
Inaccurate localisation of the target nerve structure
Use of an excessively large volume of local anaesthetic
Administering the block too far in advance of surgery

questions.explanation: A key disadvantage of non-invasive anaesthesia in complex procedures is limited pain control. Not all procedures are suitable for non-invasive anaesthesia, particularly those requiring deep pain control or extensive surgical manipulation. In some cases, non-invasive methods may fail to provide sufficient pain relief, necessitating conversion to general anaesthesia.
questions.question: Which disadvantage is MOST commonly associated with non-invasive anaesthesia techniques in complex surgical procedures?
options: Prolonged duration of action compared to invasive techniques
Increased postoperative nausea and vomiting rates
Higher incidence of respiratory depression intraoperatively
Greater incidence of postoperative nerve damage
Inability to provide adequate pain control for extensive surgery

questions.explanation: Ibuprofen is not recommended in children less than 7 kg. The recommended dose for children is 20 mg/kg body weight in divided doses. Additionally, ibuprofen should not be administered to asthmatic patients or patients with a history of peptic ulcer disease due to the risk of bronchospasm and gastrointestinal complications. Renal insufficiency and hypersensitivity reactions are also recognised adverse effects.
options: Less than 5 kg body weight minimum
Less than 3 kg body weight minimum
Less than 10 kg body weight minimum
Less than 15 kg body weight minimum
Less than 7 kg body weight minimum
questions.question: Ibuprofen as an NSAID is NOT recommended in children less than which weight?

questions.explanation: Psychological support during failed intubation should be offered to the patient and their family during this challenging situation. Failed intubation is a frightening and potentially life-threatening event for the patient and their loved ones. The nurse's role includes maintaining calm, providing clear explanations, addressing fears, and offering emotional reassurance while simultaneously supporting the clinical team.
questions.question: The psychological support aspect of nursing care during failed intubation is directed at which people?
options: The hospital administration handling incident reporting
The senior anaesthesiologist managing the difficult case
The anaesthetic nurse team experiencing the stressful situation
The surgical team waiting for airway to be secured
The patient and their family during this challenging situation

questions.explanation: Plan B in the DAS Failed Intubation Algorithm involves maintaining oxygenation with a supraglottic airway (SGA). If successful, there is an opportunity to regroup, including options to abort the procedure, use the SGA as is, or use it as a conduit to intubation. A second-generation supraglottic airway is recommended as it separates respiratory from gastrointestinal tracts and has higher cuff sealing pressures.
questions.question: According to the DAS Failed Intubation Algorithm, Plan B involves which airway management strategy?
options: Blind nasal intubation using a flexible scope
Mask ventilation with paralysis and two-person technique
Maintaining oxygenation with a supraglottic airway
Reattempting laryngoscopy with a video laryngoscope

questions.question: Capnography as a non-invasive monitoring technique measures which parameter to aid ventilation management?
questions.explanation: Capnography is a non-invasive technique that measures the concentration of carbon dioxide (CO2) in exhaled breath, providing critical information for ventilation management. Poor ventilation and hypercarbia can lead to respiratory acidosis and cardiovascular collapse, which may not be detected with pulse oximetry until very late. Capnography works alongside pulse oximetry for comprehensive respiratory monitoring.
options: Inspired oxygen concentration in the circuit
Blood pressure and cardiac output indirectly
Tidal volume and minute ventilation values
Carbon dioxide concentration in exhaled breath

questions.question: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) when administered intravenously to a child weighing between 10-50 kg should be given at which dose?
questions.explanation: Paracetamol IM/IV dosing for a child weighing 10-50 kg is 15 mg/kg/body weight every 4-6 hours. For children less than 10 kg, the dose is 7.5 mg/kg/body weight every 4-6 hours. The IV administration should be infused over 15 minutes to reduce the risk of adverse effects. Paracetamol should be used with caution in patients with hepatic impairment due to risk of hepatotoxicity.

Phantom pain sensations are reported most frequently following the amputation of a limb, though they may also occur following the removal of a breast, tongue, or internal organ, and after eye loss (phantom eye syndrome). The pain sensation, its duration, and frequency vary from individual to individual. The source of phantom pain is complex and not well understood, involving both peripheral and central mechanisms.
options: Severe spinal cord injury causing complete paralysis
Removal of internal organs like the gallbladder
Peripheral nerve injury from trauma or compression
Amputation of a limb as the most common trigger
questions.question: Phantom pain is defined as painful perception relating to a limb or organ that is not physically part of the body. This sensation is reported MOST FREQUENTLY following which event?

questions.explanation: Endobronchial intubation (also called mainstem intubation) occurs when the tracheal tube passes down one of the two bronchi that connect the trachea to each lung, rather than remaining in the trachea. This results in ventilation of only one lung, causing hypoxia and atelectasis in the unventilated lung. It can be detected by auscultating breath sounds bilaterally and confirmed by chest X-ray or bronchoscopy.
options: One of the two bronchi rather than remaining in trachea
The right pleural space causing tension pneumothorax
The nasopharynx rather than the laryngeal inlet
The subglottic space causing subglottic oedema
The oesophagus instead of the trachea during intubation
questions.question: Endobronchial intubation (mainstem intubation) occurs when the tracheal tube passes into which anatomical structure?
EEG Gamma waves (30+ Hz) are associated with which type of cognitive and neurological processing?
options: Drowsiness and early stages of sedation
Cognitive processing and higher brain function
Deep sleep and unconscious restorative processes
questions.explanation: Gamma waves (30+ Hz) are associated with cognitive processing and higher brain function. They are typically suppressed during anaesthesia along with beta waves as anaesthetic depth increases. The presence of gamma waves in the EEG during anaesthesia might indicate inadequate depth of anaesthesia. Understanding EEG frequency bands helps interpret cerebral monitoring data during anaesthesia.

For cognitively intact, communicative patients, self-report using a numerical rating scale or visual analogue scale is considered the most valid and reliable method of pain assessment, since pain is inherently subjective and the patient is the best judge of their own experience. Behavioural scales are reserved for patients unable to self-report, such as those who are non-verbal or cognitively impaired.
questions.question: For a postoperative patient who is cognitively intact and able to communicate, the MOST appropriate tool for assessing pain intensity is
options: the nurse's subjective clinical impression only
a numerical or visual analogue pain scale
a behavioural pain scale designed for non-verbal patients
reliance on the surgeon's expected pain estimate

questions.explanation: Indirectly acting sympathomimetic drugs such as ephedrine rely partly on releasing stored noradrenaline, and in patients on MAOIs, who have excess stored catecholamines due to reduced breakdown, this can precipitate a severe and potentially life-threatening hypertensive crisis. Volatile agents, neuromuscular blockers, and plain local anaesthetics do not carry this same specific dangerous interaction with MAOIs.
options: Indirectly acting sympathomimetics such as ephedrine
questions.question: A patient on long-term monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) is scheduled for surgery. The anaesthetic team must exercise particular caution with which drug class due to risk of severe hypertensive crisis?

options: Ventilation, blood glucose, circulation, and consciousness
Oxygenation, neuromuscular function, temperature, and pain
Temperature, pain score, circulation, and blood glucose
Circulation, urine output, oxygenation, and anaesthetic depth
questions.question: According to ASA Standard II, which four parameters MUST be continually evaluated during all anaesthetics?
questions.explanation: ASA Standard II requires that during all anaesthetics, the patient's oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature shall be continually evaluated. These four parameters encompass the essential physiological functions that anaesthesia and surgery can alter rapidly. Monitoring these parameters allows anaesthesia providers to detect and respond to perturbations before patient harm occurs.

The recovery position is used for unresponsive adult victims who clearly have normal breathing and effective circulation. This position maintains a patent airway and reduces the risk of airway obstruction and aspiration by placing the patient on their side with the lower arm in front of the body. It is NOT used for patients in cardiac arrest, who require CPR.
questions.question: The recovery position is used for unresponsive adult victims who demonstrate which specific condition?
options: Normal breathing and effective circulation clearly present
Irregular breathing requiring immediate ventilatory support
Absent breathing but with a palpable carotid pulse
Absent pulse but with spontaneous respiratory effort

questions.question: EEG Theta waves (4-8 Hz) are associated with which state of brain activity?
questions.explanation: EEG Theta waves (4-8 Hz) are associated with drowsiness and lighter stages of anaesthesia. They represent an intermediate state between wakefulness and deep sleep or anaesthesia. As anaesthetic depth increases, EEG frequency progressively slows from beta and alpha patterns through theta to delta, reflecting progressive brain suppression.
options: Rapid eye movement sleep during physiological rest
Active wakefulness and complex cognitive processing
Drowsiness and lighter stages of anaesthesia
Deep anaesthesia and unconscious brain suppression
To determine who is responsible for the failed attempt
To ensure all team members can perform the procedure
To arrange transfer to a higher level of care immediately
To address concerns, provide reassurance, and update on condition
To document the failure for medicolegal protection only
questions.question: Following failed intubation, maintaining clear communication with the healthcare team and the patient and their family serves which purpose?
questions.explanation: Following failed intubation, maintaining clear communication with the healthcare team includes providing updates on the patient's condition. Communication with the patient and their family involves addressing concerns and providing reassurance. This two-way communication is essential for patient safety, family-centred care, and maintaining trust during a potentially frightening and life-threatening situation.

options: leakage of gas from a correctly fitted cylinder
accidental connection of the wrong gas cylinder
overpressure damage to the cylinder valve
contamination of gas with bacterial pathogens
excessive gas flow to the patient circuit
questions.question: A pin-index safety system on anaesthetic gas cylinders is designed PRIMARILY to prevent
questions.explanation: The pin-index system uses a unique arrangement of pins and holes specific to each gas type, physically preventing a cylinder from being connected to the wrong yoke on the anaesthetic machine, thereby avoiding the serious risk of administering the incorrect gas to a patient. It does not address leakage, overpressure, contamination, or flow rate issues, which are managed by other safety features.

questions.question: A patient is prescribed tramadol postoperatively and is also taking a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for depression. The nurse should monitor closely for signs of
questions.explanation: Tramadol has serotonergic activity in addition to weak opioid receptor agonism, so combining it with an SSRI increases the risk of serotonin syndrome, presenting with agitation, hyperthermia, tremor, and autonomic instability. This drug interaction is a recognised safety concern requiring careful monitoring. Constipation is a common but far less dangerous opioid effect than serotonin syndrome in this combination.

questions.question: In diabetic patients undergoing anaesthesia, blood glucose should be monitored intra-operatively at what minimum frequency?
questions.explanation: In patients with diabetes mellitus controlled by medication, blood glucose should be monitored intra-operatively at least hourly, or more frequently if results are outside the target range. This is particularly important in patients on insulin, sulphonylureas, or meglitinides. The anaesthetic nurse is responsible for ensuring this monitoring occurs.
options: Every 2 hours or more frequently if needed
Only at the beginning and end of the procedure
At least hourly in patients with diabetes mellitus
Every 30 minutes throughout the entire procedure

questions.question: Pregnant patients beyond the mid-second trimester are at increased risk of difficult intubation PRIMARILY because of
questions.explanation: Pregnancy causes hormonally mediated capillary engorgement and oedema of the airway mucosa, including the larynx and oropharynx, which can narrow the airway and make laryngoscopy and intubation more difficult, particularly in later pregnancy or with conditions such as pre-eclampsia. Pregnant patients actually have increased, not decreased, oxygen consumption and reduced functional residual capacity, further increasing risk during airway management.

questions.question: Nociceptive pain caused by damage to body tissue is MOST characteristically described as which type of sensation?
options: Sharp, achy, or throbbing pain from tissue injury
Burning, allodynic pain from central sensitisation
Intermittent stabbing pain with normal baseline
Dull, constant background aching with fatigue
questions.explanation: Nociceptive pain caused by damage to body tissue is characteristically described as sharp, achy, or throbbing. It is often caused by an external injury such as hitting the elbow, stubbing the toe, or an ankle twist. This type of pain is experienced in the joints, muscles, skin, tendons, and bones, and can be both acute and chronic. It represents normal nociceptive function responding to tissue damage.

questions.question: Ultrasound guidance in anaesthesia PRIMARILY enhances which aspect of nerve block procedures?
options: Accuracy of needle placement near target nerves
Prevention of systemic toxicity from drug absorption
Duration of the local anaesthetic effect on nerves
Speed of onset of neuromuscular blockade
Volume of local anaesthetic required for a block
questions.explanation: Ultrasound guidance enables real-time imaging that significantly enhances accuracy and precision in localising nerves, improving the safety of interventions such as nerve blocks and vascular access. questions.question: Cardiac tamponade as a reversible cause of cardiac arrest is caused by which pathophysiological mechanism?

questions.explanation: Cardiac tamponade is a form of cardiogenic shock caused by fluid accumulation in the pericardial space. As pericardial fluid accumulates, it compresses the cardiac chambers, impairing filling and reducing cardiac output. Tamponade is a potentially reversible cause of cardiac arrest (one of the 4 H's and 4 T's) that can be treated with pericardiocentesis to release the obstructing fluid.

does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier

questions.question: A patient who has undergone invasive anaesthesia is likely to experience which SPECIFIC intraoperative advantage over those receiving non-invasive techniques?
questions.explanation: Invasive anaesthesia techniques allow for closer monitoring and control of vital signs like blood pressure and heart rate, providing greater haemodynamic stability. Higher patient satisfaction with the anaesthesia experience
Lower incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting

questions.explanation: Neonates have a large body surface area relative to their body mass, along with limited subcutaneous fat insulation and an immature ability to shiver, all of which predispose them to rapid heat loss and hypothermia during surgery, making active warming and temperature monitoring especially important in this age group. questions.question: Opioids, barbiturates, and benzodiazepines share which COMMON effect on renal function during anaesthesia?
questions.explanation: Opioids, barbiturates, and benzodiazepines contribute to a reduction in glomerular filtration rate and urine output, similar to inhalational anaesthetics. These effects are primarily mediated through their actions on cardiovascular and autonomic nervous system function, reducing renal perfusion. These perioperative changes are typically transient and clinically negligible in patients with normal renal function.

Confirmation of correct endotracheal tube placement using capnography, direct visualisation, and auscultation is essential.

The names of all witnesses present during the process
A complete assessment of the patient's psychological capacity

questions.explanation: In patients with a suspected basal skull fracture, blind nasal intubation carries the rare but catastrophic risk of the tube passing through the fracture defect into the cranial cavity, causing intracranial injury. This is why nasal intubation is generally avoided in favour of oral intubation in suspected basal skull fracture until the injury is excluded or a controlled technique is used.

questions.explanation: A sustained, characteristic capnography waveform present on multiple consecutive breaths is the most reliable confirmation of correct tracheal tube placement, since it demonstrates ongoing gas exchange from the lungs. questions.explanation: Mechanical ventilation decreases urine volume and sodium excretion, influenced by the increase in intrathoracic pressure, though ADH release, baroreceptor unloading, and renin-angiotensin system activation also play roles. These effects are important considerations for perioperative fluid management and renal function assessment in anaesthetised patients on mechanical ventilation.

questions.question: In the Isolated Forearm Technique, a positive motor response to command during IFT is termed what clinical state?
questions.explanation: A positive motor response to command during IFT is termed 'wakefulness,' indicating the patient is potentially awake and exhibiting signs of awareness but may not have recall after surgery. During most episodes of wakefulness detected by IFT, there was no increase in heart rate or blood pressure, and no sweating or tear production suggestive of inadequate anaesthesia.

questions.explanation: Multimodal prophylaxis combines antiemetics that act on different receptor pathways, such as a 5-HT3 antagonist with a dopamine antagonist or corticosteroid, to achieve a more comprehensive reduction in nausea and vomiting risk than any single agent alone, particularly in patients with multiple risk factors. Repeating the same drug at a higher dose does not broaden receptor coverage and increases side-effect risk instead.

A patient with massive intraoperative blood loss receiving multiple units of stored blood is at risk of citrate toxicity, which can manifest as
questions.explanation: Citrate, used as an anticoagulant in stored blood, chelates calcium and can cause hypocalcaemia during rapid massive transfusion, presenting with perioral tingling, muscle twitching, and in severe cases cardiac dysfunction. This is distinct from the hyperkalaemia that can occur separately from potassium leakage in stored red cells, and from malignant hyperthermia, which has a different mechanism entirely.

Beta waves (13-30 Hz) correspond to active wakefulness and are generally reduced under anaesthesia. As anaesthetic depth increases, beta wave activity is progressively suppressed. Paradoxically, certain anaesthetic agents like ketamine may maintain or increase beta wave activity despite producing clinical anaesthesia, which is an important consideration when interpreting BIS values.
questions.question: EEG Beta waves (13-30 Hz) correspond to which state of brain activity?

Active wakefulness and are generally reduced under anaesthesia
Deep sleep and profound anaesthetic suppression
Light sedation with preserved consciousness and alertness

questions.explanation: Cyclizine has anticholinergic and antihistaminic properties that can cause tachycardia and reduce cardiac efficiency, so it should be used cautiously in patients with severe heart failure, where additional cardiovascular strain is poorly tolerated. It carries less concern in well-controlled hypertension, stable angina, isolated first-degree block, or mild valvular sclerosis compared with decompensated heart failure.

Both hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia increase the risk of postoperative complications.

questions.explanation: Radicular pain (commonly known as sciatica) occurs when the spinal nerve gets compressed or inflamed, and it radiates from the back and hip into the leg by way of the spine and spinal nerve root. Symptoms include tingling, numbness, and muscle weakness in the leg. Walking, sitting, and some activities worsen sciatica. It involves the sciatic nerve, which is the most commonly affected nerve in radiculopathy.

From the lumbar spine into the groin and genitalia only
From the thoracic spine radiating around the chest wall
From the coccyx radiating into the buttock and thigh

Oxygen supply interruption during transfer could rapidly cause hypoxia and patient harm. The oxygen supply should be verified before transfer, and the portable cylinder should contain sufficient oxygen including for unexpected delays.
questions.question: Monitoring during transfer of anaesthetised patients requires which SPECIFIC equipment to be present at all times?
According to the BLS algorithm, after confirming scene safety and unresponsiveness, the NEXT step is to
questions.explanation: After confirming scene safety and establishing that the patient is unresponsive, the BLS algorithm directs the rescuer to activate the emergency response system and obtain a defibrillator before proceeding to check breathing and pulse simultaneously for no more than 10 seconds. Beginning compressions before this brief assessment, or checking a pulse for an excessively long 30 seconds, would deviate from the recommended sequence.
options: begin chest compressions immediately without checks
check for a carotid pulse for 30 seconds
open the airway with a head tilt only

questions.explanation: Mild hypothermia is defined as a core temperature between 35 and 32?C, while severe hypothermia is defined as a core temperature below 32?C. Hypothermia can cause cardiac arrest by inducing ventricular fibrillation and other arrhythmias. As one of the 4 H's (reversible causes), hypothermia must be identified and treated during resuscitation to improve survival outcomes.

Isoflurane's chemical name describes it as which type of compound with what structural characteristics?
questions.explanation: Isoflurane's chemical name is 1-chloro-2,2,2-trifluoroethyl difluoromethyl ether, classifying it as a halogenated ether. It produces anaesthetic effects and muscle relaxation but not analgesia. Side effects include decreased blood pressure and systemic vascular resistance. Adverse effects include increased bronchial secretions and increased intracranial pressure, which must be monitored during anaesthesia.

Failed tracheal intubation is defined as failure to achieve successful tracheal intubation after a maximum of how many attempts?
questions.explanation: Failed Tracheal Intubation is defined as the failure to achieve a successful tracheal intubation in a maximum of three attempts, regardless of the techniques used. It is unlikely that more than three attempts by the same clinician will be successful, and continued attempts can result in airway trauma and hypoxia. The DAS algorithm recommends a maximum of 3+1 laryngoscopy attempts.
options: After any failed attempt requiring a change in technique
After a maximum of three attempts regardless of technique
After a maximum of five attempts using different techniques
After a maximum of two attempts by a trained clinician
After a maximum of one attempt regardless of technique

questions.explanation: When clinically indicated, equipment to monitor the anaesthetic effect on the brain should be available for use on patients, especially those at high risk of awareness during general anaesthesia. Risk factors for awareness include difficult intubation, haemodynamic instability requiring reduced anaesthetic doses, prior history of awareness, and use of total intravenous anaesthesia without inhaled agents.
options: Only patients receiving total intravenous anaesthesia
All patients undergoing elective orthopaedic procedures
Patients at high risk of awareness during general anaesthesia

questions.question: A patient in theatre suddenly develops a wide-complex tachycardia with a palpable pulse and is haemodynamically unstable with a falling blood pressure. The MOST appropriate immediate management is
questions.explanation: An unstable patient with a wide-complex tachycardia and a pulse requires urgent synchronised cardioversion, which times the shock to the R wave to avoid inducing ventricular fibrillation, unlike unsynchronised defibrillation which is reserved for pulseless arrest rhythms. Adenosine and vagal manoeuvres are used for stable narrow-complex tachycardias rather than unstable wide-complex rhythms.

questions.question: When providing rescue breaths, each breath should be delivered over what duration?
questions.explanation: Each rescue breath should be delivered over 1 second, giving a sufficient tidal volume to produce visible chest rise. Taking a regular (not deep) breath before delivering the rescue breath prevents the rescuer from getting dizzy or lightheaded and prevents overinflation of the victim's lungs. The most common cause of ventilation difficulty is an improperly opened airway.
options: 0.5 seconds per breath to minimise interruption
4-5 seconds per breath in bradypnoeic patients
1 second per breath to produce visible chest rise
3-4 seconds per breath for deep lung inflation
2-3 seconds per breath for adequate filling

questions.explanation: Sugammadex is a modified gamma-cyclodextrin that selectively encapsulates aminosteroidal neuromuscular blocking agents such as rocuronium and vecuronium, forming an inactive complex that is excreted renally. It is not effective against benzylisoquinolinium agents such as atracurium or against depolarising agents such as suxamethonium, which are reversed differently or allowed to wear off spontaneously.
questions.question: Sugammadex is used to reverse neuromuscular blockade PRIMARILY produced by which class of agents?

questions.explanation: Pain associated with angina pectoris or myocardial infarction is referred to the left chest, left shoulder, and upper left arm. This referred pain pattern occurs because cardiac nociceptive signals converge in the spinal cord with somatic signals from these regions, and the brain interprets the pain as originating from somatic rather than visceral structures. Recognition of this pattern is critical for cardiac diagnosis.
options: The interscapular region of the back only
The right shoulder and upper right arm region
The left chest, left shoulder, and upper left arm
The epigastrium and central abdominal region only
The right arm and right side of the neck
questions.question: Referred pain described in cardiac angina or myocardial infarction is typically felt in which specific location?
An epidural catheter accidentally migrates into the intravascular space during a continuous postoperative infusion. The EARLIEST warning sign the nurse might observe is
options: a gradual increase in sensory block level
delayed onset of motor block only
reduced heart rate with warm extremities
sudden onset of perioral tingling or tinnitus
questions.explanation: Intravascular migration of an epidural catheter can result in systemic absorption of local anaesthetic at a rate similar to direct intravenous injection, and the earliest warning signs are typically early features of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity such as perioral tingling, tinnitus, or a metallic taste, requiring the infusion to be stopped immediately and the catheter reassessed.

Weak grip, uncoordinated jerky movements, and inability to sustain a head lift for five seconds are classic clinical signs of residual neuromuscular blockade, indicating incomplete reversal of muscle relaxants. This finding requires prompt recognition because residual paralysis increases the risk of airway obstruction, aspiration, and hypoxia in the immediate postoperative period. It is not a feature of normal recovery.

questions.explanation: Human factors contributing to failed intubation in emergency surgery include poor communication and teamwork issues, lack of planning, lack of equipment checking, and fatigue. Emergency surgery patients appear to have a higher risk of difficult or failed intubation due to these human factors in addition to the inherent urgency. These factors underscore the importance of structured team briefings and simulation training.

questions.explanation: Because true allergy to amide local anaesthetics is rare but possible, an ester-type local anaesthetic such as procaine may be selected as an alternative, since the two classes are structurally distinct and cross-reactivity is uncommon. Simply giving a higher dose of the same amide would not address a genuine allergy. Opioids and neuromuscular blockers are not substitutes for local anaesthetic action.
options: A higher dose of the same amide
A benzodiazepine as a substitute agent
An opioid injected at the same site

questions.question: Excessive ventilation during CPR is potentially HARMFUL primarily because of which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Excessive ventilation during CPR is harmful primarily because it increases intrathoracic pressure, which decreases venous return to the heart and diminishes cardiac output and survival. Excessive ventilation also causes gastric inflation and complications such as regurgitation and aspiration. During CPR, the primary purpose of assisted ventilation is to maintain adequate oxygenation while avoiding excessive volumes.

questions.question: An anaesthetic nurse preparing for a rapid sequence induction should ensure which piece of equipment is IMMEDIATELY available at the bedside?
questions.explanation: Working suction with a wide-bore (Yankauer) catheter must be immediately available during rapid sequence induction because of the significant risk of regurgitation and the need to rapidly clear the airway of vomitus or secretions to maintain airway patency and prevent aspiration. The other listed equipment, while useful in general anaesthetic practice, is not the immediate priority for this specific high-risk induction technique.

questions.question: According to the Association of Anaesthetists, the anaesthetic nurse MUST perform which ESSENTIAL role regarding minimum monitoring standards?
questions.explanation: Minimum monitoring devices must be attached before induction of anaesthesia and their use continued until the patient has recovered from the effects of anaesthesia. This is a fundamental requirement of the Association of Anaesthetists minimum standards. Starting monitoring before induction ensures baseline values are established and the equipment is functioning before the patient loses consciousness.
options: Attach minimum monitoring devices before induction and maintain until recovery
Document monitoring only at 30-minute intervals intraoperatively
Apply monitoring only during the most critical surgical phase
Remove monitoring equipment after transfer from the theatre
Delegate monitoring responsibilities to theatre nursing staff

questions.question: A patient placed in the lithotomy position for a prolonged gynaecological procedure is at increased risk of which nerve injury?
questions.explanation: In the lithotomy position, the common peroneal nerve is vulnerable to compression against the fibular head from leg supports, particularly during prolonged procedures, and can result in foot drop if unrecognised. Ulnar and radial nerve injuries are more typically associated with improper arm positioning in the supine position, while brachial plexus injury is linked to excessive arm abduction rather than leg positioning.

Common peroneal nerve injury at the fibular head
Brachial plexus injury from arm abduction
Radial nerve injury at the humeral groove
Facial nerve injury from mask pressure

questions.explanation: The femoral nerve block numbs the thigh and knee and is often used for surgeries on the hip, knee, or lower leg. It provides effective analgesia for procedures such as knee arthroplasty, femoral fractures, and hip surgeries. The sciatic nerve block may be combined with a femoral block for complete lower extremity anaesthesia below the knee.

questions.question: Acute pain is defined by its duration. It lasts from minutes to approximately how long?
questions.explanation: Acute pain implies pain short in duration, lasting from minutes to about three months (sometimes up to six months). Acute pain tends to be related to a soft-tissue injury or a temporary illness and subsides after the injury heals or illness resolves. Acute pain from an injury may evolve into chronic pain if the injury does not heal correctly or if the pain signals malfunction.

questions.explanation: Peripheral nerve stimulator monitors should be applied and used from induction, to confirm adequate muscle relaxation before endotracheal intubation, until recovery from blockade and return of consciousness. It is proposed that the brain interprets any such messages as coming from skin and muscle nerves rather than from an internal organ.

questions.question: Basic Life Support (BLS) is PRIMARILY characterised by which set of interventions?
questions.explanation: Basic Life Support is characterised by its quick emergency cardiovascular care, rescue breathing, chest compressions, and early defibrillation to restore normal breathing. BLS forms the foundation of cardiac arrest management and can be initiated by healthcare providers and trained bystanders. It bridges the gap until advanced life support providers can take over with more sophisticated interventions.
