B(ii) Explain why osteoarthritis of the hip has a lower average age of presentation than osteoarthritis of the knee at the University College Hospital, Ibadan.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Non-medical: health education; emotional support; nutritional advice; peer group discussions. Physiotherapy: range of motion exercises; muscle strengthening; gait normalization; low impact aerobic exercise; patella taping for patello-femoral OA. Orthotics: wedge insole; custom-made pick-up sticks; walking sticks; braces. Load reduction: weight reduction; shock-absorbing shoes; avoid climbing stairs. Medications: systemic analgesics/NSAIDs (tablet and topical); local/topical NSAID and intra-articular injections (steroid + local anaesthetic, or hyalagan); Disease Modifying OA Drugs (DMOAD) — Tamoxifen, Chloroquine, Glucosamine sulphate, Chondroitin sulphate; other drugs — arthocare, proteoglycans, Vitamin C. Temporary splintage (not prolonged); intra-articular hydrocortisone injection; shoe raise for limping.
A(ii) Surgical indications: rest pain; stiffness; deformity. Surgical techniques: joint debridement (osteophytes, cartilage tags, loose bodies); arthroscopic surgery; autologous cartilage grafting; realignment osteotomy (redistributes load from the damaged compartment to a healthier area of the joint); arthrodesis; arthroplasty (total knee replacement, total hip replacement); bone drilling.
B(i) Variants: (1) Monoarticular and pauciarticular OA — affects weight-bearing joints; underlying abnormality such as acetabular dysplasia, Perthes, slipped epiphysis, previous fracture, damaged ligament or menisci. (2) Polyarticular (generalised) OA — middle-aged; pain, swelling, stiffness of finger joints; hand is commonest; knobbly appearance: Heberden's nodes at distal IPJ; Bouchard's nodes at proximal IPJ. (3) Endemic OA — predisposing diseases: Kashin-Beck disease, Mseleni disease. (4) Rapidly destructive OA — possibly NSAID-induced (analgesic arthropathy); calcium crystal deposition. (5) Neuropathic joint disease (Charcot's disease) — lack of pain sensibility/joint position sense. (6) Haemophilic arthropathy.
B(ii) The lower average age of affectation of OA of the hip (49.5 years) compared to OA of the knee (59.1 years) is probably because some of the hip OA patients have secondary OA following avascular necrosis of the femoral head in patients with sickle cell anaemia.

A(i) Normal anatomy and types:
The extrahepatic biliary system comprises the right and left hepatic ducts uniting to form the common hepatic duct, which receives the cystic duct to become the common bile duct (CBD), draining into the 2nd part of the duodenum at the ampulla of Vater.
Types of biliary atresia:
(i) Atresia of CBD only
(ii) Atresia of CBD and hepatic duct
(iii) Atresia of all extrahepatic bile ducts (complete/panductal) — most severe

A(ii) Microscopic pathological changes:
- Panductal narrowed, distorted and irregular intrahepatic ducts
- Bile stasis
- Distortion of liver cell cords
- Giant cell transformation
- Focal necrosis
- Intralobular fibrosis
- Progressive over time: round cell infiltration → bile duct proliferation → liver fibrosis → cirrhosis

B) Severity and timing:
- Infants 1–3 months: obstructive jaundice, acholic stools, hepatomegaly, low-grade fever; no abdominal pain and no mass (minimal liver damage yet)
- Older children (delayed diagnosis): hepatomegaly → liver cirrhosis → portal hypertension → ascites and variceal bleeding
- Prognosis worsens with age at operation, amount of fibrous tissue present, and presence of complications

C) Functional deficits:
Portal hypertension: progressive hepatic fibrosis → portal venous obstruction → splenomegaly, ascites, variceal bleeding.
Liver cirrhosis: end-stage fibrous replacement of hepatocytes → failure of all hepatic functions.
Intracranial bleeding: malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins (bile absent in gut) → Vitamin K deficiency → coagulopathy → intracranial haemorrhage.
Liver cell carcinoma: chronic biliary stasis and hepatic fibrosis → malignant transformation (long-term complication).
Failure to thrive: malabsorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) due to absent bile flow.

questions.answerText:
(A)(i) VSD is the most common form of congenital heart defect, accounting for 15–20% of all such defects (not including those in cyanotic CHD). The magnitude of the shunt is determined by the size of the defect and the level of pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR). Small defect: large resistance to left-to-right shunt occurs at the defect and the shunt does not depend on PVR. Large VSD: resistance offered by the defect is minimal and the left-to-right shunt depends largely on PVR — the lower the PVR, the greater the shunt (dependent shunt).

(A)(ii) When a large VSD is left untreated, irreversible changes take place in pulmonary arterioles, producing pulmonary vascular obstructive disease (Eisenmenger's syndrome). As PVR approaches systemic level, the magnitude of left-to-right shunt decreases; the volume overload on the LV and LA is removed; heart size returns to normal except for a prominent PA segment; pure RVH on ECG. A bidirectional shunt causes cyanosis; the S2 is loud and single (pulmonary hypertension); murmur decreases or disappears.

(A)(iii) Clinical features: depend on size — asymptomatic; growth failure; recurrent LRTI; congestive heart failure; shortness of breath; cyanosis; pansystolic murmur; loud P2; large defects lead to pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger syndrome. Investigations: chest radiograph — cardiomegaly, enlarged LA and LV; ECG — extreme left axis, biventricular hypertrophy; ECHO — chamber size and pressures; cardiac catheter — oxygen content, PA pressures, size and number of defects.

(B) Medical: endocarditis prophylaxis; digoxin; diuretics. Surgical: before pulmonary vascular changes become irreversible; direct closure under hypothermic cardiopulmonary bypass, preferably without right ventriculotomy; most perimembranous and inlet VSDs repaired by transatrial approach; outlet (conal) defects through incision in the main PA; apical VSD may require apical right ventriculotomy.

(C) PDA: connection between PA and descending aorta; 10% of CHD. Pathophysiology: basically a consequence of left-to-right shunt; reverses if pulmonary resistance increases causing RV enlargement; large PDA — Eisenmenger syndrome can develop; significant pressure gradient between aorta and PA in both systole and diastole leads to left-to-right shunt in both phases, producing the characteristic continuous murmur. Clinical features: bounding pulse; continuous murmur; loud S2; slow growth; LRTI; dyspnoea; cyanosis depending on size and direction of flow. Investigations: CXR — cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary vascularity; ECG — left or biventricular hypertrophy; echocardiography — 2D visualises PDA, Doppler shows turbulence; cardiac catheter — PA pressures and O2 saturations. Treatment: endocarditis prophylaxis; indomethacin; surgical ligation is curative.

questions.answerText:
(i) Acute renal failure: a sudden deterioration in renal function such that neither kidney is capable of excreting body waste products (urea, creatinine, potassium), which accumulate in the blood. Fatal unless treated.
- Anuria: no urine passed.
- Oliguria: less than 0.5 ml/kg/h passed.
(ii) Causes:
- Pre-renal: shock causing reduced renal perfusion; pancreatitis.
- Intrinsic renal: shock causing renal ischaemia (ATN); nephrotoxins (aminoglycosides, myoglobin); acute glomerulonephritis; severe pyelonephritis; hypertension and diabetes mellitus.
- Post-renal: urinary tract obstruction (e.g. prostatic hypertrophy); obstructing renal calculi.
(iii) Urinary biochemistry:
- Pre-renal: urine osmolality >500 mosm/kg; UNa+ <10 mmol/l; urine/plasma urea >10/1; urine/plasma osmolality >2/1 (concentrated urine).
- Intrinsic renal: urine osmolality <400 mosm/kg; UNa+ >20 mmol/l; urine/plasma urea 3/1–1/1; urine/plasma osmolality <1.1/1 (casts, RBCs, protein in urine).
- Post-renal: normal urine findings.
(iv) Clinical features:
- Oliguric phase (may last hours/days/weeks): oliguria; uraemia (dyspnoea, confusion, drowsiness, coma); nausea, vomiting, hiccoughs, diarrhoea; anaemia, coagulopathy, GI haemorrhage; fluid retention (hypervolaemia, hypertension); hyperkalaemia (dysrhythmias); acidosis.
- Polyuric (recovery) phase (may last days/weeks): polyuria (hypovolaemia, hypotension); hyponatraemia; hypokalaemia.
(v) Management:
- Prevention: keep at-risk patients well hydrated; protect renal function with dopamine and mannitol in selected patients; monitor renal function in patients on nephrotoxic drugs.
- Identification: exclude urinary retention by catheterisation; correct hypovolaemia; bolus high-dose loop diuretics if normovolaemic; dopamine infusions if necessary.
- Treatment: maintain fluid and electrolyte balance; water intake 400 ml/day + measured losses; Na+ restricted; K+ intake nil (dextrose, insulin, and/or ion-exchange resins for hyperkalaemia); high-calorie, low-protein diet; treat infection; dialysis (peritoneal, ultrafiltration, haemodialysis) indicated for hypervolaemia, hyperkalaemia, or acidosis.
questions.question:
Describe acute renal failure (ARF) in surgical patients under the following headings:
(i) Definition, and the distinction between oliguria and anuria.
(ii) Classify the causes as pre-renal, intrinsic renal, and post-renal, with examples under each.
(iii) How to distinguish pre-renal from intrinsic renal failure using urinary biochemistry (urine osmolality, urinary sodium, urine-to-plasma urea ratio, urine-to-plasma osmolality ratio).
(iv) Clinical features of the oliguric phase and the polyuric (recovery) phase.
(v) Essential management: prevention, identification, and definitive treatment including the role of dialysis.

(A) Describe the American Thoracic Society classification of empyema thoracis in full, including the pathological and biochemical features of each stage.

(B) State the treatment of empyema thoracis under the following headings:
(i) Goals of management
(ii) Antibiotic therapy — community-acquired and hospital-acquired
(iii) Chest tube drainage criteria for removal
(iv) VATS — indications and advantages
(v) Management of chronic empyema

(C) Distinguish between the management of empyema in children and adults.
questions.answerText:
(A) Stage 1 — Exudative: increased permeability of the inflammatory and swollen pleural surface; exudative effusion; corresponds to uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion; fibrin and nuclear polymorphs may be present. Stage 2 — Fibrinopurulent: angioblastic and fibroblastic proliferation; heavy fibrin deposition on both pleura, particularly the parietal pleura; empyema established; fluid purulent; pH < 7.0; glucose < 60 mg/dL; LDH > 1000 IU/L. Stage 3 — Organizing: develops 1 week after infection; collagen organization; entrapment of underlying lung; 3–4 weeks — mature, turned peel; chronic dense fibrosis, contraction and trapping of lung, atelectasis and prolonged pulmonary infection, reduction in size of hemithorax; fibrothorax — invasion of chest wall and narrowing of intercostal spaces; the end stage.

(B)(i) Goals: (1) control infection with antibiotics; (2) evacuation of pus from pleural space; (3) obliteration of empyema cavity. Delay in drainage increases mortality from 3.4% to 16%.
(B)(ii) Community-acquired — third-generation cephalosporin; gram negative or anaerobes — third-generation cephalosporin and metronidazole/clindamycin. Hospital-acquired — guided by culture.
(B)(iii) CTTD removal criteria: clinical improvement; drainage less than 50 mL within 24 hours; radiological — adequate lung re-expansion; usually within 5–10 days; antibiotics continue for 6 weeks.
(B)(iv) VATS: primary modality for treating complicated empyema after initial therapy; 3–4 small access ports; adhesiolysis and debridement with better exposure; higher success rate (90%); shorter hospital stay, less cost; low morbidity; chest tube can be removed in 3–4 days.
(B)(v) Chronic empyema: thoracotomy, empyemectomy and decortication; Eloesser window; thoracoplasty.

(C) Children: goal of therapy — antibiotics, chest tube drainage, aggressive care; early thoracotomy — early recovery and excellent long-term results; VATS used; open drainage discouraged because of late skeletal deformities; fibrinolytic enzymes not used. Adults: intrapleural fibrinolytic agents (streptokinase 250,000 U/100 mL NS with 80% success; urokinase 100,000 U/100 mL NS with 90% success) may be used for loculated empyema; open drainage; VATS as primary modality for complicated empyema.

(i) Diagnosis: Hypospadias. Incidence: 1/300 live male births; commoner in males. Associated anomalies: undescended testis (9%); inguinal hernia (9%); significant anomalies of upper urinary tract (1–3%); ventral chordee. Type present: peno-scrotal hypospadias — urethral opening at penoscrotal junction, extreme chordee, webbed penis, cleft or bifid scrotum, associated with cryptorchidism.

(ii) Embryological basis: the urethra opens on the ventral surface of the penis proximal to the normal site of the external urethral meatus; caused by failure of fusion of the urethral folds on the ventral aspect of the penis during embryological development. Classification:
- Glandular: urethral opening seen in the portion usually occupied by the frenum (which is absent).
- Penile: opening along penile shaft — anterior or posterior (chordee present in posterior type).
- Peno-scrotal: chordee is extreme, webbed penis, cleft or bifid scrotum, associated with cryptorchidism.
- Perineal: rare; external genitalia resembles that of a female.

(iii) Management:
- Glandular hypospadias: meatal advancement and glanduloplasty.
- Other types: correction of chordee followed by urethroplasty (reconstruction of urethra to the glans).
The operation is performed when the child is able to cooperate with post-operative care; the general principle is correction of the chordee first to allow the penis to straighten, followed by urethral reconstruction.

(iv) Urinary sphincteric function: urinary sphincteric function is normal in hypospadias. If untreated, the ventral chordee prevents normal sexual intercourse; the misplaced meatus may impair directed urinary stream and fertility; severe forms with perineal hypospadias may cause difficulty in gender assignment. Differential diagnosis: perineal hypospadias with bifid scrotum and cryptorchidism may resemble female external genitalia, necessitating exclusion of female pseudohermaphroditism and intersex conditions by chromosomal and hormonal assessment.
questions.question:
A male neonate is noted at birth to have the urethral opening on the ventral surface of the penis at the penoscrotal junction. There is marked ventral curvature of the penis (chordee). The scrotum appears cleft or bifid, and an undescended testis is noted on one side.

(i) State the diagnosis with its incidence, name all associated anomalies described, and classify the type present in this infant.
(ii) Describe the predisposing embryological basis and list the full classification of hypospadias types in both the male.
(iii) Outline the full management, specifying the operation for glandular type and the operative steps for other types.
(iv) State the complications of the anomaly if untreated — citing the specific risk of urinary sphincteric function — and describe the differential diagnosis that must be excluded.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is complete left unilateral cleft lip. Using the anatomical classification it is a lateral cleft lip that is unilateral, complete (extends to the nostril), compound (associated with cleft of the alveolus), and complicated (associated with cleft palate).
(ii) The face is formed by fusion of five facial elements — frontonasal, two lateral maxillary and two mandibular segments — through mesenchymal migration between 6 and 12 weeks of intrauterine life. The upper lip is formed by fusion of the medial nasal process and the maxillary process; failure of this fusion between the nasal process and the maxillary process on the left side produces the left lateral cleft lip.
(iii) Millard's Rule of 10 requires: the child is 10 weeks old or more; the child weighs 10 pounds (4.5 kg) or more; and the child's haematocrit is 10 g/% or more. Repair is performed at 3 to 6 months of age.
(iv) The lip is repaired by Millard's rotation advancement repair, in which a rotation flap and an advancement flap are raised and interdigitated to close the cleft and restore the normal anatomy of the upper lip, including realignment of orbicularis oris.
(v) The cleft palate (secondary palate) is repaired at 6 to 18 months of age using the Von Langenbeck repair, in which bipedicle mucoperiosteal flaps are raised by longitudinal incisions along the inner aspect of each alveolar arch, based superiorly on the greater palatine vessels, and rotated medially to close the palatal defect.
questions.question:
A male neonate is noted at birth to have a gap in the upper lip on the left side extending up to the nostril, with associated defect in the alveolus and hard palate anterior to the incisive foramen.
(i) State the diagnosis and classify it precisely using the anatomical classification.
(ii) Describe the embryological basis of this condition and identify the specific processes whose failure of fusion produces the lateral variety.
(iii) State the three criteria (Millard's Rule of 10) that must be met before operative repair.
(iv) Describe the surgical repair of the lip component, naming the technique used.
(v) State when the palate component should be repaired and name the procedure used.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Bouginage (urethral dilatation) is the first-line treatment for urethral stricture; urethroplasty is embarked upon when bouginage cannot be used or fails to give lasting relief of obstructive symptoms. It is indicated for: urethral strictures from traumatic injury (e.g. fractured pelvis); some forms of hypospadias. Anatomical basis for limitation to short strictures: in excision and end-to-end anastomosis, the excised segment creates a gap; when the gap is short, the urethral ends can be approximated without tension; when the gap is long, tension at the suture line increases, causing suture breakdown and stricture recurrence. Therefore excision and anastomosis is suitable only for short strictures resulting from trauma (minimal suture-line tension).

A(ii) Anterior urethra: bulbar and pendulous (penile) segments, accessible in the perineum and along the penile shaft. Posterior urethra: prostatomembranous segment, deep in the pelvis. Safe site for scrotal flap (Orandi/Blandy procedure): the inverted U-shaped flap is raised from the scrotum, which provides good-quality, well-vascularised skin in the perineum; the scrotal skin is brought up to cover the posterior urethral stricture defect. Quatey's vascularised penile skin flap: the penile shaft skin is non-hair-bearing or sparsely hair-bearing; blood supply is maintained via a pedicle of subcutaneous tissue; therefore the graft is viable (vascularised rather than free) and produces little or no hair growth in the neourethra — reducing the risk of hair ball and calculus formation which complicates hair-bearing grafts.

B(i) Named procedures:
Anterior urethra:
- Swinney's procedure (two-stage): stage 1 — laying open the stricture end to end; stage 2 (after healing) — buried full-thickness skin graft reconstitutes the urethra.
- Island skin implantation (single-stage): strip of skin on a pedicle of subcutaneous tissue used as buried viable graft; Quatey's vascularised penile skin flap can also be used; advantage — single operation.
- Free skin graft/meshed skin graft: shorter operating time with comparable results; advantage — meshing allows the graft to cover a larger area with smaller donor skin; no requirement to raise a pedicle reduces operating time.
Posterior urethra:
- Quatey's vascularised skin flap: high graft take; little or no hair growth.
- Inverted U-shaped scrotal flap — Orandi/Blandy (two-stage): stage 1 — stricture exposed, flap of scrotal skin sewn into defect; stage 2 — full-thickness skin tube formed.

B(ii) Complications of urethroplasty: infections; haematoma; urethrocutaneous fistula; re-stenosis; hair ball formation if graft from hair-bearing skin; calculus (usually composed of hair); carcinoma of the urethra.
Urethrocutaneous fistula: when the skin graft or anastomosis breaks down due to infection, haematoma, or excessive tension, urine escapes through the defect to the skin surface, forming a fistulous tract.
Carcinoma of the urethra: chronic inflammation from recurrent strictures, infections, and the reparative process associated with multiple procedures predisposes to malignant transformation of the urethral epithelium; this is a recognised long-term complication of chronic urethral disease and repeated urethroplasty.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the indication for urethroplasty versus bouginage/urethral dilatation — state when dilatation cannot be used or fails — and explain the anatomical basis for why excision and end-to-end anastomosis is limited to short strictures.
A(ii) Describe the origin and course of the anterior and posterior urethral segments relevant to urethroplasty, state the safe site for performing the scrotal flap procedures, and explain the anatomical basis for why Quatey's vascularised penile skin flap provides superior graft take with little or no hair growth.
B(i) Describe all named surgeons and their specific operations for both anterior and posterior urethroplasty — number of stages, tissue used, and outcome advantage for each — and explain why the free skin graft/meshed skin graft offers a shorter operating time.
B(ii) Enumerate all complications of urethroplasty, explain the mechanism of urethrocutaneous fistula formation, and describe the long-term risk of carcinoma of the urethra in the context of chronic urethral disease.

A 30-year-old man presents to the plastic surgery clinic with gradual darkening and slight increase in size of a pigmented mole on his forearm over the past two months. The lesion has also started weeping and shows variegated pigmentation with satellite lesions around it.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis, and name the four types based on growth pattern.
(ii) State the risk factors (epidemiological and predisposing lesions) for this condition.
(iii) Describe the pathological staging systems used to classify depth of invasion, naming the two systems and their key levels or thresholds.
(iv) Describe the definitive surgical and non-surgical treatment options.
questions.answerText:
(i) The most likely diagnosis is malignant melanoma. The four growth pattern types are: lentigo maligna melanoma; superficial spreading melanoma; nodular melanoma; and acrolentiginous melanoma.
(ii) Risk factors include: uncommon before puberty, incidence increases with age; intermittent exposure to sunlight before age 20, classically affecting skin type I; immunosuppression; dysplastic naevi; giant naevi; and other congenital naevi. Precursors include dysplastic naevus and melanoma in situ. Malignant melanoma arises either as a change in a pre-existing naevus or de novo.
(iii) Two pathological staging systems are used:
- Breslow's classification: Thin = less than 0.76 mm depth; Moderate = intermediate; Thick = greater than 1.5 mm depth.
- Clarke's levels: Level I = confined to epidermis; Level II = invades papillary dermis; Level III = fills papillary/reticular dermis junction; Level IV = invades reticular dermis; Level V = extends below dermis (into subcutaneous fat).
(iv) Definitive treatment includes: excision with a reasonable margin, often plus skin graft for the donor defect; ray digital amputation only when the digit is involved; immunotherapy using recombinant alpha interferon, tumour infiltrating lymphocytes (TILS), and monoclonal antibodies combined with cytotoxic drugs; chemotherapy with dacarbazine (DTIC) or melphalan (limb perfusion technique); and radiotherapy. A metastatic survey (history, biopsy of suspicious lesions, CXR, chest CT, liver function tests, abdominal ultrasound and CT, brain CT/MRI, nuclear bone scan) is performed to assess extent of disease.

A(i) Arthritis denotes inflammation of the synovial joint. The synovium of the affected joint produces: increase in new vessel formation and redness (causing warmth); increased vascular permeability with leakage of fluid from new vessels causing joint swelling/effusion. Common types in Nigerian environment: septic arthritis (common in children with immune impairment from malnutrition); calcium deposition arthritic diseases (e.g. gout); inflammatory arthritides (e.g. psoriatic arthritis with joint and skin lesion); rheumatoid arthritis (autoimmune synovial hyperplasia and pannus); endocrine-related arthritis (DM, hypothyroidism, obesity); osteoarthritis (commonest type).
A(ii) Rheumatoid arthritis: it is an autoimmune lesion causing synovial hyperplasia; the hyperplastic synovium encroaches on the articular cartilage; this process is called pannus (creeping substitution); pannus destroys the articular cartilage; articular cartilage loss initiates the arthritic condition. It is part of a more generalised rheumatoid disease.
B(i) Calcium deposition arthritic diseases: commonest type in Nigeria is gouty arthritis, characterised by accumulation of uric acid in the synovium triggering an inflammatory response. Predisposing factors: red meat and wine have been incriminated. It is uncommon in the low socio-economic group — it is a disease of the affluent in society.
B(ii) Cervical spondylosis: occupation — secretaries/typists, computer operators, lecturers/teachers; qualifies as 'repetitive strain injury'. Presentations: unexplained shoulder pain radiating to arm and forearm; paraesthesia in fingers; 'dropped' thumbs (weak thumb and poor grip); dizziness (basilar artery insufficiency); occipital headache; neck stiffness. Lumbar spondylosis: occupation — linked to type of job (physical loading). Presentations: low back pain; limitation of spine movements especially extension; occasional sciatic pain radiating to legs; neurogenic claudication in severe cases (due to spinal canal stenosis).
questions.question:
Regarding types of arthritis and their pathological basis:

A(i) Describe what arthritis means anatomically, state what the synovium of an affected joint produces in inflammation, and list the common types of arthritis encountered in the Nigerian environment with their distinguishing features.
A(ii) Describe the pathological process in rheumatoid arthritis from synovial hyperplasia through pannus formation to articular cartilage loss.
B(i) Describe calcium deposition arthritic diseases, including the commonest type in Nigeria, its predisposing factors, and why it is considered a disease of the affluent.
B(ii) Distinguish between cervical spondylosis and lumbar spondylosis under the headings: occupation-related cause, clinical presentation, and neurological complications.

A(i) Describe the anatomical basis of the Brown-Séquard syndrome, naming the spinal cord tracts interrupted and explaining why the motor and sensory deficits are distributed as they are.
A(ii) Describe the anatomical basis and clinical features of the Anterior Cord Syndrome and the Posterior Cord Syndrome.
B(i) Name all the Spinal Cord Injury Syndromes, and state the anatomical level that distinguishes the Conus Medullaris syndrome from the Cauda Equina syndrome.
B(ii) Explain what is meant by the terms complete spinal cord injury and incomplete spinal cord injury, and state the anatomical structures whose injury must be assessed at the spinal level.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Brown-Séquard syndrome results from a hemicord lesion. The deficit pattern is:
- Ipsilateral upper motor neuron (UMN) paralysis — interruption of ipsilateral corticospinal tract
- Ipsilateral dorsal column deficit (loss of vibration and proprioception) — interruption of ipsilateral dorsal columns
- Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation — interruption of contralateral spinothalamic tract (which has already crossed)
- Except for a few dermatomes where there may be ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature.
A(ii) Anterior Cord Syndrome: loss of pain and temperature sense below the lesion (spinothalamic tract damage); damage to LMN of ventral horn; larger lesions may also affect corticospinal tracts. Posterior Cord Syndrome: loss of vibration and proprioception; large lesions can also damage corticospinal tracts.
B(i) Listed syndromes: neurologically intact; nerve root injury; complete spinal cord injury; incomplete spinal cord injury; anterior cord syndrome; central cord syndrome; posterior cord syndrome; Brown-Séquard syndrome; conus medullaris syndrome; cauda equina syndrome. Conus medullaris and cauda equina syndromes are distinguished primarily by their anatomical level of injury: conus medullaris syndrome results from injury to the terminal spinal cord, while cauda equina syndrome results from injury to the lumbosacral nerve roots below it.
B(ii) Complete spinal cord injury: all sensory and motor pathways are partially or completely interrupted (transverse cord lesion); dermatomes affected give the level of localisation. The structures whose injury must be assessed include: the cord, conus medullaris, cauda equina, nerve roots, and supporting elements — bone, ligament, and disc.

A(i) Fracture defined as loss of continuity in the substance of a bone. Classification of closed fractures by pattern: transverse; oblique; spiral; comminuted; segmental; greenstick fracture (in children). All may be displaced or undisplaced. Two main groups: closed fracture (traumatic or pathological) and open fracture.
A(ii) Gustillo and Anderson classification: Type I — laceration 2 cm or less, fracture not comminuted. Type II — laceration >2 cm <5 cm, fracture not comminuted. Type III — laceration >5 cm or fracture comminuted: Type IIIA — no tissue defect after wound debridement; Type IIIB — need soft tissue cover after debridement; Type IIIC — associated vascular injury requiring repair.
B(i) Conservative management: closed reduction of fracture; holding the reduction using: plaster of Paris; skin traction; skeletal traction. Operative fixation: involves exposure of fracture and accurate reduction, then stabilisation using: Kirschner wire (especially in children); plate and screws; intramedullary nail (in long bones); external fixator.
B(ii) In children, radius and ulna fractures are commonly greenstick; may have displacement and angulation but are most commonly treated conservatively (manipulation and POP application); regular weekly X-ray for 2 weeks essential; plaster removed between 3 and 6 weeks. In adults, fractures are commonly displaced with associated angulation AND rotational deformity; manipulation and POP application are usually not satisfactory because rotational deformity cannot be corrected conservatively; open reduction is essential to correct the rotational deformity; plate and screw fixation commonly used.
questions.question:
Regarding the classification and management of fractures:

A(i) Define a fracture and describe the full classification of closed fractures by pattern (morphology), distinguishing displaced from undisplaced types.
A(ii) Describe the full Gustillo and Anderson classification of open fractures with defining criteria for each type and subtype.
B(i) Describe all conservative management techniques for fractures (closed reduction and holding methods), and all operative fixation options with the indications for each.
B(ii) Explain the clinical basis for why fractures of the radius and ulna in adults require open reduction and internal fixation, while in children conservative management is usually satisfactory.

A 4-year-old girl is brought to the paediatric surgery clinic with a 3-month history of progressive abdominal swelling. On examination she has a large, firm, non-tender right-sided abdominal mass that does not cross the midline. She also has aniridia noted on eye examination.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the embryological/pathological origin of this tumour?
(ii) What associated anomalies and syndromes are linked to this condition, and what genetic feature do they share?
(iii) How would you investigate this patient, and what staging system is used?
(iv) Outline the multimodal treatment approach, including the surgical steps for tumour excision.
(v) What factors determine prognosis in this condition?
questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: Nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumour). It is the 2nd most common intra-abdominal tumour in childhood. It arises from a pathological precursor — primitive blastema/metanephric tissue/nephrogenic rest — found in 30–40% of patients with Wilms' tumour.
(ii) Associated anomalies and syndromes: Aniridia (1%), hemihypertrophy (3%), Beckwith–Wiedemann Syndrome (EMG), WAGR Syndrome (WT, aniridia, genitourinary anomaly, mental retardation), Denys–Drash Syndrome (male pseudohermaphroditism, diffuse glomerular disease, WT — 50–90% develop WT), hypospadias, undescended testis, Simpson-Golabi-Behemel Syndrome (macroglossia, visceromegaly, coarse facial features), Perlman's Syndrome (fetal gigantism, renal hamartomas, nephroblastomatosis). These are linked to hereditary WT involving a prezygotic event.
(iii) Investigations: abdominal USS, IVU, echocardiography, contrast-enhanced CT scan, CXR. Staging: Stage I — tumour confined to kidney and completely excised; Stage II — extends beyond capsule but completely excised; Stage III — extends beyond capsule with incomplete excision; Stage IV — distant metastasis to lungs, liver, bone and brain; Stage V — bilateral renal involvement.
(iv) Multimodal multidisciplinary approach: Surgery (nephrectomy) — expose, observe and palpate contralateral kidney, expose the hilum and ligate renal vessels to reduce tumour spread, low ligation of ureter to reduce urothelial tumour extension, LN sampling for staging, incomplete excision — biopsy and mark with a clip. Chemotherapy: Vincristine, Doxorubicin, Actinomycin D, Etoposide, Cyclophosphamide (NWTSG 5 Guideline, varies with patient's age, stage, tumour weight and histology). Radiotherapy is also used.
(v) Prognostic factors: Histologic type — favourable histology (FH); DNA index — worse with aneuploidy; gene expression — expression of high levels of tyrosine kinase receptor increases mortality; high levels of hyaluronan, bFGF and VEGF — worse prognosis.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man from a high TB-prevalence area presents with colicky abdominal pain, borborygmi, vomiting, and a right iliac fossa mass. He has a history of pulmonary TB.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis and specify the intestinal subtype that produces a multinodular mass through abundant inflammatory response.
(ii) State the most common complication of intestinal TB requiring clinical intervention, and name the two anatomical mechanisms by which it arises.
(iii) Describe the route by which the organism reaches the distal ileum and caecum, naming the organism in the majority of cases and the reason this region is most commonly affected.
(iv) Describe the peritoneal TB pathology type ('wet type') and the 'fibro-adhesive/plastic type', listing the key pathological findings for each.
(v) Name three less common intestinal forms of abdominal TB (beyond the ulcerative and hypertrophic types).
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: abdominal tuberculosis, intestinal type.
- The hypertrophic form, produced by abundant inflammatory response, results in a multinodular mass.

(ii) Most common complication:
- Bowel obstruction is the most common complication of intestinal TB.
- Two anatomical mechanisms: hyperplastic mural thickening and stricture formation; or due to adhesions (the plastic type causing bowel obstruction through fibrous adhesions matting bowel loops).

(iii) Route of infection and reason for site predilection:
- Primary route: swallowed sputum (ingested organism).
- Secondary routes: lympho-haematogenous spread from miliary or primary TB infection; direct spread from adjacent organs (rare).
- Organism: the majority are caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis; rarely Mycobacterium bovis.
- Reason for distal ileum and caecum predilection (90%): this region has the most well-developed lymphoid follicles (Peyer's patches), facilitating bacterial penetration and infection of submucosal lymphoid tissue.

(iv) Pathological types of peritoneal TB:
- Wet type: (1) large amount of viscous ascitic fluid — diffuse or loculated ascites; (2) whitish miliary nodules less than 5 mm.
- Fibro-adhesive (dry or plastic) type: (1) caseous nodules (cheesy yellow); (2) fibrous peritoneal reaction; (3) dense adhesions.

(v) Three less common intestinal forms:
- Tuberculous strictures: usually in the caecum and distal small gut, caused by shrinkage of a tuberculous ileocaecal mass to form a fibrous constriction.
- Tuberculous ulcers: can occur anywhere in the gut, most often in the ileum, caecum, rectum, or sigmoid colon; can cause diarrhoea; may perforate or bleed.
- Tuberculous fistulae: form occasionally.

questions.question:
Describe the following aspects of childhood lymphoma.
A(i) Classify childhood lymphomas by type and frequency, and name the subtypes of Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.
A(ii) Describe the epidemiology and aetiology of Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL) including conditions that increase its incidence.
B(i) Describe the biological behaviour and pattern of spread in NHL compared to Hodgkin's lymphoma.
B(ii) Describe Burkitt's lymphoma — including incidence, sex ratio, common primary sites, cytogenetics and form.
C(i) Describe the investigations and staging of childhood lymphoma.
C(ii) State the principles of treatment for childhood lymphoma and the factors determining favourable versus unfavourable prognosis in Hodgkin's disease.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Classification: Hodgkin's (40%); Non-Hodgkin's (60%) — subtypes: Burkitt's lymphoma (40–50%); lymphoblastic lymphoma (30–40%); large cell lymphoma (<15%) — immunoblastic (50%), anaplastic (50%).
A(ii) NHL epidemiology and aetiology: 6% of childhood cancers; 60% of childhood lymphomas; peak age 5–15; M:F ratio of 2.5:1. Conditions increasing incidence: SCID, HIV, EBV; post T-cell depleted BMT; post solid organ transplant. Factors: geographic, viral, genetic and immunologic factors.
B(i) NHL: malignant solid tumour of immune system; undifferentiated lymphoid cells; spread is aggressive, diffuse, unpredictable; involves lymphoid tissue, BM and CNS infiltration; high growth fraction and doubling time; requires rapid diagnosis and treatment; rapid chemotherapy response but tumour lysis is a concern. Hodgkin's disease: immune system malignancy involving B or T lymphocytes; Reed-Sternberg cells; spread is slow, predictable, with extension to contiguous lymph nodes; infiltration to non-lymphoid organs is rare.
B(ii) Burkitt's lymphoma: 100 new cases per year; M:F ratio of 2–3:1; mean age 11 years (in non-endemic form); most common primary site — intra-abdominal (sporadic) or jaw (endemic); cytogenetics: t(8;14) in 90%; also t(8;2) or t(8;22).
C(i) Investigations: full blood count, abdominal USS, lymph node biopsy, bone marrow aspiration/biopsy, lumbar puncture, CT scan, PET scan, bone scan. Staging (Murphy/Ann Arbor): Stage I — tumour at one site (nodal or extranodal); Stage II — two or more sites, same side of body (or resectable); Stage III — both sides of body but not Stage IV (and unresectable GI and mediastinal for NHL); Stage IV — CNS or marrow involvement for NHL (Murphy), or lung, liver, marrow, or bone for Ann Arbor.
C(ii) Treatment: chemotherapy, radiotherapy, surgery. Favourable prognosis: age <10, female, favourable subtypes (LP and NS), Stage I non-bulky disease. Unfavourable prognosis: persistently elevated ESR; lymphocyte depletion histopathology; bulky disease (largest dimension >10 cm); B symptoms.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department following a high-speed road traffic accident. He is in shock (BP <80 mmHg), has flank bruising, and is passing macroscopic haematuria. There is abdominal distension and loss of bowel sounds.

(i) State the classification of this patient's most likely urological injury and identify whether it is minor or major, giving the full classification of each category.
(ii) Identify the pathological basis for each category of injury and the investigations indicated, specifying when CT scan, IVU, and radionuclide studies are each appropriate.
(iii) Outline the full resuscitation protocol and management of blunt renal injuries, including the percentages that require surgery and nephrectomy.
(iv) State the definitive management of penetrating renal injuries and justify the approach.
questions.answerText:
(i) Classification of renal injuries: Blunt (>90%) — most common; Penetrating — less common.
Minor renal injuries: simple laceration, subcapsular haematoma, renal contusion.
Major renal injuries: renal rupture, laceration of renal artery and vein, perinephric haematoma, laceration through collecting system.
For purpose of triage: blunt injuries — most common, over 90%, may not need immediate exploration; <5% are major. Penetrating injuries — less common, usually require immediate exploration; >70% are major.

(ii) Pathological basis: blunt force causes contusion, subcapsular haematoma, or laceration depending on force; major blunt injuries disrupt the renal capsule and collecting system; penetrating injuries (missiles) directly lacerate renal parenchyma and vessels. Investigations: CT scan with/without contrast enhancement — indicated for: history of shock (BP <80 mmHg), history of microscopic haematuria plus shock, history of deceleration injury, abdominal distension/masses/flank mass, loss of bowel sounds, suspected bowel or other visceral injury, WBC >20,000/ml. When no CT scan: KUB film, inject contrast for IVU, obtain post-evacuation bladder film. IVU may miss minimal extravasation; serious renal injury may be present in the absence of shock. Radionuclide studies (99Tc-labelled DTPA, DMSA or Mag3): may show extravasation, pre-existing hydronephrosis, differential renal functions; usually not available and should not delay diagnosis.

(iii) Resuscitation: adequate airways and ventilation; vascular access and volume replacement; control of bleeders; catheter urine drainage; nasogastric drainage. History: details of injury (e.g. fall from height); history of shock (BP <80 mmHg); haematuria and urethral bleeding; history of voiding post-injury; in unconscious patient, history from witnesses. Examination: abdomen for distension, masses, bruises on flank; check for fractured ribs.
Management of blunt renal injuries: 85% of blunt renal injuries require no surgery; 5–10% will require surgery; 5% will require nephrectomy.

(iv) All penetrating renal injuries must be explored with very few exceptions. The rationale is that >70% of penetrating injuries are major, meaning they involve significant disruption of renal vasculature or collecting system that cannot be safely managed conservatively; immediate exploration allows control of haemorrhage, repair or nephrectomy as indicated.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, course, and type of neural pathways involved in penile erection — including the specific parasympathetic efferent and somatosensory afferent pathways, naming the conditions that disrupt each and the resulting clinical deficit.
A(ii) Describe the role of nitric oxide (NO) and cyclic GMP (cGMP) in the molecular mechanism of smooth muscle relaxation in the corpus cavernosum, specifying the sequence of molecular events from cavernous nerve stimulation to erection.
B(i) Describe the relationship between the endocrine axis — testosterone, hypothalamus, and nitric oxide synthase — and erectile function; state which endocrine conditions can cause ED and what percentage of ED is attributable to endocrine causes.
B(ii) State the safe diagnostic test for arteriogenic ED and for venogenic ED, and explain the anatomical basis for why arteriogenic ED in an older patient may indicate generalised atherosclerosis including coronary artery disease.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Neural pathways in penile erection:
Parasympathetic efferent pathway: arises from the parasympathetic efferent neural pathways in the sacral spinal cord; travels via the cavernous nerve (pelvic plexus) to the corpus cavernosum and helicine arteries. Disruption causes efferent neuropathy; conditions: spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, radical prostatectomy, peripheral neuropathy, other neurological diseases (e.g. Parkinson's disease).
Somatosensory afferent pathway (dorsal nerve impotence): transmits sensory stimuli from the penis centrally; disrupted by polysensory neuropathies secondary to diabetes, vitamin B12 deficiency, and lead poisoning.
Both types result in failure of the parasympathetic-mediated smooth muscle relaxation required for erection.

A(ii) Molecular mechanism:
- Sexual stimulation activates the cavernous nerve and endothelial cells.
- Nitric oxide (NO) is released.
- NO activates guanylate cyclase.
- Guanylate cyclase converts GTP to cGMP.
- cGMP activates cGMP-specific protein kinase.
- This leads to decreased intracellular Ca²⁺.
- Smooth muscle relaxation results.
- Erection occurs through lacunar engorgement.
- PDE5 degrades cGMP to 5'GMP, terminating the erection.

B(i) Testosterone acts centrally at the hypothalamus and peripherally by regulating nitric oxide synthase. Endocrine conditions causing ED: hypogonadism, hyperprolactinaemia, hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism. Endocrine factors account for 3–6% of all cases of ED. Many men with hypogonadism may have concomitant vasculogenic ED. ED is inversely correlated with serum DHEA-S (adrenal androgen precursor) and HDL.

B(ii) Arteriogenic ED: diagnosed by penile duplex ultrasound. Venogenic (cavernosal) ED: diagnosed by cavernosometry and cavernosography. In older patients, arteriogenic ED may be a component of generalised atherosclerosis; the penile arteries are small-calibre end-arteries, so atherosclerosis affecting the systemic vasculature (including the internal pudendal, internal iliac, and aortoiliac vessels) manifests first as impaired penile blood flow before larger vessel disease becomes clinically apparent; therefore arteriogenic ED may be the presenting feature of coronary artery disease, making cardiovascular evaluation essential.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset severe right iliac fossa pain, nausea, vomiting, and a low-grade fever (37.8°C). She has a flushed face, furred tongue, and rebound tenderness at McBurney's point. On PR examination there is right-sided pelvic tenderness.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the pathological basis for the condition?
(ii) List all the important differential diagnoses that must be considered in this patient.
(iii) What investigations should be requested, and what findings are expected?
(iv) What is the essential management, including options for both straightforward and complicated presentations?
(v) What complications may arise from the primary condition and from its treatment?
questions.answerText:
(i) Acute appendicitis: inflammation of the vermiform appendix. Pathological basis: either 'obstructive' — infection superimposed on luminal obstruction from any cause; or 'phlegmonous' — viral infection, lymphoid hyperplasia, ulceration, bacterial invasion without obvious cause.
(ii) Differential diagnoses:
- Pelvic: ovarian cyst, pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy, ruptured corpus luteum cyst, UTI.
- Gastrointestinal: mesenteric lymphadenitis (commonest in children), Crohn's disease, cholecystitis, perforated duodenal ulcer.
- Other: renal colic, pyelonephritis, right basal pneumonia, diabetes mellitus.
- Elderly: perforated caecal carcinoma, sigmoid diverticulitis.
(iii) Investigations:
- WCC: almost always leucocytosis; CRP: usually raised.
- Ultrasound: for appendix mass; excludes ovarian pathology.
- Laparoscopy: commonly used to exclude ovarian pathology in young women prior to appendicectomy.
- CT scan (helical): in elderly patients or where other causes are possible.
(iv) Management:
- Acute appendicitis: appendicectomy, open or laparoscopic.
- Appendix mass: IV fluids, antibiotics, close observation. If symptoms resolve — interval appendicectomy after a few months. If symptoms progress — urgent appendicectomy ± drainage.
(v) Complications: wound infection; intra-abdominal abscess (pelvic, RIF, subphrenic); adhesions; portal pyaemia; abdominal actinomycosis (rare).

(i) Erectile dysfunction (ED): the inability to achieve and/or maintain an erection adequate for satisfactory sexual performance; also referred to as erectile difficulty and impotence.

(ii) Predisposing factors and aetiological categories:
- Vasculogenic (arteriogenic): risk factors include diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, smoking, pelvic irradiation/trauma; in older patients it may be a component of generalised atherosclerosis including coronary artery disease; diagnosed by penile duplex ultrasound.
- Vasculogenic (venogenic/cavernosal): results from inadequate compression of subtunical venules due to smooth muscle dysfunction/atrophy and corporal fibrosis; same risk factors as arteriogenic ED plus Peyronie's disease; diagnosed by cavernosometry and cavernosography.
- Neurogenic (efferent neuropathy): disruption of parasympathetic efferent neural pathways; causes include spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, radical prostatectomy, peripheral neuropathy, Parkinson's disease. Afferent (somatosensory) neuropathy ("dorsal nerve impotence"): caused by polysensory neuropathies from diabetes, vitamin B12 deficiency, lead poisoning.
- Drug-related: antihypertensives — thiazide diuretics, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors; antidepressants — tricyclics, SSRIs; antiarrhythmics (digoxin); antiandrogens; H2 receptor antagonists (cimetidine); recreational agents — cigarette smoking, cocaine, marijuana.
- Psychogenic: direct inhibition of spinal centres, excessive sympathetic outflow; conditions include anxiety, depression, OCD, sexual phobias, stress.
- Endocrinological (3–6% of all cases): hypogonadism, hyperprolactinaemia, hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism; testosterone acts centrally (hypothalamus) and peripherally (nitric oxide synthase regulation); many men with hypogonadism also have concomitant vasculogenic ED.
ED is directly correlated with age, CAD, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, and smoking; inversely correlated with serum DHEA-S and HDL.

(iii) Cascade of penile erection: sexual stimulation → increased parasympathetic activity → relaxation of trabecular smooth muscle → decreased peripheral resistance → increased blood flow in cavernous and helicine arteries → increased intracavernous pressure → lacunar engorgement and penile erection. Role of NO and cGMP: cavernous nerve and endothelial cells release nitric oxide → activates guanylate cyclase → converts GTP to cGMP → cGMP-specific protein kinase activated → decreased Ca²⁺ → smooth muscle relaxation → erection. PDE5 degrades cGMP to 5'GMP, terminating erection.

(iv) Diagnostic approach (stepwise):
Step 1: Routine and recommended testing — comprehensive sexual, medical, drug, and psychosocial history; focused physical examination; recommended tests: testosterone (total, free or bioavailable), fasting glucose and serum lipids.
Step 2: Shared decision — physician-patient dialogue, patient/partner education, identification of preferences; alter modifiable risk factors and causes.
Step 3: Specialised testing if ED unresolved — nocturnal penile tumescence or vascular studies.
Step 4: Specialist treatment if still unresolved.
Treatment modalities (in order): sexual education and counselling; alter modifiable risk factors; oral agents; local therapies — intracavernosal injections, intraurethral PGE1, vacuum device; surgical treatments (implant).
questions.question:
A 55-year-old man with a background of hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents with a 2-year history of inability to achieve and/or maintain an erection adequate for satisfactory sexual performance. He smokes and takes thiazide diuretics and a beta-blocker for his hypertension.

(i) State the diagnosis and define it precisely as provided.
(ii) List all predisposing factors and aetiological categories applicable to this patient, including the specific mechanisms for each category as described.
(iii) Explain the normal physiological cascade of penile erection, including the role of nitric oxide and cGMP.
(iv) Outline the stepwise diagnostic approach and all treatment modalities in the order they are applied.

A 19-year-old female at 28 weeks gestation is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. She has abdominal tenderness, and her blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg.
(i) What is the most common blunt injury specific to the gravid abdomen, and what is the most common fetal injury in blunt trauma?
(ii) Describe the anatomical and physiological changes in pregnancy that affect the assessment of haemodynamic status.
(iii) How should this patient be packaged and positioned, and what is the reason for this?
(iv) What criteria guide the timing of perimortem caesarean section, and what is the 4-minute rule?
(v) What laboratory and monitoring investigations are indicated for fetal assessment?
questions.answerText:
(i) Abruptio placenta is the most common blunt injury to the gravid abdomen. This is because the placenta is devoid of elastic tissue while the myometrium is very elastic, predisposing to shearing forces. Fetal skull fractures are the most common fetal injury in blunt trauma.
(ii) Physiological changes affecting haemodynamic assessment: Pulse increases by 10–15 beats/minute; BP decreases by 10–15 mmHg from baseline; total blood volume increases by 45–50%. Up to 20% acute and 30–35% gradual blood loss may show no sign of instability. Therefore, normal vital signs in pregnancy must not be mistaken for absence of shock. The patient can lose 30% of blood volume before having a significant change in BP. May not have abdominal tenderness early even with significant bleeding.
(iii) Positioning: Transport with full spinal packaging. Tilt the backboard 20–30 degrees to the left. This is because the enlarging uterus can compress the inferior vena cava when the mother is in the supine position, reducing venous return and cardiac output by up to 30%. This supine hypotension syndrome is more likely after the 20th week of pregnancy.
(iv) Perimortem caesarean section: Less than 28 weeks gestation — survival chance is 0%. Maternal CPR greater than 20 minutes — fetal survival unlikely. Maternal CPR less than 5 minutes — fetal survival excellent. The 4-minute rule: maternal CPR for 4 minutes; the infant should be delivered by the 5th minute.
(v) Laboratory and monitoring investigations: Routine tests; Serum bicarbonate level; Kleihauer-Betke test to check for fetal cells in fetomaternal blood mixing — important in Rh-negative women who need Rhogam (300 micrograms). Cardiotocographic monitoring: fetal heart rate (normal 120–160), beat-to-beat variability, baseline variability, decelerations especially late, and uterine activity. If less than 1 contraction per 10 minutes for 4 hours, risk of complications drops to baseline; if greater, there is a 20% risk of placental abruption.

questions.question:
Describe gallstone disease under the following headings:
(i) Composition and types of gallstones, with their relative frequencies and predisposing factors for each type.
(ii) Pathogenesis of cholesterol stones, pigment (bilirubinate) stones, and mixed stones.
(iii) The full clinical spectrum: describe each clinical presentation, from biliary colic to obstructive jaundice, including differential diagnoses for each.
(iv) Role and findings of each key investigation.
(v) Essential management for each clinical presentation (asymptomatic stones, biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, empyema, cholangitis, obstructive jaundice).
questions.answerText:
(i) Types and frequencies:
- Cholesterol (20%): solitaire or mulberry; crystalline structure; predisposed by diabetes mellitus, pregnancy, diet, genetics.
- Pigment/bile pigment (5%): predisposed by haematological disease, Crohn's disease; commoner in the East.
- Mixed (75%): faceted; concentric structure; associated with anatomical abnormalities, stasis, previous surgery, previous infections.
(ii) Pathogenesis:
- Cholesterol stones: imbalance in bile between cholesterol, bile salts, and phospholipids, producing lithogenic bile; associated with inflammatory bowel disease.
- Bilirubinate stones: chronic haemolysis; infection with α-glucuronidase-producing bacteria.
- Mixed stones: anatomical abnormalities, stasis, previous surgery, previous infections.
(iii) Clinical presentations:
- 90% of gallstones probably asymptomatic.
- Biliary colic: severe colicky upper abdominal pain radiating around the right costal margin ± vomiting; periodicity of hours, often onset at night; spontaneously resolves. Differential: MI, peptic ulcer, GORD.
- Chronic cholecystitis: vague, intermittent right upper abdominal pain, distension, flatulence, fatty food intolerance. Differential: chronic PUD, GORD.
- Acute obstructive cholecystitis: constant right hypochondrial pain, pyrexia, nausea ± jaundice; positive Murphy's sign; leucocytosis. Differential: MI, basal pneumonia, pancreatitis, appendicitis, perforated peptic ulcer, pulmonary embolus.
- Cholangitis (Charcot's triad): abdominal pain, high fever/rigors, obstructive jaundice. Differential: MI, basal pneumonia, pancreatitis, acute hepatitis.
- Obstructive jaundice: upper abdominal pain, pale/claylike stools, dark brown urine, pruritus.
- Pancreatitis: central/epigastric pain, back pain, fever, tachycardia, epigastric tenderness.
(iv) Investigations:
- Plain X-ray: shows only 10% of gallstones.
- Ultrasound: detects 90%; assesses CBD size and CBD stones.
- ERCP: for suspected or proven CBD stones; allows stone removal or stent placement.
- OGD: to exclude PUD.
(v) Management:
- Asymptomatic: no treatment unless diabetic or on major immunosuppression.
- Biliary colic: elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
- Chronic cholecystitis: elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy only if no evidence of PUD.
- Acute cholecystitis: IV fluids, antibiotics, early or interval cholecystectomy.
- Empyema: percutaneous ultrasound/CT-guided drainage and interval cholecystectomy.
- Cholangitis: IV fluids, antibiotics, ductal drainage (usually ERCP, sphincterotomy, stone extraction).
- Obstructive jaundice: ERCP + stent insertion or percutaneous transhepatic stent.

(i) Definitions:
- Complete obstruction: total blockage of the intestinal lumen.
- Incomplete obstruction: only a partial blockage.
- Simple (mechanical): blood supply is not compromised.
- Strangulated: blood supply is compromised.
- Closed-loop obstruction: both the inlet and outlet of a bowel loop are closed off.
(ii) Causes:
- Extramural: adhesions, bands, volvulus, hernias (internal and external), compression by tumour.
- Intramural: inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease), tumours, carcinomas, lymphomas, strictures, paralytic (adynamic) ileus, intussusception.
- Intraluminal: faecal impaction, foreign bodies, bezoars, gallstone ileus.
(iii) Pathophysiology: bowel distal to obstruction collapses. Bowel proximal distends and becomes hyperactive; distension due to swallowed air and accumulating secretions. The bowel wall becomes oedematous; fluid and electrolytes accumulate in the wall and lumen (third-space loss). Bacteria proliferate in the obstructed bowel. As the bowel distends, intramural vessels become stretched, blood supply is compromised, leading to ischaemia and necrosis.
(iv) Small vs. large bowel obstruction:
- Small bowel: rapid onset; commonly due to adhesions or hernias; central loops; non-anatomical distribution; valvulae conniventes shadows cross entire width of lumen.
- Large bowel: gradual or intermittent onset; often due to carcinoma or strictures; NEVER due to adhesions; peripheral distribution; haustral shadows do not cross entire width of bowel.
(v) Essential management:
- Decompress obstructed gut: pass nasogastric tube.
- Replace fluid and electrolyte losses: Ringer's lactate or NaCl with K+ supplementation.
- Monitor patient: fluid balance, urinary catheter, regular TPR, blood tests.
- Surgical relief if: underlying causes need surgery (hernia, colonic carcinoma); patient does not improve with conservative treatment; signs of strangulation or peritonitis.
questions.question:
Describe the anatomy and pathology of intestinal obstruction under the following headings:
(i) Definitions: complete versus incomplete; simple versus strangulated; closed-loop obstruction.
(ii) Enumerate all causes, classifying them as extramural, intramural, and intraluminal.
(iii) Pathophysiology of intestinal obstruction from initial distension through to ischaemia.
(iv) Differences between small bowel and large bowel obstruction in onset, common causes, and radiological appearance.
(v) Essential management steps, and indications for surgical intervention.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Two groups: Group 1 — substances providing energy for metabolism: CHO, fats, proteins. Group 2 — substances incorporated in the synthesis of tissues: proteins, vitamins, electrolytes, trace elements.
A(ii) Basal nutritional requirements per kilogram: energy — 125–145 Joules/kg; protein — 0.7–1.0 g/kg; CHO — 4.2–6 g/kg; fat — 1.5–2 g/kg; H2O — 45–50 ml/kg (tropics), 30–35 ml/kg (temperate). Daily caloric needs: adult male — 1,800–2,000 cals/24h at bed rest (up to 2,500 with minimal activity); adult female — 15–20% less; infants and children — calories and water requirements are greater.
B(i) CHO metabolism: obligate users of glucose — brain and nervous tissues (120g/day); RBC, renal tubules, fibroblasts, neutrophils, monocytes (40g/day). Minimum glucose requirement: 160g/day.
B(ii) Protein metabolism: 10–11 kg of protein in a 70 kg man. Daily turnover: 250–300g or 3%, mainly in the gut. Proteolysis adds 50–70g to the amino acid pool. Only 25g of ingested amino acid is added to the pool; the rest of ingested amino acid is broken down as energy. The rest of the amino acid pool is produced endogenously.
C(i) Fat metabolism: 70–75% of energy expenditure comes from fat. Mainly as ketones manufactured in the liver from long-chain fatty acids. Also a source of essential fatty acids which are precursors of prostaglandins.
C(ii) Insulin: decreases muscle protein degradation, increases synthesis, increases glucose utilisation — anabolic. Glucocorticoids: increases degradation, decreases synthesis, decreases glucose utilisation — catabolic. Cytokines: increases degradation, decreases synthesis, decreases glucose utilisation — catabolic. IGF-1: decreases degradation, increases synthesis, increases glucose utilisation — anabolic. Growth hormone: no effect on degradation, increases synthesis, decreases glucose utilisation — anabolic. Thyroid hormone: increases degradation, increases synthesis, increases glucose utilisation — anabolic. Leucine: decreases degradation, increases synthesis, decreases glucose utilisation — anabolic. Fasting: increases degradation, decreases synthesis, decreases glucose utilisation — catabolic. Protein deficiency: decreases degradation, decreases synthesis, unknown effect on glucose utilisation — catabolic.
questions.question:
Describe the nutritional metabolism in surgical patients under the following headings.
A(i) State the two groups of nutritional elements and give examples of each.
A(ii) State the basal nutritional requirements per kilogram and the daily caloric needs for adults, infants and children.
B(i) Describe carbohydrate (CHO) metabolism — the obligate users of glucose, their daily requirements and the minimum daily glucose requirement.
B(ii) Describe protein metabolism — total body protein content, daily turnover, the amino acid pool and its sources.
C(i) Describe fat metabolism — the percentage of energy derived from fat, the form in which it is transported and its role as a precursor.
C(ii) Using the hormonal table, describe the roles of insulin, glucocorticoids, cytokines, IGF-1, growth hormone and thyroid hormone on muscle protein degradation, synthesis, glucose utilisation and overall effect on growth.

questions.answerText:
(i) Composition:
- Calcium oxalate: 60% — spiky, hard, discoloured by blood.
- Triple phosphate (calcium, ammonium, and magnesium phosphate): 30%+ — large 'staghorn'; soft, chalky.
- Uric acid: 5% — some pale yellow/brown, hard.
- Cystine: 1%.
(ii) Pathogenesis:
- Hypercalciuria: 65% of patients have idiopathic hypercalciuria.
- Nucleation theory: a crystal or foreign body acts as a nucleus for crystallisation of supersaturated urine.
- Stone matrix theory: a protein matrix secreted by renal tubular cells acts as a scaffold for crystallisation.
- Reduced inhibition theory: reduced urinary levels of naturally occurring inhibitors of crystallisation.
- Dehydration.
- Infection: staghorn triple phosphate calculi formed by the action of urease-producing organisms (Proteus, Klebsiella), which produce ammonia and render the urine alkaline. Schistosomiasis predisposes to bladder calculi.
(iii) Clinical presentations:
- Calyceal stones: may be asymptomatic.
- Staghorn calculi: loin pain; upper-tract UTI; recurring pyelonephritis; renal parenchymal damage.
- Ureteric colic: severe colicky pain radiating from the loin to the groin and into the testes or labia; associated gross or microscopic haematuria.
- Bladder calculi: sudden interruption of urinary stream; perineal pain; pain at the tip of the penis; haematuria; frequency.
(iv) Investigations:
- FBC, U+E, serum creatinine, calcium, phosphate, urate, proteins, alkaline phosphatase.
- Urine microscopy: haematuria and crystals.
- Plain abdominal X-ray: 90% of renal calculi are radio-opaque.
- IVU: confirms presence and identifies position of stone.
- Renogram: for staghorn calculi to assess renal function.
- 24-hour urine collection; stone analysis.
(v) Management:
- Conservative: pain relief (pethidine, diclofenac); high fluid intake; 80% of ureteric stones pass spontaneously; stones <4 mm almost always pass; stones >6 mm almost never pass.
- Non-operative: ESWL for small/medium kidney stones and upper ureteric stones; percutaneous nephrolithotomy for large kidney stones and staghorn calculi; ureteroscopy/contact lithotripsy or Dormia basket extraction for lower ureteric stones; mechanical lithotripsy for bladder stones.
- Open surgery: ureterolithotomy or nephrolithotomy (rarely required).
questions.question:
Describe renal calculi under the following headings:
(i) Composition of the main stone types and their relative frequencies.
(ii) Pathogenesis: enumerate all theories for stone formation, and explain how infective (triple phosphate) stones form.
(iii) Clinical presentations of calculi at different sites (calyceal, staghorn, ureteric, vesico-ureteric, and bladder).
(iv) Key investigations and the proportion of stones detectable on plain X-ray.
(v) Essential management: conservative, non-operative interventional procedures (ESWL, ureteroscopy, percutaneous nephrolithotomy), and indications for open surgery.

Regarding fat embolism as a complication of fractures:

A(i) Describe the pathogenesis of fat embolism, stating the conditions in which it typically occurs.
A(ii) Describe the full clinical presentation, diagnostic criteria, and the investigations required, including arterial blood gas findings and ECG changes.
B(i) State the differential diagnoses of fat embolism.
B(ii) Outline the complete treatment protocol for fat embolism and the principles of prevention.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Pathogenesis: fat released into the circulation gets deposited at the lungs, resulting in respiratory insufficiency. Typically occurs in: multiple long bone fractures; intramedullary nailing procedures.
A(ii) Clinical presentation: 98% manifest within 48 hours and 100% within 72 hours. Within 12 hours, 25% show symptoms: restlessness, incoherence, disorientation, tachycardia, tachypnoea, petechial haemorrhages (seen in light-skinned people, front and back), and cerebral hypoxia. Diagnosis: high index of suspicion required; deterioration in cerebral function. Investigations: ABG shows severe hypoxia (PO2 < 60 mmHg) and hypercapnia (PCO2 very high); examination of clotted blood shows fat globules; urine shows fat globules; ECG shows right ventricular strain.
B(i) Differential diagnoses: adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS); pulmonary thromboembolism.
B(ii) Treatment: transfer to Intensive Care Unit or High Dependence Unit (HDU); correct anaemia; assisted ventilation; heparinisation (to cause lipolysis); fluid resuscitation; Dextran (to improve capillary flow); Clofibrate (to reduce plasma lipids). Prevention: gentle fracture manipulation; early stabilization of fractures.

questions.question:
Describe the role of the surgical pathologist, the classification of biopsies, and the principles of specimen handling in surgical pathology.

A(i) Define surgical pathology and state the role of the surgical pathologist; explain why he is described as bridging the gap between the beginning and end stages of disease.
A(ii) State what information must be on the surgical pathology request card and explain the consequences of incomplete communication.
B(i) Classify biopsies according to the instrument used; state which type is least suitable for microscopic interpretation and why; describe the fixative of choice, its concentration, and the volume ratio relative to the specimen.
B(ii) State the qualities of a good surgical pathology report and explain the professional and medicolegal obligations regarding disposal of specimens.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Surgical pathology is the arm of pathology that deals with examination of both gross and histological sections of specimens from living patients to arrive at accurate diagnoses that will assist in patient management. The mainstay is examination after fixation in formalin, embedding in paraffin, and staining with Haematoxylin-Eosin. The surgical pathologist does the gross description, microscopic description, and interpretation. He bridges the gap between the beginning of a disease process and its end stages — he can correlate initial stages of disease in surgical pathology specimens with management and contribute to the body of knowledge. He is able to correlate clinical findings with pathological changes and offer advice on the biopsy received.

A(ii) The request card should be filled by a clinician familiar with the case and must contain: all facts bearing on the case; the type of biopsy (incisional or excisional) and method of obtaining it (Trucut, transrectal, transurethral etc.); if the patient has had a previous biopsy with a histological report, it should accompany the specimen; proper identification of margins (e.g. proximal and distal for intestinal biopsies; margins for soft tissue tumours). Incomplete communication between clinician and pathologist may make diagnosis difficult or impossible.

B(i) Biopsy types by instrument: cold knife, cautery, needle, or endoscopic. The type least suitable for microscopic interpretation is that obtained with a cautery, because this instrument chars and distorts the tissue and prevents proper staining. Fixative of choice: formalin; the sample should be fixed in 10% formalin, which should be nine times the volume of the specimen.

B(ii) The surgical pathology report is an important medical document that should describe as thoroughly and concisely as possible all relevant gross and microscopic features and interpret the significance for the clinician. Delivery should be prompt and timely. The mature surgical pathologist must be able to offer clinical differential diagnoses from microscopic findings and record prognostically significant data. Medicolegal obligation: all surgical biopsy specimens should be sent to the surgical pathology laboratory; discarding specimens in the trash can claiming the lesion to be insignificant amounts to professional negligence.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old man presents after a road traffic accident. On examination, a segment of the right chest wall moves inward during inspiration and outward during expiration. He is cyanosed, in respiratory distress, and in shock. Crepitus is palpable over the lateral chest wall. CXR confirms rib fractures with an underlying pulmonary contusion.

(i) State the diagnosis and give its precise definition.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiological mechanism — including mediastinal flutter and pendeluft — that produces the clinical picture.
(iii) Describe the full treatment of this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Flail chest. Definition: segmental fracture of at least 3 contiguous ribs producing a free-floating, unstable segment of the chest wall. It may be unilateral segmental fracture or bilateral on either side of the sternum. The segment moves inwards with inspiration and outwards with expiration — paradoxical movement.

(ii) The mediastinum moves from one side to the other — mediastinal flutter — impairing venous return. Air moves from one lung/lobe into the other — pendeluft. The overall effect is severe dyspnoea, cyanosis, shock, and respiratory distress.

(iii) Treatment: adequate analgesia — continuous epidural analgesia (gold standard), rib blocks, opioids; ETT with ventilation (PEEP or CPAP) in severe cases for internal pneumatic stabilization; pulmonary toileting; CTTD in haemothorax or pneumothorax; 100% oxygen; fluid restriction; effective physiotherapy; regular sputum cultures as basis for antibiotic therapy; strap flail segment with sandbag or lie on flail side; rib fixation (now replaced by PEEP).

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man is brought to the A&E following a road traffic accident. He is in severe respiratory distress with hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation to the left, absent breath sounds on the right, and hyperresonant percussion on the right side. There is no time for a chest X-ray.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) Explain the pathophysiological mechanism that produces this clinical picture.
(iii) What is the immediate resuscitative intervention and how is it performed?
(iv) What is the definitive treatment for this condition?
questions.answerText:
(i) Tension pneumothorax.

(ii) A flutter valve effect from damaged alveoli allows air to enter the pleural cavity during inspiration but no exit occurs during expiration. Pressure builds up in the pleural cavity, compressing the vena cavae and causing mediastinal shift to the opposite side with angulation at the cavo-atrial junction, reducing venous return and poor diastolic filling, leading to decreased cardiac output and circulatory collapse. Contralateral lung compression also causes parenchymal collapse, poor ventilation, and progressively severe hypoxia — collectively producing obstructive shock.

(iii) Needle thoracostomy: insert a size 14–16G cannula at the 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line; a gush of air after insertion confirms the diagnosis. This is reserved for cases presenting with shock, deviated trachea, distended neck veins, and decreased breath sounds.

(iv) Definitive treatment is chest tube thoracostomy drainage (CTTD), which is definitive in most cases.

(i) SIRS: a systemic inflammatory response characterised by two or more of the following:
- Hyperthermia >38°C or hypothermia <36°C.
- Tachycardia >90 bpm.
- Tachypnoea >20 r.p.m. or PaCO2 <4.3 kPa.
- Neutrophilia >12 × 10⁻⁹ l⁻¹ or neutropenia <4 × 10⁻⁹ l⁻¹.
(ii) Sepsis syndrome: SIRS with proven infection. Septic shock: sepsis with systemic shock. MODS: derangement of physiology such that organ function cannot maintain homeostasis; common terminal pathways include vasodilatation, capillary leak, intravascular coagulation, and endothelial cell activation.
(iii) Common surgical causes: acute pancreatitis; perforated viscus with peritonitis; fulminant colitis; multiple trauma; massive blood transfusion; aspiration pneumonia; ischaemia-reperfusion injury.
(iv) Mediators:
- TNFα: released by and activates macrophages and neutrophils; cytotoxic to endothelial and parenchymal cells.
- LPS (from Gram −ve bacteria): activates macrophages via LPS binding protein and CD14 receptors.
- IL-6 and IL-1β: cause endothelial cell activation and damage; promote complement and chemokine release.
- PAF: implicated in acute pancreatitis.
- iNOS: synthesised by activated endothelial cells; potent negative inotrope.
(v) Mortality: SIRS 7%; sepsis syndrome 14%; established septic shock 40%.
questions.question:
Describe the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) under the following headings:
(i) Definition: list all diagnostic criteria that must be present.
(ii) Definitions of sepsis syndrome, septic shock, and MODS.
(iii) Common surgical causes of SIRS.
(iv) The principal cellular and molecular mediators involved in its pathogenesis and their roles.
(v) The overall mortality rates associated with SIRS, sepsis syndrome, and septic shock.

A 22-year-old male from a road traffic accident has a grossly deformed and shortened right leg with external rotation, high energy impact mechanism, tense thigh swelling, and GCS of 14. He is haemodynamically unstable.
(i) Using the vignette findings, identify all likely injuries and determine the initial management priority according to ATLS principles as described.
(ii) What imaging should be obtained, and what anatomical structures must be evaluated?
(iii) Describe the trimodal distribution of trauma deaths and explain which peaks are preventable and how.
(iv) What are the urgent needs of the severely injured patient?
questions.answerText:
(i) Likely injuries: femoral fracture (deformed, shortened, externally rotated leg); possible head injury (GCS 14); haemorrhagic shock (haemodynamic instability). The 0.5–1 litre of blood lost into the thigh haematoma contributes to hypovolaemia. Initial management priority: ABC of resuscitation — Airway (with C-spine protection), Breathing, Circulation. Address haemodynamic instability first. 50% of severely injured patients suffer injury to the head (the most frequently injured single part of the body); 50% suffer injury to limbs; 20% to the chest; 10% to the abdomen; 5% to the spine.
(ii) Imaging and structures to evaluate: Chest X-ray; C-spine X-ray; Pelvis X-ray — these are important investigations that may be done during primary survey. Evaluate for: head injury (CT brain); femoral fracture (plain X-ray of femur); neurovascular status of the limb (distal pulse assessment; active and passive movements; limb alignment and deformities).
(iii) Trimodal distribution of trauma deaths — found in 862 trauma deaths: First peak — immediately at the site, in transit, and in A&E; due to laceration of brain, spinal cord, heart, or major blood vessel; most are not preventable. Second peak — within the first few hours; due to major internal bleeding; preventable with enhanced care. Third peak — days or weeks later; due to infection and multiple organ failure; preventable with appropriate initial care. Second and third peaks can be improved by enhanced care along the therapeutic chain.
(iv) Urgent needs of the severely injured: Establish a reliable airway; Restore the mechanics of breathing; Resuscitate the cardiovascular system; Neurological protection.
