A(i) Epidemiology and significance:
- 30,000–35,000 cases of aneurysmal SAH per year in the US.
- 10–15 million Americans harbour cerebral aneurysms; 1–2% of adults have cerebral aneurysms.
- Risk of haemorrhage from an unruptured aneurysm: 1–3% per year.
- Death or permanent disability occurs in 25–50% of patients with aneurysmal SAH.
- Risk of rehemorrhage: 20% over the next 2–3 weeks; 50% over the next 6 months; rebleeds are nearly always fatal.
- Main goal of treatment: prevent rebleed.
A(ii) Presenting symptoms: explosive or thunderclap headache — "worst headache of my life"; frequently with nausea and vomiting; decreased level of consciousness or coma; signs of meningeal irritation (nuchal rigidity, photophobia) may develop after several hours.
Sentinel haemorrhage: 40% of major SAHs are preceded by a sentinel (warning) haemorrhage of lesser intensity. A high index of suspicion for SAH must be maintained in a patient presenting with an uncharacteristic headache.
B(i) Normal vessel wall: adventitia; tunica media; internal elastic lamina; intima; endothelial cells (differs from extracranial vessels).
Aneurysmal wall: intima; fragmented internal elastic lamina; adventitia — the media is absent or deficient.
Congenital predisposing factors: medial defect; elastic defects; sites of origin of small vessels; failure of involution.
Acquired/risk factors: hypertension; atherosclerosis; contraceptive pill; substance abuse (cigarette smoking, alcohol, cocaine).
B(ii) Neurological deficit by haemorrhage site:
- Basal ganglia/internal capsule: hemiparesis; dysphasia.
- Cerebellum: ataxia; vertigo.
- Pons: cranial nerve deficits; coma.
- Cerebral cortex: hemiparesis; hemisensory loss; hemianopsia; dysphasia (depending on site within cortex).
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the epidemiology and clinical significance of aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, including annual incidence in the USA, prevalence of cerebral aneurysms, annual risk of rupture from an unruptured aneurysm, risk of rehemorrhage, and overall outcome statistics.
A(ii) Describe the presenting symptoms of aneurysmal SAH in full, including the significance of a sentinel haemorrhage and what index of suspicion this requires.
B(i) Describe the gross pathology of a cerebral aneurysm — contrasting the normal vessel wall with the aneurysmal wall — and the congenital and acquired factors that predispose to aneurysm formation.
B(ii) Describe the neurological deficit pattern after intracerebral haemorrhage based on the anatomical site of haemorrhage, naming the deficit for each of the four sites.

Describe the principles of radiation oncology relevant to surgical practice.

A(i) Define radiation oncology. Classify the types of ionising radiation used in treatment and state the units of radiation measurement.
A(ii) Describe the mechanism of cell kill by radiation (both direct and indirect pathways) and explain why adequate haemoglobin is important during radiotherapy.
B(i) Classify the modalities of cancer therapy, the types of radiotherapy (teletherapy vs brachytherapy), and the timing categories of radiotherapy.
B(ii) List the side effects of radiotherapy; state the emergency indications for radiotherapy; and list the four causes of cell injury.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Radiation oncology is a scientific and clinical discipline devoted to the management of patients with malignancies and other diseases through the use of ionising radiation alone or in combination with other modalities. Types of ionising radiation: photons (X-rays, gamma rays e.g. Cobalt-60); atomic particles (electrons, protons, neutrons — electrons are most useful). Sources: decay of radioactive substances (gamma, beta, alpha); artificial production (X-rays); naturally occurring (uranium, radium); artificial isotopes (iridium-192, cobalt-60, iodine-131). Units: Gray (Gy) — absorbed dose; Sievert (Sv) — environmental radiation; Becquerel (Bq) — nuclear medicine.

A(ii) Direct effect: radiation acts directly on DNA. Indirect effect: radiation causes hydrolysis of water, forming free radicals toxic to DNA. Reaction: H2O leads to H2O+ and e-; H2O+ leads to H2 and OH*; free radicals combine with molecular oxygen to form peroxides: 2OH* + O2 = H2O2 + H+. The indirect effect is more important. Adequate PCV is important because the indirect effect depends on oxygen; treatment in wet areas including open normal wounds leads to increased effects of radiation.

B(i) Modalities of cancer therapy: (a) surgery, (b) radiotherapy, (c) chemotherapy; others include gene therapy, hormonal therapy, and immunotherapy; over 60% of cancer patients will require radiotherapy. Types of radiotherapy: teletherapy (radiation source at a distance to the patient); brachytherapy (source close to the lesion; uses inverse square law). Timing: adjuvant, neoadjuvant, radical, concurrent radiotherapy (with chemotherapy). Intention: curative or palliative.

B(ii) Side effects: mostly inflammatory reaction on treatment fields limited to the region treated; radiation effects differ with cell radiosensitivity; teratogenesis; carcinogenesis. Emergency indications: haemostasis, spinal metastasis, severe lytic bone lesions, severe intractable pain, cerebral disease. Causes of cell injury: chemicals, infection, radiation, vibration.

A(i) Definition: inadequate thyroid hormone production and/or availability in peripheral target tissues. Primary: lack of thyroid hormone production from the gland itself — aetiology: iodine deficiency (mostly in developing nations), auto-immunity and iatrogenic following thyroidectomy or radio-iodine therapy (in developed nations). Secondary: inadequate TSH secretion from the pituitary gland. Tertiary: lack of TRH production from the hypothalamus.
A(ii) Clinical presentation: cold intolerance, fatigue, puffiness, weight gain, hair loss, dry skin, myxoedema, altered mental status, coma, bradycardia, electrolyte disorders, hypothermia, cardiomegaly, pericardial effusion, ascites, shock.
B(i) Investigations and findings: thyroid function tests — raised TSH, decreased T3, decreased T4; pituitary hormone assay; brain MRI.
B(ii) Complications: myxoedema coma. Treatment: L-thyroxine; thyroidectomy in selected cases. Follow-up: intermittent thyroid function tests, at least once every 3 months.
C(i) Hyperthyroidism: raised T3, raised T4, decreased TSH; female preponderance F:M ratio of 8:1; treatment: anti-thyroid drugs, thyroidectomy (subtotal or total), radioactive iodine therapy. Hypothyroidism: raised TSH, decreased T3, decreased T4; common disorder worldwide; treatment: L-thyroxine. Both are commoner in females than males.
C(ii) Solitary thyroid nodule on radio-isotope scan: hot — autonomous toxic nodule (functioning); warm — normally functioning nodule; cold — non-functioning nodule, 20% of which are malignant, especially in children and the elderly. Aetiology of solitary nodule: thyroid adenomas, thyroid cyst, papillary thyroid carcinoma, solitary palpable nodule in a multinodular goitre.
questions.question:
Describe the condition of hypothyroidism under the following headings.
A(i) Define hypothyroidism and classify its types (primary, secondary, tertiary) with the corresponding aetiology for each type.
A(ii) Describe the full clinical presentation of hypothyroidism.
B(i) State the investigations and their expected findings in hypothyroidism.
B(ii) Describe the complications and treatment, including follow-up.
C(i) Compare hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism in terms of TFT results, female preponderance, and treatment approach.
C(ii) Explain how solitary thyroid nodule is classified on radio-isotope scan and what the malignancy risk of each type is.

Describe the gross pathophysiology and clinical manifestations of haemoglobinopathies from a surgical perspective.

A(i) Define haemoglobinopathy, state the molecular defect in sickle cell disease (HbSS) and HbC, and describe the mode of inheritance.
A(ii) Explain the pathogenesis of a sickle cell crisis, listing the precipitating factors.
B(i) Describe the clinical manifestations of sickle cell disease across the liver, spleen, gastrointestinal tract, genitourinary, skin, and cardiorespiratory systems.
B(ii) Outline the general management principles for sickle cell disease in a surgical patient.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Haemoglobinopathies are genetically inherited disorders of the haemoglobin molecule. HbA has four subunits, which are a combination of a haem group and a globin molecule. In HbS, glutamic acid is replaced by valine in the 6th position of the B-chain; this reduces solubility and results in deformation of red cells to sickle shape. Sickle cell gene is inherited as autosomal recessive. HbC is similarly a substitution of glutamic acid by lysine in the same position. Sickle cell disease (SCD) is the inheritance of two haemoglobinopathic genes. Sickle cell anaemia results from two S genes (HbSS). Sickle cell trait is a combination of one HbS and a normal (HbA) gene.

A(ii) Pathogenesis of crisis: Decreased oxygen tension leads to sickling, then stasis, then cellular injury, then reduced circulatory volume, then increased viscosity, then further decreased oxygen tension (a vicious cycle). Precipitating factors: malaria, diarrhoea, respiratory infections, other infections, extreme temperatures, transfusion reactions, emotional reactions, physical stress.

B(i) Liver: necrosis, obstructive jaundice, cholelithiasis. Spleen: splenic atrophy, hypersplenism, splenic sequestration. GIT: intestinal infarction, adynamic ileus, peritonism. Genitourinary: hyposthenuria, haematuria, priapism. Skin: leg ulcers, subcutaneous fibrosis, possible malignant transformation. Cardiorespiratory: pneumonia, thrombosis, fat embolism, right ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary hypertension. Central nervous system: cerebral ischaemia. Ocular: retinal haemorrhage, retinal detachment, glaucoma, deteriorating vision, blindness. Bone and joints: avascular necrosis, osteoporosis (cod-fish), osteomyelitis.

B(ii) General management: analgesia; volume expansion; alkaline infusion; oxygen therapy. Regarding anaesthesia: avoid tourniquet.

questions.question:
Describe the classification of suture materials, the properties of an ideal suture, and the principles of suture selection.

A(i) List the properties of an ideal suture material.
A(ii) Distinguish between monofilament and multifilament sutures on the following properties: memory, tissue drag, wicking, knot security, and tissue reaction.
B(i) Classify suture materials as absorbable versus non-absorbable and natural versus synthetic; name at least three examples in each absorbable and non-absorbable category with a key feature of each.
B(ii) Describe suture sizing including the direction of the sizing scale and two specific examples; state the general rule for knot security (number of throws) and the exception for stainless steel.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Properties of an ideal suture: can be used in any tissue; easy to handle; good knot security; minimal tissue reaction; unfriendly to bacteria; strong yet small; will not tear through tissues; cheap.

A(ii) Properties compared:
- Memory: monofilament has more memory; multifilament is easier to handle.
- Tissue drag: monofilament has less tissue drag; multifilament has more tissue drag.
- Wicking/bacteria: monofilament does not wick; multifilament wicks and can harbour bacteria.
- Knot security: monofilament has poor knot security; multifilament has good knot security.
- Tissue reaction: monofilament causes less tissue reaction; multifilament causes more tissue reaction.

B(i) Absorbable sutures:
- Gut/Chromic gut: natural, multifilament; made of submucosa of small intestines; broken down by phagocytosis; plain lasts 3–5 days, chromic lasts 10–15 days.
- Vicryl (Polyglactin 910): braided, synthetic, absorbable; stronger than gut; broken down by enzymes; can be used in contaminated wounds.
- PDS (polydioxine): monofilament, synthetic; very good tensile strength lasting months; absorbed completely by 182 days.
Non-absorbable sutures:
- Nylon: synthetic, mono or multifilament; very little tissue reaction; poor knot security.
- Polypropylene (Prolene): monofilament, synthetic; will not lose tensile strength over time; very little tissue reaction.
- Stainless Steel: monofilament; strongest; great knot security; very little tissue reaction.

B(ii) Suture sizing: sizes run from #5 (largest) down through 0, 00 (2-0), 000 (3-0) and beyond — bigger to smaller. Small animals: 0 through 3-0. Large animals: 0 through 3. Stainless steel sized in gauges: smaller gauge = bigger, stronger (e.g. 26 gauge = 'ought'; 28 gauge = 2-0). Knot security: generally 4 throws for >90% knot security (nylon may need 5); stainless steel is an exception — 2 throws = 99% knot security.

questions.question:
Describe the pathophysiology and management of oedema and fluid homeostasis under the following headings.
A(i) Describe the body's fluid compartments, their proportions and composition.
A(ii) Define normal fluid homeostasis and state the conditions on which it depends.
B(i) Explain how inflammation causes oedema (the inflammatory category), distinguishing it from the other categories.
B(ii) Describe the clinical consequences of subcutaneous oedema and pulmonary oedema in terms of organ disease associations.
C(i) Describe the macroscopic and microscopic features of chronic hepatic congestion, including the 'nutmeg liver' appearance.
C(ii) Distinguish between petechiae and purpura in terms of size, associations and mechanisms, and explain the colour sequence of bruise resolution.
questions.answerText:
A(i) 60% of lean body weight is water. Three major fluid compartments: intracellular fluid (ICF) — fluid within cells (cytosol), constitutes 2/3 of body water; extracellular fluid (ECF) — fluid outside cells; comprising interstitial fluid (fluid surrounding cells) and plasma (fluid compartment of blood, 5% of body weight).
A(ii) Normal fluid homeostasis: maintaining blood as a liquid until such time as injury necessitates clot formation. Depends on: maintenance of vessel wall integrity; intravascular pressure; osmolarity within certain physiologic ranges.
B(i) Inflammatory oedema: Acute inflammation, chronic inflammation, and angiogenesis all cause oedema. Inflammatory oedema is due to increased vascular permeability — it is an exudate (protein-rich). This distinguishes it from other categories: increased hydrostatic pressure (venous obstruction, heart failure) and reduced plasma osmotic pressure (hypoproteinaemia) produce transudate (protein-poor); lymphatic obstruction is structural; sodium retention is a renal/hormonal mechanism.
B(ii) Subcutaneous oedema: indicates potential underlying cardiac or renal disease; can impair wound healing and when significant affects clearance of infection. Pulmonary oedema: commonly seen in left ventricular failure, renal failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and pulmonary inflammation or infection.
C(i) Chronic hepatic congestion: central areas are red and slightly depressed compared to the surrounding tan viable parenchyma, forming a 'nutmeg liver' pattern (so called because it resembles the cut surface of a nutmeg). Microscopic: centrilobular necrosis with degenerating hepatocytes and haemorrhage.
C(ii) Petechiae: minute 1–2 mm diameter skin lesions; associated with locally increased intravascular pressure, low platelet count, defective platelet function or clotting defects. Purpura: >3 mm; associated with the same disorders as petechiae, may also be due to trauma, vascular inflammation or increased vascular fragility. Bruise colour sequence: red (swollen, tender) 0–2 days; bluish-red/red-purple 2–5 days; green 5–7 days; yellow 7–10 days; brown 10–14 days; no further bruising 2–4 weeks. Mechanism: erythrocytes get degraded and phagocytosed by macrophages; haemoglobin (red-blue) is converted to bilirubin (blue-green).

questions.question:
A 5-month-old female infant presents with a 5-day history of high-grade intermittent fever, 4-day history of progressive abdominal distension, passage of scanty mucoid bloody stools, and bilious vomiting. Complementary feeding had been introduced one week prior to onset. Examination shows an acutely ill, febrile, pale child; she is tachypnoeic (rate 60/min) with a heart rate of 158/min; the abdomen is distended and soft, with tympanitic percussion notes and hypoactive bowel sounds; rectal examination reveals an empty rectum with the examining finger stained by mucoid brownish stool.

(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) State the predisposing and risk factors for this condition in these cases.
(iii) What complications arise from delayed presentation, and how does vascular compromise progress?
(iv) Outline the operative management performed in this case and the indications for surgical intervention.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Intestinal obstruction from intussusception (specifically ileocolic intussusception in this case).

(ii) Predisposing and risk factors:
- Recent dietary change (complementary feeding introduced one week before onset)
- Acute coryza
- Seasonal variation (peak in summer and mid winter)
- Rotavirus vaccine
- Familial predisposition
- Pathological lead points (in enteroenteral type): Meckel's diverticulum, enlarged mesenteric lymph node, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, coagulation dyscrasias, lymphomas, polyps, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome hamartomas

(iii) Vascular compromise progression:
- Invagination of mesentery causes intestinal obstruction
- Impedance of lymphatic return → rise in intussusceptal intramural pressure
- Rise in hydrostatic pressure → impedance of venous return
- Obstruction of arterial inflow → infarction
- Mucosa is most sensitive to ischaemia
- Transmural gangrene → perforation
- Delayed diagnosis increases mortality and need for bowel resection

(iv) Operative management and indications:
Intraoperative findings: grossly distended jejunum and ileum, ileocolic intussusception (distal 10 cm of terminal ileum, caecum, appendix and ascending colon), gangrenous intussusceptum and intussuscipiens.
Procedure: Right hemicolectomy and ileotransverse anastomosis.
Indications for surgery: established peritonitis, radiological features of perforation, failure of radiological reduction, prolonged history >24/48 hours, and presence of a lead point.

(i) Definitive procedure: Pull-Through Operation.
Three surgical components:
- Rectosigmoidectomy (resection of the aganglionic bowel)
- Pull-through (bringing the normally ganglionated bowel down)
- Colo-anal anastomosis

(ii) Three types of pull-through operations:
- Swenson's pull-through
- Duhamel's pull-through
- Soave's pull-through
(A fourth option for ultrashort segment: posterior myotomy/myectomy)

(iii) Structures at risk and consequences:
During pelvic dissection for pull-through, the pelvic autonomic nerves (parasympathetic and sympathetic) are at risk. Injury can cause:
- Urinary dysfunction (bladder dysfunction, incontinence)
- Sexual dysfunction
The vas deferens is also at risk; posterolateral dissection must avoid urethral injury. Damage to the pelvic floor musculature can lead to faecal incontinence.

(iv) Initial surgical step: Colostomy (loop or defunctioning).
Reasons: To decompress the obstructed bowel, treat or prevent enterocolitis (the most serious complication of HD, commonly fatal in neonates), allow nutritional optimisation, and permit the bowel to recover and be assessed before definitive pull-through, which is typically performed from 1 year of age.
questions.question:
A male neonate fails to pass meconium within 48 hours of birth. He has progressive abdominal distension, refusal of feeds, and vomiting. Digital rectal examination reveals an empty rectum with dramatic temporary decompression. Barium enema shows a rectosigmoid index of less than 1, and rectal biopsy confirms absence of ganglion cells. He is scheduled for a pull-through operation.

(i) Name the definitive procedure and its three surgical components.
(ii) Name the three types of pull-through operations used for this condition.
(iii) What anatomical structures are at risk during the pelvic dissection, and what are the consequences of their injury?
(iv) What initial surgical step is performed in the neonatal or acute setting before definitive surgery, and why?

questions.answerText:
A(i) Drug of choice for status epilepticus: lorazepam. Advantages over diazepam: less respiratory depression; less need for intubation; much longer anti-epileptic effect (hours vs. minutes for diazepam); absorbed rapidly IM.
A(ii) Lidocaine: 1.5–2 mg/kg IV over two minutes, repeated in five minutes if necessary, with a drip at 3–4 mg/minute. Same drug class as Dilantin (phenytoin); an excellent membrane stabiliser. Described as a "forgotten drug" in the emergency department.
Midazolam: useful in those unresponsive to full loading doses of lorazepam, phenobarbital, and phenytoin. Midazolam bolus: 170–220 mcg/kg followed by maximal infusion rates of 0.9–11 mcg/kg/min.
Fosphenytoin (Cerebyx): a prodrug of phenytoin metabolised in the liver. Advantage: rapid therapeutic level (10 minutes) when rapidly infused; can also be given IM. Cautions/limitations: no difference in cardiac side effects (in fact, more arrhythmias — 8% — must still monitor); more local pruritis and paraesthesias on infusion; cannot slow down infusion if side effects occur because lower serum drug levels result; use with caution in renal failure (large phosphate load); not a first-line drug.
B(i) Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6): for rare patients who are pyridoxine-responsive — generally children or those with isoniazid (INH) overdose. Dose: 100 mg IV if no other measures work. INH overdose: 4 g IV then 1 g IV every 30 minutes until equal to amount of INH ingested; may give IV push if the patient is seizing. For children with INH overdose: 40 mg/kg IV. Most pyridoxine-responsive seizures occur in infants but have rarely been reported in older children.
B(ii) Prolactin levels: may be elevated after a true seizure for 30–60 minutes and support the diagnosis of a seizure if present. EEG: diagnostic but may be negative. Factors that increase EEG diagnostic accuracy: sleep deprivation; use of nasopharyngeal leads. EEG is positive during a seizure; may be negative in the inter-ictal period.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the drug of choice for status epilepticus, including its advantages over diazepam. Also describe the role of lorazepam and its dosing for status epilepticus.
A(ii) Describe the use of lidocaine, midazolam, and fosphenytoin in refractory status epilepticus, including doses, routes, advantages, and specific limitations or cautions for each.
B(i) Describe the role of pyridoxine in seizures and state the specific patient groups in which it should be considered, with dosing.
B(ii) Explain the significance of prolactin levels in seizure diagnosis and state the role of EEG,. State all the factors that increase EEG diagnostic accuracy.

A patient with acute abdominal pain has a plain supine abdominal X-ray showing dilated peripheral bowel loops with thick, widely spaced haustra that do not extend fully across the bowel, containing solid faeces, with a large radius of curvature and a diameter above 5 cm.

(i) State whether these X-ray features indicate small bowel or large bowel obstruction, and list five radiological features that distinguish large bowel from small bowel dilatation on plain X-ray.
(ii) State the most common cause of large bowel obstruction, and what percentage is situated in the sigmoid colon.
(iii) Describe the plain X-ray appearance in Type 1A large bowel obstruction with a competent ileocaecal valve, including the critical caecal diameter above which danger of perforation exists.
(iv) State the plain X-ray signs of sigmoid volvulus.
questions.answerText:
(i) These features indicate large bowel obstruction.
Five distinguishing features (large bowel vs small bowel):
- Valvulae conniventes: absent in large bowel; present in jejunum in small bowel.
- Number of loops: few in large bowel; many in small bowel.
- Distribution of loops: peripheral in large bowel; central in small bowel.
- Haustra: present in large bowel (thick and widely separated, may not extend right across); absent in small bowel.
- Diameter: 5 cm or greater in large bowel; 3–5 cm in small bowel.
- Radius of curvature: large in large bowel; small in small bowel.
- Solid faeces: present in large bowel; absent in small bowel.
(Any five of the above.)

(ii) Most common cause: carcinoma, of which about 60% are situated in the sigmoid colon.

(iii) Type 1A appearance (competent ileocaecal valve):
- Dilated gas-filled colon with its haustral markings and a distended thin-walled caecum but no distension of the small bowel.
- This can lead to a massively distended caecum at higher risk of perforation secondary to ischaemia.
- A transverse caecal diameter of 9 cm has been suggested as the critical point above which the danger of perforation exists.

(iv) Plain X-ray signs of sigmoid volvulus:
- Coffee bean sign / bent inner-tube sign / omega sign (classical omega sign).
- Inverted U-shaped distended loop devoid of haustra (ahaustral).
- Liver or left flank overlap signs.
- Apex of the volvulus above T10.
- Air-fluid ratio greater than 2:1.

(i) Diagnosis: Acute appendicitis.
Anatomical position: The appendix is a colonic appendage, derivative of the midgut, 5–9 cm long, arising from the caecum; it has four layers — mucosa, submucosa (containing lymphoid tissue), muscularis, and serosa. Innervation: visceral and somatic.

(ii) Predisposing factors and aetiological categories:
Peak age: 10–12 years; rare in pre-school age and elderly; life-time appendicectomy risk 7%; affects 1:1,000 children/year.
Obstructive (70–75%): faecolith, carcinoid tumour, colonic tumour, foreign body, parasite
Non-obstructive (25–30%): lymphoid hyperplasia

(iii) Pathophysiology progression:
Obstruction → oedema → vascular and lymphatic congestion → ischaemia → localised gangrene → perforation → localised abscess → generalised peritonitis / appendiceal abscess / appendiceal mass

(iv) Treatment:
- Emergency appendicectomy (immediate surgical removal of the inflamed appendix)
- NPO
- IV fluids
- IV antibiotics
- Interval appendicectomy may be performed when there is an appendiceal mass (allows resolution first)
Post-operative complications:
- Wound infection
- Intra-abdominal abscess
- Haemorrhage
- Adhesive intestinal obstruction
questions.question:
A 10-year-old boy presents with a 24-hour history of anorexia followed by periumbilical pain that has migrated to the right iliac fossa, low-grade fever, nausea, and vomiting (which began after the onset of pain). Examination reveals tenderness at McBurney's point, a positive Rovsing's sign, positive psoas sign, and positive obturator sign.

(i) What is the diagnosis and its anatomical position?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors, and describe the two aetiological categories?
(iii) Describe the full progression of pathophysiology from obstruction to generalised peritonitis.
(iv) Outline the treatment and possible post-operative complications.

questions.answerText:
(A)(i) Erect: reproduces the normal state of the lungs and mediastinum; air rises to the apical region making pneumothorax easy to recognise (in supine film free air lies anteriorly and is difficult to detect); fluid runs downward producing a level at the base with a curved line (meniscus) — in a supine film the fluid accumulates posteriorly, making it difficult to detect and assess the amount; the diaphragms are lower showing more of the lung bases and the heart size can be accurately assessed. PA: easier to clear the scapulae from the lung fields by moving the shoulders forward; less magnification of the heart because the heart lies adjacent to the film.

(A)(ii) Assessment criteria for adequate PA CXR: patient not rotated — anterior ends of clavicles should be equidistant from the spinous processes; film taken on full inspiration — top of right diaphragm should lie below the anterior end of the 6th right rib; ribs should be sloping and not horizontal; scapulae should not overlay the lung fields; spinous processes should be faintly visible through the heart shadow; the whole of the lung fields should be fully included including the costophrenic angles and apices.

(A)(iii) Lung hilae: the left hilum normally lies 0.5–1.5 cm higher than the right; both are of similar density and size with concave borders; composed of pulmonary arteries and veins; normal lymph nodes are not seen. Mediastinum: trachea should be central; subcarinal angle normally 60–70 degrees; heart size should not exceed 14.5–15 cm in diameter in women or 15.5–16 cm in men; CT ratio should not be greater than 50%; the aorta descends just to the left of the spine.

(B) Diaphragms: smooth outline, convex upwards; right dome lies 1–2 cm higher than the left; usually at or below the level of the 10th posterior rib or 6th anterior rib; the costophrenic angle should be acute and clear. Fissures: horizontal fissure normally lies at the level of the 4th anterior rib and runs horizontally to the hilum — separates the anterior segment of the right upper lobe from the middle lobe; oblique fissures usually only seen on lateral CXR; the left fissure is steeper than the right; occasionally an accessory azygos fissure may be visible crossing the right upper lobe, containing the azygos vein.

(C) Expiratory film: taken when the patient has breathed out; helps show bronchial obstruction with air trapping (e.g., inhaled foreign body in a child). Lateral film: not part of standard chest examination; used for further assessment and localisation of abnormalities seen on PA film; earlier detection of small pleural effusions if ultrasound unavailable. Oblique views: helpful in assessing rib lesions and some pneumothoraces.
questions.question:
(A) Describe the chest X-ray assessment under the following headings:
(i) Why the film must be erect and PA — state the reasons for each
(ii) Assessment criteria for a technically adequate PA chest X-ray
(iii) The normal lung hilae and mediastinum on CXR

(B) Describe the normal diaphragms and fissures on CXR, including their position and the significance of their alteration.

(C) Explain the diagnostic difference between an expiratory film and a lateral film, and when oblique views are used.

Describe Crohn's disease under the following headings:
(i) Definition, epidemiology (sex ratio, age group, affected populations), and aetiology (all listed factors).
(ii) Pathological features: macroscopic and histological.
(iii) Clinical presentations: acute, subacute, chronic, and perianal.
(iv) Investigations required and the characteristic findings of each relevant investigation.
(v) Essential surgical indications, the surgical principle applied, and prognosis.
questions.answerText:
(i) Definition: a chronic transmural inflammatory disorder of the alimentary tract.
Epidemiology: male/female 1:1.6; young adults; high incidence among Europeans and Jewish people.
Aetiology: unknown; impaired cell-mediated immunity; genetic link probable but candidate genes unknown; no proven link to mycobacterial infection or measles virus hypersensitivity; smoking associated with recurrence.
(ii) Pathological features:
- Macroscopic: may affect any part of the alimentary tract; skip lesions in bowel; affected bowel wall and mesentery are thickened and oedematous; frequent fistulae; affected bowel characteristically 'fat wrapped'; perianal disease with perianal induration, fissure, sinus, and fistula formation.
- Histological: transmural inflammation in the form of lymphoid aggregates; non-caseating epithelioid cell granulomas with Langhans giant cells; regional nodes may also be involved.
(iii) Clinical presentations:
- Acute (uncommon): RIF peritonitis (like appendicitis); generalised peritonitis (free perforation).
- Subacute (common): RIF inflammatory mass (usually with fistulae or abscess formation); widespread ileal inflammation — general ill health, malnutrition, anaemia, abdominal pain.
- Chronic: strictures (intermittent colicky abdominal pains on eating); malabsorption (widespread disease, previous resections); growth retardation in children.
- Perianal: fissure in ano; fistula in ano; perianal sepsis.
(iv) Investigations:
- FBC: macrocytic anaemia.
- Acute phase proteins (CRP): elevated.
- Small bowel enema: narrowed terminal ileum; 'string sign' of Kantor; stricture formation; fistulae.
- Abdominal ultrasound: RIF mass; abscess formation.
- CT scan: RIF mass; abscess formation.
- Indium-labelled white-cell scan: areas of inflammation.
(v) Surgical indications: complications (peritonitis, obstruction, abscess, fistula); failure of medical treatment; persisting symptoms; growth retardation in children. Principle: resect minimum necessary.
Prognosis: 75% of patients will require surgery; 60% will require more than one operation; life expectancy is little different from the normal population.

questions.question:
Describe the post-operative management of a surgical patient with respect to pain, fluid balance, nutrition, DVT prophylaxis, and wound care.

A(i) State why post-operative pain management is important and list all pharmacological agents and routes used.
A(ii) Describe the maintenance intravenous fluid requirements in the post-operative period, including the minerals required if NPO exceeds 24 hours and the daily volume for an average adult.
B(i) Describe all the methods of DVT prophylaxis.
B(ii) State the post-operative wound care protocol, including the timing of wound inspection and the timing of suture removal for different anatomical regions.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Pain causes post-operative hypertension and shallow breathing; adequate pain management is essential to prevent these complications. Pharmacological agents: opioids are the mainstay of post-operative pain management — intravenous morphine, pethidine, and pentazocine are used. NSAIDs are used as an adjunct. Epidural analgesia and bupivacaine wound infiltration are additional options.

A(ii) Maintenance intravenous fluids: if the patient is NPO, maintenance fluids are given — usually crystalloids containing dextrose. If NPO is more than 24 hours, then maintenance minerals are needed: Na, K, Cl, Ca, HCO3. Average adult should receive about 3 litres in 24 hours. In sepsis, the maintenance fluid requirement is usually more. Hydration levels should be monitored clinically and with urine output.

B(i) DVT prophylaxis methods: early ambulation; TED (thromboembolic deterrent) stockings; limb physiotherapy; heparin; low molecular weight heparin.

B(ii) Post-operative wound care: clean wound — dressing is left until healing has occurred. Generally, the wound is inspected on the 5th day post-operatively. Suture removal timing: abdomen, thorax, and upper limb — 8th post-operative day; head and neck — 4th post-operative day; lower limb — 14th post-operative day.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old motorcyclist is brought in following a road traffic accident. He has a large wound over the right leg with bone visible, extensive soft tissue damage, and the laceration is greater than 5 cm. There is no vascular injury.

(i) Classify this open fracture and state the full Gustillo and Anderson open fracture classification system.
(ii) Describe the surgical procedure required for this fracture, including the choice of fixation device and the management principles for the wound.
(iii) What structures must be examined systematically at the initial assessment of a limb with a suspected fracture?
(iv) What are the advantages of applying a splint prior to definitive fixation, and what are the local complications that may arise from this fracture?
questions.answerText:
(i) This is a Type III B open fracture — laceration >5 cm or fracture comminuted, with need for soft tissue cover after debridement (no tissue defect capable of primary closure, but no vascular injury). Full Gustillo and Anderson classification: Type I — laceration 2 cm or less, fracture not comminuted; Type II — laceration >2 cm <5 cm, fracture not comminuted; Type III — laceration >5 cm or fracture comminuted: Type IIIA — no tissue defect after wound debridement; Type IIIB — need soft tissue cover after debridement; Type IIIC — associated vascular injury requiring repair.
(ii) Surgical procedure: involves exposure of fracture; accurate reduction; wound debridement; soft tissue coverage (Type IIIB). Fixation options: Kirschner wire (especially in children); plate and screws; intramedullary nail (in long bones); external fixator (preferred in open fractures due to wound management needs).
(iii) Systematic examination: skin — look for abrasion, blister, laceration; oedema of soft tissue; integrity of tendons; sensation over limb; vascularization — pulse, warmth, capillary refill; active and passive movement of digits; look for deformity; tenderness over soft tissue and bone; appropriate radiological views (splint limb before X-ray); elevation of the limb.
(iv) Advantages of splint: prevents continuous soft tissue injury; useful in transportation of patient; relief of pain; useful in taking appropriate radiological views. Local complications: skin/subcutaneous tissue injury; tendon/muscle injury; nerve injury (e.g. radial nerve in humeral shaft fracture); vascular injury; bone non-union, delayed union, or infection; compartment syndrome; Volkmann's ischaemic contracture; gas gangrene.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old male motorcyclist is brought in after a high-speed collision. He has a swollen, deformed left thigh, shortened and externally rotated leg, and is unable to bear weight. His pulse is 120 bpm and BP is 90/60 mmHg.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what is the estimated blood loss into the thigh from this injury?
(ii) What are the levels of femoral fracture, and what high-energy mechanisms are responsible?
(iii) Describe the ABC of resuscitation and the treatment options, distinguishing between adult and paediatric management.
(iv) What are the indications for internal fixation of femoral fractures?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis is fracture of the femur. This injury almost always results from high-energy injury. About 0.5–1 litre of blood may be lost into the thigh as a fracture haematoma. This contributes significantly to haemodynamic compromise.
(ii) Levels of fracture: Upper third; Middle third; Lower third; Supracondylar; Intercondylar. High-energy mechanisms: Road traffic accident; Fall from height; Crush injury; Pathological fracture (e.g., due to breast or kidney cancers).
(iii) Initial management: ABC of resuscitation; Trauma care; Conservative management; Surgical fixation. For adults: In advanced countries, all fractures of femur are repaired surgically with closed intramedullary nailing in adults. For children: Treatment is conservative and depends on age.
(iv) Indications for internal fixation: Associated head injury. In the absence of a satisfactory region, intramedullary nailing is not used so that epiphyses would not be damaged and thus prevent normal bone growth — in such cases, plate and screws are used.

questions.question:
A 2-year-old girl is found to have a fixed flexion deformity of her right thumb that has been present since infancy. The thumb is locked in flexion at the interphalangeal joint and cannot be fully extended. Her parents report the condition is also present in the left thumb.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State whether this condition tends to recover spontaneously if present beyond one year of age.
(iii) Describe the definitive surgical treatment, naming the specific anatomical structure released.
(iv) State the radio-ulnar synostosis: where the fusion is located, what functional deformity results, whether surgery is always indicated, and what procedure is performed when both limbs are affected.
(v) State the aetiology and associated conditions of the constriction ring syndrome, and describe the surgical treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is trigger thumb (stenosing tenosynovitis of the thumb), presenting as fixed flexion deformity of the thumb, often bilateral.
(ii) If trigger thumb is present beyond one year of age, it rarely recovers spontaneously. Surgery is therefore indicated.
(iii) The definitive surgical treatment is release of the A1 pulley, which is located at the base of the tendon sheath (the first annular pulley at the mouth of the flexor tendon sheath in the thumb).
(iv) Radio-ulnar synostosis: the fusion is located at the proximal one-third of the forearm. The functional deformity is fixed forearm pronation. It is autosomal dominant (AD) and bilateral in 60% of cases. Treatment: when unilateral or mild, it is left alone. When bilateral, a rotational osteotomy is performed in one forearm to place it in a functional position.
(v) Constriction ring syndrome (CRS), also called Streeter's syndrome, has an incidence of 1 in 15,000 live births. The aetiology is unclear and it is not genetic. CRS frequently affects both arms and all four limbs and is commonly associated with clubfoot. It is not genetic in origin. Surgical treatment: Z-plasty of the constriction band to release the circumferential constriction and restore blood flow and lymphatic drainage.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old female presents with a 4-year history of generalised body swelling, easy fatigability, dyspnoea on exertion, and orthopnoea. Examination reveals: wasted appearance, delayed secondary sexual characteristics, pulse 120/min irregular, distended neck veins, hepatomegaly, ascites, bilateral basal crepitations, and a pericardial knock. CXR shows pericardial calcification and the ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Echocardiography reveals thickened pericardium with respiratory variation of inflow velocities across AV valves.

(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) Explain the pathophysiology that produces the clinical signs of elevated systemic venous pressure and reduced cardiac output.
(iii) What is the definitive treatment, the surgical approach, and what is the intraoperative finding expected?
(iv) What are the postoperative complications of this operation?
questions.answerText:
(i) Constrictive pericarditis.

(ii) Pathophysiology: marked pericardial thickening and calcification causes a symmetrical constricting effect, producing elevation and equalization of all diastolic pressures in all chambers. Impaired ventricular filling leads to: reduced cardiac output — manifesting as fatigue, hypotension, and reflex tachycardia. Elevated systemic venous pressure manifests as jugular venous distension, hepatomegaly with marked ascites, and peripheral oedema. Respiratory intrathoracic pressure changes are not transmitted to the intracardiac chambers — during inspiration systemic venous and right atrial pressures do not fall and venous flow into the right ventricle does not increase, producing Kussmaul's sign.

(iii) Definitive treatment: pericardiectomy. Surgical approaches: anterolateral thoracotomy or median sternotomy. Intraoperative findings expected: thickened calcific pericardium; severely reduced cardiac activity during decortication; LV decortication is performed first, leaving strong/dense scarring as islands; both ventricles, atria and vena cavae are decorticated.

(iv) Postoperative complications: acute perioperative cardiac insufficiency requiring fluid substitution, catecholamines, digitalis, or intra-aortic balloon pump; ventricular wall rupture; mortality rate of 6–12% or >40% depending on myocardial involvement.

questions.question:
Describe burns injury under the following headings:
(i) Types of burns (partial and full thickness) and the differences in their characteristics and healing.
(ii) Define a major burn using all criteria given; apply Wallace's rule of nines to calculate body surface area.
(iii) Early and late complications of burns, classified by system.
(iv) Resuscitation formula for major burns (the Muir-Barclay formula): state the formula, the sequence of aliquots, and the type of fluid used.
(v) Treatment of minor and major burns, covering wound management and specific vital-area burns.
questions.answerText:
(i) Types:
- Partial thickness burn: does not destroy the skin epithelium or destroys only part of it. Colour: red; blanches; painful; light touch present; hair preserved. Usually heal with conservative management.
- Full thickness burn: destroys all sources of skin epithelial regrowth. Colour: white; no blanching; no pain; no sensation; hair lost. May require excision and skin grafting if large.
(ii) Major burn criteria: ≥20% surface area in adults (≥10% in children); OR age <5 or >60; OR airway burn; OR perineal/ocular/hand burns.
Wallace's rule of nines: head and neck 9%; each upper limb 9%; chest (front) 9%; abdomen (front) 9%; upper back 9%; lower back 9%; each lower limb 18% (front 9%, back 9%); perineum 1%. Total = 99% (approximated as 100%).
(iii) Complications:
- Immediate: compartment syndrome from circumferential burns — limb burns → limb ischaemia; thoracic burns → hypoxia from restrictive respiratory failure (prevent by urgent escharotomy).
- Early: hyperkalaemia (from cytolysis); acute renal failure (hypovolaemia, sepsis, tissue toxins); infection (beware Streptococcus); stress ulceration (Curling's ulcer).
- Local/general: laryngeal oedema; bronchospasm; ARDS; inhalational pneumonitis; acute gastric ulceration; pancreatitis; paralytic ileus; DIC; hypercatabolism and proteolysis.
- Late: contractures.
(iv) Muir-Barclay formula: % burn × wt in kg ÷ 2 = one aliquot of fluid. Give six aliquots over first 36 hours in sequence: 4 h, 4 h, 4 h, 6 h, 6 h, 12 h (from time of burn). Colloid, albumin, or plasma solutions are used.
(v) Treatment:
- Major burns: start resuscitation (ABC); give IV fluids per formula; monitor pulse, BP, temperature, urinary output; adequate analgesia IV; nasogastric tube; tetanus prophylaxis; consider referral to a burns centre.
- Minor burns: treatment by exposure (debride and leave exposed) or by dressings (tulle gras with chlorhexidine or silver sulphadiazine); debridement of eschar and split-skin grafting if needed.
- Airway burn: 100% O2; nebulised adrenaline; IPPV; laryngeal oedema treated urgently.
- Corneal burns: protective tarsorrhaphy; chloramphenicol ointment; early ophthalmological opinion.

questions.question:
Describe the following aspects of toxic shock syndrome and erysipelas.
A(i) Describe toxic shock syndrome (TSS) — its epidemiology, causative agent, toxin involved, clinical presentation, and relevant investigation findings.
A(ii) State the treatment and mortality of TSS.
B(i) Describe erysipelas — its definition, causative organism, predisposed patients, onset and clinical features including skin appearance.
B(ii) State the treatment of erysipelas and describe the differences in the involved skin layer between erysipelas and cellulitis.
C(i) Describe the pneumoperitoneum technique used in giant inguinal hernias — including the rationale, method, volumes used and the complications specific to this procedure.
C(ii) Distinguish between the advantages and opponents' arguments regarding laparoscopic herniorraphy.
questions.answerText:
A(i) TSS epidemiology: seen in menstruating women under 30 years. Associated with high-absorbency polyacrylate-containing tampons; also with female diaphragm and other barrier methods. Causative agent: Staphylococci producing TSST-1 (toxic shock syndrome toxin-1). Clinical presentation: abrupt onset of fever, macular erythema, vomiting, diarrhoea, severe muscle pain and shock. Investigation findings: negative blood cultures; anti-TSST-1 antibodies found in serum.
A(ii) Treatment: supportive; antibiotics. Mortality: 10%, mainly due to the high virulence rate of the organism.
B(i) Erysipelas: rapidly progressive acute infection involving the dermis. Causative organism: Group A Streptococci (beta-haemolytic streptococci). Predisposed patients: common at extremes of life, immunosuppressed, debilitated. Onset: abrupt onset with systemic symptoms; enlarges rapidly with sharp, raised edges; bullae rupture leaving crusts; characterised by hot, red, oedematous, brawny, and sharply defined eruptions; regional lymphadenopathy is common.
B(ii) Treatment of erysipelas: penicillin. Erysipelas involves the dermis. Cellulitis involves the deeper subcutaneous tissue, in contrast to erysipelas which is confined to the dermis.
C(i) Pneumoperitoneum in giant hernias: used for loss of right domain — serious and fatal complications may arise from repair without preparation. Popularised by Goni Moreno; gradual stretching of the peritoneal cavity. Equipment: 22G needle, 50ml syringe, 3-way stop cock. Mechanical bowel preparation. Introduce needle/catheter away from hernia site. Initial injection: 600ml of air; increase by 200ml on alternate days until 2,000–2,500ml/day by end of second week. Complications: urinary retention, subcutaneous emphysema, basilar atelectasis, respiratory distress.
C(ii) Laparoscopic herniorraphy advocates: affords excellent visualisation; earlier return to work and normal activities; minimal postoperative pain; smaller incisions with improved cosmesis. Opponents: requires general anaesthesia; more expensive; highly skilled manpower required; entrance into peritoneal cavity; no long-term follow-up to assess recurrence rates.

questions.question:
A male neonate is noticed to have an absent anus at birth. He fails to pass meconium within 24 hours. Abdominal distension progresses over the next 12 hours. An invertogram is performed at 24 hours of life.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and name the investigation performed and what it reveals?
(ii) Name the surgical procedure for a high anorectal malformation and describe its anatomical components.
(iii) What nerve or muscle complex is at risk during posterior sagittal anorectoplasty (PSARP), and what is the consequence of injury?
(iv) What is the embryological variant that determines whether the malformation is high or low, and what initial surgical step is required for high lesions?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Anorectal malformation (ARM) — high type (without fistula).
Investigation: Lateral Prone Transtrochanteric X-ray (Invertogram) — reveals the distance of the rectal gas shadow from the perineal skin, determining the level of the rectal pouch relative to the levator ani (supralevator = high; infralevator = low). A loopogram/colostogram may also be used to delineate fistula anatomy.

(ii) Procedure for high ARM: Posterior Sagittal Anorectoplasty (PSARP).
Anatomical components:
- Posterior sagittal incision from the coccyx to the perineum
- Division and identification of the voluntary muscle complex (external sphincter, levator ani)
- Identification and division of any fistula (to posterior urethra in males)
- Mobilisation of the rectal pouch
- Placement of the rectum within the muscle complex in its correct anatomical position
- Reconstruction of the muscle complex around the neo-anus

(iii) Structure at risk: The voluntary muscle complex (striated sphincteric mechanism — external sphincter and levator ani complex) and the pelvic autonomic nerves. In males, the posterior urethra is at risk.
Consequences of injury: Faecal incontinence (injury to external sphincter or muscle complex); urinary incontinence or urethral stricture (injury to posterior urethra or autonomic nerves).

(iv) Embryological variant: The level of arrest of the urorectal septum determines the height of the lesion. If the urorectal septum fails to reach the cloacal membrane, the hindgut remains high (supralevator), and a fistula to the posterior urethra persists.
Initial surgical step for high lesions: Colostomy (defunctioning colostomy to decompress the bowel and protect the urinary tract from faecal contamination), followed by PSARP at a later stage (usually after 1–3 months).

(i) Diagnosis is fat embolism. It is a relatively uncommon disorder that occurs in the first few days following trauma with a mortality rate of 10–20%. Various theories: Fat drops from bone marrow following fracture, coalesce and form emboli in pulmonary capillary beds and brain, with a secondary inflammatory cascade and platelet aggregation. Alternative theory suggests that FFAs are released as chylomicrons following hormonal changes due to trauma or sepsis. Also seen following severe burns, CPR, bone marrow transplant, and liposuction.
(ii) Risk factors: Closed fractures; Multiple fractures; Pulmonary contusion; Long bone/pelvis/rib fractures.
(iii) Clinical features: Sudden onset dyspnoea; Hypoxia; Fever; Confusion, coma, convulsions; Transient red-brown petechial rash affecting the upper body, especially the axilla. Management: Supportive treatment; Corticosteroid drugs (used in treatment; more controversial in prevention); Surgical stabilisation of fracture.
(iv) Other early systemic fracture complications to exclude: Shock; Thromboembolism (pulmonary or venous); Exacerbation of underlying diseases such as diabetes or coronary artery disease; Pneumonia.
questions.question:
A 50-year-old female on the ward develops sudden onset dyspnoea, hypoxia, fever, and confusion on the third post-operative day following a pelvic fracture repair. She has a transient red-brown petechial rash in the axilla.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what are the theories of causation?
(ii) What are the risk factors for this condition?
(iii) What are the clinical features and how is it managed?
(iv) What other early systemic complications of fractures should be excluded in this patient?

questions.answerText:
A. Definition: hand injury is the transfer of energy to the part of the upper extremity that extends from the wrist to the tip of the fingers, such that it exceeds the natural resilience of the tissues.
Classification: open or closed; open wounds (Rank and Wakefield): tidy (clean laceration from sharp object); untidy (crush, avulsion, contaminated); indeterminate.
Structures that may be injured: skin, nerves, tendons, intrinsic hand muscles, blood vessels, bones, and joints.
Aetiology: sharp objects (knives, needles, thorns, glass); machinery (dough laminating machine, fan belt, grinding mechanism, guillotine, hot press); burns (hot water, hot oils, chemicals, electricity); explosives (gunshots, knockouts, bombs).
A(i) Evaluation:
- History: identify cause of injury, duration, dominant hand, other injuries, diabetes status.
- Examination (look, feel, move): identify area of skin loss, muscle loss, severed tendon, blood vessels, or nerves and bone involvement; check function of each finger, sensation, and perfusion; examine the normal contralateral hand; check for injuries in other parts of the body.
- Investigations: haematology (PCV, group and cross-match); chemistry (U&E plus creatinine, serum protein and albumin); microbiology (wound swab for M/C/S if signs of infection); histopathology (biopsy of chronic ulcers and scars); radiograph of both hands AP and lateral to rule out fractures, dislocation, and foreign bodies.
B. Principles of treatment:
- Irrigate wound with 2 litres of saline to minimise soilage.
- Restore anatomy by tagging tissue with appropriate sutures without tension.
- Repair damaged vessels, nerves, and tendons if competent, otherwise refer.
- Dress wound regularly with saline, medical honey, and bulky/gamgee dressing and crepe bandage (not gauze bandage).
- Skin grafting or flap cover of the wound as needed.
- Apply skin traction kit and elevate affected hand on a drip stand; apply a volar cast.
- Analgesics: morphine, pethidine, or pentazocine.
- Antibiotics: Augmentin and metronidazole combination or equivalent; tetanus vaccine.
- Physiotherapy and rehabilitation; early mobilisation (e.g., Kleinert traction after tendon repair); follow-up.
B(i) Seddon's nerve injury classification:
- Neuropraxia: minimal axonal disruption; conservative treatment; complete recovery in days to months.
- Axonotmesis: total axonal disruption with intact connective tissue; conservative treatment; complete recovery in months.
- Neurotmesis: disruption of axon, endoneurium, and perineurium; requires surgical repair; moderate reduction of function.
Early complications of hand injury: haematoma, infection, stiffness, tendon rupture.
Late complications: contracture (Boutonniere deformity, swan neck deformity after tendon injury), malunion, non-union of fractures, chronic pain, and complex regional pain syndrome.
questions.question:
A. Describe the HAND INJURY under the following headings: definition; classification (open/closed and the Rank and Wakefield classification); structures that may be injured; and the aetiology of hand injuries.
A(i) Describe the systematic evaluation of the patient with a hand injury, including history, examination (using look, feel, move principles), and investigations.
B. Describe the principles of treatment for hand injury, covering wound care, repair of structures, dressing type, splintage, medications, and rehabilitation.
B(i) State the nerve injury classification (Seddon's) and its prognostic implications as given, and state the early and late complications of hand injuries and their management principles.

A 9-year-old boy presents with a 5-day history of fever, severe localized pain over the right distal tibia that is unrelieved by rest, limb held still, localised finger-tip tenderness, swelling and warmth. Full blood count shows leucocytosis. Blood culture is positive.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis and the most probable causative organism in this age group. State also what organism accounts for 25% of cases in a specific subset of patients, and identify that subset.
(ii) What are the risk factors / predisposing sources of infection, and why does the infection typically localise to the metaphysis in children?
(iii) Describe the pathogenesis from the initial infectious phase through to new bone formation (involucrum).
(iv) Outline all investigations required and the surgical management options, including the criteria for converting from intravenous to oral antibiotics and the minimum duration of treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis. Commonest organism in all age groups: Staphylococcus aureus. In sickle cell patients, Salmonella species accounts for 25% of cases — however Staphylococcus aureus remains the commonest organism (60–65%) even in sickle cell patients.
(ii) Source: haematogenous spread, commonly from minor skin abrasion; rarely from boil; bone may be infected from a wound. Metaphyseal localisation in children: more blood flow to the growing end; rapidly growing cells are unduly susceptible; delicate vessels easily injured and haematoma is a suitable medium for bacterial growth; hairpin arrangement of capillaries slows blood flow, allowing organisms to settle.
(iii) Cellulitic phase: acute inflammation with accumulation of neutrophils, oedema, exudates. Suppurative phase: abscess formation if no intervention. Bone necrosis: due to shortage of blood supply to a high number of cells. Involucrum / new bone formation: periosteum in children is thick; it moves away from the bone, resulting in new bone formation.
(iv) Investigations: FBC (leucocytosis, shift to left); ESR (high, >15 mm/hr); blood culture (positive 50%); bone aspirate for M/C/S (90% positive); X-ray (no changes for first 10–14 days; later: patchy rarefaction of metaphysis, periostitis, sclerosis, sequestra); Technetium 99 bone scan (increased uptake — hot lesion). Management: ALL patients admitted; IV antibiotics (2nd/3rd generation cephalosporins e.g. Zinacef, Rocephin + Erythromycin); convert to oral when temperature normal for 72 hours, oral drug available, good absorption, no vomiting/diarrhoea; total antibiotic duration minimum 6 weeks. Analgesics; splintage to prevent pathological fracture; surgical drainage and drilling for abscess.

questions.question:
A 4-month-old male infant is brought to the clinic with failure to thrive, vomiting, abdominal distension, and cachexia. On examination the bladder is distended and palpable; hydronephrotic kidneys and tortuous dilated ureters are felt. The urinary stream is obstructive and dribbling incontinence is noted.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis and describe the anatomical structure responsible for this condition, including its point of origin and relationship to the prostatic urethra.
(ii) State the predisposing factors and all pathological effects at the bladder, urethra, ureters, and kidneys.
(iii) Name the surgical procedure required to confirm and treat the obstructing lesion, identify the anatomical landmarks critical to the procedure, and name the structure at risk.
(iv) Outline the full resuscitation and management plan before and after relief of obstruction, including the embryological variant (posterior urethral valve type 1) and management of vesico-ureteric reflux.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Posterior urethral valves (PUV). The valves are paper-like structures arising from the verumontanum, extending downwards and laterally to the side-walls of the urethra at the apex of the prostate. They cause obstructive uropathy in the first year of life. PUV type 1 (Young type 1) are described as exaggerated semilunar urethral folds at the crista terminalis.

(ii) Degree of obstruction is variable — mild, moderate, or severe. Pathological effects: bladder — trabeculation and sacculation; urethra — posterior urethral dilatation above the valves; bladder neck — narrow but not obstructed; ureters — megaureters; kidneys — hydronephrosis, gross renal damage at birth, cystic kidneys. Clinical effects: electrolyte imbalance (natriuresis), uraemia, hyperkalaemia, septicaemia, failure to thrive, abdominal distension.

(iii) Procedures: (a) Ablative — fulguration (endoscopic) of the valves; (b) Non-operative — Fogarty or Foley catheter; urethral hook (Williams). For diagnosis: micturating cystourethrography shows dilated prostatic urethra above the obstruction; USS shows hydronephrosis and hydroureters; urethrocystoscopy with bladder filling demonstrates the valves; renal function tests. The anatomical landmark is the verumontanum from which the valves arise; the sphincter mechanism is at risk during ablation.

(iv) Resuscitation and management:
- Counsel parents on options and prognosis.
- Catheterise — watch out for post-obstructive diuresis.
- Correct fluid and electrolyte imbalance (avoid high pressure and sodium if uraemic/dehydrated).
- Treat infection with antibiotics (given empirically for infected urine).
- Improve nutrition.
- If condition fails to improve: peritoneal dialysis plus urethral drainage.
- In advanced renal deterioration or pyonephrosis: immediate bilateral nephrostomy; if condition is unilateral with a functionless kidney — nephrectomy.
- Valves resected once patient is stable.
Pathological effects and their management:
- Secondary ureterovesical obstruction: ablation of valves; reimplantation of ureters if dilatation continues or persists.
- Vesico-ureteric reflux: ablation of valves, drainage, antibiotics; if reflux continues, reimplantation after suitable surveillance period.
- Ureteric dysfunction from dilatation, stasis, and infection: remodelling or masterly inactivity.
In babies with poor general condition, poorly functioning kidneys and ureters, immediate reconstructive surgery is ineffective — perform cutaneous ureterostomy (loop or ring type).
Prognosis: nearly 50% of the infantile group die within a few months; outcome depends on degree of renal impairment; fertility is compromised.

questions.question:
A neonate is born with abdominal viscera, including the liver, protruding through a defect at the umbilicus covered by a sac composed of amnion, Wharton's jelly, and peritoneum. Echocardiography reveals a tetralogy of Fallot.

(i) State the diagnosis and classify this case by size of defect and content.
(ii) Describe the embryological basis of this condition, including the two pathological factors involved and which folds are implicated in the most common (central) form.
(iii) List four steps in the supportive management of this neonate before surgical intervention.
(iv) State the two operative management options, and explain when primary closure is not tolerated and what is used instead, including the materials used for the staged reduction.
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is omphalocele (exomphalos).
- The defect is major (greater than 4 cm) with the liver in the sac, making it a giant omphalocele.
- The most common form is centrally located and measures 4–10 cm.

(ii) Embryological basis:
- Two pathological factors: (1) reduction of the midgut from the extra-embryonic coelom, and (2) formation of the anterior abdominal wall.
- Omphalocele is due to insufficient outgrowth at the umbilical ring during the embryonic folding process.
- In the most common (central) form, lateral folds fail to close centrally, leaving the viscera in the umbilical cord and causing a large abdominal wall defect.

(iii) Supportive management steps:
- Incubator care.
- Airway and breathing support.
- Fluid resuscitation and monitoring urine output.
- Correct hypoglycaemia.
- Temperature control.
- Prophylactic antibiotics.
- Tetanus toxoid and vitamin K.
(Any four of the above.)

(iv) Operative management options:
- Primary closure: for small-to-moderate size defects, mainly intestinal content; debride to remove and clean infective layers with peritoneum intact.
- Staged reduction closure: used when primary closure cannot be tolerated (e.g., major omphalocele where increased intra-abdominal pressure would splint the diaphragm, compromise respiration, press the IVC, impair gastrointestinal circulation and motility, or impair renal perfusion).
- Materials for staged reduction: Teflon/Gortex mesh, Prolene mesh, or a silastic sheath (prosthetic silo) is shaped to reinforce the sac, sutured firmly to the fasciomuscular rim, and reduced daily as it gets loose with progressive spontaneous coelomisation of sac content, taking 7–19 days or more.

questions.question:
(A) Describe the classification of lung tumours under the following headings:
(i) Benign lung tumours — types, characteristics, and proportion of all primary lung tumours
(ii) Non-small cell carcinoma — subtypes, their location, growth characteristics, and associated conditions
(iii) Small cell carcinoma — behaviour and sites of metastasis

(B) Describe the clinical manifestations of bronchogenic carcinoma arising from (a) the primary lesion, (b) local extension, and (c) paraneoplastic syndromes.

(C) Distinguish between non-small cell and small cell carcinoma in terms of treatment approach.
questions.answerText:
(A)(i) Benign lung tumours are a heterogeneous group originating from pulmonary structures like epithelium, cartilage, and other elements; a nodule is a spot seen on CT or CXR; usually benign in young non-smokers; represent 2–5% of all primary lung tumours. The most common type is hamartoma — usually peripheral, firm and marble-like, from epithelial, fat and cartilage; other benign types include bronchial carcinoids and rare neoplasms.

(A)(ii) Non-small cell carcinoma subtypes: Squamous cell carcinoma — most common subtype worldwide; slow-growing; often located near hilum; associated with hypercalcaemia. Adenocarcinoma — WHO divides into 4 subtypes: acinar, papillary, bronchiolo-alveolar, and solid with mucin production; most common type in non-smokers. Large cell carcinoma — less differentiated tumours; often occur in periphery of lung; present as large bulky tumours. Other types — adenosquamous, giant cell, neuroendocrine, spindle cell.

(A)(iii) Small cell carcinoma includes small cell and oat cell carcinoma; it is an aggressive cancer that metastasises quickly to mediastinal nodes and metastasises to brain, bone marrow, and liver.

(B)(a) Primary lesion: cough, dyspnoea, haemoptysis, sputum, wheezing, weight loss, fever, pneumonia. (b) Local extension: chest pain; hoarseness; superior vena cava syndrome; Horner's syndrome; dysphagia; pericardial effusion; pleural effusion; diaphragm paralysis; Pancoast tumour may involve brachial plexus causing C7–T2 neuropathy with pain, numbness, and weakness. (c) Paraneoplastic syndromes: hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy; hypercalcaemia; inappropriate ADH secretion syndrome; polymyositis; subacute cerebellar degeneration; peripheral neuropathies; Cushing's syndrome.

(C) Non-small cell carcinoma: treated surgically when feasible. Small cell carcinoma: responds best to non-surgical treatment.

questions.question:
A newborn infant is noted to have failure of descent of the left scapula, which sits high and prominent in the neck-shoulder region. The paediatric surgeon notes there may be an omovertebral bony connection between the scapula and the cervical spine.
(i) State the diagnosis and the underlying developmental failure.
(ii) State the conditions that Sprengel's syndrome is associated with.
(iii) State the incidence and treatment of the MADELUNG deformity.
(iv) Describe the RADIAL CLUB HAND: its incidence, laterality, clinical features, the associated anomalies (VACTERL components applicable), and the principles of surgical treatment.
(v) Describe the congenital dislocation of the radial head: incidence, differential diagnoses that must be excluded, clinical features, radiological finding, and treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is Sprengel's syndrome (congenital elevation of the scapula). The underlying developmental failure is failure of the normal caudal migration of the scapula; in normal development the scapula descends from the neck to its thoracic position, and failure of this migration leaves the scapula elevated. In 30% of cases, the superomedial scapula is connected to the proximal cervical spinous process through an omovertebral connection (bone or cartilage).
(ii) Associated conditions: congenital scoliosis; Klippel-Feil syndrome. Treatment: surgical correction.
(iii) Madelung's deformity: epiphyseal arrest on the ulnar and volar half of the distal radius causes the wrist joint to be directed ulnarward and volarward. Autosomal dominant (AD) with variable expressivity; females are affected 4:1 over males. Wrist motion: extension and supination are limited. X-ray may show classical deformity or inferior radio-ulnar dislocation. Treatment: corrective osteotomy or physeal resection and fat graft.
(iv) Radial club hand: incidence 1 in 30,000 live births; bilateral in 60% of cases. Clinical features: absence of the radius and radial rays; bowing of the ulna. Associated anomalies (VACTERL-related components listed): anal atresia; tracheo-oesophageal fistula; radial bone absence; renal anomalies; cardiac anomalies. Principles of surgical treatment: use of serial casts (to correct radial deviation); realignment and stabilisation (lower end of ulna is transferred radially); tendon transfers (ulnar-side tendons are transferred to the radial side to provide active radial support); correction of ulnar bowing by osteotomy.
(v) Congenital dislocation of the radial head: incidence 0.16%. Differential diagnoses that must be excluded: old Monteggia fracture-dislocation; multiple endochondromatosis or exostosis; radio-ulnar synostosis. Clinical features: family history; bilateral anomaly; loss of supination. Radiological finding: hypoplasia of the capitulum; dome-shaped radial head. Treatment: if painful, excision after skeletal maturity.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old diabetic man with known HIV infection presents with multiple purple-red nodular skin lesions on both lower limbs and oral mucosa. He is aged 50 years and has no prior organ transplant history. The lesions have been present for eight months and are locally aggressive with early bone involvement.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and classify the type of this condition based on age, population at risk, and clinical course.
(ii) Describe the pathology of this tumour, naming the three histological types and stating which type is most sensitive to chemotherapy.
(iii) List the chemotherapy agents used in the treatment of this condition.
(iv) List all other treatment options available beyond chemotherapy.
(v) State what happens to the therapy-related variant of this condition when the causative drug is stopped.
questions.answerText:
(i) The most likely diagnosis is Kaposi sarcoma (idiopathic haemorrhagic sarcoma). Given the patient's age (50), HIV status, mucocutaneous and bone involvement with local aggressiveness, this most closely fits the AIDS/KS type (HIV patient, age 19–64, mucocutaneous, lymph nodes, and viscera involvement, variable course) with features of the African florid type (nodules, fungating, bone involvement, locally aggressive).
(ii) Pathology: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumour arising from the mid dermis. Histological types:
- Type I: mixed (spindle cells and vascular channels) — most sensitive to chemotherapy.
- Type II: monomorphic (spindle cells only, no vascular channels).
- Type III: anaplastic.
(iii) Chemotherapy agents used: vinblastine; etoposide; bleomycin; adriamycin (doxorubicin); methotrexate.
(iv) Other treatment options:
- Recombinant alpha interferon (immunotherapy)
- Radiotherapy
- Local therapy: excision; curettage; cryotherapy; electrodessication.
(v) In the therapy-related variant (occurring in renal transplant recipients and patients with autoimmune disease treated with immunosuppressive drugs), the lesions may regress when the causative drug is stopped.

questions.question:
Regarding acute osteomyelitis of bone:

A(i) Describe the sites of infection across age groups — children, young infants, adults, and sickle cell patients — giving the anatomical reason for metaphyseal predilection in children.
A(ii) Describe the full pathogenesis from the cellulitic phase through suppuration, bone necrosis, and involucrum formation.
B(i) Outline the investigations required for diagnosis, including the radiographic timeline and the interpretation of Technetium-99 bone scan findings.
B(ii) Distinguish between the differential diagnoses of acute osteomyelitis: acute suppurative arthritis, acute rheumatism (Still's disease), and sickle cell crisis, including the nuclear medicine finding that helps differentiate sickle cell crisis from osteomyelitis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Children: metaphysis — because more blood flow to growing end; rapidly growing cells are unduly susceptible; delicate vessels easily injured and haematoma is a suitable bacterial medium; hairpin arrangement of capillaries slows blood flow, allowing organisms to settle. Young infants: the very end of the bone may be involved. Adults: midshaft may be attacked. Sickle cell patients: diaphysis is usually involved — commoner than metaphysis.
A(ii) Cellulitic phase: acute inflammation with accumulation of neutrophils, oedema, and exudate. Suppurative phase: abscess formation if there is no intervention. Bone necrosis: results from shortage of blood supply to a high number of cells. Involucrum/new bone formation: periosteum in children is thick; it moves away from the bone, resulting in new bone formation around the infected area.
B(i) FBC: leucocytosis, shift to left. ESR: high (normal range 0–10 mm/hr; methods: Westergreen and Wintrope). Blood culture: positive in 50% of cases. Bone aspirate for M/C/S: 90% positive; replaced by ultrasound guidance. X-ray: no abnormality for first 10–14 days (50% of calcium must be lost before X-ray shows abnormality); changes include patchy rarefaction of metaphysis, periostitis (thin line parallel to shaft), sclerosis (new periosteal bone), and sequestra. Technetium-99 bone scan: shows increased uptake (hot lesion) in osteomyelitis.
B(ii) Acute suppurative/septic arthritis: pain and joint swelling (joint rather than bone). Acute rheumatism/Still's disease (JRA): fever; pain is multiple (more than one joint); child is ill-looking; ESR raised; leucocytosis not marked. Sickle cell crisis (bone infarction): Technetium-99 shows reduced uptake (cold/photodeficient lesion) — opposite of osteomyelitis where there is increased uptake. Gaucher's disease: cellular infiltration with enlarged liver.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old motorcyclist is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. He is drowsy but follows commands (GCS 10). CT brain shows a hyperdense biconvex (lens-shaped) collection over the right temporal region with midline shift.
(i) Identify the lesion and the structure most likely responsible for bleeding.
(ii) Classify head injuries by (a) mechanism and (b) severity using the Glasgow Coma Scale, including all scoring categories and their scores.
(iii) Describe the management of the elevated intracranial pressure associated with this lesion, detailing all the pharmacological and positioning measures.
(iv) State the medical therapy for head injury including anticonvulsants, the timing of seizures, and the risk factors for late seizures.
(v) Outline the surgical therapies available for head injury.
questions.answerText:
(i) Lesion: extradural (epidural) haematoma. Biconvex/lens-shaped hyperdense collection following temporal trauma most likely results from rupture of the middle meningeal artery, which runs in the extradural space.
(ii) (a) Mechanism: Closed — blunt force, RTA, falls, assaults (high or low velocity; brain not exposed). Penetrating — gunshot wounds and stab wounds (high or low velocity; brain exposure/CSF leak).
(b) Severity by GCS:
- Eye opening: spontaneous 4, to call 3, to pain 2, none 1
- Motor response: obeys commands 6, localises to pain 5, withdraws to pain 4, decorticates to pain 3, extends to pain 2, none 1
- Verbal response: oriented 5, confused 4, inappropriate 3, incomprehensible 2, none 1
Sum: best score 15, worst 3. Mild 13–15; moderate 9–12; severe 3–8.
(iii) Management of elevated ICP: intubate with modest hyperventilation to pCO2 of 30; mannitol 0.5–1.0 g/kg IV push; furosemide 5–20 mg IV; elevate head 20–30 degrees; avoid any neck vein compression; sedate and paralyse if necessary with morphine and vecuronium (struggling and coughing elevate ICP); avoid using antihypertensives to lower blood pressure.
(iv) Medical therapy: anticonvulsants — post-traumatic seizures occur in 5–15%; types are immediate, early (first week), late; prophylaxis is beneficial in the first week. Risk factors for late seizures: early seizures, depressed skull fractures, and intracranial haematoma. Other: intracranial pressure monitoring; mannitol; Lasix; barbiturates; steroids.
(v) Surgical therapy: wound debridement; evacuation of intracranial haematoma and contusions; elevation of compound depressed fracture; repair of venous sinus injuries.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man with a long history of heavy smoking and weight loss presents with a persistent productive cough, haemoptysis in 50% severity, and dyspnoea. CXR shows a central hilar mass. Bronchoscopy with biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma.

(i) List the risk factors for bronchogenic carcinoma.
(ii) Name the three macroscopic (gross) types of bronchogenic carcinoma and describe how the Pancoast tumour produces its syndrome.
(iii) Describe the routes and common sites of metastasis.
(iv) What are the available treatment options, and under what circumstance does surgical removal offer the best prospect for cure?
questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors: cigarette smoking and atmospheric pollution; arsenic, asbestos, nickel, metallic iron, iron oxides, radioactive substances; exhaust fumes, coal tar, fumes, benzopyrene, chromate and petroleum products; diffuse lung fibrosis; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
