(ii) Three macroscopic types: (a) main bronchus tumours (at main bronchi); (b) peripheral tumours (on the surface of the lungs); (c) Pancoast tumour (pulmonary sulcus or superior sulcus tumour) on the apex — it affects the brachial plexus and cervical sympathetic nerve (stellate ganglion), producing Pancoast syndrome.

(iii) Metastasis routes and sites: direct spread/local — to mediastinum, pleura, chest wall or pericardium; lymphatics — to hilar lymph nodes, subcarinal or paratracheal chain of lymph nodes; blood stream — to liver, brain, bones, adrenal glands, and skin.

(iv) Treatment options: surgical removal (offers the best prospect for cure for early-stage disease); radiotherapy (rarely for cure, mainly for palliative treatment); cytotoxic chemotherapy — cisplatin/carboplatin, etoposide, irinotecan; immunotherapy — intrapleural BCG injection to stimulate immune response; targeted therapy — crizotinib, entrectinib for ROS1 and ALK gene tumours; laser beams through flexible bronchoscope. Surgical removal offers the best prospect for cure for early-stage disease.

A. The lymphatic system of the limbs comprises three layers of vessels:
- Superficial (primary) lymphatic vessels: form a complex dermal network of capillary-like channels with no valves; these parallel the superficial veins.
- Secondary (larger) lymphatic vessels: have valves and are located in the subdermal space; they also parallel the superficial veins and drain into the third layer.
- Third (deep) layer: located in the subcutaneous fat adjacent to the fascia.
- An intramuscular system also exists, paralleling the deep arteries, draining the muscular compartment, joints, and synovium.
A(i) Chronic lymphoedema results in subcutaneous fibrosis. This fibrosis can be worsened by secondary infection. The accumulated fluid is an abnormal collection of excessive tissue proteins, oedema fluid, and products of chronic inflammation.
A(ii) Lymphoedema develops through two main mechanisms: increased capillary filtration (caused by increased capillary hydrostatic pressure, decreased tissue pressure, or increased membrane permeability) and reduced interstitial fluid absorption (caused by decreased plasma oncotic pressure, increased oncotic pressure of tissue fluid, or lymphatic obstruction). In lymphoedema, the primary cause is a defect in the lymphatic system leading to accumulation of lymph in the interstitial spaces, principally in the subcutaneous fat.
B. Primary lymphoedema subtypes by age of onset: Congenital (onset before age 1 year, familial or non-familial); Praecox (onset before age 35 years, familial or non-familial); Tarda (onset after age 35 years). Primary lymphoedema is more common in women and usually bilateral. Secondary lymphoedema has an apparent underlying cause: malignant disease; surgery (axillary surgery or groin dissection); radiotherapy; and infection (parasitic, e.g., filariasis).
B(i) Lymphoedema produces non-pitting oedema because the accumulated protein-rich interstitial fluid and subsequent fibrosis create a firmer tissue consistency that does not indent easily with pressure. Additional skin changes found on examination include hyperkeratosis and fissuring, and secondary infection of the skin.
questions.question:
A. Describe the anatomy of the LYMPHATIC SYSTEM of the limbs as presented, covering: the layers of lymphatic vessels, their valvular status, and what system each parallels.
A(i) State the pathological changes that occur in chronic lymphoedema at the tissue level.
A(ii) Explain the physiological mechanism by which lymphoedema develops, identifying the two main components that lead to accumulation of fluid in the interstitial space.
B. Describe the clinical features that distinguish PRIMARY from SECONDARY lymphoedema, including age of onset subtypes of primary lymphoedema and four common causes of secondary lymphoedema.
B(i) Explain why the oedema of lymphoedema is described as non-pitting and state two additional skin changes found on examination.

questions.answerText:
(i) Definition of infertility: inability of a couple to achieve conception after 12 months of adequate, regular unprotected sexual intercourse. Incidence: affects about 10% of all marriages. Male spermatogenic defects account for 30% of infertile marriages.

(ii) Predisposing factors in this patient:
- Mumps orchitis: causes deficiency of germ cell maturation.
- Iatrogenic damage during inguinal procedures (hernia repair at age 8): may cause damage to vas deferens, obstruction of conduction system.
- Small testes (<10 cc): suggest testicular failure or hypopituitarism.
Full aetiological categories:
- Hypopituitarism: leads to germinal aplasia; FSH low.
- Hypogonadism/testicular failure (e.g. Klinefelter's): FSH elevated, testosterone normal due to Leydig cells.
- Deficiency of germ cell maturation: mumps, trauma, X-rays, chemotherapy, radiotherapy.
- Obstruction of conduction system: absence of union between vas and epididymis, previous epididymitis, vasectomy, iatrogenic damage during inguinal procedures.
- Hyperadrenalism; varicoceles; tight clothing; undescended testes; sperm antibodies.

(iii) Investigations:
Seminal fluid analysis: volume (2.5–5 cc, up to 12 cc acceptable); count/cc (>20,000,000); morphology; motility; vitality.
Collection: abstinence >4 days; masturbation into wide-necked sterile bottle; submitted within 20 minutes; transported warm.
Hormone profile: FSH, LH, testosterone, prolactin.
Immune studies: anti-sperm antibodies.
If azoospermic: consider hormone profile — if normal, likely obstructive; if very high FSH and low testosterone, testicular failure; if hyperprolactinaemia, treat accordingly.
Testicular biopsy: anaesthesia; mid-portion of convex border of testis.
Bilateral vasography.

(iv) Treatment options (in order as listed): general measures; treatment of hypopituitarism; treatment of testicular failure; treatment of hyperprolactinaemia; surgical relief of vasal obstruction; repair of failure of vaso-epididymal union; varicocelectomy; in vitro fertilisation.
Sperm cryopreservation (banking): involves freezing and banking sperm collected through masturbation, rectal electroejaculation, testicular aspiration, or post-masturbation urine. Used before anti-cancer treatment because sperm quality may be poor before treatment (especially in testicular cancer and Hodgkin's disease); many patients must start chemotherapy soon; ICSI allows successful use of small frozen samples.
questions.question:
A 34-year-old man and his 30-year-old wife present with inability to conceive after 18 months of adequate, regular unprotected sexual intercourse. He had mumps orchitis in childhood and an inguinal hernia repair at age 8. On examination his testes are small (<10 cc), the voice is normally masculine, and there is no gynaecomastia.

(i) State the diagnosis with its precise definition and give the incidence of infertility and the proportion attributable to male factors.
(ii) List all predisposing factors applicable to this patient from the causes of male infertility, and classify them under the appropriate aetiological categories.
(iii) Describe the resuscitative and investigative steps — including seminal fluid analysis parameters, hormone profile, and the sequence of investigation if azoospermia is found.
(iv) Outline all treatment options in order as listed, and describe the role of sperm banking before anti-cancer treatment.

questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: haemorrhagic shock. Haemorrhage is the predominant cause of preventable post-injury deaths; if a patient is hypotensive, it should be assumed to be due to blood loss until this is ruled out.
(ii) Concealed haemorrhage: check chest, abdomen, retroperitoneal space, pelvis, and long bones. Chest or pelvic bleeding — X-ray or CT if stable. FAST scan to identify peritoneal haemorrhage or diagnostic peritoneal lavage.
(iii) Goals: restore circulation. Management starts from pre-hospital care ideally; arrest haemorrhage concurrently with fluid resuscitation; consensus on crystalloid, NOT colloids; prompt type-specific blood transfusion in major haemorrhage. Early use of blood products is appropriate — they maintain oxygen-carrying capacity and coagulation factor concentration. Resuscitation is not complete until acidosis is resolved.
(iv) The lethal triad: Hypothermia (T < 34°C) — use warm fluids with precision devices. Acidosis (pH < 7.2 or base deficit ≥ 8 mEq/L) — address by restoring circulation and correcting acidosis. Coagulopathy — FFP after 4 units of blood. Avoid dextrose-containing fluids; ideal fluid is Normal Saline; blood O-negative or type-specific should be used.
(v) Primary goal: identify the source of haemorrhage and control it as rapidly as possible. Inappropriately vigorous fluid resuscitation increases the rate of uncontrolled haemorrhage and may worsen survival; the most important component of resuscitation from haemorrhagic shock is source control. Monitoring: pulse, blood pressure, urine output, conjunctiva, chest.
questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman presents to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. She is hypotensive, tachycardic, with cold extremities. Bleeding is not visible externally.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what general principle should guide assessment of a hypotensive trauma patient with no visible external bleeding?
(ii) How should concealed haemorrhage be identified, and what are the possible sites?
(iii) What are the goals and principles of resuscitation, and which fluids are recommended?
(iv) What is the lethal triad in haemorrhagic shock and how is each component addressed?
(v) What is the primary goal of resuscitation, and what monitoring parameters should be used?

questions.answerText:
A(i) The three levels of microbiological investigation:
1. Pre-operative: to rule out infection that may jeopardise success of surgery. Example: conjunctival swab for M/C/S in eye surgery to rule out Staphylococcus aureus; urine for M/C/S in urological patients and gynaecological patients (especially with VVF/RVF).
2. Intra-operative: diagnosis of agents of infection. Example: cerebral abscess, pyomyositis.
3. Post-operative: diagnosis of post-operative infection.

A(ii) Determinants of good quality specimen:
- Material must be from the actual site of infection with minimum contamination from adjacent tissues or secretions.
- Optimal collection times: early morning sputum for TB; early morning urine for UTI; blood culture and blood film at the time of temperature rise.
- Sufficient quantity and number: e.g. CSF; 10 ml per blood culture set in adults with at least 2 sets; 2 samples of faeces on different days for diarrhoea.
- Appropriate sterile containers with tightly fitted screwed caps.
- Specimens for culture should be collected before administration of antibiotics.
- Proper labelling of specimen containers and request forms.

B(i) Specimens should be transported in a sterile fashion, in an environment that allows organisms to survive, and as fresh as possible for optimal isolation. For urine: should reach the microbiology laboratory within 2 hours; if delay is inevitable — refrigeration at 4 degrees C for 24–48 hours; dip-slide technique; or 1.8% boric acid in urine (preserves bacterial count and neutrophils but inhibitory to a few bacterial strains). For anaerobes: aspirate in capped syringes or stopped tubes (Vacutainer anaerobic specimen collector); Stuart's transport medium.

B(ii) Koch's postulates: (1) The micro-organism must be present in every case of the disease; (2) it can be isolated in pure culture; (3) inoculation of the pure culture into animals produces a similar disease; (4) the same species of micro-organism must be recovered from the diseased animal. Taxonomy: the branch of biology concerned with classification of all living organisms. Classification: systematic division of organisms into related groups (family, tribe, genus, species). Identification: the process by which an unknown micro-organism is confirmed as belonging to a previously established taxa. Nomenclature: there is only one correct name for an organism; all names are in Latin; the first word (genus) is capitalised; the second word (species) is not capitalised; both words are underlined or italicised.
questions.question:
Describe the pre-operative microbiological investigation of the surgical patient, the principles of quality specimen collection, and the requirements for transport.

A(i) State the three levels at which microbiological investigation is performed in the surgical patient, with an example at each level.
A(ii) List the determinants of a good-quality specimen, with specific guidance on collection timing for TB, UTI, and blood culture.
B(i) State the requirements for specimen transportation and describe the urine transport methods available when delay is inevitable.
B(ii) State Koch's postulates. Define taxonomy, classification, and identification; state the rules for binomial nomenclature of micro-organisms.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Total body water is approximately 60% of lean body mass in young men, 50% in young women and older men, and 45% in older women. 70% of body water is intracellular; 30% is extracellular, including plasma and interstitial fluid. Small amounts are present in bone, connective tissue, digestive secretions, and cerebrospinal fluid. Extracellular solutes are mainly Na+ salts (primarily NaCl and NaHCO3). Na+,K+ATPase pump on cell membranes keeps intracellular Na+ at low levels. K+ is the predominant intracellular cation, balanced by anionic charges on impermeant macromolecules.
A(ii) Between intravascular and interstitial compartments: filtration, driven by hydrostatic pressure gradient generated by cardiac contractions; oncotic pressure due to intravascular proteins. Between extracellular and intracellular compartments: osmotic forces. Isotonic saline is confined to extracellular space. Electrolyte water is distributed throughout the body, affecting both extracellular and intracellular fluid compartments and having a major impact on plasma Na+, tonicity and cell volume.
B(i) Peri-trauma fluid management depends on: type of trauma and circumstances; presence of pulmonary, cardiac, renal or hepatic disease. Monitoring: urine output, pulse rate, and BP. Note that during stress, ability to lower ADH and excrete excess water is impaired. Moderately aggressive resuscitation is best. Crystalloids remain the fluid of choice — they replete intravascular volume and enhance perfusion because of decreased blood viscosity. Crystalloids may be used to replace blood loss to a limit of 8:1; blood is needed when crystalloid infusion exceeds 50 ml/kg.
B(ii) Lactated Ringer's is better than normal saline because it buffers metabolic acidosis better. Colloids: meta-analysis has shown that use of colloids is associated with higher mortality; they are costly and may aggravate post-traumatic complications. Hypertonic saline continues to be investigated — it attenuates neutrophil-mediated injury. Administration of hypotonic solutions leads to hyponatraemia.
questions.question:
Describe the principles of fluid management in trauma under the headings of body fluid compartments, choice of fluid, and monitoring, then explain the physiological basis for the superiority of Lactated Ringer's over normal saline, and distinguish between the effects of crystalloids and colloids in trauma resuscitation.
A(i) Describe the distribution of total body water and the composition of extracellular fluid.
A(ii) Describe the mechanisms governing fluid movement between compartments.
B(i) State the principles of peri-trauma fluid management and the monitoring parameters used.
B(ii) Explain the physiological basis for the choice of Lactated Ringer's over normal saline, and distinguish between crystalloids and colloids in trauma.

A neonate (3 days old) is brought to the paediatric surgery ward with abdominal distension, failure to pass meconium, and vomiting. On examination the abdomen is distended and a tender right groin swelling is noted that appeared suddenly during vomiting. The mass is tense and irreducible.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and why does this age group carry a high risk of obstruction?
(ii) What is the embryological basis for the hernia in this sex and age group?
(iii) What immediate steps should be taken, and what circumstances warrant postponement of surgery?
(iv) What is the operative treatment and what structures are at risk during surgery?
(v) What is laparoscopic herniorraphy and what are the specific indications and techniques used?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: incarcerated inguinal hernia presenting in a neonate with intestinal obstruction. High risk of obstruction: the paediatric age group carries a high risk of obstruction. 1/3 of paediatric hernias present in the first 6 months of age; peak incidence is in infancy. Irreducibility necessitates urgent management.
(ii) Embryological basis: at 6 weeks, primitive germ cells migrate to the genital ridge; at 7–8 weeks differentiation into testis occurs; at 3 months descent commences; at 7 months the testis reaches the internal ring acquiring cord coverings. The processus vaginalis (PV) remains patent in 10% of cases — in boys this may present as a complete, funicular or bubonoiele hernia.
(iii) Immediate steps for irreducible hernia: sedation; Trendelenburg position; use of cold pack; gentle taxis. Postponement of surgery: concurrent illness; severe prematurity.
(iv) Operative treatment: herniotomy (high ligation and excision of the hernia sac). Structures at risk: ilioinguinal nerve (may be damaged); vas deferens — damage should be repaired; primary haemorrhage is a risk. Orchidopexy is required if undescended testis is found.
(v) Laparoscopic herniorraphy: advocates — affords excellent visualisation, earlier return to work and normal activities, minimal postoperative pain, smaller incisions with improved cosmesis. Opponents — requires general anaesthesia, more expensive, highly skilled manpower required, entrance into peritoneal cavity, no long-term follow-up to assess recurrence rates. Indications: repair of recurrent inguinal hernia; simultaneous repair of bilateral inguinal hernias. Techniques: TAPP; TEPA. Uses prosthetic mesh.

questions.question:
Describe the thyroid carcinoma under the following headings.
A(i) Types of primary thyroid carcinoma — name and classify all types mentioned.
A(ii) For each differentiated thyroid carcinoma (papillary, follicular, medullary), state the epidemiology, behaviour and pattern of spread.
B(i) State the investigations required in thyroid carcinoma.
B(ii) Describe the surgical options for each histological type and justify the choice.
C(i) Explain the role of non-surgical adjuvant treatments — radiotherapy, chemotherapy, radio-iodine and TSH suppression.
C(ii) Distinguish between anaplastic carcinoma and other types in terms of pathology, behaviour, spread and management.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Types of primary thyroid carcinoma: Differentiated — papillary, follicular, medullary (MTC). Undifferentiated/anaplastic. Squamous cell. Others — lymphoma, fibrosarcoma, teratoma.
A(ii) Papillary adenocarcinoma: commonest worldwide, but only 20% in Nigeria; common in children, 3rd to 4th decades; slow growing; local and distant spread; metastasis to cervical and mediastinal lymph nodes. Follicular adenocarcinoma: commonest in Nigeria (60%); highest incidence in 5th decade; slow growing; more in women; spread to bones and blood stream; forms follicles and looks like thyroid; may be minimally or widely invasive. Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC): 10%; it is an apudoma, from the C-cells, secretes calcitonin; sporadic in 75% (in a lobe or part); familial syndromes MEN IIa, MEN IIb; multicentric, secretes serotonin, prostaglandin, histamine; spreads by lymphatics and blood stream.
B(i) Investigations: FNAC; TFTs (TSH, T3, T4); USS — thyroid, liver; thyroid scan (radio-isotope 99Tc or 123 Iodine); radiographs (X-rays) — neck, thoracic inlet, CXR; laryngoscopy (flexible); serum thyroglobulin and calcitonin; CT scan, MRI, PET scan for staging; FBC, U/E, G+XM, LFTs.
B(ii) Surgery: total or near-total thyroidectomy in papillary carcinoma (well-differentiated); lobectomy + isthmusectomy ± lymph node dissection; total thyroidectomy for follicular carcinoma + radio-iodine; total thyroidectomy in MTC + lymph node excision.
C(i) Radiotherapy: for anaplastic carcinoma and lymphomata ± surgery; for metastasis to bones, especially pathological fractures. Chemotherapy: for lymphoma — cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine + external beam radiation. Radio-iodine (RAI, I-131): for hyperthyroidism; adjunct to surgery in papillary and follicular carcinoma; also if there is uptake by metastatic lesions. TSH suppression: thyroxine 0.3g/day.
C(ii) Anaplastic carcinoma: 5%; hard to feel; rapidly growing; may arise de novo; mutation of RAS proto-oncogene; local spread to trachea and oesophagus; spread to lymph nodes and blood vessels; radiosensitive. Contrast: papillary and follicular are slow growing, well differentiated, with lymphatic and haematogenous spread respectively; MTC is an apudoma; anaplastic is the most aggressive, radiosensitive, with local and vascular invasion.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man presents with difficulty swallowing and weight loss. He is found to have serum albumin of 2.5 g/100ml and a 20% loss of body weight.
(i) What nutritional status does this indicate and what clinical and laboratory parameters confirm severe malnutrition?
(ii) What are the causes of undernutrition in surgical patients?
(iii) What routes of nutritional support are available, and which should be preferred and why?
(iv) What are the calorific values of the macronutrients and the body's minimum daily glucose requirement?
(v) What monitoring parameters must be observed during TPN, and what are its complications?
questions.answerText:
(i) These parameters indicate severe protein-energy malnutrition. Clinical confirmation: fluffy hair, muscle wasting, loss of thenar eminence muscles, loose flabby skin, oedema of hypoproteinaemia, loss of body fat, pallor; weight compared to ideal for age and height; triceps skin fold thickness; mid-arm circumference. Laboratory: serum albumin value less than 3g/100ml and weight loss of 15% are key thresholds for indicating nutritional support. Red blood cell count, serum protein (albumin, pre-albumin, transferrin, retinol binding protein), nitrogen balance, hand grip dynamometry, respiratory tests, delayed cutaneous hypersensitivity or anergy, functional studies of muscle function, NMRI.
(ii) Causes: inadequate intake — inadequate supply; inability to eat (advanced cancer, chemotherapy, sepsis, post-operatively: laparotomy, gastrectomy, oesophagectomy). Excessive loss — burns, major trauma, pancreatitis, peritonitis, severe diarrhoea, copious vomiting, prolonged nasogastric suctioning, ileostomy loss, high output faecal fistula, chronic suppuration.
(iii) Routes: enteral (oral, naso-gastric, naso-duodenal, naso-jejunal, gastrostomy, jejunostomy); parenteral (intraperitoneal in children, intravenous — peripheral and central vein). Oral is the best way to correct malnutrition. Parenteral is highly invasive; complications commoner (sepsis, thrombosis, fluid and electrolyte imbalance).
(iv) Calorific values: 1g carbohydrate = 4 cals; 1g dextrose = 3.75 cals; 1g protein = 4 cals; 1g fat = 9 cals; 1g alcohol = 7 cals; 1 litre D5W = 200 cals (actually 177 cals). Minimum glucose requirement: Brain and nervous tissues — 120g/day; RBC, renal tubules, fibroblasts, neutrophils, monocytes — 40g/day; minimal glucose requirement total = 160g/day.
(v) Monitoring: daily body weight (gain expected); fluid intake and output 4–8 hourly; fractional urine sugar concentration 6-hourly (up to 3+ glycosuria acceptable); electrolytes, blood sugar and urea nitrogen daily until stable, then every 2–3 days; CBC, serum proteins, Ca, P and Mg weekly; LFT and renal function test every 2–3 weeks. Complications: due to catheter (phlebitis, pneumothorax, haemothorax, air embolism, catheter embolism, hydrothorax, ligation of brachial artery); sepsis (fungal and bacterial); hyperglycaemia (osmotic dehydration, coma, osmotic diuresis); rebound hypoglycaemia from sudden termination (termination staged: 2L with 1L N/S, then 1L with 2L N/S, then 3L D/S); allergic reaction.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the SCALP using the SCALP mnemonic. For each layer, state its content and one clinically relevant consequence of injury or disease at that layer.
A(i) Describe the SUBCUTANEOUS MUSCULOAPONEUROTIC SYSTEM (SMAS), stating its indications for use in reconstruction and in cosmetic surgery.
B. Describe Camper's and Scarpa's fasciae in the trunk as part of the subcutaneous fascial system, and explain the anatomical basis of LIPOSUCTION by describing the physiology of adipocytes, including their receptor types and the effect on lipolysis.
B(i) State the differences in fat distribution related to race and age as given.
questions.answerText:
A. SCALP mnemonic and clinical significance:
- S = Skin: outermost layer; thick and firmly bound to the layer below; skin lacerations may be deceptively small but the subcutaneous vasculature cannot retract, causing profuse bleeding.
- C = Compact subcutaneous tissue: dense fibroadipose layer firmly bound to both skin above and galea below; contains the scalp vessels in a rigid framework, preventing vascular retraction and causing profuse bleeding from scalp wounds.
- A = Aponeurosis of Galea: strong tendinous sheet; provides structural integrity; exploited in scalp rotation flaps and in SMAS face lifts.
- L = Loose areolar connective tissue: avascular cleavage plane that allows easy surgical dissection; infection or haematoma can spread widely within this plane and may extend intracranially through emissary veins.
- P = Periosteum: deepest layer, adherent to the skull's outer table; relatively avascular; loss of periosteum over bone requires flap cover as a graft will not take on bare bone.
A(i) SMAS (Subcutaneous musculoaponeurotic system): a fibromuscular layer beneath the skin and subcutaneous fat of the face and neck. Indications for use:
- Reconstruction of scalp and adjacent facial defects
- Auricular reconstruction
- Face, brow, and neck lift (the SMAS-fascia is tightened after separating it from the overlying skin and subcutaneous fat, producing a longer-lasting cosmetic result than skin-only lifts)
B. In the trunk, the subcutaneous fat is organised into superficial and deep layers separated by Scarpa's fascia (deep) and Camper's fascia (more superficial). Physiology of adipocytes for liposuction: adipocytes are connective tissue cells specialising in synthesis and storage of fat. They possess two different receptors for catecholamines: alpha-2 (α2) receptors, which block lipolysis; and alpha-1 (not beta-1) receptors, which are lipolytic and secrete lipase. Adipocytes in the deep fat layer are more receptive to glucose, incorporate it faster, take less time to enlarge, and are therefore preferentially targeted by suction lipectomy (liposuction).
B(i) Age: neonates have 20% of the adipose cell concentration of adults. The proportion of fat in the trunk generally increases with age. Extremities lose subcutaneous fat with age.
Race: Blacks experience increased fat accumulation in the buttocks compared to other races, and this pattern is magnified by the lumbar lordosis common in Blacks.

A(i) MHC antigens are coded on chromosome 6 and code polymorphic cell-surface molecules called HLAs. HLA types are class I and class II, classified by cell location and structure; inheritance is Mendelian. MHCa forms complexes with foreign proteins, which are recognised by T cells and B cells.

A(ii) Hyperacute rejection occurs immediately due to pre-formed ABO or anti-HLA antibodies causing intravascular thrombosis. Acute graft rejection occurs within 6 months and is usually reversible; mechanisms include direct and indirect pathways: CD8+ T cells release cytotoxic substances from granules; CD4+ T cells bind donor MHC allopeptides presented by APC, recruiting B cells to cause complement-mediated lysis; mononuclear cell infiltration is seen. Chronic rejection occurs after 6 months, leads to graft failure through myointimal proliferation in graft arteries causing ischaemia and fibrosis.

B(i) Classification: (1) calcineurin blockers — cyclosporin/tacrolimus; (2) antiproliferative agents — azathioprine/MMF; (3) steroids — GCC; (4) antibody therapies — ALG/ALS; (5) rapamycin (sirolimus) — binds FK-binding protein. The preferred regimen is triple therapy: calcineurin-based agent, steroids, and antiproliferative agent. Immunosuppression is highest in the first 3 months then continued indefinitely. Complications include: infections — CMV, HSV, bacterial, fungal, protozoal (Pneumocystis carinii), risk highest ≤6 months, chemoprophylaxis important; malignancy — PTLD and SQCC, requiring regular review.

B(ii) LRKD evaluation includes mixed lymphocyte culture, CT angiography of renal artery/vein/IVC/aorta, and routine workup as for recipient; inclusion criteria: age 18–65, two normally functioning kidneys, donor willingness; harvest can be laparoscopic with or without hand-assist, or open donor nephrectomy. CRD: brain death requires complete and irreversible loss of all cerebral and brainstem functions — cerebral unresponsiveness to painful stimuli, apnoea, absent brainstem reflexes (pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, oculovestibular, oropharyngeal); confirmatory tests include EEG, brain scan, cerebral angiography. Cadaveric donor preparation requires haemodynamic stability, serum osmolality monitoring, BP and CVP monitoring, 100% O₂, temperature >34°C, FFP for coagulopathy.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the immunological basis of renal transplantation, including the nature of the MHC antigens, the types of HLA, and the cellular mechanisms by which T cells and B cells recognise and respond to the graft.
A(ii) Describe the three types of graft rejection — hyperacute, acute, and chronic — including their timing, mechanisms, and pathological consequences.
B(i) Outline the classification of immunosuppressive agents used in renal transplantation, state the preferred regimen, and explain its principal complications.
B(ii) Distinguish between a living-related kidney donor (LRKD) and a cadaveric renal donor (CRD), including the criteria used to define brain death and the surgical preparation required before organ harvest.

A) Describe the enteric nerve plexuses relevant to Hirschsprung's disease under the following headings:
A(i) Names, locations, and layers of the three plexuses
A(ii) Histopathological findings in the aganglionic segment on rectal biopsy
A(iii) Pathophysiological basis of intestinal obstruction in aganglionosis

B) Explain why Hirschsprung's disease is commoner in males, what the sex ratio is by segment length, and how the segment classification is distributed.

C) Distinguish between the macroscopic appearance of the three zones of the bowel in Hirschsprung's disease.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Three enteric nerve plexuses:
- Myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus: intermuscular, between the longitudinal and circular muscle layers
- Deep Submucosal (Henle's) plexus: on the inner surface of the circular muscle layer
- Superficial Submucosal (Meissner's) plexus: close to the muscularis mucosae
All three plexuses are deficient of ganglion cells in HD.

A(ii) Rectal biopsy findings (H&E):
- Absence of ganglion cells (transition zone is hypoganglionic)
- Increased size and number of nerve fibres
- Glomeruli-like conglomeration of nerve cells occasionally seen
- Increased staining for acetylcholinesterase (ACHase)

A(iii) In aganglionosis:
- Increased number and function of cholinergic excitatory fibres
- Increased number, function, and predominance of adrenergic excitatory over inhibitory fibres
- Decreased or loss of inhibitory purinergic (NO-mediated) fibres
These three factors cause the contracted, non-relaxing state of the aganglionic segment. Normal relaxation (mediated by non-cholinergic, non-adrenergic fibres, with NO as neurotransmitter identified in 1990) is lost.

B) Overall M:F ratio is 4:1. In short-segment disease M:F = 4:1; in long-segment disease M:F = 1:1; for total colonic aganglionosis the ratio favours females. Segment distribution: short segment HD (rectosigmoid 53%, rectum 24%) = 77%; ultrashort segment = 1%; long segment = 12%; total colonic aganglionosis = 10%.

C) Three macroscopic zones:
- Proximal intestine: dilated, thickened (hypertrophied) wall, mucosal oedema and ulceration; normoganglionic
- Transition zone: cone-shaped, commonly a gradual transition; zone of hypoganglionosis
- Distal bowel: undilated, endoscopically normal gross appearance, but microscopically aganglionic

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy and pathophysiology of oedema under the following headings.
A(i) Define oedema and distinguish it from anasarca. Define exudate and transudate.
A(ii) Describe the normal mechanism of interstitial fluid formation and reabsorption, including the hydrostatic and oncotic pressure values involved.
B(i) Describe the three types of brain oedema — vasogenic, cytotoxic and interstitial — including their pathogenesis and which tissues they preferentially affect.
B(ii) Describe the morphological features of cerebral oedema at autopsy and the clinical consequences.
C(i) Distinguish between hyperaemia and congestion, including their mechanisms and tissue appearances.
C(ii) Define haemorrhage, classify the lesions by size (petechiae, purpura, ecchymosis, haematoma), and explain how bruise colour changes are used to determine age of bruise.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Oedema: abnormal increased fluid in interstitial tissue spaces and natural body cavities. Fluid in cavities is designated specially — hydrothorax, hydropericardium, hydroperitoneum (ascites). Anasarca: severe, generalised oedema with profound subcutaneous tissue swelling. Exudate: increased vascular permeability leads to inflammatory oedema rich in proteins. Transudate: oedema due to hydrodynamic derangements that is protein poor.
A(ii) Normal mechanism: outflow of fluid from the arteriolar end of the microcirculation into the interstitium, nearly balanced by inflow at the venular end; the small residual amount is drained by lymphatic vessels. The hydrostatic pressure in the arteriolar segment of the capillary is 32 mmHg; at the middle of the capillary it is 20 mmHg. Hydrostatic pressure is opposed by plasma oncotic pressure of 26 mmHg. Interstitial fluid is formed at the rate of 2 mL/min and reabsorbed by lymphatics.
B(i) Vasogenic oedema: most common variety; excess fluid in the extracellular space of the brain; results from distortion of the blood-brain barrier; associated with trauma, neoplasms, encephalitis, abscesses, infarcts, haemorrhage, toxic brain injury (e.g., lead poisoning). Cytotoxic oedema: equivalent to hydropic cell swelling (accumulation of intracellular water); usually a response to cell injury such as ischaemia; preferentially affects grey matter. Interstitial oedema: consequence of hydrocephalus — fluid accumulates in cerebral ventricles and periventricular white matter.
B(ii) Morphology: at autopsy an oedematous brain is soft and heavy; gyri are flattened and sulci narrowed; severe cerebral oedema leads to herniation of cerebral tonsils with lethal consequences. Clinical: patients suffer vomiting, disorientation, and convulsions. Brain oedema is dangerous because the rigidity of the cranium allows little room for expansion.
C(i) Hyperaemia: active process; arteriolar dilatation; engorgement of vessels with oxygenated blood. Congestion: passive process; impaired tissue outflow, venous obstruction; cyanotic (bluish) appearance with accumulation of deoxygenated blood. Congestion occurs commonly with oedema; stasis of poorly oxygenated blood leads to hypoxia; capillary rupture may occur at sites of chronic congestion leading to haemorrhage.
C(ii) Haemorrhage: extravasation of blood due to vessel rupture. Petechiae: minute 1–2 mm diameter into skin, associated with locally increased intravascular pressure, low platelet count, defective platelet function or clotting defects. Purpura: >3 mm, associated with same disorders, may be due to trauma, vascular inflammation or increased vascular fragility. Ecchymosis: larger >1–2 cm subcutaneous haematomas usually seen after trauma. Bruise colour by age: red (swollen, tender) 0–2 days; bluish-red/red-purple 2–5 days; green 5–7 days; yellow 7–10 days; brown 10–14 days; no further bruising 2–4 weeks.

(i) Diagnosis: syndactyly. Swanson classification Type II — failure of differentiation. The absent pectoralis major and syndactyly suggest Poland Syndrome (syndactyly with hypoplastic pectoralis muscles).
(ii) Embryological steps: the hand forms at the end of elongated limb buds appearing on each side of the upper trunk of the embryo at 30 days of embryonal life. By 40 days, digital rays are formed with webbing of the digits. By 46 days, the webs regress by apoptosis to form five distinct digits. Normal apical ectodermal ridge interaction, epidermal-mesenchymal interaction, and mesenchymal-mesenchymal interaction are required for normal hand formation. Failure of apoptotic web regression (failure of differentiation) produces syndactyly.
(iii) Aetiological sequences:
- Malformation sequence: an intrinsic malformation exists in the embryo (e.g., radial dysplasia).
- Deformation sequence: an abnormal external mechanical or structural force results in secondary distortion (e.g., constriction bands).
- Disruption sequence: a healthy embryo is subjected to tissue breakdown or injury (e.g., TORCH infections, thalidomide-caused deformities).
Causes include genetic, environmental, and unknown factors; warfarin, phenytoin, and alcohol are implicated. Subsequent pregnancy risk: 0–25%.
(iv) Principles of treatment: (1) improve functional ability; (2) allow unrestricted growth; (3) achieve a socially acceptable appearance.
(v) Incidence: 1 in 626 (Conway, 1956); other studies: 0.7%. The three most common are: camptodactyly, syndactyly, and polydactyly.
questions.question:
A 3-year-old child is brought to the clinic with webbing of the index and middle fingers of both hands. The digits are fused from the base to the tip, with shared nail plates. The child is otherwise healthy, but review reveals a flat chest with absent pectoralis major on the left side.
(i) State the diagnosis and the Swanson classification type to which it belongs. Name the associated syndrome suggested by the additional finding.
(ii) Describe the embryological steps in the normal formation of the hand and the point at which failure produces this deformity.
(iii) Describe the aetiological classification (sequences) recognised for congenital hand deformities, with an example of each.
(iv) State the principles of treatment of congenital hand deformities.
(v) What is the incidence of congenital hand deformities, and which three types are noted as the most common?

A(i) Describe the anatomical features of the male urethra that make catheterization challenging — its length, curvature, sphincteric mechanism, and the role of adequate anaesthesia and lubrication in negotiating each segment.
A(ii) Describe the indication, management, and anatomical basis of each cause of failed urethral catheterization — addressing catheter size, urethral anaesthesia, lubrication, and patient relaxation — and state the definitive step when all urethral manoeuvres fail.
B(i) Describe the types of urethral drainage — tidal vs. continuous — and explain the specific indications for continuous drainage in terms of the pathology being treated.
B(ii) Describe the complications of allowing rubber catheters to remain beyond 4 weeks — specifically the development of encrustation and calculus — and explain why inflation of the catheter balloon with antiseptic solutions, normal saline, or fluids other than water causes the balloon to become non-deflatable.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The male urethra has length, two curvatures (penile and perineal), and a functional sphincter at the external urethral meatus and membranous urethra. Without anaesthesia, the patient experiences pain causing him to become uncooperative, tighten the external urethral sphincter while straining, making it impossible for the catheter to pass beyond the sphincter — like trying to pass through a locked gate. Without adequate lubrication, friction between the catheter and urethral mucosa causes the catheter to coil in the urethra and prevents advancement into the bladder. 2% xylocaine jelly: squeezed into the urethra, penile clamp or manual pressure (thumb and index finger) applied for 3–5 minutes; jelly milked proximally along penile shaft.

A(ii) Causes of failed catheterization and management:
- Catheter too big: causes excess friction and trauma; catheter too small: too floppy to negotiate the urethra.
- Inadequate urethral anaesthesia: patient in pain → external sphincter closes → catheter cannot pass.
- Inadequate lubrication: friction causes catheter to coil in urethra.
- Patient not relaxed: tense patient → external sphincter closes; encourage deep breathing; ask patient to try to void at the moment of catheter passage; distract patient's attention.
- Anatomical obstruction (stricture, BPH): mount catheter on an introducer; if this fails, leave the urethra alone; perform suprapubic cystostomy; perform retrograde urethrogram thereafter to identify the nature of the obstruction.
Definitive step when all urethral manoeuvres fail: suprapubic cystostomy and retrograde urethrogram.

B(i) Tidal drainage (spigotted catheter): catheter blocked and opened only for drainage at intervals. Continuous drainage: catheter connected to a urine bag; urine drains continuously.
Indications for continuous drainage: resting the bladder in excessive disturbing urinary frequency; resting the bladder in urinary incontinence; presence of a leaking suprapubic cystostomy wound; diabetic patient in chronic retention; intensive care patients requiring urine output monitoring.

B(ii) Allowing rubber catheters beyond 4 weeks: encrustations accumulate on the portion of the catheter within the bladder; these grow into a calculus (stone) around the catheter tip, making removal impossible even after balloon deflation. Body heat over time alters the rubber material of the balloon inflation channel, causing it to become non-deflatable.
Balloon non-deflation due to fluids:
- Antiseptic solutions: corrosive to the rubber material; cause the inflation channel to glue together, preventing deflation.
- Normal saline: NaCl crystallises in the channel, blocking it.
- Sterile water is safe; ordinary clean water is adequate.
- External clamping, crushing, or kinking also damage the inflation channel.

A(i) Level distribution: 95% at L5/S1 and L4/5; 4% at L3/4; 1% at L2/3 and L1/2.
Root/motor deficits by level:
- L3/4 → L4 root: weak quadriceps; possible weak dorsiflexion
- L4/5 → L5 root: weak dorsiflexion; weak big toe extension
- L5/S1 → S1 root: weak plantar flexion; absent ankle jerk
A(ii) Clinical features:
- Pain: low back pain with radicular component; worse with coughing, straining, sitting or standing for prolonged periods; improves with bed rest; sciatica; cramping.
- Sensory: paraesthesia; numbness; sensory loss on examination.
- Motor: weakness on examination.
- Other: sphincteric dysfunction; poor erection; lumbar scoliosis.
- Spinal signs: cannot walk on toes; cannot walk on heels; positive straight leg raise (SLR) sign (Lasègue's sign, Patrick's sign, Kernig's sign on examination).
B(i) Indications for surgery:
Elective: failed conservative management; sciatica with or without deficit not responding to treatment; recurrent incapacitating low back pain and sciatica; worsening neurological deficit.
Emergency: massive midline prolapsed disc causing cauda equina compression; nerve root compression with quadriceps weakness or foot drop; sphincteric dysfunction.
B(ii) Investigations: plain radiography; MRI; CT; CT + myelogram; myelogram; electromyography; discography; epidural venography.
Operative procedures: laminectomy; microdiscectomy; percutaneous discectomy (manual, laser, or chymopapain); standard partial hemilaminectomy + microdiscectomy; percutaneous endoscopic microdiscectomy; arthroplasty.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the lumbar disc herniation level distribution, giving the percentage at each level. For each of the clinically important levels (L3/4, L4/5, L5/S1), state the nerve root affected and the specific motor deficit expected.
A(ii) Describe the clinical features of lumbar disc herniation, covering pain characteristics, sensory symptoms, motor findings, and other clinical signs including spinal findings.
B(i) Describe the indications for surgery in lumbar disc disease, distinguishing elective from emergency indications.
B(ii) List all the investigations used in prolapsed lumbar disc disease, and describe all the operative procedures available.

Describe the origin, classification and management of soft tissue infections under the following headings.
A(i) Classify soft tissue infections (STIs) based on tissue involvement and necrosis, giving examples in each category.
A(ii) State the risk factors for development of STIs.
B(i) Describe the clinical features, causative organisms, and treatment of necrotising fasciitis and gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis).
B(ii) Describe Fournier's gangrene — including definition, microbiology, phases and treatment.
C(i) Describe the investigations required in STIs and the principles of antibiotic management.
C(ii) State the measures for prevention of surgical site infection (SSI), define the types of SSI and classify surgical wounds.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Classification: Focal (localised) — non-necrotising: impetigo, folliculitis, furunculosis, SSSS, TSS; necrotising: synergistic gangrene, Fournier's gangrene, Meleney's gangrene. Diffuse — non-necrotising: erysipelas, cellulitis; necrotising: necrotising fasciitis, clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene).
A(ii) Risk factors: Trauma — lacerations, burns, abrasions, crush injuries, open fractures, IV drug use, human bite, animal bite, past streptococcal cellulitis. Disease states — diabetes mellitus, arterial insufficiency, venous insufficiency, lymphoedema, chronic renal disease, liver cirrhosis, neutropenia, immune disorders, HIV/AIDS.
B(i) Necrotising fasciitis (flesh-eating bacterial syndrome): caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, S. aureus, C. perfringens, Aeromonas hydrophila, MRSA; can be polymicrobial (mainly) or monomicrobial; symptoms: intense pain, inflammation, fever, discolouration of skin, blisters, vomiting, fluid discharge; treatment: aggressive debridement, combination of IV antibiotics, amputation if severe; has a high mortality rate. Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis): also called clostridial myonecrosis; caused by Clostridium perfringens (also C. novyi, C. septicum, C. ramnosum); occurs in contaminated fractures and foreign bodies in lacerations; onset: pain out of proportion to size of wound; oedema, pallor and dark discolouration precede gangrene; gas production, shock; crepitus is a late feature; cold, pulseless extremities late; multi-organ dysfunction syndrome; treatment: adequate debridement and antibiotics, hyperbaric oxygen considered, amputation necessary in some cases.
B(ii) Fournier's gangrene: necrotising synergistic infection between aerobic and anaerobic bacteria; involving the scrotum, external genitalia; predominantly in males; polymicrobial — Staphylococci, Streptococci, Enterobacteriaceae, Anaerobes, Fungi; hallmark: intense pain and tenderness in the genitalia. Phases: prodromal fever, malaise and lethargy 2–7 days; intense genital pain and tenderness with oedema; progressive erythema; dusky appearance with crepitus; frank gangrene and purulent drainage. Treatment: IV antibiotics and debridement.
C(i) Investigations: FBC (leucocytosis, immature WBC), serum electrolytes, creatinine, RBG, serum CPK, serum proteins, calcium, radiography, CT/MRI, USS; blood culture; microscopy, culture and sensitivity; wound swab and wound biopsy. Antibiotic management principle: on admission do not start antibiotics immediately — first take blood/aspirate for microscopy and culture; then start broad-spectrum antibiotic (3rd generation cephalosporin); when results are available, change antibiotic only if patient is not improving; if improving, do not change the course.
C(ii) SSI prevention: proper skin preparation, gentle handling of tissues, meticulous haemostasis, removal of devitalised tissues, obliterate dead spaces, adequate irrigation, use of monofilament non-absorbable sutures, wound closure without tension. Types of SSI: superficial (on the skin of the incision); deep (beneath the incisional area — muscle, fascia); organ or space. Wound classification: Class I Clean; Class II Clean-contaminated; Class III Contaminated; Class IV Dirty-infected.

A(i) Consequences of failure of neural tube closure: anencephaly; craniorachischisis totalis; spinal dysraphism; encephalocele.
Classification of spinal dysraphism (spina bifida):
Major division 1 — Spina bifida occulta: a radiological diagnosis in which there is a defect of the spinous process and/or posterior neural arch.
Major division 2 — Spina bifida aperta (cystica): types are meningocele; myelomeningocele; rachischisis (myeloschisis).
A(ii) Types of spina bifida occulta: diastematomyelia; diplomyelia; dermal sinus tracts; dermoid cysts; neurenteric cysts; fibrous bands; lipomas.
B(i) Epidemiology: ethnic differences exist; higher incidence rates in India, UK, Egypt, and Northern Ireland. In the USA, common in children of German or Irish ancestry but less common in Blacks; Hispanics have the highest rate. Geographic incidence (per 1000 births): India South 11.4, North 3.9; China/Japan 0.2–0.25; USA 0.43–0.6; UK 1.04; Spain 0.78; Nigeria 1.37; Ghana 1.15; South Africa 2.56 (White), 1.05 (Mixed), 0.95 (Black); Venezuela 2.28–5.5. Prevention: folic acid daily during early pregnancy. Recurrence rate: 2–3% for the same mother.
B(ii) Assessment: clinical assessment; ultrasound; CT; MRI; myelogram (query).
Urinary incontinence management: no urinary diversion; clean intermittent catheterisation; drugs.
Orthopaedic management: correction of talipes; braces, canes, walkers; wheelchair; physiotherapy.

questions.answerText:
(i) Ascending cholangitis secondary to common bile duct (CBD) stone obstruction. Pathological sequence: gallstones form due to altered bile composition (cholesterol, mixed, or pigment stones). A stone obstructing the CBD causes biliary ductal colic. With superimposed infection, cholangitis develops. Obstruction with infection leads to abdominal pain, high fever/rigors, and obstructive jaundice.
(ii) Charcot's triad for cholangitis: abdominal pain + high fever/rigors + obstructive jaundice; together with severe RUQ tenderness. Significance: indicates an obstructed and infected biliary system requiring urgent drainage.
(iii) Investigations:
- FBC: leucocytosis (acute inflammatory complication).
- LFTs: obstructive jaundice pattern.
- Ultrasound: detects 90% of gallstones; assesses CBD size and possible presence of CBD stones.
- ERCP: for suspected or proven CBD stones; allows stone removal or stent placement to bypass obstruction.
- OGD: to exclude peptic ulcer disease as a cause of symptoms.
(iv) Management of ascending cholangitis:
- IV fluids and antibiotics.
- Ductal drainage — now usually by ERCP, sphincterotomy, and extraction of stones.
(v) Complications of cholecystectomy: leakage of bile from cystic duct or gallbladder bed; jaundice due to retained ductal stones (retained stones can be treated by ERCP or, if a T-tube is in place, by extraction with a Dormia basket — Burhenne manoeuvre); injury to the CBD.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Osteosarcoma: affects children and adolescents (recent significant rise in age of presentation). Site: metaphyseal tumour. Clinical features: pain — constant, worse at night; mass; pathological fracture. X-ray: variable picture; 'sunburst' effect; Codman's triangle. Biopsy — histology confirms diagnosis. Treatment: neoadjuvant chemotherapy 8–12 weeks; wide resection; post-op chemotherapy 6–12 months; long-term survival 50–60%.
A(ii) Ewing's sarcoma: origin — endothelial cells of marrow; age — 10–20 years; X-ray — mid-diaphyseal lesion (in contrast to metaphyseal location of osteosarcoma). Reticulum cell sarcoma: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. Multiple myeloma: malignant B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder of the marrow — plasma cells predominating; causes plasma protein abnormalities, increased blood viscosity, anaemia, hypercalcaemia; age 45–65 years.
B(i) Chondrosarcoma: 4th–5th decade of life. It is neither chemo-sensitive nor radio-sensitive — in contrast to osteosarcoma which responds to chemotherapy (neoadjuvant and post-operative) and Ewing's sarcoma which responds to chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
B(ii) Safe site for biopsy: incisional biopsy should be done at the boundary zone of the tumour (not through uninvolved tissue). Biopsy techniques: (1) large-bone needle biopsy; (2) open biopsy — incisional (boundary zone) or excisional. Multidisciplinary team required: orthopaedic surgeon; radiologist; pathologist; oncologist; prosthetist; rehabilitation therapist. Patient must be admitted, firm diagnosis established, and patient counselled with pros and cons of treatment options.
questions.question:
Regarding primary malignant bone tumours:

A(i) For osteosarcoma, describe the typical patient age, anatomical site, clinical features (pain characteristics, mass, and pathological fracture), and the specific radiological findings.
A(ii) Describe the origin, age group, and characteristic radiological site of Ewing's sarcoma. Distinguish it from reticulum cell sarcoma and multiple myeloma.

B(ii) State the safe site principle for biopsy of a suspected malignant bone tumour, name the two biopsy techniques, and explain the cooperation required between clinical disciplines in the management of bone tumours.

A(i) Describe the functional anatomy of the oesophagus under the headings: primary function, muscle composition in the lower two-thirds, arrangement of muscle layers, and type of peristalsis produced.
A(ii) Describe the nerve supply of the oesophagus, naming the nerve, the plexus it supplies, and the two types of postganglionic neurons that differentiate from it, including the neurotransmitters each releases.
B(i) State the three physiological constriction sites of the oesophagus (as natural narrowings) and the approximate proportions of blunt foreign bodies that lodge at each site.
B(ii) Explain the anatomical reason why batteries lodging at any of these sites are particularly dangerous, naming the three mechanisms of injury they cause.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Functional anatomy:
- The oesophagus is primarily meant for aboral transport of ingested matter.
- The lower two-thirds have smooth muscle.
- It has an outer longitudinal and inner circular layer.
- Both layers run an elliptical spiral course, giving a worm-like peristalsis.

A(ii) Nerve supply:
- The vagus nerve supplies the myenteric plexus.
- The postganglionic neurons differentiate into two types:
 - Excitatory cholinergic neurons: release acetylcholine (ACH).
 - Inhibitory nitrergic neurons: release nitric oxide (NO) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP).
- The coordinated release results in a balanced contraction and relaxation.

B(i) Physiological constriction sites and proportions of blunt foreign body lodgement:
- Upper oesophageal sphincter (UOS) region: approximately 70% of blunt foreign bodies lodge here.
- Mid-oesophagus (where the aortic arch and carina overlap the oesophagus): approximately 15% lodge here.
- Lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS): approximately 15% lodge here.

B(ii) Why batteries are particularly dangerous:
- Batteries cause injury by three mechanisms: pressure necrosis, electrolysis, and alkali leakage.
- These mechanisms cause rapid perforation of the oesophageal wall, which is why batteries must be removed without any delay.

A(i) Ureteric injuries constitute less than 1% of genitourinary injuries. Penetrating injuries are the main cause; 10–20% from blunt trauma. PUJ injury is common in children due to deceleration causing hyperextensibility of the spine. High-velocity missiles can cause ureteric injury. The ureter runs from the kidney to the bladder through the retroperitoneum, passing close to major pelvic structures.
A(ii) Iatrogenic ureteric injury occurs during: splenic surgery, colonic surgery, gynaecologic surgery, or obstetric surgeries. The ureter is vulnerable because it runs in close proximity to the ovarian vessels, the uterine artery, and the lateral pelvic side wall — all areas routinely encountered during pelvic and colorectal surgery. The absence of physical signs makes early diagnosis of iatrogenic ureteric injury difficult and requires a high index of suspicion.
B(i) Clinical features of ureteric injury: Symptoms — fever 38.3–38.8°C; abdominal pain (flank, lower quadrant); abdominal distension (paralytic ileus), nausea, vomiting; urine leak due to fistula (ureterovaginal, cutaneous). Signs — febrile; hydronephrosis (flank mass); ileus causing abdominal distension; peritonitis due to extravasation; watery discharge from wound or vagina. Missed diagnosis leads to: prolonged ileus, raised BUN, persistent flank pain, abdominal mass, urinary obstruction, sepsis. Diagnosis requires high index of suspicion; haematuria is absent in 25–70% of cases.
B(ii) Investigations — Ureteric injury: USS (urinoma, hydronephrosis); IVU or retrograde ureterography; CT scan; Radionuclide scanning (delayed excretion, post-operative renal function); Intraoperative — methylene blue or indigo carmine in collecting system. Renal injury: Ultrasound scan; CT; IVU; Arteriography.

questions.answerText:
(i) Complication: Hirschsprung's-associated enterocolitis (HAEC).
It is the most serious complication of Hirschsprung's disease: it commonly pursues a rapid, fatal course in neonates, with death possible within 24 hours. It presents as a paradox of diagnostic confusion; misdiagnosis is common.

(ii) Pathophysiological sequence:
- Colonic stasis from the aganglionic segment
- Bacterial overgrowth in stagnant bowel content
- Alteration in mucin composition
- Decline in GALT (gut-associated lymphoid tissue) defence
- Entero-adherent bacteria attach to unprotected intestinal epithelium
- Invasion of bacteria into the epithelium
- Inflammatory process develops (ischaemia, mucosal ulcerations)
- Sepsis and coagulopathy develop → systemic symptoms
Plain X-ray findings: pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in the bowel wall), saw-tooth appearance of mucosa, rectosigmoid index <1.

(iii) Immediate resuscitative management:
- Stabilise: IV fluids (electrolyte correction), IV antibiotics (broad-spectrum)
- Rectal washouts to decompress the bowel
- NPO + nasogastric tube
- Monitor urinary output
- ICU care if rapid deterioration
- Emergency colostomy if conservative management fails

(iv) Definitive treatment to prevent recurrence:
- Early definitive pull-through surgery (Swenson's, Duhamel's, or Soave's procedure) after stabilisation — resects the aganglionic segment, removing the cause of colonic stasis
- Initial loop/defunctioning colostomy in the ganglionated bowel provides immediate decompression while the neonate is optimised for definitive surgery
