A 28-year-old man falls on an outstretched hand. X-ray shows a fracture of the shaft of the ulna with anterior dislocation of the radial head. A second X-ray taken on a different patient shows fracture of the shaft of the radius combined with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint.

(i) Identify both fracture-dislocation patterns and classify the first injury by its four types, stating which type is illustrated.
(ii) State the structures involved in each injury and the specific radiological assessment needed to confirm all components.
(iii) Describe the differential management approach for each injury in children versus adults.
(iv) What are the general local complications of nerve injury that can arise from closed fractures of the forearm and upper limb, and state the most commonly affected nerve and the fracture associated with it?
questions.answerText:
(i) First injury: Monteggia fracture-dislocation (fracture of ulna + dislocation of radial head). Second injury: Galeazzi fracture-dislocation (fracture of shaft of radius + dislocation of distal radioulnar joint). Monteggia types: Type I — radial head dislocated anteriorly (commonest); Type II — radial head dislocated posteriorly; Type III — radial head dislocated laterally; Type IV — Type I with fracture of the radius. Illustrated case is Type I.
(ii) Monteggia: ulnar shaft fracture + radial head dislocation at the elbow. Galeazzi: radial shaft fracture + distal radioulnar joint disruption at the wrist. Radiological assessment: AP and lateral views of the forearm, including full elbow and wrist joint views, to capture both components of each injury.
(iii) Monteggia: in children — closed reduction should be attempted; in adults — open reduction is essential for good outcome. Galeazzi: in children — closed reduction is advocated; in adults — open reduction gives excellent results. Both injuries in adults therefore require operative intervention due to the difficulty of maintaining reduction of associated joint components by closed means.
(iv) Nerve injury classifications: neuropraxia is common in closed fracture injury. Nerve compression may occur due to callous formation. Most commonly affected nerve: radial nerve — most commonly affected in humeral shaft fracture, especially at the mid-shaft level. Other complications of nerves: late entrapment by scar tissue causing neuroma.

questions.question:
Describe the origin, course, key relations, and functions of the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) in the neck, state the safe site for a surgical procedure in the neck that protects this nerve, and explain the anatomical basis of the clinical deficits that follow its injury in the context of neck trauma.
A(i) Describe the course and key relations of the vagus nerve in the neck.
A(ii) State the contents of the carotid sheath and explain why the vagus nerve is vulnerable in neck trauma.
B(i) State what deficit results from injury to the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve.
B(ii) Explain the anatomical basis for the clinical signs produced by cranial nerve injuries in Zone III neck trauma.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) is contained within the carotid sheath. The carotid sheath encloses the carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve. The nerve runs in the neck within this sheath and gives rise to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which supplies the larynx. The vagus nerve is one of the neural structures at risk in neck trauma, listed alongside the spinal cord, phrenic nerve, brachial plexus, recurrent laryngeal nerve, cranial nerves IX–XII, and stellate ganglion.
A(ii) The carotid sheath contains: the carotid artery, the internal jugular vein, and the vagus nerve. Because the majority of the important vascular and visceral organs lie within the anterior triangle bounded by the sternocleidomastoid posteriorly, the midline anteriorly, and the mandible superiorly, the vagus nerve — lying within this sheath — is directly at risk from penetrating or blunt trauma to the anterior triangle.
B(i) Injury to the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) causes hoarseness (weak voice).
B(ii) Zone III cranial nerve injury signs: Facial nerve (VII) — drooping of the corner of the mouth. Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) — dysphagia (altered gag reflex). Vagus nerve (X, recurrent laryngeal) — hoarseness (weak voice). Spinal accessory nerve (XI) — inability to shrug a shoulder and to laterally rotate the chin to the opposite shoulder. Hypoglossal nerve (XII) — deviation of the tongue with protrusion.

A(i) Epidemiology: 40 cases per 10⁶ population, or 11,000 new cases per year in the US; prevalence approximately 250,000 alive with SCI in the US. Since 2000, average age at injury is 37.6 years (previously 28.7 years). Approximately 79.6% of subjects are male; M:F = 5:1. Status at discharge: incomplete tetraplegia (34.5%), complete paraplegia (23.1%), complete tetraplegia (18.4%), and incomplete paraplegia (17.5%).
A(ii) Mechanisms of injury: vertical loading force; hyperflexion/hyperextension injury; lateral rotation injuries; flexion distraction injuries; fracture/dislocation. Acting via traction, compression, and compromise of blood supply/drainage.
Primary injuries: concussion; laceration/transection; contusion.
Secondary injuries: haematomas; hypotension; oedema; disc prolapse; electrolyte derangement; hypoxia; compression from fracture fragments.
B(i) Management principles:
- Accident site and transport: immobilise spine
- Casualty: resuscitation — airway, breathing, circulation
- Definitive: Reduction (closed or open); Immobilization (closed or open); Rehabilitation.
Four overarching principles: Resuscitation; Reduction; Immobilization; Rehabilitation.
B(ii) Supportive management of quadriplegic/paraplegic: regular turning 2-hourly or use of water bed/electric beds; expose to air; chest and limb physiotherapy; clean intermittent catheterisation; anticoagulation; psychological support.
Complications: depression; infections (UTI, chest infections, wound infections); pressure sores; genitourinary complications; DVT/pulmonary embolism.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the epidemiology of spinal cord injury, including annual incidence, prevalence, average age, sex distribution, and the distribution of neurological status at discharge.
A(ii) Describe the mechanisms of spinal cord injury, distinguishing primary injuries from secondary injuries and naming the specific types under each.
B(i) Outline the complete management principles for spinal cord injury under the headings: accident site, transport, casualty, and definitive care — including the four overarching principles.
B(ii) Describe the supportive management of quadriplegia/paraplegia and list all the recognised complications of spinal cord injury.

Describe the classification and pathophysiology of shock and burns, and explain the Jacksonian zones of local tissue injury.

A(i) Define shock and list all its types; state the ultimate consequence if shock is unrelieved.
A(ii) Describe the English and American classification of burns in full, including depth, histological layer involved, and clinical features at each level.
B(i) Describe the Jacksonian zones of burn injury at the microscopic level; state what macroscopic events are also seen locally.
B(ii) Describe the systemic metabolic and GIT changes in burns, including the specific named gastric complication and the mechanism of energy expenditure increase.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Shock is a syndrome that occurs from lack of tissue perfusion at the microvascular level. Types: haemorrhagic, hypovolaemic, endotoxic, vasovagal, cardiogenic, anaphylactic. The ultimate consequence if unrelieved: hypotension, poor perfusion of major organs, multiple organ failure, then death.

A(ii) English classification: Partial thickness burns — (a) Superficial partial thickness: extends up to the papillary dermis; heals in two weeks by regeneration of totipotential cells of sebaceous glands, hair follicles and wound edge; pain-prick sensation is intact. (b) Deep partial thickness: extends up to the reticular dermis; may form hypertrophic scar; pin-prick sensation is reduced. Full thickness burns: extends beyond the dermis; eschar is formed; no pain-prick sensation. American classification: First degree (epidermis involved); Second degree (papillary dermis); Third degree (reticular dermis); Fourth degree (beyond the dermis).

B(i) Microscopic Jacksonian zones: zone of hyperaemia (periphery); zone of stasis (intermediate); central zone of coagulative necrosis (innermost). Macroscopic events: erythema, blistering, whitish mottling of the skin, and charring. Vascular events: transient vasoconstriction followed by vasodilatation.

B(ii) Metabolic changes: resting energy expenditure of adult is 6,300–7,500 J/24 hours; in burns it increases by 40–100% or higher. Up to 250–500 g of fat may be broken down daily. Caused by catecholamines, glucagon, cortisol, and growth hormones; inhibited by insulin and prostaglandin E. GIT changes: paralytic ileus which may lead to translocation of gut micro-organisms into the systemic circulation to cause septicaemia. Named gastric complication: Curling's ulcer.

questions.question:
A patient presents with a chronic perianal discharge of seropurulent fluid mixed with flatus, and history of a recurrent perianal boil that partially heals before discharging again. On examination there is an external opening near the anus with induration and pus discharge, and an internal orifice is palpable in the anorectum.

(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Using Parks' classification, describe all four anatomical types, specifying the path of each tract relative to the sphincter complex.
(iii) List three risk factors or predisposing conditions for development of this condition.
(iv) Describe the treatment for a low-level fistula and the treatment for a high-level fistula, naming the specific procedure used for each.
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is fistula-in-ano.

(ii) Parks' classification — four anatomical types:
- Intersphincteric: the most common type; the tract is confined to the intersphincteric space.
- Trans-sphincteric: the tract connects the intersphincteric tract to the ischiorectal fossa, passing through the external sphincter.
- Supra-sphincteric: the tract loops over the external sphincter and perforates the levator ani.
- Extra-sphincteric: tracts run from the rectum to perianal skin, external to the sphincter complex.

(iii) Risk factors/predisposing conditions (any three):
- Underlying rectal disease: neoplasm, Crohn's disease, actinomycosis, tuberculosis, chlamydial infection.
- Immunoincompetence: diabetes mellitus, AIDS, patients on cytotoxic drugs.
- Trauma or surgery to the anorectum.
- Anal fissure.
- Radiotherapy for anorectal or prostate cancer.
- Inflammatory bowel disease or diverticulitis.

(iv) Treatment:
- Low-level fistula: fistulotomy with deroofing; fistulectomy for anterior non-inflamed and non-infected fistula; Parks' operation, which drains the intersphincteric region by internal sphincterotomy then lays open the part lateral to the external sphincter.
- High-level fistula: insertion of a Seton — the main track into the rectum is identified and a stout silk or linen ligature (Seton) is passed through it and tied loosely around the remaining part of the external anal sphincter; alternatively, a two-staged treatment.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man is found unresponsive at home. His wife says he complained of a severe headache before collapsing. On arrival he is unresponsive (GCS 6), has neck stiffness, and there are no focal neurological signs.
(i) Based on the clusters of signs present, state the two most likely diagnoses and the investigation that is required.
(ii) Describe the complete ABCDE systematic approach to the unconscious patient.
(iii) State the immediate pharmacological coma cocktail — listing each drug, its dose, and its indication.
(iv) Describe the signs that suggest the patient is awake but unresponsive, distinguishing the abulic state from locked-in syndrome from psychogenic unresponsiveness.
(v) In a non-trauma patient unconscious for six hours, what are the proportional causes of prolonged unconsciousness?
questions.answerText:
(i) Cluster: meningism without focal neurological signs — the two most likely diagnoses are subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm and meningitis. Required investigation: head CT scan (essential); if CT is negative but SAH is still suspected, perform lumbar puncture.
(ii) ABCDE approach:
- A (airway): ensure patient airway — airway manoeuvres, suction, and adjuncts may be required. Intubation with cuffed endotracheal tube is the definitive method of protecting the airway.
- B (breathing): ensure adequate breathing; treat problems as found.
- C (circulation): ensure adequate circulation; treat problems as found.
- D (disability): assess Glasgow Coma Score, pupils, and bedside glucose measurement.
- E (examination): full examination including notes, eye witnesses, and charts for clues to diagnosis. Consider CT brain if no diagnosis.
If stable and not intubated, consider the recovery position.
(iii) Pharmacological coma cocktail:
- Thiamine 100 mg IV — prevents Wernicke-Korsakoff encephalopathy; do not withhold glucose if thiamine unavailable.
- Glucose 25–50 g IV — to treat hypoglycaemia.
- Naloxone 2–4 ampules of 0.4 mg — to treat narcotic overdose; restrain patient if suspect narcotic withdrawal; consider in all unconscious patients.
- Flumazenil (Romazicon) 0.2 mg up to 5 mg IV — if benzodiazepine overdose suspected; do not use if concurrent tricyclic overdose or chronic benzodiazepine use suspected; may precipitate status epilepticus.
(iv) Awake but unresponsive:
- Abulic state: frontal lobe function depressed; may take several minutes to answer a question.
- Locked-in syndrome: destruction of pontine motor tracts; patient is able to look upward.
- Psychogenic unresponsiveness.
(v) In non-trauma patients unconscious for 6 hours: 40% will have taken some form of sedative. Of the remaining 60%, approximately one third have hypoxic brain injury (e.g., after cardiac arrest), one third have a cerebrovascular cause (infarct or haemorrhage), and one third have a metabolic cause (e.g., diabetes or liver disease).

questions.question:
A 22-year-old woman presents with a six-week history of right iliac fossa swelling and five months of amenorrhoea, with one week of bleeding per vaginum. She is pale and tender in the right iliac fossa.

(i) State two differential diagnoses. Using the surgical clerking framework, how would you characterise the presenting complaint of swelling?
(ii) Describe the local examination findings (palpation and percussion) using standard clerking headings.
(iii) What is the differential diagnosis framework (the standard mnemonic) for any surgical swelling, and what pathognomonic signs help classify specific types of swelling?
(iv) Describe the investigations available for soft tissue masses.
questions.answerText:
(i) Differential diagnoses: right tubo-ovarian mass and choriocarcinoma. Characterisation of swelling: Location; Onset (when and how was it noticed); Progression (increased progressively in size, static, any changes since first occurred, ever disappear); Painful; Discharge; Swelling in any other part of the body.

(ii) Palpation findings: tenderness; temperature (compare with distant skin); thrill; texture/consistency (soft, firm, hard); size (2-dimensional); pulsation; getting above and below it; fluctuancy in two axes; reducibility; emptying; fixity/mobility (attachment to surrounding structures — skin, fascia, etc.); regional lymph nodes; skin sensation; transillumination. Percussion: an indirect evaluation of size/extent (e.g. retrosternal goitre; abdomen — liver, spleen, other masses, ascites).

(iii) Differential diagnosis mnemonic — TINCABED: Trauma, Inflammatory/Infection, Neoplastic, Congenital, Angiogenic, Blood, Endocrine, Degenerative. Pathognomonic signs: Emptying sign — haemangioma; slipping sign and lobulation — lipoma; punctum — sebaceous cyst; cafe au lait spots — neurofibroma (von Recklinghausen disease); movement on swallowing — goitre; movement on tongue protrusion — thyroglossal duct cyst; reducibility — hernia, hydrocoele; transillumination (clear fluid) — hydrocoele; soft and fluctuant — cyst.

(iv) Investigations: tissue biopsy (FNAB/cytology, Trucut, incisional, excisional); FBC; ESR; urinalysis; stool microscopy; tuberculin test; tumour markers; radiology (X-rays — local and chest; ultrasound scan; CT scan; MRI; IVU; barium swallow/meal/enema); endoscopy (oesophagogastroscopy, proctosigmoidoscopy, colonoscopy, bronchoscopy, urethrocystoscopy).

A(i) Classification: Inflammation/infection — thyroiditis; hyperthyroidism — primary or secondary; hypothyroidism; goitre — various types (simple/non-toxic colloid/diffuse or nodular; toxic — toxic nodule, diffuse toxic (Graves), toxic nodular (Plummer's), or malignant toxic; inflammatory — thyroiditis, De Quervain's, Hashimoto, Riedel's; neoplastic — benign or malignant); thyroid nodule(s) — solitary or multiple; thyroid neoplasm.
A(ii) Clinical features: anterior neck mass; symptoms and signs of hyperthyroidism; symptoms and signs of hypothyroidism; signs of skin, GIT, CNS, UGS; eye signs; hoarseness of voice; features of metastatic disease.
B(i) Investigations: TFTs (T3, T4, TSH) — assess thyroid hormone levels; ultrasound scanning — morphology; thyroid scan (technetium 99m or radioactive iodine 123) — functional imaging; plain radiograph of neck + thoracic inlet, CXR — assess tracheal deviation, retrosternal extension; FNAB — cytological diagnosis; CT-Scan, MRI, PET-Scan — extent of spread of cancer; laryngoscopy — assess vocal cord function; auto-immune antibodies — identify autoimmune cause.
B(ii) WHO grading: Grade 0 — no goitre palpable or visible; Grade 1a — goitre felt but not visible even with neck extended; Grade 1b — goitre felt, visible with neck extended but not with neck in normal position; Grade 2 — goitre easily visible with neck in normal position; Grade 3 — goitre easily visible from a distance.
C(i) Thyroid diseases are commoner in females than males; however, when thyroid disease occurs in a male, the risk of malignancy is increased.
C(ii) Simple diffuse goitre (colloid goitre): persistently elevated TSH levels lead to diffuse active lobules, then TSH levels fall and lobules become inactive and filled with colloid; presentation — slowly growing bosselated anterior neck swelling, firm, non-tender, moves with swallowing but not protrusion of the tongue; normal TFTs; treated by thyroidectomy (total or subtotal). Multinodular goitre: enlarged thyroid gland with two or more nodules; most common non-toxic goitre; iodine deficiency causes diffuse follicular hyperplasia leading to nodule formation; same presentation; treated by thyroidectomy (total or subtotal); may be complicated by airway or oesophageal obstruction, toxicity, or malignant transformation.
questions.question:
Describe the thyroid gland under the following headings.
A(i) Classification of thyroid diseases — list all types as presented.
A(ii) Clinical features common to thyroid disease — list the presenting signs and symptoms.
B(i) Investigations used in thyroid disease — name every investigation mentioned and state the use of each.
B(ii) Describe the WHO grading of goitres.
C(i) State the sex distribution of thyroid disease and how the risk of malignancy differs between the sexes.
C(ii) Distinguish between simple diffuse goitre and multinodular goitre in terms of definition, pathology and treatment.

Regarding body fluid distribution and management in the peri-trauma period:

A(i) Describe the distribution of total body water between compartments (intracellular and extracellular), stating the major effective solutes in each compartment and the role of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump.
A(ii) Explain the forces governing fluid movement between the intravascular and interstitial compartments, and between the extracellular and intracellular compartments.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for preferring Lactated Ringer's over Normal Saline in trauma resuscitation, state the limit at which crystalloids must be supplemented with blood, and explain why colloids are not preferred.
B(ii) Distinguish between hypovolemia and fluid overload in the trauma patient, including the monitoring parameters used to detect each.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Total body water ~60% of lean body mass in young men; 50% in young women and older men; 45% in older women. 70% of body water is intracellular; 30% is extracellular (includes plasma and interstitial fluid; small amounts in bone, connective tissue, digestive secretions, CSF). Extracellular major solutes: Na+ salts (primarily NaCl and NaHCO3). Intracellular major solute: K+, balanced by anionic charges on impermeant macromolecules. Na+/K+ ATPase pump on cell membranes keeps intracellular Na+ at low levels; it also drives sodium reabsorption in the basolateral membrane of renal tubular cells.
A(ii) Between intravascular and interstitial compartments: filtration driven by hydrostatic pressure gradient generated by cardiac contractions; oncotic pressure due to intravascular proteins. Between extracellular and intracellular compartments: osmotic forces — some solutes like ethanol and urea are ineffective osmoles; sodium and mannitol are effective osmoles that drive water movement.
B(i) Lactated Ringer's preferred over Normal Saline because it buffers metabolic acidosis better. Crystalloids may replace blood loss to a limit of 8:1; blood is needed when crystalloid infusion exceeds 50 ml/kg. Colloids not preferred: meta-analysis shows use of colloids is associated with higher mortality; they are costly; they may aggravate post-traumatic complications.
B(ii) Hypovolemia: decrease in effective intravascular volume leading to poor perfusion from lowered preload or low Hb; age is a significant confounding factor; clinical monitoring may be impaired by anaesthesia or opiate analgesics; urine output, invasive monitoring (pulmonary artery catheter, cardiac echocardiography), serum lactate, and isotonic fluid challenge with Ringer's lactate are used. Fluid overload: associated with poor outcomes; in shock, capillary leak may cause anasarca, which can be confused with fluid overload; patients may require invasive monitoring; increased body weight may also accompany anasarca.

questions.question:
Describe the surgical management of nutritional support under the following headings.
A(i) Define protein-energy malnutrition in surgical patients and state its prevalence.
A(ii) Describe the metabolic responses to starvation — early and prolonged.
B(i) Describe the metabolic response to surgery, stating the mediators involved and the degree of catabolism for different operative insults.
B(ii) State the indications for nutritional support.
C(i) Describe the routes of nutritional support, and state the advantages of enteral feeding.
C(ii) Describe total parenteral nutrition (TPN) — its indications, routes of catheter insertion, administration schedule, monitoring and complications.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Protein-energy malnutrition is common in hospital patients — 40% of all surgical and medical admissions. Most patients will experience some malnutrition in the course of admission. There is a direct relationship between nutritional levels and surgical outcomes. Nutritional depletion leads to tissue wasting, impaired organ function, impaired immune and cardiovascular functions; the more severe the malnutrition, the more frequent the postoperative complications and deaths. Obesity had the same prognostic value as malnutrition.
A(ii) Early starvation (within 12 hours): plasma insulin levels fall, glucagon levels rise, hepatic and muscle glycogenolysis. After 24 hours: gluconeogenesis from amino acids with loss of 75g of skeletal muscles per day; gluconeogenesis in liver and kidney using glutamine, alanine, lactate and glycerol. 100g of exogenous glucose is sufficient to prevent muscle breakdown early in fasting. Prolonged fasting: lipolysis with generation of fatty acids and glycerol; adaptive ketogenesis ensues in the liver; after 2 weeks the brain adapts to using ketone bodies instead of glucose.
B(i) Metabolic response to surgery: initial and transient sympathetic activity with catecholamine release; prolonged hypermetabolic change with negative nitrogen balance. Mediators: cytokines like TNF, IL-1 and IL-6. Metabolic rate increased by 10% in average surgical procedure; increased by 50% in peritonitis; up to 100% in extensive burns. Degree of catabolism depends on extent of surgery.
B(ii) Indications for nutritional support: premorbid state; current nutritional status; age of patient; duration of starvation; degree of anticipated insult; likelihood of resuming normal intake soon; weight loss of 15%; serum albumin value less than 3g/100ml.
C(i) Routes: Enteral — oral, naso-gastric, naso-duodenal, naso-jejunal, gastrostomy, jejunostomy. Parenteral — intraperitoneal (in children), intravenous — peripheral and central vein. Oral is the best way to correct malnutrition. Advantages of enteral feeding: reduces operative complications; increases wound healing; alters gut antigen response; increases gut oxygenation; preserves gut flora; maintains immunocompetence; substrate better utilised.
C(ii) TPN indications: functionless GIT (fistulas, obstruction); pre-op preparation in malnourished patient unable to eat; GIT diseases requiring prolonged GIT rest; pre-op preparation for major procedure with high morbidity; malabsorption diseases; anorexic conditions (carcinomatosis, chemotherapy, anorexia nervosa). Routes for CVP catheter: infraclavicular percutaneous subclavian; supraclavicular percutaneous subclavian; internal jugular vein; peripheral vein at cubital fossa; catheter tip at SVC or right atrium. Administration: Day 1 — 1L/24h; Day 2 — 2L/24h; Day 3 onwards — 3L/24h. Complications: catheter-related (phlebitis, pneumothorax, haemothorax, air embolism); sepsis (fungal and bacterial); hyperglycaemia (osmotic dehydration); rebound hypoglycaemia from sudden termination; allergic reaction.

A(i) Embryological origin and sites:
- Neuroblastoma is an embryonal tumour of neural crest origin
- Arises from the adrenal medulla or sympathetic ganglion from neck to pelvis
- Sites: adrenal medulla 50% (retroperitoneal); paraspinal ganglia 25%; posterior mediastinum 20%; pelvis and neck 5%

A(ii) Pathological features:
Macroscopy:
- Purple, highly vascular and friable
- Becomes nodular as it matures or responds to therapy
Microscopy:
- Composed of neuroblasts — small round cells with prominent nucleus and small cytoplasm
- Immature tumour: no special arrangement; closely packed small spheroid cells (undifferentiated)
- More mature tumour: rosette formation; some resemble normal ganglion cells (differentiated)
Electron microscopy: neurofibrils and electron dense granules (distinguishes from PNET, rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing's tumour)

B) Safe site for tissue diagnosis: open biopsy or CT-guided biopsy; bone marrow aspiration for staging.
Tumour markers:
- VMA (Vanillylmandelic acid) = elevated in more mature NB
- HVA (Homovanillic acid) = elevated in undifferentiated NB
- NSE (Neuron-specific enolase), LDH, serum ferritin = additional markers; elevated levels associated with poor prognosis
- Tumour-derived ganglioside GD2 used for targeted immunotherapy

C) Anatomical basis of presentations:
- Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis): cervical sympathetic chain involvement
- 'Panda eyes'/bilateral orbital ecchymosis: haematogenous metastasis to the orbital bones
- 'Dancing eye syndrome' (acute cerebellar ataxia): paraneoplastic effect on the cerebellum
- Paraplegia ('dumbbell tumour'): paraspinal tumour extends through the intervertebral foramen into the spinal canal, compressing the spinal cord

A 25-year-old previously healthy woman presents with a sudden onset of severe headache that built over several minutes, followed by left-sided weakness and vomiting. She has no history of hypertension. CT brain shows a right-sided intracerebral haematoma in the parietal region without the typical basal ganglia distribution. There is no subarachnoid blood.
(i) What is the most likely underlying cause, and why does the age and location argue against the most common cause of intracerebral haemorrhage?
(ii) Describe the underlying vascular pathology of the most likely cause, including its definition, incidence, and the age group most commonly affected.
(iii) Outline the workup required for this patient, listing all imaging modalities in the order they should be performed.
(iv) Describe the treatment of elevated ICP and the definitive treatment options, including the adjunct that is not curative on its own.
(v) State the risk of rebleeding in the first year and the goal of ultimate treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely cause: ruptured arteriovenous malformation (AVM). This argues against hypertensive haemorrhage because: most hypertensive ICH patients are over 45 years old; haemorrhage in hypertensive ICH occurs in characteristic areas (basal ganglia/internal capsule 60%, cerebellar nuclei 10–15%, pons 10%, thalamus 10%); there is no history of hypertension; and AVMs should always be suspected when classic features of hypertensive haemorrhage are absent.
(ii) AVM: congenital developmental defects in the cerebral vasculature consisting of tangles of arteries feeding directly into tangles of veins without intervening capillary network. Incidence: 0.5% of population. Haemorrhages usually occur in patients between the ages of 20–40 but may occur at any age. AVMs account for 10–20% of intracerebral haemorrhages.
(iii) Workup in order: (1) head CT scan in all patients with suspected intracranial haemorrhage; (2) cerebral angiography — essential in any patient suspected of having an AVM; (3) MRI — may provide additional anatomic details.
(iv) Management of elevated ICP: intubate with modest hyperventilation to pCO2 of 30; mannitol 0.5–1.0 g/kg IV push; furosemide 5–20 mg IV; elevate head 20–30 degrees; avoid neck vein compression; sedate and paralyse with morphine and vecuronium if necessary; avoid antihypertensives to lower blood pressure. Definitive treatment options: angiographic embolisation (adjunct to surgery, not curative on its own); surgical resection; stereotactic radiosurgery in selected cases.
(v) Rebleed rate is 10% in the first year. The ultimate treatment goal is to eliminate the AVM.

A(i) Definition and types:
Intussusception: telescoping or prolapse of one segment of intestine into an adjacent segment, causing obstruction to normal flow.
Two variants:
1. Idiopathic intussusception: 90% of cases; mostly ileocolic; affects infants and toddlers
2. Enteroenteral intussusception: occurs in older children and neonates; jejunojejunal, jejunoileal, ileoileal; associated with pathological lead points

A(ii) Pathogenesis:
- Imbalance in longitudinal forces / pathological lead point / disorganised peristalsis
- Invagination of intestinal wall into lumen: invaginating segment = intussusceptum; receiving segment = intussuscipiens
- Invagination of mesentery causes intestinal obstruction
- Impedance of lymphatic return → rise in intraluminal pressure
- Rise in hydrostatic pressure → impedance of venous return
- Obstruction of arterial inflow → infarction
- Mucosa is most sensitive to ischaemia → sloughed mucosa + blood + mucus = currant jelly stool
- Transmural gangrene → perforation

B) Age and location: Predominantly affects infants aged 3–9 months; predominant cause of intestinal obstruction in persons aged 3 months to 6 years; M:F ratio 1:1 to 3:1 (at age 4 years and above, rises to 8:1 males).
Pathological lead points:
Meckel's diverticulum; enlarged mesenteric lymph node; mesenteric or intestinal tumours (lymphomas, polyps, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome hamartomas); mesenteric or duplication cysts; submucosal haematomas (Henoch-Schönlein purpura, coagulation dyscrasias); ectopic pancreatic and gastric rests; inverted appendiceal stumps; Ascaris lumbricoides; sutures and staples; cystic fibrosis; indwelling jejunal catheters

C) Empty right lower quadrant: as the intussusceptum telescopes into the colon, the caecum and ascending colon are drawn out of the right iliac fossa, leaving it empty. This produces Dance's Sign.
A sausage-shaped mass may be palpable in the right hypochondrium extending along the transverse colon.
Imaging findings:
- USS: target sign on transverse section; pseudokidney sign on longitudinal section (sensitivity and specificity 100%)
- Plain X-ray: soft tissue mass on right side; relative gaslessness in pelvis
- Barium/air enema: coiled spring sign; claw sign; can also be used therapeutically

A. Describe the BURN UNIT TREATMENT PROTOCOL for acute burn injury, covering the primary survey (ABCDE), fluid resuscitation formula, and the distribution of fluids over the first 24 hours.
A(i) Describe the special considerations for chemical burns and for electrical injuries as given.
B. State the monitoring parameters used to assess adequacy of fluid resuscitation, and state the adequate urine output target for adults and for children under 30 kg.
B(i) Describe the wound care protocol for burn injuries, including the dressings used and the special approach for burns to the face and hands. Also state the role of escharotomy and when it is indicated.
questions.answerText:
A. Primary survey (ABCDE):
- Airway maintenance with consideration of cervical spine protection.
- Breathing and ventilation: 100% O₂ via face mask (non-rebreather mask); intubate if required.
- Circulation and haemorrhage control.
- Disability: assess neurological deficit using AVPU.
- Exposure: remove sources of heat; remove clothing that is burned, soaked with chemicals, or constricting.
Secondary survey: includes scene history, physical examination, and AMPLE history.
Fluid resuscitation: estimate burn size using the Rule of Nines (or the patient's palmar surface = 1% TBSA); use the Lund and Browder chart for patients aged 13 and below. Parkland formula: Lactated Ringer's solution at 4 ml/kg/% TBSA burned (maximum 50%) = total volume in the first 24 hours. Half of this total is given in the first 8 hours post-injury; the remaining half is given in the next 16 hours. In children under 30 kg, additionally administer D5 ½ LR solution at maintenance rate.
A(i) Chemical burns: remove ALL clothing; protect self; brush powdered chemicals off wound, then flush burns for a minimum of 30 minutes with running water; irrigate burned eyes with a gentle stream of saline and obtain ophthalmology consult.
Electrical injuries: monitor distal pulses; elevate burned extremities slightly; cardiac monitoring; watch for burgundy-coloured urine (myoglobinuria).
B. Monitoring parameters: clinical response; ensure urine output; PCV; pulse oximetry.
Urine output targets: adults — at least 30 ml/hour (0.5–1 ml/kg/hr); children under 30 kg — 1–2 ml/kg/hr. Insert Foley catheter in patients with burns greater than 15% TBSA. Observe urine for burgundy colour (seen with massive or electrical injuries — indicates high risk of renal failure; give fluid bolus until output levels are achieved or urine colour changes to straw).
B(i) Wound care: apply a thin layer of Silver Sulfadiazine to open burns if dressings cannot be done immediately; occlusive wound dressing with honey; open Silver Sulfadiazine dressing for burns on the face and hands. Dressing materials: meshed gauze; cotton gauze; cotton wool; bandage. Wound debridement and dressing are performed; wound excision and skin graft are definitive.
Escharotomy: assess for circumferential full-thickness burns of the extremities or trunk. Perform escharotomy when there are decreased or absent pulses in the extremities, or when there is respiratory compromise from circumferential trunk burns.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old manual labourer presents with a 6-week history of severe low back pain with radiation down the right leg, worse on coughing and straining and on prolonged sitting or standing, but relieved by bed rest. Examination reveals weakness of right foot dorsiflexion and absent ankle jerk on the right side. Straight leg raise is positive.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and identify the disc level and nerve root most probably involved, giving the clinical basis for your answer.
(ii) List the recognised risk factors and aetiological mechanisms for this condition.
(iii) Describe the appropriate investigations.
(iv) Outline the non-operative management in full. Under what circumstances is operative management indicated, and what surgical options are available?
(v) State the complications of this condition that would mandate emergency surgery.
questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: prolapsed lumbar intervertebral disc. Weakness of dorsiflexion and absent ankle jerk point to the L4/5 disc (L5 root — weak dorsiflexion and big toe extension) or L5/S1 disc (S1 root — weak plantar flexion, absent ankle jerk). Given absent ankle jerk and weak dorsiflexion together, L5/S1 affecting S1 root is most consistent; 95% of lumbar disc herniations occur at L5/S1 and L4/5. Positive SLR (Lasègue's sign) and pain worse on coughing/straining confirm dural/nerve root irritation.
(ii) Risk factors/mechanisms: singular heavy impact; repeated minimal impact; occupational heavy lifting; poor weight-lifting posture; degenerative disc disease following disc prolapse. The disc herniation occurs through the annulus fibrosus and compresses the nerve root at its exit foramen.
(iii) Investigations: plain radiography; MRI (investigation of choice); CT; CT myelogram; myelogram; electromyography; discography; epidural venography.
(iv) Non-operative: bed rest for a few days on a firm mattress; analgesia and possible steroids; muscle relaxants; corset/physiotherapy; early exercise after pain resolves; weight reduction; correct weight-lifting posture. Operative indications: failed conservative management; sphincteric dysfunction; worsening neurological deficit. Surgical options: standard partial hemilaminectomy + microdiscectomy; laminectomy + discectomy; percutaneous endoscopic microdiscectomy; arthroplasty.
(v) Emergency surgical indications: massive midline prolapsed disc causing cauda equina compression; nerve root compression with quadriceps weakness or foot drop; sphincteric dysfunction (bowel/bladder).

questions.question:
A premature neonate is delivered and found to have a full-thickness defect located to the right of the umbilicus, with no covering sac. The eviscerated bowel is dilated, inflamed, oedematous, thickened, leathery, and shorter than normal. The umbilical cord attachment is normal. The liver is not present in the defect.

(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) State the aetiological and predisposing factors for this condition, and list the associated anomalies.
(iii) Outline the pathophysiology of the bowel changes seen.
(iv) Describe the management from stabilisation through to definitive treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Gastroschisis.

(ii) Aetiology and predisposing factors:
- Vascular accidents
- Prenatal rupture of an exomphalos
Gastroschisis is an extra-umbilical localisation of a defect. The patient is usually premature.
Associated anomalies are rare but include: intestinal atresias, malrotation of the gut, and cryptorchidism.

(iii) Pathophysiology of bowel changes:
The bowel is directly exposed to amniotic fluid without a protective sac. This leads to a chemical peritonitis causing: dilation, inflammation, oedema, thickening, leathery consistency, and foreshortening of the bowel. The eviscerated organs exclude the liver.

(iv) Management:
Stabilisation:
- Prevent hypothermia
- Wrap/protect eviscerated bowel (intestinal bag)
- Intravenous fluids
- IV antibiotics
- NPO + nasogastric tube
Definitive surgery:
- Primary closure (if feasible)
- If primary closure not possible, staged closure is performed
Prognosis is good in developed countries but poor in developing countries due to infection, severe dehydration, and hypothermia.

questions.question:
A(i) Classify abdominal tuberculosis into its main categories, and for each major category state the anatomical structures primarily involved.
A(ii) Describe the three main frequency types of abdominal TB in adults (ascitic, plastic, and glandular), stating what each type causes clinically.
B(i) Describe the pathological subtypes of peritoneal TB under the headings: wet type, fibrotic-fixed type, and fibro-adhesive (dry/plastic) type, including the key pathological findings for each.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Classification and anatomical structures:
- Peritoneal type: involves the peritoneum, omentum, and ascites.
- Mesenteric type: involves lymphadenopathy (mesenteric, para-aortic, and periportal lymph nodes).
- Intestinal type: involves the bowel in either ulcerative or hypertrophic form.
- Solid organ type: involves the liver, spleen, and other solid organs.

A(ii) Three main frequency types in adults:
- (1) Ascitic type: causes abdominal distension from large amounts of ascitic fluid.
- (2) Plastic type: causes intestinal obstruction through matted and tethered bowel loops with dense adhesions.
- (3) Glandular type: involves the mesenteric nodes, which can form palpable abdominal masses.

B(i) Pathological subtypes of peritoneal TB:
- Wet type: (1) large amount of viscous ascitic fluid — diffuse or loculated ascites; (2) whitish miliary nodules less than 5 mm.
- Fibrotic-fixed type: (1) large omental masses; (2) matted and tethered bowel loops with adhesions.
- Fibro-adhesive (dry or plastic) type: (1) caseous nodules (cheesy yellow); (2) fibrous peritoneal reaction; (3) dense adhesions.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man presents with painless total haematuria and weight loss for three months. He is a dye industry worker. On evaluation he is anaemic with a palpable suprapubic mass.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what does 'total haematuria' indicate about the site of origin?
(ii) List all the aetiological categories of haematuria and give at least two specific causes under the renal and vesical categories.
(iii) Describe the emergency presentation of haematuria and the immediate management steps.
(iv) What investigations would you order to confirm the diagnosis and plan management?
questions.answerText:
(i) The most likely diagnosis is bladder carcinoma (Ca bladder). Total haematuria — in which the entire stream is bloodstained — most likely originates from the bladder or upper urinary tract.

(ii) Aetiological categories: Renal, Pelvicalyceal and Ureteric, Vesical, Prostatic, Urethral, Sickle cell disease, Drugs, Systemic.
Renal causes include: congenital (e.g. polycystic kidneys), infections (TB, abscess, pyelonephritis, pyonephrosis, schistosomiasis), trauma, tumours, stones, vascular (hypertension, thrombosis, embolism, aneurysm), infarction.
Vesical causes include: inflammatory (TB, schistosomiasis), tumour, trauma, stone.

(iii) Emergency presentations: hypovolaemic shock, severe anaemia, and acute clot retention. Immediate management: quick evaluation and resuscitation; set 2 wide-bore IV cannulas; urgent PCV and group-and-cross-match; IV fluids (normal saline); blood transfusion; haematuric/3-way catheter; continuous saline bladder irrigation to prevent clot retention; analgesics; monitor vital signs; constant re-evaluation; serial PCV. If clot retention occurs: ensure catheter is not kinked; use bladder syringe to aspirate/flush the clot; if that fails, evacuation with Ellich's evacuator through a cystoscope sheath; if that fails, open bladder evacuation.

(iv) Investigations: Urinalysis; urine M/C/S; U/E/Cr; ESR, Hb; genotype; G6PD deficiency; ultrasound (USS-KUB); urethrography; urethroscopy; IVU; biopsy (e.g. prostatic); radiology for metastases (CXR, abdominal X-ray, pelvic/LS X-ray, skull X-ray); Tc99 bone radioisotope scan; CT, CT urogram, MRI; retrograde pyelogram; aortography.

(i) Cardiac tamponade. Beck's Triad: (1) raised JVP — elevated jugular venous pressure; (2) hypotension — reduced cardiac output from compressed ventricles; (3) muffled heart sounds — fluid surrounding the heart dampens heart sounds.

(ii) Pulsus paradoxus: a drop in systolic blood pressure by more than 10 mmHg on inspiration. Additionally, Kussmaul's sign is described as increased venous pressure on inspiration during spontaneous breathing.

(iii) Immediate resuscitation and definitive management: pericardiocentesis (to relieve tamponade acutely); pericardial window (for recurrent or chronic cases); sternotomy with repair (definitive surgical option).

questions.answerText:
(i) Extracranial (carotid) arterial disease.
- The visual episode is amaurosis fugax (transient loss of vision described as a veil coming down over the visual field) — an ipsilateral ocular TIA.
- The arm weakness is a contralateral motor TIA (transient ischaemic attack: focal neurological or ocular deficit lasting not more than 24 hours).
(ii) Pathophysiology: the commonest extracranial lesion is an atherosclerotic plaque at the carotid bifurcation. Platelet aggregation and subsequent platelet embolisation cause ocular or cerebral symptoms. Symptoms due to flow reduction are rare in the carotid territory but vertebrobasilar symptoms are usually flow related. Reversed flow in the vertebral artery in the presence of ipsilateral subclavian occlusion leads to cerebral symptoms as the arm 'steals' blood from the cerebellum — subclavian steal syndrome.
(iii) Investigations:
- Duplex scanning (B-mode scan and Doppler ultrasonic velocimetry): method of choice for assessing degree of carotid stenosis.
- Carotid angiography: no longer essential prior to surgery.
- CT or MRI brain scan: demonstrate presence of a cerebral infarct.
(iv) Indications for carotid endarterectomy:
- Carotid distribution TIA or stroke with good recovery, after 1-month delay: >70% ipsilateral stenosis; or >50% ipsilateral stenosis with ulceration.
- Asymptomatic carotid stenosis >80% (controversial).
(v) Medical treatment: aspirin (75 mg/day) inhibits platelet aggregation for the life of the platelet; clopidogril has a similar action; anticoagulation for patients with cardiac embolic disease. Carotid endarterectomy has about 5% morbidity and mortality.

A 40-year-old male manual labourer presents with a painful, swollen right hand following a machete injury to the dorsum. On examination there is tissue disruption with exposed tendon, sensory deficit over the dorsum of the index finger, loss of active extension of the index finger at the proximal interphalangeal joint, and flexion deformity at that joint. X-ray of both hands shows no fracture or dislocation.
(i) Classify the wound using the Rank and Wakefield classification and justify the classification.
(ii) Name the specific tendon deformity present, identify the structure whose insertion is disrupted, and state where this insertion is located.
(iii) Describe the classification of nerve injuries (Seddon's) relevant here and its treatment implications.
(iv) Outline the principles of treatment for this hand injury, from initial wound management to definitive repair and rehabilitation.
(v) If the amputated segment of a finger were brought by the patient, describe the correct care of the amputated part.
questions.answerText:
(i) Using the Rank and Wakefield classification, the wound is a tidy wound. It is classified as tidy because it results from a sharp object (machete/blade), has clean wound edges, and the skin involvement and degree of contamination are the key determinants; tidy wounds are suitable for primary repair.
(ii) The tendon deformity present is the Boutonniere deformity (flexion deformity at the proximal interphalangeal joint with hyperextension at the distal interphalangeal joint). This results from disrupted insertion of the central extensor slip into the base of the middle phalanx, which occurs 3 weeks after injury as the lateral bands sublux volarly.
(iii) Seddon's classification of nerve injuries:
- Neuropraxia: minimal axonal disruption; treatment is conservative; prognosis is complete recovery in days to months.
- Axonotmesis: total axonal disruption with intact endoneurium and perineurium; treatment is conservative; prognosis is complete recovery in months.
- Neurotmesis: disruption of axon, endoneurium, and perineurium; treatment requires surgical repair; prognosis is moderate reduction in function.
(iv) Principles of treatment:
- Irrigate the wound with 2 litres of saline to minimise soilage.
- Early debridement and restoration of anatomy by tagging tissues with appropriate sutures without tension.
- Repair damaged vessels, nerves, and tendons if competent, otherwise refer.
- Apply skin traction kit and elevate affected hand on a drip stand; apply a volar cast.
- Dress wound regularly with saline, medical honey, and bulky/gamgee dressing and crepe bandage (not gauze).
- Skin grafting or flap cover of the wound as needed.
- Analgesics (morphine, pethidine, or pentazocine); antibiotics (Augmentin and metronidazole or equivalent); tetanus vaccine.
- Physiotherapy, rehabilitation, and early mobilisation using regimens such as Kleinert traction after tendon repair; follow-up.
(v) Care of the amputated part: wash gently with saline; wrap in moist saline gauze; tuck into a polythene bag; and put the bag in a container of ice block and water (not placed directly on ice). This preserves the part for possible replantation.

(i) Diagnosis: cervical disc prolapse at C5/6 with C6 radiculopathy. Recommended operative procedure: anterior cervical discectomy with fusion and instrumentation (ACDF) or arthroplasty (anterior approach).
(ii) Operative indications for cervical disc disease: worsening neurological condition; myelopathy; failed conservative management.
(iii) Surgical approaches:
- Posterior approach: laminectomy; posterolateral approach for root decompression.
- Anterior approach: discectomy; discectomy + bone graft fusion; discectomy + bone graft + instrumentation; arthroplasty.
(iv) Most commonly affected levels: 60% at C6/7; 30% at C5/6. Peaks occur in the 3rd and 4th decades. Clinical syndromes: radiculopathy (nerve root compression causing pain, numbness, paraesthesia, tingling, weakness, muscle atrophy in a dermatomal/myotomal distribution); myelopathy (spinal cord compression causing clumsy gait, sphincteric anomaly, erectile dysfunction, Lhermitte's sign, upper and lower motor neuron signs); radiculomyelopathy (combined).
(v) Investigations: X-ray (AP, lateral, oblique views); CT scan; plain myelography/CT myelography; MRI; electrophysiology tests; others as indicated.

A(i) Define epispadias, state its incidence and sex distribution, describe its embryological cause, and enumerate its full classification in both the male and female with a description of each type.
A(ii) Explain the anatomical relationship between epispadias and bladder exstrophy — why complete male epispadias is always associated with ectopia vesicae, and what the dorsal chordee signifies.
B(i) Describe the clinical basis for why glandular and penile epispadias differ in severity from complete epispadias, and state the specific treatment for epispadias including the recommended timing of surgery.
B(ii) Distinguish epispadias from hypospadias on all features provided — definition, embryological cause, incidence, sex ratio, associated anomalies, and sphincteric implications.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Epispadias: congenital deformity in which the urethra opens on the dorsum of the penis at some point proximal to the glans. Incidence: 1/95,000. M:F ratio: 4:1. No familial basis. Embryological cause: failure of union of anterior walls of the urethra. Dorsal curvature of penis (chordee) is always present.
Male classification:
- Glandular: urethral opening is immediately proximal to the glans.
- Penile: urethral opening situated between the post-glandular sulcus and the suspensory ligament; occurs most often at the base of the penis.
- Complete: entire length of the dorsal wall of the urethra is absent up to the bladder neck; associated with ectopia vesicae.
Female classification:
- Clitoric.
- Subsymphyseal.
- Complete.

A(ii) Complete epispadias is always associated with ectopia vesicae because the failure of union of the anterior urethral walls extends to involve the entire anterior abdominal wall below the umbilicus — the most severe form of this developmental failure results in exposure of the bladder posterior wall. Bladder exstrophy is described as the severest form of epispadias. Dorsal chordee: the dorsal curvature is caused by fibrous tissue replacing the deficient anterior urethra on the dorsum of the penis; the penis bends dorsally towards the absent urethra.

B(i) Glandular epispadias: the defect is confined to immediately proximal to the glans; severity is minimal; continence is usually maintained. Penile epispadias: opening is along the shaft; the defect is more extensive but does not reach the bladder neck; continence may be preserved. Complete epispadias: the entire dorsal wall of the urethra is absent up to the bladder neck; urinary continence is lost. Treatment: surgical repair; operation is done when the child is over 30 months old.

B(ii) Distinction from hypospadias:
- Epispadias: urethra opens on dorsum of penis (dorsal); caused by failure of union of anterior walls of urethra; incidence 1/95,000; M:F 4:1; no familial basis; dorsal chordee always present; complete form associated with bladder exstrophy; sphincteric function impaired in complete type.
- Hypospadias: urethra opens on ventral surface of penis proximal to normal meatus; caused by failure of fusion of urethral folds on ventral aspect; incidence 1/300 live male births; much commoner than epispadias; associated with undescended testis (9%), inguinal hernia (9%), upper urinary tract anomalies (1–3%); ventral chordee present in posterior and peno-scrotal types; urinary sphincteric function is normal.

A(i) Stages of midgut rotation:
Stage I (5th–10th week of gestation): Period of physiological herniation of the bowel into the umbilical cord. Initial 180° counterclockwise rotation of the duodenojejunal and caecocolic limbs around the SMA. Both loops start in a vertical plane parallel to the SMA and end in a horizontal plane. Both loops maintain position until the bowel returns to the abdominal cavity.
Stage II (10th week): Bowel returns to the abdominal cavity. Additional 90° counterclockwise rotation (total 270°). Duodenojejunal junction moves to the left, below the SMA. Caecum moves to the right lower quadrant. A very broad pedicle is formed at the base of the mesentery.
Stage III (11 weeks to term): Descent of the caecum to the right lower quadrant. Fixation of the mesentery retroperitoneally — duodenum and colon fixed by peritoneal bands.

A(ii) Broad mesenteric base:
Fixation establishes a broad mesenteric attachment extending from the duodenojejunal junction (left upper quadrant) to the ileocaecal junction (right lower quadrant), providing a wide and stable base that prevents the midgut from twisting.

B) Three types of malrotation:
Non-rotation (commonest): arrest in Stage I; small intestine lies to the right, colon to the left; narrow mesenteric base; predisposes to volvulus.
Incomplete (arrested) rotation: Stage II arrest; peritoneal bands (Ladd's bands) from caecum to mesentery compress the duodenum; narrow mesenteric base; volvulus and mesocolic hernia can occur.
Reverse rotation: clockwise rotation; transverse colon lies behind the SMA and duodenum; causes colonic obstruction.

C) Anatomical basis of Ladd's procedure:
1. Evisceration of entire bowel: allows visualisation and assessment of all bowel.
2. Counterclockwise derotation of volvulus: reverses the clockwise twist, restoring blood supply.
3. Division of Ladd's bands: removes peritoneal adhesions compressing the duodenum, opening the duodenal lumen.
4. Mobilisation of duodenum: allows the duodenum to sit in the right lateral abdomen unobstructed.
5. Placement of caecum in left upper quadrant, duodenum in right lateral abdomen: creates the widest possible mesenteric base, reducing the risk of re-volvulus.
6. Appendicectomy: prevents atypical presentation of future appendicitis due to malpositioned appendix.
questions.question:
A) Describe the normal embryological rotation of the midgut, the axis around which it rotates, and the anatomical result of completed rotation under the following headings:
A(i) Stages of rotation: degree of rotation, timing, and what each stage accomplishes
A(ii) How fixation establishes the normal broad mesenteric base

B) Describe the three types of malrotation, the anatomical result of each type, and the clinical syndrome each produces.

C) Explain the anatomical basis of the Ladd's procedure: what each step achieves anatomically, and the anatomical reason for placing the caecum in the left upper quadrant and the duodenum in the right lateral abdomen.

questions.answerText:
(i) Spot diagnosis: botulism. Organism: Clostridium botulinum. Toxin subtypes named: A, B, E, F. The toxin is very potent and may cause rapid death following even very small ingestions.
(ii) Food sources: can be found in virtually all foods including fresh vegetables, fruits, meats, canned food, baked potatoes, and any food left out at room temperature — especially if left for over 16 hours. Most recent outbreak () from commercial cheese sauce. May also occur from contaminated wounds. Spores can withstand boiling for hours but the toxin is heat labile.
(iii) Clinical progression: incubation is 6 hours to 8 days; most occur within 18–36 hours (sooner onset, worse the paralysis). Early: alert, afebrile; dry mouth; diplopia; dysphagia; dysarthria (bulbar musculature involved early); may have nausea, vomiting, cramps, and diarrhoea. Late: descending weakness — face and upper extremities first; constipation; urinary retention. No sensory changes. May have only listlessness and hypotonia. Type A more frequently requires ventilation.
(iv) Management: supportive; anti-toxin — multivalent vaccine must be given before the patient becomes symptomatic. Laboratory data not generally helpful. CSF protein is normal; EMG is non-specific. May respond to edrophonium. Can demonstrate toxin in patient, organism in stool, and toxin in food. Mortality approximately 20%.
(v) Infant botulism: caused by colonisation of the gut by botulism organisms (rather than ingestion of pre-formed toxin). Found in honey and vegetables. The gut is colonised by bacteria which secrete toxin that is absorbed by the child. May be a cause of some cases of SIDS. Usually occurs between 1–38 weeks; heralded by constipation followed by poor suck.
questions.question:

He is alert and afebrile with a dry mouth, diplopia, dysphagia, and dysarthria. Two other family members who ate the same food have similar symptoms. There are no sensory changes.

(v) Describe infant botulism — its mechanism, the source, and its possible link to another condition —.

questions.answerText:
(i) The mass is in the anterior mediastinal compartment. Common anterior mediastinal tumours: thymoma; lymphoma; germ cell tumour.

(ii) Structures compressed and resultant features: trachea and both main-stem bronchi → airway compression causing dyspnoea; superior vena cava → SVC syndrome producing facial and neck swelling and distended neck veins; sympathetic ganglion (stellate ganglion) → Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).

(iii) Tumour markers: α-fetoprotein; β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG); lactate dehydrogenase. Investigations: complete history and physical examination; CT scan of the chest; tissue sample (certain diagnosis of thymoma requires biopsy); in patients with anterior mediastinal mass, history of ptosis, dysarthria, and muscle weakness increasing with activity suggests thymoma with myasthenia gravis; enlarged axillary, supraclavicular, and cervical lymph nodes suggest lymphoma.

(iv) Thymoma is associated with myasthenia gravis — 35% of thymoma patients present with myasthenia gravis; the syndrome is characterised by autoantibodies to acetylcholine receptors, with reduced ACH receptor concentration at the neuromuscular end plate. Staging: Stage I — intact capsule; Stage II — local invasion of pleura, phrenic nerve, or pericardium; Stage III — gross invasion (e.g., lung or aorta); Stage IVA — intrathoracic dissemination; Stage IVB — extrathoracic dissemination. Radiation is offered for Stage II or higher; chemotherapy may be used in Stage IV under clinical protocol.
questions.question:
A 22-year-old man presents with anterior chest pain, progressive dyspnoea, and ptosis of the left eye. On examination there is facial oedema, distended neck veins, and left-sided Horner's syndrome. CT chest reveals a large heterogeneous 18 cm × 8 cm × 9.8 cm anterior mediastinal mass with calcifications, multiple areas of necrosis and haemorrhage extending into the neck and right pleural space, with compression of the trachea and both main-stem bronchi.

(i) What is the anatomical compartment of the mass, and list the common tumours found in the anterior mediastinum.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Definitions:
- Memory: the ability to acquire, process, store, and retrieve information.
- Learning: a relatively permanent change in behaviour as a result of repeated practice.
- Remembering: a retrieval process in which memories are taken out of storage.
- Forgetting: the inability to retrieve stored memories.
A(ii) Neurobiology: approximately one hundred billion neurons in the brain are involved. Brain structures: hippocampus; cortex; amygdala; cerebellum; mammillary bodies; parts of the limbic system. Neural plasticity and synapses form the basis of memory.
- Short-lasting memory: may last for seconds or minutes; depends on specific synaptic events and increase in neurotransmitter release.
- Long-lasting memory: depends on new protein synthesis; physical growth of neural processes; increase in the number of synaptic connections.
B(i) Explicit (declarative) memory: factual knowledge of people, things, and events; fades in absence of practice or refreshing; recalled by conscious efforts (e.g., learning a phone number, recall in examination).
Subtypes: (1) Episodic memory — remembering personal events and experiences; (2) Semantic memory — public memory of facts or general knowledge.
Implicit memory: information memory to perform reflexive or perceptual tasks; unconsciously recalled; may last for life even without practice; includes learned behaviours such as classical conditioning and fear conditioning.
B(ii) Reasons for forgetting: repression (hiding unwanted emotions/thoughts in the unconscious); poor retrieval cues (no mental images/experience to associate with the old event); amnesia (impaired memory due to organicity, drug abuse, or severe psychological illness); interference (recall blocked by other related memories).
Short-term memory either fades with time (forgetfulness) or is reinforced and transformed into long-term memory by consolidation. Psychiatric relevance: disruption of explicit memory capacity is seen in stress-associated disorders; excessively enhanced memories are pathogenic — e.g., in PTSD and drug addiction.
questions.question:
A(i) Define memory, learning, remembering, and forgetting.
A(ii) Describe the neurobiology of memory formation and storage, stating the brain structures involved and explaining the neurobiological basis of short-lasting versus long-lasting memory.
B(i) Describe the types of memory, distinguishing explicit (declarative) memory from implicit memory, and identifying the two subtypes of explicit memory with their definitions.
B(ii) Explain the reasons for forgetting, and describe what happens to short-term memory during consolidation into long-term memory. State the psychiatric conditions in which abnormalities of memory mechanisms are relevant.

questions.answerText:
(i) The most likely diagnosis is blunt abdominal trauma with haemoperitoneum/intra-abdominal injury.
- Left rib fractures may be associated with injuries to the spleen and left kidney.

(ii) Goal and steps of resuscitation:
- Goal: adequate airway, effective breathing, and sufficient circulation.
- Steps: follow the ATLS protocol, particularly the primary survey with ABCDE of resuscitation.
 1. Ensure a patent airway and adequate ventilation.
 2. Correct hypovolaemia: establish IV line, infuse crystalloid or colloid, administer blood when available.
 3. The circulation must be restored rapidly with crystalloids or colloids while blood is being cross-matched.
 4. Establishment of invasive monitoring: urinary catheter and central venous line.

(iii) Management approach:
- This patient is in the unstable category.
- Patient is in shock and unstable with positive signs indicative of acute abdomen.
- After resuscitation steps, rapid assessment of injuries is performed.
- Immediate surgical intervention is essential for non-responders to initial resuscitation.

(iv) Diagnostic modalities and most appropriate for the unstable patient:
- Modalities available: ultrasound (FAST — focused assessment sonography for trauma), diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL), CT scan, and laparoscopy.
- For the haemodynamically unstable patient, FAST ultrasound (looking for free fluid in Morrison's pouch, pelvis, left subhepatic space, and pericardial sac) or DPL is most appropriate, as CT requires a stable patient and transfer.
questions.question:
A 28-year-old motorcyclist is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. He is in shock, not responding to initial resuscitation. Abdominal examination reveals generalised tenderness and rigid board-like abdomen. Rib fractures are noted on the left.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis and identify two specific intra-abdominal solid organs that may be injured given the left rib fractures.
(ii) Outline the goal of resuscitation and the immediate resuscitative steps in sequence.
(iii) Describe the management approach for this unstable patient and state the category he falls into (unstable or stable).
(iv) List four diagnostic modalities available for evaluation of abdominal trauma and state which is most appropriate in this haemodynamically unstable patient.

A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the anal canal and rectum, including their approximate lengths, layers, and sphincter components.
A(ii) Describe the dentate (pectinate) line under the headings: embryological significance, neurovascular supply above versus below the line, and lymphatic drainage differences.
B(i) Using the anatomy of the dentate line, explain why anal conditions below it (such as anal fissure) are exquisitely painful, and why internal haemorrhoids above it are typically painless until complicated.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Gross anatomy:
- The rectum is the distal 15 cm terminal portion of the large intestine; the anal canal is approximately 4 cm of the GI tract.
- The rectum has four layers: mucosal, submucosal, and two smooth muscle layers.
- The anal canal has an internal sphincter, an external sphincter, and an intersphincteric plane.
- The dentate line divides the neurovascular supply of the anorectum.

A(ii) Dentate line:
- Embryological significance: it marks the boundary between endodermal (columnar epithelium above) and ectodermal (squamous epithelium below) origins.
- Above the dentate line: autonomic nerve supply; venous drainage via superior rectal artery and veins with portal drainage; lymphatics drain to mesenteric nodes.
- Below the dentate line: somatic nerve supply; blood supply via inferior rectal artery and vein with systemic drainage; lymphatics drain to the inguinal nodes.

B(i) Basis for pain differences:
- Below the dentate line, the anoderm receives somatic innervation, making it exquisitely sensitive to pain, temperature, and touch; therefore anal fissures and perianal abscesses below this line cause severe pain.
- Above the dentate line, innervation is autonomic (visceral), which does not transmit sharp localised pain; therefore internal haemorrhoids above the dentate line are painless in their uncomplicated state.
- They only become painful when they prolapse, become strangulated, or thrombosed — events that involve somatic structures or cause ischaemia.

questions.question:
Regarding amputation surgery:

A(i) Describe the indications for amputation across all recognised categories, including the special consideration for tourniquet use in infection, tumour, and sickle cell disease.
A(ii) Describe the levels of amputation for both the lower limb and upper limb, from the most distal to the most proximal for each, and state the energy expenditure significance of knee joint preservation.
B(i) Describe the operative principles of bone management, nerve management, vessel ligation, drain placement, and post-operative dressing in amputation surgery.
B(ii) Explain the anatomical basis of forequarter amputation, the two surgical approaches available, and the specific complications of amputation with their management.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Indications: (1) peripheral vascular disease with diabetes (greater percentage of patients); (2) trauma — especially in men, mostly lower limbs when blood supply is irreparably damaged; open amputation often indicated with atypical flaps; (3) locally expanding tumours — usually malignant sarcomas; occasionally very large benign tumours; even with metastasis to relieve pain or treat pathological fracture; tourniquet without exsanguination used; (4) infection — chronic osteomyelitis or other severe infections; acute infections unresponsive to medical/surgical treatment (e.g. gas gangrene); open amputation required, prophylactic antibiotics, tourniquet without exsanguination; (5) congenital anomalies — fibular hemimelia, tibial hemimelia; disarticulation preferred over diaphyseal amputation; (6) nerve injuries with trophic ulcers; (7) cosmesis (rare). Tourniquet is contraindicated in ischaemic limbs; in SS with infection or tumour, tourniquet is contraindicated.
A(ii) Lower limb levels (distal to proximal): partial foot (transmetatarsal, Lisfranc, Chopart); Syme (ankle disarticulation); below-knee (BKA); through-knee (TKA); above-knee (AKA); hip disarticulation; hindquarter amputation. Upper limb levels: wrist disarticulation; below elbow; elbow disarticulation; above elbow; shoulder disarticulation; forequarter amputation. Energy significance: over 90% of below-knee amputees learn to walk with prosthesis vs. less than 60% of above-knee amputees; loss of knee joint incurs considerable increase in energy expenditure.
B(i) Bone: cut perpendicularly using bone saw or Gigli saw; bevel appropriately; cut fibula shorter than tibia; file the edges; seal ends with periosteal or muscle flaps. Nerves: gently pull down and cut at least 2 cm proximal to bone section; large nerves — isolate their vessels and ligate. Blood vessels: large — doubly ligate with absorbable or non-absorbable sutures; tiny vessels — coagulate; remove tourniquet before closure for full haemostasis. Drain: always drain using corrugated or suction drain. Dressing: strips of paraffin/tulle gras, gauze, generous roll of wool, completed with crepe bandage (soft) or plaster (rigid); rigid dressing left for at least 2 weeks; drains removed at 48–72 hours; sutures removed at 2 weeks.
B(ii) Forequarter amputation (aka shoulder girdle amputation/interscapulothoracic amputation): consists of removal of the entire upper extremity and shoulder girdle in the interval between the scapula and thoracic wall; a mutilating operation performed only for malignancy involving the joint or infiltrating the deltoid, pectoral, or subscapularis muscles. Two approaches: Berger (anterior approach with early access to major vessels); Littlewood (posterior approach, which many surgeons find easier). Complications: haematoma; infection (remove sutures for drainage, culture and treat); necrosis of skin edge or flap (go higher); neuroma (pain when neuroma is entrapped by scar); phantom sensation (disappears with regular prosthesis use); delirium tremens in alcoholics; bone spikes especially in children.

(i) The diagnosis is acute mechanical small bowel obstruction.

(ii) Four categories of aetiology with examples:
- Intraluminal causes: e.g., ascaris worm impaction (in children), faecal impaction (in elderly), intussusception.
- Extraluminal intramural causes: e.g., strictures due to inflammation, radiation therapy, or iatrogenic from gut anastomosis; carcinoma of the large bowel.
- Extraluminal extramural causes: e.g., adhesive bands, external hernias (obstructed inguinal hernia is the most common cause of acute intestinal obstruction in these parts), internal hernias, extrinsic masses.
- Paralytic ileus (adynamic): e.g., post-operative state, peritonitis, hypokalemia.

(iii) Pathophysiology of complications from strangulation:
- Strangulation occurs when the blood supply to the obstructed segment is insufficient.
- This leads to intestinal infarction, gangrene, and perforation with peritonitis.
- Fluid loss leads to dehydration, hypotension, shock, and acute renal failure.
- Electrolyte imbalance, especially hypokalaemia, leads to muscle weakness, paralytic ileus, and cardiac arrhythmias.
- Strangulation can lead to multiple organ failure and death.

(iv) Treatment:
- Resuscitation: set IV line, replace fluids and electrolytes, pass NG tube to decompress proximal GIT, pass urethral catheter to monitor urine output as a guide to adequate fluid replacement.
- Prophylactic antibiotics because of translocation or transmigration of gut bacteria.
- Surgical operation is tailored to the nature of the cause; usually an exploratory laparotomy plus the treatment of whatever is found.
questions.question:
A patient presents with colicky abdominal pain, vomiting that provides temporary relief, abdominal distension, and absolute constipation. On examination the abdomen is tense, tympanitic, and hyperactive bowel sounds are heard. An erect plain abdominal X-ray shows multiple air-fluid levels with dilated central loops that have valvulae conniventes extending right across the bowel.

(i) State the diagnosis and specify the type.
(ii) List four categories of aetiology for this condition and give one example for each.
