A 55-year-old man presents with a non-healing ulcer on the medial aspect of the lower leg, just above the medial malleolus, for eight months. Examination shows an irregular, shaggy-bordered ulcer with granulation tissue on the floor, surrounding haemosiderin pigmentation, varicose veins, and lower leg oedema. Peripheral pulses are present and ABI is 0.95.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and identify the type of ulcer based on the findings.
(ii) List four components of the pathophysiology of this type of ulcer according to causes of calf pump dysfunction.
(iii) List the complications that may arise from a chronic cutaneous ulcer of this type.
(iv) Describe the conservative management of this condition, and state the important check that must be performed before compression is applied.
(v) Name the surgical skin cover options available when granulation tissue is present, specifying the graft type most useful for large ulcers.
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is a chronic venous leg ulcer. It is a benign, chronic cutaneous ulcer located in the gaiter (malleolar) region, with characteristic irregular borders, granulation tissue, surrounding haemosiderin pigmentation, varicosities and oedema, consistent with chronic venous insufficiency.
(ii) Four components of calf pump dysfunction producing venous ulcers are:
- Deep vein insufficiency
- Deep vein obstruction
- Superficial vein insufficiency
- Perforator insufficiency
(Additionally: arteriovenous fistulae and neuromuscular dysfunction are listed.)
(iii) Complications of chronic cutaneous ulcers include: local and systemic infection; tetanus; scars and contractures; lymphoedema; bone complications (osteitis, osteomyelitis); and Marjolin's ulcer.
(iv) Conservative management involves: maintaining normal weight and avoiding smoking; correcting nutritional deficiencies and anaemia; encouraging moderate exercise; treating associated medical disease; leg elevation above the level of the heart; and applying compression immediately after elevation. Before compression bandages are applied, the ankle-brachial index (ABI) must always be measured (should be greater than 0.7 to 0.8) to avoid necrosis or gangrene of the foot in patients with arterial disease.
(v) When granulation tissue is healthy, a split-thickness skin graft (STSG) is used. For large ulcers, meshed split-thickness skin grafts are most useful as they allow greater coverage. For smaller wounds, pinch grafting is a useful option. If the bed is fibrotic, a flap is required instead of a graft.

(i) Movement on swallowing suggests goitre (thyroid swelling). Movement on tongue protrusion suggests thyroglossal duct cyst.

(ii) Local examination — palpation headings for neck swelling:
- Tenderness.
- Temperature (compare with distant skin).
- Thrill.
- Texture/consistency (soft, firm, hard).
- Size (2-dimensional).
- Pulsation.
- Getting above and below it (in the neck).
- Fluctuancy (in two axes).
- Reducibility.
- Emptying.
- Fixity/mobility — attachment to surrounding structures (skin, fascia, etc.).
- Regional lymph nodes.
- Skin sensation.
- Transillumination.
- Percussion (indirect evaluation of size/extent — e.g. retrosternal goitre).

(iii) Pathognomonic signs:
- Goitre: movement on swallowing.
- Thyroglossal duct cyst: movement on tongue protrusion.
- Sebaceous cyst: punctum.
- Lipoma: slipping sign and lobulation.
- Haemangioma: emptying sign.
- Hydrocoele: transillumination (clear fluid).
- Hernia: reducibility.
- Neurofibroma: cafe au lait spots (von Recklinghausen disease).

(iv) Imaging: X-rays (local and chest); ultrasound scan; CT scan; MRI; IVU; barium swallow, meal, enema. Biopsy: fine needle aspiration biopsy (cytology), Trucut, incisional, excisional. Endoscopy: oesophagogastroscopy, proctosigmoidoscopy, colonoscopy, bronchoscopy, urethrocystoscopy. Also: FBC, ESR, urinalysis, stool microscopy, tuberculin test, tumour markers.
questions.question:
A 58-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of progressively increasing painless swelling in the anterior neck that moves on swallowing. He has no compressive symptoms. On examination, the swelling is smooth, non-tender, and moves with swallowing and on tongue protrusion.

(i) What two diagnoses does movement on swallowing and movement on tongue protrusion suggest respectively?
(ii) Using standard local examination palpation headings, describe all the features you would assess for this neck swelling.
(iii) What specific anatomical signs (pathognomonic signs) would help you differentiate between a thyroid swelling, a thyroglossal cyst, a sebaceous cyst, a lipoma, and a haemangioma?
(iv) What imaging, biopsy, and endoscopic investigations are available for a neck swelling?

A 38-year-old female with a 6-month history of dysphagia presents. She reports that dysphagia started with solids and has now progressed to liquids. She denies any history of caustic ingestion but has had longstanding heartburn. Upper GI contrast study shows tapering of the lower oesophagus with a bird-beak deformity.

(i) Based on the nature of the dysphagia, what category of disorder does this represent — mechanical or functional — and justify your answer using the standard classification.
(ii) State the three physiological constricting points of the oesophagus with their distances from the incisor teeth.
(iii) What is the primary aim of investigating dysphagia?
(iv) What clinical features in the history should be sought when taking a history of dysphagia?
questions.answerText:
(i) The dysphagia began with solids and progressed to liquids, suggesting a mechanical disorder. Justification: dysphagia for liquids only signifies a functional disorder (oesophageal motility disorder); dysphagia for solids signifies more significant (mechanical) disease. Benign mechanical dysphagia tends to be intermittent with a history of many months or years; lower dysphagia represents a mechanical or functional disorder.

(ii) Three physiological constricting points: (1) at 15 cm from the incisor teeth — at the cricopharyngeal constriction; (2) at 25 cm — at the aortic and bronchial constriction; (3) at 40 cm — at the diaphragmatic and lower oesophageal sphincter constriction.

(iii) Primary aim of investigation: to differentiate between benign and malignant causes of dysphagia.

(iv) Clinical features to seek in history: age of the patient; duration; progression of the dysphagia; nature of dysphagia (to solids, liquids or both); whether the patient can localise the point of dysphagia; a history of high dysphagia points towards an oropharyngeal cause, often neuromuscular in origin — most common cause is cerebrovascular accident; previous history of caustic soda ingestion; reflux oesophagitis; whether dysphagia is intermittent or progressive; whether pain on swallowing (odynophagia) is an associated symptom.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man sustains a closed fracture of the mid-shaft of the right humerus following a road traffic accident. On examination, he is unable to extend his wrist or fingers, and sensation is diminished over the dorsum of the hand.

(i) State the diagnosis and identify the nerve injured. At what anatomical level is this nerve most vulnerable in this fracture, and what is the term for this type of nerve injury?
(ii) Describe the predisposing factors for this nerve to be injured at this specific location.
(iii) Outline the conservative and operative management principles for both the fracture and the nerve injury.
(iv) What are the local and general complications of fractures that may arise in this patient, including compartment syndrome and Volkmann's ischaemic contracture?
questions.answerText:
(i) Fracture of the mid-shaft of humerus with radial nerve palsy (wrist drop). The nerve injured is the radial nerve. It is most vulnerable at the mid-shaft of the humerus — where it runs in the spiral groove (radial groove) on the posterior aspect of the humerus. Type of nerve injury: neuropraxia is common in closed fracture injury.
(ii) Predisposing factors for radial nerve injury: the radial nerve runs in close contact with the humeral shaft in the spiral groove at the mid-shaft level; a fracture at this level directly endangers the nerve by compression, stretch, or entrapment between fracture fragments. Nerve compression may also occur later due to callus formation.
(iii) Management of fracture: diagnosis suspected clinically by position of limb; confirmed by radiography; conservative treatment is generally adopted in children; in adults, internal fixation using intramedullary nail or plate and screws is advocated; external fixator may also be used. Management of nerve injury: neuropraxia generally recovers spontaneously with fracture healing; nerve exploration if no recovery after expected time; nerve compression from callus may require surgical decompression.
(iv) Local complications: skin/subcutaneous tissue injury; tendon/muscle injury; nerve injury (neuropraxia — radial nerve commonest); vascular injury; bone non-union, delayed union, infection; compartment syndrome; Volkmann's ischaemic contracture (from compartment syndrome sequel). General complications: haemorrhagic shock; fat embolism (especially in multiple long bone fractures); gas gangrene; tetanus; DVT and pulmonary embolism; crush syndrome.

A. Aetiological factors of cleft lip and palate:
1. Hereditary factors: cleft lip and palate is familially transmitted as a male sex recessive gene.
2. Nutritional deficiencies: deficiencies of Vitamin A, Vitamin B, and folic acid.
3. Endocrine disorders: e.g., diabetes mellitus.
4. Maternal infections (TORCHS syndrome): Toxoplasmosis, Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Histoplasmosis, and Syphilis.
5. Drugs: e.g., corticosteroids and anticonvulsants.
6. Anoxia: e.g., resulting from threatened abortion.
7. Exposure to radiation: a potent teratogenic agent.
8. Maternal age: children delivered by mothers at late age (greater than 35 years) tend to have congenital anomalies.
9. Consanguineous marriage: tends to propagate abnormal genes leading to congenital anomalies.
A(i) Incidence:
- Africa: 1 in 2,000 live births.
- Caucasians: 1 in 1,000 live births.
- Oriental group: 1 in 500 live births.
- Indian tribes of Montana: 1 in 276 live births.
B. Anatomy of cleft lip — muscles disrupted:
- Nasolabial muscles: transverse nasalis, levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, levator labii superioris.
- Oral sphincter: orbicularis oris.
- Lower jaw muscles: depressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferioris, mentalis.
Specific deformities:
- Lip: defect in the skin and soft tissue of the upper lip; vertical soft tissue deficiency on the cleft side; abnormal attachments of lip musculature into the alar base and nasal spine.
- Alveolus: cleft in the alveolus at the site of eruption of the canine tooth.
- Hard palate: defect in the hard palate anterior to the incisive foramen.
- Nose: nasal deformity — flattened alar or reduction in height of the dome.
B(i) Cleft lip and palate as a combined entity (complicated cleft lip) is commoner in males. Isolated cleft palate is commoner in females and is often syndromic. Isolated cleft lip alone is commoner in males and accounts for 15% of presentations.

(i) Torsion of the testis: commonest in adolescence and the early twenties. Anatomical predisposing factor: high investment of the tunica vaginalis on the cord — 'bellclapper testis' — which allows free rotation of the testis.
(ii) Differential diagnoses for painful scrotal swellings:
- Torsion of testis: rapid onset; pubertal males; testis may lie high and transversely; knot may be felt in cord.
- Torsion of appendix testis (hydatid of Morgagni): mimics full torsion; early signs include a lump at the upper pole and a blue spot on transillumination; later the whole testis swells.
- Epididymo-orchitis: painful, swollen epididymis more than testis; associated erythema, fever, pyuria; pain relieved by elevating testis; unusual below age 25.
- Orchitis: confined to testis; young men (viral — mumps, glandular fever).
- Perianal haematoma / trauma: history of injury; haematocele does not transilluminate.
(iii) Investigations:
- FBC: infection.
- Ultrasound: painless, non-invasive imaging; high sensitivity and specificity for tumours; excludes torsion if blood flow confirmed.
- Doppler ultrasound: may confirm presence of blood flow where torsion is thought unlikely.
- CT scan: staging for testicular tumours.
- Surgery: may be the only way to confirm or exclude torsion in a high-risk group and should not be delayed for any other investigation if required.
(iv) Management: whenever torsion is suspected, urgent assessment and usually surgery are required. The testis must be untwisted and fixed (orchidopexy) within hours to prevent infarction; the contralateral testis is also fixed.
(v) Testicular tumour: painless swelling in younger adult men (20–50 years); may have a lax secondary hydrocele; associated abdominal lymphadenopathy; hard, irregular, non-tender testicular mass on examination; does not have rapid onset.

(i) Diagnosis: oesophageal atresia (OA) with tracheo-oesophageal fistula (TOF).
- Gas in the stomach indicates a distal fistula connecting the trachea to the distal oesophageal segment, which is Gross Type C (OA with distal TOF) — the most common type.

(ii) Spitz classification:
- This patient has a birth weight greater than 1.5 kg AND a major cardiac anomaly (VSD).
- This places the patient in Spitz Group II: birth weight greater than 1.5 kg but with a major cardiac anomaly (or alternatively birth weight less than 1.5 kg without cardiac anomaly).
- Survival rate: 59%.

(iii) Pre-operative nursing position and rationale:
- Nurse in supine 30 degrees head-up or lateral position.
- Rationale: this position reduces reflux of gastric contents through the distal fistula into the lungs, preventing aspiration pneumonia and chemical lung injury.

(iv) Four associated malformation systems and percentages:
- Cardiovascular: 29%.
- Anorectal: 14%.
- Genitourinary system (GUS): 14%.
- Gastrointestinal (GIT): 13%.
- (Also listed: Vertebral/Skeletal 10%, Respiratory 6%, Genetic 4%.)

(v) Embryological structures:
- The median laryngotracheal groove and the lateral epithelial ridges, which normally fuse to separate the tracheo-bronchial (ventral) component from the dorsal oesophagus.
- Preferential incorporation of tissue into the trachea and recanalization are also involved in normal development; failure of these processes results in OA/TOF.

questions.answerText:
(i) Breast cancer (malignant lesion of the female breast, predominantly adenocarcinoma).
Predisposing factors: strong family history of breast cancer (genetic factors — BRCA1, BRCA2); early menarche and late menopause, especially in nulliparous women; social class I and II; irradiation.
(ii) Triple assessment:
- Clinical: palpation of the breast and axilla; noting hard, irregular, fixed lump; nipple retraction and skin dimpling; peau d'orange; palpable axillary nodes.
- Radiological: mammography (ultrasound in young women with dense or large breasts); features: irregular, spiculated, radio-opaque mass with microcalcification.
- Cytological: FNAC or core biopsy; breast biopsy (excision biopsy) occasionally required.
(iii) TNM staging: IS — in situ; Stage 0 — impalpable, no nodes, no metastases; Stage 1 — <2 cm, unfixed homolateral nodes, present metastases; Stage 2 — 2–5 cm, fixed homolateral nodes; Stage 3 — 5–10 cm, contralateral or clavicular nodes; Stage 4 — >10 cm, chest wall fixed.
(iv) Early breast cancer management:
- Local treatment: lumpectomy + radiotherapy to breast; or simple mastectomy.
- Axillary treatment: axillary dissection (at time of surgery); or radiotherapy to axilla.
- Systemic prevention: hormonal therapy (e.g. tamoxifen); or adjuvant chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, 5-FU) if high risk (positive lymph nodes, bad histological features).
(v) Prognosis: early breast cancer — overall 80% 10-year survival rate. Late breast cancer — only 30–40% respond to treatment; mean survival 2 years. Prognosis depends on lymph node status, tumour size, and histological grade.

questions.answerText:
(i) Governing principle: always suspect a spinal injury in all high-priority trauma patients; when in doubt, go ahead and immobilise.
(ii) Scene assessment steps: look at the scene; properly assess the patient; determine the mechanism of injury; determine whether to immobilise — when in doubt, immobilise.
(iii) Purpose of spinal immobilisation: protects the patient's spine from further injury; serves as a total body splint; makes it easier to move the patient from the scene.
(iv) Two-responder technique:
- First responder: holds the victim's head in an in-line, neutral position to prevent movement that may cause additional injury.
- Second responder: assesses the neck — checks for signs of injury, jugular venous distension, and bruising; asks the patient about pain; then places the cervical collar around the patient's neck. The cervical collar supports the head in a neutral position and limits head movement.
After placement: maintain head in neutral position; secure to a spine board.
(v) Primary survey in multi-traumatised patient: airway maintenance and C-spine protection; breathing; circulation and control of haemorrhage; rapid neurological survey (GCS, pupils); exposure — remove all clothes; ventilate and oxygenate; reverse shock; NG and urinary catheter; ICU and theatre.

questions.answerText:
(A)(i) Anterior mediastinum: thymoma, lymphoma, germ cell tumour. Visceral compartment: fore-gut cyst, bronchogenic cyst, oesophageal and gastric origin tumours, secondary tumour of lymph node, pleuropericardial cyst, cystic lymphangioma. Paravertebral sulci: neurogenic tumour, vascular tumour, mesenchymal tumour, lymphatic lesion, fibroma, lipoma.

(A)(ii) In adults, anterior compartment masses are more likely to be malignant; masses are more often malignant in ages 30–50 years; 1/3 of tumours are symptomatic in adults. In children, posterior mediastinum masses are most common, most often benign, and 2/3 of tumours are symptomatic. In 20–40 year olds, likelihood of a mass being malignant is greater due to increased incidence of lymphoma and germ cell tumours. In infants and children, neurogenic tumours and enterogenous cysts are most common. In adults, neurogenic tumours, thymomas, and thymic cysts are most frequent.

(A)(iii) Airway compression — recurrent pulmonary infection, haemoptysis. Oesophageal compression — dysphagia. Spinal column involvement — paralysis. Phrenic nerve damage — elevated hemidiaphragm. Recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement — hoarseness. Sympathetic ganglion involvement — Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). SVC involvement — facial, neck and upper extremity swelling, dyspnoea, chest and upper extremity pain, mental status changes. Systemic diseases: thymoma — myasthenia gravis, immune deficiency, red cell aplastic anaemia; goitre — thyrotoxicosis; thymic carcinoid — Cushing's syndrome; parathyroid — hyperparathyroidism.

(B) Thymoma: 1/3 present with symptoms due to compression or invasion; 35% present with myasthenia gravis. Myasthenia gravis mechanism: autoantibodies to acetylcholine (ACH) receptors; ACH receptor concentration at neuromuscular end plate is reduced; symptoms — ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, dysarthria, dysphagia; severity of weakness increases during the day. 15% of patients with myasthenia gravis have a thymoma; 30–50% of patients with thymoma have myasthenia gravis; female-to-male ratio in myasthenia gravis is 2:1. Tensilon test (edrophonium chloride — a short-acting anticholinesterase): response within 45–60 seconds; patients may experience salivation, sweating, and nausea; blood tests for ACH receptor antibodies are elevated in most patients. Medical treatment: pyridostigmine (Mestinon); neostigmine bromide (Prostigmin); steroids; azathioprine (Imuran); cyclosporine; plasma exchange; intravenous immune globulin; thymectomy results in remission in up to 50% of patients.

(C) Staging: Stage I — intact capsule; Stage II — local invasion of pleura, phrenic nerve, or pericardium; Stage III — gross invasion (lung or aorta); Stage IVA — intrathoracic dissemination; Stage IVB — extrathoracic dissemination. Radiation offered for Stage II or higher; chemotherapy in Stage IV under clinical protocol. Management principles: excision — for teratomas, thymomas, and isolated masses likely to be benign (via VATS, median sternotomy, or thoracotomy); needle aspiration — for cystic lesions; diagnostic biopsy — procedure of choice when lymphoma, germ cell tumour, or unresectable invasive malignancy is suspected.

A(i) Zone I — the base of the neck, demarcated by the thoracic inlet inferiorly and the cricoid cartilage superiorly. Structures at risk: great vessels (subclavian vessels, brachiocephalic veins, common carotid arteries, jugular veins), aortic arch, trachea, oesophagus, lung apices, cervical spine, spinal cord, and cervical nerve roots. Zone II — from the cricoid cartilage to the angle of the mandible. Structures: carotid and vertebral arteries, jugular veins, pharynx, larynx, trachea, oesophagus, and cervical spine and spinal cord. Zone III — superior aspect, bounded by the angle of the mandible and the base of the skull. Structures: salivary and parotid glands, oesophagus, trachea, cervical spine, carotid arteries, jugular veins, and major nerves including cranial nerves IX–XII.
A(ii) Zone I: Signs of a significant injury may be hidden in the chest or mediastinum. Zone III: Injuries can prove difficult to access surgically. Zone II: injuries are the most apparent on inspection and tend not to be occult, making them easier to diagnose and explore surgically. Angiography is routinely employed to evaluate stable patients with penetrating wounds to Zones I and III.
B(i) The neck is invested by two fascial layers. The superficial fascia envelops the platysma muscle. A deeper cervical fascia envelops the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, and also demarcates: the pretracheal region (including the trachea, larynx, thyroid gland, and pericardium); the prevertebral area (containing the prevertebral muscles, phrenic nerve, brachial plexus, and axillary sheath); and the carotid sheath (enclosing the carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve).

A(i) Hypoxia and hypotension:
- Present in 20% of head injury patients.
- Aggravates spinal cord injury.
- Inversely correlated to outcome (i.e., the more hypoxia/hypotension, the worse the outcome).
- More common in death and vegetative states.
Mechanism of neural injury: hypoperfusion; microvascular damage; membrane disruption; anoxic and ischaemic cell death.
A(ii) Priorities and conflicts:
- Airway maintenance vs C-spine protection (securing airway may risk cord injury; immobilising the spine may delay airway).
- Airway maintenance vs basal skull fracture (nasal intubation risk with basal skull fracture).
- Fluid resuscitation vs brain swelling (aggressive fluid resuscitation may worsen cerebral oedema).
- Abdominal injury vs head and spine injury (surgery needed for abdomen competes with neurosurgical priorities).
- Neuroradiology in multi-trauma patients (time required for CT in a haemodynamically unstable patient).

- Good Recovery: return to pre-injury level of function.
- Moderate Disability: diminished level of function but cares for self.
- Severe Disability: unable to care for self.
- Vegetative State: no awareness of self or environment.
- Death.
B(ii) Classification of head injuries:
Scalp: scalp injuries.
Skull fractures: linear/stellate; depressed/non-depressed; basal (with or without CSF leak/cranial nerve palsies).
Intracranial lesions:
- Covering haematomas: extradural and subdural.
- Brain lesions: contusions; haematomas; diffuse axonal injury (DAI).

A 55-year-old man with weight loss and wasting presents with a haemodynamically stable episode of haemoptysis. Chest CT shows localized cavitary disease in the right upper lobe, a destroyed lobe with evidence of bronchiectasis, and organisms in the sputum confirmed on smear and culture. His preoperative FEV1 is 1.2 litres and albumin is 2.8 g/dL.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and how are the causative organisms distinguished on smear?
(ii) What patterns of disease distribution does CT show for this condition?
(iii) What is the perioperative nutritional goal, and why is nutritional rehabilitation particularly challenging in this condition?

questions.answerText:
(i) Intrathoracic tuberculosis with localized cavitary disease (or surgical complication of tuberculosis — localized cavitary disease requiring surgery). On smear, the acid-fast organisms of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) and environmental mycobacteria (EM) appear the same; culture and sensitivity data are critical for appropriate identification; the smear can estimate the infectious load and be used as a rapid method of following the patient's response to treatment.

(ii) CT patterns of disease distribution: localized cavitary disease in the upper lung field; destroyed lobe (right upper lobe preferentially) or destroyed lung (left lung preferentially for total lung destruction); localized disease in the lingula or the middle lobe.

(iii) Nutritional goal: achieve albumin level >3.0 g/dL and an anabolic state. Challenges: these patients are often cachectic and nutritionally depleted; the catabolic wasting nature of the disease makes nutritional rehabilitation extremely difficult; patients are frequently unable to orally ingest a sufficiently large caloric load; supplementation via feeding tubes and parenteral nutrition is necessary.

(iv) Conclusion on timing: whenever possible, surgery should be postponed until multidrug therapy has been administered for 3 months. Positive sputum culture despite therapy: despite 3 months of multidrug therapy, about one half (50%) of patients operated on will still have a positive sputum culture.

A male neonate presents with abdominal distension, a palpable 'golf-ball' bladder, dribbling urinary incontinence, and failure to thrive. He appears deceptively healthy-looking but has biochemical evidence of uraemia and hyperkalaemia, and the kidneys are palpable. Micturating cystourethrogram (MCU) reveals sacculation, narrow bladder neck, and posterior urethral dilatation.

(i) What is the diagnosis? Describe the pathological type and mechanism.
(ii) State the pathological effects on the urinary tract from valve obstruction downward.
(iii) Outline the immediate management steps for this neonate.
(iv) Name the definitive treatment procedure(s) and the indications for nephrostomy or ureterostomy.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Congenital posterior urethral valves (males).
Type: Exaggerated semilunar urethral folds at the crista terminalis (Young Type I), causing variable degrees of obstruction (mild, moderate, severe).
Mechanism: The valves cause obstruction to urinary outflow, leading to progressive back-pressure on the entire urinary tract.

(ii) Pathological effects:
- Trabeculation and sacculation of the urinary bladder
- Posterior urethral dilatation above the valves
- Bladder neck — narrow but not obstructed
- Megaureters (secondary uretero-vesical obstruction)
- Hydronephrosis; gross renal damage at birth; cystic kidneys
- Electrolyte imbalance (natriuresis), uraemia, hyperkalaemia
- Septicaemia, failure to thrive
- Vesicoureteric reflux (VUR)

(iii) Immediate management:
- Baby in good condition: IV fluids (avoid high pressure and high sodium); urethral drainage
- Baby dehydrated or uraemic: IV fluids, electrolyte correction
- Infected urine: antibiotics
- Failure of improvement in poor conditions: peritoneal dialysis + urethral drainage
- Advanced renal deterioration or pyonephrosis: immediate bilateral nephrostomy

(iv) Definitive treatment:
Ablation of the valves (fulguration — endoscopic) or non-operative (Fogarty or Foley catheter, urethral hook — Williams method).
Secondary uretero-vesical obstruction: reimplantation of ureters if dilatation continues after ablation.
VUR: ablation of valves → drainage → antibiotics; if reflux continues, reimplantation after surveillance.
For poor general condition, poorly functioning kidneys and ureters: cutaneous ureterostomy (loop or ring — ring preferred).

A(i) Cell type classifications: Bone — benign: Osteoid Osteoma; malignant: Osteosarcoma. Cartilage — benign: Chondroma, Osteochondroma; malignant: Chondrosarcoma. Fibrous Tissue — benign: Fibroma; malignant: Fibrosarcoma. Marrow — benign: Haemangioma; malignant: Angiosarcoma. Uncertain — benign: Giant Cell Tumour; malignant: Malignant Giant Cell Tumour. Ratio of malignant primary bone tumours to metastatic bone tumours is 1:25.
A(ii) History: onset (usually prolonged); age; asymptomatic (incidental finding); pain; swelling/lump; trauma; neurological symptoms; pathological fractures. Examination: general and loco-regional (look, feel, movement). Diagnostic imaging: plain X-rays (useful for early lesion); bone scan (skip lesions, early metastasis); CT (tumour extent); MRI (best for soft tissue tumours). Laboratory: anaemia, ESR; alkaline phosphatase; protein electrophoresis; Bence Jones protein; SAP. Biopsy: large-bone needle; open biopsy — incisional (boundary zone) or excisional.
B(i) Enneking (1986) adapted by American Joint Committee on Cancer (1997): Stage IA — low grade, intracompartmental; Stage IB — low grade, extracompartmental; Stage IIA — high grade, intracompartmental; Stage IIB — high grade, extracompartmental; Stage III — distant metastasis. Benign lesions are lowest grade. Wide margin used for Stage IA; wide resection + chemotherapy for Stage IIA. Radical (en-bloc) resection for higher-stage disease.
B(ii) Multiple myeloma is a malignant B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder of the marrow predominantly affecting plasma cells. It causes: plasma protein abnormalities leading to increased blood viscosity; anaemia from marrow replacement; hypercalcaemia from bone destruction. These systemic effects cause functional deficits in multiple organs. Age of presentation is 45–65 years.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: rupture of the posterior (prostatomembranous) urethra. The posterior urethra has two parts: prostatomembranous (posterior) and bulbar + pendulous (anterior). Specific findings: urethral bleeding; blood at urethral meatus; inability to void with full bladder; high-riding prostate on rectal examination; associated fractured pelvis. RUG confirms: extravasation of contrast at the site of rupture.

(ii) Indications for RUG: blood at external urethral meatus; perineal discoloration; fractured pelvis; failure to void. Bladder and urethral injuries are best evaluated with RUG and cystography.

(iii) Investigation for bladder rupture: cystogram with post-evacuation film.
Management:
- Intraperitoneal rupture of bladder: history includes blunt force to full bladder (RTA, fall from height), fractured pelvis, deceleration injury, lack of sensation of bladder fullness, haematuria, inability to void, diffuse lower abdominal tenderness. Management: explore within 48 hours.
- Extraperitoneal rupture: catheterize and continue continuous drainage of urine.

(iv) Anterior urethral injury: more common than posterior urethral injuries. Most often follows a fall astride or a kick to the perineum. Extravasation of blood and urine occurs at the site of rupture, leading to swelling of the penis and scrotum/perineum. This differs from posterior urethral injury in mechanism (pelvic fracture vs. perineal trauma), in urethral location (membranous vs. bulbar), and in the pattern of extravasation (perineal/scrotal swelling vs. pelvic haematoma with high-riding prostate); the high-riding prostate is specific to posterior urethral injury because the prostate is tethered by the urethra and disruption allows the prostate to float superiorly.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Coma is defined as Glasgow Coma Score less than 9. Causes:
- Coma with no localising CNS signs: metabolic insults (hypoglycaemia, uraemia, nonketotic hyperosmolar coma, Addison's disease, DKA, hypothyroidism, hepatic coma); respiratory (hypoxia, hypercapnia); intoxication (barbiturates, alcohol, opiates, carbon monoxide, benzodiazepines); infections (sepsis, pneumonia, typhoid fever); shock (hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, septic, anaphylactic); epilepsy; hypertensive encephalopathy; hyperthermia (heat stroke); hypothermia.
- Coma with meningeal irritation without localising signs: meningitis; subarachnoid haemorrhage from ruptured aneurysm; AV malformation.
- Focal brainstem or lateralising signs: pontine haemorrhage; CVA; brain abscess; subdural/epidural haemorrhage.
A(ii) Primary brain injury has already happened (stroke, head injury, meningitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage). Secondary brain injury involves cells around the primary injury that are rendered dysfunctional but not mechanically destroyed; if the environment is favourable they can recover, but hypoxaemia or ischaemia cause irreversible damage. Cerebral autoregulation: the brain autoregulates its own blood flow to maintain constant flow between a mean arterial pressure of 60 and 150 mmHg. Below 60, reduced blood flow leads to ischaemia; above 150, increased blood flow leads to oedema. Injured brains autoregulate less effectively.
B(i) Cerebral blood flow is approximately 15% of cardiac output. It is affected mainly by PaCO2, PaO2, and mean arterial pressure. The brain's metabolic rate is increased by fever and reduced by hypothermia. Hypoxaemia and hypotension are commonly found at the scene of head injury and are associated with a statistically significant worse outcome.
B(ii) The skull is a rigid box. Initially, any change in intracranial blood volume is accompanied by an opposite change in CSF volume. This compensatory mechanism is limited; brainstem herniation will eventually occur. Signs of acute raised ICP: confusion and reduced conscious level; nausea and early morning headaches (subacute onset). Raised ICP is the most common cause of death after head injury or intracerebral haemorrhage.

B(ii) Explain the mechanism of raised intracranial pressure following head injury, describe the signs of acute raised intracranial pressure, and state what the skull's compensatory mechanism is and why it is limited.

A 6-month-old infant presents with poor feeding, failure to thrive, recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, and sweating. Examination reveals tachycardia, tachypnoea, and hepatomegaly. A grade 2–3/6 systolic ejection murmur is heard at the left sternal border with widely split and fixed S2. CXR shows cardiomegaly with enlargement of the right atrium and right ventricle. ECG shows right axis deviation and mild right bundle branch block.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis and the most common anatomical type?
(ii) Explain the pathophysiology — including shunt direction, what determines the magnitude of the shunt, and why the left atrium is not enlarged.
(iii) What are the management options, including the criteria for device closure and the surgical repair technique?
questions.answerText:
(i) Atrial septal defect (ASD). The most common type is ostium secundum defect, accounting for 50–70% of all ASDs, occurring at the site of the fossa ovalis.

(ii) Pathophysiology: direction of the shunt is from left to right; magnitude of shunt is determined by the size of the defect and the relative compliance of the right ventricle (RV) and left ventricle (LV); the right atrium (RA), RV, and main pulmonary artery (PA) and its branches are dilated. The left atrium (LA) is not enlarged because the increased pulmonary venous return to the LA does not stay in that chamber — it is shunted immediately to the RA; the absence of LA enlargement is a helpful X-ray sign differentiating ASD from VSD. The PAs can handle increased blood flow for a long time without CHF because there is no direct transmission of systemic pressure to the PA; CHF and pulmonary hypertension eventually develop in the third and fourth decades of life.

(iii) Management: medical — treatment of CHF. Non-surgical/device closure — catheter-delivered closure devices (Sideris buttoned device, Angel Wings device, CardioSEAL device, Amplatzer ASD Occlusion Device); indicated for secundum ASD measuring 5 mm or more (but less than 32 mm) with significant left-to-right shunt and clinical evidence of RV volume overload. Surgical closure: indication — left-to-right shunt with pulmonary-to-systemic blood flow ratio ≥1.5:1 if device closure not appropriate; surgery usually delayed until 2–4 years of age; if CHF does not respond to medical management, surgery during infancy; traditional repair — midsternal incision under cardiopulmonary bypass by simple suture or pericardial/Teflon patch. Contraindication: pulmonary vascular resistance >10 units/m2 (>7 units/m2 with vasodilators).

questions.question:
(A) Describe constrictive pericarditis under the following headings:
(i) Definition and aetiology
(ii) Pathophysiology and haemodynamic effects on the cardiac chambers
(iii) Clinical features arising from (a) reduced cardiac output and (b) elevated systemic venous pressure

(B) State the investigations used to diagnose constrictive pericarditis, including the echocardiographic and cardiac catheterisation findings.

(C) Distinguish constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy on clinical, haemodynamic, and imaging grounds.
questions.answerText:
(A)(i) Constrictive pericarditis is chronic pericardial inflammation causing impaired ventricular filling. Aetiology: purulent; tuberculosis; idiopathic; neoplastic; irradiation; post-surgical; uraemia.

(A)(ii) Pathophysiology: marked pericardial thickening; pericardial sac obliteration; calcification of the pericardium, which may extend into myocardium; symmetrical constricting effect producing elevation and equalization of all diastolic pressures in all chambers. Right and left ventricular diastolic pressure increased and stroke volume decreased; a small increase in volume results in a considerable increase in end-diastolic pressure. Respiratory intrathoracic pressure changes are not transmitted to the pericardium and intracardiac chambers; during inspiration, systemic venous and right atrial pressures do not fall and venous flow into the right ventricle does not increase — this produces Kussmaul's sign.

(A)(iii) (a) Reduced cardiac output: fatigue, hypotension, reflex tachycardia. (b) Elevated systemic venous pressure: jugular venous distension, hepatomegaly with marked ascites and peripheral oedema.

(B) Investigations: chest X-ray (pericardial calcification); ECG (atrial fibrillation); echocardiography — pericardial thickening and calcifications, RA and LA enlargement, normal ventricles, normal systolic function, LV diameter not increasing after early rapid filling phase, restricted filling of both ventricles, respiratory variation >25% over AV valves; CT/MRI; cardiac catheterisation — dip and plateau/square root sign, equalization of LV/RV end-diastolic pressures.

(C) Constrictive pericarditis: has calcifications; respiratory variation of mitral E wave inflow velocity; preserved systolic function; no impaired ventricular or atrial filling in early diastole; pericardium thickened or calcified; end-diastolic pressures track each other. Restrictive cardiomyopathy: apical impulse +++, S3, S4, regurgitant murmurs; no calcification; no respiratory variation of mitral E wave inflow velocity; compromises both systolic and diastolic function; no surgical therapy; patients tolerate surgical stress poorly.

A. A wound is an area of compromised tissue integrity (or an area of the body whose normal integrity has been compromised). Wound healing occurs in three phases:
- Inflammatory phase: blood fills the gap and clots; fibrin in the clot holds the edges together; vascular dilatation and increased permeability occur; inflammatory exudate containing polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNLs) accumulates; monocytes transform to macrophages; lymphocytes enter last (after 72 hours); monocytes must be present to trigger fibroblast invasion and proliferation.
- Proliferative phase: commences 3 days after wounding, lasts several weeks; comprises fibroplasia (fibroblasts attracted by PDGF and TGF-β construct new extracellular matrix — initially fibronectin and hyaluronan, later collagen and proteoglycan), epithelialisation (cells at wound margins migrate and multiply, stimulated by EGF, β-FGF and KGF), and angiogenesis (capillary sprouts invade fibrin stimulated by TGF-β, PDGF, TNF-α and β-FGF, forming granulation tissue). For skin, peak tensile strength is achieved 60 days after injury.
- Maturation/remodelling phase: commences about 3 weeks after wounding; balance between collagen formation and degradation by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) produced by fibroblasts, granulocytes and macrophages; collagen orientates in an organised fashion; macrophage and fibroblast density reduce by apoptosis; acellular, avascular scar results; eventual tensile strength is only 80% of normal.
A(i) Healing by first (primary) intention occurs when the wound is clean, edges are close together, and there is no tension. Healing by second intention occurs when the wound is dirty, infected, and the gap is large; the proliferative phase is prolonged and visible as granulation tissue.
B. General factors influencing wound healing include: nutrition (especially methionine, Vitamin A and C — Vitamin C is a cofactor in hydroxylation of lysine and proline — and Vitamin E which increases breaking strength in irradiated wounds); oxygen (oxygen-carrying capacity of blood should be enhanced); oxygen radicals (degrade collagen, interfere with protein enzymes, and retard healing); drugs (NSAIDs decrease collagen synthesis); smoking (detrimental to wound healing); age (tensile strength and wound closure rate decrease with age); temperature; and diabetes mellitus.
B(i) Complications of wound healing include: wound infection; septicaemia; chronicity; hypertrophic scar; keloid; stretched scar; contractures; dyschromia (hypopigmentation and hyperpigmentation); implantation cyst; lymphoedema; bone complications (osteitis, osteomyelitis); Marjolin's ulcer; tetanus; and pressure ulcers.
questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of a WOUND and its healing process under the three phases, detailing the cellular and biochemical events occurring in each phase.
A(i) Explain the difference between healing by first intention and healing by second intention, and state the condition of the wound required for each.
B. List the general factors that influence wound healing and explain, with specific examples for two of the factors, how they impair healing.
B(i) List all the complications of wound healing.

A 70-year-old man presents to the emergency department confused, with rapid breathing, fever (39.2°C), and blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg. He is on oxygen. Arterial blood gases show pH 7.28, PO2 9.0 kPa, and elevated PCO2. He had an elective right hemicolectomy 48 hours earlier.
(i) Define hypoxia and hypoxaemia. List all the common postoperative causes of hypoxia after abdominal surgery.
(ii) What are the clinical features of hypoxia in the unconscious patient, and in the conscious patient?
(iii) What are the key investigations and their specific findings expected in postoperative hypoxia?
(iv) Describe the essential management of hypoxia covering airway, breathing, and circulatory support.
(v) Why are elderly confused patients on surgical wards considered hypoxic until proven otherwise, and what is the clinical significance of pulse oximetry saturations below 85%?
questions.answerText:
(i) Hypoxia: a lack of O2 (usually meaning lack of O2 delivery to tissues or cells). Hypoxaemia: a lack of O2 in arterial blood.
Common postoperative causes:
- CNS depression (e.g. post-anaesthesia, opiates).
- Airway obstruction (e.g. aspiration of blood or vomit).
- Poor ventilation (e.g. abdominal pain, mechanical disruption).
- Loss of functioning lung (e.g. V/Q mismatch — pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, collapse/consolidation).
Note: 80% of patients following upper abdominal surgery are hypoxic during the first 48 h postoperatively.
(ii) Clinical features:
- In the unconscious patient: central cyanosis; abnormal respirations; hypotension.
- In the conscious patient: central cyanosis; anxiety, restlessness, and confusion; tachypnoea; tachycardia, dysrhythmias (AF), and hypotension.
(iii) Key investigations:
- Pulse oximetry saturations: guide to arterial oxygenation.
- Arterial blood gases (PCO2, PO2, pH, base excess): respiratory acidosis; metabolic acidosis later.
- Chest X-ray: collapse/pneumothorax/consolidation.
- ECG: AF.
(iv) Essential management:
- Airway: triple airway manoeuvre; suction secretions; clear oropharynx; consider endotracheal intubation in CNS depression/exhausted patients (rising PCO2), neuromuscular failure; consider surgical airway (cricothyroidotomy/mini-tracheostomy) in facial trauma, upper airway obstruction.
- Breathing: position patient upright; adequate analgesia; supplemental O2 (mask/bag/ventilation); support respiratory physiology (physiotherapy, humidified gases, encourage coughing, bronchodilators).
- Circulatory support: maintain cardiac output; ensure adequate fluid resuscitation; determine and treat the cause.
(v) Acutely confused elderly patients on a surgical ward are hypoxic until proven otherwise because hypoxia causes confusion mimicking other causes. Pulse oximetry saturations <85% equate to an arterial PO2 <8 kPa and are unreliable in patients with poor peripheral perfusion.

A) Embryological origin and course:
- Thyroid diverticulum arises from the Foramen Caecum at 4th–7th week of intrauterine life
- Descends in the midline; the tract is closely related to the hyoid bone (derived from the 2nd branchial arch) during descent before obliteration
- Failure of obliteration produces a thyroglossal duct cyst
- Because the thyroglossal tract passes through or loops around the hyoid bone and is attached to the base of the tongue at the foramen caecum, the cyst moves with protrusion of the tongue (the tongue pulls the tract upward via its attachment), and is immobile while the tongue stays protruded

B) Clinical features:
- Midline cystic mass above or below the hyoid bone (60–65% adjacent to or just inferior to hyoid)
- Smooth, soft, non-tender; sometimes with a discharging sinus
- Moves with deglutition and with protrusion of the tongue
- Swelling is immobile when tongue stays protruded
- 70% of all congenital midline neck masses; most common diagnosed within the first two decades
Treatment: Sistrunk operation — removal of the cyst, the thyroglossal tract, and the central portion (body) of the hyoid bone. The hyoid body must be included because the tract passes through it; incomplete removal leads to recurrence (rate rises to near 100% if hyoid not resected).

C) Branchial cleft distinctions:
First branchial cleft cyst Type II:
- Anterior neck, suprahyoid
- Courses over the mandible and through the parotid gland
- In close relation to CN VII (facial nerve) — risk of injury
- Terminates near bony-cartilaginous junction of external ear
- Surgery may involve superficial parotidectomy
Second branchial cleft cyst (most common branchial anomaly, 90%):
- Fluctuant mass in the anterior triangle at the junction of lower and middle 2/3 of the sternocleidomastoid
- Passes between the internal and external carotid arteries
- Terminates in the tonsillar fossa
- Surgery may include tonsillectomy
questions.question:
A) Describe the embryological origin, course, and anatomical relations of the thyroglossal duct, and explain why a thyroglossal duct cyst moves with tongue protrusion.

B) Describe the clinical features of the thyroglossal duct cyst, state the safe surgical approach, and explain the anatomical basis for including the body of the hyoid bone in the excision.

C) Distinguish the anatomical basis of a first branchial cleft cyst (Type II) from a second branchial cleft cyst in terms of relations, course, and structures at risk during surgery.

questions.answerText:
(i) Predisposing factors in decreasing importance:
- Prior CRC or adenomatous polyps.
- Hereditary polyposis syndromes.
- Family history of CRC.
- Chronic active ulcerative colitis.
- Diet (low in indigestible fibre, high in animal fat).
- Increased faecal bile salts; selenium deficiency.
(ii) Pathological features:
- Site: 75% of lesions within 60 cm of the anal margin (rectum, sigmoid, left colon); 50% rectal; 5% caecal.
- Macroscopic types: polypoid, ulcerating, annular, infiltrative.
- 3% synchronous; 3% metachronous.
- Histology: adenocarcinoma (10–15% are mucinous adenocarcinoma).
- Spread: lymphatic; haematogenous (via veins to liver); peritoneal.
(iii) Dukes' staging and 5-year survival:
- A: confined to bowel wall — 80%.
- B: through bowel wall — 60%.
- C: involved lymph nodes (whatever state of primary) — 35%.
- D: distant metastases — 5%.
- Also 25% 5-year survival after successful resection of <5 liver metastases.
(iv) Surgical procedures for curative resection:
- Right hemicolectomy (no bowel preparation): lesions from caecum to splenic flexure.
- Left hemicolectomy (bowel preparation): lesions of descending and sigmoid colon.
- Anterior resection: rectal tumours.
- Abdomino-perineal resection and colostomy: very low rectal lesions.
- Hartmann's procedure: emergency surgery to left colon.
- Resection possible for liver metastases if fewer than five.
(v) Adjuvant treatments:
- Radiotherapy: to shrink rectal cancers preoperatively, or to palliate inoperable rectal cancer.
- Adjuvant chemotherapy (5-FU ± levamisole): to reduce risk of systemic recurrence in Dukes' C and some Dukes' B; to palliate liver metastases.
questions.question:
Describe colorectal carcinoma (CRC) under the following headings:
(i) Predisposing/aetiological factors in decreasing order of importance.
(ii) Pathological features: site distribution, macroscopic types, histological type, and modes of spread.
(iii) Dukes' staging system with its prognostic implications (5-year survival).
(iv) Surgical procedures available for curative resection, matched to tumour site.
(v) Non-surgical (adjuvant) treatments and their indications.

A 62-year-old man presents with change in bowel habit, haematochezia, toothpaste-calibre stools, and spurious diarrhoea for three months. Colonoscopy reveals an annular, constricting lesion in the descending colon. Barium enema shows a classical napkin-ring appearance.

(i) State the diagnosis and the specific macroscopic description of this type of lesion.
(ii) List the genetic risk factors for colorectal carcinoma, naming the specific polyposis syndromes and their features.
(iii) List four complications that may arise from this tumour at this site, including those attributable to fistula formation.
(iv) Name the definitive surgical procedure indicated for a tumour at this site, and state the operations indicated for tumours at three other specific colonic sites.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: colorectal carcinoma of the descending colon.
- Macroscopic description: annular, stenosing, or constricting lesion (producing the napkin-ring or stenosing appearance on imaging).

(ii) Genetic risk factors:
- Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP): number of polyps between 150–1000; colon cancer usually develops within 20 years of diagnosis.
- Gardner's syndrome: adenomatous polyps with soft tissue tumours and bony exostoses; malignant transformation of the polyps occurs in 100% of patients.
- Turcot's syndrome: colonic polyps plus brain tumours (usually supratentorial glioblastomas).
- Peutz-Jeghers syndrome: multiple intestinal hamartomatous polyps associated with mucocutaneous melanotic pigmentation; malignant transformation is rare.
- Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC / Lynch syndrome, types 1 and 2).
- Juvenile polyposis syndrome.

(iii) Four complications:
- Intestinal obstruction from progressive fibrosis causing stenosis.
- Perforation leading to generalised peritonitis or pericolic abscess formation.
- Profuse colonic haemorrhage.
- Fistula formation: colovesical (commonest), colovaginal, or colocutaneous fistula.

(iv) Surgical procedures by site:
- Descending colon (this tumour): left hemicolectomy.
- Caecum and ascending colon: right hemicolectomy.
- Transverse colon: transverse colectomy.
- Sigmoid colon: sigmoid colectomy.
- Proximal rectum (rectosigmoid): anterior resection.
- Distal rectum: abdomino-perineal (AP) resection (with permanent colostomy).

questions.question:
A 68-year-old man presents with progressively worsening obstructive lower urinary tract symptoms, occasional haematuria, and a six-week history of low back pain. Digital rectal examination reveals an asymmetric, hard, woody prostate with an obliterated median sulcus and a palpable seminal vesicle. PSA is elevated above 4 ng/ml.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis and identify the histological type that accounts for the majority of such tumours.
(ii) Outline the embryologic/anatomical basis of the gland's zonal architecture and explain from which zone this malignancy most commonly arises.
(iii) Describe the initial resuscitative and investigative steps required before definitive treatment.
(iv) Outline the definitive treatment options for both localised disease and the advanced disease demonstrated by this patient's skeletal metastases.
questions.answerText:
(i) Carcinoma of the prostate. Adenocarcinoma accounts for 85% of cases; other types include transitional cell carcinoma, pure primary squamous cell carcinoma, sarcomas, and lymphomas.

(ii) The prostate has peripheral, central, peri-urethral/preprostatic, and anterior zones; lobes exist only in the embryo (five lobes: two lateral, posterior, median, and anterior). Carcinoma of the prostate arises predominantly from the peripheral zone.

(iii) Investigations include: urethrocystoscopy; urine M/C/S; urea, electrolytes and creatinine (GFR), PCV; ultrasound (KUB + post-void residual); peak urine flow rate (normal ≥20 ml/s); PSA (normal 0–4 ng/ml); transrectal ultrasound-guided (TRUS) biopsy using a Trucut needle to confirm diagnosis histologically; radiology for metastases — CXR, abdominal/pelvic/lumbosacral/skull X-rays; bone radioisotope scan (Tc99-labelled); CT and MRI; LFTs; urinalysis; HIV, HBsAg, RBS; ECG.

(iv) Localised disease: watchful waiting/active surveillance; radical prostatectomy; radiotherapy; others including cryosurgery, laser, HIFU.
Advanced/metastatic disease (androgen deprivation therapy): orchidectomy; LHRH analogues (goserelin/zoladex, buserelin); anti-androgens (flutamide, bicalutamide, nilutamide); oestrogens (diethylstilboestrol — now outdated); combinations; localised radiotherapy; combinations such as radiotherapy plus hormonal therapy. Further agents in the treatment landscape include docetaxel, cabazitaxel, abiraterone, enzalutamide, radium-223, denosumab/zoledronic acid, olaparib, pembrolizumab (MSI-high), and apalutamide.

(A)(i) Preoperative risk assessment: pulmonary function testing; ventilation-perfusion scanning; room-air arterial blood gas analysis; routine laboratory evaluation; resting ECG in patients older than 40 years. Surgical candidacy criteria: no evidence of severe cardiopulmonary limitation by history and physical examination; predicted postoperative FEV1 >800 mL and preferably >1 litre; no evidence of pulmonary hypertension — specifically pulmonary artery diastolic pressure ≤20 mmHg and no elevated pulmonary vascular resistance.

(A)(ii) Medical therapy: culture-specific multidrug regimens for approximately 3 months before surgery. Standard regimen: isoniazid (INH) and rifampicin for 6 months; pyrazinamide administered for the first 2 months (until sputum cultures are negative); occasionally ethambutol or streptomycin is used. This regimen should result in negative sputum findings usually within 3 months. Persistence of sputum positivity suggests MDRTB, which is an indication for surgical resection.

(A)(iii) Nutritional rehabilitation: these patients are often cachectic and nutritionally depleted due to the catabolic wasting nature of the disease; supplementation via feeding tubes; parenteral nutrition to supplement the enteral route; megestrol acetate (Megace), human growth hormones, and anabolic steroids used to stimulate appetite. Goal: achieve albumin level >3.0 g/dL and an anabolic state.

(B) Perioperative: all patients preoperatively instructed in incentive spirometry, coughing, and deep breathing exercises. Postoperative: aggressive postoperative respiratory care is mandatory; precise fluid replacement essential; fluid administration limited to <1,500 mL/day for the first 5 postoperative days to prevent postpneumonectomy pulmonary oedema.

(C) Bronchopleural fistula: factors predisposing to BPF formation are presence of mycobacteria in sputum at time of surgery, previous chest irradiation, extensive polymicrobial superinfection, and previous thoracotomy. Management: drainage of the hemithorax to control infection and limit spillage to remaining lung; after space infection is controlled, BPF may be closed; Eloesser procedure (open-window thoracostomy); thoracoplasty is reserved for failure of all these techniques. Prevention: muscle flap (latissimus dorsi) reinforcement of bronchial stump is recommended when sputum is positive, BPF is pre-existing, or polymicrobial contamination complicates the case.
questions.question:
(A) Describe the preoperative management of a patient undergoing surgery for intrathoracic tuberculosis under the following headings:
(i) Preoperative risk assessment — investigations required and criteria for surgical candidacy
(ii) Medical therapy — drug regimen, duration, and the goal of preoperative drug treatment
(iii) Nutritional rehabilitation — goals and methods used

(B) Describe the perioperative and postoperative care requirements, including fluid management guidelines.

(C) Explain the indications for using a bronchopleural fistula (BPF) repair and what options are available when BPF occurs postoperatively.

A 60-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of progressive lower back pain associated with weight loss and fatigue. Plain X-ray of the lumbar spine shows vertebral body collapse with cod-fish vertebral morphology at L2. She has a known history of breast cancer treated 5 years ago.
(i) What vertebral body pathology is demonstrated and what is the most likely underlying cause? Distinguish this from a primary vertebral collapse in osteoporosis using the radiological morphology described.
(ii) List all the non-degenerative and non-traumatic causes of low back pain.
(iii) Describe the ligaments of the spine, naming each ligament.
(iv) Describe the spinal stability concepts and the anatomy of the vertebra and disc.
questions.answerText:
(i) Vertebral body pathology: the vertebral body collapse together with this patient's history of breast cancer is most consistent with vertebral collapse from metastatic disease. Cod-fish vertebrae with biconcave endplates are classically described in osteoporotic collapse, whereas metastatic vertebral collapse typically results from more irregular lytic bone destruction; the two are distinguished primarily on this radiological pattern together with the clinical history.
(ii) Non-degenerative/non-traumatic causes of low back pain:
- Metabolic bone disease: osteomalacia; osteoporosis; Paget's disease.
- Inflammatory disorders: ankylosing spondylitis; rheumatoid arthritis.
- Infections: pyogenic; granulomatous.
- Neoplastic disorders: benign; malignant (primary); metastatic (breast, lung, lymphoma, prostate); non-vertebral spinal tumours (intramedullary, extramedullary).
- Retroperitoneal and pelvic disorders.
(iii) Ligaments of the spine: anterior longitudinal ligament; posterior longitudinal ligament; ligamentum flavum; capsular ligament; interspinous and supraspinous ligaments; intertransverse ligament.
(iv) The vertebra articulates anteriorly via disc interposition; posterolaterally via facets; laterally and posteriorly via ligaments; with muscular support throughout. The disc is fibrocartilaginous with outer annulus fibrosus and central nucleus pulposus; nucleus pulposus contains >88% water at birth; with ageing, water reduces, thickening occurs, disc space narrows, and ossification may occur.

(i) Radiological finding: pneumoperitoneum (free gas in the peritoneal cavity).
- Presence of free gas in the peritoneal cavity always indicates perforation of a viscus.
- In over 90% of cases the cause of pneumoperitoneum will require emergency surgery.

(ii) Five supine radiograph signs of free intra-abdominal gas:
- Morison's pouch air.
- Perihepatic air.
- Rigler's (double wall) sign.
- Falciform ligament sign.
- Umbilical ligament sign.
- Urachus sign.
- The cupula sign.
- Football or air-dome sign.
(Any five.)

(iii) Commonest and less common causes:
- Commonest cause: peptic ulcer perforation.
- Less common causes: diverticulitis and malignant tumours.

(iv) Pseudo-pneumoperitoneum:
- These are radiological appearances that mimic free gas under the diaphragm but without actual perforation.
- It is important to recognise them because failure to do so may lead to an unnecessary laparotomy in search of a perforated viscus.
- Three commonest causes: Chilaiditi syndrome (hepatodiaphragmatic interposition of colon), subdiaphragmatic fat, and curvilinear pulmonary collapse.

(v) Role of CT:
- CT is the most sensitive modality for detecting pneumoperitoneum and identifying the site and cause of perforation; it is the modality of choice in acute abdominal cases as it is not hampered by overlying gas, bone, or adipose tissue.
questions.question:
A 50-year-old man presents with sudden severe epigastric pain. An erect chest X-ray shows free gas under the right hemidiaphragm. A supine abdominal X-ray shows Rigler's (double wall) sign.

(i) Name the radiological finding and state what it indicates in over 90% of cases.
(ii) List five plain X-ray signs of free intra-abdominal gas on the supine radiograph.
(iii) State the commonest cause of pneumoperitoneum and two less common causes.
(iv) Describe what pseudo-pneumoperitoneum is, state why it is important to recognise, and name its three commonest causes.
(v) State the role of CT scanning in this context.

Regarding bone as a tissue and bone loss:

A(i) Describe the functions of bone, its composition (bone matrix, mineral salt, and bone cells), and the role of each bone cell type.
A(ii) Describe the causes of macro bone loss and explain why macro bone loss is more clinically significant than micro bone loss. Describe the two types of bone (cortical/lamellar and cancellous/trabecular).
B(i) Explain how bone transport differs from callotaxis (distraction osteogenesis) and state the distraction rates for both callotaxis and chondrodiastasis.
B(ii) State why 'artificial bone' is used and describe what it is composed of, including the newer injectable preparations and their specific clinical application.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Functions of bone: protects vital organs (brain, thoracic contents); supports soft tissues; transmits load and muscular force from one part to another; mediates locomotion; is a reservoir of minerals (calcium, phosphate, and dangerous ions like lead); produces blood cells. Composition: Bone matrix — type I collagen, mucopolysaccharide ground substance, non-collagenous protein (proteoglycan, osteonectin, osteocalcin). Bone mineral salt — calcium and phosphate (crystalline hydroxyapatite), ~50% of bone volume, responsible for rigidity. Bone cells: osteoblasts — produce type I collagen and non-collagenous matrix; osteocytes — 'spent osteoblasts', relatively quiescent, maintain communication links and transmit information in response to stress and strain; osteoclasts — regulatory cells involved in organised resorption of bone.
A(ii) Causes of macro bone loss: congenital (congenital cysts, defective ossification as in pseudoarthrosis); traumatic (road traffic accidents, high-velocity gunshot wounds); post-operative (following tumour resection or resection of infected segment of bone). Macro bone loss disrupts structural integrity and mechanical function — especially critical in weight-bearing bones. Micro bone loss (e.g. osteomalacia) occurs at cellular/microscopic level without disrupting bone construct. Two types of bone: cortical (lamellar) bone — dense, forms the outer shell; cancellous (trabecular) bone — spongy internal architecture.
B(i) Bone transport: involves moving a floating bone segment to fill a defect; the floating segment is trailed by a regenerate (following callotaxis) and docks in the area of bone loss; secondary docking must be compressed for union; entire apparatus requires robust external fixator with bone transportation component. This differs from callotaxis (simple distraction osteogenesis): in callotaxis, new bone (regenerate) forms in situ at a single site; in bone transport, the floating segment leaves a trailing regenerate and has to dock secondarily. Distraction rates: callotaxis — 1 mm per day; chondrodiastasis (growth plate distraction) — 0.5 mm daily.
B(ii) Artificial bone is the inorganic component of bone — composed of hydroxyapatite composites. Newer bioactive bone cements include injectable calcium phosphate preparations, used to fill osteoporotic cavities commonly seen in the elderly. They are used to fill small defects and give remarkable support to the recipient bone once they harden at the grafted bed.

questions.question:
A 2-year-old child is brought to the plastic surgery clinic with an extra digit on the ulnar side of the right hand. The extra digit is a small, soft tissue post-axial polydactyly. The parents ask about treatment.
(i) State the Swanson classification type of this deformity and the subcategory (pre-axial versus post-axial) relevant to this case.
(ii) Describe the embryological process that normally eliminates excess digital material, and at what embryological age this normally occurs.
(iii) List the three most common congenital hand deformities.
(iv) State the principles of treatment of congenital hand deformities and explain how each applies to polydactyly.
(v) When three or more minor anomalies coexist, what is the clinical implication, and what is the recommended evaluation process?
questions.answerText:
(i) Swanson Type III — Duplication. This case represents post-axial polydactyly (extra digit on the ulnar side). The Swanson Type III classification may apply to the whole limb, mirror hand, or polydactyly. Pre-axial polydactyly involves the radial/thumb side; post-axial involves the ulnar side.
(ii) Embryological elimination of excess digital material: by 46 days of embryonal life, the digital ray webs regress by apoptosis to form five distinct digits. By 40 days, digital rays are formed with webbing; apoptosis between days 40 and 46 eliminates webbing and excess tissue to produce five distinct digits. Normal apical ectodermal ridge interaction, epidermal-mesenchymal interaction, and mesenchymal-mesenchymal interaction are required. Duplication (polydactyly) results from failure of correct apoptosis or from localised patterning defects.
(iii) The three most common congenital hand deformities: camptodactyly; syndactyly; polydactyly.
(iv) Principles of treatment: (1) improve functional ability — an extra digit on the ulnar side may impair grip or cause cosmetic embarrassment, so excision is warranted; (2) allow unrestricted growth — surgery should not restrict digital growth; (3) achieve a socially acceptable appearance — removal of the redundant digit addresses cosmesis.
(v) When three or more minor anomalies exist in a single patient, the chance of the presence of a major anomaly is 90%. The recommended evaluation process includes: pregnancy, birth, and developmental history; physical examination; laboratory and radiological investigations; genetic counselling.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man involved in a road traffic accident sustains multiple long bone fractures. In the emergency unit, he is noted to have a swollen, tender right calf with a positive Homan's sign. He is commenced on IV fluid resuscitation.

(i) What complication has developed and what is the pathophysiological mechanism responsible for its onset after trauma?
(ii) What investigations confirm this diagnosis, and what are the advantages and disadvantages of each investigative modality?
(iii) Outline the full treatment of deep vein thrombosis including monitoring parameters and duration of anticoagulation based on risk stratification.
(iv) What type of IV fluid is preferred for trauma resuscitation and what is its advantage over alternatives? State the limit at which blood transfusion becomes necessary.
questions.answerText:
(i) Deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Mechanism: following trauma, there is increased coagulability of blood due to release of thromboplastin which stimulates the coagulopathy. Note: venous thrombosis after trauma is NOT due to prolonged bed rest.
(ii) Investigations: (1) Deep venogram using a tourniquet — disadvantages: difficulty finding vein if oedema present; contrast is irritative. (2) Doppler ultrasound — non-invasive; high yield for pelvic vein DVT but low yield for calf vein DVT. (3) Radioactive I-121 + fibrinogen — high yield for calf DVT but low yield for pelvic DVT.
(iii) Treatment: restriction to bed to prevent dislodgement; heparin pump (24,000 IU); warfarin — Day 1: 10 mg; Day 2: 10 mg; use INR (standardized value of PT) maintained between 2–2.5; if INR >4, give warfarin; maintenance dose 2.5–5 mg. Duration: high risk — 6 months; low risk — 3 months.
(iv) Crystalloids are the fluid of choice. Lactated Ringer's is preferred over Normal Saline because it buffers metabolic acidosis better. Crystalloids repletes intravascular volume and enhances perfusion due to decreased blood viscosity. Crystalloids may replace blood loss up to a ratio of 8:1; blood is needed when crystalloid infusion exceeds 50 ml/kg. Meta-analysis has shown that colloids are associated with higher mortality, are costly, and may aggravate post-traumatic complications.

A(i) Definition: haemorrhagic shock is caused by significant blood loss; with hypoperfusion there is failure of adequate oxygen delivery to some tissues of the body. Leading causes worldwide: haemorrhagic shock is the leading cause of death in trauma patients worldwide; primary causes are MVRTI (motor vehicle road traffic injury), MBRTI, and gunshot wounds.
A(ii) Pathophysiology of death: haemorrhagic shock can prove fatal through the pathophysiology of organ system failure, beginning with the lungs and progressing to the renal, gut, immune and cardiovascular systems.
B(i) Classification by source: arterial — bright red, pulsatile, like a jet; venous — dark red, steady, non-pulsatile; capillary — slow, bright red. By nature: revealed — external bleeding; concealed — internal; initially concealed, later revealed.
B(ii) Management: Class I shock — oral fluids. Class II, III and IV — prompt resuscitation. Management should start from pre-hospital care ideally. Arrest haemorrhage concurrently with fluid resuscitation. Consensus on crystalloid; NOT colloids. Prompt type-specific blood transfusion in major haemorrhage. Management of trauma haemorrhage depends on a multifactorial approach: timely surgical intervention, fluid resuscitation and blood transfusion therapy.
C(i) Normal saline: indicated for traumatic head injury, need to transfuse blood and renal failure; higher osmolality than Ringer's hence less cerebral oedema in head-injured patients. Ringer's lactate: rapid infusion causes increased lactate level unrelated to acidosis. Colloids available: pentastarch, gelofusine, hypertonic saline, dextran, gelatins, perfluorocarbons (expensive). Avoid dextrose-containing fluids. Blood O-negative or type-specific is recommended for major haemorrhage.
C(ii) Routes of administration: venous (percutaneous); venous cutdown; intraosseous; subcutaneous. Clinical monitoring: pulse; blood pressure; urine output; conjunctiva; chest.
