A 72-year-old woman with COPD and osteoporosis is found on pre-operative screening (for elective right total hip replacement) to have Hb 8.5 g/dL, albumin 2.8 g/dL, and total lymphocyte count of 1,800 per uL.

(i) Using standard nutritional risk criteria, identify whether this patient is at risk of post-operative complications and state the threshold values.
(ii) What are the indications for preoperative nutritional supplementation, by what route can it be given, and how long is required?
(iii) How should her COPD be optimised pre-operatively, and what effect does smoking cessation have on pulmonary complications?
(iv) List the preoperative investigations recommended for patients aged over 50, and specify the haemoglobin thresholds for proceeding with surgery in a healthy patient versus a patient with coronary artery disease.
questions.answerText:
(i) Risk criteria for malnutrition and increased post-operative complication risk: weight loss of more than 5% in one month or of 10% or more over six months; serum albumin less than 3.2 g/dL; total lymphocyte count less than 3,000 per uL. This patient has albumin 2.8 g/dL (below 3.2 g/dL) and lymphocyte count 1,800/uL (below 3,000/uL) — she is at increased risk of post-operative complications.

(ii) Indications for preoperative nutritional supplementation: severely malnourished patients; patients who have been NPO for 3–5 days pre-operatively. Routes: oral, enteral tube feeding, or parenteral nutrition. Duration: 7–15 days of oral or intravenous supplementation is required to provide benefit in malnourished patients.

(iii) COPD optimisation: new onset of bronchospasm, dyspnoea, and reduced exercise tolerance should indicate delay of elective surgery. Continue medication; aerosol medication before surgery; risk reduction of pulmonary complications by smoking cessation; education of lung expansion manoeuvres and deep breathing exercises (incentive spirometry) for post-op; treatment of obstruction; antibiotics; hydration. Recent URTI increases airflow obstruction persisting for as long as 5 weeks — elective surgery is delayed. Smoking is associated with a nearly six-fold increase in risk for post-operative pulmonary complications. Eight weeks or more of smoking cessation was associated with a 66% reduction in post-operative pulmonary complications.

(iv) Pre-operative investigations for patients over 50: ECG (also for hypertension, CAD, cardiothoracic procedure); CXR (for major respiratory condition or cardiothoracic procedure); serum chemistry (for renal, adrenal, thyroid, diuretic therapy, chemotherapy); CBC (for genitourinary procedure); coagulation studies (for haematological/chemotherapy). Haemoglobin thresholds: Hb 7 g/dL in a healthy patient; Hb 10 g/dL in a patient with coronary artery disease.

questions.question:
A pregnant woman at 36 weeks is brought following a road traffic accident with blunt abdominal trauma. She has vaginal bleeding, uterine tenderness, and CTG shows late decelerations.
(i) What specific injury is most likely, and what anatomical factor predisposes to it?
(ii) Describe the physiological changes in pregnancy that make assessment of shock difficult.
(iii) What CTG findings indicate an increased risk of placental abruption, and what laboratory test detects fetomaternal haemorrhage?
(iv) Describe the modalities available for evaluating abdominal trauma in pregnancy and the role of radiographic studies.
questions.answerText:
(i) The most likely specific injury is abruptio placentae (placental abruption), which is the most common blunt injury in the gravid abdomen. The predisposing anatomical factor: the placenta is devoid of elastic tissue while the myometrium is very elastic, predisposing to shearing forces between the two when deceleration trauma occurs.
(ii) Physiological changes making assessment of shock difficult: Total blood volume increases by 45–50%; Up to 20% acute and 30–35% gradual blood loss may show no sign of instability; Pulse is 10–15 beats/min faster than non-pregnant baseline; BP is 10–15 mmHg lower than normal; Can lose 30% of blood volume before having significant change in BP; May not have abdominal tenderness early even with significant bleeding; The uterus is very vascular and can harbour significant occult intrauterine or abdominal bleeding.
(iii) CTG findings and fetomaternal haemorrhage: Fetal heart rate — normal 120–160. If greater than 1 contraction per 10 minutes persists for 4 hours, there is a 20% risk of placental abruption. If less than 1 contraction per 10 minutes for 4 hours, the risk of complications drops to baseline. Late decelerations are particularly significant. Kleihauer-Betke test is used to check for fetal cells in fetomaternal blood mixing — this is especially important in Rh-negative women who need Rhogam (300 micrograms).
(iv) Modalities for evaluating abdominal trauma in pregnancy: Laparotomy; CT; DPL; Ultrasound; Laparoscopy. Radiographic studies: Obtain what the patient needs — do not hold back. Avoid repeated and unnecessary studies. 0.05 to 0.1 rad is safe to the fetus. A single pelvis X-ray is less than 0.01 rad; Abdominal CT is 0.05–0.1 rad.

questions.question:
(A) Describe varicose veins of the lower limbs under the following headings:
(i) Definition, types, and gender predominance
(ii) Clinical features
(iii) Investigations

(B) State the non-operative and operative treatment options for varicose veins, including the named tests used to assess perforator and saphenofemoral competence.

(C) Describe aneurysm under the following headings: definition, types (morphological), aetiology, clinical features, investigations, and operative treatment with prognosis.
questions.answerText:
(A)(i) Varicose veins are abnormally dilated and lengthened veins. Types: (1) Primary or idiopathic — female to male ratio 2:1, accentuated by pregnancy; (2) Secondary — due to deep vein thrombosis, resulting from incompetence of valves.

(A)(ii) Clinical features: prominent veins; tiredness; aching; throbbing of deep veins; ankle swelling; tortuous veins.

(A)(iii) Investigations: FBC; urinalysis; Doppler ultrasound.

(B) Tests: Brodie-Trendelenburg test — to test the perforator veins and saphenofemoral competence. Non-operative treatment: exercise; periodic elevation; compression stockings; elastic bandaging; sclerotherapy (Asclera); laser therapy; radiofrequency. Medical treatment: NSAIDs; Daflon. Operative treatment: venous stripping and ligation of perforators. Complication: venous ulcer.

(C) Aneurysm definition: dilatation of the vessel due to weakness of the wall, containing clot. Morphological types: fusiform; saccular; false; arteriovenous (communication between adjacent artery and vein); dissecting aneurysm (blood passes through the intima — e.g., aortic aneurysm). Aetiology: degenerative; traumatic; infection (mycotic aneurysm); inflammatory. Clinical features: asymptomatic; back pain; abdominal swelling that is expansile; features depending on location; sensitive to dim light. Investigations: X-ray (may show calcification); ultrasound. Operative treatment: prosthetic graft (Dacron). Prognosis: 95% survival in elective surgery.

(i) Zone II encompasses the midportion of the neck, from the cricoid cartilage to the angle of the mandible. Important structures include: the carotid and vertebral arteries, jugular veins, pharynx, larynx, trachea, oesophagus, and cervical spine and spinal cord. Zone II injuries are the most apparent on inspection and most carotid artery injuries are associated with Zone II injuries.
(ii) Risk factors and causes: Guns and knives account for 95% of penetrating neck wounds. Motor vehicle accidents, household injuries, industrial accidents, and sporting events account for 5%. People with gunshot wounds sustain greater injury than those with stab wounds — bullets penetrate deeper and cause cavitation, damaging structures lying outside the missile tract. High-velocity bullets generate shock waves that devitalise surrounding tissues. Surgical exploration is indicated in 75% of GSW cases and only 50% of stab wounds.
(iii) Hard signs of arterial injury mandating operative repair: A large expanding haematoma; Severe active or pulsatile bleeding; Shock unresponsive to fluids; Signs of cerebral infarction; Presence of a bruit or thrill; Diminished distal pulses.
(iv) Complications: Airway obstruction (from tracheal and/or laryngeal oedema or stenosis); Vocal cord paralysis and voice change (from laryngeal trauma); Swallowing dysfunctions; Aspiration of material (e.g., blood, vomitus); Pulmonary oedema or bronchopneumonia (may follow initial strangulation injury); Soft tissue necrotising infections; Fistulas (tracheoesophageal fistula, oesophagocutaneous fistula).
questions.question:

(iv) State the complications of neck trauma that may follow after the acute phase.

questions.answerText:
(A)(i) Empyema thoracis is a condition in which pus and fluid from infected tissue collect in the pleural cavity. The most common organisms are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Staphylococcus aureus. It may also be caused by bacteria, fungi, and amoebas following pneumonia, chest wounds, chest surgery, lung abscess, or a ruptured esophagus.

(A)(ii) Stage 1 – Exudative: increased permeability of the inflamed pleural surface; exudative effusion; fibrin and nuclear polymorphs may be present; corresponds to uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion. Stage 2 – Fibrinopurulent: angioblastic and fibroblastic proliferation; heavy fibrin deposition on both pleura, particularly the parietal pleura; empyema is established. Stage 3 – Organizing: develops about 1 week after infection; collagen organization; entrapment of underlying lung; at 3–4 weeks a mature, turned peel develops; chronic dense fibrosis, contraction and trapping of the lung, atelectasis and prolonged pulmonary infection, reduction in the size of hemithorax; fibrothorax with invasion of the chest wall and narrowing of intercostal spaces — the end stage of the process.

(A)(iii) Febrile respiratory illness; prolongation of symptoms in pneumonia raises possibility of empyema; shortness of breath, cough, chest pain; aerobic empyema presents as acute febrile illness; anaerobic empyema is more indolent, usually 10 days; clinical signs of pleural effusion.

(B) At Stage 2: fluid is purulent; pH < 7.0; glucose < 60 mg/dL; LDH > 1000 IU/L. Delay in drainage increases mortality because the fibrinopurulent stage progresses to the organizing stage, resulting in entrapment of the lung, fibrothorax, chest wall invasion, and narrowing of intercostal spaces.

(C) Lung abscess is a cavity containing pus and necrotic debris within the lung parenchyma; empyema thoracis is a collection of pus within the pleural space rather than the lung parenchyma. Radiologically, lung abscess shows a cavity with an air-fluid level, with or without surrounding infiltrate; empyema shows homogeneous opacity with an inverted-D or "pregnant lady" silhouette on CXR, and chest ultrasound demonstrates loculation. CT can readily distinguish between lung abscess and an air-fluid level in an empyema cavity.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Multinodular goitre — defined as an enlarged thyroid gland containing two or more nodules; most common non-toxic goitre; incidence increases with age, most common in middle-aged females (M:F ratio 1:10). Solitary thyroid nodule: a discrete swelling in an otherwise normal thyroid gland, solitary or appearing solitary, confirmed at surgery or by pathology; it has a single palpable nodule which is usually smooth and firm.
(ii) Endemic type: iodine deficiency is the commonest cause; causes diffuse follicular hyperplasia leading to nodule formation; seen in the goitre belts of Nigeria. Sporadic type: cause is still being elucidated. Pathological mechanism: persistently elevated TSH levels lead to diffuse active lobules; TSH levels then fall and lobules become inactive and filled with colloid.
(iii) Complications of long-standing multinodular goitre: obstruction of the airway or oesophagus; toxicity; malignant transformation in long-standing cases.
(iv) Treatment: thyroidectomy (total or subtotal). Follow-up: thyroid function tests; L-thyroxine for life after total thyroidectomy.
(v) Hoarseness indicates compression of the recurrent laryngeal nerve (laryngoscopy may show vocal cord paralysis). Retrosternal goitre complications: superior vena cava obstruction; stridor from compression of tracheo-bronchial tree. Investigations for retrosternal goitre: chest x-ray, CT scan of chest, TFTs, radio-isotope scan. Differentials: mediastinal soft tissue sarcoma. Treatment: thyroidectomy through cervical incision or a median sternotomy.
questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman presents with a firm, slowly enlarging anterior neck swelling present for 8 years. The swelling moves with swallowing but not with tongue protrusion. She has no symptoms of hyper- or hypothyroidism. Ultrasound shows multiple nodules in an enlarged thyroid gland. TFTs are normal.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and how is it distinguished from a solitary thyroid nodule?
(ii) What is the aetiology and pathological mechanism of endemic versus sporadic multinodular goitre?
(iii) What are the complications of long-standing multinodular goitre?
(iv) What is the treatment and follow-up plan?

A 45-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of back pain with radiation to the left lower limb, exacerbated by activity. She had a hysterectomy 2 years ago. On examination, she has a positive straight leg raising test on the left and reduced sensation in the L5 distribution.
(i) Classify the causes of back pain into spinal and non-spinal categories, with specific examples.
(ii) What are the relevant investigations for back pain, and what does each test indicate?
(iii) What are the indications for surgical management of back pain, and what procedure is used?
(iv) What is the mechanism and clinical relevance of disc prolapse, and which spinal levels are most commonly affected?
questions.answerText:
(i) Non-spinal causes: Gynaecological — vaginal prolapse, endometriosis, fibroids. Renal causes. Other retroperitoneal pathologies — e.g., carcinoma of the head of pancreas (common in the elderly). Vascular lesions — abdominal aortic aneurysm. Peripheral nerve entrapment. Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute infective polyneuritis). Spinal and associated structures causes: Bone — fracture, primary bone tumours, metastasis/secondary deposits, blood dyscrasia. Bone and joint — infection and inflammatory causes. Soft tissue pathologies — ankylosing spondylitis (described as bamboo spine). Segmental mechanical derangement — disc degeneration/degenerative spine lesion; spondylosis leading to osteoarthritis (graded I to IV); spondylolisthesis (break in pedicle, vertebral body moves forward).
(ii) Investigations: Full blood count — anaemia suggests multiple myeloma; leucocytosis suggests infections. ESR — high in ankylosing spondylitis and infection (tuberculosis) of the spine; normal in mechanical disease. Plain radiograph (AP and lateral) — shows soft tissue shadow, disc prolapse. Serum calcium and phosphate. Alkaline phosphatase. Serum protein electrophoresis. Myelogram — for mechanical lesions. CT scan. MRI. Discography. Nerve conduction studies. Spine scintigraphy. Genotype.
(iii) Indications for surgery: Onset of neurological deficit despite conservative treatment; Onset of bladder dysfunction (neurogenic bladder). Procedure: Discectomy (fenestration).
(iv) Disc prolapse: Least occurs in the thoracic spine. Most common in the lumbar region at L5 and S1, followed by the cervical region at C5, C6, and C7. It causes root entrapment from degenerative changes and neurogenic claudication from spinal cord stenosis.

A(i) General catabolic processes: (1) Proteolytic process. (2) Conservation of extracellular fluid — reduction of water, chloride and HCO3. (3) Mobilisation of carbohydrates — 1,600 calories from carbohydrate. (4) Mobilisation of protein — protein as caloric substrate is expensive and inefficient; 1 gram N excreted equals 20 calories gained. (5) Mobilisation of fat — 300–500 g fat providing 2,700–4,500 calories.
A(ii) Endocrine effects: (1) Corticosteroids — injured cell → pituitary → ACTH → adrenal cortex → cortisol. (2) Aldosterone — four main pathways for release. (3) Catecholamines. (4) Anti-diuretic hormones (ADH). (5) Erythropoietin — produced by the kidney. (6) Sex hormone. (7) Growth hormone (not yet well-defined). (8) Thyroid hormone (not yet well-defined). (9) Renin — fall in BP → renin → angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → angiotensin II → aldosterone. (10) Glucagon — alpha cells of pancreas; hypoglycaemia → glucagon → adrenal catecholamines → glycogenolysis in liver and muscle and gluconeogenesis.
B(i) Organs most affected: (1) Kidney — failure. (2) Respiratory system — failure. (3) Cardiac system — failure, infarction.
B(ii) Clinical phases: (1) Turning point phase. (2) Anabolic phase. (3) Fat gain phase. Detrimental effects of prolonged bed rest: (1) Osteoporosis. (2) Hypercalciuria. (3) Phlebothrombosis. (4) Nitrogen and potassium loss. (5) Nephrolithiasis.

A 35-year-old male involved in an RTA presents with inability to pass urine, blood at the external urethral meatus, perineal haematoma, and suprapubic swelling. Pelvis X-ray shows a pelvic fracture.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what is the most important clinical sign?
(ii) What investigation is indicated, and why is oil-soluble contrast medium contraindicated?
(iii) Describe the immediate treatment priorities, explaining why urethral catheterisation should be avoided.
(iv) What are the treatment options available after initial suprapubic cystostomy, and what are the recognised complications of this injury?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis is urethral injury. The most important clinical sign is blood at the external urethral meatus.
(ii) Investigation: Retrograde urethrogram with water-soluble contrast medium. Oil-soluble contrast medium is contraindicated because it is irritant, causes hypersensitivity reactions, and can lead to oil embolism.
(iii) Immediate treatment: Resuscitate. Never ask the patient to pass urine — to avoid extravasation. Avoid urethral catheterisation because it could lead to: infection of a sterile haematoma; converting a partial to a complete injury. Therefore, suprapubic cystostomy is the immediate management.
(iv) Treatment options after initial suprapubic cystostomy (SPC): Trial of catheterisation — single attempt with a soft, small-size, well-lubricated catheter, by the most senior person, under sterile conditions with adequate sedation, and readiness to proceed to SPC. Rail-roading. Primary endoscopic re-alignment. Primary repair. Delayed repair. Complications: Bleeding; Extravasation and abscess; Urethral stricture; Incontinence; Impotence.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the bladder with reference to its peritoneal relations, then explain how the location of perforation determines the type of urinary extravasation, and distinguish between intraperitoneal and extraperitoneal bladder rupture in terms of investigation, presentation, and management.
A(i) Describe the peritoneal relations of the bladder and how they determine the type of injury.
A(ii) Describe the associated injuries that commonly accompany bladder rupture.
B(i) Distinguish between intraperitoneal and extraperitoneal bladder rupture in presentation and investigation.
B(ii) Describe the management of bladder injury.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The type of bladder injury depends on: the location of the perforation or laceration; its relationship with the peritoneal reflection; whether the bladder is full or empty at the time of trauma. Intraperitoneal extravasation occurs if the perforation is above the peritoneal reflection. Extraperitoneal extravasation occurs if the perforation is below the peritoneal reflection.
A(ii) Associated injuries: Pelvic fractures; Urethral injuries, especially in males; Vaginal and urethral lacerations in females; Head, spinal and visceral injuries; Long bone fractures.
B(i) Clinical features — intraperitoneal rupture: lower abdominal pain following trauma; inability to pass urine; haematuria; suprapubic tenderness; urinary peritonitis. Extraperitoneal rupture: suprapubic swelling; pelvic haematoma on DRE. Investigation: FAST — suprapubic mass may indicate extraperitoneal rupture; free peritoneal fluid indicates intraperitoneal rupture. Cystography (CT cystography combines advantages of CT and cystography). BUN — if raised but creatinine is normal, this indicates urine absorption.
B(ii) Management: Resuscitate. Conservative management by catheter placement. Operative repair: 2-layer closure with absorbable sutures; drain placed; urethral catheter left in situ. Treat associated injuries.

(i) Virchow's triad:
- Stasis: immobility, long operation, obesity, heart failure, trauma.
- Endothelial injury: trauma, intraluminal cannula, inflammation, infection.
- Hypercoagulability: polycythaemia, thrombocythaemia, leukaemia, sepsis, major trauma, diabetes, pregnancy/COCP, smoking, malignancy.
(ii) Risk factors:
- Increasing age >40 years; immobilisation; obesity; malignancy; sepsis; thrombophilia (e.g. antithrombin III/protein C/protein S deficiency, Factor V Leiden, anticardiolipin Ab); inflammatory bowel disease; trauma; heart disease; pregnancy/oestrogens.
(iii) Clinical features:
- DVT: often asymptomatic; calf tenderness, ankle oedema, mild pyrexia; phlegmasia alba/caerulea dolens.
- PE: substernal chest pain; dyspnoea; circulatory arrest; pleuritic chest pain; haemoptysis.
- PPL: history of DVT; aching limb; leg swelling; venous eczema; venous ulceration; inverted bottle-shaped leg.
(iv) Investigations:
- DVT: D-dimers; duplex imaging (suprapopliteal thrombosis); ascending venography.
- PE: ECG (S1, Q3, T3); chest X-ray (linear collapse); blood gases (hypoxia, hypocapnia); ventilation/perfusion lung scan; pulmonary angiography.
- PPL: ascending ± descending venography; duplex scanning; plethysmography; ambulatory venous pressure.
(v) Management:
- Prophylaxis: mechanical compression (TED) stockings; subcutaneous heparin 5000 iu b.d.; warfarin 1 mg/day; dextran 70 IV 500 ml/day.
- DVT treatment: anticoagulation for 6–8 weeks (IV heparin monitored by APTT; warfarin monitored by PT); thrombolysis; thrombectomy.
- PE treatment: anticoagulation for 3–6 months; thrombolysis; pulmonary embolectomy; IVC filters for recurrent PE despite treatment.
- PPL: limb elevation; compression; four-layer bandaging; graduated compression stockings; venous valve reconstruction.

(ii) Risk factors for DVT in surgical patients.
(iii) Clinical features of DVT, pulmonary embolism (PE), and the postphlebitic limb (PPL).
(iv) Investigations for DVT, PE, and PPL.

questions.answerText:
(i) Pre-operative haematological investigations:
- PCV: check whether high, low, or normal.
- FBC including WBC (total and differential) and platelet count.
- RBC indices: to detect iron deficiency anaemia, megaloblastic, combined anaemias.
- Blood film review: for inherited membrane disorders, SCD, WBC for signs of infection and malignancy.
- Hb electrophoresis: if SCD, special precautions are necessary.
- Bleeding time: 3–7 mins (IVY method); 2.5–9 mins (DUKE method).
- Clotting time (coagulation time at 37 degrees C): normal 5–11 mins.
- Prothrombin time (PT/EPW): 10–14 secs.
- Partial thromboplastin time (PTT/IPW): 35–43 secs. PTR >1.3 signifies tendency to bleed.
- Blood group phenotype: A, B, AB, O and Rhesus D positive or negative.
- Antibody identification.

(ii) Precautions for sickle cell disease in surgery and anaesthesia: special precaution is necessary once HbSS is confirmed. Avoid tourniquet. Manage volume carefully (volume expansion). Oxygen therapy is part of management. Alkaline infusion is required. Analgesia must be adequate. Precipitating factors of crisis (infection, extremes of temperature, dehydration, emotional stress) must be avoided.

(iii) Areas of overlap between haematology and surgery: priapism, gall stones, pathological fracture, chronic leg ulcer, liver biopsy, circumcision, washout syndrome.

(iv) Biosafety haematological testing is required to exclude HIV, HBV, and HCV prior to surgery, both for patient management and protection of surgical personnel.
questions.question:

(i) List the pre-operative haematological investigations required before this surgery and state the normal reference range for each coagulation test.
(ii) What precautions are necessary for anaesthesia and surgery in a patient with sickle cell disease?
(iii) What are the areas of clinical overlap between haematology and surgery?

A 3-month-old infant is brought with a swelling on the right side of the neck that transilluminates brilliantly. The swelling appeared at birth and has grown slowly. It is soft, cystic, non-tender, and located in the posterior triangle. Examination also reveals the baby has difficulty breathing in certain positions.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) List the differential diagnoses of a neck swelling in this age group that are.
(iii) State the aetiological factors responsible for head and neck craniofacial clefts as listed.
(iv) Describe the classification of craniosynostosis shapes, naming the shape, the abnormally closed suture, and the descriptive skull term for each type.
(v) List the functional problems that craniosynostosis can cause.
questions.answerText:
(i) The most likely diagnosis is cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation of the neck), presenting as a brilliantly transilluminant, soft, cystic swelling in the posterior triangle from birth.
(ii) Differential diagnoses of a neck swelling in this age group: cystic hygroma; thyroglossal cyst; cervical lymphadenopathy; cervical lipoma; and swellings arising from tumours of the head and neck including bony tissue tumours (fibrous dysplasia, Burkitt's lymphoma, osteosarcoma) and soft tissue tumours (haemangiomas, sarcomas).
(iii) Aetiological factors for head and neck craniofacial clefts:
- Radiation: causes microcephaly
- Infection: toxoplasmosis, rubella, cytomegalovirus (CMV)
- Maternal idiosyncrasies: phenylketonuria disorder; diabetes (associated with oculoauriculovertebral (OAV) spectrum)
- Chemicals / drugs: vitamin deficiency states; excess Vitamin A; isotretinoin (causes clefts and microsomia); thalidomide; diazepam (causes cleft palate and OAV); phenytoin
(iv) Classification of craniosynostosis by skull shape:
- Trigonocephaly: triangular skull shape; metopic suture prematurely closed.
- Scaphocephaly: boat-shaped skull; sagittal suture prematurely closed.
- Turricephaly: increased skull height; basal suture prematurely closed.
- Oxycephaly: pointed head; coronal suture prematurely closed.

A. Treatment procedures for wound management:
- Adjuncts: antitetanus prophylaxis; antibiotics if necessary; immobilisation; analgesics.
- Soft brushing off of sand and grits using mild soapy solution such as cetrimide and hibitane; swafeega for black smoky stains (e.g., from mechanic workshops).
- Debridement: removal of dead and dying tissues and all foreign materials.
- Irrigation: particularly jet lavage using saline in a syringe and cannula; exposed joints and bone must be lavaged.
- Wound cleansing with antiseptics (restricted to dirty, infected, or sloughy wounds; of no value in established infection): chlorhexidine (hibidil, hibitane) 0.01%–4.0%; cetrimide (Savlon, cetavlon) 1% solution; povidone iodine; hydrogen peroxide 3%–6%; hypochlorite solutions (Eusol) 0.05%–0.5%.
- Wound closure: based on timing and cleanliness, and on nature of wound.
A(i) Algorithm based on timing:
- Primary closure: clean wound seen within 12 hours.
- Delayed primary closure: wound of uncertain cleanliness seen after 12 hours or infected; wound is cleaned, dressed, and reviewed at 36 hours; if clean on review, closure is performed (usually after one week).
- Secondary closure: when the wound remains infected on review; dressing frequency individualised; closure performed when wound is clean.
B. Description of an ulcer using nine parameters:
1. Site: anatomical location.
2. Size: measured dimensions.
3. Shape: regular or irregular.
4. Edge: flat (healing); shelving/sloping (healing or benign); punched out (syphilis, ischaemia); undermined (mycobacterial/tuberculosis ulcers); raised and rolling (basal cell carcinoma); raised and everted (squamous cell carcinoma).
5. Floor and discharge: is it covered by granulation tissue or slough? Is the discharge serous, bloody, or purulent?
6. Surrounding skin: pigmentation, varicosity, induration.
7. Regional vascular status: peripheral pulses, capillary refill.
8. Regional lymph nodes: discrete, matted, tender?
9. Base (palpated): firm, hard, or soft (distinct from the floor which is what you see).
B(i) Causes of chronic cutaneous ulcers: trauma (inadequately treated traumatic ulcer — commonest cause in Nigeria); infection (acute tropical ulcer; chronic infection including tuberculosis, buruli, syphilis); vascular (venous — very common abroad; arterial — e.g., diabetic); haemoglobinopathy (HbSS and HbSC); neurotropic (trophic) ulcers (leprosy, diabetic, cord lesions, peripheral neuropathy); pressure sore; neoplastic.

A) Vas deferens — course and relations:
- The vas deferens (ductus deferens) arises from the tail of the epididymis in the scrotum
- It ascends posterior to the testis, becomes part of the spermatic cord, and passes through the external inguinal ring into the inguinal canal
- In the inguinal canal it passes medially and superiorly through the internal inguinal ring into the pelvis
- In the inguinal canal it lies among cord structures including the testicular artery, pampiniform plexus of veins, lymphatics, and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
- At herniotomy, the vas deferens must be identified and protected; if damaged it should be repaired
Structures at risk: ilioinguinal nerve, vas deferens (should be repaired if divided), vessels of the cord, causing primary haemorrhage

B) Safe approach and rationale for no posterior wall repair in children:
The safe approach in children is herniotomy (high ligation of the patent processus vaginalis at the internal ring) without repair of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.
Anatomical basis: in children, the posterior wall (conjoint tendon / transversalis fascia) is inherently strong and has not been weakened by ageing, heavy lifting, or chronic straining, so no formal repair is required. The cause is a patent processus vaginalis, not a deficiency of the posterior wall. Recurrence rates are low in children.

C) Ilioinguinal nerve injury:
- Sensory loss over the scrotum/labia majora, medial thigh, and base of the penis
- Chronic groin pain or paraesthesia in the inguinal region
- No motor deficit (the ilioinguinal nerve is primarily sensory in this region)
Why hernia is commoner on the right (55–60%):
The right testis descends later than the left, so the right processus vaginalis obliterates later and is more often patent at birth. A patent processus vaginalis predisposes to indirect inguinal hernia.

A(i) Gross anatomy and embryology:
- Embryological origin: derivative of the midgut
- Structure (4 layers): mucosa, submucosa (rich in lymphoid tissue), muscularis, serosa
- Colonic appendage; mammalian in origin; 5–9 cm long
- Innervation: visceral (via T10 sympathetic fibres — referred pain to periumbilical region) and somatic (via the overlying parietal peritoneum — localised to the right iliac fossa when inflamed)

A(ii) Aetiological categories:
Obstructive (70–75%): faecolith; carcinoid tumour; colonic tumour; foreign body; parasite
Non-obstructive (25–30%): lymphoid hyperplasia (common in children — the submucosa is rich in lymphoid tissue which can hypertrophy with viral infection)

B) Pain migration and signs:
Pain migration: Initial visceral pain (T10 — periumbilical area) from appendiceal distension; as inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, somatic pain localises to the right iliac fossa (McBurney's point — 2/3 of the distance from the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine).
McBurney's point tenderness: direct compression of the inflamed appendix at its surface marking.
Rovsing's sign: pressure in the left iliac fossa transmits to the right, compressing the appendix and eliciting right iliac fossa pain.
Psoas sign: the appendix lies on or near the right psoas muscle; hip flexion against resistance irritates an inflamed appendix posterior to the caecum (retrocaecal).
Obturator sign: internal rotation of the right hip irritates a pelvic appendix lying on the right obturator internus muscle.

C) Age distribution and treatment:
Peak age: 10–12 years; rare in pre-school and elderly (submucous lymphoid tissue is less developed in infancy, and the appendiceal lumen is wider, making obstruction less likely).
Life-time appendicectomy risk: 7%; affects 1:1,000 children/year.
Full surgical treatment:
- Emergency appendicectomy: NPO, IV fluids, IV antibiotics; then appendicectomy
- Interval appendicectomy: when an appendiceal mass is present (allow mass to resolve over 6–8 weeks, then perform elective appendicectomy to prevent future episodes)
Post-operative complications: wound infection, intra-abdominal abscess, haemorrhage, adhesive intestinal obstruction

(i) Diagnosis: Exstrophy (ectopia vesicae) of the bladder. Described as the severest form of epispadias. Epidemiology: incidence 1/10,000–50,000; M:F ratio 2:1.

(ii) Affected structures: absent bladder anterior wall; absent lower anterior abdominal wall; posterior wall of bladder and ureteric orifices exposed to the exterior; mucosa of everted posterior wall of bladder fused with skin; jets of urine observed from ureteric orifices. Associated anomalies: genital — penis is a rudimentary stump; scrotum, clitoris, and labia minora are abnormal. Neurological and anorectal abnormalities. Waddling gait is present. High incidence of ascending pyelonephritis. Higher incidence of carcinoma in these patients.

(iii) Differential pathologies of the lower urinary tract presenting at birth/early infancy:
- Congenital posterior urethral valves (males)
- Urethral stricture: congenital and acquired
- Urethral diverticulum
- Neuropathic lesions (e.g. spina bifida, sacral agenesis)
- The large smooth bladder; the lazy bladder syndrome (DeLuca); base plate deficiency (Hutch); prune belly (triad) syndrome
- Anterior urethral valves (males); foreign bodies; calculi
- Distal urethral obstruction in girls or meatal obstruction in boys
- Bladder exstrophy/epispadias complex
- Vesical agenesis/hypoplasia; duplication of bladder; congenital bladder diverticulum

(iv) Clinico-anatomical reasoning: epispadias is a congenital deformity in which the urethra opens on the dorsum of the penis proximal to the glans, caused by failure of union of the anterior walls of the urethra. Complete epispadias involves absence of the entire dorsal wall of the urethra up to the bladder neck, and is associated with ectopia vesicae. Bladder exstrophy represents the extreme end of this spectrum where not only the urethra but the entire anterior bladder wall fails to close, exposing the bladder to the exterior — hence it is the severest form.
Treatment: the defect is repaired early, within 3 days if possible; female patients show the open-bladder plate and urethra with bifid clitoris in classic bladder exstrophy. The goals of repair include bladder closure, genital reconstruction, and continence.

(A)(i) Complete transposition of the great arteries (D-TGA): the aorta arises from the right ventricle (RV) and the pulmonary artery (PA) arises from the left ventricle (LV); the normal anteroposterior relationship of the great arteries is reversed — the aorta is anterior to the PA (transposition); the aorta remains to the right of the PA (hence the prefix D for dextroposition).

(A)(ii) Pathophysiology: desaturated blood returning from the body to the RA flows out of the aorta without being oxygenated in the lungs and returns to the RA; oxygenated blood returning to the LA flows out of the PA and returns to the LA — a complete separation of the two circuits (in parallel rather than in series). This defect is incompatible with life unless communication between the two circuits occurs at the atrial, ventricular, or ductal level or any combination.

(A)(iii) Hyperoxia test: the patient inhales 100% oxygen; arterial PO2 is measured in response. Interpretation: with pulmonary disease, arterial PO2 usually rises to a level greater than 100 mmHg; when there is a significant intracardiac right-to-left shunt, arterial PO2 does not exceed 100 mmHg and the rise is usually not more than 10–30 mmHg — this helps differentiate cardiac from pulmonary cyanosis.

(B)(i) Polycythaemia: low arterial oxygen content stimulates bone marrow through erythropoietin release from the kidneys, producing increased red blood cells; resulting increase in oxygen-carrying capacity benefits cyanotic children. When the haematocrit reaches 65% or higher, a sharp increase in blood viscosity occurs and the polycythaemic response becomes disadvantageous. Clubbing is caused by soft tissue growth under the nail bed as a consequence of central cyanosis.

(B)(ii) CNS complications: due to very high haematocrit levels or iron-deficient red blood cells; brain abscesses may result from right-to-left intracardiac shunts bypassing the normally effective phagocytic filtering actions of pulmonary capillary bed; polycythaemia and high blood viscosity lead to tissue hypoxia and microinfarction of the brain, later complicated by bacterial colonisation; triad of brain abscess: fever, headache, and focal neurologic deficit.

(B)(iii) Bleeding disorders: thrombocytopenia and defective platelet aggregation most frequently noted; other abnormalities — prolonged prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time, lower levels of fibrinogen and factors V and VIII; clinical manifestations — easy bruising, petechiae, epistaxis, gingival bleeding; red cell withdrawal and replacement with equal volume of plasma corrects haemorrhagic tendency and lowers blood viscosity.

(C) TOF treatment: Palliative surgery — aimed to divert systemic blood into the pulmonary circulation to enhance pulmonary flow and oxygenation; standard operation — Modified Blalock-Taussig shunt; others — Pott's shunt and Waterston-Cooley shunt. Definitive surgery — relief of RVOT obstruction (infundibulectomy, valvotomy, patch enlargement of the RVOT); separation of systemic and pulmonary circulations by closure of the VSD under cardiopulmonary bypass. Treatment strategies: stage surgery — palliative surgery in early childhood followed by definitive surgery (usually after 3–4 years); or definitive surgery in the neonatal period or early childhood.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: varicocele-associated male infertility. Aetiology category: varicoceles (listed under causes of male infertility as a distinct category causing obstruction and/or heat-related impairment of spermatogenesis).

(ii) Predisposing factors: varicocele increases testicular temperature (scrotal temperature normally 2–3°C below core body temperature, essential for spermatogenesis); increased numbers of mast cells have been associated with different types of infertility including varicocele. From history, factors that exacerbate include: use of tight nylon underwear; tight clothing; exposure to radiation; chronic illnesses; medications (anti-cancer agents, nitrofurantoin). Surgery is the most common choice for treatment of male infertility with clinical varicocele.

(iii) Management:
General measures: treat underlying causes; correct tight clothing; stop relevant medications.
Varicocelectomy: surgical ligation/division of varicosal veins; venous drainage of the testis after varicocelectomy occurs through alternative collateral vessels. Adjunctive therapy: Zaditen (ketotifen), a mast cell blocker, improves sperm quality, chromatin integrity, and pregnancy rate when administered post-varicocelectomy (cumulative pregnancy significantly improved by 9 months post-surgery in treatment group — 41.17% vs 21.15% in control).
Other treatment options: in vitro fertilisation; general measures; treatment of hyperprolactinaemia if present.
If azoospermia: hormone profile — if normal, likely obstructive → testicular biopsy (mid-portion of convex border) and bilateral vasography; if very high FSH and low testosterone, testicular failure.

(iv) Accessory glands and their contributions:
- Seminal vesicles: secrete alkaline fluid containing fructose for sperm nutrition and energy.
- Prostate: secretes alkaline secretion that activates sperm movement.
- Bulbourethral glands: secrete alkaline mucus-like secretion for lubrication.
All three together secrete the alkaline fluid part of semen that neutralises acidity in the female reproductive tract, creating a hospitable environment for sperm survival.

A 16-year-old boy presents to the surgical outpatient clinic with a 6-month history of a painless right scrotal swelling. He was noted to have mumps at age 10. On examination, the swelling is fluctuant, transilluminates, and cannot be got above in the inguinal canal.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis? Using the SACT framework, outline the key history elements for this patient.
(ii) What does local examination reveal about this swelling, and which pathognomonic sign confirms the diagnosis?
(iii) What is the differential diagnosis using the TINCABED mnemonic, and what additional finding would suggest a varicocele?
(iv) Describe the physical examination approach (IPPA) and the specific systemic aspects relevant to a teenage male with a scrotal swelling.
questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: hydrocoele. SACT framework: Symptomatology — onset, duration, painless vs painful, progression, any discharge; Aetiology — past history of mumps infection (bilateral cheek swelling), past history of scrotal pain or swelling (torsion of testis), past history of urethral discharge, past history of groin surgery, trauma, instrumentation, occupation, cigarette smoking, alcohol, medications; Complications — infertility, associated loss of erection, ejaculatory dysfunction; Treatment — what has been done so far.

(ii) Local examination: Inspection — site (right scrotum), surface (smooth), shape (oval), surrounding skin normal. Palpation — not tender, fluctuant, cannot get above it in the inguinal canal. Transillumination: the swelling transilluminates — clear fluid. Pathognomonic sign: transillumination (clear fluid) = hydrocoele.

(iii) TINCABED differential: Trauma (haematocele); Inflammatory/Infection (epididymo-orchitis following mumps); Neoplastic (testicular tumour); Congenital (congenital hydrocoele — patent processus vaginalis); Angiogenic; Blood (haematocele); Endocrine; Degenerative. Finding that suggests varicocele: scrotal swelling with a 'feeling of bag of worms'.

(iv) IPPA: Inspection, Palpation, Percussion, Auscultation. Systemic aspects in a teenage male with scrotal swelling: CVS (pulse, BP, apex beat, heart sounds); Chest (respiratory rate, trachea, percussion, breath sounds); Abdomen (tenderness, masses — notably renal masses that can extend to the scrotum; bowel sounds; don't forget DRE); Genitalia — phallus, scrotum, testis, urethral meatus; Regional lymph nodes; General — pallor, jaundice, hydration, lymphadenopathy, oedema.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman who smokes presents with intermittent haematuria over 3 months. She works in a rubber factory. Urinalysis shows microscopic haematuria; urine cytology shows atypical cells. Cystoscopy reveals a papillary lesion at the right lateral wall of the bladder.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what are the predisposing factors for this condition?
(ii) Classify all histological types of bladder malignancy and the TNM staging for transitional cell carcinoma.
(iii) What investigations are required for staging and treatment planning?
(iv) Describe the essential management for superficial (Ta, T1) tumours, for invasive (T2, T3) tumours, and for fixed (T4) disease.
(v) What is the prognosis for each stage, and what long-term surveillance is required?
questions.answerText:
(i) Carcinoma of the bladder (transitional cell carcinoma — TCC). Predisposing factors: exposure to carcinogens in the rubber industry (1- and 2-naphthylamine, benzidine, aminobiphenyl); smoking; tryptophan metabolites; phenacetin; bladder schistosomiasis and chronic bladder stones (squamous carcinoma); congenital abnormalities (exstrophy of the bladder — adenocarcinoma).
(ii) Histological types:
- Transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) — most common.
- Squamous cell carcinoma — rare.
- Adenocarcinoma — rare.
TNM staging for TCC:
- TIS: carcinoma in situ.
- Ta: tumour confined to urothelium (superficial).
- T1: lamina propria involved (superficial).
- T2: superficial muscle invasion (invasive).
- T3a: deep muscle invasion; T3b: serosal involvement (invasive).
- T4a: invasion of prostate, uterus or vagina; T4b: fixation to pelvic wall (fixed).
(iii) Investigations:
- Urine cytology.
- IVU: occult upper tract tumours.
- Cystourethroscopy.
- FBC: anaemia.
- U+E, creatinine: renal function.
- Ultrasound: obstruction.
- CT scan: local invasion, distant metastases.
(iv) Management:
- TIS: intravesical chemotherapy; cystourethrectomy for unresponsive lesions.
- Superficial (Ta, T1): TURT and follow-up cystoscopy; if recurrences or increased risk of invasion — intravesical chemotherapy (mitomycin-C, BCG); persistent recurrences — cystourethrectomy.
- Invasive (T2, T3): TURT + radical radiotherapy; or radical cystectomy (with reconstruction or urinary diversion, e.g. ileal conduit).
- Fixed (T4): chemotherapy (MVAC, CMV, CISCA); radiotherapy and TURT for palliation.
(v) Prognosis:
- Superficial tumours: 75% 5-year survival.
- Invasive tumours: 10% 5-year survival.
- Fixed tumours and metastases: median survival 1 year.
- Long-term follow-up required for life.

(i) Common causes of goitre: physiological (puberty, pregnancy); iodine deficiency (endemic); primary hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease — circulating immunoglobulin LATS); adenomatous (nodular) goitre; thyroiditis (Hashimoto's, de Quervain's, Riedel's struma); thyroid malignancies.
Hyperthyroidism symptoms: heat intolerance and excessive sweating; increased appetite, weight loss, diarrhoea; anxiety, tiredness, palpitations; oligomenorrhoea. Signs: goitre; exophthalmos, lid lag and retraction; warm moist palms, tremor; atrial fibrillation; pretibial myxoedema.
Hypothyroidism symptoms: cold intolerance, decreased sweating; hoarseness; weight increase, constipation; slow cerebration, tiredness; muscle pains. Signs: pale/yellow skin, dry thickened skin, thin hair; periorbital puffiness, loss of outer third of eyebrow; dementia, nerve deafness, hyporeflexia; slow pulse, large tongue, peripheral oedema.
(ii) Thyroid malignancies:
- Papillary (60%): epithelial; well differentiated; lymphatic spread.
- Follicular (25%): epithelial; well differentiated; haematogenous spread.
- Anaplastic (10%): epithelial; poorly differentiated; direct, lymphatic, and haematogenous spread.
- Medullary (5%): parafollicular cell; moderate differentiation; lymphatic and haematogenous spread.
(iii) Complications of thyroidectomy:
- Intraoperative: bleeding; thyrotoxic storm (toxic glands); laryngeal oedema; pneumothorax.
- Early: hypocalcaemia; haematoma; recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy.
- Late: hypothyroidism; recurrence of thyroid disease.
(iv) Papillary carcinoma: surgery — total thyroidectomy and removal of involved lymph nodes; adjunctive — L-thyroxine postoperatively to suppress TSH; prognosis: excellent.
Follicular carcinoma: surgery — thyroid lobectomy or total thyroidectomy if metastases present; adjunctive — radioactive iodine (¹³¹I) for distant metastases and L-thyroxine to suppress TSH; prognosis — no metastases: 90% 10-year survival; with metastases: 30% 10-year survival.
(v) Anaplastic: surgery only to relieve pressure symptoms; neither radiotherapy nor chemotherapy is effective; prognosis dismal — most dead within 12 months.
Medullary: exclude phaeochromocytoma before treating (associated with MEN IIA — medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma, hyperparathyroidism; or MEN IIB — medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma, multiple mucosal neuromas, Marfanoid habitus); surgery — total thyroidectomy and excision of regional lymph nodes; prognosis — overall 50% 5-year survival.

(i) Diagnosis: vaginal hydrocele. It differs from a communicating hydrocele in the following way: a communicating hydrocele has a completely patent processus vaginalis with a small communication to the peritoneal cavity — it changes in size. A vaginal hydrocele does not communicate with the peritoneal cavity and does not change in size.
(ii) The processus vaginalis (PV) normally involutes in 90% of cases by obliteration; in 10% it remains patent. Infantile hydrocele: the PV is closed at the deep ring but fluid accumulates distally. Communicating hydrocele: the PV remains completely patent with a small communication with the peritoneal cavity; it changes in size and is difficult to reduce.
(iii) Herniography: positive-contrast peritoneography used for diagnosis of hernias in the inguinofemoral region and the pelvis (Ducharme et al. 1967). Indications: suspicion of hernia not verifiable by clinical examination; choice of procedure; follow-up. Technique: table that permits fluoroscopy and tilting; empty bladder; premedication with atropine; puncture of abdomen and testing; 50–20ml of contrast medium; turning of patient. Complications: haemorrhage, anterior abdominal wall haematoma, intestinal puncture, peritonitis, vasovagal reactions.
(iv) Treatment: Communicating hydrocele — herniotomy and hydrocelectomy. Infantile hydrocele — hydrocelectomy.
(v) Complications affecting the testis: damage to the vas deferens (should be repaired); scrotal haematoma; postoperative hydrocele; risk of testicular compromise in strangulation cases.

(i) Diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome. Full alternative name: acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculopathy.
(ii) Associated infections and vaccines: Campylobacter diarrhea (many cases); Mycoplasma; Diphtheria; Influenza; Swine flu vaccine; Rabies vaccine; Herpes zoster; acute HIV; viral hepatitis; mononucleosis; tick paralysis (similar clinical findings). 60% have antecedent URI 2–3 weeks prior to onset.
(iii) Clinical progression: begins with non-specific aches and pains and prickly paraesthesias of the feet that move proximally over hours. Weakness may progress over hours to days and moves from distal to proximal; generally stabilises after the first few days but may increase up to 14 days. May have cranial nerve and autonomic involvement (tachycardia/bradycardia, hypotension/hypertension, hypo/hyperthermia). Respiratory risk: approximately 30% have respiratory muscle involvement — patients should be admitted for observation with peak flow measurements.
(iv) CSF findings: elevated protein; normal glucose; normal cellularity. Treatment (first two weeks): plasma exchange and/or IV IgG. IV IgG is at least as good and may be better than plasma exchange; no information on additive effect. Steroids are of no use.
(v) Mortality: approximately 3%. The majority recover all function. 3% have recurrent episodes.

(i) Testicular carcinoma (germ-cell tumour). Based on AFP elevation (not elevated in pure seminoma) and β-HCG elevation, this is likely a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour.
Stage: Stage II — spread to retroperitoneal lymph nodes below the diaphragm.
Staging: Stage I — confined to scrotum; Stage II — spread to retroperitoneal lymph nodes below the diaphragm; Stage III — distant metastases.
(ii) Aetiology:
- Cryptorchidism: 50-fold increase in risk of developing testicular cancer; risk is unaffected by orchidopexy.
- Higher incidence in white men.
(iii) Classification:
- Germ-cell tumours (90%): seminoma; non-seminoma (embryonal carcinoma, teratocarcinoma, choriocarcinoma). Secrete AFP and β-HCG.
- AFP elevated: 75% embryonal, 65% teratocarcinoma; NOT elevated in pure seminoma or choriocarcinoma.
- β-HCG elevated: 100% choriocarcinoma; 60% embryonal; 60% teratocarcinoma; 10% pure seminoma.
- Stromal tumours: Leydig cell; Sertoli cell; granulosa cell — rarely metastasise.
- Metastatic tumours.
(iv) Management:
- All: radical orchidectomy (via groin incision) and histological diagnosis.
- Seminoma Stage I: radiotherapy to abdominal nodes.
- Seminoma Stage II: radiotherapy to abdominal nodes.
- Seminoma Stage III: chemotherapy (bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin).
- Non-seminoma Stage I: retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND).
- Non-seminoma Stage II: chemotherapy + RPLND.
- Non-seminoma Stage III: chemotherapy (+ RPLND if good response).
(v) Prognosis: overall cure rates are over 90%; node-negative disease has almost 100% 5-year survival. Late-stage disease also has a good prognosis with combined surgery and medical therapy.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Haemorrhage is the loss of blood from the intravascular compartment of the body from any cause. Temporal types:
- Primary: occurs during an operation; usually controlled before concluding the operation.
- Reactionary: occurs in the first 24 hours post-operatively; attributed to slippage of a ligature and/or dislodgement of a clot.
- Secondary: occurs after 1 week post-operatively; attributed to infection.

A(ii) Concealed haemorrhage occurs when there is bleeding into a body cavity (e.g. haemothorax, haemoperitoneum, intracranial haemorrhage). Revealed (overt) haemorrhage is seen escaping from a breach in tissue or a body opening. Both types may co-exist. Arterial haemorrhage spurts and is bright red oxygenated blood. Venous haemorrhage oozes and is dark deoxygenated blood. Capillary bleeding is milder oozing but oxygenated blood.

B(i) Surgical methods for control of haemorrhage: pressure, packing, positioning; ligation (sutures, clips); diathermy (heat via electricity); artery forceps (haemostats); Surgicel (topical agent); harmonic scalpel (ultrasound).

B(ii) Types of blood transfusion: whole blood transfusion, packed cell transfusion, fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate. Blood group systems: ABO system is the most important because associated antibodies occur naturally; Rhesus system is next in importance because anti-rhesus antibodies form when Rh-positive cells are introduced into Rh-negative persons; 83% of the population is Rh-positive. Immediate complications: simple febrile reactions; allergic reactions; haemolytic reactions; circulatory overload; cardiac arrest; bleeding diathesis from massive transfusion. Delayed reactions: thrombophlebitis; delayed haemolytic reaction; transmission of disease (hepatitis B and C, CMV, HIV, malaria); iron overload; immunosuppression. Massive transfusion of stored blood may cause cardiac arrhythmias due to hyperkalaemia — potassium diffuses out of RBCs during storage at a rate of 1 mmol/day.

1. Volksman's spoon (bone curette) — used for scraping bone.
2. Sinus forceps — has no ratchet unlike other forceps; used for probing sinuses.

4. Aneurysm needle — used for passing ligatures around vessels.

A(ii) Crushing intestinal clamp (Payre's): crushing/traumatic; used to crush bowel during resection of gangrenous bowel. Non-crushing intestinal clamp: curved non-crushing; used to occlude the bowel without causing trauma, preserving bowel viability.

B(i) Endotracheal tube components: graduated (to confirm depth of insertion); cuffed — (a) to prevent aspiration of gastric content and (b) to prevent wastage of anaesthetic gases or oxygen; radio-opaque line along it (makes it visible on X-ray to know tube location); Murphy's eye; pilot cuff. Indications for endotracheal intubation: (1) positive pressure ventilation; (2) need to protect the patient from aspiration; (3) emergency surgery; (4) surgery in a prone position. Laryngeal Mask Airway (LMA): a supra-glottic device. Contraindications: full stomach; emergency surgery; obese patients.

B(ii) Four commonly used methods of sterilisation: moist heat, gas, boiling water, and radiation. Tyndallisation (fractional/discontinuous sterilisation): boiling goods at 100 degrees C for 15–20 minutes a day for three consecutive days. Historical role of autoclave: Ernst Von Bergman and Shimelbus K constructed a sterilising machine for boiling instruments; metallic drums for sterilising clothes and dressings; and perfected an autoclave — this marks the beginning of the aseptic technique era. Trendelenburg in 1882 also devised a device for sterilising surgical materials and instruments with dry steam.

A(i) Classification of oesophageal foreign bodies:
- Food impaction: meat, vegetables.
- Alimentary non-edible foreign bodies: fish bones, nutshells.
- True foreign bodies: dentures/teeth, pills (with or without wrapping), metal objects (e.g., pins, clips), plastic objects, toothpicks, coins, disc/button batteries.

A(ii) Risk factors:
Patient-related factors: childhood, psychiatric disease, altered level of consciousness, drug use, alcohol use, dementia, structural abnormalities, poor vision, wearing of dentures, pathological conditions of the oesophagus.
Activity-related factors: consumption of high-risk foods (chicken bones, fish bones), professional activities (upholsterer, dressmaker), illicit activities (drug smuggling, voluntary ingestion by prisoners, concealment of forbidden objects by prisoners).

B(i) Distinctions:
- Patient group: food impaction tends to occur in older adults, often in the context of oesophageal pathology where dentures or food boluses are the common culprits; true foreign body ingestion peaks in children up to age 10 and in adults older than 50 years, with toddlers most commonly affected.
- Common site: most true (non-edible) foreign bodies lodge around the upper oesophageal sphincter region; most food impactions occur above the lower oesophageal sphincter.
- Indication for urgent extraction: failure of the foreign body to move down within 48–72 hours; objects greater than 2 cm wide and greater than 5 cm long; signs of respiratory compromise; sharp objects, coins, or battery — and a battery must be removed without any delay.

A) Describe jejunoileal atresia under the following headings:

questions.answerText:
A(i) Aetiology, incidence, associated anomalies:
- Aetiology: vascular accident (intrauterine mesenteric vascular occlusion), not a failure of recanalization
- Incidence: 1 in 330 live births; equal sex incidence
- Major cause of intestinal obstruction in neonates
Associated anomalies:
- Intestinal malrotation
- Gastroschisis
- Exomphalos

A(ii) Classification:
Type I: Stenosis or diaphragm (intraluminal membrane, bowel wall intact)
Type II: Fibrous cord connection between the two blind ends; no mesenteric defect
Type IIIa: Atresia with V-shaped mesenteric defect
Type IIIb: Atresia with apple-peel / Christmas tree appearance — the distal bowel is short, has no mesentery, and receives its blood supply in a retrograde manner from the ileocolic artery; the bowel wraps around this vessel
Type IV: Multiple atresias

B) Microcolon on barium enema:
The unused colon never receives intestinal content in utero (complete obstruction proximal to the terminal ileum), so it fails to develop its normal calibre, resulting in a microcolon (disuse atrophy). This confirms the level is in the small bowel.
Jejunal vs ileal presentation: More proximal atresia (jejunal) causes earlier and more prominent vomiting with less distension; ileal atresia causes greater abdominal distension, failure to pass meconium, and visible peristalsis because the obstruction is more distal.

C) Treatment:
Resuscitation:
- NPO
- Nasogastric tube
- IV fluids with electrolyte correction
- IV antibiotics
- Vitamin K
- Incubator care; urinary output monitoring
Surgery: Entero-enterostomy (end-to-end or end-to-oblique anastomosis after resection of the dilated proximal segment and the atretic ends; tapering of the proximal bowel may be required).

(i) Most likely diagnosis: Hodgkin's disease (Hodgkin's lymphoma). It is an immune system malignancy involving B or T lymphocytes. Pathological cell: Reed-Sternberg cells. Spread: slow, predictable, with extension to contiguous lymph nodes. Infiltration to non-lymphoid organs is rare.
(ii) Epidemiology: Hodgkin's disease accounts for 5% of childhood cancers; accounts for 40% of childhood lymphomas; bimodal peaks at 15–35 and over 50 years, rare under age 5; M:F ratio of 3:1; variation related to geography, socioeconomic status and type; increased in immunologic disorders, HIV, EBV. Prognostic subtypes: Nodular sclerosing (NS) 40–60% — lower cervical, supraclavicular, mediastinal nodes; Mixed cellularity (MC) 15–30% — advanced disease with extranodal involvement; Lymphocyte predominance (LP) 5–15% — localized disease; Lymphocyte depletion (LD) <5% — widespread disease.
(iii) Clinical presentation: painless lymph node swelling (90%) that persists despite antibiotic therapy; palpable non-tender, firm, mobile, rubbery nodes; mediastinal adenopathy (60%); superior vena cava obstruction. Bulky disease: when mass is >1/3 of thorax diameter. B symptoms: fever of >38°C for 3 days, drenching night sweats, 10% weight loss.
(iv) Investigations: full blood count, abdominal USS, lymph node biopsy, bone marrow aspiration/biopsy, lumbar puncture, CT scan, PET scan, bone scan. Staging (Ann Arbor): Stage I — tumour at one site (nodal or extranodal); Stage II — two or more sites, same side of body (or resectable); Stage III — both sides of body but not Stage IV; Stage IV — CNS or marrow involvement (Murphy) or lung, liver, marrow, or bone involvement.
(v) Treatment: chemotherapy, radiotherapy, surgery. Favourable prognosis: age <10, female, favourable subtypes (LP and NS), Stage I non-bulky disease. Unfavourable prognosis: persistently elevated ESR; lymphocyte depletion histopathology; bulky disease (largest dimension >10 cm); B symptoms.

Describe the gross anatomy and pathology of tuberculosis of the spine under the headings of pathological process, clinical features, and radiological findings, then explain why this condition may cause paralysis and distant functional deficits, and distinguish it from pyogenic spinal infection.
A(i) Describe the pathological process of tuberculosis of the spine, including the route of spread and behaviour of the abscess.
A(ii) Describe the clinical features in early and late stages of the disease, including the cervical manifestations.
B(i) Describe the radiological features on plain X-ray, CT, and MRI.
B(ii) Explain why paralysis occurs and distinguish tuberculosis from pyogenic (staphylococcal) spinal infection.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Tuberculosis of the spine is usually secondary to a primary focus. It spreads to the spine via the haematogenous route. The common site is the thoracolumbar spine. The organism is an acid-fast bacillus. It causes caseating granuloma with surrounding pus. The tubercles are composed of monocytes and epithelial cells forming minute masses with central caseation in the presence of Langhans-type giant cells. The abscess expands following the path of least resistance. Skin sinuses may form. The bone reaction to the infection varies from none to severe. The infection spares the intervertebral discs initially — unlike Staphylococcus aureus — and their involvement is a late sign. The infection spreads beneath the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments.
A(ii) Early stage: weakness, malaise, night sweats, fever, weight loss. Late stage: back pain due to bone collapse; paralysis due to pressure effect and vascular compromise — spastic type is commonest. Cervical involvement produces: hoarseness due to recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis; dysphagia; respiratory stridor (Millar's asthma).
B(i) Radiological features — Early: subtle decrease in one or more disc spaces; localised osteopaenia. Late: vertebral collapse (concertina collapse); soft tissue swelling; calcification; absent vertebral body. CT — shows more bony destruction. MRI — shows more soft tissue involvement. Biopsy and culture are also required.
B(ii) Paralysis occurs due to pressure effect and vascular compromise. Distinguished from pyogenic infection: tuberculosis spares the intervertebral discs initially, while Staphylococcus aureus involves the discs early. Differential diagnosis includes: pyogenic infection by Staphylococcus aureus or Salmonella typhi (in sickle cell patients); fungal infection (e.g., histoplasmosis duboisii); secondary metastatic disease (e.g., carcinoma of the prostate); primary bone tumours (osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, myeloma).

questions.question:
(A) Describe the spectrum of chest injuries — "the deadly dozen" — under the following headings:
(i) The lethal six identified during the primary survey, with a brief description of each
(ii) The hidden six identified during the secondary survey

(B) Describe the management of open (sucking) pneumothorax under:
(i) Pathophysiology and the critical anatomical relationship of wound size to tracheal diameter
(ii) Clinical signs during the primary survey
(iii) Treatment

(C) Describe the general principles of primary survey management in chest injury using the ABCDE framework, stating the resuscitative intervention for each step.
questions.answerText:
(A)(i) Lethal six (primary survey): (1) Airway obstruction — causes include falling tongue, dentures, expanding neck haematoma, blood, secretions, tissues, mandibular fracture; (2) Tension pneumothorax — flutter-valve effect, air enters but cannot exit, mediastinal shift, obstructive shock; (3) Open pneumothorax — sucking chest wound with air entering through defect; (4) Flail chest — segmental fracture of at least 3 contiguous ribs with paradoxical movement; (5) Massive haemothorax — blood accumulation in pleural cavity from blunt or penetrating trauma; (6) Cardiac tamponade — blood in pericardial sac compressing the heart, Beck's triad.

(A)(ii) Hidden six (secondary survey): pulmonary contusion; myocardial contusion; tracheobronchial disruption; diaphragmatic rupture; oesophageal injury; traumatic aortic rupture.

(B)(i) Air enters the pleural cavity due to negative intrapleural pressure during inspiration. When the hole size is >0.75 times that of the trachea (>75% of tracheal diameter), air preferentially flows through the defect — the less resistant path.
(B)(ii) Clinical signs: sucking air wound/bubbling is diagnostic; breathing is rapid and shallow; decreased chest expansion; increased percussion note; decreased/absent breath sounds.
(B)(iii) Treatment: 100% oxygen via face mask; apply sterile rectangular occlusive dressing; chest tube insertion; wound debridement and closure; ETT for ventilation if indicated.

(C) ABCDE framework: A — Establish a functional airway in airway obstruction by clearing the airway of secretions, foreign bodies, or ETT/tracheostomy. B — Restore normal breathing if compromised by pneumo/haemothorax or flail chest; resuscitation: needle thoracocentesis, CTTD, mechanical ventilation. C — Control life-threatening haemorrhage from massive haemothorax/cardiac tamponade; resuscitation: wide-bore cannula, samples for ABGs, FBC, GXM; volume replacement (avoid overzealous crystalloids); CTTD, pericardiocentesis, or emergency thoracotomy. D — Disability/Drugs: rule out CNS/spine injuries; antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis, analgesia as indicated. E — Exposure: examine from head to toe and treat as indicated; invite relevant specialties if polytrauma established.

A. Hand infections are classified by anatomical location into:
- Paronychia (whitlow): infection of soft tissue proximal to the nail bed; the commonest hand infection
- Felon: infection of the finger pulp
- Ulnar bursitis: infection of the ulnar bursa
- Radial bursitis: infection of the radial bursa
- Flexor sheath infection: infection of the flexor sheath
- Palmar space infection: infection of the palmar space
- Web space infection
- Infection of the space of Parona (deep to the flexor tendons in the distal forearm)
- Osteomyelitis (secondary to paronychia)
A(i) The four Kanavel signs of flexor sheath infection are: (i) fusiform swelling of the finger; (ii) semi-flexed finger position; (iii) tenderness over the flexor sheath; (iv) pain on passive extension of the finger.
A(ii) The most common pathogen in hand infection overall is Staphylococcus aureus (accounting for 80% of cases). From human bites: Eikenella corrodens and anaerobes including Peptrostreptococcus and Bacteroides. From cat, dog, and cow bites: Pasteurella multocida.
B. Management principles follow this sequence:
- Evaluate the patient with a full history (including onset, mechanism, first aid given, diabetes status) and physical examination.
- Investigations: haematology (PCV, group and cross-match), chemistry (U&E, serum protein and albumin), microbiology (wound swab for M/C/S), radiology (X-ray of both hands AP and lateral).
- Resuscitation following the ABC of resuscitation.
- Incision and drainage/debridement of any collection.
- Appropriate antimicrobials: Ampicillin/cloxacillin (Ampicilox), metronidazole, antiviral, antifungal, or antiscabies agents as appropriate.
- Tetanus vaccine; analgesics; regular saline and honey bulky dressing; elevation; physiotherapy and rehabilitation; follow-up.
B(i) Paronychia (whitlow) is infection of the soft tissue proximal to the nail bed and is the commonest hand infection. Felon is infection of the finger pulp (the fingertip pulp space).

questions.answerText:
(i) Osteosarcoma. Typical age group: children and adolescents (recent significant rise in age of presentation has also been noted). Site: metaphyseal tumour — metaphysis of long bones (e.g. around the knee — distal femur/proximal tibia). Histological basis: biopsy of tissue shows osteosarcoma on histology.
(ii) Predisposing factors: Paget's disease (giving rise to Paget's sarcoma, typically age >50 years, associated with the worst prognosis). X-ray: variable picture; 'sunburst' effect; Codman's triangle. Staging (Enneking, adapted by AJCC 1997): Stage IIA — high grade, intracompartmental; Stage IIB — high grade, extracompartmental; Stage III — distant metastasis.
(iii) Management protocol: neoadjuvant chemotherapy — 8–12 weeks pre-operatively; surgical resection — wide resection; post-operative chemotherapy — 6–12 months; long-term survival — 50–60%. Outcome has now significantly improved compared to previously.
(iv) Variants: (a) Parosteal osteosarcoma (note: dedifferentiated type exists); (b) Periosteal osteosarcoma; (c) Paget's sarcoma (age >50 years, worst prognosis). Limb-sparing surgery for bone defects: short diaphyseal defects — vascularised bone grafts; long gaps — prosthesis; osteoarticular defects — allografts, allograft prosthetic composite, or prosthesis alone; growing children — extendable implants; others — grafting, arthrodesis, distraction osteogenesis.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: end-stage renal disease from diabetic nephropathy. Procedure: renal transplantation. Gibson incision: a curved incision in the iliac fossa; approach is extraperitoneal (avoiding the peritoneal cavity). Vascular anastomoses: renal vein anastomosed to external iliac vein (RV-EIV); renal artery anastomosed to internal iliac artery or external iliac artery (RA-IIA/EIA). Urinary reconstruction: ureteroneocystostomy (donor ureter implanted into recipient bladder).

(ii) Donor evaluation: CT angiography assesses — renal artery, renal vein, IVC, and aorta (for vascular anatomy and accessory vessels). Other evaluations: mixed lymphocyte culture; routine investigations as in recipient (CBC, E/U, creatinine, liver function, blood group, HLA typing, viral serologies, urine M/C/S, CXR, ECG). Inclusion criteria: age 18–65 years; two normally functioning kidneys; donor willingness. Surgical approach: laparoscopic with or without hand-assist (HADN), or open donor nephrectomy.

(iii) Post-transplant vascular complications (6–30%):
- Renal artery stenosis: <1%.
- Renal vein thrombosis: 0.3–4%.
- Vascular anastomosis disruption.
Ureteral complications: leakage or obstruction. Bladder complications: extravasation. Lymphocele (0.6–18%): caused by division of lymphatic channels along the iliac vessels during preparation of the recipient bed; lymph accumulates in the peritransplant space, forming a cystic collection. Pelvic haematoma; infections; malignancy (lymphoma, SQCC).

(iv) Diabetic nephropathy causes ESRD through progressive glomerulosclerosis: hyperglycaemia causes thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, mesangial expansion, and eventually nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesion); this reduces the filtration surface area and increases glomerular permeability to proteins; proteinuria, hypertension, and progressive decline in GFR follow; ESRD results from complete loss of functional glomeruli.
Immunosuppressive management: the regimen is the same whether living-related or cadaveric — preferred triple regimen: calcineurin-based agent (cyclosporin or tacrolimus), steroids (GCC), and antiproliferative agent (azathioprine or MMF). Immunosuppression is highest in the first 3 months, then continued indefinitely. The living-related recipient has better HLA matching (mixed lymphocyte culture compatibility confirmed), which reduces but does not eliminate rejection risk; the same triple regimen is used. Complications of immunosuppression are the same regardless of donor type: infections (CMV, HSV, bacterial, fungal, Pneumocystis carinii — risk highest ≤6 months, chemoprophylaxis important); malignancy (PTLD, SQCC — regular review required).

A 28-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of progressive weight loss, palpitations, heat intolerance, and swelling in the front of the neck. On examination there is a diffuse smooth goitre, exophthalmos, eyelid retraction and a bruit over the thyroid.
(i) What is the diagnosis and its definition?
(ii) What are the epidemiology, aetiology, and pathophysiology of this condition?
(iii) List the full spectrum of eye signs and other system signs of this condition.
(iv) What investigations should be requested, and what are the possible complications?
(v) What are all the treatment options, and what follow-up is required?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Graves' disease (diffuse toxic goitre). Definition: autoimmune disease characterised by persistent activation of TSH receptors by anti-TSH receptor antibodies leading to increased synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones.
(ii) Epidemiology: most common cause of hyperthyroidism; commoner in females (M:F ratio of 1:8); typically between 20 and 40 years old. Aetiology: primary hyperthyroidism — diffuse toxic goitre (Graves' disease). Pathophysiology: clinical state of elevated thyroid hormone in tissues, usually due to inappropriately high secretion; can be overt (low TSH, high T3 and T4) or subclinical (low TSH, normal T3 and T4).
(iii) Eye signs: lid retraction (Dalrymple's sign); lid lag (von Graefe's sign); absence of normal blinking — staring look (Stellwag's sign); absence of forehead wrinkling (Joffroy's sign); lack of eyeball convergence (Moebius sign); increased eyelid margin pigmentation (Jellinek's sign); eyelid and conjunctiva oedema (Enroth sign); tremor of closed eyelid (Rosenbach's sign); difficulty everting upper eyelid (Gifford's sign); easy pupillary dilatation (Loewi's sign); unequal pupillary dilatation (Knie's sign); jerky pupillary contraction to light (Cowen's sign); eyeball protrusion above supra-ciliary ridge from behind (Naffziger's sign); exophthalmos. Other signs — cardiac: tachycardia, ectopic beats, pulsus paradoxus, wide pulse pressure, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation; neuromuscular: proximal myopathy, myasthenia gravis; integument: pretibial myxoedema, thyroid dermopathy, thyroid acropachy; vascular: thrill and bruits in upper pole, hepatosplenomegaly; airway: respiratory distress on compressing one side of anterior neck (Kocher's sign).
(iv) Investigations: thyroid function tests (increased T3, increased T4, decreased TSH), anti-TSH receptor antibodies, cervical x-ray (AP, lateral, thoracic inlet views), soft tissue ultrasonography of the neck, radio-isotope scan (123I or 99Tc). Complications: thyroid storm, thyrocardia.
(v) Treatment: anti-thyroid drugs (carbimazole, methimazole, propylthiouracil, propranolol, Lugol's iodine); thyroidectomy (near-total or total); radioactive iodine therapy. Prognosis excellent if given appropriate treatment. Follow-up: thyroid function tests; post total thyroidectomy patient will require L-thyroxine for life.
