A(i) Define paralytic ileus and describe the three categories of factors that cause it, giving an example of each.
A(ii) Describe the normal post-operative return of bowel activity, stating when gastric peristalsis, colonic activity, and normal bowel sounds return, and at what point a cause should be sought if ileus persists.
B(i) Explain the anatomical and physiological basis for why hypokalaemia contributes to paralytic ileus, and describe the radiological appearance of paralytic ileus on plain films.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition and three categories:
- Paralytic ileus is a state in which the intestine fails to transmit peristaltic waves due to impairment of the normal neuromuscular mechanism.
- Neural factors: e.g., the intestino-intestinal inhibitory reflex resulting from prolonged intestinal distension; excessive or rough handling of the gut by operators during abdominal surgery.
- Humoral factors: e.g., peritonitis and pus in the peritoneal cavity, suggested to cause ileus by a humoral mechanism, though the particular mediators are yet to be isolated.
- Metabolic factors: e.g., electrolyte imbalance, especially hypokalaemia; ischaemia of the intestine rapidly inhibits motility.

A(ii) Normal post-operative return of bowel activity:
- Gastric peristalsis usually returns 24–48 hours post-operatively.
- Colonic activity usually returns after 48 hours, beginning at the caecum and extending caudally.
- Normal bowel sounds should return by the 3rd to 4th post-operative day.
- Look for a cause if paralytic ileus extends beyond 4 days.

B(i) Basis of hypokalaemia and radiological appearance:
- Hypokalaemia contributes to paralytic ileus by interfering with the normal ionic movements during smooth muscle contraction.
- Radiological appearance on plain films: both small and large bowel dilatation; on horizontal-ray films, multiple fluid levels are seen.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents with right upper quadrant pain and fever. Ultrasound shows hyperechoic lesions with acoustic shadowing that are mobile, thickening of the gallbladder wall to greater than 4 mm with a hypoechoic wall, surrounding fluid, a distended gallbladder, and localised tenderness to direct probe pressure.

(i) Identify the investigation being described and state what it is the investigation of choice for in this context.
(ii) Name the specific ultrasound sign elicited by the last finding listed (localised tenderness to direct probe pressure) and state what condition it is positive for.
(iii) State what percentage of cases of acute cholecystitis develop as a complication of cholelithiasis, and what percentage of patients with gallstones will require surgery for complications within 15 years.
(iv) Name two conditions included in the acalculous group of cholecystitis and state the percentage of all acute cholecystitis cases they account for.
(v) Explain why plain radiographs are insensitive for acute cholecystitis, and name the plain film finding present in only 10% of cases.
questions.answerText:
(i) The investigation is ultrasound (USS).
- It is the investigation of choice for suspected acute cholecystitis.

(ii) The specific sign is the positive sonographic Murphy's sign.
- It is positive for acute cholecystitis.

(iii) Approximately 85–90% of cases of acute cholecystitis develop as a complication of cholelithiasis.
- Approximately 10–20% of patients with gallstones will require surgery for complications, usually cholecystitis, within 15 years after their stone disease is diagnosed.

(iv) Acalculous cholecystitis accounts for 5–15% of cases of acute cholecystitis.
- Conditions included: immunocompromised patients, critically ill patients, iatrogenic causes, and congenital causes (any two of these).

(v) Plain radiographs are insensitive for acute cholecystitis because the signs are non-specific.
- Gallstones are only seen in 10% of cases on plain film (as most are radiolucent).

A. The scalp layers are remembered by the mnemonic SCALP:
- S = Skin: the outermost layer, thick and firmly adherent.
- C = Compact subcutaneous tissue: dense fibroadipose layer firmly bound to skin and galea, containing blood vessels; lacerations here bleed profusely because vessel walls cannot retract.
- A = Aponeurosis of Galea: strong tendinous sheet linking frontalis to occipitalis; provides structural strength exploited in flap design.
- L = Loose areolar connective tissue: avascular plane that allows easy spread of infection and haematoma but also serves as the surgical dissection plane for flap elevation; infection here can spread intracranially through emissary veins.
- P = Periosteum: the deepest layer, adherent to the outer table of the skull; relatively avascular.
A(i) A scalp rotation flap is raised through the skin, compact subcutaneous tissue, and galea (S, C, and A layers), using the loose areolar layer as the plane of dissection. This technique is indicated to reconstruct scalp and adjacent facial defects when a large area of scalp is lost or exposed bone is present.
B. A skin graft is a piece of skin transferred from one part of the body to another while completely detached from its blood supply or donor site attachment; its survival depends on diffusion of nutrients from, and subsequent ingrowth of vessels from, the recipient bed, which must therefore be adequately vascular (healthy granulation tissue, vascularised subcutaneous fat, muscle, fascia, periosteum, or paratenon). A flap is a mass of tissue transferred from one part of the body to another with its blood supply intact via a vascular pedicle; it is used when the bed is not adequately vascular (e.g., bare bone, bare tendon) or when composite tissue transfer is required. One absolute contraindication to skin grafting is an avascular bed, such as exposed major vessels, bare bone without periosteum, or bare tendon without paratenon.
questions.question:
A. Describe the layers of the SCALP under the mnemonic headings used, stating what each letter represents and the clinical significance of each layer.
A(i) State the layer(s) of the scalp through which a scalp rotation flap is raised, and explain why this technique is used.
B. Distinguish between a SKIN GRAFT and a FLAP, stating the definition of each, the prerequisite condition of the recipient bed for each, and one absolute contraindication specific to skin grafting.

A 45-year-old man with a history of alcohol excess presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, and haemodynamic instability. On examination, bruising is noted in the flanks (Grey Turner's sign) and at the umbilicus (Cullen's sign).
(i) What diagnosis do the physical signs suggest, and what is their pathological basis?
(ii) State all the risk factors for pancreatic carcinoma, and how pancreatic cancer of the head of the pancreas presents differently from that of the body or tail.
(iii) Apply Courvoisier's law: state the law, explain its basis, and give all the causes of painless progressive jaundice with a palpable gallbladder.
(iv) What investigations are used for pancreatic cancer, and what finding on barium meal is characteristic?
(v) Describe the curative and palliative treatment options for pancreatic cancer.
questions.answerText:
(i) Severe/necrotising acute pancreatitis. Grey Turner's sign (flank bruising) and Cullen's sign (periumbilical bruising) indicate retroperitoneal haemorrhage from necrotising pancreatitis; they reflect spread of blood retroperitoneally and into the subcutaneous tissues around the umbilicus.
(ii) Pancreatic carcinoma risk factors: smoking; diabetes; chronic pancreatitis.
- Head/periampullary: painless, progressive jaundice with a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's law); rarely pancreatitis; rarely duodenal obstruction.
- Body: back pain; anorexia; weight loss; steatorrhoea.
- Tail: often presents with metastases; malignant ascites; or unexplained anaemia.
(iii) Courvoisier's law: a palpable gallbladder in the presence of jaundice is unlikely to be due to gallstones. Basis: gallstones cause chronic inflammation and fibrosis of the gallbladder wall, preventing it from distending; obstruction by a periampullary or pancreatic head tumour distends a previously healthy gallbladder. Causes of painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder: carcinoma of the head of pancreas; periampullary carcinoma; carcinoma of the bile duct; ampullary carcinoma.
(iv) Investigations:
- Ultrasound: may see mass in head of pancreas and distended biliary tree; facilitates needle biopsy.
- CT scan: demonstrates tumour mass; facilitates biopsy; assesses involvement of surrounding structures and local lymph node spread.
- ERCP: very accurate in making diagnosis; obtain specimen for cytology; stent may be placed to relieve jaundice.
- Barium meal: widening of the duodenal loop with medial filling defect — the reversed '3' sign.
(v) Management:
- Curative: Whipple's (pancreatico-duodenectomy) resection of small tumours of the head of pancreas if lymph nodes are not involved.
- Palliation: jaundice relieved by stent through tumour (transhepatically or via ERCP); duodenal obstruction relieved by gastrojejunostomy; pain by coeliac axis block.
- Prognosis: 90% of patients with pancreatic adenocarcinoma are dead within 12 months of diagnosis.

questions.question:
A patient presents following blunt chest trauma with tracheal deviation to the right, decreased expansion of the left side, dull percussion note on the left, decreased breath sounds on the left, and on CXR, 500 mL of blood is present in the left pleural cavity. Vitals show HR 130 bpm and BP 80/60 mmHg.

(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) Describe the initial investigations recommended, including what CXR and ultrasound findings indicate.
(iii) What is the definitive resuscitative procedure, including the chest tube size and what volume of initial drainage mandates emergency thoracotomy?
(iv) State the indications for thoracotomy in massive haemothorax.
questions.answerText:
(i) Massive haemothorax.

(ii) Investigations: CXR — a minimum of 400–500 mL is required to obliterate the costophrenic angle; USS/eFAST — can pick up small volumes < 200 mL. Signs: tracheal deviation, decreased chest expansion, dull percussion note, decreased breath sound.

(iii) Definitive resuscitative procedure: CTTD (chest tube thoracostomy drainage); chest tube size 28–32F is adequate — there is no added advantage in using a large bore tube (34–40F). Initial drainage indicating thoracotomy: immediate drainage of 1000–1500 mL (10–15 mL/kg) of blood in less than 1 hour mandates thoracotomy; continuous drainage of 200–250 mL/hr (5 mL/kg) for at least 3 consecutive hours also mandates thoracotomy.

(iv) Indications for thoracotomy: immediate drainage of 1000–1500 mL (10–15 mL/kg) of blood in <1 hr; continuous drainage of 200–250 mL/hr (5 mL/kg) for at least 3 consecutive hours; haemodynamic instability; penetrating injury with cardiac tamponade; contrast extravasation on CT-scan or rapidly expanding haematoma; large volume of haemorrhage from chest tube.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the Swanson classification of congenital hand deformities in full, listing all seven types with their Roman numeral designation, the principle underlying each type, and one clinical example for each type.
A(ii) List all the syndromes associated with congenital hand deformities, stating the defining features of each syndrome.
B(i) Describe the evaluation of a child with a congenital hand deformity.
B(ii) State the risk that three or more minor anomalies in a single patient carry, and give the subsequent pregnancy risk range for congenital hand deformities.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Swanson Classification (1968):
- Type I — Failure of formation: e.g., phocomelia.
- Type II — Failure of differentiation: e.g., syndactyly, trigger thumb, Poland syndrome, camptodactyly.
- Type III — Duplication: may apply to whole limb, mirror hand, polydactyly.
- Type IV — Overgrowth: includes hemihypertrophy and macrodactyly.
- Type V — Undergrowth: most commonly radial hypoplasia, brachysyndactyly, or brachydactyly.
- Type VI — Constriction band syndromes: Streeter hypoplasia — occurs with or without lymphoedema; involves amputation at any level.
- Type VII — Generalised anomalies and syndromes: unclassified category.
A(ii) Associated syndromes:
- Poland Syndrome: syndactyly + hypoplastic pectoralis muscles.
- Holt-Oram Syndrome: cardiac defects (ASD or VSD) + upper limb defects.
- VATER Syndrome: Vertebral defects, imperforate Anus, Tracheo-Esophageal fistula, Radial and Renal dysplasia.
- Fanconi Syndrome: pancytopenia, preaxial limb defects, renal abnormalities, hyperpigmentation, short stature, microcephaly or mental retardation.
- TAR Syndrome: Thrombocytopenia with Absent Radii (thumbs are present, unlike Fanconi).
- Aase Syndrome: triphalangeal thumb and aplastic anaemia.
- Nager Syndrome: preaxial aplasia associated with mandibulofacial dysostosis (Treacher Collins syndrome).
- Roberts Syndrome: four deficient limbs + cleft lip and palate.
B(i) Evaluation headings: pregnancy, birth, and developmental history; physical examination; laboratory and radiological investigations; genetic counselling.
B(ii) When three or more minor anomalies exist in a single patient, the chance of the presence of a major anomaly is 90%. Subsequent pregnancy risk: 0–25%.

questions.question:
(A) Describe bronchiectasis under the following headings:
(i) Definition and morphological types
(ii) The two prerequisites for induction of bronchiectasis and the pathophysiological mechanism
(iii) Conditions causing or associated with bronchiectasis

(B) Describe the clinical manifestations of bronchiectasis, including the quantity-based classification of sputum production and the physical examination findings.

(C) Explain how disease may spread or persist in bronchiectasis to cause chronic complications, and state the indications for surgical treatment.
questions.answerText:
(A)(i) Bronchiectasis is defined as "chronic dilation of the bronchi marked by fetid breath and paroxysmal coughing, with the expectoration of mucopurulent matter" — permanent abnormal dilation and destruction of bronchial walls, which may be focal or diffuse. Morphological types: cylindrical or tubular; varicose; saccular or cystic.

(A)(ii) Two prerequisites: (1) an infectious insult; (2) impairment of drainage, airway obstruction, and/or a defect in host defence. Infection produces persistent, neutrophil-dominant inflammation with pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-8, IL-1, TNF-α) and low anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-10). The affected areas show transmural inflammation, mucosal oedema, cratering and ulceration with bronchial neovascularisation, and distortion due to scarring or obstruction from repeated infection; obstruction often leads to postobstructive pneumonitis that may temporarily or permanently damage the lung parenchyma.

(A)(iii) Conditions: bacterial, mycobacterial, Aspergillus, viral (including HIV) infections; congenital — primary ciliary dyskinesia, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, cystic fibrosis, tracheobronchomegaly (Mounier-Kuhn syndrome), cartilage deficiency (Williams-Campbell syndrome), pulmonary sequestration, Marfan's syndrome; immunodeficiency — hypogammaglobulinemia; sequelae of toxic inhalation or aspiration; foreign body; rheumatic conditions — rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, Sjögren's syndrome, relapsing polychondritis, inflammatory bowel disease.

(B) Clinical manifestations: persistent or recurrent cough with purulent sputum; haemoptysis — bleeding is brisk, associated with acute infective episodes, produced by injury to superficial mucosal neovascular bronchial arterioles; dyspnoea; chest pain; malnutrition/wasting; chronic inflammation. Sputum production: mild < 15 cc/day; moderate 15–150 cc/day; severe > 150 cc/day. Physical findings: any combination of rhonchi, creps or wheezes; clubbing of digits (rare); chronic hypoxaemia → cor pulmonale → right heart failure.

(C) Spread/persistence: persistent infection leads to recurrent pneumonia in the same pulmonary segment; overwhelming purulent and viscid sputum production from a specific lung segment occurs; poorly controlled haemorrhage from neovascular bronchial arterioles; resistant organisms such as MAI or Aspergillus may harbour in bronchiectatic airways. Surgical indications: localised bronchiectasis; proximal obstructive lesion; massive haemoptysis; recurrent infections; reduction in acute infective episodes occurring in the same pulmonary segment.

(i) Diagnosis: Indirect inguinal hernia in an infant. Embryological basis: At 6 weeks, primitive germ cells migrate to the genital ridge; at 7–8 weeks differentiation into testis occurs. The gubernaculum aids descent; at 3 months descent commences, and at 7 months the testis reaches the internal ring acquiring its cord coverings. The processus vaginalis (PV) normally involutes by obliteration in 90% of cases; in 10% it remains patent, giving rise to hernias (bubonoiele, funicular, or complete) and hydroceles.
(ii) Predisposing factors: prematurity, positive family history, meconium peritonitis, chylous ascites, abdominal wall defects, exstrophy of the bladder or cloaca, undescended testis, hypospadias, epispadias, connective tissue disorders, liver disease with ascites, following VP shunt for hydrocephalus.
(iii) Intraoperative complications: damage to the ilioinguinal nerve; damage to the vas deferens (should be repaired); primary haemorrhage. Post-operative: wound infection, scrotal haematoma, postoperative hydrocele, recurrence (less common in children). Irreducible hernia — initial management: sedation, Trendelenburg position, use of cold pack, gentle taxis; postpone surgery if concurrent illness or severe prematurity is present.
(iv) Definitive operative treatment: herniotomy (ligation and excision of the hernia sac). Orchidopexy is required in cases where an undescended testis is present. In cases of obstructed hernia, treatment of obstruction takes priority.
questions.question:
A 6-week-old male infant is brought to clinic with a swelling in the right groin noticed since birth, which becomes more prominent when he cries. On examination a reducible swelling is found in the right inguinal region with a thickened cord — the 'silk glove sign' is present.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what is the embryological basis for this condition?
(ii) What predisposing factors are associated with increased incidence of this condition?
(iii) What are the complications of surgery for this condition, and how should an irreducible hernia be initially managed before surgery?
(iv) What is the definitive operative treatment, and when is orchidopexy also required?

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: incarcerated (obstructed) right inguinal hernia in a premature male infant. Predisposing factors: prematurity (5–30% of premature infants); 80–90% of paediatric hernias occur in boys; peak incidence in infancy and childhood; 1/3 present in first 6 months of age. Right-sided predominance: the right testis descends later than the left, and the processus vaginalis closes later on the right; right-sided hernias account for 55–60%, left 25%, bilateral 15%. Embryological basis: the processus vaginalis remains patent in 10% of cases; when patent it allows herniation.
(ii) Immediate management of irreducible hernia: sedation, Trendelenburg position, use of cold pack, gentle taxis. Surgery should be postponed if there is concurrent illness or severe prematurity.
(iii) Intraoperative findings and complications: the hernia sac may contain bowel. Risk of: damage to the ilioinguinal nerve; damage to the vas deferens (should be repaired if injured); primary haemorrhage.
(iv) Definitive surgical procedure: herniotomy — high ligation and excision of the hernia sac. Treatment for obstructed hernia follows priority. Orchidopexy is performed if an undescended testis is found. Postponement of surgery is considered for severe prematurity or concurrent illness. Day-case surgery is otherwise applicable.
(v) Post-operative complications: wound infection; scrotal haematoma; postoperative hydrocele; recurrence (less common in children than adults).
questions.question:
A premature male infant (32 weeks) is brought to surgery with a right inguinal swelling. On examination the hernia is irreducible and the scrotum is tender and oedematous. A diagnosis of incarcerated inguinal hernia with intestinal obstruction is made.
(i) What is the diagnosis, predisposing factors related to his age and sex, and the embryological explanation for right-sided predominance?
(ii) What immediate management steps should be taken before surgery?
(iii) What are the intraoperative findings and complications that may be encountered?
(iv) What is the definitive surgical procedure, and what special considerations apply because of his prematurity?
(v) What are the possible post-operative complications?

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is cancrum oris (noma). The child is currently in the chronic stage (the gangrenous process has demarcated and arrested).
- Acute stage: pathological processes are inflammation, gangrene, and demarcation.
- Chronic stage: pathological processes are tissue defects, fibrosis, contracture, and trismus.
(ii) Treatment in the acute stage: intravenous antibiotics; fluid replacement; correction of anaemia; correction of malnutrition.
(iii) Treatment in the chronic stage: release of trismus; release of contractures; closure of tissue defects (using appropriate flaps and reconstructive techniques).
(iv) Tumours of the head and neck:
- Soft tissue: skin tumours (squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, malignant melanoma, cylindroma); lipomas; haemangiomas; soft tissue sarcomas; salivary gland tumours (mixed parotid tumour, adenocarcinoma); gingival tumours (epulis, adenocarcinoma).
- Odontogenic tissue: cysts; ameloblastoma.
- Bony tissue: fibrous dysplasia; Burkitt's lymphoma; osteosarcoma.
(v) Management of gunshot injury to the head and neck:
Investigations: blood investigations; appropriate X-ray (AP and lateral plain X-ray); CT scan; other X-rays as indicated.
Treatment: treat shock; antitetanus prophylaxis; maintain airway; antibiotics. For soft tissue wounds: 6/0 nylon or prolene for skin sutures; remove sutures in five days; if mucosa is involved, stitch with 5/0 or 4/0 chromic catgut. If bone is exposed, a flap should be transferred. For fractures, use closed or internal fixation as necessary.
Complications: wound infection; nerve conduction disorders; ocular problems; brain damage; CSF rhinorrhoea.
questions.question:
A 5-year-old malnourished child from a rural setting presents with progressive gangrenous destruction of the right cheek and oral tissues. The overlying skin is necrotic, and there lesion has demarcated from healthy tissue. There is trismus. Intravenous antibiotics were started but the gangrenous process has now halted.
(i) State the diagnosis, identify which stage of the disease the child is currently in, and describe the pathological process at each stage.
(ii) State the treatment appropriate for the acute stage.
(iii) State the treatment required in the chronic stage, listing the specific interventions.
(iv) List the types of tumours of the head and neck, classified under soft tissue, odontogenic, and bony tissue categories.
(v) Describe the management of a gunshot injury to the head and neck, listing investigations and treatment as given.

questions.answerText:
(i) Foreign body in the airway. Types by prognosis: organic foreign bodies have a worse prognosis because they swell up; inorganic foreign bodies carry a better prognosis.

(ii) Treatment: rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia. A repeat CXR should be done just before the bronchoscopy because the foreign body can migrate. The flexible bronchoscope is not used because of its small working channel, which does not allow effective retrieval instruments.

(iii) Ventilation during the procedure: ventilation is performed using a ventilation port with the bronchoscope.

(iv) Pre-procedure CXR: repeat chest X-ray just before bronchoscopy because the foreign body can migrate. Complications of bronchoscopy: pneumothorax — a post-bronchoscopy X-ray should be done to detect this; arrhythmias — continuous pulse oximetry should be used during the procedure.
questions.question:
A 15-year-old child presents with sudden onset choking, wheezing, and dyspnoea immediately after playing with small toys. On examination there is unilateral decreased air entry. A CXR is taken and shows a radio-opaque foreign body in the right main bronchus. The child is haemodynamically stable.

(i) What is the diagnosis and the types of foreign bodies mentioned in relation to prognosis?
(ii) Describe the treatment including the type of bronchoscope used and why the flexible bronchoscope is not used.
(iii) How is ventilation maintained during the bronchoscopic procedure?
(iv) What CXR should be performed before the procedure, and what are the complications of bronchoscopy?

A 2-year-old boy is brought with a large left-sided abdominal mass, fever, and episodes of flushing and sweating. Examination reveals bilateral orbital ecchymosis ('panda eyes') and hypertension. CT scan shows a mass arising from the left adrenal medulla with stippled calcifications, crossing the midline, with bilateral lymphadenopathy. 24-hour urine collection shows elevated VMA and HVA.

(i) What is the diagnosis? Identify the organ of origin and the bilateral lymphadenopathy's significance for staging.
(ii) What other structures are compressed by a large adrenal neuroblastoma, and what are the differential diagnoses for an abdominal mass in this age group?
(iii) Explain the clinico-anatomical reasoning for the flushing, sweating, hypertension, and bilateral orbital ecchymosis.
(iv) How does the Evans staging system classify this case, and what treatment is indicated?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Neuroblastoma.
Organ of origin: Adrenal medulla (site accounts for 50% of cases).
Bilateral lymphadenopathy significance for staging: The tumour has crossed the midline with bilateral lymphadenopathy — this is Evans Stage III (tumour has crossed the midline and bilateral lymphadenopathy is present). Stage IV would require distant metastasis; IVS involves bone marrow, subcutaneous tissue, or liver in an otherwise Stage I or II patient.

(ii) Structures compressed by large adrenal neuroblastoma:
- Inferior vena cava (compression causes lower limb oedema)
- Renal vessels (causing hypertension and haematuria)
- Ureter (causing hydronephrosis — IVU may show displacement)
- Spinal cord (paraspinal extension through intervertebral foramen — paraplegia)
Differential diagnoses:
- Nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumour) — commonest renal tumour in children
- Lymphoma
- Rhabdomyosarcoma

(iii) Clinico-anatomical reasoning:
Flushing and sweating: the neuroblastoma produces catecholamines (adrenaline, noradrenaline) from the adrenal medulla → catecholamine excess → vasodilation, sweating, irritability.
Hypertension: excess catecholamine secretion causes peripheral vasoconstriction and hypertension (reported in 25%).
Bilateral orbital ecchymosis ('panda eyes'/'raccoon eyes'): haematogenous metastasis to the orbital bones causes periorbital bleeding and ecchymosis.

(iv) Evans Stage III: tumour has crossed the midline with bilateral lymphadenopathy.
Treatment: High-dose chemotherapy followed by surgery.
Chemotherapy agents: Cyclophosphamide, Doxorubicin, Vincristine, Cisplatin.
Radiotherapy: for children >1 year old; MIBG can also be used.
Outcome for Stage III: approximately 60% survival.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of worsening abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea (8 episodes per day), fever, and abdominal distension. He has a history of rectal bleeding and loose stools for 2 years, previously treated with steroids. On examination, the abdomen is distended and tender. Plain abdominal X-ray shows colonic dilatation.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the likely complication indicated by the radiological finding?
(ii) Describe the pathological features (macroscopic and histological) of the underlying condition.
(iii) List the extraintestinal manifestations, classified by system.
(iv) What are the surgical indications and the available operations, including the elective options and their outcomes?
(v) What is the long-term risk of this condition and how is it monitored?
questions.answerText:
(i) Ulcerative colitis with toxic megacolon (colonic dilatation/perforation — 'toxic megacolon'). Severe/fulminant disease: 6–20 bloody bowel motions per day; fever, anaemia, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance; colonic dilatation/perforation.
(ii) Pathology:
- Macroscopic: only the mucosa is involved with superficial ulceration, exudation, and pseudopolyposis.
- Histological: crypt abscess; inflammatory polyps; highly vascular granulation tissue; epithelial dysplasia with longstanding disease.
- Disease confined to colon; rectum always involved; may be 'backwash' ileitis.
(iii) Extraintestinal manifestations:
- Joints: arthritis (25%).
- Eye: uveitis (10%).
- Skin: erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum (10%).
- Liver: pericholangitis, fatty liver (3%).
- Ankylosing spondylitis; seronegative arthritis.
- Blood: thromboembolic disease (rare).
(iv) Surgical indications: failure of medical treatment to control chronic symptoms; complications (profuse haemorrhage, perforation/toxic megacolon); risk of cancer (greater with longer disease, more aggressive onset, more extensive disease); dysplasia or carcinoma.
Operations:
- For acute attacks/complications: total colectomy, end ileostomy, and preserved rectal stump.
- Elective: proctocolectomy with end (Brooke) ileostomy, or proctocolectomy with preservation of anal sphincter and creation of ileoanal pouch (e.g. J-shaped pouch).
(v) Long-term risk: long-term colitis carries a risk of colonic malignancy; colonoscopy is used to screen longstanding disease for dysplasia. Ulcerative colitis is a chronic problem requiring constant surveillance unless surgery, which is drastic but curative, is performed.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the lower limb relevant to hip dislocation, including the classification of types, then state the nerve at risk and the anatomical basis for this risk, and explain why the duration between dislocation and reduction determines the risk of avascular necrosis.
A(i) Classify hip dislocation by type and describe the mechanism of the commonest variety.
A(ii) Describe the nerve at risk and the method for detecting its injury clinically.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis for avascular necrosis as a complication of hip dislocation.
B(ii) Distinguish between myositis ossificans and secondary osteoarthritis as late complications of hip dislocation.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Types of hip dislocation: Posterior dislocation — constitutes about 90%. Anterior dislocation. Central dislocation — referred to as 'stove-in pelvis'. The commonest variety (posterior dislocation) is mostly due to dashboard injuries. Diagnosis: severe pain; hip is flexed, adducted, and internally rotated; radiograph; exclude sciatic nerve involvement.
A(ii) Nerve at risk: Sciatic nerve injury is a recognised complication of hip dislocation. Clinical detection: ask the patient to move the great toe. If sciatic nerve is intact, the toe can be moved; inability to do so indicates sciatic nerve involvement.
B(i) Anatomical basis for avascular necrosis: The blood supply to the femoral head is at risk when the hip is dislocated, as the vessels supplying the femoral head can be stretched, kinked, or torn during dislocation. The longer the duration between the dislocation and reduction, the greater the risk of avascular necrosis. This is because prolonged ischaemia leads to irreversible necrosis of the femoral head.
B(ii) Myositis ossificans: develops within muscle around the joint; usually involves the hip and elbow after dislocation. Treatment: avoid excessive exercise/rest; use indomethacin. Secondary osteoarthritis: osteoarthritis due to a known cause (i.e., the dislocation itself or the resulting avascular necrosis) — this is a late complication distinguished from primary/idiopathic osteoarthritis by having an identifiable preceding cause.

questions.question:
A(i) List the dietary, infective, systemic, and genetic risk factors for gastric carcinoma, organising them under these four headings.
A(ii) State the gold standard investigation for gastric carcinoma and list five other investigations used in its evaluation.
B(i) Describe the surgical treatment of gastric carcinoma, stating the aim of surgery, the choice of procedures based on tumour location (lower, middle, and upper thirds), and the criteria for endoscopic mucosal resection.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Risk factors:
Dietary: smoked or salted fish/meats, high nitrates, high-fat low-fibre diet, deficiency of antioxidants.
Infective: H. pylori infection (the most important infective risk factor).
Systemic/other: alcohol, smoking, duodeno-gastric reflux, blood group A (diffuse type), lower socio-economic class, partial gastrectomy (more than 15 years prior), pernicious anaemia, pre-malignant conditions (chronic atrophic gastritis, polyp greater than 2 cm, gastric epithelial metaplasia, rarely gastric ulcer).
Genetic: familial — 3–6-fold increased risk in first-degree relatives; mutations/loss of heterozygosity of APC gene, beta-catenin, E-cadherin; mutation of P53 gene (Li-Fraumeni syndrome); HNPCC (Lynch syndrome — family cancer syndrome); growth factor receptor overexpression/amplification (c-met, k-Sam, c-ErbB2); growth factors (TGF-α, EGF, VEGF); loss of heterozygosity BCL2 — loss of apoptosis.

A(ii) Investigations:
- Gold standard: OGD (oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy).
- Other investigations: barium meal and follow-through; endoluminal ultrasound (T-staging and lymph nodes); abdominal ultrasound (less sensitive, for metastasis workup); CT scan (mass, wall thickening, lymph node enlargement); MRI (similar to CT, more sensitive for liver metastases); PET-CT (for occult spread); laparoscopy (to detect peritoneal spread and obtain fluid for cytology).
(Any five other than the gold standard.)

B(i) Surgical treatment:
- Aim: cure or palliation, depending on resectability and operability.
- Procedures by tumour location:
 - Lower third: distal or subtotal gastrectomy.
 - Middle third: subtotal or total gastrectomy.
 - Upper third: total or radical gastrectomy.
- Resection margin classification: R0 (no residual tumour), R1, R2, R3.
- Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) criteria: early lesion, tumour less than 2 cm, elevated/polypoid, well-differentiated histology, no lymph node involvement.

(i) The presentation is consistent with a Le Fort fracture. Le Fort classification: Le Fort I — low-level fracture. Le Fort II — pyramidal or subzygomatic fracture. Le Fort III — high-level or suprazygomatic fracture.
(ii) Immediate treatment priorities: Airway — nasopharyngeal airway, endotracheal intubation, tracheostomy. Breathing. Haemorrhage control. Circulation (shock). Soft tissue injuries — within the first 8 hours, using 5/0 and 6/0 sutures. Support of bony fragments. Control of pain. Control of infection. Food and fluids.
(iii) Surgical fixation: Le Fort fractures — haloframes, box frames, transosseous wiring, bone plates. Mandibular fractures — osteosynthesis without IMF: non-compression bone plates, compression bone plates, miniplates, lag screws. Intermaxillary fixation: bonded brackets, dental wiring (direct, eyelets), archbars, capsplints. Osteosynthesis with IMF: transosseous wiring, external pin fixation, bone clamps, transfixation with Kirschner's wires.
(iv) Distinguishing clinical features: Zygomatic complex fractures — flattening of the cheek, circumorbital ecchymosis, subconjunctival ecchymosis, epistaxis, diplopia, gagging of occlusion. Le Fort fractures — gross oedema of soft tissues, bilateral circumorbital ecchymosis, chemosis, diplopia, deformity of nose and epistaxis, mobility of jaws, gagging of occlusion, CSF rhinorrhoea, difficulty in opening the mouth. The hallmark features distinguishing Le Fort from zygomatic injuries include: bilateral circumorbital involvement, CSF rhinorrhoea, and mobility of the entire mid-face — which indicate Le Fort rather than zygomatic complex fractures.
questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents to the emergency room following a road traffic accident with facial swelling, bilateral circumorbital ecchymosis, chemosis, bilateral epistaxis, CSF rhinorrhoea, and mobility of the upper jaw.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and how are Le Fort fractures classified?
(ii) What are the immediate treatment priorities in maxillofacial trauma?
(iii) Describe the surgical fixation methods used for Le Fort fractures and mandibular fractures.
(iv) What are the features that distinguish zygomatic complex fractures from Le Fort fractures clinically?

A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the prostate gland — its location, shape, zonal architecture, and embryological note on lobes — and explain why carcinoma of the prostate is commoner in men after age 50 and rarer before age 50, citing the risk factor evidence provided.
A(ii) State the normal PSA value, describe the routes and preferred method of prostatic biopsy, and distinguish the DRE findings of carcinoma from benign disease.
B(i) Describe the routes and specific sites of local, lymphatic, and haematogenous spread of carcinoma of the prostate, and explain how lymphatic spread to perineural lymphatics causes pain and how iliac nodal involvement causes lower limb oedema.
B(ii) Distinguish watchful waiting/active surveillance from radical prostatectomy and from hormonal therapy (androgen deprivation therapy), explaining the mechanism of each hormonal agent listed.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Anatomy: prostate is located in the lower part of the abdomen, behind the pubic bone, below the urinary bladder. Shape: compressed inverted cone. Zones: peripheral, central, peri-urethral (preprostatic tissue), anterior. Lobes exist only in the embryo — five lobes: two lateral, posterior, median, and anterior. Function: unknown; the fluid has electrolytes and other substances contributing to sperm fluid. Cancer arises from the peripheral zone.
Risk factors by age: age >50 is the strongest risk factor; rare before 50 but there is a steady rise after this age; latent form found in 30% of men >50 years and 60–80% of men >80 years. Post-mortem studies show 14% of males over 50 and 80% of those over 70 have the disease. 9% of prostate cancers have a hereditary basis; 3-fold increase in men whose first-degree relatives have the disease. In the US, 40% lifetime risk of developing prostate cancer, 15% risk of developing symptoms, and 3% risk of dying.

A(ii) Normal PSA: 0–4 ng/ml. Biopsy routes: transrectal using Trucut needle; transperineal using Trucut needle; transurethral using resectoscope. Preferred method: transrectal ultrasound-guided (TRUS) biopsy. DRE findings of carcinoma: asymmetry of gland; hard or woody consistency; nodule or induration; immobile mucosa; obliterated median sulcus; palpable seminal vesicle; blood on gloved finger; indistinguishable edges.

B(i) Local spread: to urethra, ureter, bladder, seminal vesicle, distal sphincter, rectum, and pelvic cellular tissue. Lymphatic spread: internal and external iliac nodes, para-aortic, mediastinal, inguinal nodes; perineural lymphatics — involvement causes pain; iliac nodal involvement may cause lower limb oedema from lymphatic obstruction and anuria from ureteric compression. Haematogenous spread: bones (vertebrae, femur, ribs, skull, sternum); spinal cord; liver, lungs, brain; skin; palate.

B(ii) Watchful waiting/active surveillance: no immediate intervention; patient monitored with DRE, PSA, and observation for symptoms; appropriate for low-risk localised disease. Radical prostatectomy: surgical removal of the prostate for localised disease. Hormonal therapy (androgen deprivation therapy) mechanisms: oestrogens (diethylstilboestrol, phosphorylated DES) — now outdated; orchidectomy — surgical castration, removes primary source of androgens; LHRH analogues (goserelin/zoladex, buserelin) — suppress LH release, reducing testosterone; anti-androgens (flutamide, bicalutamide, nilutamide) — block androgen receptors; combinations — total androgen blockade.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old woman is involved in a deceleration road traffic accident. She was wearing a seatbelt. She complains of diffuse lower abdominal pain and inability to void since the accident. On examination there is lower abdominal tenderness and guarding. Catheterisation yields minimal bloody urine. A cystogram with post-evacuation film is performed.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis, classify the type of bladder rupture most consistent with this mechanism, and give the embryological/anatomical basis for why the dome of the bladder is most vulnerable.
(ii) List all risk factors for and clinical features of the specific type of rupture in this patient, including the history elements that must be sought.
(iii) Outline the resuscitation steps and definitive management, specifying the timing of surgical exploration and the non-operative alternative.
(iv) State the definitive investigation findings on cystogram and describe the differential diagnoses of haematuria and inability to void following abdominal trauma.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: intraperitoneal rupture of the urinary bladder. Mechanism consistent: deceleration injury with seatbelt (compressive force applied to a full bladder). Anatomical basis: the dome (superior aspect) of the bladder is the only part covered by peritoneum; it is also the thinnest part and the most distensible; a sudden compressive force on a full bladder causes the intravesical pressure to rise sharply, and the dome, being the weakest point and peritonealised, ruptures into the peritoneal cavity.

(ii) Risk factors and clinical features of intraperitoneal rupture:
History: blunt force to a full bladder (RTA, fall from height); fractured pelvis; deceleration injury; lack of sensation of bladder fullness; haematuria; inability to void; diffuse lower abdominal tenderness.
Mechanism: the full bladder rises out of the pelvis into the abdomen where it is exposed to deceleration forces; the seatbelt compresses the full bladder against the spine.

(iii) Resuscitation:
- Adequate airways and ventilation.
- Vascular access and volume replacement.
- Control of bleeding.
- Catheter urine drainage.
- Nasogastric drainage.
Definitive management:
- Intraperitoneal rupture: surgical exploration within 48 hours — laparotomy, closure of the dome tear in layers, peritoneal lavage, urinary drainage.
- Extraperitoneal rupture (for completeness): catheterize and continuous drainage of urine.

(iv) Cystogram findings:
- Intraperitoneal rupture: extravasation of contrast into the peritoneal cavity, outlining loops of bowel and paracolic gutters; post-evacuation film shows retained contrast in the peritoneal space.
- Extraperitoneal rupture: flame-shaped extravasation of contrast in the perivesical space, remaining below the peritoneal reflection; does not outline bowel loops.
Differential diagnoses of haematuria and inability to void after abdominal trauma:
- Intraperitoneal bladder rupture (this patient).
- Extraperitoneal bladder rupture — associated with fractured pelvis.
- Posterior urethral rupture — blood at meatus, high-riding prostate, fractured pelvis.
- Anterior urethral injury — perineal trauma, perineal/scrotal swelling.
- Renal injury — flank bruising, flank mass.
- Ureteric injury — rare, penetrating missiles.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old child known to have homozygous HbSS presents with severe pain over the right femur, fever, tenderness over the diaphysis, and elevated WBC and ESR. Blood culture is sent.

(i) State the two diagnoses that must be distinguished and explain why this distinction matters clinically.
(ii) Describe the radiological and nuclear medicine findings that help differentiate bone infarction from bone infection in this patient.
(iii) State the organisms most likely responsible for infection in this subset of patients, ranking them in order of frequency, and explain the pathophysiological basis for why this patient is particularly susceptible to infection.
(iv) Outline the management of each condition — bone infarction and acute haematogenous osteomyelitis — in full.
questions.answerText:
(i) The two conditions are acute bone infarction (vaso-occlusive crisis) and acute haematogenous osteomyelitis. The distinction matters because management is entirely different: infarction is treated with rehydration, analgesia and rest, while osteomyelitis requires high-dose, long-term combination antibiotics, possible core decompression, and surgical intervention if abscesses develop; failure to distinguish risks inappropriate treatment and potentially fatal outcomes.
(ii) Infarction: usually diaphyseal; negative blood culture; plain radiographs inconclusive; photodeficient (cold) Technetium-99m sulphur colloid scan; quantitation of bacteria DNA by PCR — low yield. Infection: usually metaphyseal (though diaphyseal in sickle cell patients); positive culture possible; plain radiographs inconclusive; increased uptake with Technetium-99m MDP (hot scan); quantitation of bacteria DNA by PCR — high yield. MRI shows persistent foci of fat signal, persistent foci of fat signal in soft tissue, and replacement of marrow fat with fluid.
(iii) In sickle cell patients: Staphylococcus aureus — commonest (60–65%); Salmonella species — accounts for 25%. Basis of susceptibility: early loss of splenic function (functional asplenia); reduction in IgM; defective alternate complement pathway; deficiency in phagocytosis-promoting peptide.
(iv) Acute bone infarction: rehydrate; analgesics; rest the limb; residues of infarcted bone islands managed conservatively. Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis: high-dose, long-term, combination antibiotics; core decompression; management of pyaemic abscesses; address localised pathological fracture; manage bone destruction that may need amputation; prevention of/management of chronic osteomyelitis.

A(i) Sickle cell anaemia is caused by two defective genes. Point mutation: substitution of a single DNA nucleotide base. GUG (Valine) replaces GAG (Glutamic acid). The substitution is at position 6 from the N-terminal end of the beta-chain.
A(ii) Pathophysiological sequence: deoxy-HbS undergoes polymerisation → adhesion of sickled RBCs to vascular endothelium → trapping of sickled RBCs leads to intravascular haemolysis → vascular slugging/stagnation → increased blood viscosity → microcirculatory obstruction → tissue infarction and crises.
B(i) Haematological crises — sudden exaggeration of anaemia with precipitous fall in Hb: (1) aplastic — arrest of erythropoiesis; (2) splenic sequestration; (3) haemolytic — acceleration of haemolysis; (4) megaloblastic — arrest of erythropoiesis. Vaso-occlusive crises — usually preceded by infection; obstruction of microcirculation: (1) hand and foot syndrome; (2) bone pain; (3) abdominal; (4) CNS; (5) pulmonary. Infectious crises: major presenting manifestation of SCA in early childhood; susceptibility due to early loss of splenic function, reduction in IgM, defective alternate pathway, deficiency in phagocytosis-promoting peptide.
B(ii) Bone aspirate for M/C/S: 90% positive; site chosen over the point of maximal tenderness over palpable bone. The anatomical basis for diaphyseal rather than metaphyseal involvement in sickle cell patients: in non-sickle cell children, the hairpin capillary arrangement in the metaphysis slows blood flow allowing organisms to settle; in sickle cell patients, the vaso-occlusive process preferentially affects the diaphyseal vessels, causing infarction and creating a nidus for infection at the diaphysis rather than the metaphysis.
questions.question:
Regarding sickle cell disease and its musculoskeletal manifestations:

A(i) Describe the genetic basis of sickle cell anaemia, including the specific mutation, the amino acid substitution, and its position on the beta-chain.
A(ii) Describe the pathophysiological sequence that results from the genetic defect, from polymerisation of deoxy-HbS through to vascular occlusion and clinical crises.
B(i) Classify all the crises of sickle cell anaemia under haematological and vaso-occlusive types, listing the subtypes and the organ systems affected by vaso-occlusive crises.
B(ii) Explain the safe site for bone aspiration in a sickle cell patient with suspected osteomyelitis and the anatomical basis for why the diaphysis is more commonly infected in this population compared with the metaphysis in non-sickle cell children.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Recipient anatomy: incision — Gibson incision (extraperitoneal); approach — extraperitoneal (avoiding the peritoneal cavity). Structures anastomosed: renal vein to external iliac vein (RV-EIV); renal artery to internal iliac artery or external iliac artery (RA-IIA/EIA). Urinary reconstruction: ureteroneocystostomy. The kidney is placed in the iliac fossa because: the external and internal iliac vessels are accessible superficially; the iliac fossa provides a well-vascularised extraperitoneal bed; the transplant ureter is short and easily reimplanted into the bladder; reoperation in the event of complications is facilitated; the normal retroperitoneal position is occupied by the native (failed) kidney which may not have been removed.

A(ii) Exclusion criteria for recipient: active malignancy; sepsis; active TB; severe vasculitis; significant vascular disease; AIDS; active hepatitis; recent MI; active SLE; impaired mental function; extreme age (<1 year or >70 years). Age range for transplantation: 1 to 70 years.
Indications for pretransplant nephrectomy: uncontrolled hypertension; renal infection; renal calculi; upper tract obstruction; severe ureteral reflux; renal malignancy. For PCKD: massive kidney size (which would prevent placement of the transplant) or persistent infection.

B(i) Living-related kidney donor (LRKD) evaluation: (a) mixed lymphocyte culture; (b) CT angiography of renal artery, renal vein, IVC, and aorta; (c) routine investigations as in recipient.
Inclusion criteria: age 18–65 years; two normally functioning kidneys; donor willingness.
Surgical approaches for donor nephrectomy: laparoscopic with or without hand-assist (HADN); open donor nephrectomy.

B(ii) Acute graft rejection vs. chronic rejection:
Acute: occurs within 6 months; usually reversible; mechanism — direct and indirect pathways; CD8+ T cells release cytotoxic substances from granules; CD4+ T cells bind donor MHC allopeptides presented by APC, recruiting B cells causing complement-mediated lysis; pathology — mononuclear cell infiltration.
Chronic: occurs >6 months; leads to graft failure; mechanism — myointimal proliferation in graft arteries causing ischaemia and fibrosis; pathology — progressive vascular fibrosis; not reversible.
Hyperacute: occurs immediately; due to pre-formed ABO or anti-HLA antibodies; intravascular thrombosis; irreversible.
Preferred immunosuppressive regimen: triple regimen — calcineurin-based agent (cyclosporin or tacrolimus), steroids (GCC), and antiproliferative agent (azathioprine or MMF). Immunosuppression is highest in the first 3 months, then continued indefinitely.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the kidney relevant to transplantation — the recipient incision, the extraperitoneal approach, the structures anastomosed, and the urinary tract reconstruction — and explain why the kidney is placed in the iliac fossa rather than the normal retroperitoneal position.
A(ii) Describe the exclusion criteria for the renal transplant recipient and the pre-transplant conditions that require the recipient's own kidney to be removed (pretransplant nephrectomy), stating the specific indication for nephrectomy in polycystic kidney disease.
B(i) Describe all the investigations required for evaluation of a living-related kidney donor, specifying the inclusion criteria that must be satisfied and the surgical approaches available for donor nephrectomy.
B(ii) Explain how acute graft rejection differs from chronic rejection on all criteria given — timing, mechanism, cellular events, pathological finding, and reversibility — and state the preferred immunosuppressive regimen and when it is most intense.

A 7-year-old boy presents with a 3-week history of left-sided abdominal distension and vague abdominal pain. On examination there is a firm, non-tender left abdominal mass that does not move with respiration. Urinalysis shows microscopic haematuria. His blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg.
(i) What are the two most common causes of intra-abdominal solid tumours in childhood, and which is this most likely to be?
(ii) What is the pathological origin of neuroblastoma, where along the body does it arise, and what is its clinical spectrum?
(iii) What investigations are needed to work up a suspected abdominal neuroblastoma?
(iv) Describe the treatment of neuroblastoma including inductive therapy, myeloablative therapy and maintenance therapy.
(v) What factors determine prognosis in neuroblastoma?
questions.answerText:
(i) Common childhood intra-abdominal solid tumours: Wilms' tumour (nephroblastoma) and neuroblastoma. Neuroblastoma is the most common solid tumour in childhood and the most common extra-cranial solid tumour of infancy, with >50% seen in infants less than 1 year old. Given this child's age (7 years), left-sided mass and hypertension, neuroblastoma is a leading possibility; however, Wilms' tumour (peak age 4 years, 75% under 5 years) is also possible.
(ii) Pathological origin: neuroblastoma is derived from sympathogonia (neural crest) cells. It appears anywhere along the sympathetic chain and adrenal medulla. Clinical spectrum: ranges from neuroblastoma to ganglioneuroblastoma to ganglioneuroma.
(iii) Investigations: full blood count, abdominal ultrasound scan, lymph node biopsy, bone marrow aspiration/biopsy, lumbar puncture, CT scan, PET scan, and bone scan.
(iv) Treatment: multimodal approach — consists of inductive therapy and myeloablative therapy. Inductive therapy goals: induce tumour remission; decrease tumour growth; improve tumour resectability if possible; clearing of bone marrow of tumour cells allowing safer harvesting of cells for autologous transplantation; response rates vary from 60–90%. Myeloablative therapy: destroys any remaining tumour cells that survived; now recommended for all high-risk patients except those undergoing specialised protocols. Maintenance therapy: induces neuroblastoma cells to differentiate into benign cells; give 13-cis-retinoic acid for 6 months post chemotherapy. Interleukin-2 promotes immunoreactivity and cancer regression.
(v) Prognostic factors: age; stage of the disease at diagnosis; site of primary tumour; biological features — N-myc, DNA ploidy, and tyrosine kinase receptor.

(i) Fat embolism. Pathogenesis: fat released into circulation from the fracture site gets deposited at the lungs, resulting in respiratory insufficiency. Occurs in: multiple long bone fractures; intramedullary nailing.
(ii) Clinical diagnostic workup: 98% manifest within 48 hours; 100% within 72 hours; within 12 hours, 25% show symptoms. Specific findings: ABG — severe hypoxia (PO2 < 60 mmHg) and hypercapnia (PCO2 very high); ECG — right ventricular strain; examination of clotted blood — fat globules seen; urine — fat globules present; clinical: petechial haemorrhages seen in light-skinned people at front and back; deterioration in cerebral function; restlessness, incoherence, disorientation, tachycardia, tachypnoea.
(iii) Treatment: transfer to Intensive Care Unit or High Dependence Unit (HDU); correct anaemia; assisted ventilation; heparinisation (to cause lipolysis); fluid resuscitation; Dextran (to improve capillary flow); Clofibrate (to reduce plasma lipids).
(iv) Prevention: gentle fracture manipulation; early stabilization of fractures. Differential diagnoses: adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS); pulmonary thromboembolism.
questions.question:
A 28-year-old man sustains multiple long bone fractures in a road traffic accident. On day 2, he becomes restless, incoherent, tachycardic, and tachypnoeic. A petechial rash is noted over his chest and back.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis and outline the pathogenesis of this condition.
(ii) Describe the full diagnostic workup including the specific findings on ABG, ECG, blood, and urine.
(iii) Outline all treatment measures and indicate the setting in which treatment must be administered.
