Regarding the synovial joint as an organ and its relevance to osteoarthritis:

A(i) Describe the constituent structures of a synovial joint using the knee as the model, stating what makes the articular cartilage unique among joint structures.
A(ii) Explain the pathological features of osteoarthritis as recognised by the clinician, the pathologist/radiologist, the bioengineer, and the biochemist.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for why osteoarthritis is commoner with advancing age, in females, and in certain occupations.
B(ii) Distinguish between primary and secondary osteoarthritis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Constituents: (1) articulating bone ends covered with articular cartilage; (2) subchondral bone supporting the articular cartilage; (3) synovium lining the joint capsule; (4) supporting ligaments (both intra- and extra-articular); (5) surrounding muscles and tendinous attachments. The articular cartilage is unique because it has no blood vessel in it — unlike all other joint constituents — making it unable to repair once damaged (William Hunter, 1743). It is smooth, almost frictionless, and acts as load transmitter and shock absorber.
A(ii) Clinician: joint pain, joint tenderness, joint crepitus, limitation of movement. Pathologist/radiologist: articular cartilage loss, synovitis, debris/loose bodies, osteophytes. Bioengineer: altered tensile strength, altered compressive stiffness, altered shear compressive stiffness, increased cartilage permeability, marked subchondral bone stiffness. Biochemist: reduced proteoglycan (PG) concentration, altered aggregation of PG, altered matrix molecule homeostasis, altered collagen fibre size and weave, accentuated articular cartilage turnover.
B(i) Age: articular cartilage degenerative changes increase with age, visible from the 3rd decade in autopsy specimens. Female: anatomical build and fat distribution contribute, especially to knee OA; sitting posture and habits of market women propagate it. Occupation: patello-femoral joint loaded at various positions; prolonged kneeling, elite athletes, footballers, and farmers are prone.
B(ii) Primary (idiopathic) OA has no identifiable antecedent cause. Secondary OA follows antecedent joint disease — trauma, previous infection, mal-alignment, acetabular dysplasia, Perthes disease, slipped epiphysis, ligament or meniscal damage.

(i) Chronic osteomyelitis. Aetiological factors: post-traumatic and post-operative — commonest (as in this patient following road traffic accident and open fracture); sequel to acute osteomyelitis; chronic osteomyelitis of insidious onset by low-virulence organism (e.g. Staphylococcus albus — Brodie's abscess).
(ii) Clinical features: history of trauma, surgery, or previous acute osteomyelitis; pain — occurs when sinus is blocked; localised swelling; discharge — occurs later; single or multiple sinuses; skin hyperpigmentation. Radiological signs: generalised sclerosis (loss of corticomedullary differentiation); bone-in-bone appearance; irregular bone expansion; sequestrum and cloaca.
(iii) Investigations: FBC — no anaemia (except during acute flare-up); ESR — normal (except during acute flare-up); wound swab — commonest organism is Staphylococcus aureus; polymicrobial infection is uncommon. X-ray findings as above; bone scan if required.
(iv) Belfast procedure (2-stage): Stage 1 — excision of all non-viable tissue until bleeding tissue reached; excise dead bone to bleeding bone; raise flap or use bone cement as filler with antibiotics; insert drainage tube. Stage 2 — done after 6 weeks; remove bone cement; fill defect with bone graft (usually from iliac crest). Papineau technique (3–4 stages): excise all dead bone; excise all non-viable tissue; use more grafting material instead of bone cement; wound granulates then is grafted in subsequent stages. Distant complications if inadequately treated: metastatic infections — empyema thoracis; pyopericardium; lung abscess; suppurative arthritis (especially hip and knee); altered bone length.
questions.question:
A 30-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of a discharging sinus over his right tibia following a road traffic accident and open fracture treated elsewhere. The sinus discharges intermittently and is associated with localised swelling and pain when the sinus is blocked. X-ray shows generalised sclerosis and a sequestrum.

(i) State the diagnosis and outline all the aetiological factors for this condition.
(ii) Describe the full clinical features and all radiological signs.
(iii) Outline the investigations required, the most common organism on wound swab, and why polymicrobial infection is uncommon.
(iv) Describe the Belfast procedure and the Papineau technique in full, and state what distant complications this patient may develop if the condition is not adequately treated.

questions.answerText:
(i) Nosocomial infections: infections acquired within the hospital environment (not present or incubating at the time of admission). Modes of transmission (cross-infection): direct contact; theatre air; instruments; patients; staff; air; dressings; beddings; urinals; bedpans; introduction of organisms in the operating theatre.
(ii) Classification of surgical wound contamination:
- Clean: no endogenous contamination.
- Clean contaminated: entry into a viscus that does not usually contain bacteria.
- Contaminated: entry into a viscus which usually contains bacteria (e.g. colon).
- Dirty: wound is exposed to pus or visceral contents known to be infective.
(iii) Determinants of surgical wound infection:
- Microbial: concentration; virulence.
- Injury to tissue: trauma to tissue.
- Foreign material in wound.
- Resistance to antibiotics.
- Host factors (general and local): general and local host community resistance; perioperative antibiotics.
(iv) Principles of antibiotic use:
- Why: prophylactic (to prevent infection) or therapeutic (to treat established infection); antibiotics are adjunct therapy, not a substitute for indicated surgical treatment.
- When: timing relative to surgery (avoid masking of clinical features); immediately before/during operation; effective in early cellulitic and hyperaemic stage of infection.
- Which: spectrum must cover likely contaminating organisms from the viscus being cut into; parenteral or enteral route as appropriate. Precautions: drug interaction; impaired metabolism (liver/renal disease); PAE (post-antibiotic effect — aminoglycosides); side/toxic effects.
(v) Site-specific organisms:
- Cardiac/non-cardiac vascular: Staphylococcus aureus.
- Colorectal: enteric aerobes and anaerobes.
- Appendicectomy: enteric aerobes and anaerobes.
- C-section/hysterectomy: enteric aerobes and anaerobes; E. faecalis; Group B Streptococcus.
questions.question:
Describe the clinical features, diagnosis, and management of nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infections under the following headings:
(i) Define nosocomial infections and their modes of transmission (modes of cross-infection) in the hospital environment.
(ii) Classify surgical wound contamination, listing all four wound classes with their definitions.
(iii) Determinants of surgical wound infection: enumerate the microbial, injury-related, and host factors.
(iv) Principles governing the use of prophylactic and therapeutic antibiotics in surgical practice (why, when, and which antibiotic to use).
(v) Site-specific predominant organisms for cardiac, colorectal, appendicectomy, and gynaecological (C-section/hysterectomy) operations.

questions.answerText:
(i) The risk of HIV transmission per needle-stick injury is 1 in 300. Factors that increase risk in this scenario: deep injury; visible blood on the injuring device; hollow needle; high viral load of the source patient.

(ii) Post-exposure prophylaxis protocol: wash with flowing water immediately; test both patient and surgeon; start two or three drug combination antiretroviral therapy; 4-week regimen; serology monitoring at 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, and 1 year.

(iii) Hepatitis B serological markers:
(a) Active HBV infection: HBsAg (hepatitis surface antigen) = hepatitis infection present.
(b) Immunity: Anti-HBs = immunity.
(c) Previous exposure: Anti-HBc = exposure; IgM anti-HBc = last 3–6 months. HBeAg or anti-HBe = viral replication (all body fluids infectious); quantitative HBV-DNA testing is most accurate for viral load and infectivity.

(iv) Hepatitis D is a single-stranded virus that requires HBV to infect and replicate in humans; diagnosis: anti-HDV positive plus HBV infection = diagnosis. Hepatitis C: single-stranded; anti-HCV positive plus viral exposure plus elevated liver enzymes = diagnosis; sequelae risk is higher at 70%.
questions.question:
A surgeon sustains a needle-stick injury during suturing while operating on an HIV-positive patient with a viral load described as high. Blood is visible on the hollow needle.

(i) What is the risk of HIV transmission per needle-stick injury to a surgeon, and what factors in this scenario increase the risk?
(ii) Describe the post-exposure prophylaxis protocol for this surgeon step by step.
(iii) Regarding hepatitis B, describe the serological markers that indicate: (a) active HBV infection, (b) immunity, and (c) previous exposure.
(iv) Which hepatitis virus requires HBV for replication, and how is it diagnosed? State the sequelae risk for hepatitis C.

A(i) Define diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL), state the type of patient it is most useful for, and list five indications for its use.
A(ii) State the criteria that make a DPL result positive, listing all the relevant findings.
B(i) Compare DPL with FAST (Focused Assessment Sonography for Trauma) under the headings: what each looks for, the four recesses examined by FAST, and the relative advantage of each method in the setting of abdominal trauma.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition, patient type, and indications:
- DPL is a rapid and accurate test used to identify intra-abdominal injuries after blunt trauma in the hypotensive or unresponsive patient without obvious indication for abdominal exploration.
- Indications:
 1. Change in sensorium: spinal cord injury, head injury.
 2. Injury to adjacent structures.
 3. Equivocal physical examination.
 4. Prolonged loss of contact with the patient.
 5. Lap-belt sign: suspect bowel injury.
 6. No other choice.
(Any five of the above.)

A(ii) Criteria for a positive DPL:
- Aspiration of blood.
- Gastrointestinal contents.
- Bile.
- Gram's stain with bacteria.
- Red blood cells ≥ 100,000 per mm³.
- White blood cells ≥ 500 per mm³.
- Amylase value greater than 175 IU/dL.

B(i) Comparison of DPL vs FAST:
- DPL identifies intra-abdominal injuries by laboratory analysis of lavage fluid; FAST uses ultrasound to look for evidence of free fluid.
- FAST examines four recesses: Morrison's pouch, the pelvis, the left subhepatic space, and the pericardial sac.
- Relative advantage of DPL: highly accurate and quantifiable for identifying haemorrhage; useful when ultrasound is not available or inconclusive.
- Relative advantage of FAST: non-invasive, rapid, bedside procedure that can be performed without interrupting resuscitation; preferable as the first-line modality in the unstable trauma patient.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old girl with known nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumour) presents with acute onset of abdominal pain, rapid abdominal enlargement, anaemia and fever. Her CT scan shows a large right renal mass with evidence of subcapsular haemorrhage.
(i) What has occurred, and what is the staging implication of this event?
(ii) What are the histological types of Wilms' tumour and their respective prognoses?
(iii) What are the challenges in management of Wilms' tumour in developing countries?
(iv) Describe the treatment of bilateral Wilms' tumour (Stage V disease).
(v) What nephrogenic rests are and what is their relationship to Wilms' tumour?
questions.answerText:
(i) Tumour rupture has occurred, constituting acute presentation. This places the tumour at Stage III — tumour extends beyond the capsule with incomplete excision. Evidence: acute abdominal pain, rapidly enlarging abdominal mass, subcapsular haemorrhage, anaemia, and fever are all listed as features of acute presentation (tumour rupture).
(ii) Histological types: Favourable histology (FH); Unfavourable histology — anaplastic (focal or diffuse); Congenital mesoblastic nephroma (CMN) — low-grade spindle-shaped tumours seen under 1 year, rarely metastasise; Clear Cell Sarcoma of the kidney (CCSK) — bone-metastasising tumour; Malignant Rhabdoid tumour — rare with high mortality rate of 90%.
(iii) Challenges: time of presentation; unresectable tumours; socio-economic factors; paucity of epidemiological and multicentre studies; imaging techniques and drug availability; intracaval and atrial extensions; treatment compliance and follow-up.
(iv) Bilateral Wilms' tumour (Stage V): surgical management is controversial. Options: bilateral nephrectomy with renal transplantation; ex vivo tumour excision with auto-transplantation; preoperative chemotherapy with surgery — assess response after 5 weeks using CT and check for cytoreduction.
(v) Nephrogenic rests: pathological precursor — primitive blastema/metanephric tissue/nephrogenic rest. Found in 30–40% of patients with WT. Incidence of nephrogenic rests is 100 times greater than that of WT. Majority resolve spontaneously. Nephroblastomatosis — multiple or diffuse nephrogenic rests. Growth phases: incipient/dormant (few well-formed tubular structures, no proliferation, no mitoses); hyperplastic (epithelial elements with nodular expansive growth); sclerosing (stromal and epithelial elements with few blastemal nephrogenic elements).

questions.question:
A 40-year-old builder is extracted after being trapped under rubble for several hours. He passes dark coca-coloured urine. Investigations show acute renal impairment.

(i) State the diagnosis and the pathophysiological mechanism causing acute renal failure in this patient.
(ii) What initial clinical signs and monitoring parameters should be established on admission for a trauma patient with this presentation?
(iii) Outline the complete treatment protocol for this condition.
(iv) What other general complications of fractures and trauma does this patient remain at risk of, and which of these is caused by the release of thromboplastin rather than by prolonged bed rest?
questions.answerText:
(i) Crush syndrome. Mechanism: crush injuries cause the release of myoglobin; myoglobin precipitates in the kidneys as crystals, resulting in acute renal failure; the passage of coca-coloured (dark) urine is characteristic.
(ii) Monitoring parameters on admission: set intravenous line with wide bore cannula (16G or 14G — white) in the antecubital vein; withdraw 20 mls of blood for blood group and crossmatch, electrolytes and urea; monitor pulse, blood pressure, urine output (adult: 3–5/50 ml/hour; children: 1–2 ml/kg/hour); central venous pressure; pulmonary wedge pressure using Swann-Ganz catheter.
(iii) Treatment: early recognition; give intravenous fluids using Ringer's lactate; alkalinisation of urine (to prevent myoglobin crystal precipitation); adequate fluid intake to maintain urine output; monitor renal function.
(iv) Other general complications: shock (hypovolaemic/haemorrhagic) — bleeding is usually hidden, may lead to acute renal failure; occurs in multiple long bone fracture and pelvic fracture (3–4 L may be lost in pelvic fracture; 1–1.5 L in femoral shaft fracture); deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary thromboembolism — caused by release of thromboplastin stimulating coagulopathy (NOT due to prolonged bed rest); tetanus; fat embolism; delirium tremens (in alcoholics — a withdrawal symptom).

questions.question:
A 72-year-old man presents with low back pain, poor urinary stream, and nocturia for 6 months. On digital rectal examination a hard irregular nodule is felt in the prostate. PSA is markedly elevated. Bone scan shows multiple osteosclerotic lesions in the pelvis and spine.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what are all the predisposing/aetiological factors?
(ii) Describe the histological and staging features of prostatic carcinoma.
(iii) What investigations are required for staging and tissue diagnosis?
(iv) Describe the essential management for localised (T1/T2), locally advanced (T3/T4), and metastatic disease.
(v) What is the prognosis at each stage?
questions.answerText:
(i) Carcinoma of the prostate. Predisposing/aetiological factors: increasing age; more common in negro males; hormonal factors (prostate cancer growth enhanced by testosterone and inhibited by oestrogens or antiandrogens); cadmium exposure.
(ii) Pathology and staging:
- Histology: adenocarcinoma arising from glandular epithelium; Gleason grading (1–5) used for differentiation. Tumours often multicentric, located in the periphery of the gland.
- Staging: T0 (unsuspected); T1 (histological diagnosis only — clinical and radiology negative); T2 (palpable, confined within prostate); T3 (spread to seminal vesicles); T4 (spread to pelvic wall); T1–4, M1 (metastatic disease).
- Spread: direct into remainder of gland and seminal vesicles; lymphatic to iliac and periaortic nodes; haematogenous to bone (usually osteosclerotic lesions), liver, lung.
(iii) Investigations:
- FBC: anaemia.
- U+E, creatinine: renal function.
- Specific markers: PSA, alkaline and acid phosphatase.
- Transrectal ultrasound and MRI: local staging.
- Needle biopsy of the prostate: tissue diagnosis.
- Bone scan: metastases.
(iv) Management:
- T0: observation, repeated digital (or ultrasound) examination and PSA.
- T1+2: radical prostatectomy or radical radiotherapy; or interstitial radiation with ¹²⁵I or ¹⁹⁸Au.
- T3+4: external beam radiation ± hormonal therapy.
- Metastatic: hormonal manipulation; bilateral orchidectomy; stilboestrol; LH-RH agonists; antiandrogens (cyproterone acetate); radiotherapy and strontium for bony metastases.
(v) Prognosis:
- Localised tumours: 80% 5-year survival.
- Local spread: 40% 5-year survival.
- Metastases: 20% 5-year survival.

questions.question:
(A) Describe ischaemic vascular disorder under the following headings:
(i) Definition and aetiology — including the three main categories of causation
(ii) Classification into partial and complete obstruction with the features of each
(iii) Clinical features — both symptoms and signs including special vascular tests

(B) State the investigations used in ischaemic vascular disorder, including the formula for Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) and the significance of the critical level.

(C) Describe the treatment of ischaemic vascular disorder, listing all the options under restoration of blood flow and control of comorbid factors.
questions.answerText:
(A)(i) Ischaemic vascular disorder is a condition caused by impaired blood supply to the tissues that is enough to cause lack of oxygen and nutrient to the tissues for vital function. Aetiology: (1) Pressure from without — iatrogenic ligation of the main artery, tight tourniquet, bandage, and POP (plaster of Paris); (2) Occlusion from within — the lumen obstructed by embolism (80%), thrombosis (20%), atherosclerosis, Buerger's disease (thrombo-angiitis obliterans), or aneurysm; (3) Vascular disorders — vasoconstriction of the wall as in Raynaud's disease, traumatic arterial spasm, and ergot poisoning.

(A)(ii) Partial obstruction leads to chronic ischaemia characterised by loss of skin hair (which appears glossy and pits), atrophy of muscles, and osteoporosis. Complete occlusion leads to acute ischaemia characterised by severe pain, cold and dusky limb, and gangrene.

(A)(iii) Symptoms: predisposing factor (arterial injury or heart disease); pain; paralysis and sensation loss; progressive loss of temperature; pulselessness; claudication (pain in the limbs on walking or exercise). Signs: colour of limb is pale; cold; Buerger's test — elevation of affected limb causes blanching and cyanosis and the angle to the horizontal is Buerger's angle; Allen test — patient self-exsanguinates limb by making a fist then ulnar and radial arteries are occluded, then one is released at a time to demonstrate its occlusion or patency; bruit or murmur if aneurysm present.

(B) Specific investigations: X-ray (may show calcification of vessels); angiography (demonstrates obstructed vessel); magnetic resonant angiography (demonstrates vascular pathology and obstruction); Doppler ultrasound (demonstrates flow in vessels and obstruction). ABI = mean arterial pressure of arm ÷ mean arterial pressure of calf = 0.8–1 (normal); critical level is 0.45 (limb survival <50%). MAP = (2DBP + SBP) × 1/3. Non-specific: haematocrit; FBS; cholesterol assay; ECG; chest X-ray; renal function test.

(C) Restoration of blood flow: repair of injured artery; removal of occlusion within (thrombus) — thrombectomy; removal of occlusion from without (ligature or tumour); arterioplasty to widen the artery; bypass surgery to bypass obstruction. Control of comorbid factors: control of diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolaemia and hypertension; stop use of cigarette and alcohol.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old man is brought in following a fall from a height. He has an open (compound) fracture of the right femur with severe deformity and gross bleeding. He is hypotensive.
(i) Define and classify fractures by their shape, degree of comminution, and relationship to the skin and adjacent structures.
(ii) What is the primary concern, and describe the immediate management of this patient including fluid resuscitation.
(iii) List the early complications of fractures generally, and local complications of long bone fractures.
(iv) What are the late complications of fractures?
(v) How does compartment syndrome develop after a fracture, and how is it prevented?
questions.answerText:
(i) Definitions and classification:
- A fracture: a break in the continuity of a bone.
- Transverse, oblique, or spiral by shape.
- Greenstick: only one side is fractured; the other bends (immature bones).
- Comminuted: more than two fragments.
- Complicated: another structure (nerve or blood vessel) is also damaged.
- Compound (open): break in the overlying skin or nearby viscera with potential contamination of bone ends.
- Pathological: through a bone weakened by disease (e.g. metastasis).
(ii) Primary concern: haemorrhagic shock and compound fracture infection risk.
Immediate management:
- Look for shock/haemorrhage and check ABC.
- Relieve pain (opiates IV, nerve blocks, splints, traction).
- Establish good IV access; send blood for group and crossmatch.
- Compound fractures require debridement, antibiotics, and tetanus prophylaxis.
- Always consider multiple injury; always image joints above and below the fracture.
(iii) Early complications:
General: blood loss; infection; fat embolism; DVT and PE; renal failure; compartment syndrome.
Local: vascular injury (division, tear, spasm, thrombosis, aneurysm, AV fistula); nerve damage (palsy/praxia); muscle haematoma; visceral injury.
(iv) Late complications: non-union; delayed union; malunion; growth arrest; arthritis; post-traumatic sympathetic (reflex) dystrophy; avascular necrosis; joint stiffness/early OA.
(v) Compartment syndrome: circumferential burns or tight casts compress tissues; rising pressure within a fascial compartment reduces blood flow → ischaemia → oedema → further pressure rise (a vicious cycle). Prevented by urgent escharotomy for circumferential burns and by avoiding tight casts; treated by fasciotomy.

questions.question:
A(i) Define dysphagia and classify it into its two main types, explaining the mechanism of each.
A(ii) List the causes of pre-oesophageal dysphagia, and list the categories of oesophageal wall diseases that cause oesophageal dysphagia, including at least two examples from each category.
B(i) Distinguish between pulsion and traction oesophageal diverticula, naming a specific example of each type and the anatomical site of formation.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition and classification:
- Dysphagia is a subjective awareness of difficulty in swallowing due to impaired progression of matter from the pharynx to the stomach.
- Pre-oesophageal dysphagia: difficulty emptying the bolus from the oropharynx into the oesophagus.
- Oesophageal dysphagia: difficulty passing the bolus down the oesophagus.

A(ii) Causes:
Pre-oesophageal causes: myasthenia gravis, muscular dystrophy, bulbar poliomyelitis, pseudobulbar palsy, Parkinson's disease.
Oesophageal wall disease categories and examples:
- Tumours: benign (papilloma, adenomas, leiomyoma); malignant (squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma).
- Oesophagitis/stricture: corrosive burns (acids, alkalis); reflux oesophagitis.
- Oesophageal perforation: iatrogenic during endoscopy; penetrating chest trauma; Boerhaave syndrome.
- Neuromuscular dysfunction: achalasia cardia; diffuse oesophageal spasm; connective tissue diseases (scleroderma, SLE, polyarteritis nodosa).

B(i) Pulsion vs traction diverticula:
- Pulsion diverticula: caused by raised intraluminal pressure forcing mucosa through a weak point; example — Zenker's diverticulum, which forms posteriorly at Killian's dehiscence (between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus muscles at the pharyngo-oesophageal junction); also includes epiphrenic diverticulum.
- Traction diverticula: caused by external traction from adjacent inflamed lymph nodes pulling the oesophageal wall outward; example — mid-thoracic diverticulum, located at the mid-thoracic level.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old male with peripheral vascular disease and diabetes presents with a gangrenous right lower limb. After clinical assessment, the surgical team decides on a below-knee amputation.

(i) What is the indication for amputation in this patient, and what general operative principle governs tourniquet use in ischaemic limbs?
(ii) Describe the principles governing level selection, skin flaps, and muscle management during the procedure.
(iii) What post-operative complications may arise, and how should the stump be prepared for prosthetic fitting?
(iv) What is the definitive rehabilitation goal for a below-knee amputee compared with an above-knee amputee?
questions.answerText:
(i) The indication is peripheral vascular disease with diabetes. In ischaemic limbs, tourniquet is contraindicated — it should always be used except in ischaemic limbs.
(ii) Level: no longer critical with modern total contact prosthesis; save as much length as possible consistent with the pathology. Skin flaps must be marked with a marker pen; the skin at the stump end should be sensate and mobile; redundant soft tissue and dog-ears avoided. Muscles divided at least 5 cm distal to intended bone section; myodesis (suture to bone through drilled holes) or myoplasty (suture over aponeurosis) applied — myodesis avoided in ischaemic limbs.
(iii) Complications: haematoma; infection (especially in PVD/diabetes — remove sutures, culture and treat); skin edge necrosis requiring higher re-amputation; neuroma causing pain from scar entrapment; phantom sensation (disappears with regular prosthesis use); bone spikes especially in children. Stump must be ready to accept definitive prosthesis in 4–6 weeks; contractures prevented by exercise and splintage.
(iv) Over 90% of below-knee amputees learn to walk with prosthesis, while less than 60% of above-knee amputees do so. Loss of the knee joint incurs considerable increase in energy expenditure.

questions.question:
Regarding chronic osteomyelitis:

A(i) Describe the aetiology, full clinical features, and radiological findings in chronic osteomyelitis.
A(ii) Describe the Belfast procedure (two-stage) and the Papineau technique (3–4 stage) as methods of treatment, stating what each stage involves.
B(i) Explain how Brodie's abscess differs from chronic osteomyelitis in aetiology, site, clinical presentation, and radiological appearance.
B(ii) State how chronic osteomyelitis may spread to cause distant pathological complications.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Aetiology: post-traumatic and post-operative (commonest); sequel to acute osteomyelitis; chronic osteomyelitis of insidious onset by low-virulence organism (e.g. Staphylococcus albus — Brodie's abscess). Clinical features: history of trauma, surgery, or previous acute osteomyelitis; pain (when sinus is blocked); localised swelling; discharge (later); single or multiple sinuses; skin hyperpigmentation. Radiological findings: generalised sclerosis (loss of corticomedullary differentiation); bone-in-bone appearance; irregular bone expansion; sequestrum and cloaca.
A(ii) Belfast procedure (2-stage): First stage — excision of all non-viable tissue until bleeding tissue reached; excise dead bone to bleeding bone; raise flap or use bone cement as filler with antibiotics introduced; put in drainage tube. Second stage — done after 6 weeks; remove bone cement; fill defect with bone graft (usually from iliac crest). Papineau technique (3–4 stage): excise all dead bone; excise all non-viable tissue; use more grafting material instead of bone cement; wound allowed to granulate then grafted.
B(i) Brodie's abscess: caused by low virulence organism; small lesion located in metaphysis; commonest site is distal metaphysis of tibia; may be asymptomatic for years or present with recurrent attacks of pain; little swelling, tenderness. X-ray: translucent area with well-defined margin and surrounding sclerosis — contrast to chronic osteomyelitis which shows generalised sclerosis, bone-in-bone appearance, sequestrum and cloaca without a well-defined translucent focus.
B(ii) Complications of chronic osteomyelitis that spread to distant structures: metastatic infections causing empyema thoracis, pyopericardium, and lung abscess; suppurative arthritis (especially hip and knee from contiguous spread); altered length of the bone (growth disturbance in children).

questions.question:
A. Describe the anatomy of the PALATE as presented, covering: the division between primary and secondary palate, the bony components of the hard palate, and the muscular and mucosal components of the soft palate.
A(i) Explain the embryological formation of the palate, identifying the structures from which it is derived.
B. Describe the clinical problems associated with cleft palate, covering defects in: suction, dentition, speech, smell, and ear and chest complications, explaining the anatomical basis of each.
B(i) State the preoperative criteria for repair of the secondary cleft palate and name the surgical procedure used.
questions.answerText:
A. The palate is divided by the incisive foramen into the primary palate (the lip, alveolus, and hard palate anterior to the incisive foramen) and the secondary palate (all structures posterior to the incisive foramen).
Hard palate: composed of the palatine processes of the maxilla anteriorly, and the palatine bones posteriorly.
Soft palate: composed of buccal mucosa, nasal mucosa, and muscles — tensor veli palatini, levator veli palatini, and muscularis uvulae.
A(i) The face and jaws are formed by fusion of five facial elements: frontonasal process, two lateral maxillary processes, and two mandibular segments, through mesenchymal migration between 6 and 12 weeks of intrauterine life. The palate is formed by fusion of the palatine shelves of the maxillary process. The primary palate (lip and alveolus) is formed by fusion of the medial nasal processes and the maxillary process.
B. Clinical problems associated with cleft palate:
- Defective suction: negative pressure during sucking requires intact orbicularis oris and intact palate; air escapes through the defect into the nasopharynx, impairing feeding.
- Abnormal dentition: teeth protrude through the defect in the alveolus (dental anarchy).
- Defective speech: difficulty pronouncing consonants (explosive words such as G, D, M, N — the child says 'aaey' instead of 'daddy'); difficulty pronouncing sibilants (e.g., S) and fricatives (e.g., Z).
- Defective smell: constant irritation of nasal mucosa by food from the mouth impairs smell.
- Chest infection: food enters the airway during swallowing (aspiration) causing respiratory tract infections.
- Conjunctivitis: contamination of the conjunctiva with buccal flora via the lacrimal duct which drains into the nasal cavity below the inferior turbinate.
- Ear infection: regurgitation of buccal content via the Eustachian tube in the nasopharynx.
B(i) Repair of the secondary cleft palate is performed at age 6 to 18 months. The surgical procedure used is the Von Langenbeck repair, in which bipedicle mucoperiosteal flaps are raised by longitudinal incisions along the inner aspect of each alveolar arch, based superiorly on the greater palatine vessels, and rotated medially to close the palatal defect.

A(i) Minimally invasive surgery: to achieve therapeutic surgical objectives by the least stimulus so that metabolic, cardio-respiratory and physiological effects are minimal; implies a reduction in peri-operative morbidity. General principles: direct visualisation of peritoneal cavity and its contents achieved by placement of a telescope; peritoneum is a potential space developed with insufflation; video camera attached to telescope permits viewing on a monitor; trocars with sheath (5mm–10mm) introduced under direct vision. Pre-operative: same as for conventional surgery; ability to carry out the conventional open procedure is a must; consent for open procedure; empty stomach, urinary bladder and bowels; DVT prophylaxis.
A(ii) Pneumoperitoneum: Initial access — closed method using Verres (spring-loaded) needle or open method using Hasson's method. Gas: carbon dioxide — inexpensive, non-combustible, soluble, readily available, low risk of embolism. Alternatives: nitric oxide, helium, argon, air (gasless). Pressure: 15 mmHg. Flow rate: 1.5 L/minute.
B(i) Indications: Diagnostic — staging of intra-abdominal tumour, ascites of unknown origin, abdominal pain, liver disease, second-look procedure, diagnostic dilemma. Therapeutic — appendicectomy, cholecystectomy, herniorraphy, fundoplication, adrenalectomy, colectomies, etc. Contraindications: bleeding disorder, peritonitis, anterior abdominal wall sepsis, morbid obesity, intestinal obstruction, adhesions.
B(ii) Effects of pneumoperitoneum: intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH) — effects on kidney, CVS, GIT, and pulmonary systems.
C(i) Patient advantages: less trauma; less catabolism; less metabolic stress; less nitrogen balance; good cosmesis; no ileus; early ambulation; fewer wound complications; less adhesions; early return to activities of daily living. Practitioner advantages: real-time interaction; proper trainee visualisation; reduced bed occupancy rate; faster turnover; recordings for teaching; satisfaction.
C(ii) Disadvantages: high cost/low benefit ratio; capital intensive; completely different technical skill required; no tactile feedback; longer operating time; requires special training; instrument malfunction. Inherent complications: haemorrhage, viscus injury, emphysema, arrhythmias, air embolism and thermal injury.
questions.question:
Describe laparoscopic surgery under the following headings.
A(i) Define minimally invasive surgery and state the general principles of laparoscopic surgery.
A(ii) Describe the method of creating a pneumoperitoneum — access methods, gas used and its properties, pressure and flow rate.
B(i) State the indications and contraindications for laparoscopic surgery.
B(ii) Describe the effects of pneumoperitoneum on organ systems.
C(i) List the advantages for patients and for health practitioners.
C(ii) List the disadvantages of laparoscopic surgery and its inherent complications.

A 70-year-old woman with known osteoporosis is brought to hospital after a fall at home. She is unable to bear weight, has external rotation and shortening of her right lower limb, and is tender over the femoral neck and greater trochanter. Pelvic X-ray confirms an intracapsular femoral neck fracture with complete displacement and rotation of the femoral head.

(i) Classify this fracture using the Garden classification and state what type of fracture this is.
(ii) What are the risk factors for this fracture and what complications arise specifically from intracapsular displacement?
(iii) Describe all management options in the elderly for this specific Garden classification, including the prosthetic choices and the criteria for selecting total hip replacement.
(iv) State the amount of blood loss expected from a femoral shaft fracture and describe the initial resuscitation priorities.
questions.answerText:
(i) Garden Type IV — complete displacement of the fracture with full disruption. This is an intracapsular femoral neck fracture (subcapital or transcervical).
(ii) Risk factors: elderly age; female gender; osteoporosis and osteomalacia; fall at home. In younger patients (<60 years), more common in males and associated with high-energy injury. Complications specific to intracapsular displaced fractures: avascular necrosis of femoral head due to disruption of retinacular blood supply; non-union; leg length discrepancy.
(iii) In elderly patients, Garden III & IV are treated primarily with hemiarthroplasty using a Bipolar, Austin Moore, or Thompson prosthesis. In elderly patients who are fit and active, Total Hip Replacement (THR) may be done for Garden Type III & IV. THR is also done if earlier treatment with screws fails. In adults below 55 years, Garden III & IV are reduced under image intensifier and fixed with screws; if treatment fails, THR is performed.
(iv) In closed femoral shaft fracture, loss of ½ to 1 litre of blood into tissues may occur. Initial resuscitation: set intravenous line with wide bore cannula (16G or 14G — white) in the antecubital vein; before line is set, withdraw 20 mls of blood for blood group and crossmatch, electrolytes and urea; monitor vital signs — pulse, blood pressure, urine output (adult: 3–5/50 ml/hour; children: 1–2 ml/kg/hour); central venous pressure; pulmonary wedge pressure using Swann-Ganz catheter.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the anatomic classification of intracranial haemorrhage, listing all subtypes under each anatomic compartment and including the temporal subtypes of subdural haemorrhage.
A(ii) Describe the aetiologic classification of intracranial haemorrhage, distinguishing the most common from the less common causes.
B(i) Explain the two general mechanisms by which intracranial haemorrhage produces signs and symptoms, naming the specific deficits under each mechanism.
B(ii) Distinguish the clinical presentation of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage from haemorrhage due to a ruptured arteriovenous malformation (AVM), including the classical age groups, characteristic sites of haemorrhage, and the basis for suspecting an AVM.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Anatomic classification:
- Epidural haemorrhage
- Subdural haemorrhage: acute; subacute; chronic
- Subarachnoid haemorrhage
- Intracerebral haemorrhage
- Intraventricular haemorrhage
A(ii) Most common causes: trauma; arteriovenous malformation; aneurysm; hypertensive vasculopathy; coagulopathy.
Less common causes: neoplastic (haemorrhage into malignant tumour); vasculitis; infectious (bacterial or mycotic aneurysm); amyloid angiopathy; venous thrombosis; haemorrhage into infarct.
B(i) Two general mechanisms:
1. Focal deficits related to injury of a specific brain area — e.g., hemiparesis, dysphasia, visual field cut.
2. Global deficits related to elevation of intracranial pressure (ICP) — including: headache, nausea/vomiting; decreased level of consciousness (lethargy–stupor–obtundation–coma); Cushing's reflex (hypertension with bradycardia); changes in respiratory pattern; rostrocaudal motor deterioration (see Glasgow Coma Scale); cerebral herniation, pupillary dilation.
B(ii) Hypertensive ICH: most patients are over 45 years old; history of hypertension; haemorrhage occurs in characteristic areas — basal ganglia/internal capsule (60%), deep cerebellar nuclei (10–15%), pons (10%), thalamus (10%); angiography not necessary if all features are classical.
Ruptured AVM: haemorrhages usually occur between ages 20–40 (any age); AVMs are congenital developmental defects — tangles of arteries feeding directly into tangles of veins without intervening capillary network; incidence 0.5% of population; always suspect AVM if classical features of hypertensive haemorrhage are not present; requires cerebral angiography for diagnosis.

questions.question:
A male neonate is born with protrusion of abdominal viscera at the base of the umbilical cord. The defect measures 6 cm and is covered by an intact translucent membrane consisting of peritoneum, Wharton's jelly, and amnion. The membrane is avascular. Examination reveals features consistent with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and classify it by size?
(ii) What is the embryological basis of this condition, and through what mechanism does the Beckwith-Wiedemann variant arise?
(iii) Outline the immediate resuscitative steps for this neonate.
(iv) What is the definitive surgical management, and under what circumstances is conservative management chosen instead?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Exomphalos (Omphalocele). Classified as Major (defect >4 cm). Beckwith-Wiedemann Syndrome (EMG) is a syndromic form comprising Exomphalos, Macroglossia, and Gigantism (visceral and somatic).

(ii) Embryological basis: The anterior abdominal wall is formed by convergence of the cranial, caudal, and two lateral folds at the centre. Exomphalos results from failure of development of these abdominal folds, or from persistence of the body stalk. In Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, the anomaly is part of the Upper Midline Syndrome pattern, associated with chromosomal (trisomies 13, 18, 21) and syndromic anomalies, with the Pentalogy of Cantrell representing the epigastric variant.

(iii) Resuscitation for ruptured exomphalos:
- Incubator care
- Intravenous fluid
- Intravenous antibiotics
- Nasogastric tube + NPO
- Monitor urinary output
- Vitamin K
- Intestinal bag to cover eviscerated contents

(iv) Definitive surgical management:
- Primary closure
- Skin closure (may result in incisional hernia)
- Silo (staged closure)
Conservative management is chosen for major exomphalos with severe associated anomalies and intact membrane; aims to convert the exomphalos to a ventral hernia using escharotic and antimicrobial agents (e.g. 2% Silver Sulphadiazine cream, 70% Alcohol, Lugols Iodine).

A(i) The six links:
1. Etiologic agent — any micro-organism capable of producing an infectious process; depends on the number of organisms present.
2. Reservoir — the source of micro-organisms; may be other humans, plants, animals, or the general environment.
3. Portal of exit from reservoir — micro-organisms must leave the reservoir before infection can establish itself in a host.
4. Method of transmission — the means by which micro-organisms travel from reservoir to host.
5. Portal of entry — micro-organisms must enter the body; the skin is a barrier, but any break can serve as a portal of entry.
6. Susceptible host — any person at risk for infection; a compromised host is a person at increased risk.

A(ii) Three mechanisms:
- Direct transmission: immediate transfer through touching, biting, kissing, or sexual intercourse; droplet spread is also a form.
- Indirect transmission: via inanimate objects such as toys, soiled clothes, surgical instruments, water, food, blood, serum, or plasma.
- Airborne transmission: may involve droplets or dust.

B(i) Host factors increasing susceptibility: (1) Age; (2) Heredity; (3) Nature, number, and duration of physical and emotional stressors (elevated blood cortisone depletes energy stores and decreases resistance); (4) Inadequate nutritional status; (5) Some medical therapies (e.g. radiation treatments, some diagnostic procedures); (6) Certain medications (e.g. anticancer medications that depress bone marrow function, anti-inflammatory drugs, antibiotics).

B(ii) Cleaning inhibits the growth of micro-organisms by removing soiling. Disinfection is chemical or mechanical (friction) destruction of pathogens (not necessarily spores) on inanimate objects. Antisepsis is the application of a liquid antimicrobial chemical to skin or living tissue to inhibit or destroy micro-organisms. Sterilisation destroys all microbial life including highly resistant bacterial endospores. Four methods of sterilisation: moist heat, gas, boiling water, and radiation.
questions.question:
Describe the chain of infection and the factors that determine a micro-organism's ability to cause disease in a surgical patient.

A(i) Name the six links in the chain of infection and briefly describe each.
A(ii) State the three mechanisms of transmission and give an example of each.
B(i) List six host factors that increase susceptibility to infection.
B(ii) Explain how cleaning, disinfection, antisepsis, and sterilisation differ, and name four methods of sterilisation.

questions.answerText:
(i) History-taking headings for jaundice: biodata; duration; history of contact with a person with yellowness of eyes; history of blood transfusion; history of drug ingestion; family history of similar illness; genotype/history of recurrent bone pain; abdominal pain (characterised); pruritus; stool (colour, consistency, odour); urine colour; fever (characterised); tiredness; nausea/vomiting; loss of appetite; weight loss; fat intolerance.

(ii) Stool features: pale/clay-coloured stool suggests obstructive (cholestatic) jaundice due to absence of bile in the gut. Urine: dark tea-coloured urine suggests conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (obstructive or hepatocellular). Fever suggests infective aetiology (hepatitis, cholangitis, malaria). Weight loss suggests malignancy. Fat intolerance suggests biliary pathology. The combination of pale stools + dark urine + pruritus + palpable non-tender gallbladder points strongly to obstructive jaundice.

(iii) General examination: state of health; weight loss; acute distress; anaemia; jaundice; cyanosis; oedema; significant lymphadenopathy. Abdominal examination — Inspection: fullness, movement, marks, swellings, veins. Palpation: tenderness, rigidity, organs (liver, spleen, gall bladder, kidneys), other masses, specific signs (Murphy's sign). Percussion: gas, fluid, organs, masses. Auscultation: bowel sounds and bruit. Rectal examination: perianal skin, anal verge, anal sphincter, rectal wall, prostate.

(iv) Genotype/recurrent bone pain: sickle cell disease (HbSS) causes haemolytic jaundice through chronic haemolysis; a history of recurrent bone pain (vaso-occlusive crisis) and genotype (HbSS) would point to haemolytic rather than obstructive aetiology. Pathophysiological basis of pruritus in obstructive jaundice: obstruction of bile flow leads to deposition of bile salts in the skin, causing pruritus; it is therefore a symptom that points toward cholestasis.
questions.question:
A 52-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of obstructive jaundice. She has pale stools, dark urine, generalised pruritus, and a 5 kg weight loss. She is not on any medications. Examination reveals deep jaundice, a palpable non-tender gallbladder, and a smooth palpable liver edge.

(i) Using standard surgical history-taking headings, list all the symptoms and signs you would have explored for this patient presenting with jaundice.
(ii) What features of the stools, urine, and skin would you specifically enquire about, and what associated symptoms distinguish obstructive from hepatocellular and haemolytic jaundice?
(iii) Describe the general and abdominal examination findings in a patient with obstructive jaundice using standard clerking headings.
(iv) What is the significance of the genotype and recurrent bone pain history in a jaundiced patient, and what is the pathophysiological basis of pruritus in obstructive jaundice?

A 60-year-old male smoker presents with dyspnoea, haemoptysis, and SVC syndrome. CT shows a right hilar mass. Bronchoscopy reveals an obstructing lesion, and bronchoscopic biopsy confirms a diagnosis. Workup shows no distant metastasis.

(i) Name the three histological types of non-small cell lung carcinoma with their distinguishing features.
(ii) What investigations are required for the workup of lung cancer?
(iii) Describe the clinical manifestations of lung cancer caused by regional spread to hilar and mediastinal nodes.
(iv) What are the surgical and non-surgical treatment options for lung cancer?
questions.answerText:
(i) Squamous cell carcinoma — most common subtype worldwide; slow-growing; often located near hilum; associated with hypercalcaemia. Adenocarcinoma — WHO divides into 4 subtypes: acinar, papillary, bronchiolo-alveolar, and solid with mucin production; most common type in non-smokers. Large cell carcinoma — less differentiated tumours; often occur in periphery of lung; present as large bulky tumours.

(ii) Investigations: physical examination (tumour location, lymph node status, organ enlargement); chest X-ray; CT scan or MRI of the lung; CT scan or MRI of bone, brain, liver/spleen, and oesophagus; bronchoscopy; thoracoscopy; mediastinoscopy; laryngoscopy; esophagoscopy.

(iii) Regional spread to hilar and mediastinal nodes may cause: dysphagia (due to oesophageal compression); hoarseness (due to recurrent laryngeal nerve compression); Horner's syndrome (due to sympathetic nerve involvement); elevation of the hemidiaphragm (from phrenic nerve compression); SVC obstruction; phrenic or recurrent laryngeal palsy; brachial plexus compression.

(iv) Surgical: non-small cell carcinoma is treated surgically when feasible — surgical removal offers the best prospects for cure for early-stage disease. Non-surgical: small cell carcinoma responds best to non-surgical treatment; radiotherapy rarely for cure, mainly palliative; cytotoxic chemotherapy — cisplatin/carboplatin, etoposide, irinotecan; immunotherapy — intrapleural BCG injection; targeted therapy — crizotinib, entrectinib for ROS1 and ALK gene tumours; laser beams through flexible bronchoscope.

(i) Diagnosis: Malrotation of the midgut with acute midgut volvulus.
Surgical procedure: Ladd's procedure (after derotation of the volvulus).

(ii) Anatomical landmarks of Ladd's procedure:
- Evisceration of the entire bowel
- Counterclockwise derotation of the volvulus
- Examination of bowel for viability and areas of necrosis
- Release (division) of all adhesive bands (Ladd's bands) from the duodenum to the rectum
- Mobilisation of the duodenum
- Placement of the caecum in the left upper quadrant and the duodenum in the right lateral abdomen
- Appendicectomy (removes risk of atypical appendicitis presentation in future)
- Rule out other anomalies

(iii) Axis of rotation and embryological significance:
The superior mesenteric artery (SMA) is the axis of rotation. During normal development, both the duodenojejunal loop and the caecocolic loop rotate a total of 270° counterclockwise around the SMA (axis). Rotation occurs in two stages: initial 180° during physiological herniation (5th–10th week), then additional 90° on return of bowel (10th week). Fixation occurs from 12th week. The SMA supplies the entire midgut; volvulus around the SMA therefore threatens the entire midgut blood supply.

(iv) Embryological variant causing narrow base: Non-rotation (arrest in Stage I of development) — the duodenojejunal junction does not lie inferior and to the left of the SMA, and the caecum does not lie in the right lower quadrant, creating a narrow mesenteric pedicle.
Intraoperative decision for uncertain viability: If large areas of bowel are marginally viable, close and perform a second-look procedure within 36 hours. If large areas are obviously necrotic, resect and plan for parenteral nutrition and bowel transplantation.
questions.question:
A neonate presents in the first week of life with sudden onset bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, abdominal pain, haematemesis, and shock. Upper GI series shows contrast ending abruptly with a corkscrew pattern in the duodenum and loops of small bowel on the right of the abdomen. At laparotomy, a clockwise volvulus is found with a large area of marginally viable bowel.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and name the surgical procedure performed to correct the underlying rotation anomaly?
(ii) Describe the anatomical landmarks used in Ladd's procedure.
(iii) What nerve or vascular structure is the axis of rotation, and what is the embryological significance of its position?
(iv) What is the embryological variant that creates a narrow mesenteric base, and what intraoperative decision is required when the bowel viability is uncertain?

A(i) Describe the gross anatomy and components of the male reproductive system and outline the hormonal regulation of male reproductive function, specifying the role of the hypothalamus, adenohypophysis, Leydig cells, Sertoli cells, and androgen-binding protein in spermatogenesis.
A(ii) Enumerate all causes of male infertility under appropriate categories, distinguishing obstructive from non-obstructive (testicular failure) causes and specifying the hormone profiles that distinguish them in the azoospermic patient.
B(i) Describe the correct technique for seminal fluid analysis — parameters assessed, collection requirements, and submission protocol — and state the investigation sequence for the azoospermic patient including testicular biopsy site and bilateral vasography.
B(ii) State all treatment options for male infertility as listed, including the role of sperm cryopreservation and the rationale for its use before anti-cancer treatment.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Male reproductive system components: testes, epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate, bulbourethral glands, urethra.
Hormonal regulation: the hypothalamus regulates activity of the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis). The adenohypophysis synthesises LH and FSH, which modulate activity of Sertoli and Leydig cells. LH stimulates testosterone production by Leydig cells. FSH stimulates sperm production in conjunction with testosterone by regulating activity of Sertoli cells. Sertoli cells stimulated by FSH and testosterone release androgen-binding protein, which binds testosterone, thereby increasing testosterone concentration within the seminiferous tubules and stimulating spermatogenesis. Accessory glands secrete the alkaline fluid part of semen: seminal vesicles secrete alkaline fluid containing fructose for sperm nutrition and energy; prostate secretes alkaline secretion that activates sperm movement; bulbourethral glands secrete alkaline mucus-like secretion for lubrication.

A(ii) Causes of male infertility:
- Hypopituitarism: leads to germinal aplasia; FSH levels low.
- Hypogonadism/testicular failure: e.g. Klinefelter's syndrome; FSH elevated, testosterone normal due to presence of numerous Leydig cells.
- Deficiencies of germ cell maturation: from mumps, trauma, X-rays, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, hypopituitarism/hypogonadism.
- Obstruction of conduction system: absence of union between vas and epididymis, previous epididymitis, vasectomy, iatrogenic damage during inguinal procedures.
- Hyperadrenalism; varicoceles; tight clothing; undescended testes; sperm antibodies.
In the azoospermic patient: if hormone profile is normal, likely obstructive; if very high FSH and low testosterone, testicular failure; there may also be hyperprolactinaemia.

B(i) Seminal fluid analysis parameters: volume (2.5–5 cc, up to 12 cc acceptable), count/cc (>20,000,000; young people may have up to 200,000,000/cc), morphology, motility, vitality.
Collection: period of abstinence >4 days; method — masturbation; container — wide-necked sterile bottle; submission within 20 minutes; transportation — kept warm by contact with the body.
For azoospermia: (A) Testicular biopsy — anaesthesia, approach, site at mid-portion of convex border of the testis; (B) Bilateral vasography. Hormone profile: FSH, LH, testosterone, prolactin; immune studies for anti-sperm antibodies.

B(ii) Treatment options: general measures; treatment of hypopituitarism; treatment of testicular failure; treatment of hyperprolactinaemia; surgical relief of vasal obstruction; repair of failure of vaso-epididymal union; varicocelectomy; in vitro fertilisation.
Sperm cryopreservation (banking): involves freezing and banking sperm collected through masturbation, rectal electroejaculation, testicular aspiration, or post-masturbation urine. Used before anti-cancer treatment because sperm quality may be poor prior to treatment (especially in testicular cancer and Hodgkin's disease); many patients must start chemotherapy soon, limiting ejaculates; intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) allows successful use of small frozen samples.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male presents to the surgical outpatient department with a painful, pus-draining lesion along his jaw, following a tooth extraction two weeks earlier. On rotating the vial of pus, small yellow granules are visible to the naked eye.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what organism is most commonly responsible?
(ii) What are the four recognised anatomical types of this condition?
(iii) How are the characteristic granules confirmed — both at the bedside and histologically?
(iv) What is the definitive management, including the antibiotic agent and its dose?
questions.answerText:
(i) The most likely diagnosis is actinomycosis. The most common causative organism is Actinomyces israelii, which infects both man and animals and is an endogenous organism in the mouths of healthy people. Infection becomes established in traumatised tissue (e.g., after tooth abscess or extraction) and causes a suppurative infection.

(ii) The four types are: cervico-facial, thoracic, hepatic (honey-comb), and ileoceacal.

(iii) At the bedside: sterile water is run over the gauze covering the lesion; the water washes away purulent material, leaving golden granules on the gauze. Histologically: the granules appear as 'sulfur granules' surrounded by polymorphonuclear cells (PMN) forming the purulent tissue reaction. Culture for anaerobic organism is also performed.

(iv) The lesions must be surgically drained prior to antibiotic therapy. The antibiotic is Penicillin (2 million units 6-hourly).

(i) The diagnosis is primary lymphoedema, specifically the Praecox subtype (onset between 1 and 35 years of age, with a positive family history suggesting the familial variety, also known as Milroy's disease when familial and congenital).
(ii) Pathological findings in primary lymphoedema at the lymphatic vessel level:
- In 80% of cases, obliteration of distal lymphatics occurs.
- Can be due to aplasia, hypoplasia, or hyperplasia of the lymphatics.
- In 10% of cases, proximal occlusion of lymphatics in the abdomen and pelvis occurs.
- In 10% of cases, lymphatic valvular incompetence develops.
- A proportion of patients have a family history (Milroy's disease).
- Chronic lymphoedema results in subcutaneous fibrosis, which can be worsened by secondary infection.
(iii) Grading of oedema:
- 1+: oedema that is barely detectable.
- 2+: a slight indentation is visible when the skin is depressed.
- 3+: a deeper fingerprint returns to normal in 5 to 30 seconds.
- 4+: the extremity may be 1.5 to 2 times normal size.
(iv) Investigations: chronic venous insufficiency should first be excluded with Doppler ultrasound. Lymphoedema and its cause are confirmed with lymphoscintigraphy, CT or MRI scanning, and lymphangiography. The investigation of choice is lymphoscintigraphy, which has a sensitivity greater than 90% and a specificity of 100%. A normal lymphoscintigraphy excludes lymphoedema. Lymphangiography is painful and rarely required.
(v) Conservative treatment: general skin care to reduce risk of infection; elevation to reduce swelling; physiotherapy and manual lymph drainage; external pneumatic compression; compression stockings once swelling is reduced; antibiotics at the first sign of infection. Diuretics are of no proven benefit.
Surgical approaches: (1) Debulking operations: Homan's operation (elliptical excisions of skin and subcutaneous tissue with primary closure); Charles' operation (radical excision of skin and subcutaneous tissue with skin grafts). (2) Bypass operations: skin and muscle flaps; omental bridges; enteromesenteric bridges; lymphaticolymphatic anastomosis; lymphaticovenous anastomosis. Both produce good functional results though cosmesis is often poor.
questions.question:
A 25-year-old man presents with bilateral painless swelling of both lower legs that has been gradually increasing since the age of 18 years, worse on standing, and beginning distally before progressing proximally. His mother had a similar condition. Examination shows non-pitting oedema, hyperkeratosis, and skin fissuring. Doppler ultrasound excludes chronic venous insufficiency.
(i) State the diagnosis and classify the type precisely, naming the subtype by age of onset.
(ii) Describe the pathological findings in primary lymphoedema at the lymphatic vessel level.
(iii) Describe the grading of oedema (1+ to 4+) as given.
(iv) State the investigations used to confirm the diagnosis, specifying the investigation of choice and its sensitivity and specificity.
(v) Describe the conservative treatment and the two surgical approaches available, naming the specific operations under each.

(A) Describe tracheobronchial injury under the following headings:
(i) Incidence, mortality, and anatomical location of injury
(ii) Clinical features and management

(B) Describe diaphragmatic injury under the following headings:
(i) Incidence, laterality, and common cause
(ii) CXR findings and treatment

(C) Describe oesophageal injury and myocardial contusion as thoracic injuries under the following headings for each:
(i) Cause/clinical features
(ii) Key investigation or monitoring
(iii) Treatment
questions.answerText:
(A)(i) Tracheobronchial injury: rare injury but usually fatal in 30%; 80% is within 2.5 cm from the carina; presents as massive or persistent air leak into mediastinum or pleural space.
(A)(ii) Clinical features: respiratory distress, surgical emphysema, haemoptysis. Management: CTTD; suprasternal incision for mediastinal air leak (controversial); thoracotomy with repair.

(B)(i) Diaphragmatic injury: commoner in penetrating chest injuries (15%); 95% is on the left hemidiaphragm; RTA accounts for 80%.
(B)(ii) CXR may reveal: blunting of costophrenic angle; aberrant course of NG-tube; gas-filled viscera in the chest. Treatment: resuscitation; gastric decompression with NGT; surgical repair via thoracotomy or laparotomy.

(C) Oesophageal injury: (i) Rare following blunt chest injury; clinical features — chest pain, crepitus/subcutaneous emphysema, haematemesis, leakage of gastric contents via CTTD. (ii) Key investigation: upper GI contrast studies (diagnostic). (iii) Treatment: early diagnosis is key (<24 hours); antibiotics; CTTD; thoracotomy — primary repair in early stages; oesophageal exclusion in later stages.

Myocardial contusion: (i) Cause: acute deceleration injury or forceful anteroposterior chest compression; clinical features — arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, right ventricle is mostly affected, decreased cardiac output. (ii) Key monitoring: CVP monitoring. (iii) Treatment: supportive with CVP monitoring.

(i) Diagnosis: squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal/margin.
- The most common histological subtype is squamous cell carcinoma.
- Those arising below the dentate line are usually squamous (anal margin tumours); those above the dentate line are termed epidermoid carcinomas (anal canal tumours).

(ii) Risk factors:
- Direct association with HPV infection, anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN), and immunosuppression.
- High-risk groups: those infected with HPV (especially subtypes 16, 18, 31, or 33), those with HIV infection, and recipients of organ transplants.
- Pre-malignant diseases: Paget's disease, Bowen's disease, anal condylomata.
- Risk factors listed for anal carcinoma (from malignant large bowel section): HIV/AIDS, HPV, cigarette smoking, anal-receptive intercourse.

(iii) Clinical presentation of advanced tumours:
- Faecal incontinence.
- Anovaginal fistulation in women.
- On examination: malignant ulcers in the anal margin with rolled, everted edges and central ulceration; associated anal condylomata or chronic fistula-in-ano; there may be associated HPV lesions/warts; anal canal tumours are palpable as irregular indurated tender ulceration.
- Pain and bleeding are the most common symptoms; a palpable mass, pruritus, or discharge are less common; occasionally tenesmus.

(iv) Treatment:
- Squamous cell carcinomas of the anus: chemoradiotherapy (chemoradiation) is the first-line treatment.
- For other histological subtypes (e.g., adenocarcinoma, malignant melanoma): abdomino-perineal excision.
- For those with faecal incontinence or who are too ill for major surgery: a diverting loop colostomy.
questions.question:
A 52-year-old HIV-positive man presents with anal pain, bleeding, pruritus, and a palpable mass at the anal margin with rolled, everted edges and central ulceration. He also has visible anal condylomata.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis, naming the most common histological subtype and where it arises relative to the dentate line.

Describe the classification, properties, and clinical use of chemical disinfectants and antiseptics used in surgical practice.

A(i) Describe alcohol, chlorhexidine (biguanide), and iodophor compounds as antiseptics — state concentration, contact time, spectrum of activity, and limitations.
A(ii) Describe phenolic compounds and quaternary ammonium compounds (including cetrimide) and explain their limitations.
B(i) Distinguish sterilisation from disinfection; describe Tyndallisation, pasteurisation, and dry heat sterilisation including temperatures used.
B(ii) State which antiseptic is most effective against bacterial spores; which chemical requires good local exhaust ventilation and why; and explain the concept of strike-through contamination.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Alcohol (ethyl, isopropyl): concentration 70–99%; contact time 10–30 min; effective against vegetative cells, lipophilic viruses, tubercle bacilli (all very positive); less effective against hydrophilic viruses; eye irritant, toxic, flammable; inactivated by organic matter; used for work surfaces and equipment. Chlorhexidine (biguanide/Savlon): kills 99.9% of germs including bacteria and viruses; Savlon = 3% cetrimide + 0.3% chlorhexidine. Iodophor compounds: concentration 0.47%; contact time 10–30 min; effective against vegetative cells, lipophilic viruses, tubercle bacilli (very positive); less effective against hydrophilic viruses; leaves residue; corrosive; skin and eye irritant; toxic; inactivated by organic matter.

A(ii) Phenolic compounds: concentration 0.2–3%; contact time 10–30 min; effective against vegetative cells, lipophilic viruses, tubercle bacilli (very positive); less effective against hydrophilic viruses; leaves residue; corrosive; skin, eye, and respiratory irritant; toxic; inactivated by organic matter. Quaternary ammonium compounds: concentration 0.1–2%; contact time 10–30 min; effective against vegetative cells and lipophilic viruses; toxic; inactivated by organic matter. Cetrimide: mixture of tetradonium bromide + cetrimonium bromide + lautrimonium bromide; 1–3% solution.

B(i) Sterilisation destroys all microbial life including endospores; disinfection eliminates virtually all pathogenic non-spore-forming micro-organisms. Tyndallisation: boiling goods at 100 degrees C for 15–20 minutes a day for three consecutive days. Pasteurisation: mild heat (usually less than 100 degrees C) to eliminate pathogens and extend shelf life; destroys vegetative bacteria but not spores. Dry heat: 121–180 degrees C for 6 minutes to 12 hours.

B(ii) Most effective against bacterial spores: glutaraldehyde (2%; very positive response against spores). Chemical requiring good local exhaust ventilation: formaldehyde — due to its irritating characteristics and status as a carcinogen, formaldehyde should not be used without good local exhaust ventilation. Strike-through contamination: moisture carries bacteria from a non-sterile surface to a sterile surface by capillary action when moisture passes through a sterile object; this is why drapes covering instrument tables or the patient should be moisture-proof.

questions.question:
A newborn presents with excessive drooling, choking, coughing, and inability to pass a nasogastric tube beyond 10 cm. There is a history of maternal polyhydramnios. CXR shows the NGT coiled in the upper oesophageal pouch. An associated ventricular septal defect and patent ductus arteriosus are confirmed on echocardiography.

(i) What is the diagnosis and the most common anatomical variant?
(ii) Describe the embryological basis of this condition.
(iii) What proportion of infants have associated anomalies, and which are the commonest cardiac defects listed?
(iv) State the prognosis and survival rate for this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Oesophageal atresia (EA) with distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula (TEF) — the most common type, accounting for 86% of cases (Type C: EA with distal TEF).

(ii) Embryological basis: the oesophagus and trachea share a common origin from foregut derivatives; a ventral diverticulum forms at the 4th and 5th weeks; a tracheo-oesophageal septum forms by posterior deviation; isolated EA results from failure at the 8th week; failure of recanalization of the oesophagus also contributes. Types: A — isolated oesophageal atresia 8%; B — EA with proximal TEF 1%; C — EA with distal TEF 86%; D — EA with proximal and distal TEF 1%; E — H-type TEF without EA 4%; F — oesophageal stenosis.

(iii) 50% of infants have associated other midline defects. Cardiac anomalies are present in 25% of infants; the commonest cardiac defects listed are VSD, PDA, and Tetralogy of Fallot.

(iv) Prognosis and survival rates: 95–100% survival rate. Incidence: 1 of 3,000 to 5,000 births; international occurrence 0.4 to 3.6 cases per 10,000 live births; males more commonly affected than females.

A. Skin is the largest organ in the body. Its major functions are:
- Protection of deeper structures
- Thermoregulation
- Metabolism
- Immunological defence
- Sensory interface
- Psychological expression
A(i) Causes of skin defects requiring reconstructive cover:
- Trauma (surgery, road traffic accidents, gunshot wounds, burns)
- Infections
- Malignancies
- Irradiation
- Chemicals
- Drugs
- Others
B. The reconstructive ladder, from simplest to most complex:
1. Dressings alone: used for bruises, partial thickness burns, split-thickness skin graft (STSG) donor sites, and wounds where skin appendages are intact.
2. Direct closure: used for surgical incisions, lacerations, full-thickness skin graft (FTSG) donor sites; subcutaneous layer must close freely; may require undermining.
3. Skin graft: used when the defect is too large for direct closure but the floor can generate granulation tissue (i.e., vascular bed is present). Contraindicated over avascular beds, exposed major vessels or nerves, planned subsequent surgery, or when infected with B-haemolytic Streptococcus.
4. Flap: used when the bed is not adequately vascular or composite tissue transfer is required.
B(i) Specific indications for flap cover: inadequate blood supply to support STSG (e.g., bare bone, bare tendon, exposed major neurovascular bundles); second operation required in the area; to restore contour; to provide soft tissue padding; to replace unstable scar or graft; to improve skin quality.
Classification of flaps:
(a) By geometry of transfer: rotation; advancement; transposition.
(b) By tissue contained: cutaneous (skin only); fasciocutaneous (skin and fascia); myocutaneous (skin and muscle); osseous (bone); osseocutaneous (bone and skin).
(c) By blood supply: random pattern (no specific vascular pedicle, very useful on the face); axial pattern (have a direct, named superficial vascular pedicle).

A(i) List all the causes of skin defects that may require reconstructive cover.
B. Describe the RECONSTRUCTIVE LADDER, listing the options from simplest to most complex, and state for each option the type of wound for which it is appropriate.

questions.answerText:
(A)(i) Congenital heart defects are the commonest group of life-threatening anomalies — 0.5–0.8% of live births (8/1000). Aetiology: unknown, multifactorial inheritance; genetic factors implicated, high incidence in first-degree relatives; 3% have a single gene defect; 13% have associated chromosomal abnormalities; 2–4% are associated with environmental or maternal conditions and teratogenic influences. Gender differences: ASD, VSD, PDA and pulmonary stenosis are more common in girls; left-sided lesions more common in boys.

(A)(ii) Acyanotic — volume load: L–R shunts — ASD, VSD, PDA; pressure load (ventricular outflow obstruction): pulmonary/aortic valve lesions, aortic coarctation, pulmonary stenosis. Cyanotic — decreased pulmonary blood flow: TOF, pulmonary atresia, tricuspid atresia, single ventricle with pulmonic stenosis; increased pulmonary blood flow: transposition of great vessels, truncus arteriosus.

(B) Fetal circulation: gas exchange occurs at the placenta. Four shunts: placenta (gas and nutrient exchange); ductus venosus (bypasses liver); foramen ovale (right-to-left shunting at atrial level); ductus arteriosus (right-to-left shunting at arterial level). Features: high pulmonary vascular resistance; little pulmonary blood flow; ventricles work in parallel. At birth: removal of placenta increases systemic vascular resistance and closes ductus venosus; lung expansion reduces PVR, increases pulmonary blood flow, and functionally closes the foramen ovale as LA pressure exceeds RA; increased arterial oxygen saturation closes the ductus arteriosus (functional closure within 10–15 hours; anatomic closure by 2–3 weeks).

(C) TOF four components: VSD; right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction; RVH (secondary to PS); overriding of the aorta. Physiologically, the VSD is large enough to equalize pressures in both ventricles and there is RVOT stenosis. Severity of RVOT obstruction determines shunt direction — mild stenosis produces acyanotic/pink TOF (L–R shunt); severe stenosis produces right-to-left shunt and cyanosis. Hypoxic spell: excessive tachycardia or hypovolemia can narrow the RVOT and increase right-to-left shunt, causing hypoxia; the fall in arterial PO2 with increase in PCO2 and fall in pH stimulates the respiratory centre, producing hyperpnea — a vicious cycle; events precipitating it include crying, defecation, or increased physical activity that lower SVR. Squatting: increases systemic arterial oxygen saturation by trapping venous blood in lower extremities (reducing right-to-left shunt at ventricular level) and by increasing SVR, which reduces right-to-left ventricular shunt.
