questions.answerText:
(i) Gross anatomy: the kidney lies retroperitoneally in the loin. It is enclosed within Gerota's fascia (the perinephric fascia), which also contains the perirenal fat and the adrenal gland at the upper pole. The kidney has an outer cortex and inner medulla; the collecting system (pelvis and calyces) drains into the ureter at the pelvi-ureteric junction. The renal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava (IVC) on both sides (shorter on the right).
(ii) Predisposing factors: diet high in fat, oil, and milk; toxic agents (lead, cadmium, asbestos, petroleum by-products); smoking; genetic factors (oncogene on short arm of chromosome 3; HLA antigen BW-44 and DR-8); von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) syndrome; adult polycystic disease; renal dialysis patients.
Histology: adenocarcinoma arising from the proximal convoluted tubular cell (also known as hypernephroma and Grawitz tumour).
Macroscopic: yellow, smooth tumour, often at the upper pole; haemorrhagic areas; cystic change; vascular.
Microscopic: large foamy cells with attempts at tubule formation.
(iii) Robson staging:
- Stage I: tumour confined within renal capsule.
- Stage II: tumour confined by Gerota's fascia.
- Stage III: tumour to renal vein or IVC, nodes, or through Gerota's fascia.
- Stage IV: distant metastases or invasion of adjacent organs.
TNM staging applies equivalent classifications with T (primary tumour), N (nodes), and M (metastases).
(iv) Spread: direct into renal vein and perirenal tissue; lymphatic to periaortic and hilar nodes; haematogenous to lung (large 'cannon-ball' metastases), bones, and contralateral kidney. RCC characteristically invades the renal vein and extends as a tumour thrombus into the IVC and even the right atrium. Liver dysfunction (raised enzymes and prolonged PT) can occur in the absence of metastatic disease — a paraneoplastic effect mediated by tumour-derived factors causing hepatic dysfunction (Stauffer's syndrome), demonstrating that functional deficits at distant organs do not always require physical metastases.
(v) Classical triad: haematuria (50–60%); flank pain (35–50%); palpable abdominal mass (25–45%); all three present in <10% of patients.
Paraneoplastic manifestations: hypertension; polycythaemia (decreased blood flow to JGA → increased renin and erythropoietin); hypercalcaemia; ectopic hormone production (ACTH, ADH); anaemia; weight loss; PUO; liver dysfunction without metastases.
Management:
- Surgical: offers best chance of long-term survival. Partial nephrectomy if Stage I and part of VHL presentation. Radical nephrectomy: aim to remove kidney, renal vessels, upper ureter, adrenal, and Gerota's fascia. Isolated lung metastases may also be removed surgically with good results.
- Palliative: renal artery embolisation (may stop haematuria); chemotherapy (only 10% response rate); hormone therapy (only 5% response rate); immunotherapy (currently under review).
Prognosis: overall survival 40% at 5 years.
questions.question:
Describe renal cell carcinoma (RCC) under the following headings:
(i) Gross anatomy of the kidney relevant to RCC: describe the organ and the fascial envelope in which it lies.
(ii) State all the predisposing factors, the histological cell of origin, and the macroscopic and microscopic pathological features of RCC.
(iii) Describe the Robson staging system (Stages I–IV) and the TNM classification, and relate each stage to the extent of disease.
(iv) Explain how RCC spreads, including its characteristic involvement of the renal vein and inferior vena cava, and why it can cause distant functional deficits such as liver dysfunction without hepatic metastases.
(v) Describe the classical triad of clinical features, the paraneoplastic manifestations, and the essential surgical and palliative management with prognosis.

A(i) Describe haemorrhoids under the headings: definition, classification into types, and the grading system for internal haemorrhoids with the defining feature of each grade.
A(ii) State seven aetiological/predisposing factors for haemorrhoids.
B(i) List the complications of haemorrhoids, and then separately list the complications specifically attributable to haemorrhoidectomy (both early and late),.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition, classification, and grading:
- Haemorrhoids means varicosity of the haemorrhoidal venous plexus; they are also described as symptomatic anal cushions, which are normal structures universally present in all persons.
- Types: internal haemorrhoids, external haemorrhoids, and mixed haemorrhoids; also classified as primary/secondary and simple/mixed.
- Grading of internal haemorrhoids:
 - Grade I (1st degree): bleeds only; no obvious prolapse.
 - Grade II (2nd degree): bleeds, prolapses, but the prolapse remains reduced following self/manual reduction (prolapse that reduces spontaneously).
 - Grade III (3rd degree): the haemorrhoid remains permanently prolapsed (prolapse that has to be digitally reduced or remains permanently prolapsed).
 - Grade IV: permanent prolapse.

A(ii) Seven aetiological/predisposing factors:
- Constipation, pregnancy, obesity, prolonged sitting, chronic diarrhoea, chronic cough, straining (e.g., in BPH or carcinoma of the prostate), colon cancer, portal hypertension and anorectal varices, inflammatory bowel disease, rectal surgeries, familial predisposition, smoking.
(Any seven of the above.)

B(i) Complications of haemorrhoids: anaemia, strangulation, thrombosis, gangrene, infection, anal stenosis.
Complications of haemorrhoidectomy:
- Early: haemorrhage, acute urinary retention, anorectal abscess, anal fissure.
- Late: anal stenosis/stricture, incontinence.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man with a 10-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension is scheduled for an elective right hemicolectomy. His most recent fasting blood glucose is 14 mmol/L and his diastolic blood pressure is 115 mmHg.

(i) State the ASA physical status classification; which class does this patient fall into, and what implication does it have for surgery?
(ii) At what blood pressure level should elective surgery be delayed, and what is the acceptable diastolic blood pressure target for diabetic patients?
(iii) Describe the preoperative management of his diabetes mellitus on the day of surgery.
(iv) List the risk factors for postoperative myocardial infarction in this patient, and state the perioperative reinfarction rates if prior MI occurred within 6 months versus after 6 months.
questions.answerText:
(i) ASA classification: 1 = normal fit patient; 2 = well-controlled systemic illness; 3 = poorly controlled systemic illness; 4 = incapacitating disease; 5 = moribund patient. This patient has poorly controlled diabetes and hypertension and would be ASA 3. Surgery on a poorly controlled systemic illness carries increased morbidity and mortality; optimisation before elective surgery is required.

(ii) Elective surgery should be delayed if DBP is 110 mmHg or more with or without new onset of headache, but if there is no sign of end organ damage or left ventricular hypertrophy, surgery may proceed. Stage 3 hypertension (systolic 180 mmHg or more and diastolic 110 mmHg or more) should be controlled before surgery. In patients with diabetes mellitus, keep DBP below 90 mmHg.

(iii) Preoperative management of DM on the day of surgery: individual patient evaluation and instruction are required. No oral hypoglycaemics on the day of surgery. Implement GKI (glucose-potassium-insulin) regimen on the morning of major surgery. Use sliding scale management. Frequent blood sugar monitoring using glucometer.

(iv) Risk factors for postoperative MI: diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, hypertension, tobacco use, hypercholesterolaemia. Regarding prior MI: if a previous MI and subsequent surgery are separated by less than 6 months, the perioperative reinfarction rate is 5% to 86% and the mortality rate is 23% to 86%. After 6 months, the perioperative reinfarction rate stabilises at 2% to 6%.

A(i) Colonisation: presence of micro-organisms on the body surface (skin, mouth, intestines, airway) with growth and multiplication but without interaction between host and organism; occurs by acquisition of mother's genital flora during SVD or from the environment for those by C/S; in adults by migration from skin to wounds forming a biofilm inhibiting wound healing. Infection: invasion and multiplication of infective organism into the human body whether or not disease develops; there is a breach of the body immune system. Carrier: an individual harbouring a specific organism in the absence of clinical disease; a potential source of spread; could be colonised, asymptomatic infected, in incubation period, or convalescing. Bacteraemia: presence of viable bacteria in the bloodstream; may or may not be associated with active disease; may cause fever, chills, drop in BP, tachycardia; can progress to sepsis. Septicaemia: presence and active multiplication of bacteria in the blood with spread to other parts of the body; symptoms include high fever, chills, weakness, excessive sweating, hypotension. Sepsis: an overwhelming and life-threatening response of the body systems to infection that can lead to tissue damage, organ failure, and death; immune system overdrive.

A(ii) SIRS is an exaggerated defence response by the body to noxious stressors in an effort to localise and eliminate the endogenous or exogenous source of the insult. Stressors: trauma, infection, surgery, acute inflammation, ischaemia, reperfusion, malignancy.

B(i) Cleaning: removes soiling and inhibits growth of micro-organisms. Disinfection: chemical or mechanical destruction of pathogens (non-spore-forming) on inanimate objects. Sterilisation: use of a physical or chemical procedure to destroy all microbial life including highly resistant bacterial endospores.

B(ii) Alcohol (ethyl/isopropyl): 70–99%; contact time 10–30 min; effective against vegetative cells, lipophilic viruses, tubercle bacilli (all very positive); less effective against hydrophilic viruses; eye irritant, toxic, flammable; inactivated by organic matter. Glutaraldehyde: 2%; contact time 10–60 min; effective against all forms including bacterial spores; leaves residue; skin, eye and respiratory irritant; toxic. Chlorhexidine (biguanide): kills 99.9% of germs including bacteria and viruses; used in pools, spas, cosmetics. Chlorine compounds: 0.05–0.5%; contact time 10–30 min; effective against vegetative cells, lipophilic viruses, tubercle bacilli, hydrophilic viruses; less effective against bacterial spores; corrosive; inactivated by organic matter.
questions.question:
Describe the pathophysiology, classification, and surgical significance of bacteraemia, septicaemia, sepsis, and systemic inflammatory response syndrome.

A(i) Define each of the following precisely: colonisation, infection, carrier, bacteraemia, septicaemia, and sepsis.
A(ii) Define SIRS, list the stressors that trigger it, and explain the body's response.
B(i) Distinguish between infection, disinfection, and sterilisation, and explain the three levels of decontamination.
B(ii) Describe the chemical agents used in surgical antisepsis, stating concentration, contact time, spectrum of activity, and main limitations of alcohol, glutaraldehyde, chlorhexidine, and chlorine compounds.

A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the transplanted kidney in the recipient — the operative position, incision used, the vascular anastomoses performed (specifying recipient vessels used), and the urinary reconstruction performed.
A(ii) State how the zones of the donor kidney and the transplant's vascular connections relate to early post-operative complications, listing each complication with its incidence as given.
B(i) Describe the post-operative monitoring protocol for the first 48 hours — including urine output thresholds and corresponding fluid replacement regimens — and list all post-operative investigations and their timing.
B(ii) Explain why disease causing end-stage renal disease (ESRD) may spread to cause functional deficit in the transplanted kidney, and enumerate all causes of ESRD that are indications for renal transplantation as listed.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The recipient lies supine under general anaesthesia. Incision: Gibson incision (extraperitoneal). Vascular anastomoses: renal vein to external iliac vein (RV-EIV); renal artery to internal iliac artery or external iliac artery (RA-IIA/EIA). Urinary reconstruction: ureteroneocystostomy.

A(ii) Vascular complications (6–30%): renal artery stenosis <1%; renal vein thrombosis 0.3–4%; vascular anastomosis disruption. Ureteral complications: leakage or obstruction. Bladder complications: extravasation. Lymphocele: 0.6–18%. Pelvic haematoma. Infections. Malignancy: lymphoma, SQCC. The peripheral zone of the kidney is most vulnerable to ischaemia; the vascular anastomosis at the iliac vessels means kinking or stenosis at the anastomosis site directly impairs perfusion of the transplant.

B(i) Post-operative protocol:
- Bed rest × 48 hours.
- Input/output and vital signs hourly × 24 hours, then 4-hourly.
- Urine output <200 ml/hr: replace with 5% dextrose half-normal saline at 30 ml/hr.
- Urine output >200 ml/hr: replace 200 ml + two-thirds of the amount exceeding 200 ml.
- CBC, E/U every 6 hours, then daily.
- Urine M/C/S twice per week.
- Renal scan post-operative day 1.
- Renal USS post-operative day 5.
- Cystogram post-operative day 5.
- Immunosuppression as ordered.

B(ii) Disease causing ESRD may recur in the transplanted kidney because the underlying immunological, metabolic, or systemic process persists after transplantation (e.g. glomerulosclerosis, SLE, oxalosis); hypertensive nephrosclerosis recurs if hypertension is not controlled; pyelonephritis requires correction of any residual obstructive or reflux uropathy before transplant. Indications for renal transplantation (causes of ESRD): diabetic nephropathy; hypertensive nephrosclerosis; glomerulosclerosis; obstructive uropathy; analgesic nephropathy; polycystic kidney disease (PCKD); renal vascular disease; pyelonephritis; SLE; metabolic diseases (oxalosis, amyloid).

A(i) Basic anatomy of the peritoneum:
- The peritoneal membrane is a semi-permeable membrane.
- It lines the abdominal wall (parietal peritoneum) and covers the abdominal organs (visceral peritoneum).
- The membrane is a closed sac in males; the fallopian tubes and ovaries open into the peritoneal cavity in females.
- The size of the membrane approximates the body surface area (1–2 m²).
- About 100 cc of transudate (peritoneal fluid) is contained in the cavity in normal individuals.

A(ii) Additional route of infection in females:
- Because the fallopian tubes and ovaries open into the peritoneal cavity in females, organisms from the vagina can ascend through the fallopian tubes into the peritoneal cavity, providing a direct route of infection.
- In primary peritonitis, in women a likely route of infection is from the vagina through the fallopian tubes.

B(i) Chemical versus bacterial peritonitis:
- Causes: Chemical peritonitis refers to peritoneal inflammation from substances other than bacteria; sources include gastric juice, bile, blood, urine, chyle, meconium, and barium. Secondary bacterial peritonitis implies the aetiology is the result of bacterial contamination from a known source, usually from within the peritoneal cavity and often from perforation of the GIT.
- Evolution: Chemical peritonitis is initially sterile; subsequently, however, bacterial contamination supervenes.
- Most severe form: The most severe and common form of chemical peritonitis is that of perforated peptic ulcer causing a sudden outpouring of acid gastric juice, which produces an acute inflammatory response in both the visceral and parietal peritoneum.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the basic anatomy of the peritoneum under the headings: type of membrane, layers and what each lines, relationship in males versus females, approximate size, and volume of peritoneal fluid in normal individuals.
A(ii) Explain the clinical and anatomical basis for why the fallopian tubes and ovaries provide an additional route of infection of the peritoneum in females.
B(i) Distinguish between chemical (sterile) peritonitis and bacterial (secondary) peritonitis under the headings: causes, evolution over time, and the most common and severe form of chemical peritonitis.

Describe the definitions of asepsis and antisepsis, and explain the principles of surgical aseptic technique.

A(i) Define asepsis and antisepsis as used in surgical practice.
A(ii) Distinguish between medical asepsis and surgical asepsis.
B(i) State six general rules of aseptic technique in the operating room and the reason for each.
B(ii) Explain what parts of the gown are considered sterile and which are not, and state the rule on moisture and sterile drapes.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Asepsis: Prevention of sepsis by exclusion, destruction, or inhibition of growth or multiplication of microorganisms from body tissues and fluids; it is a process or procedure performed under conditions in which bacterial contamination has been minimised. Antiseptics: Inorganic chemical compounds that combat sepsis by inhibiting the growth of microorganisms without necessarily killing them; used primarily on skin to stop the growth of resident flora.

A(ii) Medical asepsis includes all practices intended to confine a specific microorganism to a specific area, limiting the number, growth, and transmission of microorganisms; objects are referred to as clean or dirty. Surgical asepsis (sterile technique) refers to keeping an area or object free of all microorganisms including spores, and is used for all procedures involving the sterile areas of the body.

B(i) Six rules and reasons:
- Surgical team members remain within the sterile area — movement out may encourage cross-contamination.
- Talking is kept to a minimum — talking releases moisture droplets laden with bacteria.
- Movement in the OR by all personnel is kept to a minimum — movement may encourage turbulent airflow, resulting in cross-contamination.
- Non-scrubbed personnel do not reach over sterile fields — dust or lint may fall on the sterile field.
- Scrubbed team members face each other and the sterile field at all times — a team member's back is not considered sterile.
- Equipment used during surgery must be sterilised — unsterile instruments may be a source of cross-contamination.

B(ii) Gowns are sterile from mid-chest to waist and from gloved hand to 2 inches above the elbow. The back of the gown is not considered sterile even if it is a wraparound gown. Drapes covering instrument tables or the patient should be moisture-proof, because moisture carries bacteria from a non-sterile surface to a sterile surface (strike-through contamination). Sterile tables are sterile only at table height; items hanging over the table edge are considered non-sterile.

A(i) Embryological development:
- The hindgut appears as the cloaca
- It is divided into the urogenital sinus (UGS) and the anorectal canal (ARC) by the urorectal septum
- The proctodaeum and cloacal membrane disintegrate and invaginate to join the ARC
- Failure of any of these steps produces anorectal malformations
- Aetiology of ARM is unknown; incidence is 1:5000 live births; males are slightly more affected; familial cases occur

A(ii) Classification:
Without fistula (or with fistula), categorised as:
- High (supralevator)
- Intermediate (supralevator)
- Low (infralevator)

B) Associated anomalies:
Seen in 50% of cases; more commonly associated with high ARM.
- GIT: Hirschsprung's disease, duodenal atresia, malrotation
- GUS: Cryptorchidism, hypospadias, vesicoureteric reflux, bicornuate uterus
- VACTERL association (Vertebral, Anal, Cardiac, Tracheo-Esophageal, Renal, Limb anomalies)

C) In high ARM, the rectum ends above the levator ani muscle. The proximity of the rectum to the urogenital sinus means fistulae commonly form to the posterior urethra in males and to the vagina in females. This causes: passage of meconium-stained urine, urinary tract infection, and urinary incontinence. Urinary tract anomalies (VUR, renal anomalies) may lead to progressive renal damage and renal functional deficit. The pelvic floor musculature is often poorly developed in high lesions, resulting in impaired sphincter function and faecal incontinence even after surgical repair.
questions.question:
A) Describe the gross anatomy of the anorectal region and the embryological basis of anorectal malformations (ARM) under the following headings:
A(i) Embryological development of the hindgut and formation of the anorectum
A(ii) Classification of ARM by level and fistula

B) State how the level of the ARM relates to the presence of associated anomalies, and list the associated anomaly groups.

C) Explain why disease may spread to distant organ systems in high ARM, and how this causes functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors applicable to this patient:
Age-related: age >50 — the strongest risk factor; rare before 50 but there is a steady rise after this age.
Familial/genetic: 9% of prostate cancers have a hereditary basis; 3-fold increase in men whose first-degree relatives have the disease; risk higher if other family members have had or have it.
Racial: more common in Blacks.
Dietary (probable): high dietary fat consumption (US > Japan); red meat increases risk; intake of fish associated with decreased risk.
Smoking: listed as a risk factor; cadmium in cigarette smoke increases risk.
Hormonal (probable): testosterone and DHT; hardly any cancer in men castrated before puberty.
Potential risk factors: obesity; high vitamin A intake; vitamin D deficiency; sexual behaviour (multiple sex partners, early sexual debut, many STDs); vasectomy before age 35 (not substantiated).

(ii) Epidemiology: commonest malignant tumour in men >65 years in the US; 2nd worldwide. Incidence in Nigeria: 127/100,000 cases (hospital incidence). Age-adjusted incidence in men ≥65 in US: 635 cases/100,000. Western world: 40% lifetime risk of developing prostate cancer; 15% risk of developing symptoms; 3% risk of dying. 1 in 6 men will be diagnosed at some time in their lives. Latent form found in 30% of men >50 years and 60–80% of men >80 years. Post-mortem: 14% of males over 50 and 80% of those over 70 have the disease.

(iii) Complications of untreated locally advanced and metastatic disease:
Local/locally advanced: LUTS (irritative — frequency, urgency, nocturia, urge incontinence, pain on micturition; obstructive — delay, straining, poor stream, overflow incontinence, dribbling, incomplete voiding, intermittency); haematuria; UTI; chronic retention with overflow incontinence; sphincter — urinary incontinence; nerves — suprapubic/perineal pain, impotence; rectum — rectal bleeding, constipation, tenesmus, obstruction.
Metastatic: lumbar spine → low back pain, sciatica; femoral neck → pathological fracture; vertebra/spinal cord → paraplegia; lymph nodes → lymphoedema of lower limbs, anuria, masses.
Widespread: cerebral → headache, nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, epilepsy, paresis; marrow → anaemia, pancytopenia; uraemia from chronic retention and ureteric obstruction; lethargy, weight loss, cachexia.

(iv) Radical prostatectomy is the most appropriate surgical option for early localised disease in a 66-year-old with positive biopsy. Justification: localised disease is the only stage at which cure is possible; radical prostatectomy removes the entire prostate gland, providing histological staging and the best chance of cure. Relative to watchful waiting: watchful waiting (active surveillance) is appropriate only for men with very low-risk disease, significant comorbidities limiting life expectancy, or patient preference; it involves monitoring with DRE, PSA, and observation without intervention. For a patient with multiple risk factors and positive biopsy, watchful waiting risks disease progression to the incurable metastatic stage; radical prostatectomy offers potential cure.
questions.question:
A 66-year-old man with a strong family history of prostate cancer (father and brother both diagnosed) presents for screening. He is an African male who smokes and consumes a high-fat diet with frequent red meat intake.

(i) List all risk factors for carcinoma of the prostate applicable to this patient, classifying them as age-related, familial/genetic, racial, dietary, hormonal, or potential risk factors.
(ii) State the epidemiological burden of the disease — worldwide ranking, incidence in Nigeria, lifetime risk in the Western world for developing symptoms and dying, and the proportion with latent disease by age group.
(iii) Outline all complications that can arise from untreated locally advanced and metastatic carcinoma of the prostate, categorising them by the anatomical structure involved.
(iv) Justify the single most appropriate surgical management option for this patient if biopsy returns positive for early localised disease, and describe its role relative to watchful waiting.

A. Describe the ANATOMY OF LYMPHATICS including the physiology of lymphoedema formation, covering: the composition of the lymphatic system layers; how clinical oedema arises from increased filtration and reduced absorption; and the five microcirculatory abnormality theories explaining the pathogenesis of venous ulceration.
A(i) Describe the WHITE CELL RHEOLOGY THEORY and the FIBRIN CUFF THEORY of Browse and Burnand in detail as given.
B. Describe the VENOUS ULCER: its morphological characteristics, common location, and associated clinical findings.
B(i) Describe the NEUROPATHIC ULCER and the ARTERIAL ULCER, contrasting their location, morphology, and specific clinical findings as given in the comparison table.
questions.answerText:
A. Lymphatic system composition: superficial (primary) lymphatic vessels form a complex dermal network of capillary-like channels with no valves, paralleling superficial veins. These drain into larger secondary lymphatic vessels with valves in the subdermal space. Both drain into a third, deeper layer in subcutaneous fat adjacent to the fascia. An intramuscular system parallels the deep arteries.
Physiology of oedema: increased capillary filtration (from increased capillary hydrostatic pressure, decreased tissue pressure, or increased membrane permeability) combined with reduced interstitial fluid absorption (from decreased plasma oncotic pressure, increased oncotic pressure of tissue fluid, or lymphatic obstruction) leads to accumulation of lymph in the interstitial spaces.
Five microcirculatory abnormality theories of venous ulceration:
1. Tissue anoxia theory of Homans (1917)
2. Arteriovenous shunting theory of Pratt
3. Fibrin cuff theory of Browse and Burnand
4. White cell rheology theory of Falanga and Eaglestein
5. Growth factor trap theory
6. Focal microvascular ischaemia theory of Bollinger
A(i) Fibrin cuff theory (Browse and Burnand): pericapillary fibrin cuffs, found in chronic venous insufficiency, act as an oxygen diffusion barrier. Persistence and continued deposition of fibrin and fibrinogen fragments may inhibit fibroblasts from producing collagen, retarding repair. Alternatively, fibrin and fibrinogen receptor breakdown products are chemotactic for fibroblasts, perpetuating the abnormal state.
White cell rheology theory (Falanga and Eaglestein): with reduced capillary blood flow in venous hypertension, trains of white blood cells cause temporary plugging of capillaries. Glycoproteins cause leukocytes to become attached to the capillary endothelium. These white cells become activated, releasing free radicals, proteolytic enzymes, and cytokines, leading to a chronic inflammatory state that, if severe enough, causes tissue damage and ulceration.
B. Venous ulcer: irregular, shaggy borders; commonly located in the gaiter area (malleolar regions); usually superficial with granulation tissue on the floor; associated findings include lower leg oedema, varicose veins, and haemosiderin pigmentation of surrounding skin.
B(i) Neuropathic ulcer: patient has a history of diabetes; complains of paraesthesia or anaesthesia; deep ulcer located over the heel or metatarsal heads (pressure sites); surrounded by a thick white rim of callus; associated with loss of sensation including light touch, vibration, and joint sense.
Arterial ulcer: suggested by diminished or absent peripheral pulses; abnormal capillary refilling; pain (and intermittent claudication); wound bed often shows a grey or black base (necrotic). ABI is less than or equal to 0.7. Located over pressure sites; morphology shows punched-out edges with a necrotic base; surrounding skin is shiny and atrophic.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old boy presents to clinic with bilateral painless enlargement of cervical lymph nodes for 4 months. He has fever, drenching night sweats and has lost 12% of his body weight. Biopsy of a lymph node reveals Reed-Sternberg cells.
(i) What is the diagnosis and what is the nature and significance of the pathological cell found?
(ii) What is the pattern of spread of this disease compared with Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma?
(iii) What staging system is used and what stage is this patient in based on the clinical information given?
(iv) What investigations are required in the workup of this patient?
(v) What treatment is offered and what features place this patient in the unfavourable prognostic group?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Hodgkin's disease (Hodgkin's lymphoma). The pathological cell is the Reed-Sternberg cell. It is an immune system malignancy involving B or T lymphocytes. Reed-Sternberg cells are the hallmark diagnostic cells of Hodgkin's disease.
(ii) Pattern of spread — Hodgkin's disease: slow, predictable, with extension to contiguous lymph nodes; infiltration to non-lymphoid organs is rare. Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma: spread is aggressive, diffuse, unpredictable; involves lymphoid tissue, bone marrow and CNS infiltration; high growth fraction and doubling time.
(iii) Staging system (Murphy/Ann Arbor): Stage I — tumour at one site (nodal or extranodal); Stage II — two or more sites, same side of body; Stage III — both sides of body but not Stage IV; Stage IV — CNS or marrow involvement (Murphy) or lung, liver, marrow, or bone (Ann Arbor). This patient has bilateral cervical lymph node enlargement plus B symptoms — he is at least Stage II or higher. The bilateral nature and B symptoms suggest Stage III or Stage IV, though CNS/marrow involvement has not been confirmed — staging investigations are needed.
(iv) Investigations: full blood count, abdominal USS, lymph node biopsy (already done — confirms RS cells), bone marrow aspiration/biopsy, lumbar puncture, CT scan, PET scan, bone scan.
(v) Treatment: chemotherapy, radiotherapy, surgery. Unfavourable prognostic features in this patient: age (15 years — above the favourable cut-off of under 10 years); male sex; B symptoms present (fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss); other unfavourable features persistently elevated ESR, lymphocyte depletion histopathology, bulky disease (largest dimension >10 cm).

(i) Diagnosis is myelomeningocele (rachischisis). Unlike a meningocele, which contains only meninges and CSF, myelomeningocele contains exposed neural tissue (the placode). Both are subtypes of spina bifida cystica, which also includes rachischisis/myeloschisis.
(ii) Embryological basis: failure of the neural tube to close results in neural tube defects; the specific form here is spina bifida aperta/cystica. Aetiology is unknown but probably multifactorial — genetic/familial, teratogens, hyperthermia, hypoxia, radiation, vascular causes, infections, trauma, drugs, and dietary factors such as vitamin (folic acid) deficiency.
(iii) Immediate steps: protect the placode from drying up; preserve all neural tissue and its vascular supply; prevent infection; assess for cardiovascular anomalies that may be life-threatening; perform clinical assessment plus US/CT/MRI as indicated; obtain informed consent of parents.
(iv) Definitive closure under general anaesthesia: protect placode from drying; preserve all neural tissue and vascular supply; avoid inclusion dermoids; avoid tethering; look for diastematomyelia and thickened filum; avoid neural compression; achieve wound closure. Timing is influenced by presence of CSF leak, level and type of lesion, degree of skin defect, and cardiovascular anomalies.
(v) Hydrocephalus is present in 80–95% of cases; 10% of cases may not need shunting. Criteria for ventriculo-peritoneal (V-P) shunt include: rapid ventricular enlargement, Chiari II malformation, developmental delay, and cosmetically unpleasant head size.
questions.question:
A newborn is noted at birth to have a sac-like protrusion over the lower spine containing neural tissue and CSF. The overlying skin is absent and the neural placode is exposed. The child has no movement in the lower limbs and the bladder is continuously dribbling urine.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and how does it differ from a meningocele?
(ii) What is the embryological basis of this condition, and what multifactorial aetiological factors are recognised?
(iii) Outline the immediate resuscitative and protective steps that must be taken before surgery.
(iv) Describe the definitive surgical closure, listing the key intraoperative principles that must be observed.
(v) What is the expected incidence of hydrocephalus in this condition, and how is it managed?

questions.answerText:
(i) Premalignant lesions and predisposing conditions for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the skin:
- Sun-damaged skin (actinic keratoses)
- Leukoplakia
- Radiation dermatitis
- Long-standing chronic ulcers and sinuses
- Unstable scars (Marjolin's ulcer)
- Radiation and arsenic/hydrocarbon exposure
(ii) Typical clinical presentations: SCC is typically papillomatous or ulcerative. Common anatomical locations in Nigeria: head and neck region; around the ankles (particularly common in the Nigerian population, often arising in chronic tropical or sickle cell ulcers).
(iii) Predictors of tumour recurrence:
- Degree of differentiation (poorly differentiated tumours recur more)
- Depth of tumour invasion
- Perineural invasion by tumour
(iv) Investigations: X-ray; CT scan; incisional biopsy (for histological diagnosis and grading).
Definitive treatment: local excision of the tumour plus skin cover (skin graft or flap as appropriate). Since there is significant regional lymphadenopathy, dissection of the involved regional lymph nodes is required. Chemotherapy may be used. Radiotherapy: only poorly differentiated lesions are reasonably sensitive.
(v) TNM staging: tumour 6 cm = T3 (tumour greater than 5 cm); regional node metastasis present = N1; no distant metastasis = M0. This corresponds to Stage III disease.
questions.question:
A 45-year-old man presents with a raised, ulcerative, papillomatous lesion around the right ankle that has been growing for two years. He gives a history of a chronic non-healing wound at the same site for five years following a road traffic accident. Biopsy reveals squamous cell carcinoma. Regional lymph nodes are enlarged and firm.
(i) List the premalignant lesions and predisposing conditions for squamous cell carcinoma of the skin.
(ii) State the typical clinical presentations and common anatomical locations in Nigerian patients.
(iii) List the predictors of tumour recurrence for this malignancy.
(iv) Describe the investigations required and the definitive treatment, including management of the regional lymphadenopathy.
(v) State the TNM staging for this lesion if the tumour is 6 cm, node metastasis is present, and there is no distant metastasis.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Embryological basis:
- The GIT forms as a straight tube at the 3rd week of IUL; rapid epithelial proliferation of the duodenum is followed by vacuolisation and recanalisation — failure of recanalisation causes duodenal atresia
- Incidence: 1 in 10,000 live births in Europe
- No familial incidence
- Associated anomalies in 50%; Down's syndrome is the commonest chromosomal anomaly
- Polyhydramnios occurs in 50% of cases due to failure of amniotic fluid absorption

A(ii) Classification by type:
Type I: Stenosis or diaphragm (most common)
Type II: Atresia with a fibrous cord joining the two ends, with intact mesentery
Type III: Atresia, no connecting fibrous cord, with a V-shaped defect in the mesentery
Location: 2nd part of duodenum in 85%, rest 15%

B) Double bubble sign:
The two bubbles represent gas-distended stomach and gas-distended proximal duodenum, with absent gas in the distal GIT (no passage of swallowed air beyond the obstruction). This finding on plain X-ray is diagnostic.
Differences from jejunoileal atresia:
- Duodenal atresia: no abdominal distension (proximal obstruction); bilious vomiting; polyhydramnios common; Down's syndrome association
- Jejunoileal atresia: abdominal distension (more distal obstruction); bilious vomiting; visible peristalsis; failure to pass meconium; barium enema shows microcolon

C) Treatment:
Not an emergency but requires:
Resuscitation: NPO, nasogastric tube, Vitamin K, IV fluids, correct electrolyte abnormalities, IV antibiotics, group and cross-match blood, incubator care, monitor urinary output.
Surgery: Duodenoduodenostomy (primary anastomosis between the two ends of the duodenum; bypasses the obstruction without resection).

A(i) Clinical presentation of intracerebral haemorrhage: rapidly progressive severe headache building over several minutes; often accompanied by focal neurological deficits; nausea and vomiting; decreased level of consciousness. History suggestive: any patient with sudden severe headache, especially if associated with nausea and vomiting, decreased level of consciousness, or focal neurological deficit.
A(ii) Classical features of hypertensive ICH:
- Most patients are over 45 years old.
- Patients have a history of hypertension (treatment may not be preventative).
- Characteristic sites:
 - Basal ganglia/internal capsule: 60%
 - Deep cerebellar nuclei: 10–15%
 - Pons: 10%
 - Thalamus: 10%
B(i) Workup: head CT scan in all patients with suspected haemorrhage; angiography not necessary if all features of classical hypertensive haemorrhage are present.
Treatment: symptomatic management of elevated intracranial pressure; surgery to reduce mass effect in selected cases. Risk of rebleed at the same site is very low.
B(ii) Rapid neurological assessment (1–3 minute exam):
- Respiration and blood pressure.
- GCS: motor function, verbal response, eye opening.
- Pupil size and reactivity: CN 2 (optic — visual input for pupil reflex) and CN 3 (oculomotor — efferent), midbrain.
- Doll's eyes (oculocephalic reflex): CN 8 (vestibulocochlear), CN 3 (oculomotor), CN 6 (abducens), medulla, pons, and midbrain.
- Corneal reflex: CN 5 (trigeminal — afferent), CN 7 (facial — efferent), pons.
- Gag reflex: CN 9 (glossopharyngeal), CN 10 (vagus), medulla.

C(ii) State the female-to-male ratio in Graves' disease and describe the role of anti-TSH receptor antibodies in its pathogenesis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: clinical state of elevated thyroid hormone in tissues, usually due to inappropriately high secretion of thyroid hormones from the thyroid gland; can be overt (decreased TSH, increased T3 and T4) or subclinical (decreased TSH, normal T3 and T4); female preponderance (F:M ratio of 8:1). Aetiology: primary/secondary hyperthyroidism; diffuse toxic goitre (Graves' disease); toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer's disease); solitary toxic nodule (Goetsch's disease); Jode-Basedow's disease (increased doses of iodides); thyrotoxicosis factitial (increased doses of thyroxine); neonatal thyrotoxicosis; struma ovarii; iatrogenic from drugs like amiodarone; thyroid carcinoma.
A(ii) Symptoms — GIT: weight loss, increased appetite, loose stools. CVS: palpitations, dyspnoea, angina. Neuromusculoskeletal: irritability, nervousness, insomnia, heat intolerance, weakness, fatigue, fine tremors, increased linear growth. Genitourinary: oligo- or amenorrhea, increased urinary frequency. Integument: hair loss, gynaecomastia, pruritus.
B(i) Investigations: TFTs (increased T3, increased T4, decreased TSH); serum thyroglobulin; serum calcitonin; cervical x-ray (AP, lateral, thoracic inlet views); soft tissue ultrasonography of the neck; indirect laryngoscopy; radio-isotope scan (123I or 99Tc); TRH assay; FBC; ECG; anti-thyroid antibodies.
B(ii) Complications: thyroid storm; thyrocardia. Treatment: anti-thyroid drugs (carbimazole, methimazole, propylthiouracil, propranolol, Lugol's iodine); thyroidectomy (subtotal or total); radioactive iodine therapy. Follow-up: thyroid function tests; post-total thyroidectomy patient will require L-thyroxine for life.
C(i) Graves' disease: autoimmune disease characterised by persistent activation of TSH receptors by anti-TSH receptor antibodies leading to increased synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones. Graves' orbitopathy: proptosis, eyelid retraction, chemosis, periorbital oedema, decreased ocular muscle motility, corneal lesions, optic nerve compression, loss of vision. Also: myxoedema, oedema of the digits (acropachy).
C(ii) Female preponderance: Graves' disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism and shows F:M ratio of 1:8 (i.e., far commoner in females), typically between 20 and 40 years old. Anti-TSH receptor antibodies persistently activate TSH receptors, leading to increased synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones — this autoimmune activation is the specific pathogenesis of Graves' disease.

A(i) Resection and primary docking: entails resection of a damaged or infected segment of bone; the bone defect following resection should not exceed 2–3 cm, otherwise there will be excessive buckling of soft tissue and unacceptable limb-length discrepancy; the resected bone ends are flushed and docked (brought together) avoiding implants; patients may need a shoe raise; following union of the primarily docked site, the bone can be distracted. It is unpopular in developed countries because of the attendant limb length discrepancies.
A(ii) Chondrodiastasis (growth plate distraction): a form of distraction osteogenesis in which the growth plate is distracted without a preceding corticotomy or osteotomy; used for either congenital or acquired limb shortening; reserved close to the end of bone growth; distraction rate is 0.5 mm daily (compared to 1 mm/day in callotaxis); the regenerate in chondrodiastasis is usually bigger and more robust than that produced by callotaxis.
B(i) Xenograft: commonest form is bovine bone chips or bovine bone granules; rendered non-reactive by rigorous chemical treatment or ionising irradiation; mechanism of action: osteoconductive (acts as scaffold for new bone formation) — chips or granules mixed with recipient blood before grafting; used for small defects only. Unpopular in developing countries because these processed bone chips are not cheap (expensive).
B(ii) Vascularised autografts are superior because: they carry their own arterial supply; they are viable right from the time of implantation (unlike non-vascularised grafts which undergo necrosis first); they behave like healing fractures at the recipient bed; they can undergo hypertrophy with appropriate loading, conferring strength and allowing early weight bearing. Three specific clinical conditions: (1) large bony defects following resection of bone tumours (usually benign); (2) reconstruction of congenital pseudoarthrosis of the tibia; (3) cases of non-union of femoral neck fractures.

A(i) Urological organs are well protected by: surrounding viscera, muscles, and skeleton; their inherent mobility. Kidneys: protected by lower ribs, lumbar muscles, perirenal fat and Gerota's fascia, and the liver and spleen anteriorly. Ureters: rarely injured — protected by their retroperitoneal position, small calibre, and mobility. Bladder: protected by the pubic bone anteriorly and pelvic viscera; when empty is entirely pelvic; when full rises into the abdomen. Urethra: the posterior urethra is fixed and vulnerable to pelvic fractures; the anterior urethra is exposed in the perineum.

A(ii) Ureteric injuries: the ureters are rarely injured; they are only very occasionally hit by penetrating missiles. Bladder rupture:
Intraperitoneal: history — blunt force to full bladder (RTA, fall from height), fractured pelvis, deceleration injury, lack of sensation of bladder fullness, haematuria, inability to void, diffuse lower abdominal tenderness. Management: explore within 48 hours (surgical repair of dome tear).
Extraperitoneal: associated with pelvic fracture, extravasation confined to perivesical space. Management: catheterize and continuous drainage of urine (conservative).
Investigation for both: cystogram; post-evacuation film.

B(i) Posterior urethra: comprises prostatomembranous urethra; fixed at the apex of the prostate by puboprostatic ligaments; disrupted by pelvic fractures.
Anterior urethra: comprises bulbar and pendulous (penile) urethra; exposed in the perineum. Mechanism of anterior injury: fall astride or kick in the perineum. Clinical pattern: extravasation of blood and urine at the site of rupture, leading to swelling of penis and scrotum/perineum.
Clinical finding unique to posterior urethral injury: high-riding prostate on rectal examination (prostate floats superiorly when urethral support is disrupted). Additional findings in posterior injury: blood at external urethral meatus; inability to void with full bladder; RUG shows extravasation of contrast at site of rupture; associated fractured pelvis.

B(ii) Injuries to the penis:
- Fractured penis (rupture of corpus cavernosum).
- Strangulating metal objects around the erect penis.
- Penile amputation.
- Degloving injury.
Management of penile amputation: (1) ice the amputated part immediately — the critical first step at the scene; (2) send to a centre where microvascular surgery can be performed for replantation.

A. Describe the PRESSURE SORE under the following headings: definition, aetiology (extrinsic and intrinsic factors), clinical grading (Grades I–IV), and treatment appropriate for each grade.
A(i) State which anatomical region accounts for the majority of pressure sores and what percentage arise there.

questions.answerText:
A. Definition: a pressure sore is due to ischaemia from prolonged pressure between a surface (e.g., bed) and an area of the body over a bony prominence. The majority develop in the lower part of the body.
Aetiology:
- Extrinsic factors: prolonged pressure (worsened by a hard or firm mattress); shear forces; friction (strips outer skin layer from inner layer).
- Intrinsic factors: infection; hypoproteinaemia; anaemia; sensory loss; impaired mobility; faecal and urinary incompetence.
Clinical grading:
- Grade I: limited to epidermis and superficial dermis.
- Grade II: full-thickness skin damage with subcutaneous tissue exposure.
- Grade III: extends down to muscle.
- Grade IV: bone or joint involvement.
Treatment by grade:
- Grades I, II, III: conservative treatment comprising control of infection, debridement, avoidance of pressure using special cushion (fenestrated foam) or special bed (Clinitron, low air loss).
- Grade IV: surgery consisting of wide excision of the ulcer with its underlying bursa and underlying bone resection; padding of residual bone and obliteration of dead space; closure with a flap (skin graft has a very limited role).
A(i) 75% of pressure sores arise in the hip/buttock area.
B. Treatment modalities for abnormal scars:
- Surgery: excisional, graft, flap, revisional, and scar release.
- Intralesional triamcinolone injection
- Superficial low-voltage radiotherapy
- Silastic gel and cream
- Pressure garment

questions.question:
A 17-year-old male is brought in following a penetrating abdominal stab wound. He is haemodynamically unstable with obvious peritoneal signs. The wound is over the right upper quadrant.
(i) What are the absolute indications for laparotomy in penetrating abdominal trauma?
(ii) What are the most commonly injured organs in stab wounds, and what proportion of stab wounds penetrate the peritoneum?
(iii) Describe the procedure and criteria for diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) in the management of this patient.
(iv) What are the complications of penetrating abdominal trauma?
questions.answerText:
(i) Absolute indications for laparotomy: Haemodynamic instability; Major vascular injuries; Pneumoperitoneum; Significant intraperitoneal blood.
(ii) Most commonly injured organs in stab wounds: Small intestine (29%), liver (28%), colon (23%). 33% of stab wounds penetrate the peritoneum; 50% of those require surgery.
(iii) Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL): 1,000 cc of warm Ringer's lactate solution (20 cc/kg for paediatric patients) is infused rapidly and allowed to return by placing the IV bag on the floor. Analysis includes: cell count, differential, Gram stain, bilirubin, amylase, vegetable matter, and faecal matter (the newspaper test). Result is positive if: 50,000–100,000 RBC count and/or 100–500 WBC count; bile or particulate debris (e.g., food fibres) is unequivocally positive. Hollow viscus injuries may yield as few as 1,000 RBCs. In unstable patients: a supine CXR followed by a FAST examination or DPL (open technique). If FAST exploration or DPL results are positive — laparotomy.
(iv) Complications: Wound failure; Intestinal injury; Malnutrition; Deep vein thrombosis; Stress ulceration; Pressure ulceration; Intra-abdominal infection; Abdominal compartment syndrome.

(i) Lung abscess — a cavity containing pus and necrotic debris in the lung parenchyma; the classic radiographic appearance is a cavity with an air-fluid level, with or without surrounding infiltrate.

(ii) Predisposing factors for aspiration lung abscess: unconsciousness; vocal cord paralysis; periodontal infection; alcoholism; seizure disorder; cerebrovascular accident (CVA); head trauma; general anaesthesia; drug addiction; dysphagia; gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD); mechanical interference with the cardiac sphincter such as nasogastric tubes and endotracheal intubation; periodontal disease and gingivitis.

(iii) Three common sites: (1) apical segment of the right lower lobe; (2) apical segment of the left lower lobe; (3) posterior segment of the right lower lobe.

(iv) A double-lumen endotracheal tube is used during operative drainage (also used in lung resection for massive haemoptysis). Surgical treatment options: pneumostomy; lobectomy.

(i) Diagnosis: Oesophageal atresia (OA) with distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula (TOF).
The classical and most common variety: blind upper pouch associated with a distal TOF, accounting for 70–80% of cases.
Frequency: 1 in 3,000–4,000 live births.

(ii) Predisposing factors and VACTERL:
- Maternal polyhydramnios
- Congenital heart lesions ("The Midline Muck-Up")
- Chromosomal anomalies 13–15 groups
- Asymptomatic crying facies
VACTERL Association:
V – Vertebral anomaly
A – Anal anomaly
C – Cardiac anomaly
T – Tracheo-oesophageal fistula
E – (implied)
R – Renal anomaly
L – Limb anomalies

(iii) Immediate pre-operative management:
- Head-up position in incubator
- Humidification with O2
- Antibiotics
- Intravenous fluids
- Replogle tube in situ
- Dutiful manual suction of pharynx hourly (physiotherapy)
- Gastrostomy if abdominal distension is causing respiratory embarrassment
- Expansion of the lung (especially RUL) in 24–48 hours

(iv) Definitive procedure: Modified Haight operation using the Denis Browne axillary incision or a postero-lateral extrapleural thoracotomy.
Post-operative complications:
- Cough
- Oesophageal stricture (stenosis)
- Anastomotic rupture
- Recurrence of TOF
- Cyanotic or 'dying' spells from laryngospasm

A 32-year-old woman presents with an extensive flame burn involving approximately 30% of the total body surface area (TBSA) following a kerosene stove explosion. She is restless, tachycardic, and thirsty.

(i) Using any two of the standard formulae, calculate the fluid requirement for this patient in the first 24 hours (assume weight 60 kg, 30% TBSA).
(ii) Describe the systemic effects of burns on the cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, renal, haematological, and immunological systems.
(iii) List the indications for admission into a burns unit.
(iv) Outline the resuscitation algorithm (ABCDE approach) and state the target urinary output.
questions.answerText:
(i) Parkland formula: 3–4 ml x 60 kg x 30% = 5,400–7,200 ml over 48 hours (based on Ringer's lactate). Half is given within 8 hours of the burn, the remaining half over the next 16 hours. Half of the fluid given in the first 24 hours is given on day 2. Evans formula: Colloids (plasma, dextran-70) = 1 ml x 60 x 30 = 1,800 ml; Crystalloids (Ringer's lactate/saline) = 1 ml x 60 x 30 = 1,800 ml, given in the same pattern as Parkland.

(ii) CVS: Hypovolaemic shock; cardiac depression from cytokines and K+ abnormalities. Respiratory: Increased respiratory rate; air hunger if there is inhalational burn with respiratory distress syndrome. GIT: Paralytic ileus, which may lead to translocation of gut micro-organisms into systemic circulation causing septicaemia; Curling's ulcer. Renal: Acute tubular necrosis leading to acute renal failure. Haematological: Anaemia due to undernutrition, damaged RBCs, daily blood loss from wound dressing, and bone marrow depression; RBC lifespan drops from 120 to 40 days. Immunological: Depression of resistance to sepsis caused by depression of plasma cells producing IgG, IgM, IgC; decrease in T4/T8 ratio impairing cellular immunity.

(iii) Indications for burns unit admission: (1) Inhalational burns; (2) Burns size >10% TBSA in <10 years or >50 years of age; (3) Burns size >20% TBSA in any age; (4) Full-thickness burns involving >5% TBSA; (5) Special burns involving the face, hands, feet, perineum, genitals, circumferential and flexural areas; (6) Associated trauma such as fractures, spinal injury, visceral injuries; (7) Comorbid conditions such as diabetes mellitus; (8) Special social situations such as abuse, psychiatric conditions.

(iv) Airway and cervical spine should be secured. Breathing and ventilation should be maintained. Circulation should be maintained. Disability (neurological status) should be ascertained. Exposure and environmental control. Fluid therapy: 14G cannula (CVL) in adults, 20G in children. Fluid should be accurate and titrated with urinary output of 0.5 ml/kg/hour in adults and 1–2 ml/kg/hour in children.

A(i) Anterior triangle: bounded by the sternocleidomastoid posteriorly, the midline anteriorly, and the mandible superiorly. Contains the majority of important vascular and visceral organs. Posterior triangle: delineated by the sternocleidomastoid, the trapezius, and the clavicle (with the exception of the region just superior to the clavicle). Except for individual nerves to specific muscles, few vital structures cross the posterior triangle.
A(ii) Clinical basis for vulnerability of anterior triangle: With the neck protected by the spine posteriorly, the head superiorly, and the chest inferiorly, the anterior and lateral regions are most exposed to injury. The larynx and trachea are situated anteriorly and are readily exposed to harm. The spinal cord lies posteriorly, cushioned by the vertebral bodies, muscles, and ligaments. The oesophagus and major blood vessels lie between the airway and spine.
B(i) Penetrating neck trauma — structures at risk: Vascular injuries — internal jugular vein (9%), carotid artery (7%). Visceral injuries — pharynx or oesophagus (5–15%), larynx or trachea (4–12%). Major nerve injury (3–8%).
B(ii) Blunt neck trauma mechanisms of blood vessel injury: Direct forces can shear the vasculature. Excessive rotation and/or hyperextension of the cervical spine causes distension and stretching of arteries and veins to the point of rupture. Intraoral trauma may extend to the blood supply. Basilar skull fractures may disrupt the intrapetrous portion of the carotid artery. Blunt impact to the anterior neck may crush the larynx or trachea, particularly at the cricoid ring, and compress the oesophagus against the posterior spinal column.

questions.answerText:
(i) Definition: tortuous, dilated, prominent superficial veins in the lower limbs, often in the anatomical distribution of the long and short saphenous veins.
Aetiology: primary or familial; pregnancy (progesterone causes passive dilatation); secondary to postphlebitic limb (perforator failure); congenital (Klippel–Trenaunay syndrome; Parkes–Weber syndrome); iatrogenic (following arteriovenous fistula).
Pathophysiology: venous valve failure, usually at the saphenofemoral junction (and sometimes in perforating veins), results in increased venous pressure in the long saphenous vein with progressive vein dilatation and further valve disruption.
(ii) Clinical features:
- Asymptomatic; cosmetic appearance.
- Dull aching leg pain; heaviness in the leg (worse in the evening or on standing for long periods); itching and eczema; superficial thrombophlebitis; bleeding; saphena varix; ulceration.
- Chronic features: venous eczema; haemosiderin deposits; lipodermatosclerosis; malleolar 'flare'; onychogryposis; venous ulceration.
(iii) Investigations:
- Clinical assessment by Trendelenburg tourniquet tests.
- Doppler velocimetry: assess sapheno-femoral junction/short sapheno-popliteal junction.
- Duplex scanning: identify recurrence site (especially recurrent varicose veins).
(iv) Venous ulcer: due to venous hypertension secondary to incompetent perforating veins or the long saphenous vein; occurs medially above the ankle; shallow with sloping edges; bleeds after minor trauma; weeps readily; associated dermatoliposclerosis; surrounding 'corona phlebectatica' of varicose veins; sloughy and painless compared with arterial ulcers.
(v) Management:
- Conservative: avoid long periods of standing; elevate limbs; wear support hosiery.
- Injection sclerotherapy (sodium tetradecyl): suitable for small veins, usually only below the knee; patients encouraged to walk several miles daily; complications: anaphylaxis and local ulceration.
- Surgical ablation: mark dilated veins with the patient standing; surgically disconnect the saphenous vein from the femoral vein; ablate perforators; remove elongated veins via multiple stab incisions; long segments above the knee removed using a vein stripper; postoperatively compression stockings worn for several weeks. Most effective for large varicose veins but recurrence rates are high.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Embryological basis:
The anterior abdominal wall is formed by the convergence of the cranial, caudal, and two lateral folds at the centre. The cephalic fold forms the epigastric region, the caudal fold the hypogastric region, and the lateral folds the central umbilical ring. Exomphalos results from failure of development of these abdominal folds (cranial, caudal, lateral), or from persistence of the body stalk, so that the bowel remains herniated at the umbilical ring. Gastroschisis results from vascular accidents or prenatal rupture of an exomphalos, causing a full-thickness wall defect lateral to the umbilicus without a sac.

A(ii) Structural differences:
Feature — Exomphalos / Gastroschisis
Location — Umbilical ring / Lateral (to the right)
Defect — 4–10 cm / <4 cm
Sac — Intact or ruptured / Absent
Cord attachment — Onto the sac / Normal
Intestinal appearance — Normal / Abnormal (dilated, inflamed, oedematous, thickened, leathery, shortened)

B) Associated anomalies, abdominal cavity, liver:
Exomphalos — Liver: often present in sac (48%); abdominal cavity: small (reduced due to herniation); associated anomalies: common (40–80%) including chromosomal (trisomies 13, 18, 21), cardiac (30%), BWS, Pentalogy of Cantrell; bowel atresia: rare.
Gastroschisis — Liver: excluded from defect (rare); abdominal cavity: normal size; associated anomalies: rare; bowel atresia: common (due to vascular compromise).

C) Management principles:
Conservative management (exomphalos): indicated for major exomphalos (>4 cm) with severe associated anomalies and intact membrane. Paint with escharotic/antimicrobial agents (70% alcohol, 2.5% formal saline, 2% silver sulphadiazine cream, Lugol's iodine, mercurochrome, GV) — aim: convert to ventral hernia; oral antibiotics.
Surgical management:
Indicated for: minor exomphalos (<4 cm), ruptured exomphalos, no significant anomalies.
Options: primary closure; skin closure (causes incisional hernia); silo (staged closure). Resuscitation precedes surgery for ruptured cases (incubator, IVF, IV antibiotics, NGT + NPO, Vitamin K, intestinal bag, monitor urinary output).

questions.answerText:
A(i) Increased hydrostatic pressure: Impaired venous return — congestive heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, ascites (liver cirrhosis), venous obstruction or compression, thrombosis, external pressure (e.g., mass), lower extremity inactivity with prolonged dependency. Arteriolar dilation — heat, neurohumoral dysregulation.
A(ii) Reduced plasma osmotic pressure (hypoproteinaemia): Protein-losing glomerulopathies (nephrotic syndrome); liver cirrhosis (ascites); malnutrition; protein-losing gastroenteropathy.
B(i) Lymphatic obstruction: Inflammatory; neoplastic; postsurgical; postirradiation.
B(ii) Sodium retention: Excessive salt intake with renal insufficiency; increased tubular reabsorption of sodium; renal hypoperfusion; increased renin-angiotensin-aldosterone secretion.
C(i) Subcutaneous oedema: finger pressure displaces interstitial fluid, leaving a depression — pitting oedema; diffuse or conspicuous in regions with high hydrostatic pressures. Lungs: often two to three times normal weight; sectioning yields frothy, blood-tinged fluid — mixture of air, oedema, and extravasated red cells. Brain: soft and heavy; gyri flattened and sulci narrowed; severe cerebral oedema leads to herniation of cerebral tonsils with lethal consequences; patients suffer vomiting, disorientation, and convulsions.
C(ii) Exudate: increased vascular permeability leads to inflammatory oedema that is rich in proteins. Transudate: oedema due to hydrodynamic derangements that is protein poor. Clinical consequences: subcutaneous oedema indicates potential underlying cardiac or renal disease, can impair wound healing and affects clearance of infection. Pulmonary oedema is commonly seen in left ventricular failure, renal failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and pulmonary inflammation or infection. Brain oedema is dangerous because the rigidity of the cranium allows little room for expansion.
