B(ii) Sodium retention — state the mechanisms.
C(i) Explain the morphological appearances of oedema in the subcutaneous tissues, lungs and brain.
C(ii) Distinguish between exudate and transudate, and state the clinical consequences of oedema at each site.

questions.answerText:
(i) Likely injured structures: larynx and/or trachea. The hallmark sign of disruption to the aerodigestive tract is crepitus.
(ii) Mechanisms of blunt injury to the larynx or trachea: A sudden increase in intratracheal pressure against a closed glottis (e.g., improper wearing of a seat belt); A crush/bruise (e.g., clothesline tackle); A rapid acceleration-deceleration action. Impact to the exposed anterior aspect of the neck may crush the larynx or trachea, particularly at the cricoid ring, or compress the oesophagus against the posterior spinal column.
(iii) Paediatric versus adult larynx: The narrowest portion of the larynx is at the C4 level in children, compared with C7 in adults. Children's necks tend to be relatively smaller than those of adults, lessening the risk of direct anterior damage to the neck. The significance: interventions such as surgical airways must account for the higher laryngeal position in children. Also, child abuse should always be considered in children with any type of neck injury.
(iv) Workup: Standard trauma blood studies (CBC, electrolytes, blood chemistry, blood type and cross-matching); coagulation profiles in those with comorbid disease or in shock; alcohol and toxicology screens when indicated. Imaging: cervical X-rays; chest X-ray; supplementary tests: CT scans, MRIs, colour flow Doppler studies, contrast studies of the oesophagus, interventional angiograms, endoscopic images. Procedures: Laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy, pharyngoscopy, and oesophagoscopy. Management priorities: Determine airway patency, breathing, and adequacy of circulation; Fully expose the patient; Airway obstruction and exsanguinating haemorrhage pose the most immediate risks to life and must be addressed first.
questions.question:
A 14-year-old boy presents to the emergency department following blunt neck trauma from a road traffic accident. He has stridor, subcutaneous emphysema, dysphonia, and pain on palpation of the anterior neck.
(i) What structures are likely injured, and what is the hallmark sign of disruption to the aerodigestive tract?
(ii) What are the mechanisms by which blunt trauma can injure the larynx or trachea?
(iii) How does the anatomy of the paediatric larynx differ from the adult, and what is the significance of this difference?
(iv) Describe the workup and initial management priorities for this patient.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is biliary atresia.

(ii) Most common type:
- Type III (atresia at the porta hepatis) accounts for 84% of cases.

(iii) Pre-operative preparation:
- Continue vitamin K administration.
- Prevent hypoglycaemia: administer a glucose load.
- Prepare bowel (to prevent hepatic encephalopathy).
- Perioperative antibiotics.
- Ensure good renal perfusion: aim for a minimum of 2 mL/kg/hour of urine output.

(iv) Definitive procedure, timing, and outcome:
- The definitive procedure is portoenterostomy (Kasai operation).
- Timing is critical: best results are achieved when done before 90 days of age.
- Outcome if done in good time:
 - 25–85% will achieve bile drainage (half of these will be cured and half will develop progressive liver problems).
 - 15–30% will have no bile flow.
 - Overall: one third will be cured, one third will deteriorate after initial bile flow, and one third will never achieve any bile flow.
questions.question:
A six-week-old infant presents with persistent jaundice since birth, pale stools, dark urine, and progressive hepatomegaly. Ultrasound shows a small or non-visualised gallbladder and a triangular cord sign at the porta hepatis. Serum conjugated bilirubin fraction is greater than 20%.

(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the most common type of this condition (by classification) and the percentage of cases it accounts for.
(iii) Describe the pre-operative preparation for surgery, including the specific steps involved.
(iv) Name the definitive surgical procedure, state the critical timing for best results, and describe the outcome if portoenterostomy is done in good time.

A 65-year-old man presents with urinary hesitancy, poor stream, and post-void dribbling for 8 months. He is now unable to void at all. On digital rectal examination, the prostate is enlarged and smooth.

(i) Using the surgical history-taking principles, list the specific symptoms you would explore and the additional symptoms that would point to different diagnoses.
(ii) What are the potential causes of difficulty in passing urine, including neurological, drug-related, and obstructive causes?
(iii) Describe the key feature that distinguishes BPH from urethral stricture when a patient strains to void.
(iv) What is the significance of haematuria in this presentation, and what questions about its character are diagnostically relevant?
questions.answerText:
(i) Specific urinary symptoms to explore: nocturia, straining, dribbling, poor stream, hesitancy, frequency, urgency, haematuria. Additional symptoms pointing to different diagnoses: back pain and weight loss (suggest malignancy); groin swelling (suggests hernia); history of urethral discharge (suggests stricture/STD); history of trauma (RTA with fracture or falling astride, suggesting urethral injury or spinal cord injury); difficulty that relieves when patient pauses to catch breath (BPH pattern); passage of only a trickle despite straining (urethral stricture pattern).

(ii) Potential causes: BPH; urethral stricture; STD; past history of surgery to the penis; past history of RTA causing spinal cord injury; constipation (faecal impaction); drugs (e.g. sedatives); circumcision (if relevant); history of falling astride (perineal trauma).

(iii) Key distinguishing feature: in BPH, the patient strains severely while passing urine, but when the patient stops to catch his breath, urine starts flowing. In urethral stricture, the patient strains and only a trickle of urine is passed regardless of rest.

(iv) In the history of haematuria: type matters diagnostically — initial haematuria (blood at start of stream) suggests urethral origin; terminal haematuria (blood at end) suggests bladder neck or prostatic urethra; total haematuria (whole stream) most likely from bladder or upper urinary tract. Duration of haematuria is also significant: haematuria of weeks suggests infection or neoplasm; months or years suggests TB, hydronephrosis, polycystic kidneys, schistosomiasis, or calculi. Past history of sickle cell disease and drugs (e.g. rifampicin, anticoagulants) should also be asked.

questions.question:
A(i) Define chronic pancreatitis and describe the ductal obstruction hypothesis for its pathophysiology, including the sequence of events from chronic alcohol use to parenchymal damage.
A(ii) Describe the toxic-metabolic hypothesis of chronic pancreatitis, listing the specific mechanisms by which alcohol causes direct injury to acinar and ductal cells.
B(i) List eight complications of chronic pancreatitis, and explain why cobalamin (vitamin B12) malabsorption occurs as one of them.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition and ductal obstruction hypothesis:
- Chronic pancreatitis is irreversible damage to the pancreas with histological evidence of inflammation, fibrosis, and destruction of exocrine (acinar) and endocrine (islets of Langerhans) tissue.
- Ductal obstruction hypothesis sequence:
 1. Chronic alcohol use affects acinar and ductal cells.
 2. Produces protein-rich pancreatic juice, low in volume and bicarbonate.
 3. Formation of protein precipitates — plug.
 4. Calcification of precipitate — ductal stone formation.
 5. Ductule obstruction.
 6. Parenchymal damage.

A(ii) Toxic-metabolic hypothesis (alcohol):
- Direct injurious effect on acinar and ductal cells.
- Increased membrane lipid peroxidation (oxidative stress) and free radical production.
- Increased acinar cell sensitivity to pathogenic stimuli.
- Stimulation of CCK production (from duodenal I cells) and activation of pro-inflammatory transcription factors.
- Activation of pancreatic stellate cells (by alcohol and cytokines) — produce proteins of the extracellular matrix.

B(i) Eight complications:
- Cobalamin malabsorption.
- Diabetes mellitus (but end organ damage of DM and DKA are rare).
- Non-DM retinopathy (peripheral) due to vitamin A and zinc deficiency.
- Pleural, peritoneal, and pericardial effusions with high amylase.
- GI bleeding (peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, pseudocyst, varices from splenic vein thrombosis).
- Cholestasis, icterus, cholangitis, biliary cirrhosis.
- Fistula (internal or external).
- Subcutaneous fat necrosis (tender red nodules on the shins).
- Pseudocyst, obstruction.
- Pancreatic carcinoma (4% lifetime risk).
- Narcotic addiction.
(Any eight.)

Cobalamin malabsorption basis: excess binding by cobalamin binding proteins other than intrinsic factor; these binding proteins are normally degraded by pancreatic enzymes, so when pancreatic enzyme secretion is deficient, these binding proteins persist and outcompete intrinsic factor for cobalamin.

(i) Diagnosis: Nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumour). Principal differential: Neuroblastoma.
Distinguishing features:
- Nephroblastoma: smooth surface; pain in 50%; usually does not cross midline; does not regress; normal urinary VMA; IVU shows calyceal/pelvic deformity.
- Neuroblastoma: knobby contour; usually painless; usually crosses midline; may regress; urinary VMA is increased; IVU shows kidney displaced with normal anatomy.

(ii) Epidemiology: 2nd commonest solid abdominal tumour in infancy and early childhood; incidence 1/200,000; accounts for 8% of renal tumours; 80% of patients are <4 years; M:F ratio equal; aetiology unknown, 1% are familial; 15% associated with other congenital anomalies including aniridia, hemihypertrophy, and genitourinary anomalies.

(iii) Staging: Stage I — tumour confined to kidney and completely resectable; Stage II — extends beyond kidney but still completely resectable; Stage III — residual tumour in abdomen after resection (local infiltration); Stage IV — spread to distant organs (lungs, liver, bone, brain); Stage V — bilateral. Most patients under 2 years have Stage I and II tumours. Distant metastasis is by bloodstream to lungs (commonest site), liver, brain, and bones. The tumour is well encapsulated until advanced; renal pelvis is involved in <half; bilateral in 5–10%.

(iv) Surgery is the mainstay, combined with radiotherapy/chemotherapy.
- Stage I (favourable histology): actinomycin D and vincristine for 6 months.
- Unfavourable Stage I or favourable Stage II: actinomycin D and vincristine for 15 months.
- Stage III or unfavourable Stage II: radiotherapy (1000 cGy) to tumour bed and whole abdomen plus chemotherapy for 15 months (actinomycin D, vincristine, adriamycin).
- Stage IV: radiotherapy plus actinomycin D, vincristine, adriamycin ± cyclophosphamide.
- Stage V: downstaging with radiotherapy/chemotherapy, then partial nephrectomy.
Investigations to guide management: IVU — establishes diagnosis, assesses contralateral kidney, distinguishes from neuroblastoma; USS and CT scan — diagnosis and detection of tumour extension; CXR — tumour extension; percutaneous needle biopsy — histology.
questions.question:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the paediatric surgery clinic with a large abdominal swelling that his mother noticed while bathing him one week ago. He has had mild abdominal pain in 50% of his activities. Examination reveals a smooth-surfaced, non-crossing abdominal mass that does not cross the midline. Urinary VMA is normal.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis and identify the principal differential diagnosis that must be excluded, distinguishing the two on all listed clinical and investigative features.
(ii) List the risk factors and epidemiological features of this tumour as provided.
(iii) Describe the staging system used for this tumour and outline the complications that arise if untreated, including routes of distant metastasis.
(iv) Outline the surgical and combined management options for each stage, justifying the choice of therapy for this patient.

A(i) Define urethroplasty, state its indication as a reconstructive procedure, and describe the two principal indications for which it is performed.
A(ii) Describe all named types of urethroplasty available for both the anterior and posterior urethra, including the number of stages, the tissue used, and any eponymous descriptions provided.
B(i) Enumerate all complications of urethroplasty and explain the clinical basis for hair ball and calculus formation when hair-bearing skin is used as a graft.
B(ii) Distinguish excision and end-to-end anastomosis from plastic surgical procedures — explain why excision and anastomosis is suitable only for short strictures, and state the advantage of island skin implantation over the two-stage procedure.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Urethroplasty in simple terms means repair of the urethra; it is a form of reconstructive surgery. It is undertaken when other modalities of treatment (e.g. bouginage) cannot be used or fail to give lasting relief of obstructive symptoms. It is a very demanding operation; quality of life after surgery is greatly improved, though like every procedure it is fraught with complications.
Principal indications: (1) urethral strictures, usually from traumatic injury e.g. fracture of the pelvis; (2) some forms of hypospadias.

A(ii) Types of urethroplasty:
Anterior urethra:
- Excision and end-to-end anastomosis: suitable for short strictures resulting from trauma; tension at suture lines is minimal, hence preventing breakdown.
- Two-stage urethroplasty (Swinney's procedure): first stage — laying open the stricture from end to end; second stage (after first stage has healed) — a buried full-thickness skin graft is used to reconstitute the urethra.
- Island skin implantation: single-stage procedure; a strip of skin left on a pedicle of subcutaneous tissue is used as a buried viable graft for repair. Quatey's vascularised penile skin flap can also be used.
- Free skin graft/meshed skin graft: takes shorter operating time with comparable results.
Posterior urethra:
- Quatey's vascularised skin flap: graft take is high with little or no hair growth.
- Inverted U-shaped scrotal flap operation (Orandi/Blandy): two-stage urethroplasty; first stage — stricture exposed and a flap of scrotal skin is sewn into the defect; second stage — a full-thickness skin tube is formed.

B(i) Complications of urethroplasty: infections; haematoma; urethrocutaneous fistula; re-stenosis; hair ball formation if graft is from hair-bearing skin; calculus, usually composed of hair; carcinoma of the urethra.
Clinical basis: when hair-bearing skin is used as a graft, hairs grow within the neourethra, accumulate, become matted, and form a hair ball; urinary salts then deposit on the hair ball forming a calculus.

B(ii) Excision and end-to-end anastomosis is suitable only for short strictures because tension at the suture line increases with the length of tissue excised; excessive tension causes suture line breakdown and recurrence of stricture. Plastic surgical procedures are required for longer strictures where direct anastomosis would be under tension.
Island skin implantation (single-stage) is advantageous over the two-stage procedure (Swinney's) because it completes the repair in one operation, reducing the total number of anaesthetics, hospital admissions, patient discomfort, and waiting time between stages. The vascularised pedicle ensures graft viability.

(i) Diagnosis: cervical spondylotic myelopathy secondary to degenerative cervical disc disease. Clinical syndrome: myelopathy. Most commonly responsible levels: 60% at C6/7; 30% at C5/6.
(ii) All clinical features:
- Pain: radicular; worse with neck movement especially extension, sneezing, coughing; headache; occipital pain; possible dizziness.
- Sensory: numbness; paraesthesia; tingling sensation.
- Motor: weakness; loss of dexterity; muscle atrophy; clumsy gait; spasm.
- Autonomic/sphincteric: sphincteric anomaly; erectile dysfunction.
- Signs: Lhermitte's sign; myotomal loss; dermatomal loss; DTR loss; upper and lower motor neuron signs.
(iii) Investigations: X-ray (AP, lateral, oblique); MRI (non-operative and pre-surgical planning); CT scan; plain myelography/CT myelography; electrophysiology tests; others as indicated.
(iv) Non-operative: rest; avoid lifting heavy objects; analgesia; antispasmodic/muscle relaxants; physiotherapy; rigid neck collar; cervical traction.
Operative indications: worsening neurological condition; myelopathy; failed conservative management.
Surgical procedures:
- Anterior: discectomy ± fusion and instrumentation; arthroplasty.
- Posterior: discectomy; laminectomy; laminoplasty.
(v) Three clinical syndromes: radiculopathy; myelopathy; radiculomyelopathy.
questions.question:
A 52-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive difficulty walking described as clumsy gait and imbalance. He also has bilateral hand numbness, weakness and loss of dexterity, and has recently noticed urinary hesitancy. Examination reveals hyperreflexia in the lower limbs, positive Lhermitte's sign, and loss of dexterity in the hands.
(i) State the diagnosis, the specific clinical syndrome, and identify the vertebral levels most commonly responsible.
(ii) List all the clinical features of cervical disc disease.
(iii) What investigations are required and in what order of preference?
(iv) Describe all non-operative management options. State the operative indications and list all the surgical procedures available for this condition under both the anterior and posterior approaches.
(v) Name the three clinical syndromes into which cervical disc prolapse may present,.

A 28-year-old woman with a 5-month history of amenorrhoea presents to the gynaecology clinic with a one-week history of bleeding per vaginum and worsening lower abdominal pain. Pelvic ultrasound shows no intra-uterine gestational sac. An excision biopsy of a right adnexal mass is performed; histology reveals malignant cytotrophoblastic and syncytiotrophoblastic cells with surrounding necrosis and haemorrhage.

(i) What is the histological diagnosis, and how does this differ from the clinical diagnosis of hydatidiform mole?
(ii) What is the correct approach to biopsy specimen handling from excision to fixation?
(iii) What is the pathologist's duty when interpreting tissue from this clinical scenario, and why must microscopic evaluation not be done in isolation?
(iv) State the medicolegal and professional obligations when handling surgical biopsy specimens.
questions.answerText:
(i) The histological diagnosis is choriocarcinoma (malignant cytotrophoblastic and syncytiotrophoblastic cells with surrounding necrosis and haemorrhage). The clinical diagnosis of hydatidiform mole is incorrect — this illustrates that clinical and histological diagnoses may differ significantly, and all surgical biopsy specimens must be submitted for pathological evaluation.

(ii) The surgical biopsy, as soon as it is taken, should be preserved in 10% formalin (nine times the volume of the specimen). Samples sent in normal saline or empty containers will undergo autolysis and no useful microscopic assessment can be made. The specimen should be properly labelled with margins identified. The type of biopsy (incisional or excisional) and method of obtaining it should be stated. If the patient has had a previous biopsy with a histological report, it should accompany the specimen.

(iii) The surgical pathologist must be able to offer clinical differential diagnoses from interpretation of microscopic findings — this is the mark of the mature surgical pathologist. He may record data that are prognostically significant or offer suggestions for pertinent clinical tests. Microscopic evaluation can sometimes be subjective; therefore practising surgical pathologists should not work in isolation. Slide review and consultations with other pathologists are very important as audit tools. Incomplete communication between clinician and pathologist may make diagnosis difficult or impossible.

(iv) Medicolegal and professional obligations: all surgical biopsy specimens should be sent to the surgical pathology laboratory for evaluation, both for medico-legal reasons and for pathological diagnosis. Several clinicians in private practice have discarded surgical biopsy specimens in the trash can claiming the lesion to be insignificant, excised for cosmetic reasons, or clinically benign — this practice is wrong and amounts to professional negligence. The surgical pathology report is an important medical document; delivery should be prompt and timely as delays negate the very essence of surgical pathology.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man presents with 3 weeks of progressive painless obstructive urinary symptoms: poor stream, hesitancy, nocturia, and terminal dribbling. On digital rectal examination the prostate is smooth and enlarged. PSA is mildly elevated. U+E shows mildly impaired renal function.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and describe the pathophysiology of the gland enlargement and its effect on the urinary tract.
(ii) What is the progression of symptoms in order as the condition worsens?
(iii) What investigations are essential, and what does each assess?
(iv) Describe the medical treatment options, with the mechanism of action of each class.
(v) What are the surgical options and the complications of surgical treatment?
questions.answerText:
(i) Benign prostatic hypertrophy (BPH): a condition of unknown aetiology characterised by increase in size of the inner zone (periurethral glands) of the prostate gland. Pathophysiology: microscopic stromal nodules develop around the periurethral glands; glandular hyperplasia originates around these nodules; as the gland increases in size, it compresses the urethra, leading to urinary tract obstruction.
(ii) Progression of symptoms:
- Initially outlet obstruction: weak stream, hesitancy, intermittency, dribbling, straining to void, acute urinary retention.
- Subsequent detrusor instability: frequency, urgency, nocturia, dysuria, urge incontinence.
- Finally detrusor failure and chronic retention: palpable (or percussible) bladder; overflow incontinence; enlarged smooth prostate on digital rectal examination.
(iii) Investigations:
- Urinalysis and urine culture: evidence of infection or haematuria.
- FBC: infection.
- U+E and serum creatinine: renal function.
- PSA: suspicion of underlying malignancy.
- Uroflowmetry and residual volume measurement (normal <100 ml): evidence of obstruction.
- Ultrasonography of kidneys and bladder: structural abnormalities.
- Transrectal ultrasound: prostate size.
- IVU: structural abnormalities. Cystoscopy.
(iv) Medical treatment:
- Alter oral fluid intake, reduce caffeine.
- α-Adrenergic blockers (e.g. phenoxybenzamine, prazosin): relax smooth muscle of bladder neck and prostate.
- Anti-androgens acting selectively at prostatic cellular level (e.g. finasteride): reduce gland size.
- Intermittent self-catheterisation if detrusor failure.
- Balloon dilatation and stenting of prostate for unfit patients.
(v) Surgical options: TURP with electrocautery or laser; thermal ablation of prostate; open prostatectomy (transvesical or retropubic) if the gland is very large.
Complications: postoperative haemorrhage and clot retention; UTI; retrograde ejaculation; impotence; TURP syndrome (hyponatraemia, hypotension, metabolic acidosis in 2%); incontinence; urethral stricture.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male is brought to the emergency room following a road traffic collision. He has haematuria, left flank pain, bruising over the left flank, and tenderness on abdominal examination. Systolic BP is 85 mmHg.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the hallmark sign of this category of injury?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors that make a patient more susceptible to renal injury following only mild trauma?
(iii) Describe the steps of initial resuscitation for this patient.
(iv) Using the grading system described, classify the grades of renal injury and state which grades are managed non-operatively.
(v) What are the operative options available, and what are the indications for operative intervention?
questions.answerText:
(i) The most likely diagnosis is renal trauma. Haematuria is the hallmark of genito-urinary tract trauma. However, the degree of haematuria does not always correlate with the severity of injury, and haematuria is absent in renal artery thrombosis or pedicle avulsion.
(ii) Predisposing factors (existing pathology): Hydronephrosis; Renal tumours; Congenital polycystic kidneys; Ectopic kidneys — due to loss of natural protection. Renal injury occurs following mild trauma in the above conditions.
(iii) Resuscitation: Quick evaluation; ABC of resuscitation; Rule out other life-threatening injuries; Stabilize patient — Systolic BP >90 mmHg; Check PCV; U/E/Creatinine; Group and crossmatch blood; Urinalysis.
(iv) Grading: Grade I — Contusion with haematuria, subcapsular haematoma, no parenchymal injury. Grade II — Parenchymal (cortical) laceration <1 cm deep. Grade III — Parenchymal (cortical) laceration >1 cm deep, no extravasation. Grade IV — Parenchymal laceration extending to medulla and collecting system; renal vascular (artery/vein) injury with contained haematoma. Grade V — Shattered kidney; vascular avulsion. Non-operative: All Grade I and II; Most Grade III and non-vascular Grade IV.
(v) Operative options: Partial nephrectomy; Total nephrectomy. Indications for operative intervention: Penetrating trauma (not absolute now); Blunt trauma with renal injury and shock; Blunt trauma with other indications for laparotomy; Vascular Grade IV (vascular) and Grade V injury; Failed conservative management.

(i) Septic arthritis (acute suppurative arthritis). Pathophysiological mechanism: the child may have acute osteomyelitis of the metaphysis of a long bone; in the hip and shoulder joints the metaphysis is intra-articular, so pus from the osteomyelitic focus leaks directly into the hip or shoulder joint, causing arthritic symptoms — pain and inability to use the joint — as the first presentation.
(ii) Risk factors and predisposing conditions: children in this environment often have underlying impairment of immune status, commonly due to malnutrition; early loss of splenic function (in sickle cell disease); reduction in IgM; defective alternate complement pathway; deficiency in phagocytosis-promoting peptide. Causative organisms: Staphylococcus aureus; Streptococcus (occasionally).
(iii) Untreated complications: destruction of articular cartilage — once the articular cartilage is damaged it cannot be repaired (William Hunter, 1743); the joint (organ) is permanently compromised; synovitis and joint effusion lead to avascular necrosis; long-term consequences include secondary osteoarthritis from articular cartilage loss, joint deformity, limb length discrepancy, and chronic disability.
(iv) Management: surgical drainage of the joint is essential; intravenous antibiotics — Staphylococcus: combination of 2nd/3rd generation cephalosporins (e.g. Zinacef, Rocephin) + Erythromycin; convert to oral antibiotics when temperature normal for 72 hours with oral drugs available, good absorption, no vomiting or diarrhoea; continue antibiotics for minimum 6 weeks; analgesics; splintage to prevent pathological fracture; joint aspiration for M/C/S (90% positive); early mobilisation to prevent stiffness and cartilage damage.
questions.question:
A 4-year-old malnourished child presents with acute onset of pain, inability to use the left hip, swelling of the hip region, and fever. The hip is held in flexion. ESR is elevated.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis and describe the pathophysiological mechanism by which the joint becomes infected in the context of this child's underlying condition.
(ii) What are the specific risk factors and predisposing conditions that make children in this environment particularly susceptible?
(iii) Outline the complications that arise if this condition is left untreated, including destruction of articular cartilage and long-term joint consequences.
(iv) Describe the surgical and medical management options for septic arthritis in this age group.

A 65-year-old female presents after a trivial fall at home. She is unable to bear weight, with pain in the right groin, and the right leg is shortened and externally rotated. She has a known history of osteoporosis.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and why is this injury more common in females above 60 years of age?
(ii) Classify the fracture using the appropriate classification system, and state which types are associated with the highest risk of avascular necrosis.
(iii) Describe the surgical treatment options, distinguishing between young, middle-aged, and elderly patients, and between intracapsular and extracapsular fractures.
(iv) What are the complications of surgery for this fracture?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis is fracture of the neck of the femur. Above 60 years, this injury is commoner in females as a result of osteoporosis and osteomalacia, which reduce bone density and make the femoral neck susceptible to fracture even with trivial trauma.
(ii) Garden's Classification — applies only to intracapsular fractures: Type I; Type II; Type III; Type IV. Types III and IV have a 90–95% possibility of avascular necrosis.
(iii) Surgical treatment: (a) Intracapsular fracture — Young patient: Garden I and II — fixation with 2 or 3 screws; Garden III and IV — reduction (to convert to I or II) then fixation with 2 or 3 screws (risk of failure if avascular necrosis occurs — explain to the patient). Middle age: Garden I and II — fixation with 2 or 3 screws; Garden III and IV — total hip replacement. Elderly: Garden I to IV — hemiarthroplasty (they are not so active). (b) Extracapsular fracture — Surgical fixation with hip sliding screw (dynamic hip screw) at an angle of 135°.
(iv) Complications of surgery: Avascular necrosis; Non-union; Screw penetration into joints; Mal-union; Dislocation — in total hip replacement (THR).

A(i) Definition and four functional uses:
- A colostomy is an artificial opening made in the large bowel to divert faeces and flatus to the exterior where it can be collected in a bag; it is a colo-cutaneous fistula designed to serve some or all the functions of the anus.
- Four uses:
 1. May replace the anus permanently.
 2. May divert the faecal stream away from a distal lesion.
 3. May decompress an obstructed colon.
 4. May protect a distal end-to-end anastomosis.

A(ii) Permanent and temporary types:
- Permanent colostomy: replaces the anus when the anus and rectum have to be removed for rectal cancer; the operation is called abdomino-perineal resection of the rectum; the stoma is usually in the left iliac fossa for easy accessibility to irrigation by the patient.
- Temporary colostomy: an interim measure pending restoration of colonic continuity; examples include transverse loop colostomy, sigmoid loop colostomy, Devine or divided stoma colostomy, double-barrel colostomy, and Hartmann's colostomy.

B(i) Complications of colostomy: retraction of the stoma, necrosis of the stoma, prolapse, stenosis, parastomal hernias, bleeding from the stoma, and colostomy diarrhoea.
Rationale for bowel preparation:
- Hard faecal masses cause local distension of bowel and at areas narrowed by repair or anastomosis may lead to ischaemia at such sites, with increased risk of rupture or dehiscence.
- The transit of faeces can cause mechanical disruption of anastomoses, especially during the first 4 days when healing is still in the lag phase.
- Collagenase activity is increased by local infection and this may prevent proper healing of the anastomosis.
questions.question:
A(i) Define a colostomy and list its four functional uses.
A(ii) Describe the two main types of colostomy (permanent and temporary), naming the specific operation that requires a permanent colostomy and stating where the stoma is usually sited and why.
B(i) List the complications of colostomy, and explain the anatomical and physiological rationale for bowel preparation before large bowel surgery, including the three risks that make bowel preparation necessary.

A 20-year-old man is brought to the emergency department following a motorcycle accident. He has an open femur fracture with exposed bone and a surrounding contaminated wound with retained foreign material.
(i) What wound class does this injury fall into, and what defines this class?
(ii) What defines each of the four surgical wound classes and what examples are given?
(iii) What risk factors for surgical site infection are relevant in this patient?
(iv) What are the types and definitions of surgical site infection?
(v) What is the classification status of communicable diseases (HIV, hepatitis, TB) in relation to wound classification?
questions.answerText:
(i) This injury falls into Class IV — Dirty/infected wound. Defined as: traumatic wound from dirty source; traumatic wound with delayed treatment; fecal contamination; foreign body; retained devitalised tissue; operative wound with acute bacterial inflammation or perforated viscus; operative wound where clean tissue is transected to gain access to a collection of pus.
(ii) Class I Clean: operative wound clean; non-traumatic, no inflammation encountered; no break in technique; respiratory, gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts not entered. Class II Clean-contaminated: non-traumatic wound with minor break in technique; GI, respiratory or GU tracts entered without significant spillage. Class III Contaminated: fresh traumatic wound from clean source; operative wound with a major break in technique; gross spillage from GI tract; entrance into GU or biliary tracts; infected urine or bile present; incision encountering acute non-purulent inflammation. Class IV Dirty/infected: as described above.
(iii) Risk factors for SSI relevant to this patient: surgery lasting more than two hours; presence of foreign bodies in wound; retained devitalised tissue; old wounds; open contaminated wound. General risk factors: elderly adult, overweight, smoking, cancer, diabetes, immunocompromised patients, emergency or abdominal surgery (the patient's specific age and sex are not in the risk factor list; the listed factors apply ).
(iv) Types of SSI: superficial — on the skin of the incision; deep — occurs beneath the incisional area, includes muscle and fascia; organ or space — infection in any area other than skin, fascia, or muscle. SSI occurs within 30 days after surgery.
(v) Communicable diseases (HIV, hepatitis, TB) are not classified under surgical wound classification. The surgical wound itself is what is being classified, not the patient's communicable disease status.

A(i) Composition, layers, size, and compartments:
- The peritoneum is the largest and most complex serous membrane in the body.
- It consists of a single layer of flattened mesothelial cells over loose areolar tissue.
- The parietal layer lines the interior surfaces of the abdominal wall, extra-peritoneal structures in the pelvis, and the undersurface of the diaphragm, then reflects onto the abdominal organs to form the visceral peritoneum.
- It thereby creates a potential space between the two layers, the peritoneal cavity.
- The connective tissue layer contains a rich network of vascular and lymphatic capillaries, nerve endings, and immune-competent cells, particularly lymphocytes and macrophages.
- Peritoneal fluid present is less than 50 mL.
- Compartments include: the pelvis, right and left paracolic gutters, right and left subphrenic spaces, right subhepatic space, lesser sac (left subhepatic), and interloop potential spaces of the small intestine.

A(ii) Clinical basis in liver disease and nephrotic syndrome:
- Primary peritonitis is observed in patients with ascites from chronic liver disease and nephrotic syndrome.
- Contamination results from translocation of bacteria across the gut wall or mesenteric lymphatics, and less frequently via haematogenous seeding in the presence of bacteraemia.
- In cirrhotic patients, the haematogenous route is most likely because portosystemic shunting diminishes hepatic clearance of bacteria.

B(i) Distinctions:
- Source: Primary peritonitis has an absence of an apparent intra-abdominal source of infection; secondary peritonitis arises from a known source, usually perforation of the gastrointestinal tract.
- Microbiology: Primary peritonitis is caused by a monomicrobial infection, most commonly gram-negative organisms; secondary peritonitis is almost always polymicrobial, containing a mixture of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria with a predominance of gram-negative organisms.
- Surgical intervention: Primary peritonitis is managed medically; secondary peritonitis is the most common form encountered by the surgeon and surgical intervention is often required.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the peritoneum under the following headings: composition, layers, size, and the compartments of the peritoneal cavity.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis for why primary peritonitis is more common in patients with chronic liver disease or nephrotic syndrome.
B(i) Distinguish between primary peritonitis and secondary peritonitis under the headings: source of infection, microbiology, and need for surgical intervention.

Describe the pathophysiology and clinical stages of cardiac arrest, the steps of basic life support (BLS) and advanced life support (ALS), and the drugs used in ALS, distinguishing between the management of shockable (VF/pulseless VT) and non-shockable (asystole/EMD) rhythms.
A(i) State the causes of cardiac arrest in the trauma setting and the signs of cardiac arrest.
A(ii) Describe the steps of basic life support including the compression-to-ventilation ratios.
B(i) Describe the management of VF/pulseless VT during ALS, including drug doses.
B(ii) Describe the management of asystole/EMD and list the reversible causes.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Causes of cardiac arrest in trauma: Airway obstruction and hypoxia; Ventilation difficulties; Severe uncorrected hypovolaemia; Untreated/unrecognised hypothermia. Signs of cardiac arrest: Loss of consciousness; Absent carotid pulse; Apnoea/gasping respiration; Dilated pupils; Cyanosis.
A(ii) Steps of BLS: Ensure safety of self and victim. Check victim's responsiveness. A — Airway patency: chin lift/jaw thrust with C-spine stabilisation; remove visible foreign body/secretions; adjuncts: oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airways. B — Breathing: look, listen and feel for 10 seconds; if not breathing — give 2 breaths using expired air ventilation. C — Circulation: check carotid pulsation; if absent — external cardiac compression; depress sternum 4–5 cm, release, then repeat; rate: 100 compressions/min. Compression-to-ventilation ratios: 1 rescuer — 15 compressions to 2 ventilations; 2 rescuers — 5 compressions to 1 ventilation.
B(i) VF/pulseless VT management: Witnessed/monitored arrest — precordial thump (once)/evaluation. Three successive DC shocks at 200 J, 200 J, 360 J (2 J/kg, 2 J/kg, 4 J/kg in children). 1 minute/10 cycles CPR. Cannulate a peripheral vein (antecubital fossa) using 14G cannula. IV epinephrine 1 mg every 3 minutes (100 mcg/kg); Intubate if skilled; Give 100% oxygen. Reassess rhythm; if pulselessness persists, repeat 3 successive shocks at 360, 360, 360 J.
B(ii) Asystole/EMD: Attach electrodes/monitor; CPR for 3 minutes; Reassess rhythm; Asystole — bolus atropine 3 mg; Consider reversible causes. Reversible causes: Hypoxia; Hypovolaemia; Hyper/hypokalaemia; Hypothermia; Tension pneumothorax; Cardiac tamponade; Thromboembolism; Toxic substances/poisoning. Drugs: Epinephrine — IV 1 mg/100 mcg/kg every 3 minutes; via ETT give 2× IV dose; refractory asystole: high bolus dose 5 mg. Atropine — single bolus 3 mg in asystole.

A(i) Types: autogenous (from one bone to another in the same patient); allogenous/allograft (from one patient to another of the same species); xenograft (from one species to another). The two repair mechanisms: osteoinduction — stimulation of osteoprogenitor cells at the recipient bed by matrix bone protein seeded by the graft, leading to new bone production; osteoconduction — the graft acts as a bridge between the bone defect ends, serving as a scaffold for new bone to be laid.
A(ii) Cancellous autograft (non-vascularized): commonest form; bone chips used to fill cavities or augment/accelerate bone union; sources include ilium, greater trochanter, proximal tibia metaphysis, distal radius, olecranon, femoral heads; fate: undergo necrosis then inflammatory response forming fibrovascular stroma; new capillaries from recipient bed initiate graft incorporation. Vascularized autograft: for large bony defects from bone tumour resection, congenital pseudoarthrosis of tibia, non-union of femoral neck fractures; sources: iliac crest (circumflex artery), fibula (peroneal artery), radial shaft mid-portion (radial artery); behave like healing fractures; can undergo hypertrophy with loading, conferring strength and allowing early weight bearing. Cortical autograft (non-vascularized): from convenient long bones (e.g. medial cortex of tibia, split fibula); augmented by cancellous chips and reinforced by plate and screws; used as onlay, inlay, or latch grafts.
B(i) Unpopular in developing countries because of lack of bone-banking facilities, unpopularity of organ donation due to beliefs of populace, and poor/non-existent bone banking systems. Advantages: offer large bone segments/quantities not obtainable from the same patient without great morbidity; articular-cartilage-bearing allografts used for joint reconstruction. Disadvantages: risk of graft rejection; transmission of infections (hepatitis, HIV); seeding of malignant tumour cells to recipient.
B(ii) Callotaxis is distraction osteogenesis using the Ilizarov technique. A careful osteotomy spares endosteal blood supply; the regenerate (new bone formed) is protected by an external fixator until strong enough for loading. Distraction rate is 1 mm per day. The external fixator device protects the regenerate and, in bone transport, includes a component for bone transportation.
questions.question:
Regarding bone graft in the management of bone loss:

A(i) Describe the types of bone graft available — autogenous, allogenous, and xenograft — and explain the two mechanisms by which a bone graft performs its repair function at the recipient site.
A(ii) Distinguish between cancellous autograft (non-vascularized), vascularized autograft, and cortical autograft (non-vascularized) stating indications, sources, and the fate of each graft at the recipient bed.
B(i) Explain why allograft is unpopular in developing countries and state both the major advantages and disadvantages of allografts.
B(ii) Describe the principle of callotaxis (distraction osteogenesis) and state the distraction rate and the role of the external fixator.

A) Describe the gross and microscopic anatomy of nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumour) under the following headings:
A(i) Macroscopic appearance and contents
A(ii) Microscopic composition and histological variants

B) State how the staging system relates to the extent of tumour spread, and explain how histological variant determines treatment intensity.

C) Explain why nephroblastoma may cause varicocele, haematuria, and hypertension, and how the tumour may spread to cause pulmonary symptoms.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Macroscopic appearance:
- Large, bulky and encapsulated tumour
- Greyish-white with fibrous septa
- Focal areas of necrosis and haemorrhage
- Sharply demarcated, variably encapsulated with haemorrhagic areas and cavitations
- Location may be central or polar

A(ii) Microscopic composition:
- Three components reflecting normal kidney differentiation: blastemal, tubular (epithelial), and stromal elements
Histological variants:
- Favourable histology: WT without anaplastic features (well differentiated)
- Unfavourable histology: presence of anaplasia — cells with nuclear enlargement, hyperchromatic nuclei and abnormal mitotic figures; anaplasia is the single most important indicator of poor prognosis

B) NWTSG Staging:
Stage I: Tumour limited to kidney and completely resected
Stage II: Tumour extends beyond kidney but completely excised
Stage III: Residual non-haematogenous tumour confined to abdomen
Stage IV: Haematogenous metastases
Stage V: Bilateral tumour
Unfavourable histology requires all modalities (surgery + chemo + radio) for all stages. Favourable histology, Stage I & II, <2 years: surgery alone; >2 years: surgery + chemotherapy; Stages III–V: all modalities.

C) Varicocele results from compression or invasion of the renal vein or inferior vena cava by the tumour, impairing venous drainage of the testicular vein. Haematuria occurs from tumour invasion into the renal collecting system. Hypertension arises from elevated renin secretion due to renal parenchymal compression. Pulmonary symptoms (cough, haemoptysis, chest pain) result from haematogenous metastases to the lungs at Stage IV.

(i) Diagnosis: hypothyroidism — iatrogenic, following thyroidectomy (not taking L-thyroxine replacement). Complication developing: myxoedema coma — this is the stated complication of hypothyroidism.
(ii) Classification by level: primary — lack of thyroid hormone production from the gland itself; this patient's type is iatrogenic primary hypothyroidism following thyroidectomy. Secondary — inadequate TSH secretion from the pituitary gland. Tertiary — lack of TRH production from the hypothalamus. Aetiology of his specific type: iatrogenic following thyroidectomy (developed nations pattern). Other aetiology: iodine deficiency (developing nations), auto-immunity.
(iii) Full spectrum of clinical features: cold intolerance, fatigue, puffiness, weight gain, hair loss, dry skin, myxoedema, altered mental status, coma, bradycardia, electrolyte disorders, hypothermia, cardiomegaly, pericardial effusion, ascites, shock.
(iv) Investigations and expected findings: thyroid function tests — raised TSH, decreased T3, decreased T4. Pituitary hormone assay. Brain MRI.
(v) Immediate and long-term management: L-thyroxine; thyroidectomy in selected cases (not applicable here as surgery has already been performed). Long-term: L-thyroxine replacement is required for life after total thyroidectomy. Follow-up: intermittent thyroid function tests, at least once every 3 months.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: myasthenia gravis. Pathophysiology: rapid fatigability of muscles caused by antibodies against acetylcholine (ACh) receptors at the neuromuscular junction — anti-ACh receptor antibodies. This results in decreased availability of ACh receptors, impaired neuromuscular transmission, and fatigable weakness. Ranges from mild isolated ocular disease to generalised life-threatening disease with loss of respiratory musculature.
(ii) Incidence: 5 per 100,000; transiently present in 20% of infants born to myasthenic patients. Women peak in their 20s; men peak in their 60s.
(iii) Tensilon test: double-blind edrophonium test — saline and active drug drawn up and labelled by a third party. If the patient is already on pyridostigmine (Mestinon), edrophonium may worsen symptoms if the current symptoms are from excess pyridostigmine; therefore, give 2 mg first and follow with 8 mg only if no response to the initial dose. Have resuscitation equipment available, as even 1–2 mg may be enough to precipitate cholinergic crisis.
(iv) Other investigations: CXR shows thymoma (note: CT has a high false-positive rate); check thyroid function tests (high rate of abnormality); EMG shows rapid fatigability with decrement; anti-ACh receptor antibodies present with generalised disease (60% with isolated ocular disease).
(v) Antibiotics to avoid: streptomycin; neomycin; kanamycin; polymyxin; bacitracin; colistin.
questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with progressive ptosis, diplopia, and nasal speech over 3 days. She is on pyridostigmine for a known condition. On examination, her facial muscles are weak and she has difficulty swallowing. Her breathing appears laboured.
(i) State the diagnosis and describe the pathophysiology including the specific antibody and receptor involved.
(ii) Describe the sex and age distribution and the overall incidence of this condition.
(iii) Describe how the Tensilon (edrophonium) test is performed safely, including the specific precaution required when the patient is already on pyridostigmine.
(iv) State the other investigations that should be performed for this condition, including those that assess for thymoma and associated endocrine pathology.
(v) List all the antibiotics that must be avoided in patients with this condition.

A 72-year-old man presents with lethargy, weight loss, and new-onset paraplegia. He had been treated for presumed benign prostatic hyperplasia for two years. A bone radioisotope scan using Tc99-labelled radioisotope shows multiple hot spots. PSA is markedly elevated. A transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma of the prostate.

(i) Identify the organ and structure most likely responsible for the paraplegia, and state the anatomical route by which carcinoma of the prostate reaches this structure.
(ii) Identify the compressed or affected structure(s) at each metastatic site observed in this patient, and list the full range of distant structures to which this cancer spreads by haematogenous and lymphatic routes.
(iii) List all differential pathologies that must be excluded before attributing the clinical picture solely to carcinoma of the prostate.
(iv) Using clinico-anatomical reasoning, explain why more than 40% of Nigerian patients present at the metastatic stage, and outline the complete hormonal and chemotherapy management cascade for this patient's stage of disease.
questions.answerText:
(i) The structure responsible for paraplegia is the spinal cord/vertebral column. The anatomical route is haematogenous spread via the Batson's vertebral venous plexus (pelvic veins communicating with vertebral veins without valves) to the vertebrae; vertebral metastases cause vertebral collapse or epidural cord compression, resulting in paraplegia. The lymphatic route involves the para-aortic and mediastinal nodes, in addition to direct haematogenous spread to the vertebrae, femur, ribs, skull, sternum, and spinal cord.

(ii) Compressed or affected structures at each site:
- Lumbar spine → low back pain, sciatica (nerve root compression).
- Femoral neck → pathological fracture.
- Vertebra/spinal cord → paraplegia.
- Lymph nodes → lymphoedema of lower limbs, anuria (from ureteric compression), palpable masses.
- Cerebral metastases → headache, nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, epilepsy, paresis.
- Bone marrow → anaemia, pancytopenia.
- Uraemia from chronic retention and ureteric obstruction.
- Lethargy, weight loss, cachexia.
Full haematogenous spread sites: bones — vertebrae, femur, ribs, skull, sternum; spinal cord; liver, lungs, brain; skin; palate.
Full lymphatic spread: internal and external iliac nodes, para-aortic, mediastinal, inguinal; perineural lymphatics (pain).

(iii) Differentials to exclude: BPH; carcinoma of the bladder; bladder calculus; urethral stricture; bladder neck obstruction; neurogenic bladder; DM; depression.

(iv) More than 40% of Nigerian patients present at the metastatic stage because PSA screening and DRE surveillance are not routinely performed; awareness is low; 1 in every 6 men will be diagnosed at some time in their lives but most present only when symptomatic (metastatic symptoms); early localised disease is largely asymptomatic.
Hormonal and chemotherapy management cascade for advanced/metastatic disease:
- Orchidectomy (surgical castration) — most accessible and cost-effective in Nigeria.
- LHRH analogues (goserelin/zoladex, buserelin) — medical castration.
- Anti-androgens (flutamide, bicalutamide, nilutamide) — androgen receptor blockade.
- Combinations — total androgen blockade.
- Localised radiotherapy for painful bone metastases.
- Treatment landscape (further agents): sipuleucel-T; docetaxel; cabazitaxel; abiraterone; enzalutamide; radium-223; denosumab/zoledronic acid; olaparib; pembrolizumab (MSI-high); apalutamide.
Most Nigerian patients undergo orchidectomy; few wealthy patients access medical therapies.

(i) Aetiology:
- Gallstones and alcohol abuse account for 95% of cases.
- Other causes: idiopathic; congenital structural abnormalities; drugs; viral infections; hypercalcaemia; hypothermia; hyperlipidaemia; trauma.
(ii) Pathological stages:
- Mild: acinar (exocrine) cell damage with enzymatic spillage, inflammatory cascade activation, and localised oedema; increased serum levels of pancreatic enzymes (amylase, lipase, colipase).
- Moderate: increasing local inflammation leads to intrapancreatic bleeding, fluid collections, and spreading local oedema involving the mesentery and retroperitoneum; activation of systemic inflammatory response leads to progressive involvement of other organs.
- Severe: progressive pancreatic destruction leads to necrosis, profound localised bleeding, and fluid collections; spread to local structures and peritoneal cavity may result in mesenteric infarction, peritonitis, and intra-abdominal fat 'saponification'. A persisting accumulation of inflammatory fluid (usually in the lesser sac) is a pseudocyst.
(iii) Imrie/Ranson criteria for severe pancreatitis (severe = 3 or more):
- WBC >16 × 10⁹/l; PaO2 <7.98 kPa; blood glucose >11.2 mmol/l; LDH >350 IU/l; SGOT >250 IU/l; PCV fall >10%; urea >1.8; Ca2+ <2.0 mmol/l.
(iv) Systemic complications:
- Respiratory: ARDS (V/Q mismatch); collapse; effusion; aspiration pneumonitis; bronchospasm.
- Renal: ATN; acute cortical necrosis.
- Haematological: DIC; DVT; haemorrhage; anaemia; leucocytosis.
- GI: stress ulceration (Curling's ulcer); paralytic ileus; mesenteric thrombosis; gastric stasis; liver dysfunction.
- Other: myocardial depression; cerebral dysfunction; hypocalcaemia; hyperglycaemia; acidosis.
(v) Management:
- Mild/moderate: IV fluids; analgesia; monitor pulse, BP, temperature.
- Severe: full resuscitation in ICU with invasive monitoring.
- Establish the cause: ultrasound to look for gallstones.
- No proven routine use for nasogastric tube or antibiotics.
- Proven CBD gallstones: urgent ERCP.
- CT scan if failure to respond or uncertain diagnosis.
- Suspected/proven infection of necrotic pancreas: antibiotics ± surgical debridement.
- Surgery has little place other than to treat severe complications (pseudocyst drainage, debridement).
questions.question:
Describe pancreatitis under the following headings:
(i) Aetiology of acute pancreatitis (all causes, in order of frequency).
(ii) Pathological stages of pancreatic injury from mild through to severe/necrotising disease.
(iii) Severity assessment: list the Imrie/Ranson criteria for severe pancreatitis.
(iv) Systemic complications of severe pancreatitis, covering respiratory, renal, haematological, and GI systems.
(v) Essential management for mild/moderate and for severe pancreatitis, including the role of ERCP and surgery.

Describe the surgical wound classification system under the following headings.
A(i) Define each of the four surgical wound classes with their defining criteria.
A(ii) Give two examples for each wound class drawn from the specialties listed.
B(i) State the 'reminders' associated with each class that indicate up-classification.
B(ii) Define surgical site infection, its time frame, and its three depth-based types with signs and symptoms.
C(i) Describe the risk factors for surgical site infection.
C(ii) Describe the measures for prevention of SSI in the operating theatre and explain why smokers should stop smoking before surgery.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Class I Clean: operative wound clean; non-traumatic, no inflammation encountered; no break in technique; respiratory, GI and GU tracts not entered. Class II Clean-contaminated: non-traumatic wound with minor break in technique; GI, respiratory or GU tracts entered without significant spillage. Class III Contaminated: fresh traumatic wound from clean source; major break in technique; gross spillage from GIT; entrance into GU or biliary tracts; infected urine or bile present; incision in acute non-purulent inflammation. Class IV Dirty/infected: traumatic wound from dirty source; delayed treatment; fecal contamination; foreign body; retained devitalised tissue; acute bacterial inflammation or perforated viscus; incision into pus collection.
A(ii) Class I examples: vascular procedures, neurological procedures, endocrine procedures, eye surgery, orthopedic procedures, penile prosthesis, mastectomy. Class II examples: GI procedures (laparoscopy, colonoscopy, gastroscopy), GYN procedures, GU procedures. Class III examples: GI procedures with gross spillage or acute inflammation, fresh accidental wounds, GI procedures with 'itis'. Class IV examples: I&D abscess, wound debridement, nose/oropharynx infected procedures.
B(i) Reminders for up-classification: Class I to II — inflammation, gross spillage, fresh accidental wound; removing old implants (wires, pins); any wound open for drainage (except total hip/knee); re-operation at same site. Class II to III — foreign bodies in a wound (bullets, etc.); Class III to IV — infected cases; I&D abscess; wound debridement.
B(ii) SSI: infections occurring in a surgically created wound, called post-operative infection; occurs within 30 days after surgery. Types: superficial — on the skin of the incision; deep — beneath the incisional area including muscle and fascia; organ or space — any area other than skin, fascia and muscle. Signs and symptoms: redness, delayed healing, fever, warmth, swelling, pain, discharge of pus. Causative organisms: Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Pseudomonas.
C(i) Risk factors for SSI: surgery lasting more than two hours; elderly adult; overweight; smoking; cancer; diabetes; immunocompromised patients; patients undergoing emergency or abdominal surgery. Smokers should quit smoking three months before a surgical operation.
C(ii) Prevention measures: proper skin preparation; gentle handling of tissues; meticulous haemostasis; removal of devitalised tissues; obliterate dead spaces; adequate irrigation; use of monofilament, non-absorbable sutures; wound closure without tension. Smokers should quit smoking 3 months before surgery to reduce the risk of surgical site infection.

(i) The diagnosis is syndactyly. It is a simple syndactyly (isolated, not complex) of the ring and little fingers. The mnemonic 5, 15, 50, 30 indicates: thumb and index finger involvement is 5%; ring and little finger involvement is 30% (the most common pairing). Syndactyly is present bilaterally in 50% of cases.
(ii) Syndactyly is more common in white males and follows autosomal dominant (AD) inheritance. It may be bilateral in 50% of cases.
(iii) The surgical technique involves marking skin flaps and using Z-plasty incisions. A dorsal butterfly flap is raised to reconstruct the web space between the separated fingers. The dorsal butterfly flap creates the new commissure. When both sides of the same digit require separation (i.e., a digit is webbed on both its radial and ulnar aspects), they must never be separated on the same day; a minimum of 6 weeks must elapse between procedures to preserve digital blood supply.
(iv) Surgery is performed at 18 months of age. Full-thickness skin grafting is almost always required to provide adequate soft tissue coverage of the raw areas created on the sides of the separated digits, as the skin available after flap creation is insufficient to cover both digit surfaces without grafting.
(v) Two syndromes in which syndactyly occurs as part of a complex are: Apert syndrome (associated with clinodactyly and characteristic facies); and Holt-Oram syndrome (associated with atrial septal defect and radial club hand). Poland's syndrome (absence of pectoralis major) is also listed.
questions.question:
A 2-year-old child is brought with webbing of the ring and little fingers on the right hand, with the two fingers fused throughout their length, sharing a common skin cover but with separate underlying bones.
(i) State the diagnosis, classify the type, and give the mnemonic stating which finger combinations are most and least commonly affected.
(ii) State the genetic inheritance and which racial group is more commonly affected.
(iii) Describe the surgical technique of correction, naming the flap used to reconstruct the web space, and state the special consideration when both sides of the same digit need to be separated.
(iv) State at what age surgery should be performed and why full-thickness skin grafting is required.
(v) Name two syndromes in which this condition may occur as part of a complex.

questions.answerText:
(i) Colles fracture. Defined as a fracture of the radius within 2.5 cm of the wrist. Most commonly seen in middle-aged and elderly women.
(ii) Predisposing factors: fall on outstretched hand; osteoporosis and osteomalacia in the older age group. Deformity: dorsal displacement and angulation with loss of radial height, producing the characteristic dinner fork deformity when displaced.
(iii) Management: commonly treated by closed reduction and application of Colles' POP (Plaster of Paris). This is the definitive conservative immobilisation technique for the majority of cases.
(iv) Late rupture of extensor pollicis longus may occur, commonly due to Colles' fracture. It occurs after 6–8 hours of injury. Mechanism: a haematoma forms which lifts up the tendon and cuts off its blood supply via the vincula longus and brevis. Treatment is replacement with extensor longus (extensor indicis proprius transfer).
questions.question:
A 62-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after a fall on an outstretched hand. Examination reveals swelling around the wrist and a characteristic dinner fork deformity.

(i) State the diagnosis, define the fracture precisely, and identify the population group most commonly affected.
(ii) Describe the predisposing factors (mechanism and patient characteristics) and the deformity pattern seen.
(iii) Outline the pathophysiology and management, including the name of the definitive immobilisation technique.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is Achalasia Cardia.

(ii) Pathological basis:
- There is an imbalance between inhibitory and excitatory neurons due to selective loss of postganglionic inhibitory neurons, leading to decreased nitric oxide (NO) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP).
- This causes impaired lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) relaxation and loss of oesophageal peristalsis.
- The postganglionic cholinergic neurons are spared, resulting in unopposed cholinergic stimulation and increased LOS pressure.

(iii) Resuscitation and supportive management:
- Correct derangements: fluid, electrolyte and nutritional derangement.
- Treat chest infection with antibiotics (for aspiration-related chest infections).
- Lifestyle changes: eating habits, sleeping posture.
- Emergency management (rare): quick initial assessment and resuscitation if aspiration causes cough, breathlessness, or stridor.

(iv) Definitive surgical treatment:
- Modified Heller's myotomy (open, laparoscopic, or VATS; transabdominal or transthoracic approach).
- Myotomy length: 8–10 cm on the oesophagus, extending 1–2 cm onto the cardia.
- An anti-reflux procedure (fundoplication) may be added to reduce post-operative gastro-oesophageal reflux.
questions.question:
A patient presents with progressive difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids, frequent regurgitation, moderate weight loss, and recurrent chest infections. On barium oesophagram, there is a dilated oesophagus with smooth distal narrowing giving a bird beak appearance, with delayed barium emptying beyond five minutes and failure of primary oesophageal wave.

(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Describe the pathological basis of this condition, including which neurons are lost and the consequence of that loss.
(iii) Outline the initial resuscitation and supportive management steps before definitive treatment.
(iv) Name and briefly describe the definitive surgical treatment option of choice for a young, low-risk patient, including the length of the myotomy.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Indications: diagnostic — cystograms/micturating cystograms; therapeutic — relieving urinary obstruction, resting the bladder in severe urinary frequency or incontinence, intravesical delivery of chemotherapeutic agents for superficial carcinoma of the bladder; monitoring urine output in intensive care patients.
Catheter materials: Rubber (amber-coloured) — most available; safe for up to 4 weeks; must be changed at 4 weeks under antibiotic cover; balloon channel damaged by antiseptic solutions, normal saline, or overstay due to body heat. Silicon (light blue) — better tolerated by the body; can remain up to 6 months, changed twice a year; expensive and not easily available. Red rubber — worst tolerated; causes chemical urethritis within hours, leading to the worst type of urethral strictures affecting the entire urethra; must be removed as soon as the bladder is emptied.

A(ii) Adult urethra accepts FG16 or FG18 for urine drainage; FG20, FG22, FG24, or FG26 for blood drainage — these must not remain beyond 24–48 hours. Oversized catheters cause strictures by: (1) overstretching the urethra, causing mucosal ischaemia and healing by fibrosis; (2) impairing drainage of periurethral glands, causing accumulated secretions, secondary infection, multiple periurethral abscesses, and ultimately fibrotic strictures. Catheters smaller than FG16 are too floppy to negotiate the urethra. Urethral catheters are available only in even-number sizes.

B(i) Patient should be supine; entire external genitalia, lower abdomen, and upper thighs cleaned with chlorhexidine (savlon); sterile drapes applied; hands washed and sterile gloves worn (sterile gown desirable but not mandatory). Iodine must never be used on external genitalia. 2% xylocaine jelly is squeezed into the urethra; a penile clamp or manual pressure with thumb and index finger is applied for 3–5 minutes; jelly is milked proximally along the shaft. Non-touch technique: catheter not touched directly; held by sterile sheet while being advanced, sheet gradually withdrawn. Entire catheter length introduced until the junction with the balloon arm abuts the meatus; balloon inflated only after confirming urine flow; balloon volume not to exceed the amount stated on the catheter; attention on the patient's face during inflation — any grimace suggests balloon is in urethra, not bladder; balloon must be immediately deflated and catheter advanced further before re-attempting inflation.

B(ii) Complications and management:
- Gram-negative septicaemia: IV normal saline run fast + IV gentamycin 280 mg or other gram-negative antibiotic; caused by catheterizing an infected urethra — purulent urethral discharge is an absolute contraindication.
- Retained catheter: managed by removing catheter with appropriate technique.
- Urethral rupture: leave the urethra alone; perform suprapubic urinary diversion; refer to a urologist.
- Urinary tract infection: appropriate antibiotics.
- Urethritis: appropriate antibiotics.
- Bladder calculus: refer to a urologist.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Gross anatomy in nephroblastoma: embryonic tumour; well encapsulated until advanced; renal pelvis is involved in <half of cases; bilateral in 5–10%. Blood-borne spread: via renal vein to inferior vena cava and then to systemic circulation. Primary site of distant metastasis: lungs (commonest). Other organs affected: liver, brain, bones.

A(ii) Staging and anatomy:
- Stage I: tumour confined to the kidney, completely resectable — capsule intact.
- Stage II: extends beyond kidney (through capsule) but still completely resectable — local perirenal involvement.
- Stage III: residual tumour in abdomen after resection — local infiltration of adjacent structures or lymph nodes; capsule disrupted.
- Stage IV: spread to distant organs (lungs, liver, bone, brain) — haematogenous dissemination.
- Stage V: bilateral — both kidneys involved.
Stage V requires partial nephrectomy (nephron-sparing surgery) after downstaging with radiotherapy/chemotherapy, because removing both kidneys would cause anephric renal failure; the goal is to preserve enough functioning renal tissue; complete nephrectomy bilaterally is incompatible with survival without dialysis/transplant. Stages I and II allow straightforward surgical excision as the primary treatment.

B(i) Spread in Stage IV and functional deficit:
- Lungs (commonest site): haematogenous emboli lodge in pulmonary capillaries → metastatic deposits → respiratory failure, pleural effusion, impaired gas exchange.
- Liver: portal and haematogenous spread → hepatic metastases → hepatic synthetic and metabolic failure, jaundice, coagulopathy.
- Bones: haematogenous spread to bone marrow and cortical bone → painful bone metastases, pathological fractures, bone marrow replacement causing anaemia and pancytopenia.
- Brain: haematogenous spread via cerebral circulation → cerebral metastases → raised intracranial pressure, seizures, focal neurological deficits.

B(ii) Distinction between nephroblastoma and neuroblastoma (all grounds):
- Surface: nephroblastoma — smooth (intact capsule); neuroblastoma — knobby contour.
- Pain: nephroblastoma — pain in 50%; neuroblastoma — usually painless.
- Midline: nephroblastoma — usually does not cross midline (confined within Gerota's fascia); neuroblastoma — usually crosses midline (arises from para-aortic sympathetic chain).
- Regression: nephroblastoma — does not regress; neuroblastoma — may regress spontaneously.
- Urinary VMA: nephroblastoma — normal; neuroblastoma — increased (catecholamine metabolite).
- IVU: nephroblastoma — calyceal/pelvic deformity (intrinsic renal tumour); neuroblastoma — kidney displaced with normal anatomy (extrinsic adrenal/retroperitoneal tumour).
- Age: nephroblastoma — 80% <4 years; neuroblastoma — older age group (also childhood).
Prognosis of nephroblastoma (survival at 2 years):
- Favourable histology: Stage I — 97%; Stage II — 92%; Stage III — 84%; Stage IV — 83%.
- Unfavourable histology: Stages I–III — 68%; Stage IV — 55%.
98% of recurrences occur within 2 years.

(i) The diagnosis is sigmoid volvulus.
- The sigmoid colon with its redundant loop and the close proximity of its points of fixation is the most frequent site.
- Colonic volvulus is a disease of the older age group, with the greatest incidence in the 6th and 7th decades.

(ii) Predisposing factors:
- A redundant segment of colon.
- Close approximation of the points of fixation of the segment to serve as a pivot for twisting.
- Malrotation of the gut whereby parts of the colon supposed to be fixed are free and mobile.
- Rarely, a hypermobile caecum may result in caecal volvulus.

(iii) Complications if untreated:
- Compromised circulation to the affected segment of bowel (as volvulus effectively causes this).
- Gangrenous bowel leading to perforation and peritonitis.
- Multiple organ failure and death (as a consequence of strangulation, intestinal infarction, gangrene, and perforation with peritonitis, as listed for intestinal obstruction complications).

(iv) Treatment options:
- Resuscitate the patient.
- Attempt reduction by rectal tube via proctoscopy, or via flexible fibreoptic sigmoidoscopy; this is only suitable in patients with a history of not more than 24 hours — justified because bowel viability is more likely to be maintained within this window, making non-operative reduction safe.
- Exploratory laparotomy, detorsion (if not gangrenous), resection and end-to-end anastomosis for cases beyond 24 hours or with gangrenous bowel.

A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the lower urinary tract in relation to obstructive uropathies in children, enumerating all causes of upper urinary tract obstruction and all causes of lower urinary tract obstruction.
A(ii) State how the zones and parts of the obstructed urinary tract relate to the pathological changes occurring at each level — bladder, posterior urethra, ureters, and kidneys — specifically for posterior urethral valves.
B(i) Describe why untreated posterior urethral obstruction may spread to cause bilateral renal impairment and the conditions under which immediate bilateral nephrostomy is indicated rather than endoscopic ablation.
B(ii) Describe the diagnosis of posterior urethral valves — the investigations performed, their specific findings, and how the radiological appearance distinguishes the obstructed from the normal urethra.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Upper urinary tract obstruction causes: ureteric stenosis; secondary megaureter(s) from VUR; idiopathic primary megaureter; retrocaval ureter; duplex systems.
Lower urinary tract obstruction causes (including both slides): congenital posterior urethral valves (males); urethral stricture (congenital and acquired e.g. traumatic, iatrogenic); urethral diverticulum (caecal type and others); neuropathic lesions (e.g. spina bifida, sacral agenesis); the large smooth bladder; the lazy bladder syndrome (DeLuca); base plate deficiency (Hutch); prune belly (triad) syndrome; anterior urethral valves (males); foreign bodies; calculi; distal urethral obstruction in girls or meatal obstruction in boys; Marion's disease (bladder neck obstruction) — noted as non-existent.

A(ii) Pathological effects of posterior urethral valves at each level:
- Urethra: posterior urethral dilatation above the valves; the valves are exaggerated semilunar folds at the crista terminalis (Young type 1); degree of obstruction is variable.
- Bladder: trabeculation and sacculation; bladder neck is narrow but not obstructed; the bladder becomes a palpable golf-ball mass.
- Ureters: megaureters develop due to back pressure; vesico-ureteric reflux occurs.
- Kidneys: hydronephrosis; gross renal damage at birth; cystic kidneys; electrolyte imbalance (natriuresis); uraemia; hyperkalaemia; septicaemia; failure to thrive.

B(i) Untreated posterior urethral obstruction spreads to cause bilateral renal impairment through sustained back pressure transmitted retrogradely from the obstructed urethra through the bladder and megaureters to both kidneys, causing progressive hydronephrosis, pyelonephritis, and renal parenchymal loss. Vesico-ureteric reflux further transmits infected urine to the kidneys. Electrolyte imbalance (natriuresis), uraemia, and hyperkalaemia develop.
Immediate bilateral nephrostomy is indicated in: advanced renal deterioration; pyonephrosis (infected, dilated collecting system). If condition is unilateral with a functionless kidney, nephrectomy is performed. Peritoneal dialysis plus urethral drainage is used when condition fails to improve with catheterisation and medical resuscitation.

B(ii) Diagnosis of posterior urethral valves:
- Micturating cystourethrography (MCU): shows dilated prostatic urethra above the obstruction; sacculation and narrowing at the bladder neck; posterior urethral dilatation.
- Ultrasonography: shows hydronephrosis and hydroureters.
- Urethrocystoscopy with bladder filling: demonstrates the valves directly.
- Renal function tests: assess degree of renal impairment.
On IVU: reveals trabeculation, sacculation, dilated posterior urethra, and can show degree of upper tract dilatation. Radiologically, the obstructed urethra shows a characteristic dilated prostatic segment above the valve with a narrow zone at the valve level, contrasting with the normal urethra which has a uniform calibre.

questions.question:

B) Describe the origin, course, and structures at risk during inguinal herniotomy in the paediatric patient, and state the safe operative approach.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Stages and timeline of testicular descent:
- 6 weeks IUL: migration of primitive germ cells to genital ridge
- 7–8 weeks: differentiation into testis or ovary; gubernaculum forms
- 3 months: commencement of descent
- 7 months: testis reaches internal ring; derivatives of cord coverings are acquired

A(ii) Fate of the processus vaginalis:
- 90% involutes by obliteration (normal)
- 10% remain patent, leading to:
 * Hernias: bubonocele, funicular, complete (inguinal hernias)
 * Hydroceles: vaginal, infantile, communicating, encysted

B) Structures at risk during inguinal herniotomy:
- Ilioinguinal nerve (damage causes sensory loss/pain)
- Vas deferens (should be repaired if damaged; primary haemorrhage risk)
- Vessels of the cord
Post-operative complications include: wound infection, scrotal haematoma, post-operative hydrocele, and recurrence (less common in children than adults).
The safe operative principle in children is herniotomy (high ligation of sac) at the internal ring; repair of the posterior wall is required in adults. Contralateral exploration is controversial.

C) Distinctions:
Communicating hydrocele: Completely patent processus vaginalis with small communication with the peritoneal cavity; changes in size; difficult to reduce; treatment is herniotomy and hydrocelectomy.
Infantile hydrocele: Processus vaginalis is closed at the deep ring but fluid is trapped; not strictly confined to infancy; does not change in size; treatment is hydrocelectomy.

(i) Diagnosis: Malrotation of the midgut (specifically incomplete rotation causing duodenal obstruction by Ladd's bands).
The structure causing duodenal obstruction is Ladd's band — peritoneal bands running from the caecum (which is malsited) across the duodenum to the mesentery, producing extrinsic compression.

(ii) Compressed/affected structures:
- Duodenum (compressed by Ladd's band)
- Proximal small bowel (dilated proximal to obstruction)
Radiological signs:
Plain X-ray: double bubble sign; absence of gas in the abdomen; multiple fluid levels with dilated small bowel; duodenal triangle in the right upper quadrant.
Upper GI series: 'bird's beak'/corkscrew in the barium column; spiral configuration of the duodenum; duodenojejunal junction on the right of the spine; loops of small bowel on the right of the abdomen.
USS: whirlpool sign — SMV and bowel loops wrapping around the SMA; inversion of SMA and SMV positions.

(iii) Differentials in neonatal bilious vomiting:
- Duodenal atresia
- Jejunoileal atresia
- Hirschsprung's disease
- Anorectal malformation
- Malrotation with volvulus

(iv) Clinico-anatomical reasoning:
In normal rotation, a broad mesenteric base is formed extending from the duodenojejunal junction (left upper quadrant) to the ileocaecal junction (right lower quadrant). In non-rotation or arrested rotation, the entire small bowel mesentery is attached along a narrow pedicle around the SMA. This narrow base allows the entire midgut to twist (volvulus) around the SMA, causing obstruction, vascular compromise, and potentially massive intestinal necrosis.
