(i) The differential diagnoses are acute bone infarction (vaso-occlusive crisis) versus acute haematogenous osteomyelitis, both occurring in sickle cell anaemia. The genetic basis: two defective genes; a point mutation — substitution of a single DNA nucleotide base. GUG (Valine) replaces GAG (Glutamic acid) at position 6 from the N-terminal end of the β-chain.
(ii) Common to both: acute bone pain; tenderness over palpable bone; warmth over tender bone; fever; features of inflammation; elevated WBC; elevated ESR; ± positive bone scan. Distinguishing features: Infarction — usually diaphyseal; negative blood culture; plain radiographs inconclusive; photodeficient 99Tc sulphur colloid scan; low yield on PCR quantitation of bacterial DNA. Infection — usually metaphyseal; ± positive culture; plain radiographs inconclusive; increased uptake with 99Tc-MDP; high yield on PCR quantitation of bacterial DNA.
(iii) Modern diagnostic tools: Magnetic resonance imaging — persistent foci of fat signal; persistent foci of fat signal in soft tissue; replacement of marrow fat with fluid. 99mTc-labelled antigranulocyte Mab Fab'2 fragments — 95% specificity. Monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) — elevated MCP-1 mRNA expression in osteoblast cultures; expression in human bone on immunohistochemistry.
(iv) Management: Acute bone infarction — rehydrate; analgesic; rest the limb; management of residues of infarcted bone islands. Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis — high-dose, long-term, combination antibiotics; core decompression; drainage of pyaemic abscesses; management of localised pathological fracture; management of bone destruction (which may necessitate amputation); prevention/treatment of chronic osteomyelitis.

(i) Using the rule of nines: anterior trunk = 18% (front half = 9%), right arm = 9%, total approximately 18% TBSA. English classification: scald with short contact time typically produces superficial or partial thickness burn — extends up to the papillary dermis; heals in two weeks by regeneration of totipotential cells of sebaceous glands, hair follicles and wound edge; pain-prick sensation is intact.

(ii) From the history: chemical, electrical, or thermal burns with prolonged contact time often lead to full thickness burns. Fluorescein dye test: normal tissue will take up the dye. Colour thermoultrasonograph: normal tissue will show warm colour variation. Histology gives the most accurate depth assessment.

(iii) First aid and pre-hospital care: (1) Safely remove patient from contact with source of burns — best done by fire-fighter team and paramedics; individuals trapped in burning buildings should crawl through covered with a wet blanket. (2) Cool burns area with copious clean water for 1–2 hours, then cover with clean dressing. (3) Take patient to hospital; oral rehydration solution or salt solution may be given on the way to help with dehydration.

(iv) Investigations: FBC — may show anaemia, raised reticulocytes, and raised WBC; up to 20% of RBCs are destroyed in major burns necessitating blood transfusion. U and E: K+ may be raised in the first 3 days of burns due to shedding of K+ from destroyed cells; urea and creatinine may be raised in dehydration and renal failure. Wound swab or biopsy for M/C/S: 1 ml of pus or 1 g of tissue with bacterial count indicates infection (organisms include Staph, Streps, Pseudomonas, Aspergillus, Candida, Herpes, cytomegalovirus). Analgesic regimen: IV morphine 10–15 mg 4-hourly.

A(i) The kidneys have natural protection due to their anatomical location. Both kidneys are at equal disposition for injury. Blunt trauma accounts for 80–90% of renal injuries; penetrating trauma accounts for 10–20%. The kidneys are covered by Gerota's fascia (perinephric fascia) and surrounded by perinephric fat. They lie in the retroperitoneum, with the lower ribs providing a degree of bony protection.
A(ii) Children are more prone to renal injury compared with adults because of: relatively large kidney size; scant perinephric fat; underdeveloped Gerota's fascia; incomplete ossification of the lower ribs. These features reduce the degree of natural protection afforded to the paediatric kidney.
B(i) Early complications: Prolonged urinary extravasation; Shock from massive blood loss; Renal infarction; Abscess formation.
B(ii) Late complications: Delayed bleeding; Arteriovenous fistula; Urinary fistula; Hydronephrosis; Renovascular hypertension; PUJ obstruction from perinephric fibrosis; Renal atrophy. Renovascular hypertension occurs as a late complication of renal trauma because perinephric fibrosis following the injury can compress the renal vasculature, activating the renin-angiotensin system and leading to secondary hypertension. This mechanism follows from the anatomical relationship of the perirenal fat and Gerota's fascia to the renal pedicle.

A 7-year-old child presents with fever, inability to walk, and swelling over the right femur. He has a history of sickle cell disease. His WBC is elevated and ESR is raised.
(i) What are the two diagnoses to consider, and what is the most common type of crisis in sickle cell anaemia that predisposes to bone pain?
(ii) Describe the genetic basis of sickle cell anaemia and the molecular events that lead to sickling.
(iii) What are the four types of haematological crises in sickle cell anaemia?
(iv) What is the management of each condition (infarction versus infection) once distinguished?
questions.answerText:
(i) The two diagnoses to consider are acute bone infarction (vaso-occlusive crisis) and acute haematogenous osteomyelitis. Vaso-occlusive crises, which cause bone pain, are the most common crisis type in sickle cell anaemia.
(ii) Genetic basis: Sickle cell anaemia is caused by two defective genes with a point mutation — substitution of a single DNA nucleotide base. GUG (Valine) replaces GAG (Glutamic acid) at position 6 from the N-terminal end of the β-chain. Molecular events: Deoxy-HbS undergoes polymerisation; adhesion of sickled RBC to vascular endothelium; trapping of sickled RBC leads to intravascular haemolysis; vascular slugging/stagnation; increased blood viscosity.
(iii) Four types of haematological crises: (1) Aplastic — arrest of erythropoiesis. (2) Splenic sequestration. (3) Haemolytic — acceleration of haemolysis. (4) Megaloblastic — arrest of erythropoiesis.
(iv) Management of acute bone infarction: Rehydrate; Analgesic; Rest the limb; Management of residues of infarcted bone islands. Management of acute haematogenous osteomyelitis: High-dose, long-term, combination antibiotics; Core decompression; Drainage of pyaemic abscesses; Management of localised pathological fracture; Management of bone destruction (which may necessitate amputation); Prevention and treatment of chronic osteomyelitis.

(i) Diagnosis is compartment syndrome. The pathophysiology: fractures of the limbs cause severe ischaemia by damage to a major artery or by increasing the osteofascial compartment pressure through swelling due to bleeding or oedema. Decreased capillary flow leads to muscle ischaemia, which leads to more oedema, which leads to more pressure, which further decreases capillary flow. This results in rapid pressure build-up leading to muscle and nerve necrosis.
(ii) Risk groups and fracture types: Tibia shaft fracture and forearm fracture carry the greatest risk. Compartment syndrome is especially common in patients aged under 35. It can also result from crush injuries (falling debris or simple compression if patient is unconscious for a length of time) or an over-tight cast.
(iii) Clinical signs — Signs of ischaemia (the 5 Ps): Pain, Paraesthesia, Pallor, Paralysis, Pulselessness. The diagnosis should be made before all these features are present. The presence of a pulse does not exclude the diagnosis. Signs of raised intracompartmental pressure: swollen arm or leg; tender muscle — calf or forearm pain on passive extension of digits; pain out of proportion to injury; redness, mottling and blisters. When uncertain, measure intracompartmental pressure directly.
(iv) Management: Remove or relieve external pressures; Prompt decompression of threatened compartments by open fasciotomy; Debride any muscle necrosis; Treat hypovolaemic shock and oliguria urgently; Renal dialysis may be necessary. Late complications if untreated: Acute renal failure secondary to rhabdomyolysis; DIC; Volkmann's contracture — where infarcted muscle is replaced by inelastic fibrous tissue.

A. Describe the anatomy of SKIN GRAFTS under the following headings: definition; types and their constituents; characteristics comparing partial (split) thickness and full thickness skin grafts in terms of graft take, contractility, resemblance to normal skin, and donor site.

questions.answerText:
A. Definition: A skin graft is a piece of skin transferred from one part of the body to another while it is completely detached from its blood supply or donor site attachment.
Types and characteristics:

Characteristic | Partial (Split) Thickness | Full Thickness
Constituents | Epidermis and part of dermis | Epidermis and whole dermis
Graft take | Better (thinner, allows better diffusion of nutrients) | Less (thicker)
Contractility | Contracts more; hence not suitable over joints | Contracts less
Resemblance to normal | Less | More pliable; contains more hair follicles and sebaceous glands
Donor site | Any suitable site, especially thigh | Areas where skin is thin, e.g., behind the ear, supraclavicular

A(i) Sources (immunological origin):
- Autograft: from the same individual
- Isograft: from the same species and isogeneic (histocompatible) individual
- Allograft: from the same species but a different individual
- Heterograft (xenograft): from a different species (e.g., pig to man) or synthetic materials (e.g., dacron for vascular grafting)
B. Stages of skin graft wound healing:
1. Plasmatic imbibition
2. Graft adherence
3. Capillary ingrowth
4. Graft contraction
5. Graft reinnervation
B(i) Factors that enhance graft take: good vascular bed (healthy granulation tissue); good approximation of graft to bed; immobilisation to prevent undue shearing; avoidance of infection at recipient site (particularly B-haemolytic Streptococcus); avoidance of haematoma and seroma.
Indications for skin grafting: significant gap in a wound that cannot be closed without tension (due to trauma, excision of tumours, or scars); treatment of non-neoplastic ulcers; treatment of full-thickness skin burns.

A(i) (a) The spinal column is the central pillar of the body; all motions and activities are anchored to it. It has a long, superior, flexible segment that supports the head, thorax, and abdomen, and a short, rigid inferior segment (pelvic portion) that carries the lower limbs. Components: bony structures, muscles, ligaments, discs, and spinal cord. Articulation: anteriorly via disc interposition; posterolaterally via facets; laterally via ligaments; posteriorly via ligaments; muscular support throughout.
(b) Regional distribution: 7 vertebrae in the neck (cervical); 12 in the thorax (thoracic); 5 in the lower back (lumbar); 5 fused vertebrae in the buttock (sacrum); 4 fused vertebrae as tailbone (coccyx).
(c) Cervical vertebrae are the smallest; lumbar vertebrae are the largest. The cervical vertebral canal is wide; the lumbar vertebral canal is small.
A(ii) Primary curvatures: thoracic and sacrococcygeal. Secondary curvatures (develop postnatally): cervical and lumbar.
B(i) Anomalies of curvature: kyphosis; lordosis; scoliosis (functional or structural). Anomalies of vertebral bodies: wedge compression; cod-fish lesions; collapse (as in osteoporosis); congenital defects.
B(ii) Disc degeneration can follow disc prolapse and, through progressive narrowing and instability, may compromise nerve roots at adjacent levels causing radicular spread of symptoms. Infective discitis in the lumbar region can cause residual deformity because the infection leads to destruction of the disc and adjacent vertebral end-plates; subsequent healing may occur with irregular bony fusion or collapse, leaving permanent angular deformity.

A. Swanson's classification of congenital upper limb deformities with examples:
1. Failure of part formation:
 - Transverse absence: congenital amputation (e.g., absence of hand at wrist)
 - Longitudinal absence: radial club hand; ulnar club hand; cleft hand
2. Failure of part differentiation: radioulnar synostosis; camptodactyly; trigger thumb; syndactyly
3. Duplication: polydactyly (pre-axial and post-axial)
4. Overgrowth: macrodactyly
5. Undergrowth: thumb hypoplasia (Blauth classification)
6. Miscellaneous: constriction ring syndrome; congenital dislocation of radial head; Madelung's deformity
A(i) Genetic factors: trisomy of chromosomes 21, 18, and 13 are associated with polydactyly and syndactyly; Apert's syndrome follows autosomal dominant (AD) inheritance. Environmental factors: drugs — thalidomide (associated with intercalary amputation, limb defects), dilantin (phenytoin), warfarin; radiation (nuclear and therapeutic) causing microcephaly; infection — TORCH syndromes (toxoplasmosis, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes). Unknown causes also exist.
B. Syndactyly types: Type I — isolated (not associated with a syndrome); Type II — complex, associated with trisomy 13, 14, 21, Apert syndrome (clinodactyly, facies), Holt-Oram syndrome (ASD, radial club hand), and Poland's syndrome (absence of pectoralis major). The mnemonic 5, 15, 50, 30 means: thumb and index = 5%; bilateral in 50%; ring and little = 30% (most common). Surgery is performed at 18 months. Full-thickness skin grafting is almost always required for soft tissue coverage. Technique: mark skin flaps with Z-plasty; dorsal butterfly flap to make the web; both sides of the same digit must never be separated on the same day (allow more than 6 weeks between procedures).
B(i) Post-axial polydactyly: located next to the little finger; is the common hand anomaly; 10 times more common in Blacks; autosomal dominant (AD) inheritance; non-syndromal.
Pre-axial polydactyly: located next to the thumb; common duplication in whites; autosomal recessive (AR) inheritance, chromosome 17; syndromal.
Treatment for both: excise the rudimentary finger.

B. For SYNDACTYLY, describe the types (I and II), the mnemonic for frequency of digital involvement, and the treatment including the timing of surgery.
B(i) For POLYDACTYLY, distinguish between the pre-axial and post-axial varieties in terms of: position, racial predominance, genetic inheritance, and whether they are syndromal or non-syndromal.

courses.title: Electrotherapy II
courses.objectives:
Superficial Heat and Infrared Radiation: Q1–9

questions.question:
A. Describe the technique of application of shortwave diathermy under the following headings: equipment preparation, patient preparation, electrode placement, parameters, dosage, and precautions.
B. Explain the rationale behind the choice of electrode spacing and size in SWD.
C. Distinguish between shortwave diathermy and microwave diathermy.
questions.answerText:
A. Equipment preparation: get the equipment and materials ready and test the machine using a hand or fluorescent/neon-filled tube to check the field before the patient is connected.
Patient preparation: question the patient thoroughly regarding contraindications, position the patient well supported, remove clothing/synthetic materials and metal fastenings from the field, and explain the treatment and sensation expected.
Electrode placement: inspect the area for rashes, infection or open wounds; test skin sensation; dry any moist skin; arrange electrodes coplanar, contraplanar or crossfire as suited to the structure; ensure correct skin-electrode distance.
Parameters: set pulse duration and pulse frequency if pulsed, then turn up the intensity/output, and set treatment time (15-30 minutes).
Dosage: gradually increase intensity to the required dosage level (I-IV), guided by the patient's subjective response, periodically asking if the heating is too vigorous.
Precautions: check contraindications, remove metal/jewellery, keep leads from touching the equipment or patient, maintain adequate spacing, and ensure the patient's feet do not touch the ground (earthing).
B. Normal spacing (about the diameter of the electrode, 2-4cm) gives a uniform field.
Closely spaced or unequal spacing concentrates the field and causes superficial heating under the closer electrode.
Electrodes should be slightly larger than the part treated for a uniform field.
Electrodes too small or of unequal size cause superficial heating, while electrodes too large cause heat loss/wastage.
C. Shortwave diathermy uses radio frequency of 27.12 MHz and penetrates deeply, up to about 5cm, and can heat deep tissue without heating superficial tissue; it covers large areas and allows hands-free application.
Microwave diathermy uses a much higher frequency (2450 MHz) with a shallower effective depth of penetration of about 3cm, and has been used for smaller body parts such as the hands.

A(i) Shortwave diathermy (SWD) is the clinical application of high frequency electromagnetic energy to the body in the radio frequency range to generate heat in deep tissues.
For therapeutic purposes a frequency of 27.12 MHz (wavelength 11.06m) is used; 13.56 MHz and 40.68 MHz are also cited as available frequencies.
A(ii) The current is produced by an oscillator (machine) circuit and transferred to a resonator (patient) circuit; it sets up an electrical field in which charged ions move from pole to pole, and a magnetic field in which a conductor exposed to a changing field develops circulating eddies.
The two circuits must be in resonance for effective energy transfer.
As the waves pass through soft tissue they meet resistance, causing molecular vibration/friction and heat.
The oscillations are of very short duration and do not stimulate motor or sensory nerves.
B(i) Physiological effects: increase in blood flow; increased white cells, histiocytes and fibroblasts in a wound; improved oedema dispersion; encouraged absorption of haematoma; reduction of the inflammatory process; more rapid fibrin fibre orientation and collagen deposition; stimulation of osteogenesis.
Non-thermal effects: restoration of normal cell function through repolarisation, increased cell growth and division, and increased sodium pump activity.
B(ii) Indications: pain relief, reduction of muscle spasm, increased localised blood flow, joint contractures, and decreased joint stiffness.
Further indications: chronic inflammatory/infective conditions (bursitis, tenosynovitis, synovitis), rheumatoid arthritis and chronic osteoarthritis.
Contraindications: implanted electronic devices (pacemaker, myoelectric prosthesis), haemorrhage, septic conditions, and malignant or undiagnosed tumours.
Further contraindications: impaired sensation, acute inflammation, pregnancy, menstruation and deep vein thrombosis.
questions.question:
A(i) Define shortwave diathermy and classify the frequencies used for therapeutic purposes.
A(ii) Describe its physical principles and waveform/characteristics.
B(i) List its physiological and therapeutic effects.
B(ii) State its indications and contraindications.

(i) A patient presents 2 days after a soft tissue injury with acute swelling and pain. State the stage of the condition.
(ii) State the modality selected for this stage and the alternative modality compared for the later stage of the same condition.
(iii) State the treatment parameters for each.
(iv) Justify the final choice of modality for the acute stage.
questions.answerText:
(i) The condition is acute, 2 days after injury, with swelling and pain.
(ii) Pulsed shortwave diathermy (PSWD) is selected for the acute stage, since acute inflammation is a contraindication to thermal (continuous) SWD; continuous SWD (CSWD) is the alternative modality that would be compared for the later, chronic stage once inflammation subsides.
(iii) PSWD parameters: pulse repetition rate 15-800Hz, pulse duration 25-500µs, peak pulse power 100-1000W, with dosage such that no heat should be felt. CSWD parameters: Dosage Level I-IV, gradually increased until warmth is just perceived, for a duration of 15-30 minutes.
(iv) PSWD is justified for the acute stage because its physiological effects are non-thermal (temperature is not appreciably raised) while increasing microvascular perfusion and tissue oxygenation, and its stated indications include soft tissue injury and control of oedema; general contraindications to thermal heating include acute inflammation, since local heat application may exacerbate the inflammatory response.

A. The erythema effect is the reddening observed following application of UVR, with a latent period of about hours; it is uniform, not mottled, with a sharp distinct edge at the junction with unexposed skin, indicating that it is the capillaries in the dermis that dilate rather than the arterioles.
Histamine and prostaglandins cause the capillary dilation; oedema and irritation of the skin become evident if the application is intense, and desquamation (peeling) of the superficial epidermis follows.
For psoriasis, the long wavelength UVA and UVB are beneficial, but not UVC; the mechanism of effect on psoriasis is not clearly understood, though the anticipated mechanism could be an immunosuppressive effect of UVR.
B. Effectiveness depends on the wavelength/band used (UVA penetrates 40-50% to the basal layer, UVB about 10%, and UVC only 40-50µm), since higher doses of UVB are needed to produce the same erythema effect as UVA.
The dose category (E0-E4) selected, which determines the latency and strength of the erythema response, and the body surface area exposed, also affect the outcome.
Condition of the mercury vapour lamp affects effectiveness: tridymite formation on the quartz tube reduces UVR emission over time, so the burner must be changed after 1000 hours of use.
C. Dangers/long-term effects: premature ageing of the skin (more prominent in fair-skinned individuals), skin becoming wrinkled and dry, decreased function of sebaceous and sweat glands, loss of elastic tissue, and increased risk of skin cancer with UVA and UVB exposure over many years.
Effects on the eyes: strong doses of UVB and UVC can cause conjunctivitis and photokeratitis, as UVB and UVC are absorbed in the cornea, while UVA can pass through to be absorbed in the eye lens and has been implicated in cataract formation.
Prevention: check contraindications (photosensitivity, active dermatological conditions, acute febrile illness) before treatment.
Do not exceed the appropriate erythema dose for the condition and skin type.
Do not expose the patient to UVC for more than 4 weeks.
Use protective measures for the eyes and monitor the skin response after treatment.
questions.question:
A. Explain the mechanism of action of ultraviolet radiation in producing the erythema effect and its use in skin conditions such as psoriasis.
B. State the factors affecting the effectiveness of UVR treatment.
C. Describe the dangers of UVR and their prevention.

(i) A patient develops eye irritation with redness and watering shortly after an ultraviolet radiation (UVR) treatment session. State the probable cause of this treatment error.
(ii) State the corrective steps that should be taken.
(iii) State the relevant contraindications or precautions that should have been observed.
(iv) State how the protocol should be modified to continue treatment safely.
questions.answerText:
(i) The probable cause is that the eyes were not adequately protected during UVR treatment; strong doses of UVB and UVC can cause conjunctivitis (inflammation of the tissue over the cornea and lining of the eyelids) and photokeratitis (inflammation of the cornea), as UVB and UVC are absorbed in the cornea.
(ii) Stop treatment, allow the eyes to rest, and ensure the patient is examined; check the erythema dose and lamp type used and whether it exceeded what was suitable for the area/condition treated.
(iii) Relevant precautions: check for contraindications such as photosensitivity and acute febrile illness before treatment; the patient must not be exposed to UVC for more than 4 weeks; UVA can pass through to be absorbed in the eye lens and has been implicated in cataract formation, so the eyes require protection whenever they are near the treatment field.
(iv) Modify the protocol by ensuring the eyes and surrounding areas not intended for treatment are shielded before every subsequent session, confirming the correct lamp (e.g. the water-cooled Kromayer lamp for local lesions, which eliminates the danger of infrared radiation) and erythema dose for the area treated, and testing skin/eye sensitivity beforehand.

questions.question:
A. Explain the mechanism of action of microwave diathermy in producing tissue heating, including the pattern of heating in tissues.
B. State the factors affecting the effectiveness of microwave diathermy treatment.
C. Describe the dangers of microwave diathermy and how they are prevented.
questions.answerText:
A. Microwave energy is produced by a magnetron and radiated toward the tissue as electromagnetic radiation; radiation that penetrates tissue only produces effect if it is absorbed.
In microwaves, there is considerable reflection at the air-skin, skin-fat and fat-muscle boundaries in the tissues.
The percentage of microwave radiation (at 2450 MHz) reflected varies with the thickness of fat and skin, from 50-70%.
The penetration depth is the depth at which 63% of the original radiation has been absorbed and 37% remains, which is 4.3cm for homogeneous tissue; the half value depth (50% absorbed) is usually 3cm.
Absorption of microwaves is lower in fat (half value 3.5cm) and higher in vascular muscle tissue (half value 0.7cm), and reflection from fat-muscle and fat-bone interfaces causes standing waves.
B. Effectiveness is affected by the thickness of fat and skin (which determines how much energy is reflected rather than absorbed), the choice and size/shape of the emitter (circular or rectangular, contact or distance emitter), and the distance between the emitter and the skin, since a diverging beam follows the inverse square law and loses intensity with distance.
Small areas are treated at 2-5cm distance with low intensity, and large areas at about 10cm distance with high intensity.
C. Dangers: burns, cataract (eye damage), and circulatory defects.
Reflectors and metal in the treatment area can render treatment ineffective or unsafe, so these should be avoided/accounted for.
Prevention: keep treatment within the stated contraindications (avoiding metal implants, pacemakers, the eyes, male gonads and overgrowing epiphysis), guide intensity by the patient's sensation of mild warmth, and use protective glasses/goggles during application.
Treatment is usually given for 20 minutes, or up to 30 minutes for significant muscle heating, to avoid excessive energy delivery.
The Specific Absorption Rate (SAR), the rate of energy absorbed per unit tissue mass, is therapeutically kept within 50-170 W/kg.

A. Equipment/tray preparation: prepare a tray containing a tape measure, two test tubes containing warm and cold water, cotton wool swabs, and soap.
Patient preparation: obtain consent, test the patient's skin sensation, and check for contraindications such as pulmonary tuberculosis, photosensitivity or acute febrile illness before treatment.
Dosage: the erythema dose scale runs from E0 to E4, based on latency period and time to erythema.
For example E1 has a latency of 6-12 hours with erythema at 2 days, while E4 has a latency of less than 2 hours with erythema in 7 days.
The body surface area exposed also varies with dose: E1 may cover the whole body, E2 about 20% of the body surface, E3 about 4%, and E4 is not usually given on intact skin, with a maximum area of 25cm² (though larger areas can be applied to an open wound).
Precautions: the patient must not be exposed to UVC for more than 4 weeks, and the mercury vapour lamp burner must be changed after 1000 hours of use and kept dry.
B. The dose is graded upward from E0 to E4 because higher doses shorten the latency period and increase the erythema/inflammatory response and its progression; the dose is therefore selected according to the desired strength of the erythema reaction for the condition treated.
Acne vulgaris is treated with an E2 dose, and eczema with an E1 or E2 dose, reflecting different tolerances of the two conditions.
C. The Hanovia lamp is an air-cooled lamp, a high pressure vapour lamp with a short wavelength of 253nm; it emits UVR, infrared and visible light and is used to treat generalised skin conditions such as acne vulgaris and psoriasis.
The Kromayer lamp is a water-cooled lamp that generates UVA and UVB.
The Kromayer lamp is used for treating local lesions such as pressure sores, ulcers and sinuses, and the danger of infrared radiation is eliminated with this lamp.
The fluorescent tube, by contrast, produces long UVA without short UVC and is mainly used for general irradiation of an individual or a group.
questions.question:
A. Describe the technique of application of ultraviolet radiation under the following headings: equipment/tray preparation, patient preparation, dosage, and precautions.
B. Explain the rationale behind the choice of erythema dose (E-dose) used.
C. Distinguish between the Hanovia lamp and the Kromayer lamp.

questions.answerText:
(i) IRR is indicated for pain relief, and low back pain and strain/sprain are specifically listed among the conditions helped, alongside osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and cervical spondylosis; the sedative action on naked nerve endings and the pain-gate mechanism support its use for the associated muscle spasm and pain.
(ii) Contraindications: haemorrhage, malignant growth, defective thermal sensation, defective arterial blood supply, scar tissue or devitalised tissue following X-ray application, and cardiovascular disease.
(iii) Dangers: burns, electric shock, eye damage (cataracts), and fainting from a fall in blood pressure due to extensive irradiation. Prevention is by keeping the correct lamp distance (luminous IRR 45-60cm; non-luminous IRR 75-90cm), limiting duration (acute conditions 10-15 minutes, chronic conditions 10-30 minutes), and testing skin sensation before treatment.
(iv) Prepare a tray with a tape measure, two test tubes of warm and cold water, cotton wool swabs and soap; test the patient's skin sensation with these before application, obtain consent, and check for the contraindications above; the patient should be positioned so the lamp does not tip and the skin is monitored throughout for overheating.
questions.question:
(i) A patient presents with chronic low back pain and associated muscle spasm. State the indications that support the use of infrared radiation (IRR) in this case.
(ii) State the contraindications and precautions that must be checked before treatment.
(iii) State the dangers/adverse effects of IRR and how they are prevented.
(iv) State the patient instructions and skin/safety checks that must be carried out.

A. Describe the technique of application of infrared radiation under the following headings: equipment/tray, patient preparation, parameters, dosage, and precautions.
B. Explain the rationale behind the choice of lamp distance and treatment duration.
C. Distinguish between luminous and non-luminous infrared generators.
questions.answerText:
A. Equipment/tray: prepare a tray with a tape measure, two test tubes containing warm and cold water, cotton wool swabs, and soap.
Patient preparation: obtain consent, test the patient's skin sensation with the warm/cold test tubes, and check for contraindications such as haemorrhage, malignant growth, defective thermal or arterial sensation, or cardiovascular disease.
Parameters: position the luminous lamp at 45-60cm from the patient, or the non-luminous lamp at 75-90cm.
Dosage: treat acute conditions for 15 minutes and chronic conditions for 30 minutes; dosage of IRR is determined by the intensity of the lamp output and the distance of the lamp from the patient.
Precautions: the properties of IRR are that it can be reflected, refracted, transmitted or absorbed, so the lamp and reflector should be positioned to direct radiation onto the treatment area only, and the patient monitored throughout for excessive heating.
B. The distance is set according to the lamp type, since the luminous lamp is positioned closer (45-60cm) and the non-luminous lamp further away (75-90cm), while the duration is set according to the stage of the condition, with a shorter time for acute conditions (15 minutes) than for chronic conditions (30 minutes).
This is consistent with dosage of IRR being governed by the intensity of the lamp output together with its distance from the patient and the duration of application.
C. Luminous IR is produced by a tungsten filament within a glass bulb containing inert gas, heated to about 3000°C, producing near infrared (780-1500nm); heat is produced instantly and no warm-up time is required.
Luminous lamps penetrate the dermis and subcutaneous fat to a depth of 5-10mm, and a red filter may be used to prevent blue and green light from passing through.
Non-luminous IR is produced by a coiled resistance wire wound or embedded in ceramic insulated material, producing far infrared (1500-12000nm) with no visible rays.
A warm-up period of 5-10 minutes is required due to the time needed to heat the core, and the power of the units may vary from 50-1000 watts.
Non-luminous IR penetrates to a depth of less than 5mm, and lacks the near-infrared/visible component that characterises luminous generators.

(i) The presentation of pink or red patchy thickened skin covered by silvery scales is psoriasis.
(ii) Ultraviolet radiation (UVR) is chosen, as psoriasis is a stated indication for UVB; the air-cooled Hanovia lamp is specifically used for generalised skin conditions such as psoriasis and acne vulgaris.
(iii) The long wavelength UVA and UVB are beneficial for the treatment of psoriasis, but not UVC. The mechanism of effect of UVR on psoriasis is not clearly understood, though the anticipated mechanism could be an immunosuppressive effect of UVR. General UVR effects that would apply include altered cell turnover in the basal layer, increased pigmentation, and the erythema reaction (reddening with a sharp distinct edge, due to dilation of dermal capillaries).
(iv) The air-cooled Hanovia lamp is used, which emits UVR, infrared and visible light and has a short wavelength of 253nm; the general dosing framework uses categories E0 to E4 based on latency and erythema time.
questions.question:
(i) A patient presents with pink or red patchy, thickened skin covered by silvery scales on the extensor surfaces. State the physiotherapy/dermatological diagnosis suggested.
(ii) Identify the electrotherapy modality chosen and give the rationale for this choice.
(iii) Describe the physiological and therapeutic effects relevant to this condition.
(iv) Describe the treatment parameters and technique of application, including lamp type.

questions.answerText:
(i) SWD indications include pain relief and rheumatoid arthritis (RhA) specifically, along with reduction of muscle spasm and decrease of joint stiffness which commonly accompany RhA.
(ii) Contraindications: implanted electronic devices such as a cardiac pacemaker, haemorrhage or risk of haemorrhage, septic conditions, malignant or undiagnosed tumours, impaired sensation, acute inflammation, severe heart disease, wetness/perspiration/damp bandaging, and pregnancy. Precautions: clothing removed, skin dried, separate skin surfaces, leads not touching the equipment or patient, and adequate spacing.
(iii) Dangers: burns from field concentration around metal or moisture, scalds from moist heat, precipitation of gangrene in impaired blood flow, overdose, electric shock, and sparking from touching an electrode. Prevention is by checking contraindications, removing metal objects, drying the skin, and keeping the patient's feet off the ground (earthing).
(iv) The patient should be told what sensation to expect (warmth), instructed to report immediately if the heating feels too vigorous, and told not to touch the electrodes or leads while the machine is running; the physiotherapist periodically asks the patient if the heating is too vigorous throughout the session.
questions.question:
(i) A patient with rheumatoid arthritis presents with joint pain. State the indications supporting the use of shortwave diathermy (SWD) in this case.
(ii) State the contraindications and precautions that must be checked before treatment.
(iii) State the dangers of SWD and how they are prevented.
(iv) State the patient instructions to be given during treatment.

questions.answerText:
A. SWD produces high frequency current that sets up an electrical field, in which charged ions move from pole to pole, and a magnetic field, in which a conductor exposed to a changing field develops circulating eddies.
As the high frequency energy passes through soft tissue it meets resistance, causing molecular/ionic vibration and friction, which generates heat.
Because the wavelengths are too short, SWD cannot produce depolarisation and contraction of muscle, so its primary thermal pathway is molecular friction rather than direct nerve or muscle stimulation.
The non-thermal (athermal) effects occur at the cell membrane, where the electromagnetic energy affects ion attraction and cell function.
These non-thermal effects restore normal function through repolarisation of damaged cells, increase cell growth and division, and reactivate the sodium pump to regain normal ionic balance.
B. Factors affecting field distribution and hence effectiveness include the spacing of electrodes: normal spacing gives a uniform field, close spacing gives superficial heating, and far spacing gives deep heating.
The size of the electrodes also matters: electrodes slightly larger than the part give a uniform field, while too-small or unequal-sized electrodes give superficial heating.
The positioning of electrodes relative to the treatment area matters: electrodes parallel to the skin give a uniform field, while non-parallel electrodes give superficial heat under the closest part.
The presence of metal in the treatment area concentrates the field and causes excessive, uneven heating, and the dosage level (I-IV) and duration selected also determine the amount of heating delivered.
C. Dangers: burns from concentration of the electric field around metal or moisture; scalds from moist heat if the treated area is moist; precipitation of gangrene if SWD is applied to an area with impaired blood flow, such as in Buerger's disease.
Further dangers: overdose if symptoms increase; electric shock from contact with a broken cable or an uncased/unearthed machine; and sparking if the patient touches an electrode while current is passing.
Prevention: check contraindications, ensure the area is completely unclothed with the skin dried, remove metal objects and jewellery, keep the patient from touching the electrodes or cables, and keep anyone with a cardiac pacemaker at least 20 feet from an inductive field or 50 feet from a capacitive field.
questions.question:
A. Explain the mechanism of action of shortwave diathermy in producing tissue heating and its non-thermal (athermal) effects.
B. State the factors affecting the effectiveness of shortwave diathermy treatment.
C. Describe the dangers of shortwave diathermy and how they are prevented.

(i) A patient presents with stiffness and pain in the small joints of the hand due to a rheumatic/arthritic condition. State the physiotherapy problem represented.
(ii) Identify the electrotherapy modality chosen and give the rationale for choosing it for this body part.
(iii) Describe the physiological and therapeutic effects relevant to this case.
(iv) Describe the treatment parameters and technique of application.
questions.answerText:
(i) The problem is joint stiffness and pain affecting a small, distal extremity, consistent with a rheumatic/arthritic condition of the hand.
(ii) Paraffin wax bath is chosen because it is best suited for the distal extremities, using its primary method of dip and wrap or dip and immerse, and it completely conforms to the treatment area, though the patient is unable to remove it during treatment.
(iii) The mineral oil added to the paraffin wax lowers its melting point, making it tolerable to immerse the hand; as a superficial heating agent using conduction, it contributes to the general interventional goals of therapeutic heat: pain reduction, control of muscle spasm, increased tissue extensibility and support for wound/tissue healing.
(iv) Paraffin is stored in double-walled thermostatically controlled stainless steel tanks at 47-54.4°C; the hand is dipped and wrapped to build a paraffin glove, then a plastic bag is placed over the wax before a towel is used to wrap it and prevent heat loss, with the wrapped hand positioned in elevation to minimise oedema formation; other methods used are brushing and bandaging, and the duration of intervention is 15-20 minutes.

(i) Low intensity laser therapy is indicated because its therapeutic effects include wound and fracture healing; using a He-Ne source at a dosage up to 4 J/cm² has reported success in healing chronic and acute surgical wounds, and wavelengths of 660nm, 820nm and 870nm encourage macrophages to release factors that stimulate fibroblast proliferation.
(ii) Contraindications and precautions: carcinoma (laser could accelerate carcinogenesis), 4-6 months following radiotherapy (radiotherapy increases tissue susceptibility to malignancy and burns), haemorrhage (laser-induced vasodilation would exacerbate it), local application to endocrine glands (alters gland function), and treatment over a pregnant uterus.
(iii) Class 3 lasers, which are commercially available therapeutic lasers, are safe for the skin but harmful to the eyes, so both therapist and patient must wear protective goggles designed for the wavelength used; using 880nm has been reported to inhibit the healing process, so this wavelength should be avoided for wound healing.
(iv) The patient and therapist must wear protective goggles for the whole session; the skin is wiped with alcohol before treatment to remove dirt that could cause scattering of the rays; the body part is positioned so the applicator's pressure does not cause movement or discomfort, and the device is switched off before the applicator is removed at the end of treatment.
questions.question:
(i) A patient has a slow-healing chronic surgical incision. State the indications supporting the use of low intensity laser therapy in this case.
(ii) State the contraindications and precautions that must be checked before treatment.
(iii) State the dangers/adverse effects of laser therapy and how they are prevented.
(iv) State the patient instructions and safety checks required during treatment.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The mechanisms by which therapeutic heat or cold is delivered to the target tissue are conduction, convection, radiation, conversion, and evaporation.
A(ii) Conduction is temperature loss or gain through direct contact between materials with a temperature difference.
Heat absorbed by the body when using a hot pack, or heat lost from a cold pack, is an example of conduction.
Convection is the transference of thermal energy to a body by the movement of air, matter or liquid around the body.
Fluidotherapy, where warm air is circulated through a bed of fine-grained cellulose particles around a body part, is a clinical example, while a freezer is a device example where the surrounding air becomes cooled rather than heated.
Radiation transfers heat through air from a warmer source to a cooler source without contact; the infrared element in a lamp is a therapeutic example, with radiant heat going only to the body area intended and the immediate vicinity of the lamp.
Conversion is a temperature change resulting from energy being transformed from one form into another, such as continuous wave therapeutic ultrasound, where sound (mechanical) energy is transformed to heat (thermal) energy absorbed by body tissue.
Evaporation is the transformation from a liquid to a gas state, with heat given off as the liquid transforms into gas.
Sweating results in cooling as it evaporates from the skin surface, and vapocoolant sprays cause cooling of the skin via evaporation.
B. The extent of temperature change results from the temperature difference between the thermal agent and the tissue area treated, the duration of exposure to the thermal agent, the thermal conductivity of the tissue area treated, and the intensity of the thermal agent.
The greater the temperature difference between the agent and the tissue, the greater the temperature change that can be produced in the tissue.
questions.question:
A(i) Define and classify the mechanisms by which therapeutic heat or cold is delivered to the target tissue.
A(ii) Describe the physical principle of each mechanism, with a clinical example.
B. State the factors affecting the extent of temperature change produced.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Ultraviolet radiation (UVR) lies between the violet end of the visible light and the X-ray region and is invisible to the human eye.
It is divided into three bands: UVA/long UV (400-315nm, penetrates to the dermis, responsible for slow natural tan), UVB/medium UV (315-280nm, erythemal, produces new pigment formation, sunburn, vitamin D synthesis), and UVC/short UV (280-100nm, germicidal, does not reach the surface of the earth).
A(ii) Physical properties of UVR: reflection, refraction, absorption and penetration.
Therapeutic UVR is produced by a mercury vapour lamp, using a straight tube or U-tube burner made of quartz, with air evacuated and argon and mercury droplets inside at low pressure; electrodes at the ends strike an arc, and gases become good conductors at the resulting high temperature and low pressure with high voltage.
Over time, tridymite (a form of silica) covers the lining of the quartz tube, reducing UVR emission because it is opaque to UVR.
B(i) Physiological effects: altered cell turnover, taking about 6 days for mitosis in the basal layer (stratum germinativum), and an epidermal transit time of about 28 days or longer for a cell to be shed as keratin flakes.
Stimulation of melanin production causing pigmentation, and the erythema effect: reddening with a latent period of hours, uniform with a sharp distinct edge, due to capillary dilation caused by histamine and prostaglandins.
Desquamation (peeling) of the superficial epidermis occurs if application is intense.
UVB also converts a sterol in the skin (7-dehydrocholesterol) to vitamin D, and opens skin pores to eliminate sebum.
B(ii) Indications: psoriasis, acne vulgaris, eczema, ulcers, pressure sore, and surgical incisions.
Further indications: vitiligo, pruritus, vitamin D deficiency and alopecia.
Contraindications: pulmonary tuberculosis, recent skin grafts, active dermatological conditions, severe diabetes (peripheral nerve damage), photosensitivity and acute febrile illness.
questions.question:
A(i) Define ultraviolet radiation and classify its three bands with their wavelength ranges.
A(ii) Describe its physical properties and how therapeutic UVR is produced.
B(i) List its physiological effects.
B(ii) State its indications and contraindications.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Microwave diathermy (MWD) is a form of electromagnetic radiation that lies between shortwaves and infrared waves; the therapeutic generators use a frequency of 2450 MHz and a wavelength of 122.5mm.
Its effective depth of penetration is about 3cm, less deep than SWD.
A(ii) A device called the magnetron produces a high frequency alternating current directly from high velocity electron motion.
This current is carried by a coaxial cable to a director/emitter (antenna) mounted in front of a metal reflector, which radiates the microwaves toward the tissue.
Circular directors give heating that is more intense on the outer portion than the centre, while rectangular directors give heating more intense in the centre.
The emitter is also called a director or applicator, and the emitter is arranged parallel to the skin surface during application.
B(i) Physiological effects (direct): increased metabolic activity, increased blood flow, stimulation of neural receptors in the skin/tissues.
Physiological effects (indirect): muscle relaxation and more efficient muscular action, general rise in temperature with dilation of superficial vessels, a fall in blood pressure, and increased sweat gland activity eliminating waste products.
Therapeutic effects: relief of pain, reduction of muscle spasm, reinforcement of the body's defence mechanism against infection, promotion of healing, and increased tissue extensibility.
B(ii) Indications: strains/sprains, muscle or tendon tears, stiffness of superficial joints, capsular lesions, rheumatic conditions, tenosynovitis/bursitis, and infected surgical incisions.
Contraindications: malignant tissue/tuberculosis, metal implants or pacemaker, overgrowing epiphysis, impaired sensation, the eyes and male gonads.
Further contraindications: haemorrhage/thrombosis/phlebitis, pregnancy, and over wet dressing or adhesive tapes.
questions.question:
A(i) Define microwave diathermy and state the frequency/wavelength used therapeutically.
A(ii) Describe how the microwave energy is produced and delivered to the tissue.
B(i) List its physiological and therapeutic effects.
B(ii) State its indications and contraindications.

(i) A patient presents with a soft tissue injury with associated swelling in the subacute stage. Identify the electrotherapy modality best suited to this presentation.
(ii) Describe the mechanism of action of this modality relevant to the swelling.
(iii) Describe the electrode/applicator placement and dosage.
(iv) Describe the progression, monitoring and end-point of treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) Pulsed shortwave diathermy (PSWD) is best suited, as its stated indications are soft tissue injury, control of oedema, and wound healing.
(ii) PSWD's physiological effects show that temperature is not appreciably raised (non-thermal); it increases microvascular perfusion, increases local tissue oxygenation and nutrient availability, which supports resolution of swelling without the risks associated with vigorous heating.
(iii) The techniques of application are the same as for continuous SWD, using the same electrode types and placement (coplanar, contraplanar or crossfire, according to the structure treated). Dosage: no heat should be felt, achieved through a combination of pulse frequency and pulse power settings.
(iv) PSWD is described as useful in post-traumatic and infective conditions; treatment can progress by monitoring for reduction of oedema and improvement of symptoms, with the physiotherapist periodically checking that no heat sensation is being produced, and continuing until the swelling/oedema is controlled.

(i) The condition is acute, being within 2 days of the ankle sprain, with active swelling and pain.
(ii) Cryotherapy (cold pack) is selected for the acute stage; hydrocollator (hot pack) is the alternative modality that would be compared for a later, chronic stage of joint stiffness in the same ankle.
(iii) Cryotherapy parameters: applied via conduction and convection, with care to avoid reducing tissue temperature to 10°C or below, over a duration guided by the hunting response cycle (12-30 minutes). Hydrocollator parameters: water storage temperature 71-79°C, covered with 4-8 layers of towelling, for a typical application of 20 minutes.
(iv) Cryotherapy is justified for the acute stage because acute inflammation and acute haemorrhage are contraindications to superficial heating agents (heat may exacerbate the inflammatory response and may prolong haemorrhage after an acute injury), whereas cryotherapy's physiological effect at this stage is vasoconstriction with decreased local blood flow, which is appropriate for controlling acute swelling; heat would only be considered once the acute stage has resolved.

questions.answerText:
A. Equipment preparation: switch on the power; after some delay the physiotherapist tests the apparatus by placing the hand or arm in front of the emitter and increasing the output until warmth is felt.
The controls are then turned to 0 and the switch turned to the standby position before the patient is treated.
Patient preparation: place the patient in a comfortable position, expose the area to be treated, clean it and make sure it is dry, and remove jewellery.
Warn the patient to avoid movement once the emitter is on, and ensure the patient wears protective glasses.
Applicator placement: arrange the emitter so its surface is parallel to the skin, avoiding areas that perspire freely or have irregular surfaces.
Parameters/dosage: up to 200 watts can be applied, guided by the patient's sensation of mild warmth, for a duration of 10-30 minutes, with weaker doses and shorter durations for acute conditions.
Precautions: remove jewellery, dry the skin, avoid irregular or perspiring surfaces, and keep the patient still once treatment begins.
B. The dosage is guided by the patient's sensation because the output controls are not precise for accurately measuring the heat delivered to the patient.
Weaker doses and shorter durations are chosen for acute conditions to avoid excessive heating of freshly injured tissue.
C. The circular director produces a heating pattern that is more intense on the outer portion than the centre.
The rectangular director produces a heating pattern that is more intense in the centre than the outer portion.
The director shape chosen therefore affects where within the treatment field the tissue is heated most intensely.

(i) The condition is chronic, with stiffness of a superficial joint rather than acute inflammation.
(ii) Microwave diathermy (MWD) is selected, with shortwave diathermy (SWD) as the alternative modality for comparison; both are indicated for stiffness of superficial joints (MWD) and decreased joint stiffness (SWD).
(iii) MWD parameters: up to 200 watts, guided by the patient's sensation of mild warmth, for a duration of 10-30 minutes. SWD parameters: dosage Level I-IV, gradually increased until warmth is just perceived, for 15-30 minutes.
(iv) MWD is justified because it has been used for smaller body parts such as the hands, and its effective depth of penetration (about 3cm) suits a superficial joint, whereas SWD's deeper penetration (several centimetres) and its use for covering larger areas make it more suited to bigger, deeper structures.

questions.answerText:
(i) Ultraviolet radiation (UVR) is best suited, as pressure sores, ulcers and surgical incisions are among its stated indications; specifically, the water-cooled Kromayer lamp is appropriate as it is used for local lesions such as pressure sores, ulcers and sinuses.
(ii) The Kromayer lamp generates UVA and UVB; using this lamp eliminates the danger of infrared radiation (IRR) that would otherwise accompany the treatment, which is a stated advantage for treating local lesions such as this.
(iii) The applicator is held close to the local lesion as appropriate for a water-cooled local lamp. The general UVR dosing framework uses erythema doses E0 to E4 with body surface area guidance (E1-whole body, E2-20% of body, E3-4% of body, E4-not usually given on intact skin, maximum area 25cm² but larger areas can be applied to an open wound).

(i) The problem is hypersensitivity and pain in a distal extremity with reduced tolerance for motion following immobilisation.
(ii) Fluidotherapy is chosen because it allows stimulation of the thermoreceptors and mechanoreceptors and can serve for simultaneous use of motion while reducing pain and hypersensitivity, unlike a static agent such as a hot pack that does not allow movement during treatment.
(iii) The method of heat transfer is convection, with natural cellulose particles enclosed in a cabinet through which dry warm air is circulated; it can be utilised therapeutically for pain relief, tissue healing, and to increase range of motion, and unlike paraffin baths and hydrocollator packs there is no loss of heat over time.
(iv) Units are thermostatically controlled between 38.8°C and 47.8°C and are fabricated to accommodate the extremities; an airtight barrier is applied before starting the unit, and the temperature is set and maintained for the period of treatment; fluidotherapy has been reported to be safe when used with splints, bandages, tape, metal implants, plastic joint replacements and artificial tendons, and exercise balls can also be used during the intervention.

questions.answerText:
(i) The condition is acute, being only 1 day after the strain injury.
(ii) Low intensity laser therapy is selected for pain management of the acute strain; for the alternative presentation of chronic tendinitis, a higher pulse repetition rate with a shorter pulse length would be used, compared with the acute case.
(iii) For the acute strain: a low pulse rate with a long pulse length is used. For chronic tendinitis: a high pulse rate with a short pulse length is used; in both cases, energy density is typically 1-10 J/cm² within the routine range of 0.5-32 J/cm², and the wavelength (visible red for superficial structures or infrared for deeper musculoskeletal structures) is selected according to the depth of the tissue.
(iv) The low pulse rate/long pulse length is justified for the acute strain because pulse repetition rate is specifically matched to the stage of the condition, with low pulse rate and long pulse length used for acute conditions, and treatment is started at a low dose, increased only if there is no change after review.

questions.question:
A. Describe the technique of application of low intensity laser therapy under the following headings: patient preparation, apparatus preparation, application of treatment, and dosage parameters.
B. Explain the rationale behind the choice of pulse repetition rate.
C. Distinguish between the visible red (He-Ne) laser and the infrared laser in terms of use.
questions.answerText:
A. Patient preparation: the patient and physiotherapist wear protective goggles; the skin to be treated is wiped with alcohol to remove dirt that can cause scattering of the rays, and the body part is positioned so pressure from the applicator does not cause movement or discomfort.
Apparatus preparation: the laser apparatus is conveniently positioned, and protective goggles designed for the particular wavelength used are provided.
Application of treatment: the applicator is applied to the surface before switching on the machine, some applicators have an indicator light showing the laser is on, and the applicator is maintained in contact with the tissue at right angles to ensure maximum penetration; if contact is not desired, as with an infected wound, the applicator is held just off the surface or covered with transparent non-reflective film.
When terminating treatment, the device is switched off before the applicator is removed.
Dosage parameters: power output is expressed in milliwatts (older machines 1-10mW, newer machines 30-200mW); irradiance (power density) is the power output divided by the treatment head size (0.1-0.125cm²); energy in Joules equals power output in watts multiplied by duration of application (e.g. 0.03W x 60 seconds = 1.8 Joules).
Energy density is measured in J/cm², with typical routine treatment ranging from 0.5-32 J/cm² and 1-10 J/cm² commonly used.
B. A low pulse rate with a long pulse length is used for acute conditions.
A high pulse rate with a short pulse length is used for chronic conditions.
The pulse repetition rate is therefore chosen according to the stage of the condition being treated.
C. Visible red laser is recommended for superficial lesions such as wounds, ulcers and skin conditions.
Infrared laser is recommended for deeper musculoskeletal structures.
The wavelength/colour of laser used is therefore matched to the depth of the tissue being targeted.

questions.question:
(i) During shortwave diathermy treatment of the lower back, a patient develops a localised burn. State the probable cause of this treatment error.
(ii) State the corrective steps that should be taken.
(iii) State the relevant contraindications or precautions that should have been observed.
(iv) State how the protocol should be modified to continue treatment safely.
questions.answerText:
(i) The probable cause is concentration of the electric field, which occurs in the presence of metal within the treatment area, or a scald from moist heat if the treated area was moist; unequal or too-close electrode spacing can also cause superficial concentration of heating under the closer or smaller electrode.
(ii) Stop the treatment, inspect and manage the burn, remove any metal objects or damp bandaging from the area, and check that the electrodes have correct, equal spacing (normal 2-4cm) before any further application.
(iii) Relevant precautions: the body area to be treated should be completely unclothed with the skin dried, particularly where perspiration accumulates in skin folds; metal objects such as jewellery, watches, keys, belt buckles and underwire bras that can be removed should be removed before treatment; wetness, perspiration or damp bandaging is a contraindication.
(iv) Modify the protocol by ensuring the skin is dry and metal-free, using normal, equal electrode spacing, setting the output according to the patient's subjective response to heat, and periodically asking the patient whether the heating is too vigorous throughout the session.

(i) The probable cause is that the doses used were inappropriately low; negative results with laser therapy for musculoskeletal disorders could be because of inappropriately low doses.
(ii) Guidance is to start at a low dose, and if there is no change to the treatment, the dose should be increased; 5 to 6 treatments are said to be adequate to achieve a response to treatment, so the treatment course and dose should be reviewed against this guidance.
(iii) Relevant contraindications to review before increasing the dose: carcinoma, 4-6 months following radiotherapy, haemorrhage (laser-induced vasodilation would exacerbate it), local application to endocrine glands, and treatment over a pregnant uterus.
(iv) Modify the protocol by gradually increasing the dose within the routine energy density range (typically 1-10 J/cm², up to 0.5-32 J/cm²), continuing to protect the eyes of both patient and therapist with wavelength-appropriate goggles, and reassessing the patient's response after the 5th or 6th treatment.

(ii) State the corrective steps that should be taken.
(iii) State the relevant contraindications or precautions that should be reviewed before continuing.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Infrared radiation (IRR) is radiation of longer wavelength than the red end of the visible spectrum, extending to the microwave region, with a wavelength range of 760nm to 1mm; any heated body emits IRR.
It is subdivided into IR-A (760-1400nm, near IR), IR-B (1400-3000nm, far IR), and IR-C (3000nm-1mm, not used in therapy).
A(ii) Luminous IR is produced by a tungsten filament within a glass bulb containing inert gas, heated to about 3000°C, producing near IR (780-1500nm); a red filter may be used to prevent blue and green light from passing through.
Luminous IR penetrates the dermis and subcutaneous fat to a depth of 5-10mm.
Non-luminous IR is produced by a coiled resistance wire wound or embedded in ceramic insulated material, producing far IR (1500-12000nm) with no visible rays, penetrating to less than 5mm depth.
B(i) Physiological effects: cutaneous vasodilation (direct and axon reflex), release of histamine, dilation of arterioles, an erythema (reddening) effect lasting 30 minutes after irradiation stops.
Increased sweat gland activity (sweat absorbs heat and evaporates, cooling the skin), and sedation of naked nerve endings producing pain relief, with increased metabolism following Van't Hoff's law.
Therapeutic effects: pain relief in conditions such as osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, cervical spondylosis, low back pain, strain and sprain, via sedation of nerve endings, the pain gate theory, and washing away of pain metabolites.
Reduction of joint stiffness, since increased soft tissue extensibility combined with stretching/mobilisation increases joint range of motion, and improved circulation aiding healing of skin lesions such as ulcers.
B(ii) Dosage guidance: luminous IRR lamp distance 45-60cm, non-luminous IRR distance 75-90cm.
Duration for acute conditions is 15 minutes and for chronic conditions 30 minutes.
Contraindications: haemorrhage, malignant growth, defective thermal sensation, defective arterial blood supply, scar tissue or devitalised tissue following X-ray application, and cardiovascular disease.

questions.answerText:
A. The initial response to cold from the surface of the body is heat loss and vasoconstriction of the superficial blood vessels.
Further cooling stimulates free nerve endings, leading to reflex vasoconstriction with decreased local blood flow, and deeper cooling may stimulate the hypothalamus, resulting in further vasoconstriction that reduces the flow of cooled blood to retain heat in the system.
The hunting response is the cycle of vasoconstriction-vasodilation lasting 12-30 minutes during cold exposure, with vasodilation occurring before the vasoconstrictive phase.
Skin vessels were shown to maximally constrict at 15°C, followed by vasodilation at temperatures below 15°C, reaching maximal vasodilation at 0°C; this cold-induced vascular response is thought to prevent local tissue injury.
B. The presence of adipose tissue is inversely proportional to the depth of cold penetration, because it acts as insulation.
Deeper cooling of muscles and joints is possible when the structures are more superficially located, but with excessive adipose tissue a longer application time is needed; tissue temperature changes to cold application have been reported at depths of 1-4cm.
C. A decrease in tissue temperature to 10°C or below may result in thermal damage to tissues.
This thermal damage may trigger an inflammatory response and result in an increase in oedema, which may explain the conflicting results seen in animal studies of the effects of cryotherapy on post-traumatic oedema.
Cold application also decreases elasticity and increases viscosity of the tissue's visco-elastic properties, so tissues that are cold may not respond as favourably to length changes, and range of motion measures taken after cold application may not be accurate.
Prevention: avoid reducing tissue temperature to 10°C or below, and account for the depth of adipose tissue when deciding the duration of application.
Monitor the skin and the patient's response throughout the treatment, particularly during the vasoconstriction-vasodilation cycle of the hunting response.
Be cautious about assessing range of motion immediately after cold application, since the results may not be an accurate reflection of the tissue's normal extensibility.

(i) A patient presents with longstanding pain and stiffness in the knee joint consistent with chronic osteoarthritis, with no signs of acute inflammation. State the physiotherapy problem this presentation represents.
(ii) Identify the electrotherapy modality most suited to this case and give the rationale for choosing it over a superficial heating agent.
(iii) Describe the physiological and therapeutic effects this modality would produce in the joint.
(iv) Describe the treatment parameters and technique of application, including electrode arrangement, spacing and dosage level.
questions.answerText:
(i) The problem is chronic joint stiffness and pain in a deeply placed joint structure (chronic osteoarthritis); the interventional goals are pain reduction, decrease of joint stiffness and increase of tissue extensibility.
(ii) Shortwave diathermy (SWD) is indicated because it produces deep heating of several centimetres, unlike superficial heating agents which penetrate less than 2-3cm; SWD's stated indications include chronic osteoarthritis and decrease of joint stiffness.
(iii) Effects: increase in tissue temperature and blood flow; decreased joint stiffness; increased cell membrane filtration and diffusion; increased metabolism; decrease in pain; muscle relaxation; decrease in inflammation. A rise of 2-3°C decreases pain and muscle spasm, while a rise of more than 3-4°C increases tissue compliance to stretch, allowing treatment of chronic connective tissue disorders.
(iv) Because the knee is deeply placed, use contraplanar electrode placement (electrodes over opposite aspects) so the electric field is directed through the deep tissue; electrodes must be parallel to the skin and not too close to each other; use flexible pad or space plate electrodes with normal spacing (2-4cm) for a uniform field; gradually increase intensity until the patient just perceives warmth, at Dosage Level III (medium, comfortable warming), for 20-30 minutes.

questions.question:
(i) A patient with chronic low back pain and limited range of motion is being considered for hydrocollator (hot pack) therapy. State the indications supporting this choice.
(ii) State the contraindications and precautions that must be checked before treatment.
(iii) State the dangers/adverse effects and how they are prevented.
(iv) State the patient instructions and skin/safety checks required.
questions.answerText:
(i) The interventional goals of superficial therapeutic heat are pain reduction and management, control of muscle spasm, and tissue extensibility, all relevant to chronic low back pain with limited range of motion.
(ii) Contraindications: acute inflammation, existing fever, malignancies, acute haemorrhage, peripheral vascular disease, tissue devitalised by x-ray therapy, undiagnosed conditions, an unconscious patient, and metal implants. Precautions: during the menstrual cycle (may increase blood flow near the low back), sensory deficit, pregnancy, superficial implants/jewellery, and mental illness.
(iii) Dangers: burns from inadequate insulation or excessive application time. Prevention: cover the hot pack with 4 to 8 layers of towelling before application, since this insulates the pack from heat loss and protects the patient from skin burn, and monitor the initial response during the first 5-10 minutes, ensuring the heat feels warm, not hot.
(iv) Adequately position and drape the patient, visually inspect the area and perform a skin sensation test, and assess the patient's ability to report sensory changes; explain to the patient what to expect from the heat and instruct them to report any unusual sensation such as overheating or burning; maximum skin temperature change is achieved within the first 10 minutes and maintained for a further 10 minutes, giving a typical application time of 20 minutes, after which the skin is re-observed and the response documented.

A(i) Cryotherapy is comprised of two Greek words, cryo (meaning cold) and therapeia (therapy, meaning cure); it refers to the use of cold temperature to treat disease.
It can be applied as cold packs, cool whirlpool, ice-wraps, and ice massage, or as a cooling agent such as a cold spray.
A(ii) The methods of thermal exchange for cryotherapy are conduction and convection.
B(i) The initial response to cold from the surface of the body is heat loss and vasoconstriction of the superficial blood vessels.
Further cooling stimulates free nerve endings, leading to reflex vasoconstriction with decreased local blood flow.
Deeper cooling may stimulate the hypothalamus, resulting in further vasoconstriction to retain heat in the system.
The hunting response is the cycle of vasoconstriction-vasodilation lasting 12-30 minutes during cold exposure, with vasodilation occurring before the vasoconstrictive phase.
Skin vessels maximally constrict at 15°C, followed by vasodilation below 15°C, reaching maximal vasodilation at 0°C.
Cold application also decreases elasticity and increases viscosity of the visco-elastic properties of tissue.
B(ii) Indications: cryotherapy is described as a mainstay therapeutic modality for a wide variety of skin conditions, sports injuries and any kind of muscle pain.
Dr Yamaguchi's whole body cryotherapy treated pain and rheumatoid arthritis using freezing treatments, with the rapid decrease in skin temperature leading to a sudden release of endorphins and decreased pain sensitivity.

questions.answerText:
A. Heating is considered mild when tissue temperature is less than 40°C and vigorous when it reaches 40-45°C; at these temperatures, hyperaemia or erythema (redness caused by increased blood flow in the capillaries of the lower skin layers) is noted.
Increase in tissue temperature increases blood flow to the area with a resultant vasodilation response in surface blood vessels; this increase in blood flow removes heat from the area because blood from a relatively cooler area flows to the heated tissue, preventing excessive heat accumulation.
Local heat application has both direct and indirect effects; for example, heat applied to the low back region results in an increase in subcutaneous blood flow and vasodilation to the distal extremities.
An increase in tissue temperature results in an increase in metabolic rate, which can facilitate tissue healing due to improved perfusion of the wound and peri-wound area, and an increase in oxygen tension of the wound allows greater clearance of bacteria from the wound site.
Temperature increase to the therapeutic level of 40-45°C can facilitate release of oxygen from the blood's haemoglobin, improving tissue nutrition and waste removal, and reflex heating in other body areas may occur if therapeutic heating levels are reached locally.
B. Selection of the appropriate heating agent is based on the size and location of the anatomic structure to be treated, the depth of the target tissue for intervention, and the intervention goals.
Superficial heating agents generally penetrate to depths of less than 2-3cm, so joint structures close to the skin surface can be adequately heated with superficial agents, whereas deeper structures require deep heating modalities.
An intervention duration of 15 to 30 minutes is necessary for a therapeutic rise in tissue temperature, and the contraindications and precautions associated with the intervention and heating agent must also guide selection.
C. Contraindications: acute inflammation (heat may exacerbate the inflammatory response), existing fever (heat may further elevate body temperature), malignancies (increased blood flow may promote metastasis), and acute haemorrhage (heat may prolong bleeding after an acute injury).
Further contraindications: peripheral vascular disease (reduced capacity to meet increased metabolic demand), devitalised tissue following x-ray therapy, undiagnosed conditions, an unconscious patient (lack of feedback), and metal implants (risk of tissue burn).
Precautions: during the menstrual cycle (may increase blood flow, especially if structures near the pelvis such as the low back are heated), sensory deficit (increased burn risk), pregnancy (effect on the foetus not fully established), superficial implants/jewellery (may accumulate heat causing thermal injury, should be removed if possible), and mental illness (feedback may be inadequate).
Temperatures above 45°C have the potential to cause thermal pain and irreversible tissue damage, so heat should be applied within the mild-to-vigorous range and the patient's skin response monitored throughout.

questions.answerText:
(i) The probable cause is inadequate insulation of the hot pack, most likely fewer than the recommended 4 to 8 layers of towelling, or a low water level/faulty thermostat in the storage unit affecting the pack's temperature, or that the patient's skin sensation was not tested and a sensory deficit went unrecognised, or the application exceeded the typical 20-minute duration without the initial 5-10 minute monitoring being carried out.
(ii) Stop the treatment, inspect and manage the burn, re-observe the skin, and document the patient's response as required for monitoring and medicolegal reasons.
(iii) Relevant contraindications/precautions: metal implants (tissue damage/burn), sensory deficit (increased potential for burn injury), an unconscious patient (lack of feedback), and mental illness (feedback may be inadequate); adequate water level in the storage unit must also be maintained to ensure optimal heat delivery.
(iv) Modify the protocol by covering the pack with the recommended 4-8 layers of towelling, performing a skin sensation test and assessing the patient's ability to report sensory changes before every application, monitoring the initial response during the first 5-10 minutes (heat should be warm, not hot), and limiting application to the typical 20 minutes, with the skin re-observed immediately after removal.

questions.answerText:
A. Low intensity laser therapy uses low output (up to about 500mW) lasers or superluminous diodes, at dosages usually less than 35 J/cm², too low to generate any detectable heating of tissue; it is therefore described as cold or soft (athermal) laser.
The biological mechanism responsible for its beneficial effects is photobiomodulation: the laser enters the tissue and interacts with the cytochrome c complex within mitochondria.
This interaction triggers a biological cascade of events that leads to an increase in cellular metabolism and a decrease in both pain and inflammation.
At the cellular level this involves short-term activation of the electron transport chain, increased ATP production, reduction of cellular pH, and increased macrophage, fibroblast and lymphocytic activity.
On nerve tissue, laser increases the rate of nerve conduction and the frequency of action potentials, and may accelerate nerve regeneration, while increased microcirculation may help accelerate wound healing.
B. Effectiveness is affected by wavelength: wavelengths of 660nm, 820nm and 870nm encourage macrophages to release factors stimulating fibroblast proliferation, while 880nm has been reported to inhibit the healing process.
The energy density (dose) used affects outcomes; negative results in some studies could be because of inappropriately low doses, and a minimal dose of 0.01 J/cm² can already alter cellular processes.
Depth of penetration also affects effectiveness: red light from a He-Ne laser penetrates 1-2mm, while infrared laser (800-900nm) penetrates 2-4mm in soft tissue, so the wavelength selected should match the depth of the target tissue.
C. Contraindications/precautions: carcinoma, since laser could accelerate carcinogenesis; 4-6 months following radiotherapy, since radiotherapy increases tissue susceptibility to malignancy and burns; haemorrhage, since laser-induced vasodilation would exacerbate it.
Further contraindications: local application to endocrine glands, since it alters gland function, and treatment over a pregnant uterus.
Class 3 lasers used in physiotherapy are safe for the skin but harmful to the eyes, so protective goggles designed for the specific wavelength must be worn by the patient and therapist.
Prevention also involves starting treatment at a low dose and increasing gradually only if there is no change, rather than beginning at a high dose.
