questions.answerText:
A. Equipment/agent: cold therapy can be delivered as cold packs, cool whirlpool, ice-wraps or ice massage.
A chemical cold pack may be activated by breaking the barrier separating water and a chemical such as ammonium chloride or ammonium nitrate, producing an endothermic reaction that keeps the pack cold for a period of time.
Patient consideration: the presence of adipose tissue is inversely proportional to the depth of cold penetration, since it acts as insulation.
Deeper cooling of muscles and joints is possible when the structures are more superficially located, but excessive adipose tissue means a longer application time is needed.
Parameters: tissue temperature changes to cold application have been reported at depths of 1-4cm, and the hunting response cycle (vasoconstriction-vasodilation) lasts 12-30 minutes during cold exposure.
Precautions: a decrease in tissue temperature to 10°C or below may result in thermal damage to tissue, which may trigger an inflammatory response and an increase in oedema, so the temperature/duration of application must be controlled to avoid this.
B. Duration is guided so as to allow the hunting response cycle (12-30 minutes) to take effect while avoiding tissue temperature falling to 10°C or below, which risks thermal damage and increased oedema rather than the intended therapeutic effect.
A chemical cold pack reaction has been described as extending up to about fifteen to twenty minutes, giving relief from inflammation and pain at the injury site.
C. A contrast bath is alternate immersion in hot and cold water, producing significant hyperaemia; it causes considerable sensory stimulation of the cutaneous thermal receptors through alternating activation, since each time neural accommodation begins, the temperature stimulation is reversed.
This strong thermal receptor stimulation is plausible to reduce pain significantly via the pain gate mechanism, and it also reduces local oedema via the alternate vasodilation and vasoconstriction.
A simple cold application uses only cold, producing sustained vasoconstriction and the hunting response cycle described above, without the alternating hot/cold stimulation and hyperaemia that a contrast bath produces.

(i) A patient presents within hours of an acute ankle sprain with pain and swelling. Identify the modality best suited to this "spot".
(ii) Describe the mechanism of action supporting its use.
(iii) Describe the applicator placement and dosage.
(iv) Describe the progression, monitoring and end-point of treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) Cryotherapy (a cold pack, cool whirlpool, ice-wrap or ice massage) is best suited, as it is described as a mainstay therapeutic modality for sports injuries and muscle pain, with thermal exchange via conduction and convection.
(ii) The initial response to the cold is heat loss and vasoconstriction of the superficial blood vessels; further cooling stimulates free nerve endings, leading to reflex vasoconstriction with decreased local blood flow, which limits swelling at the injury site; the hunting response (cycles of vasoconstriction-vasodilation lasting 12-30 minutes) also occurs during the exposure.
(iii) The agent is applied directly to the ankle via conduction/convection; tissue temperature changes with cold have been reported at depths of 1-4cm, and care must be taken not to reduce tissue temperature to 10°C or below, since this may cause thermal damage and trigger an inflammatory response with increased oedema.
(iv) Progression/monitoring is guided by the hunting response cycle (12-30 minutes) and the skin's response; note that cold decreases tissue elasticity and increases viscosity, so range of motion measured immediately after cold application may not be accurate. The end-point is control of the acute pain and swelling, after which the stage of the condition would need to change before a heating agent could be considered, since acute inflammation and acute haemorrhage are contraindications to heat.

A(i) LASER stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation; low intensity laser therapy is the application of low output (up to about 500mW) lasers and superluminous diodes for the treatment of disease and injury, usually at dosages under 35 J/cm².
Class 1 (less than 0.5mW): low power devices, not used for therapeutic purposes, used for items such as pointers and barcode readers.
Class 2 (about 1mW): visible region, safe for the skin and accidental momentary viewing but hazardous for prolonged viewing, with limited clinical applications such as He-Ne lasers.
Class 3 (1-500mW): mid power lasers used in physiotherapy, safe for the skin but harmful to the eyes, requiring protective goggles.
Class 4 (more than 500mW): high power lasers such as CO2 laser, not safe for skin or eyes, used for surgical applications.
A(ii) Physical characteristics: monochromaticity (radiation clustered around a single wavelength with a narrow bandwidth, e.g. Ruby laser at 694.3nm red light).
Collimation (rays run parallel with no divergent radiation, keeping optical power over distance and through tissue).
Coherence (light waves are in phase; the distance over which they stay in phase is the coherence length, ranging from less than 1mm to 100m).
B(i) Physiological effects: short-term activation of the electron transport chain, increased ATP production, reduction of cellular pH, and increased macrophage, fibroblast and lymphocytic activity; increased nerve conduction rate and action potential frequency.
Therapeutic effects: wound and fracture healing, arthritic conditions, musculoskeletal disorders, pain management (sprain, strain, tendinitis), and haematoma.
B(ii) Indications: chronic and acute surgical wound healing, rheumatoid and osteoarthritic pain (with reduction in morning stiffness in RA), myofascial pain syndrome and lateral epicondylitis, and chronic/musculoskeletal pain.
Contraindications: carcinoma, 4-6 months following radiotherapy, haemorrhage, local application to endocrine glands, and treatment over a pregnant uterus.
questions.question:
A(i) Define LASER and classify laser devices into their four classes by power.
A(ii) Describe the physical characteristics of laser light.
B(i) List its physiological and therapeutic effects.
B(ii) State its indications and contraindications.

(i) A patient presents with pain over the lateral epicondyle of the elbow following overuse (tennis elbow/lateral epicondylitis). Identify the electrotherapy modality best suited to this "spot".
(ii) Describe the mechanism of action supporting its use.
(iii) Describe the applicator placement and dosage.
(iv) Describe the progression, monitoring and end-point of treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) Low intensity laser therapy is best suited, as musculoskeletal disorders including lateral epicondylitis ("Tennis Elbow"), described as a tendinopathy injury involving the forearm extensor muscles, are among its treated conditions, alongside its general use for pain management in strain, sprain and tendinitis.
(ii) The mechanism is photobiomodulation: the laser enters the tissue and interacts with the cytochrome c complex within the mitochondria, triggering a biological cascade that increases cellular metabolism and decreases both pain and inflammation; laser also increases macrophage and fibroblast activity.
(iii) The applicator, about the size of a large marker pen, is applied directly to the skin over the lateral epicondyle to ensure maximum transfer of laser energy, with light pressure used to squeeze blood from superficial vessels and increase penetration; the applicator is held at right angles to the tissue.
(iv) Treatment should start at a low dose; if there is no change to the treatment, the dose should be increased, and 5 to 6 treatments are said to be adequate to achieve a response; monitoring is by assessing pain and function, with the endpoint being significant decrease in pain and improvement in function as reported with laser use for musculoskeletal conditions.

questions.question:
A. Describe the technique of application of hydrocollator (hot) packs under the following headings: equipment, patient preparation, application, and precautions.
B. Explain the rationale behind the number of towelling layers used.
C. Distinguish between hydrocollator packs and paraffin wax baths.
questions.answerText:
A. Equipment: hydrocollator packs are stored in thermostatically controlled units filled with water at 71-79°C; after use a pack needs 20-30 minutes to reheat to the storage water temperature, and low water level or a faulty thermostat can affect the pack's temperature, so adequate water level must be maintained.
Patient preparation: adequately position and drape the patient for comfort and optimal heat delivery, visually inspect the area and carry out a skin sensation test, and assess the patient's ability to report sensory changes.
Ensure the area to be treated is accessible and free of clothing and jewellery for even heating, and select a hot pack with appropriate towelling.
Application: the area to be treated should be unloaded and in a relaxed or resting position.
Explain to the patient what to expect from the heat and instruct them to report any unusual sensation such as overheating or burning.
The physiotherapist monitors the initial response during the first 5 to 10 minutes, emphasising that the heat should be warm, not hot; maximum skin temperature change is achieved within the first 10 minutes and maintained for a further 10 minutes, giving a typical application time of 20 minutes.
Precautions: re-observe the skin after removal of the pack, assess the patient's response, and document comprehensively for monitoring progress and for medicolegal reasons.
B. Before application, the hot pack is covered with 4 to 8 layers of towelling, which insulates the hot pack from heat loss and protects the patient's skin from burns.
The heat transfer mechanism is conduction, which requires optimal contact between the pack and the skin surface for effective therapeutic heat absorption, and the weight of the pack helps maintain that contact.
C. Hydrocollator packs use conduction from a hydrophilic substance (silica gel or bentonite) encased in a canvas cover, stored in water at 71-79°C, and applied over 4-8 layers of towelling for about 20 minutes.
Paraffin wax baths also use conduction, but from a mixture of paraffin wax and mineral oil stored at 47-54.4°C.
Paraffin baths are best suited to the distal extremities using a dip-and-wrap or dip-and-immerse technique, with the extremity elevated afterward, for 15-20 minutes, whereas hydrocollator packs come in various sizes and shapes to match many different body parts.

courses.title: Pharmaceutical Biotechnology II
courses.objectives:
Nucleic Acids, Plasmid DNA and DNA Isolation and Quantification: Q1–6
Gene Cloning and the Polymerase Chain Reaction: Q7–11
Recombinant Protein Production, Fermentation and Downstream Processing: Q12–20
Vaccines and Nanotechnology-Based Delivery: Q21–27
Monoclonal Antibodies, Fusion Proteins and Biosimilars: Q28–32
Formulation, Stability and Quality Control of Biotechnology Products: Q33–40

questions.answerText:
(a)
EPO is a recombinant glycoprotein for anaemia; production cell lines (e.g. CHO cells) are validated to be stable and free of contamination; media and reagents are tested for sterility, endotoxin levels and compatibility.
(b)
In-process controls: fermentation/bioreactor monitoring of pH, temperature, oxygen levels and cell density; protein expression analysis for yield and optimal conditions.
(c)
Purification monitoring: purity checks for host-cell proteins, DNA and process-related impurities; validation of chromatography steps.
(d)
• Characterisation: primary, secondary and tertiary structure by mass spectrometry and X-ray crystallography; glycosylation profiling and isoform analysis; potency/biological activity; sterility and contamination tests; stability testing; batch release.
• Regulatory frameworks: WHO (validated bioassays, glycosylation and post-translational modifications), ICH Q5A, Q5C, Q5E, Q6B, FDA 21 CFR Part 211 and EMA guidelines (host cell proteins, DNA, viral contaminants).
(e)
• Activity: EPO stimulates red blood cell production; used for anaemia from cancer chemotherapy and chronic renal failure.
• Stability: lyophilised EPO degrades with moisture, forming aggregates, so desiccants are in the packaging; glycoprotein complexity needs stringent QC.
• Safety: recombinant growth factors such as EPO are mostly well tolerated, but severe complications have been reported in patients with cancer or chronic kidney disease.
(f)
• Contamination: raw material, media and in-process sterility/endotoxin testing and contamination testing control it.
• Immunogenicity: repeated injection of recombinant homologues of human proteins such as EPO, especially aggregated or partly denatured, can break immune tolerance and produce anti-drug antibodies.
• Control: immunogenicity assessment, stability/formulation controls and consistency of glycosylation.
questions.question:
Describe the production and quality control of recombinant erythropoietin (EPO) under the following headings: (a) cell line and raw materials; (b) in-process controls; (c) purification monitoring; (d) characterisation and release.
(e) Explain the basis of its activity, stability and safety.
(f) Explain the cause and control of problems such as contamination, aggregation and immunogenicity.

questions.answerText:
(a)
QC is the testing that ensures the safety, efficacy and quality of vaccines, blood products and biotech products (interferon, EPO, GM-CSF, insulin, growth hormone) against identity, strength, purity and quality standards; it ensures batch-to-batch consistency and GMP compliance.
(b)
Components: raw material testing; in-process testing (pH, sterility, contamination); finished product testing: potency, purity, sterility and stability (shelf life, storage conditions, expiry).
(c)
Techniques: HPLC, mass spectrometry, ELISA, sterility and endotoxin (LAL) tests, mycoplasma testing, microbial limit tests, bioassays, DLS, NMR, UV-Vis, FTIR, capillary electrophoresis.
(d)
• GMP: trained personnel, validated SOPs, dedicated QC laboratories, calibrated equipment, stringent testing of raw materials, intermediates and final product, in-process controls, stability testing and deviation handling.
• Guidelines: WHO TRS 978 Annex 3; ICH Q5A (viral safety), Q5C (stability), Q5E (comparability), Q6B (specifications); FDA 21 CFR Part 211; EMA guidelines (host cell proteins, DNA, viral contaminants, glycosylation consistency).
(e)
• SDS-PAGE: proteins are denatured and then separated by size, giving molecular weight, purity and aggregation information.
• Western blot: detection using antibodies specific to the protein of interest, giving identity and post-translational modification information.
• QC challenges: large complex molecules, complicated manufacturing with living organisms, long production times, multiple fermentation runs, variable living raw materials, non-compendial requirements, genetic stability and degradation profiles.
(f)
• SDS-PAGE: purpose = molecular weight and purity; advantages: cost effective with a visual representation; limitations: semi-quantitative and low throughput.
• Western blot: purpose = protein identification; highly specific; labour intensive and limited to known targets.
• Application: SDS-PAGE for impurity analysis and aggregation assessment; Western blot for identity testing and post-translational modifications.
• Both are analytical (identification/characterisation) methods alongside HPLC, ELISA and mass spectrometry.
questions.question:
Describe the quality control of pharmaceutical biotechnology products under the following headings: (a) definition and importance; (b) key components of testing; (c) techniques; (d) regulatory and GMP considerations.
(e) Explain the scientific basis of SDS-PAGE and Western blot, and the challenges of QC for biotech products.
(f) Distinguish between SDS-PAGE and Western blot.

(a) Describe classical gene cloning, naming its five stages. (b) Name the enzymes and vectors involved.
(c) Relate the stages to the examples for restriction enzymes, vectors, host and screening. (d) Explain how blue-white screening and probe hybridisation identify the correct clone.
(e) Explain why cDNA cloning and PCR-based cloning improve on the classical approach. (f) State the trade-offs or limitations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Five stages: fragment genomic DNA with enzymes; integrate fragments into self-replicating cloning vectors (plasmids or viral DNA) to make rDNA; introduce vectors into host cells; grow cells on agar plates; screen colonies for the target gene.
(b)
Restriction endonucleases (about 800 identified) cut palindromic sites of 4, 6 or 8 bp, giving blunt (BsaAI, EcoRV) or sticky ends; the larger the site, the fewer the fragments; DNA ligase seals phosphodiester bonds.
(c)
• Vectors: plasmids (e.g. pUC18 with ampR, lacZ, lacI, ori and a 13-site polylinker), bacteriophage λ (about 48 500 bp) and BACs (very large plasmids for fragments above 100 000 bp); each must self-replicate in the host, usually E. coli.
• Host entry: transformation of E. coli with calcium chloride at 0 °C followed by 42 °C; the result is a library of clones of different genomic fragments.
(d)
• Blue-white: agar with ampicillin and X-gal; untransformed cells die; blue colonies = plasmid with no insert; white colonies = insert in lacZ (desired).
• Hybridisation: a labelled single-strand probe complementary to the gene is applied to a nitrocellulose replica of the colonies (alkali-lysed, DNA denatured), washed and detected (e.g. autoradiography) to pinpoint the colony.
• Probe sequences are known from genome projects or deduced from a partial amino acid sequence; the chosen colony is grown by submerged fermentation and the gene excised with a restriction enzyme.
(e)
• cDNA cloning: purified mRNA (oligo(dT)) is converted by reverse transcriptase into cDNA reflecting only expressed exons, so libraries are smaller and more manageable.
• PCR cloning: with sequence information from databases, flanking primers amplify the gene using heat-stable polymerase; faster and more convenient; restriction sites can be built into the primers so most clones carry the gene.
(f)
• Limitations of classical cloning: libraries can have a very large number of clones, so finding the right one is a major task.
• cDNA cloning assumes the gene is expressed in the cells; PCR is prone to sequence errors, so inserts must be sequenced from several colonies.
• Cloning vectors normally do not support expression, so the isolated gene must be moved into an expression vector for protein production.

(a)
Immunogenicity: production of anti-drug antibodies (ADAs), which can reduce efficacy and biosafety; immune-related adverse events can also occur.
(b)
• Injected foreign proteins can elicit an immune reaction; repeated injection of recombinant homologues of human proteins (IFNs, EPO), especially when aggregated or partially denatured, can break immune tolerance to self antigens.
• ADAs affect pharmacokinetics, bioavailability and efficacy, may neutralise the drug, and can cause immune complex disease, allergic reactions and severe autoimmune reactions.
(c)
• Assess immunogenicity as part of safety evaluation; limit aggregation/denaturation with stabilising formulation (e.g. polysorbate surfactant, PEG to prevent immunogenicity), gentle handling and correct storage.
• Optimise treatment through dosing schedules and multiple routes of administration; cost can be reduced using biosimilars.
(d)
• Biosimilar: nearly identical copy of an original (innovator) product made by another company using specialised biological processes; not identical to the reference, with minor differences in clinically inactive components. Generic: identical API, bioequivalent.
• Size: generic small (~150 Da) vs biosimilar large (~150,000 Da); structure simple vs complex; characterisation easy vs difficult; stability more stable vs less stable.
• Adverse immune responses lower vs higher; quality tests ≤50 vs ≥250; approval trials small in healthy volunteers vs large in patients; discovery cost low vs relatively high.
questions.question:
A patient on repeated injections of a recombinant interferon (or EPO) that was partly aggregated develops anti-drug antibodies and loss of effect.
(a) Identify the liability.
(b) Explain the underlying cause.
(c) State the formulation, handling or testing measures.
(d) Differentiate a biosimilar from a generic drug.

A pharmacy unit is asked about a recombinant alpha-interferon preparation (Rofereon-A) indicated for hepatitis B and C and Kaposi's sarcoma.
(a) Identify the product and its class, and state the types of interferon and their cell sources.
(b) State the host cell and vector used in recombinant DNA production of such a protein.
(c) Outline, in order, how the target gene is identified, cloned, introduced into the host and selected.
(d) State how the protein is recovered and purified downstream.
(e) State the key quality control tests, adverse effects and therapeutic use.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Rofereon-A (Roche) is a recombinant alpha-interferon, a biopharmaceutical; interferons are cytokines with antiviral activity and potential anticancer effects; it is a non-glycosylated protein of 165 amino acids.
• Type I = IFN-α (produced by leukocyte and lymphoblastoid cells) and IFN-β (produced by fibroblasts), made in response to viruses or double-stranded RNA; type II = IFN-γ, made mainly by natural killer cells and T cells.
(b)
The most commonly used host cell is E. coli and the most commonly used vector is the plasmid.
(c)
• Gene identification: blood from a hepatitis B-positive patient is screened by in vivo-induced antigen technology (IVIAT); DNA is extracted, amplified by PCR, visualised and purified by gel electrophoresis, sequenced, then blasted and annotated to identify the IFN-α gene.
• The target gene and the vector are cut with a restriction enzyme at a particular site and joined by DNA ligase (new phosphodiester bonds) to form recombinant DNA.
• Host cells are made competent (cold calcium chloride plus brief heat shock, or electroporation) and transformed with the recombinant plasmid.
• Selection: cells are plated on nutrient agar containing the antibiotic matching the resistance gene on the plasmid; one colony is cultured in liquid medium so the plasmid carrying the gene is replicated.
(d)
Cells are harvested (or, if the product is secreted, cells are removed and the medium kept) for bulk separation; then size exclusion, ion exchange and affinity chromatography are used.
(e)
• QC of interferon covers identity, strength, purity and quality; potency, purity, sterility and stability tests, LAL endotoxin testing and ELISA are methods.
• Adverse effects: flu-like symptoms (fever, headache, chills, myalgia); with prolonged treatment leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia and neuropsychiatric effects (fatigue, depression), sometimes needing dose reduction or stopping.
• Use: hepatitis B and C and Kaposi's sarcoma; interferons are used clinically for viral infections and cancer.

(a)
Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides; each nucleotide has a phosphate group, a pentose sugar and a nitrogenous base; purines (A, G) and pyrimidines (C, T, U); nucleotides are linked by phosphodiester bonds; a nucleoside is base plus sugar, a nucleotide adds phosphate.
(b)
DNA (Watson and Crick, 1953) is a double helix of two antiparallel strands (5'→3' and 3'→5'), sugar-phosphate outside and bases inside; A pairs with T (2 hydrogen bonds) and G with C (3 hydrogen bonds).
(c)
RNA is usually single stranded, with ribose, bases A, G, C, U (pairs A-U, G-C); folds into hairpin structures stabilised by hydrogen bonds; genetic RNA (some viruses) vs non-genetic RNA: mRNA, rRNA, tRNA.
(d)
• DNA codes for proteins (triplet codons), replicates and stores genetic information; mRNA carries information to ribosomes, rRNA forms ribosomes and catalyses peptide bonds, tRNA brings amino acids.
• Genome organisation: bacteria have a single circular chromosome plus plasmids; eukaryotes have linear chromosomes with histones in the nucleus, plus mitochondrial and chloroplast DNA.
(e)
• Complementarity (A-T, G-C) ensures fidelity of replication and underlies transcription.
• The helix is stabilised by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases and by hydrophobic stacking interactions between planar bases.
• Deoxyribose lacks the 2' -OH of ribose, making DNA chemically more stable than RNA.
(f)
• DNA: double stranded, long chain, deoxyribose, thymine, one type, found in nucleus and mitochondria, transmits genetic information.
• RNA: single stranded, short chain, ribose, uracil, several types (mRNA, rRNA, tRNA), found in cytoplasm, carries code for protein synthesis from nucleus to ribosome.
• Absorbance: nucleic acids absorb at 260 nm; A260/A280 about 1.8 for pure DNA and 2.0 for pure RNA.
• DNA triphosphate precursors (dATP, dGTP, dCTP, dTTP) are the substrates of DNA polymerase.
questions.question:
Describe the nucleic acids under the following headings: (a) chemical composition and bases; (b) structure of DNA; (c) structure and types of RNA; (d) functions.
(e) Explain the structural basis of the stability and fidelity of DNA.
(f) Distinguish between DNA and RNA.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Aerobic industrial-scale microbial fermentation: citric acid production by A. niger in 1919 was the first aerobic fermentation process.
(b)
Provision of sterile air in large quantities to support production.
(c)
• The factor: the sterile air supply (contamination control); technologies to ensure large quantities of sterile air had to be established.
• Aerobic fermentation then enabled penicillin production in World War 2 and other antibiotics; later amino acids and industrial enzymes (1960s-70s); genetic engineering (early 1970s) enabled protein pharmaceuticals.
• Production issues for biotech products: multiple fermentation runs, long production times, genetic stability of organisms, stability on scale-up.
(d)
Downstream for biotech products: harvest cells and discard medium, or remove cells and keep medium if secreted (bulk separation), then chromatography (size exclusion, ion exchange, affinity).
questions.question:
A plant plans aerobic industrial fermentation like the 1919 production of citric acid by Aspergillus niger but cannot keep the culture free from contaminants.
(a) Identify the type of fermentation involved.
(b) State the key process requirement.
(c) Identify the factor at fault or to be optimised.
(d) State the downstream recovery and purification steps.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• DNA vaccines are circular double-stranded plasmids carrying a foreign gene from a disease agent plus a promoter to start expression of the protein in the target host.
• One or more genes are isolated from the pathogen and inserted into plasmids; the plasmid is modified to produce one or two pathogen proteins and then purified for immunisation.
(b)
Delivered by injection or gene gun into muscle.
(c)
Targets investigated: HIV-AIDS, Ebola, malaria, enteric pathogens and influenza; neurological disorders such as ischaemic stroke, Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease and multiple sclerosis (a 2007 preliminary study; more trials needed).
(d)
The plasmid expresses the pathogen protein in host cells, producing a broad response: humoral immunity (antibodies) and cell-mediated immunity (especially cytotoxic T cells), with long-term cellular responses.
(e)
• Stability: stable and transportable at room temperature, allowing long-term storage; plasmids are easily propagated and stored in bacteria.
• Safety: no viral or bacterial strains are used, so no reversion to virulence; no pathogenic infection in vivo and no significant adverse effects in clinical trials.
• Production: easy, inexpensive, reproducible and scalable; decreased likelihood of replication interference.
• Several antigens can be encoded on one plasmid, or several plasmids mixed, so one vaccination can protect against multiple pathogens; neonatal immunisation despite maternal antibody is possible.
(f)
DNA vaccines are weakly immunogenic.
questions.question:
Describe the production and delivery of DNA (genetic) vaccines under the following headings: (a) source and construct; (b) delivery; (c) examples of targets and advantages.
(d) Explain the basis of their immune activity. (e) Explain the basis of their stability and safety.
(f) State their main limitation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Aggregation (interface-related), chemical instability (oxidation), loss of colloidal stability and freezing/lyophilisation concentration effects; glycation can occur if sucrose hydrolyses at pH below 6.
(b)
• Proteins are large and held in their 3-D structure by weak non-covalent interactions, so they are highly susceptible to chemical and physical degradation.
• Stabilising excipients can destabilise: polysorbates prevent interface aggregation but may introduce oxidising agents; sodium chloride reduces viscosity but harms colloidal stability and causes problems in freeze-concentrated solutions.
• Water for injection is the commonest excipient but also the medium for many degradation reactions; amorphous sugars/polyols at pH below 6 hydrolyse to glucose and fructose, causing Maillard glycation.
(c)
• Minimise and justify each excipient; use antioxidants (methionine, sodium edetate), buffers (e.g. histidine, citrate, phosphate), sugars/polyols (trehalose, sucrose, mannitol) for cryo-/lyoprotection, surfactants (polysorbate 20/80, poloxamer) and amino acids.
• Lyophilise to minimise water content; some excipients useful in liquids are detrimental in lyophilisates; avoid sucrose where hydrolysis can occur; choose primary packaging (glass, polymers, rubber, silicone) with leachables in mind.
• Use preformulation stress studies (DSC, DSF, light scattering, shaking, stirring, freeze-thaw, H2O2 oxidation) to select the formulation; real-time storage at 2-8 °C.
(d)
• Synthesis: small molecules by in vitro chemical reactions; biotech products inside living cells (e.g. genetically modified bacterial cells); purification of biotech products is more complex, needing multiple steps.
• Stability: biotech formulations are more challenging; delivery: proteins are unstable in the GIT (extreme pH, proteolytic enzymes), so oral delivery of most is not possible without specialised systems such as nanoparticle carriers.
questions.question:
A liquid therapeutic protein formulation containing polysorbate and sodium chloride shows interface-related aggregation, oxidation and poor stability on freezing.
(a) Identify the stability liabilities involved.
(b) Explain the underlying causes.
(c) State the formulation, storage or handling measures.
(d) Differentiate biotechnology-based products from conventional small-molecule drugs in synthesis, purification, stability and delivery.

(a) Describe the use of plasmid DNA in gene therapy and how it is delivered into cells. (b) State the advantage of its persistence in the cell.
(c) Relate the approach to the gene transfer methods and examples. (d) State the advantages that make plasmid DNA attractive.
(e) Explain which property plasmid DNA improves compared with other vectors. (f) Explain the trade-offs and limitations that result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Gene therapy corrects defective genes by introducing new genetic material into a patient's cells; plasmid DNA is introduced by transfection (chemical or physical methods), then transcribed to RNA and translated into a therapeutic protein.
(b)
Plasmid DNA can persist in the cell longer than some other vectors (e.g. viruses), allowing sustained expression of the therapeutic gene.
(c)
• Gene transfer methods: electroporation (high-voltage pores), microinjection (needle), lipofection (lipid-coated DNA enters by endocytosis), calcium chloride transformation, Agrobacterium-mediated transformation, and biolistics (gold/tungsten beads in a gene gun).
• Targets: genetic disorders, cancer and infectious diseases; plasmid DNA is also used to introduce therapeutic genes or produce valuable proteins.
(d)
• Advantages: low immunogenicity compared with viral vectors; large DNA capacity; stability (propagated and stored in bacteria); ease of modification.
• Further advantages: non-integrating (unlike viral vectors) and versatile delivery to a wide range of cells and tissues.
(e)
Property improved: safety (low immunogenicity, non-integrating), carrying capacity for large or multiple genes, and ease of large-scale production in bacteria.
(f)
• Limited or short gene expression, and the immune system may recognise and degrade plasmid DNA before expression; transfection efficiency can be lower than other vectors.
• Delivery barriers: limited uptake by target cells, degradation by enzymes and clearance by the immune system.
• Safety concerns: a risk of integration into the host genome with unintended mutations, and immune responses or inflammation.
• Regulatory: plasmid DNA is treated as a genetically modified organism, with ethical concerns, restrictions in some countries and a lengthy approval process.
• Manufacturing: producing plasmid DNA at large scale is challenging and costly, limiting availability.

(a)
A biosimilar ('follow-on biologic') is a biologic almost identical to an original product made by a different company, officially approved and manufactured when the originator's patent expires.
(b)
It is highly similar to a licensed reference product despite minor differences in clinically inactive components, with no clinically significant differences in safety, purity and potency.
(c)
• Generic drug: same dosage, safety, strength, administration, quality and use as the brand; identical API in same amount, bioequivalent; evaluated for therapeutic equivalence.
• Comparison: molecular size ~150 Da vs ~150,000 Da; structure simple/well-defined vs complex with variations; characterisation easy vs difficult.
• Stability: more stable vs less stable, very sensitive to surroundings; production: predictable chemical processes vs specialised biological processes; identical to reference: yes vs no.
• Immune responses: lower vs higher potential; quality tests ≤50 vs ≥250; clinical trials small in healthy volunteers vs large in patients; discovery cost low vs relatively high.
(d)
• Biosimilars are officially approved versions of original 'innovator' biopharmaceuticals; regulatory example: FDA guidance 'Quality Considerations in Demonstrating Biosimilarity to a Reference Product' highlights analytical techniques.
• Comparative stability studies compare a test product with a reference under identical conditions to show equivalence.
(e)
Cost can be reduced by using biosimilars; patent expiry allows manufacture.
(f)
• Trade-offs: complex structure with probable variation, difficult characterisation, lower stability, higher potential for adverse immune responses.
• Regulatory: need many more quality tests and large patient trials; biopharmaceuticals face specific regulatory issues owing to biological source, size, complexity and environmental sensitivity.
• Biosimilars are not identical to the reference.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the biosimilar approach and its definition. (b) State its regulatory context.
(c) Compare its features with those of generic drugs. (d) State where biosimilars fit among biopharmaceutical products.
(e) Explain which property (cost, access) biosimilars improve. (f) Explain the trade-offs and limitations that result.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Media and reagents are tested for sterility, endotoxin levels and compatibility with the process.
• Parameters tracked in production: pH, temperature, oxygen levels and cell density.
(b)
• Raw material: cell line validation (cells stable and free of contamination); media and reagents tested for sterility and endotoxin.
• In-process: protein expression analysis assesses EPO yield and ensures optimal production conditions; challenges include multiple fermentation runs, long production times, genetic stability of production organisms and variability of living raw materials.
(c)
• Downstream: harvest cells (or remove cells and keep medium if secreted), then chromatography (size exclusion, ion exchange, affinity).
• Purification monitoring: purity checks that host-cell proteins, DNA and process-related impurities are removed; validation of chromatography steps for separation efficiency.
• Characterisation: primary, secondary and tertiary structure by mass spectrometry and X-ray crystallography; glycosylation profiling and isoform analysis.
• Final steps: potency and biological activity testing, sterility and contamination testing, stability testing and batch release testing.
questions.question:
A batch of recombinant erythropoietin (EPO), a glycoprotein used for anaemia and made in CHO cells, shows poor yield and impurities.
(a) State how the media and the process parameters are monitored.
(b) Identify the factors that could be at fault and what to check or optimise.
(c) State the downstream recovery, purification and characterisation steps.

Describe the stability testing of biotech products under the following headings: (a) definition and importance; (b) purposes of stability studies; (c) types of stability study.
(d) Relate each type of study to the example conditions given. (e) Relate the factors affecting stability (temperature, humidity, light, pH, oxygen, microbial contamination) to the examples.
(f) Explain what stability studies and stabilisation measures improve for a product. (g) State the trade-offs or limitations of stress and thermal-stability testing.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Stability is the ability of a product to keep its physical, chemical and microbiological properties within limits over its shelf life; instability changes potency, purity and safety.
(b)
Purposes of stability studies: establish shelf life, assess rate and extent of degradation, detect stability-related issues (degradation, contamination, packaging) and determine optimal storage and handling.
(c)
Types: long-term, accelerated, intermediate, photo-stability, forced degradation, bracketing and matrixing, and comparative stability studies.
(d)
• Long-term: 24 months at 25 °C and 60% RH; accelerated: 40 °C and 75% RH; intermediate: 30 °C and 65% RH; photo-stability: riboflavin solutions under UV; forced degradation: paracetamol in acid; bracketing/matrixing: only highest and lowest doses; comparative: generic vs branded.
• Protein screening stresses: temperature (2-8 °C, 15, 25, 40 °C), shaking/stirring (50-500 rpm), 1-5 freeze-thaw cycles, H2O2 1-5% oxidation, humidity 0-100% RH.
(e)
• Temperature: mRNA COVID-19 vaccines need -20 °C to -80 °C; humidity: lyophilised EPO aggregates with moisture, so desiccants are used; light: riboflavin degrades to lumichrome, so amber vials; pH: insulin stable only near pH 7.
• Oxygen: methionine oxidation in trastuzumab, so antioxidants such as ascorbic acid or nitrogen; microbial contamination: Pseudomonas aeruginosa in TPN produces endotoxin.
(f)
• Improves: knowledge of shelf life, degradation pathways and the storage conditions that keep safety, efficacy and quality; forced degradation helps develop stability-indicating assays.
• Stability ensured by storage at 2-8 °C for most vaccines, 50-60% RH, light-protective and compatible container-closures; stabilisation by freeze drying, spray drying, stabilising agents and glycosylating enzymes.
(g)
• Bracketing and matrixing reduce testing volume while keeping robust data; accelerated studies simulate long-term effects in a shorter time but intermediate studies are needed when accelerated conditions alone are insufficient.
• Thermal stability assessments (DSC, DSF) are common in screening but do not consistently correlate with storage stability.
• Challenges: complexity of biotech formulations, aggregation and degradation, and stability on scale-up of production.

questions.question:
A scientist has partial sequence information for a gene of interest from a sequence database and wants to obtain large amounts of it quickly for cloning.
(a) Identify the technique.
(b) State the reaction components, enzymes, vector and host used.
(c) Outline the steps in order and how the result is verified.
(d) State the expected product and its pharmaceutical significance.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Cloning via polymerase chain reaction (PCR), now preferred because it is faster and more convenient than the classical methods.
(b)
• Two chemically synthesised oligonucleotide primers complementary to sequences flanking the gene, DNA polymerase (from Thermus aquaticus, heat stable) and dNTPs; template = total genomic DNA.
• Restriction enzyme recognition sites can be built into the primers to allow cloning of the amplified gene; vector and host as in classical cloning (plasmid, E. coli).
(c)
• Extract genomic DNA; synthesise flanking primers; heat to about 94 °C to separate strands; cool so primers anneal; extend at about 74 °C; each cycle doubles the target DNA and the cycle is repeated.
• Cut product and vector, ligate, transform and grow colonies; most clones in the library should contain the desired gene.
• Verify by direct sequencing of the insert from several colonies, to prove it is the target gene and matches the published sequence exactly, because PCR is prone to sequence errors.
(d)
• Product: large amounts of the target gene, ready for an expression vector and producer cell.
• Significance: recombinant production of a therapeutic protein starts with isolating its coding sequence, which supplies the quantities needed to evaluate a biopharmaceutical.

questions.question:
Describe the isolation of DNA from cells under the following headings: (a) definition and principle; (b) lysis methods; (c) the five basic steps; (d) applications of the purified DNA.
(e) Explain the scientific basis of silica-binding purification.
(f) Distinguish between silica-binding chemistry and ion exchange chemistry.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Nucleic acid extraction is the starting point of any molecular biology study; the first crude DNA extraction was by Friedrich Miescher in 1869 (he coined 'nuclein'); DNA can be extracted from clinical, forensic, soil, plant, animal, bacterial and yeast samples.
(b)
Lysis methods: physical (grinding with mortar and pestle under liquid nitrogen, bead beating, sonication), chemical (detergents such as SDS, chaotropes such as guanidine salts, alkaline solutions), enzymatic (lysozyme, zymolase, proteinase K, collagenase) and combinations.
(c)
• Five steps: (1) disrupt cells to make a lysate; (2) separate soluble DNA from debris by centrifugation, filtration or beads; (3) bind DNA to a purification matrix; (4) wash with alcohol-containing buffers to remove proteins and salts; (5) elute in low-ionic-strength solution (TE buffer or nuclease-free water).
• Binding chemistries: solution-based (alcohol/isopropanol precipitation), silica, cellulose and ion exchange; TE buffer's EDTA binds magnesium and helps inhibit nucleases.
(d)
Purified DNA is used for multiplex PCR, in vitro transcription/translation, transfection, sequencing, restriction digestion and cloning.
(e)
• Silica binds DNA under high-salt conditions in the presence of a chaotropic salt such as guanidine hydrochloride, which disrupts cells, deactivates nucleases and allows nucleic acid to bind.
• Washing with salt/ethanol removes proteins, lipopolysaccharides and small RNAs while DNA stays bound; low-salt elution then releases the DNA.
• Binding to silica is not DNA specific, so RNase A can be added to remove co-purified RNA; silica membrane column format is the more convenient format.
(f)
• Silica binding: high-salt chaotropic binding, salt/ethanol wash, low-salt elution; formats include paramagnetic particles or membrane columns, balancing yield and purity.
• Ion exchange: positively charged particles interact with the negatively charged DNA phosphates; DNA binds under low salt.
• In ion exchange, contaminating proteins and RNA are washed away with higher salt, the DNA is eluted under high salt and recovered by ethanol precipitation.
• Each chemistry influences efficiency, purity and binding capacity (how much nucleic acid it can bind before the system is saturated).

questions.question:
Describe the preparation of traditional vaccines under the following headings: (a) live attenuated organisms; (b) killed (inactivated) organisms; (c) requirements of an effective vaccine and storage.
(d) Explain the basis of their activity and the duration of immunity. (e) Explain why live vaccines are riskier and killed vaccines safer but less effective.
(f) Explain the cause and control of problems such as reversion to virulence, contamination and loss of potency.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Vaccination gives microorganisms in a weakened, live or killed state to stimulate antibody production and immunity (Edward Jenner used a smallpox vaccine in 1796); live vaccines use attenuated (weakened) organisms.
• Live examples: poliomyelitis (Sabin), rabies, smallpox, measles, yellow fever and BCG.
(b)
Killed vaccines use virulent strains killed so antigenicity is retained, by phenol or formaldehyde or mild heat at 50-60 °C for 1 hour; examples: cholera, measles, mumps, typhoid and poliomyelitis (Salk).
(c)
• An effective vaccine is safe and protective, induces protective antibodies, gives host defence at the point of entry (mucosal immunity), directs antibodies/T cells to the correct epitopes, and is cost effective, biologically stable with few or no side effects.
• Storage: vaccines kept at low temperatures (most vaccines at 2-8 °C).
(d)
• An antigen triggers an immune response; the immune system distinguishes foreign from own proteins and creates memory cells, so on re-exposure it quickly produces antibodies.
• Live vaccines stimulate large quantities of antibodies or T cells; persistent infection keeps memory cells stimulated, giving lifelong immunity (measles, mumps, rubella, smallpox).
(e)
Killed vaccines are quite safe but do not set up persistent infection, so they are less effective and immunity is shorter; live vaccines carry infection risk.
(f)
• Cause: live organisms may mutate and become dangerously virulent (severe infection, even death) or the vaccine may be contaminated with a virulent strain.
• Control: vaccinate only children who are not immunodeficient; do not vaccinate patients on immunosuppressive drugs or with malignant conditions; store at low temperatures.
• rDNA technology modifies the genome to attenuate disease agents, giving safer, more efficacious and cheaper vaccines; first rDNA vaccines were for rabies, foot and mouth disease and scours in animals.
• Vaccines are the most economical way to protect against epidemics, but effective vaccines are not readily available in developing nations.

questions.question:
Describe the formulation of therapeutic protein products under the following headings: (a) definition of API, drug substance and drug product; (b) critical factors; (c) excipients; (d) preformulation.
(e) Explain why an 'optimal' formulation is not simply the most stable one.
(f) Distinguish between the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) and the drug substance (DS).
questions.answerText:
(a)
Biologics are APIs from living organisms that cannot be made by conventional chemical synthesis; molecular weight typically above 1 kDa; they include viruses, peptides, proteins, nucleic acids and cell- or tissue-derived products.
(b)
Critical factors: analytical methods, API type, clinical factors, competitive landscape, dosage form, drug substance, excipients, manufacturing capabilities, phase of development, primary packaging, route of administration, target dose and type of formulation (liquid, lyophilisate, frozen liquid).
(c)
• Excipient classes: solvents (water for injection), buffers (acetate, citrate, histidine, phosphate), salts (NaCl), sugars/polyols (mannitol, sorbitol, sucrose, trehalose), surfactants (polysorbate 20/80, poloxamer), amino acids, antioxidants (methionine, sodium edetate) and preservatives (benzyl alcohol, meta-cresol, phenol).
• Principle: minimise unnecessary components; excipients can destabilise proteins and interact; novel excipients extend development time and cost through safety evaluation.
(d)
• Preformulation: establishes primary-tertiary structure, molecular weight, isoelectric point, post-translational modifications, hydrophobicity, conformational and colloidal stability, effects of pH, ionic strength and buffer species.
• Tools: DSC and DSF for thermal stability, static/dynamic light scattering and analytical ultracentrifugation for colloidal stability, and forced degradation by temperature, shaking, stirring, freeze-thaw, oxidation and humidity.
• Aims: select stress conditions and stability-indicating methods and enable stable formulations for DS, preclinical and first-in-human studies.
(e)
• The formulation must fit purposes: required stability, developmental stage, clinical and regulatory mandates, packaging/device, economics, marketing strategy and patent landscape.
• Excipients may be multifunctional (glycine as stabiliser, buffer and tonicity modifier) and some help liquids but harm lyophilisates.
(f)
• API: the molecule of interest (e.g. peptide, monoclonal antibody, enzyme), typically a solid powder in pure form, which is often impractical and unstable for most biologics.
• Drug substance: generally a liquid (sometimes frozen) formulation containing the API for storing purified bulk, derived from final purification steps such as chromatography or ultrafiltration.
• At large scale, the DS composition usually resembles the final drug product (DP), but deviations can occur while formulation development is in progress.

questions.question:
A researcher wants to clone a fragment of target DNA into E. coli using the plasmid pUC18 and identify the clones that carry the insert.
(a) Identify the technique and the class of vector used.
(b) Name the vector features, enzymes, host and selection method.
(c) Outline the steps in order, from fragmentation of DNA to identification of the clone carrying the gene of interest.
(d) Interpret the colony colours and state the expected product and its pharmaceutical significance.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Classical gene cloning with a plasmid cloning vector: a small self-replicating DNA molecule; plasmids are circular extra-chromosomal DNA found naturally in bacteria; the engineered composite molecule is recombinant DNA.
(b)
• pUC18 (2.69 kb) carries ampR (ampicillin resistance), lacZ (β-galactosidase), lacI (controls lacZ transcription) and an origin of replication; its polylinker (multiple cloning site) lies within lacZ and has cleavage sites for 13 restriction enzymes.
• Restriction endonucleases cut palindromic sequences of 4, 6 or 8 bp giving blunt or sticky ends; DNA ligase seals the plasmid by forming phosphodiester bonds; host = E. coli; selection = ampicillin plus X-gal.
(c)
• 1 Fragment genomic DNA with restriction enzymes; 2 open the vector with the same enzyme, anneal complementary sticky ends, then ligate; 3 transform E. coli (calcium chloride at 0 °C, then 42 °C temperature shock).
• 4 Spread cells on agar with ampicillin and X-gal so each cell forms a colony; 5 find the colony with the target gene by hybridisation: replica on nitrocellulose, alkali lysis, labelled single-strand probe complementary to the gene, wash, detect (e.g. autoradiography).
• The chosen colony is grown by submerged fermentation, cells lysed, vector recovered, and the cloned gene excised with a restriction enzyme and purified.
(d)
• No growth = no plasmid (no ampR); blue colony = plasmid without insert (functional β-galactosidase cleaves X-gal); white colony = insert in lacZ, no β-galactosidase = the desired cell.
• Expected product: a clone (library of clones) of E. coli carrying the cloned gene, giving larger amounts of the gene.
• Significance: isolating the gene coding for the target protein is an early step in developing a protein biopharmaceutical; cloning vectors normally do not support expression, so an expression vector and producer cell are needed next.

questions.question:
A plasmid DNA preparation must be quantified and checked for contaminating bands because absorbance readings are unreliable.
(a) Identify the technique.
(b) Explain the principle.
(c) Outline the procedure and interpretation of results.
(d) State its application.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Agarose gel electrophoresis (gel-based quantitation of DNA/RNA).
(b)
Negatively charged nucleic acids migrate toward the anode in an electric field; DNA and RNA fragments separate by size and shape, away from other impurities.
(c)
• Load the sample in a gel well in an electric field; stain with ethidium bromide (intercalates and fluoresces under UV) or SYBR Green and view on a UV transilluminator.
• Compare band intensity with standards of known amount: if 2 µL of undiluted DNA matches a 100 ng standard, the concentration is 50 ng/µL; standards should be the same size and similarly labelled as the sample.
• Contaminating bands and sheared impurities are visible, avoiding some problems of absorbance-based calculation.
(d)
• Application: quantitation of DNA/RNA for downstream transfection, cloning, PCR and NGS; gel electrophoresis is also used to visualise and purify PCR-amplified genes during gene identification.
• Alternatives: UV absorbance, fluorometry (Hoechst 33258, PicoGreen) and qPCR.

questions.question:
Describe the production of recombinant (subunit) vaccines under the following headings: (a) definition and forms; (b) host and antigen; (c) adjuvants; (d) examples.
(e) Explain the basis of their safety and specificity. (f) Explain the role of the adjuvant.
(g) Explain the problems and controls related to the antigen host and formulation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Recombinant inactivated (subunit) vaccines contain only part of the organism; they may be synthetic peptides (the most basic portion of a protein that induces an immune response) or whole proteins extracted from the disease agent or from cloned genes.
• Subunit vaccines use antigenic proteins, polysaccharides or peptides, purified from the pathogen.
(b)
Hepatitis B vaccine: the surface glycoprotein of the virus is the antigen; E. coli is not used because of improper folding, and yeast cells are used; glycosylation does not seem to affect immune stimulation.
(c)
Subunit vaccines do not replicate in the host and are usually administered with an adjuvant; only some can be formulated with aluminium-based adjuvants.
(d)
Examples: tetanus and diphtheria toxoids; recombinant protein vaccines for hepatitis B virus and human papilloma virus (HPV, linked to cervical, vulval and vaginal cancers and genital warts); recombinant subunit vaccines for herpes zoster and COVID-19.
(e)
• Safety: they contain purified parts rather than whole organisms, so they are suitable for immunocompromised patients and carry no risk of infection.
• Specificity: they can target immune responses to specific epitopes (the part of an antigen to which an antibody attaches).
(f)
Adjuvant: stimulates the immune system to respond, can protect the vaccine from rapid degradation by the host, and can enhance immunity by directly stimulating immune cells.
(g)
• Wrong host (E. coli) gives improperly folded hepatitis B antigen; control: use yeast.
• Production contaminants: harvest cells, then size exclusion, ion exchange and affinity chromatography remove contaminants of similar properties.
• Storage: vaccines need proper low-temperature storage (most 2-8 °C).

questions.question:
A parenteral biotech product made in cell culture must be tested for viable microorganisms, endotoxin and mycoplasma before release.
(a) Identify the techniques.
(b) Explain the principle of each.
(c) State how the results are interpreted.
(d) State their application and limitations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Sterility testing (direct inoculation, membrane filtration); endotoxin testing (LAL assay, recombinant Factor C assay); mycoplasma testing (PCR, cell culture-based methods); microbial limit testing (pour plate, spread plate, selective media).
(b)
Sterility: ensures freedom from viable microorganisms. LAL: Limulus amebocyte lysate detects endotoxins (lipopolysaccharides of Gram-negative bacteria). Mycoplasma testing detects contamination that standard sterility tests miss.
(c)
Interpretation: the product must be free of viable microbes and endotoxins; microbial limit testing determines bioburden in raw materials, intermediates and finished products, with selective media for pathogens such as E. coli and Salmonella.
(d)
• Application: parenteral/injectable products to prevent infection; endotoxins cause fever and other adverse reactions; mycoplasma matters in cell culture-based products such as vaccines and biologics because it affects quality and stability.
• Example of risk: contamination of TPN solutions by Pseudomonas aeruginosa leads to endotoxin production.
• Limitations: endotoxin testing is limited to endotoxins and cannot detect all pyrogens, but has high sensitivity.

questions.question:
A gene or cDNA coding for a therapeutic protein has been isolated and cloned, and the goal is now high-level production in a producer cell.
(a) Identify the type of vector needed.
(b) Name the vector elements, enzymes, host and selection method.
(c) Outline the steps in order.
(d) State the expected product and its pharmaceutical significance.
questions.answerText:
(a)
An expression vector: it supports high-level transcription and translation, unlike cloning vectors, which normally do not support expression.
(b)
• Elements: origin of replication, selectable marker (antibiotic resistance gene), promoters, translational start and stop signals.
• Each vector is tailored to a host cell type (bacterial, yeast, mammalian); approved recombinant therapeutic proteins are made in E. coli, S. cerevisiae or animal cell lines (mainly CHO or BHK).
• Restriction enzymes and DNA ligase are used for ligation; selection by antibiotic on agar; transformation by calcium chloride/heat shock or electroporation.
(c)
Identify and isolate the gene or cDNA (from genomic DNA or reverse-transcribed mRNA); amplify and sequence it; ligate into an expression vector; introduce into the producer cell; select and grow cells.
(d)
• Product: the target protein made in large quantities by the engineered cell, e.g. insulin in E. coli and S. cerevisiae, EPO in CHO cells.
• Significance: evaluation and routine medical use of a protein biopharmaceutical depend on sufficient quantities, and recombinant production has advantages over extraction from natural sources.

questions.question:
A hepatitis B vaccine antigen, the surface glycoprotein of the virus, is expressed in E. coli but the protein folds improperly.
(a) Name the host.
(b) Identify the factor at fault and how it is corrected.
(c) State the downstream recovery and purification steps and the vaccine class.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Host: yeast cells (E. coli is not used because of improper folding).
• Yeast produces both glycosylated and non-glycosylated protein; glycosylation of the antigen does not seem to affect ability to stimulate immunity significantly.
(b)
Fault: wrong host - improper folding of the glycoprotein in E. coli; corrected by production in yeast.
(c)
• Downstream: harvest host cells (medium discarded) or keep medium if secreted; contaminants with similar properties make separation difficult; chromatography (size exclusion, ion exchange, affinity) is used.
• Class: recombinant subunit vaccine; subunit vaccines do not replicate in the host, usually need an adjuvant, and only some can use aluminium-based adjuvants.
• Storage: vaccines kept at low temperature (most vaccines at 2-8 °C).

(a)
PCR is a laboratory technique that amplifies a specific segment of DNA from small amounts to millions or billions of copies, in a tube without a living cell; each cycle doubles the target DNA (Kary Mullis, 1983).
(b)
Requirements: template DNA, two chemically synthesised oligonucleotide primers complementary to sequences flanking the gene, DNA polymerase and dNTPs.
(c)
Heat to about 94 °C to separate the strands; lower the temperature so primers anneal; extension by polymerase at about 74 °C; repeat the cycle, doubling the target each time.
(d)
• Applications: amplifying a cloned gene or genomic target, adding restriction sites to the ends of a cloned gene, use of plasmid DNA as template, and verification of cloned genes.
• Cloning via PCR begins with genomic DNA extraction and flanking-primer synthesis; restriction sites in the primers allow the amplified gene to be cloned.
(e)
• The polymerase comes from the thermophile Thermus aquaticus, so it is heat stable and not inactivated at PCR operating temperatures.
• PCR is prone to sequence errors, so sequencing proves the insert is the target gene and matches the published sequence perfectly.
(f)
• Classical genomic cloning: fragment chromosomes with restriction enzymes, clone into vectors, then screen a very large library (e.g. by probe hybridisation) to find the clone.
• PCR cloning amplifies only the target region using known sequence information, so most clones contain the desired gene; it is faster and more convenient.
(g)
• cDNA cloning starts from purified eukaryotic mRNA (oligo dT) and reverse transcriptase, giving a cDNA library of exons of expressed genes only.
• PCR cloning starts from genomic DNA, needs prior sequence information, and does not require the gene to be expressed.
• Both cloning routes need a vector and host such as E. coli for the final clones.
questions.question:
Describe the polymerase chain reaction under the following headings: (a) definition and principle; (b) requirements; (c) steps and temperatures; (d) applications.
(e) Explain why a heat-stable DNA polymerase is used and why the cloned product must be sequenced.
Distinguish between cloning via PCR and (f) classical genomic DNA cloning and (g) cDNA cloning.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Receptor constructs (fusion proteins) are usually based on a naturally occurring receptor linked to an immunoglobulin frame; they are made by recombinant DNA technology.
(b)
• Etanercept (Enbrel): recombinant human TNF-receptor fusion protein (p75 soluble TNF receptor plus Fc of IgG1), a TNF antagonist for rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis and psoriasis.
• Abatacept (Orencia): immunoglobulin CTLA-4 fusion protein causing T-cell deactivation, for rheumatoid arthritis.
• Denileukin diftitox (Ontak): diphtheria toxin engineered protein combining interleukin-2 and diphtheria toxin, an IL-2 receptor binder for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
(c)
• General recombinant production and chromatography purification apply.
• General biologics QC covers potency, purity, sterility and stability.
(d)
• The receptor part provides detailed specificity, while the immunoglobulin structure gives stability and useful pharmacological features.
• Biopharmaceuticals as a class show high selectivity and low nonspecific toxicity.
(e)
• TNF antagonists (including etanercept) are mostly well tolerated, but carry risk of granulomatous infections (TB reactivation), HBV reactivation, inflammatory/autoimmune disease and increased malignancy; infection incidence is higher with infliximab and adalimumab than etanercept.
• Immunogenicity: antidrug antibodies may reduce efficacy and cause immune complex disease, allergic and autoimmune reactions; assessment of immunogenicity is part of safety evaluation.
• Control: dose reduction or cessation applies to some adverse events.
• Immune-related adverse events vary with drug, regimen and the patient's individual conditions.
questions.question:
Describe receptor construct (fusion protein) biopharmaceuticals under the following headings: (a) definition; (b) examples and indications; (c) production (source, host, vector, culture, recovery, quality control).
(d) Explain the basis of their activity and stability.
(e) Explain the cause and control of the main adverse effects and immunogenicity.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Technique devised by Kohler and Milstein in 1975: B cells from an immunised animal (typically a mouse) are fused with an immortal myeloma cell line; immunisation uses antigen plus Freund's adjuvant, repeated, with a final intravenous dose 3 days before killing.
• Spleen is removed aseptically, disrupted, and lymphocytes separated by density gradient centrifugation.
(b)
Washed lymphocytes mixed with HGPRT-defective myeloma cells, exposed to PEG briefly (toxic), washed and cultured; HAT medium for 7-10 days lets only hybridomas grow; limiting dilution to about one cell per aliquot, screening for antigen binding, then expansion of the single clone.
(c)
Protein A affinity chromatography (gold standard) with further methods for higher purity; QC: A280 for concentration, SDS-PAGE for purity, ELISA for titre.
(d)
• Each hybridoma makes one immunoglobulin from one B cell, so each antibody is specific for a single epitope; antibodies counteract or block a substance or target a cell type.
• Activity examples: anti-TNF (rheumatoid arthritis), anti-CD20 (B cell leukaemia, B cell depletion), anti-EGF receptor (cancer cells), anti-VEGF (colon cancer); diagnostic use in immunoassays and tumour staining.
(e)
Examples: trastuzumab (humanised, HER2 antagonist, breast cancer), infliximab (chimeric, TNF antagonist), adalimumab (human, TNF antagonist), rituximab (humanised, anti-CD20) and certolizumab (pegylated F(ab') fragment).
(f)
• Unwanted cells: after fusion, free myeloma cells and free lymphocytes are present; HAT medium lets only hybridomas grow; hybridomas are isolated and grown individually.
• Infusion reactions of rituximab (some fatal), tumour lysis syndrome, acute renal failure and serious infections occur.
• TNF antagonists raise the risk of granulomatous infections (TB reactivation), HBV reactivation, autoimmune disease and malignancy.
• Immunogenicity: antidrug antibodies can reduce efficacy; assessment of immunogenicity is part of safety evaluation.
questions.question:
Describe the production of monoclonal antibodies under the following headings: (a) source cells and immunisation; (b) fusion and selection; (c) purification and quality control.
(d) Explain the basis of their specificity and clinical activity. (e) Name the types of monoclonal antibody with examples.
(f) Explain the cause and control of problems such as unwanted cells in culture, infusion reactions and immunogenicity.

A pharmacy store holds lyophilised erythropoietin exposed to moisture, an mRNA vaccine kept at elevated temperature, and a light-sensitive riboflavin injection in clear vials.
(a) Identify the stability liability in each.
(b) Explain the underlying cause.
(c) State the formulation, storage or handling measures.
(d) Differentiate freeze drying from spray drying as stabilisation approaches.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Lyophilised EPO: moisture-induced degradation with aggregate formation; mRNA vaccine: denaturation of lipid nanoparticles and RNA degradation; riboflavin injection: photodegradation to lumichrome.
(b)
Moisture promotes hydrolytic reactions or microbial growth; elevated temperature accelerates chemical and physical degradation; UV and visible light cause photochemical reactions.
(c)
• EPO: desiccants in packaging and low-humidity storage (50-60% RH); mRNA vaccines: ultra-low storage (-20 °C to -80 °C); most vaccines 2-8 °C; riboflavin: amber vials or light-protective packaging.
• Handle gently to avoid physical stress; temperature-controlled storage and transport; compatible container-closures that are sterile, non-pyrogenic and non-toxic; tamper-evident packaging.
(d)
• Freeze drying (lyophilisation): freeze to about -30 to -50 °C, apply vacuum, then heat so the water sublimes, leaving the product dry.
• Spray drying: for products ending as powder (e.g. spray-dried insulin, Exubera); excipients such as trehalose, sucrose or polysorbate are added; the solution is atomised into droplets in a stream of hot gas that evaporates the water.
• Other stabilisation: buffers, chelating agents, PEG (to prevent immunogenicity), liposomes, albumin, lipids, and glycosylating enzymes (GnT, galactosyltransferase).

questions.question:
The gene for a eukaryotic therapeutic protein is to be cloned starting from the cell's messenger RNA rather than genomic DNA.
(a) Identify the technique.
(b) Name the reagents, enzymes, vector and host.
(c) Outline the steps in order.
(d) State the expected product, its advantages and its pharmaceutical significance.
questions.answerText:
(a)
cDNA cloning (construction of a cDNA library).
(b)
Oligo(dT)-cellulose beads in a column or oligo(dT)-bound magnetic beads for mRNA; low-salt buffer; ethanol; reverse transcriptase; cloning vector and host (plasmid, E. coli) as in the cloning described.
(c)
• Disrupt cells; percolate the lysate through the oligo(dT) column (or add magnetic beads to the lysate and pull out mRNA with a magnet, which is rapid and limits contact with ribonucleases).
• mRNA is retained by base pairing of its 3' poly A tail with oligo dT; wash away unbound material; desorb with low-salt buffer; precipitate with ethanol and centrifuge.
• Reverse transcriptase converts single-stranded mRNA into double-stranded cDNA; clone the fragments to make a cDNA library and identify the desired clone as in genomic cloning (labelled probe hybridisation).
(d)
• cDNA reflects only the exons of genes expressed at the time of extraction, whereas genomic DNA of a eukaryotic protein contains exons and introns.
• cDNA libraries are smaller and more manageable, assuming the gene is expressed.
• Significance: therapeutic proteins are invariably eukaryotic; the gene/cDNA is amplified, sequenced and placed in an expression vector for a producer cell.

questions.question:
A producer wants a higher-yielding antibiotic strain of a Gram-positive bacterium by genome shuffling using protoplast fusion.
(a) Identify the technique and its class.
(b) State the organisms or cells and reagents used.
(c) Outline the steps in order.
(d) State the screening of fusants, the benefits and the limitations.
(e) Differentiate it from L-form fusion.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Protoplast fusion: a method to introduce biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) or an entire chromosome into a recipient cell for genetic manipulation or directed evolution; applied to genome shuffling.
(b)
Needed mainly for Gram-positive bacteria (multi-layered peptidoglycan and teichoic acid wall); examples: Lactobacillus species, Streptomyces griseus with Micromonospora, plants; reagents: lysozyme, polyethylene glycol (PEG), osmotic protection.
(c)
• Protoplast formation with lysozyme (degrades peptidoglycan).
• PEG crowding makes protoplasts aggregate so membranes fuse.
• brief recombination between chromosomes.
• reversion to walled cells in an osmotically protected environment.
(d)
• Screening for the desired phenotype follows fusion combined with random mutagenesis.
• Benefits: higher-productivity strains (clavulanic acid, cephalosporin, enzymes, indolizomycin), activation of silent BGCs, more lactic acid and acid tolerance in Lactobacillus.
• Limitations: multiple fusion and regeneration phases, short recombination window, instability of recombinants.
(e)
• L-forms are permanently wall-deficient variants (lytic enzymes plus antibiotics in an osmotically protective environment) that propagate without a wall; fused using PEG or electrofusion with no wall regeneration.
• L-form fusion outcomes: recombination, polyploidy, heterokaryosis; protoplast fusion is followed by wall regeneration and haploid cells.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the approach of combined vaccines and their types. (b) State their principle and licensing requirement.
(c) Relate the approach to the examples. (d) State the requirements an effective vaccine must meet.
(e) Explain which properties combined vaccines improve. (f) State the trade-offs and limitations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Combined vaccines are formed by combining antigens in one vaccine; they can be live or killed.
(b)
Principle: several diseases are covered in a single administration; each combination is tested extensively before licensing.
(c)
• Examples: measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) - live; diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis (DTP) - killed.
• Other combinations: hepatitis A and B; pneumococcal and meningococcal; MMR with attenuated varicella (MMRV).
(d)
• An effective vaccine must be safe and protective and not cause illness or death, induce protective antibodies, have host defence at the point of entry, direct antibodies/T cells to the correct epitopes, and be cost effective, biologically stable with few side effects.
• Vaccination aims at an immune response and memory cells that give a quick antibody response on re-exposure.
(e)
• Properties improved: low cost, easy delivery, fewer injections and fewer visits.
• Traditional vaccines are the most cost-effective way to save lives and protect against epidemics.
(f)
• Trade-offs: reduced immunogenicity and increased side effects.
• Each combination needs extensive testing before licensing, which adds to development.
• Live component limitations: possible mutation to virulence, contamination with virulent strain, restrictions in immunodeficient or immunosuppressed patients.
• Storage requirements: proper low-temperature storage is needed (most vaccines 2-8 °C).

questions.question:
A monoclonal antibody against a target antigen is to be produced by the hybridoma method devised by Kohler and Milstein in 1975.
(a) Identify the product and its class.
(b) State the source cells used.
(c) Outline the production process in order, from immunisation to purification.
(d) State the key quality control tests.
(e) State the therapeutic and diagnostic uses.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Monoclonal antibodies are antibodies made by identical immune cells that are clones of one unique parent cell; they bind the same epitope; they are a type of recombinant-technology biopharmaceutical made to block a substance or target a cell type.
(b)
B cells (spleen lymphocytes) from an immunised animal, typically a mouse, fused with an immortal HGPRT-defective myeloma cell line.
(c)
• Immunise the mouse with antigen plus Freund's complete/incomplete adjuvant subcutaneously at multiple sites, repeated; final intravenous dose 3 days before killing; assay serum antibody; remove spleen aseptically, disrupt mechanically or enzymatically; separate lymphocytes by density gradient centrifugation.
• Mix washed lymphocytes with myeloma cells; expose to PEG for a few minutes (it is toxic), wash, culture in HAT medium for 7-10 days so only hybridomas grow.
• Dilute hybridomas to about one cell per aliquot, grow individually, screen clones for binding to the antigen, select and expand the clone; each hybridoma makes one immunoglobulin.
• Purify by Protein A affinity chromatography (the gold standard); further purification methods if higher purity is needed.
(d)
QC: antibody concentration by absorption at 280 nm (A280); purity by SDS-PAGE; titre by ELISA.
(e)
• Therapeutic: anti-TNF (rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory diseases), anti-CD20 (B cell leukaemia, depleting B cells in autoimmune disorders), anti-EGF receptor (cancer cells), anti-VEGF (colon cancer); examples trastuzumab, infliximab, adalimumab.
• Diagnostic: detect antigens or antibodies in blood, urine or tissues in immunoassays; tumour identification by staining sections; CD markers; immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence.

questions.question:
A recombinant protein made in host cells is poorly recovered because the culture contains many cell- and medium-derived contaminants with properties similar to the protein.
(a) Identify the process stage.
(b) State what the upstream stage requires.
(c) Identify the factor at fault.
(d) State the downstream recovery and purification steps with their principles.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Downstream processing, following upstream synthesis in host cells.
(b)
Upstream requires a suitable host cell and an isolated gene.
(c)
Fault: contaminants with physicochemical properties similar to the protein; the more similar, the harder the separation, so many steps are usually needed.
(d)
• Harvest cells (medium usually discarded) or, if the product is secreted, remove cells and keep the medium: the bulk separation.
• Size exclusion (gel filtration): porous beads; larger molecules elute faster, smaller ones enter pores and are slower; can also indicate molecular weight.
• Ion exchange: charged resin retains molecules of opposite charge; bound molecules released with a suitable salt concentration.
• Affinity: immobilised ligand binds the protein while contaminants pass; elute by competing molecules or changing pH while keeping the protein intact; high purification.
• Monitoring: purity checks for host-cell proteins, DNA and process-related impurities; validation of chromatography steps.

questions.question:
A gene-deleted Salmonella vaccine for sheep and poultry is described as a live genetically modified vaccine.
(a) Identify the product and its class.
(b) State the source organism.
(c) Outline how such a vaccine is produced.
(d) State the key quality requirements and precautions.
(e) State its preventive use and examples of related vaccines.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A live genetically modified (recombinant) vaccine, one of three categories of recombinant vaccines (with recombinant inactivated/subunit vaccines and genetic/DNA vaccines).
(b)
Source: bacteria or viruses with one or more genes inactivated or deleted (here Salmonella).
(c)
• rDNA technology is used to modify or delete genes that cause disease (gene isolation, nucleic acid synthesis, sequence modification, cloning): genes are extracted, modified and re-inserted to give an attenuated organism.
• Two or more genes are deleted or inactivated so the vaccine stays stable and cannot revert to a pathogenic agent.
• Alternative: an infectious clone - the entire genome of the disease agent (usually a virus) is isolated, specifically modified in the laboratory and used to re-create the live modified organism.
(d)
• An effective vaccine must be safe, protective, induce protective antibodies against correct epitopes, cost effective, biologically stable with few side effects.
• Live-vaccine dangers: organisms may mutate and become virulent or the vaccine may be contaminated with a virulent strain; precautions: not for immunodeficient patients or those on immunosuppressive drugs/with malignancy, and storage at low temperatures.
(e)
• Use: prevention of disease; live organisms stimulate large quantities of antibodies/T cells and persistent infection keeps memory cells stimulated; recombinant vaccines aim to be safer, more efficacious and less expensive.
• Related live recombinant vaccines: Salmonella typhi vaccine, BCG, vaccinia and adenovirus virus vaccines.

(a)
Plasmids are small, circular, extrachromosomal DNA molecules found mostly in bacteria (also archaea and multicellular organisms); they are not independent life, have no protective coat, and replicate independently of chromosomal DNA.
(b)
• Types: F (sex), R (resistance), Col (colicin/bacteriocin-producing), virulence and degradative (break down xenobiotics) plasmids.
• Other examples: P. aeruginosa plasmid for using camphor; B. thuringiensis plasmid for a toxin to gypsy and tent moth; Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens integrating into plant chromosomes (crown gall).
(c)
