• Isolation by boiling lysis or alkaline lysis: grown bacteria are lysed with SDS (detergent) and NaOH (strong base); at about pH 11 plasmid and chromosomal DNA are denatured.
• Rapid neutralisation with potassium acetate: chromosomal DNA forms an insoluble intra-strand aggregate, covalently closed plasmid rehybridises and stays in solution; potassium SDS precipitates protein.
(d)
Applications: cloning vector and gene transfer, gene therapy, recombinant proteins (e.g. insulin, growth hormone), DNA vaccines, restriction analysis, sequencing, PCR template and transfection.
(e)
• Replication: plasmids rely on the host cell but each controls its own replication, affecting timing of synthesis; when the bacterium divides all plasmids are copied.
• Transfer: conjugation (cell-to-cell contact, sex pili, F+ to F-; Hfr transfers only genes near the surface), transformation (naked DNA from lysed donors taken up by competent cells) and transduction.
(f)
Dangers: antibiotic resistance, pathogenicity (virulence factors), spread of traits between species in the environment, and integration into the host chromosome disrupting gene expression.
(g)
• F plasmid: fertility factor, conjugative, mostly in E. coli; transferred totally or partially; can integrate into the chromosome to give an Hfr (high frequency of recombination) male.
• R plasmid (R-factor): conjugative; gives resistance to antibiotics and metal ions (tetracycline, arsenic, streptomycin); circular DNA of 80-95 kb with resistance transfer factor (RTF) and resistance determinants.
• R plasmids have narrow (within species) and broad (between bacteria) host-range groups and spread multidrug resistance genes; F plasmids mainly enable transfer of genetic material.
questions.question:
Describe plasmid DNA under the following headings: (a) definition and features; (b) types; (c) isolation from bacterial cells; (d) applications.
(e) Explain how plasmids replicate and how they are transferred between bacteria. (f) State the dangers associated with plasmids.
(g) Distinguish between F (sex) plasmids and R plasmids.

A purified monoclonal antibody batch must be checked for concentration, purity, titre and identity.
(a) Identify the techniques suitable.
(b) Explain the principle of each.
(c) State how the results are interpreted.
(d) State their application in pharmaceutical analysis and quality control, with limitations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Absorbance at 280 nm (concentration), SDS-PAGE (purity), ELISA (titre/potency) and Western blot (identity); HPLC and mass spectrometry are also used.
(b)
• A280: aromatic amino acids in proteins absorb at 280 nm. SDS-PAGE: proteins are denatured then separated by size.
• ELISA: antigen-antibody binding is quantified via an enzymatic reaction. Western blot: detection using antibodies specific to the protein of interest.
(c)
Interpretation: A280 gives antibody concentration; SDS-PAGE gives molecular weight and purity (impurity and aggregation assessment) with a visual result; ELISA estimates titre/potency; Western blot confirms identity and post-translational modifications.
(d)
• Application: identity testing, impurity and aggregation analysis, potency assay, immunogenicity testing, so that batches meet purity, potency and consistency standards.
• Limitations: SDS-PAGE is semi-quantitative with low throughput; Western blot is labour intensive and limited to known targets; ELISA has limited dynamic range and is prone to interference.
• Advantages: SDS-PAGE is cost-effective; Western blot and ELISA are highly specific, ELISA adaptable to various targets.

(a)
Microbial contamination and endotoxin (pyrogen) contamination of an injectable.
(b)
Contamination compromises sterility and safety, causing degradation or toxin production; e.g. Pseudomonas aeruginosa in TPN solutions produces endotoxin; injections bypass natural body defences.
(c)
• Multi-dose products need preservatives (benzyl alcohol, phenol); manufacture by aseptic processing, filtration, heat sterilisation (thermally stable) or lyophilisation (thermally sensitive APIs).
• Quality requirements: sterile, pyrogen-free, isotonic, pH about 4.5-7.5, particulate-free; QC includes sterility testing, pyrogen testing, pH measurement and visual inspection.
• Container-closure systems must be sterile, non-pyrogenic, non-toxic and tamper-evident; water for injection is pyrogen-free, highly purified water.
(d)
• Sterile Water for Injection: packaged in single-dose containers, sterilised, free of antimicrobial agents.
• Bacteriostatic Water for Injection: contains antimicrobial preservatives and is suitable for multi-dose formulations.
questions.question:
A multi-dose parenteral product shows microbial growth and endotoxin, and the pharmacist must also select a suitable aqueous vehicle.
(a) Identify the liability.
(b) Explain the underlying cause.
(c) State the formulation, handling and quality control measures.
(d) Differentiate sterile water for injection from bacteriostatic water for injection.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The gene (or cDNA) for the target protein is identified and isolated, from genomic DNA or from mRNA that is reverse transcribed; it is amplified and sequenced.
(b)
The gene is placed in an rDNA expression vector and introduced into a host; all approved recombinant therapeutic proteins are made in E. coli, S. cerevisiae or animal cell lines (mainly CHO or BHK).
(c)
Upstream: host cells synthesise the protein; downstream: harvest cells (or keep the medium if secreted), then size exclusion, ion exchange and affinity chromatography.
(d)
Examples: insulin (E. coli, S. cerevisiae; Humulin approved 1982), EPO (CHO cells), growth hormone, blood factors VIII and IX, tissue plasminogen activator, interferons, interleukin-2, hepatitis B surface antigen vaccine.
(e)
• Activity: they are nearly identical to the body's key signalling proteins (erythropoietin, growth hormone, insulin and analogues); biopharmaceuticals show high selectivity and low nonspecific toxicity.
• Stability: proteins are large and held in their 3-D structure by weak non-covalent interactions, so they are susceptible to chemical and physical degradation.
• Proteins are unstable in the GIT (extreme pH, proteases), so oral delivery of most is not possible without specialised systems such as nanoparticle carriers.
(f)
• Immunogenicity: repeated injection, especially of aggregated or partly denatured protein, can produce anti-drug antibodies that alter pharmacokinetics and efficacy and may neutralise the drug.
• Control: assess immunogenicity in safety evaluation; PEG added to prevent immunogenicity; dosing schedules and administration routes.
• Formulation instability: minimise excipients, use antioxidants, buffers, sugars, surfactants and lyophilisation; polysorbate may bring oxidising agents and sodium chloride may harm colloidal stability.
• Other effects: injection of foreign proteins can cause immune-related adverse events; cost is high.
questions.question:
Describe the production of recombinant protein biopharmaceuticals under the following headings: (a) gene source; (b) vector and host; (c) culture and recovery; (d) examples.
(e) Explain the basis of their activity and the stability challenge.
(f) Explain the cause and control of immunogenicity and of formulation instability.

questions.answerText:
(a)
UV absorbance (optical density) spectrophotometry, the most common technique for nucleic acid concentration and purity.
(b)
Nucleic acids absorb UV light maximally at 260 nm (proteins at 280 nm); concentration is calculated from A260 against a blank using the Beer-Lambert equation.
(c)
• Procedure: place the sample in a quartz cuvette in the UV spectrophotometer (small-volume instruments can use as little as 1 µL on pedestals); pass UV light at a specified path length; read absorbance at 260 nm against a blank.
• A260/A280 shows protein contamination: high-quality DNA 1.7-2.0 (about 1.8 for pure DNA), RNA about 2.0; lower ratios usually indicate contaminant protein (phenol also absorbs at 280 nm).
• A260/A230 shows chemical contamination: should be >1.5 for sensitive enzyme-based assays such as qPCR and sequencing; guanidine/chaotropic salts and solvents absorb at 230 nm; the lower the ratio, the more contaminant.
• A high A260 with a low ratio suggests contaminants are raising the 260 nm reading, so the DNA amount may be overestimated.
(d)
• Application: accurate concentration matters for transfection, cloning, PCR and next-generation sequencing; inaccurate quantification increases variability; A260 also follows a purification protocol; in QC of biotech products UV-Vis spectroscopy is used for protein quantification.
• Limitations: other molecules absorb near 260 nm; UV-Vis has limited specificity and interference from impurities; alternatives are fluorometry (Hoechst 33258, PicoGreen), agarose gel electrophoresis and qPCR.
questions.question:
A silica-column purified DNA sample is to be quantified before PCR; the A260 reading is high and the A260/A280 ratio is low.
(a) Identify the technique used.
(b) Explain the principle.
(c) Outline the procedure and interpret the readings, including the 260/280 and 260/230 ratios.
(d) State its application in analysis and quality control, and its limitations.

Describe the downstream isolation and purification of biotechnology-based products under the following headings: (a) purpose and bulk separation; (b) size exclusion chromatography; (c) ion exchange chromatography; (d) affinity chromatography.
(e) Explain why purification is complex and multi-step.
(f) Distinguish between size exclusion chromatography and ion exchange chromatography.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Downstream processing isolates and purifies the compound synthesised by host cells from the cells or medium; it starts with harvesting cells (medium usually discarded) or, if secreted, removing cells and keeping the medium.
(b)
• Size exclusion (gel filtration): separation by molecular size using porous beads as stationary phase; molecules smaller than the pores enter and are hindered, larger molecules elute faster.
• Pore size can be adjusted (gels commercially available); it can also be used to estimate molecular weight.
(c)
• Ion exchange: separation by charge; resins with covalently linked negatively or positively charged groups; molecules of opposite charge are retained, neutral or same-charge molecules elute.
• Bound molecules are released with a proper salt concentration; a positively charged resin is used for a negatively charged compound and vice versa.
(d)
• Affinity: a known ligand covalently linked to a resin binds the protein; contaminants pass through; elution by competing molecules or change of pH, keeping the structure intact; high purification.
• Related uses: Protein A affinity chromatography for monoclonal antibodies; oligo(dT) affinity for mRNA; HPLC in QC separates by size, charge or hydrophobicity.
(e)
• The medium contains many cell- or medium-derived contaminants with varying similarity to the protein; the more similar, the harder the separation, so many separation methods are needed.
• Purification of biotechnology products is more complex than for chemically synthesised small molecules, needing multiple steps.
(f)
• Basis: size exclusion separates by size (larger elute first); ion exchange separates by charge (opposite-charged molecules are retained).
• Stationary phase: porous beads vs charged resin; elution: smaller molecules delayed vs release with salt concentration.
• Size exclusion can determine molecular weight; ion exchange is used frequently for biomolecules such as proteins.

(a)
Nanotechnology-based drug delivery platforms enable targeted delivery to specific tissues or cells, reducing systemic side effects and improving therapeutic efficacy.
(b)
Nanotechnology is used to prepare nanovaccines with markedly reduced consumption and side effects.
(c)
• Using nanoparticles, vaccines can be released in a controlled manner at a specific location.
• Nanovaccines can be stable at room temperature and have replaceable routes of administration.
• Such vaccines may overcome limitations of existing vaccines, giving painless, safe, effective and economic products.
(d)
• Proteins and peptides are large and unstable; in the GIT they face extreme pH and proteolytic enzymes, so oral delivery of most biotech products is not possible and needs specialised systems such as nanoparticle carriers.
• Biopharmaceuticals have different pharmacokinetics from chemical drugs, owing to large molecular size and instability.
(e)
• Improved properties: targeting, reduced systemic side effects, efficacy, controlled release, room-temperature stability, alternative routes.
• Biopharmaceuticals themselves offer high selectivity and low nonspecific toxicity.
(f)
• Trade-offs: toxicity of nanoparticles and immune responses induced by nanoparticles are the major challenges.
• Some biodegradable and biocompatible nanoparticles have been developed.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the nanotechnology approach to drug delivery. (b) Describe its use for vaccines.
(c) Relate its features to nanovaccines. (d) Explain why proteins and peptides need specialised delivery.
(e) Explain which properties nanoparticle delivery improves. (f) Explain the trade-offs and limitations that result.

questions.explanation: Ribonucleotide reductase converts all four ribonucleoside diphosphates to deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates, providing precursors for DNA synthesis. This enzyme requires thioredoxin or glutaredoxin as reducing agents and exhibits complex allosteric regulation ensuring balanced dNTP pools. Hydroxyurea inhibits this enzyme, blocking DNA replication.
questions.question: What enzyme reduces ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides?

questions.explanation: p53 activates p21 (a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor) transcription during DNA damage, arresting cell cycle for repair. p53 also induces apoptosis genes if damage is irreparable. As a tumor suppressor, p53 mutations occur in over 50% of cancers, allowing damaged cells to proliferate.
questions.question: Which transcription factor is activated by p53 during DNA damage?

questions.explanation: Receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) bind growth factors, dimerize, and autophosphorylate tyrosine residues. Phosphotyrosines recruit signaling proteins containing SH2 or PTB domains, activating pathways like MAP kinase cascades. RTK mutations or overexpression contribute to many cancers.
questions.question: Which protein family mediates most growth factor receptor signals?
What is the net ATP yield from glycolysis of one glucose molecule?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis produces four ATP molecules by substrate-level phosphorylation but consumes two ATP in the preparatory phase, giving a net yield of two ATP. Additionally, two NADH molecules are produced that can generate ATP through oxidative phosphorylation if oxygen is present. The relatively low ATP yield reflects glycolysis being an ancient anaerobic pathway.

questions.question: Iodine deficiency primarily affects:
questions.explanation: Iodine is essential for thyroid hormone (T₃, T₄) synthesis. Deficiency causes hypothyroidism, goiter (thyroid enlargement from TSH stimulation), and cretinism in infants (irreversible intellectual disability). Iodine deficiency remains common in many regions with iodine-poor soil. Salt iodization programs have largely eliminated deficiency in developed countries. Pregnant women need increased iodine to prevent fetal brain damage.

questions.question: Which drug inhibits xanthine oxidase to treat gout?
questions.explanation: Allopurinol and its metabolite oxypurinol inhibit xanthine oxidase, reducing uric acid formation and preventing gout attacks. The accumulated xanthine and hypoxanthine are more soluble than uric acid, reducing crystallization risk. This therapeutic approach addresses uric acid overproduction rather than symptoms.

Protein quality reflects amino acid composition (particularly essential amino acid content) and digestibility. Complete proteins (animal sources) contain all essential amino acids in adequate proportions. Incomplete proteins (most plant sources) are deficient in one or more essential amino acids. Protein digestibility varies: animal proteins ~95%, legumes ~80%, grains ~85%. Combining complementary proteins improves overall quality.
questions.question: Protein quality is determined by:

questions.explanation: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) serves as a cofactor for glycogen phosphorylase, though not in its usual role in amino acid metabolism. In phosphorylase, PLP participates in acid-base catalysis during the phosphorolytic cleavage reaction. The enzyme also has a serine residue that is phosphorylated for allosteric regulation.
questions.question: What cofactor is required by glycogen phosphorylase?

questions.explanation: Tetrahydrofolate derivatives carry one-carbon units at various oxidation states for nucleotide and amino acid biosynthesis. Folate is crucial for DNA replication and cell division; deficiency particularly affects rapidly dividing cells. Folate supplementation prevents neural tube defects during pregnancy by supporting proper neural development.
questions.question: Which B vitamin is essential for one-carbon transfer reactions?

questions.explanation: Approximately three protons flow through the F₀ component for each ATP synthesized at F₁. An additional proton is consumed for ATP-ADP translocase, bringing the total cost to four protons per ATP exported from mitochondria. This coupling ratio determines the P/O ratios for NADH and FADH₂.
questions.question: How many protons must flow through ATP synthase to synthesize one ATP?

questions.explanation: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase converts acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA, committing carbon to fatty acid synthesis. This biotin-dependent enzyme undergoes allosteric and hormonal regulation, controlling lipogenic flux. Citrate activates while palmitoyl-CoA inhibits the enzyme, coordinating synthesis with metabolic status.
questions.question: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of fatty acid synthesis?
The rate-limiting enzyme of fatty acid oxidation is:
questions.explanation: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT I) catalyzes the committed step for fatty acid entry into mitochondria and is inhibited by malonyl-CoA. This regulation ensures that fatty acid synthesis and oxidation do not occur simultaneously. CPT I activity determines the rate at which fatty acids are oxidized for energy production.

questions.question: Galactosemia is caused by deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Classic galactosemia (most severe) results from galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency, causing galactose-1-phosphate accumulation. Galactokinase or epimerase deficiency cause milder forms. Accumulated galactose is reduced to galactitol (lens osmotic damage causing cataracts) or oxidized to galactonic acid. Without treatment (galactose-free diet), severe liver disease, intellectual disability, and cataracts develop. Newborn screening allows early diagnosis and treatment.

Triose phosphate isomerase rapidly interconverts dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P). This allows both trioses from the aldolase reaction to proceed through the same pathway. The enzyme is extremely efficient, with catalytic perfection near the diffusion limit, ensuring minimal accumulation of DHAP.
questions.question: Triose phosphate isomerase catalyzes interconversion between:

questions.explanation: Muscle glycogen (300-400g total) serves as a reserve for muscle's own energy needs during contraction. Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and cannot release free glucose. During exercise, muscle glycogen is degraded to glucose-6-phosphate, which enters glycolysis. Glycogen depletion causes fatigue. Muscle glycogen is replenished during recovery through glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis.
questions.question: Skeletal muscle stores glycogen primarily for:
Retina metabolizes glucose via:
questions.explanation: Retina, despite high oxygen availability, uses aerobic glycolysis (Warburg effect), converting substantial glucose to lactate. This supports high biosynthetic demands of retinal cells and may reduce oxidative stress from high oxygen tension. The retinal pigment epithelium takes up and oxidizes lactate. This metabolic compartmentalization optimizes retinal function while managing oxidative stress.

questions.question: Orotic aciduria results from deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Hereditary orotic aciduria is caused by UMP synthase deficiency, which catalyzes the final two steps of de novo pyrimidine synthesis (orotate + PRPP→orotidine-5'-monophosphate→UMP). Orotic acid accumulates and is excreted in massive amounts. Patients develop megaloblastic anemia, growth retardation, and immune deficiencies. Treatment with oral uridine bypasses the enzymatic defect.

During prolonged starvation, thyroid hormone levels decrease, reducing metabolic rate to conserve energy. T₃ levels fall through decreased peripheral conversion of T₄ to T₃. Lower metabolic rate reduces protein catabolism and extends survival. Brain, heart, and liver maintain relatively constant metabolic rates. This adaptive reduction in thyroid function is part of the metabolic adaptation to starvation.
questions.question: During starvation, which tissue adapts by reducing its metabolic rate?

questions.explanation: Methotrexate competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, preventing tetrahydrofolate regeneration required for thymidylate and purine synthesis. Dividing cells with high DNA synthesis rates are most affected by this antifolate chemotherapy. Leucovorin (folinic acid) rescue provides reduced folate, protecting normal cells from toxicity.
questions.question: Why does methotrexate inhibit rapidly dividing cells?

questions.explanation: Three stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) terminate translation without encoding any amino acid. These nonsense codons are recognized by release factors rather than tRNA molecules during protein synthesis. The existence of three stop codons provides redundancy and helps ensure reliable translation termination.
questions.question: How many stop codons exist in the universal genetic code?

questions.explanation: DNA gyrase (a type II topoisomerase) relieves positive supercoiling generated by helicase-mediated unwinding. Without gyrase activity, excessive tension would halt replication fork progression and potentially damage DNA structure. This enzyme introduces negative supercoils by breaking both DNA strands temporarily and allowing relaxation.
questions.question: Which enzyme removes supercoils formed ahead of the replication fork?
What triggers increased ketogenesis during fasting?
questions.explanation: Fasting increases the glucagon/insulin ratio, promoting lipolysis and fatty acid release from adipose tissue. High glucagon also activates hepatic ketogenesis while low insulin removes inhibition of hormone-sensitive lipase. The abundant acetyl-CoA from fatty acid oxidation exceeds TCA cycle capacity, driving ketone body synthesis.

RNA primase synthesizes short RNA oligonucleotides that provide 3'-OH groups for DNA polymerase initiation. DNA polymerase cannot start synthesis de novo and requires these primers for both leading and lagging strands. The primers are later removed and replaced with DNA by DNA polymerase I.
questions.question: Which enzyme synthesizes RNA primers required for DNA replication?

questions.explanation: UV-B radiation converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin to previtamin D₃, which spontaneously isomerizes to cholecalciferol (vitamin D₃). This photoconversion is the main source of vitamin D for most people. Factors affecting synthesis include latitude, season, time of day, skin pigmentation, age, and sunscreen use. Elderly and dark-skinned individuals in northern latitudes are at high deficiency risk.
questions.question: Sunlight exposure produces vitamin D through conversion of:

questions.explanation: Familial hypercholesterolemia results from LDL receptor mutations causing impaired LDL clearance and severe hypercholesterolemia. Cholesterol deposits in tendons (xanthomas) and arteries (atherosclerosis), causing premature coronary artery disease. Statins and PCSK9 inhibitors reduce cholesterol but don't normalize levels in homozygotes.
questions.question: Which lipid disorder causes xanthomas and premature atherosclerosis?

questions.explanation: Adequate folate before conception and during early pregnancy reduces neural tube defect (spina bifida, anencephaly) risk by 50-70%. Neural tube closure occurs weeks 3-4 of gestation, often before pregnancy recognition. Folic acid fortification of grain products and periconceptional supplementation (400-800 μg daily) are key public health interventions.
questions.question: Periconceptional folate supplementation prevents:
Where does the citric acid cycle occur in eukaryotic cells?
questions.explanation: The TCA cycle enzymes (except succinate dehydrogenase) are located in the mitochondrial matrix, where substrate concentrations can be regulated independently of the cytoplasm. This compartmentalization coordinates the cycle with β-oxidation and facilitates efficient coupling to oxidative phosphorylation. Succinate dehydrogenase is embedded in the inner membrane as Complex II.

questions.question: What proteins package eukaryotic DNA into nucleosomes?
questions.explanation: Histones (H2A, H2B, H3, H4) form octameric cores around which DNA wraps to create nucleosomes. Histone modifications (acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation) regulate chromatin structure and gene accessibility. Histone-DNA interactions must be disrupted locally for transcription to proceed.

questions.question: Heart muscle preferentially uses which fuel?
questions.explanation: Heart is highly aerobic and preferentially oxidizes fatty acids (60-70% of energy) under resting conditions, with lactate, ketone bodies, and glucose providing the remainder. Heart has high mitochondrial density and oxidative capacity. During ischemia when oxygen is limited, heart must use anaerobic glycolysis, but this provides insufficient ATP. Heart can use virtually any metabolic fuel except free fatty acids during ischemia.

Hereditary fructose intolerance causes fructose-1-phosphate accumulation, depleting phosphate and inhibiting gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Symptoms include hypoglycemia, vomiting, and liver damage after fructose ingestion. Strict fructose avoidance prevents complications; natural aversion to sweet foods often develops.
questions.question: Which condition results from fructose-1-phosphate aldolase B deficiency?

questions.explanation: Phytic acid (inositol hexaphosphate) in cereals and legumes binds phosphate and minerals, forming insoluble complexes that reduce absorption. However, because phosphate is abundant in diets and absorption is relatively efficient, phytate rarely causes phosphate deficiency. Phytate's greater impact is on mineral absorption (iron, zinc, calcium). Food processing and fermentation reduce phytate content.
questions.question: Dietary phosphate absorption is impaired by:
What product results from oxidative deamination of glutamate?
questions.explanation: Glutamate dehydrogenase catalyzes oxidative deamination producing alpha-ketoglutarate, ammonia, and reduced coenzyme (NADH or NADPH). This reaction links amino acid metabolism to the citric acid cycle, providing carbon skeletons for energy generation. The reversibility allows both catabolic and anabolic roles depending on cellular conditions.

questions.question: β-Hydroxybutyrate is formed from acetoacetate by:
questions.explanation: β-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase catalyzes the reversible reduction of acetoacetate to β-hydroxybutyrate using NADH. The ratio of these two ketone bodies reflects the mitochondrial NADH/NAD+ ratio. During active fatty acid oxidation, the NADH/NAD+ ratio is high, favoring β-hydroxybutyrate formation.

β-oxidation occurs predominantly in the mitochondrial matrix where fatty acyl-CoA molecules are sequentially cleaved to generate acetyl-CoA. The process is tightly coupled to the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation for ATP production. Each cycle removes two carbons and generates FADH2 and NADH.
questions.question: Where does β-oxidation of fatty acids primarily occur in eukaryotic cells?
Which amino acid is the precursor for both dopamine and norepinephrine?
questions.explanation: Tyrosine undergoes hydroxylation (by tyrosine hydroxylase) to DOPA, decarboxylation to dopamine, hydroxylation to norepinephrine, and methylation to epinephrine. This pathway produces catecholamine neurotransmitters and hormones. Defects in tyrosine hydroxylase cause dopamine-responsive dystonia.

questions.question: During the absorptive state, the liver primarily:
questions.explanation: In the fed (absorptive) state, high insulin and glucose levels stimulate hepatic glycogen synthesis (storage) and lipogenesis (converting excess carbohydrate to fat). Gluconeogenesis is suppressed. The liver takes up glucose via GLUT2 and stores it or converts it to fatty acids for export as VLDL. Amino acids are used for protein synthesis or converted to glucose/fat.

questions.question: During pregnancy, the placenta transfers which nutrients to fetus?
questions.explanation: Placenta actively transports glucose and amino acids to fetus. Glucose is the primary fetal fuel. Maternal ketone bodies cross the placenta, especially during fasting, providing alternative fuel. Free fatty acids don't cross well; fetal liver synthesizes needed fatty acids. Maternal metabolism adapts to prioritize fetal nutrition: enhanced lipolysis provides maternal energy, sparing glucose for fetus.

questions.question: The first step of glycolysis that consumes ATP is:
questions.explanation: Hexokinase catalyzes the first ATP-consuming step, phosphorylating glucose to glucose-6-phosphate. This traps glucose in the cell because phosphorylated glucose cannot cross the plasma membrane. The reaction commits glucose to metabolism and is essentially irreversible under physiological conditions due to its large negative free energy change.

Retinol-binding protein (RBP) specifically transports retinol from liver stores to peripheral tissues. Each RBP molecule binds one retinol molecule and associates with transthyretin for stability. RBP levels reflect vitamin A status; severe protein malnutrition reduces RBP synthesis, impairing vitamin A mobilization even when hepatic stores are adequate.
questions.question: Vitamin A is transported in blood primarily bound to:
Which tripeptide is the major cellular antioxidant?
questions.explanation: Glutathione (γ-glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine) reduces oxidized proteins, degrades peroxides via glutathione peroxidase, and conjugates electrophiles for excretion. The thiol group provides reducing power; glutathione reductase regenerates reduced glutathione using NADPH. Glutathione deficiency causes oxidative stress and hemolytic anemia.

Zellweger syndrome (cerebrohepatorenal syndrome) involves absent or dysfunctional peroxisomes, impairing very long-chain fatty acid oxidation, plasmalogen synthesis, and other peroxisomal functions. Severe developmental abnormalities, neurological dysfunction, and liver disease result. Very long-chain fatty acids accumulate. The condition is usually fatal in infancy. Diagnosis involves measuring very long-chain fatty acids and identifying peroxisomal protein import defects.
questions.question: Zellweger syndrome affects which metabolic process?
The primary function of vitamin E is:
questions.explanation: Vitamin E (α-tocopherol) functions primarily as a lipid-soluble antioxidant, protecting polyunsaturated fatty acids in cell membranes from oxidative damage. It donates hydrogen to lipid peroxy radicals, breaking the chain reaction of lipid peroxidation. Vitamin E deficiency, though rare, causes neurological problems due to oxidative damage to nerve tissue.

Hyperammonemia with normal liver function suggests urea cycle enzyme deficiency (ornithine transcarbamylase, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase, others). Presentation varies from neonatal catastrophic illness to adult-onset symptoms. Ammonia is neurotoxic, causing encephalopathy, cerebral edema, and death if severe. Treatment includes protein restriction, nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylbutyrate), and arginine supplementation (depending on specific defect).
questions.question: Hyperammonemia without liver disease suggests:
HMG-CoA lyase catalyzes which step in ketogenesis?
questions.explanation: HMG-CoA lyase cleaves HMG-CoA to produce acetoacetate and acetyl-CoA. This is the final step in ketone body synthesis and is unique to liver mitochondria. Deficiency of this enzyme causes severe episodes of hypoketotic hypoglycemia during fasting because ketone bodies cannot be produced as alternative fuel.

The carnitine shuttle consists of carnitine palmitoyltransferases I and II and a translocase that together transport long-chain acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Carnitine acyltransferase I on the outer membrane transfers the acyl group from CoA to carnitine. After transport, CPT II on the inner membrane regenerates acyl-CoA in the matrix.
questions.question: Which carrier system transports activated fatty acids into mitochondria?

questions.explanation: Two ATP equivalents charge tRNA with amino acids (ATP→AMP + PPi), one GTP powers aminoacyl-tRNA delivery to A-site, and one GTP drives translocation. This high energy cost ensures translation accuracy and maintains irreversibility through coupled reactions. The substantial energy investment reflects the importance of accurate protein synthesis.
questions.question: How many ATP equivalents are consumed per peptide bond formed during translation?
Alkaptonuria is caused by deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Alkaptonuria results from homogentisate oxidase deficiency in tyrosine degradation. Homogentisic acid accumulates and polymerizes, causing dark urine on standing (ochronosis), cartilage/connective tissue pigmentation, and arthritis in later life. It's relatively benign compared to other amino acid disorders. There's no effective treatment; management focuses on arthritis symptoms. The condition provided early evidence for "one gene-one enzyme" concept.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) catalyzes the committed and rate-limiting step, oxidizing glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconolactone. The enzyme is inhibited by NADPH (product inhibition), regulating pathway flux according to NADPH needs. G6PD deficiency is the most common human enzyme deficiency, affecting over 400 million people worldwide.
questions.question: The rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway is:

questions.explanation: Normal blood ketone body concentration is about 1 mg% (0.1 mM). During prolonged fasting or untreated diabetes, levels can rise to 50-100 mg% or higher. Ketonemia is defined as elevated blood ketone levels, and ketonuria refers to ketone bodies appearing in urine when blood levels exceed renal threshold.
questions.question: Normal blood ketone body concentration is approximately:

questions.explanation: Creatine kinase is abundant in muscle and brain. Elevated CK suggests muscle damage (myositis, muscular dystrophy, intense exercise, rhabdomyolysis) or myocardial infarction. CK-MB isoform is cardiac-specific; total CK elevation with normal CK-MB suggests skeletal muscle origin. Troponins have largely replaced CK-MB for cardiac diagnosis. Statin medications can cause myopathy with CK elevation.
questions.question: Elevated serum creatine kinase (CK) suggests:
What is the product of one complete cycle of β-oxidation?
questions.explanation: Each β-oxidation cycle cleaves one acetyl-CoA while generating one FADH2 and one NADH from fatty acyl-CoA. The shortened fatty acid continues cycling until completely converted to acetyl-CoA units. Energy yield depends on chain length, with longer chains producing more reduced coenzymes.

Adult men contain about 4 grams of iron, women about 3 grams due to menstrual losses. Approximately 65% is in hemoglobin, 10% in myoglobin, 1% in enzymes (cytochromes, catalase, peroxidases), and 20-30% in storage forms (ferritin, hemosiderin). Despite relatively small total body iron, maintaining adequate iron is challenging because only about 10% of dietary iron is absorbed.
questions.question: How much iron does the average adult body contain?

questions.explanation: McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V) results from muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency, preventing muscle glycogen breakdown. Patients experience exercise intolerance, muscle cramps, and myoglobinuria after intense exercise. Blood lactate doesn't rise normally during exercise because muscle cannot break down glycogen to fuel glycolysis. The condition demonstrates muscle's dependence on glycogen for intense activity.
questions.question: McArdle disease is caused by deficiency of:
Which kinase is activated directly by cAMP?
questions.explanation: Protein kinase A (PKA) is activated when cAMP binds regulatory subunits, releasing active catalytic subunits. PKA phosphorylates serine and threonine residues on numerous substrates, mediating diverse hormonal responses. Targets include metabolic enzymes, transcription factors, and ion channels.

Cyanide and carbon monoxide bind to the iron in the heme groups of cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV), preventing oxygen reduction to water. This halts electron transport, proton pumping, and ATP synthesis. Cyanide poisoning is rapidly fatal because cells cannot produce ATP and quickly deplete energy reserves.
questions.question: Cyanide blocks ATP production by inhibiting:
What causes sickle cell disease at the molecular level?
questions.explanation: A single nucleotide substitution (GAG→GTG) replaces glutamate with valine at position 6 of β-globin. This mutation causes hemoglobin S polymerization under low oxygen, distorting red blood cells into sickle shapes. The altered cells occlude microvasculature, causing painful crises and organ damage.

questions.question: Vitamin D deficiency in children causes:
questions.explanation: Rickets results from vitamin D deficiency during skeletal growth, causing inadequate mineralization of growing bones. Clinical features include bowed legs, knock knees, delayed fontanelle closure, and rachitic rosary (enlarged costochondral junctions). Vitamin D is essential for intestinal calcium absorption; without it, calcium deposition in bone matrix is impaired despite normal matrix formation.

Diabetic ketoacidosis predominantly occurs in type 1 diabetes where absolute insulin deficiency prevents glucose utilization and allows uncontrolled lipolysis and ketogenesis. Type 2 diabetics usually retain enough insulin to suppress excessive ketone production. DKA in type 1 diabetes is often precipitated by infection, stress, or insulin omission.
questions.question: Diabetic ketoacidosis is most commonly associated with:

questions.explanation: IP3 binds receptors on endoplasmic reticulum, triggering calcium release into cytoplasm. Elevated cytoplasmic calcium activates numerous proteins including calmodulin, protein kinase C, and contractile proteins. Calcium signaling regulates diverse processes from muscle contraction to gene expression.
questions.question: What ion does IP3 mobilize from intracellular stores?
Which enzyme is responsible for unwinding the DNA double helix during replication?
questions.explanation: DNA helicase catalyzes energy-dependent unwinding of the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs. This enzyme moves along the DNA, creating replication forks where synthesis machinery can access template strands. Helicase activity is coupled to ATP hydrolysis for the energy required to separate strands.

Severe hypocalcemia (serum calcium <7.5 mg/dL) causes increased neuromuscular excitability, producing tetany (muscle spasms), paresthesias, Chvostek's sign (facial twitching with nerve tap), Trousseau's sign (carpal spasm with blood pressure cuff inflation), seizures, and laryngospasm. Ionized calcium stabilizes neuronal membranes; low levels increase membrane permeability and excitability.
questions.question: Hypocalcemia manifests clinically as:
What amino acid is the immediate precursor for nitric oxide synthesis?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide synthase converts arginine to citrulline while producing nitric oxide, a signaling molecule regulating vascular tone, neurotransmission, and immunity. This reaction requires oxygen, NADPH, and tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactor. Nitric oxide's multiple roles make arginine metabolism clinically significant.

questions.question: How is acetyl-CoA transported from mitochondria to cytoplasm for fatty acid synthesis?
questions.explanation: Acetyl-CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane, so it condenses with oxaloacetate to form citrate, which is transported to the cytoplasm. Citrate lyase cleaves citrate back to acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate in the cytoplasm. The oxaloacetate is reduced to malate, which can return to mitochondria or generate NADPH.

questions.question: Complete oxidation of glucose through the pentose phosphate pathway can yield:
questions.explanation: If all six carbons of glucose are channeled through the oxidative phase (with recycling via the non-oxidative phase), 12 NADPH molecules can be generated. This occurs when cells need maximum NADPH but minimal ribose-5-phosphate. The pathway provides metabolic flexibility, allowing independent regulation of NADPH and pentose production.

questions.question: Deficiency in which urea cycle enzyme causes ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency?
questions.explanation: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency is the most common inherited urea cycle disorder, causing accumulation of carbamoyl phosphate and ammonia. The excess carbamoyl phosphate is diverted to pyrimidine synthesis, producing elevated orotic acid in urine. OTC deficiency is X-linked and can cause severe hyperammonemia in affected males.

α-oxidation removes carbons one at a time from the carboxyl end and is essential for oxidizing branched-chain fatty acids like phytanic acid. The methyl branch at the β-carbon blocks β-oxidation. α-oxidation produces CO2 and a fatty acid shortened by one carbon, which can then undergo β-oxidation.
questions.question: α-oxidation is specialized for metabolizing which type of fatty acids?
How many molecules of water are produced per palmitic acid oxidized?
questions.explanation: Complete oxidation of palmitic acid produces metabolic water from multiple sources: 7 from β-oxidation itself, and 24 from the TCA cycle oxidation of 8 acetyl-CoA molecules. This metabolic water is physiologically important for desert animals like camels. The water production accompanies energy generation through aerobic respiration.

Azathioprine is a prodrug converted to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP), a purine analog that inhibits several enzymes in purine synthesis and is incorporated into nucleic acids. 6-MP is used as an immunosuppressant (organ transplantation, autoimmune diseases) and in leukemia treatment. The drug is inactivated by xanthine oxidase; concurrent allopurinol treatment requires dose reduction to prevent severe toxicity.
questions.question: Azathioprine is metabolized to which active immunosuppressant?
Insulin is synthesized as a precursor called:
questions.explanation: Insulin is initially synthesized as preproinsulin, containing a signal sequence that directs it to the endoplasmic reticulum. After signal sequence removal, proinsulin folds with disulfide bond formation. Proinsulin is cleaved by specific proteases, removing the C-peptide and releasing mature insulin (A and B chains linked by disulfide bonds). C-peptide measurement reflects endogenous insulin production.

questions.question: The kidney's metabolic role during prolonged fasting includes:
questions.explanation: During prolonged fasting (>3-5 days), kidney cortex becomes a significant gluconeogenic organ, contributing 20-40% of blood glucose. Renal gluconeogenesis uses lactate, glycerol, and especially glutamine (from muscle) as substrates. This adaptation is important for acid-base balance (glutamine metabolism generates bicarbonate) and nitrogen disposal. Kidney's contribution increases as hepatic glycogen is depleted.

questions.question: What transporter system moves fatty acids into mitochondria?
questions.explanation: The carnitine shuttle transfers long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs across inner mitochondrial membranes where β-oxidation occurs. Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT I) catalyzes outer membrane transfer while CPT II regenerates acyl-CoA in matrix. Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT I, coordinating synthesis and oxidation.

questions.question: The enzyme that adds glucose residues to glycogen is:
questions.explanation: Glycogen synthase catalyzes the formation of α-1,4-glycosidic bonds, adding glucose units from UDP-glucose to the growing glycogen chain. This is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogen synthesis. The enzyme exists in active (dephosphorylated) and inactive (phosphorylated) forms, with insulin promoting dephosphorylation and activation.

questions.question: What enzyme decomposes hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen?
questions.explanation: Catalase efficiently decomposes hydrogen peroxide, preventing hydroxyl radical formation through Fenton reactions. This heme-containing enzyme is abundant in peroxisomes where H2O2 is generated during fatty acid oxidation. Catalase mutations cause acatalasemia, usually benign but occasionally causing oral ulcerations.

questions.question: Metabolic syndrome is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Metabolic syndrome includes central obesity, insulin resistance, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia (elevated triglycerides, low HDL), and hypertension. It dramatically increases cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes risk. Pathophysiology involves insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, and altered adipokine secretion. Treatment focuses on weight loss, exercise, and cardiovascular risk factor management. The syndrome reflects modern lifestyle (excess calories, sedentary behavior).

questions.question: How many consecutive nucleotides constitute a codon?
questions.explanation: Three consecutive nucleotides form each codon, providing 64 possible combinations for encoding 20 amino acids. This triplet code allows for redundancy (multiple codons per amino acid) while minimizing errors. The three-base system emerged evolutionarily as optimal for balancing coding capacity and error tolerance.

IL-12 from dendritic cells and macrophages promotes Th1 differentiation, enhancing cell-mediated immunity against intracellular pathogens. Th1 cells secrete IFN-γ activating macrophages and promoting cellular responses. Th1/Th2 balance determines immune response character against different pathogen types.
questions.question: Which cytokine promotes T helper cell differentiation toward Th1 phenotype?
What molecule induces lac operon expression?
questions.explanation: Lactose (or its metabolite allolactose) acts as inducer, binding lac repressor and preventing operator occupancy. This derepression allows transcription of genes encoding β-galactosidase, permease, and transacetylase. The system exemplifies inducible gene expression responding to substrate availability.

questions.question: Which amino acid disorder causes lens dislocation and thrombosis?
questions.explanation: Homocystinuria from cystathionine β-synthase deficiency causes homocysteine accumulation affecting connective tissue (lens dislocation, skeletal abnormalities) and vascular endothelium (thrombosis). Intellectual disability may occur if untreated. Treatment includes vitamin B6 (cofactor), betaine (promotes remethylation), and dietary methionine restriction with cysteine supplementation.

questions.question: What is the template strand used during transcription also called?
questions.explanation: The antisense (template) strand runs 3' to 5' and serves as the template for RNA synthesis. This strand is complementary and antiparallel to the RNA transcript produced during transcription. The opposite strand is called the sense or coding strand because its sequence matches the RNA transcript (except T→U).

questions.question: The committed step in gluconeogenesis is catalyzed by:
questions.explanation: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase catalyzes the committed step, hydrolyzing fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to fructose-6-phosphate. This bypasses the irreversible phosphofructokinase step of glycolysis. The enzyme is inhibited by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, preventing simultaneous gluconeogenesis and glycolysis. Regulation ensures these opposing pathways don't create futile cycles.

Succinyl-CoA synthetase (also called succinate thiokinase) catalyzes substrate-level phosphorylation, converting succinyl-CoA to succinate while generating GTP (or ATP in some tissues). This is the only step in the TCA cycle that directly produces a high-energy phosphate compound. The GTP produced can be readily converted to ATP by nucleoside diphosphate kinase.
questions.question: The enzyme that directly generates GTP (or ATP) in the TCA cycle is:

questions.explanation: The 23S rRNA (in bacterial 50S subunit) forms the peptidyl transferase active site, demonstrating ribozymal catalysis. This discovery revolutionized understanding of ribosomes as RNA-based catalysts with proteins providing structural support. The catalytic mechanism involves positioning substrates and general acid-base catalysis without covalent intermediates.
questions.question: Which ribosomal RNA component catalyzes peptide bond formation?
Which force contributes least to DNA double helix stability?
questions.explanation: Covalent bonds within the sugar-phosphate backbone provide structural integrity but don't stabilize the double helix per se. Non-covalent interactions (hydrogen bonds, van der Waals forces, electrostatic interactions) maintain strand association while allowing reversible separation. This weak interaction balance permits DNA to denature and reanneal.

questions.question: Which urea cycle intermediate must be transported from mitochondria to cytoplasm?
questions.explanation: Citrulline is synthesized in the mitochondrial matrix and must be exported to the cytoplasm where the remaining urea cycle reactions occur. A specific citrulline-ornithine antiporter facilitates this exchange across the inner mitochondrial membrane. This transport step is essential for cycle continuity and couples the mitochondrial and cytoplasmic phases.

Diabetes complications result from multiple mechanisms: hyperglycemia directly damages vessels; aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol (accumulating in nerve, lens, kidney); advanced glycation end-products modify proteins; and oxidative stress injures tissues. Strict glycemic control prevents or delays complications by addressing the root cause.
questions.question: Which enzyme deficiency causes type 1 diabetes complications?
Which metabolites can serve as gluconeogenic precursors?
questions.explanation: Lactate (from muscle glycolysis), glucogenic amino acids (from protein), and glycerol (from triglyceride breakdown) are major gluconeogenic substrates. These can be converted to oxaloacetate or other TCA cycle intermediates that lead to glucose formation. Acetyl-CoA from fatty acids cannot produce net glucose because the carbons are lost as CO₂ in the TCA cycle.

Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, affecting posterior and lateral columns. Symptoms include paresthesias, ataxia, weakness, and spasticity. Demyelination results from impaired methylation reactions requiring B₁₂-dependent methionine synthase. Neurological damage can be irreversible if B₁₂ deficiency persists untreated; early recognition and treatment are essential.
questions.question: The neurological consequences of B₁₂ deficiency include:

questions.explanation: Epinephrine activates β-adrenergic receptors on adipocytes, stimulating cAMP production and hormone-sensitive lipase activation. This mobilizes fatty acids from triacylglycerol stores for oxidation in other tissues. Epinephrine's lipolytic action supports energy provision during stress or exercise.
questions.question: Which hormone promotes lipolysis in adipose tissue during fasting?
What mechanism do cancer cells use to avoid immune destruction?
questions.explanation: Cancer cells upregulate immune checkpoint molecules (PD-L1, CTLA-4) that inhibit T cell activation, evading immune destruction. Checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapies block these interactions, reactivating anti-tumor immunity. This approach has revolutionized treatment for numerous cancer types.

questions.question: The coenzyme form of thiamine is:
questions.explanation: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is the active coenzyme form, serving as a cofactor for oxidative decarboxylation reactions. TPP-dependent enzymes include pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase. The thiazole ring of TPP stabilizes carbanion intermediates through resonance, essential for breaking carbon-carbon bonds adjacent to carbonyl groups.

questions.question: Which enzyme catalyzes the transfer of amino groups from one amino acid to a keto acid?
questions.explanation: Aminotransferases (also called transaminases) are enzymes that require pyridoxal phosphate as a coenzyme and facilitate the reversible transfer of amino groups between amino acids and keto acids. This process is crucial for nitrogen metabolism and the synthesis of non-essential amino acids. The reaction involves no liberation of free ammonia, only the shuffling of amino groups among various molecules.

Molecular oxygen (O₂) is the terminal electron acceptor in aerobic respiration, being reduced to water at Complex IV. This role of oxygen is essential for maintaining electron flow through the chain. Without oxygen, electrons accumulate in carriers, NADH cannot be reoxidized, and ATP production ceases.
questions.question: The final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain is:
Which tissues can utilize ketone bodies for energy?
questions.explanation: All extrahepatic tissues with mitochondria can oxidize ketone bodies, including brain, heart, skeletal muscle, and kidney. The brain normally uses glucose but adapts to use ketone bodies during prolonged fasting, significantly reducing glucose requirements. Red blood cells lack mitochondria and cannot use ketone bodies.

Fumarate produced during urea cycle can enter citric acid cycle, linking nitrogen disposal with energy metabolism. This connection enables coordinated regulation and allows aspartate regeneration for continued urea synthesis. The bicyclic relationship demonstrates metabolic pathway integration.
questions.question: Which intermediate links the urea cycle and citric acid cycle?
Scurvy is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Scurvy results from vitamin C deficiency causing impaired collagen synthesis. Clinical features include bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, poor wound healing, bone pain, and eventually tooth loss and death. Collagen is abundant in blood vessels, skin, and connective tissue; defective collagen causes fragility and bleeding. Scurvy was historically common among sailors until citrus fruits were recognized as preventive.

questions.question: Which protein represses lac operon transcription in E. coli?
questions.explanation: Lac repressor binds the operator sequence, blocking RNA polymerase access to lac operon genes. Lactose (or allolactose) binding causes repressor conformational change, releasing DNA and permitting transcription. This classic example demonstrates negative regulation of gene expression.

questions.question: What condition promotes excessive ketone body production?
questions.explanation: Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, particularly type 1, causes excessive ketone body production due to insulin deficiency and glucagon excess. Low insulin allows unrestrained lipolysis and fatty acid oxidation. Glucagon stimulates ketogenesis while insulin deficiency prevents peripheral ketone body utilization, leading to dangerous accumulation.

questions.question: What causes Tangier disease?
questions.explanation: ABCA1 transporter deficiency prevents cholesterol efflux from cells to apoA-I, causing near-absent HDL and tissue cholesterol accumulation. Orange tonsils from cholesterol ester deposition are characteristic. Despite low HDL, atherosclerosis risk is variable. This demonstrates HDL's role in reverse cholesterol transport.

Carnitine deficiency (primary genetic or secondary to other conditions) impairs long-chain fatty acid transport into mitochondria, preventing β-oxidation. This causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia during fasting, muscle weakness, cardiomyopathy, and hepatic steatosis. Free carnitine and acylcarnitine levels are diagnostic. Treatment with oral carnitine supplementation is effective for primary deficiency. Secondary deficiency requires treating underlying cause.
questions.question: Carnitine deficiency primarily affects:
Debranching enzyme has which two catalytic activities?
questions.explanation: Debranching enzyme has two activities: transferase (moving three of four residues from a branch to another chain) and α-1,6-glucosidase (hydrolyzing the remaining α-1,6-bond to release free glucose). This bifunctional enzyme is essential for complete glycogen degradation. Deficiency causes glycogen storage disease type III with abnormal, highly branched glycogen.

MCAD deficiency impairs fatty acid oxidation, causing hypoketotic hypoglycemia during fasting. Without fatty acid oxidation, liver cannot produce ketone bodies or maintain gluconeogenesis (requires ATP from β-oxidation). This mimics fasting state biochemically but without ketone production. Sudden infant death syndrome risk is increased. Treatment requires avoiding fasting and ensuring adequate carbohydrate intake.
questions.question: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency causes:

questions.explanation: Branching enzyme (amylo-α-1,4→α-1,6-transglucosidase) transfers about 7 glucose residues from a chain of at least 11 residues to create α-1,6-glycosidic branch points. Branching increases glycogen solubility and creates more non-reducing ends for simultaneous synthesis and degradation. This structural organization allows rapid glucose mobilization when needed.
questions.question: Branching enzyme creates which type of glycosidic linkage?

questions.explanation: Pyruvate kinase catalyzes the final step of glycolysis, transferring a phosphate from phosphoenolpyruvate to ADP to generate ATP and pyruvate. This is the second substrate-level phosphorylation and another irreversible step in glycolysis. Pyruvate kinase is regulated by allosteric effectors and covalent modification, coordinating glycolysis with cellular energy status.
questions.question: Phosphoenolpyruvate is converted to pyruvate by which enzyme?

questions.explanation: Ceramides consist of sphingosine with a fatty acid attached via amide linkage to the amino group. This structural motif serves as the backbone for all sphingolipids including sphingomyelins and glycosphingolipids. Ceramides themselves function as signaling molecules regulating cell growth, differentiation, and apoptosis.
questions.question: What modification distinguishes ceramides from simple sphingosines?

questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion uses carrier proteins or channels to accelerate movement down concentration gradients without energy expenditure. This passive process increases transport rates beyond simple diffusion while maintaining thermodynamic favorability. Glucose transporters exemplify carriers mediating facilitated diffusion.
questions.question: Which transport mechanism requires no metabolic energy input?

questions.explanation: Oncogenes derive from proto-oncogenes that normally regulate cell growth but cause cancer when mutated or overexpressed. Examples include growth factors (sis), receptors (erb-B), signal transducers (ras), and transcription factors (myc). Single oncogene activation can contribute to transformation but usually requires additional mutations.
questions.question: What class of genes promotes cell division when mutated or overexpressed?

questions.explanation: Cyclic GMP produced by guanylyl cyclase mediates nitric oxide and atrial natriuretic peptide effects on smooth muscle. cGMP activates protein kinase G, phosphorylating proteins that reduce cytoplasmic calcium and promote relaxation. Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (e.g., sildenafil) enhance cGMP signaling.
questions.question: Which messenger regulates smooth muscle relaxation?

questions.explanation: Leucine and lysine degrade exclusively to acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate, unable to contribute carbon to gluconeogenesis. Most amino acids are glucogenic, forming citric acid cycle intermediates or pyruvate. Some amino acids exhibit both properties, called glucogenic and ketogenic.
questions.question: Which amino acids are purely ketogenic?

questions.explanation: Ten nucleotides occupy each 360-degree turn of the B-form DNA helix, with 34 Angstroms per complete turn. This means each nucleotide contributes 3.4 Angstroms to the helix rise and creates a 36-degree rotation. This regular spacing is fundamental to DNA structure and affects how proteins recognize DNA sequences.
questions.question: How many nucleotides complete one full turn of the DNA helix?
Transketolase requires which vitamin-derived cofactor?
questions.explanation: Transketolase uses thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) to transfer two-carbon units between sugar phosphates in the non-oxidative phase. The transketolase reaction test is used clinically to assess thiamine status. TPP deficiency impairs the non-oxidative phase, affecting the pathway's ability to adapt to varying needs for NADPH versus ribose-5-phosphate.

questions.question: What coenzyme donates methyl groups for thymidylate synthesis from dUMP?
questions.explanation: N5,N10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate provides both the methyl group and reducing equivalents for thymidylate synthase. This reaction is unique in transferring a one-carbon unit at the methylene oxidation level and reducing it to methyl. Tetrahydrofolate oxidation to dihydrofolate requires reduction by dihydrofolate reductase for continued function.

questions.question: Insulin promotes which metabolic processes?
questions.explanation: Insulin is the major anabolic hormone, promoting glucose uptake (muscle, adipose), glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis, and protein synthesis while inhibiting gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, lipolysis, and ketogenesis. Insulin signals nutrient abundance, directing metabolism toward storage. These effects are mediated by receptor tyrosine kinase activation and downstream signaling cascades affecting enzyme activity and gene expression.

Alkaptonuria results from homogentisate oxidase deficiency, causing homogentisic acid accumulation and excretion. Urine darkens upon oxidation of homogentisic acid in air. Long-term accumulation causes ochronosis (tissue pigmentation) and arthritis, though the condition is generally benign.
questions.question: Which disorder causes black urine upon air exposure?
Which fat-soluble vitamin functions as an antioxidant protecting cell membranes?
questions.explanation: Vitamin E (tocopherols) protects membrane phospholipids from oxidative damage by scavenging free radicals. Its lipophilic nature positions vitamin E within membranes where it intercepts lipid peroxyl radicals, preventing chain reactions. Vitamin E deficiency is rare but can cause neurological problems from oxidative nerve damage.

RNA polymerase II transcribes all protein-coding genes, producing mRNA precursors that undergo processing. This enzyme also transcribes many non-coding RNAs including microRNAs and long non-coding RNAs. Its activity is highly regulated through various transcription factors and chromatin modifications.
questions.question: Which RNA polymerase transcribes most protein-coding genes in eukaryotes?

questions.explanation: McArdle disease from muscle phosphorylase deficiency prevents muscle glycogen breakdown, causing exercise intolerance, muscle cramps, and myoglobinuria after intense exercise. Blood lactate doesn't rise normally with exercise (no glycolysis). Patients experience "second wind" phenomenon when alternative fuels become available. There's no hepatomegaly or hypoglycemia. Treatment involves avoiding intense exercise and ensuring adequate nutrition.
questions.question: McArdle disease (GSD V) patients experience:

questions.explanation: Sanger sequencing uses dideoxynucleotides to terminate DNA synthesis at specific positions, generating fragments of varying lengths. Fluorescent labels on different dideoxynucleotides enable automated sequence determination. This chain-termination method dominated DNA sequencing for decades before next-generation technologies emerged.
questions.question: What method sequences DNA by detecting fluorescently labeled nucleotides?
What stimulates insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells?
questions.explanation: Elevated blood glucose stimulates insulin secretion through glucose metabolism in β-cells, depolarizing membranes and triggering insulin granule exocytosis. Insulin release also responds to amino acids, gastrointestinal hormones (incretins), and autonomic nervous system input. Coordinated insulin secretion maintains postprandial glucose homeostasis.

questions.question: Which hormone stimulates milk production in mammary glands?
questions.explanation: Prolactin, secreted by anterior pituitary lactotrophs, stimulates milk synthesis in mammary epithelial cells after parturition. Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin secretion; dopamine antagonists or hypothalamic-pituitary disconnection causes hyperprolactinemia. Prolactin also affects reproductive function and immune responses.

questions.question: What role does vitamin K play in blood coagulation?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K serves as cofactor for gamma-carboxylase, which modifies glutamate residues in clotting factors to gamma-carboxyglutamate. These modified residues bind calcium ions essential for clotting factor activation on phospholipid surfaces. Vitamin K antagonists like warfarin function as anticoagulants by blocking this carboxylation.

questions.question: What type of bond links monosaccharides in disaccharides?
questions.explanation: Glycosidic bonds form between anomeric carbons and hydroxyl groups through condensation reactions releasing water. These bonds can be alpha or beta depending on anomeric carbon configuration, affecting digestibility and properties. Glycosidic linkages create immense carbohydrate diversity through varied connection points and stereochemistry.

questions.question: Palmitoyl-CoA regulates fatty acid synthesis by:
questions.explanation: Palmitoyl-CoA, the end product of fatty acid synthesis, inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase through negative feedback. It promotes dissociation of the active polymeric enzyme to inactive protomers. This prevents excessive fatty acid accumulation and coordinates synthesis with cellular needs.

Reduction of aldoses with sodium borohydride or catalytic hydrogenation converts carbonyl groups to hydroxyl groups. Glucose yields sorbitol (glucitol), galactose produces galactitol, and ribose generates ribitol. These polyols serve as sweeteners and occur naturally in various foods.
questions.question: What reaction converts aldoses to corresponding sugar alcohols?
Elevated serum aminotransferases (ALT, AST) primarily indicate:
questions.explanation: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) are released from damaged hepatocytes, making them sensitive markers of liver injury. ALT is more liver-specific; AST is also found in heart and muscle. The ALT/AST ratio helps distinguish injury types. Marked elevations suggest acute hepatitis or toxic injury. Chronic elevation indicates ongoing liver disease. Other liver function tests provide additional diagnostic information.

questions.question: What enzyme catalyzes conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid?
questions.explanation: Xanthine oxidase catalyzes sequential oxidations producing uric acid as the final purine degradation product in humans. This enzyme also generates superoxide radicals and hydrogen peroxide during catalysis, contributing to oxidative stress. Xanthine oxidase inhibitors like allopurinol treat gout by reducing uric acid production.

questions.question: Which modified monosaccharide contains an amino group at carbon 2?
questions.explanation: Glucosamine replaces the hydroxyl at carbon 2 with an amino group, often N-acetylated in biological molecules. This amino sugar appears in glycosaminoglycans, chitin, and glycoproteins. Glucosamine supplements are marketed for joint health, though efficacy remains controversial.

questions.question: What type of inhibitor increases apparent Km without affecting Vmax?
questions.explanation: Competitive inhibitors bind active sites, competing with substrate and raising apparent Km while Vmax remains unchanged. High substrate concentrations overcome inhibition by outcompeting inhibitor binding, maintaining maximum velocity potential. This reversible inhibition pattern is diagnostically important for determining inhibitor mechanisms.

Urea synthesis consumes four high-energy phosphate bonds: two ATP for carbamoyl phosphate synthesis, one ATP for argininosuccinate synthesis, and one additional ATP equivalent from fumarate regeneration. This high energy cost reflects the importance of ammonia detoxification for survival. The energy expenditure is justified because accumulated ammonia is far more toxic than the metabolic cost of its removal.
questions.question: How many ATP equivalents are consumed per molecule of urea synthesized?
In starvation, ketone bodies serve primarily to:
questions.explanation: During prolonged fasting, ketone bodies produced from adipose tissue fatty acids become the brain's primary fuel, sparing glucose. This dramatically reduces the need for gluconeogenesis from amino acids, thereby preserving muscle protein. Without this adaptation, protein wasting would be severe and unsustainable during extended food deprivation.

Vitamin E (tocopherols) intercepts lipid peroxyl radicals in membranes, preventing lipid peroxidation chain reactions. Vitamin C can regenerate vitamin E by reducing tocopheryl radicals. Vitamin E deficiency, though rare, causes neurological problems from membrane oxidative damage.
questions.question: Which vitamin functions as a lipid-soluble antioxidant in membranes?
Epinephrine binding to β-adrenergic receptors activates:
questions.explanation: Epinephrine (and norepinephrine) binding β-adrenergic receptors activates Gs proteins, which stimulate adenylyl cyclase to produce cAMP. cAMP activates protein kinase A (PKA), which phosphorylates target enzymes and transcription factors. This "fight-or-flight" response mobilizes energy stores (glycogenolysis, lipolysis), increases cardiac output, and redirects blood flow. The cAMP cascade provides signal amplification.

Secondary active transporters harness energy stored in electrochemical gradients (typically sodium or proton) established by primary active transport. Favorable ion movement down its gradient drives unfavorable solute movement against its gradient through coupled conformational changes. This indirect energy coupling achieves concentration accumulation.
questions.question: What drives secondary active transport across membranes?
Which intermediate is split by aldolase in glycolysis?
questions.explanation: Aldolase cleaves fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into two three-carbon molecules: dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. This reversible aldol cleavage is named for the enzyme and reaction type. Only glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate proceeds directly through glycolysis; dihydroxyacetone phosphate must be isomerized first.

Hydroxy amino acids such as serine, threonine, and homoserine are deaminated by PLP-dependent dehydratases (also called dehydrases) without undergoing oxidation. These enzymes remove both the hydroxyl group and the amino group as water and ammonia respectively. The reaction produces α-keto acids that can enter various metabolic pathways.
questions.question: Serine and threonine undergo non-oxidative deamination by which type of enzyme?

questions.explanation: Keratan sulfate uniquely contains galactose-N-acetylglucosamine repeating units rather than amino sugar-uronic acid pairs. The highly variable sulfation patterns and heterogeneity distinguish keratan sulfate from other glycosaminoglycans. It concentrates in cornea, cartilage, and intervertebral discs.
questions.question: Which glycosaminoglycan contains galactose instead of uronic acid?

questions.explanation: Dienoyl-CoA reductase is required in addition to enoyl-CoA isomerase for complete oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids like linoleate. The reductase uses NADPH to reduce conjugated double bonds to a single double bond. The combined action of isomerase and reductase allows polyunsaturated fatty acids to be processed through β-oxidation.
questions.question: Oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids requires which additional enzyme beyond isomerase?

questions.explanation: The glucose-alanine cycle transfers nitrogen from muscle to liver as alanine. Muscle proteins are degraded to amino acids; amino groups are transferred to pyruvate (from glycolysis) forming alanine, which travels to liver. Hepatic alanine is deaminated, yielding pyruvate for gluconeogenesis and nitrogen for urea synthesis. Glucose returns to muscle. This cycle provides glucose during fasting while removing nitrogen safely.
questions.question: The glucose-alanine cycle transfers which metabolite from muscle to liver?

questions.explanation: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) and its phosphorylated form NADP+ derive from niacin (vitamin B3). These coenzymes function as electron carriers in redox reactions throughout metabolism. Severe niacin deficiency causes pellagra, characterized by dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, and potentially death.
questions.question: What coenzyme derives from the vitamin niacin?

questions.explanation: Liver has very high pentose phosphate pathway activity because it performs extensive reductive biosynthesis (fatty acids, cholesterol) requiring large amounts of NADPH. Adipose tissue, lactating mammary gland, and adrenal cortex (steroid synthesis) also have high pathway activity. Tissues primarily generating energy through oxidation have lower activity.
questions.question: Which tissue has the highest activity of the pentose phosphate pathway?

questions.explanation: Allosteric regulation involves effector binding to sites distinct from active sites, inducing conformational changes affecting catalysis. Positive effectors increase activity while negative effectors decrease it, enabling sophisticated metabolic control. Multiple binding sites allow integration of various regulatory signals.
questions.question: What type of enzyme regulation involves protein-protein interactions at sites distant from active sites?
Which prostaglandin synthesis enzyme is selectively inhibited by COX-2 inhibitors?
questions.explanation: Cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) selective inhibitors target inflammation-induced prostaglandin synthesis while sparing COX-1-mediated gastric protection. This selectivity reduces gastrointestinal side effects associated with traditional NSAIDs that inhibit both isoforms. However, cardiovascular risks led to withdrawal of some COX-2 inhibitors from the market.

questions.question: The first step in ketone body synthesis is:
questions.explanation: Two acetyl-CoA molecules condense to form acetoacetyl-CoA, catalyzed by thiolase (also called ACAT). This reversible reaction is pulled forward by subsequent steps. Acetoacetyl-CoA is the precursor for both ketone body synthesis and cholesterol synthesis, making it a metabolic branch point.

Gluconeogenesis from two pyruvates requires six ATP equivalents: two ATP for pyruvate carboxylase, two GTP for PEPCK, and two ATP for phosphoglycerate kinase (running in reverse). This high energy cost reflects the thermodynamic challenge of reversing glycolysis. The energy expenditure is essential for maintaining blood glucose during fasting.
questions.question: How many ATP equivalents are required to synthesize one glucose from two pyruvates?
What second messenger is generated from ATP by adenylyl cyclase?
questions.explanation: Cyclic AMP (cAMP) functions as a second messenger transmitting signals from G-protein coupled receptors to intracellular targets. Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cAMP, which activates protein kinase A, phosphorylating numerous substrates. Phosphodiesterases hydrolyze cAMP, terminating signals.

questions.question: Which porphyria causes photosensitivity and liver disease?
questions.explanation: Porphyria cutanea tarda from uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency causes photosensitivity from porphyrin accumulation in skin. Liver disease results from iron overload and alcohol effects. Phlebotomy reduces iron, improving porphyrin metabolism. This is the most common porphyria type.

ADP and GDP activate glutamate dehydrogenase when energy levels are low, promoting amino acid catabolism. Conversely, ATP and GTP inhibit the enzyme when energy is abundant, conserving amino acids for biosynthesis. This allosteric regulation coordinates amino acid oxidation with cellular energy status.
questions.question: Which allosteric activators stimulate glutamate dehydrogenase activity?

questions.explanation: Amylopectin contains α(1→6) branch points approximately every 20-30 glucose residues along α(1→4) linked chains. Amylose is unbranched, consisting solely of α(1→4) linkages forming helical structures. Branching in amylopectin provides more chain ends for simultaneous enzymatic attack during starch mobilization.
questions.question: What distinguishes amylopectin from amylose structurally?

questions.explanation: Glucogenic amino acids are degraded to pyruvate or TCA cycle intermediates that can be converted to glucose through gluconeogenesis. This classification is based on metabolic fate rather than structure. Most amino acids are glucogenic, providing carbon skeletons for glucose synthesis during fasting or starvation.
questions.question: Amino acids that produce TCA cycle intermediates or pyruvate are classified as:
What technique amplifies specific DNA sequences exponentially?
questions.explanation: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) exponentially amplifies target DNA sequences through repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing, and extension. This technique revolutionized molecular biology, enabling DNA detection from minimal samples. PCR applications span diagnostics, forensics, cloning, and sequencing.

questions.question: Which amino acids can be converted to glucose during starvation?
questions.explanation: Glucogenic amino acids from protein breakdown provide carbon skeletons for glucose synthesis during prolonged fasting. Muscle protein degradation supplies amino acids to liver for gluconeogenesis, maintaining blood glucose for brain. This process causes muscle wasting during extended starvation.

About 85% of body phosphorus is in bone as hydroxyapatite, with 15% in soft tissues and extracellular fluid.
