Low calcitriol reduces calcium absorption, contributing to hypocalcemia, which stimulates PTH secretion (secondary hyperparathyroidism) and subsequent bone resorption, causing renal osteodystrophy with bone pain and pathological fractures.
questions.question: The kidney performs the final activation step of vitamin D. How does loss of this renal function in CKD contribute to skeletal complications?

questions.explanation: Vomiting and diarrhea cause prerenal AKI by depleting extracellular fluid volume, reducing effective circulating volume and renal perfusion pressure below the threshold required for adequate GFR. Prerenal AKI accounts for approximately 60–70% of all AKI cases and is fully reversible if the underlying cause (volume depletion) is corrected promptly before ischemic damage transforms it to intrinsic (intrarenal) ATN. Early volume resuscitation is the cornerstone of treatment.
options: Intrinsic (intrarenal) AKI from acute tubular necrosis
Postrenal AKI from volume depletion causing tubular casts obstructing urine flow
Renovascular AKI from dehydration-induced arterial thrombosis
Prerenal AKI from reduced effective circulating volume impairing renal perfusion
Functional AKI from reflex-mediated renal vasoconstriction only
questions.question: A dehydrated patient with severe vomiting and diarrhea develops AKI. What type of AKI does this represent and by what primary mechanism?

questions.explanation: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy results from multiple mechanisms of chronic hyperglycemic injury: polyol pathway activation (excess glucose converted to sorbitol by aldose reductase, causing osmotic stress), formation of advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) damaging nerve proteins and blood vessels, oxidative stress from mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired nerve blood flow from endoneurial capillary disease. These mechanisms together cause axonal degeneration and demyelination.
questions.question: Which mechanism most accurately explains the development of diabetic peripheral neuropathy?
options: Hyperglycemia directly damages the myelin sheath by precipitating calcium in Schwann cells
Chronic hyperglycemia causes polyol pathway activation, AGE formation, oxidative stress
Insulin deficiency prevents peripheral nerve myelination in adult neurons
Hyperosmolarity from hyperglycemia directly shrinks Schwann cells causing demyelination
Elevated free fatty acids from lipolysis directly deposit in peripheral nerves causing inflammation

questions.explanation: The ionotropic GABA-A receptor mediates primary CNS inhibition by increasing chloride conductance, leading to neuronal hyperpolarization. NMDA, AMPA, and kainate receptors mediate excitation via glutamate. Nicotinic receptors respond to acetylcholine in the peripheral and central nervous systems.
questions.question: Inhibitory neurotransmission in the CNS is primarily mediated via which receptor?

questions.explanation: HLA-B1502 is strongly associated with carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN in Han Chinese, Southeast Asian, and South Asian populations. This pharmacogenomic association is so strong that many regulatory agencies mandate HLA-B1502 screening before carbamazepine initiation in patients of relevant ancestry. HLA-A3101 is associated with carbamazepine hypersensitivity in European populations.
questions.question: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) as a severe cutaneous adverse reaction to AEDs is most strongly associated with which HLA allele particularly relevant in Asian populations?
options: HLA-B5701 associated with carbamazepine in Han Chinese
HLA-B1502 associated with carbamazepine in Han Chinese and Southeast Asians
HLA-B5801 associated with allopurinol in Asian populations
HLA-DRB107 associated with phenytoin in all populations
HLA-A3101 associated with valproate in European populations
Reduced GFR ? decreased calcium reabsorption ? hypercalcemia ? soft tissue calcification
Reduced GFR ? excessive aldosterone ? sodium retention ? bone mineral loss
Reduced GFR ? elevated renin ? angiotensin II ? parathyroid suppression ? demineralization
Reduced GFR ? excess vitamin D ? hypercalcemia ? parathyroid suppression ? thinning bones
Reduced GFR ? phosphate retention ? hyperphosphatemia ? hypocalcemia ? secondary hyperparathyroidism ?
questions.question: CKD causes renal osteodystrophy through disrupted calcium-phosphate metabolism. What is the correct sequence of pathophysiological events linking CKD to renal osteodystrophy?
questions.explanation: In CKD: reduced GFR causes phosphate retention and hyperphosphatemia. Elevated phosphate combines with calcium, lowering ionized calcium (hypocalcemia). Additionally, reduced 1-alpha-hydroxylation of vitamin D (deficient calcitriol) further reduces gut calcium absorption. Both hyperphosphatemia and low calcitriol stimulate PTH secretion (secondary hyperparathyroidism). Chronically elevated PTH mobilizes calcium from bone, causing renal osteodystrophy, bone pain, and pathological fractures.

Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing toxic acetaldehyde to accumulate when alcohol is consumed, producing flushing, nausea, vomiting, and hypotension; this aversive reaction serves as a behavioural deterrent to drinking in motivated patients.
options: Direct blockade of alcohol absorption in the gut
Inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase causing acetaldehyde accumulation
Inhibition of alcohol dehydrogenase reducing ethanol metabolism
Direct stimulation of the vomiting centre independent of alcohol
questions.question: Disulfiram is used as an adjunct in alcohol use disorder treatment because it produces an unpleasant reaction upon alcohol ingestion through which mechanism?

options: Dopamine D3 receptor in the nucleus accumbens
Noradrenaline beta-1 receptor in the locus coeruleus
Histamine H2 receptor in the hypothalamus
Serotonin 5-HT1A receptor in the raphe nuclei and hippocampus
questions.explanation: Chronic SSRI/SNRI use desensitises presynaptic 5-HT1A autoreceptors in the dorsal raphe nucleus, allowing sustained increases in serotonin release. Postsynaptic 5-HT1A receptors in the hippocampus and amygdala mediate anxiolytic responses. This autoreceptor desensitisation contributes to the 2-4 week delay in anxiolytic onset, as early SSRI use can temporarily worsen anxiety before adaptation occurs.
questions.question: Which receptor is primarily responsible for the anxiolytic component of antidepressant action in generalised anxiety disorder?

options: Naloxone, the opioid antagonist with no intrinsic activity
Fentanyl and its class, which incorporate large N-substituents enhancing receptor affinity
Etorphine, which is approximately 1000 times more potent than morphine
Codeine, produced by N-methylation of morphine's nitrogen
Methadone, which lacks the piperidine ring entirely
questions.question: N-phenethyl substitution on morphine's piperidine nitrogen produces a 14-fold increase in activity. This structure-activity relationship finding is clinically relevant because it led to the development of:
questions.explanation: SAR studies showed that replacing the N-methyl group on morphine with larger substituents (N-phenethyl: 14-fold increase; N-phenethyl in the 4-phenylpiperidine scaffold: basis for fentanyl) dramatically increases mu opioid receptor affinity and potency. This relationship underpins the development of fentanyl and its analogues (sufentanil, alfentanil, remifentanil) - among the most potent opioids in clinical use.

questions.question: Which antidepressant has the longest plasma half-life among SSRIs, making discontinuation syndrome least likely and allowing for less frequent dosing?
options: Fluoxetine (t1/2 ~4-6 days, active metabolite norfluoxetine 4-16 days)
questions.explanation: Fluoxetine has the longest half-life of all SSRIs (~4-6 days) and its active metabolite norfluoxetine has an even longer half-life (4-16 days). This provides a built-in gradual taper when the drug is stopped, making discontinuation syndrome virtually absent. It can also be given as a once-weekly dose for maintenance therapy. Paroxetine has the shortest half-life and highest discontinuation syndrome risk.

ACE inhibitor cough results from accumulated bradykinin because ACE also degrades bradykinin. ARBs act at the angiotensin II receptor and do not affect ACE, so bradykinin levels remain normal. This receptor-selective mechanism eliminates the cough seen with ACE inhibitors.
questions.question: A hypertensive diabetic patient develops a dry, persistent cough on lisinopril. Her physician switches her to losartan. Why does this switch resolve the cough?
options: Losartan blocks the same enzyme but with a shorter duration of action
Losartan reduces bradykinin synthesis at the pulmonary endothelium directly
Losartan raises bradykinin levels less than lisinopril because it is renally cleared
Losartan increases bradykinin breakdown through hepatic enzyme induction
Losartan does not raise bradykinin levels since it blocks receptors, not the enzyme

questions.explanation: The involvement of serotonin in schizophrenia is supported by the fact that 5-HT2A agonists such as LSD and psilocybin produce hallucinations, thought disorder, and reality distortion resembling schizophrenic positive symptoms in normal subjects. This, combined with the efficacy of combined D2/5-HT2A antagonists (atypicals), implicates serotonergic dysregulation in schizophrenia pathophysiology.
options: Fluoxetine (an SSRI) reduces positive symptoms of schizophrenia
All antipsychotics must block 5-HT2A receptors to be effective
LSD and psilocybin (5-HT2A agonists) produce hallucinations similar to schizophrenia
Serum serotonin levels are always elevated in schizophrenic patients
Serotonin exclusively controls dopaminergic tone in all brain pathways
questions.question: Serotonergic dysfunction is increasingly implicated in schizophrenia pathogenesis because:

options: Enhancement of GABA-A receptor chloride conductance
Blockade of T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons
Blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels stabilising neuronal membranes
Direct antagonism of NMDA glutamate receptors
questions.explanation: Phenytoin stabilises hyperexcitable neuronal membranes by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels in a use-dependent manner, preventing sustained repetitive firing. Its characteristic adverse effects of gingival hyperplasia and coarse facies are unrelated to this mechanism but are well-recognised chronic toxicities.
questions.question: A patient with generalised tonic-clonic seizures is started on phenytoin and later develops gum hyperplasia and coarsening of facial features. Which mechanism underlies phenytoin's anticonvulsant action?

options: Activity in the aglycone; more hydroxyl groups on sugars increase polarity, reducing protein binding and duration of action
Activity in the sugar moiety; pharmacokinetics modified by the aglycone
Activity equally distributed; both portions contribute equally to both activity and pharmacokinetics
Activity in the lactone ring only; sugar and steroid nucleus modify absorption only
Activity only when both portions are bonded; separation completely abolishes activity
questions.explanation: The inotropic pharmacological activity resides in the aglycone (steroid nucleus with lactone ring). The sugar moiety modifies pharmacokinetics: more hydroxyl groups increase polarity, reducing protein binding, hepatic metabolism, and tubular reabsorption, resulting in shorter duration of action and increased renal excretion. Digitoxin (fewest OH groups) = slowest onset, longest duration; digoxin (moderate OH groups) = intermediate; ouabain (most OH groups) = fastest onset, shortest duration, parenteral only.
questions.question: The pharmacological activity of cardiac glycosides resides in one structural component while the other modifies pharmacokinetics. More hydroxyl groups on sugars inversely affect duration of action. What is this pharmacokinetic relationship?

options: Any synthetic compound with morphine-like properties
Any compound that reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression
An endogenous peptide produced in the brain (e.g., endorphin)
A naturally occurring compound derived from opium (e.g., morphine, codeine)
A semi-synthetic compound with modifications to the natural structure
questions.question: The correct distinction between an 'opiate' and an 'opioid' is that an opiate is:
questions.explanation: An opiate refers specifically to naturally occurring opioid compounds derived from the opium poppy (Papaver somniferum) - primarily morphine, codeine, thebaine, and noscapine. 'Opioid' is the broader term encompassing all compounds (natural, semi-synthetic, synthetic, and endogenous peptides) that bind opioid receptors. Heroin is a semi-synthetic opioid; fentanyl is a synthetic opioid.

options: Failure to respond to one antipsychotic trial of any duration
Inadequate response to at least two antipsychotics at adequate doses from different classes
Schizophrenia that is unresponsive to clozapine after 12 weeks
Schizophrenia with predominant negative symptoms unresponsive to atypicals
Positive symptoms persisting despite doses above the therapeutic range
questions.question: Which of the following correctly characterises 'treatment-resistant schizophrenia' (TRS)?
questions.explanation: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS) is defined as inadequate response (insufficient reduction in positive symptoms and/or global functioning) to at least two adequate antipsychotic trials of different chemical classes, each at adequate doses (equivalent to 400-600 mg chlorpromazine/day) for at least 6 weeks. TRS is an indication for clozapine, the gold standard treatment.

questions.question: Remifentanil differs from other fentanyl analogues primarily because:
options: It has a much longer duration of action due to slow hepatic metabolism
It is the only fentanyl analogue active via the oral route
It is a partial mu agonist with a ceiling effect on respiratory depression
It does not cross the blood-brain barrier due to its hydrophilic structure
It is hydrolysed by plasma and tissue esterases producing an ultra-short action independent of organ function
questions.explanation: Remifentanil has a unique ester linkage in its structure, making it susceptible to rapid hydrolysis by non-specific blood and tissue esterases to an inactive carboxylic acid metabolite. This produces an extremely short duration of action (context-sensitive half-life ~3 minutes), independent of liver or kidney function. It is infused continuously in anaesthesia and must be replaced by another analgesic at procedure end as its analgesia dissipates within minutes of stopping.

Uraemic neuropathy from accumulated toxins typically becomes clinically apparent in advanced CKD, generally stage 4 to 5, correlating with a significant decline in GFR. Earlier stages are usually asymptomatic neurologically, which is why neuropathy is considered a late manifestation of significant renal impairment.
questions.question: A patient with CKD develops progressively worsening peripheral neuropathy manifesting as burning feet and restless legs. At what stage of CKD do such neurological manifestations typically become apparent?
options: Immediately upon any GFR decline below normal
Only after initiation of dialysis, never before
Exclusively in CKD caused by diabetes mellitus

questions.question: A patient with resistant hypertension is found to have paroxysmal episodes of headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis with markedly elevated blood pressure. Which secondary cause should be prioritised for investigation?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of episodic headache, palpitations, and sweating accompanying severe paroxysmal hypertension strongly suggests catecholamine excess from a phaeochromocytoma. This adrenal medullary tumour secretes catecholamines intermittently, producing the characteristic episodic rather than sustained pattern of severe hypertension.

questions.question: A patient on thionamide therapy for Graves' disease develops fever and sore throat after 2 months. What is the most important immediate action?
questions.explanation: Agranulocytosis is the most serious adverse effect of thionamide drugs, occurring in 0.1-0.5% of patients. It typically presents with sudden high fever, severe sore throat, and signs of infection, usually within the first 3 months of treatment. An urgent full blood count is mandatory. If agranulocytosis is confirmed (neutrophils <0.5 x 10^9/L), the thionamide must be stopped immediately, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics started, and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) administered. All patients starting thionamides must be warned to seek urgent review if they develop fever or sore throat.
options: Perform an urgent full blood count; if agranulocytosis confirmed, stop thionamide immediately
Reduce the dose of thionamide and add an antibiotic empirically
Switch from PTU to carbimazole as the fever indicates PTU-induced thyroid storm
Administer radioiodine therapy immediately to replace the failing thionamide therapy
Prescribe paracetamol and continue the thionamide as fever is a common side effect

questions.explanation: Triazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine (t1/2 <6 hours), not a long-acting one. The long-acting benzodiazepines (t1/2 24-72 hours) include chlorazepate, diazepam, quazepam, nitrazepam, chlordiazepoxide, flurazepam, and prazepam. These agents accumulate with repeated dosing and can cause prolonged sedation, especially in the elderly.
questions.question: Long-acting benzodiazepines in the mnemonic 'CDQNCP' include all of the following EXCEPT:
A schizophrenic patient with predominant negative symptoms, such as social withdrawal and blunted affect, is most likely to benefit from which class of antipsychotic?
questions.explanation: Atypical antipsychotics, through combined serotonin-dopamine antagonism, are generally more effective for negative and cognitive symptoms than typical agents, which predominantly target positive symptoms via pure D2 blockade in the mesolimbic pathway.

questions.question: A patient develops visual disturbances described as yellow-green halos around lights, along with nausea and confusion, while on digoxin. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Xanthopsia, or yellow-green visual halos, along with nausea, vomiting, confusion, and arrhythmias, is a classic feature of digoxin toxicity resulting from its effect on retinal cone cells and the central nervous system. Serum digoxin levels should be checked and the drug withheld pending evaluation.
options: Acute glaucoma precipitated by a coexisting anticholinergic drug
An unrelated ophthalmologic condition requiring separate referral
Digoxin toxicity affecting the central nervous system and retina
A normal, expected effect of digoxin unrelated to dosage
Migraine with visual aura triggered by cardiac medication

questions.explanation: Furosemide has variable and often reduced oral bioavailability, particularly in heart failure patients with bowel wall oedema, leading to unpredictable diuretic response. Torsemide has higher and more consistent oral bioavailability, providing more reliable diuresis in patients switched from oral furosemide.
questions.question: A patient on torsemide for heart failure switches from furosemide due to inconsistent diuretic response. What pharmacokinetic property explains torsemide's more predictable effect?
options: Selective action on the proximal tubule rather than the loop of Henle
Higher and more consistent oral bioavailability than furosemide
Greater potency requiring substantially higher milligram doses
Significantly shorter half-life allowing more frequent dosing flexibility
Complete renal elimination unlike furosemide's hepatic metabolism

questions.explanation: DKA is defined by: hyperglycemia (glucose usually >14 mmol/L), ketonemia and ketonuria (from unrestrained lipolysis due to absolute insulin deficiency), and metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3 and bicarbonate <15 mEq/L from ketoacid accumulation). This results from absolute insulin deficiency allowing unopposed glucagon action, causing excessive hepatic glucose production, lipolysis, and ketogenesis that overwhelms the body's buffering capacity.
options: Hyperglycemia, hyperosmolarity, and absence of ketones
Hyperglycemia, elevated ketone bodies, and metabolic acidosis
questions.question: What metabolic triad defines diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), which predominantly occurs in Type 1 diabetes?
Venlafaxine at higher doses produces additional noradrenergic effects distinguishing it from pure SSRIs, most notably causing which adverse effect requiring monitoring?
questions.explanation: As an SNRI, venlafaxine inhibits both serotonin and, at higher doses, norepinephrine reuptake; the added noradrenergic activity can cause dose-dependent hypertension, necessitating blood pressure monitoring, unlike pure SSRIs which lack this cardiovascular effect.
options: Marked weight gain within the first week
Severe sleep apnoea and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Acute alcohol withdrawal in a monitored inpatient setting
Sleep-onset insomnia in otherwise healthy adults
Generalised anxiety disorder with no respiratory comorbidity
questions.question: The clinical indication where benzodiazepines are contraindicated due to risk of respiratory depression is:
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines cause dose-dependent respiratory depression and muscle relaxation, which can precipitate respiratory failure in patients with severe sleep apnoea (by worsening upper airway obstruction) or COPD (by reducing hypoxic respiratory drive). They are relatively safe in healthy subjects but must be used cautiously in compromised respiratory states.

options: All COPD patients with FEV1 below 50% predicted regardless of other features
COPD patients with a chronic bronchitis phenotype exclusively, regardless of eosinophil count
COPD patients with blood eosinophil count >=300 cells/uL and history of frequent exacerbations
COPD patients who are currently smokers only, as ICS reduces tobacco-related inflammation
COPD patients with concurrent asthma-COPD overlap (ACO) only, as this is the sole approved indication
questions.question: In which COPD patient profile does evidence most strongly support ICS addition to LABA/LAMA dual bronchodilator therapy?
questions.explanation: ICS addition to LABA/LAMA (triple therapy) in COPD is most evidence-based in patients with: (1) blood eosinophil count >=300 cells/uL (indicating eosinophilic inflammation that responds to corticosteroids and predicts ICS benefit per GOLD guidelines), AND (2) frequent exacerbations (>=2 moderate exacerbations or >=1 hospitalization per year) despite dual bronchodilator therapy. The IMPACT trial showed greatest ICS benefit in patients with higher eosinophil counts. ICS should be withheld or withdrawn in patients with eosinophil counts <100 cells/uL where harm (pneumonia risk) outweighs benefit.

questions.question: St. John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum), an herbal antidepressant, acts primarily through:
questions.explanation: St. John's Wort's active ingredient hyperforin weakly inhibits reuptake of serotonin, noradrenaline, dopamine, GABA, and glutamate. It also activates TRPC6 sodium channels, which may contribute to its antidepressant effect. Its clinical efficacy is comparable to prescribed antidepressants for mild-to-moderate depression. A critical interaction concern is CYP3A4 induction, reducing levels of many co-prescribed drugs (HIV antiretrovirals, oral contraceptives, warfarin).
options: Irreversible MAO-A inhibition similar to phenelzine
Weak monoamine reuptake inhibition via hyperforin plus other actions
Potentiation of benzodiazepine binding to GABA-A receptors
Direct stimulation of adenylate cyclase increasing neuronal cAMP

questions.question: Disulfiram (Antabuse) works as an aversive therapy for alcohol dependence by:
questions.explanation: Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH2), the enzyme responsible for oxidising acetaldehyde (the first metabolite of ethanol) to acetate. When a patient on disulfiram drinks alcohol, acetaldehyde accumulates to toxic levels, causing flushing, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, hypotension - the disulfiram-alcohol reaction. This aversive consequence deters drinking. Compliance is the major limitation of disulfiram therapy.
options: Inhibiting acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, causing toxic acetaldehyde accumulation when alcohol is consumed
Blocking alcohol's GABA-A potentiation, eliminating its pleasurable effects
Stimulating mu opioid receptors to reduce alcohol craving
Blocking ethanol absorption in the gastrointestinal tract
Enhancing hepatic first-pass metabolism of ethanol to inactive metabolites

questions.question: What is the most critical long-term complication of untreated congenital hypothyroidism?
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormone is absolutely essential for normal brain development in the perinatal period. Untreated congenital hypothyroidism causes irreversible intellectual disability (cretinism), impaired myelination of the nervous system, deafness, speech delay, and stunted growth. Treatment must begin within the first 2-4 weeks of life for optimal neurological outcomes, which is why neonatal screening programs (heel-prick test for TSH and T4) are conducted universally in developed countries.
options: Severe growth retardation with normal intelligence
Severe systolic heart failure from neonatal cardiomyopathy
Progressive deafness and visual loss from cranial nerve damage
Irreversible intellectual disability and neurological damage if untreated in the first weeks of
Diabetes mellitus from neonatal pancreatic destruction associated with hypothyroidism

questions.question: DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins) lower blood glucose by a specific mechanism. How does sitagliptin reduce blood glucose?
questions.explanation: DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin, saxagliptin, linagliptin, alogliptin) inhibit dipeptidyl peptidase-4, which normally rapidly degrades the incretin hormones GLP-1 and GIP within minutes of their secretion. By inhibiting DPP-4, these drugs prolong endogenous GLP-1 and GIP action, enhancing glucose-dependent insulin secretion and reducing glucagon. The glucose-dependent mechanism means DPP-4 inhibitors have low risk of hypoglycemia and are generally well tolerated.
options: They directly stimulate insulin secretion from beta cells by activating adenylyl cyclase
They competitively inhibit pancreatic glucagon release by blocking alpha-cell glucagon receptors
They inhibit dipeptidyl peptidase-4, which degrades active GLP-1 and GIP
They reduce hepatic glucose output by inhibiting glycogen phosphorylase in hepatocytes
They improve insulin sensitivity in peripheral tissues by inhibiting adipocyte lipolysis

questions.question: Which antiepileptic drug is contraindicated in pregnancy due to a 'spina bifida' (neural tube defect) risk approximately 10-20 times higher than baseline?
questions.explanation: Valproic acid causes neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly) in approximately 1-2% of exposed pregnancies, a risk 10-20 times higher than the general population. This is attributed to folate metabolism interference and HDAC (histone deacetylase) inhibition. Valproate is the most teratogenic AED and should be avoided in women of childbearing age. High-dose folic acid supplementation reduces (but does not eliminate) neural tube defect risk.

Tardive dyskinesia arises from chronic dopamine receptor blockade causing receptor upregulation, producing involuntary orofacial movements after prolonged therapy. Unlike acute dystonia, it is often irreversible and abrupt withdrawal can worsen symptoms, so cautious tapering or switching agents is preferred.
options: Acute dystonia; treat with intravenous anticholinergics immediately
Akathisia; switch to a beta-blocker promptly
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; give dantrolene urgently
Tardive dyskinesia; the causative drug should be tapered cautiously
questions.question: A patient on long-term typical antipsychotic therapy develops involuntary lip smacking and tongue protrusion after two years of treatment. Which condition is this, and what is the key management principle?

options: Direct toxic injury of the ACE inhibitor on renal tubular cells
Loss of angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction reduces GFR
Excessive systemic hypotension reducing overall renal blood flow
Increased renal vascular resistance from reflex sympathetic activation
Precipitation of drug crystals within the renal collecting system
questions.explanation: In bilateral renal artery stenosis, glomerular filtration is critically dependent on angiotensin II-mediated constriction of the efferent arteriole to maintain filtration pressure. ACE inhibitors abolish this compensatory constriction, causing a sharp fall in GFR and acute kidney injury in this specific setting.
questions.question: A patient with hypertension and CKD stage 3 develops worsening renal function and a rise in creatinine after starting an ACE inhibitor. Renal artery duplex ultrasound reveals bilateral renal artery stenosis. What is the mechanism of the deterioration?

options: Start insulin immediately regardless of the potassium level
Give a single dose of oral potassium and continue as planned
Begin potassium replacement before starting the insulin infusion
Withhold both insulin and potassium until glucose normalizes
Administer calcium gluconate instead of correcting potassium
questions.explanation: Insulin drives potassium intracellularly, which can precipitate life-threatening hypokalemia and cardiac arrhythmia if the starting potassium is already low. When serum potassium is below approximately 3.3 mEq/L, potassium replacement should be initiated before or alongside insulin therapy in DKA management.
questions.question: A patient in DKA being treated with IV insulin infusion is found to have a serum potassium of 3.1 mEq/L before insulin has been started. What is the appropriate action?
A patient presents with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure with bilateral infiltrates following sepsis. Which ventilation strategy reduces mortality in moderate-severe ARDS?
questions.explanation: The ARMA trial established low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg ideal body weight, plateau pressure <=30 cmH2O) as the cornerstone of ARDS ventilation, reducing mortality by 22% compared to conventional tidal volumes (12 mL/kg). In moderate-severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150 mmHg), prone positioning for >=16 hours/day was shown in the PROSEVA trial to reduce 28-day mortality from 32.8% to 16.0%. These strategies limit ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI) from overdistension and cyclical collapse-reopening of lung units (atelectrauma). Permissive hypercapnia (accepting elevated PaCO2) is an acceptable consequence of lung-protective ventilation.
options: Lung-protective ventilation using low tidal volume (6 mL/kg IBW) to prevent ventilator-induced lung injury
High tidal volume ventilation (12-15 mL/kg IBW) to maintain normocapnia and minimize respiratory acidosis
High PEEP (20-25 cmH2O) with normal tidal volumes to maximize alveolar recruitment
Prone positioning alone without tidal volume limitation in patients with mild ARDS
Oscillatory high-frequency ventilation as the first-line mode for all ARDS patients

questions.question: Morphine is less effective than pure morphine for pain when administered as crude opium because:
questions.explanation: Crude opium contains numerous alkaloids, pigments, and organic acids that collectively slow and render inconsistent the absorption of morphine when ingested. This pharmacokinetic variability makes crude opium less predictable and effective as an analgesic than purified morphine at equivalent morphine doses. Historically, opium was used for its constipating and anxiolytic effects more than precise analgesia.
options: Opium is slowly and inconsistently absorbed due to its complex alkaloid mixture and formulation
Opium contains GABA antagonists that reduce morphine's CNS effects
Thebaine in opium competitively antagonises morphine at mu receptors
Papaverine in opium blocks dopamine receptors reducing analgesia
Noscapine in opium is a serotonin agonist counteracting opioid analgesia

questions.explanation: Codeine is a prodrug that undergoes O-demethylation by CYP2D6 (approximately 10% of dose) to form morphine, which is responsible for its analgesic effect. In CYP2D6 poor metabolisers (approximately 7-10% of Caucasians), codeine produces inadequate analgesia. In ultra-rapid metabolisers, excessive morphine formation has caused fatal respiratory depression in children and breastfed infants. This led to codeine restrictions in paediatrics.
questions.question: Codeine's analgesic activity depends primarily on its metabolism by which enzyme?

questions.explanation: Chloral hydrate is rapidly reduced in the liver (and erythrocytes) to trichloroethanol by the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase. Trichloroethanol is the pharmacologically active CNS depressant metabolite. This is why chloral hydrate and ethanol potentiate each other - both compete for the same metabolic pathway and share CNS depressant properties.
options: Reduction to trichloroethanol by alcohol dehydrogenase
questions.question: The sedative-hypnotic drug 'chloral hydrate' is metabolised to its active form by:
Systolic heart failure has a specific pathophysiological basis distinguishing it from diastolic heart failure. Which abnormality most directly defines systolic heart failure?
options: Impaired myocardial relaxation causing a stiff ventricle unable to fill adequately
Valvular stenosis reducing cardiac output without primary myocardial dysfunction
Reduced ventricular contractility (reduced ejection fraction <40%) resulting in decreased cardiac output
Pericardial tamponade compressing the heart and reducing ventricular filling
Severe hypertension increasing afterload, overwhelming otherwise normal contractility
questions.explanation: Systolic heart failure (HFrEF) is defined by impaired ventricular contractility with ejection fraction <40%. The ventricle cannot generate sufficient force to eject an adequate stroke volume meeting the body's metabolic needs. This causes the clinical syndrome of reduced cardiac output, dyspnea, fatigue, and fluid retention. It differs fundamentally from diastolic (HFpEF) where systolic function is preserved but the stiff ventricle fails to fill adequately. HFrEF responds best to neurohormonal blockade, positive inotropes, and diuretics.

options: Bronchial hyperresponsiveness consistent with underlying asthma
Fixed, irreversible airflow obstruction consistent with COPD
Normal airway reactivity, effectively excluding asthma
A restrictive rather than obstructive ventilatory pattern
Established pulmonary fibrosis with reduced lung compliance
questions.question: A patient with a suspected diagnosis of asthma undergoes a methacholine challenge test. What does a positive result, defined as a significant fall in FEV1, indicate?
questions.explanation: Methacholine is a bronchoconstrictor agent used to provoke airway narrowing in susceptible individuals. A significant fall in FEV1 in response to a low dose indicates bronchial hyperresponsiveness, a hallmark feature of asthma, and supports the diagnosis when spirometry findings are otherwise inconclusive.

Although SSRIs block SERT within hours, antidepressant effects require 2-4 weeks. This is attributed to adaptive neuroplastic changes: desensitisation of presynaptic 5-HT1A autoreceptors (which initially dampen the benefit of SERT blockade), receptor downregulation, altered gene expression (BDNF upregulation), and synaptic remodelling. These adaptive changes explain the clinical lag period.
questions.question: The onset of clinical antidepressant effect typically requires 2-4 weeks despite immediate monoamine reuptake blockade. This delay is best explained by:
options: Slow drug absorption and distribution to CNS over several weeks
Requirement for receptor upregulation before synaptic transmission improves
Need for gene expression changes and neuroplasticity rather than simple receptor occupancy
First-pass metabolism requiring dose accumulation to therapeutic levels
Direct NMDA receptor mechanism that requires weeks for full channel blockade

questions.question: Which diuretic agent specifically blocks carbonic anhydrase in the early proximal convoluted tubule rather than acting on the loop, distal tubule, or collecting duct?
questions.explanation: Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor acting in the early proximal convoluted tubule. It prevents H? secretion and HCO3? reabsorption, causing bicarbonate diuresis and metabolic acidosis. While primarily used for glaucoma, altitude sickness, and certain seizure disorders, it is classified among diuretics. It is distinct from loop diuretics (TALH), thiazides (early DCT), osmotic agents (proximal tubule passively), and potassium-sparing agents (collecting duct).

options: Overproduction of TSH by the pituitary gland causing secondary hyperthyroidism
Stimulating autoantibodies that bind and activate TSH receptors on thyroid follicular cells
Autonomous thyroid nodules that produce thyroid hormone independent of TSH regulation
Excessive dietary iodine intake causing uncontrolled thyroid hormone synthesis
Ectopic thyroid hormone production from struma ovarii
questions.explanation: Graves' disease is caused by stimulating thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI, also called TRAb) that bind the TSH receptor on thyroid follicular cells, activating it just like TSH but without feedback regulation. This causes uncontrolled thyroid hormone synthesis and secretion, thyroid hypertrophy (diffuse goiter), and the extrathyroidal features unique to Graves' disease: exophthalmos (from retro-orbital glycosaminoglycan accumulation) and pretibial myxedema.
questions.question: What is the pathophysiological mechanism that makes Graves' disease unique among thyroid disorders?
Which AED is the drug of choice for trigeminal neuralgia (as well as focal epilepsy)?
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine is the first-line treatment for trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux) as well as focal epilepsy. Its sodium channel-blocking mechanism stabilises hyperexcitable trigeminal nerve afferents generating the characteristic lancinating facial pain. Oxcarbazepine is an alternative. Valproate and other AEDs have less evidence for trigeminal neuralgia. This dual indication makes carbamazepine clinically significant.

questions.question: A patient presents with acute ischemic stroke and BP of 185/100 mmHg. Why is it generally inadvisable to aggressively lower blood pressure in the acute phase of ischemic stroke?
options: Elevated blood pressure post-stroke prevents cerebral edema formation
Lowering blood pressure increases hemorrhagic transformation risk by reducing clot formation
Antihypertensive medications are direct contraindications to tPA administration
Acute hypertension is protective against cerebral vasospasm in the first 24 hours
questions.explanation: In acute ischemic stroke, aggressive BP lowering can extend the infarct because the penumbra (potentially salvageable neurons surrounding the ischemic core) depends on elevated BP to maintain collateral perfusion. Cerebral autoregulation is impaired in and around the infarct, making local blood flow pressure-dependent. BP is only lowered acutely if extremely elevated (>220/120 mmHg without tPA or >185/110 mmHg if tPA is planned), with gradual careful reduction.

Naltrexone has a longer half-life (approximately 4-13 hours for parent drug, active metabolite 6-beta-naltrexol has longer duration), good oral bioavailability, and is used for maintaining abstinence in detoxified opioid-dependent patients and in alcohol use disorder. Naloxone has a very short half-life (~60-90 minutes), poor oral bioavailability, and is used parenterally for acute overdose reversal.
questions.question: Naltrexone differs from naloxone in that naltrexone:
options: Has a shorter duration of action and is preferred for acute overdose reversal
Is a partial mu agonist rather than a pure antagonist
Is selective for kappa opioid receptors without mu antagonism
Has a longer duration of action, oral bioavailability, and is used for opioid dependence maintenance
Is inactivated by first-pass hepatic metabolism and cannot be given orally
Acute hypoxic respiratory failure following pneumonia with bilateral infiltrates on CXR
Acute onset within 1 week of a clinical insult, bilateral opacities on imaging, PaO2/FiO2 ratio <300 mmHg
Chronic progressive hypoxemia with bilateral ground-glass opacities without an identifiable cause
Post-operative respiratory failure with atelectasis and pleural effusions within 72 hours of surgery
Any bilateral pneumonia with PaO2 <60 mmHg on room air regardless of onset timing
questions.question: What is the Berlin definition of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)?
questions.explanation: The Berlin definition (2012) defines ARDS by: (1) Timing—acute onset within 1 week of a known clinical insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms; (2) Imaging—bilateral opacities on CXR or CT not fully explained by effusions, lobar/lung collapse, or nodules; (3) Origin of edema—respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload; (4) Oxygenation—with PEEP/CPAP >=5 cmH2O: Mild ARDS (PF ratio 200-300), Moderate ARDS (PF ratio 100-200), Severe ARDS (PF ratio <100). Treatment includes low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg IBW) and prone positioning for moderate-severe ARDS.

The mesolimbic pathway, connecting the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens, mediates reward and reinforcement, and its dysregulation by drugs of abuse underlies craving and dependence. The nigrostriatal pathway instead governs motor control, not reward processing.
questions.question: Which neurotransmitter system, when dysfunctional, is most implicated in the reward and reinforcement pathways underlying substance dependence?
Which anxiolytic mechanism is shared by both benzodiazepines and barbiturates at the molecular level?
options: Enhancement of GABA-A receptor mediated chloride conductance
Stimulation of adenylate cyclase via beta receptors
questions.explanation: Both drug classes act allosterically on the GABA-A receptor complex to increase chloride ion conductance, producing neuronal hyperpolarisation and CNS depression, though at distinct binding sites with different mechanisms of channel activation at high doses.

Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS, activating ionotropic receptors (NMDA, AMPA, kainate) to depolarize neurons. GABA serves the opposite inhibitory role, while dopamine and serotonin are modulatory. Disruption of glutamate signalling underlies many neurological disorders.
questions.question: Which neurotransmitter is primarily responsible for excitatory neurotransmission in the CNS?
What is the recommended immediate treatment for mild-to-moderate hypoglycemia in a conscious diabetic patient?
options: Intravenous dextrose 50% at a dose of 50 mL immediately
Oral sucrose 50 g immediately dissolved in water
Oral administration of 15-20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
Subcutaneous insulin dose adjustment to prevent further hypoglycemia
questions.explanation: For mild-to-moderate hypoglycemia in a conscious patient who can swallow, the recommended immediate treatment is the '15-15 rule': 15-20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate (glucose tablets, fruit juice, regular soda, or sugar), followed by reassessment of blood glucose after 15 minutes. If glucose remains below 4 mmol/L, the treatment is repeated. Once blood glucose normalizes, a complex carbohydrate snack is recommended to prevent recurrence.

questions.question: Which neurotransmitter system is primarily implicated in the extrapyramidal side effects of antipsychotic drugs?
questions.explanation: Extrapyramidal side effects (EPS) arise from dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway by antipsychotic drugs. This disrupts the normal balance between dopamine and acetylcholine in the basal ganglia, producing movement disorders such as parkinsonism, dystonia, and akathisia.

options: Direct blockade of renal potassium channels by the drug
Increased aldosterone secretion raises distal tubular sodium reabsorption
Enhanced renin release stimulating potassium retention
Increased angiotensin II activity enhancing potassium secretion
Reduced aldosterone secretion decreases distal tubular potassium excretion
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin II formation, which normally stimulates aldosterone release. Reduced aldosterone lowers the sodium-potassium exchange in the distal nephron, decreasing potassium excretion. This effect is amplified in patients with pre-existing CKD, requiring close potassium monitoring.
questions.question: A patient with hypertension and chronic kidney disease is prescribed an ACE inhibitor for renoprotection. Two weeks later, potassium rises to 5.8 mEq/L. What is the underlying mechanism?

questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors block conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, but ACE also normally degrades bradykinin. Inhibited ACE causes bradykinin accumulation, which stimulates prostaglandin and substance P release in the airway, resulting in a dry persistent cough. This differentiates ACE inhibitors from ARBs, which do not inhibit bradykinin degradation and thus do not cause cough.
questions.question: A clinical pharmacist counsels a patient on ACE inhibitors. Which adverse effect results specifically from bradykinin accumulation caused by ACE inhibition?

questions.explanation: Cyclic AMP (cAMP) is a second messenger generated by adenylate cyclase upon G-protein activation. It amplifies receptor signals by activating protein kinase A (PKA), which phosphorylates target proteins to alter cellular responses. Ionotropic receptors act directly as ion channels without second messengers.
options: It directly opens ion channels without receptor involvement
It forms the basis of ionotropic receptor activity
It degrades neurotransmitters in the synaptic cleft
It acts as an intracellular amplifier linking receptor activation to cellular response
It blocks sodium influx during neuronal excitation
questions.question: What is the significance of the 'second messenger' cAMP in CNS drug action?
The 'dopamine D2 receptor occupancy' required for antipsychotic efficacy is approximately:
questions.explanation: PET studies demonstrate that approximately 65-80% D2 receptor occupancy is required for antipsychotic efficacy. Occupancy above 80% significantly increases EPS risk. Atypical antipsychotics (clozapine, quetiapine) achieve efficacy at lower occupancies or transiently. This has revolutionised the dosing philosophy of antipsychotics, supporting the lowest effective dose strategy.

options: Is a selective D2 antagonist that prevents dopamine-mediated mood swings
Inhibits serotonin reuptake similar to SSRIs when used at low doses
Directly stimulates 5-HT1A receptors to produce antidepressant effects
Has active metabolite norquetiapine that inhibits noradrenaline reuptake
Blocks H1 receptors causing increased deep-wave sleep
questions.explanation: Quetiapine's active metabolite norquetiapine inhibits the noradrenaline transporter (NET), contributing antidepressant activity. Additionally, quetiapine's 5-HT2A antagonism and partial 5-HT1A agonism contribute to its antidepressant profile. These properties, beyond simple D2 blockade, explain its regulatory approval for bipolar depression and as an adjunct in major depression.
questions.question: Quetiapine (Seroquel) is clinically useful for bipolar depression in addition to psychosis because it:

questions.explanation: Prostaglandins maintain afferent arteriolar vasodilation to preserve renal perfusion, particularly when renal blood flow is compromised; NSAID-mediated prostaglandin inhibition removes this compensatory vasodilation, reducing glomerular filtration and precipitating acute kidney injury in vulnerable patients.
options: Inhibition of prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar vasodilation
Direct nephrotoxic crystal deposition in renal tubules
Excessive efferent arteriolar vasodilation reducing filtration
Direct immune complex deposition in glomeruli
Increased renal blood flow overwhelming filtration capacity
questions.question: A patient with chronic kidney disease is prescribed an NSAID for osteoarthritis pain. Which mechanism explains the risk of acute kidney injury in this setting?
Which statement correctly differentiates ionotropic from metabotropic neurotransmitter receptors?
questions.explanation: Ionotropic receptors, such as GABA-A and NMDA, form ligand-gated ion channels producing rapid millisecond responses. Metabotropic receptors, such as GABA-B and dopamine receptors, couple to G-proteins and second messengers, producing slower, longer-lasting modulatory effects.
options: Ionotropic receptors act only in the periphery, metabotropic only centrally
Ionotropic receptors directly gate ion channels, while metabotropic receptors act via G-proteins
Metabotropic receptors always produce faster responses than ionotropic
Ionotropic receptors require second messengers, metabotropic do not
Both receptor types always produce identical response kinetics

questions.question: A 70-year-old man with hypertension and symptomatic bradycardia is being considered for antihypertensive therapy. Which drug class should be avoided?
questions.explanation: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as verapamil and diltiazem slow AV nodal conduction and depress sinus node automaticity. In a patient with pre-existing bradycardia, this can worsen conduction block or precipitate symptomatic bradyarrhythmia. Dihydropyridines lack significant nodal effects.

questions.explanation: Ventilator-associated pneumonia typically develops from microaspiration of contaminated oropharyngeal or gastric secretions that pool around the endotracheal tube cuff and are subsequently aspirated into the lower respiratory tract, introducing pathogenic bacteria into an already vulnerable ventilated lung.

Score 0-1: low risk, outpatient treatment; Score 2: moderate risk, consider admission; Score 3-5: high risk, hospital admission recommended, with ICU for score 4-5.

Slower dissociation from cardiac sodium channels

questions.explanation: Bupivacaine binds cardiac sodium channels with high affinity and dissociates slowly, particularly during diastole, leading to a higher risk of severe, treatment-resistant arrhythmias and cardiac arrest compared with lidocaine, which dissociates more rapidly.
questions.question: Bupivacaine carries a greater risk of cardiotoxicity compared with lidocaine at equipotent doses primarily because of which property?
Valproic acid used as a mood stabiliser carries a black box warning for which serious adverse effect, particularly in young children?
questions.explanation: Valproic acid can cause severe, sometimes fatal hepatotoxicity, with the highest risk in children under two years old, especially those on polytherapy or with underlying metabolic disorders, necessitating liver function monitoring during therapy.

questions.question: A 52-year-old Nigerian man presents with BP 155/95 mmHg confirmed on two separate clinic visits. Which stage of hypertension does this represent according to AHA classification?
questions.explanation: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as systolic BP =140 mmHg or diastolic BP =90 mmHg. A reading of 155/95 mmHg satisfies this since 155 = 140 mmHg. AHA 2017 guidelines require confirmation on at least two separate occasions, which is fulfilled here. The patient has no features of hypertensive urgency or emergency.

questions.question: A patient on phenytoin therapy has a serum level checked and it returns significantly elevated despite no dose change, after starting fluconazole. Which mechanism explains this interaction?
options: Induction of phenytoin metabolism by fluconazole
Displacement of phenytoin from plasma albumin only
Inhibition of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes metabolising phenytoin
questions.explanation: Fluconazole inhibits cytochrome P450 enzymes responsible for phenytoin metabolism, leading to elevated phenytoin levels and risk of toxicity such as nystagmus, ataxia, and diplopia. Careful monitoring or dose adjustment is required when azole antifungals are co-administered.

Approximately 25-30% of untreated DVT cases progress to pulmonary embolism, as thrombi fragment and embolize through the venous circulation to the right heart and pulmonary arteries. DVTs in the proximal leg veins (above the knee: popliteal, femoral, iliac) carry the greatest risk of embolization. This high rate of PE from untreated DVT is the primary rationale for anticoagulation therapy in DVT, which dramatically reduces the risk of PE and its potentially fatal consequences.

questions.explanation: Myxedema coma is a rare life-threatening emergency from extreme hypothyroidism characterized by: hypothermia (temperature <35C), bradycardia, profound altered consciousness or coma, hypoventilation with hypercapnia and hypoxia, hyponatremia, and hypoglycemia. It is typically precipitated by a stressor (infection, cold exposure, sedatives) in a severely hypothyroid patient. Treatment includes IV levothyroxine or liothyronine, IV hydrocortisone (coexisting adrenal insufficiency), glucose, and supportive care.

questions.question: A patient with COPD on long-term azithromycin prophylaxis for recurrent exacerbations should be monitored for which specific cardiac risk associated with this therapy?
questions.explanation: Macrolides, including azithromycin, can prolong the cardiac QT interval by blocking potassium channels involved in ventricular repolarization, increasing the risk of torsades de pointes, particularly in patients with other QT-prolonging risk factors. Baseline ECG assessment is recommended before starting chronic prophylactic macrolide therapy.

questions.explanation: Losartan is preferred in hypertensive patients with gout because it blocks URAT1, increasing renal uric acid excretion and lowering serum urate. Hydrochlorothiazide and other thiazides should be avoided because they compete with uric acid at the renal tubular secretion site, reducing uric acid excretion and worsening hyperuricemia, potentially precipitating acute gout attacks. This pharmacological understanding guides rational drug selection in comorbid conditions.

options: Prefer amlodipine; avoid spironolactone due to hyperuricemia induction
Prefer furosemide for uric acid excretion; avoid enalapril due to uric acid retention

questions.explanation: Barbiturates bind a specific allosteric site on GABA-A receptors (distinct from the benzodiazepine site) and increase the duration of Cl- channel opening. At high doses, they can directly activate GABA-A channels without GABA present. Benzodiazepines increase frequency (not duration) of channel opening. This mechanistic difference explains barbiturates' higher toxicity in overdose compared to benzodiazepines.

options: Increasing frequency of chloride channel opening without affecting duration
Increasing duration of chloride channel opening and at high doses directly activating channels
Binding the benzodiazepine allosteric site on GABA-A receptors
Blocking GABA reuptake transporters GAT-1 and GAT-3

questions.explanation: Chloral hydrate is one of the oldest synthetic hypnotics, classified as a miscellaneous CNS depressant. It acts primarily by potentiating GABA-A function. It has a rapid onset and is metabolised to trichloroethanol, which is the active form. Due to its narrow therapeutic window and abuse potential, it is now rarely used.

A hypnotic drug produces drowsiness and facilitates sleep onset and maintenance. Both classes show dose-dependent CNS depression - a hypnotic dose of a sedative produces sleep.

Has no effect on the GABA-A receptor

questions.explanation: Stimulant withdrawal is characterised primarily by a 'crash' of fatigue, dysphoria, increased appetite, and hypersomnia due to depleted monoamine stores, and is generally not medically dangerous, unlike the life-threatening withdrawal syndromes associated with sedative-hypnotics or alcohol.
questions.question: Abrupt cessation of chronic stimulant use, such as amphetamine, typically produces which withdrawal presentation, in contrast to opioid or sedative withdrawal?

Causes include pneumonia, ARDS, pulmonary edema, pulmonary fibrosis. Type 2 (hypercapnic) respiratory failure is PaO2 <8 kPa with PaCO2 >6 kPa (>45 mmHg), indicating failure of alveolar ventilation. questions.explanation: Digoxin is most beneficial in 'low output heart failure' (systolic/HFrEF). The positive inotropic effect significantly improves cardiac output and reduces the compensatory neurohormonal activation. In normal hearts, the inotropic effect is smaller because baseline contractility is already adequate. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, digoxin is contraindicated—increasing contractility can worsen dynamic outflow obstruction. The drug is the of choice for 'low output CHF' as specifically stated in clinical pharmacology references.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with dynamic left ventricular outflow obstruction

questions.explanation: Despite different primary molecular targets, all major dependence-inducing drugs ultimately increase extracellular dopamine concentration in the nucleus accumbens (the 'reward centre') via the mesolimbic pathway. Cocaine and amphetamine act directly on DAT; opioids disinhibit VTA neurons; nicotine activates nAChRs on VTA dopamine neurons; alcohol potentiates GABA and inhibits NMDA, indirectly increasing mesolimbic dopamine. This commonality is the neurobiological basis of addiction.
options: Blockade of dopamine D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway
Enhancement of GABA-A inhibitory neurotransmission in the cortex
Increase of extracellular dopamine in the nucleus accumbens via the mesolimbic pathway

Which antidepressant should be used with particular caution in a patient with a known seizure disorder due to its dose-dependent lowering of seizure threshold?
questions.explanation: Bupropion carries a well-documented dose-dependent risk of lowering seizure threshold, particularly at higher doses or with immediate-release formulations, making it relatively contraindicated in patients with epilepsy compared to SSRIs which have minimal proconvulsant activity.

questions.question: A patient with CKD is found to have persistently low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D despite adequate dietary vitamin D intake. What is the underlying mechanism?
questions.explanation: The kidney performs the final activation step of vitamin D, converting 25-hydroxyvitamin D to the active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D via 1-alpha-hydroxylase. In CKD, loss of functioning renal mass reduces this enzymatic activity, leading to functional vitamin D deficiency despite normal precursor levels, contributing to secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Adequate iron stores are essential for erythropoiesis to respond to erythropoietin-stimulating agents. Functional or absolute iron deficiency is common in CKD and blunts the haematologic response, so iron studies should be checked and repleted before or alongside initiating erythropoiesis-stimulating therapy.

questions.question: What is the pharmacological rationale for using levothyroxine (T4) rather than directly administering liothyronine (T3) for hypothyroidism treatment?
questions.explanation: Levothyroxine (synthetic T4) is preferred because T4 has a much longer half-life (~7 days versus T3's ~1 day), allowing once-daily dosing and maintaining stable thyroid hormone levels. The body's own deiodinase enzymes regulate peripheral conversion of T4 to active T3 according to tissue needs. T3 therapy produces supraphysiological T3 peaks that can cause cardiac adverse effects (tachycardia, arrhythmias) and requires multiple daily dosing.

T3 is hepatotoxic when administered orally while T4 is not
T4 bypasses the pituitary feedback mechanism, making dose adjustment easier

questions.question: Dobutamine is a commonly used inotrope in acute heart failure. What is dobutamine's mechanism of action and how does it differ from dopamine at low doses?
questions.explanation: Dobutamine is primarily a selective beta-1 adrenergic agonist (with mild beta-2 and weak alpha-1 activity). At therapeutic doses, it predominantly stimulates cardiac beta-1 receptors, increasing contractility and output with relatively modest heart rate increase. Unlike dopamine, dobutamine does not activate dopamine receptors and does not produce selective renal vasodilation at any dose. Dobutamine is the preferred inotrope in acute decompensated heart failure with low output and elevated filling pressures.

It is effective against tonic-clonic and focal seizures.

options: Hot nodules demonstrate increased radionuclide uptake indicating autonomous functioning thyroid tissue
Hot nodules have increased blood flow; cold nodules have reduced blood flow on Doppler ultrasound
Hot nodules are malignant; cold nodules are always benign cysts
Hot nodules contain more calcium (psammoma bodies); cold nodules contain more colloid
Hot nodules are seen exclusively in Hashimoto's thyroiditis; cold nodules only in Graves' disease
questions.explanation: On radionuclide thyroid scintigraphy (using 99mTc-pertechnetate or 123I), hot (hyperfunctioning) nodules demonstrate increased tracer uptake, indicating autonomously functioning thyroid tissue that traps iodine independently of TSH regulation. Hot nodules are almost never malignant but may cause hyperthyroidism. Cold (hypofunctioning) nodules demonstrate absent or reduced uptake. Approximately 10-20% of cold nodules are malignant, necessitating fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) for histological evaluation when clinically indicated.

The mesolimbic dopamine pathway projects from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens and limbic structures. It is the primary reward pathway, mediating euphoria, motivation, and reinforcement of behaviour. All major drugs of abuse ultimately increase dopamine in this pathway, driving addiction.

questions.explanation: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is an immune reaction against platelet factor 4-heparin complexes that paradoxically activates platelets, causing thrombocytopenia alongside arterial or venous thrombosis. It typically develops 5 to 10 days after exposure and requires immediate heparin discontinuation and alternative anticoagulation.

questions.question: Cardiac glycosides have a two-component chemical structure. What are the two structural portions that compose a cardiac glycoside molecule?
questions.explanation: Cardiac glycosides consist of two portions: the aglycone (genin)—a steroidal nucleus (tetracyclic cyclopentanoperhidrophenanthrene) with a lactone ring at C-17 and hydroxyl groups at C-3 and C-14—and the glycone (sugar moiety) attached at C-3 via a glycosidic bond. The pharmacological inotropic activity resides in the aglycone, while attached sugars modify solubility, cell permeability, protein binding, and pharmacokinetic behaviour.

Glucagon directly stimulates glucose absorption from the gastrointestinal tract into the portal circulation

questions.question: Glucagon is used to treat severe hypoglycemia when IV access is unavailable. What is the mechanism by which glucagon reverses hypoglycemia?
questions.explanation: Glucagon binds hepatic glucagon receptors (G-protein-coupled receptors), activating adenylyl cyclase and increasing intracellular cAMP. Elevated cAMP activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase (initiating glycogenolysis) and inhibits glycogen synthase. Glucagon also promotes gluconeogenesis. The net result is rapid release of glucose from hepatic glycogen stores, correcting hypoglycemia. Glucagon requires adequate hepatic glycogen stores to be effective and therefore fails in severely starved or alcohol-intoxicated patients.

questions.question: Which renal biopsy lesion is pathognomonic for diabetic nephropathy, distinguishing it from other glomerular diseases?
questions.explanation: Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions (nodular glomerulosclerosis) are pathognomonic for diabetic nephropathy on renal biopsy. These are ovoid or spherical accumulations of PAS-positive extracellular matrix material that develop in the periphery of the glomerular tuft. They are seen in advanced diabetic nephropathy. The more common lesion is diffuse glomerulosclerosis (diffuse increase in mesangial matrix), which is not pathognomonic as it can also occur in other glomerulopathies such as hypertensive nephrosclerosis.

They are not suitable for long-term anxiety or insomnia due to high tolerance and dependence potential.

options: Dupilumab blocks IgE preventing its binding to mast cell Fc receptors
Dupilumab blocks IL-5, reducing eosinophil maturation in the bone marrow
Dupilumab is a monoclonal antibody blocking the shared alpha subunit of the IL-4 receptor
Dupilumab blocks TSLP, preventing upstream type-2 sensitization from the epithelium
Dupilumab blocks the IL-33 receptor (ST2) preventing alarmin-driven type-2 inflammation
questions.explanation: Dupilumab is a monoclonal antibody targeting the IL-4 receptor alpha subunit (IL-4Ralpha), which is the shared signaling component for both the IL-4 receptor and the IL-13 receptor. By blocking IL-4Ralpha, dupilumab simultaneously inhibits both IL-4 signaling (driving Th2 differentiation, IgE class switching, and mucus production) and IL-13 signaling (driving airway smooth muscle contraction, goblet cell metaplasia, and fibrosis). It is effective in severe eosinophilic and type-2 asthma, atopic dermatitis, and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps.
questions.question: Dupilumab is a newer biological agent used in severe eosinophilic and type-2 asthma. What is its specific mechanism of action?
Topiramate's multiple anticonvulsant mechanisms include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Topiramate's polypharmacological mechanisms include sodium channel blockade, positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors, kainate/AMPA glutamate receptor antagonism, and carbonic anhydrase inhibition. T-type calcium channel blockade (primary mechanism of ethosuximide) is not a topiramate mechanism. Topiramate's cognitive side effects (word-finding difficulties, 'Dopamax') limit its tolerability.
options: Selective T-type calcium channel blockade as its primary mechanism

questions.question: Metformin is first-line pharmacological treatment for Type 2 diabetes. What is its primary mechanism of action?
options: Stimulates insulin secretion by closing K-ATP channels in beta cells
Inhibits intestinal alpha-glucosidase enzymes to slow carbohydrate absorption
Binds to PPAR-gamma receptors to increase glucose transporter expression
Inhibits DPP-4 enzyme to increase active incretin levels
Activates AMPK, reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis and improving peripheral insulin sensitivity
questions.explanation: Metformin primarily activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and inhibits mitochondrial respiratory chain complex I, reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis (its main action) and improving peripheral insulin sensitivity. Importantly, metformin does not stimulate insulin secretion, does not cause hypoglycemia as monotherapy, and is weight-neutral or promotes modest weight loss—major advantages over sulfonylureas and insulin.

questions.question: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) is not classified as a true NSAID because it:
options: Inhibits COX-3 enzyme selectively in peripheral tissues only
Blocks prostaglandin synthesis only in inflamed tissues
Has only slight peripheral anti-inflammatory activity, acting mainly by COX-2 inhibition in the CNS to reduce fever and pain
Potentiates endocannabinoid pathways for pain relief without COX inhibition
Irreversibly inhibits COX-1 only in the liver
questions.explanation: Paracetamol has minimal anti-inflammatory activity (distinguishing it from NSAIDs) because it is inactivated by peroxides present in inflamed tissues. It acts primarily in the CNS to reduce fever (hypothalamus) and modulate pain perception, predominantly through central COX-2 inhibition. It may also act via the endocannabinoid system (AM404 metabolite). Its analgesic-antipyretic profile without peripheral anti-inflammatory effect makes it uniquely positioned among analgesics.

questions.question: The Diel's Alder reaction using thebaine as the diene is important in opioid chemistry because it allows synthesis of which class of highly potent opioids?
questions.explanation: Thebaine undergoes a Diels-Alder [4+2] cycloaddition with dienophiles (e.g., vinyl methyl ketone for etorphine synthesis) to form a Diels-Alder adduct. Subsequent Grignard reaction introduces additional substituents, yielding oripavine derivatives. Etorphine (1000x morphine), buprenorphine (a partial agonist), and diprenorphine are all oripavine derivatives synthesised via this route from thebaine.

The most important interventions for slowing CKD progression are: aggressive blood pressure control (target <130/80 mmHg), ACE inhibitors or ARBs in proteinuric CKD (renoprotective through reducing intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria), optimal glycemic control in diabetics (target HbA1c <7%), and moderate protein restriction to reduce nitrogenous waste load and intraglomerular hyperfiltration. These interventions together significantly reduce the rate of GFR decline and delay ESRD.
questions.question: Management of CKD aims to slow progression. Which interventions are most important for slowing CKD progression in a diabetic patient with hypertension and proteinuria?
options: High protein diet to compensate for urinary protein losses
High potassium diet to counteract urinary potassium loss in CKD
High phosphate supplementation to correct hypophosphatemia in CKD
Fluid restriction in all CKD stages regardless of urine output

A direct vasodilator combined with a beta-blocker and a diuretic

questions.question: Direct vasodilators like hydralazine and minoxidil trigger reflex tachycardia and sodium retention. Which drug combination is specifically employed to counteract these compensatory adverse reactions?
questions.explanation: Direct vasodilators trigger reflex sympathetic activation (causing tachycardia and increased cardiac output) and neurohormonal sodium/water retention via RAAS/sympathetic stimulation. A beta-blocker suppresses the reflex tachycardia and increased cardiac output, while a diuretic counteracts the sodium and water retention. This triple combination (vasodilator + beta-blocker + diuretic) maximizes antihypertensive efficacy while managing the compensatory reflexes that would otherwise reduce efficacy or cause harm.

questions.question: CKD typically causes characteristic changes in kidney size detectable on imaging. What renal size finding on ultrasound specifically supports a diagnosis of CKD?
questions.explanation: CKD characteristically shows bilaterally small kidneys (<8 cm on ultrasound) due to progressive nephron loss and replacement by fibrotic tissue. As nephrons are destroyed, the parenchyma shrinks, producing bilaterally small fibrotic kidneys. This finding supports CKD diagnosis. Notable exceptions are diabetic nephropathy and HIV nephropathy (kidneys may remain normal or enlarged), and polycystic kidney disease (markedly enlarged). Bilateral small kidneys suggest irreversible damage, supporting conservative or renal replacement therapy planning.
options: Enlarged kidneys (>12 cm) with normal cortical thickness
Polycystic appearance with multiple uniformly sized cysts
Normal kidney size with focal areas of cortical thinning only
Small kidneys representing fibrotic replacement of lost nephrons

questions.explanation: Lipid solubility largely determines local anaesthetic potency because the drug must cross the lipid-rich nerve membrane to reach its intracellular binding site on the sodium channel; more lipophilic agents like bupivacaine are more potent than less lipophilic ones like procaine.
questions.question: Which factor most determines the potency of a local anaesthetic agent?
options: Degree of ionisation at physiological pH only
Molecular weight of the compound alone
Lipid solubility of the drug molecule
Complete reversal available instantly with any antidote at any time
Shorter half-life requiring more frequent dosing for safety
Exclusively renal elimination unaffected by any patient factors

questions.explanation: Low molecular weight heparins have more predictable bioavailability and a more consistent anticoagulant response than unfractionated heparin, allowing weight-based fixed dosing without routine coagulation monitoring in most patients. This predictability makes them suitable for outpatient treatment of DVT.
questions.question: A patient with DVT is started on therapeutic enoxaparin. What is the primary pharmacological advantage of low molecular weight heparin over unfractionated heparin in this outpatient setting?

questions.explanation: Naltrexone has good oral bioavailability and a considerably longer duration of action than naloxone, allowing once-daily or extended-release monthly dosing to maintain opioid blockade and support relapse prevention in opioid use disorder, unlike naloxone, which is reserved for acute reversal.
options: Much shorter duration of action than naloxone
Partial rather than full antagonist activity
Longer oral bioavailability and duration of action
Selective action only at kappa receptors
questions.question: Naltrexone differs from naloxone primarily in which pharmacokinetic characteristic, making it suitable for maintenance therapy in opioid use disorder?

questions.explanation: Amiodarone contains approximately 37% iodine by molecular weight and can cause both amiodarone-induced hypothyroidism (from the Wolff-Chaikoff effect) and amiodarone-induced hyperthyroidism (from excess iodine providing substrate for hormone synthesis, or from a direct destructive thyroiditis). Additionally, amiodarone inhibits peripheral Type 1 deiodinase, blocking T4 to T3 conversion, causing uniquely elevated T4, elevated reverse T3, and normal or low T3.
options: Amiodarone selectively stimulates TSH receptors causing hyperthyroidism only
Amiodarone can cause both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism
Amiodarone activates thyroid peroxidase, increasing thyroid hormone synthesis exclusively
Amiodarone blocks TSH secretion from the pituitary, causing secondary hypothyroidism only
Amiodarone has no effect on thyroid function regardless of dose or duration
questions.question: What is the relationship between amiodarone and thyroid dysfunction?

questions.explanation: In intubated asthmatic patients, the primary ventilatory concern is air trapping (auto-PEEP or intrinsic PEEP) from severe expiratory airflow obstruction. Air cannot exit completely before the next breath begins, causing progressive lung hyperinflation, increasing intrathoracic pressure, circulatory compromise, and risk of barotrauma. The recommended strategy is: low respiratory rate (10-14 breaths/min) allowing more time for exhalation, low tidal volume (6-8 mL/kg IBW), prolonged expiratory time (I:E ratio 1:4 or 1:5), minimal or no added PEEP, and acceptance of permissive hypercapnia to avoid the dangers of dynamic hyperinflation.
options: High respiratory rate (25-30 breaths/min) with large tidal volumes to maximally ventilate and rapidly correct acidosis
High PEEP ventilation (>15 cmH2O) to keep airways open throughout the respiratory cycle
Permissive hypercapnia strategy using low respiratory rate, low tidal volume
Prone positioning for 16 hours per day as for ARDS to improve oxygenation in severe asthma
High-frequency oscillatory ventilation as first-line mode for all intubated asthmatic patients
questions.question: Severe acute asthma can require ventilatory support. Which ventilation strategy specifically prevents air trapping and dynamic hyperinflation in ventilated asthmatic patients?

questions.explanation: KDIGO defines CKD as GFR <60 mL/min/1.73m² OR urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio >65 mg/mmol OR protein-creatinine ratio >100 mg/mmol persisting for more than 3 months. GFR <60 represents loss of more than 50% of normal kidney function. A GFR =60 with markers of kidney damage (proteinuria, hematuria, imaging abnormalities) also qualifies as CKD stages 1–2 if present =3 months. The 3-month criterion distinguishes CKD from transient AKI.
questions.question: CKD is defined by KDIGO criteria. Which GFR threshold, persisting for more than 3 months, defines the presence of CKD?

questions.explanation: Fentanyl is highly lipophilic, allowing rapid crossing of the blood-brain barrier and quick onset of analgesic effect, in contrast to the more hydrophilic morphine, which crosses more slowly, delaying peak central nervous system effect despite comparable potency once equilibrated.
questions.question: Fentanyl's rapid onset of action compared with morphine when given intravenously is primarily explained by which property?
options: Lower receptor binding affinity permitting faster diffusion
Greater plasma protein binding delaying onset
Significantly larger molecular size aiding penetration
Higher lipid solubility allowing faster blood-brain barrier penetration
Exclusively oral route enhancing systemic absorption

questions.explanation: Arteriosclerosis—thickening, loss of elasticity, and calcification of arterial walls—develops in association with aging, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus. Diabetes accelerates arterial stiffening through advanced glycation end-products, while hypertension causes mechanical stress promoting arterial wall hypertrophy. These changes reduce arterial compliance and impair blood supply particularly to the cerebrum and lower extremities, predisposing to IHD, stroke, and peripheral arterial disease.
options: Marfan syndrome and systemic lupus exclusively
Giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis alone
questions.question: Arteriosclerosis predisposes patients to IHD and its complications. Which combination of conditions is specifically associated with the development of arteriosclerosis?

questions.explanation: Short-acting benzodiazepines are cleared quickly, so plasma levels fall rapidly overnight, and the abrupt loss of GABAergic potentiation can trigger rebound anxiety or early awakening. Longer-acting agents avoid this by maintaining more stable plasma concentrations.
questions.question: A patient prescribed a short-acting benzodiazepine for sleep reports early morning rebound anxiety. Which pharmacokinetic property is most responsible?
options: Accumulation of the drug from a very long half-life
Formation of an active metabolite with longer action
Poor oral bioavailability of the parent drug
Rapid decline in plasma concentration overnight

questions.explanation: Lorazepam IV is a first-line treatment for status epilepticus due to its rapid onset, effective anticonvulsant duration (12-24 hours), and favourable pharmacokinetic profile. Diazepam IV is also used but has shorter anticonvulsant duration due to redistribution. Alprazolam is used for anxiety; temazepam and oxazepam are for insomnia, not emergency seizure management.
questions.question: Which of the following benzodiazepines is the drug of choice for status epilepticus administered intravenously?

options: Subepithelial 'spike and dome' deposits on microscopy
Crescent formation within the majority of glomeruli
Diffuse linear IgG deposition along the basement membrane
