The substantia nigra pars compacta projects to the striatum via the nigrostriatal pathway, controlling voluntary movement. Locus coeruleus is noradrenergic, and raphe nuclei are serotonergic.

questions.question: A pregnant hypertensive woman at 28 weeks gestation requires antihypertensive therapy. Which of the following is contraindicated because of fetal renal toxicity?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors like enalapril cross the placenta and impair fetal renal function, causing oligohydramnios, renal dysgenesis, and fetal skull defects when used in the second and third trimesters. Methyldopa, labetalol, nifedipine, and hydralazine are considered safer alternatives in pregnancy.

questions.question: Which antipsychotic is associated with the highest risk of agranulocytosis requiring mandatory blood count monitoring?
questions.explanation: Clozapine carries a 1-2% risk of agranulocytosis (potentially fatal reduction in white blood cells), which requires mandatory weekly to fortnightly white blood cell count monitoring. Despite this, clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Regular haematological surveillance is compulsory during clozapine therapy.

questions.question: A pregnant patient on lithium in the first trimester is counselled about which specific fetal risk?
questions.explanation: Lithium use during the first trimester carries an increased, though relatively small, risk of Ebstein's anomaly, a malformation of the tricuspid valve. This risk must be weighed against the danger of untreated bipolar relapse when counselling pregnant patients.
options: Ebstein's anomaly, a congenital cardiac malformation
Neural tube defects such as spina bifida
Craniofacial dysmorphism identical to fetal alcohol syndrome

questions.explanation: During opioid withdrawal, opioid receptor-suppressed locus coeruleus (LC) noradrenergic neurons rebound with hyperactivity, producing excessive noradrenaline release - causing tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, anxiety, and diarrhoea. Clonidine activates presynaptic alpha2 adrenoceptors (autoreceptors) on LC neurons, suppressing this noradrenergic hyperactivity and ameliorating withdrawal symptoms without producing opioid-like euphoria or dependence.
questions.question: Clonidine (an alpha-2 agonist) is used in opioid withdrawal management because it:
options: Acts as a partial opioid receptor agonist reducing withdrawal severity
Reduces noradrenergic hyperactivity from the locus coeruleus that mediates physical withdrawal symptoms
Blocks dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens preventing relapse
Potentiates endogenous opioid peptide release reducing craving
Inhibits cortisol release preventing HPA axis hyperactivity in withdrawal

questions.explanation: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis results from a combined type III and type IV immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to repeatedly inhaled organic antigens, such as those found in mouldy hay, causing episodic inflammatory lung injury that classically improves with removal from the causative exposure.
questions.question: A patient with occupational exposure to mouldy hay develops recurrent episodes of fever, cough, and dyspnoea occurring hours after exposure, with imaging showing diffuse infiltrates that resolve with avoidance. What is the underlying immune mechanism?
options: Immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to inhaled organic antigens
Direct fungal invasion and destruction of lung parenchyma
Chemical irritant injury from inhaled ammonia in decomposing hay
Bacterial superinfection following inhalation of contaminated hay

questions.question: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors such as acarbose work in the gastrointestinal tract. What is their mechanism and a major adverse effect?
questions.explanation: Acarbose and miglitol competitively inhibit alpha-glucosidase enzymes (sucrase, maltase, glucoamylase) on the brush border of the small intestinal enterocytes, delaying and reducing the postprandial glucose peak. The undigested carbohydrates pass to the colon where fermentation by colonic bacteria produces gas, causing the characteristic adverse effects of flatulence, bloating, and diarrhea.
options: They inhibit pancreatic amylase exclusively; major adverse effect is hepatitis
They stimulate GLP-1 secretion from intestinal L-cells; major adverse effect is acute pancreatitis
They competitively inhibit intestinal alpha-glucosidase enzymes, slowing digestion and absorption of dietary
They block intestinal SGLT1 glucose transporter; major adverse effect is osmotic diarrhea
They reduce gastric acid secretion to slow carbohydrate exposure; major adverse effect is hypergastrinemia

questions.question: Psychological dependence differs from physical dependence in that it involves:
questions.explanation: Psychological dependence is characterised by an emotional or mental need for a drug - manifesting as intense craving, compulsive drug-seeking, and inability to function without the drug - without necessarily involving physical withdrawal syndrome. Stimulants (cocaine, amphetamine) classically produce strong psychological dependence with less pronounced physical withdrawal. The memory of drug-induced reward states (positive reinforcement) drives craving.
options: Physiological hyperarousal requiring hospitalisation on drug cessation
The presence of a measurable biochemical withdrawal marker in blood
Emotional distress, craving, and compulsive drug-seeking without necessarily a physical withdrawal syndrome
Exclusively genetic predisposition without any environmental component
Physical tolerance requiring dose escalation to avoid withdrawal
Autoimmune lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of thyroid follicular cells, mediated by
Stimulating autoantibodies against TSH receptors causing hyperthyroidism
Autoantibodies against the sodium-iodide symporter blocking iodine uptake
Complement-mediated destruction of thyroid C-cells producing autoimmune hypothyroidism
IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction against thyroid follicle epithelial cells
questions.question: What is the autoimmune mechanism underlying Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
questions.explanation: Hashimoto's thyroiditis involves T-lymphocyte (CD8+ cytotoxic T-cells and CD4+ helper T-cells) infiltration of the thyroid gland, leading to follicular cell apoptosis and destruction. Anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies (present in >95% of patients) and anti-thyroglobulin (anti-Tg) antibodies serve as markers of the autoimmune process. Progressive destruction leads to goiter initially, followed by thyroid atrophy and hypothyroidism.

options: Isolated systolic hypertension in the elderly
Hypertension with peripheral edema and Raynaud's phenomenon
Hypertension in pregnancy requiring safe maternal drug
Resistant hypertension requiring maximal peripheral vasodilation
questions.question: Verapamil and nifedipine are both calcium channel blockers used for hypertension. In which specific clinical situation is verapamil clearly preferred over nifedipine?
questions.explanation: Non-dihydropyridine CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem) have significant negative chronotropic and dromotropic effects on cardiac conduction, slowing AV nodal conduction. This makes them useful for rate control in supraventricular tachyarrhythmias (SVT, atrial fibrillation) alongside their antihypertensive effect. Dihydropyridines like nifedipine primarily act on vascular smooth muscle with minimal cardiac conduction effects and may cause reflex tachycardia, making them less appropriate for SVT management.

In a conscious patient with mild-to-moderate hypoglycemia, oral fast-acting carbohydrate is the first-line treatment, followed by a complex carbohydrate snack to prevent recurrence. Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia can be prolonged and recurrent, so such patients require observation even after initial recovery.
options: Withholding all treatment until symptoms resolve spontaneously
Administration of an additional sulfonylurea dose to stabilize levels
Oral fast-acting carbohydrate such as glucose tablets or juice
Immediate hospital admission for intravenous dextrose only
Intramuscular glucagon injection as the first-line treatment
questions.question: A patient on glibenclamide skips a meal after taking the morning dose and develops sweating, tremor, and confusion. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment for this conscious patient?
A patient with acute MI is given streptokinase. What is the precise mechanism of action of thrombolytic agents such as streptokinase and alteplase in dissolving coronary thrombi?
questions.explanation: Thrombolytics (fibrinolytics) activate plasminogen to plasmin, the endogenous enzyme responsible for fibrinolysis. Plasmin breaks down the fibrin mesh holding the thrombus together, dissolving the clot and restoring coronary blood flow. Streptokinase forms a complex with plasminogen to activate it, while alteplase (tPA) directly activates fibrin-bound plasminogen with greater clot selectivity and theoretically fewer systemic bleeding complications.
options: They activate the coagulation cascade to form a new protective fibrin cap over the thrombus
They block glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors to prevent platelet aggregation
They convert plasminogen to plasmin, which degrades the fibrin mesh and dissolves the coronary thrombus
They inhibit vitamin K-dependent clotting factors to prevent thrombus extension
They directly lyse atheromatous plaques using proteolytic enzymes

questions.explanation: Vigabatrin carries a well-documented risk of permanent concentric visual field constriction, believed related to retinal GABA accumulation, requiring regular ophthalmological monitoring and generally restricting its use to refractory epilepsy such as infantile spasms.
options: Progressive and potentially permanent visual field constriction
questions.question: Vigabatrin's irreversible inhibition of GABA transaminase increases synaptic GABA levels but is limited in use because of which serious adverse effect?
A patient using cocaine develops chest pain and is found to have myocardial infarction despite having no significant coronary atherosclerosis. Which mechanism best explains this presentation?
questions.explanation: Cocaine blocks norepinephrine reuptake, causing excessive sympathetic stimulation that can provoke coronary artery vasospasm, increased myocardial oxygen demand, and thrombosis, precipitating myocardial infarction even in patients without significant underlying atherosclerotic disease.
options: Direct toxic destruction of cardiac myocytes only
Embolic occlusion from cocaine-induced clot formation in the aorta
Coronary vasospasm from excessive sympathetic stimulation
Direct viral myocarditis triggered by cocaine use

questions.question: What is the mechanism by which radioiodine (131I) therapy ablates the hyperactive thyroid gland?
questions.explanation: Radioiodine (131I) is administered orally and actively taken up into thyroid follicular cells via the sodium-iodide symporter. Within the cells, 131I emits beta radiation that causes direct DNA damage and chromosomal breaks, resulting in progressive thyroid cell destruction over weeks to months. The major long-term consequence is hypothyroidism, which develops in most patients and requires lifelong levothyroxine replacement.
options: 131I competitively inhibits thyroid peroxidase, reducing organification of normal iodide
131I stimulates an immune response against thyroid cells causing autoimmune ablation
131I blocks T4 synthesis by competing with T4 for thyroglobulin binding sites
131I causes hyperviscosity of thyroid colloid, preventing thyroid hormone release
131I is taken up by the sodium-iodide symporter into thyroid follicular cells

questions.question: Ester-type local anaesthetics such as procaine are more likely than amide types to cause allergic reactions because they are metabolised to which compound?
questions.explanation: Ester local anaesthetics are hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase to para-aminobenzoic acid, a known allergen, accounting for their higher allergic potential compared with amide anaesthetics, which are metabolised hepatically and rarely provoke true allergic reactions.

options: Acute pancreatitis presenting atypically with oedema
A normal, expected, and clinically insignificant finding
An unrelated allergic reaction requiring drug discontinuation
Fluid retention associated with thiazolidinedione therapy
questions.explanation: Thiazolidinediones cause sodium and fluid retention through effects on renal tubular sodium channels, which can precipitate or worsen peripheral oedema and heart failure. This adverse effect is a specific caution in patients with pre-existing heart failure, in whom TZDs are generally avoided.
questions.question: A patient with type 2 diabetes started on pioglitazone develops new bilateral ankle swelling and mild dyspnoea on exertion. What is the most likely explanation?
Obesity is a major controllable risk factor for IHD. Which mechanism most directly and comprehensively links obesity to increased IHD risk?
questions.explanation: Obesity promotes cardiovascular risk through multiple interrelated mechanisms: insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome produce elevated triglycerides, low HDL, and small dense LDL; hypertension results from sodium retention, sympathetic activation, and RAAS stimulation; systemic inflammation from adipose-derived cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6) accelerates endothelial dysfunction and atherogenesis; and obstructive sleep apnea further increases cardiovascular risk. This multifactorial pathophysiology explains obesity's potency as a cardiovascular risk factor.
options: Obesity directly compresses cardiac myocytes through mechanical pressure from surrounding adipose tissue
Obesity promotes insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hypertension
Obesity exclusively increases IHD risk through elevated LDL cholesterol production alone
Which mechanism most directly and comprehensively links obesity to increased IHD risk?
Obesity causes mechanical valvular damage from cardiac compression by surrounding adipose tissue

questions.question: In Nigeria, approximately 160,000 people suffer a stroke each year. Among survivors, approximately what proportion can return to their previous level of activity without limitation?
questions.explanation: Among stroke survivors, approximately 10% can return to their previous level of activity without limitation. About 50% regain enough function to return home with limited assistance, and approximately 40% remain institutionalized or require significant ongoing care. This poor functional outcome underscores the critical importance of primary prevention (controlling hypertension, managing risk factors) and early effective acute stroke treatment to minimize brain damage and disability.

Clopidogrel is a thienopyridine prodrug requiring activation by hepatic CYP2C19. The active metabolite irreversibly blocks the P2Y12 ADP receptor on platelets, preventing ADP-induced activation and aggregation for the platelet's lifespan. CYP2C19 poor metabolizers may have reduced activation and diminished antiplatelet effect, which is clinically relevant in PCI patients where inadequate platelet inhibition increases stent thrombosis risk. Ticagrelor is a direct-acting P2Y12 inhibitor not requiring metabolic activation.

questions.question: Nalorphine (N-allyl morphine) is a mixed agonist-antagonist not used clinically as an agonist because:
questions.explanation: Nalorphine (N-allyl morphine) was the first opioid antagonist/partial agonist discovered. As a kappa opioid agonist, it produces analgesia but also severe dysphoria, anxiety, and psychotomimetic effects (hallucinations) that make it clinically unacceptable as an analgesic. It can compete with stronger mu agonists and precipitate withdrawal in dependent patients. It was superseded by pure antagonists (naloxone) and better-tolerated partial agonists.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with hypertension and gout is started on an antihypertensive that subsequently precipitates an acute gouty attack. Which drug class most likely caused this?
questions.explanation: Thiazide diuretics reduce renal urate excretion by competing for the same organic anion transporter, raising serum uric acid. This can precipitate acute gouty arthritis in predisposed patients. Losartan is unique among ARBs in having mild uricosuric properties instead.

questions.question: A patient has predominantly very high triglycerides as the main lipid abnormality. Which class of lipid-lowering drug is most effective for markedly elevated triglycerides?
questions.explanation: Fibrates (fenofibrate, gemfibrozil) are most effective for reducing elevated triglycerides. They activate PPAR-alpha nuclear receptors, increasing lipoprotein lipase activity (increasing triglyceride clearance from VLDL and chylomicrons) and reducing hepatic VLDL synthesis. Fibrates also modestly raise HDL. While statins primarily target LDL reduction, fibrates primarily target hypertriglyceridemia and are the drug of choice when this is the predominant lipid disorder.

Non-selective NSAIDs inhibit COX-1, which normally produces prostaglandins that maintain gastric mucosal blood flow, mucus, and bicarbonate secretion; loss of this protection predisposes to erosions and peptic ulceration, a risk reduced but not eliminated by COX-2 selective agents.

Increased gastric mucus production causing ulceration

Enhanced gastric blood flow damaging the mucosa

Direct toxic damage to bronchial epithelium

questions.question: An asthmatic patient develops bronchospasm after taking aspirin. Which mechanism best explains this reaction, known as aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease?

To directly dissolve the existing thrombus through fibrinolytic activation
To immediately restore blood flow through the thrombosed vessel
To prevent platelet aggregation at the existing thrombus surface
To reduce vascular wall inflammation surrounding the thrombus
questions.explanation: Anticoagulants do not directly dissolve existing clots—that is the role of thrombolytics. Anticoagulation prevents the existing thrombus from propagating and prevents new thrombus formation, allowing the body's own fibrinolytic system to gradually dissolve the existing clot over days to weeks. This is sufficient for most DVT and PE cases. Systemic thrombolysis is reserved for life-threatening massive PE with haemodynamic compromise where the time needed for natural fibrinolysis is too long.
questions.question: Anticoagulation is the cornerstone of DVT treatment. What is the primary therapeutic goal of anticoagulation in managing established DVT?

Stimulates platelet disaggregation through ADP receptor blockade
Inhibits platelet COX-1 irreversibly reducing thromboxane A2 without substantially affecting endothelial prostacyclin

This pharmacokinetic selectivity - platelets are exposed to higher aspirin concentrations in the portal circulation before aspirin is hydrolysed systemically - explains low-dose aspirin's antiplatelet benefit.

questions.explanation: Minoxidil causes hypertrichosis—diffuse excessive growth of fine hair over the body. While cosmetically distressing for hypertensive patients, this side effect has been exploited therapeutically as a topical preparation for male-pattern baldness (androgenetic alopecia). Oral minoxidil also causes reflex tachycardia and sodium-water retention, requiring co-administration of a beta-blocker and diuretic to counteract these compensatory effects.

Suppression of bone marrow platelet production

Propranolol has the additional benefit of inhibiting peripheral deiodinase-1, reducing T4 conversion to active T3.

Beta-blockers reduce thyroid vascularity by alpha-1 receptor blockade, reducing surgical risk
Beta-blockers block TSH receptors, reducing thyroid stimulation in Graves' disease
Beta-blockers directly reduce iodine organification, reducing thyroid hormone synthesis
Beta-blockers rapidly control adrenergic symptoms of hyperthyroidism while awaiting slower-onset antithyroid drug effects

questions.question: Which statement is most accurate regarding G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) in CNS pharmacology?
questions.explanation: GPCRs are seven-transmembrane domain receptors coupled to G-proteins that activate intracellular signalling cascades (cAMP, IP3/DAG, etc.), producing slower but longer-lasting cellular responses than ionotropic receptors. They are targeted by many CNS drugs including antipsychotics, antidepressants, opioids, and anxiolytics.

Minimal change disease results from T-lymphocyte-mediated production of a circulating permeability factor (possibly soluble urokinase-type plasminogen activator receptor) that damages podocyte foot processes, increasing glomerular protein permeability. Corticosteroids suppress this T-cell-mediated immune process, reducing permeability factor production. The result is restoration of normal podocyte morphology and resolution of massive proteinuria. Minimal change disease has an excellent response rate to corticosteroids, particularly in children.
questions.question: Corticosteroids are first-line treatment in minimal change disease causing nephrotic syndrome. What is the pharmacological basis for using corticosteroids in this condition?

Corticosteroids stimulate hepatic albumin synthesis to replace urinary protein losses

questions.question: A patient with proteinuric CKD is started on an ACE inhibitor even though blood pressure is only mildly elevated. What is the specific renoprotective rationale beyond blood pressure control?
options: Increased glomerular filtration rate directly repairs damaged nephrons
Suppression of erythropoietin reduces workload on damaged nephrons
Direct antibacterial activity reduces risk of recurrent pyelonephritis
Enhanced renal blood flow reverses established glomerular scarring
Reduced intraglomerular pressure lowers proteinuria and slows CKD progression
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors preferentially dilate the efferent arteriole, reducing intraglomerular pressure and hyperfiltration. This proteinuria-lowering, renoprotective effect occurs independent of systemic blood pressure reduction and is why ACE inhibitors and ARBs are first-line agents in proteinuric CKD even with only mild hypertension.

Amitriptyline's analgesic properties (used for neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, migraine prevention) arise from spinal noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake inhibition, augmenting the descending pain inhibitory pathway. At the spinal cord level, increased NA and 5-HT activate inhibitory interneurons that suppress nociceptive transmission. This mechanism is separate from its antidepressant effect and occurs at lower doses.
options: Blocks spinal noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake, enhancing descending pain inhibition
Is a prodrug converted to an opioid receptor agonist
Directly inhibits prostaglandin synthesis via COX inhibition

questions.explanation: Diabetic nephropathy (diabetic kidney disease) and systemic hypertension are the two most common causes of CKD worldwide, together accounting for the majority of ESRD cases. Diabetes damages the glomerular filtration barrier through AGEs and hemodynamic changes; hypertension causes hypertensive nephrosclerosis through pressure-mediated glomerular injury. In Nigeria specifically, hypertension ranks first as a cause of CKD, with diabetes as the third most common cause of ESRD.

Absorbed tyramine displaces noradrenaline from sympathetic nerve terminals, causing massive NA release, severe hypertension, hyperpyrexia, and potentially fatal intracranial haemorrhage - the 'cheese reaction'. Patients must avoid tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, red wine, cured meats).

Which fasting plasma glucose value meets the diagnostic threshold for diabetes mellitus on two separate occasions or once with symptoms?
questions.explanation: The WHO and ADA diagnostic criterion for diabetes mellitus using fasting plasma glucose is FPG >= 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL), confirmed on two separate occasions. If classic symptoms are present, a single FPG >= 7.0 mmol/L suffices. FPG 5.6-6.9 mmol/L is classified as impaired fasting glucose (prediabetes).

questions.question: In acute ischemic stroke management, IV alteplase (tPA) is a time-sensitive intervention. What is the critical time window for administering IV tPA after stroke symptom onset?
options: Within 6 hours exclusively via intra-arterial route
questions.explanation: IV alteplase must be administered within 3–4.5 hours of stroke symptom onset. After this window, the risk of hemorrhagic transformation of infarcted brain tissue exceeds the benefit of reperfusion. The 'time is brain' principle holds that approximately 1.9 million neurons die per minute of stroke. Haemorrhagic stroke must first be excluded by CT imaging. Eligibility criteria include blood pressure <185/110 mmHg and no contraindications to thrombolysis.

questions.question: Which pharmacokinetic property of diazepam explains its rapid initial CNS effect but short duration of single-dose action?
options: Low lipid solubility resulting in slow BBB penetration
High water solubility and renal elimination
Extensive first-pass metabolism to inactive compounds
High lipid solubility causing rapid brain entry followed by redistribution to fat
questions.explanation: Diazepam is highly lipid-soluble, crossing the blood-brain barrier rapidly and producing a quick onset of action. However, following peak brain concentration, it redistributes into adipose tissue and muscle, reducing brain levels and shortening the duration of a single dose despite its very long plasma half-life (24-72 hours), which matters more with repeated dosing.

Insulin glargine is a long-acting insulin analogue with duration of action of approximately 20-24 hours, providing a relatively peakless, stable basal insulin level, ideal for basal therapy with once-daily injection. Insulin lispro, aspart, and glulisine are rapid-acting analogues for meal-time coverage. Regular insulin has intermediate onset and duration. NPH insulin has a peak effect, making hypoglycemia more likely compared to glargine.

questions.explanation: Acetylcholine (ACh) in the CNS plays critical roles in arousal, attention, memory formation, and cognitive function via muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. The basal forebrain cholinergic system projecting to the hippocampus and cortex is severely degenerated in Alzheimer's disease. ACh is distinct from the dopaminergic reward system.

questions.question: Nitroglycerin is used to acutely relieve angina. What is the primary pharmacodynamic mechanism by which nitroglycerin reduces myocardial oxygen demand?
questions.explanation: Nitroglycerin is metabolized to nitric oxide (NO) in vascular smooth muscle. NO activates guanylyl cyclase, increasing cGMP and causing smooth muscle relaxation. At therapeutic doses, the predominant effect is venodilation, reducing venous return (preload), decreasing end-diastolic volume and ventricular wall tension, thereby reducing myocardial oxygen demand. Coronary artery dilation also improves blood supply and is particularly relevant in Prinzmetal angina from vasospasm.
options: Directly blocking calcium entry into coronary artery smooth muscle cells
Converting to nitric oxide (NO) activating guanylyl cyclase, causing venodilation and reducing cardiac preload
Blocking beta-1 receptors in the heart to reduce myocardial contractility
Inhibiting thromboxane A2 synthesis to prevent platelet aggregation in coronary arteries
Increasing erythropoietin production to improve oxygen delivery to myocardium

questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines have largely replaced barbiturates in clinical practice because they have a much wider therapeutic index - a patient taking many times the therapeutic dose of a benzodiazepine alone rarely dies, whereas barbiturate overdose is frequently fatal due to direct GABA-A activation and profound respiratory depression. questions.question: Chronic opioid use commonly causes constipation with little tolerance developing to this effect, in contrast to respiratory depression and euphoria. Which mechanism explains this persistent effect?
questions.explanation: Opioid receptors are densely expressed in the enteric nervous system, and their sustained activation reduces peristalsis and increases sphincter tone; unlike CNS effects, tolerance to this peripheral action develops slowly or minimally, making constipation a persistent problem requiring co-prescribed laxatives.

questions.question: What is the mechanism of action of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) in reducing sputum viscosity?
questions.explanation: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is a thiol compound that provides free sulfhydryl (SH) groups. Mucus viscosity is largely determined by disulfide (S-S) bonds that cross-link mucin glycoprotein chains. NAC's free thiol groups break these disulfide bonds through a thiol-disulfide exchange reaction, reducing the molecular weight and degree of cross-linking of mucin polymers, thereby decreasing mucus viscosity (mucolytic effect). NAC also replenishes intracellular glutathione.

questions.explanation: Daily low-dose azithromycin (a macrolide) has been shown in randomized trials (ALBERT trial) to reduce COPD exacerbations when used as prophylaxis in high-risk patients. questions.explanation: Varenicline (Champix/Chantix) is the most effective single pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation, achieving abstinence rates approximately twice those of nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) and 1.5 times those of bupropion in clinical trials. It works as a partial agonist at alpha4-beta2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, reducing nicotine cravings and withdrawal symptoms (partial agonism) while blocking the rewarding effects of smoking (competitive antagonism with nicotine). Combination NRT (patch plus short-acting) is also highly effective. Smoking cessation is the only intervention proven to slow FEV1 decline in COPD.

Inhaled beta-2 agonists to reduce the pleasure response to nicotine in the lung

questions.question: Furosemide is a loop diuretic with a specific nephron site of action that differs from thiazide diuretics. At which exact nephron segment does furosemide exert its primary pharmacological effect?
options: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
questions.explanation: Furosemide inhibits the Na?/K?/2Cl? co-transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle (TALH), where 25–30% of filtered sodium is normally reabsorbed. Blocking this transporter prevents creation of the medullary osmotic gradient needed for water reabsorption, producing large volumes of dilute urine. This distinguishes loop diuretics from thiazides (early DCT) and potassium-sparing diuretics (collecting duct).

questions.question: A patient on lithium therapy presents with coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, and vomiting after starting a thiazide diuretic. Which mechanism explains this presentation?
options: Displacement of lithium from plasma proteins
Direct hepatotoxic interaction between the two drugs
Reduced renal lithium clearance causing toxic accumulation
questions.explanation: Thiazide diuretics cause sodium depletion, prompting increased proximal tubular reabsorption of sodium along with lithium, reducing its renal clearance and precipitating toxicity. This is a critical interaction requiring lithium level monitoring whenever diuretics are co-prescribed.

questions.question: A patient on furosemide develops muscle cramps, weakness, and arrhythmias with severe hypokalemia. Which specific electrolyte replacement should be administered to correct this diuretic-induced abnormality?
questions.explanation: Loop diuretics cause significant urinary potassium loss (kaliuresis). Potassium chloride (oral for mild, IV for severe hypokalemia) is required to correct the deficit. Severe hypokalemia risks life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias and muscle paralysis. Importantly, hypomagnesemia often coexists with hypokalemia and impairs potassium repletion; magnesium must also be corrected. The KCl form is preferred because loop diuretics also cause metabolic alkalosis (hypochloremia), and chloride replacement helps correct this.
options: Magnesium sulfate alone without addressing potassium
Calcium gluconate infusion as first-line treatment
Oral or IV potassium chloride supplementation based on severity
Full antagonist at dopamine D2 receptors only
Pure agonist at dopamine D2 receptors
Partial agonist at dopamine D2 receptors

questions.question: A patient with hypertension and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is prescribed carvedilol. What property distinguishes carvedilol from metoprolol in this setting?

questions.question: Withdrawal syndrome from CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, barbiturates, alcohol) is life-threatening because cessation causes:
questions.explanation: Chronic CNS depressant (alcohol, benzodiazepine, barbiturate) use leads to compensatory upregulation of NMDA glutamate receptors and downregulation of GABA-A receptors. Upon abrupt cessation, the brain becomes hyperexcitable - unopposed by GABA and hyperactivated by NMDA - producing tremor, anxiety, autonomic instability, psychosis (delirium tremens), and potentially fatal generalised seizures. Management requires substitution with a long-acting benzodiazepine and gradual tapering.

questions.question: Mepolizumab is a biological agent used in severe eosinophilic asthma. What is its mechanism of action and what biomarker guides its use?
options: Mepolizumab blocks IgE; guided by total serum IgE level
Mepolizumab blocks the IL-4 receptor (IL-4Ralpha), inhibiting both IL-4 and IL-13 signaling
Mepolizumab is a monoclonal antibody against interleukin-5, blocking eosinophil maturation and survival
Mepolizumab blocks TNF-alpha, reducing neutrophilic inflammation; guided by neutrophil count
Mepolizumab blocks thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP) preventing Th2 sensitization
questions.explanation: Mepolizumab is a monoclonal antibody that specifically targets interleukin-5 (IL-5), the key cytokine responsible for eosinophil maturation in the bone marrow, recruitment to the lungs, and survival in the airway. By blocking IL-5, mepolizumab significantly reduces blood and tissue eosinophils. Its use is guided by blood eosinophil count (>=300 cells/uL); indicated for severe eosinophilic asthma not controlled by high-dose ICS/LABA

options: FEV1/FVC ratio >0.80 with reduced FVC suggesting restrictive lung disease
FEV1 <80% predicted with normal FEV1/FVC ratio
Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio <0.70, confirming persistent airflow limitation
FVC <70% predicted with elevated FEV1/FVC ratio
PEFR <50% predicted with normal spirometry at rest
questions.question: What spirometric criterion defines COPD by post-bronchodilator spirometry?
questions.explanation: COPD is defined spirometrically by a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio of less than 0.70 (70%), confirming persistent airflow limitation not fully reversible, as per GOLD guidelines. This criterion distinguishes COPD from asthma (where obstruction is largely reversible). The severity of COPD is then classified by FEV1 percent predicted (GOLD 1: >=80%, GOLD 2: 50-79%, GOLD 3: 30-49%, GOLD 4: <30%).

questions.question: Hydrochlorothiazide is prescribed for a hypertensive patient. At which nephron segment does hydrochlorothiazide inhibit sodium reabsorption?
questions.explanation: Thiazide diuretics inhibit the Na?/Cl? co-transporter in the early distal convoluted tubule (DCT), responsible for approximately 3–5% of sodium reabsorption. This distinguishes thiazides from loop diuretics (TALH) and potassium-sparing agents (collecting duct). The DCT is also where thiazides paradoxically enhance calcium reabsorption, making them useful in patients with hypercalciuria and calcium oxalate kidney stones.

questions.question: Ketamine is particularly useful as an induction agent in haemodynamically unstable trauma patients because, unlike most anaesthetics, it:
questions.explanation: Ketamine indirectly stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, increasing heart rate and blood pressure, unlike propofol or thiopental which cause cardiovascular depression, making it advantageous in hypovolaemic or haemodynamically unstable patients requiring induction.

Depresses respiratory drive more than other agents
Stimulates sympathetic outflow, maintaining blood pressure and heart rate
Produces complete loss of airway reflexes immediately

questions.question:
A) Describe the thermal and non-thermal physiological effects of therapeutic ultrasound.
B) State the therapeutic effects/indications of ultrasound.
C) State the contraindications and dangers of ultrasound.
questions.answerText:
A) Thermal effects: ultrasound waves absorbed by tissue are converted into heat; the amount of heat depends on tissue absorption (protein absorbs more), the number of passes of the treatment head, and circulation efficiency; continuous ultrasound produces heat directly proportional to intensity and duration, while pulsed ultrasound produces less heat, with a 1:4 ratio producing less heat than 1:1.
A) Non-thermal effects: cavitation is the oscillatory activity of compressible bodies (gas/vapour voids); stable cavitation causes microstreaming (unidirectional fluid movement influencing membrane permeability), while unstable/transient cavitation involves rapid bubble collapse causing a local rise in temperature and is potentially dangerous.
A) The mechanical effect (micro-massage) arises from compression and rarefaction of cells affecting tissue fluid movement in interstitial spaces, helping reduce oedema, and, combined with the thermal effect, makes stretching of scars and adhesions easier.
A) Biological effect on repair: in the inflammatory stage, ultrasound increases lysosome membrane fragility, enhancing enzyme release to clear debris; in the proliferative stage, Ca++ ions are driven into fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, increasing mobility and collagen production; in remodelling, ultrasound increases the tensile strength of the scar by affecting fibre direction, strength and elasticity.
B) Ultrasound is used after soft tissue injuries as its mechanical effects help remove traumatic exudates and reduce the danger of adhesion formation.
B) It makes scar tissue more pliable, allowing more effective stretching of contracted scars, and its mechanical effects help treat chronic indurated oedema.
B) Ultrasound is found effective in promoting the healing of varicose ulcers and pressure sores, and has been investigated for its effect on blood flow.
C) Vascular conditions such as thrombophlebitis are contraindicated because insonation may break off emboli; acute sepsis should be treated cautiously due to the danger of spreading infection.
C) Ultrasound is not applied to a radiated area within six months of radiotherapy, and tumours are not insonated because they may be stimulated or metastasize.
C) A pregnant uterus is not treated, so the back and abdomen should not be treated during pregnancy; other contraindications include cardiac disease and haemorrhage.
C) Further contraindications: severely ischaemic tissue, the fluid-filled eye and gonads (testes/ovary), metal implants, plastics used in replacement surgery, and anaesthetic areas.
C) Dangers: burns from a stationary continuous beam causing excess heat accumulation; unstable cavitation; overdose causing exacerbation of symptoms; and damage to the equipment/crystal if the head is switched on while not in contact with a transmitting medium.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the components of the pool plant and its purpose.
A(ii) Describe the disinfectants used in hydrotherapy pools.
B) Explain the clinical basis for why sodium hypochlorite is the most commonly used chlorine donor.
C) Distinguish between the conventional method and the Bad Ragaz method of pool exercise.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The pool plant serves the purpose of disinfecting the pool regularly, maintaining the pool at a constant temperature, filtering the water regularly to control dirt, and recycling the pool water regularly.
A(i) Components of the pool plant include the circulating pump, filter (sand filter, diatomaceous filter, disposable filter), calorifiers (heaters), and chlorine dosing pump.
A(ii) Chlorine is the main disinfectant, introduced directly as gaseous chlorine or via chlorine donors such as sodium hypochlorite, calcium hypochlorite and chloro-iso-cyanurate; bromine has also been used but is linked with eczematous dermatoses; ozone is a powerful but expensive disinfectant.
A(ii) Sodium hypochlorite (household/laundry bleach, trade name chloros/bridos) is about 15% available chlorine; calcium hypochlorite has about 65% available chlorine and is 95% soluble; chloro-iso-cyanurate is 100% soluble and introduced as hand chlorination.
A(ii) The pool area is ventilated by extracting, plenum or balanced ventilating systems, or by air conditioning which automatically adjusts temperature and humidity; pool size is usually 15m² or 20m² with a depth of 1.0-1.2m, a traditionally sloping floor or steps, and mechanical, hydraulic or electrical hoists.
B) Sodium hypochlorite is commonly used because it is readily available as household/laundry bleach and provides an adequate available chlorine concentration for pool disinfection.
B) By contrast, calcium hypochlorite offers a higher percentage of available chlorine but different solubility, and chloro-iso-cyanurate offers full solubility with a hand-chlorination method, giving therapists a choice depending on the required disinfection method.
B) Chlorine and pH levels must be tested two or three times a day and bacteriological testing performed regularly, regardless of which chlorine donor is chosen, to ensure the disinfection method remains effective.
C) The course content lists the conventional method and the Bad Ragaz method as the two methods of exercise in therapeutic pools.
C) In the Bad Ragaz Ring Method, the patient floats horizontally in the water supported by rings or floats around the neck, arms, pelvis and knees, with the extremities used as levers to activate trunk muscles, the physiotherapist supporting the patient in the pool, and buoyancy used purely as support (not assisting or resisting); muscle activity can be isometric, isotonic or isokinetic, based on PNF principles.
C) The conventional method, as distinguished from Bad Ragaz in the course content, is the standard approach to pool exercise not built on the PNF-based ring-supported floating technique.
C) Course content also lists disinfection among the safety measures needed alongside whichever exercise method (conventional or Bad Ragaz) is used, since both methods are performed in the same treated pool water.

A(i) The Halliwick method was developed by James McMillan in 1950; it encourages active participation without floatation devices, using a sequential 10-point programme originally developed for teaching children with disabilities to swim.
A(i) The 10-point programme includes mental adjustment, disengagement, transversal rotation control, sagittal rotation control, longitudinal rotation control, combined rotation control, upthrust and mental inversion, balance in stillness, turbulent gliding, and simple progression/basic swimming movement.
A(i) Indications for Halliwick include balance disorder, scoliosis, CVA and cerebral palsy.
A(ii) Watsu was developed by Harold Dull in 1980 as the first form of aquatic body work; it is a one-on-one technique in which the therapist gently moves, stretches and massages the patient in chest-deep warm water.
A(ii) Benefits of Watsu include deep relaxation, reduced pain/stress/fatigue and increased ROM; indications include fibromyalgia and neurological impairment.
A(ii) The Bad Ragaz Ring Method is an aquatic therapy based on the PNF technique, in which therapist-assisted strengthening and mobilising exercises are performed with the patient lying horizontally supported by rings or floats around the neck, arms, pelvis and legs; indications include orthopaedic and rheumatology conditions, soft tissue injuries and neurological conditions.
B) The Bad Ragaz Ring Method is designed as a water-based strengthening and mobilising resistive exercise model using PNF patterns and therapist-assisted resistance, making it the more direct choice for muscle strengthening.
B) Watsu, by contrast, is characterised as a form of deep relaxation and passive aquatic therapy, aimed at relaxation, pain/stress/fatigue reduction and ROM rather than resisted strengthening.
C) Ai Chi is a form of aquatic exercise for relaxation, fitness and physical rehabilitation that combines deep breathing and slow broad movement while standing in chest-deep water; indications include osteoporosis and balance deficits.
C) The Burdenko method, developed by Dr Igor Burdenko, is designed to improve balance, coordination, flexibility, speed and strength, and is a complete system combining both water and land exercises.
C) Water Pilates, created by Joseph Pilates, adapts pilates exercises for the pool to improve strength, flexibility and ROM, and encourages musculoskeletal alignment and abdominal strengthening.
C) Back Hab Aquatic therapy is designed for individuals with back pain, hamstring injuries or to increase abdominal strength, based on walking programmes in the pool.

questions.answerText:
(i) Ultrasound is indicated for the soft tissue lesion, but the water bath method is used because direct contact is not possible due to the irregular shape of the part and tenderness.
(ii) The water bath method of ultrasound application, reasonably applied to the hand, ankle or foot.
(iii) A water bath filled with degassed water is used if possible, since ordinary tap water allows gas bubbles to dissociate, accumulate on the skin and treatment head, and reflect the beam; the patient is seated with the part immersed in water of a comfortable temperature, suitably supported.
(iv) The treatment head is placed in the water and held 1 cm from the skin, moved in small concentric circles, with the front kept parallel to the skin surface to reduce reflection to a minimum; mode/frequency/intensity/duration are chosen per the lesion (e.g. 0.1-0.25 W/cm² for acute conditions, 0.25-1 W/cm² for chronic conditions, 1-5 minutes).
(v) The head is never switched on unless in contact with a transmitting medium (the water); the intensity is returned to zero before the transducer is removed from the water; the transducer is cleaned after use with a noncorrosive, nonabrasive antiseptic lotion.
(vi) An alternative for an irregular surface that cannot conventionally be placed in a water bath is the water bag method, using a plastic or rubber bag filled with degassed water as a cushion between the treatment head and the skin, with a coupling medium applied both between the bag and skin and the bag and treatment head.

questions.answerText:
A) Phonophoresis relies on perturbation of the tissue causing more rapid particle movement, encouraging absorption of the drug.
A) The thermal effects of ultrasound increase tissue permeability, and the acoustic pressure created by the ultrasonic beam drives the medication into the tissues, so the medication follows the path of the beam.
A) Continuous ultrasound at an intensity great enough to produce thermal effects may induce a pro-inflammatory response, whereas pulsed ultrasound with a low spatial-averaged temporal peak intensity may be best if the goal is to decrease inflammation.
A) The depth to which drugs penetrate is uncertain; once past the epidermis, dispersal depends on tissue vascularity; 3 MHz has been shown to be more effective than 0.75 MHz or 1 MHz for achieving absorption of local anaesthetic.
B) The anti-inflammatory drug hydrocortisone has been widely used, with high-concentration (10%) ointments more effective than 1% when driven with relatively high-intensity ultrasound.
B) NSAIDs used include methyl salicylate and diclofenac sodium/potassium.
B) It is defined as the movement of drugs through the skin into the subcutaneous tissues under the influence of ultrasound, otherwise called sonophoresis or ultrasonophoresis.
C) The same considerations apply as for giving ultrasound for its intrinsic effects, with additional attention to allergies and sensitivities to the substance being driven into the skin.
C) A patient who cannot eat seafood should not be treated with iodine; if skin irritation or itching occurs, an antihistamine is the usual antidote and an alternative should be selected in future.
C) A patient sensitive to metals should not be treated with zinc, as they may have reactions even to metallic jewellery, requiring dermatologic consultation and a nonmetallic substitute.
C) A reaction to mecholyl with vasomotor shifting is treated with a simple stimulant such as black coffee; a patient sensitive to aspirin should not be treated with salicylates.
C) Reactions to hydrocortisone are uncommon and are usually due to base chemicals (e.g. novocaine) rather than the steroid itself, treated with an antihistamine skin lotion for dermal irritation.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Water in the pure state has a neutral pH, which changes when a substance dissolves in it; water is a universal solvent.
A(i) Water molecules exist in liquid form over a wide range of temperature, 0-100°C; body cells are about 75% water, blood about 90% water, and muscle about 80% water.
A(i) Pool temperature is 34-37°C (94-98°F).
A(ii) Water is colourless, odourless and tasteless.
A(ii) It has high thermal conductivity/specific heat capacity, absorbing 4.184 Joules (4.2 J/g) of heat to raise 1 gram of water by 1°C.
A(ii) Viscosity is a measure of a fluid's resistance to flow, often referred to as the thickness of the fluid.
A(ii) Surface tension depends on whether cohesive force is greater or less than adhesive force, as shown with water-wax, water-glass and mercury-glass interactions.
B) Archimedes' principle states that a body immersed in a fluid experiences an apparent loss of weight equal to the weight of fluid displaced.
B) Hydrostatic pressure is the ratio of the force exerted by the fluid per body surface area and depends on the depth of the submerged part; it increases in proportion to depth.
B) Because hydrostatic pressure increases with depth and density, motion is performed more easily near the surface of the water than at greater depths.
C) Laminar flow is a hydrodynamic property described alongside turbulent flow, forming part of the properties of water used for exercise in the pool (streamline position and speed).
C) Turbulent flow is the contrasting hydrodynamic property; the properties of water used for pool exercise include turbulence (streamline position, speed), upthrust, specific heat capacity and hydrostatic pressure.

questions.answerText:
(i) Rheumatoid arthritis is a listed indication for hydrotherapy.
(ii) Hydrophobia (fear of water) is itself listed as requiring precaution - breathing control must be taught; hydrophobia is also listed among the contraindications for hydrotherapy in the course content, so a careful decision balancing indication versus fear of water is required.
(iii) Dangers/complications include water-borne disease risk (e.g. gastrointestinal infection, skin infections such as folliculitis or otitis externa), and pool safety hazards if the patient panics in water.
(iv) A whirlpool bath (extremity or low boy tank) could be justified as a modified choice, since whirlpool therapy induces relaxation of spastic muscle, relieves pain and spasm, and allows easier exercise due to buoyancy, while requiring less full-body immersion than a therapeutic pool, and breathing control can be taught before progressing to fuller immersion.

questions.answerText:
A) UVR's antibiotic effect, via action on the reticuloendothelial system, increases body resistance to infection; short ultraviolet rays can destroy bacteria and other small organisms such as fungi found in wounds.
A) Erythema and desquamation effects help clear infected material and stimulate granulation tissue in non-infected wounds.
B) For infected wounds, UVR is used to destroy bacteria, remove infected dead material, promote repair and increase healing, generally using UVB via a Kromayer's lamp with E3 or E4 doses.
B) For non-infected wounds, UVR stimulates the growth of granulation tissue and promotes repair, generally using UVA with a filter such as cellophane.
B) For alopecia, suberythemal or E1 doses are given daily for 6-8 treatments to improve general health and hair follicle nutrition; individual patches can be treated with E2 or E3 doses via Kromayer's lamp twice a day.
B) For rickets, UVR converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to vitamin D, which is necessary for calcium absorption and bone/teeth formation, helping reduce osteoporosis and fractures, and is beneficial for bed-ridden, elderly or chronically debilitated patients.
C) Rickets dosage: the patient is positioned in oblique side-lying (45° inclination) and given a suberythemal dose; general debilitating conditions are similarly positioned in oblique side-lying with a suberythemal dose.
C) Wound dosage: for an infected wound the base is given an E2 dose with edges screened, repeated two or three times a week, and an indolent ulcer floor is given an E4 dose; distances of 36 inches are used for related conditions such as ulcers.
C) Alopecia dosage: suberythema/E1 daily for 6-8 treatments generally, with E2 dose specifically noted for alopecia and E2/E3 for promotion of nutrition via Kromayer's lamp.
C) General contraindications applicable across these conditions include acute skin conditions, hypersensitivity to sunlight, prior deep X-ray/cobalt therapy, recent skin grafting, pulmonary tuberculosis, cardiac/kidney/liver disease and fever.
C) Overdose risk factors (too long exposure, lamp moved closer, changing lamp without new E1, careless sensitizer use) apply to treatment of all these conditions.
C) Eye protection with goggles is also required across these treatments, since UVB and UVC are absorbed by the cornea and UVA by the lens, risking conjunctivitis or cataract.

questions.answerText:
(i) Scar tissue made pliable by ultrasound allows more effective stretching of contracted scars, which is the therapeutic basis for use in this patient.
(ii) Direct contact ultrasound with a coupling medium.
(iii) A coupling medium is applied to the skin to eliminate air and transmit the beam; the treatment head is moved in small concentric circles over the skin to avoid concentration at one point, keeping the whole front plate in contact; this method is suitable for areas up to three times the size of the treatment head.
(iv) Intensity for chronic conditions/scar tissue is 0.25-1 W/cm², with a duration of 1-5 minutes; mode can be continuous (for thermal effect on collagen extensibility) and frequency chosen as 1 or 3 MHz depending on the depth of the lesion.
(v) The treatment head is never switched on unless in contact with a transmitting medium; the emitting surface is kept parallel to the skin and pressed firmly to exclude air, with movement slow enough for tissue deformation but fast enough to avoid hot spots.
(vi) An alternative is the water bag method if the scar is on an irregular surface that cannot be treated by direct contact, using a plastic or rubber bag filled with degassed water as a coupling cushion between the treatment head and the skin.

questions.answerText:
(i) Hydrotherapy (pool therapy) is indicated; osteoarthritis is one of the listed indications for hydrotherapy.
(ii) Buoyancy partially supports the body weight and reduces the load on the affected joints and tissue, allowing greater freedom of movement.
(ii) The warmth of the water allows muscles to relax and eases pain in the joints; this gives a sedative, pain-relieving effect with increased blood flow.
(iii) Pool temperature is maintained at 34-37°C (94-98°F).
(iii) The fundamental starting position is modified by the word "support" when the patient is supported on a plinth or half-plinth.
(iii) Exercise makes use of the properties of water used in pool exercise - turbulence, upthrust/buoyancy, specific heat capacity and hydrostatic pressure.
(iii) Buoyancy can be used to assist movement of the knee and minimise stress on the joint, or work can be done against the assistance of buoyancy to create resistance.
(iv) Precautions: check for contraindications such as open infected wounds, tinea pedis, renal and faecal incontinence, and hydrophobia before starting.
(iv) Pool safety measures must be observed - non-slip floor, handrails, tested and maintained hoists.
(iv) Progression uses the different effects of buoyancy (assisting, resisting, supporting), alteration of the length of the weight arm of the moving part, and use of floats.
(iv) Buoyancy-resisting progression proceeds from a short weight arm, to a short weight arm plus float, to a long weight arm, to a long weight arm plus float, to increasing the size or number of floats.
questions.question:
A 58-year-old woman with osteoarthritis of both knees complains of joint pain and stiffness that makes exercising on land difficult. She is referred for pool-based physiotherapy.

questions.answerText:
(i) Ultrasound is indicated as it is often used after soft tissue injuries, as its mechanical effects help remove traumatic exudates and reduce the danger of adhesion formation; pulsed ultrasound is applied when a non-thermal effect is desired, as for acute soft tissue injuries.
(ii) The mechanical effect (micro-massage) from the longitudinal compression waves affects the movement of tissue fluid in interstitial spaces, helping to reduce oedema; in the inflammatory stage of repair, ultrasound increases lysosome membrane fragility, enhancing enzyme release to clear debris.
(iii) Intensity for acute and immediate post-traumatic conditions is 0.1-0.25 W/cm², duration 1-5 minutes, using pulsed mode; the treatment head is moved continuously with even pressure, kept parallel to the skin, in overlapping strokes or circles.
(iv) A coupling medium is always used and the head is never switched on out of contact with tissue; the acute condition should be treated cautiously to prevent exacerbation of symptoms, with the initial stage using a low dose (intensity 0.25-0.5 W/cm², time 2-3 minutes) and progressing as the inflammatory stage resolves toward the proliferative and remodelling stages of repair.

A pregnant woman in her third trimester presents with low back pain and is being considered for either ultrasound or another physical modality.
(i) What are the indications that would normally support use of ultrasound for back pain?

(iii) What dangers/complications must be guarded against?

questions.answerText:
(i) Ultrasound is generally indicated for soft tissue injury, chronic indurated oedema, and conditions where mechanical/thermal effects assist healing and pain reduction.
(ii) Pregnancy is a contraindication: a pregnant uterus is not treated as insonation may cause damage to the fetus; consequently, during pregnancy the back and abdomen should not be treated with ultrasound.
(iii) The danger is damage to the fetus if the pregnant uterus (back/abdomen area) is insonated.
(iv) Given that the back and abdomen should not be treated with ultrasound during pregnancy, an alternative modality or a non-insonated area/technique should be chosen.

A(i) Generators include the high-pressure mercury vapour lamp, the Kromayer's lamp, fluorescent tubes, the Theraktin tunnel, and PUVA apparatus.
A(i) The mercury vapour lamp is a gas discharge lamp using an electric arc through vaporised mercury to produce light; it was invented by Peter Cooper Hewitt in 1901.
A(i) Lamps may be air-cooled (for individual/group treatment) or water-cooled (for treatment of cavities); these are also called high-altitude lamps as the ultraviolet resembles that found in UV-rich sunlight at high altitude.
A(ii) A U-shaped glass tube filled with argon gas at low pressure encloses mercury and is sealed at both ends; the burner is made of quartz, which allows passage of UV rays and withstands high temperatures.
A(ii) A step-up transformer applies a high potential difference (400 volts) across the metal caps at each end, ionizing the argon gas.
A(ii) Further collisions ionize mercury vapour, and ultraviolet rays are produced by argon ionization, mercury vaporization and mercury ionization, taking about 5 minutes to reach peak output.
A(ii) With prolonged use, some quartz changes to tridymite, which is opaque to UV rays; total lamp output gradually decreases as tridymite proportion increases, and around 1000 hours the burner tube needs replacement.
B) The Kromayer's lamp is a water-cooled mercury vapour lamp, and the circulating distilled water absorbs the harmful infrared rays, eliminating the danger of burns, so it can be used in contact with the skin and inside body cavities.
B) The high-pressure mercury vapour lamp is not water-cooled and so retains infrared rays that could burn the skin if used in direct contact, and is therefore used at a distance rather than in contact.
C) UVA has a wavelength of 315-400 nm and produces erythemal effects without pigmentation.
C) UVB has a wavelength of 280-315 nm and produces erythemal effects, formation of vitamin D, and skin tanning (blister/burn).
C) UVC has a wavelength below 280 nm and can kill bacteria as well as contribute to vitamin D formation and skin tanning (blister/burn).
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the types of generators used to produce therapeutic ultraviolet radiation.
A(ii) Describe the construction/production process of the high-pressure mercury vapour lamp.
B) Explain the clinical basis for why the Kromayer's lamp can be used in contact with body tissue while the high-pressure mercury vapour lamp cannot.

A) Describe the technique of describing and applying an exercise in the pool (starting position, apparatus, repetition, analysis, progression).
B) State the safety rules for safe practice in the pool.
C) Explain the basis of buoyancy-related progression and how overload/adverse strain is prevented.
questions.answerText:
A) An exercise is described by naming and describing the starting position, the apparatus used, the number of repetitions, an analysis of the muscle work and which property of water is used, and a description of the progression of the exercise.
A) Starting positions on land include standing, sitting, kneeling, lying and hanging; in water, the word "support" is added when the patient is supported on a plinth or half-plinth.
A) Example exercises: water walking/jogging (chest-deep water, alternating walking/jogging for 5 minutes), forward lunges (waist-deep water, 3 sets of 10 each leg), single leg balance (aiming for 30 seconds per leg, 5 sets), side stepping (20 steps down the pool, repeated 3 times each direction), and deep water bicycle (using a flotation belt or noodle).
A) Further examples: push-ups at the pool edge (3 sets of 10, made easier/harder by moving to deeper/shallower water), arm raises in neck-deep water (3 sets of 10), standing donkey kicks at the pool wall (3 sets of 10 each leg), and standing knee lifts (3 sets of 10 each leg).
B) The maximum time for a physiotherapist to be in the water without a break is 2 hours, and therapists treating patients regularly should not be in the water for longer than 1.5 hours without a break.
B) The pool floor must be non-slip, with handrails on both sides of steps, an emergency bell cord situated over the pool, and hoists tested and maintained regularly.
B) Water temperature should be 34-37°C (94-98°F), chlorine 1.5-3.00 ppm, and pH 7.2-7.8, tested two or three times a day, with a complete water turnover every 4 hours.
C) Progression uses the different effects of buoyancy (assisting, resisting, supporting), alteration of the length of the weight arm of the moving body part, and use of floats.
C) In buoyancy-supporting progression, the body is moved in a streamlined position slowly at first, then the speed is increased to increase turbulence; alternatively the body is made unstreamlined with slow movement, then speed of movement is increased.
C) In buoyancy-resisting progression, the sequence moves from a short weight arm, to a short weight arm plus float, to a long weight arm, to a long weight arm plus float, to increasing the size or number of floats.
C) This graded progression allows load to be increased gradually rather than abruptly, helping to prevent overload or adverse strain on the muscle being trained.
C) Overshoes must be provided and worn within designated pool areas, and all staff must be trained and regularly tested in emergency and resuscitation procedures, to further support safe practice during progression of exercise.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the whirlpool bath under the headings of principle, construction and types.
A(ii) Describe the equipment/components involved in a Hubbard tank.
B) Explain the clinical basis for why the Kromayer's lamp is more hazardous to the skin than the high-pressure mercury vapour lamp when not correctly used (relate lamp construction to tissue proximity).
C) Distinguish between the extremity tank and the Hubbard tank.
questions.answerText:
A(i) A whirlpool is a large tub filled with water agitated by a small built-in motor; the part to be treated is immersed while the water is agitated, combining the effect of temperature with the mechanical effects of water; a jet of water or air stream is produced by an electrical motor incorporated into the apparatus.
A(i) Extremity tank: the smallest, used for the distal upper or lower extremity, capacity 10-45 gallons.
A(i) Low boy/buoy tank: allows submersion from the waist down in long sitting, capacity 75-105 gallons; high boy/buoy tank: large enough for both lower extremity and trunk in short sitting, capacity 60-105 gallons.
A(i) Hubbard tank: allows full body immersion, capacity 200 to more than 400 gallons, with larger tanks having more than one turbine for agitation.
A(ii) The Hubbard tank allows full body immersion with the patient lowered gradually to allow acclimatisation to water temperature; the head is kept out of the water using an inflatable neck ring and head support, while the rest of the body floats free in the circulating water.
A(ii) The Hubbard tank is suitable for acute/subacute rheumatoid arthritis with multiple joint pain, whole body burn injury, and paraplegia in ill patients in unstable condition with severe pain or serious infections.
B) The Kromayer's lamp is designed to be used in direct contact with the tissues since it is water-cooled and the circulating water absorbs infrared rays, eliminating burn danger, and it can be used both on the skin surface and inside body cavities.
B) The high-pressure mercury vapour lamp is used at a distance rather than in contact, and is less hazardous in this respect because it is not applied directly to the tissue, though it lacks the water-cooling that protects against infrared burns at close range.
B) A pump and cooling fan are incorporated into the Kromayer lamp body to cool the water, and water circulation should be continued for five minutes after the burner is switched off to cool the lamp.
C) The extremity tank is the smallest whirlpool type, used only for the distal upper or lower extremity, with a capacity of 10-45 gallons.
C) The low boy and high boy tanks sit between these two extremes in both capacity (60-105 gallons) and body coverage (waist-down or lower extremity plus trunk), distinguishing them from the extremity tank and the Hubbard tank.
C) Indications for whirlpool generally include multiple joint stiffness, pain, disuse atrophy, wound debridement in burns, paralytic conditions, rheumatism of skeletal and soft tissue, and spasm/spastic muscle, with tank type chosen according to how much of the body needs treatment.

questions.question:
A woman aged between 50 and 70 years presents with a chronic ulcer on the lower two-thirds of the leg, associated with varicose veins and long periods of standing at work.
(i) What is the condition?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors and the pathophysiological features of this condition?
(iii) Describe the physiotherapy management of this condition using ultrasound.
questions.answerText:
(i) A venous ulcer.
(ii) Predisposing factors: venous congestion associated with varicose veins or DVT, occupations demanding prolonged standing, and poor personal hygiene and malnutrition.
(ii) The floor of the ulcer may be pale and anaemic with watery discharge (indolent ulcer), green/yellow discharge (infected ulcer), or pink/purple with red spots (granulating ulcer); the wall and base show further features of chronicity, spreading or healing, and there may be oedema, pain on walking, limited ankle/foot movement, and calf muscle weakness/atrophy with loss of the pumping action.
(iii) Ultrasound can be used, but is contraindicated in DVT; it is given at 0.25-0.5 W/cm² for 5-10 minutes.
(iii) A pulsed beam is used for a small area and a continuous beam for a large area.
(iii) Ultrasound is given with coupling cream to the surrounding skin, or in a sterile saline bath, applied to both the ulcer and the surrounding area.
(iii) Other modalities used alongside include pulsed electromagnetic energy (PEME), laser, compression bandaging/support, and active exercise (noting the complication risk of superficial and deep vein thrombosis); UV rays may also be used, with an E2 dose to the base for an infected ulcer or an E4 dose to the floor for an indolent ulcer.

A) Preparation of the patient: the skin is washed and hairs removed, and the nature of the treatment, need for a couplant, and stability of the area are explained; the treatment head is not switched on until it is in contact with the skin.
A) The skin surface is inspected and inflammatory skin conditions avoided; a couplant is applied to the skin surface.
A) Three factors determine dosage: size of the treatment area, depth of the lesion from the surface, and nature of the lesion.
A) Parameters: mode (pulse or continuous), frequency (1 or 3 MHz), intensity (0.1-0.25 W/cm² for acute/post-traumatic lesions; 0.25-1 W/cm² for chronic/scar tissue), and duration of 1-5 minutes.
A) The treatment head is moved continuously with even pressure, kept parallel to the skin, in overlapping parallel strokes, circles or figures of eight.
B) The treatment head is never switched on unless it is in contact with a transmitting medium, since air reflects the beam and can set up standing waves.
B) The transducer is placed on the skin before the output is turned on, to avoid damage from reflected energy.
B) The intensity is returned to zero, manually or automatically, before the transducer is removed from the water bath or tissue contact.
B) The transducer is cleaned after each use with a noncorrosive, nonabrasive antiseptic lotion.
C) Burns occur if a continuous beam is allowed to remain stationary, so that excess heat accumulates in the tissues; this is prevented by continuous, even movement of the head.
C) Unstable cavitation is dangerous because rapid bubble collapse causes a great local rise in temperature; appropriate mode/intensity selection helps prevent this.
C) Overdose causes exacerbation of symptoms, and equipment damage occurs if the head is held in air while switched on (reflected energy sets up standing waves that can damage the crystal), so the head must always be in contact with a transmitting material when switched on.
