A patient scheduled for pool therapy has an open infected wound on the leg and a history of tinea pedis that has not yet cleared.
(i) Identify whether pool immersion is suitable or unsuitable for this patient.
(ii) What tissues/structures are of concern if immersion proceeds?
(iii) What alternative modalities could be considered?
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for the decision.
questions.answerText:
(i) Pool immersion is unsuitable; open infected wounds and tinea pedis are both listed contraindications/precautions for hydrotherapy.
(ii) The skin and soft tissue at the wound and the feet (site of tinea pedis) are of concern, as immersion could spread infection through the pool water to other users and worsen the patient's own condition.
(iii) For tinea pedis or verrucas, pool therapy must be delayed until the condition has cleared, or special socks may be worn.
(iv) Open infected wounds and burns with infection are listed contraindications for hydrotherapy, and precautions require tinea pedis to be cleared (or special socks worn) before pool therapy, so treatment should be delayed until the wound and tinea pedis have resolved, or an alternative non-immersion modality used in the meantime.

A) Water temperature should be 34-37°C (94-98°F), chlorine levels 1.5-3.00 parts per million, and water pH 7.2-7.8.
A) Chlorine and pH levels must be tested two or three times a day, there must be a complete water turnover every 4 hours, and bacteriological testing and backwashing must be performed regularly, with results recorded meticulously.
A) Air temperature should be 25°C (78°F) and humidity 55%, with overshoes provided and worn within designated areas.
B) The pool floor must be non-slip with handrails on both sides of steps, an emergency bell cord situated over the pool, and hoists tested and maintained regularly; a footbath must be near the pool entry.
B) All staff must be trained and regularly tested in emergency and resuscitation procedures; a physiotherapist should not be in the water for longer than 2 hours without a break (1.5 hours if treating patients regularly).
B) Precautions are needed for patients with tinea pedis/verrucas, AIDS with skin cuts, hydrophobia, contact lenses, hearing aids, allergy to chlorine, haemophilia and severe mental retardation.
C) Water-related disease includes waterborne disease caused by microbiological pathogens or chemical contaminants, and risk of illness is linked to faecal contamination of pool water from bathers, contaminated source water, or animal contamination.
C) Faecal matter enters water through accidental faecal release or residual faecal material washed off swimmers; non-faecal shedding (vomit, mucus, saliva, skin) is another source of pathogens.
C) Organisms of concern include faecally-derived viruses (adenovirus, rotavirus, norovirus, hepatitis A) and bacteria (Shigella, E. coli) and protozoa (Giardia, Cryptosporidium).
C) Non-faecally-derived organisms of concern include Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Legionella spp., Staphylococcus aureus and non-tuberculous mycobacteria, plus fungi such as Trichophyton and Epidermophyton causing tinea pedis (athlete's foot).
C) Modes of transmission include direct contact (as required for hydrotherapy), ingestion, indirect contact, inhalation of aerosols, and aspiration.
C) Prevention includes pool and poolside maintenance, water and air quality control with routine monitoring and filtration, proper disinfection, water temperature regulation, minimising accidental faecal releases and vomit, education of pool users, and pre-swim hygiene.
questions.question:
A) Describe the technique/procedure for maintaining a safe hydrotherapy pool environment (temperature, disinfection, testing frequency).
B) State the safety rules for safe practice for staff and patients using the pool.
C) Explain the basis of water-borne disease risk in pools and how it is prevented.

A(i) Describe the physical principles and properties of ultrasound waves.
A(ii) Describe how ultrasound is produced and the equipment/components involved.
B) Explain the clinical basis for choosing 1 MHz versus 3 MHz for a given treatment.
C) Distinguish between continuous ultrasound and pulsed ultrasound.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Sonic waves are longitudinal waves, a series of mechanical compressions and rarefactions in the direction of travel, occurring in solids, liquids and gases.
A(i) As sound waves pass through matter their energy is dissipated/attenuated, and molecular agitation is measured as heat.
A(i) Velocity is higher in solids and liquids than in gases: air 344 m/s, water 1410 m/s, muscle 1540 m/s, bone 3500 m/s.
A(ii) A vibrating source (for 1 MHz, one million cycles per second) is produced using a quartz, barium titanate, lead zirconate or nickel-cobalt ferrite crystal, which deforms under a varying potential difference (the piezoelectric effect).
A(ii) Langevin discovered that vibrating a quartz crystal with high-frequency alternating current produces ultrasound (the reversed piezoelectric effect).
A(ii) A source of high-frequency current is conveyed by a coaxial cable to a transducer circuit/treatment head, where the crystal is fused to a metal front plate; a change in crystal shape moves the front plate, producing ultrasonic waves whose frequency depends on crystal size and current frequency.
A(ii) The effective radiating area (ERA), the area of the faceplate/crystal, is an important parameter in determining the true intensity delivered.
B) At 1 MHz, energy is transmitted through more superficial tissue and absorbed primarily in deeper tissue at depths of 3-5 cm, making it useful for patients with a high percentage of cutaneous fat or where deeper structures are the treatment target.
B) At 3 MHz, energy is absorbed more superficially, with a depth of penetration between 1 and 2 cm, because the higher frequency gives a lower depth of penetration and greater scatter/attenuation in superficial tissue.
B) The lower the frequency (within limits), the higher the depth of penetration, so 1 MHz produces more heat in deep layers due to less superficial scatter allowing more energy to reach deeper tissue.
C) Continuous ultrasound is applied to achieve thermal effects, used for chronic conditions.
C) Pulsed ultrasound is applied when a non-thermal effect is desired, such as for acute soft tissue injuries; the duty cycle (fraction of time the energy is on) determines the acoustic energy and heat produced, with a duty cycle of 51-99% producing less acoustic energy and heat.

questions.question:
A) Describe the physiological effects of ultraviolet radiation (UVR) on the skin.
B) State the therapeutic uses/indications of UVR.
C) State the contraindications, precautions and dangers of UVR.
questions.answerText:
A) Carcinogenesis: prolonged exposure to UVB or UVC can affect DNA and cell replication, so treatment should not exceed four weeks.
A) Erythema: UVR causes dilatation of superficial dermal blood vessels; the smallest dose producing erythema detectable 8-24 hours after exposure is the minimal erythema dose (MED).
A) Pigmentation develops within two days as UVR stimulates melanocytes to produce melanin, which forms an umbrella over the cell nucleus; pigmentation is greater in dark skin.
A) Thickening of the epidermis (hyperplasia), up to three times normal thickness, followed by desquamation (peeling) which reduces the skin's resistance to further UVR.
A) Production of vitamin D from 7-dehydrocholesterol, helping to reduce osteoporosis and fractures; effects on the eyes include irritation, conjunctivitis, photokeratitis, or cataract with UVA in PUVA.
A) Accelerated ageing with continuous exposure; an antibiotic effect via the reticuloendothelial system that can destroy bacteria and fungi in wounds.
B) Indications include infected and non-infected wounds, acne vulgaris, psoriasis, alopecia and rickets, and general debilitating conditions.
B) For wounds, infected wounds are treated to destroy bacteria and promote healing, while non-infected wounds are treated to stimulate granulation tissue.
C) Contraindications: acute skin conditions (skin cancer, acute eczema, dermatitis, lupus erythematosus, herpes simplex), hypersensitivity to sunlight, prior deep X-ray or cobalt therapy, recent skin grafting, pulmonary tuberculosis, cardiac/kidney/liver disease, and fever.
C) Precautions include checking for use of sensitizing drugs and protecting the eyes with goggles.
C) Dangers include overdose from too long an exposure, the lamp being moved too close, changing lamps without recording a new E1, and careless use of sensitizers.
C) Long-term/chronic effects include solar elastosis (premature ageing of the skin) and cancer, hence the course of treatment should not exceed four weeks.

(i) Hydrotherapy is indicated; it has been demonstrated to increase the muscle strength of the paretic leg in stroke patients and to improve balance, gait, aerobic endurance and agility, using hands-on techniques such as joint mobilisation, stretching and relaxation.
(ii) The temperature of the water plays a role in relaxing muscles and joints and encourages spastic or contracted muscle to relax, which is why many stroke patients prefer aquatic therapy over land-based treatment.
(iii) Concepts used in stroke management include the Halliwick method (balance and stability exercises), the Bad Ragaz Ring method (muscle strengthening based on PNF), and the Watsu method (relaxation), among others (Ai Chi, Burdenko method, Water Pilates, Back Hab Aquatic techniques).
(iii) In Bad Ragaz, the patient floats horizontally supported by rings/floats at the neck, arms, pelvis and legs, with the therapist providing support and buoyancy used as support rather than assisting or resisting.
(iv) Precautions: check contraindications such as renal/faecal incontinence, hydrophobia, open infected wounds and tinea pedis; ensure pool safety measures are in place.
(iv) Progression can use different effects of buoyancy (assisting, resisting, supporting), altering the weight arm length, and use of floats, moving from short weight arm to long weight arm with floats and increasing float size/number as appropriate.

A 62-year-old man with left-sided hemiparesis following a stroke has reduced balance and gait, and prefers exercising in warm water over land-based exercise.

questions.answerText:
(i) Ultrasound to an anaesthetic area is a contraindication/requires great caution.
(ii) If ultrasonic energy is given to an anaesthetic area, the patient will not experience any pain or heat sensation, which could lead to burns of the skin and underlying tissue without the patient being aware.
(iii) Because pain or heat sensation acts as a warning of excessive heating, and this warning is absent in an anaesthetic area, ultrasound risks causing an unnoticed burn; treatment to such an area should therefore be avoided or given with extreme caution and reduced intensity/monitoring.

questions.answerText:
A) The drug to be driven into the tissue is combined in a suitable gel or cream forming the couplant, and smeared onto the part using a spatula rather than by the patient's fingers.
A) The treatment head is used on the skin in the usual manner; relatively high intensities of 1 to 1.5 W/cm² have been used.
A) The depth of the target tissue determines the frequency used, and the time of treatment depends on the area to be treated; about 1 minute of treatment per 10 cm² of area is reasonable.
A) Drugs used include hydrocortisone (a 10% ointment is more effective than 1%) and NSAIDs such as methyl salicylate, diclofenac sodium and diclofenac potassium; both pulsed and continuous ultrasound have been used.
B) Continuous ultrasound at a thermal intensity may induce a pro-inflammatory response, so if the goal is to decrease inflammation, pulsed ultrasound with a low spatial-averaged temporal peak intensity is the better choice.
B) After treatment, the drug must be removed from both the patient's skin and the transducer head, so that it is not unknowingly applied to another patient with the same treatment head.
B) Gels are more efficient coupling agents than creams, particularly for higher-frequency ultrasound (1.5 and 3 MHz).
C) The same considerations apply as for ultrasound given for its intrinsic effects; allergies and sensitivities to the substance used contraindicate its use, for example a patient who cannot eat seafood should not be treated with iodine.
C) If skin irritation or itching occurs it should be reported; the usual antidote is an antihistamine, and an alternative substance should be selected for future treatment.
C) Patients sensitive to metals should not be treated with zinc, since they may react even to metallic jewellery or watch bands; dermatologic consultation should be sought and a nonmetallic substance substituted.
C) A reaction to mecholyl with vasomotor shifting is treated with a simple stimulant such as black coffee, and vertigo from orthostatic adjustment is usually momentary.
C) A patient sensitive to aspirin should not be treated with salicylates, and medical consultation should be sought for the specific treatment of symptoms.

questions.answerText:
A) Whirlpool bath combines the effect of temperature with the mechanical effects of water; a jet of water or air stream produced by an electrical motor creates turbulence in the water.
A) The whirlpool treatment relaxes muscle tension and provides a feeling of comfort; especially in post-surgical patients, it decreases pain, reduces complications, and helps bring forward the discharge date.
A) The water temperature can be warm or cold depending on the treatment goal, with typical warm whirlpool temperatures of 98-110°F for 10-15 minutes (up to 20-30 minutes).
B) Indications: multiple joint stiffness, pain, disuse atrophy, wound debridement in burns, paralytic conditions (poliomyelitis), rheumatism of skeletal and soft tissue, and spasm/spastic muscle.
B) Therapeutic uses: inducing relaxation especially in spastic muscle prior to exercise, relief of pain and spasm, easier exercise due to buoyancy, debridement of dead tissue from the wound surface, and heating of soft tissue around a joint prior to mobilisation.
B) Whirlpools are recommended as a treatment for reducing pain in patients with osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.
C) Contraindications: circulatory deficiency, diminished thermal sensation, deep vein thrombosis, malignancy, and bleeding disorder.
C) Further contraindications: severe swelling, recent skin graft, acute traumatic and inflammatory lesions of the musculoskeletal system, and local or general infections.
C) Hubbard tank use is nonetheless suited to ill patients in unstable condition, with severe pain or serious infections, for whole-body immersion despite the general infection caution, and it is used for acute/subacute rheumatoid arthritis with multiple joint pain and whole-body burn injury.
C) Care should be taken to keep the patient's head out of water, using an inflatable neck ring and head support, when using the Hubbard tank.
C) The patient should be lowered gradually into the tank to allow acclimatisation to the water temperature.
C) Whirlpool treatment was first started by the French army during the First World War and is currently used in many countries for medical and surgical conditions.
questions.question:

B) State the therapeutic uses/indications of whirlpool bath.

A) Describe the technique of application of UVR-based regimens for psoriasis (Goeckerman, Leeds/Ingram and PUVA), including dosage and duration.
B) State the safety rules for safe practice with these regimens.
C) Explain the basis of adverse effects of these regimens and how they are prevented.
questions.answerText:
A) Goeckerman regimen: coal tar application 2-3 times a day with general (total body) UVB radiation given once a day as a suberythemal or E1 dose.
A) Leeds/Ingram regimen: the skin's sensitivity is increased by local application of coal tar (added to the bath before treatment), lesions are covered with dithranol cream (inhibiting DNA synthesis), cleaned off the next day, and the process repeated; a suberythemal E1 dose is given daily via Theraktin tunnel or air-cooled lamp at 100 cm, increased daily at 12.5%.
A) PUVA: 8-methoxypsoralen tablets are taken with milk two hours before UVA exposure.
A) Posture reference points for PUVA include the midpoint of the line joining the inferior angles of the scapulae (upper trunk) and the midpoint of the line joining the two popliteal fossae (lower trunk), with the greater trochanters used for the sides.
A) UVA doses in PUVA are graded by skin type from type I (always burns, never tans) to type VI (black skin).
B) Precautions for PUVA: do not take psoralens on an empty stomach; protective goggles/polaroid sunglasses must be worn from taking the psoralen to at least 12 hours after treatment.
B) Stop using all ointments during PUVA; simple oil or lubricating lotion may be used if the skin is dry.
B) If the patient feels pain during treatment, the physiotherapist must be called immediately.
C) The aim of UVR in psoriasis is to decrease the rate of DNA synthesis in the skin cells, slowing their proliferation, which is what the coal tar/dithranol/psoralen agents in each regimen are designed to support.
C) Long-term/chronic adverse effects of UVR include solar elastosis (premature ageing of the skin) and cancer risk from influence on DNA and cell replication.
C) The course of treatment should therefore not exceed four weeks, to reduce the risk of these long-term effects.
C) Overdose is prevented by accurate timing, correct lamp distance using the inverse-square law, and careful recording of E1 for each lamp used.

questions.question:
A) Describe the technique of application of ultraviolet radiation, including calculation of the test dose and general irradiation.
B) State the safety rules for safe practice with UVR.
C) Explain the basis of the dangers of UVR and how they are prevented.
questions.answerText:
A) The test dose is assessed using the individual patient's reaction to UVR; the flexor aspect of the forearm is used, the skin washed to remove dust/grease, and three differently shaped holes (about 2 cm × 2 cm in the middle, one larger, one smaller) are cut in card, paper or lint.
A) E1 is the dose that appears last and disappears first; from E1, other doses are calculated: suberythemal = 75% of E1, E2 = E1 × 2.5, E3 = E1 × 5, E4 = E1 × 10, and double E4 = E4 plus 20 × E1.
A) For general irradiation with an air-cooled lamp, the patient is positioned in oblique side-lying with goggles worn; the fractional method divides the body at the ASIS/PSIS line into upper and lower halves, each treated separately at 100 cm, and a suberythemal dose (half the patient's E1) is used for a total body exposure.
A) The lamp is placed at a standard distance from the patient (about 50 cm), warmed up before use, switched on for the required time, then the patient is turned to expose the opposite aspect for equal radiation.
B) The nature and effect of the treatment are explained, contraindications are checked, and a test dose is determined before treatment begins.
B) Protective goggles are worn by the patient and the therapist; soft structures (lips, ear lobes, eyelids, nipples, navel) are screened with petroleum jelly, and the rest of the body not being treated is covered with a thick blanket.
B) The patient is warned to keep still and not to touch the lamp during treatment.
C) Eye damage (conjunctivitis or cataract) is a danger because UVB/UVC are absorbed by the cornea and UVA by the lens; this is prevented by the consistent wearing of suitable goggles.
C) Overdose can occur from too long an exposure; a proper timer with an audible sound and auto-cut device is used to prevent this.
C) Overdose can also occur if the lamp is moved closer to the patient; the patient is instructed not to move, and the therapist calculates distance using the inverse-square law.
C) Changing the lamp can cause overdose if the new lamp's E1 is not recorded and used, so average E1 must be carefully recorded and marked on every lamp.
C) Careless use of sensitizing drugs can cause an exaggerated reaction, so sensitizers must be administered and used carefully.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old presents with comedones, papules and pustules blocking the hair follicles and sebaceous glands of the face, back and chest, with a diet high in butter, cream, sugar and chocolate.
(i) What is the condition?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors and pathology of this condition?
(iii) Describe the physiotherapy management using UVR.
questions.answerText:
(i) Acne vulgaris.
(ii) Predisposing factors: puberty, lack of fitness/exercise/fresh air, poor health/constipation, diet high in butter, cream, sugar, chocolate or alcohol, sweating, endocrine abnormalities involving testosterone, anxiety, and skin type/dark complexion/heredity.
(ii) Pathology: sebum production and keratin block the pilosebaceous duct and hair follicle; the exposed surface becomes oxidized and blackened, inflammation and bacterial infection cause swelling/distension and pus formation (pustule); once pus is discharged the duct/follicle shrink and heal, but repeated attacks can result in scar tissue.
(iii) Positioning: sitting, with two pillows for the back of the head and neckline/hairline maintenance, the remaining part covered and cotton wool worn on the eyes.
(iii) UVR spectrum 190-390 nm, distance 18 inches, dose E2, with the focusing point at the tip of the nose; dosage depends on the patient's weight and skin type; the patient washes the affected area twice a day with oil-free soap and rinses with cool water.

(i) Ultrasound is unsuitable at the site of the DVT and requires caution at the implant site; vascular conditions such as thrombophlebitis (where insonation may cause emboli to be broken off) are not treated with ultrasound, and metal implants reflect ultrasound at their interfaces.
(ii) Over a metal implant, ultrasound would be reflected at the tissue-metal interface, leading to more energy absorption in that area; over the DVT area, the vascular tissue and any emboli risk being disturbed by insonation.
(iii) Vascular conditions such as thrombophlebitis are a contraindication to ultrasound because insonation may cause emboli to be broken off, and metal implants reflect ultrasound at their interfaces leading to increased and unpredictable energy absorption in the tissue; treatment should therefore avoid the implant and vascular area until these risks are addressed.
questions.question:
A patient with a metal implant in the treatment area and a recent history of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is being assessed for treatment of a soft tissue lesion near the affected limb.
(i) Identify whether ultrasound is a suitable or unsuitable modality here.
(ii) What tissues/structures would be affected if ultrasound were applied over the implant or the vascular area?
(iii) Give the clinical reasoning for the decision.

A patient with acute/subacute disease presenting with multiple joint pains across several joints, without infection, is referred for full-body immersion hydrotherapy.
(i) What is the likely condition category being treated?
(ii) What are the predisposing/associated features described for this presentation?
(iii) Describe the physiotherapy management using the Hubbard tank.
questions.answerText:
(i) Acute or subacute rheumatoid arthritis presenting with multiple joint pains, one of the conditions for which the Hubbard tank (full body immersion) is suitable.
(ii) The Hubbard tank is also suitable for whole body burn injury and for paraplegia in ill patients in unstable condition, with severe pain or serious infections, indicating this modality is chosen for widespread, severe or multi-system presentations.
(iii) The patient is lowered gradually into the tank to allow acclimatisation to the water temperature; the head is kept out of the water using an inflatable neck ring and head support, while the rest of the body floats free in the circulating water.
(iii) The typical warm whirlpool temperature is 98-110°F for 10-15 minutes (up to 20-30 minutes); therapeutic effects include induced relaxation especially in spastic muscle prior to exercise, relief of pain and spasm, and easier exercise due to buoyancy; whirlpools are specifically recommended for reducing pain in rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.question:
An immobile 70-year-old bed-bound patient develops a pressure injury over the heel, exposing a shallow cavity with a pink, vascular floor and surrounding skin that is red.
(i) What is the diagnosis and why is ultraviolet radiation (UVR) indicated?
(ii) What is the physiological basis of UVR's effect on this lesion?
(iii) Describe the treatment technique and parameters.
(iv) State the precautions and how treatment would be progressed.
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is a pressure sore; pressure sores are treated with UVR, with external factors (postoperative pain, immobility, unconsciousness, prolonged bedrest) and internal factors (muscle tone, incontinence, diabetes, trophic ulcer) as the cause.
(ii) UVR produces erythema (dilatation of superficial dermal blood vessels) which brings blood to the area, and desquamation which helps clear the floor of the sore; the antibiotic effect of short ultraviolet rays helps destroy bacteria and other organisms in the wound.
(iii) The patient is positioned in oblique side-lying (45°).
(iii) Dosage: floor E4 dose, wall E3 dose, base E2 dose, at a distance of 36 inches.
(iv) Precautions: the therapist must check for local contraindications such as the skin condition of the sore and avoid overdose by accurate timing, correct lamp distance (applying the inverse-square law), and careful recording of E1 for the lamp used.
(iv) Progression of UVR dosage follows: suberythemal - previous dose plus 12.5%; E1 - previous dose plus 25%; E2 - previous dose plus 50%; E3 - previous dose plus 75%; note that dosage on open wounds (E4) is not progressed because there is no epidermis to thicken.

questions.question:
A patient with acute eczema who is also taking a thiazide diuretic is being considered for ultraviolet radiation (UVR) treatment for a skin lesion.
(i) Identify whether UVR is a suitable or unsuitable modality for this patient.
(ii) What tissues/structures would be affected by UVR if applied?
(iii) Give the clinical reasoning for your decision.
questions.answerText:
(i) UVR is unsuitable in this patient; acute skin conditions such as acute eczema are a contraindication to UVR, and thiazide diuretics are listed among the drugs that sensitize the skin to UVR.
(ii) If applied, UVR would affect the epidermis (causing erythema, thickening/hyperplasia and desquamation), the melanocytes (pigmentation), and, with sensitizer use, could provoke an exaggerated skin reaction.
(iii) Acute skin conditions such as acute eczema must be avoided for UVR irradiation, and the use of sensitizers such as thiazide diuretics must be administered and used carefully to avoid harmful effects, so treatment should not proceed until the eczema has resolved and the sensitizing drug issue has been addressed with the prescriber.

questions.question:
A) Describe the physiological and therapeutic effects of hydrotherapy.
B) State the therapeutic uses/indications of hydrotherapy.
C) State the contraindications and dangers of hydrotherapy.
questions.answerText:
A) Water's thermal conductivity/high specific heat capacity allows it to absorb a large amount of heat before its temperature changes significantly; the pool temperature of 34-37°C (94-98°F) means the human body gains heat from the water.
A) Effects include pain relief through a sedative effect and increased blood flow, and muscle (elasticity) relaxation, with increased blood flow in the superficial vessels.
A) The physiological and therapeutic effects are grouped under musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, respiratory, renal and psychological effects.
B) Indications include osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, obesity, post-immobilisation fracture, stroke, hemiparesis and hemiplegia, low back pain, sports injuries (ACL, PCL), multiple sclerosis, oedema, injection palsy and ankylosing spondylitis.
B) Advantages of pool therapy include partial support of body weight, reduced load on affected joints/tissue, greater freedom of movement, reduced fear of falling, a psychological boost, and warmth that relaxes muscles and eases joint pain.
C) Contraindications include renal and faecal incontinence, hydrophobia, open infected wounds, burns with infection, and tinea pedis.
C) Precautions are needed for patients with tinea pedis or verrucas (delay therapy or wear special socks), AIDS (not treated if skin cuts are present), hydrophobia (breathing control must be taught), contact lenses, hearing aids, allergy to chlorine, haemophilia and severe mental retardation.
C) Dangers include water-borne diseases; water-related disease is any significant adverse effect on health caused directly or indirectly by the condition or quality of water.
C) The commonest water-related illness is gastrointestinal infection; other categories include respiratory infections and skin or systemic disorders.
C) Modes of transmission of water-related disease include direct contact (e.g. that required for hydrotherapy), ingestion, indirect contact, inhalation of aerosols, and aspiration of contaminated water.
C) Organisms of concern include faecal-derived viruses/bacteria/protozoa (e.g. rotavirus, E. coli, Giardia, Cryptosporidium) and non-faecally derived organisms (e.g. Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Legionella spp., Staphylococcus aureus, non-tuberculous mycobacteria).
C) Prevention includes pool and poolside maintenance, water and air quality control, proper disinfection, water temperature regulation, minimising accidental faecal releases, and education of pool users.

(i) Wound debridement in burns is a listed indication for whirlpool therapy, and heating of the soft tissue around a joint prior to mobilisation is a therapeutic use of whirlpool.
(ii) An extremity tank, the smallest type, used for the distal upper or lower extremity.
(iii) The extremity tank has a capacity of 10 to 45 gallons of water; a jet of water or air stream is produced by an electrical motor built into the apparatus, creating turbulence.
(iv) The typical warm whirlpool temperature is 98-110°F, with a treatment duration of 10-15 minutes (up to 20-30 minutes).
(v) Care must be taken with contraindications such as circulatory deficiency, diminished thermal sensation, DVT, malignancy, bleeding disorder, severe swelling or recent skin graft, acute traumatic/inflammatory lesions, and local or general infection.
(vi) An alternative or modification could be to use a low boy or high boy tank if a larger area (e.g. lower extremity and trunk) needed treatment, or to combine whirlpool with debridement of dead tissue from the wound surface before mobilisation.
questions.question:
A patient recovering from a localised hand burn is referred for whirlpool therapy to assist wound debridement before mobilisation exercises.
(i) What is the treatment indication/diagnosis-related basis for whirlpool use here?
(ii) Name the type of whirlpool tank suited to this patient.
(iii) Describe the equipment and set-up required.

questions.answerText:
(i) Acne vulgaris - a chronic inflammatory disease of the sebaceous glands, typically affecting the face, chest and upper back, starting between 9 and 17 years and associated with puberty, poor health, and diet high in butter, cream, sugar, chocolate or alcohol.
(ii) Ultraviolet radiation (UVR).
(iii) The patient sits on a stool with the back supported against a wall, with two pillows for head support and the neck/hairline maintained; cotton wool is worn on the eyes; the focusing point is the tip of the nose.
(iv) UVR spectrum 190-390 nm, distance 18 inches, dose E2; dosage depends on the patient's weight and skin type.
(v) The affected area is washed at least twice a day with oil-free soap and rinsed with cool water; the intensity of dose needed can be painful and cosmetically unacceptable, so this must be discussed with the patient, and treatment is only palliative.
(vi) General management (topical sulphur-based ointment, salicylic acid-based ointment, or benzoyl peroxide gel, and general antibiotics) can be used as an alternative or adjunct to UVR.

A patient with whole-body burn injury is referred for hydrotherapy using a Hubbard tank.
(i) What is the treatment goal/diagnosis-related indication for this patient?
(ii) Name the modality/technique to be used.
(iii) Describe the equipment and set-up required.
(iv) State the treatment parameters and dosage.
(v) State the safety measures for the patient and the therapist.
(vi) Suggest an alternative technique or modification.
questions.answerText:
(i) Whole body burn injury is a listed indication for Hubbard tank/whirlpool hydrotherapy, used for wound debridement in burns and to induce relaxation and relief of pain and spasm.
(ii) The Hubbard tank (full body immersion whirlpool).
(iii) The Hubbard tank allows for full body immersion, with a capacity of 200 to more than 400 gallons; larger tanks may have more than one turbine for agitation; an inflatable neck ring and head support are used to keep the head out of the water.
(iv) The patient is lowered gradually into the tank to allow acclimatisation to the water temperature; the typical warm whirlpool temperature is 98-110°F, with a treatment duration of 10-15 minutes (up to 20-30 minutes).
(v) The rest of the body is allowed to float free in the circulating water while the head is kept out of the water; care should be taken with patients who are ill, unstable, in severe pain, or who have serious infections, as the Hubbard tank is suited to such cases but requires close monitoring.
(vi) An alternative is to use a smaller whirlpool tank (extremity, low boy or high boy) if only part of the body requires treatment, or to combine whirlpool debridement with heating of the soft tissue around a joint prior to mobilisation.

A) Hydrostatic pressure effects include promoting circulation or alleviating peripheral oedema due to venous or lymphatic insufficiency, reducing/limiting effusion, helping to brace unstable joints or weak muscles, inducing bradycardia, and centralising peripheral blood flow.
A) The greatest hydrostatic pressure effects occur with vertical positioning, and there are no hydrostatic pressure effects with non-immersion hydrotherapy techniques.
A) Surface tension means an extremity moving through the surface performs more work than if kept under water, and using equipment at the surface increases resistance.
A) Viscosity creates resistance to all active movements that is velocity-dependent, making water a safe and effective strengthening/conditioning medium; resistance falls to zero when motion stops (a safety feature), and can be increased by increasing speed or frontal area, which is also useful for debriding and cleansing wounds.
B) Buoyancy provides relative weightlessness and joint unloading, allowing active motion with increased ease, and provides resistance to movement when an extremity moves against buoyancy, useful for strengthening.
B) Buoyancy allows the therapist three-dimensional access to the patient and assists in supporting the patient's body weight during therapeutic activities.
B) As speed of movement through water increases, resistance (drag) increases; moving water past the patient requires more effort to maintain position, and equipment such as gloves, paddles or boots increases drag and resistance.
C) Fear of water can limit the effectiveness of activity and increase symptoms during/after immersion due to muscle guarding.
C) Neurological disorders such as ataxia present increased difficulty controlling purposeful movement, and multiple sclerosis patients are heat intolerant and fatigue with immersion in temperatures greater than 33°C.
C) Cardiac dysfunction such as angina or high blood pressure is a precaution, and small open wounds/tracheostomies require waterproof dressing coverage.
C) Contraindications include cardiac failure and unstable angina, and severe peripheral vascular disease.
C) Further contraindications: danger of bleeding or haemorrhage, open wounds and skin infection, uncontrolled seizures, water/airborne infections, and severe kidney disease.

A(i) Describe coupling media used in ultrasound therapy and their characteristics.
A(ii) Describe attenuation of the ultrasound beam and the effective radiating area (ERA).
B) Explain the clinical basis for why the treatment head must never be switched on without a transmitting medium in contact.
C) Distinguish between the near field (Fresnel zone) and the distant field (Fraunhofer zone).
questions.answerText:
A(i) Ultrasonic waves are not transmitted by air, so a couplant must be interposed between the treatment head and the patient's skin; no couplant gives perfect transmission, and even the most efficient reduces the applied dose by about a quarter.
A(i) Transmission efficiencies given are: aqua sonic gel 72.6%, glycerol 67%, distilled water 59%, liquid paraffin 19%, petroleum jelly 0%, air 0%.
A(i) Characteristics of a good coupling medium: acoustic impedance similar to the tissue, high transmissivity for ultrasound, and high viscosity.
A(i) Further characteristics: low susceptibility to bubble formation, chemically inactive, hypoallergic, relatively sterile, cheap, and able to act as a lubricant so the head moves smoothly over the skin.
A(ii) Attenuation is the gradual reduction in intensity of the ultrasonic beam once it has left the treatment head, due to absorption (converted to heat, contributing the thermal effect) and scatter (beam deflected by reflection at interfaces, bubbles or particles).
A(ii) The effective radiating area (ERA) is the area of the faceplate/crystal size, which is smaller relative to the soundhead, and its determination is essential for a true indication of intensity.
B) Air has zero transmission and will reflect the ultrasound beam back into the treatment head; this can set up a standing wave that might damage the crystal.
B) Consequently, the treatment head is never left switched on when not in contact with a transmitting medium, to protect the crystal from this reflected-energy damage.
C) The near field (Fresnel zone) is close to the transducer face, where some waves cancel each other while others reinforce, producing an irregular pattern of sonic waves.
C) The distant field (Fraunhofer zone) lies beyond the near field, away from the transducer head.
C) These two fields relate to the depth of penetration and intensity distribution of the ultrasonic beam.
C) Understanding these fields helps explain why beam intensity and effect are not uniform close to versus further from the treatment head.

questions.question:
A child presents with loss of reflexes, loose and floppy limbs, progressive muscle weakness, pain and fatigue following a febrile illness.
(i) What is the condition?
(ii) What are the predisposing/staging features and pathophysiology of this condition?
(iii) Describe the physiotherapy management of this condition using hydrotherapy.
questions.answerText:
(i) Poliomyelitis (the paralytic/post-polio syndrome).
(ii) Polio is a viral disease that destroys the nerve cells in the spinal cord, causing muscle weakness or paralysis; the disease is classified into an acute stage (febrile illness), a convalescent stage (starting 48 hours after the febrile illness and extending for about 16 months, subdivided into a sensitive phase with muscle sensitivity/spasm and a nonsensitive phase), and a chronic stage; symptoms vary from mild viral illness without paralysis to quadriplegia and respiratory failure.
(iii) During the acute/sensitive phase, moist heat is used since muscles are sensitive to stretching and handling, with spasm often leading to hypertonic and myostatic contracture; a warm bath (Hubbard tub) is used, with water temperature between 98-101°F (occasionally 104°F), for a duration not more than 20 minutes, once daily, combined with hot packs on stiff/painful joints at other times.
(iii) Treatment by stage: acute preparalytic - complete rest; paralytic - hot pack to relieve spasm followed by passive movement; convalescent - rest by positioning with moist heat/hubbard tub immersion, passive movement replaced by active movement; asensitive stage - heat if stiffness persists, passive movement becoming passive stretching, with muscle re-education in the pool (standing/walking re-education using splints and crutches); chronic stage - muscle re-education, functional training, standing exercises and gait retraining.

(i) The condition is psoriasis; UVR is indicated because the aim of treatment is to decrease the rate of DNA synthesis in the skin cells and slow their proliferation, which is accelerated in psoriasis (maturation of 21-29 days shortened to about 4 days).
(ii) Contraindications/precautions: acute skin conditions such as skin cancer, acute eczema, dermatitis, lupus erythematosus or herpes simplex; hypersensitivity to sunlight; prior deep X-ray or cobalt therapy; recent skin grafting; pulmonary tuberculosis; cardiac, kidney and liver disease; fever.
(iii) Dangers: eye damage (conjunctivitis or cataract) if goggles are not worn; overdose from too long an exposure, the lamp being moved closer to the patient, changing the lamp without re-checking E1, or careless use of sensitizers; the course of treatment should not exceed four weeks because of the carcinogenic risk from prolonged exposure.
(iv) The Leeds (Ingram) regimen is justified: sensitivity of the skin is increased by local application of coal tar added to the bath before treatment, the lesions are covered with dithranol cream which inhibits DNA synthesis and is cleaned off the next day, and a suberythemal E1 dose is given daily via a Theraktin tunnel or air-cooled lamp at 100 cm, increased daily by 12.5%; alternatively, PUVA (8-methoxypsoralen taken with milk two hours before UVA exposure) can be justified for the same DNA-synthesis-inhibiting aim.

questions.question:
Describe the pharmacology of methotrexate:
(a) Class
(b) Mechanism of action
(c) Pharmacokinetics
(d) Uses
(e) Adverse effects
State the basis of its selectivity and effect on immune cells and mediators:
(f) Why it is effective at a lower dose in rheumatoid arthritis
(g) Its effect on cytokines and cellular immunity
(h) Its safe combination with NSAIDs
Explain the basis of toxicity and drug interaction:
(i) The pattern of toxicity
(j) The interaction with co-trimoxazole
(k) The interaction with azathioprine or leflunomide
questions.answerText:
(a)
A folic acid (folate) antagonist with cytotoxic, immunosuppressant and anti-rheumatoid activity; a non-biologic DMARD.
(b)
Folate antagonism; decreases chemotaxis and adhesion of inflammatory cells and inhibits pro-inflammatory cytokine production.
(c)
Metabolized in the liver; peak plasma concentration at 1-2 hours after low-dose administration; mainly renally excreted; given orally or subcutaneously.
(d)
Rheumatoid arthritis (monotherapy or with hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, infliximab), pemphigus, myasthenia gravis, uveitis; also immunosuppression in autoimmune disease.
(e)
Nausea, mouth ulcer, hair loss, cytopenias, elevated liver enzymes, rarely pneumonitis, bone marrow suppression.
(f)
Its anti-rheumatoid activity is achieved at a dose lower than that needed in cancer chemotherapy.
(g)
It markedly suppresses cytokine production and cellular immunity and has an anti-inflammatory effect.
(h)
NSAIDs can be safely used in conjunction with methotrexate for RA symptom control.
(i)
Nausea, mouth ulcer, hair loss, cytopenias, raised liver enzymes, pneumonitis and bone marrow suppression.
(j)
Use with co-trimoxazole causes pancytopenia.
(k)
Combination with azathioprine or leflunomide causes liver and lung complications.

questions.question:
A patient with rheumatoid arthritis who tests positive for hepatitis B serology is treated with a chimeric human monoclonal antibody directed against CD20, and develops fulminant reactivation of hepatitis B.
(a) Identify the cause.
(b) Explain the underlying immunological or pharmacological basis.
(c) Differentiate the drug from other biologic classes used in rheumatoid arthritis.
(d) Reason to the management decision.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Viral reactivation after B-cell depletion by rituximab.
(b)
B lymphocytes contribute to initiation and maintenance of the inflammatory cascade by antigen presentation and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
• Rituximab, directed against CD20, depletes B cells by cell-mediation, complement-dependent cytotoxicity and the promotion of apoptosis and growth arrest.
(c)
TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept, certolizumab, golimumab): all increase risk of serious infections. Tocilizumab: IL-6 receptor blocker with CYP450 interaction. Anakinra: IL-1 receptor blocker given daily.
(d)
Rituximab is contraindicated in patients with hepatitis B positive serology.
• The other biologic target families available are TNF inhibitors, IL-6 receptor blockers and IL-1 receptor blockers.

questions.question:
Describe the pharmacology of cyclosporin:
(a) Class and source
(b) Mechanism of action
(c) Uses
(d) Adverse effects
State the basis of its selectivity and its effect on specific immune cells and mediators:
(e) Which arm of immunity it suppresses and which it leaves intact
(f) Its effect on lymphocytes in the cell cycle
(g) The pathway it halts, from T-cell stimulation to cytokine production
Explain the basis of its toxicity and drug interactions:
(h) Pattern of organ toxicity
(i) Interactions that increase toxicity
(j) Interactions that lower or raise its levels
questions.answerText:
(a)
An immunosuppressant extracted from a soil fungus.
(b)
It binds the intracellular protein cyclophyllin, and this complex inhibits the calcium-calmodulin activated enzyme calcineurin.
(c)
Autoimmune diseases; most effective in graft rejection reactions; renal, hepatic, cardiac and bone marrow transplantation.
(d)
Sustained hypertension, diabetes, seizures, gum hyperplasia, viral infection, tremors, hirsutism.
(e)
It suppresses cell-mediated immunity and prevents graft rejection, yet leaves the recipient with enough (humoral) immunity to combat bacterial infection.
(f)
Lymphocytes are arrested in the G0 or G1 phase of the cell cycle.
(g)
T-cell receptor stimulation raises Ca2+, which binds calmodulin to activate calcineurin; calcineurin dephosphorylates NFAT, which migrates to the nucleus for transcription of cytokine genes (IL-2, TNF-alpha, GM-CSF). Cyclosporin halts these pathways, so IL-2 production and cytotoxic T-cell stimulation and proliferation fail.
(h)
It is nephrotoxic and hepatotoxic but not toxic to bone marrow, and it leaves humoral immunity intact.
(i)
All nephrotoxic drugs such as vancomycin, amphotericin B and NSAIDs increase its toxicity. By depressing renal function it can reduce the excretion of many drugs.
(j)
Enzyme inducers decrease its levels (transplant rejection); erythromycin, ketoconazole and related drugs increase its levels (toxicity).

questions.question:
Describe the pharmacology of cromolyn (sodium cromoglycate):
(a) Class and related drugs
(b) Mechanism of action
(c) Pharmacokinetics
(d) Indications
(e) Adverse effects
State the basis of its selectivity and effect on immune cells and mediators:
(f) The cell it acts on
(g) The immune reaction it interrupts
(h) Its effect on airways
Explain the basis of its route of administration and toxicity:
(i) The basis of its route of administration
(j) Its adverse effects
questions.answerText:
(a)
A mast cell stabiliser; related agents are nedocromil sodium and ketotifen.
(b)
It inhibits the release of inflammatory chemicals from mast cells and makes the airways less likely to narrow.
(c)
Unabsorbed orally, so given as an aerosol; a small fraction of the inhaled drug is absorbed systemically and rapidly excreted unchanged in urine and bile.
(d)
Bronchial asthma and allergic rhinitis.
(e)
Cough, flushing, palpitation, chest pain, nasal congestion, nausea, fatigue, migraine, sneezing, dysphagia, oesophageal spasm, tinnitus, pharyngitis.
(f)
Mast cells (release inhibitors).
(g)
Mast cell degranulation caused by antigen-IgE interaction (IgE cross-linking releases histamine, leukotrienes and prostaglandins).
(h)
The airways are less likely to narrow, as release of bronchoconstrictor mediators from mast cells is reduced.
(i)
It is not absorbed orally, so it is effective only by inhalation; aerosol delivery is site specific and enhances the therapeutic ratio.
(j)
The adverse effects described above, such as cough, flushing and palpitation.

(a)
Genetically engineered protein molecules that block inflammatory cytokines: TNF inhibitors, IL-6 receptor blockers, IL-1 receptor blockers, and anti-CD20.
(b)
TNF inhibitors block TNF binding to its receptors; tocilizumab blocks IL-6 receptor signalling; anakinra blocks the IL-1 receptor; rituximab depletes B cells (cell-mediation, complement-dependent cytotoxicity, apoptosis, growth arrest).
(c)
Infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept, certolizumab, golimumab; tocilizumab; anakinra, rilonacept, canakinumab; rituximab.
(d)
RA, and also Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, chronic psoriasis (anti-TNF agents).
(e)
All anti-TNF agents increase the risk of serious infections; rituximab: hepatitis B reactivation; tocilizumab: upper respiratory infection, headache, hypertension, injection site reaction, raised liver enzymes; anakinra: injection-site rash.
(f)
RA is mediated by pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1 and TNF-alpha have a major role; macrophage IL-1/TNF-alpha degrade the joint), and B cells contribute to the inflammatory cascade by antigen presentation and cytokine production.
(g)
They are expensive to produce (sterile conditions, multiple purification steps), have limited shelf life, need controlled storage, and are typically given by a physician; anakinra needs daily injection.
(h)
Cytokine networks are balanced; inhibiting pro-inflammatory cytokines can compromise host defence against infection.
(i)
Infliximab is a monoclonal chimeric human-mouse anti-TNF antibody; etanercept contains the human TNF receptor and the Fc portion of human IgG1.
(j)
Infliximab binds soluble TNF trimers with high affinity (both monomeric and trimeric forms); etanercept binds mainly the active trimeric form less stably, and TNF-beta.
(k)
Infliximab is given by intravenous infusion, typically with methotrexate; adalimumab is a fully human monoclonal anti-TNF antibody given subcutaneously.
(l)
The Fc portion of infliximab promotes complement activation and antibody-mediated apoptosis and cellular cytotoxicity of activated T lymphocytes and macrophages.
questions.question:
Describe the biologic disease modifying anti-rheumatoid drugs under the following headings:
(a) Classification
(b) Mechanism of action
(c) Examples
(d) Uses
(e) Adverse effects
Explain the pharmacological basis of efficacy and limitation:
(f) Why cytokine and B-cell targets are effective in rheumatoid arthritis
(g) Why they are less convenient than conventional drugs
(h) Why they raise infection risk
Distinguish between related drugs:
(i) Infliximab and etanercept in structure
(j) Their binding of TNF
(k) Infliximab and adalimumab in route and nature

Describe the pharmacology of infliximab:
(a) Class
(b) Mechanism of action
(c) Route and combination
(d) Uses
(e) Adverse effects
State the basis of its selectivity and effect on specific immune cells and mediators:
(f) Which forms of TNF it binds
(g) The role of its Fc portion
(h) How it differs from etanercept
Explain the basis of toxicity and drug interaction:
(i) The infection risk
(j) The consequence of inhibiting pro-inflammatory cytokines
(k) The combination with methotrexate
questions.answerText:
(a)
A monoclonal chimeric human-mouse anti-TNF antibody; a biologic DMARD (TNF inhibitor).
(b)
It binds soluble TNF trimers with high affinity, preventing the cytokine from binding its receptors.
(c)
Administered as an intravenous infusion; typically used in combination with methotrexate to enhance its therapeutic effects.
(d)
Severe Crohn's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, ulcerative colitis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis.
(e)
All anti-TNF agents increase the risk of serious infections.
(f)
It binds both monomeric and trimeric forms of TNF (the inactive and active forms).
(g)
The Fc portion promotes complement activation and antibody-mediated apoptosis and cellular cytotoxicity of activated T lymphocytes and macrophages.
(h)
Etanercept (human TNF receptor plus Fc of human IgG1, given subcutaneously) binds mainly the active trimeric form less stably and also binds TNF-beta.
(i)
All anti-TNF agents increase the risk of serious infections.
(j)
Inhibiting pro-inflammatory cytokines can compromise host defence against infection.
(k)
Infliximab is typically combined with methotrexate to enhance its therapeutic effects.

questions.question:
A patient with an autoimmune disease in which autoreactive T cells attack myelin (or with Crohn's disease) is given a humanized monoclonal antibody directed against an integrin on leukocytes.
(a) Identify the drug.
(b) State the molecular and cellular target and mechanism of action.
(c) Describe the effect on the immune response.
(d) State the therapeutic use and how a related drug differs in side effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Natalizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody against alpha-4 integrin.
(b)
It interferes with the alpha4-beta1 integrin (VLA-4) interaction with VCAM-1 on vascular endothelial cells, which facilitates extravasation (diapedesis) of CD4+ T cells; it also prevents alpha4-beta7 integrin binding to MAdCAM-1 on endothelial cells of venules.
(c)
It blocks diapedesis of autoreactive T cells into the brain and so prevents attack on the myelin sheath; blocking effector-cell entry into inflammatory sites (diapedesis steps: chemoattraction, rolling adhesion, tight adhesion, transmigration) has high therapeutic potential.
(d)
• Uses: chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease of the brain (multiple sclerosis) and Crohn's disease (alpha4-beta7/MAdCAM-1 blockade).
• Vedolizumab (approved for Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis) produces fewer side effects due to its alpha4-beta7-restricted binding.

(a)
Glucocorticoids (steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs).
• Short-acting: hydrocortisone, cortisone. Intermediate-acting: prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone, triamcinolone. Long-acting: betamethasone, dexamethasone, paramethasone. Topical: beclomethasone dipropionate, budesonide, fluocinolone acetonide, fluocortolone.
(b)
They inhibit MHC II expression and proliferation of T lymphocytes.
• They also act by indirect inhibition of phospholipase A2: they induce synthesis of the protein lipocortin-1, which inhibits phospholipase A2, so arachidonic acid and prostaglandin formation falls.
(c)
Production of IL-1, IL-2 and IL-6 is decreased, so helper T cells are not activated.
• A lymphopenic effect results from sequestration of T lymphocytes in tissues.
(d)
Used with cyclosporine to prevent graft rejection; autoimmune diseases (RA, SLE), haematological conditions, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, eye conditions.
• Also adrenal insufficiency, collagen diseases, bronchial asthma, severe allergic reactions, skin diseases, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, cerebral oedema, organ transplantation and skin allograft, septic shock.
(e)
Susceptibility to infections (linked to the immunosuppressive and lymphopenic action), delayed wound healing, osteoporosis, growth retardation in children.
• Peptic ulceration, Cushing habitus (moon face, buffalo hump), hyperglycaemia, muscular weakness, psychiatric disorders, withdrawal syndrome.
questions.question:
A transplant recipient is given a drug class that is usually combined with cyclosporine to prevent graft rejection. The drugs inhibit MHC II expression and T-lymphocyte proliferation, lower IL-1, IL-2 and IL-6 production, and cause lymphopenia through sequestration of T lymphocytes in tissues. The same class is also used in rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and eye conditions.
(a) Identify the drug class and give examples.
(b) State the molecular and cellular target and mechanism of action.
(c) Describe the effect on the immune response.
(d) State the therapeutic uses.
(e) State the key adverse effects, including those linked to the mechanism.

Describe the H1-receptor antagonists (antihistamines) under the following headings:
(a) Classification
(b) Mechanism of action
(c) Examples
(d) Uses
(e) Adverse effects
Explain the pharmacological basis of efficacy and limitation:
(f) Why first-generation agents are sedating with many side effects
(g) Why second-generation agents are non-sedating and longer acting
(h) Why antihistamines are not indicated for asthma
Distinguish between related drugs or classes:
(i) Loratadine
(j) Cetirizine and fexofenadine
(k) First- versus second-generation agents as sleep aids and for motion sickness
(l) First-generation drug interactions
questions.answerText:
(a)
First generation: ethanolamines, ethylenediamines, alkylamines, phenothiazines, piperazines, piperidines. Second generation: piperidines and piperazines (non-sedating).
(b)
They competitively block histamine or act as inverse agonists at histamine receptors (G protein-coupled).
(c)
First generation: diphenhydramine, clemastine, tripelennamine/pyrilamine, chlorpheniramine, promethazine, hydroxyzine, cyclizine, meclizine, cyproheptadine. Second generation: loratadine, fexofenadine, cetirizine, desloratadine, azelastine, astemizole, acrivastine.
(d)
Allergic rhinitis, urticaria, dermatoses, contact dermatitis, allergic conjunctivitis (ophthalmic agents); adjunct in anaphylaxis; first-generation also as sedatives and for motion sickness, nausea and vertigo.
(e)
First generation: sedation (paradoxical excitation in children), dizziness, fatigue, antimuscarinic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention), overdose with excitation, tremors, hallucination, hypotension; they cross the placenta.
(f)
They penetrate the CNS and have low specificity, interacting with muscarinic, alpha-adrenergic and serotonin receptors as well as histamine receptors.
(g)
They are lipophobic with low capacity to cross the blood-brain barrier, higher H1 selectivity with no anticholinergic effects, and a duration of action of 4-24 h; some also act on leukotrienes or as anti-platelet-activating factor.
(h)
Histamine is only one of several mediators of the bronchial reaction; second-generation compounds are used only as adjuncts in asthmatics with rhinitis, urticaria or dermatitis.
(i)
Loratadine undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism by CYP3A4 to the active desloratadine; CYP inhibitors (macrolides, imidazole antifungals) raise its level and can cause toxicity.
(j)
Cetirizine and fexofenadine are not subject to these drug interactions.
(k)
First-generation agents (diphenhydramine, doxylamine) are sedative and used for insomnia and motion sickness (diphenhydramine, dimenhydrinate, cyclizine, meclizine, promethazine); second-generation agents have no value as somnifacients.
(l)
First-generation drugs potentiate CNS depressants (alcohol, opioids, sedatives), are additive with antimuscarinics, should not be taken with MAOIs, and may decrease the effect of cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine).

questions.question:
A person is stung by a bee and soon develops a fall in blood pressure, difficulty in breathing and shock.
(a) Identify the immunological mechanism and hypersensitivity type involved.
(b) Name the drug classes or agents used for management.
(c) Justify the choice of each through its mechanism.
(d) State the main adverse effects of the agents named.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity, anaphylactic shock. The individual must first be sensitized; the reaction is caused by inappropriate IgE production, and IgE has an affinity for mast cells and basophils.
• A bee sting introduces allergen directly into the circulation. When IgE meets its specific allergen, the mast cell discharges vasoactive substances (histamine is the mediator of allergy); the massive release causes fall in blood pressure, shock and difficulty in breathing.
(b)
Epinephrine (physiologic antagonist), H1-receptor antagonists as adjuncts (together with an H2 antagonist and epinephrine), and corticosteroids (severe allergic reactions). Mast cell stabilisers (cromolyn, nedocromil) are release inhibitors.
(c)
Epinephrine has smooth muscle actions opposite those of histamine, acting via different receptors, and is life-saving in systemic anaphylaxis.
• H1 antagonists competitively block histamine or act as inverse agonists; release inhibitors reduce mast cell degranulation caused by antigen-IgE interaction.
• Corticosteroids inhibit phospholipase A2 (via lipocortin-1), reducing prostaglandin and leukotriene synthesis.
(d)
First-generation H1 antagonists: sedation (paradoxical excitation in children), dizziness, fatigue, antimuscarinic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention).
• Corticosteroids: susceptibility to infections, delayed wound healing, osteoporosis, hyperglycaemia, peptic ulceration, Cushing habitus.

(a)
Muromonab CD3.
(b)
It binds the CD3 antigen near the TCR on helper T cells; this obstructs the binding of MHC II antigen to the TCR.
(c)
Participation of T cells in the immune response is prevented; T cells disappear from circulation, leading to an immune blocked state.
(d)
Use: acute organ transplant rejection.
• Key adverse effect: cytokine release syndrome with flu-like symptoms (chills, rigor, wheezing, fever, headache, tremor, myalgia, arthralgia, weakness); occasionally aseptic meningitis, intragraft thrombosis, pulmonary oedema, seizures and a shock-like state.
• Pre-treatment with a high dose of corticosteroid reduces the reaction.

questions.answerText:
(a)
A propionic acid derivative NSAID.
(b)
The same mechanism and pharmacological actions as aspirin, except that it is a reversible inhibitor of the COX enzymes.
(c)
Rapidly absorbed after oral ingestion; half-life 1-2 h; highly bound to plasma proteins; excreted through the kidney as metabolites.
(d)
Analgesic, antipyretic, anti-inflammatory, acute gouty arthritis, patent ductus arteriosus, dysmenorrhoea. Preparations: oral, topical cream for osteoarthritis, liquid gel for post-surgical dental pain, intravenous for patent ductus arteriosus.
(e)
Gastric upset (less frequent than aspirin), fluid retention, hypersensitivity reactions, ocular disturbances, rare haematologic effects (agranulocytosis and aplastic anaemia).
(f)
Classical NSAIDs inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2 (reversibly, except aspirin); ibuprofen is not COX-2 selective.
(g)
Inhibiting COX reduces PG production; PGs sensitize nociceptors to stimulation (e.g. by 5-HT, bradykinin), and IL-1 induces COX-2 in the brain with PGE production and fever, so NSAIDs are analgesic and antipyretic.
(h)
It is more potent as an anti-inflammatory than aspirin.
(i)
Inhibition of COX-1 reduces house-keeping PGs, giving gastrointestinal side effects and bronchospasm; loss of PGE2/PGI2 cytoprotection leads to mucosal ulceration.
(j)
Concomitant ibuprofen antagonizes the irreversible platelet inhibition of aspirin, limiting aspirin's cardioprotective effect.
(k)
Contraindicated in peptic ulcer, aspirin allergy, kidney impairment, liver disease, pregnancy and haemophilia.

A widely used, effective and inexpensive ethanolamine antihistamine penetrates the CNS and produces relatively strong sedation; it is also used for motion sickness and as a sleep aid.
(a) Identify the agent and its class.
(b) State the pharmacokinetic features.
(c) State the relevant drug interactions or metabolic considerations.
(d) State the clinical consequence.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diphenhydramine, a first-generation H1-receptor antagonist (ethanolamine) that competitively blocks histamine or acts as an inverse agonist.
(b)
Well absorbed after oral administration, peak blood levels in 1-2 h, therapeutic effect lasting 4-6 h; generally metabolized in the liver through hydroxylation; metabolites and a small amount of parent compound are excreted in the urine.
• Children tend to eliminate antihistamines more rapidly than adults; hepatic impairment slows elimination.
(c)
Potentiates other CNS depressants (alcohol, opioids, sedatives); additive with classical antimuscarinics; patients taking MAOIs should not take antihistamines; its anticholinergic action may decrease the effectiveness of cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine).
(d)
Sedation, diminished alertness and motor incoordination; paradoxical hyperactivity in young children; antimuscarinic effects (dryness, blurred vision, urine retention, constipation).
• Acute overdose: central excitation, tremors, hallucination, hypotension, features of belladonna poisoning, and death from respiratory or cardiovascular failure. It can cross the placenta (caution in pregnancy) and is contraindicated where wakefulness is critical.

questions.question:
Describe the prostaglandin analogues under the following headings:
(a) Classification
(b) Mechanism of action
(c) Examples
(d) Uses
(e) Adverse effects
Explain the pharmacological basis of efficacy and limitation:
(f) Why misoprostol prevents NSAID-induced ulcer
(g) Why epoprostenol (PGI2) is used in pulmonary hypertension and extracorporeal circulation
(h) Why latanoprost lowers eye pressure
Distinguish between related drugs or classes:
(i) Dinoprostone and alprostadil
(j) Alprostadil in impotence versus patent ductus arteriosus
(k) PGI2 versus TXA2
(l) PGE2 effects on platelets by dose
questions.answerText:
(a)
Analogues of PGE1 (misoprostol, alprostadil), PGE2 (dinoprostone), PGI2 (epoprostenol) and PGF2-alpha (latanoprost, a stable PGF2-alpha).
(b)
They mimic prostanoid actions: PGI2 and PGE2 raise cAMP and lower smooth muscle intracellular calcium (vasodilation); PGE2 and PGF2-alpha contract the uterus; PGE1 relaxes corpora cavernosa smooth muscle.
(c)
Dinoprostone, alprostadil, misoprostol, epoprostenol, latanoprost.
(d)
Dinoprostone: promote labour via cervical ripening. Alprostadil: impotence (replaced by PDE-V inhibitors), maintain patency of the neonatal ductus arteriosus until surgery. Misoprostol: prevent NSAID ulcer. Epoprostenol: primary and secondary pulmonary hypertension, heparin replacement in some haemodialysis, prevent platelet aggregation in extracorporeal circuits. Latanoprost: glaucoma.
(e)
Misoprostol is not used in pregnant women or those planning pregnancy, and with diclofenac it gives diarrhoea.
(f)
NSAIDs cause loss of PGE2 and PGI2 mediated inhibition of acid secretion and cytoprotection; misoprostol, a synthetic methyl ester analogue of PGE1, is used to prevent NSAID-induced ulcer.
(g)
PGI2 lowers peripheral, pulmonary and coronary vascular resistance, is a vasodilator and inhibits platelet aggregation.
(h)
Prostaglandin derivatives of PGE2, PGF2-alpha and PGD2 lower intraocular pressure; latanoprost is a stable PGF2-alpha with an ocular hypotensive effect.
(i)
Dinoprostone (PGE2 analogue) promotes labour through cervical ripening; alprostadil (PGE1) is used in impotence and to keep the ductus arteriosus patent.
(j)
In impotence alprostadil has been replaced by PDE-V inhibitors; in neonates it maintains ductus patency until corrective surgery.
(k)
PGI2 (endothelium) is a vasodilator and inhibits platelet aggregation, opposing TXA2 (platelets), which causes vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation and is inhibited by aspirin.
(l)
PGE2 at low dose enhances platelet aggregation and at higher concentration inhibits it; PGI2 and PGD2 inhibit aggregation.

questions.question:
A patient with bronchial asthma is given an oral drug that competitively blocks leukotriene receptors in the airway (a second agent in the same setting directly inhibits 5-lipoxygenase).
(a) Identify the drug class and agents.
(b) State the molecular and cellular target and mechanism of action.
(c) Describe the effect on the immune response.
(d) State the therapeutic use and key adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Leukotriene receptor antagonists: montelukast and zafirlukast; the 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor is zileuton.
(b)
They block the leukotriene (CysLT1) receptor in the airway, functionally decreasing the ability of mast cells to degranulate; zileuton directly inhibits the enzyme 5-lipoxygenase, which synthesizes leukotrienes.
(c)
Leukotrienes cause bronchospasm, mucus secretion, microvascular permeability and airway oedema; LTB4 is a chemoattractant for neutrophils, eosinophils, T lymphocytes and monocytes. Blocking them dampens the inflammatory response.
(d)
Use: bronchial asthma. Pharmacokinetics: well absorbed orally, highly plasma protein bound, metabolized by CYP2C9 (montelukast also by CYP3A4); half-life montelukast 3-6 h, zafirlukast 8-12 h.
• Adverse effects: headache, abdominal pain, eczema, dizziness, dyspepsia, fever, gastroenteritis, nasal congestion, rash, urticaria, bronchitis, cough, upper respiratory tract infection, allergic granulomatous angiitis (Churg-Strauss syndrome). Zileuton use is limited by elevated liver enzymes.

(a)
Beta-2 sympathomimetics (short-acting and long-acting), anticholinergics, and methylxanthines.
(b)
Beta-2 agonists stimulate beta-2 receptors, raising cAMP in bronchial muscle cells and causing relaxation. Anticholinergics block muscarinic cholinergic receptors, decreasing cGMP and smooth muscle contractility. Methylxanthines decrease TNF-alpha and leukotriene release and relax smooth muscle.
(c)
Short-acting: salbutamol, terbutaline. Long-acting: salmeterol, formoterol. Anticholinergics: ipratropium bromide, tiotropium bromide. Methylxanthine: theophylline (naturally occurring with caffeine and theobromine).
(d)
Asthma; short-acting beta-2 agonists abort and terminate attacks; ipratropium combined with a beta-2 agonist can be used in severe asthma.
(e)
Beta-2 agonists: muscle tremors (dose related), downregulation of bronchial beta-2 receptors, cardiac arrhythmias, palpitation, restlessness, nervousness, throat irritation, ankle oedema. Anticholinergics: dry mouth, constipation. Theophylline: rapid heartbeat, nausea, palpitation, agitation, vomiting, seizures.
(f)
They act directly on the beta-2 adrenoceptors of bronchial smooth muscle; they also inhibit mediator release from mast cells and TNF-alpha release from monocytes and increase mucus clearance through action on cilia.
(g)
Methylxanthine use has declined because of the high risk of severe life-threatening toxicity and numerous drug interactions.
(h)
Tremors, downregulation of bronchial beta-2 receptors, arrhythmia and other side effects limit their use.
(i)
Short-acting (salbutamol, terbutaline): maximum effect within 30 min, duration 3-5 h. Long-acting (salmeterol, formoterol): duration 8-12 h.
(j)
Ipratropium acts through muscarinic block (decreased cGMP) whereas beta-2 agonists act through raised cAMP; the combination produces more marked and longer-lasting bronchodilatation.
(k)
Theophylline is well absorbed orally, distributed in all tissues, crosses the placenta and is secreted in milk; half-life 7-12 h in adults, 3-5 h in children; erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, oral contraceptives and allopurinol decrease its metabolism and raise its level.
(l)
Cromolyn, salmeterol, ipratropium bromide and formoterol are only effective by inhalation; inhaled aerosol delivery is site specific and enhances the therapeutic ratio.

(a)
Etanercept.
(b)
A biologic DMARD (genetically engineered protein molecule that blocks inflammatory cytokines) in the TNF-inhibitor family.
(c)
It binds TNF-alpha, preventing it from interacting with its receptors.
• It differs from infliximab and adalimumab: infliximab binds both monomeric and trimeric (inactive and active) TNF, whereas etanercept binds mainly the active trimeric form in a less stable manner, and also binds TNF-beta.
(d)
Route: subcutaneous.
• Recombinant cytokines and antibodies in general have limited shelf life, require special/controlled storage and are typically administered by a physician; production requires sterile conditions and multiple purification stages.

questions.question:
A patient with active rheumatoid arthritis, in whom IL-1 and TNF-alpha have a major pathogenic role, is given a subcutaneous biologic that contains both the human TNF receptor and the Fc portion of human IgG1.
(a) Identify the biologic.
(b) Classify it.
(c) Outline the pathway it blocks.
(d) State the route of administration and the storage or handling needs.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Prophylactic or therapeutic products: vaccines (live, killed), toxoids, immune sera, human immunoglobulins, in-vivo diagnostics, antibody-targeted therapeutics, diagnostics.
(b)
They modify the immune status of the recipient by providing immunity to infectious disease or by provoking an indication of immune status; vaccines stimulate active immunity, immune sera and immunoglobulins give passive immunity.
(c)
Live: Sabin polio, smallpox, measles, yellow fever, rabies, BCG. Killed: pertussis, Salk polio, rabies, typhoid, cholera, measles, mumps. Toxoids: diphtheria, tetanus, botulinum. Sera: diphtheria and botulinum antitoxin, equine tetanus antitoxin, anti-venins.
(d)
Live and killed vaccines and toxoids prevent disease (toxoids for tetanus, diphtheria, botulism and clostridial infections); immune sera for prophylaxis and treatment of venomous bites and stings; immunoglobulins in IM, IV (tetanus) and intravenous forms.
(e)
Live vaccines: mutation making the organism highly virulent, and contamination with virulent strains. Killed vaccines: poor protection and toxicity.
(f)
Live vaccines contain attenuated living organisms that retain immunogenicity, but the organism can mutate to high virulence or the vaccine can be contaminated with virulent strains.
(g)
Killed vaccines may lose protective antigens during killing, so each dose must contain sufficient antigen; they contain all components and can be toxic, so the total amount is divided into several doses over days or weeks.
(h)
Immune sera are antibodies from immunised animals (horses, mules, donkeys, sheep, goats); the immunity they confer is passive, and their use is limited nowadays.
(i)
A toxoid is a bacterial toxin whose toxicity has been inactivated by chemical or gentle heat treatment while immunogenicity is kept, and it does not revert to a toxin; killed vaccines are whole inactivated organisms.
(j)
Normal immunoglobulin has low antibody titres representative of the population (pooled from 1000 or more individuals); specific immunoglobulin has high titres of a particular antibody from people recently infected or immunised.
(k)
IgG crosses the placenta, neutralises toxins and coats bacteria for phagocytosis; IgA is found in mucous membrane secretions and coats infective agents to prevent binding to mucosal cells.
(l)
Tuberculin, brucellin, histoplasmin, mullein and coccidioidin demonstrate immune response and previous exposure; the Schick test detects protective immunity to diphtheria; the Mantoux test detects sensitization by mycobacterial proteins.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Short-acting (hydrocortisone, cortisone); intermediate (prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone, triamcinolone); long-acting (betamethasone, dexamethasone, paramethasone); topical (beclomethasone dipropionate, budesonide, fluocinolone acetonide, fluocortolone).
(b)
They induce lipocortin-1, which inhibits phospholipase A2, so arachidonic acid, prostaglandins, thromboxane, prostacyclin and leukotrienes are not formed. They also inhibit MHC II expression, T-lymphocyte proliferation and IL-1, IL-2, IL-6 production.
(c)
Adrenal insufficiency, arthritis, collagen diseases (SLE, scleroderma), bronchial asthma, severe allergic reactions, autoimmune diseases, skin diseases, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, cerebral oedema, organ transplantation and skin allograft, septic shock.
(d)
Susceptibility to infections, delayed wound healing, osteoporosis, growth retardation in children, peptic ulceration, Cushing habitus, hyperglycaemia, muscular weakness, psychiatric disorders, withdrawal syndrome.
(e)
Used for a short period at low doses during flares; bone thinning (calcium and vitamin D supplements advised), weight gain, diabetes and immunosuppression; low-dose steroids may be an alternative to more toxic DMARDs in pregnant, elderly or debilitated patients.
(f)
Relative anti-inflammatory potency (cortisol = 1): prednisone 4, prednisolone 5, methylprednisolone 5, triamcinolone 5, paramethasone 10, betamethasone 25-40, dexamethasone 30.
(g)
By blocking phospholipase A2 they act above both the cyclo-oxygenase and lipoxygenase pathways. NSAIDs do not inhibit lipoxygenase at clinical doses and push more substrate to the LOX pathway, increasing leukotriene formation; corticosteroids inhibit eicosanoid synthesis and so limit leukotrienes.
(h)
Their side effects are more pronounced than those of NSAIDs, so they are indicated only for a short period at low doses during RA flares.
(i)
Hydrocortisone (short-acting, natural) has anti-inflammatory potency 1 versus 30 for dexamethasone (long-acting).
(j)
Hydrocortisone salt-retaining activity 1.0; dexamethasone 0.
(k)
Fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid) has anti-inflammatory activity 10 but salt retention 250, whereas the long-acting glucocorticoids have 0.
(l)
Corticosteroids have more pronounced side effects than NSAIDs; NSAID effects centre on ulcer, GIT disturbance and bronchospasm.
