Describe immunodeficiency as an abnormality of the immune system:
(a) Its types
(b) Primary immunodeficiency
(c) Secondary immunodeficiency
(d) AIDS
Relate its parts to examples and clinical features:
(e) Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
(f) B-cell deficiency
(g) T-cell deficiency
(h) NK cell deficiency
Explain the clinical implications and what trade-off or limitation results:
(i) The role of drugs and therapy in causing deficiency
(j) Why HIV control fails
(k) The parallel with ageing
(l) The choice of active or passive immunity
questions.answerText:
(a)
Primary immunodeficiency syndrome, secondary immunodeficiency syndrome, and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
(b)
A hereditary deficiency of cellular, humoral or both mechanisms: agammaglobulinaemia or dysgammaglobulinaemia from B-cell deficiency, thymic dysplasia giving T-cell deficiency, and Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (combined).
(c)
Results from another disease: lymphoid tumours, haematologic disorders involving phagocytes, protein-losing conditions (nephrotic syndrome), diabetes mellitus and renal failure (mechanisms not well understood), and drugs and irradiation for cancer therapy.
(d)
T-cell dysfunction due to a viral agent; loss of T-cell activity makes the patient susceptible to a wide variety of rare or unusual infections; HIV depletes CD4+ T cells.
(e)
X-linked recessive (almost exclusively boys); persistent thrombocytopenia, small platelets, eczema/atopy, cellular and humoral immunodeficiency, risk of autoimmune disease and haematologic malignancy; commonly IgM deficiency.
(f)
The host cannot make antibodies and presents with recurrent bacterial infections; opsonization does not occur and phagocytes cannot compete with growing bacteria.
(g)
Recurrent infections with parasites, viruses and intracellular bacteria; seen in transplant patients suppressed to prevent rejection and in HIV infection.
(h)
A girl without NK cells had life-threatening chickenpox, recurrent ear infections, disseminated CMV and herpes simplex; NK cells are important in controlling herpes viruses, which downregulate MHC I.
(i)
Many therapeutically used immunosuppressive drugs, particularly after transplant surgery, and cancer drugs and irradiation, may affect immunologic function.
(j)
The immune system initially controls HIV-1 then fails: viral escape by mutations in CTL epitopes, functional impairment of HIV-specific CD8+ T cells, and high immune activation.
(k)
Lifespan of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells is shortened to about a third; terminally differentiated cells accumulate (immunosenescence); AIDS is much more severe immunosenescence than normal ageing.
(l)
Active immunity is not applicable in the immunodeficient, whereas passive immunity (ready-made antibody) is applicable in them.

(a)
Cytokines are low molecular weight regulatory proteins produced by many cell types (activated lymphocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, endothelial, epithelial and connective tissue cells) that mediate and regulate immune and inflammatory reactions.
(b)
Pro-inflammatory (IL-6, IL-1, TNF-alpha) and anti-inflammatory (IL-10, TGF-beta); also interleukins, interferons (IFN-alpha antiviral, IFN-beta anti-tumour), TNF, colony stimulating factors and TGF.
(c)
Pleiotropic, redundant, can synergize or antagonize each other, can stimulate production of other cytokines and influence expression of cytokine receptors.
(d)
Autocrine and paracrine actions, rarely endocrine.
(e)
IFN-alpha is used in chronic hepatitis C and cancer; IL-2 and IFN enhance T-cell activation in immunodeficiency disease.
(f)
Filgrastim, a synthetic colony stimulating factor, is used in neutropenia.
(g)
Anakinra (recombinant IL-1 antagonist) is used in rheumatoid arthritis; infliximab (anti-TNF-alpha) in severe Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.
(h)
TNF-alpha mediates local inflammation; IL-1 acts on endothelium; TNF-alpha, IL-6 and IL-1 cause fever (brain); IL-6 and IL-1 drive acute phase proteins (liver); TNF-alpha and IL-6 drive leukocyte production (bone marrow).
(i)
Specific proteins that mediate inflammation can be inhibited, unlike with chemical drugs; their activity is well studied in animal models; recombinant proteins are easier and cheaper to make than before.
(j)
Pleiotropy means several processes are affected in parallel; redundancy means blocking one cytokine can be compensated by others, although a different cytokine blocker can be substituted in incomplete remission or intolerance.
(k)
Production is expensive (sterile conditions, multiple purification stages); biologics have limited shelf life, need controlled storage and are typically given by a physician.
(l)
Inhibiting pro-inflammatory cytokines can compromise host defence against infection; inhibiting regulatory cytokines can result in autoimmunity or tissue damage.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Inhibition of COX-1 by the NSAID, with loss of house-keeping prostaglandins; gastric peptic ulcer is especially linked to aspirin and GI bleeding especially to indomethacin.
(b)
COX-1 is constitutive with gastric epithelial cytoprotection; loss of PGE2 and PGI2 mediated inhibition of acid secretion and cytoprotection, and of PGI2 inhibition of LTB4-mediated neutrophil adhesion and activation, increases leukocyte-endothelial interaction, capillary obstruction, ischaemic cell injury, proteases and oxygen radicals, and mucosal ulceration.
(c)
Non-selective NSAIDs inhibit COX-1 and COX-2; preferential COX-2 inhibitors (nimesulide, meloxicam, nabumetone) and selective COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib, parecoxib, rofecoxib) cause little gastric damage and do not inhibit platelet aggregation.
• Selective COX-2 inhibitors have renal toxicity (not recommended in severe renal insufficiency) and a high incidence of cardiovascular thrombotic events with some, such as rofecoxib.
(d)
NSAIDs are contraindicated in peptic ulcers. Diclofenac with misoprostol decreases upper GI ulceration but results in diarrhoea; diclofenac with omeprazole prevents recurrent bleeding; selective COX-2 inhibitors have a lower incidence of gastric upset.

A patient has recurrent reversible airway obstruction with bronchial hyper-reactivity and airway inflammation, triggered by viral infection, exercise or atmospheric pollutants; an early reaction occurs 10-30 minutes after trigger exposure and a late reaction after 6-9 hours.
(a) Identify the immunological mechanism and hypersensitivity type involved.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Asthma, a chronic inflammatory condition; asthma is classed among Type I (IgE-mediated) atopic allergies.
• Early phase: IgE binds mast cells and basophils; on re-exposure, cross-linking releases histamine, proinflammatory cytokines, leukotrienes and prostaglandins, causing smooth muscle contraction, vascular permeability and mucus secretion. Late phase: neutrophils and other inflammatory cells are attracted by chemotaxis into inflamed airways.
(b)
Bronchodilators (beta-2 agonists, anticholinergics, methylxanthines) and anti-inflammatory agents (inhaled corticosteroids), plus mast cell stabilisers, leukotriene modifiers and anti-IgE antibody.
(c)
Pharmacotherapy aims to reverse bronchial smooth muscle constriction and airway inflammation. Beta-2 agonists raise cAMP, relax bronchial muscle and inhibit mast cell mediator release.
• Inhaled corticosteroids decrease cytokines that recruit and activate eosinophils and promote IgE production and IgE receptor expression, and reduce mucus, oedema and exudation; effect peaks after 4-7 days.
(d)
Systemic steroids are indicated for acute severe exacerbations not responding to initial inhaled beta-2 agonists every 20 minutes for 3-4 doses.
(e)
Beta-2 agonists: tremors, receptor downregulation, arrhythmias, palpitation. Inhaled corticosteroids: oral candidiasis, dysphonia, throat irritation, endocrine suppression. Anticholinergics: dry mouth, constipation.

(a)
Rheumatoid arthritis, a chronic autoimmune illness; it is classed among chronic immune complex diseases (Type III hypersensitivity).
• Activated CD4+ T cells infiltrate the joint and release IL-2, IL-6 and IFN-gamma, which attract B cells and macrophages; plasma cells release rheumatoid factor, initiating cartilage and bone damage; macrophages release IL-1 and TNF-alpha, causing synovial endothelial cell and fibroblast proliferation, neovascularization and remodelling.
(b)
NSAIDs (first line), corticosteroids (short courses during flares), DMARDs (non-biologic: methotrexate, sulfasalazine, chloroquine, cyclophosphamide, leflunomide; biologic).
(c)
NSAIDs inhibit COX and so reduce prostaglandin and thromboxane; corticosteroids reduce inflammation by acting on phospholipase A2 and eicosanoid synthesis.
• DMARDs are slow-acting and promote remission by slowing joint destruction; methotrexate suppresses cytokine production; biologics block TNF, IL-6, IL-1 or CD20 B cells.
(d)
Calcium and vitamin D supplements are advised alongside corticosteroids.
(e)
NSAIDs: ulcer, GI upset. Corticosteroids: bone thinning, weight gain, diabetes, immunosuppression.
• Methotrexate: nausea, mouth ulcer, hair loss, cytopenias, elevated liver enzymes, pneumonitis, bone marrow suppression. Anti-TNF agents: serious infections.
questions.question:
A patient has chronic joint stiffness, synovium inflammation with thickening and excessive synovial fluid, with periods of remission and flares.
(a) Identify the immunological mechanism and hypersensitivity category involved.
(b) Name the drug classes used for management.
(c) Justify the choices through mechanism.
(d) State the supportive measures advised alongside corticosteroids.
(e) State the main adverse effects.

questions.answerText:
(a)
A complex of a sulfonamide (sulfapyridine) and salicylate; a non-biologic DMARD.
(b)
It is a prodrug metabolized to sulfapyridine and 5-aminosalicylic acid; sulfapyridine is thought to reduce secretion of interleukin (IL)-8 and monocyte chemoattractant protein (MCP).
(c)
About 10-20% of an oral dose is absorbed; half-life 6-17 h.
(d)
Typically used in irritable bowel disease and causes remission in active rheumatoid arthritis.
(e)
Nausea, vomiting, headache, rash, hemolytic anaemia.
(f)
Sulfapyridine is thought to reduce IL-8 and MCP secretion.
(g)
DMARDs are slow-acting drugs that promote remission by slowing or stopping progression of joint destruction and deformity.
(h)
Methotrexate may be used with other DMARDs such as hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine.
(i)
Hemolytic anaemia along with nausea, vomiting, headache and rash.
(j)
Only a small part (10-20%) of an oral dose is absorbed.
questions.question:
Describe the pharmacology of sulfasalazine:
(a) Class
(b) Mechanism of action
(c) Pharmacokinetics
(d) Uses
(e) Adverse effects
State the basis of its selectivity and effect on mediators:
(f) The effect of its active moiety on chemokines and cytokines
(g) The type of antirheumatic drug and speed of action
(h) Its use with other drugs
Explain the basis of toxicity and absorption:
(i) The toxicity pattern
(j) The extent of its absorption

questions.answerText:
(a)
A primary signal from the TCR engaging peptide-MHC (TCR-CD3 complex, with CD4/CD8 coreceptors) and a costimulatory signal from CD28 binding B7-1 (CD80)/B7-2 (CD86), both on the same activated professional APC.
(b)
TCR engagement induces NFAT, AP-1 and NF-kB; a key downstream product is IL-2, essential for T-cell proliferation and survival; CD25 (IL-2 receptor) is expressed on activated T cells.
(c)
Ca2+ binds calmodulin to activate calcineurin, which dephosphorylates NFAT; NFAT moves to the nucleus and transcribes IL-2, TNF-alpha and GM-CSF, leading to cytotoxic T-cell stimulation and proliferation.
(d)
CTLA-4 binds B7 with higher affinity than CD28 and dampens activation; PD1 and PSGL-1 fine-tune the response; T cells that engage peptide-MHC without costimulation become anergic.
(e)
Cyclosporin (via cyclophyllin) and tacrolimus (via FKBP) inhibit calcineurin, halting cytokine gene transcription and IL-2 production; lymphocytes arrest in G0/G1.
(f)
Muromonab CD3 binds CD3 near the TCR and obstructs MHC II antigen binding to the TCR; T cells disappear from circulation.
(g)
Glucocorticoids inhibit MHC II expression and T-cell proliferation and reduce IL-1, IL-2 and IL-6 so helper T cells are not activated.
(h)
Numerous activating or blocking monoclonal antibodies interfere with the fine-tuning of TCR signalling, allowing pharmacological modulation of the immune response.
(i)
Suppressing T-cell activation prevents graft rejection and treats autoimmune disease.
(j)
Cyclosporin suppresses cell-mediated immunity yet leaves enough humoral immunity to combat bacterial infection and is not toxic to bone marrow.
(k)
T-cell deficiency gives recurrent infections with parasites, viruses and intracellular bacteria, as seen in transplant patients suppressed to prevent rejection; glucocorticoids cause lymphopenia and susceptibility to infection.
(l)
Muromonab CD3 produces cytokine release syndrome (flu-like symptoms, shock-like state), reduced by high-dose corticosteroid pre-treatment.

(b) The intracellular signal pathway to cytokine production
(c) The calcium-calcineurin step
(d) The negative regulators
Relate its parts to examples of drugs acting at these points:
(e) Cyclosporin and tacrolimus
(f) Muromonab CD3
(g) Glucocorticoids
(h) Monoclonal antibodies that modulate TCR signalling
Explain why the strategy works clinically and what trade-off or limitation results:
(i) The clinical goal
(j) The advantage of selective T-cell suppression
(k) The consequence of T-cell deficiency
(l) The specific toxicity of the antibody approach

A patient with rheumatoid arthritis whose disease is refractory to, or who cannot take, anti-IL-6 or anti-TNF biologics is given a once-daily injectable that is a non-glycosylated recombinant protein.
(a) Identify the biologic.
(b) Classify it.
(c) Outline the pathway it modulates.
(d) State the route of administration, the dosing frequency and the storage or handling needs.
(e) Identify the toxicity or risk linked to its use.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Anakinra.
(b)
A biologic DMARD: a non-glycosylated recombinant form of the IL-1 receptor antagonist (an IL-1 receptor blocker). Related IL-1 agents: rilonacept (a fusion protein that binds IL-1, being evaluated for gout) and canakinumab (being evaluated for COPD).
(c)
It binds the IL-1 receptor and decreases the activity of IL-1 alpha and IL-1 beta; IL-1 and TNF-alpha are the primary inflammatory cytokines in RA pathogenesis.
• It can be used as monotherapy or with anti-TNF agents.
(d)
Once-daily injection (the daily injection is a disadvantage).
• Recombinant proteins in general have limited shelf life, need special/controlled storage, and are typically administered by a physician.
(e)
An itchy rash may appear at the injection site.
• Inhibiting a pro-inflammatory cytokine can compromise host defence against infection.

questions.question:
Describe the pharmacology of diclofenac:
(a) Class
(b) Mechanism of action
(c) Clinical uses
(d) Preparations
(e) Adverse effects
State the basis of its selectivity and its effect on mediators:
(f) Its COX selectivity
(g) Its relative anti-inflammatory versus analgesic potency
(h) The basis of its gastric effect
Explain the basis of toxicity and drug interaction:
(i) Renal and hepatic toxicity
(j) Combination with misoprostol or omeprazole
(k) Interactions and contraindications shared by NSAIDs
questions.answerText:
(a)
An aryl (acetic acid) derivative NSAID, given as diclofenac sodium.
(b)
A non-selective inhibitor of COX-1 and COX-2.
(c)
Any inflammatory condition, musculoskeletal pain, dysmenorrhoea, acute gouty arthritis, fever, post-ophthalmic inflammation (local), solar keratoses (topical gel).
(d)
Diclofenac with misoprostol, diclofenac with omeprazole, 1% ophthalmic preparation, 3% topical gel for solar keratoses, rectal suppository for analgesia or post-operative nausea.
(e)
Gastric upset, renal impairment, elevation of serum aminotransferase, salt and water retention.
(f)
It inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2 non-selectively.
(g)
It is more potent as an anti-inflammatory than as an analgesic or antipyretic.
(h)
COX inhibition lowers PGs: loss of PGE2 and PGI2 inhibition of acid secretion and cytoprotection, and of PGI2 inhibition of LTB4-mediated neutrophil adhesion, leads to mucosal ulceration.
(i)
Renal impairment, elevated serum aminotransferase and salt and water retention are the toxicities.
(j)
Diclofenac with misoprostol decreases upper gastrointestinal ulceration but results in diarrhoea; diclofenac with omeprazole is used to prevent recurrent bleeding.
(k)
NSAIDs potentiate the gastric irritant effect of alcohol and the hypoglycaemic effect of oral hypoglycaemic drugs; contraindicated in pregnancy, haemophilia, hypersensitivity, viral infections (mainly in children) and peptic ulcers.

questions.question:
A transplant recipient maintained on cyclosporin rejects the graft after an enzyme-inducing drug is added. Another recipient on cyclosporin develops toxicity after treatment with erythromycin or ketoconazole, or with vancomycin, amphotericin B or an NSAID.
(a) Identify the cause.
(b) Explain the underlying pharmacological basis.
(c) Differentiate cyclosporin from the related drug tacrolimus.
(d) Reason to the management decision.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A drug interaction altering cyclosporin exposure.
(b)
Enzyme inducers decrease cyclosporin levels, giving transplant rejection; erythromycin, ketoconazole and related drugs increase its levels, giving toxicity.
• Nephrotoxic drugs (vancomycin, amphotericin B, NSAIDs) increase its toxicity; cyclosporin depresses renal function and can reduce excretion of many drugs.
• Cyclosporin binds cyclophyllin, inhibits calcineurin, and halts NFAT-driven IL-2 production; it is nephrotoxic and hepatotoxic but spares bone marrow.
(c)
Tacrolimus (FK506): chemically different, isolated from a soil fungus, same mechanism, 100 times more potent, binds the cytoplasmic protein FKBP and inhibits T cells via calcineurin; clinical efficacy and toxicity are similar to cyclosporine.
• Tacrolimus causes less hypertension, hirsutism and gum hyperplasia than cyclosporin, but is more likely to precipitate diabetes, neurotoxicity, alopecia and diarrhoea.
(d)
Avoid or adjust co-administered enzyme inducers, CYP-inhibiting drugs (erythromycin, ketoconazole) and nephrotoxic drugs, because they change levels or toxicity.

(a)
Immunological unresponsiveness to self, called tolerance or self-tolerance, is very important to human health.
(b)
Cells with receptors for self-antigens are destroyed in the thymus or bone marrow.
(c)
Self-reacting lymphocytes are made non-responsive (anergy) or induced to self-destruct.
(d)
In the thymic cortex, positive selection keeps T cells whose TCRs recognise self-MHC; in the medulla, negative selection deletes T cells recognising self-peptides with high affinity. Over 98% of thymocytes die by apoptosis in the thymus.
(e)
A T cell engaging peptide-MHC without enough CD28 costimulation becomes anergic: it cannot proliferate because IL-2 is not produced.
(f)
CTLA-4 binds B7 with higher affinity than CD28 and dampens T-cell activation; PD1 and PSGL-1 also fine-tune the response.
(g)
TReg cells maintain peripheral tolerance and suppress proliferation of effector T cells.
(h)
B cells whose receptors recognise bone marrow components are negatively selected and die by apoptosis; negative selection of self-reactive T cells also prevents activation of the matching B cells.
(i)
Tolerance prevents the immune system attacking self-cells and tissues; the immune system also needs to regulate the length and size of a response.
(j)
If tolerance is not balanced well it leads to autoimmunity (diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, multiple sclerosis); recognition of self-peptides by autoreactive T cells can result in autoimmunity.
(k)
Long-term inflammation is destructive to the host.
(l)
Chronic immune infections (CMV, HIV) cause premature ageing of the immune system; in toxic shock syndrome, large numbers of activated T cells and massive cytokines shut down organ systems and can cause death.

A bronchodilator used in asthma is one of three naturally occurring methylated xanthines (with caffeine and theobromine). It decreases the production and release of pro-inflammatory signals such as TNF-alpha and leukotriene and promotes smooth muscle relaxation, but its use has declined.
(a) Identify the agent and its class.
(b) State its pharmacokinetic features (absorption, distribution and half-life).
(c) State the relevant drug interactions or metabolic considerations.
(d) State the clinical consequence.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Theophylline, a methylxanthine.
• It decreases the production and release of TNF-alpha and leukotriene, effectively decreasing inflammation, and promotes smooth muscle relaxation and dilation of the bronchioles, especially in asthmatics.
(b)
Well absorbed orally, distributed in all tissues, crosses the placenta and is secreted in milk.
• Half-life 7-12 h in adults and 3-5 h in children.
(c)
Erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, oral contraceptives and allopurinol decrease its metabolism, thereby increasing its plasma level.
(d)
Raised plasma levels bring side effects: rapid heartbeat, nausea, palpitation, agitation, vomiting and seizures.
• Its use has declined because of the high risk of severe life-threatening toxicity and numerous drug interactions.

questions.question:
Describe the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) under the following headings:
(a) Classification
(b) Mechanism of action
(c) Examples
(d) Clinical uses
(e) Adverse effects
Explain the pharmacological basis of their efficacy and limitation:
(f) The basis of the anti-inflammatory, analgesic and antipyretic actions
(g) The basis of gastrointestinal toxicity
(h) Why selective COX-2 inhibitors damage the gastric mucosa less, and the limitations they carry
Distinguish between aspirin and ibuprofen:
(i) Mechanism of COX inhibition
(j) Anti-inflammatory potency and dose tolerance
(k) Pharmacokinetics
(l) Distinctive adverse effects and interaction
questions.answerText:
(a)
Nonselective COX inhibitors: salicylates, pyrazolone derivatives, indole derivatives, propionic acid derivatives, anthranilic acid derivatives, aryl-acetic acid derivatives, oxicam derivatives, dihydropyrrolizine carboxylic acid derivative. Selective COX inhibitors: preferential COX-2 and selective COX-2 inhibitors.
(b)
They inhibit cyclo-oxygenases (COX), so prostaglandin (PG) production is reduced. COX-1 is constitutive (house-keeping); COX-2 is induced by pro-inflammatory factors (TNF-alpha, IL-1).
(c)
Aspirin, salicylamide, phenylbutazone, metamizol, indomethacin, naproxen, mefenamic acid, diclofenac, piroxicam, ketorolac; nimesulide, meloxicam, nabumetone; celecoxib, parecoxib, rofecoxib.
(d)
Pain (headache, toothache, myalgia, back pain), fever, arthritis (rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, gout, ankylosing spondylitis), dysmenorrhoea, closure of the patent ductus arteriosus, prevention of MI, stroke and reinfarction (aspirin).
(e)
GIT disturbances (epigastric pain, nausea, peptic ulcer, GI bleeding), CNS disturbances, leukopenia/agranulocytosis, water and sodium retention/oedema, hypersensitivity reactions, Reye's syndrome and bronchospasm (aspirin).
(f)
PGs do not cause pain but sensitize nociceptors to stimulation (e.g. by 5-HT, bradykinin). IL-1 from activated macrophages induces COX-2 in the brain, giving PGE production, altered thermoregulation and fever, so NSAIDs are antipyretic. Inhibition of COX-2 is thought to underlie the anti-inflammatory action.
(g)
Classical NSAIDs inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2, so house-keeping PGs fall (gastrointestinal effects, bronchospasm). Loss of PGE2 and PGI2 mediated inhibition of acid secretion and cytoprotection, plus loss of PGI2 inhibition of LTB4-mediated neutrophil adhesion and activation, leads to proteases, oxygen radicals and mucosal ulceration.
(h)
Selective COX-2 drugs spare COX-1, so they cause little gastric mucosa damage and do not inhibit platelet aggregation. Limitations: renal toxicity (not recommended in severe renal insufficiency) and a high incidence of cardiovascular thrombotic events with some, such as rofecoxib.
(i)
Aspirin inhibits COX irreversibly; ibuprofen has the same mechanism and actions but is a reversible COX inhibitor.
(j)
Ibuprofen is more potent as an anti-inflammatory than aspirin. Aspirin needs a high dose (5-8 g/day) for anti-inflammatory use, which many patients cannot tolerate (GIT), so propionic acid derivatives such as ibuprofen and naproxen are tried first.
(k)
Aspirin: weak acid (pKa about 3.5), non-ionized in the stomach and easily absorbed, duration about 4 h, hydrolysed to active salicylate. Ibuprofen: rapidly absorbed orally, half-life 1-2 h, highly plasma protein bound, excreted by the kidney as metabolites.
(l)
Aspirin: Reye's syndrome, bronchospasm, peptic ulcer. Ibuprofen: gastric upset less frequent than aspirin, fluid retention, ocular disturbances, rare agranulocytosis and aplastic anaemia; it antagonizes the irreversible platelet inhibition of aspirin, limiting aspirin's cardioprotective effect.

(a)
Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid), a salicylate NSAID that irreversibly inhibits COX.
(b)
Non-ionized in the stomach and so easily absorbed; hydrolysed by esterases in tissues and blood to salicylate (active) and acetic acid; most salicylate is converted in the liver to water-soluble conjugates that are rapidly excreted by the kidneys; duration about 4 h.
(c)
Concomitant ibuprofen antagonizes its irreversible platelet inhibition, limiting its cardioprotective effect.
• It potentiates the gastric irritant effect of alcohol and the hypoglycaemic effect of oral hypoglycaemic drugs.
(d)
Anti-inflammatory use needs a high dose (5-8 g/day) that many patients cannot tolerate (GIT), so propionic acid derivatives are tried first.
• Gastric peptic ulcer, Reye's syndrome and bronchospasm include; contraindicated in pregnancy, haemophilia, hypersensitivity and viral infections in children. Low-dose use prophylaxes platelet aggregation diseases and pre-eclampsia (excess TXA2).
questions.question:
An orally taken weak acid (pKa about 3.5), non-ionized in the stomach and easily absorbed, with a duration of action of about 4 hours, is hydrolysed by esterases in tissues and blood to an active salicylate and acetic acid.
(a) Identify the agent and its mechanism.
(b) State its pharmacokinetic features.
(c) State the relevant drug interactions or metabolic considerations.
(d) State the clinical consequence.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Piroxicam, an oxicam derivative NSAID.
• Mechanism: non-selective inhibition of COX-1 and COX-2, trapping of free radicals, inhibition of polymorphonuclear leukocyte migration and inhibition of lymphocyte function.
(b)
Well absorbed orally; half-life 45 hours; given once daily.
(c)
NSAIDs as a class potentiate the gastric irritant effect of alcohol and the hypoglycaemic effects of oral hypoglycaemic drugs.
(d)
Gastric upset is less frequent (20%); other adverse effects are dizziness, tinnitus, headache and allergy.
• As a non-selective COX inhibitor it reduces house-keeping prostaglandins, with the class risks of GIT disturbance and bronchospasm; NSAID contraindications include pregnancy, haemophilia, hypersensitivity and peptic ulcers.
questions.question:
An oxicam NSAID that is a non-selective COX-1 and COX-2 inhibitor, traps free radicals, inhibits polymorphonuclear leukocyte migration and inhibits lymphocyte function is well absorbed orally and given once daily.
(a) Identify the agent and its class.
(b) State the pharmacokinetic features.
(c) State the relevant drug interactions.
(d) State the clinical consequence.

Describe active and passive immunity as strategies of immune protection:
(a) The types of acquired immunity
(b) Active immunity
(c) Passive immunity
(d) The properties that separate them
Relate their parts to common examples:
(e) Natural and artificial active immunity
(f) Natural passive immunity
(g) Artificial passive immunity
(h) Products used to provide immunity
Explain why each works clinically and what trade-off or limitation results:
(i) The advantage of active immunity
(j) Its limitation
(k) The advantage of passive immunity
(l) Its limitation
questions.answerText:
(a)
Acquired (adaptive) immunity is divided into active immunity (natural, artificial) and passive immunity (natural, artificial).
(b)
Active immunity is produced actively by the host's immune system and induced by infection or by immunogens.
(c)
Passive immunity is received passively with no active host participation; it is ready-made antibody treatment.
(d)
Active: durable protection, lag period, immunological memory, booster effect, may have a negative phase, not applicable in the immunodeficient. Passive: transient, immediate, no memory, subsequent dose less effective, no negative phase, applicable in the immunodeficient.
(e)
Natural: from disease. Artificial: from injection or purposeful exposure to antigen, e.g. measles vaccine.
(f)
Transfer of maternal antibody across the placenta (IgG) to the fetus, or by colostrum.
(g)
Hepatitis B immune globulin (gamma globulin) given after exposure to hepatitis B; immune sera (antitoxins, anti-venins) from immunised animals.
(h)
Vaccines, toxoids, immune sera and human immunoglobulins; vaccines, immune sera and immunoglobulins are each specific to one infection, so monospecific preparations can be combined.
(i)
Active immunity gives durable, effective protection with memory and a booster effect on a subsequent dose; memory is the basis of vaccination.
(j)
It is effective only after a lag period, a negative phase may occur, and it is not applicable in the immunodeficient.
(k)
Passive immunity is immediate and can be used in the immunodeficient.
(l)
It is transient and less effective, has no memory, and a subsequent dose is less effective; the use of immune sera is limited nowadays.

questions.question:
Describe the immunostimulants under the following headings:
(a) Classification
(b) Mechanism of action
(c) Examples
(d) Uses
Explain the pharmacological basis of efficacy and limitation:
(e) Why cytokines can stimulate immunity
(f) Why microbial products are used as adjuvants
(g) The status of the evidence for these agents
Distinguish between related agents:
(h) Cytokines and levamisole
(i) Levamisole and BCG
(j) Interferon-gamma and IL-2 in innate cells
(k) Immunostimulants and immunosuppressants
questions.answerText:
(a)
Cytokines (interleukins, TNF, haemopoietic growth factors); levamisole (an antihelminthic); BCG and other adjuvants/microbial products.
(b)
Cytokines are available by rDNA technology; levamisole appears to enhance the magnitude of T-cell mediated immunity; BCG and microbial products probably act by activation of macrophages.
(c)
G-CSF, M-CSF, GM-CSF, interleukins, TNF; levamisole; BCG, picibanil, lentinan, pachymaran.
(d)
Cytokines: viral infections, autoimmune and neoplastic disease. Levamisole: tried in some immunodeficiency diseases, RA, post-surgery and colorectal cancer.
(e)
Cytokines control proliferation and activation of immune cells, increase antibody production and inflammation (interleukins), kill cancer cells (TNF) and produce an antiviral state (interferons).
(f)
They probably activate macrophages.
(g)
BCG and other microbial products are 'being tried' and 'probably' act on macrophages; levamisole 'has been tried' and 'appears' to enhance T-cell immunity, so their mechanism is not firmly established.
(h)
Cytokines are recombinant proteins with multiple effects; levamisole is an antihelminthic that enhances T-cell mediated immunity.
(i)
Levamisole enhances T-cell mediated immunity; BCG and related microbial products act as adjuvants probably by macrophage activation.
(j)
IFN-gamma is the best cytokine for activating macrophages to kill ingested organisms; IL-2 is needed for NK cells to differentiate into activated killer cells.
(k)
Immunostimulants strengthen immune steps (infection, neoplasia); immunosuppressants inhibit cellular/humoral immunity (transplantation, autoimmune disease).

questions.question:
Describe the inhibitors of eicosanoid synthesis and action under the following headings:
(a) Classification
(b) Mechanism of action
(c) Examples
(d) Uses
(e) Adverse effects
Explain the pharmacological basis of efficacy and limitation:
(f) Why NSAIDs increase leukotriene formation
(g) Why corticosteroids limit leukotrienes
(h) Why low-dose aspirin is selective for platelets
Distinguish between related drugs or classes:
(i) Zileuton and montelukast/zafirlukast
(j) COX-1 and COX-2
(k) TXA2 and PGI2
(l) Leukotrienes and histamine
questions.answerText:
(a)
Inhibitors of prostaglandin synthesis (corticosteroids; non-selective and selective COX-2 NSAIDs; aspirin, an irreversible COX inhibitor) and inhibitors of leukotrienes (corticosteroids, CysLT1 receptor antagonists, 5-LOX inhibitor).
(b)
Corticosteroids inhibit PLA2 (which releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids); NSAIDs inhibit COX, preventing synthesis of the parent prostaglandin PGH2; CysLT1 antagonists block the receptor; zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase.
(c)
Corticosteroids; aspirin, non-selective NSAIDs, selective COX-2 inhibitors; zafirlukast, montelukast; zileuton.
(d)
NSAIDs: inflammation, pain, fever, platelet aggregation prevention; corticosteroids and leukotriene inhibitors: asthma.
(e)
NSAIDs: GI ulcer, bleeding, bronchospasm, hypersensitivity, renal effects. Leukotriene agents: headache, Churg-Strauss syndrome (montelukast/zafirlukast), raised liver enzymes (zileuton). Corticosteroid effects: infections, osteoporosis, hyperglycaemia.
(f)
NSAIDs do not inhibit lipoxygenase activity at clinical doses; they cause more substrate to be metabolized through the LOX pathway, increasing formation of inflammatory and proliferative leukotrienes.
(g)
Corticosteroids inhibit eicosanoid synthesis, thus limiting the amount of leukotrienes formed; useful in asthma.
(h)
Chronic low-dose aspirin selectively and irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1 and TXA2 without modifying the systemic activity of COX-1 and COX-2.
(i)
Zileuton blocks leukotriene synthesis (5-LOX); montelukast and zafirlukast block CysLT1 receptors. Zileuton's use is limited by elevated liver enzymes.
(j)
COX-1 is constitutive and has house-keeping functions such as gastric epithelial cytoprotection; COX-2 is inducible (cytokines, shear stress, growth factors) and a major source of prostanoids in inflammation and cancer.
(k)
TXA2 (platelets) causes vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation, and is inhibited by aspirin; PGI2 (endothelium) is a vasodilator and inhibits platelet aggregation.
(l)
Histamine is produced rapidly and transiently while the more potent leukotrienes are synthesized; LTC4 and LTD4 form SRS-A, causing slow and sustained bronchiolar constriction.

questions.question:
A patient with resistant asthma, positive skin tests or raised IgE levels, and frequent hospitalization is started on an injectable biologic that binds the Fc portion of IgE.
(a) Identify the drug.
(b) State the molecular and cellular target and mechanism of action.
(c) Describe the effect on the immune response.
(d) State the therapeutic use and the key adverse effect linked to its use.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Omalizumab, an anti-IgE antibody.
(b)
It binds the Fc portion of IgE (the main immunoglobulin involved in binding and degranulation of mast cells), preventing IgE from binding the mast cell Fc epsilon receptor I (FcεRI).
• FcεRI is also on basophils, lymphocytes, monocytes and eosinophils, so inhibiting IgE binding to these cells also contributes to the therapeutic effect.
(c)
In asthma, receptor-bound IgE cross-linking on re-exposure releases histamine, cytokines, leukotrienes and prostaglandins from mast cells; blocking IgE binding therefore reduces this IgE-mediated mast cell response.
(d)
Use is reserved for resistant asthma with positive skin tests or raised IgE who require frequent hospitalization; it is very expensive.
• Adverse effect: injection site reaction.

questions.question:
An Rh D-negative woman has just delivered (or aborted) an Rh-positive baby (or fetus).
(a) Identify the immunological mechanism or hypersensitivity type that threatens future offspring.
(b) Name the agent used for management.
(c) Justify the choice through its mechanism.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Hemolytic disease of the newborn, classified under Type II (cytotoxic) hypersensitivity: IgG or IgM antibodies destroy cell surface molecules, and antigen-antibody binding activates complement and destroys the cell to which the antigen is bound.
(b)
Anti-D immunoglobulin: human IgG with a high titre of antibody against Rh D antigen.
(c)
It binds Rho antigens, preventing antibody formation in Rh-negative individuals.
• Use: to prevent post-partum or post-abortion formation of antibody in Rho-D negative women who delivered or aborted an Rho-positive baby or fetus; it prevents Rh hemolytic disease in future offspring.
• Timing: it should be given within 72 hours of delivery or abortion.

questions.question:
Describe immunomodulation as a pharmacological strategy:
(a) The definition of an immunomodulator
(b) The steps of the immune response that drugs may modulate
(c) The role of immunosuppressants
Relate its parts to the common examples:
(d) Glucocorticoids
(e) Cyclosporin
(f) Muromonab CD3 and anti-thymocyte globulin
(g) Cyclophosphamide and methotrexate
(h) Immunostimulants
Explain why the strategy works clinically and what trade-off or limitation results:
(i) The clinical rationale
(j) The selectivity of cyclosporin
(k) The consequence of T-cell suppression
(l) The need for balance in the immune response
questions.answerText:
(a)
An immunomodulator is a substance (e.g. a drug) that has an effect on the immune system; the effect could either stimulate or suppress it.
(b)
Drugs may suppress or stimulate: antigen recognition and phagocytosis; lymphocyte proliferation/differentiation; synthesis of antibodies and Ag-Ab interaction; release of mediators due to the immune response; modification of target tissue response.
(c)
Immunosuppressants inhibit cellular/humoral immunity and are useful in organ transplantation and autoimmune disorders.
(d)
Glucocorticoids inhibit MHC II expression and T-lymphocyte proliferation and reduce IL-1, IL-2 and IL-6, so helper T cells are not activated; used with cyclosporine to prevent graft rejection and in RA, SLE, psoriasis, IBD.
(e)
Cyclosporin inhibits calcineurin (via cyclophyllin) and so halts NFAT-driven cytokine gene transcription and IL-2 production; it suppresses cell-mediated immunity.
(f)
Muromonab CD3 (murine anti-CD3 antibody) obstructs MHC II antigen binding to the TCR and T cells disappear from circulation (acute organ transplant rejection). Anti-thymocyte globulin (horse or rabbit polyclonal) binds and depletes T lymphocytes (steroid-resistant graft rejection).
(g)
Cyclophosphamide has more effect on B cells and humoral immunity than on T cells (bone marrow transplantation, SLE maintenance). Methotrexate, a folate antagonist, markedly suppresses cytokine production and cellular immunity (RA, pemphigus, myasthenia gravis, uveitis).
(h)
Immunostimulants: cytokines (interleukins, TNF, G-CSF, M-CSF, GM-CSF made by rDNA technology), levamisole (enhances T-cell mediated immunity), BCG and microbial products (picibanil, lentinan, pachymaran) that probably activate macrophages.
(i)
Suppressing cellular/humoral immunity prevents graft rejection and controls autoimmune disease; stimulating it is tried in viral infections, immunodeficiency and neoplastic disease.
(j)
Cyclosporin suppresses cell-mediated immunity yet leaves enough humoral immunity to combat bacterial infection.
(k)
T-cell immune deficiency gives recurrent infections with parasites, viruses and intracellular bacteria, seen in transplant patients suppressed to prevent rejection; glucocorticoids also cause lymphopenia and susceptibility to infection.
(l)
There should always be a balance: an immune response that cannot be activated when needed gives infection, whereas one activated without a real threat or not switched off gives allergy and autoimmune disease.

questions.question:
A patient with rheumatoid arthritis (or Crohn's disease) is given a subcutaneous biologic that is a fully human monoclonal antibody against TNF.
(a) Identify the biologic.
(b) Classify it.
(c) Outline the pathway it blocks.
(d) State the route of administration and the storage or handling needs.
(e) Identify the toxicity or risk linked to its use.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Adalimumab.
(b)
A biologic DMARD and TNF inhibitor; a fully human monoclonal antibody against TNF.
(c)
It targets TNF, the pro-inflammatory cytokine with a major role (with IL-1) in rheumatoid arthritis, which is produced by activated macrophages in the synovium.
(d)
Route: subcutaneous.
• Biologics in general have limited shelf life, need special/controlled storage and are typically administered by a physician.
(e)
All anti-TNF agents increase the risk of serious infections; inhibiting pro-inflammatory cytokines can compromise host defence.
• Indications: rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, moderate-to-severe chronic psoriasis.

(a)
Interferon-alpha (chronic hepatitis C and cancer) and filgrastim (neutropenia).
(b)
Recombinant cytokines made by rDNA technology; interferons are glycoproteins; filgrastim is a synthetic colony stimulating factor (haemopoietic growth factor).
(c)
Infected cells release IFN, which warns neighbouring cells so they enter an antiviral state; virus ds-RNA activates a host protein that inhibits host protein synthesis, so the virus cannot replicate.
• Colony stimulating factors (G-CSF, M-CSF, GM-CSF) direct pluripotent stem cells to differentiate into PMN cells or monocytes in the bone marrow.
(d)
Recombinant cytokines need sterile production with multiple purification stages, have limited shelf life, require special/controlled storage and are typically administered by a physician.
(e)
Cytokines are pleiotropic (several processes affected in parallel) and redundant; the cytokine network is balanced, and altering it may impair the immune response.
questions.question:
A patient with chronic hepatitis C is treated with a recombinant interferon, and another patient with neutropenia is treated with a synthetic colony stimulating factor.
(a) Identify the biologics.
(b) Classify them.
(c) Outline the pathway they modulate.
(d) State the storage or handling needs.
(e) Identify the risk linked to their use.

Describe inflammation as a biological process:
(a) Its definition
(b) Its causes
(c) Its temporal phases
(d) Its cardinal signs
Relate its parts to the examples and mediators and the points of pharmacological intervention:
(e) The vascular response
(f) The cellular response
(g) The chemical mediators
(h) The intervention points of anti-inflammatory drugs
Explain why the response works clinically and what trade-off or limitation results:
(i) The benefits of acute inflammation
(j) The harm of chronic inflammation
(k) The mechanisms that terminate inflammation
(l) The effect of failed resolution
questions.answerText:
(a)
A non-specific, localized immune reaction that tries to localize the pathogenic agent; a response to an injurious stimulus and a self-defence mechanism.
(b)
Exogenous: physical (mechanical, thermal), chemical, biological agents. Endogenous: circulation disorders (thrombosis, infarction, haemorrhage), enzyme activation (acute pancreatitis), deposits of metabolic products (uric acid, urea).
(c)
Acute phase (transient vasodilation and increased capillary permeability); subacute phase (infiltration of leukocytes and phagocytic cells); proliferative phase (tissue degeneration and fibrosis).
(d)
Rubor (redness), tumor (swelling), calor (heat), dolor (pain), functio laesa (loss of function).
(e)
Stage I brief vasoconstriction; stage II active vasodilation (redness, heat); stage III passive vasodilation with fluid exudation (swelling, pain, impaired function); exudation dilutes the offending agent and clotting localizes spread of microorganisms.
(f)
Granulocytes and monocytes: pavementing (adhesion molecules), emigration, chemotaxis (cytokines, C3a, C5a), and phagocytosis (adherence plus opsonization, engulfment, intracellular killing).
(g)
TNF-alpha and IL-1 first (fever, IL-6, IL-8, IFN-gamma; IL-6 drives CRP); histamine (H1); prostaglandins (COX pathway); leukotrienes (lipoxygenase; LTC4/LTD4 form SRS-A); PAF; kinins (bradykinin); complement fragments.
(h)
Corticosteroids inhibit phospholipase A2; NSAIDs inhibit COX; leukotriene receptor antagonists and zileuton act on the leukotriene pathway; antihistamines block histamine receptors.
(i)
Acute inflammation initiates phagocytosis and killing of pathogens, limits the spread of infection, stimulates the adaptive immune response and initiates tissue repair.
(j)
Chronic inflammation causes tissue damage: macrophages release toxins including reactive oxygen species that injure tissue and can cause DNA mutation and cancer.
(k)
Short half-life of mediators; TGF-beta from macrophages; downregulation of leukotrienes; IL-1 receptor antagonist and soluble TNF receptor; apoptosis of pro-inflammatory cells; IL-4 and IL-10; lipoxins, resolvins and protectins that end neutrophil infiltration.
(l)
Failure to terminate the response results in chronic inflammation and cellular destruction; an exaggerated, sustained response can have severe adverse consequences without apparent benefit.

(a)
Hypersensitivity (serum sickness or anaphylaxis) to anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG), an animal-derived antibody.
(b)
ATG binds T lymphocytes and depletes them; it has the potential to produce serum sickness or anaphylaxis.
• Serum sickness is the systemic Type III reaction due to circulating immune complexes; anaphylaxis is Type I (IgE-mediated), as with horse gamma globulin given to patients sensitized to horse protein.
(c)
Muromonab CD3 is a murine monoclonal antibody against CD3 near the TCR on helper T cells that blocks MHC II antigen binding to the TCR; its adverse effect is cytokine release syndrome (reduced by high-dose corticosteroid pre-treatment). ATG is polyclonal and less expensive than muromonab CD3.
(d)
ATG is used in steroid-resistant cases to suppress acute graft rejection; muromonab CD3 is used for acute organ transplant rejection.
questions.question:
A patient with steroid-resistant acute graft rejection is given a polyclonal antibody purified from a horse (or rabbit) immunized with human thymic lymphocytes, and develops features of serum sickness or anaphylaxis.
(a) Identify the cause.
(b) Explain the underlying immunological or pharmacological basis.
(c) Differentiate the drug from the related T-cell directed antibody.
(d) Reason to the management decision.

questions.answerText:
(a)
A non-biologic (synthetic) disease modifying anti-rheumatoid drug (DMARD).
(b)
Its metabolite reversibly inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, decreasing ribonucleotide synthesis, so activation and proliferation of immune cells fall and stimulated cells arrest in the G1 phase.
(c)
Rheumatoid arthritis (a non-biologic DMARD).
(d)
Elevated liver enzymes, leukopenia, thrombopenia, headache, rash, itching, loss of hair and body weight, hypertension and chest pain.
(e)
Reduced ribonucleotide synthesis decreases activation and proliferation of immune cells and arrests stimulated cells in G1.
(f)
The active metabolite teriflunomide also inhibits tyrosine kinases responsible for early T-cell and B-cell signalling.
(g)
DMARDs are slow-acting drugs that promote remission by slowing or stopping progression of joint destruction and deformity.
(h)
Liver enzyme elevation, leukopenia and thrombopenia, together with the other adverse effects described above.
(i)
Contraindicated in pregnant and lactating women.
(j)
Combination of methotrexate with leflunomide (or azathioprine) causes liver and lung complications.
questions.question:
Describe the pharmacology of leflunomide:
(a) Class
(b) Mechanism of action
(c) Use
(d) Adverse effects
State the basis of its selectivity and effect on immune cells and mediators:
(e) The enzyme step it affects and the consequence for immune cells
(f) The effect of its active metabolite at higher doses
(g) The type of drug and speed of action
Explain the basis of toxicity and drug interaction:
(h) The pattern of toxicity
(i) The contraindication
(j) The interaction with methotrexate

questions.answerText:
(a)
Type III (immune complex mediated) hypersensitivity; chronic immune complex diseases include systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), acute glomerulonephritis, rheumatic fever and rheumatoid arthritis.
• Soluble complexes with excess antigen lodge on the basement membrane and activate complement; chemotactic products attract neutrophils, which release lysosomal enzymes that damage the vessel, giving vasculitis (local: Arthus reaction; systemic: serum sickness).
(b)
Glucocorticoids (used in collagen diseases such as SLE) and cyclophosphamide (maintenance therapy in SLE).
(c)
Glucocorticoids inhibit MHC II expression and T-lymphocyte proliferation, lower IL-1, IL-2 and IL-6, and inhibit phospholipase A2 via lipocortin-1.
• Cyclophosphamide has more effect on B cells and humoral immunity than on T cells and cell-mediated immunity.
(d)
Glucocorticoids: susceptibility to infections, delayed wound healing, osteoporosis, hyperglycaemia, peptic ulceration, Cushing habitus, muscular weakness, psychiatric disorders, withdrawal syndrome.
questions.question:
A patient has a chronic disease in which immune complexes and complement are deposited in tissues, producing vasculitis that affects the joints and kidneys (arthritis and glomerulonephritis).
(a) Identify the immunological mechanism and hypersensitivity type involved.
(b) Name the drug classes or agents used for management.
(c) Justify the choices through mechanism.
(d) State the main adverse effects of the glucocorticoids.

A patient with rheumatoid arthritis who takes warfarin (or cyclosporine) starts a biologic that binds both soluble and membrane-bound IL-6 receptor, and the levels of the co-administered drug change.
(a) Identify the cause.
(b) Explain the underlying immunological or pharmacological basis.
(c) Differentiate the biologic from other biologic classes used in rheumatoid arthritis.
(d) Reason to the management decision.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A drug-drug interaction with tocilizumab (an IL-6 receptor blocker).
(b)
Tocilizumab binds soluble and membrane-bound IL-6 receptor and inhibits IL-6 mediated signalling; inhibiting IL-6 may restore CYP450 activities to higher levels.
• Hence CYP450 substrates with a narrow therapeutic window, such as cyclosporine or warfarin, may need dosage adjustment.
(c)
TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept, certolizumab, golimumab): all increase risk of serious infections. Anakinra: blocks IL-1 receptor, daily injection, itchy injection-site rash. Rituximab: anti-CD20, depletes B cells, hepatitis B reactivation.
• Tocilizumab can be used with non-biologic DMARDs or as monotherapy; its side effects include upper respiratory tract infection, headache, hypertension, injection site reaction and elevated liver enzymes.
(d)
Adjust the dose of narrow-therapeutic-window CYP450 substrates (cyclosporine, warfarin).

questions.question:
An immunological product consists of a suspension of bacteria or viruses that have been killed or inactivated but keep adequate immunogenic properties (for example pertussis, inactivated poliomyelitis (Salk), rabies, typhoid and cholera preparations).
(a) Identify the product.
(b) Classify it.
(c) Outline the immune pathway it stimulates.
(d) State the dosing requirements.
(e) Identify the toxicity, immunogenicity or risk linked to its use.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A killed (inactivated) vaccine.
(b)
An immunological product with a prophylactic effect, in the vaccine group (alongside live attenuated vaccines and toxoids); examples also include measles and mumps preparations.
(c)
It stimulates a protective immune response and active immunity, with immunological memory and a booster effect on a subsequent dose; memory is the basis of vaccination.
(d)
Each dose must contain sufficient antigenic material to stimulate a protective response, so killed vaccine suspensions are relatively concentrated; the total amount needed is divided into several doses at intervals of a few days or weeks.
(e)
Killed vaccines are quite safe: they cannot replicate or set up persistent infection.
• Limitations: they often give poor protection, possibly from partial destruction of protective antigens during killing, and because they contain all components of the micro-organism they can be toxic at times.

questions.question:
Describe hypersensitivity reactions as a concept:
(a) The definition and prerequisite
(b) Type I
(c) Types II and III
(d) Type IV
Relate their parts to the common examples:
(e) Type I examples
(f) Type II examples
(g) Type III examples
(h) Type IV examples
Explain the clinical significance and what limitation or trade-off results:
(i) Immediate versus delayed reactions
(j) The severity of Type I reactions
(k) The basis of damage in Type III
(l) The pharmacological management of allergy
questions.answerText:
(a)
Hypersensitivity denotes increased reactivity of the host to an antigen that damages the host; the individual must first be sensitized by previous exposure, and on later exposure symptoms occur immediately or after several days.
(b)
Type I (immediate): inappropriate IgE with affinity for mast cells and basophils; the allergen causes mast cells to discharge vasoactive substances (sneezing, runny nose, red watery eyes, wheezing).
(c)
Type II (cytotoxic): IgG or IgM antibodies against cell surface or tissue components activate complement and destroy the cell. Type III (immune complex): persisting circulating complexes lodge on vessel basement membranes, activate complement and attract neutrophils, causing vasculitis.
(d)
Type IV (delayed): cell-mediated, T-lymphocyte reaction; takes about 12 hours or more to develop, accumulates lymphocytes and macrophages, not mediated by histamine, no antibodies involved.
(e)
Hay fever, asthma, food allergies, eczema, anaphylactic shock (bee or wasp stings, penicillin, horse gamma globulin, peanuts, shellfish).
(f)
Transfusion reaction due to ABO incompatibility, immune hemolytic anaemias, hemolytic disease of the newborn, Goodpasture syndrome, drugs acting as haptens (penicillin).
(g)
SLE, acute glomerulonephritis, rheumatic fever, rheumatoid arthritis; Arthus reaction (local) and serum sickness (systemic).
(h)
Positive tuberculin (PPD/Koch) test with induration of 5 mm or more within 48 hours; contact dermatitis, graft rejection, autoimmune disease, drug allergy and allergic response to insect bites and stings.
(i)
Immediate hypersensitivity refers to antibody-mediated reactions, delayed hypersensitivity to cell-mediated immunity.
(j)
Type I ranges from mild food allergy to life-threatening anaphylactic shock, with massive vasoactive release causing a fall in blood pressure, shock and difficulty in breathing; it is the most common immunological abnormality in medical practice.
(k)
The size of complexes determines whether they are eliminated quickly or retained long enough to damage vessels, particularly in joints and kidney (arthritis, glomerulonephritis).
(l)
Anti-allergic drugs: antihistaminics, corticosteroids, mast cell stabilisers and antileukotriene drugs; epinephrine is life-saving in systemic anaphylaxis.

(a)
Loratadine, a second-generation H1-receptor antagonist (lipophobic, low capacity to cross the blood-brain barrier, higher H1 specificity, no anticholinergic effects).
(b)
Rapidly absorbed, with peak plasma concentrations in 1-3 h and duration of action generally 4-24 h; extensive first-pass metabolism by CYP3A4 to active desloratadine.
• Children tend to eliminate antihistamines more rapidly than adults; hepatic impairment slows elimination.
(c)
CYP inhibitors such as macrolide antibiotics or imidazole antifungals increase H1-antagonist levels, leading to toxicity; cetirizine and fexofenadine are not subject to these interactions.
• Long-term use may reduce effectiveness, probably through induction of hepatic drug-metabolizing enzymes.
(d)
Toxicity risk with CYP inhibitors, lessening of effect over prolonged use, and altered dosing considerations in children and hepatic impairment; less CNS depression than first-generation drugs.
• Used for allergic rhinitis and urticaria; not indicated in asthma alone but useful as an adjunct in asthmatic patients with rhinitis, urticaria or dermatitis.
questions.question:
A non-sedating antiallergic drug that is a piperidine antihistamine undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism, converted by CYP3A4 isozymes to an active metabolite, desloratadine.
(a) Identify the agent and its class.
(b) State the pharmacokinetic features.
(c) State the relevant drug interactions or metabolic considerations.
(d) State the clinical consequence.
