questions.explanation: Clean intermittent catheterisation is the standard approach for managing neurogenic bladder dysfunction in myelomeningocele, helping prevent urinary retention and reduce infection risk. This is generally preferred over permanent indwelling catheters for long-term management. Family education and a consistent schedule are essential for successful bladder programmes.
options: Fluid restriction as the sole strategy

questions.question: A 3-month-old in Pavlik harness for DDH has hip flexion of 130 degrees. The physiotherapist must alert the orthopaedist because exceeding 120 degrees risks:
questions.explanation: Hip flexion exceeding 120 degrees in the Pavlik harness may compromise femoral head blood supply through excessive compression of posterior capsular vessels and stretch of the retinacular arteries, causing avascular necrosis. This serious complication significantly worsens long-term hip prognosis. Physiotherapists monitoring Pavlik harness use must check flexion angles at each assessment and communicate promptly with the orthopaedist.
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Growth and development are identical concepts with no distinction
Development refers only to height and weight changes
Growth refers to physical size changes while development refers to functional skill progression
Growth and development are entirely unrelated processes
Growth refers only to cognitive skill acquisition
questions.explanation: Growth describes the physical, anatomical changes in body size and composition, while development refers to the progressive acquisition of functional skills and abilities across domains. Though distinct, growth and development are closely interrelated, since physical growth supports and is influenced by functional developmental progress. Distinguishing these terms supports accurate documentation and communication in paediatric assessment.
questions.question: Which statement accurately reflects the relationship between growth and development in children?
Serial casting may be used in arthrogryposis management to achieve which effect?
options: Prevention of any future physiotherapy involvement
Gradual, progressive correction of joint contracture
Permanent immobilisation with no further correction intended
Treatment of an unrelated skin infection
Immediate full correction within a single application
questions.explanation: Serial casting applies gradual, incremental stretch to a contracted joint over successive cast changes, slowly improving range of motion in conditions like arthrogryposis. It is not intended to achieve full correction in one application, nor to replace ongoing physiotherapy. This staged approach respects the tissue's limited elasticity while working toward functional gains.

questions.question: An infant is being assessed for developmental progress. The therapist wants to test cephalocaudal development. Which comparison is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Cephalocaudal development compares proximal-to-distal progression along the head-to-tail axis, so head control versus leg control is the correct comparison. Shoulder-to-hand reflects the proximodistal principle instead. Understanding which axis is tested avoids confusing the two developmental principles.
options: Comparing head control to leg control acquisition
Comparing shoulder control to hand control
Comparing right hand to left hand skill

questions.question: The term 'containment' in Legg-Calve-Perthes management refers to which treatment principle?
questions.explanation: Containment refers to positioning or bracing strategies aimed at keeping the softened femoral head well-seated within the acetabulum during the healing process, using the acetabulum as a mould to preserve a spherical shape. This principle underlies both conservative bracing and surgical containment procedures. Successful containment improves long-term hip joint congruency and function.
options: Placing the child in isolation to prevent infection
Completely removing the femoral head surgically
Keeping the femoral head well-seated within the acetabulum during healing
Restricting the child to bed rest indefinitely

questions.explanation: Legg-Calve-Perthes syndrome results from disrupted blood supply to the proximal femoral head, most often via the medial femoral circumflex artery, leading to avascular necrosis. This causes softening and potential collapse of the femoral head over time. Understanding the vascular basis explains why weight-bearing precautions are important during the disease course.
questions.question: Legg-Calve-Perthes syndrome results from interruption of blood flow to which structure?

options: Stop all gross motor therapy immediately
Continue monitoring since gross and fine motor rates can differ
Conclude the child has global developmental delay
questions.explanation: Since gross and fine motor domains can mature at slightly different rates within normal variation, an isolated fine motor lag alongside on-track gross motor skills does not necessarily indicate global delay. Continued monitoring with reassessment is appropriate before broader diagnostic conclusions. Domain-specific tracking avoids premature labelling.
questions.question: A child demonstrates crawling but has not yet developed a mature pincer grasp at 9 months. How should the physiotherapist proceed?

questions.explanation: Genu valgum, commonly known as knock-knee, describes a lower limb alignment where the knees angle inward and touch while the ankles remain apart. This differs from genu varum, or bow-leg, where the knees angle outward. Some degree of physiological genu valgum is normal in early childhood and often resolves with growth.
options: Knock-knee deformity with knees angled inward
Fixed flexion contracture of the hip
Bow-leg deformity with knees angled outward
Complete absence of the knee joint
questions.question: Genu valgum refers to which lower limb alignment abnormality?

questions.explanation: A heel-strike gait with coordinated arm swing, rather than a flat-footed high-guard pattern, indicates a mature walking pattern, typically established by around age 3. Earlier toddler gait is normally less refined. Recognising mature gait helps distinguish normal variation from a pathological pattern.
questions.question: An 18-month-old walks with a heel-strike pattern and coordinated arm swing rather than a flat-footed, high-guard pattern. This represents:
Two infants present with brachial plexus injury, one with neurapraxia and one with avulsion. The type with the best prognosis for spontaneous recovery is:
questions.explanation: Neurapraxia, a mild stretch injury without axonal disruption, carries the best prognosis for spontaneous recovery among brachial plexus injury types. Avulsion and neurotmesis involve more severe axonal or root damage with poorer natural recovery. This distinction guides the timing of surgical referral.

options: A long spinal cord lesion spanning three or more vertebral segments
Complete absence of any spinal cord signal change
A short lesion spanning less than one segment
Normal spinal imaging with brain-only lesions
questions.explanation: Longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesions spanning three or more vertebral segments are a hallmark imaging feature supporting Neuromyelitis Optica over typical multiple sclerosis, which usually shows shorter lesions. This imaging pattern, combined with clinical and antibody findings, guides accurate diagnosis. Correct differentiation impacts long-term treatment choice.
questions.question: A child with suspected Neuromyelitis Optica is being differentiated from multiple sclerosis. Which spinal imaging finding would most support the NMO diagnosis?
Complete trisomy 18 accounting for 95% of Edwards syndrome cases results from non-disjunction producing an extra chromosome 18. This chromosomal error typically occurs during:
questions.explanation: Non-disjunction causing complete trisomy 18 most commonly occurs during maternal meiosis II when homologous chromosome 18 pairs fail to separate, producing an egg with two copies of chromosome 18. Advanced maternal age increases the risk of this meiotic error. Understanding the genetic mechanism informs family counselling and prenatal testing options, providing context for physiotherapy's role in comprehensive care.

options: Guaranteed normal joint development regardless of treatment
Early degenerative hip osteoarthritis and gait abnormality
Improved hip joint function over time
questions.explanation: Untreated or inadequately managed DDH can progress to chronic hip instability, abnormal joint loading and early degenerative osteoarthritis, along with a persistent limp or abnormal gait pattern. This underscores the importance of early screening and appropriate management. Long-term outcomes are significantly improved with timely intervention.
questions.question: Left untreated, severe Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip can lead to which long-term complication?
ADEM characteristically shows multiple bilateral asymmetric white matter lesions on MRI. This best distinguishes ADEM from MS because MS lesions are typically:
questions.explanation: MS characteristically produces discrete, well-defined periventricular lesions on MRI, contrasting with ADEM's diffuse, bilateral, poorly demarcated white matter lesions reflecting widespread post-infectious demyelination. This imaging distinction is critical for differential diagnosis and influences prognosis and treatment planning. ADEM lesions may also involve deep grey matter unlike typical MS.

The described one-sided bending and cracking pattern is characteristic of a greenstick fracture, common in children due to the flexibility of immature bone. This fracture type generally has a favourable healing prognosis with appropriate immobilisation. Recognising this pattern helps guide expected management, typically closed reduction and casting.
questions.question: A 5-year-old presents with a forearm fracture that bends and cracks on one side of the bone only, seen on X-ray. Which fracture type is this?

questions.explanation: Because hydrocephalus is common in myelomeningocele and often managed with a shunt, signs such as irritability, vomiting and bulging fontanelle suggest possible shunt malfunction and raised intracranial pressure. This is a medical emergency requiring urgent referral rather than routine therapy continuation. Prompt recognition can prevent serious neurological complications.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices a child with myelomeningocele suddenly develops irritability, vomiting and a bulging fontanelle. What should be suspected?
options: Shunt malfunction causing raised intracranial pressure

questions.question: A physiotherapist is designing a session for a 2-year-old who becomes disengaged with repetitive structured drills. What modification is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Embedding functional movement goals within engaging, play-based activities maintains therapeutic structure while significantly improving motivation and cooperation in young children, who typically respond better to play than repetitive drills. Abandoning structured goals entirely would reduce the session's therapeutic value. This balanced, play-integrated approach reflects developmentally appropriate paediatric physiotherapy practice.
options: Discontinue therapy since the child cannot cooperate
Remove all structure and abandon goal-directed practice entirely
Continue the identical repetitive drills regardless of engagement
Assume disengagement means no therapy is possible at this age
Embed the same functional movement goals within play-based activities

questions.question: During acute ADEM with altered consciousness in a child, the physiotherapist's priority intervention is:
questions.explanation: During acute ADEM, passive ROM and positioning prevent contracture formation while the autoimmune inflammatory process is active. Aggressive interventions risk exacerbating neurological symptoms in an unstable patient. Positioning also prevents pressure injuries and maintains joint integrity during periods of altered consciousness.

Sickle cell disease is a recognised risk factor for ischaemic stroke specifically relevant in children, related to vaso-occlusion and abnormal blood flow dynamics, unlike the more typical adult risk factors of long-term hypertension or atherosclerosis. This distinct risk factor profile is important when considering paediatric stroke aetiology. Screening and preventive strategies differ accordingly in at-risk paediatric populations.
questions.question: In children, which condition is a recognised risk factor for ischaemic stroke that is less common in adult stroke populations?

questions.explanation: Correctly identifying the level of measurement, whether nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio, determines which statistical methods are appropriate and valid for analysing the data collected, since inappropriate methods can lead to misleading conclusions. This underpins sound evidence-based practice in outcome measurement and research. Selecting the correct approach protects the validity and reliability of clinical and research findings.
questions.question: Why is it important for a physiotherapist to correctly identify the level of measurement of an outcome tool before analysis?
options: It determines the colour of the assessment form
It is only relevant for adult patients, not children
It has no bearing on statistical analysis at all
It only matters for billing purposes
It determines which statistical methods are valid to apply

questions.explanation: Post-meningitic cerebellar inflammation or infarction produces ataxia characterised by wide-based gait, intention tremor, and dysmetria, distinctly different from the hemiplegia of cortical damage or the involuntary movements of basal ganglia involvement. Physiotherapy for post-meningitic cerebellar ataxia emphasises balance training, coordination exercises, and provision of appropriate mobility aids during recovery. Neuroanatomical recognition directs appropriate rehabilitation targeting.
questions.question: Following acute meningitis, a 5-year-old develops wide-based ataxic gait with intention tremor. This pattern indicates damage to which brain structure?

questions.explanation: Since children in the sensorimotor stage learn primarily through direct sensory and motor exploration, hands-on activities involving movement and sensory feedback align best with this developmental stage. Abstract or verbal reasoning tasks are more appropriate for older children in later cognitive stages. Matching activity type to cognitive stage supports more effective engagement and learning during therapy.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is planning a therapy activity for an 18-month-old and wants to align it with Piaget's sensorimotor stage. Which activity type is most appropriate?
options: Purely passive observation with no interaction
Hands-on exploratory play involving movement and sensory feedback

questions.explanation: Severe neonatal jaundice can lead to cerebral palsy through bilirubin-induced injury to the basal ganglia, a mechanism known as kernicterus. This differs from infective, nutritional, or purely traumatic causes of CP. Recognising this link underlines the importance of timely jaundice management in newborns.
questions.question: A newborn with severe jaundice requiring exchange transfusion is later found to have cerebral palsy. The likely underlying mechanism linking jaundice to CP is:

questions.explanation: The lumbosacral region is the most frequently affected site in myelomeningocele, more so than the cervical, thoracic, or sacrococcygeal regions. The neurological level at this site largely determines the pattern of motor and sensory loss. This anatomical knowledge underpins functional prognosis counselling.
questions.question: An infant is found to have myelomeningocele at the spinal region most frequently affected by this condition. This region is the:

questions.explanation: A shortened right sternocleidomastoid pulls the head into lateral tilt toward the right shoulder while rotating the chin toward the left, the opposite side. Recognising this classic postural pattern helps confirm the clinical diagnosis. Early stretching aims to correct both the tilt and the rotational component.
questions.question: Which head posture is classically seen in congenital muscular torticollis affecting the right sternocleidomastoid?
options: Head held in pure flexion with no rotation
Head tilted to the right with rotation to the left
Symmetrical head position with no tilt or rotation
Head held in pure extension with no tilt
Head tilted to the left with rotation to the right

questions.question: A physiotherapist working with a family who has limited resources for equipment is planning a home programme for a child with hypotonia. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Ignore the family's resource constraints entirely
Insist on expensive specialised equipment with no alternative
Design low-cost, functional activities using household items and daily routines
Recommend only clinic-based sessions with no home component
Discontinue therapy planning until equipment can be purchased
questions.explanation: Designing a home programme that uses low-cost, accessible household items and integrates activities into daily routines respects the family's resource constraints while still supporting meaningful therapeutic practice between sessions. Insisting on expensive equipment without considering feasibility could reduce programme adherence. Practical, resource-sensitive planning reflects responsive, family-centred paediatric physiotherapy practice.

questions.question: A newborn shows strong flexor posturing of the limbs at rest. As the infant matures over the first months, this physiological flexion is expected to:
questions.explanation: Physiological flexor tone present at birth gradually decreases over the first few months as the nervous system matures and extensor control develops. It does not disappear suddenly or convert directly into spasticity in typical development. Tracking this gradual change is part of routine developmental assessment.

questions.question: A teenager with cerebral palsy is approaching school transition. Effective goal-setting in paediatric therapy at this stage should primarily involve:
questions.explanation: Effective goal-setting for a teenager with cerebral palsy approaching school transition should involve collaboration between the child, family, and the wider care team. This reflects family- and patient-centred practice rather than unilateral decision-making by any single party. Shared goal-setting improves engagement and relevance of the resulting care plan.
options: Collaboration between child, family, and team

questions.question: Aquatic therapy for a child with spastic cerebral palsy is preferred because warm water at 33-36 degrees Celsius:
questions.explanation: Warm water at therapeutic temperatures inhibits alpha motor neurone activity, reducing spasticity and facilitating more normal movement patterns in cerebral palsy. Buoyancy simultaneously reduces the effect of gravity on postural muscles, enabling more independent movement for children with significant motor impairment. Hydrotherapy is an evidence-supported adjunct to land-based physiotherapy in paediatric neurological rehabilitation.
options: Inhibits alpha motor neurons reducing spasticity
Permanent muscle paralysis unrelated to bone growth
Limb length discrepancy or angular deformity from growth arrest
No possible long-term consequence at all
Guaranteed symmetric growth with no risk
questions.question: Which growth-related complication is a specific concern following a fracture through the epiphyseal growth plate?
questions.explanation: Injury to the growth plate carries a specific risk of partial or complete growth arrest, which can result in limb length discrepancy or angular deformity as the child continues to grow. This risk varies depending on the Salter-Harris classification of the injury. Long-term monitoring of growth is therefore important following physeal fractures.

options: Chronic joint pain and reduced range of motion from repeated vaso-occlusion
questions.explanation: Repeated vaso-occlusive episodes over time can lead to chronic joint pain, reduced range of motion and complications such as avascular necrosis in children with sickle cell disease. This differs from the other listed conditions, which have separate distinct aetiologies. Ongoing musculoskeletal monitoring is an important part of comprehensive sickle cell care.
questions.question: Chronic complications of sickle cell disease that physiotherapists should monitor for include which musculoskeletal issue?

questions.explanation: When development never advances beyond strong primitive reflexes, the child remains functionally bound to reflexive movement rather than progressing to righting, equilibrium, and voluntary control. This reflects the normal reflex hierarchy of development. Early identification allows for timely intervention to support higher-level motor progression.
questions.question: An infant continues to show only strong primitive reflexes with no voluntary movement at 9 months. If unresolved, this predicts the infant remaining at the:

questions.explanation: Early weight-bearing through the affected side provides somatosensory input that stimulates cortical reorganisation and motor recovery during the critical neuroplasticity window after meningitic brain injury. Learned non-use of the affected limb significantly worsens long-term functional outcomes and must be actively prevented. Constraint-induced movement therapy principles build on this early affected-side activation approach.
options: Increases spasticity in the affected limb
Stimulates cortical reorganisation through somatosensory input
Eliminates the need for gait aids
questions.question: During post-meningitic hemiplegia rehabilitation in a 4-year-old, early affected-side weight-bearing is prioritised because it:
In paediatric physiotherapy practice, why is play often incorporated into therapy sessions for young children?
questions.explanation: Incorporating play into therapy sessions increases a young child's engagement and motivation, allowing functional and motor skills to be practised meaningfully within a naturally rewarding context. This does not replace structured, goal-directed therapy but rather enhances its delivery for this age group. Play-based intervention is widely recognised as developmentally appropriate practice in paediatric physiotherapy.
options: It increases engagement and motivation while practising functional skills
It has no therapeutic value and is purely for entertainment
It replaces the need for any goal-directed therapy
It should always be avoided during structured sessions
It is only appropriate for children over school age

questions.explanation: Spina bifida is a neural tube defect caused by incomplete closure of the neural tube, which normally develops into the brain and spinal cord. Closure normally occurs by around the 28th day of pregnancy. Failure at the caudal end produces the spinal defect seen in spina bifida.
questions.question: Spina bifida results from failure of closure of which embryonic structure?

questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease is caused by a mutation in the HBB gene, which encodes the beta subunit of haemoglobin, leading to abnormal haemoglobin S formation. Alpha-globin gene mutations instead cause alpha-thalassemia, a different condition. This genetic basis explains the inherited, autosomal recessive pattern of sickle cell disease.
questions.question: Sickle cell disease results from a mutation in which gene?

questions.explanation: Children with spina bifida at the L4-L5 level typically retain enough hip and knee musculature to achieve ambulation with aids or braces, rather than being fully wheelchair-dependent or achieving normal gait. This functional outcome depends on the specific neurological level of the lesion. Setting realistic expectations supports appropriate goal-setting.
questions.question: A child with spina bifida at L4-L5 is undergoing repeated functional reassessment. The therapist's expectation for eventual community mobility is:
Which combination of structures is included under the umbrella of CNS infections?
options: Brain, spinal cord, optic nerves and their covering membranes
questions.explanation: CNS infections encompass the brain, spinal cord, optic nerves and their protective membranes such as the meninges, reflecting the anatomical scope of the central nervous system. This is distinct from peripheral nervous system or non-neural organ infections. Understanding this scope helps clarify why symptoms can vary widely depending on the structure involved.

options: They may impair prostaglandin-mediated bone healing
They are required for full fracture rehabilitation
questions.question: NSAIDs manage fracture pain through COX enzyme inhibition. A physiotherapy consideration regarding prolonged NSAID use is:
questions.explanation: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin synthesis through COX inhibition; since prostaglandins mediate early inflammatory bone repair including osteoblast recruitment, prolonged NSAID use may theoretically impair healing, particularly during the first two weeks. Physiotherapists should be aware of medication timing and duration when planning rehabilitation progressions. Short-term use is generally considered safe while prolonged administration warrants consideration.

Independent sitting with reach typically emerges around 6-8 months as trunk control matures sufficiently to free the hands for tasks. Achieving this earlier or considerably later may warrant closer developmental review. This milestone reflects developing postural control against gravity.
questions.question: A child sits unsupported on the floor while reaching for a toy with both hands. This skill is typically achieved by:

questions.explanation: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head is a known complication of both untreated DDH and its treatment, particularly from excessive Pavlik harness flexion exceeding 120 degrees or closed reduction, making serial radiological surveillance essential to detect early changes before femoral head deformation becomes established. Clinical signs including restricted hip ROM, limp, or groin pain warrant urgent orthopaedic review. Post-treatment surveillance is a fundamental long-term management component.
questions.question: A physiotherapist reviews a 3-year-old who completed Pavlik harness treatment for DDH 6 months ago. Long-term follow-up is required primarily to monitor for:
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

questions.explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by a deficiency or absence of dystrophin, a protein essential for maintaining muscle cell membrane integrity during contraction. Its absence leads to progressive muscle fibre damage and replacement with fibrotic and fatty tissue. This molecular basis distinguishes it from other myopathies with different underlying protein defects.
questions.question: Duchenne muscular dystrophy results from a deficiency of which protein?

questions.explanation: Circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus can emerge from the live attenuated oral polio vaccine in under-immunised populations, where the weakened virus can regain virulence through prolonged circulation. The inactivated polio vaccine, being non-live, does not carry this risk. This distinction is important in outbreak surveillance and vaccination policy.
questions.question: Vaccine-derived poliovirus outbreaks are most closely associated with which vaccine type when population immunity is low?
A 7-year-old with L3 myelomeningocele can community ambulate with HKAFOs. The physiotherapy focus for maintaining this ambulation level includes:
questions.explanation: Maximising available L3 and above muscle function through hip flexor, adductor, and partial quadriceps strengthening directly supports HKAFO ambulation capacity. Gait training optimises energy efficiency within the orthotic framework and builds walking endurance. The physiotherapist's role is to maximise functional ambulation potential within the neurological level while also ensuring appropriate wheelchair provision for longer distances.
options: Hip flexor and quadriceps strengthening with gait training
Restricting ambulation to reduce energy expenditure
No effect on gross motor skills
Interference with normal weight shifting needed for walking
questions.explanation: A retained positive support reflex causes stiff, extended leg posturing that blocks the flexible weight shifting required for a mature walking pattern. This can contribute to a stiff-legged or toe-walking gait. Therapy aims to inhibit the reflex while facilitating dynamic weight transfer.
questions.question: A 14-month-old still demonstrates a strong positive support reflex when placed in standing, causing rigid extended legs. What is the likely impact on function?
A 5-month-old is observed bringing both hands together at midline to explore a toy with hands and feet. This skill is best described as:
questions.explanation: Bringing the hands together at midline to explore a toy along with the feet is best described as hand and foot play, an exploratory milestone distinct from pincer grasp, cruising, or crawling. This behaviour typically emerges around 5 months. It reflects developing midline orientation and body awareness.

options: Reassure that this will definitely self-correct with no referral
Support orthopaedic referral since this is beyond the typical self-resolving age
Recommend only shoe inserts with no further evaluation
Assume this is unrelated to any underlying condition
Ignore the finding since it is always benign
questions.question: A child with persistent, worsening genu valgum at age 10 is referred for physiotherapy assessment. What is the most appropriate action given this age and pattern?
questions.explanation: Because physiological genu valgum typically resolves by around 7 years, persistent or worsening deformity at age 10 falls outside the normal pattern and should prompt orthopaedic referral to exclude pathological causes. Reassurance alone without further evaluation could delay appropriate management. Collaborative referral ensures accurate diagnosis and timely treatment planning.

questions.question: Intellectual disability is best described using which broad diagnostic term?
questions.explanation: Intellectual disability is a generalised disorder affecting both cognitive functioning and adaptive behaviour, persisting rather than being a temporary or purely physical or infectious condition. This broad, generalised nature affects multiple areas of a child's functioning and development. Recognising this comprehensive scope supports appropriately holistic, multidisciplinary management planning.
options: A generalized disorder of cognitive and adaptive functioning
A purely temporary childhood illness that always resolves
A condition limited only to sensory organs

questions.explanation: Although the brain lesion itself does not progress, secondary musculoskeletal changes such as contractures can develop as the child grows, requiring active management through stretching, positioning or serial casting. Ignoring such changes risks worsening deformity. Addressing evolving impairments is a core part of cerebral palsy management.
options: Discontinuing all therapy since no lesion change occurred
Stretching and serial casting to manage evolving contracture
Ignoring the finding since the lesion is non-progressive
questions.question: A toddler with cerebral palsy is noted to have progressively tightening heel cords limiting ankle dorsiflexion. What is the most appropriate physiotherapy focus?
Physiological genu valgum in early childhood is generally considered normal up to approximately what age before requiring closer evaluation if persistent?
questions.explanation: Mild physiological genu valgum is common in young children and typically self-corrects by around 7 years of age as normal growth proceeds. Persistence or worsening beyond this age, or asymmetric involvement, warrants further orthopaedic evaluation. Understanding this natural developmental pattern helps avoid unnecessary early intervention.

options: Complete rigid immobilisation of the fracture site
Load-sharing internal splinting allowing earlier mobilisation
Antibiotic delivery to the fracture site
questions.question: The primary purpose of intramedullary nail fixation in femoral shaft fractures is to provide:
questions.explanation: Intramedullary nails are inserted into the medullary canal, providing load-sharing internal splinting that allows progressive weight-bearing and joint mobilisation while the fracture heals. This load-sharing property reduces the risk of disuse complications associated with complete immobilisation. Early physiotherapy following intramedullary fixation is central to preventing joint stiffness and muscle atrophy.

As ambulation declines and fall risk increases, physiotherapy should shift toward contracture prevention, appropriate mobility aids, and strategies to manage fall risk safely, reflecting the progressive nature of the condition. Discontinuing therapy entirely would neglect ongoing needs for function and safety. Proactive, stage-appropriate planning supports the best possible quality of life.
questions.question: A 10-year-old with Duchenne muscular dystrophy is beginning to show reduced ambulation endurance and increased falls. What should the physiotherapy plan now emphasise?
options: Discontinuing all physiotherapy since decline is inevitable
Contracture prevention, mobility aids and fall risk management
Focusing exclusively on academic tuition with no physical input
Ignoring the falls since they are expected and harmless

questions.explanation: Rapid spontaneous improvement within weeks is typical of neuropraxia, the mildest nerve injury involving temporary conduction block without structural nerve disruption. More severe injuries such as neurotmesis or avulsion generally show minimal or no spontaneous recovery. This distinction guides expectations for further intervention.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is grading nerve injury severity in a child with brachial plexus palsy and finds spontaneous improvement within the first month. Which injury type is most consistent?

questions.explanation: Shoulder dystocia, where the baby's shoulder becomes lodged during delivery, is a major risk factor for obstetric brachial plexus injury due to excessive traction forces applied to free the shoulder. Uncomplicated caesarean delivery generally carries lower risk. Recognising risk factors helps anticipate which newborns need early nerve function assessment.
options: Elective caesarean section with no complications
Post-term pregnancy alone with no dystocia
Breech presentation with no traction applied
questions.question: Which risk factor is most associated with obstetric brachial plexus injury during delivery?

questions.explanation: Atlanto-axial joint instability is a specific orthopaedic risk in Down syndrome related to ligamentous laxity at the upper cervical spine. Screening for this before vigorous activity is essential to prevent serious neurological injury. This precaution is a key safety consideration unique to this population.
questions.question: A child with Down syndrome is being screened for orthopaedic risk before starting a new exercise programme. A key structural measurement the therapist should specifically check is:

questions.explanation: Spastic hemiplegia affects one side of the body, usually with the arm more involved than the leg, often following a focal vascular insult or cortical injury. This contrasts with diplegia, which affects both legs, and quadriplegia, which affects all limbs. Recognising the pattern helps target upper limb versus gait interventions.
questions.question: Hemiplegic cerebral palsy typically involves which pattern of body involvement?
options: Both arms only, sparing the legs
One side of the body, arm more than leg
Both legs equally, sparing the arms
All four limbs with trunk involvement

questions.explanation: Head lifting briefly in prone position is an expected skill at around 3 months of age, reflecting early extensor control of the neck. Achieving it earlier or much later than this would be atypical. This milestone forms part of routine developmental screening.
questions.question: A mother reports her infant can lift the head briefly while lying prone. This skill is expected at approximately:
Early physiotherapy management following sciatic nerve palsy primarily focuses on which goal?
options: Preventing contracture and maintaining joint range of motion
Aggressive resisted strengthening from the first day regardless of nerve status
Immediate return to unrestricted competitive sport
Complete immobilisation of the entire limb
Ignoring the affected limb until spontaneous recovery
questions.explanation: Early management focuses on maintaining joint range of motion and preventing contracture in the denervated limb, since muscles without adequate innervation are vulnerable to shortening and stiffness if left unaddressed. Aggressive strengthening is not appropriate until adequate nerve recovery or reinnervation has occurred. This approach supports the best functional outcome as recovery progresses.

questions.question: Karyotyping shows a child's Down syndrome resulted from nondisjunction during meiosis. This mechanism accounts for approximately what proportion of all Down syndrome cases?
questions.explanation: Trisomy 21 from nondisjunction accounts for approximately 95% of all Down syndrome cases, making it by far the most common mechanism. Translocation and mosaic forms make up the remaining smaller proportion. This distinction has implications for genetic counselling and recurrence risk.

questions.question: A child becomes anxious and clingy whenever the primary caregiver leaves the room, but is easily soothed upon their return. This pattern is best explained by Bowlby's theory of:
questions.explanation: Distress on separation followed by being readily comforted on reunion reflects Bowlby's concept of secure attachment. This pattern differs from avoidant or resistant attachment styles described in attachment theory. Recognising secure attachment is reassuring regarding the caregiver-child bond.

Sciatic nerve palsy can result from direct trauma including pressure, stretching or a cut to the nerve, in addition to spinal or iatrogenic causes such as injections. This broad range of aetiologies means a thorough history is important to identify the underlying mechanism. Correct identification of cause guides both prevention and management strategies.
questions.question: Which category broadly describes non-spinal, non-iatrogenic causes of sciatic nerve palsy?
options: Only congenital absence of the nerve
Direct trauma such as pressure, stretching or a cut to the nerve
Only viral infections of the nerve

questions.explanation: Recording both the distribution of limb involvement and the quality of muscle tone reflects a combined topographic and physiological classification of cerebral palsy. This dual approach gives a fuller clinical picture than either system alone. It informs prognosis and guides individualized treatment planning.
questions.question: A therapist records a child's cerebral palsy using both limb distribution and tone quality. This reflects use of:

options: Restrict the child to a wheelchair permanently
Ignore the discrepancy since it will self-correct
Apply a rigid full-leg cast indefinitely
Shoe raise or orthotic adjustment to correct the discrepancy
questions.explanation: Leg length discrepancy from asymmetric growth after motor neuron damage can be managed with shoe raises or orthotic modifications to improve gait symmetry and reduce compensatory strain. It does not typically self-correct without intervention. A multidisciplinary approach involving orthotics optimises long-term mobility.
questions.question: A child with residual polio weakness in one leg has developed a leg length discrepancy affecting gait symmetry. What is the most appropriate management consideration?

questions.explanation: Extension of Erb's palsy to involve the hand and fingers suggests additional injury to the C7 root, beyond the classic C5-C6 pattern. This extended involvement changes the clinical picture and prognosis. Identifying the specific roots involved guides targeted assessment and management planning.
questions.question: An infant with Erb's palsy also develops ipsilateral hand and finger weakness in addition to the shoulder and elbow deficit. This extended pattern suggests involvement of which additional root?

options: A progressive muscle-wasting genetic disease of adulthood
An isolated skin condition with no joint involvement
Congenital contracture of multiple joints in a fixed position
questions.question: Arthrogryposis is best defined as which type of condition?
questions.explanation: Arthrogryposis describes congenital contracture of joints, typically in a flexed or fixed position, present from birth and affecting multiple joints. It is classified as a hereditary disorder of fibrous tissues rather than an acquired infection. Recognising this congenital, multi-joint pattern distinguishes it from other acquired paediatric conditions.

questions.question: Postaxial polydactyly characterising Patau syndrome involves extra digits on which side of the hand?
questions.explanation: Postaxial polydactyly in Patau syndrome involves extra digits on the ulnar side of the hand or fibular side of the foot, reflecting disrupted sonic hedgehog signalling in limb pattern formation. This contrasts with preaxial polydactyly occurring on the radial/tibial side with different genetic associations. Documentation of polydactyly type contributes to differential diagnosis of multiple congenital anomaly syndromes.

options: Symmetrical head movement in all directions
Age-appropriate head control with full neck rotation
Persistent head tilt to one side with limited neck rotation
questions.question: Which finding would most appropriately prompt referral for further assessment of possible torticollis in a 2-month-old?
questions.explanation: A persistent head tilt combined with limited active or passive neck rotation in early infancy is a key clinical sign prompting further assessment for torticollis, ideally identified and treated early for the best outcomes. Symmetrical movement and full rotation would be reassuring, normal findings. Early recognition and referral support timely initiation of stretching-based physiotherapy management.

questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease and chronic hip avascular necrosis is being assessed for a long-term exercise programme. Which principle should guide the plan?
questions.explanation: For chronic avascular necrosis, exercise planning should balance protecting the compromised joint from excessive loading while still maintaining functional mobility and strength through appropriate low-impact activity. Complete immobilisation risks stiffness and deconditioning, while high-impact loading could worsen joint damage. An individualised, joint-protective approach is key.
options: Ignore joint status and use standard paediatric protocols
Balance joint protection with maintaining functional mobility
Maximise high-impact loading regardless of joint status

questions.question: When assessing an infant with obstetric brachial plexus injury, the therapist compares movement quality on the affected side against the infant's own primitive reflexes mainly to help:
questions.explanation: Comparing an infant's affected-side movement quality against the child's own primitive reflex responses helps the therapist distinguish true muscle weakness from simple reflex absence in obstetric brachial plexus injury. This comparison improves diagnostic accuracy. It supports a more targeted approach to ongoing assessment and treatment planning.

options: Hearing impairment as the only possibility
Language delay warranting speech therapy referral
Normal variation for bilingual children only
questions.explanation: Two-word combinations absent at 28 months, significantly beyond the typical 18-24 month window, represents language delay warranting speech therapy evaluation and screening for conditions commonly comorbid with language delay including autism spectrum disorder, hearing impairment, and cognitive developmental delay. Interdisciplinary awareness enables timely referrals within paediatric rehabilitation teams. Language development monitoring is part of comprehensive paediatric physiotherapy assessment.
questions.question: Two-word combinations typically emerge at 18-24 months. Absence of two-word phrases at 28 months suggests:
Which broad category divides the two main types of stroke based on underlying mechanism?
questions.explanation: Stroke is broadly classified as ischaemic, caused by blocked blood flow, or haemorrhagic, caused by bleeding into or around the brain tissue. This distinction is critical because management approaches differ significantly between the two types. Accurate classification, usually via imaging, guides both acute medical treatment and rehabilitation planning.

A birth weight greater than 4 kg is a recognised significant risk factor for obstetric brachial plexus injury, reflecting the increased likelihood of shoulder dystocia during delivery of a large infant. Lower birth weights do not carry this same elevated risk. Awareness of this threshold supports anticipatory clinical vigilance.
questions.question: A delivery is complicated by macrosomia, with the baby's birth weight noted as a key risk factor for obstetric brachial plexus injury. The clinically significant threshold is birth weight over:

options: Hip subluxation or dislocation causing pain
questions.explanation: Progressive lateral migration of the femoral head in cerebral palsy from spasticity and muscle imbalance can lead to subluxation or complete dislocation, causing chronic pain, sitting difficulties, and care complications. Hip surveillance programmes using annual X-rays to measure migration percentage enable preventive intervention before irreversible dislocation occurs. Physiotherapy contributes through standing programmes, hip abductor strengthening, and appropriate positioning.
questions.question: A 7-year-old with cerebral palsy receives orthopaedic review. Hip surveillance is recommended because progressive femoral head migration can lead to:

options: Monitor for corticosteroid-related side effects such as weight gain affecting mobility
Physiotherapy should stop entirely once medication begins
This medication only affects unrelated organ systems
Corticosteroids have no relevance to physiotherapy management
Corticosteroids eliminate the need for any further monitoring
questions.explanation: Corticosteroid therapy, while beneficial in slowing disease progression, can cause side effects such as weight gain that may affect mobility and load on already weakened muscles, making this a relevant physiotherapy monitoring consideration. Physiotherapy input remains important throughout medical treatment rather than being replaced by it. Coordinated multidisciplinary care optimises overall outcomes.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is coordinating care for a boy with Duchenne muscular dystrophy who is starting corticosteroid therapy. What is a relevant physiotherapy consideration?

questions.explanation: New neurological symptoms in a child with known spina bifida occulta during growth periods may indicate tethered cord syndrome, where rapid spinal growth stretches the spinal cord fixed at its caudal attachment, causing progressive neurological injury. This requires urgent neuroimaging and neurosurgical referral to prevent irreversible damage. Physiotherapists recognising this red flag pattern play a critical role in preventing permanent neurological deterioration.
questions.question: A child with spina bifida occulta presents with new foot weakness and back pain during a growth spurt. The physiotherapist should suspect:

questions.explanation: Because dystrophin-deficient muscle fibres are especially vulnerable to damage from high-force eccentric contractions, high-intensity eccentric resistance exercise is generally avoided as it can accelerate muscle fibre breakdown in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Instead, moderate, submaximal activity is generally favoured to maintain function without excessive damage. This exercise precaution is a key consideration in tailoring physiotherapy programmes for this population.
options: It reverses the underlying genetic defect
It is only relevant to cardiac muscle, not skeletal muscle
It is universally recommended as first-line treatment
It can accelerate muscle fibre damage in dystrophin-deficient muscle
It has no effect on dystrophic muscle at all
questions.question: Why is high-intensity eccentric resistance exercise generally avoided in children with Duchenne muscular dystrophy?

questions.explanation: Involuntary mirrored movement appearing in the unaffected limb during an effortful task in spastic hemiplegia is termed an associated reaction, distinct from protective, righting, or equilibrium responses. These movements are involuntary rather than purposeful. Recognising associated reactions helps differentiate them from genuine voluntary improvement.
questions.question: During an effortful reaching task, a child with spastic hemiplegia shows involuntary mirrored movement in the unaffected arm. This phenomenon is known as:
A therapist tests ventral suspension in a 5-month-old and finds no head, trunk or limb extension response. What should be suspected?
questions.explanation: Because the Landau reflex should be emerging by around 3 months, its absence at 5 months is atypical and warrants closer neurological evaluation. It may point toward hypotonia or delayed central nervous system maturation. Serial assessment helps determine whether the delay resolves or persists.
options: Completely normal development for this age
Delayed or absent Landau reflex needing further neuro assessment

questions.question: Which term describes the adaptive functioning skills needed to live independently, such as self-care and communication?
questions.explanation: Adaptive behaviours refer specifically to the practical skills required for independent living, including self-care, communication and social interaction, which are assessed alongside cognitive functioning in diagnosing intellectual disability. This term is distinct from motor reflexes or developmental principles discussed elsewhere in paediatric assessment. Understanding this terminology supports accurate multidisciplinary communication and documentation.

Increasing supervised tummy time during awake periods and varying head positioning helps reduce sustained pressure on one area of the skull, addressing positional plagiocephaly while supporting overall motor development. Continuing unchanged supine positioning would likely worsen the flattening. Family education on safe sleep alongside positional variation during awake time is key to management.
questions.question: A caregiver reports their 4-month-old spends most of the day lying on their back and now has a flattened area on the back of the skull. What is the most appropriate physiotherapy advice?
options: Keep the infant supine at all times with no change
Recommend permanent side-lying with no variation
Avoid all interaction with the infant's head position
Increase supervised tummy time and vary head positioning

questions.explanation: Using the thumb and index fingertip to pick up a small object is the defining feature of a pincer grasp, distinct from the cruder palmar or raking grasp patterns. This refined grasp typically emerges around 9-10 months. Its presence reflects maturing fine motor control.
questions.question: A 10-month-old picks up a small raisin using the thumb and index finger tip. This skill is known as:

questions.explanation: Family-centred practice actively involves caregivers as partners throughout assessment, goal-setting and intervention, recognising that consistent family involvement, especially through home programmes, is critical to therapy success in children. Excluding families or ignoring their input undermines both engagement and outcomes. This collaborative approach is a foundational principle across paediatric physiotherapy practice.
questions.question: A key principle in family-centred paediatric physiotherapy practice is which of the following?
options: Excluding caregivers from all therapy sessions
Assuming family preferences are irrelevant to therapy planning
Actively involving caregivers as partners in assessment and intervention planning
Making all decisions without any family input
Treating the child in complete isolation from family context
Assume the child cannot participate in any motor therapy
Increase instruction complexity to challenge the child
Break the task into single, simple steps with demonstration
Continue using the same complex instructions regardless
Refuse to modify the session format at all
questions.explanation: Simplifying instructions into single steps with visual demonstration supports better understanding and participation for a child with intellectual disability, matching the teaching approach to the child's cognitive processing needs. Maintaining unmodified complex instructions would likely reduce engagement and successful task completion. Practical, individualised communication adaptations improve therapy effectiveness.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing a 6-year-old with intellectual disability who struggles to follow multi-step verbal instructions during a gross motor task. What is the most appropriate adaptation?

options: A fibrous mass or tightness within the muscle
A viral infection unrelated to the muscle
An acute bacterial infection of the muscle
A malignant tumour of the muscle
questions.explanation: Congenital muscular torticollis is most often caused by a fibrous mass or shortening within the sternocleidomastoid muscle, leading to lateral neck flexion toward and rotation away from the affected side. It is not typically caused by infection or malignancy. Early physiotherapy stretching is the mainstay of conservative management.
questions.question: Congenital muscular torticollis in infants is most commonly caused by which finding in the sternocleidomastoid muscle?
Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder characteristically causes inflammatory attacks in which two CNS regions?
questions.explanation: Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder is characterised by inflammatory demyelinating attacks primarily targeting the optic nerves and spinal cord, distinguishing it from classic multiple sclerosis. This produces visual loss alongside motor and sensory spinal cord symptoms. Correct localisation of attacks aids differential diagnosis from other demyelinating disorders.
options: Only the peripheral retina without spinal involvement

questions.explanation: An ordinal scale ranks data in a meaningful order, such as mild, moderate or severe pain, but the intervals between ranks are not necessarily equal. This differs from interval and ratio scales, which have consistent, measurable intervals between values. Many clinical outcome measures, such as functional grading scales, use ordinal data.
questions.question: Which level of measurement ranks data in order but does not guarantee equal intervals between ranks?
During a sickle cell disease exercise programme, which combination of conditions must be avoided to prevent vasoocclusive crisis?
questions.explanation: Dehydration, hypoxia, and sustained high-intensity exercise causing lactic acidosis promote deoxygenation of haemoglobin, triggering HbS polymerisation and sickling in the microvasculature. Physiotherapy exercise programmes must ensure adequate hydration, appropriate exercise intensity with rest periods, and avoidance of hypoxic environments including high altitude. Moderate-intensity aerobic exercise is safe when these precautions are maintained consistently.

questions.question: A child recovering from ADEM develops chronic fatigue 3 months post-onset. The most appropriate physiotherapy strategy is:
questions.explanation: Post-ADEM chronic fatigue is managed through graded exercise programmes incorporating activity pacing and energy conservation, incrementally building tolerance while preventing boom-bust cycles. Abrupt cessation worsens deconditioning and fatigue perpetuating factors. Physiotherapists apply evidence-based fatigue management principles from post-inflammatory neurological rehabilitation literature.

questions.question: A child with Duchenne muscular dystrophy is encouraged to participate in vigorous, high-intensity sport. This is discouraged primarily because overexertion in this condition may:
questions.explanation: Vigorous, high-intensity activity is discouraged in Duchenne muscular dystrophy because overexertion can accelerate muscle fibre damage in already vulnerable dystrophin-deficient muscle. This is the opposite of improving dystrophin production or reversing progression. Exercise prescription must therefore balance activity benefits against this specific risk.

options: Prolonged supine positioning with limited position variation
questions.question: Positional plagiocephaly in infants is most closely associated with which practice?
questions.explanation: Positional plagiocephaly, or flattening of the skull, is associated with prolonged time spent in one position, particularly supine sleeping without adequate variation or tummy time during awake hours. Supervised tummy time is actually protective by reducing sustained pressure on one area of the skull. Physiotherapists often recommend repositioning strategies and tummy time to help manage this condition.

options: Ordinary teething irritability in an infant
Mild seasonal cough with no other symptoms
Sudden onset facial droop, arm weakness or speech difficulty
Gradual weight gain over several months
Slow, chronic decline in appetite over a year
questions.question: Which of these is a recognised acute warning sign of stroke in children that should prompt emergency evaluation?
questions.explanation: Sudden onset of facial droop, arm weakness or speech difficulty are classic acute stroke warning signs that apply to children as well as adults, requiring emergency medical evaluation. These signs reflect an acute focal neurological event rather than gradual, chronic changes. Prompt recognition and urgent referral are critical to minimise long-term disability.

questions.question: A 6-week-old infant is brought in with the head persistently tilted to the left and rotated to the right. What is the most likely diagnosis and initial management approach?
options: Erb's palsy managed with elbow splinting
Congenital muscular torticollis managed with gentle stretching
Sciatic nerve palsy managed with an ankle-foot orthosis
DDH managed with a Pavlik harness
questions.explanation: The described head tilt and rotation pattern is classic for congenital muscular torticollis affecting the left sternocleidomastoid, and gentle, consistent stretching is the standard first-line physiotherapy management. Early intervention improves the likelihood of full resolution without surgery. Family education on positioning and handling techniques supports the home stretching programme.

options: Wrist extensors and intrinsic hand muscles
questions.question: In Erb's palsy from C5-C6 injury, the 'waiter's tip' posture reflects unopposed action of which muscle group?
questions.explanation: C5-C6 nerve root damage paralyses shoulder abductors and external rotators, allowing intact adductors and internal rotators to dominate, holding the arm adducted, internally rotated with elbow extended. The resulting posture resembles a waiter expecting a tip. Recognising this pattern guides targeted physiotherapy to prevent contracture of the dominant unopposed muscle groups.

Congenital talipes equinovarus, commonly known as clubfoot, presents with the foot turned inward and downward at birth due to abnormal positioning of the foot and ankle joints. This differs from genu valgum, which affects knee alignment, and DDH, which affects the hip. The Ponseti method of serial casting is a well-established conservative treatment approach.
questions.question: Which paediatric foot deformity is characterised by the foot being turned inward and downward at birth?

questions.explanation: Multiple fractures at different healing stages with an inconsistent history are significant red flags for non-accidental injury, requiring the clinician to raise concerns through proper child protection and safeguarding channels rather than direct confrontation or dismissal. This is a critical safety responsibility for all healthcare providers working with children. Prompt, appropriate escalation protects the child's welfare.
options: Discharge the child with no further action
Raise safeguarding concerns through appropriate child protection channels
Assume this is a coincidental normal finding
Confront the caregivers directly without involving appropriate services
Ignore the pattern and proceed with routine therapy only
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices an infant with multiple fractures at different healing stages and an inconsistent history from caregivers. What is the most appropriate action?

questions.explanation: Vaso-occlusive crises occur when sickle-shaped red blood cells become rigid and obstruct microvascular blood flow, causing tissue ischaemia and pain. This is the hallmark acute complication of sickle cell disease. Management focuses on hydration, pain control and addressing any triggering factors such as infection or dehydration.
options: Viral destruction of red cell precursors
Bacterial infection of bone marrow directly
Sickled red cells obstructing small blood vessels
questions.question: A painful vaso-occlusive crisis in sickle cell disease is primarily caused by which process?

questions.explanation: Height measured in centimetres is a ratio-level variable because it has a true zero point and allows meaningful ratio comparisons, such as saying one child is twice as tall as another. This classification is important because it permits the widest range of valid statistical operations, including means and ratios. Correctly identifying height as ratio data supports accurate growth tracking analysis.
options: Nominal scale, since it has no order or meaning
Ordinal scale, since only ranking is possible
Ratio scale, since it has a true zero and meaningful ratios between values
It cannot be classified using standard measurement scales
Interval scale, since there is no true zero for height
questions.question: A physiotherapist records a child's height in centimetres for tracking growth. Which level of measurement does this represent, and why is this classification important?

questions.explanation: A nominal scale classifies data into distinct categories without any implied order or ranking, such as blood type or sex. This is the most basic level of measurement among the four classic scales. Understanding scale type is essential for selecting appropriate statistical analysis methods in outcome measurement.
questions.question: Which level of measurement classifies data into categories with no inherent order, such as blood type?
A newborn has a bony vertebral defect with no visible sac and no neurological deficit. This presentation is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: A bony vertebral defect without a visible sac or neurological deficit is characteristic of spina bifida occulta, the mildest and often asymptomatic form. This contrasts with meningocele and myelomeningocele, which involve a visible sac. Recognising this distinction avoids unnecessary alarm in asymptomatic cases.

options: Adaptive behaviours needed for independent living
questions.question: Intellectual disability is generally characterised by significantly impaired cognitive functioning along with deficits in which additional area?
questions.explanation: Intellectual disability involves significantly impaired cognitive functioning combined with deficits in adaptive behaviours, which are the practical skills needed for independent daily living such as communication, self-care and social skills. This dual criterion distinguishes it from isolated sensory or physical impairments. Comprehensive assessment addresses both cognitive and adaptive functioning domains.

options: Associated Horner's syndrome from sympathetic chain involvement
Sign of good prognosis for full recovery
questions.question: A child with Klumpke's palsy is noted to also have drooping of one eyelid and a smaller pupil on the same side. What does this combination suggest?
questions.explanation: Ptosis and miosis alongside Klumpke's palsy suggest Horner's syndrome from sympathetic fibre disruption near the T1 nerve root, indicating more extensive plexus involvement. This combination is generally associated with a more guarded prognosis. It should prompt closer specialist monitoring and assessment.

options: Allow unrestricted maximal exertion with no precautions
Ignore the child's disease status during planning
Encourage graded participation with hydration and rest breaks
Recommend only bed rest as the safest option
questions.explanation: Graded participation with attention to adequate hydration, avoiding overheating, and built-in rest breaks allows children with sickle cell disease to safely engage in physical activity while minimising crisis triggers. Complete prohibition is overly restrictive and can affect psychosocial wellbeing. Individualised, informed activity planning balances safety with participation.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is designing an activity plan for a child with sickle cell disease who wants to join a school sports team. What guidance is most appropriate?

questions.explanation: Legg-Calve-Perthes syndrome typically presents in children between approximately 4 and 8 years of age, with boys affected more often than girls. This age-specific vulnerability relates to the pattern of femoral head blood supply during growth. Recognising the typical age range assists in clinical suspicion during assessment.
questions.question: Legg-Calve-Perthes syndrome most commonly affects children within which age range?

questions.explanation: Children with Legg-Calve-Perthes syndrome often present with an insidious, painless or mildly painful limp rather than acute severe symptoms, which can delay diagnosis. High fever and joint redness would suggest an infectious process such as septic arthritis instead. Recognising the typically subtle presentation supports timely orthopaedic referral.
options: Immediate total loss of hip motion
Sudden complete paralysis of the leg
questions.question: Which symptom is a common early presentation of Legg-Calve-Perthes syndrome?
During assessment, a 10-month-old fails to extend the arms protectively when tipped sideways while sitting. What is the clinical significance?
questions.explanation: Since the protective extension reaction should be present by 6 to 9 months, its absence at 10 months signals a possible neuromotor deficit. This reaction is essential for safe sitting and fall prevention. Prompt referral for comprehensive neurodevelopmental assessment is indicated.
options: This is unrelated to motor development
This indicates only a hearing problem
Absent protective extension is a red flag for neuromotor dysfunction
This is expected and requires no action

questions.question: During assessment, a 10-month-old uses a raking motion instead of a pincer grasp to pick up a raisin. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: This is an emergency requiring immediate surgery
This confirms a definite diagnosis of cerebral palsy
This means the child is deaf
This indicates normal advanced fine motor skill
This may represent a mild fine motor delay needing monitoring
questions.explanation: Since the pincer grasp typically emerges by 9 months, persistence of a raking pattern at 10 months is a mild delay that should be monitored with reassessment. It does not on its own confirm a neurological diagnosis. Serial observation guides whether further referral is needed.

questions.question: A boy with muscular dystrophy is asked to record every time he stumbles or falls at home. This fall diary is primarily kept by:
questions.explanation: A fall diary in muscular dystrophy is typically kept by the family or caregiver at home, providing the clinical team with real-world data on frequency and circumstances of falls. This information supports monitoring of disease progression between clinic visits. It also helps guide timely adjustments to mobility aids or safety precautions.

Because dyskinetic cerebral palsy frequently involves orofacial involuntary movements, feeding and swallowing difficulties are common and should prompt a specific oromotor and feeding assessment. This is not something to dismiss or assume is normal. Collaborative management with speech-language therapy protects nutritional safety.
questions.question: An infant with a known perinatal hypoxic event develops fluctuating tone and orofacial involuntary movements by age one. What immediate implication does this raise for feeding therapy?
options: Confirmation that feeding is completely normal
No relevance to feeding at all
Sign that speech therapy is contraindicated
Risk of oromotor dysfunction requiring feeding assessment
Indication for immediate tube feeding without assessment

questions.explanation: Following the acute inflammatory phase of ADEM, physiotherapy focuses on rehabilitating any residual motor, balance or cognitive deficits, since many children make significant but sometimes incomplete recovery. Immediate return to full activity without assessment risks missing ongoing impairments. Individualised rehabilitation planning supports optimal long-term function.
questions.question: A key physiotherapy consideration after resolution of the acute phase of ADEM is which of the following?
options: Rehabilitation of residual motor and cognitive deficits
Immediate return to competitive sport with no assessment
No further physiotherapy is ever needed
Avoiding all physical activity for years

questions.question: Which primitive reflex is elicited by turning an infant's head to one side, causing extension of the limbs on the face side and flexion on the skull side?
questions.explanation: The asymmetric tonic neck reflex produces the classic fencing posture when the head is turned, with limb extension on the chin side and flexion on the occiput side. It normally integrates by 4 to 6 months. Its persistence beyond this age can interfere with rolling and midline hand use.

questions.question: A child with developmental delay continues to show strong primitive reflexes well beyond the expected age of integration. A likely functional consequence of this persistence is:
questions.explanation: Persistent primitive reflexes beyond the expected age of integration commonly interfere with the development of voluntary, purposeful movement rather than enhancing it. This persistence is a clinical red flag for neuromotor delay. Early identification allows for targeted intervention to support functional progress.

questions.question: A child with spastic hemiplegia favours the unaffected hand for all tasks, causing the affected hand to be underused. Which intervention approach directly addresses this pattern?
options: Complete immobilisation of the unaffected hand permanently
questions.explanation: Constraint-induced movement therapy restricts the unaffected limb temporarily to encourage active use of the affected hand, addressing learned non-use common in hemiplegia. This differs from simply strengthening unrelated muscle groups. It has strong evidence for improving upper limb function in hemiplegic cerebral palsy.

options: Complete absence of any joint movement
Normal reflexes with no change at all
questions.explanation: Hypotonia is characterised by reduced resistance to passive movement, often accompanied by increased joint range and a 'floppy' presentation on handling. This contrasts with hypertonia, where resistance to passive movement is increased. Correctly distinguishing tone abnormalities supports accurate diagnosis and appropriately targeted intervention.
questions.question: A paediatric physiotherapist assessing hypotonia should expect to find which characteristic on examination?

options: Focus solely on passive range of motion with no active balance work
Improve dynamic sitting and standing balance for daily function
Discharge without any functional goal setting
Avoid all balance training to prevent falls
Achieve competitive gymnastics level balance immediately
questions.explanation: Realistic, functional goals such as improving dynamic sitting and standing balance directly address the residual trunk ataxia while supporting safe daily activity participation. Overly ambitious goals unrelated to current ability are not appropriate at this stage. Structured, progressive goal-setting supports measurable rehabilitation outcomes.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is planning discharge goals for a child recovering from ADEM with mild residual trunk ataxia. Which goal is most appropriate?
A caregiver asks why their child's sciatic nerve palsy is being managed conservatively rather than with immediate surgery. What is the most appropriate explanation?
options: Surgery is always the first-line treatment for any nerve injury
Conservative management is never appropriate for nerve injuries
Many cases show partial or full spontaneous recovery, so conservative management is trialled first
Nerve injuries never recover without surgical intervention
There is no rationale for this treatment approach
questions.explanation: Many sciatic nerve injuries, depending on severity and cause, show partial or complete spontaneous recovery over time, so conservative management with monitoring and supportive therapy is often trialled before considering surgical exploration. Surgery is generally reserved for cases without adequate recovery within an expected timeframe or with confirmed nerve transection. Explaining this staged approach helps families understand the treatment rationale.

questions.question: Resistance exercise prescribed for a young child with Duchenne muscular dystrophy should generally be:
questions.explanation: Resistance exercise for a young child with Duchenne muscular dystrophy should be kept light and submaximal to avoid accelerating muscle fibre breakdown. Maximal or eccentric high-load training carries particular risk in this dystrophin-deficient muscle. This cautious approach balances functional benefit against potential harm.

options: Complete immobilisation of the entire limb long-term
Passive range of motion and positioning to prevent contracture
Aggressive resisted strengthening of denervated muscles
questions.question: An early-phase physiotherapy plan is being developed for a child with new sciatic nerve palsy following a traumatic injury. What should be prioritised in this phase?
questions.explanation: In the early phase following nerve injury, passive range of motion and appropriate positioning help prevent contracture in the denervated muscle groups while nerve recovery is awaited or monitored. Aggressive strengthening of muscles without adequate innervation is not effective or appropriate at this stage. This cautious early approach supports optimal recovery potential.

questions.question: Spastic cerebral palsy accounts for 80% of cases. Spasticity is characterised by which examination finding distinguishing it from rigidity?
questions.explanation: Spasticity is defined as velocity-dependent increased resistance to passive stretch of muscle from upper motor neurone lesion hyperexcitability. This velocity-dependence clinically distinguishes spasticity from rigidity, which shows equal resistance at all speeds. Clinical recognition guides appropriate physiotherapy interventions including speed-controlled stretching, serial casting, and hydrotherapy for spasticity reduction.
options: No increase in tone at any speed

questions.question: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is inherited in which pattern?
questions.explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy follows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern, resulting from mutations in the dystrophin gene, which predominantly affects males while females are typically carriers. This inheritance pattern explains why the condition is rarely seen in girls. Understanding the genetics supports appropriate family counselling and screening of at-risk relatives.

questions.question: Ataxic cerebral palsy primarily results from damage to which brain structure?
questions.explanation: Ataxic cerebral palsy results from cerebellar injury, producing poor coordination, unsteady gait and difficulty with balance and fine motor precision. Basal ganglia injury instead produces dyskinetic features, while corticospinal tract damage produces spasticity. Identifying the lesion site helps explain the clinical presentation.

Splinting in obstetric brachial plexus injury is generally reserved for specific deformity prevention rather than applied universally regardless of severity. Overuse of splints without clear indication can limit active movement and function. Targeted use balances protection against contracture with promotion of active use.
questions.question: Parents ask whether splinting is needed for their infant's mild obstetric brachial plexus injury with good spontaneous movement. Splinting in OBPI is generally reserved for:

questions.explanation: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development describes the difference between what a child can achieve independently and what they can achieve with guidance from a more skilled other, emphasising the role of social interaction in learning. This concept supports the therapeutic use of scaffolded, guided practice in paediatric physiotherapy. Applying this idea helps therapists calibrate the right level of support during skill teaching.
questions.question: Vygotsky's concept of the 'zone of proximal development' refers to which idea?
options: An area of the brain responsible for language only
A fixed stage of purely physical growth
A measurement of muscle tone in infants
The exact age at which walking begins
The gap between what a child can do alone and with guided support
No further treatment is needed once the first cast is removed
A series of gentle casts gradually correct the position over several weeks, followed by bracing
The method has a very low success rate and is rarely used
Casting is painful and should be avoided if at all possible
A single cast will immediately and permanently correct the deformity
questions.question: A family is anxious about starting Ponseti casting for their newborn's clubfoot and asks about the expected process. What is the most appropriate explanation?
questions.explanation: Explaining that the Ponseti method involves a series of gentle, sequential casts over several weeks to gradually correct the foot position, followed by a bracing programme to maintain correction, helps set realistic expectations for the family. It is a well-established, generally well-tolerated method with high success rates worldwide. Clear explanation supports family confidence and adherence to the full treatment programme, including the bracing phase.
