questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the urease test.
(b) State the principle of the mannitol motility test.
(c) List the materials required for each test.
(d) Describe the procedure for each test.
(e) State how results of each test are reported, with examples.
(f) Explain why these tests are useful in bacterial identification.
(g) Distinguish the urease test from the mannitol motility test.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Urease principle: urease is a hydrolytic enzyme that attacks the nitrogen-carbon bond in amide compounds such as urea, forming the alkaline end product ammonia; urea broth/agar contains phenol red as indicator.
(b)
Mannitol motility principle: this is a semisolid agar medium; motile bacteria swarm to give diffused spreading growth, while non-motile bacteria give growth confined to the stab line with sharply defined margins; it also detects mannitol fermentation via a phenol red colour change.
(c)
Materials (urease): bacterial broth cultures, Christensen's urea agar slant, inoculation loop. Materials (mannitol motility): bacterial culture broth, mannitol fermentation (semisolid) medium, inoculation loop.
(d)
• Urease procedure: inoculate the medium with the test organism by loop inoculation; keep an uninoculated tube as control; incubate at 37°C for 24 hours and observe.
• Mannitol motility procedure: inoculate the medium by stab inoculation; keep an uninoculated tube as control; incubate at 37°C for 24-48 hours; observe for motility pattern and colour change.
(e)
• Urease reporting: a deep pink colour is positive (e.g. Klebsiella sp., Proteus sp.); no colour change is negative (e.g. E. coli, Salmonella sp.).
• Mannitol motility reporting: diffuse, hazy growth is motile (e.g. Pseudomonas sp.); growth confined to the stab line only is non-motile (e.g. Staphylococcus aureus); red colour is mannitol non-fermenting (e.g. Bacillus cereus); yellow colour is mannitol fermenting (e.g. E. coli).
(f)
Why used: the urease test aids identification of organisms such as Proteus and Klebsiella, while the mannitol motility test provides both motility and mannitol fermentation information in a single medium.
(g)
• Distinguishing feature: urease testing relies on ammonia production raising pH (phenol red turns pink), a purely chemical colour reaction.
• Mannitol motility testing combines a physical observation (spreading growth pattern indicating motility) with a separate acid-fermentation colour change (red to yellow) in the same semisolid medium.
• Both tests are read after overnight incubation at 37°C and compared against an uninoculated control tube.
• Both tests contribute biochemical/physiological information that is combined with other tests (e.g. indole, citrate) to complete identification of an isolate.

questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the skin snip technique for onchocerciasis.
(b) Describe the procedure, including apparatus used.
(c) State a precaution/limitation of the technique.
(d) State how stool samples are generally collected and handled for parasitological examination.
(e) Explain why correct specimen handling is important in both techniques.
(f) Distinguish the skin snip technique from routine stool sample collection.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Principle: a skin snip is used to detect microfilariae (larvae) that migrate to the skin in onchocerciasis; incubating the tissue in saline allows the microfilariae to emerge for microscopic identification.
(b)
• Apparatus: a razor blade or biopsy punch (e.g. sclerocorneal) is used to remove tiny skin samples (3-5mg) from multiple sites (e.g. iliac crests, shoulder blades) by elevating a small cone of skin.
• Procedure: the tissue is incubated in normal saline at room temperature for 24 hours to allow microfilariae to emerge, then examined microscopically; nucleic acid amplification can also be used on skin-snip specimens.
(c)
Precaution/limitation: sensitivity is low in the early disease stage and in geographic areas of low prevalence, so a negative result does not exclude infection.
(d)
• Stool collection principle: freshly passed stool samples are preferred over specimens from a bed pan; a sterile or clean container (not cleaned with disinfectant) preserves organism viability.
• Stool handling: samples are sometimes examined fresh (for amoeba, ciliates), with liquid/soft stool examined within 15 minutes; the sample must not be mixed with urine or disinfectant, as these kill trophozoites; specimens from enema or laxatives are often positive for worm eggs or adult worms.
• Stool preservation: samples may be mixed with 10% formalin or polyvinyl chloride (3 parts stool to 1 part preservative), or left unpreserved for antigen detection/PCR; storage is at 4°C, or -15°C for antigen/PCR.
(e)
• Why correct handling matters (both): both procedures are designed to preserve the viability or detectability of the target organism (microfilariae or stool pathogens) from the time of collection to the time of laboratory examination.
• Reasoning: killing trophozoites through improper handling (e.g. disinfectant contact) or allowing microfilariae to remain undetected through insufficient incubation time would both result in a false-negative finding despite true infection being present.
(f)
• Distinguishing feature: the skin snip procedure requires an incubation step (24 hours in saline) to let the organism migrate out of the tissue before it can be seen, whereas stool collection principally requires correct timing, container, preservative and temperature to keep organisms viable or detectable, without an equivalent incubation step.
• Both procedures require prompt transport/handling to the laboratory to avoid deterioration of the specimen or loss of the diagnostic organism.
• Both are examples of how the biology of the target parasite (tissue-migrating microfilariae versus intestinal trophozoites/eggs) determines the specific collection and handling method required.

questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the Gram stain.
(b) List the reagents/materials required for Gram staining.
(c) Describe the procedure for Gram staining.
(d) State a precaution relevant to interpreting Gram stain results.
(e) State how Gram stain results are reported.
(f) Explain why the Gram stain is used/preferred as a starting point in bacterial identification.
(g) Distinguish the Gram stain from the acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen) stain.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principle: dye retention depends on the physical properties (thickness, density, porosity) and chemical composition of the bacterial cell wall.
• Gram-positive bacteria have thick, dense, relatively non-porous walls; Gram-negative bacteria have thin walls surrounded by lipid-rich membranes.
(b)
Materials: crystal violet (primary stain), iodine solution (mordant), decolorizer (ethanol and acetone mixture), safranin (counterstain), water.
(c)
• Procedure step 1: heat-fix the specimen on a slide, then stain with crystal violet; both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria appear purple at this stage.
• Procedure step 2: apply Gram's iodine (mordant), forming an insoluble crystal violet-iodine complex ("iodine lake"); both groups remain purple.
• Procedure step 3: decolorize with the ethanol/acetone mixture; Gram-positive organisms retain the crystal violet-iodine complex, Gram-negative organisms are decolorized.
• Procedure step 4: counterstain with safranin; Gram-negative organisms take up the red counterstain, Gram-positive organisms remain purple.
(d)
Precaution: over-decolorization can cause Gram-positive organisms, or aged/damaged cells, to stain falsely Gram-negative.
(e)
Reporting: organisms are reported as Gram-positive (purple) or Gram-negative (red), together with their shape and arrangement.
(f)
Why preferred: it improves visibility by contrast, differentiates morphological types, and divides bacteria into Gram-positive and Gram-negative groups, forming the starting point for bacterial identification.
(g)
• Distinguishing feature: the acid-fast stain uses carbol fuchsin, acid-alcohol as decolorizer, and methylene blue as counterstain, unlike the crystal violet/iodine/safranin sequence of the Gram stain.
• The acid-fast reaction depends on the lipid-rich, mycolic-acid-containing cell wall of organisms such as Mycobacterium resisting decolorization by acid-alcohol, a property that Gram-positive/negative differentiation does not test for.

(a)
• Structure/features: fungi are eukaryotic organisms with a membrane-bound nucleus, endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria (unlike prokaryotic bacteria); they are heterotrophic and are either saprophytes (living on dead organic matter) or parasites (living on living organisms).
• Moulds show filamentous growth while yeasts show pasty or mucoid growth; saprophytic moulds are grouped by mycelium type: septate versus aseptate, and hyaline (colourless) versus dematiaceous (pigmented, dark, grey to black).
• Identifying characteristics - hyaline septate members: Aspergillus spp. have septate, hyaline mycelium with unbranched conidiophores (A. fumigatus a potential pathogen, especially from a pulmonary source); Penicillium spp. have brush-shaped conidiophores with flask-shaped sterigmata.
(b)
• Identifying characteristics - dematiaceous members: Alternaria spp. develop very dark colonies with age and bear chains of large brown conidia; Cladosporium spp. have septate dematiaceous mycelium, conidia in chains, and green colonies with a black reverse.
• Identifying characteristics - aseptate members: all are susceptible to cycloheximide and are rapid growers; some (e.g. Rhizopus spp.) have root-like rhizoids, and spore-bearing structures are called sporangiophores.
(c)
• Standard method/setting: fungal culturing uses tubed media (rather than plates) because there is less chance of spore release into the environment, less chance of dehydration, and ease of storage; tube agar is inoculated in a straight line, plate agar in a large "S" pattern.
• Cultures are incubated aerobically (and anaerobically if Actinomycetes are suspected) at room temperature, and also at 37°C if dimorphic fungi are suspected; cultures are kept for 4 weeks and examined every other day, with systemic pathogens often needing 10 days to 2 weeks.
(d)
• Specimens are processed for recovery accordingly: skin, nails and hair undergo direct examination following KOH preparation; pleural fluid, sputum and bronchial aspirates must be fresh, as saprophytes would overgrow pathogens such as Histoplasma capsulatum.
• Precaution/safety reasoning: because dimorphic fungal cultures, especially Coccidioides immitis, produce arthroconidia that are very easily inhaled, caution must be taken when handling such cultures, and transport packaging must state "WARNING: POTENTIAL PATHOGEN" on the outside label.
• Using tubed rather than plated media for suspect pathogenic fungi is itself a safety precaution, since it reduces the chance of spores becoming airborne during examination or handling.
• Correct recognition of septate versus aseptate, and hyaline versus dematiaceous mycelium, guides identification, since misclassifying these basic structural features can group an isolate with the wrong saprophyte or pathogen category.
• Overall, correct culture handling (tubed media, appropriate incubation temperature/duration) together with safety precautions (avoiding inhalation of arthroconidia, correct specimen labelling) is essential when working with fungal cultures.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the structural classification of fungal saprophyte mycelium (septate/aseptate, hyaline/dematiaceous).
(b) State identifying microscopic and colonial characteristics used to place an isolate into these groups, with examples.
(c) State the standard setting/method in which fungal cultures are handled in the laboratory.
(d) Explain the reasoning behind the safety precaution taken with cultures suspected of containing Coccidioides immitis.

(a) State the general classification of trematodes of medical importance and the specimens used to diagnose them.
(b) State how the diagnostic method is applied/selected according to the trematode and stage of infection.
(c) Explain why a basic error in specimen selection leads to an inaccurate or invalid diagnosis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Trematodes are typically flattened and leaf-shaped with two muscular suckers, a bifurcated gut, and both circular and longitudinal muscles; unlike nematodes, they lack a cuticle and have a syncytial epithelium instead.
• Trematodes of medical importance include Schistosoma species (causing renal tract and intestinal disease, affecting about 200 million people) and the family Fasciolidae, including Fasciola hepatica and Fasciolopsis buski, found in the intestine and biliary tract of humans and herbivorous animals.
(b)
• How each type is applied/selected diagnostically: for Schistosoma, eggs are demonstrated in urine (for S. haematobium, via centrifuged deposit or filtration) or stool (Kato-Katz smear technique), with species identified by the characteristic position of spines on the egg; vesical and rectal biopsy may also be used.
• For Fasciola hepatica, stool microscopy demonstrates large, ovoid, bile-stained eggs; this is useful in chronic fascioliasis but not useful in acute fascioliasis, because eggs are rarely excreted in the faeces at that stage.
• For Fasciola hepatica, stool antigen detection (an EIA-based test for copro-antigen) can diagnose chronic fascioliasis; immunodiagnosis can detect infection 4-8 weeks before eggs appear in stool; molecular diagnosis (DNA probes and PCR) has also been evaluated.
• For Fasciolopsis buski, presumptive diagnosis is based on detection of large operculated eggs in the faeces by microscopy; because these eggs are similar to those of F. hepatica, specific diagnosis requires identification of the expelled adult fluke.
• For a trematode causing pulmonary disease, sputum is the specimen of choice, with eggs detected only 2-3 months after infection, and Charcot-Leyden crystals described as a consistent microscopic finding in egg-positive sputum; immunodiagnosis is also used.
(c)
• Why a basic error leads to an inaccurate or invalid result: relying on stool microscopy alone in suspected acute fascioliasis would give a false-negative result, since eggs are rarely excreted in the faeces at that early stage; antigen detection or immunodiagnosis should be considered instead.
• Choosing urine rather than stool (or vice versa) as the specimen for a given Schistosoma species without first identifying the species/likely site of infection could result in the target eggs not being present in the specimen examined.
• Failing to collect a midday urine specimen for suspected urinary schistosomiasis (eggs are typically shed in urine around midday) could reduce the chance of detecting eggs, since timing of collection affects egg yield.
• Because F. hepatica and F. buski eggs are morphologically very similar, relying on stool egg microscopy alone without further identification of the expelled fluke, where necessary, could result in a species-level misidentification.
• Correctly matching the specimen type and diagnostic method to the suspected trematode and stage of infection is therefore essential to obtain a valid result.

questions.question:
A Giemsa-stained thin blood film from a febrile patient shows red blood cells containing ring-shaped structures.
(a) Identify the organism and form suggested by this finding.
(b) State the technique used, and the role of the corresponding thick film.
(c) State how the finding should be recorded.
(d) State a follow-up practical step where microscopy is inconclusive.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Ring forms within red blood cells on a Giemsa-stained film are trophozoites of a Plasmodium species (the malaria parasite).
(b)
Microscopic examination of a Giemsa-stained blood film is the gold standard; the thin film shown here is used for speciation, while a thick film (also prepared) is used for parasite identification and estimating parasite density.
(c)
The finding is recorded as "ring forms seen" with the parasite density from the thick film, and the species identified from the thin film.
(d)
Where microscopy is inconclusive, further methods such as the Quantitative Buffy Coat test, rapid diagnostic tests (e.g. based on PfHRP-2 or pLDH), or PCR may be used to confirm and speciate the parasite.

questions.question:
A patient with suspected onchocerciasis presents for skin snip sampling to demonstrate microfilariae.
(a) Identify the apparatus and specimen involved.
(b) State the principle behind the technique.
(c) Describe the step-by-step procedure.
(d) State the expected finding and a limitation of the technique.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A razor blade or biopsy punch (e.g. sclerocorneal) is used to obtain the specimen, which is a tiny skin sample (3-5 mg).
(b)
In onchocerciasis, microfilariae (larvae) migrate to the skin; incubating a small skin sample in saline allows the microfilariae to emerge from the tissue for microscopic identification.
(c)
Remove tiny skin samples from multiple sites (e.g. iliac crests, shoulder blades) by elevating a small cone of skin with the razor blade or biopsy punch; incubate the tissue in normal saline at room temperature for 24 hours to allow the microfilariae to emerge; examine microscopically.
(d)
Microfilariae seen on microscopy confirm onchocerciasis; sensitivity is low in the early disease stage and in areas of low prevalence, so skin-snip specimens can also be examined by nucleic acid amplification for greater sensitivity.

questions.question:
A febrile adult patient with suspected bloodstream infection requires a blood culture to be set up in the laboratory.
(a) Identify the specimen type and apparatus required, and state the appropriate volume to collect from an adult.
(b) State the principle behind aseptic collection and the accepted timing of collection relative to the fever.
(c) Describe the step-by-step procedure for collecting and processing the specimen, including what should be done if bacterial endocarditis is suspected.
(d) State the expected observation in a bottle that has become positive, and how this should be interpreted.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Venous blood is the specimen required; it is collected aseptically into a nutrient (blood culture) medium; for an adult, 5-10 ml should be collected (0.5-2 ml for infants, 2-5 ml for children).
(b)
Aseptic technique must be used to avoid contamination; specimens should be obtained early, preferably before antimicrobial treatment, and collected within 10 minutes of fever onset.
(c)
Explain the procedure to the patient; use aseptic technique for venipuncture; collect the appropriate volume for age; if bacterial endocarditis is suspected, collect 3 sets of blood cultures; introduce (inoculate) the sample into the nutrient medium and incubate at 35-37°C.
(d)
A positive bottle shows observable growth as turbidity, gas formation, or discrete colonies; this indicates viable organisms are present in the blood and the isolate should be further identified and tested for antimicrobial susceptibility.

(a)
• Composition: culture media contain water (source of hydrogen and oxygen), electrolytes (e.g. NaCl), peptone (partially digested proteins), meat/yeast extract (protein degradation products, carbohydrates, inorganic salts, growth factors), and where required, blood or serum (5-10% defibrinated horse or sheep blood).
• Agar, derived from seaweed (Algae - Gelidium species), is composed of carbohydrates, protein-like material and fatty acids (2-3%); it acts merely as a solidifying agent and provides no nutrition to bacteria.
(b)
Identifying properties of agar: it melts at 95-100°C and solidifies at 42-45°C; it remains solid at all incubation temperatures; it is transparent; it is not heat-labile, so it can be easily sterilized; it should be unaffected by almost all bacteria.
(c)
• Media are also classified by physical state: liquid (broth), solid (1.5-30% agar), and semisolid (0.05-0.3% agar, useful for motility testing and for culturing anaerobic/microaerophilic organisms, since it forms an oxygen gradient).
• Nutrients originally supplied as meat infusions can be replaced by beef or yeast extract; peptone provides a readily available nitrogen and carbon source, since most organisms can use the amino acids and simpler nitrogenous compounds it contains.
• A defined (chemically defined/synthetic) medium has known quantities of all ingredients and is used for research; an undefined medium has complex ingredients (e.g. yeast extract, casein hydrolysate) in unknown proportions.
• Standard method/setting: choice between defined and undefined media in practice depends on whether known, controlled composition is required (defined, for research) or general growth support is sufficient (undefined, for routine diagnostic work).
• In practice, agar-containing media are pre-warmed to dissolve the agar before sterilization, but should not be heated so extensively that essential components are destroyed.
(d)
• Precaution reasoning: because agar melts at 95-100°C but solidifies only at 42-45°C, heat-labile supplements should be added after the medium has cooled to about 50°C, with the supplement itself at room temperature before mixing in.
• If a very cold liquid supplement is added, the agar can gel prematurely or form visible transparent flakes, as seen in blood-enriched agar, spoiling the medium.
• A related precaution in preparation is to adequately soak agar-containing media with agitation before heating and to adjust pH before dispensing into containers for sterilization, since deviations affect nutrient availability and growth.
• Correct handling of raw materials (e.g. distilled or deionized water, slightly acidic pH) is emphasized because the quality of the medium depends directly on the quality of its raw materials.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition of culture media, including the role of agar.
(b) State the identifying properties of agar that make it suitable for bacteriological media.
(c) State the standard setting in which the choice between defined and undefined media is made in practice.
(d) Explain the reasoning behind the precaution of adding heat-labile supplements only after cooling the medium.

(a) Describe the external morphology of Sarcoptes scabiei.
(b) State the identifying features used to recognize the mite and its ova microscopically.
(c) State the standard setting in which scabies is diagnosed and managed.
(d) Explain the reasoning behind treating all household members and close contacts simultaneously.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Structure/composition: Sarcoptes scabiei, the human itch mite, is a member of family Sarcoptidae within order Acarina; it is characteristically oval, ventrally flattened and dorsally convex, tortoise-like in shape.
(b)
• Size: adult females measure 0.30-0.45mm; adult males measure 0.2-2.5mm long, with a flattened oval body; males are distinguished from females by their smaller size.
• Identifying characteristics: the dorsal surface is covered with numerous small peg-like protuberances and a few bristles; adults have four pairs of short cylindrical legs divided into five ring-like segments.
• The first two pairs of legs end in short stalks called pedicels, terminating in thin-walled roundish structures termed "suckers" (pulvilli), which help the mite grip the host's skin and aid movement; in the female, the posterior two pairs of legs lack suckers but end in long, conspicuous bristles.
(c)
• Standard method/setting: diagnosis is made by scraping burrows, mounting the scraping in 20% KOH under a cover slip, and examining under low power microscopy for the mite and its ova; the mite forms a tunnel in the skin in which the female lays eggs in discharged stages of development.
• Scabies is a widespread skin disease and an important public health problem particularly in underdeveloped countries with poverty, poor hygiene, social deprivation and overcrowded conditions; at least 300 million cases occur annually.
(d)
• Precaution: regular housekeeping, frequent bed linen changes, and stringent hygienic standards (e.g. in nursing homes) are recommended, along with minimizing contamination of inanimate objects.
• Higher room temperatures have been shown to result in higher mite mortality due to desiccation; simple washing of bed sheets and pillow cases in hot water with sufficient disinfectant renders these items safer for reuse.
• Treatment (e.g. 5% benzyl benzoate lotion, 1% gamma benzene hexachloride/lindane, malathion) is given to all members of the household and all close contacts simultaneously.
• Reasoning behind simultaneous treatment: untreated contacts remaining infested could re-infest a treated individual, so this precaution is aimed at breaking the chain of transmission within a household.
• Because Sarcoptes scabiei is one of only a few true human-parasitic mites (alongside chigger mites and the human follicle mite), correctly identifying it on microscopy (versus a free-living or animal-associated mite) is essential before treatment is initiated.
• Overall, recognition of the mite's distinctive morphology (pedicels/suckers, dorsal protuberances, size) together with adherence to hygiene/treatment precautions guides safe and effective management of scabies.

questions.question:
A stool culture on MacConkey agar produces two colony types: pink colonies and colourless colonies.
(a) Identify what each colony colour indicates about the organisms present.
(b) State the type of medium and the basis of the colour reaction.
(c) State how the finding should be recorded.
(d) State the follow-up practical step needed to identify the isolate(s) further.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pink colonies indicate lactose-fermenting organisms (e.g. coliforms such as E. coli); colourless colonies indicate non-lactose-fermenting organisms (e.g. Salmonella, Shigella).
(b)
MacConkey agar is a selective and indicator (differential) medium containing lactose, bile salts and a pH indicator (neutral red), used to distinguish lactose fermenters from non-fermenters.
(c)
The finding is recorded as colony colour (pink or colourless) together with colony morphology on MacConkey agar.
(d)
Subculture suspect non-lactose-fermenting colonies onto identification media such as TSI, and carry out further biochemical tests (e.g. indole, citrate, urease) to confirm identity.

(a)
• Parasites fall into two major groups: parasitic protozoa (unicellular eukaryotes) and parasitic helminths (Metazoa, belonging to phyla Nematoda and Platyhelminthes).
• Protozoa are classified into four traditional groups based on locomotion and reproduction: flagellates (e.g. Giardia, Trichomonas intestinally/genitourinary; Trypanosoma, Leishmania in blood/tissue), amoebae (move by pseudopodia, e.g. Entamoeba, Naegleria, Acanthamoeba), sporozoa (complex alternating life cycle, e.g. Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Toxoplasma, and Plasmodium species), and ciliates (bear cilia, e.g. Balantidium coli, the only human parasite of this group).
• Blood protozoa are further grouped as Mastigophora (flagellates/haemoflagellates, e.g. Trypanosoma and Leishmania) and Coccidia/Sporozoa (e.g. Plasmodium species and Babesia species).
(b)
• How each type is matched to a diagnostic method: microscopy (Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood films) is the gold standard for blood/tissue flagellates and sporozoa such as Plasmodium and Trypanosoma, while stool microscopy (direct wet mount, concentration methods, permanent stains) is used for intestinal amoebae, flagellates and ciliates.
• Culture methods are used for selected protozoa, including Amoeba, Leishmania, Trypanosoma, and the malarial parasite.
• Immunodiagnostic (antigen detection) methods are selected for specific protozoa, such as EIA kits detecting the galactose-inhibitable adherence protein of pathogenic Entamoeba histolytica, or DFA assays using FITC-labelled monoclonal antibody for Giardia cysts.
• Serological tests (e.g. ELISA) are useful for amoebiasis, malaria and toxoplasmosis, while molecular methods (PCR, with RFLP or DNA sequencing) are used when unequivocal identification cannot be made by other means.
(c)
• Why a basic error leads to an inaccurate/invalid result: mixing a stool sample with urine or disinfectant kills trophozoites, so amoebic or flagellate trophozoites would be missed on subsequent microscopy even though originally present.
• Examining liquid or soft stool later than 15 minutes after passage risks trophozoites losing motility or disintegrating before identification, similarly producing a false-negative result.
• Refrigerating a thin blood film smear (rather than keeping it at ambient temperature for transport within 24 hours) can alter cell morphology, which could lead to misidentification or a missed diagnosis of blood protozoa.
• Because some antigen-detection kits for the Entamoeba histolytica/E. dispar group are not specific for the pathogenic species, using a non-specific kit and reporting a positive result as pathogenic E. histolytica would be a misapplication leading to an inaccurate report.
• Correctly matching the diagnostic method (microscopy, culture, antigen detection, serology, or molecular) to the group of protozoa and the stage of infection is therefore essential, since each method has different sensitivity and specimen requirements.
questions.question:
(a) State the general classification of parasitic protozoa, and the further grouping of blood protozoa.
(b) State how each protozoan group is matched to a diagnostic method in the laboratory.
(c) Explain why a basic error in specimen handling leads to an inaccurate or invalid result for protozoan diagnosis.

A Gram-negative bacillus isolated on a differential stool culture medium is inoculated onto Triple Sugar Iron (TSI) agar for further characterisation.
(a) Identify the medium and apparatus used.
(b) State the principle of the test.
(c) Describe the step-by-step procedure.
(d) State how the reaction pattern is read, with an example organism for two different patterns.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A TSI agar slant and an inoculation loop are used, with a pure bacterial broth culture as the specimen.
(b)
TSI differentiates Enterobacteriaceae based on their ability to ferment glucose, lactose and sucrose and to produce hydrogen sulphide (H2S); phenol red indicator changes colour with acid production, and sodium thiosulfate/ferrous ammonium sulfate detect H2S as a black precipitate in the butt.
(c)
Inoculate the TSI slant with the test organism by stab and streak inoculation; keep an uninoculated tube as control; incubate both tubes at 37°C for 24 hours; observe the colour of the slant and butt and any gas production or blackening.
(d)
An A/A pattern with gas and no H2S (e.g. E. coli, Klebsiella) shows fermentation of glucose and lactose/sucrose; a K/A pattern with H2S (e.g. Salmonella typhi) shows fermentation of glucose only, with hydrogen sulphide production.

(a)
Retention of the red carbol fuchsin despite acid-alcohol decolorization identifies the organism as acid-fast, most commonly a Mycobacterium species (e.g. M. tuberculosis); Nocardia may also show partial acid-fastness.
(b)
The Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) stain: the heat-fixed smear is flooded with heated carbol fuchsin, decolorized with acid-alcohol, and counterstained with methylene blue.
(c)
The finding is recorded/reported as "acid-fast bacilli (AFB) seen".
(d)
Process the specimen further by culture, noting that mycobacteria may require as long as 6-8 weeks of incubation, and use molecular/nucleic acid amplification methods for confirmation where available.
questions.question:
A sputum smear stained by the Ziehl-Neelsen method shows bright red bacilli against a blue background under oil immersion.
(a) Identify the organism grouping suggested by this finding.
(b) State the technique used to obtain this finding.
(c) State how the finding should be recorded.
(d) State the follow-up practical step needed to confirm identification.

(a) State the general classification of antimicrobial susceptibility testing methods.
(b) State how each method is applied/selected in the laboratory.
(c) Explain why a basic error in performing any of these methods leads to an inaccurate or invalid result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Antimicrobial susceptibility testing techniques are broadly classified as dilution techniques (agar or broth based, measuring MIC and, where applicable, MBC) and diffusion techniques.
• Diffusion techniques include the Kirby-Bauer method (qualitative disc diffusion, reporting sensitive, intermediate or resistant), the Stokes method (test and control organisms on the same plate, with zones compared directly - a major pitfall being lack of standardization), and the antimicrobial gradient method (e.g. the E-test, establishing a concentration gradient in agar, also usable to determine MIC).
• Other methods include automated instrument systems (using optical detection to detect subtle changes in bacterial growth and generate rapid results, e.g. Vitek 2, BD Phoenix) and genotypic methods (detecting specific antibiotic-resistance genes using PCR and DNA hybridization).
(b)
• How each type is applied/selected: broth or agar dilution is selected when a precise, quantitative MIC (and/or MBC) value is required to guide dosing, particularly where a categorical result alone is insufficient.
• The Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion method is selected for routine, practical screening of an isolate against multiple antibiotics simultaneously, giving a categorical (sensitive/intermediate/resistant) result compared against an interpretative chart.
• The Stokes method may be selected where a rapid, direct comparison between a test organism and a known control organism is convenient, though its lack of standardization is recognized as a major limitation.
• The E-test/antimicrobial gradient method is selected when a quantitative MIC value is wanted but a broth/agar dilution set-up is not practical, since it combines diffusion convenience with a numerical result.
• Automated instrument systems are selected where rapid throughput and reduced hands-on time are priorities, while genotypic methods are selected when detection of a specific resistance mechanism (rather than a phenotypic growth response) is required.
(c)
• Why a basic error leads to an inaccurate/invalid result: in disc diffusion, an incorrect inoculum turbidity (not matched to the 0.5 McFarland standard) or incorrect disc spacing/distance from the plate edge can distort zone sizes and give a false sensitive or resistant report.
• In broth dilution, using an incorrectly standardized inoculum (outside the 1-5 ×10⁵ CFU/ml range) can shift the apparent MIC, leading to an inaccurate assessment of susceptibility.
• In the Stokes method specifically, lack of standardization between the test and control organism inoculum or conditions is itself recognized as a source of unreliable, non-reproducible results.
• Because the results of susceptibility testing directly influence the choice of drug for treatment of an infection, an error in performing any of these methods can lead to a clinically inappropriate antibiotic choice.

questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen) stain.
(b) List the materials required.
(c) Describe the procedure.
(d) State a precaution relevant to interpreting results.
(e) State how results are reported.
(f) Explain why the acid-fast stain is used/preferred for certain organisms.
(g) Distinguish the acid-fast stain from the Gram stain.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principle: acid-fast bacteria resist decolorization with acidified organic solvents (acid-alcohol) once stained; this depends on their lipid-rich cell walls being relatively impermeable to basic dyes unless combined with phenol.
• It is thought some stain becomes trapped within the cell and some forms a complex with mycolic acids in the cell wall.
(b)
Materials: Mycobacterium culture/smear, carbol fuchsin, acid-alcohol solution (70% ethanol with 0.5% hydrochloric acid), methylene blue counterstain.
(c)
• Procedure: prepare the bacterial smear as for Gram staining, air-dry and heat-fix; flood with heated carbol fuchsin and allow contact for 5 minutes; rinse with deionized water.
• Decolorize with acid-alcohol until the colour runs from the smear; wash with deionized water.
• Counterstain for 30 seconds with 1% methylene blue; rinse, blot dry, and examine under oil immersion.
(d)
Precaution: organisms with disrupted cell walls or shorter-chain mycolic acids (e.g. Nocardia) may stain only weakly acid-fast, so results should be interpreted with this in mind.
(e)
Reporting: acid-fast bacteria appear an intense red (retaining carbol fuchsin); other materials appear blue from the methylene blue counterstain.
(f)
Why used: it is the primary clinical stain to detect Mycobacterium (e.g. M. tuberculosis, the most common pathogen of this group) and other acid-fast organisms such as Nocardia.
(g)
• Distinguishing feature: unlike the Gram stain (crystal violet/iodine/alcohol/safranin), the acid-fast stain uses heated carbol fuchsin as primary stain, acid-alcohol as the differentiating decolorizer, and methylene blue as counterstain.
• The two stains differentiate different properties: the Gram stain separates organisms by cell wall thickness/porosity into Gram-positive/negative, while the acid-fast stain specifically detects the mycolic-acid-rich walls of Mycobacteria and related organisms.
• Mycobacteria are not reliably classified by the Gram method because of their large lipid content, which is why the dedicated acid-fast technique is required for these organisms.

questions.question:
A patient with intensely itchy burrows on the finger webs is suspected of having scabies, and a skin scraping is taken for microscopy.
(a) Identify the apparatus and reagent required.
(b) State the principle of the technique.
(c) Describe the step-by-step procedure.
(d) State the expected finding and the follow-up action once a positive result is confirmed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A clean microscope slide, a cover slip, a 20% potassium hydroxide (KOH) solution, and a blade or scalpel for scraping the burrow are required.
(b)
Sarcoptes scabiei mites and their ova can be visualised microscopically once KOH has cleared the keratin/skin debris from a burrow scraping.
(c)
Make scrapings from the burrows; place the scraping on a clean microscope slide; add 1-2 drops of 20% KOH solution; cover with a cover slip; examine under a low power microscope, looking for the mite and the ova.
(d)
Identification of the mite and/or its ova on microscopy confirms scabies; treatment (e.g. 5% benzyl benzoate lotion, 1% gamma benzene hexachloride, or malathion) should be given to the patient and to all household members and close contacts simultaneously.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the basic morphological classification of bacteria (shape and arrangement), with examples.
(b) State the identifying characteristic that determines whether an organism is reliably classified by the Gram method.
(c) State the standard setting in which morphology and Gram reaction are used together in practice.
(d) Explain the reasoning behind using an alternative staining technique for certain organisms.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Bacteria are classified into basic shapes - cocci (spherical), bacilli (rod-shaped), spiral (spirilla), and vibrio (comma-shaped) - existing as single cells, pairs, chains, or clusters.
• Cocci are further classified by arrangement: monococcus/micrococcus (single round cells, e.g. Micrococcus flavus); diplococcus (cells divide once, remain attached in pairs, e.g. Diplococcus pneumoniae); streptococcus (repeated division in one plane forming chains, e.g. Streptococcus pyogenes).
• Further coccal arrangements: tetracoccus (four cells dividing in two planes at right angles, e.g. Gaffkya tetragena); staphylococcus (division in three planes forming grape-like clusters, e.g. Staphylococcus aureus); sarcina (division in three planes forming a cube-like configuration of 8-16 cells, e.g. Sarcina lutea).
• Bacilli are rod-shaped bacteria occurring singly or in pairs (e.g. Bacillus cereus); vibrios are curved, comma-shaped bacteria (e.g. Vibrio cholerae); spirilla are spiral/spring-like with multiple curvature and terminal flagella (e.g. Spirillum volutans).
• Other forms: Actinomycetes are branching filamentous bacteria; Mycoplasmas are cell-wall-deficient bacteria without a stable morphology, occurring as round/oval bodies or interlacing filaments.
(b)
Identifying characteristic: morphology and Gram staining are two of the most important classification systems, with the nature of the cell wall as the initial criterion; bacteria with rigid, thick walls are subdivided by shape and staining reaction, while spirochetes (thin flexible walls) and mycoplasmas (no cell wall) form separate units.
(c)
• Standard method/setting: in practice, morphological classification (cell shape and arrangement on a stained smear) is combined with the Gram reaction as an initial step, before biochemical identification tests are selected.
• The difference between Gram-positive and Gram-negative groups is attributed to a much larger peptidoglycan layer in Gram-positive organisms, in which iodine and crystal violet precipitate and are not eluted by alcohol, unlike in Gram-negative organisms.
(d)
• Reasoning for an alternative technique: because Mycobacteria are not reliably stained by the Gram method due to their large lipid content, alternative staining techniques (Kinyoun or Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast stain) must be used, otherwise this important pathogen group could be missed or misclassified.
• Correctly recognizing cell arrangement (e.g. clusters versus chains) on a smear guides which further tests are selected (e.g. catalase/coagulase for clustered cocci, versus haemolysis pattern for chained cocci).
• Recognizing basic shape and Gram reaction together therefore narrows the identity of an isolate before more specific biochemical or serological tests are applied.
• This combined approach (shape, arrangement, Gram reaction, and awareness of exceptions such as Mycobacteria) is the standard first step of bacterial identification in the routine laboratory.

(a)
The disc with a zone at or below the resistant breakpoint indicates the organism is resistant to that antibiotic; the disc with a large zone above the sensitive breakpoint indicates the organism is sensitive to that antibiotic.
(b)
The zone of inhibition diameter for each disc is measured and compared against the standards in the interpretative chart; each antibiotic is reported as Sensitive, Resistant, or Intermediate.
(c)
The results indicate the in vitro activity of each antimicrobial agent against the isolate, which has a direct influence on the choice of drug for treatment of the infection.
(d)
Where a reading is intermediate/borderline, confirmatory testing such as MIC determination may be considered before a final treatment decision.
questions.question:
After incubating a disc diffusion plate, the zone of inhibition around one antibiotic disc measures at the resistant breakpoint on the interpretative chart, while a second disc shows a large zone above the sensitive breakpoint.
(a) Interpret what each of these two readings means.
(b) State how the results should be recorded/reported.
(c) State what the results indicate about choice of treatment.
(d) State the follow-up action for a borderline (intermediate) reading.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Structure/features: ticks belong to Class Arachnida, Order Acarina, superfamily Ixodoidea, comprising Ixodidae (hard ticks) and Argasidae (soft ticks); the body is compressed dorso-ventrally, cephalothorax and abdomen fused (unsegmented), four pairs of legs in adults/nymphs (three pairs in the larva), no wings, no antennae.
• The capitulum (false head) carries the mouthparts and pedipalps: the hypostome (ventral, elongated, backwardly directed teeth), chelicerae (two, dorsal, hooked, in a sheath), and pedipalps (two, four-segmented, lateral to the chelicerae).
• Identifying features - hard ticks: capitulum projects from the anterior end (seen dorsally); a scutum (chitinous plate) is present, covering the whole dorsal surface in the male and a small anterior portion in the female; pulvilli are present; respiratory spiracles lie behind the last coxae.
• Identifying features - soft ticks: capitulum lies on the ventral surface (not seen dorsally); scutum is absent; pulvilli are absent; respiratory spiracles lie between the third and fourth coxae.
• Hard ticks are short-lived (males die after mating, females after egg-laying) and lay eggs as a single large patch; soft ticks are long-lived and lay eggs in several patches at intervals; hard ticks are permanent ectoparasites (dropping off only to moult/lay eggs), while soft ticks are temporary ectoparasites (visiting only for a blood meal).
(b)
Larval-stage features: hard tick larvae have a small anterior scutum, are oval and brownish, with a single nymphal instar stage; soft tick larvae lack a scutum and pulvilli, are round and yellowish, with several (4-5) nymphal stages.
(c)
Standard method/setting: recognizing whether a tick specimen is hard or soft, based on capitulum position, presence/absence of scutum, and spiracle position, is the basis for laboratory or field identification of ticks of medical importance and for assessing likely attachment duration.
(d)
• Precaution/safety reasoning: because ticks are blood-feeding vectors of disease (e.g. Babesia species, typically transmitted by the nymph stage of Ixodes scapularis), avoidance of tick bites and appropriate control measures reduce infection risk.
• Control measures include applying permethrin products to clothing/boots, not to the skin, which is the specific application method stated for this control product.
• The reasoning behind applying permethrin to clothing/boots rather than skin is that this is the way the product is intended to be used to repel/kill ticks before they reach the skin, so applying it incorrectly (directly to skin) would not follow the correct control method.
• Correctly differentiating hard versus soft ticks also matters clinically, since their differing behaviour (permanent versus temporary parasitism) affects the likely site and duration of attachment relevant to risk assessment.
• The three orders of medical importance within Class Arachnida are Acarina (ticks and mites), Araneida (spiders) and Scorpionida (scorpions), so correct order/family identification is the first step before species-level work and targeted control.

(a) Describe the external morphology of hard ticks (Ixodidae) and soft ticks (Argasidae).
(b) State the identifying features that distinguish them, including at the larval stage.
(c) State the standard setting in which correct hard/soft tick identification is applied.
(d) Explain the reasoning behind the precaution of applying tick-control products to clothing/boots rather than to the skin.

(a) State the principle of autoclaving as a sterilization method for culture media.
(b) State the parameters required for effective autoclaving.
(c) Describe the procedure and precautions for autoclaving liquid media.
(d) State how sterility of a sterilized batch is monitored.
(e) Explain why autoclaving is the preferred method for most culture media.
(f) Distinguish autoclaving from steaming and from filtration as sterilization methods.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Principle: autoclaving is the method used for the majority of culture media, using a combination of steam, pressure and time to destroy bacterial endospores and vegetative cells.
(b)
Parameters: the autoclave must reach and maintain 121°C for at least 15-30 minutes using saturated steam under at least 15 psi of pressure; 15 minutes is the thermal death time recommended for liquid media volumes up to 1 litre.
(c)
• Procedure/precaution: no liquid should be sealed in a container and autoclaved; fill containers two-thirds full and loosen caps; allow liquids to cool before tightening caps; tubes are placed in racks or packed loosely in a basket; a maximum of 15 minutes is recommended for carbohydrate media in tubes for fermentation studies.
• Further precaution: over-autoclaving can cause precipitation, alteration of pH and destruction of essential components (and increased acidity); under-autoclaving can result in an unsterile medium, which must be discarded.
(d)
• Sterility monitoring: chemical indicators (e.g. autoclave tape) must be used with each load, though tape alone is not an adequate monitor; biological indicators (e.g. Bacillus/Geobacillus stearothermophilus spore strips) must be used at least monthly to validate spore-killing efficacy.
• Reporting: each batch of media should be clearly labeled after sterilization, and a representative sample (about 5%) tested for sterility, typically incubated for about 48 hours at 35°C; more than 2 colonies per plate means the whole batch is discarded.
(e)
Why preferred: autoclaving is effective at destroying both vegetative cells and resistant endospores, making it suitable for the majority of routine media.
(f)
• Steaming at 100°C: used for media containing ingredients that would be broken down at temperatures above 100°C (e.g. Cary-Blair transport medium), and for re-melting previously bottled sterile agar media, using perforated trays above boiling water.
• Filtration: removes bacteria from fluids using membrane filters; used mainly for heat-sensitive additives that cannot be autoclaved (e.g. enzymes, serum, urea, certain carbohydrates).
• Distinguishing feature: unlike autoclaving, steaming does not reach temperatures sufficient to destroy all endospores and is reserved for heat-labile media; filtration involves no heat at all and instead physically removes organisms, suiting only heat-sensitive components.
• The volume of media in one sterilization batch should be kept small (ideally two litres) to ensure even heat penetration, regardless of the method used.
• Choice of method depends on the heat stability of the medium's ingredients: robust media are autoclaved, heat-labile media are steamed or filter-sterilized.

questions.question:
A pure bacterial isolate is to be tested for susceptibility to several antibiotics using the disc diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) method.
(a) Identify the medium, standard and apparatus required.
(b) State the principle of the method.
(c) Describe the step-by-step procedure, including disc spacing and incubation conditions.
(d) State how the result is read and reported.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Mueller-Hinton agar, a 0.5 McFarland turbidity standard, antimicrobial discs, and a 90 mm or 120 mm petri dish are required.
(b)
This is a qualitative agar diffusion method used to determine whether an organism is sensitive, intermediate or resistant to an antimicrobial agent, based on diffusion of the drug from the disc into the agar.
(c)
Prepare the inoculum by emulsifying 4-5 colonies in broth; compare turbidity with the 0.5 McFarland standard; swab the surface of Mueller-Hinton agar with the suspension; place discs on the surface 20 mm apart and 25 mm from the edge of the plate (6 discs for a 90 mm dish, 9 discs for a 120 mm dish); incubate aerobically at 35°C for 18-24 hours.
(d)
Measure the zone of inhibition around each disc and compare it with standards in an interpretative chart; report each antibiotic as Sensitive, Resistant, or Intermediate.

questions.question:
(a) State the general classification of immunity into active and passive, and natural and acquired.
(b) State how each type is applied/selected/recognized in assessing a patient's protection.
(c) Explain why a basic error in interpreting the type of immunity or a serological result leads to an inaccurate conclusion.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Immunity is classified into active immunity (resistance developed in response to an antigen - an infecting agent or a vaccine - characterized by antibody production by the host) and passive immunity (immunity conferred by antibody produced in another host, acquired naturally or artificially).
• Active immunity may follow clinical or subclinical infection (natural) or follow vaccination (acquired); passive immunity may involve transfer of maternal antibodies through the placenta or milk (natural), or administration of immunoglobulin/antiserum (acquired).
• Innate (non-specific) immunity comprises mechanical barriers, biochemical factors, phagocytosis, and action of the reticuloendothelial system, and does not depend on prior exposure to a specific antigen.
• Specific (acquired) immunity is cell-mediated and humoral, acquired by the host's response to a particular antigen; antigens/immunoglobulins such as IgG and IgA are found in serum, forming primary antigen-antibody complexes.
(b)
• How each type is applied/selected: active immunization is used where durable, long-term protection built through the host's own immune memory is the aim, whereas passive immunization is used where immediate, though typically shorter-lived, protection is required.
• Recognizing whether a patient's protection is natural or acquired informs decisions such as whether further vaccination or booster doses are needed.
(c)
• Why a basic error leads to an inaccurate or invalid result: assuming a patient has durable, active immunity when they have in fact only received passive antibody would be an error, since passive immunity does not involve the host's own memory response and wanes once the transferred antibody is cleared.
• Mistaking evidence of an innate (non-specific) response, such as phagocytosis, for evidence of specific acquired immunity to a particular antigen would be an error in interpreting a patient's immune status.
• Because agglutination and precipitin formation are both primary antigen-antibody reactions used in serology, an error in distinguishing which reaction is being observed (agglutinins against particulate antigens versus precipitins against soluble antigens) could lead to misinterpretation of a serological test result.
• In immunofluorescence-based diagnosis, an error in reagent labelling or technique could produce a false result in tests such as the fluorescent treponemal antibody-absorption test used to diagnose Treponema pallidum infection.
• Serology has the recognized limitation that there is usually a lag between onset of infection and development of antibodies, so an error in timing of serological testing (too early after exposure) could give a false-negative result even where infection is present.
• A high antibody titre may simply reflect a past infection rather than a current one, so failing to consider this when interpreting a single serological result could lead to an inaccurate conclusion about current infection status.

(a)
• Principle: the citrate test determines the ability of a microorganism to utilize citrate as its sole source of carbon (and ammonium salt as sole nitrogen source); a citrase enzyme facilitates transport of citrate into the cell.
• Citrate, a Krebs cycle intermediate, is enzymatically converted to pyruvic acid and carbon dioxide; the medium becomes alkaline as CO2 combines with sodium and water to form carbonate, changing bromothymol blue from green to Prussian blue.
(b)
Materials: bacterial broth, Simmons citrate agar slants (or Koser's citrate medium, liquid), inoculation loop.
(c)
Procedure: inoculate a Simmons citrate agar slant with the test organism by stab and streak inoculation; keep an uninoculated tube as control; incubate both at 37°C for 24-48 hours and observe.
(d)
Precaution: the test is performed on a synthetic medium in which sodium citrate is the only carbon source, so contamination with another carbon source (e.g. carry-over on the loop) can give a false positive.
(e)
Reporting: colour change to blue is a positive result; the medium remaining green, with no growth, is a negative result.
(f)
Why used: it is used to differentiate among enteric bacteria based on their ability to utilize citrate, helping to further distinguish organisms already grouped as Enterobacteriaceae on TSI.
(g)
• Distinguishing feature: TSI tests fermentation of three sugars (glucose, sucrose, lactose in different concentrations) and hydrogen sulphide production, using a phenol red indicator in a butt/slant format, rather than a citrate-utilization principle.
• TSI reporting differentiates patterns such as A/A (glucose and lactose/sucrose fermented), K/A (glucose only fermented), K/K (non-fermenter), and blackening (H2S production).
• Both tests use members of the Enterobacteriaceae as reference organisms and both require an uninoculated control tube for comparison.
• Citrate utilization is typically applied after TSI to further narrow the identity of an isolate within the Enterobacteriaceae.
• Citrate testing gives a single colour end-point (green to blue), whereas TSI gives a combination of slant colour, butt colour, gas and blackening reactions.

(b) List the materials required.
(c) Describe the procedure.
