(f) Explain why the citrate test is used in identification of enteric bacteria.
(g) Distinguish the citrate test from the TSI test.

A blood agar plate inoculated with a throat swab shows colonies surrounded by a complete, clear zone in which the red blood cells have been fully lysed.
(a) Identify the haemolytic pattern and an organism associated with it.
(b) State the technique/medium used to obtain this finding.
(c) State how the finding should be recorded.
(d) State the follow-up practical step needed to identify the organism further.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A complete, clear zone of lysis around the colony represents beta-haemolysis, seen with organisms such as Streptococcus pyogenes.
(b)
Culture on blood (enriched) agar, which is enriched by adding blood, serum or egg, followed by incubation to allow colony growth and development of the haemolytic pattern.
(c)
The finding is recorded as the haemolysis pattern observed (e.g. "beta-haemolysis: complete clearing") together with the colony morphology.
(d)
Proceed with Gram staining and appropriate biochemical/serological identification tests based on the haemolysis pattern and colony morphology observed.

questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the oxidase test.
(b) List the materials required.
(c) Describe the procedure.
(d) State the precautions relevant to the test.
(e) State how results are reported.
(f) Explain why the oxidase test is used in bacterial identification.
(g) Distinguish the oxidase test from the catalase test.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principle: the oxidase test detects the enzyme cytochrome oxidase, involved in the reduction of oxygen at the end of the electron transport chain in aerobic respiration.
• The colourless redox reagent (tetramethyl-p-phenylenediamine dihydrochloride) reacts with the enzyme and oxygen, forming the coloured compound indophenol blue (a purple colour change).
(b)
Materials: oxidase disc (reagent-impregnated filter paper), 24-hour-old test organism, applicator stick or glass rod.
(c)
Procedure: rub the test organism over the reagent-impregnated disc using a sterile applicator stick or glass rod; include controls; observe the reaction within 10 seconds.
(d)
Precautions: acidity inhibits oxidase enzyme activity, so the test must not be performed on colonies from carbohydrate-fermenting media such as MacConkey agar; the reagent must be freshly prepared; a nichrome wire should not be used; cultures should not be very cold; the colour change must be read within the prescribed time.
(e)
Reporting: formation of a purple colour within the prescribed time is a positive test (e.g. Pseudomonas sp., Vibrio sp.); no colour change is a negative test (e.g. E. coli, Klebsiella).
(f)
Why used: the oxidase test is a key test to differentiate the family Pseudomonadaceae (oxidase positive) from Enterobacteriaceae (oxidase negative), and is useful for speciation of many other bacteria.
(g)
• Distinguishing feature: catalase testing uses 3% hydrogen peroxide and reads gas bubble formation, distinguishing Staphylococcus (positive) from Streptococcus/Enterococcus (negative), rather than distinguishing Pseudomonadaceae from Enterobacteriaceae.
• Both tests are rapid bench (phenotypic) tests read within seconds of adding the reagent.
• Oxidase testing is particularly useful when an isolate is already known to be a Gram-negative rod that grew poorly or did not ferment sugars typically seen with Enterobacteriaceae.
• Catalase precautions include avoiding a metal loop (false positive, corrodes metal) and avoiding scraping blood agar (red blood cell catalase gives false positive), whereas oxidase precautions centre on avoiding acidic/fermenting media and metal (nichrome) wires.
• Both tests are used together with the Gram stain and other biochemical tests to build a complete identification profile of a bacterial isolate.

(a)
• Culture media are classified by consistency (solid media, used for isolating bacteria as pure culture using agar; liquid media, used for profuse growth such as blood culture, in which mixed organisms cannot be separated) and by chemical composition (routine laboratory media and synthetic/chemically defined media used for research).
• Routine laboratory media are classified into basic media (support growth without special enrichment, e.g. nutrient broth, nutrient agar, peptone water - Staphylococcus and Enterobacteriaceae grow in these), enriched media (enriched with blood, serum or egg, e.g. blood agar, chocolate agar, Lowenstein-Jensen - Streptococci grow in blood agar), selective media (favour a particular organism by inhibiting others, e.g. MacConkey agar, Lowenstein-Jensen), indicator/differential media (contain an indicator such as blood, neutral red or tellurite, e.g. blood agar, MacConkey agar), transport media (used when a specimen cannot be cultured soon after collection, e.g. Cary-Blair, Amies, Stuart, viral transport medium), and storage media (for long-term storage, e.g. egg saline medium, chalk cooked meat broth, glycerol).
• Other functional types include enrichment media (fluid selective media inhibiting unwanted organisms while stimulating the organism of interest, e.g. alkaline peptone water, Selenite-F broth, tetrathionate broth) and identification media (contain substrates/chemicals to help identify isolated bacteria, e.g. peptone water sugars, urea broth, Kligler iron agar).
(b)
• How each type is applied/selected: basic media are used to maintain stock cultures of control strains and to subculture pathogens from differential/selective media before biochemical/serological testing; enriched media are chosen for fastidious organisms with exacting growth requirements (e.g. Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria species, some Streptococcus species).
• Selective media are chosen when culturing a specimen from a site with normal flora, to prevent contaminants overgrowing the pathogen (e.g. TCBS, containing bile salt favouring Vibrio cholerae); differential/indicator media are chosen to visually distinguish organism properties on the same plate (e.g. MacConkey agar distinguishing lactose fermenters, pink, from non-fermenters, colourless).
• Transport media are selected when a specimen cannot be cultured immediately, to prevent overgrowth of commensals and maintain pathogen viability without allowing multiplication; identification media are selected only after an organism has been isolated in pure culture, to reveal specific biochemical properties.
(c)
• Why a basic error leads to an inaccurate/invalid result: an enrichment medium that is insufficiently nutritious to support the target pathogen will result in many false-negative cultures.
• A selective medium that is too inhibitory may suppress both the pathogen and the normal flora, while an insufficiently inhibitory medium allows commensal organisms to overgrow the plate and obscure the target pathogen.
• Errors in raw material quality, water quality, or storage of dehydrated media (e.g. caking or darkening) similarly compromise the medium's ability to support or select for the intended organisms, leading to unreliable culture results.
• Using the wrong functional type of medium for a given task, such as using a storage medium where an enriched medium is needed for isolation, defeats the purpose for which the medium was designed and can yield a false-negative or misleading result.
• Failing to maintain the correct storage temperature or shelf-life for prepared media can degrade selective or indicator components, leading to poor selectivity or false colour reactions.
• The overall reasoning is that each type of medium is designed for a specific purpose, so a basic error in choosing or preparing the wrong type undermines the validity of the culture result obtained from it.
questions.question:
(a) State the general classification of culture media by consistency and by chemical composition/functional type.
(b) State how each functional type of medium is applied/selected in the laboratory.
(c) Explain why a basic error in choosing or preparing a medium leads to an inaccurate or invalid culture result.

(a) State the principle of the endospore stain (Schaeffer-Fulton method).
(b) State the principle of the capsule stain (Hiss method).
(c) Describe the procedure for each.
(d) State how results of each stain are reported.
(e) Explain why each of these special stains is used in bacteriology.
(f) Distinguish the endospore stain from the capsule stain.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Endospore stain principle: spores are normally impervious to stains; under the light microscope, endospores show high light refractivity indicative of high protein content, so special methods are needed to stain them.
• In the Schaeffer-Fulton method, malachite green (primary stain) is forced to permeate the spore wall by heating (acting as mordant); washing with water removes stain from vegetative cells but not from the spore wall.
• Endospore stain procedure: the endospores retain the primary dye (malachite green), while vegetative cells lose the primary stain and take up the red colour of the counterstain (safranin).
• Other endospore staining methods mentioned include the modified Ziehl-Neelsen method (using 0.25-0.5% sulphuric acid as decolorizing agent) and the Barthelomew-Mittwar method.
• Endospore stain reporting: spores stain green (from malachite green) within a red/pink vegetative cell body when observed microscopically.
(b)
• Capsule stain principle: the capsule is non-ionic, so it is not stained by an acidic stain, but a basic stain such as crystal violet stains both the cell and the capsule.
• Capsule stain procedure: treat with a hypertonic solution, 20% copper sulphate, which serves the dual role of decolorizing agent and counterstain; the hypertonic copper sulphate causes diffusion of stain toward the outer surface of the cell.
(c)
After drying, the stain not diffused out of the capsular layer is retained there, and the copper sulphate decolorizes the capsule.
(d)
Capsule stain reporting: the capsule appears as a faint blue halo around a purple cell.
(e)
Why used: capsule staining is diagnostically useful because the capsule is a virulence factor (e.g. in pneumococci); endospore staining is used to demonstrate spore-forming organisms (e.g. Bacillus, Clostridium).
(f)
• Distinguishing feature: capsules may also be demonstrated by negative staining (Nigrosin or India ink), since capsules are non-ionic and repel both acidic and basic stains, whereas endospores actively retain malachite green once heat-mordanted.
• Both are examples of special/differential staining techniques (alongside Gram and acid-fast stains) used to visualize specific bacterial structures rather than simply classify organisms into two groups.

questions.question:
Doubling dilutions of an antibiotic (0, 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 µg/ml) are set up in broth inoculated with a standardized bacterial suspension; after overnight incubation, the tube containing 2 µg/ml is the lowest concentration with no visible turbidity, and a subculture from that tube onto drug-free agar shows no growth.
(a) Interpret what these two readings represent.
(b) State how each reading is recorded.
(c) State what the results indicate about the organism's susceptibility.
(d) State the action the results are used for.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The lowest concentration of antibiotic that prevented visible growth (2 µg/ml) is the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC); since the subculture from that tube onto drug-free agar shows no growth, the drug has also killed the organism at that concentration, giving the Minimum Bactericidal Concentration (MBC).
(b)
The MIC is recorded as the lowest concentration with no visible growth (turbidity); the MBC is recorded as the lowest concentration whose subculture inhibits at least 99.9% of the bacterial colonies (shows no growth) on the drug-free plate.
(c)
The more susceptible the organism is to the antimicrobial agent, the lower the MIC (and MBC); this indicates the antimicrobial concentration needed to inhibit or kill the isolate.
(d)
The MIC/MBC values are used to guide the selection and dosing of the antimicrobial agent for treatment of the infection.

(a)
• Fungal saprophytes/contaminant moulds are grouped by mycelium type: septate versus aseptate, and hyaline (colourless) versus dematiaceous (pigmented, dark, grey to black); aseptate members are additionally susceptible to cycloheximide.
• Hyaline septate members include Aspergillus spp. (unbranched conidiophores; A. fumigatus a potential pathogen especially from pulmonary sources), Paecilomyces spp. (brush-like conidiophores, long tapered sterigmata), Penicillium spp. (brush-shaped conidiophores, flask-shaped sterigmata), Scopulariopsis spp. (coarsely roughened sterigmata), Trichoderma spp. (flask-shaped conidiophores, clustered conidia), and Fusarium spp. (oval to sickle-shaped conidia, reported to cause eye infections).
• Dematiaceous members include Alternaria spp. (dark conidiophores bearing chains of large brown conidia), Curvularia spp. (spirally arranged brown conidia), and Cladosporium spp. (green colonies with a black reverse, conidia in chains).
• Aseptate members include Mucor spp. (unbranched sporangiophores, no rhizoids, very rapid growth), Rhizopus spp. (rhizoids present, nodal sporangiophores), and Syncephalastrum spp. (short, branched sporangiophores with tubular sporangia containing chains of spores).
(b)
How each type is applied/selected in identification: colony growth rate, surface texture (cottony, granular, chalky, velvety, powdery, silky, glabrous, waxy) and pigmentation (obverse and reverse colour) are used together with microscopic features (conidiophore and sterigmata shape, conidial arrangement) to assign an isolate to hyaline or dematiaceous, septate or aseptate groups, and then to genus.
(c)
• Teased preparations (with lactophenol cotton blue stain), slide culture techniques, and transparent tape preparations are the standard microscopic methods used to examine these structures without disturbing colony morphology.
• Why a basic error leads to an inaccurate or invalid result: because saprophytic contaminant fungi and potential opportunistic pathogens can resemble each other superficially, failing to correctly examine microscopic features could result in a contaminant being wrongly reported as a pathogen, or vice versa.
• Confusing Aspergillus (septate, unbranched conidiophores) with a similar-appearing but aseptate mould such as Syncephalastrum, without checking septation, is specifically noted as a possible source of error.
• Because most saprophytes are inhibited by cycloheximide, using a medium containing cycloheximide (such as Mycosel agar) when a cycloheximide-susceptible pathogen (e.g. some yeasts, including Cryptococcus neoformans) needs to be recovered would prevent growth of the target organism.
• Incorrect incubation conditions (e.g. not incubating at 37°C when a dimorphic fungus is suspected, or not maintaining cultures for the recommended 4 weeks, with systemic pathogens sometimes requiring 10 days to 2 weeks) could result in a false-negative culture.
• Because pigmentation can diffuse into the agar and must be assessed on both the obverse (top) and reverse (underside) of the colony, examining only one side could lead to missing a key identifying feature and a misclassification.
• Correct, systematic assessment of colony and microscopic morphology together is therefore essential to avoid misclassifying fungal isolates within these saprophyte categories.
questions.question:
(a) State the general classification of fungal saprophytes by mycelium type (septate/aseptate, hyaline/dematiaceous).
(b) State how these classifications are applied/selected in identifying a fungal isolate.
(c) Explain why a basic error in examining colony or microscopic features leads to an inaccurate or invalid identification.

After adding Kovac's reagent to a peptone water culture, a cherry red colour develops in the top reagent layer; the uninoculated control tube shows no colour change.
(a) Interpret this result.
(b) State how the result should be recorded.
(c) State what the result indicates, with an example organism.
(d) State the follow-up action needed to complete identification.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Development of a cherry red colour in the top reagent layer is a positive indole test, showing that the organism hydrolysed tryptophan to indole.
(b)
The culture is recorded as "indole positive".
(c)
Indole-positive organisms include E. coli and Proteus vulgaris (Klebsiella sp. and Proteus mirabilis are typically indole negative); this helps in identifying members of the Enterobacteriaceae.
(d)
The indole result is combined with other biochemical tests (methyl red, Voges-Proskauer, citrate) to complete identification of the isolate.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the basic composition of a stain, and the roles of a mordant, an accentuator and a decolorizer in staining.
(b) State the identifying structural features that make Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial cell walls behave differently on staining.
(c) State the standard method/setting in which these staining reagents are used in practice.
(d) Explain the reasoning behind the precaution of correctly timed fixation and decolorization when staining.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Composition: a stain is an organic compound containing a benzene ring plus a chromophore (imparts colour) and an auxochrome group (confers ionization/salt-forming ability and binds to fibres or tissues); a dye is a general-purpose colouring agent, while a stain specifically colours biological material.
(b)
• A mordant is a chemical that forms an insoluble complex with the stain, fixing it or helping it penetrate more deeply into the cell (e.g. Gram's iodine, phenol in Ziehl-Neelsen staining).
• An accentuator is added to a stain to make the reaction more selective and intense (e.g. potassium hydroxide added to Loeffler's methylene blue).
• A decolorizer is a chemical used to remove excess stain in indirect/regressive staining (e.g. ethanol in Gram's staining).
• Most stains used for bacteria are basic, since bacterial nucleic acid attracts positive ions (e.g. methylene blue, crystal violet); acidic stains are used for background staining.
• Structural features: Gram-positive bacteria have thick, dense, relatively non-porous walls, while Gram-negative bacteria have thin walls surrounded by lipid-rich membranes; these physical properties, with chemical composition, determine dye retention.
• Some non-bacterial organisms with thick cell walls (e.g. some yeasts) also stain Gram-positive; Gram-positive bacteria that have lost wall integrity through aging or damage may stain Gram-negative.
• Bacteria carry a slight negative charge overall; basic dyes (positively charged colour portion) react with this charge to directly stain the organism, while acidic dyes (negatively charged colour portion) are repelled and instead stain the background.
(c)
• Standard method/setting: in practice, these reagents are combined in the four-part Gram stain procedure (crystal violet, iodine, decolorizer, safranin) applied as the routine first-line stain to almost all bacteriological specimens and cultures.
• It is used to determine the staining characteristic of an organism, at times directing diagnosis of disease, and to demonstrate the purity of a culture.
(d)
• Precaution reasoning: fixation (by heat) kills the organism, causes it to adhere to the slide, and alters it so it more readily accepts stains; over-heating during fixation is avoided since excessive heat may distort morphology and introduce artefacts.
• Because decolorization is the most technique-sensitive step, incomplete or excessive decolorization can misclassify an organism's Gram reaction and mislead subsequent identification, so correct timing of this step is emphasized as good laboratory practice.

(a)
Principle: catalase is an enzyme produced by organisms living in oxygenated environments to neutralize toxic hydrogen peroxide, breaking it into oxygen and water; anaerobes generally lack catalase.
(b)
Materials: 24-hour bacterial culture, clean dry glass slide (or petri dish), 3% hydrogen peroxide, applicator sticks.
(c)
• Procedure: transfer a small amount of bacterial colony to a clean dry glass slide using a loop or sterile wooden stick.
• Place a drop of 3% H2O2 on the slide and mix; a positive result is rapid evolution of oxygen bubbles within 5-10 seconds; a negative result shows no bubbles or only a few scattered bubbles.
(d)
• Precaution 1: do not use a metal loop or needle with H2O2, as it gives a false positive and degrades the metal.
• Precaution 2: avoid scraping blood agar when taking the colony, as red blood cells are catalase positive and can give a false positive.
(e)
Reporting: the isolate is reported as catalase positive or catalase negative, based on bubble formation.
(f)
Why used: it is primarily used to distinguish among Gram-positive cocci, since Staphylococcus is catalase positive while Streptococcus and Enterococcus are catalase negative; it also differentiates Clostridium (negative) from Bacillus (positive) and aids identification of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Enterobacteriaceae.
(g)
• Distinguishing feature: the coagulase test uses plasma (EDTA or citrated human/rabbit plasma) rather than hydrogen peroxide.
• The coagulase test detects clot formation (tube test) or clumping (slide test) caused by the enzyme coagulase, produced by Staphylococcus aureus.
• The coagulase test distinguishes coagulase-producing S. aureus from other, coagulase-negative species of Staphylococcus, whereas catalase testing distinguishes staphylococci as a genus from streptococci/enterococci.
• Both are simple bench (phenotypic) tests important in the identification pathway for Gram-positive cocci seen on a smear.
questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the catalase test.
(b) List the materials required.
(c) Describe the procedure.
(d) State two precautions relevant to the test.
(e) State how results are reported.
(f) Explain why the catalase test is used in bacterial identification.
(g) Distinguish the catalase test from the coagulase test.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Myiasis, the invasion of tissues of animals or humans by the larval stages of dipterous flies, is classified according to fly habit into specific (obligatory) myiasis (larvae develop only in living tissue, e.g. Dermatobia, Hypoderma), semispecific (facultative) myiasis (larvae develop in living or dead tissue, attracted by discharge from diseased/necrotic tissue but may also attack living tissue, e.g. Calliphora, Sarcophaga), and accidental myiasis (larvae do not normally develop in a host but may accidentally do so if ingested or deposited near orifices, e.g. Musca, Fannia).
• Myiasis is also classified by tissue invaded: cutaneous myiasis (traumatic, furuncular/nodular, or creeping eruption), ocular myiasis, aural (ear) myiasis, nasopharyngeal myiasis, urogenital myiasis, and intestinal/gastric myiasis.
(b)
• How each type is applied/selected: recognizing traumatic cutaneous myiasis (flies attracted by blood or pus from a wound, e.g. Chrysomya, Calliphora, Sarcophaga) versus furuncular myiasis (larvae burrowing into intact skin forming painful nodules, e.g. Dermatobia, Cordylobia) guides the clinical picture expected.
• Recognizing creeping eruption (larvae migrating in a tortuous channel through the skin, causing local itching and pain during migration, e.g. Hypoderma, Gastrophilus) as distinct from furuncular myiasis is important, since the presentation differs.
• Ocular myiasis is divided into external (conjunctivitis) and internal (larvae invading the eye, potentially destroying the eye, orbit, or reaching the brain, e.g. Sarcophaga, Wohlfahrtia, Calliphora); recognizing which form is present is important because of the differing severity and urgency involved.
• Aural myiasis is recognized by discharge from an infected ear attracting flies, with larvae potentially reaching the middle ear, internal ear and brain, causing pain, tinnitus, bad odour, perforation of the drum and deafness (e.g. Wohlfahrtia); nasopharyngeal myiasis is recognized by pain, oedema, purulent discharge and occlusion of the nose (e.g. Wohlfahrtia, Sarcophaga).
• Urogenital myiasis is recognized where flies deposit eggs or larvae in the urethral opening, with larvae migrating to the urethra and, in females, potentially to the vagina.
(c)
• Why a basic error leads to an inaccurate or invalid result: failing to distinguish specific (obligatory) myiasis, which occurs on living tissue regardless of prior injury, from semispecific (facultative) myiasis, typically associated with decaying or necrotic tissue, could lead to an incorrect assumption about the underlying wound condition or fly species involved.
• Mistaking accidental myiasis (where larvae do not normally develop in the host) for specific or semispecific myiasis could lead to an incorrect assessment of the likely clinical course and expected tissue involvement.
• Failing to recognize internal ocular myiasis, and instead treating it as external (conjunctival) myiasis only, would be a serious error given the risk of the larvae destroying the eye, orbit, or reaching the brain.
• Misclassifying aural or nasopharyngeal myiasis based only on the presenting symptom, without considering that larvae can progress to the middle ear, internal ear and brain (aural), could result in under-treatment of a potentially serious infestation.
• Correctly applying the classification of myiasis (by fly habit and by tissue invaded) is therefore essential, since the expected clinical course, tissue involvement and potential complications differ substantially between the categories.
questions.question:
(a) State the general classification of myiasis according to the habits of the fly, and according to the tissue invaded.
(b) State how each classification is applied/selected in recognizing the clinical presentation.
(c) Explain why a basic error in classifying myiasis leads to an inaccurate or invalid diagnosis.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principle: TSI differentiates Enterobacteriaceae (Gram-negative bacilli capable of fermenting glucose with acid production) from other Gram-negative intestinal bacilli, based on differences in carbohydrate fermentation patterns and hydrogen sulphide production.
• TSI contains lactose and sucrose at 1% concentration and glucose at 0.1% concentration, with phenol red as the acid-base indicator, and sodium thiosulfate/ferrous ammonium sulfate to detect H2S.
(b)
Materials: bacterial broth cultures, TSI agar slants, inoculation loop.
(c)
Procedure: inoculate the TSI slant with the test organism by stab and streak inoculation; keep an uninoculated tube as control; incubate both tubes at 37°C for 24 hours.
(d)
Precaution: the cap should be closed loosely (not tightly) to allow free exchange of air, so the slant can revert to alkaline once the limited glucose is exhausted; a tightly closed tube can give a misleadingly acid slant.
(e)
• Observation: observe the colour of both the butt and slant, and gas production (cracks/bubbles) or blackening of the butt (H2S).
• Interpretation: A/A (with or without gas) means glucose and either sucrose or lactose (or both) are fermented; K/A means glucose only is fermented; K/K means the organism is a non-fermenter; a black precipitate in the stab indicates H2S production.
(f)
Why used: TSI allows presumptive identification of enteric bacteria in a single tube by combining three sugar-fermentation reactions with H2S detection.
(g)
• Distinguishing feature: unlike the citrate test, which uses a single carbon source (citrate) and a single colour end-point (green to blue), TSI uses three sugars at different concentrations in a slant/butt format to give a combination of colour, gas and blackening reactions.
• TSI is generally performed before citrate testing, using the sugar-fermentation/H2S pattern to narrow down the likely genus before citrate utilization is tested to further distinguish closely related organisms.
• Both tests require an uninoculated control tube incubated alongside the test tube for valid comparison.
• Both are part of the routine biochemical identification pathway used for Gram-negative bacilli isolated on differential/selective media such as MacConkey agar.
questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the Triple Sugar Iron (TSI) test.

(a) Describe the preparation/technology behind subunit, attenuated and vector vaccines.
(b) State the identifying limitations of traditional (older) vaccine technology.
(c) State the standard setting in which active and passive immunizing agents (vaccines, immunoglobulins, antisera) are used.
(d) Explain the reasoning behind deleting (rather than merely modifying) virulence genes in attenuated vaccine design.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Structure/composition: a vaccine renders the recipient resistant to infection; it is injected or given orally, and the host produces antibodies to a particular pathogen so that, on further exposure, the pathogen is inactivated and disease is prevented.
• Traditional vaccine technology grew the pathogen in animals (e.g. vaccinia in calves for smallpox, rabbit brains for rabies), by simple bacterial culture then inactivation (e.g. cholera vibrio), or in eggs (e.g. influenza, vaccinia) followed by inactivation.
• Subunit (protein) vaccines use components of the pathogen rather than the whole organism, avoiding extraneous pathogenic particles but raising questions of cost and whether the protein matches the natural form; examples of proteins shown to elicit immune responses include herpes simplex virus envelope glycoprotein, foot-and-mouth disease virus capsid protein (VP1), and extracellular proteins of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
• Attenuated vaccines consist of pathogenic strains with virulence genes deleted or modified; live vaccines are generally more effective than killed/subunit vaccines; an example is a live cholera vaccine constructed by deleting part of the A peptide gene of the cholera enterotoxin from Vibrio cholerae.
• Vector vaccines use a vector (e.g. vaccinia virus) to carry an antigen gene from another pathogen; the antigen DNA sequence is inserted into a plasmid beside the vaccinia virus promoter, and recombination transfers the gene into the vaccinia virus genome, which can then be used as a vaccine for that antigen.
(b)
Identifying limitations of traditional vaccines: inability to grow all organisms in culture, safety risk to laboratory personnel, expense, insufficient attenuation, possible reversion to an infectious state, need for refrigeration, ineffectiveness for some infectious agents, and immature immune response in infants/children.
(c)
• Standard method/setting: immunization is classified as active immunity (antibody production by the host, following infection or vaccination) and passive immunity (antibody transferred from another host, naturally via placenta/milk, or artificially by immunoglobulin/antiserum).
• Immunizing agents used in practice comprise vaccines, immunoglobulins and antisera; there are five immunoglobulin classes (IgM, IgA, IgG, IgE, IgD), and two immunoglobulin preparations for passive immunization - normal human immunoglobulin and specific (hyper-immune) human immunoglobulin.
• Antisera (non-human) are prepared in animals such as horses, used for conditions such as diphtheria, tetanus, gas gangrene, botulism and rabies.
(d)
• Precaution/safety reasoning: because attenuated (live) vaccines carry a risk of reversion to an infectious state, virulence genes are specifically deleted (not merely weakened) so that the organism cannot revert, which is the key safety rationale behind recombinant attenuated vaccine design.
• The reasoning for the recombinant approach generally is that if a virulence gene is only modified/weakened rather than removed, the organism retains a route back to a pathogenic form, whereas deletion (as in the live cholera vaccine example, with 550 base pairs of the A peptide removed) prevents such reversion.
• The traditional need for refrigeration of many vaccines is a practical limitation that recombinant/subunit approaches aim to address, reflecting the ongoing reasoning behind moving from older culture/inactivation-based vaccine technology to newer recombinant approaches.

questions.question:
(a) State the general classification of staining techniques into simple and differential staining, and their subtypes.
(b) State how each type of staining is applied/selected in the laboratory.
(c) Explain why a basic error in a staining procedure leads to an inaccurate or invalid result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Staining techniques are classified into simple staining (use of a single stain) and differential staining (use of two contrasting stains); simple staining is divided into direct/positive staining (stains the object) and indirect/negative staining (stains the background).
• Differential staining is used either for separation into groups (e.g. Gram stain and acid-fast stain) or for visualization of structures (e.g. capsule stain, spore stain, flagella stain).
• In simple staining, only a single staining step is used and everything is stained with the same colour; simple stains are used to stain whole cells or specific cellular components.
• In direct (positive) staining, basic dyes (e.g. methylene blue, crystal violet, basic fuchsin) react with the negatively charged bacterial cytoplasm (opposite charges attract) and the organism becomes directly stained.
• In indirect (negative) staining, an acidic dye (e.g. nigrosin or Indian ink), also negatively charged, is repelled by the negatively charged bacterial surface and instead deposits around the organism, leaving it colourless/transparent against a stained background.
(b)
• How each type is applied/selected: direct/positive simple staining is chosen when the aim is simply to improve visibility and observe general morphology; indirect/negative staining is chosen for structures (such as capsules) that do not readily take up either acidic or basic stains directly.
• Differential staining for separation into groups (Gram, acid-fast) is chosen when the aim is to classify an organism into a recognized category; differential staining for structure visualization (capsule, spore, flagella stains) is chosen when a specific structure, rather than the organism's group, needs to be demonstrated.
• The general technique for most staining methods follows the same basic sequence: smear, air dry, heat fix, stain, examine; fixation kills the organism, causes it to adhere to the slide, and alters it so it more readily accepts stains.
(c)
• Why a basic error leads to an inaccurate or invalid result: omitting or shortening the fixation step can allow the smear to wash off the slide during staining, or leave organisms in an altered state that does not take up stain properly.
• In differential staining, an error in the timing of the decolorization step (e.g. in Gram staining) can cause an organism to be wrongly classified from one group to the other, directly changing the reported identity of the isolate.
• Using an acidic stain where a basic stain was needed (or vice versa) would fail to demonstrate the intended structure, since the stain's ionic charge must be appropriate to what is being stained (cell body versus background versus a non-ionic structure like a capsule).
• Because staining is often the first step in bacterial identification, an error at this stage propagates forward into every subsequent step, making accurate execution of the chosen staining technique essential.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the structural features of lice, and the two orders into which they are classified.
(b) State the identifying features that distinguish the head, body and crab louse of humans.
(c) State the standard setting in which lice are transmitted and controlled in practice.
(d) Explain the reasoning behind advising against sharing personal items such as combs and headphones.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Structure/features: lice are small (1-8mm), wingless, dorsoventrally flattened, generally host-specific ectoparasites of mammals and birds; there are two orders, Mallophaga (biting/chewing lice) and Anoplura (sucking lice).
• Sucking lice (Anoplura) are considered important vectors of pathogens because they are blood-feeding ectoparasites of placental mammals, with sucking mouthparts and tibiotarsal claws adapted to grasping host hairs; biting lice (Mallophaga) infest the pelage of birds or mammals and have chewing mandibulate mouthparts.
(b)
• Three human lice are recognized: the head louse (Pediculus humanus capitis), the body louse (Pediculus humanus), and the crab louse (Pthirus pubis).
• Identifying features - head louse: occurs on the scalp and hair, with females depositing eggs on individual hairs close to the base of the hair shaft (within about 1mm of the skin), typically near the nape or behind the ears.
• Identifying features - body louse: tends to be larger than the other human lice, infests body and associated hairs but is also found in clothing, and uniquely deposits its eggs on or near clothing seams rather than on the host.
• Identifying features - crab louse: has tibiotarsal claws adapted for grasping coarser hairs, most commonly found in the pubic region, though it may also infest eyelashes, eyebrows, beard, moustache and chest hairs, and occasionally the scalp of babies.
(c)
• Standard method/setting: under optimal conditions, human lice can complete one generation in a month; transmission occurs through close host physical contact, and head lice can also be transferred via shared objects such as caps, combs, hairbrushes or headphones.
• Diseases associated with lice include endemic (louse-borne) typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii), trench fever (Bartonella quintana), and louse-borne (epidemic) relapsing fever (Borrelia recurrentis, transmitted when an infected louse is crushed and abraded into the skin).
(d)
• Precaution/safety reasoning: chemicals that kill lice (pediculicides, e.g. gels, shampoos, sprays, fogs) are used for control, alongside behavioural control such as avoiding close physical contact and avoiding sharing clothes, sheets, headphones, hats, combs and hairbrushes.
• Washing clothes of louse-infested individuals in hot, soapy water is recommended because it will usually kill lice; this follows from lice being unable to survive for more than a few days off the host.
• Reasoning behind avoiding shared items: because head lice can be transferred via shared objects such as caps, combs, hairbrushes and headphones, in addition to close physical contact, avoidance of sharing such items removes this additional route of transfer.
• Control of rats and their lice in domestic settings, and exclusion of flying squirrels from attics, may decrease the incidence of endemic typhus and sporadic epidemic typhus respectively, since these lice can transmit pathogens between reservoir hosts and humans.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the technique of the germ tube test and the chlamydospore test for Candida albicans under the headings: principle, materials, procedure.
(b) State a precaution and how results are reported.
(c) Explain why these tests are used/preferred as a first step in identifying Candida albicans.
(d) Distinguish these morphological tests from carbohydrate assimilation/fermentation testing.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principle: Candida albicans and C. stellatoidea characteristically produce a germ tube (a short tube-like outgrowth) when incubated briefly in a protein medium, and later, when grown on cornmeal agar with Tween 80, produce thick-walled resting structures called chlamydospores.
• Materials: a yeast isolate, a protein medium (e.g. serum) for the germ tube test; cornmeal agar with Tween 80 for the chlamydospore test.
• Procedure for the germ tube test: the yeast is incubated briefly in the protein medium and examined microscopically for germ tube formation.
• Procedure for the chlamydospore test: the yeast is inoculated by jabbing into cornmeal agar with Tween 80; cultures are observed every 24 hours for 3 days, looking for chlamydospore production.
(b)
• Precaution: germ tubes must be distinguished from early pseudohyphae, which can superficially resemble them, so a short, defined incubation time is used for the germ tube test to avoid a false reading.
• Reporting: an isolate is reported as germ tube positive and/or chlamydospore positive, supporting identification as Candida albicans (or C. stellatoidea).
(c)
Why used/preferred: these are rapid, simple presumptive tests used specifically to identify Candida albicans among yeast isolates without requiring more elaborate biochemical work-up.
(d)
• Distinguishing feature from carbohydrate assimilation/fermentation testing: the germ tube and chlamydospore tests rely on a specific morphological response of the organism to particular media/conditions, whereas carbohydrate assimilation and fermentation tests measure utilization of a carbohydrate (under anaerobic conditions for fermentation) as determined by acid and gas production, using bromcresol purple as an indicator.
• In carbohydrate fermentation testing for yeasts, specimens are inoculated beneath broth, with acid production turning the purple broth to yellow and gas detected as bubbles trapped in a fermentation tube, observed every 48 hours for 14 days.
• Nitrogen assimilation testing uses three tubes with different nitrogen sources and bromthymol blue as indicator (blue to yellow indicating a positive reaction).
• The germ tube/chlamydospore tests give a same-day or few-day answer based on morphology, whereas carbohydrate assimilation/fermentation testing requires observation over a longer period (up to 14 days) and is based on biochemical utilization rather than morphology.
• Both approaches are used within medical mycology to identify yeasts and yeast-like organisms, with the morphological tests often used first as rapid presumptive tests before biochemical confirmation if needed.

questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the indole test.
(b) State the principle of the methyl red and Voges-Proskauer tests.
(c) List the materials required for these tests.
(d) Describe the procedure for the indole test.
(e) State how results of all three tests are reported, with examples.
(f) Explain why these tests are used together in identification of Enterobacteriaceae.
(g) Distinguish the indole test from the methyl red/Voges-Proskauer tests.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Indole test principle: tryptophan is oxidized by some bacteria via the enzyme tryptophanase, forming indole, pyruvic acid and ammonia; the medium contains tryptophan as substrate, and indole is detected using Kovac's reagent.
(b)
• Methyl red principle: enteric organisms oxidize glucose for energy; the methyl red indicator detects large concentrations of acidic end products maintained at the end of incubation (positive in organisms such as E. coli, which maintains a stable low pH of about 4).
• Voges-Proskauer principle: detects the ability of organisms to produce acetyl methyl carbinol (acetoin) during glucose fermentation, using Barrett's reagent (alcoholic alpha-naphthol and potassium hydroxide).
(c)
Materials: test tubes, bacterial culture, peptone water and Kovac's reagent (indole); MR broth and methyl red indicator (MR); VP broth and Barrett's reagents A and B (VP); inoculating loop for all.
(d)
Indole procedure: inoculate peptone water tubes with bacterial broth culture using sterile needle technique; keep an uninoculated control tube; incubate at 37°C for 24-48 hours; add 1 ml of Kovac's reagent and shake gently after 10-15 minutes.
(e)
• Indole reporting: a cherry red colour in the top reagent layer is indole positive (e.g. E. coli, Proteus vulgaris); absence of red colour is indole negative (e.g. Klebsiella sp., Proteus mirabilis).
• MR reporting: red colour throughout the tube is MR positive (e.g. E. coli, Proteus sp., Salmonella sp.); a yellow colour is MR negative (e.g. Klebsiella, Enterobacter sp.).
• VP reporting: development of a pink/rose or crimson red colour is VP positive (e.g. Klebsiella sp., Enterobacter); absence of colour change is VP negative (e.g. E. coli, Proteus sp.).
(f)
Why used together: the indole, methyl red, Voges-Proskauer and citrate ("IMViC") tests are used together to differentiate members of the Enterobacteriaceae, and MR specifically differentiates E. coli from Enterobacter aerogenes as water/food sanitary indicators.
(g)
• Distinguishing feature: the indole test detects tryptophan breakdown using Kovac's reagent, while MR and VP tests detect different glucose-fermentation end products (stable acid versus neutral acetoin) using different reagents in a similar broth base.
• Ehrlich's reagent is an alternative to Kovac's reagent for the indole test, recommended for anaerobic and non-fermentative Gram-negative organisms, and considered more sensitive.
• E. coli and Enterobacter aerogenes typically give opposite MR and VP results to each other, which is exploited in differentiating these two coliforms.

questions.question:
After incubation, a TSI slant inoculated with a stool isolate shows a black precipitate in the butt of the tube.
(a) Identify what this finding indicates.
(b) State the basis of the reaction in the medium.
(c) State how the finding should be recorded.
(d) State the follow-up practical step needed to confirm identification.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Blackening of the butt indicates hydrogen sulphide (H2S) production, seen with organisms such as Salmonella typhi.
(b)
Sodium thiosulfate and ferrous ammonium sulfate present in the TSI medium react with H2S produced during fermentation, forming the black precipitate.
(c)
The tube is recorded as H2S positive, together with the slant/butt colour pattern (e.g. K/A with H2S production).
(d)
Carry out further biochemical tests and, where relevant, serological (agglutination) tests to confirm the specific identity of the H2S-producing organism.

(a)
• Structure/composition: TSI agar contains lactose and sucrose at 1% concentration and glucose at 0.1% concentration, with phenol red as the pH indicator, and sodium thiosulfate and ferrous ammonium sulfate to detect hydrogen sulphide (seen as a black precipitate in the butt).
• MacConkey agar is a selective and indicator medium containing lactose, bile salts and a pH indicator (neutral red), used to identify lactose fermenters (pink) from non-lactose fermenters (colourless).
• Simmons citrate agar (solid) or Koser's citrate medium (liquid) contains sodium citrate as the only source of carbon and energy, with bromothymol blue as the pH indicator, green when acidic (pH 6.8 and below) and blue when alkaline (pH 7.6 and above).
(b)
Identifying feature: because the glucose concentration in TSI is one-tenth that of lactose or sucrose, organisms that ferment only glucose exhaust it quickly, and the acid produced in the slant oxidizes rapidly, causing the slant to revert to (or remain) an alkaline red, while the butt (under lower oxygen tension) remains acidic (yellow).
(c)
• Standard method/setting: these media are used sequentially in identifying Enterobacteriaceae and other Gram-negative bacilli - MacConkey agar is typically used first to separate lactose from non-lactose fermenters, TSI is then used for sugar fermentation and H2S production, and citrate utilization further differentiates isolates.
• In practice, organisms used to inoculate identification media (TSI, citrate, urea media) must first be isolated in pure culture from a primary or selective/differential medium.
(d)
• Precaution reasoning: on TSI, a tightly closed cap prevents free exchange of air, and an acid reaction caused solely by glucose fermentation may also involve the slant, giving a misleading (falsely acid) slant reading; the cap should therefore be closed loosely, allowing the alkaline condition of the slant to develop correctly once glucose is exhausted.
• On the oxidase test, acidity inhibits oxidase enzyme activity, so the test must not be performed on colonies from carbohydrate-fermenting media such as MacConkey agar, since this could give a false negative result.
• On citrate agar, because sodium citrate is the sole carbon source, contamination of the medium or carry-over of nutrients from a non-citrate medium on the inoculating loop could produce a false positive.
• Including an uninoculated control tube alongside TSI and citrate media allows comparison of colour and growth, ensuring that any colour change or growth in the test tube is genuinely due to the organism's metabolism.
• A basic handling error, such as stabbing too deep or too shallow into TSI, or failing to streak the slant surface adequately, can produce an ambiguous or inaccurate slant/butt reading that does not reflect the organism's true fermentation pattern.
• Correct preparation and use of these differential/selective media, each with a defined composition and indicator system, is central to accurate identification of Gram-negative enteric bacilli.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition of TSI agar, MacConkey agar, and Simmons citrate/Koser's citrate medium.
(b) State the identifying feature of TSI that allows detection of glucose-only fermenters.
(c) State the standard setting/order in which these media are used together in practice.
(d) Explain the reasoning behind the precaution of closing a TSI tube cap loosely rather than tightly.

(a) State the general classification of bacteria by oxygen requirement.
(b) State how each type is applied/selected when choosing culture atmosphere and duration.
(c) Explain why a basic error in providing the wrong atmosphere or incubation time leads to an inaccurate or invalid culture result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Bacteria are classified by oxygen requirement into obligate aerobes (require oxygen to live, e.g. Pseudomonas), facultative anaerobes (can use oxygen but can also grow in its absence, e.g. E. coli, Staphylococcus, yeasts, many intestinal bacteria), obligate anaerobes (cannot use oxygen and are harmed by toxic forms of oxygen, e.g. Clostridium species causing tetanus and botulism), aerotolerant anaerobes (cannot use oxygen but tolerate its presence, e.g. Lactobacillus, which ferments regardless of oxygen), and microaerophiles (require oxygen but at low concentrations and are sensitive to toxic oxygen forms, e.g. Campylobacter).
• Culture atmospheres in practice are provided at 35-37°C in ambient air, air supplemented with carbon dioxide (3-10%), reduced oxygen (microaerophilic conditions), or no oxygen (anaerobic conditions), depending on the organism's requirements.
• Anaerobic conditions in a medium can be achieved by adding reducing substances (e.g. in thioglycollate broth or Robertson's cooked meat broth), displacing air with carbon dioxide, absorbing oxygen chemically, removing oxygen by direct oxidation, or inoculating into deeper layers of solid media or under a layer of oil in liquid media.
(b)
• How each type is applied/selected: clinical specimens from bacterial infections often contain aerobic, facultative anaerobic and anaerobic bacteria together, so such specimens are usually inoculated onto a variety of general-purpose, differential and selective media and incubated under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions.
• Semisolid media (0.05-0.3% agar) are selected for anaerobic and microaerophilic organisms, since they form an oxygen gradient in the tube, allowing all degrees of oxygen tension to exist within the same culture vessel.
(c)
• Duration of incubation is matched to the organism: most aerobic and anaerobic bacteria grow overnight, whereas some mycobacteria require as many as 6-8 weeks.
• Why a basic error leads to an inaccurate/invalid result: incubating a specimen only under aerobic conditions when an obligate anaerobe (e.g. Clostridium) is present would fail to recover that organism, since obligate anaerobes are harmed by oxygen.
• Conversely, failing to provide oxygen for an obligate aerobe (e.g. Pseudomonas) would prevent its growth, since it specifically requires oxygen to live.
• Not providing a reduced-oxygen (microaerophilic) atmosphere for an organism such as Campylobacter could result in failure to isolate the organism even though it is present in the specimen.
• Discontinuing incubation too early (e.g. after only overnight incubation) when a slow-growing organism such as a mycobacterium is suspected, rather than allowing the recommended 6-8 weeks, would give a false-negative culture result.
• Because clinical specimens often contain a mixture of aerobic, facultative and anaerobic organisms, inoculating onto only one type of medium/atmosphere rather than a range of media under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions would risk missing part of the true microbial picture.
• Correctly classifying the likely oxygen requirement of a suspected organism, and providing the matching incubation atmosphere and duration, is therefore essential to obtaining a valid culture result.

(a)
EDTA anticoagulant human plasma (or citrated/diluted rabbit plasma), a clean glass slide, test tubes, pipettes, distilled water, and an inoculation loop are required.
(b)
Staphylococcus aureus produces coagulase (free and bound), which clots plasma in a tube or agglutinates cocci on a slide; bound coagulase (clumping factor) cross-links fibrinogen chains, while free coagulase acts with a plasma factor to convert fibrinogen to fibrin.
(c)
Slide test: make dense suspensions of the organism on two ends of a slide labelled "test" and "control"; add a drop of citrated plasma to the test suspension and mix. Tube test: label three tubes "test", "negative control" and "positive control", each with 0.5 ml of diluted plasma; add 0.1 ml of the relevant broth culture to each tube and incubate at 37°C, observing up to four hours (overnight at room temperature if still negative).
(d)
Slide test: clumping within 5-10 seconds is positive; no clumping is negative (strains negative here should be confirmed by the tube test). Tube test: gelling of the plasma that remains in place on inverting the tube is positive; no clot formation is negative.
questions.question:
A catalase-positive, Gram-positive coccus isolated in clusters from a wound needs to be confirmed as Staphylococcus aureus using the coagulase test.
(a) Identify the reagents and apparatus needed for both the slide and tube versions of the test.
(b) State the principle of the test.
(c) Describe the step-by-step procedure for the slide test and the tube test.
(d) State how each version of the test is read and interpreted as positive or negative.

(a) Describe the two microscopy-based forms of blood film examination used in malaria diagnosis.
(b) State the identifying features/purpose of the thick and the thin film respectively.
(c) State the standard setting in which blood film smears are collected and handled.
(d) Explain the reasoning behind the precaution against refrigerating blood smear slides.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Structure/features: laboratory diagnosis of malaria is definitive and more reliable than clinical diagnosis (which is presumptive, based on fever, anorexia, malaise); microscopic examination of a Giemsa-stained blood film is the gold standard.
• Two film types are used: the thick blood film, used for parasite identification and estimating parasite density, and the thin film, used for speciation of the parasite.
(b)
• Identifying characteristics: malaria is caused by Plasmodium falciparum, P. malariae, P. ovale, P. vivax and P. knowlesi, transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito; P. falciparum (malignant tertian) has developed resistance to almost all categories of antimalarial drugs currently in use.
• Other microscopy-based tests mentioned include the Quantitative Buffy Coat (QBC) test, fluorescence microscopy, and Benzothiocarboxypurine (BCP) staining.
• In the QBC test, blood is mixed with acridine orange, centrifuged in a capillary tube, and read directly with a fluorescent microscope, allowing visualization of the layered blood components (platelets, lymphocytes, granulocytes, red blood cells).
(c)
• Standard method/setting: thick and thin films are prepared, stained with Giemsa, and examined under oil immersion; rapid diagnostic tests (e.g. ParaSight-F, ICT/Malpac, OptiMAL) based on antigen detection (PfHRP-2, pLDH) provide additional, faster options in many clinical settings.
• Collection: blood film smears are collected as capillary blood from a finger prick; the thin film is fixed with methanol or another fixative.
• Handling/transport: slides should be transported within 24 hours and should not be refrigerated, as refrigeration can alter cell morphology.
(d)
• Precaution reasoning: because thin films require chemical fixation before staining while thick films are examined unfixed (to allow lysis of red cells and concentration of parasites), the two film types must be prepared and handled differently even on slides taken at the same time.
• The precaution against refrigerating blood smear slides exists because altered cell (and parasite) morphology could lead to misidentification of species or a missed diagnosis on later examination.
• Other investigations performed alongside microscopy include full blood count (PCV, WBC, platelet count, coagulation tests), blood glucose, blood chemistry, urinalysis (haemoglobinuria, proteinuria) and screening for G6PD deficiency, relevant before certain antimalarial drugs are given.
• Correct film preparation and handling is essential because microscopy remains the reference (gold standard) method against which rapid diagnostic tests and other methods are validated.

questions.question:
A slide coagulase test is set up with "test" and "control" suspensions of a Gram-positive coccus; within 8 seconds, visible clumping is seen in the test suspension but not in the control.
(a) Interpret this result.
(b) State how the result should be recorded.
(c) State what the result indicates about the organism's identity.
(d) State the follow-up action if a strain does not show this reaction.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Agglutination/clumping of the test suspension within 5-10 seconds, with no clumping in the control (ruling out auto-agglutination), is a positive slide coagulase result.
(b)
The isolate is recorded as "slide coagulase positive".
(c)
A positive result indicates the organism produces bound coagulase (clumping factor), consistent with Staphylococcus aureus.
(d)
Strains that do not produce bound coagulase (and so give no clumping) must be confirmed by the tube coagulase test before being ruled out as S. aureus.

(a)
• Ticks (superfamily Ixodoidea) are classified into two families: Ixodidae (hard ticks) and Argasidae (soft ticks), distinguished by capitulum position, presence/absence of a scutum, position of respiratory spiracles, presence/absence of pulvilli, longevity, and parasitism pattern (permanent versus temporary), as well as by egg-laying pattern.
• Their life cycle is further classified by the number of hosts involved: one-host ticks (e.g. Boophilus decoloratus), two-host ticks (e.g. Hyalomma truncatum), and three-host ticks (e.g. Amblyomma variegatum).
(b)
How each classification is applied/selected: recognizing whether a specimen is a hard or soft tick, and how many hosts its life cycle involves, informs the likely pattern of host contact (how long it remains attached, whether it returns to the same host) and therefore the disease transmission risk and appropriate control approach.
(c)
• Larval-stage identification is also used: hard tick larvae have a small, anterior scutum, are oval and brownish, with a single nymphal instar stage; soft tick larvae lack a scutum and pulvilli, are round and yellowish, with several (4-5) nymphal stages.
• Why a basic error leads to an inaccurate or invalid result: mistaking a soft tick for a hard tick (or vice versa) because the capitulum position or scutum was not correctly assessed would lead to an incorrect assumption about how long the tick remains attached, affecting interpretation of exposure and disease risk.
• An error in recognizing the nymphal stage of a tick (e.g. failing to recognize Ixodes scapularis nymphs as the stage typically transmitting Babesia microti) could lead to control measures being directed at the wrong life stage, reducing their effectiveness.
• Applying a permethrin-based control product directly to skin, rather than to clothing/boots as intended, would be an error in the correct application of the stated control measure, potentially reducing its safety or effectiveness.
• Failing to correctly identify the tick family before choosing a control strategy could also mean that a strategy suited to a permanent ectoparasite is wrongly applied to a temporary ectoparasite, or vice versa.
• Because ticks are vectors of multiple pathogens (e.g. Babesia species via Ixodes scapularis), correct family- and stage-level identification underlies accurate risk assessment for tick-borne disease.
• The classification of ticks by number of hosts in the life cycle is applied to understanding transmission dynamics, since a one-host tick completes its whole life cycle on a single host animal, unlike two- or three-host ticks.
• An error in distinguishing tick life-cycle type could lead to an incorrect assumption about where in the environment (on the host versus between hosts) intervention would be most effective.
• Overall, correct application of tick classification (family, host number, life stage) is central to both accurate specimen identification and effective, correctly targeted control measures.
questions.question:
(a) State the general classification of ticks by family and by number of hosts in the life cycle.
(b) State how these classifications are applied/selected in assessing risk and control.
(c) Explain why a basic error in tick identification leads to an inaccurate or invalid assessment of risk/control.

(a) State the principle of antimicrobial susceptibility testing.
(b) Describe the Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion method under the headings: materials, procedure, reporting.
(c) Describe the broth dilution method under the headings: materials, procedure, reporting.
(d) State a precaution common to both methods.
(e) Explain why both categories of method (diffusion and dilution) are used in the laboratory.
(f) Distinguish disc diffusion from dilution (MIC/MBC) testing.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Principle: antimicrobial susceptibility testing determines the sensitivity of an isolate to various antimicrobial agents, directly influencing the choice of drug for treatment; two broad technique groups are dilution and diffusion.
(b)
• Kirby-Bauer materials: Mueller-Hinton agar, 0.5 McFarland standard, antimicrobial discs, 90mm/120mm petri dish.
• Kirby-Bauer procedure: prepare inoculum by emulsifying 4-5 colonies in broth, compare turbidity with the McFarland standard, swab Mueller-Hinton agar, place discs 20mm apart and 25mm from the plate edge (6 discs for a 90mm dish, 9 for a 120mm dish), incubate aerobically at 35°C for 18-24 hours.
• Kirby-Bauer reporting: measure the zone of inhibition around each disc and compare with an interpretative chart; report as Sensitive, Resistant or Intermediate.
(c)
• Broth dilution materials: doubling dilutions of the antibiotic in liquid growth medium, a standardized bacterial suspension (1-5 ×10⁵ CFU/ml).
• Broth dilution procedure: make doubling dilutions (e.g. 0,1,2,4,8,16 µg/ml); inoculate with the standardized suspension; incubate overnight at 35°C; examine tubes for visible growth (turbidity).
• Broth dilution reporting: the lowest concentration with no visible growth is the MIC; a subculture from that tube onto drug-free agar with no growth (inhibiting at least 99.9% of colonies) gives the MBC.
(d)
Precaution common to both: a standardized inoculum (McFarland standard or CFU count) is essential for valid, reproducible results in either method.
(e)
Why used: dilution methods give quantitative MIC/MBC values useful for precise dosing, while disc diffusion is a simpler qualitative screening method widely used for its practicality in testing multiple antibiotics at once.
(f)
• Distinguishing feature: disc diffusion reads a zone diameter around a fixed-concentration disc and reports a categorical result (S/I/R); dilution methods read growth/no-growth across a concentration gradient and report a numerical MIC (and MBC) value.
• Other related methods include the Stokes method (test and control organisms on the same plate, limited by lack of standardization) and the antimicrobial gradient method (e.g. E-test), which estimates MIC using an agar diffusion format.
• Newer approaches include automated instrument systems (e.g. Vitek 2, BD Phoenix) using optical detection, and genotypic methods detecting resistance genes by PCR and DNA hybridization.

questions.question:
(a) State the general classification of immunizing agents into vaccines, immunoglobulins and antisera, and the subtypes of each.
(b) State how each type is applied/selected for active or passive protection.
(c) Explain why a basic error in selecting the wrong immunizing agent leads to an inappropriate outcome.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Immunizing agents are classified into three types: vaccines, immunoglobulins, and antisera (antitoxins).
• Immunoglobulin preparations for passive immunization are of two types: normal human immunoglobulin (e.g. for hepatitis A, measles, rabies, tetanus, mumps) and specific (hyper-immune) human immunoglobulin (e.g. for hepatitis B, varicella, diphtheria).
• Antisera (non-human immunoglobulin, prepared in animals such as horses) are used for conditions such as diphtheria, tetanus, gas gangrene, and botulism, and also rabies.
• Vaccines are further classified as subunit/peptide vaccines, attenuated vaccines, and vector vaccines, each produced by a different technology (purified pathogen components, live modified pathogen with deleted virulence genes, or a carrier virus/bacterium bearing an inserted antigen gene).
(b)
How each type is applied/selected: vaccines are selected for active immunization, to stimulate the host's own antibody response ahead of exposure; immunoglobulins and antisera are selected for passive immunization, providing ready-made antibodies for immediate, typically shorter-lived, protection.
(c)
• Within immunoglobulins, normal human immunoglobulin is selected when broad, pooled antibody coverage against common infections is needed, while specific hyper-immune human immunoglobulin is selected when targeted, high-titre antibody against a particular pathogen is required.
• Antisera (animal-derived) are selected specifically for conditions such as diphtheria, tetanus, gas gangrene and botulism, where human-derived immunoglobulin preparations are not listed as the standard option.
• Why a basic error leads to an inaccurate/invalid result: selecting an active immunizing agent (a vaccine) when immediate protection is required would be an error, since active immunity takes time to develop as the host's own antibody response builds up, unlike passive immunity, which is immediate.
• Conversely, relying only on passive immunization when long-term protection is needed would be an error, since passive immunity is not maintained by the host's own memory response.
• Using a normal human immunoglobulin preparation where a specific (hyper-immune) preparation was required (or vice versa) would not provide the intended, appropriately targeted level of antibody protection for the specific pathogen involved.
• Because attenuated (live) vaccines require virulence genes to be deleted rather than merely reduced, insufficient attenuation is noted as a limitation of some traditional vaccine approaches, which could result in the vaccine itself causing disease.
• Correctly distinguishing between the different immunizing agents, and their subtypes, and matching them to whether active or passive, immediate or long-term protection is required, is therefore essential to avoid an inappropriate immunization choice.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the physical and microbiological quality control parameters checked in prepared culture media.
(b) State the identifying features examined under physical characteristics of prepared media.
(c) State the standard setting/schedule in which sterility and performance testing are carried out.
(d) Explain the reasoning behind discarding a batch of media that shows more than 2 colonies per plate on sterility testing.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Structure/features assessed: quality control of culture media covers growth-supporting characteristics, physical characteristics, gel strength, and sterility (batch contamination), because the accuracy of a laboratory's reporting depends on the quality of the media used.
(b)
• Physical characteristics examined include depth (thickness of the medium in the plate, which should be 4.0mm), avoidance of unequal filling of plates, smoothness of appearance, clarity, haemolysis, bubbles, contamination, freezing/crystallization, cracked medium/plate, and pH of the medium.
• Identifying characteristics of good raw material quality: the most important raw material is water, which should be distilled or deionized with a slightly acidic pH; dehydrated media should be ordered for 6 months to 1 year, packed to be used within 1-2 months, dated on receipt/opening, and stored in a dark, cool, well-ventilated place.
(c)
• Standard method/setting: documentation for each batch should record the number/amount prepared, source of each ingredient, lot number, preparation date, expiration date, and sterilization method.
• Sterilization is generally by autoclaving, with time and quantity closely regulated and temperature/pressure constantly monitored; batch volume should be kept small (ideally two litres); biological indicators such as Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores check spore-killing efficacy.
• Sterility checking schedule: about 5% of any batch is tested; sterility is routinely checked by incubating the medium for about 48 hours at 35°C (or alternatively room temperature for at least three days).
• Performance testing (growth-supporting characteristics) is the most important microbiological parameter: each medium is tested with organisms expected to give a positive reaction and with organisms expected not to grow or to give a negative reaction, using standard inoculating procedures and stock organisms (e.g. E. coli ATCC 25922, Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 25923, Neisseria gonorrhoeae ATCC 49226).
• An example given is the blood agar performance test, checked for haemolysis and growth using S. pyogenes, S. pneumoniae and E. faecalis.
(d)
• Precaution/safety reasoning: equipment (e.g. autoclaves) should be calibrated before use and at regular intervals, with clear operating and cleaning instructions and service sheets, since poorly maintained equipment could compromise sterilization and therefore media quality.
• Specimen and media containers should be inspected regularly, especially caps for missing or worn liners, and defective units discarded, since defects could allow contamination or loss of sterility.
• Personnel should be appropriately trained, with ongoing training and retraining, because inconsistent technique by untrained staff is itself a source of quality-control failure.
• Reasoning for discarding a batch with more than 2 colonies per plate on sterility testing: this indicates the batch as a whole cannot be relied upon to be sterile, so using it could introduce contaminating organisms into subsequent cultures and produce inaccurate results.

questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the coagulase test.
(b) List the materials required.
(c) Describe the slide and tube procedures.
(d) State how the slide test differs in use from the tube test.
(e) State how results are reported.
(f) Explain why the coagulase test is used in bacterial identification.
(g) Distinguish the coagulase test from the catalase test.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principle: Staphylococcus aureus produces coagulase, which can clot plasma into a gel in a tube or agglutinate cocci on a slide; this differentiates S. aureus from other species of Staphylococcus.
• Free coagulase is a secreted, heat-labile enzyme detected by the tube test; bound coagulase (clumping factor) is a heat-stable, cell-wall-associated protein detected by the slide test.
(b)
Materials: EDTA anticoagulant human plasma or 1 in 10 diluted rabbit plasma, clean glass slide, test tubes, pipettes, distilled water, inoculation loop.
(c)
• Slide procedure: make dense suspensions of staphylococci on two ends of a slide labelled "test" and "control"; treat the test suspension with a drop of citrated plasma and mix; the control rules out auto-agglutination.
• Tube procedure: three tubes ("test", "negative control", "positive control") each filled with 0.5 ml of diluted plasma; add 0.1 ml of the relevant broth culture to each; incubate at 37°C and observe up to four hours, then overnight at room temperature if still negative.
(d)
Use: slide coagulase is used to screen isolates of S. aureus, while tube coagulase is used for confirmation, especially where the slide test is negative.
(e)
Reporting: slide test - agglutination/clumping within 5-10 seconds is positive; tube test - gelling of plasma that remains in place on inverting the tube is positive; absence of either is negative.
(f)
Why used: the test is useful in differentiating S. aureus from other coagulase-negative staphylococci, an important step in clinical identification.
(g)
• Distinguishing feature: unlike the catalase test, which uses hydrogen peroxide and reads bubble formation within seconds, the coagulase test uses plasma and reads clumping (slide, seconds) or clot formation (tube, up to hours/overnight).
• Catalase differentiates staphylococci from streptococci/enterococci at the genus level, while coagulase differentiates S. aureus specifically from other staphylococcal species.
• Both tests are part of the standard biochemical identification pathway following Gram staining of Gram-positive cocci seen in clusters.
• Both tests use small amounts of bacterial growth mixed with a reagent but detect different enzyme activities (peroxide breakdown versus plasma clotting).

questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the Kato-Katz stool technique.
(b) State the principle of concentration techniques (flotation and sedimentation).
(c) Describe general stool microscopy procedure, including the direct wet mount.
(d) State a precaution relevant to stool microscopy.
(e) Explain why concentration methods are used alongside direct examination.
(f) Distinguish flotation from sedimentation concentration techniques.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Kato-Katz principle: this stool smear technique is used to demonstrate schistosome eggs for microscopy, allowing species to be identified from characteristic egg spines.
(b)
• Flotation principle: uses a solution of high specific gravity so that eggs and cysts float; examples are saturated sodium chloride (for Ascaris spp., hookworms) and zinc sulphate centrifugation flotation (for cysts, nematodes).
• Sedimentation principle: uses a solution of low specific gravity, e.g. formol-ether, and can be used for egg counts in a gram of stool.
(c)
• Direct wet mount procedure: a thin emulsion of a small amount of faeces is made with a few drops of saline; lugol's iodine may be added to reveal nuclear detail and the glycogen vacuole in cysts; this demonstrates protozoa (trophozoites), cysts, eggs and larvae.
• General procedure: the sample is collected in a clean, dry container; a preservative (10% formalin) is sometimes used; samples are sometimes examined fresh (for amoeba, ciliates); liquid/soft stool is examined within 15 minutes.
(d)
• Precaution: the sample must not be mixed with urine or disinfectant, as these kill trophozoites; specimens obtained by enema or laxatives are often positive for worm eggs or adult worms and should be interpreted with this in mind.
• Reporting: results may be reported as gross findings (e.g. mucoid, blood-stained stool suggesting acute amoebic dysentery) and/or microscopic findings (e.g. named eggs, cysts, trophozoites seen).
(e)
Why concentration is used: concentration methods (flotation, sedimentation) increase the chance of detecting scanty parasites compared with a direct wet mount alone, while Kato-Katz specifically enables demonstration and quantification of schistosome eggs.
(f)
• Distinguishing feature: flotation relies on a high-specific-gravity solution to bring light eggs/cysts to the surface, whereas sedimentation (e.g. formol-ether) relies on a low-specific-gravity solution and produces a sediment used for direct examination and egg counts.
• Permanent stained smears (e.g. trichrome or iron haematoxylin staining) may additionally be used to visualize protozoan trophozoites such as those of Giardia.
• Selection of technique depends on the suspected parasite: flotation and Kato-Katz suit eggs/cysts of nematodes and schistosomes, while fresh unpreserved samples and wet mounts are needed for fragile trophozoites of amoebae and ciliates.
• Both flotation and sedimentation are used specifically when parasites are scanty in a sample, unlike the direct wet mount, which is used as a first, rapid examination.

(a)
This pattern (K/A with gas, without H2S) indicates that the organism ferments glucose only (not lactose or sucrose), with gas production, and does not produce hydrogen sulphide.
(b)
The reaction is recorded as "K/A with gas production, no H2S production".
(c)
This pattern is consistent with an organism such as Salmonella paratyphi A among the Enterobacteriaceae.
(d)
