questions.question:
A person is found with pinpoint pupils, drowsiness and slow breathing after taking a large amount of an opioid analgesic.
(a) Identify the offending drug class.
(b) Explain the mechanism of toxicity.
(c) State the specific antidote and its properties.
(d) Identify at-risk patients and preventive measures.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Opioid (narcotic) analgesics such as morphine, heroin, methadone, fentanyl, pethidine
(b)
• Binding to central opioid receptors produces sedation, respiratory depression, miosis, reduced heart rate and BP
• Fentanyl is about 500 times as potent as pethidine and heroin 2-3 times as potent as morphine through greater lipid solubility and CNS penetration; potency raises overdose risk
(c)
• Naloxone, a pure antagonist, is commonly used to treat narcotic overdose
• Naloxone is N-allyl 14-beta-hydroxydihydromorphinone; naltrexone is similar but has weak agonist activity
• Nalorphine, a mixed agonist-antagonist, competes with agonists and can cause withdrawal and has psychotomimetic effects
(d)
• Paediatric use of diphenoxylate-atropine needs strict dosing because of opioid intoxication and death
• Tolerant users who take more than their normal dose may show 'on the nod' semiconscious sleep

(a)
Organic nitrates (simple nitric or nitrous acid esters of polyalcohols); the prototype given sublingually is nitroglycerine
(b)
• Nitroglycerine has very low oral bioavailability (10-20%) because of a marked first-pass effect, so it is given sublingually; total duration of effect is 15-30 minutes
• Isosorbide dinitrate is also given sublingually, its earlier metabolites are active; transdermal and buccal slow-release preparations are other routes
• Amyl nitrate is a highly volatile liquid in fragile glass ampules, crushed and inhaled; absorption is very rapid with effect in seconds, half-life 2-8 minutes, active partly denitrated metabolite half-life up to 3 hours
• Isosorbide 5-mononitrate (metabolite of the dinitrate) has bioavailability of almost 100% and is excreted as glucuronide by the kidney
(c)
• Nitroglycerine is metabolised in the liver by organic nitrate reductase, which removes nitrate groups stepwise until fully inactivated
• It may lose potency in storage through volatilisation and adsorbs to plastic, so it is stored in a tightly closed glass container; it is not light sensitive
(d)
• Sublingual route avoids first-pass loss and gives relief of angina of effort that usually subsides with rest or nitroglycerin
• Amyl nitrate is very useful in emergency situations because of its rapid effect
• Poor storage (volatilisation or plastic adsorption) can leave the drug with reduced potency
• Tolerance is a feature of organic nitrates
questions.question:
A patient with angina takes a drug sublingually. The patient also asks about swallowing the same drug and about an inhaled alternative for emergencies.
(a) Identify the drug class and the prototype used by the sublingual route.
(b) Explain how route, first-pass metabolism and drug form affect bioavailability, onset and duration for the sublingual, oral and inhaled forms.
(c) State how the drug is metabolised, how it must be stored, and the monitoring or dose adjustment points.
(d) State the clinical consequences of these pharmacokinetic features.

A. Describe the neurobiology of anxiety and the relationship between dose and CNS depression for sedative-hypnotics.
(a) State the GABAergic mechanism and the stages of CNS depression with increasing dose.
(b) Relate these to examples of drugs and sleep effects.
(c) Explain the clinical significance.
(d) State the limitations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• CNS equilibrium depends on balance between excitation (glutamate) and inhibition (GABA); GABAA receptor activation increases Cl- conductance and hyperpolarises the neuron
• Dose-dependent depression: relief of anxiety → sedation → hypnosis → confusion, delirium, ataxia → surgical anaesthesia → coma with respiratory and vasomotor depression → death
• Sedative versus hypnotic difference is usually dose: lower dose calming, higher dose sleep
(b)
• Benzodiazepines increase channel opening frequency; barbiturates increase opening duration; both raise receptor affinity for GABA
• Normal sleep: NREM (70-75%, four stages) and REM cycling over 90 minutes
• Sedative-hypnotics shorten sleep latency, lengthen stage 2 NREM, decrease REM and slow-wave sleep; tolerance after 1-2 weeks
(c)
• Hypnotic effects can be obtained with most anxiolytics by increasing dose; barbiturates have a steep dose-response from sedation to respiratory depression, benzodiazepines are safer
• Barbiturates thiopental and methohexital are used as adjuncts in anaesthesia because of fast onset and short duration
• All these drugs alter the normal sleep cycle and are for symptomatic, short-term use (days or weeks, never months)
(d)
• Buspirone separates anxiolysis from sedation
• Distinction between pathological and normal anxiety is hard to draw
• Rebound REM increase and nightmares follow withdrawal

questions.question:
A patient taking phenelzine eats a large portion of ripe cheese and develops a severe throbbing headache and a sharp rise in blood pressure.
(a) Identify the type of interaction and the offending drug class.
(b) Explain the mechanism.
(c) Predict the clinical outcome and the danger.
(d) State how to manage or avoid it and name safer options.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pharmacodynamic drug-food interaction (the 'cheese reaction') with irreversible, non-selective monoamine oxidase inhibitors (phenelzine, tranylcypromine, iproniazid)
(b)
• Tyramine from fermentation is normally metabolised by MAO in gut wall and liver; MAO inhibition allows absorption and enhances its sympathomimetic effect
• MAOIs raise the cytoplasmic monoamine pool in nerve terminals, increasing release by indirectly acting amines such as tyramine and amphetamine
(c)
• Acute hypertension with severe throbbing headache and occasionally intracranial haemorrhage; at least 10 mg tyramine needed; main danger from ripe cheese and concentrated yeast products (Marmite)
• Indirectly acting sympathomimetics (ephedrine, amphetamine) also cause severe hypertension
(d)
• Avoid tyramine-rich foods and indirectly acting sympathomimetics; avoid TCAs simultaneously
• Moclobemide, a reversible MAO-A-selective inhibitor, does not cause the cheese reaction (MAO-B still metabolises tyramine); MAOIs are now largely superseded

questions.question:
A patient with liver dysfunction is given an amide local anaesthetic, while another patient with a plasma esterase-sensitive agent develops an allergic reaction. The prescriber also asks why bupivacaine lasts longer than mepivacaine.
(a) Identify the pharmacokinetic processes involved.
(b) Explain the effect on onset, duration and accumulation for amides and esters.
(c) State the dosing adjustment and the role of vasoconstrictors.
(d) Name the clinical consequence.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Hepatic biotransformation of amides versus plasma esterase hydrolysis of esters; plasma protein binding determines duration
(b)
• Amides are metabolised in the liver, more slowly in liver dysfunction; esters are rapidly hydrolysed by plasma esterases in the blood
• Duration depends on plasma protein binding: bupivacaine 95% protein bound lasts longer than mepivacaine 55%
• Potency relates to lipid solubility; higher solubility allows lower concentration and less toxicity
(c)
Epinephrine or felypressin is added as vasoconstrictor to restrict systemic absorption and prolong action (e.g. lidocaine 120 min to 240 min)
(d)
• Hydrolysis of ester-linked anaesthetics forms para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), usually allergenic; amides rarely cause hypersensitivity
• Prilocaine can cause methaemoglobinaemia and is not used for obstetric analgesia because of neonatal methaemoglobinaemia

(a)
• Migraine is a neurovascular disorder with prodrome, aura (up to 1 h), unilateral throbbing headache (up to 72 h) and postdrome; with aura in one third, without aura about 80%
• Theories: vascular (meningeal vessel dilatation), cortical spreading depression, and neuronal (trigeminal nociceptor sensitisation); trigeminal nerves release CGRP, substance P and neurokinin A causing plasma extravasation
• Acute drugs: triptans, ergot alkaloids, NSAIDs, lasmiditan, CGRP antagonists (olcegepant, rimegepant); antiemetics occasionally
(b)
• 5-HT1 receptor binding inhibits neuronal firing, 5-HT2 binding excites; descending 5-HT pain inhibition is deficient
• Prophylaxis: propranolol (blocks 5-HT2, reduces firing), amitriptyline, verapamil, flunarizine, valproic acid, topiramate, pizotifen (5-HT2 antagonist); SSRIs and 5-HT2A/2C antagonists (methysergide, trazodone, risperidone, ketanserin) also named
• Familial hemiplegic migraine arises from mutations in the alpha-1A subunit of the voltage-gated calcium channel (chromosome 19); migraine is inherited with about a 50% chance
(c)
• Triptans first-line in acute severe attacks; NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) for analgesia; ergots for restricted cases
• Prophylactics (propranolol, TCAs, CCBs, antiseizure agents, antiemetics) are not for acute attacks
• Pizotifen: drowsiness, appetite stimulation, weight gain
(d)
• Propranolol should not be given with triptans or ergotamine
• Pizotifen is not used with MAOIs and potentiates sedatives
• Triptans should not be combined with ergotamine, MAOIs, lithium or SSRIs

A patient with heart failure is on digoxin together with a loop diuretic or thiazide diuretic. The patient later develops a cardiac arrhythmia.
(a) Identify the type of interaction and the electrolyte disturbance involved.
(b) Explain the mechanism, including the role of potassium, calcium and magnesium.
(c) Predict the clinical outcome.
(d) State how to manage or avoid it, and name other drugs that act similarly.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pharmacodynamic interaction: diuretics lower serum potassium (hypokalaemia), which enhances digitalis cardiotoxicity; corticosteroids act the same way
(b)
• Potassium and digitalis inhibit each other's binding to Na+/K+ ATPase, so hypokalaemia facilitates the enzyme-inhibiting action of the glycoside while hyperkalaemia reduces it
• Abnormal cardiac automaticity is inhibited by hyperkalaemia, so moderately raised extracellular K+ reduces digitalis effects, especially toxic effects
• Calcium facilitates toxicity by accelerating overloading of intracellular calcium stores that causes digitalis-induced abnormal automaticity; hypercalcaemia raises arrhythmia risk
• Magnesium acts opposite to calcium; hypomagnesaemia is a risk factor for arrhythmias
(c)
• Increased risk of digoxin toxicity: bradycardia, partial or complete heart block, extrasystoles, coupled beats, ventricular fibrillation and fatal arrhythmias
• Increased excitability can lead to ventricular tachycardia and ultimately ventricular fibrillation at toxic concentrations
(d)
• Monitor and manage potassium levels and evaluate serum electrolytes in patients with digitalis-induced arrhythmias
• Severe intoxication: digitalis antibodies (Fab fragments), raised against digoxin and also recognising digitoxin and ouabain
• Other drugs that raise toxicity by displacing digitalis from protein binding: amiodarone, quinidine, verapamil, tetracyclines, erythromycin
• Patients should not take non-prescription cough or cold medicines, antacids, laxatives or antidiarrheals without consulting the physician

questions.question:
A. Describe the antipsychotic drugs as a therapeutic group.
(a) State the biochemical basis of psychosis and classify the drugs.
(b) Give the mechanism of each group.
(c) Compare the groups by use, adverse effects.
(d) State precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Psychosis: distorted or absent sense of reality (hallucinations, delusions, disorganised speech and behaviour); seen in schizophrenia, mood disorders, substance-induced, dementia and delirium
• Dopamine hypothesis (Arvid Carlsson): overactivity of dopaminergic function; serotonin and probably glutamate are also involved
• Positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations) and negative symptoms (flat affect, poor eye contact, lack of goal-directed activity)
(b)
• Typical: D2 antagonists (also muscarinic, histamine and alpha blockade); atypical: 5-HT2A antagonism with lesser D2 antagonism; aripiprazole partial agonist at 5-HT2A and D2
• Pimozide is a miscellaneous agent for Tourette syndrome (tics)
(c)
• Other uses: anxiety, autism, antiemetic (D2 block in CTZ; atypicals less effective), refractory hiccups (chlorpromazine); no analgesic effect
• Typical: EPS, hyperprolactinaemia; atypical: metabolic effects, weight gain, agranulocytosis with clozapine
• Olanzapine major weight gain; quetiapine and aripiprazole suicidality black-box warning in children; ziprasidone no weight gain
(d)
• Regular full blood counts with clozapine; QT prolongation (typicals, quetiapine, ziprasidone)
• Increased cerebrovascular events and mortality in dementia; lowers seizure threshold; neuroleptic malignant syndrome
• Antimuscarinics for high-EPS agents; elderly at 5-fold risk of tardive dyskinesia
• Risk of acute dystonia highest in the first weeks, in the young and antipsychotic-naive

(a)
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a fatal idiosyncratic adverse reaction of antipsychotics (low or high potency, typical or atypical)
(b)
• Characterised by mental status changes, muscle rigidity, hyperthermia and autonomic dysfunction
• It is an adverse effect of dopamine blockade
(c)
Differentiate from acute dystonia, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia and dementia, which lack the fever, rigidity and autonomic features
(d)
Related monitoring for antipsychotic toxicity: regular full blood counts with clozapine (agranulocytosis, first 6 months); QT prolongation risk with some agents
questions.question:
A woman with schizophrenia who has long been on antipsychotics arrives with a temperature of 103.2 F, blood pressure 180/99, heavy sweating, muscular rigidity, mutism and obtundation.
(a) Identify the condition and the offending drug class.
(b) State the features and the mechanism where given.
(c) State the management and any specific antidote.
(d) Identify at-risk patients and monitoring or preventive measures.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Morphine, a natural opium alkaloid (about 10-15% of opium) from Papaver somniferum; opioid analgesic
(b)
Opioids bind opioid receptors, which are G-protein coupled, in the brain, spinal cord and periphery, reducing the perception of pain
(c)
• Use: one of the most effective drugs for pain, e.g. terminal illness and cancer pain; given orally, IM, SC or IV; long-acting oral forms (Oramorph, MS Contin, Avinza)
• Effects: euphoria, mental clouding, drowsiness, apathy, reduced heart rate and BP, constipation, miosis, nausea and vomiting, dysphoria, itching, respiratory depression, antitussive effect
• Less common: confusion, hallucinations, delirium, hypothermia, bradycardia or tachycardia, raised intracranial pressure
(d)
• High addiction liability; physical dependence is an automatic consequence of long-term use and withdrawal follows abrupt stopping; Schedule II/III controlled drug
• Tolerance and dose escalation occur, although many pain specialists do not regard tolerance as a problem in chronic pain
• Opioids have no ceiling effect, unlike non-opioid analgesics, and are used for severe pain with no anti-inflammatory effect
questions.question:
A patient with terminal cancer has severe pain that has not responded to milder analgesics. The doctor prescribes the principal alkaloid of opium. Over days the patient becomes constipated, nauseated and drowsy with small pupils.
(a) Identify the drug and its class.
(b) State the mechanism of action at the receptor target.
(c) State the therapeutic use and the key adverse effects.

A young child is brought in with coma and convulsions, hyperventilation, high temperature, tinnitus and vomiting after swallowing many tablets of a common analgesic-antipyretic.
(a) Identify the offending drug and the condition.
(b) Explain the mechanism of toxicity.
(c) State the management and whether a specific antidote exists.
(d) Identify at-risk patients and monitoring or preventive measures.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Aspirin (salicylate) poisoning, a medical emergency that often occurs in children; mild chronic intoxication is called salicylism
(b)
• Increased peripheral CO2 production with compensatory hyperventilation gives serious acid-base imbalance and respiratory acidosis; respiratory failure is the usual cause of death
• Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation produces excessive heat and hyperthermia, particularly in children
• CNS effects: convulsions, confusion, dizziness, tinnitus (plasma 200-450 mg/mL, resolves in 2-3 days), vertigo, high-tone deafness, delirium, stupor, coma
(c)
• There is no specific antidote; use the ABCD approach (airway, breathing, circulation, decontamination)
• Aggressive IV volume repletion for large-volume diuresis; activated charcoal to prevent further absorption (important with enteric-coated aspirin)
• Sodium bicarbonate to keep blood pH 7.5-7.55 and urine pH above 8; alkalinisation increases excretion
• Haemodialysis if measures fail, deterioration, or plasma salicylate above 1000 mg/mL
(d)
Consider in any young child with coma, convulsions or cardiovascular collapse; Reye's syndrome risk in viral infections in children under 12; monitoring of acid-base status implied

(a)
A barbiturate (acidic drugs such as phenobarbital, pentobarbital)
(b)
• Barbiturates prolong GABA-gated chloride channel opening and at high concentrations act directly (GABA-mimetic), causing marked CNS depression
• Depression of the medullary respiratory centres is the usual cause of death; also loss of brainstem vasomotor control and myocardial depression
(c)
• Treatment: support respiration and circulation; alkalinise the urine and promote diuresis (acidic drugs are excreted faster in alkaline urine); haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis
• No medication against barbiturate overdose; flumazenil is not effective against barbiturates
• Overdose can also cause renal failure and cardiovascular collapse
(d)
• Narrow safety margin and strong physiological dependence on long-term use; drugs with quick onset are most abused
• Combined alcohol or other CNS depressants add to toxicity; elderly and those with limited hepatic function need reduced dosage
• Contraindicated in patients with porphyria
• Withdrawal: increased anxiety, insomnia, CNS excitability and convulsions; long half-life drugs give the mildest withdrawal
questions.question:
A person is brought in comatose after taking a large amount of an acidic sedative-hypnotic, with severe respiratory depression, hypotension and diminished reflexes.
(a) Identify the class of the offending drug.
(b) Explain the mechanism of toxicity and the usual cause of death.
(c) State the management and whether a specific antidote exists.

A patient taking a warfarin anticoagulant is given a sedative for insomnia and then also drinks alcohol.
(a) Identify the sedative implicated in the interaction and the type of interaction.
(b) Explain the mechanisms, including alcohol and enzyme effects.
(c) Predict the clinical outcome.
(d) State how to manage or avoid it.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Chloral hydrate: the only sedative noted with a clinically important protein-binding interaction (displaces warfarin from plasma proteins) - a pharmacokinetic interaction
(b)
• Chloral hydrate displaces warfarin from plasma protein binding sites; it undergoes extensive biotransformation
• Alcohol and other CNS depressants (narcotics) add to sedative effects of benzodiazepines, barbiturates and zolpidem/zaleplon - a pharmacodynamic additive effect
• Barbiturates (phenobarbital) and meprobamate induce liver enzymes and cause autometabolism; benzodiazepines have few significant interactions despite 60-95% protein binding
(c)
• Increased effect of warfarin is implied by displacement
• Alcohol with benzodiazepines greatly reduces the margin of safety; respiratory support may be needed in toxicity when taken with another CNS depressant
(d)
• Avoid combination of chloral hydrate and warfarin; chloral hydrate is used mainly in children, the elderly and when other drugs fail
• Avoid alcohol, narcotics, over-the-counter antihistamines and anticholinergics with benzodiazepines
• Avoid combining anxiolytic drugs

(a)
• Three shared properties of narcotic analgesics: pain relief; withdrawal signs when stopped after chronic use; suppression of withdrawal of chronic morphine administration (so they can substitute for each other)
• Physical dependence is an automatic consequence of long-term use; tolerance is the loss of pain-relieving effect needing larger doses
• Dose escalation occurs with long-term use; tolerance is not considered a problem by most pain specialists in chronic pain
(b)
• Short-term: euphoria, mental clouding, drowsiness, apathy, reduced heart rate and BP, constipation, miosis, nausea, vomiting, dysphoria, itching, increased pain sensitivity once effects wear off
• Less common: confusion, hallucinations, delirium, hypothermia, bradycardia, tachycardia, raised intracranial pressure
• Respiratory depression and sedation are notable adverse effects
(c)
• Tolerant users given more than their normal dose may be 'on the nod', a semiconscious sleep
• Withdrawal appears when the drug is abruptly stopped or the dose reduced
(d)
• Methadone is used as a weaning drug for opioids or heroin and for maintenance
• Naloxone treats overdose; nalorphine and naltrexone are antagonists
• Opioids are controlled drugs (Schedule II/III)
• Codeine is very rarely abused because analgesia is mild and side effects such as convulsions are marked
questions.question:
A. Describe tolerance, dependence and adverse effects of opioid analgesics.
(a) Classify the effects and give the mechanisms with examples.
(b) State the short-term and less common effects.
(c) State how they are recognised.

A. Compare tricyclic antidepressants and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
(a) State the classification, mechanism of action and pharmacokinetics of each.
(b) State the pharmacological actions.
(c) State the therapeutic uses and adverse effects.
(d) Distinguish the two groups from each other.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• TCAs: imipramine, desipramine, amitriptyline, nortriptyline, clomipramine (related to phenothiazines, first made 1949); SSRIs: fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram, sertraline
• TCAs block noradrenaline and 5-HT uptake by competing for the amine transporter site, with little effect on dopamine uptake; SSRIs selectively block 5-HT reuptake
• TCA PK: rapid absorption, 90-95% albumin bound, volume 10-50 L/kg, hepatic N-demethylation and hydroxylation, active metabolites, half-life 10-80 h; SSRI half-life 18-24 h (fluoxetine 24-96 h)
(b)
• TCAs also block muscarinic, histamine and 5-HT receptors; antimuscarinic effects do not contribute to antidepressant effect
• Both show a 2-4 week delay before therapeutic effect
(c)
• TCA uses: depression (still widely used), neuropathic pain, enuresis, chronic pain; SSRI uses: depression, anxiety, OCD
• TCA adverse effects: sedation, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, postural hypotension, QT prolongation, sudden cardiac death risk
• SSRI adverse effects: nausea, anorexia, insomnia, loss of libido, failure of orgasm
(d)
• SSRIs have fewer anticholinergic effects, are safer in overdose, and cause no cheese reaction
• SSRIs are as effective as TCAs in moderate depression but probably less effective in severe depression
• TCAs are dangerous in overdose; haemodialysis is ineffective
• Paroxetine and fluoxetine inhibit CYP2D6 and are not combined with TCAs

(a)
• Symptomatic: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, tacrine, rivastigmine, galantamine) and NMDA receptor antagonist (memantine); disease-modifying approaches; other therapies
• AChE inhibitors reduce acetylcholine breakdown within the CNS, raising its concentration and improving cholinergic transmission; they must cross the blood-brain barrier
• Memantine is an NMDA receptor antagonist that prevents excitotoxicity from overstimulation of glutamate receptors
(b)
• AChE inhibitors: more beneficial in early stages; galantamine (from daffodils or snowdrop bulbs) and rivastigmine for mild to moderate dementia
• Donepezil has shown benefits in behaviour and cognition, though there is no proof it slows progression; tacrine was the first approved drug in 1993
• Memantine can slow memory loss, even with moderate to severe cognitive loss
(c)
• AChE inhibitors: anorexia, muscle cramps, diarrhoea; with long-term use bradycardia, hypotension, hypersecretion, bronchoconstriction, GI hypermotility, decreased intraocular pressure
• Memantine is well tolerated with few dose-related effects, including confusion and restlessness
(d)
• Tacrine is no longer used clinically because of extreme toxicity
• None of the current agents alter the underlying neurodegenerative process
• Psychotic symptoms in later stages are treated with antidepressants, anti-anxiety medicine and antipsychotics

A. Describe the drugs used in Alzheimer disease as a therapeutic group.

A young child has acute diarrhoea. A clinician is choosing between a weak opioid agonist combined with atropine and another opioid acting on the gut wall.
(a) Select the drug or class and justify it.
(b) State the mechanism and expected pharmacodynamic effect.
(c) Name the drug to avoid or use with strict dosing, and why.
(d) State the alternative agent and the monitoring required.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Loperamide (Imodium) is used in acute and chronic diarrhoea
(b)
• Loperamide has a methadone-like structure on a piperidine nitrogen and binds opiate receptors in the gut wall
• Opioids historically used for constipating action (opium was valued for it)
(c)
• Diphenoxylate is a weak opioid agonist combined with atropine; paediatric use has strict dosing guidelines because of opioid intoxication and death
• Codeine is also used in anti-diarrhoeal preparations; very rarely abused but severe side effects such as convulsions can occur
(d)
• Alternative: diphenoxylate with atropine in older patients with strict dosing
• Monitoring for opioid toxicity (drowsiness, respiratory depression, miosis)

(a)
Amantadine, the only drug licensed as an antidyskinetic in advanced disease; daily doses 100-400 mg
(b)
Possible actions: facilitating presynaptic dopamine release, blocking dopamine reuptake, an anticholinergic (nicotinic antagonist) effect and weak NMDA receptor antagonism
(c)
• Antimuscarinics (trihexyphenidyl, orphenadrine) reduce tremor but not bradykinesia and cause constipation, urinary retention, cognitive impairment and toxic confusion
• Ergot-derived cabergoline risks pleuropulmonary fibrosis and is no longer routinely used; tolcapone is hepatotoxic
• Amantadine side effects: toxic confusional state, peripheral and corneal oedema, livedo reticularis, more frequent at higher doses
(d)
• Alternatives: COMT inhibitors (entacapone preferred, may exacerbate dyskinesia), MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline 5 or 10 mg daily, rasagiline), non-ergot dopamine agonists (ropinirole, pramipexole, rotigotine), apomorphine (45-60 min effect), deep brain stimulation
• Monitoring: no routine monitoring for amantadine but attention to sudden visual changes; strict liver monitoring for tolcapone
questions.question:
A patient with advanced Parkinson disease on levodopa has major motor fluctuations and involuntary movements (dyskinesia).
(a) Select the drug or class and justify it.
(b) State the mechanism and expected pharmacodynamic effect.
(c) Name drugs to avoid or use with caution and why.
(d) State alternative agents and monitoring.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Cardiac glycoside from Digitalis lanata/purpurea: aglycone (steroid nucleus with lactone ring at C-17) plus sugars at C-3; activity resides in the aglycone, sugars modify solubility and permeability
• Inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase → rise in intracellular Na+ → reduced Ca2+ expulsion by the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger → more free Ca2+ for actin-myosin interaction → increased contractile force; also stimulates vagal action
• PK: well absorbed orally; about 10% of people have gut bacteria that inactivate it; widely distributed including CNS; not extensively metabolised; about two thirds excreted unchanged by kidneys; half-life 36-40 hours with normal renal function; once-daily tablet
(b)
• Actions: positive inotropic (without increased oxygen consumption), negative chronotropic, negative dromotropic (slower AV node conduction), shortened systole and prolonged diastole; diuresis only through improved circulation
• Uses: congestive heart failure (low-output), paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, atrial flutter and fibrillation (slows ventricular rate), dilated heart, heart failure symptomatic despite diuretics and ACE inhibitor
(c)
• Adverse effects: anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea; headache, fatigue, blurred vision, loss of colour perception, disorientation, hallucinations in the elderly; rarely gynaecomastia
• Cautions: hypokalaemia, renal impairment, hypothyroidism, myocarditis, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia, pulmonary disease, ventricular fibrillation, pregnancy
• Interactions: enhanced toxicity with amiodarone, quinidine, verapamil, tetracyclines, erythromycin and K+-lowering diuretics/corticosteroids; reduced effect with phenytoin, phenobarbitone, antacids, sucralfate, neomycin, cholestyramine
(d)
• Narrow therapeutic index: minor changes in bioavailability can cause serious toxicity or loss of effect; antibiotics can raise levels in patients whose gut bacteria inactivate digoxin
• Toxic concentrations shorten the action potential and refractory period → increased excitability → ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation
• Extracardiac effects need only dose reduction; severe intoxication is treated with digitalis antibodies (Fab fragments)
• Monitoring includes serum digoxin level (0.5-2 ng/mL) and electrolytes, especially potassium
questions.question:
A. Describe the pharmacology of digoxin.
(a) State its source, class, mechanism of action and pharmacokinetics.
(b) State its pharmacological actions and therapeutic uses.
(c) State its adverse effects, contraindications or cautions and interactions.
(d) Explain the basis of its toxicity and the principle of management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Tolerance: decreased pharmacological effect on repeated administration, developing over time
• Dependence: adaptive state from repeated administration, with tolerance and withdrawal symptoms on stopping that propel relapse; use becomes compulsive
• Physical dependence: characteristic withdrawal syndromes (myalgia, tremors, sweating, convulsions), from resetting of homeostatic mechanisms; psychological dependence: emotional distress, craving and compulsive seeking after stopping
• Addiction: persistent use despite harm, combining mental and physical dependence with uncontrollable seeking behaviour
(b)
• Dependence is marked by strong compulsion, difficulty controlling use, withdrawal, tolerance, and neglect of other pleasures
• Risk factors: host variables (gene polymorphisms in enzymes and receptors, inherited susceptibility) and environmental variables (societal norms, peer pressure)
(c)
• CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids) show physical dependence; stimulants (heroin, amphetamine, cocaine) more psychological dependence
• Opioids and cocaine are strong reinforcers, benzodiazepines weak; craving is triggered by environmental cues or drug paraphernalia
• Dependence-producing drugs: anaesthetics (propofol, ketamine), sedatives, opioids, psychostimulants, hallucinogens (LSD, mescaline, PCP), nicotine, ethanol, GHB, MDMA
(d)
• The appearance of a withdrawal syndrome on termination is the only actual evidence of physical dependence
• Patients taking medicine for proper indications at correct doses may still show tolerance and withdrawal if it is stopped abruptly rather than gradually
• Common mechanism: reward through the mesolimbic dopaminergic pathway, raising dopamine in the nucleus accumbens
questions.question:
A. Describe the principles of tolerance, dependence and addiction.
(a) Define tolerance, physical dependence, psychological dependence and addiction.
(b) State the signs of dependence and risk factors.
(c) Relate these to the drugs given as examples.
(d) Explain the clinical significance and limitation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Alzheimer disease features loss of cortical and subcortical cholinergic neurons, atrophy of cerebral cortex, beginning in the hippocampus and spreading
• Hallmarks: amyloid plaques (beta-amyloid) outside neurons and neurofibrillary tangles (hyperphosphorylated tau) inside neurons
• Three hypotheses: amyloid cascade, tau, cholinergic
(b)
• Amyloid cascade: excess A-beta from APP, presenilin 1 and 2 mutations or metabolic failure, causing inflammation, free radical formation and plaques
• Tau: hyperphosphorylated tau detaches from microtubules and forms tangles, so the neuron's transport system collapses
• Cholinergic: acetylcholine biosynthesis falls in the presence of plaques and tangles, leading to neuron loss
(c)
• Cholinergic loss is the target of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine); NMDA overstimulation (excitotoxicity) is the target of memantine
• Disease-modifying approaches inhibit amyloid formation, A-beta aggregation, and tau phosphorylation
• Risk factors: age, genetics, lifestyle, head trauma, depression, Down syndrome, environmental toxins
(d)
• Current treatment is palliative with modest short-term benefit and none alters the underlying neurodegeneration
• Disease is treatable but incurable
• Other options: ginkgo biloba, oestrogen, aspirin, lifestyle changes and antipsychotics, antidepressants and anxiolytics in later stages
questions.question:
A. Describe the pathogenic hypotheses of Alzheimer disease and their link to drug therapy.
(a) State the hallmarks and the three hypotheses.
(b) State the cellular events in each hypothesis.
(c) Relate these to drug examples given.
(d) Explain the clinical significance and limitation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Non-selective: salicylates, propionic acids (ibuprofen, naproxen), fenamates, oxicams, ketorolac, indomethacin, sulindac, phenylbutazone; preferential COX-2: nimesulide, meloxicam, nabumetone, diclofenac, aceclofenac; selective COX-2: celecoxib, etoricoxib, parecoxib
• NSAIDs inhibit COX, reducing PGs, PGI2 and TXA2; they do not inhibit lipoxygenase, so leukotrienes are not suppressed; most inhibit COX-1 and COX-2 reversibly, aspirin irreversibly
• Actions: analgesia, antipyresis (PGE2 in hypothalamus), anti-inflammation, antiplatelet effect
(b)
• Aspirin: well absorbed, protein bound, hydrolysed to salicylate, half-life 3-6 h rising to 15-30 h with dose; non-aspirin NSAIDs' duration relates to drug disposition
• Paracetamol (analgesic-antipyretic with poor anti-inflammatory action) is a weak COX inhibitor, with COX-3 in brain proposed as its site
(c)
• Uses: inflammatory pain (arthritis), mild-moderate pain, fever, dysmenorrhoea, antiplatelet use for aspirin; they treat symptoms but do not affect disease progression
• Adverse effects: gastric damage and bleeding, platelet inhibition, renal blood flow and Na+/water retention, delayed labour, asthma and anaphylactoid reactions, premature closure of fetal ductus arteriosus
• No physical dependence and no abuse liability
(d)
• COX-1 is constitutive and housekeeping (gastric cytoprotection, platelets, renal flow); COX-2 is inducible at inflammation sites and also constitutive in kidney and brain
• Selective COX-2 inhibitors are relatively safer for the stomach; rofecoxib and valdecoxib are noted (rofecoxib withdrawn)
• Selective inhibitors do not inhibit COX-1 platelet TXA2, so they lack the aspirin antiplatelet effect (implied by the COX-1 role)
• Paracetamol is practically free of gastric toxicity
questions.question:
A. Compare non-selective and selective cyclooxygenase inhibitors.
(a) State the classification, mechanism of action and pharmacological actions.
(b) State the pharmacokinetic features given.
(c) State the therapeutic uses and adverse effects.
(d) Distinguish the groups from each other.

questions.answerText:
(a)
A selective COX-2 inhibitor such as celecoxib or etoricoxib, which is relatively safer for the stomach
(b)
• COX-2 is inducible at inflammatory sites and mediates analgesic, antipyretic and anti-inflammatory actions, while COX-1 produces gastroprotective prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2)
• Selective COX-2 inhibition spares COX-1, so there is less loss of mucus and bicarbonate secretion and less mucosal erosion
(c)
• Avoid aspirin and non-selective NSAIDs: peptic ulcer is a contraindication; COX-1 inhibition causes gastric erosion, ulceration, blood loss
• Avoid in chronic kidney disease or asthma-prone patients because of renal and anaphylactoid reactions
(d)
• Alternative: paracetamol, practically free of gastric toxicity, though with poor anti-inflammatory action
• Monitor for GI bleeding, renal function (Na+ and water retention) and bleeding time
questions.question:
An older patient with osteoarthritis has a history of peptic ulcer disease and needs an anti-inflammatory analgesic.
(a) Select the drug class and justify it.
(b) State the mechanism and expected pharmacodynamic effect.
(c) Name drugs to avoid and why.
(d) State the alternative agent and the monitoring required.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Inhaled gases (nitrous oxide, xenon), volatile liquids (halothane, isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane), IV agents (propofol, thiopental, ketamine), opioid and benzodiazepine adjuncts
• Propofol enhances GABA-mediated inhibition; inhalational agents are small lipid-soluble molecules crossing alveolar membranes, potency expressed as minimum alveolar concentration (MAC)
• General anaesthesia produces unconsciousness, amnesia, analgesia with or without muscle relaxation, like a medically induced controlled coma
(b)
• Stage 1 induction; stage 2 excitement (delirium, erratic breathing, risk of choking); stage 3 surgical (muscles relax, breathing depressed); stage 4 overdose (medullary suppression, respiratory and cardiovascular collapse)
• Pre-, intra- and post-operative phases; NPO fasting times (clear liquids 2 h, light meal 6 h, full meal 8 h)
(c)
• Nitrous oxide 50:50 with oxygen as labour analgesic; sevoflurane: cough, nausea, shivering; propofol: hypotension, apnoea
• Muscle relaxants: depolarising (suxamethonium) and non-depolarising (alcuronium, vecuronium) need mechanical ventilation and reversal with neostigmine only for non-depolarising
• Premedication: reduces anxiety, secretions, gastric volume and nausea
(d)
• Malignant hyperthermia: lethal temperature rise, hypercarbia, acidosis, hyperkalaemia; common events: nausea, vomiting, sore throat, emergence delirium in children
• Withhold on the morning of surgery: anticoagulants, metformin, MAO inhibitors, ACE inhibitors; continue beta blockers in high-risk patients
• Neostigmine must not be used with suxamethonium
• General anaesthesia is preferred for long procedures, significant blood loss, chest operations, and young patients
questions.question:
A. Describe the general anaesthetics and adjuncts as a therapeutic group.
(a) Classify the agents and give the mechanism of each group.
(b) State the stages of anaesthesia and the phases of care.
(c) Compare the groups by use and adverse effects.
(d) State the precautions.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Triptans (5-HT1B/1D agonists, e.g. sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan); oral sumatriptan undergoes substantial pre-systemic hepatic metabolism
(b)
• Oral bioavailability of sumatriptan is only 14%, the lowest of the triptans; subcutaneous bioavailability is about 97%
• Oral peak plasma concentration is reached within 1-2 hours; sumatriptan may be given subcutaneously, by mouth or as a nasal spray
• Rizatriptan is given orally; zolmitriptan orally or intranasally
(c)
• Subcutaneous or nasal routes bypass first-pass loss and give more reliable effect in acute attacks
• Triptans are not intended for prophylaxis of migraine
questions.question:
A patient with severe acute migraine is considering a triptan by mouth, by nasal spray or by injection under the skin, because oral dosing seems to work poorly.
(a) Identify the drug class and the pharmacokinetic process that limits oral use.
(b) Explain the effect of route on onset, bioavailability and accumulation.
(c) Name the clinical consequence.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Sodium valproate is broad-spectrum and of particular value in idiopathic generalised epilepsies, but it is more teratogenic than other commonly used AEDs and should be avoided in women of childbearing age
(b)
• Acts on voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels and on GABA turnover
• Treatment aim: control seizures with one drug at the lowest effective dose with fewest side effects
(c)
• Valproate adverse effects: nausea, diarrhoea, weight gain, alopecia, skin rash, thrombocytopenia
• Carbamazepine should be avoided in absence and myoclonic seizures
(d)
• Alternatives for generalised tonic-clonic seizures: lamotrigine, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine (with levetiracetam, clobazam, topiramate as adjuncts); for myoclonic: levetiracetam, clonazepam, topiramate, piracetam
• Therapeutic drug monitoring for valproate only for suspected toxicity, deterioration in control, adherence or interactions; abrupt withdrawal must be avoided (200-400 mg every 2-4 weeks)
questions.question:
A woman of childbearing age has idiopathic generalised epilepsy and needs long-term antiepileptic therapy.
(a) Identify the broad-spectrum drug that is effective in idiopathic generalised epilepsy and the reason it is a problem in this patient.
(b) State the mechanism and expected pharmacodynamic effect of that drug.
(c) Name the drug to avoid and its adverse effects.
(d) State alternative agents and monitoring.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Absorption interference by dietary protein and a short duration of effect leading to end-of-dose wearing-off
(b)
• Protein diet can critically interfere with levodopa absorption, so IR levodopa is taken 30 minutes before food
• Immediate-release bioavailability is 90-100%; controlled-release bioavailability is 60-70%
• CR preparations (Sinemet CR 50/200, Half Sinemet CR 25/100; Madopar CR) simplify regimens, relieve nocturnal akinesia and, co-prescribed with IR levodopa by day, relieve end-of-dose deterioration
(c)
• IR levodopa starts at 50 mg three times daily and is titrated to a maximum of 600 mg/day
• Entacapone 200 mg is given with each levodopa dose (up to 10 doses/day) to increase levodopa reaching the CNS by peripheral COMT inhibition
• Patient diaries relating bradykinesia and dyskinesia to drug and food intake are helpful
(d)
Wearing-off and dyskinesia typically appear after years of treatment, relating to disease duration
questions.question:
A patient with Parkinson disease on immediate-release levodopa complains that the effect wears off before the next dose, and eats a high-protein diet. A controlled-release form is considered.
(a) Identify the pharmacokinetic problem.
(b) Explain the effect of formulation and food on absorption, onset, duration and bioavailability.
(c) State the dose and dosing adjustments with monitoring.
(d) Name the clinical consequence.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids; COX forms prostanoids, lipoxygenase forms leukotrienes, epoxygenases form EETs
• Prostanoids are 20-carbon fatty acid derivatives: prostaglandins, prostacyclin (PGI2) and thromboxane A2 (TXA2)
• Prostaglandins sensitise peripheral nociceptors to pain; NSAIDs reduce or reverse this and also suppress prostanoid formation in spinal cord and brain
(b)
• COX-1: constitutive, non-inducible, widely distributed (GIT, platelets, vascular smooth muscle, renal medulla); produces gastroprotective PGs and TXA2
• COX-2: inducible by cytokines at inflammation sites; constitutive in kidney and neurons; produces PGI2 in blood vessels
• COX-3: recently identified in brain; proposed site of paracetamol action
(c)
• PGE2: vasodilatation, decreased gastric acid, increased mucus, natriuresis, pyrogenic effect, uterine contraction; TXA2: vasoconstriction, platelet aggregation; PGI2: vasodilatation, anti-aggregatory
• Fever: pyrogens induce hypothalamic PGE2 raising the set point; NSAIDs reset it, causing vasodilatation and heat loss
• Inhibition of COX-1 largely accounts for GI adverse effects; COX-2 inhibition mediates analgesia and anti-inflammatory effect
(d)
• Inhibition of COX with diversion of arachidonic acid to leukotrienes may explain aspirin-induced asthma (no proof)
• COX-2 inhibitors showed some positive effects in Alzheimer disease; COX-2 may be involved in neurodegeneration
• Anti-inflammatory potency roughly matches COX-2 inhibition potency
questions.question:
A. Describe prostanoid synthesis and the cyclooxygenase isoforms as the basis of NSAID action.
(a) State the pathway from arachidonic acid and the products.
(b) State the properties and distribution of COX-1, COX-2 and COX-3.
(c) Relate these to the actions of the prostanoids and to NSAID effects.
(d) Explain the clinical significance and limitation.

A. Compare ergot alkaloids and triptans in migraine.
(a) State the classification, mechanism of action and pharmacological actions.
(b) State the pharmacokinetics of each.
(c) State the therapeutic uses and adverse effects.
(d) Distinguish the two groups from each other.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Ergot alkaloids: ergotamine, ergonovine, methysergide (LSD is an ergot derivative); triptans (5-HT1 agonists): sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan; lasmiditan is a 5-HT1F agonist
• Ergots act on prejunctional neuronal 5-HT receptors (5-HT1B/1D) as partial agonists and are potent vasoconstrictors; triptans stimulate 5-HT1B/1D receptors in the cranial circulation, inhibit neuronal firing and block neurogenic plasma extravasation in dura mater
• Both prevent vasodilation and stretching of pain nerve endings; triptans also reduce nausea and vomiting
(b)
• Ergotamine: oral, sublingual, rectal, inhaler; low oral levels from first-pass; liver metabolism with 90% of metabolites in bile; plasma half-life about 2 h but vasoconstriction lasts 24 h or more
• Sumatriptan: peak 1-2 h orally, oral bioavailability 14%, subcutaneous about 97%; rizatriptan oral; zolmitriptan oral or intranasal
(c)
• Ergots: acute migraine, restricted to frequent moderate or infrequent severe attacks; not analgesic for other conditions; adverse effects diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, weakness, prolonged vasospasm
• Triptans: first-line for acute severe migraine and cluster headache (sumatriptan), not for prophylaxis; vasoconstriction in coronary and pulmonary beds
• Neither group should be combined with serotonergic drugs
(d)
• Triptans are more selective than ergot alkaloids
• Ergot vasoconstriction is cumulative and long-lasting
• Ergot is most effective early in an attack; triptans are first-line
• Propranolol potentiates the vasoconstriction of both groups

(a)
• Ramipril, an ACE inhibitor; the prodrug is converted to the active metabolite ramiprilat by carboxylesterase 1
• ACE inhibitors are grouped as thiol-containing (captopril), dicarboxyl-containing (enalapril, lisinopril, benazepril, quinapril, ramipril) and phosphorus-containing (fosinopril)
(b)
• ACE is a zinc-containing enzyme; ACE inhibitors block conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II (a potent vasoconstrictor and stimulator of aldosterone secretion)
• Less angiotensin II → relaxation of arteriolar smooth muscle → lower total peripheral resistance → lower BP
• They also decrease the breakdown of bradykinin; this effect on bradykinin is responsible for the dry cough
(c)
• Use: treatment of hypertension
• Adverse effects: shakiness, dry cough, dizziness and light-headedness from low BP, fatigue, early mouth dryness, nausea, fainting, chest pain, neutropenia (fever, chills, persistent sore throat), impotence, hyperkalaemia
• Serious: allergic reaction/angioedema (rash, swelling of face, mouth, tongue or throat); in extreme cases potentially fatal liver problems
(d)
• Contraindicated in renovascular disease, severe renal impairment (especially one kidney or bilateral renal artery stenosis), volume depletion, history of angioedema on an ACE inhibitor, pregnancy and hypotension
• Ramiprilat half-life is variable (3-16 hours) and prolonged by heart, liver and kidney failure
• Potassium monitoring is essential because of hyperkalaemia
questions.question:
A hypertensive patient is started on an oral prodrug whose active metabolite is formed by carboxylesterase 1 and is mostly excreted by the kidneys. After some days the patient complains of a dry cough and dizziness.
(a) Identify the drug and its class, and state how this class is divided structurally.
(b) State the mechanism of action at the molecular target and explain why the cough occurs.
(c) State the therapeutic use and the key adverse effects.
(d) State the contraindications and precautions.

A. Describe the renal handling of sodium, water and urate and the processes of renal function.
(a) State the four basic processes of renal function and the endocrine and regulatory functions of the kidney.
(b) State sodium handling by each nephron segment and the site of action of each diuretic class.
(c) Relate these to examples of drugs affecting the process.
(d) Explain the clinical significance and limitation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Four basic processes: glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption, tubular secretion, urinary excretion
• Kidneys regulate water and electrolyte balance, arterial BP (renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system), acid-base balance; they produce renin, erythropoietin and 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol; gluconeogenesis is the 4th function
(b)
• Proximal tubule reabsorbs about 67% of Na+ (carbonic anhydrase inhibitors early PCT, osmotic diuretics late PCT); thick ascending limb 25-30% (loop diuretics)
• Distal convoluted tubule 3-5% (thiazides at early DCT); collecting duct 3-5% (K+-sparing diuretics: spironolactone, amiloride, triamterene)
• Principal cells: aldosterone raises Na+ reabsorption through epithelial Na+ channels and K+ secretion; ADH raises water reabsorption
(c)
• Acetazolamide blocks carbonic anhydrase → less H+ secretion and Na+ reabsorption → diuresis and acidosis; mannitol and urea are osmotic diuretics
• Spironolactone is an aldosterone receptor antagonist (anti-androgenic effects, contraindicated in males); amiloride/triamterene block ENaC → hyperkalaemia and acidosis
• Uric acid: most is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, a small amount secreted; probenecid and sulfinpyrazone inhibit urate reabsorption, allopurinol inhibits synthesis; thiazides reduce urate excretion
• SGLT-2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin) block proximal tubule glucose reabsorption
(d)
• Loop diuretics: oedema in cardiac, hepatic, renal disease, pulmonary oedema, heart failure, hypercalcaemia, hyperkalaemia; adverse effects: volume depletion, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, ototoxicity
• Erythropoietin falls in renal disease → anaemia of chronic renal disease
• Spironolactone improves survival in advanced heart, kidney or liver failure; limitation: hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis

questions.question:
A patient with hypertension on a thiazide diuretic starts taking an NSAID regularly for joint pain.
(a) Identify the type of interaction.
(b) Explain the mechanism involving prostaglandins and the kidney.
(c) Predict the clinical outcome.
(d) State how to manage or avoid it.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pharmacodynamic interaction: NSAIDs blunt the blood-pressure-lowering effect of thiazides
(b)
• PGE2 and PGI2 maintain renal blood flow; NSAIDs impair COX-dependent renal blood flow and reduce glomerular filtration rate
• Na+ and water retention follow juxtaglomerular COX-2 (probably COX-1) inhibition, opposing diuretic-driven BP lowering
(c)
• Reduced antihypertensive effect, fluid retention, worsening renal insufficiency in susceptible patients
• Thiazides themselves cause hypokalaemia, hyperuricaemia and may aggravate diabetes
(d)
• Avoid or monitor concomitant NSAIDs with thiazide treatment; concomitant use of thiazides with ACE inhibitors can be beneficial
• Paracetamol is a very weak COX inhibitor and practically free of gastric and renal effects

(a)
• Neurochemical effects of antidepressants are fast (monoamine uptake inhibition, MAO inhibition) but clinical benefit is delayed by weeks
• Clinical effect is usually measured by subjective rating scales such as the 17-item Hamilton scale; trials show weak effects after large placebo responses
(b)
• Beta-1 and alpha-2 adrenoceptors are downregulated after chronic antidepressant treatment (and ECT); relevance is unclear because beta blockers are not antidepressant
• SSRIs: raised 5-HT activates somatodendritic 5-HT1A autoreceptors reducing release; these desensitise with chronic treatment, explaining slow onset
• Alpha-2 antagonists enhance noradrenaline release and indirectly 5-HT release via alpha-1 excitation of raphe neurons and removal of presynaptic inhibition
• Intracellular signalling: activation of the transcription factor CREB, Fos and NF-kB, and hippocampal neurogenesis may account for slow onset
(c)
• Pindolol (beta blocker with 5-HT1A affinity) combined with SSRIs to speed onset; mirtazapine and mianserin block alpha-2 receptors
• Combined 5-HT1A antagonist/SSRI drugs were not effective in man, perhaps by blocking postsynaptic receptors too
• Venlafaxine efficacy increases with dose as weak noradrenaline reuptake inhibition adds to 5-HT uptake inhibition
(d)
• No animal condition corresponds to inherited human depression; existing models are of questionable similarity
• 30-40% of patients show no improvement, possibly genetic
• Non-drug therapies (ECT, deep brain stimulation, vagus stimulation) have a more rapid onset
questions.question:
A. Describe the mechanisms proposed for the delayed onset of antidepressant action.
(a) State the neurochemical effects that occur rapidly and the clinical lag.
(b) State the adaptive changes proposed.
(c) Relate these to examples of drugs.
(d) Explain the clinical significance and limitations.

A patient with hallucinations, delusions and disorganised speech is started on a first-generation butyrophenone or phenothiazine. After some weeks the patient develops restlessness, slow movements with tremor and rigidity, and breast secretion with missed periods.
(a) Identify the drug class and give examples.
(b) State the mechanism of action and explain the movement and endocrine effects.
(c) State the therapeutic uses and other key adverse effects.
(d) State the contraindications, precautions and measures for the movement disorders.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Typical (first-generation) antipsychotics: phenothiazines (chlorpromazine), butyrophenones (haloperidol), thioxanthenes (flupentixol); fluphenazine and pimozide are other examples
(b)
• Predominantly antagonise brain dopamine D2 receptors; also block muscarinic, histamine and alpha-adrenergic receptors
• Extrapyramidal effects (akathisia, parkinsonism, acute dystonia, tardive dyskinesia) arise from D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway (dopamine/acetylcholine imbalance); higher D2 potency gives greater EPS
• D2 blockade in the tuberohypophyseal pathway raises prolactin → gynaecomastia, galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, sexual dysfunction or infertility
(c)
• Uses: psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia, antiemetic (D2 block in chemoreceptor trigger zone), intractable hiccups (chlorpromazine), pimozide for Tourette syndrome; no analgesic effect
• Other effects: dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, loss of accommodation (anticholinergic); orthostatic hypotension, sexual dysfunction (alpha-1); sedation, weight gain (H1); QT prolongation; lowered seizure threshold
(d)
• Acute dystonia is high risk in the first few weeks, in the young and antipsychotic-naive; tardive dyskinesia develops after months or years in 20-40% and may be irreversible
• Antimuscarinic drugs can be used for agents with high EPS; increased cerebrovascular events and mortality in dementia patients
• Elderly have a 5-fold greater risk of tardive dyskinesia

questions.question:
A patient with hypertension also has a history of calcium kidney stones from idiopathic hypercalciuria.
(a) Select the drug class and justify it.
(b) State the mechanism and expected pharmacodynamic effect on urinary electrolytes and BP.
(c) Name the conditions and drugs to avoid or use with caution and why.
(d) State the alternative agent and the monitoring required.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Thiazide diuretics (for example hydrochlorothiazide): first-line for hypertension and first-line for idiopathic hypercalciuria to reduce calcium stone formation
(b)
• Inhibit the Na+-Cl- co-transporter on the luminal membrane of the early distal convoluted tubule (binding the Cl- site), which accounts for 3-5% of Na+ reabsorption
• Raised Na+ and Cl- delivery to the late distal tubule promotes K+ excretion; thiazides increase urinary Na+, K+, Cl- but decrease urinary calcium (increase Ca2+ reabsorption)
• BP effect: first through diuresis and volume regulation; later lower peripheral resistance from vascular remodelling
(c)
• Adverse effects: hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia, hyperuricaemia (gout), aggravated diabetes mellitus, photosensitivity, reduced libido, GIT disturbance
• NSAIDs reduce the BP-lowering effect; hypokalaemia raises digoxin toxicity; thiazides reduce uric acid excretion by sharing the organic anion transporter with urate
• Thiazides tend to potentiate dihydropyridine CCBs; concomitant ACE inhibitors can be beneficial
(d)
• Alternative: loop diuretics (inhibit Na+-K+-2Cl- co-transporter in thick ascending limb) for severe hypertension; K+-sparing diuretics (amiloride, triamterene) as adjuncts
• Monitoring: potassium, magnesium, sodium, calcium, uric acid and glucose

(a)
Calcium channel blockers; nifedipine (a dihydropyridine) is the example with grapefruit warning for extended-release forms
(b)
• Block voltage-sensitive L-type calcium channels, reducing extracellular Ca2+ entry → relaxation of cardiac and vascular smooth muscle → vasodilatation and lower BP; they also dilate coronary vessels
• Verapamil is relatively cardioselective, dihydropyridines are relatively smooth-muscle selective, diltiazem is intermediate; nifedipine causes marked vasodilation with little cardiac depression, verapamil and diltiazem depress SA/AV nodes
(c)
• Uses: angina, hypertension, supraventricular arrhythmias (atrial flutter, fibrillation, paroxysmal SVT)
• Adverse effects: flushing, headache, dizziness, tachycardia, bradycardia, constipation, gingival hyperplasia and peripheral oedema
• Ankle oedema is due to a rise in intracapillary pressure from selective precapillary arteriolar dilatation, not sodium retention, and is relieved by bed rest
(d)
• Nifedipine is rapidly and fully absorbed, protein bound 92-98%, metabolised mainly by CYP3A4; 60-80% of dose appears in urine as inactive metabolites
• Extended-release forms are taken on an empty stomach and grapefruit or its juice must be avoided
• Short-acting forms (immediate-release nifedipine, nicardipine) should be avoided; amlodipine (half-life 30-50 h) allows once-daily dosing
• Pregnancy: use only when absolutely indicated; the drug enters breast milk
questions.question:
A patient with hypertension is treated with a drug that blocks L-type calcium channels, and the patient also drinks grapefruit juice while taking an extended-release preparation. The patient develops ankle swelling, headache and flushing.
(a) Identify the drug class and the example described.
(b) State the mechanism and the relative cardiac versus vascular selectivity of the examples.
(c) State the therapeutic uses and adverse effects, including the ankle swelling.
(d) State the pharmacokinetic and precaution points, including formulation and pregnancy.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Clozapine, the atypical antipsychotic with efficacy against negative symptoms and the drug ultimately used in refractory schizophrenia
(b)
• Predominant antagonism of 5-HT2A receptors with lesser D2 antagonism; 5-HT2A blockade increases striatal dopamine, so extrapyramidal effects are considerably less than with typical drugs
• Atypicals bind less avidly to D2 receptors in striatum and hypothalamus (less EPS and endocrine disturbance) and appear to improve cognitive function
(c)
• Agranulocytosis is common with clozapine, especially in the first 6 months
• High risk of new-onset diabetes and diabetic ketoacidosis with clozapine and olanzapine; weight gain
• Typical high-potency agents (haloperidol) carry high EPS; thioridazine causes severe orthostatic hypotension through alpha-1 blockade
(d)
• Alternatives: risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole (partial agonist at 5-HT2A and D2), ziprasidone (oral and injectable)
• Regular full blood count monitoring is essential; monitor glucose and weight; olanzapine weight gain, quetiapine and aripiprazole suicidality warning in children, ziprasidone and quetiapine QT prolongation
questions.question:
A patient with schizophrenia has not responded to other medications, and negative symptoms such as flat affect and lack of goal-directed activity remain.
(a) Select the drug and justify it.
(b) State the mechanism and expected pharmacodynamic effect.
(c) Name drugs or effects to avoid or be cautious about and why.
(d) State alternative agents and the monitoring required.

A child has brief episodes of blank staring lasting a few seconds with eyelid fluttering, after which normal activity resumes as if nothing had happened.
(a) Identify the seizure type and the drug of first choice.
(b) State the mechanism of action at the molecular target.
(c) State the dosing, therapeutic scope and key adverse effects.
(d) State the contraindications or precautions and the drug that must be avoided.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Typical absence (petit mal) seizure, seen almost exclusively in childhood and early adolescence; ethosuximide is the drug of first choice for generalised absence seizures
• Other first-line options for absence: clobazam and lamotrigine; adjuncts: clonazepam, sodium valproate, levetiracetam, topiramate, zonisamide
(b)
Ethosuximide blocks low-voltage-activated (T-type) calcium channels
(c)
• Initial dose 500 mg daily in two divided doses, increased by 250 mg every 5-7 days; absorption is complete and syrup and capsule bioavailability are equivalent
• It has no useful effect against any other seizure type; tolerance does not seem to be a problem
• Adverse effects: gastrointestinal symptoms early in therapy, behaviour disorders, anorexia, fatigue, sleep disturbances, headache
(d)
• Carbamazepine is not effective in absence and myoclonic seizures and may even be deleterious; barbiturates cannot be used for absence seizures
• Withdraw slowly (ethosuximide 125-250 mg every 2 weeks when changing drug, every 4 weeks for total withdrawal) to avoid rebound seizures

(a)
• Methyl is the optimal nitrogen substituent for agonist activity; bulky groups (propyl, allyl, cyclopropylmethyl) produce antagonists; quaternary ammonium derivatives lack analgesia
• N-phenethyl increases activity about 14-fold over morphine; secondary amine is much less active than tertiary
(b)
• Common features: tertiary nitrogen with small alkyl group, a quaternary carbon, a phenyl attached to it, and a 2-carbon spacer to the nitrogen
• The opioid receptor has an anionic site for the charged nitrogen, a cavity for the piperidine ring and a flat surface for the aromatic ring
(c)
• Conversion of 3-OH to 3-OCH3 (codeine) reduces activity to 15%; acetylation of 3- and 6-OH (heroin) increases potency 2-3 times by lipid solubility
• Naloxone and naltrexone are N-substituted antagonists; nalorphine is a mixed agonist-antagonist; etorphine is about 1000 times morphine (animal use); pentazocine is the only benzomorphan used clinically
• Pethidine (4-phenylpiperidine) is about 20% of morphine; fentanyl is 100 times meperidine; dextromethorphan is an NMDA antagonist in cough preparations
• Loperamide and diphenoxylate are antidiarrhoeal piperidines
(d)
• Small structural changes can alter activity dramatically, so derivatives with better bioavailability and lower addiction were sought
• Tramadol resembles codeine with rings B, D and E removed and has multiple mechanisms
• Methadone and propoxyphene: propoxyphene is mild with low addiction liability
• Open-chain analogues cannot yield antagonists
questions.question:
A. Describe structure-activity relationships among opioid analgesics.
(a) State the principle linking structure to potency and agonist or antagonist activity.
(b) State the structural features common to opioids.
(c) Relate these to the examples given.
(d) Explain the clinical significance and limitation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Aim: control seizures with one drug at the lowest effective dose and fewest side effects; therapy is long term (usually at least 3 years, sometimes life)
• Start slowly with a small dose to avoid early side effects that undermine confidence; a gradual introduction gives the same effect as rapid introduction for most drugs
• Phenytoin serum level-dose relationship is non-linear, so small dose changes may produce large serum changes
(b)
• Valproate is more teratogenic and avoided in women of childbearing age; TDM is useful in pregnant and elderly patients and the acutely unwell
• Newer AEDs (levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine as first-line exceptions) are second-line generally and better tolerated, not more effective
• Brand consistency is recommended; generic prescribing is controversial
(c)
• Therapeutic drug monitoring: poor control, sudden change, adherence, side effects, interactions; stable patients about once a year
• Rebound seizures follow abrupt withdrawal, greatest with barbiturates (phenobarbital, primidone) and benzodiazepines (clobazam, clonazepam)
(d)
• Withdraw stepwise over 2-3 months; carbamazepine 100-200 mg, phenytoin 50 mg, valproate 200-400 mg, ethosuximide 125-250 mg per 2-4 weeks
• A benzodiazepine can cover the withdrawal phase if rapid withdrawal is needed
• Patient education on adherence is essential; poor adherence causes admissions
• Status epilepticus (over 5 minutes) treated with IV lorazepam, or diazepam, or buccal midazolam 10 mg
questions.question:
A. Describe the principles of antiepileptic prescribing, monitoring and withdrawal.
(a) Classify the principles and give the rationale with examples.
(b) State the special-population and adverse-effect considerations.
(c) State how problems are recognised.
(d) State how they are prevented or managed.

A. Compare amide-linked and ester-linked local anaesthetics.
(a) State the classification, mechanism of action and pharmacological actions.
(b) State the pharmacokinetics of each.
(c) State the therapeutic uses and adverse effects of examples.
(d) Distinguish the two groups from each other.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Esters: cocaine, procaine, chloroprocaine, tetracaine, benzocaine; amides: lidocaine, mepivacaine, bupivacaine, prilocaine, etidocaine, ropivacaine, levobupivacaine (amides contain 'i' twice, esters once)
• Structure: lipophilic aromatic group joined by an ester or amide linkage to a hydrophilic ionisable amine; weak bases with pKa 8-9
• Mechanism: reversible block of sodium channels, preventing depolarisation and action potential initiation and propagation
(b)
• Esters are hydrolysed by plasma esterases to PABA (allergenic); amides are biotransformed in the liver (slower in liver dysfunction)
• Duration relates to protein binding (bupivacaine 95% vs mepivacaine 55%); potency relates to lipid solubility
• Lidocaine clearance depends on hepatic blood flow; propranolol reduces it
(c)
• Lidocaine: most widely used, dental, spinal, epidural; bupivacaine: long-acting, cardiotoxic; ropivacaine and levobupivacaine less cardiotoxic
• Prilocaine: methaemoglobinaemia and not for obstetric use; cocaine: topical vasoconstriction only, corneal clouding and toxicity
• Spinal/epidural risks: bradycardia, hypotension, respiratory depression
(d)
• Amides are preferred: not hydrolysed by plasma esterases and rarely cause hypersensitivity, with no cross-sensitivity with esters
• Esters have short duration (procaine 45 minutes) and cause allergy through PABA
• Surface anaesthesia: lidocaine, tetracaine, dibucaine, benzocaine; risk of systemic toxicity with large areas

questions.question:
A. Describe the pharmacology of anxiolytics, sedatives and hypnotics as a therapeutic group.
(a) Classify the drugs and give the mechanism of each group.
(b) State the uses of each group.
(c) Compare the groups by adverse effects.
(d) State the precautions for each group.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Groups: benzodiazepines, barbiturates, 'Z' compounds (zolpidem, zaleplon), chloral hydrate, buspirone, melatonin congeners (ramelteon), plus propranolol, clonidine, antidepressants and antihistamines
• Benzodiazepines, barbiturates and Z-drugs enhance GABAA receptor Cl- channel function; buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist; ramelteon is an M1 and M2 melatonin receptor agonist
• Zolpidem and zaleplon bind BZ1 receptors, are antagonised by flumazenil, and have rapid onset, half-life 2-3 hours
(b)
• Benzodiazepines: anxiety, insomnia, convulsions, spasm, pre-anaesthesia; barbiturates: IV anaesthesia (thiopental); zolpidem/zaleplon: short-term insomnia
• Chloral hydrate induces sleep in half an hour for about 6 hours (children, elderly, failure of other drugs); melatonin and ramelteon: sleep-wake disturbance, jet lag
• Propranolol: anxiety with autonomic symptoms; clonidine: panic attacks and withdrawal anxiety; SSRIs/clomipramine: obsessive-compulsive behaviour; TCAs/MAOIs: panic
(c)
• Benzodiazepines: sedation, amnesia, tolerance, dependence; barbiturates: hangover, dependence, respiratory depression; Z-drugs: GIT upset, drowsiness, dizziness
• Buspirone: tachycardia, nervousness, GI distress; ramelteon: no high abuse potential
(d)
• Barbiturates are contraindicated in porphyria; clonidine withdrawal may cause life-threatening hypertensive crisis
• Ramelteon: caution in liver disease, sleep apnoea, depression or suicidal thoughts, over 65 years
• Melatonin: caution in liver or renal problems
• All are for short-term symptomatic use only

(a)
• Buspirone: the most selective anxiolytic available, no sedation, no sedative-hypnotic or muscle relaxant effects, no dependence or withdrawal, no alcohol interaction, no impairment of driving
• Well tolerated by the elderly but clearance may be slow
(b)
• Partial agonist at 5-HT1A receptors, presynaptically inhibiting serotonin release
• Anxiolytic effect takes 1-2 weeks (several weeks) to develop, so it suits chronic anxiety, not acute anxiety
(c)
• Avoid barbiturates: narrow safety margin, abuse liability, enzyme induction, hangover
• Avoid benzodiazepines for long-term use: sedation, ataxia, amnesia, tolerance and dependence; benzodiazepines plus alcohol greatly reduce the margin of safety
(d)
• Alternative: a benzodiazepine for short-term use (diazepam, lorazepam, alprazolam) at reduced dose in elderly; propranolol for prominent physical symptoms
• Monitoring: side effects such as tachycardia, nervousness, GI distress
questions.question:
An elderly patient with chronic generalised anxiety, who drives and drinks alcohol occasionally, needs an anxiolytic without sedation, abuse potential or dependence.
(a) Select the drug and justify it.
(b) State its mechanism and expected pharmacodynamic effect.
(c) Name drugs or classes to avoid and why.
(d) State the alternative agent and the monitoring needed.

A. Compare angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers.
(a) Give the classification, mechanism of action and pharmacological actions of each group.
(b) State the pharmacokinetic features given for examples of each group.
(c) State the therapeutic uses and adverse effects of each group.
(d) Distinguish the two groups from each other.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• ACE inhibitors: thiol (captopril), dicarboxyl (enalapril, lisinopril, benazepril, quinapril, ramipril) and phosphorus (fosinopril) groups; they differ in potency, prodrug status and pharmacokinetics
• ACE inhibitors block conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II and block bradykinin degradation
• ARBs (losartan, valsartan, candesartan, telmisartan, irbesartan) are non-peptide imidazole derivatives, acidic drugs that competitively block the angiotensin type 1 (AT1) receptor → vasodilatory effect; losartan lowers afterload and preload
(b)
• Captopril: onset 0.25-0.5 h, duration 6-10 h, half-life under 2 h, not a prodrug; enalapril and ramipril are prodrugs; lisinopril acts 24 h with 100% renal elimination
• Losartan: bioavailability about 33%, first-pass metabolism by CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 to active EXP3174 (10-40 times more potent at AT1), half-life 6-9 h, protein binding 98.7%
• Telmisartan half-life 24 h, protein binding over 99%, daily dose 40-80 mg; all ARBs have low but adequate oral bioavailability
(c)
• Both groups are used for hypertension and are first-line (A of the 'ACD' drugs); losartan is also uricosuric by inhibiting URAT1
• ACE inhibitor adverse effects: dry cough, hyperkalaemia, angioedema, hypotension, neutropenia; both groups are contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal toxicity)
• ARB adverse effects: upper respiratory infection or stuffy nose, dizziness, back pain, hypotension, hyperkalaemia, allergic reactions
(d)
• ACE inhibitors block only the renin-angiotensin pathway, whereas ARBs antagonise angiotensin II generated by either pathway (including chymase)
• ARBs do not block bradykinin breakdown, so there is no dry cough and angioedema is less common than with ACE inhibitors
• Both can cause hyperkalaemia, so potassium supplements or potassium-containing salt substitutes need physician monitoring

questions.question:
A. Describe aspirin.
(a) State its class, mechanism of action and pharmacokinetic features given.
(b) State its uses and doses.
(c) State its adverse effects and contraindications.
(d) Explain the basis of toxicity and the principle of management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Acetylsalicylic acid, the prototype salicylate; hydrolyses easily, unstable in aqueous media and affected by moisture; more stable salicylates are diflunisal, salsalate and choline salicylate
• Irreversibly and non-selectively inhibits COX-1 and COX-2, preventing conversion of arachidonic acid to PGH2 and so prostaglandins and thromboxane; inhibits COX-1 more than COX-2
• COX-2 inhibition accounts for analgesic, antipyretic and anti-inflammatory effects; COX-1 inhibition accounts for antiplatelet effect and gastric effects
(b)
• Analgesic/antipyretic/anti-inflammatory: adult dose 325-975 mg; antiplatelet dose 70-100 mg; prophylaxis of myocardial infarction
• Methyl salicylate is a topical counter-irritant; sulfasalazine, olsalazine, mesalamine for inflammatory bowel disease
(c)
• Gastric irritation → bleeding → ulceration → perforation; increased depth of respiration; excessive bleeding; uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation, hyperglycaemia, glycosuria
• Delayed onset of labour; low daily doses (2 g) decrease renal urate excretion
• Contraindicated in children under 8 years, peptic ulcer, bleeding disorder and late pregnancy
(d)
• Loss of prostaglandin protection (mucus, blood supply and bicarbonate increase, acid decrease) causes mucosal irritation
• Thromboxane inhibition gives bleeding tendency
• Alternatives for patients unable to tolerate salicylates: paracetamol

questions.question:
A man who drinks heavily stops suddenly and 12-48 hours later has tremor, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension, hallucinations and then seizures.
(a) Identify the condition and the offending substance.
(b) Explain the mechanism of the dependence and the timing of features.
(c) State the management and drugs used.
(d) Identify at-risk patients and monitoring or preventive measures.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Alcohol (ethanol) withdrawal syndrome after physical dependence
(b)
• Ethanol is a CNS depressant; its initial effects can be perceived as stimulation through suppression of inhibitory systems; heavy users acquire tolerance and physical dependence
• Features: craving, irritability, nausea, tremor, sleep disturbance, tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, dilated pupils; hallucinations 12-48 hours; seizures 6-48 hours; delirium tremens 48-96 hours
• Ethanol shows positive reinforcement (euphoria, anxiolysis) and raises dopamine in the nucleus accumbens
(c)
• Detoxification: attention to hydration and electrolytes, vitamins especially high-dose thiamine, and a sedating cross-tolerant drug
• Short-acting benzodiazepine such as oxazepam 15-30 mg every 4-6 hours according to stage and severity; other options chlordiazepoxide, clorazepate, diazepam and some barbiturates
(d)
• Alcohol also produces cross-tolerance to benzodiazepines, which can be lethal in combination with alcohol in overdose
• Nutritional deficiency (thiamine) causes memory impairment; liver, cardiovascular, endocrine, GI damage; high suicide risk; long-term prevention uses disulfiram, naltrexone, acamprosate and behavioural therapy

(a)
Zolpidem (imidazopyridine non-benzodiazepine hypnotic): hepatic CYP450 metabolism to inactive metabolites
(b)
• Rapidly absorbed, onset within about 15 minutes, short duration (2-4 hours, half-life 2-3 hours)
• Cimetidine increases zolpidem half-life; rifampicin decreases it (enzyme induction)
• Zaleplon behaves similarly: rapid onset, duration about 1 hour, metabolism inhibited by cimetidine
(c)
• Dose should be reduced in hepatic dysfunction, the elderly and patients taking cimetidine
• Monitoring: drowsiness, dizziness, GIT upset
(d)
• Consequence of reduced clearance: exaggerated drowsiness and respiratory depression at high dose with other CNS depressants such as ethanol
• Benefits: no hangover, minimal tolerance, dependence and rebound insomnia; use short term for insomnia; flumazenil can reverse overdose
questions.question:
An elderly patient with limited hepatic function needs a hypnotic. The prescriber considers a drug that is rapidly metabolised by the liver to inactive metabolites, and notes that cimetidine and rifampicin are also on the patient's list.
(a) Identify the drug and the pharmacokinetic process involved.
(b) Explain the effect on onset, duration and accumulation, and the effect of the co-administered drugs.
(c) State the dose adjustment and monitoring.
(d) Name the clinical consequence.

A. Describe the calcium channel blockers.
(a) Give the classification, mechanism of action and pharmacological actions.
(b) State the pharmacokinetics of the main examples.
(c) State the therapeutic uses and adverse effects.
(d) Distinguish dihydropyridines from verapamil and diltiazem.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Three structural classes: phenylalkylamines (verapamil), dihydropyridines (nifedipine, amlodipine, felodipine, isradipine, nicardipine, nimodipine), benzothiazepines (diltiazem)
• Block voltage-sensitive L-type calcium channels, reducing entry of extracellular calcium; relax arteriolar smooth muscle and reduce peripheral resistance; dilate coronary arteries
• Non-dihydropyridines also depress SA and AV node and lower heart rate and cardiac contractility
(b)
• Verapamil: oral absorption over 90%, bioavailability 10-35%, protein bound 83-92%, half-life 2.8-6.3 h; diltiazem bioavailability 41-67%, half-life 3.5-7 h
