• Nifedipine: bioavailability 45-86%, protein bound 92-98%, half-life 1.9-5.8 h; amlodipine: bioavailability 64-90%, half-life 30-50 h
• Nifedipine is metabolised mainly by CYP3A4
(c)
• Uses: angina, hypertension, supraventricular arrhythmias
• Adverse effects: flushing, peripheral oedema, tachycardia, bradycardia, heart block, headache, dizziness, constipation (verapamil), nausea, vomiting, gum hypertrophy
(d)
• Verapamil depresses cardiac contractility, SA and AV nodes most; diltiazem is intermediate; nifedipine gives the strongest vasodilation with little cardiac depression
• Dihydropyridines are more potent peripheral vasodilators and cause reflex sympathetic discharge; verapamil and diltiazem decrease heart rate and contraction
• Structure-activity: 1,4-DHP ring is an absolute requirement, a bulky substituent at position 4 is essential, and nitro-DHPs are photosensitive
• Digoxin level rises with verapamil/diltiazem; thiazides potentiate dihydropyridines

questions.question:
A. Describe withdrawal syndromes of CNS depressant drugs.
(a) Classify the withdrawal syndromes and give the mechanism with examples.
(b) State the features of alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal.
(c) State how they are recognised.
(d) State how they are prevented or managed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Withdrawal syndromes appear when a physically dependent person stops abruptly; they reflect resetting of homeostatic mechanisms from tolerance (negative reinforcement)
• Examples: benzodiazepines, opioids, barbiturates, alcohol; barbiturate withdrawal gives anxiety, insomnia, CNS excitability, convulsions
(b)
• Alcohol: craving, irritability, nausea, tremor, tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, hallucinations, seizures, delirium tremens
• Benzodiazepines: anxiety, agitation, increased sensitivity to light and sound, paraesthesias, muscle cramps, myoclonic jerks; with high doses seizures and delirium; also insomnia, anorexia, tremor
• Serious benzodiazepine withdrawal may include convulsions and death
(c)
• Timing for alcohol: seizures 6-48 hours, hallucinations 12-48 hours, delirium tremens 48-96 hours
• The appearance of a withdrawal syndrome is the only actual evidence of physical dependence
• Drugs with long half-lives give the mildest withdrawal (barbiturates)
(d)
• Reduce gradually: for benzodiazepines 25% dose reduction per week until 50% reached, then 1/8 every 4-7 days
• Alcohol withdrawal: short-acting benzodiazepine, thiamine, fluids and electrolytes
• Opioid withdrawal can be covered by substituting methadone
• Flumazenil may precipitate withdrawal symptoms

questions.question:
A patient on propranolol receives an amide local anaesthetic containing adrenaline for a procedure, and the patient also has ischaemic heart disease.
(a) Identify the type of interaction.
(b) Explain the mechanisms.
(c) Predict the clinical outcome.
(d) State how to manage or avoid it.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pharmacokinetic (beta blocker with amide local anaesthetic) and pharmacodynamic (adrenaline with beta blocker and cardiac disease)
(b)
• Propranolol and probably other beta blockers reduce metabolism of lidocaine and other amide anaesthetics by reducing hepatic blood flow; lidocaine clearance is highly dependent on hepatic blood flow
• Adrenaline is added to restrict systemic absorption and toxicity, but is hazardous in ischaemic heart disease, arrhythmia and uncontrolled hypertension
(c)
• Higher local anaesthetic levels and greater systemic toxicity (CNS depression, drowsiness, tinnitus; cardiotoxicity especially with bupivacaine)
• Vasoconstrictor-related cardiac stress in a patient with ischaemic heart disease
(d)
• Avoid vasoconstrictor-containing preparations in these patients and those on beta blockers
• Use lower doses within maximum limits
• Esters are hydrolysed by plasma esterases, so hepatic blood flow matters less (but give PABA allergy)

(a)
Tricyclic antidepressants (imipramine, amitriptyline, nortriptyline, clomipramine and others)
(b)
• Main effects on the CNS and heart: excitement, delirium and convulsions, then coma and respiratory depression lasting days; pronounced atropine-like effects (dry mouth and skin, mydriasis, inhibition of gut and bladder)
• Antimuscarinic action at muscarinic receptors causes the atropine-like effects; ventricular dysrhythmias are linked to QT prolongation; sudden death from ventricular fibrillation is rare
(c)
• Haemodialysis is ineffective because of extravascular sequestration and strong albumin binding (90-95%)
• Anticholinesterase drugs have been used to counter the atropine-like effects but are no longer recommended
(d)
• TCAs were once commonly used for suicide attempts; safer antidepressants (SSRIs) are less dangerous in overdose
• Elderly patients have longer half-lives; paroxetine/fluoxetine raise TCA levels via CYP2D6; therapeutic usual doses slightly raise the risk of sudden cardiac death
questions.question:
A patient who attempted suicide with a common older antidepressant is admitted with excitement and delirium, convulsions, then coma and respiratory depression, with dry mouth and skin, dilated pupils and cardiac arrhythmias.
(a) Identify the offending drug class.
(b) Explain the mechanism of toxicity.
(c) State the management and what is not helpful.
(d) Identify at-risk patients and monitoring or preventive measures.

A patient on a drug that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels develops a skin rash, dizziness, blurred vision, ataxia and hyponatraemia.
(a) Identify the offending drug.
(b) Explain the nature of the adverse reactions and mechanism.
(c) State the management and whether a specific antidote exists.
(d) Identify at-risk patients and monitoring or preventive measures.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Carbamazepine, a first-line drug for generalised tonic-clonic and focal seizures acting by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels
(b)
• Dose-related reactions: ataxia, dizziness, blurred vision, diplopia are common
• Idiosyncratic reactions: skin rash in up to 10%, rarely severe skin eruptions such as erythema multiforme and Stevens-Johnson syndrome; gastrointestinal disturbance and hyponatraemia can force withdrawal
(c)
Only about 5% of adverse events require drug withdrawal; withdraw slowly (100-200 mg every 4 weeks for total withdrawal); a benzodiazepine can cover withdrawal if rapid withdrawal is needed
(d)
• Serious but extremely uncommon events: hepatic failure and bone marrow depression
• Introduce at low dose and increase over a month; therapeutic drug monitoring; avoid in absence and myoclonic seizures where it may be harmful

(a)
• Detoxification drugs (short-acting benzodiazepines such as oxazepam, chlordiazepoxide, clorazepate, diazepam, some barbiturates) and relapse-prevention drugs (disulfiram, naltrexone, acamprosate)
• Benzodiazepines are cross-tolerant sedatives that block or diminish withdrawal symptoms
• Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing acetaldehyde accumulation and flushing on drinking; naltrexone is an opioid antagonist blocking reinforcing properties of alcohol; acamprosate is a competitive NMDA glutamate receptor inhibitor normalising dysregulated neurotransmission
(b)
• Severe withdrawal needs hydration, electrolytes, vitamins (especially high-dose thiamine) and a sedating medication; oxazepam 15-30 mg every 4-6 hours
• Complete abstinence is the goal of long-term therapy, achieved mainly by behavioural approaches
• Naltrexone decreases relapse rate in most cases; acamprosate promotes abstinence alone or with naltrexone
(c)
• Disulfiram causes an unpleasant flushing reaction and is not effective in controlled trials because of non-compliance
• Naltrexone works best with behavioural programmes; a 30-day depot preparation improves adherence, the main problem
(d)
• Alcohol withdrawal: seizures (6-48 h), hallucinations (12-48 h), delirium tremens (48-96 h) need monitoring
• Benzodiazepines are potentially lethal in overdose when combined with alcohol
• Alcoholics have complications of liver, cardiovascular, endocrine and GI disease and high suicide risk
questions.question:
A. Describe the pharmacological management of alcohol dependence and withdrawal.
(a) Classify the drugs and give the mechanism of each.
(b) State the uses.
(c) Compare the drugs by adverse effects and limitations.
(d) State the precautions.

A patient with generalised anxiety is prescribed a drug that facilitates GABA-gated chloride channel opening at a regulatory site distinct from the GABA site. The patient later reports drowsiness, poor coordination and memory loss for events after the dose.
(a) Identify the drug class and give examples.
(b) State the mechanism of action at the receptor and the resulting neuronal effect.
(c) State the therapeutic uses and key adverse effects.
(d) State the contraindications, precautions and withdrawal advice.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Benzodiazepines (e.g. diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, lorazepam, alprazolam, oxazepam, triazolam, clonazepam, temazepam)
(b)
• Bind the GABAA receptor (a ligand-gated Cl- channel) allosterically at a site distinct from GABA, increasing the frequency of channel opening and receptor affinity for GABA
• Greater Cl- influx → hyperpolarisation of the neuronal membrane → decreased excitability; BZ1 mediates sedation, anticonvulsant effect and amnesia, BZ2 anxiolysis and muscle relaxation
(c)
• Uses: anxiety (alprazolam in panic/phobic disorders), sedation of excitement, insomnia (triazolam sleep induction, temazepam maintenance, flurazepam early waking), IV diazepam in status epilepticus, clonazepam in other epilepsy, muscle spasm, alcohol withdrawal, pre-anaesthesia (midazolam preferred)
• Adverse effects: sedation (hangover), ataxia, anterograde amnesia, confusion, muscle weakness, tolerance (receptor down-regulation), dependence; paradoxical excitability can occur
• Serious withdrawal syndrome: anxiety, insomnia, anorexia, tremor, twitching, sweating, convulsions, delirium; may cause death
(d)
• Additive effects with alcohol and other CNS depressants greatly reduce the margin of safety; avoid combining anxiolytics and avoid over-the-counter antihistamines and anticholinergics
• Use short term only; withdraw gradually (reduce dose 25% per week until 50% reached, then 1/8 every 4-7 days)
• Cross the placenta and are found in breast milk; take care in impaired hepatic function and children (respiratory effects)

questions.question:
A. Describe the pharmacology of the antiepileptic drugs as a therapeutic group.
(a) Classify the drugs by chemical and clinical grouping and give the mechanisms.
(b) State which drugs are used for each seizure type.
(c) Compare the main drugs by use, adverse effects and cautions.
(d) State the precautions common to the group.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Chemical classes include barbiturates, benzodiazepines, carboxamides, fatty acids, GABA analogues (gabapentin, pregabalin), hydantoins (phenytoin), succinimides (ethosuximide), pyrrolidines (levetiracetam), triazines (lamotrigine) and others
• Clinically: drugs for major attacks (phenytoin, carbamazepine, mephobarbital, primidone) and for minor attacks (ethosuximide, acetazolamide, clonazepam, trimethadione, valproic acid)
• Three mechanisms: modulation of voltage-gated ion channels, enhancement of GABA-mediated inhibition, attenuation of glutamate-mediated excitation
(b)
• Tonic-clonic: carbamazepine, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, valproate (adjunct levetiracetam, clobazam, topiramate); absence: ethosuximide, clobazam, lamotrigine; myoclonic: levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam, topiramate, piracetam
• Focal: carbamazepine, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, valproate; status epilepticus: IV lorazepam, then diazepam or buccal midazolam, then IV phenytoin, valproate or phenobarbital, then anaesthesia
(c)
• Phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine act on sodium channels; ethosuximide on calcium channels; levetiracetam binds synaptic vesicle protein 2A; gabapentin blocks high-voltage calcium channels
• Gabapentin is mostly used for neuropathic pain; phenytoin serum level-dose relationship is non-linear and it is rarely used
• Carbamazepine: rash, hyponatraemia, auto-induction; valproate: weight gain, alopecia, teratogenicity; ethosuximide: GI upset, behaviour change
(d)
• Use one drug at the lowest effective dose, start low and increase slowly; newer AEDs are better tolerated but not more effective
• Withdraw slowly over 2-3 months, particularly barbiturates and benzodiazepines
• Therapeutic drug monitoring for phenytoin and carbamazepine; keep the same brand
• Therapy is long term, usually at least 3 years; poor adherence is a major cause of admission

questions.question:
A. Describe morphine.
(a) State its source, class, mechanism of action and pharmacokinetics.
(b) State its uses.
(c) State its adverse effects, contraindications and interactions.
(d) Explain the basis of dependence and tolerance and the principle of management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principal alkaloid of opium (10-15%), discovered in 1809 by Serturner, from the opium poppy Papaver somniferum; a 4,5-epoxymorphinan opioid agonist
• Acts on G-protein coupled opioid receptors in brain and spinal cord to reduce pain perception
• Routes: oral (including controlled-release), IM, SC, IV; codeine is the 3-methoxy analogue with 15% of morphine's activity
(b)
• One of the most effective analgesics, used in terminal illness and cancer pain; acute and moderate chronic pain
• Substituting dihydro derivatives increases activity (dihydromorphinone 6 times dihydromorphine)
(c)
• Increased tolerance to pain, euphoria, antitussive effect, respiratory depression, constipation, emesis; miosis and itching
• Less common: confusion, hallucinations, delirium, hypothermia, bradycardia, raised intracranial pressure
(d)
• High addiction liability; physical dependence is an automatic consequence of long-term use; abrupt stopping or dose reduction causes withdrawal reactions
• Tolerance is the need for larger doses for the same analgesia; chronic pain patients may escalate dose
• Naloxone treats overdose; methadone can substitute to suppress withdrawal
• Derivatives were sought with better oral bioavailability and reduced addiction liability

questions.question:
A patient needs a minor dental procedure under an amide-linked local anaesthetic that blocks sodium channels, with adrenaline added. The patient later reports drowsiness, altered taste and ringing in the ears.
(a) Identify the drug and its class.
(b) State the mechanism of action at the molecular target.
(c) State the therapeutic uses and the key adverse effects.
(d) State the contraindications and precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Lidocaine (lignocaine), the most widely used local anaesthetic; amide-linked; 2% with or without adrenaline is the most popular dental anaesthetic
(b)
• Reversibly binds and inactivates sodium channels, preventing Na+ influx, depolarisation and propagation of the action potential, so nerve conduction is blocked
• Weak base (pKa 8-9) so activity is pH dependent; the ionised form binds from inside after the drug reaches the inner axonal membrane through open Na+ channels or the membrane
(c)
• Uses: surface (topical), infiltration, nerve block, spinal and epidural anaesthesia; the clinical sequence is sympathetic block, then loss of pain and temperature, proprioception, touch, and motor function
• Early central effects are depressant: drowsiness, mental clouding, dysphoria, altered taste, tinnitus; injection may be painful but local tissue toxicity is low
• Cross-sensitivity with ester local anaesthetics is not seen; hypersensitivity is rare
(d)
• Avoid adrenaline-containing preparations in ischaemic heart disease, cardiac arrhythmia, uncontrolled hypertension and in patients on beta blockers
• Maximum dose 4.5 mg/kg (7 mg/kg with epinephrine) with duration 120 minutes (240 minutes with epinephrine)
• Clearance depends on hepatic blood flow

questions.question:
A. Describe the pharmacology of nitroglycerine.
(a) State its drug class, mechanism of action and pharmacokinetics.
(b) State its uses in the types of angina and the basis of its clinical effect.
(c) State its adverse effects, contraindication and interactions or special effects of nitrates.
(d) Explain the basis of nitrate toxicity and its management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Prototype organic nitrate, a nitric/nitrous acid ester of a polyalcohol; given sublingually
• Mechanism: denitrated by glutathione S-transferase → free nitrite ion → nitric oxide → activates guanylyl cyclase → increased cGMP → smooth muscle relaxation → vasodilatation
• PK: oral bioavailability 10-20% (marked first-pass); metabolised in liver by organic nitrate reductase; duration 15-30 minutes; slow-release transdermal and buccal forms exist
(b)
• Angina of effort: lowers myocardial oxygen requirement via decreased venous return, reduced intracardiac volume, decreased arterial BP and decreased intraventricular pressure and left ventricular volume
• Variant angina: relaxes epicardial coronary artery smooth muscle and relieves coronary spasm
• Unstable angina: dilates epicardial coronary arteries, reduces oxygen demand, and decreased platelet aggregation may be important
(c)
• Acute toxicity is an extension of vasodilatation: orthostatic hypotension, tachycardia and throbbing headache
• Contraindicated in raised intracranial pressure
• Industrial exposure produces tolerance ('Monday morning sickness') and dependence; nitrates decrease platelet aggregation and enhance erection through NO release
(d)
• Nitrite ion reacts with haemoglobin to form methaemoglobin; the concentration is usually too low to matter and this effect is used in cyanide poisoning (sodium nitrite)
• Excessive methaemoglobinaemia is treated with methylene blue
• Animal studies link nitrosamines to cancer but not in humans; small angina doses are not shown to give significant nitrosamine levels

(a)
Propofol (Diprivan 10 mg/ml), the most common induction agent; non-barbiturate IV anaesthetic that has displaced barbiturates; can also maintain anaesthesia by slow infusion
(b)
• Increases GABA-mediated inhibitory tone by decreasing the rate of dissociation of GABA from its receptor, prolonging chloride channel opening and hyperpolarisation
• Associated with less postoperative nausea and vomiting and more rapid return to consciousness
(c)
• Side effects: fall in blood pressure, depressed or stopped breathing, pain on injection; lipid emulsion can support bacterial growth without aseptic care
• Malignant hyperthermia is a rare inherited reaction to some anaesthetics; medicines to avoid on the morning of surgery include anticoagulants, metformin, MAO inhibitors, ACE inhibitors; beta blockers are continued in high-risk patients
(d)
• Alternatives: thiopental, ketamine (IV); sevoflurane (well-tolerated vapour allowing inhalation induction), desflurane; nitrous oxide with oxygen
• Opioids (fentanyl, remifentanil) work synergistically with induction agents; neostigmine reverses non-depolarising blockers but not suxamethonium
• Monitoring: recovery in PACU until activity, circulation, consciousness, oxygen saturation and respiration criteria are met
questions.question:
A patient is scheduled for elective surgery under general anaesthesia and the anaesthetist wants a rapid induction with less postoperative nausea and vomiting, and a well-tolerated vapour for maintenance.
(a) Select the induction agent and justify it.
(b) State the mechanism and expected pharmacodynamic effect.
(c) Name agents or conditions to be careful about and why.
(d) State alternative agents and monitoring.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Acetaminophen (paracetamol), a p-aminophenol derivative, is used primarily for analgesic and antipyretic activity, particularly in patients unable to tolerate salicylates; no gastric irritation
(b)
• Inhibits central prostaglandin synthesis, presumably through selectivity for COX-2 with little or no COX-1 activity; analgesic and antipyretic
• Non-opioids have a ceiling effect on analgesia, so raising the dose will not give further relief
(c)
• Avoid aspirin in children under 8 years, peptic ulcer, bleeding disorder and late pregnancy
• Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX-1 and COX-2, giving antiplatelet effect, gastric irritation and bleeding
• Paracetamol adverse effects: skin rash, haemolytic anaemia, renal dysfunction and tubular necrosis
(d)
• Alternatives: other non-opioids (ibuprofen, diclofenac, mefenamic acid), COX-2 selective NSAIDs, or opioids for severe pain
• Monitoring: gastric and bleeding signs, renal function
questions.question:
A patient with pain and fever cannot tolerate salicylates because of gastric irritation, and another patient is a child under 8 years old with a bleeding disorder.
(a) Select the drug and justify it.
(b) State the mechanism and expected pharmacodynamic effect.
(c) Name the drug to avoid and why.
(d) State alternative agents and monitoring.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Pharmacodynamic interaction: additive vasoconstriction
(b)
Beta-adrenoceptor blockers like propranolol (which block 5-HT2 receptors and reduce neuronal firing) potentiate the peripheral vasoconstriction caused by triptans or ergotamine
(c)
• Excess peripheral vasoconstriction; ergot vasoconstriction is long-lasting and cumulative with repeated dosing
• Prolonged vasospasm is not easily reversed by serotonin antagonists
(d)
• Propranolol and triptans or ergotamine should not be given concurrently
• Alternative prophylactics: pizotifen (especially if beta blockers are contraindicated; side effects drowsiness, appetite stimulation, weight gain), amitriptyline, verapamil, flunarizine, valproic acid, topiramate
• Prophylactic drugs are effective for prophylaxis only, not for acute attacks
questions.question:
A migraine patient taking propranolol for prophylaxis develops an acute attack and is given ergotamine or a triptan at the same time.
(a) Identify the type of interaction.
(b) Explain the mechanism.
(c) Predict the clinical outcome.
(d) State how to manage or avoid it and name an alternative prophylactic.

A. Describe the dopamine agonists used in Parkinson disease.
(a) State the classification, mechanism of action and pharmacological actions.
(b) State the pharmacokinetic features given.
(c) State the therapeutic uses and adverse effects.
(d) Distinguish ergot from non-ergot agonists and compare with levodopa.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Ergot derived (cabergoline) and non-ergot (ropinirole, pramipexole, rotigotine); apomorphine is the most potent non-selective agonist
• They stimulate dopamine receptors, post- and presynaptically, bypassing the degenerating nigrostriatal neurons; they differ in affinity for D2 and D3 subtypes
• Compared with levodopa they are less potent and less well tolerated
(b)
• Cabergoline is given once daily, plasma half-life 63-68 hours
• Apomorphine has a short half-life; a single bolus lasts 45-60 minutes
(c)
• Uses: Parkinson disease, with non-ergot agonists the agonists of choice; apomorphine for advanced disease
• Adverse effects: nausea, vomiting, postural hypotension, hallucinations, confusion, impulse control disorders
(d)
• Ergot derivatives risk pleuropulmonary fibrosis and are not routinely used
• Apomorphine: rare irreversible Coombs haemolytic anaemia with entacapone
• Levodopa is the most effective first-line drug but causes wearing-off and dyskinesia; agonists have impulse-control risks
• Treatment is wholly symptomatic; no drug is proven neuroprotective

questions.question:
A. Describe the pain pathway and the sites of action of analgesic drugs.
(a) State the nociceptors, fibre types and the ascending and descending pathways.
(b) State the modulation mechanisms (gate control and descending inhibition).
(c) Relate these to examples of analgesic drugs given.
(d) Explain the clinical significance and limitation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Nociceptors are free nerve endings of A-delta and C primary afferent fibres, activated by mechanical, thermal or chemical stimuli; inflammatory mediators (bradykinin, serotonin, prostaglandins, cytokines, H+) lower their threshold (primary sensitisation)
• A-beta fibres carry light touch; A-delta fibres carry rapid sharp localised pain; unmyelinated C fibres carry slow, burning, dull pain
• A-delta and C fibres synapse in dorsal horn laminae I and II releasing glutamate and substance P; glycine and GABA act at inhibitory interneurones
• Spinothalamic tract carries pain localisation to thalamus and somatosensory cortex; spinoreticular tract carries the emotional aspects of pain
(b)
• Gate control theory: A-beta stimulation activates dorsal horn inhibitory interneurones and inhibits C fibre transmission; TENS is based on it
• Descending inhibition arises from the periaqueductal grey and rostral ventromedial medulla, rich in opioid receptors, using noradrenaline and serotonin
(c)
• NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin production by inhibiting COX, reducing nociceptor sensitisation; COX-2 inhibitors (parecoxib) have lower GI bleeding risk
• Opioids act on mu receptors, inhibit excitatory neurotransmitter release in the dorsal horn and enhance descending inhibition in the PAG; paracetamol acts centrally on brain COX
• Local anaesthetics (bupivacaine, lidocaine) reversibly inhibit action potential propagation; TCAs (amitriptyline), duloxetine and gabapentin are used in neuropathic pain
(d)
• Neuropathic pain (allodynia, hyperalgesia, burning pain) is difficult to treat and responds to antidepressants and anticonvulsants
• Multimodal analgesia combines drugs of different actions to lower doses and side effects (NSAID plus opioid for postoperative pain)
• Side effects: NSAIDs bleeding, ulcer, renal impairment, bronchospasm; opioids respiratory depression, constipation, nausea, sedation; local anaesthetics CNS and cardiovascular toxicity

questions.question:
A. Describe the adverse effects, interactions and dependence of sedative-hypnotics.
(a) Classify the adverse reactions and give the mechanism with examples.
(b) State the drug interactions.
(c) State how overdose and withdrawal are recognised.
(d) State how they are prevented or managed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• CNS depressant effects: sedation and hangover, ataxia, anterograde amnesia, confusion, muscle weakness
• Tolerance: benzodiazepine tolerance relates to receptor down-regulation; barbiturate tolerance to receptor down-regulation and induction of hepatic enzymes; hypnotic tolerance after 1-2 weeks
• Dependence is psychological (drug craving) and physical (withdrawal when stopped)
• Paradoxical hyperexcitability can occur with benzodiazepines; barbiturates cause porphyria and skin eruptions
(b)
• Additive effects with narcotics and alcohol; benzodiazepines reduce effect of antiepileptics; SSRIs and oral contraceptives decrease benzodiazepine metabolism
• Chloral hydrate displaces warfarin from plasma proteins; phenobarbital induces liver enzymes; rifampicin shortens and cimetidine lengthens zolpidem half-life
(c)
• Withdrawal mimics anxiety: anxiety, insomnia, anorexia, tremor, sweating, hypersensitivity to light and noise, convulsions, delirium
• Overdose: prolonged sleep with little respiratory depression for benzodiazepines; coma, severe respiratory depression, hypotension with barbiturates
(d)
• Benzodiazepine overdose treated with flumazenil with respiratory support, though seizures and arrhythmias may follow if tricyclic antidepressants were taken
• Use for short-term treatment only (days or weeks); withdraw gradually; avoid combination of anxiolytics
• Reduce dose in elderly and hepatic dysfunction
• Barbiturate overdose: support, alkalinise urine, dialysis

questions.question:
A. Describe buspirone.
(a) State its drug class, mechanism of action and pharmacokinetics.
(b) State its uses, advantages and disadvantages.
(c) State its adverse effects and cautions.
(d) Relate its profile to other anxiolytic and sedative-hypnotic drugs.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Azaspirodecanedione; selective anxiolytic and partial agonist at 5-HT1A receptors, presynaptically inhibiting serotonin release
• Rapidly absorbed orally; extensive hepatic metabolism (hydroxylation and dealkylation) to active metabolites such as 1-(2-pyrimidyl)-piperazine (1-PP), which has alpha-2 blocking action
• Short half-life about 2.5 h, so given two or three times daily; clearance may be slow in elderly though well tolerated
(b)
• Uses: generalised anxiety disorder / chronic anxiety; not effective in panic disorders; not for acute anxiety because onset takes 1-2 weeks (effect takes several weeks to develop)
• Advantages: no physical dependence or withdrawal, no abuse potential, less sedation and psychomotor impairment, no interaction with alcohol, no rebound anxiety
• Disadvantages: slow onset (1-2 weeks) and short half-life requiring repeated daily dosing
(c)
• Side effects: tachycardia, palpitations, nervousness, gastrointestinal distress, paraesthesias, dose-dependent pupillary constriction
• Does not have sedative, anticonvulsant or muscle relaxant effects and does not potentiate CNS depressants
(d)
• Relatively high margin of safety unlike barbiturates; no abuse liability unlike benzodiazepines
• Analogues: ipsapirone, gepirone, tandospirone
• Other anxiolytic options: benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, alprazolam) for GAD; TCAs and MAOIs for panic; clomipramine and SSRIs for obsessive-compulsive behaviour
• Propranolol is used when autonomic anxiety symptoms are severe (adverse effects: lethargy, vivid dreams, hallucinations)

questions.question:
A. Describe the mechanisms underlying seizures and antiepileptic drug action.
(a) State the cellular basis of a seizure and epilepsy.
(b) State the three major mechanisms of antiepileptic drugs.
(c) Relate these to examples of drugs and their seizure-type efficacy.
(d) Explain the clinical significance and limitation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Seizure: sudden, brief disruption of normal neuronal function; epilepsy: recurrent unprovoked seizures; excessive or oversynchronised discharge of cortical neurons
• GABA receptor mediated inhibition terminates a seizure; NMDA (glutamate) receptor activation is required for propagation, and reduced GABA receptor function favours seizures
• The epileptic focus is where abnormal discharge starts; it may spread via cortical and subcortical routes; epilepsy has no pathognomonic lesion
(b)
• Modulation of voltage-gated ion channels
• Enhancement of GABA-mediated inhibitory neurotransmission
• Attenuation of glutamate-mediated excitatory neurotransmission
(c)
• Phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine: sodium channels (effective in focal seizures only); lamotrigine: sodium and calcium channels, broad efficacy
• Ethosuximide: calcium channels, effective in primary generalised (absence) only; valproate: sodium, calcium and GABA, broad
• Barbiturates promote GABA binding, prolong chloride channel opening and reduce glutamate excitation; felbamate and topiramate act at all four sites
(d)
• Drug choice depends on seizure type, so accurate classification is essential
• Seizures may recur with poor adherence, sleep deprivation, stress, hypoglycaemia, alcohol, hormonal change and flashing lights
• Surgery or vagus nerve stimulation is considered when drugs fail and a focus is identifiable

(a)
• Groups: levodopa preparations, dopamine agonists, COMT inhibitors (tolcapone, entacapone), MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline, rasagiline), amantadine, antimuscarinics (trihexyphenidyl, orphenadrine), apomorphine
• COMT inhibitors act mainly peripherally, blocking conversion of levodopa to 3-O-methyldopa and increasing levodopa entering CNS; MAO-B inhibitors slow dopamine breakdown (levodopa-sparing)
• Pathophysiology: loss of dopaminergic nigral neurons; more than 50% lost before motor features appear
(b)
• MAO-B inhibitors: de novo or adjunctive (selegiline 5 or 10 mg daily); entacapone with each levodopa dose; amantadine antidyskinetic; antimuscarinics reduce tremor, not bradykinesia
• Levodopa is first-line; non-ergot agonists are agonists of choice; apomorphine for advanced disease
(c)
• COMT inhibitors: dyskinesia exacerbation, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dry mouth, urine discolouration; tolcapone hepatotoxic
• Antimuscarinics: constipation, urinary retention, cognitive impairment, toxic confusional states
• Amantadine: confusion, oedema, livedo reticularis; agonists: nausea, hypotension, hallucinations, impulse control disorders
(d)
• Tolcapone needs strict liver function monitoring; entacapone has not shown liver derangement
• Antimuscarinics need close monitoring and suit selected younger patients
• Non-motor features (hypotension, constipation, depression, dementia) need attention; tricyclic antidepressant may help sleep
• Education, diaries linking symptoms to drug and food intake, and carer support are part of care
questions.question:
A. Describe the drugs used in Parkinson disease as a therapeutic group.
(a) Classify the drugs and give the mechanism of each group.
(b) State the uses of each group.
(c) Compare the groups by adverse effects.
(d) State the precautions and monitoring for each group.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Bupivacaine: more lipophilic, more potent, long-acting amide; protein binding 95%
(b)
• More prone to prolong the QTc interval, induce ventricular tachycardia and cause cardiac depression; cardiac toxicity limits general use
• Toxicity depends on relative rates of absorption and metabolism: drugs rapidly absorbed but slowly metabolised are more toxic
(c)
Safer alternatives: ropivacaine (less cardiotoxicity) and levobupivacaine (lower affinity for cardiac channels, less cardiotoxicity and CNS depression than the racemate)
(d)
• Vasoconstrictors such as epinephrine restrict systemic absorption and toxicity; maximum dose bupivacaine 2.5 mg/kg (3 mg/kg with epinephrine)
• Amides are metabolised more slowly in liver dysfunction; propranolol and other beta blockers reduce metabolism of lidocaine and other amide anaesthetics by reducing hepatic blood flow
• Risk of systemic toxicity increases with high concentrations over large areas for surface anaesthesia
questions.question:
A patient given a high dose of a long-acting, highly lipophilic amide local anaesthetic develops ventricular tachycardia and cardiac depression.
(a) Identify the likely offending drug.
(b) Explain the mechanism and factors raising toxicity.
(c) State management or safer alternatives and any antidote.
(d) Identify at-risk patients and preventive measures.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Typical: phenothiazines (chlorpromazine), butyrophenones (haloperidol), thioxanthenes (flupentixol); atypical: clozapine, risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole, ziprasidone
• Typical drugs predominantly antagonise D2 receptors and also block muscarinic, histamine and alpha-adrenergic receptors; atypicals predominantly antagonise 5-HT2A with lesser D2 antagonism
• PK of typicals: rapid oral absorption, highly lipophilic, large volumes of distribution, extensive CYP phase 1 metabolism then conjugation, excretion in urine and some bile
(b)
• Aripiprazole is a partial agonist at 5-HT2A and D2; atypicals bind less avidly to striatal and hypothalamic D2 receptors
• 5-HT2A blockade raises striatal dopamine, preventing extrapyramidal effects
(c)
• Uses: psychosis; typicals also antiemetic and for hiccups; atypicals effective against negative symptoms (especially clozapine) and increasingly drugs of choice
• Typical adverse effects: EPS, tardive dyskinesia, hyperprolactinaemia, anticholinergic and antiadrenergic effects, sedation, QT prolongation, neuroleptic malignant syndrome
• Atypical adverse effects: weight gain, diabetes and ketoacidosis (clozapine, olanzapine), agranulocytosis (clozapine), less QT prolongation at therapeutic doses
(d)
• Atypicals produce considerably less EPS and endocrine disturbance and may improve cognition
• Atypicals carry more metabolic and weight problems; typicals more EPS and higher cardiac QT risk
• High-potency typical (haloperidol, fluphenazine) have more EPS; low-potency (chlorpromazine, thioridazine) fewer EPS but more sedation, hypotension
• Warnings: antipsychotics increase cerebrovascular events and mortality in dementia
questions.question:
A. Compare typical and atypical antipsychotic drugs.
(a) State the classification, mechanism of action and pharmacokinetics of each.
(b) State the pharmacological profile at receptors.
(c) State the therapeutic uses and adverse effects of each.
(d) Distinguish the two groups from each other.

A patient in an alcohol rehabilitation programme is taking disulfiram and drinks alcohol, developing an unpleasant flushing reaction. Another patient taking naltrexone is also advised about alcohol.
(a) Identify the type of interaction.
(b) Explain the mechanism.
(c) Predict the clinical outcome and therapeutic purpose.
(d) State the limitations, how to manage or avoid problems and other drugs used.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pharmacokinetic (metabolic enzyme inhibition) drug-alcohol interaction, deliberately used therapeutically
(b)
Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, the second step of ethanol metabolism, so acetaldehyde accumulates
(c)
• Accumulated acetaldehyde produces an unpleasant flushing reaction when alcohol is ingested; knowledge of the reaction helps the patient resist drinking
• Naltrexone, an opioid antagonist, blocks some of the reinforcing properties of alcohol and decreases relapse rate, best with behavioural programmes; a 30-day depot preparation improves adherence
(d)
• Disulfiram is pharmacologically effective but not effective in controlled trials because many patients are non-compliant
• Acamprosate, a competitive NMDA-type glutamate receptor inhibitor, normalises dysregulated neurotransmission and promotes abstinence alone or with naltrexone
• Complete abstinence is the long-term goal, achieved mainly by behavioural approaches

(a)
Ergot alkaloids (ergotamine, ergonovine, methysergide)
(b)
• Ergotamine is a strong vasoconstrictor; the effect is long-lasting (24 hours or longer despite plasma half-life about 2 hours) and cumulative with repeated use
• Diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting come from activation of the medullary vomiting centre and GIT serotonin receptors; weakness at extremities also occurs
• Overdose of ergotamine and ergonovine causes prolonged vasospasm
(c)
• The vasospasm is not easily reversed by serotonin antagonists
• Ergot alkaloids are most effective given early in an attack
(d)
• Restrict to patients with frequent moderate or infrequent severe attacks; do not combine with beta blockers or triptans
• Oral ergotamine has low bioavailability due to first-pass metabolism; caffeine (100 mg per 1 mg ergotamine, Cafergot) improves absorption
questions.question:
A migraine patient who has been repeatedly taking an ergot alkaloid for severe attacks presents with cold, weak extremities, diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting.
(a) Identify the offending drug class.
(b) Explain the mechanism of toxicity.
(c) State the management and any limits of antagonists.
(d) Identify at-risk patients and preventive points.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Strong albumin binding, extensive tissue distribution and hepatic metabolism with long elimination half-life
(b)
• Rapidly absorbed orally; 90-95% bound to plasma albumin at therapeutic concentrations; binds extravascular tissues giving very large distribution volumes (10-50 L/kg) and low elimination rates
• Metabolised in the liver by N-demethylation and ring hydroxylation; metabolites are often active (imipramine → desipramine, amitriptyline → nortriptyline); glucuronides excreted in urine
• Half-lives range 10-20 h for imipramine and desipramine to about 80 h for protriptyline, and are longer in the elderly
(c)
• Gradual accumulation leads to slowly developing side effects; antidepressant effect takes 2-4 weeks like other antidepressants
• Nortriptyline shows a narrow therapeutic window: too high a plasma concentration reduces the antidepressant effect
(d)
• Haemodialysis is ineffective for increasing elimination because of tissue sequestration and albumin binding
• Side effects: sedation, atropine-like effects, postural hypotension, QT prolongation
questions.question:
An elderly patient is prescribed a tricyclic antidepressant. Side effects such as daytime drowsiness develop slowly, and the prescriber asks whether dialysis would remove the drug in overdose.
(a) Identify the pharmacokinetic processes involved.
(b) Explain the effect on absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, onset and accumulation.
(c) State the dosing and monitoring points.
(d) Name the clinical consequence.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Benzodiazepines: short (triazolam, midazolam), intermediate (oxazepam, temazepam, lorazepam, alprazolam) and long acting (diazepam, clonazepam, flurazepam, nitrazepam); barbiturates: ultrashort (thiopental), short (pentobarbital), intermediate (amobarbital), long (phenobarbital)
• Benzodiazepines increase frequency of GABA-Cl- channel opening; barbiturates bind a different site and prolong the duration of opening, and at high concentration are GABA-mimetic
• Benzodiazepine actions: anxiolytic, sedative, hypnotic, anticonvulsant, central muscle relaxation, anterograde amnesia; barbiturates also depress excitatory transmitters and act on RAS and cortex
(b)
• Benzodiazepines: well absorbed, protein bound 60-95%, lipid soluble, hepatic CYP oxidation and glucuronide conjugation, many active metabolites, cross placenta and enter breast milk; diazepam half-life 20-80 h
• Barbiturates: well absorbed, redistributed from brain to muscle and fat; hepatic microsomal metabolism (phenobarbital largely excreted unchanged); excretion increased in alkaline urine; powerful enzyme inducers
(c)
• Benzodiazepine uses: anxiety, insomnia, seizures, spasm, alcohol withdrawal, pre-anaesthesia; adverse effects: sedation, ataxia, amnesia, tolerance, dependence
• Barbiturate uses: ultrashort-acting thiopental for IV anaesthesia; no longer used as sedative-hypnotics or antiepileptic (phenobarbital) because safer drugs exist
• Barbiturate adverse effects: hangover, tolerance, dependence, respiratory depression, skin eruptions, porphyria, placental transfer
(d)
• Benzodiazepines have a wide safety margin, lower abuse liability, no hepatic enzyme induction, little REM depression, and flumazenil as antagonist
• Barbiturates have a narrow safety margin, high abuse liability, strong enzyme induction, REM depression with rebound and nightmares, and no specific antagonist
• Flumazenil is not effective against barbiturate overdose
• Barbiturate overdose is managed by supporting respiration and circulation, alkalinising urine, promoting diuresis, and dialysis
questions.question:
A. Compare benzodiazepines and barbiturates.
(a) State the classification, mechanism of action and pharmacological actions of each.
(b) State the pharmacokinetics of each.
(c) State the therapeutic uses and adverse effects.
(d) Distinguish the two groups from each other.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Auto-induction: carbamazepine induces its own metabolism and the metabolism of other drugs
(b)
• Because of auto-induction, serum concentrations fall as metabolism increases, and other drugs' metabolism is also increased
• The slow-release preparation (Tegretol CR 200 mg, 400 mg) allows twice-daily ingestion and avoids high peak serum concentrations
(c)
• Introduce at low dosage and increase steadily over about a month
• Therapeutic drug monitoring is an integral component of management with phenytoin and carbamazepine; check when control is poor, with sudden changes in control, for adherence and interactions; stabilised patients may be checked once a year
(d)
• Rapid introduction can cause side effects; adverse events occur in up to a third of patients, only about 5% need withdrawal
• Dose-related effects: ataxia, dizziness, blurred vision, diplopia; poor control may follow induction of its own metabolism
questions.question:
A patient newly started on carbamazepine has falling drug levels after a few weeks and is also taking other medicines. The prescriber considers a slow-release formulation.
(a) Identify the pharmacokinetic process involved.
(b) Explain the effect on onset, duration, accumulation and co-administered drugs.
(c) State the dose adjustment and monitoring.
(d) Name the clinical consequence.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Methyldopa: widely used in the past, its main application now is management of hypertension during pregnancy
(b)
• Methyldopa → alpha-methyldopamine → alpha-methylnorepinephrine, stored and released on stimulation; stimulates central alpha-2 receptors → reduced peripheral sympathetic outflow
• It enters the brain via an aromatic amino acid transporter; half-life 2 h but effect persists 24 h or more; bioavailability 25%; maximum effect at 2 g daily in divided doses
• The vasomotor centres retain sensitivity to baroreceptor control, so postural hypotension is not uncommon
(c)
• Avoid ACE inhibitors, ARBs and aliskiren: contraindicated in pregnancy; ARBs show fetal toxicity especially in the second and third trimesters
• Calcium channel blockers are used in pregnancy only when absolutely indicated, when benefit outweighs risk, and they enter breast milk
(d)
• Adverse effects: sedation, mental slowing, nightmares, vertigo, depression, lactation, raised prolactin, positive Coombs test (10-20% after 12 months), haemolytic anaemia, hepatitis, drug fever
• Alternative agents named for hypertension in general: first-line ACE inhibitors/ARBs, calcium channel antagonists, thiazides; second-line beta blockers, alpha blockers; hydralazine and clonidine are others
questions.question:
A hypertensive patient is also pregnant. A prescriber is choosing between several antihypertensive classes.
(a) Select the drug that is the main application in pregnancy and justify it.
(b) State its mechanism of action and expected pharmacodynamic effect.
(c) Name the drug classes to avoid in pregnancy and why, and mention the position on calcium channel blockers.
(d) State the adverse effects of the chosen drug to be monitored and the alternative agents given.

A patient with epilepsy on phenytoin has a small dose increase and the serum level rises disproportionately, with signs of toxicity.
(a) Identify the pharmacokinetic process involved.
(b) Explain the effect on serum concentration, accumulation and metabolism.
(c) State the dose adjustment and monitoring.
(d) Name the clinical consequence and the formulation point for parenteral use.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Non-linear dose-serum level relationship of phenytoin, which is metabolised in the liver
(b)
• Small dose changes may produce considerable changes in serum level, so accumulation can occur
• Metabolism is mainly by CYP2C9 and CYP2C10 and to a lesser extent CYP2C19, by para-hydroxylation of the phenyl groups to inactive metabolites that are conjugated with glucuronic acid and excreted in urine
(c)
• Therapeutic drug monitoring is an integral part of management with phenytoin and carbamazepine; stabilised patients may be checked once a year
• Withdraw slowly (50 mg every 2 weeks when changing drug, every 4 weeks for total withdrawal); phenytoin is currently rarely used
(d)
• Consequence: toxicity or loss of seizure control from small dose changes; it alters Na+, K+ and Ca2+ conductance and membrane potential
• Fosphenytoin is a more soluble phosphate ester prodrug for parenteral use, rapidly converted to phenytoin in plasma

questions.question:
A patient with Parkinson disease taking levodopa with carbidopa is also given a non-selective monoamine oxidase inhibitor, an antihypertensive, oral iron tablets and an antipsychotic.
(a) Identify the type of each interaction.
(b) Explain the mechanism of each.
(c) Predict the clinical outcome.
(d) State how to manage or avoid them.
questions.answerText:
(a)
MAO-A inhibitor (e.g. phenelzine) with levodopa: pharmacodynamic; antihypertensives: additive pharmacodynamic; antipsychotics: pharmacodynamic antagonism; oral iron: pharmacokinetic (absorption)
(b)
• Levodopa is converted by aromatic amino acid decarboxylase to dopamine; with MAO-A inhibitors this produces a hypertensive crisis
• Levodopa can enhance the hypotensive effect of antihypertensive agents and may antagonise the action of antipsychotics
• Concomitant oral iron preparations may reduce levodopa absorption
(c)
• Hypertensive crisis with MAO-A inhibitors; extra hypotension (orthostatic) with antihypertensives; reduced antipsychotic effect; reduced levodopa effect with iron
• Levodopa itself commonly causes nausea, vomiting and orthostatic hypotension
(d)
• Avoid levodopa for at least 2 weeks after stopping an MAO-A inhibitor (non-selective forms are rarely prescribed now)
• Levodopa should be taken 30 minutes before food because dietary protein interferes with absorption; domperidone 10 or 20 mg three times daily may control nausea

questions.question:
A. Describe the mechanism of local anaesthetic action and the factors governing potency, onset and duration.
(a) State the sequence of events at the nerve and the clinical sequence of block.
(b) State the physicochemical determinants.
(c) Relate these to examples given.
(d) Explain the clinical significance and limitation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Local anaesthetics reach the inner axonal membrane through open Na+ channels or directly through the membrane and bind sodium channels, blocking initiation and propagation of the action potential by preventing depolarisation
• Sequence of block: sympathetic block (vasodilatation), loss of pain and temperature, proprioception, touch and pressure, then motor function
• Local anaesthetics cause reversible conduction block, so the person remains conscious
(b)
• Potency relates to lipid solubility; duration relates to plasma protein binding
• They are weak bases (pKa 8-9), so activity is strongly pH dependent; ionised forms are important for binding
• Vasoconstrictors (adrenaline, felypressin) restrict absorption, prolonging action and reducing toxicity
(c)
• Bupivacaine (95% bound) lasts longer than lidocaine and mepivacaine; bupivacaine 4 h vs lidocaine 120 min
• Epidural and spinal routes: bradycardia, hypotension, respiratory depression from sympathetic block
• Surface agents (lidocaine, tetracaine) have systemic toxicity risk with large areas
(d)
• Regional block (lidocaine 1%, bupivacaine 0.5%) numbs an entire body portion and needs training
• Esters are allergenic via PABA; amides preferred
• Toxicity increases if rapidly absorbed but slowly metabolised

(a)
• Fatty acid antiepileptic (valproic acid and amide derivatives valpromide, valnoctamide)
• Broad mechanism: acts on voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels and on GABA turnover
• Broad-spectrum, effective across the complete range of seizure types with particular value in idiopathic generalised epilepsies
(b)
• First-line for generalised tonic-clonic seizures and focal seizures; first-line for tonic/atonic seizures; absence and myoclonic seizures (adjunct for absence, first-line for myoclonic)
• Available as Epilim 200 mg and Epilim Chrono 500 mg; intravenous valproate is second-line in status epilepticus
• Valproic acid is among drugs effective in minor attacks
(c)
• Adverse effects: nausea, diarrhoea, weight gain, alopecia, skin rash, thrombocytopenia
• More teratogenic than other commonly used AEDs; avoid in women of childbearing age
• TDM only for suspected toxicity, deterioration in control, adherence or interactions
(d)
• Withdraw slowly (200-400 mg every 2 weeks when changing drug, every 4 weeks for total withdrawal)
• Compared with ethosuximide it is not restricted to absence seizures
• Compared with carbamazepine it is effective in absence and myoclonic seizures where carbamazepine may be harmful

A patient takes aspirin first at an analgesic dose and later at a high anti-inflammatory dose, and develops tinnitus. The prescriber considers changing urine pH.
(a) Identify the pharmacokinetic processes involved.
(b) Explain the effect of dose on elimination, half-life and accumulation, and the effect of urine pH.
(c) State dosing adjustment and monitoring.
(d) Name the clinical consequence.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Rapid hydrolysis of aspirin to salicylate (first-pass), glucuronide/glycine conjugation, dose-dependent renal elimination
(b)
• Well absorbed from stomach and duodenum, peak plasma level in 1-2 hours; highly protein bound; crosses the blood-brain barrier
• About 75% of salicylate is conjugated to glucuronic acid and glycine (salicyluric acid is the glycine conjugate); 25% is excreted unchanged
• Half-life is 3-6 hours at analgesic doses (first-order kinetics) and 15-30 hours at anti-inflammatory doses (zero-order kinetics), so accumulation occurs at high doses
• Alkalinisation of the urine increases excretion
(c)
• Take with food; capsules, tablets, enteric-coated tablets and suppositories are available
• Tinnitus occurs at plasma levels of 200-450 mg/mL and resolves 2-3 days after withdrawal, a sign of salicylism
(d)
Higher doses risk salicylism and toxicity because elimination saturates

(a)
• Four classes: natural alkaloids (morphine, codeine, thebaine); semi-synthetic (heroin, oxycodone, hydrocodone, hydromorphone); synthetic (pethidine, methadone, fentanyl, tramadol, pentazocine, buprenorphine); endogenous peptides (endorphins, dynorphins, enkephalins)
• Bind G-protein coupled opioid receptors in brain, spinal cord and periphery, lowering pain perception; all share analgesia, withdrawal on stopping and suppression of morphine withdrawal
• Effects: euphoria, drowsiness, miosis, reduced heart rate and BP, constipation, nausea, antitussive effect
(b)
• Opium is slowly absorbed and less effective than pure morphine; codeine is 1-2% of opium and 15% as active as morphine; heroin is 2-3 times as potent via lipid solubility
• Fentanyl patch lasts up to 72 hours; methadone accumulates in lipid tissue with long duration; tramadol has minimal effect on respiratory rate, heart rate, BP or GI transit at recommended dose
(c)
• Uses: acute and moderate chronic pain; codeine in cough suppressants and antidiarrhoeals; loperamide and diphenoxylate in diarrhoea; methadone in addiction maintenance; remifentanil/alfentanil in anaesthesia
• Adverse effects: sedation, respiratory depression, constipation, miosis, nausea, dependence, tolerance; raised intracranial pressure rarely
• Naloxone treats overdose; naltrexone and nalorphine are other antagonists
(d)
• Opioids act centrally, cause dependence, are controlled drugs, have no ceiling and no anti-inflammatory effect, and are used for severe pain
• Non-opioids act peripherally, have anti-inflammatory effect, have a ceiling effect, cause no dependence and are used for mild to moderate pain
• Non-opioid adverse effects: gastric irritation, bleeding problems
• Tramadol should not be used by patients allergic to codeine

questions.answerText:
(a)
Parkinson disease treated with levodopa plus carbidopa (co-careldopa, Sinemet) or benserazide (co-beneldopa, Madopar)
(b)
• Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons from substantia nigra pars compacta to striatum reduces dopamine; levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted by aromatic amino acid decarboxylase to dopamine stored in surviving nigrostriatal terminals
• The decarboxylase inhibitor blocks peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine, allowing a lower levodopa dose
(c)
• Use: first-line symptomatic therapy; no drug has proven disease-modifying effect
• Common adverse effects: nausea, vomiting, orthostatic hypotension; later vivid dreams, nightmares, confusional state (may indicate PD dementia)
• Long term: wearing-off effect, response fluctuations and dyskinesia after years of treatment
(d)
• Avoid for at least 2 weeks after stopping MAO-A inhibitors (hypertensive crisis); enhances antihypertensive effect; antagonises antipsychotics; absorption reduced by oral iron
• IR start 50 mg three times daily, maximum 600 mg/day, taken 30 minutes before food

A. Describe the adverse reactions of NSAIDs.
(a) Classify the reactions and give the mechanism with examples.
(b) State the aspirin-specific and non-prostaglandin-mediated reactions.
(c) State how they are recognised.
(d) State how they are prevented or managed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• GI: decreased PG synthesis reduces mucus and HCO3- secretion and enhances acid secretion, giving erosion, ulceration, blood loss, occult bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia
• Platelet: inhibition of proaggregatory TXA2 predominates → prolonged bleeding time
• Renal: impaired renal blood flow and GFR, Na+ and water retention, renal insufficiency in susceptible patients
• Obstetric/fetal: delay or prolongation of labour, premature closure of fetal ductus arteriosus
(b)
• Hypersensitivity: aspirin-precipitated asthma, urticaria, angioneurotic swelling, rhinitis, nasal polyps, anaphylactoid reactions
• Reye's syndrome: fulminant hepatitis with cerebral oedema in children with viral infections, especially under 12
• Hepatic, dermal (photosensitivity, Stevens-Johnson, toxic epidermal necrolysis) and CNS (headache, tinnitus, deafness, confusion) effects unrelated to PG inhibition
(c)
GI pain and occult blood loss; tinnitus signals salicylate excess; bleeding tendency; oedema
(d)
• Take aspirin with food; use enteric-coated forms
• Avoid in peptic ulcer, asthma, viral infection in children, chronic kidney disease, allergy
• COX-2 selective inhibitors and paracetamol are relatively safer for the stomach
• Salicylate poisoning: no antidote; ABCD, IV fluids, charcoal, bicarbonate to urine pH above 8, dialysis if needed

(a)
Clonidine (centrally acting sympatholytic; hypertensive crisis on sudden withdrawal)
(b)
Reduces sympathetic outflow by stimulating central alpha-2 adrenoceptors: lowers cardiac output (reduced heart rate and relaxed capacitance vessels) and peripheral vascular resistance; renal blood flow is maintained
(c)
• Management of the hypertensive crisis: clonidine plus alpha- and beta-adrenoceptor blocking agents
• Tricyclic antidepressants block its antihypertensive effect
(d)
• Symptoms occur after omitting 1-2 doses; abrupt discontinuation can lead to hypertensive crisis
• Contraindicated in patients with depression; adverse effects include sedation
• PK: oral and transdermal forms (transdermal effective for 7 days, less sedation but more skin reactions); half-life 8-12 h, bioavailability 95%, dosed twice daily
• Withdrawal should be avoided

A. Describe carbamazepine.
(a) State its class, mechanism of action and pharmacokinetics.
(b) State its uses and dose practice.
(c) State its adverse effects, interactions and cautions.
(d) Explain the basis of toxicity and the principle of its management and monitoring.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Carboxamide antiepileptic drug acting by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels
• PK: exhibits auto-induction, inducing its own metabolism and that of other drugs; slow-release form allows twice-daily dosing and avoids high peak levels
(b)
• First-line for generalised tonic-clonic and focal seizures; also in the group effective for major attacks (with phenytoin, primidone)
• Not effective in absence and myoclonic seizures, where it may be deleterious
• Introduce at low dosage and increase steadily over a month
(c)
• Adverse events in up to a third of patients; about 5% require withdrawal (skin rash, gastrointestinal upset, hyponatraemia)
• Dose-related: ataxia, dizziness, blurred vision, diplopia; idiosyncratic skin rash in up to 10%; rarely erythema multiforme and Stevens-Johnson syndrome
• Hepatic failure and bone marrow depression are extremely uncommon
(d)
• Induction of metabolism produces interactions with other drugs; therapeutic drug monitoring is integral and useful for adherence and interactions
• Withdraw gradually (100-200 mg every 2 or 4 weeks) to avoid rebound seizures
• A benzodiazepine can cover rapid withdrawal if life-threatening side effects occur

(a)
• Five groups: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, niacin, fibrates, bile acid-binding resins, and inhibitors of intestinal sterol absorption
• Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase; niacin reduces VLDL secretion and adipose lipase flux of free fatty acids; fibrates are PPAR-alpha ligands increasing lipoprotein lipase hydrolysis of triglyceride
• Resins (colestipol, cholestyramine, colesevelam) bind bile acids and prevent reabsorption; ezetimibe selectively inhibits phytosterol and cholesterol reabsorption
(b)
• Statins: raised aminotransferases, rare myopathy; niacin: prostaglandin-mediated flushing, dizziness, palpitations
• Fibrates (gemfibrozil, fenofibrate): rashes, GIT symptoms, myopathy, arrhythmias, hypokalaemia, raised aminotransferases/alkaline phosphatase, rhabdomyolysis
• Resins: nausea, bloating, constipation or diarrhoea, fatty stool and hyperchloraemic acidosis in large doses; ezetimibe: rarely myositis
(c)
• Resins impair absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, digitalis, thiazides, warfarin, tetracycline, thyroxine, fluvastatin, iron, penicillin; colestyramine reduces coumarin anticoagulant effect
• Myopathy risk rises when fibrates or niacin are added to a statin
• Combinations: niacin + statin (familial combined hyperlipoproteinaemia); statin + ezetimibe (highly synergistic); statin + fenofibrate (raised LDL and VLDL); resins + ezetimibe + niacin + statin for severe raised LDL
(d)
• Use the lowest effective doses and monitor closely for toxicity; monitor liver with statin + fenofibrate
• Give other drugs at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after the resin
• Statins are not given in pregnancy and are used with caution in liver disease
questions.question:
A. Describe the lipid-lowering drugs as a group.
(a) Classify them and state the mechanism of action of each group.
(b) State the main adverse effects of each group.
(c) State the drug interactions and the useful combinations.
(d) Explain how toxicity is monitored and prevented.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Methadone (accumulation in lipid tissue) and fentanyl (lollipop and patch)
(b)
• Methadone accumulates in lipid tissue outside the CNS, giving slow onset and long duration; used as a weaning drug and for long-term maintenance of addiction
• Fentanyl is a short-acting analgesic (500x pethidine); lollipop form for breakthrough pain, long-acting patch effective up to 72 hours
• Alfentanil is ultrashort acting; remifentanil is shortest acting with rapid offset after prolonged infusion; sufentanil is 5-10 times fentanyl
(c)
• Methadone is used as the racemate; the R-isomer is 7-50 times as potent as the S-isomer
• Short-acting opioids work within an hour for about 4 hours; long-acting controlled-release forms release over 8 to 12 hours or longer, taken at regular times such as every 12 hours
(d)
• Methadone can substitute for other opioids because narcotic analgesics suppress each other's withdrawal signs
• Heroin's greater lipid solubility gives rapid CNS penetration

A. Describe the adverse reactions and interactions of the diuretics.
(a) Classify the diuretics and give the mechanism of toxicity with examples.
(b) State the electrolyte and metabolic effects of each group.
(c) State the drug interactions and how the problems are recognised.
(d) State how they are prevented or managed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Groups: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide), osmotic diuretics (mannitol, urea), loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide, ethacrynic acid), thiazides (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorothiazide), K+-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, amiloride, triamterene)
• Loop diuretics inhibit the Na+-K+-2Cl- co-transporter in the thick ascending limb; thiazides inhibit the Na+-Cl- co-transporter in the early distal tubule; amiloride and triamterene block ENaC; spironolactone antagonises aldosterone
(b)
• Loop: volume depletion, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia; ototoxicity with IV or high doses or with aminoglycosides, ethacrynic acid worse
• Thiazides: hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia, hyperuricaemia and gout, worsened diabetes, photosensitivity, reduced libido
• K+-sparing: hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis; spironolactone has anti-androgenic effects (low libido, gynaecomastia) and is contraindicated in males
• Acetazolamide causes acidosis; sulfonamide loop diuretics are contraindicated in sulfa hypersensitivity
(c)
• NSAIDs reduce BP-lowering effect of thiazides; ACE inhibitors may be beneficial with them
• Diuretic-induced hypokalaemia raises digoxin toxicity; thiazides and urate share the organic anion transporter, reducing urate excretion
• Gynaecomastia, ototoxicity and gout flare are recognisable clinical signs; electrolyte tests are implied
(d)
• K+-sparing diuretics are combined with thiazides (HCTZ/amiloride, HCTZ/triamterene) to counter potassium loss
• Avoid ethacrynic acid and high-dose IV loop diuretics with aminoglycosides to avoid hearing loss

questions.question:
A. Describe the antidepressant drugs as a therapeutic group.
(a) Classify the drugs and give the mechanism of each group.
(b) State the clinical uses of each group.
(c) Compare the groups by adverse effects.
(d) State the precautions and non-drug options.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Groups: MAO inhibitors; monoamine uptake inhibitors (SSRIs, TCAs, SNRIs, noradrenaline/dopamine uptake inhibitors); monoamine receptor antagonists (mirtazapine, trazodone, mianserin); St John's wort
• MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine irreversible; moclobemide reversible MAO-A-selective) raise cytoplasmic monoamines; SNRIs (venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, duloxetine, milnacipran) block 5-HT and noradrenaline uptake
• Bupropion inhibits noradrenaline and dopamine uptake; reboxetine and atomoxetine selectively block noradrenaline uptake; mirtazapine blocks alpha-2, 5-HT2C, 5-HT2A, 5-HT3 and H1 receptors
(b)
• Depression, anxiety (venlafaxine, duloxetine), OCD (SSRIs), neuropathic pain/fibromyalgia (duloxetine, milnacipran), bupropion for nicotine dependence, atomoxetine for ADHD, desvenlafaxine for hot flushes, duloxetine urinary incontinence
• Lithium and carbamazepine for bipolar disorder; fluoxetine for bulimia; TCAs for enuresis and chronic pain
(c)
• MAOIs: hypotension, tremor, insomnia, weight gain, atropine-like effects, rare hydrazine hepatotoxicity, cheese reaction
• TCAs: sedation, atropine-like effects, postural hypotension, QT prolongation; SNRIs: headache, insomnia, sexual dysfunction, dry mouth; duloxetine hepatotoxic
• Mianserin: bone marrow depression requiring blood counts; mirtazapine: sedation via H1 block
(d)
• Overdose: TCAs dangerous; SNRIs CNS depression, serotonin toxicity, seizures; duloxetine contraindicated in hepatic impairment
• 30-40% of patients show no improvement; effects take weeks, with receptor adaptation (beta-1 and alpha-2 downregulation) and neurogenesis proposed
• Non-drug options: electroconvulsive therapy, electromagnetic therapy, deep brain stimulation, vagus stimulation with more rapid onset
• Atypical antidepressants have fewer sedative and anticholinergic effects and lower toxicity in overdose

questions.question:
A. Describe fluoxetine.
(a) State its class, mechanism of action and pharmacokinetics.
(b) State its uses.
(c) State its adverse effects, contraindications and interactions.
(d) Explain the delayed therapeutic effect and the principle of its safe use.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, among the most commonly prescribed antidepressants
• Blocks 5-HT reuptake; also has 5-HT2C antagonist activity, shared with mirtazapine, which may contribute to its effect in anorexia and bulimia
• PK: well absorbed; plasma half-life 24-96 h (longer acting than other SSRIs)
(b)
• Uses: depression and anxiety disorders, obsessive compulsive disorder, bulimia
• Not as effective as TCAs in severe depression; individual patients may respond better to one SSRI than another
(c)
• Adverse effects: nausea, anorexia, insomnia, loss of libido and failure of orgasm; reports of aggression and violence not confirmed by controlled studies
• Inhibits TCA metabolism through CYP2D6, so it is not combined with TCAs (increased TCA toxicity)
• With MAOIs it can cause serotonin syndrome with tremor, hyperthermia and cardiovascular collapse; deaths have occurred
• Not recommended for depression under 18 years (doubtful efficacy, excitement, insomnia, aggression, suicidal ideation concern)
(d)
• Acute 5-HT rise activates somatodendritic 5-HT1A autoreceptors, limiting release; desensitisation on prolonged treatment explains the 2-4 week delay
• Pindolol (5-HT1A affinity) has been used with SSRIs to speed onset
• Safer in overdose than TCAs and with fewer anticholinergic effects

questions.question:
A patient with moderate depression and an anxiety disorder is started on a drug that inhibits the serotonin transporter. Nausea, insomnia and loss of libido develop, and no benefit is seen in the first two weeks.
(a) Identify the drug class and give examples.
(b) State the mechanism of action and explain the delayed onset.
(c) State the therapeutic uses and key adverse effects.
(d) State the contraindications or precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors: fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, paroxetine, sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram; the most commonly prescribed antidepressants
(b)
• Block 5-HT reuptake; acutely, rise in synaptic 5-HT is limited because increased 5-HT activates somatodendritic 5-HT1A autoreceptors on raphe neurons, inhibiting 5-HT release
• On prolonged treatment these 5-HT1A receptors desensitise, so 5-HT release rises; a delay of 2-4 weeks precedes therapeutic effect
(c)
• Uses: depression (as effective as TCAs and MAOIs in moderate depression, probably less than TCAs in severe), anxiety disorders, obsessive compulsive disorder; fluoxetine in bulimia
• Adverse effects: nausea, anorexia, insomnia, loss of libido, failure of orgasm (postsynaptic 5-HT2, 5-HT3, 5-HT4 stimulation); fewer anticholinergic effects and safer in overdose than TCAs; no cheese reaction
(d)
• Not recommended for depression in children under 18 (doubtful efficacy; excitement, insomnia, aggression, possible suicidal ideation)
• With MAOIs: serotonin syndrome (tremor, hyperthermia, cardiovascular collapse); paroxetine and fluoxetine inhibit TCA metabolism via CYP2D6
• Plasma half-lives 18-24 h; fluoxetine 24-96 h

(a)
• Non-barbiturate intravenous anaesthetic, 10 mg/ml injectable lipid emulsion (Diprivan)
• Increases GABA-mediated inhibitory tone by decreasing dissociation of GABA from the receptor, prolonging chloride channel opening and hyperpolarising cells
(b)
• Most common induction agent in current use; can maintain anaesthesia by slow IV infusion instead of inhaled agents
• Associated with less postoperative nausea and vomiting and more rapid return to consciousness
(c)
• Decreases blood pressure, depresses or even stops breathing, causes pain on injection
• Lipid emulsion can be a medium for rapid bacterial growth without meticulous aseptic precautions
(d)
• It has displaced barbiturates (thiopental) in many practices; other IV agents: ketamine, fentanyl, midazolam (amnesia)
• Inhaled agents: nitrous oxide, halothane, sevoflurane, desflurane, isoflurane; sevoflurane allows inhalation induction in adults
• Balanced anaesthesia combines inhaled and IV drugs
• Opioids work synergistically with induction agents

A. Describe the adverse reactions of antipsychotic drugs.
(a) Classify the adverse reactions and give the mechanism with examples.
(b) State the endocrine, cardiac and metabolic effects.
(c) State how the reactions are recognised.
(d) State how they are prevented or managed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Extrapyramidal effects from D2 blockade in nigrostriatal pathway: acute dystonia (spasm of tongue, face, neck, back), akathisia (restlessness), parkinsonism (bradykinesia, tremor, rigidity), tardive dyskinesia (repetitive oral-facial and choreiform movements)
• Anticholinergic: dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, loss of accommodation, glaucoma aggravation; alpha-1 block: orthostatic hypotension, sexual dysfunction; H1 block: sedation, weight gain
(b)
• Endocrine: D2 blockade in tuberohypophyseal pathway raises prolactin → gynaecomastia, galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, infertility
• Cardiac: K+ channel block prolongs QT → ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death
• Metabolic: raised triglycerides, hyperglycaemia and diabetes (more with atypicals, especially clozapine and olanzapine); lowered seizure threshold
(c)
• Tardive dyskinesia occurs after months or years in 20-40% on first-generation drugs; acute dystonia in the first weeks
• Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: mental status change, rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic dysfunction (fatal, idiosyncratic)
• Hyperprolactinaemia case: amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea with high-potency haloperidol most likely
(d)
• Antimuscarinic drugs blunt excitatory tone for EPS; atypicals give less EPS
• Regular full blood counts for clozapine (agranulocytosis, first 6 months)
• Tardive dyskinesia may be irreversible and may worsen when therapy is stopped
• Dementia patients have increased cerebrovascular events and mortality

(a)
• Dopamine precursor, the most effective first-line oral symptomatic treatment for Parkinson disease; given with peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor carbidopa or benserazide
• Crosses the blood-brain barrier, converted by aromatic amino acid decarboxylase to dopamine stored in surviving nigrostriatal terminals; peripheral conversion is blocked by the inhibitor, allowing lower doses
• Bioavailability: IR 90-100%, CR 60-70%; protein diet interferes with absorption; COMT converts levodopa peripherally to inert 3-O-methyldopa
(b)
• IR start 50 mg three times daily to maximum 600 mg/day; take 30 minutes before food
• CR forms help nocturnal akinesia and end-of-dose deterioration
(c)
• Adverse effects: nausea, vomiting, orthostatic hypotension, vivid dreams, nightmares, confusional state
• Interactions: MAO-A inhibitors (hypertensive crisis; avoid 2 weeks), antihypertensives, antipsychotics, oral iron
• Increase the dose slowly or co-prescribe domperidone 10 or 20 mg three times daily for nausea
(d)
• After years of treatment: wearing-off and response fluctuations, dyskinesia, related as much to disease duration
• Add-ons: entacapone 200 mg with each dose (peripheral COMT inhibition), MAO-B inhibitors, controlled-release levodopa
• Amantadine is the only drug licensed as antidyskinetic
• Surgery (lesioning, deep brain stimulation) helps motor fluctuations or dyskinesia
