questions.answerText:
(a)
• Irreversible non-selective: phenelzine, tranylcypromine, iproniazid; reversible MAO-A-selective: moclobemide
• They raise 5-HT most, noradrenaline and dopamine least in brain and periphery, mainly in the cytoplasmic pool, increasing spontaneous leakage and release by indirectly acting amines
(b)
• Hypotension (accumulated false amines such as octopamine displace noradrenaline), tremor, excitement, insomnia, convulsions in overdose
• Increased appetite and weight gain; atropine-like effects; rare hydrazine hepatotoxicity (phenelzine, iproniazid; under 1 in 10 000)
• Effects on amine metabolism develop rapidly and a single dose lasts several days; antidepressant effect is delayed
(c)
• Cheese reaction with tyramine (at least 10 mg) from ripe cheeses and yeast extracts such as Marmite
• Severe hypertension with ephedrine and amphetamine; hypertensive episodes with TCAs; serotonin syndrome with SSRIs; levodopa with MAO-A inhibitors
• MAOIs inhibit enzymes involved in the metabolism of other drugs
(d)
• Recognise cheese reaction by acute hypertension, severe throbbing headache and possible intracranial haemorrhage
• Prevent by dietary restriction and avoidance of sympathomimetics and other antidepressants; use moclobemide to reduce interactions
• Avoid in liver disease
• Use has declined because of interactions

(a)
TCA + paroxetine/fluoxetine: pharmacokinetic (inhibited metabolism); MAOI + SSRI: pharmacodynamic; MAOI + tyramine-rich food: drug-food pharmacodynamic
(b)
• Paroxetine and fluoxetine inhibit TCA hepatic metabolism through CYP2D6
• SSRIs plus MAOIs raise serotonin excessively; MAO inhibition lets dietary tyramine (normally metabolised by MAO in gut wall and liver) be absorbed and enhances its sympathomimetic effect
(c)
• Increased TCA toxicity; serotonin syndrome with tremor, hyperthermia and cardiovascular collapse, from which deaths have occurred
• Cheese reaction: acute hypertension, severe throbbing headache, occasionally intracranial haemorrhage; at least 10 mg tyramine is needed
• Hypertensive episodes also reported with TCA plus MAOI together
(d)
• Do not combine paroxetine or fluoxetine with TCAs; avoid SSRIs with MAOIs; avoid ripe cheeses and concentrated yeast products (Marmite) on MAOIs
• Avoid indirectly acting sympathomimetics (ephedrine, amphetamine); directly acting noradrenaline is not hazardous; moclobemide (MAO-A reversible) does not cause the cheese reaction because MAO-B can still metabolise tyramine
questions.question:
A patient on a tricyclic antidepressant is given fluoxetine or paroxetine for added effect; another patient on an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor receives an SSRI and also eats ripe cheese.
(a) Identify the type of each interaction.
(b) Explain the mechanisms.
(c) Predict the clinical outcome.
(d) State how to manage or avoid them.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Classes: diuretics, sympatholytics (beta blockers, alpha-1 blockers, centrally acting drugs, adrenergic neuron blockers), calcium channel blockers, vasodilators, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, renin inhibitor (aliskiren)
• Diuretics reduce blood volume and cardiac output; ACE inhibitors/ARBs block angiotensin II; CCBs block L-type calcium channels, relax arteriolar smooth muscle and reduce peripheral resistance
• Beta blockers reduce cardiac output and renin release; alpha-1 blockers (prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin) dilate arterioles and veins; clonidine and methyldopa stimulate central alpha-2 receptors; minoxidil opens K+ channels; hydralazine dilates arterioles
(b)
• BP categories: normal below 120/80; pre-hypertension 120-139/80-89; stage 1 140-159/90-99; stage 2 160 or above/100 or above
• First-line ACD: ACE inhibitors/ARBs, calcium channel antagonists, thiazide diuretics; second line: beta blockers, aldosterone antagonists, alpha blockers, loop diuretics; direct vasodilators last line
(c)
• Thiazides: mild to moderate HTN, loop diuretics: severe HTN and emergencies; thiazide adverse effects: hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperuricaemia, glucose intolerance, raised serum lipids
• CCB adverse effects: flushing, headache, dizziness, peripheral oedema, gum hypertrophy, constipation (verapamil), tachycardia or bradycardia and heart block
• ACE inhibitors: dry cough, hyperkalaemia, angioedema; ARBs: no dry cough; beta blockers: heart block, bronchoconstriction, vivid dreams; alpha-1 blockers: postural hypotension
(d)
• Beta blockers: caution in heart block, diabetes, bronchoconstriction; clonidine contraindicated in depression and abrupt withdrawal can cause hypertensive crisis
• Vasodilators give reflex tachycardia and fluid retention and work best combined with other antihypertensive drugs
• Short-acting dihydropyridines (immediate-release nifedipine, nicardipine) should be avoided; amlodipine and felodipine allow once-daily dosing
• ACE inhibitors, ARBs and aliskiren are contraindicated in pregnancy
questions.question:
A. Describe the antihypertensive drug classes.
(a) Classify the drugs and give the mechanism of each group.
(b) Give the blood-pressure categories and the first- and second-line agents.
(c) Compare the groups by uses and adverse effects.
(d) State the precautions for each group.

A patient with raised LDL cholesterol is given a drug that is best taken in the evening and that blocks the first committed step of sterol synthesis.
(a) Identify the drug class and give examples.
(b) State the mechanism of action and the expected effect on lipids and LDL receptors.
(c) State the therapeutic role and the key adverse effects.
(d) State the contraindications and precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins): lovastatin, atorvastatin, fluvastatin, pravastatin, simvastatin, rosuvastatin
(b)
• Structural analogues of the HMG-CoA intermediate; competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting first committed step in sterol synthesis (mevalonate formation)
• Reduced hepatocyte cholesterol → increased expression of LDL receptors → greater clearance of cholesterol from plasma; most effective in lowering LDL
• Other effects: decreased oxidative stress and vascular inflammation, increased stability of atherosclerotic lesions; maximal effect in one month
(c)
• Usually the drug of first choice; lower total and LDL cholesterol; reduce coronary events and total mortality; few side effects; can be combined with resins, niacin or ezetimibe
• Evening dosing, except atorvastatin and rosuvastatin, because cholesterol synthesis is greatest at night (midnight to 2 am)
• Adverse effects: elevated serum aminotransferases; rarely myopathy, more likely with niacin or fibrates
(d)
• Not for pregnant women (cholesterol is essential for fetal development); not for homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (no LDL receptors)
• Use with caution and reduced dosage in hepatic parenchymal disease and in the elderly
• Stop temporarily in serious illness, trauma or major surgery; daily doses are lovastatin 10-80 mg, pravastatin maximum 80 mg, simvastatin 5-80 mg, rosuvastatin 5-40 mg

questions.question:
A migraine patient taking a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, or an MAO inhibitor, or lithium, or ergotamine is prescribed sumatriptan.
(a) Identify the type of interaction.
(b) Explain the mechanisms, including the vascular effects.
(c) Predict the clinical outcome.
(d) State how to manage or avoid it.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pharmacodynamic interaction between serotonergic drugs
(b)
• Triptans stimulate 5-HT1B/1D receptors, causing intracranial vasoconstriction and inhibiting neuronal firing; ergot alkaloids are also 5-HT1B/1D agonists and potent vasoconstrictors
• Triptans can also cause vasoconstriction in other vascular beds, notably the coronary and pulmonary vasculature
• SSRIs, MAOIs and lithium are other serotonergic drugs that should not be combined with triptans
(c)
Additive serotonergic and vasoconstrictor effects; ergotamine overdose can give prolonged vasospasm; combination with SSRIs/MAOIs can cause serotonin syndrome
(d)
• Do not combine triptans with ergotamine, MAOIs, lithium or SSRIs
• Pizotifen potentiates sedation of sedatives and antidepressants and should not be used with MAO inhibitors

(a)
• Centrally acting: methyldopa, clonidine, guanabenz, guanfacine; they lower sympathetic outflow from brainstem vasomotor centres and keep baroreceptor sensitivity
• Methyldopa becomes alpha-methylnorepinephrine, stimulating central alpha-2 receptors; clonidine lowers cardiac output and peripheral resistance
• Vasodilators: minoxidil (arteriolar only, active metabolite minoxidil sulfate opens K+ channels), hydralazine (arterioles not veins), nitroprusside and diazoxide IV in hypertensive emergencies
(b)
• Methyldopa: sedation, mental slowing, nightmares, vertigo, depression, raised prolactin, positive Coombs test, haemolytic anaemia, hepatitis, drug fever
• Clonidine: sedation, depression, hypertensive crisis on sudden withdrawal
• Minoxidil: tachycardia, palpitation, angina, oedema, headache, sweating, hypertrichosis
• Hydralazine: headache, nausea, anorexia, palpitations, sweating, flushing; lupus-like syndrome (arthralgia, rash, fever) at 400 mg/day or more, mainly slow acetylators
(c)
• Recognise withdrawal by nervousness, tachycardia, headache, sweating; treat with clonidine and alpha plus beta blockers
• Reflex tachycardia and fluid retention are counteracted by combining vasodilators with beta blockers and diuretics; in ischaemic heart disease reflex tachycardia may provoke ischaemic arrhythmia
(d)
• Tricyclic antidepressants block clonidine's effect; methyldopa is mainly used in pregnancy
• Hydralazine: bioavailability about 25%, fast acetylators have higher first-pass effect and weaker antihypertensive effect; dose 40-200 mg/day in 2-3 divided doses
• Minoxidil is useful in renal impairment needing maximal dilatation; half-life about 4 h with effect about 24 h

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Histoplasmosis is also known as: Cave disease; Darling's disease; Ohio valley disease; Reticuloendotheliosis; and Caver's disease. It was discovered in 1905 by Darling. It was previously misdiagnosed as tuberculosis (TB).

A(ii)
Epidemiology: Histoplasma capsulatum is found throughout the world. It is endemic in certain parts of the United States, e.g., Ohio river valley and the lower Mississippi river. It is commonly found in caves in southern and East Africa. 90% of the people in endemic areas have positive histoplasmin skin tests. Histoplasmosis is not contagious but is contracted by inhalation of the spores from disturbed soil or guano.

B(i)
Complications of histoplasmosis:
• Enlarged lymph nodes
• Severe scarring
• Adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease)

B(ii)
Fungi are eukaryotes which possess a thick chitin-containing cell wall and an ergosterol-containing cell membrane. They can grow either as budding yeast cells or slender filamentous hyphae. The hyphae may be septate or aseptate. Some of the important pathogenic fungi exhibit thermal dimorphism — hyphal form at room temperature and yeast forms at body temperature. Few fungi are pathogenic in man whereas most plant diseases are caused by fungi. They may cause superficial or deep infections.
questions.question:
Describe histoplasmosis under the following headings:

A(i) State the full names by which histoplasmosis is also known, who discovered it and when, and what disease it was previously misdiagnosed as.
A(ii) Describe the epidemiology of histoplasmosis, including where the organism is found geographically and the significance of endemic areas.
B(i) Describe the complications of histoplasmosis.
B(ii) Describe the fungi in general — their cell structure, the form in which they grow, the significance of septate versus aseptate hyphae, and the concept of thermal dimorphism.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
An amalgam is a special type of alloy in which mercury is one of the component. Dental amalgam is the most widely used filling material for posterior teeth.
Indications (Applications):
• Class I and Class II cavities
• Class V cavities where aesthetics is not important
• In combination with retentive pins to restore a crown
• For making dies
• In retrograde root canal fillings
• As a core material
Contraindications (Disadvantages as clinical limit): frank pulpal infection; mutilated tooth; severe discoloration; poor or inadequate enamel available

A(ii)
Supplied as: bulk powder and mercury; alloy and mercury in disposable capsule; preweighed alloy as tablet in tubes and mercury in sachets.
Trituration: the process of wetting all the surfaces of the alloy particles.
• Manual trituration: by hand using glass mortar and pestle
• Mechanical trituration: by mechanical amalgamator
Advantages of mechanical trituration:
• Shorter mixing time
• More standardized procedure
• Less mercury

B(i)
Advantages of amalgam restoration:
• Reasonably easy to insert
• Not too technique sensitive
• Maintains anatomic form well
• Has adequate resistance to fracture
• After a period of time prevents marginal leakage
• Has reasonably long service life
Disadvantages:
• The colour does not match tooth structure
• More brittle and can fracture if incorrectly placed
• Subject to corrosion and galvanic shock
• Eventually shows marginal breakdown
• Does not bond to tooth structure
• Risk of mercury toxicity

B(ii)
Immediate causes of amalgam failure (within a few weeks of restoration):
• Postoperative pain and hypersensitivity: occurs in unlined cavities when the thickness of the remaining pulpal dentine is less than 1mm; the dentinal thickness is therefore critical — if it is less than 1mm, the cavity must be lined to protect the pulp
• Fracture of restoration: if unsupported by healthy dentine
• Fracture of portion of remaining natural teeth: when enamel margins of the cavity are not supported by healthy dentine
questions.question:
Describe dental amalgam under the following headings:

A(i) Define amalgam and state its indications and contraindications for use as a restorative material.
A(ii) Describe how amalgam is supplied and the process of trituration, including the manual and mechanical methods and the advantages of mechanical trituration.
B(i) State the advantages and disadvantages of amalgam restoration.
B(ii) Describe the immediate causes of amalgam failure, and explain the histopathological basis for the requirement of adequate dentinal thickness for a cavity liner.

Describe candidiasis of the oral cavity under the following headings:

A(i) Describe the organism responsible for oral candidiasis, including its nature, the principal and other species involved, and its normal habitat.
A(ii) Describe the pathogenesis of candidiasis, including how the organism produces virulence factors and how the immune system responds.
B(i) Describe the diagnosis of oral candidiasis in full — clinical, microscopic, and cultural components.
B(ii) Describe angular chelitis and median rhomboid glossitis as specific forms of oral candidal infection — include predisposing factors, clinical appearance, histological findings, and management for each.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Candida is a dimorphic fungus. The principal species associated with infection is Candida albicans; others include C. glabrata, C. krusei, and C. parapsilosis. They are commensals commonly found in the mouth, vagina, throat, and large bowel. Oral carriage varies in the healthy population (about 20%). Denture wearing, pregnancy, tobacco smoking, and DM increase the carriage rate.

A(ii)
Pathogenesis: Candida is capable of shifting between different phenotypes in a reversible manner. It produces a large number of functionally distinct adhesins. Innate immunity and T cells respond to superficial infections, while neutrophils and mononuclear phagocytes play an important role in deep infections. Candida produces several substances aiding disease establishment: proteinases which encourage invasiveness; catalases that aid intracellular survival and resist oxidative killing by phagocytes; adenosine which blocks neutrophil oxygen radical production and degranulation. It is weakly pathogenic — local or systemic predisposing factors are essential. The exact mechanism by which disease is caused is unknown but may be as a result of a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to its antigen.

B(i)
Diagnosis of oral candidiasis:
• Clinical: often diagnosed on clinical presentation
• Microscopic: confirmed by microscopic studies of scrapings stained by KOH/Gram stain
• Culture: involves both quantitation (plating on Candida chromogenic agar, incubating, and counting colony-forming units) and qualitation (germ tube growth for C. albicans and carbohydrate assimilation for other species)

B(ii)
Angular chelitis: multifactorial disease of infectious origin, seen in about 30% of patients with denture stomatitis. Beta-haemolytic Streptococcus/S. aureus in patients without candidiasis; combination of these organisms seen in some cases. Clinically: erythema, fissuring, and soreness at the angle of the mouth; it is painful. Predisposing factors: deep skin folds at the angle of the mouth due to reduced vertical height; iron deficiency, riboflavin, folic acid, and B12 deficiency.
Median rhomboid glossitis: appears white to reddish in colour, smooth, nodular, or fissured midline lesion on the dorsum of the tongue, just anterior to the foramen caecum; roughly rhomboidal/oval in shape and depapillated; pathogenesis uncertain. In some patients, usually smokers, an opposing (kissing) lesion is seen on the palate. Histology: area devoid of lingual papilla with a surface covered by parakeratotic acanthotic squamous epithelium; neutrophil and lymphocytic infiltration of the epithelium together with presence of Candidal hyphae; lymphocytic infiltration of the lamina propria; thick fibrous band separating epithelium from underlying connective tissue. Antifungal treatment does not often return the papillae of the affected area.

(i)
Specific aetiological factors in this patient:
• Habits: thumb sucking (a pressure habit under Graber's general factors) contributing to anterior open bite and upper anterior spacing
• Soft tissue factors: forward tongue posture maintaining the open bite
• Space excess: leading to upper and lower anterior segment spacing
• Skeletal: possible defects of jaw growth in the vertical plane (anterior deficiency producing anterior open bite)

(ii)
Soft tissue neutral zone: tongue posture, tongue size, lips and cheek are all listed as soft tissue factors. The neutral zone is the zone where forces from the tongue on one side and the lips and cheeks on the other side are balanced. Abnormal tongue posture can push teeth outward; abnormal lip or cheek forces can push teeth inward, both resulting in malocclusion.

(iii)
Habits and malocclusion:
• Thumb or finger sucking: produces anterior open bite and anterior spacing
• Foreign objects: contribute to pressure habit-related malocclusion
• Tongue thrusting: produces anterior open bite
• Lip or cheek biting: displaces teeth through abnormal pressure
• Mentalis muscle strain (hyperactive mentalis muscle): contributes to lower labial segment malocclusion
These habits apply abnormal pressure forces that alter tooth and alveolar bone position.

(iv)
Skeletal factors:
• Congenital: sickle cell disease; Pierre Robin syndrome; Crouzon syndrome; hemi-facial macrosomia/microsomia; cleft lip and palate.
• Infectious: TMJ osteomyelitis (in the young).
• Traumatic: TMJ ankylosis; other trauma-related malocclusion.
Defects of jaw growth in three planes:
• Vertical: anterior deficiency or posterior excess — anterior open bite; reverse — deep bite
• Transverse: mandibular deficiency or maxillary excess — crossbite; reverse — scissors bite
• Antero-posterior: maxillary excess or mandibular deficiency — Class II; reverse — Class III

(v)
Space excess: tooth size arch length discrepancy in which there is more arch space than tooth material; leads to upper and lower anterior segment spacing. Space deficiency: tooth size arch length discrepancy in which there is less arch space than tooth material; leads to severe anterior segment crowding.
questions.question:
A 19-year-old male presents with a slowly progressive anterior open bite following a history of prolonged thumb sucking in childhood. He also has spacing in the upper and lower anterior segments. On examination, the clinician notes forward tongue posture and a narrow, high-arched palate.

(i) What are the specific aetiological factors contributing to this patient's malocclusion, drawn from the classification of causes?
(ii) Describe the full soft tissue neutral zone concept and how tongue posture, tongue size, and lips and cheeks each contribute to malocclusion.
(iii) State all the habits that cause malocclusion and describe the type of malocclusion each produces, where known.
(iv) List all the skeletal factors — congenital and otherwise — that cause malocclusion, including specific named syndromes.
(v) Explain space excess and space deficiency as causes of malocclusion, and link them to the types of malocclusion each produces.

Describe the classification and management of tooth discolouration in children under the following headings:
A(i) Classify tooth discolouration in children.
A(ii) Describe the causes, clinical distribution, and management of all forms of intrinsic tooth discolouration in children.
B(i) Describe the types, timing, and clinical features of tetracycline staining.
B(ii) Describe amelogenesis imperfecta and dentinogenesis imperfecta.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Classification of tooth discolouration: Extrinsic; Intrinsic.

A(ii)
Intrinsic tooth discolouration:
• Non-vital tooth discolouration: occurs in non-vital teeth.
• Enamel hypoplasia: defective enamel formation — randomly pitted, vertically grooved, very thin, though hard and translucent; defects tend to become stained but are not prone to caries unless enamel is very thin and damaged.
• Chronological enamel hypoplasia: commonest type; represents defective enamel formation as a result of systemic disorders or an insult on ameloblasts. Causes: Nutritional deficiency (Vit. A, C, D); Exanthematous disease (measles, chicken pox); Local infection or trauma; Birth injury; Prematurity; Rhesus haemolytic disease; Systemic infection; Inborn errors of metabolism e.g. phenylketonuria; Excess exposure to irradiation.
• Fluorosis: includes diffuse and dense forms.

B(i)
Tetracycline staining: May be due to prenatal, neonatal, or postnatal ingestion. Tetracycline is contraindicated from utero to 12 years postnatal. Discolouration depends on type of tetracycline: Chlortetracycline — greyish brown; Oxytetracycline — yellowish discolouration.

B(ii)
Amelogenesis imperfecta: hereditary disorder of enamel. Enamel may be randomly pitted; vertically grooved; very thin; though hard and translucent; defects tend to become stained but are not prone to caries unless enamel is very thin and damaged.
Dentinogenesis imperfecta: hereditary disorder of dentine.

questions.question:
Describe dental caries under the following headings:
A(i) Definition and nature of the disease.
A(ii) Aetiological factors.
B(i) Explain the dynamic balance between demineralisation and remineralisation, including factors that favour each.
B(ii) Distinguish between the microscopic zones of enamel caries progression.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Dental caries is a localized progressive destruction of the hard tissue of the teeth that starts from the external surface of the tooth. It is caused by demineralisation/destruction of the hard tissue of the tooth surface. It is a form of bacterial infection caused by acidogenic bacteria. It is a multifactorial disease. It is a dynamic condition — whichever process (demineralisation or remineralisation) exceeds dictates what happens to the tooth surface.

A(ii)
Aetiological factors: Microbial factor — plaque harbouring acidogenic micro-organisms (Streptococcus mutans, Lactobacilli); Dietary factor — sugar substrate (intrinsic and extrinsic); Tooth surface — pit and fissures more liable than smooth surfaces; Time — frequency of intake of cariogenic substrate is important.

B(i)
Demineralisation and remineralisation occur simultaneously. Periods of demineralisation by organic acids of microbial origin alternate with remineralisation by salivary components or therapeutic agents e.g. fluoride. The outcome tilts to whichever factor prevails overall in the oral environment.
Demineralisation factors: Sugar; Plaque; Reduced saliva; Poor oral hygiene practice.
Remineralisation factors: Fluoride; Increased salivary flow; Good oral hygiene practice to remove plaque; Buffering effect of saliva.

B(ii)
Microscopic zones of spread:
• Translucent zone: innermost part of the lesion.
• Dark zone: 2nd layer.
• Body of lesion: area of maximum demineralisation.
• Surface zone: partial demineralisation — about 10% mineral loss occurs in this layer.

questions.question:
A patient with a multilocular radiolucency of the jaw has an aspiration that yields a golden-yellow shimmering fluid.
(i) What does this finding suggest and what chair-side investigations are available for evaluating this lesion?
(ii) Describe what biopsies can confirm, distinguishing between incisional and excisional biopsy.
(iii) List all extraoral radiographic views available and state the specific view used for sinus assessment.
(iv) State what haematological tests should be requested if the lesion is suspected to be associated with a bleeding disorder.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The golden-yellow shimmering fluid suggests a cystic lesion. Chair-side investigations: Aspiration of cystic fluid (which may be golden yellow, dirty white, or blood); Shimmering test; Toluidine (vital) staining.

(ii)
Incisional biopsy: a procedure in which a small area of tissue is taken to identify the composition (or make-up) of a lesion or abnormality. Excisional biopsy: a more involved procedure where the entire abnormality or area of interest is removed. Histology is used to confirm the diagnosis. Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC) is also available.

(iii)
Extraoral radiographic views: Postero-anterior view of the jaws [and skull]; Antero-posterior view of the jaws; Occipito-mental radiograph [Sinus view or Waters view] — used for sinus assessment; Submento-vertex radiograph [jug-handle view]; Orthopantomogram; CT; MRI; Sialography.

(iv)
For a bleeding disorder: Clotting profile — used as a baseline investigation before a surgical procedure.

A(i)
Definition: Restorative interventions aim at repairing damaged, injured, diseased or discoloured teeth to retain the tooth as a functional and aesthetically acceptable unit of the arch. They involve placement of a biomaterial in an adequately prepared tooth.
Indications:
• Following destruction from a carious lesion.
• When there is need to replace or repair restorations with serious defects such as improper proximal contact, overhanging, defective open margins or poor aesthetics.
• To restore proper form and contour of fractured teeth.
• To restore proper form and function of congenitally malformed teeth e.g. peg-shaped laterals, amelogenesis imperfecta.
• Aesthetic desires of patients to improve appearance e.g. tooth discolorations.
• As part of other restorative needs e.g. in a bridge.
• Tooth wear lesions (attrition, abrasion, erosion, abfraction).

A(ii)
Intracoronal restorations: placed within a cavity prepared in the crown of a tooth; can be direct (amalgam/composite) or indirect (inlays — fabricated in the laboratory and cemented). Examples: Amalgam fillings; Tooth-coloured restorations (composite, glass ionomer cements, compomers, ceramic inlays); Cast metal restorations (gold inlays and onlays).
Extracoronal restorations: placed around (outside) the tooth; fabricated from metallic alloys or tooth-coloured materials or combination. Examples: Veneers, crowns, bridges, implant-retained prostheses.

B(i)
Principles of amalgam intracoronal preparation:
• Outline form: shape of cavosurface margin should comprise smooth flowing curves determined by size and location of carious lesion.
• Convenience form: cavity should be large enough to admit operative instruments.
• Retention form: ability to withstand occlusally directed force; tooth should be occlusally convergent with retentive features such as undercuts and grooves.
• Resistance form: to withstand obliquely directed forces; smooth flat floor and depth of 2 mm for amalgam.
• Cavity toileting: prepared cavity should be cleaned with an air-water jet to remove debris.

B(ii)
Conventional tooth preparation: requires specific wall forms, depths, and marginal forms; used for amalgam, gold, and ceramics restorations. Modified tooth preparation: used for bonded direct restorations (Composite, GIC, etc.); exhibits greater variability, non-uniform depths, more shallow depths, preparation walls of varying heights or widths, marginal angles of 90° or greater, more enamel bevel, and less or no need for retention and resistance form features (locks, slots, pins, grooves).
questions.question:
Describe the types and principles of dental restorations under the following headings:
A(i) Define dental restorations and state all the indications for restorations.
A(ii) Classify dental restorations by location (intracoronal vs extracoronal) with examples of each.
B(i) Describe the principles of tooth preparation for amalgam intracoronal restorations.
B(ii) Distinguish between conventional and modified tooth preparation.

A 28-year-old patient presents with progressive difficulty chewing and recent tooth fracture following a road traffic accident. After radiographic examination, the clinician plans surgical management. The patient also has a history of Paget's disease.

(i) What intraoperative difficulty might be anticipated, and what are all the causes of difficult tooth extraction?
(ii) State all the instruments necessary for simple forceps extraction and describe the components and function of the extraction forceps.
(iii) Describe the correct extraction movements for mandibular versus maxillary teeth, specifying direction of primary pressure for each group.
(iv) Describe the post-extraction care, including digital compression and postoperative instruction.
(v) What are all the indications for surgical (transalveolar) exodontia rather than simple intra-alveolar extraction?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Difficulty anticipated: sclerosis of bone in Paget's disease makes bone harder and teeth more brittle ('glass in concrete'). All causes of difficult extraction:
• Excessively strong supporting tissues, e.g., in heavily built patients, Blacks
• Misshapen roots: divergent or hooked roots; hypercementosis may give rise to large bulbous roots
• Easily detached crowns: may be due to large restorations, deep cervical caries, or abrasion
• Brittle teeth: with increasing age teeth become brittle and bone becomes harder; root-filled teeth and teeth involved in chronic periodontitis may break easily
• Sclerosis of bone: e.g., in long-standing chronic inflammation or Paget's disease
• Buried and impacted teeth
• Ankylosis and geminated teeth
• Inadequate access, e.g., in patients with trismus

(ii)
Instruments for simple forceps extraction: examination set; local anaesthesia syringe (dental), needle and ampoule of local anaesthetic; extraction forceps (depending on the tooth to be removed) and elevators; sterile gauze; suction tip, towel clamp, artery forceps.
Components and function of extraction forceps: each forceps is composed of two parts — the handle (above the hinge) and the beaks (below the hinge). The handle is held in the hand upon which pressure is exerted. The beaks are the functional component that grasp the tooth at the cervical region and remove it from the alveolar socket. Because tooth anatomy varies, forceps with specially designed beaks are manufactured for specific teeth.

(iii)
Extraction movements:
• Maxillary teeth: buccal pressure is greater than the corresponding palatal or lingual pressure. For all maxillary teeth the dentist is to the front and right of the patient.
• Mandibular premolars, 1st and 2nd molars: buccal movement is more.
• Mandibular 3rd molar: lingual movement is more.
• For single, conical roots: rotational force may be applied in addition to buccolingual pressure.
These movements expand the alveolar bone and sever the periodontal ligament fibres; slight traction is also employed simultaneously.

(iv)
Post-extraction care:
• Compress socket walls with fingers (digital pressure)
• Put gauze pack over socket and ask patient to bite hard on the gauze roll
• After haemostasis is achieved, give postoperative instructions

(v)
Indications for surgical (transalveolar) exodontia rather than simple extraction include situations where simple forceps technique is expected to fail or cause greater damage — these are exactly the situations listed as causes of difficult extraction: buried and impacted teeth; grossly broken-down or brittle teeth; misshapen or hypercementosed roots; sclerotic bone; ankylosed teeth; inadequate access.

questions.question:
A patient presents with a missing upper left central incisor following trauma. The treating dentist plans to restore the space with a fixed bridge using adjacent natural teeth.
(i) State the definition of a dental bridge and its advantages over removable prostheses.
(ii) State all the disadvantages of bridges.
(iii) Describe a dental implant as an alternative option, including its disadvantages and advantages.
(iv) State the role of a denture as a prosthetic option, describing all five roles of dentures.
questions.answerText:
(i)
A bridge is an artificial tooth or teeth attached to natural teeth on either side of the gap. Advantages: Dental bridges appear and function similar to natural teeth; they remain in the mouth at all times.

(ii)
Disadvantages of bridges: The natural teeth need to be trimmed down so that the bridge can be attached by cementation — this can weaken, break or cause pulp death in these (abutment) teeth; Bridges are relatively costly compared to dentures; Crown (caps) that connect to the supporting teeth can become loose if not cemented or fitted well, making the natural teeth susceptible to decay.

(iii)
A dental implant is a metal rod that is placed in the jaw bone to hold an artificial tooth or teeth in place. Dentures or bridges can be screwed onto the implant.
Disadvantages: More expensive than dentures and bridges; Requires surgery; Need to have healthy and adequate bone.
Advantages: Can be used to support fixed bridges even if no natural teeth remain in the mouth; Can support removable partial dentures, making them far more comfortable to wear; Crowns and bridges anchored by implants are made to look natural and to match surrounding teeth.

(iv)
Roles of dentures:
• Mastication: chewing ability is improved by replacing edentulous areas with denture teeth.
• Aesthetics: denture provides support for the lips and cheeks, corrects the collapsed appearance that occurs after tooth loss, and improves facial appearance.
• Phonetics: by replacing missing teeth, especially anterior, patients are better able to pronounce some words.
• Self-esteem: patients feel better about themselves.
• Dental harmony: denture prevents drifting and supraeruption of adjacent or opposing teeth into the edentulous space.

(i)
Acquired gingival hyperplasia (drug-induced gingival enlargement). Commonly seen in children on phenytoin (used for epilepsy). Side effect of immunosuppressive drug cyclosporin (used to prevent rejection following transplantation of tissue or organ) is also noted.

(ii)
Drugs causing similar gingival changes: phenytoin and cyclosporin.

(iii)
Management:
• Efficient plaque control.
• Use of chlorhexidine mouthwash.
• If severe, gingivectomy can be done.
• Consult child's physician for consideration of other alternative drug.

(iv)
Other gingival conditions:
• Hereditary gingival fibromatosis: generalised but sometimes localised fibrous enlargement of gingival tissue; gross enlargement may interfere with occlusion; if anterior, it is unsightly.
• Gingivitis: inflammation of the gingiva; associated with plaque around erupting teeth and increased susceptibility of gingival tissue to bacterial irritation; prevalence also increases during puberty associated with commencement of sex hormone secretion.
• Fibrous epulis: presents as a mass on the gingiva; colour varies from pink to red depending on degree of vascularity; consists of inflammatory cell infiltrate and mature fibrous tissue.
questions.question:
A 12-year-old boy on phenytoin for epilepsy presents with generalised enlargement of gum tissue that is interfering with his occlusion.
(i) State the diagnosis and its cause.
(ii) List other drugs known to cause similar changes.
(iii) Describe the full management of this condition.
(iv) List the other conditions of the gingiva in children, together with their associated findings.

Describe the surgical anatomy and diseases of the temporomandibular joint under the following headings:

A(i) Describe the surgical anatomy of the TMJ, including the type of joint, the components of the joint, the disc (meniscus), the ligaments, and the articular surface of the temporal bone.
A(ii) Describe the condyle in terms of shape and axis orientation, and state how the disc and its attachments relate to the movement of the condyle.
B(i) State the full classification of diseases of the TMJ, listing all categories and subcategories.
B(ii) Describe the classification, aetiology, and radiological features of TMJ ankylosis, including what each radiological view contributes.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Surgical anatomy:
• Synovial joint between the mandible and the undersurface of the squamous part of the temporal bone
• Separated into upper and lower cavities by a fibrous disc within the joint
• Capsule attached high up on the neck of the mandible around the articular margin of the condyle; it is lax but strong
• Disc attached around the periphery to the inside of the capsule; anteriorly attached near the condyle (moves forward with condyle); posteriorly attached nearer the temporal bone and therefore cannot move so freely; the posterior end has less dense texture than elsewhere
• Fibres can elongate and recoil a little; the disc has an undulating contour
• Anterior margin of the disc and adjoining capsule receive the insertion of the upper fibres of the lateral pterygoid muscle
Ligaments: Temporomandibular ligament — a stout band of fibrous tissue from the lower border of the zygoma to the posterior border of the neck and ramus of the mandible; tightens in retrusion and protrusion. Sphenomandibular ligament — attached to the axis of rotation of the mandible; limits movement but remains constant in length and tension in all positions.
Articular surface: composed of the concave articular fossa and the convex articular eminence.

A(ii)
The condyle is elliptically shaped with its long axis oriented mediolaterally. The meniscus is a fibrous, saddle-shaped structure that separates the condyle and the temporal bone. Anteriorly, the disc is attached near the condyle and moves forward with the condyle; posteriorly it is attached nearer the temporal bone and cannot move so freely.

B(i)
Classification of diseases of the TMJ:
• Traumatic: intracapsular fracture, birth injury, haemarthrosis
• Infective: ankylosing spondylitis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, infective arthritis, osteoarthritis
• Metabolic: gout
• Neoplasms: chondroma, osteoma
• Developmental: condylar hyperplasia, condylar hypoplasia, bifid condyle, condylar agenesis
• Internal disc displacement: anterior disc displacement with reduction; anterior disc displacement without reduction
• Genetically determined: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, pseudoxanthoma elasticum, Marfan's syndrome, Treacher-Collins syndrome
• Pain dysfunction syndrome
• Ankylosis of the temporomandibular joint
• Dislocation of the joint

B(ii)
Classification of ankylosis: false or true; unilateral or bilateral; fibrous or bony; extraarticular and intraarticular; partial and complete.
Aetiology: Trauma (congenital, forceps delivery, condylar fractures, glenoid fossa fractures); Infection (arthritis, osteomyelitis, otitis media, parotitis, tonsillitis, abscess around the joint, actinomycosis); Inflammation (rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, septic arthritis); Scar tissue (burns, irradiation); Systemic diseases (smallpox, scarlet fever, typhoid, gonococcal arthritis).
Radiological features by view:
• PA view: mediolateral extent of bony mass; graphical record of asymmetry
• Lateral oblique view: anteroposterior dimension of condylar mass
• Panoramic view: antegonial notching and inferior arching; rough assessment of caries and periodontal disease
• Cephalometry: evaluates associated skeletal malformations
• Submentovertex: coronoid process involvement; diameter of condylar mass
• TMJ views (open and close): movement of condyle; narrowing of joint space; proliferation within bony compartment; complete bony ankylosis shows overall obliteration of temporomandibular area with dense sclerotic bone
• CT scan: delineation of bony mass

questions.question:
Describe direct restorative materials as used in dentistry under the following headings:

A(i) Define direct restoration and state all the types of direct restorative materials with their examples.
A(ii) For dental amalgam: state its definition, composition (all constituents), the function of each constituent, and the applications.
B(i) For composite resins: state their definition, uses, types (by curing mechanism), composition, and the properties of the set material.
B(ii) For glass ionomer cement: state its definition, general properties, and how it differs from direct filling gold in terms of applications and material characteristics.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Direct restoration is the process of placement of dental restorative materials directly on the tooth structure for the purpose of repairing a defect or modifying the existing structure to normal morphology and function. The material is placed on the tooth directly in the clinic without laboratory procedure involvement.
Types of direct restorative materials:
• Amalgam
• Composite resins
• Glass ionomer cement
• Dental cements for restoration
• Direct filling gold
• Dental ceramics

A(ii)
Amalgam is defined as a special type of alloy in which mercury is one of the component. It is the most widely used filling material for posterior teeth.
Composition and functions:
• Silver: major element in the reaction; whitens the alloy; decreases creep; increases strength; increases expansion on setting; increases tarnish resistance
• Tin: controls the reaction between silver and mercury (otherwise too fast); reduces strength and hardness; reduces resistance to tarnish and corrosion
• Copper: hardness and strength; setting expansion
• Zinc: acts as scavenger/deoxidizer
• Platinum: hardens the alloy and resistance to corrosion
• Palladium: hardens and whitens the alloy
Applications: Class I, II (posterior) and Class V cavities where aesthetics is not important; in combination with retentive pins to restore a crown; for making dies; in retrograde root canal fillings; as a core material

B(i)
Composite resins are tooth-coloured restorative materials made up of resins strengthened by the addition of silica particles called fillers.
Uses: restoration of anterior and posterior teeth; to veneer metal crown and fixed partial denture; to build up cores; bonding of orthodontic brackets, etched cast restoration, ceramic crowns; pits and fissure sealants; aesthetic laminates; repair of chipped porcelain restoration.
Types by curing mechanism: chemically activated; light activated; dual cure.
Composition: resin matrix or binder — Bis GMA or urethane dimethacrylate; filler — quartz, colloidal silica or metal glasses; coupling agent — organosilanes.
Properties: hardness (not as amalgam); undergoes polymerization shrinkage (varying, based on resin to filler ratio); may undergo slow expansion associated with water sorption; do not adhere chemically to tooth structure but through micromechanical retention and bonding agents.

B(ii)
Glass ionomer cement is a tooth-coloured restorative material consisting of polymer materials surrounding glass-reinforced filler particles. The set material has good adhesion and prevents recurrent caries by slow and continuous release of fluoride ions.
General properties: aesthetically acceptable; anticariogenic effect; biocompatible and milder irritant to pulp than silicate; bonds to both enamel and dentin; poor fracture and abrasion resistance when unfilled compared to composite; dimensionally stable; insoluble in oral fluids; restorations can be easily repaired and replaced.
Direct filling gold: not widely used due to alternatives; it is malleable and the most noble of metals. Applications: pits and small Class I restorations; repair of casting margins; Class II, V, and VI restoration; repair of perforations in gold crowns. Contraindications: teeth with very large pulp chambers; severely periodontally weakened teeth; root canal filled teeth (because these teeth become brittle).

A(i)
The odontogenic keratocyst (OKC) is an uncommon jaw cyst with a strong tendency to recur after removal. The mandible is usually affected, with 50% occurring in the angle of the mandible. It forms intraosseously and may grow around the crown of a tooth. It spreads extensively along the marrow spaces before expanding the jaw — growth is by finger-like projection into marrow spaces rather than by expansion (mural growth rather than by osmotic pressure effect). Clinical signs may not occur until the cyst is well advanced.

A(ii)
Radiographic features: appears as well-defined radiolucent areas, either more or less rounded with scalloped margin or multiloculated, simulating ameloblastoma. Clinical and radiographic features may allow for a fairly accurate preoperative diagnosis but definitive diagnosis is only by histology.
Histological types — Two types:
• Parakeratotic: higher tendency to recur; epithelial lining of uniform thickness; epithelial lining weakly attached to fibrous wall; inflammatory cells typically scanty or absent
• Orthokeratotic: clearly defined basal cell layer of basal cells with prekeratin; well-defined granular cell layer with abundant orthokeratin formation; lower recurrence tendency

B(i)
OKC has a strong tendency to recur; treatment is by enucleation with treatment of the bone (mechanical or chemical).
Gorlin-Goltz syndrome (syndrome of multiple jaw cysts and basal cell carcinoma):
• Heritable as an autosomal dominant trait
• Frontal and parietal bossing and broad nasal root
• Multiple keratocysts of the jaws
• Multiple naevoid basal cell carcinomas of the skin
• Skeletal anomalies (usually minor)
• Intracranial anomalies
• Main oral importance: likelihood of development of multiple cysts

B(ii)
Comparison — OKC vs Dentigerous cyst:
• OKC: uncommon; forms intraosseously; grows along marrow spaces; may grow around crown of tooth; mandible most affected (50% at angle); histological lining with uniform thickness epithelium weakly attached to wall; treatment: enucleation with bone treatment.
• Dentigerous cyst: forms from remains of enamel organ after enamel formation is complete; forms around the crown of a tooth (dilation of the follicle); attached to the neck of the tooth; most usually associated with unerupted 3rd molars and canines; commoner in males; age 20–50 years; lumen characteristically lined with cuboidal epithelium surrounded by wall of connective tissue; inflammatory cells usually lacking; treatment: enucleation (marsupialization for very large cysts); usually does not recur after treatment.
questions.question:
Describe the odontogenic keratocyst (OKC) under the following headings:

A(i) Define the lesion, state its frequency, typical site of occurrence, and mode of growth.
A(ii) Describe the radiographic and histological features, including the two histological types and the distinguishing microscopic features of each.
B(i) Explain the clinical significance of the OKC's tendency to recur, state the treatment of choice, and describe the Gorlin-Goltz syndrome in full — including its mode of inheritance and all associated features.
B(ii) Distinguish the OKC from the dentigerous cyst in terms of origin, site, typical relationship to teeth, age and sex predilection, histological lining, and treatment.

questions.answerText:
A.
Components of the periodontium: alveolar bone; cementum; periodontal ligament; gingiva (gum).

B.
Clinical assessment criteria:
• Colour — Health: coral pink (brown variation); Factor: vascular supply/keratinisation; Disease: shades of red or blue; Factor: inflammation/stasis; Condition: chronic gingivitis.
• Contour — Health: scalloped and knife-edged margin; Factor: shape of tooth and alignment in arch; Disease: rolled margin; Factor: inflammatory changes; Condition: chronic gingivitis.
• Consistency — Health: firm and resilient; Factor: collagenous nature of lamina propria; Disease: soggy puffiness that pits on pressure; Factor: infiltration by fluids and cells of inflammatory exudate; Condition: chronic gingivitis.
• Size — Health: normal; Factor: sum total of bulk of cellular and intercellular elements; Disease: increased; Condition: gingival enlargement (increased fibres and decreased cells OR decreased fibres and increased cells).
• Surface texture — Health: smooth margin; stippling on attached gingiva; Factor: attachment of gingival fibres to underlying bone; Disease: loss of stippling — smooth and shiny; Factor: destruction of gingival fibres as a result of inflammation; Condition: gingivitis.
• Position — Health: 1mm above CEJ; Factor: position of tooth in the arch; Disease: apically placed (gingival recession) or coronally placed (pseudo-pockets); Factor: toothbrush trauma, inflammation, tooth malpositon; Condition: gingival recession / pseudo-pockets.

C.
Chronic marginal gingivitis is the most common form. It has a slow onset and long duration and is usually painless. It is usually due to accumulation of plaque and calculus. Treatment: oral hygiene instructions/motivations in home care, scaling and polishing. Meticulous removal of plaque will usually result in resolution without residual tissue destruction.
Acute ulcerative gingivitis (AUG): sudden onset, short duration and painful. Clinical features: bleeding, halitosis, punched-out crater-like ulceration, pain, metallic taste. Common among children and adolescents. Associated with malnutrition, stress, cigarette smoking, and host immunity. Treatment: OHI, debridement, antibiotics, scaling and polishing, treatment of predisposing factors.
questions.question:
Describe the periodontal tissues under the following headings:

A. Components and their arrangement
B. Clinical assessment criteria for the gingiva in health and in disease — for each criterion, state the healthy appearance, the factor responsible for the healthy appearance, the diseased appearance, the factor responsible for the diseased change, and the disease condition involved
C. Explain why chronic marginal gingivitis is the most common form of gingivitis, and distinguish it from acute ulcerative gingivitis in terms of onset, course, clinical features, and treatment

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Surgery is defined as 'the art or practice of treating injuries, deformities and other disorders by manual operation or instrumental appliances' (Oxford English Dictionary). Also: 'a medical procedure involving an incision with instruments; performed to repair damage or arrest disease in a living body.' OMS deals with surgical conditions of the face, jaws, and oral cavity.
Basic necessities for surgery: adequate visibility; assistance.
Adequate visibility requires: adequate access (mouth opening, surgical exposure, retraction); adequate light; surgical field free of excess blood and other fluids.

A(ii)
Asepsis is the attempt to keep patients, health care staff, and objects free from infectious agents. Surgical asepsis describes efforts aimed at preventing microbes from gaining access into surgically created wounds. The oral cavity is dirty but organisms are normal flora; introduction of organisms from outside can result in infection. Universal precautions are applied to prevent sepsis. Efforts fall under: instrument sterilization; operatory disinfection; surgical staff preparation (hand and arm preparation — clean technique and sterile technique).

B(i)
Principles of incisions: use a sharp blade of proper size; use firm continuous strokes; avoid cutting vital structures; incise perpendicular to the epithelial surface; intraoral incisions should be properly placed.
Flap design: correct flap design helps prevent flap necrosis, flap dehiscence, and flap tearing.
Tissue handling: careful flap design and incision technique must be combined with careful tissue handling. Excessive crushing, pulling, extremes of temperature, desiccation, and harsh chemicals damage tissues and should be avoided. Toothed forceps and skin hooks are preferred to forceps that crush wound edges. Avoid excessive pulling forces when retracting tissue. Use copious irrigation when drilling or cutting bone. Protect soft tissue when drilling or cutting.
Haemostasis: no effort should be spared to minimize blood loss. Methods: apply pressure on a bleeding vessel or a haemostat (assists natural clotting); thermal coagulation (heat); suture ligation; pressure on the wound; use of vasoconstrictors.

B(ii)
Preoperative period:
• Purposes of surgery: diagnostic; curative; restorative; palliative (makes patient more comfortable); cosmetic (reconstructs skin and underlying structures).
• Assessment history and data collection: age; drug and substance use; medical history including cardiac and pulmonary histories; previous surgery and anaesthesia; blood donations; discharge planning.
• Physical assessment: obtain baseline vital signs; focus on problem areas identified by the patient's history; report any abnormal findings to surgeon and anaesthesia personnel. Systems: cardiovascular; respiratory; renal/urinary; neurological; musculoskeletal; nutritional status; psychosocial assessment.
• Laboratory assessment: urinalysis; blood type and crossmatch; complete blood count or haemoglobin and haematocrit; clotting studies; electrolyte levels; serum creatinine level; pregnancy test; chest x-ray; electrocardiogram (EKG or ECG).
• Informed consent: the surgeon is responsible for obtaining signed consent before sedation and surgery; patient must be given all information including risks and complications.
• NPO: patient given nothing by mouth for 6 to 8 hours before surgery; decreases risk for aspiration.
questions.question:
Describe the basic principles of oral and maxillofacial surgery under the following headings:

A(i) Define surgery and state the basic necessities for surgical practice, including what adequate visibility requires.
A(ii) Describe the principles of aseptic technique, universal precautions, and the categories under which efforts against sepsis fall.
B(i) Describe the principles of incision, flap design (including what correct flap design prevents), tissue handling, and haemostasis in oral and maxillofacial surgery.
B(ii) Describe the preoperative period in full — including the purposes of surgery, the components of preoperative assessment (history and physical), and the laboratory investigations required before surgery.

A patient presents with a tooth that cannot be removed with routine forceps extraction due to thick dense bone and hypercementosis.
(i) State what procedure is indicated and list all other indications for this procedure.
(ii) Describe the principles of simple forceps extraction, including the mechanical principles applied.
(iii) State the five types of forces used with forceps to expand the socket and luxate the tooth.
(iv) Describe the three elevator principles used in exodontia.
(v) List the postoperative instructions that should be given to the patient after tooth extraction.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Transalveolar surgery (disimpaction) is indicated. Other indications:
• Failure to remove a tooth with forceps or routine extraction.
• Presence of thick dense bone, particularly buccocortical.
• Presence of short clinical crowns with signs of severe attrition.
• Hypercementosis.
• Teeth with long and divergent roots.
• Presence of large pneumatized maxillary sinus.
• Teeth with extensive caries, root caries, or large amalgam restorations.
• Erupted mandibular third molars with limited access.
• Endodontically treated teeth.

(ii)
Extraction requires expansion of the alveolar socket and separation of the periodontal and gingival soft tissues. Controlled force is delivered with elevators and forceps to expand and fracture the alveolar socket without fracturing the alveolar process, roots or crown. Forceps should firmly engage the tooth as apically as possible without injuring adjacent structures. Mechanical principles: lever, wedge, and rotating wheel and axle.

(iii)
Five types of forces:
• Apical pressure — to expand bony socket and displace the centre of tooth rotation apically.
• Buccal force — to expand the buccal crestal bone.
• Lingual force — to expand the lingual crestal bone.
• Rotational force — to cause internal expansion; useful for tooth with single conical root.
• Tractional force — applied last, gently, to deliver the tooth from the socket after adequate bony expansion.

(iv)
Elevator principles:
• Lever principle: lever of 1st order where fulcrum is between effort and resistance.
• Wedge principle: elevator forced between root of tooth and investing bony tissue parallel to the root.
• Wheel and axle principle: modification of lever principle, used in combination with lever or wedge.

(v)
Postoperative instructions: Avoid excessive exercise and alcohol for the remainder of the day. Eat and drink normally but avoid getting food in the socket. Take over-the-counter pain killers early before pain becomes severe. Hot salt-water mouthwashes starting 24 hours after extraction — a teaspoon of salt in a mug of hot water, before and after every meal and last thing at night. If significant bleeding, sit up, place a rolled gauze over the socket and bite down for 10 minutes. Contact the clinic if bleeding or pain cannot be controlled.

questions.question:
A patient presents with a dome-shaped bluish swelling approximately 0.8 cm in diameter on the buccal gingiva. It has been present for two months and is not associated with any symptoms. There is no history of trauma to the area. The adjacent teeth test vital.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the key distinguishing feature of the lesion from the common periodontal cyst?
(ii) State the full classification of cysts of the oral and maxillofacial region.
(iii) Give the relative frequency of all jaw cysts, and explain why the radicular cyst is the most common cause of major chronic jaw swelling.
(iv) Describe all the cysts without epithelial lining (pseudocysts) and all the soft tissue cysts of the oral region.
(v) Compare the eruption cyst with the dentigerous cyst in terms of tissue of origin, presentation, age group, teeth involved, and treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Most likely diagnosis: Gingival cyst of adults. It is rare and forms dome-shaped swellings less than 1 cm in diameter; it may erode underlying bone. The key distinguishing feature from the common periodontal cyst: gingival cyst of adults does not recur after enucleation, and the adjacent teeth test vital (unlike radicular cyst which is associated with a non-vital tooth).

(ii)
Full classification of cysts of the oral and maxillofacial region:
• Odontogenic cysts — Developmental: dentigerous cyst, eruption cyst, odontogenic keratocyst, gingival cyst, lateral periodontal cyst; Inflammatory: radicular cyst, paradental cyst; Neoplastic: cystic ameloblastoma, calcifying odontogenic (ghost cell) cyst
• Non-odontogenic cysts: nasopalatine cyst, nasolabial cyst
• Cysts without epithelial lining (pseudocyst): solitary (simple) bone cyst, aneurysmal bone cyst

(iii)
Relative frequency of jaw cysts:
• Radicular (periodontal): 65–70%
• Dentigerous: 15–18%
• Nasopalatine: 5–10%
• Keratocysts: 3–5%
• Lateral periodontal: less than 1%
• Paradental: less than 1%
The radicular cyst is the most common cause of major chronic jaw swelling because it is the most prevalent cyst (65–70%), arising by epithelial proliferation in an apical granuloma at the root apex of a non-vital tooth, and it grows as a slowly progressive painless swelling that remains asymptomatic until large enough to be conspicuous.

(iv)
Pseudocysts (cysts without epithelial lining): solitary (simple) bone cyst; aneurysmal bone cyst.
Soft tissue cysts: mucoceles (extravasation or retention) — most common soft tissue cyst, most frequently on lower lip, usually caused by damage to the duct and extravasation of saliva; saliva leaking into surrounding tissues causes mild inflammation and pulls up to form cysts with connective tissue lining. Ranula — uncommon type of mucocele arising from sublingual or submandibular salivary glands; usually unilateral about 2–3 cm in diameter; may extend across the whole floor of the mouth; bluish, soft and fluctuant; typically painless but may interfere with speech and mastication. Sublingual dermoid cyst — develops between the hyoid and the mandible or beneath the tongue; may be filled with desquamated keratin. Cysts from abnormality of development of the branchial arches and pharyngeal pouches.
Treatment: mucocele — excision with underlying gland; ranula — marsupialization with removal of related gland; simple incision leads to recurrence.

(v)
Comparison: Eruption cyst vs Dentigerous cyst:
• Origin: eruption cyst — similar to dentigerous cyst (related to the crown of an erupting tooth); dentigerous cyst — forms from remains of enamel organ after enamel formation is complete, as a dilation of the follicle
• Presentation: eruption cyst — presents in the soft tissue around the crown of an erupting tooth as a rounded bluish swelling; dentigerous cyst — slowly progressive painless swelling in the jaw, asymptomatic until conspicuous
• Age: eruption cyst — affects children; dentigerous cyst — uncommon in children, age 20–50 years
• Teeth involved: eruption cyst — involves teeth having no predecessor (deciduous or permanent); dentigerous cyst — most usually associated with unerupted 3rd molars and canines
• Treatment: eruption cyst — most burst spontaneously; occasionally the cyst roof may be removed to allow the tooth to erupt; dentigerous cyst — enucleation (marsupialization for very large cysts); usually does not recur

questions.question:
A patient presents with a painless, slowly progressive swelling in the anterior mandible. Radiography reveals a well-defined radiolucency at the apex of a tooth in the region, with a corticated margin. The tooth in question tests non-vital. The cystic fluid is described as watery and opalescent with a shimmering quality.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and state its relative frequency among jaw cysts.
(ii) State all the risk factors, predisposing conditions, and patient demographics associated with this lesion.
(iii) Describe the pathogenesis of this lesion, including the epithelial source and the mechanism of enlargement.
(iv) List the full differential diagnosis with the distinguishing features for each differential.
(v) State the treatment options available and the expected outcome after treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Radicular (periodontal) cyst. It is the most common cause of major chronic jaw swelling. Relative frequency: 65–70% of all jaw cysts.

(ii)
Demographics and features:
• Rare below 10 years of age
• Common between 20–60 years of age
• More common in males
• Associated with a non-vital tooth of origin
• Forms in bone in relation to the root of a non-vital tooth
• Arises by epithelial proliferation in an apical granuloma

(iii)
Pathogenesis:
• Arises by epithelial proliferation within an apical granuloma
• Forms in bone in relation to the root of a non-vital tooth
• Presents as a slowly progressive, painless swelling; asymptomatic until large enough to be conspicuous
• Swelling is rounded and may have different consistencies: bony hard, ping-pong, egg-cracking, soft and fluctuant
• If infected, becomes painful and rapidly enlarges
• Histologically: cystic lining consists of stratified squamous epithelium of variable thickness lacking basal cell epithelium; capsule consists of collagenous fibrous connective tissue with varying amounts of inflammatory cells
• Cystic fluid: watery and opalescent, or viscid and yellowish, sometimes shimmering (cholesterol crystals — not of diagnostic importance)

(iv)
Differential diagnosis:
• Anatomic structures: maxillary antrum and foramina
• Cysts of other types
• Neoplasms
• Ameloblastoma: suggested by resorption of adjacent teeth
• Secondary tumour deposit: distinguished by hazy outline and solid mass appearance

(v)
Treatment:
• Enucleation with primary closure
• Rarely: marsupialization for exceptionally large cysts
• Does not recur after complete enucleation
• A residual cyst can remain after the causative tooth has been extracted, making diagnosis less obvious

questions.question:
Describe the clinical features and management of dental anomalies in children under the following headings:
A(i) List the categories of dental anomalies, and describe anomalies of tooth number.
A(ii) Describe extra cusps — their location and clinical significance.
B(i) Describe Hutchinson's incisors and mulberry molars, including the causative organism and the pathway of infection.
B(ii) Describe macrodontia and microdontia.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Categories of dental anomalies: Tooth number; Size; Form; Structure. These variations may be exclusively genetic, environmental, or a combination. Both deciduous and permanent dentitions may be affected.
Anomalies of tooth number:
• Hypodontia: fewer than normal number as a result of failure of development.
• Anodontia: complete absence of teeth.
• Oligodontia: multiple teeth missing (more than six teeth).

A(ii)
Extra cusps:
• Cusp of Carabelli: found on palatal surface of 1st molars.
• Talon's cusp: found on palatal surface of anterior teeth.
These cusps encourage food stagnation and hence rampant caries.

B(i)
Hutchinson's incisor and mulberry molar: one of the later signs of congenital syphilis. Treponema pallidum from infected mother can cross the placenta during the 2nd trimester.
Hutchinson's incisors: characterised by peg-shaped deformity of the upper central incisor of the permanent dentition; the tooth is wider at the cervical margin than at the incisal edge with notching at the tip.
Mulberry molars: the molars have multiple cusps and may also be hypoplastic.

B(ii)
Macrodontia: large teeth. Generalised form is rare but it can be unilateral, associated with hemifacial hypertrophy.
Microdontia: small teeth, typically occurring in the lateral incisors.

questions.question:
Describe the categories of investigations used in oral pathology under the following headings:
A(i) List all categories of investigations and all intraoral radiographic types.
A(ii) List all extraoral radiographic views.
B(i) Distinguish between incisional and excisional biopsy.
B(ii) Describe exfoliative cytology, chair-side investigations, and haematological investigations, including the specific clinical indications for each haematological test.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Categories of investigations: Radiography; Biopsy; Chair-side investigations; Haematological investigations (e.g. FBC, WBC + Differentials, FPG + 2HPP, Clotting profile, retroviral screening).
Intraoral radiography: Periapical radiograph; Bite-wing radiograph; Occlusal radiograph.

A(ii)
Extraoral radiography: Postero-anterior view of the jaws [and skull]; Antero-posterior view of the jaws; Occipito-mental radiograph [Sinus view or Waters view]; Submento-vertex radiograph [jug-handle view]; Orthopantomogram; CT; MRI; Sialography.

B(i)
Incisional biopsy: a procedure in which a small area of tissue is taken to identify the composition (or make-up) of a lesion or abnormality. Excisional biopsy: a more involved procedure where the entire abnormality or area of interest is removed.

B(ii)
Exfoliative cytology: cells are collected after they have been either spontaneously shed by the body (spontaneous exfoliation) or manually scraped/brushed off a surface of the body (mechanical exfoliation). Chair-side investigations: Aspiration of cystic fluid (golden yellow, dirty white, or blood); Shimmering test; Toluidine (vital) staining. Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC) is also available.
Haematological investigations and their indications:
• FBC and WBC + Differentials: general workup.
• FPG + 2HPP: suspected DM cases with oral manifestations, poorly controlled DM.
• Clotting profile: bleeding disorders; as a baseline investigation before a surgical procedure.
• Retroviral screening: suspected cases with candida, bilateral parotid gland enlargement, recalcitrant and extensive oral aphthous ulcerations.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old patient presents to the dental clinic following a road traffic accident with a fracture of the jaw. The attending clinician plans surgical extraction of the tooth in the fracture line. After reviewing the patient's full medical history, the dentist proceeds to perform a maxillary tooth extraction.

(i) State all the indications for dental extraction relevant to this scenario and in general.
(ii) Describe the full preoperative assessment required, including clinical, radiographic, and patient preparation components.
(iii) State the correct patient and surgeon positions for maxillary tooth extraction, including the precise chair angle.
(iv) Describe the complete extraction technique using forceps, including how to hold the forceps for maxillary teeth, the sequence of movements applied, and why each movement is used.
(v) Describe the healing stages of an extraction wound in the correct order, and list all the causes of delayed healing.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Indications for extraction:
• Gross caries where restoration is impractical
• Pulpitis where endodontic treatment is impractical
• Apical periodontitis, especially posterior teeth where endodontic treatment is impractical or hazardous
• Periodontal disease — advanced disease
• Fractured teeth — fracture passing through the coronal half of the crown
• Fracture of the jaw — tooth in fracture line (except when needed for stabilization)
• Misplaced and impacted teeth — if carious or damaging adjacent teeth
• Orthodontic treatment
• Retained deciduous teeth when the permanent successor is in a good position to erupt
• Prosthetic consideration — if interfering with fitting of denture or detracting from appearance
• Supernumerary and supplemental teeth — if interfering with eruption or causing crowding
• Gross neglect
• At risk from certain systemic diseases, e.g., haemophilia
• Preparation for radiotherapy

(ii)
Preoperative assessment:
• Presurgical medical assessment
• General patient assessment: biodata, demeanor, build, extraoral and intraoral examination
• Clinical evaluation: access to tooth, mobility, condition of crown
• Radiographic examination: tooth anatomy, relationship of associated vital structures, configuration of roots, condition of surrounding bone
• Patient preparation: protective clothing, face mask, protective eyewear, sterile gloves after hand washing; proper patient positioning; draping

(iii)
Patient position: For maxillary tooth extraction, the patient's mouth must be at the same height as the dentist's elbow; the angle between the dental chair and the horizontal (floor) must be approximately 120°; the occlusal surface of the maxillary teeth must be at a 45° angle compared to horizontal when the mouth is open.
Dentist position: for all maxillary teeth, the dentist is to the front and right (and to the left, for left-handed dentists) of the patient.

(iv)
Forceps holding: For maxillary forceps, the handle is held so the thumb stays on top of the handle while the other four fingers support the handle from below. Technique: beaks forced into the gingival crevice, positioned at the cervical line parallel to the long axis, without grasping bone or gingiva. Apical force (apical thrust) applied to engage part of the root, to expand crestal bone, and to displace the centre of rotation as far apically as possible. Initial extraction movements are gentle; slow pressure applied buccally then lingually (buccolingual). Movements increase gradually; buccal pressure is greater than palatal/lingual for maxillary teeth. For single conical roots, rotational force may be added. These movements expand the alveolar bone and sever the periodontal ligament fibres. Slight traction is also employed simultaneously.

(v)
Healing stages in order:
• Formation of blood clot filling the socket
• Organization of the clot
• Epithelialization of the surface of the wound
• Formation of woven bone in the connective tissue filling the socket
• Replacement of woven bone by trabecular bone and remodelling of the alveolus
Causes of delayed healing: infection; prolonged bleeding due to a clotting defect; formation of an oro-antral fistula; proliferation of a malignant tumour; radiotherapy; immunodeficiency; underlying systemic disease (e.g., diabetes mellitus, liver disease); scurvy

questions.question:
Describe the structure and function of dental radiography under the following headings:
A(i) Describe the theoretical basis and step-by-step technique of the paralleling cone technique for periapical radiography.
A(ii) Describe the theoretical basis and step-by-step technique of the bisecting angle technique.
B(i) Describe the main clinical indications for occlusal radiography and the available projections for both maxilla and mandible.
B(ii) Describe the step-by-step technique for performing the lower standard occlusal radiograph.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Paralleling cone technique (also called long cone or right angle technique): The central ray of the X-ray beam is directed at right angles to the teeth and the film. The X-ray film is kept parallel to the long axis of the teeth using special holders. A long cone of 12 inches is used.
Theory:
• Film packet is placed in a holder and positioned parallel to the long axis of the tooth under investigation.
• The X-ray tubehead is then aimed at right angles (vertically and horizontally) to both the tooth and the film packet.
• By using a film holder with fixed film packet and X-ray tubehead positions, the technique is reproducible.

A(ii)
Bisecting angle technique theory:
• Film packet is placed as close to the tooth under investigation as possible without bending the packet.
• The angle formed between the long axis of the tooth and the long axis of the film packet is assessed and mentally bisected.
• The X-ray tubehead is positioned at right angles to this bisecting line with the central ray aimed through the tooth apex.
• Using the geometrical principle of similar triangles, the actual length of the tooth in the mouth equals the length of the image of the tooth on the film.

B(i)
Main clinical indications for occlusal radiography:
• Periapical assessment of upper anterior teeth, especially in children and adults unable to tolerate periapical films.
• Detecting the presence of unerupted canines, supernumeraries and odontomes.
• As the midline view, using the parallax method for determining the bucco/palatal position of unerupted canines.
• Evaluation of the size and extent of lesions such as cysts or tumours in the anterior maxilla.
• Assessment of fractures of the anterior teeth and alveolar bone.
Projections — Maxillary: Upper standard occlusal; Upper oblique occlusal; Vertex occlusal.
Mandibular: Lower 90° occlusal (true occlusal); Lower 45° occlusal (standard occlusal); Lower oblique occlusal.

B(ii)
Technique for lower standard occlusal:
• Patient seated with head supported, occlusal plane horizontal and parallel to the floor, asked to support a protective thyroid shield.
• Film packet, white (pebbly) surface facing uppermost, placed flat into the mouth on to the occlusal surfaces of the lower teeth. Patient bites together gently. Film placed centrally — long axis crossways in adults, anteroposteriorly in children.
• X-ray tubehead positioned above patient in the midline, aiming downwards through the bridge of the nose at an angle of 65°-70° to the film packet.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman presents with a painless swelling of the lower lip for 6 months. The swelling is soft, bluish, and approximately 1 cm in diameter. There is a history of repeated trauma to the lip from biting. Aspiration yields a mucoid fluid.

(i) What is the diagnosis and what is the pathogenesis of this specific type?
(ii) Distinguish this lesion from all other similar soft tissue swellings of the oral cavity that arise from salivary glands or ducts, and state the treatment for each, where known.
(iii) Describe the ranula — its origin, clinical features, and treatment.
(iv) Describe all the non-odontogenic cysts of the oral and maxillofacial region, including origin, clinical features, and treatment for each.
(v) State all the gingival cysts — including gingival cysts of newborns and their variants, and gingival cysts of adults.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Mucocele (extravasation type). Pathogenesis: usually caused by damage to the duct and extravasation of saliva. Saliva leaking into surrounding tissues causes mild inflammation. Saliva eventually pools up to form a cyst with connective tissue lining (not an epithelial lining).

(ii)
Distinction from similar swellings:
• Mucocele (extravasation): most common soft tissue cyst; most frequently on lower lip; caused by damage to the duct and extravasation of saliva; connective tissue lining; treatment — excision with underlying gland.
• Mucocele (retention type): rare; due to duct obstruction and dilatation forming a retention cyst with an epithelial lining; treatment — excision with underlying gland.
• Ranula: uncommon type of mucocele arising from the sublingual or submandibular salivary glands; usually has an epithelial lining; treatment — marsupialization with removal of related gland; enucleation is difficult because of the very thin wall; simple incision leads to recurrence.
• Dermoid cyst: develops between the hyoid and the mandible or beneath the tongue; may be filled with desquamated keratin.

(iii)
Ranula: originates from the sublingual or submandibular salivary glands. Structure: similar to mucocele though there is usually an epithelial lining. Clinical features: usually unilateral, about 2–3 cm in diameter; may extend across the whole floor of the mouth; bluish, soft, and fluctuant; typically painless but may interfere with speech and mastication. Treatment: marsupialization with removal of the related gland; enucleation is difficult because of the very thin wall; simple incision leads to recurrence.

(iv)
Non-odontogenic cysts:
• Nasopalatine duct cyst: arises from vestiges of the nasopalatine duct; present in the midline of the anterior maxilla; slow growing; occasional discharge; radiographically — well-circumscribed radiolucency in the anterior part of the midline of the maxilla; must be differentiated from the anterior palatine fossa (max 6–7mm).
• Nasolabial cyst: uncommon; occurs deep to the nasolabial fold; probably arises from remnants of the nasolacrimal duct; occasionally bilateral; may present as swelling of the upper lip and may distort the nostril; treatment — simple excision.

(v)
