Gingival cysts:
• Dental lamina cysts of newborns (Bohn's nodules): up to 80% of infants have small nodules or cysts in the gingivae; caused by proliferation of epithelial cells of Serres.
• Epstein's pearls (non-odontogenic): appear as cream-coloured swellings along the midpalatine raphe; resolve spontaneously in a matter of months.
• Gingival cysts of adults: rare; form dome-shaped swellings less than 1 cm in diameter; may erode underlying bone; do not recur after enucleation.

A(i)
Oral and Maxillofacial Radiology is the specialty of Dentistry concerned with performance and interpretation of diagnostic imaging used for examining the craniofacial, dental and adjacent structures. Radiographs are often referred to as the clinician's main diagnostic aid because the use of X-rays is an integral part of clinical dentistry, with some form of radiographic examinations necessary on the majority of patients.

A(ii)
Reasons radiographs are used in dentistry:
• To detect pathology associated with teeth and their supporting structures (caries, periodontal disease, periapical pathology).
• To detect anomalies/injuries associated with teeth, supporting structures, maxilla and mandible.
• To determine presence/absence of teeth and to localise unerupted teeth.
• To measure length of roots before endodontic therapy.
• To detect presence/absence of radio-opaque salivary calculi and foreign bodies.
• To detect anomalies/injuries/pathology of adjacent facial structures.
• To evaluate skeletal and/or soft tissues before orthodontic treatment.
• To monitor progression of orthodontic treatment and dental disease.
• To enable preoperative assessment of skeletal and soft tissue patterns before orthognathic surgery.
• To assess bony healing and effectiveness of surgical treatment postoperatively.

B(i)
Bitewing radiography: a lateral view of the posterior regions of the jaws; demonstrates the crowns of the teeth and the alveolar crestal bone of the premolar and molar regions of both maxilla and mandible.
Periapical radiography: a lateral projection displaying both the crown and the root of the tooth and the surrounding bone.
Occlusal radiography: a number of views in which the film is positioned in the occlusal plane.

B(ii)
Panoramic radiography: produces an image of both jaws and their respective dentitions on a single extra-oral film. Oblique lateral radiography: demonstrates large areas of the maxilla and mandible, with the region imaged dependent on the technique chosen. Cephalometry: employs techniques to produce standardised and reproducible films of the facial bones for use in orthodontic, orthognathic and implant treatment.
questions.question:
Describe the radiographic features and types of dental radiography under the following headings:
A(i) Define dental/maxillofacial radiology and state why radiographs are referred to as the clinician's main diagnostic aid.
A(ii) List all the reasons radiographs are used in dentistry.
B(i) Define and distinguish between bitewing, periapical, and occlusal intraoral radiography.
B(ii) Define and distinguish between the three main extra-oral projections — panoramic, oblique lateral, and cephalometry.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Ankylosis of the temporomandibular joint (bony type). An opening of less than 5mm is considered to indicate full bony union, supporting this diagnosis.

(ii)
Aetiological factors:
• Trauma: Congenital, forceps delivery, condylar fractures, glenoid fossa fractures
• Infection: Arthritis, osteomyelitis, otitis media, parotitis, tonsillitis, abscess around the joint, actinomycosis
• Inflammation: Rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, septic arthritis
• Scar tissue: Burns, irradiation
• Systemic diseases: Smallpox, scarlet fever, typhoid, gonococcal arthritis

(iii)
Unilateral: Obvious facial asymmetry; deviation of mandible and chin toward affected side; recession of chin with hypoplastic mandible on affected side; roundness and fullness on affected side; flatness and elongation on unaffected side; antegonial notch on affected side; crossbite; Class II Angles malocclusion on affected side plus unilateral posterior crossbite; absent condylar movements on affected side. Bilateral: Symmetrical but micrognathic mandible; Class II malocclusion; no gliding movement; no asymmetry. Oral findings in both: malocclusion, anterior open bite, crossbite, malposed teeth.

(iv)
Radiological investigations:
• Posteroanterior view: mediolateral extent of the bony mass; graphical record of asymmetry
• Lateral oblique view: anteroposterior dimension of condylar mass
• Panoramic view: antegonial notching, inferior arching of body of mandible; rough assessment of caries and periodontal disease
• Cephalometry: evaluates associated skeletal malformations
• Submentovertex: evaluates coronoid process involvement and diameter of condylar mass
• Orthopantomograph: comparison of two sides; presence of antegonial notch
• TMJ views (open and close): movement of condyle, narrowing of joint space, proliferation within bony compartment
• CT scan: delineation of bony mass

(v)
Treatment objectives: restoration of function; correction of deformity; prevention of recurrence; restoration of normal growth pattern; improvement of esthetics.
Methods of treatment:
• Extraarticular fibrous ankylosis: excision of fibrous tissue; closure with flap or graft; jaw exercises
• Intraarticular ankylosis: brisement force; condylectomy; osteoarthroplasty (gap or interpositional arthroplasty)
• Distraction osteogenesis
questions.question:
A 35-year-old male presents with inability to open his mouth. He gives a history of a fall that injured his chin in childhood, followed by progressive difficulty opening the jaw. On examination, the mandible deviates toward one side, with fullness on that side and relative flattening on the other. There is a tell-tale scar on the chin. Interincisal opening measures 4mm. Radiographs reveal obliteration of the temporomandibular area with dense sclerotic bone.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and how does the interincisal opening finding support it?
(ii) State all the aetiological factors that can lead to this condition.
(iii) What are the full clinical features, including oral findings, that distinguish unilateral from bilateral presentations?
(iv) List all radiological investigations required and state what each contributes to diagnosis.
(v) State the treatment objectives and all methods of treatment available for this condition.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Classification of periodontal diseases:
• Gingival Diseases — (a) Dental plaque-induced gingival diseases; (b) Non-plaque-induced gingival lesions
• Chronic Periodontitis — (a) Localized; (b) Generalized
• Aggressive Periodontitis — (a) Localized; (b) Generalized
• Periodontitis as a Manifestation of Systemic Diseases — (A) Associated with hematological disorders: acquired neutropenia, leukemias, other; (B) Associated with genetic disorders: familial and cyclic neutropenia, Down syndrome, other; (C) Not otherwise specified
• Necrotizing Periodontal Diseases — (A) Necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (NUG); (B) Necrotizing ulcerative periodontitis (NUP)
• Abscesses of the Periodontium — (A) Gingival abscess; (B) Periodontal abscess; (C) Pericoronal abscess
• Periodontitis Associated With Endodontic Lesions — Endodontic-periodontal lesion; periodontal-endodontic lesion; combined lesions
• Developmental or Acquired Deformities and Conditions — (A) Localized tooth-related factors; (B) Mucogingival deformities around teeth including gingival recession, lack of keratinized gingiva, decreased vestibular depth, gingival excess; (C) Mucogingival deformities on edentulous ridges; (D) Occlusal trauma: primary and secondary.

A(ii)
Histopathological stages:
• Initial lesion: acute exudative inflammatory response in the connective tissue subjacent to the coronal portion of the junctional epithelium; changes include vascular and perivascular collagen destruction with characteristic neutrophilic infiltration
• Early lesion: characterized by T-lymphocytes; more collagen loss
• Established lesion: dominated by B-lymphocytes and plasma cells
• Progression is likely orchestrated by cytokines responsible for recruitment, differentiation, and growth of characteristic cell types with progressive chronicity

B(i)
Periodontitis is the inflammatory lesion of the tooth-supporting tissues. It often follows an apical extension of gingivitis with associated alveolar bone loss and formation of a periodontal pocket. It eventually leads to mobility and tooth loss in some cases. Gingivitis, by contrast, is inflammation of the gingivae without concomitant involvement of the underlying tooth-supporting structures.

B(ii)
Plaque-induced gingivitis types:
• Acute: sudden onset, short duration, painful; may be bacterial, viral, or fungal in origin, mostly bacterial
• Subacute: less severe than the acute phase
• Recurrent: an inflammatory process that reappears after treatment or disappears spontaneously and then reappears
• Chronic: most common form; slow onset, long duration, usually painless
questions.question:
Describe the classification of periodontal diseases under the following headings:

A(i) State the major categories and their subcategories as per the full classification of periodontal diseases and conditions, including all numbered divisions.
A(ii) Describe the histopathological stages of the gingivitis lesion, naming the characteristic cells and tissue changes at each stage.
B(i) Explain the progression from gingivitis to periodontitis, including the key distinguishing features and the consequences of untreated periodontitis.
B(ii) Distinguish between the four clinical types of plaque-induced gingivitis in terms of onset, duration, and painful nature.

Describe the acquired causes of tooth loss and the effects of tooth loss under the following headings:
A(i) List all acquired causes of tooth loss.
A(ii) Describe periodontal disease as a cause of tooth loss, including the form seen in teenagers.
B(i) Describe the effects of tooth loss on the patient across all domains.
B(ii) Describe all three methods of tooth notation, with examples.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Acquired causes of tooth loss: Physical trauma or injury; Periodontal (gum) disease; Dental caries and sequelae; Infection (osteomyelitis); Tumour (benign or malignant); Others: orthodontic, prosthetic.

A(ii)
Periodontal (gum) disease: leading cause of tooth loss in adults. Dental caries and sequelae are described as an irreversible microbial disease involving the softening of the hard dental tissues and proceeding to cavity formation in the tooth. Aggressive periodontitis is the form seen in teenagers.

B(i)
Effects of tooth loss:
• Facial appearance.
• Mastication/Nutrition.
• Teeth arrangement.
• Effect on jaw bones.
• Speech.
• Psychological and social well-being.

B(ii)
Tooth notation methods:
• FDI notation: Permanent teeth — 18 to 11/21 to 28 (upper) and 48 to 41/31 to 38 (lower). Deciduous — 55 to 51/61 to 65 (upper) and 85 to 81/71 to 75 (lower).
• Zsigmondy-Palmer notation: Permanent teeth — 8-1/1-8 (upper and lower). Deciduous — E-A/A-E (upper and lower).
• Universal notation.

A(i)
Edentulism is the medical term to describe the condition of missing teeth. Partial edentulism (partial tooth loss): one tooth or few teeth missing in the upper or lower arch or both. Complete edentulism (complete tooth loss): all the teeth are missing in the upper or lower arch or both.

A(ii)
Types of tooth replacement: All acrylic denture; Metallic denture; Flexible denture; Bridges; Implants; Obturator denture.

B(i)
Classification of dentures:
• By number of teeth replaced: Partial dentures; Complete dentures.
• By material used: Acrylic denture; Metallic denture; Flexible denture.
• By ease of removal: Removable denture (Complete denture; Immediate denture); Fixed denture (Teeth retained/bridge; Implant retained); Fixed removable denture.
A denture is a dental prosthesis that replaces one or more missing teeth or the entire dentition/teeth and associated structures in the maxillary or mandibular or both arches.

B(ii)
Obturator: A prosthesis that covers an oronasal fistula (or 'holes') in the roof of the mouth, providing the wearer with a plastic/acrylic, removable roof of the mouth, which aids in speech, eating, and proper air flow.
questions.question:
Describe the classification and types of tooth replacement prostheses under the following headings:
A(i) Define edentulism and distinguish between partial and complete edentulism.
A(ii) List all the types of tooth replacement options available.
B(i) Classify dentures by number of teeth replaced, material used, and ease of removal, giving examples under each.
B(ii) Describe obturators — their definition, function, and clinical indication.

A patient presents with recurrent episodes of inability to close the jaw after yawning. On examination, there are bilateral hollows anterior to the tragi, the chin is protruding, the muscles of mastication are tense, there is excessive salivation, and the centre line is intact. The patient is otherwise healthy.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and what is its relative frequency among all joint dislocations?
(ii) State all the causes of this condition, covering traumatic, physiological, iatrogenic, and constitutional factors.
(iii) Describe the full clinical features of this presentation.
(iv) State all the surgical operations involving the joint directly that are used in management, and distinguish between early and chronic case management.
(v) State the full range of investigations used and the incisions employed for surgical access to the temporomandibular joint.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: anterior dislocation of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ). Constitutes about 3–6% of all joint dislocations. Anterior displacement is the commonest type.

(ii)
Causes:
• Traumatic: falls, fits, road traffic accidents, assaults
• Physiological: excessive yawning, shouting
• Iatrogenic: excessive opening during dental and ENT treatment
• Drugs: drugs of the phenothiazine group
• Constitutional factors: flattened articular eminence, loose capsule and ligament system, hyperfunction of lateral pterygoid, hypofunction of distal fibres of temporalis, underdeveloped joint cartilage, abnormal contour and developmental disorder of condylar head

(iii)
Full clinical features of anterior dislocation:
• Opened mouth
• Protruding chin
• Tense muscles of mastication
• Excessive salivation
• Speech deformity
• Pain in the area of the TMJ
• Hollows on both sides of the face anterior to the tragi
• Centre line is intact
• Inability to close the mouth
• Excessive lengthening of the face
• Inability of the anterior teeth to close together
• Dimple in front of the ears
• Can be acute, chronic, or recurrent

(iv)
Surgical operations involving the joint directly:
• Lateral pterygoid myotomy
• Mechanical tightening of capsule
• Dautrey's procedure
• Eminectomy
• Augmentation of eminence with Proplast, Silastic, bone grafts
• Coronoidectomy
• Osteotomy: horizontal ramus, vertical subsigmoid, modified vertical subsigmoid, inverted L-shaped osteotomy of the ramus, intraoral sagittal split technique
Management by stage:
• Early cases (manual): manual reduction; under muscle relaxants; injection of local anaesthetic; under general anaesthesia — Hippocratic manoeuvre (conservative manual manipulation)
• Chronic cases: open reduction; condylectomy; condyloctomy

(v)
Investigations: cephalometry; PA view; lateral skull radiograph; model casts.
Incisions for surgical access: preauricular; postauricular; temporal; submandibular; intraoral; endaural.

questions.question:
Describe the gross features and clinical relevance of dental caries under the following headings:
A(i) Describe the spread of dental caries through the tooth from enamel to pulp.
A(ii) Describe the microscopic zones of the carious lesion and what each represents.
B(i) Explain how dental caries progresses to produce each of the sequelae, from reversible pulpitis to death.
B(ii) Explain why certain patients are more susceptible to caries, including all patient-related and tooth-related factors that influence the decision to restore a tooth.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Spread of dental caries: Enamel → Dentine (lateral spread and faster) → Pulp.

A(ii)
Microscopic zones:
a) Translucent zone: innermost part of the lesion.
b) Dark zone: 2nd layer.
c) Body of lesion: area of maximum demineralisation.
d) Surface zone: partial demineralisation — about 10% mineral loss occurs in this layer.

B(i)
Sequelae progression:
Pain → Reversible pulpitis → Irreversible pulpitis → Apical periodontitis (apical granuloma/cyst) → Periapical abscess → Dentoalveolar abscess → Tooth loss → Osteomyelitis → Cellulitis/space infection from spread of infections e.g. Ludwig's angina → Death (ignorance and unmanaged/poorly managed dental disease).
Rate of progression: Incipient caries to clinical caries (cavitation) on smooth surfaces takes 18 months ± 6 months. Poor oral hygiene and frequent exposures to sucrose can produce incipient lesions in as little as 3 weeks. Caries development in healthy individuals is usually slow in comparison to compromised persons.

B(ii)
General patient factors influencing susceptibility and restoration decision: Exposure to fluoride; Caries status; General health; Parafunctional habit; Age (particularly child/adult); Xerostomia; Socio-economic status; Diet.
Tooth factors: Tooth location/type/size; Cavity design/type; Dentition; Occlusal load; Tooth quality e.g. hypoplasia.
Operator and restoration process factors: Material type (physical properties, quality of finish); Moisture control; Anaesthesia during restoration; Expertise and training.

questions.question:
Describe indirect restorative materials under the following headings:

A(i) Define indirect restorative materials, list all the types, and explain why gold is considered the gold standard, including its properties and current limitations.
A(ii) Describe porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM): its position as a restorative material, its advantages, its limitations, and what restorations it cannot be used for.
B(i) Describe zirconia and lithium disilicate as restorative materials — state what makes each material notable, its applications, and for lithium disilicate state the only commercially available product.
B(ii) Explain the indications and clinical situations for choosing an inlay versus an onlay, and state which materials are suitable for each.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
An indirect restorative material is a dental material that can be used to fabricate a restoration outside the mouth (i.e., in the laboratory) and is then brought back into the clinic and cemented onto the tooth/teeth in the patient's mouth.
Types: 1. Gold alloy; 2. Base metal alloy; 3. Porcelain fused to metal (PFM); 4. Composite resins; 5. Ceramics.
Gold as gold standard: numerous polls confirm that dentists would choose gold for indirect restoration in their own mouths. Properties: durable; allows minimal preparation design; excellent marginal adaptation; excellent biocompatible properties. Limitations: colour (patients demand tooth-coloured options); price has skyrocketed above $1,500 per ounce, increasing cost from lab to dentist to patients; as a result, gold is being used less often.

A(ii)
PFM (porcelain-fused-to-metal): for many years, PFM has been the most common indirect restoration for posterior teeth. It meets patient demands for tooth-coloured restoration while providing dentists with the strength and fit they require. Advantages: time-proven material; tooth-coloured; provides strength. Limitations: challenges in its ability to create a final restoration that simulates a natural tooth; ceramists can more closely replicate a natural tooth with newer materials. Cannot be used for: inlays and onlays — dentists are limited to crown and bridge restorations with PFM.

B(i)
Zirconia: an extremely strong material with the benefit of being white; introduced as a substructure to replace traditional metal substructures in PFM; now also used for anterior and limited posterior bridges; early zirconia restorations continue to show promise.
Lithium disilicate (eMax, Ivoclar): the only currently available product of this type; presents with esthetic properties approaching or equaling leucite-reinforced glass materials; significantly better strength properties; provides a high level of esthetic restoration for posterior restorations.

B(ii)
Inlay indications: a large Class II preparation where the proximal contact and/or contours are challenging; the ability to work on a model indirectly provides the opportunity to create more ideal anatomy. Materials suitable: gold, indirect composite, and lithium disilicate.
Onlay indications: a damaged tooth that presents with a lot of healthy tooth structure remaining but one or two cusps require full coverage; provides opportunity for a more conservative restoration while strengthening a compromised tooth. Materials suitable: gold, indirect composite, and lithium disilicate.

questions.question:
Describe the gingiva and its normal architecture under the following headings:

A(i) State why knowledge of the normal appearance of the gingiva is essential, and describe all the components of the periodontium.
A(ii) Describe the clinical features of healthy gingiva under all six assessment criteria, including what each feature looks like and the anatomical or physiological factor responsible for that appearance.
B(i) Describe Stillman's cleft and gingival recession — what they represent, their causes, and their position classification in the context of gingival position assessment.
B(ii) Describe gingival abscesses and all the types of periodontal abscesses listed in the classification of periodontal diseases, and explain how Nifedipine and inflammation each cause gingival size changes through different mechanisms.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Knowledge of the normal appearance of the gingiva is essential for: appreciation of normal variation; detection of any change in case of disease; diagnosis and prompt treatment of disease; follow-up of patients. Danger exists in inadequate knowledge of normal architecture of gingivae.
Components of the periodontium: alveolar bone; cementum; periodontal ligament; gingiva (gum).

A(ii)
Clinical features of healthy gingiva:
• Colour: coral pink (brown variation); factor responsible: vascular supply and keratinisation
• Contour: scalloped and knife-edged margin; factor responsible: shape of tooth and alignment in arch
• Consistency: firm and resilient; factor responsible: collagenous nature of lamina propria
• Size: normal; factor responsible: sum total of bulk of cellular and intercellular elements
• Surface texture: smooth margin with stippling on attached gingiva; factor responsible: attachment of gingival fibres to underlying bone
• Position: 1mm above the cemento-enamel junction (CEJ); factor responsible: position of tooth in the arch

B(i)
Stillman's cleft: an abnormality of gingival contour. Gingival recession: the position of the gingiva is apically placed (below normal); causes include toothbrush trauma, inflammation, and tooth malpositon. Pseudo-pockets: the position of the gingiva is coronally placed (above normal); cause is inflammation. Position is normally 1mm above CEJ; apical placement constitutes recession; coronal placement constitutes pseudo-pocket.

B(ii)
Abscesses of the periodontium (from the full classification):
• Gingival abscess
• Periodontal abscess
• Pericoronal abscess
Gingival size changes and mechanisms:
• Nifedipine-related gingival enlargement: associated with increased fibres and decreased cells (fibrous overgrowth mechanism)
• Inflammation-related gingival enlargement: associated with decreased fibres and increased cells (infiltration by fluids and cells of the inflammatory exudate produces soggy puffiness that pits on pressure in chronic gingivitis)
Thus, the two mechanisms are fundamentally opposite at the cellular level: drug-induced enlargement is fibrotic while inflammatory enlargement is exudative/cellular.

(i)
Dry socket (alveolar osteitis).

(ii)
Birn's hypothesis:
Trauma and infection → Inflammation of bone marrow → Release of tissue activator → Plasminogen in clot gets converted to plasmin (fibrinolytic agent) → Clot is displaced and kinins are released from kininogen (from the clot) → Pain.

(iii)
Complications:
• Local — Immediate: Fractured crown, root, alveolus, tuberosity, mandible, adjacent tooth; Tear of gingiva, alveolar mucosa; Oroantral communication; Fractured instrument.
• Local — Delayed: Dry socket; Local infection; Delayed or secondary haemorrhage; Osteonecrosis.
• Local — Late: Alveolar atrophy; Osteomyelitis; Actinomycosis.
• Regional/distant — Immediate: Crushed or burnt lip; Injury to mandible, adjacent inferior dental or lingual nerves; Lacerated tongue/mucosa/palate; Swallowed or inhaled instrument; Injection track haematoma.
• Regional/distant — Delayed: Spreading infection; Myofascial pain dysfunction.

(iv)
Systemic absolute contraindications: Leukemia; Renal failure; Cirrhosis of liver; Cardiac failure.
questions.question:
A child who had a tooth extracted one week ago returns with severe pain in the extraction socket. There is no evidence of clot in the socket.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiological sequence (Birn's hypothesis) leading to the development of this complication.
(iii) State the classification of complications following exodontia under the headings of timing (immediate, delayed, late) and location (local, regional/distant).
(iv) State all systemic absolute contraindications to exodontia.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Candidal leucoplakia (chronic hyperplastic candidosis). Specific predisposing factors in this patient: denture wearing; tobacco smoking (strongly associated with tobacco smoking); the combination of both is a recognised association in this condition.

(ii)
Macroscopic appearance: characteristically presents as a dense opaque white lesion with irregular density and thickness; may have a rough or nodular surface. It cannot be scraped off. Most commonly seen on the buccal mucosa, at the commissure of the lips, as a roughly triangular lesion, often associated with angular chelitis. Usually asymptomatic.

(iii)
Histological findings: an oedematous epithelium exhibiting hyperparakeratosis and irregular acanthosis; Candidal hyphae seen at right angles to the surface but often do not penetrate to the prickle cell layer; variable numbers of acute and chronic inflammatory cells in the lamina propria; micro-abscesses may be seen.
Premalignant significance: considered a premalignant lesion; about 50% of cases show some features of atypia — these features resolve with treatment in some cases; in about 15% of cases it progresses to dysplastic lesions; the risk of progression is highest in speckled lesions; Candida species can generate carcinogens (nitrosamines).

(iv)
Systemic diseases predisposing to candidiasis: HIV/AIDS; iron deficiency anaemia; megaloblastic anaemia; DM; burns; acute leukaemia and other immunodeficiency states. Xerostomia due to Sjögren's disease or radiotherapy also predisposes.
Mechanism of resistance to phagocytic killing: Candida produces catalases that aid intracellular survival and resist oxidative killing by phagocytes; it also secretes adenosine which blocks neutrophil oxygen radical production and degranulation.

(v)
Common clinical features: burning sensation; altered taste and smell; dysphagia; red/white patches. Oral candidiasis may be associated with candidiasis of skin, nail, and other mucosal sites.
Diagnosis — clinical: often on clinical presentation. Microscopic: scrapings stained by KOH/Gram stain. Cultural (quantitation): plating on Candida chromogenic agar, incubating, and counting colony-forming units. Cultural (qualitation): germ tube growth for C. albicans, and carbohydrate assimilation for other species.
questions.question:
A 55-year-old male with a history of denture wearing presents with a painless white lesion at the commissure of his lips bilaterally, which cannot be scraped off. He is a heavy tobacco smoker. Biopsy is taken and histology reveals hyperparakeratosis, irregular acanthosis, and the presence of candidal hyphae.

(i) What is the diagnosis and what are the specific predisposing factors in this patient?
(ii) Describe the full macroscopic appearance of this lesion and its most common site of occurrence.
(iii) Describe the histological findings of this lesion in detail and explain its premalignant significance.
(iv) State all the systemic diseases and immunosuppressive conditions that predispose to candidiasis, and explain the mechanism by which Candida resists killing by phagocytes.
(v) Describe the clinical features (burning sensation, taste changes, and mucosal appearance) common to oral candidiasis, and describe the diagnosis including the cultural methods used.

A patient with a damaged posterior tooth presents to the clinic. The tooth has lost one cusp but retains a significant amount of healthy tooth structure. The clinician decides that a direct composite restoration would be under too great an occlusal load, yet a full-coverage crown is considered too aggressive. A laboratory-fabricated indirect restoration is chosen.

(i) State the diagnosis/treatment scenario and identify the material options appropriate for this restoration.
(ii) State the full indications and contraindications for indirect composite resin restorations.
(iii) Describe the physical properties that make indirect composites superior to direct composites, and explain why polymerization shrinkage is dramatically reduced.
(iv) Compare the advantages of indirect composite over direct composite in terms of tooth structure conservation, interproximal contours, and aesthetics.
(v) Describe the role of CAD/CAM technology in indirect restorations, including its benefits and current limitations.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Treatment scenario: The tooth is moderately broken down with one or two cusps requiring full coverage but with healthy tooth structure remaining. An onlay is the appropriate restoration. Material options: gold, indirect composite, and lithium disilicate are all suitable for an onlay restoration.

(ii)
Indications for indirect composite:
• Moderately broken down tooth where the lesion is too large or the restoration will be under too great an occlusal load for a direct composite (or nonsupporting amalgam), yet placement of a full-coverage crown is considered too aggressive
Contraindications:
• Incipient lesions
• Severely broken down teeth
• Bruxers
• Higher cost (two visits required, plus laboratory fees)

(iii)
Physical properties:
• Superior wear, strength, longevity, and margins compared to direct composites
• Dramatically reduced polymerization shrinkage due to better and more complete curing methods
• Curing methods include combinations of heat, pressure (in nitrogen atmosphere, water, etc.), light, and vacuum, outside the oral cavity
• In most cases, these indirect materials are microhybrid composite variations on proven direct composite resin systems (e.g., Herculite XRV and belleGlass HP)

(iv)
Advantages over direct composite:
• Tooth conservation for inlays is less for indirect composites compared to direct composites because of a divergent preparation and other reduction requirements
• Conservation of tooth structure is greater with indirect composite onlays than with full-coverage crowns
• Interproximal contours are superior because they are fabricated on removable dies by a skilled dental technician
• Aesthetics are superior because they are created outside the oral cavity by skilled dental technicians

(v)
CAD/CAM technology:
• CAD/CAM uses computer-aided design and computer-aided manufacturing to improve design and creation of dental restorations
• Applications include crowns, veneers, inlays, onlays, fixed bridges, implant restorations, dentures, and orthodontic appliances
• Benefits: increased speed; increased convenience; decreased labour costs; precision
• Makes possible restorations otherwise infeasible; reduces unit cost
• Uses subtractive processes (CNC milling) and additive processes (3D printing)
• Limitation: chairside CAD/CAM often involves extra time on the part of the dentist; fee is often at least two times higher than conventional lab treatments
• Superficial layers are 60 to 100 micrometers thick (not comparable to traditionally fabricated restorations with 25–50 micrometer multiple layers); rely on superficial staining rather than deep-set coloration of hand-layered porcelain

A(i)
Dental plaque is a colourless, soft, sticky coating that tenaciously adheres to teeth. It forms almost immediately after brushing. Plaque remains attached to the tooth despite movements of the tongue, water rinsing, water spray, or less than thorough brushing. Formation of plaque concentrates millions of microorganisms on the tooth. It harbours acidogenic micro-organisms — majorly Streptococcus mutans and Lactobacilli. Others include S. sanguis, S. salivarius, Actinomyces, S. sobrinus (more important in smooth-surface decay and associated with rampant caries).

A(ii)
Streptococcus mutans converts sucrose and fructose to extracellular polysaccharides (glucans and fructans respectively). These are long-chain, high-molecular-mass polymers that: aid adherence of micro-organisms to the tooth surface; are water insoluble and act as diffusion barriers trapping organic acid on the tooth; increase plaque thickness and aid acid retention. Micro-organisms act on sugary substrate by fermentation, produce acid that decreases pH of the oral environment, causing loss of minerals in the tooth and leading to dissolution and cavity formation.

B(i)
Black's classification: based on surface/site of involvement (Class I–VI). Other classifications:
• By surface affected: Smooth surface; Pit and fissure; Root caries/cemental caries.
• By tooth/period: Early childhood caries/nursing bottle caries (deciduous teeth); Rampant caries (rapid, sudden formation involving usually protected teeth).
• By rate of progression: Acute/chronic; Active/arrested/recurrent/residual.
• By part of tooth affected: Enamel/dentinal caries/cemental caries.

B(ii)
Sequelae: Pain; Reversible pulpitis; Irreversible pulpitis; Apical periodontitis — apical granuloma/cyst; Periapical abscess; Dentoalveolar abscess; Tooth loss; Osteomyelitis; Cellulitis/space infection e.g. Ludwig's angina; Death (ignorance and unmanaged or poorly managed dental disease).
questions.question:
Describe the process of dental plaque formation and its role in caries development under the following headings:
A(i) Composition and properties of dental plaque.
A(ii) Role of Streptococcus mutans in caries initiation.
B(i) Describe the classification of dental caries by Black and by other criteria.
B(ii) Distinguish between the sequelae of untreated dental caries, from earliest to most severe.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Odontogenic tumours are lesions derived from epithelial, ectomesenchymal or mesenchymal elements that are or have been part of the tooth-forming apparatus. They are found almost exclusively within the maxillofacial skeleton (intraosseous), and occasionally in the soft tissue (gingiva) or alveolar mucosa in edentulous regions (extraosseous).

A(ii)
Classification of FOL: Fibro-osseous lesions are a diverse group generally characterised by replacement of normal bone by fibrous connective tissue with an admixture of mineralised products including osteoid, mature bone, and/or cementum-like calcification.
• Developmental e.g. Cherubism.
• Reactive or dysplastic: osseous dysplasias — Periapical cementoosseous dysplasia, Focal cementoosseous dysplasia, Florid cementoosseous dysplasia, Familial gigantiform cementoma.
• Neoplastic e.g. Ossifying fibroma.
• Fibrous dysplasia (some classify under reactive/dysplastic).

B(i)
Fibrous dysplasia:
• Clinical: Monostotic type commonly affects jaw bones (maxilla more than mandible), also ribs and femur; no sex predilection; seen mainly in first and second decades; slowly growing. Polyostotic type affects multiple bones simultaneously; more common in females. Syndromes: Jaffe-Lichtenstein (polyostotic FD + skin pigmentations/café-au-lait macules); McCune-Albright (polyostotic FD + skin pigmentations + endocrine disorders mainly precocious puberty); Mazabraud (polyostotic FD + intramuscular myxomas).
• Radiographic: Early — cystic; Middle — ground glass/orange peel; Late — pagetoid/cotton wool.
• Histological: slight to moderate cellular fibrous connective tissue stroma containing foci of irregularly shaped trabeculae of immature bone, typically described as Chinese lettering appearance.

B(ii)
Fibrous dysplasia stabilises after puberty and grows much more slowly afterwards. Treatment: surgical recontouring; surgical excision.
questions.question:
Describe the gross features and classification of odontogenic tumours under the following headings:
A(i) Definition and origin of odontogenic tumours.
A(ii) Classification of fibro-osseous lesions (FOL) with examples of each type.
B(i) Describe the clinical, radiographic, and histological features of fibrous dysplasia.
B(ii) Explain why fibrous dysplasia stabilises after a certain period and state the treatment options.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Graber general (extrinsic) factors: heredity; congenital defects; environment; predisposing metabolic climate and disease; diet; abnormal pressure habits; posture; trauma.
Role of heredity — Two facts:
• For each individual there is a basic pattern or blueprint for dentofacial development which may be masked but not really changed (unless by surgery)
• Racial and familial characteristics repeat
Hereditably determined characteristics: tooth size; arch length and width; height of the palatal vault; crowding or spacing; overbite and overjet; position and configuration of muscles; tongue size and shape; character of the oral mucosa.
Heredity also plays a role in: congenital deformities; facial asymmetry; size and position of the jaws; oligodontia and anodontia; supernumerary teeth; variations in tooth shape.

A(ii)
Environmental factors — Prenatal: trauma; maternal diet; maternal metabolism and diseases; fetal posture; maternal consumption of alcohol and drugs. Postnatal: birth injuries; TMJ injuries; accidents, fractures; avulsion or displacement of teeth.
Metabolic factors and diseases: acute febrile disease (e.g., measles, mumps, chicken-pox); diseases of muscle dysfunction (e.g., muscular dystrophy, cerebral palsy, polio); endocrine disorders (e.g., pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid).

B(i)
McCoy and Shepard (1956) classification:
a) Direct (determining) factors
b) Indirect (predisposing) factors
Salzman classification:
a) Prenatal
b) Postnatal

B(ii)
Diet: Poor diet may cause deficiency diseases such as rickets, beri-beri, scurvy, etc. These may cause severe malocclusion due to interference with craniofacial growth and development, in addition to periodontal problems associated with significant bone loss.
Posture: not an important factor; may be a contributing factor; seldom considered a primary cause.
Three facial typing profiles (linked to heredity):
• Brachycephalic: short, broad face; convex profile; Class Two (protrusive maxilla or retrusive mandible) or Class I bimaxillary
• Dolicocephalic: narrow, tapering, long face; concave profile; Class Three (protrusive mandible or retrusive maxilla)
• Mesocephalic: round, oval face; flat profile; Class One (denture bases in harmony)
questions.question:
Describe the aetiology and classification of malocclusion under the following headings:

A(i) State the Graber (1972) classification of general (extrinsic) factors contributing to malocclusion, and describe the role of heredity in detail, including the dentofacial characteristics that are hereditably determined.
A(ii) Describe environmental factors — both prenatal and postnatal — as well as metabolic factors and diseases that contribute to malocclusion.
B(i) Describe the McCoy and Shepard classification and the Salzman classification of aetiological factors in malocclusion.
B(ii) Explain the role of diet and posture in the aetiology of malocclusion, and describe the three facial typing profiles linked to heredity.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Nasopalatine duct cyst:
• Origin: arises from vestiges of the nasopalatine duct. Alternative names depending on position relative to the postulated line of the incisive canal: nasopalatine cyst, incisive canal cyst, medial palatine cyst, palatine papilla cyst, and median alveolar cyst.
• Site: present in the midline of the anterior maxilla.
• Clinical features: slow growing; occasional discharge.
• Radiographic appearance: well-circumscribed radiolucency in the anterior part of midline of the maxilla.
• Differentiation from normal anatomical structure: must be differentiated from the anterior palatine fossa — the anterior palatine fossa is considered normal up to a maximum of 6–7mm.

A(ii)
Nasolabial cyst:
• Origin: probably arises from remnants of the nasolacrimal duct.
• Site: occurs deep to the nasolabial fold.
• Laterality: uncommon; occasionally bilateral.
• Clinical features: may present as a swelling of the upper lip and may distort the nostril.
• Treatment: simple excision.

B(i)
Soft tissue cysts of the oral region:
• Mucoceles (extravasation or retention)
• Ranula (originating in minor salivary glands)
• Sublingual dermoid cyst
• Cysts from abnormality of development of the branchial arches and pharyngeal pouches
Mucocele — most common soft tissue cyst; most frequently on the lower lip. Extravasation type (usual): caused by damage to the duct and extravasation of saliva; saliva leaks into surrounding tissues causing mild inflammation; saliva eventually pools up to form a cyst with connective tissue lining (not epithelial). Retention type (rare): due to duct obstruction and dilatation, forming a retention cyst with an epithelial lining.
Treatment of mucocele: excision with the underlying gland.

B(ii)
Ranula:
• Origin: uncommon type of mucocele arising from the sublingual or submandibular salivary glands.
• Distinguishing features from simple mucocele: structure similar to mucocele though there is usually an epithelial lining; usually unilateral about 2–3 cm in diameter (larger than typical mucocele); may extend across the whole floor of the mouth; bluish, soft, and fluctuant; typically painless but may interfere with speech and mastication.
• Treatment: marsupialization with removal of the related gland; enucleation is difficult because of the very thin wall; simple incision leads to recurrence.
Dermoid cyst (floor of mouth):
• Development location: develops between the hyoid and the mandible, or beneath the tongue.
• Contents: may be filled with desquamated keratin.
questions.question:
Describe the nasopalatine duct cyst, nasolabial cyst, and all cysts of the soft tissues under the following headings:

A(i) Describe the nasopalatine duct cyst — state its origin, alternative names, site, clinical features, radiographic appearance, and how it is differentiated from a normal anatomical structure.
A(ii) Describe the nasolabial cyst — state its origin, site, laterality, clinical features, and treatment.
B(i) List all the soft tissue cysts of the oral region, state the origin of each, and describe the full clinical features and treatment of the mucocele (extravasation and retention types).
B(ii) Describe the ranula — its origin, clinical features distinguishing it from a simple mucocele, and its treatment; and describe the dermoid cyst of the floor of the mouth in terms of its developmental location and contents.

Describe the full scope of exodontia under the following headings:
A(i) Define exodontia, including the approaches available, its frequency among oral surgical procedures, and the principle of irreversibility.
A(ii) List all the indications for tooth extraction.
B(i) List all systemic and local contraindications (relative and absolute) to exodontia.
B(ii) Describe all four principles of exodontia.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Exodontia is the painless removal of a whole tooth, teeth, or tooth root with minimal trauma to investing tissues, so that the wound heals uneventfully and with no postoperative preprosthetic problems. It is a surgical procedure accomplished with either an intraalveolar approach (using forceps, elevators) or a transalveolar approach (disimpaction). It is the most frequent oral surgical procedure worldwide: the simplest of procedures and the most technically challenging. It is irreversible and should be employed only when all alternatives have been excluded.

A(ii)
Indications for extraction: Beyond restoration due to caries; Periodontal disease; Fracture; Tooth surface loss; Pulpal necrosis or apical infection not amenable to endodontics and liable to cause symptoms; Significant risk of distant infection; Partly erupted teeth causing symptoms; Before transalveolar exodontia; Traumatizing mucosa; Tooth excessive for the size of arch or position cannot be corrected by orthodontics; Interference with satisfactory construction of a prosthesis; Associated disease treatable only if the tooth is removed; Over-retained deciduous teeth; Teeth involved in the foci of infection; Supernumerary teeth; Before radiotherapy; Economics, aesthetic, hygiene.

B(i)
Relative systemic contraindications: Severe dental anxiety; Haemophilia or other coagulopathies; Uncontrolled metabolic diseases; Uncontrolled hypertension and cardiac diseases; Ongoing radio-/chemotherapy; Patients on anticoagulant drugs, cancer medication, glucocorticoids, immunosuppressants.
Relative local contraindications: Ongoing acute inflammatory or infectious process; Teeth within the area of a tumour.
Absolute local: Teeth involved in arteriovenous malformations.
Absolute systemic: Leukemia; Renal failure; Cirrhosis of liver; Cardiac failure.

B(ii)
Principles of exodontia:
• Applying displacing force to a tooth or root: done directly using forceps or indirectly via a fulcrum using an elevator.
• Expansion of the socket: to make surrounding bone loose to facilitate easy removal of tooth.
• Removal of bone surrounding the root: done in cases where expansion of bone is not possible.
• Sectioning the tooth: done in extreme cases where the tooth is not being delivered otherwise.

A(i)
Developmental absence of one or more teeth in the primary or permanent dentition is called hypodontia. Classification by severity:
• Mild to moderate hypodontia: absence of usually two or more but fewer than six teeth.
• Severe hypodontia: absence of six or more teeth excluding third molar.
• Oligodontia: absence of multiple teeth usually associated with systemic manifestation.
• Anodontia: complete absence of all teeth. Rare.

A(ii)
Local causes of isolated hypodontia: Early irradiation of the tooth germ; Hormonal (hypoparathyroidism); Metabolic influences; Trauma affecting tooth germ; Infection (measles, rubella).
Syndromic/systemic causes: Ectodermal dysplasia; Cleft lip and palate; Down's syndrome (genetic).

B(i)
Associated clinical features:
• Microdontic teeth.
• Delayed or abnormal eruption of permanent teeth.
• Disruption of the plane of occlusion.
• Alveolar ridge atrophy.
• Reduced lower facial height.

B(ii)
Syndromes:
• Cleft lip and palate: cleft lip, hard and soft palate, or combination.
• Ectodermal dysplasia: defect of the hair, skin, nails etc.
• Down Syndrome: mental retardation, mongoloid face, macroglossia, delayed eruption of teeth, and heart defects.
Treatment: Requires several phases and interdisciplinary care involving various dental and medical specialties to achieve excellent aesthetics and function.
questions.question:
Describe hypodontia and its consequences under the following headings:
A(i) Define hypodontia and classify it by severity.
A(ii) List all the local and systemic (syndromic) causes of hypodontia.
B(i) Describe the associated clinical features of hypodontia leading to aesthetic and functional disability.
B(ii) Describe the features of three named syndromes associated with hypodontia, and state the approach to treatment.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Palmer notation (also called Zsigmondy-Palmer system, chevron system, or set square system): Each dental quadrant extends from the midline of the oral cavity posteriorly, corresponding to the upper left and right quadrants in the maxilla and lower left and right in the mandible. Depicted schematically with a vertical line between the central maxillary and mandibular incisors and a horizontal line between the maxilla and mandible, dividing the oral cavity into four quadrants. Clinicians use these vertical and horizontal lines to denote the quadrant of the tooth/teeth to be radiographed. Convention is used to distinguish between permanent and deciduous dentitions.

A(ii)
FDI notation: identifies each tooth using two digits. The dentition is divided into four quadrants, assigned numbers 1-4 for permanent teeth and 5-8 for deciduous dentition. Quadrants follow numerically starting from upper right, to upper left, to lower left, to lower right. The quadrant number precedes the tooth number. Individual teeth numbered sequentially from 1 (central incisor) to the most distal molar (1-8 in permanent; 1-5 in deciduous).
Examples: 53 — upper right deciduous canine; 37, 38 — lower left second and third molars.

B(i)
The FDI method is preferred by some clinicians to avoid the typographical errors that can sometimes affect the Palmer system.

B(ii)
In edentulous patients (no teeth visible within the dental arches), a clinician will continue to use the dental formula to denote the part of the oral cavity requiring radiography. The third notation system is the Universal notation system.
questions.question:
Describe the principles and clinical application of dental tooth notation under the following headings:
A(i) Describe the Palmer notation system, including its design, how quadrants are represented, and how permanent and deciduous dentitions are distinguished.
A(ii) Describe the FDI notation system, including how quadrants are numbered, how teeth are numbered, with examples.
B(i) Compare Palmer and FDI notation systems — advantages of FDI over Palmer.
B(ii) State when dental notation is still used even in the absence of teeth, and name the third notation system.

A 45-year-old male presents with a painless jaw swelling. Radiography reveals a multiloculated radiolucency simulating ameloblastoma, with a scalloped margin. Biopsy confirms the diagnosis of an odontogenic keratocyst. He also has multiple naevoid skin lesions and multiple jaw cysts on family history review.

(i) What is the full diagnosis, including the syndromic component, and what is its mode of inheritance?
(ii) State all the clinical, radiographic, and histological features of the odontogenic keratocyst.
(iii) Describe all the features of the associated syndrome, and explain its main oral importance.
(iv) Compare the recurrence risk and treatment of the two histological subtypes of OKC, justifying the difference.
(v) Give the full differential diagnosis for multiloculated jaw radiolucency and the distinguishing feature that separates this lesion from ameloblastoma on clinical and imaging grounds.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Odontogenic keratocyst as part of the Gorlin-Goltz syndrome (syndrome of multiple jaw cysts and basal cell carcinoma). Mode of inheritance: heritable as an autosomal dominant trait.

(ii)
Features of OKC:
• Clinical: uncommon; strong tendency to recur after removal; mandible usually affected (50% in angle of mandible); forms intraosseously; may grow around the crown of a tooth; spreads extensively along marrow spaces before expanding the jaw; clinical signs may not occur until the cyst is well advanced
• Radiographic: appears as well-defined radiolucent areas, either more or less rounded with scalloped margin or multiloculated simulating ameloblastoma; growth by finger-like projection into marrow spaces (mural growth) rather than by osmotic pressure effect
• Histological: epithelial lining of uniform thickness; epithelial lining weakly attached to fibrous wall; inflammatory cells typically scanty or absent; parakeratotic type: higher tendency to recur; orthokeratotic type: clearly defined basal cell layer with prekeratin; well-defined granular cell layer with abundant orthokeratin formation

(iii)
Gorlin-Goltz syndrome features:
• Heritable as an autosomal dominant trait
• Frontal and parietal bossing and broad nasal root
• Multiple keratocysts of the jaws
• Multiple naevoid basal cell carcinomas of the skin
• Skeletal anomalies (usually minor in nature)
• Intracranial anomalies
• Main oral importance: likelihood of development of multiple cysts

(iv)
Parakeratotic OKC: higher tendency to recur; treatment requires enucleation with additional treatment of the bone (mechanical or chemical) to reduce recurrence. Orthokeratotic OKC: lower tendency to recur. The greater recurrence of the parakeratotic type justifies the more aggressive treatment of the bone cavity.

(v)
Differential diagnosis for multiloculated jaw radiolucency:
• Ameloblastoma: distinguished by resorption of adjacent teeth on radiograph
• Other cysts of different types
• Secondary tumour deposit: distinguished by hazy outline and solid mass appearance
• Anatomic structures (maxillary antrum and foramina) for anterior lesions
The OKC is distinguished from ameloblastoma primarily by its histological features (uniform epithelial lining weakly attached to wall, scanty inflammatory cells) and by its growth pattern along marrow spaces (mural/finger-like) rather than by expansion.

questions.question:
Describe the periapical radiograph under the following headings:
A(i) Definition of periapical radiography and what it demonstrates.
A(ii) The main clinical indications for requesting a periapical radiograph.
B(i) Describe the two radiographic techniques used for periapical radiography, including the theoretical basis of each.
B(ii) Explain the principal difference in film/tooth relationship between the two techniques.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Periapical radiography is a lateral projection displaying both the crown and the root of the tooth and the surrounding bone.

A(ii)
Main clinical indications:
• Detection of apical infection/inflammation
• Assessment of the periodontal status
• After trauma to the teeth and associated alveolar bone
• Assessment of the presence and position of unerupted teeth
• Assessment of root morphology before extractions
• During endodontics
• Preoperative assessment and postoperative appraisal of apical surgery
• Detailed evaluation of apical cysts and other lesions within the alveolar bone
• Evaluation of implants postoperatively

B(i)
Paralleling (long cone) technique: The film packet is placed in a holder positioned parallel to the long axis of the tooth. The X-ray tubehead is aimed at right angles (vertically and horizontally) to both the tooth and film. A cone of 12 inches is used. The technique is reproducible using a film holder with fixed positions.
Bisecting angle technique: The film packet is placed as close to the tooth as possible without bending it. The angle formed between the long axis of the tooth and the long axis of the film packet is assessed and mentally bisected. The X-ray tubehead is positioned at right angles to this bisecting line with the central ray aimed through the tooth apex. Based on the geometrical principle of similar triangles, the actual tooth length equals the image length on the film.

B(ii)
In the paralleling technique, the film is parallel to the long axis of the tooth and the beam is perpendicular to both. In the bisecting angle technique, an angle exists between the tooth and film, and the beam is directed perpendicular to the bisecting line between them.

(i)
Diagnosis: Pseudomembranous candidiasis (thrush). Predisposing factors in this patient: HIV/AIDS (immunodeficiency state), prolonged use of broad-spectrum antibiotics.

(ii)
Predisposing factors:
• Local: mucosal trauma, denture wearing, poor denture hygiene, ill-fitting dentures, tobacco smoking, carbohydrate-rich diet
• Age: extremes of age (neonates, infants, and old age)
• Drugs: prolonged use of broad-spectrum antibiotics, local or systemic use of steroids
• Xerostomia: due to Sjögren's disease, radiotherapy
• Systemic diseases: HIV/AIDS, iron deficiency anaemia, megaloblastic anaemia, DM, burns, acute leukaemia and other immunodeficiency states

(iii)
Pseudomembranous candidiasis (thrush):
• Also known as thrush; affects 5% of newborn infants (from the birth canal), 10% of old debilitated patients
• Presents as soft white plaques which can be scraped off leaving a red bleeding base
• Any part of the oral mucosa can be affected; favoured sites include buccal mucosa, mucobuccal folds, oropharynx, and lateral aspect of tongue
• Symptoms minimal if pseudomembrane is intact; otherwise patient complains of tenderness, burning, and dysphagia
• Histology: necrotic and desquamating parakeratotic epithelium infiltrated by Candida hyphae, yeast forms, and acute inflammatory cells

(iv)
Other oral forms:
• Erythematous candidiasis (antibiotic stomatitis/glossitis): most favoured site is tongue followed by palate; seen in patients on prolonged antibiotic therapy/steroids; presents as red painful areas of mucosa; if dorsum of tongue — appears depapillated; complaints of pain, burning sensation, and dysphagia; histology: inflamed mucosa with areas of erosion/ulceration
• Candidal leucoplakia (chronic hyperplastic candidosis): may occur in individuals with no systemic predisposition; strong association with tobacco smoking; presents as dense opaque white lesion with irregular density and thickness, may have rough or nodular surface; cannot be scraped off; most frequently seen on buccal mucosa (commissure of lips, as roughly triangular lesion); considered a premalignant lesion — about 15% progress to dysplastic lesions; Candida can generate carcinogens (nitrosamines)
• Chronic atrophic candidosis (denture stomatitis): about 65% of geriatrics using full maxillary dentures; predisposition: poor denture fit, poor denture hygiene, failure to remove at nights; area appears red, oedematous and demarcated by denture outline; three forms of inflammation: pinpoint, diffuse, granular/multinodular; usually symptomless; histology: atrophic epithelium that is oedematous; management: improved denture hygiene

(v)
Treatment:
• Topical: nystatin 500,000 units/5mls used 5 times daily — caution in dentate patients, especially if xerostomic, since it is sucrose-sweetened; nystatin powder (100mg/g) in spray container may be applied on denture fitting surfaces
• Amphotericin B: 100mg/ml — swish 1ml and swallow every 6 hours
• Clotrimazole oral troche (mycelex): 10mg dissolved in the mouth 5 times daily
• Systemic: fluconazole and the azole group are better absorbed in acidic pH, so best taken with food; amphotericin B: nephrotoxic, given IV

A 38-year-old male with HIV/AIDS presents with white patches on the buccal mucosa, which can be scraped off leaving a red, bleeding base. He also complains of burning and dysphagia. He has been on prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics for a chest infection.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and what predisposing factors are present in this patient?
(ii) State all the local and systemic predisposing factors for this condition in general.
(iii) Describe the full clinical features of this specific type of the condition, including the histological findings.
(iv) Distinguish this presentation from three other oral forms of the same disease, describing the clinical and histological features of each.
(v) Describe the full treatment regimen, including topical and systemic agents with doses, and cautions.

Describe the aetiology, clinical features, and management of Acute Oral Candidiasis (Thrush) under the following headings:
A(i) Causative agent, its normal habitat, and conditions under which disease occurs.
A(ii) Full clinical features including distribution of lesions and what happens when plaque is removed.
B(i) Describe angular stomatitis in children — causes and treatment.
B(ii) Describe the common intraoral soft tissue conditions of the tongue in children, including geographic tongue and ankyloglossia.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Acute oral candidiasis (Thrush) is caused by Candida albicans, a yeast-like fungus. Candida albicans is a normal commensal of the oral cavity and GIT. This condition occurs as a result of actual penetration of tissues under certain conditions.

A(ii)
Clinical features: Oral lesions are characterised by appearance of soft, white, slightly elevated plaques on oral mucosa. Most frequently occurring site: buccal mucosa and tongue; although it can be seen on palate, gingiva, and floor of the mouth. When the plaque is stripped from the surface, it leaves a raw bleeding surface.

B(i)
Angular stomatitis: Deep fissures that bleed and ulcerate at the commissure of the mouth. Causes: mouth breathers; chronic licking of the lip; oral Candida infection.
Treatment: Lubrication of lips with antibiotic/antifungal ointment; stop habit.

B(ii)
Ankyloglossia (tongue tie): present at birth; short lingual frenum or anterior attachment of frenum to the tip of the tongue; does not prevent child from talking but from talking properly.
Treatment: Frenectomy.
Geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis): normally symptomless; patients may complain of discomfort with spicy foods; certain areas appear shiny and red due to loss of filiform papillae; red patches are surrounded by white margins; these areas disappear before reappearing in other regions of the tongue.
Treatment: Benign and requires no treatment — reassurance.

(i)
Diagnosis: Gorlin-Goltz syndrome (syndrome of multiple jaw cysts and basal cell carcinoma). The single most important oral implication is the likelihood of development of multiple cysts.

(ii)
Types of jaw cysts — full classification:
• Odontogenic cysts — Developmental: dentigerous cyst, eruption cyst, odontogenic keratocyst, gingival cyst, lateral periodontal cyst; Inflammatory: radicular cyst, paradental cyst; Neoplastic: cystic ameloblastoma, calcifying odontogenic (ghost cell) cyst
• Non-odontogenic cysts: nasopalatine cyst, nasolabial cyst
• Cysts without epithelial lining (pseudocyst): solitary (simple) bone cyst, aneurysmal bone cyst

(iii)
Histological features of the OKC (most associated with the syndrome):
• Epithelial lining of uniform thickness
• Clearly defined basal cell layer of basal cells with prekeratin in orthokeratotic type
• Epithelial lining weakly attached to fibrous wall
• Well-defined granular cell layer with abundant orthokeratin formation in orthokeratotic type
• Inflammatory cells typically scanty or absent
• Parakeratotic type: higher tendency to recur; epithelial lining weakly attached
• Growth is by finger-like projection into marrow spaces (mural growth) rather than by osmotic pressure effect
The tendency to recur is explained by: the weak attachment of the epithelial lining to the fibrous wall (making complete removal difficult); the mural growth pattern into marrow spaces; and the parakeratotic type's intrinsic biological behaviour.

(iv)
Other associated features of Gorlin-Goltz syndrome (apart from jaw cysts and skin lesions):
• Heritable as an autosomal dominant trait
• Frontal and parietal bossing and broad nasal root
• Skeletal anomalies (usually minor in nature)
• Intracranial anomalies

(v)
Nasopalatine duct cyst:
Origin: arises from vestiges of nasopalatine duct; named variants depending on position in relation to postulated line of incisive canal: nasopalatine, incisive canal, medial palatine, palatine papilla, and median alveolar cyst. Site: present in the midline of the anterior maxilla; slow growing; occasional discharge. Radiographic: well-circumscribed radiolucency in the anterior part of midline of the maxilla; must be differentiated from anterior palatine fossa (max 6–7mm).
Nasolabial cyst:
Origin: probably arise from remnants of nasolacrimal duct. Site: occurs deep to the nasolabial fold; occasionally bilateral. Clinical: may present as a swelling of the upper lip and may distort the nostril. Treatment: simple excision.
questions.question:
A young child presents with a family history of frontal and parietal bossing. On examination, multiple naevoid basal cell carcinomas are found on the skin. A panoramic radiograph reveals multiple radiolucent lesions in both jaws. Genetic testing confirms an autosomal dominant disorder.

(i) What is the diagnosis and what is the single most important oral implication?
(ii) State all the types of jaw cysts that may be encountered and their complete classification.
(iii) For the jaw cyst most associated with this syndrome, describe its full histological features and explain why it tends to recur.
(iv) Describe all the other associated features of this syndrome apart from the jaw cysts and skin lesions.
(v) Describe the nasopalatine duct cyst and the nasolabial cyst — including origin, site, clinical features, radiographic appearance, and treatment.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Mumps. Acute viral infection of salivary gland, commoner in the parotid gland. Causative agent: not specifically identified; the condition is an acute viral infection. Incubation period: 21 days. It is the commonest parotid swelling in children and is highly infectious. It mainly affects children.

(ii)
Clinical features: Headache; Malaise; Fever; Swelling of parotid gland — starts on one side and later the second side, hence bilateral presentation; Reduced saliva flow, leading to ascending infection which can cause bacterial infection, hence pus discharge from gland duct.

(iii)
Other organs can be affected e.g. testicles and ovaries, leading to ovaritis and orchitis.

(iv)
It is highly contagious; therefore the affected child should be isolated and materials used should be separated.
questions.question:
A child presents with acute bilateral painful swelling of the parotid glands following a prodrome of headache, malaise, and fever.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis, the causative agent, and the incubation period.
(ii) Describe the full clinical features and the mechanism by which secondary bacterial infection can occur.

Describe fibrous dysplasia with its systemic associations under the following headings:
A(i) Define fibrous dysplasia and distinguish between the monostotic and polyostotic forms, including sites affected and demographic features.
A(ii) Describe the radiographic changes at each stage of fibrous dysplasia.
B(i) Name and describe three syndromes associated with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, including all their components.
B(ii) Describe the histological appearance and the treatment of fibrous dysplasia.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Fibrous dysplasia is a benign fibro-osseous disease that frequently affects the jawbones.
Monostotic: commonly affects jaw bones; may also affect the ribs and femur; affects maxilla more than mandible; no sex predilection; seen mainly in first and second decades of life; slowly growing.
Polyostotic: affects multiple bones simultaneously (jaw bones, ribs, femur); more common in females than males.

A(ii)
Radiographic features depend on stage:
• Early: cystic.
• Middle: ground glass or orange peel.
• Late: pagetoid or cotton wool appearance.

B(i)
Syndromes:
• Jaffe-Lichtenstein syndrome: Polyostotic FD + skin pigmentations (café-au-lait macules).
• McCune-Albright syndrome: Polyostotic FD + skin pigmentations + Endocrine disorders mainly precocious puberty.
• Mazabraud syndrome: Polyostotic FD + intramuscular myxomas.

B(ii)
Histological appearance: slight to moderate cellular fibrous connective tissue stroma that contains foci of irregularly shaped trabeculae of immature bone, typically described as Chinese lettering appearance.
Treatment: Fibrous dysplasia stabilises after puberty and grows much more slowly afterwards. Options: Surgical recontouring; Surgical excision.

questions.question:
Describe the principles of wound care and oral dressings used in oral and maxillofacial surgery under the following headings:

A(i) Describe the composition of BIPP pack in full — stating the exact proportions of each constituent, the chemical role of each constituent, and the clinical situations in which it is used.
A(ii) Describe Whitehead's varnish in full — state all its constituents, the mechanism by which it provides its antibacterial effect, its waterproofing property, and its clinical uses.
B(i) Describe asepsis in oral surgery, including the definition, the particular challenge posed by the oral cavity, and all the categories under which universal precautions are applied.
B(ii) Describe the perioperative periods in oral and maxillofacial surgery — state all three periods, explain what NPO means and why it is required, and list the categories of regularly scheduled medications that must be specifically addressed before surgery.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
BIPP pack: a sterile gauze (ribbon) impregnated with a paste containing:
• One part bismuth subnitrate
• Two parts iodoform
• One part sterile liquid paraffin by weight
Role of bismuth subnitrate: it is a topical astringent and antiseptic; soluble in weak acid but insoluble in water and alcohol; contributes to the antibacterial properties of BIPP pack by releasing dilute nitric acid on hydrolysis.
Clinical uses: extraction sockets (dry sockets); large bone defects.

A(ii)
Whitehead's varnish — constituents:
• Iodoform
• Benzoin
• Starch
• Natural Balsam
• Ether
Mechanism of antibacterial effect: its constituent aromatic resins break down to produce benzoic acid, which is antiseptic.
Waterproofing property: its waterproofing property confers additional advantage in oral wound protection.
Clinical uses: extraction sockets (dry sockets); large bone defects.

B(i)
Asepsis is the attempt to keep patients, health care staff, and objects free from infectious agents. Surgical asepsis describes the efforts aimed at preventing microbes from gaining access into surgically created wounds. The oral cavity is dirty but organisms are normal flora; introduction of organisms from outside can result in infection. Universal precautions are applied to prevent sepsis under: instrument sterilization; operatory disinfection; surgical staff preparation — including hand and arm preparation (clean technique and sterile technique).

B(ii)
Perioperative periods:
• Preoperative period: before surgery
• Intraoperative period: during surgery
• Postoperative period: after surgery
NPO (nothing by mouth): the patient is given nothing by mouth for 6 to 8 hours before surgery. NPO status decreases the risk for aspiration. Failure to adhere may result in cancellation of surgery or increase the risk of aspiration during or after surgery.
Regularly scheduled medications requiring specific address:
• Diabetes medications
• Cardiac medications
• Anticoagulants
• Corticosteroids
The physician and anaesthesia provider must be notified for instructions about these medications.

questions.question:
A patient presents with a slowly growing, painless jaw swelling associated with a multilocular radiolucency on radiograph described as a soap-bubble appearance, with root resorption of adjacent teeth.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and where in the jaws this condition most frequently occurs.
(ii) State all the biological subtypes, including their distinguishing features.
(iii) Describe the histological pattern most commonly seen.
(iv) Outline the treatment options, relating each to the biological subtype.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Ameloblastoma. Approximately 80% occur in the mandible, with a marked predilection for the posterior region. In Black Africans, any region of the mandible may be involved, particularly the symphysis.

(ii)
Biological subtypes:
• Solid/conventional: slowly growing, locally invasive epithelial odontogenic tumour with high recurrence if treated conservatively; virtually no tendency to metastasise. Most cases diagnosed between 30 and 60 years. No gender predilection.
• Peripheral (extraosseous): occurs in the gingiva and very rarely buccal mucosa; seen in older adults aged 40-60; benign, nonaggressive, generally does not invade underlying bone; recurrence is rare.
• Unicystic (cystic ameloblastoma): presents as a cyst; mean age significantly lower than solid type — peak in 2nd and 3rd decades; no gender predilection; usually unilocular; 3 histologic types: luminal, intraluminal, and mural.
• Malignant: two types — Metastasising ameloblastoma (no specific features different from non-metastasising; diagnosis made in retrospect after metastatic deposits, mostly in the lung) and Ameloblastic carcinoma (shows features of malignancy).

(iii)
The follicular pattern is commonest: islands of odontogenic epithelium within a fibrous stroma. Basal cells are columnar, hyperchromatic, lined up in palisaded fashion with nuclei displaced away from the basement membrane. Central cells may be loosely arranged resembling stellate reticulum. The plexiform pattern contains basal cells in anastomosing strands with inconspicuous stellate reticulum.

(iv)
Treatment depends on biologic variant: Cystic type may require just enucleation; Solid types require surgical excision; Malignant variants are treated as carcinomas. Mandibular ameloblastoma has better prognosis than maxillary ameloblastoma.

questions.question:
A child presents with soreness in the mouth, gum bleeding on minimal trauma such as during tooth brushing, drooling of saliva, halitosis, and signs of malnutrition.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) State all the predisposing factors — bacteriological, local tissue changes, and systemic.
(iii) List the complications that can arise from this condition.
(iv) State the predisposing illnesses associated with the identified complication that destroys oral soft and hard tissue.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis.

(ii)
Predisposing factors:
• Bacteriological: Borrelia vincenti, Fusobacterium nucleatum, Bacteroides e.g. Bacteroides melaninogenicus.
• Local tissue changes: Pre-existing gingivitis due to poor oral hygiene; Trauma or injury to the gingiva; Sepsis.
• Systemic: Debilitating illness e.g. malaria, exanthematous fever like measles; Child with herpetic gingivostomatitis; Nutritional deficiency — tissue resistance reduces with deficiency of essential vitamins e.g. Vit. A, B, C; Psychosomatic factors e.g. neglect of a child (induces stress).

(iii)
Complications: Cancrum oris; Osteomyelitis.

(iv)
Cancrum Oris: A devastating infection that destroys oral soft and hard tissue, affecting young malnourished children recovering from serious debilitating illness. It is characterised by well demarcated gangrene affecting the gum, oral mucosa and soft tissue of the face, often with extensive destruction of the skin and bony skeleton.
Predisposing illnesses: Measles, Diarrhoea and vomiting, Malaria, Small pox, Typhoid fever, Tuberculosis, Chicken pox, Whooping cough, Burkitt Lymphoma.

A(i)
Malocclusion is defined as any occlusal pattern which bears significant deviation from the ideal and is associated with either aesthetic and/or functional disability. It can occur in three planes:
• Vertical plane: anterior deficiency or posterior excess produces anterior open bite (AOB); reverse produces deep bite
• Transverse plane: mandibular deficiency or maxillary excess produces crossbite; reverse produces scissors bite
• Antero-posterior plane: maxillary excess or mandibular deficiency produces Class II malocclusion; reverse produces Class III

A(ii)
Classification of aetiological factors:
• Skeletal factors — Congenital: sickle cell disease, Pierre Robin syndrome, Crouzon syndrome, hemi-facial macrosomia/microsomia, cleft lip and palate; Infectious: TMJ osteomyelitis (in the young); Traumatic: TMJ ankylosis, other trauma-related malocclusion; Other defects of jaw growth in the three planes as above.
• Soft tissue factors: neutral zone; tongue posture; tongue size; lips and cheek
• Space excess or deficiency: tooth size arch length discrepancy
• Local factors: anomalies of tooth number; anomalies of tooth size; anomalies of tooth shape; early loss of deciduous teeth; premature loss of permanent teeth; retention of primary teeth; habits; abnormal tooth position (displacements, rotations, transpositions)
Graber classification:
• General (extrinsic) factors: heredity; congenital defects; environment; predisposing metabolic climate and disease; diet; abnormal pressure habits; posture; trauma
• Local (intrinsic) factors: as under local factors above

B(i)
Soft tissue neutral zone: tongue posture, tongue size, and lips and cheek form part of the soft tissue factors. Habits that contribute to malocclusion include: thumb or finger sucking; foreign objects; tongue thrusting; lip or cheek biting; mentalis muscle strain. These habits apply abnormal pressure forces to teeth and alveolar bone, altering their position and resulting in malocclusion.

B(ii)
Local factors:
• Congenital absence of teeth (oligodontia/anodontia)
• Anomalies of tooth size (e.g., peg-shaped lateral incisors, tooth size arch length discrepancy)
• Anomalies of tooth shape
• Abnormal labial frenum
• Premature loss of deciduous teeth
• Supernumerary teeth
• Abnormal resorption of deciduous teeth
• Delayed eruption of permanent teeth
• Abnormal eruptive path
• Ankylosis of deciduous teeth
• Proximal caries
• Improperly contoured restorations
• Retention of primary teeth (when permanent successor is in a good position to erupt)
