A patient requiring a tooth restoration is found to have moderate tooth structure loss following caries removal. The clinician considers all direct restorative materials available.

(i) State all the uses of composite resin as a direct restorative material.
(ii) Describe the microfilled composite and hybrid composite — how they differ from conventional composite in surface smoothness and mechanical properties, and in which clinical situations each is preferred.
(iii) Describe dental ceramics as a direct restorative material, stating the properties that make them distinct from other direct materials.
(iv) Describe the causes of tooth structure loss that make restorative materials necessary.
(v) State the indications and contraindications for direct restorations in general.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Uses of composite resin:
• Restoration of anterior and posterior teeth
• To veneer metal crown and fixed partial denture
• To build up cores
• Bonding of orthodontic brackets, etched cast restoration, ceramic crowns
• Pits and fissure sealants
• Aesthetic laminates
• Repair of chipped porcelain restoration
• Restoring aesthetics
• Improving mastication

(ii)
Microfilled composite:
• Better surface smoothness than conventional composite
• Inferior mechanical properties compared to conventional composite
• Used for aesthetic purposes in stress-free areas
Hybrid composite:
• Better surface smoothness (than conventional)
• Equal mechanical properties (to conventional)

(iii)
Dental ceramics: more excellent aesthetic properties; higher strength; hardness; stability of colour.

(iv)
Causes of tooth structure loss:
• Dental caries (tooth decay) — most common cause
• Trauma (tooth/teeth fracture)
• Developmental anomalies, e.g., amelogenesis imperfecta, dentinogenesis imperfecta, peg-shaped lateral incisors

(v)
Indications for direct restoration:
• Prevention of caries developing
• Dental caries
• Trauma
• Tooth shape and size malformations
• Mild to moderate discolorations
Contraindications for direct restoration:
• Poor oral hygiene
• Pulpal exposure
• Gross tooth destruction
• Inadequate tooth structure for retention
• Lack of qualitative and quantitative enamel for bonding
• Severe tooth discoloration

questions.question:
A 10-year-old boy presents with dark staining on all surfaces of his teeth. On history, he has been on iron supplements.
(i) State the type of tooth discolouration and its classification.
(ii) List all the causes of extrinsic tooth discolouration in children, with the colour associated with each cause.
(iii) State the clinical distribution pattern of staining for each cause of extrinsic discolouration.
(iv) State the management for each cause of extrinsic tooth discolouration.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Extrinsic tooth discolouration. Classification: Extrinsic (occurring on the outer surface) vs. Intrinsic.

(ii)
Causes of extrinsic tooth discolouration and associated colours:
• Beverages/food: specific colour varies and is not further specified.
• Poor oral hygiene (chromogenic bacteria): green/orange stains.
• Drugs: Iron supplements — black; Chlorhexidine — brown/black; Rifabutin — red.

(iii)
Clinical distribution:
• Poor oral hygiene: stains follow the gingival contour at cervical ⅓ of the tooth.
• Beverages/food: affects all surfaces of the tooth.
• Drugs: affects all surfaces of the tooth.

(iv)
Management:
• Beverages/food/drugs: removed by prophylaxis.
• Poor oral hygiene: Oral hygiene instructions and motivation.

questions.question:
A patient who is a farmer presents with fever, dry cough, muscle aches, headache, and chest pain three weeks after spending time in a bat cave. A chest radiograph is done and the patient is subsequently referred for further management. He later develops adrenal insufficiency and oral ulceration.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and by what mechanism is the infection acquired?
(ii) State all the population groups at risk of infection and at risk of severe disease.
(iii) Describe the pathogenesis of this infection from the point of inhalation of spores.
(iv) Describe all the clinical forms of this disease, including the symptoms of each form, and state which form is usually fatal if untreated.
(v) Describe the diagnosis and treatment of this disease, including the agents used and the adverse effects of each.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Histoplasmosis (also known as Cave disease, Darling's disease, Ohio valley disease, Reticuloendotheliosis, and Caver's disease). Infection is acquired by inhalation of spores from disturbed soil or guano; it is not contagious.

(ii)
At risk of infection: farmers; pest control workers; poultry keepers; landscapers and gardeners; people who monitor bird populations or have contact with bats or bat caves; archaeologists; geologists.
At risk of severe disease: infants and very young children; older adults; people with HIV or AIDS; people receiving chemotherapy or long-term treatment with corticosteroid drugs such as prednisone; people who have had organ transplants and are taking anti-rejection medications.

(iii)
Pathogenesis: Inhaled spores are phagocytosed by macrophages after opsonisation by antibodies. They replicate in the macrophages and lyse them. T cells secrete interferon-γ which activates macrophages to kill intracellular fungi. Histoplasma also stimulates macrophages to secrete TNF which recruits other macrophages to kill the organism. Patients lacking cellular immunity are prone to disseminated disease. Symptoms start within 3 to 17 days after exposure (average 12–14 days).

(iv)
Clinical forms:
• Asymptomatic primary histoplasmosis: most common presentation; seen in otherwise healthy individuals; the only sign of infection is a lung scar
• Acute symptomatic pulmonary histoplasmosis: occurs in otherwise healthy people with intense exposure; symptoms — fever, muscle aches, headache, dry cough, chills, chest pain, loss of appetite, sweats
• Chronic pulmonary histoplasmosis: affects people with underlying lung disease such as emphysema; signs — fever, night sweats, a cough that may bring up blood, shortness of breath, weight loss
• Disseminated histoplasmosis: primarily infants/immunocompromised; can affect nearly any part of the body — eyes, liver, bone marrow, central nervous system, skin, adrenal glands, intestinal tract; symptoms — fever, weight loss, enlarged spleen/liver, pneumonia, pericarditis, meningitis, adrenal insufficiency, ulcers of the mouth, tongue or intestinal tract. Untreated disseminated histoplasmosis is usually fatal.

(v)
Diagnosis: fungal culture (gold standard — blood, mucus, or tissue sample; takes about 4 weeks); antigen detection in blood or urine samples by ELISA or PCR; antibody detection (formed 2–6 weeks after infection).
Treatment: asymptomatic cases need no treatment; amphotericin B (given IV; adverse effect: nephrotoxic); itraconazole (adverse effects: headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhoea).
Prevention: spray contaminated soil with water to prevent spores from being released into the air; use an effective face mask.

questions.question:
Describe the cause, pathophysiology, clinical features, and management of primary herpetic gingivostomatitis under the following headings:
A(i) Aetiological agent and forms of infection (primary vs. recurrent).
A(ii) Full clinical features and diagnostic criteria.
B(i) Describe hand, foot and mouth disease — aetiology, incubation period, and all clinical features.
B(ii) Compare the oral manifestations of measles with its systemic features, including timing and characteristics of oral lesions.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis is caused by Herpes simplex type 1. Primary infection presents as acute stomatitis. Recurrent infection is in the form of herpes labialis and occurs at the corner of the mouth. After the primary infection, the herpes virus remains dormant in the epithelial cells of the host.

A(ii)
Clinical features and diagnosis:
• Presence of vesicles.
• Lesions on any part of the mucosa.
• Enlarged and tender lymph nodes.
• Systemic upset.

B(i)
Hand, foot and mouth disease: highly contagious epidemic disease of young children. Caused by coxsackie virus A-16. Incubation period: 2-6 days. Coxsackie virus A-16 produces a maculopapular rash on the hands and feet. Clinical features: Sudden onset of low-grade fever; Sore throat; Headache; Anorexia; Pains in the limbs; Vesicular exanthematous lesions distributed over buccal mucosa, tongue, hard palate, hands, feet and nappy area.

B(ii)
Measles: acute contagious dermato-tropic viral infection primarily affecting children, occurring in epidemic form. Causative agent: a myxovirus. Incubation period: 7-14 days.
Systemic features: onset of fever; malaise; cough; conjunctivitis; photophobia; lacrimation; eruptive skin lesions starting on the face in the hairline and behind the ears, spreading to neck, chest, back and extremities — appear as tiny macules or papules that enlarge and coalesce.
Oral lesions (Koplik's spots): occur 2-3 days BEFORE the skin rash; appear on the buccal mucosa as small irregularly shaped white flecks surrounded by red margin.
Management of mouth lesions: recommend a soft diet; cold rather than hot food; use of orabase (carboxymethyl cellulose gelatin paste) — a paste that adheres to mucous membrane and covers the ulcer to produce relief from pain.
Complications: Encephalitis; Otitis media; Bronchial pneumonia.

questions.question:
A child presents with a painless, dome-shaped, fluctuant enlargement overlying an erupting permanent first molar. The area becomes tender on pressing.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Describe the treatment.
(iii) Define pericoronitis and explain its pathogenesis.
(iv) Describe two other problems associated with eruption in children — congenital and acquired.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Eruption cyst: a localised, dome-shaped, fluctuant enlargement overlying an erupting tooth. It is tender if inflamed.

(ii)
Treatment: No treatment required. Excised if symptomatic to allow eruption.

(iii)
Pericoronitis: incomplete eruption of a tooth may produce an opening through the overlying gum (a pocket). This pocket forms a large stagnation area which can easily become infected through the opening, causing pericoronitis.

(iv)
Other eruption problems:
• Hutchinson's incisors and mulberry molars: one of the later signs of congenital syphilis. Treponema pallidum from infected mother can cross the placenta during the 2nd trimester. Hutchinson's incisors: characterised by peg-shaped deformity of the upper central incisor of the permanent dentition; the tooth is wider at the cervical margin than at the incisal edge with notching at the tip. Mulberry molars: the molars have multiple cusps and may also be hypoplastic.
• Extra cusps: Cusp of Carabelli — found on palatal surface of 1st molars; Talon's cusp — found on palatal surface of anterior teeth. These cusps encourage food stagnation and hence rampant caries.

(i)
Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis, caused by Herpes simplex type 1.

(ii)
Primary infection presents as acute stomatitis with vesicles on any part of the mucosa, enlarged and tender lymph nodes, and systemic upset. Recurrent infection is called herpes labialis and occurs at the corner of the mouth.

(iii)
Diagnostic criteria for primary form:
• Presence of vesicles.
• Lesions on any part of the mucosa.
• Enlarged and tender lymph nodes.
• Systemic upset.

(iv)
After the primary infection, the herpes virus remains dormant in the epithelial cells of the host, and recurrent infection (herpes labialis) subsequently occurs at the corner of the mouth.
