questions.answerText:
1. Atelectasis, most likely resorptive/obstructive type given the post-operative setting (though other types include passive, adhesive, compressive, and cicatrization atelectasis).
2. Deep breathing exercises, segmental breathing, incentive spirometry exercises, and coughing, as these can respond to acute postoperative or hospitalised atelectasis.
3. Incentive spirometry is a therapeutic modality and outcome measure that relies on the patient's own effort to perform a hyperinflation manoeuvre while receiving biofeedback on inspired volume, encouraging progressively deeper inhalation; deep breathing and segmental breathing are directed at re-expanding the collapsed lung segment; coughing clears any associated secretions.
4. Monitor for tachycardia and cyanosis persisting or worsening, and for signs that the atelectasis is not resolving (continued absent breath sounds, opacification), which would warrant escalation; chest radiograph in significant collapse also shows shift of the mediastinum toward the affected side and decreased size of rib interspaces over the affected hemithorax, which should be watched for.
5. In a mechanically ventilated patient unable to cooperate with active incentive spirometry, fibre-optic bronchoscopy may be used to suction secretions causing the atelectasis, and manual hyperinflation via the ventilator circuit can be used, as the deep inflation this provides recruits alveoli 'unused' during tidal ventilation, helping to prevent and reverse atelectasis and promote full aeration of the alveoli.
questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman, three days post-abdominal surgery, develops decreased chest movement and absent breath sounds over the right lower lobe, with tachycardia. Chest radiograph shows opacification of the affected segment with elevation of the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) Name the specific physiotherapy techniques indicated.
(iii) State the indications, positioning and technique for the named interventions.
(iv) State the precautions/adverse responses to monitor.
(v) State how management would be modified if this occurred in a mechanically ventilated ICU patient.

A(i) Define restrictive lung dysfunction (RLD).
A(ii) State its aetiology/classification.
A(iii) Describe its pathophysiology.
A(iv) State its clinical manifestations.
A(v) State the investigations used to identify it.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why RLD is more severe in certain groups (e.g. neuromuscular disease).
C. Distinguish between restrictive lung dysfunction and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
questions.answerText:
A(i) Restrictive lung dysfunction (RLD) is an abnormal reduction in pulmonary ventilation due to restriction of expansion by the chest wall or the lungs; lung expansion is restricted so the volume of air/gas moving in and out is decreased. It is not a disease itself but may result from many different diseases of the pulmonary system or almost any other body system.
A(ii) May be classified as permanent (spinal cord injury) or progressive (idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis); acute and reversible (pneumothorax) or chronic but reversible (Guillain-Barre syndrome); and pulmonary or extrapulmonary. Causes include interstitial (pulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis, bronchiolitis obliterans), infectious (pneumonia), neoplastic (bronchogenic carcinoma), pleural (pleural effusion, atelectasis, ARDS), cardiovascular (pulmonary oedema, pulmonary emboli), neuromuscular (spinal cord injury, ALS, poliomyelitis, myasthenia gravis, tetanus, muscular dystrophy), musculoskeletal (ankylosing spondylitis, kyphoscoliosis, pectus excavatum/carinatum), connective tissue (rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, scleroderma, polymyositis), traumatic (crush injuries, penetrating wounds, pulmonary lacerations), and pharmaceutical causes.
A(iii) Three major aspects of pulmonary ventilation are involved: compliance of the lung and chest wall, lung volumes and capacities, and the work of breathing. Decreased pulmonary compliance means the lungs are stiffer and more difficult to expand, increasing resistance to lung expansion and requiring increased pressure to maintain adequate ventilation. All lung volumes eventually decrease, with IRV and ERV most markedly affected; RV is usually decreased but may be increased in neuromuscular causes. Because all volumes decrease, all capacities (including TLC and VC) decrease, and the work of breathing increases.
A(iv) Tachypnoea; hypoxaemia from ventilation-perfusion mismatch; decreased breath sounds with dry inspiratory crackles (from atelectatic alveoli opening at end inspiration, heard mostly at lung bases); decreased lung volumes/capacities on spirometry; decreased diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) from widened interstitial spaces due to scar tissue, capillary fibrosis and ventilation-perfusion abnormalities; possible cor pulmonale from hypoxaemia, fibrosis and capillary compression; dyspnoea, an irritating dry nonproductive cough, and a wasted, emaciated appearance as disease progresses.
A(v) Pulmonary function tests (spirometry) showing decreased TLC and VC as the two most common spirometric measurements used to identify RLD.
B. Neuromuscular causes such as spinal cord injury, ALS, poliomyelitis, myasthenia gravis, tetanus and muscular dystrophy are specifically noted to sometimes cause an increase (rather than the usual decrease) in residual volume, reflecting the different mechanism (respiratory muscle weakness rather than parenchymal stiffness) by which these groups develop RLD, which can affect its severity and presentation compared with other causes.
C. In COPD the pathology is obstruction to airflow affecting the airways, mainly impairing expiration and gas exchange capability, with increased work of breathing due to hyperinflation and useful measurement via flow rates; in RLD the pathology is difficulty expanding the lungs, affecting the lung parenchyma and thoracic pump, mainly impairing inspiration and reducing lung volume, with increased work of breathing due to decreased lung compliance and volume, and useful measurement via volumes or capacities.

1. Progressive constriction of the coronary arteries is the underlying cause; cardiac pain appears when the load on the heart becomes too great in relation to coronary blood flow, so risk factors mirror those of coronary heart disease/atherosclerosis producing that constriction.
2. If severe, the patient may be scheduled for coronary bypass surgery to restore normal coronary blood flow; angina is a life-threatening condition requiring vigilant management, and medications must remain within visible access during physiotherapy as the patient may develop angina during treatment.
3. Positions of recumbency increase the volume of fluid shifted to the central circulation, increasing venous return and the work of the heart, so upright body positions are selected during exercise and at rest afterwards to minimise cardiac work; medications must not be expired and must be kept within visible access during physiotherapy.
4. Options: in less severe cases, conservative medication (e.g. sublingual nitroglycerin, nitroglycerin patch), education and physiotherapy; beta-blockers to reduce cardiac load, potassium channel activators to relieve angina; after stabilisation, a graded exercise tolerance test under supervision in a cardiac stress testing facility with ECG monitoring to quantify the angina threshold as a basis for exercise prescription; long-term goals include maximising quality of life and general health, educating regarding heart disease, self-management, nutrition, weight control, smoking cessation and reduction, alcohol consumption, anger and stress management, disease prevention, risk factors, medication use, physical activity and exercise, and relaxation.
I would prioritise the graded, ECG-monitored exercise tolerance test to establish the angina threshold, since this quantifiable threshold then safely underpins an individualised exercise prescription rather than generic activity advice.
questions.question:
A 55-year-old man reports recurrent episodes of pain beneath the upper sternum, radiating to the left shoulder and arm, brought on by exertion and relieved by rest. He has known coronary artery narrowing.

(i) State the risk factors relevant to this condition.
(ii) State the complications that may arise.
(iii) State the precautions relevant to his physiotherapy care.
(iv) Outline the physiotherapy management options, justifying the one you would prioritise.

A patient on intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV) via an endotracheal tube in the ICU develops increasing bronchial secretions and is unable to cough effectively due to the presence of the tube.

(i) State the underlying problem/diagnosis.
(ii) Name the specific physiotherapy technique indicated.
(iii) State the indications, positioning/set-up and technique for the named intervention.
(iv) State how positioning would be modified for this patient if unconscious or paralysed.
questions.answerText:
1. Risk of chest infection secondary to IPPV: the endotracheal/tracheostomy tube causes irritation of the tracheal mucous membrane increasing mucus secretion; secretions become dry and crusted because the upper respiratory tract's normal humidification is bypassed; the patient cannot cough effectively due to the tube; there is reduction/paralysis of normal ciliary action; and there is loss of the normal sigh mechanism. The longer a patient receives IPPV, the greater the likelihood of secretion and infection problems.
2. Manual hyperinflation technique.
3. Manual inflation is delivered as a deep inflation that recruits alveoli left 'unused' during the tidal volume of IPPV, re-expanding them, which helps prevent and reverse atelectasis and promotes full alveolar aeration; the fast expiratory flow rate generated is enhanced by vibration and shaking, which loosens and moves secretions towards the main airways for removal by suction.
4. The unconscious or paralysed patient usually requires prolonged care and, where possible, should be nursed in full side-lying and turned 2-hourly, allowing for chest and pressure area care as well as accurate joint positioning; the two legs are separated with pillows, the lower leg extended while the upper leg is flexed at the hip and knee, both feet kept at right angles using sandbags and/or pillows, and the lower shoulder positioned so the patient is not lying on the pressure point of the shoulder, with the forearm resting on a pillow; limb positions are regularly reversed as the patient is turned 2-hourly throughout the 24 hours.

questions.question:
A(i) State the three domains into which respiratory/cardiopulmonary outcome measures are grouped.
A(ii) State examples of behavioural domain measures.
A(iii) State examples of clinical domain measures (physical, psychological, social, medical utilisation).
A(iv) State examples of health domain measures.
B. State how these outcome measures relate to common cardiopulmonary pathologies.
C. Explain why an abnormal result on one of these measures (e.g. a low functional walk test distance) indicates a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Health domain, clinical domain, and behavioural domain.
A(ii) Behavioural outcomes include lifestyle changes important in managing chronic conditions, such as smoking cessation, stress management, adherence with exercise, physiotherapy, diet and medication; assessed by diary, interview or questionnaire, and self-efficacy measures (the individual's judgement of their capability of achieving designated performances).
A(iii) Physical measures: weighing scale, sphygmomanometer, dyspnoea intensity scale, rating of perceived exertion scale, VO2 max, pulmonary function tests, chest radiograph, arterial blood gases, breathing pattern, breath sounds, sputum profile, visual analogue scale. Psychological measures: Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI). Social measures: structured questionnaire, interview. Medical utilisation measures: structured questionnaire, interview (covering time lost from work/studies, number of hospitalisations, number of GP consultations).
A(iv) Health-related quality of life measures such as the Short Form Health Survey-12 (SF-12), Short Form Health Survey-36 (SF-36), Sickness Impact Profile (SIP), Chronic Respiratory Questionnaire (CRQ), and the McGill COPD Quality of Life Questionnaire; the health domain also comprises measures of mortality and morbidity.
B. Clinical domain physical measures such as chest radiograph, arterial blood gases, breathing pattern, breath sounds and sputum profile are directly used to assess conditions such as pneumonia, pulmonary fibrosis, pleural effusion and atelectasis, while functional exercise capacity tests (chair rise test, seated step test, self-paced walk test, 2/3/6/12-minute walk tests, modified shuttle test, treadmill endurance test, 10-metre walk velocity test, 200-metre fast walk test) are used where VO2 max equipment (the gold standard) is unavailable, with the 3MWT and 6MWT being most common, following American Thoracic Society guidelines for the 6MWT; chair rise tests give a baseline where a patient cannot tolerate a walk test.
C. Since measurement of quality of life is very important to evaluating physiotherapy intervention (there being at times only a weak correlation between physiological measures and quality of life), a poor result on a functional measure such as a walk test reflects a reduced functional exercise capacity that corresponds to the underlying cardiopulmonary limitation, and outcome measures should be selected from more than one domain, chosen for validity, reproducibility, patient acceptability, efficiency and low cost, with the physiotherapist possessing the expertise required to use them.

questions.question:
A(i) State the principles of breathing exercises and cough/huff technique.
A(ii) State their mechanism of action.
A(iii) State their indications.
A(iv) State the procedure.
A(v) State the precautions.
B. State the safe parameters/monitoring criteria for their use.
C. Explain the physiological basis of their effects.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Breathing exercises (controlled deep breathing) and cough/huff are treatment techniques used in physiotherapy for the respiratory system, alongside postural drainage and manual techniques.
A(ii) Controlled deep breathing exercises can be combined with other manual techniques for maximal clearance of bronchial secretion; cough/huff assists expulsion of loosened secretions from the airway.
A(iii) Breathing exercises may be used for conscious patients who have just undergone open heart surgery or those who have recently been weaned from the ventilator. Cough/huff is used for patients who are conscious.
A(iv) Controlled deep breathing exercises are performed by the conscious patient, combined where appropriate with manual techniques (percussion, shaking, vibration, postural drainage) for maximal clearance of bronchial secretion; cough/huff is performed by the conscious patient to expel loosened secretions.
A(v) As with other respiratory techniques, the chest should be auscultated before and after treatment to check breath sounds, and the breathing pattern and chest expansion observed.
B. These techniques require the patient to be conscious and able to cooperate (following open heart surgery or recent weaning from the ventilator for breathing exercises; conscious state for cough/huff); monitoring is via auscultation of breath sounds before and after treatment.
C. Controlled deep breathing increases lung expansion and, combined with the mechanical loosening effect of manual techniques, helps move secretions towards the main airways; the cough/huff manoeuvre then generates the expiratory airflow needed to expel these loosened secretions from the airway, which is why the two are used together for maximal clearance of bronchial secretion in conscious, cooperative patients.

A(i) Valvular heart disease is when any valve responsible for controlling blood flow between the heart chambers is damaged or diseased, occurring when one or more valves do not open or close properly; when more than one valve is affected it is called multiple valvular heart disease. Any valve can become diseased, but the aortic valve is most commonly affected.
A(ii) Congenital (present at birth, e.g. atresia, Ebstein anomaly, aortic/pulmonary atresia) or acquired later in life; causes include calcification of valves leading to atherosclerosis, annular dilation, breakage of chordae tendinae, valve degeneration (as in connective tissue disorders), and infections such as endocarditis.
A(iii) Older age, history of heart infections such as endocarditis, history of heart disease or heart attack, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and diabetes, congenital heart disease, pregnancy, and autoimmune disorders.
A(iv) Dyspnoea, oedema, angina, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, heart murmurs, chest pain, fatigue, dizziness or fainting, irregular heartbeat, and inability to maintain a regular activity level.
A(v) History (chest pain, shortness of breath, exercise intolerance, chronic cough, syncope, palpitations); physical examination (jugular venous distension, atrial heart sounds S3 and S4, changes in blood pressure, irregular pulse, murmurs); tests (electrocardiogram, chest X-ray, with echocardiogram/cardiac catheterisation as the gold standard).
B. The aortic valve is the most commonly affected valve; aortic stenosis (senile calcific aortic stenosis) is characterised by calcification of the aortic leaflets from chronic mechanical stress, and mitral stenosis similarly results from age-related degenerative changes with chronic mechanical stress promoting calcific degeneration, explaining why older patients are more prevalently and severely affected as this is a cumulative, stress-related degenerative process.
C. In valvular stenosis, there is a reduction in the diameter of the valve orifice pathway, restricting forward flow (e.g. mitral stenosis, tricuspid stenosis, aortic stenosis); in valvular insufficiency (also called incompetent, regurgitant, or prolapsed valvular heart disease), the valve does not close properly, allowing backward flow of blood (e.g. mitral regurgitation with ballooning of the valve cusps into the left atrium during systole, tricuspid regurgitation with backflow to the right atrium during systole, aortic regurgitation with backflow into the left ventricle during diastole, and pulmonary regurgitation with backflow into the right ventricle).
questions.question:
A(i) Define valvular heart disease.
A(ii) State its causes.
A(iii) State its risk factors.
A(iv) State its clinical features.
A(v) State the investigations used to diagnose it.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why the aortic valve is most commonly affected and why calcific degeneration is more prevalent in older patients.
C. Distinguish between valvular stenosis and valvular insufficiency (regurgitation).

A newborn infant shows a bluish discolouration of the lips and fingertips that worsens with crying and feeding. On examination a loud murmur is heard, and the infant tires easily during feeds.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis suggested by this classic presentation.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
questions.answerText:
1. Tetralogy of Fallot, the most common cause of cyanosis in which most of the blood fails to flow through the lungs.
2. Predisposing factor: viral infection in the mother during the first trimester of pregnancy, when the fetal heart is being formed, is one of the most common causes of congenital heart defects such as this.
3. Four abnormalities occur simultaneously: transposition of the great vessels, stenosis of the pulmonary artery, ventricular septal defect, and hypertrophy of the right ventricle. Together these cause most blood to bypass the lungs and enter the systemic circulation deoxygenated, producing cyanosis.

A(i) High blood pressure (hypertension), high blood cholesterol, cigarette smoking, sedentary lifestyle, diabetes mellitus, obesity, stress (can elevate blood pressure over an extended period and trigger release of high levels of clot-forming platelets), and occupation. Hypertension is noted as the most prevalent cardiovascular disease and one of the most powerful contributors to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.
A(ii) Heredity, male sex, increasing age, and race.
A(iii) Improvement in exercise tolerance without significant complications; reduction in number and severity of symptoms; improved lipid levels; reduction in cigarette smoking; reduction in rates of death; improvement in psychosocial wellbeing; improved quality of life; enhanced return to work; reduced costs for subsequent hospital treatment; improved respiratory capacity during exercise; improved functional capacity of exercising muscles; greater difference in oxygen levels between arterial and venous blood (more efficient oxygen extraction); increased glucose tolerance; maintenance of ideal body weight; adherence to prudent living habits; reduced strain and nervous tension; improved self-confidence and sense of wellbeing.
A(iv) Special consideration should be given to women, people on low incomes, the elderly, and people with physical disability.
B. Atherosclerosis (build-up of fatty plaque in artery walls narrowing medium and large arteries) is directly linked to modifiable risk factors such as high cholesterol and hypertension, while coronary heart disease, myocardial infarction, and peripheral arterial disease are all associated with these same modifiable risk factors, alongside contributions from the non-modifiable factors of heredity, sex, age and race.
C. Without rehabilitation and risk factor modification, high blood pressure and high blood cholesterol persist as major contributors to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, and stress continues to elevate blood pressure and trigger clot-forming platelet release; this abnormal, unmanaged physiological state increases the risk of further cardiac events and limits exercise tolerance and functional capacity, which is precisely what the benefits of cardiac rehabilitation (improved lipid levels, improved exercise tolerance, reduced symptom severity) are designed to reverse.
questions.question:
A(i) State the modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular disease.
A(ii) State the non-modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular disease.
A(iii) State the benefits of cardiac rehabilitation.
A(iv) State the special populations requiring special consideration.
B. State how these risk factors relate to common cardiovascular pathologies.
C. Explain why an abnormal lipid/blood pressure response may occur without rehabilitation and the functional deficit this causes.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Medical surveillance for continued management of complications and further stabilising the patient; risk factor modification focusing on dietary change, smoking cessation and stress management; general counselling in the form of psychological and vocational counselling and behavioural intervention; exercise training to improve functional capacity, ensure early return to independent life, and remove the harmful effects of prolonged bed rest.
A(ii) Inpatient rehabilitation is carried out in a number of stages, started 3-5 days after the cardiac event or when the patient is certified stable: Stage 1 (partial self-care, dangling legs, sitting in chair 15 minutes 1-2x/day, active/passive ROM), Stage 2 (complete self-care in bed, sitting 15-30 minutes 2-3x/day, active ROM sitting on bed), Stage 3 (sitting as often as possible, body stretching, walking 50m at slow pace), Stage 4 (walk to bathroom with supervision, walk 75m at average pace, teach pulse counting), Stage 5 (walk to waiting room/corridor, walk 300m 2x/day, check pulse counting, practise stair steps), Stage 6 (shower/tub bath with supervision, walk 500m 2x/day, continue stairs, begin home exercise instruction), Stage 7 (continue all previous activities, walk 500m 2-3x/day, walk up/down a flight of steps, continue outpatient/home programme).
A(iii) Frequency 3-4 times a week; duration 10-15 minutes initially, 30-60 minutes per session as fitness improves; types of exercise vary (single mode may cause boredom/poor adherence, so different modes such as cycle and arm ergometry, walking, bench-stepping and treadmill should be incorporated); circuit-type training is recommended in initial stages, continuous conditioning training (walking, swimming, cycling) introduced later, and interval training (putting rest intervals between work intervals) may be adopted at any stage to allow a higher intensity at each work station.
A(iv) Regular check-ups including monitored exercise performance throughout the rehabilitation period; pulse counting taught to the patient; monitoring of haemodynamic response (blood pressure, heart rate, rate pressure product) before, during, and after exercise, particularly aerobic and strengthening exercise.
B. Cardiac rehabilitation programmes were originally designed for patients recovering from acute myocardial infarction, and have since been expanded to patients recovering from coronary artery bypass graft surgery, angioplasty, and heart transplantation, those with stable angina or silent ischaemia, those with chronic arrhythmias, congestive heart failure and valvular heart disease, and as primary prevention for patients with a high risk factor profile for a future cardiovascular event.
C. Patients with cardiac disease are haemodynamically unstable, so their haemodynamic response such as blood pressure, heart rate and rate pressure product must be monitored before, during and after exercise; heavy lifting, static exercises and straining are avoided, and upright body positions are selected for exercise and for rest afterwards, because positions of recumbency increase the volume of fluid shifted to the central circulation from the periphery, increasing venous return and the work of the heart, which can provoke an abnormal (excessive) haemodynamic response and limit functional exercise capacity.
questions.question:
A(i) State the components of a cardiac rehabilitation programme.
A(ii) State the phases/stages of inpatient cardiac rehabilitation.
A(iii) State the principles of outpatient exercise prescription.
A(iv) State the outcome measures/monitoring used.
B. State how the findings/stages relate to common pathologies requiring cardiac rehabilitation.
C. Explain why an abnormal haemodynamic response may occur during rehabilitation and the functional deficit it causes.

questions.answerText:
1. Patient A's pattern (abrupt onset, high fever, productive cough, pleuritic pain, chills, leukocytosis, lobar consolidation) is typical of bacterial pneumonia. Patient B's pattern (insidious onset, moderate fever, nonproductive cough, myalgia, normal white blood cell count, patchy diffuse bronchopulmonary infiltrates) is typical of viral pneumonia.
2. In both cases the lung parenchyma is affected, as pneumonia is an inflammatory process of the lung parenchyma usually beginning with infection in the lower respiratory tract, most commonly acquired by inhalation or aspiration.
3. Bacterial pneumonia causative organisms include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, Haemophilus influenzae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Staphylococcus aureus. Viral pneumonia causative organisms include cytomegalovirus, varicella zoster, herpes simplex, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus, adenovirus, and influenza virus (fungal and chlamydial organisms such as Pneumocystis jiroveci and Chlamydia psittaci are also recognised causes of pneumonia generally).
4. Drug therapy is the primary treatment focus for both; supportive physiotherapy (postural drainage, percussion, vibration, and assisted coughing techniques for output over 30 ml/day or impaired cough) would be more prominently indicated for Patient A given the productive cough and higher secretion burden, while adequate hydration and nutrition remain important for both, with treatment intensity guided by the clinical manifestations (breath sounds, ABG, PFT changes, tachypnoea, raised heart rate) seen in pneumonia.
questions.question:
Two patients present with pneumonia. Patient A has abrupt onset, high fever, productive cough, pleuritic pain, and leukocytosis. Patient B has an insidious onset, moderate fever, nonproductive cough, myalgia, and a normal white blood cell count.

(i) Interpret the findings for each patient.
(ii) State the structure/system affected in both cases.
(iii) List the differential causative organism groups for each pattern.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan for each.

questions.answerText:
1. Post-myocardial infarction inpatient cardiac rehabilitation.
2. The staged inpatient cardiac rehabilitation protocol (ward activities and supervised exercise), which can be started 3-5 days after the cardiac event or when the patient is certified stable by both clinical judgement and the physician.
3. Stage 1: partial self-care (ADL), self-feeding, dangling legs on side of bed, sitting in chair for 15 minutes once or twice a day, active and passive ROM exercises for all extremities in bed, ankle dorsi-/plantar-flexion repeated hourly when awake. Stage 2: complete self-care in bed, sitting in chair 15-30 minutes 2-3 times a day, active ROM exercises while sitting on the side of the bed. Stage 3: sitting in chair as often as possible, body stretching, walking 50m at a slow pace. Stage 4: walking to bathroom with supervision, walking 75m at average pace, teaching pulse counting. Stage 5: walking to waiting room or ward corridor, walking 300m twice a day, checking pulse counting, practising a few stair steps. Stage 6: shower/tub bath with supervision, walking 500m twice a day, continuing stair practice, beginning home exercise instruction. Stage 7: continuing all previous ward activities, walking 500m two to three times a day, walking up and down a flight of steps, continuing outpatient/home exercise programme.
4. Regular check-ups including monitored exercise performance are advisable throughout the rehabilitation period; special consideration should be given to women, people on low incomes, the elderly, and people with physical disability.
5. Patients should not exercise if they are generally unwell, symptomatic, or clinically unstable on arrival; progression through the stages should be held back or slowed accordingly until stability is regained, with medical surveillance continuing for management of complications.
questions.question:
A patient is now three days post-myocardial infarction, certified stable by both the clinical judgment of the physiotherapist and the physician, and is commenced on inpatient cardiac rehabilitation.

(i) State the diagnosis/context.
(ii) Name the specific physiotherapy approach/technique indicated.
(iii) State the indications, positioning and technique/progression for the named intervention.
(iv) State the precautions to monitor throughout.
(v) State how the programme would be modified for a patient who remains symptomatic or clinically unstable.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Postural drainage is one of the treatment techniques used in physiotherapy for the respiratory system, listed alongside manual techniques such as chest percussion, breathing exercises, cough/huff, mechanical ventilation/manual hyperinflation, and suction.
A(ii) It uses gravity-assisted positioning of the patient to help drain secretions from specific segments of the lung towards the central airways for clearance.
A(iii) It is indicated for patients with retained secretions, such as those with pneumonia (as supportive therapy alongside drug therapy) or patients in the ICU requiring assistance with secretion clearance.
A(iv) The patient is positioned to use gravity to assist drainage of the affected lung segment(s), and this is typically combined with manual techniques such as percussion, shaking or vibration for a fuller effect; auscultation before and after treatment helps evaluate its effect.
A(v) Listen to the patient's chest with a stethoscope, noting whether breath sounds are normal, reduced, absent, or whether there are added sounds; also listen to heart sounds; it is advisable to listen both before and after treatment; observe expansion of the chest and the breathing pattern, and note evidence of other injuries that may affect positioning.
B. Auscultation of breath and heart sounds before and after treatment; observation of chest expansion and breathing pattern.
C. By positioning the patient so that gravity assists the flow of secretions from smaller, more peripheral airways towards the larger central airways, postural drainage promotes more effective mobilisation and subsequent clearance (by cough or suction) of retained bronchial secretions; where positioning cannot be safely achieved because of other injuries (for example, a fractured shaft of femur requiring a Thomas's splint, or a neck injury requiring skull traction), inappropriate positioning risks aggravating those injuries, which is why evidence of other injuries must be checked before treatment.
questions.question:
A(i) State the principles of postural drainage.
A(ii) State its mechanism of action.
A(iii) State its indications.
A(iv) State the procedure.
A(v) State the precautions.
B. State the safe parameters/monitoring criteria for its use.
C. Explain the physiological basis of its effects, and of the complications that may follow if misapplied.

A 65-year-old woman presents with progressive breathlessness on exertion, orthopnoea, and bilateral ankle swelling. On examination there are bibasal crackles and raised jugular venous pressure. She is diagnosed with congestive heart failure.

(i) State the risk factors relevant to this condition.
(ii) State the complications that may arise.
(iii) State the precautions/contraindications relevant to her physiotherapy care.
(iv) Outline the physiotherapy management options available, justifying the one you would prioritise.
questions.answerText:
1. Risk factors: hypertension, coronary heart disease, valvular heart disease, myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, and other causes of impaired cardiac function.
2. Complications: left-sided heart failure with pulmonary congestion and low cardiac output from accumulation of blood from the left ventricle to the left atrium and lungs; right-sided heart failure with increased pressure load on the right ventricle and higher pulmonary vascular pressure; biventricular heart failure with severe left ventricular pathology producing pulmonary accumulation, increased pulmonary pressure and right ventricular signs of failure.
3. She should not exercise if generally unwell, symptomatic, or clinically unstable on arrival; haemodynamic response (BP, heart rate, rate pressure product) should be monitored before, during and after exercise, particularly aerobic and strengthening exercise; heavy lifting, static exercise and straining should be avoided; fluid should be restricted in the presence of congestive heart failure.
4. Options: activities of daily living training and patient education on avoiding excessive stress; upright body positions selected for exercise and rest, as positions of recumbency increase the volume of fluid shifted to the central circulation and increase venous return and cardiac work; individualised, closely monitored aerobic exercise once stable; non-pharmacological measures including promoting adherence to recommendations, maintaining an adequate diet, maintaining a normal weight, avoiding added sodium, maintaining optimal blood cholesterol and blood sugar, maintaining normal blood pressure, avoiding smoking, exercising regularly, and restricting alcohol.
I would prioritise upright positioning with closely monitored, individualised aerobic exercise, since positions of recumbency directly increase cardiac work in this haemodynamically unstable population, while monitored exercise addresses deconditioning without provoking decompensation.

1. This describes atrial fibrillation, a common heart rhythm disorder characterised by irregular and often rapid heartbeat, in which irregular and rapid electrical activity in the atria (upper chambers) disrupts normal coordination between the atria and ventricles, leading to inefficient blood pumping; it is grouped among the arrhythmias, which also include bradycardia (heart rate under 60 bpm) and tachycardia (heart rate over 100 bpm).
2. Atrial fibrillation can increase the risk of stroke and heart failure.
3. As with other unstable cardiac rhythm/pump conditions, vital signs and haemodynamic response should be monitored before, during and after exercise, and the patient should not exercise while generally unwell, symptomatic, or clinically unstable; heavy lifting, static exercise and straining should be avoided given the risk of provoking further rhythm disturbance or decompensation.
4. Options: pharmacological anti-arrhythmic medication to control the heart's rhythm (used in valvular disease pharmacological management and applicable to arrhythmia control generally), anticoagulation given the stroke risk, and closely monitored, individualised graded activity within a cardiac rehabilitation framework, using upright positioning to minimise cardiac work.
I would prioritise close haemodynamic monitoring alongside anticoagulation-appropriate, low-risk graded activity, since the primary danger (stroke, heart failure) is systemic rather than purely exertional, making safe monitoring paramount before progressing exercise intensity.
questions.question:
A 70-year-old man presents with palpitations and an irregularly irregular pulse. He is found to have irregular, rapid electrical activity in the upper chambers of the heart.

(i) State the risk factors/underlying mechanism.
(ii) State the complications that may arise.
(iii) State the precautions relevant to his physiotherapy care.
(iv) Outline the physiotherapy management options, justifying the one you would prioritise.

A(i) Define the key pressures involved in breathing (intrapulmonary, atmospheric, intrapleural, transmural).
A(ii) State the relationship governing airflow through the airway.
A(iii) State the factors affecting airway resistance.
A(iv) State the physical properties of the lung.
A(v) Describe what happens on inspiration and expiration.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why the upper respiratory tract is the site of greatest airflow resistance.
C. Distinguish between compliance and elasticity of the lung.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Intrapulmonary/alveolar pressure is the pressure within the lungs. Atmospheric pressure is the total pressure of the mixture of gases (79.04% nitrogen, 20.93% oxygen, 0.03% carbon dioxide) present in the atmosphere. Intrapleural/intrathoracic pressure is the pressure in the pleural space. Transmural pressure is the difference between the alveolar and intrapleural pressure, and is the driving pressure responsible for inflating the lungs.
A(ii) Airflow through the conducting airway is directly proportional to the pressure difference created between the ends of the airway and inversely proportional to the resistance within the airway.
A(iii) The bifurcation and branching of airways; the size (diameter) of the lumen of each airway, which can be reduced by mucus or oedema in the airways, contraction of smooth muscles, and the degree of elasticity/distensibility of the lung parenchyma. Normally airways widen during inspiration and narrow during expiration; as diameter decreases, resistance to airflow increases; diseases causing bronchospasm (asthma) or increased mucus production (chronic bronchitis) further increase airway resistance, particularly during expiration.
A(iv) Compliance (distensibility of lung tissue, the ability to stretch and expand, allowing the lung to stretch during inspiration, defined as change in lung volume per change in transmural/transpulmonary pressure); elasticity (tendency of a structure to return to its initial size after being distended, playing a role in resisting lung distension/compliance); surface tension (acts to collapse the alveolus and increase the pressure of air within it, occurring during expiration).
A(v) On inspiration, when the diaphragm and external intercostals contract, they increase the volume of the thoracic cavity and lung, with a concomitant reduction in intrapulmonary pressure (Boyle's law), termed a subatmospheric/negative intrapulmonary pressure; this pressure difference between atmosphere and lungs facilitates airflow into the lungs to normalise the pressure difference. Expiration occurs when intrapulmonary pressure exceeds atmospheric pressure, allowing the lungs to recoil inward and expel air.
B. The site of greatest airflow resistance is the upper respiratory tract because it is more narrow, and airflow is more turbulent there, compared with the more distal, progressively branching airways.
C. Compliance describes the distensibility of lung tissue, i.e. its ability to stretch and expand (allowing the lung to stretch during inspiration), expressed as the change in lung volume per change in transmural pressure; elasticity is the opposite tendency, the tendency of a structure to return to its initial size after being distended, which plays a role in resisting lung distension or compliance.

questions.question:
A(i) Define atelectasis.
A(ii) State the five types/classification of atelectasis.
A(iii) State its clinical features.
A(iv) State its treatment.
A(v) State the chest radiograph findings.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why postoperative and hospitalised patients are prone to atelectasis.
C. Distinguish between resorptive (obstructive) and compressive atelectasis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Atelectasis, meaning "incomplete expansion," describes a state where a region of the lung parenchyma is collapsed and non-aerated; there are several pulmonary and chest disorders associated with this pathological condition.
A(ii) Resorptive/obstructive atelectasis (most common type, often due to an obstruction such as a tumour, foreign body, or mucus plug, with resorption of alveolar air distal to the obstruction); passive atelectasis (loss of lung volume caused by simple pneumothorax or diaphragmatic dysfunction); adhesive atelectasis (occurs with surfactant deficiency, giving alveoli a greater tendency to collapse); compressive atelectasis (results from compression of the lung by a space-occupying lesion, such as pleural effusion, pleural tumour, or empyema, squeezing air out of the alveoli); cicatrization atelectasis (volume loss due to decreased pulmonary compliance from fibrosis).
A(iii) Tachycardia, cyanosis, decreased chest movement over the affected area, absent breath sound over the collapsed lung area.
A(iv) Deep breathing exercises, segmental breathing, incentive spirometry exercises, coughing; acute atelectasis (as in postoperative or other hospitalised patients) can respond to these measures; fibre-optic bronchoscopy may be used to suction secretions causing the atelectasis.
A(v) The chest radiograph may show opacification of the atelectatic segment or lobe; with significant lung collapse, it will show elevation of the hemidiaphragm on the affected side, shift of the mediastinum toward the affected side, and a decrease in size of the rib interspaces over the affected hemithorax.
B. Resorptive/obstructive atelectasis, the most common type, often results from obstruction by a mucus plug or foreign body, and adhesive atelectasis can occur with surfactant deficiency; postoperative and hospitalised patients are prone to reduced deep breathing, retained secretions (mucus plugging) and reduced surfactant activity, all of which predispose to alveolar collapse, which is why deep breathing exercises, segmental breathing, incentive spirometry and coughing are the first-line responses in this group.
C. Resorptive (obstructive) atelectasis is caused by an obstruction (tumour, foreign body, mucus plug) with resorption of alveolar air distal to the block, whereas compressive atelectasis results from an external space-occupying lesion (such as pleural effusion, pleural tumour, or empyema) compressing the lung and squeezing air out of the alveoli, without an intraluminal obstruction being the primary cause.

1. Aortic aneurysm, a bulge or weakening in the aorta, the main artery carrying blood from the heart.
2. It is a weakening of the aortic wall producing a bulge; if it ruptures, it can be life-threatening, reflecting the seriousness of unrecognised or unmanaged aneurysmal disease.
questions.question:
An elderly patient is found incidentally to have a bulge in the wall of the main artery leaving the heart, with concern about the risk of rupture.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis suggested by this presentation.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiology.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Incentive spirometry is a therapeutic modality, and also an outcome measure, that relies on the patient's own effort to perform a hyperinflation manoeuvre while providing biofeedback to the patient; deep breathing exercises and segmental breathing are related techniques for the treatment of atelectasis.
A(ii) When the patient observes their inspired volume via the spirometer, they can be encouraged to work by inhaling more and more, progressively increasing lung expansion.
A(iii) Deep breathing exercises, segmental breathing, incentive spirometry exercises, and coughing are indicated in acute atelectasis, such as in postoperative or other hospitalised patients.
A(iv) The patient performs a hyperinflation manoeuvre using the incentive spirometer, observing their own inspired volume as biofeedback and being encouraged to inhale progressively more; deep breathing and segmental breathing are performed to target re-expansion of the affected lung segment(s), combined with coughing to clear associated secretions.
A(v) Incentive spirometry functions both as a therapeutic modality and as an outcome measure.
B. Response is monitored by the patient's own observed inspired volume on the spirometer (the biofeedback mechanism); these techniques are indicated for acute atelectasis in postoperative or hospitalised patients, which can respond to these measures.
C. Atelectasis describes a collapsed, non-aerated region of lung parenchyma; deep breathing exercises and incentive spirometry work by encouraging progressively deeper inspiration, which increases lung volume and helps re-expand the collapsed alveoli, while coughing clears any secretions contributing to the collapse; where these active techniques are insufficient, fibre-optic bronchoscopy may be used to suction secretions causing the atelectasis.
questions.question:
A(i) State the principles of deep breathing exercises and incentive spirometry.
A(ii) State their mechanism of action.
A(iii) State their indications.
A(iv) State the procedure.
A(v) State what incentive spirometry additionally functions as.
B. State the safe parameters/monitoring criteria for their use.
C. Explain the physiological basis of their effects in treating/preventing atelectasis.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Physicians, nurses, physiotherapists and other paramedics who have training in critical/intensive care medicine are referred to as intensivists; the physiotherapist working in an ICU has an important role to play both as an individual and as a team member.
A(ii) Suction pumps, drains and catheters, and a wide array of drugs including broad spectrum antibiotics and analgesics; the physiotherapist needs to be competent in handling this equipment and should be able to interpret and analyse the recorded data relevant to their assessment before treating patients.
A(iii) ICU monitoring systems should be used to determine the indications and contraindications for treatment, define parameters of treatment on the FITT principles, determine whether response to treatment is appropriate, determine whether treatment should be modified or discontinued, and determine appropriate patient positioning during and after treatment.
A(iv) Meticulous hand washing (scrubbing and rinsing) between patients; washing after contact with infected wounds, blood, vomitus, urine, pus or stool; routine wearing of gowns, gloves, caps and masks.
B. For proper treatment of ICU patients, each patient should be thoroughly assessed at each visit and treatment given accordingly, with routine treatments to be avoided; assessment covers nine key systems in alphabetical order: cardiovascular, central nervous system, endocrine, gastrointestinal tract, haematology, microbiology (including sepsis status), peripheries (and skin), renal (and metabolic), and respiratory system.
C. Patients in the ICU are prone to infection, so personal hygiene and good hygienic practice are essential; without meticulous infection control (hand washing between patients, washing after contact with infected wounds/blood/vomitus/urine/pus/stool, and routine protective wear), the already vulnerable ICU patient is placed at heightened risk of hospital-acquired infection, compounding their existing critical illness and undermining efforts to make the ICU a healing environment in which physical, psychosocial and technological factors are all considered to hasten recovery.
questions.question:
A(i) State the role of the physiotherapist as a member of the ICU team.
A(ii) State the equipment the ICU physiotherapist needs to be competent in handling.
A(iii) State the purpose of ICU monitoring in relation to the FITT principle.
A(iv) State the infection control measures required in the ICU.
B. State how these roles/measures relate to common ICU pathologies/patient states.
C. Explain why infection control is particularly critical in this environment and the functional/risk deficit its absence causes.

A(i) Define congenital heart disease.
A(ii) State its aetiology.
A(iii) List the common types of congenital heart disease.
A(iv) Describe the pathophysiology of Tetralogy of Fallot.
A(v) Describe the pathophysiology of coarctation of the aorta.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why maternal viral infection in the first trimester causes these defects.
C. Distinguish between atrial septal defect and ventricular septal defect.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Congenital heart diseases are diseases that result from the malformation of the heart or its associated blood vessels during fetal life.
A(ii) One of the most common causes of congenital heart defects is a viral infection in the mother during the first trimester of pregnancy, when the fetal heart is being formed.
A(iii) Patent ductus arteriosus, Tetralogy of Fallot, atrial septal defect, coarctation of the aorta, ventricular septal defect, atrioventricular canal defect, truncus arteriosus, Ebstein anomaly, pulmonary atresia, and tricuspid atresia.
A(iv) Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cause of cyanosis in which most of the blood fails to flow through the lungs; four abnormalities occur simultaneously: transposition of the great vessels, stenosis of the pulmonary artery, ventricular septal defect, and hypertrophy of the right ventricle.
A(v) Coarctation of the aorta occurs when there is a narrowing of the aorta, mostly just beyond the left subclavian artery, though it can occur at other locations of the aortic arch or in the thoracic or abdominal aorta; the narrowing raises upper body blood pressure, causing upper extremity hypertension; it is seen in 6-8% of patients with congenital heart disease.
B. The fetal heart is formed during the first trimester of pregnancy, so a viral infection in the mother during this critical developmental window is one of the most common causes of congenital heart defects, as the infection can interfere with normal cardiac formation at this stage.
C. Atrial septal defect is a hole in the wall of the heart between the left and right atria (upper chambers), causing blood to flow from the left atrium and mix with the right atrium instead of going to the rest of the body, and is considered a simple defect because the hole may close on its own as the heart grows during childhood. Ventricular septal defect is a hole in the wall between the left and right ventricles (lower chambers), causing blood to flow from the left ventricle and mix with the right ventricle; if the hole is large, the heart and lungs may need to work harder to pump blood and fluid may build up in the lungs.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old man presents with sudden, severe central chest pain radiating to the left arm and shoulder, lasting more than 30 minutes and associated with sweating and breathlessness. He has a background history of hypertension and cigarette smoking. He is admitted, stabilised medically, and referred for physiotherapy once cardiac troponin has peaked.

(i) State the most likely clinical impression.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiology underlying this condition.
(iii) State the physiotherapy assessment findings you would expect.
(iv) Draw up a problem list and goals of treatment.
(v) Outline the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
1. Myocardial infarction (MI) resulting from prolonged myocardial ischaemia.
2. MI is the death of an area of myocardium due to occlusion of one or more coronary arteries; ischaemia is reversible but infarction denotes cell death. Injured cells may recover or die during the healing period, with the next six weeks being crucial. Infarcts occur mainly in the ventricles (left more than right); greater severity raises the risk of ventricular insufficiency, acute pulmonary oedema and left ventricular failure, with usual hypoxaemia from impaired pumping. Healed myocardium retains scarring affecting electrical excitability (dysrhythmia) and mechanical function, predisposing to hypoxia.
3. Chest pain, altered vital signs (heart rate, blood pressure), ECG changes, and reduced exercise tolerance on assessment.
4. Problem list: reduced exercise tolerance, risk of further cardiac events, harmful effects of bed rest, anxiety/depression. Goals: initiate early physical activity, allay anxiety and depression, offset harmful effects of bed rest, return to activities of daily living, initiate patient/family education, promote risk factor reduction.
5. Multidisciplinary cardiac rehabilitation with medical surveillance and risk factor modification (dietary change, smoking cessation, stress management).
Inpatient rehabilitation progressed through graded stages: partial self-care and dangling legs, sitting out of bed, active/passive ROM exercises, progressing to walking 50m, 75m, 300m and up to 500m two to three times a day, and practising stairs.
Activity restricted to 5 METs or 70% of maximal heart rate for 4 to 6 weeks after MI.
Outpatient rehabilitation with individualised exercise prescription: frequency 3-4 times a week, duration 10-15 minutes initially increasing to 30-60 minutes as fitness improves.
Circuit-type training in early stages, continuous conditioning training (walking, swimming, cycling) later, and interval training with rest between work periods.
Patient and family education on outlining the course of rehabilitation, planning resumption of life at home, and promoting risk factor reduction.

questions.question:
An infant presents with poor feeding, breathlessness and failure to thrive. Investigation reveals a hole in the wall between the two lower chambers of the heart, and the heart and lungs appear to be working harder than normal.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis suggested by this presentation.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
questions.answerText:
1. Ventricular septal defect (VSD), a hole in the wall between the left and right ventricles.
2. A common predisposing factor for congenital heart defects generally, including VSD, is maternal viral infection in the first trimester of pregnancy, when the fetal heart is being formed.
3. Blood may flow from the left ventricle and mix with blood in the right ventricle instead of going to the rest of the body. If the hole is large, the heart and lungs may need to work harder to pump blood, and fluid may build up in the lungs, which is consistent with this infant's breathlessness and poor feeding/failure to thrive.

questions.question:
A(i) Define peripheral heart/vascular disease.
A(ii) List the common arterial diseases.
A(iii) List the common venous diseases.
A(iv) List the common lymphatic diseases.
A(v) State the aetiology of the arterial diseases listed.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why cold exposure and emotional stress trigger Raynaud's disease episodes.
C. Distinguish between arterial disease and venous disease of the peripheries.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Peripheral heart diseases are diseases that affect the blood vessels that supply the body, most commonly affecting arteries and veins in the arms and legs; they are classified into arterial disease, venous disease, and lymphatic disease.
A(ii) Occlusive peripheral arterial disease (chronic, occlusive arterial disease of medium and large sized vessels from peripheral atherosclerosis, associated with hypertension and hyperlipidaemia); Raynaud's disease (episodic spasm of small arteries and arterioles); Buerger's disease/thromboangiitis obliterans (chronic inflammatory vascular occlusive disease of small arteries beginning distally and progressing proximally); diabetic angiopathy (inappropriate elevation of blood glucose with accelerated atherosclerosis, a major complication being neuropathy).
A(iii) Varicose veins (distended, swollen, tortuous superficial veins that may lead to varicose ulcers); thrombophlebitis (clot formation and acute inflammation in a superficial or deep vein); chronic venous incompetence (venous valvular insufficiency from fibroelastic degeneration of valve tissue and venous dilation).
A(iv) Lymphadenopathy (enlargement of lymph nodes with or without tenderness); lymphedema (chronic disorder with excessive fluid accumulation due to obstruction of lymphatics or removal of lymph nodes); acute lymphangitis (acute bacterial infection spreading through the lymphatic system).
A(v) Occlusive PAD results from peripheral atherosclerosis and is associated with hypertension and hyperlipidaemia; Raynaud's disease is exacerbated by exposure to cold or emotional stress; Buerger's disease begins distally and progresses proximally in both upper and lower extremities; diabetic angiopathy results from inappropriate elevation of blood glucose and accelerated atherosclerosis.
B. Raynaud's disease is an episodic spasm of small arteries and arterioles that is specifically exacerbated by exposure to cold or emotional stress, so these triggers precipitate the vasospastic episodes that produce the characteristic finger tip pallor and cyanosis.
C. Arterial disease (occlusive PAD, Raynaud's, Buerger's, diabetic angiopathy) involves compromised blood supply to the tissues through narrowed, spastic or occluded arteries, whereas venous disease (varicose veins, thrombophlebitis, chronic venous incompetence) involves impaired return of blood from the tissues through distended, clotted, or valvularly incompetent veins.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old woman who stands for long periods at work presents with distended, tortuous superficial veins in both legs, with some areas of skin breakdown.

(i) State the most likely clinical impression.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiology underlying this condition.
(iii) State the physiotherapy assessment findings expected.
(iv) Draw up a problem list and goals of treatment.
questions.answerText:
1. Varicose veins, potentially progressing to chronic venous incompetence.
2. Varicose veins are distended, swollen superficial veins that appear tortuous and may lead to varicose ulcers. Chronic venous incompetence is venous valvular insufficiency that results from fibroelastic degeneration of valve tissue and venous dilation, which can follow prolonged venous distension of this kind.
3. The skin breakdown/ulceration described is consistent with the varicose ulcers noted as a recognised consequence of varicose veins.
4. Problem list: venous distension and tortuosity, risk of/existing skin breakdown (ulceration), occupational standing as a contributing factor. Goals: prevent progression to chronic venous incompetence and ulceration, address the occupational contributing factor.

questions.question:
A(i) State the principles of airway suction.
A(ii) State its mechanism of action.
A(iii) State its indications.
A(iv) State the equipment involved.
A(v) State the circumstances under which suction should be given.
B. State the safe parameters/monitoring criteria for its use.
C. Explain the physiological basis for why suction is frequently required in the ICU.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Airway suction is a treatment technique used in physiotherapy for the respiratory system in the ICU, done via suction equipment to facilitate the removal of bronchial secretions.
A(ii) It removes secretions directly from the airway that the patient may be unable to clear by coughing, particularly in the presence of an endotracheal or tracheostomy tube.
A(iii) Airway suction is frequently required for the ICU patient to facilitate the removal of bronchial secretions.
A(iv) Suction pumps, among the equipment the ICU physiotherapist needs to be competent in handling, alongside drains and catheters, and a wide array of drugs including broad spectrum antibiotics and analgesics.
A(v) Suction should be given whenever secretions can be heard in an intubated patient, and for retained secretions in the spontaneously breathing patient who is unable to cough and expectorate efficiently.
B. Suction is indicated whenever secretions can be heard in an intubated patient, or for retained secretions in a spontaneously breathing patient unable to cough and expectorate efficiently; the physiotherapist should be familiar with monitoring facilities to allay apprehension and optimise assessment and treatment effectiveness.
C. Patients receiving IPPV via an endotracheal or tracheostomy tube develop increased mucus secretion from tracheal irritation, secretions become dry and crusted because normal upper airway humidification is bypassed, the patient cannot cough effectively due to the tube, ciliary action is reduced/paralysed, and the normal sigh mechanism is lost; the longer a patient receives IPPV, the more likely secretion and infection problems become, which is why suction, alongside manual hyperinflation, is frequently required in this setting.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male heavy smoker presents with pain and colour changes in the toes of both feet, with the problem having started distally and progressed proximally.

(i) State the most likely clinical impression.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiology underlying this condition.
(iii) State the physiotherapy assessment findings expected.
(iv) Draw up a problem list and goals of treatment.
questions.answerText:
1. Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans).
2. It is a chronic inflammatory vascular occlusive disease of small arteries that begins distally and progresses proximally in both upper and lower extremities, consistent with this patient's pattern.
3. Assessment would reveal signs of arterial disease affecting the digits given the small-artery occlusive process, with the condition progressing proximally over time if unaddressed.
4. Problem list: distal ischaemic pain, risk of progression to more proximal involvement, ongoing tobacco exposure as a driver of the disease. Goals: limit disease progression, manage pain, address the smoking behaviour that is closely linked to this condition.

1. This presentation is consistent with cor pulmonale, right-sided heart failure due to hypoxaemia, fibrosis, and compression of the pulmonary capillaries, which leads to pulmonary hypertension; this is a recognised consequence of restrictive lung dysfunction (RLD).
2. The pulmonary vasculature and right side of the heart are primarily affected, secondary to the underlying restrictive pulmonary process; RLD is not itself a disease but a dysfunction resulting from many different diseases of the pulmonary system or almost any other body system.
3. Differential causes of RLD include interstitial disease (pulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis, bronchiolitis obliterans), infectious causes (pneumonia), neoplastic causes (bronchogenic carcinoma), pleural disease (pleural effusion, atelectasis, ARDS), cardiovascular causes (pulmonary oedema, pulmonary emboli), neuromuscular causes (spinal cord injury, ALS, poliomyelitis, myasthenia gravis, tetanus, muscular dystrophy), musculoskeletal causes (ankylosing spondylitis, kyphoscoliosis, pectus excavatum/carinatum), and connective tissue causes (rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, scleroderma, polymyositis).
4. Because RLD reduces lung volumes and capacities, increases the work of breathing, and can progress to cor pulmonale with right ventricular dysfunction, the physiotherapy plan should be based on the classic clinical manifestations (tachypnoea, hypoxaemia from ventilation-perfusion mismatch, decreased breath sounds with dry inspiratory crackles, decreased lung volumes/capacities on spirometry, decreased DLCO) and dyspnoea, dry cough and wasting symptoms, grading treatment intensity to the degree of hypoxaemia and cardiac strain present.
questions.question:
A patient with long-standing restrictive lung dysfunction is found to have signs of right-sided heart strain. Investigations show elevated pulmonary pressures and right ventricular dysfunction.

(i) Interpret the findings given.
(ii) State the structure/system primarily affected.
(iii) List the differential/underlying conditions that could produce restrictive lung dysfunction of this severity.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan.

A(i) State the gold standard measure of functional exercise capacity.
A(ii) State the alternative functional exercise capacity measures used by physiotherapists.
A(iii) State which of these tests are most common and the guideline body for one of them.
A(iv) State the value of the chair rise test.
B. State how these outcome measures relate to pathology severity.
C. Explain why an abnormal (reduced) result on a functional walk test indicates a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Measurement of volume of oxygen consumption (VO2 max) is the gold standard for measurement of functional exercise capacity, although many therapists will not have access to the equipment needed for this measurement in their day-to-day treatment environment.
A(ii) The chair rise test, the seated step test, the self-paced walk test, the 2-minute (2MWT), 3-minute (3MWT), 6-minute (6MWT), and 12-minute (12MWT) walk tests, the modified shuttle test, the treadmill endurance test, the 10-metre walk velocity test, and the 200-metre fast walk test.
A(iii) The 3MWT and the 6MWT are the most common; the instructions for the 6MWT are based on guidelines created by the American Thoracic Society.
A(iv) Chair rise tests are objective measures that can give a baseline of functional capacity and lower extremity strength in a population that may not be able to tolerate the demands of a walk test.
B. Given the range of outcome measures available, the physiotherapist is required to select, for an individual patient or group of patients, those measures that are the most valid and reproducible, have high patient acceptability, are efficient in terms of time and equipment needed, and are inexpensive, with selection including measures from more than one domain where possible, appropriate to the severity and tolerance level of the patient's underlying pathology.
C. Because VO2 max testing equipment is often unavailable, these alternative functional exercise capacity tests are used as practical proxies for a patient's true aerobic/functional capacity; a reduced result on any of them reflects a genuine limitation in the patient's ability to sustain physical activity, which is why the physiotherapist must possess the required expertise to use the outcome measures selected and interpret the functional deficit they reveal.

questions.question:
A(i) Define pneumonia.
A(ii) State its aetiology/categories.
A(iii) Describe its pathophysiology (clinical manifestation findings).
A(iv) State its clinical features.
A(v) State the investigations/findings used to identify it.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why nosocomial pneumonia is more common in certain hospitalised groups.
C. Distinguish between bacterial and viral pneumonia.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Pneumonia is an inflammatory process of the lung parenchyma that usually begins with an infection in the lower respiratory tract.
A(ii) Major causative agents include bacteria and viruses; it may also be caused by fungi or mycoplasmas. There are four categories: community-acquired pneumonia, hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP), health care-associated pneumonia (HCAP), and ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP); the latter three are known as nosocomial pneumonia. The most common routes for infection are inhalation and aspiration.
A(iii) Findings: decreased lung volumes, decreased lung compliance, decreased gas exchange, increased work of breathing, decreased oxygen uptake, pulmonary capillary leakage; resolution may result in fibrosis and scarring; usually increased heart rate, especially with fever.
A(iv) Bacterial pneumonia: abrupt onset, lobar consolidation, high fever, dyspnoea, tachypnoea, productive cough, pleuritic pain, leukocytosis, chills. Viral pneumonia: insidious onset, patchy diffuse bronchopulmonary infiltrates, moderate fever, dyspnoea, tachypnoea, nonproductive cough, myalgia, normal white blood cell count.
A(v) Decreased PaO2 on ABG (PaCO2 may be altered depending on breathing pattern); breath sounds may show bronchial sounds above lobar pneumonia, absent breath sounds over pneumonia, dullness to percussion, bubbling rales, rhonchi, decreased or absent sounds, egophony, and whispering pectoriloquy.
B. Nosocomial pneumonia is defined as infection in the lower respiratory tract with onset 72 hours or more after hospitalisation, and risk factors include nasogastric tube placement, intubation, dysphagia, tracheostomy, mechanical ventilation, lung injury, diabetes, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, intra-abdominal infection, uraemia, shock, history of smoking, advanced age, poor nutritional status, thoracoabdominal surgery, and therapeutic interventions such as broad-spectrum antibiotics, corticosteroids, antacids, or high oxygen concentrations, so patients with these exposures are more commonly and more severely affected.
C. Bacterial pneumonia has an abrupt onset with lobar consolidation, high fever, productive cough, pleuritic pain and leukocytosis, with Streptococcus pneumoniae being the most common community-acquired cause; viral pneumonia has an insidious onset with patchy diffuse bronchopulmonary infiltrates, moderate fever, nonproductive cough, myalgia and a normal white blood cell count, caused by organisms such as cytomegalovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus, adenovirus and influenza virus.

questions.question:
A(i) Define acquired heart disease.
A(ii) List the common acquired heart diseases.
A(iii) State the epidemiology of cardiovascular disease in Nigeria.
A(iv) Describe the pathophysiology of atherosclerosis.
A(v) State the types of arrhythmia.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why CVDs are a leading global cause of death.
C. Distinguish between angina pectoris and myocardial infarction.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Acquired heart diseases are heart diseases that develop during a person's lifetime, as opposed to congenital heart diseases which result from malformation during fetal life.
A(ii) Atherosclerosis, heart failure (left-sided/congestive, right-sided, biventricular), myocardial infarction, angina pectoris, arrhythmia (bradycardia, tachycardia, irregular rhythm), coronary heart disease, carditis (endocarditis, pericarditis, myocarditis), atrial fibrillation, cardiomyopathy (dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive, arrhythmogenic), and aortic aneurysm.
A(iii) In Nigeria, the mortality rate due to heart failure is 12.3%; hypertension, cardiomyopathies and rheumatic disease are the most common types of CVDs from a current-to-future health perspective, and Nigeria has the highest global burden of peripartum cardiomyopathy.
A(iv) Atherosclerosis is a condition characterised by the build-up of fatty plaque in the walls of the arteries; it narrows medium sized and large arteries, making the flow of blood difficult, and a blood clot formed on the plaque can block the flow of blood.
A(v) Bradycardia (heart rate too slow, under 60 beats per minute), tachycardia (heart rate too fast, over 100 beats per minute), and irregular rhythm (the heart may not pump enough blood to meet the body's needs).
B. According to the World Health Organization, the prevalence of CVDs is one of the leading causes of death globally as these diseases do not discriminate based on geography or socioeconomic status; more than four out of five CVD deaths are due to heart attacks, and one third of these deaths occur in people under 70 years of age.
C. In angina pectoris, cardiac pain begins to appear when the load on the heart becomes too great in relation to coronary blood flow in persons with progressive constriction of their coronary arteries, with pain usually felt beneath the upper sternum and referred to the left shoulder and arm; this represents reversible ischaemia. Myocardial infarction occurs as a result of prolonged myocardial ischaemia and is the death of an area of the myocardium due to occlusion of one or more coronary arteries, representing irreversible cell death rather than the reversible pain of angina.

1. Thrombophlebitis occurs when there is clot formation and acute inflammation in a superficial or deep vein; recent immobility (as after surgery) is a recognised setting for venous clot formation.
2. Complications relate to the venous disease group: varicose veins (distended, swollen, tortuous superficial veins that may lead to varicose ulcers) and chronic venous incompetence (venous valvular insufficiency from fibroelastic degeneration of valve tissue and venous dilation) are related venous conditions that can follow venous damage.
questions.question:
A 55-year-old woman, recently immobile after surgery, develops unilateral calf swelling, warmth and tenderness.

(i) State the risk factors relevant to this condition.

A 50-year-old woman is found on routine screening to have persistently elevated blood pressure. She has a sedentary lifestyle and a family history of cardiovascular disease.

(i) State the risk factors relevant to this condition.
(ii) State the complications that may arise if unmanaged.
(iii) State the precautions relevant to her physiotherapy exercise programme.
(iv) Outline the physiotherapy management options, justifying the one you would prioritise.
questions.answerText:
1. Modifiable risk factors: high blood cholesterol, cigarette smoking, sedentary lifestyle, diabetes mellitus, obesity, stress, and occupation. Non-modifiable risk factors: heredity, male sex, increasing age, and race. Hypertension itself is noted as the most prevalent cardiovascular disease and one of the most powerful contributors to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.
2. Uncontrolled hypertension is a contributor to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality and is listed among the acquired heart diseases/pathophysiological conditions affecting the cardiovascular system, alongside coronary heart disease, valvular heart disease, myocardial infarction and arrhythmia.
3. Effects must be monitored closely to ensure desired effects are being achieved (whether from medication or exercise); an exercise prescription should include generalised aerobic exercise at an intensity that is optimally therapeutic and not associated with any untoward haemodynamic response.
4. Options: pharmacological management using vasodilators (reduce afterload), diuretics (reduce plasma volume), and beta-blocking agents; non-pharmacological management including physiotherapy, which is an effective intervention with the primary goal of eliminating the need for medication, or secondarily reducing the need for or potency of medication required; the exercise prescription may be supplemented with relaxation techniques and breathing control; other recommendations include nutrition, weight control, exercise, smoking cessation, and stress management.
I would prioritise the physiotherapy-led non-pharmacological exercise prescription (generalised aerobic exercise at a therapeutic, haemodynamically safe intensity) since it directly targets the primary goal of reducing or eliminating medication need while also addressing the modifiable risk factors of sedentary lifestyle and obesity.

A(i) Assisted coughing techniques are supportive therapy used in the treatment of pneumonia (and other conditions with excess secretions), alongside postural drainage, percussion and vibration.
A(ii) It assists the patient in expelling mucus/secretions from the airway when their own cough mechanism is inadequate to do so.
A(iii) It is specifically indicated for patients who are producing more than 30 ml of mucus per day, or who have an impaired cough mechanism.
A(iv) Applied alongside the other supportive techniques (postural drainage, percussion, vibration) and combined with adequate hydration and nutrition, which are also important in this context.
A(v) As with the related manual techniques, auscultation of the chest before and after treatment, and observation of breathing pattern and chest expansion, are used to guide safe application.
B. The threshold for adding assisted coughing techniques is more than 30 ml of mucus per day, or the presence of an impaired cough mechanism.
C. In a patient with more than 30 ml of mucus production per day or an impaired cough mechanism, the normal physiological clearance process is insufficient to expel the secretion load, risking secretion retention, atelectasis, and infection; assisted coughing techniques compensate for this deficit by externally assisting the generation of adequate expiratory flow to expel the loosened secretions, working alongside postural drainage, percussion and vibration which mobilise the secretions toward the central airways in the first place.
questions.question:
A(i) State the principles of assisted coughing/cough-huff technique.
A(ii) State its mechanism of action.
A(iii) State its specific indication.
A(iv) State the procedure.
A(v) State the precautions.
B. State the safe parameters/monitoring criteria (secretion volume threshold) for its use.
