questions.answerText:
A(i) Pleural effusion is an excessive or abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pleural cavity, which normally contains between 10 and 25 mL of fluid.
A(ii) The fluid is a transudate if it has a low protein content and accumulates due to changes in hydrostatic pressure within the pleural capillaries; it is an exudate if it has a high protein content and accumulates because of changes in the permeability of the pleural surfaces.
A(iii) The most common causes are cardiac failure, pneumonia, and malignant neoplasm; other causes include tuberculosis, pulmonary infarction, and bronchiectasis.
A(iv) Empyema (collection of pus in the pleural cavity); pneumothorax (air collects between the visceral and parietal pleura, allowing the lung to move away from the chest wall and partially deflate); haemothorax (haemorrhage into the pleural space); haemoptysis (expectoration of sputum containing blood, varying from slight streaking to frank bleeding); haematemesis (blood is vomited, characterised by acidity and dark red blood).
A(v) Identify and treat the underlying cause; aspiration of excess fluid via diagnostic thoracentesis or thoracoscopy. Physiotherapy management includes positioning on the normal side to improve the ventilation-perfusion ratio and help with movement and drainage on the affected side, breathing exercises (diaphragmatic and localised breathing exercise), and aerobic exercises.
B. Cardiac failure produces changes in hydrostatic pressure within the pleural capillaries, generating a transudate effusion, while pneumonia (an inflammatory infective process) alters the permeability of the pleural surfaces, generating an exudate effusion; both are listed among the most common causes of pleural effusion alongside malignant neoplasm.
C. A transudate has low protein content and results from altered hydrostatic pressure in the pleural capillaries (as in cardiac failure); an exudate has high protein content and results from altered permeability of the pleural surfaces (as in infective or inflammatory conditions such as pneumonia).
questions.question:
A(i) Define pleural effusion.
A(ii) State the difference between a transudate and an exudate.
A(iii) State its aetiology.
A(iv) State the related terminology associated with pleural effusion.
A(v) State its treatment.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why cardiac failure and pneumonia commonly cause pleural effusion.
C. Distinguish between a transudate and an exudate pleural effusion.

questions.answerText:
A(i) ACE inhibitors (e.g. enalapril), which inhibit the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, decreasing sodium retention and vasoconstriction to decrease blood pressure; beta-adrenergic blockers (e.g. atenolol), which reduce myocardial demand by decreasing heart rate and contractility, controlling arrhythmia, reducing blood pressure and chest pain; aspirin, which decreases platelet aggregation, thereby preventing the occurrence of myocardial infarction.
A(ii) Coronary artery bypass graft, heart valve surgery (valvuloplasty), and coronary angioplasty.
A(iii) Thrombolytic therapy is administered for acute myocardial infarction; it activates the body's fibrinolytic system, dissolving the clot and restoring coronary blood flow (e.g. streptokinase, tissue plasminogen activator).
A(iv) In managing acute myocardial infarction, activity can be increased once the acute phase has stopped (peak in cardiac troponin levels); activity should be restricted to 5 METs or 70% of maximal heart rate for 4 to 6 weeks after myocardial infarction.
B. ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers are used for blood pressure/arrhythmia and chest pain control relevant to hypertension and angina/arrhythmia; aspirin and thrombolytic therapy are specifically relevant to preventing/treating myocardial infarction; surgical options (bypass graft, valvuloplasty, angioplasty) address coronary artery disease and valvular heart disease respectively.
C. Following myocardial infarction, activity is restricted to 5 METs or 70% of maximal heart rate for 4 to 6 weeks because increasing activity can only safely begin once the acute phase has stopped, as indicated by the peak in cardiac troponin levels; this restriction is designed to prevent excessive myocardial oxygen demand and workload being placed on a heart muscle that is still healing (the six weeks after infarction being crucial for minimising further damage and maximising healing), thereby preventing further ischaemic injury or complications during this vulnerable recovery window.
questions.question:
A(i) State the pharmacological medications used in the management of CVD.
A(ii) State the surgical treatment options for CVD.
A(iii) State the use of thrombolytic therapy.
A(iv) State the activity restriction guidance following myocardial infarction.
B. State how these treatments relate to specific cardiac pathologies.
C. Explain why activity restriction is necessary in the weeks following myocardial infarction and the functional deficit it is designed to prevent.

questions.answerText:
1. Occlusive peripheral arterial disease (PAD).
2. PAD is a chronic, occlusive arterial disease of medium and large sized vessels resulting from peripheral atherosclerosis, and is associated with hypertension and hyperlipidaemia; atherosclerosis is a condition characterised by build-up of fatty plaque in artery walls that narrows medium and large arteries, making blood flow difficult, and a blood clot formed on the plaque can block flow.
3. The Ankle Brachial Index (ABI) is the relevant outcome measure, a noninvasive, economical objective measure used to examine perfusion of the lower extremities in individuals at high risk of cardiovascular disease or PAD; it compares an average systolic blood pressure of the lower extremity with an average systolic blood pressure of the upper extremity, using a stethoscope or handheld Doppler ultrasound, and has high validity, reliability, sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing lower extremity ischaemia.
4. Problem list: reduced walking tolerance from claudication, impaired lower limb perfusion, cardiovascular risk factors (smoking, diabetes). Goals: improve functional walking capacity, reduce cardiovascular risk factor burden, protect the limb from ischaemic complications.
questions.question:
A 62-year-old man with diabetes and a long smoking history complains of cramping pain in his calves on walking, relieved by rest. On examination, his lower limb pulses are diminished and the skin is cool and pale on elevation.

(i) State the most likely clinical impression.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiology underlying this condition.
(iii) State the physiotherapy assessment findings/tool expected.
(iv) Draw up a problem list and goals of treatment.

A(i) State the components of clinical assessment of the patient in the ICU.
A(ii) State the systems assessed via case notes, charts and radiographs.
A(iii) State the purpose of ICU monitoring systems.
A(iv) State the nine key intensive care systems assessed.
B. State how these assessment findings relate to common ICU pathologies.
C. Explain why an abnormal response (such as fluctuating intracranial pressure) may occur and the functional/treatment deficit it causes.
questions.answerText:
A(i) For proper treatment, each patient should be thoroughly assessed at each visit and treatment given accordingly; routine treatments are to be avoided. Neurological system assessment notes that fluctuating intracranial pressure (ICP) may occur from physiotherapy procedures and environmental stimuli in the poorly sedated patient, and consistent levels of ICP are necessary for physiotherapy intervention.
A(ii) Important information is obtained from recordings in the case notes, intensive care charts, and radiographs; the physiotherapist should read the patient's case notes, view the charts and radiographs each time they want to treat the patient. Case notes give the patient's present condition, past medical condition, operation notes, and progress made since admission. Fluid balance is noted (dehydration may cause difficulty expectorating secretions due to increased viscosity and may cause confusion; a large positive balance may produce wet lungs/pulmonary oedema). Drugs prescribed, their dosages and administration times should also be noted.
A(iii) An essential component of managing the ICU patient is monitoring of cardiopulmonary function and oxygen transport; the physiotherapist should be familiar with the extensive monitoring facilities to allay apprehension and because quality care in the ICU depends on harnessing the monitoring equipment to optimise assessment, treatment effectiveness, and reduce untoward risk to the patient. Monitoring should be used to determine the indications and contraindications for treatment, define treatment parameters on the FITT principle, determine whether response to treatment is appropriate, determine whether treatment should be modified or discontinued, and determine appropriate patient positioning during and after treatment.
A(iv) Cardiovascular, central nervous system, endocrine system, gastrointestinal tract, haematology, microbiology (including sepsis status), peripheries (and skin), renal (and metabolic), and respiratory system.
B. Infection control is a key consideration as ICU patients are prone to infection, requiring meticulous hand washing between patients, washing after contact with infected wounds, blood, vomitus, urine, pus or stool, and routine wearing of gowns, gloves, caps and masks; making the ICU a healing environment requires that all physical, psychosocial and technological factors be considered to hasten the patient's recovery.
C. Fluctuating ICP may occur from physiotherapy procedures and environmental stimuli in the poorly sedated patient; because consistent ICP levels are necessary for physiotherapy intervention to proceed safely, an abnormal (fluctuating) ICP response represents a functional deficit that limits or delays the physiotherapist's ability to treat the patient until levels stabilise, underscoring why routine treatments are to be avoided and each patient thoroughly assessed at each visit before treatment is given.

1. Mitral stenosis, a valvular stenotic lesion.
2. Valvular stenosis occurs because the heart valves are essentially orifices allowing blood to move between chambers; any reduction in the diameter of this pathway is a stenotic valvular disease. Age-related degenerative changes are a leading cause of mitral stenosis, similar to aortic stenosis, where chronic mechanical stress on the valve promotes calcific degeneration; other causes include annular dilation, breakage of chordae tendinae, valve degeneration (as in connective tissue disorders), and infections such as endocarditis.
3. Dyspnoea, oedema, angina, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, heart murmurs, chest pain, fatigue, dizziness or fainting, irregular heartbeat, and inability to maintain a regular activity level; on physical examination, jugular venous distension, atrial heart sounds S3 and S4, changes in blood pressure, irregular pulse and murmurs.
4. Problem list: reduced exercise tolerance, dyspnoea, risk of further valve/cardiac damage. Goals: protect the valve from further damage, lessen symptoms, maintain activities of daily living within safe limits, avoid excessive stress.
5. Rehabilitation team focus on activities of daily living and education on avoiding excessive stress; patient should remain relatively rested until treatment of comorbid conditions or post-operative complications is complete; patient should not exercise if generally unwell, symptomatic, or clinically unstable on arrival; caution should be taken in prescribing exercise so as not to aggravate symptoms, alongside protecting the valve from infection (prompt attention to sore throat, fever, general body aches, and good dental hygiene).

A 40-year-old woman with a childhood history of rheumatic fever presents with progressive dyspnoea, fatigue, and episodes of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. On auscultation a murmur is heard, and there is a history of exercise intolerance and palpitations.

(i) State the most likely clinical impression.

A 50-year-old man with known cardiac failure develops worsening breathlessness. Chest examination reveals reduced breath sounds and stony dullness to percussion at the right lung base.

(i) Interpret the examination findings given.
(ii) State the structure/system primarily affected.
(iii) List the differential conditions that could account for this presentation.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan.
questions.answerText:
1. Reduced breath sounds with dullness at the lung base in a patient with cardiac failure is consistent with pleural effusion, an excessive or abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pleural cavity, which normally contains only 10-25 mL of fluid.
2. The pleural cavity/pleural space is primarily affected; whether the fluid is a transudate (low protein, from changes in hydrostatic pressure within the pleural capillaries, as typically occurs in cardiac failure) or an exudate (high protein, from changes in pleural surface permeability) depends on the underlying cause.
3. The most common causes of pleural effusion are cardiac failure, pneumonia, and malignant neoplasm; other causes include tuberculosis, pulmonary infarction, and bronchiectasis. Related terminology to differentiate includes empyema (pus in the pleural cavity), pneumothorax (air between visceral and parietal pleura), haemothorax (haemorrhage into the pleural space), haemoptysis (blood-streaked sputum) and haematemesis (vomited blood).
4. The underlying cause must first be identified and treated, with aspiration of excess fluid via diagnostic thoracentesis or thoracoscopy; the physiotherapy plan should position the patient on the normal (unaffected) side to improve the ventilation-perfusion ratio and assist movement and drainage on the affected side, combined with diaphragmatic and localized breathing exercises and aerobic exercise, given the cardiac failure background.

questions.question:
A child is found on routine examination to have significantly higher blood pressure in the arms than in the legs, with diminished femoral pulses.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis suggested by this classic presentation.
(ii) State the predisposing factors and prevalence.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
questions.answerText:
1. Coarctation of the aorta.
2. It is seen in 6-8% of patients with congenital heart diseases; a common predisposing mechanism for congenital heart defects generally is a viral infection in the mother during the first trimester of pregnancy, when the fetal heart is being formed.
3. Coarctation occurs when there is a narrowing of the aorta, most often just beyond the left subclavian artery, though it can occur at various other locations of the aortic arch or in the thoracic or abdominal aorta. The narrowing raises upper body blood pressure, causing upper extremity hypertension, which explains the arm-leg blood pressure discrepancy found on examination.

A(i) The heart lies obliquely in the mediastinum, two-thirds left of the midsagittal plane; the base (formed by the two atria) is broad and lies at the level of the second intercostal space, while the apex (tip of the left ventricle) projects into the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line. The wall has three layers: the pericardium (outermost, a double-walled sac), the myocardium (middle layer, facilitates pumping), and the endocardium (innermost, lines the chambers). The heart is divided into right and left halves, each with an atrium (superior) and ventricle (inferior); four valves control flow: tricuspid (right atrium to right ventricle), pulmonary (right ventricle to pulmonary artery), mitral/bicuspid (left atrium to left ventricle), and aortic (left ventricle to aorta).
A(ii) Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium through the superior and inferior vena cava; the right atrium contracts, pushing blood through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle; the right ventricle contracts, forcing blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary artery, which carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs, where carbon dioxide is exchanged for oxygen.
A(iii) Oxygenated blood returns via the pulmonary veins to the left atrium; the left atrium contracts, sending blood through the mitral (bicuspid) valve into the left ventricle; the left ventricle contracts, pumping blood through the aortic valve into the aorta, which branches into arteries delivering oxygenated blood to all parts of the body; capillaries exchange oxygen/nutrients for carbon dioxide/waste; deoxygenated blood returns via veins to the right atrium, restarting the pulmonary circuit.
A(iv) Coronary circulation supplies oxygen and nutrients to the heart (especially the myocardium) via the right and left coronary arteries, with coronary veins carrying deoxygenated blood away; the right coronary artery supplies the right ventricle, right atrium, lower wall of the left ventricle, and upper posterior interventricular septum; the left coronary artery divides into the ramus circumflexus and ramus interventricularis anterior (RIA), which together supply the rest of the left ventricle, the anterior interventricular septum, and the entire left atrium; venous drainage is mainly through the coronary sinus.
B. Left-sided (congestive) heart failure is characterised by pulmonary congestion and low cardiac output due to accumulation of blood from the left ventricle back to the left atrium and lungs, consistent with the left heart's role of receiving oxygenated blood from the lungs and pumping it systemically; right-sided heart failure is characterised by increased pressure load on the right ventricle with higher pulmonary vascular pressure, consistent with the right heart's role of receiving deoxygenated systemic blood and pumping it to the lungs.
C. Because the right side of the heart specifically drives the pulmonary circuit, increased pressure load and higher pulmonary vascular pressure in right-sided failure impede forward flow into the lungs, causing blood to back up systemically; this abnormal circulatory pattern produces the functional deficit of systemic venous congestion, whereas the analogous problem on the left side produces pulmonary congestion and reduced systemic cardiac output, underscoring why the two sides of failure present with different clinical pictures despite arising from the same basic pump-failure mechanism.
questions.question:
A(i) State the structure of the heart (chambers, valves, wall layers).
A(ii) Describe the pulmonary circuit.
A(iii) Describe the systemic circuit.
A(iv) Describe coronary circulation.
B. State how this circulatory anatomy relates to right-sided versus left-sided heart failure findings.
C. Explain why an abnormal circulation pattern (e.g. in right-sided failure) produces a functional deficit.

A patient presents with dyspnoea and fatigue. On echocardiogram, one of the mitral valve cusps is seen ballooning into the left atrium during ventricular systole.

(i) Interpret the findings given.
(ii) State the structure primarily affected.
(iii) List the differential valvular lesions that share this clinical presentation.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan.
questions.answerText:
1. Ballooning of one or both mitral valve cusps into the left atrium during ventricular systole is consistent with mitral regurgitation, a degenerative process producing this appearance; mitral regurgitation, tricuspid regurgitation, aortic regurgitation and pulmonary regurgitation are together classed as valvular insufficiency, in which the valves do not close properly (also called incompetent, regurgitant, or prolapsed valvular heart disease).
2. The mitral valve (between the left atrium and left ventricle) is primarily affected.
3. Differential valvular lesions sharing overlapping symptoms (dyspnoea, oedema, angina, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, murmurs, chest pain, fatigue, dizziness/fainting, irregular heartbeat) include mitral stenosis, aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, tricuspid stenosis, tricuspid regurgitation, and pulmonary regurgitation, distinguished by history, physical examination (jugular venous distension, S3/S4, blood pressure changes, irregular pulse, murmurs) and tests (ECG, chest X-ray, echocardiogram/cardiac catheterisation as gold standard).
4. The physiotherapy plan should focus on protecting the valve from further damage (prompt treatment of infection symptoms, dental hygiene), lessening symptoms, keeping the patient relatively rested until comorbid conditions/post-operative complications are treated, avoiding exercise if generally unwell, symptomatic or clinically unstable, and using caution in exercise prescription so as not to aggravate symptoms.

questions.question:
A young infant is noted to have a continuous murmur and mild breathlessness on feeding, but no cyanosis at this stage. Investigation shows a persistent connection between the pulmonary artery and the aorta.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis suggested by this presentation.
(ii) State the predisposing factors and prevalence.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
questions.answerText:
1. Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).
2. The ductus arteriosus is present in the fetus and normally allows immediate recirculation of blood through the fetal systemic arteries; in about 1 of every 5500 babies the ductus never closes after birth, causing PDA. A common predisposing factor for congenital heart defects generally is maternal viral infection in the first trimester of pregnancy, when the fetal heart is being formed.
3. The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery with the aorta, bypassing the lungs, so that in the fetus almost all pulmonary arterial blood flows through this vessel; when it fails to close, this abnormal connection persists after birth. Persons with this condition do not show cyanosis until late in life, when the heart fails or the lungs become congested, explaining the absence of cyanosis in this infant.

questions.question:
A(i) State the principles of positioning the unconscious/paralysed ICU patient.
A(ii) State its purpose.
A(iii) State the detailed positioning technique.
A(iv) State the turning frequency.
A(v) State the precautions.
B. State the safe parameters/monitoring criteria (turning interval) for its use.
C. Explain the physiological basis for why this positioning approach is used.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The unconscious or paralysed patient usually requires prolonged care; where possible, they will be nursed in side-lying and turned 2-hourly.
A(ii) Full side-lying allows for chest and pressure area care as well as accurate joint position, and is usually the correct position for the unconscious or paralysed patient.
A(iii) The two legs are separated with pillows; the lower leg is extended while the upper leg is flexed at the hip and knee; both feet are kept at right angles using sandbags and/or pillows; the lower shoulder is positioned so the patient is not lying on the pressure point of the shoulder, with the forearm resting on a pillow; the upper hand and forearm rest either on the patient's thigh or on a pillow.
A(iv) The patient is turned 2-hourly throughout the 24 hours, with the position of the limbs regularly reversed as this occurs.
A(v) Pillows and sandbags should be suitably placed to prevent the patient from rolling onto their back; positioning of the patient is the joint responsibility of the nursing and physiotherapy staff.
B. Turning and repositioning occurs 2-hourly throughout the 24-hour period.
C. Prolonged immobility in the unconscious or paralysed patient creates risk to pressure areas, joint position, and chest status; nursing the patient in full side-lying with 2-hourly turning and careful limb/pillow positioning simultaneously protects the skin from pressure damage, maintains accurate joint alignment to prevent contracture, and facilitates chest care, which is why this is described as usually the correct position for such patients and why it is a shared, joint responsibility of nursing and physiotherapy staff to maintain consistently.

questions.question:
A(i) State the principles of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).
A(ii) State when CPR is needed.
A(iii) State the procedure for CPR.
A(iv) State the compression-to-ventilation ratio.
A(v) State the precautions.
B. State the safe parameters (compression rate and depth) for CPR.
C. Explain the physiological basis for why CPR is needed and how it maintains circulation/breathing.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is a way of maintaining the pumping function of the heart and the breathing function of the lungs when they fail, involving applying external cardiac compression and doing mouth-to-mouth breathing (artificial respiration).
A(ii) CPR is needed when there is loss of consciousness but the patient still breathes and the pulse can still be felt (no CPR needed, only observation); when the pulse is still felt but there is no breathing (mouth-to-mouth breathing alone needed); and when there is no breathing and no pulse felt (full CPR needed).
A(iii) Before starting CPR, check that circulation and breathing have been lost, and check that the airway is clear, removing any obstruction such as vomited substances or broken teeth before CPR starts. If a pulse is felt but breathing has stopped: lay the patient on the back, pinch the nose, perform head-tilt and chin-lift to open the airway (this keeps the tongue out of the way), kneel at the patient's side, take a deep breath, place your lips over the patient's mouth and forcibly breathe out (or use a mask held tightly against the face covering nose and mouth, with head-tilt/chin-lift). If there is no pulse, cardiac compression is also required: kneeling at the side, remove clothing covering the chest to expose the skin, place the heel of one hand on top of the other with fingers interlocked on the bare chest between the nipples, and push hard and fast.
A(iv) A universal compression-to-ventilation ratio of 30 compressions to 2 breaths is given to victims of all ages except children and infants, who are given a ratio of 15:2; 5 cycles of compression and ventilation are performed.
A(v) At the end of each compression, allow the chest to re-expand completely, as this allows more blood to refill the heart between compressions and incomplete chest recoil reduces the blood flow created by compressions; compressions should not be interrupted often or for long; before starting CPR, send for expert help.
B. Press down about 1.5 to 2 inches with each compression, keeping the elbows straight and bringing body weight directly over the hands; deliver compressions in a smooth fashion at a rate of 100 compressions per minute.
C. Usually the heart fails to pump adequate blood to all organs of the body when there is myocardial infarction, and blood flow to the brain fails; after a few seconds this causes loss of consciousness and collapse, and after a minute or two breathing also stops as it is controlled by the brain; CPR is therefore designed to keep both the circulation and the breathing going artificially, by mechanically compressing the heart to circulate blood and by providing artificial respiration (there is enough oxygen in the air breathed out by the rescuer for a patient receiving mouth-to-mouth breathing).

questions.question:
A(i) State the principles of manual hyperinflation.
A(ii) State its mechanism of action/main effects.
A(iii) State its indications.
A(iv) State the procedure/context of use.
B. Explain the physiological basis of its effects.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Manual hyperinflation is a technique used by the physiotherapist to help remove secretions in patients receiving intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV), who are at risk of developing increased bronchial secretions and possible chest infection.
A(ii) Its main effects are: the deep inflation recruits alveoli that are 'unused' during the tidal volume of IPPV, re-expanding them, which helps both prevent and reverse atelectasis and promotes full aeration of the alveoli; and the fast expiratory flow rate generated, enhanced by vibration and shaking, loosens and moves secretions towards the main airways.
A(iii) Indicated for ventilated (IPPV) patients at risk of retained secretions and atelectasis, particularly the longer a patient is receiving IPPV, as this increases the likelihood of problems with secretions and infection.
A(iv) Applied via the ventilator circuit/manual inflation to deliver a deep inflation to the ventilated patient, combined with vibration and shaking during the expiratory flow to help move secretions towards the main airways for subsequent removal (e.g. by suction).
B. In a patient on IPPV, the endotracheal or tracheostomy tube irritates the tracheal mucous membrane, increasing mucus secretion; secretions become dry and crusted because the upper respiratory tract's normal humidification is bypassed; the patient cannot cough effectively because of the tube; there is reduction/paralysis of normal ciliary action; and there is loss of the normal sigh mechanism. Manual hyperinflation counters these effects physiologically by providing a deep inflation that re-expands under-ventilated alveoli (preventing/reversing atelectasis) and by generating an enhanced expiratory flow that mechanically mobilises secretions toward the central airways.

A(i) pH: 7.35-7.45; PaCO2: 4.7-6.0 kPa (35-45 mmHg); PaO2: 10.7-13.3 kPa (80-100 mmHg); HCO3: 22-26 mmol/l; base excess: -2 to +2.
A(ii) Hypoxaemia is a deficiency of oxygen in arterial blood (PaO2 < 8 kPa/60 mmHg, SaO2 < 90%). Hypoxia is a deficiency of oxygen at tissue level. Hypocapnia/hypocarbia is a deficiency of CO2 in arterial blood. Hypercapnia/hypercarbia is excess CO2 in arterial blood. Clinical features of hypoxaemia include cyanosis, tachypnoea, tachycardia (arrhythmias/bradycardia), peripheral vasoconstriction, and restlessness progressing to confusion/coma. Clinical features of hypercapnia include flapping tremor of the hands, tachypnoea, tachycardia/bradycardia, peripheral vasodilation with warm hands, headache, sweating, and drowsiness/hallucinations progressing to coma.
A(iii) PFTs measure lung volumes and capacities to evaluate the mechanical function of the lungs; values are related to age, weight, sex, and body position, and altered by disease; PFT values are used to predict the severity of the disease process on lung function and are combined with other objective tests to determine the person's functional level.
A(iv) Obstructive pathologies are routinely diagnosed by forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and forced vital capacity (FVC); restrictive pathologies are examined via inspiratory capacity (IC) and total lung capacity (TLC), with TLC and vital capacity (VC) being the two most common spirometric measurements used to identify restrictive lung dysfunction.
B. Reduced PaO2 (hypoxaemia) with normal or reduced PaCO2 and reduced TLC/VC/FRC on PFT are seen in restrictive conditions such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and pneumonia, while COPD-type obstructive pathology is assessed via FEV1/FVC.
C. Arterial blood gas analysis and interpretation is used to ascertain the state of a patient's respiratory and metabolic function and acid-base balance, and it is beneficial to observe trends or a series of samples rather than one result in isolation; an abnormal PaO2 (hypoxaemia) reflects inadequate gas exchange at the alveolar-capillary membrane, producing the tissue-level functional deficits described (restlessness, confusion, cyanosis, tachycardia), while abnormal PFT volumes/capacities reflect the mechanical restriction or obstruction present, directly limiting the patient's functional exercise capacity.
questions.question:
A(i) State the normal values of arterial blood gases.
A(ii) Define hypoxaemia, hypoxia, hypocapnia and hypercapnia.
A(iii) State the role and use of pulmonary function tests (PFTs).
A(iv) State which PFT measurements are used for obstructive versus restrictive pathologies.
B. State how these findings relate to common cardiopulmonary pathologies.
C. Explain why an abnormal PaO2/PaCO2 or PFT result occurs and the functional deficit it causes.

A(i) State the principles of Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP).
A(ii) State its mechanism of action.
A(iii) State its indications.
A(iv) State the population it is used with.
A(v) State the main goals of its use.
B. State the safe parameters/monitoring criteria (functional residual capacity, PaO2) for its use.
C. Explain the physiological basis of its effects.
questions.answerText:
A(i) CPAP (Continuous Positive Airway Pressure) is a system used in the spontaneously breathing patient, used as an adjunct to physiotherapy treatment.
A(ii) It may be effective in the treatment of certain respiratory conditions such as postoperative atelectasis.
A(iii) It is indicated for certain respiratory conditions such as postoperative atelectasis, used as an adjunct to physiotherapy treatment.
A(iv) It is used in the spontaneously breathing patient (as distinct from mechanical ventilation/manual hyperinflation, which is used in the ventilated patient).
A(v) The main goals are to increase functional residual capacity (FRC) accompanied by an increase in PaO2, and to decrease the work of breathing and improve oxygen consumption.
B. The main goals being monitored are an increase in functional residual capacity (FRC) accompanied by an increase in PaO2, and a decrease in the work of breathing with improved oxygen consumption.
C. By maintaining a continuous positive pressure in the airway throughout the breathing cycle, CPAP helps keep alveoli open (increasing functional residual capacity), which improves the surface area available for gas exchange (raising PaO2), while also reducing the effort the patient must make with each breath (decreasing the work of breathing) and thereby improving oxygen consumption, which is particularly effective in conditions such as postoperative atelectasis where alveolar collapse is the underlying problem.

1. Positioning of the unconscious/paralysed patient to prevent pressure area damage while maintaining chest care and accurate joint position during prolonged ICU care.
2. Full side-lying positioning with regular turning.
3. Where possible the patient is nursed in full side-lying, allowing for chest and pressure area care as well as accurate joint position; the two legs are separated with pillows, the lower leg extended while the upper leg is flexed at the hip and knee; both feet are kept at right angles using sandbags and/or pillows; the lower shoulder is positioned so the patient is not lying on the pressure point of the shoulder, with the forearm resting on a pillow; the upper hand and forearm rest either on the patient's thigh or on a pillow.
4. The patient should be turned 2-hourly, with the position of the limbs regularly reversed as the patient is turned throughout the 24 hours; pillows and sandbags should be suitably placed to prevent the patient from rolling onto their back.
5. Positioning of the patient is the joint responsibility of the nursing and physiotherapy staff.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
1. Bacterial (community-acquired) pneumonia, given the abrupt onset, high fever, productive cough, pleuritic pain and lobar consolidation pattern.
2. Postural drainage, percussion and vibration, as supportive therapy alongside drug therapy which is the primary treatment focus.
3. Postural drainage uses positioning to drain secretions with the aid of gravity. Percussion (chest clapping) is a manual technique used with postural drainage. Vibration/shaking is applied throughout the expiratory phase to help move secretions towards the main airways. Adequate hydration and nutrition should accompany these techniques.
4. Percussion should not be used in the presence of rib fractures, acute pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, osteoporosis, metastasis, or pulmonary tuberculosis. Shaking should not be used in osteoporosis or metastasis in the ribs and spine, haemoptysis, or acute pleuritic pain. Vibration is contraindicated where the other two techniques are also contraindicated, and specifically in the presence of metastasis of the ribs or spine.
5. Assisted coughing techniques should be added for patients producing more than 30 ml of mucus per day or with an impaired cough mechanism; breathing exercises (controlled deep breathing) and cough/huff can be combined with manual techniques for maximal clearance of bronchial secretion, particularly if the patient becomes too unwell to tolerate positioning alone.
questions.question:
A 45-year-old man is admitted with abrupt-onset high fever, chills, productive cough, dyspnoea, tachypnoea and pleuritic chest pain. Chest examination reveals bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right lower lobe.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.

A(i) Define idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
A(ii) State its aetiology.
A(iii) Describe its pathophysiology.
A(iv) State its clinical features (pulmonary function test, arterial blood gas, breath sound and symptom findings).
A(v) State the investigations/findings used to identify it.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why this condition is more severe in certain groups.
C. Distinguish between idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and pneumonia.
questions.answerText:
A(i) A chronic, progressive, irreversible, and usually lethal lung disease, characterised by progressive worsening of dyspnoea and lung function; it occurs mostly in older adults.
A(ii) The most important environmental risk factors are cigarette smoking and exposure to metal and wood dust; it can also result from an atypical reparative process after injury to the lung epithelium.
A(iii) Marked by proliferation and accumulation of fibroblasts or myofibroblasts and excessive deposition of extracellular matrix, resulting in scarring and destruction of the lung architecture.
A(iv) PFT: decreased TLC, VC, FRC, RV, with normal or decreased flow rates; as disease progresses, tidal volume decreases and respiratory rate increases. ABG: decreased PaO2 with normal PaCO2; hypoxaemic with exercise early in disease, hypoxaemic at rest as disease progresses. Breath sounds: bibasilar end-inspiratory dry rales, decreased breath sounds. Symptoms: dyspnoea on exertion progressing to dyspnoea at rest, repetitive nonproductive cough, weight loss, decreased appetite, fatigue, sleep disturbance with loss of REM sleep. One-third of patients develop pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular dysfunction and cor pulmonale.
A(v) Pulmonary function tests, arterial blood gas analysis, and auscultation for the characteristic bibasilar dry rales.
B. It occurs mostly in older adults, and the most important environmental risk factors are cigarette smoking and exposure to metal and wood dust, so groups with heavier or longer smoking histories and greater occupational dust exposure are more severely and more commonly affected.
C. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a chronic, progressive, irreversible restrictive disease of insidious onset caused by fibroblast proliferation and scarring, whereas pneumonia is an inflammatory process of the lung parenchyma usually beginning with an infection in the lower respiratory tract, which may be acute (sudden onset over hours to days) or chronic (gradually worsening over days to months), and is caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, or mycoplasmas rather than a fibrotic reparative process.

questions.question:
A(i) State the types of exercise used in outpatient cardiac rehabilitation.
A(ii) State the principles of circuit-type training and its components.
A(iii) State the principles of continuous conditioning training.
A(iv) State the principles of interval training.
B. State how these exercise types relate to a patient's stage of recovery/risk stratification.
C. Explain the functional deficit that interval training specifically addresses.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Use of a single mode of exercise (e.g. walking) may be boring and lead to poor adherence, so different modes of aerobic exercise such as cycle and arm ergometry, walking, bench-stepping and treadmill should be incorporated.
A(ii) Circuit-type training is recommended in the initial stages, involving several modes of exercise such as cycle and arm ergometry, walking, bench-stepping and treadmill; components of a typical circuit training programme include high knee stepping on the spot, arm cycles, spot steps/step-ups, push-away from the wall, half squats, body stretching, chest press with ball, side steps/split squats, lateral arm raises with ball, and shuttle walking.
A(iii) Continuous conditioning training, such as walking, swimming, and cycling, may be introduced in the later stages of rehabilitation.
A(iv) Interval training may be adopted at any stage; it involves putting rest intervals between work intervals, which allows the patient to attain a higher intensity at each work station.
B. Circuit training with its varied, lower-intensity component exercises suits the initial stages of rehabilitation when tolerance is still being established, continuous conditioning training suits later stages once fitness and tolerance have improved, and interval training, being adaptable to any stage via its rest periods, can be used across the recovery continuum to allow controlled higher-intensity work without exceeding the patient's tolerance.
C. Because standard continuous exercise at a higher intensity may exceed a cardiac patient's safe tolerance, interval training addresses this functional deficit by inserting rest intervals between work intervals, which allows the patient to attain a higher work intensity at each station than would be tolerated in continuous training, without breaching the haemodynamic limits that must be monitored in cardiac patients.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old child is found on examination to have a murmur, with mild breathlessness on exertion but no cyanosis. Investigation reveals a hole in the wall between the two upper chambers of the heart.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis suggested by this presentation.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
questions.answerText:
1. Atrial septal defect (ASD), a hole in the wall of the heart between the left and right atria.
2. A common predisposing factor for congenital heart defects generally, including ASD, is a viral infection in the mother during the first trimester of pregnancy, when the fetal heart is being formed.
3. The hole causes blood to flow from the left atrium and mix with the right atrium instead of going to the rest of the body. ASD is considered a simple congenital heart defect because the hole may close on its own as the heart grows during childhood, which explains the relatively mild presentation without cyanosis in this child.

1. The reduction in TLC, VC and FRC with normal or reduced (not increased) flow rates, together with reduced PaO2 and normal PaCO2 and bibasilar dry rales, indicates a restrictive rather than obstructive ventilatory defect, consistent with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; hypoxaemia is present on exertion early in the disease and at rest as it progresses.
2. The lung parenchyma/interstitium is primarily affected, with proliferation and accumulation of fibroblasts or myofibroblasts and excessive extracellular matrix deposition causing scarring and destruction of lung architecture and decreased lung compliance.
3. Differential restrictive lung dysfunction causes include other interstitial diseases (sarcoidosis, bronchiolitis obliterans), infectious causes (pneumonia), neoplastic causes (bronchogenic carcinoma), pleural diseases (pleural effusion, atelectasis, ARDS), cardiovascular causes (pulmonary oedema, pulmonary emboli), neuromuscular causes (spinal cord injury, ALS, poliomyelitis, myasthenia gravis, tetanus, muscular dystrophy), musculoskeletal causes (ankylosing spondylitis, kyphoscoliosis, pectus excavatum/carinatum), and connective tissue causes (rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, scleroderma, polymyositis).
4. As one-third of patients develop pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular dysfunction and cor pulmonale, and hypoxaemia worsens with exercise progressing to rest, the physiotherapy plan should be guided by monitoring oxygenation, providing supplemental oxygen as required, considering pulmonary rehabilitation, and grading activity to the patient's hypoxaemic response rather than by flow-rate-based obstructive disease parameters.
questions.question:
A 68-year-old man with a long smoking history presents with progressively worsening dyspnoea on exertion and a repetitive nonproductive cough. Examination reveals bibasilar end-inspiratory dry rales. Pulmonary function testing shows reduced TLC, VC and FRC with normal or reduced flow rates. Arterial blood gas shows reduced PaO2 with normal PaCO2.

(i) Interpret the test and examination findings given.
(ii) State the structure/system primarily affected.
(iii) List the differential conditions that could produce this pattern.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan.

questions.answerText:
1. Cardiac arrest, requiring cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), which is needed when there is no breathing and no pulse felt (also needed if there is loss of consciousness but the patient still breathes and has a pulse, or if the pulse is felt but there is no breathing).
2. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR): a way of maintaining the pumping function of the heart and the breathing function of the lungs when they fail, applying external cardiac compression and mouth-to-mouth breathing (artificial respiration).
3. Before starting, check that circulation and breathing have genuinely been lost and that the airway is clear, removing any obstruction such as vomited substances or broken teeth. If a pulse is felt but breathing has stopped, mouth-to-mouth artificial respiration alone is given: lay the patient on the back, pinch the nose, perform head-tilt and chin-lift to open the airway, kneel at the patient's side, take a deep breath, place your lips over the patient's mouth (or use a mask held tightly over nose and mouth with head-tilt/chin-lift) and forcibly breathe out. If there is no pulse, cardiac compression is added: kneel at the side, expose the bare chest, place the heel of one hand on top of the other with fingers interlocked between the nipples, and push hard and fast, compressing about 1.5 to 2 inches with each compression, keeping the elbows straight and bringing body weight directly over the hands, delivering compressions smoothly at a rate of 100 per minute, allowing full chest re-expansion between compressions, and not interrupting compressions often or for long. Before starting CPR, send for expert help.
4. Ensure complete chest recoil between compressions, as incomplete recoil reduces the blood flow created by compressions; compressions should not be interrupted often or for long.
5. The universal compression-to-ventilation ratio is 30 compressions to 2 breaths for victims of all ages, except children and infants, for whom the ratio is 15:2; five cycles of compression and ventilation are performed.
questions.question:
A man collapses suddenly in the street. He is unresponsive, and on checking you find there is no breathing and no pulse.

questions.answerText:
1. This describes cardiomyopathy, a condition affecting the heart muscle in which the heart chambers become stretched, thickened or stiff, making it harder for the heart to pump blood; it can be dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive, or arrhythmogenic.
2. Impaired cardiac function affecting the heart's ability to pump blood effectively; cardiomyopathy is listed among conditions that can affect blood flow through the heart, alongside hypertension, coronary heart disease, valvular heart disease, myocardial infarction, arrhythmia and coronary embolism, any of which may compound the clinical picture.
3. As with other unstable cardiac conditions, haemodynamic response (blood pressure, heart rate, rate pressure product) should be monitored before, during and after exercise, particularly aerobic and strengthening exercise, and heavy lifting, static exercise and straining should be avoided; the patient should not exercise while generally unwell, symptomatic, or clinically unstable.
4. Options: upright body positioning for exercise and rest, since recumbent positions increase central fluid shift, venous return and cardiac work; individualised, closely monitored graded exercise once stable; general cardiovascular risk factor and lifestyle modification (diet, weight control, smoking cessation, stress management).
I would prioritise closely monitored, upright, individualised exercise given the impaired pump function, since it directly addresses the haemodynamic vulnerability described for cardiac patients while still working towards functional improvement.

An elderly patient presents with exertional dyspnoea, chest pain and episodes of dizziness/fainting. On auscultation there is a murmur, and calcification of the valve leaflets is confirmed on echocardiogram.

(i) Interpret the findings given.
(ii) State the structure primarily affected.
(iii) List the differential valvular lesions that could produce a similar clinical picture.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan.
questions.answerText:
1. This presentation (dyspnoea, chest pain, dizziness/fainting, murmur, valve calcification) is consistent with aortic stenosis, also known as senile calcific aortic stenosis, characterised by calcification of the aortic leaflets; it is described as the most common lesion affecting the heart valves.
2. The aortic valve is primarily affected; the aortic valve is noted as the valve most commonly affected in valvular heart disease generally.
3. Related valvular lesions producing overlapping clinical features (dyspnoea, oedema, angina, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, murmurs, chest pain, fatigue, dizziness/fainting, irregular heartbeat) include mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, tricuspid stenosis, tricuspid regurgitation, aortic regurgitation, and pulmonary regurgitation, diagnosed via history, physical examination (jugular venous distension, S3/S4, blood pressure changes, irregular pulse, murmurs) and tests (ECG, chest X-ray, and the gold standard echocardiogram/cardiac catheterisation).
4. Given the risk of dizziness/fainting and chest pain, physiotherapy management should protect the valve from further damage (prompt attention to infection, dental hygiene), lessen symptoms alongside pharmacological treatment, and ensure the patient does not exercise while generally unwell, symptomatic, or clinically unstable, with caution in exercise prescription so as not to aggravate symptoms.

A(i) These are manual treatment techniques used in physiotherapy, alongside postural drainage, for clearance of the respiratory system.
A(ii) Percussion (chest clapping) and vibration/shaking loosen and move bronchial secretions towards the main airways; shaking is applied throughout the expiratory phase; vibration has a finer action than percussion and shaking.
A(iii) They are indicated for patients with retained bronchial secretions requiring assistance with clearance, such as in pneumonia (as supportive therapy alongside drug therapy) and in ICU patients.
A(iv) Percussion should not be used in the presence of rib fractures, acute pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, osteoporosis, metastasis, or pulmonary tuberculosis. Shaking should not be used in osteoporosis or metastasis in the ribs and spine, haemoptysis, or acute pleuritic pain. Vibration is contraindicated when the other two techniques are also contraindicated, particularly in the presence of metastasis of the ribs or spine.
A(v) Percussion (clapping) is applied to the chest wall over the affected area; shaking is applied throughout the expiratory phase and is often more appropriate for ventilated patients; vibration is applied with a finer action than the other two, used when the other two are contraindicated.
A(vi) Listen to the patient's chest with a stethoscope before and after treatment, noting whether breath sounds are normal, reduced, absent, or whether added sounds are present; observe chest expansion and breathing pattern; note evidence of other injuries (such as a fractured shaft of femur with Thomas's splint or skull traction for neck injury) that may limit positioning.
B. Auscultation before and after treatment to assess breath sounds; observation of the breathing pattern and chest expansion; avoidance of use where rib fractures, acute pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, osteoporosis, metastasis or pulmonary tuberculosis are present, as listed under contraindications.
C. These techniques work by mechanically loosening secretions adherent to the airway walls and using the generated vibration/shaking to help move them towards the larger, more central airways where they can be cleared by coughing or suction. If misapplied in the presence of the listed contraindications, the mechanical force involved risks precipitating or worsening rib fracture, provoking bleeding (haemoptysis), or displacing pathological bone (metastasis, osteoporosis), which is why these conditions exclude their safe use.

A young woman notices that her fingertips repeatedly turn pale then blue on exposure to cold weather or during periods of emotional stress, with the episodes being intermittent.

(i) State the most likely clinical impression.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiology underlying this condition.
(iii) State the physiotherapy assessment findings expected.
(iv) Draw up a problem list and goals of treatment.
questions.answerText:
1. Raynaud's disease.
2. It is an episodic spasm of small arteries and arterioles, exacerbated by exposure to cold or emotional stress, which matches this patient's trigger pattern.
3. The finger tips develop pallor and cyanosis during episodes, consistent with the arterial spasm described.
4. Problem list: episodic digital ischaemia triggered by cold/stress, potential impact on hand function during episodes. Goals: reduce frequency/severity of vasospastic episodes, patient education on trigger avoidance.

questions.explanation: Elevated basal FSH, low AMH, and reduced antral follicle count together indicate diminished ovarian reserve, reflecting a reduced pool of remaining oocytes and reduced responsiveness to gonadotrophin stimulation, which affects prognosis for both natural conception and assisted reproduction success. Polycystic ovaries would instead typically show high antral follicle counts and normal or elevated AMH. This combination of markers is used together, rather than individually, for more accurate reserve assessment.
questions.question: A couple experiencing infertility undergoes evaluation of the female partner. Serum day-3 FSH is markedly elevated with low AMH and reduced antral follicle count. What does this combination of findings MOST likely indicate?
In a woman with an obstructed urinary tract from uterovaginal prolapse, which investigation would best delineate the size, shape, and position of the kidneys, bladder, and ureters?
questions.explanation: Intravenous pyelogram (IVP) provides dynamic imaging of the urinary tract and shows the size, shape, and position of the kidneys, bladder, ureters, and urethra. It is particularly valuable when obstructive uropathy complicates prolapse. Cystoscopy evaluates the interior of the bladder and urethra but does not delineate the upper urinary tract.

questions.question: A woman with TWO or more first- or second-degree relatives with ovarian cancer has an estimated lifetime risk of developing ovarian cancer of up to:
questions.explanation: Women with two or more first- or second-degree relatives with ovarian cancer may carry the BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene mutation, conferring a lifetime risk of developing ovarian cancer of up to 50%. These high-risk individuals require specialised genetic counselling and may opt for prophylactic oophorectomy.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman is diagnosed with PID and is treated as an outpatient. The Criteria for HOSPITAL ADMISSION of a PID patient include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Mild PID without systemic features in a reliable, compliant patient who can be followed up is appropriate for outpatient oral antibiotic treatment. Indications for hospital admission include: inability to exclude a surgical emergency, failure of outpatient therapy, inability to tolerate oral medications, tubo-ovarian abscess, pregnancy, and severe systemic illness. The distinction is important because inpatient IV antibiotics achieve higher tissue concentrations and allow closer monitoring.
options: Severe illness, nausea, vomiting, or high fever
Mild PID without systemic features in compliant patient
Surgical emergency cannot be excluded (ruptured ectopic, appendicitis)

questions.question: A 21-year-old male presents to an infertility clinic unable to smell. His testosterone is low, FSH and LH are low, and testicular volume is reduced. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Kallman's syndrome is the combination of isolated GnRH deficiency and anosmia (inability to smell) caused by failure of GnRH neurons and olfactory neurons to migrate from the olfactory placode to the hypothalamus during embryogenesis. The low gonadotropins and hypogonadism without anosmia would suggest hypothalamic amenorrhoea/hypogonadism; the anosmia is the pathognomonic feature. Treatment with pulsatile GnRH or gonadotropin replacement can restore fertility.

Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine adhesions/synechiae) is categorized under uterine defects as a cause of spontaneous abortion. It typically results from aggressive curettage or infection following previous uterine surgery. The adhesions prevent normal implantation and can cause recurrent pregnancy loss, amenorrhoea, and infertility.
questions.question: Among the causes of spontaneous abortion, Asherman's syndrome is listed under which broad category?

options: Bone age reflects cumulative steroid exposure and skeletal maturation
Chronological age underestimates puberty in boys
Chronological age is unreliable in developing countries
Bone age predicts final adult height in all conditions
It can be measured without radiological equipment
questions.question: Bone age is considered SUPERIOR to chronological age for assessing pubertal progress because:
questions.explanation: Bone age, assessed by wrist X-ray comparing epiphyseal maturation to standard atlases, reflects cumulative exposure to sex steroids and growth hormone and thus accurately represents the child's physiological stage of maturation. It is more informative than chronological age because children of the same chronological age can have markedly different hormonal exposures and developmental stages. Puberty in girls occurs approximately 2 years earlier than boys (bone age-adjusted).

options: Increased gap junction formation between cells
Reduced gap junction and oxytocin receptor expression
questions.question: During the luteal phase, progesterone suppresses myometrial contractility. Which mechanism MOST directly explains this relaxant effect on uterine smooth muscle?
questions.explanation: Progesterone downregulates myometrial gap junction proteins and oxytocin receptors, reducing electrical coupling between myocytes and limiting coordinated contractions. This quiescent effect maintains uterine relaxation during the luteal phase and early pregnancy. Oestrogen, by contrast, promotes gap junction and oxytocin receptor expression in preparation for labour.

Normal appearance of the contralateral ovary

questions.explanation: If intraoperative findings such as capsule rupture, dense adhesions, or suspicious peritoneal deposits are encountered during laparoscopic surgery for a suspected ovarian malignancy, conversion to open laparotomy is recommended to allow safe, complete, and oncologically sound tumour removal.
questions.question: A patient with a suspected malignant ovarian mass planned for laparoscopic surgery should have the procedure converted to laparotomy if which intraoperative finding occurs?
Among those requiring surgery for ovarian tumours, what percentage is malignant in postmenopausal women compared to premenopausal women?
questions.explanation: Among ovarian tumours requiring surgery, 45% are malignant in postmenopausal women compared to only 13% in premenopausal women. This dramatic difference underscores the importance of age as a risk factor for ovarian malignancy and the need for a lower threshold of surgical intervention in older women.

questions.question: In lymphocyte culture for chromosome analysis, blood is incubated for how many days and chromosomes are counted in how many cells?
questions.explanation: For lymphocyte culture, 2-3 mL of venous blood is placed directly into culture medium or collected in a heparinized bottle and incubated for 2-3 days. Cells are then harvested for chromosomal preparations. Chromosomes are counted in approximately 30 cells and fully analysed in about 10 cells. This technique is used in gynaecological cases of intersex and chromosomal disorders.

questions.question: Non-contraceptive benefits of the levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS/Mirena) include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Complete protection against sexually transmitted infections
Prevention of endometrial hyperplasia during estrogen HRT
questions.explanation: The LNG-IUS has multiple well-established non-contraceptive benefits: first-line treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding (achieving 70–90% reduction), symptom relief in endometriosis, protection of the endometrium from hyperplasia in women on estrogen-only HRT, and reduction of adenomyosis-related dysmenorrhoea. It does NOT protect against STIs — no intrauterine device or hormonal method prevents sexually transmitted infections. Condoms remain necessary for STI prevention.

options: FSH surge causing premature ovulation from small follicles
Prolactin elevation from reduced dopamine activity
Androgen accumulation causing hirsutism, acne, and follicular inhibition
questions.question: In PCOD, elevated LH causes excessive theca cell androgen production. The androstenedione produced is then aromatized in granulosa cells to oestradiol. However, this aromatization step is impaired in PCOD. What is the primary consequence of this impaired aromatization?
questions.explanation: In PCOD, impaired granulosa cell aromatase activity (due to insufficient FSH stimulation) prevents adequate conversion of androstenedione to oestradiol, allowing androgens to accumulate in the follicle and blood. Excess androgens cause follicular atresia (preventing dominant follicle selection), hirsutism, and acne. The resulting chronic anovulation with elevated oestrone (from peripheral conversion) creates a self-perpetuating cycle maintaining the abnormal LH:FSH ratio.

questions.question: Liquid Based Cytology (LBC) is listed as a recent advance in cytology. What is its primary advantage over conventional smear preparation?
questions.explanation: Liquid-Based Cytology (LBC) is a modern advancement over conventional Pap smear preparation. The primary advantages include: significantly reduced inadequate sample rates (because cells are evenly distributed in the liquid medium), improved cellular preservation and morphology, and compatibility with computer-assisted (automated) reading systems. LBC has largely replaced conventional smears in organised screening programmes in developed countries.
options: It is cheaper than conventional smears
It eliminates the need for fixation
It can diagnose colposcopic abnormalities directly
It replaces histology for CIN diagnosis
It reduces inadequate samples and allows computer-assisted reading
Systemic hormonal suppression of tubal function
Direct mechanical erosion of the fallopian tubes by the device
Permanent alteration of oocyte chromosome number
Increased risk of ascending pelvic infection causing tubal damage
Direct toxic effect of copper on the endometrium causing tubal scarring
questions.question: A woman with a history of IUCD insertion presents with infertility and is found on investigation to have tubal blockage. Which mechanism links IUCD use to this outcome?
questions.explanation: Intrauterine device use, particularly around the time of insertion or with pre-existing undiagnosed infection, is associated with an increased risk of ascending pelvic infection, which can cause tubal damage and subsequent infertility if untreated. This risk is highest in the weeks following insertion and in women with an increased baseline STI risk. Screening for infection before insertion reduces this complication.

options: Salpingectomy is technically more difficult in all cases
Salpingotomy is always the faster procedure regardless of findings
Preservation of the only functioning tube to maximise future natural fertility potential
Salpingotomy has a lower overall complication rate in every patient
Salpingotomy avoids the need for any hCG follow-up
questions.explanation: In a woman whose only remaining functional tube is affected by the ectopic pregnancy, salpingotomy (tube-conserving surgery) is favoured to preserve the chance of future natural conception, despite carrying a higher risk of persistent trophoblastic tissue requiring hCG surveillance and possible further treatment. This decision balances future fertility desire against procedural risk. Careful counselling and follow-up hCG monitoring are essential after salpingotomy.
questions.question: In a comparison of salpingectomy versus salpingotomy for tubal ectopic pregnancy in a patient with a contralateral damaged tube, which factor most strongly favours salpingotomy despite its higher risk of persistent trophoblastic tissue?

questions.explanation: Oestrogen normally restrains osteoclast-mediated bone resorption; as oestrogen levels fall during the menopausal transition, this restraint is lost, causing bone remodelling to shift toward net resorption and accelerated bone loss, increasing osteoporosis and fracture risk. This mechanism underlies the rationale for HRT or other anti-resorptive therapies in preventing postmenopausal bone loss in appropriately selected women. Weight-bearing exercise and adequate calcium and vitamin D intake are also important adjuncts.
questions.question: A woman is counselled that bone loss accelerates significantly in the years around menopause. What is the underlying physiological reason for this accelerated bone loss?
options: Increased vitamin D synthesis at menopause
Increased dietary calcium absorption at menopause
Loss of oestrogen's restraint on osteoclast-driven resorption
Decreased parathyroid hormone secretion at menopause
It is hydatidiform mole, a form of gestational trophoblastic disease
It is a form of missed abortion with hydropic degeneration
It is a form of threatened abortion requiring bedrest
It is a complete abortion with retained placenta
It is inevitable abortion with placenta praevia
questions.explanation: Hydatidiform mole is gestational trophoblastic disease characterized by markedly elevated hCG, uterus larger than dates, hyperemesis gravidarum, and the characteristic snowstorm ultrasound pattern from hydropic villi. Though involving pregnancy loss (usually no viable fetus in complete mole), it is classified separately from simple abortion due to its malignant potential and need for hCG surveillance post-evacuation. It must be distinguished from missed abortion to ensure proper follow-up.
questions.question: A patient at 10 weeks reports that her symptoms of pregnancy (nausea, vomiting) are more severe than expected and her uterus is larger than dates. hCG is extremely elevated. Ultrasound shows a snowstorm pattern. How does this condition relate to the abortion classification?

options: Postpartum cycles are frequently irregular, making cycle length-based predictions inaccurate
The uterus has not fully involuted and cannot support implantation
Breastfeeding estrogen suppresses calendar-based ovulation permanently
The first postpartum period always coincides with ovulation
Postpartum women are immunologically protected against pregnancy for 3 months
questions.explanation: The calendar (rhythm) method requires knowledge of several previous cycle lengths to predict fertile windows. Postpartum cycles are frequently irregular for many months, making cycle length predictions unreliable. Ovulation may occur unexpectedly early or late compared to pre-pregnancy cycle patterns. Until at least 6–12 regular cycles are recorded after postpartum return of menses, the calendar method is not dependable.
questions.question: After delivery, the calendar method of periodic abstinence is unreliable in the first several postpartum cycles because:

A 50-year-old with endometrial cancer confined to the uterus undergoes total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Which additional risk factor in her history would MOST strongly have justified pelvic lymphadenectomy at the time of surgery?
options: Family history of breast cancer only
Body mass index of 24 without diabetes
Deep myometrial invasion on frozen section
questions.explanation: Deep myometrial invasion, high tumour grade, or larger tumour size are recognised indications for pelvic (and sometimes para-aortic) lymphadenectomy in endometrial cancer surgery, since these features correlate with increased risk of nodal metastasis. Nulliparity, early menarche, and family history of breast cancer are epidemiological risk factors for developing endometrial cancer but do not by themselves indicate a need for lymphadenectomy at surgery. Frozen section assessment during surgery helps guide this intraoperative decision.

options: From superior to inferior along the vaginal wall only
In a single non-layered mass closure
From the skin inward toward the rectal mucosa only
From lateral to medial across the perineum
In layers, from the rectal mucosa outward toward the perineal skin
questions.question: During primary repair of a 3rd degree perineal tear, the surgeon closes the rectal wall defect first before repairing the sphincter and perineal body. In what direction relative to tissue planes should this rectal repair generally proceed?
questions.explanation: Repair of a 3rd degree tear proceeds systematically in layers, beginning with closure of the rectal mucosa and wall, followed by identification and repair of the anal sphincter, and finally the perineal muscles and skin. This layered approach ensures each anatomical structure is accurately reapproximated, minimising the risk of fistula formation or persistent incontinence. Meticulous technique at each layer is essential for good functional outcome.

questions.question: A 6-year-old girl develops breast budding and vaginal bleeding. Investigations reveal suppressed gonadotrophins with elevated oestradiol, and café-au-lait skin patches with irregular borders are noted. What is the MOST likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: McCune-Albright syndrome causes peripheral precocious puberty through autonomous ovarian oestrogen production independent of gonadotrophin stimulation, explaining the suppressed gonadotrophins despite high oestradiol, combined with characteristic irregular-bordered café-au-lait skin pigmentation and fibrous dysplasia of bone. Central precocious puberty would instead show elevated, not suppressed, gonadotrophins. Recognising the skin finding is a key diagnostic clue distinguishing this peripheral cause from central causes.

questions.question: A patient develops oliguria in the immediate postoperative period following major gynaecological surgery. The MOST appropriate initial assessment is:
questions.explanation: Oliguria after major surgery is most commonly due to inadequate intravascular volume, so the initial assessment should focus on fluid balance, blood pressure, and signs of hypovolaemia before considering other causes such as urinary catheter obstruction or, rarely, acute kidney injury.
options: Review of fluid balance and intravascular volume status
Administration of a loop diuretic without further assessment
Complete and permanent loss of erectile function
A temporary inability to achieve another erection or orgasm
Persistent painful erection lasting several hours
questions.question: The refractory period following male orgasm is characterised by which physiological feature?
questions.explanation: The male refractory period is a temporary physiological state following orgasm during which further erection and orgasm cannot occur, varying in duration between individuals and generally lengthening with age, distinguishing the male sexual response cycle from the typically shorter or absent refractory period in women.

options: Bicornuate uterus with recurrent pregnancy loss
Unicornuate uterus with no rudimentary horn
questions.question: Abdominal metroplasty (Strassman procedure) is specifically indicated for which Müllerian anomaly to improve reproductive outcomes?
questions.explanation: Abdominal metroplasty (Strassman procedure) — unification of the two uterine horns into a single cavity — is the surgical correction specifically performed for a bicornuate uterus when there are recurrent pregnancy losses or preterm deliveries attributable to the anomaly. For a septate uterus, hysteroscopic resection of the septum is preferred (less invasive). Arcuate uterus generally does not require surgery. Didelphys repair is rarely performed.

options: High rates of viral infections occur during pregnancy
Environmental toxins interfere with sex steroid synthesis
questions.explanation: Autosomal recessive intersex conditions (such as 21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH and 5-alpha-reductase deficiency) are more common in communities where inter-marriage (consanguinity) is prevalent. Consanguinity increases the probability that both parents carry the same recessive gene, raising the risk that offspring inherit two copies of the defective allele. This explains the higher prevalence of these conditions in certain isolated or endogamous populations.
questions.question: In intersex conditions, the incidence is approximately 1 in 2,000. Conditions with AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE inheritance are most common in communities where:
The most characteristic short-term symptom of menopause is the vasomotor symptom. Which description BEST characterizes this symptom and its natural course?
options: Persistent, lifelong daily episodes of profuse sweating without flush
Hot flushes that permanently worsen without treatment
Chronic generalized burning sensation unrelated to hormonal changes
Night sweats only, never occurring during the day
Sudden episodic heat sensations that are self-limiting
questions.explanation: Hot flushes are the most characteristic symptom of menopause, occurring in up to 75% of menopausal women, caused by hypothalamic thermoregulatory centre dysfunction from oestrogen withdrawal. They are described as sudden episodic sensations of heat spreading from the trunk and face, often with sweating and palpitations. Hot flushes are self-limiting, resolving spontaneously in most women within 2–5 years though some persist longer.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about ovarian cancer prevention is correct?
questions.explanation: Oral contraceptive pill (OCP) use is a well-established chemoprophylactic agent that reduces ovarian cancer risk, with the benefit persisting for years after cessation. Screening has not been proven to reduce mortality. Prophylactic oophorectomy is reserved for high-risk (BRCA-mutation) women, not all women.
options: Screening has been proven to reduce mortality in general population
Prophylactic oophorectomy is recommended for all women after 40 years
Talc use in the perineum is protective against ovarian cancer
Asbestos exposure reduces ovarian cancer risk

questions.question: A woman with symptomatic stage 2 uterine prolapse wishes to avoid surgery due to future pregnancy plans. Which conservative management option is MOST appropriate as first-line therapy?
questions.explanation: A vaginal pessary provides mechanical support to reduce prolapse symptoms without surgery, making it appropriate first-line management for women wishing to preserve fertility or avoid surgical intervention. Surgical options such as hysterectomy or mesh procedures are generally deferred until childbearing is complete, given the risk of prolapse recurrence with subsequent pregnancy. Pessaries can be used temporarily or long-term depending on patient preference.

options: Normal aging-related decline in sexual function
questions.explanation: Erectile dysfunction (ED) is defined as the persistent inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual performance. The duration criterion is typically 6 months and problem on =75% of attempts. ED is distinct from occasional failure (normal) and must be distinguished from decreased desire (HSDD) or ejaculatory disorders.
questions.question: A 45-year-old man reports an inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual performance on more than 75% of attempts over 6 months. This MOST likely represents:
A woman's infertility is attributed to cervical mucus hostility. Which mechanism mediates this cause of cervical factor infertility?
questions.explanation: Cervical mucus hostility is caused by anti-sperm antibodies (IgA and IgG) in the cervical mucus that agglutinate, immobilize, or prevent sperm penetration. The postcoital test (PCT) demonstrates this by showing sperm that are present but non-progressive or dead in otherwise good-quality mid-cycle mucus. Treatment options include corticosteroids to suppress antibody production or bypassing the cervix through intrauterine insemination (IUI).
options: Cervical mucus physically blocks sperm entry regardless of immune factors
Progesterone-induced mucus prevents sperm penetration at mid-cycle
Anti-sperm antibodies in cervical mucus immobilize or agglutinate sperm
Bacterial vaginosis changes mucus pH causing sperm death
Estrogen deficiency reduces mucus volume below adequate levels
En-bloc vulvectomy with bilateral groin dissection
Simple excision of the affected labia
questions.explanation: Radical vulvectomy historically referred to en-bloc resection of the entire vulva with bilateral inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy. Though still used for advanced disease, the trend has shifted to more conservative surgery (wide local excision with separate groin incisions) to reduce morbidity (wound breakdown, lymphoedema) while maintaining oncological outcomes.
questions.question: The term 'radical vulvectomy' historically referred to:

options: Negative pressure suction removing products of conception
Sharp curettage of endometrial lining by mechanical scraping
Osmotic dilation followed by forceps extraction
CO2 insufflation into the uterine cavity for visualization
questions.question: The Karman (vacuum) curette used in MVA achieves uterine evacuation by which physical principle?
questions.explanation: Manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) uses a hand-held syringe to generate negative pressure (vacuum/suction) that is transmitted through a flexible cannula into the uterine cavity, aspirating the products of conception without sharp curettage. This suction mechanism causes less uterine trauma than sharp curettage, reducing the risk of Asherman's syndrome. MVA can be performed under local anaesthesia as an outpatient or clinic-based procedure.

options: Enlarged testes with normal secondary sexual characteristics
Absent facial hair with normal testicular size
