This is distinct from colposcopy (which provides direct magnified visualisation), colpomicroscopy (which achieves higher magnification with staining), and standard cervical cytology.
options: Magnified digital photography using a colposcope
questions.question: Cervicography as a diagnostic tool for CIN involves which specific technique?

options: Jaundice and right upper quadrant pain only
questions.question: Brain metastases from choriocarcinoma may present as:
questions.explanation: CNS metastases from choriocarcinoma present as acute focal neurological deficits, seizures (epilepsy), or psychiatric manifestations (psychosis). CT/MRI of the brain is essential in staging. The CSF hCG to plasma ratio above 60:1 is suggestive of CNS disease. Whole-brain irradiation may be needed alongside chemotherapy.

questions.question: A 31-year-old nulliparous woman with heavy menstrual bleeding wants to preserve fertility and avoid surgery. Investigations show no structural pathology. Which first-line medical therapy is MOST appropriate?
questions.explanation: The levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system is recommended as first-line medical therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding without structural pathology in women wishing to preserve fertility, as it reduces menstrual blood loss substantially while being reversible. Surgical options such as ablation or hysterectomy are inappropriate for a woman wanting future fertility. Since no structural lesion exists, myomectomy and embolisation are not indicated.

options: Normal ovarian reserve for her age
questions.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with 2 years of secondary infertility. Her serum FSH on Day 3 of the cycle is markedly elevated. What does this finding most directly indicate about her fertility potential?
questions.explanation: A markedly elevated Day 3 FSH level reflects reduced negative feedback from a diminishing pool of ovarian follicles, indicating diminished ovarian reserve, which becomes increasingly common with advancing maternal age and significantly affects the likelihood of successful conception, whether natural or through assisted reproduction. This finding helps guide realistic counselling and the choice and urgency of fertility treatment. Other markers such as anti-Müllerian hormone are often used alongside FSH for a fuller picture of ovarian reserve.

options: FSH below 5 IU/L with regular cycles
LH below FSH with normal cycles
questions.question: A woman is diagnosed with premature ovarian insufficiency at age 32. Which laboratory finding would be MOST expected to confirm this diagnosis on two occasions a month apart?
questions.explanation: Premature ovarian insufficiency is confirmed by persistently elevated FSH, typically above 25 IU/L, measured on two occasions at least a month apart in a woman under 40 with amenorrhoea. This reflects loss of negative feedback from a depleted follicular pool. Low FSH or elevated oestradiol would be inconsistent with ovarian failure.

The timing of fistula repair depends on the aetiology. Direct operative injury fistulae should be repaired immediately at the time of recognition because the tissues are well-vascularised, uninfected, and amenable to primary repair. Ischaemic necrosis fistulae (from pressure necrosis after obstructed labour) must be delayed 2-3 months until the effects of trauma and superadded infection have completely subsided and tissues have returned to normal.
questions.question: A fistula caused by direct operative injury should be managed differently from one caused by ischaemic necrosis. Direct injury fistulae are repaired:
options: Electively after the next menstrual period
Immediately at the time of recognition

questions.explanation: Postoperative fever in the first 24–48 hours is most commonly due to physiological atelectasis (collapse of small airway units) causing a respiratory inflammatory response. The mnemonic '5 Ws' (Wind—atelectasis, Water—UTI, Wound, Walking—DVT, Wonder drugs—drug fever) helps categorise fever timing and likely cause postoperatively.
questions.question: Postoperative fever occurring on day 1–2 after major surgery is MOST commonly caused by:

questions.explanation: In Klinefelter syndrome, approximately 50% of men have focal areas of residual spermatogenesis despite overall seminiferous tubule failure. Surgical testicular sperm extraction (TESE or microTESE) can retrieve sperm from these focal areas in approximately 30–50% of cases, enabling ICSI. Testosterone replacement is contraindicated as it further suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular axis. This option should be discussed before testosterone therapy is commenced.
questions.question: A 28-year-old man with primary male factor infertility is found to have 47,XXY karyotype (Klinefelter syndrome). He produces very small testes with a volume of 2mL bilaterally. What is his BEST reproductive option?
options: Surgical testicular sperm extraction (TESE) combined with ICSI
Hormonal stimulation with FSH to increase testicular sperm production
Clomiphene citrate to stimulate endogenous gonadotropins

questions.explanation: Daily suppressive aciclovir from around 36 weeks gestation reduces the likelihood of a recurrent outbreak and viral shedding at the time of labour, thereby increasing the chance of safe vaginal delivery for women who acquired primary herpes earlier in pregnancy. Elective caesarean at the time of initial diagnosis is unnecessary since delivery is not imminent. This management balances effective risk reduction with minimising unnecessary surgical intervention.
options: Avoiding all antiviral therapy in pregnancy
questions.question: A woman is diagnosed with primary genital herpes at 30 weeks gestation. Which additional management is MOST appropriate to reduce the risk of a recurrence at the time of labour?

questions.explanation: A pessary is a removable device placed in the vagina to keep pelvic structures in place. Follow-up after pessary insertion includes giving antibiotics, seeing the patient every 3-6 months, and changing the pessary every 6 months. Regular follow-up is essential to prevent complications such as vaginal ulceration, erosion, or fistula formation.
questions.question: A pessary is considered a temporary measure for prolapse. What is the recommended follow-up interval for a patient using a pessary?
options: Weekly review for the first month, then yearly
Review every 2 years with change as needed

questions.explanation: A pregnancy test is the mandatory first investigation in any woman of reproductive age with abnormal uterine bleeding, because pregnancy complications (ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, gestational trophoblastic disease) are life-threatening and must be excluded before any other investigation or treatment is undertaken. Missing an ectopic pregnancy by proceeding directly to hormonal therapy without a pregnancy test can be fatal. This is the most critical 'rule out first' in DUB evaluation.
questions.question: In the DIAGNOSIS of DUB, which of the following represents a MANDATORY investigation before any treatment is initiated?

options: Vaginal discharge algorithm only — treating candidiasis and BV
Urethral discharge algorithm using single-dose gonorrhoea therapy alone
Genital ulcer algorithm as lower abdominal pain may represent perianal syphilis
Lower abdominal pain / PID algorithm covering gonorrhoea, chlamydia, anaerobes with combination antibiotic therapy and follow-up within 72 hours
No specific algorithm exists; all patients with lower abdominal pain are referred to hospital
questions.question: In a resource-limited setting like Nigeria, which syndromic management algorithm is used for a woman presenting with lower abdominal pain, vaginal discharge, and cervical motion tenderness?
questions.explanation: The WHO syndromic management lower abdominal pain algorithm is triggered by a combination of lower abdominal pain, vaginal/cervical discharge, and cervical motion tenderness — the triad suggesting PID. Treatment targets the common PID pathogens: N. gonorrhoeae (single-dose IM ceftriaxone), C. trachomatis (doxycycline 100mg BD for 14 days), and anaerobes (metronidazole 400mg BD for 14 days). A review at 72 hours is mandatory to assess treatment response and decide on inpatient admission if no improvement.

options: Pre-menopausal women; fibroids compressing the bladder
Adolescent girls; congenital pelvic floor weakness
questions.question: Which population group has a higher prevalence of urinary incontinence, and what factor specifically contributes to this increased prevalence?
questions.explanation: Urinary incontinence has a higher prevalence with increasing age. In older women, the ageing process (decreased muscle tone, impaired neural control), menopause (hypoestrogenism causing urethral and bladder atrophy), childbirth injuries, obesity, prolapse, and previous gynaecological surgery all contribute to increased prevalence. This multi-factorial aetiology explains why incontinence becomes increasingly common in post-menopausal women.

questions.question: A male condom breaks during intercourse. In advising the female partner, the MOST time-critical recommendation for pregnancy prevention is:
options: Take levonorgestrel emergency contraception ideally within 72 hours
Begin combined oral contraceptives immediately with no waiting period
Use a second condom immediately for residual protection
Schedule an intrauterine device fitting within 7 days at the earliest
questions.explanation: Emergency contraception with levonorgestrel 1.5mg is most effective when taken as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse, ideally within 72 hours, though it retains some efficacy up to 120 hours. Copper IUD insertion (even more effective) can be done up to 5 days (120 hours) post-exposure. Vaginal douching is ineffective and potentially harmful. Starting regular OCP without a waiting period does not constitute emergency contraception.

options: Bilateral ejaculatory duct obstruction absent seminal vesicle
Primary testicular failure with complete azoospermia
Partial vas deferens obstruction from previous vasectomy
questions.explanation: Very low volume (< 1mL), acidic pH semen with azoospermia suggests bilateral ejaculatory duct obstruction or congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, as the alkaline seminal vesicle and prostatic secretions (which make up 90% of semen volume) are absent. Normal semen is alkaline (pH 7.2–8.0) from seminal vesicle bicarbonate secretions. This pattern, combined with normal testicular size and FSH, points to obstructive azoospermia rather than testicular failure.
questions.question: A man reports that his ejaculation feels normal but semen analysis shows absent sperm with a very low semen volume (0.5mL) and acidic pH. What does this pattern suggest?

options: Pelvic inflammatory disease with periadnexal adhesions
questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents with menorrhagia, dysmenorrhoea, and worsening dyspareunia. She has cyclical rectal pain during menstruation. CA-125 is mildly elevated. Laparoscopy reveals powder-burn lesions on the pouch of Douglas and ovaries. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Endometriosis is characterized by ectopic endometrial glands and stroma implanting outside the uterus, classically on the ovaries, pouch of Douglas, and utero-sacral ligaments. The clinical triad of cyclical dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia (cyclical rectal pain) combined with laparoscopic powder-burn or blue-black lesions is diagnostic. It is listed as a cause of infertility through tuboperitoneal adhesions and ovarian endometriomas.

options: The cervical cap is more effective than the diaphragm in all women
The cervical cap does not require fitting by a healthcare provider
The cervical cap provides protection against sexually transmitted infections
The cervical cap is only suitable for parous women
The cervical cap can remain in place for up to 48 hours without additional spermicide for subsequent acts of intercourse
questions.question: The cervical cap differs from the diaphragm in which IMPORTANT clinical way?
questions.explanation: The cervical cap can be left in place for up to 48 hours (compared to the diaphragm's maximum 24 hours) without adding additional spermicide for each subsequent act of intercourse. This is a practical advantage. However, its efficacy is significantly reduced in parous women (who have a larger, more irregular cervical os) compared to nulliparous women, which is the reverse of the diaphragm's relatively consistent efficacy.

Tubal reanastomosis success (live birth rate) ranges from approximately 40–85% depending on: the original sterilization method (clips have best reversal outcomes as they cause minimal tubal destruction; salpingectomy cannot be reversed), the length of remaining tube, woman's age, and baseline fertility of the couple. Despite variable success, the irreversible counselling message is appropriate because reversal is expensive, often unavailable in Nigeria, and success is uncertain.
options: Near 100% success rates making tubal ligation effectively reversible for all women
Reversal is universally unsuccessful if more than 12 months have elapsed since sterilization
Success rates are identical regardless of whether clips, rings, or salpingectomy was performed
Success rates of 40–85% depending on method of sterilization, extent of tubal destruction, woman's age and fertility status at time of reversal
Reversal is technically impossible and IVF is the only option after tubal ligation
questions.question: Which of the following CORRECTLY identifies the pregnancy rates after reversal of female sterilization (tubal reanastomosis)?

questions.explanation: Some women continue to experience localised vaginal atrophy symptoms despite systemic hormone replacement therapy, and adding local vaginal oestrogen preparations directly targets vaginal tissue more effectively, often providing additional symptom relief for dryness and dyspareunia beyond systemic treatment alone.
questions.question: A postmenopausal woman on systemic hormone replacement therapy who continues to experience vaginal dryness and dyspareunia despite treatment should be advised to consider:
options: Increasing the systemic oestrogen dose without limit
Avoiding any further evaluation since symptoms are expected
Switching to combined oral contraceptives instead

questions.explanation: Small cell carcinoma of the hypercalcaemic type is a rare, aggressive ovarian tumour predominantly affecting young women, often associated with paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia. Its aggressive behaviour and poor prognosis contrast with most other ovarian tumours in this age group.
questions.question: Small cell carcinoma of the ovary with hypercalcaemia MOST typically affects which age group?
Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome causes primary amenorrhoea due to a specific embryological defect. Which developmental structures fail to form normally in this condition?
questions.explanation: MRKH syndrome results from agenesis or hypoplasia of the Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts, which normally give rise to the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina, while the ovaries, which develop from a separate embryological origin, remain functionally normal. This explains why affected women have normal secondary sexual characteristics and hormone levels but lack a uterus and present with primary amenorrhoea. Renal anomalies are also commonly associated due to the close embryological relationship between Müllerian and mesonephric structures.
options: The urogenital sinus, resulting in ambiguous genitalia
The gonadal ridge, resulting in absent ovaries
The Wolffian ducts, resulting in absent vas deferens
The Müllerian ducts, resulting in absence of the uterus and upper vagina
The neural tube, resulting in spina bifida

questions.question: The Type 1 endometrial carcinoma phenotype is classically described as:
options: Thin, multiparous, African-American women with poorly differentiated tumours
Obese nulliparous white women with well-differentiated tumours
Postmenopausal women with no identifiable risk factors
Women with BRCA mutations and serous histology
questions.explanation: Type 1 endometrial carcinoma occurs classically in obese, nulliparous, white women with signs of hyperoestrogenism and late menopause. These tumours tend to be well-differentiated, superficially invasive, progesterone-sensitive, carry a very favourable prognosis, and extrauterine disease is unusual.

options: Uterine incision to remove the pregnancy
Chemical instillation into the amniotic cavity
questions.question: A patient undergoes hysterotomy for a 20-week pregnancy. In the classification of surgical methods for induced abortion, hysterotomy is MOST appropriately described as:
questions.explanation: Hysterotomy involves making a surgical incision into the uterus (similar to a mini-Caesarean section) to remove the pregnancy and is reserved for cases where other methods have failed or are contraindicated. It carries higher morbidity than other methods and is rarely performed. It is distinguished from hysterectomy (complete uterine removal), which is only used in life-threatening situations.

Organised mass screening programmes systematically invite an entire eligible population with structured call and recall systems, reducing the number of high-risk women who are missed compared with relying on opportunistic individual screening, while also benefiting from economies of scale in sample processing. This population-level structure improves overall cost-effectiveness and cancer detection rates. It underpins national cervical screening programmes worldwide.
options: Individual screening requires no laboratory infrastructure
Systematic population coverage improves detection efficiency
Mass screening uses cheaper, less accurate test kits
Mass screening eliminates the need for any follow-up of abnormal results
Individual screening always detects more cancers per test performed
questions.question: A national mass cervical cytology screening programme is compared with individual opportunistic screening in terms of resource use. Which factor most explains why organised mass screening is generally more cost-effective at a population level?

questions.explanation: In a woman who has completed childbearing, vaginal hysterectomy combined with anterior and posterior repair addresses uterine descent and associated compartment defects definitively in a single procedure. Fertility preservation is not a concern, making this the most direct definitive option. Ligament plication is performed concurrently to restore vault support.
questions.question: A woman with completed family and third-degree uterovaginal prolapse is being counselled on definitive surgery. Why is vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair generally preferred over uterus-conserving options in this scenario?
options: It avoids the need for any anaesthesia
It removes the uterus and repairs all defects simultaneously
It is always safer than any conservative repair regardless of fertility wishes
It eliminates the need for postoperative catheterisation
It is the only operation that treats cystocele

questions.explanation: HCG is selectively produced by syncytiotrophoblast, with a normal titre of 20–30 mIU/ml. It is a glycoprotein with molecular weight 36,000–40,000 Daltons and a half-life of 32–37 hours. Its beta fraction is specific and measured by RIA and enzyme immunoassay, while the alpha fraction shares immunological similarity with pituitary gonadotrophins.
questions.question: HCG as a tumour marker is selectively produced by which cell type?

questions.explanation: Establishing differential renal function before major reconstructive fistula surgery is essential, since a non-functioning kidney may require separate management, such as nephrectomy, and affects overall surgical and anaesthetic risk assessment. This information also helps set realistic expectations about postoperative renal function. Renal scintigraphy or intravenous urography is typically used to assess this.
options: It determines the choice of anaesthetic agent only
It is only relevant if the patient is diabetic
It has no bearing on fistula surgery outcomes
It replaces the need for any urinary tract imaging
Guides overall surgical planning and prognosis
questions.question: A patient with a non-functioning kidney secondary to urinary tract injury from obstructed labour is being planned for definitive fistula surgery. Why is preoperative assessment of individual renal function on each side particularly important in this scenario?
Second primary malignancy risk after successful treatment of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia with etoposide-containing regimens is MOST notably increased for which cancer?
questions.explanation: Etoposide, used in regimens such as EMA-CO for high-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, carries a recognised long-term risk of secondary acute myeloid leukaemia, which should be discussed with patients as part of informed consent for treatment.

options: Dry days or sticky, cloudy, white/yellow scant secretion
Abundant, clear, slippery, and stretchy mucus with egg-white consistency
Moderate amounts of white mucus with creamy consistency throughout the cycle
Any mucus present regardless of consistency indicates the fertile phase
Thick mucus with a strong odour indicating hostile cervical conditions
questions.explanation: In the Billings Ovulation Method, infertile days are characterised by either complete dryness (no mucus sensation or visible secretion) or the presence of thick, sticky, cloudy, white or yellowish, scant secretion without the slippery/lubricative sensation of fertile mucus. These characteristics reflect progesterone dominance or low estrogen states. Only the wet, slippery, transparent mucus indicates fertility.
questions.question: The 'infertile days' in the Billings Ovulation Method are characterized by which mucus description?

questions.explanation: Epispadias with an abnormally positioned urethral meatus results in semen being deposited away from the cervix during intercourse, reducing the chance of sperm reaching the cervical mucus and upper reproductive tract, even though spermatogenesis itself may be entirely normal. This anatomical rather than spermatogenic cause of infertility may be amenable to surgical correction or bypassed using assisted insemination techniques. Semen analysis in these men may otherwise be normal.
questions.question: A couple presents after 3 years of infertility. Investigation reveals the male partner has epispadias with malpositioned external urethral meatus. Through which mechanism does this anatomical anomaly most directly cause infertility?
options: Semen deposited away from the cervix
Complete obstruction of the vas deferens

questions.question: An adequate chemotherapy response in choriocarcinoma is defined as a serum hCG fall of:
questions.explanation: An adequate response to chemotherapy in choriocarcinoma is defined as a fall of serum hCG by one log (10-fold decrease). If hCG does not decline by one log within 18 days of completing the first chemotherapy course, a second course is required with dose escalation if the first course response was inadequate.

questions.question: Which of the following is MOST correct regarding hormonal emergency contraception (EC) with levonorgestrel?
questions.explanation: Levonorgestrel EC acts primarily by inhibiting or delaying ovulation, preventing the sperm from meeting an egg. There is no conclusive evidence that it prevents implantation of a fertilized egg. It has no effect on an established pregnancy and is not an abortifacient. Efficacy is highest when taken immediately after unprotected intercourse and decreases with time; it does not provide ongoing protection for subsequent unprotected acts.
options: It works by terminating an established pregnancy (abortifacient)
It is equally effective regardless of when in the cycle it is taken
It prevents pregnancy mainly by delaying or inhibiting ovulation, not by disrupting implantation
It provides ongoing contraceptive protection for 7 days after use
It is contraindicated in women who have previously been pregnant

questions.question: In the management of acute severe uterine bleeding, the MOST rapid non-surgical medical therapy to control bleeding is:
questions.explanation: For acute heavy uterine bleeding, intravenous conjugated equine oestrogens (25 mg IV every 4 hours for up to 24 hours or until bleeding is controlled) is the most rapid-acting medical therapy. Oestrogen causes vasospasm of uterine arteries, rapid endometrial proliferation to cover denuded surfaces, and stimulates clotting at the capillary level. It is followed by oral progestins to stabilise the regrown endometrium. Oral progestins alone act too slowly in acute emergencies.
options: Antifibrinolytic agents such as tranexamic acid

questions.explanation: An endometrial thickness below the accepted threshold on transvaginal ultrasound has a high negative predictive value, making significant endometrial pathology unlikely, though persistent or recurrent bleeding still warrants further evaluation such as biopsy.
questions.question: Transvaginal ultrasound measurement of endometrial thickness is MOST useful in postmenopausal bleeding because a thin endometrium:
options: Excludes the need for any further investigation ever
Has a high negative predictive value for carcinoma

questions.explanation: Human menopausal gonadotrophins (hMG = FSH + LH) combined with hCG (to trigger ovulation) are used for ovulation induction in anovulatory DUB when simpler agents (clomiphene, tamoxifen) have failed. They are most appropriate for WHO Group II anovulation (normogonadotrophic, normoprolactinaemic anovulation — such as PCOS) where endogenous gonadotrophins are present but inadequate. They require ultrasound monitoring to prevent hyperstimulation and multiple pregnancy. They should not be used in hypergonadotrophic states (where the ovary cannot respond).
questions.question: Ovulatory induction with human menopausal gonadotrophins (hMG) combined with hCG in DUB is most appropriate for:
options: Women with corpus luteum insufficiency from ovulatory DUB
WHO Group II anovulation (PCOS) after failed clomiphene

questions.explanation: Hysterectomy provides the definitive advantage of complete cure and simultaneous removal of the uterus (including any concurrent pathology such as fibroids, adenomyosis, or missed hyperplasia/carcinoma not detected on pre-operative sampling). Endometrial ablation, while more conservative, is not 100% effective, may leave residual endometrium that can progress to carcinoma, and has a significant reoperation rate. Hysterectomy's higher mortality, morbidity, and cost are its limitations.
options: Faster recovery with fewer hospital days
Preservation of fertility if desired later
questions.question: Hysterectomy in DUB provides which SPECIFIC advantage over endometrial ablation?

questions.explanation: Treatment by stage: Stage Ia (microinvasive) - cone biopsy or simple hysterectomy. Stage Ib - radical surgery OR radiotherapy (both are primary options). Stage IIa - radiotherapy OR radical surgery. Stages IIb, III - radiotherapy. Stage IV - palliative treatment. The choice between surgery and radiotherapy for stage Ib depends on patient factors including age, medical fitness, and centre expertise.
questions.question: Which stage of cervical carcinoma is treated by radical surgery or radiotherapy as primary alternatives?

options: Absent secondary sexual characteristics and ambiguous genitalia
Secondary amenorrhoea with normal uterus on imaging
Recurrent spontaneous abortions with a normal vagina
Primary amenorrhoea, normal secondary characteristics, absent vagina
questions.question: A girl with aplasia of the uterus due to complete failure of Müllerian duct development will MOST likely have which clinical features?
questions.explanation: Aplasia of the uterus results from complete failure of Müllerian duct development, so the fallopian tubes, uterus, and upper third of the vagina are all absent. Ovarian function is normal and independent of Müllerian development, so secondary sexual characteristics (oestrogen-driven breast development, body fat distribution) develop normally. Primary amenorrhoea follows because there is no endometrium to shed.

questions.question: DMPA administered correctly at 12-week intervals has a typical-use failure rate of approximately:
options: Less than 1 per 100 women per year
questions.explanation: DMPA has a typical-use failure rate of approximately 4–6 per 100 women per year, primarily because some women receive late injections beyond the 13-week grace period, allowing ovulation to escape suppression. With perfect use (every 12 weeks precisely), the failure rate is less than 0.3%. Its excellent typical-use efficacy compared to pills reflects that it requires only 4 injections per year rather than daily adherence.

One of the listed components of reproductive health explicitly covers promotion of healthy sexual maturation beginning from pre-adolescence, responsible and safe sexual behaviour throughout life, and promotion of gender equality. This component recognizes that reproductive health spans the entire lifecycle and includes adolescent and sexual health education. Safe motherhood and fertility management are separate components.
questions.question: Which component of reproductive health care specifically includes promotion of healthy sexual maturation from pre-adolescence and responsible sex throughout the lifetime?

questions.explanation: Rectal injury during pelvic procedures including vaginal hysterectomy and pelvic floor repair (PFR) is listed as an aetiology of rectovaginal fistula. When pelvic surgery is complicated by scarring from pelvic sepsis or endometriosis, normal planes are distorted, increasing the risk of rectal injury during posterior dissection. The resulting RVF requires careful pre-operative planning for repair.
questions.question: A woman with endometriosis undergoes pelvic floor repair (PFR). She subsequently develops a fistula. Which type is most likely?
options: Rectovaginal fistula from rectal injury during PFR

questions.question: A patient with a known ectopic pregnancy of 6 weeks and stable haemodynamics has a serum hCG of 1,800 mIU/mL with no cardiac activity on ultrasound. Which treatment is MOST appropriate?
questions.explanation: Medical management with methotrexate (a folate antagonist that inhibits trophoblast proliferation) is appropriate for haemodynamically stable, unruptured ectopic pregnancies with hCG below 5,000 mIU/mL, no cardiac activity, and small size. Success rates exceed 85% in carefully selected patients. It avoids surgery and preserves the fallopian tube for future fertility.

options: Antibiotics alone indefinitely without any drainage procedure
Surgical or radiological drainage combined with continued antibiotics
Immediate hysterectomy in every case regardless of severity
questions.question: A woman with untreated pelvic inflammatory disease develops a tubo-ovarian abscess. Which management approach is indicated if she remains clinically unstable or fails to respond to antibiotics alone?
questions.explanation: A tubo-ovarian abscess that fails to respond to antibiotics alone, or in a clinically unstable patient, requires drainage, either surgically or via image-guided percutaneous approaches, combined with continued appropriate antibiotic therapy to achieve source control and prevent progression to sepsis or rupture. This escalation reflects the need for definitive management of a localised collection that antibiotics alone may not adequately penetrate. Close monitoring guides the timing and threshold for intervention.

Birth spacing of at least 24–36 months between births (interpregnancy interval from delivery to next conception of =18 months) is associated with reduced maternal nutritional depletion, improved child survival, and better breastfeeding outcomes. Interpregnancy intervals under 18 months are associated with preterm birth, low birth weight, and maternal anaemia. Family planning supports optimal spacing.
options: Achieving a desired family size of exactly two children
Ensuring all family members are born in the same hospital
Reducing the interval between pregnancies to within 12 months
Limiting family size based on government-set quotas
At least a 3-year interval between births to optimize maternal and child health
questions.question: The concept of 'spacing' in family planning most directly aims to achieve:

options: A twin pregnancy with one sac resorbing
Likely ectopic or abnormal, given the hCG level
Normal variation requiring no further action
A completely normal early intrauterine pregnancy
questions.explanation: At hCG levels above the discriminatory zone, a normal intrauterine pregnancy should be visible on transvaginal ultrasound; absence of an intrauterine sac at this level strongly suggests an ectopic pregnancy or a failing pregnancy, warranting further evaluation. This combination is used clinically to guide urgent further investigation rather than reassurance. Serial hCG trends and repeat scanning help clarify the diagnosis if it remains uncertain.
questions.question: A woman with a 6-week ectopic pregnancy has a serum hCG of 6,500 mIU/mL with no intrauterine sac seen on transvaginal ultrasound. What does the combination of hCG level and absent intrauterine sac specifically suggest?
A 70-year-old woman has a 2 cm well-differentiated vulval squamous cell carcinoma with no palpable lymph nodes. FIGO staging would classify this as:
questions.explanation: A 2 cm vulval squamous cell carcinoma confined to the vulva and/or perineum with no lymph node involvement is classified as FIGO Stage I (specifically Stage IA if stromal invasion is 1 mm or less, or Stage IB if greater than 1 mm but still confined to vulva/perineum). Stage II involves adjacent perineal structures; Stage III involves inguinal nodes.

options: Is inserted by the partner, not the user
Cannot be used with additional spermicide
Requires no spermicide use for effectiveness
Fits snugly over the cervix by suction alone
Gives complete protection against all infections
questions.explanation: The cervical cap is a smaller device that fits directly over the cervix and is held in place partly by suction, in contrast to the diaphragm, which spans the vaginal fornices and rests against the pubic bone anteriorly, generally requiring spermicide use with both devices for effectiveness.
questions.question: The cervical cap differs from the diaphragm in that it:

questions.explanation: The recurrence rate for ectopic pregnancy is 15% after the first ectopic and rises to 25% after two ectopic pregnancies. This reflects the underlying tubal damage that predisposed to the first ectopic, which often affects both tubes. Women should be counselled about this risk and offered early ultrasound in subsequent pregnancies.
questions.question: In Nigeria, ectopic pregnancy accounts for 2–3% of gynaecological emergencies. After a FIRST ectopic pregnancy, what is the recurrence risk for a subsequent ectopic?
Hypothyroidism as a cause of DUB and menorrhagia is diagnosed by:
questions.explanation: Thyroid function tests (TSH, T3, T4) diagnose hypothyroidism, which causes menorrhagia through mechanisms including anovulation from hypothalamic suppression, coagulation factor deficiency, and impaired fibrinolysis. TSH is the most sensitive initial screening test — an elevated TSH with low free T4 confirms primary hypothyroidism. Treatment with thyroid hormone replacement frequently resolves the menorrhagia without specific gynaecological intervention. This is why thyroid function is a standard DUB investigation.

The primary and most important mechanism of COCs is ovulation suppression through inhibition of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis. Exogenous estrogen and progestogen provide negative feedback, suppressing GnRH pulsatility and the pituitary FSH/LH surges required for follicular development and ovulation. Secondary mechanisms include cervical mucus thickening and endometrial changes, but ovulation suppression is the primary mechanism.
questions.question: The PRIMARY mechanism by which combined oral contraceptives (COCs) prevent pregnancy is:
options: Thickening cervical mucus to prevent sperm penetration
Suppression of ovulation through inhibition of FSH and LH surges
Inducing corpus luteum insufficiency after ovulation

questions.explanation: The standard cut-off level for CA-125 is 35 u/ml. A level above this is strongly suggestive of ovarian cancer, particularly in postmenopausal women. However, CA-125 can also be elevated in endometriosis, PID, liver disease, and other non-gynaecological conditions.
questions.question: The cut-off level of CA-125 that is considered the upper limit of normal is:

The partner should also be treated to prevent reinfection
Treatment of the partner is optional and rarely beneficial
The partner does not require any assessment or treatment
questions.explanation: Partner notification and treatment are essential components of managing curable sexually transmitted infections, since failure to treat a partner risks reinfection of the index patient and continued transmission within the sexual network, undermining the benefit of the initial treatment.
questions.question: A woman diagnosed with a curable sexually transmitted infection should MOST importantly be advised regarding her sexual partner that:

Laser therapy for CIN is described as requiring no formal anaesthesia in many cases and achieving healing within a defined time frame. Approximately how many days does healing typically take after laser treatment?
options: Healing does not occur without additional surgery
questions.explanation: After laser ablation or conisation for CIN, cervical re-epithelialisation and healing typically takes around 4 to 6 weeks, during which the patient is advised to avoid intercourse and tampon use to reduce infection risk. Follow-up cytology is then performed after adequate healing has occurred. This timeframe is similar to other ablative and excisional cervical procedures.

questions.question: A woman has had three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages. Investigations reveal a balanced reciprocal translocation in one partner's karyotype. What is the MOST appropriate next step in her management?
questions.explanation: A balanced translocation can produce unbalanced gametes leading to recurrent miscarriage, so genetic counselling is essential to explain recurrence risk and discuss reproductive options such as preimplantation genetic testing. Heparin and progesterone are more relevant to antiphospholipid syndrome or luteal insufficiency, not chromosomal translocations. Cerclage addresses cervical weakness, an unrelated mechanism.

questions.question: The MOST important instruction to give a couple when one partner is newly diagnosed with a curable STI (e.g., gonorrhoea or chlamydia) is:
questions.explanation: Partner notification and simultaneous treatment of all sexual partners is the cornerstone of STI management. Without treating both partners simultaneously, 'ping-pong' reinfection occurs — the treated partner is reinfected by the untreated partner immediately upon resuming sexual activity. Abstinence or consistent condom use until both partners have completed treatment and are symptom-free prevents reinfection. Partner treatment also prevents the untreated partner's complications.
options: Treat only the symptomatic partner and advise condom use for 3 months
The partner's infection will resolve spontaneously without treatment in most cases
The uninfected partner needs testing only if they develop symptoms within 2 weeks
Condom use alone during treatment is sufficient to prevent reinfection without treating the partner
Both partners must be simultaneously treated to prevent reinfection, and sexual intercourse should be avoided until both partners have completed treatment

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman is counselled about non-hormonal options for managing menopausal hot flushes due to a history of breast cancer. Which class of medication has evidence for reducing vasomotor symptoms in this context?
questions.explanation: For women in whom systemic hormone therapy is contraindicated, such as those with a history of hormone-sensitive breast cancer, selective serotonin or noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors have evidence for reducing the frequency and severity of vasomotor symptoms through central neurotransmitter effects on thermoregulation. This provides an important non-hormonal alternative for symptom relief. Lifestyle measures and other non-hormonal options may also be used alongside or instead of medication.
options: Oestrogen-only vaginal cream in high systemic doses
Incorporates urinary hormone monitoring using a fertility monitor alongside mucus and BBT observations
Uses only calendar calculation without any biological monitoring
Relies exclusively on Mittelschmerz as its single fertility marker
Is designed only for women with polycystic ovary syndrome
Requires monthly blood hormone testing by a laboratory
questions.question: The Marquette Model of natural family planning differs from other NFP methods in that it:
questions.explanation: The Marquette Model (developed at Marquette University) uniquely incorporates the ClearBlue Fertility Monitor, which measures urinary estrogen and LH metabolites to objectively identify the fertile window. This is used alongside mucus observations and optionally BBT. The addition of objective hormonal monitoring reduces user uncertainty and may improve effectiveness, particularly for women with difficult-to-interpret mucus patterns or those new to fertility awareness.

options: Right and left levator ani muscles
questions.question: A rectocele develops due to a gap or weakness between which structures?
questions.explanation: Rectocele develops when there is a gap or weakness between the right and left portions of the levator ani muscles posteriorly, allowing the rectum to herniate forward into the vaginal wall. This is distinct from an enterocele, which occurs due to failure to support the cardinal ligament or correct enterocele at hysterectomy.

The proliferative phase of the endometrial cycle corresponds to the follicular phase of the ovarian cycle. During this phase, rising FSH drives follicular development and oestrogen production from the granulosa cells; this oestrogen stimulates endometrial proliferation. The two terms (follicular/proliferative) describe the same time period from the perspective of the ovary and uterus respectively, covering approximately days 1–13 of a 28-day cycle.
questions.question: The proliferative phase of the menstrual cycle corresponds to which ovarian phase?
Which of the following MOST accurately distinguishes the copper IUD from the levonorgestrel intrauterine system in terms of effect on menstrual bleeding?
questions.explanation: The copper IUD can increase menstrual blood loss and cramping due to its local inflammatory mechanism, whereas the levonorgestrel intrauterine system suppresses the endometrium and typically reduces menstrual blood loss, a key counselling point when helping women choose between the two devices.
options: The copper IUD may increase menstrual blood loss, while the LNG-IUS typically reduces it
The copper IUD reduces bleeding while the LNG-IUS increases it
Both devices reliably increase menstrual blood loss equally
Both devices reliably reduce menstrual blood loss equally
Neither device has any effect on menstrual bleeding patterns

questions.explanation: Regular menstruation is evidence of ovulation in approximately 80% of cases; the remaining 20% of regular bleeders may have anovulatory cycles with unopposed oestrogen causing irregular shedding rather than progesterone-withdrawal menstruation. This distinction is important because regular cycles do not guarantee fertility. In infertility work-up, ovulation must be confirmed biochemically (mid-luteal progesterone) even in women with regular cycles.
questions.question: Normal menstruation is considered evidence of ovulation in what percentage of cases?

The pregnancy protects against tumour progression
Treatment proceeds without delay; delivery timing is individualised
Pregnancy must always be terminated immediately regardless of gestation
Treatment is always deferred until spontaneous labour at term
questions.explanation: Management of cervical carcinoma in late pregnancy requires balancing the urgency of cancer treatment against fetal maturity, often allowing a short, carefully monitored delay to improve fetal viability before definitive treatment, especially in early-stage disease. Multidisciplinary discussion involving oncology and obstetrics determines the safest individualised plan. Undue delay in advanced disease is avoided as it worsens maternal prognosis.
questions.question: A woman diagnosed with invasive cervical carcinoma in the early third trimester of pregnancy is counselled about management. What is the generally accepted principle guiding her treatment?

questions.explanation: Hormonal effects on acne through combined oral contraceptive use develop gradually as androgen suppression and other hormonal changes take effect on the skin, so women should be counselled that noticeable improvement typically takes several months of consistent pill use rather than an immediate effect.
options: Improvement occurs only after five years of continuous use
questions.question: A 22-year-old woman on the combined oral contraceptive pill for acne management asks how long she should expect to wait before seeing clinical improvement. She should be advised that visible benefit typically takes:

options: Transverse vaginal septum causing outflow obstruction
Mullerian agenesis with absent vagina (partial MRKH)
questions.explanation: A transverse vaginal septum causes primary amenorrhoea with cryptomenorrhoea (menstrual blood trapped above the septum), normal secondary sexual characteristics, normal uterus and ovaries, and a structurally absent portion of the vaginal canal on MRI. Unlike imperforate hymen (which affects only the hymen), a transverse septum involves the vaginal wall itself. Treatment is surgical septum excision and vaginal reconstruction.
questions.question: A 22-year-old with primary amenorrhoea has normal female secondary sexual characteristics, a normal uterus, and bilateral ovaries on ultrasound. Her karyotype is 46,XX. MRI shows an absent vaginal canal below the cervix. FSH and LH are normal. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?

options: Whole pelvic external beam radiotherapy alone
Unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with uterine and contralateral ovary preservation
Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
questions.explanation: In early-stage germ cell tumours such as immature teratoma, fertility-sparing surgery with unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy while preserving the uterus and contralateral ovary is appropriate in young women, since these tumours are usually chemosensitive if recurrence occurs.
questions.question: A young woman with a stage IA immature ovarian teratoma wishing to preserve fertility should MOST appropriately undergo:

questions.explanation: Suction curettage under general anaesthesia is the treatment of choice for complete hydatidiform mole evacuation. It carries lower risk of metastasis than sharp curettage (D&C). The uterus must be completely emptied, and oxytocin is commenced prior to the procedure. Histological examination of the evacuated tissue is mandatory.
questions.question: The GOLD STANDARD initial management of a complete hydatidiform mole is:

questions.explanation: The gubernaculum guides gonadal descent in both sexes; in females it persists as the ovarian ligament proximally and the round ligament of the uterus distally, since ovarian descent halts within the pelvis. The processus vaginalis is the peritoneal outpouching relevant mainly to testicular descent through the inguinal canal. Persistent mesonephric duct remnants instead form structures such as Gartner duct cysts.
questions.question: The ovaries develop from the genital ridge and descend into the pelvis, unlike the testes which descend into the scrotum. What structure guides ovarian descent and later becomes the ovarian ligament?

options: Acute urinary retention from periurethral oedema
questions.explanation: Surgical manipulation and oedema around the bladder neck and urethra after prolapse repair can precipitate acute urinary retention. A period of catheter drainage allows swelling to settle and prevents bladder overdistension. Early mobilisation and catheter removal are then guided by residual urine volumes.
questions.question: Following surgical correction of prolapse, a urethral catheter is left in situ for 24 to 48 hours. What immediate postoperative complication is this measure primarily intended to prevent?
Choriocarcinoma differs histologically from hydatidiform mole in that it:
options: Arises only after a normal term pregnancy
Is composed purely of cytotrophoblast without syncytiotrophoblast
questions.explanation: Choriocarcinoma is composed of sheets of anaplastic cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast without chorionic villi, distinguishing it histologically from hydatidiform mole and invasive mole, both of which retain villous architecture even when invading the myometrium.

questions.question: A patient with cervical carcinoma shows a bullous oedema of the bladder on cystoscopy. What FIGO stage does this indicate?
questions.explanation: FIGO staging specifically states that a bullous oedema of the bladder does NOT constitute stage IV disease. Stage IVa is only diagnosed when there is actual involvement (invasion) of the mucosa of the bladder or rectum. Stage IV also includes disease that has extended beyond the true pelvis. Bullous oedema alone remains classified as stage III and should not be upstaged to IVa.

options: Yes; any two spontaneous abortions constitute recurrent abortion
Yes; recurrent abortion is 2 or more consecutive spontaneous abortions
No; recurrent abortion requires THREE or more consecutive losses
No; chromosomally abnormal losses are excluded from the recurrent abortion definition
Yes; but only if both losses were in the same trimester
questions.explanation: Recurrent abortion is defined as two or more CONSECUTIVE spontaneous abortions — both consecutive and spontaneous losses qualify regardless of chromosomal findings, gestational age, or trimester. With two consecutive losses, this patient meets the definition and full investigation is warranted. The majority of women diagnosed with recurrent abortion ultimately achieve successful pregnancy with or without treatment, which is important counselling information.
questions.question: A 24-year-old woman reports two previous abortions: the first at 8 weeks (products of conception showed normal karyotype) and the second at 14 weeks (trisomy 18 on karyotype). She is now 6 weeks pregnant and requests reassurance. According to the definition of recurrent abortion, does she qualify?

options: A hyperandrogenic state with no effect on the pituitary axis
A pseudopregnancy state with high progesterone alone
A pseudomenopausal state through suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis
questions.explanation: Danazol suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis and has androgenic properties, creating a pseudomenopausal, hypo-oestrogenic state that causes atrophy of endometriotic implants and relief of associated symptoms. Its use has declined due to significant androgenic side effects such as weight gain, acne, and voice changes, with other medical therapies now often preferred. It remains of historical and occasionally niche clinical relevance in endometriosis management.
questions.question: Danazol has historically been used for endometriosis treatment. Its mechanism involves creating a specific hormonal state. What is this state called?

questions.explanation: Diaphragm-associated UTIs result from two mechanisms: (1) the anterior rim pressing against the urethra, causing incomplete bladder emptying and urinary stasis favoring bacterial growth, and (2) spermicide (particularly nonoxynol-9) disrupting normal vaginal flora by killing Lactobacillus species, allowing E. coli and other uropathogens to colonize the vaginal vestibule and ascend to the bladder.
questions.question: A woman with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) is using a diaphragm. The MOST likely mechanism by which diaphragm use increases UTI risk is:
options: Latex components colonize the bladder with pathogens
Anterior rim pressure on the urethra impairs complete bladder emptying
Spermicide reduces vaginal Lactobacillus, promoting colonization with uropathogens
Diaphragm insertion introduces bowel flora directly into the bladder

questions.explanation: Luteinized unruptured follicle (LUF) syndrome occurs when the dominant follicle undergoes luteinization and progesterone secretion (giving basal body temperature rise and positive Day 21 progesterone) without actually releasing the oocyte. BBT charts and serum progesterone appear to indicate ovulation, but no ovum is available for fertilization. LUF is a cause of apparent ovulatory infertility and is diagnosed by serial ultrasound folliculometry.
questions.question: A woman is found to have a luteinized unruptured follicle (LUF) syndrome. She is investigated for infertility. Which ovarian factor does this represent, and what is its functional significance?
options: Follicle luteinizes without releasing the ovum
Anovulation from PCOD with elevated androgens
Premature ovarian failure with elevated FSH
Corpus luteum insufficiency with low progesterone
Empty follicle syndrome from gonadotropin excess

questions.explanation: A cystocele descends through the pubocervical fascia, which normally supports the bladder and lies between the cardinal ligament and pubis. When this fascia is deficient, the bladder herniates into the anterior vaginal wall. Additionally, the uretero-vesical junctions may also be affected, risking ureteric obstruction, which is a surgical caution during anterior colporrhaphy.
questions.question: A cystocele descends through defects in which fascia?

questions.explanation: The correct temporal sequence of the menstrual cycle is: menstrual phase (shedding, days 1–5) ? follicular/proliferative phase (follicular development and endometrial proliferation, days 1–13) ? ovulatory phase (LH surge and ovulation, day 14 in a 28-day cycle) ? luteal/secretory phase (corpus luteum function and secretory endometrium, days 15–28). The proliferative and follicular phases are synonymous, as are secretory and luteal.

Sensate focus exercises used in psychosexual therapy are PRIMARILY designed to:
options: Provide a definitive cure for all forms of sexual dysfunction
Reduce performance anxiety by removing pressure to achieve orgasm
Diagnose an underlying hormonal cause of dysfunction
Replace the need for any medical evaluation
Increase the frequency of penetrative intercourse immediately
questions.explanation: Sensate focus exercises involve structured, non-genital touching exercises that gradually progress, deliberately removing the goal of orgasm or intercourse, thereby reducing performance anxiety and helping couples reconnect with pleasurable touch as part of psychosexual therapy.

questions.question: The Adjustable Continence Therapy (ACT) device for stress incontinence consists of which components?
questions.explanation: The Adjustable Continence Therapy (ACT) consists of silicone balloons with subcutaneous ports placed bilaterally in the periurethral position. Saline is used for balloon adjustment (inflation/deflation) through the subcutaneous ports to modify urethral closure pressure as needed. This adjustability distinguishes it from fixed slings and colposuspension, allowing individualised post-operative urethral support.
options: Silicone balloons in periurethral position, saline-adjusted
A prolene mesh sling from groin to groin under the urethra
A retropubic suture from vaginal wall to pectineal ligament
An electrode through the sacral foramen
A ring pessary placed at the bladder neck

questions.explanation: Recurrent candidiasis should prompt screening for poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, since hyperglycaemia promotes fungal overgrowth by increasing glucose availability in vaginal secretions and impairing local immune defences. The other listed conditions are not established risk factors for recurrent candidal infection. Identifying and managing underlying diabetes is essential to prevent ongoing recurrence.
questions.question: A woman with recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, defined as four or more episodes yearly, is being evaluated. Which underlying condition should MOST specifically be excluded?

options: All levator muscles relax together to allow defaecation
Puborectalis contracts harder to force stool through
Puborectalis relaxes while other levator muscles contract during defaecation
The internal anal sphincter relaxes alone to initiate defaecation
Levator ani plays no role; only the external sphincter matters
questions.question: Compared to the vagina, which of the following is true of the levator ani muscle's role in defaecation?
questions.explanation: Defaecation requires coordinated relaxation of the puborectalis (which normally maintains the anorectal angle) while the other levator muscles contract. This dual action straightens the anorectal junction by widening the angle and simultaneously raises the pelvic diaphragm to facilitate passage of stool.

questions.question: Paget disease of the vulva is characterised histologically by which specific cell type?
questions.explanation: Paget disease of the vulva is characterised histologically by large pale cells with abundant cytoplasm (Paget cells) scattered throughout the epidermis—an intraepithelial adenocarcinoma. It presents as an erythematous, eczematoid, pruritic lesion and may be associated with an underlying invasive adenocarcinoma of the vulva or Bartholin gland.

options: Primary amenorrhoea, absent secondary characteristics, and short stature
Secondary amenorrhoea after a period of normal menstrual function
Recurrent pregnancy loss with normal puberty
questions.question: Turner's syndrome (45,XO) most commonly presents clinically in a young woman as:
questions.explanation: Turner's syndrome (45,X) is the commonest sex chromosome abnormality in females and the commonest cause of primary amenorrhoea. It presents with streak gonads, absent secondary sexual development, short stature (due to absent second sex chromosome genes for height), and primary amenorrhoea. The female phenotype is preserved because without testicular tissue, neither testosterone nor AMH is produced.

questions.question: A woman treated for pelvic inflammatory disease three years ago now presents with chronic pelvic pain and infertility. Which long-term complication MOST directly explains her infertility?
questions.explanation: Pelvic inflammatory disease causes inflammatory damage and scarring of the fallopian tubes, leading to tubal occlusion or distorted architecture that impairs ovum transport and fertilisation, the leading cause of tubal factor infertility. Ovarian function is not typically directly destroyed by ascending pelvic infection. Uterine synechiae are more classically associated with intrauterine instrumentation such as curettage, not PID.

options: Leave the IUD in situ as it provides no further risk once pregnancy is confirmed
Immediate surgical termination of pregnancy is mandatory
Only remove after 12 weeks gestation when the risk of procedural miscarriage is lower
Administer systemic methotrexate to treat the IUD-related pregnancy
Remove the IUD if the threads are accessible, as leaving it in situ increases risk of second-trimester miscarriage, infection, preterm labour
questions.question: A woman with a copper IUD in situ is found to have a positive pregnancy test. After excluding ectopic pregnancy, the MOST appropriate management is:
questions.explanation: When intrauterine pregnancy is confirmed with an IUD in situ, the IUD should be removed as early as possible if the threads are accessible in the cervical canal. Leaving the IUD in place significantly increases risk of second-trimester miscarriage (~50%), septic abortion, chorioamnionitis, and preterm labour. If threads are not accessible, conservative management with close surveillance is required and removal may need ultrasound guidance.

ABO blood group associations in GTD include: group A women with group O husbands having an adverse prognosis, while group AB women have the poorest overall prognosis. These associations may reflect immunological interactions between maternal and paternal antigens in the trophoblastic tissue.
options: Blood group O with O partner
Blood group AB with blood group A partners
Blood group A with O partner
questions.question: Which of the following is MOST closely associated with an ABO blood group risk factor for GTD prognosis?

questions.explanation: Above the discriminatory zone (1,500–2,000 mIU/mL for transvaginal ultrasound), a viable intrauterine pregnancy should always be visible. Absence of an intrauterine gestational sac at hCG levels above this threshold indicates either a failing intrauterine pregnancy (incomplete/missed abortion) or an ectopic pregnancy — both require urgent evaluation and management. This principle is the cornerstone of early ectopic pregnancy diagnosis.
questions.question: A primigravida at 8 weeks presents with right adnexal tenderness and a complex adnexal mass on ultrasound. Her serum hCG is 3,200 mIU/mL but no intrauterine gestational sac is seen. The discriminatory zone for transvaginal ultrasound is 1,500–2,000 mIU/mL. What does the absence of an intrauterine sac above this discriminatory zone indicate?
options: Failing intrauterine pregnancy or ectopic pregnancy
Twin pregnancy with one failed gestational sac

questions.question: A vesicovaginal fistula developing after radical hysterectomy for cervical carcinoma most likely results from:
questions.explanation: Vesicovaginal fistula after radical hysterectomy most commonly results from inadvertent bladder injury during dissection or devascularisation of the bladder base from extensive parametrial dissection. The incidence is higher after radical (Wertheim) hysterectomy than simple hysterectomy due to the extensive bladder mobilisation required.

The mean cycle length decreases with age, from approximately 30 days at age 20 to 27 days by age 40, primarily because the follicular phase shortens as ovarian reserve declines. With fewer follicles, the dominant follicle matures faster (perhaps due to higher ambient FSH from reduced inhibin), resulting in earlier ovulation. The luteal phase remains relatively constant. This is a normal age-related change, not pathological, until it becomes excessive.
options: Shortened follicular phase from declining ovarian reserve
A shortened luteal phase from corpus luteum insufficiency
Increasing progesterone sensitivity in the endometrium
questions.question: A woman in her mid-30s has a cycle length that has shortened to 24 days compared to 28 days in her 20s. This is MOST consistent with:

questions.explanation: In subsequent pregnancies following GTD treatment, hCG levels should be measured 6–8 weeks after termination of pregnancy to detect any recurrence. Additionally, early ultrasound should confirm normal pregnancy, and histological examination of the placenta or products of conception should be performed to exclude recurrent trophoblastic disease.
questions.question: After delivery of the placenta in a patient previously treated for GTD, which monitoring step is MOST important at 6 weeks postpartum?

options: Douching with acidic solutions immediately after intercourse
questions.explanation: The female condom is the only woman-controlled barrier contraceptive available without prescription or provider fitting that also offers meaningful STI protection. While its perfect-use failure rate (~5%) and typical-use rate (~21%) are higher than prescription methods, it provides dual protection from pregnancy and STIs. Spermicide alone is significantly less effective and provides no STI protection. Douching is ineffective and potentially harmful.
questions.question: The MOST effective non-prescription barrier contraceptive method available to women who cannot access healthcare providers is:
A patient on aspirin for cardiac protection requires non-urgent major gynaecological surgery. Aspirin should be:
options: Continued at full dose throughout the perioperative period
Stopped only on the morning of surgery
questions.explanation: Aspirin used for secondary cardiac prevention should ideally be stopped 7–10 days before major surgery to reduce haemorrhagic risk, provided the cardiac risk of stopping allows it. For patients at high cardiovascular risk (e.g., recent coronary stent), the risk of thrombosis from stopping aspirin must be weighed against bleeding risk, often requiring cardiology consultation.

Sudden severe unilateral pain with an enlarged ovary and absent Doppler flow strongly indicates ovarian torsion, a surgical emergency where the ovarian pedicle twists and compromises blood supply, requiring urgent laparoscopic detorsion to salvage the ovary. Absent flow specifically distinguishes torsion from other causes of acute pelvic pain, which typically preserve some vascularity. Delay in diagnosis risks irreversible ovarian necrosis.
questions.question: A 45-year-old presents with sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain, nausea, and vomiting. Ultrasound shows an enlarged ovary with absent Doppler flow. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Cystoscopy allows direct visualisation of the bladder mucosa, enabling identification of a fistulous opening, tumour, stone, or inflammatory change that could explain haematuria and reduced bladder capacity. It complements imaging studies and is often essential before planning fistula repair. Biopsy of any suspicious lesion can also be taken during the procedure.
questions.question: A woman with unexplained haematuria and a small-capacity bladder on imaging is being investigated further. Which investigation is specifically indicated to directly visualise the bladder mucosa and identify a possible fistulous opening or other lesion?
A woman who has had a previous hydatidiform mole has what increased risk of mole in subsequent pregnancies?
questions.explanation: After a hydatidiform mole, the risk of mole in subsequent pregnancies is increased approximately 10-fold. These women require close monitoring in subsequent pregnancies with early ultrasound confirmation of normal intrauterine pregnancy and histological examination of the placenta or products of conception.

questions.question: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is a miscellaneous endocrine cause of amenorrhoea. In non-classical (late-onset) CAH, the excess adrenal androgen production is caused by deficiency of which enzyme?
questions.explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for over 90% of CAH cases, including the non-classical form that presents in adolescence or adulthood with hyperandrogenism, oligomenorrhoea/amenorrhoea, and hirsutism — closely mimicking PCOD. The enzyme block diverts steroidogenesis toward androgens (DHEA, androstenedione) instead of cortisol and aldosterone. Diagnosis requires a stimulated 17-hydroxyprogesterone level; treatment is low-dose glucocorticoid replacement to suppress ACTH-driven adrenal androgen excess.

Unilateral adnexal tenderness with peritoneal signs (cervical excitation, shoulder tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation) is the hallmark feature distinguishing ectopic pregnancy from threatened abortion. Ectopic pregnancy should always be excluded in the differential diagnosis of threatened abortion, as stated in teaching materials. Heavy bleeding with open os and products visible suggests incomplete abortion rather than ectopic pregnancy.
questions.question: A second-year student is asked to identify the MOST common presenting symptom that raises the suspicion of ectopic versus threatened abortion in a patient with a positive pregnancy test and vaginal bleeding. Which feature MOST strongly favours ectopic pregnancy?
options: Open cervical os with products visible
Unilateral adnexal tenderness with peritoneal signs

questions.question: Sterilization counselling should emphasize which of the following points ABOVE all others?
options: The procedure is most cost-effective after three children
The partner must provide written consent before the procedure
Sterilization eliminates menstrual periods in women
Vasectomy is medically safer than tubal ligation in all circumstances
Sterilization must be considered permanent and irreversible, and the decision must be freely made
questions.explanation: Pre-sterilization counselling must emphasize irreversibility as the central message. Although reversal procedures exist, they are expensive, technically demanding, and have unpredictable success rates. Decisions must be made without coercion, pressure, or dependency on a partner's consent (though partner discussion is encouraged). The counsellor must ensure the individual has no ambivalence about permanent contraception, particularly in younger patients.

questions.question: Postoperative wound dehiscence following gynaecological laparotomy is MOST strongly associated with which risk factor?
options: Use of absorbable suture material alone
Use of a transverse rather than midline incision
Poor nutritional status and wound infection
Short duration of the surgical procedure
questions.explanation: Wound dehiscence is strongly associated with factors that impair tissue healing, particularly malnutrition, infection, and increased intra-abdominal pressure, whereas surgical technique factors such as suture choice and incision type play a comparatively smaller role when these risk factors are well controlled.

questions.question: A couple has been trying for 2 years. The man's testicular examination reveals a soft left testicular swelling with a 'bag of worms' appearance on palpation in the standing position. Which clinical condition does this describe?
questions.explanation: Varicocele presents classically as a 'bag of worms' sensation in the scrotum due to dilated, tortuous veins of the pampiniform plexus, best felt with the patient standing (gravitational venous filling). It is more common on the left (>90%) due to the perpendicular insertion of the left testicular vein into the left renal vein, creating higher venous pressure. Varicocele is found in approximately 40% of infertile males.

options: Return for re-fitting as significant weight change may alter vaginal dimensions and the correct size
Discontinue diaphragm use as weight gain makes it ineffective
Continue using the same diaphragm as weight does not affect fit
Switch to a larger size using home measurement kits
Add extra spermicide to compensate for any fit change
questions.explanation: Significant weight change (gain or loss of more than 3–4 kg) can alter vaginal dimensions and the pubococcygeal measurement used to size a diaphragm. Re-fitting is recommended after significant weight change, delivery, abortion, pelvic surgery, and annually at routine check-ups. Using an incorrectly sized diaphragm (too small — dislodges; too large — uncomfortable and gaps) significantly increases failure risk.
questions.question: A 32-year-old woman using a diaphragm gains 8kg over 6 months. She should be advised to:

options: The white opaque colour of estrogenic mucus
The ferning pattern seen on dried mucus under microscopy
The quantity of mucus secreted per day during the fertile phase
The stretchability or thread-forming property of fertile cervical mucus, indicating high water content and sperm penetrability
The pH neutrality of periovulatory cervical secretions
questions.explanation: Spinnbarkeit (German: 'spinnability') is the property of peak fertile cervical mucus to form a long, thin, elastic thread when stretched between two surfaces. Periovulatory mucus under estrogen stimulation has high water content (>95%), low viscosity, and high elasticity — properties that facilitate sperm transport. Spinnbarkeit of 6 cm or more indicates peak fertility. Post-ovulatory progesterone converts mucus to thick, inelastic, impenetrable secretions.
questions.question: Spinnbarkeit refers to which characteristic of cervical mucus that indicates peak fertility?

options: Direct viral damage to the seminiferous tubules impairing spermatogenesis
Obstruction of the epididymis without testicular damage
Autoimmune destruction of Leydig cells only, sparing sperm production
questions.explanation: Mumps orchitis occurring after puberty can cause direct viral inflammatory damage to the seminiferous tubules where spermatogenesis occurs, potentially resulting in azoospermia if damage is severe and bilateral. This differs from prepubertal mumps infection, which less commonly affects fertility since spermatogenesis has not yet begun. Testicular biopsy and hormonal assessment help characterise the extent of damage in affected men.
questions.question: A man presents with infertility following mumps orchitis at age 19. Semen analysis shows azoospermia. What is the mechanism by which mumps orchitis in adulthood leads to this outcome?
A bicornuate uterus results from which embryological error?
options: Complete failure of Müllerian duct development
Partial Müllerian fusion failure with two uterine horns
Failure of canalization of the fused Müllerian ducts
Persistence of a midline septum within a normally fused uterus
questions.explanation: Bicornuate uterus occurs when the lower portions of the Müllerian ducts fuse incompletely, leaving two partially separated uterine horns sharing a common lower uterine segment and cervix. It differs from septate uterus (normal external outline, internal septum) and didelphys (two completely separate uteri, each with its own cervix). Bicornuate uterus is associated with recurrent miscarriage and preterm birth.

questions.question: In stress urinary incontinence, the predominant risk factors listed are obesity, childbirth, and gender. Which specific mechanism links childbirth to SUI?
options: Increased BMI postpartum causing intra-abdominal hypertension
Hormonal changes in the puerperium reducing sphincter tone
Retained products of conception compressing the bladder
Urethral hypermobility during abdominal pressure increase
questions.explanation: The pathophysiology of SUI involves urethral hypermobility, where the urethra is displaced during sudden increases in abdominal pressure (coughing, sneezing, lifting), decreasing pressure transmission to the urethra. Childbirth causes this by traumatising the pelvic floor muscles, connective tissue, and pudendal nerve innervation, impairing the normal mechanism that equalises pressure between the bladder and urethra during stress activities.

options: Reassurance and further evaluation only if bleeding persists or worsens
Insertion of a second device to control the bleeding
Immediate removal without any further discussion
questions.question: A woman with a well-positioned IUD and no current infection requests removal because of a single episode of intermenstrual spotting. The MOST appropriate initial approach is:
questions.explanation: A single episode of intermenstrual spotting in an otherwise asymptomatic woman with a correctly positioned IUD is common and usually self-limiting, so reassurance and counselling are appropriate initially, reserving further investigation or removal for persistent, worsening, or otherwise concerning bleeding patterns.

Advanced endometriosis can reduce ovarian reserve, particularly if endometriomas have previously been surgically excised, and distorted pelvic anatomy can complicate oocyte retrieval, while the inflammatory pelvic environment may also impair embryo implantation, together reducing overall IVF success rates compared with women without endometriosis. This informs counselling about realistic expectations and may influence decisions about surgical management before IVF. Individualised treatment planning is important given this variability in impact.
questions.question: A 29-year-old with stage IV endometriosis undergoing IVF is counselled about the impact of her disease on treatment. Which mechanism explains why advanced endometriosis can reduce IVF success rates?
options: Endometriosis only affects male partners' fertility
Endometriosis has no effect on fertility outcomes
Endometriosis always causes complete infertility making IVF pointless
Endometriosis improves implantation rates through inflammatory signalling
Reduced ovarian reserve and altered pelvic anatomy

questions.question: The etonogestrel subdermal implant is inserted into which anatomical layer of the upper arm?
questions.explanation: The etonogestrel implant is inserted just beneath the skin into the subdermal subcutaneous tissue of the inner upper arm using a specialised applicator, allowing sustained release of progestogen over its duration of action while remaining palpable for later removal.

options: The uterus is absent in MRKH  but also absent in CAIS
Secondary sexual characteristics are absent in MRKH but normal in CAIS
The ovaries are absent in MRKH but testes are present in CAIS
Pubic and axillary hair are absent in MRKH as in CAIS
questions.question: Congenital absence of the vagina (vaginal agenesis) associated with MRKH syndrome differs from absence of the vagina in testicular feminization (CAIS) in that in MRKH:
questions.explanation: In MRKH (46,XX, Müllerian agenesis), the uterus and upper vagina are absent because of failure of Müllerian duct development, while the ovaries are present and functional. In CAIS (46,XY), the uterus is absent because AMH produced by the testes caused Müllerian regression. In both conditions the uterus is absent; the key differences are karyotype (XX vs. XY), the gonads (ovaries vs. testes), and the presence of pubic/axillary hair (present in MRKH, absent in CAIS).

options: Only through the placenta during the second trimester
Exclusively through breastfeeding after 6 months of age
Transplacental, during labour and delivery, and through breastfeeding
Only through contaminated instruments during delivery
Airborne transmission in the delivery room from maternal blood droplets
questions.explanation: Mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV occurs through three routes: transplacentally during pregnancy (especially the third trimester), during labour and delivery when the infant is exposed to maternal blood and secretions, and postnatally through breastfeeding. Complete cART dramatically reduces all three routes. Breastfeeding is safe while on ART with undetectable viral load.
questions.question: Vertical transmission of HIV from mother to child can occur through which of the following routes?

options: Immediately remove the IUD without antibiotic treatment
Treat with antibiotics and remove the IUD only if there is no response within 72 hours
Admit for IV antibiotics; if clinical response occurs, the IUD can remain; remove only if no response
Continue IUD use and manage PID with outpatient oral antibiotics
Remove the IUD and withhold antibiotics awaiting culture results
