questions.question: A physiotherapist is about to apply phonophoresis drug-containing couplant to the treatment area. How should this be applied?
questions.explanation: The drug-containing phonophoresis couplant is applied to the treatment area using a spatula to ensure an even, adequate layer of gel or ointment that fills all surface contours and creates complete acoustic coupling between the transducer and skin. Using a spatula prevents contamination of the drug preparation and ensures consistent application thickness. The transducer is then moved through the drug medium throughout the treatment period.

questions.question: A patient receives UV therapy for psoriasis using coal tar application. Which treatment protocol specifically combines coal tar with UVB radiation?
questions.explanation: The Goeckerman regimen combines the application of coal tar preparations with UVB radiation to treat psoriasis, where coal tar acts as a photosensitiser enhancing the therapeutic effect of UVB on hyperproliferating keratinocytes. This regimen has been used for over a century and remains effective. The Ingram or Leeds protocol differs by using dithranol cream combined with UVB.

questions.question: A regulatory inspector reviews a facility's water-testing logbook. Bacteriological testing of pool water must be performed:
options: Never, if chlorine levels seem adequate
Only once when the pool first opens
Only after a visible outbreak occurs
At regular scheduled intervals, typically weekly or more often
questions.explanation: Bacteriological testing of pool water must be performed at regular scheduled intervals, typically weekly or more frequently, rather than only at opening or after a visible problem occurs. Regular testing allows early detection of contamination before it becomes a clinical risk. This routine monitoring is a cornerstone of pool safety management.

questions.question: A therapist wants to make a buoyancy-resisted shoulder exercise progressively harder over several weeks. Altering the weight arm length to progress this exercise involves:
options: Moving the resistance closer to the joint axis only
Switching the patient to a dry-land programme entirely
Moving the resistance further from the joint axis
questions.explanation: Moving the resistance further from the joint axis increases the weight arm length and therefore the resistance torque during a buoyancy-resisted exercise. This is distinct from changing chemical or environmental factors like pH or chlorine, which have no bearing on mechanical resistance. This biomechanical principle underlies progressive aquatic strength training.

options: Prone closed-chain squatting on pool floor
Vertical floating supported by a flotation belt
Standing under a UVR lamp near the pool
questions.question: A patient with a load-sensitive lumbar disc herniation wants pain relief through aquatic therapy. Which positioning is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Vertical floating with a flotation belt unloads the spinal intra-articular structures and relaxes the paraspinal muscles, benefiting load-sensitive disc conditions. Closed-chain squatting or rapid running would increase spinal loading, worsening symptoms. This targeted positioning uses buoyancy therapeutically for spinal unloading.

questions.question: A therapist attaches a flotation belt around a patient's waist for a standing exercise. This equipment shifts the centre of buoyancy:
questions.explanation: Adding a flotation belt around the waist shifts the centre of buoyancy toward the belt's location, since the float introduces a strong buoyant force at that point. This can be used deliberately to support or destabilize particular body segments. Understanding this helps therapists position equipment for specific therapeutic goals.
options: Below the centre of gravity always

questions.question: Rheumatoid arthritis presenting with multiple joint pain and whole-body burn injury are indications for which whirlpool type?
questions.explanation: The Hubbard tank allows full body immersion, making it suitable for conditions affecting multiple joints or extensive body surface areas such as widespread burns. Extremity and low boy tanks are limited to smaller body regions. Selection depends on the extent of the area requiring treatment.

options: Removing buoyancy completely at all depths
Adjusting water depth to control buoyant support
questions.explanation: Adjusting water depth allows the therapist to control the degree of buoyant support and therefore grade weight-bearing load gradually as a fracture heals. Standing in shallower water increases load, while deeper water reduces it. This adjustable progression is harder to replicate precisely with land-based methods alone.
questions.question: A patient with a healing lower-limb fracture is progressed from non-weight-bearing to partial weight-bearing more gradually in the pool than would be possible on land. This graded loading is made possible by:

questions.explanation: Ultrasound is contraindicated over an area within six months of radiotherapy because radiation has a devitalizing effect on tissue, increasing risk of complications. This precaution reflects the time needed for tissue recovery after radiotherapy. Screening treatment history is therefore part of ultrasound patient assessment.
questions.question: Ultrasound should not be applied over an irradiated area within how many months of radiotherapy?
A patient sensitive to aspirin is prescribed salicylate-containing phonophoresis. What specific adverse reaction risk must be communicated?
questions.explanation: Patients with aspirin sensitivity may develop allergic reactions to salicylate-containing phonophoresis preparations because acoustic-driven transdermal delivery introduces sufficient salicylate to trigger hypersensitivity responses including urticaria, bronchospasm, or anaphylaxis in sensitive individuals. Aspirin sensitivity must be screened for before prescribing any salicylate-based phonophoresis. Alternative anti-inflammatory preparations without salicylates should be substituted.

questions.question: A clinician explains why most people float fairly easily in water. This relates to the human body's specific gravity compared with water being approximately:
questions.explanation: The human body's specific gravity is slightly less than that of water, which explains why most people float relatively easily when relaxed. This differs markedly from denser materials like lead. This property underpins the buoyant support patients experience during aquatic therapy.

questions.question: Which factor is NOT among the primary determinants of UVR dose received by the skin according to standard technique?
questions.explanation: UVR dose depends on lamp output, distance, angle of incidence, and duration of exposure, all of which directly affect the quantity of energy delivered. Clothing colour outside the exposed field has no bearing on the dose received by exposed skin. Understanding these factors prevents accidental overdose.
options: Angle of radiation on the skin

questions.explanation: A suberythemal dose (75-85% of E1) is the appropriate UV dose for treating rickets because it stimulates adequate conversion of 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin to vitamin D3 without producing erythema or tissue damage. Erythema-producing doses are unnecessary and potentially harmful for this indication. Suberythemal doses for rickets are administered using general body irradiation techniques to maximise skin surface exposure.
questions.question: A patient with rickets is referred for UV therapy. Which erythema dose is administered to optimise vitamin D synthesis?
Which skin type classification, according to biological effects on skin used in PUVA dosing, always burns and never tans?
questions.explanation: Skin Type I always burns and never tans, appearing as the most UV-sensitive category among the classifications used for PUVA dosing. Type IV never burns and always tans, representing lower sensitivity. This classification guides individualized dosing to reduce burn risk.

Open or infected wounds are a contraindication to hydrotherapy due to infection transmission risk, so the therapist must verify wound status before pool immersion. Age, water temperature preference, and swimming ability are not the primary safety concern here. Wound assessment is a required step in the pre-treatment screening process.
questions.question: A patient with a healing pressure sore on the sacrum is also considered for hydrotherapy. What must the therapist verify first?
options: That the patient is under 30 years old
That the pool has a low boy tank
That the wound is not open or infected
That the patient can swim independently
No, only UVA can ever be used for vitiligo
Yes, UVB from the theraktin can be tried with a suberythemal dose
Yes, but only with double the psoralen dose
No, vitiligo cannot be treated with UVR at all
Yes, but only using the Kromayer lamp underwater
questions.question: A patient undergoing PUVA for vitiligo asks whether UVB alone can be used if UVA is unavailable. What is the correct response?
questions.explanation: If a UVA source is unavailable, UVB delivered via the theraktin tunnel can be successful for vitiligo, using a suberythemal dose tried once or twice weekly for six to eight weeks. This provides an alternative when UVA equipment is not accessible. Understanding treatment flexibility helps therapists adapt care to available resources.

Ai Chi, combining slow movement and deep breathing in chest-deep water, is indicated for patients with balance deficits or osteoporosis due to its gentle, controlled nature. Conditions like uncontrolled epilepsy or cardiac failure remain contraindications for most aquatic therapy. Appropriate patient selection ensures safe application.
questions.question: Ai Chi is particularly indicated for patients presenting with which condition?

options: Coal tar has no effect on UVR sensitivity
Coal tar cancels the need for further UVR
Coal tar always requires doubling the dose
Coal tar use is irrelevant to safety planning
Coal tar is a sensitizer that may require dose adjustment
questions.question: A patient completing UVR treatment for psoriasis also uses coal tar ointment at home. What should the therapist consider regarding future dosing?
questions.explanation: Coal tar is listed among substances that sensitize the skin to ultraviolet radiation, so its concurrent use should be considered when planning UVR dosing to avoid unexpected overreaction. This does not mean UVR should be automatically doubled or discontinued, but rather monitored carefully. Recognizing sensitizer use supports safe, individualized dose planning.

questions.question: How is the E3 dose calculated relative to the E1 dose in ultraviolet radiation therapy?
options: E1 multiplied by two and a half
questions.explanation: The E3 dose is calculated as E1 multiplied by five, producing a stronger erythemal reaction than E2, which is E1 multiplied by two and a half. E4, the strongest standard dose, is E1 multiplied by ten. This proportional scale allows graded dosing based on individual skin sensitivity.

Ultraviolet rays convert 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin into vitamin D, which is essential for calcium absorption and bone formation. Melanin instead relates to pigmentation, not vitamin D synthesis. This physiological effect underlies UVR's use in conditions like rickets.
questions.question: Vitamin D synthesis following UVR exposure results from the conversion of which skin compound?
What is the recommended air humidity level for a hydrotherapy pool area?
questions.explanation: A humidity level of approximately 55% is recommended for the pool area to maintain patient and staff comfort while limiting excessive moisture. Levels too low cause dryness, while levels too high promote mold and discomfort. This is monitored alongside air temperature control.

A whirlpool bath is fundamentally an agitated water treatment tank, distinct from static immersion tanks or dry heat chambers. The agitation provides both a mechanical and thermal therapeutic effect. Understanding this basic definition underlies appropriate clinical use of whirlpool equipment.
questions.question: A patient asks the therapist to explain, in basic terms, what a whirlpool bath actually is before starting treatment. A whirlpool bath is fundamentally:

options: Use of visible light instead of sound
Total lack of any frequency setting
Purpose of imaging versus tissue treatment
questions.explanation: Diagnostic ultrasound is used for imaging purposes, such as visualizing a fetus, while therapeutic ultrasound aims to produce physiological tissue effects for rehabilitation. Both use mechanical sound waves above the audible range, but their clinical applications differ substantially. This distinction clarifies why the same physical principle serves different clinical goals.
questions.question: Diagnostic ultrasound used to image a fetus during pregnancy differs from therapeutic ultrasound mainly in what aspect?
A physiotherapist explains transient cavitation to a student. What dangerous consequence distinguishes it from stable cavitation?
options: Transient cavitation causes local temperature spikes
questions.explanation: Transient cavitation involves the rapid and violent collapse of gas-filled microbubbles under intense acoustic pressure, generating extremely localised temperature spikes, shock waves, and free radical production that can cause significant tissue damage. This is distinct from stable cavitation where bubbles oscillate without collapsing. Transient cavitation is an undesirable and potentially harmful effect in therapeutic ultrasound and is avoided by using appropriate intensities and pulsed modes.

Aquatic therapy suits elderly patients particularly well because it combines reduced joint loading with a lower risk of injurious falls, allowing safer active movement than land-based exercise alone. This is not a claim that supervision becomes unnecessary or that it is limited to younger patients. This combination of safety and activity makes it well suited to frail older adults.
questions.question: A frail elderly patient with multiple joint problems is referred for an exercise programme that minimizes fall risk while still allowing active movement. Why is aquatic therapy particularly suitable for elderly patients?
options: It is more dangerous than land exercise for this group
It is suitable only for young athletic patients
It requires high-impact loading on every joint
It eliminates the need for any supervision
It combines reduced joint load with a lower risk of injurious falls

questions.explanation: Resistance in aquatic exercise is strongly influenced by the speed of limb movement through the water, with faster movement producing dramatically more resistance. This relationship allows therapists to grade intensity without needing extra equipment. It is a fundamental principle underlying water-based strength training.
questions.question: A therapist notices that moving a limb quickly through water dramatically increases the workload compared with a slow, controlled movement. This illustrates that, in aquatic exercise, resistance is strongly influenced by:

questions.explanation: The fluid-filled eye provides exceptional ultrasound transmission with minimal attenuation, allowing energy to concentrate in the intraocular structures and retina at potentially damaging intensity levels. This exceptional acoustic transparency means standard therapeutic intensities become hazardous within ocular tissue. Ultrasound must never be applied over the eyes, and careful shielding must prevent beam passage through ocular tissue during periorbital treatment.
options: The lens cannot regenerate UV damage
questions.question: A patient with fluid-filled eyes and a history of retinal detachment is referred for facial ultrasound. What specific danger applies?

questions.explanation: Wheelchair accessibility throughout rest, changing, and utility areas is essential to accommodate patients with disabilities using hydrotherapy services. Adequate privacy and security for valuables are also required. These facility standards support safe and dignified access to treatment.
questions.question: Which general facility feature is essential for a hydrotherapy department to accommodate patients with disabilities?
Continuous mode ultrasound is primarily selected to achieve which type of effect?
questions.explanation: Continuous mode ultrasound delivers energy throughout the treatment period, producing predominantly thermal effects useful for chronic conditions. Pulsed mode instead emphasizes non-thermal mechanical effects, more suitable for acute injuries. Selecting the correct mode depends on the stage and nature of the condition being treated.

questions.question: A patient presents for general UV irradiation of a large body area. At what standard distance should the lamp be positioned?
questions.explanation: For general UV irradiation of large body areas, the lamp is positioned at 100 cm from the skin surface, with the rays striking perpendicular to the skin at 90 degrees for maximum absorption. This greater distance compared to localised treatment allows uniform irradiation across a wider skin surface. The physiotherapist must then calculate the exposure time based on the test dose and this standard treatment distance.

Pulsed ultrasound with low spatial-averaged temporal peak intensity is preferred when the goal is to decrease inflammation, since continuous ultrasound at higher intensity may induce a proinflammatory response. This distinction guides mode selection based on treatment goals. Matching mode to desired biological effect optimizes phonophoresis outcomes.
questions.question: Which ultrasound mode is preferred in phonophoresis when the treatment goal is to decrease inflammation?
A physiotherapist is treating a patient with metal implants in the hip with ultrasound. What specific concern must be addressed?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound energy is partially reflected at the metal-tissue interface due to the large acoustic impedance mismatch, causing energy to accumulate at the implant surface. This reflection increases local energy intensity beyond safe thermal limits, risking periosteal burns and potential implant heating. Physiotherapists must exercise extreme caution or avoid direct ultrasound application over metal implants, particularly with continuous high-intensity modes.
options: Reflection increases energy at the interface

questions.question: The E1 dose in ultraviolet radiation therapy is defined by which characteristic response on the test dose cutouts?
questions.explanation: The E1 dose is identified as the cutout area where erythema appears last and disappears first, representing the mildest detectable reaction. This response is used as the baseline for calculating stronger doses such as E2 through E4. Accurate identification of E1 is essential for safe dose progression.
options: Appears immediately and persists a week

questions.explanation: Patients must avoid washing the UV-irradiated area after treatment to preserve the photochemical products and photosensitising reactions that continue to exert therapeutic effects in the skin following exposure. Washing removes these biologically active compounds before they are fully utilised. This is a consistent post-treatment instruction for all UV therapy applications regardless of the treated condition.
questions.question: A physiotherapist applies UV to a patient with deep acne scarring. After the session, what instruction should be given regarding the irradiated skin?
options: Apply ice pack to cool skin

questions.explanation: Pseudomonas folliculitis rash typically appears one to two days after exposure to contaminated water, reflecting the time needed for bacterial proliferation and immune response in the skin. This delayed onset is an important clue in outbreak investigations linked to hot tubs or pools. Recognising this timeline supports accurate clinical diagnosis.
questions.question: A group of swimmers develop a itchy, red, bumpy rash on the trunk a day or two after using a poorly maintained hot tub. This Pseudomonas folliculitis rash typically appears approximately:
options: Within minutes of leaving the water permanently

questions.question: A physiotherapist documents coupling agent details after ultrasound treatment. What specific coupling agent information must be recorded?
questions.explanation: Post-treatment documentation must include the type of coupling agent used during ultrasound or phonophoresis, as this information is essential for tracking allergic reactions, ensuring consistency between treatment sessions, and providing medicolegal accountability. In phonophoresis, the drug agent used is particularly important to document for medication record-keeping and adverse event reporting. Incomplete documentation compromises patient safety and professional standards.

questions.question: Which protective measure is essential for both patient and therapist during ultraviolet radiation treatment sessions?
options: Applying heavy oil to all skin
questions.explanation: Goggles must be worn by both patient and therapist during UVR treatment to protect the eyes from conjunctivitis or cataract risk associated with ultraviolet exposure. Only the area to be treated is exposed, with the rest of the body appropriately screened. This protective measure is standard practice across all UVR applications.

Moving closer to the lamp increases intensity received according to the inverse-square law, risking overdose and burns. This is precisely why patients are instructed to remain still throughout treatment. The therapist must reposition the patient and reassess the treatment distance immediately.
questions.question: A patient moves closer to the UVR lamp during treatment because they feel cold. What immediate risk does this pose?
options: No risk since distance does not affect dose
Automatic dose correction by the lamp
Overdose due to increased intensity at reduced distance
Improved uniformity of the dose received

questions.explanation: Because the Kromayer lamp is used in direct skin contact, much smaller cutout holes of about 0.25 cm by 0.25 cm with short exposure times are used, unlike the standard 2 cm by 2 cm holes for the air-cooled lamp or 4 cm by 4 cm for the theraktin tunnel. This size adjustment reflects the different intensity delivered by contact application. Correct technique selection prevents inaccurate dose calculation.
questions.question: A therapist is calculating the test dose using a Kromayer lamp, which requires contact with the skin. How should the cutout hole size differ from the standard air-cooled lamp method?
options: Identical hole sizes of 2 cm by 2 cm
Much smaller cutout holes of about 0.25 cm by 0.25 cm
Larger holes of 4 cm by 4 cm
No cutout holes are needed at all
Holes sized according to patient's age only

questions.explanation: Kromayer's lamp is water-cooled, absorbing harmful infrared rays through circulating distilled water, allowing safe direct contact with skin or body cavities. The high-pressure air-cooled lamp is used at a distance for general or group treatment instead. This design difference determines their respective clinical applications.
questions.question: Which mercury vapour lamp type is specifically designed for use in direct contact with body cavities?
In the paralytic stage of poliomyelitis, hot packs are used mainly to achieve what effect before movement?
questions.explanation: Hot packs applied during the paralytic stage relieve muscle spasm, preparing the muscles for subsequent passive movement. This is followed by passive movement rather than active exercise at this early stage. The goal is comfort and preparation, not increasing tone or restricting motion.

options: Decrease the water depth to ankle level only
Switch off the pool filtration system
Increase the lever arm length using equipment
Remove the patient from the water entirely
questions.question: A therapist progressing a buoyancy-resisted exercise wants to make the movement harder without changing the patient's position. One way to alter buoyancy effects to progress exercise is to:
questions.explanation: Increasing the lever arm length using equipment, such as moving a float further from the joint, is one way to progress a buoyancy-resisted exercise without changing the patient's overall position. This increases the resistance torque experienced at the joint. This principle allows fine control over exercise difficulty.

options: Lower and closely monitor pool water temperature
Ignore the report and continue as planned
questions.explanation: Patients with multiple sclerosis are heat intolerant and fatigue in water above 33 degrees Celsius, so temperature should be kept below this threshold and monitored closely. Increasing temperature would worsen fatigue, while permanent discontinuation is unnecessarily restrictive. Individualized temperature control allows safe continued participation.
questions.question: A patient with multiple sclerosis reports fatigue whenever pool sessions run above 33?C. What is the most appropriate therapist action?
Which factor primarily determines whether a patient should perform buoyancy-assisted rather than buoyancy-resisted pool exercises?
questions.explanation: Patients with muscle power below a fair grade, meaning they cannot move the limb fully against gravity, should perform buoyancy-assisted or buoyancy-supported exercises. Those with fair grade or above can perform buoyancy-resisted exercises for strengthening. This grading guides safe and effective exercise prescription in the pool.

options: Whirlpool warming and debridement followed by stretching exercises
Stretching first followed by cold whirlpool only
Simultaneous UVR and stretching without whirlpool
Whirlpool only, avoiding any stretching activity
questions.explanation: Whirlpool therapy warms tissue and assists debridement, creating favorable conditions for subsequent stretching exercises to improve joint mobility affected by burn-related stiffness. Reversing this order or omitting either component would reduce treatment effectiveness. This logical sequencing reflects the combined thermal and mechanical benefits of whirlpool before stretching.
questions.question: A patient recovering from a burn injury with associated joint stiffness is considered for combined whirlpool and stretching. What sequence best supports treatment goals?

questions.explanation: Acute and immediate post-traumatic conditions are treated cautiously with lower intensities of 0.1 to 0.25 W/cm2 to avoid exacerbating symptoms. Chronic conditions and scar tissue may tolerate higher intensities of 0.25 to 1 W/cm2. Matching intensity to injury stage reduces risk of adverse reactions.
questions.question: For acute or immediate post-traumatic conditions, which ultrasound intensity range is generally recommended?

questions.explanation: The human body has a specific gravity of about 0.974, slightly less than that of water, which is why the body generally floats. Objects with specific gravity below 1.0 float, while those above 1.0 sink. This underlies the buoyant support water provides during exercise.
questions.question: The specific gravity of the average human body is approximately what value, allowing it to float in water?

questions.explanation: The effective radiating area is the area of the crystal faceplate, which is typically smaller than the visible soundhead, and is essential for accurately calculating delivered intensity. This parameter directly affects dose calculations for treatment. Ignoring ERA can lead to inaccurate intensity settings.
questions.question: The effective radiating area of an ultrasound treatment head refers to what?
options: The entire surface of the treatment table
The size of the coupling gel container
The total room area used for treatment
The diameter of the patient's limb
The area of the crystal faceplate producing energy

questions.explanation: The ultrasound transducer should be moved at a rate of approximately 4 cm per second during direct contact application to ensure uniform energy distribution across the treatment area without allowing energy to concentrate in any single location. Moving too slowly risks focal overheating and standing wave formation, while moving too rapidly reduces the total energy delivered to each area. Consistent movement speed is a critical technical parameter for safe and effective ultrasound delivery.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is using ultrasound at 1 MHz on the quadriceps following knee surgery. At what rate should the transducer be moved to ensure safe and uniform energy delivery?
A patient recovering from a stroke has significant spasticity in the affected leg and needs PNF-based resisted strengthening in water. Which technique is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: The Bad Ragaz Ring method uses PNF-based patterns for therapist-assisted strengthening while the patient floats supported by rings, making it appropriate for neuromuscular strengthening in stroke rehabilitation. Watsu and Ai Chi are more passive or relaxation-focused. Matching technique to therapeutic goal ensures effective rehabilitation.

questions.question: Which aquatic method uses a structured ten-point program developed to teach swimming and balance to children with disabilities?
questions.explanation: The Halliwick method, developed by James McMillan, uses a sequential ten-point program encouraging active participation without floatation devices. It focuses on mental adjustment, balance, and rotation control. This differs from Watsu, which centers on passive relaxation and stretching by the therapist.

questions.question: A therapist is unsure whether to use 1 MHz or 3 MHz ultrasound for a patient with a superficial tendon lesion just under the skin. Which frequency is correct and why?
options: 1 MHz because it always penetrates deepest
3 MHz because it always penetrates deepest
3 MHz because it targets superficial tissue at 1 to 2 cm depth
1 MHz because frequency has no depth effect
Neither frequency is appropriate for tendons
questions.explanation: 3 MHz ultrasound is absorbed in more superficial tissues at depths of 1 to 2 cm, making it appropriate for a superficial tendon lesion, whereas 1 MHz targets deeper structures at 3 to 5 cm. Frequency selection directly relates to lesion depth. Correct frequency choice ensures the treatment energy reaches the intended tissue.

In the convalescent stage, passive movement is progressively replaced with active movement as sensitivity and spasm subside. This reflects a graded rehabilitation approach matching tissue tolerance. Complete discontinuation or surgical replacement is not part of this described progression.
questions.question: During the convalescent sensitive phase of poliomyelitis, which treatment progression typically occurs?
options: Active exercise changes to bed rest
Passive movement changes to active movement

questions.explanation: Ultrasound's thermal effect increases the extensibility of collagen, making stretching of scars and adhesions easier, a key therapeutic application for chronic indurated scar tissue. It does not remove scar tissue entirely or cause paralysis. This mechanism underlies ultrasound's use in scar and adhesion management.
questions.question: A therapist plans to treat a chronic indurated scar with ultrasound to improve extensibility. Which combined effect is being targeted?
options: Complete removal of the scar tissue

questions.question: A patient with osteoarthritis of multiple joints finds land-based exercise too painful to sustain regularly. What makes aquatic exercise particularly valuable for arthritic patients?
options: Aquatic exercise is identical to land exercise in every way
Reduced joint loading allows pain-free movement
Arthritic patients cannot exercise in water at all
questions.explanation: Aquatic exercise is particularly valuable for arthritic patients because reduced joint loading allows pain-free movement that may not be tolerable on land. This is a genuine biomechanical benefit rather than a permanent cure for the underlying disease. This makes water-based exercise a practical option for sustaining activity in arthritic patients.

questions.question: Which anti-inflammatory drug is widely used in phonophoresis, often at higher ointment concentration for effectiveness?
questions.explanation: Hydrocortisone is widely used in phonophoresis, with higher concentration ointments such as 10% found more effective than 1% when driven through the skin using ultrasound. Insulin, penicillin, and other drugs listed are not standard phonophoresis agents. This anti-inflammatory application targets localized musculoskeletal conditions.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the pool plant's circulating pump and filter system?
questions.explanation: The pool plant components, including the circulating pump and filters, work together to disinfect, filter, and recycle pool water continuously. This maintains water hygiene rather than serving any exercise or diagnostic function. Regular maintenance of these components is essential for patient safety.
options: To heat only the changing rooms
To generate underwater turbulence for exercise
To maintain clean, filtered, recycled water

questions.question: A therapist switches on the ultrasound treatment head before placing it in contact with the patient's skin. What is the primary risk of this error?
questions.explanation: Switching on the treatment head while not in contact with a transmitting medium risks reflecting the beam back into the head, potentially damaging the crystal through standing wave formation. The head should always be placed in contact with the patient or medium before activation. This is a fundamental safe-practice rule for ultrasound equipment.
options: Reflected energy could damage the transducer crystal
The machine will not turn on at all

questions.explanation: Patients unable to eat seafood typically have iodine allergy; therefore, iodine-containing phonophoresis coupling agents must be avoided as the acoustic-driven drug delivery could cause systemic allergic reactions including anaphylaxis. Alternative drug preparations without iodine must be substituted. A thorough allergy history including seafood and iodine sensitivity must be taken before phonophoresis with any potentially iodine-containing preparation.
options: Do not treat with iodine-based agents
questions.question: A patient who cannot eat seafood is scheduled for phonophoresis. What specific phonophoresis precaution applies to this patient?

questions.explanation: UV therapy produces a general sense of well-being in patients beyond its cutaneous therapeutic effects, attributed to endorphin release stimulated by UV exposure and the psychological benefits of skin improvement in conditions affecting self-image such as psoriasis and vitiligo. This psychological benefit is a documented secondary outcome of UV therapy courses. Physiotherapists should include it in patient education to enhance treatment engagement.
questions.question: A patient reports a general sense of well-being following a course of UV therapy. What psychological benefit of UV treatment does this represent?
A therapist has just completed ultrasound treatment and needs to prepare the equipment for the next patient. What is the correct final step?
questions.explanation: After treatment, the transducer should be cleaned of coupling medium and all controls returned to zero, ensuring hygiene and safe starting conditions for the next patient. Leaving settings active or skipping cleaning risks cross-contamination or accidental overdose. This standard closing procedure is part of safe ultrasound practice.
options: Leave all settings as used for convenience
Immediately begin the next patient without cleaning
Increase the intensity setting for the next patient
Store the transducer while still switched on
Clean the transducer and return all controls to zero

questions.explanation: Acute sepsis or spreading infection requires cautious modality selection, since both UVR and ultrasound carry specific infection-related contraindications or precautions that must be weighed against expected benefit. This clinical reasoning, not scheduling or unrelated factors, should guide the decision. Careful assessment of infection status is central to safe modality choice.
options: The colour of the patient's clothing
The distance from the treatment room door
The time of day the appointment occurs
Presence of acute spreading infection favoring cautious modality choice
questions.question: A therapist is choosing between UVR and ultrasound for an infected wound with surrounding cellulitis. Which factor most influences modality selection?
A patient has a muscle graded below fair strength and cannot yet move the limb fully against gravity on land. In the pool, this muscle should initially perform exercise of which type?
questions.explanation: A muscle graded below fair strength cannot move the limb fully against gravity on land, so in water it should begin with buoyancy-assisted exercise, where buoyancy supports rather than resists the movement. This allows safe, gravity-reduced practice for very weak muscles. Progression to resisted work occurs only once strength improves.

Courses of ultraviolet therapy should not exceed four weeks because prolonged exposure to UVB or UVC increases the risk of carcinogenesis by affecting DNA and cell replication. This time limit balances therapeutic benefit against long-term skin cancer risk. Monitoring cumulative exposure is essential in clinical practice.
questions.question: Prolonged ultraviolet therapy courses should generally not exceed which duration due to carcinogenesis risk?

questions.explanation: An oblique side-lying position at 45 degrees is recommended for treating sacral pressure sores with UV because it presents the wound surface perpendicular to the UV lamp beam for maximum absorption while avoiding pressure on the wound and maintaining patient comfort and dignity. Direct prone or supine positioning would either place pressure on the wound or fail to expose it optimally to the UV beam.
questions.question: A patient with a pressure sore on the sacral region is to be treated with UV. What patient positioning is recommended?

questions.explanation: A maximum duration of approximately 20 minutes is typically recommended for a paralysed patient's session in a large agitated treatment tub, balancing therapeutic benefit against fatigue and cardiovascular strain. Far longer durations risk overexertion in a vulnerable patient. This time limit reflects a key safety consideration in tub-based treatment.
questions.question: Facility protocols specify a time limit for a paralysed patient's session in the large agitated treatment tub. The maximum recommended duration in this tub is approximately:
A 3 MHz ultrasound frequency is most appropriate for treating tissue at which approximate depth?
questions.explanation: At 3 MHz, ultrasound energy is absorbed in more superficial tissues with penetration depth of about 1 to 2 cm, making it suitable for superficial structures. In contrast, 1 MHz penetrates to 3 to 5 cm for deeper tissue treatment. Frequency selection therefore depends on the depth of the target lesion.

The biomechanics of closed and open chain exercises differ in water because buoyancy changes the loading pattern, so what is closed-chain on land may become open-chain in deep water, as with running in a flotation vest. This requires the therapist to understand these biomechanical differences. Joint loading is reduced, not entirely eliminated.
questions.question: Closed-chain exercise in water differs from closed-chain exercise on land primarily because of what factor?

questions.explanation: PUVA therapy, combining the photoactive drug psoralen with UVA radiation, is the most successful treatment modality for vitiligo, stimulating melanocyte proliferation and migration into depigmented patches. The psoralen is taken orally two hours before UVA exposure to maximise photosensitisation. Standard UV sources without psoralen sensitisation achieve inferior repigmentation outcomes in vitiligo.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with vitiligo. Which UV modality has shown the greatest therapeutic success for this condition?

questions.explanation: Duration in the Hubbard tub should not exceed twenty minutes to prevent overheating or fatigue while still allowing effective exercise and pain relief. Longer durations risk cardiovascular strain, particularly in medically vulnerable patients. This time limit balances therapeutic benefit with safety.
questions.question: What is the recommended maximum duration a patient should remain in a Hubbard tub during polio treatment?

questions.explanation: Metal implants reflect ultrasound at their interfaces, potentially increasing energy absorption at that specific location, which requires caution during treatment planning near such areas. This differs from claims that implants have no effect or that ultrasound damages the implant itself. Awareness of this interaction guides safe intensity and technique selection near implants.
options: Reflection of ultrasound at the implant interface increasing local energy absorption
Metal implants have no effect on ultrasound at all
Implants eliminate the need for coupling medium
questions.question: A therapist notices a metal implant is present in the area a patient wants treated with ultrasound. What consideration is most relevant?
A duty cycle between 51% and 99% in pulsed ultrasound produces which relative effect?
questions.explanation: A duty cycle of 51% to 99% during pulsed ultrasound produces less acoustic energy and consequently less heat than continuous mode, favoring non-thermal mechanical effects. This differs from continuous mode, which maximizes thermal build-up. Selecting duty cycle allows the therapist to tailor thermal versus non-thermal emphasis.
options: Less acoustic energy and less heat
Delay treatment until cleared or wear special socks
Shorten the session to five minutes
questions.question: Tinea pedis requires which precaution before a patient enters the hydrotherapy pool?
questions.explanation: Tinea pedis, a fungal foot infection, requires delaying pool therapy until resolved or having the patient wear protective socks to prevent transmission. Simply adjusting temperature or chlorine levels does not address the contagion risk. This precaution protects both the patient and other pool users.

Rickets is a disease of disordered calcium metabolism in infants and young children, producing characteristic bone changes. UVR promotes vitamin D synthesis, which supports calcium absorption to address this deficiency. This distinguishes rickets from disorders of other mineral balances.
questions.question: Rickets is primarily a disorder of which mineral metabolism affecting bone development in children?
A physiotherapist treats a patient with chronic indurated oedema of the lower limb with ultrasound. What mechanical effect clears this condition?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound produces a mechanical clearing effect on chronic indurated oedema by using its pressure wave action to break down the protein-rich fibrous matrix that characterises long-standing tissue oedema, improving fluid mobility and reabsorption. This mechanical dispersal is enhanced by microstreaming effects around cells. The result is softening of indurated tissue, improvement in tissue mobility, and reduction in chronic lymphatic congestion.

questions.question: A therapist lowers a patient into the pool and asks them to predict what will happen to their limb. According to Archimedes' principle, the immersed limb will experience an upward force equal to the:
questions.explanation: Archimedes' principle states that an immersed body experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the water it displaces. This is distinct from the body's own total weight or the surrounding air pressure. Understanding this principle underlies how buoyancy assists or resists movement in pool exercise.

The inverse square law states that intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance; when distance is halved, intensity increases fourfold, so the required exposure time must be reduced to one quarter to deliver the same dose. This law is fundamental to UV dosimetry calculations. Failure to adjust exposure time when changing lamp distance risks delivering inadvertent overdose causing severe erythema or burns.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is calculating a new UV dose after halving the treatment distance. According to the inverse square law, what change occurs to the required exposure time?
Which drug class listed among UVR sensitizers includes agents such as Terramycin and Achromycin?
questions.explanation: Terramycin and Achromycin are examples of tetracycline antibiotics listed among substances that sensitize skin to ultraviolet radiation. Barbiturates and sulphonamides represent separate drug categories with their own listed examples. Identifying sensitizer use is part of the pre-treatment assessment for UVR therapy.

questions.question: Which of the following is a recognized contraindication to ultraviolet radiation therapy?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary tuberculosis is contraindicated for UVR because the treatment may exacerbate the condition by reducing resistance to microbial activity. Rickets, alopecia, psoriasis, and acne vulgaris are established indications for ultraviolet therapy instead. Correct screening prevents worsening of infectious respiratory disease.

questions.question: Which factor makes aquatic exercise particularly useful for rheumatoid arthritis management?
questions.explanation: Water's ability to retain heat combined with reduced joint loading makes it clinically useful for rheumatoid arthritis, promoting vasodilation, increased circulation, and improved range of motion. It does not cure the underlying autoimmune disease. This combination supports symptom management rather than disease modification.
options: Permanent cure of the underlying disease
Combination of heat retention and reduced joint loading

questions.question: A Theraktin tunnel is being set up for whole-body UV irradiation. How many fluorescent tubes are typically mounted in this device?
questions.explanation: The Theraktin tunnel contains four fluorescent UV tubes arranged around the treatment tunnel to provide circumferential irradiation of the patient positioned within it. This arrangement enables efficient whole-body UV treatment for conditions such as psoriasis and generalised skin disorders. The fluorescent tube design was specifically developed to eliminate short-wave UV production while delivering therapeutic UVB wavelengths.

questions.question: A patient with a varicose ulcer on the lower leg is treated with ultrasound. What is the primary mechanism promoting ulcer healing?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound promotes varicose ulcer healing primarily by enhancing granulation tissue formation and improving local circulation through its biological and mechanical effects on fibroblasts, macrophages, and microvascular endothelium. The combination of increased fibroblast activity and improved blood flow to the ischaemic wound bed accelerates tissue repair. Ultrasound also has mild bacteriostatic effects that support the healing environment.

questions.question: Which factor determines the appropriate ultrasound frequency selected for phonophoresis of a drug to a specific tissue depth?
questions.explanation: The depth of the target tissue determines the frequency selected for phonophoresis, since higher frequencies like 3 MHz favor superficial absorption while lower frequencies penetrate deeper. This mirrors general ultrasound frequency selection principles. Matching frequency to target depth maximizes drug delivery effectiveness.

questions.question: A therapist calculates the expected pressure at a patient's feet during standing immersion in a pool roughly 120 cm deep. The approximate pressure at this depth would be close to:
questions.explanation: Hydrostatic pressure increases by roughly 0.74 mmHg per centimetre of water depth, so a depth of about 120 cm produces a pressure close to 89 mmHg. This calculation allows therapists to estimate pressure effects at different body levels during standing immersion. Understanding this relationship supports clinical reasoning about treatment positioning.

options: Reduces fear of falling and supports movement
Is always faster than land therapy
Eliminates the need for any exercise repetition
Removes the need for any therapist supervision
questions.question: Many stroke patients report greater willingness to move and exercise in the pool compared with the same exercises attempted on land. This is largely because aquatic therapy:
questions.explanation: Many stroke patients are more willing to move in the pool because the supportive, buoyant environment reduces fear of falling compared with land-based practice. This increased confidence supports more active participation in therapy. The psychological as well as physical support of water contributes to this preference.

UVA (315-400 nm) penetrates the deepest of all UV components, reaching as far as the capillary loops in the upper dermis, which explains its greater ability to stimulate melanocytes, produce deep tanning, and contribute to photoageing and dermal collagen damage. UVB is largely absorbed in the epidermis, and UVC is almost entirely absorbed in the stratum corneum and superficial epidermis. Penetration depth determines both therapeutic applications and damage potential.
questions.question: A physiotherapist determines that UVB wavelengths penetrate to the level of capillary loops in the dermis. Which UV component penetrates to this dermal depth?

options: Double the usual UV dose prescribed
Monitor carefully for increased burning risk
Decrease the drug dosage before treatment
questions.explanation: Photosensitising medications including certain antibiotics, diuretics, and antifungals lower the erythema threshold, meaning a standard UV dose will produce a more intense or accelerated erythema response and increased burn risk. The physiotherapist must significantly reduce the UV dose and monitor the patient closely for exaggerated reactions. A modified test dose should be performed to determine the actual erythema threshold in these patients.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notes that a patient is taking photosensitising medication. What precaution must be specifically applied?

questions.explanation: Attenuation describes the gradual reduction in ultrasound beam intensity due to absorption, where tissue converts energy to heat, and scatter, where the beam is deflected by interfaces or bubbles. These two factors together explain declining intensity with tissue depth. This is distinct from hydrostatic or dermatological phenomena seen in other modalities.
questions.question: Attenuation of an ultrasound beam is primarily caused by which two factors?
A patient reports a history of taking deep X-ray therapy six months ago and is now referred for facial UVR. What should the therapist consider?
options: No relevance to current UVR treatment
Automatic approval since six months have passed
Increased skin hypersensitivity as a possible contraindication
Requirement to double the standard dose
Immediate discontinuation of all future care
questions.explanation: Patients who have had deep X-ray or cobalt therapy may have devitalized tissue and hypersensitive skin, making this a relevant contraindication or caution for subsequent UVR treatment regardless of the time elapsed. This history must be carefully considered during assessment rather than dismissed. Appropriate caution protects the patient from adverse skin reactions.

questions.question: Which distance from the skin is standard for general ultraviolet irradiation using the air-cooled lamp?
questions.explanation: The standard distance for general ultraviolet irradiation with the air-cooled lamp is 50 centimeters from the patient's skin surface. Deviating from this distance changes the dose received according to the inverse-square law. Accurate distance measurement is therefore critical for dose consistency.

options: E2 dose applied to floor only
No dose since UVR is contraindicated
questions.question: A patient with an infected open wound on the leg is scheduled for pressure sore management using UVR. Which dose is applied to the wound floor?
questions.explanation: The floor of a pressure sore or ulcer receives the E4 dose to promote debridement and destroy bacteria in infected wounds, while the wall receives E3 and the base receives E2. UVR is indicated, not contraindicated, for treating pressure sores and infected wounds through this graded dosing approach. Matching dose to tissue depth optimizes healing.

questions.question: The Bad Ragaz Ring Method is primarily based on which therapeutic approach?
questions.explanation: The Bad Ragaz Ring Method uses patterns derived from proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation to improve active and passive range of motion and neuromuscular function. The patient floats horizontally supported by rings while the therapist provides resistance. This distinguishes it from techniques like joint mobilization, which are manual, not aquatic-based.

questions.question: A patient with a healthy immune system develops diarrhoeal illness after pool exposure, later confirmed as cryptosporidiosis. In an immunocompetent patient, this illness typically lasts approximately:
questions.explanation: Cryptosporidiosis typically lasts one to two weeks in an immunocompetent patient, reflecting a self-limiting but uncomfortable gastrointestinal illness. This contrasts with much shorter or much longer durations seen with other conditions. Recognising this expected course helps guide patient counselling and recovery expectations.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is explaining UVB effects on the skin. By what factor can the stratum corneum increase in thickness following UV exposure?
questions.explanation: UV exposure can stimulate epidermal hyperplasia, causing the stratum corneum to increase in thickness up to five times its normal dimension as a photoprotective adaptive response. This thickening reduces UV penetration to deeper layers and represents the skin's natural adaptation to repeated UV exposure. It is the basis for the tanning and hardening effect seen with regular UV exposure and is exploited therapeutically in conditions requiring increased skin tolerance.

questions.question: Therapeutic ultrasound frequencies typically used in physiotherapy fall within which range?
questions.explanation: Therapeutic ultrasound in physiotherapy typically ranges from 0.5 to 5 MHz, well above the audible range of 20 to 20000 Hz that defines ordinary sound. This frequency range allows effective tissue penetration and heating. Selecting the frequency within this range depends on the target tissue depth.

options: Soft tissue warming and relaxation effects
Removal of all body weight effects
Increased friction against the pool floor
questions.explanation: Warm water promotes relaxation and soft tissue warming, along with ease of positioning, which improves tolerance to stretching compared to land-based stretching. It does not eliminate sensation or muscle tone entirely. These combined effects make aquatic stretching a valuable rehabilitation tool.
questions.question: Why might patients tolerate stretching exercises better in water than on land?
A patient with acne vulgaris is scheduled for UVR therapy focused on the nose. Which focusing point and distance combination is correct?
questions.explanation: Acne vulgaris treatment focuses on the tip of the nose at a distance of 18 inches using an E2 dose, following standard positioning protocols for this condition. Using an incorrect distance or dose could result in ineffective treatment or burns. Precise focusing point selection is part of standard acne UVR technique.
options: Tip of the nose at 18 inches with an E2 dose
Forehead at 50 cm with an E4 dose
Chin at 100 cm with a suberythemal dose
Cheek at 5 cm with an E1 dose
Nose at 90 cm with double E4 dose

questions.question: Which factor most directly determines the amount of pressure exerted on a submerged body part?
questions.explanation: Hydrostatic pressure increases proportionally with the depth of immersion due to the increasing weight of water above a given point. Floating devices affect buoyancy, not the underlying pressure relationship. This principle explains why deeper body parts experience greater compressive force.

questions.question: A patient lies supine while a therapist gently guides the hip into flexion, letting the limb float upward with minimal effort. This is best described as a buoyancy-assisted hip flexor exercise because the limb moves:
questions.explanation: A buoyancy-assisted hip flexor exercise is defined by the limb moving with the buoyant force, rising toward the water surface with minimal patient effort. This differs from buoyancy-resisted work, where the limb moves against the upward force. Recognising this distinction allows correct exercise selection for very weak muscles.
options: Only when fully out of the water
Only when resisted by a float
With the buoyant force, toward the surface

questions.explanation: Ai Chi is specifically performed standing in chest-deep water to combine partial buoyant support with deep breathing and slow movement while keeping the head above water for breath control. Full submersion would prevent the breathing component central to this method. This positioning is intentional and specific to Ai Chi's methodology.
questions.question: A patient asks why the therapist keeps them at chest depth during Ai Chi rather than fully submerged. What is the correct explanation?
options: Full submersion is required for all aquatic therapy
Chest-deep water allows standing breathing exercises with partial buoyant support
Chest depth prevents any buoyancy effect entirely
It has no effect on the exercise outcome
Deeper water always improves balance training

questions.explanation: Anaesthetic (sensory-deficient) skin is a contraindication for ultrasound because the patient cannot detect thermal pain that normally provides the physiotherapist with a safety signal indicating that tissue temperature is reaching dangerous levels. This eliminates a critical protective feedback mechanism, making inadvertent thermal burns possible without patient warning. The physiotherapist must use objective temperature monitoring or avoid treatment in areas of established sensory loss.
questions.question: A patient with an anesthetic lower limb requires ultrasound treatment. Why is sensory impairment a contraindication?
options: Equipment is likely to be damaged
Cannot detect pain or excessive heat

questions.question: Which patient population is specifically noted to be heat intolerant during hydrotherapy above 33?C?
questions.explanation: Patients with multiple sclerosis are heat intolerant and may fatigue when immersed in water above 33 degrees Celsius, so pool temperature must be carefully controlled for this group. Other listed conditions do not carry this specific thermal sensitivity. This precaution guides individualized dosing of water temperature.

The Bad Ragaz Ring Method is based on using fixed support points, often at the pool wall, combined with the therapist guiding the patient through resisted, rhythmic patterns. This differs from methods centred on relaxation or independent swimming skill development. It is widely used for proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation-based strengthening.
questions.question: A therapist uses fixed support points at the pool wall along with rhythmic patterns of resisted movement to retrain trunk and limb stability. This describes the basis of the:

questions.explanation: The Leeds or Ingram regimen for psoriasis uses dithranol cream, which inhibits DNA synthesis in the abnormally hyperproliferating keratinocytes of psoriatic plaques, combined with UVB irradiation. Dithranol's antiproliferative mechanism complements the UVB-induced apoptosis of activated T-cells driving psoriatic inflammation. This combination produces superior plaque clearance compared to either modality alone.
questions.question: A patient with psoriasis is being treated with the Ingram protocol. Which active agent is applied to inhibit DNA synthesis in hyperproliferative keratinocytes?

options: A reason to increase water temperature further
questions.explanation: Severe, unstable heart failure is generally considered a contraindication to aquatic therapy because of the cardiovascular demands placed on the body by immersion. This differs from milder, well-controlled cardiac conditions, which may only require precautions. Recognising contraindications protects patients from significant clinical risk.
questions.question: A patient with severe unstable heart failure is referred for pool therapy. This condition is best classified in relation to aquatic therapy as:
A therapist wants to progress a patient's buoyancy-resisted shoulder abduction exercise in the pool. Which modification best achieves this?
questions.explanation: Progressing buoyancy-resisted exercise involves increasing the weight arm length or adding floats, both of which increase resistive torque against the moving limb. Decreasing speed would reduce, not increase, resistance. This systematic progression allows controlled strengthening as tolerance improves.
options: Increase the lever arm length or add a float
Move the exercise to shallow water only
Shorten the lever arm without floats

questions.question: A post-fracture patient needs graded weight bearing during aquatic rehabilitation. How can the therapist best control the load on the healing limb?
options: Vary the depth of water immersion
Add extra chlorine to the water
Use a louder background sound system
questions.explanation: Weight bearing can be graded by varying immersion depth, since deeper water increases buoyant support and reduces load on the limb. Shallower water increases the proportion of body weight borne. This method provides a controlled way to progress loading during fracture rehabilitation.

questions.question: A patient with epilepsy is referred for electrophysical agent therapy. Why is this condition listed as a precautionary contraindication?
options: Sensory stimulation may trigger seizure episodes
questions.explanation: Epilepsy is listed as a precautionary contraindication for certain electrophysical agents because sensory stimulation, electrical currents, or light flicker from some devices may trigger seizure activity in susceptible patients. The physiotherapist must assess seizure type, frequency, and triggers before treatment, ensure appropriate safety measures are in place, and have a clear seizure management protocol. Not all modalities carry equal risk, and individual risk assessment is required.

questions.question: In hydrotherapy, movement of water molecules that remain parallel to one another during slow flow is termed what?
questions.explanation: Laminar flow describes fluid movement where molecules travel in parallel layers, typically occurring at slower speeds. Turbulent flow occurs when molecules move irregularly, usually at higher speeds, increasing resistance. Understanding this distinction helps therapists grade exercise intensity in the pool.

questions.question: A patient asks why their psoriasis treatment dose is being increased by 25% each session using E1. What should the therapist explain?
questions.explanation: E1 dosing progression follows a standard rate of increasing the previous dose by 25% per session, distinct from suberythemal progression at 12.5% or E3 progression at 75%. This systematic increase accounts for the skin's adaptive thickening response to prevent overdose. Explaining the rationale reassures the patient this progression is deliberate and evidence based.
options: Doses never increase once treatment starts
This is an error and should be corrected
E1 doses always double every session
This reflects the standard progression rate for E1 dosing
Progression rate has no clinical basis
Reduced joint loading and warmth-related pain relief
questions.question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis reports significantly less joint pain during pool-based exercise than during equivalent land exercise. Water benefits rheumatoid arthritis treatment mainly through:
questions.explanation: Water benefits rheumatoid arthritis treatment mainly through reduced joint loading combined with warmth-related pain relief and muscle relaxation. This is far more clinically meaningful than claims of curing the disease or fusing joints. These combined effects make aquatic exercise a valuable option for arthritic patients.

questions.question: Which type of rickets results from defects in renal function typically seen in children above five years?
questions.explanation: Renal rickets results from defects in renal function affecting calcium metabolism, typically occurring in children above five years old. Nutritional rickets instead results from dietary deficiency in children under four years. Celiac rickets is due to malabsorption in intestinal disease, a distinct mechanism.

questions.question: A therapist is selecting a whirlpool tank for a patient with a whole-body burn injury requiring full immersion. Which tank should be selected?
questions.explanation: The Hubbard tank permits full body immersion, making it appropriate for whole-body burn injury requiring extensive treatment area coverage. Extremity, low boy, and high boy tanks are limited to smaller body regions. Selecting the correct tank size ensures the entire affected area receives treatment.

questions.question: Which application method is preferred for treating irregularly shaped areas like the hand or foot with ultrasound?
questions.explanation: The water bath method immerses the irregular body part in water, allowing the treatment head to be held close without requiring perfect skin contact, ideal for joints of the hand, wrist, foot, and ankle. Direct contact with cream is used mainly for regular surfaces. This method accommodates anatomical irregularity effectively.

questions.question: A therapist has calculated a patient's E1 as 90 seconds. What is the calculated E3 dose for this patient?
questions.explanation: E3 is calculated as E1 multiplied by five, so 90 seconds multiplied by five equals 450 seconds. E2 would instead be E1 multiplied by two and a half, giving 225 seconds. Accurate calculation prevents accidental overdose or underdose during subsequent treatments.

questions.question: A patient's feet immersed under water experience pressure that increases with depth mainly because of which principle?
questions.explanation: Hydrostatic pressure is the pressure exerted by a fluid at rest, increasing proportionally with depth due to the weight of fluid above. It differs from buoyancy, which is an upward force rather than a depth-dependent pressure. This principle governs why deeper immersion increases pressure on tissues.

questions.question: Which erythema dose level produces painful blisters and thick sheet-like desquamation lasting about a week?
questions.explanation: The E4 dose produces an angry red appearance with painful blisters and thick sheet-like desquamation lasting around a week, representing the strongest standard erythemal dose. E1 produces only mild pinkness with no discomfort. This dose is typically reserved for open wounds where epidermal thickening is not a concern.

Warmth from pool immersion reduces muscle tone and guarding, which explains the subjective looser feeling reported after time in a warm pool. This is a temporary physiological response rather than a permanent structural change. Recognising this effect supports appropriate use of warm water for tightness and spasm management.
questions.question: A patient with chronically tight hamstrings reports feeling noticeably looser after ten minutes in a warm pool. The musculoskeletal effect responsible for this is:
options: Warmth-induced reduction in muscle tone and guarding
Permanent shortening of the muscle fibres

questions.explanation: The ultrasound treatment head should be tested before patient treatment by placing it in water and observing the rippling and agitation of the water surface, confirming that the transducer is producing sound energy. If no water movement is observed, the equipment is faulty and must not be used. This simple test confirms transducer function without exposing the therapist or patient to uncertain energy output.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is testing the ultrasound equipment before patient treatment. What is the correct testing method?
options: Place head underwater and observe ripples
Apply to the therapist's own hand

questions.explanation: The water bath method is appropriate for irregularly shaped or tender areas like the ankle, allowing the treatment head to be held near the skin without direct pressure. Direct contact would be uncomfortable and difficult to maintain evenly on irregular surfaces. This method ensures effective energy transfer while minimizing patient discomfort.
questions.question: A therapist is treating a patient's irregularly shaped ankle joint where direct contact is uncomfortable due to tenderness. Which application method should be used?

questions.explanation: During the sensitive, tender phase of early convalescent poliomyelitis, treatment should focus on gentle, pain-free positioning and support rather than vigorous stretching or resistance. Aggressive intervention at this stage risks further tissue damage and pain. A cautious approach protects recovering tissue during this vulnerable period.
questions.question: During the early convalescent stage of poliomyelitis, a child's limbs are extremely tender to touch and movement. The appropriate treatment focus during this sensitive phase is:

options: Distance from the electrical power source
Colour of the coupling gel used
Wave interference patterns close to the transducer
questions.question: Which factor primarily determines the near field, or Fresnel zone, characteristics of an ultrasound beam?
questions.explanation: The near field, or Fresnel zone, is characterized by irregular wave interference patterns close to the transducer face, where some waves cancel and others reinforce. Beyond this lies the distant field, or Fraunhofer zone, with more uniform beam characteristics. Understanding these zones helps explain variable heating patterns near the treatment head.

The Burdenko method, developed by Dr Igor Burdenko, is a complete system combining both water and land exercises to improve balance, coordination, flexibility, speed, and strength. It does not incorporate ultraviolet or ultrasound modalities. This dual environment approach differentiates it from purely aquatic methods.
questions.question: The Burdenko method combines which two environments in its rehabilitation approach?

questions.explanation: The choice of buoyancy exercise type, whether assisted, supported, or resisted, should be based primarily on the patient's current muscle grade rather than unrelated factors. Matching exercise type to strength level ensures safe and effective progression. This individualized approach underlies sound aquatic exercise prescription.
questions.question: A therapist deciding which buoyancy exercise type to prescribe for a given patient bases this choice primarily on the patient's:

options: Excess buoyancy at the wound site
questions.explanation: Open wounds and active skin infections are contraindicated for pool entry mainly due to the risk of spreading infection to the patient and other pool users. This is unrelated to any benefit from chlorine exposure. Protecting wound integrity and pool hygiene both depend on respecting this contraindication.
questions.question: A patient with a fresh, unhealed surgical wound asks why they cannot start pool therapy yet. Open wounds and active skin infections are contraindicated for pool entry mainly because of the risk of:

options: Proceed using continuous mode at high intensity
Apply ultrasound directly over the affected vein
Avoid ultrasound due to embolism risk
Increase intensity to relieve tightness faster
questions.explanation: Thrombophlebitis is a contraindication to ultrasound because insonation may dislodge emboli from the affected vessel, posing serious medical risk. The therapist should avoid treatment and refer for medical assessment instead. Recognizing vascular contraindications is essential before proceeding with ultrasound therapy.
questions.question: A patient with thrombophlebitis in the calf requests ultrasound therapy for calf tightness. What should the therapist do?

questions.question:
Answer the following on the structure and function of the heart:
1. Describe the functions of the heart under these headings: wall layers and pericardium, chambers and valves, pathway of blood, coronary circulation and cardiac muscle properties.
2. State how its components relate to common pathologies of excess and deficiency (valve disease, coronary artery disease, congenital defects).
3. Explain why heart failure may affect distant organs and cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• The heart is a hollow muscular four-chamber pump; the right side receives deoxygenated blood at low pressure and pumps it to the lungs, and the left receives oxygenated blood and pumps it at high pressure around the body.
• Wall: epicardium (serous covering), myocardium (contracts) and endocardium (lining); the double-walled pericardium (fibrous and serous, with parietal and visceral layers around a fluid-filled cavity) protects and anchors the heart, prevents overfilling and allows friction-free work.
• Valves: the tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral and aortic valves are one-way gates; AV valves are anchored by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles.
• Pathway: right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, pulmonary arteries, lungs, pulmonary veins, left atrium, bicuspid valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta.
• The left ventricular wall is thickest to supply the systemic circulation; coronary arteries supply the heart muscle with collateral routes.
• Cardiac muscle is striated and branched with intercalated discs, a functional syncytium with a long refractory period (250 ms).
2. Pathologies:
• Valve disease: regurgitation (leakage) or stenosis (narrowing); mitral valve prolapse.
• Coronary artery disease: insufficient blood supply from atherosclerosis, artery spasm or clot; myocardial infarction is death of heart muscle from lack of oxygen, replaced by scar tissue; angina pectoris is heart pain from ischaemia; treatment includes clot-dissolving drugs (streptokinase, t-PA, heparin), angioplasty and bypass graft.
• Congenital defects: atrial septal defect and ventricular septal defect; the fetal foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus bypass the pulmonary circulation.
3. Distant effects:
• Left-sided failure: blood backs up into the lungs as pulmonary oedema, with suffocation and lack of oxygen to the tissues.
• Right-sided failure: fluid builds up in tissues as peripheral oedema.
• Causes of CHF include coronary artery disease, hypertension, myocardial infarction, valve disorders and congenital defects.

1. Haemostasis:
• Definition: if a blood vessel wall breaks, a series of reactions is set in motion to accomplish haemostasis, the stoppage of bleeding; the response is fast, localized and carefully controlled, and involves clotting factors in plasma plus substances released by platelets and injured tissue cells.
• Vascular spasm: the damaged vessel constricts (vasoconstriction), reducing blood loss; triggers are direct injury to vascular smooth muscle, chemicals released by endothelial cells and platelets, and reflexes from local pain receptors.
• Platelet plug formation: intact endothelium releases nitric oxide and prostacyclin (PGI2), which prevent platelet aggregation in undamaged tissue; when the endothelium is damaged and collagen is exposed, platelets adhere to the collagen, stabilised by von Willebrand factor; platelets swell, form spiked processes, become stickier and release ADP (a potent aggregating agent), serotonin and thromboxane A2 (enhance vascular spasm and aggregation) in a positive feedback cycle; a plug is built within one minute but is loosely knit, so larger breaks need reinforcement.
• Coagulation: fibrin threads reinforce the platelet plug (the thrombin system forms fibrin, the "red clot", while the platelet plug is the "white clot"); blood changes from liquid to gel through clotting factors (procoagulants), most of them plasma proteins made by the liver, numbered I to XIII in order of discovery, all (except tissue factor) circulating in inactive form; vitamin K is required for the synthesis of four of the clotting factors.
• Phase 1: the intrinsic or extrinsic pathway converges on factor X, which with calcium ions, PF3 (platelet phosphatidylserine) and factor V forms prothrombin activator (usually the slowest step; once present the clot forms in 10 to 15 seconds).
• Phase 2: prothrombin activator converts prothrombin to the enzyme thrombin.
• Phase 3: thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen to fibrin, which polymerises into insoluble strands; with calcium ions thrombin activates factor XIII (fibrin stabilizing factor), which cross-links the fibrin into a mesh; clot formation is normally complete within 3 to 6 minutes.
• Clot retraction and repair: within 30 to 60 minutes platelets, which contain actin and myosin, contract, squeezing out serum and drawing the vessel edges together; platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) stimulates smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts to divide and rebuild the wall, and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) stimulates endothelial cells to restore the lining.
• Fibrinolysis: plasmin, produced when plasminogen is activated (tissue plasminogen activator from endothelial cells, activated factor XII and thrombin), digests fibrin; it begins within two days and continues over several days; without it vessels would gradually block.
• Limiting clot growth: swift removal of clotting factors and inhibition of activated clotting factors; heparin (from basophil and mast cell granules and found on endothelial cells) enhances antithrombin III, which inhibits thrombin and factors IXa, Xa, XIa and XIIa; other thrombin inhibitors are alpha2-macroglobulin, heparin cofactor II and alpha1-antitrypsin.
2. Basis of thromboembolic disorders:
• A thrombus is a clot that develops and persists in an unbroken vessel; if it breaks away and floats it is an embolus, which becomes an embolism when it lodges in a vessel too narrow to pass (pulmonary embolism impairs oxygen uptake; cerebral embolism may cause a stroke; coronary thrombosis may kill heart muscle).
• Conditions that roughen the vessel endothelium (atherosclerosis, inflammation) allow platelets to gain a foothold.
• Slowly flowing blood or stasis (bedridden patients, long economy-class flights) means clotting factors are not washed away and accumulate until a clot forms.
