• Aspirin is an antiprostaglandin drug that inhibits thromboxane A2 formation, blocking platelet aggregation and plug formation; heparin binds antithrombin and enhances its inhibition of thrombin (IIa), Xa and IXa and is the anticoagulant most used in hospital; warfarin, taken orally, interferes with the action of vitamin K in the production of some procoagulants.
3. Intrinsic versus extrinsic pathway:
• Intrinsic: triggered by negatively charged surfaces such as activated platelets, collagen or glass (so it can clot blood in a test tube); called intrinsic because the factors are within the blood; slower because it has many intermediate steps; requires factors VIII, IX, X, XI, XII, prekallikrein, high-molecular-weight kininogen, calcium and platelet phospholipids.
• Extrinsic: triggered by tissue factor (TF, factor III) from beneath damaged endothelium, which is outside the blood; faster because it bypasses several intrinsic steps (clot in about 15 seconds in severe trauma); the TF-VIIa complex is a principal step.
• The two meet at the activation of factor X to Xa.
questions.question:
Answer the following on haemostasis and blood clotting:
1. Describe the process of haemostasis under these headings: definition, vascular spasm, platelet plug formation, coagulation (intrinsic pathway, extrinsic pathway, common pathway, role of clotting factors), clot retraction and repair, fibrinolysis, and the factors limiting clot growth.
2. Explain the physiological basis of thromboembolic disorders: why undesirable intravascular clotting is commoner or more dangerous in certain states, and how aspirin, heparin and warfarin prevent it.
3. Distinguish between the intrinsic and the extrinsic pathways of coagulation.

questions.answerText:
1. Functions of leucocytes:
• Production (leukopoiesis) is stimulated by glycoprotein messengers, the interleukins and colony-stimulating factors (CSFs); WBCs average 5,000 to 10,000 per mm3.
• Neutrophils (40 to 70% of WBCs, 2 to 6 lobes): phagocytosis, degranulation and neutrophil extracellular traps; they release lysozyme, oxidants and defensins, congregate at infection sites and amplify inflammation through cytokines.
• Eosinophils (2 to 3%): release histaminase, phagocytose antigen-antibody complexes, act against parasitic worms and help break apart clots.
• Basophils (0.5 to 1%): become mast cells that liberate heparin, histamine and serotonin; they intensify inflammation and mediate hypersensitivity.
• Lymphocytes: smallest WBCs (8 to 10 micrometre); T cells, B cells and NK cells; B cells release antibodies, cytotoxic T cells release cytotoxic granules, helper T cells signal other cells, and memory cells respond to the same antigen later.
• Monocytes (3 to 8%, largest WBC): reach infection later than neutrophils but in larger numbers and differentiate into macrophages.
• Innate immunity is non-specific (barriers, chemicals, phagocytes); acquired immunity is specific, adaptive and has memory.
2. Excess and deficiency:
• Leukocytosis is an increase in WBC number; leukopenia is a count below 5,000/mm3.
• High neutrophils: bacterial infection, burns, stress, inflammation; low: radiation, chemotherapy drugs, vitamin B12 deficiency, systemic lupus erythematosus.
• High eosinophils: allergic reactions, parasitic infection, autoimmune disease, adrenal insufficiency; low: certain drugs, stress, Cushing's syndrome.
• Basophils rise with stress and allergies; high monocytes: viral or fungal infection, tuberculosis, some leukaemias, chronic disease; a low monocyte count rarely occurs.
3. Distant effects:
• Eosinophil changes point to the adrenal glands (adrenal insufficiency or Cushing's syndrome).
• Neutrophil changes may reflect vitamin B12 deficiency, radiation, drugs or systemic disease.
• Basophil-mediated hypersensitivity may appear as anaphylaxis, asthma, atopic dermatitis and hay fever.
• WBCs live in blood, skin and mucosa of the respiratory tract and circulate to lymphoid organs, so their changes signal disease at these distant sites.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the white blood cells:
1. Describe the functions of the leucocytes under these headings: production and its regulation, granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils), agranulocytes (lymphocytes, monocytes), and innate and acquired immunity.
2. State how the counts of each cell type relate to pathologies of excess and deficiency (leukocytosis, leukopenia and the raised or lowered counts of each type).
3. Explain why a disturbance of white cell counts may reflect disease in a distant organ or system.

Answer the following on the nerve impulse:
1. Describe the nerve impulse under these headings: resting potential and how it is maintained, the action potential and its ionic basis, threshold and the all-or-none law, propagation, refractory periods and conduction velocity.
2. Explain why the refractory period is physiologically important and why conduction is faster in some fibres.
3. Distinguish between the absolute and relative refractory periods, and between conduction in myelinated and unmyelinated fibres.
questions.answerText:
1. Nerve impulse:
• Resting potential: the inside of the neurone is negative, about -70 mV (range -50 to -90 mV), maintained by the Na+/K+ ATPase pump (3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in) and by many more K+ channels than Na+ channels.
• Action potential: stimulation (mechanical, chemical, thermal or electrical) makes the membrane suddenly permeable to Na+, which rushes in, causing further depolarisation (positive feedback) to about +40 mV; permeability to Na+ then falls and K+ moves out slowly until repolarisation to -70 mV within about 2 ms.
• Threshold: the minimum stimulus, generally 5 to 15 mV less negative than resting potential, opens all voltage-gated Na+ channels; the all-or-none law means the amplitude does not change with stimulus size or distance, only frequency changes.
• Propagation: local circuits at the leading edge excite the next part of the axon.
• Conduction velocity: 1 to 120 m/s, increasing with fibre diameter, temperature and the presence of myelin.
2. Importance:
• The refractory period ensures impulses flow in only one direction because the region behind cannot be depolarised, and limits the frequency of impulses.
• Myelin acts as an insulator so action potentials occur only at nodes of Ranvier, giving saltatory conduction.
3. Distinctions:
• Absolute refractory period: about 1 ms during which no impulse can be propagated however intense the stimulus; relative refractory period: about 5 ms during which a new impulse needs a stimulus more intense than normal threshold.
• Myelinated fibres conduct much faster by jumping from node to node; unmyelinated fibres conduct more slowly (for example C fibres at 0.5 to 2 m/s versus A-delta at 12 to 30 m/s).

questions.question:
Answer the following on the anterolateral pathway and pain:
1. Describe the anterolateral pathway as a control system: receptors, fibre types, dorsal horn, tracts, brainstem and thalamic relays and cortical interpretation, for fast and slow pain and for thermal sensation.
2. State the fibre conduction values and the stimuli that raise pain, the causes of visceral pain, and the compensatory analgesia system.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the signs and symptoms of damage (thalamic syndrome, hyperalgesia and Brown-Sequard syndrome).
questions.answerText:
1. Pathway:
• It transmits pain, heat, cold, crude touch, tickle, itch and sexual sensations; pain is a protective mechanism.
• Receptors are free nerve endings in skin, periosteum, arterial walls, joint surfaces and the falx and tentorium; fast pain (sharp, pricking) is carried by A-delta fibres, which secrete glutamate and end in laminae I and V; slow pain (aching, throbbing) is carried by C fibres, which secrete substance P and end in laminae I and II; both end in the dorsal horn, which acts as a gate.
• Fibres originate mainly in laminae I, IV, V and VI, cross in the anterior commissure, and ascend as the anterior and lateral spinothalamic tracts (fast), the spinoreticular pathway (slow) and the spinotectal tract.
• Fast fibres end in brainstem reticular nuclei and the ventrobasal complex; slow fibres end in the reticular nuclei of the medulla, pons and mesencephalon, the tectal area and the periaqueductal grey.
• Thermal: cold receptors use A-delta fibres and warm receptors use C fibres, travelling in the tract of Lissauer to laminae I to III, crossing and ascending in the pathway.
2. Values and modifiers:
• A-delta fibres 2 to 5 micrometre, 12 to 30 m/s; C fibres 0.4 to 1.2 micrometre, 0.5 to 2 m/s; the pathway conducts at 8 to 40 m/s, with poor localisation and gradation compared with the dorsal column pathway.
• Chemicals that raise slow pain: bradykinin, serotonin, histamine, K+, acetylcholine and substance P; visceral pain follows ischaemia, spasm, distension of a hollow viscus and stretching of ligaments, carried by C fibres.
• Compensation: the analgesia system of the brain and spinal cord suppresses pain input.
3. Damage:
• Thalamic syndrome: loss of pain from the opposite side, ataxia and enhanced pain sensitivity.
• Primary hyperalgesia is excessive sensitivity of nociceptors (for example histamine release after a heat burn); secondary hyperalgesia follows a lesion in the spinal cord or thalamus.
• Brown-Sequard syndrome: pain, heat and cold are lost on the opposite side, 2 to 6 segments below the transection.

1. Visual pathway:
• Retina: pigment layer, rods and cones, bipolar cells (excitatory or inhibitory), horizontal cells (inhibitory, lateral inhibition to enhance contrast), amacrine cells and ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve.
• After leaving the retinas impulses pass through the optic nerves; at the optic chiasm fibres from the nasal halves of the retinas cross and join the temporal fibres of the other eye to form the optic tract.
• Fibres of each tract synapse in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (six layers: P ganglion cells project to layers 3 to 6 and M ganglion cells to layers 1 and 2), and the geniculocalcarine fibres pass by the optic radiation to the primary visual cortex of the occipital lobe, with onward transmission to secondary visual areas.
• Other projections: fibres go from the optic tracts to the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus to control circadian rhythm.
2. Values and adaptation:
• About 6 million cones and 120 million rods supply 1.2 million optic nerve fibres (convergence about 105:1).
• Visual acuity is tested with the Snellen chart at 20 ft (6 m); normal is 20/20, 20/15 is better than normal and 20/100 is subnormal.
• Dark adaptation is an increase in retinal sensitivity on moving to dim light, maximal in about 20 minutes, cones adapting first and rods later; retinal, opsins and vitamin A are converted back to rhodopsin.
• Light adaptation: after hours in bright light the photochemicals are reduced to retinal and opsins (and retinal to vitamin A), so sensitivity falls.
• Radiologists and pilots wear red goggles in bright light to avoid waiting 20 minutes to become dark-adapted.
3. Deficits:
• Colour blindness: dichromates lack one cone type (protanope lacks red, deuteranope green, tritanope blue) and monochromates have one type; red-green colour blindness occurs almost exclusively in males (8% of women are carriers); blue-green defects occur in people taking sildenafil.
• Nyctalopia (night blindness) is linked to the rhodopsin-retinal visual cycle; the pigment layer stores vitamin A, a precursor of rhodopsin.
• After a lesion of the pathway, fibres from the macula are spared.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the central visual pathway:
1. Describe the visual pathway as a control system: photoreceptors and retinal processing, the optic nerve, chiasm, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiation, visual cortex and other projections.
2. State the normal values (photoreceptor numbers, visual acuity), the factors that raise or lower retinal sensitivity and the compensatory adaptation responses.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the visual deficits when the pathway or the receptors fail.

Answer the following on the functions of the respiratory tract and lungs:
1. Describe the functions of the air passages, lungs and pulmonary circulation under these headings: pathway of air, mucus and cilia (mucociliary escalator), alveoli and surfactant, and the respiratory muscles.
2. State how the components relate to common respiratory disorders (airway, lung tissue and lung circulation disease) and the factors that cause them.
3. Explain why a respiratory disturbance may affect a distant organ or system.
questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• Air passages: nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, primary bronchi, secondary (lobar), tertiary (segmental) bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles (each bronchiole gives rise to 50 to 80), respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs; they filter, moisten, warm and conduct air; the conducting portion ends at the terminal bronchioles.
• Mucus from goblet cells and submucosal glands humidifies and filters air; ciliated epithelium (about 200 cilia per cell beating 10 to 20 times per second, upward in the lower tract and downward in the nose) moves trapped particles, forming the mucociliary escalator.
• Alveoli: about 300 million, area about 70 m2, each in a basket of capillaries; type I cells permit rapid diffusion and type II cells (5%) secrete surfactant that prevents collapse; the pulmonary circulation and alveoli together form the respiratory membrane.
• Muscles: diaphragm and external intercostals (inspiration); internal intercostals and abdominal muscles in forced expiration.
2. Disorders:
• Respiratory disorders are irregular or abnormal functioning, physiological or anatomical, resulting from genetics, allergies, lifestyle (smoking), air pollution and infections.
• Categories: airway disease, lung tissue disease and lung circulation disease; examples are asthma, COPD, emphysema, occupational disorders, sinusitis and lung cancer.
• Restrictive diseases (fibrosis, sarcoidosis) reduce volumes; obstructive diseases (emphysema, chronic bronchitis, asthma) increase residual volume; emphysema destroys alveolar walls.
• Drug groups: bronchodilators, antihistamines, antitussives, decongestants, expectorants, leukotriene modifiers, lung surfactants and mucolytics.
3. Distant effects:
• Impaired gas exchange reduces oxygen delivery to all tissues and reduces CO2 removal, changing blood pH.
• Pulmonary embolism dangerously impairs the ability to obtain oxygen; left heart failure backs blood into the lungs as pulmonary oedema.
• Smoking raises carbon monoxide occupancy of haemoglobin to as much as 10%.

1. Control of heart rate:
• Effector: the SA node sets the rhythm; without neural influences the heart beats according to the SA node rhythm, but sympathetic and parasympathetic fibres are continuously active and modify the rate of spontaneous depolarisation.
• Receptors and afferent input: pressure receptors (baroreceptors) in the aorta and carotid arteries give sensory feedback; higher brain centres also act on the centre.
• Integrating centre: the cardiac control centre (CCC) in the medulla oblongata coordinates autonomic activity of the heart.
• Efferent pathway: the sympathetic cardioacceleratory centre stimulates the heart and the parasympathetic cardioinhibitory centre (vagus) inhibits it.
• Sympathetic action: norepinephrine (sympathetic endings) and epinephrine (adrenal medulla) open Na+ and Ca2+ channels in SA node cells, increasing the pacemaker potential and firing rate.
• Parasympathetic action: acetylcholine opens K+ channels, hyperpolarising the SA node and slowing its firing.
• Feedback: the pace at any time is the net effect of these antagonistic influences; mechanisms that raise the rate are positive chronotropic and those that lower it are negative chronotropic; autonomic innervation of the SA node is the major means of regulating heart rate.
2. Normal values, modifiers and compensation:
• Normal values: resting heart rate about 70 beats per minute (the SA node generates about 75 impulses per minute); stroke volume about 70 to 80 ml per beat; cardiac output = SV x HR, for example 75 ml x 70 = 5,250 ml/min, about 5 L/min (normal range 4 to 6 L/min).
• Raise heart rate: sympathetic stimulation (stress, anxiety, excitement, exercise), norepinephrine, epinephrine, thyroxine, caffeine (positive chronotropic).
• Lower heart rate: acetylcholine and vagal tone, sedatives (negative chronotropic); the resting bradycardia of endurance-trained athletes is largely due to high vagus nerve activity.
• Compensation in exercise: heart rate rises first through decreased vagal inhibition of the SA node, then further through increased sympathetic stimulation; the sympatho-adrenal effect on cardiac output acts through a positive chronotropic effect on heart rate and a positive inotropic effect on contractility; intra- and extracellular ion concentrations must be maintained for normal heart function.
3. Basis of changes when the pathway fails:
• The parasympathetic (vagal) influence dominates at rest and produces vagal tone; if the vagus nerve were cut the heart would lose its tone and the heart rate would increase by about 25 beats per minute.
• In the complete absence of neural influences the SA node keeps the heart beating at its own rhythm because the conducting cells are self-exciting (automaticity).
• Loss of the sympathetic drive would remove the positive chronotropic and inotropic effects that increase cardiac output in exercise.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the control of heart rate:
1. Describe the control system for heart rate: receptors, afferent input, integrating centre, efferent pathway, effector and feedback, including the cellular actions of the transmitters on the pacemaker cells.
2. State the normal values for heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output, the factors that raise or lower heart rate, and the compensatory response during exercise.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the changes seen when the autonomic supply to the heart fails or is removed.

questions.answerText:
1. Regulation of stroke volume:
• Three variables regulate SV: end diastolic volume (EDV, preload), total peripheral resistance (TPR, which creates the afterload) and cardiac contractility.
• Frank-Starling law: the strength of ventricular contraction varies directly with EDV, an intrinsic property of heart muscle; SV is directly proportional to preload and to contractility and inversely proportional to TPR (MAP = TPR x CO).
• Extrinsic control: sympathetic stimuli and the sympatho-adrenal effect (norepinephrine and adrenaline) give a positive inotropic effect on contractility independent of stretch and EDV.
• Venous return determines preload; it depends on blood volume and venous pressure and is aided by sympathetic venous constriction, the skeletal muscle pump and the thoracic-abdominal pressure difference.
2. Values, modifiers and compensation:
• Values: EDV about 110 to 130 ml, SV about 70 to 80 ml, ejection fraction about 60% (EF = SV/EDV x 100); about 80 ml remains in the ventricle at end of systole; SV = EDV minus ESV.
• Raise SV: slow heartbeat and exercise (increase venous return), sympathetic stimuli, certain hormones, calcium and some drugs.
• Lower SV: blood loss and extremely rapid heartbeat; acidosis, increased extracellular K+ and calcium channel blockers lower contractility; higher TPR (afterload) lowers SV.
• Compensation: the Frank-Starling response (more filling gives stronger contraction) and sympatho-adrenal stimulation; cardiac reserve is the difference between resting and maximal cardiac output.
3. Basis of heart failure signs:
• Congestive heart failure is caused by coronary atherosclerosis, persistent high blood pressure, multiple myocardial infarcts and dilated cardiomyopathy (dilated chambers that contract poorly).
• Left-sided failure: a less effective pump leaves more blood in the ventricle, the heart is overstretched, blood backs up into the lungs as pulmonary oedema, leading to suffocation and lack of oxygen to the tissues.
• Right-sided failure: fluid builds up in tissues as peripheral oedema.
• Ageing brings sclerosis of the valve flaps, a decline in cardiac reserve, fibrosis of cardiac muscle and atherosclerosis.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the regulation of stroke volume:
1. Describe the system regulating stroke volume: the variables (preload, afterload, contractility), the intrinsic Frank-Starling mechanism, the extrinsic sympathetic control and the role of venous return.
2. State the normal values (end-diastolic volume, stroke volume, ejection fraction), the factors that raise or lower stroke volume and the compensatory responses.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the signs and symptoms when the pump fails (congestive heart failure).

questions.answerText:
1. Pathway:
• It carries sensations that must be transmitted rapidly with high temporal and spatial fidelity: touch (light torch), vibration, position, movement against the skin and pressure, in large myelinated fibres.
• First-order neurones (medial branch) pass uninterrupted to the medulla and synapse in the dorsal column nuclei (cuneate and gracile); a lateral branch re-enters the dorsal column (15%), forms the spinocervical tract or the spinocerebellar tract, and many elicit local cord reflexes.
• Second-order neurones decussate and continue through the medial lemnisci to the thalamus; fibres from the trigeminal sensory nuclei join the medial lemniscus.
• Thalamus: all fibres end in the ventrobasal complex (ventral posterolateral nucleus for medial lemniscal fibres, ventral posteromedial for trigeminal fibres).
• Third-order neurones project to the postcentral gyrus (SSA 1); because the medial lemnisci cross, the left side of the body is represented on the right thalamus and the right side on the left.
2. Values and cortex:
• Velocity 30 to 120 m/s.
• SSA 1 (Brodmann 3, 1, 2) localises sensations, judges pressure, weight, shape and texture; the association areas (Brodmann 5 and 7) decipher the sensory information.
• Removal of the association areas causes amorphosynthesis; inability to judge shape is astereognosis.
3. Damage:
• Brown-Sequard syndrome (one half of the cord transected): motor function is blocked on the side of the lesion below it; kinesthetic, position and vibration sensations, light touch, discrete localisation and two-point discrimination are lost on the same side; pain, heat and cold are lost on the opposite side.
• Thalamic damage affects the relay of tactile information to the cortex.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway:
1. Describe the pathway as a control system: receptors and the sensations carried, first-, second- and third-order neurones, the thalamic relay, the cortical target and the branches of the first-order fibre.
2. State the conduction velocity, the functions of the somatic sensory cortex and the effects of removing the association areas.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the deficits when the pathway is damaged (including hemisection of the cord).

questions.answerText:
1. Pain modulation:
• The synaptic junctions between nociceptor fibres and dorsal horn cells are sites of plasticity where pain impulses can be modified; the dorsal horn is referred to as a gate.
• The analgesia system is the brain's capability to suppress input of pain signals; it consists of the periaqueductal grey and periventricular areas of the mesencephalon and upper pons, which project to the raphe magnus nucleus (lower pons and upper medulla) and the nucleus reticularis paragigantocellularis, which project to a pain inhibitory complex in the dorsal horns; other connections are the periventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and the medial forebrain bundle.
• Most fibres secrete enkephalins and serotonin; painful stimulation releases substance P from afferent fibres, and this release is blocked by the descending system using axo-axonic synapses on the afferent neurone.
2. Modifiers and compensation:
• Raise pain: bradykinin, serotonin, histamine, K+, acetylcholine and substance P; tissue damage.
• Compensation: the opiate system; morphine-like agents cause analgesia when injected into any part of the analgesia system by activating opiate receptors; the opiate substances include beta-endorphin, met-enkephalin, leu-enkephalin and dynorphin.
3. Failure:
• Facilitation of transmission from a cord or thalamic lesion causes secondary hyperalgesia, and sensitised nociceptors cause primary hyperalgesia.
questions.question:
Answer the following on pain modulation (gating and the analgesia system):
1. Describe the pain modulation system as a control pathway: the dorsal horn gate, the brain and brainstem components of the analgesia system, the transmitters and the feedback onto the primary afferent.
2. State the factors that raise pain and the compensatory response, including the role of the opiate system.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the effects when the pathway fails or is overactive.

questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• Meninges: three layers from outside inward, the dura mater (thick, lines the skull), the arachnoid mater (thin, web-like; the subdural space lies between them) and the pia mater (follows the folds; the subarachnoid space lies between arachnoid and pia).
• CSF: clear colourless fluid produced by ependymal cells in the choroid plexuses and absorbed in the arachnoid granulations; volume about 150 ml, production about 550 ml/day, turnover about 3.7 times per day.
• Formation: plasma is passively filtered across the choroidal capillary endothelium, then water and ions are secreted across the choroidal epithelium (HCO3-, Cl- and K+ through apical channels, with aquaporins for water); CSF is nearly protein-free.
• Circulation: lateral ventricles, interventricular foramina, third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, fourth ventricle, then the subarachnoid space through the median and lateral apertures and the central canal of the cord.
• Functions: buoyancy (brain of about 1500 g behaves as 25 to 50 g), protection as a shock absorber, prevention of ischaemia (reducing CSF lowers intracranial pressure and aids perfusion), homeostasis and removal of waste.
• Blood-brain barrier: a selective semipermeable border formed by tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells and choroid epithelial cells, with astrocyte end-feet and pericytes; it keeps out pathogens, limits large or hydrophilic molecules, allows hydrophobic molecules (O2, CO2, hormones) and small polar molecules, and actively transports glucose.
2. Pathologies:
• Clinical significance: hydrocephalus, lumbar puncture, anaesthesia and chemotherapy, kernicterus and drug administration.
• Causes of CNS disorders: trauma, infections (cryptococcal meningitis, malaria, leprosy, viruses), degeneration (Parkinson's disease), structural defects (anencephaly), tumours, autoimmune disorders (acute disseminated encephalomyelitis attacks myelin) and stroke.
• Cerebral oedema (swelling from the inflammatory response) may compress and kill brain tissue.
3. Distant effects:
• Metabolic waste diffuses into CSF and is removed into the blood as CSF is absorbed, so failure of drainage affects the whole brain.
• Stroke from interrupted blood supply kills tissue in the affected area, giving loss of function.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the cerebrospinal fluid, meninges and blood-brain barrier:
1. Describe the functions of the meninges, cerebrospinal fluid (formation, circulation, functions) and blood-brain barrier (structure, functions).
2. State how the components relate to common pathologies of excess and deficiency and the causes of CNS disorders.
3. Explain why a disturbance of these protective systems may affect distant parts of the nervous system and cause a functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
1. Cough reflex:
• Stimulus: irritant agents; receptors are situated in several locations.
• Afferent fibres pass via the vagus, trigeminal, glossopharyngeal and phrenic nerves to the centre in the medulla oblongata.
• Efferent fibres arise from the medullary centre and pass through the vagus, phrenic and spinal motor nerves to activate the primary and accessory respiratory muscles; the effectors are the muscles of inspiration.
• Sequence: about 2 to 5 litres of air is inspired, the epiglottis and vocal cords close tightly, abdominal and intercostal muscles contract forcefully against the diaphragm, then sudden wide opening of the cords and epiglottis makes air explode outward carrying the foreign body from the bronchi and trachea.
2. Values and comparison:
• Values: pressure in the lungs rises to about 100 mmHg.
• Compensation: the reflex clears foreign material from the trachea and bronchi; the mucociliary escalator (cilia beating 10 to 20 times per second with mucus) also removes trapped particles.
• Sneeze: stimulated by irritants in the nasal mucosa; receptors are olfactory receptors and trigeminal endings; afferents run in the trigeminal and olfactory nerves to the medullary centre; efferents run through the trigeminal, facial, glossopharyngeal, vagus and intercostal nerves to pharyngeal, tracheal and respiratory muscles; it resembles the cough but the uvula is depressed so air passes rapidly through the nose to clear the nasal passages.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the cough and sneeze reflexes:
1. Describe the cough reflex as a control pathway: stimulus, receptors, afferent nerves, medullary centre, efferent nerves, effectors and the sequence of the act.
2. State the normal values in the act of coughing, the factors that trigger it and how it compensates for irritants, and compare with the sneeze reflex.

Answer the following on the regulation of body pH:
1. Describe the regulation of body pH under these headings: sources of volatile and fixed acids, chemical buffering, the respiratory response and the renal response (bicarbonate handling and urinary buffers).
2. Explain why fixed acids accumulate in certain states (uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, starvation, alcoholism, protein metabolism).
3. Distinguish between carbonic (volatile) acid and non-carbonic (fixed) acids, and between the three lines of defence.
questions.answerText:
1. Regulation of pH:
• Acids are produced continuously and threaten the pH of extracellular and intracellular fluids; H2CO3 is in equilibrium with CO2, which leaves through the lungs, so arterial H2CO3 is set by respiratory activity.
• Chemical buffering in extracellular and intracellular fluids and bone is the first line of defence; it minimises pH change but removes no acid or base.
• Respiratory response is the second line: breathing removes CO2 as fast as it forms and large acid loads stimulate breathing, lowering H2CO3.
• Renal response: the burden of removing excess H+ falls on the kidneys, which excrete H+ combined with urinary buffers (for example phosphate), add new HCO3- to the ECF, reabsorb filtered bicarbonate through carbonic anhydrase-dependent steps and excrete the anions liberated from strong acids (phosphate, chloride, sulphate); the kidneys also excrete H+ in excess acid or HCO3- in excess base.
2. Basis of accumulation:
• Incomplete fatty acid oxidation in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, starvation and alcoholism produces ketone body acids (acetoacetic and hydroxybutyric acids); incomplete carbohydrate metabolism produces lactate.
• Oxidation of proteins and amino acids produces strong acids such as H2SO4, HCl and H3PO4.
3. Distinctions:
• Carbonic acid is volatile and removed by the lungs; non-carbonic (fixed) acids are unaffected by breathing, are buffered and are excreted by the kidneys.
• First line: chemical buffers; second: respiratory; third: renal.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the lymphatic system:
1. Describe the functions of the lymphatic system under these headings: components, lymph formation and return, transport of fat, and defence, including the structure of a lymph node.
2. State how the lymphatic system and its organs relate to common pathologies of excess and deficiency.
3. Explain why a disturbance of the lymphatic system may affect a distant organ.
questions.answerText:
1. Functions of the lymphatic system:
• Components: lymphatic vessels (similar to veins and capillaries), lymph nodes, tonsils, adenoids, spleen and thymus; there are hundreds of lymph nodes.
• Fluid return: the circulation filters an average of 20 litres per day; about 17 litres are reabsorbed and about 3 litres stay in the interstitial fluid, so the lymph system provides an accessory return route for the surplus three litres.
• Other functions: absorbs and transports fatty acids and fats as chyle from the digestive system, transports white blood cells to and from the nodes, and carries antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells to the nodes.
• Lymph is similar to plasma and contains lymphocytes, waste, cellular debris, bacteria and proteins; lymphoid organs are sites of lymphocyte production.
• Lymph node: several afferent vessels bring in lymph, which percolates through the node and leaves by an efferent vessel; the cortex contains lymphoid follicles and the medulla lies inside; follicles expand significantly when they meet a foreign antigen.
2. Pathologies:
• Cancers of the lymphocytes (lymphomas) and spleen disorders are listed among blood disorders.
3. Distant effects:
• Lacteals absorb lipids and lymphatic vessels transport them to the bloodstream.
• Lymph carries white cells and antigen-presenting cells between nodes and tissues, so an immune response begins in nodes away from the infection.
• Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue defends the digestive tract.

1. Gas exchange:
• Air compositions: alveolar air is partially replaced by atmospheric air at each breath, oxygen constantly diffuses into the capillaries, carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into alveolar air, and dry inspired air is humidified in the passages.
• Respiratory membrane: a fluid layer with surfactant, alveolar epithelium, epithelial basement membrane, thin interstitial space, capillary basement membrane and capillary endothelium; thickness averages about 0.6 micrometre and is as little as 0.2 micrometre in places.
• Fick's law: diffusing capacity is proportional to pressure gradient x surface area / thickness; solubility and molecular weight give the diffusion coefficient (proportional to S/square root of MW); diffusing capacity is the volume of gas that diffuses each minute for a 1 mmHg pressure difference.
• Values: for oxygen 21 ml/min/mmHg at rest, rising to about 65 (three times); for CO2 about 400 to 450 at rest, rising to about 1200 to 1300 in exercise.
• Alveoli: about 300 million alveoli of 0.3 to 0.5 mm diameter with total area about 70 square metres, each in a basket of pulmonary capillaries; type I cells allow rapid diffusion and type II cells secrete surfactant.
2. Impaired exchange and exercise:
• Removing a lung halves the surface area; in emphysema alveolar walls dissolve and area falls up to fivefold, and with a fall to one third or one quarter of normal exchange is impeded even at rest.
• Oedema and fibrosis increase membrane thickness; a thickness of two to three times normal interferes significantly with exchange.
• Exercise raises diffusing capacity by opening previously dormant capillaries or dilating open ones, increasing surface area, and by a better ventilation-perfusion ratio.
3. Distinctions:
• Alveolar versus inspired air: partial replacement per breath, continual O2 uptake, CO2 addition and humidification.
• Alveolar versus expired air: dead space air mixes with alveolar air, so expired air has higher oxygen tension and lower carbon dioxide tension than alveolar air.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide (mechanism of gaseous exchange):
1. Describe gas exchange between the alveoli and the pulmonary capillaries under these headings: composition of inspired, alveolar and expired air, the respiratory membrane, Fick's law and the factors governing diffusing capacity, and normal diffusing capacities.
2. Explain why gas exchange is impaired in certain states (emphysema, oedema, fibrosis, removal of a lung) and how diffusing capacity increases in exercise.
3. Distinguish between alveolar air and inspired air, and between alveolar air and expired air.

Answer the following on the functions of the small and large intestines:
1. Describe the functions of the small and large intestines under these headings: motility, secretions, digestion and absorption (carbohydrate, protein, lipid, water) and the bacterial flora.
2. State how these functions relate to common pathologies (diarrhoea and its causes, types and treatment).
3. Explain why intestinal disturbance may affect a distant organ or system and cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• Small intestine motility: segmentation and peristalsis mix contents with enzymes, maximise exposure to the intestinal membrane and propel contents into the large intestine.
• Small intestine secretion: 1 to 3 L per day from duodenal and intestinal glands, containing ions, mucoprotein, IgA and enzymes (enterokinase, peptidase, sucrase, lipase); functions are protection by mucus, digestion and dilution.
• Absorption: by simple and facilitated diffusion, active transport, endocytosis and paracellular transport; the surface area is increased by folds, villi and microvilli; glucose and galactose enter by Na-dependent secondary active transport and fructose by facilitated transport; amino acids and di- and tripeptides enter by Na-dependent secondary active transport; fats are absorbed as micelles, re-packed into chylomicrons or VLDL and leave via lymph vessels or the venous system.
• Large intestine: segmentation mixes contents, mass movement propels them onward and defecation evacuates them; colonic alkaline secretion neutralises acids from bacteria, mucus lubricates faeces, and bacterial flora make vitamins B and K.
2. Pathologies:
• Diarrhoea is the passage of loose, liquid or watery stool (three or more in 24 hours or more frequent than normal for the individual); the change in consistency matters more than the number.
• Causes: bacteria (Shigella, E. coli, Salmonella), viruses (rotavirus, adenoviruses), parasites (Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia), metabolic disease, hyperthyroidism, diabetes mellitus, pancreatic insufficiency, food allergy, lactose intolerance, antibiotics and irritable bowel syndrome.
• Types: watery diarrhoea, dysentery (blood or mucus in stool) and persistent diarrhoea (14 days or more); transmission is mostly faecal-oral.
• Treatment: rehydration to replace fluid and electrolytes, antimotility agents (loperamide), antibiotics by pathogen, probiotics and zinc supplementation.
3. Distant effects:
• Diarrhoea causes loss of fluid and electrolytes, requiring rehydration; severe vomiting and diarrhoea change plasma CO2 and blood acidity.
• Endocrine and metabolic disorders (hyperthyroidism, diabetes) can cause diarrhoea, and others (hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia) cause constipation.
• Impaired fat absorption reduces absorption of fat-soluble vitamin K, causing bleeding, and bacterial vitamin K production in the large intestine supports clotting.

questions.question:
Answer the following on olfaction (smell):
1. Describe the olfactory pathway as a control system: receptor cells and epithelium, transduction, olfactory bulb, olfactory tract, olfactory cortex and central connections.
2. State the normal features (numbers, adaptation), the factors that raise or lower olfactory sensitivity and the adaptation response.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the abnormalities of smell.
questions.answerText:
1. Olfactory pathway:
• The olfactory epithelium (about 5 cm2 in the roof of the nasal cavity) has 10 to 20 million bipolar olfactory sensory neurons among supporting (sustentacular) cells and basal stem cells; each neuron has a dendrite ending in a knob with 10 to 20 cilia bearing odorant receptors, covered by mucus from Bowman's glands.
• Transduction: odorants dissolve in mucus and bind G-protein-coupled receptors, which activate adenylyl cyclase and cAMP, opening cation channels; Na+ and Ca2+ enter and depolarise the cell.
• Axons pass through the cribriform plate into the olfactory bulb, where they contact mitral and tufted cell dendrites in glomeruli; mitral and tufted axons run through the intermediate and lateral olfactory striae to the olfactory cortex (anterior olfactory nucleus, olfactory tubercle, piriform cortex, amygdala, entorhinal cortex).
• There is no thalamic relay in the primary smell pathway; conscious discrimination depends on the pathway to the orbitofrontal cortex (greater on the right); the amygdala pathway gives emotional responses and the entorhinal cortex olfactory memories; olfactory cortex also projects via the hypothalamus.
2. Modifiers and adaptation:
• Rapid adaptation is mediated by Ca2+ acting through calmodulin on cyclic nucleotide-gated channels.
• The olfactory threshold increases with age: more than 75% of humans over 80 have impaired ability to identify smells; pregnancy commonly gives oversensitivity (hyperosmia).
3. Abnormalities:
• Anosmia (absence), hyposmia (diminished) and dysosmia (distorted); anosmia is associated with hypogonadism (Kallmann's syndrome).
• Causes: nasal congestion, fracture of the cribriform plate, tumours (neuroblastoma, meningioma), infections and abscesses, and Alzheimer's disease; dysosmia arises from sinus infections, partial nerve damage and poor dental hygiene.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the liver and biliary system:
1. Describe the functions of the liver, bile and gallbladder under these headings: metabolic and haematological functions, synthesis and secretion of bile, storage and concentration of bile, and delivery to the duodenum.
2. State how liver and biliary function relate to pathologies of deficiency, especially of clotting and fat absorption.
3. Explain why liver disturbance may affect distant organs and cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• Liver: metabolic regulation (stores absorbed nutrients and vitamins and releases them as needed), haematological regulation (plasma protein production and removal of old RBCs), bile production, detoxification of toxins and heparin formation.
• Bile: secreted by liver cells at a constant rate of about 40 ml per hour; required for fat digestion and absorption; between meals the sphincter of Oddi is closed and bile is stored and concentrated in the gallbladder, then delivered to the duodenum.
• Gallbladder: a pear-shaped sac under the liver (fundus, body, neck) with capacity of 30 to 50 ml; it concentrates bile by absorbing water, stores bile, selectively absorbs bile salts, keeps the bile acid, excretes cholesterol and secretes mucus; the neck continues as the cystic duct, which joins the common hepatic duct to form the bile duct.
• The biliary system consists of the liver, gallbladder and bile ducts.
2. Pathologies:
• Most clotting factors are plasma proteins synthesised by the liver; when the liver cannot make its usual procoagulants abnormal and often severe bleeding occurs.
• Causes range from an easily resolved vitamin K deficiency (common in newborns and after systemic antibiotics) to near-total loss of liver function as in hepatitis or cirrhosis.
• Vitamin K is fat-soluble and absorbed with fats; in liver disease the failing cells make neither procoagulants nor the bile needed for fat and vitamin K absorption.
• Bilirubin and enzymes such as aspartate transaminase and alkaline phosphatase are markers of liver damage; excess bilirubin from red cell breakdown is taken up by the liver and secreted in bile.
3. Distant effects:
• Liver failure shows as bleeding because clotting factors are synthesised in the liver.
• Impaired bile flow causes vitamin K deficiency, and bacteria in the large intestine, which normally produce vitamin K, cannot compensate if fat absorption is impaired.
• Liver cirrhosis is listed as a cause of blood disorders, and the liver's failure to make plasma proteins and remove old RBCs affects the blood.

1. Reticular activating system:
• The RAS is part of the reticular formation in the anterior brainstem; the reticular formation receives input from the spinal cord, sensory pathways, thalamus and cortex and has efferent connections throughout the nervous system.
• Components: the locus coeruleus (upper dorsolateral pons; releases norepinephrine widely to the cortex; active on waking and arousal), the raphe nuclei (serotonergic; pain sensation, mood, circadian rhythm through the suprachiasmatic nucleus, arousal), the posterior tuberomammillary hypothalamus (histaminergic; wakefulness and cognition) and the pedunculopontine tegmentum (cholinergic; projects to the thalamus and cortex).
• Activation: the lateral hypothalamus releases orexin in response to light hitting the eyes, activating the locus coeruleus and stimulating the transition from sleep to waking.
2. Functions and EEG:
• The RAS is responsible for wakefulness, the ability to focus, the fight-flight response, attention, arousal and modulation of muscle tone, and acts as a gatekeeper of what reaches consciousness.
• Cholinergic neurons promote desynchronisation of the brain, switching from slow sleep rhythms to high-frequency, low-amplitude wake rhythms, seen on the EEG.
• Collateral fibres of the auditory pathway also reach the RAS.
3. Failure:
• Depressants increase theta and delta waves and sleep; abnormal delta activity is linked with difficulty maintaining conscious awareness, as in brain injury.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the reticular activating system:
1. Describe the reticular activating system as a control system: inputs, its four component nuclear groups, their transmitters and their projections to the thalamus and cortex.
2. State the functions it controls, the factors that activate it and the changes it produces in the EEG.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the effects on arousal and consciousness when the system fails or is damaged.

questions.answerText:
1. Functions of the pancreas:
• Endocrine: secretes insulin and glucagon from the islets of Langerhans.
• Exocrine: secretes pancreatic juice with an aqueous component (contains HCO3-, neutralises stomach acid in the duodenum so enzymes can function) and an enzymatic component (trypsin, chymotrypsin, lipase and amylase) essential for digesting and absorbing carbohydrates, fats and proteins.
• Enzyme actions: pancreatic amylase converts starch to maltose and maltotriose (pH 7.0); lipase with colipase converts triglyceride to monoglyceride and fatty acids (pH 8.0); enterokinase converts trypsinogen to trypsin and chymotrypsinogen to chymotrypsin, which reduce protein to polypeptides, and carboxypeptidase yields amino acids.
2. Pathologies:
• Diabetes mellitus (Type 1 IDDM and Type 2 NIDDM) is shown by raised plasma glucose.
• Pancreatic insufficiency is listed as a cause of diarrhoea.
3. Distant effects:
• Incomplete fatty acid oxidation in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus produces ketone body acids, adding a non-volatile acid load for the kidneys and buffers to handle.
• Lipids, proteins and lipoproteins are markers in diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease.
• Insulin and glucagon are degraded by the kidneys.
• Loss of pancreatic enzymes and bicarbonate impairs digestion and absorption in the intestine, producing diarrhoea.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the functions of the pancreas:
1. Describe the functions of the pancreas under these headings: endocrine secretion, exocrine secretion (aqueous and enzymatic components), actions in the duodenum and regulation.
2. State how the pancreatic components relate to common pathologies of excess and deficiency.
3. Explain why a disturbance of the pancreas may affect a distant organ or system.

Answer the following on the nervous control of respiration:
1. Describe the control pathway for breathing: receptors, afferent pathways, integrating centres in the brain, efferent nerves, effector muscles and feedback reflexes.
2. State the normal values for breathing, the factors that raise or lower ventilation and the compensatory response during exercise.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the signs and symptoms when the pathway is disturbed.
questions.answerText:
1. Nervous control of respiration:
• Voluntary control is through the motor cortex of the cerebrum, with inputs from the limbic system and hypothalamus; involuntary control is by neurons in the pons and medulla.
• Medullary respiratory centre: sets the basic rhythm; the dorsal respiratory group (DRG) integrates input from stretch receptors and peripheral chemoreceptors and maintains the rhythm by stimulating the diaphragm and intercostals (inspiration); when DRG activity ceases the muscles relax (expiration); the ventral respiratory group (VRG) generates the rhythm, is involved in forced breathing and stimulates accessory muscles of forced inspiration and expiration.
• Pontine respiratory group: the apneustic centre stimulates the DRG, controlling the depth of inspiration; the pneumotaxic centre inhibits the DRG, allowing relaxation after inspiration and controlling the overall rate.
• Efferent and effectors: phrenic and intercostal nerves stimulate the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles to contract, producing inspiration; when stimulation stops the muscles relax and expiration occurs.
• Feedback and receptors: aortic and carotid bodies monitor PCO2, PO2 and pH; the hypothalamus monitors emotional state and body temperature; proprioceptors report joint and muscle movement; the inflation reflex protects the lungs from over-inflating and pulmonary irritant reflexes protect the respiratory zones from foreign material.
2. Values, modifiers and compensation:
• Values: adult respiratory rate about 12 to 18 breaths per minute (about 18 to 30 in a 10-year-old); tidal volume 500 ml and pulmonary ventilation 12 x 500 = 6000 ml/min.
• Factors affecting respiration: exercise, temperature, smoking, quantity and quality of air, internal ratio of CO2 and O2, blood pH, respiratory disorders, and drugs including alcohol.
• Compensation in exercise: oxygen demand rises, so tidal volume and breathing rate increase; chemoreceptors (aortic arch and carotid arteries, detecting blood acidity) and proprioceptors (joint and muscle movement) send messages to the medulla oblongata.
3. Disturbance:
• The mechanisms available to protect the lungs are the cough reflex, the sneeze reflex, the inflation reflex and the pulmonary irritant reflexes.

questions.question:
Answer the following on lung volumes and capacities:
1. Describe lung volumes and capacities under these headings: spirometry, the four volumes, the four capacities, minute and alveolar ventilation, and dead space.
2. Explain how restrictive and obstructive lung diseases alter the volumes and capacities.
3. Distinguish between anatomical and physiological dead space, and between pulmonary ventilation and alveolar ventilation.
questions.answerText:
1. Volumes and capacities:
• Spirometry measures air volumes and capacities; a volume is one phase of the respiratory cycle and a capacity is the sum of two or more volumes.
• Tidal volume about 500 ml; inspiratory reserve volume about 3000 ml; expiratory reserve volume about 1100 ml; residual volume about 1200 ml.
• Inspiratory capacity = TV + IRV = 3500 ml; vital capacity = TV + IRV + ERV = 4600 ml; functional residual capacity = RV + ERV = 2300 ml; total lung capacity = RV + ERV + TV + IRV = 5800 ml.
• Pulmonary ventilation = respiratory rate x tidal volume = 12 x 500 = 6000 ml/min; alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume - dead space) x respiratory rate = (500 - 150) x 12 per minute.
• All volumes and capacities are about 20 to 25% less in women than in men and greater in athletic persons than in small asthenic persons.
2. Disease patterns:
• Restrictive disease makes it harder to get air in: decreased VC, TLC, RV and FRC; examples are fibrosis, sarcoidosis, muscular diseases and chest wall deformities.
• Obstructive disease makes it harder to get air out: decreased VC but increased TLC, RV and FRC; examples are emphysema, chronic bronchitis and asthma.
3. Distinctions:
• Anatomical dead space is the volume of all passageways from the nose to the terminal bronchiole; physiological dead space adds non-functioning and poorly perfused alveoli, and in normal lungs the two are equal.
• Pulmonary ventilation is the total air moved per minute; alveolar ventilation is the air reaching the gas exchange areas per minute, that is with the dead space subtracted.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the transport of carbon dioxide in the blood:
1. Describe carbon dioxide transport under these headings: the three chemical forms, the reactions in the red cell, the chloride shift, and the reverse reactions in the lungs.
2. Explain why active tissues unload more oxygen (the link between CO2 loading, hydrogen ions and oxygen dissociation).
3. Distinguish between the chloride shift and the reverse chloride shift, and between carbaminohaemoglobin and bicarbonate transport.
questions.answerText:
1. CO2 transport:
• About 4 ml of CO2 is transported from tissues to lungs in each 100 ml of blood: 10% dissolved, 30% combined with haemoglobin and plasma proteins as carbamino-Hb (CO2 reacts with the amino group), and 60% as HCO3-.
• In the red cell dissolved CO2 reacts with water to form carbonic acid, catalysed by carbonic anhydrase (about 5000-fold faster); carbonic acid dissociates into H+ and HCO3-; most H+ combine with haemoglobin.
• Chloride shift: bicarbonate diffuses out of the red cell into plasma while chloride diffuses in, so venous red cells contain more chloride than arterial cells.
• In the lungs the reactions reverse: as haemoglobin loads oxygen its affinity for H+ declines, H+ dissociates and combines with HCO3- entering the red cell, chloride moves out (reverse chloride shift), free CO2 is regenerated and diffuses into the alveolus, together with CO2 released from carbaminohaemoglobin and dissolved CO2.
2. Link to oxygen unloading:
• Active tissues generate extra CO2, which raises H+ and lowers pH; this shifts the oxygen-haemoglobin curve to the right (Bohr effect) and promotes oxygen availability.
• CO2 loading releases hydrogen ions in the erythrocyte, and hydrogen ions promote O2 dissociation.
3. Distinctions:
• Chloride shift occurs in the tissues (HCO3- out, Cl- in); the reverse chloride shift occurs in the lungs (Cl- out, HCO3- in).
• Carbaminohaemoglobin carries about 30% of CO2 bound to the amino group of Hb; bicarbonate carries about 60%, formed through carbonic anhydrase.

1. Conducting system:
• The system consists of special conducting cells and fibres (not nervous tissue) that self-excite, conduct rapidly and coordinate the chambers; both atria contract together and first, then both ventricles.
• SA node: primary impulse initiator and physiological pacemaker; generates about 75 impulses per minute.
• AV node: secondary pacemaker and conduit; the atria are separated from the ventricles by a cartilaginous septum that cannot conduct, so the AV node is the only pathway; it delays the impulse about 0.1 second.
• Bundle of His: the initial segment penetrating the fibrous trigone into the interventricular septum; it allows only forward movement of action potentials and bifurcates into right and left bundle branches.
• Purkinje fibres: subendocardial branches extending to the apex and then up the ventricular walls; they have many more gap junctions than AV nodal cells, giving almost instantaneous transmission to the ventricle.
• ECG: electrodes on the skin record current spreading from the heart; there are bipolar leads (I, II, III), unipolar limb leads (aVR, aVL, aVF) and chest leads V1 to V6, twelve in all.
2. Normal values and modifiers:
• P wave (atrial depolarisation) 0.1 s, 0.1 to 0.12 mV; QRS (ventricular depolarisation) 0.08 to 0.10 s; T wave (ventricular repolarisation) 0.2 s, 0.3 mV; PR interval 0.12 to 0.2 s; ST segment 0.08 s; RR interval 0.8 s (one cardiac cycle, used for heart rate).
• Compensation: the rapid Purkinje conduction compensates for the delay at the AV node and lets the ventricles contract shortly after the atria.
• Ion levels and other factors that change the trace include potassium (hyperkalemia, hypokalemia), calcium and thyrotoxicosis.
3. Basis of ECG changes in failure:
• P wave: taller and wider in atrial enlargement; absent in hyperkalemia, atrial fibrillation or sinoatrial block.
• PR interval: prolonged in bradycardia and first degree heart block; shortened in tachycardia.
• QRS: prolonged in bundle branch block and hyperkalemia.
• ST segment: elevated in myocardial infarction, left bundle branch block, acute pericarditis; depressed in acute myocardial ischaemia, posterior infarction, ventricular hypertrophy, hypokalemia.
• T wave: tall and broad-based in acute ischaemia; flat or inverted in myocardial infarction, ventricular hypertrophy, pericarditis; U wave prominent in hypokalemia.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the conducting system of the heart and the electrocardiogram:
1. Describe the conducting system as a control pathway: initiator (pacemaker), conduction route through the SA node, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches and Purkinje fibres, and how ECG leads record it.
2. State the normal ECG values (durations and amplitudes of waves, intervals and segments), the factors that alter them and the compensatory role of the Purkinje fibres.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the ECG changes when the pathway fails or is damaged.

questions.answerText:
1. Phototransduction:
• Each photoreceptor has an outer segment (stacked saccules with photochemical, modified cilium), inner segment (rich in mitochondria), nucleus and synaptic body.
• Rods contain rhodopsin (scotopsin plus 11-cis retinal), which decomposes when it absorbs light; cones contain colour pigments.
• Cascade: light forms metarhodopsin II, which activates transducin, which activates phosphodiesterase, which hydrolyses cGMP; cGMP separates from the Na+ channel, so the channels close and Na+ conductance into the outer segment falls; metarhodopsin II is inactivated by rhodopsin kinase.
• Receptor potential: more Na+ leaves than leaks in, so the inside becomes more negative (hyperpolarisation from about -40 mV in dark to -70/-80 mV in light), greater with more light energy.
• The pigment layer contains melanin, which prevents reflection of light, and stores vitamin A, a precursor of rhodopsin.
2. Basis of sensitivity changes:
• Nyctalopia (night blindness) is named in the rhodopsin-retinal visual cycle; the pigment layer stores vitamin A, a precursor of rhodopsin, and dark adaptation reforms rhodopsin from retinal, opsins and vitamin A.
• In dark adaptation retinal, opsins and vitamin A are converted back to rhodopsin (maximal in about 20 minutes; cones adapt first and rods later, more lastingly); in light adaptation much of the photochemical is reduced to retinal and opsins and retinal to vitamin A, lowering sensitivity.
• Sildenafil inhibits retinal phosphodiesterase and can cause blue-green colour blindness.
3. Rods versus cones:
• Rods: rhodopsin, vision at low light levels (scotopic), no colour vision, about 120 million; discs are separate from the plasma membrane.
• Cones: colour pigments (blue 445 nm, green 535 nm, red 570 nm), active at higher light levels (photopic), colour vision, about 6 million, concentrated in the fovea; membrane is continuous with the plasma membrane.
questions.question:
Answer the following on phototransduction in the retina:
1. Describe phototransduction under these headings: structure of rods and cones, rhodopsin and the visual cycle, the biochemical cascade, the receptor potential, and the differences between rods and cones.
2. Explain the physiological basis of night blindness and of retinal sensitivity changes in light and dark.
3. Distinguish between rods and cones.

Answer the following on erythropoiesis:
1. Describe erythropoiesis under these headings: sites, stem cells and growth factors, stages of red cell development, regulation by tissue oxygenation and erythropoietin, and the dietary requirements for red cell maturation.
2. Explain the basis of the anaemias that arise from disturbed red cell production: why deficiency of vitamin B12, folic acid or iron produces anaemia and why it is commoner in some people.
3. Distinguish between megaloblastic (pernicious) anaemia and iron-deficiency anaemia.
questions.answerText:
1. Erythropoiesis:
• Sites: haemopoiesis occurs in embryonic sites (yolk sac, liver, spleen, thymus, lymph nodes, bone marrow) and after birth in the red bone marrow.
• Stem cells: blood cells arise from a common pluripotent haemopoietic stem cell that can self-renew or differentiate into committed progenitors (the colony-forming unit-erythrocyte, CFU-E, for red cells); interleukin-3 promotes proliferation of pluripotent stem cells and CFU-E; differentiation is stimulated by differentiation inducers.
• Erythropoietin (EPO): made mainly by the kidneys and in small amounts by the liver; it stimulates production of proerythroblasts from CFU-E.
• Stages: pluripotent stem cell, pronormoblast (earliest recognised cell; large, basophilic, about 1% Hb), basophilic normoblast, polychromatophilic normoblast (Hb production), orthochromatic normoblast (final nucleated stage), reticulocyte (no nucleus, about 95% Hb, circulates 1 to 2 days) and then mature RBC.
• Regulation: the basic regulator is tissue oxygenation; RBC production is proportional to 1/tissue oxygenation, so anaemia from haemorrhage, low atmospheric oxygen, lung disease, blood doping or altitude increases production.
• Requirements: amino acids, iron (for haem), vitamin B12 and folic acid (final maturation and DNA synthesis), vitamin B6 (DNA and haem synthesis), vitamin C (folate metabolism and iron absorption); copper and cobalt are essential in other animals but not shown in humans.
2. Basis of anaemia from disturbed production:
• Lack of vitamin B12 or folic acid slows proliferation of erythroblasts, so cells develop into large, irregular or oval erythrocytes with higher fragility and shorter life, leading to megaloblastic anaemia; these vitamins are needed for purine and pyrimidine synthesis and DNA, and a great demand is made in adult erythropoiesis (10 to 20 g of cells formed per day).
• Vitamin B12 absorption needs intrinsic factor from the stomach mucosa; in most pernicious anaemia intrinsic factor is deficient, in an autoimmune disease with atrophy of the stomach mucosa that most often affects the elderly; diet is rarely the problem except for strict vegetarians.
• Iron-deficiency anaemia is generally a secondary result of haemorrhagic anaemias but also results from inadequate intake of iron-containing foods and impaired iron absorption.
• Anaemia is a sign of some disorder, with blood oxygen levels inadequate to support metabolism; anaemic individuals are fatigued, pale, short of breath and chilly.
3. Megaloblastic versus iron-deficiency anaemia:
• Megaloblastic (pernicious): due to lack of vitamin B12 or folic acid, developing erythrocytes grow but do not divide, giving large pale macrocytes.
• Iron-deficiency: haemoglobin content is low, and the erythrocytes produced are small and pale microcytes.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the control of glomerular filtration:
1. Describe the control system for glomerular filtration: the filtration barrier, the receptor (macula densa), the effector (afferent arteriole), vasoactive substances and feedback.
2. State the normal values (renal plasma flow, GFR, fraction filtered, reabsorbed, urine flow), the factors that raise or lower GFR and the compensatory response.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the changes when filtration control is disturbed.
questions.answerText:
1. Control of filtration:
• Filtration barrier: a substance must pass through the pores between glomerular capillary endothelial cells, an acellular basement membrane and the filtration slits between the podocyte foot processes; small electrolytes and glucose are freely filtered, but the negatively charged basement membrane repels negatively charged molecules such as albumin.
• Sensing and feedback: a rise in arterial pressure raises glomerular capillary pressure and GFR, which raises tubular flow; macula densa cells are stimulated to release chemicals that cause afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, reducing flow into the glomerulus and returning capillary pressure and GFR to normal (autoregulation).
• Effectors: vasodilators (nitric oxide, bradykinin, prostacyclin) dilate the afferent arteriole and raise volume and pressure entering the glomerulus; vasoconstrictors (epinephrine, norepinephrine, angiotensin II) do the reverse.
2. Values and modifiers:
• About 20% of plasma entering the kidney is filtered (80% leaves by the efferent arteriole); renal plasma flow is 625 ml/min and GFR 125 ml/min; about 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed and urine flow is about 1 ml/min.
• Raise GFR: higher arterial pressure, higher glomerular hydrostatic pressure, afferent dilation; lower GFR: afferent vasoconstriction.
• GFR is measured as clearance of inulin, which is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted; PAH clearance measures total renal blood flow because PAH is cleared by filtration and secretion.
3. Disturbance:
• GFR reflects the efficiency of the kidney in filtration and is an index of its functionality.

questions.question:
Answer the following on hearing and the auditory pathway:
1. Describe the auditory system as a control pathway: conduction of sound through the external, middle and inner ear, the receptor (hair cells), the afferent pathway to the cortex and the collateral connections.
2. State how loudness and pitch are coded, the protective mechanism against loud sound and how direction is determined.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the signs of conduction deafness and nerve deafness.
questions.answerText:
1. Auditory pathway:
• Ear structure: the external ear (pinna, meatus, tympanic membrane) gathers sound; the middle ear (auditory tube, ossicles, oval and round windows, tensor tympani and stapedius) transmits it; the cochlea has three coiled tubes, scala vestibuli, scala media and scala tympani, with Reissner's membrane between the first two and the basilar membrane, carrying the organ of Corti, between the last two.
• Receptors: one row of inner hair cells and 3 to 4 rows of outer hair cells, on the basilar membrane and embedded in the tectorial membrane; when the basilar membrane vibrates the cilia bend, mechanically gated cation channels open and K+ and Ca2+ enter, depolarising the cell (resting potential about -60 mV), voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open, transmitter is released and the cochlear nerve endings fire; bending towards the scala tympani hyperpolarises.
• Pathway: first-order neurons synapse, second-order neurons cross, then the lateral lemniscus, another synapse and the auditory radiation; collateral fibres run to the reticular activating system and the vermis of the cerebellum.
2. Coding and protection:
• Loudness is coded by amplitude, frequency of firing and recruitment of new hair cells; pitch by frequency.
• The tensor tympani and stapedius protect against loud noise and mask low-frequency sounds in loud environments.
• Direction of sound is determined by the time lag between the ears and by the difference in intensity between the ears.
3. Deafness:
• Conduction deafness: impaired sound transmission in the external or middle ear, from a wax plug, foreign bodies, destruction of ossicles or a thickened eardrum.
• Nerve deafness: damage to the hair cells or neural pathways, from aminoglycoside antibiotics, loud noise, a tumour of cranial nerve VIII or vascular damage in the medulla.

questions.question:
Answer the following on taste (gustation):
1. Describe the gustatory pathway as a control system: taste buds and receptor cells, transduction for each taste modality, first-order nerves, brainstem relay, thalamus and cortex.
2. State the normal features (numbers of buds and fibres, adaptation) and the factors that alter taste sensitivity.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the taste abnormalities.
questions.answerText:
1. Gustatory pathway:
• Taste buds lie in papillae of the tongue (fungiform, foliate, circumvallate) and in the epiglottis, palate and pharynx; a bud (50 to 100 cells) contains basal, sustentacular and gustatory receptor cells around a taste pore; each is innervated by about 50 nerve fibres.
• Modalities: salty (Na+ through ENaC, blocked by amiloride, releasing glutamate), sour (H+ through ENaC and HCN channels), umami (glutamate on metabotropic mGluR4), bitter (T2R G-protein-coupled receptors and gustducin) and sweet (T1R3 receptors coupled to gustducin).
• First-order neurons: anterior two-thirds through the chorda tympani of the facial nerve, posterior one-third through the glossopharyngeal nerve, other parts through the vagus nerve; fibres pass to the nucleus of the solitary tract, then to the thalamus, then to the gustatory cortex at the foot of the postcentral gyrus and the insula; taste reflex fibres run to the salivatory nuclei.
2. Modifiers:
• Receptor potentials rise with tastant concentration; the response adapts to a lower level within seconds and the tastant is washed away by saliva; smell and food texture contribute to flavour.
• Aging and tobacco abuse diminish taste, and drugs (cisplatin, penicillamine, captopril, vitamin B3) and zinc deficiency can cause ageusia.
3. Abnormalities:
• Ageusia (absence), hypogeusia (diminished) and dysgeusia or parageusia (disturbed).
• Damage to the lingual or glossopharyngeal nerve causes ageusia and hypogeusia; neurological disorders (vestibular schwannoma, Bell palsy, familial dysautonomia, multiple sclerosis, some infections) also impair taste.

1. Functions of the kidney:
• The renal system produces, transports and stores urine (kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra and their muscles).
• Regulates osmolality of body fluids by excreting dilute or concentrated urine; regulates plasma Na+, K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, Cl-, bicarbonate, phosphate and sulphate; regulates extracellular fluid volume by controlling Na+ and water excretion; helps regulate arterial pressure by adjusting Na+ excretion and producing renin.
• Acid-base balance: excretes H+ when there is excess acid or HCO3- when there is excess base; synthesises ammonia.
• Eliminates urea, uric acid (purine metabolism) and creatinine (muscle metabolism), and excretes drugs and toxic compounds.
• Hormones: major production sites of erythropoietin and 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D3; degrades insulin, glucagon and parathyroid hormone; synthesises prostaglandins, thromboxane A2 and kallikrein (which leads to kinins).
• Nephron: glomerulus filters protein-free plasma into Bowman's capsule; proximal tubule does uncontrolled reabsorption and secretion; loop of Henle sets the medullary osmotic gradient; distal tubule and collecting duct do variable, controlled reabsorption of Na+ and water and secretion of K+ and H+; the juxtaglomerular apparatus produces substances that control kidney function.
2. Pathologies:
• Plasma urea nitrogen and creatinine are measures of kidney function, and GFR is an index of the kidneys' functionality (normal 125 ml/min).
• Hypercalcaemia occurs, for example, in renal failure; alkaline phosphatase is raised in kidney disorders.
3. Distant effects:
• Erythropoietin is made mainly by the kidneys and stimulates red cell production, so kidney function links to blood.
• The kidneys convert vitamin D into its active form, allowing calcium absorption in the small intestine.
• Kidney control of Na+, water and renin affects arterial blood pressure and extracellular fluid volume; acid-base regulation depends on kidney excretion of H+ and addition of HCO3- to the ECF.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the functions of the kidney:
1. Describe the functions of the kidney under these headings: excretion, regulation of fluid, ions and acid-base balance, hormones synthesised or degraded, and the roles of the parts of the nephron.
2. State how the regulatory components of the nephron and the kidney's hormonal roles relate to common pathologies of excess and deficiency.
3. Explain why kidney disturbance may affect a distant organ or system and cause a functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• The cerebrum (telencephalon) is the largest part of the brain, with the cortex divided into two hemispheres and subcortical structures such as the hippocampus, basal ganglia and olfactory bulb.
• The hemispheres are joined by the corpus callosum; each controls the opposite side of the body; the left hemisphere controls speech, comprehension, arithmetic and writing and the right creativity, spatial ability, artistic and musical skills; the left is dominant for hand use and language in about 92% of people.
• Lobes: frontal (attention, reward, short-term memory, motivation, planning), temporal (sensory input with emotional meaning, long-term memory, language perception), parietal (touch, spatial awareness, navigation, language) and occipital (visual processing).
• Somatosensory cortex: sensory signals from all modalities end in the cortex behind the central sulcus; SSA 1 localises sensations and judges pressure, weight, shape and texture; association areas 5 and 7 interpret them.
• Prefrontal and orbital frontal cortex: judgment, insight, motivation, mood and conditioned emotional reactions.
2. Pathologies:
• Damage to the prefrontal area causes difficulty with abstract reasoning, judgment, mood and puzzle solving, and tactless behaviour; alcohol strongly affects it; depression is associated with increased activity in the medial frontal regions.
• Inability to judge shapes is astereognosis; removal of the association areas causes amorphosynthesis.
• Stroke (interruption of blood supply), Alzheimer's disease and tumours also disturb cortical function.
3. Distant effects:
• Because each hemisphere controls the opposite side, a lesion affects the contralateral body.
• A cerebrovascular accident from a ruptured vessel kills the tissue supplied, with loss of some functions or death.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the functions of the cerebral cortex:
1. Describe the functions of the cerebrum under these headings: hemispheres and corpus callosum, lobes and their functions, somatosensory areas and the limbic (prefrontal) cortex.
2. State how regions of the cortex relate to common pathologies of excess and deficiency of function.
3. Explain why a cortical lesion may cause a functional deficit in a distant part of the body.

Answer the following on the erythrocyte and haemoglobin:
1. Describe the functions of the erythrocyte and haemoglobin under these headings: structure, production and its regulation, oxygen and carbon dioxide transport, acid-base role, life span and destruction.
2. State how erythrocyte and haemoglobin disorders relate to pathologies of deficiency (the anaemias) and of excess (polycythaemia), including the abnormal haemoglobins.
3. Explain why these disturbances produce effects in distant organs and a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Erythrocyte functions:
• Structure: biconcave disc (6 to 9 micrometre diameter, 1 to 2 micrometre thick), deformable to pass the smallest vessels, no nucleus or mitochondria, about 33% haemoglobin; over 97% of the dry cell is haemoglobin.
• Haemoglobin: globin (two alpha and two beta chains) bound to haem, each haem bearing an iron atom that binds one O2 reversibly, so one Hb carries four O2; one cell holds about 250 million Hb molecules; normal Hb is 13 to 18 g/100 ml in adult males, 12 to 16 in females and 14 to 20 in infants.
• Functions: transport oxygen and assist CO2 transport, regulate acid-base balance to prevent large pH changes, assist clot formation; erythrocytes are the major factor in blood viscosity.
• Production: stimulated by erythropoietin (made mainly by the kidneys) in response to tissue oxygenation; a 70 kg man produces about 2.3 x 10^6 red cells per second.
• Destruction: life span 100 to 120 days; anucleate cells cannot synthesise protein, become rigid and fragile and are trapped in the spleen (the red blood cell graveyard) and engulfed by macrophages; haem is split from globin, globin to amino acids, iron stored as ferritin or haemosiderin and haem to bilirubin, carried on albumin, taken up by liver, secreted in bile and metabolised to urobilinogen and stercobilin in faeces; spilled Hb is captured by haptoglobin.
2. Deficiency and excess:
• Anaemia: blood with abnormally low oxygen-carrying capacity, from insufficient red cells (haemorrhagic, haemolytic, aplastic), from low Hb content (iron-deficiency, pernicious) or from abnormal Hb.
• Abnormal Hb: in thalassaemia one globin chain is absent or faulty and cells are thin and deficient in Hb; in sickle-cell anaemia one of 146 amino acids in a beta chain is changed, so HbS links into stiff rods under low oxygen and cells become spiky.
• Polycythaemia: an abnormal excess of erythrocytes that increases viscosity so blood sludges; polycythaemia vera, a bone marrow cancer, has 8 to 11 million cells/microlitre and haematocrit up to 80%, with dizziness.
3. Distant effects:
• Because the erythrocyte delivers oxygen to every tissue, anaemia leaves oxygen inadequate for normal metabolism and gives fatigue, pallor, breathlessness and chilliness.
• Sickle cells interfere with oxygen delivery, leaving victims gasping for air and in extreme pain.
• Aplastic anaemia from marrow destruction (drugs, radiation, viruses) impairs formation of all formed elements, so anaemia is one sign among several.
• Sluggish flow in polycythaemia impairs circulation generally.

1. Functions and composition:
• Blood is a connective tissue with formed elements suspended in a plasma matrix but no fibre elements; it is the medium for metabolic activities, transport (oxygen, nutrients, carbon dioxide, nitrogenous wastes, hormones), protection (prevents fluid loss from damaged vessels, phagocytic WBCs, plasma antibodies) and homeostasis.
• Organisation: plasma is 55% of whole blood (a straw-coloured liquid, 91.5 to 92% water, 7 to 9% proteins, 1% solutes with Na+ the major solute) and formed elements 45% (mainly RBCs, plus leucocytes and platelets).
• Plasma constituents: organic nutrients (glucose, fats, amino acids, vitamins), inorganic ions (bicarbonate, phosphate, sulphate, chloride, calcium, potassium, sodium, magnesium), secretions such as enzymes (ALT, AST, SOD) and hormones, dissolved gases (O2, CO2), metabolic products (urea, bilirubin, creatinine) and plasma proteins (about 7%; fibrinogen, albumin, globulin and antibodies).
• Functions of plasma: transport of cells, food, waste and hormones; fibrinogen for clotting; homeostasis; globulin gives rise to antibodies for immunity.
• Formed elements: RBCs transport oxygen, help carry CO2, regulate acid-base balance and assist clot formation; neutrophils phagocytose and prevent spread of infection; eosinophils attack parasites and phagocytose antigen-antibody complexes; basophils secrete substances mediating hypersensitivity; lymphocytes mediate specific immunity (B cells humoral, T cells cellular); platelets initiate clotting and plug damaged vessels.
