Causes: Chlamydia trachomatis (most common), Neisseria gonorrhoeae, streptococcus and herpes simplex virus; risk factors include maternal infections, HIV-infected mothers, premature rupture of membranes, inadequate ocular prophylaxis, silver nitrate exposure, ocular trauma during delivery, mechanical ventilation, prematurity, poor prenatal care and poor hygienic delivery.
(c)
Infected birth canal during vaginal birth, transmembrane transmission and transplacental transmission.
(d)
• Gram stain, cultures (blood agar, chocolate agar, Thayer-Martin), Giemsa stain and PCR; gonococcal shows Gram-negative intracellular diplococci; chlamydial shows basophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions; viral uses viral culture, direct fluorescent antibody and PCR.
• Imaging is not associated, but CT or MRI help for complications like orbital cellulitis, meningitis, encephalitis and pneumonia.
(e)
• Babies of mothers with sexually transmitted infections are predisposed; an infant of a Chlamydia-positive mother has a 30-40% chance of conjunctivitis and a 10-12% chance of pneumonia.
• Premature, ventilated infants and those exposed to silver nitrate or without adequate prophylaxis are also at risk.
(f)
• Gonococcal: within 2-5 days, severe white bilateral discharge, tearing, lid swelling; prompt treatment prevents corneal ulceration.
• Chlamydial: 5-14 days, redness, watery discharge, lid swelling; needs systemic treatment to eradicate nasopharyngeal bacteria.
• Herpetic: within 2 weeks, following systemic and CNS infection, watery discharge, lid margin skin lesions; systemic acyclovir is needed.
• Chemical: within 24 hours of silver nitrate instillation, lid swelling, redness and tearing, resolving spontaneously within a few days.
questions.question:
Ophthalmia neonatorum:
(a) Define it.
(b) State its causes and risk factors.
(c) State its routes of transmission.
(d) Describe its diagnostic investigations.
(e) Explain why certain infants are more vulnerable.
(f) Distinguish gonococcal, chlamydial, herpetic and chemical types.

Corneal abrasion:
(a) Describe its pathophysiology.
(b) State how its healing stages relate to clinical manifestations and diagnostic findings.
(c) Explain how it may progress to other complications and functional deficit.
(d) State the nursing care plan, health education and management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A scratch or injury on the surface of the cornea; causes include dust, sand or metal particles, fingernails, contact lenses, cosmetic brushes, improper lens use and sports or accident injuries.
• The corneal epithelium is disrupted, exposing nerve endings (pain); loss of epithelial integrity compromises transparency and refraction, causing visual disturbance.
(b)
• Latent phase immediately after injury; migration phase within the first few hours as edge cells cover the wound; proliferation phase in the first 24 to 48 hours; epithelial reattachment phase, when pain eases and vision improves.
• Signs: gritty or foreign body sensation, redness, tearing, photophobia, blurred vision and blepharospasm.
• Diagnosis: slit lamp inspection, fluorescein staining highlighting epithelial damage, and visual acuity and intraocular pressure.
(c)
Untreated, it can lead to keratitis (infection), corneal ulceration, scarring and vision loss; it is common in construction workers, athletes and those in dusty environments.
(d)
• Medical: topical antibiotics, lubricating drops or ointments, cycloplegics for pain and photophobia, oral analgesics and sometimes patching.
• Nursing diagnoses: acute pain related to corneal injury, and risk for infection related to compromised corneal integrity.
• Care plan: assess pain with a standard scale and describe discomfort; the objective is relief of pain after 20 to 30 minutes, evaluated as relief reported after 25 minutes.
• Education: avoid eye rubbing, correct contact lens hygiene, correct use of eye medicines and eye protection.
• Regular assessment of pain, visual acuity, infection and healing.

questions.question:
Hypertensive retinopathy:
(a) Describe its pathophysiology.
(b) State how its stages relate to clinical manifestations and diagnostic findings.
(c) Explain how it progresses to other systems or causes functional deficit.
(d) State the nursing care plan, health education and management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Long-standing high blood pressure makes retinal vessels tighten (vasospasm), narrowing the lumen and limiting blood flow; over time vessels grow stiff and thick, and continued hypertension causes vision loss.
• The higher the pressure and the longer it has been high, the more severe the damage.
(b)
• Stage 1: brighter arteriolar reflexes, vascular distension and tortuosity (silver wiring), no parenchymal changes. Stage 2: generalized narrowing, arteriovenous nicking, distended tortuous venules, fine retinal hemorrhages.
• Stage 3: thin threadlike arterioles, rosary-like constrictions, Siegrist's streaks, cotton wool spots, hard exudates (macular star), hemorrhages and optic disk edema. Stage 4: stage 3 changes over the entire fundus, bilateral papilledema, retinal edema and exudative detachment.
• Symptoms: double or dim vision, headaches, visual disturbances, sudden vision loss; tests: ophthalmoscopy, fluorescein angiography, fundus photography, optical coherence tomography and blood pressure measurement.
(c)
• Optic disc edema from severely elevated blood pressure can indicate impending stroke or death; hypertension is a risk factor for cardiac, cerebrovascular, renal and eye disease.
• Complications: worsening vision or blindness, macular edema, ischemic optic neuropathy, retinal detachment, retinal artery or vein occlusion and malignant hypertension.
(d)
• Nursing: comprehensive assessment (visual acuity, intraocular pressure, fundoscopy, blood pressure history), regular blood pressure monitoring, medication management, documentation, follow-up and referral.
• Education: importance of blood pressure control, adherence to antihypertensives, lifestyle change (quit smoking, exercise, weight loss, fruit, vegetables, less salt, caffeine and alcohol) and medicines such as diuretics, beta-blockers or ACE inhibitors.
• Prevention: yearly check-ups, managing blood pressure, avoiding smoking, regular exercise.
• Nursing diagnoses: decreased cardiac output related to vasospasm of retinal vessels, and deficient knowledge.

questions.question:
Ophthalmic drug administration:
(a) Describe the routes and forms of ocular drugs.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities and rationale for eye drop instillation.
(c) Explain why drug loss occurs and how absorption is improved.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Local routes: topical, intravitreous, subconjunctival, subtenon, retrobulbar and intracameral; systemic routes also exist; the blood-aqueous and blood-retinal barriers limit entry.
• Forms: solution and suspension (most common), ointment and gel.
• Solutions and suspensions are easily instilled, interfere less with vision and have fewer complications, but have short ocular contact time, imprecise delivery, frequent contamination and a possibility of ocular injury.
(b)
• One drop is enough because the cul-de-sac holds only 7 to 10 microlitres and a drop is about 50 microlitres; only about 20% of the instilled drug is retained.
• Apply digital pressure at the medial canthal area and keep the eyes closed for 5 minutes after drops to improve ocular and decrease systemic absorption; wait 10 minutes between drops.
• Frequency relates to duration of action and order of use relates to pH.
(c)
• Drug is eliminated by the lacrimal gland (tear production, turnover rate 16% per minute), dilution, overflow, drainage, and the nasal cavity with its large surface area; irritating drugs stimulate reflex tearing.
• Factors determining corneal penetration: drug concentration, viscosity, lipid and water solubility, pH, surfactants, reflex tearing, preservative and form.

questions.question:
A patient with an eye tumour has chronic pain from pressure on nerve endings, fatigue, anxiety and bulging of the eye, and surgical removal of the eye (enucleation) is planned.
(a) State the presentation and diagnosis.
(b) State the diagnostic tests and what nurses monitor.
(c) Name the treatment or procedure.
(d) State the pre-operative and post-operative nursing care.
(e) State the complications to watch for.
(f) State the discharge teaching.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Ocular tumour, which may be benign or malignant; warning signs are reduced eyesight, intraocular hemorrhage, bulging eyes, change in iris colour, flashes or double vision and eye pain; often it is initially asymptomatic.
(b)
Physical examination, CT, MRI, ultrasonography and biopsy (used less often); nurses monitor vital signs two hourly during chemotherapy and radiation.
(c)
Radiation therapy (proton beam or plaque), chemotherapy, cryotherapy, brachytherapy and enucleation, followed by reconstruction with an artificial eye or implant.
(d)
• Pre-operative diagnoses: chronic pain (assess pain with a 0 to 10 scale, comfort measures, hot or cold compress, analgesics such as morphine), anxiety (encourage sharing of feelings, calm environment, accurate information) and ineffective health maintenance.
• Post-operative: acute pain, disturbed visual sensory perception and situational low self-esteem; orient to the environment, remove extra furniture, encourage expression of loss, provide sufficient lighting and large print, discuss body-image concerns.
(e)
Risk for injury from impaired vision; sterile wound dressing with normal saline to prevent infection.
(f)
Lie on the back or unoperated side to reduce intraocular pressure; discourage straining at defecation, bending down, hard coughing, sneezing or vomiting; assess visual status in the unaffected eye; adaptation to visual changes within about 2 weeks; free of injury for seven days.

questions.question:
Perioperative hypothermia:
(a) Describe its pathophysiology and risk factors.
(b) State how its stages relate to clinical manifestations.
(c) Explain how it may progress to other systems and cause complications.
(d) State the nursing care and prevention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Hypothermia occurs when the body loses heat faster than it can produce it, causing a dangerous drop in body temperature.
• Risk factors: anesthesia-induced vasodilation (propofol, halothane, isoflurane, desflurane, sevoflurane, nitroglycerin, nitroprusside), exposure of the body cavity, cold operating room, cold infused fluids and poor peripheral circulation.
(b)
• Mild (35 to 32°C): shivering, numbness and confusion.
• Moderate (32 to 28°C): shivering stops, confusion increases and coordination is impaired.
• Severe (below 28°C): loss of consciousness, coma and death.
• Signs include shivering or none in severe cases, disorientation, drowsiness, slurred speech, slow or weak pulse and unresponsiveness.
(c)
Consequences: cardiac arrhythmias and arrest, coagulopathy and bleeding disorders, impaired wound healing and surgical site infections, increased postoperative complications and prolonged recovery and ICU stay.
(d)
• Monitor patient temperature closely and continuously during surgery.
• Prevention: pre-operative warming, intra-operative warming devices (forced-air, warming mattresses), warm IV fluids and irrigation, and a warm operating room.
• In PACU, warming blankets or cooling measures maintain normothermia.

(a)
• Trichiasis is a condition in which lashes grow inwards and rub on the cornea; it may follow blepharitis, trauma or lid surgery; often the cause is unknown but may include blepharitis, infection or entropion.
• Aim of treatment: removal of the offending lashes; options are epilation with forceps (repeated regularly), electrolysis, cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen), argon laser ablation and others.
• Treatment is rarely complete and usually needs repeating at regular intervals.
(b)
• Before: prepare local anaesthetic injection and drops, and assist the doctor or specialist nurse with electrolysis, in which an electrode is introduced into each offending follicle to destroy it.
• After: instil antibiotic ointment following the procedure and inform the patient the eye will be uncomfortable for a few days.
• Check the cornea for abrasions from the ingrowing lashes; if present, use prescribed antibiotic ointment three times a day for three or four days.
• Instruct the patient to return for further epilation as soon as the eye becomes irritated, so complications can be avoided by prompt treatment.
(c)
• Signs: red irritated eye, foreign body sensation, watering, pain on exposure to light; if persistent, corneal scarring can occur.
• Complications: corneal abrasions, corneal ulceration, corneal opacities and vascularisation of the cornea.
• Prevention: prompt repeat epilation when irritation recurs.
questions.question:
Trichiasis:
(a) Describe the medical management and procedures.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities and rationale before, during and after treatment.
(c) Explain the basis of complications and how they are prevented.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors: advanced age, diabetes or kidney disease, family history of malignant hyperthermia, heart disease, hypertension or stroke, lung disease (asthma, COPD), obesity (BMI 30 or more), seizures or neurological disorders, sleep apnea and smoking.
(b)
• Anesthetic awareness: about 1 in 1,000 under general anesthesia are aware of surroundings but unable to move or communicate.
• Atelectasis (collapsed lung); malignant hyperthermia, an inherited dangerous reaction with fever and muscle contractions during surgery; nerve damage causing numbness, weakness or neuropathic pain; postoperative delirium, with confusion lasting about a week in older people.
• Common side effects: drowsiness, sore throat, nausea and vomiting, chills from hypothermia, difficulty urinating, headache, itching, back or muscle pain, and fatigue, usually gone within 24 hours.
(c)
• Four categories: general (unconscious), regional (spinal, epidural, nerve blocks), sedation (mild, moderate, deep) and local anesthesia (for example lidocaine).
• Emergency management and complications handling: general principle that the team monitors patients; Pre-operative: assessment of physical and emotional status, medical history, allergies and cognitive abilities, and teaching on anesthesia and post-operative care.
questions.question:
A patient who is elderly, obese, has diabetes, a history of smoking and sleep apnea, and a family history of malignant hyperthermia, is scheduled for surgery under anesthesia.
(a) State the risk factors for anesthesia complications.
(b) State the potential complications and how to recognize them.
(c) State the nursing and anesthesia management options (by type of anesthesia).

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pharmacological: anti-emetics (ondansetron, metoclopramide, granisetron, dolasetron), anxiolytics (midazolam, lorazepam, diazepam), antihistamines (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine), dexamethasone, and motility agents such as metoclopramide.
• Non-pharmacological: gentle surgical technique, minimal stimulation, adequate hydration, avoiding triggers (opioids, inhalational anesthetics), adequate anesthesia depth, avoiding hypotension and excessive fluid, and monitoring for complications.
(b)
• Administer rescue anti-emetics as needed and monitor and document IONV episodes.
• Give emotional support and reassurance; collaborate with anesthesia and surgical teams to adjust techniques; consider acupressure or acupuncture; manage pain with non-opioid analgesics.
• Continue monitoring for IONV.
(c)
• Pathophysiology is serotonin-mediated stimulation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone then the vomiting center; triggers include anesthetic agents, surgical stimulation and patient factors.
• Complications: aspiration pneumonia, dehydration and electrolyte imbalance, delayed recovery, postoperative complications, anxiety, increased bleeding risk through raised blood pressure, equipment damage, staff exposure to fluids and lengthened stay.
• Prevention: avoiding triggers and non-pharmacological measures above and anti-emetic prophylaxis.
questions.question:
Intraoperative nausea and vomiting:
(a) Describe the medical management.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities.
(c) Explain the basis of complications and how they are prevented.

Pterygium:
(a) Describe the medical management.
(b) Describe the surgical techniques and intra-operative and post-operative care.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities before, during and after treatment.
(d) Explain the basis of the complications and how they are prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Lubricating drops (artificial tears) improve comfort and redness; short-term NSAID or steroid anti-inflammatory drops are used for an inflamed pterygium under an eye specialist's supervision.
(b)
• Surgery is the main treatment if severe or vision is affected; techniques include bare sclera, rotational conjunctival flap, limbal conjunctival autograft, amniotic membrane graft and free conjunctival autograft.
• Intra-operative: usually local anaesthetic as a day-stay procedure taking about half an hour; the pterygium is excised and healthy conjunctival tissue from under the upper lid is transplanted, held by fibrin glue or stitches, lowering recurrence to about one in fifty.
• Post-operative: an eye patch overnight, drops about four times daily for 4 to 8 weeks, painkillers for the first one to two days, and the eye may look red for up to a month.
(c)
• Before: take health history and assess; reassure and allay fears; educate patient and relatives on the disease and treatment; ensure informed consent; explain the procedure and post-operative instructions.
• During and after: encourage adherence to drops and eye patch use; give prescribed post-operative pain relief; assist with activities of daily living if vision is impaired.
• Education and comfort: teach UV protection (sunglasses, hats), regular eye exams, eye hygiene and lubrication; discourage scratching, contact lens use or other irritants for patient comfort.
(d)
• Complications: recurrence after removal, corneal ulcers or perforation, vision loss or blindness if untreated, and chronic eye irritation.
• Recurrence arises from reactivation of the inflammatory process, sometimes enhanced by surgical trauma; the graft reduces the recurrence risk.
• Prevention: UV-protective sunglasses, eye protection from dust and wind, avoiding eye rubbing, and keeping eyes moist with artificial tears.
• Early detection and treatment help alleviate symptoms and prevent complications.

questions.question:
A patient has red, irritated, watering eyes with a foreign body sensation and pain in light because eyelashes grow inwards and rub on the cornea; destruction of the lash follicles is planned.
(a) State the diagnosis and presentation.
(b) State what nurses monitor.
(c) Name the procedures.
(d) State the pre-operative, intra-operative and post-operative nursing care.
(e) State the complications to watch for.
(f) State the discharge teaching.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Trichiasis, in which lashes grow inwards and rub on the cornea, often following blepharitis, trauma or lid surgery; the eye is red and irritated with foreign body sensation, watering and pain in light.
(b)
Nurses check the cornea for abrasions from the ingrowing lashes.
(c)
Epilation with forceps (repeated regularly); electrolysis, where an electrode is introduced to each offending follicle to destroy it; cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen; argon laser ablation.
(d)
• Pre-operative: prepare local anaesthetic injection and drops.
• Intra-operative: assist the doctor or specialist nurse in performing electrolysis.
• Post-operative: instil antibiotic ointment and tell the patient the eye will be uncomfortable for a few days.
(e)
Corneal abrasions, corneal ulceration, corneal opacities and vascularisation; scarring of the cornea if the condition persists.
(f)
• If abrasions have occurred, use antibiotic ointment three times a day for three or four days; return for further lash epilation as soon as irritation recurs.
• Treatment is rarely completely curative and usually needs repeating at regular intervals.

questions.question:
Glaucoma:
(a) Describe its pathophysiology.
(b) State how the types relate to clinical manifestations and diagnostic findings.
(c) Explain how it progresses to functional deficit.
(d) State the nursing care plan, health education and complications.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve; aqueous humor normally drains through the drainage angle to keep intraocular pressure stable.
• When the angle does not work or is blocked, fluid builds up, pressure rises and the optic nerve, made of over a million fibers, is damaged; blind spots develop and are not noticed until most fibers have died.
(b)
• Open-angle glaucoma, the most common type, is gradual and painless with no early vision changes; slow loss of peripheral (tunnel) vision is the main loss, which is why it is called the "silent thief of sight".
• Angle-closure glaucoma occurs when the iris blocks the drainage angle; an acute attack brings sudden blurry vision, severe eye or forehead pain, redness, headache, nausea, vomiting and rainbow halos; chronic angle-closure is symptom-free at first.
• Other types: normal-tension (optic nerve damage with normal pressure), congenital (present at birth), and secondary (steroids, uveitis, diabetes, eye injury).
• Diagnosis needs a complete eye exam: tonometry, gonioscopy, dilated exam, optical coherence tomography, pachymetry, slit-lamp, visual acuity and visual field (perimetry).
(c)
As fibers die, peripheral vision is lost, advanced glaucoma leads to blindness and all damage is permanent; about 1 in 10 people develop some visual impairment and 5% blindness.
(d)
• Nursing care plan: provide patient safety, assess vision, educate on eye-drop compliance and follow-up, and manage anxiety; Management includes daily pressure-lowering eye drops and surgery: laser trabeculoplasty (open-angle), laser iridotomy (angle-closure), trabeculectomy with a filtration bleb, cataract surgery for narrow angles, and drainage implants.
• Health education: regular screening (every 1 to 3 years for high-risk people after 35, more often with age) and reporting drop side effects.
• Complication summary: visual impairment and blindness.

questions.question:
Post-anaesthesia care:
(a) Describe the medical management and phases of care.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities and rationale on admission, during recovery and at discharge from the PACU.
(c) Explain the basis of complications and how they are prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Post-anaesthesia care manages patients after surgery and anaesthesia in the PACU, aiming to return the patient to a safe physiologic level.
• Phase 1: immediate post-anaesthesia period with one-on-one care; Phase 2: continued recovery when consciousness returns to baseline and pulmonary, cardiac and renal functions are stable; Phase 3: extended observation.
• Medical management after a colon resection: pain medicines, clear liquids advancing to regular diet, wound care, activity to prevent clots and physical therapy; pre-surgical bowel preparation and antibiotics.
(b)
• Admission: the circulating nurse calls the PACU nurse; hand-off report from anesthesia provider, surgeon and circulating nurse; then rapid assessment of airway, breathing and circulation, vital signs, pain, neurological status, nausea and vomiting, urine output and dressing and drains.
• During recovery: frequent vital signs, reassess pain, turn and ambulate to prevent pneumonia and clots, maintain IV fluids and normothermia, manage nausea with antiemetics, document and act as advocate.
• Discharge criteria: stable vital signs, pain control, adequate oxygenation and ability to meet basic needs; a physician is responsible for discharge.
(c)
• Benefits: early detection of complications, reduced morbidity and mortality, shorter stays and fewer infections.
• Watch for respiratory depression, bleeding or allergic reactions; continuous monitoring allows early prevention.
• Nursing diagnoses: ineffective breathing pattern related to anesthetic agent and risk for surgical site infection.

questions.question:
A child has an eye that deviates inward while the other looks straight ahead, and surgery to realign the eye muscles is planned.
(a) State the diagnosis and presentation.
(b) State the diagnostic tests and what nurses monitor.
(c) Name the medication or surgical procedures.
(d) State the pre-operative and post-operative nursing care.
(e) State the complications to watch for.
(f) State the discharge teaching.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Strabismus (esotropia, an inward deviation of the eye); symptoms include double vision, eye strain, headaches, inability to read comfortably and unstable vision; the brain may ignore one eye, causing loss of depth perception.
(b)
General eye exam (ptosis, pupil irregularities), visual acuity tests suited to age, stereoacuity tests, the Hirschberg test (corneal light reflex) for manifest strabismus, and the Krimsky test for angle of deviation; nurses check for amblyopia, impaired binocularity and incomitance.
(c)
Glasses, prism lenses, exercises, botulinum toxin injections, patching and orthoptic therapy; surgery: recession, resection, plication, transposition, adjustable suture, minimally invasive and robotic-assisted surgery.
(d)
• Pre-operative: history of risk factors (prematurity, family history, perinatal complications) and physical exam; orientation to surroundings.
• Prevent injury: call light within reach, respond immediately, place near nurses' station, bright labels for important places.
(e)
Constant unilateral strabismus risks amblyopia in children.
(f)
Teach safe ambulation at home with handrails and labelled places; patch therapy and vision therapy; health education tailored to learning style, including caregivers.

(a)
• Medical: inspection first to know severity; cleansing and repair of wounds; cold compresses early followed by warm compresses; NSAIDs and corticosteroids.
• Surgical: hematomas causing significant orbital pressure may be surgically drained or evacuated; orbital fractures most often need repair.
• Surgery is usually non-emergent, done 10 to 14 days after injury to let the ophthalmologist assess ocular function (extraocular muscles, nasolacrimal duct); emergency repair is unusual unless the globe is displaced into the maxillary sinus.
• Repair frees entrapped ocular structures and restores orbital floor integrity; cosmetic surgery for deformities and enophthalmos may follow after 4 to 6 months.
(b)
• Take history as soon as the patient stabilizes (duration, nature of work, exposure to risk); assess the globe and meticulously assess the face for underlying fractures, always suspected in blunt trauma.
• Position semi-Fowler at 30 degrees to reduce intracranial pressure; monitor vital signs for a hint of impending trouble.
• Give protein- and vitamin-rich food for wound healing; give analgesics, antibiotics for foreign objects and anti-inflammatories; encourage rest.
(c)
• Orbital roof fractures endanger the brain; blow-out fractures may entrap the inferior rectus, causing enophthalmos; blunt injuries carry more retinal detachment and herniation.
• Retained copper, iron or vegetable foreign bodies cause purulent infection and are removed.
• Prevention is preferable to treatment of injury; MRI is contraindicated if a foreign body is metallic.
• Nursing diagnoses: acute pain and risk for injury.
questions.question:
Ocular and orbital trauma:
(a) Describe the medical and surgical management.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities and rationale.
(c) Explain the basis of complications and how they are prevented.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Assess pain with a standard intensity scale and ask the patient to describe the discomfort; assess for signs of infection, visual acuity and intraocular pressure; findings are gritty sensation, redness, tearing, photophobia, blurred vision and blepharospasm.
(b)
• Acute pain related to corneal injury secondary to abrasion, evidenced by patient report of pain.
• Risk for infection related to compromised corneal integrity and exposure to environmental contaminants.
(c)
The protective corneal epithelium is disrupted, exposing nerve endings (pain) and impairing transparency and refraction; healing goes through latent, migration, proliferation and reattachment phases.
(d)
• Pain: assess pain with a scale (baseline data), modify the environment to minimize discomfort, change position within limits (reduces pressure), and administer prescribed analgesics such as paracetamol (pharmacological pain relief).
• Infection: assess for signs and history of surgery (breaks in the first line of defence), monitor and report redness, swelling and increased pain, monitor white blood cell count, and assess nutritional status, weight and serum albumin.
• Also give topical antibiotics, lubricating drops, cycloplegics and patching as prescribed; teach avoiding eye rubbing and contact lens hygiene.
(e)
• Outcomes: relief of pain after 20 to 30 minutes; no sign of infection during hospitalization.
• Evaluation: patient verbalized relief of pain after 25 minutes and did not show any sign of infection during hospitalization.
questions.question:
A patient has a corneal abrasion from a scratch to the surface of the eye, with a gritty sensation, redness, tearing, photophobia and blurred vision.
(a) State the priority nursing assessment findings.
(b) State the nursing diagnoses.
(c) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(d) State the priority nursing interventions with rationale.
(e) State the expected outcomes and evaluation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Significant and potentially life-threatening bleeding during surgery, arising from vessel trauma, surgical errors or underlying medical conditions.
(b)
Trauma to blood vessels, poor surgical technique (inadequate hemostasis), coagulopathy, infection, hypotension, vascular abnormalities, organ injury, systemic diseases such as liver disease or hematological disorders, and improper instrumentation.
(c)
Hypotension, tachycardia, pale skin, cool and clammy skin, decreased urine output, restlessness or anxiety, altered mental status, oliguria or anuria, and visible bleeding in the field or drains.
(d)
• Uncontrolled bleeding causes hemodilution, hypothermia, consumption of clotting factors and acidosis, which worsen clotting in a vicious cycle.
• Investigations: CBC, coagulation profile (PT, APTT, fibrinogen), blood gas analysis, ultrasound, CT scan and X-ray.
(e)
Patients with coagulopathy (pre-existing or induced by medications or conditions), liver disease, hematological disorders, infection or vascular abnormalities are more vulnerable.
(f)
• WHO grading: Grade 0 no bleeding; 1 petechial; 2 mild clinically significant loss; 3 gross loss requiring transfusion; 4 debilitating loss, retinal or cerebral, associated with fatality.
• ATLS Class I: up to 15% blood volume, no change in vital signs; Class II: 15 to 30%, tachycardia and narrowed pulse pressure.
• Class III: 30 to 40%, blood pressure drops, heart rate rises, perfusion and mental status worsen; Class IV: over 40%, limit of compensation reached and aggressive resuscitation needed.
• WHO grades severity of bleeding, whereas ATLS classes are based on percentage of blood volume lost.
• Consequences include hypovolemic shock, organ dysfunction, coagulopathy and metabolic acidosis.
questions.question:
Major intraoperative hemorrhage:
(a) Define it and describe its classification.
(b) State its causes.
(c) State its clinical manifestations.
(d) Describe its pathophysiology and diagnostic investigations.
(e) Explain why certain patients are more vulnerable.
(f) Distinguish between the WHO and the ATLS classifications.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Blepharitis is an acute or chronic inflammation of the lid margins, usually bilateral, classified as anterior or posterior; causes are staphylococcal chronic infection and seborrhoeic excessive lipid secretion from meibomian glands.
• Possible associations: dandruff, poor hygiene, eczema, allergy to make-up or drugs.
(b)
• Signs: red swollen lid margins, scales and crusted lashes, irritation, burning, itching, loss of lashes, watery eyes, sticking eyelids and blurred vision improving with blinking.
• Complications: conjunctivitis, trichiasis, entropion or ectropion of the lower lid in severe cases, and corneal ulcer.
(c)
• Cleaning the eyelids: irrigate and clean lid margin and lashes with normal saline using good quality cotton swabs; antibiotic ointment along the lid margin two or three times a day if severe.
• Treat dandruff with antidandruff shampoo; stop or change make-up, remove all make-up at day's end, discard eye make-up including mascara every 3 months; stop causative drugs.
• Teach hygiene to hair, face and hands; apply a warm clean face cloth over closed eyelids for soreness and itching, repeating when heat goes.
• Priority: lid cleaning and hygiene, which are central to treatment, aimed at relief of itchiness, discharge and burning.
questions.question:
A patient has red, swollen lid margins with scales on the lashes, burning, itching, eyelids sticking together and blurred vision that improves with blinking; the patient uses eye make-up, has dandruff and poor hygiene.
(a) State the risk factors.
(b) State the potential complications and how they are recognized.
(c) State the nursing and medical management options and justify the priority intervention.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Prevention needs early diagnosis and physical medicine such as passive range of motion and splinting before contractures are present or while mild.
• Prophylaxis: daily standing or walking, passive stretching of muscles and joints, positioning to promote extension and oppose flexion, and splinting to prevent or delay contractures.
• Occupational therapy management of wrist and hand range of motion slows contractures and maintains fine motor skills.
• Advanced contractures become fixed, respond little to stretching or splinting and may require surgery.
(b)
• Prophylaxis aims to maintain function, range of motion and skin integrity.
• Symptom assessment: pain, joint and muscle rigidity, reduced movements, weakness and limited use.
(c)
• Contracture develops when elastic tissue is replaced by nonstretchy fiber-like tissue; after injury, muscles contract protectively and stay contracted.
• Extrinsic factors: reduced use, static positioning for prolonged periods and muscle imbalance; intrinsic factors: fibrotic changes to muscle; also scarring after trauma or burns and congenital myopathies.
• Lower limb contractures are much more prevalent than upper limb; contractures are inevitable in some neuromuscular diseases.
• Static positioning is an important cause, so regular positioning and movement prevent formation.
questions.question:
Contractures:
(a) Describe the medical and surgical management and prevention.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities and rationale.
(c) Explain the basis of contracture and how it is prevented.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pre-operative teaching is a nursing intervention that improves patients' knowledge, health behaviors and outcomes before surgery by explaining the procedure, anesthesia and recovery.
• Goals: reduce anxiety and fear, promote understanding, improve post-operative outcomes, enhance cooperation, support informed consent, pain management, wound care and infection prevention, medication management and lifestyle modification.
(b)
Components: assessment, information sharing, demonstration and return demonstration, written instructions, emotional support, family involvement, cultural sensitivity and evaluation.
(c)
Methods: face-to-face education, written instructions, visual aids, group classes, telehealth, demonstrations, return demonstrations, teaching aids, computer-based learning and family involvement.
(d)
• Challenges: limited time and resources, patient anxiety and stress, complexity of procedures, limited health literacy, language barriers, cultural and individual differences, cognitive or sensory impairments, high patient volume and outdated materials.
• Difficulty evaluating patient understanding is also a challenge.
(e)
• Demonstration showcases equipment, techniques or self-care activities such as wound dressing.
• Return demonstration has patients perform a task themselves (for example injecting insulin) to show understanding.
• Strategies: individualized and multimodal teaching, simplification, active learning and technology.
• Perioperative nurses assess, educate, prepare, support, advocate, coordinate, document and evaluate.
questions.question:
Pre-operative teaching:
(a) Define it and state its goals.
(b) State its components.
(c) State its methods.
(d) Explain the challenges that make certain patients harder to teach.
(e) Distinguish demonstration from return demonstration.

Strain:
(a) Describe its pathophysiology.
(b) State how its classification relates to clinical manifestations and diagnostic findings.
(c) Explain how it may progress to complications and functional deficit.
(d) State the nursing care plan, health education and management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• With sudden eccentric muscle tension, damage occurs beneath the epimysium and at the muscle attachment to the periosteum; creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase are released.
• Inflammatory mediators (histamine, serotonin, bradykinin, prostaglandin) increase capillary permeability and stimulate pain receptors, causing edema; acute inflammation lasts 3 to 4 days.
• Phases: destruction (myofibril necrosis and hematoma), repair and remodeling (phagocytosis and scar tissue), and remodeling (maturation and recovery of function).
(b)
• First degree: few fibers torn, mild tenderness, no strength loss; second degree: nearly half torn, painful with limited motion; third degree: complete rupture with severe pain or limited movement.
• Signs: swelling, bruising, pain at rest and on use, and weakness; diagnosis is by examination and X-ray to exclude fracture.
(c)
Early complications are deep vein thrombosis and compartment syndrome; intermediate are early recurrences, myositis ossificans, rhabdomyolysis and infection; delayed is post-traumatic fibrosis.
(d)
• Care: RICE (cold 20 to 30 minutes in the first 24 to 48 hours, compression, elevation), acetaminophen, heat after 24 to 48 hours, progressive exercises in 2 to 5 days; severe strains need 1 to 3 weeks of immobilization.
• Nursing diagnoses: acute pain, impaired physical mobility and activity intolerance; nursing care includes reassuring, supporting the area with pillows, teaching ambulatory devices, assisting with daily living, and a calcium, vitamin and protein diet.
• Care plan goals: pain reduction within 30 to 45 minutes and improved mobility within 3 to 4 days.
• Excessive early exercise delays recovery; strains take weeks to months to heal.

questions.question:
Diabetic retinopathy:
(a) Describe its pathophysiology.
(b) State how its stages relate to clinical manifestations and diagnostic findings.
(c) Explain how it progresses to cause complications and functional deficit.
(d) State the nursing care, health education and medical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Diabetes causes abnormal glucose metabolism, and high blood glucose shunts glucose into the aldose reductase pathway, producing sorbitol that affects the pericytes of retinal capillaries.
• Pericytes lose their autoregulation function, causing weakness and saccular outpouching of capillary walls; these microaneurysms are the earliest detectable sign.
(b)
• NPDR, the early stage: tiny vessels leak and the retina swells; macular swelling (macular edema) is the most common reason for vision loss; vessels may close (macular ischemia) and exudates form, blurring vision.
• PDR, the advanced stage: neovascularization, with fragile new vessels bleeding into the vitreous (few dark floaters if slight, blocked vision if heavy); scar tissue forms and can cause macular problems or retinal detachment, stealing central and peripheral vision.
• Signs: blurry or double vision, dark or floating spots, flashing lights, blank spots, trouble seeing in the dark; tests: visual acuity, tonometry, pupil dilation, ophthalmoscopy, fluorescein angiography and optical coherence tomography.
(c)
• Complications: vitreous hemorrhage, glaucoma from new vessels, retinal detachment from scar tissue pulling the retina, and macular edema with severe, sometimes permanent, vision impairment.
• The longer a person has diabetes, especially if poorly controlled, the more likely retinopathy; it usually affects both eyes.
(d)
• Medical: laser to treat new vessels (stabilizes but rarely improves vision), anti-VEGF injections (ranibizumab, aflibercept), dexamethasone intravitreal implant, and vitreoretinal surgery for blood or scar tissue.
• Nursing: monitor blood pressure and respiratory rate, monitor for hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, promote a healthy weight, and promote physical activity, which lowers blood glucose.
• Education: teach home glucose monitoring, assist with meal planning (less carbohydrate, processed food and sugar; more fruit, vegetables, lean protein and whole grains).
• Screening: encourage ophthalmologist eye screening at six months and reporting worsening symptoms.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old first-time mother with no significant past medical history, a non-smoker who drinks occasionally, is to have an elective Cesarean section under spinal or epidural anesthesia.
(a) State the presentation and diagnosis or indication.
(b) State what nurses monitor and assess.
(c) State the procedure and anesthesia named.
(d) State the pre-operative and post-operative nursing care.
(e) State the complications to watch for.
(f) State the discharge teaching.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Yemi is a generally healthy 28-year-old with a first pregnancy, uncomplicated until the decision for a Cesarean section.
(b)
Pre-operative: baseline vital signs and fetal heart rate; ensure she understands the procedure and post-operative expectations. Post-operative: vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation), uterine contraction, lochia and pain levels.
(c)
Cesarean section under spinal or epidural anesthesia so that she is awake and alert during the birth.
(d)
• Pre-operative: emotional support to reduce anxiety.
• Immediate post-operative: IV pain medicine, keep the airway open and breathing comfortable, assist bonding and breastfeeding, explain procedures, and newborn APGAR, temperature and breastfeeding support.
• Postpartum ward: oral pain medicines (acetaminophen, ibuprofen), IV fluids until oral intake, early mobilization, clear liquids advancing to regular diet, deep breathing exercises.
• Ongoing: regular pain assessment, daily wound inspection with dressing changes per protocol, compression stockings and early ambulation, incentive spirometry and deep breathing.
(e)
Hemorrhage or adverse reactions to anesthesia; signs of infection (redness, swelling, discharge); blood clots; atelectasis and pneumonia.
(f)
• Discharge criteria: stable vital signs, pain controlled on oral medicines, tolerating oral intake, ambulating independently or with minimal help, feeding initiated.
• Teach medication regimen, avoiding heavy lifting for at least 6 weeks, keeping the wound clean and dry, postpartum depression, infection signs, baby care, and follow-up with the obstetrician and pediatrician.
• Provide contact information for questions after discharge.

questions.question:
A patient has had a surgical procedure and on the fifth post-operative day the wound shows signs of infection.
(a) State the risk factors for surgical site infection.
(b) State the potential complications and how they are recognized.
(c) State the nursing and medical management options and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Most infections arise from the patient's own flora on skin, mucous membranes or hollow viscera; the incision is the portal of entry, and contaminated surfaces, instruments and hands can be reservoirs or modes of transmission.
• Patient factors: poorly controlled glucose, poor nutrition, smoking and stress; immunocompromised patients are susceptible to fungi such as Candida.
(b)
• Recognition: superficial infection (skin and subcutaneous tissue) shows purulent discharge, organism identified or surgeon diagnosis; deep infection shows purulent discharge, dehiscence or abscess on CT; organ/space infection shows drain pus or CT abscess.
• Consequences: morbidity, poor cosmetic outcomes, persistent pain and itching, restricted movement and emotional impact.
(c)
• Prevention: antibiotic prophylaxis (for example cefazolin), chlorhexidine skin preparation, clipping rather than shaving hair, strict aseptic technique and hand hygiene, sterile dressings and wound care.
• Optimizing glucose, nutritional support, preoperative smoking cessation and stress reduction; change gloves and instruments before closure.
• Nursing: assess for signs of infection such as erythema, edema, abnormal discharge and foul odor, monitor drainage, use aseptic dressing techniques, give antibiotics and educate the patient on wound care.
• Priority: aseptic technique and hand hygiene, because they break the chain of infection at each stage.

(a)
• Take baseline vital signs and a history of injury, including the mechanism of injury, to determine severity; take a health history because sprains can be confused with fractures or bone bruises.
• Expected findings: intense pain, swelling, bruising or hematoma, joint instability, restricted mobility, difficulty bearing weight, decreased range of motion, and a cracking or popping sound when a ligament ruptures.
(b)
• Acute pain related to pressure on nerve endings, evidenced by patient report of pain.
• Impaired physical mobility related to joint instability, evidenced by inability to walk with the affected limb.
• Deficient knowledge related to unfamiliarity with treatment modalities, evidenced by questions such as "will I be able to walk again".
(c)
A sprain is stretching or tearing of a ligament; grade I is minor stretching with mild swelling and no instability; grade II is a partial tear with moderate swelling and some instability; grade III is a complete rupture (sometimes avulsing bone) with severe instability. A ligament takes about six weeks to heal.
(d)
• Pain: assess vital signs, pain level and characteristics (baseline data); ensure bed rest and reposition (optimal comfort); teach deep breathing and diversional therapy such as music (reduce pain); give prescribed analgesics (block the pain pathway).
• RICE: rest to reduce inflammation; ice pack wrapped in a wet cloth for 15 minutes every 2 hours for 24 hours (reduces pain and swelling); firm elastic compression bandage (support, reduces swelling); elevation (reduces swelling, promotes circulation); brace or cast in severe cases.
• Mobility: assess mobility level (early recognition), reassure (relieves anxiety), change position 3 hourly (enhances circulation), assist range-of-motion exercises (reduce muscle rigidity), give a calorie- and protein-rich diet (energy and cell regeneration).
• Knowledge: assess level of knowledge and best mode of learning, reassure, and educate on the condition and treatment (improves understanding and cooperation).
(e)
• Outcomes: pain reduced to 2/10 within 40 minutes; assisted with activities of daily living at first and later performs mobility gradually within range of motion; verbalizes increased knowledge within 45 to 60 minutes.
• Evaluation: patient verbalized pain reduction, performed activities of daily living without assistance, and verbalized increased knowledge on the condition and treatment after nursing intervention.
questions.question:
A patient presents with pain, swelling, bruising, an unstable joint and difficulty bearing weight after the joint was suddenly forced beyond its usual range of movement; a cracking or popping sound was heard at the time of injury.
(a) State the priority nursing assessment findings you would collect.
(b) Identify the nursing diagnoses.
(c) Explain the pathophysiological basis of the condition, including its grades.
(d) State the priority nursing interventions with the rationale for each.
(e) State the expected outcomes and how you would evaluate them.

During surgery a patient has sudden pulsatile bleeding, swelling around the injured area, a pale cool limb, an absent distal pulse and numbness after accidental damage to a blood vessel.
(a) State the risk factors or causes.
(b) State the potential complications and how they are recognized.
(c) State the nursing and medical management options and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Vascular injury from surgical trauma (accidental cutting, tearing or puncturing), clamping or ligating errors, electrocautery complications, graft handling, compression or tension from retractors, poor visualization, and inadvertent dissection.
(b)
• Recognition: external or pulsatile bleeding, pain, swelling, pallor, pulselessness, numbness or tingling and decreased range of motion.
• Consequences: hemorrhage leading to hypovolemic shock, loss of perfusion with limb ischemia or loss, organ dysfunction, infection, delayed recovery, long-term complications and increased mortality.
(c)
• Medical: immediate recognition; control hemorrhage by direct pressure or clamping proximal and distal to the injury; notify vascular surgery; fluid resuscitation; imaging (CT angiography or ultrasound); blood products; prophylactic antibiotics.
• Nursing: monitor vital signs for shock, inspect the site, do a neurovascular assessment (distal pulses, capillary refill); inform the surgical team; apply direct pressure with sterile gauze and elevate the limb; tourniquets only under surgical guidance.
• Prepare equipment (blood products, IV fluids, clamps, suture materials), ensure IV access, and monitor urine output and compartment syndrome.
• Document baseline vital signs, time of injury recognition and responses; support and educate the patient and family.
• Priority: control of bleeding with direct pressure, because time is critical in preventing ischemic complications and the first medical step is direct pressure.

questions.question:
Mrs L, a 45-year-old woman admitted for elective surgery for chronic abdominal pain, was found to be in labour with a breech baby and went to theatre, where a vascular injury occurred, leaving her in pain with weak peripheral pulses and acute blood loss.
(a) State the priority nursing assessment findings.
(b) State the nursing diagnoses.
(c) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(d) State the priority nursing interventions with rationale.
(e) State the expected outcomes.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Continuous vital signs for shock (hypotension, tachycardia); inspect for bleeding, swelling or bruising at the site; neurovascular assessment of distal pulses, capillary refill and neurological status; facial expression of pain; absent or weak peripheral pulses; signs of respiratory distress and tachycardia.
(b)
• Acute pain related to vascular system blockage, evidenced by facial expression of pain.
• Ineffective tissue perfusion related to reduced blood flow, evidenced by absent or weak peripheral pulses.
• Risk for decreased cardiac output, evidenced by acute blood loss; risk for impaired gas exchange, evidenced by respiratory distress and tachycardia.
(c)
Direct trauma from instruments, cuts or retraction can range from minor tears to complete lacerations of a vessel wall; penetrating injury involves direct penetration of the vessel wall including by surgical incisions.
(d)
• Apply direct pressure with sterile gauze, elevate the limb, and use pressure dressings or tourniquets only under surgical guidance; inform the surgical team and anesthesia immediately.
• Prepare blood products, IV fluids, clamps and sutures; ensure IV access; monitor urine output and oxygen saturation; monitor for compartment syndrome; document; support and educate the family.
(e)
Outcomes: verbalizes reduced pain within 30 to 45 minutes of nursing intervention; demonstrates adequate tissue perfusion with 3+ peripheral pulses.

questions.question:
On fundoscopy a patient with raised blood pressure has arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nicking, cotton wool spots, hard exudates in a macular star, hemorrhages and swelling of the optic disk.
(a) Identify the affected organ or system.
(b) State the expected changes at each stage and the investigations.
(c) State the complications.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for nursing priorities and escalation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The retina (hypertensive retinopathy), damage from blood pressure higher than the eye can tolerate; it is a target-organ effect of hypertension along with cardiac, cerebrovascular and renal disease.
(b)
• These findings correspond to stage 3: thin threadlike arterioles, rosary-like constrictions, Siegrist's streaks, cotton wool spots, macular star, hemorrhages and optic disk edema; stage 4 adds changes over the entire fundus, bilateral papilledema and exudative retinal detachment.
• Investigations: ophthalmoscopy, fluorescein angiography, fundus photography, OCT and blood pressure measurement.
(c)
Complications: macular edema, ischemic optic neuropathy, retinal detachment, retinal artery or vein occlusion and malignant hypertension.
(d)
• Optic disc edema from severely elevated pressure can indicate impending stroke or death, so this is an escalation trigger.
• Priority: regular blood pressure monitoring and collaboration with the team to set target pressures; administer antihypertensives and monitor side effects.
• Educate on adherence, lifestyle changes (quit smoking, exercise, weight loss, diet) and follow-up.
• Refer to ophthalmologists or retinal specialists for evaluation; close monitoring prevents vision loss.
• Sudden vision loss and headache are symptoms to report; document findings.

questions.question:
Hypoxia in the perioperative period:
(a) Define it and state its classification.
(b) State its causes.
(c) Describe its pathophysiology and consequences.
(d) Explain how it may progress to other systems.
(e) State the prevention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Hypoxia occurs when blood cannot carry enough oxygen to tissues; it is failure of oxygenation at the tissue level; symptoms include rapid breathing, shortness of breath, slower heart rate and changes in skin colour.
• Hypoxemia is arterial oxygen tension below normal (PaO2 80 to 100 mmHg); the two may or may not occur together, though hypoxemia is by far the commonest cause of tissue hypoxia.
• Classes: hypoxemic (insufficient oxygen reaching blood), stagnant or circulatory (decreased flow), anaemic (decreased carrying capacity) and histotoxic (impaired utilisation).
(b)
Causes of hypoxemia are grouped into problems with the oxygen delivery system and problems with the patient.
(c)
• Incidence: even in advanced settings, about 1 in 15 patients experience hypoxia for at least two consecutive minutes during surgery.
• Reduced cerebral oxygen saturation correlates with postoperative complications.
(d)
Consequences: acute heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, acute renal failure, reduced cognitive function and permanent brain damage; time to organ failure depends on the level of oxygen deprivation.
(e)
• Prevention: check the anaesthesia machine before every anesthetic, use machines with an O2 pressure failure alarm, hypoxic guard, oxygen proportioning devices, flow meter tubes downstream and a check valve.
• Related events: intraoperative pneumothorax and hypercapnia (respiratory acidosis) are described as respiratory complications.

(a)
The orbit: orbital cellulitis, an acute purulent inflammation of the cellular tissue of the orbit, and an ophthalmic emergency because of optic nerve compression.
(b)
• Expected changes: proptosis, red inflamed lids, chemosis, reduced visual acuity and colour vision, relative afferent pupil defect, possible double vision, painful limited ocular movements, malaise and fever.
• Investigations: full blood count, urea, electrolytes and glucose; CT scan for subperiosteal and orbital collections and adjacent sinus disease; intraconal opacity without sinus disease suggests trauma or foreign body.
(c)
Preseptal cellulitis (infection of the eyelids only, not beyond the orbital septum); lid oedema is also linked with conjunctivitis, stye, chalazion and drug allergy.
(d)
• Admit, arrange urgent CT of paranasal sinuses, orbits and brain, and refer urgently to ENT; give prescribed antibiotics and analgesia; monitor optic nerve function (visual acuity, pupils, colour vision, light brightness).
• Escalate because infection can spread to the brain (cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess) and cause optic atrophy, panophthalmitis and central retinal vessel occlusion.
• Prepare for incision and drainage if an abscess forms.
questions.question:
A patient with swelling and redness of the eyelids, a bulging eye pushed forward, fever, painful limited eye movements and reduced vision has blood tests and a CT scan requested.
(a) Identify the affected organ or system.
(b) State the expected changes or abnormalities and the investigations.
(c) State the differential conditions.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for nursing priorities and escalation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The musculoskeletal system (ligament, muscle and tendon, or joint).
(b)
• Sprain: ligament stretch or tear with pain, swelling, bruising, instability and popping; X-ray rules out fracture, MRI shows soft tissue and ligaments, CT shows bone detail, and ultrasound shows ligament or tendon condition.
• Strain: muscle or tendon tear at the musculotendinous junction with swelling, bruising, pain at rest and on use, and weakness; X-ray excludes bone break.
• Dislocation: visibly deformed joint, numbness, swelling, limited movement and intense pain; X-ray is the most common test; CT and MRI if needed; nerve conduction and EMG for nerve and muscle.
(c)
Sprains can be confused with fractures or bone bruises; other differentials: fracture and compartment syndrome.
(d)
• Do a neurovascular assessment (pulse, sensation, movement) and monitor for compartment syndrome and infection, which are escalation triggers.
• Manage pain, immobilize with splint, elevate and apply ice; RICE applies to sprain and strain.
• Escalate for severe sprains needing immobilization or surgery, for grade 3 strains needing repair, and for dislocation needing closed reduction or open reduction if that fails.
• Antecedent steps: take history of mechanism of injury to determine severity.
questions.question:
A patient has a painful swollen ankle after a sudden twist; clinicians need to distinguish a ligament injury, a muscle or tendon injury and a displaced joint, and X-ray, MRI and ultrasound are requested.
(a) Identify the affected system.
(b) State the expected changes and investigations for each.
(c) State the differential conditions.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for nursing priorities and escalation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Osteoarthritis, also called osteoarthrosis, is the most common and most disabling degenerative musculoskeletal disease, frequently over-treated or under-treated, with its impact on elderly quality of life often ignored.
(b)
Causes: increased age, obesity, previous joint damage and repetitive use in occupation or recreation.
(c)
• Mechanical injury of the articular cartilage, subchondral bone and synovium; chondrocyte response, cytokine release, and stimulation of proteolytic enzymes, metalloproteases and collagenase; damage triggers further response.
• Degenerative diseases reduce the weight-bearing capacity of the affected organ.
(d)
• Pain from inflamed synovium, stretched capsule, irritated periosteal nerve endings, microfracture and muscle spasm; stiffness in the morning lasting under 30 minutes and easing with movement; functional impairment.
• Diagnosis: physical assessment shows tender swollen joints; X-ray shows narrowed joint space from progressive loss of cartilage; only 30% of patients with X-ray changes report symptoms.
(e)
• Onset often begins in the third decade and peaks in the fifth and sixth; by 40 years 90% have degenerative changes in weight-bearing joints; prevalence is 50 to 80% in the elderly.
• Obese people wear out weight-bearing joints; previous joint damage and congenital hip disease predispose.
(f)
• Primary (idiopathic) osteoarthritis has no prior event or disease related to it.
• Secondary osteoarthritis results from previous joint injury or inflammatory disease.
• Management of each type differs only as given for osteoarthritis generally: heat, weight loss, rest, orthotics, analgesics, osteotomy and arthroplasty.
questions.question:
Osteoarthritis:
(a) Define it and state its classification.
(b) State its causes.
(c) Describe its pathophysiology.
(d) State its clinical manifestations and diagnostic findings.
(e) Explain why certain patients are more vulnerable.
(f) Distinguish between primary and secondary osteoarthritis.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Deformities are deviations from normal body architecture; vertebral types are scoliosis, kyphosis and lordosis; skull deformities come from premature closure of sutures and fontanelles, mainly in children.
• Skull types: plagiocephaly (asymmetry from premature fusion of the coronal or lambdoid suture), trigonocephaly (wedge shape, metopic suture), scaphocephaly (boat shape, sagittal suture) and brachycephaly (wide, both coronal sutures).
(b)
General causes: congenital factors, traumatic injuries, medical conditions and developmental abnormalities.
(c)
Visible alterations in appearance, functional limitations, skeletal misalignments, joint restrictions, muscle imbalances and impaired range of motion; manifestations depend on the nature and origin of the deformity.
(d)
• Scoliosis is most often diagnosed in childhood or early adolescence; lordosis is caused by neuromuscular conditions such as spina bifida and cerebral palsy, congenital issues, hip or pelvic conditions, previous back surgery and poor posture.
• Skull deformities mostly affect children.
(e)
• Scoliosis is an abnormal lateral curvature of the spine treated with braces (milder forms) or surgery.
• Kyphosis (hunchback) is an increased roundness of the thoracic curve (over 50 degrees); cause is undetermined; treatment: physical therapy, lifestyle change, braces for up to a year and surgery.
• Lordosis is excessive curvature giving a "swayback" appearance, mostly lumbar.
• Some lordosis is normal in the neck and low back; it is a problem when excessive.
questions.question:
Deformities of the spine and skull:
(a) Define deformities and describe vertebral and skull types.
(b) State the causes.
(c) State the clinical manifestations.
(d) Explain why certain patients are more vulnerable.
(e) Distinguish kyphosis from lordosis and scoliosis.

A patient struck in the eye by a blunt object has pain and difficulty moving the eye, double vision, bruising and swelling of the eyelids, facial numbness, a sunken eyeball, and nausea and vomiting worsened by eye movement.
(a) Identify the affected structures.
(b) State the expected changes and the investigations.
(c) State the differential injury types.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for nursing priorities and escalation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The orbit and its contents: a blow-out fracture of the orbital floor, where compression of soft tissue and sudden rise in orbital pressure transmit force to the orbital floor (area of least resistance).
(b)
• The inferior rectus and inferior oblique muscles, fat and fascia may become entrapped and the globe displaced inward (enophthalmos); typical causes are blunt small objects such as a fist, knee, elbow, tennis or golf balls.
• Manifestations: pain and difficulty moving the eye, blurred or double vision, bruising, eyelid swelling, facial numbness, nausea or vomiting worsened by eye movement, bulging or sunken eyeballs and lacerations.
• Investigations: complete eye examination, facial X-rays, CT scan, ultrasonography, slit-lamp and indirect ophthalmoscopy for intraocular foreign bodies, and MRI (contraindicated if the foreign body is metallic).
(c)
Differentials: orbital roof fracture (dangerous for the brain), zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture, soft tissue injury with subconjunctival hemorrhage, orbital or intraocular foreign bodies, penetrating injury, blunt injury (hyphema, retinal detachment) and ocular contusion.
(d)
• Suspect underlying fractures in all blunt trauma; take history once stable; assess the globe and face meticulously.
• Position semi-Fowler at about 30 degrees to reduce intracranial pressure and monitor vital signs, which hint at impending trouble.
• Give analgesics, antibiotics if a foreign body and anti-inflammatories; cold then warm compresses; encourage rest and protein and vitamin-rich food.
• Escalation: orbital roof fracture risk to the brain, globe displaced into the maxillary sinus (emergency repair), expanding hematoma causing significant orbital pressure (drainage); otherwise repair is non-emergent at 10 to 14 days.

(a)
Abnormal cells divide and multiply, starting with DNA mutations that activate oncogenes or inactivate tumour suppressor genes, cell cycle dysregulation, avoidance of apoptosis, sustained growth signals and angiogenesis.
(b)
• Types: benign (chalazion, nevi, hemangioma) and malignant (choroidal melanoma, the commonest primary malignant tumour in adults, and retinoblastoma in children).
• WHO classification: epithelial tumours (most common, ocular surface), melanocytic tumours, hematolymphoid tumours, soft tissue tumours, hamartomas and choristomas, and secondary tumours.
• Warning signs: reduced eyesight, intraocular hemorrhage, bulging eyes, change in iris colour, light flashes or double vision and eye pain; tests: physical exam, CT, MRI, ultrasonography and biopsy (used less often).
(c)
• Invasion occurs when cells degrade the extracellular matrix, lose adhesion and enter the bloodstream to form secondary tumours at distant sites.
• Tumours in the eye are usually secondary from breast, lung, bowel or prostate cancer.
(d)
• Pre-operative nursing diagnoses: chronic pain, fatigue and anxiety; post-operative: acute pain, disturbed sensory perception (visual) and situational low self-esteem.
• Care: sterile dressing with saline and non-adhesive pads, adequate diet, two-hourly vital signs during chemotherapy and radiation, help with daily living, analgesics, education and emotional support.
• Post-enucleation: lie on the back or unoperated side, avoid straining, bending and coughing, orient to the environment and remove extra furniture.
• Rehabilitation: reconstructive surgery with artificial eye or implants; sufficient lighting and large print; adaptation within 2 weeks.
questions.question:
Ocular tumours:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology.
(b) State how the types and WHO classification relate to clinical manifestations and diagnostic findings.
(c) Explain how they may progress or spread.
(d) State the nursing care plan, health education and rehabilitation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Osteomyelitis is a bone infection; bacteria travel through the bloodstream from an infection elsewhere (pneumonia, abscessed tooth, urinary tract infection), or an open fracture, surgery or open wound over a bone exposes the bone.
• Risk factors that weaken the immune system: diabetes (most cases stem from diabetes), sickle cell disease, HIV or AIDS, rheumatoid arthritis, intravenous drug use, alcoholism, long-term steroids, hemodialysis, poor blood supply and recent injury.
• Open wounds over bone are most common with peripheral vascular disease, peripheral neuropathy or diabetes; it affects about 2 in every 10,000 people.
(b)
• Recognition: fever, irritability, fatigue, nausea, tenderness, redness and warmth, swelling around the bone and lost range of motion; vertebral infection shows severe back pain, especially at night; acute osteomyelitis develops over 7 to 10 days.
• Complications: the infection can spread further or become so severe that amputation is the only remaining option.
(c)
• Investigations: X-rays, blood tests, bone scans, and a bone biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and identify the organism so the right medicine is prescribed.
• Treatment aims to stop infection and preserve function with antibiotics, surgery or both; antibiotics are given for several weeks through an IV then as pills and often avoid surgery.
• More serious or chronic osteomyelitis needs surgery to remove infected tissue and bone.
• Priority: antibiotics, which bring the infection under control; surgery prevents spread or amputation.
questions.question:
A patient with diabetes and an open wound over a bone has fever, fatigue, tenderness, redness, warmth and swelling near a bone and lost range of motion; osteomyelitis is diagnosed.
(a) State the risk factors.
(b) State the potential complications and how they are recognized.
(c) State the nursing and medical or surgical management options and justify the priority intervention.

A patient with moderate to severe osteoarthritis of a weight-bearing joint has severe pain and loss of function, and surgery is being considered.
(a) State the presentation and diagnosis.
(b) State the diagnostic tests and what nurses monitor.
(c) Name the medications and surgical procedures.
(d) State the pre-operative, intra-operative and post-operative nursing care.
(e) State the discharge teaching.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Osteoarthritis with pain, morning stiffness under 30 minutes easing with movement, and functional impairment.
(b)
Physical assessment for tender, swollen joints; X-ray showing narrowing of the joint space; ultrasound; nurses assess pain, BMI, posture, gait, range of motion, crepitus and ability to perform daily activities, and vital signs after activity.
(c)
Acetaminophen first, then NSAIDs, COX-2 blockers, opioids and intra-articular corticosteroids; heat, weight loss, joint rest and orthotics; surgery: osteotomy (alters weight distribution) and arthroplasty (replaces diseased joint components).
(d)
• Pre-operative: assess, reassure, prepare the patient for diagnostic tests; intra-operative: assist during surgical procedures such as osteotomy and arthroplasty.
• Post-operative: pain and analgesic teaching, walking aids, positioning with pillows.
(e)
Teach analgesic and anti-inflammatory side effects, use of a cane in the contralateral hand, weight reduction, footwear, physical and occupational therapy referral, and assessing home barriers such as multiple flights of stairs.

questions.question:
Cataract in diabetic patients:
(a) Describe the medical and surgical management.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities and rationale before, during and after treatment.
(c) Explain the basis of complications and how they are prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Cataract is clouding of the lens; surgery removes the cloudy lens and replaces it with an artificial lens, after which vision is generally better and a new glasses prescription may be needed.
• Diagnosis: visual acuity test, slit lamp eye structure exam, dilated retinal exam, and applanation tonometry.
• Laser treatment (photocoagulation), anti-VEGF medicines and vitrectomy are described for diabetic eye disease: focal/grid laser for macular edema, scatter laser (panretinal photocoagulation) for abnormal vessels, and vitrectomy for severe bleeding or scar tissue.
(b)
• Pre-operative assessment: evaluate diabetes control, medical history and overall health.
• Blood sugar control: keep levels optimal before, during and after surgery; infection prevention through strict infection control to reduce postoperative infection.
• Pain management to prevent complications; wound care with proper dressing changes to promote healing; medication management of diabetes and postoperative medicines.
• Patient education on post-operative care, diabetes management and follow-up; collaborate with surgeon, anesthetist and other professionals.
(c)
• Retrobulbar hemorrhage can result from retrobulbar anaesthetic infiltration if the short ciliary artery is located by the injection.
• Acute bacterial endophthalmitis is a devastating complication occurring in about 1 in 1000 cases; toxic anterior segment syndrome is non-infectious inflammation after anterior chamber surgery.
• Prevention: manage blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol, quit smoking, eat a balanced antioxidant-rich diet, exercise, and have dilated eye exams.
• Good metabolic control may reverse cataract in young diabetics.

(a)
A traumatic force leads to ligamentous injury; the joint capsule is damaged; muscle and tendon involvement causes pain and spasm; the articular cartilage may be damaged; in severe cases bones fracture.
(b)
• Complete dislocation (luxation) separates the bones totally; subluxation is partial.
• Clinical: visibly deformed joint, numbness, swelling, limited movement and intense pain.
• Diagnosis: X-ray, CT for inconclusive X-ray or suspected fracture, MRI for soft tissue damage, nerve conduction studies for nerve damage and EMG for muscle electrical activity.
(c)
• Progression: neurovascular complications where nerves and vessels are compressed or injured, causing sensory changes, numbness and vascular compromise; long-term joint problems from cartilage damage.
• Commonly dislocated joints: fingers, shoulders, knees, elbows, hips and jaws.
(d)
• Nursing diagnoses: acute pain, impaired physical mobility and risk for fall; care includes immobilization, cold in the first 24 to 72 hours, analgesics and range-of-motion exercises.
• Care plan goals: reduce pain after 20 minutes, maintain mobility at the highest possible level after 8 hours, and no falls.
• Health education: diagnosis, treatment and expected recovery time.
• Rehabilitation: physical therapy exercises once healing starts to regain strength, flexibility and range of motion.
• Immobilization lasts from a few weeks to several months.
questions.question:
Dislocation:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology.
(b) State how the types relate to clinical manifestations and diagnostic findings.
(c) Explain how it may progress to other structures and cause functional deficit.
(d) State the nursing care plan, health education and rehabilitation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Assess and record pain intensity with scales such as Wong-Baker FACES, visual analog scale and FLACC; assess the degree of mobility produced by bone displacement, the patient's perception of immobility, and the level of instability.
• Findings: visibly deformed joint, numbness, swelling, limited ability to move, intense pain; neurovascular status (pulse, sensation, movement).
(b)
Acute pain related to soft tissue injury, evidenced by verbalization; impaired physical mobility related to musculoskeletal impairment (dislocation), evidenced by inability to move around; risk for fall evidenced by instability and reduced mobility.
(c)
Traumatic force stretches or tears ligaments, damaging the capsule and allowing bones out of position; muscle and tendon involvement causes pain and spasm; cartilage and bone may be damaged; nerves and vessels may be compressed.
(d)
• Immobilize with bed rest, cast, splint or traction (relieves pain, prevents bone displacement); cold or ice pack in the first 24 to 72 hours (reduces edema and hematoma); analgesics (morphine, ibuprofen 400 mg, ketorolac) block the pain pathway; diversional activities reduce boredom.
• Footboard maintains functional position; active or passive range-of-motion exercises maintain joint motility and prevent contracture or atrophy; self-care enhances control; fluids 2000 to 3000 ml/day reduce urinary infection, stones and constipation.
• Risk for fall: bed rest or limb rest, support the dislocated joint, bed board or orthopedic bed, and side rails.
(e)
• Pain: reduction after 20 minutes of nursing intervention. Mobility: maintain mobility at the highest possible level after 8 hours. Falls: none during hospitalization.
• Evaluation: patient verbalized reduction in pain after 20 minutes, maintained mobility at the highest possible level after 8 hours, and did not experience a fall.
questions.question:
Mrs B has a dislocated hip and has been admitted with pain, inability to move around and an unstable joint.
(a) State the priority nursing assessment findings.
(b) State the nursing diagnoses.
(c) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(d) State the priority nursing interventions with rationale.
(e) State the expected outcomes and evaluation.

Scleritis:
(a) Define it and describe its types.
(b) State its causes and risk factors.
(c) Describe its pathophysiology.
(d) List its clinical manifestations and diagnosis.
(e) Explain why certain patients are more vulnerable.
(f) Distinguish scleritis from episcleritis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Scleritis is a severe, potentially sight-threatening inflammatory disease of the sclera; anterior scleritis is 90% of cases (non-necrotising 75% of these, diffuse or nodular; necrotising 15%, the most severe), and posterior scleritis is 10%.
• Scleromalacia perforans is a painless necrotizing form with a white, avascular, thin sclera where choroidal exposure and staphyloma may occur.
(b)
Idiopathic or associated with autoimmune disease (rheumatoid arthritis most common, vasculitides, lupus, Sjögren's, inflammatory bowel disease), infections (herpes zoster ophthalmicus, Pseudomonas, syphilis, tuberculosis), surgery such as pterygiectomy or cataract surgery, and drugs, most strongly bisphosphonates.
(c)
In autoimmune disease there is zonal scleral necrosis surrounded by granulomatous inflammation and vasculitis, with T-cells and macrophages infiltrating the deep episcleral tissue; infectious scleritis may show microabscesses.
(d)
• Violet-bluish hue with scleral edema; severe dull, boring pain worse with eye movement and at night, radiating to ear, scalp, face and jaw; the globe is tender; posterior disease may show retinal detachment or optic nerve edema.
• Diagnosis is clinical by slit lamp; ultrasonography or CT confirms posterior scleritis; biopsy excludes neoplastic or infective causes.
(e)
• Patients are usually aged 40 to 60, with a male to female ratio of 2:3.
• About 30 to 40% of cases are linked to autoimmune disease and 50% of patients have an autoimmune condition, sometimes undiagnosed; 4 to 10% are infectious.
• Patients after ocular surgery may develop surgery-induced necrotizing scleritis, often with Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
(f)
• Episcleritis is a more superficial inflammation treated with topical medicines such as NSAID drops; scleritis is much more painful and can cause vision loss or illness from an underlying collagen vascular disease.
• Inflamed scleral vessels are adherent and cannot be moved with a cotton-tipped applicator, and deep vessels do not blanch with 2.5 to 10% phenylephrine, unlike superficial episcleral vessels.

questions.question:
Uveitis:
(a) Define it and state its types.
(b) State its causes.
(c) Describe its clinical manifestations and complications.
(d) State its diagnostic evaluation.
(e) Explain why certain patients are more vulnerable or misdiagnosed.
(f) Distinguish acute anterior uveitis from intermediate and posterior uveitis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Inflammation of the uveal tract (iris, ciliary body, choroid); types: anterior (most common, acute anterior uveitis), intermediate (pars plana and vitreous), posterior (vitreous and chorioretinal layers, least common) and panuveitis (all three).
(b)
