Genetic, traumatic, systemic immune-mediated or infectious causes; HLA-B27-associated anterior uveitis is the commonest noninfectious type (ankylosing spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriatic arthritis, Reiter's); also sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, Lyme, syphilis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, CMV, VZV, HSV and toxoplasmosis; up to 60% idiopathic.
(c)
• Acute anterior: pain, redness with ciliary flush, photophobia, blurred vision, epiphora, miosis or irregular pupil.
• Complications: band keratopathy, posterior synechiae, cataracts, intraocular hypertension, glaucoma, cystoid macular edema, optic nerve atrophy and permanent vision loss.
(d)
Slit-lamp exam and dilated fundus exam; keratic precipitates are pathognomonic for anterior uveitis; blood tests (CBC, ESR, ANA, HLA-B27, HIV, etc.) guided by suspected cause.
(e)
• Uveitis is often misdiagnosed and treated as pink eye; 90% of cases were reported in primary care settings, and it affects adults aged 20 to 50, with HLA-B27 uveitis more common in young adults.
• Patients with chronic uveitis and older age have higher rates of complications and vision loss (29.9% of chronic cases had long-term vision loss).
(f)
• Acute anterior: pain over hours to days, redness, photophobia, limbal flush and miosis; chronic anterior: blurred vision and mild redness.
• Intermediate and posterior: painless, floaters or reduced acuity, redness not prominent, no photophobia.
• Diagnostic findings: anterior shows keratic precipitates, cells and flare, posterior synechiae and hypopyon; intermediate/posterior shows active chorioretinal inflammation and "snowbanks" at the pars plana.
• Posterior uveitis is the most responsible for profound vision loss if untreated.

(a)
Osteoarthritis, the most common and most disabling degenerative joint disease (also called osteoarthrosis), classified as primary (idiopathic) or secondary (after joint injury or inflammatory disease).
(b)
• Predisposing factors: increased age (cartilage loses ability to resist microfracture), obesity, previous joint damage, and repetitive occupational or recreational use.
• Pathophysiology: mechanical injury of the articular cartilage, subchondral bone and synovium, then chondrocyte response, cytokine release and stimulation of proteolytic enzymes, metalloproteases and collagenase; the damage predisposes to further damage.
(c)
• Assess joint pain, stiffness, swelling, tenderness, limited range of motion, crepitus, weight, BMI, posture and gait; reassure the patient that pain is acknowledged.
• Support joints slightly flexed with pillows or rolls; teach use of a cane (in the contralateral hand for hip or knee), walker, crutches or wheelchair; encourage weight loss; promote proper footwear.
• Monitor vital signs after activity; give vitamin-rich foods; assess ability to perform activities of daily living; prepare the patient for diagnostic tests and assist during surgery.
• Teach prescribed analgesics and anti-inflammatory medicines and their side effects; refer to physical and occupational therapy, psychologist and social worker, and community resources such as the Arthritis Foundation.
• Assess home barriers to mobility, such as multiple flights of stairs, and role in the family.
• Education: prevention includes weight reduction, preventing injuries and perinatal screening for congenital hip disease; no treatment stops the degenerative process.
questions.question:
A patient of advanced age has joint pain that worsens with movement, morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes that eases with movement, and reduced ability to perform daily activities; an X-ray shows a narrowed joint space.
(a) Name the diagnosis.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiology.
(c) Describe the nursing management including patient and family education.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The cardiovascular system and circulating volume: major intraoperative hemorrhage, which can cause hypovolemic shock.
(b)
• Expected: hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, cool clammy skin, oliguria, restlessness and altered mental status from poor cerebral perfusion.
• Investigations: CBC, coagulation profile (PT, APTT, fibrinogen), blood gas for acidosis, ultrasound, CT and X-ray.
(c)
• Stages by ATLS: Class I up to 15% blood loss with no vital sign change; Class II 15 to 30% with tachycardia and narrowed pulse pressure; Class III 30 to 40% with falling pressure; Class IV above 40%.
• Associated coagulopathy, hypothermia and acidosis form a vicious cycle; vascular injury is a cause to consider.
(d)
• Monitor vital signs, assess the surgical site and estimate blood loss; start rapid crystalloids and consider blood products by laboratory values.
• Inform the surgical team promptly and coordinate with anesthesia for vasopressors or hemostatic agents; give tranexamic acid as ordered.
• Monitor urine output and CVP for fluid status and shock signs.
• Consequences to prevent: hemodynamic instability, hypovolemic shock, organ dysfunction, coagulopathy and metabolic acidosis.
• Document blood loss, fluids, products and response.
questions.question:
During surgery a patient has falling blood pressure, rapid heart rate, cool clammy skin, reduced urine output, restlessness and confusion; blood loss is visible in the field.
(a) Identify the affected system and the likely problem.
(b) State the expected abnormalities and the investigations.
(c) State the differential considerations and stages.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for nursing priorities and escalation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors: age, contact lens wear, compromised immune system, allergies, environmental exposure, eye trauma, and underlying conditions such as SLE and STD.
(b)
• Corneal involvement (ulcers or abrasions) is recognized by pain, photophobia and visual disturbances.
• Recurrent infections occur especially with weakened immunity, causing chronic inflammation and discomfort; conjunctival scarring follows chronic or recurrent inflammation and may affect the eye surface and impair vision.
• Secondary bacterial infections may need extra antibiotics; herpes simplex viral conjunctivitis can progress to herpetic keratitis.
• Chronic irritation from allergens or contact lenses forms conjunctival papillae (giant papillary conjunctivitis); neonates with chlamydial or gonococcal infection risk scarring, corneal ulceration or blindness.
(c)
• Bacterial: antibiotic drops or ointments (erythromycin, bacitracin, polymyxin B) for 5 to 7 days. Viral: self-limiting in 1 to 2 weeks; artificial tears and cold compresses; antiviral drops if herpes simplex.
• Allergic: antihistamine drops, mast cell stabilizers, NSAID drops, allergen avoidance, cool compresses. Giant papillary: stop contact lens wear, switch to daily disposables, ensure lens hygiene, mast cell stabilizer or antihistamine drops.
• Nursing: assess symptoms, onset, duration, exposure and previous treatment; give cool compresses and lubricating drops for comfort; administer prescribed medicines; monitor response, adverse reactions and corneal or secondary infection; schedule follow-up and referral; document.
• Priority: patient education and prevention of spread, covering hand hygiene, avoiding eye rubbing, not sharing towels, eye makeup or drops, contact lens hygiene (no overnight or water exposure), avoiding irritants and allergens, and isolation precautions if necessary.
questions.question:
A patient who wears contact lenses and has a weakened immune system presents with a red, irritated eye with discharge.
(a) Identify the risk factors for conjunctivitis that apply to this patient and others.
(b) State the potential complications and how you would recognize them.
(c) Outline the nursing and medical management options by type of conjunctivitis and justify the priority nursing intervention.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Muscle atrophy, specifically physiologic atrophy from not using the muscles enough.
(b)
• Predisposing: seated jobs, health problems limiting movement, reduced activity, being bedridden, inability to move limbs because of stroke or other brain disease, and lack of gravity as in space flight.
• Pathophysiology: protein degradation exceeds protein synthesis, leading to reduced cross-sectional area of myofibers and decreased muscle strength; it manifests as reduced force production, easy fatigue and decreased exercise capability.
• Physiologic atrophy can often be reversed with exercise and better nutrition.
(c)
• Exercise is widely acknowledged as the most effective therapy but is not applicable to all patients.
• Signs to assess: reduced muscle mass, one limb smaller, weakness, numbness or tingling, trouble walking, swallowing or speaking.
• Related care for immobility: range-of-motion exercises and adequate nutrition are given in related topics.
• Other types: pathologic (aging, starvation, Cushing disease) and neurogenic (most severe, nerve injury or disease).
questions.question:
A bedridden patient who cannot move the limbs because of a stroke has one arm smaller than the other, weakness, and reduced muscle mass.
(a) Name the diagnosis.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiology.
(c) Describe the nursing management.

Psychosocial issues in orthopedic rehabilitation:
(a) Describe the issues and how they arise.
(b) State how they relate to recovery and adherence.
(c) Explain how they affect function and relationships.
(d) State the preventive measures, nursing care and rehabilitation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Psychosocial issues complicate rehabilitation, affecting emotional well-being and recovery, with heightened stress and anxiety from physical limitations and social isolation.
• Main issues: fear of re-injury, social isolation, depression and anxiety, and self-esteem issues from changes in appearance or perceived loss of independence.
• Others: financial strain, chronic pain, sleep disturbances, role changes, communication challenges, frustration and impatience, coping with uncertainty, dependency on pain medications and disruption of daily routine.
(b)
Fear of re-injury reduces motivation and engagement; adherence to treatment is a challenge, and lack of a robust support system hinders coping and adherence.
(c)
Impact on relationships, limited leisure activities, loss of productivity, grief and loss, body functional concerns and employment issues.
(d)
• Early identification of psychosocial risk factors, including assessing pre-existing mental health conditions.
• Patient education and counseling to address psychosocial aspects.
• Proactive, patient-centered communication so patients understand the rehabilitation process and fears are addressed.
• Social support and psychosocial support programs such as peer support or counseling mitigate distress.

(a)
• Intraoperative pneumothorax is a rare but potentially lethal complication.
• Causes: congenital defect of the diaphragm, rupture of a bulla, endobronchial intubation and creation of pneumoperitoneum.
(b)
• Accumulated air in the pleural space puts positive pressure on the lung and prevents proper expansion, causing respiratory distress.
• Negative pressure pulmonary edema is a noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, also called post-extubation, post-obstructive or laryngospasm-related pulmonary edema.
(c)
• As air continues to accumulate the trachea and other structures shift, leading to respiratory failure; hypercapnia (raised arterial CO2) results in respiratory acidosis, showing as elevated ETCO2.
• Complications of pneumothorax: another collapsed lung in future, and shock if there are serious injuries, infection, severe inflammation or fluid in the lung.
(d)
• Prevention of pulmonary edema: intra-operative muscle relaxant, topical or spray lidocaine and steroids in at-risk patients.
• Clear the airway of retained blood or secretions by suctioning the oropharynx and extubate at a very deep or very light level of anesthesia.
• Bronchospasm is a joint event during intubation, especially in patients with respiratory disease, and mostly resolves without complications.
questions.question:
Intraoperative pneumothorax and negative pressure pulmonary edema:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology.
(b) State how causes relate to clinical findings.
(c) Explain how respiratory failure and other effects develop.
(d) State prevention and nursing care.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Orbital cellulitis is an acute purulent inflammation of the cellular tissue of the orbit; it is an ophthalmic emergency because of optic nerve compression, is more common in children and is usually unilateral.
• Causes: spread of infection from neighbouring structures such as the nasal sinus, sepsis after penetrating injuries, septic operations such as enucleation, facial erysipelas and spread of pyaemia (pneumococcus, Staphylococcus, Streptococcus).
(b)
• Signs: proptosis, red inflamed lids, chemosis, abscess over the upper lid, reduced visual acuity and colour vision, relative afferent pupil defect, possible double vision, limited and painful eye movements, malaise and fever.
• Investigations: full blood count, urea, electrolytes and glucose; CT scan to look for subperiosteal and orbital collections and adjacent sinus disease; intraconal opacity without sinus disease suggests trauma or a foreign body.
(c)
Infection may spread backward into the brain: cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess; also panophthalmitis, sinus formation, optic atrophy, subperiorbital abscess, central retinal vein or artery occlusion, raised intraocular pressure and exposure keratopathy.
(d)
• Nursing: admit, arrange urgent CT of paranasal sinuses, orbits and brain, arrange urgent ENT referral, and give analgesia (local heat may comfort), nasal decongestant, fan or tepid sponging for fever, and nourishing fluids with a light diet.
• Give prescribed antibiotics (for example oral clindamycin, ciprofloxacin, chloramphenicol drops, IV in severe cases), continued up to 6 weeks orally; dress any abscess and prepare for incision and drainage; send pus for analysis.
• Monitor optic nerve function by visual acuity, pupillary reactions, colour vision and light brightness appreciation.
• Preseptal cellulitis is infection of the eyelids only, not spreading beyond the orbital septum.
• ENT specialists are involved in joint care.
questions.question:
Orbital cellulitis:
(a) Describe its pathophysiology and causes.
(b) State how its signs relate to diagnostic findings.
(c) Explain how it may progress or spread to other systems and cause functional deficit.
(d) State the nursing care plan.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The orbit (eye socket), which houses the eyeball, muscles, nerves and tissues: an orbital tumour, which may push the eye forward and cause it to bulge.
(b)
• Expected: bulging eye, double vision or vision loss, droopy or swollen eyelid, pressure, numbness or tingling, and pain and inflammation.
• Investigations: visual assessment, CT scan, MRI, ultrasonography and biopsy (used less often).
(c)
• Types: cysts, vascular lesions, lymphomas, neurogenic tumours and secondary tumours from sinuses, cranium or metastasis (breast, lung, prostate, melanoma).
• Children: dermoid cysts, capillary hemangiomas, rhabdomyosarcoma; adults: lymphoid tumours, cavernous hemangiomas, meningiomas.
• Risk: Graves' disease (thyroid eye disease), age and abnormal development.
(d)
• A tumour that causes pain or vision problems needs treatment; otherwise it is monitored; options include antibiotics, corticosteroids, radiation, chemotherapy and surgery (removal, reduction, cyst drainage, reconstruction).
• Nursing: assessment and history, sterile dressing with normal saline, adequate diet, two-hourly vital signs during chemotherapy and radiation, analgesics, education and emotional support.
questions.question:
A patient has bulging of one eye, double vision, a droopy swollen eyelid, a feeling of pressure in the eye, and numbness or tingling around the eye.
(a) Identify the affected structure.
(b) State the expected changes and investigations.
(c) State the differential causes.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for nursing priorities and escalation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Rickets, a condition affecting bone development in children; the adult equivalent is osteomalacia or soft bones.
(b)
• The most common cause is a lack of vitamin D or calcium; vitamin D largely comes from exposing the skin to sunlight and is also found in oily fish and eggs.
• Vitamin D is essential for the formation of strong and healthy bones in children; deficiency causes bone pain, poor growth and soft, weak bones that can lead to bone deformities.
(c)
• For most children, rickets is successfully treated by ensuring they eat foods containing calcium and vitamin D or by taking vitamin supplements.
• Provide dietary supplements of calcium and vitamin D, ensure a balanced diet high in fiber and fluids to stimulate gastric motility, and maintain a safe environment.
• Assess the patient's and family's understanding and health educate them; monitor vital signs; assist with self-care activities such as bathing.
• Promote mobility by ensuring prescribed exercises are performed, observe for skin irritation, and provide emotional support.
• Call on an interdisciplinary team (surgeons, physical therapists); deformities may need surgical correction or reconstruction and pharmacological pain management.
• Nursing diagnoses may include impaired physical mobility, chronic pain and disturbed body image.
questions.question:
A child has bone pain, poor growth and soft, weak bones with bowing of the legs (genu valgum or genu varum).
(a) Name the diagnosis.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiology.
(c) Describe the nursing management including patient and family education.

A patient has a painless swelling of the upper eyelid caused by a blocked gland duct; it fluctuates in size and one swelling is large enough to press on the cornea and blur vision.
(a) Name the diagnosis.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiology.
(c) Describe the nursing management including patient and family education.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Chalazion, a swelling of a meibomian gland due to blockage of its duct; it can affect the upper or lower lid.
(b)
• It is commonly caused by Staphylococci; it may become infected and is then called an internal hordeolum.
• The swelling may fluctuate in size, may point to the skin surface, and a large one can obstruct vision or press on the cornea and cause astigmatism.
(c)
• Aim: relieve the swollen eyelid causing pain and discomfort, and relieve any sticky discharge.
• Cleanse the eyes with warm water; apply antibiotic ointment (chloramphenicol three to four times a day for 14 days) if the chalazion is infected.
• Education: keep eyelids clean by washing off crusts and discharge with warm water twice a day; return if the swelling does not subside.
• If swelling does not subside, a simple operation of incision and curettage can remove remaining material.

(a)
• Airway, breathing and circulation first; vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature), pain, level of consciousness, urine output and nausea and vomiting.
• Surgical site: erythema, edema, abnormal discharge and foul odor; colour, amount and consistency of drainage; dressing and drains.
(b)
• Ineffective breathing pattern related to effects of the anesthetic agent, evidenced by labored breathing.
• Risk for surgical site infection related to the surgical incision.
(c)
Anesthetic effects on breathing: the effects of the anesthetic agent are the cause; the incision is a direct portal of entry for pathogens.
(d)
• Breathing: reassure by explaining the procedure and its benefits (alleviates fear); check SpO2 (to know oxygen saturation); give oxygen therapy (improves saturation and breathing pattern); keep the environment neat and tidy (prevents obstruction by dust and maintains airflow).
• Infection: assess for signs of infection (early recognition allows prompt intervention); monitor drainage (early detection); use aseptic technique for dressings (reduces introduction of pathogens); give antibiotics as prescribed (prevent infection).
(e)
• Outcomes: easy breathing without obstruction after 15 to 30 minutes of nursing intervention; surgical site free of infection.
• Evaluation: patient verbalized easy breathing after 15 to 30 minutes, and the surgical site did not show any sign of infection.
questions.question:
After a major abdominal operation under anesthesia, a patient in the recovery area has labored breathing and a fresh surgical incision.
(a) State the priority nursing assessment findings.
(b) State the nursing diagnoses.
(c) Explain the pathophysiological basis of the risks.
(d) State the priority nursing interventions with rationale.
(e) State the expected outcomes and evaluation.

Dislocation:
(a) Describe the medical and surgical management.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities and rationale before, during and after treatment.
(c) Explain the basis of complications and how they are prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation) reduces pain, swelling and damage; a splint, cast or brace immobilizes the joint for a few weeks to several months; ibuprofen or acetaminophen manage pain.
• Closed reduction, where the joint is manually manipulated into place, is the most common approach; open reduction surgery is rarely needed if closed reduction fails.
• Rehabilitation with physical therapy regains strength, flexibility and range of motion.
(b)
• Admit the patient, monitor vital signs, take history and do a neurovascular assessment (pulse, sensation, movement distal to the injury), and assess and treat pain.
• Immobilize with a splint, brace or sling, elevate the limb above heart level, apply ice for 20 minutes at a time several times a day, and give nutritional counseling and smoking cessation advice.
• Rationale: pain assessment determines effectiveness of interventions; immobilization relieves pain and prevents bone displacement; ice for the first 24 to 72 hours reduces edema, hematoma and pain; range-of-motion exercises maintain motility and prevent contracture or atrophy.
• Give fluids of 2000 to 3000 ml/day within cardiac tolerance to reduce urinary infection, stone formation and constipation; provide a bed board or orthopedic bed and side rails.
(c)
• Nerves and vessels around the joint may be compressed or injured, causing sensory changes and vascular compromise; monitor for infection or compartment syndrome.
• Prevention: warm up, proper technique, healthy weight, strengthening muscles and protective gear.
• Nursing diagnoses: acute pain, impaired physical mobility and risk for fall.
• Health education on diagnosis, treatment and expected recovery time.

questions.question:
Glaucoma:
(a) Define it and state its types.
(b) State its causes and risk factors.
(c) Describe its clinical manifestations.
(d) State its diagnostic tests.
(e) Explain why certain patients are more vulnerable.
(f) Distinguish open-angle from angle-closure glaucoma.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve; major types are open-angle and angle-closure, with normal-tension, congenital and secondary glaucoma also described.
(b)
• Drainage angle malfunction or blockage raises intraocular pressure; secondary causes include corticosteroids, uveitis, diabetes and eye injury.
• Risk: age over 40, family history, African, Hispanic or Asian heritage, high eye pressure, farsightedness or nearsightedness, eye injury, long-term steroids, thin corneas, optic nerve thinning, diabetes, migraines, high blood pressure and poor circulation.
(c)
General: eye pain or pressure, headaches, halos, low, blurred or tunnel vision or blind spots, nausea and vomiting, red eyes.
(d)
Tonometry, gonioscopy, dilated exam, optical coherence tomography, pachymetry, slit lamp, visual acuity and visual field tests; screening pressure alone is not enough.
(e)
• Normal-tension glaucoma is more common among people of Asian descent, and some people have optic nerves sensitive to normal pressure; congenital glaucoma often runs in families and is present at birth.
• Glaucoma is a leading cause of blindness over age 60.
(f)
• Open-angle: the most common, gradual drainage failure like a clogged drain, painless, no early vision change, slow loss of peripheral vision.
• Angle-closure: the iris blocks the drainage angle like paper over a sink drain; pressure rises quickly in an acute attack with sudden blurry vision, severe pain, headache, nausea, vomiting and halos; it is a true emergency.
• Chronic angle-closure develops slowly without symptoms until damage or an attack.
• Treatment differs: laser trabeculoplasty for open-angle and laser iridotomy for angle-closure.

questions.question:
Sprain:
(a) Define it and state its grades.
(b) State its causes.
(c) Describe its pathophysiology.
(d) List its clinical manifestations and diagnostic investigations.
(e) Explain why certain patients are more vulnerable.
(f) Distinguish a sprain from a strain.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A sprain is an injury to a ligament, the collagen band connecting bones at a joint, which gives passive stabilization and proprioception; the joint is forced suddenly beyond its usual range and the inelastic fibres are overstretched.
• Grade I: microscopic damage, slight tenderness, no instability; Grade II: partial tear with visible swelling and tenderness, no or mild instability; Grade III: complete rupture with significant swelling and instability.
(b)
Sports injuries, falls, lifting heavy objects beyond one's limit, slipping and catching oneself, rolling an ankle or twisting a knee, and repetitive strain.
(c)
The ligament is stretched or torn, from minor stretching (first degree) to partial tear (second) to complete rupture that may avulse bone (third); the most common sites are the ankles, knees and wrists; ligaments take about six weeks to heal.
(d)
• Manifestations: intense pain, swelling, bruising, joint instability, restricted mobility, difficulty bearing weight, decreased range of motion, and a popping sound.
• Diagnosis: physical examination (tenderness, swelling, grading), X-ray (rules out fracture), MRI (soft tissue including ligaments), CT scan and ultrasound (ligament or tendon condition).
(e)
Vulnerable groups are those in sports, repetitive joint use at work or hobby, heavy lifting and those prone to falls.
(f)
• A strain is a "muscle pull", a microscopic incomplete tear of muscle or tendon from overuse or overstretching, at the musculotendinous junction; a sprain affects a ligament.
• Strains most commonly occur in the foot, leg or back and arise from improper body mechanics, poor flexibility, fatigue or poor warm-up.
• Strains are classified first degree (few fibres torn), second degree (nearly half torn) and third degree (complete rupture); both are managed with RICE.

questions.question:
Anaphylaxis during anesthesia:
(a) Describe its pathophysiology and diagnostic criteria.
(b) State how its triggers relate to clinical manifestations.
(c) Explain how it may progress to other systems and cause complications.
(d) State the treatment.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Anaphylactic reactions are caused by the sudden release of mediators (histamine, tryptase, chymase, cathepsin) from basophils and mast cells after exposure to a trigger; they are very rare at 1 in 4,000 to 1 in 25,000.
• WAO diagnostic criteria: acute skin or mucosal reaction with respiratory compromise, hypotension or end-organ dysfunction; or at least two of skin or mucosa involvement, respiratory compromise, hypotension or persistent gastrointestinal symptoms after exposure; or hypotension after a known allergen.
(b)
• Triggers: antibiotics (beta-lactams account for about 70%), neuromuscular blocking agents (succinylcholine and rocuronium most common; IgE-mediated), sugammadex, latex, chlorhexidine; almost all agents except inhalational agents have been implicated.
• Most frequent presenting sign was hypotension (46%), with bronchospasm also common, and diagnosis is difficult because of overlap with the effects of anesthesia.
(c)
• Mortality is 3% to 10%; profound vasodilation causes hypotension and end-organ dysfunction.
• Progression to other systems is through respiratory compromise and cardiovascular collapse.
(d)
• Stop the suspected agent and give 100% oxygen.
• Epinephrine is the drug of choice, causing vasoconstriction that raises venous return and cardiac output, with positive inotropic effects.
• Vasopressin (2-unit bolus) for refractory cases; methylene blue has been used in unresponsive cases; glucagon (1 mg bolus) for patients on beta-blockers.
• Fluid replacement counteracts vasodilation; whether to proceed with surgery is individualized by severity.

questions.question:
After a fall, a patient has a visibly deformed joint that looks out of place, with intense pain, swelling, numbness and limited ability to move it.
(a) Name the diagnosis.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiology.
(c) Describe the nursing management including patient and family education.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Dislocation, in which the articular surfaces of the joint are no longer in anatomic contact (bones "out of joint"); complete dislocation (luxation) or partial (subluxation).
(b)
• Predisposing factors: trauma (falls, motor vehicle accidents, sports injuries, direct blows), repetitive stress weakening ligaments, muscle weakness, and joint hypermobility.
• Traumatic force stretches or tears ligaments, allowing the bones out of position with capsular damage; muscle and tendon involvement causes pain and spasm; cartilage and bone may be damaged or fractured.
• Nerves and blood vessels may be compressed, causing sensory changes, numbness and vascular compromise.
(c)
• Admit, monitor vital signs, do a neurovascular assessment of pulse, sensation and movement distal to the injury, manage pain, immobilize the joint with a splint, brace or sling, and elevate the limb.
• Apply ice for 20 minutes at a time several times a day, monitor for infection or compartment syndrome, and encourage healthy diet and smoking cessation, as smoking delays healing.
• Health education: clear, concise information on diagnosis, treatment plan and expected recovery time.
• Prevention teaching: warm up before exercise, proper technique, healthy weight, strengthening muscles around the joints and protective gear.
• Nursing diagnoses: acute pain, impaired physical mobility and risk for fall.

questions.question:
Miss O has a muscle strain in the ankle region with pain, limited range of motion, loss of strength and fatigue.
(a) State the priority nursing assessment findings.
(b) State the nursing diagnoses.
(c) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(d) State the priority nursing interventions with rationale.
(e) State the expected outcomes and evaluation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Assess level of pain and deformity of the affected part, activity tolerance, neurovascular status, swelling, bruising or redness, pain at rest or on use, and muscle weakness.
(b)
Acute pain related to stretching of the affected ligaments, evidenced by verbalization; impaired physical mobility related to limited range of motion, evidenced by pain and discomfort with movement; activity intolerance related to fatigue, evidenced by loss of strength in the ankle due to reduced range of motion.
(c)
A strain is an incomplete microscopic tear of muscle or tendon at the musculotendinous junction; mediators such as histamine, serotonin, bradykinin and prostaglandin cause edema, heat, redness and pain; phases are destruction, repair and remodeling.
(d)
• Pain: immobilize the affected area (reduces pain), apply ice (reduces pain and swelling), elevate (lowers local vessel pressure), rest (promotes recovery), analgesic such as paracetamol (reduces pain).
• Mobility: maintain neutral positioning (prevents stress at the strain site), assist position changes and transfers (encourages active participation), offer encouragement with exercise regimen (reconditioning is uncomfortable and fatiguing), supervise safe use of ambulatory aids, and change positions often (relieves pressure).
• Activity tolerance: assess tolerance (baseline), schedule activities around rest (improves circulation), allow the patient to determine best exercise times, promote nutrition and hydration (malnourishment prevents recovery), and give passive range-of-motion exercises (prevent contractures and muscle weakness).
(e)
• Outcomes: pain reduced within 30 to 45 minutes; improved mobility by performing previously limiting movements within 3 to 4 days; a measurable progressive increase in activity tolerance during hospitalization.
• Evaluation: verbalized reduction in pain after 40 minutes, improved mobility after 3 days, and reported a progressive increase in activity tolerance.

questions.question:
Orthopaedic deformities:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology.
(b) State how the classifications relate to clinical manifestations and diagnostic findings.
(c) Explain how deformities lead to functional deficit.
(d) State the nursing care plan, health education and rehabilitation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Deformities are deviations from normal body architecture with structural irregularities affecting form and function, from congenital, traumatic, chronic medical or developmental causes.
• Growth normally follows a well-orchestrated plan; disruption from genetic factors, events during pregnancy or childhood affects bones and soft tissue, producing biomechanical imbalances and impaired movement.
(b)
• Classes: vertebral (scoliosis, kyphosis, lordosis), skull (plagiocephaly, trigonocephaly, scaphocephaly, brachycephaly from premature suture fusion), congenital (talipes equinovarus, polydactyly), post-traumatic and those due to medical conditions (Dupuytren contracture, rheumatoid hand, rickets, osteoporosis).
• Manifestations: visible alteration in appearance, functional limitations, skeletal misalignment, joint restrictions, muscle imbalances and impaired range of motion.
• Diagnostics: X-ray, CT and MRI, genetic testing for congenital deformities, and blood tests for metabolic or inflammatory conditions.
(c)
• Joints may not bend and muscles do not work smoothly, causing pain and difficulty with regular activities; hand deformities occur in about 90% of rheumatoid arthritis patients.
• Treatment: surgery for correction, physical therapy and pharmacologic pain relief; some can only be managed by palliative nursing care.
(d)
• Nursing diagnoses: impaired physical mobility, chronic pain and disturbed body image; care includes passive or active range-of-motion exercises, flotation mattress, massage, analgesics and support groups.
• Education and care: assess patient and family understanding, educate, assist with self-care, prevent skin irritation, give a high fiber and fluid diet, calcium and vitamin D supplements, keep a safe environment and call on the interdisciplinary team.
• Rehabilitation: physical therapy and prescribed exercises; rheumatoid hand rehabilitation is a long-term process.

questions.question:
Conjunctivitis:
(a) Define it and state how it is classified.
(b) State its causes.
(c) State its risk factors.
(d) Describe its pathophysiology.
(e) List its clinical manifestations.
(f) List its diagnostic investigations.
(g) Explain why certain patients are more vulnerable to conjunctivitis and its complications.
(h) Distinguish between bacterial, viral, allergic and giant papillary conjunctivitis in terms of cause, features and management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Inflammation of the conjunctival tissue with engorged vessels, pain and ocular discharge; acute (3 to 4 weeks, usually 1 to 2 weeks) or chronic (more than 4 weeks), and infectious or noninfectious.
(b)
Bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae), viruses (especially adenovirus), allergens, irritants (smoke, pollution, chlorine, harsh chemicals), contact lens misuse, sexually transmitted infections (chlamydia, gonorrhea) and autoimmune disorders (rheumatoid arthritis, SLE).
(c)
Risk factors: age, contact lens wear, compromised immune system, allergies, environmental exposure, eye trauma, and underlying conditions such as SLE and STD.
(d)
Inflammation dilates conjunctival vessels, causing redness (hyperemia) and swelling; the conjunctival epithelium is the primary defence, and secondary defences are tear film immunoglobulins, lysozyme, conjunctival vasculature, and the rinsing action of blinking and lacrimation.
(e)
Redness, watery discharge, gritty or foreign body sensation, itching, burning or stinging, swelling, pus or mucus discharge, photophobia, crusting of eyelids, and blurry vision.
(f)
History taking, physical examination, visual acuity test, slit lamp examination, fluorescein staining, allergy testing, microbiological culture (severe or recurrent bacterial cases) and blood tests for systemic or autoimmune conditions.
(g)
• Newborns who acquire chlamydia or gonorrhea during childbirth may develop conjunctival scarring, corneal ulceration or blindness if untreated; people with weakened immune systems or underlying conditions get recurrent infections.
• Contact lens wearers are prone to giant papillary conjunctivitis; susceptible individuals exposed to pollen, dust or pet dander develop allergic conjunctivitis.
(h)
• Bacterial: Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pneumoniae; redness, irritation, thick yellowish or greenish discharge and crusting; antibiotic drops or ointments (erythromycin, bacitracin, polymyxin B) for 5 to 7 days.
• Viral: usually adenovirus, highly contagious, with redness, watery discharge and discomfort; self-limiting in 1 to 2 weeks, treated with artificial tears and cold compresses, with antiviral drops if herpes simplex virus is the cause.
• Allergic: triggered by pollen, dust or pet dander; itching, redness and watery discharge; treated with antihistamine drops, mast cell stabilizers, NSAID drops, allergen avoidance and cool compresses.
• Giant papillary: from mechanical irritation by contact lenses, with discomfort, itching and mucous discharge; treated by stopping lens wear or using daily disposables, ensuring lens hygiene, and using mast cell stabilizer or antihistamine drops.

questions.question:
Surgical site infection:
(a) Define it and state its classification.
(b) State its causes and the chain of infection.
(c) State its consequences.
(d) Explain why certain patients are more vulnerable.
(e) Distinguish superficial incisional, deep incisional and organ/space infections.
questions.answerText:
(a)
SSIs are a common and significant complication of invasive surgery and a large share of healthcare-associated infections; CDC classifies them as superficial, deep incisional or organ/space.
(b)
• Most originate from endogenous flora on mucous membranes, skin or hollow viscera; common bacteria are Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA), E. coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterococcus.
• The chain: infectious agent, reservoir (human skin, hospital environment and instruments), portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry (the surgical incision) and susceptible host.
(c)
Morbidity, poor cosmetic outcomes, persistent pain and itching, restricted movement and emotional impact.
(d)
• Immunocompromised patients are vulnerable to fungi such as Candida; patients themselves can be reservoirs like MRSA; poorly optimized comorbidities (glucose) raise risk.
• Prevention includes managing comorbidities, optimizing glucose, nutritional support, smoking cessation and stress reduction.
(e)
• Superficial: skin and subcutaneous tissue only (over 50% of SSIs), with purulent discharge, organism, surgeon's diagnosis or deliberate opening with symptoms.
• Deep incisional: soft tissues including muscle and fascia, with purulent discharge, dehiscence, re-opening with positive culture or abscess on CT.
• Organ/space: beyond the fascial or muscle layers, including implant-related infection; purulent drain discharge, isolated organism or abscess on CT.
• A stitch abscess, localized cellulitis or infected superficial stab puncture alone is not counted.
• Prevention: antibiotic prophylaxis, chlorhexidine skin antisepsis, hair clipping not shaving, strict aseptic technique and hand hygiene.

questions.question:
A young adult with ankylosing spondylitis has gradual eye pain, redness around the cornea, photophobia, watery eyes and blurred vision, which was first treated as pink eye.
(a) State the risk factors.
(b) State the potential complications and how they are recognized.
(c) State the nursing and medical management options and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Uveitis (acute anterior uveitis) is triggered by genetic, traumatic, systemic immune-mediated or infectious causes; HLA-B27-associated anterior uveitis is most common noninfectious type, with ankylosing spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriatic arthritis and Reiter's syndrome.
• Others: sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, Lyme disease, syphilis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, CMV, VZV, HSV and toxoplasmosis; older age raises complication and vision loss rates.
(b)
• Recognition: pain, hyperemia with ciliary flush, photophobia, blurred vision, epiphora and miosis or an irregular pupil; posterior types show floaters or decreased acuity.
• Complications: band keratopathy, posterior synechiae, cataracts, intraocular hypertension, glaucoma, cystoid macular edema, optic nerve atrophy and permanent vision loss.
• Keratic precipitates on slit-lamp examination indicate anterior uveitis.
(c)
• Medical: topical cycloplegics (homatropine, cyclopentolate) for pain and photophobia; topical corticosteroid (prednisolone) first choice for noninfectious anterior uveitis; antivirals for HSV and VZV; antibiotics are generally not indicated; immunomodulators.
• Nursing and primary care: identify the condition, start first-line therapy, provide pain relief, and refer to an ophthalmologist within 24 hours.
• Use the mnemonic RSVP (persistent Redness, Sensitivity to light, Visual change, Pain) to identify referral need; treatment should start within 24 hours.
• Justification: earlier diagnosis by an ophthalmologist gives a better prognosis and chance of preserving vision; teach medication adherence and urgent follow-up regardless of symptoms.

(a)
• Immediate recognition, control of hemorrhage by direct pressure or proximal and distal clamping, and immediate consultation with vascular surgery because time is critical in preventing ischemic complications.
• Fluid resuscitation while avoiding excessive volume that could worsen bleeding; continuous monitoring of vital signs, urine output and limb perfusion; imaging if the patient is stable.
• Blood products (packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma, platelets) to correct coagulopathy, and prophylactic antibiotics in significant contamination.
(b)
• Monitor vital signs continuously to detect shock, inspect for bleeding, and do neurovascular checks of pulses, capillary refill and neurological status.
• Inform the surgical team and anesthesia providers immediately; apply direct pressure with sterile gauze, elevate the limb, and use tourniquets only under surgical guidance.
• Prepare blood products, IV fluids, clamps and sutures; ensure IV access; document; monitor for compartment syndrome; emotional support and education for the patient and family.
(c)
• Injury arises from direct trauma to vessel walls from instruments, cuts or retractors, ranging from minor tears to complete lacerations.
• Consequences: hemorrhage and hypovolemic shock, limb ischemia or loss, organ dysfunction, infection, delayed recovery, long-term complications and mortality.
• Prevention depends on avoiding the causes: improper clamping, electrocautery misuse, poor visualization and improper retraction.
• Diagnostic tests such as ultrasonography, CT angiography, angiography and ankle-brachial index assess the extent of injury.
• Intra-operative nursing role is described by the actions above.
questions.question:
Intraoperative vascular injury:
(a) Describe the medical management.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities and rationale.
(c) Explain the basis of complications and how they are prevented.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Handover is the transfer of information and professional responsibility and accountability between individuals and teams; it is critical for continuity, quality and safety of care.
• SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is an evidence-based communication technique that encourages preparation and supports escalation; handovers should be verbal and written and documented.
• Three parts: anaesthetist to recovery practitioner, scrub practitioner to recovery practitioner, and recovery practitioner to ward practitioner.
(b)
• Before transfer the patient should be physiologically stable; a qualified practitioner accompanies the patient and keeps them covered to protect dignity; the anaesthetist formally hands over care to a trained recovery staff member.
• On arrival give oxygen as needed and monitor oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure, ECG, temperature and level of consciousness; one-to-one care until the patient maintains the airway and communicates.
• Handover content includes name, operation, theatre, past history, allergies, anaesthetic technique, analgesia, antiemetics and instructions; scrub handover includes complications, items left in situ (drains, packs, catheter), skin closure and dressing.
• Discharge criteria: acceptable observations (NEWS), comfort, wound not bleeding excessively, drains without excessive drainage, and a minimum of 20 minutes in recovery after the final morphine dose.
(c)
• Handover failures can lead to diagnostic and therapeutic delays and adverse events.
• Residual drugs left in IV cannulae have caused cardiac and respiratory arrest, so lines are flushed with normal saline, documented and handed over.
• Ward handover covers anaesthetic type, vital signs, blood sugar, analgesia, antibiotics, drains and dressings.
questions.question:
Post-operative handover:
(a) Describe the handover procedure and its structure (SBAR).
(b) State the nursing responsibilities and rationale.
(c) Explain the basis of complications and how they are prevented.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Dupuytren contracture, a benign, progressive disease of the palmar fascia causing shortening, thickening and fibrosis of the fascia and aponeurosis of the palm.
(b)
• It is driven by myofibroblastic proliferation, is a genetic disorder and rarely affects Africans.
• Deformities are due to structural irregularities impacting form and function; pain and impaired range of motion may follow.
(c)
• Treatment options: observation, needle aponeurotomy, collagenase injection and surgical resection and fasciectomy.
• General deformity nursing care: assess pain, functional limitations and psychosocial issues; assess understanding of the patient and family and educate them; assist with self-care; promote prescribed exercises; maintain a safe environment; give emotional support; call on an interdisciplinary team.
• Nursing diagnoses may include impaired physical mobility, chronic pain and disturbed body image.
questions.question:
A patient with a genetic condition has a progressive thickening and shortening of the palm tissue with fibrosis, so that the fingers cannot be straightened.
(a) Name the diagnosis.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiology.
(c) Describe the nursing management including patient and family education.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Assess pain characteristics (location, frequency, duration, intensity) with a 0 to 10 scale, vital signs, and visual acuity using Snellen's eye chart; assess thoughts and feelings about the diagnosis.
(b)
• Chronic pain related to pressure of tumour on nerve endings, evidenced by verbalization.
• Anxiety related to unknown outcome of disease, evidenced by verbalization.
• Ineffective health maintenance related to diabetic self-care activities, evidenced by reported blurred vision.
(c)
Uncontrolled blood glucose can increase damage to retinal blood vessels; pressure from the tumour on nerve endings causes pain; detailed pathophysiology of the tumour is in the general ocular tumour account.
(d)
• Pain: non-pharmacological comfort measures (massage, repositioning, diversion) promote relaxation; hot or cold compress; allow the patient to voice pain; analgesics such as morphine.
• Anxiety: encourage sharing of thoughts (examine fears and misconceptions), calm open environment, frequent contact, accurate consistent information and explanation of procedures.
• Health maintenance: adhere strictly to blood sugar monitoring and insulin; visit the ophthalmologist for eye screening six months; report any worsening of symptoms (prevents worsening of retinopathy).
(e)
• Outcomes: pain reduced from 8 to 4 within 15 to 20 minutes; anxiety to a manageable level after 30 minutes; understanding of how to prevent worsening vision after two hours.
• Evaluation: patient verbalized a decrease of pain from 8 to 4, reduced anxiety, and understanding of how to prevent worsening of vision.
questions.question:
A patient with diabetes has an eye problem; her care plan includes chronic pain from pressure of a tumour on nerve endings, anxiety about the unknown outcome of the disease, and blurred vision reported to be related to diabetic self-care activities, and she is awaiting eye surgery.
(a) State the priority nursing assessment findings.
(b) State the nursing diagnoses.
(c) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(d) State the priority nursing interventions with rationale.
(e) State the expected outcomes and evaluation.

Hazards of the surgical environment:
(a) Define the types of hazards.
(b) State the causes.
(c) State the consequences for staff.
(d) Explain why surgical staff are vulnerable.
(e) Distinguish biological hazards from chemical hazards.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Physical hazards: cuts, pricks, electrical shocks, burns and falls.
• Biological hazards: contact with blood and body fluids; chemical hazards: waste anesthetic gases and disinfectants; other hazards: long hours standing and stress.
(b)
Examples: scalpel cuts, hitting the head on lights over the table, slips on wet floors or without slip-resistant footwear, needlesticks, leaks in connective tubing from anesthetic equipment and exposure to cleaning agents.
(c)
Exposure to diseases including HIV and hepatitis after a cut or prick; illness or injury from chemical exposure; stress wearing down a professional over time.
(d)
• Team members regularly contact blood and body fluids, 50 percent of exposures occur after use of an item, and surgery is often performed in life or death situations where the slightest mistake can cost a life.
• Anesthetic equipment can malfunction during surgery.
(e)
• Biological hazards come from blood and body fluids and infectious agents; chemical hazards come from waste anesthetic gases leaking from tubing and from disinfectants and sanitizing agents.
• Control: PPE, hand hygiene and environmental controls.

questions.question:
Patient G, an 83-year-old man, has undergone a colon resection for removal of cancerous nodes and has been transferred to the PACU.
(a) State the presentation and indication.
(b) State what nurses monitor.
(c) State the procedure named and medical management.
(d) State the pre-operative and post-operative nursing care.
(e) State the complications to watch for.
(f) State the discharge teaching.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Patient G, 83, had a colon resection for cancerous nodes; the operation proceeded without complications.
(b)
Nurses monitor blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature (frequently, every 5 minutes at first), level of consciousness, pain and surgical site for bleeding, swelling or infection.
(c)
Colon resection. Pre-surgical prep: bowel preparation with clear liquids and laxatives, antibiotics, adjusting blood thinners and dietary counseling; post-surgical: pain medicine, diet progression, wound care, walking to prevent clots and physical therapy.
(d)
• Pre-operative: review past surgeries, illnesses, allergies and medications; nursing diagnoses acute pain and anxiety (reassure and assess pain).
• Post-operative: airway management, oxygen, pain scales, antiemetics, IV fluids and thermoregulation, bowel function monitoring, dietary counseling, documentation, and emotional support.
(e)
Respiratory depression, bleeding, allergic reactions, nausea and vomiting, infection at the surgical site and ineffective breathing pattern.
(f)
Discharge teaching from the PACU: pain management strategies, activity restrictions and follow-up appointments; dietary guidance from a dietitian; signs of infection.

questions.question:
A baby a few days old has a raised temperature of 38.2°C, chest in-drawing, swollen eyelids and eye discharge; the mother has a sexually transmitted infection, and the baby is diagnosed with ophthalmia neonatorum.
(a) State the priority nursing assessment findings.
(b) State the nursing diagnoses.
(c) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(d) State the priority nursing interventions with rationale.
(e) State the expected outcomes and evaluation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Assess vital signs and temperature, respiratory rate, depth and ease of respiration, and breath sounds for decreased sounds, crackles or wheezes; eye findings depend on type: gonococcal (2-5 days after birth, severe bilateral discharge, tearing, lid swelling) or chlamydial (5-14 days, redness, watery discharge, lid swelling).
(b)
• Hyperthermia related to inflammatory processes, evidenced by temperature of 38.2°C.
• Ineffective breathing pattern related to increase in secretions in the airway, evidenced by chest in-drawing.
• Interrupted breastfeeding related to the neonate's present illness, evidenced by separation of mother from infant.
(c)
Ophthalmia neonatorum is severe conjunctivitis in a baby under 28 days old, acquired from the birth canal from Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae or herpes simplex virus; routes are the infected birth canal, transmembrane and transplacental transmission; silver nitrate can cause chemical conjunctivitis.
(d)
• Hyperthermia: monitor temperature and promote surface cooling by undressing or light clothes (heat loss by radiation and conduction); tepid sponge and cool cloth to the head; antipyretics as ordered, but no aspirin as it may cause Reye's syndrome; bed rest to reduce metabolic demand; antibiotics to treat the underlying cause.
• Breathing: assess respiratory rate, depth and ease and auscultate (prompt intervention); upright semi-Fowler's position (lung expansion); suction (removes secretions and clears the airway); oxygen as ordered (corrects dyspnea).
• Also: explain the condition sensitively to both parents, screen both parents at the genito-urinary medicine clinic, teach eye cleaning and instillation of antibiotics; strict handwashing.
(e)
• Outcome: temperature returns to 37.2°C after an hour of effective nursing intervention; respiratory rate stays within acceptable range (25-30) during hospitalization.
• Evaluation: infant's temperature reduced to 37.2°C after an hour; respiratory rate remained within acceptable range during the period of hospitalization.

(a)
• Physical hazards: cuts, pricks, electrical shocks, burns and falls, including head injuries on lights and slips on wet floors without slip-resistant footwear.
• Biological hazards: contact with blood and body fluids with exposure to diseases including HIV and hepatitis after a cut or prick; 50 percent of blood and fluid exposures occur after use.
• Chemical hazards: leaks in anesthetic tubing expose everyone to waste anesthetic gases; disinfectants and cleaning agents can cause sickness or injury.
• Other: surgeons spend long hours on their feet and face stress from life-or-death situations.
(b)
Consequences: physical injury, bloodborne infections, harm from waste anesthetic gases and chemical exposure, and long-term wear from stress.
(c)
Use PPE according to standard precautions, hand hygiene, clean and disinfect equipment and the environment, and use environmental controls (airflow, temperature, humidity).
questions.question:
A theatre nurse is concerned about injuries and illness among operating room staff from sharps, exposure to blood, leaking anesthetic gases, cleaning agents and stress.
(a) State the types of hazards (risk factors).
(b) State the potential consequences.
(c) State the management options.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Open-angle glaucoma, which is painless with no vision changes at first, then slow loss of peripheral (tunnel) vision; most people do not notice until damage is severe.
(b)
Tonometry, gonioscopy, dilated exam, OCT, pachymetry, slit lamp, visual acuity and perimetry; nurses assess vision and safety.
(c)
Daily pressure-lowering eye drops; laser trabeculoplasty; trabeculectomy (a tiny scleral flap and a conjunctival filtration bleb hidden under the upper eyelid that drains aqueous and lowers pressure); cataract surgery for narrow angles; glaucoma drainage devices.
(d)
General nursing: provide patient safety, assess vision, educate about glaucoma and eye drops, and manage anxiety.
(e)
Visual impairment affects about 1 in 10 and blindness 5%; drops can cause stinging, red eyes, changes in pulse and breathing, dry mouth and blurred vision.
(f)
Educate on eye-drop compliance and the importance of follow-up; teach that glaucoma damage is permanent; testing every 6 to 12 months after age 65.
questions.question:
A patient has gradual loss of side vision without pain and is found to have raised eye pressure with optic nerve damage; glaucoma surgery (a filtration flap procedure) is planned.
(a) State the diagnosis and presentation.
(b) State the diagnostic tests and what nurses monitor.
(c) Name the medication or procedures.
(d) State the general nursing care.
(e) State the complications to watch for.
(f) State the discharge teaching.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Treatments are cycloplegics, antimicrobials, topical or systemic corticosteroids and immunomodulatory drugs, started within 24 hours.
• Topical cycloplegics relieve pain and photophobia by relaxing ciliary spasm: cyclopentolate (1% one drop three times daily) and homatropine (1 to 2 drops every 3 to 4 hours), preferred because it lasts longer.
• Topical corticosteroid, such as prednisolone acetate 1% 2 to 4 times daily, is the first choice for noninfectious anterior uveitis.
• Acyclovir, valacyclovir and famciclovir for HSV and VZV; valganciclovir for CMV; antibiotics generally not indicated.
(b)
• Identify the condition promptly, start first-line therapy, relieve pain, and refer to an ophthalmologist within 24 hours, using RSVP.
• Take a detailed history and review of systems (back pain, joint swelling, arthritis) because a slit lamp exam may not be available in primary care.
• Teach medication adherence and urgent follow-up regardless of symptoms; adverse effects discussed.
(c)
• Complications: glaucoma, cataracts, posterior synechiae, band keratopathy and macular edema; chronic uveitis has the highest rate of long-term vision loss.
• Early diagnosis and early intervention give a better chance of preserving vision; monitor every 1 to 7 days then co-manage every 1 to 6 months after stabilization.
questions.question:
Uveitis:
(a) Describe the medical management.
(b) State the nursing and primary care responsibilities and rationale.
(c) Explain the basis of complications and how they are prevented.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The sclera; scleritis, a severe ocular inflammation whose most common autoimmune association is rheumatoid arthritis.
(b)
• Violet-bluish hue with scleral edema and dilatation; on slit-lamp the inflamed scleral vessels are criss-crossed, adherent and immobile to a cotton-tipped applicator; the globe is tender; the conjunctival and superficial vessels blanch with 2.5 to 10% phenylephrine but deep vessels do not.
• Anterior segment associations: keratitis, corneal infiltrates or thinning, uveitis and trabeculitis; posterior: chorioretinal granulomas, retinal vasculitis, serous retinal detachment, optic nerve edema.
• Ultrasonography or CT confirms posterior scleritis and biopsy may exclude neoplastic or infective causes.
(c)
Episcleritis (more superficial, less painful, treated with topical NSAIDs); infectious scleritis (herpes zoster ophthalmicus, Pseudomonas, fungal, syphilis, tuberculosis) and surgery-induced or drug-induced scleritis.
(d)
• The pain is severe and can be sight-threatening; 75% of necrotizing cases will have visual impairment, so pain control comes first.
• Give prescribed pain medicine and medications (oral NSAIDs first line for mild to moderate scleritis, with warnings on gastric bleeding and renal toxicity; systemic corticosteroids for posterior or necrotizing disease).
• Monitor for signs of vision loss or perforation of the sclera and escalate these promptly.
• Because 50% have autoimmune disease, refer for the underlying condition; immunosuppressive drugs may be used in severe scleritis.
• Provide eye protection teaching, emotional support and education on side effects, including raised intraocular pressure, infection risk, gastric irritation and osteoporosis with steroids.
questions.question:
A patient in the middle age group with rheumatoid arthritis has a red eye with a violet-bluish hue, severe boring pain that is worse at night and on eye movement, and a tender globe.
(a) Identify the affected structure and the likely diagnosis.
(b) State the expected changes or abnormalities on examination and investigation.
(c) State the differential conditions.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for nursing priorities and escalation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Anesthesia-induced vasodilation (propofol, halothane, isoflurane, desflurane, sevoflurane, nitroglycerin and sodium nitroprusside can cause vasodilation), exposure of the body cavity, cold operating room environment, infusion of cold fluids and poor peripheral circulation.
(b)
• Recognition by stage: mild (35 to 32°C) shivering, numbness, confusion; moderate (32 to 28°C) shivering stops, confusion increases, coordination impaired; severe (below 28°C) loss of consciousness, coma and death.
• Signs: shivering or none in severe cases, disorientation, drowsiness, slurred speech, slow or weak pulse, unresponsiveness.
• Complications: cardiac arrhythmias and arrest, coagulopathy and bleeding disorders, impaired wound healing and surgical site infections, increased postoperative complications, prolonged recovery and ICU stay.
(c)
• Continuous temperature monitoring and pre-operative warming.
• Intra-operative warming devices such as forced-air warming and warming mattresses; warm IV fluids and irrigation solutions; maintaining a warm operating room.
• In the recovery period, warming blankets or cooling measures maintain normothermia.
• Priority: close temperature monitoring, because it is the way to detect hypothermia early.
questions.question:
A patient is having a long surgery in a cold operating room under anesthesia with vasodilating drugs, cold fluids are being infused and the body cavity is exposed.
(a) State the risk factors for hypothermia.
(b) State the potential complications and how they are recognized.
(c) State the nursing management and prevention options and justify the priority intervention.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Contracture develops when normally stretchy tissue is replaced by nonstretchy fiber-like tissue; causes are multifactorial, both extrinsic and intrinsic.
• Reduced use (lack of mobility or injury): decreased ability to move a limb through full range, static positioning for prolonged periods, and agonist-antagonist muscle imbalance; weakness preventing full active joint mobilization is the single most frequent factor.
• Severe muscle and bone injuries (myopathic conditions give more severe contractures than neuropathic disorders, with fibrotic changes), scarring after traumatic injury or burns, and congenital factors such as muscular dystrophies with hypotonia and early contractures.
(b)
• Recognition: pain, joint and muscle rigidity, reduced movements, muscle weakness and limited use of the affected area; contractures reduce joint mobility.
• Advanced contractures become fixed and respond little to stretching or splinting; lower limb contractures are much more prevalent than upper limb.
(c)
• Prevention needs early diagnosis and physical medicine such as passive range of motion and splinting while contractures are absent or mild.
• Regular daily standing or walking, passive stretching of muscles and joints, positioning the limbs to promote extension and oppose flexion, and splinting to prevent or delay contractures.
• Occupational therapy of wrist and hand range of motion slows contractures and keeps fine motor skills; advanced fixed contractures may need surgery.
• Priority: early passive range of motion and splinting, because static positioning is an important cause and mild contractures respond best.
questions.question:
A patient has been immobilized for a long period after a serious injury; a joint is becoming stiff and painful with limited movement, and the muscles remain contracted even though the injury has resolved.
(a) State the risk factors.
(b) State the potential complications and how they are recognized.
(c) State the nursing and medical or surgical management options and justify the priority intervention.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Osteomyelitis is an infection of the bone, a rare but serious condition, occurring in infants, children and adults, with different bacteria typically affecting different age groups.
(b)
Bacteria travel through the bloodstream (bacteremia) from an infection elsewhere, such as pneumonia, an abscessed tooth or a urinary tract infection; an open fracture, surgery or open wound over a bone also exposes the bone.
(c)
Diabetes (most cases), sickle cell disease, HIV or AIDS, rheumatoid arthritis, intravenous drug use, alcoholism, long-term steroids, hemodialysis, poor blood supply and recent injury; only 2 of every 10,000 people get it.
(d)
Fever, irritability, fatigue, nausea, tenderness, redness and warmth, swelling around the bone, and lost range of motion; acute osteomyelitis develops over 7 to 10 days and symptoms of acute and chronic forms are very similar.
(e)
X-rays, blood tests, bone scans, and a bone biopsy needed to confirm the diagnosis and determine the organism.
(f)
• Conditions and behaviours that weaken the immune system raise risk, as in diabetes, sickle cell disease and HIV.
• An open wound over a bone with underlying peripheral vascular disease, peripheral neuropathy or diabetes can lead to osteomyelitis.
(g)
• In children it most commonly occurs at the ends of the long bones of the arms and legs, affecting the hips, knees, shoulders and wrists.
• In adults it is more common in the bones of the spine (vertebrae), feet or pelvis, with vertebral disease showing severe back pain especially at night.
• Management: several weeks of IV antibiotics then pills; surgery removes infected tissue and bone in serious or chronic cases.
questions.question:
Osteomyelitis:
(a) Define it.
(b) State its causes.
(c) State its risk factors.
(d) List its symptoms.
(e) List its investigations.
(f) Explain why certain patients are more vulnerable.
(g) Distinguish between how it presents in children and in adults.

An older patient has an inward-turned lower eyelid with a feeling of a foreign body, red watering eyes, blurred vision, light sensitivity and crusting.
(a) State the diagnosis and presentation.
(b) State the causes and assessment.
(c) Name the treatment and procedures.
(d) State the complications to watch for.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Entropion, turning inwards of the eyelid, usually the lower lid; symptoms: foreign body sensation, red eyes, tearing, blurred vision, pain, itching, sensitivity to light and wind, and drainage or crusting.
(b)
Lower eyelid laxity is the usual cause; scarring (cicatricial), age over 60 as eyelid supports weaken, spasm of the orbicularis muscle (spastic), eye injury, infection or previous eye surgery.
(c)
• Nonsurgical treatment relieves symptoms and protects the eye: ocular lubrication and tear preparations; in spastic entropion the lid may realign as inflamed or infected eye is treated.
• Eyelid hygiene, antibiotics and corticosteroids help blepharitis-related entropion; surgery is generally required to fully correct entropion.
(d)
Complications: if tissue scarring has occurred, entropion may persist even after the other condition is treated; trichiasis and corneal injury from lashes rubbing are described in related conditions.

questions.question:
A child has a rounded upper back with a forward curve of more than 50 degrees; another patient has a sideways curvature of the spine; a third has an excessive lumbar "swayback" curve.
(a) Identify the affected system.
(b) State the expected changes and abnormalities.
(c) State the differential conditions.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for nursing priorities and escalation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The musculoskeletal system, specifically the vertebral column: deformities of the spine.
(b)
• Kyphosis (hunchback): increased convexity of the thoracic curve, more than 50 degrees; cause undetermined (genetics, abnormal ossification, medical or postural defects).
• Scoliosis: abnormal lateral curvature, most often diagnosed in childhood or early adolescence; lordosis: excessive curvature giving a swayback, mostly lumbar.
(c)
• Differentials: scoliosis, kyphosis and lordosis; lordosis may come from spina bifida, cerebral palsy, congenital issues, hip or pelvic conditions, previous back surgery and poor posture.
• Investigations: X-rays, CT and MRI to assess structural abnormalities; genetic testing and blood tests where relevant.
(d)
• Priorities: assess neurologic and respiratory function, pain, functional limitations and psychosocial issues; promote mobility and prescribed exercises; assess for skin irritation.
• Treatments: braces for milder scoliosis, and for kyphosis physical therapy, lifestyle modification, braces for up to a year and surgery.
• Nursing diagnoses: impaired physical mobility, chronic pain and disturbed body image.

(a)
• General anesthesia: unconscious with no awareness; regional anesthesia numbs an area (spinal, epidural, nerve blocks such as femoral and brachial plexus); sedation or monitored anesthesia care (mild, moderate, deep); local anesthesia (for example lidocaine).
• Mild sedation is often used for eye surgery with the patient awake and responding; deep sedation is nearly the same as general anesthesia, with the patient breathing unassisted.
• Agents: inhaled (nitrous oxide, sevoflurane, desflurane, isoflurane), intravenous (propofol, thiopental, etomidate, ketamine), regional (lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine); sedatives (midazolam, propofol, dexmedetomidine).
(b)
The nursing roles in the PACU and in pre-operative teaching are assessment, education, emotional support and documentation.
(c)
• Side effects: back or muscle pain, chills (hypothermia), difficulty urinating, fatigue, headache, itching, nausea and vomiting, injection site pain and sore throat, usually passing within 24 hours.
• Complications: anesthetic awareness (about 1 in 1,000), atelectasis, malignant hyperthermia, nerve damage and postoperative delirium.
• At risk: advanced age, diabetes, kidney, heart or lung disease, obesity, seizures, sleep apnea and smoking.
• Benzodiazepines such as midazolam are used as premedication and provide anxiolysis.
• Midazolam is the most commonly used preoperative sedative; diazepam causes veno-irritation on injection.
• Synthetic opioids can cause miosis and respiratory depression.
questions.question:
Anesthesia and sedation:
(a) Describe the types of anesthesia and levels of sedation.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities and rationale.
(c) Explain the basis of complications and how they are prevented.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Bone tumour (benign or malignant, such as osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma or chondrosarcoma); signs are bone pain, swelling and tenderness, weakened bone leading to fracture, fatigue, unintended weight loss, gait abnormality and paresthesia.
(b)
X-rays (cannot tell benign from malignant), MRI and CT for location and size, PET-CT, bone scan, and biopsy (aspiration, core or open, incisional or excisional); nurses assess pain and characteristics and monitor vital signs.
(c)
Limb salvage surgery removes the cancerous bone with a margin of healthy tissue and replaces it with a metal prosthesis or bone transplant; amputation is considered when the tumour is large or nerves and vessels are involved; chemotherapy and radiation therapy may be combined.
(d)
• Pre-operative: admit, reassure, monitor vital signs, rest, high carbohydrate and protein diet, educate patient and family, and prepare and support the patient during diagnostic procedures.
• Post-operative: assess pain and give analgesics; handle the affected extremity gently with splints for protection; assist with body image changes after surgery or amputation; encourage expression of fears, refer to a psychologist or spiritual advisor; involve the family.
(e)
Pathologic fracture from weakened bone and relapse.
(f)
After treatment, further X-rays and imaging confirm the tumour is gone; regular visits every few months; monitor the body for relapse; assist the patient in planning daily activities.
questions.question:
A patient with a bone tumour has bone pain, swelling and tenderness, weight loss, fatigue and a weakened bone; surgery with limb salvage or amputation is being considered.
(a) State the diagnosis and presentation.
(b) State the diagnostic tests and what nurses monitor.
(c) Name the procedure or treatment.
(d) State the pre-operative and post-operative nursing care.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Holistic physical assessment to discern type and extent, covering pain, functional limitations and psychosocial issues; assess neurologic and respiratory functions; assess the patient's and family's understanding; assess mobility status, pain using a rating scale, and perception of change in body part.
• Clinical findings: visible alterations in appearance, skeletal misalignments, joint restrictions, muscle imbalances and impaired range of motion.
(b)
• Impaired physical mobility related to joint displacement, evidenced by being confined to bed.
• Chronic pain related to pressure on nerve endings, evidenced by verbalization.
• Disturbed body image related to congenital abnormality, evidenced by change in social behaviour.
(c)
Growth disruption from genetic factors, events in pregnancy or childhood leads to tissue changes where bones and soft tissues do not form properly, causing biomechanical imbalances (some parts too tight, others too weak), impaired movement, pain and reduced functionality.
(d)
• Mobility: assess mobility and need for help (guides best plan); safe environment (reduces accidental falls); passive or active range-of-motion exercises (prevent stiffness, improve strength); flotation mattress (decreases skin pressure).
• Pain: pain rating scale (early detection); massage and alternative comfort measures (improve circulation, reduce pressure and fatigue); analgesics (reduce pain).
• Body image: assess perception of change, need for a support group (part of rehabilitation), encourage talking about feelings (enhances coping), and use clothing to enhance appearance (boosts self-image and confidence).
(e)
• Mobility outcome: moves extremities after 45 to 60 minutes of nursing intervention. Pain outcome: verbalizes a reduction after 15 to 30 minutes.
• Body image outcome: demonstrates enhanced body image and self-esteem after 45 to 60 minutes; evaluation records each objective as achieved.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
(a)
Assess the patient's ability to see and perform activities (baseline for changes affecting visual acuity); symptoms: cloudy or blurry vision, double vision in one eye, halos, glare sensitivity, poor night vision and faded colours.
(b)
• Disturbed visual sensory perception related to altered state of the sense organ (eye), evidenced by blurred vision.
• Anxiety related to uncertainty or distress caused by floaters.
(c)
• Aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol through the polyol pathway; sorbitol accumulates, causing osmotic changes; lens fibers become hydropic, degenerate and form sugar cataracts.
• High blood sugar over time also damages eye blood vessels and raises aqueous glucose, swelling the lens.
(d)
• Make the room safe with adequate lighting and furniture moved toward the walls (reduces injury); keep glasses and call bell within reach (optimal visual acuity); teach the patient and family about a safe environment; give prescribed medicines.
• Anxiety: let the patient express concerns (deal with reality and clarify misconceptions); promote a calm, soothing environment with soft lighting and less noise; teach coping mechanisms and positive self-talk (builds confidence and lowers anxiety).
• Also control blood sugar, prevent infection, manage pain and educate on diabetes management and follow-up.
(e)
• Outcome: visual perception improves within 3 days of nursing intervention; the client appears relaxed and reports anxiety reduced to a manageable level.
• Evaluation: visual perception improved within 3 days, and the client appeared relaxed and reported reduced anxiety.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Medical: glasses or contact lenses for refractive errors, prism lenses to align the eyes, eye exercises, botulinum toxin injections to temporarily relax muscles, orthoptic therapy, vision therapy, and patching of the stronger eye.
• Surgery realigns or strengthens extraocular muscles: recession (weakening by reattaching farther back), resection (strengthening by removing a portion), plication, transposition, adjustable suture surgery, minimally invasive surgery, robotic-assisted surgery and bilateral surgery.
(b)
• History: prematurity, family history, perinatal complications, systemic disorders, neonatal oxygen, systemic medicines and male sex are risk factors; physical exam looks for amblyopia, impaired binocularity, central scotomas and incomitance.
• Prevent injury: orient the patient, keep the call light within reach, respond immediately, place injury-prone patients near the nurses' station, teach safe ambulation at home, and label significant places with bright colours.
• Patch therapy: covering the stronger eye forces the weaker eye to work harder; vision therapy changes how eyes process visual information rather than strengthening muscles.
• Health education: note misconceptions, consider learning style, include the patient or caregiver in teaching goals, and give clear explanations and demonstrations.
(c)
• Constant unilateral strabismus causes constant suppression, a risk for amblyopia in children; double vision may lead the brain to ignore one eye with loss of depth perception.
• Crowded visual acuity tests are preferred for detecting amblyopia because they are more accurate.
• Prevention of amblyopia depends on early patching and correcting refractive error.
• The Hirschberg test detects manifest strabismus and the Krimsky test measures the angle of deviation.
