During anesthesia a patient suddenly develops hypotension and bronchospasm shortly after a neuromuscular blocking agent and an antibiotic are given.
(a) Name the diagnosis.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiology.
(c) Describe the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Anaphylaxis during anesthesia, which is very rare (1 in 4,000 to 1 in 25,000) with a mortality of 3% to 10% and is difficult to diagnose.
• The most frequent presenting sign was hypotension (46% of cases), with bronchospasm also reported.
(b)
• Triggers: almost all agents used in the operating room except inhalational agents; antibiotics (most commonly beta-lactams such as penicillins and cephalosporins, 70%), neuromuscular blocking agents (succinylcholine and rocuronium most common), sugammadex, latex and chlorhexidine.
• Pathophysiology: sudden release of mediators (histamine, tryptase, chymase, cathepsin) from basophils and mast cells after exposure to the trigger; NMBA reactions are mainly IgE-mediated.
(c)
• Discontinue the suspected agent and give 100% oxygen; epinephrine is the drug of choice; vasopressin for refractory cases; glucagon for patients on beta-blockers; fluid replacement for vasodilation.
• Diagnosis by World Allergy Organization criteria (skin or mucosal reaction with respiratory compromise or hypotension, two or more systems after exposure, or hypotension after a known allergen).
• Whether to proceed with surgery is decided individually based on reaction severity.

questions.question:
Rickets, osteomalacia and osteoporosis:
(a) Define each.
(b) State causes and risk factors.
(c) Describe clinical manifestations.
(d) State prevention and treatment.
(e) Explain why certain patients are more vulnerable.
(f) Distinguish between the three conditions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Rickets affects bone development in children, causing bone pain, poor growth and soft, weak bones that can lead to deformities such as genu valgum and genu varum.
• Osteomalacia is the similar condition in adults (soft bones); osteoporosis is weakened bones with reduced bone mineral density, more susceptible to fractures.
(b)
• Rickets: most commonly lack of vitamin D or calcium; vitamin D is from sunlight, oily fish and eggs.
• Osteoporosis: if the body cannot maintain adequate bone formation, bones lose density; risk factors are aging, hormonal changes, lack of physical activity and certain medications.
(c)
Bone pain, poor growth, soft bones and deformities in rickets; fragility and fractures in osteoporosis.
(d)
• Rickets is treated in most children by foods containing calcium and vitamin D or vitamin supplements.
• Osteoporosis prevention: early detection by bone density testing, diet rich in calcium and vitamin D, weight-bearing exercises and medication when necessary.
(e)
• Osteoporosis develops gradually and is more common in older adults; immobilization and reduced weight-bearing during orthopedic rehabilitation cause bone mineral density loss.
• Children lacking vitamin D or calcium are vulnerable to rickets.
(f)
• Rickets is in children; osteomalacia is its adult counterpart; osteoporosis involves reduced bone mineral density from inadequate bone formation with increased resorption.
• Nurses assess risk, use weight-bearing exercises, give calcium and vitamin D supplementation and educate patients.

(a)
Acute angle-closure glaucoma attack, a true eye emergency that should be treated immediately or blindness may occur.
(b)
• Predisposing factors: age over 40, family history of glaucoma, African, Hispanic or Asian heritage, high eye pressure, being farsighted or nearsighted, previous eye injury, long-term steroid use, thin central corneas, thinning of the optic nerve, and diabetes, migraines, high blood pressure or poor circulation.
• The eye constantly makes aqueous humor that drains through the drainage angle to keep intraocular pressure stable.
• In angle-closure glaucoma the iris sits very close to the drainage angle and blocks it, like paper over a sink drain; when completely blocked eye pressure rises very quickly and damages the optic nerve.
• As nerve fibers die, blind spots develop; glaucoma damage is permanent and cannot be reversed.
(c)
• Provide patient safety and assess vision.
• Educate the patient on eye-drop compliance: drops used daily lower eye pressure, and side effects can include stinging, red eyes, changes in pulse, breathing changes (especially with asthma), dry mouth, blurred vision and eyelash growth.
• Educate the patient about glaucoma and on the importance of follow-up; manage anxiety.
• Teach that early detection through routine eye exams is the best protection; testing every six to twelve months after age 65.
• Treatments the family should know of: eye drops, laser (trabeculoplasty, iridotomy), trabeculectomy, cataract surgery for narrow angles, drainage devices.

A patient who spends much time outdoors in sun, wind and dust presents with a triangular fold of tissue growing onto the cornea from the side nearest the nose, with redness, burning, tearing and blurred vision, and surgery is planned.
(a) Identify the diagnosis and describe its presentation.
(b) Name the diagnostic tests and what the nurse monitors.
(c) Name the medical treatment and the surgical procedure.
(d) State the pre-operative, intra-operative and post-operative nursing care.
(e) State the complications to watch for.
(f) State the discharge teaching.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pterygium (Surfer's Eye), a non-cancerous fibrovascular outgrowth of conjunctiva over the cornea; early it is asymptomatic, later redness, discomfort, blurry vision, burning, irritation, tearing and corneal astigmatism.
(b)
Tests: comprehensive ocular exam, slit-lamp biomicroscopy, conjunctival scrapings or biopsy, refraction for astigmatism, and Schirmer's test or tear film break-up time to rule out dry eye; size is graded 1 (0-2 mm), 2 (2-4 mm) and 3 (more than 4 mm).
(c)
Medical: lubricating drops and short-term anti-inflammatory drops; surgery is the main treatment if severe or vision is affected, with free conjunctival autograft or other techniques, usually under local anaesthetic as a day-stay procedure of about half an hour.
(d)
• Pre-operative: health history and physical assessment, reassurance, education on the disease and treatment, informed consent, and explanation of the procedure and post-operative instructions.
• Intra-operative: the pterygium is excised and a small piece of healthy conjunctiva from under the upper lid is transplanted, held with fibrin glue or stitches; Post-operative: eye patch overnight, drops about four times daily for 4 to 8 weeks, analgesics for the first one to two days, assist with daily living if vision is impaired.
(e)
Recurrence, corneal ulcers or perforation, vision loss or blindness if untreated, and chronic eye irritation; the eye may look red up to a month with mild swelling.
(f)
Adhere to eye drops and use of the patch; UV protection with sunglasses and hats; eye protection in dust or wind; avoid rubbing the eyes; keep eyes moist with artificial tears; regular eye exams; proper eye hygiene; avoid scratching, contact lenses or irritants.

(a)
• Trauma is an emotional response to a terrible event such as an accident, rape or natural disaster, or to a physically or emotionally threatening or harmful event.
• Types: acute (a single stressful or dangerous event), chronic (repeated and prolonged exposure, for example child abuse, bullying, domestic violence) and complex trauma (exposure to multiple events).
(b)
• Causes: fall from height, domestic violence, road traffic accidents, natural disaster and man-made disaster.
• Manifestations: pain, hemorrhage, respiratory issues, fracture, palpitation, shock, anxiety, depression, confusion, loss of consciousness and post-traumatic stress syndrome.
(c)
Mechanism of injury is the way damage to skin, muscles, organs and bones happens; it helps clinicians determine severity and develop a treatment plan; main types are penetrating, blunt and sharp, and deceleration trauma.
(d)
Progression includes shock, psychological responses such as depression and post-traumatic stress syndrome, and systemic effects of hemorrhage and respiratory problems.
(e)
• Phases: triage (I), primary survey and resuscitation (II), secondary survey (III), stabilization (IV), transfer (V) and definitive care (VI).
• Assessment begins before arrival with information gathering, forming the trauma team and preparing equipment; on arrival, triage and primary survey assess airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure.
• Interventions: endotracheal intubation, CPR, bleeding control, blood transfusion, fracture immobilization, oxygen, IV access, fluids and medicines, psychological support; cricothyroidotomy for urgent airway access, converted to a tracheostomy within 72 hours to prevent subglottic stenosis.
• Guiding principles: safety, choice, collaboration, trustworthiness and empowerment.

Medical and surgical asepsis:
(a) Define asepsis and describe the two types.
(b) State their principles and components.
(c) State the five moments of hand hygiene.
(d) Explain why compliance matters and why staff fail to comply.
(e) Distinguish between medical asepsis and surgical asepsis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Asepsis is the absence of pathogenic microorganisms that can cause infection; aseptic technique prevents their transfer; it is required for wound dressing and insertion and maintenance of invasive devices.
• The two forms are medical asepsis (clean technique) and surgical asepsis (sterile technique).
(b)
• Medical asepsis components: knowing what is dirty, clean and sterile, keeping them separate, and remedying contamination immediately; principles: hand hygiene, PPE per standard precautions, cleaning and disinfecting shared equipment and the environment.
• Surgical asepsis principles: sterile field, hand hygiene, PPE (sterile gowns, gloves, masks, eye protection), sterilization of instruments, environmental controls (airflow, temperature, humidity) and aseptic techniques such as minimizing talking in the OR.
(c)
Five moments: before touching a patient, before a procedure, after a procedure or body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching a patient's surroundings.
(d)
• Significance: prevents surgical site infections, protects patient and healthcare worker safety, meets regulatory compliance and improves quality of care.
• Reasons for non-compliance: inaccessible hand hygiene supplies, skin irritation, being too busy, glove use, not thinking about it and lack of knowledge.
(e)
• Medical asepsis aims to control the number of micro-organisms and is used for all clinical patient care; surgical asepsis aims to remove all micro-organisms and is used for all surgical or sterile procedures.
• Healthcare providers should keep immunizations current, maintain personal hygiene and not work when sick.

(a)
The respiratory system: hypoxia (oxygen failing to reach tissues) with hypercapnia, and a suspected intraoperative pneumothorax.
(b)
• Hypoxia: rapid breathing, shortness of breath, slower heart rate and changes in skin colour; hypoxemia is arterial oxygen tension below normal (normal PaO2 80 to 100 mmHg) and is the commonest cause of tissue hypoxia.
• Hypercapnia: increased arterial CO2 resulting in respiratory acidosis, presenting as elevated end-tidal CO2.
• Pneumothorax: accumulated air in the pleural space puts positive pressure on the lung and prevents expansion, causing respiratory distress; as air accumulates the trachea and other structures may shift.
(c)
Pneumothorax (from diaphragm defect, rupture of a bulla, endobronchial intubation or creation of pneumoperitoneum), negative pressure pulmonary edema after extubation, bronchospasm, and the four hypoxia classes (hypoxemic, stagnant, anaemic, histotoxic).
(d)
• Hypoxia can cause acute heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, acute renal failure, reduced cognitive function and permanent brain damage, so early recognition is a priority.
• Prevention of hypoxia: check the anaesthesia machine before every procedure and use alarms, hypoxic guard and oxygen proportioning devices.
questions.question:
During general anesthesia a patient's oxygen saturation falls and end-tidal carbon dioxide rises, with respiratory distress; air in the pleural space after a pneumoperitoneum is suspected.
(a) Identify the affected organ or system.
(b) State the expected changes or abnormalities.
(c) State the differential conditions.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for nursing priorities and escalation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The retina, where high blood sugar damages the light-sensitive retinal blood vessels: diabetic retinopathy, which usually affects both eyes.
(b)
• Expected changes: microaneurysms first; in NPDR leaking vessels, macular edema, macular ischemia and exudates; in PDR neovascularization with vitreous bleeding and scar tissue.
• Investigations: visual acuity test, tonometry, pupil dilation, ophthalmoscopy, fluorescein angiography (dye shows leaking or non-supplying vessels) and optical coherence tomography.
(c)
• Four diabetic eye diseases threaten sight: diabetic retinopathy, cataract (clouding of the lens from sorbitol swelling), glaucoma (raised pressure damaging the optic nerve) and diabetic macular edema.
• Cataract features: cloudy or blurry vision, halos, glare and faded colours; glaucoma features: eye pain or pressure, halos and tunnel vision.
(d)
• Escalate new floaters or flashing lights because bleeding can block vision, and a sudden onset of floaters or severe vision loss suggests retinal detachment needing emergency surgery.
• Raised eye pain or pressure suggests glaucoma from new vessels.
• Priority nursing: monitor blood pressure and glucose for hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, since uncontrolled glucose raises the risk of PDR.
• Teach home glucose monitoring, meal planning and physical activity; arrange ophthalmologist screening and reporting of worsening symptoms.
• Laser and anti-VEGF injections stabilize changes; laser usually does not improve sight, so early referral matters.
